# About This Book

## Welcome

ROOTED is a chapter-by-chapter commentary on the entire New Testament, from *Matthew 1* to *Revelation 22*. It is written for readers who want to understand Scripture deeply but may not have formal theological training. The goal is to walk through each chapter the way a patient Bible teacher would: explaining what is happening, who is speaking and why, what the words meant to their first hearers, and how the teaching applies to life today.

## How Each Chapter Is Organized

Every chapter study follows the same pattern. It begins with a **Chapter Theme** and a short summary of the **Main Teaching**. The **Chapter Background and Story** then walks through the whole chapter in order, explaining people, places, customs, and the flow of the narrative or argument. Under **Important Verses Explained**, two to four key verses are studied in depth, each with a Simple Explanation, a Deeper Spiritual Meaning, and a section on Applying This Teaching to Life Today. A wider section, **How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today**, shows how the chapter’s teachings work together in everyday life. Each chapter closes with a single **Chapter Prayer**.

## About the Scripture Quotations

Scripture quotations are from the World English Bible (WEB), a modern English translation in the public domain. Every key verse and every quoted phrase in this book was checked word for word against the WEB text published by eBible.org. Quotations from Scripture appear in italics, and references are italicized as well. Short words and phrases are sometimes quoted from within a longer verse; the full verse can be read through the link at the top of each chapter. Some verses mentioned in the commentary are absent from many early manuscripts, and where that matters, the commentary says so.

## About Interpretation

The commentary tries to explain what each passage actually says in its own setting before drawing out its spiritual meaning. Where faithful Christians have understood a passage in different ways, such as on the Lord’s Supper, baptism, church leadership, divorce and remarriage, or the details of end-times prophecy, the main views are described briefly and fairly rather than presented as settled. Passages about suffering, submission, forgiveness, and marriage are never meant to require anyone to remain in danger or to tolerate abuse; seeking safety, protection, and help is consistent with faithfulness to Christ.

## About the Cover

This edition keeps the original ROOTED cover artwork. The cover’s reference to the Navigators 5x5x5 method comes from an earlier workbook edition; this edition is a reading commentary rather than a workbook, so it contains explanations and applications instead of exercises, quizzes, or review schedules.

# Matthew

## About This Gospel

The Gospel of Matthew opens the New Testament and serves as a bridge between the Old Testament and the story of Jesus. Early Christian tradition consistently names Matthew, the tax collector whom Jesus called to follow Him (*Matthew 9:9*), as its author. It was probably written in the second half of the first century, for a community that included many Jewish believers who knew the Scriptures of Israel well.

Matthew’s central concern is to show that Jesus is the Messiah promised to Israel, the Son of David and the Son of Abraham, and that in Him God’s promises are fulfilled. More than any other Gospel, Matthew points out how events in Jesus’ life fulfill the Old Testament, often with the phrase “that it might be fulfilled.” He presents Jesus as a new and greater Moses who teaches God’s will with authority, as the true Son of God who remains faithful where Israel failed, and as “God with us.”

## How the Book Is Arranged

Matthew organizes Jesus’ teaching into five major sections, each ending with a phrase like “When Jesus had finished these words”: the Sermon on the Mount (chapters 5–7), the mission instructions to the Twelve (chapter 10), the parables of the kingdom (chapter 13), teaching on life in the community of disciples (chapter 18), and teaching about the end of the age (chapters 24–25). Between these teaching sections come narratives of Jesus’ miracles, conflicts, and journeys. The book moves from His birth and early ministry in Galilee to His final week in Jerusalem, His death, and His resurrection.

## Themes to Watch For

The kingdom of heaven is Matthew’s great theme: God’s reign arriving in Jesus, calling for repentance and a righteousness that goes deeper than outward rule-keeping. Matthew also emphasizes that Jesus’ mission, first directed to Israel, is meant for all nations, a theme that begins with the visit of the wise men and ends with the command to make disciples of all nations. The book is framed by the promise of Immanuel, “God with us” (*1:23*), and Jesus’ final promise, “I am with you always” (*28:20*).

# Matthew — Chapter 1

Chapter Theme: The Promised King Enters a Real Family

[Read Matthew 1 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/MAT01.htm)

Main Teaching

Matthew opens his Gospel by tracing Jesus’ family line through David and Abraham, showing that God’s long history of promises with Israel is now reaching its goal. He then tells how Joseph, a righteous man faced with a painful dilemma, obeys God’s word and receives Mary’s child as his own. The child is named Jesus because He will save His people from their sins, and He is Immanuel, “God with us.”

## Chapter Background and Story

Matthew was written for readers who knew the Scriptures of Israel well, and its opening chapter is built to speak directly to them. For centuries Israel had been waiting. God had promised Abraham that through his family all the nations of the earth would be blessed (*Genesis 12:3*). He had promised David that a son of his would reign on a throne that would last forever (*2 Samuel 7:12–16*). Yet by the time of Jesus, no descendant of David had ruled for nearly six hundred years. The nation had been conquered by Babylon, had returned from exile in small numbers, and now lived under Roman power and the rule of Herod, a king appointed by Rome who was not from David’s line. Many Jews longed for the Messiah, the anointed king God had promised. Matthew’s first sentence answers that longing.

### The Genealogy of Jesus the Messiah (*1:1–17*)

Matthew begins, “*The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham*” (*v. 1*). “Christ” is not a surname; it is the Greek form of the Hebrew title “Messiah,” meaning “anointed one.” Calling Jesus “the son of David” identifies Him as the rightful heir to David’s throne. Calling Him “the son of Abraham” ties Him to the very first promise God made to Israel’s ancestor. The phrase “the book of the genealogy” also echoes the way Genesis introduces family histories (*Genesis 2:4*; *5:1*), hinting that something as significant as a new beginning is taking place.

Modern readers often skip genealogies, but in the ancient world a family record established identity, inheritance, and legitimacy. Matthew’s list moves from Abraham to David, from David to the exile in Babylon, and from the exile to Jesus. He arranges it into three groups of fourteen generations (v. 17). He has selected and arranged the names deliberately, which was a common and accepted practice; his purpose is not to list every ancestor but to show the shape of Israel’s history. It rose to its height with King David, fell to its lowest point in the exile, and now arrives at the Messiah. Some scholars also note that the numerical value of David’s name in Hebrew letters is fourteen, which would make the whole list a subtle emphasis on David’s royal line.

The genealogy contains some surprises. Ancient genealogies usually listed only fathers, but Matthew names four women before Mary: Tamar (v. 3), Rahab (v. 5), Ruth (v. 5), and “*her who had been Uriah’s wife*” (*v. 6*), that is, Bathsheba. Each one has an unusual story. Tamar was involved in a scandalous episode with her father-in-law Judah (*Genesis 38*). Rahab was a Canaanite woman of Jericho who sheltered Israel’s spies (*Joshua 2*). Ruth was a Moabite, from a people often hostile to Israel. Bathsheba is not even named; she is called the wife of Uriah, a Hittite, which reminds readers of David’s adultery and his murder of her husband (*2 Samuel 11*). By including these women, Matthew shows that God’s saving purpose has always worked through outsiders, through broken family stories, and even through serious sin. The Messiah’s family tree is not polished, and that is part of the good news.

The list also includes faithful kings like Hezekiah and Josiah alongside wicked ones like Manasseh and Ahaz. It passes through the shame of the exile (vv. 11–12). Matthew is telling Israel’s whole story, failures included, and saying that God has been faithful through all of it.

At the end, the pattern changes. For forty generations the wording has been “A became the father of B.” But when Matthew reaches Joseph, he writes that Joseph was “*the husband of Mary, from whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ*” (*v. 16*). In the Greek, “from whom” is feminine, referring to Mary. Matthew is carefully preparing for what he explains next: Joseph is Jesus’ legal father, giving Him the royal line of David, but Joseph is not His biological father.

### Joseph’s Dilemma and the Angel’s Message (*1:18–25*)

Matthew now tells how the birth came about. Mary was “*engaged to Joseph*” (*v. 18*). Jewish betrothal was much more binding than a modern engagement. It was a legal commitment, usually arranged between families, that could only be ended by a formal divorce, and the couple could be called husband and wife even though they did not yet live together or have sexual relations. The wedding, when the bride moved into the husband’s home, typically came about a year later. During this period Mary was found to be pregnant. Matthew immediately tells the reader that the child was “*by the Holy Spirit*” (*v. 18*), but Joseph did not yet know this.

From Joseph’s point of view, the only explanation was that Mary had been unfaithful. The law of Moses treated this very seriously. Joseph had options: he could expose her publicly, bringing great shame on her and possibly a legal trial, or he could divorce her quietly before a couple of witnesses. Matthew describes Joseph as a “*righteous man*” (*v. 19*) who was “*not willing to make her a public example*” (*v. 19*), so he decided to end the betrothal privately. His righteousness included both respect for God’s law and mercy toward Mary.

While he was considering this, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream. The angel addressed him as “*Joseph, son of David*” (*v. 20*), reminding him of his royal ancestry and the role he was about to play. He told him not to be afraid to take Mary as his wife, because the child had been conceived by the Holy Spirit. He told Joseph that Mary would give birth to a son and that Joseph was to name Him Jesus. In that culture, naming a child was the father’s right and an act of legally acknowledging the child as his own. By naming Jesus, Joseph would adopt Him into the line of David.

Matthew then explains that this fulfilled the words of the prophet Isaiah: the virgin would conceive and bear a son, called Immanuel, which means “*God with us*” (*v. 23*). This is the first of many times Matthew says that something happened “that it might be fulfilled,” showing how Jesus completes the story and hopes of the Old Testament.

Joseph’s response is immediate and complete. He “*did as the angel of the Lord commanded him*” (*v. 24*). He took Mary home as his wife, accepting whatever gossip might follow, and he did not have sexual relations with her until after Jesus was born, which confirms that Jesus’ conception was entirely the work of God. Then “*He named him Jesus*” (*v. 25*). Joseph never speaks a word in Matthew’s Gospel, but his obedience speaks loudly. Without fanfare, he protected Mary, received her child, and gave Jesus a home and a family name.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Matthew 1:19* — Joseph’s Righteousness and Mercy

> *“Joseph, her husband, being a righteous man, and not willing to make her a public example, intended to put her away secretly.”*
>
> — *Matthew 1:19* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse describes Joseph’s response when he learned that Mary, his betrothed wife, was pregnant. Since he knew he was not the father, he would naturally have concluded that she had been unfaithful. Matthew has already told the reader that the child was from the Holy Spirit (v. 18), but Joseph had not yet been told. This verse captures him at the moment of greatest heartbreak and confusion, before the angel appears.

Matthew calls Joseph “her husband” even though they were not yet married in the full sense, because Jewish betrothal was a legally binding union. Ending it required a formal divorce. That is why Matthew says Joseph “intended to put her away,” which means to divorce her.

Two qualities are mentioned. First, Joseph was “a righteous man.” In Jewish thought, a righteous person was someone who lived faithfully according to God’s law. Joseph took the commandments seriously, and he believed he could not simply go ahead with the marriage as if nothing had happened. Second, he was “*not willing to make her a public example*” (*v. 19*). He could have brought the matter before the community and shamed Mary publicly. Instead he chose to act quietly, with only the minimum witnesses required, to protect her as much as possible.

This tells us that Joseph’s righteousness was not harsh. He did not use the law as a weapon to punish someone who, as far as he knew, had wronged him deeply. He combined faithfulness to God with compassion toward Mary. This prepares the way for the angel’s message, which will ask him to go further still: to trust God’s explanation and take Mary as his wife.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Joseph’s story shows that true righteousness and mercy belong together. Later in Matthew, Jesus will criticize religious leaders who were careful about small rules but neglected “*justice, mercy, and faith*” (*Matthew 23:23*), and He will quote God’s words through Hosea, “*I desire mercy, and not sacrifice*” (*Matthew 9:13*). Joseph, the man who raised Jesus, already embodied that kind of righteousness. He cared about God’s law, but he did not separate obedience from kindness.

The verse also shows a man making a hard decision with incomplete information. Joseph acted as wisely and as kindly as he could with what he knew, and then God gave him more light. Faithfulness often works this way. God does not always explain everything at once, but He guides those who are seeking to do what is right. When the angel spoke, Joseph was ready to change his plan, which shows that his commitment was to God’s will rather than to his own sense of what was respectable.

It is worth noticing how much Joseph was asked to give up. Taking Mary as his wife meant sharing in whatever suspicion and gossip surrounded her pregnancy. He laid aside his reputation in order to obey God and protect a vulnerable woman and her child. In this he foreshadows the self-giving love that Jesus Himself would show.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Joseph’s example teaches believers to hold firm convictions with a merciful heart. When someone has wronged us, or appears to have done so, we often feel entitled to expose them or make sure everyone knows. Joseph shows another way. It is possible to take right and wrong seriously while still refusing to humiliate another person. This applies to conflicts in families, workplaces, and churches: deal with problems honestly, but do not use them to shame others or to make ourselves look better.

His example also encourages patience before reaching final conclusions. Joseph’s first judgment, while understandable, turned out to be mistaken. Many painful situations have explanations we do not yet know. Taking time, praying, and remaining open to God’s direction can keep us from decisions we would later regret.

Finally, Joseph shows the kind of obedience that is willing to bear misunderstanding. Doing what God asks may sometimes cost us comfort or reputation. Believers can trust that quiet, faithful obedience matters to God even when no one else notices it.

### *Matthew 1:21* — The Name That Means Salvation

> *“She shall give birth to a son. You shall name him Jesus, for it is he who shall save his people from their sins.”*
>
> — *Matthew 1:21* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These words are part of the angel’s message to Joseph in his dream. Joseph has been told not to be afraid to take Mary as his wife because her child has been conceived by the Holy Spirit. Now he is told two things about the child: Mary will give birth to a son, and Joseph is to give Him the name Jesus.

The instruction “You shall name him” is significant. In Jewish custom, the father named his son, and by doing so he publicly claimed the child as his own. By naming Jesus, Joseph would make Him his legal son and heir, placing Him in the royal line of David that Matthew traced in verses 1–16.

The name itself carries the meaning of the verse. “Jesus” is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Yeshua (Joshua), which means “the LORD saves” or “the LORD is salvation.” It was a common name at the time, but the angel explains why it fits this child in a unique way: “*for it is he who shall save his people from their sins*” (*v. 21*).

Many Jews of that time hoped the Messiah would save Israel from its political enemies, especially Rome. The angel defines salvation more deeply. Israel’s greatest problem was not foreign rule but sin, the rebellion against God that had led to the exile in the first place and that separates every human being from God. Jesus will deal with that root problem. “His people” refers first to Israel, but as Matthew’s Gospel unfolds, Jesus’ people will include all who follow Him from every nation (*Matthew 28:19*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse summarizes the purpose of Jesus’ life before He is even born. Matthew’s Gospel will show Jesus teaching, healing, and confronting evil, but all of it moves toward the cross, where He gives His life “*as a ransom for many*” (*Matthew 20:28*) and where His blood is poured out “*for the remission of sins*” (*Matthew 26:28*). The name Jesus already points to that goal.

The verse also says something important about who Jesus is. In the Old Testament, it is the LORD Himself who promises to redeem Israel from all their iniquities (*Psalm 130:8*). Here the angel says that Jesus Himself will save His people from their sins. Matthew is quietly preparing readers for the truth announced two verses later: in Jesus, God has come to be with His people.

Salvation from sin includes forgiveness, but it is broader than that. It means being rescued from sin’s guilt and also from its power, being restored to God and gradually transformed to live as God intends. The New Testament presents this salvation as God’s gift, received through faith in Jesus, not as a reward earned by good behavior.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites readers to see their deepest need clearly. Many people want help with circumstances, relationships, health, or finances, and God cares about all of these. But the angel names sin as the problem Jesus came to address at the root. Being honest about our own wrongdoing, rather than excusing it or blaming others, is the first step to receiving what Jesus offers.

It also calls believers to trust Jesus as Savior rather than trying to save themselves. When guilt weighs heavily, the answer is not to try harder to make up for it but to come to the One whose very name means “the LORD saves.” Confessing sin to Him and receiving His forgiveness brings real freedom.

Finally, because Jesus saves people from sin and not only its penalty, His followers can expect and seek real change. Habits, attitudes, and patterns that once seemed fixed can be confronted with His help. Growth may be gradual, but the One who saves is also at work to make His people new.

### *Matthew 1:23* — Immanuel, God With Us

> *“‘Behold, the virgin shall be with child, and shall give birth to a son. They shall call his name Immanuel,’ which is, being interpreted, ‘God with us.’”*
>
> — *Matthew 1:23* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse is Matthew’s comment on the events he has just described. After telling how the angel instructed Joseph, Matthew explains that all of this happened to fulfill what the Lord had spoken through the prophet. The words come from *Isaiah 7:14*, and Matthew quotes them in the form found in the Greek translation of the Old Testament, which used the word “virgin.”

In Isaiah’s own day, the prophecy was given to King Ahaz of Judah around 735 B.C., when Judah was threatened by an alliance between Syria and the northern kingdom of Israel. Ahaz was afraid and refused to trust God. Isaiah told him that God would give a sign: a young woman would conceive and bear a son named Immanuel, and before the child grew old enough to know right from wrong, the threatening kings would be gone. Many interpreters believe this sign had a first fulfillment in Isaiah’s time. But Isaiah’s prophecy continues in chapters 8–11 to speak of a child who would be called “*Mighty God*” (*Isaiah 9:6*) and who would sit on David’s throne forever. Matthew sees the fullest meaning of Isaiah’s words in Jesus, whose birth from a virgin is far more than a sign about a temporary political crisis.

The name “Immanuel” comes from two Hebrew words: “immanu” (with us) and “El” (God). Matthew translates it for his readers: “God with us.” Jesus was not literally called Immanuel as His everyday name; His name was Jesus. “Immanuel” describes who He is. In Him, God is present with His people.

Matthew emphasizes that Jesus’ conception happened without a human father. Mary was a virgin, and the child was conceived by the Holy Spirit (vv. 18, 20). This is not a small detail. It shows that Jesus’ coming was a unique act of God, not simply the birth of a gifted human being.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

“God with us” is one of the central themes of Matthew’s Gospel. It appears at the beginning of the book in this verse, in the middle when Jesus promises to be present wherever two or three gather in His name (*Matthew 18:20*), and at the very end when the risen Jesus tells His disciples, “*I am with you always, even to the end of the age*” (*Matthew 28:20*). Matthew frames his entire Gospel with the truth that, in Jesus, God has come near and remains near.

Throughout the Old Testament, God’s presence among His people was precious and holy. He dwelt in the tabernacle and later in the temple, and the prophets promised a day when God would dwell among His people in a new way. Christians confess that in Jesus this promise was fulfilled in the most personal way possible: God took on human nature. The doctrine called the incarnation teaches that Jesus is fully God and fully human, one person who can truly represent humanity before God and truly reveal God to humanity.

Christians have long understood the virgin birth as a sign of this mystery. Jesus did not begin as an ordinary man who later became divine. From His conception, He was the Son of God entering human life. This is why His presence, His teaching, and His saving work carry God’s own authority.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

“God with us” means believers are never truly alone. Jesus did not save from a distance; He entered human life, with its weakness, sorrow, and pain. When believers face loneliness, fear, or suffering, they can bring it to a God who understands from the inside and who has promised His continuing presence through His Spirit.

The truth of Immanuel also shapes how believers live. If God is with His people, then every part of life, including work, family, rest, and relationships, is lived in His presence. That encourages integrity in private as well as in public, and gratitude in ordinary moments as well as special ones.

Finally, Isaiah’s original prophecy was given to a frightened king who refused to trust God. The sign of Immanuel was God’s answer to fear. Believers facing threatening situations today can remember that God’s presence is the deepest answer to fear, and they can choose to trust Him rather than rely only on their own plans and alliances, as Ahaz did.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Matthew 1* reminds readers that God keeps His promises across long stretches of time. Generations lived and died between Abraham and Jesus, and between David and Jesus. Many of them saw little evidence that God’s promises were moving forward. Yet God was faithful through every generation, including the dark years of exile. Believers who are waiting on God, whether for answered prayer, for change in a difficult situation, or for the fulfillment of His purposes, can take courage from this. God’s timing is often slower than ours, but His faithfulness does not fail.

The genealogy also speaks to anyone who feels their family history or personal past disqualifies them from God’s purposes. The Messiah’s family line included foreigners, people with scandalous stories, and kings who did great evil. God did not hide these names. He worked through and beyond them. No one’s background places them beyond the reach of God’s grace. This does not excuse sin, but it means that the past does not have to have the last word.

Joseph’s example gives a picture of quiet, practical faithfulness. He was asked to do something that would cost him reputation and comfort, and he obeyed without delay. His righteousness included mercy, and his obedience was expressed in protecting and caring for others. Many of the most important acts of faith are like this: unseen, costly, and steady. Believers can ask God for the same kind of integrity in their families and responsibilities, choosing compassion over humiliation and obedience over self-protection.

Above all, the chapter presents Jesus as the Savior from sin and as God with us. These two truths belong together. Because Jesus is God with us, He is able to save; and because He saves His people from their sins, His presence brings forgiveness rather than fear. The right response is to trust Him, to bring honest confession of sin to Him, and to live each day aware that He is present and at work.

## Chapter Prayer

Faithful God, thank You for keeping Your promises through all the generations, through times of strength and times of failure, until You sent Jesus, the Son of David and the Son of Abraham. Thank You that His family line includes people with broken and surprising stories, and that Your grace reaches people no one else would have chosen.

Give me a heart like Joseph’s, that holds firmly to what is right and still refuses to shame others, and that obeys You promptly even when it costs me something. Thank You that Jesus came to save His people from their sins. Help me to be honest about my sin and to trust Him rather than my own efforts. Thank You that He is Immanuel, God with us. When I feel afraid or alone, remind me that You are near, and teach me to live every part of my life in Your presence. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

# Matthew — Chapter 2

Chapter Theme: The True King Is Worshiped by Strangers and Hunted by a Tyrant

[Read Matthew 2 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/MAT02.htm)

Main Teaching

Wise men from the east travel to worship the newborn King of the Jews, while King Herod, threatened by the child, tries to destroy Him. God protects Jesus through dreams given to the wise men and to Joseph, leading the family to Egypt and then to Nazareth. Matthew shows that Jesus relives Israel’s story and fulfills its Scriptures, and that God’s purposes cannot be stopped by violent human power.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Matthew 2* moves forward from the birth of Jesus to events that took place some time afterward, probably within the first two years of His life. Matthew does not describe the birth itself in detail. Instead he focuses on how different people responded to the news that the King of the Jews had been born. Some came from far away to worship Him. Others, who should have welcomed Him, ignored Him or tried to kill Him.

The political background is important. Herod the Great ruled Judea from 37 to 4 B.C. as a client king of Rome. He was an Idumean (an Edomite by ancestry) whose family had converted to Judaism, so many Jews never fully accepted him as a legitimate king. He was a brilliant builder who expanded the Jerusalem temple magnificently, but he was also deeply paranoid and brutal. He executed one of his wives, her mother, and three of his own sons because he suspected them of plotting against him. A man like this would not react calmly to news that someone else had been “born King of the Jews.” Because Herod died in 4 B.C., Jesus must have been born a little before that date. (The calendar system dividing B.C. and A.D. was calculated centuries later and contained a small error.)

### The Visit of the Wise Men (*2:1–12*)

Matthew tells us that Jesus was born “*in Bethlehem of Judea*” (*v. 1*), the small town about six miles south of Jerusalem that was David’s hometown. Wise men, or “magi,” arrived in Jerusalem from the east. The magi were a class of learned advisers in Persia and Babylon, known for studying the stars and interpreting dreams. Babylon had hosted a large Jewish community since the exile, so it is possible that such scholars knew of Jewish hopes for a coming king. Matthew does not tell us how many magi there were; the tradition of three comes from the three gifts. Nor were they kings, though later tradition often pictured them that way.

They asked, “*Where is he who is born King of the Jews? For we saw his star in the east, and have come to worship him*” (*v. 2*). Many explanations have been offered for the star, including a comet, a conjunction of planets, or a supernatural light. Matthew’s interest is not astronomical. He wants readers to see that God used a sign these Gentile scholars could understand to draw them to His Son. Some readers also connect the star to *Numbers 24:17*, where the prophet Balaam, himself a man from the east, foresaw that “*A star will come out of Jacob*” (*Numbers 24:17*).

Their question alarmed Herod, “*and all Jerusalem with him*” (*v. 3*). Jerusalem’s leaders and people knew how Herod responded to threats, and they feared what might follow. Herod called together the chief priests and scribes, the experts in the Scriptures, and asked where the Messiah was to be born. They answered immediately: Bethlehem, quoting *Micah 5:2* together with words from *2 Samuel 5:2* about a ruler who would shepherd God’s people Israel. The irony is striking. The religious experts knew exactly where the Messiah would be born, yet none of them made the six-mile journey to see. The foreigners traveled hundreds of miles to worship; the scholars stayed home.

Herod secretly met the magi to find out exactly when the star had appeared. Then he sent them to Bethlehem, asking them to report back so that he too could come and worship. His words were a lie; his real plan was murder. The magi set out, and the star went ahead of them until it stood over the place where the child was. Matthew says they “*rejoiced with exceedingly great joy*” (*v. 10*), piling up words to describe their delight.

They entered “*the house*” (*v. 11*), which suggests the family was by now living in a home in Bethlehem rather than in the place where Jesus was born. They saw the child with Mary His mother, bowed down, and worshiped Him. Then they opened their treasures and gave Him gold, frankincense, and myrrh, gifts fit for royalty. Warned in a dream not to return to Herod, they went home by another route.

### The Escape to Egypt (*2:13–15*)

After the magi left, an angel appeared to Joseph in a dream and told him to take the child and His mother and flee to Egypt, because Herod was about to search for the child to kill Him. Egypt was a natural place of refuge. It lay outside Herod’s control, and large Jewish communities lived there, especially in Alexandria. Joseph obeyed at once, leaving “*by night*” (*v. 14*). The gifts of the magi may well have helped to pay for the journey and the time in a foreign land.

Matthew says that the family remained in Egypt until Herod’s death, fulfilling the words, “*Out of Egypt I called my son*” (*v. 15*). These words come from *Hosea 11:1*, where they originally referred to Israel. God had called Israel His “son” at the time of the exodus (*Exodus 4:22*) and brought the nation out of slavery in Egypt. Matthew is not saying that Hosea was predicting Jesus’ trip to Egypt in the way a fortune-teller predicts events. He is showing that Jesus relives and completes Israel’s story. Israel, God’s son, went down to Egypt and was brought out; Jesus, God’s true Son, does the same. Where Israel often failed, Jesus will be faithful.

### The Massacre at Bethlehem (*2:16–18*)

When Herod realized the magi had not returned, he was furious. He ordered the killing of all boys two years old and under in Bethlehem and its surrounding area, based on the time the magi had told him the star appeared. Bethlehem was a small village, so the number of children killed may have been relatively small, perhaps a dozen or two. That is why the event is not mentioned by other historians of the period, but it fits exactly with what is known of Herod’s character.

Matthew connects this tragedy with *Jeremiah 31:15*, where Rachel, the ancestral mother of Israel who was buried near Bethlehem, is pictured weeping for her children as they were taken into exile. The passage in Jeremiah expressed the grief of the nation at its darkest hour, but it is immediately followed by God’s promise of hope, restoration, and a new covenant (*Jeremiah 31:16–34*). By citing this verse, Matthew acknowledges the horror and grief of Bethlehem’s mothers without minimizing it, while also hinting that God’s plan of redemption is moving forward even through such sorrow.

### The Return to Nazareth (*2:19–23*)

After Herod died, an angel again appeared to Joseph in Egypt and told him to return to the land of Israel. Joseph obeyed, but when he learned that Herod’s son Archelaus was ruling Judea, he was afraid to go there. Archelaus had a reputation for cruelty equal to his father’s; he began his reign by massacring around three thousand people in the temple courts, and Rome eventually removed him in A.D. 6. Warned again in a dream, Joseph took the family north to the region of Galilee, ruled by another of Herod’s sons, Antipas, and settled in the small town of Nazareth.

Matthew says this fulfilled what was spoken through the prophets, that “*he will be called a Nazarene*” (*v. 23*). No Old Testament verse contains these exact words, and Matthew speaks of “the prophets” in the plural, suggesting he is summarizing a theme rather than quoting one passage. Many interpreters connect “Nazarene” with the Hebrew word “netzer,” meaning “branch,” used in *Isaiah 11:1* for the shoot that would grow from the family of Jesse, David’s father. Others note that Nazareth was an obscure and somewhat despised town (*John 1:46*), so that being called a “Nazarene” fits the prophetic picture of a Messiah who would be humble and rejected (*Isaiah 53:2–3*). Both ideas may be in view.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Matthew 2:2* — Strangers Seeking the King

> *“‘Where is he who is born King of the Jews? For we saw his star in the east, and have come to worship him.’”*
>
> — *Matthew 2:2* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These are the first words spoken by the magi when they arrive in Jerusalem. They have traveled a long distance from the east, likely from Persia or Babylon, a journey that could have taken weeks or months. They come to the capital city, naturally expecting that the royal court would know about the birth of a new king.

Their question contains three important claims. First, they say this child is “born King of the Jews.” Herod held the title “King of the Jews,” given to him by the Roman Senate, but he had not been born to it. The magi’s words imply that this child is the rightful king by birth, which is why Herod is so disturbed. Second, they say, “*we saw his star in the east*” (*v. 2*). In the ancient world, people commonly believed that the birth of great rulers was marked by signs in the heavens. God used something these astrologers were watching to draw them to Jesus. Third, they say they have come “*to worship him*” (*v. 2*). The Greek word used here can mean to bow down in respect before a king, but Matthew uses it repeatedly for the worship given to Jesus (for example, *Matthew 14:33*; *28:9*, 17).

The irony of this verse is powerful. The title “King of the Jews” will appear again at the end of Matthew, written above Jesus’ head on the cross as the charge against Him (*Matthew 27:37*). From the beginning to the end of His life, Jesus is recognized as king by outsiders while being rejected by the powerful in Jerusalem.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The magi are the first worshipers of Jesus in Matthew’s Gospel, and they are Gentiles. This anticipates the end of the book, where the risen Jesus sends His disciples to “*make disciples of all nations*” (*Matthew 28:19*). The Old Testament prophets had foreseen that nations would come to Israel’s light and bring gifts to honor God (*Isaiah 60:3*, 6; *Psalm 72:10–11*). Matthew shows this beginning to happen in the infancy of Jesus.

The verse also shows how God meets people where they are. The magi were not familiar with Israel’s Scriptures in the way the priests and scribes were. They had only a star and a question. Yet God led them, first through the sign in the sky, then through the Scriptures that pointed to Bethlehem, and finally through a dream that protected them. Their search was imperfect but sincere, and God honored it.

At the same time, the contrast with Jerusalem’s leaders is a warning. Knowing the right answers about the Messiah did not lead the scribes to seek Him. Religious knowledge without a heart to respond can leave a person unmoved even when God is doing something remarkable nearby.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

The magi’s example encourages anyone who is searching for God, even with limited understanding. God is able to use whatever light a person has to lead them toward Jesus. Honest seeking, combined with willingness to learn from Scripture, is the path the magi followed, and it led them to worship.

For those who already know a great deal about the Bible, the scribes are a sober reminder. It is possible to know where Jesus can be found and never actually come to Him. Knowledge should lead to action: worship, obedience, and a willingness to go where He is, even when it is inconvenient.

The magi also show that worship involves effort and sacrifice. They traveled far and gave valuable gifts. Coming to Jesus may require believers to rearrange priorities, set aside time, and offer what is precious to them. Worship is not only what happens in a service; it is the orientation of a whole life toward Christ as King.

### *Matthew 2:11* — Worship and Gifts for the Child King

> *“They came into the house and saw the young child with Mary, his mother, and they fell down and worshiped him. Opening their treasures, they offered to him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh.”*
>
> — *Matthew 2:11* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse describes the moment the magi finally reach Jesus. Having followed the star from Jerusalem to Bethlehem, they enter the house where the family is living. They find “*the young child with Mary, his mother*” (*v. 11*). Matthew’s wording keeps the focus on Jesus. He is the one the magi worship, while Mary is mentioned as His mother.

The magi “*fell down and worshiped him*” (*v. 11*). Bowing to the ground was the posture of people coming before a great king. These distinguished men from the east humble themselves before a small child living in a modest home in a village. Then they open their treasure chests and present gifts. Gold was the most precious metal and was associated with royalty. Frankincense was a fragrant resin burned in worship, including in the temple. Myrrh was a costly perfume used in anointing oil and also for embalming the dead.

Since early in church history, Christians have seen symbolic meaning in these gifts: gold for a king, frankincense for one who is worshiped as God, and myrrh pointing to His death and burial. Matthew himself does not explain the gifts this way, so such interpretations should be held as reflections rather than as the text’s direct claim. What the text does make clear is that these were royal gifts offered in worship, fitting for the King of the Jews.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This scene echoes Old Testament passages that pictured the nations bringing gifts to God’s king. *Psalm 72*, a prayer for the king of David’s line, says that the kings of Sheba and Seba will bring gifts and all nations will serve him. *Isaiah 60:6* speaks of nations bringing “*gold and frankincense*” (*Isaiah 60:6*) and proclaiming the praises of the LORD. Matthew shows these hopes beginning to come true as Gentile visitors worship the Messiah.

The verse also reveals the kind of king Jesus is. He is honored with royal gifts, yet He is found not in a palace but in an ordinary house in a small town. God’s King comes in humility. This pattern will run through His whole life, until He is crowned with thorns. True worship recognizes His majesty even when it is hidden in lowliness.

Finally, it is noteworthy that worship comes before giving. The magi bow down first and then open their treasures. Their gifts are an expression of their worship, not a substitute for it.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse calls believers to give Jesus the honor that belongs to a king. Worship begins with humility, recognizing that He is greater than we are, and then expresses itself in giving. The magi gave their best, not their leftovers. Believers can ask what it would mean to offer Christ their best time, abilities, resources, and attention rather than whatever remains after everything else.

It also teaches that worship should come from the heart before it reaches the hands. Giving money, serving, or performing religious duties has value when it flows from honoring Jesus. Without that, generosity can become a way of seeking approval or feeling good about ourselves. Beginning with genuine worship keeps our gifts in the right place.

Finally, the humble setting reminds believers not to overlook Christ in ordinary places. He is present in small churches, humble homes, and in people the world considers unimportant. Learning to recognize and honor Him in such settings is part of true worship.

### *Matthew 2:13* — God’s Protection in a Dangerous World

> *“Now when they had departed, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream, saying, ‘Arise and take the young child and his mother, and flee into Egypt, and stay there until I tell you, for Herod will seek the young child to destroy him.’”*
>
> — *Matthew 2:13* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse comes just after the magi have departed, having been warned not to return to Herod. Joseph, who has already received a message from an angel in a dream (*Matthew 1:20*), now receives a second one. This time the message is urgent: “*Arise and take the young child and his mother, and flee into Egypt*” (*v. 13*).

The reason is given plainly: “*for Herod will seek the young child to destroy him*” (*v. 13*). Herod has been tricked by the magi and is about to act. The angel tells Joseph to stay in Egypt until further notice. The journey from Bethlehem to the Egyptian border was roughly a hundred miles across desert country, a difficult trip for a family with a young child, and life as refugees in a foreign land would have been uncertain.

Joseph’s response, described in the next verse, is immediate. He got up and left that very night. Once again he says nothing; he simply obeys. His obedience saves the life of Jesus. Shortly afterward, Herod’s soldiers carried out the massacre in Bethlehem.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that God’s protection does not always come in the form of removing danger. God did not stop Herod from ruling or from acting violently. Instead He warned Joseph and provided a way of escape. God’s care for His Son worked through human obedience, through a difficult journey, and through life in exile.

The flight to Egypt also connects Jesus to the story of Israel. Long before, Jacob’s family had gone down to Egypt to survive famine, and later God brought Israel out of Egypt in the exodus. There are also echoes of Moses: just as Pharaoh ordered Hebrew baby boys killed and Moses was spared (*Exodus 1–2*), Herod orders the killing of Bethlehem’s boys and Jesus is spared. Matthew presents Jesus as the one who will lead a greater exodus, rescuing people from sin and death.

The passage does not explain why God spared Jesus while other children died. Matthew does not hide that tragedy or explain it away. He places it within the larger story of a God who will one day judge all injustice and who sent His Son, in the end, to suffer and die Himself. The suffering of the innocent is a real mystery, but the cross shows that God does not stand at a distance from it.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Joseph’s example shows that faithfulness to God sometimes includes taking practical action to protect the vulnerable. Joseph did not stay in Bethlehem and assume nothing bad would happen. He took the warning seriously and moved his family to safety. Trusting God and acting wisely are not opposites. Believers who face danger, whether from abusive people, unsafe situations, or threatening circumstances, can see in Joseph a model of faith that acts to protect life.

The verse also speaks to those who have been displaced, who have had to leave home, or who live as refugees. Jesus Himself spent part of His childhood as a refugee in a foreign land. Believers can remember that He understands such experiences, and the church has good reason to show compassion and practical care for people forced from their homes.

Finally, Joseph’s quick obedience encourages believers to act on what God makes clear without unnecessary delay. When God’s will is plain, such as caring for those entrusted to us, telling the truth, or leaving behind sin, hesitation can be costly.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Matthew 2* contrasts three responses to Jesus. The magi searched for Him, rejoiced when they found Him, and worshiped Him with costly gifts. Herod saw Jesus as a threat to his own power and tried to destroy Him. The chief priests and scribes knew the Scriptures well but showed no interest in seeking the Messiah. These responses are still present today. Some people seek Christ wholeheartedly. Some resist Him because He challenges their control over their own lives. And some know a great deal about Him but remain indifferent. This chapter invites each reader to consider which response describes their own heart, and to choose the path of the magi.

The chapter also teaches that God’s purposes cannot be defeated by human power. Herod was ruthless, cunning, and politically powerful, and he set out to kill the child. Yet God guided the magi, warned Joseph, and preserved Jesus. Herod died, and Jesus lived. When believers see injustice and violence in the world, or when they feel small before powerful forces, they can remember that God’s kingdom will outlast every earthly throne.

At the same time, *Matthew 2* does not pretend that following God means a life free from danger or grief. Jesus’ family became refugees. The mothers of Bethlehem wept for their children. God’s protection came through warnings, hard journeys, and the faithful obedience of ordinary people. Believers should expect that faithfulness may involve difficulty and should not interpret hardship as a sign that God has abandoned them. They should also take seriously their responsibility to act wisely and protect those in their care.

Finally, the repeated pattern of Joseph’s obedience offers a practical model. Three times he received direction and three times he acted promptly. His faith was expressed in decisions about where to live, when to travel, and how to keep his family safe. Following Christ is lived out in such ordinary decisions, made prayerfully and in obedience to what God has shown.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord God, thank You for drawing the magi from a distant land to worship Your Son, and for showing that Jesus is the King not only of Israel but of all nations. Give me a heart that seeks Him as they did, that rejoices to find Him, and that offers Him my very best in worship.

Keep me from the hardness of Herod, who saw Jesus as a threat to his own control, and from the indifference of those who knew the Scriptures but never went to Bethlehem. Thank You for protecting Jesus through Joseph’s quick obedience. Help me to listen and obey promptly when You make Your will clear, and to act wisely to protect those You have placed in my care. Comfort all who grieve because of violence and injustice, and remind me that every earthly throne will pass away, but the kingdom of Your Son will stand forever. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Matthew · Chapter 3 of 28

# Matthew — Chapter 3

Chapter Theme: The Call to Repent and the Beloved Son Revealed

[Read Matthew 3 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/MAT03.htm)

Main Teaching

John the Baptist prepares the way for the Messiah by calling Israel to repentance and warning that genuine change must show itself in a changed life. Jesus then comes to be baptized, identifying Himself with the people He came to save, and the Father publicly declares Him to be His beloved Son as the Spirit comes upon Him.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Matthew 3* jumps forward about thirty years from the end of chapter 2. Jesus has grown up in Nazareth, and now a new figure appears on the scene: John the Baptist. Luke’s Gospel tells us that John was a relative of Jesus, the son of an elderly priest named Zechariah and his wife Elizabeth, born just a few months before Jesus (*Luke 1*). Matthew introduces him simply as the one who came “*preaching in the wilderness of Judea*” (*v. 1*).

To understand why John’s ministry caused such a stir, it helps to know that many Jews believed God had not sent a true prophet for centuries. The last of the Old Testament prophets, Malachi, had promised that God would send a messenger to prepare His way, and that Elijah would come before the great day of the LORD (*Malachi 3:1*; *4:5*). The people lived with a sense that God was silent, waiting for Him to act again. Then suddenly, in the barren region near the Jordan River, a man dressed like Elijah began calling the whole nation to prepare for God’s coming.

### John the Baptist’s Message and Lifestyle (*3:1–6*)

John’s message was short and urgent: “*Repent, for the Kingdom of Heaven is at hand!*” (*v. 2*) Matthew usually says “Kingdom of Heaven” where Mark and Luke say “Kingdom of God.” Many Jews avoided saying God’s name out of reverence, sometimes replacing it with “Heaven,” so the two phrases mean the same thing. The kingdom is God’s rule, His reign breaking into the world to set things right, as the prophets had promised.

Matthew identifies John with the voice of *Isaiah 40:3*, crying out in the wilderness to prepare the way of the Lord. In Isaiah, that voice announced the end of Israel’s exile and God’s return to rescue His people. Ancient roads were prepared for the arrival of a king by leveling and straightening them. John’s work was to prepare people’s hearts in the same way, removing obstacles so they would be ready for the Lord.

John’s appearance reinforced his message. He wore clothing made of camel’s hair and a leather belt, which deliberately recalls Elijah, who is described in *2 Kings 1:8* as wearing a garment of hair with a leather belt. His diet of locusts (permitted as food under *Leviticus 11:22*) and wild honey was the simple fare of the desert. He lived outside the comforts and structures of society, and his whole life said that something was wrong and needed to change.

People came to him in great numbers from Jerusalem, Judea, and the Jordan region. They were baptized by him in the river, confessing their sins. Jewish people knew of ritual washings for purification, and Gentiles who converted to Judaism were sometimes immersed as part of their entry into Israel. John’s baptism was striking because he called Jews, God’s covenant people, to undergo a washing of repentance, as if they needed to begin again. The location was meaningful too. Israel had entered the promised land by crossing the Jordan; now the people were returning to the river to prepare for a new act of God.

### John’s Warning to the Religious Leaders (*3:7–12*)

Among the crowds came many Pharisees and Sadducees. The Pharisees were a popular movement devoted to careful observance of the law of Moses, including many traditions about how to apply it. The Sadducees were a smaller, wealthier group associated with the priestly aristocracy and the temple, who rejected beliefs such as the resurrection of the dead. These groups often disagreed with each other, but both held positions of religious influence.

John greeted them with shocking words: “*You offspring of vipers, who warned you to flee from the wrath to come?*” (*v. 7*) The image is of snakes fleeing a brush fire. John suspected they were coming for baptism as a kind of insurance against judgment, without any real change of heart. He told them to “*produce fruit worthy of repentance*” (*v. 8*), meaning that genuine repentance would show itself in changed behavior.

He also warned them not to rely on being descendants of Abraham. Many believed that belonging to Abraham’s family guaranteed a place among God’s people. John said that God could raise up children for Abraham from the stones lying on the ground. (In Hebrew and Aramaic, the words for “children” and “stones” sound similar, which may have made the saying memorable.) Family heritage could not replace a living relationship with God.

John used two agricultural images of judgment. The ax was already lying at the root of the trees, ready to cut down any tree that did not bear good fruit. And the one coming after him would hold a winnowing fork. At harvest, farmers tossed threshed grain into the air with a fork; the wind blew the light chaff away while the heavier wheat fell back to the threshing floor. The wheat was gathered and stored, and the chaff was burned. John was saying that the coming one would separate the genuine from the false.

John insisted that this coming one was far greater than he was. John was not even worthy to carry His sandals, a task done by the lowest servants. John baptized with water, but the coming one would “*baptize you in the Holy Spirit*” (*v. 11*) and with fire. The prophets had promised that in the last days God would pour out His Spirit on His people (*Joel 2:28*; *Ezekiel 36:26–27*). Fire could represent both purification and judgment, and in John’s words both seem to be in view: the Messiah would purify those who repent and judge those who refuse.

### The Baptism of Jesus (*3:13–17*)

Then Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan to be baptized by John. John tried to stop Him, saying, “*I need to be baptized by you, and you come to me?*” (*v. 14*) John recognized that Jesus was greater and had no sins to confess. Why should the one who would baptize with the Spirit be baptized by a mere prophet?

Jesus answered, “*Allow it now, for this is the fitting way for us to fulfill all righteousness*” (*v. 15*). These are the first words Jesus speaks in Matthew’s Gospel. He did not need to repent, but He chose to stand with sinful people in their act of repentance, identifying fully with the people He came to save. By doing what God was calling Israel to do through John, He was carrying out God’s righteous plan in every respect. His baptism also anticipates the cross, where the sinless one would take the place of sinners. Some interpreters also see in it His public dedication to His mission, much as priests and kings in Israel were consecrated before beginning their service.

As Jesus came up out of the water, the heavens were opened, and He saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and resting on Him. Then a voice from heaven declared, “*This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased*” (*v. 17*). In this scene the Father speaks, the Son is baptized, and the Spirit descends. Christians have long seen here a revelation of the one God as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, a truth that Matthew will make explicit at the end of his Gospel in the command to baptize “*in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit*” (*Matthew 28:19*).

## Important Verses Explained

### *Matthew 3:2* — Repent, for the Kingdom Is Near

> *“‘Repent, for the Kingdom of Heaven is at hand!’”*
>
> — *Matthew 3:2* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse is John the Baptist’s summary message. He preached it in the wilderness of Judea, a dry and rugged region between Jerusalem and the Dead Sea, to the crowds who came out to hear him. Matthew will later show Jesus beginning His own ministry with exactly the same words (*Matthew 4:17*), which tells us how central this call is.

“Repent” translates a Greek word meaning to change one’s mind, but in the Bible it carries the fuller meaning of the Hebrew idea of turning around. To repent is to turn away from sin and turn back to God. It involves a change of thinking, attitude, and direction. It is not simply feeling sorry; it is a reorientation of one’s life. That is why John later insists on fruit that shows repentance is real.

The reason for repentance is that “*the Kingdom of Heaven is at hand*” (*v. 2*). “At hand” means it has come near; it is about to arrive or is already arriving. The Jews hoped for the day when God would act decisively to establish His rule, defeat evil, and restore His people. John announced that this day was upon them. But he gave the announcement a surprising twist: the coming of God’s kingdom is not automatically good news for everyone. It means God will set things right, which includes judging sin. To be ready, people needed to turn from their sins.

The crowds who heard John understood his message as urgent. Many responded by confessing their sins and being baptized. The call was addressed not only to obvious sinners but to the whole nation, including the religious and respectable.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The kingdom of heaven is the central theme of Jesus’ teaching in Matthew. It refers to God’s reign: His saving and ruling power coming into the world through Jesus. The kingdom has a present dimension, seen when Jesus forgives sins, heals the sick, and drives out demons, and a future dimension, which will be complete when Christ returns. John stood at the threshold of this new era, announcing that it was about to begin.

Repentance is the doorway into the kingdom. Throughout Scripture, God calls His people to return to Him (for example, *Isaiah 55:7* and *Joel 2:12–13*), always with the promise that He is gracious and ready to forgive. Repentance is not a way of earning God’s favor; it is the response of someone who realizes they have been going the wrong way and turns back to the God who welcomes them. In the New Testament, repentance and faith go together, as two sides of turning from sin to God.

It is important that John’s message was given to religious people. Repentance is not only for those whose sins are obvious. Pride, self-righteousness, and religious complacency also need to be repented of. Everyone needs to turn to God.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Repentance is not a one-time event but a lasting posture for believers. Martin Luther began his famous Ninety-Five Theses with the observation that when Jesus called people to repent, He meant that the entire life of believers should be one of repentance. Followers of Christ continually recognize areas where they have turned from God and choose to turn back to Him.

Practically, repentance means naming sin honestly rather than minimizing it, confessing it to God, and making specific changes. If we have wronged someone, repentance may include apologizing and making things right. If a habit is pulling us away from God, it means taking concrete steps away from it. Feeling regret without changing direction is not yet repentance.

The nearness of God’s kingdom also gives repentance hope. We do not turn from sin into emptiness; we turn toward the God whose rule brings forgiveness, healing, and new life. Repentance is the doorway to joy, not just to sorrow.

### *Matthew 3:8* — Fruit That Shows Repentance Is Real

> *“Therefore produce fruit worthy of repentance!”*
>
> — *Matthew 3:8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

John speaks these words directly to the Pharisees and Sadducees who came to the place where he was baptizing. He had just called them “*offspring of vipers*” (*v. 7*) and asked who had warned them to flee from the coming judgment. John perceived that many of them were not coming in genuine repentance. They may have wanted to appear righteous before the crowds, or to protect themselves from judgment, without truly changing.

“Fruit” is a common biblical image for the visible results of what is inside a person. Just as a tree is known by the fruit it produces, a person’s repentance is shown by the way they live. John was saying that baptism, as an outward act, was not enough. If their repentance was real, it would produce evidence: changed behavior, humility, justice, and mercy.

Luke’s Gospel records examples of the kind of fruit John meant. He told those with two coats to share with someone who had none; he told tax collectors to collect no more than they were authorized; and he told soldiers not to extort money or accuse people falsely (*Luke 3:10–14*). Repentance touched practical matters like money, honesty, and the treatment of others.

John then warned them not to rely on their status as descendants of Abraham. Being part of God’s chosen people did not exempt them from the need for genuine repentance. He followed this with the image of the ax at the root of the trees, ready to cut down every tree that did not produce good fruit.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse teaches that true repentance cannot be separated from transformed living. Scripture consistently connects inner faith and outward obedience. Jesus will later say, “*by their fruits you will know them*” (*Matthew 7:20*), and James will insist that faith without works is dead (*James 2:17*). Christians believe that people are saved by God’s grace, not by their good works, but they also believe that genuine faith and repentance always produce a changed life.

The warning about relying on Abraham as father addresses a danger that every religious community faces: assuming that belonging to the right group, family, or church guarantees a right standing with God. Heritage and community are gifts, but they are not a substitute for personal turning to God. Paul later explains that Abraham’s true children are those who share his faith (*Galatians 3:7*).

At the same time, the image of fruit is hopeful. Fruit grows gradually. God does not expect immediate perfection from those who repent, but He does expect real growth. Where there is genuine life, fruit will appear.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse calls believers to examine whether their faith is making a difference in how they live. It is possible to attend church, use the right words, and participate in religious practices without real change. Genuine repentance will eventually show itself in how we spend money, how we speak, how we treat those with less power, and whether we keep our commitments.

It also warns against relying on spiritual background. Growing up in a Christian family, attending a particular church, or having been baptized years ago are not substitutes for a present, living faith. Each person must respond to God personally.

Finally, the call to bear fruit encourages specific, practical steps. If there is someone we have wronged, fruit might mean seeking reconciliation. If we have been dishonest, it might mean making restitution. If we have neglected those in need, it might mean beginning to give generously. Small, concrete changes are the evidence of a heart that has truly turned to God.

### *Matthew 3:17* — “*This Is My Beloved Son*” (*v. 17*)

> *“Behold, a voice out of the heavens said, ‘This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased.’”*
>
> — *Matthew 3:17* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse records the voice of God the Father speaking from heaven immediately after Jesus’ baptism. Jesus had come to John to be baptized, and when John hesitated, Jesus insisted that it was right “*to fulfill all righteousness*” (*v. 15*). As Jesus came up out of the water, the heavens opened, and He saw the Spirit of God descending on Him like a dove. Then the Father spoke.

The Father’s words echo two important Old Testament passages. The first is *Psalm 2:7*, where God says to His anointed king, “*You are my son*” (*Psalm 2:7*). This psalm was understood as describing the Messiah, the king of David’s line. The second is *Isaiah 42:1*, where God introduces His Servant: “*my chosen, in whom my soul delights*” (*Isaiah 42:1*). In Isaiah, the Servant is the one who will bring justice to the nations and, later in the book, suffer for the sins of others (*Isaiah 53*). The Father’s words combine these two figures: Jesus is the royal Son and the suffering Servant.

The word “beloved” emphasizes the deep love between the Father and the Son. Some also hear an echo of *Genesis 22:2*, where God speaks of Isaac as Abraham’s son, “*your only son, Isaac, whom you love*” (*Genesis 22:2*), the son Abraham was asked to offer. The phrase “*with whom I am well pleased*” (*v. 17*) expresses the Father’s approval of Jesus. At this point Jesus has not yet preached a sermon or performed a miracle. The Father’s pleasure rests on who Jesus is and on His willingness to take up His mission.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse is one of the clearest revelations in Scripture of Jesus’ identity. He is not merely a prophet like John or a good teacher. He is the beloved Son of God. Matthew’s Gospel will continue to build on this truth, and the same words will be spoken again at the transfiguration, with the added command, “*Listen to him*” (*Matthew 17:5*).

The scene also reveals the relationship within the one God. The Father speaks, the Son is baptized, and the Spirit descends. This does not explain the mystery of the Trinity, but it shows that the Father, Son, and Spirit are distinct and act together in the work of salvation.

The timing of these words is significant. They come right after Jesus identifies with sinners in baptism and right before He goes into the wilderness to be tempted. The Father’s affirmation strengthens Jesus for the trial ahead. In chapter 4 the devil will twice say, “If you are the Son of God,” trying to make Jesus prove His identity on the devil’s terms. Jesus does not need to prove it. He has already heard His Father’s voice.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse calls readers first to recognize who Jesus is. The Father Himself has declared Jesus to be His beloved Son. That means His words carry God’s authority, His life reveals God’s character, and His mission accomplishes God’s purposes. The appropriate response is to listen to Him, trust Him, and follow Him.

It also offers a picture of the identity God gives to those who belong to Christ. The New Testament teaches that believers are adopted as God’s children through Jesus (*Galatians 4:4–7*). Jesus’ sonship is unique, but believers share in the Father’s love through Him. This means believers can draw their sense of worth from God’s love rather than from achievement, approval, or performance.

Finally, the order of events is a lesson. The Father’s love and approval came before Jesus’ public ministry and before His time of testing. In the same way, believers do not serve God in order to earn His love; they serve from the security of being loved. When temptation or hardship comes, remembering that we belong to God can steady us, just as Jesus faced the devil secure in His Father’s words.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Matthew 3* brings together two great themes: the call to repentance and the revelation of Jesus as God’s beloved Son. They belong together. John prepared people for Jesus by calling them to turn from sin, and Jesus Himself stepped into the water alongside repentant sinners. The chapter invites readers to come to God honestly, admitting their need, and to discover that the one who is coming in power to judge is also the one who stands with sinners to save them.

The chapter warns against empty religion. John was severe with religious leaders who came for baptism without real repentance and who trusted in their heritage. This warning still applies to anyone who relies on church attendance, religious upbringing, or outward practices instead of a living, obedient relationship with God. The remedy is not to abandon spiritual practices but to let them be expressions of a heart truly turned to God, producing fruit in everyday life.

John’s humility offers another lesson. He had large crowds, great influence, and a powerful message, but he insisted that he was not worthy even to carry Jesus’ sandals. He understood that his role was to point to someone greater. Believers who serve in any capacity, whether in families, churches, or communities, can learn from John to keep attention on Christ rather than on themselves.

Finally, Jesus’ willingness to be baptized shows the humility of God’s Son. He did not hold Himself apart from sinful people; He joined them. His followers are called to the same kind of humble solidarity with others, refusing to look down on those who are struggling, and remembering that every believer stands before God only because Jesus chose to stand with us. Living from the Father’s love, rather than striving to earn it, allows believers to face temptation and serve others with steady confidence.

## Chapter Prayer

Heavenly Father, thank You for sending John to prepare the way for Your Son, and for the clear call to repent because Your kingdom has come near. Search my heart and show me where I have turned away from You. Give me grace to turn back fully, not only with words or outward actions but with a changed life that bears real fruit.

Keep me from trusting in my background, my reputation, or my religious habits instead of in You. Thank You that Jesus, though He had no sin, stepped into the water with sinners and identified Himself with people like me. Thank You for declaring Him Your beloved Son. Help me to listen to Him, to follow Him, and to live in the security of being loved by You through Him, so that I may face temptation and serve others with humility and confidence. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
