Matthew · Chapter 4 of 28

# Matthew — Chapter 4

Chapter Theme: The Faithful Son in the Wilderness and the Call to Follow

[Read Matthew 4 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/MAT04.htm)

Main Teaching

Led by the Spirit into the wilderness, Jesus resists the devil’s temptations by trusting and obeying God’s Word, succeeding where Israel had failed. He then begins His public ministry in Galilee, announcing the kingdom of heaven, calling fishermen to follow Him, and showing the kingdom’s power by teaching and healing.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Matthew 4* follows directly from Jesus’ baptism. The Father had just declared from heaven, “*This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased*” (*Matthew 3:17*), and the Spirit had come upon Jesus. Now that same Spirit leads Him into the wilderness, where His identity as God’s Son will be tested. This order matters: Jesus faces temptation not to earn His Father’s approval, but as the beloved Son who must show what kind of Son He is.

The chapter divides into two main parts. The first is the temptation in the wilderness (vv. 1–11). The second is the beginning of Jesus’ ministry in Galilee (vv. 12–25), including His move to Capernaum, His first preaching, the calling of His first disciples, and a summary of His teaching and healing.

### The Temptation in the Wilderness (*4:1–11*)

Matthew says that Jesus “*was led up by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil*” (*v. 1*). The Greek word for “tempted” can also mean “tested.” From God’s perspective this was a test that would reveal Jesus’ faithfulness; from the devil’s perspective it was an attempt to make Him fall. The wilderness was the barren region of Judea, a place associated in Israel’s memory with the forty years their ancestors wandered after leaving Egypt.

The parallels with Israel’s history are deliberate. Israel passed through the waters of the Red Sea and then spent forty years in the wilderness, where they were tested and repeatedly failed: they complained about food, tested God, and worshiped a golden calf. Jesus passes through the waters of baptism and then spends forty days in the wilderness, where He is tested and remains faithful. All three of His replies to the devil come from *Deuteronomy 6–8*, the chapters in which Moses reflected on Israel’s wilderness years. Matthew is showing that Jesus is the true, faithful Son of God, succeeding where Israel had failed. There is also an echo of Moses himself, who fasted forty days and nights on Mount Sinai (*Exodus 34:28*).

After fasting forty days and nights, Jesus was hungry. The tempter came and said, “*If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become bread*” (*v. 3*). The word “if” does not express doubt so much as challenge: “Since you are God’s Son, use your power for yourself.” The temptation was to satisfy a real need by using His divine authority independently of the Father’s will. Jesus answered from *Deuteronomy 8:3*, which says that God let Israel hunger in the wilderness and fed them with manna to teach them that people live not by bread alone but by every word from God’s mouth.

Next the devil took Jesus to “*the pinnacle of the temple*” (*v. 5*), probably a high corner of the temple complex overlooking a steep drop into the Kidron Valley. This time the devil quoted Scripture himself, *Psalm 91:11–12*, which promises that God’s angels will guard His people. He urged Jesus to throw Himself down and let God rescue Him. Such a spectacular rescue might also have impressed crowds at the temple. Jesus replied with *Deuteronomy 6:16*: “*You shall not test the Lord, your God*” (*v. 7*). That verse refers to the time at Massah when the Israelites demanded that God prove His presence by giving them water (*Exodus 17:1–7*). Putting oneself in danger to force God to act is not faith but presumption.

Finally, the devil took Jesus to a very high mountain and showed Him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory. He offered them all if Jesus would bow down and worship him. This was a temptation to gain the kingdom without the cross, to reach the goal of ruling the nations by taking a shortcut that bypassed obedience and suffering. Jesus responded firmly: “*Get behind me, Satan!*” (*v. 10*) and quoted *Deuteronomy 6:13*, that God alone is to be worshiped and served. Then the devil left Him, and angels came and served Him.

### Jesus Begins His Ministry in Galilee (*4:12–17*)

Some time later, Jesus heard that John the Baptist had been arrested. (Matthew will explain the reason in chapter 14: John had condemned Herod Antipas for marrying his brother’s wife.) Jesus withdrew to Galilee, the northern region where He had grown up. He left Nazareth and made His home in Capernaum, a fishing town on the northwest shore of the Sea of Galilee.

Matthew sees this move as fulfilling *Isaiah 9:1–2*. The tribal territories of Zebulun and Naphtali, in the north of Israel, had been the first to fall when Assyria invaded in the eighth century B.C., and the region had a mixed population, which is why Isaiah calls it “*Galilee of the Gentiles*” (*v. 15*). Isaiah promised that this region, which had first experienced darkness, would be the first to see a great light. That passage continues with the promise of a child born to reign on David’s throne (*Isaiah 9:6–7*). Matthew says the light has now dawned in Jesus.

From that time, Jesus began to preach the same message John had preached: “*Repent! For the Kingdom of Heaven is at hand*” (*v. 17*). The phrase “from that time” marks a turning point in Matthew’s Gospel, the beginning of Jesus’ public ministry.

### The Calling of the First Disciples (*4:18–22*)

Walking along the shore of the Sea of Galilee, Jesus saw two brothers, Simon (later called Peter) and Andrew, casting a net into the water. He said to them, “*Come after me, and I will make you fishers for men*” (*v. 19*). They immediately left their nets and followed Him. A little farther on, He saw James and John, the sons of Zebedee, in a boat with their father, mending their nets. He called them, and they immediately left the boat and their father and followed Him.

John’s Gospel tells us that at least some of these men had already met Jesus earlier, when they were associated with John the Baptist (*John 1:35–42*). Their response by the lake was therefore not entirely without background. Still, their decision was costly. Fishing on the Sea of Galilee was a significant business; Mark notes that Zebedee had hired servants (*Mark 1:20*). Leaving the boat and their father meant leaving livelihood, family business, and security to attach themselves to Jesus.

It was unusual for a rabbi to call his disciples. Normally students sought out a teacher. Jesus took the initiative and called these men to follow Him personally, not simply to learn a body of teaching.

### Teaching, Preaching, and Healing (*4:23–25*)

Matthew closes the chapter with a summary of Jesus’ early ministry. He went throughout Galilee “*teaching in their synagogues, preaching the Good News of the Kingdom, and healing every disease and every sickness among the people*” (*v. 23*). Synagogues were local gathering places for prayer and the reading and teaching of Scripture, and visiting teachers were often invited to speak. Jesus’ teaching explained the meaning of God’s Word; His preaching announced the arrival of the kingdom; and His healings demonstrated what the kingdom looks like, with the effects of sin and evil being reversed.

News about Jesus spread throughout Syria, the larger Roman province that included Galilee. People brought those suffering from all kinds of conditions: diseases, pain, demon possession, seizures, and paralysis. He healed them. Great crowds followed Him from Galilee, from the Decapolis (a league of ten largely Gentile cities east of the Jordan), from Jerusalem and Judea, and from beyond the Jordan. This summary sets the stage for the Sermon on the Mount, which begins in the next chapter as Jesus sees the crowds and goes up the mountainside to teach.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Matthew 4:4* — Living by Every Word From God

> *“But he answered, ‘It is written, “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds out of God’s mouth.”’”*
>
> — *Matthew 4:4* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This is Jesus’ answer to the first temptation. He had fasted for forty days in the wilderness and was hungry. The devil came and suggested that, as the Son of God, Jesus should turn the stones around Him into bread. The wilderness of Judea was full of rounded limestone rocks that might even resemble small loaves. The suggestion seemed reasonable. Jesus had the power, and He had a genuine need.

But Jesus saw what the temptation really was. The Spirit had led Him into the wilderness, and the Father had not told Him to end His fast by making bread. To use His power to provide for Himself would be to act independently of His Father, putting His physical needs above His trust in God. It would also set a pattern of using His power for His own comfort rather than for His mission.

Jesus answered by quoting *Deuteronomy 8:3*. In that chapter Moses reminded Israel that God had led them through the wilderness for forty years to humble them and test them. God let them hunger and then fed them with manna, a food they had never known, to teach them that “*man does not live by bread only, but man lives by every word that proceeds out of the LORD’s mouth*” (*Deuteronomy 8:3*). Israel had often failed this test, complaining and doubting God’s care. Jesus, facing the same kind of test, chose to trust His Father.

Jesus was not saying that bread is unimportant. He was saying that life depends ultimately on God and on obedience to His Word. He would rather remain hungry in obedience than be filled through disobedience.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows Jesus as the faithful Son who succeeds where Israel failed. Throughout the temptation narrative, Jesus relives Israel’s wilderness experience and remains faithful at every point. This is not only an example for believers but part of His saving work: He is the obedient one whose faithfulness counts for those who belong to Him. *Hebrews 4:15* says that He was “*in all points tempted like we are, yet without sin*” (*Hebrews 4:15*).

The verse also shows the importance of Scripture in spiritual life. Jesus did not argue with the devil or rely on His own reasoning. He responded with God’s Word, which He clearly knew deeply and understood in its context. Paul later calls the Word of God “*the sword of the Spirit*” (*Ephesians 6:17*). Knowing and trusting Scripture equips believers to recognize and resist temptation.

The temptation also teaches something about the nature of sin. Many temptations are not to do something obviously evil but to meet legitimate needs in illegitimate ways. Hunger was a real need. The question was whether Jesus would meet it by trusting His Father or by acting on His own.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to recognize that their deepest life comes from God, not only from physical provision. In a world that measures well-being mostly by material comfort, Jesus reminds His followers that relationship with God and obedience to His Word are essential for true life. Making time to read, understand, and live by Scripture is not an optional extra; it is nourishment.

It also helps believers recognize temptations to meet legitimate needs in wrong ways. The desire for security, affection, recognition, rest, or provision is not wrong. Temptation comes when we pursue these things through dishonesty, compromise, or disobedience. Jesus shows that it is better to wait on God, even through hardship, than to grab at what we need in a way that dishonors Him.

Finally, Jesus’ example shows the value of knowing Scripture well. When temptation comes, it is too late to begin learning God’s Word. Regular reading, reflection, and memorizing key passages prepare believers to recognize lies and respond with truth.

### *Matthew 4:10* — Worship God Alone

> *“Then Jesus said to him, ‘Get behind me, Satan! For it is written, “You shall worship the Lord your God, and you shall serve him only.”’”*
>
> — *Matthew 4:10* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This is Jesus’ response to the third and final temptation. The devil had taken Him to a very high mountain and shown Him all the kingdoms of the world in their splendor. He promised to give them all to Jesus if Jesus would fall down and worship him. This temptation was the most direct of the three. It offered Jesus the authority over the nations that, according to *Psalm 2:8*, God had promised to give His Son, but it offered it on the devil’s terms: without suffering, without the cross, and at the price of worshiping someone other than God.

Jesus replied, “*Get behind me, Satan!*” (*v. 10*) This was a command to leave. “Satan” is a Hebrew word meaning “adversary” or “accuser.” Then Jesus quoted *Deuteronomy 6:13*, where Moses commanded Israel to fear the LORD and serve Him alone, warning them not to follow other gods once they entered the land. Matthew’s wording, “worship” and “serve him only,” emphasizes that God alone is worthy of devotion.

After this the devil left Jesus, and angels came and served Him. The test was over, and Jesus had remained faithful at every point. Later in Matthew, Jesus will use similar words to Peter when Peter tries to talk Him out of going to the cross (*Matthew 16:23*). The temptation to avoid suffering on the way to glory would return, but Jesus would reject it again.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This temptation reveals what is at stake in worship. The devil’s ultimate goal was to receive the worship that belongs to God alone. Idolatry, giving ultimate devotion to anything other than God, lies at the heart of all sin. Israel’s great failure in the wilderness was making a golden calf and worshiping it (*Exodus 32*). Jesus, the faithful Son, refuses any rival to God.

The temptation also reveals the difference between the devil’s way to power and God’s way. The devil offered glory without suffering. God’s way led through the cross. After His resurrection, Jesus would say to His disciples, “*All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth*” (*Matthew 28:18*). He received the kingdom the devil had offered, but He received it from the Father, through obedience and sacrifice. The kingdoms of this world will become His, not because He compromised, but because He was faithful.

This verse shows that there are no shortcuts in God’s kingdom that bypass obedience. The end does not justify the means. Even a good goal pursued by sinful methods is a form of serving another master.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse calls believers to examine what they truly worship. Few people today are tempted to bow before the devil literally, but many are tempted to give ultimate devotion to success, money, power, approval, comfort, or relationships. Whatever we are willing to compromise our integrity for has become a rival to God. Recognizing these rivals honestly is the first step to turning away from them.

It also warns against shortcuts. Many temptations promise good results by questionable means: advancing a career through dishonesty, gaining influence through manipulation, or achieving a goal by cutting moral corners. Jesus’ example teaches believers to pursue good ends only by good means, trusting God with the results.

Finally, Jesus’ firm response, “Get behind me, Satan!”, shows that some temptations should not be negotiated with. Believers can decide in advance that certain things are not up for discussion, and respond to temptation with clear refusal rather than prolonged consideration.

### *Matthew 4:19* — “*Come After Me*” (*v. 19*)

> *“He said to them, ‘Come after me, and I will make you fishers for men.’”*
>
> — *Matthew 4:19* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus speaks these words to Simon Peter and his brother Andrew as He walks along the shore of the Sea of Galilee. They are casting a net into the water, doing the ordinary work of their family trade. Fishing was hard, physical labor, often done at night, and it was an important industry around the lake. These men were not religious scholars or members of the elite. They were working men in a busy lakeside economy.

Jesus’ call has two parts. The first is a command: “Come after me.” This is the language of discipleship. In Jewish culture, a disciple literally followed his teacher, walking behind him, learning from his words and his way of life, and imitating him. But Jesus’ call is unusual. Rabbis did not normally go looking for disciples; students chose their teachers. Jesus takes the initiative, and He calls them not to study the law under Him but to attach themselves to Him personally.

The second part is a promise: “*I will make you fishers for men*” (*v. 19*). Jesus uses the language of their own work to describe their new calling. Instead of gathering fish, they will gather people into God’s kingdom. The phrase “I will make you” shows that Jesus Himself will train and shape them. They do not yet know how to do this work, but He will teach them.

Their response is immediate: “*They immediately left their nets and followed him*” (*v. 20*). The same happens with James and John, who leave the boat and their father. Matthew presents these responses as models of wholehearted discipleship.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that following Jesus begins with His call, not with our qualifications. He chose ordinary fishermen, not the most educated or influential people. Paul later reminds the Corinthians that God chose what the world considers foolish and weak (*1 Corinthians 1:26–29*). Jesus calls people as they are and promises to make them into what He intends.

The image of fishing for people may echo *Jeremiah 16:16*, where God says He will send fishermen to gather His people (though in that passage the context is judgment). In Jesus’ ministry the image becomes one of gathering people into God’s saving kingdom. Discipleship is not only about personal growth; it includes being sent to bring others to Jesus.

The call also shows the priority of Jesus over every other loyalty. Leaving nets, boats, and even a father represented a radical reordering of life. This does not mean that every disciple must abandon their job or family. Many followers of Jesus in the Gospels stayed in their homes and trades. But it does mean that Jesus’ claim on a person’s life comes first, and every other commitment must be held under His lordship.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Jesus’ call still comes to people in the middle of ordinary life. He did not wait for these fishermen to become religious professionals. Believers can expect Him to meet them in their work, homes, and daily routines, and to call them to follow Him there.

Following Jesus means more than believing certain facts about Him; it means learning from Him, imitating Him, and obeying Him day by day. Practically, this involves spending time with His words in Scripture, praying, joining with other believers, and allowing Him to shape priorities, decisions, and relationships.

The promise “I will make you” is also an encouragement. Many believers feel unqualified to share their faith or to serve. Jesus did not call the fishermen because they were already skilled at fishing for people; He promised to make them so. Believers can step forward in faith, trusting that He will equip them as they follow. And when following Him requires leaving something behind, whether a habit, an ambition, or a source of security, the example of these disciples encourages a prompt and wholehearted response.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Matthew 4* shows how Jesus faced temptation and how He began calling others to follow Him. Both parts of the chapter speak to everyday life. In the wilderness, Jesus faced temptations that targeted His physical needs, His trust in God, and His mission. Believers face similar pressures: to meet needs in wrong ways, to test God rather than trust Him, and to pursue good goals through compromise. Jesus’ consistent response was to rely on God’s Word and to refuse anything that would draw Him away from His Father. Knowing Scripture, recognizing temptation for what it is, and holding firm convictions are practical ways believers can follow His example.

The chapter also shows that testing often comes after spiritual high points. Jesus went into the wilderness right after hearing His Father’s voice at His baptism. Believers sometimes experience their hardest struggles after times of blessing or growth. Recognizing this pattern can help them stay alert and avoid becoming overconfident.

The calling of the fishermen reminds readers that Jesus’ invitation is personal and life-changing. He did not merely invite people to agree with Him; He called them to follow Him. That call reshaped their priorities, their work, and their relationships. Believers today can ask what following Jesus requires of them in their current circumstances, and respond with the same readiness the first disciples showed.

Finally, the summary of Jesus’ ministry, teaching, preaching, and healing, shows what kind of kingdom He brings. It is a kingdom that addresses both the soul and the body, bringing truth, forgiveness, and restoration. Those who follow Jesus are called to share in this kind of ministry: speaking truthfully about God, showing compassion to those who suffer, and bringing others to the One who can heal and save.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for remaining faithful in the wilderness when You were hungry, alone, and tempted. Thank You for trusting Your Father’s Word, refusing to test Him, and worshiping Him alone. Teach me to live by every word that comes from God, and help me to know Scripture so well that I recognize temptation and answer it with truth.

Show me where I am tempted to meet good needs in wrong ways or to seek good goals through compromise, and give me strength to refuse the shortcuts that dishonor You. Thank You for calling ordinary people to follow You. Help me to hear Your call in the middle of my everyday life and to respond without delay. Make me into the person You want me to be, and use me to bring others to You. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Matthew · Chapter 5 of 28

# Matthew — Chapter 5

Chapter Theme: The Blessed Life and the Deeper Righteousness of the Kingdom

[Read Matthew 5 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/MAT05.htm)

Main Teaching

In the opening of the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus describes the kind of people who are blessed in God’s kingdom and calls His followers to be salt and light in the world. He explains that He came to fulfill the Law, and He shows that God’s will reaches beyond outward actions to the heart, calling His disciples to a righteousness marked by reconciliation, purity, faithfulness, truthfulness, and love even for enemies.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Matthew 5–7* is known as the Sermon on the Mount, the longest single block of Jesus’ teaching in the Gospels. At the end of chapter 4, Matthew described large crowds following Jesus from Galilee, the Decapolis, Jerusalem, Judea, and beyond the Jordan, drawn by His teaching and healing. Now Jesus, seeing those crowds, goes up onto a mountainside, sits down (the normal posture for a Jewish teacher), and His disciples gather around Him. The crowds are listening too (*Matthew 7:28*), but the sermon is addressed first to those who have begun to follow Him. It describes the life of people who belong to God’s kingdom.

Many readers have noticed the parallel with Moses. Just as Moses went up Mount Sinai and brought God’s law to Israel, Jesus goes up a mountain and teaches what God’s will means for His people. But Jesus does not speak as Moses did, relaying God’s words. He speaks with His own authority: “You have heard that it was said... but I tell you.” Matthew wants readers to see Jesus as the one greater than Moses, who reveals the true meaning of God’s law.

### The Beatitudes (*5:1–12*)

Jesus begins with a series of statements each starting with “Blessed are.” These are called the Beatitudes, from the Latin word for “blessed.” The word “blessed” does not mean simply “happy” in a passing emotional sense. It describes people who are in a good and enviable position because God’s favor rests on them. Jesus is not giving a list of requirements to earn blessing; He is announcing who is truly well off in God’s kingdom, often turning the world’s values upside down.

He begins with “*the poor in spirit*” (*v. 3*), those who recognize their spiritual poverty and dependence on God. He continues with those who mourn (over sin and the brokenness of the world), the gentle (humble people who do not grasp for power), those who hunger and thirst for righteousness (who long for God’s will to be done in their lives and in the world), the merciful, the pure in heart, the peacemakers, and those persecuted for righteousness. Each statement includes a promise: comfort, inheriting the earth, being filled, receiving mercy, seeing God, being called God’s children. The first and eighth beatitudes share the same promise, “*theirs is the Kingdom of Heaven*” (*v. 3*), framing the list.

Many of these phrases echo the Old Testament. The promise that the gentle will inherit the earth echoes “*But the humble shall inherit the land*” (*Psalm 37:11*). The comfort for those who mourn recalls *Isaiah 61:1–3*, where the Lord’s anointed one is sent to comfort all who mourn and proclaim good news to the poor. Jesus is announcing that the promises of the prophets are being fulfilled in His ministry.

The final beatitude shifts from “those who” to “you.” Jesus tells His disciples that they will be insulted and persecuted because of Him, and that they should rejoice because their reward in heaven is great, just as the prophets before them were persecuted. He is preparing them for the reality that following Him will bring opposition.

### Salt and Light (*5:13–16*)

Jesus then tells His disciples, “*You are the salt of the earth*” (*v. 13*) and “*You are the light of the world*” (*v. 14*). In the ancient world, salt was used to flavor food and to preserve it from decay. Salt in Palestine was often taken from the Dead Sea area mixed with other minerals; if the sodium chloride dissolved away, what remained was tasteless and useless. Jesus warns that disciples who lose their distinctive character are like salt that has lost its flavor.

Light, similarly, exists to be seen. A city on a hill cannot be hidden, and nobody lights an oil lamp and puts it under a basket. Disciples are to let their light shine so that others see their good works and glorify their Father in heaven. Israel had been called to be a light to the nations (*Isaiah 42:6*; *49:6*). Now Jesus gives this calling to His followers.

### Jesus and the Law (*5:17–20*)

Jesus then addresses a question His listeners may have had. His authoritative teaching and His conflicts with religious leaders might suggest that He was setting aside the Scriptures. He says plainly, “*Don’t think that I came to destroy the law or the prophets. I didn’t come to destroy, but to fulfill*” (*v. 17*). “The law and the prophets” was a way of referring to the whole Old Testament.

He insists that not even “*one smallest letter or one tiny pen stroke*” (*v. 18*) will pass from the law until everything is accomplished. The “smallest letter” refers to the Hebrew letter yod, the smallest in the alphabet, and the “pen stroke” to the tiny marks that distinguish some Hebrew letters from others. Jesus takes the Scriptures with complete seriousness.

He then says something that would have astonished His hearers: unless their righteousness exceeded that of the scribes and Pharisees, they would never enter the kingdom. The Pharisees were known for their careful observance of the law. Jesus is not calling for more rules but for a deeper righteousness, one that reaches the heart and reflects the true intention of God’s commands. The rest of the chapter shows what that looks like.

### Six Illustrations of Deeper Righteousness (*5:21–48*)

Jesus gives six examples, each following the pattern “You have heard that it was said... but I tell you.” In each case He addresses a commandment or a common interpretation of it, and then shows God’s deeper purpose.

**Anger and reconciliation (*5:21–26*).** The command “*You shall not murder*” (*Exodus 20:13*) forbids taking life. Jesus says that anger, contempt, and insulting words are also deadly in God’s sight. “Raca” was an Aramaic insult meaning something like “empty-head.” “Gehenna” was the name of the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, once associated with child sacrifice and later used as a symbol of final judgment. Jesus then gives two practical examples: if you are bringing an offering to the altar and remember that someone has something against you, leave the gift and go be reconciled first; and settle disputes quickly before they reach court. Relationships with others matter so much that they take priority over religious ritual.

**Lust and purity (*5:27–30*).** The command “*You shall not commit adultery*” (*Exodus 20:14*) forbids sexual unfaithfulness. Jesus says that looking at someone with the intention of lusting after them is already adultery in the heart. He then uses vivid exaggeration: if your right eye or right hand causes you to sin, tear it out or cut it off. Jesus is not commanding literal self-harm. He is using a well-known teaching method of overstatement to show how seriously sin must be dealt with. Whatever leads us into sin should be removed decisively.

**Divorce (*5:31–32*).** *Deuteronomy 24:1–4* regulated divorce by requiring a man to give his wife a certificate of divorce, which protected her by allowing her to remarry. In Jesus’ day, some teachers interpreted the grounds for divorce very broadly, allowing a man to divorce his wife for almost any reason. Jesus says that divorcing a wife, except for sexual immorality, makes her an adulteress (since she would likely be forced to remarry for survival), and whoever marries her commits adultery. His point is that marriage is a lifelong covenant, not something to be discarded casually, and that the casual divorce of His day harmed women in particular. Christians have differed on how to apply this teaching, including whether other grounds such as abandonment (*1 Corinthians 7:15*) or abuse may justify separation or divorce. The passage itself focuses on protecting the permanence of marriage against easy divorce; it should not be used to trap someone in a situation of danger or abuse. Jesus returns to this subject in more detail in *Matthew 19*.

**Oaths and truthfulness (*5:33–37*).** The law required that vows made to the Lord be kept (*Numbers 30:2*). In Jesus’ day, people had developed systems of oaths, swearing by heaven, by earth, by Jerusalem, or by one’s own head, with some oaths considered more binding than others. This created loopholes for dishonesty. Jesus says not to swear at all in this manipulative way, but to let “yes” mean yes and “no” mean no. Truthfulness should be so consistent that oaths become unnecessary. (Many Christians understand this as forbidding casual or evasive oaths rather than formal oaths in a court of law; others, such as Quakers and Mennonites, have historically refused all oaths.)

**Retaliation (*5:38–42*).** “*An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth*” (*v. 38*) (see *Exodus 21:24*) was a principle for courts, meant to limit punishment so that it fit the crime rather than escalating into revenge. Some had turned it into a justification for personal retaliation. Jesus tells His disciples not to retaliate against an evil person. He gives examples: turning the other cheek when struck on the right cheek (a backhanded slap, which was an insult rather than a violent assault), giving your cloak as well as your coat when sued, and going a second mile when compelled to go one (Roman soldiers could legally force civilians to carry their gear for one mile). Jesus is teaching His followers to refuse revenge and to respond to insult and imposition with generous, surprising goodness. This teaching is about personal retaliation, not about whether governments should maintain justice (see *Romans 13:1–4*), and it does not require a person to remain in an abusive situation or to refuse protection. It calls disciples to break the cycle of revenge.

**Love for enemies (*5:43–48*).** The law commanded, “*You shall love your neighbor as yourself*” (*Leviticus 19:18*). The words “and hate your enemy” are not in the Old Testament, but some people had concluded that if you must love your neighbor, you may hate those who are not your neighbor. Jesus says, “*love your enemies*” (*v. 44*) and pray for those who persecute you. This reflects the character of God, who sends sun and rain on both the good and the evil. Jesus concludes, “*Therefore you shall be perfect, just as your Father in heaven is perfect*” (*v. 48*). The word “perfect” means complete, whole, or mature. In context, it refers especially to love that is complete, not partial, extending even to enemies as God’s love does.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Matthew 5:3* — Blessed Are the Poor in Spirit

> *“Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the Kingdom of Heaven.”*
>
> — *Matthew 5:3* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This is the first statement of the Sermon on the Mount. Jesus has gone up the mountainside, sat down to teach, and begun to speak to His disciples while the crowds listen. Many in the crowd were poor, sick, or burdened, people who had followed Him because He healed and taught with compassion (*Matthew 4:23–25*). Jesus begins His teaching by telling them who is truly blessed.

“Blessed” describes a state of well-being that comes from God’s favor. Jesus is not describing a feeling but a reality: these people are in a good position before God, even if they do not appear to be by worldly standards.

“Poor in spirit” refers to people who recognize their spiritual need. In the Old Testament, “the poor” often referred to humble, faithful people who were oppressed and depended entirely on God for help (for example, *Psalm 34:6* and *Isaiah 66:2*). Being poor in spirit means acknowledging that we have nothing to offer God on our own merit. It is the opposite of spiritual pride and self-sufficiency. Luke’s version of this beatitude says simply “*Blessed are you who are poor*” (*Luke 6:20*), showing that Jesus cared about the materially poor as well. Matthew emphasizes the inner attitude of humble dependence.

The promise is that “*theirs is the Kingdom of Heaven*” (*v. 3*). The kingdom does not belong to those who think they deserve it, but to those who know they do not. Notice that this promise is in the present tense: the kingdom already belongs to the poor in spirit.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This beatitude stands at the head of the list because it describes the doorway into the kingdom. Every other quality in the Beatitudes grows from this recognition of need. A person cannot mourn over sin, hunger for righteousness, or show mercy without first knowing their own poverty before God.

This truth runs throughout the Bible. God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble (*James 4:6*; *Proverbs 3:34*). Jesus later tells a parable about a Pharisee who boasted of his goodness and a tax collector who simply prayed, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner,” and says it was the tax collector who went home justified (*Luke 18:9–14*). Salvation is received, not achieved.

This beatitude also turns the world’s values upside down. The world tends to honor the strong, the confident, and the self-sufficient. Jesus says that the kingdom belongs to those who know they are weak and needy. This is not a call to poor self-esteem but to honest humility before God.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This beatitude invites believers to come to God with empty hands. Prayer, worship, and confession begin not with what we bring to God but with what we need from Him. Recognizing our dependence on God is not weakness; it is the beginning of blessing.

It also guards against spiritual pride. Believers who grow in knowledge and service can slowly begin to think of themselves as spiritually rich and look down on others. Remembering that every blessing in the kingdom is a gift keeps believers humble and gracious toward others who are struggling.

Finally, those who feel spiritually poor, who struggle with doubt, weakness, or a sense of failure, can take comfort here. Jesus does not begin by blessing the spiritually accomplished. He begins with those who know they need Him. That need is not a barrier to the kingdom; it is the way in.

### *Matthew 5:16* — Let Your Light Shine

> *“Even so, let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.”*
>
> — *Matthew 5:16* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse concludes Jesus’ short teaching about salt and light. He has just told His disciples, “*You are the light of the world*” (*v. 14*), and He has used two images: a city built on a hill, whose lights can be seen from far away at night, and a household oil lamp, which is placed on a stand so it can light the whole room rather than hidden under a measuring basket. In a small one-room house of that time, a single lamp on a stand could provide light for everyone.

Now Jesus applies the images: “*let your light shine before men*” (*v. 16*). The disciples’ light is their “good works,” their visible acts of goodness, faithfulness, and love. These are not meant to be hidden. The purpose, however, is crucial: “*that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven*” (*v. 16*). The goal is not that people will admire the disciples but that they will give glory to God.

This verse comes right after the Beatitudes, which describe the inner character of kingdom people, and just before the passages showing what that character looks like in action. It also comes right after Jesus warns that disciples will be persecuted. Jesus does not tell His followers to withdraw from the world to avoid opposition. They are to remain visible, showing God’s goodness through their lives.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Light is a major biblical image for God’s presence, truth, and salvation. God created light at the beginning (*Genesis 1:3*). Israel was called to be a light to the nations, displaying God’s character to the world (*Isaiah 49:6*). Jesus Himself is described as the light of the world (*John 8:12*), and in *Matthew 4:16* He is the great light dawning on those in darkness. His followers reflect His light, as the moon reflects the sun.

There seems to be a tension between this verse and *Matthew 6:1*, where Jesus warns against doing good deeds to be seen by others. The difference lies in motive and purpose. In *Matthew 6*, the problem is seeking praise for oneself. Here, the purpose is that God would be glorified. Believers are not to hide their faith or their good works, but neither should they perform them for applause.

The verse also shows that good works have a witnessing function. Peter makes the same point in *1 Peter 2:12*, urging believers to live honorably among unbelievers so that, seeing their good deeds, they may glorify God. The credibility of the gospel is often connected to the lives of those who proclaim it.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse calls believers to live visibly good lives in ordinary settings: at work, at home, in neighborhoods, and online. Honesty, kindness, generosity, faithfulness, and care for those in need are light that others can see. Believers do not need a special platform to shine; they need to live consistently where God has placed them.

It also calls for examining motives. Good works done to build a reputation or gain approval point attention to ourselves. Good works done in love and gratitude to God point others to Him. Believers can ask God to purify their motives and to keep them from seeking credit.

Finally, the image of a lamp under a basket warns against hiding faith out of fear or embarrassment. Believers need wisdom about when and how to speak about their faith, but they should not conceal who they are. When people notice something different and ask about it, believers can gently point them to the Father who is the source of all goodness.

### *Matthew 5:17* — Jesus Came to Fulfill the Law

> *“Don’t think that I came to destroy the law or the prophets. I didn’t come to destroy, but to fulfill.”*
>
> — *Matthew 5:17* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus speaks these words right after describing His disciples as salt and light, and right before He begins to explain the deeper meaning of the commandments. His listeners may have wondered whether Jesus’ new teaching was meant to replace the Scriptures they knew. Some religious leaders were already suspicious of Him. Jesus addresses the issue directly: “*Don’t think that I came to destroy the law or the prophets*” (*v. 17*).

“The law or the prophets” refers to the Hebrew Scriptures, what Christians call the Old Testament. The “law” (in Hebrew, Torah) refers especially to the first five books, including the commandments given through Moses. The “prophets” includes the historical and prophetic books. Together they represent all of God’s revelation to Israel up to that time.

Jesus says, “*I didn’t come to destroy, but to fulfill*” (*v. 17*). To “fulfill” means more than simply to obey. It means to bring to completion, to accomplish the purpose, and to reveal the full meaning. Jesus fulfills the prophets by being the one they pointed to. He fulfills the law by perfectly obeying it, by revealing its deepest intention (as He does in the rest of this chapter), and by accomplishing what the sacrifices and rituals of the law anticipated.

In the following verses, Jesus affirms that the law will not pass away until everything is accomplished, and He warns against teaching others to break even the least commandment. He also says His disciples’ righteousness must exceed that of the scribes and Pharisees, not by keeping more rules, but by obeying from the heart.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse is important for understanding how Christians relate to the Old Testament. Jesus does not discard God’s earlier revelation. He completes it. The whole Old Testament story, with its covenants, laws, sacrifices, and prophecies, points to Him. After His resurrection, Jesus will explain to His disciples how everything written about Him in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms had to be fulfilled (*Luke 24:44*).

Christians have long discussed how the various parts of the law apply after Christ’s coming. The New Testament teaches that some aspects of the law, such as the sacrificial system, food laws, and rituals that set Israel apart, have been fulfilled in Christ and are no longer binding in the same way (see *Hebrews 10:1–14*; *Mark 7:19*; *Acts 10*). The moral heart of the law, such as love for God and neighbor, faithfulness, truthfulness, and justice, continues to express God’s will and is deepened by Jesus’ teaching. Christians in different traditions explain this relationship in somewhat different ways, but all agree that Jesus is the key to understanding the law.

This verse also shows that grace does not mean God’s moral standards have been lowered. Jesus calls His disciples to a higher righteousness than the Pharisees, one that reaches the heart. That righteousness is impossible by human effort alone; it is the fruit of a new heart given by God’s Spirit, as the prophets promised (*Jeremiah 31:33*; *Ezekiel 36:26–27*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to value the whole Bible, including the Old Testament. Its stories, laws, psalms, and prophecies are not outdated; they reveal God’s character and point to Christ. Reading them in light of Jesus gives them their full meaning and enriches faith.

It also calls believers to take God’s moral will seriously. Some people assume that because salvation is by grace, obedience does not matter much. Jesus teaches the opposite: those who belong to His kingdom will seek to do God’s will from the heart. Grace frees believers not to ignore God’s commands but to obey them out of love.

Finally, Jesus’ approach guards against legalism. The scribes and Pharisees focused on external rules and sometimes created loopholes. Jesus looks at the heart. Believers can ask not only “What am I allowed to do?” but “What does God desire, and what reflects His love?” That question leads to deeper and more joyful obedience.

### *Matthew 5:44* — Love Your Enemies

> *“But I tell you, love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who mistreat you and persecute you,”*
>
> — *Matthew 5:44* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse is the final and most demanding of the six illustrations in which Jesus contrasts what His listeners had heard with what He teaches. In verse 43 He quotes a common saying: “*You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy*” (*v. 43*). The first half comes from *Leviticus 19:18*. The second half is not in Scripture; it was a conclusion some people drew, assuming that if they were commanded to love their neighbor (understood as a fellow Israelite or a member of their own group), they were free to hate outsiders and opponents.

Jesus responds with four commands: love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who mistreat and persecute you. (Some of these phrases are not found in all ancient manuscripts of Matthew but appear in *Luke 6:27–28*.) Each command describes an active response. Love here is not merely a feeling of affection but a commitment to seek another person’s good. Jesus asks His disciples to bless rather than curse, to do good rather than harm, and to pray rather than plot revenge.

His listeners lived under Roman occupation. They knew enemies who taxed them, insulted them, and sometimes brutalized them. Some groups of the time hoped to drive out the Romans by force. Jesus’ teaching was radical in that setting. He also knew His disciples would face persecution because of Him (vv. 10–12), and He was preparing them to respond as children of God.

In the next verse, Jesus gives the reason: to be “*children of your Father who is in heaven*” (*v. 45*), who sends sun and rain on both the evil and the good. God shows kindness even to those who reject Him, and His children are to reflect His character.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Love for enemies is one of the most distinctive features of Jesus’ teaching, and He lived it out Himself. On the cross He prayed for those who crucified Him: “*Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing*” (*Luke 23:34*). Paul writes that God showed His love for us “*while we were yet sinners*” (*Romans 5:8*), and that we were reconciled to God while we were His enemies (*Romans 5:10*). The gospel itself is the story of God loving His enemies.

This teaching reveals that love for enemies is not natural human behavior. Jesus says that even tax collectors, who were despised as collaborators, love those who love them. Loving enemies requires a love that comes from God. It reflects the character of the Father and is possible only through His grace.

It is important to understand what this command does not mean. Loving an enemy does not mean approving of their wrongdoing, pretending harm did not happen, or remaining in a situation where we are endangered. It does not cancel the role of governments and courts in restraining evil and pursuing justice. Love may include setting boundaries, seeking legal protection, or confronting wrongdoing. What it rules out is hatred, revenge, and the desire to see an enemy destroyed. It calls believers to want the enemy’s ultimate good, including their repentance and reconciliation with God.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse calls believers to identify the people they consider enemies or opponents: those who have hurt them, insulted them, opposed them, or simply disagree with them deeply. Jesus asks His followers to respond to such people not with hatred but with active goodwill. That may begin with refusing to speak contemptuously about them, refusing to wish them harm, and choosing to treat them with basic respect.

Prayer is one of the most practical ways to obey this command. Praying sincerely for someone who has wronged us, asking God to bless them and bring them to good, gradually changes our own hearts. It is difficult to keep hating someone we are honestly praying for.

Finally, loving enemies takes wisdom. In some situations, love means maintaining distance and boundaries for safety, while refusing bitterness. In others, it means acts of kindness that surprise and disarm. In a world full of division, especially political and social hostility, followers of Jesus can show a different way: firm in truth, yet refusing to dehumanize or hate those on the other side.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Matthew 5* presents a picture of life in God’s kingdom that is both beautiful and challenging. The Beatitudes show that God’s blessing rests on those the world often overlooks: the humble, the grieving, the gentle, the merciful, the peacemakers, and the persecuted. Believers can measure their lives not by the world’s standards of success but by these qualities, asking God to make them more poor in spirit, more hungry for righteousness, and more merciful.

The calling to be salt and light reminds believers that their faith is not private. It is meant to affect the world around them, preserving what is good, resisting decay, and showing God’s goodness in practical ways. This happens through ordinary faithfulness: honesty at work, kindness in the family, fairness in business, and care for neighbors.

The six illustrations show that God cares about the heart. Avoiding murder is not enough if we harbor contempt. Avoiding adultery is not enough if lust controls our thoughts. Keeping technical promises is not enough if we are habitually dishonest. Jesus calls His followers to examine their anger, their desires, their commitments, their speech, their responses to mistreatment, and their attitudes toward enemies. In each area He offers a better way: seeking reconciliation quickly, dealing decisively with sources of temptation, honoring the covenant of marriage, speaking plainly and truthfully, refusing revenge, and actively loving those who oppose us.

No one can live this way perfectly by willpower. The Sermon on the Mount shows the depth of our need for grace, which brings readers back to the first beatitude: blessed are the poor in spirit. Jesus came to fulfill the law, and through Him believers receive both forgiveness for falling short and the Spirit who changes hearts. The right response is to come to Him humbly, to ask for His help, and to take concrete steps of obedience in the areas where His words have touched us most directly.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for describing so clearly the life of Your kingdom, and for blessing people who are poor in spirit, who mourn, and who hunger for righteousness. I confess that I often value what the world values. Make me humble and dependent on You, merciful toward others, and pure in heart.

Help me to be salt and light where You have placed me, so that people may see goodness in my life and glorify my Father in heaven, not me. Search my heart for hidden anger, lust, dishonesty, and the desire for revenge. Give me courage to seek reconciliation quickly, to keep my word, and to answer insult with grace. Teach me to love my enemies and pray for those who hurt me, with wisdom to set right boundaries and without bitterness. Thank You that You fulfilled the law perfectly for me; fill me with Your Spirit so that I may obey from the heart. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Matthew · Chapter 6 of 28

# Matthew — Chapter 6

Chapter Theme: Living Before the Father, Not for the Audience

[Read Matthew 6 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/MAT06.htm)

Main Teaching

Jesus teaches that giving, prayer, and fasting should be done for God, who sees in secret, rather than to impress other people. He gives His disciples a model prayer, warns that wealth can capture the heart, and calls them to replace anxious striving with trust in their heavenly Father by seeking His kingdom first.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Matthew 6* continues the Sermon on the Mount. In chapter 5 Jesus described the character of kingdom people and showed that God’s commands reach the heart: anger, lust, dishonesty, revenge, and hatred of enemies. He ended that chapter by saying His disciples should be complete in love, as their heavenly Father is. Chapter 6 turns to another area where the heart is revealed: religious practice and the use of money. The phrase “your Father” appears again and again in this chapter. Jesus wants His followers to live with a constant awareness that they are children of a Father who sees, knows, and cares.

The first half of the chapter (vv. 1–18) addresses three practices that were central to Jewish devotion: giving to the poor, prayer, and fasting. Jesus does not question whether His disciples should do these things; He assumes they will. His concern is why and how they do them. The second half (vv. 19–34) addresses money, possessions, and anxiety, showing how the heart can become divided between God and wealth.

### The Warning About Performing for Others (*6:1*)

Jesus begins with a general principle: “*Be careful that you don’t do your charitable giving before men, to be seen by them, or else you have no reward from your Father who is in heaven*” (*v. 1*). The word translated “charitable giving” in some manuscripts is literally “righteousness,” referring to acts of devotion in general. The problem is not being seen; Jesus told His disciples in *Matthew 5:16* to let their light shine. The problem is doing good deeds in order to be seen and praised. When that is the goal, the praise of people is the only reward one receives.

### Giving to the Poor (*6:2–4*)

Jesus describes “hypocrites” who announce their giving with a trumpet in the synagogues and streets. The word “hypocrite” originally referred to an actor in the Greek theater who wore a mask and played a role. Whether Jesus means a literal trumpet or uses the phrase as a vivid image for self-promotion, the point is clear: some people gave in a way designed to win admiration. Jesus says, “*they have received their reward*” (*v. 2*). The verb was used in commercial receipts to mean “paid in full.” They wanted applause, they got it, and that is all they will get.

Instead, His disciples are not to let their left hand know what their right hand is doing. This is a vivid way of saying that giving should be so unselfconscious that we do not even keep score for ourselves. The Father, who sees in secret, will reward them.

### Prayer (*6:5–15*)

Jesus then applies the same principle to prayer. Some people liked to pray standing in the synagogues and on street corners so that others would see them. Jewish people often prayed at set times of the day, and someone who arranged to be in a public place at those times could make a show of their devotion. Jesus tells His disciples to go into their “*inner room*” (*v. 6*), close the door, and pray to the Father in secret. In a typical home, the inner room was often a storeroom, the only room with a door. The point is not that public prayer is wrong (Jesus Himself prayed publicly), but that prayer is conversation with God, not a performance for an audience.

He also warns against babbling “*vain repetitions as the Gentiles do*” (*v. 7*). In many pagan religions, worshipers piled up the names of gods and repeated formulas, hoping to secure the gods’ attention. Jesus says that the Father already knows what His children need before they ask. Prayer is not a technique for persuading a reluctant deity; it is trusting communication with a Father who cares.

Then Jesus gives a model prayer, often called the Lord’s Prayer, which is studied in detail below. After the prayer, He adds a comment on one line of it: if we forgive others, the Father will forgive us; if we refuse to forgive, neither will the Father forgive us. This does not mean that we earn God’s forgiveness by forgiving others. It means that a person who has truly received God’s mercy cannot hold onto unforgiveness toward others without contradicting the very mercy they claim to have received. Jesus will illustrate this with a parable in *Matthew 18:21–35*.

### Fasting (*6:16–18*)

Fasting, going without food for a period of time to devote oneself to God, was a regular part of Jewish piety. The law required fasting on the Day of Atonement, and devout people like the Pharisees fasted twice a week (*Luke 18:12*). Some made sure others knew it by looking gloomy and neglecting their appearance. Jesus tells His disciples to wash their faces and groom themselves normally so that their fasting is seen only by the Father. Again, the reward comes from God, not from people.

### Treasure in Heaven (*6:19–24*)

The second half of the chapter turns to wealth. Jesus warns against storing up treasures on earth, where “*moth and rust consume, and where thieves break through and steal*” (*v. 19*). In the ancient world, wealth was often kept in fine clothing (vulnerable to moths), metals and grain (which could corrode or be eaten by pests), and stored valuables (which thieves could steal by digging through mud-brick walls). Earthly wealth is insecure. Instead, His disciples should store up treasure in heaven, where it is safe.

He then speaks of the eye as the lamp of the body. If the eye is “sound” (or “single,” focused and generous), the whole body is full of light; if the eye is “evil,” the body is full of darkness. In Jewish idiom, a “good eye” described a generous person and an “evil eye” described someone stingy or envious (see *Proverbs 22:9*; *28:22*). Jesus is saying that how we look at money and possessions affects our whole life.

Finally, He says no one can serve two masters. A slave could not truly belong to two owners with competing demands. “*You can’t serve both God and Mammon*” (*v. 24*). “Mammon” is an Aramaic word for wealth or property. Jesus personifies it as a rival master that demands loyalty. The issue is not owning things, but who or what rules the heart.

### Anxiety and Trust (*6:25–34*)

Because no one can serve both God and money, Jesus says, “*don’t be anxious for your life*” (*v. 25*). Many of His listeners were poor farmers and laborers for whom food and clothing were real daily concerns. Jesus does not dismiss these needs. He points to the birds, which do not sow or reap yet are fed by the Father, and to the wildflowers, which are more beautifully clothed than Solomon in all his royal splendor, though they bloom for only a short time and are then used as fuel for ovens. If God cares for birds and flowers, He will certainly care for His children.

Jesus gently rebukes His listeners as people of “*little faith*” (*v. 30*) and points out that worry accomplishes nothing; it cannot add a single moment to a person’s life. Anxious striving after food, drink, and clothing is what “*the Gentiles seek after*” (*v. 32*), meaning people who do not know God as their Father. Disciples know that their Father knows what they need. So instead of being ruled by anxiety, they are to seek first God’s kingdom and His righteousness, and these needs will be provided. The chapter ends with practical wisdom: do not worry about tomorrow, because each day has enough trouble of its own.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Matthew 6:9–13* — The Prayer Jesus Taught

> *“Pray like this: “Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy. Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven. Give us today our daily bread. Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors. Bring us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one. For yours is the Kingdom, the power, and the glory forever. Amen.””*
>
> — *Matthew 6:9–13* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus gives this prayer in the middle of His teaching about prayer. He has just warned against praying to be seen by others and against heaping up empty words as though God could be manipulated by long speeches. Now He says, “*Pray like this*” (*v. 9*). The prayer is a model showing what true prayer includes, though Christians have also prayed these exact words together from the earliest days of the church. Luke records a shorter version, given when a disciple asked Jesus to teach them to pray (*Luke 11:1–4*).

The prayer begins, “Our Father in heaven.” Jews sometimes called God “Father” in prayer, but Jesus’ constant use of this name, and His invitation to His disciples to share in it, was distinctive. “Our” reminds disciples that they pray as part of a family. “In heaven” reminds them that the Father is also the sovereign Lord above all. The first request, “*may your name be kept holy*” (*v. 9*), asks that God’s name, meaning His character and reputation, be honored and treated as holy by everyone.

The next two requests continue that focus: “*Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven*” (*v. 10*). These ask God to establish His rule fully on earth, so that the world is set right and His will is done here as completely as it is in heaven. The prayer begins with God’s glory and purposes before turning to personal needs.

Then come three requests for daily needs. “Give us today our daily bread” asks for the provision needed for each day, reminding disciples to depend on God one day at a time, as Israel depended on manna in the wilderness. “*Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors*” (*v. 12*) asks for forgiveness of sin, which is pictured as a debt owed to God, and acknowledges that those who receive forgiveness forgive others. “*Bring us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one*” (*v. 13*) asks God to keep His children from being overwhelmed by testing and to rescue them from the devil’s power. The closing words of praise, “For yours is the Kingdom, the power, and the glory forever. Amen,” are not found in the oldest manuscripts of Matthew, but they were used in early Christian worship and echo *1 Chronicles 29:11*.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The structure of this prayer teaches believers what matters most. It begins with God: His name, His kingdom, His will. Only then does it turn to human needs. This order reshapes the way people pray. Prayer is not primarily a way to get what we want but a way of aligning our lives with God’s purposes. Yet the prayer also shows that God cares about the most basic needs: food, forgiveness, and protection.

The prayer is deeply communal. Every request uses “us” and “our.” Even when praying alone in a closed room, disciples pray as members of God’s family, concerned for the needs of others as well as their own.

The prayer also holds together the present and the future. Asking for God’s kingdom to come looks toward the day when Christ returns and all evil is removed. Asking for daily bread and forgiveness today recognizes that we live now, in a world not yet made whole, dependent on God’s grace each day. The prayer gives believers both hope for the future and help for the present.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This prayer offers a pattern that can shape daily prayer. Believers can begin by honoring God and asking that His name be respected in their own lives, families, and communities. They can pray for His will to be done in specific situations, including in their own choices. Then they can bring their needs, confess their sins, and ask for protection, all with confidence that the Father hears.

The prayer also challenges believers to examine their relationships. Praying “as we also forgive our debtors” while holding onto bitterness is a contradiction. If there is someone we refuse to forgive, this prayer brings that to light and invites us to release it to God. Forgiveness does not mean pretending wrongdoing did not happen or necessarily restoring trust immediately, but it does mean giving up the desire for revenge and leaving judgment to God.

Finally, the request for daily bread encourages contentment and trust. Rather than demanding security for years ahead, believers can ask God for what they need today and trust Him again tomorrow. And the request for deliverance from temptation encourages humility: believers do not presume on their own strength but ask God to guard them.

### *Matthew 6:21* — Where Your Treasure Is

> *“for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.”*
>
> — *Matthew 6:21* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse concludes Jesus’ short teaching about treasures in verses 19–21. He has told His disciples not to store up treasures on earth, where moths, rust, and thieves can destroy or take them, but to store up treasures in heaven, where nothing can damage or steal them. Now He gives the reason: “*for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also*” (*v. 21*).

In biblical thought, the “heart” is not merely the seat of emotions but the center of a person’s thoughts, desires, choices, and loyalties. Jesus is saying that what we value most will capture our hearts. Our attention, affection, and energy naturally follow what we treasure.

Jesus’ listeners understood earthly treasure: fine clothes, stored grain, precious metals, and land. Many of them had very little, while some, like the religious leaders, were comfortable. “Treasure in heaven” refers to what has lasting value before God, such as faithfulness, generosity, acts of mercy, and devotion to God’s kingdom. Elsewhere Jesus speaks of selling possessions and giving to the poor as a way of storing treasure in heaven (*Matthew 19:21*; *Luke 12:33*).

This verse connects the private devotion described earlier in the chapter with the use of money. Just as the hypocrites wanted the reward of human praise, people can set their hearts on earthly wealth. In both cases, the question is the same: what are we really living for?

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals the close connection between money and spiritual life. Jesus speaks about wealth often because it so easily becomes a rival to God. Paul writes that “*the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil*” (*1 Timothy 6:10*), and warns that those who are eager to be rich fall into many temptations. Possessions are not evil in themselves, but they can easily claim the heart.

The verse also teaches that the heart follows investment. We often think we must first feel love for something before we give to it, but Jesus suggests that where we place our treasure shapes what we love. Giving generously to God’s purposes draws the heart toward those purposes. Hoarding draws the heart toward possessions.

Treasure in heaven also speaks of hope. Earthly wealth is temporary; it cannot be taken beyond death. Treasure in heaven lasts forever. Jesus calls His followers to live with eternity in view, valuing what God values and investing in what will endure.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to look honestly at where their time, money, and attention go. Bank statements, calendars, and daily thoughts often reveal what we truly treasure. If most of our energy is spent pursuing financial security, comfort, or possessions, our hearts will follow.

It also calls believers to practice generosity as a spiritual discipline. Giving to the church, supporting those in need, and contributing to work that advances God’s kingdom are ways of storing treasure in heaven. Generosity loosens the grip of money on the heart and directs affection toward God’s purposes. This does not mean neglecting responsible care for family or necessities; Scripture also commends providing for one’s household (*1 Timothy 5:8*). It means keeping possessions in their proper place.

Finally, this verse offers freedom. Those who place their treasure in heaven do not have to live in fear of losing everything. Economic changes, theft, or loss can still hurt, but they cannot touch the treasure that matters most.

### *Matthew 6:33* — Seek First His Kingdom

> *“But seek first God’s Kingdom and his righteousness; and all these things will be given to you as well.”*
>
> — *Matthew 6:33* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse is the climax of Jesus’ teaching about anxiety in verses 25–34. He has told His disciples not to worry about food, drink, and clothing. He has pointed to the birds and wildflowers as evidence of God’s care, and He has reminded them that worry cannot add a moment to their lives. He has also said that anxious pursuit of these things is characteristic of “*the Gentiles*” (*v. 32*), meaning people who do not know God as Father, whereas His disciples have a Father who knows what they need.

Now Jesus tells them what to do instead of worrying: “*But seek first God’s Kingdom and his righteousness*” (*v. 33*). To “seek” means to pursue something as a priority, to make it the goal of one’s efforts. “First” means first in importance, not merely first in a sequence. God’s kingdom is His rule and saving reign through Jesus. “His righteousness” refers to the way of life that reflects God’s will, which Jesus has been describing throughout the Sermon on the Mount.

Then comes a promise: “*and all these things will be given to you as well*” (*v. 33*). “All these things” refers specifically to the necessities Jesus has been discussing: food, drink, and clothing. Jesus promises that the Father will provide what His children truly need when they make His kingdom their priority.

The final verse of the chapter adds practical wisdom: do not worry about tomorrow, because each day has enough trouble of its own. Disciples are to live faithfully in the present, trusting God with the future.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse addresses the root of anxiety. Worry often comes from making our own security the center of life. When we are ultimately responsible for providing everything we need, anxiety is natural. Jesus offers a different center: God’s kingdom. When God’s purposes take first place, our needs are placed in His hands, and He has promised to care for His children.

This promise must be understood carefully. Jesus is not promising wealth or luxury, nor is He saying that believers will never experience hardship or need. Christians in the New Testament sometimes went hungry and suffered poverty (*2 Corinthians 11:27*; *Philippians 4:12*). The promise is that God will provide what His children truly need to live and to do His will, and that nothing can separate them from His care. Paul expresses the same confidence: “*My God will supply every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus*” (*Philippians 4:19*).

The verse also teaches that God’s kingdom and righteousness belong together. Seeking the kingdom does not only mean religious activity; it means pursuing a life that reflects God’s justice, mercy, and holiness in every area, including work, money, and relationships.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse calls believers to examine their priorities. Many decisions about work, finances, time, and relationships reveal what we are seeking first. Seeking God’s kingdom first might mean choosing honesty when dishonesty would be more profitable, giving generously even when finances are tight, or making time for worship and service when other activities compete for attention.

It also offers a practical response to anxiety. When worries arise about money, health, or the future, believers can turn them into prayer, bringing their needs to the Father who knows them. Then they can focus on what God has given them to do today, rather than trying to control tomorrow. Responsible planning is not forbidden; Scripture praises wise preparation (*Proverbs 6:6–8*). What Jesus forbids is anxious striving that forgets God.

Finally, this verse invites trust in God’s character. The Father who feeds birds and clothes flowers knows and loves His children. Believers can rest in His care, even when circumstances are uncertain, and find freedom to live generously and faithfully rather than fearfully.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Matthew 6* confronts one of the most subtle temptations in spiritual life: doing the right things for the wrong reasons. Giving, praying, and fasting are good, but they can become ways of building a reputation or feeling superior. Jesus calls His followers to live before an audience of One. In practice, this might mean giving quietly without seeking recognition, praying honestly in private rather than only in public, and practicing spiritual disciplines without advertising them. It also means examining motives regularly and asking God to purify them.

The chapter also teaches believers how to pray. The Lord’s Prayer provides a framework that keeps God’s glory central while bringing real needs before Him. It reminds believers to depend on God daily, to confess sin honestly, to forgive others, and to ask for protection from temptation and evil. Using this pattern regularly can deepen prayer and keep it from becoming either self-centered or mechanical.

Jesus’ teaching about money is especially relevant in cultures shaped by consumerism and financial pressure. He warns that wealth can capture the heart and become a rival master. Believers can respond by practicing generosity, holding possessions loosely, and evaluating major financial decisions in light of God’s kingdom. The question is not only “Can I afford this?” but “Does this reflect what I treasure most?”

Finally, the chapter speaks directly to anxiety. Jesus does not shame people for their worries, but He invites them to trust their Father. He reminds them of God’s care for creation, the uselessness of worry, and the priority of God’s kingdom. Anxiety may sometimes require practical help, including counsel or medical care, and seeking such help is consistent with trusting God. But the deepest answer to fear is knowing the Father’s love and choosing, day by day, to seek His kingdom first and leave tomorrow in His hands.

## Chapter Prayer

Father in heaven, thank You that You see what is done in secret and that I can live my life before You rather than for the approval of others. Forgive me for the times I have given, prayed, or served to be noticed. Purify my motives so that I seek Your reward and not human praise.

Teach me to pray as Jesus taught: to honor Your name, to long for Your kingdom, to seek Your will, to depend on You for daily bread, to confess my sins and forgive those who have wronged me, and to ask You to keep me from evil. Guard my heart from the love of money, and help me to store up treasure in heaven through generosity and faithfulness. When I am anxious about tomorrow, remind me that You know what I need. Help me to seek Your kingdom and righteousness first, and to trust You with everything else. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
