Matthew · Chapter 7 of 28

# Matthew — Chapter 7

Chapter Theme: Two Ways, Two Trees, Two Foundations

[Read Matthew 7 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/MAT07.htm)

Main Teaching

Jesus concludes the Sermon on the Mount by warning against hypocritical judgment, encouraging persistent prayer to a generous Father, and summarizing God’s will in the Golden Rule. He then presents a series of choices: the narrow and the wide road, true and false prophets, genuine and empty confession, and building on rock or on sand. Hearing His words is not enough; the wise person puts them into practice.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Matthew 7* is the final chapter of the Sermon on the Mount, which began in *Matthew 5* when Jesus sat down on a mountainside to teach His disciples while the crowds listened. In chapter 5 He described the character of kingdom people and showed that God’s commands reach the heart. In chapter 6 He warned against religious performance and against letting money and anxiety rule the heart. Now He addresses how disciples should treat others and how they should respond to His teaching as a whole.

The chapter moves from relationships (judging others, the Golden Rule) to prayer and then to a series of sharp contrasts. Jewish wisdom teaching often ended with a choice between two ways, as in *Psalm 1* and *Deuteronomy 30:15–20*, where Moses set before Israel life and death, blessing and curse. Jesus ends His sermon the same way, presenting His hearers with a decision.

### Judging Others (*7:1–6*)

Jesus begins, “*Don’t judge, so that you won’t be judged*” (*v. 1*). This famous saying is often misunderstood. Jesus is not forbidding all moral evaluation; in the same chapter He tells His disciples to recognize false prophets by their fruit (vv. 15–20), which requires discernment. What He forbids is the harsh, condemning, self-righteous judgment that looks down on others while ignoring one’s own faults. He warns that the standard we use for others will be used for us.

He illustrates with a humorous and exaggerated picture: someone with a beam (a large wooden plank used in building) sticking out of his own eye trying to remove a speck of sawdust from his brother’s eye. As a carpenter’s son, Jesus may have known this image well. The point is not that we should never help others with their faults. Jesus says, “*First remove the beam out of your own eye, and then you can see clearly to remove the speck out of your brother’s eye*” (*v. 5*). Honest self-examination and repentance come first, and they make us both humble and clear-sighted enough to help others gently.

Verse 6 adds a balancing warning: “*Don’t give that which is holy to the dogs, neither throw your pearls before the pigs*” (*v. 6*). In Jewish culture, dogs (usually wild scavengers, not pets) and pigs were unclean animals. Holy things, such as food offered to God, were not to be thrown to dogs. Pearls were extremely valuable, but pigs would see them only as inedible and trample them. Jesus seems to be saying that while disciples should not be judgmental, they also need discernment. Some people persistently and violently reject what is holy, and disciples are not required to keep pressing sacred truth on those who will only scorn and attack it. Jesus later tells His disciples to shake the dust off their feet when a town refuses their message (*Matthew 10:14*).

### Asking, Seeking, Knocking (*7:7–11*)

Jesus then encourages His disciples to pray: “*Ask, and it will be given you. Seek, and you will find. Knock, and it will be opened for you*” (*v. 7*). The verbs in Greek suggest continuing action: keep asking, keep seeking, keep knocking. He supports this with an argument from everyday life. No father would give his hungry son a stone that looks like a loaf of bread or a snake instead of a fish. If sinful human parents know how to give good gifts to their children, how much more will the heavenly Father give good things to those who ask Him? (Luke’s parallel says the Father will give “*the Holy Spirit*” (*Luke 11:13*), the greatest good gift.)

The placement of this teaching is significant. Jesus has just set out the demanding standards of the kingdom. The disciples might wonder how they could ever live this way. Jesus’ answer is prayer: ask the Father for what you need, including the grace to obey.

### The Golden Rule (*7:12*)

Jesus then gives what has become known as the Golden Rule: “*whatever you desire for men to do to you, you shall also do to them*” (*v. 12*). He adds, “*for this is the law and the prophets*” (*v. 12*), meaning that this principle summarizes the moral teaching of the whole Old Testament. Versions of this principle in negative form (“do not do to others what you would not want done to you”) existed in Judaism and other cultures, including a saying attributed to the rabbi Hillel. Jesus’ positive form is more demanding: it requires actively doing good, not just avoiding harm.

### The Narrow Gate (*7:13–14*)

Jesus now begins His concluding warnings. He describes two gates and two roads. The wide gate and broad road lead to destruction, and many travel on it. The narrow gate and restricted road lead to life, and few find it. The image is of a choice between an easy, popular path and a demanding one. Following Jesus is not the default direction of life; it requires a deliberate decision and continuing commitment. The word translated “restricted” can carry the sense of pressure or hardship, hinting that the way of discipleship includes difficulty.

### False Prophets and Their Fruit (*7:15–20*)

Jesus warns against false prophets who come “*in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravening wolves*” (*v. 15*). They appear to be part of God’s flock, but their real aim is to harm and exploit it. The Old Testament warned frequently about prophets who spoke falsely in God’s name (*Jeremiah 23:16*; *Ezekiel 22:27*). Jesus says they can be recognized by their fruit. Just as a thornbush cannot produce grapes, a corrupt person’s life and teaching will eventually reveal what is inside. A good tree produces good fruit; a bad tree produces bad fruit. Fruit includes both conduct and the effects of a teacher’s message on others.

### Saying “Lord, Lord” (*7:21–23*)

Jesus then gives one of the most sobering warnings in the Gospels. Not everyone who calls Him “Lord, Lord” will enter the kingdom, but only those who do the will of His Father. On “that day,” the day of judgment, many will point to impressive religious activity: prophesying, casting out demons, and doing mighty works in His name. Jesus will say to them, “*I never knew you. Depart from me, you who work iniquity*” (*v. 23*).

Notice that Jesus presents Himself as the one who will judge on the last day and whose personal relationship with a person determines their destiny. The problem with these people is not that they did no religious works but that they never truly knew Christ, and their lives were marked by lawlessness. Religious activity, even spectacular activity, cannot replace genuine relationship with Jesus and obedience to the Father.

### The Wise and Foolish Builders (*7:24–27*)

Jesus ends the sermon with a parable. Everyone who hears His words and does them is like a wise man who built his house on rock. When the rain fell, the rivers flooded, and the winds beat against the house, it stood firm. Everyone who hears His words and does not do them is like a foolish man who built on sand. When the storm came, the house collapsed.

In Palestine, dry riverbeds (wadis) could fill suddenly with rushing water during winter rains. A house built on the sandy floor of such a valley might look fine in the dry season, but it would be swept away when the floods came. The two houses might look the same from outside; the difference was only revealed by the storm.

### The Crowd’s Reaction (*7:28–29*)

When Jesus finished, the crowds were astonished, because He taught “*with authority, and not like the scribes*” (*v. 29*). The scribes, the experts in the law, usually taught by citing earlier authorities and traditions. Jesus spoke on His own authority: “I tell you.” He claimed that obeying His words was the foundation of life and that He would judge the world. The crowds sensed that someone extraordinary was speaking.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Matthew 7:1* — Do Not Judge

> *“Don’t judge, so that you won’t be judged.”*
>
> — *Matthew 7:1* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse begins the final chapter of the Sermon on the Mount. Jesus has just finished teaching about anxiety and trusting God, and now He turns to how His disciples treat others. The command is short and direct, and the next verse explains it: “*For with whatever judgment you judge, you will be judged; and with whatever measure you measure, it will be measured to you*” (*v. 2*).

The word “judge” in Greek can mean to evaluate, to discern, or to condemn. The context shows that Jesus is warning against a particular kind of judging: a critical, condemning attitude that focuses on other people’s faults while ignoring one’s own. The picture of the person with a beam in his eye trying to remove a speck from his brother’s eye (vv. 3–5) shows that the problem is hypocrisy and self-righteousness.

Jesus is not forbidding all moral discernment. In this same chapter He tells His disciples to beware of false prophets and to recognize them by their fruit (vv. 15–20), and in *Matthew 18:15–17* He gives instructions for confronting a brother who sins. The issue is not whether we notice wrong but how we respond to it: with humility, honesty about ourselves, and a desire to help, or with pride, harshness, and condemnation.

His listeners lived in a culture where religious groups often judged one another, and where some looked down on “sinners,” tax collectors, and Gentiles. Jesus warns that those who use harsh standards for others will face the same standards themselves before God.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse connects with Jesus’ teaching on mercy throughout the Sermon. Earlier He said, “*Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy*” (*Matthew 5:7*), and in the Lord’s Prayer He taught His disciples to ask forgiveness as they forgive others (*Matthew 6:12*). The principle is consistent: the way we treat others reveals whether we have truly understood God’s mercy toward us.

Ultimately, only God is the righteous judge. Paul writes, “*why do you judge your brother?*” (*Romans 14:10*) and reminds believers that all will stand before God’s judgment seat. James adds that there is only one lawgiver and judge (*James 4:12*). When we condemn others, we take a role that belongs to God alone.

At the same time, Scripture calls believers to discernment, to distinguish truth from error and right from wrong, and to lovingly correct one another (*Galatians 6:1*). The key is that correction must begin with self-examination and be carried out in humility and gentleness, with the goal of restoration rather than condemnation.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to notice how quickly they criticize others. Before pointing out someone else’s faults, they can ask God to reveal their own. Often the faults that irritate us most in others are ones we struggle with ourselves.

It also calls for a different tone when correction is necessary. Confronting wrongdoing is sometimes an act of love, especially when someone is harming themselves or others. But it should be done privately when possible, gently, and with a genuine desire to help, not to shame. Believers should be as eager to extend grace as they would want grace extended to them.

Finally, this verse warns against the habit of speaking negatively about others, whether in conversation, online, or in our thoughts. Assuming the worst about people, labeling them, or writing them off reflects the judgmental spirit Jesus forbids. Choosing to assume the best where possible, and leaving final judgment to God, frees believers from a burden they were never meant to carry.

### *Matthew 7:7* — Ask, Seek, and Knock

> *“Ask, and it will be given you. Seek, and you will find. Knock, and it will be opened for you.”*
>
> — *Matthew 7:7* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus speaks these words after warning about judging others and about giving holy things to those who scorn them. He now turns to prayer, encouraging His disciples to come to God with confidence. The three verbs, ask, seek, and knock, form a progression of increasing intensity. Asking is making a request; seeking involves effort and searching; knocking is persistent pursuit, like someone standing at a door until it is opened.

In Greek, these commands are in the present tense, suggesting ongoing action: keep on asking, keep on seeking, keep on knocking. Jesus is encouraging persistence in prayer. Luke places a similar saying right after a parable about a man who keeps knocking on his friend’s door at midnight until the friend gets up and gives him bread (*Luke 11:5–10*).

Jesus then explains why prayer is worthwhile. The Father is generous. Using a comparison His listeners would understand immediately, He asks which father would give his son a stone when he asks for bread, or a snake when he asks for fish. In Galilee, bread was a basic food and fish was common from the lake. No loving father would deceive his child with something useless or dangerous. If sinful human parents know how to give good gifts, “*how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him!*” (*v. 11*)

This teaching comes near the end of a sermon full of demanding commands. It reassures the disciples that they do not have to live the kingdom life by their own strength. They can ask the Father for everything they need.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals God’s character as a generous Father. Prayer is not an attempt to wear down a reluctant God; it is the natural expression of children who trust a Father who delights to give good gifts. James writes that “*Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights*” (*James 1:17*).

It is important to read the promise in context. Jesus promises that the Father will give “good things” to those who ask. This does not mean that God will grant every specific request exactly as we ask it. A wise father does not give his children everything they want, especially if it would harm them. Sometimes God’s answer is different from our request because He knows what is truly good. Jesus Himself prayed in Gethsemane for the cup to pass from Him, and the Father’s answer was not removal but strength to obey (*Matthew 26:39*).

The greatest good gift the Father gives is Himself: His presence, His Spirit, and His kingdom. Prayer that seeks God Himself, and not only His gifts, will never be disappointed.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to pray with confidence and persistence. When a need remains or a prayer seems unanswered, the call is not to give up but to keep asking, seeking, and knocking, while trusting God’s wisdom about the answer. Persistent prayer often deepens our understanding of what we truly need and shapes our hearts toward God’s will.

It also invites believers to bring every kind of need to God, including the need for grace to live the life Jesus describes. Struggles with anger, lust, worry, or unforgiveness are exactly the kinds of things to bring to the Father, asking for help.

Finally, this verse invites trust in God’s goodness when answers differ from our hopes. Remembering that the Father gives good gifts helps believers interpret disappointments without concluding that God does not care. He may be giving something better, or working in ways we cannot yet see.

### *Matthew 7:12* — The Golden Rule

> *“Therefore, whatever you desire for men to do to you, you shall also do to them; for this is the law and the prophets.”*
>
> — *Matthew 7:12* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse is often called the Golden Rule, and it serves as a summary of much of the Sermon on the Mount. The word “therefore” links it to what came before. Jesus has just said that the Father gives good gifts to those who ask. Because God is so generous to us, we should treat others with the same generosity.

The principle is simple: think about how you would want others to treat you, and then treat them that way. If we want to be listened to, we should listen. If we want to be forgiven, we should forgive. If we want others to be honest and fair with us, we should be honest and fair with them. If we would want help in a time of need, we should help others in their need.

Jesus adds, “*for this is the law and the prophets*” (*v. 12*). This phrase echoes *Matthew 5:17*, where He said He came to fulfill the law and the prophets. Here He says that this rule sums up their moral teaching. Later, Jesus will say that the whole law and the prophets depend on the two great commandments: love God with all your heart, and love your neighbor as yourself (*Matthew 22:37–40*). The Golden Rule is a practical way of living out love for neighbor.

Similar sayings existed in Jewish and other ancient traditions, usually in negative form, such as “What is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbor.” Jesus’ version is positive: it is not enough to avoid harming others; disciples must actively do good to them.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The Golden Rule reflects God’s own character. God does not wait for people to earn His kindness; He takes the initiative to do good, sending sun and rain on the just and unjust (*Matthew 5:45*). When believers treat others as they would like to be treated, they reflect the generous heart of their Father.

The rule also provides a practical guide for countless situations that are not specifically addressed in Scripture. Rather than requiring a detailed rule for every circumstance, Jesus gives a principle that can be applied everywhere: at home, at work, in business, in conflict, and in caring for the needy.

At the same time, the Golden Rule must be understood within the whole of Jesus’ teaching. It does not mean giving people whatever they want, or approving of everything they do. Love sometimes requires telling the truth or setting boundaries. The question is what we would truly want if we were in the other person’s place and thinking clearly about what is good.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

The Golden Rule invites believers to practice empathy deliberately. Before responding to someone, especially in a difficult situation, they can pause and ask how they would want to be treated if their positions were reversed. This simple question can transform conversations, decisions, and relationships.

It applies in practical ways: speaking respectfully about people who are not present, treating employees and coworkers fairly, paying debts on time, being patient with those who are slow or struggling, and showing hospitality to strangers. It also applies to how we treat people who cannot benefit us, such as the poor, the elderly, children, and those on the margins.

Finally, the Golden Rule challenges passivity. It is not enough to avoid harming others. Jesus calls His disciples to take initiative in doing good, looking for ways to bless others as they would want to be blessed.

### *Matthew 7:24* — Building on the Rock

> *“Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine and does them, I will liken him to a wise man who built his house on the rock.”*
>
> — *Matthew 7:24* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse begins the final parable of the Sermon on the Mount. Jesus has just warned that not everyone who calls Him “Lord” will enter the kingdom, but only those who do the Father’s will. Now He gives a picture of the difference between true and false discipleship.

He says that “*Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine and does them*” (*v. 24*) is like a wise man who built his house on rock. “These words of mine” refers to the whole Sermon on the Mount, including the Beatitudes, the teaching on anger, lust, truthfulness, and love for enemies, the warnings about hypocrisy and money, and the call to trust the Father. Jesus places His own words at the foundation of life, something only God’s Word could claim.

The key phrase is “and does them.” Both builders in the parable hear Jesus’ words. The difference is that one acts on them and the other does not. In Palestine, a sudden winter storm could turn a dry valley into a rushing river. A house built on the sandy ground in such a valley would be destroyed, while a house built on bedrock would stand. The storm reveals which foundation each builder chose.

Jesus’ hearers would have understood the storm as a picture of testing, both the trials of life and, especially, the final judgment. The question is whether one’s life will stand when it is tested.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This parable teaches that hearing God’s Word is not enough; it must be obeyed. James makes the same point: “*But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves*” (*James 1:22*). Knowledge of Scripture, attendance at teaching, and agreement with Jesus’ words do not by themselves form a foundation. Obedience does.

This does not mean that salvation is earned by good works. The Sermon on the Mount begins with blessings for the poor in spirit, those who know they cannot save themselves. But genuine faith in Jesus always leads to obedience. Those who truly trust Him will seek to do what He says. A life that never changes despite hearing His words reveals that the person has not truly built on Him.

The parable also shows that Jesus Himself is the rock. Throughout Scripture, God is called the rock of His people (*Psalm 18:2*; *Isaiah 26:4*). By saying that a life built on His words will stand, Jesus is claiming to be the sure foundation God provides.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse calls believers to move from hearing to doing. After reading Scripture or hearing it taught, a helpful response is to identify specific ways to obey: someone to forgive, a habit to change, a person to help, a truth to trust. Small acts of obedience, repeated over time, build a foundation that will stand.

It also prepares believers for storms. Hardships, temptations, losses, and crises come to everyone. Those who have built their lives on Jesus’ words are not exempt from storms, but they can withstand them. The time to build a strong foundation is before the storm arrives, through consistent faithfulness in ordinary days.

Finally, this parable invites honest self-examination. Two houses may look alike from the outside. Similarly, two people may appear equally religious. The real question is whether Jesus’ words are actually shaping how we live. If they are not, the remedy is to come to Him humbly, ask for His help, and begin to put His words into practice.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Matthew 7* brings the Sermon on the Mount to a practical and decisive conclusion. Jesus has described a way of life marked by humility, purity, mercy, truthfulness, generosity, and love. Now He asks His listeners to respond, not merely by admiring His teaching, but by living it.

The chapter’s teaching on judging others is especially relevant in a culture quick to criticize. Jesus calls His followers to look first at their own faults, to correct others only with humility and gentleness, and to leave final judgment to God. This does not mean abandoning discernment; believers must still recognize false teaching and harmful behavior. But their posture toward others should be marked by mercy rather than condemnation.

The encouragement to ask, seek, and knock reminds believers that the kingdom life is not lived by willpower alone. The Father is generous and ready to give good things, including the strength to obey. Regular, persistent prayer is the way disciples draw on His help. The Golden Rule then gives a practical test for daily life: treat others as you would want to be treated, actively doing good rather than merely avoiding harm.

Finally, Jesus presents a series of choices that call for honest reflection. The narrow road and the wide road, good fruit and bad fruit, genuine obedience and empty words, rock and sand: each contrast asks whether His teaching is truly shaping a person’s life. Religious activity, impressive gifts, and correct words are not enough. What matters is knowing Jesus and doing the Father’s will. Believers can respond by examining their lives, confessing where they have heard without doing, and taking concrete steps to build on the rock while there is still time.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for teaching with authority and for giving me words on which I can build my whole life. Forgive me for the times I have judged others harshly while ignoring my own faults. Show me the beam in my own eye, and give me humility and gentleness when I need to help someone else.

Thank You that my Father in heaven gives good gifts to those who ask. Teach me to keep asking, seeking, and knocking, and to trust His goodness when His answers are different from what I expected. Help me to treat others as I would want to be treated, and to take the initiative in doing good. Keep me on the narrow road that leads to life, guard me from false teachers, and let my life bear good fruit. Do not let me be someone who only hears Your words; make me someone who does them, so that my house stands firm when the storms come. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Matthew · Chapter 8 of 28

# Matthew — Chapter 8

Chapter Theme: The Authority of Jesus Over Sickness, Storm, and Evil

[Read Matthew 8 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/MAT08.htm)

Main Teaching

After teaching with authority on the mountain, Jesus demonstrates that same authority in action. He cleanses a leper, heals a Gentile officer’s servant from a distance, restores Peter’s mother-in-law, calms a violent storm, and frees two men from demons. Along the way He shows that faith means trusting His word, and that following Him comes before every other claim.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Matthew 8* begins immediately after the Sermon on the Mount. At the end of chapter 7, the crowds were astonished that Jesus taught “*with authority*” (*Matthew 7:29*). Matthew now shows that Jesus’ authority is not only in His words but in His deeds. Chapters 8 and 9 together contain ten miracle stories, grouped carefully. They show Jesus’ power over disease, nature, demons, and even death, and they reveal how different people respond to Him. Matthew’s arrangement is more thematic than strictly chronological; he gathers similar events together to show who Jesus is.

The people Jesus helps in this chapter are striking: a leper, a Roman centurion, and a woman. In Jewish society these were all people at the margins of religious life in different ways. Lepers were ritually unclean and excluded from community; Gentiles were outside God’s covenant people; and women had limited status in public religious life. Jesus’ compassion reaches them first.

### The Cleansing of a Leper (*8:1–4*)

As Jesus came down the mountain, a man with leprosy approached, knelt before Him, and said, “*Lord, if you want to, you can make me clean*” (*v. 2*). In the Bible, “leprosy” referred to a range of skin diseases, not only what is today called Hansen’s disease. Under the law of Moses (*Leviticus 13–14*), anyone with such a condition was declared unclean and had to live apart from others, wearing torn clothes and calling out “Unclean!” to warn people away. The disease brought physical suffering, social isolation, and religious exclusion. Touching a leper made a person ritually unclean.

The man did not doubt Jesus’ power; he wondered whether Jesus was willing. Jesus answered by doing what no one else would do: He touched him. “*I want to. Be made clean.*” (*v. 3*) Instead of Jesus becoming unclean, the man became clean. Jesus then told him to tell no one but to go to the priest and offer the sacrifice prescribed in *Leviticus 14*. This would officially restore the man to the community and serve “*as a testimony to them*” (*v. 4*), evidence to the priests of what had happened. Jesus’ instruction to keep quiet reflects His concern, seen throughout the Gospels, that people would misunderstand His mission if they saw Him only as a miracle-worker.

### The Centurion’s Faith (*8:5–13*)

In Capernaum, a centurion came to Jesus. A centurion was a Roman army officer in charge of about a hundred soldiers. He may have served Herod Antipas rather than Rome directly, but either way he was a Gentile and a representative of foreign power. He told Jesus that his servant was at home paralyzed and suffering terribly. Luke tells us that this centurion was respected by the local Jewish leaders because he had built their synagogue (*Luke 7:1–10*).

Jesus immediately offered to come. The centurion replied, “*Lord, I’m not worthy for you to come under my roof. Just say the word, and my servant will be healed*” (*v. 8*). Devout Jews generally avoided entering Gentile homes because it would make them ritually unclean. The centurion may have been sparing Jesus that problem, but he also expressed deep humility. He explained his reasoning: as an officer, he understood authority. He gave orders and soldiers obeyed. He believed Jesus had the same kind of authority over sickness, so that a word from Him would be enough.

Jesus was amazed. He said He had not found such great faith anywhere in Israel. Then He made a startling prediction: many would come from east and west, meaning Gentiles from distant nations, and would feast with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven, while “*the children of the Kingdom*” (*v. 12*), those who assumed they belonged because of their heritage, would be thrown out. The image of a banquet with the patriarchs draws on prophetic hopes such as *Isaiah 25:6–8*. “Weeping and gnashing of teeth” describes grief and anguish at being excluded. Jesus then told the centurion to go, and the servant was healed at that very hour.

### Healing at Peter’s House (*8:14–17*)

Jesus went to Peter’s house in Capernaum (archaeologists have uncovered a house there that early Christians venerated as Peter’s home). Peter’s mother-in-law was in bed with a fever. Jesus touched her hand, the fever left, and she got up and began to serve Him. Her immediate service shows both the completeness of the healing and a fitting response to Jesus.

That evening, people brought many who were demon-possessed and sick. Jesus drove out the spirits with a word and healed all the sick. Matthew sees this as fulfilling *Isaiah 53:4*: “*He took our infirmities and bore our diseases*” (*v. 17*). *Isaiah 53* describes the Suffering Servant who bears the sins and griefs of others. Matthew shows that Jesus’ healing ministry is part of His work as that Servant, a foretaste of the complete restoration His death and resurrection will bring.

### The Cost of Following Jesus (*8:18–22*)

When Jesus saw the crowds, He gave orders to cross to the other side of the lake. Before they left, two people spoke to Him about following Him. A scribe said enthusiastically, “*Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go*” (*v. 19*). Jesus replied that foxes have dens and birds have nests, but “*the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head*” (*v. 20*). “Son of Man” is the title Jesus used most often for Himself. It could simply mean “a human being,” but it also recalls *Daniel 7:13–14*, where “*one like a son of man*” (*Daniel 7:13*) receives everlasting dominion from God. Jesus’ point to the scribe was that following Him meant sharing a life without security or comfort.

Another disciple said, “*Lord, allow me first to go and bury my father*” (*v. 21*). Burying one’s parents was a sacred duty in Jewish culture. The man’s father may not yet have died; the phrase could mean, “Let me wait until my father dies and I have fulfilled my family obligations.” Either way, Jesus’ reply was shocking: “*Follow me, and leave the dead to bury their own dead*” (*v. 22*). He meant that those who are spiritually dead could take care of such matters, while the call to follow Him took priority. Jesus was not teaching disrespect for parents; elsewhere He rebuked those who neglected them (*Matthew 15:3–6*). He was teaching that His claim comes before even the most important human obligations.

### Calming the Storm (*8:23–27*)

Jesus got into a boat, and His disciples followed Him. Matthew’s wording links this scene to the preceding sayings: this is what following Jesus looks like. A violent storm arose on the lake, so that the waves covered the boat. The Sea of Galilee lies about seven hundred feet below sea level, surrounded by hills, and winds can sweep down suddenly and stir up dangerous storms. Several of the disciples were experienced fishermen, and they were terrified. Meanwhile, Jesus was asleep.

They woke Him, crying, “*Save us, Lord! We are dying!*” (*v. 25*) Jesus first addressed their fear: “*Why are you fearful, O you of little faith?*” (*v. 26*) Then He rose and rebuked the wind and waves, and there was a great calm. The disciples were amazed: “*What kind of man is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?*” (*v. 27*) In the Old Testament, it is God who rules the raging sea and stills its waves (*Psalm 89:9*; *107:28–29*). The disciples were beginning to realize that Jesus was far more than a teacher or healer.

### The Demon-Possessed Men in the Gadarene Region (*8:28–34*)

On the other side of the lake, in the region Matthew calls the country of the Gergesenes (other manuscripts and Gospels read Gadarenes or Gerasenes; the names refer to towns in the same largely Gentile region), two demon-possessed men came out of the tombs to meet Jesus. They were so violent that no one could pass that way. Mark and Luke focus on one of the men, while Matthew mentions both.

The demons recognized Jesus immediately: “*What do we have to do with you, Jesus, Son of God? Have you come here to torment us before the time?*” (*v. 29*) They knew that God had appointed a time of final judgment for evil spirits, and they were alarmed that Jesus had come to confront them already. A large herd of pigs was feeding nearby, which confirms that this was Gentile territory, since Jews did not raise pigs. The demons begged to be sent into the pigs. Jesus said one word, “Go!” The demons left the men and entered the pigs, and the whole herd rushed down the steep bank into the lake and drowned.

The herdsmen ran into the town and reported everything. The whole town came out to meet Jesus, but instead of welcoming Him, they begged Him to leave their region. They had seen His power, but they were more concerned about their economic loss and their fear than about the freedom of two tormented men. The chapter ends with this sad response: people who preferred to keep their lives as they were rather than have Jesus among them.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Matthew 8:3* — “*I Want To. Be Made Clean*” (*v. 3*).

> *“Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him, saying, ‘I want to. Be made clean.’ Immediately his leprosy was cleansed.”*
>
> — *Matthew 8:3* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse describes the first miracle Matthew records after the Sermon on the Mount. A man with leprosy came to Jesus as He came down the mountain with great crowds following. Under the law of Moses, such a man was considered unclean and was required to live apart from others (*Leviticus 13:45–46*). He would not have been allowed to approach crowds, and certainly not to come near a teacher. His approach was itself an act of desperate faith.

The man knelt before Jesus and said, “*Lord, if you want to, you can make me clean*” (*v. 2*). He was confident in Jesus’ power but unsure of His willingness. Perhaps years of rejection had taught him to expect that no one wanted to come near him.

Jesus’ response came in action before words: He “*stretched out his hand and touched him*” (*v. 3*). This touch was remarkable. According to the law, touching an unclean person made the one who touched unclean. Jesus could have healed with a word, as He would for the centurion’s servant. Instead, He chose to touch a man who may not have been touched by anyone in a long time. Then He answered the man’s exact question: “I want to.” He was willing. “Be made clean.” Immediately the leprosy disappeared.

The direction of contagion was reversed. Normally uncleanness spread from the unclean to the clean. With Jesus, cleanness spread from Him to the unclean. He was not defiled; the man was healed.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals the heart of Jesus toward the excluded and the ashamed. The leper’s question, “if you want to,” is one many people ask about God. They believe God is powerful, but they wonder whether He cares about them. Jesus’ answer, in word and touch, is clear: He is willing.

In the Old Testament, leprosy was not only a physical condition but a picture of uncleanness that separated a person from God’s presence and His people. Throughout Scripture, God’s holiness required separation from uncleanness. Jesus shows that God’s holiness is not merely a barrier that excludes; in Christ, it becomes a power that cleanses and restores. This anticipates the deeper cleansing from sin that Jesus came to bring. As *1 John 1:7* says, “*the blood of Jesus Christ, his Son, cleanses us from all sin*” (*1 John 1:7*).

Jesus’ instruction to go to the priest also shows that He respected the law of Moses and wanted the man fully restored to community life. Healing was not only about the body; it included restored relationships and full participation in worship.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites anyone who feels unclean, ashamed, or unworthy to come to Jesus with confidence. Whatever sense of defilement a person carries, whether from their own sin, from what others have done to them, or from circumstances that have made them feel excluded, Jesus is willing to cleanse and restore. The question is not whether He is able or willing; it is whether we will come.

It also challenges believers to imitate Jesus’ compassion. In every community there are people who feel untouchable: the sick, the stigmatized, the lonely, and those whose past makes others keep their distance. Followers of Jesus can show His love through practical presence, kindness, and inclusion, while taking appropriate care for health and safety.

Finally, Jesus’ concern for the man’s restoration to community reminds believers that healing includes belonging. The church is called to welcome people who have been restored by Christ and help them find their place among God’s people.

### *Matthew 8:10* — Great Faith From an Unexpected Place

> *“When Jesus heard it, he marveled and said to those who followed, Most certainly I tell you, I haven’t found so great a faith, not even in Israel.”*
>
> — *Matthew 8:10* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse records Jesus’ reaction to the Roman centurion in Capernaum. The centurion had asked Jesus to heal his servant, who was paralyzed and suffering. When Jesus offered to come to his house, the centurion said he was not worthy to have Jesus under his roof. He asked Jesus simply to say the word, explaining that he understood authority: as an officer, he gave orders and they were carried out. He believed Jesus’ word had that same authority over sickness.

Matthew says that Jesus “*marveled*” (*v. 10*). Only twice in the Gospels is Jesus said to be amazed: here at a Gentile’s faith, and in *Mark 6:6* at the unbelief of the people in His hometown of Nazareth. Jesus turned to the crowd following Him and said that He had not found faith like this anywhere in Israel.

What made this faith great? First, it was humble: the centurion, a man of power and position, said he was not worthy. Second, it was confident: he believed that Jesus’ word alone was enough, without any need for Jesus to be physically present. Third, it was perceptive: he recognized that Jesus’ authority came from God, just as his own authority came from Rome. He understood that sickness had to obey Jesus’ command.

The original listeners would have been surprised. They might have expected great faith from religious leaders or devout Israelites, not from a Gentile officer associated with foreign occupation. Jesus’ praise turned their expectations upside down, and His next words warned that many Gentiles would share in the kingdom while some who assumed they belonged would be excluded.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that faith, not ethnicity or religious status, is what connects a person to God’s kingdom. The centurion had no covenant privileges as a Gentile, yet he received Jesus’ blessing because he trusted Him. This anticipates the great theme of the New Testament that Gentiles are welcomed into God’s people through faith in Christ (*Romans 1:16*; *Ephesians 2:11–22*).

The verse also teaches what faith is. Faith is not a feeling of certainty that something will happen, or a technique for obtaining results. It is trust in the person and authority of Jesus. The centurion’s faith rested entirely on who Jesus was and what His word could do.

At the same time, Jesus’ warning in the following verses shows that privilege without faith is dangerous. Those who grew up with God’s promises can take them for granted and miss the One the promises point to. Religious heritage is a gift, but it must lead to personal trust in Christ.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to trust the authority of Jesus’ word. Much of Christian life involves trusting His promises when we cannot see Him physically present or the outcome yet. Scripture records His words so that believers can rely on them, just as the centurion relied on Jesus’ spoken command.

It also teaches humility in faith. The centurion did not think he deserved Jesus’ help; he trusted Jesus’ goodness and power. Believers can come to God not on the basis of their own worthiness but on the basis of His grace.

Finally, the centurion’s request was on behalf of someone else, a servant who in that culture would have had little status. His faith expressed itself in compassion. Believers can bring the needs of others to Jesus in prayer and act on their behalf, especially for those who have no one else to speak for them.

### *Matthew 8:26* — Fear and Faith in the Storm

> *“He said to them, ‘Why are you fearful, O you of little faith?’ Then he got up, rebuked the wind and the sea, and there was a great calm.”*
>
> — *Matthew 8:26* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse comes in the middle of the storm on the Sea of Galilee. Jesus had told His disciples to cross the lake, and they followed Him into the boat. Suddenly a violent storm arose, so severe that the waves were covering the boat. The disciples, some of whom were experienced fishermen who knew these waters, believed they were going to die. Meanwhile, Jesus was asleep, likely exhausted after a long day of teaching and healing.

The disciples woke Him, crying, “*Save us, Lord! We are dying!*” (*v. 25*) Their prayer was urgent and sincere. They turned to the right person. Yet Jesus’ first words were a gentle rebuke: “*Why are you fearful, O you of little faith?*” (*v. 26*) Note the order in Matthew’s account: Jesus speaks to their fear before He calms the storm. The phrase “little faith” appears several times in Matthew (*6:30*; *14:31*; *16:8*; *17:20*). It does not mean no faith; the disciples did turn to Jesus. It means faith that was not strong enough to overcome their fear. They had seen His power, yet in the crisis they acted as if He might let them drown.

Then Jesus “*got up, rebuked the wind and the sea, and there was a great calm*” (*v. 26*). The word “rebuked” is the same word used when Jesus rebukes demons. He spoke to the storm as to a force under His command. The sudden calm, rather than a gradual lessening of the wind, showed that this was not a natural change in the weather.

The disciples’ response was awe: “*What kind of man is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?*” (*v. 27*) In the Old Testament, only God controls the seas (*Psalm 107:23–30*). The disciples were beginning to see that Jesus shared God’s own authority over creation.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals that following Jesus does not guarantee calm waters. The disciples were in the storm precisely because they obeyed Jesus’ instruction to cross the lake. Faithfulness can lead into difficulty. Yet Jesus was with them in the boat, and He was not anxious. His sleep reflected perfect trust in His Father’s care, the same trust He described in *Matthew 6*.

The calming of the storm also reveals Jesus’ identity. He commands the forces of nature as only the Creator can. Matthew wants readers to share the disciples’ question, “What kind of man is this?” and to arrive at the answer: He is the Son of God, with authority over all creation.

Jesus’ rebuke of the disciples’ fear is not harsh condemnation. It is a teacher’s challenge, calling them to grow. Faith does not mean never feeling afraid, but it means that fear does not have the final word because we know who is with us.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Many believers face storms: illness, financial crisis, family conflict, grief, or danger. This verse reminds them that Jesus is present in those storms. Like the disciples, they can cry out to Him honestly. He welcomes such prayers.

It also invites believers to examine their fear. Fear often reveals what we believe about God when we are under pressure. If we believe He has forgotten us or does not care, fear will dominate. If we remember His power and His presence, faith can steady us even before circumstances change.

Finally, this story encourages growth in faith over time. The disciples’ faith was small, but Jesus kept teaching them. Believers can learn from each storm, recalling how God has been faithful in the past and building confidence for the future. Faith grows as we see, repeatedly, that the One in the boat with us has authority over the wind and the waves.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Matthew 8* shows Jesus’ authority over every kind of brokenness: disease, distance, demonic oppression, and the forces of nature. This means that no situation is outside His reach. Believers can bring every need to Him, confident that He is both able and willing to act, even when His answer comes in a different way or at a different time than they expect.

The chapter also shows the kinds of people Jesus welcomes. He touched a leper, praised the faith of a Gentile soldier, and healed a woman in her home. He crossed into Gentile territory to free two men whom everyone else feared. His compassion broke through social and religious barriers. Believers today are called to the same kind of love, reaching out to people who are excluded, feared, or overlooked, and treating them with dignity.

Faith is a central theme throughout the chapter. The leper believed in Jesus’ power; the centurion trusted His word; the disciples had “little faith” in the storm. Faith grows when it rests on who Jesus is rather than on our circumstances or feelings. Believers can strengthen their faith by remembering His authority, trusting His promises in Scripture, and bringing their fears honestly to Him in prayer.

The chapter also includes a sober reminder about the cost of discipleship. Jesus told one would-be follower that He had nowhere to lay His head and told another that following Him came before even family obligations. Following Jesus requires putting Him first. And the chapter ends with a town that asked Jesus to leave because His presence had disrupted their economy. Every reader must decide whether to welcome Jesus’ authority, even when it costs something, or to send Him away in order to keep life as it is.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for Your authority over sickness, storms, and every power of evil. Thank You that You were willing to touch the man no one else would touch, and that You still welcome those who feel unclean or unworthy. Cleanse me, Lord, and help me to show Your compassion to people others avoid.

Give me faith like the centurion’s, humble and confident in Your word. When storms rise in my life and I feel afraid, remind me that You are with me in the boat and that the wind and waves obey You. Help my small faith to grow. Teach me to follow You even when it costs me comfort or security, and keep me from ever asking You to leave because Your presence disrupts what I want to protect. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Matthew · Chapter 9 of 28

# Matthew — Chapter 9

Chapter Theme: Authority to Forgive and Compassion for the Lost

[Read Matthew 9 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/MAT09.htm)

Main Teaching

Jesus shows that His authority reaches beyond physical healing to the forgiveness of sins. He calls a tax collector to follow Him, eats with sinners, explains that His coming brings something new, and restores the sick, the blind, the mute, and even a girl who has died. Moved with compassion for crowds who are like sheep without a shepherd, He asks His disciples to pray for workers for God’s harvest.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Matthew 9* continues the series of miracles that began in chapter 8. Having shown Jesus’ power over disease, storms, and demons, Matthew now adds His authority to forgive sin and to raise the dead. Alongside these miracles runs a growing conflict with religious leaders, especially scribes and Pharisees, who object to Jesus’ claims and His friendships. The chapter ends with Jesus’ deep compassion for the crowds and His call to prayer for laborers, which leads directly into chapter 10, where He sends out the Twelve.

### The Paralyzed Man Forgiven and Healed (*9:1–8*)

Jesus crossed the lake back to “*his own city*” (*v. 1*), meaning Capernaum, where He had made His home (*Matthew 4:13*). Some people brought a paralyzed man lying on a mat. Mark and Luke add the memorable detail that his friends opened up the roof to lower him down because of the crowd (*Mark 2:1–12*). Matthew keeps the account short and focuses on what Jesus said.

Seeing their faith (the faith of the friends as well as the man), Jesus said, “*Son, cheer up! Your sins are forgiven you*” (*v. 2*). This must have surprised everyone. The man came for healing, and Jesus spoke first about forgiveness. Many in that culture assumed a connection between sin and sickness. Jesus did not say this man’s paralysis was caused by a specific sin, but He addressed the man’s deepest need first.

Some scribes thought to themselves, “*This man blasphemes*” (*v. 3*). In their view, only God could forgive sins, because all sin is ultimately against God. If Jesus claimed to forgive sins, He was claiming God’s prerogative. Their reasoning was correct, but their conclusion was wrong. Jesus knew their thoughts and asked which was easier: to say “Your sins are forgiven” or “Get up and walk.” Anyone could say the first words, since no one could see whether forgiveness had happened. Saying the second could be tested immediately. So Jesus did the visible miracle to prove the invisible one. He told the man to get up, take his mat, and go home, and the man did. The crowds were filled with awe and praised God for giving such authority.

### The Call of Matthew (*9:9–13*)

As Jesus walked on, He saw a man named Matthew sitting at the tax booth. (Mark and Luke call him Levi; he likely had both names.) Tax collectors in Galilee worked for Herod Antipas, collecting tolls and customs on goods passing through Capernaum, which lay on a trade route. They were notorious for overcharging and were seen as collaborators with oppressive rulers. Devout Jews considered them unclean and excluded them from religious life. Jesus said to him, “*Follow me*” (*v. 9*), and Matthew got up and followed. Unlike the fishermen, who could return to fishing, Matthew walked away from a lucrative position he could not easily get back.

Matthew then hosted a meal at his house, and many tax collectors and “sinners” came to eat with Jesus and His disciples. “Sinners” referred to people known for immoral lives or who did not observe the law as the Pharisees did. In that culture, sharing a meal expressed acceptance and fellowship. The Pharisees objected, asking the disciples why their teacher ate with such people.

Jesus answered with a proverb: healthy people do not need a doctor; sick people do. Then He quoted *Hosea 6:6*: “*I desire mercy, and not sacrifice*” (*v. 13*), telling the Pharisees to go and learn what it means. In Hosea, God criticized Israel for offering sacrifices while lacking faithful love. Jesus applied it to the Pharisees, who were careful about religious purity but lacked mercy toward sinners. He concluded that He came to call not the righteous but sinners to repentance.

### The Question About Fasting (*9:14–17*)

Next, disciples of John the Baptist asked Jesus why they and the Pharisees fasted often but His disciples did not. Jesus answered with an image from a wedding. Wedding celebrations in that culture lasted a week, and the groom’s friends were free from religious duties like fasting during the celebration. It would be absurd for them to mourn while the bridegroom was present. Jesus identified Himself as the bridegroom, an image the Old Testament used for God in relation to His people (*Isaiah 62:5*; *Hosea 2:19–20*). But He added a somber note: “*the days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast*” (*v. 15*), His first hint in Matthew of His coming death.

He then gave two short parables. No one sews a patch of unshrunk cloth onto an old garment, because when it gets wet the new patch shrinks and tears the old fabric. And no one pours new, still-fermenting wine into old, brittle wineskins, because the expanding wine would burst them. New wine needs new wineskins. Jesus was saying that the new reality He brought could not simply be added onto old patterns of religion. The kingdom He announced required new ways of living.

### A Ruler’s Daughter and a Suffering Woman (*9:18–26*)

While Jesus was speaking, a ruler came, knelt before Him, and said, “*My daughter has just died, but come and lay your hand on her, and she will live*” (*v. 18*). Mark and Luke tell us his name was Jairus and that he was a leader of the synagogue. Matthew’s shorter account says that the girl had already died, emphasizing the man’s remarkable faith. Jesus got up and went with him.

On the way, a woman who had suffered from bleeding for twelve years came up behind Jesus and touched the fringe of His garment. Under *Leviticus 15:25–27*, a woman with ongoing bleeding was considered ritually unclean, and anyone she touched became unclean. For twelve years she had lived in isolation, unable to participate fully in worship or community. Jewish men wore tassels on the corners of their garments as reminders of God’s commands (*Numbers 15:38–40*). She thought, “*If I just touch his garment, I will be made well*” (*v. 21*). Jesus turned, saw her, and said, “*Daughter, cheer up! Your faith has made you well*” (*v. 22*). He called her “daughter,” welcoming her into the family of God, and publicly affirmed her healing.

When Jesus reached the ruler’s house, professional mourners were already there. Families, even poor ones, hired flute players and wailing women for funerals. Jesus told them to leave because “*the girl isn’t dead, but sleeping*” (*v. 24*). They laughed at Him because they knew she was dead. Jesus was not denying that she had died; He was saying that death, in His presence, is like sleep from which a person can be awakened. He sent the crowd out, took her by the hand, and she got up. News of this spread throughout the region.

### Two Blind Men and a Mute Man (*9:27–34*)

As Jesus went on, two blind men followed Him, calling, “*Have mercy on us, son of David!*” (*v. 27*) This is the first time someone in Matthew calls Jesus “Son of David” in a request, recognizing Him as the promised Messiah. The prophets had said that when God came to save His people, the eyes of the blind would be opened (*Isaiah 35:5*). Jesus asked them, “*Do you believe that I am able to do this?*” (*v. 28*) They said, “Yes, Lord.” He touched their eyes and said, “*According to your faith be it done to you*” (*v. 29*). Their eyes were opened. Jesus sternly told them not to tell anyone, perhaps because He did not want to be seen as a political messiah, but they spread the news everywhere.

Then a man who was mute because of a demon was brought to Him. When Jesus cast out the demon, the man spoke. The crowds were amazed, saying nothing like this had ever happened in Israel. But the Pharisees said, “*By the prince of the demons, he casts out demons*” (*v. 34*). They could not deny the miracles, so they attributed them to Satan. This accusation will return in *Matthew 12*, where Jesus responds to it directly.

### Compassion for the Crowds (*9:35–38*)

Matthew closes with a summary that echoes *Matthew 4:23*: Jesus went through all the towns and villages, teaching, preaching the kingdom, and healing every disease. When He saw the crowds, “*he was moved with compassion for them because they were harassed and scattered, like sheep without a shepherd*” (*v. 36*). Then He told His disciples that the harvest was plentiful but the workers few, and He asked them to pray for the Lord of the harvest to send out workers. In the next chapter, Jesus will send these same disciples out as the answer to that prayer.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Matthew 9:6* — Authority to Forgive Sins

> *“But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins— (then he said to the paralytic), ‘Get up, and take up your mat, and go to your house.’”*
>
> — *Matthew 9:6* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse is the turning point of the healing of the paralyzed man in Capernaum. His friends had brought him to Jesus on a mat, hoping for healing. Instead, Jesus first said, “*Son, cheer up! Your sins are forgiven you*” (*v. 2*). Some scribes, experts in the law, silently accused Jesus of blasphemy, because they knew that only God can forgive sins. Jesus knew their thoughts and challenged them with a question: which is easier to say, “Your sins are forgiven” or “Get up and walk”?

The point of the question is that forgiveness cannot be seen, so anyone could claim to forgive sins without being proven wrong. Healing paralysis, however, can be seen immediately. Jesus now says that He will do the visible miracle so that they may know He has the invisible authority: “*But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins*” (*v. 6*). Then He turns to the paralyzed man and commands him to get up, take his mat, and go home.

The title “Son of Man” comes from *Daniel 7:13–14*, where one like a son of man comes before God and receives authority, glory, and an everlasting kingdom. By using this title, Jesus claims that heavenly authority. The phrase “on earth” is important: forgiveness, which was understood as something God granted from heaven, was now being given on earth through Jesus.

The man stood up and went home, proving that Jesus’ words had real power. The crowds were filled with awe and glorified God.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse makes one of the clearest claims in the Gospels about Jesus’ identity. The scribes were right that only God can forgive sins. Jesus did not deny that; He demonstrated that He has the authority to do what only God can do. Matthew’s readers are meant to draw the conclusion that Jesus shares God’s authority because He is “*God with us*” (*Matthew 1:23*).

The verse also shows that forgiveness is our deepest need. The paralyzed man and his friends wanted physical healing, and Jesus gave it. But He addressed the man’s relationship with God first. Physical healing was temporary; the man would eventually die. Forgiveness of sins restored him to God forever. Jesus’ healing ministry serves as a sign pointing to His greater work of saving people from sin, which He will accomplish through His death (*Matthew 26:28*).

Finally, the verse connects forgiveness and new life. The man who was forgiven got up and walked. In a similar way, God’s forgiveness is not only the removal of guilt but the beginning of a new life of obedience and freedom.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse assures believers that Jesus has full authority to forgive sins. Many people carry guilt for things they have done, wondering whether they can ever be truly free. Jesus’ words to the paralyzed man, “Your sins are forgiven,” are words He still speaks to those who come to Him in faith. Believers can confess their sins honestly and trust that His forgiveness is real and complete.

It also invites believers to keep their priorities in line with Jesus’. It is natural to pray mostly for physical needs and circumstances, and God cares about these. But Jesus shows that our relationship with God is the most important matter. Praying for forgiveness, spiritual renewal, and reconciliation with God deserves a central place.

Finally, those who have been forgiven are called to “get up and walk,” living new lives. Forgiveness is not permission to keep sinning but the freedom to begin again, leaving behind what once held us down.

### *Matthew 9:13* — Mercy, Not Sacrifice

> *“But you go and learn what this means: “I desire mercy, and not sacrifice,” for I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.”*
>
> — *Matthew 9:13* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus speaks these words to the Pharisees after they criticize Him for eating with tax collectors and sinners at Matthew’s house. Matthew, a tax collector, had just left his tax booth to follow Jesus, and he invited his friends, other tax collectors and people with bad reputations, to a meal with Jesus. The Pharisees, who carefully avoided contact with people they considered unclean, asked Jesus’ disciples why their teacher ate with such people.

Jesus first answered with a proverb: “*Those who are healthy have no need for a physician, but those who are sick do*” (*v. 12*). A doctor who avoided sick people would be useless. Jesus came for those who know they need help.

Then He told the Pharisees, “*But you go and learn what this means*” (*v. 13*). This phrase was a common way rabbis sent students back to study Scripture more carefully. It carried a gentle irony: these experts in the law needed to learn its meaning. Jesus quoted *Hosea 6:6*: “*I desire mercy, and not sacrifice*” (*v. 13*). In Hosea, God was rebuking Israel for continuing to offer sacrifices while their lives lacked loyalty and love. God was not rejecting sacrifices entirely, since He had commanded them. He was saying that rituals without mercy are empty, and mercy is what He values most.

Jesus applied this to the Pharisees. They were concerned with ritual purity and separation from sinners, but they lacked compassion. Jesus concluded, “*for I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance*” (*v. 13*). He came to call those who know they are sinners. The “righteous” may refer to those who consider themselves righteous and therefore see no need for Him.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals the heart of God toward sinners. God is not repelled by sinful people in the way the Pharisees were. He seeks them out, invites them, and offers them restoration. Jesus’ table fellowship with tax collectors and sinners was a living picture of God’s welcome. *Luke 15* contains three parables, the lost sheep, the lost coin, and the lost son, that make the same point: heaven rejoices when sinners repent.

The verse also warns against religious practice without mercy. Jesus quotes *Hosea 6:6* again in *Matthew 12:7*, showing how central this principle is to His teaching. Religious activities, such as worship, giving, and moral discipline, matter, but they become distorted when they make people proud, harsh, or unwilling to help those who are struggling.

Notice that Jesus calls sinners “to repentance.” His welcome is not approval of sin; it is an invitation to change. Matthew’s own life shows this: he left his tax booth to follow Jesus. Mercy and the call to repentance go together. Jesus accepts people as they are, but He does not leave them as they are.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse calls believers to show mercy to people the world, or the church, may look down on. Followers of Jesus can build genuine friendships with people far from God, sharing meals, listening, and caring for them, not to look down on them but because they too have been shown mercy. This does not mean joining in sin, but it does mean refusing to keep people at a distance because of their reputation.

It also invites believers to examine whether their religion has become more about rules and appearances than about love. If someone is more concerned with being seen as respectable than with helping those in need, Jesus’ words apply.

Finally, the verse is good news for anyone who feels too sinful for God. Jesus came for sinners. The first step is simply to recognize one’s need, like a sick person who goes to a physician, and come to Him. His welcome is real, and His call to repentance is the path to new life.

### *Matthew 9:36* — Sheep Without a Shepherd

> *“But when he saw the multitudes, he was moved with compassion for them because they were harassed and scattered, like sheep without a shepherd.”*
>
> — *Matthew 9:36* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse comes at the end of a long section describing Jesus’ ministry. Matthew has just summarized that Jesus went through all the towns and villages, teaching in synagogues, preaching the kingdom, and healing every kind of disease. Everywhere He went, crowds gathered: the sick, the poor, the oppressed, and the curious. Now Matthew tells us how Jesus saw them.

“*He was moved with compassion for them*” (*v. 36*). The Greek word used for compassion is very strong; it refers literally to the inner organs and describes a deep, gut-level feeling of pity and love. Jesus did not look at the crowds as an inconvenience or merely as an audience. He felt their need deeply.

Matthew describes the crowds as “*harassed and scattered*” (*v. 36*). “Harassed” means troubled, weary, or mistreated. “Scattered” can mean thrown down or helpless. They were burdened by sickness, poverty, oppression, and religious leaders who loaded them with heavy requirements without helping them (*Matthew 23:4*).

They were “*like sheep without a shepherd*” (*v. 36*). This phrase comes from the Old Testament. Moses asked God to provide a leader so that Israel would not be “*as sheep which have no shepherd*” (*Numbers 27:17*). In *Ezekiel 34*, God condemned Israel’s leaders as bad shepherds who fed themselves instead of the flock, and He promised that He Himself would shepherd His people and set over them one shepherd, His servant David. Jesus is the fulfillment of that promise: the Good Shepherd who cares for the lost and scattered sheep.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals the heart of Jesus, and through Him the heart of God, toward suffering people. God is not distant or indifferent. He sees human need and is moved by it. The compassion of Jesus is not only an emotion; it leads to action. In this case, it leads Him to call His disciples to pray for workers and then to send them out to minister (*Matthew 10*).

The image of a shepherd was widely used in the ancient world for kings and leaders. A good shepherd protected, fed, guided, and cared for the flock, even at personal risk. Israel’s leaders had often failed in this role. Jesus came as the true shepherd, and in *John 10:11* He says that the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.

This verse also connects compassion with mission. Seeing people as harassed and helpless led Jesus to speak of a harvest. People’s needs are not only a reason for sadness but an opportunity for God’s kingdom to reach them through His workers.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to see people the way Jesus does. Crowds in cities, neighbors, coworkers, and even difficult people can be seen as harassed and helpless, burdened by needs that are often hidden. Asking God for a heart of compassion can transform how believers relate to those around them, replacing irritation or indifference with care.

It also calls believers to act on compassion. Jesus’ compassion led to prayer and to sending workers. Believers can pray for people in need, for their communities, and for those who serve them. They can also look for ways to help, whether by meeting practical needs, offering friendship, or sharing the good news of Jesus.

Finally, this verse offers comfort to those who feel harassed and helpless themselves. Jesus sees such people with compassion, not disappointment. He is the Shepherd who seeks the scattered sheep and invites them to come to Him for care and rest.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Matthew 9* presents Jesus as the one who brings forgiveness, mercy, and new life to people who need it most. He forgives a paralyzed man, calls a despised tax collector, eats with sinners, heals a woman isolated for twelve years, raises a dead girl, and gives sight to the blind. Each story shows that no one is beyond His reach. Believers can bring their deepest needs to Him, beginning with the need for forgiveness, and trust that He has authority to meet them.

The chapter also challenges religious attitudes that keep people at a distance. The Pharisees objected when Jesus forgave sins and when He ate with sinners. Jesus answered that God desires mercy more than ritual, and that He came for the sick, not the healthy. Churches and individual believers can ask whether they welcome people with messy lives or quietly keep them away. Showing mercy does not mean ignoring sin, but it does mean treating others as people Jesus came to save.

The teaching about new wine and new wineskins reminds believers that following Jesus brings real change. Faith in Him is not simply adding a religious layer to an old life; it creates a new way of living. Habits, attitudes, and priorities may need to be reshaped to fit the life of the kingdom.

Finally, the chapter ends with Jesus’ compassion for the crowds and His call to pray for workers. Believers today are called to share His compassion and to join His mission. This can begin with prayer for the people around us, and continue with willingness to be part of the answer: serving, helping, and speaking about the One who forgives, heals, and shepherds His people.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for Your authority to forgive sins and for the mercy You show to people the world looks down on. Thank You that You came for the sick and not the healthy, and that You call sinners like me to repentance and new life. Forgive my sins, and help me to rise and walk in the freedom You give.

Keep me from religion that values appearances more than mercy. Give me Your heart for people who are harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd. Teach me to welcome those others avoid, to show compassion in practical ways, and to share the good news of Your forgiveness. Lord of the harvest, send out workers into Your harvest, and make me willing to be one of them. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
