Matthew · Chapter 13 of 28

# Matthew — Chapter 13

Chapter Theme: The Hidden Growth of God’s Kingdom

[Read Matthew 13 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/MAT13.htm)

Main Teaching

Jesus teaches in parables that reveal how God’s kingdom works: the message is received in different ways depending on the condition of the heart, good and evil will grow together until the final harvest, the kingdom begins small but grows great, and it is worth more than everything else a person owns. The chapter closes with His own hometown rejecting Him because they cannot see past His ordinary background.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Matthew 13* is the third of Jesus’ five major teaching sections in Matthew. It comes after two chapters of mounting opposition. John the Baptist questioned Jesus from prison, towns that saw His miracles did not repent, and the Pharisees plotted to destroy Him and accused Him of working by Satan’s power (*Matthew 11–12*). A natural question arises: if Jesus is the Messiah and God’s kingdom has arrived, why are so many people rejecting Him? Why hasn’t the kingdom simply overpowered all opposition? The parables in this chapter answer those questions.

A parable is a short story or comparison drawn from everyday life, used to teach a spiritual truth. Jesus’ parables used familiar images from Galilean life: farming, fishing, baking, and buying. Parables could make a truth vivid and memorable, but they also required hearers to think and respond. As Jesus explains in this chapter, parables revealed truth to those who were open and concealed it from those who had already hardened their hearts.

### The Parable of the Sower (*13:1–9*)

The same day as the events of chapter 12, Jesus went out and sat by the Sea of Galilee. So many people gathered that He got into a boat and taught from the water while the crowd stood on the shore. The natural slope of the shoreline could carry His voice to a large crowd.

He told about a farmer sowing seed. In Palestine, farmers often scattered seed by hand across a field before plowing it into the soil. Some seed fell along the hard-packed path, where birds ate it. Some fell on rocky ground, where a thin layer of soil covered limestone bedrock; it sprang up quickly but withered in the sun because it had no root. Some fell among thorns, which grew up and choked it. Some fell on good soil and produced a crop of a hundred, sixty, or thirty times what was sown, an extraordinary harvest by ancient standards. Jesus ended with, “*He who has ears to hear, let him hear*” (*v. 9*), a call to listen carefully and respond.

### Why Jesus Speaks in Parables (*13:10–17*)

The disciples asked why He spoke to the crowds in parables. Jesus replied that the “*mysteries of the Kingdom of Heaven*” (*v. 11*) had been given to them but not to others. In the New Testament, a “mystery” is not a puzzle but a truth that was once hidden and is now revealed by God. Those who had responded to Jesus would receive more understanding; those who had rejected Him would lose even what they had.

Jesus quoted *Isaiah 6:9–10*, where God told Isaiah that his preaching would harden a people who refused to listen. Jesus’ parables had a similar effect: for those whose hearts were already closed, they remained puzzling stories. But Jesus also said, “*But blessed are your eyes, for they see; and your ears, for they hear*” (*v. 16*). The disciples were privileged to see what prophets and righteous people had longed to see: the arrival of God’s promised kingdom in Jesus.

### The Sower Explained (*13:18–23*)

Jesus then explained the parable. The seed is “*the word of the Kingdom*” (*v. 19*), the message about God’s reign through Jesus. The different soils represent different responses. The path stands for those who hear but do not understand, so the evil one snatches the message away. The rocky ground stands for those who receive the word with joy but have no root, so they fall away when trouble or persecution comes. The thorny ground stands for those whose response is choked by “*the cares of this age and the deceitfulness of riches*” (*v. 22*). The good soil stands for those who hear, understand, and bear fruit. The details of this parable are studied below.

### The Wheat and the Weeds (*13:24–30*, 36–43)

Jesus told another parable. A man sowed good seed in his field, but at night an enemy sowed darnel among the wheat. Darnel is a weed that looks very similar to wheat in its early stages and can be poisonous. Deliberately sowing weeds in someone’s field was a known form of revenge in the ancient world; Roman law even had penalties for it. When the plants grew and the weeds became visible, the servants offered to pull them up. The owner refused, because pulling the weeds might uproot the wheat, whose roots were intertwined. Both would grow together until harvest, when the weeds would be gathered and burned and the wheat gathered into the barn.

Later, in the house, Jesus explained this parable to His disciples. The sower is the Son of Man; the field is the world; the good seed represents the people of the kingdom; the weeds represent the people of the evil one; the enemy is the devil; the harvest is the end of the age; and the reapers are angels. At the end, the Son of Man will send His angels to remove everything that causes sin and all who do evil, and “*the righteous will shine like the sun in the Kingdom of their Father*” (*v. 43*).

### The Mustard Seed and the Yeast (*13:31–35*)

Two short parables describe the kingdom’s growth. The mustard seed was proverbially tiny, yet the plant could grow to ten feet or more in Galilee, large enough for birds to perch in. The kingdom began small, with a carpenter from Nazareth and a handful of disciples, but it would grow far beyond its beginnings. The image of birds nesting in branches echoes Old Testament pictures of great kingdoms sheltering the nations (*Ezekiel 17:23*; *Daniel 4:12*).

The yeast parable makes a similar point. A woman mixed a small amount of yeast into three measures of flour, about sixty pounds, enough to feed a hundred people, and it worked through the whole batch. The kingdom works quietly and invisibly, but it transforms everything it touches. (Yeast is often a symbol of evil in Scripture, but here Jesus uses it simply as an image of hidden, pervasive influence.)

Matthew notes that Jesus spoke to the crowds only in parables, fulfilling *Psalm 78:2*, which speaks of uttering things hidden from long ago.

### The Treasure, the Pearl, and the Net (*13:44–50*)

Jesus told His disciples three more parables. The kingdom is like treasure hidden in a field; a man found it, hid it again, and joyfully sold everything to buy the field. It is like a merchant who searched for fine pearls and, finding one of great value, sold everything to buy it. These parables are studied below.

The kingdom is also like a dragnet, a large net drawn between boats or from the shore, which caught all kinds of fish. The fishermen sorted the good fish from the bad, perhaps those that were inedible or ritually unclean (*Leviticus 11:9–12*). So at the end of the age, the angels will separate the wicked from the righteous. Like the parable of the weeds, this one teaches that judgment will come, but it belongs to God at the end.

### New and Old Treasures (*13:51–52*)

Jesus asked whether His disciples understood, and they said yes. He then compared every scribe trained for the kingdom to a homeowner who brings out of his storeroom things new and old. A disciple who understands Jesus’ teaching values both the Old Testament Scriptures and the new revelation that Jesus brings, seeing how they fit together. Some have suggested that Matthew himself, with his careful use of Old Testament fulfillment, is an example of such a scribe.

### Rejection at Nazareth (*13:53–58*)

Jesus returned to His hometown of Nazareth and taught in the synagogue. The people were amazed at His wisdom and miracles, but they could not accept Him. They asked, “*Isn’t this the carpenter’s son?*” (*v. 55*) The word translated “carpenter” can refer to a builder who worked with wood or stone. They named His mother and His brothers, James, Joses, Simon, and Judas, and mentioned His sisters. (Christians have understood these “brothers and sisters” in different ways: as children of Mary and Joseph born after Jesus, as children of Joseph from an earlier marriage, or as cousins, since the word could be used broadly for relatives. The point of the passage is not affected.) They knew Him too well, or thought they did, and “*They were offended by him*” (*v. 57*).

Jesus responded with a proverb: “*A prophet is not without honor, except in his own country and in his own house*” (*v. 57*). Matthew concludes that Jesus did not do many miracles there because of their unbelief. Their lack of faith did not limit His power, but it closed them off from receiving what He offered.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Matthew 13:23* — The Good Soil That Bears Fruit

> *“What was sown on the good ground, this is he who hears the word and understands it, who most certainly bears fruit and produces, some one hundred times as much, some sixty, and some thirty.”*
>
> — *Matthew 13:23* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse is the final part of Jesus’ explanation of the parable of the sower. He spoke the parable to a large crowd from a boat, then explained it privately to His disciples. The parable describes four kinds of ground on which seed falls, and Jesus identifies the seed as the word of the kingdom, His message about God’s reign.

The first three soils show ways the message fails to take root. The hard path represents people who hear without understanding, so the evil one snatches the message away. The rocky ground represents people who respond enthusiastically at first but fall away when following Jesus brings trouble or persecution. The thorny ground represents people whose faith is gradually choked by worries and the deceptive attraction of wealth.

This verse describes the good soil: the person “*who hears the word and understands it, who most certainly bears fruit*” (*v. 23*). Three things mark the good soil. First, they hear the word. Second, they understand it. In Matthew, understanding is more than intellectual knowledge; it means grasping the message and taking it to heart. Third, they bear fruit, meaning their lives are changed and produce results that reflect God’s kingdom.

The yield of a hundred, sixty, or thirty times is remarkable. An ordinary harvest in that region might produce seven to ten times what was sown. Jesus describes an abundant, even miraculous harvest. The different amounts show that not everyone bears the same amount of fruit, but all who receive the word in good soil are fruitful.

The parable also explains why Jesus’ ministry met with so much rejection. The problem was not with the seed or the sower, but with the condition of the soil.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This parable teaches that the condition of the heart determines how a person responds to God’s Word. The same message produces very different results in different people. This explains why some respond to the gospel with lasting faith while others reject it, drift away, or let it be crowded out.

The parable also warns about different dangers to faith. Some people never understand because they do not truly listen. Others have shallow faith that cannot withstand pressure. Others allow worries and the desire for wealth to choke their spiritual life. These dangers are not only for unbelievers; believers can also experience hardness, shallowness, or distraction at different times.

At the same time, the parable gives hope. Despite the losses, the harvest is great. God’s kingdom will produce abundant fruit in those who receive it. The New Testament describes this fruit in many ways: transformed character (*Galatians 5:22–23*), good works, faithful witness, and people brought to faith. Jesus says in *John 15:5* that those who remain in Him will bear much fruit.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to consider the condition of their own hearts. Do they listen to God’s Word with a desire to understand and obey, or do they let it bounce off a hard surface? Is their faith deeply rooted, or does it fade when following Jesus becomes difficult? Are worries or the pursuit of money slowly choking their spiritual life?

Practical steps can help cultivate good soil. Reading Scripture attentively, asking God for understanding, and reflecting on how to apply it help the word take root. Developing deep roots through prayer, fellowship, and perseverance in hard times prepares believers for trials. Identifying and dealing with the “thorns” of anxiety and materialism, perhaps by simplifying life, practicing generosity, or bringing worries to God, keeps faith from being choked.

Finally, this parable encourages those who share God’s Word. Not everyone will respond, and some responses will be disappointing. But the sower keeps sowing, trusting that God will bring a harvest. Believers can share their faith faithfully, leaving the results to God.

### *Matthew 13:30* — Growing Together Until the Harvest

> *“Let both grow together until the harvest, and in the harvest time I will tell the reapers, ‘First, gather up the darnel weeds, and bind them in bundles to burn them; but gather the wheat into my barn.’’”*
>
> — *Matthew 13:30* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse is the final instruction of the landowner in the parable of the wheat and the weeds. A man had sown good seed in his field, but an enemy secretly sowed darnel weeds among the wheat at night. When the crops grew, the servants discovered the weeds and asked whether they should pull them up. The owner said no, because pulling the weeds might uproot the wheat with them. Darnel and wheat look nearly identical in their early growth, and their roots could be tangled together.

So the owner said, “*Let both grow together until the harvest*” (*v. 30*). At harvest time, he would tell the reapers to gather the weeds first, bind them in bundles to be burned, and gather the wheat into his barn. At harvest, when the plants were mature, the difference between them would be clear, and separation would be safe.

Jesus later explained the parable to His disciples. The field is the world, the good seed is the people of the kingdom, the weeds are the people of the evil one, the enemy is the devil, the harvest is the end of the age, and the reapers are angels. The point is that good and evil will exist side by side in the world until the final judgment. God will separate them at the end, not now, and not through His servants’ efforts.

This parable answered a question many in Jesus’ day had. If the kingdom had come, why was evil still present? Why didn’t the Messiah immediately destroy all the wicked? The answer is that the kingdom comes in stages. It has come in Jesus, but the final judgment awaits the end of the age.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This parable teaches patience in the face of evil. God’s delay in judging is not weakness or indifference. Peter explains that the Lord is “*patient with us, not wishing that anyone should perish, but that all should come to repentance*” (*2 Peter 3:9*). God gives time for repentance and protects His people from harm in the process.

The parable also warns against attempting to purify the world or the church by force. Throughout history, some have tried to root out evil by violence, persecution, or harsh judgment, often harming innocent people in the process. Jesus teaches that final separation belongs to God and His angels at the end of the age.

This does not mean that believers should ignore sin or that the church should never exercise discipline. Elsewhere Jesus gives instructions for dealing with sin among believers (*Matthew 18:15–17*), and Paul instructs churches to address serious, unrepentant sin (*1 Corinthians 5*). The parable’s field is “the world,” and its main point is that God will deal with evil completely and justly at the end. Until then, believers live alongside evil, resist it, and trust God for final judgment.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to be patient and trust God’s justice when they see evil in the world. It is natural to want immediate justice, and Scripture affirms the cry for justice. But believers can trust that God will set everything right at the proper time. That trust frees them from bitterness and from taking vengeance into their own hands.

It also calls for humility in judging others. The servants could not reliably tell wheat from weeds, and pulling up weeds would damage the wheat. Believers are often poor judges of who truly belongs to God. They can address wrongdoing where they have responsibility, through appropriate means, while leaving ultimate judgment to God.

Finally, this verse reminds believers that the harvest is coming. Life is not endless, and the world as it is will not continue forever. This calls for faithful living and readiness. Believers can live as wheat, bearing good fruit, knowing that the Lord of the harvest sees and will gather His own.

### *Matthew 13:44* — The Treasure Worth Everything

> *“Again, the Kingdom of Heaven is like treasure hidden in the field, which a man found and hid. In his joy, he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field.”*
>
> — *Matthew 13:44* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This parable is one of two short stories Jesus told His disciples privately about the value of the kingdom. In the ancient world there were no banks as we know them, and people often buried their valuables in the ground for safekeeping, especially in times of war or danger. If the owner died or was taken away, the treasure might remain hidden for years until someone discovered it.

In the parable, a man finds such a treasure in a field. He hides it again and, “*In his joy*” (*v. 44*), sells everything he owns to buy the field. Under some customs of the time, buying the field would give him rights to whatever was in it. Jesus does not comment on the ethics of the man’s actions; His point is the man’s response. He recognized that the treasure was worth far more than everything he had, and he gladly gave up everything to obtain it.

The parable that follows makes a similar point. A merchant searching for fine pearls finds one of great value and sells everything to buy it. In the first parable, the man stumbles upon the treasure unexpectedly. In the second, the merchant finds it after a deliberate search. Both respond in the same way.

The key phrase is “in his joy.” The man does not sell everything with regret or sorrow. He is thrilled, because what he gains is worth infinitely more than what he gives up.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This parable teaches that God’s kingdom, meaning life under God’s reign through Jesus, is the most valuable thing a person can have. It is worth more than possessions, status, comfort, or any other pursuit. Paul expressed the same conviction: “*I count all things to be a loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus, my Lord*” (*Philippians 3:8*).

The parable also teaches that following Jesus involves wholehearted commitment. The man sold everything. Jesus elsewhere calls His disciples to put Him above family, possessions, and even their own lives (*Matthew 10:37–39*). Yet the parable shows that this commitment is not a grim sacrifice but a joyful exchange. People who understand the value of the kingdom do not feel cheated by what they give up.

This parable does not teach that salvation can be bought. The kingdom is God’s gift, received by faith. The parable is about recognizing its surpassing value and responding with total commitment. Some interpreters also see in it a picture of Christ, who gave up everything to purchase His people (*2 Corinthians 8:9*), though Jesus’ explanation focuses on the response of the one who finds the kingdom.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to consider how they value God’s kingdom. Do they treat their relationship with Christ as one priority among many, or as the treasure that gives everything else its meaning? The way people spend their time, money, and energy often reveals what they truly treasure.

It also encourages joyful generosity and sacrifice. When following Jesus requires giving something up, whether a habit, an ambition, a possession, or comfort, believers can remember that what they gain in Christ is worth far more. Approaching sacrifice with joy rather than resentment reflects a true understanding of the kingdom’s value.

Finally, the parable reminds believers that God’s kingdom may be found unexpectedly, as with the man in the field, or after long searching, as with the merchant. Either way, the right response is the same: recognize the treasure and commit wholeheartedly to Jesus.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Matthew 13* helps believers understand how God’s kingdom works in the world. It does not come in a sudden display of overwhelming force but grows gradually, sometimes hidden, often opposed, yet unstoppable. This perspective helps believers stay faithful when they see little visible progress. The mustard seed and the yeast remind them that small beginnings can lead to great results, and that God works quietly in ways that may not be immediately obvious.

The parable of the sower invites ongoing self-examination. The condition of the heart matters. Believers can cultivate good soil by listening attentively to God’s Word, putting down deep roots through prayer and obedience, and guarding against the worries and riches that choke spiritual life. They can also be patient and hopeful when sharing their faith, knowing that the results depend on God working in hearts.

The parables of the weeds and the net teach both patience and seriousness. Good and evil will exist together until the end, and believers are not called to root out evil by force or to judge others’ final destiny. But judgment is coming, and it will be complete and just. This calls believers to live faithfully, bearing good fruit, and to trust God’s justice.

The parables of the treasure and the pearl call for wholehearted, joyful commitment. Nothing in life compares with the value of knowing Christ and belonging to His kingdom. Finally, the rejection at Nazareth warns against allowing familiarity or prejudice to blind us to God’s work. The people of Nazareth thought they knew Jesus, but their assumptions kept them from receiving Him. Believers can ask God to keep them open and humble, ready to recognize and receive Him wherever and however He works.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for teaching in parables that reveal the hidden ways of Your kingdom. Make my heart good soil that hears Your word, understands it, and bears lasting fruit. Soften any hard places, deepen my roots so that I stand firm in trouble, and clear away the worries and desires that choke my faith.

Give me patience when I see evil growing alongside good, and help me trust that You will bring perfect justice at the harvest. Keep me from judging others harshly, and help me to live faithfully as Your wheat. Thank You that Your kingdom, though it began small, is growing throughout the world. Teach me to value You as the treasure worth more than everything I own, and to follow You with joy. Guard me from the familiarity and unbelief that kept Your hometown from receiving You. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Matthew · Chapter 14 of 28

# Matthew — Chapter 14

Chapter Theme: Two Kings, Two Banquets, and the Lord of the Sea

[Read Matthew 14 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/MAT14.htm)

Main Teaching

Matthew contrasts the corrupt banquet of Herod, where John the Baptist is executed to keep a careless oath, with the banquet in the wilderness, where Jesus feeds thousands out of compassion. That night Jesus walks on the stormy sea, calls Peter to come to Him, rescues him when he sinks, and is worshiped by His disciples as the Son of God.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Matthew 14* follows the parables of the kingdom and the rejection of Jesus at Nazareth (*Matthew 13*). It begins a section in which Jesus increasingly withdraws from public conflict and focuses on teaching His disciples. The chapter is built around a striking contrast between two rulers. Herod Antipas, who held the title of king in the popular sense, throws a lavish birthday feast that ends in murder. Jesus, the true King, hosts a simple meal in a deserted place that ends in abundance and healing.

### The Death of John the Baptist (*14:1–12*)

Herod the tetrarch was Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great (who tried to kill the infant Jesus in *Matthew 2*). After his father’s death, Antipas ruled Galilee and Perea from 4 B.C. to A.D. 39. “Tetrarch” originally meant a ruler of a quarter of a territory, and it came to mean a minor ruler under Roman authority. People sometimes called him “king” (v. 9), though Rome never gave him that title.

When Herod heard reports about Jesus, he said, “*This is John the Baptizer. He is risen from the dead*” (*v. 2*). His guilty conscience made him fear that the prophet he had killed had come back. Matthew then tells the story in a flashback. Herod had arrested John because John told him, “*It is not lawful for you to have her*” (*v. 4*). Herod had divorced his first wife to marry Herodias, who was his brother’s wife (and also his niece). *Leviticus 18:16* and *20:21* forbade marrying a brother’s wife while the brother was alive. John spoke the truth to a powerful man, knowing the danger.

Herod wanted to kill John but was afraid of the people, who considered John a prophet. At Herod’s birthday celebration, the daughter of Herodias danced before the guests and pleased Herod. (The historian Josephus names her Salome.) Herod, probably drunk and eager to impress his guests, promised with an oath to give her anything she asked. Prompted by her mother, she asked for the head of John the Baptist on a platter. Herod was grieved, but because of his oaths and his guests, he ordered John beheaded. The head was brought on a platter, like another dish at the feast, and given to the girl, who gave it to her mother.

John’s disciples came, took his body, buried it, and went to tell Jesus. John’s death foreshadowed Jesus’ own: both were faithful messengers of God, executed by rulers who knew they were innocent but acted to protect their reputations.

### Feeding the Five Thousand (*14:13–21*)

When Jesus heard the news, He withdrew by boat to a deserted place. He may have been grieving His cousin and forerunner, and He may also have been withdrawing from Herod’s territory to avoid premature conflict. But the crowds heard where He was going and followed on foot around the lake. When Jesus landed and saw them, “*He had compassion on them and healed their sick*” (*v. 14*).

As evening came, the disciples urged Jesus to send the crowds away so they could buy food in the villages. Jesus answered, “*They don’t need to go away. You give them something to eat*” (*v. 16*). The disciples had only five loaves and two fish. These were probably small barley loaves, the bread of the poor, and dried or pickled fish. Jesus told them to bring the food to Him. He had the people sit down on the grass, took the loaves and fish, looked up to heaven, blessed God, broke the loaves, and gave them to the disciples, who distributed them to the crowd.

Everyone ate and was satisfied. The disciples gathered twelve baskets of leftovers, one for each of the twelve tribes of Israel or one for each disciple. The number fed was about five thousand men, besides women and children, so the total may have been well over ten thousand.

This miracle carries rich Old Testament echoes. God fed Israel with manna in the wilderness (*Exodus 16*), and the prophet Elisha fed a hundred men with twenty barley loaves, with some left over (*2 Kings 4:42–44*). *Psalm 23* speaks of the shepherd who makes his sheep lie down in green pastures. The actions of taking, blessing, breaking, and giving bread also anticipate the Last Supper (*Matthew 26:26*). Matthew presents Jesus as the shepherd-king who provides for His people.

### Jesus Walks on the Water (*14:22–33*)

Immediately after the meal, Jesus made His disciples get into the boat and cross the lake ahead of Him while He dismissed the crowd. John’s Gospel tells us that the crowd wanted to make Jesus king by force (*John 6:15*), which may explain why He sent the disciples away so quickly. Then He went up the mountain alone to pray.

Meanwhile, the boat was far from land, battered by waves because the wind was against it. During “*the fourth watch of the night*” (*v. 25*), between three and six in the morning, Jesus came to them walking on the sea. The disciples had been rowing against the wind for hours. When they saw Him, they were terrified and cried out, “*It’s a ghost!*” (*v. 26*) Jesus immediately spoke to them: “*Cheer up! It is I! Don’t be afraid*” (*v. 27*).

Peter answered, “*Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the waters*” (*v. 28*). Jesus said, “Come.” Peter got out of the boat and walked on the water toward Jesus. But when he saw the wind, he became afraid, began to sink, and cried out, “*Lord, save me!*” (*v. 30*) Jesus immediately reached out His hand, caught him, and said, “*You of little faith, why did you doubt?*” (*v. 31*) When they climbed into the boat, the wind stopped.

The disciples in the boat worshiped Jesus, saying, “*You are truly the Son of God!*” (*v. 33*) This is a significant moment. In *Matthew 8*, after Jesus calmed a storm, they asked, “What kind of man is this?” Now they answer their own question.

### Healings at Gennesaret (*14:34–36*)

After crossing the lake, they landed at Gennesaret, a fertile plain on the northwest shore of the Sea of Galilee. When the people recognized Jesus, they sent word throughout the region and brought all their sick to Him. They begged to touch even the fringe of His garment, as the woman with the bleeding had done (*Matthew 9:20*), and all who touched it were healed. The chapter ends as it began its second half, with Jesus’ compassionate healing.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Matthew 14:14* — Compassion in a Time of Grief

> *“Jesus went out, and he saw a great multitude. He had compassion on them and healed their sick.”*
>
> — *Matthew 14:14* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse comes right after Jesus hears that John the Baptist has been executed by Herod. John was Jesus’ relative, the prophet who had prepared His way and baptized Him. His death was brutal and unjust. Matthew tells us that when Jesus heard the news, “*he withdrew from there in a boat to a deserted place apart*” (*v. 13*). He seems to have wanted time alone, perhaps to grieve, to pray, and to step away from Herod’s attention.

But the crowds heard where He was going and followed Him on foot from the towns around the lake. When Jesus stepped out of the boat, He did not find the quiet place He had sought. Instead, a great crowd was waiting.

Matthew tells us how Jesus responded: “*He had compassion on them and healed their sick*” (*v. 14*). The word for compassion is the same strong word used in *Matthew 9:36*, describing a deep inner response of pity and love. Jesus did not resent the crowd’s interruption. He saw their need and responded with care, healing the sick among them. Later in the day, His compassion extended to feeding them all.

This verse shows Jesus’ heart in a moment when He might have been expected to focus on His own grief. Instead of turning the crowd away, He gave Himself to meet their needs.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals the depth of Jesus’ compassion. He was fully human and surely felt sorrow at John’s death. Elsewhere He wept at the grave of His friend Lazarus (*John 11:35*). Yet His grief did not close His heart to others. His compassion flowed even in a time of personal loss.

The verse also shows Jesus as the true shepherd of God’s people. The crowds were like sheep without a shepherd (*Matthew 9:36*), and Herod, their earthly ruler, had just shown himself to be a destroyer rather than a shepherd. Jesus’ care for the people stands in sharp contrast to Herod’s self-centered feast. The true King is the one who gives Himself for the needs of others.

It is worth noticing that Jesus did seek solitude, and after feeding the crowd He went up the mountain alone to pray (v. 23). His compassion for others did not mean He neglected His own need for time with the Father. Both belong together in a healthy life of service.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse offers comfort to those who are grieving. Jesus knows what it is to lose someone, and He does not stand at a distance from human sorrow. Believers can bring their grief honestly to Him.

It also offers an example for believers who serve others while carrying their own burdens. Compassion does not require pretending that everything is fine. Jesus grieved, sought solitude, and still met the needs in front of Him. Believers can ask God for the strength to love others even in difficult seasons, while also making room for rest, prayer, and their own healing.

Finally, the pattern of Jesus’ day, withdrawal, service, and then prayer, offers wisdom for sustainable compassion. People who constantly give without receiving from God can become exhausted. Regular time alone with God prepares believers to respond to interruptions and needs with genuine compassion rather than resentment.

### *Matthew 14:27* — “*It Is I. Don't Be Afraid*” (*v. 27*).

> *“But immediately Jesus spoke to them, saying, ‘Cheer up! It is I! Don’t be afraid.’”*
>
> — *Matthew 14:27* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These words are spoken by Jesus to His disciples in the middle of the night on the Sea of Galilee. After feeding the five thousand, Jesus sent the disciples ahead by boat while He dismissed the crowd and went up the mountain to pray. During the night, the wind turned against them and the waves battered the boat. They were stuck in the middle of the lake, rowing hard and making little progress.

In the early hours of the morning, between three and six, Jesus came toward them, walking on the water. In the darkness and the storm, the disciples did not recognize Him. They thought He was a ghost, and they screamed in fear. Many people in that time believed in spirits that haunted the sea.

Jesus immediately spoke to calm them: “*Cheer up! It is I! Don’t be afraid*” (*v. 27*). “Cheer up” means “take courage.” “It is I” in Greek is literally “I am” (ego eimi). In ordinary speech this simply means “It’s me.” But in the Old Testament, God revealed His name to Moses as “*I AM*” (*Exodus 3:14*), and in Isaiah God repeatedly says “I am he” to comfort His people (*Isaiah 43:10–13*; *51:12*). Jesus is walking on the sea, something the Old Testament says only God does: God alone “*treads on the waves of the sea*” (*Job 9:8*). In this setting, Jesus’ words carry a deeper meaning: the One who is coming to them across the waters is the very presence of God.

His first concern was their fear. Before calming the storm, He calmed their hearts with His presence and His word.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals Jesus’ identity as the Son of God who shares God’s power over creation. The disciples’ worship at the end of the scene, “*You are truly the Son of God!*” (*v. 33*), shows that they began to understand this.

It also reveals how God meets His people in their fear. The phrase “Do not be afraid” appears often in Scripture, usually when God or His messengers appear to people in frightening circumstances. The basis for courage is not that the danger is small, but that God is present. *Isaiah 43:2* promises, “*When you pass through the waters, I will be with you*” (*Isaiah 43:2*).

The setting matters too. The disciples were in the storm because they had obeyed Jesus’ instruction to cross the lake. Obedience does not guarantee calm waters. But Jesus was watching over them from the mountain, and He came to them at the right time. His delay was not abandonment.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse speaks to believers who feel caught in a storm, whether in health, finances, relationships, or uncertainty about the future. Like the disciples, they may struggle for hours, even years, against contrary winds. Jesus’ words invite them to take courage, not because the storm is unreal, but because He is present.

It also reminds believers that fear can distort how they see God’s presence. The disciples saw Jesus and thought He was a ghost. In difficult times, people sometimes misread God’s work or fail to recognize Him. Listening to His word in Scripture helps believers recognize His presence when circumstances are confusing.

Finally, believers can hold onto the truth that Jesus sees them in the storm. He watched the disciples from the mountain and came to them. Believers can pray honestly in hard times, trusting that He knows where they are and will come to them in His time and in His way.

### *Matthew 14:30–31* — Sinking Faith and the Saving Hand

> *“But when he saw that the wind was strong, he was afraid, and beginning to sink, he cried out, saying, ‘Lord, save me!’ Immediately Jesus stretched out his hand, took hold of him, and said to him, ‘You of little faith, why did you doubt?’”*
>
> — *Matthew 14:30–31* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These verses describe what happened after Peter stepped out of the boat. When Jesus came to the disciples walking on the water and said, “It is I,” Peter responded boldly: “*Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the waters*” (*v. 28*). Peter wanted to be where Jesus was and to share in what Jesus was doing. Jesus said, “Come,” and Peter climbed over the side of the boat and actually walked on the water toward Jesus.

Then “*when he saw that the wind was strong, he was afraid*” (*v. 30*). The wind had been blowing all along, but Peter’s attention shifted from Jesus to the danger around him. Fear took over, and he began to sink. In desperation, he cried out, “*Lord, save me!*” (*v. 30*) This short prayer echoes the disciples’ cry in the earlier storm (*Matthew 8:25*).

Jesus responded “*Immediately*” (*v. 31*). He reached out His hand and caught Peter. Then He said, “*You of little faith, why did you doubt?*” (*v. 31*) “Little faith” does not mean no faith. Peter had enough faith to step out of the boat, which none of the others did. But his faith wavered when he looked at the storm. The word translated “doubt” means to waver or be divided, pulled in two directions. Peter was torn between trust in Jesus and fear of the wind.

Jesus’ question is not harsh condemnation but gentle correction. He had already saved Peter before asking it. When they climbed into the boat, the wind stopped.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show both the possibility and the fragility of faith. Peter’s step onto the water shows that faith in Jesus can lead people to do what they could never do on their own. His sinking shows how quickly fear can overwhelm faith when attention shifts from Jesus to circumstances.

The most important truth in these verses is that Jesus saves those who call on Him, even when their faith is weak. Peter did not rescue himself, and Jesus did not let him drown as a lesson. Jesus reached out immediately. Paul writes that “*whoever will call on the name of the Lord will be saved*” (*Romans 10:13*). Salvation depends not on the strength of our faith but on the strength of the One we trust.

This scene also anticipates Peter’s later story. He would again be bold, promising never to deny Jesus, and would again fail when fear took hold (*Matthew 26:69–75*). And again, Jesus would restore him. Peter’s life shows that failures of faith need not be final when we cry out to Jesus.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to take steps of faith in response to Jesus’ call. Following Him may involve stepping out of comfortable places, such as serving in new ways, forgiving someone, taking a risk for the sake of the gospel, or obeying God when the outcome is uncertain. Like Peter, believers can step out when Jesus says, “Come.”

They also show how important it is to keep one’s focus on Jesus. Difficulties do not disappear when we trust Him, but faith grows stronger when we focus on His power and presence rather than on the size of the problem. Regular prayer, remembering God’s past faithfulness, and meditating on Scripture help keep attention on Him.

Finally, these verses offer hope when faith falters. Everyone experiences moments of fear and doubt. The right response is not to hide or despair but to cry out, “Lord, save me!” Jesus reaches out to those who call on Him. Believers can learn from their moments of sinking, trusting that the same hand that caught Peter will catch them.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Matthew 14* sets two kinds of leadership side by side. Herod’s feast shows power driven by pride, fear of embarrassment, and self-indulgence. He knew John was a prophet, but he executed him rather than lose face before his guests. Jesus’ meal in the wilderness shows power used for compassion and provision. Believers who have any kind of influence, whether in families, workplaces, churches, or communities, can ask which kind of leadership their lives resemble. Do they protect their image at the expense of what is right, or do they use their influence to serve others?

John the Baptist’s courage is also an example. He told Herod the truth about his sin, even though it cost him his freedom and his life. Few believers face such extreme consequences, but many face pressure to stay silent about what is right. Speaking truth with courage and love remains part of faithful discipleship.

The feeding of the five thousand teaches that Jesus can do much with little. The disciples had only five loaves and two fish, far too little for the need. But when they brought what they had to Jesus, He multiplied it. Believers often feel their resources, abilities, or time are insufficient to make a difference. The call is to bring what they have to Jesus and let Him use it.

Finally, the storm and Peter’s walk on the water speak to fear and faith. Jesus comes to His people in their storms, speaks words of courage, and reaches out to save those who call on Him. Believers can step out in faith when He calls, keep their eyes on Him in difficulty, and cry out to Him when they begin to sink. Like the disciples in the boat, their experiences of His rescue can lead them to deeper worship of Him as the Son of God.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for John the Baptist’s faithful courage, and help me speak truth with love even when it is costly. Guard me from the pride and fear of embarrassment that led Herod to do what he knew was wrong. Teach me to use whatever influence I have to serve others, as You did.

Thank You for Your compassion, even in Your own grief, and for feeding the hungry crowd from so little. I bring You what I have, small as it is; use it for Your purposes. When storms rise and the wind is against me, help me hear Your voice saying, “*Cheer up! It is I! Don’t be afraid*”. Give me faith to step out when You call, and when fear makes me sink, let me cry out to You and feel Your hand catching me. Like Your disciples in the boat, I worship You as the Son of God. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Matthew · Chapter 15 of 28

# Matthew — Chapter 15

Chapter Theme: Clean Hands, Unclean Hearts, and Faith From the Outside

[Read Matthew 15 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/MAT15.htm)

Main Teaching

Jesus confronts religious leaders who use human traditions to cancel God’s commands, teaching that true defilement comes from the heart, not from unwashed hands or food. He then honors the persistent faith of a Gentile woman and feeds a large crowd in Gentile territory, showing that God’s mercy reaches beyond Israel’s borders to all who come to Him in need.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Matthew 15* continues the pattern of the previous chapters: Jesus faces growing opposition from religious leaders while showing compassion to ordinary people, including outsiders. A delegation of Pharisees and scribes now arrives from Jerusalem, the center of religious authority, which shows that official concern about Jesus is increasing. The chapter is arranged so that its first half is about what truly makes a person “clean” or “unclean,” and its second half shows Jesus welcoming people whom many Jews considered unclean: a Canaanite woman and Gentile crowds.

### The Tradition of the Elders (*15:1–9*)

The Pharisees and scribes asked Jesus, “*Why do your disciples disobey the tradition of the elders? For they don’t wash their hands when they eat bread*” (*v. 2*). The “tradition of the elders” was a large body of oral teachings that interpreted and applied the law of Moses. The Pharisees believed these traditions had been passed down from Moses and were authoritative. They were later written down in the Mishnah around A.D. 200.

The handwashing in question was not about hygiene but ritual purity. The law of Moses required priests to wash before serving in the tabernacle (*Exodus 30:17–21*). The Pharisees extended this to ordinary meals for all Israelites, pouring water over the hands in a prescribed way to remove any ritual defilement picked up through contact with unclean things or people.

Jesus responded with a counter-question: “*Why do you also disobey the commandment of God because of your tradition?*” (*v. 3*) He gave an example. God commanded, “*Honor your father and your mother*” (*Exodus 20:12*), and warned against speaking evil of parents (*Exodus 21:17*). Honoring parents included supporting them financially in their old age. But some used a vow called “*Corban*” (*Mark 7:11*), declaring money or property “devoted to God.” Once declared, those resources could not be used to help parents, though the person might still keep using them. In this way, a religious tradition provided a loophole that cancelled one of the Ten Commandments.

Jesus called them “*hypocrites*” (*v. 7*) and quoted *Isaiah 29:13*: “*These people draw near to me with their mouth, and honor me with their lips; but their heart is far from me*” (*v. 8*). Their worship was outwardly correct but inwardly empty, and they treated human rules as if they were God’s commands.

### What Truly Defiles (*15:10–20*)

Jesus then called the crowd and gave a principle: “*That which enters into the mouth doesn’t defile the man; but that which proceeds out of the mouth, this defiles the man*” (*v. 11*). This was a startling statement. The law of Moses contained detailed food laws (*Leviticus 11*), and many Jews had suffered and even died rather than eat forbidden food (as recorded in 1 Maccabees 1:62–63). Jesus was not merely criticizing handwashing traditions; He was teaching that the deepest problem of uncleanness is not external but internal.

The disciples told Jesus that the Pharisees were offended. Jesus replied that every plant His Father did not plant would be uprooted, and He called the Pharisees “*blind guides of the blind*” (*v. 14*). Those who follow blind guides will fall into a pit with them.

Peter asked Jesus to explain. Jesus pointed out that food passes through the digestive system and out of the body; it does not touch the heart. But what comes out of the mouth comes from the heart: “*evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, sexual sins, thefts, false testimony, and blasphemies*” (*v. 19*). These are what make a person unclean before God. In Mark’s account the saying ends with the words “*making all foods clean*” (*Mark 7:19*), which many translations treat as Mark’s own comment on what Jesus’ teaching meant. The early church later recognized that the food laws, which had marked Israel as distinct, no longer applied to followers of Jesus (*Acts 10:9–16*).

### The Canaanite Woman’s Faith (*15:21–28*)

Jesus then withdrew to the region of Tyre and Sidon, Gentile cities on the Mediterranean coast north of Galilee, in what is now Lebanon. A Canaanite woman from that area came to Him, crying out, “*Have mercy on me, Lord, you son of David! My daughter is severely possessed by a demon!*” (*v. 22*)

Matthew calls her a “Canaanite,” an old term that recalls Israel’s ancient enemies in the land, people the Israelites had been told to drive out. Yet she addressed Jesus as “Lord” and “Son of David,” recognizing Him as Israel’s Messiah, which many in Israel had refused to do.

At first Jesus did not answer her at all. The disciples, annoyed by her persistent crying, urged Him to send her away. Jesus said, “*I wasn’t sent to anyone but the lost sheep of the house of Israel*” (*v. 24*), echoing His instructions to the Twelve (*Matthew 10:6*). His earthly mission was focused first on Israel, in keeping with God’s plan.

But the woman came, knelt before Him, and said simply, “*Lord, help me*” (*v. 25*). Jesus replied, “*It is not appropriate to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs*” (*v. 26*). The “children” were Israel; “dogs” was a term Jews sometimes used for Gentiles. The Greek word Jesus used refers to small household dogs rather than wild scavengers, which softens the image somewhat, but the statement still sounds harsh.

The woman did not argue or take offense. She accepted the comparison and turned it into an appeal: “*Yes, Lord, but even the dogs eat the crumbs which fall from their masters’ table*” (*v. 27*). She did not claim the children’s place; she asked only for crumbs, trusting that even a crumb of Jesus’ mercy would be enough.

Jesus answered, “*Woman, great is your faith! Be it done to you even as you desire*” (*v. 28*). Her daughter was healed at that moment. Many interpreters believe Jesus’ initial silence and hard words were a test that drew out and displayed the woman’s faith, in contrast to the unbelief of Israel’s leaders in the first part of the chapter. Her faith, like the centurion’s in *Matthew 8*, is called great.

### Healing and Feeding Many (*15:29–39*)

Jesus returned toward the Sea of Galilee, apparently to its eastern side, in the Decapolis region, which had a largely Gentile population (*Mark 7:31*). He went up a mountain and sat down. Great crowds brought the lame, blind, mute, crippled, and many others and laid them at His feet, and He healed them. The crowds were amazed and “*glorified the God of Israel*” (*v. 31*), a phrase that suggests many in the crowd were Gentiles praising Israel’s God.

Jesus then told His disciples that He had compassion on the crowd, which had been with Him for three days and had nothing to eat. He did not want to send them away hungry. The disciples asked where they could find enough bread in such a remote place, apparently forgetting the earlier feeding of the five thousand. They had seven loaves and a few small fish. Jesus gave thanks, broke the bread, and gave it to the disciples to distribute. Everyone ate and was satisfied, and seven large baskets of leftovers were collected. About four thousand men were fed, besides women and children.

This second feeding is similar to the first (*Matthew 14*), but its setting among Gentiles is significant. The first feeding, with twelve baskets left over, took place among Jews. The second, with seven baskets, took place in largely Gentile territory. Some see in the number seven a symbol of completeness, suggesting that Jesus’ provision extends to the whole world. Jesus then sent the crowds away and went by boat to the region of Magdala.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Matthew 15:8* — Lips Near, Hearts Far

> *“‘These people draw near to me with their mouth, and honor me with their lips; but their heart is far from me.”*
>
> — *Matthew 15:8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus speaks these words to the Pharisees and scribes who came from Jerusalem to criticize His disciples for not washing their hands ritually before eating. Jesus had just shown how their tradition of “Corban” allowed people to avoid supporting their aging parents by declaring their resources devoted to God. In this way, they kept a human tradition while breaking God’s clear command to honor father and mother.

After calling them hypocrites, Jesus quoted *Isaiah 29:13*. In Isaiah’s day, around 700 B.C., the people of Jerusalem continued to offer sacrifices, keep festivals, and say the right words in worship, but their lives showed that they did not truly love or trust God. God said through Isaiah that the people “*draw near to me with their mouth, and honor me with their lips; but their heart is far from me*” (*v. 8*).

Jesus applied these words to the religious leaders of His own time. They were very careful about outward religious practices. They spoke about God, kept many rules, and appeared devout. But their hearts were distant from God. Their concern for tradition had become more important than God’s actual commands and more important than love for people.

The next verse completes the quotation: “*And they worship me in vain, teaching as doctrine rules made by men*” (*v. 9*). Their worship was empty because it was not rooted in a heart devoted to God, and because they had elevated human rules to the level of divine commands.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals that God looks at the heart. Throughout Scripture, God makes clear that outward religion without inward devotion is unacceptable to Him. When Samuel looked for a king among Jesse’s sons, God told him, “*man looks at the outward appearance, but the LORD looks at the heart*” (*1 Samuel 16:7*). The prophets repeatedly criticized Israel for offering sacrifices while practicing injustice (*Isaiah 1:10–17*; *Amos 5:21–24*).

The verse also warns about the danger of tradition. Traditions can be helpful; they preserve wisdom and give structure to worship and life. But when traditions are treated as equal to or above God’s Word, they can distort faith and even contradict God’s commands. Jesus does not reject all tradition, but He insists that God’s Word must judge every human practice.

Finally, the verse shows that hypocrisy is not only a problem of the Pharisees. Every religious person faces the temptation to say the right words and perform the right rituals while their heart is elsewhere. Jesus’ warning applies to all who worship.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to examine whether their worship comes from the heart. It is possible to sing songs, recite prayers, attend services, and use religious language while the heart is distracted, indifferent, or even resistant to God. Worship becomes real when it involves honest love for God, a desire to obey Him, and a willingness to let Him change us.

It also calls believers to examine their traditions. Every church and family has practices and expectations, some written and some unspoken. These can be good, but they should be tested by Scripture. Believers can ask whether any tradition is preventing them from obeying God’s clear commands, such as caring for family, loving neighbors, or showing mercy.

Finally, Jesus’ specific example, neglecting parents through a religious loophole, shows that genuine faith includes practical care for family. Honoring parents, especially as they age, is part of honoring God. Religious activity should never become an excuse to neglect the people God has placed in our lives.

### *Matthew 15:18–19* — What Comes From the Heart

> *“But the things which proceed out of the mouth come out of the heart, and they defile the man. For out of the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, sexual sins, thefts, false testimony, and blasphemies.”*
>
> — *Matthew 15:18–19* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus speaks these words to His disciples after Peter asks Him to explain His saying about defilement. Earlier, Jesus told the crowd that what goes into the mouth does not defile a person, but what comes out of the mouth does. The disciples were concerned because the Pharisees had been offended. Peter asked for an explanation, and Jesus expressed surprise that they still did not understand.

He explained with a simple illustration. Food enters the mouth, goes into the stomach, and passes out of the body. It never reaches the heart, so it cannot make a person morally unclean. But “*the things which proceed out of the mouth come out of the heart, and they defile the man*” (*v. 18*).

Then Jesus listed what comes from the heart: “*evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, sexual sins, thefts, false testimony, and blasphemies*” (*v. 19*). The list begins with evil thoughts, the inner source from which other sins grow. The rest closely follows the second half of the Ten Commandments: murder (the sixth commandment), adultery and sexual immorality (the seventh), theft (the eighth), false testimony (the ninth), and blasphemy, or slander, which damages others with words. These sins are not caused by external contamination. They come from within.

Jesus concludes in the next verse that these are what defile a person, but eating with unwashed hands does not. The Pharisees were focused on keeping their hands clean while their hearts produced the very things that make people unclean before God.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This teaching reveals the true source of sin: the human heart. Jeremiah wrote, “*The heart is deceitful above all things and it is exceedingly corrupt*” (*Jeremiah 17:9*). Sin is not merely a matter of bad surroundings or bad influences; it arises from within. This means that external rules, however carefully kept, cannot solve the problem of sin. A new heart is needed.

The Old Testament prophets promised that God would one day give His people new hearts. Through Ezekiel, God said, “*I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you*” (*Ezekiel 36:26*). The New Testament teaches that this promise is fulfilled through Jesus and the Holy Spirit. Only God can cleanse the heart.

This teaching also had significant consequences for the early church. Jesus’ words about food helped the first Christians understand that the food laws, which had separated Jews from Gentiles, no longer needed to divide believers. What matters before God is not the food on one’s plate but the condition of one’s heart.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses call believers to look beneath their outward behavior to the condition of their hearts. It is possible to avoid obvious sins while harboring bitterness, lust, greed, or contempt. Jesus teaches that such thoughts are the roots of sinful actions. Honest self-examination, asking God to reveal what is hidden, is the beginning of real change.

They also warn against blaming outside forces entirely for our sins. While circumstances and influences matter, Jesus places responsibility on the heart. Believers can take ownership of their sins, confess them honestly, and ask God for inner transformation rather than only changing external habits.

Finally, these verses encourage believers to seek God’s cleansing. Because the problem is in the heart, the solution must reach the heart. Through prayer, confession, Scripture, and the work of the Holy Spirit, God renews people from within. Believers can pray as David did, “*Create in me a clean heart, O God*” (*Psalm 51:10*), and trust that God answers such prayers.

### *Matthew 15:28* — “*Woman, Great Is Your Faith*” (*v. 28*)

> *“Then Jesus answered her, ‘Woman, great is your faith! Be it done to you even as you desire.’ And her daughter was healed from that hour.”*
>
> — *Matthew 15:28* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse concludes Jesus’ encounter with the Canaanite woman in the region of Tyre and Sidon. She had come to Jesus crying out for mercy because her daughter was severely tormented by a demon. She called Him “Lord” and “Son of David,” recognizing Him as Israel’s Messiah.

The conversation that followed was difficult. At first Jesus did not answer her. The disciples wanted Him to send her away. Jesus said that He was sent only to the lost sheep of Israel. When she knelt and pleaded, “Lord, help me,” He said it was not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs. She answered with humility and quick wit: even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from the master’s table.

Now Jesus responds with admiration: “*Woman, great is your faith!*” (*v. 28*) He grants her request, and her daughter is healed at that very moment.

Why does Jesus call her faith great? First, she was persistent. She kept asking despite silence, the disciples’ resistance, and apparent refusal. Second, she was humble. She did not demand her rights or claim to be worthy. She accepted her place as an outsider and asked only for crumbs. Third, she trusted Jesus’ power and goodness completely. She believed that even a crumb of His mercy would be enough to heal her daughter.

Her faith stands in sharp contrast to the Pharisees in the first part of the chapter. They were Israel’s religious leaders, yet their hearts were far from God. She was a Gentile, from a people associated with Israel’s ancient enemies, yet she showed great faith.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This story shows that God’s mercy is not limited by ethnicity, background, or status. Although Jesus’ earthly mission was focused first on Israel, He responded to faith wherever He found it. This anticipates the spread of the gospel to all nations after His resurrection (*Matthew 28:19*). Paul later teaches that in Christ there is no distinction between Jew and Greek, for “*the same Lord is Lord of all, and is rich to all who call on him*” (*Romans 10:12*).

The story also shows the nature of persistent faith. Jesus’ initial silence and words were not a rejection of the woman. They gave her the opportunity to express her faith clearly and publicly. Elsewhere Jesus teaches His followers to keep asking and not lose heart (*Luke 18:1–8*). Faith sometimes means holding on to God’s goodness even when His response seems slow or unclear.

Finally, the woman’s humility is a picture of how all people come to God. No one has a right to God’s mercy. Everyone comes, in a sense, asking for crumbs from the Master’s table. Yet God, in His grace, gives not crumbs but the full bread of life.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to keep praying when answers are delayed. The woman did not give up when Jesus was silent or when His words were hard to hear. Believers who have prayed for a long time for a loved one, for healing, or for change can continue to bring their requests to God, trusting His goodness even when they do not understand His timing.

It also calls for humility in prayer. The woman did not argue that she deserved help. She appealed to Jesus’ mercy. Believers can come to God not on the basis of their own worthiness but on the basis of His grace.

Finally, the story challenges believers to recognize faith in unexpected places. The disciples wanted to send the woman away; Jesus praised her. Churches and individuals can be quick to dismiss people who seem like outsiders. Jesus’ example calls believers to welcome all who seek Him and to recognize that genuine faith may be found in people they would least expect.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Matthew 15* calls believers to examine the relationship between outward religion and inward reality. The Pharisees were careful about ritual washing but neglected God’s command to care for their parents. Their lips honored God while their hearts were far from Him. Believers can ask whether any of their religious habits have become a substitute for genuine love for God and others. Worship that pleases God comes from the heart and shows itself in obedience and mercy.

The chapter also teaches that the source of sin is within. External rules and appearances cannot cleanse a heart that produces evil thoughts, sexual sin, dishonesty, and slander. The solution is not merely trying harder to behave better but asking God to change the heart. Confession, repentance, and dependence on the Holy Spirit are essential parts of genuine spiritual growth.

The story of the Canaanite woman provides a powerful example of persistent, humble faith. She kept asking despite obstacles and trusted that even a crumb of Jesus’ mercy would be enough. Believers facing unanswered prayers or difficult circumstances can learn from her persistence and humility. They can also learn from Jesus’ response to her: He welcomed someone others wanted to send away.

Finally, the healing and feeding of Gentile crowds show that God’s compassion extends to all people. Followers of Jesus are called to share that compassion across ethnic, cultural, and social boundaries. The chapter invites believers to welcome outsiders, care for the needy, and recognize that God’s table is open to everyone who comes to Him in faith.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, You see past my words and outward habits to the condition of my heart. Forgive me for the times I have honored You with my lips while my heart was far from You. Show me where I have let traditions or appearances take the place of real love for You and for others, especially those in my own family.

Create in me a clean heart. Remove the evil thoughts, impurity, dishonesty, and harsh words that come from within, and fill me with Your Spirit. Give me the persistent, humble faith of the Canaanite woman, who kept asking and trusted that even a crumb of Your mercy was enough. Help me to welcome those whom others overlook and to share Your compassion with people of every background. Thank You that Your table is open to all who come to You in faith. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
