Matthew · Chapter 16 of 28

# Matthew — Chapter 16

Chapter Theme: Who Jesus Is and What It Costs to Follow Him

[Read Matthew 16 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/MAT16.htm)

Main Teaching

Religious leaders demand a sign while missing the signs already before them, and the disciples misunderstand Jesus’ warning about false teaching. At Caesarea Philippi, Peter confesses that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God, and Jesus promises to build His church. But when Jesus explains that the Messiah must suffer, die, and rise, Peter resists, and Jesus teaches that following Him means denying oneself and taking up the cross.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Matthew 16* is a turning point in the Gospel. Up to this point, Matthew has been building toward the question of Jesus’ identity: who is this man who teaches with authority, heals the sick, calms storms, and forgives sins? In this chapter, Peter gives the answer on behalf of the disciples. But immediately afterward, Jesus reveals something they did not expect: the Messiah must suffer and die. From this point on, the story moves steadily toward Jerusalem and the cross.

### Demanding a Sign (*16:1–4*)

The Pharisees and Sadducees came together to test Jesus. These two groups usually disagreed sharply: the Pharisees emphasized strict observance of the law and oral traditions, while the Sadducees were wealthy, politically connected, associated with the temple priesthood, and rejected the resurrection. Their cooperation shows how much they both felt threatened by Jesus. They asked Him for “*a sign from heaven*” (*v. 1*), something dramatic that would prove His authority beyond question, perhaps a sign in the sky.

Jesus answered with an example from everyday life. They could predict the weather by looking at the sky: a red sky in the evening meant fair weather, while a red sky in the morning meant a storm. (Some early manuscripts do not contain verses 2–3, but the saying fits the context.) They could read weather signs, but they could not read “*the signs of the times*” (*v. 3*). Jesus’ miracles, His teaching, and the fulfillment of prophecy were all around them, yet they did not see what God was doing.

He repeated what He had said in *Matthew 12:39*: an evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, but no sign will be given except the sign of Jonah, which points to His death and resurrection. Then He left them.

### The Yeast of the Pharisees and Sadducees (*16:5–12*)

When the disciples crossed the lake, they realized they had forgotten to bring bread. Jesus warned them, “*Take heed and beware of the yeast of the Pharisees and Sadducees*” (*v. 6*). Yeast is a small amount of fermented dough that spreads through an entire batch. In Scripture it often represents a corrupting influence that spreads quietly.

The disciples thought Jesus was talking about their lack of bread. Jesus rebuked their “little faith” and reminded them of the two miraculous feedings. Did they not remember the five loaves for five thousand and the twelve baskets left over, and the seven loaves for four thousand and the seven baskets left over? Jesus could easily provide bread. His concern was something else. Then they understood that He was warning them about the “*teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees*” (*v. 12*). Their false teaching, hypocrisy, and unbelief could spread like yeast among His followers.

### Peter’s Confession (*16:13–20*)

Jesus then took His disciples to the region of Caesarea Philippi, about twenty-five miles north of the Sea of Galilee, near the foot of Mount Hermon. This was largely Gentile territory. The city had been rebuilt by Herod’s son Philip and named in honor of Caesar Augustus. It had a temple dedicated to Caesar and a cave shrine to the Greek god Pan, from which a spring flowed that was one of the sources of the Jordan River. In this setting, surrounded by claims of other gods and earthly power, Jesus asked who people said He was.

The disciples reported various opinions: some said John the Baptist (as Herod believed), others Elijah (whom Malachi said would return), others Jeremiah or one of the prophets. These were high opinions; people saw Jesus as a great prophet. But Jesus pressed further: “*But who do you say that I am?*” (*v. 15*)

Peter answered, “*You are the Christ, the Son of the living God*” (*v. 16*). Jesus blessed Peter, saying that this truth had been revealed to him by the Father, not by human reasoning. Then Jesus made His famous statement about Peter and the church, which is studied in detail below. He gave Peter “*the keys of the Kingdom of Heaven*” (*v. 19*) and the authority to “bind” and “loose.” Finally, He told the disciples not to tell anyone yet that He was the Messiah, since popular expectations of a political, military Messiah could lead to misunderstanding.

### Jesus Predicts His Death (*16:21–23*)

“*From that time, Jesus began to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things from the elders, chief priests, and scribes, and be killed, and the third day be raised up*” (*v. 21*). The phrase “from that time” marks a major turning point, echoing *Matthew 4:17*, where Jesus began His public ministry. Now begins a new emphasis: the road to the cross. The word “must” shows that His suffering was part of God’s plan, not an accident.

Peter, who had just confessed Jesus as the Messiah, took Him aside and rebuked Him: “*Far be it from you, Lord! This will never be done to you*” (*v. 22*). In Peter’s mind, the Messiah was supposed to triumph, not suffer and die. Jesus turned and said, “*Get behind me, Satan! You are a stumbling block to me, for you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of men*” (*v. 23*).

These are some of Jesus’ harshest words to a disciple, and they echo what He said to Satan in the wilderness (*Matthew 4:10*). Satan had offered Jesus the kingdoms of the world without the cross. Now Peter, without realizing it, was offering the same temptation. The irony is striking: a few verses earlier, Jesus called Peter a “rock” on which He would build His church; now Peter is a “stumbling block,” literally a rock to trip over.

### The Cost of Discipleship (*16:24–28*)

Jesus then told His disciples that if anyone wanted to follow Him, they must deny themselves, take up their cross, and follow Him. Whoever tries to save their life will lose it, but whoever loses their life for Jesus’ sake will find it. He asked what good it would be to gain the whole world and lose one’s soul.

He added that the Son of Man will come in His Father’s glory with His angels and will repay each person according to what they have done. Then He said that some standing there would not die before they saw “*the Son of Man coming in his Kingdom*” (*v. 28*). This saying has been understood in several ways. Many connect it with the transfiguration, which immediately follows in *Matthew 17*, where three disciples see Jesus’ glory. Others connect it with His resurrection and ascension, the coming of the Spirit at Pentecost, or the judgment on Jerusalem in A.D. 70, all of which showed His kingdom’s power within the disciples’ lifetimes. The main point is that the kingdom of the suffering Messiah would soon be revealed in power.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Matthew 16:16* — “*You Are the Christ, the Son of the Living God*” (*v. 16*)

> *“Simon Peter answered, ‘You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.’”*
>
> — *Matthew 16:16* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These words are Peter’s answer to Jesus’ question at Caesarea Philippi. Jesus had taken His disciples to this region far north of Galilee, a place filled with temples to Caesar and to pagan gods. There He asked them who people said He was. The disciples reported that people thought He was John the Baptist, Elijah, Jeremiah, or another prophet. Then Jesus asked them directly: “*But who do you say that I am?*” (*v. 15*) Peter, often the spokesman for the group, answered.

His answer has two parts. First, “You are the Christ.” “Christ” is the Greek form of “Messiah,” meaning “anointed one.” In Israel, kings and priests were anointed with oil when they took office. The Jews hoped for a Messiah, an anointed king from David’s line, whom God would send to save His people and establish His kingdom. Peter recognized that Jesus was this long-awaited king.

Second, “the Son of the living God.” In the Old Testament, the king of Israel could be called God’s son (*2 Samuel 7:14*; *Psalm 2:7*), so the phrase could be a royal title. But in Matthew’s Gospel, it carries a deeper meaning. The Father declared Jesus His beloved Son at His baptism (*Matthew 3:17*), and the disciples worshiped Him as the Son of God after He walked on water (*Matthew 14:33*). Peter’s confession points to Jesus’ unique relationship with God. “The living God” contrasts with the lifeless idols worshiped in that region.

Jesus responded that Peter was blessed, because this insight had not come from human reasoning but from the Father Himself.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Peter’s confession is at the heart of the Christian faith. To believe in Jesus is to believe that He is the Messiah promised in Scripture and the Son of God. John wrote his Gospel so that readers “*may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing, you may have life in his name*” (*John 20:31*).

Jesus’ response shows that true understanding of His identity comes by God’s revelation. People can study Jesus, admire Him, and form many opinions about Him, but recognizing Him as Lord and Savior is a gift from God. Paul writes that “*no one can say, “Jesus is Lord,” but by the Holy Spirit*” (*1 Corinthians 12:3*).

The setting is also significant. In a place where Caesar was worshiped as a god and pagan shrines filled the landscape, Peter declared that Jesus, a poor teacher from Galilee, was the Son of the living God. Faith in Christ has always meant choosing Him above every competing claim to ultimate authority.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Jesus’ question, “Who do you say that I am?”, is still the most important question anyone can answer. It is not enough to know what others say about Jesus, whether scholars, friends, or culture. Each person must answer for themselves. Believers can reaffirm their own confession of faith and consider how it shapes their lives.

This confession also has practical implications. If Jesus is the Messiah, the King, then He has authority over every part of life. If He is the Son of the living God, then His words carry divine weight. Believers can ask whether their decisions, priorities, and relationships reflect the truth that Jesus is Lord.

Finally, Peter’s confession was made in a setting full of competing loyalties. Believers today also live surrounded by competing claims: success, wealth, political power, pleasure, and other ideologies. Confessing Jesus as Lord means giving Him the place that no other loyalty can take.

### *Matthew 16:18* — “*On This Rock I Will Build My Assembly*” (*v. 18*)

> *“I also tell you that you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my assembly, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it.”*
>
> — *Matthew 16:18* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus speaks these words immediately after Peter’s confession that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God. Jesus has just told Peter that he is blessed because the Father revealed this truth to him. Now Jesus says something about Peter and about His plans for the future.

“*you are Peter*” (*v. 18*). Simon had been given the name Peter, meaning “rock” (Greek “Petros”; Aramaic “Cephas”). Jesus now explains the significance of that name: “*on this rock I will build my assembly*” (*v. 18*). “Assembly” translates the Greek word “ekklesia,” usually translated “church.” It refers to a gathered community of God’s people. In the Greek Old Testament, this word was used for the assembly of Israel. Jesus is saying that He will build a new community of His followers.

Christians have interpreted “this rock” in different ways. Roman Catholics understand it to refer to Peter himself, as the leader of the apostles, and see this as the foundation for the authority of Peter’s successors. Many Protestants understand the rock to be Peter’s confession of faith, the truth that Jesus is the Christ, or Jesus Himself, who is elsewhere called the foundation and cornerstone (*1 Corinthians 3:11*; *Ephesians 2:20*). Others hold that the rock is Peter as the first confessor and leading apostle, whose foundational role in the early church is seen in Acts, without implying a line of successors. The wordplay suggests that Peter is closely connected to the rock, and in Acts he does take a leading role in founding the church, preaching at Pentecost and opening the door to Gentiles.

Jesus adds a promise: “*the gates of Hades will not prevail against it*” (*v. 18*). Hades was the realm of the dead. “Gates” represent its power. Death and all the forces of evil will not be able to overcome the church Jesus builds.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals that Jesus’ mission includes forming a community. Following Jesus is not merely an individual commitment; it means belonging to His people, the church. Jesus speaks of “my” assembly, showing that the church belongs to Him, and He is the one who builds it.

The promise that the gates of Hades will not prevail gives the church great confidence. Throughout history, the church has faced persecution, internal failures, false teaching, and opposition. Yet it has endured, not because of human strength, but because Christ keeps His promise. This promise is ultimately grounded in His own victory over death through His resurrection.

The verse also shows that the church is founded on the truth about who Jesus is. Whatever one’s view of Peter’s role, the church exists because people confess that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God. When this confession is lost, the foundation is lost.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to value the church as Christ’s own community. Churches are imperfect, made up of flawed people, but Jesus builds them and loves them. Believers can commit themselves to a local church, participating in its worship, fellowship, and mission, rather than trying to follow Jesus in isolation.

It also offers encouragement when the church seems weak or under attack. Christ has promised that His church will endure. Believers can serve faithfully and hopefully, even in difficult times, knowing that the church’s future rests in Christ’s hands.

Finally, this verse calls believers to build their faith on the truth about Jesus. In a culture with many opinions about Him, the church stands on the confession that He is the Christ, the Son of the living God. Believers can make this confession central to their lives and to their communities.

### *Matthew 16:24* — Deny Yourself, Take Up Your Cross, and Follow

> *“Then Jesus said to his disciples, If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.”*
>
> — *Matthew 16:24* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse comes right after Jesus rebukes Peter. Jesus had begun to explain that He must go to Jerusalem, suffer, be killed, and rise on the third day. Peter objected strongly, saying this would never happen to Him. Jesus responded, “Get behind me, Satan!” because Peter was thinking in human terms, not God’s. Now Jesus explains to all His disciples what following Him requires.

“*If anyone desires to come after me*” (*v. 24*) is an invitation, not a command forced on anyone. Jesus is speaking to those who want to be His disciples. He gives three requirements.

First, “*let him deny himself*” (*v. 24*). Denying oneself does not mean hating oneself or merely giving up certain pleasures. It means refusing to make oneself the center of life, saying “no” to self-will in order to say “yes” to God’s will.

Second, “*take up his cross*” (*v. 24*). Everyone in Jesus’ time knew what this meant. The Romans crucified criminals and rebels, forcing them to carry their own crossbeam to the place of execution. A person carrying a cross was on the way to death. Jesus is saying that following Him requires a willingness to die, whether literally or by putting to death one’s own self-centered ambitions. Peter wanted a Messiah without a cross. Jesus says that both the Messiah and His followers will carry one.

Third, “*follow me*” (*v. 24*). Discipleship means continuing to walk after Jesus, going where He goes, and living as He lives. Since He is going to the cross, following Him means walking that same path of self-giving obedience.

In the following verses, Jesus explains why this is worthwhile: those who lose their lives for Him will find them, and gaining the whole world is worthless if one loses one’s soul.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that the cross is central not only to Jesus’ mission but to the life of His followers. Jesus did not die so that His followers could live comfortable, self-centered lives. He died to save them and to transform them into people who live for God. Paul writes, “*I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me*” (*Galatians 2:20*).

This teaching also clarifies what kind of Messiah Jesus is. Peter expected a triumphant king. Jesus revealed a suffering servant who would win victory through sacrifice. His followers share in both His suffering and His victory. The path of the cross leads to resurrection.

At the same time, taking up the cross does not mean seeking suffering for its own sake or accepting abuse as if it were God’s will. The cross Jesus speaks of is suffering that comes because of loyalty to Him and faithfulness to God’s will. It is a willing surrender of oneself to God, not passive acceptance of injustice.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse calls believers to identify areas where they are living for themselves rather than for Christ. Denying oneself might mean putting others’ needs ahead of personal convenience, choosing obedience over comfort, letting go of resentment, or giving up habits that dishonor God. These daily decisions are part of what it means to take up the cross.

It also prepares believers for the cost of faithfulness. Following Jesus may lead to misunderstanding, rejection, or loss. In some parts of the world, it leads to persecution and death. Jesus does not hide these costs. Believers can face them with courage, knowing that they are following the One who walked the same path.

Finally, this verse invites believers to trust Jesus’ promise. Losing one’s life for Him is not a tragic loss but the path to true life. What seems like sacrifice in the moment leads to lasting joy. Believers can follow Jesus wholeheartedly, confident that nothing given up for Him is wasted.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Matthew 16* asks the most important question in the Gospels: “Who do you say that I am?” Every person must answer it. Peter’s confession, that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God, is the foundation of Christian faith and of the church. Believers can return regularly to this confession, letting it shape their priorities and loyalties in a world full of competing claims.

The chapter also warns against spiritual blindness and false influence. The Pharisees and Sadducees could read the sky but not the signs of God’s work. Their teaching spread like yeast. Believers need discernment to recognize teaching that distorts the truth about God and to resist influences that subtly lead them away from Christ. Remembering what Jesus has done, as the disciples were told to remember the feedings, strengthens faith against such influences.

Peter’s story in this chapter shows how quickly a person can move from insight to error. He confessed Jesus truly and then tried to steer Jesus away from the cross. Believers can confess correct truths about Jesus while still resisting His way of suffering and self-giving. They need humility to accept God’s ways when those ways are different from their own expectations.

Finally, the chapter calls for costly discipleship. Following Jesus means denying oneself, taking up the cross, and following Him. This shapes how believers handle ambition, comfort, possessions, and relationships. It invites them to ask what good it would be to gain the whole world and lose their soul. Jesus promises that those who lose their lives for His sake will find true life. The cross is not the end of the story; it leads to resurrection and to the coming of His kingdom in glory.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, I confess with Peter that You are the Christ, the Son of the living God. Thank You for revealing this truth to me, and help me to live in a way that shows You are Lord over every part of my life. Guard me from the yeast of false teaching and from the blindness that misses what You are doing.

Thank You for building Your church and for promising that the gates of death will not overcome it. Help me to love and serve Your people faithfully. When I resist Your ways because I am thinking as people think rather than as God thinks, correct me and draw me back. Give me grace to deny myself, take up my cross, and follow You. When following You costs me something, remind me that whoever loses their life for You will find it. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Matthew · Chapter 17 of 28

# Matthew — Chapter 17

Chapter Theme: Glory on the Mountain, Struggle in the Valley

[Read Matthew 17 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/MAT17.htm)

Main Teaching

On a high mountain, three disciples see Jesus transfigured in glory, meet Moses and Elijah, and hear the Father command them to listen to His Son. Coming down, they face a suffering boy whom the other disciples could not help, and Jesus teaches that even small, genuine faith in God can accomplish what seems impossible. Jesus again predicts His death and resurrection and, in the matter of the temple tax, shows both His unique Sonship and His willingness to avoid needless offense.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Matthew 17* follows directly from chapter 16, where Peter confessed Jesus as the Christ, the Son of the living God, and Jesus revealed that He must suffer, die, and rise. He then told His disciples that following Him meant taking up the cross, and He promised that some of them would see the Son of Man coming in His kingdom (*Matthew 16:28*). Six days later, three of them saw a glimpse of that glory. The transfiguration confirmed Peter’s confession and reassured the disciples that the path of suffering Jesus described would lead to glory.

### The Transfiguration (*17:1–8*)

Jesus took Peter, James, and John up “*a high mountain by themselves*” (*v. 1*). Matthew does not name the mountain. Tradition has identified it as Mount Tabor in lower Galilee, but many scholars think Mount Hermon, near Caesarea Philippi, is more likely, since that is where the previous events took place. These three disciples formed an inner circle; they would later be the ones Jesus took with Him into Gethsemane (*Matthew 26:37*).

There Jesus “*was changed before them*” (*v. 2*). The Greek word is “metamorphoo,” from which we get “metamorphosis.” His face shone like the sun, and His clothes became as white as light. This was not a reflected glow, as when Moses’ face shone after speaking with God (*Exodus 34:29–35*), but a revelation of Jesus’ own glory, usually hidden during His earthly life.

Moses and Elijah appeared, talking with Him. Moses represented the Law, through which God gave Israel His covenant; Elijah represented the Prophets, and he was expected to return before the day of the Lord. Both had met God on a mountain (Sinai, also called Horeb), and both had unusual departures from this life: Moses was buried by God Himself (*Deuteronomy 34:5–6*), and Elijah was taken up in a whirlwind (*2 Kings 2:11*). Luke tells us they spoke with Jesus about His “departure” (literally “exodus”) that He was about to accomplish in Jerusalem (*Luke 9:31*). Their presence showed that the whole Old Testament pointed to Jesus and His coming death.

Peter, overwhelmed, offered to build three shelters, one each for Jesus, Moses, and Elijah. These may have been like the booths built during the Feast of Tabernacles, which celebrated God’s presence with Israel in the wilderness. Peter may have wanted to prolong the moment, or he may have thought the kingdom had fully arrived. But his suggestion placed Jesus on the same level as Moses and Elijah.

While Peter was still speaking, a bright cloud overshadowed them, and a voice spoke from it: “*This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him*” (*v. 5*). The cloud recalls the cloud of God’s presence that led Israel in the wilderness and filled the tabernacle and temple (*Exodus 40:34–35*; *1 Kings 8:10–11*). The words repeat what the Father said at Jesus’ baptism, with an added command.

The disciples fell on their faces in fear. Jesus came, touched them, and said, “*Get up, and don’t be afraid*” (*v. 7*). When they looked up, they saw only Jesus. Moses and Elijah had gone. The scene ended with Jesus alone, as the one to whom they must now listen.

### The Question About Elijah (*17:9–13*)

As they came down the mountain, Jesus told them not to tell anyone about the vision until after His resurrection. Before that, people would misunderstand it. The disciples asked about the teaching of the scribes that Elijah must come first, based on *Malachi 4:5–6*. If Jesus was the Messiah, where was Elijah?

Jesus agreed that Elijah comes first to restore all things, but He said Elijah had already come, and people did not recognize him; they did to him whatever they wanted. In the same way, the Son of Man would suffer at their hands. The disciples understood that He was speaking about John the Baptist, who had been executed by Herod (*Matthew 14*). John’s fate foreshadowed Jesus’ own.

### The Boy the Disciples Could Not Heal (*17:14–21*)

When they reached the crowd, a man knelt before Jesus and begged Him to have mercy on his son. The boy was “*epileptic*” (*v. 15*) (literally “moonstruck,” a term people then used for seizures, which they associated with the moon) and suffered terribly, often falling into fire or water. Matthew tells us that a demon was the cause in this case (v. 18). This should not be taken to mean that epilepsy in general is caused by demons. The Gospels distinguish between ordinary illnesses and demonic oppression (*Matthew 4:24* lists them separately), and in this particular case the boy’s seizures were connected with a demon.

The father had brought the boy to the disciples, but they could not heal him. Jesus responded with frustration: “*Faithless and perverse generation! How long will I be with you? How long will I bear with you?*” (*v. 17*) His words were addressed to the generation as a whole, including the disciples, the crowd, and the scribes who were arguing (*Mark 9:14*). He then told them to bring the boy to Him, rebuked the demon, and the boy was healed at that moment.

Privately, the disciples asked why they had failed. Jesus told them it was because of their unbelief (literally, “little faith”). He then gave a vivid promise about faith as small as a mustard seed, which is studied below. Verse 21, “*But this kind doesn’t go out except by prayer and fasting*” (*v. 21*), is not found in many of the oldest manuscripts of Matthew and may have been added from *Mark 9:29*, where Jesus says this kind can come out only by prayer. Either way, the point is that the disciples had been relying on themselves rather than depending on God.

### Second Prediction of the Passion (*17:22–23*)

While they were gathering in Galilee, Jesus again told His disciples that He would be betrayed into human hands, killed, and raised on the third day. This was the second of three major predictions (see *Matthew 16:21* and *20:17–19*). This time the disciples did not argue; they were “*exceedingly sorry*” (*v. 23*). They seemed to hear the part about His death more clearly than the promise of His resurrection.

### The Temple Tax (*17:24–27*)

When they returned to Capernaum, the collectors of the “*didrachma*” (*v. 24*) (the two-drachma temple tax) asked Peter whether his teacher paid it. Every Jewish man over twenty was expected to pay this annual tax of half a shekel for the upkeep of the temple, based on *Exodus 30:13–16*. Peter immediately said yes.

When Peter came into the house, Jesus spoke first, asking him whether kings collect taxes from their own children or from others. Peter answered, “From others.” Jesus said, “*Therefore the children are exempt*” (*v. 26*). The point was that Jesus, as the Son of God, was not obligated to pay a tax for His Father’s house. By extension, His followers, as God’s children, shared in that freedom.

Nevertheless, Jesus did not want to cause offense. He told Peter to go to the lake, cast a line, and take the first fish he caught. In its mouth he would find a “stater,” a coin worth four drachmas, exactly enough to pay the tax for both Jesus and Peter. Matthew does not record Peter actually catching the fish, but the instruction shows Jesus’ authority and provision. It also shows His willingness to set aside His rights for the sake of others.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Matthew 17:5* — “*Listen to Him*” (*v. 5*)

> *“While he was still speaking, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them. Behold, a voice came out of the cloud, saying, ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him.’”*
>
> — *Matthew 17:5* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse describes the high point of the transfiguration. Jesus had taken Peter, James, and John up a high mountain, where He was transformed before them, His face shining like the sun and His clothes white as light. Moses and Elijah appeared and spoke with Him. Peter, not knowing what to say, offered to build three shelters, one for each of them.

“*While he was still speaking*” (*v. 5*), God interrupted Peter. A bright cloud overshadowed them. In the Old Testament, God’s presence was often revealed in a cloud: it led Israel through the wilderness, rested on Mount Sinai when God gave the law, and filled the tabernacle and temple. The disciples would have understood that God Himself was present.

A voice spoke from the cloud: “*This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased*” (*v. 5*). These are the same words the Father spoke at Jesus’ baptism (*Matthew 3:17*), echoing *Psalm 2:7* (the royal Son) and *Isaiah 42:1* (the chosen Servant). The Father again affirmed Jesus’ identity.

Then He added a new command: “*Listen to him*” (*v. 5*). This phrase recalls *Deuteronomy 18:15*, where Moses promised that God would raise up a prophet like him, and said, “*You shall listen to him*” (*Deuteronomy 18:15*). Jesus is that prophet, and more. The command also corrected Peter’s suggestion. Peter wanted to honor Jesus alongside Moses and Elijah; the Father declared that Jesus alone is His Son and the one to whom they must listen. The command was especially fitting after Peter had resisted Jesus’ teaching about the cross in chapter 16. The disciples needed to listen to Jesus even when His words were hard to accept.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse affirms the supremacy of Jesus over even the greatest figures of the Old Testament. Moses and Elijah were honored servants of God, but Jesus is God’s Son. The Law and the Prophets pointed to Him, and now He is the final and complete revelation of God. *Hebrews 1:1–2* says that God spoke in the past through the prophets, but in these last days “*has at the end of these days spoken to us by his Son*” (*Hebrews 1:2*).

The transfiguration also strengthened the disciples for what lay ahead. They had just heard that Jesus must suffer and die. The glimpse of His glory showed them that the cross would not be the end. Peter later wrote about this experience, saying that they were eyewitnesses of His majesty when they heard the voice from heaven on the holy mountain (*2 Peter 1:16–18*).

The command “Listen to him” also reminds believers that hearing God’s voice now means attending to Jesus. His words, recorded in the Gospels and explained by His apostles, are the way God speaks to His people.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse calls believers to listen to Jesus above all other voices. Many voices compete for attention: culture, media, friends, personal desires, and even religious traditions. The Father’s command is clear: listen to His Son. Believers can make it a priority to read and reflect on Jesus’ words regularly, letting them shape their thoughts and decisions.

Listening to Jesus also means obeying Him. In the Bible, to “listen” or “hear” often includes the idea of obeying. Believers can ask not only “What did Jesus say?” but “How should I respond?” This is especially important when His words are difficult or challenge their preferences, as Peter discovered.

Finally, this verse offers encouragement in difficult seasons. The disciples were about to face the shock of Jesus’ arrest and crucifixion. The memory of His glory would help sustain them. Believers can remember that the Jesus they follow is the glorious Son of God, and that suffering in this life will give way to glory.

### *Matthew 17:20* — Faith Like a Mustard Seed

> *“He said to them, Because of your unbelief. For most certainly I tell you, if you have faith as a grain of mustard seed, you will tell this mountain, “Move from here to there,” and it will move; and nothing will be impossible for you.”*
>
> — *Matthew 17:20* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse is Jesus’ answer to His disciples’ question about why they could not heal the boy. While Jesus was on the mountain with Peter, James, and John, the other disciples had tried to drive out the demon that was tormenting the boy, but they failed. Earlier, Jesus had given the Twelve authority to cast out demons (*Matthew 10:1*, 8), and they had done so before. Now they were puzzled.

Jesus answered, “*Because of your unbelief*” (*v. 20*). Many manuscripts read “little faith,” the word Jesus often used for His disciples’ wavering trust (*Matthew 6:30*; *8:26*; *14:31*; *16:8*). The problem was not that they lacked a technique but that they were not truly relying on God. Perhaps they had begun to think the power was theirs.

Then Jesus said, “*if you have faith as a grain of mustard seed, you will tell this mountain, ‘Move from here to there,’ and it will move*” (*v. 20*). The mustard seed was proverbially tiny, as Jesus had said in the parable of *Matthew 13:31–32*. His point is that the size of faith matters less than its object. Even very small faith, if it is genuine trust in God, can accomplish great things, because God is the one who acts.

“Move this mountain” was a common Jewish expression for doing something that seemed impossible. Jesus was probably pointing to the mountain they had just come down from. He was not encouraging people to rearrange landscapes but using a vivid image for overcoming impossible obstacles. He concluded, “*nothing will be impossible for you*” (*v. 20*), meaning nothing that is within God’s will for His servants to accomplish.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse teaches that the power of faith lies not in the believer but in God. Faith is not a force we generate or a technique for getting what we want. It is trust in God, and God is the one who does the impossible. That is why even small faith, if it is real, can achieve great things. Jesus elsewhere says, “*With men this is impossible, but with God all things are possible*” (*Matthew 19:26*).

The context also shows that faith grows through dependence on God, expressed in prayer. Mark’s version of this account records Jesus saying that this kind can only come out by prayer (*Mark 9:29*). The disciples may have treated their earlier success as their own ability. Faith that depends on God will naturally pray.

At the same time, this verse must be read alongside the rest of Scripture. It does not mean that believers will receive whatever they want if they have enough faith, or that unanswered prayers are always due to a lack of faith. Paul prayed three times for his “thorn in the flesh” to be removed, and God’s answer was, “*My grace is sufficient for you*” (*2 Corinthians 12:9*). Faith trusts God’s power and God’s wisdom together.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers who feel that their faith is small. Jesus does not require great faith before God can act. He invites people to trust God with whatever faith they have. Believers facing overwhelming situations can bring them to God, trusting that He is able to do what they cannot.

It also calls believers to depend on God rather than on their own abilities, experience, or past success. Even long-time believers can drift into self-reliance in their spiritual lives and ministries. Regular prayer, honest acknowledgment of weakness, and seeking God’s help keep faith directed toward Him.

Finally, believers can hold this promise together with trust in God’s wisdom. When prayers are not answered in the way they hoped, they need not conclude that their faith was too small. They can continue to trust God, who sometimes moves mountains and sometimes gives grace to endure them.

### *Matthew 17:27* — Free, Yet Willing to Avoid Offense

> *“But, lest we cause them to stumble, go to the sea, cast a hook, and take up the first fish that comes up. When you have opened its mouth, you will find a stater coin. Take that, and give it to them for me and you.”*
>
> — *Matthew 17:27* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse concludes a short episode in Capernaum about the temple tax. Each Jewish man was expected to pay half a shekel each year for the support of the temple in Jerusalem, a practice based on *Exodus 30:13–16*. When the tax collectors asked Peter whether Jesus paid it, Peter quickly said yes.

When Peter came into the house, Jesus raised the issue first. He asked whether kings collect taxes from their own children or from others. Peter answered that kings tax others, not their own families. Jesus concluded, “*Therefore the children are exempt*” (*v. 26*). Since the temple was His Father’s house, Jesus, as God’s Son, should not have to pay a tax for its upkeep. He was making a claim about His unique relationship with God.

But then Jesus said, “*But, lest we cause them to stumble*” (*v. 27*). To “cause to stumble” means to give offense or become an obstacle to someone’s faith. If Jesus refused to pay, the tax collectors and others might think He did not respect the temple or God’s law. That could become an unnecessary barrier to their receiving His message. So Jesus chose to pay, even though He was not obligated.

He told Peter to go to the lake, cast a hook, and take the first fish that came up. In its mouth he would find a “stater,” a silver coin worth four drachmas, exactly enough to pay the two-drachma tax for both Jesus and Peter. Jesus included Peter in the payment, showing His care for His disciple and including him among God’s children.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This short story reveals two truths about Jesus. First, He is the Son of God, with a unique relationship to the Father and authority over the temple. Earlier He had said that “*one greater than the temple is here*” (*Matthew 12:6*). Second, He was willing to set aside His rights for the sake of others. This anticipates His greatest act of self-giving on the cross. Paul describes Jesus as one who, though He was in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be used for His own advantage, but emptied Himself (*Philippians 2:6–7*).

The verse also teaches a principle that the apostle Paul developed later. Believers have freedom in Christ, but they should be willing to limit their freedom for the sake of others, so as not to cause unnecessary offense or hinder someone’s faith (*1 Corinthians 8:9–13*; *9:19–23*). Christian freedom is not about insisting on rights but about loving others.

Finally, the miraculous provision shows that Jesus can meet His followers’ needs, often in unexpected ways. The Lord who commands the sea and its creatures provided what was needed.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to consider how they use their freedom. There may be many things believers are free to do, but they can ask whether exercising that freedom would cause unnecessary offense or become a stumbling block for others. Sometimes love means setting aside personal rights to serve others or to avoid harming someone’s faith.

It also encourages believers to fulfill civic and community responsibilities in a way that honors Christ. Paying taxes, keeping commitments, and respecting legitimate authority can be part of a good witness. Jesus’ example shows that believers should not create needless conflict over matters that do not compromise their faith.

Finally, this verse reminds believers that God provides for His people. When they choose to act in love and integrity, even at personal cost, they can trust that God will supply what they need.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Matthew 17* moves from the mountaintop to the valley, and both settings speak to the life of faith. On the mountain, the disciples saw Jesus’ glory and heard the Father’s command to listen to Him. Believers today may experience times of special closeness to God, but even ordinary days are lived in the presence of the glorious Son of God. The Father’s command, “Listen to him,” remains the guiding principle for every season. Making time to hear Jesus’ words in Scripture, and responding with obedience, keeps believers centered on Him.

The valley shows the reality of struggle. The disciples could not help the suffering boy because their faith had drifted from dependence on God. Believers often experience similar failures when they rely on their own abilities, routines, or past successes. Jesus’ answer is not to try harder but to trust God, even with small faith, and to depend on Him in prayer. This applies to ministry, family responsibilities, and personal struggles.

The chapter also continues to prepare the disciples for the cross. Jesus repeated that He would be betrayed, killed, and raised. The transfiguration showed them that suffering would lead to glory. Believers facing hardship can remember that the path of following Jesus may include suffering, but it leads to resurrection and glory.

Finally, the temple tax story teaches a balance between freedom and love. Jesus was free from the obligation but chose to pay to avoid needless offense. Believers can follow His example by setting aside their rights for the sake of others, fulfilling responsibilities with integrity, and trusting God to provide what they need.

## Chapter Prayer

Father, thank You for revealing the glory of Your beloved Son on the mountain and for commanding us to listen to Him. Help me to hear His voice above all the other voices in my life and to obey what He says, even when His words are hard to accept.

When I face situations that seem impossible, remind me that even small faith in You can move mountains, because nothing is too hard for You. Forgive me for relying on my own strength, and teach me to depend on You in prayer. Strengthen my hope when I walk through suffering, knowing that the cross leads to glory. Help me to use my freedom with love, setting aside my rights when doing so will help others, and to trust You to provide all I need. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Matthew · Chapter 18 of 28

# Matthew — Chapter 18

Chapter Theme: Humility, Care for the Vulnerable, and Forgiveness in God’s Family

[Read Matthew 18 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/MAT18.htm)

Main Teaching

When the disciples ask who is greatest, Jesus answers by setting a child among them and teaching that greatness comes through humility. He warns severely against causing vulnerable believers to stumble, describes the Father’s search for every lost sheep, gives a careful process for addressing sin within the community, and teaches through a parable that those who have been forgiven an unpayable debt must forgive others from the heart.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Matthew 18* is the fourth of Jesus’ five major teaching sections in Matthew. It is often called the Community Discourse, because it deals with how Jesus’ followers should live together. After His transfiguration and His second prediction of His death (*Matthew 17*), Jesus turns to the relationships among His disciples. The previous chapter ended with Jesus paying the temple tax to avoid causing offense. This chapter develops that concern: how should members of God’s family treat one another, especially the weak, the wandering, and those who sin against them?

### Who Is the Greatest? (*18:1–5*)

The disciples came to Jesus and asked, “*Who then is greatest in the Kingdom of Heaven?*” (*v. 1*) Mark and Luke tell us that this question arose from an argument among them about which of them was the greatest (*Mark 9:33–34*; *Luke 9:46*). Despite Jesus’ teaching about taking up the cross, they were still thinking about rank and status.

Jesus called a little child and placed the child in the middle of them. In the ancient world, children had little status. They were loved by their families, but they had no legal rights, no power, and no social standing. Jesus said that unless they turned and became like children, they would never enter the kingdom. Whoever humbles himself like this child is the greatest in the kingdom. Then He added that whoever welcomes such a child in His name welcomes Him. The disciples were asking about greatness; Jesus answered by pointing to the lowliest.

### Warnings About Causing Others to Stumble (*18:6–9*)

Jesus then gave a severe warning: whoever causes “*one of these little ones who believe in me*” (*v. 6*) to stumble would be better off having a large millstone hung around his neck and being drowned in the sea. “Little ones” here includes children and also humble, vulnerable believers. A “huge millstone” was the large stone turned by a donkey to grind grain; it weighed hundreds of pounds. Drowning was considered a dreadful death, especially without burial. Jesus’ point is that leading a vulnerable believer into sin or away from faith is extremely serious in God’s eyes.

He acknowledged that in a fallen world, causes of stumbling will come, but He pronounced woe on the person through whom they come. Then He repeated, in slightly different form, the vivid language from *Matthew 5:29–30*: if your hand, foot, or eye causes you to sin, cut it off or tear it out. As before, this is not a command for literal self-injury but a dramatic way of saying that whatever leads us into sin must be dealt with decisively, because sin’s consequences are eternal.

### The Lost Sheep (*18:10–14*)

Jesus warned His disciples not to despise these little ones, adding that “*in heaven their angels always see the face of my Father*” (*v. 10*). This suggests that God’s attention is constantly directed toward the most vulnerable members of His family. (Verse 11, about the Son of Man coming to save the lost, is not in many early manuscripts and may have been added from *Luke 19:10*.)

He then told a parable. If a man has a hundred sheep and one wanders away, does he not leave the ninety-nine on the hillside to search for the one that strayed? When he finds it, he rejoices more over that one than over the ninety-nine that never wandered. In the same way, “*it is not the will of your Father who is in heaven that one of these little ones should perish*” (*v. 14*). In *Luke 15*, Jesus tells a similar parable about sinners who repent. Here in Matthew, the emphasis is on the community’s responsibility to care for believers who wander away.

### Addressing Sin in the Community (*18:15–20*)

Jesus then gave instructions for what to do when a fellow believer sins. These instructions are studied in detail below. The process moves from a private conversation, to a small group of witnesses, to the whole church, with the goal of restoring the brother or sister.

Jesus gave the community authority to “bind” and “loose,” the same authority given to Peter in *Matthew 16:19*. In Jewish teaching, these terms referred to forbidding and permitting, and to making decisions about discipline. The community’s decisions, made faithfully, reflect heaven’s will. Jesus added that if two of them agree on earth about anything they ask, it will be done by the Father, and “*where two or three are gathered together in my name, there I am in the middle of them*” (*v. 20*). In this context, the promise especially concerns the community gathered to seek God’s will in matters of discipline and reconciliation. Jesus promises to be present, guiding and confirming their decisions. The promise also assures believers more broadly of His presence whenever they gather in His name.

### How Often Should I Forgive? (*18:21–35*)

Peter then asked how many times he should forgive a brother who sins against him. Was seven times enough? Some rabbis taught that a person should forgive the same offense three times, so Peter thought he was being generous. Jesus answered, “*I don’t tell you until seven times, but, until seventy times seven*” (*v. 22*). The Greek can mean seventy-seven times or seventy times seven, but the point is the same: forgiveness should not be counted. This may echo *Genesis 4:24*, where Lamech boasted that he would take vengeance seventy-seven times. Jesus reverses unlimited revenge into unlimited forgiveness.

He then told a parable. A king wanted to settle accounts with his servants. One servant owed ten thousand talents. A talent was the largest unit of money in that world, equal to about twenty years’ wages for a laborer. Ten thousand talents was an unimaginable sum, more than the annual tax revenue of entire provinces. The servant could never repay it. The king ordered that he, his wife, his children, and everything he owned be sold to recover part of the debt, a practice known in the ancient world. The servant fell on his knees and begged for patience, promising to repay everything, an impossible promise. The king, moved with compassion, cancelled the entire debt.

That same servant then went out and found a fellow servant who owed him a hundred denarii, about a hundred days’ wages. This was a real debt but tiny compared to what he had been forgiven. He grabbed his fellow servant by the throat and demanded payment. The fellow servant fell down and begged for patience, using almost the same words the first servant had used. But the first servant refused and had him thrown into prison until he could pay.

The other servants were deeply distressed and reported what happened to the king. The king called the first servant in and said, “*You wicked servant! I forgave you all that debt because you begged me*” (*v. 32*), and asked whether he should not have shown mercy to his fellow servant as the king had shown mercy to him. In anger, the king handed him over to the jailers until he paid everything he owed. Jesus concluded: “*So my heavenly Father will also do to you, if you don’t each forgive your brother from your hearts for his misdeeds*” (*v. 35*).

## Important Verses Explained

### *Matthew 18:3–4* — Becoming Like a Child

> *“and said, Most certainly I tell you, unless you turn and become as little children, you will in no way enter into the Kingdom of Heaven. Whoever therefore humbles himself as this little child is the greatest in the Kingdom of Heaven.”*
>
> — *Matthew 18:3–4* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus speaks these words in response to the disciples’ question, “*Who then is greatest in the Kingdom of Heaven?*” (*v. 1*) The disciples had been arguing about rank. They had just seen Peter, James, and John go up the mountain with Jesus, and perhaps that sparked rivalry. Despite everything Jesus had taught about humility and the cross, they were still thinking in terms of status and position.

Jesus answered by calling a little child and placing the child in the middle of them. Then He said, “*unless you turn and become as little children, you will in no way enter into the Kingdom of Heaven*” (*v. 3*). The word “turn” means to change direction, a word closely related to repentance. Jesus was saying that the disciples needed to turn away from their focus on greatness. More than that, the question was not who would be greatest in the kingdom but whether they would enter it at all.

What does it mean to become like a child? Jesus explains in verse 4: “*Whoever therefore humbles himself as this little child is the greatest in the Kingdom of Heaven*” (*v. 4*). The key quality is humility. In that culture, children were not admired for innocence or purity as they often are today. They were valued by their families, but socially they were among the least important members of society. They were dependent, without power, and unable to claim status. To become like a child means accepting a lowly position, depending on God rather than oneself, and giving up the quest for importance.

Jesus turned the disciples’ question upside down. They wanted to know who would be at the top; He told them that greatness belongs to those willing to be at the bottom.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses reveal that entrance into God’s kingdom requires humility. No one can earn a place in the kingdom by achievement or status. People enter it as dependent children, receiving it as a gift. This connects with the first Beatitude: “*Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the Kingdom of Heaven*” (*Matthew 5:3*).

The teaching also redefines greatness. The world measures greatness by power, influence, wealth, and recognition. Jesus measures it by humility and service. He Himself is the supreme example. Later He says that the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve and to give His life (*Matthew 20:28*). Paul writes that Jesus humbled Himself and became obedient to death on a cross, and therefore God highly exalted Him (*Philippians 2:8–9*).

Becoming like a child does not mean being childish, naive, or immature. Paul urges believers to be mature in their thinking (*1 Corinthians 14:20*). Rather, it means relating to God with humble trust and dependence, and relating to others without seeking status over them.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses invite believers to examine their desire for recognition and status. In workplaces, churches, families, and social settings, it is easy to compare oneself with others, seek credit, or want to be seen as important. Jesus calls His followers to let go of such ambitions and to take the lower place willingly.

They also call believers to depend on God like children depend on their parents. This means bringing needs to Him in prayer, trusting His care, and acknowledging that everything good comes from Him. Pride says, “I can handle this”; childlike faith says, “Father, I need You.”

Finally, these verses encourage believers to value those whom society overlooks. Jesus placed a child, someone of little status, at the center of His teaching. Followers of Jesus can give attention, respect, and care to children and to others who lack power or influence, recognizing that such people are honored in God’s kingdom.

### *Matthew 18:15* — Going to a Brother Who Has Sinned

> *“If your brother sins against you, go, show him his fault between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained back your brother.”*
>
> — *Matthew 18:15* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse begins Jesus’ instructions for dealing with sin within the community of His followers. It comes right after the parable of the lost sheep, in which Jesus said that the Father does not want any of His little ones to perish. The instructions that follow are a practical way of seeking a wandering brother or sister.

“*If your brother sins against you*” (*v. 15*). “Brother” refers to a fellow member of God’s family, a fellow believer. Some ancient manuscripts do not include “against you,” which would make the instruction about any sin a fellow believer commits, but the following conversation with Peter about forgiving a brother who sins “against me” suggests that personal offenses are especially in view.

Jesus says, “*go, show him his fault between you and him alone*” (*v. 15*). The first step is private. Rather than gossiping, complaining to others, or nursing resentment, the offended person is to go directly to the one who sinned. “Show him his fault” means to help him see what he has done wrong. Keeping it private protects the person’s dignity and gives the best opportunity for repentance.

“*If he listens to you, you have gained back your brother*” (*v. 15*). The goal is not winning an argument or getting revenge but restoring a relationship. “Gained” means won back, as the shepherd recovered the lost sheep.

If the private conversation fails, Jesus describes further steps (vv. 16–17). Bring one or two others, following the principle in *Deuteronomy 19:15* that matters should be established by two or three witnesses. If the person still refuses, tell the church. If he refuses to listen even to the church, treat him as “*a Gentile or a tax collector*” (*v. 17*), that is, as someone outside the community. Even this final step has the goal of restoration, since Jesus Himself sought out Gentiles and tax collectors with mercy.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that sin within the community matters to God. Followers of Jesus are not to ignore sin or pretend it does not exist. Love sometimes requires honest confrontation. Paul writes, “*Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness*” (*Galatians 6:1*).

At the same time, the process is designed to protect people. Keeping the matter private at first prevents gossip and public shame. Involving witnesses ensures fairness and helps clarify whether there truly is a sin or a misunderstanding. Bringing it to the church happens only after other steps have failed. The process reflects both justice and mercy.

The goal throughout is restoration. Jesus’ instructions come right after the parable of the lost sheep and right before His teaching on unlimited forgiveness. Discipline in God’s family is never meant to be harsh or vindictive but to bring back those who have wandered.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse calls believers to handle conflict directly and privately when possible. It is tempting to complain to others, post vague criticisms online, or avoid the person entirely. Jesus calls His followers to go to the person who has wronged them, with humility and a desire for reconciliation. Before doing so, believers can examine their own hearts, remembering Jesus’ teaching about removing the beam from one’s own eye (*Matthew 7:3–5*).

It also requires wisdom. This teaching applies to ordinary sins and conflicts within the church. It does not require a victim of abuse or a crime to meet privately with an abuser, or to keep serious wrongdoing secret. In such cases, safety, the involvement of appropriate leaders, and reporting to civil authorities are right and necessary. Jesus’ concern for protecting “little ones” in this same chapter supports this.

Finally, the goal of “gaining your brother” should shape the tone of any confrontation. Believers can speak truthfully but gently, listen carefully, be open to correction themselves, and rejoice when relationships are restored.

### *Matthew 18:21–22* — Forgiveness Without Counting

> *“Then Peter came and said to him, ‘Lord, how often shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? Until seven times?’ Jesus said to him, I don’t tell you until seven times, but, until seventy times seven.”*
>
> — *Matthew 18:21–22* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These verses record Peter’s question and Jesus’ answer about forgiveness. Jesus had just taught about confronting a brother who sins and about the church’s role in restoring wandering believers. Peter, thinking about this, asked a practical question: “*Lord, how often shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? Until seven times?*” (*v. 21*)

Peter’s suggestion seemed generous. Some Jewish teachers taught that a person should forgive someone three times for the same offense, based on passages in Amos where God judges nations after “three transgressions, and for four.” Peter doubled that and added one, reaching seven, a number associated with completeness.

Jesus answered, “*I don’t tell you until seven times, but, until seventy times seven*” (*v. 22*). Whether the number means seventy-seven or four hundred ninety, the point is that forgiveness is not something to count. Anyone keeping track of how many times they have forgiven has missed the point. Jesus’ words may intentionally reverse *Genesis 4:24*, where Lamech, a descendant of Cain, boasted that if Cain was avenged sevenfold, he would be avenged seventy-sevenfold. Lamech wanted unlimited revenge; Jesus calls His followers to unlimited forgiveness.

Jesus then told the parable of the unforgiving servant to explain why forgiveness must be so generous. The servant who had been forgiven an impossible debt refused to forgive a much smaller one. The parable ends with Jesus’ warning that the Father will not forgive those who refuse to forgive others from their hearts.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses, together with the parable, show that forgiveness flows from having been forgiven. The ten thousand talents represent the enormous debt of sin each person owes to God, a debt no one could ever repay. God’s forgiveness through Christ cancels that debt completely. In comparison, the wrongs others commit against us, though real and sometimes very painful, are small. Paul writes, “*forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you*” (*Ephesians 4:32*).

The warning at the end of the parable is serious. It does not mean that people earn God’s forgiveness by forgiving others. It means that a person who has truly received God’s mercy will be changed by it. A persistent refusal to forgive reveals that someone has not really understood or received God’s grace. This echoes Jesus’ teaching on the Lord’s Prayer (*Matthew 6:12*, 14–15).

It is important to understand what forgiveness is and is not. Forgiveness means releasing the debt, giving up the right to revenge, and leaving justice to God. It does not mean pretending the wrong did not happen, excusing it, or necessarily trusting the person again immediately. Reconciliation requires repentance and rebuilt trust, and in some cases, especially where there has been abuse, it may not be safe or wise to restore a relationship. Forgiveness also does not cancel the need for legal or civil consequences for serious wrongdoing. A person can forgive from the heart while still maintaining boundaries and seeking justice through proper channels.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses call believers to stop keeping score. Many people forgive once or twice but then keep a mental record of offenses, ready to bring them up later. Jesus calls His followers to release such records. This may require ongoing effort, especially for deep wounds. Forgiveness is often a process, and it may need to be renewed each time painful memories return.

Remembering how much God has forgiven is the key to forgiving others. When believers reflect on the debt of sin they have been released from, it becomes easier to release others from what they owe. Praying for those who have hurt us, and asking God for help to forgive, are practical ways of beginning.

Finally, believers can forgive while also using wisdom. Forgiveness does not require remaining in harmful situations or allowing someone to continue causing harm. Believers can forgive from the heart, refuse bitterness and revenge, and still protect themselves and others, set boundaries, and seek help when needed.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Matthew 18* gives practical teaching about life in God’s family. It begins with humility. The disciples wanted to know who was the greatest; Jesus told them to become like children. Believers can apply this by letting go of the desire for status, serving others without seeking recognition, and relating to God with humble dependence. Churches can reflect this by honoring those who are often overlooked and refusing to organize their life around power and prestige.

The chapter calls for deep care for the vulnerable. Jesus warns severely against causing little ones to stumble. This includes children and new or struggling believers. Churches and believers are responsible for protecting children, for being careful about how their words and actions affect others, and for never using authority to harm. Any form of abuse within a community of faith is a grave betrayal of Jesus’ teaching, and it must be stopped, reported, and addressed.

The parable of the lost sheep and the instructions for addressing sin show that God cares about those who wander. Believers are called to seek out those who are drifting, to address sin honestly but gently, and always to aim for restoration. This requires courage to speak truthfully, humility to listen, and patience to keep seeking those who have strayed.

Finally, the chapter ends with forgiveness. Believers who have been forgiven an unpayable debt by God are called to forgive others from the heart, without counting. This is one of the hardest commands Jesus gives, and it cannot be obeyed without God’s grace. But it brings freedom from bitterness and reflects the mercy believers have received. At the same time, forgiveness can coexist with wise boundaries and the pursuit of justice. The heart releases revenge, while wisdom protects against further harm.

## Chapter Prayer

Father, forgive me for the times I have sought to be great rather than humble. Teach me to come to You like a child, depending on You for everything, and help me to honor those whom the world overlooks. Make me careful never to cause one of Your little ones to stumble, and give me courage to protect the vulnerable.

Thank You that You seek every lost sheep and rejoice when one is found. Give me a heart that cares for those who wander, and wisdom to speak truth gently when a brother or sister has sinned, always with the hope of restoration. Thank You for forgiving the enormous debt of my sin through Jesus. Help me to forgive others from my heart, without keeping count, and to release the desire for revenge. Give me wisdom to set right boundaries where needed, and fill me with the mercy You have shown me. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
