Matthew · Chapter 19 of 28

# Matthew — Chapter 19

Chapter Theme: Marriage, Children, Riches, and the Impossible Made Possible

[Read Matthew 19 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/MAT19.htm)

Main Teaching

As Jesus travels toward Jerusalem, He answers a test question about divorce by pointing back to God’s design for marriage at creation. He welcomes children whom His disciples try to turn away, and He tells a wealthy young man to sell his possessions and follow Him. When the disciples wonder who can be saved, Jesus answers that salvation is impossible for people but possible for God, and He promises that no sacrifice made for His sake will be lost.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Matthew 19* marks a geographical turning point. Jesus has finished His ministry in Galilee and now heads south toward Jerusalem, where He will be crucified. He crosses into “*the borders of Judea beyond the Jordan*” (*v. 1*), the region east of the Jordan River known as Perea, which was also ruled by Herod Antipas. This was the same territory where John the Baptist had been arrested for criticizing Herod’s marriage. Large crowds follow Jesus, and He heals them.

Chapters 19 and 20 address questions about family, wealth, status, and reward in God’s kingdom. Several encounters reveal how the values of the kingdom differ from the values of the world, and they continue the theme of humility and dependence from chapter 18.

### The Question About Divorce (*19:1–12*)

Some Pharisees came to test Jesus: “*Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife for any reason?*” (*v. 3*) This was a debated issue. The law of Moses in *Deuteronomy 24:1–4* allowed a man to divorce his wife if he found “some unseemly thing” in her and required him to give her a certificate of divorce. Two famous rabbinic schools disagreed about what “some unseemly thing” meant. The school of Shammai taught that it referred to serious sexual immorality. The school of Hillel interpreted it broadly, allowing divorce for almost any reason, even burning a meal or finding a more attractive woman. In practice, only men could initiate divorce in most Jewish settings, which left women very vulnerable. The question may also have been a trap, since Herod Antipas, ruler of the region, had divorced his wife to marry Herodias.

Jesus did not begin with the debate about Deuteronomy. He went back to creation. God made humanity male and female (*Genesis 1:27*) and said that a man would leave his parents, be joined to his wife, and the two would become one flesh (*Genesis 2:24*). Jesus concluded: “*What therefore God has joined together, don’t let man tear apart*” (*v. 6*). Marriage is God’s work, a lifelong covenant union.

The Pharisees asked why Moses commanded a certificate of divorce. Jesus corrected them: Moses did not command divorce; he permitted it “*because of the hardness of your hearts*” (*v. 8*). The certificate was a regulation in a sinful world, protecting a divorced woman by allowing her to remarry. But “*from the beginning it has not been so*” (*v. 8*). God’s original design was permanence.

Jesus then said that whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another commits adultery. The Greek word for sexual immorality, “porneia,” is a broad term covering various kinds of sexual sin. Jesus’ teaching was stricter than both rabbinic schools in practice, since it ruled out divorce for trivial reasons entirely.

The disciples were stunned: if marriage was this binding, maybe it was better not to marry. Jesus replied that not everyone can accept this teaching, only those to whom it is given. He spoke of eunuchs: some were born unable to marry or have children, some were made so by others (as servants in royal courts sometimes were), and some had chosen to remain unmarried “*for the Kingdom of Heaven’s sake*” (*v. 12*). In a culture where marriage and children were expected, Jesus honored those who remained single in service to God. Jesus Himself was unmarried, and Paul later spoke of singleness as a gift (*1 Corinthians 7:7*).

### Jesus Blesses the Children (*19:13–15*)

People brought little children to Jesus so that He would lay His hands on them and pray. It was a common practice to ask respected rabbis to bless children. The disciples rebuked those who brought them, perhaps thinking Jesus was too important or too busy for children. Jesus said, “*Allow the little children, and don’t forbid them to come to me; for the Kingdom of Heaven belongs to ones like these*” (*v. 14*). He laid His hands on them and blessed them. This scene echoes His teaching in *Matthew 18:3–5*: the kingdom belongs to those who receive it with childlike dependence, and those who welcome children welcome Him.

### The Rich Young Man (*19:16–22*)

A man came to Jesus and asked, “*Good teacher, what good thing shall I do, that I may have eternal life?*” (*v. 16*) Matthew tells us he was young (v. 20) and wealthy (v. 22); Luke adds that he was a ruler (*Luke 18:18*). His question assumed that eternal life could be gained by doing some good deed.

Jesus responded, “*Why do you call me good? No one is good but one, that is, God*” (*v. 17*). Jesus was not denying His own goodness but challenging the man to think about what “good” really means. True goodness belongs to God alone. Then Jesus said that if he wanted to enter life, he should keep the commandments. When the man asked which ones, Jesus listed several of the Ten Commandments dealing with relationships with others, adding, “*You shall love your neighbor as yourself*” (*v. 19*) (*Leviticus 19:18*).

The man replied that he had kept all these and asked, “*What do I still lack?*” (*v. 20*) His question suggests that despite his outward obedience, he sensed something was missing. Jesus answered that if he wanted to be complete, he should sell his possessions, give to the poor, and he would have treasure in heaven; then he should come and follow Jesus. The young man went away sad, because he had great wealth.

### The Danger of Riches (*19:23–26*)

Jesus told His disciples that it is hard for a rich person to enter the kingdom of heaven. He added a startling image: “*it is easier for a camel to go through a needle’s eye than for a rich man to enter into God’s Kingdom*” (*v. 24*). The camel was the largest animal in Palestine, and the eye of a needle was the smallest opening. Some have suggested that “the eye of a needle” referred to a small gate in Jerusalem, but there is no evidence that such a gate existed in Jesus’ time. Jesus was using deliberate exaggeration, as He often did, to describe something humanly impossible.

The disciples were “*exceedingly astonished*” (*v. 25*). Many people in that culture believed wealth was a sign of God’s blessing. If the rich, who seemed favored by God, could not be saved, who could? Jesus answered, “*With men this is impossible, but with God all things are possible*” (*v. 26*). This is studied below.

### The Reward for Following Jesus (*19:27–30*)

Peter, perhaps thinking of the contrast with the rich young man, said, “*Behold, we have left everything and followed you. What then will we have?*” (*v. 27*) Jesus responded with a promise. In “*the regeneration*” (*v. 28*), the renewal of all things when the Son of Man sits on His glorious throne, the twelve apostles will sit on twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel. Their sacrifice would be honored in the kingdom.

Jesus then extended the promise to everyone who has left houses, family members, or lands for His sake: they will receive a hundred times as much and inherit eternal life. Mark adds that they will receive these things “now in this time,” with persecutions, referring to the new family of believers (*Mark 10:30*). Finally Jesus said, “*But many will be last who are first, and first who are last*” (*v. 30*). This saying, which also ends the parable in chapter 20, warns that God’s evaluation often reverses human expectations.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Matthew 19:6* — What God Has Joined Together

> *“So that they are no more two, but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, don’t let man tear apart.”*
>
> — *Matthew 19:6* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus speaks these words in response to a question from the Pharisees designed to test Him. They asked whether it was lawful for a man to divorce his wife “for any reason.” In Jesus’ time, many teachers allowed men to divorce their wives for trivial reasons, and women had little ability to object or protect themselves. The Pharisees may also have hoped Jesus would say something that would get Him in trouble with Herod Antipas, who had divorced his wife to marry his brother’s wife.

Jesus took the discussion back to the beginning. He reminded them that God made human beings male and female and that God declared a man would leave his parents and be joined to his wife, and the two would become one flesh (*Genesis 1:27*; *2:24*). Then He drew the conclusion in this verse: “*So that they are no more two, but one flesh*” (*v. 6*). Marriage creates a profound union of two lives, physically, emotionally, and socially.

“*What therefore God has joined together, don’t let man tear apart*” (*v. 6*). Jesus teaches that marriage is not merely a human contract that can be dissolved at will. God Himself joins a husband and wife together. Human beings, whether the spouses themselves or others, should not break apart what God has united.

When the Pharisees asked why Moses allowed divorce, Jesus explained that Moses permitted it because of the hardness of human hearts, but that this was not God’s original intention. He then stated that divorce and remarriage, except in cases of sexual immorality, amounts to adultery.

His listeners, including His own disciples, found this teaching shocking. They had grown up in a culture where divorce was relatively easy for men. Jesus was restoring God’s design for marriage and protecting women from being discarded.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals that marriage is part of God’s good design for creation. It is a covenant relationship, a solemn commitment made before God, that reflects His own faithfulness. The prophets used marriage as an image of God’s covenant love for Israel, and the New Testament presents marriage as a picture of the relationship between Christ and the church (*Ephesians 5:31–32*).

Jesus’ teaching also shows how God’s law accommodates human sinfulness without approving it. Divorce was permitted in the law because of hard hearts, to limit the damage sin causes. But the ideal remains lifelong faithfulness. This pattern helps believers understand that some biblical laws regulate a broken world rather than express God’s highest desire.

Christians have understood the application of Jesus’ teaching in different ways. Some traditions, such as the Roman Catholic Church, teach that a valid sacramental marriage cannot be dissolved, though an annulment may declare that a valid marriage never existed. Many Protestants believe divorce is permitted for sexual unfaithfulness and also for abandonment by an unbelieving spouse (*1 Corinthians 7:15*), and many also believe that abuse, which violates the covenant at its core, can be grounds for separation and divorce. Traditions also differ on remarriage after divorce. These questions require careful study and pastoral wisdom, and they should be handled with compassion for those whose marriages have been broken.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse calls married believers to treat their marriage as a sacred covenant joined by God. That means investing in the relationship, keeping promises, practicing forgiveness, seeking help when problems arise, and refusing to treat divorce as an easy escape from ordinary difficulties. It also means guarding marriage against unfaithfulness in thought and action.

For those considering marriage, this verse encourages careful thought and prayer. Marriage is a lifelong commitment, and entering it wisely is part of honoring God’s design.

At the same time, this teaching must never be used to trap someone in danger. God’s design for marriage includes love, faithfulness, and protection, and abuse betrays that design. A person facing abuse should seek safety and help, and the church should support them. Jesus’ teaching protected vulnerable spouses from being cast aside; it should not be used to harm them. Those who have experienced divorce, whatever the circumstances, can find in Christ forgiveness, healing, and a welcome in God’s family.

### *Matthew 19:21* — What the Rich Young Man Lacked

> *“Jesus said to him, ‘If you want to be perfect, go, sell what you have, and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.’”*
>
> — *Matthew 19:21* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus speaks these words to a wealthy young man who had come asking what good thing he must do to receive eternal life. Jesus had told him to keep the commandments and listed several of them, including honoring parents and loving one’s neighbor as oneself. The young man replied that he had kept all these from his youth, and then asked, “*What do I still lack?*” (*v. 20*)

The man was sincere. He seems to have lived an outwardly moral life. Yet he sensed that something was missing. Jesus answered, “*If you want to be perfect, go, sell what you have, and give to the poor*” (*v. 21*). “Perfect” means complete or whole, the same word used in *Matthew 5:48*. Jesus was showing him what would make his obedience complete.

The command to sell everything was specific to this man. Jesus had listed commandments about loving others, and the man claimed to have kept them. But his wealth had a hold on his heart that kept him from loving his neighbor fully and from loving God above all. Jesus put His finger on the one thing the man could not give up.

Jesus promised that if he did this, “*you will have treasure in heaven*” (*v. 21*), echoing His teaching in *Matthew 6:19–21* about storing up lasting treasure. Then came the most important part: “*and come, follow me*” (*v. 21*). Giving away possessions was not an end in itself; it was a way of freeing the man to follow Jesus.

The young man’s response was sad: he went away grieving because he had great possessions. He wanted eternal life, but not at the cost of his wealth. His possessions, in reality, possessed him.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This encounter reveals that outward obedience is not the same as wholehearted devotion to God. The young man had kept many commandments, but his wealth had become an idol. Jesus’ command exposed what truly ruled his heart. The first commandment, to have no other gods before the LORD, was the one he was breaking.

The story also shows that eternal life cannot be earned by doing “good things.” The man asked what good thing he should do. Jesus’ answer showed him that he could not reach completeness on his own. What he needed was not one more good deed but a new allegiance: following Jesus.

It is important to note that Jesus does not command every believer to sell everything. Some of His followers, such as Zacchaeus, gave away much but not all (*Luke 19:8*), and some wealthy followers supported Jesus’ ministry (*Luke 8:3*). But Jesus does call every believer to put Him above all possessions and to be willing to give up whatever stands between them and Him. Generosity toward the poor is a consistent mark of faithful discipleship throughout Scripture.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to ask what might be holding them back from following Jesus wholeheartedly. For the rich young man it was wealth. For others it might be comfort, a relationship, a career, a reputation, or an ambition. Jesus lovingly identifies these idols and calls His followers to let them go.

It also challenges believers’ relationship with money. In many societies, financial security and material comfort are highly valued. Believers can examine whether their possessions serve God’s purposes or have become sources of identity and security. Practical steps include giving generously, living simply, caring for the poor, and holding possessions with open hands.

Finally, the story warns against assuming that moral respectability is enough. Many people live decent lives but have never surrendered themselves to Jesus. Following Him means more than avoiding wrongdoing; it means making Him Lord over everything.

### *Matthew 19:26* — With God All Things Are Possible

> *“Looking at them, Jesus said, ‘With men this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.’”*
>
> — *Matthew 19:26* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus speaks these words after the rich young man has gone away sad, unwilling to give up his possessions to follow Jesus. Jesus then told His disciples that it is hard for a rich person to enter the kingdom of heaven, easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle. The image describes something completely impossible.

The disciples were astonished and asked, “*Who then can be saved?*” (*v. 25*) In their culture, wealth was often seen as a sign of God’s favor. If even the rich, who seemed blessed by God, could not enter the kingdom, what hope was there for anyone?

Jesus looked at them and said, “*With men this is impossible, but with God all things are possible*” (*v. 26*). The phrase “looking at them” suggests a moment of deliberate emphasis. Jesus did not soften His teaching about the danger of wealth. He agreed that salvation is impossible from a human standpoint. No one, rich or poor, can save themselves by their own efforts, goodness, or resources.

But God can do what people cannot. Salvation is God’s work. He can change a heart that is attached to wealth, as He later did with Zacchaeus, a rich tax collector who gave half his possessions to the poor (*Luke 19:1–10*). He can bring anyone into His kingdom.

The phrase echoes *Genesis 18:14*, where God asked Abraham, “*Is anything too hard for the LORD?*” (*Genesis 18:14*) when promising a son to elderly Sarah. Jesus applies the same truth to salvation.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse expresses the heart of the gospel: salvation is by God’s grace, not by human achievement. The rich young man asked what good thing he could do to earn eternal life. Jesus’ answer to the disciples makes clear that no human effort is enough. Paul later wrote, “*for by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God*” (*Ephesians 2:8*).

This truth humbles everyone. The rich cannot buy their way in; the moral cannot earn their way in; the religious cannot qualify themselves. Every person depends entirely on God’s mercy. Yet the same truth gives hope to everyone. No one is beyond God’s reach. Those who seem least likely to be saved can be transformed by His power.

The verse is sometimes quoted as a general promise that God will do anything a person wants. In context, it is specifically about salvation: God can do what is impossible for humans by bringing people into His kingdom. It reveals God’s power, but it should be applied according to His will and purposes, not as a guarantee of every human desire.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse calls believers to stop relying on themselves for salvation. Whether through moral effort, religious activity, or good deeds, people often try to earn God’s acceptance. Jesus says this is impossible. The right response is to trust God’s grace and receive salvation as His gift.

It also gives hope for those who seem far from God, including family members and friends. Believers sometimes give up praying for people they think will never change. Jesus’ words remind them that God can do what seems impossible. They can keep praying and keep loving, trusting God to work.

Finally, this verse encourages believers in their own struggles with sin and attachment to the things of this world. Letting go of idols, such as wealth, comfort, or control, may feel impossible. But God can change hearts. Believers can ask Him to free them from whatever holds them back, trusting His power to do what they cannot.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Matthew 19* addresses some of the most personal areas of life: marriage, children, money, and reward. In each area, Jesus calls His followers to see things from God’s perspective rather than from the perspective of their culture.

On marriage, Jesus points back to God’s design at creation. Marriage is a lifelong covenant joined by God, not a contract to be dissolved for convenience. Believers who are married can honor their covenant through faithfulness, forgiveness, and seeking help when needed. Those who are single can find dignity and purpose in serving God, as Jesus honored those who remain unmarried for the kingdom. And those whose marriages have been broken, including through abuse or abandonment, can find compassion and healing in Christ and in His church. Jesus’ teaching protects the vulnerable; it must never be used to keep someone in danger.

Jesus’ welcome of children reminds believers that no one is too small or insignificant for Him. Churches and families can make room for children, value them, and help them come to Jesus. It also reminds every believer to approach God with childlike trust.

The rich young man’s story challenges believers’ relationship with wealth. Possessions can become idols that keep people from following Jesus wholeheartedly. Believers can examine what they are unwilling to give up and ask God to free them. Generosity, simplicity, and care for the poor are practical expressions of a heart that treasures Christ above all.

Finally, Jesus’ words about salvation and reward offer hope. Salvation is impossible for people but possible for God, and no sacrifice made for Jesus’ sake will go unrewarded. Believers can trust God’s grace for their salvation and follow Jesus generously, knowing that God’s kingdom often reverses the world’s rankings and that what is given up for Him will be repaid many times over.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for showing me Your good design for marriage and for honoring both those who marry and those who remain single for Your kingdom. Help me to keep my promises, to honor the covenants I make, and to treat others with faithfulness and love. Comfort those whose marriages have been broken, and protect those who are in danger.

Thank You for welcoming little children. Give me a childlike faith that depends on You. Show me anything I am holding onto more tightly than I hold onto You, and give me grace to let it go. Free me from trusting in wealth or my own goodness. I confess that salvation is impossible for me by my own efforts, but I thank You that with God all things are possible. Help me to follow You wholeheartedly, trusting that nothing I give up for Your sake will be lost. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Matthew · Chapter 20 of 28

# Matthew — Chapter 20

Chapter Theme: Grace That Overturns Ranking, and the Servant King

[Read Matthew 20 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/MAT20.htm)

Main Teaching

Through the parable of the vineyard workers, Jesus teaches that God’s kingdom runs on generous grace, not on earning and comparison. On the road to Jerusalem He predicts His death a third time, then answers a request for places of honor by teaching that greatness means service, because He came to give His life as a ransom for many. Leaving Jericho, He stops for two blind men whom the crowd tries to silence and gives them sight.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Matthew 20* continues directly from chapter 19. Peter had just asked what the disciples would receive for leaving everything to follow Jesus, and Jesus promised a great reward, adding, “*But many will be last who are first, and first who are last*” (*Matthew 19:30*). The parable that opens chapter 20 explains that saying, and it ends with the same words reversed (v. 16). The whole chapter is about how the kingdom of heaven turns human ideas of status, merit, and greatness upside down.

### The Parable of the Workers in the Vineyard (*20:1–16*)

Jesus told of a landowner who went out early in the morning to hire workers for his vineyard. In Palestine, day laborers gathered in the marketplace hoping to be hired. They were among the poorest people in society, often landless, depending on daily work to feed their families. The landowner agreed to pay them a denarius for the day, the standard wage for a day’s labor and roughly what a family needed to live for a day.

He went out again at the third hour (about 9 a.m.), the sixth (noon), and the ninth (3 p.m.), hiring more workers and promising to pay what was right. Finally, at the eleventh hour (about 5 p.m.), with only an hour of daylight left, he found others still standing around. When he asked why they had been idle all day, they replied, “*Because no one has hired us*” (*v. 7*). These were likely the least desirable workers, perhaps older, weaker, or less skilled. He sent them into the vineyard too.

At evening, the law required that day laborers be paid before sunset (*Deuteronomy 24:14–15*). The owner told his manager to pay the workers, starting with the last ones hired. Those who had worked only one hour received a full denarius. When those hired first came forward, they expected more. But they also received one denarius. They grumbled against the owner: “*These last have spent one hour, and you have made them equal to us who have borne the burden of the day and the scorching heat!*” (*v. 12*)

The owner replied to one of them, calling him “*Friend*” (*v. 13*), that he had done him no wrong; they had agreed on a denarius. He was free to be generous with what belonged to him. Then he asked, “*Or is your eye evil, because I am good?*” (*v. 15*) Jesus concluded, “*So the last will be first, and the first last*” (*v. 16*). (Some manuscripts add “For many are called, but few are chosen,” a saying that also appears in *Matthew 22:14*.)

The parable answers Peter’s question about reward. The disciples would indeed be rewarded, but they must not think that God’s kingdom works like a system of wages based on merit and seniority. God gives generously, and those who come late receive the same grace as those who came early. The parable also had a wider application in Jesus’ setting: tax collectors, sinners, and later Gentiles were coming into the kingdom alongside the religious people who had long served God, and some resented it.

### Third Prediction of the Passion (*20:17–19*)

As Jesus was going up to Jerusalem (the city sits on hills, so travelers always “went up” to it), He took the Twelve aside and told them for the third time what would happen. This prediction is the most detailed. He would be handed over to the chief priests and scribes, condemned to death, handed over to the Gentiles (the Romans) to be mocked, flogged, and crucified, and on the third day He would be raised. For the first time Jesus specified that He would be crucified, the Roman method of execution reserved for slaves, rebels, and the worst criminals.

### A Request for Places of Honor (*20:20–28*)

Immediately after this solemn prediction, the mother of James and John (the sons of Zebedee) came to Jesus with her sons, knelt, and asked a favor. Some have suggested from comparing *Matthew 27:56* with *Mark 15:40* and *John 19:25* that she may have been Salome, possibly the sister of Jesus’ mother, which would make James and John Jesus’ cousins, though this is uncertain. She asked that her two sons sit at Jesus’ right and left in His kingdom, the positions of highest honor next to a king. Mark’s account has James and John ask directly (*Mark 10:35–37*), showing that the request was theirs as well.

Jesus answered, “*You don’t know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I am about to drink?*” (*v. 22*) The “cup” was an Old Testament image for suffering and especially for God’s judgment (*Isaiah 51:17*; *Jeremiah 25:15*). Jesus was about to drink that cup on the cross. They confidently said, “We are able.” Jesus told them they would indeed drink His cup. James was later executed by Herod Agrippa I (*Acts 12:2*), the first of the apostles to be martyred; John suffered persecution and exile (*Revelation 1:9*). But the places at His right and left were not His to give; they belonged to those for whom the Father had prepared them. Ironically, the next time Matthew mentions people on Jesus’ right and left, they are two criminals crucified beside Him (*Matthew 27:38*).

The other ten disciples were indignant with the two brothers, probably because they wanted those positions themselves. Jesus called them together and contrasted the kingdom with the world’s systems of power. Gentile rulers “*lord it over them*” (*v. 25*), and their great ones exercise authority over others. “*It shall not be so among you*” (*v. 26*). Whoever wants to be great must be a servant, and whoever wants to be first must be a slave. A “bondservant” or slave had the lowest position in society, with no rights of his own. Jesus grounded this teaching in His own mission: the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many.

### Two Blind Men Near Jericho (*20:29–34*)

As Jesus and His disciples left Jericho, about fifteen miles northeast of Jerusalem, a large crowd followed. Pilgrims traveling to Jerusalem for Passover often passed through Jericho. Two blind men sitting by the road heard that Jesus was passing and cried out, “*Lord, have mercy on us, you son of David!*” (*v. 30*) (Mark and Luke mention one man, Bartimaeus; Matthew, as he sometimes does, mentions two.) By calling Jesus “Son of David,” they recognized Him as the Messiah, the heir of David’s throne.

The crowd rebuked them and told them to be quiet. Blind beggars were considered a nuisance, and perhaps the crowd thought Jesus had more important things to do on His way to Jerusalem. But the men cried out even louder. Jesus stopped, called them, and asked, “*What do you want me to do for you?*” (*v. 32*) They answered, “*Lord, that our eyes may be opened*” (*v. 33*). Moved with compassion, Jesus touched their eyes. Immediately they could see, and they followed Him.

The contrast with the request of James and John is striking. Jesus asks both groups essentially the same question (compare v. 21). The disciples, who could see physically, asked for power and position. The blind men asked for mercy. Their request was granted, and they followed Jesus on the road to Jerusalem, the road to the cross.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Matthew 20:15* — Resenting God’s Generosity

> *“Isn’t it lawful for me to do what I want to with what I own? Or is your eye evil, because I am good?’”*
>
> — *Matthew 20:15* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse is the landowner’s reply to the workers who complained at the end of the day. They had worked from early morning, through the heat of the day, and received the denarius they had agreed to. But when they saw that those who had worked only one hour received the same amount, they grumbled. They felt they had been treated unfairly.

The landowner first pointed out that he had done them no wrong; he had paid them exactly what they agreed to (v. 13). Then he asked two questions. “*Isn’t it lawful for me to do what I want to with what I own?*” (*v. 15*) The money was his, and he had the right to be generous with it. Paying the latecomers a full day’s wage did not take anything away from those who worked longer.

The second question went deeper: “*Or is your eye evil, because I am good?*” (*v. 15*) In Jewish idiom, an “evil eye” meant envy or stinginess, a resentful attitude toward someone else’s good fortune (see *Matthew 6:23*). The landowner was exposing the real problem. The workers were not upset because they had been cheated, but because someone else had received generosity they felt was undeserved. Their envy had turned the owner’s goodness into a cause for complaint.

Jesus’ listeners would have understood the workers’ complaint; it seems natural. That is why the parable is so powerful. It shows how human ideas of fairness, based on what people deserve, can clash with God’s generosity, based on grace.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This parable reveals that God’s kingdom is based on grace, not on merit. No one earns eternal life by working long and hard enough. Those who come to God late in life receive the same gift as those who have served Him for decades. The thief on the cross, who turned to Jesus in his last hours, received the promise of paradise (*Luke 23:43*).

The verse also exposes a danger for those who have followed God for a long time: resenting God’s grace to others. Jesus tells a similar story in the parable of the prodigal son, where the older brother is angry when his father welcomes the younger son home with a celebration (*Luke 15:25–32*). Religious people can begin to think they deserve more than others because of their faithfulness, and then resent God’s kindness to sinners.

Finally, the verse shows that envy is a spiritual problem. It distorts how we see God and others. Instead of rejoicing in God’s goodness, envy complains about it. The cure for envy is remembering that we, too, have received grace we did not deserve.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to examine whether they ever resent God’s generosity to others. This might show up in feeling bitter when someone who has lived a careless life comes to faith and is welcomed, when a new believer receives attention or opportunities, or when others are blessed in ways we feel we deserved more. Recognizing envy and confessing it is the first step toward freedom.

It also calls believers to rejoice in God’s grace wherever it appears. When someone turns to God late in life, or when a person with a troubled past is restored, believers can celebrate rather than compare. Every person in God’s kingdom is there by grace.

Finally, this verse encourages humility about service. Long years of faithfulness are good and will be rewarded, but they do not make anyone more deserving of God’s love than others. Believers can serve with gratitude rather than with a sense of entitlement, remembering that the privilege of working in God’s vineyard is itself a gift.

### *Matthew 20:28* — The Son of Man Came to Serve

> *“even as the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.”*
>
> — *Matthew 20:28* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus speaks these words to all twelve disciples after a conflict about status. James and John, along with their mother, had asked for the places of highest honor in Jesus’ kingdom. The other ten disciples were angry with them, likely because they wanted those places too. Jesus had just told them for the third time that He was going to Jerusalem to be condemned, mocked, flogged, and crucified. Yet His disciples were arguing about who would be greatest.

Jesus called them together and explained that His kingdom works differently from worldly power. Among the nations, rulers dominate and use authority over others. Among His followers, greatness means serving, and being first means becoming a slave. Then Jesus gave the reason, pointing to Himself: “*even as the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve*” (*v. 28*).

“Son of Man” is the title from *Daniel 7*, where one like a son of man receives authority, glory, and a kingdom, and all peoples serve Him. Jesus is that glorious figure, and yet He came not to be served but to serve. The one who deserves the worship of all nations takes the role of a servant.

He adds, “*and to give his life as a ransom for many*” (*v. 28*). A ransom was a price paid to set someone free, such as a slave or a prisoner of war. Jesus is saying that His death will be the price that sets people free. “For many” echoes *Isaiah 53:11–12*, where the Suffering Servant bears the sins of many. The word “for” can mean “in place of,” suggesting that Jesus’ death is substitutionary: He dies in place of those He saves.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse is one of the clearest statements in the Gospels about why Jesus came and why He died. His entire life was service, and His death was the ultimate act of service, giving His life to set others free. Christians have understood this ransom in various ways: as freedom from sin’s power, from the penalty of guilt, and from death and the devil. The New Testament presents all these aspects, and Christians emphasize them differently. The central truth is that Jesus’ death accomplished what humans could not do for themselves: their liberation and reconciliation with God.

This verse also shows that Jesus’ example and His saving work belong together. He is the model for His followers’ service, but He is more than a model. His service as a ransom is unique; no one else can give their life for the sins of many. Believers serve others in response to His saving service for them.

Finally, the verse redefines greatness. In God’s kingdom, the greatest one of all, the Son of Man, is the one who serves most completely. Greatness is measured not by how many people serve us but by how fully we give ourselves to serve others.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse calls believers to adopt a servant mindset in every area of life. In families, it means putting others’ needs before one’s own. In churches, it means leaders who serve rather than dominate, and members who look for ways to help rather than seek recognition. In workplaces, it means working with integrity and caring for colleagues and customers, not merely seeking advancement.

It also challenges believers’ views of leadership. Those who hold authority, whether parents, managers, pastors, or public officials, are called to use it for the good of others, not for personal gain. Jesus’ words, “It shall not be so among you,” rule out abusive, self-serving uses of power among His people.

Finally, this verse invites gratitude. Jesus gave His life as a ransom for many. Believers can receive this gift with thankfulness, and let that gratitude become the motivation for serving others. Service flows best not from duty or a desire for reward, but from knowing how much one has been served by Christ.

### *Matthew 20:32* — “*What Do You Want Me to Do for You?*” (*v. 32*)

> *“Jesus stood still and called them, and asked, ‘What do you want me to do for you?’”*
>
> — *Matthew 20:32* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse comes in the final scene of the chapter. Jesus and His disciples were leaving Jericho with a large crowd, heading toward Jerusalem for Passover. Two blind men sitting by the road heard that Jesus was passing by and began shouting, “*Lord, have mercy on us, you son of David!*” (*v. 30*) Calling Him “Son of David” showed that they recognized Him as the Messiah.

The crowd told them to be quiet. Perhaps they thought the blind beggars were embarrassing or unimportant, or that Jesus, on His way to Jerusalem, should not be bothered. But the men cried out even louder.

Then “*Jesus stood still*” (*v. 32*). Jesus was on His way to the most important events of His life: His death and resurrection. Yet He stopped for two blind beggars whom the crowd wanted to ignore. He called them and asked, “What do you want me to do for you?” Jesus surely knew what they needed, but He invited them to express their request. This gave them dignity and allowed them to state their faith.

They answered, “*Lord, that our eyes may be opened*” (*v. 33*). Matthew tells us Jesus was “*moved with compassion*” (*v. 34*), touched their eyes, and immediately they could see. Then they followed Him, joining His journey toward Jerusalem.

The question in this verse echoes the question Jesus asked the mother of James and John in verse 21. She asked for power and position for her sons. The blind men asked for mercy and sight. Their request was granted, and they became followers.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that Jesus is never too busy for people in need. Even on His way to the cross, He stopped for those others overlooked. This reveals God’s attentiveness to individuals, especially the poor and powerless. The crowd’s attempt to silence the blind men stands in contrast to Jesus’ welcome.

The story also illustrates the kind of prayer Jesus honors. The blind men’s cry for mercy reflects the attitude of the poor in spirit, those who know they cannot help themselves. Their persistence, crying out louder despite opposition, recalls the Canaanite woman in *Matthew 15*. Jesus responds to such humble, persistent faith.

Spiritually, the healing of blindness often symbolizes the opening of eyes to see who Jesus is. The blind men could “see” that Jesus was the Son of David even before their physical sight was restored, while many with physical sight, including the religious leaders, remained spiritually blind. After receiving sight, the men followed Jesus, showing the response that true spiritual sight produces.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to bring their requests to Jesus honestly. He asks, “What do you want me to do for you?” Believers can answer specifically in prayer, naming their needs, hopes, and struggles. God already knows, but He welcomes His children’s requests.

It also encourages persistence when others try to silence our cries for help. Sometimes people, circumstances, or even our own doubts tell us to stop praying or that our needs are not important. The blind men’s example encourages believers to keep calling out to Jesus.

Finally, this verse challenges believers to stop for people in need. Like the crowd, it is easy to see certain people as interruptions. Jesus’ example calls His followers to notice those who are overlooked, to listen to them, to ask what they need, and to respond with compassion.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Matthew 20* challenges the way people naturally think about fairness, status, and greatness. The parable of the vineyard workers teaches that God’s kingdom is based on generous grace, not on earning and comparison. Believers can let go of the habit of measuring themselves against others and resenting God’s kindness to people they think are less deserving. Everyone in God’s kingdom is there by grace, and that is cause for celebration, not envy.

The request of James and John shows how easily even devoted followers can seek status and recognition. Jesus’ answer redefines greatness as service. This applies in every sphere of life: family, church, work, and community. Believers can look for ways to serve others, especially in unnoticed ways, and can resist the desire for titles, positions, and praise. Those with authority are called to use it for the good of others, never to dominate.

At the center of the chapter is Jesus’ statement that He came to serve and to give His life as a ransom for many. This is both the foundation of salvation and the model for Christian life. Believers can receive His sacrifice with gratitude and allow it to shape how they treat others.

Finally, the healing of the blind men shows Jesus’ compassion for the overlooked. He stopped for those others tried to silence. Believers can bring their needs to Jesus with humble persistence, trusting His compassion. They can also follow His example by noticing and responding to people in need, even when it is inconvenient. Like the blind men who followed Jesus after receiving sight, those who have experienced His mercy are called to follow Him on the road He walked.

## Chapter Prayer

Father, thank You for the generous grace of Your kingdom, where those who come late are welcomed as fully as those who came early. Forgive me for the times I have compared myself with others or resented Your kindness to them. Help me to rejoice whenever anyone receives Your mercy, remembering that I too have received what I did not deserve.

Lord Jesus, thank You for coming not to be served but to serve, and for giving Your life as a ransom for many, including me. Free me from seeking status and recognition. Teach me to serve others gladly, and to use any influence I have for their good. Thank You for stopping for the blind men when others wanted them silenced. Help me to bring my needs to You honestly and persistently, to notice people others overlook, and to follow You wherever You lead. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Matthew · Chapter 21 of 28

# Matthew — Chapter 21

Chapter Theme: The King Comes to His City and His Temple

[Read Matthew 21 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/MAT21.htm)

Main Teaching

Jesus enters Jerusalem as the humble King foretold by Zechariah, welcomed by crowds shouting “Hosanna.” He clears the temple of trade, heals the blind and lame there, and curses a fruitless fig tree as a sign of judgment on empty religion. When the religious leaders challenge His authority, He answers with parables showing that genuine obedience, not outward profession, marks those who belong to God, and that rejecting God’s Son brings serious consequences.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Matthew 21* begins the final week of Jesus’ earthly life, often called Holy Week or Passion Week. Chapters 21–28 cover only about a week, yet they make up nearly a third of Matthew’s Gospel, showing how central these events are. Jesus has traveled from Galilee through Perea and Jericho, and now He approaches Jerusalem for the Passover festival. The city was crowded with pilgrims, possibly hundreds of thousands, and expectations were high. Many hoped the Messiah would appear and deliver Israel from Roman rule.

Jesus’ actions in this chapter are deliberate and symbolic. He enters the city in a way that fulfills prophecy, He acts with authority in the temple, and He confronts the religious leaders. Each action raises the same question the crowd asks in verse 10: “*Who is this?*” (*v. 10*)

### The Triumphal Entry (*21:1–11*)

As Jesus and His disciples approached Jerusalem, they came to Bethphage on the Mount of Olives, east of the city. Jesus sent two disciples into the village to bring a donkey and her colt, telling them that if anyone asked, they should say, “*The Lord needs them*” (*v. 3*). This may reflect prior arrangements or Jesus’ supernatural knowledge; either way, Jesus is directing events.

Matthew explains that this fulfilled the prophecy of *Zechariah 9:9* (combined with a phrase from *Isaiah 62:11*): “*Tell the daughter of Zion, behold, your King comes to you, humble, and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey*” (*v. 5*). Conquering kings usually rode war horses; a king coming in peace might ride a donkey. Zechariah’s prophecy continues by describing a king who brings peace to the nations. Jesus was claiming to be Israel’s King, but a humble King of peace, not a military conqueror. Matthew mentions both the donkey and the colt; the young colt may have been more willing to be ridden with its mother nearby.

The disciples put their cloaks on the animals, and Jesus sat on them. A very large crowd spread their cloaks on the road, an act of honor for a king (as in *2 Kings 9:13*), and others cut branches from trees and spread them on the road. John tells us these were palm branches (*John 12:13*), a symbol of Jewish national victory. The crowds shouted, “*Hosanna to the son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest!*” (*v. 9*) These words come from *Psalm 118*, one of the psalms sung by pilgrims at Passover.

When Jesus entered the city, all Jerusalem was stirred, asking, “Who is this?” The crowds answered, “*This is the prophet, Jesus, from Nazareth of Galilee*” (*v. 11*). Their answer was true but incomplete. Within a week, many in the city would call for His crucifixion.

### Cleansing the Temple (*21:12–17*)

Jesus entered the temple courts and drove out those who were buying and selling. The temple complex was huge, and its outer area, the Court of the Gentiles, was the only place where non-Jews could come to worship. Here merchants sold animals for sacrifice, and money changers exchanged foreign currency for the Tyrian shekels required for the temple tax. These services had a practical purpose for pilgrims who traveled long distances. But the trade had filled the space intended for prayer, and there is evidence that some of these businesses, connected with the high priestly families, overcharged worshipers.

Jesus overturned the tables of the money changers and the seats of those selling doves. Doves were the sacrifice offered by the poor (*Leviticus 12:8*), so those exploiting the trade in doves were taking advantage of the most vulnerable worshipers. Jesus quoted *Isaiah 56:7*, “*My house shall be called a house of prayer*” (*v. 13*), and *Jeremiah 7:11*, saying they had made it “*a den of robbers*” (*v. 13*). This action is studied in detail below.

Then the blind and the lame came to Jesus in the temple, and He healed them. According to *2 Samuel 5:8*, a saying arose that the blind and the lame would not enter the house. Jesus welcomed them. Children were shouting in the temple courts, “*Hosanna to the son of David!*” (*v. 15*) The chief priests and scribes were indignant and asked Jesus whether He heard what the children were saying. Jesus answered by quoting *Psalm 8:2*: “*Out of the mouth of children and nursing babies, you have perfected praise*” (*v. 16*). In that psalm, the praise is directed to God. Jesus was accepting praise that belongs to God. He then left the city and spent the night in Bethany, where His friends Mary, Martha, and Lazarus lived.

### The Fig Tree (*21:18–22*)

The next morning, as Jesus returned to the city, He was hungry. He saw a fig tree by the road with leaves but no fruit. Fig trees in that region often produced small early fruit along with their leaves, so a tree in full leaf suggested there should be something to eat. Finding nothing, Jesus said, “*Let there be no fruit from you forever!*” (*v. 19*) and the tree withered immediately.

This was an acted parable. In the Old Testament, the fig tree sometimes symbolized Israel (*Jeremiah 8:13*; *Hosea 9:10*; *Micah 7:1*). The tree had the appearance of life but no fruit, like the temple worship Jesus had just confronted: busy and impressive but lacking the fruit of genuine faithfulness. Jesus’ action warned of judgment on a religion that looks alive but produces nothing for God.

The disciples were amazed. Jesus told them that if they had faith and did not doubt, they could do even greater things, such as telling a mountain to be thrown into the sea. The “mountain” may have been a reference to the Mount of Olives or the temple mount itself. He added, “*All things, whatever you ask in prayer, believing, you will receive*” (*v. 22*). This promise is about prayer that trusts God fully, and it must be understood alongside Jesus’ other teaching that prayer seeks God’s will (*Matthew 6:10*; *26:39*). It is not a formula to obtain anything a person wants, but an encouragement to pray with confident dependence on God.

### The Question of Authority (*21:23–27*)

When Jesus returned to the temple and began teaching, the chief priests and elders challenged Him: “*By what authority do you do these things? Who gave you this authority?*” (*v. 23*) They were the official authorities over the temple, and Jesus had acted without their permission.

Jesus answered with a question: was John’s baptism from heaven or from human origin? The leaders discussed it among themselves. If they said “from heaven,” Jesus would ask why they had not believed John. If they said “from men,” they feared the crowd, who considered John a prophet. So they answered, “*We don’t know*” (*v. 27*). Jesus replied that He would not tell them by what authority He acted. His question was not a dodge. John had pointed to Jesus as the Coming One. If they had accepted John’s authority, they would have known the answer to their own question.

### The Parable of the Two Sons (*21:28–32*)

Jesus then told a parable. A man had two sons. He told the first to go work in the vineyard. The son said, “I will not,” but later changed his mind and went. The father told the second son the same thing. That son said, “I’m going, sir,” but did not go. Jesus asked which son did his father’s will. The leaders answered, “The first.”

Jesus applied the parable directly: “*the tax collectors and the prostitutes are entering into God’s Kingdom before you*” (*v. 31*). Tax collectors and prostitutes had openly lived in disobedience, like the first son’s initial refusal, but many had repented when John preached and believed him. The religious leaders had professed obedience to God, like the second son, but had not repented or believed. This parable is studied below.

### The Parable of the Tenants (*21:33–46*)

Jesus told another parable. A landowner planted a vineyard, put a wall around it, dug a winepress, and built a watchtower, details that echo *Isaiah 5:1–7*, where the vineyard represents Israel. He leased it to tenant farmers and went away. At harvest time, he sent servants to collect his share of the fruit. The tenants beat one, killed another, and stoned another. He sent more servants, and they did the same. Finally he sent his son, thinking, “*They will respect my son*” (*v. 37*). But the tenants said, “*This is the heir. Come, let’s kill him and seize his inheritance*” (*v. 38*). They threw him out of the vineyard and killed him.

Jesus asked what the owner would do. The leaders answered that he would destroy those evil men and lease the vineyard to others who would give him the fruit. Jesus then quoted *Psalm 118:22–23*: “*The stone which the builders rejected was made the head of the corner*” (*v. 42*). The “builders” were Israel’s leaders; the rejected stone was Jesus, who would become the cornerstone of God’s new work. He declared that God’s kingdom would be taken away from them and given to “*a nation producing its fruit*” (*v. 43*). Anyone who falls on this stone will be broken, and anyone on whom it falls will be crushed.

The meaning is clear in context. The servants represent the prophets God sent to Israel, many of whom were rejected and persecuted. The son represents Jesus Himself. The tenants are the religious leaders, who would soon kill Him. The “nation producing its fruit” refers to the community of all who follow Jesus, both Jews and Gentiles. This parable was directed at the leaders who rejected Jesus, not at the Jewish people as a whole; Jesus’ first followers were Jews. Christians have sometimes misused passages like this to justify contempt for Jewish people, which is a grave distortion of the text.

The chief priests and Pharisees realized He was talking about them. They wanted to arrest Him, but they feared the crowds, who considered Him a prophet.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Matthew 21:9* — “*Hosanna to the Son of David!*” (*v. 9*)

> *“The multitudes who went in front of him, and those who followed, kept shouting, ‘Hosanna to the son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest!’”*
>
> — *Matthew 21:9* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse records the shouts of the crowds as Jesus rode into Jerusalem on a donkey. Thousands of pilgrims were traveling to the city for Passover, the festival celebrating God’s deliverance of Israel from Egypt. Many had followed Jesus from Galilee and had seen His miracles, including the healing of two blind men at Jericho just before. As Jesus rode toward the city, the crowd in front and the crowd behind Him began to shout.

“Hosanna” is a Hebrew expression meaning “Save, please!” or “Save now!” It comes from *Psalm 118:25*. Over time, it had also become a shout of praise and celebration. The crowd shouted, “Hosanna to the son of David!” acknowledging Jesus as the Messiah, the heir of King David who would restore Israel’s kingdom.

“*Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!*” (*v. 9*) comes from *Psalm 118:26*. This psalm was sung by pilgrims as they approached Jerusalem and the temple, especially at Passover. Originally it may have been a blessing on the king or on worshipers entering the temple. Now the crowd applied it to Jesus. “In the name of the Lord” means coming with God’s authority, as His representative.

“*Hosanna in the highest!*” (*v. 9*) means something like “Save us, you who live in the highest heaven!” or “Praise in the highest!”

The crowd’s welcome expressed genuine hope that Jesus was the Messiah. But many likely expected Him to lead a political revolution against Rome. When Jesus did not do that, many turned against Him. Within days, a crowd in Jerusalem would be shouting, “Let him be crucified!” (*Matthew 27:22–23*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows Jesus publicly accepting the title of Messiah. For most of His ministry, He had avoided public declarations about His identity. Now, at the end, He deliberately fulfilled Zechariah’s prophecy and accepted the crowd’s praise. He was presenting Himself to Jerusalem as its King.

But Jesus was a different kind of king than many expected. He came humble, riding a donkey, not a war horse. He came to save, but not primarily from Rome. The crowd’s cry, “Save now!”, would be answered in a way they did not expect: through His death on the cross, where He would save His people from their sins (*Matthew 1:21*).

Christians have long used this verse in worship, especially on Palm Sunday, the Sunday before Easter. It reminds believers that Jesus is the King who comes in God’s name, and it invites them to welcome Him with praise. At the same time, it is a warning about the fickleness of enthusiasm. Praise that depends on Jesus fulfilling our expectations can quickly turn into rejection when He does not.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to welcome Jesus as King. Praising Him in worship is fitting and good. But true welcome goes beyond enthusiasm; it means accepting Him as the King He truly is, not the king we want Him to be.

It also calls believers to examine their expectations of Jesus. Many people follow Jesus hoping He will solve their problems in a particular way, bring them success, or align with their political views. When He does not meet those expectations, they may become disillusioned. Jesus came to save from sin and to establish God’s kingdom in His own way. Believers can trust Him even when His ways differ from their hopes.

Finally, the cry “Hosanna” (“Save now!”) can be a genuine prayer for believers. In times of need, they can call on Jesus as the Savior who came in God’s name. He hears that cry, and He has already accomplished the greatest salvation through the cross.

### *Matthew 21:13* — A House of Prayer

> *“He said to them, ‘It is written, “My house shall be called a house of prayer,” but you have made it a den of robbers!’”*
>
> — *Matthew 21:13* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus speaks these words after driving out the merchants and money changers from the temple courts. The temple in Jerusalem was the center of Jewish worship, the place where God’s presence was believed to dwell in a special way. Its outer court, the Court of the Gentiles, was the only area where non-Jews could come to pray to the God of Israel.

During Passover, this court was filled with people selling animals for sacrifice and changing money for the temple tax. Pilgrims needed animals that met the law’s requirements, and they needed the correct currency. But the trade had taken over the space meant for prayer, and some merchants exploited worshipers by charging excessive prices. Those selling doves, the sacrifice of the poor, were especially taking advantage of vulnerable people.

Jesus overturned their tables and drove them out. Then He quoted two passages from the prophets. The first was *Isaiah 56:7*: “*My house shall be called a house of prayer*” (*v. 13*). In Isaiah, the full verse says the temple would be a house of prayer “*for all peoples*” (*Isaiah 56:7*). God intended His house to be a place where all nations could come to pray. By filling the Court of the Gentiles with commerce, the temple authorities were blocking the very people God wanted to welcome.

The second quotation came from *Jeremiah 7:11*: “*but you have made it a den of robbers*” (*v. 13*). In Jeremiah’s time, the people of Judah practiced injustice and idolatry during the week and then came to the temple thinking they were safe because of it. Jeremiah warned that the temple had become like a cave where robbers hide after committing their crimes. God would judge it, and the first temple was destroyed by Babylon in 586 B.C. Jesus’ words carried the same warning.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals God’s purpose for worship: a place where people meet Him in prayer, open to all nations. It also reveals His anger at worship that has been corrupted by greed and exploitation. Religious activity can become a cover for injustice, and God takes this very seriously.

Jesus’ action also showed His authority over the temple. As the Son of God, He had the right to cleanse His Father’s house. This act anticipated His later teaching that He Himself would replace the temple as the place where people meet God (*John 2:19–21*). After His death and resurrection, the New Testament teaches that believers, individually and together, become God’s temple through the Holy Spirit (*1 Corinthians 3:16*; *6:19*). The temple in Jerusalem was destroyed by the Romans in A.D. 70, about forty years after Jesus’ warning.

Finally, Jesus’ cleansing of the temple shows that zeal for God can include righteous anger against injustice. Jesus was not out of control; His actions were deliberate and purposeful. His anger was directed at the exploitation of worshipers and the obstruction of prayer.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse calls churches and believers to keep worship centered on prayer and on God Himself. Churches can examine whether their activities, programs, or finances have crowded out prayer and genuine encounter with God. Worship should be a place where people meet God, not a place driven by commercial interests or personal gain.

It also calls for concern for outsiders. The Court of the Gentiles was meant for those outside Israel. Churches can ask whether they welcome outsiders, newcomers, the poor, and people from other cultures, or whether their practices make it hard for such people to come and worship.

Finally, this verse warns against using religion as a cover for wrongdoing. Believers can examine whether they practice dishonesty, exploitation, or injustice while maintaining an appearance of devotion. Jesus’ words call for integrity: worship and daily life must match. Since believers are now God’s temple, they can also ask whether their own lives are “houses of prayer,” places where God is honored rather than spaces filled with other priorities.

### *Matthew 21:31* — Doing the Father’s Will

> *“Which of the two did the will of his father? They said to him, ‘The first.’ Jesus said to them, Most certainly I tell you that the tax collectors and the prostitutes are entering into God’s Kingdom before you.”*
>
> — *Matthew 21:31* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse is Jesus’ application of the parable of the two sons. He told this parable to the chief priests and elders after they challenged His authority in the temple. They had refused to say whether John the Baptist’s ministry came from God, because either answer would expose them.

In the parable, a father asked his first son to work in the vineyard. The son refused but later changed his mind and went. The father asked the second son, who said, “I’m going, sir,” but never went. Jesus asked, “*Which of the two did the will of his father?*” (*v. 31*) The leaders answered correctly: “The first.” Words without action are worthless; action after repentance is what matters.

Then Jesus applied it: “*the tax collectors and the prostitutes are entering into God’s Kingdom before you*” (*v. 31*). Tax collectors were considered traitors and thieves; prostitutes were viewed as the most morally compromised members of society. Both groups had openly said “no” to God by their lifestyles. But when John the Baptist came preaching repentance, many of them believed him and changed. Like the first son, they had refused at first but then obeyed.

The religious leaders were like the second son. They said “yes” to God by their religious profession, careful observance, and positions of leadership. But when God sent John, they did not believe him. Even after seeing tax collectors and prostitutes repent, they still did not change their minds (v. 32).

The phrase “entering into God’s Kingdom before you” may mean “instead of you” or “ahead of you.” Either way, it was a shocking statement to religious leaders who assumed they were closest to God.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse teaches that God values genuine repentance and obedience over outward religious profession. Saying the right words, holding the right positions, or maintaining a respectable reputation does not make someone right with God. What matters is responding to God’s call with a changed heart and life. This echoes Jesus’ warning in *Matthew 7:21* that not everyone who says “*Lord, Lord*” (*Matthew 7:21*) will enter the kingdom, but only those who do the Father’s will.

It also shows the hope available to people with the worst reputations. Those whom society, and religious people, had written off were entering the kingdom. No past is too dark for God’s grace when someone truly repents. Throughout the Gospels, Jesus welcomed tax collectors and sinners, and many of them responded with faith.

At the same time, the verse is a warning to the religious. Familiarity with God’s things can harden the heart. The religious leaders had seen God’s work through John and through Jesus, and they still refused to repent. The greatest danger is not past sin but present refusal to turn to God.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse calls believers to examine whether their actions match their words. It is possible to sing, pray, and speak about obeying God while ignoring what He has clearly asked. Believers can ask where they have said “yes” to God without following through, whether in forgiving someone, serving others, giving generously, or changing a sinful habit.

It also encourages those who have said “no” to God in the past. Whatever someone’s history, they can still change their mind and obey. God welcomes those who repent, regardless of how long they have resisted.

Finally, this verse warns against spiritual pride. Believers can avoid looking down on people whose lives seem far from God, remembering that such people may respond to God’s grace more readily than those who are comfortable in their religion. Humility, repentance, and obedience are the marks of those who truly do the Father’s will.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Matthew 21* presents Jesus as the King who comes to His city and His temple, and it calls every reader to respond to Him. The crowds welcomed Him with praise but did not understand the kind of King He was. Believers can welcome Jesus with genuine worship while letting Him define His kingship. He is the humble King who brings peace and who saves through the cross, not a king who exists to fulfill our political or personal agendas.

The cleansing of the temple challenges the way worship and money mix. Jesus was angered that a place of prayer for all nations had become a marketplace that exploited the poor. Churches and believers can examine whether their worship is centered on God, whether they welcome outsiders, and whether their practices treat people fairly. Individual believers, as temples of the Holy Spirit, can also ask whether their lives are marked by prayer or crowded with other priorities.

The fig tree and the parables warn against religion that looks impressive but bears no fruit. The religious leaders had the appearance of devotion but rejected God’s messengers and His Son. Believers can look for evidence of genuine fruit in their lives: repentance, obedience, love, and faithfulness. Saying the right words is not enough; doing the Father’s will is what matters.

Finally, the chapter offers hope to those who have said “no” to God. Tax collectors and prostitutes were entering the kingdom because they repented and believed. No one is beyond God’s grace. At the same time, the chapter warns that rejecting Jesus, the cornerstone, has serious consequences. The right response is to receive Him as King, turn from sin, and bear the fruit of His kingdom.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, You are the humble King who came to Jerusalem riding on a donkey, bringing peace and salvation. I welcome You with praise, and I ask You to be the King You truly are in my life, not the king I would design for myself. Save me, Lord, and help me to trust Your ways when they are different from my expectations.

Cleanse my heart as You cleansed the temple. Remove the greed, distraction, and empty religion that crowd out prayer, and make my life a house of prayer. Help me and Your church to welcome people of every nation and background. Keep me from being like the son who said yes and did not go. Give me a repentant heart that turns to You and does the Father’s will. Thank You that tax collectors and sinners are welcomed into Your kingdom, and that Your grace reaches me too. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
