Matthew · Chapter 22 of 28

# Matthew — Chapter 22

Chapter Theme: Invited to the Feast, Tested in the Temple

[Read Matthew 22 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/MAT22.htm)

Main Teaching

Jesus tells a parable of a royal wedding feast to show that God’s invitation, rejected by many who were first invited, goes out to everyone, while still requiring a fitting response. In the temple courts, His opponents try to trap Him with questions about taxes, the resurrection, and the greatest commandment. Jesus answers each with wisdom that exposes their errors, summarizes the law as love for God and neighbor, and finally asks a question about the Messiah that no one can answer.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Matthew 22* continues the confrontation in the temple courts during the final week before Jesus’ death. In chapter 21, the chief priests and elders challenged Jesus’ authority, and He responded with parables about two sons and wicked tenants that exposed their rejection of God’s messengers. They wanted to arrest Him but feared the crowds. In chapter 22, Jesus tells one more parable, and then different groups of opponents come with questions designed to trap Him. Each attempt fails, and by the end of the chapter, no one dares ask Him anything more.

### The Parable of the Wedding Feast (*22:1–14*)

Jesus compared the kingdom of heaven to a king who prepared a wedding feast for his son. In the ancient Near East, a royal wedding feast was a grand occasion that could last for days. Invitations were typically sent twice: once well in advance, and then again when everything was ready. Refusing a king’s invitation after initially accepting was a serious insult.

The king sent his servants to call the invited guests, but they would not come. He sent more servants with a warm appeal: the dinner was prepared, the cattle were slaughtered, everything was ready. But the guests “*made light of it*” (*v. 5*) and went off to their farms and businesses. Others seized the servants, mistreated them, and killed them. The king was furious, sent his army, destroyed the murderers, and burned their city.

Then he told his servants to go to the main roads and invite everyone they found. They gathered “*both bad and good*” (*v. 10*), and the wedding hall was filled with guests. But when the king came in, he saw a man without wedding clothes. He asked, “*Friend, how did you come in here not wearing wedding clothing?*” (*v. 12*) The man was speechless. The king ordered him bound and thrown into the outer darkness. Jesus concluded, “*For many are called, but few chosen*” (*v. 14*).

The parable continues the themes of chapter 21. The king is God; the son is Jesus; the wedding feast represents the joy of God’s kingdom, a common image in Jewish hope (*Isaiah 25:6–9*). The first invited guests represent the religious leaders and those in Israel who rejected God’s call through the prophets, John, and Jesus. The destruction of the city may point to the destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans in A.D. 70, which many early Christians understood as a judgment connected with the rejection of Jesus. The invitation to everyone on the roads represents the gospel going out to all people, including sinners and Gentiles.

The man without wedding clothes shows that accepting the invitation requires a fitting response. Some interpreters suggest that hosts sometimes provided garments for guests, so refusing to wear one was an insult. Whether or not that custom applied, the point is that those who come to God’s feast must be transformed by His grace. Many interpreters connect the wedding garment with the righteousness that comes from God and shows itself in a changed life (compare *Revelation 19:8*). Being “called” means receiving the invitation; being “chosen” refers to those who truly respond and belong to God.

### Paying Taxes to Caesar (*22:15–22*)

The Pharisees then plotted to trap Jesus in His words. They sent their disciples together with the Herodians, supporters of Herod’s family who cooperated with Rome. These two groups normally opposed each other, but they united against Jesus. They began with flattery, praising His honesty and impartiality. Then they asked, “*Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not?*” (*v. 17*)

This was a carefully designed trap. The tax in question was the poll tax paid directly to the Roman emperor, which had sparked a revolt led by Judas the Galilean in A.D. 6. Many Jews hated it as a sign of foreign domination. If Jesus said “pay it,” He would lose the support of the crowds who resented Rome. If He said “don’t pay it,” the Herodians could report Him to the Romans as a rebel.

Jesus saw through their scheme and called them hypocrites. He asked to see the coin used for the tax. They brought a denarius, which showed it was in their possession. Jesus asked whose image and inscription were on it. They said, “Caesar’s.” The denarius of that time likely bore the image of Emperor Tiberius and an inscription calling him “son of the divine Augustus.” Jesus then said, “*Give therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s*” (*v. 21*). His opponents were amazed and left. This saying is studied below.

### The Question About the Resurrection (*22:23–33*)

That same day, the Sadducees came. Matthew explains that they “*say that there is no resurrection*” (*v. 23*). The Sadducees accepted only the first five books of Moses as authoritative and believed that those books did not teach resurrection. They presented a scenario based on the law of levirate marriage (*Deuteronomy 25:5–6*), which required a man to marry his brother’s widow if the brother died childless, to continue the family line. Seven brothers married the same woman in turn, each dying without children. In the resurrection, whose wife would she be? The Sadducees intended to show that the idea of resurrection was absurd.

Jesus answered, “*You are mistaken, not knowing the Scriptures, nor the power of God*” (*v. 29*). First, they misunderstood God’s power. In the resurrection, people will not marry, but will be like the angels. Life in the age to come is not simply a continuation of earthly life with the same arrangements; God will transform it. Second, they misunderstood the Scriptures. Jesus quoted from the books the Sadducees accepted, *Exodus 3:6*, where God says to Moses at the burning bush, “*I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob*” (*Exodus 3:6*). God spoke these words centuries after the patriarchs died, yet He said “I am,” not “I was.” “*God is not the God of the dead, but of the living*” (*v. 32*). Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are still alive to God, and their relationship with Him guarantees their future resurrection. The crowds were astonished.

### The Greatest Commandment (*22:34–40*)

When the Pharisees heard that Jesus had silenced the Sadducees, they gathered together. One of them, an expert in the law, asked Him a question to test Him: “*Teacher, which is the greatest commandment in the law?*” (*v. 36*) Jewish teachers counted 613 commandments in the law of Moses and often debated which were “heavy” and which were “light.”

Jesus answered by quoting *Deuteronomy 6:5*, the heart of the Shema, the confession of faith that devout Jews recited daily: “*You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind*” (*v. 37*). This is the first and greatest commandment. Then He added a second, like it, from *Leviticus 19:18*: “*You shall love your neighbor as yourself*” (*v. 39*). He concluded that all the Law and the Prophets depend on these two commandments. This is studied below.

### Whose Son Is the Messiah? (*22:41–46*)

While the Pharisees were still gathered, Jesus asked them a question: “*What do you think of the Christ? Whose son is he?*” (*v. 42*) They answered, “Of David,” which was the standard expectation. The Messiah would be a descendant of King David.

Jesus then asked how David, speaking by the Spirit, could call the Messiah “Lord” in *Psalm 110:1*: “*The Lord said to my Lord, sit on my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet*” (*v. 44*). In that psalm, “The LORD” (God) speaks to “my Lord” (the Messiah). In that culture, a father would not call his son “lord”; a son honored his father. If David called the Messiah “Lord,” then the Messiah must be more than David’s son. He must be greater than David.

The Pharisees could not answer. Jesus was pointing to His own identity: He is David’s son by human descent, but He is also David’s Lord, the Son of God who would sit at God’s right hand. *Psalm 110:1* became one of the most quoted Old Testament verses in the New Testament, used to describe Jesus’ exaltation after His resurrection (*Acts 2:34–36*; *Hebrews 1:13*). After this, no one dared ask Him any more questions.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Matthew 22:21* — Caesar’s and God’s

> *“They said to him, ‘Caesar’s.’ Then he said to them, ‘Give therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.’”*
>
> — *Matthew 22:21* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse contains Jesus’ answer to one of the most carefully planned traps of His ministry. The Pharisees and Herodians came together to ask whether it was lawful to pay taxes to Caesar. These groups had different views on Roman rule, but they united to test Jesus. The question seemed to have no safe answer. Saying “yes” would make Jesus appear to support foreign oppression and lose the crowd’s support. Saying “no” would make Him guilty of rebellion against Rome.

Jesus asked them to show Him the coin used to pay the tax. They brought a denarius, a Roman silver coin. Jesus asked whose image and inscription were on it. They answered, “Caesar’s.” The coin bore the image of Emperor Tiberius and likely an inscription calling him the son of the divine Augustus. Many devout Jews were troubled by such coins because of their claims of divinity and because images could be seen as violating the second commandment. The fact that Jesus’ questioners had one in their possession, even in the temple courts, was telling.

Jesus then said, “*Give therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s*” (*v. 21*). The word “give” here means “give back” or “pay what is owed.” Since the coin bears Caesar’s image and was produced by his government, it belongs to his sphere. Paying taxes is a legitimate obligation. But Jesus added that people must also give to God what belongs to Him.

This answer avoided both traps. Jesus affirmed that taxes should be paid, so He could not be accused of rebellion. But He also placed Caesar under God. Caesar’s coin was Caesar’s, but Caesar was not divine, and he had no claim on what belongs only to God. His opponents were amazed and went away.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse teaches that believers have real obligations to governing authorities, but those obligations are limited. Paul later explains that governments are established by God to maintain order and that Christians should pay taxes and give honor to those in authority (*Romans 13:1–7*). Peter also urges believers to honor the emperor (*1 Peter 2:17*). Yet both apostles also insisted on obeying God rather than human authorities when the two conflict (*Acts 5:29*).

The deeper point lies in the word “image.” The coin bore Caesar’s image, so it belonged to him. *Genesis 1:27* teaches that human beings are made in the image of God. If what bears Caesar’s image belongs to Caesar, then what bears God’s image, human beings themselves, belongs to God. Caesar can claim taxes, but God claims the whole person: heart, soul, mind, and strength.

This saying does not create two completely separate spheres, as if God has no interest in public life. Everything ultimately belongs to God (*Psalm 24:1*), and governments are accountable to Him. But it does mean that believers can participate in civic life and fulfill their responsibilities while recognizing that their ultimate loyalty belongs to God alone.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse calls believers to be responsible citizens. Paying taxes honestly, obeying just laws, and respecting those in authority are part of faithful living. Christian faith does not exempt believers from civic duties.

It also calls believers to keep their ultimate loyalty for God. No government, political party, nation, or leader deserves the devotion that belongs only to God. When political loyalties become all-consuming, or when governments demand what conflicts with God’s commands, believers must remember that they belong to God first.

Finally, this verse invites each believer to consider what they are giving to God. If they bear God’s image, then their lives belong to Him. That includes time, abilities, relationships, and resources. Jesus’ words challenge believers not only to pay what they owe to the state, but to give themselves wholly to God.

### *Matthew 22:32* — The God of the Living

> *““I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob”? God is not the God of the dead, but of the living.”*
>
> — *Matthew 22:32* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus speaks these words to the Sadducees, a group of religious leaders who denied the resurrection of the dead. They had tried to make the resurrection look ridiculous with a story about a woman who married seven brothers in turn, according to the law of levirate marriage. They asked whose wife she would be in the resurrection.

Jesus told them they were mistaken because they did not know the Scriptures or the power of God. He first explained that resurrection life is different from earthly life; people will not marry then. Then He turned to the Scriptures. The Sadducees accepted the five books of Moses as their highest authority, so Jesus quoted from *Exodus 3:6*, where God spoke to Moses from the burning bush: “*I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob*” (*v. 32*).

By the time God spoke these words to Moses, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob had been dead for centuries. Yet God did not say “I was their God” but “I am their God.” Jesus drew the conclusion: “*God is not the God of the dead, but of the living*” (*v. 32*). If God still identifies Himself as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, then they must still be alive in relationship with Him. And God’s covenant relationship with them, which included promises for their bodies and their descendants, requires that He will raise them.

The crowds who heard this were astonished. Jesus had answered the Sadducees from the very books they claimed to honor.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse teaches that God’s relationship with His people does not end at death. The covenant God makes with those who belong to Him is stronger than death. Those who die in faith are still alive to God, and they await the resurrection of the body. Luke’s account adds, “*for all are alive to him*” (*Luke 20:38*).

The verse also shows how Jesus read Scripture. He paid attention to the precise wording and to the character of God revealed in it. The God who calls Himself the God of Abraham would not abandon Abraham to permanent death. God’s faithfulness guarantees resurrection.

Jesus’ own resurrection, a few days after this conversation, would be the decisive proof. Paul says Christ “*became the first fruit of those who are asleep*” (*1 Corinthians 15:20*), the beginning of the great resurrection harvest. The Christian hope is not merely that the soul survives death, but that God will raise His people bodily, transforming them to share in His eternal life.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse brings comfort to those who have lost loved ones who trusted in God. Death is real and painful, but it does not end the relationship between God and His people. Believers who have died are alive to God, and they will be raised. Grief can be held together with hope.

It also shapes how believers face their own mortality. Because God is the God of the living, death is not the final word. Believers can live with courage and purpose, knowing that their future is secure in God’s faithfulness.

Finally, this verse encourages careful reading of Scripture. Jesus rebuked the Sadducees for not knowing the Scriptures or the power of God. Believers can study the Bible attentively and humbly, allowing it to correct their assumptions, and they can trust that God’s power is greater than their limited understanding.

### *Matthew 22:37–39* — Love God, Love Your Neighbor

> *“Jesus said to him, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind.” This is the first and great commandment. A second likewise is this, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.””*
>
> — *Matthew 22:37–39* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These verses contain Jesus’ answer to a question from an expert in the law. The Pharisees had gathered after Jesus silenced the Sadducees, and one of them asked Him which commandment in the law was the greatest. Jewish teachers often debated how to rank the many commandments of the law. The question may have been a test to see whether Jesus would downplay some part of the law.

Jesus answered by quoting *Deuteronomy 6:5*: “*You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind*” (*v. 37*). This verse was part of the Shema, the daily confession of faith that begins, “*Hear, Israel: the LORD is our God. The LORD is one*” (*Deuteronomy 6:4*). Every devout Jew knew these words. “Heart, soul, and mind” together mean the whole person: emotions, will, life, and thoughts. Love for God must involve every part of a person’s being. (Deuteronomy says “heart, soul, and might”; the other Gospels include both “mind” and “strength,” showing that the point is total devotion.)

Jesus said this is “*the first and great commandment*” (*v. 38*). Then He added a second that is “*likewise*” (*v. 39*), meaning similar in nature and importance: “*You shall love your neighbor as yourself*” (*v. 39*), from *Leviticus 19:18*. In Leviticus, “*neighbor*” (*Leviticus 19:18*) referred to fellow Israelites, but the same chapter also commands love for foreigners living among them (*Leviticus 19:34*), and Jesus expanded “neighbor” to include anyone in need, even enemies (*Luke 10:25–37*; *Matthew 5:44*).

In the next verse, Jesus says that all the Law and the Prophets depend on these two commandments, the way a door hangs on its hinges. Every other commandment in Scripture is an expression of love for God or love for neighbor.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses summarize the heart of God’s will for human life. God is not primarily interested in rule-keeping for its own sake; He desires love. The Ten Commandments themselves are divided into duties toward God and duties toward others. Paul writes, “*Love therefore is the fulfillment of the law*” (*Romans 13:10*).

The order matters. Love for God comes first. When God is loved above all, love for others flows from that relationship and is shaped by it. But the two cannot be separated. John writes that anyone who says he loves God but hates his brother is a liar (*1 John 4:20*). Love for God is shown in love for those made in His image.

These commands also reveal humanity’s need for grace. No one has loved God with all their heart, soul, and mind, or loved their neighbor perfectly as themselves. The commandments show the standard, and they reveal how far everyone falls short. Jesus alone fulfilled them perfectly, and through Him believers receive forgiveness and the Holy Spirit, who pours God’s love into their hearts (*Romans 5:5*) and enables them to love.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses offer a simple but demanding guide for daily life. Believers can ask, in any situation, “How can I love God here?” and “How can I love my neighbor here?” These questions apply to decisions about time, money, work, relationships, speech, and priorities.

Loving God with the whole heart, soul, and mind means worship that engages emotions, will, and intellect. It includes prayer, obedience, trusting Him in hardship, and thinking carefully about His Word. It means giving Him first place in every area of life.

Loving one’s neighbor as oneself means caring for others’ well-being with the same attention we naturally give our own. It includes kindness, honesty, generosity, patience, and forgiveness, and extends to people we find difficult, people different from us, and people in need. This love is not merely a feeling; it is expressed in practical action.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Matthew 22* begins with an invitation. God invites people to the joy of His kingdom, pictured as a royal wedding feast. Many reject the invitation because they are busy with other concerns, and some respond with hostility. But God extends the invitation to everyone, good and bad alike. Believers can receive this invitation with gratitude and share it widely, knowing that God welcomes people from every background. At the same time, the man without wedding clothes reminds them that accepting God’s invitation means being transformed by His grace, not continuing as though nothing has changed.

The questions in the temple courts show Jesus’ wisdom and challenge believers in practical ways. The question about taxes teaches that believers have real responsibilities to governing authorities, but their ultimate loyalty belongs to God, in whose image they are made. Believers can be good citizens without giving any government or political cause the devotion that belongs to God alone.

The question about the resurrection reminds believers that God is the God of the living. Death does not end the relationship between God and His people, and the hope of resurrection can sustain believers in grief and in the face of their own mortality. It also challenges believers to know the Scriptures and trust God’s power.

At the center of the chapter is the greatest commandment: love God with all your heart, soul, and mind, and love your neighbor as yourself. This summary of God’s will can guide every part of life. Believers can measure their priorities, decisions, and relationships by these two commandments, and when they fall short, they can turn to Jesus, who fulfilled them perfectly, and ask for His Spirit to fill them with love.

## Chapter Prayer

Gracious King, thank You for inviting me to the feast of Your kingdom. Forgive me for the times I have been too busy or distracted to respond to Your call. Clothe me with the righteousness You provide, and change my life so that it fits the grace I have received. Help me to share Your invitation with everyone, knowing that You welcome people from every road.

Teach me to fulfill my responsibilities to those in authority while giving my whole self to You, because I bear Your image. Thank You that You are the God of the living, and that those who trust in You are alive to You even in death. Strengthen my hope in the resurrection. Above all, help me to love You with all my heart, soul, and mind, and to love my neighbor as myself. Where I fall short, fill me with Your Spirit and Your love. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Matthew · Chapter 23 of 28

# Matthew — Chapter 23

Chapter Theme: Warnings Against Hypocrisy and the Lament Over Jerusalem

[Read Matthew 23 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/MAT23.htm)

Main Teaching

In His final public teaching, Jesus warns the crowds and His disciples about religious leaders who teach God’s law but do not live it, who seek honor, burden others, and focus on small details while neglecting justice, mercy, and faithfulness. He pronounces a series of woes on their hypocrisy, then grieves over Jerusalem with the heart of a mother hen longing to gather her chicks, warning that their house will be left desolate.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Matthew 23* is Jesus’ last public address in Matthew’s Gospel. It comes at the end of a series of confrontations in the temple courts during His final week (*Matthew 21–22*). The chief priests, elders, Pharisees, Sadducees, and Herodians had all tried to trap Him, and each time He silenced them. Now Jesus turns to the crowds and His disciples and speaks openly about the scribes and Pharisees. After this chapter, He leaves the temple for the last time (*Matthew 24:1*).

It is important to read this chapter carefully. Jesus’ sharp words are aimed at the hypocrisy of particular religious leaders who were opposing Him, not at Jewish people as a whole or even at every Pharisee. Some Pharisees were sincere seekers, such as Nicodemus (*John 3*) and Joseph of Arimathea, and Paul himself was a Pharisee before following Christ. Christians have sometimes misused this chapter to fuel prejudice against Jewish people, which is a terrible distortion. The warnings here apply to religious hypocrisy wherever it is found, including in the church.

### Practice What They Preach, Not What They Do (*23:1–12*)

Jesus began, “*The scribes and the Pharisees sit on Moses’ seat*” (*v. 2*). In synagogues, a special stone chair was sometimes reserved for the teacher who read and explained the law of Moses. “Sitting on Moses’ seat” meant having the role of teaching the law. Jesus told the people to observe what they taught, insofar as it faithfully conveyed God’s law, but not to follow their example, because “*they say, and don’t do*” (*v. 3*).

He gave several examples. They tied up heavy burdens, rules and requirements, and laid them on others without lifting a finger to help. They did their works to be seen. They made their “*phylacteries*” (*v. 5*) broad and lengthened the tassels on their garments. Phylacteries were small leather boxes containing Scripture passages, worn on the forehead and arm in obedience to *Deuteronomy 6:8*. Tassels were worn on the corners of garments according to *Numbers 15:38–39*. Both were meant to remind the wearer of God’s commands, but some made them larger to display their devotion. They loved the places of honor at banquets, the best seats in the synagogues, respectful greetings in the marketplaces, and being called “Rabbi,” meaning “my great one” or “teacher.”

Jesus told His disciples not to seek such titles. They should not be called “Rabbi,” because they have one Teacher, the Christ, and they are all brothers. They should call no one on earth “father” in the sense of a spiritual authority who replaces God, because they have one Father in heaven. They should not be called “masters” or “instructors,” because they have one Master, the Christ. Jesus was not banning ordinary uses of these words (Paul calls himself a spiritual father in *1 Corinthians 4:15*), but warning against titles that elevate some believers over others and take honor that belongs to God.

He concluded with the principle He had taught before: “*But he who is greatest among you will be your servant*” (*v. 11*). Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.

### The Seven Woes (*23:13–36*)

Jesus then pronounced a series of “woes.” A woe is a solemn declaration of grief and coming judgment, used often by the Old Testament prophets (*Isaiah 5:8–23*). It expresses both sorrow and warning. (The WEB places one woe as verse 13 about devouring widows’ houses; this verse is not found in many early manuscripts of Matthew and appears in *Mark 12:40* and *Luke 20:47*.)

The first woe concerns shutting the kingdom of heaven in people’s faces. The religious leaders did not enter themselves, and by their teaching and opposition to Jesus they kept others from entering. The next concerns their zeal for converts. They would travel over land and sea to make one convert, a Gentile who became a full Jewish proselyte, but then make that person “*twice as much a son of Gehenna*” (*v. 15*) as themselves, passing on their own legalism and hypocrisy.

Another woe addresses their rules about oaths. They taught that swearing by the temple meant nothing, but swearing by the gold of the temple was binding; swearing by the altar meant nothing, but swearing by the gift on the altar was binding. These distinctions created loopholes for dishonesty. Jesus called them “*blind fools*” (*v. 17*), pointing out that the temple makes the gold holy and the altar makes the gift holy, and that all oaths are ultimately made before God. This echoes His teaching in *Matthew 5:33–37* about simple truthfulness.

The next woe concerns tithing. The law required giving a tenth of the harvest (*Leviticus 27:30*; *Deuteronomy 14:22*). The Pharisees tithed even small garden herbs like mint, dill, and cumin, but neglected “*the weightier matters of the law: justice, mercy, and faith*” (*v. 23*). Jesus said they should have practiced the latter without neglecting the former. He compared them to people who carefully strain a tiny gnat out of their drink (gnats were unclean under the food laws) but swallow a camel, the largest unclean animal. This woe is studied below.

Two woes contrast outward appearance with inner reality. They cleaned the outside of the cup and dish, but inside they were full of greed and self-indulgence. Jesus told them to clean the inside first, and the outside would also be clean. They were like “*whitened tombs*” (*v. 27*). Before Passover, tombs were often painted with whitewash so that pilgrims would not accidentally touch them and become ritually unclean (*Numbers 19:16*). The tombs looked clean and bright on the outside, but inside they were full of dead bones. In the same way, the leaders appeared righteous outwardly but were full of hypocrisy and lawlessness inside.

The final woe concerns the tombs of the prophets. The leaders built and decorated monuments to prophets whom earlier generations had killed, and they claimed they would never have done such things. But by plotting against Jesus, they were showing that they were truly the descendants of those who killed the prophets. Jesus said, “*Fill up, then, the measure of your fathers*” (*v. 32*), meaning they would complete their ancestors’ sin by rejecting and killing Him. He called them “*You serpents, you offspring of vipers*” (*v. 33*), the same words John the Baptist had used (*Matthew 3:7*).

Jesus said He would send prophets, wise men, and teachers, His own messengers, and they would kill some, crucify some, flog some in synagogues, and pursue others from town to town. The book of Acts records such persecution. All the righteous blood shed on earth, from Abel (the first murder victim, *Genesis 4*) to Zechariah (whose murder in the temple court is recorded in *2 Chronicles 24:20–22*, the last book in the traditional order of the Hebrew Bible), would come upon this generation. In other words, the whole history of rejecting God’s messengers was reaching its climax in the rejection of His Son. (Matthew calls Zechariah “son of Barachiah,” while 2 Chronicles calls him the son of Jehoiada; scholars have offered several explanations, including that Jehoiada was his grandfather or that two figures are being linked.)

### The Lament Over Jerusalem (*23:37–39*)

The chapter ends not with anger but with grief. Jesus cried out, “*Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to her!*” (*v. 37*) He longed to gather the city’s children together as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, but they were not willing. As a result, “*your house is left to you desolate*” (*v. 38*). “Your house” likely refers to the temple, and perhaps to the city as a whole. About forty years later, in A.D. 70, the Romans destroyed the temple and much of Jerusalem.

Jesus concluded that they would not see Him again until they said, “*Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!*” (*v. 39*), the words of *Psalm 118:26* that the crowds had shouted at His entry into Jerusalem. This may point to His return, when He will be recognized as Lord. Paul expresses hope for Israel’s future turning to Christ (*Romans 11:25–27*), and many interpreters see that hope reflected here. These words close Jesus’ public ministry with both judgment and a door of hope left open.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Matthew 23:11–12* — Greatness Through Humble Service

> *“But he who is greatest among you will be your servant. Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.”*
>
> — *Matthew 23:11–12* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These verses conclude the first part of Jesus’ teaching in this chapter, where He warns the crowds and His disciples about the behavior of the scribes and Pharisees. Jesus has just described how these leaders loved public recognition: wearing enlarged phylacteries and long tassels, taking the best seats at banquets and in synagogues, receiving respectful greetings in public, and being called “Rabbi.” Their religion had become a way of gaining honor.

Jesus told His disciples not to seek such titles and recognition, because they have only one Teacher, one Father, and one Master. They are all brothers and sisters, equals before God. Then He gave the principle that should guide them: “*But he who is greatest among you will be your servant*” (*v. 11*).

This repeats what Jesus taught just days earlier when James and John asked for the best positions in His kingdom (*Matthew 20:26–28*). Greatness in God’s kingdom is measured not by status, titles, or honor, but by humble service to others.

Verse 12 adds a promise and a warning: “*Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted*” (*v. 12*). Those who promote themselves and seek honor will eventually be brought low, whether in this life or at the final judgment. Those who humble themselves will be lifted up by God. This principle appears often in Scripture, from *Proverbs 29:23* to *James 4:10*.

The scribes and Pharisees in Jesus’ day were respected and honored. His disciples were mostly ordinary people with no status. Jesus was telling them not to envy or imitate the leaders’ pursuit of honor, but to follow a different path.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses describe a reversal that runs throughout Scripture. Mary sang that God “*has put down princes from their thrones, and has exalted the lowly*” (*Luke 1:52*). Jesus taught that the last will be first and the first last. This reversal reflects God’s character: He opposes the proud and gives grace to the humble.

Jesus is the supreme example of this principle. Though He was the Son of God, He humbled Himself to become a servant and died on a cross. Paul writes that because of this, “*God also highly exalted him*” (*Philippians 2:9*). The path to exaltation in God’s kingdom always passes through humility.

These verses also warn against the danger of religious leadership becoming a platform for pride. Those who teach and lead God’s people can easily begin to seek honor and recognition. Jesus calls leaders to remember that they are servants and that all believers are equals before God.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses call believers to examine their desire for recognition. It is natural to want to be noticed, respected, and honored. But Jesus calls His followers to find their worth in God’s approval, not in human praise. Believers can ask whether they serve in order to be seen and whether they feel hurt when their contributions go unrecognized.

They also encourage believers to look for ways to serve others, especially in tasks that are not glamorous or noticed. Serving in humble ways, helping those who cannot return the favor, and putting others’ needs first reflect the character of Christ.

Finally, these verses offer encouragement to those who serve faithfully without recognition. God sees and will honor them. Humility is not a loss; it is the path God blesses. Believers can trust that God will lift them up in His time and in His way.

### *Matthew 23:23* — Justice, Mercy, and Faithfulness

> *“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you tithe mint, dill, and cumin, and have left undone the weightier matters of the law: justice, mercy, and faith. But you ought to have done these, and not to have left the other undone.”*
>
> — *Matthew 23:23* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse is one of the woes Jesus pronounced on the scribes and Pharisees. It focuses on how they practiced the law of tithing. The law of Moses required Israelites to give a tenth of their produce, such as grain, wine, and oil, to support the Levites and the temple (*Deuteronomy 14:22–29*). The Pharisees applied this command with great care, even tithing small herbs grown in their gardens: “*mint, dill, and cumin*” (*v. 23*). They would count out one leaf of every ten to give to God.

Jesus did not criticize their careful tithing in itself. He said they ought to do it. The problem was that they “*have left undone the weightier matters of the law: justice, mercy, and faith*” (*v. 23*). “Weightier” means more important, more central. “Justice” means fairness and right treatment of others, especially the poor and powerless. “Mercy” means compassion and kindness, especially toward those in need. “Faith” can also be translated “faithfulness,” meaning loyalty to God and trustworthiness in relationships.

These three qualities echo the prophet Micah, who said that God requires His people “*to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God*” (*Micah 6:8*). The prophets often condemned Israel for keeping religious rituals while neglecting justice and compassion.

Jesus followed this with a vivid image: “*You blind guides, who strain out a gnat, and swallow a camel!*” (*v. 24*) Strict Pharisees would strain wine through cloth to make sure no tiny gnat, an unclean insect, got into their drink. Yet they were “swallowing” a camel, the largest unclean animal, by neglecting justice and mercy. The exaggeration made the point unforgettable.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse teaches that God’s commands are not all equal in weight. Some matters are central to God’s heart, and others are secondary. Faithful obedience pays attention to small things, but never at the expense of the great things. The center of God’s law is love for God and neighbor (*Matthew 22:37–40*), expressed through justice, mercy, and faithfulness.

It also shows how religious people can lose sight of what matters most. Careful attention to rules can give a sense of righteousness while the heart grows cold toward people. This danger is not limited to the Pharisees; it affects every religious tradition, including Christian churches. People can be precise about doctrine, worship styles, or personal habits while neglecting the poor, treating others unfairly, or being unkind.

At the same time, Jesus’ words, “*But you ought to have done these, and not to have left the other undone*” (*v. 23*), show that He did not dismiss the smaller matters. Faithfulness in small things is good. The problem is when small things replace the weightier ones.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse calls believers to examine their priorities. Are they careful about the details of religious practice but neglectful of justice, mercy, and faithfulness? Believers can ask whether they treat others fairly in business and work, whether they show compassion to people in need, and whether they are trustworthy in their relationships and commitments.

It also encourages believers to care about justice in their communities. This includes treating employees fairly, paying debts, being honest in dealings, standing up for those who are mistreated, and supporting efforts to help the poor and vulnerable.

Finally, the image of straining out a gnat while swallowing a camel invites believers to notice where they major on minor issues. Churches and individuals can become consumed with secondary matters, arguing over small differences while neglecting love, mercy, and the needs of the world. Keeping the “weightier matters” at the center helps believers keep a right perspective.

### *Matthew 23:37* — The Mother Hen’s Lament

> *“Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to her! How often I would have gathered your children together, even as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you would not!”*
>
> — *Matthew 23:37* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse comes at the very end of Jesus’ public teaching, right after His long series of woes against the scribes and Pharisees. Having spoken sharply about their hypocrisy and warned of judgment, Jesus now expresses deep grief over Jerusalem.

“*Jerusalem, Jerusalem*” (*v. 37*). The repetition of the name expresses strong emotion, like David’s lament over his son: “*Absalom, my son, my son*” (*2 Samuel 18:33*). Jerusalem was the holy city, the place where God had chosen to put His name and where the temple stood. Yet Jesus describes it as the city “*who kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to her*” (*v. 37*). Throughout Israel’s history, prophets sent by God had been rejected and sometimes killed in Jerusalem. Jeremiah was threatened with death there; Zechariah was stoned in the temple court (*2 Chronicles 24:21*). Now the city was about to reject and kill God’s own Son.

Then Jesus uses a tender image: “*How often I would have gathered your children together, even as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you would not!*” (*v. 37*) A mother hen spreads her wings over her chicks to protect them from danger, such as a predator or fire, even at the cost of her own life. The Old Testament uses similar language for God’s protection: “*He will cover you with his feathers. Under his wings you will take refuge*” (*Psalm 91:4*). Jesus speaks as God would speak, longing to protect and gather His people.

“How often” suggests that Jesus had repeatedly sought to gather Jerusalem, through His own ministry and through the prophets who came before. But the response was, “you would not.” The people were unwilling.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals the heart of God toward those who reject Him. Jesus had just pronounced severe judgment, but His words were not those of a harsh judge eager to condemn. They came from a grieving heart that longed to save. God’s judgment is real, but it is never His first desire. Through Ezekiel, God said, “*I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live*” (*Ezekiel 33:11*).

The verse also shows the reality of human responsibility. Jesus wanted to gather Jerusalem, “and you would not.” God does not force people into His care. Those who refuse His invitation bear responsibility for their choice. The following verse warns that their house would be left desolate, a prediction fulfilled in the destruction of the temple in A.D. 70.

Finally, the image of the mother hen points toward the cross. A hen protects her chicks by covering them with her own body. Jesus would soon give His life to protect and save His people. His willingness to gather them meant His willingness to die for them.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites anyone who has been resisting God to come under His protection. Jesus’ longing to gather Jerusalem shows His longing to gather every person. Whatever someone’s history of rejecting God, His invitation remains open. The question is whether they will be willing.

It also shapes how believers view people who reject God. Jesus grieved over Jerusalem rather than gloating over its coming judgment. Believers can approach those who reject the faith with compassion and prayer rather than anger or contempt. Even when they must speak hard truths, they can do so with a grieving heart that longs for others to come to God.

Finally, this image offers comfort to believers. Those who come to Jesus find shelter under His wings. In times of danger, fear, or uncertainty, believers can rest in His protection, trusting that the One who gave His life for them will keep them safe in His care.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Matthew 23* is a sobering chapter that challenges anyone involved in religious life. Jesus’ warnings were aimed at leaders who taught God’s law but did not live it, who sought honor and recognition, who burdened others without helping them, and who focused on small rules while neglecting justice, mercy, and faithfulness. These temptations are present in every generation and every church. Believers, and especially those who teach or lead, can examine themselves honestly in light of Jesus’ words.

The chapter calls for integrity, the match between what one says and what one does. Hypocrisy is dangerous because it deceives others and the hypocrite himself. Believers can ask God to show them where their outward life does not match their inner reality and to cleanse them from the inside out. Being the same person in private as in public is a mark of genuine faith.

The chapter also calls for humility and service. The desire for titles, recognition, and the best seats is common, but Jesus teaches that greatness comes through serving others. Churches can reflect this by treating all believers as brothers and sisters, refusing to build hierarchies of prestige, and honoring humble service.

Jesus’ emphasis on justice, mercy, and faithfulness reminds believers of what matters most to God. Careful religious practices are good, but they must never replace fairness, compassion, and trustworthiness. Finally, the lament over Jerusalem shows that God’s warnings come from a heart of love. Jesus longs to gather people under His protection. Believers can respond to His invitation, find shelter in Him, and share His compassion with those who are still resisting.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, You see past outward appearances to the heart. Forgive me for the times I have said one thing and done another, sought recognition for my service, or placed burdens on others without helping them. Cleanse me from the inside out, so that my private life matches what I profess in public.

Teach me to serve humbly rather than seek honor, remembering that I have one Teacher, one Father, and one Master. Help me not to strain out gnats while swallowing camels, but to give my attention to justice, mercy, and faithfulness. Thank You for Your heart that grieves over those who reject You and longs to gather them like a mother hen gathers her chicks. Gather me under Your wings, and give me Your compassion for those who are still far from You. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Matthew · Chapter 24 of 28

# Matthew — Chapter 24

Chapter Theme: Watchful and Faithful Until the Son of Man Comes

[Read Matthew 24 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/MAT24.htm)

Main Teaching

As Jesus leaves the temple, He predicts its destruction, and His disciples ask when this will happen and what will signal His coming and the end of the age. Jesus warns them not to be deceived, prepares them for wars, persecution, and the coming devastation of Jerusalem, and describes His glorious return. Because no one knows the day or hour, His followers must stay alert and remain faithful in their responsibilities until He comes.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Matthew 24–25* make up the fifth and final major teaching section in Matthew, often called the Olivet Discourse because Jesus delivered it on the Mount of Olives. It follows directly from chapter 23, where Jesus ended His public ministry by lamenting over Jerusalem and declaring, “*Behold, your house is left to you desolate*” (*Matthew 23:38*). Now He leaves the temple for the last time.

This is one of the most debated chapters in the Bible, and readers should approach it with care and humility. Jesus’ words address two connected events: the destruction of the Jerusalem temple, which happened in A.D. 70 when Roman armies under Titus besieged and burned the city, and His own return at the end of the age. Christians interpret the relationship between these two events in different ways. Some (often called preterists) believe that most of the chapter, through verse 34, was fulfilled in the events of A.D. 70. Others (futurists) believe that much of it describes events still to come before Christ’s return. Many interpreters hold a combined view: that Jesus’ words had a first fulfillment in A.D. 70 and point forward to a final fulfillment at the end of history. Whatever view one takes, the chapter’s main practical teaching is clear: do not be deceived, endure faithfully, and be ready.

### The Prediction and the Question (*24:1–3*)

As Jesus left the temple, His disciples pointed out its buildings. Herod the Great had begun a massive renovation of the temple around 20 B.C., and work was still continuing. The temple complex was one of the wonders of the ancient world, built with enormous white stones, some over forty feet long, and decorated with gold. The Jewish historian Josephus wrote that from a distance it looked like a mountain covered with snow.

Jesus answered, “*there will not be left here one stone on another, that will not be thrown down*” (*v. 2*). This was a shocking prediction. About forty years later, the Romans destroyed the temple so completely that only parts of its retaining walls remained, including the section known today as the Western Wall.

Later, as Jesus sat on the Mount of Olives overlooking the temple, the disciples asked privately, “*Tell us, when will these things be? What is the sign of your coming, and of the end of the age?*” (*v. 3*) They may have assumed that the destruction of the temple and the end of the world would happen together. Jesus’ answer addresses both.

### Do Not Be Deceived (*24:4–14*)

Jesus began with a warning: “*Be careful that no one leads you astray*” (*v. 4*). Many would come claiming to be the Messiah and would deceive many. They would hear of wars and rumors of wars, but these should not alarm them; such things must happen, but “*the end is not yet*” (*v. 6*). Nations would fight, and there would be famines and earthquakes. These were only “*the beginning of birth pains*” (*v. 8*). In Jewish thought, the “birth pains of the Messiah” were troubles expected before the arrival of the new age. Jesus’ point was that disasters are not signs that the end has immediately arrived; they are part of the long, painful process leading to it.

His followers would be persecuted, hated by all nations because of His name, and some would be killed. Many would fall away, betray one another, and hate each other. False prophets would mislead many. Because lawlessness would increase, “*the love of many will grow cold*” (*v. 12*). But “*he who endures to the end will be saved*” (*v. 13*). Meanwhile, the gospel of the kingdom would be preached throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations, and then the end would come.

### The Abomination of Desolation and the Great Distress (*24:15–28*)

Jesus then spoke of “*the abomination of desolation*” (*v. 15*), a phrase from Daniel (*Daniel 9:27*; *11:31*; *12:11*). In Daniel, it referred to a desecration of the temple. Many Jews saw an early fulfillment in 167 B.C., when the Greek king Antiochus IV Epiphanes set up an altar to Zeus in the temple and sacrificed a pig on it. Jesus said that something similar would happen again. Luke’s parallel says, “*But when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, then know that its desolation is at hand*” (*Luke 21:20*), which suggests that the Roman siege of Jerusalem was in view. The phrase “let the reader understand” calls readers to pay attention.

When this happened, those in Judea should flee to the mountains immediately. Someone on a housetop (flat roofs were used as living space) should not go inside to get possessions; someone in the field should not go back for a cloak. Jesus expressed special compassion for pregnant women and nursing mothers, for whom flight would be especially difficult, and told His followers to pray that their flight would not be in winter, when travel was harder, or on a Sabbath, when traveling was restricted and gates might be closed. According to the early church historian Eusebius, Christians in Jerusalem heeded such a warning and fled to Pella, east of the Jordan, before the city’s destruction.

Jesus described “*great suffering, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now*” (*v. 21*). Josephus records the horrors of the siege of Jerusalem, including starvation, internal violence, and the deaths of hundreds of thousands. Many interpreters believe Jesus’ words also point beyond A.D. 70 to a final time of tribulation before His return. For the sake of the chosen, those days would be shortened.

He warned again about false messiahs and false prophets who would perform great signs to deceive even the chosen, if possible. If anyone said the Messiah was in the wilderness or in an inner room, they should not believe it. His coming would not be secret: “*For as the lightning flashes from the east, and is seen even to the west, so will the coming of the Son of Man be*” (*v. 27*). It would be unmistakable and visible to all.

### The Coming of the Son of Man (*24:29–31*)

“*But immediately after the suffering of those days*” (*v. 29*), the sun would be darkened, the moon would not give light, the stars would fall, and the powers of heaven would be shaken. This language comes from Old Testament prophecies of God’s judgment (*Isaiah 13:10*; *34:4*; *Joel 2:10*). Some interpreters understand it as symbolic language for the collapse of earthly powers; others take it as describing literal cosmic events at the end of history.

Then “*the sign of the Son of Man will appear in the sky*” (*v. 30*), and all the peoples of the earth would mourn. They would see the Son of Man coming on the clouds with power and great glory, language from *Daniel 7:13–14*. He would send His angels with a loud trumpet call to gather His chosen ones from the four winds. This describes Jesus’ return in glory to gather His people.

### The Lesson of the Fig Tree (*24:32–35*)

Jesus told His disciples to learn from the fig tree. When its branches become tender and its leaves appear, summer is near. In the same way, when they saw “all these things,” they would know that He was near, right at the door. He added, “*this generation will not pass away until all these things are accomplished*” (*v. 34*). This verse is part of the debate about the chapter. Those who see much of it as fulfilled in A.D. 70 note that this happened within a generation of Jesus’ words. Others suggest “generation” means the kind of people or the generation that sees the final signs. Jesus then affirmed, “*Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away*” (*v. 35*).

### No One Knows the Day or Hour (*24:36–51*)

Jesus then emphasized that the exact time of His coming is unknown: “*But no one knows of that day and hour, not even the angels of heaven, but my Father only*” (*v. 36*). This is studied below.

He compared His coming to the days of Noah. People were going about ordinary life, eating, drinking, and marrying, until the flood came and swept them away. They did not expect it. So it will be when the Son of Man comes. Two men will be in the field; one will be taken and one left. Two women will be grinding grain; one will be taken and one left. These images show that His coming will divide people suddenly. (Interpreters differ on whether “taken” means taken in judgment, as the flood “took them all away,” or taken to be with Christ.)

Therefore, Jesus said, keep watch. If a homeowner knew when a thief was coming, he would stay awake. Since no one knows when Christ will come, His followers must always be ready.

Finally, Jesus told a parable about a servant put in charge of a household. If the master returns and finds him faithfully caring for the household, the master will reward him. But if the servant thinks, “*My lord is delaying his coming*” (*v. 48*), and begins to abuse his fellow servants and live carelessly, the master will come unexpectedly and punish him severely. The final words describe the fate of hypocrites.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Matthew 24:4* — Do Not Be Led Astray

> *“Jesus answered them, Be careful that no one leads you astray.”*
>
> — *Matthew 24:4* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These are Jesus’ first words in response to His disciples’ question about when the temple would be destroyed and what would be the sign of His coming and the end of the age. The disciples wanted information about timing and signs. Jesus began not with a timetable but with a warning: “*Be careful that no one leads you astray*” (*v. 4*).

To be “led astray” means to be deceived, misled, or caused to wander from the truth. Jesus immediately explained the danger: “*For many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am the Christ,’ and will lead many astray*” (*v. 5*). In the decades after Jesus’ ascension, several men did claim to be messiahs or prophets and led followers into failed revolts against Rome. The book of Acts mentions Theudas and Judas the Galilean (*Acts 5:36–37*) and an Egyptian who led thousands into the wilderness (*Acts 21:38*).

Jesus repeated this warning throughout the chapter. False prophets would arise and deceive many (v. 11). False messiahs would perform great signs (v. 24). People would claim that Christ was in the wilderness or in secret rooms (v. 26). Deception is the danger Jesus mentions most often in this discourse.

He also warned against misinterpreting world events. Wars, famines, and earthquakes would happen, but they would not mean the end had come. People in every generation have been tempted to see current events as proof that the end is immediately at hand. Jesus told His disciples not to be alarmed or misled by such interpretations.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that one of the greatest threats to faith is deception. Persecution can harm the body, but deception can lead people away from Christ. Paul similarly warned about those who would come in with false teaching (*Acts 20:29–30*), and John wrote that many antichrists had already appeared (*1 John 2:18*).

The verse also shows that Jesus cared more about His disciples’ faithfulness than about satisfying their curiosity. He did give information about future events, but His main concern was that they would remain faithful and not be misled. The purpose of biblical prophecy is not to provide material for speculation but to prepare God’s people to live faithfully.

Finally, Jesus’ warning reveals that deception often comes “in my name.” False teachers and false messiahs use Jesus’ name and Christian language. This means believers need discernment, testing teaching and claims by Scripture and by the character of Christ.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse calls believers to be discerning. Many voices claim to speak for God, offer new revelations, predict the date of Christ’s return, or promise special knowledge. Believers can test such claims by comparing them with Scripture and with the teaching of Jesus and the apostles. Any teaching that contradicts the clear message of the Bible, or that sets dates for Christ’s return, should be rejected.

It also calls believers not to be alarmed by world events. Wars, disasters, and crises are painful and real, and believers should respond to them with compassion and prayer. But they should not let fear or speculation take over. Jesus said, “*See that you aren’t troubled*” (*v. 6*).

Finally, the best protection against deception is knowing Jesus and His Word well. Regular reading of Scripture, participation in a faithful church, and humility before God help believers recognize what is true and resist what is false.

### *Matthew 24:36* — No One Knows the Day or Hour

> *“But no one knows of that day and hour, not even the angels of heaven, but my Father only.”*
>
> — *Matthew 24:36* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus speaks these words after describing His glorious return and telling His disciples to learn from the fig tree. He has spoken of signs and events that would precede the end. Now He makes clear that, despite these signs, the exact time of His coming cannot be known.

“*But no one knows of that day and hour*” (*v. 36*). “That day” refers to the day of His return. Jesus says plainly that no human being knows when it will be. Then He adds, “*not even the angels of heaven*” (*v. 36*). Even the angels, who stand in God’s presence, do not know. Mark’s Gospel also adds “*nor the Son*” (*Mark 13:32*), and many manuscripts of Matthew include those words too. Christians have understood this to mean that during His earthly life, in His humanity, Jesus voluntarily limited His knowledge, so that this particular knowledge belonged to the Father alone. “*but my Father only*” (*v. 36*).

Jesus followed this statement with the example of Noah. People before the flood were living normal lives, eating, drinking, and marrying, with no awareness of the coming judgment until it arrived. Christ’s return will come in the same unexpected way.

This verse would have been surprising to disciples who wanted a timeline. Jesus did not give one. Instead, He told them to be ready at all times.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse teaches that the timing of Christ’s return belongs to God alone. Throughout history, many people have tried to calculate the date of Jesus’ return, often causing confusion, disappointment, and damage to the church’s witness. Jesus’ clear words rule out such date-setting. Before His ascension, Jesus told His disciples again, “*It isn’t for you to know times or seasons which the Father has set within his own authority*” (*Acts 1:7*).

The verse also reveals the purpose of not knowing. If people knew the exact day, they might live carelessly until shortly before it. Because the time is unknown, believers are called to live faithfully every day. The uncertainty of the timing is meant to produce constant readiness, not anxiety.

Finally, this verse points to the trust believers can place in the Father’s wisdom. God knows the right time. His timing is perfect, and believers can rest in His knowledge rather than trying to know what He has not revealed.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse calls believers to reject speculation and date-setting about Christ’s return. When people claim to know when Jesus will come back, believers can respond with Jesus’ clear words: no one knows. This protects them from being misled or discouraged.

It also calls believers to live in readiness. Since Christ could return at any time, believers can live each day as if it might be the day: faithful in their responsibilities, at peace with God, reconciled with others, and actively serving. This is not a call to fear but to faithfulness.

Finally, this verse encourages believers to trust God with the future. Many people feel anxious about what is coming. Believers can rest in knowing that the Father holds the timing in His hands. They do not need to know when Christ will come; they need to know Him and be found faithful.

### *Matthew 24:45–46* — The Faithful Servant

> *“Who then is the faithful and wise servant, whom his lord has set over his household, to give them their food in due season? Blessed is that servant whom his lord finds doing so when he comes.”*
>
> — *Matthew 24:45–46* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These verses begin a short parable that concludes Jesus’ teaching in this chapter. He has just told His disciples to stay alert because they do not know when He will come, and He compared His coming to a thief arriving unexpectedly. Now He describes what readiness looks like.

“*Who then is the faithful and wise servant, whom his lord has set over his household, to give them their food in due season?*” (*v. 45*) In wealthy households of that time, a trusted servant or slave was often put in charge of the household’s affairs while the master was away, including distributing food to the other servants. This was a position of responsibility and trust.

The servant is described as “faithful,” meaning reliable and trustworthy, and “wise,” meaning sensible and prudent. His wisdom shows in his understanding that the master will return and that his responsibility is to care for others in the meantime.

“*Blessed is that servant whom his lord finds doing so when he comes*” (*v. 46*). The servant is blessed because the master finds him carrying out his responsibilities. He is not idle, not careless, and not taking advantage of the master’s absence. He is faithfully doing his job. The next verse says the master will put him in charge of all his possessions, a great reward.

In contrast, Jesus describes a wicked servant who thinks, “*My lord is delaying his coming*” (*v. 48*), and begins to beat his fellow servants and eat and drink with drunkards. The master will return unexpectedly and punish him severely.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This parable shows that readiness for Christ’s return is not about calculating dates or withdrawing from ordinary life. It is about faithfully doing what Christ has entrusted to us. Being ready means being found at work: caring for others, serving well, and living with integrity.

The parable also highlights how believers treat other people. The faithful servant feeds the household; the wicked servant abuses his fellow servants. The way believers treat others, especially those under their care, reveals whether they are truly ready for the Lord’s return. This anticipates the parable of the sheep and the goats in *Matthew 25*, where the Son of Man judges people according to how they treated the least of His brothers and sisters.

Finally, the parable warns about the danger of delay. The wicked servant reasoned that the master was delayed and used that as an excuse for careless living. Believers can be tempted to think that because Christ has not yet returned, it does not matter how they live. Jesus warns that such thinking is dangerous.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses invite believers to consider what Christ has entrusted to them. This might include responsibilities in their families, workplaces, churches, and communities. Faithfulness means carrying out these responsibilities well: caring for children, working honestly, serving others, and using their gifts for God’s purposes.

They also call believers, especially those in positions of authority, to treat others with care. Parents, employers, church leaders, teachers, and anyone with influence over others are like the servant in charge of the household. They are called to provide for and protect those under their care, never to abuse them.

Finally, these verses encourage believers to live with a long-term perspective. Christ’s return may seem delayed, but believers can remain faithful day after day, year after year. The reward for faithfulness is great, and the Master will surely come.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Matthew 24* deals with the future, but its purpose is to shape how believers live in the present. Jesus did not give His disciples a detailed timetable; He prepared them to remain faithful in a world marked by deception, conflict, persecution, and uncertainty.

The first application is discernment. Jesus warned repeatedly about false messiahs and false prophets. Believers today encounter many voices claiming to speak for God, offering new revelations, or predicting the end. They can test these claims by Scripture, refuse to follow anyone who sets dates for Christ’s return, and hold firmly to the teaching of Jesus.

The second is endurance. Jesus warned that His followers would face hatred, persecution, betrayal, and the temptation to let their love grow cold. Believers in many parts of the world experience this directly. Others face subtler pressures. In every setting, Jesus calls His followers to endure to the end, keeping their love warm and their faith firm, while continuing to share the gospel with all nations.

The third is calm trust. Wars, disasters, and crises are real, but Jesus told His followers not to be alarmed. They can respond to world events with compassion and prayer without being controlled by fear or speculation, trusting that the Father holds the timing of history in His hands.

The fourth is readiness through faithfulness. Because no one knows the day or hour, believers are called to live faithfully every day. This means doing what Christ has entrusted to them, caring for those in their charge, and refusing to live carelessly because His return seems delayed. The best way to be ready for Christ’s coming is to be found faithfully serving Him when He comes.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for warning Your followers about the dangers ahead and for promising that You will return in power and glory. Guard me from deception. Give me discernment to recognize false teaching, and keep me anchored in Your Word, which will never pass away.

When I hear of wars, disasters, and troubles, keep me from fear and give me compassion and trust. Strengthen me to endure to the end and keep my love from growing cold. Thank You that the Father knows the day and hour of Your coming. Help me to trust Him with the future and to live each day ready to meet You. Make me a faithful and wise servant, caring well for the people and responsibilities You have given me, so that when You come, You will find me doing Your will. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
