Matthew · Chapter 25 of 28

# Matthew — Chapter 25

Chapter Theme: Ready, Faithful, and Merciful When the King Returns

[Read Matthew 25 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/MAT25.htm)

Main Teaching

Jesus completes His teaching about His return with three pictures of what readiness means. The parable of the ten virgins calls for prepared, lasting faith; the parable of the talents calls for faithful use of what God has entrusted; and the scene of the sheep and the goats shows that the King will judge people by how they treated the least of His brothers and sisters, because what is done for them is done for Him.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Matthew 25* continues the Olivet Discourse that began in chapter 24. Jesus is still on the Mount of Olives with His disciples, a few days before His crucifixion. In chapter 24 He warned about deception, predicted the destruction of the temple, described His glorious return, and stressed that no one knows the day or hour. He ended with a short parable about a faithful servant who is found caring for the household when his master returns. Chapter 25 expands on what it means to be ready through two longer parables and a vivid picture of the final judgment.

Each section adds a different emphasis. The first parable focuses on preparation over time, especially when the bridegroom is delayed. The second focuses on responsibility and active faithfulness. The third focuses on mercy toward those in need. Together they show that readiness for Christ’s return is not passive waiting but faithful, active, compassionate living.

### The Parable of the Ten Virgins (*25:1–13*)

Jesus compared the kingdom of heaven to ten young women, bridesmaids, who took their lamps and went out to meet the bridegroom. In Jewish weddings of that time, the groom would go to the bride’s family home, sometimes after negotiations that took hours, and then lead a procession back to his own home for the wedding feast. Friends of the bride would wait to join the procession, carrying lamps or torches, which were needed for a nighttime celebration. The lamps were probably torches with oil-soaked rags or small clay oil lamps that needed regular refilling.

Five of the young women were foolish and took no extra oil. Five were wise and brought flasks of oil. The bridegroom was delayed, and all of them grew drowsy and fell asleep. Notice that all ten slept; sleeping was not the problem. At midnight someone shouted that the bridegroom was coming. All ten got up and trimmed their lamps. The foolish ones realized their lamps were going out and asked the wise ones to share. The wise said there would not be enough for everyone and told them to go buy oil. While they were gone, the bridegroom arrived. Those who were ready went in with him to the wedding feast, and the door was shut.

Later the other bridesmaids came, saying, “*Lord, Lord, open to us*” (*v. 11*). He replied, “*Most certainly I tell you, I don’t know you*” (*v. 12*). These words echo Jesus’ warning in *Matthew 7:21–23*. Jesus concluded, “*Watch therefore, for you don’t know the day nor the hour in which the Son of Man is coming*” (*v. 13*). This parable is studied below.

### The Parable of the Talents (*25:14–30*)

Jesus told another parable. A man going on a journey entrusted his wealth to his servants. To one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one, “*to each according to his own ability*” (*v. 15*). A talent was a large sum of money, equal to about twenty years’ wages for a laborer. Even one talent was a great deal. (The English word “talent,” meaning a natural ability, actually comes from this parable.)

The servant with five talents immediately put the money to work and gained five more. The one with two gained two more. But the servant with one talent dug a hole and buried his master’s money. Burying money was considered a safe way to protect it in that culture, but it produced no gain.

After a long time, the master returned and settled accounts. The first two servants reported their gains, and the master praised each with the same words: “*Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your lord*” (*v. 21*).

The third servant came and said, “*Lord, I knew you that you are a hard man*” (*v. 24*), who reaped where he did not sow. He said he was afraid and so he hid the talent. Now here it was, returned. The master called him “*wicked and slothful*” (*v. 26*). If he truly believed his master was demanding, he should at least have put the money in the bank to earn interest. The master took the talent and gave it to the servant with ten. He declared that those who have will receive more, and those who do not have will lose even what they have. The worthless servant was thrown into the outer darkness.

The third servant’s problem was not that he had less, but that he did nothing with what he had been given. His view of his master as harsh led to fear, and fear led to inaction. Faithfulness means using what God entrusts to us for His purposes.

### The Sheep and the Goats (*25:31–46*)

Jesus concluded the discourse with a description of the final judgment. When the Son of Man comes in His glory, with all His angels, He will sit on His glorious throne. All the nations will be gathered before Him, and He will separate them as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats. In Palestine, shepherds often grazed sheep and goats together during the day but separated them at night, since goats needed more warmth. Sheep were generally more valuable and sometimes associated with blessing.

The King, as Jesus now calls the Son of Man, will say to those on His right, “*Come, blessed of my Father, inherit the Kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world*” (*v. 34*). Then He explains why: they fed Him when He was hungry, gave Him drink when He was thirsty, welcomed Him as a stranger, clothed Him, cared for Him when sick, and visited Him in prison.

The righteous are surprised. They ask when they ever saw Him in such need. The King answers, “*because you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me*” (*v. 40*). This verse is studied below.

Then the King will say to those on His left, “*Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire which is prepared for the devil and his angels*” (*v. 41*). They did not feed, welcome, clothe, or visit Him. They also ask when they saw Him in need and did not help. He answers that whatever they did not do for the least of these, they did not do for Him. The chapter ends with a solemn statement: “*These will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life*” (*v. 46*).

Notice that the eternal fire was “*prepared for the devil and his angels*” (*v. 41*), not for human beings. The kingdom, by contrast, was prepared for the blessed from the foundation of the world. God’s original intention for humanity is blessing, not judgment.

After this, *Matthew 26* begins the account of Jesus’ arrest and crucifixion. The King who will one day sit on the throne of glory first goes to the cross, where He will Himself be hungry, thirsty, stripped, treated as a stranger, and imprisoned.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Matthew 25:13* — Keep Watch, Because You Do Not Know the Hour

> *“Watch therefore, for you don’t know the day nor the hour in which the Son of Man is coming.”*
>
> — *Matthew 25:13* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse concludes the parable of the ten virgins. In the story, ten bridesmaids were waiting for a bridegroom to arrive so they could join the wedding procession and celebration. Five were wise and brought extra oil for their lamps. Five were foolish and did not. When the bridegroom was delayed, all of them fell asleep. At midnight the announcement came: the bridegroom was coming. The foolish bridesmaids discovered that their lamps were going out. While they went to buy oil, the bridegroom arrived, the wise bridesmaids went in with him, and the door was shut. When the foolish ones returned, the bridegroom said he did not know them.

Jesus then applied the parable: “*Watch therefore, for you don’t know the day nor the hour in which the Son of Man is coming*” (*v. 13*). “Watch” means to stay alert and ready. In the story, both groups slept, so “watching” does not mean never resting. It means being prepared so that, whenever the bridegroom comes, you are ready to go in.

The key difference between the wise and the foolish was preparation for a delay. The foolish bridesmaids were ready if the bridegroom came quickly, but not if he took longer than expected. The wise ones had planned for the long wait.

Jesus’ disciples, and Matthew’s first readers, may have expected Jesus to return very soon. This parable prepared them for the possibility of a long delay. Faith that is ready only for a quick return may run out when the wait is long.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This parable teaches that spiritual readiness cannot be borrowed. The wise bridesmaids could not share their oil, not because they were selfish, but because each person must be prepared for themselves. Many interpreters understand the oil as representing genuine faith, a living relationship with God, or a life that bears fruit, things that cannot be transferred from one person to another. A person cannot rely on the faith of their parents, spouse, or church.

The parable also warns that there will be a point when it is too late. The door was shut. This reflects the seriousness of Jesus’ return. The opportunity to respond to God’s invitation is open now, but it will not remain open forever. The bridegroom’s words, “I don’t know you,” echo Jesus’ warning in *Matthew 7:23* to those who called Him “Lord” but did not truly know Him.

At the same time, the parable is a picture of joy. The goal is a wedding feast, a celebration. Christ’s return is not only a time of judgment but the beginning of the great celebration of God’s kingdom. Those who are ready will share in His joy.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse calls believers to prepare for a long journey of faith. It is easy to be enthusiastic at first and then fade over time. Believers can develop habits that sustain faith over many years: regular prayer, Scripture reading, worship, fellowship, and service. These are like oil that keeps the lamp burning even when the wait is long.

It also reminds each person that their relationship with God is personal. Being surrounded by believers, attending church, or growing up in a Christian family is valuable, but it cannot replace personal faith. Each person must come to Christ for themselves.

Finally, this verse encourages believers not to put off what matters most. If someone has been delaying a decision to follow Christ, to reconcile with someone, or to deal with sin, now is the time. The door is open today, and the bridegroom could come at any time.

### *Matthew 25:21* — “*Well Done, Good and Faithful Servant*” (*v. 21*)

> *“His lord said to him, “Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your lord.””*
>
> — *Matthew 25:21* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These words are spoken by the master in the parable of the talents to the servant who had received five talents. Before leaving on a long journey, the master entrusted his wealth to three servants according to their abilities: five talents to one, two to another, and one to the third. A talent was a very large amount of money, about twenty years of wages for a laborer. The master expected the servants to manage his wealth wisely while he was gone.

The first servant immediately went and put the money to work, probably through trade or investment, and doubled it. When the master returned after a long time and asked for an account, the servant reported that he had gained five more talents.

The master responded, “*Well done, good and faithful servant*” (*v. 21*). “Good” describes the servant’s character; “faithful” describes his reliability in carrying out his responsibility. The master then said, “*You have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things*” (*v. 21*). Five talents was a huge sum, yet the master calls it “a few things.” Compared to what he would now receive, even this great responsibility was small. Faithfulness leads to greater responsibility.

Finally, the master said, “*Enter into the joy of your lord*” (*v. 21*). The reward was not only more responsibility but a share in the master’s joy, a welcome into close fellowship with him.

The servant with two talents also doubled his amount and received exactly the same words of praise (v. 23). The master did not compare the two servants. Each was praised for faithfulness with what he had been given.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows what God values in His servants: goodness and faithfulness. God does not measure people by the size of their gifts or the scale of their results but by their faithfulness with what He has entrusted to them. The servant with two talents received the same praise as the one with five. Paul writes, “*it is required of stewards that they be found faithful*” (*1 Corinthians 4:2*).

The parable also teaches that everything believers have is entrusted by God. Abilities, opportunities, resources, time, relationships, and the gospel itself are gifts from the Master. Believers are stewards, not owners, and they are accountable for how they use what has been given to them.

Finally, the master’s words reveal the joy that awaits faithful servants. Serving God is not a grim duty followed by a cold evaluation. It leads to a welcome into the Master’s joy. The reward of faithful service is deeper fellowship with God Himself.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to consider what God has entrusted to them. Everyone has received something: abilities, education, time, money, relationships, experiences, and spiritual gifts. The question is not how much we have compared to others, but whether we are using what we have for God’s purposes.

It also encourages believers who feel their gifts are small. The servant with two talents received the same praise as the one with five. God does not expect people to produce what He has not given them. He looks for faithfulness. A person who faithfully cares for one family member, serves in a small role, or uses modest resources generously is just as pleasing to God as someone with greater visibility.

Finally, this verse warns against fear and inaction. The third servant buried his talent because he was afraid. Many believers hold back from serving because they fear failure or think their contribution doesn’t matter. Jesus’ parable encourages them to step out and use their gifts, trusting that God values faithful effort and that their work for Him is never wasted.

### *Matthew 25:40* — Done for the Least, Done for Christ

> *“The King will answer them, “Most certainly I tell you, because you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.””*
>
> — *Matthew 25:40* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse is the King’s explanation to the righteous at the final judgment. Jesus describes the scene: the Son of Man sitting on His glorious throne, all nations gathered before Him, and the people separated like sheep and goats. To those on His right, the King says they are blessed and will inherit the kingdom, because when He was hungry, thirsty, a stranger, naked, sick, and in prison, they cared for Him.

The righteous are surprised. They ask when they ever saw Him in such situations. They do not remember serving the King. The King answers, “*Most certainly I tell you, because you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me*” (*v. 40*).

“The least of these” refers to people who are small, insignificant, and powerless in the world’s eyes. The six needs mentioned, hunger, thirst, being a stranger, lacking clothing, sickness, and imprisonment, describe people in desperate circumstances. In that culture, prisoners often depended on family and friends to bring food, and visiting them could be risky. Strangers had no community to protect them.

Jesus calls these people “my brothers.” Christians have interpreted this phrase in two main ways. Some understand “the least of these my brothers” to refer to Jesus’ disciples, especially those who are poor, persecuted, or traveling as messengers of the gospel, since Matthew elsewhere uses “brothers” for Jesus’ followers (*Matthew 12:50*; *28:10*) and “little ones” for disciples (*Matthew 10:42*). Others understand it to include all people in need, since Jesus identifies with suffering humanity. Both views agree that Jesus identifies Himself personally with those who suffer and that acts of mercy toward them are acts of service to Him. Scripture elsewhere commands care for all people in need (*Galatians 6:10*).

The righteous did not serve in order to be seen by the King or to earn a reward. Their acts of compassion flowed naturally from their character, and they were surprised to learn their significance.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals Jesus’ deep identification with the poor and suffering. The King of glory, seated on His throne, says that when the hungry are fed and the prisoner is visited, it is done to Him. This echoes the Old Testament, where God declares Himself the defender of the poor, the widow, the orphan, and the stranger (*Deuteronomy 10:18*; *Proverbs 19:17*).

It also shows that genuine faith is seen in practical mercy. The parable does not teach that people are saved by doing good works; elsewhere Matthew makes clear that salvation comes through Jesus, who gives His life as a ransom (*Matthew 20:28*; *26:28*). But it does show that those who truly belong to the King will reflect His compassion. Mercy toward the needy is evidence of a heart transformed by God. James writes that faith without works is dead (*James 2:14–17*).

Finally, the passage gives dignity to ordinary acts of kindness. Feeding someone, giving water, welcoming a stranger, providing clothing, visiting the sick, and going to see a prisoner are not dramatic acts. They are simple, practical, and available to almost everyone. Yet the King treats them as service done to Himself.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse calls believers to see Christ in those who are in need. When believers encounter someone who is hungry, lonely, sick, a stranger, poorly clothed, or in prison, they are meeting someone with whom Jesus identifies. Serving such people is a way of serving Him.

Practical applications include supporting food banks and shelters, welcoming immigrants and newcomers, visiting the sick and elderly, caring for people in prison and their families, giving clothing and resources, and simply noticing people who are often ignored. Churches can organize ministries that meet these needs, and individuals can look for opportunities in their daily lives.

Finally, this verse encourages believers to serve without seeking recognition. The righteous were surprised by the King’s words because they had not been keeping score. Believers can serve with humble, unselfconscious love, trusting that the King sees every act of mercy, even those no one else notices.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Matthew 25* gives three pictures of what it means to be ready for Christ’s return, and each applies to daily life. The parable of the ten virgins calls for lasting faith. The Christian life is often longer and more ordinary than expected, and enthusiasm alone will not sustain it. Believers can build habits of prayer, worship, Scripture, and fellowship that keep their faith alive over many years. They can also remember that each person must be ready for themselves; faith cannot be borrowed from others.

The parable of the talents calls for faithful use of what God has entrusted. Every believer has received gifts, opportunities, and resources from God. The question is not how much one has compared with others, but whether one is using it faithfully. Fear and comparison can lead to inaction, but God praises those who step out in faith and serve with what they have. The reward is not only greater responsibility but the joy of sharing in the Master’s joy.

The scene of the sheep and the goats calls for mercy toward the needy. Jesus identifies Himself with the hungry, thirsty, stranger, naked, sick, and imprisoned. Believers can look for practical ways to care for such people, recognizing that in serving them, they serve Christ. This mercy should flow naturally from hearts transformed by God’s grace, not from a desire for recognition.

Together, these three pictures show that waiting for Christ is not passive. It involves preparation, faithfulness, and compassion. The final words of the chapter are sobering: there are two destinies, eternal punishment and eternal life. But the kingdom was prepared for God’s people from the foundation of the world, and the King who will judge is the same One who went to the cross to save. Believers can live with hope, readiness, and love as they wait for His return.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, You are the Bridegroom and the King who will come again in glory. Keep my faith alive through long seasons of waiting, and help me to be ready whenever You come. I know that I cannot borrow faith from others, so draw me close to You and fill my life with what only You can give.

Thank You for everything You have entrusted to me. Free me from fear and comparison, and help me to use my time, abilities, and resources faithfully for Your purposes. I long to hear You say, “Well done, good and faithful servant.” Open my eyes to see You in the hungry, the thirsty, the stranger, the poorly clothed, the sick, and the prisoner. Give me a heart of mercy that serves them as I would serve You, without seeking praise. Thank You for preparing a kingdom for Your people, and for going to the cross so that I could share in it. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Matthew · Chapter 26 of 28

# Matthew — Chapter 26

Chapter Theme: The Willing Sacrifice on the Night of Betrayal

[Read Matthew 26 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/MAT26.htm)

Main Teaching

As the Passover approaches, Jesus is anointed for burial, betrayed for thirty pieces of silver, and shares a final meal in which He explains His death as the blood of the new covenant poured out for the forgiveness of sins. In Gethsemane He submits His will to the Father; at His arrest He refuses violence and rescue; before the council He openly declares His identity; and in the courtyard Peter denies Him three times. Throughout, Matthew shows that Jesus goes to His death knowingly and willingly, in fulfillment of Scripture.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Matthew 26* begins the account of Jesus’ passion, the events of His suffering and death. The first verse marks the transition: “*When Jesus had finished all these words*” (*v. 1*). This phrase closes each of Jesus’ five major teaching sections in Matthew (*7:28*; *11:1*; *13:53*; *19:1*), and here it says “all these words,” signaling that His teaching ministry is now complete. What follows is the climax of the Gospel.

Matthew’s account closely parallels *Mark 14*, but Matthew adds details that highlight two themes: Jesus’ full awareness and control of what is happening, and the fulfillment of Scripture. Jesus is not a victim caught by surprise. He predicts each step, and He chooses to walk the path the Father has given Him.

### The Plot and the Anointing (*26:1–16*)

Jesus told His disciples, “*You know that after two days the Passover is coming, and the Son of Man will be delivered up to be crucified*” (*v. 2*). Passover remembered God’s rescue of Israel from Egypt, when the blood of a lamb protected each household from judgment (*Exodus 12*). Jesus connected His death directly with this festival.

At the same time, the chief priests and elders met in the palace of the high priest, Caiaphas. Caiaphas served as high priest from about A.D. 18 to 36, an unusually long tenure that suggests he worked closely with the Roman authorities. In 1990, archaeologists discovered an ornate ossuary (bone box) inscribed “Joseph son of Caiaphas,” which many believe belonged to him. The leaders plotted to arrest Jesus by deception and kill Him, but not during the festival, fearing a riot among the crowds.

In Bethany, at the home of Simon the leper, a woman poured a jar of very expensive perfume on Jesus’ head. The disciples were indignant at the “waste,” since it could have been sold and the money given to the poor. Jesus defended her, saying she had done a beautiful thing and had prepared His body for burial, and that her deed would be remembered wherever the gospel was preached. This scene is studied below.

Then Judas Iscariot, one of the Twelve, went to the chief priests and asked, “*What are you willing to give me if I deliver him to you?*” (*v. 15*) They weighed out thirty pieces of silver. Matthew alone mentions the amount. In *Exodus 21:32*, thirty shekels was the compensation paid for a slave gored by an ox. In *Zechariah 11:12–13*, it was the insulting wage paid to God’s rejected shepherd, which was thrown to the potter in the temple. Matthew will return to this prophecy in chapter 27. The price shows how little the religious leaders valued Jesus.

### The Last Supper (*26:17–30*)

On the first day of the Feast of Unleavened Bread, Jesus sent His disciples to prepare the Passover meal at a certain man’s house in Jerusalem, with the message, “*My time is at hand*” (*v. 18*). Jesus knew His appointed hour had come.

That evening, as they reclined at the table (the customary posture for festive meals), Jesus announced that one of them would betray Him. The disciples were deeply grieved and asked one by one, “*It isn’t me, is it, Lord?*” (*v. 22*) Jesus said that the one who dipped his hand into the dish with Him would betray Him, and He pronounced a solemn woe on the betrayer. Matthew alone records Judas asking, “*It isn’t me, is it, Rabbi?*” (*v. 25*) Notice that the other disciples called Jesus “Lord,” while Judas called Him “Rabbi,” a respectful title but one that never appears on the lips of Jesus’ faithful followers in Matthew. Jesus answered, “*You said it*” (*v. 25*), a way of saying, “Yes, it is as you say.”

During the meal, Jesus took bread, gave thanks, broke it, and gave it to the disciples, saying, “*Take, eat; this is my body*” (*v. 26*). Then He took a cup, gave thanks, and gave it to them, saying, “*All of you drink it*” (*v. 27*), and explaining that it was His blood of the new covenant poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins. This is studied below. He added that He would not drink wine again until He drank it new with them in His Father’s kingdom.

After singing a hymn, likely from the Hallel Psalms (*Psalms 113–118*) traditionally sung at Passover, they went out to the Mount of Olives.

### Peter’s Denial Predicted (*26:31–35*)

On the way, Jesus told them that all of them would fall away that night, quoting *Zechariah 13:7*: “*I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered*” (*v. 31*). But He promised that after He was raised, He would go ahead of them to Galilee. Peter insisted that even if everyone else fell away, he never would. Jesus told him that before the rooster crowed that night, he would deny Him three times. Peter replied that even if he had to die with Jesus, he would never deny Him, and all the disciples said the same.

### Gethsemane (*26:36–46*)

They came to Gethsemane, an olive grove whose name means “oil press.” Jesus took Peter, James, and John with Him and began to be sorrowful and deeply distressed. He told them, “*My soul is exceedingly sorrowful, even to death. Stay here and watch with me*” (*v. 38*). Matthew alone includes the words “with me,” emphasizing Jesus’ desire for companionship in His agony.

He went a little farther, fell on His face, and prayed, “*My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass away from me; nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire*” (*v. 39*). Returning, He found the disciples sleeping and asked Peter whether they could not watch with Him for one hour. He urged them to watch and pray so they would not enter into temptation, because the spirit is willing but the flesh is weak. (*Mark 14* treats this warning in depth; in Matthew the emphasis falls on Jesus’ own progression in prayer, studied below.)

He went away a second time and prayed, “*My Father, if this cup can’t pass away from me unless I drink it, your desire be done*” (*v. 42*). Again He found them asleep. He prayed a third time, saying the same words. Then He returned and told them that the hour had come, the Son of Man was being betrayed, and the betrayer was near.

### The Arrest (*26:47–56*)

Judas arrived with a large crowd armed with swords and clubs, sent by the chief priests and elders. He had arranged a signal: the one he kissed was the man to arrest. He came to Jesus, said, “*Greetings, Rabbi!*” (*v. 49*), and kissed Him. Matthew alone records Jesus’ reply: “*Friend, why are you here?*” (*v. 50*) Even in the moment of betrayal, Jesus addressed Judas as “friend,” though the word could also carry a tone of reproach, as in *Matthew 20:13* and *22:12*.

One of Jesus’ companions (*John 18:10* identifies him as Peter) drew a sword and cut off the ear of the high priest’s servant. Jesus told him to put the sword away, because those who take the sword will die by the sword. He added that He could ask His Father, who would immediately send more than twelve legions of angels. A Roman legion had about six thousand soldiers, so twelve legions would be over seventy thousand angels. But then, He asked, how would the Scriptures be fulfilled? This scene is studied below.

Jesus then asked the crowd why they came with weapons as though He were a robber, when He had taught in the temple every day. All this happened to fulfill the writings of the prophets. Then all the disciples deserted Him and fled.

### The Trial Before Caiaphas (*26:57–68*)

Jesus was taken to Caiaphas, where the scribes and elders had gathered. Peter followed at a distance into the courtyard to see what would happen. The council looked for false testimony to justify a death sentence but could not find agreeing witnesses, as the law required (*Deuteronomy 19:15*). Finally two came forward and claimed Jesus had said He could destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days, a distortion of something He had said about His body (*John 2:19–21*).

Jesus remained silent, fulfilling *Isaiah 53:7*. Then Caiaphas said, “*I adjure you by the living God that you tell us whether you are the Christ, the Son of God*” (*v. 63*). To “adjure” someone was to put them under a solemn oath. Under oath, Jesus answered, “*You have said so*” (*v. 64*), meaning yes, and added that they would see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven, combining *Psalm 110:1* and *Daniel 7:13*. Jesus was claiming to be the divine King who would judge them.

The high priest tore his clothes and declared that Jesus had spoken blasphemy. The council agreed that He deserved death. They spat in His face, struck Him, and mocked Him, demanding that He prophesy who hit Him.

### Peter’s Denials (*26:69–75*)

Meanwhile, in the courtyard, a servant girl said that Peter had been with Jesus the Galilean. He denied it before everyone. At the gateway, another girl said the same, and Peter denied it with an oath: “*I don’t know the man*” (*v. 72*). A little later, bystanders said his Galilean accent gave him away. He began to curse and swear, “I don’t know the man!” Immediately the rooster crowed. Peter remembered Jesus’ words, went outside, and “*wept bitterly*” (*v. 75*).

The contrast is deliberate. Inside, under oath, Jesus told the truth about Himself, knowing it would cost Him His life. Outside, Peter swore falsely to save himself. Yet Matthew’s Gospel does not end with Peter’s failure; the risen Jesus will gather His scattered disciples in Galilee (*Matthew 28:16–20*).

## Important Verses Explained

### *Matthew 26:13* — A Gift Remembered Wherever the Gospel Goes

> *“Most certainly I tell you, wherever this Good News is preached in the whole world, what this woman has done will also be spoken of as a memorial of her.”*
>
> — *Matthew 26:13* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus speaks these words in Bethany, two days before Passover, at the home of Simon the leper. A woman (identified in *John 12:3* as Mary, the sister of Martha and Lazarus) had come to Him with an alabaster jar of very expensive perfume and poured it on His head while He reclined at the table. Anointing a guest’s head with a little oil was a gesture of hospitality, but this woman used a whole jar of costly perfume, an extravagant act of devotion.

The disciples were indignant. They asked, “*Why this waste?*” (*v. 8*) and pointed out that the perfume could have been sold for a large sum and given to the poor. Their objection sounded reasonable and even righteous.

Jesus defended her. He said she had done “*a good work for me*” (*v. 10*). The poor would always be with them, giving them many opportunities to help, but He would not always be with them. Then He explained the deeper meaning of her act: “*in pouring this ointment on my body, she did it to prepare me for burial*” (*v. 12*). In Jewish custom, bodies were anointed with spices and perfumes before burial. Jesus had just told His disciples that He would be crucified in two days. Whether the woman fully understood or not, her gift became a preparation for His death.

Then Jesus made a remarkable promise in this verse: “*wherever this Good News is preached in the whole world, what this woman has done will also be spoken of as a memorial of her*” (*v. 13*). Jesus expected the gospel to be preached throughout the whole world, and He said her act would be part of that story. The promise has been fulfilled; her deed is recorded in three Gospels and remembered by Christians everywhere.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows the value Jesus places on wholehearted devotion. The disciples measured the woman’s act by its cost and practical usefulness. Jesus measured it by its love. Her gift was not wasteful, because nothing given to Jesus out of love is wasted.

The scene also shows that the gospel is centered on Jesus’ death. Her anointing pointed to His burial, and Jesus connected her act with the preaching of the gospel. The good news that would go to the whole world is the news of His death and resurrection.

Matthew places this story between the leaders’ plot and Judas’s betrayal. The contrast is sharp: the leaders scheme, Judas sells Jesus for thirty pieces of silver, and this woman pours out something precious for Him. Every person must decide whether Jesus is worth everything or worth a small price.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to express their love for Jesus wholeheartedly. Worship, time, resources, and service given to Him are never wasted, even if others do not understand. Believers can ask what it would look like to give Christ their best rather than their leftovers.

It also warns against a critical spirit toward others’ devotion. The disciples criticized the woman with arguments that sounded practical and spiritual. Believers can be slow to judge how others express their love for Christ, recognizing that God sees the heart.

Finally, this verse holds devotion to Christ and care for the poor together. Jesus did not dismiss care for the poor; He assumed His followers would continue to help them. Love for Jesus is the root, and generosity toward others is one of its fruits. Both belong in the life of a disciple.

### *Matthew 26:28* — Blood Poured Out for the Forgiveness of Sins

> *“for this is my blood of the new covenant, which is poured out for many for the remission of sins.”*
>
> — *Matthew 26:28* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus speaks these words during the Last Supper, the Passover meal He shared with His twelve disciples on the night before His death. The Passover meal included bread, wine, and the Passover lamb, and the leader explained the meaning of the elements in light of Israel’s deliverance from Egypt. Jesus had just taken bread, given thanks, broken it, and said, “Take, eat; this is my body.” Now He took a cup of wine, gave thanks, and told all of them to drink from it.

He explained: “*for this is my blood of the new covenant, which is poured out for many for the remission of sins*” (*v. 28*). “Blood of the covenant” recalls *Exodus 24:8*, where Moses sprinkled sacrificial blood on the people to seal the covenant at Mount Sinai. “New covenant” recalls *Jeremiah 31:31–34*, where God promised a new covenant in which He would forgive His people’s sins and write His law on their hearts. “Poured out for many” echoes *Isaiah 53:12*, where the Servant poured out His life to death and bore the sins of many.

Matthew alone includes the phrase “*for the remission of sins*” (*v. 28*). “Remission” means forgiveness, the cancellation of a debt. This phrase connects the cup directly with the angel’s announcement at the beginning of Matthew’s Gospel that Jesus would “*save his people from their sins*” (*Matthew 1:21*). The purpose of Jesus’ death is forgiveness.

The disciples would have known that Jesus was speaking about His death, since He had predicted it repeatedly. But they could not yet understand how His death would accomplish forgiveness. That understanding came after the resurrection and the gift of the Spirit.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse explains the meaning of Jesus’ death in His own words. His blood, His life given in death, establishes the new covenant and brings forgiveness of sins. In the Old Testament sacrificial system, blood represented life given in place of the sinner (*Leviticus 17:11*). Hebrews explains that “*Apart from shedding of blood there is no remission*” (*Hebrews 9:22*), and that Christ’s sacrifice accomplished what animal sacrifices could only picture.

The command, “All of you drink it,” is significant. Every disciple, including those who would soon deny and desert Him, was included. Forgiveness is offered to all who come to Christ, regardless of their failures.

Christians have understood the Lord’s Supper in different ways, from belief in Christ’s real presence in the bread and wine, to a spiritual presence received by faith, to a memorial of His death. All Christian traditions agree that the meal proclaims Jesus’ death for the forgiveness of sins and points forward to the day when He will drink it new in His Father’s kingdom.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to trust that their sins are truly forgiven through Christ’s death. Guilt and shame can linger even after confession, but Jesus said His blood was poured out for the forgiveness of sins. Believers can rest in what He has accomplished rather than trying to earn forgiveness through their own efforts.

It also calls believers to take the Lord’s Supper seriously. Each time they share the bread and cup, they remember His sacrifice, receive His grace, examine their hearts, and look forward to His return. Coming to the table with gratitude and honest repentance deepens faith.

Finally, this verse reminds believers that they belong to a covenant community. The cup was shared among all the disciples. Those forgiven by Christ are joined to one another, and they are called to extend forgiveness to each other as they have been forgiven.

### *Matthew 26:39* — “My Father, … Not What I Desire”

> *“He went forward a little, fell on his face, and prayed, saying, ‘My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass away from me; nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire.’”*
>
> — *Matthew 26:39* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse records Jesus’ first prayer in Gethsemane, an olive grove on the Mount of Olives where He went after the Last Supper. He had taken Peter, James, and John with Him and told them that His soul was overwhelmed with sorrow to the point of death. He asked them to stay and keep watch with Him. Then He went a little farther and “*fell on his face*” (*v. 39*), the posture of complete humility and desperate prayer.

He addressed God as “*My Father*” (*v. 39*). Matthew emphasizes the personal relationship: Jesus prays as the Son speaking to His Father. He asked, “*if it is possible, let this cup pass away from me*” (*v. 39*). The “cup” represents the suffering He was about to endure, including the cup of God’s judgment against sin, an image used by the prophets (*Isaiah 51:17*). Jesus genuinely desired that, if there were any other way, He might be spared this suffering.

But He immediately added, “*nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire*” (*v. 39*). He placed His own desire under the Father’s will.

Matthew’s account highlights a progression in Jesus’ prayers. In His second prayer, the wording changes: “*My Father, if this cup can’t pass away from me unless I drink it, your desire be done*” (*v. 42*). The first prayer asks whether the cup might pass; the second accepts that it will not, and embraces the Father’s will. This echoes the words Jesus taught His disciples in the Lord’s Prayer: “*Let your will be done*” (*Matthew 6:10*). He prayed a third time with the same words. When He rose from prayer, He went to meet His betrayer with calm resolve.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This prayer reveals the depth of Jesus’ humanity and the strength of His obedience. He felt the full horror of what was coming. He did not face the cross with indifference or stoic detachment. Yet He chose obedience. *Hebrews 5:8* says that He “*learned obedience by the things which he suffered*” (*Hebrews 5:8*).

The progression in His prayers shows how honest prayer can lead to peace in God’s will. Jesus did not pretend to want the cup. He expressed His desire honestly. But as He continued in prayer, His request moved toward acceptance. Prayer did not change the Father’s plan, but it prepared Jesus to walk the path ahead.

It is important to note what Jesus’ submission does and does not mean. He submitted to a specific purpose: giving His life for the salvation of the world. His submission does not teach that believers must passively accept every suffering or injustice as God’s will. Those who arrested and condemned Jesus were acting wickedly, and Scripture consistently calls for resisting evil and protecting the vulnerable. Jesus’ obedience was a willing choice to fulfill His saving mission.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse teaches believers to pray honestly. They can bring their fears, desires, and requests to God openly, even repeatedly, as Jesus did. God welcomes honest prayer from His children.

It also teaches believers to surrender their will to God’s. After expressing their desires, they can say, “Not what I desire, but what You desire.” This surrender is not resignation but trust that the Father’s will is good, even when it is hard. In practice, it may mean accepting a closed door, persevering in a difficult calling, or choosing obedience when it is costly.

Finally, this verse shows that prayer can bring strength to face what lies ahead. Jesus emerged from Gethsemane ready to face His arrest. Believers facing difficult decisions or trials can spend time in prayer, asking not only for deliverance but for strength to do God’s will, and wisdom to recognize when God’s will includes seeking help, protection, or change.

### *Matthew 26:52* — Put Away the Sword

> *“Then Jesus said to him, Put your sword back into its place, for all those who take the sword will die by the sword.”*
>
> — *Matthew 26:52* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse comes at the moment of Jesus’ arrest in Gethsemane. Judas had arrived with a large armed crowd sent by the chief priests and elders. He identified Jesus with a kiss, and the crowd seized Him. In that moment, one of Jesus’ companions drew a sword and struck the servant of the high priest, cutting off his ear. John’s Gospel tells us that the swordsman was Peter and the servant’s name was Malchus (*John 18:10*). Luke adds that Jesus touched the man’s ear and healed him (*Luke 22:51*).

Jesus immediately said, “*Put your sword back into its place, for all those who take the sword will die by the sword*” (*v. 52*). Jesus rejected violence as a way of defending Him or advancing His kingdom. Violence leads to more violence.

Then Jesus explained that He did not need human defense: “*Or do you think that I couldn’t ask my Father, and he would even now send me more than twelve legions of angels?*” (*v. 53*) A Roman legion had about six thousand soldiers, so twelve legions would be a vast heavenly army. Jesus was not helpless. He could have been rescued in an instant. But He asked, “*How then would the Scriptures be fulfilled that it must be so?*” (*v. 54*) He chose not to call for help because His death was the fulfillment of God’s plan revealed in Scripture.

Peter’s action showed sincere loyalty but misunderstood Jesus’ mission. Peter was ready to fight for Jesus, but he was not ready to watch Jesus willingly go to the cross.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that Jesus’ kingdom does not advance through violence. Jesus later told Pilate, “*My Kingdom is not of this world. If my Kingdom were of this world, then my servants would fight*” (*John 18:36*). His kingdom comes through truth, love, and self-sacrifice. This connects with His teaching in the Sermon on the Mount about not retaliating and loving enemies (*Matthew 5:38–44*).

It also shows that Jesus’ death was voluntary. He was not overpowered. He had access to unlimited power and chose not to use it. He laid down His life willingly, as He said in *John 10:18*. This makes His sacrifice an act of love and obedience, not merely a tragedy.

Christians have applied this verse in different ways to questions of war, self-defense, and the role of government. Some believe it supports a commitment to nonviolence in all circumstances. Others believe it forbids using violence to advance Christ’s kingdom or for personal revenge, while allowing governments to use force to restrain evil (*Romans 13:4*) and allowing the protection of the innocent. In its immediate context, Jesus was rejecting armed resistance to His own arrest, because He came to give His life.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse calls believers to reject violence and force as ways of advancing their faith or defending Christ’s honor. History contains many sad examples of people using violence in Jesus’ name. His words, “Put your sword back,” stand against all such efforts.

It also calls believers to break cycles of retaliation in their own lives. Whether in families, communities, or online conflict, responding to hostility with hostility usually escalates harm. Following Jesus means seeking peace, responding to wrongs with justice and restraint rather than revenge.

Finally, this verse invites believers to trust God’s power and plan. Peter thought he needed to defend Jesus with a sword. Jesus knew that His Father’s power was available and that His Father’s plan was good. Believers can trust God in situations that seem out of control, remembering that God’s purposes are often accomplished through ways that look like weakness.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Matthew 26* shows a range of responses to Jesus as He approaches the cross. A woman pours out a costly gift in love. Judas sells Him for thirty pieces of silver. The disciples promise loyalty and then sleep, fight, flee, and deny. The religious leaders plot, bribe, and condemn. In the middle of all this, Jesus moves forward with clear purpose and willing obedience. Readers are invited to see themselves in these responses and to ask how they are responding to Jesus.

The chapter calls believers to wholehearted devotion. The woman at Bethany gave something precious without calculating its cost. Believers can ask whether they give Jesus their best, whether in worship, time, resources, or service, and whether they are quick to criticize others’ devotion.

The Last Supper reminds believers that Jesus’ death was for the forgiveness of sins. The new covenant rests on His blood, not on their faithfulness. This gives assurance and humility. Believers who have failed can return to Christ, confident that His blood was poured out for people like them, including disciples who would deny Him that very night.

Gethsemane teaches believers how to face hard things: with honest prayer, persistent seeking of God’s will, and surrender to the Father. It also teaches watchfulness, since the disciples’ failure to pray left them unprepared for the test. Jesus’ response at His arrest teaches the rejection of violence and retaliation, and trust in God’s power and plan.

Finally, Peter’s denial and bitter weeping show both the danger of self-confidence and the hope of restoration. Believers can recognize their weakness, depend on God’s strength, and, when they fail, turn back to Jesus with genuine repentance. The One who went willingly to the cross did so for disciples who had failed Him, and His grace is greater than their failures.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for walking willingly toward the cross, knowing everything that would happen to You. Give me a heart like the woman at Bethany, who poured out her best for You without counting the cost. Keep me from valuing You cheaply, as Judas did, and from criticizing the devotion of others.

Thank You for the cup of the new covenant, Your blood poured out for the forgiveness of my sins. Help me to rest in Your forgiveness and to share it with others. When I face my own Gethsemane, teach me to pray honestly and to say, “Your will be done.” Keep me watchful and prayerful, aware of my weakness. Help me to put away every sword of retaliation and to trust Your power and plan. When I fail You, as Peter did, let my sorrow lead me back to You, the Savior who gave Himself for me. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Matthew · Chapter 27 of 28

# Matthew — Chapter 27

Chapter Theme: The King Crucified

[Read Matthew 27 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/MAT27.htm)

Main Teaching

Jesus is handed over to Pilate, rejected in favor of Barabbas, mocked as a king, and crucified between two robbers. Judas dies in despair, the crowds and leaders taunt Jesus to save Himself, and Jesus cries out the words of *Psalm 22* before giving up His spirit. At His death the temple curtain is torn, the earth shakes, and a Roman centurion confesses Him as the Son of God. His body is buried in a rich man’s tomb, which is sealed and guarded.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Matthew 27* records the most important day in human history from Matthew’s perspective: the crucifixion of Jesus. During the previous night, Jesus had been arrested in Gethsemane, tried before the Jewish council led by Caiaphas, and condemned for claiming to be the Messiah and the Son of God, while Peter denied Him in the courtyard (*Matthew 26*). Now, early in the morning, the council finalized its decision and handed Jesus over to the Roman governor.

The Jewish council could condemn Jesus by its own law, but under Roman rule it did not have the authority to carry out executions (*John 18:31*). Only the Roman governor could do that. The council therefore needed to present Jesus to Pilate in a way that would convince him that Jesus deserved death under Roman law. A charge of blasphemy would not interest Pilate, but a claim to be “King of the Jews” could be presented as rebellion against Caesar.

Throughout this chapter, Matthew emphasizes three themes: Jesus’ innocence, His identity as King and Son of God, and the fulfillment of Scripture. He also shows a range of human responses: Judas’s despair, Pilate’s cowardice, the crowd’s manipulation, the soldiers’ mockery, the leaders’ contempt, and finally the centurion’s confession and the women’s faithful presence.

### Jesus Handed Over to Pilate (*27:1–2*)

When morning came, the chief priests and elders formally decided to put Jesus to death. They bound Him and handed Him over to Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor (prefect) of Judea from A.D. 26 to 36. Historical sources describe Pilate as harsh and insensitive to Jewish customs, but also wary of complaints reaching Rome. An inscription bearing his name was discovered at Caesarea in 1961, confirming his historical role. Governors normally lived in Caesarea on the coast but came to Jerusalem during festivals to keep order.

### The Death of Judas (*27:3–10*)

When Judas saw that Jesus had been condemned, he was seized with remorse. He brought back the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders and said, “*I have sinned in that I betrayed innocent blood*” (*v. 4*). His confession is one more testimony to Jesus’ innocence. But the leaders replied coldly, “*What is that to us? You see to it*” (*v. 4*). They had used Judas and now discarded him. Judas threw the money into the temple and went away and hanged himself.

The chief priests, who had paid the money to arrange Jesus’ death, now became scrupulous about the law. They said it was not lawful to put the money into the temple treasury because it was “*the price of blood*” (*v. 6*). They used it to buy a potter’s field as a burial place for foreigners, and it became known as the Field of Blood. (*Acts 1:18–19* gives a complementary account of Judas’s death and the field.)

Matthew says this fulfilled what was spoken by Jeremiah the prophet. The wording draws mainly on *Zechariah 11:12–13*, where thirty pieces of silver, the price set on God’s rejected shepherd, are thrown to the potter in the temple. But Matthew also has in mind passages in Jeremiah about a potter’s house and the purchase of a field (*Jeremiah 18–19*; *32:6–15*), especially *Jeremiah 19*, where a potter’s vessel is broken in the Valley of Hinnom, renamed a valley of slaughter. Jewish writers sometimes combined prophecies and named only the more prominent prophet. Matthew is showing that the betrayal and its aftermath fit the pattern of God’s rejected shepherd and the judgment that follows.

### Jesus Before Pilate (*27:11–26*)

Pilate asked Jesus, “*Are you the King of the Jews?*” (*v. 11*) Jesus answered, “*So you say*” (*v. 11*), affirming it but in a way that suggested Pilate did not fully understand what kind of king He was. When the chief priests and elders accused Him, Jesus said nothing. Pilate was amazed that He did not defend Himself.

It was Pilate’s custom at the festival to release one prisoner chosen by the crowd. There was a notorious prisoner named Barabbas. (Some manuscripts give his full name as “Jesus Barabbas,” which would make Pilate’s question even more striking: which Jesus do you want?) Mark and Luke tell us Barabbas had been involved in an insurrection and murder (*Mark 15:7*). Pilate asked the crowd whether they wanted Barabbas or Jesus, knowing that the leaders had handed Jesus over out of envy.

While Pilate was sitting on the judgment seat, his wife sent him a message: “*Have nothing to do with that righteous man, for I have suffered many things today in a dream because of him*” (*v. 19*). Matthew alone records this. Even a Gentile woman recognized Jesus’ innocence.

Meanwhile, the chief priests and elders persuaded the crowd to ask for Barabbas and to have Jesus executed. When Pilate asked again, they shouted for Barabbas. When he asked what to do with Jesus, they cried, “*Let him be crucified!*” (*v. 22*) Pilate asked what evil Jesus had done, but they only shouted louder.

Seeing that a riot was starting, Pilate took water and washed his hands before the crowd, saying, “*I am innocent of the blood of this righteous person. You see to it*” (*v. 24*). Hand-washing was a symbolic act declaring innocence (*Deuteronomy 21:6–9*). But Pilate was not innocent. He had the authority to release Jesus and chose not to, out of fear of unrest. Washing his hands could not remove his responsibility.

The people answered, “*May his blood be on us and on our children!*” (*v. 25*) This verse has been tragically misused throughout history to blame the Jewish people as a whole for Jesus’ death and to justify persecution. Such use is a grave misreading. The words were spoken by a particular crowd in Jerusalem, stirred up by its leaders, on a particular day. The New Testament teaches that Jesus’ death was the result of human sin in general, involving Jewish leaders, Roman authorities, His own disciples, and ultimately all people, and that His death happened according to God’s plan to save (*Acts 4:27–28*). Jesus Himself prayed for those who crucified Him (*Luke 23:34*), and the apostles preached forgiveness to the very people of Jerusalem (*Acts 2:36–41*). Matthew may also intend a deeper irony: Jesus’ blood, which the crowd called down in judgment, is the blood “*poured out for many for the remission of sins*” (*Matthew 26:28*).

Pilate released Barabbas and had Jesus flogged. Roman flogging was brutal, done with whips embedded with pieces of bone or metal, and it sometimes killed prisoners before crucifixion. Then Pilate handed Him over to be crucified.

### The Soldiers Mock Jesus (*27:27–31*)

The governor’s soldiers took Jesus into the Praetorium, the governor’s headquarters, and gathered the whole cohort around Him, possibly several hundred soldiers. They stripped Him and put a scarlet robe on Him, likely a soldier’s red cloak, imitating a royal purple robe. They twisted a crown out of thorns and put it on His head, put a reed in His right hand as a mock scepter, and knelt before Him, saying, “*Hail, King of the Jews!*” (*v. 29*) They spat on Him and struck Him on the head with the reed. Then they put His own clothes back on Him and led Him away to be crucified.

The irony is profound. The soldiers mocked Jesus as a false king, but Matthew’s readers know He truly is the King. The crown of thorns, meant as a joke, became a symbol of the King who wore the curse of human sin.

### The Crucifixion (*27:32–44*)

As they went out, they forced a man from Cyrene (in North Africa) named Simon to carry Jesus’ cross. Jesus, weakened by the flogging, apparently could not carry the crossbeam all the way. Mark notes that Simon was the father of Alexander and Rufus (*Mark 15:21*), suggesting that his sons became known in the early church.

They came to Golgotha, which means “Place of a Skull,” probably a rocky area just outside the city walls. They offered Jesus wine mixed with gall, a bitter substance, perhaps intended as a mild sedative. Jesus tasted it but refused to drink, choosing to face His suffering with full awareness. The scene recalls *Psalm 69:21*.

They crucified Him. Crucifixion was a Roman form of execution designed to be slow, painful, and humiliating, reserved for slaves, rebels, and the worst criminals. The victim was nailed or tied to a cross and left to die of exhaustion and suffocation, sometimes over days. Matthew does not describe the physical details; his readers knew them all too well.

The soldiers divided His clothes by casting lots, fulfilling *Psalm 22:18*. They sat down to keep watch. Above His head they placed the written charge: “*THIS IS JESUS, THE KING OF THE JEWS*” (*v. 37*). Two robbers (or rebels) were crucified with Him, one on His right and one on His left, the very places James and John had requested in His kingdom (*Matthew 20:21*).

People passing by shook their heads and mocked Him, using His own words against Him: “*You who destroy the temple and build it in three days, save yourself! If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross!*” (*v. 40*) These words echo the devil’s temptation in the wilderness: “If you are the Son of God” (*Matthew 4:3*, 6). The chief priests, scribes, and elders also mocked Him: “*He saved others, but he can’t save himself*” (*v. 42*). Their words were unintentionally true: precisely because He was saving others, He would not save Himself. They added, “*He trusts in God. Let God deliver him now, if he wants him*” (*v. 43*), echoing *Psalm 22:8*, the psalm of the righteous sufferer. Even the robbers crucified with Him insulted Him.

### The Death of Jesus (*27:45–56*)

From the sixth hour (noon) until the ninth hour (3 p.m.), darkness covered the land. In Scripture, darkness often signals God’s judgment (*Exodus 10:21–23*; *Amos 8:9*). About three o’clock, Jesus cried out with a loud voice, “*Eli, Eli, lima sabachthani?*” (*v. 46*), which means, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” This is studied below.

Some bystanders thought He was calling Elijah, perhaps mishearing “Eli.” One ran and offered Him sour wine on a sponge. Others said to wait and see whether Elijah would come to save Him. Then Jesus cried out again with a loud voice and “*yielded up his spirit*” (*v. 50*). Matthew’s wording suggests that Jesus gave up His life willingly; it was not simply taken from Him.

At that moment, extraordinary things happened. The curtain of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom. The earth shook, rocks split, tombs were opened, and many holy people who had died were raised. Matthew says they came out of the tombs after Jesus’ resurrection and appeared to many in Jerusalem. This unusual event, found only in Matthew, signals that Jesus’ death and resurrection have broken the power of death. Interpreters have discussed how to understand it, but Matthew presents it as a sign that the resurrection age has begun. The torn curtain and the centurion’s confession are studied below.

Many women were watching from a distance, women who had followed Jesus from Galilee and cared for His needs. Among them were Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joseph, and the mother of Zebedee’s sons. While the male disciples had fled, these women remained.

### The Burial (*27:57–61*)

When evening came, a rich man from Arimathea named Joseph, who had become a disciple of Jesus, went to Pilate and asked for Jesus’ body. Normally the bodies of crucified criminals were left on crosses or thrown into common graves. Jewish law required that the body of an executed person be buried before nightfall (*Deuteronomy 21:22–23*), especially before the Sabbath. Joseph took a risk by publicly identifying with Jesus. Pilate granted his request.

Joseph wrapped the body in clean linen and placed it in his own new tomb cut into the rock. He rolled a large stone in front of the entrance. *Isaiah 53:9* says the Servant was buried “*with a rich man in his death*” (*Isaiah 53:9*). Mary Magdalene and the other Mary sat opposite the tomb, watching. They knew exactly where Jesus was buried.

### The Guard at the Tomb (*27:62–66*)

The next day, the Sabbath, the chief priests and Pharisees went to Pilate. They remembered that Jesus had said He would rise after three days. Calling Him “*that deceiver*” (*v. 63*), they asked Pilate to secure the tomb so that His disciples could not steal the body and claim He had risen. Pilate told them to take a guard and make it as secure as they could. They sealed the stone and posted guards. Ironically, their efforts to prevent a fraudulent resurrection claim would provide evidence for the real resurrection: a sealed, guarded tomb that would be found empty.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Matthew 27:46* — “*My God, My God, Why Have You Forsaken Me?*” (*v. 46*)

> *“About the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, ‘Eli, Eli, lima sabachthani?’ That is, ‘My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?’”*
>
> — *Matthew 27:46* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse records one of the most solemn moments in the Bible. Jesus had been hanging on the cross since about nine in the morning (*Mark 15:25*). From noon until three in the afternoon, darkness covered the land. Throughout these hours He had been mocked by passersby, religious leaders, soldiers, and even the robbers crucified with Him. Now, around three o’clock, He cried out with a loud voice.

His words were in Aramaic, the everyday language of Jesus and His disciples, with “Eli” (“my God”) in Hebrew form: “*Eli, Eli, lima sabachthani?*” (*v. 46*) Matthew translates them: “*My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?*” (*v. 46*) These words are the opening line of *Psalm 22*, a psalm of David that describes a righteous man suffering intense agony and mockery, crying out to God, and then ending in confidence and praise as God delivers him and the nations turn to the Lord.

Matthew has already shown connections between *Psalm 22* and the crucifixion. The mockers shook their heads (*Psalm 22:7*), said “*He trusts in God. Let God deliver him now*” (*v. 43*) (compare *Psalm 22:8*), and the soldiers divided His garments by casting lots (*Psalm 22:18*). Now Jesus Himself prays the psalm’s opening words.

The cry expresses real anguish. Jesus, who had always lived in perfect communion with His Father and who addressed Him as “My Father” in Gethsemane, now cries “My God,” expressing a profound experience of abandonment. Some bystanders misunderstood, thinking He was calling for Elijah.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Christians have reflected deeply on what this cry means. Many understand it to express the reality that Jesus was bearing the judgment for sin on behalf of others. Paul writes, “*For him who knew no sin he made to be sin on our behalf, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God*” (*2 Corinthians 5:21*). On the cross, Jesus experienced the separation from God that sin brings, so that those who trust in Him would never be separated from God. The darkness over the land points to this judgment.

At the same time, interpreters caution against concluding that the Trinity was broken or that the Father stopped loving the Son. Jesus still addressed Him as “My God,” a cry of faith even in agony. By quoting the beginning of *Psalm 22*, Jesus may also have been pointing to the whole psalm, which moves from abandonment to vindication: “*neither has he hidden his face from him; but when he cried to him, he heard*” (*Psalm 22:24*). Jesus’ cry is both a real experience of forsakenness and a prayer of trust.

The verse also shows that Jesus fully entered human suffering, including the experience of feeling abandoned by God. Believers who feel forsaken in their own suffering can know that Jesus understands that experience from the inside.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse shows that it is not wrong to bring the deepest anguish to God in honest words. Jesus prayed the words of a psalm of lament, a prayer that asks God “why.” Believers who are suffering, grieving, or feeling abandoned can bring their cries to God, using the psalms as Jesus did. Honest lament is an act of faith, because it is addressed to God.

It also gives believers deep assurance. Because Jesus experienced forsakenness on the cross, those who trust in Him will never be forsaken by God. Hebrews quotes God’s promise, “*I will in no way leave you, neither will I in any way forsake you*” (*Hebrews 13:5*). Even when believers feel far from God, they can trust that He has not abandoned them.

Finally, this verse calls believers to gratitude and worship. The cost of their salvation was immense. Jesus endured not only physical pain but spiritual anguish to bring them to God. Remembering this can deepen love for Him and strengthen resolve to follow Him.

### *Matthew 27:51* — The Temple Curtain Torn in Two

> *“Behold, the veil of the temple was torn in two from the top to the bottom. The earth quaked and the rocks were split.”*
>
> — *Matthew 27:51* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse describes what happened at the very moment Jesus died. He had cried out with a loud voice and yielded up His spirit. Immediately, “*the veil of the temple was torn in two from the top to the bottom*” (*v. 51*).

The temple in Jerusalem had curtains separating its sacred spaces. The most important curtain separated the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place, the innermost room where God’s presence was believed to dwell in a special way. In the original tabernacle, this room held the ark of the covenant (*Exodus 26:31–33*). Only the high priest could enter it, and only once a year, on the Day of Atonement, bringing the blood of a sacrifice to atone for the sins of the people (*Leviticus 16*). The curtain was a powerful symbol of the separation between a holy God and sinful people. According to later Jewish tradition, it was very thick and very large.

Matthew says the curtain was torn “*from the top to the bottom*” (*v. 51*). This detail suggests that the tearing was God’s act, not a human one. No person standing on the ground could tear such a curtain from the top.

Matthew adds that the earth shook and the rocks split. Earthquakes in the Old Testament often accompanied God’s appearances and acts of judgment (*Exodus 19:18*; *Psalm 18:7*). Jesus’ death was a world-shaking event.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The tearing of the curtain shows that Jesus’ death opened the way into God’s presence. The book of Hebrews explains this meaning: believers can now enter the Most Holy Place “*by the way which he dedicated for us, a new and living way, through the veil, that is to say, his flesh*” (*Hebrews 10:20*). Jesus’ body, torn on the cross, is the true curtain through which people come to God. The barrier of sin has been removed by His sacrifice.

The torn curtain also signals that the temple’s sacrificial system had reached its fulfillment. Jesus had predicted the temple’s destruction (*Matthew 24:2*), and He had said that something greater than the temple was here (*Matthew 12:6*). His death accomplished what all the temple’s sacrifices pointed to. Some interpreters also see the torn curtain as a sign of judgment on the temple itself, which would be destroyed about forty years later.

Finally, this event reveals that access to God is now open to everyone who comes through Christ, not only priests, and not only Israel. In the very next verses, a Gentile centurion confesses Jesus as the Son of God.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to approach God with confidence. Because the curtain has been torn, they do not need a human priest or a sacrifice to come into God’s presence. Hebrews encourages believers, “*Let’s therefore draw near with boldness to the throne of grace*” (*Hebrews 4:16*). Prayer is a privilege made possible by Jesus’ death.

It also reminds believers that their access to God depends entirely on Jesus. They do not come to God on the basis of their own goodness, but through what Christ has done. This brings both humility and assurance.

Finally, this verse encourages believers to welcome others into God’s presence. The barrier between God and people has been removed for all who come through Christ. Believers can share this good news with anyone, regardless of background, inviting them to come near to God through Jesus.

### *Matthew 27:54* — “*Truly This Was the Son of God*” (*v. 54*)

> *“Now the centurion and those who were with him watching Jesus, when they saw the earthquake and the things that were done, were terrified, saying, ‘Truly this was the Son of God!’”*
>
> — *Matthew 27:54* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse records the reaction of the Roman soldiers who carried out Jesus’ crucifixion. A centurion was an officer in charge of about a hundred soldiers. He and his men had been responsible for the execution. They had likely participated in mocking Jesus, dividing His clothing, and keeping watch over Him as He died. To them, He was just another condemned man, a Jewish prisoner accused of claiming to be a king.

But they had seen how Jesus died. They had watched the darkness cover the land, heard His loud cry, and felt the earthquake. Matthew says that when they saw the earthquake and everything that happened, “*were terrified*” (*v. 54*). Then they said, “*Truly this was the Son of God!*” (*v. 54*)

The irony is striking. The religious leaders had mocked Jesus for claiming to be the Son of God (v. 43). The passersby had challenged Him: “If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross!” (v. 40). Jesus did not come down. Yet it was precisely in His death, not by escaping it, that these Gentile soldiers recognized who He was.

For a Roman soldier, “son of a god” might have meant a divine or extraordinary man, a phrase sometimes used for emperors. But Matthew’s readers understand that the centurion spoke a greater truth than he may have realized. The Father had declared Jesus His beloved Son at His baptism (*Matthew 3:17*) and transfiguration (*Matthew 17:5*). Peter had confessed Him as the Son of the living God (*Matthew 16:16*). Now, at the cross, Gentile soldiers confess the same.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that the cross reveals who Jesus truly is. Many expected that if Jesus were really the Son of God, He would come down from the cross and prove it by saving Himself. Instead, the cross itself is where His identity as God’s Son is most clearly displayed: the Son who obeys the Father to the point of death and gives His life for others.

The confession of the Gentile soldiers also anticipates the spread of the gospel to all nations. At the beginning of Matthew, Gentile magi came to worship the newborn King of the Jews. Now, at the end, Gentile soldiers confess Him as the Son of God. Soon, the risen Jesus will send His disciples to make disciples of all nations (*Matthew 28:19*).

Finally, this verse shows that no one is beyond the reach of God’s revelation. These soldiers had been instruments of Jesus’ execution. Yet they came to recognize Him. God can open the eyes of even the most unlikely people.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites readers to look at the cross and recognize who Jesus is. Many people today have ideas about Jesus as a good teacher, a prophet, or a moral example. The cross reveals that He is the Son of God who gave Himself for the world. Believers can reflect on the cross regularly, allowing it to deepen their understanding of Jesus and their love for Him.

It also encourages believers to hope for those who seem far from God. If Roman soldiers who crucified Jesus could confess Him as the Son of God, then anyone can come to faith. Believers can keep praying for and sharing Christ with people who seem hostile or indifferent.

Finally, this verse reminds believers that God’s power is often revealed in what looks like weakness. The world expected strength to come by escaping the cross. God revealed His Son through the cross. Believers can trust that God works through humility, sacrifice, and suffering in ways that the world does not expect.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Matthew 27* invites readers to stand at the foot of the cross and consider their own response to Jesus. The chapter presents many responses: Judas’s despair, the leaders’ hatred, Pilate’s cowardice, the crowd’s manipulation, the soldiers’ mockery, the bystanders’ taunts, the centurion’s confession, Joseph’s courage, and the women’s faithful presence. Every reader can ask which of these responses reflects their own heart and choose the path of confession, courage, and faithfulness.

The contrast between Judas and Peter is especially important. Both failed Jesus seriously. Judas felt remorse but went to the religious leaders, who offered no help, and he died in despair. Peter wept bitterly but was later restored by the risen Jesus. Believers who have failed can learn from this: remorse alone is not enough, but turning back to Jesus brings forgiveness and restoration.

Pilate’s story warns against trying to avoid responsibility. He knew Jesus was innocent, but he gave in to pressure and tried to wash his hands of the decision. Believers face many situations where it is tempting to go along with the crowd or avoid taking a stand for what is right. Washing one’s hands does not remove responsibility. Integrity requires courage.

The mockery at the cross reveals that Jesus chose not to save Himself so that He could save others. Believers can respond with gratitude and worship, remembering the cost of their salvation. They can also bring their own suffering, abandonment, and grief to God, as Jesus did in the words of *Psalm 22*, trusting that He hears.

Finally, the torn curtain and the centurion’s confession show the results of Jesus’ death: open access to God for all who come through Christ, and a gospel that reaches all nations. Believers can approach God with confidence, share the good news with anyone, and follow the example of Joseph and the women, who stayed faithful when others fled.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, I stand at the foot of Your cross in awe and gratitude. You were betrayed, condemned though innocent, mocked as a king, and crucified between robbers. You chose not to save Yourself so that You could save me. Thank You for bearing the darkness and the forsakenness I deserved, so that I will never be forsaken.

Forgive me for the times I have acted like Pilate, avoiding responsibility, or like the crowd, going along with what is wrong. When I fail, keep me from despair and draw me back to You. Thank You for tearing the curtain and opening the way into God’s presence. Help me to draw near with confidence. Like the centurion, I confess that You are truly the Son of God. Give me the courage of Joseph and the faithfulness of the women who stayed near You. Help me to live in grateful love for the King who wore a crown of thorns for me. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
