Matthew · Chapter 28 of 28

# Matthew — Chapter 28

Chapter Theme: The Risen King Sends His Disciples to All Nations

[Read Matthew 28 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/MAT28.htm)

Main Teaching

Early on the first day of the week, women who come to the tomb find it empty and hear from an angel that Jesus has risen, just as He said. Jesus meets them, and the religious leaders bribe the guards to spread a false story. On a mountain in Galilee, the risen Jesus declares that all authority belongs to Him, sends His followers to make disciples of all nations, and promises to be with them always.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Matthew 28* is the climax and conclusion of Matthew’s Gospel. Jesus had been crucified on Friday and buried in Joseph of Arimathea’s tomb before sunset (*Matthew 27:57–61*). The chief priests and Pharisees, remembering that Jesus had predicted His resurrection, persuaded Pilate to seal the tomb and post a guard (*27:62–66*). Saturday was the Sabbath, a day of rest. *Matthew 28* opens at dawn on Sunday, the first day of the week.

Jesus had repeatedly told His disciples that He would be killed and raised on the third day (*Matthew 16:21*; *17:23*; *20:19*). He had also promised that after He was raised, He would go ahead of them into Galilee (*26:32*). Yet none of the disciples seem to have expected the resurrection. The women came to visit a grave, and the men were in hiding. The events of this chapter took them by surprise.

### The Empty Tomb (*28:1–8*)

As the first day of the week was dawning, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary (the mother of James and Joseph, *27:56*) went to see the tomb. These were the same women who had watched Jesus die and seen where He was buried (*27:55–61*). Mark and Luke tell us they brought spices to anoint the body (*Mark 16:1*; *Luke 24:1*).

Suddenly there was a great earthquake. An angel of the Lord came down from heaven, rolled back the stone, and sat on it. His appearance was like lightning, and his clothes were white as snow. The guards were so afraid that they shook and became like dead men. The irony is striking: the guards posted to keep the dead man in the tomb became like dead men, while the one who had died was alive.

The angel did not roll away the stone to let Jesus out, but to let the witnesses in. He said to the women, “*Don’t be afraid, for I know that you seek Jesus, who has been crucified*” (*v. 5*). Then he announced the news that is studied below: “*He is not here, for he has risen, just like he said*” (*v. 6*). He invited them to see the place where He had lain, and then told them to go quickly and tell the disciples that Jesus had risen and was going ahead of them to Galilee.

The women hurried away from the tomb “*with fear and great joy*” (*v. 8*), running to tell the disciples. In that culture, women’s testimony was often given less weight than men’s, especially in legal matters. If the early church had invented the resurrection story, it would have been unlikely to make women the first witnesses. Their prominence in all four Gospels is one of the marks of historical honesty.

### Jesus Appears to the Women (*28:9–10*)

As the women went, Jesus Himself met them and greeted them with the ordinary word, “*Rejoice!*” (*v. 9*), which was also a common greeting meaning something like “Hello” or “Greetings.” They came to Him, took hold of His feet, and worshiped Him. Holding His feet shows that He was physically present, not a ghost or vision. Their worship shows that they recognized Him as more than a teacher.

Jesus repeated the angel’s message with a tender change: “*Don’t be afraid. Go tell my brothers that they should go into Galilee, and there they will see me*” (*v. 10*). He called the disciples who had deserted Him “my brothers.” Their failure had not ended their relationship with Him.

### The Guards’ Report (*28:11–15*)

While the women were on their way, some of the guards went into the city and reported to the chief priests everything that had happened. The chief priests met with the elders and devised a plan. They gave the soldiers a large sum of money and told them to say, “*His disciples came by night and stole him away while we slept*” (*v. 13*). They promised to protect the soldiers if the story reached Pilate, since sleeping on duty could be punished severely.

The story had obvious problems. If the guards were asleep, how could they know who took the body? And it is hard to imagine that the frightened disciples, who had fled at Jesus’ arrest, would overpower or sneak past a guard and break a seal. Matthew notes that this story was still being told among some Jews at the time he wrote his Gospel. His account explains where the rumor came from. Notably, the story assumes that the tomb was empty; the dispute was over how it became empty.

The religious leaders had paid thirty pieces of silver to arrange Jesus’ death. Now they paid a large sum to cover up His resurrection. Money could buy a betrayal and a lie, but it could not keep Jesus in the grave.

### The Great Commission (*28:16–20*)

The eleven disciples, now without Judas, went to Galilee, to the mountain Jesus had designated. Matthew’s Gospel often places important moments on mountains: the temptation (*4:8*), the Sermon on the Mount (*5:1*), the feeding of the four thousand (*15:29*), and the transfiguration (*17:1*). This final mountain scene brings the Gospel to its conclusion.

When they saw Jesus, they worshiped Him, “*but some doubted*” (*v. 17*). This honest detail is studied below. Jesus came to them and spoke words that form the climax of the whole Gospel: “*All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth*” (*v. 18*). In the wilderness, the devil had offered Jesus the kingdoms of the world if He would worship him (*4:8–9*). Jesus refused and took the path of the cross. Now, through His obedience, death, and resurrection, He has received all authority from the Father, not only over the earth but over heaven as well. This fulfills *Daniel 7:13–14*, where the Son of Man receives dominion over all peoples.

On the basis of this authority, Jesus gave His disciples their mission: to go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and teaching them to obey everything He commanded. Then He gave a promise: “*Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age*” (*v. 20*). These verses are studied below.

Matthew’s Gospel began with the promise that Jesus would be called “Immanuel,” meaning “*God with us*” (*Matthew 1:23*). It ends with Jesus’ promise to be with His disciples always. The whole Gospel is framed by the truth that in Jesus, God is with His people.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Matthew 28:6* — “*He Has Risen, Just Like He Said*” (*v. 6*)

> *“He is not here, for he has risen, just like he said. Come, see the place where the Lord was lying.”*
>
> — *Matthew 28:6* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These words are spoken by an angel to Mary Magdalene and the other Mary at Jesus’ tomb early on Sunday morning. The women had come to visit the grave, expecting to find Jesus’ body. Instead, there was a great earthquake, and an angel rolled back the stone and sat on it. The Roman guards were terrified and became like dead men. The angel told the women not to be afraid, because he knew they were looking for Jesus, who had been crucified.

Then came the announcement: “*He is not here, for he has risen, just like he said*” (*v. 6*). Each part of this statement is important. “He is not here” declares the empty tomb. “He has risen” explains why; the body was not stolen or moved, but Jesus had been raised from the dead by God’s power. The verb form emphasizes that God raised Him. “Just like he said” reminds the women that Jesus had predicted this. Three times He had told His disciples that He would be killed and raised on the third day (*Matthew 16:21*; *17:23*; *20:19*). His words had come true.

The angel then invited them, “*Come, see the place where the Lord was lying*” (*v. 6*). The women could see for themselves that the body was gone. The resurrection was not just a spiritual idea but a bodily event that left an empty tomb.

Immediately afterward, the angel sent them to tell the disciples. Then Jesus Himself met them, and they took hold of His feet and worshiped Him, confirming that He was truly and physically alive.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The resurrection is the foundation of the Christian faith. Paul writes, “*If Christ has not been raised, your faith is vain; you are still in your sins*” (*1 Corinthians 15:17*). The resurrection shows that God accepted Jesus’ sacrifice, that His death really accomplished forgiveness, and that death has been defeated. It vindicates Jesus’ claims to be the Messiah and Son of God.

The phrase “just like he said” also teaches that Jesus’ words can be trusted. Everything He predicted about His death and resurrection came to pass. If He kept His word about this, believers can trust His other promises, including His promise to return and to raise His people.

The resurrection also gives hope for believers’ future. Jesus’ resurrection is the beginning of the resurrection of all who belong to Him. Because He lives, they will live. Death is not the end for those who trust in Christ.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse calls believers to live with resurrection hope. Grief, suffering, and death are real, but they are not final. Believers can face loss and their own mortality with confidence that Jesus has conquered death and will raise His people.

It also encourages believers to trust Jesus’ words. When His promises seem slow to be fulfilled, believers can remember that He did exactly what He said about rising from the dead. His faithfulness in the past gives confidence for the future.

Finally, the angel’s message led immediately to a mission: go and tell. The good news of the resurrection is meant to be shared. Believers can share this hope with others, especially those who are grieving or searching for meaning, by speaking about the risen Jesus and living in a way that reflects His victory.

### *Matthew 28:17* — Worship and Doubt on the Mountain

> *“When they saw him, they bowed down to him; but some doubted.”*
>
> — *Matthew 28:17* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse describes the moment when the eleven disciples saw the risen Jesus on the mountain in Galilee. The women had delivered the message from the angel and from Jesus, and the disciples had obeyed by going to Galilee. Now Jesus appeared to them.

“*When they saw him, they bowed down to him*” (*v. 17*). The word means they worshiped Him, falling down before Him as one worships God. These men had followed Jesus for years, and now they recognized Him as far more than a teacher.

Then Matthew adds a surprising phrase: “*but some doubted*” (*v. 17*). The word translated “doubted” is the same word used when Peter began to sink in the water: “*why did you doubt?*” (*Matthew 14:31*) It describes hesitation or being divided in mind, rather than outright unbelief. Some of the disciples, even while seeing Jesus, struggled to take it all in. Perhaps they were overwhelmed, uncertain, or still processing their own failure and the shock of the past days. Matthew does not say who doubted or how long their doubt lasted.

What Jesus did next is significant. He did not send away the doubters or wait until everyone was certain. “*Jesus came to them and spoke to them*” (*v. 18*). He drew near to the whole group, worshipers and doubters alike, and gave them His commission.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals the honesty of Matthew’s Gospel. Matthew could have presented the disciples as perfectly confident at this climactic moment, but he records that some doubted. This honesty strengthens the credibility of the account. The early church did not hide the weaknesses of its leaders.

The verse also shows that worship and doubt can exist together in the same group and even in the same heart. Faith is not always free of questions. The disciples had experienced trauma, failure, and an event unlike anything in human experience. Their hesitation is understandable.

Most importantly, the verse shows Jesus’ response to doubt. He came near and spoke to them. He entrusted His mission to people who were still growing in faith. Jesus’ work in the world does not depend on His followers’ perfect certainty but on His authority and His presence with them.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers who struggle with doubt. Many sincere believers have times of questioning, uncertainty, or hesitation. These experiences do not mean they are excluded from Jesus’ presence or purposes. Like the disciples, they can continue to worship, bring their questions to Him, and stay close to the community of faith.

It also encourages believers to welcome others who doubt. Churches can be places where honest questions are allowed and where people with uncertain faith are invited to keep seeking Jesus. Jesus did not wait for perfect faith before drawing near.

Finally, this verse reminds believers that Jesus’ mission is carried out by imperfect people. Believers do not need to have all their questions answered before they serve and share their faith. They can step forward in obedience, trusting Jesus’ authority and His promise to be with them.

### *Matthew 28:19–20* — Make Disciples of All Nations

> *“Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all things that I commanded you. Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age. Amen.”*
>
> — *Matthew 28:19–20* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These verses contain Jesus’ final words in Matthew’s Gospel, often called the Great Commission. Jesus has just declared, “*All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth*” (*v. 18*). The word “Go” in verse 19 is connected to that authority: because Jesus has all authority, He sends His followers out with His mission.

The main command is “*make disciples*” (*v. 19*). A disciple is a learner and follower of a teacher. Jesus is not only telling His followers to win converts but to make people who follow Him in their whole lives. The command includes three supporting actions: going, baptizing, and teaching.

“Go” means that disciples must move outward to reach others rather than waiting for people to come to them. “*of all nations*” (*v. 19*) marks a major expansion. During His earthly ministry, Jesus had told the Twelve to go only to the lost sheep of Israel (*Matthew 10:5–6*). Now the mission extends to every people group in the world, fulfilling God’s promise to Abraham that through his offspring “*all the nations of the earth will be blessed*” (*Genesis 22:18*).

“Baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” describes the act by which new disciples are publicly identified with the triune God and with His people. “Name” is singular, suggesting the one God revealed as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

“*teaching them to observe all things that I commanded you*” (*v. 20*). Discipleship includes ongoing instruction in Jesus’ teaching. Matthew’s Gospel contains five major blocks of Jesus’ teaching (chapters 5–7, 10, 13, 18, 24–25), and these provide much of the content disciples are to learn and obey. The goal is not merely to know His commands but to “observe” or obey them.

Finally comes the promise: “*Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age*” (*v. 20*). Jesus will not be physically present in the same way, but He will be with His disciples through every day until His return.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses reveal the global scope of God’s plan. From Genesis onward, God intended to bless all nations through Abraham’s family. Jesus, the son of Abraham (*Matthew 1:1*), now sends His disciples to bring that blessing to the whole world. The church’s mission is rooted in God’s eternal purpose.

The Great Commission also shows that discipleship is comprehensive. It begins with going to people where they are, continues with baptism into the life of God’s people, and grows through lifelong learning and obedience. It is not merely a decision but a transformation of life under Jesus’ authority.

The promise of Jesus’ presence is the foundation of the whole mission. The disciples were not sent out alone or in their own strength. The same Jesus who was “God with us” at His birth (*1:23*) promises to be “with you always.” This presence is fulfilled through the Holy Spirit, whom Jesus promised to send (*John 14:16–18*; *Acts 1:8*). The mission is sustained by His authority and His presence.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses call every believer to participate in making disciples. Not everyone is called to travel to distant countries, but every believer can help others know and follow Jesus. This might include sharing their faith with friends, family, and coworkers; supporting missionaries; welcoming people from other cultures; and helping new believers grow.

They also call believers to take discipleship seriously in their own lives. Being a disciple means continually learning and obeying Jesus’ teaching. Believers can make a habit of studying His words, applying them to daily decisions, and helping others do the same. Churches can focus on helping people grow in obedience, not merely in knowledge.

Finally, these verses give believers confidence. The task of reaching all nations is enormous, and believers may feel inadequate. But Jesus has all authority, and He has promised to be with His people always. Believers can obey His commission with courage and joy, knowing that He goes with them every day, until the end of the age.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Matthew 28* transforms everything that came before it. The crucified King is alive. The tomb is empty. Jesus’ words have proven true. This means that believers can trust His promises, face death with hope, and know that His sacrifice has truly accomplished forgiveness. The resurrection is not only a past event but a present reality: Jesus is alive and active today.

The chapter shows the right responses to the risen Jesus. The women responded with fear and great joy, worship, and obedience as they ran to tell others. The disciples worshiped, even with some doubt. The religious leaders responded with bribery and lies to suppress the truth. Every person must decide how to respond to the claim that Jesus has risen. Believers can respond with worship, trust, and joyful obedience.

Jesus’ tenderness toward His failed disciples is also striking. He called them “my brothers” after they had deserted Him, and He entrusted His mission to them even though some still doubted. Believers who feel unworthy or uncertain can take heart: Jesus does not wait for perfect people to carry out His work.

Finally, the Great Commission gives every believer a purpose. Jesus has all authority, and He sends His followers to make disciples of all nations, baptizing them and teaching them to obey His commands. This mission shapes how believers live, how churches use their resources, and how Christians relate to people of other nations and cultures. And it is sustained by His promise: “I am with you always, even to the end of the age.” The story Matthew began with “God with us” ends with Jesus’ promise to remain with His people forever.

## Chapter Prayer

Risen Lord Jesus, thank You that the tomb is empty and that You have risen just as You said. Thank You for conquering death and for proving that Your sacrifice was accepted for my sins. Fill me with the same fear and great joy that the women felt, and help me to run and tell others the good news.

Thank You for calling Your failing disciples “my brothers” and for drawing near even to those who doubted. When I struggle with doubt, help me to keep worshiping You and to trust Your presence. You have all authority in heaven and on earth. Send me out to help others become Your disciples, to welcome them into Your family, and to teach them to obey everything You have commanded. Give me courage, compassion for people of every nation, and confidence in Your promise that You are with me always, even to the end of the age. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Book 2 of 27

# Mark

## About This Gospel

Mark is the shortest of the four Gospels and probably the first to be written. Early Christian writers, beginning with Papias in the early second century, report that John Mark, a companion of Peter and Paul (*Acts 12:12*, 25; *1 Peter 5:13*), wrote down Peter’s preaching about Jesus. Many scholars date the book to the 60s A.D., likely written in Rome for Christians who faced suspicion and persecution under Nero. Mark often explains Jewish customs and translates Aramaic words, which suggests that many of his readers were Gentiles.

## The Shape of the Book

Mark tells the story with urgency. His favorite word, “immediately,” moves the narrative quickly from scene to scene. The first half of the book (chapters 1–8) shows Jesus’ authority in Galilee as He teaches, heals, casts out demons, and calms storms, while the disciples and the crowds keep asking, “Who is this?” At Caesarea Philippi, Peter confesses that Jesus is the Christ (*8:29*). The second half (chapters 8–16) follows Jesus “on the way” to Jerusalem as He teaches that the Son of Man must suffer, die, and rise, and as He calls His followers to take up their cross. Roughly a third of the book describes Jesus’ final week.

## Themes to Watch For

Mark presents Jesus as the Son of God (*1:1*; *15:39*) whose identity is most clearly revealed at the cross. He emphasizes that Jesus came “not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (*10:45*). Mark is honest about the disciples’ fear, misunderstanding, and failure, and equally clear about Jesus’ patient grace toward them. His vivid details, such as the cushion in the boat, the green grass at the feeding of the five thousand, and Jesus’ Aramaic words “Talitha cumi” and “Ephphatha,” give the book the feel of eyewitness memory.

Mark · Chapter 1 of 16

# Mark — Chapter 1

Chapter Theme: The Good News Begins, and the Kingdom Breaks In

[Read Mark 1 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/MRK01.htm)

Main Teaching

Mark begins abruptly with the announcement that his book is the good news about Jesus Christ, the Son of God. After John the Baptist prepares the way and Jesus is baptized and tested, Jesus bursts onto the scene in Galilee, calling people to repent and believe, summoning fishermen to follow Him, driving out demons, healing the sick, and withdrawing to pray. His authority amazes everyone, yet He refuses to let popularity set His agenda.

## Chapter Background and Story

Mark is the shortest of the four Gospels and probably the earliest. Early Christian tradition, recorded by writers such as Papias in the early second century, says that Mark (also called John Mark, *Acts 12:12*) wrote down the preaching of the apostle Peter, likely in Rome in the 60s A.D. The book is written in fast-moving, vivid Greek. One of Mark’s favorite words is “immediately,” which appears eleven times in chapter 1 alone. The pace gives the impression of urgency: God’s kingdom is breaking into the world, and there is no time to waste.

Unlike Matthew and Luke, Mark includes no birth stories or genealogy. He begins with Jesus as an adult and moves quickly from His baptism into His ministry. Mark often explains Jewish customs and translates Aramaic words, which suggests he was writing mainly for Gentile readers, possibly Christians in Rome who were facing suspicion and, before long, persecution under the emperor Nero.

### The Beginning of the Good News (*1:1–8*)

Mark’s first sentence serves as the title and theme of his whole book: “*The beginning of the Good News of Jesus Christ, the Son of God*” (*v. 1*). This verse is studied below.

Mark then quotes the prophets. The words come from *Malachi 3:1* and *Isaiah 40:3*, but Mark names Isaiah, the more prominent prophet, which was a common way of citing combined texts. Both passages promise a messenger who would prepare the way for the Lord’s coming. Mark identifies that messenger as John the Baptist.

John appeared in the wilderness, “*preaching the baptism of repentance for forgiveness of sins*” (*v. 4*). People came from all over Judea and Jerusalem to be baptized in the Jordan River, confessing their sins. John’s clothing of camel’s hair and leather belt recalled the prophet Elijah (*2 Kings 1:8*), and his diet of locusts and wild honey reflected life in the desert. John pointed beyond himself: someone mightier was coming, whose sandal strap he was not worthy to stoop down and untie. Untying sandals was a task for the lowest slave. John baptized with water, but the coming one “*will baptize you in the Holy Spirit*” (*v. 8*), fulfilling the prophets’ promise that God would pour out His Spirit (*Joel 2:28*; *Ezekiel 36:26–27*).

### Jesus’ Baptism and Testing (*1:9–13*)

Jesus came from Nazareth, a small, obscure village in Galilee, and was baptized by John in the Jordan. As He came up out of the water, He saw “*the heavens parting*” (*v. 10*). Mark uses a strong word meaning “torn open,” the same word he uses at the end of the Gospel when the temple curtain is torn in two (*Mark 15:38*). Isaiah had prayed, “*Oh that you would tear the heavens, that you would come down*” (*Isaiah 64:1*). Now heaven was torn open, the Spirit descended on Jesus like a dove, and a voice declared, “*You are my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased*” (*v. 11*).

Immediately the Spirit “*drove him out into the wilderness*” (*v. 12*), where He was tempted by Satan for forty days. Mark’s account is very brief compared with Matthew and Luke, but it includes a detail they do not: Jesus “*was with the wild animals*” (*v. 13*), and angels served Him. The wilderness was dangerous, but Jesus was protected there. Some interpreters see an echo of Adam, who lived peacefully with the animals before sin, and of the prophetic hope that the Messiah’s reign would bring peace even among wild creatures (*Isaiah 11:6–9*).

### The Message of the Kingdom (*1:14–15*)

After John was arrested, Jesus went into Galilee preaching the good news of God. His message is summarized in verse 15: “*The time is fulfilled, and God’s Kingdom is at hand! Repent, and believe in the Good News*” (*v. 15*). This message is studied below.

### Calling the First Disciples (*1:16–20*)

Walking beside the Sea of Galilee, Jesus saw Simon and his brother Andrew casting their nets. He said, “*Come after me, and I will make you into fishers for men*” (*v. 17*), and they immediately left their nets and followed Him. A little farther on, He called James and John, the sons of Zebedee, who were mending nets in their boat. They left their father in the boat “*with the hired servants*” (*v. 20*). That detail, unique to Mark, tells us that Zebedee had a family business large enough to employ workers. These men left a measure of financial security to follow Jesus. (*Matthew 4:19* is studied in depth in Matthew’s commentary.)

### Authority in the Synagogue at Capernaum (*1:21–28*)

They went to Capernaum, a fishing town on the northwest shore of the lake, which became Jesus’ home base. On the Sabbath, Jesus taught in the synagogue. The people were astonished because “*he taught them as having authority, and not as the scribes*” (*v. 22*). Scribes usually taught by quoting earlier authorities. Jesus taught as one who spoke with God’s own authority.

Suddenly a man with an unclean spirit cried out, “*What do we have to do with you, Jesus, you Nazarene? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are: the Holy One of God!*” (*v. 24*) The demon recognized who Jesus was and knew that His coming meant defeat for the forces of evil. Jesus rebuked the spirit, saying, “*Be quiet, and come out of him!*” (*v. 25*) The spirit shook the man violently and came out with a shriek. The people were amazed that Jesus’ authority extended even to evil spirits, and news about Him spread throughout Galilee.

Jesus’ command for the demon to be quiet is the first instance of what scholars call the “messianic secret” in Mark: Jesus repeatedly silences demons and tells people not to publicize His identity or His miracles. He did not want His identity proclaimed by demons, and He did not want people to misunderstand His mission as merely that of a miracle-worker or political liberator before they understood that He had come to suffer and die.

### Healing at Peter’s House and at Sunset (*1:29–34*)

Leaving the synagogue, they went to the home of Simon and Andrew. Simon’s mother-in-law was in bed with a fever. Jesus took her by the hand and raised her up, and the fever left her. She began to serve them. That evening, after sunset (when the Sabbath ended and people could carry the sick without breaking Sabbath rules), the whole town gathered at the door. Jesus healed many and drove out many demons, again not allowing the demons to speak because they knew who He was.

### Withdrawing to Pray (*1:35–39*)

Very early the next morning, while it was still dark, Jesus went to a solitary place to pray. Simon and the others searched for Him and, when they found Him, said, “*Everyone is looking for you*” (*v. 37*). They expected Jesus to return to Capernaum and build on His popularity. Instead, He said, “*Let’s go elsewhere into the next towns, that I may preach there also, because I came out for this reason*” (*v. 38*). This scene is studied below.

### Cleansing a Leper (*1:40–45*)

A man with leprosy came to Jesus, knelt, and begged, “*If you want to, you can make me clean*” (*v. 40*). Mark says Jesus was “*moved with compassion*” (*v. 41*) (some manuscripts say He was “indignant,” perhaps at the disease and the suffering it caused). He reached out and touched the man, which no one would normally do because touching a leper made a person ritually unclean, and said, “*I want to. Be made clean*” (*v. 41*). The leprosy left him immediately. (Matthew’s parallel account of this healing is explored in depth at *Matthew 8:3*.)

Jesus sternly warned the man not to tell anyone but to show himself to the priest and offer the sacrifices required by Moses (*Leviticus 14*). But the man went out and talked freely, spreading the news everywhere. As a result, Jesus could no longer enter a town openly and stayed in deserted places. The chapter ends with an ironic reversal: the man who had been forced to live outside the towns because of his disease could now enter them, while Jesus, who had touched him, was now the one staying in lonely places. Yet people still came to Him from everywhere.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Mark 1:1* — The Beginning of the Good News

> *“The beginning of the Good News of Jesus Christ, the Son of God.”*
>
> — *Mark 1:1* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This short verse is Mark’s opening line, and it works like a title for his entire book. Unlike Matthew, who begins with a genealogy, or Luke, who begins with a formal introduction, Mark plunges straight into his subject.

“*The beginning*” (*v. 1*) may refer to the start of Mark’s account, but it also echoes the first words of the Bible: “*In the beginning, God created*” (*Genesis 1:1*). Mark may be hinting that something as momentous as a new creation is starting with Jesus.

“Good News” translates the Greek word “euangelion,” from which we get “evangelism” and “evangelical.” In the Roman world, this word was used for important public announcements, such as the birth of an emperor or a military victory. An inscription from 9 B.C. celebrated the birthday of Caesar Augustus as “the beginning of the good news for the world.” Mark’s readers in the Roman Empire would have heard his opening as a bold claim: the truly good news for the world is not about Caesar but about Jesus. In the Old Testament, Isaiah used the same idea to announce God’s coming to save His people (*Isaiah 40:9*; *52:7*).

“*of Jesus Christ*” (*v. 1*) names the subject. “Jesus” was His personal name, meaning “the LORD saves.” “Christ” is the Greek translation of “Messiah,” meaning the anointed king promised by God.

“*the Son of God*” (*v. 1*). (A few early manuscripts omit these words, but most include them.) This title frames the whole Gospel. The Father declares Jesus His beloved Son at the baptism (*1:11*) and the transfiguration (*9:7*), demons recognize Him as God’s Son (*3:11*; *5:7*), and at the climax, a Roman centurion at the cross says, “*Truly this man was the Son of God!*” (*Mark 15:39*) Mark’s Gospel moves from this opening claim to that confession.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse tells readers that Mark’s book is not merely biography but proclamation. It announces good news that calls for a response. The message centers on a person: Jesus, the Messiah and Son of God. The gospel is not first a set of ideas or rules but the announcement of who Jesus is and what God has done through Him.

The word “beginning” also suggests that the whole of Mark’s story, from John’s preaching to the empty tomb, is only the beginning. The good news continues to spread through Jesus’ followers into the world. Mark’s Gospel famously ends abruptly, with the women fleeing from the empty tomb (*Mark 16:8*), as if inviting readers to continue the story themselves.

Finally, by using language associated with Caesar, Mark makes a quiet but powerful claim: Jesus, not any earthly ruler, is the true King whose coming brings good news to the world. This claim would cost many early Christians their lives, yet they believed it was true.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites readers to receive the story of Jesus as good news, not just as religious information. The life, death, and resurrection of Jesus are news that changes everything: forgiveness is offered, God’s kingdom has come near, and death has been defeated. Believers can let this good news shape their outlook, especially in times of discouragement.

It also challenges believers to consider what they treat as the “good news” in their lives. Many people look to political leaders, economic success, or personal achievements as the source of hope. Mark insists that the deepest good news is found in Jesus, the Son of God.

Finally, this verse encourages believers to see themselves as part of the continuing story. The gospel’s “beginning” in Jesus continues as His followers share it with others. Believers can tell the story of Jesus in their own words and live in a way that shows it is truly good news.

### *Mark 1:15* — Repent and Believe the Good News

> *“and saying, ‘The time is fulfilled, and God’s Kingdom is at hand! Repent, and believe in the Good News.’”*
>
> — *Mark 1:15* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse summarizes Jesus’ message as He began His public ministry in Galilee. Mark says that after John the Baptist was arrested, Jesus came into Galilee, “*preaching the Good News of God’s Kingdom*” (*v. 14*). The timing is significant: John’s ministry of preparation had ended, and Jesus’ ministry of fulfillment was beginning.

Jesus’ message has two announcements and two commands. The first announcement is “*The time is fulfilled*” (*v. 15*). The word for “time” here means a decisive moment or appointed season, not just chronological time. God’s long-awaited moment had arrived. All the centuries of promise and waiting were reaching their goal.

The second announcement is “*God’s Kingdom is at hand*” (*v. 15*). God’s kingdom means His reign, His saving and ruling power coming to set the world right. “At hand” means it has come near; in Jesus, it is arriving. The miracles in the rest of the chapter, driving out demons, healing the sick, cleansing a leper, show what the kingdom’s arrival looks like.

Then come the two commands: “*Repent, and believe in the Good News*” (*v. 15*). To repent means to turn around, to change one’s mind and direction, turning away from sin and self-rule and toward God. To believe means to trust and rely on the good news, placing one’s confidence in what God is doing through Jesus. Matthew’s summary emphasizes repentance (*Matthew 4:17*); Mark adds the explicit call to believe. Repentance and faith are two sides of one response: turning from sin and turning to God in trust.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse captures the heart of the gospel. God has acted in history; His appointed time has come; His kingdom is breaking into the world through Jesus. The proper response is not to earn God’s favor but to turn from sin and trust His good news. Paul summarizes his own preaching the same way: “*repentance toward God, and faith toward our Lord Jesus*” (*Acts 20:21*).

The order is important. The announcements come first, and the commands follow. Repentance and faith are not ways of making God’s kingdom come; they are responses to the kingdom that God is already bringing. Grace comes first, and human response follows.

The verse also shows that the gospel is both good news and a summons. It announces what God has done, but it also calls for a change of life. Believing the good news without repenting would be like hearing that a doctor has a cure and refusing to take it. Repenting without believing would be like trying to cure oneself. Both belong together.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse calls every person to respond to Jesus. For those who have never trusted Him, it is an invitation to turn from going their own way and to trust the good news about Jesus. This is not a matter of becoming religious but of turning to God and relying on what He has done.

For believers, repentance and faith continue throughout life. They can regularly turn away from sins God reveals and renew their trust in His promises. Each day offers fresh opportunities to repent of specific attitudes and actions and to rely on God’s grace rather than their own efforts.

Finally, the announcement that “the time is fulfilled” encourages believers to recognize the urgency of the gospel. God’s kingdom has come near in Jesus. This is not a message to put off until later. Believers can respond wholeheartedly now and share the invitation with others who need to hear it.

### *Mark 1:35* — Jesus Withdraws to Pray

> *“Early in the morning, while it was still dark, he rose up and went out, and departed into a deserted place, and prayed there.”*
>
> — *Mark 1:35* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse comes after one of the busiest days of Jesus’ ministry recorded in Mark. On the Sabbath in Capernaum, He had taught in the synagogue, driven out an unclean spirit, healed Peter’s mother-in-law, and then, after sunset, healed many sick people and cast out many demons as the whole town gathered at the door. It would have been late at night before the crowds left.

Yet “*Early in the morning, while it was still dark*” (*v. 35*), Jesus got up and went out to “*a deserted place*” (*v. 35*) to pray. The Greek phrase suggests very early, perhaps between three and six in the morning. Mark uses the word “deserted” or “wilderness,” the same word used for the place where Jesus was tested in verses 12–13. Jesus deliberately sought solitude away from the crowds and even from His disciples.

Mark does not tell us what Jesus prayed. But the following verses show what resulted. Simon and the others searched for Jesus and, when they found Him, said, “*Everyone is looking for you*” (*v. 37*). They expected Him to return to Capernaum and continue the successful ministry there. But Jesus answered that they should go to other towns so that He could preach there too, “*because I came out for this reason*” (*v. 38*). His time in prayer seems to have clarified His mission and kept Him from being directed by popular demand.

Mark records Jesus withdrawing to pray at three key moments: here at the beginning of His ministry, after feeding the five thousand (*6:46*), and in Gethsemane before His death (*14:32–42*). Each time, He was facing a temptation to turn from His mission: popularity, political expectations, and suffering.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that Jesus, though He was the Son of God, lived in constant dependence on His Father through prayer. If Jesus needed time alone with the Father, His followers need it even more. Prayer is not an optional extra for especially spiritual people; it is the source of strength and direction for the life of faith.

The verse also shows the connection between prayer and faithfulness to one’s calling. Success in Capernaum could have pulled Jesus into a different agenda. Through prayer, He remained focused on what the Father had sent Him to do. Prayer helps believers discern between what is merely urgent or popular and what God is truly calling them to.

Finally, Jesus’ example reveals a rhythm of engagement and withdrawal. He gave Himself fully to people’s needs, and He withdrew to be alone with God. Both were necessary. Service without prayer leads to exhaustion and drift; prayer without service becomes self-focused. Jesus held both together.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to make regular time for prayer, especially in busy seasons. Many people find that early morning, before the demands of the day begin, is a good time to pray, as Jesus did. Others may find different times. What matters is setting aside time to be alone with God, away from distractions.

It also encourages believers to seek solitude. Modern life is full of noise, screens, and constant demands. Finding a quiet place, turning off devices, and being still before God can be difficult but deeply restorative.

Finally, Jesus’ example shows the value of prayer for discernment. When opportunities, pressures, or expectations pull believers in many directions, prayer helps them recognize what God is calling them to do. Believers can bring their decisions to God in prayer, asking Him to keep them faithful to His purposes rather than driven by others’ expectations or their own desire for success.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Mark 1* moves quickly, and its pace conveys urgency. The good news of Jesus is not a leisurely idea to be considered someday; it is an announcement that God’s time has come and His kingdom is breaking in. Readers are called to respond by repenting and believing. For those who have not yet trusted Jesus, this chapter is an invitation to turn to Him. For believers, it is a reminder to keep turning from sin and trusting the good news every day.

The chapter shows the authority of Jesus over every area of life: He teaches with authority, commands evil spirits, heals diseases, and touches the untouchable. Believers can bring every part of their lives under His authority, trusting that no problem, fear, or burden is beyond His power. His compassion for the leper shows that His authority is joined with tender love for those who are suffering and excluded.

The calling of the fishermen shows that following Jesus involves real decisions and real costs. James and John left a family business with hired workers. Following Jesus may require believers to reorder priorities, leave behind security, or step into unfamiliar paths. Jesus’ promise, “I will make you,” assures them that He will shape them for His purposes.

Finally, Jesus’ early morning prayer offers a model for sustainable discipleship. He was busy, popular, and in demand, yet He made time to be alone with the Father, and that time kept Him focused on His mission. Believers can build regular rhythms of prayer into their lives, especially in busy seasons, so that their activity flows from communion with God rather than from pressure or the desire for approval.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for the good news that in You God’s appointed time has come and His kingdom has drawn near. I turn from my own way and trust in You. Help me to keep repenting and believing every day, not only once, and to live as one who has heard the best news in the world.

Thank You for Your authority over evil, sickness, and everything that harms Your people, and for Your compassion that reaches out to touch the untouchable. Make me willing to follow You when You call, even when it means leaving security behind. Teach me to rise and seek You in prayer as You sought Your Father, so that I may stay faithful to Your purposes and not be driven by pressure or praise. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Mark · Chapter 2 of 16

# Mark — Chapter 2

Chapter Theme: New Wine That Old Religion Cannot Contain

[Read Mark 2 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/MRK02.htm)

Main Teaching

*Mark 2* brings together five scenes in which Jesus’ words and actions provoke questions from religious leaders. He forgives a paralyzed man before healing him, calls a tax collector and eats with sinners, explains why His disciples do not fast, and defends them for picking grain on the Sabbath. In each scene Jesus reveals that something new has arrived: the Son of Man who forgives sins, welcomes sinners, brings joy like a bridegroom, and is Lord of the Sabbath.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Mark 1* showed Jesus’ authority and growing popularity in Galilee. *Mark 2:1–3:6* presents a series of five controversy stories, carefully arranged, in which Jesus’ actions are challenged by scribes and Pharisees. The stories move from silent objection (*2:6–7*), to questions directed at the disciples (*2:16*), to questions addressed to Jesus (*2:18*, 24), and finally, in *Mark 3:6*, to a plot to kill Him. Mark shows how opposition to Jesus grew step by step.

The scribes were experts in the law of Moses who taught and interpreted it. The Pharisees were a popular movement devoted to careful observance of the law and the traditions that applied it to daily life, especially regarding purity, tithing, fasting, and the Sabbath. Many of them were sincere, but their system of rules often left little room for mercy toward people who did not measure up. Jesus’ teaching and actions challenged their assumptions about who could be forgiven, who could be welcomed, and what God truly required.

### The Paralyzed Man Lowered Through the Roof (*2:1–12*)

Jesus returned to Capernaum, and word spread that He was “*at home*” (*v. 1*), probably at Peter’s house. So many people gathered that there was no room left, not even outside the door. While Jesus was speaking, four men arrived carrying a paralyzed man on a mat. Unable to reach Jesus through the crowd, they climbed onto the roof, dug through it, and lowered the man down in front of Jesus.

Homes in Galilee typically had flat roofs made of wooden beams covered with branches, reeds, and packed clay. An outside staircase often led to the roof, which was used for storage, work, and sleeping in hot weather. Digging through it would have been messy and disruptive, with dirt falling on the crowd below. But the men were determined.

Jesus, “*seeing their faith*” (*v. 5*), said to the paralyzed man, “*Son, your sins are forgiven you*” (*v. 5*). This verse is studied below. Some scribes sitting there thought to themselves, “*Who can forgive sins but God alone?*” (*v. 7*) They believed Jesus was committing blasphemy by claiming God’s authority. Jesus knew their thoughts and asked which was easier to say: “Your sins are forgiven” or “Get up and walk.” To demonstrate that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins, He told the man to get up, take his mat, and go home. The man did so in front of everyone, and they were all amazed and praised God, saying, “*We never saw anything like this!*” (*v. 12*) (Matthew’s account of this event is studied at *Matthew 9:6*.)

### The Call of Levi and the Meal With Sinners (*2:13–17*)

Jesus went out again beside the lake and taught the crowds. As He walked along, He saw Levi, the son of Alphaeus, sitting at the tax booth. Levi is also called Matthew (*Matthew 9:9*). Capernaum was located on a trade route and near the border between the territories of Herod Antipas and his brother Philip, so a toll station there collected customs on goods passing through. Tax collectors were widely despised because they worked for the ruling powers and often enriched themselves by overcharging. Jesus said to Levi, “*Follow me*” (*v. 14*), and Levi got up and followed Him.

Later, Jesus was eating at Levi’s house with many tax collectors and “sinners,” people known for immoral lives or for not keeping the law as the Pharisees did. Mark adds that “*there were many, and they followed him*” (*v. 15*). When the scribes of the Pharisees saw this, they asked Jesus’ disciples why He ate with such people. Sharing a meal signaled acceptance and fellowship, and the Pharisees believed that associating closely with sinners would make a person unclean.

Jesus answered, “*Those who are healthy have no need for a physician, but those who are sick. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance*” (*v. 17*). A doctor goes where the sick are. Jesus came for those who know they need Him. (Matthew’s account adds Jesus’ quotation of *Hosea 6:6*, studied at *Matthew 9:13*.)

### The Question About Fasting (*2:18–22*)

At that time, John’s disciples and the Pharisees were fasting. The law required fasting only on the Day of Atonement, but devout groups fasted more often; the Pharisees fasted twice a week (*Luke 18:12*). Some people asked Jesus why His disciples did not fast.

Jesus answered with a picture from a wedding: “*Can the groomsmen fast while the bridegroom is with them?*” (*v. 19*) Jewish weddings were joyful celebrations lasting up to a week, and the bridegroom’s friends were free from religious duties like fasting during the celebration. Fasting was associated with mourning, and it would be absurd to mourn at a wedding. Jesus’ presence was like a wedding feast. In the Old Testament, God is pictured as the bridegroom of His people (*Isaiah 62:5*; *Hosea 2:19–20*), so Jesus’ use of this image is a quiet claim about His identity. But He added, “*the days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast in that day*” (*v. 20*). This is the first hint in Mark of Jesus’ death.

Then Jesus gave two short parables about new cloth and new wine, studied below. The new reality He was bringing could not simply be added onto the old patterns of religion.

### Picking Grain on the Sabbath (*2:23–28*)

On a Sabbath, Jesus and His disciples were walking through grain fields, and the disciples began to pick heads of grain. The law allowed travelers to pick grain by hand from a neighbor’s field (*Deuteronomy 23:25*), but the Pharisees considered picking grain on the Sabbath a form of harvesting, which was forbidden work.

Jesus responded by reminding them of David. When David and his men were hungry and fleeing from King Saul, David entered the house of God and ate the consecrated bread, which only priests were allowed to eat (*1 Samuel 21:1–6*). Mark says this happened “*at the time of Abiathar the high priest*” (*v. 26*). In 1 Samuel the priest who gave David the bread was Ahimelech, Abiathar’s father. Many scholars explain that Jesus was referring to the section of Scripture known by Abiathar’s name or to the general period of Abiathar, who was the better-known high priest of David’s time. Jesus’ point was that human need took priority over a ceremonial rule, and David was not condemned.

Then Jesus stated a principle found only in Mark: “*The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath*” (*v. 27*). He concluded, “*Therefore the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath*” (*v. 28*). This saying is studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Mark 2:5* — Faith That Breaks Through Roofs

> *“Jesus, seeing their faith, said to the paralytic, ‘Son, your sins are forgiven you.’”*
>
> — *Mark 2:5* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse comes at the moment the paralyzed man is lowered into the room where Jesus is teaching. The scene was dramatic. The house in Capernaum was so crowded that no one else could get in, not even near the door. Four men had carried their paralyzed friend on a mat, but they could not get near Jesus. Instead of giving up, they climbed onto the flat roof, dug through the layers of clay, branches, and beams, and lowered the man down right in front of Jesus. Pieces of roof must have fallen on the people below. It was a bold, disruptive, determined act.

Mark tells us, “*Jesus, seeing their faith*” (*v. 5*). Notice the word “their.” Jesus saw the faith of the four friends as well as the paralyzed man. Their faith was visible in their actions: they believed Jesus could help, and they refused to let obstacles stop them from bringing their friend to Him.

Then Jesus said something unexpected: “*Son, your sins are forgiven you*” (*v. 5*). The friends had brought the man for healing. Jesus began with forgiveness. He called the man “son” (literally “child”), a term of tender affection. Jesus was not saying that this man’s paralysis was caused by a particular sin. Rather, He was addressing the man’s deepest need first: his relationship with God.

This statement provoked the scribes, who silently accused Jesus of blasphemy, because only God can forgive sins. Jesus then healed the man to prove that He had authority to forgive. The visible healing confirmed the invisible forgiveness.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that faith is often expressed in action. The four friends did not merely feel sympathy or say they believed; they acted, overcoming obstacles to bring their friend to Jesus. James writes that faith without works is dead (*James 2:17*). Real faith moves people to do something.

It also shows the power of intercessory faith, faith exercised on behalf of someone else. The paralyzed man could not get to Jesus by himself. His friends carried him. Jesus honored their faith. This encourages believers to bring others to Jesus through prayer and practical help, especially those who cannot come on their own.

Finally, the verse reveals that forgiveness is humanity’s deepest need. Jesus healed the man’s body, but He first healed his relationship with God. Physical healing would last a lifetime; forgiveness would last forever. Jesus’ authority to forgive sins shows that He shares the authority of God Himself.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse calls believers to be like the four friends, bringing others to Jesus. Many people are spiritually or physically unable to come on their own because of illness, despair, doubt, or circumstances. Believers can carry them through prayer, practical care, invitations, encouragement, and persistent love.

It also encourages believers not to give up when obstacles arise. The crowd blocked the door, but the friends found another way. When bringing people to Jesus seems difficult, believers can be creative and persistent, trusting that their efforts matter.

Finally, this verse reminds believers that Jesus cares about their deepest needs. People often come to God for help with circumstances, and He does care about these. But He also offers something greater: forgiveness and restored relationship with God. Believers can receive His forgiveness with gratitude and seek it for others as well.

### *Mark 2:22* — New Wine Needs New Wineskins

> *“No one puts new wine into old wineskins; or else the new wine will burst the skins, and the wine pours out, and the skins will be destroyed; but they put new wine into fresh wineskins.”*
>
> — *Mark 2:22* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse is the second of two short parables Jesus told when He was asked why His disciples did not fast like the disciples of John and the Pharisees. Jesus had answered that the friends of the bridegroom cannot fast while He is with them. His presence was a time of celebration, not mourning. Then He gave two images to explain what His coming meant.

The first image (v. 21) was of a patch. No one sews a piece of new, unshrunk cloth onto an old garment. When washed, the new patch would shrink and tear away from the old fabric, making the hole worse.

The second image is in this verse. In the ancient world, wine was stored in containers made from animal skins, usually goatskins. New wine was still fermenting, producing gas that stretched the container. A new wineskin was flexible and could expand. An old wineskin had already been stretched and had become dry and brittle. If new wine were poured into it, the skin would burst, and both the wine and the skin would be lost. “*but they put new wine into fresh wineskins*” (*v. 22*).

Jesus’ point was that the new reality He brought could not be contained within old religious forms. The joy of the kingdom, the forgiveness of sinners, the welcome of outcasts, and the presence of the Bridegroom required new ways of thinking and living. Trying to squeeze Jesus’ message into the rigid patterns of the Pharisees’ traditions would damage both.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse teaches that Jesus did not come merely to reform or patch up existing religion. He came to bring something new: the arrival of God’s kingdom, the new covenant, and the gift of the Spirit. The Old Testament itself pointed toward this newness, as when God said through Isaiah, “*Behold, I will do a new thing*” (*Isaiah 43:19*).

This does not mean that Jesus rejected the Old Testament. He fulfilled it (*Matthew 5:17*). But the way God’s people related to Him would change: through faith in Jesus rather than through the ceremonial system, with the Spirit writing God’s law on their hearts, and with Gentiles welcomed alongside Jews. The early church wrestled with these changes, as the book of Acts and Paul’s letters show.

The parable also has a broader principle. Whenever God works in fresh ways, rigid patterns and traditions can resist His work. The problem is not tradition itself, but inflexibility that cannot receive what God is doing.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to examine whether their habits and traditions help or hinder them from receiving what God is doing. Traditions can be valuable when they express faith, but they become “old wineskins” when they are held so rigidly that they block the joy, grace, and mission of Jesus.

It also invites individuals to be open to transformation. When people come to Christ, He does not simply add religion to their old lives; He makes them new. Paul writes, “*if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation*” (*2 Corinthians 5:17*). Believers can allow Jesus to reshape their attitudes, priorities, and ways of living rather than trying to fit Him into old patterns.

Finally, this verse encourages churches to remain flexible in their methods while faithful to the unchanging gospel. The message of Jesus does not change, but the ways it is expressed and shared may need to adapt to reach new people and situations.

### *Mark 2:27* — The Sabbath Was Made for People

> *“He said to them, The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.”*
>
> — *Mark 2:27* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus speaks these words in response to the Pharisees, who criticized His disciples for picking grain as they walked through fields on the Sabbath. The Pharisees viewed this as a form of harvesting, one of the types of work forbidden on the Sabbath according to their interpretation of the law. Jesus had already answered by reminding them that David ate the consecrated bread when he and his men were hungry, showing that human need could take priority over ceremonial rules.

Now He gives a principle that only Mark records: “*The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath*” (*v. 27*). The Sabbath was established by God at creation, when He rested on the seventh day (*Genesis 2:2–3*), and it was commanded in the Ten Commandments (*Exodus 20:8–11*). *Deuteronomy 5:12–15* adds that the Sabbath reminded Israel that they had been slaves in Egypt and that God had freed them. The Sabbath was a gift: a day of rest from labor, a day to remember God’s goodness, and a protection for servants, animals, and even foreigners from endless work.

By Jesus’ time, many rules had been developed to define what counted as work on the Sabbath. The intention was to protect the commandment, but the result was often a heavy burden. The Pharisees treated the Sabbath as if people existed to serve it. Jesus reversed this: the Sabbath exists to serve people. It was made for their good.

Then Jesus added, “*Therefore the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath*” (*v. 28*). As the Son of Man, He has authority over the Sabbath and the right to determine its true meaning. (This claim is discussed further at *Matthew 12:8*.)

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals God’s purpose behind His commands. God’s laws are not arbitrary burdens but expressions of His love and care for human beings. The Sabbath was designed for rest, worship, freedom, and delight. When religious rules are applied in ways that harm people or ignore their genuine needs, they have been twisted from God’s purpose.

The verse also shows the connection between rest and Jesus Himself. As Lord of the Sabbath, Jesus offers true rest. In *Matthew 11:28*, He invites the weary to come to Him for rest. *Hebrews 4* teaches that a Sabbath rest remains for God’s people, entered through faith in Christ. The weekly Sabbath pointed toward this deeper rest of the soul in God.

Christians differ in how they apply the Sabbath today. Some keep Saturday as the Sabbath; most worship on Sunday, the day of Jesus’ resurrection; some see the Sabbath principle as calling for a regular day of rest; others see it as fulfilled entirely in Christ. Whatever the practice, Jesus’ principle applies: rest and worship are gifts meant for human good, not burdens to be used against others.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to receive rest as a gift from God. Many people live without regular rest, driven by work, responsibilities, and constant connection. God designed human beings to need rest, and honoring that need is part of trusting Him. Setting aside regular time for rest and worship acknowledges that life depends on God, not on endless effort.

It also warns against using religious practices to burden or judge others. Believers can examine whether they impose rules on others that go beyond God’s intention, or whether they criticize others for not following their particular practices. God’s commands are meant to bring life and freedom.

Finally, this verse encourages believers to look at the purpose behind God’s commands. When they read Scripture, they can ask not only what God commands but why, and how His commands express His love for people. This understanding leads to obedience that is joyful rather than burdensome.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Mark 2* shows Jesus doing things that surprised and offended religious people: forgiving sins, eating with sinners, celebrating instead of fasting, and defending His disciples on the Sabbath. In each case, He revealed that something new had arrived with Him. This chapter invites believers to examine whether they, like the Pharisees, have become more attached to religious rules and appearances than to the grace and joy Jesus brings.

The story of the paralyzed man and his friends offers a picture of compassionate, determined faith. Believers are called to bring others to Jesus, especially those who cannot come on their own. This may involve prayer, practical help, and persistence when obstacles arise. It also reminds believers that Jesus offers forgiveness, the deepest healing anyone can receive.

The call of Levi and the meal with sinners challenge believers to welcome people the world or the church may reject. Jesus came for the sick, not the healthy. Churches and individual believers can ask whether people with messy lives feel welcome among them, and whether they are willing to share meals and friendship with those who are far from God.

The images of the bridegroom, the new patch, and new wine remind believers that following Jesus is a joyful and transforming reality, not just an addition to old patterns. Believers can allow Him to reshape their lives and remain open to His work. Finally, Jesus’ teaching on the Sabbath shows that God’s commands are given for human good. Believers can receive rest as a gift, honor God with regular rhythms of worship, and refuse to use religious rules as burdens for others.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You that You have authority to forgive sins and that You came to call sinners, not the righteous. Thank You for welcoming people the world rejects, and for welcoming me. Give me the determined faith of the four friends, who would not let any obstacle keep them from bringing someone to You. Show me who I can carry to You through prayer and practical love.

Keep me from treating my traditions and habits as more important than Your grace. Make me a new wineskin, flexible and open to the new life You bring. Thank You that You are the Bridegroom whose presence fills life with joy. Teach me to receive rest as Your gift, to honor You with regular times of worship, and never to use religious rules to burden others. You are Lord of the Sabbath and Lord of my life. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
