Mark · Chapter 3 of 16

# Mark — Chapter 3

Chapter Theme: Hard Hearts, Chosen Friends, and the True Family of Jesus

[Read Mark 3 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/MRK03.htm)

Main Teaching

Jesus heals a man’s withered hand on the Sabbath, grieved and angered by the hard hearts of those watching to accuse Him, and they begin plotting His death. As crowds pour in from every direction, He appoints twelve apostles to be with Him and to be sent out. His own family thinks He is out of His mind, and scribes from Jerusalem say He works by Satan’s power, but Jesus shows that He has come to bind the strong man and declares that whoever does God’s will is His true family.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Mark 3* completes the series of five conflict stories that began in *Mark 2*. Jesus had forgiven sins, eaten with tax collectors, explained why His disciples did not fast, and defended them for picking grain on the Sabbath. Each time, religious leaders objected. In the first scene of chapter 3, the opposition reaches a turning point: the Pharisees join with their political rivals to plan Jesus’ death.

The rest of the chapter shows two very different circles around Jesus. On the one hand, huge crowds come to Him, and He chooses twelve men to be His closest companions. On the other hand, His own family misunderstands Him, and religious authorities from Jerusalem accuse Him of being in league with the devil. Mark uses a favorite technique here, called a “sandwich,” in which he begins one story, interrupts it with another, and then finishes the first. The account of Jesus’ family (vv. 20–21, 31–35) surrounds the accusation by the scribes (vv. 22–30), inviting readers to compare the two kinds of misunderstanding.

### The Man With the Withered Hand (*3:1–6*)

Jesus went into a synagogue on the Sabbath, where there was a man with a withered, possibly paralyzed hand. Some people were watching Jesus closely to see whether He would heal on the Sabbath, so that they could accuse Him. Mark later identifies them as Pharisees (v. 6). In their view, healing a non-life-threatening condition was work that should wait until after the Sabbath.

Jesus told the man, “*Stand up*” (*v. 3*), literally “rise into the middle,” bringing him before everyone. Then He asked the watchers, “*Is it lawful on the Sabbath day to do good or to do harm? To save a life or to kill?*” (*v. 4*) The question exposed the real issue. Failing to do good when one can is a form of harm. And the question carried an irony: Jesus was seeking to heal on the Sabbath, while they were seeking a way to destroy Him. They remained silent.

Jesus looked around at them “*with anger, being grieved at the hardening of their hearts*” (*v. 5*). This is studied below. He told the man to stretch out his hand, and it was completely restored.

Immediately the Pharisees went out and began plotting with the Herodians how to destroy Jesus. The Herodians were supporters of the Herod family, especially Herod Antipas, who ruled Galilee under Roman authority. The Pharisees normally opposed them, since they saw cooperation with Rome as compromise. Their alliance against Jesus shows how threatened both groups felt. Herod had already arrested John the Baptist, so this was a dangerous partnership.

### Crowds From Every Region (*3:7–12*)

Jesus withdrew with His disciples to the Sea of Galilee. A huge crowd followed Him, not only from Galilee but from Judea, Jerusalem, Idumea (the region far to the south), across the Jordan, and around Tyre and Sidon (Gentile cities to the northwest). Mark’s list covers nearly every direction, showing that Jesus’ reputation had spread throughout the land and beyond Jewish territory.

The crowds were so large and eager that Jesus asked His disciples to keep a small boat ready so He would not be crushed. People with diseases pushed forward to touch Him. Whenever unclean spirits saw Him, they fell down and cried out, “*You are the Son of God!*” (*v. 11*) Jesus sternly ordered them not to make Him known. He did not want His identity proclaimed by demons, nor did He want to be known simply as a miracle-worker before people understood His mission.

### The Appointment of the Twelve (*3:13–19*)

Jesus went up on a mountainside and called to Himself those He wanted, and they came. He appointed twelve, “*that they might be with him, and that he might send them out to preach*” (*v. 14*), and to have authority to drive out demons. This is studied below.

Mark lists the Twelve. Simon was given the name Peter, which means “rock.” James and John, the sons of Zebedee, were named “*Boanerges, which means, Sons of Thunder*” (*v. 17*), perhaps because of their fiery personalities; in *Luke 9:54* they offered to call down fire on a Samaritan village. The others were Andrew, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Thomas, James the son of Alphaeus, Thaddaeus, Simon the Zealot, and Judas Iscariot, “*who also betrayed him*” (*v. 19*). The group included fishermen, a tax collector (Matthew), and a Zealot (Simon), whose political loyalties were opposed. Jesus formed them into one community.

The number twelve is significant. Israel had twelve tribes, descended from the twelve sons of Jacob. By choosing twelve apostles, Jesus was signaling the renewal of God’s people. Mark’s mention of Judas’s betrayal at the very beginning reminds readers that even in this chosen circle, the shadow of the cross was present.

### Jesus’ Family Thinks He Is Out of His Mind (*3:20–21*)

Jesus went home, and again the crowd gathered so that He and His disciples could not even eat. When His family heard about it, they went to take charge of Him, because they said, “*He is insane*” (*v. 21*). The word “friends” in the WEB here refers to those close to Him, most likely His family, as verse 31 shows. They probably thought He had become overwhelmed, unbalanced, or dangerously caught up in His mission. Their concern may have been sincere, but they did not understand who He was. *John 7:5* tells us that at this time even His brothers did not believe in Him.

### The Scribes’ Accusation and the Strong Man (*3:22–30*)

Meanwhile, scribes who had come down from Jerusalem, likely official representatives of the religious authorities, said, “*He has Beelzebul*” (*v. 22*), and that He cast out demons by the prince of demons. They could not deny His power, so they attributed it to Satan.

Jesus called them over and answered with parables. How can Satan drive out Satan? A kingdom or household divided against itself cannot stand. If Satan were fighting against himself, his rule would be coming to an end. Then Jesus gave a short parable that explains His exorcisms: “*But no one can enter into the house of the strong man to plunder unless he first binds the strong man; then he will plunder his house*” (*v. 27*). Satan is the strong man who has held people captive. Jesus is the stronger one who has come to bind him and set his captives free. His victory over demons shows that He is more powerful than Satan. This echoes *Isaiah 49:24–25*, where God promises to take captives from the mighty.

Jesus then warned that all sins and blasphemies people commit can be forgiven, but whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will never be forgiven. Mark explains why Jesus said this: “*because they said, “He has an unclean spirit.”*” (*v. 30*) The scribes were looking at the clear work of God’s Spirit in freeing people from evil and calling it the work of Satan. (This warning is studied in depth at *Matthew 12:31–32*.)

### Jesus’ True Family (*3:31–35*)

Now Jesus’ mother and brothers arrived and stood outside, sending someone in to call Him. The crowd sitting around Jesus told Him that His mother, brothers, and sisters were outside looking for Him. Jesus asked, “*Who are my mother and my brothers?*” (*v. 33*) Looking at those seated in a circle around Him, He said, “*Behold, my mother and my brothers!*” (*v. 34*) and then explained who belongs to His family. This is studied below.

Notice the contrast in this scene. Jesus’ family stood outside, trying to take Him away. His disciples sat inside, around Him, listening. Physical closeness to Jesus did not guarantee understanding; responding to Him did.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Mark 3:5* — Anger and Grief at Hard Hearts

> *“When he had looked around at them with anger, being grieved at the hardening of their hearts, he said to the man, ‘Stretch out your hand.’ He stretched it out, and his hand was restored as healthy as the other.”*
>
> — *Mark 3:5* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse describes Jesus’ emotional response in the synagogue on the Sabbath. A man with a withered hand was present, and the Pharisees were watching to see whether Jesus would heal him so they could accuse Him of breaking the Sabbath. Jesus brought the man into the middle of the room and asked the watchers a direct question: “*Is it lawful on the Sabbath day to do good or to do harm? To save a life or to kill?*” (*v. 4*) They refused to answer.

Mark then gives us a rare glimpse into Jesus’ feelings. He “*looked around at them with anger*” (*v. 5*). Jesus made eye contact with each of them, and His anger was visible. But Mark immediately adds, “*being grieved at the hardening of their hearts*” (*v. 5*). His anger was mixed with sorrow. The word “hardening” describes something that has become stiff, insensitive, or calloused. Their hearts had become so focused on rules and on defeating Jesus that they had no compassion for a suffering man.

Matthew and Luke tell this story but do not mention Jesus’ anger and grief. Mark, likely drawing on Peter’s eyewitness memory, preserves this emotional detail.

Then Jesus said to the man, “*Stretch out your hand*” (*v. 5*). He did not touch him or do anything that could be considered “work.” He simply spoke, and the man obeyed. As he stretched out his hand, it was fully restored. The man’s obedience is part of the miracle; he did what he could not do until Jesus commanded it.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that Jesus experienced real human emotions, including anger. His anger was not sinful. It was a righteous response to cruelty disguised as religion. Paul writes, “*Be angry, and don’t sin*” (*Ephesians 4:26*). Jesus’ anger was directed at injustice and hardness, not at personal offense, and it was joined with grief, a sorrow that these people were missing God’s heart.

The verse also reveals the danger of a hardened heart. The Pharisees were religious, knowledgeable, and committed, yet they could watch a suffering man and care only about catching Jesus in a violation. Hardness of heart is a recurring warning in Scripture. *Psalm 95:8* says, “*Don’t harden your heart*” (*Psalm 95:8*). In Mark, even the disciples will be warned about hardened hearts (*Mark 6:52*; *8:17*). It is a danger for everyone, not just for Jesus’ opponents.

Finally, the healing shows God’s purpose for the Sabbath and for all His commands: to do good and to save life. Jesus’ question exposed the real choice. Refusing to help when one is able is not neutral; it is a failure to do good.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to examine their own hearts for hardness. It is possible to know a great deal about God and to be active in religious life while becoming calloused toward the needs of others. Believers can ask God to soften their hearts and to make them sensitive to suffering, especially when rules or routines make it easy to look away.

It also shows that some anger is appropriate. Believers can feel righteous anger at cruelty, injustice, and the mistreatment of vulnerable people. But Jesus’ example shows that such anger should be joined with grief, directed at wrongdoing rather than personal offense, and expressed in ways that bring healing rather than revenge.

Finally, Jesus’ question, “*Is it lawful on the Sabbath day to do good or to do harm?*” (*v. 4*), challenges believers to act when they can help. Choosing not to help someone in need is not truly neutral. Believers can look for opportunities to do good, even when it is inconvenient or when others criticize them for it.

### *Mark 3:14* — Chosen to Be With Him and Sent Out

> *“He appointed twelve, that they might be with him, and that he might send them out to preach”*
>
> — *Mark 3:14* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse describes the appointment of the twelve apostles. Mark says that Jesus went up on a mountainside and “*called to himself those whom he wanted*” (*v. 13*). The initiative was entirely His. These men did not apply or compete for the position; Jesus chose them.

He “*appointed twelve*” (*v. 14*). The number deliberately recalls the twelve tribes of Israel. Jesus was forming the core of a renewed people of God.

Mark gives two purposes for their appointment. First, “*that they might be with him*” (*v. 14*). Before they did anything for Jesus, they were called simply to be with Him. They would travel with Him, eat with Him, listen to His teaching, watch how He treated people, see His miracles, and learn from His example. Discipleship in that culture meant living closely with one’s teacher, learning both from words and from life.

Second, “*that he might send them out to preach*” (*v. 14*). The word “apostle” means “one who is sent.” Jesus would send them as His messengers to proclaim the kingdom of God. Verse 15 adds that they would have authority to drive out demons. Their mission would continue His own work.

The order matters. Being with Jesus comes first; being sent comes second. Their effectiveness in preaching and ministry would grow out of their relationship with Him. Later, after Pentecost, the religious leaders noticed Peter and John’s boldness and “*recognized that they had been with Jesus*” (*Acts 4:13*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals the heart of discipleship: a relationship with Jesus that leads to mission. Jesus did not choose the Twelve primarily as employees or students of a program. He chose them to share His life. Their service would flow from their companionship with Him.

It also shows that God’s call is based on His choice, not human merit. Jesus called “those whom he wanted.” The Twelve were ordinary men, including fishermen, a tax collector, and a political zealot. Even Judas, who would betray Him, was among them. God’s call rests on His grace and purposes, not on the qualifications of those He calls.

The two purposes, being with Jesus and being sent by Him, apply to all believers, not just the apostles. Jesus’ final words in Matthew combine these same themes: He sends His followers to make disciples, and He promises, “I am with you always” (*Matthew 28:19–20*). The apostles had a unique, foundational role, but every believer is called into relationship with Christ and into His mission.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse calls believers to prioritize being with Jesus. Service, ministry, and activity can easily crowd out time with Him. Yet fruitful ministry grows from close relationship. Believers can spend time in prayer, in Scripture, and in worship, simply being in His presence, before and alongside their service.

It also reminds believers that they are sent. Being with Jesus is not meant to end in private spirituality. He sends His followers into the world to share the good news and to continue His work of compassion and freedom. Every believer has a place in that mission, whether in their home, workplace, community, or beyond.

Finally, this verse offers encouragement to those who feel unqualified. Jesus chose ordinary people and shaped them by being with them. Believers can trust that the same Lord who called them will also equip them as they spend time with Him and step out in obedience.

### *Mark 3:35* — Whoever Does God’s Will Is My Family

> *“For whoever does the will of God is my brother, my sister, and mother.”*
>
> — *Mark 3:35* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse concludes a scene that began earlier in the chapter. In verse 21, Jesus’ family heard that He was so busy with the crowds that He could not even eat, and they set out to take charge of Him, saying He had lost His mind. Mark then told of the scribes accusing Jesus of working by Satan’s power. Now Jesus’ mother and brothers arrive. They stand outside the crowded house and send someone in to call Him.

The people sitting around Jesus told Him, “*Behold, your mother, your brothers, and your sisters are outside looking for you*” (*v. 32*). In that culture, family loyalty was extremely important. Many expected Jesus to stop what He was doing and go to His family.

Instead, Jesus asked, “Who are my mother and my brothers?” Then He looked around at those seated in a circle around Him, the people listening to His teaching, and said, “Behold, my mother and my brothers!” Then He explained: “*For whoever does the will of God is my brother, my sister, and mother*” (*v. 35*).

Jesus was not rejecting His mother and brothers. He cared for His mother even from the cross (*John 19:26–27*), and His brother James later became a leader in the Jerusalem church (*Acts 15:13*; *Galatians 1:19*). Rather, Jesus was redefining family in the kingdom of God. The deepest family bond is formed not by blood but by doing God’s will. Notice that He added “sister,” including women among His disciples, which was significant in a culture where religious teachers did not usually have female students.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals that God’s kingdom creates a new family. Those who follow Jesus become brothers and sisters to Him and to one another. Throughout the New Testament, believers call each other “brothers” and “sisters,” reflecting this new identity. Paul describes the church as “*the household of God*” (*Ephesians 2:19*).

The verse also shows that belonging to Jesus’ family is defined by response, not by status. His physical family, standing outside, had not yet understood or accepted Him. The crowd sitting at His feet, listening and responding, were closer to Him. Doing God’s will is the mark of His family. This includes believing in Jesus, whom God sent, and following His teaching.

This teaching is especially meaningful for those who have lost natural family ties or whose families reject them because of their faith. In God’s family, they find a home. At the same time, it does not cancel the responsibility to honor and care for one’s natural family, which Jesus affirmed elsewhere (*Mark 7:9–13*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to see the church as their family. Fellow believers are brothers and sisters, and relationships within the church can reflect the loyalty, care, and love of a family. Believers can welcome others, share their lives, support one another in need, and treat each other with the commitment family members show.

It also encourages those who feel alone or rejected. Whether because of family conflict, loss, or isolation, many people lack close family relationships. In Christ, they belong to a larger family. Churches can be places where such people find genuine belonging.

Finally, this verse calls believers to do God’s will. Being in Jesus’ family is not about outward association but about listening to Him and responding with obedience. Believers can sit at His feet like those in the crowd, learning from Him and seeking to do what pleases the Father.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Mark 3* shows how people respond to Jesus in different ways, and each response invites reflection. The Pharisees watched Jesus with hard hearts, more interested in catching Him than in seeing a suffering man healed. Believers can ask God to keep their hearts soft and compassionate, and to help them choose to do good when they have the opportunity, even when religious habits or the criticism of others make it difficult.

The crowds came from every direction to see Jesus, but many came only for what He could do for them. The Twelve were called into a deeper relationship: to be with Him and to be sent by Him. Believers are invited into this same pattern of discipleship. Spending time with Jesus through prayer and Scripture is the foundation for serving Him in the world.

Jesus’ family misunderstood Him, and the scribes slandered Him. Both responses show that closeness to religious tradition or even to Jesus Himself does not guarantee understanding. Believers can stay humble and teachable, refusing to dismiss God’s work simply because it does not fit their expectations. The parable of the strong man also gives hope: Jesus has bound the power of evil and sets captives free. No bondage is beyond His power.

Finally, Jesus’ declaration that whoever does God’s will is His family gives believers a new identity and a new community. They belong to God’s family, with brothers and sisters in Christ. This calls them to love one another, welcome the lonely, and live as members of a household centered on doing God’s will.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for doing good and saving life, even when others were watching to accuse You. Soften any hardness in my heart, and give me Your compassion for those who are suffering. Help me to feel grief and righteous anger at what harms people, and to respond with healing rather than revenge.

Thank You for calling ordinary people to be with You and to be sent by You. Draw me close to You, so that my service flows from time spent in Your presence. Thank You that You have bound the strong man and that You set captives free. Keep me humble and open to Your work, even when it surprises me. Thank You for making me part of Your family. Help me to do the Father’s will and to love Your people as my brothers and sisters. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Mark · Chapter 4 of 16

# Mark — Chapter 4

Chapter Theme: The Kingdom That Grows in Secret and the Lord Who Stills the Storm

[Read Mark 4 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/MRK04.htm)

Main Teaching

Teaching from a boat, Jesus uses parables to show how God’s kingdom grows: the word is received differently by different hearts, what is hidden will be revealed, the kingdom grows mysteriously by God’s power, and it begins small but becomes great. That evening, when a violent storm threatens to sink the disciples’ boat, Jesus calms the wind and waves with a word, and the disciples are left asking who He really is.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Mark 4* is one of only two long teaching sections in Mark’s Gospel (the other is *Mark 13*). Mark generally emphasizes what Jesus did more than what He said, but here he gathers several of Jesus’ parables about the kingdom of God. The setting follows the tension of chapter 3: the religious leaders were plotting against Jesus, scribes from Jerusalem had accused Him of working by Satan’s power, and His own family thought He was out of His mind. Yet crowds kept coming. Why were people responding so differently to Jesus? And if God’s kingdom had truly arrived, why did it seem so small and so opposed? The parables in this chapter address those questions.

### The Parable of the Sower (*4:1–9*)

Jesus began teaching by the Sea of Galilee. The crowd was so large that He got into a boat and sat down in it on the water, while the people stood on the shore. Coves along the lake form natural amphitheaters where a speaker’s voice carries well.

He began with a command: “*Listen!*” (*v. 3*) Then He told of a farmer scattering seed. Some fell on the hard path, where birds ate it. Some fell on rocky ground with shallow soil, sprang up quickly, and withered in the sun because it had no root. Some fell among thorns, which choked it so it produced no grain. Some fell on good soil and produced a harvest of thirty, sixty, or a hundred times what was sown. Jesus ended, “*Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear*” (*v. 9*). The command to “listen” at the beginning and “hear” at the end frames the parable: it is about how people hear God’s word.

### Why Parables? (*4:10–12*)

When Jesus was alone, His followers and the Twelve asked about the parables. He told them, “*To you is given the mystery of God’s Kingdom, but to those who are outside, all things are done in parables*” (*v. 11*). In the Bible, a “mystery” is a truth once hidden but now revealed by God. The disciples had been given insight into God’s kingdom because they had come close to Jesus. Those “outside” heard only stories.

Jesus then quoted *Isaiah 6:9–10*, where God told Isaiah that his preaching would harden a people who refused to listen. These words are difficult. They do not mean that Jesus wanted people to remain in sin. Rather, parables both reveal and conceal. For those who come to Jesus wanting to understand, parables open up the truth. For those who have already hardened their hearts, parables remain puzzling, and their rejection is confirmed. The parables test the heart.

### The Sower Explained (*4:13–20*)

Jesus asked, “*Don’t you understand this parable? How will you understand all of the parables?*” (*v. 13*) The sower parable is a key to the rest, because it is about how people receive God’s word.

He explained that the farmer sows the word. The path represents people from whom Satan immediately takes away the word. The rocky ground represents people who receive the word with joy but have no root, so they fall away when trouble or persecution comes. The thorny ground represents those whose response is choked by “*the cares of this age, and the deceitfulness of riches, and the lusts of other things*” (*v. 19*). Mark’s list adds “desires for other things,” a broad category that includes anything that competes with God for a person’s heart. The good soil represents those who hear the word, accept it, and bear fruit. (This parable is studied in depth at *Matthew 13:23*.)

### The Lamp and the Measure (*4:21–25*)

Jesus continued with short sayings. A lamp is not brought into a room to be put under a basket or bed, but on a stand. Though the kingdom’s truth is now partly hidden in parables, it is meant to be revealed. Nothing is hidden except to be brought into the open.

He then said, “*Take heed what you hear*” (*v. 24*), and gave a principle about how listening works. This saying is studied below.

### The Seed Growing Secretly (*4:26–29*)

Mark alone records this parable. A man scatters seed on the ground. Night and day, whether he sleeps or gets up, the seed sprouts and grows, though he does not know how. The soil produces grain by itself: first the stalk, then the head, then the full kernel. When the grain is ripe, he puts in the sickle, because the harvest has come. This parable is studied below.

### The Mustard Seed (*4:30–34*)

Jesus asked how to describe God’s kingdom. It is like a mustard seed, the smallest seed farmers commonly planted in Palestine. Yet when it grows, it becomes the largest of garden plants, with branches big enough for birds to nest in its shade. The kingdom’s beginnings in Jesus’ ministry looked small and insignificant, but it would grow into something great, offering shelter to many. The image of birds nesting in branches echoes Old Testament pictures of a great kingdom that shelters the nations (*Ezekiel 17:23*; *Daniel 4:12*).

Mark notes that Jesus spoke to the people with many parables like these, “*as they were able to hear it*” (*v. 33*). He adapted His teaching to what His hearers could receive. In private, He explained everything to His disciples.

### Calming the Storm (*4:35–41*)

That evening, Jesus said, “*Let’s go over to the other side*” (*v. 35*). They left the crowd and took Jesus along in the boat “*even as he was*” (*v. 36*), suggesting He was tired after a long day of teaching. Other boats were with them. A violent windstorm arose, and the waves broke over the boat so that it was nearly swamped. The Sea of Galilee lies about seven hundred feet below sea level, surrounded by hills, and cool air rushing down through the valleys can suddenly stir up fierce storms.

Jesus was in the stern, “*asleep on the cushion*” (*v. 38*). Only Mark mentions the cushion, a vivid detail likely remembered by an eyewitness. The disciples woke Him and said, “*Teacher, don’t you care that we are dying?*” (*v. 38*) This question is studied below.

Jesus got up, rebuked the wind, and said to the sea, “*Peace! Be still!*” (*v. 39*) The words literally mean “Be silent! Be muzzled!”, the same kind of command He gave to demons (*Mark 1:25*). The wind stopped, and there was a great calm. Then He asked them, “*Why are you so afraid? How is it that you have no faith?*” (*v. 40*)

The disciples were filled with a different kind of fear, awe at what they had witnessed. They asked one another, “*Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?*” (*v. 41*) In the Old Testament, it is God who rules the raging sea and calms the storm (*Psalm 89:9*; *107:28–29*). The disciples were beginning to realize that Jesus possessed the authority of God Himself. Their question echoes through Mark’s Gospel until it is answered at the cross and the empty tomb.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Mark 4:24* — Take Heed What You Hear

> *“He said to them, Take heed what you hear. With whatever measure you measure, it will be measured to you; and more will be given to you who hear.”*
>
> — *Mark 4:24* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus speaks these words to His disciples as part of a series of short sayings following the parable of the sower. He has just explained that the farmer’s seed is God’s word, and that different kinds of hearers respond in different ways. He has also said that a lamp is meant to be put on a stand, not hidden, meaning that the truth of God’s kingdom is meant to be revealed. Now He gives a warning and a promise about listening.

“*Take heed what you hear*” (*v. 24*). The phrase means “pay attention to what you are hearing” or “be careful how you listen.” In Luke’s version, Jesus says, “*Be careful therefore how you hear*” (*Luke 8:18*). Both emphases matter: what we listen to and how we listen.

Then Jesus uses a common saying from the marketplace: “*With whatever measure you measure, it will be measured to you*” (*v. 24*). In buying and selling grain, merchants used measuring containers. A generous merchant would fill the measure full; a stingy one would fill it loosely. Jesus applies this to listening. The attention and openness people give to God’s word determine how much understanding they receive. Those who listen carefully and respond receive more.

Jesus adds, “*and more will be given to you who hear*” (*v. 24*). God is generous. Those who respond to His word receive even more than they give. The next verse explains: “*For whoever has, to him more will be given; and he who doesn’t have, even that which he has will be taken away from him*” (*v. 25*). Those who receive and use God’s truth grow in understanding. Those who neglect it lose even what they once had.

In context, this saying explains the difference between the disciples and the outsiders. The disciples had drawn near to Jesus and wanted to understand, so they received more explanation. Those who only heard stories and did not seek further understanding remained outside.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse teaches that spiritual understanding grows through attentive, responsive listening. God’s word is not meant to be heard passively. It calls for a response. When people listen with openness and act on what they hear, God gives them greater understanding. When people ignore what they hear, their hearts gradually become harder and their understanding fades.

This principle appears throughout Scripture. James writes that those who look into God’s law and do what it says will be blessed, while those who hear without doing deceive themselves (*James 1:22–25*). Proverbs repeatedly urges the hearer to incline the ear and apply the heart to wisdom.

The verse also reveals God’s generosity. He does not give exactly what people give Him; He gives more. Those who respond to His word, even in small ways, find that He multiplies their understanding and fruitfulness.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to be careful listeners. In a world full of voices, believers can pay attention to what they allow into their minds and hearts. They can prioritize listening to God’s word through Scripture reading, preaching, and reflection, and they can be discerning about other influences that compete for their attention.

It also calls believers to listen with the intention of responding. Reading the Bible or hearing a sermon can become routine. Believers can approach God’s word asking, “What is God saying to me, and how should I respond?” Acting on even small insights leads to greater understanding over time.

Finally, this verse warns against neglect. Faith that is not nourished and applied can weaken. Believers who have drifted from regular engagement with God’s word can return, trusting that God is generous and will give more to those who seek Him.

### *Mark 4:26–29* — The Seed That Grows by Itself

> *“He said, ‘God’s Kingdom is as if a man should cast seed on the earth, and should sleep and rise night and day, and the seed should spring up and grow, though he doesn’t know how. For the earth bears fruit by itself: first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear. But when the fruit is ripe, immediately he puts in the sickle, because the harvest has come.’”*
>
> — *Mark 4:26–29* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This parable is found only in Mark’s Gospel. It follows the parable of the sower and the sayings about the lamp and the measure. Like the sower, it uses the image of seed, but its emphasis is different.

A man “*should cast seed on the earth*” (*v. 26*). After planting, he goes on with his normal life: “*and should sleep and rise night and day*” (*v. 27*). Meanwhile, the seed sprouts and grows, “*though he doesn’t know how*” (*v. 27*). Ancient farmers did not understand the biology of plant growth. They knew that seeds grew, but the process was a mystery to them.

“*For the earth bears fruit by itself*” (*v. 28*). The Greek word translated “by itself” is “automate,” from which we get “automatic.” The growth happens without the farmer’s direct effort. Jesus describes the stages: first the blade (the green shoot), then the ear (the head of grain), then the full grain in the ear. Growth happens gradually, step by step.

Finally, “*But when the fruit is ripe, immediately he puts in the sickle, because the harvest has come*” (*v. 29*). The farmer’s role returns at the end: he harvests. The language of the sickle and harvest echoes *Joel 3:13*, where the harvest is an image of God’s final judgment and the climax of His purposes.

Jesus’ disciples may have been discouraged. The kingdom of God did not seem to be advancing quickly. Opposition was growing, and many people were not responding. This parable assured them that God’s kingdom was growing, even when they could not see it or explain it.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This parable teaches that the growth of God’s kingdom depends on God’s power, not human effort. The farmer plants, but he cannot make the seed grow. Paul expresses the same truth: “*I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase*” (*1 Corinthians 3:6*). Believers are responsible to sow the word faithfully, but the results belong to God.

It also teaches that God’s work is often hidden and gradual. Much growth happens underground, unseen. The kingdom does not always advance in dramatic, visible ways. Sometimes it grows quietly in hearts, families, and communities over long periods of time.

Finally, the parable points to a certain harvest. Growth is not endless; it moves toward a goal. God will bring His kingdom to completion, and there will be a final harvest at the end of the age. This gives believers both patience in the present and hope for the future.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This parable relieves believers of the pressure to produce spiritual results by their own power. Parents raising children, believers sharing their faith, teachers, pastors, and anyone who serves can plant seeds faithfully and then trust God with the growth. They can rest, as the farmer slept, knowing that God is at work even when they cannot see it.

It also encourages patience with spiritual growth, both in others and in oneself. Growth happens in stages: first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain. Believers can be patient with new Christians, with struggling friends, and with their own slow progress, trusting that God is working gradually toward maturity.

Finally, this parable encourages faithfulness in sowing. The farmer did not know how the seed grew, but he did plant it. Believers can keep sharing God’s word, praying, serving, and living faithfully, confident that God will bring the harvest in His time.

### *Mark 4:38* — “*Teacher, Don't You Care?*” (*v. 38*)

> *“He himself was in the stern, asleep on the cushion; and they woke him up and asked him, ‘Teacher, don’t you care that we are dying?’”*
>
> — *Mark 4:38* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse comes in the middle of the storm on the Sea of Galilee. At the end of a long day of teaching, Jesus had told His disciples to cross to the other side of the lake. They set out in the evening, with other boats following. Suddenly a violent windstorm arose. The waves broke over the boat, and it was filling with water. Several of the disciples were experienced fishermen who knew this lake, and they were terrified.

Meanwhile, “*He himself was in the stern, asleep on the cushion*” (*v. 38*). The stern, at the back of the boat, was where the helmsman sat, and a cushion was sometimes kept there. Jesus was so exhausted, and so at peace, that He slept through the storm.

The disciples woke Him and said, “*Teacher, don’t you care that we are dying?*” (*v. 38*) Mark records the question in its rawest form. Matthew’s version is a prayer, “*Save us, Lord!*” (*Matthew 8:25*), and Luke’s is a cry of alarm. Mark preserves the disciples’ accusation: Jesus’ sleep seemed to them like indifference. How could He rest while they were about to drown?

Jesus did not answer their question with words at first. He got up, rebuked the wind, and commanded the sea to be still, and there was a great calm. Then He asked them, “*Why are you so afraid? How is it that you have no faith?*” (*v. 40*) His action answered their question. He did care, and He was in control all along.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse expresses a question that many believers ask in times of suffering: “God, don’t You care?” When God seems silent or inactive while trouble rages, it can feel as though He is indifferent. The psalms are full of similar cries: “*Wake up! Why do you sleep, Lord?*” (*Psalm 44:23*) Scripture does not hide these honest questions.

Jesus’ response shows that His apparent inactivity was not indifference. He was present in the boat, sharing the same danger as His disciples. His rest reflected perfect trust in His Father, not lack of concern. When He acted, He showed that He had complete authority over the storm.

The story also teaches that fear and faith are closely connected. Jesus asked why they had no faith. Their fear came from forgetting who was in the boat with them. Faith does not mean storms will never come, but it means trusting that the One who is with us is greater than any storm.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse gives believers permission to bring honest questions to God. When life feels overwhelming and God seems silent, they can cry out to Him, even with the words, “Don’t You care?” God is not offended by honest prayer. He invites His children to bring their fears to Him.

It also reminds believers that God’s silence is not His absence. Jesus was in the boat the whole time. In seasons when God seems quiet, believers can remember His promises, His past faithfulness, and His presence with them, trusting that He cares even when they cannot feel it.

Finally, this verse encourages believers to grow in faith through storms. The disciples learned more about who Jesus was through this frightening experience. Believers can look back on hard seasons and see how God was present and powerful, building confidence for future storms.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Mark 4* helps believers understand how God’s kingdom works and how they should respond to it. The parable of the sower shows that the condition of the heart affects how people receive God’s word. Believers can examine whether their hearts are hard, shallow, crowded with worries and desires, or open and fruitful. They can ask God to make them good soil, and they can deal honestly with whatever is choking their spiritual life.

The sayings about the lamp and the measure call believers to listen carefully and respond. God’s truth is meant to be revealed, and those who receive it with attention and obedience are given more. Regular engagement with Scripture, combined with a willingness to act on what one hears, leads to growing understanding.

The parables of the growing seed and the mustard seed give hope and patience. God’s kingdom grows by His power, often slowly and invisibly, but it will grow into something great and will reach its harvest. Believers can plant seeds faithfully in their families, workplaces, and communities, trusting God for the results and refusing to be discouraged by small beginnings or slow progress.

Finally, the storm on the lake shows that following Jesus does not mean avoiding storms. The disciples were in danger precisely because they obeyed His instruction to cross the lake. Yet Jesus was with them, and He had authority over the wind and waves. Believers can bring their fears and even their questions to Him, trusting that He cares and that He is greater than any storm they face. Each experience of His faithfulness can deepen their answer to the disciples’ question: “Who then is this?”

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for sowing the word of Your kingdom in my heart. Make me good soil that receives Your word, holds onto it, and bears fruit. Clear away the worries, the deceitfulness of riches, and the desires for other things that choke my faith. Help me to listen carefully and to respond to what I hear.

Thank You that Your kingdom grows by Your power, even when I cannot see how. Give me patience with my own slow growth and with others, and help me to keep planting seeds faithfully, trusting You for the harvest. When storms rise and I wonder whether You care, remind me that You are with me in the boat and that the wind and sea obey You. Turn my fear into faith and my questions into worship. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Mark · Chapter 5 of 16

# Mark — Chapter 5

Chapter Theme: Restored, Healed, and Raised: Jesus and the Desperate

[Read Mark 5 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/MRK05.htm)

Main Teaching

Jesus meets three people in situations no one else could change: a man tormented by many demons living among the tombs, a woman who has suffered from bleeding for twelve years, and a synagogue leader whose daughter dies before Jesus arrives. He frees the man and sends him home to tell what God has done, calls the trembling woman “daughter” and declares her healed, and raises the girl from death with a tender command. Jesus’ power reaches into places of uncleanness, shame, and death.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Mark 5* follows directly from the end of *Mark 4*, where Jesus calmed a violent storm on the Sea of Galilee and the disciples asked, “*Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?*” (*Mark 4:41*) *Mark 5* continues to answer that question. Having shown Jesus’ authority over nature, Mark now shows His authority over demonic powers, chronic disease, and death itself.

All three stories in this chapter involve people who were considered ritually unclean under the law of Moses. The man lived among tombs, in Gentile territory, near pigs, and was possessed by unclean spirits. The woman had a bleeding condition that made her unclean according to *Leviticus 15:25–27*. The girl died, and touching a corpse made a person unclean (*Numbers 19:11*). In each case, Jesus does not become unclean by contact; instead, His holiness and power restore what was broken.

### The Man With a Legion of Demons (*5:1–20*)

Jesus and His disciples crossed to the eastern shore of the lake, into the region of the Gadarenes (the manuscripts vary between Gerasenes, Gadarenes, and Gergesenes, names connected with towns in the area). This was the Decapolis, a league of largely Gentile cities with Greek culture. As soon as Jesus stepped out of the boat, a man with an unclean spirit came out of the tombs to meet Him.

Mark describes the man’s condition in painful detail. He lived among the burial caves. People had tried to restrain him with chains and shackles, but he tore the chains apart and broke the shackles. No one was strong enough to subdue him. Night and day, among the tombs and in the hills, he cried out and cut himself with stones. He was isolated, tormented, self-destructive, and feared by everyone. (The Gospels distinguish demonic oppression from ordinary illness; readers today should not assume that mental illness or self-harm is always caused by demons. Mark presents this specific case as spiritual bondage, and he shows Jesus’ compassion for a man everyone else had given up on.)

When the man saw Jesus from a distance, he ran and fell on his knees before Him. The demon shouted, “*What have I to do with you, Jesus, you Son of the Most High God? I adjure you by God, don’t torment me*” (*v. 7*). “Most High God” was a title often used by Gentiles for the God of Israel. Ironically, the demon tried to use a solemn oath to control Jesus, but it had no power over Him. Jesus had already commanded the spirit to come out.

Jesus asked its name. The answer was, “*My name is Legion, for we are many*” (*v. 9*). A Roman legion contained about six thousand soldiers. The name suggested a vast number of spirits and evoked the image of an occupying army, a powerful picture for people living under Roman rule. The demons begged Jesus not to send them out of the area. A large herd of about two thousand pigs was feeding on the nearby hillside. The demons begged to be sent into the pigs. Jesus gave them permission, and the whole herd rushed down the steep bank into the lake and drowned.

Readers sometimes wonder why Jesus allowed the destruction of the pigs. The text does not explain fully, but it shows the destructive nature of the demons and the reality of the man’s deliverance. The pigs’ fate made visible what the demons intended for the man. It also shows that one human being was worth more to Jesus than a large herd of animals.

The herdsmen ran and reported what had happened in the town and countryside. People came out and found the man “*sitting, clothed, and in his right mind*” (*v. 15*). This description is a complete reversal of his former condition: instead of wandering, he was sitting; instead of naked (*Luke 8:27*), he was clothed; instead of tormented, he was sane. Yet the people were afraid. When they heard what had happened, including the loss of the pigs, they begged Jesus to leave their region. They valued their economic security and their comfort over the presence of the One who had freed a tormented man.

As Jesus was getting into the boat, the man who had been freed begged to go with Him. Jesus did not allow it but gave him a different mission, studied below. The man went away and began to proclaim in the Decapolis how much Jesus had done for him, and everyone was amazed.

### Jairus and the Woman (*5:21–43*)

Jesus crossed back to the western shore, and a large crowd gathered. One of the synagogue leaders, named Jairus, came and fell at His feet. A synagogue leader was a respected layman responsible for organizing worship services. Jairus pleaded earnestly, “*My little daughter is at the point of death. Please come and lay your hands on her, that she may be made healthy, and live*” (*v. 23*). Jesus went with him, and the crowd pressed in around Him.

Mark now uses his “sandwich” technique, interrupting one story with another so that each helps interpret the other. In the crowd was a woman who had suffered from bleeding for twelve years, the same number of years Jairus’s daughter had been alive. Mark describes her suffering vividly: she “*had suffered many things by many physicians, and had spent all that she had, and was no better, but rather grew worse*” (*v. 26*). Her condition made her ritually unclean, so she would have been excluded from worship and close contact with others. Anyone she touched would become unclean. She had lost her health, her money, her community, and likely her hope.

She had heard about Jesus. She came up behind Him in the crowd and touched His clothes, thinking, “*If I just touch his clothes, I will be made well*” (*v. 28*). Immediately her bleeding stopped, and she felt in her body that she was healed.

Jesus immediately realized that power had gone out from Him. He turned around and asked, “*Who touched my clothes?*” (*v. 30*) The disciples thought the question was absurd, since the crowd was pressing in on Him from every side. But Jesus kept looking around to see who had done it. The woman, trembling with fear, came and fell at His feet and told Him the whole truth. She may have feared rebuke for touching Him while unclean. Instead, Jesus spoke words of blessing, studied below.

While Jesus was still speaking, messengers arrived from Jairus’s house: “*Your daughter is dead. Why bother the Teacher any more?*” (*v. 35*) The delay caused by the woman seemed to have cost the girl her life. But Jesus overheard and told Jairus, “*Don’t be afraid, only believe*” (*v. 36*). This is studied below.

Jesus allowed only Peter, James, and John to follow Him. At the house, there was a commotion of people weeping and wailing loudly. Professional mourners were common in that culture, and even poor families hired flute players and wailing women. Jesus said, “*Why do you make an uproar and weep? The child is not dead, but is asleep*” (*v. 39*). They laughed at Him, because they knew she was dead. Jesus was not denying that she had died; He was saying that in His presence, death is like sleep, from which He can awaken her.

He put them all outside and took only the girl’s parents and His three disciples into the room. He took her by the hand and said, “*Talitha cumi!*” (*v. 41*) Mark preserves the Aramaic words Jesus actually spoke, likely as Peter remembered them, and translates them: “*Girl, I tell you, get up!*” (*v. 41*) “Talitha” was a tender word, like “little girl” or “little lamb.” Immediately she stood up and began to walk. Mark adds, “*for she was twelve years old*” (*v. 42*). Everyone was completely astonished.

Jesus gave strict orders that no one should know about this, and He told them to give her something to eat. This practical instruction shows His tender care, and it also confirms that she was truly alive and well.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Mark 5:19* — Go Home and Tell What the Lord Has Done

> *“He didn’t allow him, but said to him, ‘Go to your house, to your friends, and tell them what great things the Lord has done for you and how he had mercy on you.’”*
>
> — *Mark 5:19* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus speaks these words to the man He had just freed from a legion of demons. Only hours earlier, this man had been living among the tombs, screaming day and night, cutting himself with stones, and breaking every chain people used to restrain him. Now he was sitting quietly, clothed, and in his right mind. The people of the region, frightened by what had happened and upset about the loss of their pigs, had begged Jesus to leave.

As Jesus was getting into the boat, the man begged to go with Him. This was a natural desire. Jesus had rescued him, and the people of his town were afraid. He wanted to stay with the One who had set him free and become one of His followers.

“*He didn’t allow him*” (*v. 19*). This is surprising. Jesus often called people to follow Him. But for this man, Jesus had a different calling: “*Go to your house, to your friends, and tell them what great things the Lord has done for you and how he had mercy on you*” (*v. 19*).

Jesus sent him back to the very people who had known him in his tormented state. His family and friends had probably given up on him. Now they would see the change in his life and hear his story. Jesus told him to tell them what “the Lord” had done, pointing to God. Notice also that Jesus had told others to keep quiet about His miracles, but He told this man to speak. In this largely Gentile region, there was less danger of people misunderstanding Jesus as a political messiah, and the man’s testimony would prepare the way for Jesus’ later ministry there (*Mark 7:31*).

Verse 20 tells us the man obeyed. He went throughout the Decapolis, a region of ten cities, proclaiming how much Jesus had done for him, and everyone was amazed. Mark notes that he spoke of what “Jesus” had done, showing that he understood that God’s mercy had come through Jesus.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that every believer has a story of God’s mercy to tell. The man did not have theological training. He had not been with Jesus long. But he had experienced Jesus’ power and mercy, and that was enough to make him a witness. Personal testimony, describing what God has done, is one of the most powerful ways the gospel spreads.

It also shows that Jesus’ calling looks different for different people. Some are called to leave their homes and travel with Him. Others are called to stay and witness among the people who know them best. Both callings are valuable. Faithfulness means accepting the calling Jesus gives, even if it differs from what we would choose.

Finally, the verse highlights mercy. The man’s freedom was not something he earned; it was mercy. Testimony about God is ultimately testimony about His mercy toward people who could not help themselves.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to tell others what God has done for them. They do not need to have all the answers or be skilled speakers. They can share honestly how Jesus has shown them mercy, forgiven them, changed them, or helped them through difficulty. Personal stories often open doors that arguments cannot.

It also reminds believers that home is often the first mission field. Family members, friends, neighbors, and coworkers are the people who know us best. They can see the difference Christ makes in our lives over time. Living faithfully among them and sharing our story with them is an important part of following Jesus.

Finally, this verse teaches believers to accept God’s calling even when it differs from their desires. Some may wish for a dramatic ministry elsewhere, but God may call them to serve faithfully where they are. Obedience in the place God puts us is a true form of discipleship.

### *Mark 5:34* — “*Daughter, Your Faith Has Made You Well*” (*v. 34*)

> *“He said to her, ‘Daughter, your faith has made you well. Go in peace, and be cured of your disease.’”*
>
> — *Mark 5:34* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus speaks these words to the woman who had suffered from bleeding for twelve years. She had spent all her money on doctors and only grown worse. Under the law of Moses, her condition made her ritually unclean (*Leviticus 15:25–27*), which meant she could not participate fully in worship, and anyone she touched would become unclean. For twelve years she had lived with physical weakness, poverty, and social isolation.

She came up behind Jesus in the crowd, believing that if she could just touch His clothes, she would be healed. When she did, her bleeding stopped immediately. Jesus felt that power had gone out from Him and asked who had touched Him. Although the disciples thought the question was strange, Jesus kept looking for her. The woman came forward, trembling with fear, fell at His feet, and told Him the whole truth.

Jesus then said, “*Daughter, your faith has made you well. Go in peace, and be cured of your disease*” (*v. 34*). Every part of this response is significant.

“Daughter” is the only time in the Gospels that Jesus addresses a woman this way. For someone who had been isolated for years, this word welcomed her into a relationship of belonging and affection.

“*your faith has made you well*” (*v. 34*). The word translated “made well” can also mean “saved.” Jesus credits her faith, not the touch itself, as the means of her healing. Her faith had reached out to Him, and His power had responded. Calling attention to her faith publicly also restored her reputation. Everyone now knew she was healed and could be welcomed back into community life.

“*Go in peace*” (*v. 34*). This was a common Jewish blessing (“Go in shalom”), wishing someone wholeness and well-being.

“*and be cured of your disease*” (*v. 34*). Jesus confirmed that her healing was complete and lasting.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that Jesus cares about the whole person: body, relationships, and soul. He could have let the woman slip away healed but unnoticed. Instead, He sought her out to give her more than physical healing. He gave her a public declaration of restoration, a new identity as a daughter, and a blessing of peace.

It also shows the nature of faith. The woman’s faith was imperfect; she may have thought of Jesus’ clothes almost as having magical power. Yet Jesus honored her faith because it was directed toward Him. Faith does not need to be perfectly informed to be real. What matters is that it reaches out to Jesus.

Finally, Jesus’ encounter with an “unclean” woman shows that His holiness is contagious in a new way. Instead of becoming unclean by her touch, He made her clean. This anticipates the deeper cleansing He brings through His death, removing the barriers of sin and shame that separate people from God.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse offers hope to anyone who has suffered for a long time or exhausted every other option. Like the woman, they can bring their need to Jesus. He sees them, cares about their suffering, and responds to faith that reaches out to Him.

It also encourages those who feel ashamed or excluded. Jesus did not shame the woman; He called her “daughter.” Believers who carry shame because of illness, past sin, or circumstances can find in Jesus a welcome that restores dignity and belonging.

Finally, this verse invites believers to see people as Jesus does. In a crowded world, it is easy to overlook those who are suffering quietly. Jesus stopped for one hidden, ashamed woman. Believers can slow down, notice people others ignore, and offer them dignity, kindness, and a place to belong.

### *Mark 5:36* — “*Don't Be Afraid, Only Believe*” (*v. 36*)

> *“But Jesus, when he heard the message spoken, immediately said to the ruler of the synagogue, ‘Don’t be afraid, only believe.’”*
>
> — *Mark 5:36* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus speaks these words to Jairus, a synagogue leader whose twelve-year-old daughter had been dying. Jairus had come to Jesus, fallen at His feet, and begged Him to come and lay His hands on her so she would live. Jesus agreed and went with him. But on the way, the crowd slowed them down, and Jesus stopped to speak with the woman who had been healed of bleeding.

While Jesus was still speaking to her, messengers came from Jairus’s house with terrible news: “*Your daughter is dead. Why bother the Teacher any more?*” (*v. 35*) From their point of view, it was over. Jesus could heal the sick, but there was nothing to be done for the dead.

Jesus heard what they said and immediately spoke to Jairus: “*Don’t be afraid, only believe*” (*v. 36*). The Greek suggests “stop being afraid” and “keep on believing.” Jairus had already shown faith by coming to Jesus. Now Jesus called him to continue trusting even in the face of death.

Imagine Jairus’s emotions. He had just watched Jesus stop for someone else while his own daughter was dying. Now he heard that she was dead. He may have felt despair, grief, perhaps even anger. Jesus did not ask him to stop grieving or to pretend the news was false. He asked him to keep believing in Jesus’ power, even when all hope seemed gone.

Jesus went with Jairus to his house. When the mourners laughed at Jesus’ statement that the child was only sleeping, He put them out, took the parents and three disciples into the room, took the girl’s hand, and raised her to life.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that faith in Jesus can persist even when circumstances seem hopeless. Death seemed to have the final word, but Jesus had power over death. This scene anticipates Jesus’ own resurrection and His promise to raise all who belong to Him. For those who trust in Jesus, death is not the end.

The verse also shows the relationship between fear and faith. Fear is natural when facing devastating news. But Jesus calls His followers not to let fear rule them. The opposite of fear here is not courage based on circumstances, but trust in Jesus’ power and character.

Finally, the delay in this story teaches something about God’s timing. Jesus stopped to help the woman, and the delay seemed to cost the girl her life. But the delay led to an even greater miracle. Sometimes God’s delays, which feel painful at the time, serve purposes we cannot see.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse speaks to believers facing frightening news, whether about health, family, finances, or the future. Jesus’ words, “Don’t be afraid, only believe,” invite them to keep trusting Him even when the situation seems beyond hope. This does not mean denying grief or pretending everything is fine. It means holding onto Jesus in the midst of fear.

It also offers comfort to those who have lost loved ones. Jesus raised Jairus’s daughter as a sign of His power over death. While not every loved one is restored to life in this world, believers can trust that those who die in Christ will be raised to eternal life. Grief can be held together with hope.

Finally, this verse encourages believers to trust God’s timing when He seems to delay. When prayers seem unanswered or help seems late, believers can keep believing, trusting that Jesus is still at work and that His purposes are good.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Mark 5* shows Jesus meeting people at their lowest points: a man tormented beyond human help, a woman exhausted by years of illness and isolation, and a father whose child had died. In each case, Jesus brought restoration that no one else could provide. This chapter invites believers to bring their most desperate situations to Him, trusting that no condition is beyond His reach.

The chapter also shows how differently people respond to Jesus’ power. The townspeople begged Him to leave because His presence disrupted their economy and frightened them. The freed man begged to go with Him. Jairus fell at His feet, and the woman reached out in faith. Believers can examine whether they welcome Jesus’ work in their lives, even when it disrupts their comfort, or whether they try to keep Him at a distance.

Each person in this chapter received not only healing but restored relationships. The man was sent home to his family and community. The woman was called “daughter” and restored to her community. The girl was returned to her parents. Jesus cares about belonging as well as healing. Churches can reflect this by welcoming people who have been isolated, ashamed, or excluded, and by helping them find a place in God’s family.

Finally, the chapter calls believers to persistent faith and bold witness. Jairus was told to keep believing even after hearing that his daughter had died. The freed man was told to go and tell what the Lord had done. Believers can trust Jesus in the face of fear and loss, and they can share their own stories of His mercy with the people who know them best.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You that no one is beyond the reach of Your power and compassion. You freed the man whom everyone feared, You healed the woman whom everyone avoided, and You raised the girl when everyone said it was too late. I bring You the situations in my life and in the lives of those I love that seem hopeless. Meet us there with Your power and mercy.

Keep me from asking You to leave when Your work disrupts my comfort. Thank You for calling me Your child and for removing my shame. When I hear frightening news, help me to hear Your voice saying, “Don’t be afraid, only believe.” Give me courage to tell my family and friends what great things You have done for me and how You have had mercy on me. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
