Mark · Chapter 9 of 16

# Mark — Chapter 9

Chapter Theme: Glory Revealed, Faith Stretched, and the Way of the Servant

[Read Mark 9 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/MRK09.htm)

Main Teaching

Three disciples see Jesus transfigured in glory and hear the Father say, “Listen to him.” At the foot of the mountain, a desperate father whose son is tormented cries out, “I believe. Help my unbelief!” and Jesus frees the boy. As Jesus again predicts His death, the disciples argue about greatness, try to stop an outsider who heals in Jesus’ name, and are warned to take sin seriously and to live at peace with one another.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Mark 9* continues the second half of Mark’s Gospel, which began at Caesarea Philippi when Peter confessed that Jesus is the Christ and Jesus revealed that the Christ must suffer, die, and rise (*Mark 8:27–38*). Jesus had called His followers to take up the cross. Now the disciples receive a glimpse of the glory that lies beyond suffering, and then they return to a world of struggle, unbelief, and their own pride. Throughout the chapter, the disciples continue to misunderstand, but Jesus patiently teaches them what it means to follow a suffering Messiah.

### The Transfiguration (*9:1–13*)

Jesus said that some standing there would not die before they saw “*God’s Kingdom come with power*” (*v. 1*). Six days later, the transfiguration gave three of them such a glimpse. (*Matthew 16:28* and its discussion note other ways this saying has been understood.)

Jesus took Peter, James, and John up a high mountain, and He was transfigured before them. His clothes became dazzling white, “*such as no launderer on earth can whiten them*” (*v. 3*), a vivid detail only Mark includes, likely from Peter’s memory. Elijah and Moses appeared, talking with Jesus. Moses represented the Law, and Elijah represented the Prophets; both pointed to Jesus.

Peter said, “Rabbi, it is good for us to be here,” and suggested building three shelters. Mark explains, “*For he didn’t know what to say, for they were very afraid*” (*v. 6*). A cloud overshadowed them, and a voice came from the cloud: “*This is my beloved Son. Listen to him*” (*v. 7*). Suddenly they saw only Jesus. (This scene is studied in depth at *Matthew 17:5*.)

On the way down, Jesus told them not to tell anyone until the Son of Man had risen from the dead. They kept the matter to themselves, “*questioning what the “rising from the dead” meant*” (*v. 10*). Jews who believed in resurrection expected it at the end of history for all the righteous, not for one person in the middle of history. The disciples could not yet grasp what Jesus meant.

They asked why the scribes said Elijah must come first (based on *Malachi 4:5*). Jesus agreed that Elijah comes first to restore all things, but He asked how it could also be written that the Son of Man must suffer much and be rejected. Then He said that Elijah had already come, and people did to him whatever they wanted. He was referring to John the Baptist, who had been executed by Herod (*Mark 6:14–29*). John’s suffering foreshadowed Jesus’ own.

### The Boy With an Unclean Spirit (*9:14–29*)

When they returned to the other disciples, they found a large crowd and some scribes arguing with them. When the crowd saw Jesus, they were amazed and ran to greet Him. Jesus asked what they were arguing about. A man in the crowd explained that he had brought his son, who had a spirit that made him mute. The spirit would seize him, throw him to the ground, make him foam at the mouth, grind his teeth, and become rigid. The father had asked the disciples to drive it out, but they could not.

Jesus responded, “*Unbelieving generation, how long shall I be with you? How long shall I bear with you? Bring him to me*” (*v. 19*). His frustration was directed at the general lack of faith, including the disciples’. When they brought the boy, the spirit immediately threw him into a convulsion. He fell to the ground and rolled around, foaming at the mouth.

Mark alone records the conversation that followed. Jesus asked the father how long this had been happening. “*From childhood*” (*v. 21*), the father said. The spirit had often thrown him into fire or water to kill him. (As in Matthew’s account, the Gospel attributes these seizures to a demon in this particular case; this should not be generalized to mean that epilepsy is always demonic.) Then the father pleaded, “*But if you can do anything, have compassion on us and help us*” (*v. 22*).

Jesus repeated the father’s words back to him: “*If you can believe, all things are possible to him who believes*” (*v. 23*). The question was not whether Jesus could help, but whether the father would trust Him. The father’s response is studied below.

Seeing a crowd running together, Jesus rebuked the spirit: “*You mute and deaf spirit, I command you, come out of him, and never enter him again!*” (*v. 25*) The spirit shrieked, convulsed the boy violently, and came out. The boy lay so still that many said he was dead. But Jesus took him by the hand and lifted him up, and he stood.

Later, in private, the disciples asked why they could not drive it out. Jesus answered, “*This kind can come out by nothing but by prayer and fasting*” (*v. 29*). (The words “and fasting” are not found in some of the oldest manuscripts.) The disciples had previously cast out demons (*Mark 6:13*), but perhaps they had begun to rely on their own authority rather than on God. Dependence on God expressed in prayer was essential.

### Second Prediction of the Passion (*9:30–32*)

Jesus and His disciples passed through Galilee, and He did not want anyone to know, because He was teaching His disciples. He told them, “*The Son of Man is being handed over to the hands of men, and they will kill him; and when he is killed, on the third day he will rise again*” (*v. 31*). This was His second prediction of His death. But “*they didn’t understand the saying, and were afraid to ask him*” (*v. 32*). Perhaps they remembered how Jesus rebuked Peter the last time, or perhaps they did not want to face what He was saying.

### Who Is the Greatest? (*9:33–37*)

When they reached Capernaum and were in the house, Jesus asked what they had been arguing about on the road. They were silent, because they had been arguing about who was the greatest. The contrast is stark: Jesus was speaking about His suffering and death, while they were competing for status.

Jesus sat down, the posture of a teacher, called the Twelve, and said, “*If any man wants to be first, he shall be last of all, and servant of all*” (*v. 35*). Then He took a little child, placed the child among them, and took the child in His arms. In that culture, children had little status. Jesus said that whoever welcomes such a child in His name welcomes Him, and whoever welcomes Him welcomes the Father who sent Him. Greatness in God’s kingdom is measured by humble service to those with no status. (Matthew’s parallel is studied at *Matthew 18:3–4*.)

### The Outsider Who Cast Out Demons (*9:38–41*)

John then told Jesus that they had seen someone driving out demons in Jesus’ name and tried to stop him “*because he doesn’t follow us*” (*v. 38*). Notice that John said “follow us,” not “follow you.” The disciples were concerned about their group’s status, and perhaps they were embarrassed that an outsider succeeded where they had just failed (vv. 18, 28).

Jesus said not to stop him, because no one who does a miracle in His name can quickly speak evil of Him. He added, “*For whoever is not against us is on our side*” (*v. 40*). This is studied below. Jesus then said that anyone who gives His followers even a cup of water in His name because they belong to Christ will not lose their reward.

### Warnings About Causing Sin (*9:42–50*)

Jesus then warned that whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in Him to stumble would be better off thrown into the sea with a millstone around his neck. “Little ones” includes children and humble, vulnerable believers. A millstone was a heavy stone turned by a donkey to grind grain.

He then used vivid exaggeration: if your hand, foot, or eye causes you to sin, cut it off or tear it out. It is better to enter life maimed than to go into Gehenna. Gehenna was the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, once associated with child sacrifice (*Jeremiah 7:31*) and later used as a symbol of final judgment. Jesus quoted *Isaiah 66:24* about the worm that does not die and the fire that is not quenched. (Verses 44 and 46, which repeat this quotation, are absent from many early manuscripts.) Jesus was not commanding literal self-mutilation but showing how seriously sin must be dealt with. Whatever leads us into sin must be removed decisively.

The chapter ends with sayings about salt, studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Mark 9:24* — “*I Believe. Help My Unbelief!*” (*v. 24*)

> *“Immediately the father of the child cried out with tears, ‘I believe. Help my unbelief!’”*
>
> — *Mark 9:24* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse records the cry of a desperate father. His son had been tormented by a spirit since childhood. It made the boy unable to speak, threw him to the ground in violent convulsions, and often threw him into fire or water to kill him. The father had brought his son to Jesus’ disciples while Jesus was on the mountain, but they could not help. By the time Jesus arrived, the father had experienced years of suffering and one more disappointment.

When the boy was brought to Jesus, the spirit threw him into another convulsion. The father pleaded, “But if you can do anything, have compassion on us and help us.” His words reveal both hope and doubt. He hoped Jesus might help, but he was not sure.

Jesus responded, “*If you can believe, all things are possible to him who believes*” (*v. 23*). Jesus turned the father’s “if you can” back to him. The question was not about Jesus’ ability but about the father’s trust.

Then comes this verse: “*Immediately the father of the child cried out with tears, “I believe. Help my unbelief!”*” (*v. 24*) The word “immediately” shows the urgency of his response. “With tears” (found in many manuscripts) shows his emotion. His words are deeply honest. He declares, “I believe,” affirming that he does trust Jesus. But in the same breath, he admits that his faith is mixed with doubt: “Help my unbelief.” He does not pretend to have perfect faith. He asks Jesus to strengthen the faith he has.

Jesus did not reject him because his faith was imperfect. He immediately commanded the spirit to leave the boy, and the boy was freed.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse is one of the most honest prayers in the Bible. It shows that faith and doubt can exist together in the same heart. The father believed enough to bring his son to Jesus and to ask for help, but he also struggled with doubt after years of suffering and the disciples’ failure. Jesus accepted his mixed faith and responded with power.

It also shows that faith itself can be a gift that we ask God to strengthen. The father asked Jesus not only to heal his son but to help his unbelief. Believers can ask God to increase their faith, just as the disciples later asked, “*Increase our faith*” (*Luke 17:5*). God is not waiting for people to produce perfect faith before He acts; He helps them believe.

Finally, the verse shows that the power lies in Jesus, not in the strength of the believer’s faith. Earlier Jesus taught that even faith as small as a mustard seed can move mountains (*Matthew 17:20*). The father’s faith was weak, but it was directed toward the right person.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers who struggle with doubt. Many people feel guilty because their faith is not stronger, especially in prolonged suffering or after repeated disappointments. The father’s prayer shows that it is acceptable to come to Jesus with mixed faith. Believers can be honest with God about their doubts and ask Him to strengthen their trust.

It also provides a simple, powerful prayer for difficult times: “I believe. Help my unbelief.” When believers face situations that test their faith, such as illness, loss, or unanswered prayers, they can use these words, affirming their trust while asking God to help them where they are weak.

Finally, this verse encourages believers to keep bringing their needs to Jesus even after disappointments. The father had been let down by the disciples, but he did not give up. Believers who have been discouraged by unanswered prayers or by the failures of others can still come to Jesus Himself, trusting His compassion and power.

### *Mark 9:40* — “*Whoever Is Not Against Us Is on Our Side*” (*v. 40*)

> *“For whoever is not against us is on our side.”*
>
> — *Mark 9:40* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus speaks these words in response to a report from John, one of the Twelve. John told Jesus, “*Teacher, we saw someone who doesn’t follow us casting out demons in your name; and we forbade him, because he doesn’t follow us*” (*v. 38*).

The context is important. Just before this, the disciples had failed to cast out a demon from a boy (vv. 14–29), and they had been arguing about which of them was the greatest (vv. 33–34). Now they had encountered someone outside their group who was successfully casting out demons using Jesus’ name. They tried to stop him. Notice that John said “he doesn’t follow us,” not “he doesn’t follow you.” The disciples’ concern seems to have been about their group’s authority and status.

Jesus answered, “*Don’t forbid him, for there is no one who will do a mighty work in my name and be able quickly to speak evil of me*” (*v. 39*). Someone who was genuinely doing good in Jesus’ name was not going to turn quickly against Him. Then Jesus gave the principle in this verse: “*For whoever is not against us is on our side*” (*v. 40*).

Jesus was teaching His disciples not to be exclusive or territorial. The man was working on behalf of Jesus’ kingdom, even though he was not part of their particular group. They should welcome such allies rather than oppose them.

Jesus followed this with a promise: even someone who gives His followers a cup of water in His name because they belong to Christ will not lose their reward (v. 41). Small acts of support for His people are valued by God.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse warns against a narrow, possessive spirit among believers. The disciples assumed that God’s work had to happen through their group. Jesus corrected them, showing that God’s kingdom is larger than any one group of followers. This applies to the church today, where believers from different traditions, denominations, and ministries serve Christ in different ways.

In *Matthew 12:30*, Jesus said, “*He who is not with me is against me*” (*Matthew 12:30*). These sayings are not contradictory. In *Matthew 12*, Jesus was speaking about people’s personal response to Him: there is no neutral ground regarding Jesus Himself. In *Mark 9*, He is speaking about how His disciples should treat others who are working in His name: they should not oppose those who are doing His work simply because they belong to a different group.

The verse also highlights the danger of pride and rivalry among believers. The disciples had just been arguing about who was the greatest, and now they were trying to stop someone else’s ministry. Pride often shows itself in a desire to control and to be recognized as the only legitimate ones.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse calls believers to be generous toward other Christians who serve Jesus differently. Churches and ministries can easily become competitive, suspicious, or dismissive of others. Believers can rejoice when the gospel is preached, the poor are served, and people are helped in Jesus’ name, even if it is done by people outside their own church or tradition.

This does not mean ignoring false teaching. Scripture calls believers to test teaching and to reject what contradicts the gospel (*1 John 4:1*). But disagreements on secondary matters, or differences in methods and styles, should not lead believers to oppose others who are genuinely serving Christ.

Finally, this verse invites believers to examine their motives. Are they more concerned with Christ’s work being done or with their own group getting credit? Humility allows believers to celebrate God’s work wherever it happens.

### *Mark 9:50* — Have Salt in Yourselves and Be at Peace

> *“Salt is good, but if the salt has lost its saltiness, with what will you season it? Have salt in yourselves, and be at peace with one another.”*
>
> — *Mark 9:50* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse concludes a series of sayings in which Jesus warned His disciples about the seriousness of sin. He had told them that causing a little one to stumble deserves severe judgment, and that they should remove anything that causes them to sin, even if it is as valuable as a hand, foot, or eye. In verse 49, He said, “*For everyone will be salted with fire*” (*v. 49*), a difficult saying that may refer to the testing and purifying trials that believers will face, or to sacrifices in the Old Testament, which were offered with salt (*Leviticus 2:13*).

Now Jesus speaks about salt in a more positive way: “*Salt is good*” (*v. 50*). In the ancient world, salt was valuable for flavoring and preserving food. But Jesus asks what happens if salt loses its saltiness. Salt in that region was often mixed with impurities, and if the actual salt dissolved away, what remained was useless. Jesus asks, “*with what will you season it?*” (*v. 50*)

Then He gives two commands: “*Have salt in yourselves, and be at peace with one another*” (*v. 50*). “Have salt in yourselves” means to maintain the distinctive qualities of discipleship, such as purity, faithfulness, and devotion to God, that make believers like valuable salt. Salt was also associated with covenants in the Old Testament (“a covenant of salt,” *Numbers 18:19*), representing faithfulness and loyalty.

“Be at peace with one another” brings the teaching back to where it started. The disciples had been arguing about who was the greatest (v. 34) and had tried to stop someone outside their group (v. 38). Jesus ends this section of teaching by calling them to peace. The qualities that make them “salt” should lead to harmony, not rivalry.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse connects personal holiness with peaceful relationships. Disciples who are truly “salty,” devoted to God and faithful to His ways, will live at peace with others. Pride, rivalry, and competition destroy this peace. Paul later urges believers to “*as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men*” (*Romans 12:18*).

The image of salt losing its saltiness warns against losing the distinctive character of discipleship. Believers can drift into the attitudes and values of the world, becoming indistinguishable from those around them. When this happens, they lose their ability to influence others for good.

Finally, the call to “have salt in yourselves” may also point to the purifying work of God in believers’ lives. The “fire” of trials and the “salt” of God’s covenant faithfulness work together to make believers holy and useful to God.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse calls believers to maintain their distinctive Christian character. In a world that pressures people to conform, believers can remain faithful to Christ’s teaching in their speech, integrity, generosity, and relationships. This distinctiveness is what makes them valuable to the world, like salt that preserves and flavors.

It also calls believers to pursue peace with one another. Churches, families, and friendships are often damaged by competition, pride, and conflict. Believers can take practical steps toward peace: apologizing when they have wronged others, refusing to gossip, letting go of the need to be right, and seeking reconciliation.

Finally, this verse connects holiness and harmony. Believers can examine whether their pursuit of righteousness has made them proud or harsh, or whether it has made them more humble and peaceful. True holiness produces peace.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Mark 9* moves from the glory of the mountaintop to the struggles of the valley, and both speak to everyday life. The transfiguration reminds believers that Jesus is the glorious Son of God, and the Father’s command, “Listen to him,” remains the guiding principle for discipleship. Even when life is difficult or confusing, believers can trust that the One they follow is glorious, and that the path of the cross leads to resurrection.

The father of the tormented boy shows that faith can be weak and still be real. Believers who struggle with doubt can come to Jesus honestly, praying, “I believe. Help my unbelief.” They can also learn from the disciples’ failure that spiritual power depends on prayerful dependence on God rather than on past experience or personal ability.

The disciples’ argument about greatness and their attempt to stop the outsider reveal the persistent temptations of pride and rivalry. Jesus answers with a child in His arms and a call to be servant of all. Believers can look for ways to serve those with little status, celebrate God’s work through others, and resist the urge to compete for recognition.

Finally, Jesus’ warnings about sin call for seriousness. Whatever leads believers or others into sin should be dealt with decisively. Believers should be especially careful not to cause vulnerable people to stumble. And Jesus’ closing words bring these teachings together: have salt in yourselves, maintaining a distinctive faithfulness to God, and be at peace with one another.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for revealing Your glory on the mountain and for the Father’s command to listen to You. Help me to hear Your voice above all others. When I face situations that seem hopeless, I come to You as the father of the tormented boy did. I believe; help my unbelief. Strengthen my faith, and teach me to depend on You in prayer.

Forgive me for wanting to be great and for competing with others. Make me a servant of all, willing to welcome the least important for Your sake. Help me to rejoice when Your work is done through people outside my own circle. Give me courage to deal seriously with sin in my life, and keep me from causing anyone to stumble. Keep me salty with faithfulness to You, and help me to live at peace with others. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Mark · Chapter 10 of 16

# Mark — Chapter 10

Chapter Theme: On the Road to Jerusalem: Receiving the Kingdom Like a Child

[Read Mark 10 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/MRK10.htm)

Main Teaching

As Jesus travels toward Jerusalem, He teaches about marriage, welcomes children, and lovingly calls a rich man to give up his wealth and follow Him. He warns that riches make entering the kingdom hard, promises that no sacrifice for Him will be lost, predicts His death for the third time, and corrects His disciples’ desire for status by declaring that He came to serve and give His life as a ransom. The chapter ends with blind Bartimaeus throwing off his cloak, receiving his sight, and following Jesus on the road.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Mark 10* continues Jesus’ journey south from Galilee toward Jerusalem, where He will be crucified. Mark often describes Jesus and His disciples as being “on the way” (vv. 17, 32, 46, 52). The phrase is literal, describing their travel, but it also carries a deeper meaning: following Jesus means walking with Him on the way to the cross. The early Christians were sometimes called followers of “*the Way*” (*Acts 9:2*).

This chapter parallels *Matthew 19–20*, but Mark adds vivid personal details, such as Jesus’ indignation at the disciples, His love for the rich man, and the name and actions of the blind beggar Bartimaeus. The chapter is also framed by two encounters with Jesus’ question, “What do you want me to do for you?” (vv. 36, 51), asked first to James and John, who want power, and then to Bartimaeus, who wants sight.

### Teaching About Divorce (*10:1–12*)

Jesus left Galilee and went into Judea and the region east of the Jordan River. Crowds gathered again, and He taught them. Some Pharisees came to test Him with a question: “*Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife?*” (*v. 2*) This region was ruled by Herod Antipas, who had divorced his wife to marry Herodias and had executed John the Baptist for criticizing that marriage. The question may have been a trap.

Jesus asked what Moses commanded. They answered that Moses permitted a man to write a certificate of divorce and send his wife away (*Deuteronomy 24:1–4*). Jesus explained that Moses wrote this command “*For your hardness of heart*” (*v. 5*). The law regulated divorce in a sinful world, but it did not represent God’s original design. Jesus pointed back to creation: God made humanity male and female, and a man leaves his parents and is joined to his wife, and the two become one flesh. Therefore, “*What therefore God has joined together, let no man separate*” (*v. 9*).

Later, in the house, the disciples asked Him about this again. Jesus said that whoever divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery against her, and a woman who divorces her husband and marries another commits adultery. Mark’s version mentions a woman divorcing her husband, which was possible under Roman law but rarely under Jewish law; Mark’s Gentile readers in Rome would have needed this application. Notice also that Jesus said a man who divorces commits adultery “against her,” treating the wife as a person who could be wronged, at a time when many viewed adultery mainly as an offense against a husband. Mark does not include the exception for sexual immorality found in Matthew. (Christian traditions differ on how to apply these teachings, including in cases of abandonment and abuse; see the discussion at *Matthew 19:6*. Jesus’ teaching protects the vulnerable and must not be used to keep anyone in danger.)

### Jesus Blesses the Children (*10:13–16*)

People were bringing little children to Jesus so that He would touch them. The disciples rebuked them, perhaps thinking Jesus was too important or busy for children. Mark alone tells us that Jesus “*was moved with indignation*” (*v. 14*) at the disciples. He said, “*Allow the little children to come to me! Don’t forbid them, for God’s Kingdom belongs to such as these*” (*v. 14*). Then He added a principle studied below. Mark also tells us that Jesus took the children in His arms, laid His hands on them, and blessed them. His tenderness toward children contrasts with His disciples’ dismissiveness.

### The Rich Man (*10:17–27*)

As Jesus set out on His way, a man ran up, knelt before Him, and asked, “*Good Teacher, what shall I do that I may inherit eternal life?*” (*v. 17*) Matthew calls him young, and Luke calls him a ruler. His running and kneeling showed eagerness and respect.

Jesus asked why he called Him good, since no one is good except God alone. Then He reminded him of the commandments dealing with relationships with others, including one unique to Mark’s list: “*Do not defraud*” (*v. 19*), perhaps a pointed reference to how wealth could be gained unjustly. The man said he had kept all these since his youth.

Then Mark records something the other Gospels omit: “*Jesus looking at him loved him*” (*v. 21*). Jesus told him he lacked one thing: he should sell everything, give to the poor, and he would have treasure in heaven; then he should come and follow Jesus. The man’s face fell, and he went away sad, because he had great wealth. This verse is studied below.

Jesus looked around and said to His disciples how hard it is for the wealthy to enter God’s kingdom. The disciples were amazed, because many people assumed wealth was a sign of God’s blessing. Jesus repeated, calling them “*Children*” (*v. 24*), a tender term, and said that it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter God’s kingdom. The disciples were even more astonished: “*Then who can be saved?*” (*v. 26*) Jesus looked at them and said, “*With men it is impossible, but not with God, for all things are possible with God*” (*v. 27*). (These sayings are studied at *Matthew 19:21* and *19:26*.)

### The Reward of Following Jesus (*10:28–31*)

Peter said, “*Behold, we have left all and have followed you*” (*v. 28*). Jesus promised that no one who had left home, family, or land for His sake and the gospel’s would fail to receive a hundred times as much in this present age, including houses, brothers, sisters, mothers, children, and fields, “*with persecutions*” (*v. 30*), and in the age to come, eternal life.

This promise shows that those who leave family and possessions for Christ gain a new, much larger family: the community of believers who share homes, resources, and love. Mark alone adds “with persecutions,” a realistic reminder that following Jesus brings hardship as well as blessing. Mark’s first readers in Rome knew this well. Jesus ended with a reversal: “*many who are first will be last, and the last first*” (*v. 31*).

### The Third Prediction of the Passion (*10:32–34*)

Mark gives a striking picture: they were on the road going up to Jerusalem, with Jesus walking ahead of them. The disciples were astonished, and those who followed were afraid. Jesus was walking deliberately toward His death, and His followers sensed the danger.

Jesus took the Twelve aside and told them, for the third time, what would happen. This is the most detailed of His predictions: He would be handed over to the chief priests and scribes, condemned to death, handed over to the Gentiles (the Romans), mocked, spat on, flogged, and killed. And on the third day He would rise again. Every detail would be fulfilled in *Mark 14–16*.

### James and John’s Request (*10:35–45*)

Immediately after this prediction, James and John came to Jesus and said, “*Teacher, we want you to do for us whatever we will ask*” (*v. 35*). Jesus asked, “*What do you want me to do for you?*” (*v. 36*) They asked to sit at His right and left in His glory, the positions of highest honor. (In Matthew’s account, their mother made the request on their behalf.)

Jesus told them they did not know what they were asking, and He asked whether they could drink His cup and be baptized with His baptism. The “cup” was an Old Testament image for suffering and God’s judgment, and “baptism” here pictures being overwhelmed or immersed in suffering. They confidently said they could. Jesus told them they would indeed share His suffering, but the places at His right and left were not His to give.

The other ten were indignant with James and John. Jesus called them together and contrasted the way of the world, where rulers lord it over others, with the way of His kingdom, where the great are servants and the first are slaves of all. He concluded, “*For the Son of Man also came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many*” (*v. 45*). (This verse, central to Mark’s Gospel, is studied in depth at *Matthew 20:28*.)

### Blind Bartimaeus (*10:46–52*)

They came to Jericho, about fifteen miles northeast of Jerusalem, the last major stop before the climb to the city. As Jesus was leaving with His disciples and a large crowd, a blind beggar named Bartimaeus, the son of Timaeus, was sitting by the road. Mark is the only Gospel writer to give his name, which suggests he may have become known to the early church.

When Bartimaeus heard that Jesus of Nazareth was passing by, he began to shout, “*Jesus, you son of David, have mercy on me!*” (*v. 47*) “Son of David” was a title for the Messiah, the heir to David’s throne. Bartimaeus, though physically blind, saw who Jesus was. Many people rebuked him and told him to be quiet, but he shouted even louder.

Jesus stopped and said, “Call him.” The people now said to Bartimaeus, “*Cheer up! Get up. He is calling you!*” (*v. 49*) Bartimaeus threw off his cloak, jumped up, and came to Jesus. This is studied below. Jesus asked him, “*What do you want me to do for you?*” (*v. 51*), the same question He had asked James and John. Bartimaeus answered, “*Rabboni, that I may see again*” (*v. 51*). “Rabboni” means “my teacher,” a respectful and personal title. Jesus said, “*Go your way. Your faith has made you well*” (*v. 52*). Immediately he received his sight “*and followed Jesus on the way*” (*v. 52*).

The final phrase is significant. Bartimaeus followed Jesus “on the way,” the road to Jerusalem and the cross. He became a model disciple: seeing Jesus clearly, asking for mercy rather than status, and following Him.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Mark 10:15* — Receiving the Kingdom Like a Little Child

> *“Most certainly I tell you, whoever will not receive God’s Kingdom like a little child, he will in no way enter into it.”*
>
> — *Mark 10:15* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus speaks these words after His disciples tried to stop people from bringing children to Him. Parents were bringing their little children so that Jesus would touch them and bless them, a common practice with respected teachers. But the disciples rebuked them. Perhaps they thought Jesus had more important things to do, or that children were not worth His time.

Mark tells us that when Jesus saw this, He was “*moved with indignation*” (*v. 14*). This is the only time in the Gospels that Jesus is described as indignant with His own disciples. He told them to let the children come and not to hinder them, “*for God’s Kingdom belongs to such as these*” (*v. 14*).

Then Jesus added the solemn statement in this verse: “*whoever will not receive God’s Kingdom like a little child, he will in no way enter into it*” (*v. 15*). “Receive” means to welcome or accept a gift. The kingdom of God is not earned or achieved; it is received. Jesus says it must be received the way a little child receives.

How does a child receive? In Jesus’ culture, children were dependent and had no status or achievements to offer. A child receives gifts simply and gladly, without thinking they must earn them. A child trusts the giver. This is the attitude Jesus calls for: humble dependence, trust, and openness to God’s gift.

The next verse adds a beautiful scene: Jesus “*took them in his arms and blessed them, laying his hands on them*” (*v. 16*). Jesus showed by His actions that the children were welcome.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse teaches that entrance into God’s kingdom is by grace, received with humble trust. No one can enter by their own merit, achievement, or status. This connects directly with the next scene, where a rich man asks what he must do to inherit eternal life. He comes thinking of achievement; Jesus has just said the kingdom must be received like a child.

The verse also shows the value Jesus places on children. In a culture that often overlooked them, Jesus welcomed, embraced, and blessed them. He made them examples of how to receive the kingdom. This reveals God’s heart for the small, weak, and dependent.

Finally, Jesus’ indignation shows that hindering people from coming to Him is a serious matter. The disciples thought they were protecting Jesus’ time, but they were blocking the very people who represented the kingdom. Religious people can sometimes become obstacles to others coming to Christ.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse calls believers to approach God with childlike trust. Rather than trying to earn God’s favor or relying on accomplishments, believers can receive His grace as a gift. This means admitting dependence on Him, trusting His goodness, and coming to Him with openness rather than pride.

It also calls believers to value children and help them come to Jesus. Churches and families can make room for children, take their faith seriously, teach them about Jesus, and show them His love. Children are not merely the church of the future; they are welcomed by Jesus now.

Finally, this verse warns against hindering anyone from coming to Christ. Believers can examine whether their attitudes, traditions, or behavior make it harder for others, whether children, newcomers, or people from different backgrounds, to come to Jesus. Jesus wants all to come to Him.

### *Mark 10:21* — Jesus Looked at Him and Loved Him

> *“Jesus looking at him loved him, and said to him, ‘One thing you lack. Go, sell whatever you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me, taking up the cross.’”*
>
> — *Mark 10:21* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse is the heart of Jesus’ encounter with the rich man. The man had run up to Jesus, knelt, and asked what he must do to inherit eternal life. Jesus reminded him of the commandments about relationships with others, and the man said he had kept them all since his youth. He seems to have been sincere, a man who had tried to live a good life.

Then Mark gives a detail the other Gospels do not include: “*Jesus looking at him loved him*” (*v. 21*). Jesus looked carefully at this man, seeing his sincerity and his need, and He felt genuine love for him. Everything Jesus said next was spoken in love.

“*One thing you lack*” (*v. 21*). Despite his moral life, the man was missing something essential. Jesus identified it: “*Go, sell whatever you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me, taking up the cross*” (*v. 21*). (The last phrase is found in some manuscripts.)

The command had several parts. Selling his possessions would free him from what was holding his heart. Giving to the poor would express love for his neighbor in a costly way. Treasure in heaven would replace earthly treasure. And following Jesus was the ultimate goal. The man’s wealth had become an idol that kept him from wholehearted devotion to God.

The man’s response was heartbreaking: “*But his face fell at that saying, and he went away sorrowful, for he was one who had great possessions*” (*v. 22*). He wanted eternal life, but not at the cost of his wealth.

Matthew’s version of this story is studied at *Matthew 19:21*, focusing on the danger of wealth. Mark’s detail about Jesus’ love adds another dimension: even His most demanding call comes from love.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that Jesus’ commands, even the hard ones, come from love. Jesus did not ask the man to give up his wealth to punish him or to make following Him difficult. He asked because He loved him and saw what was keeping him from true life. Jesus’ call to give up idols is an invitation to freedom.

It also shows that Jesus sees each person clearly. He knew exactly what this man needed to hear. For another person, the “one thing” might be different: a relationship, a habit, an ambition, or a grudge. Jesus lovingly identifies what stands between each person and wholehearted devotion to God.

Finally, the man’s sad departure shows that Jesus does not force anyone to follow Him. He loved the man, but He let him go. Love respects the freedom to choose, even when the choice is tragic. Mark does not tell us whether the man later changed his mind; the story leaves the reader to consider their own response.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to trust that Jesus’ commands come from love. When God asks them to give up something, whether a possession, a habit, a relationship, or a plan, they can trust that He is not trying to take away their joy but to give them something better. His demands are expressions of His love.

It also invites believers to ask what “one thing” might be holding them back. Many people live respectable lives but hold onto something that competes with God for their hearts. Believers can ask Jesus to show them what that is and to give them courage to let it go.

Finally, this verse encourages believers to speak hard truths in love. Jesus told the man something difficult, but He did it from genuine love. When believers need to challenge someone, they can follow Jesus’ example, looking at the person with love and speaking truth for their good, not to condemn them.

### *Mark 10:50* — Throwing Off the Cloak

> *“He, casting away his cloak, sprang up, and came to Jesus.”*
>
> — *Mark 10:50* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse describes Bartimaeus’s response when Jesus called him. Bartimaeus was a blind beggar sitting by the road outside Jericho. When he heard that Jesus of Nazareth was passing by, he began shouting, “*Jesus, you son of David, have mercy on me!*” (*v. 47*) The crowd told him to be quiet, but he shouted even louder. Jesus stopped and told the people to call him. The same people who had told him to be quiet now said, “*Cheer up! Get up. He is calling you!*” (*v. 49*)

Bartimaeus responded immediately: “*He, casting away his cloak, sprang up, and came to Jesus*” (*v. 50*). Each action is significant.

“*casting away his cloak*” (*v. 50*). For a poor beggar, a cloak was one of his most important possessions. It kept him warm at night and served as his blanket. He may also have spread it on the ground to collect coins from passersby. The law of Moses protected a poor person’s cloak, requiring that it be returned before sunset if taken as a pledge (*Exodus 22:26–27*). Throwing it aside showed his eagerness to get to Jesus and his willingness to leave behind what had been his security. A blind man who throws aside his cloak may not be able to find it again.

“*sprang up*” (*v. 50*). He did not hesitate or move slowly. He jumped up with excitement and hope.

“*came to Jesus*” (*v. 50*). Though blind, he made his way to Jesus, likely guided by the voices of those around him.

Jesus asked him, “What do you want me to do for you?” Bartimaeus answered, “Rabboni, that I may see again.” Jesus told him his faith had made him well. Immediately he received his sight and followed Jesus on the way.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse provides a picture of how people respond to Jesus’ call. Bartimaeus’s actions contrast sharply with the rich man earlier in the chapter. The rich man came to Jesus eagerly but went away sad because he could not let go of his great possessions. Bartimaeus, a poor beggar, threw away his only possession to come to Jesus. The rich man held onto his wealth; the beggar let go of his cloak.

It also shows the contrast with James and John. When Jesus asked them, “What do you want me to do for you?”, they asked for positions of power. When He asked Bartimaeus the same question, he asked for mercy and sight. Bartimaeus understood his need and came to Jesus with humility.

Finally, Bartimaeus’s story ends with discipleship. He did not simply receive healing and go home; he followed Jesus “on the way,” the road to Jerusalem and the cross. His healing led to following. He becomes a model for all believers: recognizing Jesus, crying out for mercy, letting go of what holds us back, and following Him.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to respond to Jesus’ call with eagerness. When Jesus calls, through Scripture, through conviction, or through an opportunity to serve, believers can respond without delay, as Bartimaeus did.

It also challenges believers to consider what “cloak” they might need to throw aside to come to Jesus. It may be a source of security, a habit, a way of thinking, or something that seems necessary but is holding them back. Letting go of such things can be frightening, but Jesus offers far more than what we leave behind.

Finally, Bartimaeus’s persistence encourages believers to keep calling out to Jesus even when others discourage them. Many people face voices that tell them to be quiet about their faith or their needs. Bartimaeus shouted louder. Believers can keep seeking Jesus and bringing their needs to Him, trusting that He will stop and call them.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Mark 10* is about what it means to follow Jesus “on the way” to Jerusalem and the cross. Jesus’ teaching on marriage calls believers to honor God’s design for lifelong covenant faithfulness, while His treatment of women as persons who can be wronged reminds them that this teaching protects the vulnerable rather than trapping them in harm.

His welcome of children shows that the kingdom must be received with humble, trusting dependence. Believers can approach God not with achievements but with open hands, and they can make room for children and others who are easily overlooked, never hindering anyone from coming to Jesus.

The rich man’s story and Jesus’ teaching on wealth confront believers with the power possessions can have over the heart. Jesus looked at the man with love and called him to let go of what held him. Believers can ask what holds their hearts, trust that Jesus’ demands come from love, and remember that salvation, though impossible for people, is possible with God. They can also trust Jesus’ promise that nothing given up for Him is lost, even though following Him includes persecutions.

James and John’s request and the disciples’ indignation show how easily even devoted followers seek status. Jesus’ answer, that He came to serve and give His life as a ransom, redefines greatness for every believer. Finally, Bartimaeus shows the response Jesus desires: recognizing Him, crying out for mercy, throwing aside whatever holds us back, and following Him on the way. Believers can walk the road of discipleship with the same eagerness and humility.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for welcoming little children into Your arms. Teach me to receive Your kingdom like a child, with humble trust and open hands, and keep me from ever hindering others from coming to You. Thank You for looking at me with love, even when You call me to give up what I hold too tightly. Show me the one thing that stands between me and wholehearted devotion to You, and give me courage to let it go.

Free me from seeking greatness and status. Teach me to serve as You served, You who gave Your life as a ransom for many. Like Bartimaeus, I cry out for Your mercy. Help me to throw aside whatever holds me back, to come to You eagerly, and to follow You on the way, wherever it leads. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Mark · Chapter 11 of 16

# Mark — Chapter 11

Chapter Theme: The King Enters, the Temple Is Judged, and Faith Is Called For

[Read Mark 11 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/MRK11.htm)

Main Teaching

Jesus enters Jerusalem on a colt to shouts of “Hosanna,” then looks over the temple and returns the next day to drive out the merchants, declaring that God’s house should be a house of prayer for all nations. Mark wraps this action inside the story of a leafy but fruitless fig tree that Jesus curses and that withers, showing that God’s judgment rests on empty religion. Jesus calls His disciples to faith in God and to forgiveness in prayer, and He refuses to answer leaders who will not admit the truth about John the Baptist.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Mark 11* begins the final week of Jesus’ earthly life. *Mark 11–16* covers only about eight days, yet it fills more than a third of Mark’s Gospel. Jesus has traveled from Galilee to Jericho and now climbs the steep road to Jerusalem for Passover. The city was filled with pilgrims, and Messianic hopes were high. Jesus had predicted three times that He would be rejected, killed, and raised in Jerusalem (*Mark 8:31*; *9:31*; *10:33–34*). Now He arrives.

Mark arranges this chapter carefully. He tells about Jesus’ entry, then His first look at the temple, then the cursing of the fig tree, then the cleansing of the temple, then the withered fig tree. This “sandwich” structure, in which the fig tree story surrounds the temple scene, shows that the two events interpret each other. (Matthew’s account of these events is studied at *Matthew 21*; this chapter focuses on details distinctive to Mark.)

### The Entry Into Jerusalem (*11:1–11*)

As they approached Jerusalem, near the villages of Bethphage and Bethany on the Mount of Olives, Jesus sent two disciples ahead to a village to find “*a young donkey tied, on which no one has sat*” (*v. 2*). Animals that had never been used were considered suitable for sacred purposes (*Numbers 19:2*; *1 Samuel 6:7*). If anyone asked, they were to say, “*The Lord needs him*” (*v. 3*), and that He would send it back. Everything happened exactly as Jesus said, showing that He was in control of the events of His final week.

They brought the colt, threw their cloaks on it, and Jesus sat on it. This act fulfilled *Zechariah 9:9*, which describes Israel’s king coming humbly, riding on a donkey’s colt. Many people spread their cloaks on the road, and others spread leafy branches cut from the fields. Those in front and behind shouted, “*Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!*” (*v. 9*), words from *Psalm 118:25–26*, a psalm sung by pilgrims at Passover. Mark adds a shout found only in his Gospel: “*Blessed is the kingdom of our father David that is coming in the name of the Lord!*” (*v. 10*) The crowd was hoping for the restoration of David’s kingdom, probably imagining political liberation from Rome.

Mark’s account of the entry ends quietly. Jesus entered the temple, “*looked around at everything*” (*v. 11*), and since it was already late, went back to Bethany with the Twelve. Mark alone records this inspection. Jesus was like a king surveying His house before acting. What He saw would lead to His action the next day.

### The Fig Tree Cursed (*11:12–14*)

The next morning, as they were leaving Bethany, Jesus was hungry. Seeing a fig tree in leaf at a distance, He went to see if it had any fruit. He found nothing but leaves, “*for it was not the season for figs*” (*v. 13*). Jesus said to it, “*May no one ever eat fruit from you again!*” (*v. 14*), and His disciples heard it. This puzzling episode is studied below.

### Cleansing the Temple (*11:15–19*)

In Jerusalem, Jesus entered the temple courts and began driving out those who were buying and selling. He overturned the tables of the money changers and the seats of those selling doves. The money changers exchanged foreign coins for the Tyrian silver coins required for the temple tax, and doves were the sacrifice of the poor (*Leviticus 12:8*). Mark adds a detail found only in his account: Jesus “*would not allow anyone to carry a container through the temple*” (*v. 16*). People apparently used the outer court as a shortcut, carrying goods through the sacred space. Jesus stopped it all.

He then taught, quoting *Isaiah 56:7*: “*My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations*” (*v. 17*). Mark alone includes “for all the nations.” The commercial activity was taking place in the Court of the Gentiles, the only area where non-Jews could come to worship. By turning it into a marketplace, the temple authorities were blocking the very people God wanted to welcome. Then Jesus quoted *Jeremiah 7:11*: “*But you have made it a den of robbers!*” (*v. 17*) In Jeremiah’s day, God had warned that the temple would be destroyed because people practiced injustice and then used the temple as a hiding place, the way robbers retreat to a den. (This action is studied in depth at *Matthew 21:13*.)

The chief priests and scribes heard this and looked for a way to kill Jesus. But they feared Him, because the whole crowd was amazed at His teaching. When evening came, Jesus and His disciples left the city.

### The Withered Fig Tree and the Lesson on Faith (*11:20–26*)

The next morning, as they passed by, they saw the fig tree withered from the roots. Peter remembered and said, “*Rabbi, look! The fig tree which you cursed has withered away*” (*v. 21*). Jesus responded with teaching about faith and prayer, studied below. He then added an important condition for prayer: forgiveness, also studied below. (Verse 26 is not found in many early manuscripts.)

### The Question of Authority (*11:27–33*)

Back in the temple courts, the chief priests, scribes, and elders, representing the Sanhedrin, the ruling council, came to Jesus and demanded, “*By what authority do you do these things? Or who gave you this authority to do these things?*” (*v. 28*) They were the official authorities over the temple. Jesus had acted without their permission.

Jesus said He would answer if they answered one question: was John’s baptism from heaven or from men? They discussed it among themselves. If they said “from heaven,” Jesus would ask why they had not believed John. If they said “from men,” they feared the people, who all considered John a prophet. So they answered, “*We don’t know*” (*v. 33*). Jesus replied that He would not tell them by what authority He acted.

Jesus’ question was not an evasion. John had testified that Jesus was the Coming One. If the leaders had acknowledged John’s authority, they would have known the source of Jesus’ authority too. Their refusal to answer honestly exposed their unwillingness to accept the truth. They were more concerned with protecting their position and avoiding public embarrassment than with discovering what God was doing.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Mark 11:13–14* — The Fruitless Fig Tree

> *“Seeing a fig tree afar off having leaves, he came to see if perhaps he might find anything on it. When he came to it, he found nothing but leaves, for it was not the season for figs. Jesus told it, ‘May no one ever eat fruit from you again!’ and his disciples heard it.”*
>
> — *Mark 11:13–14* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These verses describe one of the most puzzling events in Jesus’ ministry. On the morning after His entry into Jerusalem, as Jesus left Bethany, He was hungry. He saw a fig tree in the distance that was in leaf, and He went to see whether it had any fruit. When He reached it, He found nothing but leaves. Mark adds, “*for it was not the season for figs*” (*v. 13*). Then Jesus said to the tree, “*May no one ever eat fruit from you again!*” (*v. 14*) The next morning, the disciples saw the tree withered from the roots (v. 20).

Many readers wonder why Jesus would curse a tree for not having fruit when it was not the season. The answer lies in understanding both fig trees and Mark’s purpose.

Fig trees in that region usually produced their leaves in spring, around Passover. Along with the leaves, many fig trees produced small early knobs of fruit, called “paggim,” which were edible, though not as good as the main crop that came later in summer. A tree full of leaves but without any of these early knobs was a sign that it would not produce fruit that year. The tree’s leaves advertised fruit, but it had none. Its appearance was misleading.

More importantly, Mark presents this event as an acted parable, a symbolic action like those of the Old Testament prophets, who sometimes performed actions to illustrate God’s message. Mark places the cursing of the fig tree right before the cleansing of the temple and the discovery of the withered tree right after it. The fig tree represents the temple and the religious system centered on it. Like the tree, the temple was impressive and busy, full of activity and appearance, but it was not producing the fruit God desired: prayer, justice, and welcome for the nations. Jesus’ curse on the tree pictured God’s judgment on fruitless religion. The temple was destroyed by the Romans about forty years later, in A.D. 70.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This passage connects with the Old Testament, where the fig tree and vine often represent Israel. The prophets used fig trees to describe God’s disappointment when He looked for fruit among His people and found none. Jeremiah wrote, “*No grapes will be on the vine, no figs on the fig tree, and the leaf will fade*” (*Jeremiah 8:13*), describing God’s judgment. Micah lamented that there was no early fig to eat (*Micah 7:1*). Jesus’ action stands in this prophetic tradition.

The passage warns that outward religious activity without genuine fruit is dangerous. The temple had magnificent buildings, constant sacrifices, and crowds of worshipers, yet it had become a place of commerce and exploitation rather than prayer. God looks for the fruit of faithfulness, justice, mercy, and true worship, not merely leaves of religious appearance.

The fig tree also shows that Jesus has authority to pronounce judgment. The same Jesus who healed and welcomed sinners also confronted religious hypocrisy with God’s judgment. His love and His holiness belong together.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage invites believers to examine whether their lives bear real fruit or only leaves. It is possible to be active in church, use religious language, and appear devout while lacking genuine love for God and others. Believers can ask whether their faith produces fruit such as prayer, love, honesty, generosity, and humility, or whether it is mostly outward appearance.

It also challenges churches to evaluate their life together. Are they houses of prayer, places where all people, including outsiders, are welcome to meet God? Or have they become focused on activity, buildings, or programs while neglecting what matters most to God?

Finally, this passage encourages believers to take God’s judgment seriously while trusting His grace. Jesus’ warning is not meant to drive people to despair but to call them to repentance and genuine faith. Those who abide in Christ will bear fruit (*John 15:5*), not by their own effort, but by His life in them.

### *Mark 11:22–24* — Have Faith in God

> *“Jesus answered them, Have faith in God. For most certainly I tell you, whoever may tell this mountain, “Be taken up and cast into the sea,” and doesn’t doubt in his heart, but believes that what he says is happening, he shall have whatever he says. Therefore I tell you, all things whatever you pray and ask for, believe that you have received them, and you shall have them.”*
>
> — *Mark 11:22–24* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These verses contain Jesus’ response when Peter pointed out that the fig tree Jesus had cursed had withered from the roots. The disciples were amazed that the tree had died so quickly. Jesus turned their attention from the miracle to its source: “*Have faith in God*” (*v. 22*).

The phrase is simple but central. Jesus did not say “have faith in faith” or “have faith in your words.” He said “have faith in God.” The power that withered the fig tree came from God, and faith is trust directed toward Him.

Then Jesus gave a vivid illustration: whoever says to “*this mountain*” (*v. 23*), “*Be taken up and cast into the sea*” (*v. 23*), and does not doubt but believes, will have it done. Jesus and His disciples were near Jerusalem, and “this mountain” may refer to the Mount of Olives or the temple mount itself. The sea might be the Dead Sea, visible from the Mount of Olives. “Moving mountains” was a common Jewish expression for doing something seemingly impossible. If Jesus was pointing to the temple mount, His words may have connected to the judgment He had just pronounced on the temple.

Jesus continued: “*all things whatever you pray and ask for, believe that you have received them, and you shall have them*” (*v. 24*). This is a bold promise about prayer offered in faith.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses teach that prayer rooted in faith in God is powerful. Believers are invited to pray boldly, trusting that God can do what seems impossible. Faith is not wishful thinking but confident trust in God’s power and character.

However, these verses must be understood in the context of the whole Bible’s teaching on prayer. They do not mean that believers can obtain anything they want simply by believing hard enough. Jesus Himself prayed in Gethsemane, “*Not what I desire, but what you desire*” (*Mark 14:36*), and the Father did not remove the cup. Paul prayed three times for his thorn to be removed, and God said no (*2 Corinthians 12:7–9*). John teaches that God hears prayers that are “*according to his will*” (*1 John 5:14*). Faith in God includes trusting His wisdom when His answer differs from our request.

These verses also must not be used to blame people for unanswered prayers by suggesting that they did not have enough faith. Many faithful believers have prayed for healing or deliverance and not received it in this life. Scripture honors such people (*Hebrews 11:35–39*). The point of Jesus’ teaching is to encourage bold, trusting prayer, not to create a formula that guarantees results.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to pray boldly. They can bring to God situations that seem impossible: broken relationships, deep sin, serious illness, injustice, or spiritual darkness. God is able to do far more than they imagine. Faith means trusting His power rather than being limited by what seems possible.

They also call believers to direct their faith toward God, not toward their own feelings or words. The focus is not on how strongly one believes, but on whom one believes in. Believers can pray with confidence because God is good, powerful, and faithful.

Finally, these verses invite believers to trust God’s wisdom alongside His power. When answers to prayer differ from what they hoped, they can continue to have faith in God, knowing that His purposes are good even when they do not understand them. They can also comfort others who are suffering without suggesting that their faith was lacking.

### *Mark 11:25* — Forgive When You Pray

> *“Whenever you stand praying, forgive, if you have anything against anyone; so that your Father, who is in heaven, may also forgive you your transgressions.”*
>
> — *Mark 11:25* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus speaks these words right after encouraging His disciples to have faith in God and to pray boldly. He has promised that whatever they ask in prayer, believing, they will receive. Now He adds an important condition that shapes how they pray: “*Whenever you stand praying, forgive, if you have anything against anyone*” (*v. 25*).

“Stand praying” reflects the common Jewish posture for prayer, standing with hands raised. Jesus says that whenever His followers pray, they must deal with any resentment they hold against others. “Anything against anyone” covers every grievance and every person.

The purpose is given: “*so that your Father, who is in heaven, may also forgive you your transgressions*” (*v. 25*). “Transgressions” are wrongdoings, stepping over the line God has set. Those who pray to God for forgiveness and help must themselves be willing to forgive.

This teaching connects with the cleansing of the temple and the fig tree. The temple was meant to be a house of prayer, but it had become corrupt. Now Jesus teaches His disciples what true prayer involves: faith in God and a forgiving heart. Prayer is not merely about getting what we ask for; it is about being in right relationship with God and others.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse teaches that forgiveness is essential to a healthy relationship with God. Jesus consistently connects receiving God’s forgiveness with forgiving others. In the Lord’s Prayer, He taught His followers to pray, “*Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors*” (*Matthew 6:12*). In the parable of the unforgiving servant, He showed that those who have been forgiven much must forgive others (*Matthew 18:21–35*).

This does not mean that people earn God’s forgiveness by forgiving others. God’s forgiveness is a gift of grace. But a heart that has truly received God’s forgiveness will be changed by it. Refusing to forgive others while asking God for forgiveness reveals a heart that has not fully understood or received God’s mercy.

The placement of this verse right after the promise about powerful prayer is significant. Bold faith and bitter resentment cannot coexist comfortably. Unforgiveness hinders prayer because it damages our relationship with God. Peter later writes that husbands who mistreat their wives may find their prayers hindered (*1 Peter 3:7*), showing that relationships with others affect relationships with God.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to examine their hearts whenever they pray. Before bringing requests to God, they can ask whether they are holding resentment against anyone. If so, they can bring that resentment to God and choose to forgive, releasing the debt and the desire for revenge.

It also helps believers understand forgiveness correctly. Forgiving someone does not mean pretending the wrong did not happen, excusing it, or necessarily restoring trust immediately. In cases of abuse or ongoing harm, forgiveness can coexist with protective boundaries and with seeking justice through appropriate channels. Forgiveness means giving up the right to personal revenge and leaving judgment to God.

Finally, this verse encourages believers to make forgiveness a regular part of their spiritual lives. Forgiveness is often not a one-time act but a process, especially for deep wounds. Each time believers pray, they can renew their decision to forgive, asking God for the strength to let go and for healing in their hearts.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Mark 11* shows Jesus arriving in Jerusalem as King and Judge. The crowds welcomed Him with hopes of a political kingdom, but Jesus came humbly on a colt and then turned His attention to the temple. Believers can welcome Jesus as King while allowing Him to define what His kingdom means. He is not a king who exists to fulfill their agendas but one who calls them to genuine faith and fruitful lives.

The fig tree and the temple warn against religion that is all leaves and no fruit. Believers can examine whether their faith produces genuine fruit: prayer, love, justice, and welcome for others. Churches can ask whether they are truly houses of prayer for all nations, places where outsiders are welcomed to meet God, or whether other activities have crowded out what matters most.

Jesus’ teaching on faith calls believers to trust God boldly in prayer. Nothing is too difficult for Him. Yet faith also trusts His wisdom when His answers differ from their requests. Believers can pray with confidence, avoid turning faith into a formula, and comfort others without blaming them for unanswered prayers.

The call to forgive when praying reminds believers that their relationship with God cannot be separated from their relationships with others. Resentment hinders prayer. Believers can regularly examine their hearts and release grudges to God, while using wisdom about boundaries and justice. Finally, the leaders’ refusal to answer honestly about John shows the danger of protecting one’s position instead of admitting truth. Believers can choose honesty and humility, even when the truth is costly.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, You came to Jerusalem as the humble King, riding on a colt. I welcome You as my King, and I ask You to reign in my life on Your terms, not mine. Search my life as You searched the temple. Where I have leaves without fruit, appearance without reality, forgive me and make me fruitful.

Make my life and Your church a house of prayer for all nations, open to everyone who seeks You. Teach me to have faith in God, to pray boldly, and to trust Your wisdom when Your answers are different from my requests. Show me anyone I am holding resentment against, and give me grace to forgive as You have forgiven me. Keep me honest and humble, willing to accept the truth even when it costs me. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
