Mark · Chapter 14 of 16

# Mark — Chapter 14

Chapter Theme: Anointed, Betrayed, and Abandoned — The Night Before the Cross

[Read Mark 14 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/MRK14.htm)

Main Teaching

On the night before His death, Jesus is honored by a woman’s costly devotion, gives His disciples bread and wine as signs of His body and blood, wrestles in prayer in Gethsemane, and is arrested, tried, and denied. The chapter places His steady obedience to the Father beside the weakness, fear, and failure of the people closest to Him, and shows that His sacrifice is given for exactly such people.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Mark 14* opens the final movement of Mark’s Gospel. Jesus has entered Jerusalem riding a colt (*Mark 11*), cleared the temple courts of trading, and spent several days teaching in the temple while the religious leaders tried to trap Him with questions about authority, taxes, resurrection, and the greatest commandment (*Mark 11–12*). In *Mark 13* He sat on the Mount of Olives and warned His disciples that the temple would be destroyed and that hard days were coming, closing with the repeated command to “watch.” That word becomes important again in this chapter, because the disciples are about to face their own hour of testing, and they will not be ready.

The setting is the Passover season. Passover was the great annual festival remembering how God rescued Israel from slavery in Egypt, when the blood of a lamb on the doorposts meant that judgment “passed over” the household (*Exodus 12*). It was followed immediately by the seven-day Feast of Unleavened Bread, so the two names were often used together. Jerusalem’s population swelled with pilgrims, national hopes of freedom ran high, and the Roman authorities kept a nervous watch for unrest. This explains a great deal of what happens in the chapter: the leaders want Jesus dead, but they fear the crowds who admire Him, so they need a quiet arrest away from public view.

### The Plot and the Anointing at Bethany (*14:1–11*)

Mark begins by telling us that the chief priests and scribes were looking for a way to seize Jesus “*by deception and kill him*” (*v. 1*). Their hesitation was practical rather than moral: “*Not during the feast, because there might be a riot among the people*” (*v. 2*). Mark then deliberately places a story of extravagant love between two scenes of plotting, a technique he uses elsewhere to let one story interpret another.

At Bethany, a village about two miles from Jerusalem on the far slope of the Mount of Olives, Jesus is eating in the house of “*Simon the leper*” (*v. 3*), probably a man Jesus had healed and who was still known by his old condition. An unnamed woman (*John 12:3* identifies her as Mary, the sister of Martha and Lazarus) breaks open an alabaster jar of pure nard, a fragrant oil imported from the Himalayan region, and pours it over His head. Breaking the jar meant the whole amount was used at once. Some of those present calculated its value at more than three hundred denarii. Since a denarius was roughly a day’s wage for a laborer, this was close to a year’s income. Their complaint sounded righteous: the money could have been given to the poor, and giving to the poor was a recognized act of devotion at Passover.

Jesus defends her. He does not dismiss the poor; His words echo *Deuteronomy 15:11*, which assumes that God’s people will keep opening their hands to the needy. His point is that this moment is unique. He will not always be physically present with them, and the woman has done something fitting for this hour. Whether or not she fully understood it, she has “*anointed my body beforehand for the burying*” (*v. 8*). In Jesus’ own interpretation, her gift becomes preparation for His death, and He promises that wherever the gospel is preached, her act will be remembered.

The contrast that follows is sharp. Immediately after a woman gives something precious to honor Jesus, Judas Iscariot, “*one of the twelve*” (*v. 10*), goes to the chief priests to hand Jesus over, and they promise him money. Mark does not explain Judas’s motives in detail. He simply lets the reader see two responses to Jesus side by side: one pours out a treasure for Him, the other sells Him.

### Preparing and Sharing the Passover Meal (*14:12–25*)

On the day the Passover lambs were sacrificed at the temple, the disciples ask where they should prepare the meal. Jesus sends two of them into the city with unusual directions: they will meet a man carrying a jar of water (normally a woman’s task, so he would be easy to spot), follow him to a house, and find a large upper room already furnished. The details suggest prior arrangement and also Jesus’ calm control over events. He is not being swept toward the cross by accident.

During the meal, Jesus announces that one of the Twelve, someone eating with Him, will betray Him. In that culture, sharing a meal created a bond of friendship and trust, which made betrayal by a table companion especially painful (*Psalm 41:9* speaks of exactly this grief). The disciples respond with sorrow, each asking, “*Surely not I?*” (*v. 19*) Jesus says that the Son of Man goes “*as it is written about him*” (*v. 21*), meaning His death fulfills God’s purpose revealed in Scripture, yet the betrayer remains fully responsible for what he chooses to do.

Then Jesus does something that reshapes the Passover. The meal normally retold the story of the exodus, interpreting the lamb, the unleavened bread, and the bitter herbs. Jesus takes the bread, blesses it, breaks it, and says, “*Take, eat. This is my body*” (*v. 22*). He takes the cup and calls it “*my blood of the new covenant, which is poured out for many*” (*v. 24*). He is explaining His coming death in terms of Israel’s story of rescue and covenant. Just as the first Passover marked God’s deliverance from Egypt, His death will mark a new and greater deliverance. He then vows not to drink wine again until He drinks it “*anew in God’s Kingdom*” (*v. 25*), a statement that looks beyond the cross to the future feast of God’s kingdom.

### Predicting Desertion and Peter’s Confident Promise (*14:26–31*)

After singing a hymn (very likely from *Psalms 113–118*, the songs traditionally sung at Passover), they walk out to the Mount of Olives. On the way, Jesus quotes *Zechariah 13:7*: “*I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered*” (*v. 27*). All of them will stumble that night. Yet He immediately adds a promise: after He is raised, He will go ahead of them into Galilee. Even before they fail, He tells them that their failure will not be the end of the relationship.

Peter objects strongly: “*Although all will be offended, yet I will not*” (*v. 29*). Jesus answers with a precise prediction: before the rooster crows twice, Peter will deny Him three times. Peter insists even more forcefully that he would die rather than deny Him, and “*They all said the same thing*” (*v. 31*). This exchange is the key to understanding Gethsemane. The disciples are sincere. They really do intend to stay loyal. But they are confident in their own strength, and they do not yet see how frightened, tired, and vulnerable they will be within a few hours.

### Gethsemane: Agony and Prayer (*14:32–42*)

Gethsemane, a name meaning “oil press,” was an olive grove on the lower slope of the Mount of Olives. Jesus leaves most of the disciples near the entrance and takes Peter, James, and John further in, the same three who had seen His glory on the mountain of transfiguration (*Mark 9:2*). Mark uses strong words to describe His state: He “*began to be greatly troubled and distressed*” (*v. 33*). He tells them, “*My soul is exceedingly sorrowful, even to death*” (*v. 34*), language that echoes the laments of *Psalms 42–43*. He asks them to stay and keep watch.

Going a little farther, He falls to the ground and prays that, if possible, “*the hour might pass away from him*” (*v. 35*). His prayer, studied in detail below, is a cry of real anguish combined with real surrender. When He returns, He finds the disciples asleep and speaks directly to Peter, using his old name, Simon. The man who had just promised to die for Jesus could not stay awake for one hour. Jesus warns them to watch and pray so they will not fall when testing comes. This happens three times. Each time Jesus prays, and each time they sleep. Mark notes that “*they didn’t know what to answer him*” (*v. 40*). Finally Jesus says that the hour has come and the betrayer is near.

### The Arrest (*14:43–52*)

Judas arrives with an armed crowd sent by the chief priests, scribes, and elders. His prearranged signal is a kiss, the ordinary greeting a disciple might give a respected teacher. The warmth of the gesture makes the betrayal even more painful. One of those standing by draws a sword and cuts off the ear of the high priest’s servant (*John 18:10* identifies the swordsman as Peter). Jesus points out the absurdity of coming for Him with weapons as if He were a violent bandit, when He had taught openly in the temple every day. He accepts what is happening as the fulfillment of Scripture.

Then comes one of the saddest sentences in Mark: “*They all left him, and fled*” (*v. 50*). The prediction of verse 27 comes true. Mark adds a strange detail found in no other Gospel: a young man, wearing only a linen cloth, follows, is grabbed, and runs away naked. Many have suggested this young man was Mark himself, though the text does not say so. Either way, the image underlines the point: every follower runs, even at the cost of shame.

### The Trial Before the Council (*14:53–65*)

Jesus is taken to the high priest (Caiaphas, according to *Matthew 26:57*), where the chief priests, elders, and scribes have gathered. This is the Sanhedrin, the ruling council of Jewish leaders in Jerusalem. They look for testimony to justify a death sentence, but the witnesses contradict one another. Under the law of Moses, a charge required agreeing witnesses (*Deuteronomy 19:15*), so their case falls apart. Some twist Jesus’ words about the temple. Through all of it, Jesus stays silent, recalling the Servant of *Isaiah 53:7* who did not open his mouth before his accusers.

Finally the high priest asks directly: “*Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?*” (*v. 61*) (“the Blessed” was a reverent way of referring to God without saying His name). For most of Mark’s Gospel, Jesus has avoided public declarations of His identity. Now, at the moment when it will cost Him His life, He answers plainly: “*I am*” (*v. 62*). He adds that they will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power and coming with the clouds, combining *Psalm 110:1* and *Daniel 7:13*. He is claiming to be the one who will share God’s throne and judge the world, including the men now judging Him. The high priest tears his clothes, a traditional sign of grief at hearing blasphemy, and the council condemns Him. They spit on Him, blindfold Him, beat Him, and mockingly demand that He “prophesy.”

### Peter’s Denials (*14:66–72*)

Meanwhile Peter has followed at a distance into the high priest’s courtyard and is warming himself at the fire. Mark has arranged the scenes so that, while Jesus is boldly confessing the truth upstairs, Peter is denying the truth downstairs. A servant girl recognizes him as one of Jesus’ companions. Peter denies it. She tells the bystanders, and he denies it again. Then the bystanders notice that he is a Galilean (his northern accent gave him away) and press him. Peter begins to call down curses and swear an oath that he does not know “*this man of whom you speak*” (*v. 71*). He will not even say Jesus’ name.

At that moment the rooster crows a second time. Peter remembers Jesus’ words, and he breaks down and weeps. The chapter ends not with a speech but with the sound of a grown man’s tears. Yet the reader already knows from verse 28 that Jesus has promised to meet His scattered followers again in Galilee, and in *Mark 16:7* the angel will tell the women to give that message to “*his disciples and Peter*”, naming Peter specifically.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Mark 14:24* — The Blood of the New Covenant

> *“He said to them, This is my blood of the new covenant, which is poured out for many.”*
>
> — *Mark 14:24* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These words are spoken during the Passover meal, in the upper room in Jerusalem, on the last evening before Jesus’ death. He is speaking to the Twelve, including Judas, whose betrayal He has just announced. The Passover meal was full of symbolic actions, and the head of the table explained what the food meant. Jesus uses that familiar moment to explain what His own death will mean. Having said the bread is His body, He now gives them the cup of wine, and after they have all drunk from it, He interprets it.

The phrase “blood of the covenant” comes from *Exodus 24:8*. When God made His covenant with Israel at Mount Sinai, Moses sprinkled the blood of sacrifices on the people and said, “*Look, this is the blood of the covenant*” (*Exodus 24:8*). A covenant was a binding relationship established by solemn promises, and in the ancient world it was often sealed with a sacrifice. By using this language, Jesus is saying that His death will establish a covenant relationship between God and His people. The word “new” points to *Jeremiah 31:31–34*, where God promised a new covenant in which He would write His law on His people’s hearts and “*remember their sin no more*” (*Jeremiah 31:34*).

The phrase “*poured out for many*” (*v. 24*) tells the disciples that His death is not a tragic accident but a giving of His life on behalf of others. Earlier, Jesus had said that He came “*to give his life as a ransom for many*” (*Mark 10:45*), and both statements echo *Isaiah 53*, where the Servant of the Lord “*bore the sins of many*” (*Isaiah 53:12*). In Hebrew idiom, “many” stresses the great number of people who benefit, not a limited group; it contrasts the one who dies with the multitude for whom He dies.

The disciples would have understood that Jesus was speaking about His death, because He had told them three times on the road to Jerusalem that He would be killed and would rise (*Mark 8:31*; *9:31*; *10:33–34*). What they could not yet grasp was how His death could be the center of God’s plan. Only after the resurrection would they begin to see that the cross was the sacrifice that opened the new covenant.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse explains why Christians understand the death of Jesus as the foundation of their relationship with God. The new covenant promised forgiveness and a changed heart, and Jesus says that His blood is what brings that covenant into being. The Letter to the Hebrews develops this at length, describing Jesus as both the priest and the sacrifice of a better covenant (*Hebrews 8–9*). Salvation, in this light, is not first of all our promise to God, but God’s promise to us, sealed at the cost of His Son’s life.

It is significant that Jesus gives this cup to men who are about to fail Him. Judas will betray Him, Peter will deny Him, and all of them will run. Yet the covenant meal is shared with all of them before any of that happens. The grace of the new covenant was not earned by the disciples’ faithfulness; it was offered in full knowledge of their weakness.

Christians have understood the Lord’s Supper in different ways. Roman Catholic and Orthodox Christians believe Christ is truly and substantially present in the bread and wine; Lutherans also affirm a real presence; many Reformed believers speak of a spiritual presence received by faith; and many other Protestants emphasize the meal as a memorial and proclamation of His death (*1 Corinthians 11:26*). All agree on what the passage itself makes clear: Jesus interpreted His death as a sacrifice that establishes the new covenant, and He gave His followers a meal to keep that at the center of their life together.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse calls believers to build their confidence before God on what Jesus has done rather than on how well they have performed. When guilt or failure presses in, the new covenant offers solid ground: forgiveness was secured by the giving of His life, not by our ability to make up for what we have done wrong. That is a reason to confess sin honestly instead of hiding it, because the basis of acceptance is already settled.

It also means taking the Lord’s Supper seriously as more than a routine. When a church shares the bread and cup, it is remembering a covenant sealed by blood and declaring that it belongs to Christ. Coming to that table thoughtfully, with honest repentance and gratitude, keeps the cross from becoming a distant idea.

Finally, a covenant creates a people, not only individuals. The cup was shared. Those who belong to Christ are bound to one another through Him, which calls for patience, forgiveness, and practical care within the church, especially toward those who have failed and returned.

### *Mark 14:36* — “*Not What I Desire, but What You Desire*” (*v. 36*)

> *“He said, ‘Abba, Father, all things are possible to you. Please remove this cup from me. However, not what I desire, but what you desire.’”*
>
> — *Mark 14:36* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus speaks these words in Gethsemane, the olive grove at the foot of the Mount of Olives, only a short time before Judas arrives with the armed crowd. He has just told Peter, James, and John that His soul is overwhelmed with sorrow “*even to death*” (*v. 34*), and He has gone a little farther on to pray alone, falling to the ground. Mark first summarizes the prayer (He asked that, if possible, the hour might pass from Him) and then gives His actual words. This is one of the most personal glimpses into Jesus’ inner life anywhere in the Gospels.

He addresses God as “*Abba, Father*” (*v. 36*). “Abba” is the Aramaic word a child would use for his father, expressing closeness and trust. Mark keeps the original Aramaic word because it was so striking that the early church remembered it (Paul uses it in *Romans 8:15* and *Galatians 4:6* to describe the believer’s relationship with God). Jesus then affirms, “*all things are possible to you*” (*v. 36*), and asks, “*Please remove this cup from me*” (*v. 36*).

“The cup” is a familiar image from the Old Testament prophets, where it often stands for the cup of God’s judgment against sin (for example, *Isaiah 51:17* and *Jeremiah 25:15*). Earlier, Jesus had asked James and John whether they could “*drink the cup that I drink*” (*Mark 10:38*), referring to His approaching suffering. In Gethsemane, the cup is the whole ordeal ahead: betrayal, abandonment, mockery, torture, crucifixion, and the bearing of sin that the cross involves. Jesus’ request is genuine. He is not acting out a script. He feels the horror of what is coming and asks the Father, if there is any other way, to take it from Him.

Then comes the turning point of the prayer: “*However, not what I desire, but what you desire*” (*v. 36*). Jesus places His own desire honestly before the Father and then submits it to the Father’s will. He does not pretend the suffering is easy, and He does not pretend He wants it. He chooses to trust and obey the Father. Mark tells us He prayed “*saying the same words*” (*v. 39*) a second time, and *Matthew 26:42–44* shows Him praying a third time. When He rises from prayer, He goes out to meet the arresting crowd without running, resisting, or calling for rescue.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This prayer reveals both the true humanity of Jesus and the depth of His obedience. Christians confess that Jesus is fully God and fully human, and Gethsemane shows the human side vividly: He was distressed, He was sorrowful, and He had a will that shrank from suffering. *Hebrews 5:7–8* seems to look back on this scene when it describes Jesus offering up prayers “*with strong crying and tears*” (*Hebrews 5:7*) and learning obedience through what He suffered. His obedience was not effortless; it was chosen in anguish.

The prayer also shows what faithful prayer looks like. Jesus prays with total honesty and total trust. He does not hide His desire, and He does not demand that God fulfill it. The phrase “all things are possible to you” is not a formula that forces God’s hand; it is a confession of God’s power, joined with a willingness to accept God’s wisdom when God’s answer is different from our request. The Father did not remove the cup. Jesus’ prayer was answered not by escape but by strength to go forward, and through His suffering came the salvation of the world.

It is important to read this verse carefully. Jesus’ submission is to a specific purpose of the Father: to give His life for sinners. It does not teach that whatever painful thing happens to a person must be accepted as God’s will. Scripture repeatedly condemns injustice and cruelty, and in this very scene the people arresting and condemning Jesus are doing wrong, even as God works through it. Surrendering to God’s will never means pretending wrongdoing is good, accepting abuse, or refusing protection, medical care, or help that God provides through others.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Jesus’ prayer gives believers permission to be honest with God. There is no need to hide fear, grief, or the strong wish that a painful situation would go away. Bringing those desires to God plainly, even repeatedly as Jesus did, is not a lack of faith. Faith speaks honestly and then entrusts the outcome to the Father.

The prayer also teaches a deeper surrender than simply asking for what we want. “Not what I desire, but what you desire” is a sentence that can shape daily decisions: when we face a choice between what is comfortable and what is right, when obedience will cost something, or when God’s answer is not the one we hoped for. Saying it sincerely means holding plans and preferences with an open hand and committing ourselves to do what God shows to be right, even when it is costly.

At the same time, seeking God’s will includes using the wisdom and resources He gives. It is consistent with this prayer to seek counsel, see a doctor, report wrongdoing, leave a dangerous situation, or ask for help. Jesus’ surrender was not passivity; it was active obedience to a clear calling. For believers, surrender means trusting God enough to do what is right in the situation, not resigning ourselves to harm that God’s Word calls us to resist.

### *Mark 14:38* — Watch and Pray: Good Intentions Under Pressure

> *“Watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.”*
>
> — *Mark 14:38* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

To understand this verse, it helps to remember what has just happened. Only an hour or two earlier, Jesus warned the disciples that all of them would fall away that night. Peter insisted that he would never deny Jesus, even if he had to die, and the others said the same. Then in Gethsemane, Jesus told Peter, James, and John that He was deeply distressed and asked them to stay and keep watch while He prayed. When He returned, He found them asleep. He spoke directly to Peter: “*Simon, are you sleeping? Couldn’t you watch one hour?*” (*v. 37*) Then He gave the warning in this verse.

“Watch” means to stay awake and alert, but it is also the word Jesus used repeatedly in *Mark 13* when He told His disciples to be spiritually ready. “Temptation” here means a time of testing, a moment of pressure in which a person may be drawn to give up faithfulness to God. Jesus knows exactly what test is coming: within the hour, the arresting crowd will arrive, and the disciples will have to decide whether to stand with Him or save themselves. He tells them to watch and pray so that they will not “enter into” that temptation, meaning not be overcome by it when it arrives.

Then Jesus explains why prayer is necessary: “*The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak*” (*v. 38*). “Spirit” here refers to the disciples’ inner desire and intention. They really are willing; their promises were sincere. “Flesh” refers to their human weakness, their physical exhaustion, their fear, and their natural instinct to protect themselves. Jesus is not merely scolding them for being tired late at night. He is describing the gap between what they sincerely want to do and the strength they will actually need when the pressure comes.

The rest of the chapter proves Jesus right. The disciples sleep a second and third time. When the crowd arrives, one of them grabs a sword, and then they all flee. Peter follows at a distance, but when a servant girl questions him, he denies even knowing Jesus, and finally swears that he does not know “*this man of whom you speak*” (*v. 71*). The man who had been most confident in his loyalty fails most visibly. Meanwhile Jesus, who spent that hour in prayer, faces arrest, false accusations, and beatings without wavering.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse holds together two truths: human beings can sincerely desire to be faithful, and sincere desire is not enough by itself. Peter’s failure did not come from a lack of love for Jesus. It came from confidence in his own strength and from not taking seriously his need for God’s help. Scripture warns about this repeatedly; Paul writes, “*let him who thinks he stands be careful that he doesn’t fall*” (*1 Corinthians 10:12*). Recognizing our weakness is not pessimism; it is the beginning of wisdom.

Prayer, in this passage, is the way the willing spirit leans on God’s strength. Jesus Himself models it. Facing the hardest test of His life, He does not rely on His own resolve; He spends the hour in honest prayer to the Father, and He emerges ready. This does not mean that prayer automatically guarantees that we will never stumble, or that prayer works like a technique. It means that prayer is how dependent people stay connected to the One who can hold them up, and that those who ignore their need for God are especially exposed when trouble comes.

The story also carries great hope. Jesus knew the disciples would fail, and He had already promised to meet them in Galilee after His resurrection (v. 28). Peter wept bitterly, but his story did not end in that courtyard. He was restored (*John 21:15–19*) and later stood boldly before the same council that condemned Jesus (*Acts 4*). The flesh is weak, but Christ’s grace is stronger than our failures.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse calls believers to be honest about their vulnerabilities. Most people who fall into serious wrongdoing did not plan to; they meant well but were caught unprepared by fatigue, fear, pressure, or desire. Knowing the situations in which we are most likely to give in, whether exhaustion, loneliness, anger, peer pressure, or fear of what others think, allows us to pray specifically about them and to prepare wisely rather than assume we will be fine.

“Watch and pray” also means preparing before the test arrives, not only during it. Jesus prayed in the garden before the soldiers came. Believers who know that a difficult conversation, a major decision, a season of temptation, or a time of suffering is approaching can bring it to God ahead of time, ask for strength and wisdom, and decide in advance what faithfulness will look like. Practical steps belong with prayer: rest when the body needs it, seek the support of trusted fellow believers, and avoid placing ourselves in situations where we know we are weak.

Finally, this verse warns against relying on good intentions alone. Promises like Peter’s (“I will never”) are easy to make when life is calm. Real faithfulness grows from humble dependence on God. When we do fail, as Peter did, the right response is not despair but honest repentance and a return to Jesus, who already knew our weakness and still calls us back.

### *Mark 14:72* — Peter Remembers and Weeps

> *“The rooster crowed the second time. Peter remembered the words that Jesus said to him, ‘Before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times.’ When he thought about that, he wept.”*
>
> — *Mark 14:72* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse closes the chapter at the lowest point of Peter’s life. Peter had followed Jesus at a distance after the arrest and slipped into the courtyard of the high priest’s house, where he sat with the guards by the fire. While Jesus was inside being falsely accused and openly confessing that He is the Christ, Peter was outside being questioned by a servant girl and the bystanders. Three times he denied any connection with Jesus, and the third time he began “*to curse and to swear*” (*v. 71*), meaning he called down curses on himself if he was lying and swore an oath that he did not know Jesus.

Immediately the rooster crowed for the second time. Mark alone records that the rooster crowed twice, matching exactly what Jesus had said in verse 30. Hearing it, Peter remembered Jesus’ words. The prediction he had argued against so confidently had come true in every detail, and he could no longer pretend otherwise.

The final phrase is simple: “*When he thought about that, he wept*” (*v. 72*). Mark does not describe a formal confession or an immediate restoration. He shows us a man who suddenly sees the truth about himself. The weeping is the grief of someone who loved Jesus and failed Him, and who realizes that Jesus knew it would happen and loved him anyway.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Peter’s tears show the difference between worldly sorrow and godly sorrow. Judas also came to regret what he had done (*Matthew 27:3–5*), but his regret led to despair. Peter’s grief, painful as it was, eventually led him back to Jesus. Paul later describes this distinction: “*godly sorrow produces repentance leading to salvation*” (*2 Corinthians 7:10*), while worldly sorrow leads to death. The difference is not the depth of the failure but whether the sorrowing person turns toward the Lord.

It is striking that this story is recorded at all. Early Christian tradition connects Mark’s Gospel with Peter’s preaching, which would mean that Peter himself told this story about his worst moment. The church did not hide the failures of its leaders. The gospel is not a story of strong people who never fell, but of a faithful Savior who rescues and restores weak people.

The contrast between Jesus and Peter in this chapter is intentional. Jesus prayed and stood firm; Peter slept and fell. Jesus confessed the truth at the cost of His life; Peter denied it to save his own. Yet Jesus’ faithfulness was not only an example for Peter to copy. It was the faithfulness by which Peter would be saved. The one who stood firm went to the cross for the one who did not.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to let the truth about their failures lead them to repentance rather than to hiding or despair. When the “rooster crows” in our own lives, when we suddenly see that we have betrayed what we believe, it hurts. That pain can be the beginning of healing if it brings us honestly back to God.

It also calls for humility in how we view others who fail. The church is made up of people like Peter. Remembering that the most prominent apostle once denied Jesus with curses should make believers slower to write people off and quicker to hope for their restoration, while still taking wrongdoing seriously and allowing real repentance to bear fruit over time.

Finally, Peter’s story is a reminder that a moment of failure does not have to define the rest of a life. Jesus’ promise to go before His disciples to Galilee was given before they failed. Believers who have stumbled can return to Christ, accept His forgiveness, make right what can be made right, and continue to follow Him.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Mark 14* places a series of human responses beside Jesus’ steady obedience: a woman’s lavish devotion, Judas’s calculated betrayal, the disciples’ sincere but fragile promises, the council’s injustice, and Peter’s denial. Seeing all of them together helps believers recognize themselves honestly. Most of us are not Judas, but many of us are much more like the sleeping disciples than we want to admit. We love Jesus and mean well, yet we are easily overwhelmed by fatigue, fear, or the desire to protect ourselves. The chapter calls for humility rather than self-confidence, and for prayerful dependence rather than bold promises.

The anointing at Bethany shows that love for Jesus is sometimes extravagant and misunderstood. The woman’s gift seemed wasteful to practical observers, yet Jesus called it beautiful. Generosity to the poor remains important, and Jesus never dismissed it; but devotion to Him is the root from which all other good works grow. Believers can ask God to make their love for Christ wholehearted, and they can be slow to criticize others whose devotion takes a form they do not understand.

Gethsemane teaches how to face hard things. Jesus brought His fear honestly to the Father, prayed more than once, accepted the Father’s will, and then acted with courage. That pattern applies to illness, grief, difficult obedience, hard conversations, and major decisions. It also guards against two errors: pretending we are not afraid, and assuming that God’s will requires us to accept whatever harm comes our way. Jesus’ submission was purposeful obedience to His saving mission, not passivity in the face of wrongdoing.

The trial scene shows the cost of integrity. Jesus refused to answer false accusations, but when asked directly who He was, He told the truth, knowing it would lead to His death. Believers may face pressure, sometimes small and sometimes serious, to stay quiet about their faith or to bend the truth to protect themselves. Peter’s denials show how quickly fear can lead to dishonesty when we are unprepared. Prayer, honest self-knowledge, and the support of fellow believers help build the courage to remain truthful when it is costly.

Above all, the chapter points to grace. Jesus shared the covenant cup with the very disciples who would abandon Him, and He promised to meet them again before they failed. Whatever our failures, the blood of the new covenant was poured out for people like us. That is the reason to return to Him after we fall, to extend patient grace to others who fail, and to keep following Him with greater humility than before.

## Chapter Prayer

Father, thank You for the love of Jesus, who knew that His friends would fail Him and still gave them the bread and the cup and poured out His life for them. Thank You that the new covenant rests on His faithfulness and not on my strength. Make my devotion to Him wholehearted, like the woman who broke her jar of ointment, and keep me from the hardness that calculates what love costs.

When I face what I fear, teach me to pray as Jesus prayed in Gethsemane: honestly, without hiding my desires, and with a heart willing to say, “Not what I desire, but what You desire.” Give me wisdom to tell the difference between faithful obedience and passively accepting what is wrong. Show me where I am weak, and help me to watch and pray instead of trusting my own good intentions. When I fail, as Peter did, let my sorrow lead me back to You and not into despair. Strengthen me to speak the truth about Jesus even when it is costly. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Mark · Chapter 15 of 16

# Mark — Chapter 15

Chapter Theme: The King Who Would Not Save Himself

[Read Mark 15 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/MRK15.htm)

Main Teaching

Handed over to Pilate, Jesus stands silent while a crowd chooses the rebel Barabbas, and Pilate, wanting to please the crowd, sends Jesus to be flogged and crucified. Soldiers mock Him as king, a passerby named Simon carries His cross, and leaders taunt Him to save Himself. After crying out the words of *Psalm 22*, Jesus dies; the temple curtain tears and a Roman centurion confesses Him as the Son of God. Joseph of Arimathea boldly asks for His body and buries Him while faithful women watch.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Mark 15* follows the night of Jesus’ arrest and trial before the Jewish council, during which Peter denied Him three times (*Mark 14*). Early in the morning, the council finalized its decision. The Jewish leaders could condemn Jesus under their law, but Roman authority reserved the power of execution, so they needed Pilate’s verdict. They brought Jesus to him with a charge that would matter to Rome: claiming to be “King of the Jews,” which sounded like rebellion against Caesar.

Mark tells the story of the crucifixion with restraint and power. He does not dwell on physical details, which his readers knew all too well. Instead, he highlights the irony that runs through the chapter: Jesus is mocked as a king, yet He truly is the King; He is taunted to save Himself, but He stays on the cross precisely to save others; and the one who finally recognizes Him is not a disciple or a religious leader but the Roman officer in charge of His execution. (Matthew’s parallel account is studied at *Matthew 27*, including the cry of abandonment, the torn curtain, and the centurion’s confession.)

### Jesus Before Pilate (*15:1–15*)

Very early in the morning, the chief priests, elders, scribes, and the whole council reached their decision. They bound Jesus, led Him away, and handed Him over to Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor of Judea from A.D. 26 to 36. Pilate usually lived in Caesarea on the coast but came to Jerusalem during festivals to maintain order.

Pilate asked, “*Are you the King of the Jews?*” (*v. 2*) Jesus answered, “*So you say*” (*v. 2*), affirming the title but suggesting that Pilate did not understand what kind of king He was. The chief priests accused Him of many things. Pilate asked whether He would answer, but Jesus made no further reply, and Pilate was amazed. His silence fulfilled *Isaiah 53:7*, which describes the Servant as silent before His accusers like a lamb led to slaughter.

At the festival, Pilate customarily released a prisoner chosen by the crowd. A man named Barabbas was in prison with rebels who had committed murder during an uprising. His name means “son of the father,” an irony that early Christians noticed: the guilty “son of the father” was released, while the innocent Son of the Father was condemned.

The crowd came and asked Pilate to follow his custom. Pilate asked whether they wanted him to release “the King of the Jews,” because he knew the chief priests had handed Jesus over out of envy. But the chief priests stirred up the crowd to ask for Barabbas. When Pilate asked what to do with Jesus, they shouted, “*Crucify him!*” (*v. 13*) Pilate asked what evil He had done, but they shouted louder. Pilate, “*wishing to please the multitude*” (*v. 15*), released Barabbas, had Jesus flogged, and handed Him over to be crucified. This verse is studied below.

Roman flogging was brutal. The victim was stripped and beaten with a whip of leather straps embedded with pieces of bone or metal. It often tore flesh to the bone and sometimes killed the prisoner before crucifixion.

### The Soldiers’ Mockery (*15:16–20*)

The soldiers led Jesus into the courtyard of the palace, the Praetorium, and called together the whole cohort, a unit that could include several hundred men. They dressed Him in purple, the color of royalty, twisted together a crown of thorns, and put it on Him. They saluted Him, “Hail, King of the Jews!” struck His head with a reed, spat on Him, and knelt before Him in mock homage. Then they put His own clothes back on Him and led Him out to crucify Him.

The soldiers meant all of this as a cruel joke. But Mark’s readers know that their words were true. Jesus is the King, and one day every knee will bow before Him in genuine worship (*Philippians 2:10*).

### Simon of Cyrene and the Crucifixion (*15:21–32*)

On the way, the soldiers forced a man passing by, Simon of Cyrene, to carry Jesus’ cross. Cyrene was a city in North Africa with a significant Jewish population. Simon may have been a pilgrim in Jerusalem for Passover, “*coming from the country*” (*v. 21*). Roman soldiers had the right to compel civilians to carry loads. Jesus, weakened by the flogging, was apparently unable to carry the crossbeam the whole way.

Mark adds that Simon was “*the father of Alexander and Rufus*” (*v. 21*). This detail suggests that Mark’s readers knew Simon’s sons, who may have become members of the early church. Paul greets a Rufus in Rome (*Romans 16:13*), possibly the same person. If so, Simon’s unwilling encounter with Jesus’ cross may have led to his family’s faith. Simon became a picture of discipleship: literally taking up the cross and following Jesus (*Mark 8:34*).

They brought Jesus to Golgotha, meaning “Place of a Skull,” likely a rocky hill outside the city walls. They offered Him wine mixed with myrrh, which may have been intended to dull the pain, but He did not take it. He chose to face His suffering with full awareness.

They crucified Him and divided His clothes by casting lots, fulfilling *Psalm 22:18*. Mark notes, “*It was the third hour when they crucified him*” (*v. 25*), about nine in the morning. The written charge above Him read, “*THE KING OF THE JEWS*” (*v. 26*). Two robbers (probably rebels, like Barabbas’s companions) were crucified with Him, one on His right and one on His left. (Verse 28, quoting *Isaiah 53:12*, “He was counted with transgressors,” is not found in many early manuscripts of Mark, though *Luke 22:37* records Jesus applying this verse to Himself.)

People passing by insulted Him, shaking their heads, and taunting Him with His own words about destroying and rebuilding the temple: “*save yourself, and come down from the cross!*” (*v. 30*) The chief priests and scribes also mocked Him among themselves: “*He saved others. He can’t save himself*” (*v. 31*). This verse is studied below. They added that if He came down from the cross, they would see and believe. Even the men crucified with Him insulted Him.

### The Death of Jesus (*15:33–41*)

At noon, darkness covered the whole land until three in the afternoon. At three o’clock, Jesus cried out with a loud voice, “*Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani?*” (*v. 34*), which means, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” These are the opening words of *Psalm 22*, spoken in Aramaic. (This cry is studied in depth at *Matthew 27:46*.) Some bystanders thought He was calling Elijah. One ran, filled a sponge with sour wine, put it on a reed, and offered it to Him, saying they should wait to see if Elijah would come to take Him down.

Then Jesus let out a loud cry and breathed His last. At that moment, the curtain of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom. Mark uses the same Greek verb for tearing that he used at Jesus’ baptism, when Jesus saw the heavens parting (*Mark 1:10*). At the beginning and end of Jesus’ ministry, a barrier between God and humanity is ripped apart. (The torn curtain is studied at *Matthew 27:51*.)

The centurion standing in front of Jesus saw how He died and said, “*Truly this man was the Son of God!*” (*v. 39*) Mark’s Gospel began by announcing “Jesus Christ, the Son of God” (*1:1*). The Father declared Him His Son at His baptism and transfiguration. Demons recognized Him as God’s Son. But the first human being in Mark’s Gospel to confess Him as the Son of God is a Gentile soldier watching Him die. Mark’s message is clear: Jesus is most fully revealed as the Son of God on the cross.

Some women were watching from a distance, including Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James the younger and Joses, and Salome. These women had followed Jesus in Galilee and cared for His needs, and many other women had come up with Him to Jerusalem. The male disciples had fled, but the women remained. They would also witness His burial and become the first witnesses of His resurrection.

### The Burial (*15:42–47*)

It was the day of Preparation, the day before the Sabbath. The Sabbath began at sunset on Friday, and Jewish law required that bodies not remain on crosses overnight (*Deuteronomy 21:22–23*), especially on the Sabbath. Joseph of Arimathea, a prominent member of the council who was waiting for the kingdom of God, went boldly to Pilate and asked for Jesus’ body. This is studied below.

Pilate was surprised that Jesus was already dead, since crucified men often lingered for days. He summoned the centurion to confirm it. When the centurion confirmed that Jesus was dead, Pilate gave the body to Joseph. This official confirmation is important: Jesus truly died. Joseph bought linen cloth, took the body down, wrapped it, and placed it in a tomb cut out of rock. He rolled a stone against the entrance. Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses saw where He was laid.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Mark 15:15* — Wishing to Please the Crowd

> *“Pilate, wishing to please the multitude, released Barabbas to them, and handed over Jesus, when he had flogged him, to be crucified.”*
>
> — *Mark 15:15* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse records the moment Pilate condemned Jesus. Pilate had questioned Jesus and was amazed at His silence. He recognized that the chief priests had handed Jesus over “*for envy*” (*v. 10*). He asked the crowd whether they wanted him to release “the King of the Jews,” apparently hoping they would choose Jesus. But the chief priests stirred up the crowd to demand Barabbas, a rebel involved in a murderous uprising. When Pilate asked what crime Jesus had committed, the crowd only shouted louder, “Crucify him!”

Mark then gives the reason for Pilate’s decision: “*Pilate, wishing to please the multitude*” (*v. 15*). Pilate was not convinced Jesus was guilty. He knew the charges came from envy. But he wanted to satisfy the crowd. Roman governors were responsible for keeping peace in their provinces, and a riot during Passover, with Jerusalem crowded with pilgrims, could have threatened his position. Historical sources tell us that Pilate had already offended the Jewish population several times and had been reported to the emperor. He likely feared further trouble.

So Pilate “*released Barabbas to them*” (*v. 15*), a man guilty of violent rebellion. Then he had Jesus flogged and “*handed over Jesus, when he had flogged him, to be crucified*” (*v. 15*). The innocent man was condemned, and the guilty man was released.

The phrase “handed over” appears repeatedly in Mark’s passion narrative. Judas handed Jesus over to the chief priests (*14:10*), the chief priests handed Him over to Pilate (*15:1*), and Pilate handed Him over to be crucified (*15:15*). Each person passed responsibility to the next. Yet Jesus had predicted this very sequence (*10:33*), showing that it was also part of God’s plan.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows the danger of fearing people more than God. Pilate had the authority and the knowledge to release Jesus, but he chose to please the crowd. His decision reveals how the desire for approval, safety, or position can lead people to do what they know is wrong. *Proverbs 29:25* warns, “*The fear of man proves to be a snare, but whoever puts his trust in the LORD is kept safe*” (*Proverbs 29:25*).

The exchange of Barabbas for Jesus also carries a deep meaning. Barabbas, guilty of rebellion and murder, went free because Jesus took his place. Christians have long seen in this a picture of the gospel: Jesus, the innocent one, was condemned so that the guilty could go free. Peter later reminded the people of Jerusalem that they had “*denied the Holy and Righteous One and asked for a murderer to be granted to you*” (*Acts 3:14*), yet he called them to repentance and forgiveness.

Finally, the verse shows that human responsibility and God’s plan work together. Pilate, the chief priests, and the crowd were responsible for their choices, yet God was working through these events to accomplish salvation (*Acts 2:23*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse calls believers to examine whether they are ruled by the desire to please others. Many people make decisions based on what will keep others happy, avoid conflict, or protect their reputation, even when they know it is wrong. Believers can ask God for the courage to do what is right, trusting Him with the consequences.

It also challenges those in positions of authority. Leaders in families, workplaces, churches, and communities often face pressure to make popular decisions rather than just ones. Pilate’s example shows the cost of choosing popularity over justice. Believers in leadership can seek to protect the innocent and act with integrity.

Finally, this verse invites believers to see themselves in Barabbas. Everyone is guilty before God, and Jesus took the place of the guilty. This should lead to gratitude and humility, and to a willingness to extend grace to others, since all have been freed by the same Savior.

### *Mark 15:31* — “*He Saved Others; He Can't Save Himself*” (*v. 31*)

> *“Likewise, also the chief priests mocking among themselves with the scribes said, He saved others. He can’t save himself.”*
>
> — *Mark 15:31* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse records the mockery of the chief priests and scribes as Jesus hung on the cross. Throughout the crucifixion, Jesus was insulted from every side. People passing by shook their heads and taunted Him to save Himself and come down from the cross. The religious leaders joined in, speaking “*among themselves*” (*v. 31*), mocking Him to one another.

They said, “*He saved others. He can’t save himself*” (*v. 31*). The word “saved” can mean rescued, healed, or delivered. The leaders admitted, perhaps sarcastically, that Jesus had saved others. Throughout Mark’s Gospel, Jesus had healed the sick, cast out demons, and raised the dead. The word “save” was often used for these healings (*Mark 5:34*; *10:52*). Now, the leaders said, He could not save Himself.

They continued, “*Let the Christ, the King of Israel, now come down from the cross, that we may see and believe him*” (*v. 32*). They used His titles mockingly. They claimed that if He performed one more miracle, coming down from the cross, they would believe. But they had already seen many miracles and had refused to believe.

The tragic irony is that their mockery spoke a profound truth. Jesus could have saved Himself. He said in Gethsemane that the Father could send legions of angels (*Matthew 26:53*). But if He saved Himself, He could not save others. He stayed on the cross precisely because He was saving others. His refusal to come down was not weakness but love.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals the heart of the gospel. Jesus came “*to give his life as a ransom for many*” (*Mark 10:45*). Saving others required Him to give up His own life. If He had come down from the cross, there would have been no sacrifice for sin, no ransom, and no salvation.

It also shows the difference between human and divine power. The leaders thought that power meant self-preservation and spectacular displays. Jesus revealed that God’s power is shown in self-giving love. Paul writes that the message of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to those being saved, it is the power of God (*1 Corinthians 1:18*).

Finally, the demand “*now come down from the cross, that we may see and believe him*” (*v. 32*) echoes Satan’s temptation in the wilderness and Peter’s rebuke at Caesarea Philippi. The temptation to avoid the cross followed Jesus to the very end. Each time, He chose the Father’s will.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to deep gratitude. Jesus could have saved Himself, but He chose to stay on the cross to save them. Every believer’s salvation depended on His refusal to come down. Remembering this can transform how believers view their own worth and God’s love.

It also calls believers to follow Jesus’ example of self-giving love. In small and large ways, loving others often requires giving up self-protection, comfort, or advantage. Parents sacrifice for children, friends give time for one another, and believers serve those in need. Jesus’ example shows that true love is willing to lose in order to help others.

Finally, this verse challenges the demand for proof on our own terms. The leaders said they would believe if Jesus came down from the cross. Many people today say they would believe if God did something spectacular for them. But faith rests on what God has already done, especially in the cross and resurrection of Jesus.

### *Mark 15:43* — Joseph’s Bold Request

> *“Joseph of Arimathaea, a prominent council member who also himself was looking for God’s Kingdom, came. He boldly went in to Pilate, and asked for Jesus’ body.”*
>
> — *Mark 15:43* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse introduces Joseph of Arimathea, who appears in all four Gospels only at Jesus’ burial. Jesus had died on the cross around three in the afternoon. It was Friday, the day of Preparation before the Sabbath. The Sabbath would begin at sunset, and Jewish law required that executed bodies be buried before nightfall (*Deuteronomy 21:22–23*). Without intervention, Jesus’ body might have been left on the cross or thrown into a common grave, as often happened with crucified criminals.

Mark describes Joseph in three ways. First, he was from “*Arimathaea*” (*v. 43*), a town in Judea. Second, he was “*a prominent council member*” (*v. 43*), a respected member of the Sanhedrin, the council that had just condemned Jesus. Luke tells us that he had not agreed with their decision (*Luke 23:51*). Third, he “*also himself was looking for God’s Kingdom*” (*v. 43*), meaning he was waiting expectantly for God to establish His reign. John tells us he was a secret disciple of Jesus because he feared the Jewish leaders (*John 19:38*).

Then Mark says, “*He boldly went in to Pilate, and asked for Jesus’ body*” (*v. 43*). The word “boldly” (literally “having dared”) shows that this was a risky act. Approaching the Roman governor to request the body of a man executed for treason could raise suspicion that Joseph was a sympathizer. Identifying with Jesus could also cost him his standing among the council members who had just condemned Him. Touching a corpse would make him ritually unclean during Passover. Yet Joseph acted.

Pilate, surprised that Jesus had died so quickly, confirmed His death with the centurion and then gave the body to Joseph. Joseph bought linen, took the body down, wrapped it, and laid it in a tomb cut from rock.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that Jesus’ death moved a secret disciple to public courage. While Jesus was alive, Joseph had kept his faith hidden. But after the crucifixion, when the disciples had fled and it seemed that Jesus’ mission had failed, Joseph stepped forward. The cross, which scattered many followers, drew him into the open.

It also shows God’s care for His Son even in death. *Isaiah 53:9* says the Servant would be “*with a rich man in his death*” (*Isaiah 53:9*). Through Joseph, Jesus received an honorable burial in a new tomb rather than a criminal’s grave. The details of the burial also confirm that Jesus truly died, which is essential for the reality of His resurrection.

Finally, Joseph is described as someone “looking for God’s kingdom.” His action of love came from hope, even when that hope seemed shattered. He did not know that in three days Jesus would rise, but he honored Him anyway.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers who have kept their faith hidden to step forward. Many people believe in Jesus but are afraid to identify with Him publicly because of what family, friends, or colleagues might think. Joseph’s example shows that it is never too late to take a stand for Christ.

It also shows that faithfulness sometimes means acting when others have given up. When the disciples had scattered, Joseph and the women remained. Believers can show faithfulness in difficult times, serving and honoring Christ even when circumstances seem hopeless.

Finally, Joseph’s example invites believers to use their resources and position for Christ. Joseph used his influence to approach Pilate and his wealth to provide a tomb. Believers can ask how their own resources, connections, and abilities can be used to honor Jesus and serve others.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Mark 15* confronts readers with the cross of Jesus and invites them to consider their response. The chapter shows many responses: the leaders’ envy, Pilate’s cowardice, the crowd’s manipulation, the soldiers’ mockery, the bystanders’ scorn, the centurion’s confession, the women’s faithful presence, and Joseph’s bold love. Each reader can ask where they stand.

Pilate’s decision warns against letting the desire to please others override what is right. Believers face many pressures to go along with the crowd. The fear of people can lead to injustice and compromise. Believers can choose to fear God rather than people, trusting Him with the consequences of doing right.

The exchange of Barabbas and the mocking cry, “*He saved others. He can’t save himself*” (*v. 31*), reveal the heart of the gospel. Jesus took the place of the guilty and refused to save Himself so that He could save others. Believers can respond with gratitude, humility, and a willingness to love others in self-giving ways.

The centurion’s confession shows that the cross is where Jesus is most clearly revealed as the Son of God. Believers can return again and again to the cross to understand God’s love and Jesus’ identity. Finally, the women and Joseph show faithfulness when others had fled. Simon of Cyrene, who carried the cross, may have become a believer with his family. Believers can follow these examples: staying near Jesus in hard times, taking up their cross, and stepping out publicly in love for Him.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, You stood silent before Your accusers, were rejected in favor of a guilty man, and were mocked as a king. You could have saved Yourself, but You stayed on the cross to save me. I thank You with all my heart. Like Barabbas, I am guilty, and You took my place.

Keep me from Pilate’s fear of the crowd, and give me courage to do what is right even when it is unpopular. Help me to take up my cross and follow You, as Simon carried Yours. Like the centurion, I confess that You are truly the Son of God. Give me the faithfulness of the women who stayed near You and the boldness of Joseph, who stepped forward to honor You. Help me to live in grateful love for the King who would not save Himself. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
