Mark · Chapter 16 of 16

# Mark — Chapter 16

Chapter Theme: He Has Risen: Good News for Frightened Followers

[Read Mark 16 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/MRK16.htm)

Main Teaching

At dawn on the first day of the week, three women come to anoint Jesus’ body and find the stone rolled away and a messenger announcing that He has risen. They are told to tell the disciples “and Peter” that Jesus is going ahead of them to Galilee, but they flee in fear and astonishment. The longer ending, found in many manuscripts, records appearances of the risen Jesus, the disciples’ slowness to believe, His commission to preach the good news to all creation, and His ascension.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Mark 16* is the climax of Mark’s Gospel. Jesus had been crucified on Friday and buried before sunset in a tomb belonging to Joseph of Arimathea (*Mark 15:42–47*). Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses had watched where He was laid. The Sabbath followed, from sunset Friday to sunset Saturday, a day of rest when no work could be done.

Throughout Mark’s Gospel, Jesus had predicted that He would be killed and would rise on the third day (*8:31*; *9:31*; *10:34*). The disciples had not understood. Now the prediction is fulfilled.

### A Note on the Ending of Mark

Before looking at the chapter, it is important to know that the ending of Mark is one of the best-known questions in the study of the New Testament text. The two oldest complete Greek manuscripts of the New Testament, Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, both from the fourth century, end Mark’s Gospel at verse 8. Some early church writers, such as Eusebius and Jerome, also noted that the most accurate copies they knew ended there. Other manuscripts, including the majority of later ones, contain verses 9–20, known as the “longer ending.” A few manuscripts contain a short alternative ending, and some contain both.

Many scholars believe that verses 9–20 were added early in the church’s history to give Mark a fuller conclusion, drawing on resurrection accounts found in the other Gospels and Acts. Others defend the longer ending as original or believe Mark’s original ending was lost. Most modern Bibles, including the WEB, print verses 9–20 with a note explaining the situation. The longer ending has been read in churches for many centuries and contains nothing that contradicts the rest of the New Testament, though some of its details (such as handling snakes and drinking poison) should be read with particular care. This commentary treats verses 1–8 as the core of Mark’s account and explains verses 9–20 as an early summary of the resurrection appearances and the church’s mission.

### The Empty Tomb (*16:1–8*)

When the Sabbath was over, on Saturday evening, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome bought spices to anoint Jesus’ body. Anointing with aromatic oils and spices was a way of honoring the dead and reducing the odor of decay. Because Jesus had been buried hurriedly before the Sabbath, these women wanted to complete the task. Very early on Sunday morning, just after sunrise, they went to the tomb.

On the way, they asked one another, “*Who will roll away the stone from the door of the tomb for us?*” (*v. 3*) Tombs cut into rock were often sealed with a large, disk-shaped stone that rolled in a channel in front of the entrance. Mark notes that it was very large. The women had come out of love, without a plan for this obstacle.

But when they looked up, they saw that the stone had already been rolled back. Entering the tomb, they saw “*a young man sitting on the right side, dressed in a white robe*” (*v. 5*), and they were alarmed. Matthew identifies him as an angel (*Matthew 28:2*). His white robe indicates heavenly glory, as at Jesus’ transfiguration (*Mark 9:3*).

He said, “*Don’t be amazed. You seek Jesus, the Nazarene, who has been crucified. He has risen! He is not here. See the place where they laid him!*” (*v. 6*) This is studied below.

Then he gave them a commission: “*But go, tell his disciples and Peter, ‘He goes before you into Galilee. There you will see him, as he said to you.’*” (*v. 7*) Jesus had promised on the night of His arrest that after He was raised, He would go ahead of them into Galilee (*Mark 14:28*). This verse is studied below.

The women “*went out, and fled from the tomb, for trembling and astonishment had come on them. They said nothing to anyone; for they were afraid*” (*v. 8*). If Mark’s Gospel originally ended here, it is a startling conclusion. This verse is studied below.

### The Longer Ending: Appearances, Commission, and Ascension (*16:9–20*)

The longer ending begins by stating that Jesus, having risen early on the first day of the week, appeared first to Mary Magdalene, “*from whom he had cast out seven demons*” (*v. 9*) (see *Luke 8:2*). She went and told those who had been with Him, who were mourning and weeping. But when they heard that He was alive and had been seen by her, they did not believe it. (*John 20:11–18* tells this story in detail.)

Afterward, He appeared in a different form to two of them as they were walking in the country. They went back and told the others, but they did not believe them either. (*Luke 24:13–35* tells this story of the two disciples on the road to Emmaus.)

Later, Jesus appeared to the Eleven as they were eating. He “*rebuked them for their unbelief and hardness of heart*” (*v. 14*), because they had not believed those who saw Him after He rose. This theme of the disciples’ slowness to believe runs throughout Mark’s Gospel and appears in the other resurrection accounts too (*Luke 24:11*, 25; *John 20:24–29*).

Then Jesus commissioned them: “*Go into all the world and preach the Good News to the whole creation*” (*v. 15*). This is studied below. He added, “*He who believes and is baptized will be saved; but he who disbelieves will be condemned*” (*v. 16*). The emphasis falls on belief; condemnation is connected with unbelief, not with lack of baptism. Christians have generally understood baptism as the normal outward expression of faith, while recognizing that salvation rests on faith in Christ (compare the thief on the cross in *Luke 23:43*).

Jesus said that certain signs would accompany those who believe: casting out demons in His name, speaking in new languages, picking up snakes, being unharmed if they drank anything deadly, and healing the sick by laying hands on them. The book of Acts records the apostles casting out demons, speaking in other languages at Pentecost (*Acts 2*), healing the sick, and Paul surviving a viper’s bite (*Acts 28:3–6*). These verses describe signs that God gave to confirm the apostles’ message. They are not commands to deliberately handle snakes or drink poison to test God, which Jesus Himself refused to do (*Matthew 4:5–7*). Tragically, some groups have taken these verses as instructions to handle venomous snakes in worship, resulting in deaths. That practice misreads the passage.

After speaking to them, the Lord Jesus was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God, the place of supreme authority, fulfilling *Psalm 110:1*, which Jesus had quoted (*Mark 12:36*; *14:62*). The disciples went out and preached everywhere, and the Lord worked with them, confirming His word by the signs that accompanied it.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Mark 16:6* — “*He Has Risen! He Is Not Here*” (*v. 6*)

> *“He said to them, Don’t be amazed. You seek Jesus, the Nazarene, who has been crucified. He has risen! He is not here. See the place where they laid him!”*
>
> — *Mark 16:6* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These words are spoken by a young man in a white robe to three women at Jesus’ tomb. Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome had come very early on Sunday morning with spices to anoint Jesus’ body. They had watched Him die on Friday and had seen where He was buried. They came expecting to care for a corpse. On the way, they worried about who would roll away the heavy stone. But they found it already rolled back, and inside the tomb sat a young man in white. They were alarmed.

The messenger said, “*Don’t be amazed*” (*v. 6*). Then he identified exactly whom they were looking for: “*You seek Jesus, the Nazarene, who has been crucified*” (*v. 6*). He described Jesus by His hometown, Nazareth, and by His death, crucifixion. There was no mistake about identity. The same Jesus who had been crucified was the one he was speaking about.

“*He has risen!*” (*v. 6*) In Greek, this is a single word in the passive voice, meaning “He has been raised,” emphasizing that God raised Him. Then: “*He is not here*” (*v. 6*). The body was gone. Then the invitation: “*See the place where they laid him!*” (*v. 6*) The women could see the empty place where Jesus’ body had been. The evidence was before their eyes.

Jesus had predicted this three times. Each time, He said that after being killed, He would rise again (*Mark 8:31*; *9:31*; *10:34*). The disciples had not understood. Now His word was fulfilled.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse announces the heart of the Christian faith: Jesus, who was crucified, has risen from the dead. The resurrection shows that Jesus is who He claimed to be, the Son of God. It shows that His death was not a defeat but a victory, the ransom He came to give (*Mark 10:45*). It shows that God accepted His sacrifice. And it shows that death itself has been defeated.

The phrase “who has been crucified” is significant. The risen Jesus is still the crucified one. The resurrection does not erase the cross; it vindicates it. Paul preached “*Christ crucified*” (*1 Corinthians 1:23*) because the risen Lord is the one who died for sins.

The empty tomb is also important evidence. The women saw the place where Jesus had been laid, and it was empty. Christian faith rests not on a spiritual idea alone but on a historical event: Jesus’ body was raised from the dead.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse calls believers to live in the reality of the resurrection. Because Jesus is risen, His promises are true, His sacrifice is effective, and death is not the end. Believers can face fear, suffering, and grief with hope.

It also invites believers to come and see. The messenger invited the women to see the empty tomb. Believers can examine the evidence for the resurrection and grow in confidence that their faith rests on solid ground. They can also invite others to “come and see” who Jesus is.

Finally, this verse reminds believers that Jesus is not among the dead. He is alive and active today. Faith is not merely honoring a great teacher of the past but following a living Lord who is present with His people.

### *Mark 16:7* — “*Tell His Disciples and Peter*” (*v. 7*)

> *“But go, tell his disciples and Peter, “He goes before you into Galilee. There you will see him, as he said to you.””*
>
> — *Mark 16:7* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These words continue the message the young man gave the women at the empty tomb. After announcing that Jesus had risen, he gave them a mission: “*But go, tell his disciples and Peter*” (*v. 7*). The women would be the first messengers of the resurrection.

Notice the specific mention of Peter. Peter was one of the disciples, so why name him separately? Only a few days earlier, Peter had denied Jesus three times in the courtyard of the high priest, even calling down curses and swearing that he did not know Him (*Mark 14:66–72*). When the rooster crowed, Peter remembered Jesus’ prediction and broke down weeping. He had promised that he would never deny Jesus, even if he had to die with Him. He had failed completely.

Peter may have wondered whether he was still a disciple at all, or whether Jesus would ever want to see him again. The message “and Peter” answered that question. Jesus specifically included him. Peter was not cut off. He was still wanted.

The message continued: “*He goes before you into Galilee. There you will see him, as he said to you*” (*v. 7*). On the night of His arrest, Jesus had predicted that all the disciples would fall away, but He had also promised, “*However, after I am raised up, I will go before you into Galilee*” (*Mark 14:28*). That promise was given before they failed, and it was still in effect after they failed. Jesus, the Shepherd who had been struck, would gather His scattered sheep again.

Galilee was where the disciples had first been called, where Jesus had taught and healed, and where their journey with Him had begun. Jesus would meet them there to begin again.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse is one of the most tender in Mark’s Gospel. It shows that Jesus’ grace is greater than His followers’ failures. Peter had denied Him, and all the disciples had fled. Yet the risen Jesus sent a message specifically including Peter and promising to meet them all again. Early Christian tradition connects Mark’s Gospel with Peter’s preaching. If that is true, Peter himself may have often told how the angel said, “and Peter,” as a testimony to Jesus’ grace toward him.

It also shows that Jesus keeps His promises. He had said He would go ahead of them to Galilee. Their failure did not cancel His promise. God’s faithfulness does not depend on human faithfulness. Paul writes, “*If we are faithless, he remains faithful*” (*2 Timothy 2:13*).

Finally, the verse points to restoration. *John 21* tells how the risen Jesus met Peter by the Sea of Galilee and three times asked him, “Do you love me?”, matching his three denials, and then commissioned him to feed His sheep. The message at the tomb was the beginning of that restoration.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse brings hope to anyone who has failed Jesus. Many believers carry guilt over times they denied Christ, compromised their faith, or acted in ways that dishonored Him. They may wonder if Jesus still wants them. The words “and Peter” show that He does. Believers can return to Him, confess their failures, and receive His forgiveness and restoration.

It also encourages believers to extend grace to others who have failed. If Jesus specifically reached out to Peter after his denial, believers can reach out to those who have stumbled, offering welcome rather than rejection, while still taking wrongdoing seriously.

Finally, this verse reminds believers that Jesus keeps His promises. Even when they have been unfaithful, He remains faithful. They can trust His promises of forgiveness, His presence, and His future return, knowing that their failures do not cancel His faithfulness.

### *Mark 16:8* — Fear, Trembling, and Silence

> *“They went out, and fled from the tomb, for trembling and astonishment had come on them. They said nothing to anyone; for they were afraid.”*
>
> — *Mark 16:8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse describes the women’s response to the angel’s message. They had come to the tomb expecting to anoint a dead body. Instead, they found the stone rolled away, the tomb empty, and a heavenly messenger who told them that Jesus had risen and that they should tell the disciples and Peter.

Mark tells us: “*They went out, and fled from the tomb, for trembling and astonishment had come on them*” (*v. 8*). The women were overwhelmed. “Trembling” describes physical shaking from fear; “astonishment” describes being beside oneself with amazement. They had encountered something completely beyond their expectations: a heavenly messenger and the news that the dead had been raised.

“*They said nothing to anyone; for they were afraid*” (*v. 8*). At first, they were too frightened to speak. Of course, the other Gospels tell us that the women did eventually tell the disciples (*Matthew 28:8*; *Luke 24:9*), and Mark’s own longer ending says that Mary Magdalene went and told them (v. 10). The point of verse 8 is their immediate reaction of awe and fear.

If Mark’s Gospel originally ended at this verse, as the oldest manuscripts suggest, it is an unusual and powerful conclusion. Throughout Mark, people who were told to keep silent often spread the news anyway. Now, at the end, those who were told to speak are silent out of fear. The ending leaves the story open, inviting readers to consider their own response. Will they, too, be overwhelmed into silence, or will they go and tell?

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that the resurrection is an overwhelming event. It is not a comforting idea that fits easily into ordinary life. It is a world-changing act of God that produces awe and even fear. In the Bible, encounters with God’s power and holiness often cause fear (*Isaiah 6:5*; *Mark 4:41*; *9:6*). The resurrection is the greatest revelation of God’s power.

It also shows that even faithful followers can respond with fear and hesitation. These women had stayed with Jesus at the cross when the male disciples fled. They were among the most faithful followers in Mark’s Gospel. Yet even they were overwhelmed. This honesty is part of the Gospels’ credibility. The early church did not invent heroic stories about its first witnesses; it told the truth about their fear.

Finally, an ending at verse 8 would invite readers to complete the story. Mark began his Gospel with “the beginning of the Good News” (*1:1*). The rest of the story continues as believers go and tell. The message entrusted to the women is now entrusted to every reader.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse acknowledges that fear can keep believers from sharing their faith. Many believers know the good news of Jesus’ resurrection but are afraid to speak about it because of what others might think, fear of not knowing what to say, or uncertainty about how it will be received. The women’s fear shows that this struggle is common.

It also invites believers to move beyond fear. The women’s silence was not the end of the story; they did eventually tell the disciples, and the message spread throughout the world. Believers can ask God for courage to share what He has done, trusting that He works through ordinary, even frightened, messengers.

Finally, this verse encourages believers to respond to the resurrection with awe. In a world that often treats Jesus casually, the resurrection calls for wonder and worship. Believers can take time to reflect on the astonishing truth that Jesus has risen, allowing it to fill them with reverent joy.

### *Mark 16:15* — Go Into All the World

> *“He said to them, Go into all the world and preach the Good News to the whole creation.”*
>
> — *Mark 16:15* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse is part of the longer ending of Mark, which many early manuscripts include and which has been read in churches for centuries, though it is absent from the oldest complete manuscripts. In this section, the risen Jesus appears to the eleven disciples while they are eating. He rebukes them for their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they had not believed those who saw Him after He rose. Then He gives them their mission.

“*Go into all the world*” (*v. 15*). The disciples were not to stay in Jerusalem or even in Israel. Their mission was to extend to every nation and people. This echoes Jesus’ teaching that the gospel must first be preached to all nations (*Mark 13:10*).

“*and preach the Good News*” (*v. 15*). “Preach” means to proclaim publicly like a herald announcing important news. “Good News” (gospel) is the message about Jesus: His life, death, and resurrection, and the salvation He offers. Mark’s Gospel began with “*The beginning of the Good News of Jesus Christ, the Son of God*” (*Mark 1:1*). Now the disciples are sent to continue proclaiming it.

“*to the whole creation*” (*v. 15*). This phrase emphasizes the universal scope of the mission. The good news is for everyone, everywhere.

The following verses describe the response to this preaching (belief and baptism lead to salvation; unbelief leads to condemnation) and signs that would accompany believers. The section ends with Jesus’ ascension and the disciples going out to preach everywhere, with the Lord working with them.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse expresses the same mission found at the end of Matthew (*Matthew 28:19–20*), Luke (*Luke 24:47*), John (*John 20:21*), and Acts (*Acts 1:8*). In each Gospel, the risen Jesus sends His followers into the world with His message. This consistent testimony shows that mission is central to the church’s identity. The good news is not meant to be kept within a small group but shared with all people.

It also shows that Jesus entrusted His mission to imperfect people. Just before giving this command, He rebuked the disciples for their unbelief. Yet He still sent them. God does not wait for His followers to become perfect before using them. He sends them in their weakness and works through them.

Finally, the verses that follow show that the Lord works with His messengers: “*the Lord working with them and confirming the word by the signs that followed*” (*v. 20*). The mission is not accomplished by human effort alone but by Christ’s continuing presence and power.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse calls every believer to participate in sharing the good news. Not everyone will travel to distant countries, but everyone can share the gospel with people around them, support those who go to other places, and pray for the spread of the good news throughout the world.

It also encourages believers who feel inadequate. Jesus sent disciples who had just been rebuked for unbelief. He uses imperfect people. Believers can share their faith not because they are perfect but because the message is true and the Lord works with them.

Finally, this verse reminds believers that the gospel is for the whole creation. No person or people group is outside its reach. Believers can pray for and care about people of every nation, culture, and background, and seek to make the good news known to them.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Mark 16* announces the most important news in the world: Jesus, who was crucified, has risen from the dead. Everything in the Christian faith depends on this event. Believers can live with confidence that Jesus’ promises are true, His sacrifice is effective, and death is defeated. In times of grief, fear, or uncertainty, they can hold onto the hope of the resurrection.

The message “and Peter” shows the depth of Jesus’ grace. Peter had denied Jesus, yet he was specifically included in the invitation to meet the risen Lord. Believers who have failed can know that Jesus still wants them and offers restoration. They can also extend that same grace to others who have stumbled.

The women’s fear and silence acknowledge that the resurrection is overwhelming and that sharing it can be frightening. Believers often struggle with fear when it comes to speaking about their faith. Yet the story does not end with silence. The message spread from frightened women and doubting disciples to the whole world. Believers can ask God for courage to share the good news.

Finally, Jesus’ commission to go into all the world and preach the gospel to all creation is the mission of the church. Believers can participate by sharing their faith, supporting others in mission, and praying for the spread of the gospel. They do so with confidence that the Lord works with them, confirming His word. Mark began with “the beginning of the Good News,” and the rest of the story continues through every believer who carries that news to others.

## Chapter Prayer

Risen Lord Jesus, thank You that the tomb is empty and that You have been raised from the dead, just as You said. Thank You that the crucified One is alive, and that Your death has won forgiveness and Your resurrection has defeated death. Fill me with awe and joy at this good news.

Thank You for the words “and Peter,” which show that You do not abandon those who fail You. When I have denied You in word or action, draw me back and restore me. Help me to show the same grace to others. When fear makes me silent, give me courage to speak. Send me into the world to share the good news, and work through me as You worked through Your first disciples. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Book 3 of 27

# Luke

## About This Gospel

Luke is the longest of the four Gospels and the first of a two-volume work; its sequel is the book of Acts. Both are addressed to a man named Theophilus (*Luke 1:3*; *Acts 1:1*). Early Christian tradition identifies the author as Luke, a physician and traveling companion of the apostle Paul (*Colossians 4:14*; *2 Timothy 4:11*). Luke was likely a Gentile, and he wrote in polished Greek. He tells us that he carefully investigated everything from the beginning, drawing on eyewitnesses, so that his readers could know the certainty of what they had been taught (*Luke 1:1–4*). Many scholars date the book to the 60s–80s A.D.

## The Shape of the Book

Luke begins with the births of John the Baptist and Jesus, told from Mary’s perspective, and records Jesus’ ministry in Galilee (chapters 4–9). At *Luke 9:51*, Jesus “set his face to go to Jerusalem,” and much of the middle of the book (*9:51–19*:27) is a long journey filled with parables and teachings found only in Luke, including the Good Samaritan, the lost sheep, the lost coin, the prodigal son, the rich man and Lazarus, and the Pharisee and the tax collector. The book ends with Jesus’ death, resurrection, and ascension in Jerusalem.

## Themes to Watch For

Luke presents Jesus as the Savior of all people, especially those the world overlooks: the poor, women, Samaritans, Gentiles, tax collectors, and sinners. Jesus summarizes His mission: “the Son of Man came to seek and to save that which was lost” (*19:10*). Luke emphasizes prayer, showing Jesus praying at every major turning point, and the work of the Holy Spirit. Joy and praise run through the book from the angels’ song at Jesus’ birth to the disciples’ worship at His ascension. Luke also gives careful attention to money and possessions, warning against greed and calling for generosity to the poor.

# Luke — Chapter 1

Chapter Theme: God Remembers His Promises: Two Miraculous Births Announced

[Read Luke 1 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/LUK01.htm)

Main Teaching

Luke opens his carefully researched account by telling how the angel Gabriel announced two births: John, son of the elderly priest Zechariah and his wife Elizabeth, who would prepare the way for the Lord; and Jesus, conceived by the Holy Spirit in the virgin Mary, who would reign forever on David’s throne. Mary responds with humble trust and a song of praise to the God who lifts up the lowly, and Zechariah, his voice restored, praises God for remembering His covenant and sending salvation.

## Chapter Background and Story

Luke is the longest of the four Gospels, and it is the first of two volumes by the same author; the second is the book of Acts. Together they make up more than a quarter of the New Testament. Early Christian tradition identifies the author as Luke, a physician and companion of the apostle Paul (*Colossians 4:14*; *2 Timothy 4:11*; *Philemon 24*). Luke was likely a Gentile, and he wrote in polished Greek for a broad audience. He gives special attention to people often overlooked in the ancient world: women, the poor, Samaritans, Gentiles, and sinners. He also emphasizes prayer, the Holy Spirit, and joy.

*Luke 1* is unique among the Gospels. It tells the stories of John the Baptist’s and Jesus’ births side by side, showing that both were part of God’s plan. The chapter is filled with Old Testament echoes. Elderly, childless couples receiving miraculous children recall Abraham and Sarah (*Genesis 18*) and Hannah, mother of Samuel (*1 Samuel 1–2*). The songs of Mary and Zechariah are woven from the language of the Psalms and the Prophets. Luke wants his readers to see that God is fulfilling the promises He made to Israel.

### Luke’s Purpose (*1:1–4*)

Luke begins with a formal introduction, the kind found in Greek historical and scientific writings of the time. He notes that many had already written accounts of the events “*which have been fulfilled among us*” (*v. 1*), based on the testimony of eyewitnesses and servants of the word. Luke himself had investigated everything carefully from the beginning and decided to write an orderly account for “*most excellent Theophilus*” (*v. 3*). This prologue is studied below.

### Zechariah and Elizabeth (*1:5–25*)

Luke sets the story “*in the days of Herod, the king of Judea*” (*v. 5*), Herod the Great, who ruled from 37 to 4 B.C. A priest named Zechariah belonged to the priestly division of Abijah. King David had organized the priests into twenty-four divisions (*1 Chronicles 24*), and each served in the temple for one week twice a year. Zechariah’s wife, Elizabeth, was also from a priestly family, a descendant of Aaron. Both were “*righteous before God*” (*v. 6*), living faithfully according to God’s commands. But they had no children, because Elizabeth was unable to conceive, and both were now old.

In that culture, childlessness was often considered a disgrace and sometimes even assumed to be a sign of God’s disfavor. Luke makes clear that this was not the case for Zechariah and Elizabeth: they were righteous. Their story recalls Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah, and Hannah, all of whom waited long for children whom God gave in His time.

While Zechariah’s division was serving, he was chosen by lot to enter the temple and burn incense on the altar in the Holy Place. There were so many priests that this was likely a once-in-a-lifetime honor. Incense was offered every morning and evening, and its rising smoke symbolized the prayers of God’s people (*Psalm 141:2*). Outside, a crowd of worshipers was praying.

Suddenly an angel of the Lord appeared, standing at the right side of the altar. Zechariah was terrified. The angel said, “*Don’t be afraid, Zacharias, because your request has been heard. Your wife, Elizabeth, will bear you a son, and you shall call his name John*” (*v. 13*). “John” means “the LORD is gracious.” The angel described the child’s future: he would bring joy to many, be great in God’s sight, never drink wine or strong drink (like a Nazirite, *Numbers 6:1–4*), and be filled with the Holy Spirit even before birth. He would turn many Israelites back to God and go before the Lord “*in the spirit and power of Elijah*” (*v. 17*), fulfilling *Malachi 4:5–6*, to prepare a people for the Lord.

Zechariah asked how he could be sure of this, since he and his wife were old. The angel identified himself: “*I am Gabriel, who stands in the presence of God*” (*v. 19*). Gabriel had appeared to the prophet Daniel centuries earlier (*Daniel 8:16*; *9:21*). Because Zechariah did not believe, he would be unable to speak until the promise was fulfilled.

The people waiting outside wondered why Zechariah was taking so long. When he finally came out, he could not speak to give the customary priestly blessing. They realized he had seen a vision. After his service ended, he went home. Elizabeth became pregnant and stayed in seclusion for five months, saying, “*Thus has the Lord done to me in the days in which he looked at me, to take away my reproach among men*” (*v. 25*).

### The Announcement to Mary (*1:26–38*)

In Elizabeth’s sixth month of pregnancy, God sent Gabriel to Nazareth, a small, obscure village in Galilee. Gabriel came to a virgin named Mary, who was pledged to be married to Joseph, a descendant of King David. Jewish betrothal was a binding commitment, usually arranged when the girl was quite young, often in her early to middle teens. The marriage would be completed about a year later when the bride moved to her husband’s home.

The contrast with the previous scene is striking. Zechariah was an elderly priest in the temple in Jerusalem, the holiest place in Israel. Mary was a young woman in an insignificant village, with no religious position. Yet Gabriel greeted her, “*Rejoice, you highly favored one! The Lord is with you*” (*v. 28*). “Highly favored” means that she had received grace from God, not that she was the source of grace.

Mary was greatly troubled and wondered what this greeting meant. Gabriel said, “*Don’t be afraid, Mary, for you have found favor with God*” (*v. 30*). She would conceive and give birth to a son and name Him Jesus. He would be great, would be called the Son of the Most High, and God would give Him the throne of His father David. He would reign over the house of Jacob forever, and His kingdom would never end. These words fulfill God’s promise to David that his descendant would reign forever (*2 Samuel 7:12–16*).

Mary asked, “*How can this be, seeing I am a virgin?*” (*v. 34*) Her question differs from Zechariah’s. He asked for proof; she asked how it would happen. Gabriel explained: “*The Holy Spirit will come on you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you*” (*v. 35*). The word “overshadow” recalls the cloud of God’s presence that covered the tabernacle (*Exodus 40:35*). Therefore, the child would be called holy, the Son of God. Gabriel also told her that her relative Elizabeth, who had been called barren, was six months pregnant, and concluded, “*For nothing spoken by God is impossible*” (*v. 37*).

Mary’s response is studied below.

### Mary Visits Elizabeth (*1:39–56*)

Mary hurried to the hill country of Judea to visit Elizabeth, likely a journey of several days. When Mary greeted her, the baby leaped in Elizabeth’s womb, and Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit. She exclaimed, “*Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb!*” (*v. 42*) and asked why she was so favored that “*the mother of my Lord*” (*v. 43*) should come to her. Elizabeth, inspired by the Spirit, recognized the child Mary carried as her Lord. Even the unborn John responded with joy. Elizabeth added, “*Blessed is she who believed*” (*v. 45*), contrasting Mary’s faith with her husband’s doubt.

Mary responded with a song of praise, often called the Magnificat from its first word in Latin. It is studied below. Mary stayed with Elizabeth about three months, likely until John’s birth, and then returned home.

### The Birth and Naming of John (*1:57–66*)

Elizabeth gave birth to a son, and her neighbors and relatives rejoiced with her. On the eighth day, they came to circumcise the child, as the law required (*Genesis 17:12*; *Leviticus 12:3*), and they assumed he would be named after his father. Elizabeth said, “*Not so; but he will be called John*” (*v. 60*). They objected, since no one in the family had that name, and they made signs to Zechariah, suggesting that he may have been deaf as well as mute. He asked for a writing tablet and wrote, “*His name is John*” (*v. 63*). Immediately his mouth was opened, and he began to speak, praising God.

Fear came on all the neighbors, and these events were talked about throughout the hill country of Judea. People wondered, “*What then will this child be?*” (*v. 66*), because the Lord’s hand was clearly with him.

### Zechariah’s Song (*1:67–80*)

Zechariah was filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied. His song, often called the Benedictus from its first word in Latin, praises God for visiting and redeeming His people. God had raised up “*a horn of salvation*” (*v. 69*) in the house of David. “Horn” was an image of strength, like the horns of a powerful animal. God was keeping His promises spoken by the prophets, showing mercy, remembering His covenant with Abraham, and rescuing His people so that they could serve Him without fear, in holiness and righteousness.

Then Zechariah turned to his son. John would be called a prophet of the Most High, going before the Lord to prepare His way and to give His people knowledge of salvation through the forgiveness of sins. The song ends with a beautiful image of God’s tender mercy, studied below.

The chapter closes with a summary: the child grew and became strong in spirit, and he lived in the wilderness until he appeared publicly to Israel.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Luke 1:3–4* — Certainty About What You Have Been Taught

> *“it seemed good to me also, having traced the course of all things accurately from the first, to write to you in order, most excellent Theophilus; that you might know the certainty concerning the things in which you were instructed.”*
>
> — *Luke 1:3–4* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These verses are part of Luke’s introduction to his Gospel, a single, carefully constructed sentence in Greek (vv. 1–4). In verse 1, Luke acknowledged that many others had already written accounts of the events concerning Jesus. In verse 2, he explained that these accounts were based on the testimony of “*those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and servants of the word*” (*v. 2*), people who had seen Jesus’ ministry firsthand and had become messengers of the gospel.

Now Luke explains his own work: “*it seemed good to me also, having traced the course of all things accurately from the first, to write to you in order*” (*v. 3*). Several important claims are packed into this sentence. Luke “traced” or investigated the events, suggesting research and inquiry. He did so “accurately,” carefully checking information. He went back “from the first,” to the very beginning of the story. And he wrote “in order,” an organized account, though not necessarily in strict chronological sequence in every detail.

He wrote for “*most excellent Theophilus*” (*v. 3*). The name means “friend of God” or “loved by God.” “Most excellent” was a title of respect used for officials of high rank (*Acts 24:3*; *26:25*). Theophilus may have been a Roman official or a wealthy patron who sponsored Luke’s writing. Some have suggested the name represents any reader who loves God, though most scholars think he was a real person.

Luke’s purpose: “*that you might know the certainty concerning the things in which you were instructed*” (*v. 4*). Theophilus had already been taught about Jesus, perhaps as a new believer or an interested inquirer. Luke wanted him to have confidence that what he had learned was reliable.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that the Christian faith is rooted in history. Luke did not present a collection of myths or private visions. He wrote about real events that happened in real places, among real people, and he based his account on eyewitness testimony and careful investigation. Throughout Luke and Acts, he anchors events in history by naming rulers and officials (*Luke 2:1–2*; *3:1–2*).

They also show that faith and careful thinking go together. Luke did not ask Theophilus to believe without reason. He provided evidence and an orderly account so that Theophilus could have certainty. Christianity invites people to examine its claims.

Finally, the verses show that the gospel is meant to be passed on faithfully. The eyewitnesses delivered the message, Luke carefully recorded it, and Theophilus received it. This chain of faithful transmission continues as believers today read Scripture and pass on its message to others.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers who have doubts or questions about their faith. Like Theophilus, they can seek certainty by studying the Gospels carefully, learning about their historical background, and considering the testimony of the eyewitnesses. Faith does not require ignoring questions; it can grow stronger through honest investigation.

They also encourage believers to value careful study of Scripture. Luke took great care to write accurately. Believers can read the Bible with similar care, paying attention to context, history, and the order of events, rather than reading verses in isolation.

Finally, these verses remind believers that they are part of a long chain of faithful witnesses. They can pass on what they have received to others, especially to new believers who, like Theophilus, need to know the certainty of what they have been taught.

### *Luke 1:38* — “*Behold, the Servant of the Lord*” (*v. 38*)

> *“Mary said, ‘Behold, the servant of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word.’ Then the angel departed from her.”*
>
> — *Luke 1:38* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These words are Mary’s response to the angel Gabriel’s announcement. Gabriel had told her that she would conceive and give birth to a son named Jesus, who would be called the Son of the Most High and would reign on David’s throne forever. When Mary asked how this could happen since she was a virgin, Gabriel explained that the Holy Spirit would come upon her and the power of the Most High would overshadow her. He told her that her elderly relative Elizabeth was also pregnant, and he declared, “For nothing spoken by God is impossible.”

Mary’s answer is simple and profound: “*Behold, the servant of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word*” (*v. 38*).

“Servant” translates a word that means a female slave or bondservant. Mary described herself as someone who belonged entirely to God and was ready to do His will. This was a statement of humble submission.

“*let it be done to me according to your word*” (*v. 38*) expressed her acceptance of God’s plan. She did not fully understand how it would happen or what it would cost. Being pregnant before her marriage to Joseph was complete could bring suspicion, shame, and the risk that Joseph would end the betrothal. Under the law, she could even face severe consequences if accused of unfaithfulness. Yet Mary trusted God and accepted His word.

Mary’s response contrasts with Zechariah’s. When Gabriel announced John’s birth to Zechariah, an elderly priest serving in the temple, Zechariah asked for proof and was made unable to speak because of his unbelief. Mary, a young woman from an insignificant village, responded with faith.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse presents Mary as a model of faith and surrender to God. Her words echo the prayer Jesus would later teach, “*Let your will be done*” (*Matthew 6:10*), and His own prayer in Gethsemane, “*not what I desire, but what you desire*” (*Mark 14:36*). Mary shows that true faith involves both trusting God’s promises and submitting to His will.

The verse also reveals how God works through humble people. Mary had no wealth, position, or fame. She lived in Nazareth, a village of little importance. Yet God chose her for the most important role in history: to be the mother of the Messiah. God often chooses the lowly to accomplish His purposes, as Mary herself celebrated in her song (*Luke 1:48*, 52).

Christians have honored Mary throughout history for her faith and obedience. Catholic and Orthodox traditions give her special veneration; Protestant traditions emphasize her as an example of faith. All Christians can agree that her response to God’s word is a beautiful model of humble trust.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to respond to God’s word with trust and surrender. God’s plans may not always be what believers expected, and they may involve uncertainty or cost. Like Mary, believers can say, “Let it be done to me according to your word,” trusting that God is good and that His purposes are best.

It also encourages believers to see themselves as servants of the Lord. Their lives belong to God, and their purpose is to do His will. This perspective shapes how they make decisions, handle challenges, and use their time and abilities.

Finally, Mary’s response shows that faith does not require complete understanding. She did not know everything that lay ahead, but she trusted the God who spoke. Believers facing uncertainty can trust God’s character even when they do not see the full picture.

### *Luke 1:46–48* — “*My Soul Magnifies the Lord*” (*v. 46*)

> *“Mary said, My soul magnifies the Lord. My spirit has rejoiced in God my Savior, for he has looked at the humble state of his servant. For behold, from now on, all generations will call me blessed.”*
>
> — *Luke 1:46–48* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These verses begin Mary’s song of praise, known as the Magnificat. Mary had traveled to visit her relative Elizabeth, who was pregnant with John. When Mary arrived and greeted her, Elizabeth’s baby leaped in her womb, and Elizabeth, filled with the Holy Spirit, blessed Mary and the child she carried, calling Mary “*the mother of my Lord*” (*v. 43*). In response, Mary burst into praise.

“*My soul magnifies the Lord*” (*v. 46*). To “magnify” means to make great or to declare greatness. Mary’s whole being praised God. “*My spirit has rejoiced in God my Savior*” (*v. 47*). Mary called God “my Savior,” recognizing her own need for salvation and celebrating God’s saving work.

She gave the reason for her praise: “*for he has looked at the humble state of his servant*” (*v. 48*). “Humble state” describes Mary’s low social position. She was young, female, poor, and from an obscure village. Yet God had looked on her with favor. “*For behold, from now on, all generations will call me blessed*” (*v. 48*). Mary recognized that her role would be remembered throughout history, not because of her own greatness, but because of what God had done.

Mary’s song draws heavily on the Old Testament, especially the song of Hannah in *1 Samuel 2:1–10*. Hannah, who had been childless, praised God after He gave her a son, Samuel. Mary’s song echoes Hannah’s themes: God’s holiness, His care for the lowly, and His reversal of human power. Mary’s song also contains phrases from many psalms, showing how deeply she knew the Scriptures.

In the rest of the song (vv. 49–55), Mary praises God’s mighty deeds, His mercy, and His reversal of fortunes: scattering the proud, bringing down rulers, lifting up the humble, filling the hungry, and sending the rich away empty. She ends by celebrating God’s faithfulness to His promises to Abraham and his descendants.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This song reveals the character of God. He is mighty, holy, merciful, and faithful. He notices the lowly and lifts them up. He opposes the proud and brings down the powerful who abuse their power. He keeps His promises across generations. These themes run throughout Luke’s Gospel, where Jesus brings good news to the poor and welcomes the outcast.

Mary’s song also shows that true worship begins with recognizing God’s greatness and one’s own need. Mary did not boast about being chosen. She magnified God and called Him her Savior. Her humility made her a fitting vessel for God’s work.

Finally, the song is both personal and corporate. Mary praises God for what He has done for her, and then she praises Him for what He is doing for all His people. Personal experiences of God’s grace connect believers to God’s larger story of salvation.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses invite believers to make praise a central part of their lives. Like Mary, they can respond to God’s goodness with worship that involves their whole being. Praising God for His character and His work reminds believers of His greatness and lifts their hearts above their circumstances.

They also encourage believers who feel insignificant. God noticed Mary in her humble state. He sees those who are overlooked by the world, and He can use them for His purposes. No one is too small or unimportant for God’s attention.

Finally, Mary’s song challenges believers to share God’s concern for the lowly and His opposition to pride and injustice. Believers can humble themselves before God, care for the hungry and poor, and refuse to trust in wealth or power. Mary’s song describes God’s kingdom values, and believers are called to live by them.

### *Luke 1:78–79* — The Dawn From on High

> *“because of the tender mercy of our God, by which the dawn from on high will visit us, to shine on those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death; to guide our feet into the way of peace.”*
>
> — *Luke 1:78–79* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These verses conclude Zechariah’s song of praise, called the Benedictus. Zechariah had been unable to speak for about nine months because he doubted the angel’s message. When his son was born and he wrote, “His name is John,” his speech returned, and he was filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied.

In the first part of his song, Zechariah praised God for keeping His promises to David and Abraham by raising up a Savior. Then he addressed his infant son, saying that John would be a prophet who would prepare the way for the Lord and give knowledge of salvation through the forgiveness of sins. These final verses explain why all this was happening.

“*because of the tender mercy of our God*” (*v. 78*). Salvation comes not because people deserve it but because of God’s compassionate heart. The phrase “tender mercy” literally refers to the inner parts, the deepest feelings of compassion.

“*by which the dawn from on high will visit us*” (*v. 78*). “Dawn” (or “sunrise”) is an image of the coming Messiah. *Malachi 4:2* promised that “*shall the sun of righteousness arise with healing in its wings*” (*Malachi 4:2*). *Isaiah 9:2* promised that people walking in darkness would see a great light. Zechariah was saying that God was about to send the Messiah, like the sun rising after a long, dark night.

“*to shine on those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death*” (*v. 79*). This echoes *Isaiah 9:2*. “*Darkness*” (*Isaiah 9:2*) represents ignorance, sin, and despair. “The shadow of death” describes the fear and hopelessness of people facing death without God. The Messiah would bring light into this darkness.

“*to guide our feet into the way of peace*” (*v. 79*). The final image is of travelers who, now that the sun has risen, can see the path and walk safely. “Peace” in the Hebrew sense (shalom) means wholeness, well-being, and right relationship with God and others.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses reveal that salvation flows from God’s tender mercy. God did not send His Son grudgingly or reluctantly; He sent Him out of deep compassion for people trapped in darkness. This is the heart of the gospel: “*For God so loved the world, that he gave his only born Son*” (*John 3:16*).

The image of sunrise shows what Jesus brings to the world. Before the dawn, people sit in darkness, unable to see their way, afraid of death. Jesus comes like the rising sun, bringing light, warmth, and life. Later Jesus would say, “*I am the light of the world*” (*John 8:12*). Those who follow Him do not walk in darkness.

Finally, these verses show that salvation leads to peace. The goal is not merely escaping darkness but walking in the way of peace: peace with God through forgiveness, peace within through trust, and peace with others through love.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses offer hope to anyone sitting in darkness, whether the darkness of sin, grief, depression, fear, or confusion. Jesus came as the dawn from on high to shine on such people. Believers can bring their darkness to Him, trusting that His light can reach even the deepest shadows.

They also encourage believers to rest in God’s tender mercy. Salvation is not earned; it is a gift from a compassionate God. When believers feel unworthy, they can remember that God’s mercy, not their merit, is the source of their salvation.

Finally, these verses call believers to walk in the way of peace. Having received God’s light, they can follow Jesus’ guidance in their decisions and relationships, seeking peace with God and with others. They can also be bearers of light, sharing the hope of the dawn with those who are still in darkness.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Luke 1* shows that God keeps His promises, even after long periods of silence and waiting. Zechariah and Elizabeth had prayed for a child for years, and Israel had waited centuries for the Messiah. God answered both in His time. Believers who are waiting on God for answered prayer, for change, or for His promises to be fulfilled can trust that He remembers them and that His timing is perfect.

The chapter contrasts two responses to God’s word. Zechariah, a respected priest, doubted and was silenced. Mary, a young woman from an obscure village, believed and surrendered herself to God’s will. Believers can choose Mary’s response: “Behold, the servant of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word.” This kind of faith trusts God even when His plans are surprising and costly.

The songs of Mary and Zechariah teach believers how to praise God. They magnify His holiness, His mercy, His power, and His faithfulness. They celebrate His care for the lowly and His opposition to pride. Believers can make praise a regular part of their lives and allow these songs to shape their values, caring for the humble and hungry and refusing to trust in wealth or power.

Finally, Luke’s careful introduction reminds believers that their faith rests on historical events and reliable testimony. They can study Scripture with confidence, grow in certainty about what they have been taught, and pass on the good news faithfully to others. The dawn from on high has visited the world in Jesus, and believers are called to walk in His light and share it with those in darkness.

## Chapter Prayer

Faithful God, thank You for keeping Your promises across generations and for remembering those who wait on You. Thank You for the careful testimony of eyewitnesses and for the Scriptures that give me certainty about what I believe. When I wait for answers to prayer, help me to trust Your perfect timing.

Give me faith like Mary’s, so that I respond to Your word with humble trust and say, “Let it be done to me according to Your word.” Forgive me for the times I have doubted like Zechariah. Fill my heart with praise like Mary’s song, so that my soul magnifies You and rejoices in You, my Savior. Thank You for looking on the lowly and lifting them up. Thank You for Your tender mercy, by which the dawn from on high has visited us in Jesus. Shine on me in my darkness, and guide my feet into the way of peace. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
