Luke · Chapter 2 of 24

# Luke — Chapter 2

Chapter Theme: Good News of Great Joy for All People

[Read Luke 2 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/LUK02.htm)

Main Teaching

Jesus is born in Bethlehem in humble circumstances, and angels announce His birth to shepherds as good news of great joy for all people. In the temple, the aged Simeon and Anna recognize the infant as God’s promised salvation, a light for the nations and the glory of Israel, while Simeon warns Mary of sorrow to come. At twelve, Jesus stays behind in the temple, showing His awareness that He must be in His Father’s house, and then returns to Nazareth to grow in wisdom and favor.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Luke 2* contains the most familiar account of Jesus’ birth. Matthew’s Gospel tells the story from Joseph’s perspective and includes the visit of the wise men (*Matthew 1–2*). Luke tells it from Mary’s perspective and focuses on humble people: shepherds, an elderly man, and a widow. Throughout the chapter, Luke shows that Jesus was born into the real world of Roman power and Jewish law, that His family was devout and observed the law faithfully, and that God revealed His Son first to the lowly.

### The Birth of Jesus (*2:1–7*)

Luke places Jesus’ birth in its historical setting: “*a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that all the world should be enrolled*” (*v. 1*). Augustus was the first Roman emperor, ruling from 27 B.C. to A.D. 14. He was celebrated as a bringer of peace, and some inscriptions called him “savior” and his birthday “good news.” Luke’s account quietly sets Jesus over against Augustus: the true Savior and bringer of peace is the child born in Bethlehem.

The enrollment was a census for tax purposes. Luke says it was “*the first enrollment made when Quirinius was governor of Syria*” (*v. 2*). Historians have discussed this detail, since Quirinius is known to have conducted a census around A.D. 6, about ten years after Herod’s death. Various explanations have been proposed: that Quirinius held an earlier administrative role, that the Greek word can mean “before” Quirinius’s census, or that the census process began earlier and was completed later. Luke’s careful historical habits elsewhere suggest that he had reasons for his statement, even if the details are not fully known today.

Everyone went to register in their ancestral towns. Joseph, a descendant of David, traveled from Nazareth in Galilee to Bethlehem in Judea, about ninety miles, with Mary, who was pledged to him and was pregnant. The journey would have taken several days. God used the emperor’s decree to bring Jesus to be born in Bethlehem, the town of David, fulfilling *Micah 5:2*.

While they were there, Mary gave birth to her firstborn son. She “*wrapped him in bands of cloth and laid him in a feeding trough, because there was no room for them in the inn*” (*v. 7*). Wrapping a newborn tightly in strips of cloth was a common practice. A feeding trough, or manger, was used to hold food for animals. The word translated “inn” can also mean “guest room.” Many houses in Bethlehem had a main living area, a guest room, and a lower level where animals were kept at night. If the guest room was full, perhaps with relatives also in town for the census, the family may have stayed in the area with the animals. Either way, Jesus’ birth took place in humble circumstances, not in a palace.

### The Shepherds and the Angels (*2:8–20*)

In the fields nearby, shepherds were keeping watch over their flocks at night. Shepherds had a low social status. Their work kept them outdoors and away from religious observances, and they were sometimes viewed as unreliable. Yet God chose them to receive the first announcement of the Messiah’s birth. There is also a fitting connection: David, from whom the Messiah descended, had been a shepherd in the same region.

An angel of the Lord appeared, and the glory of the Lord shone around them. They were terrified. The angel said, “*Don’t be afraid, for behold, I bring you good news of great joy which will be to all the people*” (*v. 10*), and announced the birth of a Savior, Christ the Lord. This is studied below. The sign would be a baby wrapped in cloths and lying in a manger, an unexpected sign for the Messiah.

Suddenly a great company of angels appeared, praising God: “*Glory to God in the highest, on earth peace, good will toward men*” (*v. 14*). (Many manuscripts read “peace among people with whom he is pleased,” emphasizing that peace comes through God’s favor.) The angels’ song declared that the birth of Jesus brings glory to God and peace to the earth.

When the angels left, the shepherds said, “*Let’s go to Bethlehem, now, and see this thing that has happened*” (*v. 15*). They hurried and found Mary, Joseph, and the baby lying in the manger. After seeing Him, they told everyone what they had been told about the child, and all who heard were amazed. “*But Mary kept all these sayings, pondering them in her heart*” (*v. 19*). This is studied below. The shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for everything they had heard and seen.

### Jesus Presented in the Temple (*2:21–24*)

On the eighth day, Jesus was circumcised and named Jesus, the name given by the angel. Then, when the time of purification required by the law of Moses was completed, His parents took Him to Jerusalem to present Him to the Lord.

Luke mentions two different laws. First, after giving birth to a son, a woman was considered ritually unclean for forty days and then offered a sacrifice for purification (*Leviticus 12:1–8*). Second, every firstborn son was to be dedicated to the Lord, recalling how God spared Israel’s firstborn at the exodus (*Exodus 13:2*, 12–15). Mary and Joseph offered “*A pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons*” (*v. 24*), the offering permitted for those who could not afford a lamb (*Leviticus 12:8*). This detail shows that Jesus was born into a poor family. Luke emphasizes that Jesus’ parents carefully obeyed the law.

### Simeon’s Song (*2:25–35*)

In Jerusalem there was a man named Simeon, who was righteous and devout. He was “*looking for the consolation of Israel*” (*v. 25*), waiting for God to comfort His people by sending the Messiah, as promised in *Isaiah 40:1*. The Holy Spirit was on him, and the Spirit had revealed to him that he would not die before he had seen the Lord’s Christ.

Guided by the Spirit, Simeon came into the temple courts just as Mary and Joseph brought in Jesus. He took the child in his arms and praised God. His song, called the Nunc Dimittis from its first words in Latin, is studied below.

Mary and Joseph marveled at what was said. Then Simeon blessed them and spoke to Mary: “*Behold, this child is appointed for the falling and the rising of many in Israel, and for a sign which is spoken against*” (*v. 34*). Jesus would divide people. Some would stumble over Him and fall; others would be raised up through faith in Him. He would be opposed. Then Simeon added, “*Yes, a sword will pierce through your own soul*” (*v. 35*). Mary would suffer deep grief, which was fulfilled as she watched her Son die on the cross (*John 19:25*). Through Jesus, the thoughts of many hearts would be revealed.

### Anna the Prophetess (*2:36–38*)

There was also a prophetess named Anna, the daughter of Phanuel, from the tribe of Asher. She was very old. She had been married for seven years before her husband died, and then she had been a widow until she was eighty-four (or, as the Greek may mean, for eighty-four years, which would make her over a hundred). She never left the temple but worshiped there night and day with fasting and prayer. At that very moment, she came up, gave thanks to God, and spoke about the child to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem.

Luke often pairs a man and a woman in his stories (Zechariah and Mary, Simeon and Anna). Both Simeon and Anna were faithful, elderly, and waiting for God to act. Their long patience was rewarded.

### The Return to Nazareth (*2:39–40*)

When Joseph and Mary had done everything required by the law, they returned to Nazareth in Galilee. (Luke does not mention the visit of the wise men or the flight to Egypt recorded in *Matthew 2*; the two Gospels focus on different episodes.) The child grew and became strong, filled with wisdom, and the grace of God was upon Him.

### The Boy Jesus in the Temple (*2:41–52*)

Every year Jesus’ parents traveled to Jerusalem for the Passover festival. When Jesus was twelve, they went as usual. Twelve was the age when Jewish boys began preparing to take on the full responsibilities of the law (the later bar mitzvah ceremony takes place at thirteen). After the festival, as His parents started home, Jesus stayed behind in Jerusalem without their knowledge. Pilgrims often traveled in large groups of relatives and neighbors, so they assumed He was somewhere in the caravan. After a day’s journey, they looked for Him among their relatives and friends. Not finding Him, they returned to Jerusalem.

After three days, they found Him in the temple courts, sitting among the teachers, listening to them and asking questions. Everyone who heard Him was amazed at His understanding and answers. His parents were astonished. Mary said, “*Son, why have you treated us this way? Behold, your father and I were anxiously looking for you*” (*v. 48*). Jesus answered with the first words He speaks in Luke’s Gospel, studied below. They did not understand what He meant.

Jesus went down with them to Nazareth and “*was subject to them*” (*v. 51*), obeying His parents. Mary again treasured all these things in her heart. The chapter ends with a summary: “*And Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and men*” (*v. 52*). This verse shows that Jesus grew as a real human being, developing in understanding, physically, spiritually, and socially. It echoes the description of the boy Samuel, who grew in favor with the LORD and with people (*1 Samuel 2:26*).

## Important Verses Explained

### *Luke 2:10–11* — Good News of Great Joy

> *“The angel said to them, Don’t be afraid, for behold, I bring you good news of great joy which will be to all the people. For there is born to you today, in David’s city, a Savior, who is Christ the Lord.”*
>
> — *Luke 2:10–11* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These words are spoken by an angel to shepherds in the fields near Bethlehem on the night Jesus was born. The shepherds were watching their flocks, likely protecting them from predators and thieves. Suddenly an angel appeared, and the glory of the Lord shone around them. They were terrified, as people in the Bible usually are when they encounter God’s glory.

The angel began, “*Don’t be afraid*” (*v. 10*). Then he explained why fear was unnecessary: “*for behold, I bring you good news of great joy which will be to all the people*” (*v. 10*). “Good news” translates the same Greek word used for the gospel. In the Roman world, it was used for announcements of important events, such as a victory or the birth of an emperor. The angel announced news that would bring “great joy,” not just to a few, but to “all the people,” meaning all of Israel and ultimately the whole world.

Then the angel told them what the news was: “*For there is born to you today, in David’s city, a Savior, who is Christ the Lord*” (*v. 11*).

Each phrase is important. “To you” makes the news personal; the Savior was born for these shepherds. “Today” emphasizes that the long-awaited moment had arrived. “In David’s city” identifies Bethlehem, connecting Jesus to King David and to the prophecy of *Micah 5:2*. “A Savior” describes Jesus’ mission: to rescue people from sin and its consequences. “Christ” means the Messiah, the anointed King promised by God. “Lord” is a title that in the Greek Old Testament often translated God’s own name. Together, these titles declare that this baby is the promised King and the divine Lord who has come to save.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses announce the heart of the Christian message. The birth of Jesus is good news because He is the Savior. People need saving from sin, guilt, death, and separation from God, and God has sent His Son to rescue them.

It is significant that the announcement came to shepherds. They were ordinary working people with low social status. God chose to reveal the birth of His Son not to the powerful in Rome or the religious leaders in Jerusalem, but to humble shepherds. This fits Mary’s song, which praised God for lifting up the lowly (*Luke 1:52*). The gospel is for everyone, beginning with those the world overlooks.

The contrast with Caesar Augustus is also meaningful. Augustus was celebrated as a savior who brought peace to the world. But the angel announced that the true Savior had been born, not in a palace in Rome but in a humble place in Bethlehem. The angels then proclaimed peace on earth through this child. God’s way of saving the world is very different from the world’s way.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses invite believers to receive the birth of Jesus as genuinely good news. In a world full of bad news, the message that a Savior has come remains the best news anyone can hear. Believers can let this truth fill them with joy and shape their outlook on life, especially in difficult times.

They also remind believers that the gospel is “to you.” It is not merely a general truth but a personal message. Each person can receive Jesus as their Savior, Christ, and Lord.

Finally, these verses encourage believers to share this good news with everyone. The angel said the news was for all the people. Believers can share the message of Jesus with those around them, especially with those who, like the shepherds, are overlooked or considered unimportant by others.

### *Luke 2:19* — Mary Treasured and Pondered These Things

> *“But Mary kept all these sayings, pondering them in her heart.”*
>
> — *Luke 2:19* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse comes after the shepherds visited the newborn Jesus. They had seen angels in the fields and heard the announcement of a Savior’s birth. They hurried to Bethlehem and found the baby lying in a manger, just as the angel had said. Then they told everyone what they had heard about this child, and all who heard were amazed.

In contrast to the excited shepherds and the amazed crowd, Mary responded differently: “*But Mary kept all these sayings, pondering them in her heart*” (*v. 19*).

“Kept” means she treasured or preserved these things carefully, like valuable possessions. “Pondering” means she thought deeply about them, turning them over in her mind and trying to put the pieces together. The word suggests comparing and reflecting, considering how the events fit together.

Mary had much to ponder. An angel had told her she would bear the Son of God. Her elderly relative had miraculously become pregnant. Now shepherds came saying angels had announced her baby’s birth as the Savior, Christ the Lord. Yet her son had been born in humble circumstances and laid in a feeding trough. Mary did not understand everything, but she held onto these experiences and reflected on their meaning.

Luke repeats this idea in verse 51, after the twelve-year-old Jesus says He must be in His Father’s house: “*his mother kept all these sayings in her heart*” (*v. 51*). Many scholars believe these verses hint at Luke’s source. Mary may have been one of the eyewitnesses Luke consulted (*Luke 1:2*), sharing memories she had treasured for decades.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows a contemplative response to God’s work. Excitement and amazement are natural responses to God’s acts, but Mary models something deeper: careful, ongoing reflection that seeks to understand what God is doing. This kind of reflection allows God’s truth to sink deeply into the heart.

It also shows that understanding God’s ways often takes time. Mary did not grasp everything at once. She kept these experiences in her heart, and over the years, especially through Jesus’ death and resurrection, their meaning became clearer. Faith involves living with some mysteries, trusting God while continuing to seek understanding.

Finally, Mary’s pondering is connected with her role as a faithful witness. Her treasured memories became part of the testimony that has been passed down to the church through the Gospels.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to take time to reflect on God’s work in their lives. In a busy and noisy world, it is easy to move quickly from one experience to the next without considering what God might be saying. Setting aside time for quiet reflection, prayer, and journaling can help believers notice and remember God’s faithfulness.

It also encourages believers to meditate on Scripture. Rather than reading quickly and moving on, they can ponder what they read, asking what it reveals about God and how it applies to their lives. *Psalm 1* describes the blessed person as one who meditates on God’s law day and night.

Finally, this verse offers comfort to those who do not understand what God is doing. Mary did not have all the answers, but she trusted God and held onto what He had shown her. Believers can do the same, trusting that understanding will come in God’s time.

### *Luke 2:30–32* — “*My Eyes Have Seen Your Salvation*” (*v. 30*)

> *“for my eyes have seen your salvation, which you have prepared before the face of all peoples; a light for revelation to the nations, and the glory of your people Israel.”*
>
> — *Luke 2:30–32* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These verses are part of the song Simeon sang when he held the infant Jesus in the temple. Simeon was a righteous and devout man who had been waiting for the “consolation of Israel,” the comfort God promised to send His people through the Messiah. The Holy Spirit had revealed to him that he would not die before seeing the Lord’s Christ.

When Mary and Joseph brought forty-day-old Jesus to the temple to present Him to the Lord, the Spirit led Simeon there at that very moment. He took the child in his arms and praised God. He began, “*Now you are releasing your servant, Master, according to your word, in peace*” (*v. 29*). Simeon saw himself as a servant who had been standing watch, and now God was releasing him from his duty. He could die in peace because God had kept His promise.

The reason for his peace is in these verses: “*for my eyes have seen your salvation*” (*v. 30*). Simeon was holding a baby, yet he said he had seen God’s salvation. Salvation was not merely an idea or event; it was embodied in this child. Jesus’ name means “the LORD saves.”

“*which you have prepared before the face of all peoples*” (*v. 31*). God had been preparing this salvation for a long time, and it was not hidden in a corner. It was for all peoples to see.

“*a light for revelation to the nations, and the glory of your people Israel*” (*v. 32*). Simeon declared that Jesus would be a light to the Gentiles, revealing God to nations who did not know Him. This echoes *Isaiah 42:6* and *49:6*, where God’s Servant is called a light for the nations. Jesus would also be the glory of Israel, the fulfillment of God’s promises to His chosen people.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that salvation is found in a person, Jesus. Simeon did not see a program or a set of rules; he saw a child and recognized Him as God’s salvation. The Christian faith centers on a relationship with Jesus, who saves.

They also highlight the universal scope of God’s salvation. Simeon, a devout Jew, declared that Jesus was a light for the Gentiles as well as the glory of Israel. This theme runs through Luke and Acts, which tell how the gospel spread from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth (*Acts 1:8*). God’s salvation was always intended for the whole world.

Finally, Simeon shows how faith can bring peace even in the face of death. Having seen God’s salvation, he was ready to die. Those who know Christ can face death without fear, knowing that God has kept His promises.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers who are waiting on God’s promises. Simeon waited faithfully for years, and God fulfilled His word. Believers can continue to trust and wait, knowing that God keeps His promises in His time.

They also invite believers to find peace in Jesus. Like Simeon, believers can face life’s uncertainties and even death with peace, because they have seen God’s salvation in Christ. This peace comes not from circumstances but from knowing that God is faithful.

Finally, these verses call believers to share Christ as a light to all nations. If Jesus is the light for the Gentiles, believers can support the spread of the gospel among every people group and welcome people from every background into the community of faith.

### *Luke 2:49* — “*I Must Be in My Father's House*” (*v. 49*)

> *“He said to them, ‘Why were you looking for me? Didn’t you know that I must be in my Father’s house?’”*
>
> — *Luke 2:49* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These are the first words Jesus speaks in Luke’s Gospel. He was twelve years old. His family had traveled to Jerusalem for the Passover festival, as they did every year. When the festival ended and they began the journey home, Jesus stayed behind without their knowledge. His parents assumed He was traveling with relatives or friends in the large caravan. After a full day, they realized He was missing and returned to Jerusalem.

For three days they searched for Him. Imagine their fear: a twelve-year-old boy alone in a crowded city. Finally, they found Him in the temple courts, sitting among the teachers, listening and asking questions. Everyone who heard Him was amazed at His understanding.

Mary said, “*Son, why have you treated us this way? Behold, your father and I were anxiously looking for you*” (*v. 48*). Her words express real distress and perhaps a mild rebuke.

Jesus answered, “*Why were you looking for me? Didn’t you know that I must be in my Father’s house?*” (*v. 49*) The phrase “my Father’s house” can also be translated “about my Father’s business” or “among my Father’s things.” Either way, Jesus’ words show His awareness of a unique relationship with God. Mary had said, “your father and I,” referring to Joseph. Jesus gently pointed to another Father, God Himself. The word “must” shows a sense of divine purpose and necessity, a word Jesus will use throughout Luke to describe His mission (*Luke 4:43*; *9:22*; *24:7*).

“*They didn’t understand the saying which he spoke to them*” (*v. 50*). Even Mary and Joseph, who knew about His miraculous conception, did not fully grasp what He meant. Yet Jesus returned with them to Nazareth and was obedient to them.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals that even as a boy, Jesus was aware of His unique identity as the Son of God. His relationship with the Father was the center of His life. This awareness shaped His entire ministry and led Him eventually to the cross, always doing what the Father had sent Him to do.

It also shows the balance of Jesus’ life. He knew His heavenly Father’s claim on Him, yet He submitted to His earthly parents. He did not use His identity as an excuse to disobey them. This shows that honoring God and honoring parents go together.

Finally, the verse shows Jesus’ love for God’s house and God’s Word. He was found listening to teachers and asking questions, eager to learn. The child who would become the great Teacher first sat among teachers as a learner.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to make their relationship with God the center of their lives. Like Jesus, they can find their identity and purpose in being children of the Father. This shapes their priorities, choices, and sense of calling.

It also encourages believers, especially young people, to love God’s house and His Word. Jesus found joy in being in the temple and learning about God. Believers can cultivate a love for worship, learning Scripture, and asking good questions about faith.

Finally, Jesus’ example of obedience to His parents reminds believers that devotion to God includes honoring family relationships and responsibilities. Faithfulness to God should make believers better sons, daughters, parents, and family members, not more neglectful ones.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Luke 2* shows that God works in the ordinary and the humble. The Son of God was born to a poor family, laid in a feeding trough, and first announced to shepherds. Believers can look for God’s presence in ordinary places and among ordinary people, and they can take comfort that God notices and values those the world overlooks.

The chapter presents the good news in its simplest form: a Savior has been born who is Christ the Lord. This news brings great joy and peace, and it is for all people. Believers can receive it personally and share it widely, like the shepherds who told everyone what they had seen.

The examples of Mary, Simeon, and Anna show different aspects of faithful living. Mary treasured and pondered God’s work in her heart, reflecting deeply on what He was doing. Simeon and Anna waited patiently for many years, filled with the Spirit and devoted to prayer and worship. Believers can cultivate reflection, patience, and devotion, trusting that God fulfills His promises in His time.

Simeon’s warning to Mary reminds believers that following Jesus includes both joy and sorrow. Jesus would be opposed, and Mary would suffer. Faith does not remove pain, but it gives hope. Finally, the boy Jesus in the temple shows the importance of putting God first while honoring family. Like Jesus, believers can grow in wisdom, maturity, and favor with God and people as they seek to be about their Father’s business.

## Chapter Prayer

Father, thank You for the good news of great joy: that a Savior has been born, who is Christ the Lord. Thank You for sending Your Son in humility, laid in a manger and announced to shepherds. Help me to receive this news with joy and to share it with everyone around me, especially those who feel overlooked.

Like Mary, teach me to treasure and ponder Your work in my heart. Like Simeon and Anna, give me patience to wait for Your promises and a heart devoted to worship and prayer. Thank You that my eyes have seen Your salvation in Jesus, a light for all nations. Help me to put You first in my life, as Jesus did, while honoring the people You have placed around me. Let me grow in wisdom and in favor with You and with others. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Luke · Chapter 3 of 24

# Luke — Chapter 3

Chapter Theme: Prepare the Way: Repentance That Changes Everyday Life

[Read Luke 3 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/LUK03.htm)

Main Teaching

In a precisely dated moment of history, God’s word comes to John the Baptist, who calls people to a repentance that shows itself in generosity, honesty, and justice. John points beyond himself to the One who will baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire, and he is imprisoned for confronting Herod. Jesus is baptized while praying, the Spirit descends, and the Father declares Him His beloved Son. Luke then traces Jesus’ ancestry all the way back to Adam, showing that He belongs to all humanity.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Luke 3* moves forward about eighteen years from the end of *Luke 2*, where the twelve-year-old Jesus was found in the temple and then returned to Nazareth to grow in wisdom and stature. Now John the Baptist begins his public ministry, and Jesus is baptized and begins His work. Luke’s account parallels *Matthew 3* and *Mark 1*, but he adds several distinctive features: a detailed historical setting, John’s practical instructions to different groups, the mention of Jesus praying at His baptism, and a genealogy that traces Jesus’ family back to Adam. (*Matthew 3:2*, *3:8*, and *3:17* are studied in depth in Matthew’s commentary.)

### The Historical Setting (*3:1–2*)

Luke begins with a remarkable list of rulers, the kind of dating a careful historian would use. It was “*in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar*” (*v. 1*), the Roman emperor who succeeded Augustus. Depending on how the years were counted, this was around A.D. 27–29. Pontius Pilate was governor of Judea (A.D. 26–36). Herod Antipas was tetrarch of Galilee; his brother Philip ruled the regions northeast of Galilee; and Lysanias ruled Abilene, northwest of Damascus. The high priests were Annas and Caiaphas. Annas had been high priest from A.D. 6 to 15 and was removed by the Romans, but he remained very influential; his son-in-law Caiaphas held the office during Jesus’ ministry (*John 18:13*).

This list of powerful men, emperors, governors, tetrarchs, and high priests, sets the stage for something surprising: “*the word of God came to John, the son of Zacharias, in the wilderness*” (*v. 2*). God’s word did not come to the palace in Rome or the temple in Jerusalem, but to a man in the desert. This phrase echoes the way the Old Testament introduces prophets: “the word of the LORD came to” Jeremiah, Hosea, and others. After centuries without a prophet, God was speaking again.

### John’s Preaching (*3:3–9*)

John went throughout the region around the Jordan River, “*preaching the baptism of repentance for remission of sins*” (*v. 3*). Baptism in water was a sign of turning away from sin and turning to God. Luke quotes *Isaiah 40:3–5* at greater length than Matthew or Mark. Isaiah described a voice crying in the wilderness to prepare the way for the Lord: valleys would be filled, mountains leveled, crooked roads made straight, and rough ways smooth. In the ancient world, roads were prepared this way for the arrival of a king. Luke continues the quotation to include its climax: “*All flesh will see God’s salvation*” (*v. 6*). This verse is studied below.

John spoke bluntly to the crowds coming for baptism: “*You offspring of vipers, who warned you to flee from the wrath to come?*” (*v. 7*) Like snakes fleeing a fire, many were coming to escape judgment without real change. He told them to produce fruit that showed their repentance and not to rely on being descendants of Abraham. God could raise up children for Abraham from stones. The ax was already at the root of the trees, ready to cut down any that did not bear good fruit.

### What Should We Do? (*3:10–14*)

Luke alone records the practical questions people asked John and his specific answers. The crowds asked, “*What then must we do?*” (*v. 10*) John answered that anyone with two tunics should share with someone who had none, and anyone with food should do the same. Tax collectors asked what they should do. John told them, “*Collect no more than that which is appointed to you*” (*v. 13*). Soldiers asked the same question, and John told them, “*Extort from no one by violence, neither accuse anyone wrongfully. Be content with your wages*” (*v. 14*). This section is studied below.

### John Points to the Messiah (*3:15–20*)

The people were filled with expectation and wondered whether John might be the Messiah. John answered that he baptized with water, but someone more powerful was coming, whose sandal straps John was not worthy to untie. That one “*will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire*” (*v. 16*). The Holy Spirit would be poured out on God’s people, as the prophets had promised (*Joel 2:28*). Fire could signify both purification and judgment. John described the coming one with a winnowing fork in His hand, separating wheat from chaff, gathering the wheat into His barn and burning the chaff with unquenchable fire.

With many other words, John “*preached good news to the people*” (*v. 18*). Even his warnings of judgment were part of good news, because they called people to turn to God before it was too late.

Then Luke briefly tells how John’s ministry ended. John rebuked Herod Antipas for marrying Herodias, his brother’s wife, and for all the other evil things he had done. Herod added to his sins by locking John up in prison. Luke mentions this here, before Jesus’ baptism, to close John’s story and turn the focus fully to Jesus. (*Mark 6:14–29* tells the full story of John’s death.)

### The Baptism of Jesus (*3:21–22*)

When all the people were being baptized, Jesus was baptized too. Luke adds a detail found only in his Gospel: Jesus “*was praying*” (*v. 21*). Luke emphasizes Jesus’ prayer life throughout his Gospel, showing Him praying at key moments (*5:16*; *6:12*; *9:18*, 28–29; *22:41–44*). As Jesus prayed, heaven was opened, and the Holy Spirit descended on Him “*in a bodily form like a dove*” (*v. 22*). Luke’s phrase “in bodily form” emphasizes that this was a visible event. A voice came from heaven: “*You are my beloved Son. In you I am well pleased*” (*v. 22*).

The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are all present in this scene. The Spirit’s coming on Jesus anointed Him for His mission, as He will announce in the synagogue at Nazareth: “*The Spirit of the Lord is on me, because he has anointed me to preach good news to the poor*” (*Luke 4:18*).

### The Genealogy of Jesus (*3:23–38*)

Luke notes that Jesus was “*about thirty years old*” (*v. 23*) when He began His ministry. Thirty was the age when priests began their service (*Numbers 4:3*) and when David became king (*2 Samuel 5:4*). Luke describes Jesus as “*the son (as was supposed) of Joseph*” (*v. 23*), acknowledging that Joseph was His legal father, though not His biological father, since Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit (*Luke 1:35*).

Luke’s genealogy differs from Matthew’s in several ways. Matthew begins with Abraham and moves forward to Jesus, emphasizing that Jesus is the son of Abraham and the son of David, the fulfillment of Israel’s hope (*Matthew 1:1–17*). Luke begins with Jesus and moves backward, past David and Abraham, all the way to Adam, “*the son of God*” (*v. 38*). Between David and Joseph, the two lists name different ancestors: Matthew traces the line through Solomon, Luke through David’s son Nathan. Scholars have offered several explanations. One common view is that Luke records Mary’s genealogy (with Joseph named as the son-in-law of Heli), while Matthew records Joseph’s. Another is that Matthew gives the royal legal line and Luke the biological line of Joseph, with differences explained by customs such as levirate marriage, in which a man could be the legal son of one man and the biological son of another. Ancient genealogies served different purposes, and both Gospels agree that Jesus is a descendant of David.

Luke’s genealogy is studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Luke 3:6* — All Flesh Will See God’s Salvation

> *“All flesh will see God’s salvation.’”*
>
> — *Luke 3:6* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse concludes the passage from Isaiah that Luke quotes to describe John the Baptist’s ministry. Matthew and Mark quote only the first part of *Isaiah 40:3*, about the voice crying in the wilderness to prepare the way of the Lord. Luke continues the quotation through *Isaiah 40:5*, ending with this line: “*All flesh will see God’s salvation*” (*v. 6*).

In Isaiah’s original context, around the time of the Babylonian exile, these words announced that God would come to rescue His people and bring them home. *Isaiah 40* begins, “Comfort, comfort my people.” The image of a highway in the wilderness, with valleys raised and mountains lowered, pictured God returning to His people in power. The prophecy ended with the promise that all people would see God’s glory and salvation.

“All flesh” means all humanity, every person, not just Israel. Luke’s decision to include this phrase is deliberate. One of his major themes is that the good news of Jesus is for everyone: Jews and Gentiles, rich and poor, men and women, righteous and sinners. Simeon had already declared that Jesus would be “*a light for revelation to the nations*” (*Luke 2:32*). Now Luke shows that John’s ministry was preparing the way for a salvation that would reach the entire world.

“God’s salvation” refers to God’s rescue of His people from sin, death, and everything that separates them from Him. In Luke’s Gospel, this salvation is embodied in Jesus Himself. When Simeon held the infant Jesus, he said, “*for my eyes have seen your salvation*” (*Luke 2:30*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals the universal reach of the gospel. God’s plan was never limited to one nation. From His promise to Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him (*Genesis 12:3*), God intended to bring salvation to all peoples. Luke’s two volumes, the Gospel and Acts, trace how this salvation moved from a small group of Jewish followers in Jerusalem to Gentiles throughout the Roman world (*Acts 1:8*; *28:28*).

The verse also shows the purpose of repentance. John called people to prepare the way by repenting, leveling the mountains of pride and filling the valleys of despair, straightening crooked paths of sin. Repentance clears the way for people to see and receive God’s salvation.

Finally, the verse reflects the hope that one day God’s salvation will be visible to all. Christians look forward to the return of Christ, when every knee will bow and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord (*Philippians 2:10–11*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse calls believers to share the good news with all people. If God’s salvation is for all flesh, believers should not limit their love and witness to people who are like them. They can reach out across cultural, social, economic, and ethnic barriers, recognizing that every person needs and can receive God’s salvation.

It also invites believers to examine whether anything in their lives is blocking the way. Pride, bitterness, dishonesty, or other sins can act like mountains and crooked roads, hindering their relationship with God and their witness to others. Repentance clears the way.

Finally, this verse offers hope. No person is beyond the reach of God’s salvation. Believers can pray for and share Christ with those who seem far from God, trusting that God desires all people to see His salvation.

### *Luke 3:10–11* — “*What Then Must We Do?*” (*v. 10*)

> *“The multitudes asked him, ‘What then must we do?’ He answered them, ‘He who has two coats, let him give to him who has none. He who has food, let him do likewise.’”*
>
> — *Luke 3:10–11* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These verses begin a section found only in Luke’s Gospel. John the Baptist had been preaching powerfully, calling people to repent and warning them that they must produce fruit showing their repentance was genuine. He told them not to rely on being descendants of Abraham, and he warned that every tree not producing good fruit would be cut down and thrown into the fire.

The crowds responded with a sincere question: “*What then must we do?*” (*v. 10*) They wanted to know what repentance looked like in practice. John’s answer was simple and concrete: “*He who has two coats, let him give to him who has none. He who has food, let him do likewise*” (*v. 11*).

The “coat” was a tunic, the basic garment worn next to the skin. Many poor people had only one. Having two tunics meant having more than one needed. John told those with extra to share with those without. The same applied to food. Repentance meant generosity toward the needy.

Then specific groups asked the same question. Tax collectors asked what they should do. They worked for the ruling authorities and were known for overcharging and keeping the extra for themselves. John did not tell them to quit their jobs; he told them, “*Collect no more than that which is appointed to you*” (*v. 13*). Repentance for them meant honesty and fairness in their work.

Soldiers also asked. These may have been Jewish soldiers serving Herod Antipas or soldiers attached to Roman officials. Soldiers were poorly paid and sometimes used their power to extort money from civilians by threats or false accusations. John told them, “*Extort from no one by violence, neither accuse anyone wrongfully. Be content with your wages*” (*v. 14*). Repentance meant refusing to abuse power.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that repentance is not merely a religious feeling or ritual. It touches the most practical areas of life: possessions, money, work, and the use of power. True repentance changes how people treat others. This connects with the prophets, who repeatedly taught that God desires justice and mercy more than religious rituals (*Isaiah 1:16–17*; *Amos 5:24*; *Micah 6:8*).

It is significant that John did not tell tax collectors or soldiers to abandon their professions. He told them to do their work with integrity. Faith is meant to be lived out in ordinary jobs and everyday responsibilities. Believers can honor God in whatever legitimate work they do by being honest, fair, and generous.

The common thread in John’s answers is love for neighbor. Sharing clothing and food, collecting only what is fair, and refusing to exploit others are all ways of treating others as one would want to be treated. These are the fruits that show that a heart has truly turned to God.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses invite believers to ask John’s question for themselves: “What then must we do?” Repentance is not complete until it reaches daily life. Believers can consider how their faith should change the way they use money and possessions, how they do their jobs, and how they use whatever power or influence they have.

Practically, this might mean sharing extra clothing, food, or resources with those in need; being honest in business, taxes, and financial dealings; treating employees, customers, and coworkers fairly; refusing to use positions of authority to intimidate or take advantage of others; and practicing contentment rather than constant striving for more.

Finally, these verses encourage believers to serve God where they are. They do not need to leave their jobs to follow God faithfully. Whether they are teachers, business owners, factory workers, nurses, soldiers, or parents, they can bring integrity, generosity, and compassion into their daily work.

### *Luke 3:38* — The Son of Adam, the Son of God

> *“the son of Enos, the son of Seth, the son of Adam, the son of God.”*
>
> — *Luke 3:38* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse concludes the genealogy of Jesus in Luke’s Gospel. Luke’s list begins in verse 23 with Jesus, “*being the son (as was supposed) of Joseph*” (*v. 23*), and then traces His ancestors backward through seventy-seven generations. It passes through King David, Abraham, and Noah, finally reaching “*the son of Enos, the son of Seth, the son of Adam, the son of God*” (*v. 38*).

Adam was the first human being, created directly by God (*Genesis 2:7*). Luke calls Adam “the son of God,” not in the same sense that Jesus is the Son of God, but because Adam owed his existence directly to God, without a human father.

The placement of this genealogy is significant. It comes immediately after Jesus’ baptism, where the voice from heaven declared, “You are my beloved Son.” And it comes immediately before the temptation in the wilderness, where the devil says, “*If you are the Son of God*” (*Luke 4:3*). Luke surrounds the genealogy with declarations about Jesus’ sonship.

Matthew’s genealogy begins with Abraham, emphasizing that Jesus is the Messiah of Israel. Luke goes further back, to Adam, emphasizing that Jesus belongs to all humanity. He is not only the son of Abraham and David, but the son of Adam, connected to every human being. This fits Luke’s emphasis on the universal reach of the gospel.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse presents Jesus as the representative of all humanity. Paul develops this idea, describing Adam as the head of the old humanity, through whom sin and death entered the world, and Christ as the head of a new humanity, through whom life and righteousness come (*Romans 5:12–21*; *1 Corinthians 15:22*, 45). Where Adam, the first “son of God,” failed when tempted in the garden, Jesus, the true Son of God, remains faithful when tempted in the wilderness (*Luke 4:1–13*).

The genealogy also affirms that Jesus was fully human. He had real ancestors and belonged to a real family history. He was not a phantom or a heavenly being disguised as a man. He shared the human story from its very beginning.

Finally, by tracing Jesus back to Adam, Luke shows that the gospel addresses the human condition as a whole. Every person descends from Adam and shares in the brokenness that entered the world through sin. Jesus came to restore what was lost, offering salvation to all of Adam’s descendants.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse reminds believers that Jesus belongs to every person and every people. No ethnic group, nation, or social class has a special claim on Him. Believers can approach people of every background with the confidence that Jesus came for them too.

It also offers comfort to those who feel their family history disqualifies them. Jesus’ family tree, traced back to Adam, includes every kind of person. God works through human history, with all its failures, to accomplish His purposes.

Finally, this verse invites believers to see Jesus as the one who succeeds where humanity has failed. Every person, like Adam, has sinned. Jesus, the faithful Son, offers a new beginning. Believers can find their identity not in their connection to Adam’s failure, but in their union with Christ, the true Son of God.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Luke 3* shows that God’s word often comes in unexpected places. The rulers of the world held the power and the titles, but God spoke to a prophet in the wilderness. Believers can remain open to hearing God’s voice in humble and unexpected ways, and they can trust that God’s purposes move forward regardless of who holds earthly power.

John’s preaching calls for genuine repentance. Like the crowds, believers can ask, “What then must we do?” The answer touches everyday life: sharing with those in need, being honest in work and money, refusing to abuse power, and being content. Repentance is not only a feeling of sorrow but a change in how people live and treat others.

John’s humility is also an example. Though people wondered if he was the Messiah, he pointed beyond himself to Jesus. Believers can serve faithfully while directing attention to Christ rather than themselves. John’s courage in confronting Herod reminds them that faithfulness sometimes means speaking truth to those in power, even at great cost.

Jesus’ baptism, marked by prayer and the Father’s declaration of love, shows the importance of prayer and the security of knowing one’s identity in God. Finally, Luke’s genealogy, reaching back to Adam, reminds believers that Jesus came for all humanity. The salvation John announced is for “all flesh,” and believers are called to share that good news with everyone.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord God, thank You for speaking Your word in the wilderness and for sending John to prepare the way for Jesus. Search my heart and show me the mountains of pride, the valleys of despair, and the crooked paths of sin that need to be made straight. Help me to repent in ways that change how I live.

Show me what I must do. Give me a generous heart to share with those in need, integrity in my work and in my dealings with money, and humility in how I use any power or influence I have. Teach me to be content. Thank You that Jesus, Your beloved Son, came for all people, and that His salvation reaches every son and daughter of Adam. Help me to point others to Him, as John did, and to share the good news that all flesh may see Your salvation. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Luke · Chapter 4 of 24

# Luke — Chapter 4

Chapter Theme: Anointed by the Spirit: Good News for the Poor and the Outsider

[Read Luke 4 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/LUK04.htm)

Main Teaching

Full of the Holy Spirit, Jesus resists the devil’s temptations in the wilderness and returns to Galilee in the Spirit’s power. In His hometown synagogue He reads Isaiah’s prophecy of good news for the poor, freedom for captives, and sight for the blind, and announces that it is fulfilled in Him. When He reminds His neighbors that God’s prophets showed mercy to Gentiles, they try to kill Him. In Capernaum He drives out demons and heals the sick, and then moves on, because He was sent to preach the kingdom in other towns too.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Luke 4* marks the beginning of Jesus’ public ministry. In chapter 3, Jesus was baptized while praying, the Holy Spirit descended on Him, and the Father declared Him His beloved Son. Luke then traced His genealogy back to Adam, “the son of God.” Now Luke shows the Son of God tested in the wilderness and then launching His mission in Galilee. Throughout this chapter, Luke emphasizes the Holy Spirit’s role: Jesus is “*full of the Holy Spirit*” (*v. 1*), “*led by the Spirit*” (*v. 1*), returns “*in the power of the Spirit*” (*v. 14*), and declares, “*The Spirit of the Lord is on me*” (*v. 18*).

### The Temptation in the Wilderness (*4:1–13*)

Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, was led by the Spirit into the wilderness, where He was tempted by the devil for forty days. He ate nothing during that time, and afterward He was hungry. Luke’s account closely parallels Matthew’s (studied at *Matthew 4:4* and *4:10*), but Luke places the temptations in a different order. Matthew ends with the temptation on the mountain, where the devil offers the kingdoms of the world. Luke ends with the temptation at the temple in Jerusalem. This fits Luke’s emphasis on Jerusalem, where his Gospel begins (with Zechariah in the temple) and ends (with the disciples worshiping in the temple), and where Jesus’ mission will reach its climax.

The devil’s first temptation was to turn a stone into bread. Jesus answered from *Deuteronomy 8:3* that people do not live by bread alone. The devil then showed Jesus all the kingdoms of the world and said, “*I will give you all this authority and their glory, for it has been delivered to me*” (*v. 6*). Luke alone includes this boast. The devil claimed authority over the world’s kingdoms; Scripture elsewhere calls him “*the prince of this world*” (*John 12:31*). But his offer required Jesus to worship him. Jesus answered from *Deuteronomy 6:13* that God alone is to be worshiped and served.

Finally, the devil took Jesus to the highest point of the temple and, quoting *Psalm 91*, urged Him to throw Himself down and let angels catch Him. Jesus answered from *Deuteronomy 6:16*, “*You shall not tempt the Lord your God*” (*v. 12*).

Luke concludes, “*When the devil had completed every temptation, he departed from him until another time*” (*v. 13*). The phrase “until another time” (or “until an opportune time”) signals that the battle was not over. Satan would return. In *Luke 22:3*, as the crucifixion approaches, Luke writes that Satan entered Judas. Jesus’ victory in the wilderness was the first round in a conflict that would culminate at the cross.

### Return to Galilee (*4:14–15*)

Jesus returned to Galilee in the power of the Spirit. News about Him spread through the whole region. He taught in their synagogues, and everyone praised Him. These summary verses show His early popularity, which makes the rejection at Nazareth all the more striking.

### Rejected at Nazareth (*4:16–30*)

Jesus went to Nazareth, where He had grown up. On the Sabbath He went to the synagogue, “*as was his custom*” (*v. 16*). Jesus regularly participated in synagogue worship. A synagogue service typically included prayers, readings from the Law and the Prophets, and a sermon or explanation, often given by a visiting teacher.

Jesus stood up to read, and the scroll of the prophet Isaiah was handed to Him. He unrolled it and found the passage from *Isaiah 61:1–2* (with a phrase from *Isaiah 58:6*). He read, “*The Spirit of the Lord is on me, because he has anointed me to preach good news to the poor*” (*v. 18*). This passage is studied below.

Then He rolled up the scroll, gave it back to the attendant, and sat down, the customary position for teaching. Every eye in the synagogue was fixed on Him. He said, “*Today, this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing*” (*v. 21*). Jesus was claiming to be the one Isaiah described, the Spirit-anointed messenger bringing God’s salvation.

Notice where Jesus stopped reading. *Isaiah 61:2* continues, “*and the day of vengeance of our God*” (*Isaiah 61:2*). Jesus stopped after “to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord.” His first coming was focused on grace and salvation. Judgment would come later.

At first the people were impressed. They “*wondered at the gracious words which proceeded out of his mouth*” (*v. 22*). But they also asked, “*Isn’t this Joseph’s son?*” (*v. 22*) They knew Him as a local carpenter’s son. How could He be the fulfillment of Isaiah’s prophecy?

Jesus anticipated their thoughts. He quoted a proverb, “*Physician, heal yourself!*” (*v. 23*), meaning they wanted Him to do the miracles in Nazareth that He had done in Capernaum. He said, “*no prophet is acceptable in his hometown*” (*v. 24*). Then He gave two examples from Israel’s history, studied below. Elijah was sent to a widow in Sidon, a Gentile, during a famine, rather than to the many widows in Israel. Elisha healed Naaman the Syrian, a Gentile, rather than the many lepers in Israel.

The people’s mood changed instantly. They were furious. They drove Jesus out of town and took Him to the edge of the hill on which Nazareth was built, intending to throw Him off the cliff. Nazareth sits on a hillside with steep slopes nearby. Throwing someone off a cliff could also be the first step of a stoning. But Jesus “*passing through the middle of them, went his way*” (*v. 30*). Luke does not explain how. Jesus’ time had not yet come.

### Authority in Capernaum (*4:31–41*)

Jesus went down to Capernaum, a town on the northwest shore of the Sea of Galilee. On the Sabbath, He taught in the synagogue, and the people were amazed because His words had authority.

In the synagogue was a man possessed by an unclean demon, who cried out, “*Ah! what have we to do with you, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are: the Holy One of God!*” (*v. 34*) Jesus rebuked the demon: “*Be silent and come out of him!*” (*v. 35*) The demon threw the man down in front of everyone and came out without injuring him. Luke the physician notes that the man was unharmed. The people were amazed at Jesus’ authority and power over unclean spirits, and news about Him spread throughout the region.

Jesus then went to Simon’s house. Simon’s mother-in-law was suffering from a high fever, and they asked Jesus to help her. Luke, possibly drawing on his medical knowledge, specifies “a great fever.” Jesus stood over her and “*rebuked the fever*” (*v. 39*), treating it almost as a hostile force. The fever left her, and she immediately got up and began to serve them.

At sunset, when the Sabbath ended, people brought all their sick to Jesus. Luke notes that He “*laid his hands on every one of them*” (*v. 40*), giving each person individual attention. Demons came out of many, shouting, “*You are the Christ, the Son of God!*” (*v. 41*) Jesus rebuked them and would not let them speak, because they knew He was the Messiah. He did not want His identity proclaimed by demons or misunderstood by the crowds.

### Moving On to Other Towns (*4:42–44*)

At daybreak, Jesus went to a solitary place. The crowds searched for Him and tried to keep Him from leaving. But He said, “*I must preach the good news of God’s Kingdom to the other cities also. For this reason I have been sent*” (*v. 43*). This is studied below. He continued preaching in the synagogues of Judea (some manuscripts read “Galilee”; Luke sometimes uses “Judea” for the whole land of the Jews).

## Important Verses Explained

### *Luke 4:18–19* — The Spirit of the Lord Is on Me

> *“‘The Spirit of the Lord is on me, because he has anointed me to preach good news to the poor. He has sent me to heal the broken hearted, to proclaim release to the captives, recovering of sight to the blind, to deliver those who are crushed, and to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord.’”*
>
> — *Luke 4:18–19* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These verses contain the words Jesus read in the synagogue at Nazareth, His hometown. It was the Sabbath, and Jesus had returned from the wilderness full of the Spirit’s power, with news about Him spreading throughout Galilee. In the synagogue service, He stood to read from the Scriptures, and He was handed the scroll of Isaiah. He found *Isaiah 61:1–2* and read it aloud.

“*The Spirit of the Lord is on me, because he has anointed me*” (*v. 18*). In the Old Testament, prophets, priests, and kings were anointed with oil to set them apart for God’s service. Here, the anointing is with the Spirit. Jesus had just been anointed with the Spirit at His baptism (*Luke 3:22*). The title “Messiah” or “Christ” means “anointed one.”

The passage then describes the anointed one’s mission:

“*to preach good news to the poor*” (*v. 18*). “The poor” includes people who are economically poor and also those who are humble, oppressed, and dependent on God. Luke’s Gospel shows special concern for the poor (*Luke 6:20*; *14:13*; *16:19–31*).

“*He has sent me to heal the broken hearted, to proclaim release to the captives*” (*v. 18*). “Release” can mean freedom from prison, but it is also the word used for forgiveness of sins. Jesus brings freedom from every kind of bondage, including sin and demonic oppression.

“*recovering of sight to the blind*” (*v. 18*). Jesus would heal physically blind people (*Luke 18:35–43*) and also open spiritually blind eyes.

“*to deliver those who are crushed*” (*v. 18*). This phrase from *Isaiah 58:6* describes setting free the oppressed and broken.

“*and to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord*” (*v. 19*). This refers to the year of the Lord’s favor, recalling the Year of Jubilee (*Leviticus 25*), when every fifty years debts were cancelled, slaves were freed, and land was returned to its original owners. Jesus was announcing a time of God’s grace and restoration.

After reading, Jesus sat down and said, “Today, this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.” He was claiming that He was the one Isaiah had described.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses serve as Jesus’ mission statement in Luke’s Gospel. Everything He does in the following chapters, preaching good news, healing, freeing people from demons, forgiving sins, welcoming outcasts, fulfills this passage. His ministry addresses the whole person: body, soul, and social situation.

The passage also shows that Jesus’ mission is empowered by the Holy Spirit. Luke emphasizes the Spirit’s role in Jesus’ life, and later in Acts, he shows the same Spirit empowering Jesus’ followers to continue His mission (*Acts 1:8*; *2:1–4*).

Finally, the phrase “the acceptable year of the Lord” points to a time of grace. Jesus stopped reading before “the day of vengeance of our God.” His first coming was focused on salvation, forgiveness, and restoration. Christians understand that judgment will come at His return, but now is the time of God’s favor. As Paul writes, “*Behold, now is the acceptable time. Behold, now is the day of salvation*” (*2 Corinthians 6:2*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses invite believers to receive Jesus’ good news personally. Whether they are poor in resources or in spirit, broken-hearted, captive to sin or addiction, blind to God’s truth, or crushed by life, Jesus came to bring them freedom and healing. They can come to Him with their needs.

They also show believers what it means to follow Jesus. If Jesus’ mission focused on the poor, the broken, the captive, and the oppressed, His followers should care about these people too. Churches and believers can share the good news in words while also showing compassion through practical care, healing, and efforts to free people from bondage.

Finally, these verses remind believers that they serve in the power of the Spirit. Jesus’ mission was empowered by the Spirit, and believers’ service must be as well. They can depend on the Holy Spirit rather than on their own strength as they seek to share Christ’s love with others.

### *Luke 4:26–27* — Mercy for the Widow of Zarephath and Naaman

> *“Elijah was sent to none of them, except to Zarephath, in the land of Sidon, to a woman who was a widow. There were many lepers in Israel in the time of Elisha the prophet, yet not one of them was cleansed, except Naaman, the Syrian.”*
>
> — *Luke 4:26–27* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These verses come at the turning point of Jesus’ sermon in Nazareth. Jesus had read from Isaiah and declared that the prophecy was fulfilled in Him. At first, the people spoke well of Him and were amazed at His gracious words. But they also questioned how Joseph’s son could make such claims. Jesus perceived that they wanted Him to perform miracles in Nazareth as He had in Capernaum, and He said, “No prophet is acceptable in his hometown.”

Then Jesus gave two examples from the Old Testament. First, during the time of the prophet Elijah, there was a terrible famine in Israel lasting three and a half years. There were many widows in Israel, yet “*Elijah was sent to none of them, except to Zarephath, in the land of Sidon, to a woman who was a widow*” (*v. 26*). Zarephath was a town in Phoenicia, Gentile territory. God sent Elijah to a Gentile widow, who cared for him and whose son he raised from the dead (*1 Kings 17:8–24*).

Second, during the time of the prophet Elisha, “*There were many lepers in Israel*” (*v. 27*), yet none of them was healed “*except Naaman, the Syrian*” (*v. 27*). Naaman was the commander of the army of Aram (Syria), an enemy nation. Through Elisha, God healed Naaman of his leprosy after he washed in the Jordan River (*2 Kings 5:1–14*).

Jesus’ point was that when Israel rejected God’s prophets, God showed mercy to Gentiles who responded in faith. The people of Nazareth were rejecting Jesus, and His words implied that God’s blessings might go to outsiders instead.

The reaction was immediate and violent. The people were filled with rage, drove Jesus out of town, and tried to throw Him off a cliff. They were angry that Jesus suggested God’s favor might extend to Gentiles, and that their own familiarity with Him might lead them to miss what God was doing.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses reveal that God’s mercy has always reached beyond Israel’s boundaries. Even in the Old Testament, God showed kindness to Gentiles like the widow of Zarephath and Naaman. This anticipates the gospel’s spread to all nations, a major theme in Luke and Acts. Simeon had called Jesus “*a light for revelation to the nations*” (*Luke 2:32*).

They also show the danger of assuming special privilege. The people of Nazareth thought they had a special claim on Jesus because He grew up among them. They expected Him to benefit their town. Jesus challenged this attitude. God’s grace is not owed to anyone because of their background, nationality, or familiarity with religious things.

Finally, the people’s violent reaction foreshadows Jesus’ rejection and death. Rejected in His hometown at the beginning of His ministry, He would be rejected in Jerusalem at the end. Yet even rejection could not stop God’s purposes; Jesus passed through the crowd and continued His mission.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses challenge believers to examine whether they assume God’s favor belongs only to people like them. Churches can become comfortable with insiders and resistant to outsiders. Jesus’ examples remind believers that God delights to show mercy to unexpected people, including those from different cultures, nations, and backgrounds.

They also warn against familiarity breeding contempt. People who have grown up in church or around Christianity may take Jesus for granted, as the people of Nazareth did. Believers can ask God to keep their hearts open and responsive, so that familiarity never blinds them to His work.

Finally, these verses encourage believers to rejoice when God works among people they did not expect. Instead of resenting God’s mercy to outsiders, they can celebrate it and participate in sharing God’s love with everyone.

### *Luke 4:43* — “I Must Preach the Good News to Other Cities Also”

> *“But he said to them, ‘I must preach the good news of God’s Kingdom to the other cities also. For this reason I have been sent.’”*
>
> — *Luke 4:43* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse comes at the end of an extraordinary day in Capernaum. Jesus had taught with authority in the synagogue, cast out a demon, healed Simon’s mother-in-law, and then, after sunset, healed many sick people, laying His hands on each one. Demons came out of many. The whole town was amazed.

At daybreak, Jesus went to a solitary place. The crowds searched for Him and, when they found Him, “*held on to him, so that he wouldn’t go away from them*” (*v. 42*). They wanted Him to stay in Capernaum, perhaps to keep healing and teaching them. It would have been natural for Jesus to settle where He was so welcomed.

But Jesus said, “*I must preach the good news of God’s Kingdom to the other cities also. For this reason I have been sent*” (*v. 43*).

The word “must” expresses divine necessity. Jesus’ mission was determined by the Father, not by popular demand. “Preach the good news” connects with the Isaiah passage He read in Nazareth: He was anointed to preach good news. This is the first time Luke uses the phrase “the kingdom of God,” which becomes the central theme of Jesus’ teaching. The kingdom is God’s reign, His saving rule breaking into the world through Jesus. “For this reason I have been sent” shows that Jesus understood Himself as sent by God with a specific purpose.

Notice also the contrast between Nazareth and Capernaum. Nazareth tried to kill Jesus; Capernaum tried to keep Him. Both, in different ways, tried to control Him. But Jesus followed His Father’s purpose, not the crowd’s wishes.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that Jesus’ priority was preaching the good news of the kingdom. His healings and miracles were important; they demonstrated the kingdom’s power and showed God’s compassion. But they served a larger purpose: announcing that God’s reign had arrived and calling people to respond. Jesus did not want to be known only as a healer.

It also shows that Jesus’ mission was directed by the Father, not by popularity. The crowds wanted Him to stay; the Father had sent Him to other towns. Jesus regularly withdrew to pray (*Luke 5:16*), and prayer kept Him focused on His mission. Mark’s parallel account mentions that Jesus had gone out early to pray before saying these words (*Mark 1:35–38*).

Finally, the verse reveals the expansive nature of the gospel. Jesus’ message was not meant to stay in one place. It was meant to spread to other towns, and eventually, through His followers, to all nations. This anticipates the mission of the church described in Acts.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to keep the good news at the center of their lives and ministries. Churches and Christians do many good things, but proclaiming the good news of God’s kingdom should remain central. Practical care and compassion are important, and they are most powerful when connected to the message of Jesus.

It also encourages believers to be guided by God’s purposes rather than by the expectations of others. Even good opportunities and popularity can pull people away from what God has called them to do. Through prayer, believers can discern God’s direction and have the courage to follow it.

Finally, this verse reminds believers that the gospel is meant to spread. Believers can look beyond their own community, supporting and participating in efforts to share the good news with other towns, cities, and nations.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Luke 4* shows Jesus beginning His ministry in the power of the Holy Spirit. He resisted temptation in the wilderness by relying on God’s Word, and He launched His mission by declaring that the Spirit had anointed Him to bring good news to the poor and freedom to the oppressed. Believers can rely on the same Spirit to help them resist temptation and serve others faithfully.

The temptation account reminds believers that spiritual battles are real and ongoing. The devil left Jesus “until another time.” Believers should not assume that one victory means the struggle is over. Staying close to God through Scripture and prayer prepares them for future tests.

The sermon at Nazareth calls believers to embrace Jesus’ mission. He came for the poor, the broken-hearted, the captive, the blind, and the oppressed. His followers can share His good news in words and show His compassion in action. At the same time, the people of Nazareth’s rejection warns against familiarity and against assuming that God’s favor belongs only to people like us. God delights to show mercy to outsiders, and believers should rejoice in that.

The healings in Capernaum show Jesus’ authority over evil and sickness, and His personal care for each individual. Finally, His decision to leave Capernaum shows the priority of preaching the kingdom and of following God’s direction rather than popular demand. Believers can keep the gospel central, seek God’s guidance in prayer, and help the good news spread beyond their own community.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for resisting the devil in the wilderness and for relying on God’s Word. Help me to stand firm when I am tempted, knowing that the struggle continues, and fill me with the Holy Spirit as You were filled. Thank You for coming to bring good news to the poor, healing to the broken-hearted, freedom to captives, sight to the blind, and liberty to the oppressed. Bring that freedom and healing into my life.

Keep me from the familiarity and pride that made Your hometown reject You. Help me to rejoice when You show mercy to people I would not expect. Give me Your compassion for those who are suffering, and help me to care for them in Your name. Keep the good news of Your kingdom at the center of my life, and guide me by Your Spirit to go where You send me. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
