Luke · Chapter 5 of 24

# Luke — Chapter 5

Chapter Theme: From Empty Nets to Full Lives: Jesus Calls Sinners

[Read Luke 5 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/LUK05.htm)

Main Teaching

After a fruitless night of fishing, Simon obeys Jesus’ word, catches an overwhelming number of fish, and falls at Jesus’ knees confessing his sinfulness; Jesus calls him to catch people instead. Jesus cleanses a leper, regularly withdraws to pray, forgives and heals a paralyzed man, calls the tax collector Levi, and eats with sinners. He explains that He came for the sick, and that the new life He brings cannot be squeezed into old patterns.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Luke 5* continues Jesus’ early ministry in Galilee. In chapter 4, He announced His mission in Nazareth, was rejected there, and then taught and healed in Capernaum with great authority. Now Luke shows Jesus calling His first disciples and encountering people at the margins: a fisherman who feels unworthy, a man with leprosy, a paralyzed man, and a tax collector. At the same time, the Pharisees and teachers of the law begin to watch Jesus closely and raise objections. Several of these stories also appear in Matthew and Mark (see *Matthew 8:3*, *Matthew 9:6*, *Matthew 9:13*, *Mark 2:5*, and *Mark 2:22*), but Luke tells the calling of Peter in a distinctive way that is found only in his Gospel.

### The Miraculous Catch and the Call of Simon (*5:1–11*)

Jesus was standing beside the “*lake of Gennesaret*” (*v. 1*), Luke’s name for the Sea of Galilee, taken from the fertile plain on its northwest shore. The crowd was pressing in on Him to hear the word of God. He saw two boats at the water’s edge; the fishermen had left them and were washing their nets. Fishermen on the lake typically worked at night, when fish came closer to the surface, and cleaned and repaired their nets in the morning.

Jesus got into one of the boats, which belonged to Simon (later called Peter), and asked him to push out a little from shore. Then He sat down and taught the crowd from the boat. Sitting in a boat slightly offshore allowed His voice to carry over the water to the people on the beach.

When He finished speaking, He said to Simon, “*Put out into the deep and let down your nets for a catch*” (*v. 4*). Simon answered with honest reluctance, then obedience. This is studied below. They caught so many fish that their nets began to tear. They signaled their partners in the other boat to come help, and they filled both boats so full that they began to sink.

When Simon Peter saw this, he fell at Jesus’ knees and said, “*Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, Lord*” (*v. 8*). This response is studied below. Simon and all his companions, including James and John, the sons of Zebedee, were astonished. Jesus said to Simon, “*Don’t be afraid. From now on you will be catching people alive*” (*v. 10*). The phrase “catching people alive” uses a word that means to capture alive, rather than to kill, as fish were. Simon would gather people into God’s kingdom for life.

They brought their boats to shore, “*left everything, and followed him*” (*v. 11*). Having just made the greatest catch of their careers, they left it all behind. The miracle that could have made them wealthy became the moment they gave up their business to follow Jesus.

(Mark and Matthew record a briefer call of these fishermen by the lake, studied at *Matthew 4:19* and *Mark 1:16–20*. Luke’s fuller account may describe the same event in more detail or a related occasion. Many readers see Luke’s version as explaining why the fishermen were willing to follow so readily: they had witnessed Jesus’ power and been confronted with their own unworthiness.)

### Cleansing a Man With Leprosy (*5:12–16*)

In one of the towns, a man “*full of leprosy*” (*v. 12*) came to Jesus. Luke the physician notes the severity of the disease. The man fell on his face and begged, “Lord, if you want to, you can make me clean.” Jesus reached out, touched him, and said, “I want to. Be made clean.” Immediately the leprosy left him. (This healing is studied at *Matthew 8:3*.) Jesus told him not to tell anyone but to show himself to the priest and offer the sacrifices Moses commanded as a testimony.

Despite this, news about Jesus spread even more, and large crowds came to hear Him and to be healed. Then Luke adds a sentence that reveals something essential about Jesus’ life: “*But he withdrew himself into the desert and prayed*” (*v. 16*). This is studied below.

### Forgiving and Healing a Paralyzed Man (*5:17–26*)

One day as Jesus was teaching, Pharisees and teachers of the law were sitting there. They had come from every village of Galilee, Judea, and Jerusalem. Their presence shows that Jesus’ ministry was attracting the attention of religious authorities from far and wide. Luke adds, “*The power of the Lord was with him to heal them*” (*v. 17*).

Some men brought a paralyzed man on a mat, but they could not get him in because of the crowd. So they went up on the roof and lowered him through the tiles, right in front of Jesus. Luke mentions “tiles,” which suggests a roof of clay tiles, a type more familiar to his Greek readers than the packed-earth roofs common in Galilee.

Seeing their faith, Jesus said, “*Man, your sins are forgiven you*” (*v. 20*). The scribes and Pharisees began reasoning that this was blasphemy, since only God can forgive sins. Jesus knew their thoughts and asked which was easier to say: “Your sins are forgiven” or “Get up and walk.” To prove that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins, He told the man to get up, take his mat, and go home. Immediately the man stood up, picked up the mat, and went home “*glorifying God*” (*v. 25*). Everyone was amazed and gave glory to God, saying, “*We have seen strange things today*” (*v. 26*). (This event is studied at *Matthew 9:6* and *Mark 2:5*.)

### The Call of Levi (*5:27–32*)

Jesus went out and saw a tax collector named Levi sitting at his tax booth. He said, “Follow me!” Luke adds that Levi “*left everything*” (*v. 28*). For a tax collector, this was a dramatic step. Fishermen could return to their boats, but a tax collector who abandoned his post could not easily get it back.

Levi then held a great banquet for Jesus at his house, with a large crowd of tax collectors and others. The Pharisees and their scribes complained to Jesus’ disciples: “*Why do you eat and drink with the tax collectors and sinners?*” (*v. 30*) Jesus answered, “*Those who are healthy have no need for a physician, but those who are sick do*” (*v. 31*). Then He added, “*I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners, to repentance*” (*v. 32*). Luke alone includes the words “to repentance,” making clear that Jesus’ welcome of sinners was an invitation to turn to God and be changed. (This saying is studied at *Matthew 9:13*.)

### The Question About Fasting and the New Wine (*5:33–39*)

The Pharisees then said that John’s disciples and their own disciples often fasted and prayed, but Jesus’ disciples ate and drank. Jesus answered that the friends of the bridegroom cannot fast while He is with them, but the days would come when the bridegroom would be taken away, and then they would fast.

He told a parable about new and old. No one tears a patch from a new garment to fix an old one; doing so ruins the new garment, and the patch does not match the old. No one puts new wine into old wineskins, or the skins will burst. New wine must go into new wineskins. (This saying is studied at *Mark 2:22*.)

Luke alone adds a final saying: “*No man having drunk old wine immediately desires new, for he says, ‘The old is better.’*” (*v. 39*) This is a gentle, perhaps humorous, observation about human nature. People who are used to the old often resist the new, preferring what is familiar. Jesus was explaining why many religious people resisted His message. They were comfortable with their traditions and did not want the new thing God was doing. The saying is both a warning and an expression of understanding: resistance to change is natural, but it can cause people to miss God’s work.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Luke 5:5* — “*But at Your Word I Will Let Down the Net*” (*v. 5*)

> *“Simon answered him, ‘Master, we worked all night and caught nothing; but at your word I will let down the net.’”*
>
> — *Luke 5:5* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse records Simon’s response when Jesus told him to go out into deep water and let down his nets for a catch. The setting is important. Simon was a professional fisherman on the Sea of Galilee. He and his partners had worked hard all night, the best time for fishing, and had caught nothing. Now it was morning, and they were cleaning their nets, ready to go home. Jesus had just used Simon’s boat as a platform to teach the crowds.

When Jesus told him to put out into the deep and let down the nets, Simon answered, “*Master, we worked all night and caught nothing*” (*v. 5*). This was an honest statement of the facts. Fishing in the daytime, in deep water, after a night of failure, made no sense from a fisherman’s perspective. Jesus was a teacher, perhaps a carpenter’s son, not a fisherman. Simon could have dismissed His instruction.

But Simon continued, “*but at your word I will let down the net*” (*v. 5*). He obeyed, not because the instruction made sense to him, but because Jesus said it. Simon called Jesus “Master,” a word used for a person in authority, such as a commander or overseer. Luke uses this word only on the lips of disciples.

The result was overwhelming. They caught so many fish that their nets began to break, and they needed their partners’ help. Both boats were filled so full that they began to sink.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that obedience to Jesus’ word is the path to fruitfulness. Simon’s own expertise and effort had produced nothing. But when he obeyed Jesus’ word, even against his own judgment, the result was abundance. This echoes Jesus’ teaching that apart from Him, His followers can do nothing (*John 15:5*).

It also shows that faith and honest doubt can coexist. Simon did not pretend that Jesus’ instruction made sense. He stated his reservations honestly. But he chose to obey anyway. Faith is not the absence of questions; it is trust that acts on Jesus’ word even when questions remain.

Finally, the abundant catch is a picture of what Jesus would do through Simon’s life. Jesus told him that from now on he would catch people. In *Acts 2*, after Peter preached on the day of Pentecost, about three thousand people believed and were baptized, an abundant “catch” that came through obedience to Jesus.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers who feel that their efforts have been fruitless. Many people work hard in their jobs, families, ministries, or personal growth and see little result. Jesus’ word to Simon invites them to keep listening to Him and to obey, trusting that He can bring fruit where their efforts alone have failed.

It also invites believers to obey Jesus even when His instructions do not make sense to them. Scripture sometimes calls believers to forgive when it seems foolish, to give when they feel they have little, or to wait when they want to act. Like Simon, they can say, “At your word, I will,” trusting that Jesus knows better than they do.

Finally, this verse shows that honest prayer is welcome. Believers can tell Jesus their doubts and frustrations, as Simon did, and then choose to trust and obey. Honesty and obedience can go together.

### *Luke 5:8* — “*Depart From Me, for I Am a Sinful Man*” (*v. 8*)

> *“But Simon Peter, when he saw it, fell down at Jesus’ knees, saying, ‘Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, Lord.’”*
>
> — *Luke 5:8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse records Simon Peter’s reaction to the miraculous catch of fish. Moments earlier, Simon had told Jesus that he and his partners had fished all night and caught nothing, but he obeyed Jesus’ instruction to let down the nets again. The result was a catch so large that the nets began to tear and two boats began to sink.

Simon’s response was not excitement about the profit or pride in the catch. Instead, “*when he saw it, fell down at Jesus’ knees*” (*v. 8*). Falling to his knees in a crowded, fish-filled boat shows how overwhelmed he was. He said, “*Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, Lord*” (*v. 8*).

Notice that Simon changed how he addressed Jesus. In verse 5, he called Him “Master.” Now he called Him “Lord.” Something about the miracle revealed to Simon that Jesus was more than a teacher. He sensed God’s presence and power in Jesus, and that awareness made him painfully aware of his own sinfulness.

This kind of reaction appears elsewhere in Scripture. When Isaiah saw the Lord in the temple, he cried, “*Woe is me! For I am undone, because I am a man of unclean lips*” (*Isaiah 6:5*). When people encounter God’s holiness, they become aware of their own unworthiness.

Simon asked Jesus to leave him, not because he did not want Jesus, but because he felt unworthy to be near Him. Jesus did not leave. Instead, He said, “*Don’t be afraid. From now on you will be catching people alive*” (*v. 10*). Jesus responded to Simon’s confession of sin not with rejection but with a calling.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that a true encounter with Jesus reveals both His holiness and our sinfulness. Simon did not need a sermon about sin; he simply saw Jesus’ power and recognized his own unworthiness. Genuine spiritual awakening often begins with this kind of humbling realization.

It also shows Jesus’ grace. Simon asked Jesus to go away, but Jesus drew closer and called him into His service. Jesus did not wait for Simon to become worthy before calling him. He called him in his unworthiness. This is the pattern of grace throughout Scripture: God calls sinners, forgives them, and uses them for His purposes.

Finally, Simon’s story shows that those who know their sinfulness are often the ones God uses most. Later in Luke, Jesus says that one who has been forgiven much loves much (*Luke 7:47*). Peter would fail again, denying Jesus three times, and again Jesus would restore him and use him to lead the early church.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to approach Jesus with humility. Recognizing one’s sinfulness is not a sign of weak faith; it is often the beginning of genuine faith. Believers can come to Jesus honestly, acknowledging their sins, and trust that He responds with grace.

It also encourages those who feel too sinful to be used by God. Many people think they must clean up their lives before God can use them. Simon’s story shows that Jesus calls people in their unworthiness and transforms them. The proper response is not to push Jesus away but to receive His call.

Finally, this verse shows that fear can be replaced by purpose. Jesus told Simon, “Don’t be afraid,” and then gave him a mission. Believers who feel unworthy or afraid can hear Jesus’ words of reassurance and step into the purpose He has for them.

### *Luke 5:16* — Jesus Withdrew to Pray

> *“But he withdrew himself into the desert and prayed.”*
>
> — *Luke 5:16* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse appears in the middle of a period of great popularity in Jesus’ ministry. He had just healed a man full of leprosy and told him not to tell anyone. Instead, news about Jesus spread even more, and “*great multitudes came together to hear and to be healed by him of their infirmities*” (*v. 15*). The demands on Jesus were increasing. People came from everywhere, wanting healing and teaching.

Then Luke adds, “*But he withdrew himself into the desert and prayed*” (*v. 16*). The word “but” shows a contrast: while crowds were gathering, Jesus withdrew. “Desert” refers to lonely, uninhabited places, away from towns and crowds.

The verb forms in Greek suggest that this was a regular habit, not a one-time event. A natural way to translate it is, “But he would often withdraw to lonely places and pray.” Jesus made a practice of seeking solitude with His Father, especially when the demands of ministry were greatest.

Luke emphasizes Jesus’ prayer life more than any other Gospel writer. He records Jesus praying at His baptism (*3:21*), before choosing the twelve apostles (*6:12*), before Peter’s confession (*9:18*), at the transfiguration (*9:28–29*), before teaching the Lord’s Prayer (*11:1*), in Gethsemane (*22:41–44*), and on the cross (*23:34*, 46). Prayer was the foundation of Jesus’ ministry.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals that Jesus, though He was the Son of God, lived in dependence on His Father through prayer. His power to heal and teach flowed from His relationship with the Father. If Jesus needed regular time alone with God, His followers need it even more.

It also shows that popularity and success can be spiritually dangerous. Crowds can create pressure, distraction, and the temptation to measure success by numbers or approval. Jesus’ habit of withdrawing kept Him focused on His Father’s will rather than on public demands. Prayer was His anchor in the midst of activity.

Finally, the verse shows the importance of rhythms in spiritual life. Jesus moved between public ministry and private prayer. Both were essential. Service flowed from communion with God, and communion with God prepared Him for service.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to make prayer a regular habit, not just something done in emergencies. Setting aside consistent time to be alone with God, away from distractions, helps believers stay connected to Him and receive strength and direction.

It is especially relevant for busy seasons. When responsibilities increase, prayer is often the first thing to be neglected. Jesus’ example shows that busy times are when prayer is most needed. Believers can protect time for prayer, even when it feels like there is too much to do.

Finally, this verse invites believers to seek solitude. Modern life is filled with noise, screens, and constant connection. Finding a quiet place and time, whether early in the morning, during a walk, or in a quiet room, can create space to hear God and be renewed by Him.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Luke 5* shows Jesus calling unlikely people into His kingdom: a fisherman who knew he was sinful, a man with leprosy who was excluded from community, a paralyzed man who could not come on his own, and a tax collector who was despised by others. In every case, Jesus responded with grace, power, and a call to new life. Believers can take encouragement that Jesus calls people as they are and transforms them.

The miraculous catch teaches that obedience to Jesus’ word leads to fruitfulness, even when His instructions seem unreasonable. Believers can bring their honest doubts to Him and then choose to obey, trusting that He knows better. The catch also shows that encountering Jesus’ power reveals human sinfulness, and that Jesus meets confession with mercy and calling rather than rejection.

Jesus’ habit of withdrawing to pray provides a model for balancing activity and devotion. In busy seasons especially, believers need time alone with God to stay grounded and to discern His will. Prayer is not a luxury but the foundation of fruitful service.

The call of Levi and the banquet with sinners show that Jesus came for those who know they need Him. Believers can welcome people who feel far from God and invite them to repentance and new life, rather than keeping them at a distance. Finally, the sayings about new wine remind believers that Jesus’ new life cannot be contained in old patterns, and that people often prefer the familiar. Believers can ask God to keep them open to His work, even when it challenges their comfort.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for meeting Simon in his empty boat and filling his nets beyond what he could imagine. When my efforts seem fruitless, help me to listen to Your word and to obey, even when I do not understand. Like Simon, I confess that I am a sinful person. Thank You that You do not turn away from sinners, but draw near and call us to follow You.

Teach me to follow Your example of withdrawing to pray, especially when life is busy and demanding. Thank You for touching the untouchable, forgiving the paralyzed man, and calling Levi. Help me to welcome those who feel far from You and to invite them to repentance and new life. Keep me from clinging to old patterns when You are doing something new, and make my heart a fresh wineskin for Your new life. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Luke · Chapter 6 of 24

# Luke — Chapter 6

Chapter Theme: The Sermon on the Plain: Kingdom Blessings and Radical Mercy

[Read Luke 6 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/LUK06.htm)

Main Teaching

Jesus faces criticism over the Sabbath, heals a man’s withered hand, and spends a whole night in prayer before choosing twelve apostles. Coming down to a level place among a great crowd, He pronounces blessings on the poor, hungry, grieving, and persecuted and woes on the rich and comfortable. He calls His followers to love enemies, show mercy as the Father is merciful, give generously, avoid hypocritical judgment, and build their lives by doing what He says.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Luke 6* contains two Sabbath controversies, the choosing of the Twelve, and Jesus’ great sermon often called the Sermon on the Plain, because Luke says Jesus delivered it on “*a level place*” (*v. 17*). This sermon has much in common with Matthew’s Sermon on the Mount (*Matthew 5–7*). Jesus likely taught similar themes on many occasions, and the Gospel writers selected and arranged His teaching for their own purposes. Luke’s version is shorter and more direct, and it includes woes alongside the blessings. (Several parallel teachings are studied in depth in Matthew’s commentary: the Sabbath at *Matthew 12:8*, the Beatitudes at *Matthew 5:3*, love for enemies at *Matthew 5:44*, the Golden Rule at *Matthew 7:12*, judging at *Matthew 7:1*, and the wise builder at *Matthew 7:24*.)

### Lord of the Sabbath (*6:1–11*)

On a Sabbath, Jesus’ disciples were walking through grain fields, picking heads of grain, rubbing them in their hands to remove the husks, and eating. Some Pharisees objected that they were breaking the Sabbath by harvesting and threshing. Jesus reminded them that David and his men ate the consecrated bread from God’s house when they were hungry (*1 Samuel 21:1–6*). Then He declared, “*The Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath*” (*v. 5*).

On another Sabbath, Jesus was teaching in a synagogue where there was a man whose “*right hand was withered*” (*v. 6*). Luke, the physician, specifies that it was the right hand, the hand most people would need for work. The scribes and Pharisees watched closely to see whether Jesus would heal on the Sabbath, so they could accuse Him. Jesus knew their thoughts. He told the man to stand up in front of everyone. Then He asked, “*Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good, or to do harm? To save a life, or to kill?*” (*v. 9*) He looked around at them all and told the man to stretch out his hand. It was completely restored.

The religious leaders “*were filled with rage*” (*v. 11*) and began discussing what they might do to Jesus. (*Mark 3:5* records Jesus’ anger and grief at their hardened hearts.)

### Choosing the Twelve After a Night of Prayer (*6:12–16*)

Luke then records something found only in his Gospel: “*In these days, he went out to the mountain to pray, and he continued all night in prayer to God*” (*v. 12*). This is studied below. When morning came, Jesus called His disciples and chose twelve of them, whom He named apostles, meaning “those who are sent.”

Luke’s list includes Simon Peter, Andrew, James, John, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Thomas, James son of Alphaeus, Simon the Zealot, Judas son of James (called Thaddaeus in Matthew and Mark), and Judas Iscariot, “*who also became a traitor*” (*v. 16*). The phrase “became a traitor” suggests that Judas was not a traitor when chosen, but became one later.

### The Crowd on the Plain (*6:17–19*)

Jesus came down with the Twelve and stood on a level place. A large crowd of His disciples was there, along with a great number of people from all over Judea, from Jerusalem, and from the coastal region of Tyre and Sidon, a Gentile area. They came to hear Him and to be healed. Those troubled by unclean spirits were healed, and the whole crowd tried to touch Him, “*for power came out of him and healed them all*” (*v. 19*). The scene shows Jesus surrounded by needy people from many backgrounds, including Gentiles, as He begins His teaching.

### Blessings and Woes (*6:20–26*)

Looking at His disciples, Jesus said, “*Blessed are you who are poor, for God’s Kingdom is yours*” (*v. 20*). He continued with blessings on those who are hungry now, who weep now, and who are hated, excluded, insulted, and rejected because of the Son of Man. These blessings are studied below.

Then, unlike Matthew’s version, Luke records four woes that mirror the four blessings: “*But woe to you who are rich! For you have received your consolation*” (*v. 24*). Woe to those who are well fed now, for they will be hungry. Woe to those who laugh now, for they will mourn and weep. And woe when everyone speaks well of you, for that is how their ancestors treated the false prophets.

A “woe” is an expression of grief and warning, used by the Old Testament prophets to announce coming judgment (*Isaiah 5:8–23*). Jesus was not saying that wealth, food, or laughter are evil in themselves. He was warning those who find all their comfort in these things now and have no need for God. Their “consolation,” their comfort, is already received in full. By contrast, the poor, hungry, and grieving who look to God will receive His kingdom, His filling, and His joy.

### Love Your Enemies (*6:27–36*)

Jesus then turned to “*you who hear*” (*v. 27*), those who are listening and willing to respond. He commanded, “*love your enemies, do good to those who hate you*” (*v. 27*), and to bless those who curse them and pray for those who mistreat them. He gave examples: turn the other cheek to someone who strikes you, do not withhold your shirt from someone who takes your coat, give to everyone who asks, and do not demand back what is taken. (As discussed at *Matthew 5:44*, these commands address personal retaliation and generosity; they do not require anyone to remain in danger or forbid seeking protection.)

Jesus stated the Golden Rule: “*As you would like people to do to you, do exactly so to them*” (*v. 31*). He explained that loving those who love you, doing good to those who do good to you, and lending to those who will repay you is no different from what sinners do. Instead, His followers should love their enemies, do good, and lend without expecting anything back. Then their reward will be great, and they will be “*children of the Most High; for he is kind toward the unthankful and evil*” (*v. 35*). He concluded with a call to imitate God, studied below: “*Therefore be merciful, even as your Father is also merciful*” (*v. 36*).

### Do Not Judge, and Give Generously (*6:37–42*)

Jesus continued: “*Don’t judge, and you won’t be judged. Don’t condemn, and you won’t be condemned. Set free, and you will be set free*” (*v. 37*). “Set free” can also mean “forgive” or “release.” Then He gave a promise about generosity, studied below.

He told a parable: can a blind person guide a blind person? Both will fall into a pit. A disciple is not above the teacher, but everyone who is fully trained will become like the teacher. This means that disciples will resemble their teachers. Following a blind guide leads to blindness; following Jesus leads to becoming like Him.

He then warned against hypocritical judging, using the image of someone with a beam in his own eye trying to remove a speck from his brother’s eye. First, remove the beam from your own eye, and then you will see clearly to help your brother.

### Good Fruit and a Firm Foundation (*6:43–49*)

A good tree does not produce bad fruit, and a bad tree does not produce good fruit. Each tree is known by its fruit. People do not gather figs from thorns or grapes from briers. In the same way, a good person brings good things out of the good stored up in the heart, and an evil person brings evil things out of evil stored up in the heart, “*for out of the abundance of the heart, his mouth speaks*” (*v. 45*).

Jesus asked, “*Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and don’t do the things which I say?*” (*v. 46*) Calling Jesus “Lord” while ignoring His teaching is a contradiction. He ended with a parable: everyone who comes to Him, hears His words, and does them is like a man who dug deep and laid a foundation on rock. When a flood came, the house stood firm. But the one who hears and does not obey is like a man who built a house on the ground without a foundation. When the flood came, it collapsed, and its destruction was great. Luke’s version emphasizes digging deep, a detail that suggests effort and commitment in building a life on Jesus’ words.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Luke 6:12* — A Night of Prayer Before Choosing the Twelve

> *“In these days, he went out to the mountain to pray, and he continued all night in prayer to God.”*
>
> — *Luke 6:12* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse describes what Jesus did before one of the most important decisions of His ministry: choosing the twelve apostles. It comes right after conflict with the religious leaders. Jesus had healed a man with a withered hand on the Sabbath, and the scribes and Pharisees were “*filled with rage*” (*v. 11*), discussing what they might do to Him. Opposition was growing.

Luke writes, “*In these days, he went out to the mountain to pray, and he continued all night in prayer to God*” (*v. 12*). Mountains in Scripture are often places of encounter with God. Moses received the law on Mount Sinai; Elijah met God on Mount Horeb. Jesus went to a mountain to be alone with His Father.

He prayed “all night.” This was not a quick prayer but an extended time of communion with God, lasting until morning. Only Luke records this detail. The phrase “prayer to God” emphasizes the focus of His prayer: He was seeking His Father.

The next verse explains what happened after the night of prayer: “*When it was day, he called his disciples, and from them he chose twelve, whom he also named apostles*” (*v. 13*). Jesus chose the Twelve after a night of prayer. These men would be His closest companions, would carry His message after His resurrection, and would lay the foundation of the church. The choice was so important that Jesus sought His Father’s guidance in extended prayer.

Interestingly, among those chosen after this night of prayer was Judas Iscariot, who would betray Jesus. Jesus’ prayerful choice did not mean that everything would go smoothly. God’s purposes would be accomplished even through betrayal.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that Jesus made important decisions in dependence on His Father. Though He was the Son of God, He did not act independently. He sought the Father’s will in prayer. In John’s Gospel, Jesus says, “*the Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing*” (*John 5:19*). Prayer was how Jesus aligned His actions with the Father’s will.

It also shows the seriousness of leadership in God’s kingdom. The apostles would be foundational to the church (*Ephesians 2:20*). Jesus did not choose them casually. The early church followed this example, praying before selecting leaders and sending missionaries (*Acts 1:24–26*; *13:2–3*; *14:23*).

Finally, the verse shows that prayer often comes before and during times of opposition. As hostility grew, Jesus withdrew to pray. Prayer gave Him strength, clarity, and peace in the face of conflict.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to pray before making important decisions. Choices about relationships, careers, moves, ministries, and leadership deserve careful prayer. While not every decision requires an all-night prayer vigil, believers can follow Jesus’ example by seeking God’s guidance seriously and patiently.

It also encourages churches to pray when choosing leaders. Selecting pastors, elders, teachers, or ministry leaders should be done prayerfully, seeking God’s will rather than relying only on human judgment or popularity.

Finally, this verse reminds believers that prayer is especially important in times of conflict and pressure. When facing opposition, criticism, or difficult circumstances, they can follow Jesus’ example by withdrawing to pray, seeking God’s strength and wisdom.

### *Luke 6:20–21* — Blessed Are You Who Are Poor

> *“He lifted up his eyes to his disciples, and said: Blessed are you who are poor, for God’s Kingdom is yours. Blessed are you who hunger now, for you will be filled. Blessed are you who weep now, for you will laugh.”*
>
> — *Luke 6:20–21* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These verses begin the Sermon on the Plain. Jesus had just come down from the mountain where He spent the night in prayer and chose the Twelve. He stood on a level place surrounded by a large crowd of disciples and people from all over Judea, Jerusalem, and the Gentile coast of Tyre and Sidon. Many had come to be healed. Luke says Jesus “*lifted up his eyes to his disciples*” (*v. 20*), indicating that He was speaking especially to those who had chosen to follow Him.

He said, “*Blessed are you who are poor, for God’s Kingdom is yours*” (*v. 20*). Notice that Luke records Jesus speaking directly: “you who are poor,” rather than Matthew’s “the poor in spirit.” Luke’s wording emphasizes the actual poverty of many of Jesus’ followers. Many of the people listening were materially poor: fishermen, laborers, the sick, and the marginalized. Jesus told them that God’s kingdom belongs to them.

“*Blessed are you who hunger now, for you will be filled*” (*v. 21*). Many in the crowd knew real hunger. Jesus promised that God would satisfy them. “*Blessed are you who weep now, for you will laugh*” (*v. 21*). Those who grieve now will know joy in God’s kingdom.

The word “now” is important. Jesus contrasts the present situation with the future reversal God will bring. Those who are poor, hungry, and weeping now will be blessed in God’s kingdom. Then, in the woes that follow, Jesus warns those who are rich, full, and laughing now that their situation will be reversed.

These blessings echo Mary’s song in *Luke 1*, where she praised God for filling the hungry with good things and sending the rich away empty (*Luke 1:53*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses reveal God’s special concern for the poor, hungry, and grieving. Throughout Scripture, God shows Himself as the defender of the weak and oppressed. Jesus’ mission statement in *Luke 4:18* was to preach good news to the poor. These blessings fulfill that mission.

They also teach that God’s kingdom reverses the world’s values. The world sees the poor, hungry, and grieving as unfortunate; Jesus calls them blessed, not because poverty is good in itself, but because God is with them and His kingdom belongs to them. Those who are poor often recognize their need for God more readily than those who are comfortable.

Christians have discussed how Luke’s “you who are poor” relates to Matthew’s “poor in spirit.” The two are complementary. Luke emphasizes God’s care for the materially poor; Matthew emphasizes the spiritual humility that recognizes dependence on God. Both are true. God cares about physical poverty, and He also welcomes all who come to Him with empty hands.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses bring hope to those who are poor, hungry, or grieving. God sees them, cares for them, and promises that their situation is not the end of the story. His kingdom belongs to them, and He will satisfy and comfort them.

They also challenge believers to share God’s concern for the poor. If God blesses the poor and hungry, His people should care for them in practical ways: sharing food, resources, and compassion; advocating for justice; and treating the poor with dignity.

Finally, these verses, together with the woes, invite believers to examine where they find their comfort. Wealth, comfort, and popularity can lead people to feel they have no need for God. Believers can hold these things loosely and find their true security in God’s kingdom.

### *Luke 6:36* — Be Merciful as Your Father Is Merciful

> *“Therefore be merciful, even as your Father is also merciful.”*
>
> — *Luke 6:36* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse summarizes Jesus’ teaching about love for enemies. He has just told His followers to love their enemies, do good to those who hate them, bless those who curse them, and pray for those who mistreat them. He has told them to give to everyone who asks, to treat others as they want to be treated, and to lend without expecting anything back. He explained that ordinary people love those who love them, but His followers should go further, loving even the ungrateful and wicked. If they do, they will be “*children of the Most High; for he is kind toward the unthankful and evil*” (*v. 35*).

Then Jesus gives this summary command: “*Therefore be merciful, even as your Father is also merciful*” (*v. 36*).

“Merciful” means showing compassion, kindness, and forgiveness, especially toward those who do not deserve it. Mercy goes beyond fairness; it gives what is needed rather than what is earned.

The standard is God Himself: “*even as your Father is also merciful*” (*v. 36*). God is described throughout Scripture as merciful. When He revealed Himself to Moses, He proclaimed, “*The LORD! The LORD, a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth*” (*Exodus 34:6*). God shows kindness even to those who reject Him, sending sun and rain on the just and the unjust. His children are called to reflect His character.

Matthew’s parallel says, “*you shall be perfect, just as your Father in heaven is perfect*” (*Matthew 5:48*). Luke’s version focuses specifically on mercy, showing that the perfection Jesus calls for is especially the perfection of merciful love.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals that mercy is at the heart of God’s character and the Christian life. Believers have received God’s mercy: forgiveness for their sins, adoption into His family, and grace they did not deserve. Having received mercy, they are called to show mercy to others. Jesus taught, “*Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy*” (*Matthew 5:7*).

The verse also shows that Christian ethics flow from God’s character. Believers do not love enemies merely because it is a rule. They do it because they are children of a merciful Father, and children resemble their parents. The goal of the Christian life is to become like God in His love and mercy.

Finally, the verse sets a high standard that no one can meet perfectly. God’s mercy is infinite; human mercy is limited. This drives believers back to God’s grace, depending on Him to make them more merciful through His Spirit.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse calls believers to show mercy in everyday relationships. Mercy might mean forgiving someone who has wronged them, being patient with someone who is difficult, helping someone who cannot repay, or giving someone a second chance. It means responding to others not according to what they deserve, but according to the mercy God has shown.

It also encourages believers to remember God’s mercy toward them. When it is hard to show mercy to others, believers can reflect on how much God has forgiven them. Gratitude for God’s mercy softens the heart and makes it easier to extend mercy to others.

Finally, mercy requires wisdom. Showing mercy does not mean ignoring wrongdoing, enabling harmful behavior, or remaining in dangerous situations. God’s mercy is joined with His justice and truth. Believers can show mercy while still setting healthy boundaries and seeking justice where needed.

### *Luke 6:38* — Give, and It Will Be Given to You

> *“‘Give, and it will be given to you: good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over, will be given to you. For with the same measure you measure it will be measured back to you.’”*
>
> — *Luke 6:38* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse comes in the section of Jesus’ sermon about mercy and judgment. He has just said, “*Don’t judge, and you won’t be judged. Don’t condemn, and you won’t be condemned. Set free, and you will be set free*” (*v. 37*). Now He adds a positive command and promise: “*Give, and it will be given to you*” (*v. 38*).

Jesus uses a vivid picture from the grain market: “*good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over, will be given to you*” (*v. 38*). In the ancient world, grain was sold by volume, using a measuring container. A generous merchant would fill the measure, press the grain down, shake it to settle it, and then keep filling until it overflowed. The buyer would hold the grain in a fold of his robe, which was used like a large pocket. The image is of extravagant generosity.

Then Jesus states the principle: “*For with the same measure you measure it will be measured back to you*” (*v. 38*). The way people treat others will come back to them. Those who are generous, merciful, and forgiving will receive generosity, mercy, and forgiveness.

In context, “giving” refers broadly to generosity: forgiving, not condemning, showing mercy, and sharing resources. Jesus has just spoken of lending without expecting repayment and giving to anyone who asks. The verse applies to all these forms of generosity.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals God’s generous character. He is not stingy. When His people give, He responds with overflowing generosity. Paul writes, “*he who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly. He who sows bountifully will also reap bountifully*” (*2 Corinthians 9:6*).

It is important to understand this verse correctly. Jesus is not teaching a formula for getting rich by giving money. Some teachers have used this verse to promise financial wealth to those who give to their ministries. That distorts Jesus’ meaning. The context is about mercy, forgiveness, and generosity toward others, not about investment strategies. The reward God gives may include material provision, but it also includes spiritual blessings, joy, relationships, and eternal reward.

The verse also connects with Jesus’ teaching that the measure people use for others will be used for them. Those who judge harshly will be judged; those who show mercy will receive mercy. God responds to people in ways that reflect how they treat others.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to be generous in every area of life. They can be generous with forgiveness, giving others the benefit of the doubt. They can be generous with time, attention, and encouragement. They can be generous with resources, sharing with those in need.

It also frees believers from anxiety about generosity. Many people hesitate to give because they fear they will not have enough. Jesus promises that God will provide abundantly for those who give. Believers can trust Him and give freely.

Finally, believers can guard against misusing this verse. Generosity should flow from love for God and others, not from a desire to get something back. The joy of giving and the knowledge that God sees and rewards are motivations enough. Believers can also be cautious about teachers who use this verse to pressure people into giving for personal gain.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Luke 6* presents a picture of life in God’s kingdom that challenges the world’s values at every point. Jesus begins by praying all night before choosing His apostles, showing believers the importance of seeking God before important decisions and in times of opposition.

The blessings and woes call believers to see life from God’s perspective. God cares deeply for the poor, hungry, grieving, and persecuted, and He warns those who find their comfort in wealth and popularity. Believers can care for those in need, hold their possessions loosely, and find their security in God rather than in comfort or approval.

The command to love enemies and be merciful as the Father is merciful lies at the heart of the chapter. Believers are called to respond to hatred with love, to curses with blessings, and to mistreatment with prayer. This is impossible by human strength alone, but it becomes possible as believers reflect on God’s mercy toward them and depend on His Spirit. Mercy should be joined with wisdom, setting boundaries where necessary while refusing bitterness and revenge.

Jesus’ teaching about judging and giving calls for humility and generosity. Believers should examine themselves before criticizing others, forgive freely, and give generously, trusting God’s overflowing generosity in return. Finally, the parable of the two builders reminds believers that hearing Jesus’ words is not enough. Calling Him “Lord” means doing what He says. Those who dig deep and build on His teaching will stand firm when life’s floods come.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for showing me how to pray before making important decisions. Teach me to seek my Father’s will in prayer, especially when I face difficult choices or opposition. Thank You for blessing the poor, the hungry, and those who weep. Help me to share Your concern for them, and keep me from finding my comfort in wealth, comfort, or the approval of others.

Give me grace to love my enemies, to do good to those who hate me, and to pray for those who mistreat me. Make me merciful as my Father is merciful. Keep me from judging and condemning others, and help me to forgive freely. Make me generous in every way. Above all, do not let me call You “Lord” without doing what You say. Help me to dig deep and build my life on Your words, so that I stand firm when the storms come. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Luke · Chapter 7 of 24

# Luke — Chapter 7

Chapter Theme: Great Faith, Deep Compassion, and Much Love

[Read Luke 7 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/LUK07.htm)

Main Teaching

Jesus heals the servant of a humble Gentile centurion, raises the only son of a grieving widow at Nain, and reassures the imprisoned John the Baptist by pointing to His works of mercy. At a Pharisee’s dinner, a woman known as a sinner washes Jesus’ feet with her tears; Jesus teaches through a parable that those forgiven much love much, declares her sins forgiven, and sends her away in peace.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Luke 7* follows the Sermon on the Plain, in which Jesus taught about loving enemies, showing mercy, and building life on His words. This chapter shows Jesus living out that teaching. He responds to a Gentile soldier, a grieving widow, a doubting prophet, and a sinful woman. Each story reveals His compassion for people at the edges of society and His authority to heal, raise the dead, and forgive sins. The chapter also contrasts those who receive Jesus with humble faith and those who reject Him with proud self-righteousness. (The centurion’s faith is studied at *Matthew 8:10*, and John’s question at *Matthew 11:3*.)

### The Centurion’s Servant (*7:1–10*)

After finishing His sermon, Jesus entered Capernaum. A centurion there had a servant who was “*dear to him*” (*v. 2*) and was sick and near death. A centurion was a Roman officer in charge of about a hundred soldiers. In Galilee, he may have served Herod Antipas, but he was certainly a Gentile.

Luke’s version includes details not found in Matthew. The centurion did not come to Jesus personally at first; he sent Jewish elders to ask Jesus to come and heal his servant. The elders urged Jesus to help, saying, “*He is worthy for you to do this for him, for he loves our nation, and he built our synagogue for us*” (*vv. 4–5*). This Gentile officer had shown respect and generosity toward the Jewish people.

Jesus went with them. But before He reached the house, the centurion sent friends with a message: “*Lord, don’t trouble yourself, for I am not worthy for you to come under my roof*” (*v. 6*). The elders said he was “worthy,” but the centurion said he was “not worthy.” His humility was genuine. He explained that he understood authority. As an officer, he gave orders and they were carried out. He believed Jesus could simply say the word and his servant would be healed.

Jesus was amazed and said to the crowd, “*I tell you, I have not found such great faith, no, not in Israel*” (*v. 9*). When the messengers returned, they found the servant well.

### Raising the Widow’s Son at Nain (*7:11–17*)

Soon afterward, Jesus went to a town called Nain, about six miles southeast of Nazareth. His disciples and a large crowd went with Him. As He approached the town gate, a funeral procession was coming out. The dead man was “*the only born son of his mother, and she was a widow*” (*v. 12*). A large crowd from the town was with her. This scene, found only in Luke, is studied below.

Jesus had compassion on her and said, “*Don’t cry*” (*v. 13*). He went up and touched the bier (an open coffin or stretcher used to carry the body). The bearers stood still. Jesus said, “*Young man, I tell you, arise!*” (*v. 14*) The dead man sat up and began to speak, and Jesus gave him back to his mother.

Everyone was filled with awe and praised God, saying, “*A great prophet has arisen among us!*” (*v. 16*) and “*God has visited his people!*” (*v. 16*) The people may have remembered that the prophet Elijah raised the son of a widow in Zarephath (*1 Kings 17:17–24*), and Elisha raised the son of a woman in Shunem, a village just a few miles from Nain (*2 Kings 4:32–37*). Jesus was acting like the great prophets, but with even greater authority; He raised the young man with a simple command. News about Him spread throughout Judea and the surrounding region.

### John the Baptist’s Question (*7:18–35*)

John’s disciples told him about all these things. John was in prison (*Luke 3:20*). He sent two of his disciples to ask Jesus, “*Are you the one who is coming, or should we look for another?*” (*v. 19*) Luke adds that at that very time Jesus cured many people of diseases, afflictions, and evil spirits, and gave sight to many who were blind. Then He told John’s messengers to report what they had seen and heard: the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the poor have good news preached to them. These were the signs of the Messiah’s age described in Isaiah (*Isaiah 35:5–6*; *61:1*). He added, “*Blessed is he who finds no occasion for stumbling in me*” (*v. 23*).

After John’s messengers left, Jesus spoke to the crowds about John, calling him more than a prophet and the messenger promised in *Malachi 3:1*. No one born of women was greater than John, yet the least in God’s kingdom is greater than he.

Luke adds a comment not found in Matthew: “*When all the people and the tax collectors heard this, they declared God to be just, having been baptized with John’s baptism*” (*v. 29*). Those who had responded to John’s call to repentance acknowledged that God’s way was right. “*But the Pharisees and the lawyers rejected the counsel of God, not being baptized by him themselves*” (*v. 30*). By refusing John’s baptism, they rejected God’s purpose for them.

Jesus compared His generation to children in the marketplace who complain that others will not play their games. John came fasting, and they said he had a demon. Jesus came eating and drinking, and they called Him a glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners. Whatever God sent, they rejected. But “*Wisdom is justified by all her children*” (*v. 35*); those who accept God’s wisdom show that it is right.

### The Sinful Woman at the Pharisee’s House (*7:36–50*)

One of the Pharisees, named Simon, invited Jesus to eat with him. Jesus went and reclined at the table. At formal meals, guests reclined on cushions or couches around a low table, leaning on one elbow with their feet stretched away from the table. Such meals were often semi-public; uninvited people could come in and watch.

A woman in that town “*who was a sinner*” (*v. 37*) learned that Jesus was eating there. Luke does not say what her sin was, but she was known in the town for an immoral life. She brought an alabaster jar of perfume. Standing behind Jesus at His feet, weeping, she began to wet His feet with her tears and wipe them with her hair. She kissed His feet and poured perfume on them. Letting her hair down in public was considered improper for a woman, and her actions would have shocked the guests. (This event is different from the anointing at Bethany shortly before Jesus’ death, recorded in *Matthew 26*, *Mark 14*, and *John 12*.)

Simon the Pharisee thought to himself, “*This man, if he were a prophet, would have perceived who and what kind of woman this is who touches him, that she is a sinner*” (*v. 39*). In Simon’s view, a true prophet would know her reputation and would not allow her to touch Him.

Jesus knew Simon’s thoughts and said, “Simon, I have something to tell you.” He told a parable about two debtors. One owed a moneylender five hundred denarii, about a year and a half’s wages. The other owed fifty denarii. Neither could pay, so the lender cancelled both debts. Jesus asked which would love him more. Simon answered, “*He, I suppose, to whom he forgave the most*” (*v. 43*). Jesus said he had judged correctly.

Then Jesus turned toward the woman and said to Simon, “*Do you see this woman?*” (*v. 44*) This question is studied below. Jesus pointed out that Simon had neglected the customary courtesies of hospitality: he gave no water for Jesus’ feet, no kiss of greeting, and no oil for His head. But the woman had washed His feet with her tears, kissed them continually, and anointed them with perfume.

Then Jesus said, “*Therefore I tell you, her sins, which are many, are forgiven, for she loved much. But one to whom little is forgiven, loves little*” (*v. 47*). This verse is studied below. Jesus told the woman, “*Your sins are forgiven*” (*v. 48*). The other guests began to say among themselves, “*Who is this who even forgives sins?*” (*v. 49*) Jesus said to the woman, “*Your faith has saved you. Go in peace*” (*v. 50*).

## Important Verses Explained

### *Luke 7:13* — Compassion for a Grieving Widow

> *“When the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her and said to her, ‘Don’t cry.’”*
>
> — *Luke 7:13* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse is at the heart of the story of the widow of Nain, found only in Luke’s Gospel. Jesus was approaching the gate of the town of Nain, accompanied by His disciples and a large crowd. At the same time, a funeral procession was coming out of the town. In Jewish custom, burial took place on the same day as death, usually outside the town. Mourners, often including hired flute players and wailing women, would follow the body.

The dead man was “*the only born son of his mother, and she was a widow*” (*v. 12*). Luke’s description reveals the depth of this woman’s tragedy. She had already lost her husband. Now she had lost her only son. In that society, a widow without a son had no one to provide for her or protect her. She faced not only grief but also poverty and vulnerability. A large crowd from the town was with her, showing community sympathy, but no one could change her situation.

Then Luke writes, “*When the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her and said to her, “Don’t cry.”*” (*v. 13*) Several details are significant.

Luke calls Jesus “the Lord” here, the first time he uses this title by itself in his own narration. It emphasizes Jesus’ divine authority, which He is about to demonstrate.

“*saw her*” (*v. 13*). Jesus noticed her. In the large crowd, His attention was on the grieving mother.

“*he had compassion on her*” (*v. 13*). The Greek word means a deep, gut-level feeling of pity and love. No one asked Jesus to help. The widow did not request a miracle. Jesus acted entirely out of His own compassion.

“*Don’t cry*” (*v. 13*). These words could sound harsh if spoken by anyone else. But Jesus said them because He was about to remove the cause of her tears.

Jesus then touched the bier, which would normally make a person ritually unclean, and commanded the young man to rise. The man sat up and began to speak, and Jesus “*gave him to his mother*” (*v. 15*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals the compassionate heart of Jesus. He sees human suffering and is moved by it. His miracles were not merely demonstrations of power; they flowed from love. This compassion reflects the character of God, who is described as the defender of widows (*Psalm 68:5*).

The story also shows Jesus’ authority over death. He did not pray for the young man to be raised, as Elijah and Elisha did; He commanded him to rise. This anticipates Jesus’ own resurrection and His promise to raise all who belong to Him. Death is not the final word when Jesus is present.

Finally, the phrase “gave him to his mother” shows that Jesus restored not only life but also relationship and security. The widow’s future was restored along with her son. Jesus cares about the whole person and their circumstances.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse brings comfort to those who are grieving. Jesus sees their sorrow and has compassion on them. While He may not reverse every loss in this life, He promises that death will not have the final word. Those who belong to Him will be raised, and He will wipe away every tear (*Revelation 21:4*).

It also invites believers to notice those who are suffering. Jesus saw the widow in the crowd. Believers can pay attention to people who are grieving, lonely, or vulnerable, especially widows, the elderly, and those who have lost family support, and respond with compassion and practical help. James writes that pure religion includes caring for widows in their affliction (*James 1:27*).

Finally, this verse reminds believers that Jesus acts out of compassion even when people do not ask. God’s grace often comes before we seek it. Believers can trust that Jesus cares about them even when they are too overwhelmed to pray.

### *Luke 7:44* — “*Do You See This Woman?*” (*v. 44*)

> *“Turning to the woman, he said to Simon, Do you see this woman? I entered into your house, and you gave me no water for my feet, but she has wet my feet with her tears, and wiped them with the hair of her head.”*
>
> — *Luke 7:44* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse comes in the middle of a tense dinner at the home of Simon, a Pharisee who had invited Jesus to eat with him. During the meal, a woman known in the town as a sinner came in and began weeping at Jesus’ feet, wetting them with her tears, wiping them with her hair, kissing them, and anointing them with perfume. Simon was offended and thought that if Jesus were a prophet, He would know what kind of woman was touching Him.

Jesus responded by telling Simon a parable about two debtors, one forgiven a large debt and one a small debt, and asked which would love the lender more. Simon correctly answered that the one forgiven more would love more.

Then Jesus “*Turning to the woman*” (*v. 44*), said to Simon, “*Do you see this woman?*” (*v. 44*) Jesus physically turned toward her while speaking to Simon. This gesture directed Simon’s attention to her as a person. Simon saw her only as “a sinner,” a category that defined and dismissed her. Jesus asked him to truly see her.

Jesus continued, contrasting Simon’s behavior with hers. “*I entered into your house, and you gave me no water for my feet*” (*v. 44*). In that culture, a host would normally provide water for guests to wash their feet after walking on dusty roads. Simon had not done this. “*but she has wet my feet with her tears, and wiped them with the hair of her head*” (*v. 44*). The woman had done far more than Simon, using her own tears and hair.

In the next verses, Jesus noted that Simon gave Him no kiss of greeting, but she had not stopped kissing His feet; Simon did not anoint His head with oil, but she had anointed His feet with perfume. Simon, the respectable host, had been cold and neglectful. The woman, the known sinner, had shown overflowing love.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that Jesus sees people as they truly are, beyond their reputations and labels. Simon saw a sinner; Jesus saw a woman who loved much because she had been forgiven much. God looks at the heart, not at outward appearances or social status (*1 Samuel 16:7*).

It also reveals the blindness of self-righteousness. Simon was religious, respectable, and careful about purity. But he failed to see his own lack of love and his own need for forgiveness. He judged the woman while neglecting basic hospitality to Jesus. Self-righteousness often makes people blind to their own faults and to the worth of others.

Finally, the verse shows Jesus’ defense of the vulnerable. In front of the respected guests, Jesus honored this woman and rebuked the host. He took her side against the judgment of the religious community. Jesus consistently welcomed and defended those whom society rejected.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to see people as Jesus sees them. It is easy to label people by their past, their reputation, or their appearance, and then dismiss them. Jesus calls His followers to look beyond labels and see each person as someone made in God’s image, capable of love and repentance.

It also challenges believers to examine their own hearts for self-righteousness. Simon was more concerned with the woman’s sins than with his own coldness. Believers can ask whether they are quick to judge others while overlooking their own lack of love, gratitude, or hospitality.

Finally, this verse encourages believers to defend and honor those whom others look down on. Like Jesus, they can speak up for people who are being judged unfairly and treat them with dignity and kindness, especially in religious settings where such people may feel unwelcome.

### *Luke 7:47* — Forgiven Much, She Loved Much

> *“Therefore I tell you, her sins, which are many, are forgiven, for she loved much. But one to whom little is forgiven, loves little.”*
>
> — *Luke 7:47* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse is the conclusion of Jesus’ response to Simon the Pharisee. A woman known as a sinner had come into Simon’s house and shown extravagant love to Jesus by washing His feet with her tears, kissing them, and anointing them with perfume. Simon was offended. Jesus told a parable about two debtors: one owed five hundred denarii and the other fifty, and the lender forgave both. Simon agreed that the one forgiven more would love more. Jesus then contrasted Simon’s cold hospitality with the woman’s overflowing love.

Now Jesus draws the conclusion: “*Therefore I tell you, her sins, which are many, are forgiven, for she loved much*” (*v. 47*). This sentence can be misunderstood. It might sound as if her love earned her forgiveness. But the parable shows the opposite order. In the parable, the debtors were forgiven first, and their love came as a result. The woman’s great love was the evidence that she had been forgiven, not the cause. She had likely encountered Jesus or His message before, received His forgiveness, and now came to express her gratitude. Her love showed how much she had been forgiven.

Then Jesus said, “*But one to whom little is forgiven, loves little*” (*v. 47*). This was aimed at Simon. Simon did not think he needed much forgiveness, so he showed little love. The problem was not that Simon had fewer sins, but that he did not recognize his need.

Jesus then said directly to the woman, “*Your sins are forgiven*” (*v. 48*), confirming publicly what had already happened. The guests asked, “Who is this who even forgives sins?” Jesus told her, “*Your faith has saved you. Go in peace*” (*v. 50*). Her salvation came through faith in Jesus, and her love was its fruit.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals the connection between forgiveness and love. Those who understand how much they have been forgiven respond with deep love and gratitude toward God. Love for God is not a way of earning forgiveness; it is the natural response to forgiveness received. John writes, “*We love him, because he first loved us*” (*1 John 4:19*).

It also shows that everyone needs forgiveness. Simon thought he owed little; the woman knew she owed much. But in reality, both were debtors who could not pay. The difference was in their awareness of their need. Those who think they are good enough often have little love for God, because they do not grasp the depth of His mercy.

Finally, the verse shows that Jesus has authority to forgive sins. The guests’ question, “Who is this who even forgives sins?”, points to His divine identity. Only God can forgive sins, and Jesus forgave this woman’s many sins.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to remember how much they have been forgiven. When love for God grows cold, it is often because believers have forgotten the depth of their sin and the greatness of God’s mercy. Reflecting on God’s forgiveness can rekindle gratitude and love.

It also warns believers against self-righteousness. Those who think they have little need of forgiveness will love little. Believers can ask God to help them see their sin honestly, not to drive them to despair, but to deepen their appreciation of His grace.

Finally, this verse offers hope to those who feel their sins are too many. The woman’s sins were many, yet they were forgiven. No one is beyond Jesus’ mercy. Those who come to Him in faith can hear His words: “*Your sins are forgiven*” (*v. 48*) and “*Your faith has saved you. Go in peace*” (*v. 50*).

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Luke 7* shows Jesus reaching out to people others overlooked or rejected: a Gentile soldier, a poor widow, a doubting prophet, and a sinful woman. In each case, He responded with compassion, power, and grace. Believers can take comfort that Jesus sees them in their need and responds with love, whatever their background or situation.

The centurion’s humble faith teaches believers to trust Jesus’ authority and to approach Him with humility rather than a sense of entitlement. The widow of Nain shows that Jesus notices suffering and acts out of compassion, even before being asked. Believers can bring their grief to Him and trust His power over death. They can also follow His example by noticing and caring for those who are grieving and vulnerable.

John’s question and Jesus’ answer show that honest doubt can be brought to Jesus, and that He responds by pointing to His works. The contrast between the tax collectors who accepted God’s way and the Pharisees who rejected it warns believers against pride and the refusal to repent.

Finally, the story of the sinful woman reveals the heart of the gospel. Those who are forgiven much love much. Believers can remember the depth of God’s forgiveness and respond with grateful love. They can also learn to see people as Jesus sees them, looking beyond labels and reputations, and refuse the self-righteousness that keeps people from recognizing their own need for grace.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for Your compassion toward people the world overlooks. Like the centurion, I am not worthy for You to come under my roof, yet I trust that You can say the word and bring healing. Thank You for seeing the widow of Nain in her grief and restoring her son. Comfort all who grieve, and help me to notice and care for those who are suffering.

When I have questions and doubts, help me to bring them to You and to look at what You have done. Keep me from the pride that rejects Your ways. Thank You for forgiving my many sins. Help me never to forget how much I have been forgiven, so that I may love You much. Teach me to see people as You see them, beyond their labels and reputations, and to welcome them with Your grace. Thank You that my faith in You has saved me and that I can go in peace. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
