Luke · Chapter 8 of 24

# Luke — Chapter 8

Chapter Theme: Hearing the Word and Holding It Fast

[Read Luke 8 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/LUK08.htm)

Main Teaching

Supported by women whom He had healed, Jesus travels from town to town preaching the kingdom. He teaches that God’s word bears fruit in honest and good hearts that hold it fast with perseverance, and that His true family are those who hear and do God’s word. He then calms a storm, frees a man tormented by many demons, heals a woman who had suffered for twelve years, and raises a synagogue leader’s daughter, showing His power over nature, evil, disease, and death.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Luke 8* continues Jesus’ ministry in Galilee. The previous chapter ended with a woman known as a sinner washing Jesus’ feet with her tears and receiving His forgiveness. *Luke 8* begins by mentioning other women who followed Jesus, and much of the chapter focuses on hearing God’s word rightly. The second half contains a series of miracles that answer the disciples’ question in the storm: “*Who is this then, that he commands even the winds and the water, and they obey him?*” (*v. 25*)

Many events in this chapter are also recorded in Matthew and Mark and are studied in depth there: the parable of the sower (*Matthew 13:23*; *Mark 4:24*), the storm (*Matthew 8:26*; *Mark 4:38*), the man with a legion of demons (*Mark 5:19*), and the healing of Jairus’s daughter and the woman with bleeding (*Mark 5:34*, *5:36*). This chapter highlights details distinctive to Luke.

### The Women Who Followed Jesus (*8:1–3*)

Jesus traveled through towns and villages, proclaiming the good news of the kingdom of God. The Twelve were with Him, and so were “*certain women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities*” (*v. 2*). Luke names three: Mary called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out; Joanna, the wife of Chuza, the manager of Herod’s household; and Susanna. There were many others too, and they “*served them from their possessions*” (*v. 3*). This passage, found only in Luke, is studied below.

### The Parable of the Sower (*8:4–15*)

A large crowd gathered from many towns, and Jesus told a parable about a farmer sowing seed. Some fell on the path and was trampled and eaten by birds. Some fell on rock and withered because it had no moisture. Some fell among thorns and was choked. Some fell on good soil and produced a hundred times as much. Jesus called out, “*He who has ears to hear, let him hear!*” (*v. 8*)

When the disciples asked what it meant, Jesus said they had been given knowledge of the secrets of the kingdom, but others heard only parables. Then He explained: “*The seed is the word of God*” (*v. 11*). Those along the path hear, but the devil takes the word away “*that they may not believe and be saved*” (*v. 12*). Those on the rock receive the word with joy but have no root; they believe for a while and fall away in time of testing. Those among the thorns hear but are choked by worries, riches, and pleasures of life, and their fruit does not mature. Those on good soil hear the word with an honest and good heart, hold it fast, and bear fruit with perseverance. Luke’s wording of this last description is studied below.

### The Lamp and Careful Hearing (*8:16–18*)

No one lights a lamp and hides it under a jar or a bed; it is put on a stand so people can see. Nothing hidden will remain hidden. Then Jesus warned, “*Be careful therefore how you hear. For whoever has, to him will be given; and whoever doesn’t have, from him will be taken away even that which he thinks he has*” (*v. 18*). Luke’s phrase “even what he thinks he has” suggests that some people believe they possess spiritual understanding, but if they do not truly receive and act on the word, even that illusion will be taken away. (A similar saying is studied at *Mark 4:24*.)

### Jesus’ True Family (*8:19–21*)

Jesus’ mother and brothers came to see Him but could not get near because of the crowd. When told they were outside, He said, “*My mother and my brothers are these who hear the word of God and do it*” (*v. 21*). This saying fits the chapter’s theme perfectly. The good soil is the person who hears the word and holds it fast; Jesus’ family are those who hear God’s word and do it. Luke’s version is gentler than Mark’s, where Jesus’ family had come thinking He was out of His mind (*Mark 3:21*). Luke had already presented Mary as one who heard and believed God’s word (*Luke 1:38*, 45). (See also *Mark 3:35*.)

### Calming the Storm (*8:22–25*)

Jesus and His disciples got into a boat to cross the lake. As they sailed, Jesus fell asleep. A windstorm came down on the lake, and the boat was filling with water and in danger. The disciples woke Him, crying, “*Master, Master, we are dying!*” (*v. 24*) Jesus got up and rebuked the wind and the raging water, and they became calm. Then He asked, “*Where is your faith?*” (*v. 25*) This question is studied below. The disciples, afraid and amazed, asked one another who this was, whom even the wind and water obey.

### The Man With Many Demons (*8:26–39*)

They sailed to the region of the Gerasenes, across the lake from Galilee, a largely Gentile area. A man from the town who had been possessed by demons for a long time met Jesus. He wore no clothes and lived among the tombs rather than in a house. When he saw Jesus, he cried out, fell down before Him, and shouted, “*What do I have to do with you, Jesus, you Son of the Most High God? I beg you, don’t torment me!*” (*v. 28*) Luke explains that the unclean spirit had often seized him, and though he had been kept under guard and chained, he broke the chains and was driven by the demon into the wilderness.

Jesus asked his name, and he said, “Legion,” because many demons had entered him. The demons begged Jesus not to order them into “*the abyss*” (*v. 31*), the place of confinement for evil spirits (*Revelation 9:1–2*; *20:1–3*). They asked to enter a large herd of pigs, and Jesus allowed it. The pigs rushed down the steep bank into the lake and drowned.

When the people of the region came and found the man “*sitting at Jesus’ feet, clothed and in his right mind*” (*v. 35*), they were afraid. Luke’s phrase “sitting at Jesus’ feet” describes the posture of a disciple learning from a teacher, the same posture Mary of Bethany takes in *Luke 10:39*. The man who had been wild and naked had become a learner of Jesus. But the people asked Jesus to leave because they were overcome with fear.

The healed man begged to go with Jesus, but Jesus told him, “*Return to your house, and declare what great things God has done for you*” (*v. 39*). The man went and proclaimed throughout the town “*what great things Jesus had done for him*” (*v. 39*). Notice that Jesus said “God,” and the man said “Jesus.” Luke may be showing that what Jesus did was the work of God.

### A Dying Girl and a Suffering Woman (*8:40–56*)

When Jesus returned, the crowd welcomed Him. Jairus, a ruler of the synagogue, fell at His feet and begged Him to come to his house, because his only daughter, about twelve years old, was dying. As Jesus went, the crowds pressed around Him.

A woman who had suffered from bleeding for twelve years, and who had spent all her money on doctors without being healed, came up behind Him and touched the fringe of His cloak. Luke, the physician, records honestly that she “*could not be healed by any*” (*v. 43*). Immediately her bleeding stopped. Jesus asked who touched Him. Peter pointed out that the crowds were pressing against Him from every side. But Jesus said, “*Someone did touch me, for I perceived that power has gone out of me*” (*v. 46*). The woman, realizing she could not remain hidden, came trembling and told everyone why she had touched Him and how she had been healed. Jesus said, “*Daughter, cheer up. Your faith has made you well. Go in peace*” (*v. 48*).

While He was speaking, someone came from Jairus’s house and said the girl had died. Jesus told Jairus, “*Don’t be afraid. Only believe, and she will be healed*” (*v. 50*). At the house, He allowed only Peter, John, James, and the girl’s parents to come in. Everyone was weeping, but Jesus said she was not dead but sleeping. They laughed at Him. He took her by the hand and called, “*Child, arise!*” (*v. 54*) Luke says “*Her spirit returned*” (*v. 55*), and she got up at once. Jesus told them to give her something to eat, and told her astonished parents not to tell anyone what had happened.

The two stories are woven together. A twelve-year-old girl and a woman who had suffered for twelve years both received new life through Jesus. Both were called “daughter” in effect, and both were restored to their families and communities.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Luke 8:2–3* — The Women Who Provided for Jesus

> *“and certain women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities: Mary who was called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out; and Joanna, the wife of Chuzas, Herod’s steward; Susanna; and many others who served them from their possessions.”*
>
> — *Luke 8:2–3* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These verses describe some of the people who traveled with Jesus as He went from town to town preaching the good news of God’s kingdom. Luke has just said that the Twelve were with Him. Now he adds that “*certain women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities*” (*v. 2*) were also with Him.

Luke names three of them. First, “*Mary who was called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out*” (*v. 2*). “Magdalene” means she came from Magdala, a fishing town on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee. Jesus had freed her from severe demonic oppression; “seven” suggests the completeness or severity of her bondage. (There is no biblical evidence that Mary Magdalene was the sinful woman of *Luke 7* or a prostitute, a later tradition that has been widely questioned.) Mary Magdalene would be present at Jesus’ crucifixion and burial and would be the first witness to His resurrection (*Luke 24:10*; *John 20:1–18*).

Second, “*Joanna, the wife of Chuzas, Herod’s steward*” (*v. 3*). Chuza managed the household or estate of Herod Antipas, the ruler of Galilee. This was a position of wealth and influence. Joanna’s presence shows that Jesus’ followers included people from Herod’s court. She would also be among the women at the empty tomb (*Luke 24:10*).

Third, Susanna, mentioned only here.

Luke adds that there were “*many others who served them from their possessions*” (*v. 3*). These women used their own money and resources to support Jesus and His disciples as they traveled. They were not merely followers; they were partners in His ministry.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that women played a significant role in Jesus’ ministry. In first-century Jewish culture, it was unusual for women to travel with a religious teacher. Rabbis did not usually have female disciples. Jesus welcomed women as followers and partners. Luke, more than any other Gospel writer, highlights women: Elizabeth, Mary, Anna, the widow of Nain, the sinful woman, Mary and Martha, and the women at the cross and tomb.

They also show that grace leads to gratitude and service. These women had been healed and set free by Jesus. Their response was to follow Him and support His work generously. Those who have received God’s grace naturally want to give back in love.

Finally, these verses reveal that Jesus’ ministry was supported by ordinary people’s generosity. Jesus did not perform miracles to supply His own needs; He depended on the generosity of His followers. God works through the gifts of His people to advance His kingdom.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to respond to God’s grace with gratitude and service. Like these women, believers who have been forgiven, healed, or set free can follow Jesus and use their resources to support His work.

They also affirm the valuable role of women in God’s kingdom. Churches can recognize, honor, and encourage women’s contributions to ministry, as Jesus did. The women who supported Jesus were faithful when many others were not; they stayed at the cross and were first at the empty tomb.

Finally, these verses encourage generosity in supporting the spread of the gospel. Believers can support pastors, missionaries, and ministries with their resources, seeing this as a way of partnering in Jesus’ mission, just as these women did.

### *Luke 8:15* — An Honest and Good Heart That Holds Fast

> *“Those in the good ground, these are those who with an honest and good heart, having heard the word, hold it tightly, and produce fruit with perseverance.”*
>
> — *Luke 8:15* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse is Jesus’ explanation of the good soil in the parable of the sower. In the parable, a farmer scattered seed, which represents “*the word of God*” (*v. 11*). Some fell on the path, where the devil took it away. Some fell on rock, where it sprang up but withered because it had no root, representing those who believe for a while but fall away when tested. Some fell among thorns, where worries, riches, and pleasures choked it so its fruit never matured.

Then Jesus described the good soil: “*Those in the good ground, these are those who with an honest and good heart, having heard the word, hold it tightly, and produce fruit with perseverance*” (*v. 15*). Luke’s wording adds details not found in Matthew or Mark. (The parable is studied from Matthew’s perspective at *Matthew 13:23*.)

“*with an honest and good heart*” (*v. 15*). The phrase “honest and good” was a common Greek expression for a person of noble character. Here it describes a heart that is sincere, open, and ready to receive God’s word without deceit or resistance.

“*having heard the word, hold it tightly*” (*v. 15*). To “hold tightly” means to keep firmly, to retain and not let go. Unlike the path, where the word was snatched away, and the rock, where it was quickly lost, the good soil holds onto the word.

“*and produce fruit with perseverance*” (*v. 15*). “Perseverance” means patient endurance, steady faithfulness over time, especially through difficulty. Fruit takes time to grow. The good soil does not produce a crop overnight; it keeps holding onto the word through seasons of testing until fruit matures.

Luke’s emphasis on perseverance contrasts with the rocky soil, which fell away “*in time of temptation*” (*v. 13*), and the thorny soil, whose fruit did not mature. The good hearer keeps going.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse teaches that fruitful faith requires both openness and endurance. An honest heart receives God’s word sincerely. Holding it fast means continuing to believe and obey it. Perseverance means remaining faithful through trials, temptations, and the passing of time. Jesus said elsewhere that the one who endures to the end will be saved (*Mark 13:13*).

It also shows that spiritual fruit takes time. Believers sometimes become discouraged when they do not see immediate change in themselves or others. But fruit grows slowly. The good soil produces fruit “with perseverance,” through patient faithfulness over the long haul.

Finally, the verse connects the condition of the heart with the outcome of faith. Hearing is the same for all four soils; the difference is the heart. This calls believers to examine their hearts and ask God to make them honest and good soil.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to receive God’s word with honest hearts. That means approaching Scripture not to find support for what they already want, but to hear what God is truly saying, even when it challenges them.

It also calls believers to hold God’s word tightly. In a world full of distractions and competing messages, it is easy to forget what God has said. Believers can hold onto His word through regular reading, memorization, reflection, and obedience.

Finally, this verse encourages patience and perseverance. Spiritual growth is often slow, and fruit may take years to mature. Believers can keep trusting and obeying God through dry seasons, trials, and temptations, confident that God will bring fruit in His time.

### *Luke 8:25* — “*Where Is Your Faith?*” (*v. 25*)

> *“He said to them, ‘Where is your faith?’ Being afraid, they marveled, saying to one another, ‘Who is this then, that he commands even the winds and the water, and they obey him?’”*
>
> — *Luke 8:25* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse comes immediately after Jesus calms a violent storm on the Sea of Galilee. Jesus had told His disciples, “Let’s go over to the other side of the lake.” As they sailed, He fell asleep. A windstorm swept down on the lake, and the boat began filling with water. Several of the disciples were experienced fishermen, but they were terrified. They woke Jesus, crying, “Master, Master, we are dying!” Jesus got up, rebuked the wind and the raging water, and everything became calm.

Then Jesus asked them, “*Where is your faith?*” (*v. 25*) Luke’s version of this question differs slightly from Matthew’s (“Why are you fearful, O you of little faith?”) and Mark’s (“How is it that you have no faith?”). Luke’s wording suggests that the disciples did have faith, but in the moment of crisis, they did not use it. Their faith was somewhere else; it had not been brought to bear on the storm.

The disciples responded with fear and amazement: “*Who is this then, that he commands even the winds and the water, and they obey him?*” (*v. 25*) They had seen Jesus heal the sick and cast out demons, but this display of power over nature filled them with awe. In the Old Testament, only God controls the wind and the sea (*Psalm 107:29*).

The setting is significant. The disciples were in the storm because they had followed Jesus’ instruction to cross the lake. Jesus was with them in the boat. His question invited them to remember who was with them and to trust Him even in danger.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that faith is not only something we possess but something we must exercise. The disciples believed in Jesus, but in the storm, fear overwhelmed their trust. Faith must be brought into the real situations of life, especially the frightening ones.

It also shows that Jesus is the Lord of creation. The disciples’ question, “Who is this?”, runs throughout the Gospels. Jesus’ power over the wind and water reveals that He shares God’s authority. The One who created the world has authority over it.

Finally, the question “Where is your faith?” is gentle rather than harsh. Jesus did not abandon His frightened disciples; He calmed the storm and then invited them to grow. He continues to patiently teach His followers to trust Him.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to ask themselves where their faith is when trouble comes. It is easy to trust God when life is calm, but storms reveal whether faith is active. When fear rises, believers can remind themselves of who Jesus is and choose to trust Him.

It also encourages believers to bring their fears to Jesus. The disciples were afraid, but they went to the right person. Believers can cry out to Jesus in their storms, trusting that He hears and cares.

Finally, this verse reminds believers that storms can deepen their understanding of Jesus. The disciples came away from the storm asking, “Who is this?” Each experience of Jesus’ faithfulness in difficulty can strengthen believers’ faith and deepen their awe of Him.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Luke 8* centers on how people respond to God’s word and to Jesus Himself. The parable of the sower shows that the same word produces different results depending on the condition of the heart. Believers can ask God to make their hearts honest and good, receiving His word sincerely, holding it fast, and bearing fruit with perseverance. This involves guarding against distractions, worries, riches, and pleasures that choke spiritual growth.

The chapter emphasizes that hearing must lead to doing. Jesus’ true family are those who hear God’s word and do it. Believers can move beyond knowing about God’s word to living it out in daily obedience.

The women who followed Jesus show that grace leads to gratitude and service. Those who have been healed, forgiven, and freed by Jesus can respond by following Him and using their resources to support His work. Their example also affirms the valuable role of women in God’s kingdom.

The miracles in the second half of the chapter reveal Jesus’ authority over storms, demons, disease, and death. Believers can trust Him in every kind of crisis. When fear rises, they can ask themselves, “Where is my faith?” and turn to Jesus. The healed man’s commission to tell what God had done reminds believers to share their stories of Jesus’ work in their lives. Finally, the stories of the woman and Jairus show that Jesus sees individuals, honors persistent faith, and gives new life even when all hope seems gone.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for sowing the word of God in my heart. Make my heart honest and good soil that receives Your word, holds it fast, and bears fruit with perseverance. Guard me from the worries, riches, and pleasures that choke my faith, and help me to be careful how I hear. Make me part of Your family by hearing God’s word and doing it.

Thank You for the women who followed and supported You out of gratitude. Help me to respond to Your grace with generous service. When storms rise in my life, remind me that You are with me, and when You ask, “Where is your faith?”, help me to trust You. Thank You for Your power over evil, sickness, and death. Help me to tell others what great things You have done for me. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Luke · Chapter 9 of 24

# Luke — Chapter 9

Chapter Theme: Who Jesus Is, and the Road He Sets His Face Toward

[Read Luke 9 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/LUK09.htm)

Main Teaching

Jesus sends out the Twelve, feeds five thousand, and hears Peter confess Him as the Christ of God, then teaches that He must suffer and that His followers must take up their cross. On the mountain, while He prays, His glory is revealed and Moses and Elijah speak of the “departure” He will accomplish in Jerusalem. After further lessons in humility and mercy, Jesus resolutely sets His face toward Jerusalem and warns that following Him requires wholehearted, forward-looking commitment.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Luke 9* is a hinge chapter in Luke’s Gospel. Its first half concludes Jesus’ ministry in Galilee, focusing on His identity: Herod asks who He is, Peter confesses Him as the Christ, and the Father declares Him His beloved Son. Its second half begins the long journey to Jerusalem, which occupies *Luke 9:51–19:27*, often called the “travel narrative.” Much of Jesus’ teaching found only in Luke appears during this journey.

Several events in this chapter are studied in depth in Matthew’s and Mark’s commentaries: the feeding of the five thousand (*Mark 6:31*), Peter’s confession (*Matthew 16:16*), taking up the cross (*Matthew 16:24*), the cost of gaining the world (*Mark 8:36*), the transfiguration (*Matthew 17:5*), the healing of the boy (*Mark 9:24*), greatness and the child (*Matthew 18:3–4*), and the outsider who cast out demons (*Mark 9:40*). This chapter highlights Luke’s distinctive emphases.

### The Mission of the Twelve (*9:1–6*)

Jesus called the Twelve together and gave them “*power and authority over all demons, and to cure diseases*” (*v. 1*). He sent them out to proclaim the kingdom of God and to heal. They were to take nothing for the journey: no staff, bag, bread, money, or extra tunic. They were to stay in whatever house welcomed them, and if a town rejected them, they were to shake the dust off their feet as a testimony. They went from village to village, preaching the gospel and healing everywhere.

### Herod’s Question (*9:7–9*)

Herod Antipas heard about everything that was happening and was perplexed. Some said John had been raised from the dead; others said Elijah had appeared; others said one of the ancient prophets had come back to life. Herod said, “*I beheaded John, but who is this about whom I hear such things?*” (*v. 9*) He wanted to see Jesus. Herod’s question, “Who is this?”, introduces the chapter’s central theme. Herod would finally see Jesus during His trial, hoping to see a miracle, but would only mock Him (*Luke 23:8–11*).

### Feeding the Five Thousand (*9:10–17*)

When the apostles returned, they told Jesus what they had done. He took them privately toward a town called Bethsaida, but the crowds followed. Jesus “*welcomed them*” (*v. 11*), spoke to them about the kingdom of God, and healed those who needed it. Luke’s word “welcomed” shows Jesus’ openness even when His plans for rest were interrupted.

Late in the day, the Twelve urged Him to send the crowd away to find food and lodging. Jesus said, “*You give them something to eat*” (*v. 13*). They had only five loaves and two fish. Jesus had the people sit in groups of about fifty, took the loaves and fish, looked up to heaven, blessed and broke them, and gave them to the disciples to distribute. Everyone ate and was satisfied, and twelve baskets of leftovers were collected.

### Peter’s Confession and the Call to Follow (*9:18–27*)

Luke alone tells us that Jesus asked His disciples about His identity “*As he was praying alone*” (*v. 18*). Prayer comes before every major turning point in Luke’s account. Jesus asked who the crowds said He was. They gave the same answers Herod had heard: John the Baptist, Elijah, or an ancient prophet. Then He asked, “*But who do you say that I am?*” (*v. 20*) Peter answered, “*The Christ of God*” (*v. 20*), meaning God’s anointed Messiah.

Jesus warned them not to tell anyone and explained that “*The Son of Man must suffer many things*” (*v. 22*), be rejected, be killed, and be raised on the third day. Then He said to everyone, “*If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me*” (*v. 23*). (Many manuscripts of Luke add the word “daily,” emphasizing that cross-bearing is an everyday commitment.) Whoever tries to save their life will lose it, but whoever loses their life for Jesus’ sake will save it. What good is it to gain the whole world and lose oneself? Whoever is ashamed of Jesus and His words, the Son of Man will be ashamed of when He comes in glory. Finally, He said some standing there would not die before they saw the kingdom of God.

### The Transfiguration (*9:28–36*)

About eight days later, Jesus took Peter, John, and James up a mountain “*to pray*” (*v. 28*). Again Luke emphasizes prayer. “*As he was praying, the appearance of his face was altered, and his clothing became white and dazzling*” (*v. 29*). Moses and Elijah appeared in glory and talked with Jesus about “*his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem*” (*v. 31*). This detail, found only in Luke, is studied below.

Peter and his companions had been very sleepy, but they woke fully and saw Jesus’ glory. As Moses and Elijah were leaving, Peter suggested building three shelters, “*not knowing what he said*” (*v. 33*). A cloud came and covered them, and they were afraid. A voice from the cloud said, “*This is my beloved Son. Listen to him!*” (*v. 35*) (Many manuscripts read “my Chosen One.”) When the voice had spoken, Jesus was alone. The disciples kept silent about what they had seen.

### The Boy With an Unclean Spirit (*9:37–43*a)

The next day, a man in the crowd begged Jesus to look at his son, “*for he is my only born child*” (*v. 38*), a detail Luke adds that deepens the father’s anguish. A spirit seized the boy and threw him into convulsions, and the disciples had been unable to drive it out. Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit, healed the boy, and “*gave him back to his father*” (*v. 42*), an echo of how He gave the widow’s son back to his mother in *Luke 7:15*. Everyone was amazed at the greatness of God.

### Misunderstanding and Pride (*9:43*b–50)

While everyone marveled, Jesus told His disciples, “*Let these words sink into your ears, for the Son of Man will be delivered up into the hands of men*” (*v. 44*). But they did not understand, and Luke says the meaning “*was concealed from them*” (*v. 45*); they were afraid to ask Him about it. The full meaning of the cross would be understood only after the resurrection (*Luke 24:25–27*, 45).

Then an argument started among the disciples about which of them was the greatest. Jesus took a little child, stood the child beside Him, and said that whoever welcomes such a child in His name welcomes Him, and whoever welcomes Him welcomes the Father. “*For whoever is least among you all, this one will be great*” (*v. 48*). John then mentioned someone casting out demons in Jesus’ name whom they had tried to stop, because he was not one of their group. Jesus said, “*Don’t forbid him, for he who is not against us is for us*” (*v. 50*).

### Setting His Face Toward Jerusalem (*9:51–56*)

Now comes the turning point of Luke’s Gospel: “*It came to pass, when the days were near that he should be taken up, he intently set his face to go to Jerusalem*” (*v. 51*). This verse is studied below.

Jesus sent messengers ahead to a Samaritan village to prepare for His arrival. Samaritans lived in the region between Galilee and Judea. They were descendants of Israelites who had intermarried with other peoples after the Assyrian conquest centuries earlier, and they worshiped on Mount Gerizim rather than in Jerusalem. Jews and Samaritans had a long history of hostility. The Samaritans did not welcome Jesus “*because he was traveling with his face set toward Jerusalem*” (*v. 53*). They resented pilgrims heading to the Jerusalem temple.

James and John asked, “*Lord, do you want us to command fire to come down from the sky and destroy them, just as Elijah did?*” (*v. 54*) They were thinking of Elijah calling down fire on soldiers sent by a king of Samaria (*2 Kings 1:9–12*). Mark tells us Jesus had nicknamed them “*Sons of Thunder*” (*Mark 3:17*). But Jesus turned and rebuked them. Many manuscripts add His words, “*You don’t know of what kind of spirit you are*” (*v. 55*), and “*For the Son of Man didn’t come to destroy men’s lives, but to save them*” (*v. 56*). They went on to another village. Jesus refused to respond to rejection with violence. Later in Luke’s writings, Samaritans would receive the gospel with joy (*Acts 8:4–25*), and John himself would go to Samaria to pray for them to receive the Holy Spirit (*Acts 8:14–17*).

### The Cost of Following Jesus (*9:57–62*)

As they traveled, three people spoke with Jesus about following Him. One said, “*I want to follow you wherever you go, Lord*” (*v. 57*). Jesus replied that foxes have dens and birds have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay His head. Following Him meant giving up security.

Jesus said to another, “Follow me!” The man asked first to go and bury his father. Jesus answered, “*Leave the dead to bury their own dead, but you go and announce God’s Kingdom*” (*v. 60*). As discussed at *Matthew 8:22*, the man may have meant waiting until his father died, which could take years. Jesus’ point was that the call of the kingdom takes priority.

A third said, “*I want to follow you, Lord, but first allow me to say good-bye to those who are at my house*” (*v. 61*). This request recalls Elisha, who asked Elijah for permission to say goodbye to his parents before following him (*1 Kings 19:19–21*). Jesus’ answer is studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Luke 9:31* — The “*Departure*” (*v. 31*) Jesus Would Accomplish

> *“who appeared in glory and spoke of his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem.”*
>
> — *Luke 9:31* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse is part of Luke’s account of the transfiguration. About eight days after Peter confessed Jesus as the Christ of God, and after Jesus taught that He must suffer, die, and rise, Jesus took Peter, John, and James up a mountain to pray. While He was praying, His face changed and His clothes became dazzling white. Two men appeared and talked with Him: Moses and Elijah.

Only Luke tells us what they talked about: “*who appeared in glory and spoke of his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem*” (*v. 31*).

The word translated “departure” is the Greek word “exodos,” from which we get “exodus.” It can simply mean “departure” or “death,” but in a Jewish context, it would immediately recall the great exodus, when God delivered Israel from slavery in Egypt through Moses. The presence of Moses, the leader of the first exodus, makes the connection even stronger.

Jesus’ “exodus” included His death, resurrection, and ascension, His departure from this world back to the Father. Just as the first exodus freed Israel from bondage in Egypt, Jesus’ exodus would free His people from bondage to sin and death.

Notice that Luke says this departure was something Jesus would “*accomplish*” (*v. 31*). The word means to fulfill or complete. Jesus’ death was not an accident or defeat; it was the fulfillment of God’s plan, something Jesus would actively carry out.

The setting is also important. The transfiguration took place between Jesus’ first prediction of His death (*9:22*) and His decision to set His face toward Jerusalem (*9:51*). Moses and Elijah, representing the Law and the Prophets, confirmed that Jesus’ coming death was in line with all of Scripture.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals that Jesus’ death and resurrection are the new and greater exodus. Throughout the Old Testament, the exodus was the defining act of God’s salvation. The prophets looked forward to a new exodus, when God would again rescue His people (*Isaiah 43:16–19*). Jesus fulfilled this hope. Paul calls Christ “*our Passover*” (*1 Corinthians 5:7*), linking His sacrifice to the Passover lamb that marked the first exodus.

The verse also shows that the cross was central to God’s plan. Even on the mountain of glory, the conversation was about Jesus’ death. Glory and suffering are not opposites in Jesus’ story; His glory is revealed through His suffering. This prepared the disciples, though they did not yet understand, for the events in Jerusalem.

Finally, the presence of Moses and Elijah shows that the whole Old Testament points to Jesus. After His resurrection, Jesus explained to His disciples how everything written about Him in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms had to be fulfilled (*Luke 24:44*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to see Jesus’ death and resurrection as their exodus from slavery. Just as Israel was freed from Egypt, believers have been freed from the power of sin and death through Christ. They can live as free people, no longer slaves to sin.

It also reminds believers that God’s plans often include suffering on the way to glory. Jesus’ path led through the cross to the resurrection. Believers facing hardship can trust that God is working, and that suffering is not the end of their story.

Finally, this verse encourages believers to read the Old Testament in light of Jesus. The stories of Moses, the exodus, and the prophets all point to Him. Reading Scripture this way deepens understanding of God’s unfolding plan of salvation.

### *Luke 9:51* — He Set His Face to Go to Jerusalem

> *“It came to pass, when the days were near that he should be taken up, he intently set his face to go to Jerusalem”*
>
> — *Luke 9:51* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse marks the turning point of Luke’s Gospel. Until now, most of Jesus’ ministry has taken place in Galilee. From this point on, Luke describes Jesus as traveling toward Jerusalem, a journey that continues for ten chapters until His arrival in the city (*Luke 19:28*). Along the way, Jesus teaches many parables and lessons found only in Luke.

“*It came to pass, when the days were near that he should be taken up*” (*v. 51*). “Taken up” refers to Jesus’ ascension into heaven, but it may also include the whole series of events: His death, resurrection, and ascension. The time for these events was approaching. Just as Moses and Elijah had spoken of His “departure” (*9:31*), Luke now says the time of His being “taken up” was near.

“*he intently set his face to go to Jerusalem*” (*v. 51*). To “set one’s face” means to be firmly determined, to resolve with unwavering commitment. The phrase echoes *Isaiah 50:7*, where the Servant of the Lord says, “*Therefore I have set my face like a flint, and I know that I won’t be disappointed*” (*Isaiah 50:7*). The Servant in that passage faces mocking and suffering but trusts God to vindicate Him.

Jesus knew what awaited Him in Jerusalem: rejection, suffering, and death. He had told His disciples this repeatedly (*9:22*, 44). Yet He did not turn away. He resolutely set out toward the city where He would die.

In the very next verses, Jesus faced rejection from a Samaritan village because He was heading toward Jerusalem. His determination to go there cost Him even on the way.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals Jesus’ willing obedience and determination to fulfill His mission. He was not dragged to the cross against His will; He chose it. In John’s Gospel, Jesus says, “*No one takes it away from me, but I lay it down by myself*” (*John 10:18*). His resolute face toward Jerusalem shows His love for His Father and for the people He came to save.

It also shows that faithfulness sometimes requires steadfast determination in the face of difficulty. Jesus knew the path ahead was painful, but He did not waver. Hebrews describes Jesus as one who, “*for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising its shame*” (*Hebrews 12:2*).

Finally, the verse reminds believers that Jesus’ journey to Jerusalem was a journey toward their salvation. Every step He took brought Him closer to the cross where He would give His life for them.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to follow Jesus with determination. Following Christ may involve difficult paths: standing for truth when it is unpopular, serving when it is costly, or persevering through suffering. Believers can set their faces to obey God, trusting Him with the outcome.

It also encourages believers to remain focused on God’s purposes despite distractions and opposition. Jesus faced rejection on the way to Jerusalem, but He did not turn back. Believers may face obstacles and discouragement, but they can keep moving forward in faithfulness.

Finally, this verse invites believers to gratitude. Jesus resolutely walked toward the cross for their sake. Reflecting on His determination to save them can deepen their love for Him and strengthen their own commitment to follow Him.

### *Luke 9:62* — No Looking Back From the Plow

> *“But Jesus said to him, ‘No one, having put his hand to the plow and looking back, is fit for God’s Kingdom.’”*
>
> — *Luke 9:62* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse concludes a short series of encounters between Jesus and people who wanted to follow Him, found at the beginning of His journey to Jerusalem. One man offered to follow Jesus wherever He went, and Jesus warned that He had no place to lay His head. Another was called by Jesus but asked to bury his father first, and Jesus told him to proclaim the kingdom instead.

A third man said, “*I want to follow you, Lord, but first allow me to say good-bye to those who are at my house*” (*v. 61*). This request seems reasonable. It recalls the prophet Elisha, who, when called by Elijah, asked permission to kiss his father and mother goodbye. Elijah allowed it, and Elisha then slaughtered his oxen, burned his plowing equipment, and followed Elijah (*1 Kings 19:19–21*).

Jesus responded with an image from farming: “*No one, having put his hand to the plow and looking back, is fit for God’s Kingdom*” (*v. 62*). In the ancient world, plows were simple tools pulled by oxen. The farmer guided the plow with one hand, keeping his eyes fixed on a point ahead to plow a straight furrow. If he looked back over his shoulder, the furrow would become crooked, and the work would be ruined.

Jesus was not condemning saying goodbye to one’s family. He was addressing the heart attitude behind the request. The phrase “first allow me” suggests divided loyalty. The man wanted to follow Jesus, but on his own terms and timetable. Jesus warned that following Him requires wholehearted commitment and a forward focus, not constant looking back to what was left behind.

“Fit” means useful or suitable. A plowman who keeps looking back is not suited for the job. Similarly, a disciple whose heart is divided between following Jesus and clinging to the past is not ready for the work of God’s kingdom.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse teaches that discipleship requires undivided commitment. Jesus does not want halfhearted followers who keep one eye on Him and the other on what they have left behind. He calls for wholehearted devotion. This echoes the first commandment, to love God with all one’s heart.

It also warns against the danger of looking back. In *Genesis 19:26*, Lot’s wife looked back at Sodom and became a pillar of salt. Jesus later warns, “*Remember Lot’s wife!*” (*Luke 17:32*) Looking back with longing at the old life can draw people away from following Jesus.

Finally, the verse shows that Jesus’ call is urgent. The kingdom of God is breaking into the world, and Jesus is on His way to Jerusalem. There is work to be done. Disciples must be focused on what lies ahead.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to examine whether their commitment to Jesus is wholehearted. Are there areas of life they are holding back, or past ways of living they keep looking back on with longing? Believers can ask God to help them follow Jesus with undivided hearts.

It also encourages believers to keep their eyes forward. Regret, nostalgia, or longing for former sins can distract believers from God’s present calling. Like a farmer plowing a straight furrow, believers can fix their eyes on Jesus and the work He has given them. Paul writes about “*forgetting the things which are behind, and stretching forward to the things which are before*” (*Philippians 3:13*).

Finally, this verse does not mean believers should neglect their families or relationships. Elsewhere Jesus affirms honoring parents and caring for family. The point is about priority and focus: Jesus must come first, and following Him should not be postponed or divided.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Luke 9* focuses on two great questions: Who is Jesus, and what does it mean to follow Him? Herod asked, “Who is this?” Peter answered, “The Christ of God,” and the Father declared, “This is my beloved Son. Listen to him!” Believers can affirm this confession personally and listen to Jesus above every other voice.

The chapter shows that Jesus’ identity is inseparable from His mission of suffering. Even in His glory on the mountain, the conversation was about His “exodus” in Jerusalem. His followers are called to take up their cross, deny themselves, and follow Him. Believers can embrace the path of self-giving love, trusting that it leads to life.

Luke’s emphasis on prayer reminds believers that Jesus prayed before Peter’s confession and at the transfiguration. Prayer was the setting for revelation. Believers can make prayer central to their lives, especially at important moments.

The disciples’ failures, their inability to heal the boy, their argument about greatness, their exclusiveness, and their desire to call down fire, show how slowly even close followers learn Jesus’ ways. Believers can examine themselves for pride, rivalry, and a desire for revenge, and learn from Jesus’ rebukes. He came not to destroy but to save.

Finally, Jesus set His face toward Jerusalem with determination, and He calls His followers to the same wholehearted commitment. Following Him means giving up security, putting His kingdom first, and keeping one’s hand on the plow without looking back. Believers can follow Jesus resolutely, with undivided hearts, on the road He walked.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, I confess with Peter that You are the Christ of God. Thank You for revealing Your glory on the mountain and for the Father’s command to listen to You. Thank You for the exodus You accomplished in Jerusalem, setting me free from slavery to sin and death. Help me to deny myself, take up my cross, and follow You.

Forgive me for the pride that seeks to be greatest, the exclusiveness that resents others serving You, and the anger that wants to call down fire on those who reject You. Teach me that You came not to destroy but to save. Thank You for setting Your face toward Jerusalem for my sake. Give me the same determination to follow You wholeheartedly. Keep my hand on the plow and my eyes fixed on You, without looking back. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Luke · Chapter 10 of 24

# Luke — Chapter 10

Chapter Theme: Sent Out, Showing Mercy, and Sitting at Jesus’ Feet

[Read Luke 10 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/LUK10.htm)

Main Teaching

Jesus sends out seventy messengers to prepare His way and, when they return rejoicing over their power, tells them to rejoice instead that their names are written in heaven. Asked by a lawyer who counts as a neighbor, He tells the parable of the Good Samaritan, showing that being a neighbor means showing mercy to anyone in need. At the home of Martha and Mary, He gently teaches that listening to Him is the one thing most needed.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Luke 10* continues the journey to Jerusalem that began in *Luke 9:51*, when Jesus “*intently set his face to go to Jerusalem*” (*Luke 9:51*). Much of the material in this chapter is found only in Luke, including the mission of the seventy, the parable of the Good Samaritan, and the visit to Martha and Mary. The chapter moves from mission (going out to others), to love for neighbor (showing mercy), to devotion (sitting at Jesus’ feet). Together these three scenes show what a disciple’s life looks like: serving, loving, and listening.

### The Mission of the Seventy (*10:1–16*)

After choosing and sending the Twelve (*Luke 9:1–6*), Jesus “*appointed seventy others*” (*v. 1*) and sent them two by two ahead of Him into every town He planned to visit. (Some manuscripts read seventy-two.) The number may recall the seventy elders who helped Moses (*Numbers 11:16–25*) or the seventy nations listed in *Genesis 10*, suggesting that the mission would eventually reach all peoples.

Jesus told them, “*The harvest is indeed plentiful, but the laborers are few. Pray therefore to the Lord of the harvest, that he may send out laborers into his harvest*” (*v. 2*). He warned them that He was sending them “*as lambs among wolves*” (*v. 3*), vulnerable in a hostile world. They were to travel light, carrying no purse, bag, or sandals, and not stop to exchange long greetings on the road, a sign of urgency.

When they entered a house, they were to say, “*Peace be to this house*” (*v. 5*). If someone of peace lived there, a person open to God’s message, their peace would rest on that home. They were to stay in the same house, eating whatever was offered, because “*the laborer is worthy of his wages*” (*v. 7*). Paul later quotes this saying (*1 Timothy 5:18*). They were to heal the sick and announce, “*God’s Kingdom has come near to you*” (*v. 9*).

If a town rejected them, they were to wipe its dust off their feet as a warning and still declare that the kingdom had come near. Jesus pronounced woes on Chorazin, Bethsaida, and Capernaum, towns that had seen His miracles but had not repented (see *Matthew 11:20–24*). He concluded, “*Whoever listens to you listens to me, and whoever rejects you rejects me. Whoever rejects me rejects him who sent me*” (*v. 16*). The messengers represented Jesus Himself.

### The Return of the Seventy (*10:17–24*)

The seventy returned with joy, saying, “*Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name!*” (*v. 17*) Jesus replied, “*I saw Satan having fallen like lightning from heaven*” (*v. 18*). Their success over demons was a sign that Satan’s power was being broken by the coming of God’s kingdom. Jesus had given them authority to “*tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy*” (*v. 19*). Serpents and scorpions were symbols of evil and danger (compare *Psalm 91:13*). Then He redirected their joy, a teaching studied below.

“*In that same hour, Jesus rejoiced in the Holy Spirit*” (*v. 21*). Luke alone records that Jesus was full of joy in the Spirit. He thanked the Father for hiding these things from the wise and learned and revealing them to little children, people with humble, childlike faith. He declared that all things had been entrusted to Him by the Father, and that only the Son truly knows the Father and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him. Then He told His disciples privately that they were blessed to see what they were seeing, because many prophets and kings had longed to see and hear these things but had not.

### The Parable of the Good Samaritan (*10:25–37*)

An expert in the law stood up to test Jesus: “*Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?*” (*v. 25*) Jesus asked what the law said. The man answered by combining *Deuteronomy 6:5* and *Leviticus 19:18*: love God with all your heart, soul, strength, and mind, and love your neighbor as yourself. Jesus said, “*You have answered correctly. Do this, and you will live*” (*v. 28*).

But the man, “*desiring to justify himself*” (*v. 29*), asked, “*Who is my neighbor?*” (*v. 29*) He wanted to define “neighbor” narrowly so that he could be sure he had fulfilled the command. Many Jews of that time understood “neighbor” to mean fellow Jews, especially those who kept the law.

Jesus answered with a story. A man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho. The road descended about 3,300 feet over roughly seventeen miles through rocky, desolate terrain, and it was known for robbers. The man was attacked, stripped, beaten, and left half dead.

A priest happened to be going down the same road. He saw the man and passed by on the other side. A Levite, a temple assistant, did the same. Both were religious leaders who served in the temple. They may have feared that the man was dead, since touching a corpse would make them ritually unclean (*Numbers 19:11–16*), or they may have feared that robbers were nearby. Whatever their reasons, they did not help.

Then a Samaritan came along. Jews and Samaritans despised each other. Just one chapter earlier, a Samaritan village had refused to welcome Jesus, and James and John wanted to call down fire on it (*Luke 9:52–54*). Jesus’ listeners would have expected the Samaritan to be the villain. Instead, the Samaritan was the hero. This parable is studied below.

Jesus asked which of the three proved to be a neighbor to the man. The lawyer answered, “*He who showed mercy on him*” (*v. 37*); he could not bring himself to say “the Samaritan.” Jesus told him, “*Go and do likewise*” (*v. 37*).

### Martha and Mary (*10:38–42*)

As Jesus and His disciples continued their journey, they came to a village where a woman named Martha welcomed Him into her home. John’s Gospel tells us that this village was Bethany, near Jerusalem, and that Martha and Mary had a brother named Lazarus (*John 11:1*). Martha’s sister Mary “*sat at Jesus’ feet and heard his word*” (*v. 39*). Sitting at a teacher’s feet was the posture of a disciple. In that culture, it was unusual for a woman to take this place, which was normally reserved for men studying under a rabbi.

Martha was “*distracted with much serving*” (*v. 40*), busy preparing food and hospitality for Jesus and likely His disciples, a large group. She came to Jesus and said, “*Lord, don’t you care that my sister left me to serve alone? Ask her therefore to help me*” (*v. 40*). Jesus’ answer is studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Luke 10:20* — Rejoice That Your Names Are Written in Heaven

> *“Nevertheless, don’t rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.”*
>
> — *Luke 10:20* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse comes when the seventy messengers returned from their mission. Jesus had sent them out in pairs to towns He planned to visit, with authority to heal the sick and announce that God’s kingdom had come near. They came back full of excitement: “*Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name!*” (*v. 17*)

Jesus affirmed that their success was real and significant. He said He saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven, meaning that their victories over demons showed the defeat of Satan’s power. He confirmed that He had given them authority over the enemy’s power.

But then He redirected their joy: “*Nevertheless, don’t rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven*” (*v. 20*).

The idea of names written in heaven appears throughout Scripture. Moses spoke of God’s book (*Exodus 32:32–33*), Daniel mentioned people whose names are written in the book (*Daniel 12:1*), and Revelation speaks of the Lamb’s book of life (*Revelation 21:27*). Having one’s name written in heaven means belonging to God, being a citizen of His kingdom, and being assured of eternal life.

Jesus was not saying that the disciples’ ministry success did not matter. He was saying it should not be the primary source of their joy. Ministry success can come and go; some missions succeed and others fail. But their relationship with God, their names written in heaven, was secure and permanent.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse teaches that a believer’s deepest joy should come from belonging to God, not from achievements, even spiritual ones. It is possible to find identity and satisfaction in ministry success, spiritual gifts, or results. But these can lead to pride when things go well and despair when they do not. Jesus points His followers to something more secure: God’s grace in choosing them and writing their names in heaven.

It also guards against a dangerous misunderstanding. Elsewhere, Jesus warned that some who did mighty works in His name, even casting out demons, would be rejected because He never knew them (*Matthew 7:22–23*). Spiritual power is not proof of salvation. What matters is a genuine relationship with God.

Finally, the verse shows that salvation is God’s work. Names are written in heaven by God, not by human effort. This truth is a source of humble joy and security.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to examine where they find their joy. If their joy depends on how well their ministry, work, or spiritual life seems to be going, it will rise and fall with circumstances. Believers can root their joy in the unchanging truth that they belong to God.

It also encourages those who feel their service is unsuccessful. Pastors, missionaries, teachers, parents, and others who serve faithfully may see little visible fruit. They can rejoice that their names are written in heaven, and that their worth before God does not depend on their results.

Finally, this verse warns believers against pride in spiritual achievements. Gifts and successes come from God. Believers can be grateful for them while keeping their hearts focused on the greater gift of salvation.

### *Luke 10:33–34* — The Samaritan Who Showed Compassion

> *“But a certain Samaritan, as he traveled, came where he was. When he saw him, he was moved with compassion, came to him, and bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. He set him on his own animal, brought him to an inn, and took care of him.”*
>
> — *Luke 10:33–34* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These verses describe the turning point of the parable of the Good Samaritan. Jesus told this story in response to a lawyer who asked, “Who is my neighbor?” In the story, a man traveling from Jerusalem to Jericho was attacked by robbers, stripped, beaten, and left half dead by the road. A priest came by and passed on the other side. A Levite did the same. Both were religious leaders who served in God’s temple, yet both avoided the wounded man.

Then Jesus said, “*But a certain Samaritan, as he traveled, came where he was*” (*v. 33*). Jesus’ listeners would have been shocked. Samaritans were despised by Jews as religious heretics and ethnic outsiders. The hostility went both ways. A Samaritan would have been the last person they expected to be the hero.

“*When he saw him, he was moved with compassion*” (*v. 33*). The priest and Levite also “saw” the man, but they passed by. The Samaritan saw him and was moved with deep compassion, the same word used for Jesus’ compassion for the widow of Nain (*Luke 7:13*).

Then Jesus describes the Samaritan’s actions in detail: he “*came to him, and bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine*” (*v. 34*). Oil soothed wounds, and wine acted as an antiseptic. He “*set him on his own animal*” (*v. 34*), meaning the Samaritan walked so the injured man could ride. He “*brought him to an inn, and took care of him*” (*v. 34*). The next day, he gave the innkeeper two denarii, about two days’ wages, and promised to repay any additional expenses when he returned.

The Samaritan’s compassion was practical, personal, costly, and continuing. He risked his own safety on a dangerous road, used his own supplies, gave up his own comfort, spent his own money, and committed to future care for a stranger who was likely Jewish, someone from a people who despised him.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This parable transforms the question, “Who is my neighbor?” The lawyer wanted to know the limits of his obligation, whom he was required to love. Jesus turned the question around. At the end, He asked, “*Now which of these three do you think seemed to be a neighbor to him who fell among the robbers?*” (*v. 36*) The question is not “Who deserves my love?” but “Will I be a neighbor to anyone in need?” Love does not set boundaries based on ethnicity, religion, or social status.

It also exposes the danger of religion without compassion. The priest and Levite were respected religious figures, but they failed the test of love. The Samaritan, an outsider, fulfilled God’s law. This echoes Jesus’ teaching that God desires mercy, not sacrifice.

Many Christians throughout history have also seen in the Good Samaritan a picture of Jesus Himself. Humanity lies wounded and helpless by the road of life, and Jesus, rejected and despised, comes near, binds up wounds, and pays the cost of healing. While this is not the main point of the parable, it reflects the compassion Jesus showed throughout His ministry.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses challenge believers to show compassion to anyone in need, regardless of who they are. Believers can ask themselves who might be lying “by the road” in their own lives: a neighbor who is struggling, a coworker in crisis, a stranger in trouble, or someone from a group they find difficult to love.

They also show that compassion must be practical. The Samaritan did not just feel sorry for the man; he acted. Believers can look for concrete ways to help: giving time, resources, practical assistance, and ongoing support. Compassion often costs something.

Finally, these verses warn against excuses. The priest and Levite may have had reasons, such as religious duties, fear, or busyness. Believers can examine whether they use similar excuses to avoid helping others. Jesus’ command is clear: “Go and do likewise.”

### *Luke 10:41–42* — One Thing Is Needed

> *“Jesus answered her, ‘Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is needed. Mary has chosen the good part, which will not be taken away from her.’”*
>
> — *Luke 10:41–42* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These verses are Jesus’ response to Martha, who had welcomed Him into her home. Martha was busy with all the work of hospitality, likely preparing a large meal for Jesus and His disciples. Her sister Mary sat at Jesus’ feet, listening to His teaching. Martha became frustrated and came to Jesus, saying, “*Lord, don’t you care that my sister left me to serve alone? Ask her therefore to help me*” (*v. 40*).

Martha’s frustration is understandable. Hospitality was an important duty in that culture, and serving a large group was hard work. She was doing something good. But her complaint revealed that her service had become a burden that made her anxious and resentful, even toward Jesus.

Jesus answered gently, repeating her name: “*Martha, Martha*” (*v. 41*). Repeating a name in Scripture often expresses affection and concern (compare “Simon, Simon,” *Luke 22:31*). Then He said, “*you are anxious and troubled about many things*” (*v. 41*). “Anxious” means worried, pulled in different directions. “Troubled” means upset or disturbed. Martha’s mind was divided by many concerns.

“*but one thing is needed*” (*v. 42*). Out of all the things Martha was worried about, only one thing was truly necessary. “*Mary has chosen the good part, which will not be taken away from her*” (*v. 42*). Mary had chosen to sit at Jesus’ feet and listen to His word. This was the “good part,” and Jesus would not take it from her by sending her to help in the kitchen.

Jesus was not condemning Martha’s service or saying that work does not matter. Elsewhere, Luke presents service positively (*Luke 8:3*; *22:27*). Rather, He was saying that listening to Him comes first, and that service done in anxiety and distraction loses its joy.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses teach that relationship with Jesus is the most important thing in life. Activity, even good activity done for Jesus, cannot replace time spent with Him. Mary’s posture at Jesus’ feet shows the priority of listening to His word.

They also show that busyness can be a spiritual danger. Martha was doing good things, but she was “distracted.” Her service had become a source of anxiety and comparison. When believers serve without first spending time with Jesus, their service can become a burden and their hearts can grow resentful.

Finally, Jesus’ defense of Mary is significant. In that culture, women were not usually allowed to sit at a rabbi’s feet as disciples. Jesus affirmed Mary’s choice and would not send her back to traditional roles. He welcomed women as His learners and disciples.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses invite believers to make time to sit at Jesus’ feet. In busy lives full of responsibilities, it is easy to neglect prayer, Scripture, and quiet time with God. Believers can prioritize listening to Jesus, trusting that, as Jesus said, “*one thing is needed*” (*v. 42*).

They also invite believers to examine their service. Are they serving with joy, or with anxiety and resentment? If service has become a burden, it may be a sign that they need to return to Jesus’ feet and be renewed in His presence.

Finally, these verses warn against comparing oneself with others. Martha compared her work with Mary’s and felt unfairly treated. Believers can avoid judging others’ devotion and instead focus on their own relationship with Jesus.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Luke 10* presents three aspects of discipleship: going out on mission, loving one’s neighbor, and listening to Jesus. All three are essential, and they work together.

The mission of the seventy reminds believers that Jesus sends His followers into the world to share the good news and show God’s kingdom. The harvest is large, and workers are few. Believers can pray for more workers and be willing to go themselves. They can also remember that their deepest joy is not in ministry success but in belonging to God, with their names written in heaven.

The parable of the Good Samaritan challenges believers to be neighbors to anyone in need. Love does not ask, “Who deserves my help?” but “How can I help this person?” This love crosses boundaries of ethnicity, religion, and social status, and it is shown in practical, costly action. Believers can look for the wounded people along their own roads and respond with compassion.

The story of Martha and Mary reminds believers that sitting at Jesus’ feet is the “one thing needed.” Mission and service flow from relationship with Him. Without time in His presence, service can become anxious and burdensome. Believers can build regular time for listening to Jesus into their lives and serve from a place of rest rather than worry.

Taken together, the chapter shows a balanced life of discipleship: going out to share the good news, showing mercy to those in need, and returning regularly to sit at Jesus’ feet.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord of the harvest, the harvest is great and the workers are few. Send out workers into Your harvest, and make me willing to go where You send me. Thank You that my name is written in heaven. Help me to find my deepest joy in belonging to You, not in my successes or achievements.

Give me the compassion of the Good Samaritan. Open my eyes to the wounded people along my road, and keep me from passing by on the other side. Help me to show mercy in practical, generous ways to anyone in need, even to those I find hard to love. And Lord, when I become anxious and troubled about many things, call me back to the one thing needed. Teach me to sit at Your feet and listen to Your word, so that my service flows from love and not from worry. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
