Luke · Chapter 11 of 24

# Luke — Chapter 11

Chapter Theme: Teach Us to Pray: Bold Asking and True Blessedness

[Read Luke 11 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/LUK11.htm)

Main Teaching

When His disciples ask Him to teach them to pray, Jesus gives them a model prayer and a parable about a friend at midnight, encouraging bold, persistent asking of a Father who gives the Holy Spirit. He answers critics who claim He works by Satan’s power, says that true blessedness belongs to those who hear and keep God’s word, warns a generation that demands signs, and rebukes religious leaders whose outward correctness hides neglect of justice and love for God.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Luke 11* continues Jesus’ journey toward Jerusalem. The previous chapter ended with Mary sitting at Jesus’ feet, listening to His word, and Jesus saying this was the one thing needed (*Luke 10:42*). *Luke 11* begins with prayer, another way of being in God’s presence. The chapter then moves to conflict, as Jesus faces accusations and confronts the hypocrisy of religious leaders.

Some of the teaching in this chapter also appears in Matthew, often in different settings. Jesus likely taught similar themes on multiple occasions. (The Lord’s Prayer is studied at *Matthew 6:9–13*; asking, seeking, and knocking at *Matthew 7:7*; the Beelzebul controversy and blasphemy against the Spirit at *Matthew 12:31–32*; and the woes on the Pharisees at *Matthew 23:23*.) This chapter focuses on Luke’s distinctive emphases.

### Teach Us to Pray (*11:1–4*)

Luke sets the scene: Jesus “*finished praying in a certain place*” (*v. 1*). Throughout Luke’s Gospel, Jesus prays at important moments. His disciples had watched Him pray, and one of them asked, “*Lord, teach us to pray, just as John also taught his disciples*” (*v. 1*). Religious teachers in that time often gave their followers distinctive prayers that expressed their community’s identity.

Jesus gave them a prayer that is shorter than the version in *Matthew 6:9–13*. It begins, “*Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy. May your Kingdom come*” (*v. 2*). (Many manuscripts read simply “Father,” the intimate address Jesus Himself used.) The disciples were to ask God for daily bread, for forgiveness of sins as they forgive everyone indebted to them, and for protection from temptation. Luke’s version says, “*Forgive us our sins, for we ourselves also forgive everyone who is indebted to us*” (*v. 4*), connecting God’s forgiveness of sins with the believer’s forgiveness of others’ debts.

### The Friend at Midnight (*11:5–8*)

Jesus then told a parable found only in Luke. Imagine going to a friend at midnight and asking to borrow three loaves of bread because a traveler has arrived and you have nothing to offer him. Hospitality was a sacred duty in that culture; failing to feed a guest would bring shame on the whole household and village. Travelers often journeyed in the evening to avoid the heat, so a late arrival was not unusual. Families typically baked bread daily, so having none left at midnight was a real problem.

The friend inside answers, “*Don’t bother me. The door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed. I can’t get up and give it to you*” (*v. 7*). In a typical one-room peasant home, the whole family slept together on mats on a raised platform. Getting up meant waking everyone. Yet Jesus said that the friend would get up and give what was needed, not because of friendship, but because of the asker’s “*persistence*” (*v. 8*). This is studied below.

### Ask, Seek, Knock (*11:9–13*)

Jesus applied the parable: “*keep asking, and it will be given you. Keep seeking, and you will find. Keep knocking, and it will be opened to you*” (*v. 9*). The WEB’s wording “keep asking” captures the ongoing sense of the Greek verbs. Everyone who asks receives, seeks finds, and knocks has the door opened.

Then He reasoned from human fathers. What father would give his son a snake when he asks for a fish, or a scorpion when he asks for an egg? Even sinful parents know how to give good gifts. Then Jesus concluded with a promise unique to Luke’s wording, studied below: the heavenly Father will give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him.

### Jesus and Beelzebul (*11:14–28*)

Jesus cast out a demon that made a man mute. When the demon left, the man spoke, and the crowds were amazed. But some said, “*He casts out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of the demons*” (*v. 15*). Others tested Him by asking for a sign from heaven.

Jesus answered that a kingdom divided against itself falls. If Satan were fighting himself, his kingdom could not stand. He added, “*But if I by God’s finger cast out demons, then God’s Kingdom has come to you*” (*v. 20*). The phrase “finger of God” recalls *Exodus 8:19*, where Pharaoh’s magicians, unable to copy Moses’ miracle, admitted, “This is God’s finger.” Jesus’ power came directly from God, and it showed that God’s kingdom had arrived.

He told of a strong man, fully armed, guarding his house; but when someone stronger attacks and overpowers him, the stronger one takes away his armor and divides the spoils. Jesus is the stronger one who has come to defeat Satan. He then said, “*He who is not with me is against me*” (*v. 23*), and warned that an unclean spirit who leaves a person may return with seven others worse than itself if the “house” remains empty. Being cleaned up is not enough; a person must be filled with God’s presence.

As Jesus said these things, a woman in the crowd called out, “*Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts which nursed you!*” (*v. 27*) Jesus replied, “*On the contrary, blessed are those who hear the word of God, and keep it*” (*v. 28*). This exchange, found only in Luke, is studied below.

### The Sign of Jonah and the Lamp of the Body (*11:29–36*)

As crowds grew, Jesus called His generation evil because it sought a sign. The only sign given would be the sign of Jonah. Just as Jonah was a sign to the people of Nineveh, who repented at his preaching, the Son of Man would be a sign to this generation. The Queen of the South and the people of Nineveh would condemn this generation at the judgment, because they responded to lesser messengers, while “*one greater than Solomon is here*” (*v. 31*) and “*one greater than Jonah is here*” (*v. 32*).

Jesus then said that no one lights a lamp and hides it. The eye is the lamp of the body. When the eye is healthy, the whole body is full of light; when it is bad, the body is full of darkness. He warned, “*Therefore see whether the light that is in you isn’t darkness*” (*v. 35*). The problem was not a lack of light from Jesus but the spiritual condition of those who refused to see it.

### Woes Against Pharisees and Lawyers (*11:37–54*)

A Pharisee invited Jesus to dinner. Jesus went in and reclined at the table without first performing the ritual washing before the meal, and the Pharisee was surprised. Jesus said, “*Now you Pharisees cleanse the outside of the cup and of the platter, but your inward part is full of extortion and wickedness*” (*v. 39*). God made both the outside and the inside. Then He gave a surprising instruction: “*But give for gifts to the needy those things which are within, and behold, all things will be clean to you*” (*v. 41*). Generosity from the heart, rather than ritual washing, makes a person clean.

Jesus pronounced three woes on the Pharisees: for tithing small herbs while neglecting “*justice and God’s love*” (*v. 42*); for loving the best seats and public greetings; and for being like unmarked graves that people walk over without knowing, becoming unclean (*Numbers 19:16*). The Pharisees appeared clean but secretly spread defilement.

One of the experts in the law said, “*Teacher, in saying this you insult us also*” (*v. 45*). Jesus pronounced three woes on the lawyers: for loading people with burdens they did not help carry; for building tombs for the prophets their ancestors killed, showing that they shared their ancestors’ attitude; and for taking away “*the key of knowledge*” (*v. 52*). They had the Scriptures, which pointed to God’s kingdom, but they neither entered it themselves nor allowed others to enter.

When Jesus left, the scribes and Pharisees became fiercely hostile and began questioning Him aggressively, “*lying in wait for him, and seeking to catch him in something he might say*” (*v. 54*). Opposition was growing as Jesus journeyed toward Jerusalem.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Luke 11:8* — Bold Persistence in Prayer

> *“I tell you, although he will not rise and give it to him because he is his friend, yet because of his persistence, he will get up and give him as many as he needs.”*
>
> — *Luke 11:8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse concludes a parable Jesus told right after teaching His disciples the Lord’s Prayer. In the story, a man has an unexpected guest arrive at midnight and has no bread to offer. In that culture, hospitality was a serious obligation; failing to provide food for a guest would bring shame. So the man goes to a friend’s house and asks to borrow three loaves.

The friend inside does not want to help. His door is locked, his children are asleep with him, and getting up would disturb the whole family. He says, “Don’t bother me.”

Then Jesus says, “*I tell you, although he will not rise and give it to him because he is his friend, yet because of his persistence, he will get up and give him as many as he needs*” (*v. 8*).

The word translated “persistence” literally means “shamelessness” or “boldness.” It describes the man’s willingness to keep asking without embarrassment, even at an inconvenient time. Some interpreters understand the word to refer to the sleeping friend’s desire to avoid shame. In a small village, refusing to help a neighbor with a guest would bring dishonor on him too. Either way, the result is that the friend gets up and gives him “*as many as he needs*” (*v. 8*), not just the minimum.

The parable uses a “how much more” argument. If a reluctant friend will help because of bold persistence, how much more will God, who is not reluctant at all, respond to His children’s prayers? Jesus is not saying God is like the sleepy friend. He is saying God is far better.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse teaches that believers can pray boldly and persistently. God is not irritated by His children’s requests. He invites them to ask, seek, and knock. The man in the parable asked for bread for someone else, a guest. This suggests that prayer for others’ needs is especially welcome to God.

It also shows that God’s response is generous. The friend gave “as many as he needs.” God does not give grudgingly or minimally. He gives abundantly according to His wisdom.

The parable must be read alongside Jesus’ teaching that God is a loving Father who knows what His children need (*Luke 12:30*). Persistence in prayer does not change God’s mind as if He were reluctant; rather, it expresses faith, deepens dependence, and shapes the one who prays. Luke later records a similar parable about a persistent widow, told “*that they must always pray, and not give up*” (*Luke 18:1*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to keep praying when answers seem delayed. Many believers give up praying for a need after a short time. Jesus invites them to keep asking with bold confidence that God hears.

It also encourages believers to pray for others. The man in the parable asked for bread to feed a guest. Believers can bring the needs of friends, family, neighbors, and even strangers to God, persistently and boldly.

Finally, this verse invites believers to approach God without shame. Some people hesitate to pray because they feel unworthy or worry that they are bothering God. Jesus’ parable encourages bold, “shameless” prayer, rooted in confidence in God’s goodness.

### *Luke 11:13* — The Father Gives the Holy Spirit

> *“If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him?”*
>
> — *Luke 11:13* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse concludes Jesus’ teaching on prayer that began with the disciples’ request, “Lord, teach us to pray.” Jesus had given them a model prayer, told the parable of the friend at midnight, and encouraged them to keep asking, seeking, and knocking.

Then He used an illustration from family life. Which father, if his son asked for a fish, would give him a snake? Or if he asked for an egg, would give him a scorpion? A snake might resemble a certain type of fish, and a scorpion curled up might look somewhat like an egg. No loving father would trick his child with something harmful.

Then comes this verse: “*If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him?*” (*v. 13*)

“Being evil” is a reminder that all humans are sinful, yet even sinful parents care for their children. The phrase “how much more” contrasts imperfect human parents with the perfect heavenly Father. If imperfect parents give good gifts, God will give far better gifts.

Matthew’s parallel says that the Father will give “good things” to those who ask (*Matthew 7:11*). Luke specifies the greatest good gift: “*the Holy Spirit*” (*v. 13*). The Holy Spirit is God’s own presence, dwelling in His people, empowering them, guiding them, and transforming them. Luke emphasizes the Holy Spirit throughout his Gospel and especially in Acts, where the Spirit is poured out on believers at Pentecost and throughout the early church.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals that God’s greatest gift to His children is Himself, through His Holy Spirit. Prayer is not merely a way to get things from God; it is a way to receive more of God. When believers pray, the Father gives them His presence and power.

It also reveals God’s character as a loving Father. He is not stingy or deceptive. He does not trick His children or give them harmful things. Even when He does not give exactly what they ask for, He gives what is good. The best gift is the Spirit, who helps believers in every circumstance.

In Luke’s second volume, Acts, this promise is fulfilled in remarkable ways. The disciples prayed, and the Spirit was poured out (*Acts 1:14*; *2:1–4*). Believers prayed, and the place was shaken, and they were filled with the Spirit (*Acts 4:31*). Prayer and the gift of the Spirit go together.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to ask God for the Holy Spirit. Believers who have trusted Christ already have the Spirit dwelling in them (*Romans 8:9*). Yet the New Testament also speaks of being filled with the Spirit repeatedly (*Ephesians 5:18*). Believers can ask God to fill them, guide them, strengthen them, and work through them by His Spirit.

It also encourages believers to trust God’s goodness in prayer. When God’s answers differ from their requests, they can trust that He is giving good gifts, not harmful ones. Their heavenly Father loves them and knows what they need.

Finally, this verse invites believers to seek God Himself, not only His gifts. Prayer is about relationship. The greatest answer to prayer is more of God’s presence in one’s life.

### *Luke 11:28* — Blessed Are Those Who Hear and Keep God’s Word

> *“But he said, ‘On the contrary, blessed are those who hear the word of God, and keep it.’”*
>
> — *Luke 11:28* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse records a brief exchange found only in Luke’s Gospel. Jesus had just been teaching about His victory over Satan and warning about the danger of an empty house that evil spirits can reoccupy. As He was speaking, “*a certain woman out of the multitude lifted up her voice and said to him, “Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts which nursed you!”*” (*v. 27*)

The woman was praising Jesus by praising His mother. In that culture, a woman’s honor was often tied to her children. Saying that the mother of such a son was blessed was a way of honoring the son. It was a sincere compliment, and it echoed what Elizabeth had said to Mary (*Luke 1:42*) and what Mary herself had sung, “*from now on, all generations will call me blessed*” (*Luke 1:48*).

Jesus responded, “*On the contrary, blessed are those who hear the word of God, and keep it*” (*v. 28*). The word translated “on the contrary” can also mean “rather” or “even more.” Jesus was not denying that His mother was blessed. Instead, He redirected the focus. The greatest blessing is not physical relationship to Jesus but hearing and obeying God’s word.

Interestingly, Mary herself is the model of this blessing in Luke’s Gospel. She heard God’s word through the angel and responded, “*Let it be done to me according to your word*” (*Luke 1:38*). She treasured God’s works in her heart (*Luke 2:19*, 51). Elizabeth said, “*Blessed is she who believed*” (*Luke 1:45*). Mary was blessed not only because she gave birth to Jesus but because she heard God’s word and kept it.

This saying echoes *Luke 8:21*, where Jesus said His mother and brothers are those who hear God’s word and do it.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse teaches that true blessedness is available to everyone. Physical closeness to Jesus, being His mother or brother, was a privilege only a few could have. But hearing and obeying God’s word is open to all. Anyone can receive the blessing Jesus describes.

It also shows that hearing alone is not enough. Jesus says blessed are those who hear the word and “keep” it, meaning guard it, obey it, and live by it. This connects with the parable of the sower, where the good soil hears the word and holds it fast (*Luke 8:15*), and with the parable of the builders, where the wise person hears and does Jesus’ words (*Luke 6:47–48*).

Finally, the verse places God’s word at the center of the life of faith. Relationship with Jesus is expressed through attentive listening and faithful obedience to what God has said.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to pursue the blessing Jesus describes. Believers can make hearing God’s word a regular part of their lives through Scripture reading, preaching, and reflection. They can also commit to keeping it, applying it to their decisions and relationships.

It also corrects any tendency to rely on religious connections or heritage. Being raised in a Christian family, belonging to a church, or having religious experiences are not substitutes for hearing and obeying God’s word personally.

Finally, this verse reminds believers that blessing is found in obedience. When they keep God’s word, even when it is difficult, they experience the blessedness Jesus promised: a life rooted in God’s truth and filled with His presence.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Luke 11* begins with prayer and ends with conflict, and both speak to the life of faith. The disciples’ request, “Lord, teach us to pray,” is one every believer can make. Jesus gave a simple pattern: address God as Father, seek His glory and kingdom, ask for daily needs, receive and extend forgiveness, and ask for protection from temptation. Believers can use this pattern to shape their prayers.

The parable of the friend at midnight and Jesus’ teaching on asking, seeking, and knocking encourage bold, persistent prayer. God is not reluctant; He is a loving Father who gives good gifts, especially the gift of the Holy Spirit. Believers can pray with confidence, especially for the needs of others, and seek God Himself above all His gifts.

The controversy over Beelzebul reminds believers that Jesus is stronger than Satan, and that neutrality toward Jesus is impossible. Being cleaned up without being filled with God’s presence leaves a person vulnerable. Believers can invite Christ to fill every part of their lives.

Jesus’ response to the woman in the crowd reminds believers that true blessedness comes from hearing and keeping God’s word. Finally, the woes against the Pharisees and lawyers warn against religion that focuses on outward appearance while neglecting justice, love for God, and generosity. Believers can examine their hearts, give generously to those in need, and make sure they are helping rather than hindering others from entering God’s kingdom.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, as Your disciples asked, I ask You: teach me to pray. Help me to call God my Father, to seek His glory and His kingdom, to depend on Him for daily bread, to receive His forgiveness and forgive others, and to ask for His protection from temptation. Give me boldness and persistence in prayer, especially for the needs of others.

Thank You that my heavenly Father gives good gifts and the greatest gift of all, the Holy Spirit. Fill me with Your Spirit, and keep my life from being an empty house. Thank You that You are stronger than every power of evil. Make me one of those who hear the word of God and keep it. Cleanse me from the inside, free me from hypocrisy, and teach me to practice justice, love for God, and generosity. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Luke · Chapter 12 of 24

# Luke — Chapter 12

Chapter Theme: Rich Toward God, Free From Fear, Ready for the Master

[Read Luke 12 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/LUK12.htm)

Main Teaching

Before a huge crowd, Jesus warns His disciples against hypocrisy and the fear of people, assuring them of the Father’s care. When a man asks Him to settle an inheritance dispute, Jesus warns against greed and tells the parable of the rich fool who stored up goods but was not rich toward God. He calls His “little flock” to trust the Father who delights to give them the kingdom, to be ready for the Master’s return, and to remember that much will be required from those entrusted with much.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Luke 12* continues Jesus’ journey to Jerusalem. At the end of *Luke 11*, Jesus had confronted the Pharisees and lawyers, and they began “*lying in wait for him*” (*Luke 11:54*). Now crowds of “*many thousands*” (*v. 1*) gather, so many that people are trampling one another. Yet Jesus speaks “*first of all*” (*v. 1*) to His disciples. The chapter’s teachings revolve around three dangers that threaten faithful discipleship: hypocrisy, greed, and spiritual carelessness. Running through all of them is Jesus’ answer to fear: the Father’s care and the promise of His kingdom.

Some of this teaching parallels Matthew (studied there: sparrows and fear at *Matthew 10:29–31*; anxiety and seeking the kingdom at *Matthew 6:33*; treasure in heaven at *Matthew 6:21*; the faithful servant at *Matthew 24:45–46*; division in families at *Matthew 10:34–39*). This chapter focuses on what is distinctive in Luke.

### Beware of Hypocrisy, Do Not Fear People (*12:1–12*)

Jesus warned, “*Beware of the yeast of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy*” (*v. 1*). Like yeast that silently spreads through dough, hypocrisy, pretending to be something one is not, spreads quietly and corrupts. Jesus reminded them that nothing hidden will stay hidden; what is whispered in private will be proclaimed from the housetops. Hypocrisy is not only wrong but ultimately futile, because God will bring everything into the open.

Then He addressed fear. He called His disciples “*my friends*” (*v. 4*), the only time in the first three Gospels that Jesus uses this word for His disciples. They should not fear those who can kill the body and then can do nothing more. Instead, they should fear God, who has authority over eternal destiny. Yet this holy fear is joined with deep comfort: five sparrows are sold for two small coins, yet “*Not one of them is forgotten by God*” (*v. 6*), and the hairs of their heads are all counted. Matthew’s version mentions two sparrows sold for one coin; Luke’s five for two suggests a fifth was thrown in free, the least valuable of all, and still not forgotten.

Jesus promised that whoever acknowledges Him before others, He will acknowledge before God’s angels, and whoever denies Him will be denied. He warned about blasphemy against the Holy Spirit (see *Matthew 12:31–32*). And He promised that when they were brought before synagogues and rulers, “*the Holy Spirit will teach you in that same hour what you must say*” (*v. 12*).

### The Rich Fool (*12:13–21*)

Someone in the crowd called out, “*Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me*” (*v. 13*). Rabbis were sometimes asked to settle legal disputes, since Jewish law covered inheritance (*Deuteronomy 21:17* gave the eldest son a double share). Jesus declined: “*Man, who made me a judge or an arbitrator over you?*” (*v. 14*) He saw a deeper problem than the legal question. He warned the whole crowd against greed, a warning studied below.

Then He told a parable found only in Luke. A rich man’s land produced an abundant harvest. He thought to himself, “*What will I do, because I don’t have room to store my crops?*” (*v. 17*) He decided to tear down his barns and build bigger ones, store everything there, and say to himself, “*Soul, you have many goods laid up for many years. Take your ease, eat, drink, and be merry*” (*v. 19*).

Notice how the man spoke only to himself. He used “I” and “my” repeatedly: my crops, my barns, my grain, my goods, my soul. He never thought of God or of others in need. In a land where many people lived on the edge of hunger, he planned only for his own comfort.

But God said to him, “*You foolish one, tonight your soul is required of you. The things which you have prepared—whose will they be?*” (*v. 20*) This is the only parable in which God Himself speaks directly. The man who planned for “many years” did not have even one more night. Jesus concluded, “*So is he who lays up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God*” (*v. 21*). This is studied below.

### Do Not Worry; Seek the Kingdom (*12:22–34*)

Turning to His disciples, Jesus said they should not worry about what they will eat or wear. Life is more than food, and the body more than clothing. He pointed to ravens, birds considered unclean in the law of Moses (*Leviticus 11:15*), which neither sow nor reap, yet God feeds them. He pointed to lilies that neither toil nor spin, yet are dressed more beautifully than King Solomon. Worrying cannot add an hour to one’s life. Instead, they should seek God’s kingdom, and these things would be given to them as well.

Then Jesus spoke one of the most tender sentences in the Gospels, studied below: “*Don’t be afraid, little flock, for it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the Kingdom*” (*v. 32*). Because the Father gives them the kingdom, they can be generous: “*Sell what you have and give gifts to the needy*” (*v. 33*), making purses that do not wear out and treasure in heaven that thieves cannot steal and moths cannot destroy. “*For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also*” (*v. 34*).

### Ready for the Master’s Return (*12:35–48*)

Jesus called His followers to readiness: “*Let your waist be dressed and your lamps burning*” (*v. 35*). In that culture, people wore long robes and tucked them into a belt when they needed to work or move quickly. Lamps burning meant being prepared even at night. They should be like servants waiting for their master to return from a wedding feast, ready to open the door the moment he knocks.

Then Jesus said something astonishing: when the master finds his servants watching, “*he will dress himself, make them recline, and will come and serve them*” (*v. 37*). In every normal household, servants waited on masters. Here the master serves the servants. This picture anticipates Jesus washing His disciples’ feet (*John 13*) and His words at the Last Supper: “*But I am among you as one who serves*” (*Luke 22:27*).

Jesus compared His return to a thief coming at an unexpected hour. Peter asked whether this parable was for the disciples or for everyone. Jesus answered with the image of a faithful and wise steward put in charge of a household, giving others their food at the right time. If the master finds him doing this, he will put him in charge of everything. But if the servant decides the master is delayed and begins beating the other servants and getting drunk, the master will return unexpectedly and punish him severely.

Jesus added a principle about responsibility, found only in Luke and studied below: the servant who knew the master’s will and did not do it will be punished more severely than one who did not know. “*To whomever much is given, of him will much be required*” (*v. 48*).

### Fire, Baptism, and Division (*12:49–53*)

Jesus said, “*I came to throw fire on the earth. I wish it were already kindled*” (*v. 49*). Fire in Scripture can mean judgment or purification, and John the Baptist had said Jesus would baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire (*Luke 3:16*). Then Jesus spoke of “*a baptism to be baptized with*” (*v. 50*), referring to His coming suffering and death, like being overwhelmed by deep waters. He said, “*how distressed I am until it is accomplished!*” (*v. 50*) Jesus felt the weight of the cross ahead of Him.

He warned that His coming would bring division rather than easy peace, even within families: father against son, mother against daughter. This does not mean Jesus wants families divided. It means that loyalty to Him would cause conflict when some family members followed Him and others opposed Him. Jesus does bring peace with God, but that peace may cost earthly peace.

### Reading the Times (*12:54–59*)

Jesus told the crowds that they could predict the weather: a cloud rising from the west, from the Mediterranean Sea, meant rain; a south wind from the desert meant heat. “*You hypocrites! You know how to interpret the appearance of the earth and the sky, but how is it that you don’t interpret this time?*” (*v. 56*) They could read weather signs but not the significance of Jesus’ presence among them.

He urged them to settle matters with an accuser on the way to court before it was too late, or they would be thrown into prison until the last penny was paid. The application was urgent: they were all on their way to God’s judgment. Now was the time to make things right with God through repentance, before the opportunity passed.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Luke 12:15* — Life Is Not Measured by Possessions

> *“He said to them, ‘Beware! Keep yourselves from covetousness, for a man’s life doesn’t consist of the abundance of the things which he possesses.’”*
>
> — *Luke 12:15* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus speaks these words after a man in the crowd asked Him to tell his brother to divide the family inheritance. Jesus had been teaching His disciples about weighty matters: hypocrisy, fearing God rather than people, and confessing Him before others. In the middle of this, the man interrupted with a request about money. Perhaps his older brother was holding onto the family property, and he felt cheated.

Jesus refused to act as a judge in the case. Instead, He addressed the attitude underneath the request, speaking to the whole crowd: “*Beware! Keep yourselves from covetousness*” (*v. 15*). The word “Beware” means to be watchful, and “keep yourselves” means to guard. Jesus used two strong verbs, suggesting that greed is a danger that can creep in unnoticed and requires constant vigilance. “Covetousness” (often translated “greed”) means the desire for more, an endless craving to have and accumulate. Jesus warned against “*covetousness*” (*v. 15*) in every form, not only obvious materialism but every subtle kind of wanting more.

Then He gave the reason: “*for a man’s life doesn’t consist of the abundance of the things which he possesses*” (*v. 15*). A person’s true life, their worth, identity, and meaning, is not measured by how much they own. Even having an abundance does not secure life. The parable of the rich fool that follows illustrates this vividly: the man had more than enough, but he lost his life that very night.

Jesus was not saying that the man’s concern for fairness was wrong in itself. Inheritance disputes can involve real injustice. But Jesus saw that the man’s heart was focused on possessions, and He warned everyone about the danger of letting the pursuit of things define their lives.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse exposes one of the most common and least recognized sins. Greed is rarely confessed, because people tend to measure themselves against those who have more and conclude that they are not greedy. Paul calls covetousness a form of idolatry (*Colossians 3:5*), because it gives to possessions the trust and devotion that belong to God. The tenth commandment forbids coveting (*Exodus 20:17*), showing that God cares about the desires of the heart, not only outward actions.

It also teaches a different definition of life. The world often measures success by wealth and possessions. Jesus says true life is found elsewhere: in relationship with God, in being rich toward Him, in love and generosity. Jesus Himself had nowhere to lay His head, yet He lived the fullest life ever lived.

Finally, the verse shows how greed damages relationships. The man was in conflict with his brother over money. Greed often divides families and friends, as people put possessions above people.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to watch carefully for greed in their own hearts. It can show up as constant dissatisfaction, envy of others’ possessions, anxiety about money, an inability to give generously, or conflict with family over inheritances and property. Naming these patterns honestly is the first step toward freedom.

It also encourages believers to define their lives by something other than possessions. They can find their identity in being children of God and their purpose in loving Him and others. Practicing contentment, gratitude, and generosity helps loosen greed’s grip.

Finally, this verse speaks to family conflicts over money. Believers can seek fairness while refusing to let possessions destroy relationships. Sometimes the wiser choice is to let go of what one is owed rather than lose a brother or sister. Where real injustice exists, believers can pursue it through fair means without letting bitterness take over.

### *Luke 12:20–21* — The Rich Fool

> *“‘But God said to him, “You foolish one, tonight your soul is required of you. The things which you have prepared—whose will they be?” So is he who lays up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God.’”*
>
> — *Luke 12:20–21* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These verses are the climax of the parable of the rich fool, which Jesus told after warning against greed. In the parable, a rich man’s land produced an abundant harvest. He had so much that his barns could not hold it. He decided to tear down his barns, build bigger ones, store everything, and then relax: eat, drink, and enjoy himself for many years.

The man’s plan seemed sensible. Storing a large harvest is not wrong in itself; Joseph stored grain in Egypt to prepare for famine (*Genesis 41*). The problem was his attitude. He spoke only to himself, planned only for himself, and thought only of his own comfort. He did not thank God for the harvest, did not consider those in need, and did not think about eternity.

Then “*But God said to him, ‘You foolish one, tonight your soul is required of you.’*” (*v. 20*) The word “foolish” in the Bible does not mean unintelligent. It describes someone who lives as though God does not matter (*Psalm 14:1*). The man was successful by worldly standards but foolish by God’s. “Your soul is required of you” uses the language of a loan being called in. His life was not his own; it had been lent to him by God, and now God was asking for it back.

“*The things which you have prepared—whose will they be?*” (*v. 20*) All his careful planning would benefit someone else. He could not take any of it with him. Ecclesiastes reflects on this same problem: a person works hard and then leaves everything to someone who did not work for it (*Ecclesiastes 2:18–21*).

Jesus concluded, “*So is he who lays up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God*” (*v. 21*). The contrast is between treasure stored “for himself” and being “rich toward God.” Being rich toward God means investing one’s life in what matters to God: loving Him, serving others, and generously sharing what He has given.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This parable teaches that life is short and uncertain, and that possessions cannot secure the future. James writes, “*For what is your life? For you are a vapor that appears for a little time, and then vanishes away*” (*James 4:14*). The rich man made plans for many years but did not have one more day. Wise living takes the shortness of life seriously.

It also reveals that everything people have is on loan from God. The man spoke of “my crops” and “my goods,” but his very soul was required of him. Believers are stewards, not owners, of their time, money, abilities, and lives.

Finally, the parable invites people to consider what it means to be “rich toward God.” Jesus explains in the following verses: seek God’s kingdom, give to the needy, and store up treasure in heaven (vv. 31–34). True wealth is measured by love for God and generosity toward others.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses invite believers to examine their plans and priorities. Are they planning their lives as if God does not matter? Are they focused only on their own comfort and security? Believers can plan responsibly while holding their plans humbly before God and keeping eternity in view.

They also challenge believers to use their abundance for God’s purposes. When God provides more than they need, believers can ask whether they are building bigger barns or sharing with those in need. Generosity is a way of being rich toward God.

Finally, these verses encourage believers to live with an awareness that life is short. This awareness is not meant to produce fear, but wisdom: investing in relationships, faithfulness, and God’s kingdom rather than in things that cannot last.

### *Luke 12:32* — “*Don't Be Afraid, Little Flock*” (*v. 32*)

> *“Don’t be afraid, little flock, for it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the Kingdom.”*
>
> — *Luke 12:32* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse comes at the end of Jesus’ teaching about worry. He had told His disciples not to be anxious about food and clothing, pointing to ravens that God feeds and lilies that God clothes. He reminded them that worry cannot add an hour to life. He told them that the nations of the world chase after these things, but their Father knows what they need. Instead, they should seek God’s kingdom, and these things would be added to them.

Then He spoke these words: “*Don’t be afraid, little flock, for it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the Kingdom*” (*v. 32*).

“*Don’t be afraid*” (*v. 32*). This command appears throughout Scripture, often when God reassures His people. Jesus knew His disciples faced many reasons for fear: poverty, persecution, uncertainty, and the dangers of following Him to Jerusalem.

“*little flock*” (*v. 32*). This phrase is tender. A flock is a group of sheep, dependent on their shepherd for protection, food, and guidance. “Little” emphasizes how small and vulnerable Jesus’ followers were: a handful of ordinary people in a world of powerful empires and hostile religious leaders. In the Old Testament, God often described Himself as the shepherd of Israel (*Psalm 23*; *Ezekiel 34*). Jesus is the shepherd who cares for His small and vulnerable flock.

“*for it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the Kingdom*” (*v. 32*). “Good pleasure” means delight, what God is glad to do. God is not reluctantly giving His people the kingdom; He delights to give it. “The Kingdom” is God’s reign, His salvation, His presence, and every blessing that comes with belonging to Him. This is the greatest gift possible.

The connection with the previous verses is important. If the Father is giving them the kingdom, surely He will also provide food and clothing. And because they have such a great treasure, they can be generous with earthly possessions (v. 33).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals the heart of God toward His people. He is not a harsh master but a loving Father who delights to give. Fear and anxiety often grow from a belief that God is distant, stingy, or unwilling to care for us. Jesus corrects this belief by showing God’s generous heart.

It also shows that the kingdom is a gift, not an achievement. The disciples do not earn the kingdom by their efforts; the Father gives it. This grace is the foundation of security for believers.

Finally, the verse connects freedom from fear with generosity. The next verse calls the disciples to sell possessions and give to the needy. People who are afraid tend to hoard. People who know that the Father has given them the kingdom are free to give generously.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse speaks to believers who feel small, vulnerable, or afraid. Whether facing financial uncertainty, health concerns, opposition, or an uncertain future, they can hear Jesus’ tender words: “Don’t be afraid, little flock.” They belong to the Good Shepherd, and their Father delights to give them the kingdom.

It also invites believers to trust God’s generosity. When they worry about their needs, they can remember that God has already given them the greatest gift. He will not withhold what they truly need.

Finally, this verse encourages generosity. Believers who are secure in the Father’s love and in the gift of the kingdom can hold their possessions loosely and share freely with others. Fear leads to hoarding; trust leads to generosity.

### *Luke 12:48* — Much Given, Much Required

> *“but he who didn’t know, and did things worthy of stripes, will be beaten with few stripes. To whomever much is given, of him will much be required; and to whom much was entrusted, of him more will be asked.”*
>
> — *Luke 12:48* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse concludes Jesus’ teaching about faithful and unfaithful servants. Jesus had described a steward put in charge of a household while the master was away. If the master returns and finds the steward faithfully caring for the other servants, he will be rewarded. But if the steward decides the master is delayed and begins abusing others and living carelessly, he will be severely punished.

Peter had asked whether this parable was for the disciples or for everyone (v. 41). Jesus’ answer suggests that it applies especially to leaders, those entrusted with responsibility over others, but its principle applies to all.

Jesus then explained that punishment would be proportional to knowledge. “*That servant who knew his lord’s will, and didn’t prepare nor do what he wanted, will be beaten with many stripes*” (*v. 47*), while “*he who didn’t know, and did things worthy of stripes, will be beaten with few stripes*” (*v. 48*). Both are accountable, but the one who knew more is more accountable.

Then He gave the principle: “*To whomever much is given, of him will much be required; and to whom much was entrusted, of him more will be asked*” (*v. 48*).

This statement applies to every kind of gift and resource: knowledge of God’s will, spiritual gifts, opportunities, money, abilities, influence, and positions of leadership. The more a person has received from God, the greater their responsibility to use it faithfully.

The disciples had received much: they had walked with Jesus, heard His teaching, seen His miracles, and been given authority. Their responsibility was correspondingly great.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse teaches that God’s judgment is fair and proportional. He takes into account what each person knew and what each person was given. This reflects God’s justice, which Scripture describes as perfect (*Deuteronomy 32:4*). Those who have greater knowledge and privilege bear greater responsibility.

It also teaches that every gift from God comes with a calling. Gifts are not given merely for personal enjoyment or advancement; they are entrusted for God’s purposes and for the good of others. The steward in the parable was given authority so that he could feed the household.

Finally, this verse speaks especially to leaders. James writes, “*Let not many of you be teachers, my brothers, knowing that we will receive heavier judgment*” (*James 3:1*). Those who lead God’s people are accountable for how they care for them.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to take inventory of what they have been given. Many believers have received a great deal: access to Scripture, freedom to worship, education, resources, health, relationships, and spiritual gifts. These are not merely privileges but responsibilities. Believers can ask how they are using what God has entrusted to them.

It especially challenges those who know God’s will. Believers who have heard much teaching and know what God desires are more accountable for obeying it. Knowledge should lead to action.

Finally, this verse calls leaders, whether parents, pastors, teachers, employers, or others with influence, to faithful stewardship. They are entrusted with the care of others, and they will give an account. This is a sobering responsibility, but it also gives purpose and dignity to their roles.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Luke 12* addresses three great dangers in the life of faith: hypocrisy, greed, and spiritual carelessness. Against hypocrisy, Jesus reminds believers that nothing hidden will remain hidden, so they can live with integrity, the same in private as in public. Against the fear of people, He reminds them that God holds ultimate authority and cares for them in every detail. Believers can confess Christ openly and trust the Holy Spirit to help them when they are challenged.

Against greed, Jesus warns that life does not consist in possessions. The parable of the rich fool calls believers to examine their plans, refuse to live as though God does not matter, and use their abundance to be rich toward God. Contentment, gratitude, and generosity are practical ways to resist greed. In family disputes over money and property, believers can pursue fairness without letting possessions destroy relationships.

Against anxiety, Jesus offers the Father’s care. The Father feeds ravens and clothes lilies, and He delights to give His little flock the kingdom. Believers can bring their worries to Him, seek His kingdom first, and find freedom to be generous because they are secure in His love.

Against spiritual carelessness, Jesus calls for readiness. Believers can live each day prepared for the Master’s return, faithfully caring for the people and responsibilities entrusted to them. They can remember that much is required from those who have been given much, and that the Master who returns will Himself serve His faithful servants. Finally, Jesus’ call to read the times and settle accounts urges believers not to delay in making things right with God and with others.

## Chapter Prayer

Father, thank You that You see everything and that nothing is hidden from You. Free me from hypocrisy, and help me to live the same way in private as I do in public. Thank You that You do not forget even one sparrow and that You know every hair on my head. Help me not to fear people, but to honor You and confess Jesus before others.

Guard my heart from greed in all its forms. Remind me that my life does not consist in the abundance of my possessions. Keep me from being like the rich fool, and teach me to be rich toward You. When I am anxious, help me to hear Jesus say, “Don’t be afraid, little flock, for it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the kingdom.” Make me generous, ready for Christ’s return, and faithful with everything You have entrusted to me. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Luke · Chapter 13 of 24

# Luke — Chapter 13

Chapter Theme: Time to Repent, Freedom for the Bound, and the Narrow Door

[Read Luke 13 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/LUK13.htm)

Main Teaching

When people ask about victims of violence and disaster, Jesus refuses to treat tragedy as proof of greater guilt and instead calls everyone to repent, illustrating God’s patience with the parable of a fruitless fig tree given one more year. He frees a woman bent over for eighteen years and defends healing her on the Sabbath. He describes God’s kingdom as growing from small beginnings, urges people to strive to enter through the narrow door while it is open, and laments over Jerusalem.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Luke 13* continues Jesus’ journey toward Jerusalem, and its themes follow naturally from the end of *Luke 12*, where Jesus urged the crowds to read the signs of the times and to settle accounts before reaching the judge. The chapter returns again and again to urgency: the time to repent is now, God’s patience is real but not endless, and the door to the kingdom will not stay open forever. At the same time, the healing of the bent woman shows the compassion that lies behind every warning.

### Tragedy and Repentance (*13:1–5*)

Some people told Jesus about Galileans “*whose blood Pilate had mixed with their sacrifices*” (*v. 1*). No other ancient source records this event, but it fits what is known of Pilate, who sometimes used violent force against crowds. Apparently Roman soldiers had killed some Galilean pilgrims while they were offering sacrifices at the temple, so that their blood mingled with the blood of their animals.

Many people in that time believed that disaster was always a direct punishment for a particular sin. Job’s friends assumed this about Job; the disciples assumed it about a man born blind (*John 9:2*). Jesus addressed this assumption directly, and then mentioned a second tragedy: eighteen people killed when a tower in Siloam, in the southern part of Jerusalem near the pool of Siloam, collapsed on them. One tragedy was caused by human cruelty, the other by an accident. In both cases, Jesus said the victims were not worse sinners than others. This teaching is studied below.

### The Parable of the Barren Fig Tree (*13:6–9*)

Jesus then told a parable found only in Luke. A man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard. For three years he came looking for fruit and found none. Fig trees normally began bearing within a few years of planting, so three years without fruit suggested the tree was not going to produce. He told the gardener to cut it down: “*Why does it waste the soil?*” (*v. 7*) A fruitless tree took up space and drew nutrients from ground that could support something productive.

But the gardener asked for one more year to dig around it and fertilize it. If it bore fruit, good; if not, it could be cut down. This parable is studied below. It follows naturally from Jesus’ call to repent: God is patient, giving time and care to bring about fruit, but the time of patience will end.

### Healing a Woman Bent Over (*13:10–17*)

On a Sabbath, Jesus was teaching in a synagogue. This is the last time Luke records Jesus teaching in a synagogue. A woman was there who had been crippled by “*a spirit of infirmity eighteen years*” (*v. 11*). She was bent over and could not straighten up at all. Luke the physician describes her condition carefully; it may have been a severe spinal disorder, and Luke connects it with a spiritual cause.

When Jesus saw her, He called her forward and said, “*Woman, you are freed from your infirmity*” (*v. 12*). He laid His hands on her, and immediately she straightened up and began praising God.

The synagogue leader was indignant because Jesus had healed on the Sabbath. Notice that he did not speak directly to Jesus. He spoke to the crowd: “*There are six days in which men ought to work. Therefore come on those days and be healed, and not on the Sabbath day!*” (*v. 14*) He treated healing as work that violated the Sabbath (*Exodus 20:9–10*).

Jesus answered, “*You hypocrites!*” (*v. 15*) He pointed out that each of them would untie his ox or donkey on the Sabbath and lead it to water. Jewish teachers allowed this kind of care for animals. Then He drew the conclusion that is studied below. His opponents were humiliated, and the whole crowd rejoiced at all the wonderful things He was doing.

### The Mustard Seed and the Yeast (*13:18–21*)

Jesus asked what God’s kingdom was like. It is like a mustard seed planted in a garden that grows into a tree large enough for birds to nest in its branches. It is also like yeast that a woman mixed into about sixty pounds of flour until all of it was leavened. Placed right after the healing of one bent woman in an ordinary synagogue, these parables suggest that the kingdom’s work, though it may look small, is growing and will transform everything. (See *Matthew 13* and *Mark 4:30–32*.)

### The Narrow Door (*13:22–30*)

Luke reminds readers that Jesus was traveling through towns and villages, teaching, as He made His way to Jerusalem. Someone asked, “*Lord, are they few who are saved?*” (*v. 23*) This was a debated question among Jewish teachers. Jesus did not give a number. Instead, He turned the question into a personal challenge, studied below.

He warned that once the owner of the house gets up and shuts the door, people will stand outside knocking and saying, “Lord, open to us!” He will answer, “*I don’t know you or where you come from*” (*v. 25*). They will protest, “*We ate and drank in your presence, and you taught in our streets*” (*v. 26*). Casual acquaintance with Jesus, having been around Him or heard Him teach, is not the same as knowing Him. He will tell them to depart.

There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth when they see Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and all the prophets in God’s kingdom while they themselves are thrown out. Meanwhile, people will come “*from the east, west, north, and south*” (*v. 29*), Gentiles from every direction, and sit down at the feast in God’s kingdom. “*Behold, there are some who are last who will be first, and there are some who are first who will be last*” (*v. 30*).

### Herod and the Lament Over Jerusalem (*13:31–35*)

At that time, some Pharisees came and told Jesus to leave, because Herod Antipas wanted to kill Him. Not all Pharisees were hostile to Jesus; these may have been genuinely warning Him, or they may have wanted Him out of their area. Herod had already executed John the Baptist.

Jesus replied, “*Go and tell that fox*” (*v. 32*). A fox was seen as a sly, destructive animal, and perhaps also a small, insignificant one compared to a lion. Jesus was not intimidated. He would continue driving out demons and healing people today and tomorrow, and on the third day He would reach His goal. He must keep going, “*for it can’t be that a prophet would perish outside of Jerusalem*” (*v. 33*). Jesus spoke with sorrowful irony: Jerusalem was the city where prophets were killed. His death would happen there, on God’s timetable, not Herod’s.

Then Jesus lamented over Jerusalem, longing to gather its children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, though they were unwilling. Their house would be left desolate, and they would not see Him until they said, “*Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!*” (*v. 35*) (This lament is studied at *Matthew 23:37*.) In Luke, these words come before Jesus’ entry into Jerusalem, where the crowds will indeed shout these words of *Psalm 118* (*Luke 19:38*).

## Important Verses Explained

### *Luke 13:2–3* — Tragedy and the Call to Repent

> *“Jesus answered them, Do you think that these Galileans were worse sinners than all the other Galileans, because they suffered such things? I tell you, no, but unless you repent, you will all perish in the same way.”*
>
> — *Luke 13:2–3* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These verses are Jesus’ response to people who told Him about a tragic event. Some Galilean worshipers had been killed by Pilate’s soldiers while offering sacrifices, so that their blood mixed with the blood of their animals. The people who reported this may have expected Jesus to condemn Pilate, or they may have been wondering what these Galileans had done to deserve such a fate.

Jesus addressed the assumption behind their report: “*Do you think that these Galileans were worse sinners than all the other Galileans, because they suffered such things?*” (*v. 2*) Many people in that time believed that terrible suffering was proof of terrible sin. If something awful happened to someone, they must have deserved it.

Jesus answered His own question firmly: “*I tell you, no*” (*v. 3*). The victims were not worse sinners than other people. Their suffering was not a sign of special guilt. Jesus then mentioned another tragedy, the collapse of the tower in Siloam that killed eighteen people, and gave the same answer: they were not worse offenders than everyone else in Jerusalem.

But Jesus did not stop there. He turned the question back to His listeners: “*but unless you repent, you will all perish in the same way*” (*v. 3*). Instead of speculating about why others suffered, His listeners needed to examine their own hearts. Everyone is a sinner who needs to repent. The tragedies were reminders that life is uncertain and death can come suddenly. The proper response was not to judge the victims but to turn to God while there was still time.

The phrase “perish in the same way” may also have had a more specific meaning. If the nation continued on its path of rejecting God and pursuing violent rebellion against Rome, many would die by Roman swords and falling buildings, as happened when Jerusalem was destroyed in A.D. 70.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses correct a common and harmful way of thinking about suffering. Scripture does teach that sin has consequences, and sometimes suffering results from specific wrongdoing. But Jesus clearly rejects the idea that every tragedy is a sign of special guilt. The book of Job makes the same point: Job suffered greatly, yet God declared him righteous. In *John 9:3*, Jesus said of the man born blind that neither he nor his parents had sinned to cause his blindness.

At the same time, Jesus refuses to let His listeners avoid their own need for repentance. All people are sinners (*Romans 3:23*), and all need to turn to God. Tragedies remind everyone that life is fragile and that they will one day stand before God.

Finally, these verses show Jesus’ compassion and honesty together. He did not blame victims, and He did not give easy explanations for suffering. But He did speak urgently about the need for repentance, because He cared about His listeners’ eternal destiny.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses warn believers against blaming people for their suffering. When someone experiences illness, accident, violence, or natural disaster, believers should not assume that they are being punished for some hidden sin. Such assumptions can deeply wound people who are already hurting. Instead, believers can respond with compassion, prayer, and practical help.

They also invite believers to examine their own lives. When tragedies happen, it is natural to ask why. Jesus redirects the question: “What does this mean for me?” Tragedies remind people that life is short and uncertain, and they call everyone to be ready to meet God.

Finally, these verses encourage believers not to delay repentance. Many people intend to make things right with God someday. Jesus’ words show that there may not be a “someday.” Now is the time to turn to Him.

### *Luke 13:8* — One More Year: The Patience of God

> *“He answered, ‘Lord, leave it alone this year also, until I dig around it and fertilize it.”*
>
> — *Luke 13:8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse is the gardener’s plea in the parable of the barren fig tree. Jesus told this parable right after calling His listeners to repent. In the story, a man had a fig tree in his vineyard. Fig trees were often planted in vineyards, where the soil was good. For three years the owner came looking for figs and found none. He told the gardener, “*Cut it down! Why does it waste the soil?*” (*v. 7*) The tree was taking up good ground and nutrients without producing anything.

The gardener answered, “*Lord, leave it alone this year also, until I dig around it and fertilize it*” (*v. 8*). He asked for one more year. During that year, he would give the tree special care: digging around its roots to loosen the soil and let in water and air, and adding manure to nourish it. Then, as the next verse says, “*If it bears fruit, fine; but if not, after that, you can cut it down*” (*v. 9*).

In the Old Testament, the fig tree and the vineyard were images for Israel (*Isaiah 5:1–7*; *Hosea 9:10*). In the context of Jesus’ ministry, the parable described Israel, and especially Jerusalem, which had received God’s care through the prophets and now through Jesus Himself, yet had not produced the fruit of repentance. Some interpreters connect the “three years” with the approximate length of Jesus’ ministry, though the parable does not say this directly.

The gardener’s plea shows God’s patience and mercy. Judgment was deserved, but more time and more care were given. Yet the parable does not end with a guarantee. It leaves the outcome open: will the tree bear fruit?

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals God’s patience with people who have not yet responded to Him. Peter writes that God “*is patient with us, not wishing that anyone should perish, but that all should come to repentance*” (*2 Peter 3:9*). God’s delay in judgment is not weakness or indifference; it is an opportunity for repentance.

The gardener’s work also shows that God does not merely wait passively. He digs and fertilizes. He actively works to bring about fruit through His Word, His Spirit, circumstances, and the people He sends. Many believers can look back and see how God patiently worked in their lives before they responded to Him.

At the same time, the parable warns that God’s patience has a limit. The tree is given one more year, not unlimited time. Grace should not be taken for granted. The opportunity to repent and bear fruit is real, and it is urgent.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to respond to God’s patience with repentance and fruitfulness. If God has been patiently working in their lives, perhaps through difficulties, sermons, conversations, or quiet conviction, they can respond now rather than delay.

It also offers hope to those who feel spiritually unfruitful. God has not given up on them. He continues to work, digging around and nourishing their lives. Believers can cooperate with His work by spending time in His Word, prayer, and fellowship, allowing Him to bring fruit.

Finally, this verse encourages believers to be patient with others, as God is patient. Like the gardener, they can pray for and care for people who have not yet borne fruit, rather than giving up on them quickly.

### *Luke 13:16* — A Daughter of Abraham Set Free

> *“Ought not this woman, being a daughter of Abraham whom Satan had bound eighteen long years, be freed from this bondage on the Sabbath day?”*
>
> — *Luke 13:16* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse is the climax of Jesus’ response to a synagogue leader who objected to Him healing on the Sabbath. Jesus had been teaching in a synagogue when He saw a woman who had been bent over for eighteen years, unable to straighten up. He called her forward, declared her free from her disability, and laid His hands on her. Immediately she stood up straight and praised God.

The synagogue leader was indignant and told the crowd that there were six days for work, so people should come to be healed on those days and not on the Sabbath. Jesus called His critics hypocrites and pointed out that they untied their oxen and donkeys on the Sabbath to lead them to water. Then He said, “*Ought not this woman, being a daughter of Abraham whom Satan had bound eighteen long years, be freed from this bondage on the Sabbath day?*” (*v. 16*)

Several phrases are significant. “*this woman, being a daughter of Abraham*” (*v. 16*). The phrase “son of Abraham” was common for Jewish men, but “daughter of Abraham” was rare. Jesus honored her as a full member of God’s covenant people, worthy of care and dignity. If an ox deserves to be untied on the Sabbath, surely a daughter of Abraham deserves more.

“*whom Satan had bound eighteen long years*” (*v. 16*). Jesus revealed that her condition was connected to Satan’s oppression. Luke had described her as having “a spirit of infirmity.” The word “bound” connects with the image of untying animals.

“*be freed from this bondage on the Sabbath day?*” (*v. 16*) Jesus argued that the Sabbath was the most fitting day for her release. The Sabbath celebrated God’s rest and Israel’s freedom from slavery in Egypt (*Deuteronomy 5:15*). Setting a captive free was exactly in keeping with the Sabbath’s purpose.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that Jesus came to set people free from every kind of bondage. In His first sermon at Nazareth, He announced that He was sent “*to proclaim release to the captives*” (*Luke 4:18*) and “*to deliver those who are crushed*” (*Luke 4:18*). The healing of the bent woman was a living fulfillment of that mission.

It also shows Jesus’ compassion for those who suffer long. The woman had been bound for eighteen years. Jesus noticed her, called her, touched her, and restored her. He also restored her dignity, calling her a daughter of Abraham in front of the whole synagogue.

Finally, the verse exposes the danger of valuing religious rules above people. The synagogue leader was more concerned about the Sabbath rules than about the woman’s suffering. Jesus showed that God’s commands are meant to bring life and freedom, not to keep people bound.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages anyone who has been burdened for a long time, whether by illness, depression, addiction, grief, or spiritual oppression. Jesus sees them and has the power to set them free. They can bring their burdens to Him, trusting His compassion and authority.

It also reminds believers to honor people’s dignity. Jesus called the woman a “daughter of Abraham,” affirming her value. Believers can treat people who are suffering or marginalized with respect and remind them of their worth before God.

Finally, this verse challenges believers to examine whether their religious practices ever stand in the way of compassion. Churches can make sure that their traditions and schedules serve people rather than burden them, and that they are quick to help those in need.

### *Luke 13:24* — Strive to Enter Through the Narrow Door

> *“Strive to enter in by the narrow door, for many, I tell you, will seek to enter in and will not be able.”*
>
> — *Luke 13:24* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse is Jesus’ answer to a question asked as He traveled through towns and villages on His way to Jerusalem. Someone asked, “*Lord, are they few who are saved?*” (*v. 23*) This was a common topic of discussion among Jewish teachers. Some believed that all Israel would share in the age to come; others believed only a faithful remnant would.

Jesus did not answer the question directly. Instead, He turned it into a personal challenge: “*Strive to enter in by the narrow door, for many, I tell you, will seek to enter in and will not be able*” (*v. 24*).

“*Strive*” (*v. 24*) translates a Greek word from which we get “agonize.” It was used for athletes competing in contests. Jesus calls for serious, wholehearted effort. Entering the kingdom is not something to approach casually.

“*the narrow door*” (*v. 24*). A narrow door allows only one person at a time and requires effort to pass through. In *Matthew 7:13–14*, Jesus speaks of a narrow gate and a hard road leading to life. The narrow door represents the way of repentance and faith in Jesus Himself. In *John 10:9*, Jesus says, “*I am the door*” (*John 10:9*).

“*for many, I tell you, will seek to enter in and will not be able*” (*v. 24*). In the following verses, Jesus explains why. There will come a time when the owner of the house shuts the door. Then those outside will knock and claim that they ate and drank with Him and heard Him teach in their streets. But He will say He does not know them. Many will try to enter too late, or on their own terms, relying on casual association with Jesus rather than genuine relationship with Him.

Jesus’ answer shifted the focus from curiosity about others to urgency about oneself. The important question is not “How many will be saved?” but “Am I entering?”

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse teaches that salvation requires a personal, wholehearted response to Jesus. The word “strive” does not mean that people earn salvation by effort; salvation is God’s gift of grace (*Ephesians 2:8–9*). Rather, it means taking God’s invitation seriously, turning from sin, and committing oneself to Jesus with urgency and sincerity.

It also warns against false security. Those outside the door claimed familiarity with Jesus: they had eaten with Him and heard Him teach. But familiarity is not the same as faith. Many people today know about Jesus, attend church occasionally, or grew up in Christian families, but have never personally entered through the narrow door.

Finally, the following verses show that the kingdom will include people from every direction: east, west, north, and south. Many who considered themselves insiders will be outside, while outsiders from the nations will sit at the feast. God’s kingdom will surprise people.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites each person to make sure they have entered through the narrow door. Instead of speculating about others’ salvation, believers can examine their own relationship with Jesus. Do they truly know Him, trust Him, and follow Him?

It also encourages believers not to delay. The door will not stay open forever. Those who have been putting off a decision to follow Jesus can respond now while the opportunity remains.

Finally, this verse calls believers to humility and hope. They should not assume that religious familiarity guarantees salvation, and they should rejoice that God’s kingdom will include people from every nation who come to Him in faith. Believers can share the invitation widely, urging others to enter while the door is open.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Luke 13* brings together urgent warnings and tender compassion. Jesus’ response to the tragedies of the slain Galileans and the fallen tower teaches believers not to blame victims for their suffering, while reminding everyone that life is uncertain and repentance cannot wait. Believers can respond to tragedy with compassion for those who suffer and with honest self-examination.

The parable of the barren fig tree reveals God’s patience. He gives time and care to bring about fruit. Believers can respond to that patience by repenting and bearing fruit, and they can show similar patience toward others who have not yet responded to God.

The healing of the bent woman shows Jesus’ compassion for those who have suffered for a long time and His power to set people free. It also challenges any religious attitude that values rules above people. Believers can honor the dignity of those who suffer and make sure their practices help rather than hinder compassion.

The parables of the mustard seed and yeast encourage believers that God’s kingdom grows from small beginnings. The teaching about the narrow door calls each person to enter through Jesus with wholehearted commitment, not relying on familiarity with religion. And the warning about Herod and the lament over Jerusalem show Jesus’ courage in following God’s plan and His grief over those who refuse to come to Him. Believers can follow Him with courage and share His longing for people to be gathered into His care.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, keep me from judging those who suffer as if their pain proved their guilt. Give me compassion for the hurting, and help me to hear Your call to repentance in my own life. Thank You for Your patience with me, like the gardener who asked for one more year. Work in my life to make me fruitful, and help me to respond to Your care without delay.

Thank You for setting free the woman who was bent over for eighteen years. Set me free from whatever binds me, and help me to treat every person with the dignity You give them. Help me to strive to enter through the narrow door, to truly know You and not merely know about You. Give me courage to follow Your path as You followed the Father’s plan, and share with me Your longing to gather people under Your wings. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
