Luke · Chapter 14 of 24

# Luke — Chapter 14

Chapter Theme: The Banquet of the Kingdom and the Cost of Coming

[Read Luke 14 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/LUK14.htm)

Main Teaching

At a Sabbath meal in a Pharisee’s home, Jesus heals a man and then teaches about humility, telling guests not to grab the best seats and hosts to invite the poor and disabled who cannot repay them. Through the parable of the great banquet, He shows that God’s invitation goes out to the outcasts after the invited guests make excuses. Then, turning to the crowds following Him, He warns that discipleship requires putting Him above every other love and counting the cost before beginning.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Luke 14* is set mostly around a dinner table. Meals in the ancient world were important social events that reflected and reinforced people’s status. Where you sat, who invited you, and whom you invited all showed your place in society. Guests reclined on couches arranged around tables, with the most honored places closest to the host. Hosts often invited people who could invite them back, creating networks of social obligation. Jesus uses this setting to teach about God’s kingdom, where these values are turned upside down.

The chapter continues Jesus’ journey to Jerusalem. In *Luke 13*, He spoke of people coming from east and west to feast in God’s kingdom while some who expected to be inside would be shut out (*Luke 13:29–30*). *Luke 14* develops this theme of the kingdom banquet.

### Healing on the Sabbath (*14:1–6*)

On a Sabbath, Jesus went to eat at the house of a leading Pharisee. Sabbath meals were often special occasions with guests. Luke notes ominously, “*they were watching him*” (*v. 1*). In front of Jesus was a man suffering from “*dropsy*” (*v. 2*), a condition in which the body swells with fluid, often a sign of serious heart, kidney, or liver disease. Some interpreters wonder whether the man had been placed there deliberately to test Jesus.

Jesus asked the lawyers and Pharisees, “*Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?*” (*v. 3*) They said nothing. Jesus took hold of the man, healed him, and sent him away. Then He asked which of them, if a son or an ox fell into a well on the Sabbath, would not immediately pull him out. They had no answer. This is the fourth Sabbath healing in Luke (see 4:31–39; *6:6–11*; *13:10–17*), and each time Jesus shows that doing good on the Sabbath fulfills its purpose.

### Taking the Lowest Place (*14:7–11*)

Jesus noticed how the guests chose the places of honor at the table. He told them a parable. At a wedding feast, do not take the place of honor, because someone more distinguished may arrive, and the host may ask you to give up your seat. Then, embarrassed, you would have to move to the lowest place. Instead, take the lowest place, so that the host may say, “*Friend, move up higher*” (*v. 10*), and you will be honored in front of everyone.

This was practical wisdom, echoing *Proverbs 25:6–7*. But Jesus was teaching something deeper about God’s kingdom: “*For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted*” (*v. 11*). In God’s kingdom, honor is not grasped but given. Those who humble themselves will be lifted up by God. (A similar saying is studied at *Matthew 23:11–12*.)

### Inviting Those Who Cannot Repay (*14:12–14*)

Then Jesus spoke to the host. When you give a lunch or a dinner, do not invite friends, relatives, or rich neighbors, who may invite you back and repay you. Instead, invite “*the poor, the maimed, the lame, or the blind*” (*v. 13*). This is studied below. Jesus’ list matters: in some Jewish groups of the time, people with physical disabilities were excluded from certain religious gatherings. Jesus told the host to welcome exactly these people.

### The Parable of the Great Banquet (*14:15–24*)

Hearing this, one of the guests said, “*Blessed is he who will feast in God’s Kingdom!*” (*v. 15*) Jews looked forward to the great banquet God would host at the end of the age (*Isaiah 25:6*). The guest seemed to assume that he and others like him would certainly be there.

Jesus responded with a parable. A man prepared a great banquet and invited many guests. As was customary, guests received an initial invitation, and when everything was ready, the host sent a servant to tell them, “*Come, for everything is ready now*” (*v. 17*). Accepting the first invitation and then refusing the second was a serious insult.

But they all began to make excuses. One had bought a field and needed to see it. Another had bought five pairs of oxen and needed to test them. A third had just married. These excuses were weak. No one would buy a field without seeing it first, or oxen without testing them. Even the newly married man could have come; the law exempted new husbands from military service (*Deuteronomy 24:5*), not from dinners. The excuses revealed that the guests simply did not value the invitation.

The host was angry and sent his servant out to the streets and alleys of the town to bring in “*the poor, maimed, blind, and lame*” (*v. 21*), the same people Jesus told the Pharisee to invite. This is studied below. When there was still room, the master sent the servant to the roads and country lanes outside the town to “*compel them to come in*” (*v. 23*). The word “compel” does not mean force; it means urge strongly. People from outside the town, perhaps travelers or outcasts, would be reluctant to believe that the invitation was really for them, so the servant needed to persuade them. The master said that none of the originally invited guests would taste his banquet.

The parable describes how the religious leaders and many in Israel, who had been invited through the prophets, were refusing Jesus’ invitation, while outcasts and sinners within Israel, and then Gentiles from outside, were coming in. (A similar parable is studied at *Matthew 22*, where it is set at a king’s wedding feast.)

### The Cost of Discipleship (*14:25–35*)

Large crowds were traveling with Jesus. He turned to them and spoke words that would have stopped many in their tracks: “*If anyone comes to me, and doesn’t disregard his own father, mother, wife, children, brothers, and sisters, yes, and his own life also, he can’t be my disciple*” (*v. 26*). This verse is studied below. He added, “*Whoever doesn’t bear his own cross and come after me, can’t be my disciple*” (*v. 27*).

Then Jesus told two short parables about counting the cost. Someone who wants to build a tower first sits down and estimates the cost, to see if he has enough to finish it; otherwise people will mock him for starting something he could not complete. And a king going to war against another king first considers whether his ten thousand soldiers can defeat twenty thousand; if not, he sends a delegation to ask for terms of peace. The first of these is studied below.

Jesus concluded, “*So therefore, whoever of you who doesn’t renounce all that he has, he can’t be my disciple*” (*v. 33*). Following Jesus means placing everything one has under His lordship.

Finally, Jesus spoke about salt. Salt is good, but if it loses its saltiness, it is useless, not fit even for the soil or the manure pile; it is thrown out. Salt in that region was often mixed with other minerals, and if the actual salt dissolved away, the remaining substance was worthless. A disciple who loses commitment to Jesus loses the very quality that makes them useful. Jesus ended, “*He who has ears to hear, let him hear*” (*v. 35*).

## Important Verses Explained

### *Luke 14:13–14* — Invite Those Who Cannot Repay You

> *“But when you make a feast, ask the poor, the maimed, the lame, or the blind; and you will be blessed, because they don’t have the resources to repay you. For you will be repaid in the resurrection of the righteous.”*
>
> — *Luke 14:13–14* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus speaks these words to the host of a dinner party, a leading Pharisee who had invited Jesus to a Sabbath meal. Jesus had just watched the guests compete for the best seats and had told them to take the lowest places instead. Now He turned to the host and addressed the guest list itself.

In verse 12, Jesus told him not to invite friends, brothers, relatives, or rich neighbors, because they might invite him back and repay him. In that culture, meals were part of a system of social exchange. People invited those of equal or higher status, and they expected to be invited in return. Hospitality built networks of influence and honor.

Then Jesus said, “*But when you make a feast, ask the poor, the maimed, the lame, or the blind*” (*v. 13*). These were people at the bottom of society. The poor could not return the invitation. The disabled were often excluded from social and even religious life. Some Jewish writings of the time excluded people with such conditions from certain community gatherings. Inviting them would bring no social advantage.

“*and you will be blessed, because they don’t have the resources to repay you. For you will be repaid in the resurrection of the righteous*” (*v. 14*). The blessing comes precisely because they cannot repay. Generosity that expects a return is merely exchange. True generosity gives without expecting anything back. God Himself will reward such generosity at the resurrection of the righteous, when He raises His people and establishes His kingdom.

Jesus was not saying it is wrong to share meals with family and friends. He used a common Jewish style of overstatement (“not this, but that”) to make a point: generosity should especially reach those who cannot give back.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This teaching reflects God’s own generosity. God invites people into His kingdom who have nothing to offer Him. Every believer is like the poor, the crippled, the lame, and the blind, welcomed to God’s table by grace, not by merit. When believers invite those who cannot repay, they imitate the God who invited them.

It also fulfills Jesus’ mission. In His first sermon, He announced good news to the poor and sight to the blind (*Luke 4:18*). In His answer to John the Baptist, He pointed to the blind seeing and the lame walking (*Luke 7:22*). His followers are called to share this concern for those on the margins.

Finally, the promise of repayment “in the resurrection of the righteous” shows that believers live with an eternal perspective. They do not need to be repaid now, because God will reward faithfulness in the age to come. This frees them to give generously without calculating what they will get back.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses challenge believers to examine their hospitality and generosity. Do they mostly share their homes, time, and resources with people who can return the favor? Jesus calls His followers to welcome people who cannot repay them: the poor, the lonely, people with disabilities, the elderly, refugees, and others often left out.

Practical expressions might include inviting a lonely neighbor to a meal, including people with disabilities in church and community life, serving at a food ministry, or befriending someone who has few friends. These acts reflect the generous heart of God.

Finally, these verses encourage believers to give without seeking recognition or return. When they help those who cannot repay, they can trust that God sees and will reward them.

### *Luke 14:21* — Bring In the Poor, the Maimed, the Blind, and the Lame

> *“That servant came, and told his lord these things. Then the master of the house, being angry, said to his servant, “Go out quickly into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in the poor, maimed, blind, and lame.””*
>
> — *Luke 14:21* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse is the turning point in the parable of the great banquet. Jesus told this parable after a guest at a dinner said, “Blessed is he who will feast in God’s Kingdom!” The guest assumed that people like him would be at that feast.

In the parable, a man prepared a great banquet and invited many guests. When the meal was ready, he sent his servant to tell them to come. But one after another, they made excuses: one had bought a field, one had bought oxen, one had just married. These excuses showed that they did not value the invitation.

Then “*That servant came, and told his lord these things*” (*v. 21*). The master was angry. His invitation had been rejected and his honor insulted. But instead of canceling the banquet, he said to his servant, “*Go out quickly into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in the poor, maimed, blind, and lame*” (*v. 21*).

“Quickly” shows urgency. The banquet was ready, and the master wanted it filled. “Streets and lanes” were where the poor and outcast lived and begged. The list, “the poor, maimed, blind, and lame,” exactly matches the list Jesus had just given to the host in verse 13. The master in the parable did what Jesus told the host to do.

In the context of Jesus’ ministry, the first invited guests represent the religious leaders and those in Israel who assumed they belonged in God’s kingdom but rejected Jesus’ invitation. The poor and disabled from the town represent the outcasts and sinners within Israel who were responding to Jesus: tax collectors, prostitutes, the sick, and the poor. Then, in verse 23, the servant goes outside the town to the highways and hedges, which many interpreters understand as representing Gentiles.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals that God’s grace reaches those whom society overlooks. The kingdom of God is not reserved for the respectable and powerful. It is filled with people who know their need. Paul writes that God chose the foolish, the weak, and the lowly of this world (*1 Corinthians 1:26–29*).

It also shows the seriousness of rejecting God’s invitation. The first guests were not rejected because they were sinful but because they were preoccupied with other things: property, business, and family. These were not evil in themselves, but they were valued above the master’s invitation. Many people miss God’s kingdom not because of terrible sins but because ordinary concerns crowd out their response to Him.

Finally, the master’s determination to fill his house shows God’s desire for many to come. God’s banquet will not be empty. He keeps sending out invitations until His house is full.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to see themselves among the poor, crippled, blind, and lame, people who have nothing to offer God but are welcomed by grace. This understanding produces humility and gratitude.

It also challenges believers to examine whether ordinary concerns are keeping them from responding to God. Work, possessions, and family are good gifts, but they can become excuses for neglecting God. Believers can ask whether they are making excuses when God calls them to deeper commitment or service.

Finally, this verse calls believers and churches to go to the streets and lanes, reaching people on the margins with God’s invitation. The master sent his servant out quickly and urgently. Believers can share the good news with those who feel excluded, assuring them that there is room at God’s table.

### *Luke 14:26* — Loving Jesus Above All

> *“If anyone comes to me, and doesn’t disregard his own father, mother, wife, children, brothers, and sisters, yes, and his own life also, he can’t be my disciple.”*
>
> — *Luke 14:26* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus speaks these words to large crowds who were traveling with Him toward Jerusalem. Many were enthusiastic about Jesus, perhaps hoping for miracles or expecting Him to establish a political kingdom. Jesus turned and spoke to them about what it really means to be His disciple.

“*If anyone comes to me, and doesn’t disregard his own father, mother, wife, children, brothers, and sisters, yes, and his own life also, he can’t be my disciple*” (*v. 26*). The WEB uses “disregard,” but the Greek word literally means “hate.” This shocking statement must be understood in its context and culture.

In Jewish and Semitic idiom, “love” and “hate” were often used as strong comparisons meaning “love more” and “love less.” For example, *Genesis 29:30–31* says Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah, and then says Leah was “hated,” meaning less loved. *Malachi 1:2–3* says God loved Jacob and hated Esau, describing His choice of one over the other. Matthew’s parallel saying makes the meaning clear: “*He who loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me*” (*Matthew 10:37*).

Jesus was not commanding His followers to feel hatred toward their families. Elsewhere He affirmed the command to honor parents (*Luke 18:20*) and condemned those who used religious excuses to neglect their parents (*Mark 7:9–13*). He also commanded love for enemies, so He certainly did not command hatred for family. Rather, He was saying that love for Him must be so great that, by comparison, all other loves look like hatred. When loyalty to family conflicts with loyalty to Jesus, Jesus must come first.

“*yes, and his own life also*” (*v. 26*). Even one’s own life must be held under Jesus’ lordship. This connects with the next verse about carrying one’s cross.

In that culture, family loyalty was extremely strong. Following Jesus could lead to rejection by family, loss of inheritance, and social isolation. Jesus wanted the crowds to understand the potential cost before deciding to follow Him.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse teaches that Jesus demands first place in His followers’ lives. No other relationship, not even the closest family bonds, can take precedence over Him. This is a claim that only God can rightly make. In the Old Testament, God commanded His people to love Him with all their heart, soul, and strength (*Deuteronomy 6:5*). Jesus makes the same claim for Himself.

It also shows that following Jesus may be costly. In many parts of the world today, people who become Christians face rejection by their families, loss of community, and even danger. Jesus’ words prepare His followers for such costs and assure them that He is worth it.

Finally, putting Jesus first does not reduce love for family; it reorders it. When Jesus is first, believers love their families more truly, with His love, His patience, and His wisdom, rather than less. Family relationships flourish best when they are not made into idols.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to examine whether anything or anyone has taken first place in their hearts above Jesus. Family, romantic relationships, children, careers, and personal ambitions can all become rivals to Christ. Believers can ask God to help them love Him above all.

It also encourages believers who face family opposition because of their faith. Some are rejected or pressured by family members for following Jesus. Jesus knows this cost, and He promises a new family of believers (*Luke 18:29–30*). Believers can remain loving and respectful toward their families while staying faithful to Christ.

Finally, this verse must never be used as an excuse to neglect or mistreat family members. Jesus calls His followers to honor parents, love spouses, and care for children. Putting Jesus first should make believers better family members, not worse ones.

### *Luke 14:28* — Count the Cost

> *“For which of you, desiring to build a tower, doesn’t first sit down and count the cost, to see if he has enough to complete it?”*
>
> — *Luke 14:28* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse begins the first of two short parables Jesus told about the cost of discipleship. He had just told the large crowds following Him that anyone who does not love Him above family and even their own life, and does not carry their own cross, cannot be His disciple. Now He uses everyday examples to explain why people should think carefully before committing to follow Him.

“*For which of you, desiring to build a tower, doesn’t first sit down and count the cost, to see if he has enough to complete it?*” (*v. 28*) A tower might be a watchtower in a vineyard, used to protect crops, or a farm building. Anyone planning such a project would first calculate the cost of materials and labor. If he began without enough resources, he might lay the foundation and then be unable to finish.

The next verses describe the consequences: “*everyone who sees begins to mock him*” (*v. 29*), saying, “*This man began to build and wasn’t able to finish*” (*v. 30*). An unfinished building would be a public embarrassment, a visible sign of poor planning.

Jesus then told a second parable about a king considering whether his army of ten thousand could defeat an opponent with twenty thousand. If not, he would seek peace while the enemy was still far away.

Jesus applied both parables: “*So therefore, whoever of you who doesn’t renounce all that he has, he can’t be my disciple*” (*v. 33*). Following Jesus is a serious commitment that requires giving Him everything. Before starting, people should understand what it will require.

The crowds following Jesus were large and enthusiastic. But many were following for the wrong reasons or without understanding where He was going. Jesus was going to the cross. He wanted followers who were committed, not people who would start enthusiastically and then fall away when following became difficult.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse teaches that discipleship is a lifelong commitment that should be entered thoughtfully. Jesus does not want shallow enthusiasm that fades when trials come. The parable of the sower describes people who receive the word with joy but fall away in time of testing (*Luke 8:13*). Counting the cost helps prevent this.

It is important to understand that counting the cost does not mean earning salvation through effort. Salvation is a gift of grace. But receiving that gift means surrendering one’s life to Jesus as Lord. Grace is free, but it is not cheap; it costs us our self-rule.

The verse also suggests that Jesus is honest with His followers. He does not hide the cost to attract more people. Instead, He tells them the truth: following Him may cost family relationships, possessions, comfort, and even life. Yet He is worth it, as the parable of the treasure in the field teaches (*Matthew 13:44*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages people considering faith in Jesus to think seriously about what it means. Following Jesus is not just adding religion to one’s life; it is giving Him lordship over everything. Those who come to Him should do so with understanding and wholehearted commitment.

It also invites believers to renew their commitment regularly. Over time, believers may grow lukewarm or discouraged. Counting the cost again, remembering what Jesus asks and what He offers, can renew their resolve to keep following Him.

Finally, this verse guides how believers share their faith. Rather than presenting Christianity as a way to make life easy, believers can honestly explain both the cost and the incomparable worth of following Jesus. This honesty produces disciples who endure.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Luke 14* challenges the world’s values of status, exchange, and self-interest. At the Pharisee’s table, Jesus taught humility: take the lower seat and let God lift you up. Believers can resist the desire for recognition and status, trusting that God honors those who humble themselves.

He also taught generosity toward those who cannot repay. Believers can open their homes and lives to the poor, the disabled, the lonely, and the overlooked, imitating the God who welcomes them without merit. Such generosity is rewarded not by social return but by God at the resurrection of the righteous.

The parable of the great banquet warns against making excuses when God invites. Ordinary concerns like work, property, and family can crowd out a response to God. Believers can examine their priorities and respond wholeheartedly to God’s invitation. The parable also shows God’s determination to fill His house with outcasts and outsiders, calling believers to share the invitation with those on the margins.

Finally, Jesus’ teaching on the cost of discipleship calls for wholehearted commitment. He must come first, above even the closest family relationships and one’s own life. Followers must carry their cross and surrender all they have to Him. Before starting, they should count the cost, and they should keep their commitment strong so that they do not become like salt that has lost its saltiness. Jesus is honest about the cost because He wants disciples who will finish the journey with Him.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, You healed the sick on the Sabbath and taught that the humble will be exalted. Free me from the desire for status and the best seats, and teach me to take the lower place. Give me a generous heart that welcomes the poor, the disabled, and the lonely, without expecting anything in return.

Thank You for inviting me to Your banquet, though I had nothing to offer. Forgive me for the times I have made excuses when You called. Help me to share Your invitation with those on the streets and in the lanes, those who think there is no room for them. Help me to love You above everyone and everything, even my own life. Give me courage to carry my cross and follow You, and help me to count the cost and stay faithful to the end. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Luke · Chapter 15 of 24

# Luke — Chapter 15

Chapter Theme: Lost and Found: The Joy of God Over Repentant Sinners

[Read Luke 15 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/LUK15.htm)

Main Teaching

When religious leaders grumble that Jesus welcomes sinners and eats with them, He answers with three parables about lost things: a sheep, a coin, and a son. In each, the one who searches rejoices when the lost is found, showing heaven’s joy over one sinner who repents. The story of the father and his two sons reveals a father who runs to welcome a returning son and pleads with an angry older son to join the celebration.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Luke 15* is one of the best-loved chapters in the Bible. It contains three parables, the last of which, often called the parable of the prodigal son, is one of the most famous stories Jesus ever told. All three parables answer a single complaint.

The setting is described in the first two verses: “*Now all the tax collectors and sinners were coming close to him to hear him*” (*v. 1*). Tax collectors were despised as collaborators who enriched themselves at others’ expense. “Sinners” referred to people known for immoral lives or who did not keep the law as religious leaders expected. These people were drawn to Jesus.

But “*The Pharisees and the scribes murmured, saying, “This man welcomes sinners, and eats with them.”*” (*v. 2*) The word “murmured” recalls Israel grumbling against God in the wilderness (*Exodus 16:2*). In that culture, eating with someone signaled acceptance and fellowship. The religious leaders believed that a holy teacher should separate himself from sinners. Jesus’ table fellowship with them seemed to approve of their sin. Jesus answered with three parables that reveal God’s heart toward the lost.

### The Lost Sheep (*15:3–7*)

Jesus asked which of them, having a hundred sheep and losing one, would not leave the ninety-nine in the open country and search for the lost one until he found it. A flock of a hundred was a medium-sized flock, probably belonging to a family or village. Shepherds counted their sheep each evening, and a missing sheep meant a real loss. The shepherd would leave the others in the care of other shepherds and search the wilderness.

When he finds it, “*he carries it on his shoulders, rejoicing*” (*v. 5*). A lost sheep would often lie down helpless and frightened, unable or unwilling to move. The shepherd carries it home himself. Then he calls his friends and neighbors to celebrate. Jesus concluded with the lesson that is studied below: there is more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous people who need no repentance.

Jesus had addressed His critics directly: “Which of you men...?” Many of the Pharisees would have considered shepherds lowly and ritually unreliable people. Yet Jesus asked them to imagine themselves as shepherds, and He used the image to describe God, the great Shepherd of Israel (*Psalm 23*; *Ezekiel 34:11–16*).

### The Lost Coin (*15:8–10*)

The second parable features a woman with ten silver coins, called drachmas, each worth about a day’s wage. Losing one was significant for a poor household. These coins may have been her savings or part of her dowry, sometimes worn as a headdress. Village houses had few small windows and dirt floors, so a lost coin would be hard to find. She lit a lamp, swept the house, and searched carefully until she found it. Then she called her friends and neighbors to rejoice with her.

Jesus said, “*Even so, I tell you, there is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner repenting*” (*v. 10*). “In the presence of the angels” is a reverent way of referring to God Himself rejoicing. Notice that Jesus used a woman to represent God’s searching love, pairing her with the male shepherd, as Luke often pairs men and women in his Gospel.

### The Lost Son (*15:11–24*)

The third parable is longer and more personal. A man had two sons. The younger said, “*Father, give me my share of your property*” (*v. 12*). Under Jewish law, the younger of two sons would inherit one-third of the estate (*Deuteronomy 21:17* gave the firstborn a double share). But inheritance normally came at the father’s death. Asking for it early was deeply insulting, almost like wishing his father dead. It also meant breaking up the family property, which might include land and livestock that would have to be sold. Remarkably, the father agreed and divided his property between the sons.

Not long after, the younger son gathered everything, turned it into cash, and traveled to “*a far country*” (*v. 13*), a Gentile land far from family and faith. There he wasted his money in reckless, wild living. When everything was gone, a severe famine struck. He became desperate and hired himself out to a citizen of that country, who sent him to feed pigs. For a Jewish young man, this was utter degradation; pigs were unclean animals (*Leviticus 11:7*). He was so hungry that he longed to eat the pods the pigs were eating, probably carob pods, a cheap animal feed. No one gave him anything.

Then “*he came to himself*” (*v. 17*). This turning point is studied below. He decided to return to his father, confess his sin, and ask to be treated as a hired servant.

He got up and went home. “*But while he was still far off, his father saw him and was moved with compassion, and ran, fell on his neck, and kissed him*” (*v. 20*). The father’s response is studied below. The son began his prepared speech, but the father interrupted before he could ask to become a servant. He told his servants to bring the best robe, a ring for his hand, and sandals for his feet, and to kill the fattened calf for a celebration. The robe signified honor, the ring authority and family membership, and the sandals showed he was a son, since servants often went barefoot. A fattened calf was saved for the most important occasions and could feed an entire village. The father explained, “*for this, my son, was dead and is alive again. He was lost and is found*” (*v. 24*).

### The Older Son (*15:25–32*)

Meanwhile, the older son was working in the field. As he came near the house, he heard music and dancing. A servant told him that his brother had returned and that the father had killed the fattened calf. The older son became angry and refused to go in.

The father came out and pleaded with him, just as he had gone out to meet the younger son. The older son complained, “*Behold, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed a commandment of yours, but you never gave me a goat, that I might celebrate with my friends*” (*v. 29*). He referred to his brother as “*this your son*” (*v. 30*), refusing to call him “my brother,” and accused him of wasting the father’s wealth on prostitutes, a detail not mentioned earlier.

The father’s answer is studied below. The parable ends without telling us whether the older son went in to the celebration. Jesus leaves the story open, because the older son represents the Pharisees and scribes who were grumbling about Jesus welcoming sinners. The question was whether they would join the celebration of God’s grace.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Luke 15:7* — Joy in Heaven Over One Sinner Who Repents

> *“I tell you that even so there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents, than over ninety-nine righteous people who need no repentance.”*
>
> — *Luke 15:7* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse concludes the parable of the lost sheep. Jesus told this parable because the Pharisees and scribes were complaining that He welcomed sinners and ate with them. They believed a holy teacher should avoid such people. Jesus responded by asking them to imagine being a shepherd who has a hundred sheep and loses one. Would he not leave the ninety-nine and search for the lost one until he found it? When he finds it, he carries it home on his shoulders, rejoicing, and calls his friends and neighbors to celebrate with him.

Then Jesus applied the parable: “*I tell you that even so there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents, than over ninety-nine righteous people who need no repentance*” (*v. 7*).

“Joy in heaven” refers to God’s own joy and the joy of all in His presence. When a sinner repents, God celebrates. This was a striking picture of God. The religious leaders thought God would be pleased by separation from sinners; Jesus said God rejoices when sinners are found and brought home.

“*one sinner who repents*” (*v. 7*). The lost sheep represents a sinner, someone who has wandered away from God. Repentance means turning back to God. In the parable, the sheep does not find its own way home; the shepherd searches for it and carries it. This shows that repentance is a response to God’s seeking grace.

“*than over ninety-nine righteous people who need no repentance*” (*v. 7*). This phrase contains gentle irony. Everyone needs repentance (*Romans 3:23*). The “righteous people who need no repentance” likely refers to those who think they do not need it, like the Pharisees who were grumbling. They saw themselves as the ninety-nine safe sheep. Jesus’ words invited them to recognize that heaven’s joy is focused on the lost being found.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals that God actively seeks the lost. He is like a shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine to search for one sheep. God takes the initiative in salvation. Jesus later summarized His mission: “*For the Son of Man came to seek and to save that which was lost*” (*Luke 19:10*).

It also reveals that God’s heart is full of joy over repentance. God does not grudgingly accept repentant sinners; He celebrates. This corrects the image of God as harsh or reluctant to forgive. The prophet Zephaniah described God rejoicing over His people with singing (*Zephaniah 3:17*).

Finally, the verse challenges those who see themselves as righteous. If God rejoices over sinners who repent, His people should share that joy rather than resent it. Self-righteousness can make people blind to God’s heart and to their own need.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse offers hope to anyone who feels lost. God is not waiting with anger; He is searching with love. Those who have wandered from God can turn back to Him, knowing that heaven will rejoice at their return.

It also invites believers to share God’s joy over repentance. When someone comes to faith or returns to God, believers can celebrate wholeheartedly, regardless of that person’s past.

Finally, this verse calls believers to join God’s search for the lost. Like the shepherd, they can reach out to people who have wandered from God, showing patience and love, and helping bring them home.

### *Luke 15:17–18* — “*When He Came to Himself*” (*v. 17*)

> *“But when he came to himself, he said, ‘How many hired servants of my father’s have bread enough to spare, and I’m dying with hunger! I will get up and go to my father, and will tell him, Father, I have sinned against heaven and in your sight.”*
>
> — *Luke 15:17–18* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These verses describe the turning point in the life of the younger son in Jesus’ parable. He had demanded his inheritance from his father while his father was still alive, a deeply insulting request. Then he traveled to a distant country and wasted everything in reckless living. When a severe famine struck, he had nothing left. He hired himself out to a local citizen who sent him to feed pigs, unclean animals in Jewish law. He was so hungry that he wanted to eat the pigs’ food, but no one gave him anything. He had reached rock bottom.

Then “*But when he came to himself*” (*v. 17*). This phrase means he came to his senses, he woke up to reality. Up to this point, he had been living in a kind of illusion, thinking that freedom from his father and money would bring happiness. Now he saw clearly.

He reasoned, “*How many hired servants of my father’s have bread enough to spare, and I’m dying with hunger!*” (*v. 17*) Even his father’s hired workers, day laborers who had the least security, had more than enough food. He was starving.

Then he decided: “*I will get up and go to my father, and will tell him, “Father, I have sinned against heaven and in your sight.”*” (*v. 18*) He planned to admit his sin honestly. “Against heaven” means against God; “in your sight” means against his father. He recognized that his actions had wronged both God and his father. In the next verse, he planned to say he was no longer worthy to be called a son and to ask to be made a hired servant.

His repentance involved several steps: recognizing his true condition, remembering his father’s goodness, deciding to return, and planning to confess his sin honestly without excuses.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses describe what genuine repentance looks like. It begins with “coming to oneself,” seeing one’s situation truthfully. Sin often involves self-deception, believing that life apart from God will bring freedom and joy. Repentance begins when that illusion is broken.

The son’s motivation is worth noticing. His first thought was hunger, a practical need. His motives were not perfectly pure. Yet the father received him anyway. God welcomes people who come to Him even with mixed motives, and He transforms them through His grace.

These verses also show that true repentance involves honest confession. The son did not blame others or make excuses. He said simply, “I have sinned.” This echoes David’s confession in *Psalm 51:4*. Honest confession is the doorway to restoration.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses invite anyone who has wandered from God to “come to themselves.” Sometimes it takes hardship, emptiness, or loss to make people see the truth about their lives. Those who find themselves in a “far country,” whether through addiction, broken relationships, or simply drifting from God, can stop, consider their situation honestly, and remember the Father’s goodness.

They also encourage honest confession. Believers can bring their sins to God without excuses or blame, simply saying, “I have sinned.” God welcomes honest hearts.

Finally, these verses show that it is never too late to return. The son had wasted everything and fallen as low as he could imagine. Yet the way home was still open. No one has gone too far to come back to God.

### *Luke 15:20* — The Father Who Ran

> *“He arose and came to his father. But while he was still far off, his father saw him and was moved with compassion, and ran, fell on his neck, and kissed him.”*
>
> — *Luke 15:20* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse is the emotional heart of the parable. The younger son had wasted his inheritance, fallen to the lowest point of his life, and decided to return home to confess his sin and ask to be a hired servant. He had a speech prepared. He may have been nervous about how his father would respond. In that culture, a son who shamed his family this way could expect rejection, and the village might also treat him with contempt.

“*He arose and came to his father*” (*v. 20*). He acted on his decision.

“*But while he was still far off, his father saw him*” (*v. 20*). The father saw him from a distance, suggesting that he had been watching and waiting, hoping for his son’s return.

“*and was moved with compassion*” (*v. 20*). The father’s first response was not anger but deep compassion, the same word used of Jesus’ compassion for the widow of Nain and of the Samaritan’s compassion for the wounded man.

“*and ran*” (*v. 20*). In that culture, a dignified older man did not run. Running required lifting one’s long robes and exposing one’s legs, which was considered undignified. Yet the father ran. He set aside his own dignity to reach his son. Some interpreters suggest he also ran to reach his son before the villagers could mock or reject him, protecting him from shame.

“*fell on his neck, and kissed him*” (*v. 20*). He embraced his son and kissed him repeatedly, a sign of forgiveness and reconciliation (compare Esau and Jacob, *Genesis 33:4*). The father welcomed him before the son could even finish his confession.

When the son began his speech, the father interrupted him, calling for the best robe, a ring, sandals, and a feast. The son had planned to ask to be a servant; the father restored him fully as a son.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals the heart of God toward repentant sinners. God is not a reluctant judge waiting for sinners to prove themselves. He is a Father who watches, longs, and runs to welcome them home. Jesus was answering the Pharisees’ complaint by showing that His welcome of sinners reflected the Father’s own heart.

It also shows the extravagance of God’s grace. The son expected to be a servant; the father restored him as a son. God does not merely tolerate repentant sinners; He restores them to full relationship as His children. Paul writes that believers have received “*the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, “Abba! Father!”*” (*Romans 8:15*)

Finally, the father’s running suggests the humility of God’s love. Just as the father set aside his dignity to embrace his son, God in Christ humbled Himself to come to sinners. The ultimate expression of this is the cross, where Jesus bore shame to bring sinners home.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse assures anyone who is afraid to return to God that He is waiting with compassion. Whatever they have done, the Father is ready to run to them and embrace them. They do not need to clean themselves up first; they can simply come home.

It also helps believers understand their identity. Through Christ, they are not servants trying to earn their place, but beloved children, fully restored. They can live with the security of being welcomed and loved.

Finally, this verse calls believers to reflect the Father’s heart toward others. When people who have wandered return to faith or turn to God for the first time, believers can welcome them warmly, without suspicion or condescension, as the father welcomed his son.

### *Luke 15:31–32* — The Father’s Plea to the Older Son

> *“‘He said to him, “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. But it was appropriate to celebrate and be glad, for this, your brother, was dead, and is alive again. He was lost, and is found.”’”*
>
> — *Luke 15:31–32* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These verses are the father’s response to his older son. While the household celebrated the younger son’s return, the older son came in from working in the field and heard music and dancing. When he learned that his father had thrown a feast for his wayward brother, he became angry and refused to go in.

The father came out and pleaded with him, just as he had gone out to meet the younger son. The older son complained bitterly. He had served his father for years, never disobeyed, and never received even a young goat for a party with his friends. But when “*this your son*” (*v. 30*) came home after wasting the father’s money on prostitutes, the father killed the fattened calf. His words revealed resentment, pride, and a sense that he had earned more than he received. He also showed that he thought of himself as a servant rather than a son (“I have served you”).

The father answered gently: “*Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours*” (*v. 31*). He addressed him with an affectionate word for “child.” He reminded him that he had always enjoyed the father’s presence and that everything the father had belonged to him. The older son had not lost anything by his brother’s return. His inheritance was secure.

Then the father explained: “*But it was appropriate to celebrate and be glad, for this, your brother, was dead, and is alive again. He was lost, and is found*” (*v. 32*). Notice the father’s words: “this, your brother.” The older son had said “*this your son*” (*v. 30*), refusing to acknowledge his brother. The father reminded him of their relationship. Celebration was “appropriate,” the right and fitting response, because a brother who was as good as dead had come back to life.

The parable ends here. We are not told whether the older son went in to the celebration. Jesus left the ending open.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses reveal that the older son was also lost, though he never left home. He was physically near his father, but his heart was far from him. He saw his relationship with his father as service and reward rather than love. This describes the Pharisees and scribes who grumbled that Jesus welcomed sinners. They were religious and obedient outwardly, but they did not share the Father’s heart.

The verses also show that God’s love reaches out to the self-righteous as well as to the openly sinful. The father went out to both sons. God invites religious people who resent His grace to come in and join the celebration.

Finally, the open ending invites a response. The older son represents anyone who thinks they deserve God’s favor because of their obedience, and who resents God’s generosity toward others. The question remains: will they come in and rejoice?

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses challenge believers who have been faithful for a long time. It is possible to serve God outwardly while losing sight of His love and becoming resentful of His grace to others. Believers can examine whether they see themselves as servants earning rewards or as beloved children who already share everything the Father has.

They also call believers to celebrate when others come to God, regardless of their past. Believers can welcome repentant sinners as brothers and sisters, not as people who must prove themselves first.

Finally, these verses offer comfort to those who have always stayed close to God but sometimes feel overlooked. The Father says, “You are always with me, and all that is mine is yours.” Their faithfulness is not forgotten, and their inheritance is secure. Joy at others’ return does not diminish God’s love for them.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Luke 15* reveals the heart of God more clearly than almost any other chapter in the Bible. God is a shepherd who searches for lost sheep, a woman who sweeps the house for a lost coin, and a father who runs to welcome his wayward son. He rejoices when the lost are found. Anyone who feels far from God can take courage: He is searching for them and longs for their return.

The younger son’s story shows what repentance looks like: coming to one’s senses, remembering the Father’s goodness, getting up, and confessing honestly. It also shows that God’s welcome is far greater than anyone expects. He does not make repentant sinners into servants; He restores them as sons and daughters. Believers can rest in this identity and live as beloved children.

The older son’s story warns against self-righteousness. It is possible to stay close to God outwardly while resenting His grace to others. Believers who have served faithfully can guard against bitterness and comparison, remembering that everything the Father has is theirs. They can join the celebration when others come home.

Finally, the chapter calls believers to share God’s heart. Like the shepherd and the woman, they can seek those who are lost. Like the father, they can welcome returning sinners with open arms. And like heaven itself, they can rejoice over every sinner who repents.

## Chapter Prayer

Father, thank You for searching for me like a shepherd seeks a lost sheep and a woman searches for a lost coin. Thank You that there is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents. When I have wandered into a far country, help me to come to my senses, remember Your goodness, and return to You with honest confession.

Thank You for running to meet me, embracing me, and restoring me as Your child, not as a servant. Help me to live in the security of Your love. Guard me from the resentment of the older son. When others return to You, help me to rejoice with You and welcome them as my brothers and sisters. Give me Your heart for the lost, and help me to join You in seeking and welcoming them home. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Luke · Chapter 16 of 24

# Luke — Chapter 16

Chapter Theme: Faithful With Money, Rich Toward the Poor, Listening to God’s Word

[Read Luke 16 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/LUK16.htm)

Main Teaching

Through the puzzling parable of a dishonest manager, Jesus urges His followers to use money shrewdly with eternity in view and to be faithful in small things, since no one can serve both God and wealth. When money-loving Pharisees scoff, He warns that God sees the heart. Then, in the story of a rich man and the beggar Lazarus, He shows the eternal consequences of ignoring the poor and of refusing to listen to the Scriptures God has already given.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Luke 16* continues Jesus’ teaching on the way to Jerusalem and follows directly from the three parables of the lost in *Luke 15*. Those parables answered religious leaders who grumbled that Jesus welcomed sinners. *Luke 16* turns to money, a subject Jesus addressed often. It includes two parables, both beginning with the words “*There was a certain rich man*” (*v. 1*) (v. 1) and “*there was a certain rich man*” (*v. 19*) (v. 19). The first is addressed to the disciples; the second responds to Pharisees who “*were lovers of money*” (*v. 14*). Together they teach that money is a test of faithfulness and that how people use wealth has eternal consequences.

### The Parable of the Shrewd Manager (*16:1–8*)

A rich man had a manager, or steward, who handled his business affairs. Wealthy landowners often employed managers to oversee their estates, collect rents, and handle contracts. Someone accused the manager of wasting his master’s property. The master called him in and said, “*Give an accounting of your management, for you can no longer be manager*” (*v. 2*).

The manager thought to himself about his options. He was not strong enough to do hard manual labor and was ashamed to beg. Then he came up with a plan. Before word of his dismissal spread, he called in his master’s debtors one by one. These were likely tenant farmers or merchants who owed the master large amounts of produce. One owed a hundred measures of olive oil (around 800 gallons); the manager told him to change his bill to fifty. Another owed a hundred measures of wheat (perhaps a thousand bushels); the manager told him to change it to eighty. These were substantial reductions. The debtors would be grateful to the manager, and he hoped they would welcome him into their homes after he lost his job.

Then comes the surprising line: “*His lord commended the dishonest manager because he had done wisely*” (*v. 8*). The master did not praise the manager’s dishonesty; Jesus Himself calls him “the dishonest manager.” He praised his shrewdness, his ability to see his situation clearly and act decisively to secure his future. Some interpreters suggest the manager may have been cancelling his own commission or illegal interest, which would make his actions less dishonest, but the text still calls him dishonest. The point is not his ethics but his foresight.

Jesus drew the lesson: “*for the children of this world are, in their own generation, wiser than the children of the light*” (*v. 8*). People of the world are often more clever about securing their earthly future than God’s people are about preparing for eternity. This parable is studied below.

### Faithful With Little and Much (*16:9–13*)

Jesus continued, “*make for yourselves friends by means of unrighteous mammon, so that when you fail, they may receive you into the eternal tents*” (*v. 9*). “Mammon” is an Aramaic word for wealth or possessions. Jesus calls it “unrighteous” because money so easily becomes tied up with injustice and greed, and because it belongs to this passing age. “When you fail” means when money runs out or when life ends. Just as the manager used his master’s money to make friends who would receive him, believers should use money in ways that bless others and store up treasure in heaven.

Then Jesus gave a principle about faithfulness, studied below: “*He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much*” (*v. 10*). If people are not trustworthy with worldly wealth, who will trust them with true riches? If they are not faithful with what belongs to someone else (and all possessions ultimately belong to God), who will give them something of their own?

He concluded, “*No servant can serve two masters*” (*v. 13*). A person will love one and hate the other. “*You aren’t able to serve God and Mammon*” (*v. 13*). Money is a rival master, demanding loyalty that belongs to God alone. (This saying is studied at *Matthew 6:21–24*.)

### The Pharisees Scoff (*16:14–18*)

The Pharisees heard all this and “*scoffed at him*” (*v. 14*). Luke describes them as “*lovers of money*” (*v. 14*). Many people in that time believed that wealth was a sign of God’s blessing and righteousness. The Pharisees may have thought Jesus’ warnings about money were foolish, especially coming from a poor teacher.

Jesus answered, “*You are those who justify yourselves in the sight of men, but God knows your hearts. For that which is exalted among men is an abomination in the sight of God*” (*v. 15*). The Pharisees made themselves look righteous before others, but God saw their hearts. What people admire, such as wealth, status, and religious reputation, can be detestable to God when it springs from pride and greed.

Jesus then made three brief statements. First, “*The law and the prophets were until John*” (*v. 16*). John the Baptist marked a turning point; since then, the good news of God’s kingdom has been preached, and everyone is pressing urgently into it. Second, this does not mean the law is cancelled: “*it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one tiny stroke of a pen in the law to fall*” (*v. 17*). Jesus fulfills the law, and its moral demands remain. Third, as an example of the law’s continuing force, He spoke about divorce: whoever divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery. (This teaching is discussed at *Matthew 19:6* and *Mark 10*, including how Christian traditions apply it and the protection of those in danger.) The Pharisees who prided themselves on keeping the law were in fact loosening its moral standards where it suited them, as with the easy divorce practices of the time.

### The Rich Man and Lazarus (*16:19–31*)

Jesus then told a story found only in Luke. There was a rich man who dressed in purple and fine linen and feasted lavishly every day. Purple cloth was extremely expensive, dyed with a substance taken from shellfish, and it was associated with royalty. Fine linen was often imported from Egypt. This man lived in luxury.

At his gate lay a beggar named Lazarus, covered with sores. Lazarus is the only character in Jesus’ parables given a name. The name is a form of Eleazar, meaning “God helps.” Lazarus longed to eat the scraps that fell from the rich man’s table. Wealthy people sometimes wiped their hands on bread during meals and then threw it on the floor. Even the dogs came and licked his sores; he was too weak to drive them away. The rich man passed Lazarus every day at his gate but did nothing.

Both men died. Lazarus was carried by angels to “*Abraham’s bosom*” (*v. 22*), a place of honor and comfort, like reclining next to Abraham at a banquet. The rich man was buried, and in Hades he was in torment. He looked up and saw Abraham far away with Lazarus beside him. He called out, “*Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue!*” (*v. 24*) Notice that he still thought of Lazarus as a servant to be sent on errands.

Abraham replied, “*Son, remember that you, in your lifetime, received your good things, and Lazarus, in the same way, bad things. But here he is now comforted and you are in anguish*” (*v. 25*). The reversal echoes Mary’s song (*Luke 1:52–53*) and Jesus’ blessings and woes (*Luke 6:20–26*). Abraham added that a great chasm separated them, so that no one could cross from one side to the other.

The rich man then begged Abraham to send Lazarus to warn his five brothers. Abraham answered, “*They have Moses and the prophets. Let them listen to them*” (*v. 29*). The rich man insisted that if someone came from the dead, they would repent. Abraham’s reply is studied below.

A note on interpretation: this story uses imagery common in Jewish thinking of the time about the afterlife, such as Abraham’s side, Hades, and a great gulf. Christians differ on how literally to take the details of the afterlife in this story, since it functions as a parable. But its central lessons are clear: choices in this life have eternal consequences, the way people treat the poor matters to God, and the Scriptures are sufficient to lead people to repentance.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Luke 16:8–9* — Using Wealth Wisely With Eternity in View

> *“His lord commended the dishonest manager because he had done wisely, for the children of this world are, in their own generation, wiser than the children of the light. I tell you, make for yourselves friends by means of unrighteous mammon, so that when you fail, they may receive you into the eternal tents.”*
>
> — *Luke 16:8–9* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These verses contain the lesson of the parable of the shrewd manager, one of the most puzzling parables Jesus told. A manager was about to be fired for wasting his master’s money. Thinking quickly about his future, he called in his master’s debtors and reduced their bills significantly, making them grateful to him so that they would welcome him into their homes after he lost his job.

Then “*His lord commended the dishonest manager because he had done wisely*” (*v. 8*). Many readers are troubled by this. Was Jesus praising dishonesty? No. The parable calls him “the dishonest manager,” and Jesus does not approve of his cheating. What the master commended was his shrewdness: he recognized that his time was short, understood his situation, and acted decisively to prepare for the future. The word translated “wisely” means shrewdly or prudently.

Jesus then drew the lesson: “*for the children of this world are, in their own generation, wiser than the children of the light*” (*v. 8*). “Children of this world” are people whose concerns are limited to this life. “Children of the light” are God’s people. Jesus observed that worldly people are often more thoughtful and energetic about securing their earthly futures than God’s people are about preparing for eternity.

“*I tell you, make for yourselves friends by means of unrighteous mammon*” (*v. 9*). “Mammon” means money or wealth. Jesus calls it “unrighteous” because wealth is so often gained or used unjustly and because it belongs to this passing world. Yet it can be used for good. Believers should use money to “make friends,” to help people, especially the poor, and to support God’s work.

“*so that when you fail, they may receive you into the eternal tents*” (*v. 9*). “When you fail” means when money runs out, or when life ends. “Eternal tents” refers to eternal dwellings in God’s kingdom. The picture may be of people who have been helped by believers’ generosity welcoming them into eternity, or of God Himself receiving them. The point is that money used generously in this life has eternal significance.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This parable teaches that this life is a time of stewardship, and it will end. Like the manager, every person will one day give an account. The wise response is to use what God has entrusted, especially money, with that day in view.

It also teaches that money can be used for eternal purposes. Money itself is temporary, but the good done with it can have lasting effects: people fed, the gospel shared, the poor helped, relationships built. Jesus taught elsewhere that giving to the needy stores up treasure in heaven (*Luke 12:33*).

Finally, the parable challenges believers’ priorities. Worldly people often plan carefully for retirement, careers, and comfort. Believers should be at least as thoughtful about eternal matters. This does not mean neglecting responsible planning, but it means placing eternal priorities first.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses invite believers to think strategically about how they use money. Rather than spending everything on personal comfort or saving everything for themselves, they can ask how their resources might bless others and advance God’s kingdom.

Practical applications include generous giving to those in need, supporting ministries and missions, helping neighbors and friends in crisis, and using hospitality to build relationships. These are ways of “making friends” with money that will matter in eternity.

Finally, these verses remind believers that life is short. Just as the manager knew his time was limited, believers can live with an awareness that their opportunity to use earthly resources for God’s purposes will one day end. Acting wisely now has eternal value.

### *Luke 16:10* — Faithful in Little, Faithful in Much

> *“He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much. He who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much.”*
>
> — *Luke 16:10* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse follows the parable of the shrewd manager, in which a manager about to lose his job used his master’s money to secure his future. Jesus had just told His disciples to use money wisely, with eternity in view. Now He states a principle about faithfulness: “*He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much. He who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much*” (*v. 10*).

“Faithful” means trustworthy, reliable, and dependable. “A very little” refers to small things, which in this context especially means money and earthly possessions. Jesus says that faithfulness in small things reveals character. A person who is trustworthy in small matters is likely to be trustworthy in larger ones. Similarly, a person who is dishonest in small things will be dishonest in larger things too.

In the following verses, Jesus applies this to money and spiritual life. “*If therefore you have not been faithful in the unrighteous mammon, who will commit to your trust the true riches?*” (*v. 11*) Worldly wealth is the “very little”; “true riches” are spiritual blessings and responsibilities in God’s kingdom. If people cannot be trusted with money, God will not entrust them with greater spiritual treasures.

“*If you have not been faithful in that which is another’s, who will give you that which is your own?*” (*v. 12*) Everything people possess on earth ultimately belongs to God; they are stewards of His property. If they are not faithful with what belongs to God, they cannot expect to receive the eternal inheritance He promises.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse teaches that character is revealed in small things. Many people think that small compromises do not matter, such as a small lie, a little cheating, or careless use of money. Jesus teaches that these small things reveal and shape character. Faithfulness in daily, ordinary matters prepares a person for greater responsibility.

It also shows that money is a spiritual test. How people handle money reveals their hearts. Generosity, honesty, and responsible stewardship show faithfulness to God. Greed, dishonesty, and waste show that money has become a master. Jesus’ parables about talents and minas make a similar point (*Matthew 25:21*; *Luke 19:17*).

Finally, the verse points to the generosity of God’s rewards. Those who are faithful with “very little” will be entrusted with “much.” God rewards faithfulness far beyond what is earned.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to be faithful in small things. Honesty in small financial matters, keeping small promises, doing small tasks well, and treating people kindly in everyday interactions all matter to God. These small faithfulnesses build a character that can be trusted with more.

It also encourages believers to see their finances as a matter of spiritual faithfulness. Budgeting responsibly, paying debts, giving generously, avoiding dishonest gain, and caring for what they have are ways of being faithful with what belongs to God.

Finally, this verse warns against excusing small sins. Believers can examine whether they have been dishonest in small ways, such as exaggerating, cutting corners, or taking what isn’t theirs, and repent, knowing that small dishonesty can grow into larger unfaithfulness.

### *Luke 16:31* — “*Neither Will They Be Persuaded if One Rises From the Dead*” (*v. 31*)

> *“‘He said to him, “If they don’t listen to Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded if one rises from the dead.”’”*
>
> — *Luke 16:31* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse is the final line of the story of the rich man and Lazarus. In the story, a rich man lived in luxury while a poor beggar named Lazarus lay at his gate, hungry and covered with sores. Both died. Lazarus was carried to Abraham’s side, while the rich man found himself in torment in Hades. He begged Abraham to send Lazarus to cool his tongue, but Abraham said that a great chasm separated them.

Then the rich man made another request. He asked Abraham to send Lazarus to his father’s house to warn his five brothers so they would not end up in the same place of torment. Abraham answered, “*They have Moses and the prophets. Let them listen to them*” (*v. 29*). “Moses and the prophets” refers to the Scriptures, the Old Testament. The Scriptures already taught God’s will clearly, including care for the poor (*Deuteronomy 15:7–11*; *Isaiah 58:6–7*; *Amos 4:1–2*).

The rich man protested, “*No, father Abraham, but if one goes to them from the dead, they will repent*” (*v. 30*). He believed that a miraculous sign would convince his brothers where Scripture had not.

Abraham’s final answer: “*If they don’t listen to Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded if one rises from the dead*” (*v. 31*).

The problem was not a lack of evidence but a lack of willingness to listen. If people refuse to obey what God has already clearly revealed, a miracle will not change their hearts. They will find a way to explain it away.

This verse carries powerful irony. Jesus Himself would soon rise from the dead, yet many would still refuse to believe. In *John 11*, Jesus raised another man named Lazarus from the dead, and instead of believing, the chief priests plotted to kill Lazarus too (*John 12:10–11*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse teaches that Scripture is sufficient to lead people to repentance and faith. God has revealed His will clearly in His Word. Paul writes that the Scriptures are “*able to make you wise for salvation through faith, which is in Christ Jesus*” (*2 Timothy 3:15*). People do not need more spectacular signs; they need to listen to what God has already said.

It also reveals that unbelief is often a matter of the will rather than the mind. People sometimes say they would believe if they had more evidence. But Jesus’ story suggests that hearts closed to God’s Word will remain closed even to miracles. Faith requires a willingness to listen and obey.

Finally, the verse points toward Jesus’ resurrection. One did rise from the dead. The question for every reader is whether they will listen to Moses, the prophets, and the risen Jesus, or whether they will continue to refuse.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to take Scripture seriously. They do not need to wait for a dramatic sign to know God’s will. Much of what God wants is already clear in His Word, including caring for the poor, loving neighbors, and repenting of sin. The question is whether they will obey.

It also helps believers understand people who refuse to believe. Sometimes believers think that if they could just present the right evidence, others would believe. While evidence and reasoning are valuable, faith also requires an open heart. Believers can pray for God to soften hearts while faithfully sharing His Word.

Finally, this verse, together with the whole story, calls believers to notice the “Lazarus at their gate.” The rich man’s sin was not his wealth alone, but his indifference to the suffering person right outside his door. Believers can open their eyes to the needy around them and respond with compassion, obeying what Moses and the prophets, and Jesus, have clearly taught.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Luke 16* teaches that money is a test of the heart and that how people use it has eternal consequences. The parable of the shrewd manager challenges believers to use their resources wisely with eternity in view: helping others, giving generously, and investing in what lasts. Worldly people often plan carefully for their earthly futures; believers should be even more thoughtful about their eternal futures.

Jesus’ principle about faithfulness in little things reminds believers that character is revealed in everyday choices. Honesty in small matters, careful stewardship, and generosity with modest resources prepare believers for greater responsibilities in God’s kingdom. And no one can serve two masters. Believers must decide whether God or money will rule their hearts.

The Pharisees’ scoffing reveals how easily religious people can love money while appearing righteous. God sees the heart, and what people admire may be detestable to Him. Believers can examine their hearts for love of money and pride in appearances.

Finally, the story of the rich man and Lazarus shows the eternal seriousness of ignoring the poor. The rich man did not harm Lazarus directly; he simply ignored him. Believers can open their eyes to the needy around them and respond with compassion. The story also teaches that Scripture is sufficient to lead people to God. Believers can listen to God’s Word, obey it, and share it, trusting that it has the power to change hearts, while praying for those whose hearts remain closed.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, everything I have belongs to You. Teach me to be a faithful and wise steward, using my money and possessions with eternity in view. Help me to be faithful in small things, honest in every detail, and generous toward others. Free me from serving money, and help me to serve You alone.

Search my heart, Lord, and show me where I have loved money or sought the approval of others more than Your approval. Open my eyes to the Lazarus at my gate, the people in need whom I may have overlooked, and give me compassion and courage to help them. Thank You for the Scriptures that show me Your will. Help me to listen to Your Word and obey it, and to trust that it has power to lead people to repentance and life. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
