Luke · Chapter 17 of 24

# Luke — Chapter 17

Chapter Theme: Forgiveness, Humble Service, Gratitude, and Readiness for the Kingdom

[Read Luke 17 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/LUK17.htm)

Main Teaching

Jesus warns against causing others to stumble, calls His disciples to rebuke and forgive repeatedly, and teaches that faith grows as humble servants do their duty without seeking praise. Of ten men He heals of leprosy, only one, a Samaritan, returns to thank Him. When asked when God’s kingdom will come, Jesus says it is already present among them, and then warns that the Son of Man’s coming will be sudden, like the flood in Noah’s day.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Luke 17* continues Jesus’ journey to Jerusalem. Luke reminds us of this in verse 11: “*As he was on his way to Jerusalem*” (*v. 11*). The chapter begins with short teachings for the disciples about relationships within the community (vv. 1–10), then records the healing of ten lepers (vv. 11–19), and ends with teaching about the coming of God’s kingdom and the return of the Son of Man (vv. 20–37). Its themes include forgiveness, faith, humility, gratitude, and readiness.

### Stumbling Blocks and Forgiveness (*17:1–4*)

Jesus told His disciples that “*It is impossible that no occasions of stumbling should come*” (*v. 1*). In a fallen world, temptations and causes of sin are inevitable. But “*woe to him through whom they come!*” (*v. 1*) It would be better for such a person to be thrown into the sea with a millstone around his neck than to cause one of these “*little ones*” (*v. 2*) to stumble. “Little ones” refers to vulnerable believers, especially those who are young in faith. (See the discussion at *Matthew 18:6* and *Mark 9:42*.)

Then Jesus said, “*Be careful*” (*v. 3*), and gave instructions about how to respond when a fellow believer sins. This is studied below.

### Increase Our Faith (*17:5–10*)

The apostles responded, “*Increase our faith*” (*v. 5*). Perhaps they felt overwhelmed by Jesus’ demanding teaching on forgiveness. Jesus answered, “*If you had faith like a grain of mustard seed, you would tell this sycamore tree, ‘Be uprooted and be planted in the sea,’ and it would obey you*” (*v. 6*). The mulberry or sycamine tree had deep, extensive roots and was very hard to uproot. Jesus’ point was that the size of faith is less important than its object. Even small faith in a great God can accomplish what seems impossible, including the “impossible” task of forgiving repeatedly. (A similar saying is studied at *Matthew 17:20*.)

Jesus then told a short parable about a servant. When a servant comes in from plowing or tending sheep, his master does not tell him to sit down and eat; he tells him to prepare supper and serve him first. The master does not thank the servant for doing what he was told. Jesus concluded, “*Even so you also, when you have done all the things that are commanded you, say, ‘We are unworthy servants. We have done our duty.’*” (*v. 10*)

This parable is not about how God treats His people; elsewhere Jesus describes the master serving his faithful servants (*Luke 12:37*). It is about the attitude disciples should have. They should not think that obeying God earns them special credit or puts God in their debt. Obedience is simply what servants owe their Lord. “Unworthy” here means something like “ordinary” or “not deserving of special reward.” This teaching guards against pride. Even after forgiving seven times a day, the disciples should not think they have done something remarkable; they have simply done their duty.

### The Ten Lepers (*17:11–19*)

As Jesus traveled along the border between Samaria and Galilee, He entered a village. Ten men with leprosy met Him, standing at a distance as the law required (*Leviticus 13:45–46*). In the Bible, “leprosy” referred to various skin diseases that made a person ritually unclean and excluded them from the community. These ten had formed their own group, bound together by shared suffering. Their group included both Jews and at least one Samaritan; their common disease had broken down ethnic barriers.

They called out, “*Jesus, Master, have mercy on us!*” (*v. 13*) Jesus told them, “*Go and show yourselves to the priests*” (*v. 14*). According to the law, a person healed of a skin disease had to be examined by a priest before being declared clean and allowed back into community life (*Leviticus 14*). Jesus sent them before they were healed, testing their faith. “*As they went, they were cleansed*” (*v. 14*).

One of them, when he saw that he was healed, turned back, praising God with a loud voice. He fell on his face at Jesus’ feet and thanked Him. Luke adds, “*and he was a Samaritan*” (*v. 16*). This is studied below. Jesus asked where the other nine were, and whether no one except this foreigner returned to give glory to God. Then He said to the Samaritan, “*Get up, and go your way. Your faith has healed you*” (*v. 19*). The word for “healed” can also mean “saved.” All ten were cleansed of leprosy, but the Samaritan who returned received something more: a relationship with Jesus and a declaration of salvation.

### The Coming of the Kingdom (*17:20–37*)

The Pharisees asked Jesus when God’s kingdom would come. Many Jews expected the kingdom to arrive with dramatic signs, such as the overthrow of Rome and the restoration of Israel’s independence. Jesus answered, “*God’s Kingdom doesn’t come with observation*” (*v. 20*), meaning not with signs that can be tracked and calculated. People will not say, “Here it is!” or “There it is!” “*for behold, God’s Kingdom is within you*” (*v. 21*). This is studied below.

Then Jesus turned to His disciples and spoke about the future. A time would come when they would long to see one of the days of the Son of Man but would not see it. People would claim, “*Look, here!*” (*v. 23*) or “*Look, there!*” (*v. 23*) They should not follow such claims. When the Son of Man comes, it will be like lightning flashing across the sky, sudden and visible to all. “*But first, he must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation*” (*v. 25*). The cross had to come before the glory.

Jesus compared His coming to the days of Noah and Lot. People were going about ordinary life, eating, drinking, marrying, buying, selling, planting, building, until judgment came suddenly: the flood in Noah’s day, and fire and sulfur on Sodom in Lot’s day. They were not wicked because they ate and built; their problem was that they lived as though God did not matter and ignored His warnings. So it will be when the Son of Man is revealed.

On that day, a person on the housetop should not go down to get his belongings, and a person in the field should not turn back. “*Remember Lot’s wife!*” (*v. 32*) As she fled Sodom, she looked back with longing and became a pillar of salt (*Genesis 19:26*). Jesus warned against clinging to the things of this world. “*Whoever seeks to save his life loses it, but whoever loses his life preserves it*” (*v. 33*).

Jesus said that on that night, two people will be in one bed; one will be taken and the other left. Two women will be grinding grain together; one will be taken and the other left. (Verse 36, about two in a field, is missing from the oldest manuscripts.) The disciples asked, “*Where, Lord?*” (*v. 37*) Jesus answered with a proverb: “*Where the body is, there the vultures will also be gathered together*” (*v. 37*). Just as vultures inevitably gather where there is a carcass, judgment will come wherever it is deserved. The coming of the Son of Man will be unmistakable. (See the discussion of similar teaching at *Matthew 24*.)

## Important Verses Explained

### *Luke 17:3–4* — Rebuke and Forgive

> *“Be careful. If your brother sins against you, rebuke him. If he repents, forgive him. If he sins against you seven times in the day, and seven times returns, saying, “I repent,” you shall forgive him.”*
>
> — *Luke 17:3–4* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus speaks these words to His disciples right after warning them about causing others to stumble. He had said that it would be better for someone to be thrown into the sea with a millstone around his neck than to cause a vulnerable believer to sin. Now He turns to the other side of community life: how to respond when someone sins against you.

“*Be careful*” (*v. 3*). This means “watch yourselves” or “pay attention to yourselves.” It may refer back to the warning about causing others to stumble, or forward to the teaching that follows. Either way, Jesus calls His followers to watchfulness in their relationships.

“*If your brother sins against you, rebuke him*” (*v. 3*). “Brother” refers to a fellow disciple. To “rebuke” means to point out the wrong honestly. Jesus does not tell His followers to ignore sin or pretend it did not happen. Love sometimes requires honest confrontation. (*Matthew 18:15* gives fuller instructions about going privately to the person.)

“*If he repents, forgive him*” (*v. 3*). When the person acknowledges the wrong and turns from it, the response must be forgiveness. Forgiveness means releasing the debt and giving up the right to hold the offense against them.

“*If he sins against you seven times in the day, and seven times returns, saying, ‘I repent,’ you shall forgive him*” (*v. 4*). “Seven times in a day” is a striking picture of repeated offenses, almost absurdly frequent. The number seven suggests completeness. Jesus means that there is no limit to forgiveness when someone sincerely repents. In *Matthew 18:22*, Jesus tells Peter to forgive not seven times but seventy times seven.

The apostles’ immediate response was, “*Increase our faith*” (*v. 5*). They recognized that this kind of forgiveness required more faith than they had.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses hold together truth and grace. Jesus does not call His followers to ignore sin, nor to hold grudges. He calls them to honest confrontation and generous forgiveness. Both are expressions of love. Rebuke without forgiveness becomes harsh; forgiveness without honesty can enable ongoing harm.

They also reflect God’s own forgiveness. God forgives His people repeatedly when they repent. Believers who have received such forgiveness are called to extend it to others. Paul writes, “*even as Christ forgave you, so you also do*” (*Colossians 3:13*).

It is important to understand that forgiveness does not always mean immediate restoration of trust, especially when someone has caused serious harm. Forgiveness releases the desire for revenge and the debt owed; rebuilding trust may take time and evidence of real change. In cases of abuse, forgiveness can coexist with protective boundaries and with seeking justice through appropriate authorities.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses invite believers to address wrongs honestly rather than holding silent resentment or gossiping about others. When someone has sinned against them, they can speak to that person directly and gently, with the goal of restoration.

They also call believers to forgive generously when others repent. It can be difficult to forgive someone who keeps failing in the same way. Jesus asks His followers to keep forgiving, trusting God for the strength to do so.

Finally, these verses encourage believers to ask God for more faith, as the apostles did. Forgiveness is often beyond human strength. Believers can pray for God’s help to forgive and to love those who hurt them, while also using wisdom about trust and boundaries.

### *Luke 17:10* — “*We Are Unworthy Servants*” (*v. 10*)

> *“Even so you also, when you have done all the things that are commanded you, say, “We are unworthy servants. We have done our duty.””*
>
> — *Luke 17:10* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse concludes a short parable Jesus told after the apostles asked Him to increase their faith. He had just taught them to forgive repeatedly, even seven times in a day, and He had told them that even faith as small as a mustard seed could uproot a tree.

Then He told a parable about a servant. Imagine having a servant who has been out plowing or tending sheep all day. When he comes in, the master would not say, “*Come immediately and sit down at the table*” (*v. 7*). Instead, he would say, “*Prepare my supper, clothe yourself properly, and serve me while I eat and drink. Afterward you shall eat and drink*” (*v. 8*). The master would not thank the servant for doing what he was told, because that was simply the servant’s job.

Jesus applied this: “*Even so you also, when you have done all the things that are commanded you, say, ‘We are unworthy servants. We have done our duty.’*” (*v. 10*)

“Unworthy servants” does not mean worthless people. It means servants who have no special claim on their master, who have not earned extra reward. They have simply done what they were supposed to do.

The parable addresses the disciples’ attitude. After hearing Jesus’ demanding teaching on forgiveness, the disciples might have thought that if they managed to forgive seven times a day, they would deserve special credit. Jesus warned against that kind of thinking. Obedience to God is not a way of putting God in their debt; it is simply the right response of servants to their Lord.

In the ancient world, servants (or slaves) were expected to obey without receiving thanks. Jesus used this familiar arrangement to make a point about humility, not to approve of slavery or to describe God’s character as harsh. Elsewhere, Jesus says that the faithful servant will be welcomed by the master, who will even serve him (*Luke 12:37*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse teaches humility in service. Believers can be tempted to think that their good works earn them special favor with God, or to keep score of their obedience. Jesus corrects this attitude. Salvation and all of God’s blessings are gifts of grace, not wages earned. Paul writes, “*Now to him who works, the reward is not counted as grace, but as something owed*” (*Romans 4:4*). God owes no one anything.

It also guards against spiritual pride. When believers serve faithfully, give generously, or forgive repeatedly, they may be tempted to feel superior to others. Jesus’ words remind them that they have only done what they should.

At the same time, this verse should be read alongside Jesus’ other teachings. God does reward His faithful servants generously (*Luke 19:17*), not because they have earned it, but because He is gracious. The attitude of humble servanthood frees believers from pride and from the burden of trying to earn God’s favor.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to serve God without seeking praise or recognition. Whether they serve in church, care for family, or help others, they can do so humbly, recognizing that they are simply doing what God asks.

It also frees believers from keeping score. They do not need to track their good deeds or compare them with others. Their relationship with God rests on His grace, not on their performance.

Finally, this verse encourages believers to find joy in obedience itself. Serving God is a privilege, not a burden to be rewarded. Believers can say with humility and gladness, “We have done our duty,” and trust God’s generous heart.

### *Luke 17:15–16* — The One Who Returned to Give Thanks

> *“One of them, when he saw that he was healed, turned back, glorifying God with a loud voice. He fell on his face at Jesus’ feet, giving him thanks; and he was a Samaritan.”*
>
> — *Luke 17:15–16* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These verses describe the response of one man among ten who were healed of leprosy. As Jesus traveled along the border between Samaria and Galilee on His way to Jerusalem, ten men with leprosy met Him. They stood at a distance, as required by law, and called out, “Jesus, Master, have mercy on us!” Jesus told them to go and show themselves to the priests, who could declare them clean and allow them to return to their families and communities. As they went, they were healed.

Then “*One of them, when he saw that he was healed, turned back, glorifying God with a loud voice*” (*v. 15*). He did not continue to the priests immediately. He turned around and came back to Jesus. He had probably called out to Jesus from a distance before; now he praised God loudly, no longer ashamed or isolated.

“*He fell on his face at Jesus’ feet, giving him thanks*” (*v. 16*). Falling at someone’s feet showed deep humility and worship. He thanked Jesus personally for his healing. Notice that he glorified God and thanked Jesus, suggesting that he recognized God’s power working through Jesus.

Then Luke adds the surprise: “*and he was a Samaritan*” (*v. 16*). Samaritans were despised by Jews as religious heretics and ethnic outsiders. Yet this Samaritan was the only one who returned to give thanks. The other nine, presumably Jews, received healing but did not return.

Jesus asked, “*Weren’t the ten cleansed? But where are the nine?*” (*v. 17*) and “*Were there none found who returned to give glory to God, except this foreigner?*” (*v. 18*) Then He told the Samaritan, “*Get up, and go your way. Your faith has healed you*” (*v. 19*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses reveal that gratitude is a mark of genuine faith. All ten were healed physically, but only one returned to thank Jesus. The word Jesus used to the Samaritan, “Your faith has healed you,” can also mean “saved you.” The Samaritan received more than physical healing; he received a personal encounter with Jesus and a declaration of salvation.

They also show that God’s grace reaches outsiders. Luke repeatedly highlights Samaritans responding to God: the Good Samaritan in Jesus’ parable (*Luke 10:30–37*) and now this healed man. In Acts, Samaritans would receive the gospel with joy (*Acts 8:4–8*). God’s kingdom crosses ethnic and religious boundaries.

Finally, the story warns against taking God’s blessings for granted. The nine may have been grateful in their hearts, or they may have been eager to return to normal life. Either way, they did not come back to honor the one who healed them. It is possible to receive God’s gifts without truly turning to God.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses invite believers to practice gratitude. Every good thing in life comes from God: health, provision, relationships, salvation, and countless daily mercies. Believers can make a habit of returning to God in thanksgiving, both in private prayer and in public worship.

They also challenge believers not to be like the nine, who received blessings but moved on without acknowledging God. When prayers are answered or difficulties are resolved, believers can pause to thank God before rushing back to normal life.

Finally, these verses remind believers that people they consider outsiders may show greater faith and gratitude than those who seem to be insiders. Believers can welcome and learn from people of every background who respond to God with sincere hearts.

### *Luke 17:21* — God’s Kingdom Is in Your Midst

> *“neither will they say, “Look, here!” or, “Look, there!” for behold, God’s Kingdom is within you.”*
>
> — *Luke 17:21* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse is part of Jesus’ answer to a question from the Pharisees. They asked Him when God’s kingdom would come. Many Jews of that time expected the kingdom to arrive with dramatic signs: the defeat of Israel’s enemies, the restoration of David’s throne, and visible cosmic events. They may have expected Jesus to give them a timeline or a list of signs to watch for.

Jesus answered, “*God’s Kingdom doesn’t come with observation*” (*v. 20*). The word “observation” refers to watching carefully, the way someone watches for signs to calculate a date. The kingdom would not arrive in a way that could be tracked and predicted by signs.

“*neither will they say, ‘Look, here!’ or, ‘Look, there!’*” (*v. 21*) People would not be able to point to one location and say, “The kingdom is over there.”

“*for behold, God’s Kingdom is within you*” (*v. 21*). The Greek phrase translated “within you” can also mean “among you” or “in your midst.” Many scholars prefer “among you” in this context, because Jesus was speaking to Pharisees who opposed Him; it seems unlikely that He meant the kingdom was in their hearts. He likely meant that the kingdom was already present among them in His own person and ministry. The King had come, and His healings, exorcisms, and teaching showed that God’s reign was breaking into the world. Others take “within you” to emphasize the inward, spiritual nature of the kingdom: it begins in people’s hearts as they submit to God’s rule. Both truths are taught in Scripture.

The Pharisees were looking for a future political event, while the kingdom was already standing in front of them in Jesus. Yet in the following verses, Jesus also spoke to His disciples about a future coming of the Son of Man, which would be sudden and visible to all. The kingdom has both a present reality and a future fulfillment.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse teaches that God’s kingdom is present wherever Jesus is. It is not merely a future hope but a present reality. Wherever people submit to Jesus as King, wherever the sick are healed and sinners forgiven, the kingdom is at work. Earlier Jesus said, “*But if I by God’s finger cast out demons, then God’s Kingdom has come to you*” (*Luke 11:20*).

It also warns against being so focused on future signs that one misses God’s present work. The Pharisees wanted dramatic signs but failed to recognize the King standing among them. People today can become absorbed in speculation about the end times while ignoring Jesus’ call to follow Him now.

Finally, the verse, together with the following teaching, shows the “already and not yet” nature of the kingdom. It has already come in Jesus, but it will be fully revealed when He returns. Believers live between these two realities, experiencing the kingdom now while waiting for its completion.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to recognize God’s kingdom in the present. They do not need to wait for some future event to experience God’s reign. They can submit to Jesus as King today, allowing His rule to shape their thoughts, words, and actions.

It also encourages believers to look for signs of God’s kingdom around them: lives transformed, relationships restored, the poor cared for, and the gospel spreading. These are evidence that the kingdom is at work.

Finally, this verse warns against being consumed by speculation about the future. While Jesus will return, and believers should be ready, their primary focus should be on following Him faithfully now. The kingdom is “in your midst,” calling for a response today.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Luke 17* covers several aspects of discipleship. It begins with relationships within the community of faith. Believers must be careful not to cause others, especially vulnerable believers, to stumble. When others sin against them, they should speak honestly and forgive generously whenever there is repentance, even repeatedly. This kind of forgiveness requires faith, and believers can ask God to increase it.

The parable of the servant teaches humility. Believers should serve God faithfully without expecting special praise or thinking that their obedience earns them favor. Everything they have is a gift of grace. This humility frees them from pride and from the burden of trying to earn God’s love.

The story of the ten lepers calls believers to gratitude. All ten were healed, but only one returned to give thanks, and he was a Samaritan. Believers can make a habit of returning to God in thanksgiving and can welcome people of every background who respond to God with sincere faith.

Finally, Jesus’ teaching about the kingdom reminds believers that God’s reign is already present in Jesus, and that it will be fully revealed when He returns. His return will be sudden and unmistakable, like the flood in Noah’s day. Believers can live faithfully now, not clinging to the things of this world like Lot’s wife, but ready at all times to meet the Son of Man.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, keep me from causing anyone to stumble, especially those who are young or vulnerable in faith. Give me the courage to speak honestly when someone wrongs me, and the grace to forgive them whenever they repent, even again and again. Increase my faith, because I cannot forgive like this by my own strength.

Teach me to serve You with humility, without seeking praise or thinking that I have earned Your favor. Make me like the Samaritan who returned to thank You, and keep me from taking Your blessings for granted. Thank You that Your kingdom is present wherever You reign. Help me to live under Your rule today, and keep me ready for the day of Your return, not clinging to the things of this world. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Luke · Chapter 18 of 24

# Luke — Chapter 18

Chapter Theme: Persistent Prayer and Humble Hearts

[Read Luke 18 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/LUK18.htm)

Main Teaching

Jesus tells a parable about a widow who keeps pleading with an unjust judge, teaching His followers always to pray and not give up, because God will bring justice to His people. Through the parable of the Pharisee and the tax collector, He shows that God accepts the humble who plead for mercy, not the proud who trust in their own righteousness. He welcomes little children, calls a rich ruler to give up his wealth, predicts His death again, and gives sight to a blind man who cries out for mercy.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Luke 18* continues Jesus’ journey to Jerusalem and brings it near its goal. By the end of the chapter, Jesus is approaching Jericho, the last major town before the climb to Jerusalem. The chapter opens with two parables found only in Luke, both about prayer and both concerning people’s attitudes toward God. It then includes events also recorded in Matthew and Mark: Jesus blessing children, the rich ruler, the third prediction of His death, and the healing of a blind man. (These are studied in depth at *Mark 10:15*, *Mark 10:21*, *Matthew 19:26*, *Matthew 20:28*, and *Mark 10:50*.)

The chapter follows Jesus’ teaching at the end of *Luke 17* about the sudden coming of the Son of Man. His followers would face a long wait, often in difficult circumstances, and they would need persistent prayer and humble faith.

### The Persistent Widow and the Unjust Judge (*18:1–8*)

Luke explains the purpose of this parable before Jesus tells it: “*that they must always pray and not give up*” (*v. 1*). This is studied below.

In a certain town there was a judge who “*didn’t fear God and didn’t respect man*” (*v. 2*). In the Old Testament, judges were commanded to judge fairly, to fear God, and to protect the vulnerable (*Deuteronomy 16:18–20*; *2 Chronicles 19:6–7*). This judge did none of that. He was corrupt and callous.

A widow in that town kept coming to him, saying, “*Defend me from my adversary!*” (*v. 3*) Widows were among the most vulnerable people in ancient society. With no husband to support or defend them, they were easily exploited. The law of Moses repeatedly commanded care and justice for widows (*Exodus 22:22–24*). This widow had no money for bribes and no powerful connections. All she had was persistence.

For a while the judge refused. But eventually he said to himself, “*Though I neither fear God nor respect man*” (*v. 4*), “*yet because this widow bothers me, I will defend her, or else she will wear me out by her continual coming*” (*v. 5*). The phrase “wear me out” can literally mean “give me a black eye,” a humorous exaggeration suggesting the judge felt worn down, as if beaten, by her constant appeals.

Jesus then drew the lesson, studied below. If even an unjust judge would grant justice to a persistent widow, how much more will God, who is perfectly just and loving, respond to His people who cry out to Him? Then Jesus asked a probing question: “*Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on the earth?*” (*v. 8*)

### The Pharisee and the Tax Collector (*18:9–14*)

Jesus told another parable “*to certain people who were convinced of their own righteousness, and who despised all others*” (*v. 9*). Two men went up to the temple to pray. People often went to the temple at the times of the morning and afternoon sacrifices to pray. One was a Pharisee, a respected religious man known for careful observance of the law. The other was a tax collector, despised as a collaborator with Rome and often dishonest.

The Pharisee stood and prayed “*by himself*” (*v. 11*), which may mean he prayed silently about himself, or stood apart from others. His prayer began with thanks to God but quickly turned to self-praise: he was not like other people, robbers, evildoers, adulterers, or even this tax collector. He listed his religious achievements: “*I fast twice a week. I give tithes of all that I get*” (*v. 12*). The law required only one annual fast, on the Day of Atonement, but devout Pharisees fasted twice a week. The law required tithing certain produce, but he tithed everything. He went beyond what was required.

Yet his prayer contained no request, no confession, and no real need for God. He was comparing himself to others and congratulating himself.

The tax collector stood at a distance. He would not even look up to heaven, but beat his chest, a sign of deep grief and repentance, and prayed, “*God, be merciful to me, a sinner!*” (*v. 13*) This prayer is studied below. Jesus declared that this man, not the Pharisee, went home “*justified*” (*v. 14*), declared righteous before God. “*for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but he who humbles himself will be exalted*” (*v. 14*).

### Jesus Blesses the Children (*18:15–17*)

People were bringing even their babies to Jesus for Him to touch them. Luke uses a word for infants. The disciples rebuked the people, thinking Jesus should not be bothered. But Jesus called the children to Him and said, “*Allow the little children to come to me, and don’t hinder them, for God’s Kingdom belongs to such as these*” (*v. 16*). Whoever does not receive God’s kingdom like a little child will never enter it. Placed right after the parable of the tax collector, this scene reinforces the lesson: the kingdom belongs to the humble and dependent, not the self-sufficient. (See *Mark 10:15*.)

### The Rich Ruler (*18:18–30*)

A certain ruler asked Jesus, “*Good Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?*” (*v. 18*) Jesus questioned why he called Him good, since only God is good, and listed several commandments. The ruler said he had kept them all since his youth. Jesus said, “*You still lack one thing. Sell all that you have and distribute it to the poor. Then you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me*” (*v. 22*). The man became very sad, because he was very rich.

The contrast with the previous scenes is clear. The tax collector came with nothing but a plea for mercy. Little children came with nothing to offer. The rich ruler came with his record of obedience and his wealth, and he could not let go of them. Jesus said how hard it is for the rich to enter God’s kingdom, harder than for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle. When the listeners asked who could be saved, Jesus answered, “*The things which are impossible with men are possible with God*” (*v. 27*). He promised that anyone who has left home or family for God’s kingdom will receive much more in this age and eternal life in the age to come. (See *Matthew 19:21–26* and *Mark 10:21*.)

### Third Prediction of the Passion (*18:31–34*)

Jesus took the Twelve aside and told them that they were going up to Jerusalem, where everything written by the prophets about the Son of Man would be fulfilled. He would be handed over to the Gentiles, mocked, insulted, spit on, flogged, and killed, and on the third day He would rise again. Luke emphasizes the disciples’ lack of understanding three times in one verse: “*They understood none of these things. This saying was hidden from them, and they didn’t understand the things that were said*” (*v. 34*). Only after the resurrection would Jesus open their minds to understand the Scriptures (*Luke 24:45*).

### The Blind Man Near Jericho (*18:35–43*)

As Jesus approached Jericho, a blind man was sitting by the road begging. Hearing the crowd, he asked what was happening and was told that Jesus of Nazareth was passing by. He called out, “*Jesus, you son of David, have mercy on me!*” (*v. 38*) People told him to be quiet, but he shouted all the more. Jesus stopped and had him brought near, and asked, “*What do you want me to do?*” (*v. 41*) He answered, “*Lord, that I may see again*” (*v. 41*). Jesus said, “*Receive your sight. Your faith has healed you*” (*v. 42*). Immediately he could see, and he followed Jesus, praising God, and all the people praised God too.

This man’s prayer, “have mercy on me,” echoes the tax collector’s prayer, “be merciful to me.” Both men came to God with nothing but their need, and both were received. The blind beggar saw who Jesus was, the Son of David, more clearly than the disciples, who did not understand what Jesus had just told them. (Mark’s account, which names him Bartimaeus, is studied at *Mark 10:50*.)

## Important Verses Explained

### *Luke 18:1* — Always Pray and Do Not Give Up

> *“He also spoke a parable to them that they must always pray and not give up,”*
>
> — *Luke 18:1* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse introduces the parable of the persistent widow, and unusually, Luke tells readers the parable’s purpose before it begins: “*He also spoke a parable to them that they must always pray and not give up*” (*v. 1*).

The context is important. At the end of *Luke 17*, Jesus had been speaking about the coming of the Son of Man. He told His disciples that there would be days when they would long to see the Son of Man but would not see Him, and that His coming would be sudden. Between Jesus’ first coming and His return, His followers would live in a world where injustice continued and where they would often suffer. They would be tempted to lose hope and stop praying.

“*that they must always pray*” (*v. 1*). “Always” does not mean that believers must be speaking prayers every moment, but that prayer should be a constant and persistent part of life, especially in times of difficulty. Paul expresses a similar idea: “*pray without ceasing*” (*1 Thessalonians 5:17*).

“*and not give up*” (*v. 1*). The phrase means not to lose heart, not to become discouraged, not to grow weary. When prayers seem unanswered and justice seems delayed, it is tempting to stop praying. Jesus warns against this.

The parable that follows illustrates the point. A widow kept coming to an unjust judge asking for justice, and he finally gave in because of her persistence. If persistence works even with an unjust judge, how much more should believers persist in prayer to a just and loving God?

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that persistent prayer is an expression of faith. When believers keep praying, they demonstrate that they still trust God, even when they do not see answers. Giving up on prayer often means giving up hope that God will act.

It also shows that Jesus understands the difficulty of prayer. He knew His followers would face times when prayer seemed fruitless and they would be tempted to quit. He did not ignore this struggle; He addressed it directly with encouragement.

Finally, the verse connects prayer with the hope of Christ’s return. Believers pray in a world that is not yet fully set right. They pray, as Jesus taught, “Your kingdom come.” Persistent prayer keeps their hope alive until He returns.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers who feel discouraged in prayer. Perhaps they have prayed for a loved one’s salvation, for healing, for justice, or for a change in circumstances, and nothing seems to happen. Jesus’ words invite them to keep praying and not lose heart.

It also encourages believers to build habits of regular prayer that sustain them through difficult seasons. Prayer is not only for emergencies; it is an ongoing relationship with God. Setting aside regular times for prayer and bringing needs to God throughout the day can help believers pray “always.”

Finally, this verse reminds believers that persistent prayer is not about manipulating God. God is not reluctant like the unjust judge. Persistence reflects faith, deepens dependence, and keeps believers connected to God while they wait for His answers.

### *Luke 18:7–8* — Will God Not Bring Justice to His Chosen Ones?

> *“Won’t God avenge his chosen ones who are crying out to him day and night, and yet he exercises patience with them? I tell you that he will avenge them quickly. Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on the earth?”*
>
> — *Luke 18:7–8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These verses are Jesus’ application of the parable of the persistent widow. In the story, a judge who did not fear God or respect people refused to help a widow who kept asking for justice against her adversary. Eventually, he gave in, not because he cared about justice, but because she kept bothering him. Jesus said, “*Listen to what the unrighteous judge says*” (*v. 6*). Then He drew the lesson.

“*Won’t God avenge his chosen ones who are crying out to him day and night*” (*v. 7*). The argument moves from lesser to greater. If even an unjust judge would eventually give justice to a persistent widow he did not care about, how much more will God, who is perfectly just and who loves His people, bring justice to His chosen ones? God is not like the unjust judge; He is the opposite. The word “avenge” here means to vindicate or bring justice, to set things right for those who have been wronged.

“His chosen ones” refers to God’s people, those He has called to belong to Him. They are not strangers to God, as the widow was to the judge. They are His beloved children.

“*and yet he exercises patience with them?*” (*v. 7*) This phrase is difficult to translate. It may mean, “Will He delay long over them?”, a question expecting the answer “no.” Or it may refer to God’s patience, His willingness to wait so that more people may repent (*2 Peter 3:9*).

“*I tell you that he will avenge them quickly*” (*v. 8*). God will act decisively. “Quickly” may mean that when God acts, He acts suddenly, or that from God’s perspective, the wait is short, even when it feels long to His suffering people.

Then Jesus asked a sobering question: “*Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on the earth?*” (*v. 8*) The real issue is not whether God will be faithful, but whether His people will remain faithful in prayer and trust while they wait.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses reveal God’s commitment to justice. God sees the oppression and suffering of His people, and He will set things right. Throughout Scripture, God is described as the defender of the widow, the orphan, and the oppressed (*Psalm 68:5*; *146:7–9*). The cry for justice is not ignored.

They also acknowledge the reality of waiting. God’s people cry out “day and night,” which implies a long and painful wait. Revelation pictures martyrs crying out, “*How long, Master, the holy and true, until you judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?*” (*Revelation 6:10*) God’s timing often differs from ours, but His justice is certain.

Finally, Jesus’ question about faith turns the focus to believers’ responsibility. God will be faithful; the question is whether His people will keep trusting and praying until He comes. Persistent prayer is how faith endures through the long wait.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses offer comfort to those who suffer injustice. Whether facing persecution, mistreatment, abuse, or systemic injustice, believers can bring their cries to God, knowing that He hears and will act. They do not need to take revenge into their own hands; they can trust God’s justice (*Romans 12:19*). This trust is compatible with seeking justice through appropriate channels, such as reporting wrongdoing and seeking help.

They also encourage believers to keep praying for justice in the world. Believers can pray for persecuted Christians, oppressed people, victims of violence, and those who have no one to defend them, trusting that God cares about these things.

Finally, Jesus’ question invites self-examination: will He find faith in me? Believers can ask God to strengthen their faith so that they remain faithful in prayer and trust until Christ returns.

### *Luke 18:13–14* — “*God, Be Merciful to Me, a Sinner*” (*v. 13*)

> *“But the tax collector, standing far away, wouldn’t even lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his chest, saying, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner!” I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other; for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but he who humbles himself will be exalted.”*
>
> — *Luke 18:13–14* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These verses are the climax of the parable of the Pharisee and the tax collector. Jesus told this parable to people who trusted in their own righteousness and looked down on others. Two men went to the temple to pray. The Pharisee stood and prayed about himself, thanking God that he was not like other people, especially the tax collector, and listing his religious achievements: fasting twice a week and tithing everything he received.

“*But the tax collector, standing far away*” (*v. 13*). He stood at a distance, perhaps in the outer court, feeling unworthy to come close to God’s presence. Tax collectors were despised as traitors and cheats, and this man seems to have known that he deserved that reputation.

“*wouldn’t even lift up his eyes to heaven*” (*v. 13*). People often prayed with eyes and hands lifted toward heaven. He could not bring himself to look up, overwhelmed by shame.

“*but beat his chest*” (*v. 13*). This was a gesture of intense grief and repentance, usually associated with mourning. The heart was considered the source of sin, and beating the chest expressed deep sorrow over one’s own heart.

“*saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner!’*” (*v. 13*) His prayer was short and simple. He did not list good deeds or compare himself with others. He confessed that he was a sinner and asked for mercy. The word for “be merciful” is related to the word for atonement; it means “be propitiated toward me” or “let your wrath be turned away from me.” He was asking God to forgive him on the basis of mercy, possibly thinking of the sacrifice being offered in the temple at that hour. In Greek, the phrase is literally “the sinner,” as if he thought of himself as the worst of all.

Then Jesus gave His verdict: “*I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other*” (*v. 14*). “Justified” means declared righteous before God, accepted by Him. The tax collector, who confessed his sin and asked for mercy, was accepted. The Pharisee, who trusted in his own righteousness, was not.

Jesus concluded with the principle: “*for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but he who humbles himself will be exalted*” (*v. 14*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses reveal the heart of the gospel: people are made right with God not by their own righteousness but by God’s mercy. The Pharisee’s religious achievements did not justify him, because he trusted in them rather than in God. The tax collector had nothing to offer except his need, and God justified him. Paul later explains this truth: “*being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus*” (*Romans 3:24*).

They also expose the danger of self-righteousness and contempt for others. The Pharisee was not wrong to fast or tithe. His problem was that he trusted in these things and looked down on others. Pride blinds people to their own need for mercy.

Finally, the tax collector’s prayer has been treasured throughout Christian history. In Eastern Orthodox tradition, it became the basis for the “Jesus Prayer”: “Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner.” It expresses the posture of every person who comes to God: humble, honest, and dependent on mercy.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses invite believers to examine how they approach God. Do they come trusting in their good deeds, church attendance, or moral record? Or do they come humbly, acknowledging their need for mercy? God accepts those who come to Him honestly and humbly.

They also warn against comparing oneself to others. It is easy to feel spiritually superior to people who struggle with obvious sins. Jesus’ parable shows that such comparisons are dangerous. Every person stands before God in need of mercy.

Finally, these verses offer hope to those who feel unworthy to approach God. Like the tax collector, they can come with nothing but their need and pray, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner.” Jesus promises that such prayers are heard and that those who pray them go home justified.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Luke 18* is about how people approach God. The parable of the persistent widow teaches believers to pray always and not give up, especially when facing injustice and long delays. God is not like the unjust judge; He is a loving Father who will bring justice to His people. Believers can bring their cries to Him persistently, trusting His character and timing, while asking whether He will find faith in them when He comes.

The parable of the Pharisee and the tax collector teaches that God accepts the humble, not the self-righteous. Believers can come to God not on the basis of their achievements but on the basis of His mercy. They can guard against comparing themselves to others and looking down on those who struggle, remembering that they too need God’s mercy every day.

The welcome of little children reinforces this lesson. God’s kingdom belongs to those who receive it like children, with dependence and trust. The rich ruler shows the opposite: someone who could not let go of his wealth and his record of obedience. Believers can examine what they are clinging to and trust that what is impossible for people is possible with God.

Finally, the blind man near Jericho shows the right response to Jesus: crying out for mercy, persisting despite opposition, recognizing Jesus as the Son of David, and following Him with praise. Believers can approach Jesus the same way, with honest need, persistent faith, and grateful worship.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, teach me to pray always and not to lose heart. When I am waiting for answers and justice seems delayed, help me to keep crying out to You, trusting that You hear and that You will act. When You return, may You find faith in me.

I come to You not with my achievements, but with my need. God, be merciful to me, a sinner. Keep me from pride and from looking down on others. Help me to receive Your kingdom like a little child, with trust and dependence. Show me anything I am clinging to more than You, and give me grace to let it go. Like the blind man near Jericho, I cry out for Your mercy. Open my eyes, and help me to follow You with praise. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Luke · Chapter 19 of 24

# Luke — Chapter 19

Chapter Theme: Seeking the Lost and Weeping Over the City

[Read Luke 19 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/LUK19.htm)

Main Teaching

In Jericho, Jesus invites Himself to the home of Zacchaeus, a rich chief tax collector, whose encounter with Jesus leads him to give generously and repay those he cheated; Jesus declares that He came to seek and save the lost. Through the parable of the minas, He teaches faithful service while His followers wait for His kingdom. As He enters Jerusalem to the praise of His disciples, He weeps over the city that did not recognize the time of God’s visitation, and He cleanses the temple.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Luke 19* brings Jesus’ long journey to Jerusalem, which began in *Luke 9:51*, to its destination. Jesus passes through Jericho, about fifteen miles northeast of Jerusalem, and then climbs the steep road to the city, arriving at the Mount of Olives. From there He descends into Jerusalem for the final week of His earthly life.

The chapter contains one of the most beloved stories in Luke, the conversion of Zacchaeus, and ends with Jesus’ lament over Jerusalem and the cleansing of the temple. Throughout the chapter, Jesus appears as the seeking Savior, the coming King, and the grieving Lord.

### Zacchaeus (*19:1–10*)

Jesus entered Jericho and was passing through. Jericho was a wealthy city on an important trade route, with palm groves and balsam plantations, and it was a center for collecting taxes and customs. A man named Zacchaeus lived there. He was “*a chief tax collector, and he was rich*” (*v. 2*). As a chief tax collector, he supervised other tax collectors and likely profited from their work as well as his own. Tax collectors bid for the right to collect taxes for the Roman authorities and made their money by charging more than was required. Zacchaeus had become rich this way, and his neighbors would have despised him as a traitor and a thief. His name, ironically, comes from a Hebrew word meaning “pure” or “righteous.”

Zacchaeus wanted to see who Jesus was, but he was short and could not see over the crowd. So he ran ahead and climbed a sycamore-fig tree along the route. Sycamore-figs had low, spreading branches that were easy to climb. For a wealthy, important man, running and climbing a tree was undignified, showing how eager he was.

When Jesus reached the spot, He looked up and said, “*Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for today I must stay at your house*” (*v. 5*). Jesus called him by name, though they had apparently never met. He invited Himself to Zacchaeus’s home, saying He “must” stay there, the same word Luke uses for divine necessity in Jesus’ mission. Zacchaeus hurried down and welcomed Him joyfully.

But the crowd grumbled, “*He has gone in to lodge with a man who is a sinner*” (*v. 7*). As in *Luke 15:2*, people were upset that Jesus associated with sinners.

Then Zacchaeus stood up and made a remarkable declaration, studied below. Jesus responded, “*Today, salvation has come to this house, because he also is a son of Abraham*” (*v. 9*). Despite his sins, Zacchaeus was a descendant of Abraham, part of God’s covenant people, and he had now shown the faith of Abraham. Then Jesus summarized His whole mission in one sentence, also studied below: “*For the Son of Man came to seek and to save that which was lost*” (*v. 10*).

Notice the contrast with the rich ruler in *Luke 18:18–23*. That ruler was respected and law-abiding but went away sad because he would not give up his wealth. Zacchaeus was despised and dishonest, yet he gave much of his wealth away with joy. What seemed impossible for the rich, entering God’s kingdom (*Luke 18:24–27*), became possible by God’s grace.

### The Parable of the Minas (*19:11–27*)

While the people were listening, Jesus told a parable, “*because he was near Jerusalem, and they supposed that God’s Kingdom would be revealed immediately*” (*v. 11*). Many expected that when Jesus reached Jerusalem, He would immediately establish His kingdom in power. Jesus told a parable to correct this expectation.

A nobleman went to a distant country to be appointed king and then return. This would have reminded listeners of Archelaus, a son of Herod the Great, who traveled to Rome in 4 B.C. to have his kingship confirmed by Caesar. A delegation of Jews followed him to Rome to oppose his appointment. When Archelaus returned, he took revenge on his opponents.

Before leaving, the nobleman gave ten servants one mina each and told them, “*Conduct business until I come*” (*v. 13*). A mina was worth about a hundred days’ wages, a significant but not enormous sum, much less than the talents in Matthew’s similar parable (*Matthew 25:14–30*). Meanwhile, his citizens hated him and sent a delegation after him saying, “*We don’t want this man to reign over us*” (*v. 14*).

When the nobleman returned as king, he called the servants to account. The first had earned ten more minas, and the king said, “*Well done, you good servant! Because you were found faithful with very little, you shall have authority over ten cities*” (*v. 17*). The second had earned five and was given five cities. A third had kept his mina wrapped in a cloth because he feared the king as a harsh man. The king condemned him from his own words: if he believed the king was harsh, he should at least have put the money in the bank to earn interest. The king took his mina and gave it to the one with ten. Finally, the king ordered that his enemies who did not want him to reign be brought and killed before him.

The parable taught several lessons. First, the kingdom would not appear immediately; there would be a period of waiting while the King was away. Second, during that time, His servants must faithfully use what He has entrusted to them. Third, the King would return and hold everyone accountable. Fourth, those who rejected His rule would face judgment. The parable anticipated both Jesus’ ascension and return, and the rejection He was about to face in Jerusalem. (A similar parable is studied at *Matthew 25:21*.)

### The Triumphal Entry (*19:28–40*)

After telling the parable, Jesus went on ahead, going up to Jerusalem. Near Bethphage and Bethany on the Mount of Olives, He sent two disciples to bring a colt that had never been ridden, telling them to say, “*The Lord needs it*” (*v. 31*). Everything happened as He said. They put their cloaks on the colt and set Jesus on it, fulfilling *Zechariah 9:9*, and people spread their cloaks on the road.

As He came to the descent of the Mount of Olives, from which the whole city of Jerusalem and the temple come into view, “*the whole multitude of the disciples began to rejoice and praise God with a loud voice for all the mighty works which they had seen*” (*v. 37*). They shouted, “*Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord! Peace in heaven, and glory in the highest!*” (*v. 38*) Luke’s wording echoes the angels’ song at Jesus’ birth (*Luke 2:14*). Luke emphasizes that Jesus is “the King,” connecting with the parable just told.

Some Pharisees in the crowd told Jesus to rebuke His disciples. They may have feared that such royal language would provoke Roman retaliation, or they may have objected to the claim itself. Jesus answered, “*I tell you that if these were silent, the stones would cry out*” (*v. 40*). Creation itself would proclaim the King if His people were silent.

### Jesus Weeps Over Jerusalem (*19:41–44*)

As He came near and saw the city, Jesus wept over it. This scene, found only in Luke, is studied below. Jesus predicted that enemies would build an embankment around the city, surround it, crush it and its children, and not leave one stone on another, “*because you didn’t know the time of your visitation*” (*v. 44*). This was fulfilled in A.D. 70, when Roman armies besieged and destroyed Jerusalem.

### Cleansing the Temple (*19:45–48*)

Jesus entered the temple and began driving out those who were selling, saying, “*It is written, ‘My house is a house of prayer,’ but you have made it a ‘den of robbers’!*” (*v. 46*) (This event is studied at *Matthew 21:13* and *Mark 11:13–14*.) He taught in the temple every day. The chief priests, scribes, and leaders of the people were trying to kill Him, but they could not find a way, “*for all the people hung on to every word that he said*” (*v. 48*).

## Important Verses Explained

### *Luke 19:8* — Zacchaeus’s Changed Heart

> *“Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord, ‘Behold, Lord, half of my goods I give to the poor. If I have wrongfully exacted anything of anyone, I restore four times as much.’”*
>
> — *Luke 19:8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse records Zacchaeus’s response after Jesus invited Himself to his home. Zacchaeus was a chief tax collector in Jericho, a wealthy man who had gained much of his wealth by overcharging people. His neighbors despised him. When Jesus came to town, Zacchaeus climbed a tree to see Him. To everyone’s surprise, Jesus stopped, called him by name, and said He must stay at his house. Zacchaeus welcomed Him joyfully, while the crowd grumbled that Jesus was going to be the guest of a sinner.

Then “*Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord*” (*v. 8*). Standing suggests a formal, public declaration. He addressed Jesus as “Lord,” showing respect and submission.

“*Behold, Lord, half of my goods I give to the poor*” (*v. 8*). This was extraordinary generosity. Jewish teachers of that time often recommended giving no more than a fifth of one’s possessions to charity to avoid becoming poor oneself. Zacchaeus gave half.

“*If I have wrongfully exacted anything of anyone, I restore four times as much*” (*v. 8*). “If” here does not suggest doubt; Zacchaeus knew he had cheated people. The phrase means “whomever I have defrauded.” The law of Moses required someone who had stolen and confessed to repay the amount plus one-fifth (*Leviticus 6:1–5*; *Numbers 5:6–7*). Fourfold restitution was required only in certain cases of theft, such as stealing a sheep (*Exodus 22:1*). Zacchaeus went far beyond what the law required.

Notice that Jesus did not demand any of this. Zacchaeus responded freely to Jesus’ grace. Jesus’ acceptance came first; Zacchaeus’s transformation followed. The man who had been known for taking now became known for giving.

Jesus declared, “*Today, salvation has come to this house*” (*v. 9*). Zacchaeus’s generosity did not earn salvation; it was the evidence that salvation had arrived.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows what genuine repentance looks like. It is not merely feeling sorry or saying the right words. It involves concrete changes: generosity to the poor and restitution to those one has wronged. John the Baptist had told tax collectors to collect no more than required (*Luke 3:12–13*); Zacchaeus went much further.

It also shows the transforming power of grace. Zacchaeus was not changed by condemnation or lectures. He was changed by Jesus’ acceptance. Jesus called him by name and chose to stay in his home, despite the crowd’s disapproval. This undeserved welcome melted Zacchaeus’s heart. Paul writes that God’s kindness leads people to repentance (*Romans 2:4*).

Finally, the verse shows that salvation affects how people handle money. Many of Jesus’ teachings in Luke deal with wealth. The rich fool hoarded; the rich man ignored Lazarus; the rich ruler could not let go. Zacchaeus, transformed by Jesus, used his wealth to bless others and make things right.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to let their faith change how they use money. Generosity to the poor and fairness in financial dealings are signs of a heart transformed by Christ. Believers can ask how their encounter with Jesus should shape their giving and spending.

It also calls believers to make restitution where possible. If they have wronged others, whether by cheating, stealing, lying, or harming them, repentance may include making things right: apologizing, repaying, or repairing damage. This shows that repentance is real.

Finally, this verse shows believers how to help others change. Zacchaeus was transformed not by judgment but by grace. Believers can show acceptance and love to people whom others despise, trusting that God’s grace can change hearts.

### *Luke 19:10* — To Seek and Save the Lost

> *“For the Son of Man came to seek and to save that which was lost.”*
>
> — *Luke 19:10* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse is Jesus’ explanation of why He went to the house of Zacchaeus. The crowd had grumbled that Jesus was staying with a sinner. Zacchaeus had responded to Jesus’ grace by giving half his possessions to the poor and promising to repay fourfold anyone he had cheated. Jesus declared that salvation had come to his house because he was a son of Abraham.

Then Jesus explained His mission: “*For the Son of Man came to seek and to save that which was lost*” (*v. 10*).

“*the Son of Man*” (*v. 10*) is Jesus’ favorite title for Himself, drawn from *Daniel 7:13–14*, where one like a son of man receives an everlasting kingdom. The glorious Son of Man came on a mission of rescue.

“*came*” (*v. 10*). This word implies that Jesus came from somewhere, sent with a purpose. His coming was intentional.

“*to seek*” (*v. 10*). Jesus actively searches for lost people. He did not wait for Zacchaeus to come to Him; He stopped, looked up, called him by name, and invited Himself to his home. This echoes the parables of *Luke 15*, where the shepherd searches for the lost sheep and the woman searches for the lost coin.

“*and to save*” (*v. 10*). Jesus not only finds the lost; He rescues them. Salvation includes forgiveness, restoration to God, and transformation, as seen in Zacchaeus’s life.

“*that which was lost*” (*v. 10*). “Lost” describes people who are separated from God, wandering, and unable to find their way back on their own. In *Ezekiel 34*, God criticized Israel’s leaders for not seeking the lost sheep and promised, “*I will seek that which was lost*” (*Ezekiel 34:16*). Jesus fulfills this promise.

This verse summarizes the whole of Luke’s Gospel. From the beginning, Jesus came for the poor, the outcast, sinners, and the lost. He welcomed tax collectors, touched lepers, defended a sinful woman, and told stories of a seeking shepherd and a waiting father.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals the heart of Jesus’ mission. He did not come primarily to condemn, to establish a political kingdom, or to reward the righteous. He came to seek and save the lost. This is the good news: God takes the initiative to rescue people who cannot rescue themselves.

It also reveals that everyone is in some sense lost apart from Christ. Zacchaeus was obviously lost, but the respectable rich ruler was also lost, unable to let go of his wealth. The grumbling crowd, who looked down on Zacchaeus, needed to see that they too needed a Savior.

Finally, the verse defines the mission of Jesus’ followers. If Jesus came to seek and save the lost, His people are called to join Him in that mission, reaching out to those far from God with the same love and initiative He showed.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse offers hope to anyone who feels lost. Jesus is seeking them. They do not need to find their own way back to God; Jesus comes looking for them, calls them by name, and invites them into relationship.

It also challenges believers to share Jesus’ mission. They can look for the “Zacchaeuses” in their communities, people who are despised, overlooked, or far from God, and reach out to them with kindness and the good news. This may mean going where respectable people would not go, as Jesus did.

Finally, this verse warns against the attitude of the grumbling crowd. Believers can resist the temptation to judge those Jesus seeks, and instead rejoice when the lost are found.

### *Luke 19:41–42* — Jesus Weeps Over Jerusalem

> *“When he came near, he saw the city and wept over it, saying, If you, even you, had known today the things which belong to your peace! But now, they are hidden from your eyes.”*
>
> — *Luke 19:41–42* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This scene, found only in Luke, takes place during Jesus’ entry into Jerusalem. Jesus was riding a colt down the Mount of Olives, and a crowd of disciples was joyfully praising God, shouting, “Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord!” It was a moment of celebration.

Then “*When he came near, he saw the city and wept over it*” (*v. 41*). From the Mount of Olives, the whole city of Jerusalem spreads out below, with the temple prominent in view. In the middle of the celebration, Jesus wept. The word used means loud, audible weeping, not just quiet tears. It is a different and stronger word than the one used when Jesus wept at Lazarus’s tomb (*John 11:35*).

Jesus said, “*If you, even you, had known today the things which belong to your peace!*” (*v. 42*) The name “Jerusalem” is often understood to mean “city of peace.” Yet the city did not recognize the way to true peace, which was standing before it in Jesus. The crowds had just shouted “peace in heaven,” but Jerusalem as a whole, especially its leaders, would reject the King who brought peace with God.

“*But now, they are hidden from your eyes*” (*v. 42*). Because they had refused to recognize Jesus, the truth was now hidden from them. Repeated rejection had led to spiritual blindness.

In the following verses, Jesus predicted the city’s destruction: enemies would build embankments, surround the city, crush its people, and leave not one stone on another, “*because you didn’t know the time of your visitation*” (*v. 44*). “Visitation” refers to God coming to His people, which happened in Jesus. Zechariah had sung that God had visited His people (*Luke 1:68*). But Jerusalem did not recognize the visit. This prophecy was fulfilled in A.D. 70, when Roman armies besieged and destroyed Jerusalem.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals the heart of Jesus toward those who reject Him. He was about to be betrayed, condemned, and crucified in this city. Yet He did not respond with anger or satisfaction at their coming judgment. He wept. God’s judgment is real, but He takes no pleasure in it. Through Ezekiel, God said, “*I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked*” (*Ezekiel 33:11*).

It also shows the seriousness of missing God’s visitation. Jerusalem had the Scriptures, the temple, and the prophets, and then the Messiah Himself came. But they did not recognize Him. Privilege brings responsibility, and rejecting God’s gracious visit has consequences.

Finally, Jesus’ tears show that He fully shared human emotion. He was not a detached figure. He felt deep grief over the city He loved, the city that would kill Him. His love for people continued even as they rejected Him.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses invite believers to recognize the times when God visits them. God works in people’s lives through His Word, His Spirit, circumstances, and other people. Believers can be attentive to God’s work and respond rather than letting opportunities pass.

They also call believers to share Jesus’ heart for people who reject Him. It is easy to become angry or dismissive toward those who oppose the gospel. Jesus wept over them. Believers can pray with compassion for their communities, cities, and nations, grieving over sin and longing for people to find peace with God.

Finally, these verses remind believers that peace comes through Jesus. Many people seek peace through politics, wealth, achievement, or distraction. True peace, with God and within, is found in recognizing and receiving Jesus. Believers can point others to Him as the source of the peace they seek.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Luke 19* brings together the seeking love of Jesus and the seriousness of how people respond to Him. Zacchaeus shows that no one is too lost or too despised for Jesus to seek. Jesus called him by name, entered his home, and transformed his life. Believers can take comfort that Jesus seeks them, and they can join His mission of seeking the lost, reaching out to people others avoid.

Zacchaeus’s response also shows what real repentance looks like: generosity to the poor and restitution to those one has wronged. Believers can allow their encounter with Jesus to change how they handle money and how they make things right with others.

The parable of the minas reminds believers that they live in a time of waiting between Jesus’ ascension and His return. During this time, they are called to faithfully use what He has entrusted to them. They will give an account when the King returns. Faithfulness in small things leads to greater responsibility in His kingdom.

The triumphal entry shows that Jesus is the King who comes in the name of the Lord, deserving praise even if the stones must cry out. And His tears over Jerusalem show His grief over those who reject Him and miss the time of God’s visitation. Believers can welcome Jesus as King, recognize God’s work in their lives, and share His compassion for people who do not yet know the way of peace.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for seeking me as You sought Zacchaeus, calling me by name and coming into my life. Thank You that You came to seek and to save the lost. Let Your grace change my heart as it changed his, so that I give generously and make things right with those I have wronged.

Help me to be faithful with everything You have entrusted to me while I wait for Your return. I welcome You as the King who comes in the name of the Lord. Give me Your heart for those who do not yet know You, a heart that weeps over their lostness rather than condemning them. Help me to recognize when You are working in my life, and keep me from missing the time of Your visitation. Lead me and many others into the things that make for peace. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
