Luke · Chapter 20 of 24

# Luke — Chapter 20

Chapter Theme: The Beloved Son, the Rejected Stone, and the Children of the Resurrection

[Read Luke 20 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/LUK20.htm)

Main Teaching

Teaching daily in the temple, Jesus is challenged about His authority and answers with a parable in which a vineyard owner sends his beloved son to tenants who kill him. He declares that the stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. He silences traps about taxes and the resurrection, teaching that those raised from the dead become children of the resurrection, alive to God. He then points to the Messiah as David’s Lord and warns against religious leaders who exploit the vulnerable.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Luke 20* takes place in the temple courts during Jesus’ final days in Jerusalem. At the end of chapter 19, Jesus had wept over the city, cleansed the temple, and begun teaching there every day, while the chief priests, scribes, and leaders sought to destroy Him but could not, because “*all the people hung on to every word that he said*” (*Luke 19:48*). In chapter 20, the leaders try a different approach: public challenges designed to discredit Jesus or give them grounds to hand Him over to the Roman governor.

Each of the events in this chapter also appears in Matthew and Mark, where they are studied in depth: the question of authority (*Matthew 21:23–27*), the parable of the tenants (*Matthew 21:33–46*; *Mark 12:10*), taxes to Caesar (*Matthew 22:21*), the resurrection question (*Matthew 22:32*), David’s Lord (*Matthew 22:41–46*), and the warning about scribes (*Mark 12:38–40*). This chapter focuses on the details Luke emphasizes.

### The Question of Authority (*20:1–8*)

Luke notes that Jesus was “*teaching the people in the temple and preaching the Good News*” (*v. 1*). Even in the midst of mounting danger, Jesus continued His mission of proclaiming the good news.

The chief priests and scribes, together with the elders, the three groups that made up the Sanhedrin, the ruling council, came and asked, “*by what authority do you do these things? Or who is giving you this authority?*” (*v. 2*) “These things” probably included His cleansing of the temple and His teaching. They held official authority over the temple, and Jesus had acted without their permission.

Jesus answered with a question about John’s baptism: was it from heaven or from men? The leaders realized they were trapped. If they said “from heaven,” Jesus would ask why they had not believed John. If they said “from men,” Luke adds, “*all the people will stone us, for they are persuaded that John was a prophet*” (*v. 6*). So they said they did not know. Jesus replied that He would not tell them by what authority He acted. Their refusal to answer honestly showed that they were not genuinely seeking the truth.

### The Parable of the Tenants (*20:9–19*)

Jesus then told the people a parable. A man planted a vineyard, leased it to tenant farmers, and went away for a long time. At harvest, he sent a servant to collect his share of the fruit, but the tenants beat him and sent him away empty-handed. He sent a second servant, whom they beat and treated shamefully, and a third, whom they wounded and threw out. These servants represent the prophets God sent to Israel, many of whom were mistreated and rejected.

Then the owner said, “*What shall I do? I will send my beloved son. It may be that seeing him, they will respect him*” (*v. 13*). This verse is studied below. But the tenants reasoned, “*This is the heir. Come, let’s kill him, that the inheritance may be ours*” (*v. 14*). They threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. Jesus asked what the owner would do: he would come, destroy those tenants, and give the vineyard to others.

When the people heard this, they said, “*May that never be!*” (*v. 16*) Luke alone records this horrified response. They understood the seriousness of what Jesus was describing. Then Jesus looked directly at them and quoted *Psalm 118:22*, studied below.

The chief priests and scribes wanted to arrest Him at that very hour, because they knew the parable was about them. But they feared the people.

### Taxes to Caesar (*20:20–26*)

The leaders watched Jesus closely and sent spies who “*pretended to be righteous*” (*v. 20*), hoping to trap Him in His words so that they could hand Him over to the governor, Pilate. Luke makes their purpose explicit: they wanted a political charge that Rome would take seriously.

The spies flattered Jesus and asked whether it was lawful to pay taxes to Caesar. Jesus saw through their trickery. He asked to see a denarius and asked whose image and inscription were on it. They said, “Caesar’s.” He said, “*Then give to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s*” (*v. 25*). They could not trap Him, and they were amazed and fell silent. Ironically, at His trial before Pilate, the leaders would falsely accuse Jesus of “*forbidding paying taxes to Caesar*” (*Luke 23:2*), the very thing He had refused to do.

### The Question About Resurrection (*20:27–40*)

Some Sadducees, who denied the resurrection, came with a scenario about a woman who married seven brothers in turn and asked whose wife she would be in the resurrection. Luke’s version of Jesus’ answer includes details not found in Matthew or Mark, studied below. Jesus then pointed to the burning bush, where God called Himself “the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob,” and concluded, “*Now he is not the God of the dead, but of the living, for all are alive to him*” (*v. 38*). Luke alone adds “for all are alive to him.”

Some of the scribes, who as Pharisees believed in the resurrection, said, “*Teacher, you speak well*” (*v. 39*). After that, no one dared to ask Him any more questions.

### David’s Son and David’s Lord (*20:41–44*)

Jesus then asked how people could say that the Messiah is David’s son, when David himself calls Him “Lord” in *Psalm 110:1*: “*The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand,*” (*v. 42*) “*until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet.”*” (*v. 43*) If David calls the Messiah “Lord,” how can He merely be David’s son? Jesus was pointing to His own identity as greater than David, the Son of God who would be exalted to God’s right hand. Peter later quoted this same psalm at Pentecost to explain Jesus’ resurrection and ascension (*Acts 2:34–36*).

### Beware of the Scribes (*20:45–47*)

In the hearing of all the people, Jesus warned His disciples about scribes who liked to walk around in long robes, loved respectful greetings in the marketplaces, the best seats in the synagogues, and places of honor at banquets. They “*devour widows’ houses, and for a pretense make long prayers*” (*v. 47*). They would receive greater condemnation. This warning leads directly into the next scene in *Luke 21*, where Jesus notices a poor widow giving her last coins.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Luke 20:13* — “*I Will Send My Beloved Son*” (*v. 13*)

> *“The lord of the vineyard said, “What shall I do? I will send my beloved son. It may be that seeing him, they will respect him.””*
>
> — *Luke 20:13* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse is the turning point of the parable of the tenants, which Jesus told in the temple courts shortly after the religious leaders challenged His authority. In the parable, a man planted a vineyard and rented it to tenant farmers before going away for a long time. When harvest came, he sent servants to collect his share of the fruit. One after another, the tenants beat the servants, treated them shamefully, wounded them, and sent them away with nothing.

Then “*The lord of the vineyard said, ‘What shall I do?’*” (*v. 13*). The owner paused to consider. This question expresses the patience and the pain of the owner, who had been rejected again and again.

“*I will send my beloved son*” (*v. 13*). The owner decided to send the one closest to his heart. The phrase “beloved son” is the same phrase the Father used at Jesus’ baptism (*Luke 3:22*) and transfiguration (*Luke 9:35*). Jesus’ listeners who knew those events, and Luke’s readers, would recognize that Jesus was speaking about Himself.

“*It may be that seeing him, they will respect him*” (*v. 13*). Luke alone includes the word “It may be” (or “perhaps”). The owner hoped the tenants would respect his son even though they had rejected the servants. This expresses God’s patient hope that His people would receive His Son.

But the tenants saw the son as an opportunity. They said, “This is the heir. Come, let’s kill him, that the inheritance may be ours.” They threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. Jesus was predicting His own death at the hands of the religious leaders, outside the city walls of Jerusalem.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals the depth of God’s patience and love. Throughout Israel’s history, God sent prophet after prophet, and many were rejected. Yet God did not give up. He sent His own Son. *Hebrews 1:1–2* describes this: God spoke through the prophets in many ways, but in these last days He has spoken through His Son.

It also shows that sending the Son was God’s greatest act of love. The owner sent the one dearest to him. *John 3:16* says that God so loved the world that He gave His only Son. The sending of the beloved Son was costly; it led to his death.

Finally, the verse shows the tragedy of rejecting God’s Son. The tenants saw the son as an obstacle to their own control and possession. Many people today reject Jesus for similar reasons: they want to keep control of their lives, rather than submit to God as the rightful owner.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to receive God’s Son with honor and gratitude. God sent His beloved Son to us. The right response is to respect Him, listen to Him, and give Him the fruit of our lives.

It also reminds believers that everything belongs to God. The tenants acted as though the vineyard was theirs. Believers are stewards, not owners, of their lives, gifts, and resources. They can give God the “fruit” He deserves: worship, obedience, and lives that honor Him.

Finally, this verse invites believers to marvel at God’s patience. Despite repeated rejection, God kept reaching out. He continues to show patience today, giving people time to turn to Him. Believers can respond to that patience with repentance and gratitude, and they can share God’s patient love with others.

### *Luke 20:17–18* — The Rejected Stone

> *“But he looked at them and said, ‘Then what is this that is written, “The stone which the builders rejected was made the chief cornerstone”? Everyone who falls on that stone will be broken to pieces, but it will crush whomever it falls on to dust.’”*
>
> — *Luke 20:17–18* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These verses come immediately after the parable of the tenants. Jesus had described tenant farmers who killed the owner’s beloved son, and He said the owner would destroy them and give the vineyard to others. The people listening were horrified and said, “May that never be!”

Then “*But he looked at them*” (*v. 17*). Luke emphasizes Jesus’ direct, searching gaze, which gave His next words great weight.

“*Then what is this that is written, ‘The stone which the builders rejected was made the chief cornerstone’?*” (*v. 17*) Jesus quoted *Psalm 118:22*. The same psalm had been sung by the crowds at His entry into Jerusalem a few days earlier (“Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord,” *Psalm 118:26*). In the psalm, the builders rejected a stone as unsuitable, but God made it the most important stone in the building. The cornerstone held the walls together and set the alignment for the entire structure.

Jesus was applying this to Himself. The “builders,” Israel’s religious leaders, were rejecting Him. But God would make Him the cornerstone of His new work. The parable ended with the son’s death; the psalm pointed beyond death to vindication. Jesus’ rejection and death would lead to His exaltation.

Then Jesus added a warning in verse 18, using imagery that may draw on *Isaiah 8:14–15* and *Daniel 2:34–35*: “*Everyone who falls on that stone will be broken to pieces, but it will crush whomever it falls on to dust*” (*v. 18*). Those who stumble over Jesus, rejecting Him, will be broken. And when the stone falls in judgment, it will crush those who oppose it. In Daniel, a stone cut without hands strikes and destroys earthly kingdoms and becomes a great mountain, representing God’s everlasting kingdom.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses reveal that God turns human rejection into His triumph. The leaders thought they could get rid of Jesus by killing Him. Instead, His death and resurrection made Him the cornerstone of God’s people. Peter later proclaimed this very verse to the Sanhedrin (*Acts 4:10–12*) and in his letter (*1 Peter 2:4–8*).

They also show that no one can remain neutral toward Jesus. He is either the cornerstone on which people build their lives or the stone over which they stumble. Rejecting Him has serious consequences.

Finally, these verses connect with the hope of God’s kingdom. Like the stone in Daniel’s vision, Jesus’ kingdom will ultimately prevail over every earthly power.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses call believers to build their lives on Jesus as the cornerstone. Their values, decisions, and relationships should be aligned with Him. A life built on any other foundation will not stand.

They also warn those who are rejecting Jesus. Stumbling over Him leads to brokenness. The invitation remains to turn to Him while there is time.

Finally, these verses encourage believers who feel rejected for their faith. Jesus was rejected by the powerful, but God exalted Him. Believers can trust that God sees and will vindicate those who belong to Him.

### *Luke 20:35–36* — Children of the Resurrection

> *“But those who are considered worthy to attain to that age and the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage. For they can’t die any more, for they are like the angels and are children of God, being children of the resurrection.”*
>
> — *Luke 20:35–36* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These verses are part of Jesus’ answer to the Sadducees, a group of religious leaders who denied the resurrection of the dead. They had presented a scenario about a woman who married seven brothers in succession according to the law of levirate marriage (*Deuteronomy 25:5–6*), asking whose wife she would be in the resurrection. They intended to show that belief in resurrection was absurd.

Jesus first said, “*The children of this age marry and are given in marriage*” (*v. 34*). Marriage belongs to life in the present age. Then He described the age to come: “*But those who are considered worthy to attain to that age and the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage*” (*v. 35*).

“Considered worthy” does not mean that people earn the resurrection by their merit. It describes those whom God counts as belonging to the age to come, those who are His. “That age” refers to the coming age of God’s kingdom, after the resurrection.

“*For they can’t die any more*” (*v. 36*). Luke alone includes this explanation. In this present age, marriage and children are needed partly because people die; new generations carry on life. In the age to come, death will be no more, so marriage in its earthly form will no longer serve the same purpose.

“*for they are like the angels*” (*v. 36*). Jesus does not say people become angels; He says they will be like angels in that they will not die and will not marry.

“*and are children of God, being children of the resurrection*” (*v. 36*). Those raised to eternal life will be fully revealed as God’s children. Their identity will be defined by resurrection life.

Jesus’ answer shows that the Sadducees’ scenario was based on a misunderstanding. They assumed that resurrection life would simply continue earthly arrangements. But God’s power will transform life in the age to come.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses affirm the reality of the resurrection. Jesus taught clearly that the dead will be raised and that those who belong to God will live forever. His own resurrection a few days later would confirm this teaching. Paul writes that believers will be raised with transformed, imperishable bodies (*1 Corinthians 15:42–44*).

They also show that resurrection life is not merely a continuation of earthly life but a transformation. Relationships, including marriage, will be transformed. This does not mean that the love between spouses will be lost; it means that all relationships will be fulfilled in the greater reality of being God’s children together in His presence.

Finally, the phrase “children of the resurrection” describes believers’ ultimate identity. They are God’s children, destined for resurrection life. This identity gives hope that death is not the end and that God’s family will be gathered forever.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses offer hope to believers facing death or grieving loved ones. Death is not final for those who belong to God. They will be raised, will never die again, and will live as God’s children forever.

They also help believers hold earthly relationships in proper perspective. Marriage and family are precious gifts in this age, but they are not ultimate. Single believers, widows, widowers, and those whose marriages have been painful can find comfort in knowing that their deepest identity is as children of God and children of the resurrection.

Finally, these verses encourage believers to live now in light of the age to come. Knowing that they are destined for resurrection life can shape how they spend their time, treat others, and face suffering, with hope and confidence in God’s power.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Luke 20* shows Jesus facing mounting opposition with wisdom, courage, and truth. The religious leaders refused to answer honestly about John’s baptism, revealing that they were not seeking truth. Believers can examine whether they are open to truth even when it is uncomfortable or costly.

The parable of the tenants reveals God’s patience and love, sending prophet after prophet and finally His beloved Son. It also shows the tragedy of rejecting Him to keep control of what belongs to God. Believers can receive Jesus with honor, give God the fruit of their lives, and build on Him as the cornerstone.

The question about taxes teaches that believers can fulfill their responsibilities in society while giving their whole selves to God, in whose image they are made. The answer to the Sadducees gives believers confident hope in the resurrection: those who belong to God are alive to Him and will be raised as children of the resurrection, never to die again.

Finally, Jesus’ question about David’s Lord points to His divine identity, and His warning about the scribes calls believers to humility and to the protection of the vulnerable. Religious leaders who seek honor while exploiting widows face greater judgment. Believers, especially those in leadership, can serve humbly, protect those who are weak, and pray sincerely rather than for show.

## Chapter Prayer

Father, thank You for Your patience in sending prophet after prophet, and finally Your beloved Son. Forgive me for the times I have acted as though my life were my own. I receive Jesus with honor, and I want to give You the fruit You deserve. Help me to build my life on Jesus, the cornerstone, and never to stumble over Him.

Help me to fulfill my responsibilities in the world while giving my whole self to You. Thank You for the hope of the resurrection, and that all who belong to You are alive to You. Comfort me and all who grieve with the promise that Your children will never die again. Keep me humble, honest, and caring toward the vulnerable, and free me from seeking honor for myself. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Luke · Chapter 21 of 24

# Luke — Chapter 21

Chapter Theme: Endure, Look Up, and Stay Alert

[Read Luke 21 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/LUK21.htm)

Main Teaching

After praising a poor widow’s gift, Jesus predicts the destruction of the temple and prepares His followers for deception, wars, persecution, and the fall of Jerusalem. He promises them wisdom when they are put on trial and assures them that by endurance they will gain their lives. When the signs of the end appear, they are to lift up their heads because redemption is near, and meanwhile they must guard their hearts and pray, staying ready to stand before the Son of Man.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Luke 21* concludes Jesus’ public teaching in the temple during His final week in Jerusalem. It parallels *Matthew 24* and *Mark 13*, the “Olivet Discourse,” which are studied in depth in those commentaries (*Matthew 24:4*, *24:36*, *24:45–46*; *Mark 13:11*, *13:31*, *13:37*). Luke’s version has several distinctive emphases: it clearly separates the destruction of Jerusalem from the final coming of the Son of Man, it gives specific words of encouragement for believers facing persecution, and it ends with a warning against being weighed down by the cares of life.

As with the parallel chapters, Christians interpret the details of this prophecy in different ways. Luke’s wording makes it especially clear that part of Jesus’ prophecy concerned the Roman siege and destruction of Jerusalem in A.D. 70, while other parts look forward to His return at the end of the age.

### The Widow’s Offering (*21:1–4*)

The chapter opens in the temple, where Jesus watched rich people putting gifts into the treasury. He saw a poor widow put in two small copper coins. He said she had put in more than all the others, because they gave out of their abundance, but she, out of her poverty, put in “*all that she had to live on*” (*v. 4*). This scene follows directly after Jesus’ warning about scribes who “*devour widows’ houses*” (*Luke 20:47*). (The widow’s gift is studied at *Mark 12:43–44*.) Her total devotion stands in contrast to the temple’s outward splendor, which is described next.

### The Temple Will Be Destroyed (*21:5–7*)

Some people were admiring the temple, “*how it was decorated with beautiful stones and gifts*” (*v. 5*). Herod the Great’s rebuilt temple was magnificent, with gleaming white stone and gold. Wealthy donors had given gifts to adorn it, such as a golden vine with grape clusters described by the historian Josephus. Jesus said, “*the days will come in which there will not be left here one stone on another that will not be thrown down*” (*v. 6*). They asked when this would happen and what sign would show it was about to take place.

### Do Not Be Deceived or Terrified (*21:8–11*)

Jesus warned, “*Watch out that you don’t get led astray*” (*v. 8*). Many would come in His name, claiming, “I am he,” and, “*The time is at hand*” (*v. 8*). Luke alone includes this second claim. False teachers would proclaim that the end was imminent. Jesus said, “*Therefore don’t follow them*” (*v. 8*). When they heard of wars and uprisings, they should not be terrified, because these things must happen first, “*but the end won’t come immediately*” (*v. 9*). Nations would fight, and there would be earthquakes, famines, plagues, and frightening signs in the sky.

### Persecution and Promised Help (*21:12–19*)

“*But before all these things*” (*v. 12*), Jesus said, His followers would be arrested and persecuted, handed over to synagogues and prisons, and brought before kings and governors because of His name. The book of Acts, Luke’s second volume, records this happening: Peter and John before the Sanhedrin (*Acts 4*), Paul before governors Felix and Festus and King Agrippa (*Acts 24–26*).

“*It will turn out as a testimony for you*” (*v. 13*). Their trials would become opportunities to bear witness to Jesus. They should resolve not to prepare their defense in advance, “*for I will give you a mouth and wisdom which all your adversaries will not be able to withstand or to contradict*” (*v. 15*). In *Mark 13:11*, this promise is connected to the Holy Spirit; here Jesus says He Himself will give them words and wisdom. In *Acts 6:10*, Stephen’s opponents “*weren’t able to withstand the wisdom and the Spirit by which he spoke*” (*Acts 6:10*).

Jesus warned that they would be betrayed even by parents, brothers, relatives, and friends, and some would be put to death. They would be hated by everyone because of His name. Then He gave a promise and a call to endurance, studied below.

### The Fall of Jerusalem (*21:20–24*)

Luke’s version is especially specific about Jerusalem: “*But when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, then know that its desolation is at hand*” (*v. 20*). Where Matthew and Mark speak of “the abomination of desolation,” Luke describes the siege directly. When they saw this, people in Judea should flee to the mountains, those in the city should get out, and those in the countryside should not enter the city.

“*For these are days of vengeance, that all things which are written may be fulfilled*” (*v. 22*). The destruction would be God’s judgment, fulfilling prophetic warnings about the consequences of rejecting Him. Jesus expressed compassion for pregnant women and nursing mothers. There would be great distress and wrath on the people. They would fall by the sword and be taken as captives to all nations, and “*Jerusalem will be trampled down by the Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled*” (*v. 24*).

This prophecy was fulfilled in A.D. 70, when Roman armies under Titus surrounded Jerusalem, besieged it, and destroyed the city and temple. Josephus records that over a million people died and nearly a hundred thousand were taken captive. Early church writers report that Christians in Jerusalem heeded Jesus’ warning and fled before the final siege.

The phrase “until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled” indicates a period during which Gentiles would dominate Jerusalem, but it also suggests that this period has a limit set by God. Christians have understood it in different ways. Some connect it with the period of the gospel going to the Gentiles (*Romans 11:25*), others with Gentile political control of Jerusalem until the end of the age.

### The Coming of the Son of Man (*21:25–28*)

Jesus then spoke of signs in the sun, moon, and stars, and on earth, nations in anguish and perplexity at the roaring of the sea and waves. People would faint from fear and foreboding of what was coming on the world, for the powers of the heavens would be shaken. “*Then they will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and great glory*” (*v. 27*), language from *Daniel 7:13–14*. Then came a word of encouragement for believers, studied below.

### The Fig Tree and Jesus’ Words (*21:29–33*)

Jesus told them to look at the fig tree and all the trees. When they sprout leaves, people know summer is near. In the same way, when they saw these things happening, they would know that “*God’s Kingdom is near*” (*v. 31*). He said this generation would not pass away until all things had happened (see the discussion at *Matthew 24:34*), and declared, “*Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will by no means pass away*” (*v. 33*). (This verse is studied at *Mark 13:31*.)

### Watch and Pray (*21:34–38*)

Jesus ended with a warning unique to Luke, studied below: “*So be careful, or your hearts will be loaded down with carousing, drunkenness, and cares of this life, and that day will come on you suddenly*” (*v. 34*). That day would come on everyone on earth like a trap. Therefore they should always be watchful, praying for strength to escape what was coming and “*to stand before the Son of Man*” (*v. 36*).

Luke concludes the section with a summary: every day Jesus taught in the temple, and every night He went out and spent the night on the Mount of Olives. All the people came early in the morning to hear Him in the temple. These peaceful days would soon end as the events of His betrayal and death began in chapter 22.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Luke 21:18–19* — Not a Hair Will Perish; Endurance Wins Life

> *“And not a hair of your head will perish. By your endurance you will win your lives.”*
>
> — *Luke 21:18–19* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These verses come at the end of Jesus’ warnings about persecution. He had told His disciples that they would be arrested, imprisoned, and brought before kings and governors because of Him. They would be betrayed by parents, brothers, relatives, and friends. “*They will cause some of you to be put to death*” (*v. 16*). They would be hated by everyone because of His name.

Then Jesus said, “*And not a hair of your head will perish*” (*v. 18*). This seems puzzling, since He had just said that some of them would be killed. How can both be true?

The answer is that Jesus was speaking of ultimate safety, not physical safety in every case. Some of His followers would die, but nothing could destroy them in the deepest sense. Their lives were secure in God’s hands. Earlier, Jesus had said, “*don’t be afraid of those who kill the body, and after that have no more that they can do*” (*Luke 12:4*), and that even the hairs of their heads are counted (*Luke 12:7*). God’s care for them would extend beyond death to the resurrection. Not even the smallest part of who they are would be lost to God.

“*By your endurance you will win your lives*” (*v. 19*). “Endurance” means patient perseverance, steadfastness under pressure, continuing to trust and follow Jesus through suffering. “Win your lives” (or “gain your souls”) means that by remaining faithful, they would secure true and eternal life. Elsewhere Jesus says, “*he who endures to the end will be saved*” (*Mark 13:13*).

This promise does not mean that people earn salvation by enduring. It means that genuine faith perseveres, and that those who belong to Christ will be kept through trials. Endurance is the way faith shows itself in hard times.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses reveal that believers’ security rests in God, not in circumstances. Persecution, betrayal, and even death cannot ultimately harm those who belong to Christ. Paul expresses the same confidence: nothing, not tribulation, persecution, danger, or death, can separate believers from the love of God in Christ Jesus (*Romans 8:35–39*).

They also show that endurance is essential to the Christian life. Faith is not only a one-time decision but a lifelong journey of trust. In the parable of the sower, the good soil represents those who “*produce fruit with perseverance*” (*Luke 8:15*). The early church faced intense persecution, and these words gave them courage to remain faithful.

Finally, the verses hold together honesty and hope. Jesus did not promise His followers an easy life or physical protection from every harm. He told them plainly that some would die. But He also promised that nothing could take away their true life.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers who face opposition, persecution, or suffering for their faith. In many parts of the world, Christians are imprisoned, rejected by family, or killed. Others face lesser but real hostility. Jesus’ words assure them that their ultimate safety is secure in God’s care.

They also call believers to endurance. When faith is tested by suffering, disappointment, or long waiting, believers can keep trusting and following Jesus. Perseverance is not about grim willpower but about holding onto Christ, who holds onto them.

Finally, these verses help believers face fear. Fear of loss, pain, or death can paralyze. Remembering that not a hair of their head will perish in God’s ultimate care can give believers courage to live faithfully.

### *Luke 21:28* — Look Up, Your Redemption Is Near

> *“But when these things begin to happen, look up and lift up your heads, because your redemption is near.”*
>
> — *Luke 21:28* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse comes after Jesus described frightening events that would precede His return. He spoke of signs in the sun, moon, and stars; nations in anguish and confusion at the roaring of the sea; and people fainting from fear and foreboding of what was coming on the world. The powers of the heavens would be shaken. Then the Son of Man would come in a cloud with power and great glory.

While the world would respond to these events with terror, Jesus told His followers to respond differently: “*But when these things begin to happen, look up and lift up your heads, because your redemption is near*” (*v. 28*).

“*look up and lift up your heads*” (*v. 28*). People who are afraid or ashamed often bow their heads and look down. Jesus told His followers to look up with confidence and hope. Lifting the head was a sign of joy and expectation.

“*because your redemption is near*” (*v. 28*). “Redemption” means release or deliverance, the act of being set free, like a slave being freed or a captive being ransomed. For believers, the return of the Son of Man means final deliverance from sin, suffering, death, and every evil. What terrifies the world brings hope to God’s people.

This verse shows a striking contrast. The same events produce fear in some and hope in others. The difference is relationship with the coming King. For those who belong to Him, His coming is the moment they have longed for.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals that the Christian hope is not escape from the world’s troubles but redemption through them. Believers do not need to fear the end of the age, because it brings the completion of their salvation. Paul writes that believers are “*waiting for adoption, the redemption of our body*” (*Romans 8:23*). Jesus’ return will bring that final redemption.

It also shows that believers can face frightening times with a different perspective. When the world seems to be shaking, believers can look beyond the chaos to the coming King. Their hope is not in the stability of the world but in the faithfulness of God.

Finally, the verse encourages believers to live with expectation. Like people waiting for a long-awaited guest, they can keep their eyes on the horizon, ready to welcome Christ.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse offers hope to believers in troubled times. Wars, disasters, pandemics, and social upheaval can produce fear and anxiety. Believers can acknowledge the reality of these troubles while lifting their heads in hope, knowing that God is working out His purposes and that their redemption is near.

It also invites believers to examine their response to world events. Do they react with the same fear and despair as the world, or with confident hope in Christ? Regular reflection on Christ’s promised return can shape their outlook.

Finally, this verse encourages believers to share their hope with others. When people around them are fainting with fear, believers can point them to the One who brings redemption.

### *Luke 21:34* — Guard Your Hearts

> *“So be careful, or your hearts will be loaded down with carousing, drunkenness, and cares of this life, and that day will come on you suddenly.”*
>
> — *Luke 21:34* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse begins the final warning of Jesus’ teaching about the end times, found only in Luke. Jesus had described the destruction of Jerusalem, cosmic signs, and the coming of the Son of Man. He had told His followers to lift up their heads because their redemption was near. Now He turned to how they should live while they wait.

“*So be careful*” (*v. 34*). Jesus called His followers to watchfulness over their own lives.

“*or your hearts will be loaded down*” (*v. 34*). The word means weighed down, burdened, or dulled. Jesus warned that their hearts could become so heavy that they would lose spiritual alertness.

Jesus named three things that could weigh down the heart. “*carousing*” (*v. 34*) refers to excessive partying and indulgence, and the dullness that follows it. “*drunkenness*” (*v. 34*) is self-explanatory. “*and cares of this life*” (*v. 34*) refers to anxieties about daily needs, worries about money, health, and the future. Notice that Jesus put ordinary worries alongside drunkenness. Both indulgence and anxiety can dull spiritual awareness.

“*and that day will come on you suddenly*” (*v. 34*). “That day” is the day of the Son of Man’s return. If their hearts were dulled, it would catch them by surprise. The next verse adds that it will come “*like a snare*” (*v. 35*) on everyone on earth, a trap that springs without warning.

Then Jesus gave the remedy: “*Therefore be watchful all the time, praying that you may be counted worthy to escape all these things that will happen, and to stand before the Son of Man*” (*v. 36*). Watchfulness and prayer keep the heart alert.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals that spiritual danger often comes not from dramatic persecution but from ordinary life. The disciples might face prisons and kings, but they might also simply drift into spiritual sleep through indulgence or worry. Many believers fall away not because of a single crisis but through slow distraction.

It also connects with the parable of the sower, where the seed among thorns is choked by “*cares, riches, and pleasures of life*” (*Luke 8:14*). Both pleasures and worries can choke spiritual life. Jesus warns against both.

Finally, the verse shows the goal of watchfulness: to stand before the Son of Man. Believers will one day stand before Christ. Living with that day in view shapes how they live now.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to examine what weighs down their hearts. It may be indulgence, such as excessive entertainment, alcohol, or pleasure-seeking that dulls spiritual sensitivity. Or it may be anxiety about work, money, family, or the future. Believers can identify these weights and bring them to God.

It also encourages believers to practice watchfulness and prayer. Regular prayer, Scripture reading, worship, and fellowship help keep the heart alert. Prayer specifically for strength to remain faithful is a practical response to Jesus’ warning.

Finally, this verse calls believers to live with eternity in view. They will stand before the Son of Man. This awareness is not meant to produce fear but focus, helping them live faithfully each day and resist the distractions that would draw them away from Christ.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Luke 21* prepares believers to live faithfully in a world of turmoil while waiting for Christ’s return. The poor widow’s offering reminds them that God values wholehearted devotion more than outward splendor. The magnificent temple would be destroyed, but the widow’s gift was precious to God.

Jesus’ warnings about deception call believers to discernment. Many will claim to speak for Christ or announce that the end is near. Believers can test such claims by Scripture and refuse to follow them. When they hear of wars and disasters, they need not be terrified.

The promises about persecution offer courage. Believers who face opposition for their faith can trust that Jesus will give them words and wisdom, that their trials can become opportunities for testimony, and that their ultimate safety is secure in God’s care. By endurance they will gain their lives.

The fall of Jerusalem shows that Jesus’ words come true, which gives confidence that His promises about the future will also be fulfilled. When the world shakes, believers can lift up their heads in hope, because their redemption is near.

Finally, Jesus’ closing warning calls believers to guard their hearts against both indulgence and anxiety, and to stay watchful in prayer. Each day can be lived with the awareness that they will stand before the Son of Man, a hope that brings focus, courage, and joy.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for the poor widow’s example of wholehearted devotion. Help me to give You my best and all that I have. Guard me from deception, and keep me from being terrified by wars and disasters. When I face opposition for my faith, give me words and wisdom, and help me to see my trials as opportunities to testify about You.

Thank You that not a hair of my head will perish outside Your care, and that by endurance I will gain my life. When the world is shaken, help me to lift up my head, because my redemption is near. Keep my heart from being weighed down by indulgence or worry. Help me to stay watchful and prayerful, so that I may be ready to stand before You when You come. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Luke · Chapter 22 of 24

# Luke — Chapter 22

Chapter Theme: The Last Supper, the Garden, and the Look That Broke Peter’s Heart

[Read Luke 22 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/LUK22.htm)

Main Teaching

As Passover arrives, Satan enters Judas, who agrees to betray Jesus. At the Last Supper, Jesus gives the bread and cup as signs of His body given and His blood poured out for His disciples, and when they argue about greatness, He reminds them that He is among them as one who serves. He tells Peter that He has prayed for him in the coming test, prays in agony on the Mount of Olives, heals a servant’s ear at His arrest, and, after Peter’s denials, turns and looks at Peter, who goes out and weeps bitterly.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Luke 22* begins the account of Jesus’ suffering and death. Throughout his Gospel, Luke has shown Jesus traveling toward Jerusalem with determination, knowing what awaited Him there (*Luke 9:51*). Now the time has come. Luke’s account parallels *Matthew 26* and *Mark 14*, but it includes many distinctive details: Satan entering Judas, Jesus’ longing to eat the Passover, His teaching about service at the table, His prayer for Peter, the angel strengthening Him in the garden, His healing of the servant’s ear, and His look at Peter. (The anointing, the institution of the Lord’s Supper, Gethsemane, and Peter’s denials are studied in *Mark 14:24*, *14:36*, *14:38*, *14:72* and *Matthew 26:28*, *26:39*, *26:52*.)

### The Plot and Judas’s Betrayal (*22:1–6*)

The Feast of Unleavened Bread, called the Passover, was approaching. Jerusalem was crowded with pilgrims. The chief priests and scribes were looking for a way to kill Jesus, but they feared the people.

Luke writes, “*Satan entered into Judas, who was also called Iscariot, who was counted with the twelve*” (*v. 3*). This recalls *Luke 4:13*, where the devil left Jesus after the temptations “*until another time*” (*Luke 4:13*). That time had now come. Luke does not excuse Judas; he chose to go to the chief priests and temple officers and discuss how to hand Jesus over. But Luke shows that the betrayal was part of a larger spiritual battle. The leaders were glad and agreed to give Judas money. He looked for an opportunity to betray Jesus when no crowd was present.

### Preparing the Passover (*22:7–13*)

On the day when the Passover lamb had to be sacrificed, Jesus sent Peter and John to prepare the meal. He told them they would meet a man carrying a jar of water, which would have been unusual since women usually carried water. They were to follow him to a house and ask the owner for the guest room. The owner would show them a large, furnished upper room. They found everything as Jesus had said and prepared the Passover.

### The Last Supper (*22:14–23*)

When the hour came, Jesus reclined at the table with the apostles. He said, “*I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer*” (*v. 15*). The Greek phrase expresses deep longing: “With desire I have desired.” Jesus had looked forward to this final meal with His friends. He said He would not eat it again until it was fulfilled in God’s kingdom.

Luke’s account mentions two cups. The Passover meal included several cups of wine. Jesus took a cup, gave thanks, and told them to share it, saying He would not drink of the fruit of the vine again until God’s kingdom came. Then He took bread, gave thanks, broke it, and gave it to them, saying, “*This is my body which is given for you. Do this in memory of me*” (*v. 19*). This is studied below. After supper, He took the cup and said, “*This cup is the new covenant in my blood, which is poured out for you*” (*v. 20*). (Some early manuscripts omit part of verses 19–20, but most include them, and Paul’s account in *1 Corinthians 11:23–25* closely matches Luke’s.)

Then Jesus said that the hand of His betrayer was with Him on the table. The Son of Man would go as God had determined, but woe to the one who betrayed Him. The disciples began to ask each other which of them it could be.

### The Dispute About Greatness (*22:24–30*)

Shockingly, right after the Last Supper, an argument arose among the disciples about which of them was the greatest. Jesus answered that the kings of the Gentiles lord it over their people, and those in authority call themselves “*benefactors*” (*v. 25*), a title rulers used to advertise their generosity. “*But not so with you*” (*v. 26*). The greatest should be like the youngest, and the leader like one who serves. This is studied below.

Then Jesus spoke kindly to them: “*But you are those who have continued with me in my trials*” (*v. 28*). Despite their failures, they had stayed with Him. He promised them a kingdom, that they would eat and drink at His table and sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel.

### Jesus Prays for Peter (*22:31–38*)

Then Jesus spoke directly to Peter: “*Simon, Simon, behold, Satan asked to have all of you, that he might sift you as wheat*” (*v. 31*). This verse and the next are studied below. Peter declared, “*Lord, I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death!*” (*v. 33*) Jesus told him that before the rooster crowed that day, he would deny three times that he knew Him.

Jesus then reminded them that when He sent them out without purse, bag, or sandals, they lacked nothing (*Luke 9:3*; *10:4*). “*But now*” (*v. 36*), He said, things would be different. They should take a purse and bag, and whoever had no sword should sell his cloak and buy one. He explained that the Scripture “*He was counted with transgressors*” (*v. 37*) (*Isaiah 53:12*) must be fulfilled in Him. The disciples said, “*Lord, behold, here are two swords*” (*v. 38*), and He replied, “*That is enough*” (*v. 38*).

This passage is often misunderstood. Jesus was not instructing His disciples to take up arms; a few hours later He rebuked the use of the sword and healed the man who was struck (vv. 49–51). Many interpreters understand His words as a vivid way of saying that times of hostility were coming, when His followers would no longer be welcomed and would need to provide for themselves. When the disciples took Him literally and produced two swords, His reply, “That is enough,” may mean “Enough of this talk,” ending a conversation they had misunderstood.

### Prayer on the Mount of Olives (*22:39–46*)

Jesus went out, “*as his custom was*” (*v. 39*), to the Mount of Olives, and His disciples followed. Luke does not name Gethsemane but notes that Jesus regularly went there. He told them, “*Pray that you don’t enter into temptation*” (*v. 40*). He withdrew about a stone’s throw, knelt down, and prayed, “*Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done*” (*v. 42*). (This prayer is studied at *Mark 14:36* and *Matthew 26:39*.)

Luke alone records, “*An angel from heaven appeared to him, strengthening him*” (*v. 43*). “*Being in agony, he prayed more earnestly. His sweat became like great drops of blood falling down on the ground*” (*v. 44*). (Some early manuscripts do not include verses 43–44, but many do, and they were known to early Christian writers in the second century.) Luke the physician describes Jesus’ intense distress. The phrase “like great drops of blood” may mean that His sweat fell like drops of blood, or it may describe a rare medical condition in which extreme stress causes blood vessels to rupture into sweat glands. Either way, Luke shows the depth of Jesus’ anguish.

When Jesus rose from prayer, He found the disciples asleep, “*because of grief*” (*v. 45*). Luke gently explains their sleep as a result of sorrow. Jesus said, “*Why do you sleep? Rise and pray that you may not enter into temptation*” (*v. 46*).

### The Arrest (*22:47–53*)

While He was still speaking, a crowd arrived, led by Judas. He approached Jesus to kiss Him. Jesus said, “*Judas, do you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?*” (*v. 48*) A kiss was a sign of friendship and respect; Judas used it as a signal for betrayal.

The disciples asked, “*Lord, shall we strike with the sword?*” (*v. 49*) Before Jesus could answer, one of them struck the high priest’s servant and cut off his right ear. Jesus said, “*Let me at least do this*” (*v. 51*) (or “No more of this!”), and He touched the man’s ear and healed him. Luke alone records this healing. Even while being arrested, Jesus showed mercy to one of those arresting Him.

Jesus said to the chief priests, temple officers, and elders who had come for Him that they had not arrested Him when He taught daily in the temple. “*But this is your hour, and the power of darkness*” (*v. 53*). For a short time, evil would seem to triumph.

### Peter’s Denials and Jesus’ Look (*22:54–62*)

They seized Jesus and took Him to the high priest’s house. Peter followed at a distance. In the courtyard, people lit a fire and sat around it, and Peter sat among them. A servant girl looked closely at him in the firelight and said, “*This man also was with him*” (*v. 56*). Peter denied it: “*Woman, I don’t know him*” (*v. 57*). A little later someone else said he was one of them, and Peter said, “*Man, I am not!*” (*v. 58*) About an hour later another insisted that he was a Galilean. Peter said, “*Man, I don’t know what you are talking about!*” (*v. 60*) Immediately, while he was still speaking, a rooster crowed.

Then comes a detail found only in Luke: “*The Lord turned and looked at Peter*” (*v. 61*). This is studied below. Peter remembered Jesus’ words, went out, and wept bitterly.

### Jesus Before the Council (*22:63–71*)

The men guarding Jesus mocked and beat Him. They blindfolded Him, struck Him, and demanded, “*Prophesy! Who is the one who struck you?*” (*v. 64*) At daybreak, the council of elders, chief priests, and scribes gathered and questioned Him. They asked whether He was the Christ. He said that if He told them, they would not believe. Then He declared, “*From now on, the Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of the power of God*” (*v. 69*), echoing *Psalm 110:1* and *Daniel 7:13*. They asked, “Are you then the Son of God?” He answered, “*You say it, because I am*” (*v. 70*). They concluded they needed no more witnesses.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Luke 22:19* — “*Do This in Memory of Me*” (*v. 19*)

> *“He took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke and gave it to them, saying, ‘This is my body which is given for you. Do this in memory of me.’”*
>
> — *Luke 22:19* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse records the moment Jesus gave the bread to His disciples during the Last Supper. It was Passover, the annual festival when Jews remembered God’s deliverance of Israel from slavery in Egypt. The Passover meal included unleavened bread, bitter herbs, wine, and the Passover lamb, each with symbolic meaning, and the father or leader explained them as part of retelling the story of the exodus.

Jesus had told His disciples that He had eagerly desired to eat this Passover with them before He suffered. During the meal, “*He took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke and gave it to them*” (*v. 19*). These actions, taking, giving thanks, breaking, and giving, echo how Jesus fed the five thousand (*Luke 9:16*) and how He would break bread with the two disciples at Emmaus after His resurrection (*Luke 24:30*).

Then He said, “*This is my body which is given for you*” (*v. 19*). Jesus gave new meaning to the Passover bread. It now represented His own body, which would be given in death the next day. “For you” emphasizes that His death would be on behalf of His disciples, for their benefit. Luke alone records the words “which is given for you” in connection with the bread.

“*Do this in memory of me*” (*v. 19*). Jesus commanded His disciples to continue this practice. Just as Passover helped Israel remember the exodus, this meal would help Jesus’ followers remember His death and the new deliverance He accomplished. “Memory” in the Bible is more than mental recall. It means bringing a past event into the present so that it shapes life now. When believers eat the bread, they remember and proclaim His saving death.

Paul’s account of the Lord’s Supper, written in the 50s A.D., includes these same words (*1 Corinthians 11:24*), showing that the early church practiced this meal from the beginning.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals that Jesus’ death was a voluntary gift. His body was “given,” not merely taken. He gave Himself for His people. *Isaiah 53* describes the Servant who poured out His life for others, and Jesus saw Himself fulfilling that role.

It also shows that the Lord’s Supper is central to Christian worship. From the earliest days, believers gathered to break bread (*Acts 2:42*). Christians have understood the Lord’s Supper in different ways: some believe Christ is truly present in the bread and wine, some emphasize a spiritual presence received by faith, and some see it primarily as a memorial. All agree that it calls believers to remember Jesus’ sacrifice and to receive it with gratitude.

Finally, the command “Do this in memory of me” shows that remembering Jesus’ death is essential to the life of faith. Believers are prone to forget. Regular participation in the Lord’s Supper keeps the cross at the center of their faith.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to participate in the Lord’s Supper with reverence and gratitude. Each time they take the bread, they can remember that Jesus gave His body for them personally. This remembrance can deepen love for Him and renew commitment to follow Him.

It also encourages believers to make remembrance of Jesus’ sacrifice a regular part of their lives, not only in church but in daily reflection. Remembering the cross can bring comfort in guilt, humility in pride, and courage in difficulty.

Finally, this verse reminds believers that the Lord’s Supper is shared. Jesus gave the bread to all His disciples, including those who would fail Him that very night. It is a meal of grace for imperfect people, uniting believers as one body in Christ.

### *Luke 22:27* — “*I Am Among You as One Who Serves*” (*v. 27*)

> *“For who is greater, one who sits at the table, or one who serves? Isn’t it he who sits at the table? But I am among you as one who serves.”*
>
> — *Luke 22:27* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse comes in a surprising moment. Jesus had just shared the Last Supper with His disciples, giving them the bread and cup as signs of His body and blood. He had told them that one of them would betray Him. And immediately afterward, “*A dispute also arose among them, which of them was considered to be greatest*” (*v. 24*). While Jesus was facing death, His disciples were arguing about rank.

Jesus responded by contrasting the world’s way of leadership with His kingdom’s way. The kings of the Gentiles lord it over others, and those in authority call themselves “benefactors,” taking credit for their supposed generosity. “*But not so with you*” (*v. 26*). The greatest among them should become like the youngest, who in that culture had the least status, and the leader should be like one who serves.

Then Jesus asked a question: “*For who is greater, one who sits at the table, or one who serves?*” (*v. 27*) In that culture, the answer was obvious: the one reclining at the table, being served, was greater than the servant waiting on him. Jesus acknowledged this: “*Isn’t it he who sits at the table?*” (*v. 27*)

Then He pointed to Himself: “*But I am among you as one who serves*” (*v. 27*). Jesus, the Lord and Teacher, the King who would be seated at the right hand of God, had taken the role of a servant. John’s Gospel tells us that at this same meal, Jesus washed His disciples’ feet, a task assigned to the lowest servant (*John 13:1–17*). And within hours, He would give His life for them.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals the heart of Jesus’ mission. He came not to be served but to serve and to give His life (*Mark 10:45*, studied at *Matthew 20:28*). His whole life was service, culminating in the cross. Paul describes Jesus as taking the form of a servant and humbling Himself to death on a cross (*Philippians 2:7–8*).

It also reveals how slow the disciples were to understand. Even at the Last Supper, they were competing for status. Jesus did not reject them; He patiently taught them again, and He commended them for having stayed with Him in His trials. Grace meets people in their failures.

Finally, this verse redefines greatness for all believers. In God’s kingdom, greatness is measured by service. Leaders are servants. This turns upside down the world’s understanding of power and status.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse calls believers to follow Jesus’ example of service. In families, workplaces, churches, and communities, they can look for ways to serve others rather than seeking recognition or status. This may mean doing humble tasks, putting others’ needs first, or using authority to help rather than to dominate.

It especially challenges leaders. Pastors, parents, managers, and others in authority are called to lead as servants, not as people who expect to be served. Christian leadership is measured by how well leaders care for others.

Finally, this verse invites believers to receive Jesus’ service. He is still “among you as one who serves.” Believers can come to Him with their needs, trusting that He gives Himself for their good.

### *Luke 22:31–32* — “I Prayed for You That Your Faith Wouldn’t Fail”

> *“The Lord said, ‘Simon, Simon, behold, Satan asked to have all of you, that he might sift you as wheat, but I prayed for you, that your faith wouldn’t fail. You, when once you have turned again, establish your brothers.’”*
>
> — *Luke 22:31–32* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus speaks these words to Peter during the Last Supper, shortly before His arrest. The disciples had just been arguing about who was the greatest. Jesus had taught them about servant leadership and promised them a place in His kingdom. Now He turned to Peter with a warning and a promise.

“*Simon, Simon*” (*v. 31*). Jesus repeated his name, a sign of deep concern and affection. He used his original name, Simon, rather than Peter, “rock,” perhaps hinting at the weakness Peter was about to show.

“*behold, Satan asked to have all of you, that he might sift you as wheat*” (*v. 31*). The word “you” here is plural in Greek, meaning all the disciples. Satan had demanded permission to test them severely. This recalls the book of Job, where Satan asked permission to test Job (*Job 1:6–12*). “Sift as wheat” pictures grain being shaken violently in a sieve to separate it from chaff. The disciples were about to be shaken by fear, confusion, and failure.

“*but I prayed for you, that your faith wouldn’t fail*” (*v. 32*). Here “you” is singular, referring to Peter specifically. Jesus had prayed for Peter personally. He did not pray that Peter would avoid the test or never fail. He prayed that Peter’s faith would not fail completely, that even after falling, he would not abandon his faith altogether.

“*You, when once you have turned again, establish your brothers*” (*v. 32*). Jesus knew Peter would fall, but He also knew Peter would return. “Turned again” means repent and come back. Then Peter would have a responsibility: to strengthen the other disciples. His experience of failure and restoration would equip him to help others.

Peter responded with confidence: “Lord, I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death!” Jesus told him that before the rooster crowed, he would deny Him three times. Within hours, it happened.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses reveal that believers face real spiritual opposition. Satan seeks to shake and destroy faith. Peter writes later, “*Be sober and self-controlled. Be watchful. Your adversary, the devil, walks around like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour*” (*1 Peter 5:8*). Peter knew from experience what it meant to be sifted.

They also reveal Jesus’ intercession for His people. Jesus prayed for Peter before Peter failed. His prayer was the reason Peter’s faith did not ultimately collapse. The New Testament teaches that the risen Jesus continues to intercede for believers (*Romans 8:34*; *Hebrews 7:25*). Believers’ perseverance depends not only on their own strength but on Christ’s prayers for them.

Finally, the verses show that failure is not the end of usefulness. Jesus expected Peter to fail, but He also expected him to return and to strengthen others. Peter became a leader of the early church, preaching at Pentecost and caring for believers. His failure made him humble and compassionate.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers facing spiritual testing. Trials, temptations, and doubts can shake faith severely. Believers can take comfort that Jesus is praying for them, that their faith may not fail.

They also offer hope to those who have failed. Like Peter, believers may have denied Jesus in word or action. Jesus’ words show that failure does not have to be final. They can turn back to Him, receive forgiveness, and continue following Him.

Finally, these verses call restored believers to strengthen others. Those who have experienced failure and God’s restoring grace are often best equipped to help others who are struggling. Believers can use their own stories to encourage, support, and strengthen fellow believers.

### *Luke 22:61* — The Lord Turned and Looked at Peter

> *“The Lord turned and looked at Peter. Then Peter remembered the Lord’s word, how he said to him, ‘Before the rooster crows you will deny me three times.’”*
>
> — *Luke 22:61* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse, found only in Luke, describes the moment immediately after Peter’s third denial. Jesus had been arrested on the Mount of Olives and taken to the high priest’s house. Peter followed at a distance and sat with others around a fire in the courtyard. A servant girl recognized him and said he had been with Jesus. Peter denied it. A little later, someone else accused him, and he denied it again. About an hour later, another person insisted that Peter was a Galilean and had been with Jesus. Peter said, “*Man, I don’t know what you are talking about!*” (*v. 60*) Immediately, while he was still speaking, a rooster crowed.

Then “*The Lord turned and looked at Peter*” (*v. 61*). Jesus was apparently being held somewhere within sight of the courtyard, perhaps being led from one place to another in the high priest’s house. At the very moment of Peter’s third denial and the rooster’s crow, Jesus turned and looked at him.

Luke does not describe Jesus’ expression. But the look was enough. “*Then Peter remembered the Lord’s word, how he said to him, “Before the rooster crows you will deny me three times.”*” (*v. 61*) Only a few hours earlier, Peter had boldly declared that he was ready to go with Jesus to prison and death. Jesus had warned him he would deny Him three times. Now it had happened, exactly as Jesus said.

“*He went out, and wept bitterly*” (*v. 62*). Peter left the courtyard and broke down in tears. His weeping showed genuine sorrow and grief over what he had done.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals that Jesus knows His followers’ failures. He saw Peter at the very moment of his denial. Nothing is hidden from Him. Yet His look seems to have been one of sorrow and love rather than anger. Jesus had already prayed for Peter (v. 32) and had already told him that he would turn back. The look was an invitation to remember Jesus’ words, both the warning and the promise.

It also shows how conviction can lead to repentance. Peter’s tears were the beginning of his restoration. Unlike Judas, whose remorse led to despair (*Matthew 27:3–5*), Peter’s grief led him back to Jesus. After the resurrection, the risen Lord appeared to Peter (*Luke 24:34*) and restored him (*John 21:15–19*).

Finally, the verse shows the contrast between Jesus and Peter on that night. Jesus faced His accusers with courage and truth; Peter denied Him out of fear. Yet Jesus’ faithfulness was not only an example for Peter but the very means of his salvation. Jesus went to the cross for the one who denied Him.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to let Jesus’ gaze bring them to repentance. When they fail Him, whether through denial, compromise, or sin, they can remember that He sees them with sorrowful love. His look is not one of rejection but of invitation to return.

It also encourages believers to allow godly sorrow to lead them back to Christ. Tears over sin are not the end; they are the beginning of restoration when they lead to repentance and trust in Jesus’ forgiveness.

Finally, this verse reminds believers to be humble about their own strength. Peter was sure he would never deny Jesus. Believers can learn from his story to depend on Christ’s prayers and grace rather than on their own confidence, and to pray, as Jesus urged, that they will not enter into temptation.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Luke 22* shows the night before Jesus’ death, and it reveals both His faithfulness and human weakness. Judas, influenced by Satan and his own greed, betrayed Jesus. The disciples argued about greatness at the Last Supper. Peter denied Him three times. Yet through it all, Jesus remained faithful, loving, and in control.

The Last Supper calls believers to remember Jesus’ sacrifice regularly. His body was given and His blood poured out “for you.” Participating in the Lord’s Supper with reverence and gratitude keeps the cross at the center of faith and unites believers as one body.

Jesus’ response to the disciples’ argument calls believers to servant leadership. In God’s kingdom, greatness is measured by service, and Jesus Himself is among His people as one who serves. Believers can look for ways to serve others humbly and to use any authority they have for others’ good.

Jesus’ words to Peter remind believers that spiritual testing is real, but Jesus intercedes for His people. Failure need not be final. Those who fall can turn back to Him and then strengthen others. His prayer in the garden shows the importance of watchful prayer in times of temptation and distress.

Finally, Jesus’ healing of the servant’s ear and His look at Peter reveal His mercy even toward those who opposed or failed Him. Believers can receive His mercy when they fail and extend it to others, including their enemies.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for eagerly desiring to share the Passover with Your disciples, and for giving Your body and pouring out Your blood for me. Help me to remember Your sacrifice with gratitude every time I share the bread and cup. Forgive me for seeking greatness and recognition, and teach me to serve as You served.

Thank You for praying for Peter, and for praying for me, that my faith may not fail. When I am tested, keep me watchful and prayerful. When I fail, as Peter did, let Your look of sorrowful love bring me to repentance and back to You, and then use my story to strengthen others. Thank You for healing even those who came to arrest You. Make me merciful, as You are merciful. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
