Luke · Chapter 23 of 24

# Luke — Chapter 23

Chapter Theme: The Innocent King Who Forgave, Saved, and Entrusted Himself to the Father

[Read Luke 23 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/LUK23.htm)

Main Teaching

Pilate and Herod both find Jesus innocent, yet Pilate gives in to the crowd and hands Him over to be crucified. On the way to the cross Jesus grieves for the women of Jerusalem, and on the cross He prays for His executioners’ forgiveness, promises paradise to a repentant criminal, and dies entrusting His spirit to the Father. A centurion declares Him righteous, and Joseph of Arimathea buries Him while faithful women watch.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Luke 23* records Jesus’ trials before Pilate and Herod, His crucifixion, death, and burial. Luke’s account parallels *Matthew 27* and *Mark 15* (studied at *Matthew 27:46*, *27:51*, *27:54* and *Mark 15:15*, *15:31*, *15:43*), but it has several distinctive emphases. Luke repeatedly stresses Jesus’ innocence: Pilate declares Him innocent three times, Herod finds no guilt, a criminal says He has done nothing wrong, and the centurion calls Him righteous. Luke also records three sayings of Jesus from the cross found in no other Gospel, each revealing His heart: forgiveness for His enemies, salvation for a dying criminal, and trust in His Father.

### Before Pilate (*23:1–7*)

After the council condemned Jesus at daybreak (*Luke 22:66–71*), the whole assembly brought Him to Pilate, the Roman governor. They accused Him of three things: “*perverting the nation, forbidding paying taxes to Caesar, and saying that he himself is Christ, a king*” (*v. 2*). These charges were framed to sound like rebellion against Rome. The second was false; Jesus had said the opposite (*Luke 20:25*). The third twisted His claim to be the Messiah into a political threat.

Pilate asked, “*Are you the King of the Jews?*” (*v. 3*) Jesus answered, “*So you say*” (*v. 3*). Pilate then said to the chief priests and the crowd, “*I find no basis for a charge against this man*” (*v. 4*). This was the first of Pilate’s three declarations of Jesus’ innocence. The accusers insisted that Jesus was stirring up the people from Galilee to Jerusalem. When Pilate heard “Galilee,” he learned that Jesus was from Herod Antipas’s territory, and since Herod was in Jerusalem for the Passover, Pilate sent Jesus to him.

### Before Herod (*23:8–12*)

Luke alone records this episode. Herod Antipas, who had beheaded John the Baptist, was very glad to see Jesus. He had wanted to see Him for a long time and “*hoped to see some miracle done by him*” (*v. 8*). Herod treated Jesus like an entertainer. He questioned Him at length, but Jesus gave no answer at all. The chief priests and scribes stood there accusing Him vehemently. Herod and his soldiers then treated Jesus with contempt and mocked Him, dressed Him in an elegant robe, and sent Him back to Pilate.

Luke notes, “*Herod and Pilate became friends with each other that very day, for before that they were enemies with each other*” (*v. 12*). Two rulers who had been rivals found common ground in their dismissal of Jesus. In *Acts 4:27*, the early church prays about how Herod and Pilate, with the Gentiles and the people of Israel, gathered against Jesus, fulfilling *Psalm 2*.

### Pilate Gives In (*23:13–25*)

Pilate called together the chief priests, rulers, and people and told them that neither he nor Herod had found Jesus guilty of the charges. “*nothing worthy of death has been done by him*” (*v. 15*). He proposed to have Jesus punished, probably by flogging, and then release Him. (Verse 17, about releasing a prisoner at the feast, is missing from many early manuscripts.)

But the crowd shouted together, “*Away with this man! Release to us Barabbas!*” (*v. 18*) Barabbas had been imprisoned for an uprising in the city and for murder. Pilate, wanting to release Jesus, appealed to them again, but they kept shouting, “*Crucify! Crucify him!*” (*v. 21*) A third time Pilate asked, “*Why? What evil has this man done? I have found no capital crime in him*” (*v. 22*). But they insisted with loud shouts, and “*Their voices and the voices of the chief priests prevailed*” (*v. 23*).

Pilate granted their demand. He released the man guilty of rebellion and murder, “*but he delivered Jesus up to their will*” (*v. 25*). Luke’s account highlights the injustice: the innocent man was condemned and the guilty man freed. (Pilate’s decision is studied at *Mark 15:15*.)

### The Way to the Cross (*23:26–31*)

As they led Jesus away, they seized Simon of Cyrene, who was coming in from the country, and made him carry the cross behind Jesus. Luke’s wording, “after Jesus,” presents Simon as a picture of discipleship: taking up the cross and following Jesus (*Luke 9:23*).

A large crowd followed, including women who were mourning and wailing for Him. Jesus turned to them and said, “*Daughters of Jerusalem, don’t weep for me, but weep for yourselves and for your children*” (*v. 28*). Even on His way to death, Jesus’ concern was for others. He foresaw the coming destruction of Jerusalem (*Luke 19:41–44*; *21:20–24*), when the suffering would be so terrible that people would call childless women blessed and would beg the mountains to fall on them (echoing *Hosea 10:8*). Then He said, “*For if they do these things in the green tree, what will be done in the dry?*” (*v. 31*) This proverb means that if such things happen to an innocent man (green wood, which does not burn easily), how much worse will judgment be for the guilty (dry wood, which burns readily)?

### The Crucifixion (*23:32–43*)

Two criminals were led out to be executed with Jesus. At the place called “The Skull,” they crucified Him with the criminals on His right and left, fulfilling *Isaiah 53:12*, which Jesus had quoted the night before (*Luke 22:37*).

Then Jesus said, “*Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing*” (*v. 34*). This prayer is studied below. (Some early manuscripts lack this verse, but it is widely attested and fits Luke’s portrait of Jesus perfectly.) The soldiers divided His clothes by casting lots, fulfilling *Psalm 22:18*.

The people stood watching. The rulers sneered, “*He saved others. Let him save himself, if this is the Christ of God, his chosen one!*” (*v. 35*) The soldiers mocked Him too, offering Him sour wine and saying, “*If you are the King of the Jews, save yourself!*” (*v. 37*) Above Him was an inscription: “*THIS IS THE KING OF THE JEWS*” (*v. 38*).

One of the criminals hanging beside Him also insulted Him: “*If you are the Christ, save yourself and us!*” (*v. 39*) But the other criminal rebuked him. Their exchange and Jesus’ response are studied below.

### The Death of Jesus (*23:44–49*)

It was about noon, and darkness came over the whole land until three in the afternoon, “*The sun was darkened*” (*v. 45*). The curtain of the temple was torn in two. (The torn curtain is studied at *Matthew 27:51*.) Then Jesus cried out with a loud voice, “*Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!*” (*v. 46*) and breathed His last. This saying is studied below.

The centurion who saw what happened “*glorified God, saying, “Certainly this was a righteous man.”*” (*v. 47*) Where Matthew and Mark record him saying “Truly this was the Son of God,” Luke emphasizes the word “righteous” or “innocent,” which fits his theme of Jesus’ innocence. The Gentile officer recognized the truth that Pilate had declared and that the leaders had rejected.

The crowds who had gathered to watch went home “*beating their chests*” (*v. 48*), a sign of grief and perhaps of repentance. All those who knew Jesus, including the women who had followed Him from Galilee, stood at a distance watching.

### The Burial (*23:50–56*)

A man named Joseph, a member of the council, “*a good and righteous man*” (*v. 50*) from the town of Arimathea, “*he had not consented to their counsel and deed*” (*v. 51*). Luke makes clear that not every council member agreed with condemning Jesus. Joseph was waiting for God’s kingdom. He went to Pilate and asked for Jesus’ body, took it down, wrapped it in linen, and placed it in a tomb cut in the rock, where no one had yet been laid.

It was the day of Preparation, and the Sabbath was about to begin at sunset. The women who had come with Jesus from Galilee followed and saw the tomb and how His body was laid. They went home and prepared spices and perfumes, and then “*On the Sabbath they rested according to the commandment*” (*v. 56*). Their faithful presence at the cross and the tomb would make them the first witnesses of the resurrection.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Luke 23:34* — “*Father, Forgive Them*” (*v. 34*)

> *“Jesus said, ‘Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing.’ Dividing his garments among them, they cast lots.”*
>
> — *Luke 23:34* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These are the first words Jesus spoke from the cross in Luke’s Gospel. He had been betrayed by Judas, denied by Peter, falsely accused before the council, mocked by Herod’s soldiers, condemned by Pilate despite being declared innocent, and handed over to be crucified. Roman soldiers had nailed Him to a cross between two criminals. Crucifixion was one of the most painful and humiliating forms of execution ever devised.

In this moment of agony, Jesus prayed: “*Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing*” (*v. 34*).

“*Father*” (*v. 34*). Even on the cross, Jesus addressed God with intimacy and trust. Throughout Luke, Jesus prayed to His Father at every crucial moment.

“*forgive them*” (*v. 34*). “Them” likely includes the Roman soldiers who were crucifying Him, and possibly all who were responsible for His death: the religious leaders, Pilate, and the crowd. Jesus did not call down judgment on them. He asked the Father to forgive them.

“*for they don’t know what they are doing*” (*v. 34*). The soldiers were carrying out orders without understanding that they were crucifying the Son of God. The leaders and crowds, too, did not fully understand who Jesus was. Peter later said to the people of Jerusalem, “*I know that you did this in ignorance, as did also your rulers*” (*Acts 3:17*). Their ignorance did not make them innocent, since they still needed forgiveness, but it was a reason Jesus appealed for mercy.

Immediately after this prayer, Luke notes that the soldiers divided His clothes by casting lots. Even as Jesus prayed for them, they continued their cruel work.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This prayer reveals the heart of Jesus and the heart of God. Jesus had taught His followers to love their enemies, bless those who curse them, and pray for those who mistreat them (*Luke 6:27–28*). On the cross, He did exactly that. His teaching was not just words; He lived it in the most extreme circumstances.

It also reveals the purpose of the cross. Jesus died so that sinners could be forgiven. His prayer for His executioners points to the forgiveness He was making possible for all people through His death. Even those who crucified Him could be forgiven. In *Acts 2*, many of the people of Jerusalem who had called for His crucifixion repented and were forgiven.

Finally, this prayer became a model for Jesus’ followers. Stephen, the first Christian martyr, prayed as he was being stoned, “*Lord, don’t hold this sin against them!*” (*Acts 7:60*) Throughout history, many believers facing persecution have prayed for their persecutors, following Jesus’ example.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse calls believers to forgive those who hurt them. If Jesus could forgive those who were crucifying Him, believers can ask for His grace to forgive those who have wronged them. Forgiveness may be difficult and may take time, but Jesus shows that it is possible.

It also encourages believers to pray for those who hurt them. Praying for enemies softens the heart and reflects God’s love. It does not mean pretending wrongs did not happen or remaining in harmful situations; believers can pursue safety and justice while still refusing hatred and praying for the good of those who harmed them.

Finally, this verse gives assurance to anyone who wonders whether they can be forgiven. If Jesus prayed for the forgiveness of those crucifying Him, no one is beyond the reach of His mercy. Believers can come to Him confident that He desires to forgive.

### *Luke 23:42–43* — “Today You Will Be With Me in Paradise”

> *“He said to Jesus, ‘Lord, remember me when you come into your Kingdom.’ Jesus said to him, ‘Assuredly I tell you, today you will be with me in Paradise.’”*
>
> — *Luke 23:42–43* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These verses record a conversation between Jesus and one of the two criminals crucified beside Him. Both men had been condemned to death, likely for violent crimes such as robbery or rebellion. One of them joined the crowd in mocking Jesus: “*If you are the Christ, save yourself and us!*” (*v. 39*)

But the other criminal rebuked him: “*Don’t you even fear God, seeing you are under the same condemnation?*” (*v. 40*) He continued, “*And we indeed justly, for we receive the due reward for our deeds, but this man has done nothing wrong*” (*v. 41*). This criminal recognized three things: he feared God; he admitted that he deserved his punishment; and he declared that Jesus was innocent.

Then he turned to Jesus and said, “*Lord, remember me when you come into your Kingdom*” (*v. 42*). Some manuscripts read simply “Jesus, remember me.” This is remarkable faith. Jesus was dying on a cross, mocked and apparently powerless. Yet this man believed that Jesus was a king who would come into His kingdom. He asked only to be remembered, a humble request.

Jesus answered, “*Assuredly I tell you, today you will be with me in Paradise*” (*v. 43*). “Assuredly” (or “Truly”) emphasizes certainty. “Today” means that very day, not at some distant future time. “With me” promises personal fellowship with Jesus. “Paradise” is a Persian word for a garden, used in Jewish writings for the place of blessedness where the righteous dead are with God, recalling the garden of Eden. The man asked to be remembered in the future; Jesus promised him far more, immediately.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses reveal that salvation is by grace through faith, not by works. This man had no time to do good deeds, be baptized, or make restitution. He had lived a life deserving death. Yet he turned to Jesus in faith and repentance, and Jesus promised him paradise. Paul writes that salvation is “*not of yourselves; it is the gift of God*” (*Ephesians 2:8*).

They also show what genuine repentance looks like. The man feared God, admitted his guilt without excuse, recognized Jesus’ innocence, and trusted Jesus as King. These are the marks of true faith.

Finally, these verses provide comfort about death. Jesus promised the criminal that he would be with Him that very day. Many Christians understand this as teaching that believers who die go immediately into the presence of Christ, as Paul says, “*having the desire to depart and be with Christ*” (*Philippians 1:23*). Christians have different views about the details of life after death before the final resurrection, but all affirm that believers are safe with Christ.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses offer hope to anyone who thinks it is too late to turn to God. The criminal turned to Jesus in his final hours and was welcomed. No matter what someone has done or how much time has passed, they can come to Jesus in faith.

They also invite believers to approach Jesus with the same honest repentance: admitting their sin, recognizing His righteousness, and asking for His mercy. Salvation does not depend on a record of good works but on trusting Jesus.

Finally, these verses comfort those facing death or grieving loved ones who trusted in Christ. Jesus’ promise, “Today you will be with me,” assures believers that death does not separate them from Him.

### *Luke 23:46* — “*Father, Into Your Hands I Commit My Spirit*” (*v. 46*)

> *“Jesus, crying with a loud voice, said, ‘Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!’ Having said this, he breathed his last.”*
>
> — *Luke 23:46* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These are Jesus’ final words before His death in Luke’s Gospel. He had been on the cross for hours. From noon until three in the afternoon, darkness covered the land, and the curtain in the temple was torn in two. Then “*Jesus, crying with a loud voice, said, “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!”*” (*v. 46*)

“*crying with a loud voice*” (*v. 46*). Crucified victims usually grew weaker until they could barely speak. Jesus’ loud cry suggests that He was not simply overcome by death but actively gave up His life.

“*Father*” (*v. 46*). As in His first words on the cross (v. 34), Jesus addressed God as Father. His relationship with the Father remained the center of His life even in death.

“*into your hands I commit my spirit*” (*v. 46*). These words come from *Psalm 31:5*, a psalm of trust in God amid suffering and danger. Jewish people sometimes prayed this psalm as an evening prayer before sleep. Jesus added “Father” to the psalm’s words. “Commit” means to entrust or hand over something valuable to someone’s safekeeping. Jesus entrusted His life to His Father, confident that the Father would receive Him and raise Him.

“*Having said this, he breathed his last*” (*v. 46*). Jesus died after entrusting Himself to God.

Luke’s account of Jesus’ death emphasizes peace and trust. Matthew and Mark record Jesus’ cry, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (studied at *Matthew 27:46*). Luke records this final word of trust. Both are true: Jesus experienced the depths of forsakenness as He bore sin, and He died entrusting Himself fully to His Father.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals Jesus’ perfect trust in His Father, even in death. Throughout His life, He had lived in dependence on the Father, praying at every crucial moment. In death, He entrusted Himself completely to God. Peter later wrote that Jesus, when He suffered, “*committed himself to him who judges righteously*” (*1 Peter 2:23*).

It also shows that Jesus’ death was voluntary. He gave up His spirit; it was not simply taken from Him. In *John 10:18*, Jesus says that no one takes His life from Him; He lays it down of His own accord.

Finally, this verse gives believers a model for facing death. Stephen, as he was being stoned, prayed, “*Lord Jesus, receive my spirit!*” (*Acts 7:59*) Throughout Christian history, many believers have prayed these words of *Psalm 31* as they died. Because Jesus entrusted His spirit to the Father and was raised, believers can entrust their spirits to God with confidence.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to entrust their lives to God every day. “Into your hands I commit my spirit” can be a prayer at the beginning or end of each day, expressing trust in God’s care. It is fitting for times of uncertainty, fear, illness, or danger.

It also comforts believers facing death, whether their own or that of loved ones. Jesus has gone before them through death and has shown that the Father’s hands are safe. Believers can face death not with terror but with trust.

Finally, this verse encourages believers to trust God when they cannot see the outcome. Jesus entrusted Himself to the Father before the resurrection, in the darkness of the cross. Believers can trust God in their own dark moments, believing that He is faithful and will bring life out of death.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Luke 23* presents Jesus as the innocent King who suffered unjustly. Pilate, Herod, the criminal, and the centurion all recognized His innocence, yet He was condemned to satisfy a crowd. Believers can respond with gratitude, recognizing that the innocent one died in the place of the guilty, just as Barabbas was released while Jesus was crucified.

The chapter also warns against the failures of those who opposed Jesus. Pilate gave in to pressure despite knowing the truth. Herod treated Jesus as entertainment. The crowd was swayed by its leaders. Believers can ask God for courage to stand for truth, to take Jesus seriously, and to resist going along with the crowd.

Jesus’ words from the cross teach believers how to live and die. His prayer, “Father, forgive them,” calls believers to forgive those who hurt them and to pray for their enemies. His promise to the criminal, “Today you will be with me in Paradise,” gives hope to anyone who turns to Him in faith, no matter how late. And His final prayer, “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit,” teaches believers to entrust their lives and their deaths to God.

Finally, the examples of Simon, the mourning women, Joseph of Arimathea, and the women from Galilee show different forms of faithfulness. Believers can carry the cross after Jesus, grieve over sin, act courageously for Him even when others oppose Him, and remain present in faithful love. These quiet acts of faithfulness prepare the way for the joy of the resurrection.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, You were innocent, yet You were condemned in my place. Thank You for bearing the cross for me. Forgive me for the times I have gone along with the crowd or failed to take You seriously. Give me courage to stand for what is true and right.

Thank You for praying, “Father, forgive them,” even as You were being crucified. Help me to forgive those who have hurt me and to pray for their good. Like the criminal beside You, I confess that I deserve judgment, and I ask You to remember me in Your kingdom. Thank You for Your promise of paradise to all who trust in You. Teach me to entrust my life to the Father each day, and when my time comes, help me to say with You, “Father, into Your hands I commit my spirit.” In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Luke · Chapter 24 of 24

# Luke — Chapter 24

Chapter Theme: He Is Risen: Burning Hearts, Opened Minds, and a Mission to All Nations

[Read Luke 24 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/LUK24.htm)

Main Teaching

Women find the tomb empty and hear angels ask why they seek the living among the dead. The risen Jesus walks unrecognized with two grieving disciples on the road to Emmaus, explains how all the Scriptures point to Him, and is recognized as He breaks bread. He appears to the gathered disciples, shows them His wounded hands and feet, eats with them, opens their minds to understand the Scriptures, commissions them to preach repentance and forgiveness to all nations, promises the Spirit’s power, and ascends to heaven as they worship with great joy.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Luke 24* is the triumphant conclusion of Luke’s Gospel. Jesus had been crucified on Friday and buried in Joseph of Arimathea’s tomb. The women who had followed Him from Galilee saw where He was laid, prepared spices, and rested on the Sabbath (*Luke 23:55–56*). Now, on the first day of the week, everything changes.

The entire chapter takes place on a single day, the day of resurrection, at least until the ascension at the end, which *Acts 1:3* tells us happened forty days later; Luke compresses the time in his Gospel and describes it more fully in Acts. Luke’s resurrection account has several distinctive emphases: the fulfillment of Scripture, the physical reality of Jesus’ risen body, the gradual movement of the disciples from confusion and doubt to understanding and joy, and the mission that will continue in Luke’s second volume, Acts.

### The Empty Tomb (*24:1–12*)

Very early on Sunday morning, the women came to the tomb with the spices they had prepared. They found the stone rolled away. When they went in, they did not find the body of the Lord Jesus. While they were puzzled, two men in dazzling clothing appeared beside them. The women were terrified and bowed with their faces to the ground. The men said, “*Why do you seek the living among the dead?*” (*v. 5*) This question, with the announcement that follows, is studied below.

The angels reminded the women of what Jesus had told them in Galilee: the Son of Man must be handed over to sinful men, be crucified, and rise on the third day. “*They remembered his words*” (*v. 8*). They returned from the tomb and told everything to the eleven and the others. Luke names them: “*Mary Magdalene, Joanna, and Mary the mother of James*” (*v. 10*), and other women. These are the same women who had supported Jesus’ ministry (*Luke 8:2–3*) and stayed near the cross (*Luke 23:49*).

But the apostles thought their words were “*nonsense*” (*v. 11*), and they did not believe them. In that culture, women’s testimony was often given less weight. The disciples’ unbelief shows that they were not expecting a resurrection; they were not inventing a story they wanted to believe. Peter, however, got up and ran to the tomb. He looked in and saw the linen cloths lying by themselves, and he went home wondering what had happened.

### The Road to Emmaus (*24:13–35*)

That same day, two of Jesus’ followers were walking to a village called Emmaus, about seven miles from Jerusalem (sixty stadia). They were discussing everything that had happened. As they talked, Jesus Himself came near and walked with them, “*But their eyes were kept from recognizing him*” (*v. 16*).

Jesus asked what they were discussing. They stopped, their faces downcast. One of them, named Cleopas, asked whether He was the only visitor in Jerusalem who did not know what had happened. Jesus asked, “*What things?*” (*v. 19*) They told Him about Jesus of Nazareth, “*a prophet mighty in deed and word before God and all the people*” (*v. 19*), whom the chief priests and rulers had handed over to be crucified. Then they said, “*But we were hoping that it was he who would redeem Israel*” (*v. 21*). Their hope had died with Jesus. They also told Him about the women’s report of an empty tomb and angels saying He was alive, and that some had gone to the tomb and found it empty, but had not seen Him.

Jesus said, “*Foolish people, and slow of heart to believe in all that the prophets have spoken!*” (*v. 25*) He asked, “*Didn’t the Christ have to suffer these things and to enter into his glory?*” (*v. 26*) Then, “*Beginning from Moses and from all the prophets, he explained to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself*” (*v. 27*). Jesus showed them that the whole Old Testament pointed to a Messiah who would suffer and then be glorified. Their problem was not that the cross contradicted Scripture, but that they had read Scripture selectively, expecting only a triumphant king.

As they approached the village, Jesus acted as if He would go farther. They urged Him to stay, because it was evening. He went in with them. When He was at the table with them, “*he took the bread and gave thanks. Breaking it, he gave it to them*” (*v. 30*). These actions echo the feeding of the five thousand (*Luke 9:16*) and the Last Supper (*Luke 22:19*). “*Their eyes were opened and they recognized him; then he vanished out of their sight*” (*v. 31*).

They said to each other, “*Weren’t our hearts burning within us while he spoke to us along the way, and while he opened the Scriptures to us?*” (*v. 32*) This verse is studied below. They got up immediately and returned to Jerusalem, a seven-mile walk at night. They found the Eleven and others gathered together, who told them, “*The Lord is risen indeed, and has appeared to Simon!*” (*v. 34*) Paul also mentions this appearance to Peter (*1 Corinthians 15:5*). Then the two told what had happened on the road and how Jesus was recognized by them “*in the breaking of the bread*” (*v. 35*).

### Jesus Appears to the Disciples (*24:36–43*)

While they were still talking, Jesus Himself stood among them and said, “*Peace be to you*” (*v. 36*). They were startled and frightened, thinking they were seeing a ghost. Jesus asked why they were troubled and why doubts arose in their hearts. He invited them to look at His hands and feet and to touch Him, showing that He was not a spirit. This is studied below.

Luke adds, “*While they still didn’t believe for joy, and wondered*” (*v. 41*). Their joy was so great that it seemed too good to be true. Then Jesus asked, “*Do you have anything here to eat?*” (*v. 41*) They gave Him a piece of broiled fish, and He ate it in front of them, further proving that He was physically alive.

### Opening Their Minds and Commissioning Them (*24:44–49*)

Jesus reminded them of what He had told them while He was still with them: “*that all things which are written in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms concerning me must be fulfilled*” (*v. 44*). These three groups covered the whole Hebrew Bible. “*Then he opened their minds, that they might understand the Scriptures*” (*v. 45*). Throughout Luke, the disciples had not understood Jesus’ predictions of His death (*Luke 9:45*; *18:34*). Now Jesus opened their minds.

He told them that the Scriptures taught that the Messiah would suffer and rise on the third day, and that repentance and forgiveness of sins would be proclaimed in His name to all nations, beginning at Jerusalem. This is studied below. He said, “*You are witnesses of these things*” (*v. 48*). They had seen His life, death, and resurrection, and they would testify about Him.

Then He gave a promise: “*Behold, I send out the promise of my Father on you. But wait in the city of Jerusalem until you are clothed with power from on high*” (*v. 49*). “The promise of my Father” is the Holy Spirit, whom the prophets had promised (*Joel 2:28*). *Acts 2* records the fulfillment of this promise on the day of Pentecost.

### The Ascension (*24:50–53*)

Jesus led them out as far as Bethany, on the Mount of Olives. He lifted up His hands and blessed them, the posture of a priest pronouncing a blessing (*Leviticus 9:22*). “*While he blessed them, he withdrew from them and was carried up into heaven*” (*v. 51*). Jesus’ last action on earth was to bless His followers.

“*They worshiped him and returned to Jerusalem with great joy*” (*v. 52*). This is the first time in Luke that the disciples are said to worship Jesus, recognizing Him as Lord and God. They were not sad that He had left; they were filled with joy. “*and were continually in the temple, praising and blessing God*” (*v. 53*). Luke’s Gospel began in the temple, with Zechariah offering incense (*Luke 1:8–9*), and it ends in the temple, with Jesus’ followers praising God. The story continues in Acts.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Luke 24:5–6* — “*Why Do You Seek the Living Among the Dead?*” (*v. 5*)

> *“Becoming terrified, they bowed their faces down to the earth. The men said to them, Why do you seek the living among the dead? He isn’t here, but is risen. Remember what he told you when he was still in Galilee,”*
>
> — *Luke 24:5–6* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These verses record the angels’ message to the women at Jesus’ tomb. Early on Sunday morning, the first day of the week, the women who had followed Jesus from Galilee came to the tomb with spices to anoint His body. They had watched Him die on Friday and had seen where He was buried. They came expecting to care for a corpse.

But they found the stone rolled away, and when they entered, Jesus’ body was not there. While they stood perplexed, two men in dazzling clothing stood beside them. Luke later identifies them as angels (v. 23). The women were terrified and bowed their faces to the ground.

The angels asked, “*Why do you seek the living among the dead?*” (*v. 5*) Tombs were for the dead. The women had come to a place of death looking for someone who was alive. The question gently corrects their expectations: they were looking in the wrong place, because Jesus was no longer dead.

“*He isn’t here, but is risen*” (*v. 6*). This is the central announcement of the Christian faith. The word “risen” is a passive form meaning “has been raised,” emphasizing that God raised Him from the dead.

“*Remember what he told you when he was still in Galilee*” (*v. 6*). The angels reminded the women that Jesus had predicted His death and resurrection. In Luke, Jesus predicted this several times (*Luke 9:22*, 44; *18:31–33*). The women had heard His words but had not understood them. Now the angels called them to remember.

Verse 8 records their response: “*They remembered his words*” (*v. 8*). Remembering Jesus’ words transformed their confusion into understanding. They went back and told the apostles everything.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses announce that Jesus is alive. He is not a dead teacher whose memory people honor, but a living Lord. Christianity is not primarily a set of moral teachings or a remembrance of a great person; it is a relationship with the risen Jesus, who is alive today.

They also show the importance of remembering Jesus’ words. The women’s confusion turned to understanding when they remembered what Jesus had said. Throughout *Luke 24*, understanding comes as people recall and understand Jesus’ words and the Scriptures.

Finally, the angels’ question challenges people who look for Jesus in the wrong places. Some look for Him only in history, as a figure of the past. Others look for Him in religious rituals without a living relationship. The angels remind everyone that Jesus is alive and must be sought as the living Lord.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses invite believers to relate to Jesus as alive, not merely as a historical figure. They can pray to Him, trust Him, and follow Him, knowing that He is present and active.

They also encourage believers to remember Jesus’ words, especially in times of confusion or grief. Like the women at the tomb, believers can find clarity and hope when they recall what Jesus has said in Scripture.

Finally, these verses bring hope to those who grieve. The tomb could not hold Jesus. His resurrection is the promise that death will not have the final word for those who belong to Him. Believers can face loss with confidence that the living Lord will raise His people.

### *Luke 24:32* — “*Weren't Our Hearts Burning Within Us?*” (*v. 32*)

> *“They said to one another, ‘Weren’t our hearts burning within us while he spoke to us along the way, and while he opened the Scriptures to us?’”*
>
> — *Luke 24:32* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse records the words of two disciples after they recognized the risen Jesus. Earlier that day, they had been walking from Jerusalem to the village of Emmaus, discouraged and confused. Their hopes that Jesus would redeem Israel had been crushed by His crucifixion. They had heard reports from the women that the tomb was empty and that angels said He was alive, but they did not know what to make of it.

As they walked, Jesus joined them, but they did not recognize Him. When they explained their sadness, Jesus called them slow to believe the prophets, and then He explained to them, beginning with Moses and all the prophets, everything in the Scriptures about Himself. When they reached Emmaus, they invited Him to stay. At the table, He took bread, gave thanks, broke it, and gave it to them. Their eyes were opened, they recognized Him, and He disappeared.

Then they said to each other, “*Weren’t our hearts burning within us while he spoke to us along the way, and while he opened the Scriptures to us?*” (*v. 32*)

“Our hearts burning within us” describes an inner warmth, excitement, and conviction. Even before they recognized Jesus, something stirred in them as He explained the Scriptures. Jeremiah described God’s word as “*a burning fire shut up in my bones*” (*Jeremiah 20:9*). The disciples’ hearts were set on fire by the truth.

“*while he opened the Scriptures to us*” (*v. 32*). The word “opened” means explained or unlocked the meaning. They had known the Scriptures, but Jesus showed them how the whole Old Testament pointed to Him, especially to a Messiah who would suffer before entering His glory.

The disciples’ response was immediate. They got up that very hour and walked seven miles back to Jerusalem in the dark to tell the other disciples.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals that Jesus is the key to understanding Scripture. The whole Bible, Old and New Testaments, points to Him. When people understand the Scriptures in light of Jesus, they come alive. Jesus later said the same thing to all the disciples (v. 44).

It also shows that Scripture and Jesus’ presence work together. The disciples’ hearts burned as He explained the Scriptures, and their eyes were opened when He broke bread. In the church’s life, Jesus continues to make Himself known through the Word and through the shared life of believers, including the Lord’s Supper.

Finally, this verse shows that encountering the risen Jesus transforms people. The disciples went from discouragement to joy, from walking away from Jerusalem to running back to share the news.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to read Scripture with Jesus at the center. When they read the Old Testament, they can look for how it points to Christ; when they read the New Testament, they can see how He fulfills God’s promises. This kind of reading can set hearts on fire.

It also invites believers to ask Jesus to open the Scriptures to them. Before reading the Bible, they can pray for understanding, trusting that the risen Lord, through His Spirit, can make His Word come alive.

Finally, this verse offers hope to those who are discouraged. Like the two disciples on the road, believers may feel that their hopes have been crushed. Jesus walks with them, even when they do not recognize Him, and He can turn their sorrow into joy.

### *Luke 24:39* — “*See My Hands and My Feet*” (*v. 39*)

> *“See my hands and my feet, that it is truly me. Touch me and see, for a spirit doesn’t have flesh and bones, as you see that I have.”*
>
> — *Luke 24:39* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse records Jesus’ words when He appeared to the gathered disciples on the evening of His resurrection. The two disciples from Emmaus had just returned and were telling the others how they had recognized Jesus. While they were still speaking, Jesus suddenly stood among them and said, “Peace be to you.” They were startled and terrified, thinking they were seeing a spirit or ghost.

Jesus asked them why they were troubled and why doubts were arising in their hearts. Then He said, “*See my hands and my feet, that it is truly me*” (*v. 39*). His hands and feet bore the marks of the nails from the crucifixion. These wounds proved that the risen Jesus was the same person who had been crucified. John’s Gospel records Jesus showing His wounds to Thomas as well (*John 20:27*).

“*Touch me and see, for a spirit doesn’t have flesh and bones, as you see that I have*” (*v. 39*). Jesus invited them to touch Him and confirm that He had a real, physical body. He was not a ghost, a vision, or a spirit. He had been raised bodily.

Luke then records that Jesus showed them His hands and feet. Even then, “*While they still didn’t believe for joy, and wondered*” (*v. 41*), He asked for something to eat. They gave Him broiled fish, and He ate it in their presence. Eating provided further proof of His physical resurrection.

Luke, the physician and careful historian, emphasizes this bodily reality. Some people in the Greek world believed that the body was unimportant or even evil, and that only the soul mattered. Others might have thought the disciples saw a vision. Luke shows clearly that Jesus’ resurrection was physical.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse teaches that Jesus was raised bodily. His resurrection was not merely spiritual survival but the transformation of His physical body. This is essential to the Christian faith. Paul writes that if Christ has not been raised, faith is useless (*1 Corinthians 15:14–17*). Jesus’ bodily resurrection is the guarantee that believers will also be raised bodily (*1 Corinthians 15:20–23*).

It also shows that the risen Jesus still bears the marks of the cross. His wounds were not erased. They became signs of His victory and His love. In *Revelation 5:6*, Jesus is seen as a Lamb that appears to have been slain. The crucified one is the risen one.

Finally, the verse shows Jesus’ patience with doubt. The disciples were frightened and doubtful, yet He did not rebuke them harshly. He gave them evidence: His wounds, His touch, and His eating. Jesus meets honest doubt with patient reassurance.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse gives believers confidence in the reality of the resurrection. Their faith rests on a real event: Jesus was raised bodily from the dead. This truth can strengthen faith in times of doubt.

It also gives hope for the future. Because Jesus was raised bodily, believers can look forward to their own bodily resurrection. God cares about the whole person, body and soul, and will one day restore all things.

Finally, this verse encourages believers who struggle with doubt. Jesus does not reject those who doubt. He invites them to look and see. Believers can bring their questions to Him and examine the evidence, trusting that He will strengthen their faith.

### *Luke 24:46–47* — Repentance and Forgiveness Proclaimed to All Nations

> *“He said to them, Thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead the third day, and that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name to all the nations, beginning at Jerusalem.”*
>
> — *Luke 24:46–47* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These verses contain Jesus’ summary of the message His followers would proclaim. He had appeared to the gathered disciples, shown them His hands and feet, and eaten with them. Then He reminded them of what He had told them before His death: everything written about Him in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms must be fulfilled. “*Then he opened their minds, that they might understand the Scriptures*” (*v. 45*).

Jesus summarized what the Scriptures taught: “*Thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead the third day*” (*v. 46*). The suffering and resurrection of the Messiah were not accidents or failures; they were God’s plan, revealed in Scripture. Passages like *Isaiah 53*, *Psalm 22*, and *Psalm 16* point to a Messiah who would suffer and be raised.

Then Jesus described what would follow: “*and that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name to all the nations, beginning at Jerusalem*” (*v. 47*).

“*repentance and remission of sins*” (*v. 47*). This is the heart of the message. “Repentance” means turning away from sin and turning to God. “Remission” means forgiveness, the cancellation of the debt of sin. Because of Jesus’ death and resurrection, forgiveness is available to all who repent.

“*preached in his name*” (*v. 47*). The message would be proclaimed by Jesus’ authority and centered on Him.

“*to all the nations*” (*v. 47*). The message is for everyone, Jews and Gentiles alike. This fulfills Simeon’s prophecy that Jesus would be a light for the Gentiles (*Luke 2:32*) and the promise that all flesh would see God’s salvation (*Luke 3:6*).

“*beginning at Jerusalem*” (*v. 47*). The mission would start in Jerusalem, the city where Jesus was crucified. The book of Acts follows exactly this pattern: the gospel spreads from Jerusalem to Judea, Samaria, and the ends of the earth (*Acts 1:8*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses summarize the gospel: the Messiah suffered, died, and rose again, and through Him forgiveness is offered to all who repent. This message is not a human invention but the fulfillment of God’s plan revealed throughout Scripture.

They also reveal the mission of the church. Jesus’ followers are called to proclaim this message to all nations. This mission continues today. The phrase “beginning at Jerusalem” is significant: the message started in the very city that rejected Jesus. God’s grace was offered first to those who had crucified Him.

Finally, these verses show that the message of forgiveness requires the response of repentance. Forgiveness is freely offered, but it is received by turning to God. Jesus’ message is both an invitation and a call to change.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses invite believers to receive the message of repentance and forgiveness personally. Whatever sins they have committed, forgiveness is available in Jesus’ name to all who turn to Him.

They also call believers to participate in proclaiming this message. Every believer is a witness to what Jesus has done. They can share the good news of forgiveness with family, friends, neighbors, and people of other nations, and support the work of spreading the gospel worldwide.

Finally, these verses remind believers that their message is rooted in Scripture. They can study how the whole Bible points to Christ, so that they can understand and share the good news with confidence.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Luke 24* announces the greatest news in history: Jesus is risen. The women found an empty tomb and heard the angels say, “Why do you seek the living among the dead?” Believers can relate to Jesus as their living Lord, present and active today, and they can face grief and death with the hope of resurrection.

The chapter shows how people move from confusion to faith. The women remembered Jesus’ words. The disciples on the road to Emmaus had their hearts set on fire as Jesus explained the Scriptures. The gathered disciples saw His wounds and watched Him eat. In each case, Jesus patiently met people in their doubt and discouragement. Believers who struggle with doubt can bring their questions to Jesus, study the Scriptures, and trust that He will open their eyes.

The chapter also emphasizes that Jesus is the key to all Scripture. He opened the minds of His disciples to understand how the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms pointed to Him. Believers can read the Bible with Christ at the center, and they can ask Him to make His Word come alive in their hearts.

Finally, Jesus commissioned His followers to proclaim repentance and forgiveness in His name to all nations, promising the power of the Holy Spirit. Believers are witnesses of these things. Like the first disciples, they can worship Jesus with great joy, praise God continually, and share the good news with others. The story that began in Luke continues in Acts, and it continues today through every believer who bears witness to the risen Lord.

## Chapter Prayer

Risen Lord Jesus, thank You that You are not among the dead, but alive forever. Thank You for conquering death and for keeping every promise You made. When I am discouraged like the disciples on the road to Emmaus, walk with me, open the Scriptures to me, and set my heart on fire with Your truth.

Thank You for showing Your hands and feet, the marks of Your love, and for proving that You are truly risen. Help me to trust You when I doubt. Open my mind to understand the Scriptures and to see You at the center of them. Thank You that repentance and forgiveness of sins are offered in Your name to all nations. Make me a faithful witness, fill me with the power of Your Spirit, and let my life overflow with joy and praise to God. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Book 4 of 27

# John

## About This Gospel

The Gospel of John is the fourth Gospel and the most reflective of the four. Its author describes himself as “the disciple whom Jesus loved” (*John 21:20–24*), and early Christian tradition identifies him as John the son of Zebedee, one of the Twelve. Most scholars date the book to the last decades of the first century, and tradition connects it with the church in Ephesus. John tells us plainly why he wrote: “*these are written, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name*” (*John 20:31*).

## The Shape of the Book

John opens with a majestic prologue about the eternal Word who became flesh (*1:1–18*). The first half of the book (chapters 1–12) is sometimes called the Book of Signs. It records seven miracles, beginning with water turned into wine at Cana and ending with the raising of Lazarus, and it places Jesus at the great Jewish feasts in Jerusalem. The second half (chapters 13–21) is sometimes called the Book of Glory. It slows down to cover Jesus’ final evening with His disciples, His long farewell teaching and prayer (chapters 13–17), and then His arrest, crucifixion, and resurrection appearances. About ninety percent of John’s material is not found in Matthew, Mark, or Luke.

## Themes to Watch For

John presents Jesus as the eternal Son who reveals the Father. Seven times Jesus says “I am” with a picture: the bread of life, the light of the world, the door, the good shepherd, the resurrection and the life, the way, the truth and the life, and the true vine. These sayings echo God’s name revealed to Moses. Key words recur through the book: believe, life, light, truth, love, witness, abide, and glory. John shows that faith is a personal response to Jesus, that eternal life begins now in knowing God (*17:3*), and that the Holy Spirit, the Counselor, continues Jesus’ presence with His people after He returns to the Father.

John · Chapter 1 of 21

# John — Chapter 1

Chapter Theme: The Word Became Flesh: God Revealed in Jesus

[Read John 1 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/JHN01.htm)

Main Teaching

John opens his Gospel by declaring that the eternal Word, who was with God and was God, through whom all things were made, became flesh and lived among us, full of grace and truth. John the Baptist testifies that he is not the Messiah but the voice preparing the way, and he points to Jesus as the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world. The first disciples begin to follow Jesus, inviting others to “come and see.”

## Chapter Background and Story

The Gospel of John is different in style from Matthew, Mark, and Luke. Early Christian tradition identifies its author as John the apostle, the son of Zebedee, “the disciple whom Jesus loved” (*John 21:20–24*), writing probably near the end of the first century, likely in Ephesus. John includes many events and teachings not found in the other Gospels, such as the wedding at Cana, Jesus’ conversations with Nicodemus and the Samaritan woman, the raising of Lazarus, and Jesus’ long farewell discourse. John explains his purpose near the end of the book: “*these are written, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name*” (*John 20:31*).

*John 1* has two main parts. The first (vv. 1–18), often called the Prologue, is a profound reflection on who Jesus is, written in poetic, deeply theological language. The second (vv. 19–51) tells how John the Baptist testified about Jesus and how the first disciples came to follow Him.

### The Word Who Was God (*1:1–5*)

John begins with words that deliberately echo *Genesis 1:1*: “*In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God*” (*v. 1*). This verse is studied below. John uses the term “Word” (Greek “Logos”) to describe the eternal Son of God before He became human. The Word was the agent of creation: “*All things were made through him. Without him, nothing was made that has been made*” (*v. 3*). In the Word was life, and that life was the light of all people. “*The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness hasn’t overcome it*” (*v. 5*). The word “overcome” can also mean “understood” or “grasped.” Darkness has neither understood the light nor been able to extinguish it. This anticipates the conflict throughout John’s Gospel between light and darkness, which reaches its climax at the cross, where the darkness seems to win but is defeated by the resurrection.

### John the Witness (*1:6–8*)

John (the writer always calls him simply “John,” never “John the Baptist”) was “*a man sent from God*” (*v. 6*). He came as a witness to testify about the light, so that all might believe through him. “*He was not the light*” (*v. 8*). The Gospel writer is careful to show that John the Baptist, though important, was only a witness pointing to Jesus. Some people in the first century continued to follow John the Baptist as though he were the Messiah (*Acts 19:1–7*), so the Gospel writer clarifies his role.

### The Light Came Into the World (*1:9–13*)

The true light, which gives light to everyone, was coming into the world. “*He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world didn’t recognize him*” (*v. 10*). The tragedy is that the Creator came into His own creation, and the creation did not know Him. “*He came to his own, and those who were his own didn’t receive him*” (*v. 11*). “His own” first refers to Israel, God’s chosen people, many of whom rejected Him. But there is good news, studied below: “*But as many as received him, to them he gave the right to become God’s children, to those who believe in his name*” (*v. 12*).

### The Word Became Flesh (*1:14–18*)

Then comes the climax of the Prologue: “*The Word became flesh and lived among us*” (*v. 14*). This verse is studied below. John the Baptist testified that Jesus, though He came after John in time, existed before him. From His fullness, believers have all received “*grace upon grace*” (*v. 16*), one blessing after another, an unending supply.

“*For the law was given through Moses. Grace and truth were realized through Jesus Christ*” (*v. 17*). The law was itself a gift of God, but in Jesus, God’s grace and truth were revealed in their fullness. “*No one has seen God at any time*” (*v. 18*). Even Moses was not allowed to see God’s face (*Exodus 33:20*). But “*The only born Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has declared him*” (*v. 18*). (Many manuscripts read “the only begotten God.”) Jesus, who shares the closest relationship with the Father, has made God known. To see Jesus is to see what God is like.

### John’s Testimony About Himself (*1:19–28*)

The religious authorities in Jerusalem sent priests and Levites to ask John, “Who are you?” John said plainly, “*I am not the Christ*” (*v. 20*). They asked if he was Elijah, whom *Malachi 4:5* said would return before the day of the Lord. He said no. (Jesus later said John fulfilled Elijah’s role, *Matthew 11:14*, but John did not claim this title for himself.) They asked if he was “the Prophet,” the prophet like Moses promised in *Deuteronomy 18:15*. He said no.

Finally John answered, “*I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness, ‘Make straight the way of the Lord,’ as Isaiah the prophet said*” (*v. 23*). John saw himself as only a voice, a messenger whose importance came entirely from the one he announced. When asked why he baptized, John said he baptized with water, but “*among you stands one whom you don’t know*” (*v. 26*). He was not worthy even to untie His sandal strap, the task of the lowest servant. These events took place at Bethany beyond the Jordan, a different Bethany from the village near Jerusalem.

### The Lamb of God (*1:29–34*)

The next day, John saw Jesus coming toward him and said, “*Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!*” (*v. 29*) This declaration is studied below. John explained that he had not known who the Messiah would be, but God had told him that the one on whom he saw the Spirit descend and remain would be the one who baptizes with the Holy Spirit. John had seen the Spirit descend like a dove and remain on Jesus. “*I have seen and have testified that this is the Son of God*” (*v. 34*).

### The First Disciples (*1:35–51*)

The following day, John was standing with two of his disciples when Jesus walked by. John said again, “*Behold, the Lamb of God!*” (*v. 36*) The two disciples heard this and followed Jesus. Jesus turned and asked them, “*What are you looking for?*” (*v. 38*) These are the first words Jesus speaks in John’s Gospel, and they are a question every reader must answer. The disciples asked where He was staying. Jesus said, “*Come and see*” (*v. 39*). They went and stayed with Him that day. It was about four in the afternoon, a detail that suggests an eyewitness memory.

One of the two was Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother. (The other is unnamed, and many believe he was John, the Gospel’s author.) Andrew first found his brother Simon and told him, “*We have found the Messiah!*” (*v. 41*) He brought Simon to Jesus. Jesus looked at him and said, “*You are Simon the son of Jonah. You shall be called Cephas*” (*v. 42*), which means “rock” in Aramaic, or Peter in Greek. Jesus saw not only who Simon was but who he would become.

The next day Jesus found Philip and said, “Follow me.” Philip found Nathanael and told him they had found the one Moses and the prophets wrote about: Jesus of Nazareth. Nathanael was skeptical: “*Can any good thing come out of Nazareth?*” (*v. 46*) Nazareth was a small, insignificant village. Philip replied simply, “*Come and see*” (*v. 46*).

When Jesus saw Nathanael coming, He said, “*Behold, an Israelite indeed, in whom is no deceit!*” (*v. 47*) Nathanael was surprised and asked how Jesus knew him. Jesus said He had seen him under the fig tree before Philip called him. Sitting under a fig tree was sometimes associated with studying Scripture and meditating. Nathanael was amazed and declared, “*Rabbi, you are the Son of God! You are King of Israel!*” (*v. 49*) Jesus said he would see greater things: “*hereafter you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man*” (*v. 51*). This recalls Jacob’s dream of a ladder reaching to heaven with angels going up and down on it (*Genesis 28:12*). Jesus is the true connection between heaven and earth, the meeting place of God and humanity.

## Important Verses Explained

### *John 1:1* — In the Beginning Was the Word

> *“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”*
>
> — *John 1:1* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This is the opening sentence of John’s Gospel, and it is one of the most important sentences in the Bible. Matthew begins with Jesus’ genealogy, Mark with John the Baptist, and Luke with the births of John and Jesus. John begins before time itself.

“*In the beginning*” (*v. 1*). These words deliberately echo the first words of the Bible, *Genesis 1:1*: “*In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth*” (*Genesis 1:1*). John takes his readers back before creation, to eternity.

“*was the Word*” (*v. 1*). The Greek word “Logos” means “word,” “message,” or “reason.” For Jewish readers, “word” recalled God’s creative word in Genesis (“God said, ‘Let there be light’”), His word that came to the prophets, and the personified Wisdom of God in passages like *Proverbs 8*, which was with God before creation. For Greek readers, “Logos” was a philosophical term for the rational principle that orders the universe. John uses a term both audiences would recognize, and then fills it with new meaning: the Word is a person, Jesus Christ. Notice that “was” describes ongoing existence. When the beginning began, the Word already existed. The Word did not come into being; He always was.

“*and the Word was with God*” (*v. 1*). The Word was in close relationship with God. The phrase suggests face-to-face fellowship. The Word is distinct from the Father, yet in intimate communion with Him.

“*and the Word was God*” (*v. 1*). The Word is not merely like God or a lesser divine being; He is God. In Greek, the word order emphasizes “God”: “and God was the Word.” This shows that the Word shares fully in God’s nature. Some groups have translated this “the Word was a god,” but this translation does not fit the grammar or the context of John’s Gospel, which repeatedly affirms Jesus’ full deity (*John 20:28*).

Together, the second and third clauses describe a mystery: the Word is distinct from God (He was “with God”) and yet is God. This is one of the foundations of the Christian doctrine of the Trinity: one God existing eternally as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

In verse 14, John identifies the Word: “The Word became flesh and lived among us.” The Word is Jesus.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals that Jesus is eternal and divine. He did not begin to exist at His birth in Bethlehem. He existed before creation, in perfect fellowship with the Father, and He is fully God. Jesus later said, “*before Abraham came into existence, I AM*” (*John 8:58*), and Thomas would confess Him as “*My Lord and my God!*” (*John 20:28*)

It also reveals that God has always been relational. Before creation, the Word was “with God,” in loving fellowship. God did not create the world because He was lonely; He created out of the overflow of the love that eternally existed within Himself.

Finally, the verse shows that God has spoken. The Word is God’s self-expression, His communication to the world. In Jesus, God has spoken most clearly and completely (*Hebrews 1:1–2*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to worship Jesus as God. He is not merely a great teacher or prophet but the eternal Word, worthy of worship and complete trust. Believers can approach Him with reverence and love.

It also gives believers confidence that God has revealed Himself. They do not have to guess what God is like. They can look at Jesus, the Word, and know God. Reading the Gospels and meditating on Jesus’ life and teaching is the clearest way to know God.

Finally, this verse invites believers to listen to God’s Word. If Jesus is God’s Word, then His teaching carries God’s authority. Believers can listen to Him and let His words shape their lives.

### *John 1:12* — The Right to Become God’s Children

> *“But as many as received him, to them he gave the right to become God’s children, to those who believe in his name:”*
>
> — *John 1:12* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse comes right after a sad statement. John had written that the Word, through whom the world was made, came into the world, but the world did not recognize Him (v. 10). He came to His own people, Israel, and they did not receive Him (v. 11). Many rejected Jesus.

But this verse begins with the word “*But*” (*v. 12*), introducing hope. Not everyone rejected Him. “*as many as received him*” (*v. 12*). “Received” means welcomed or accepted. Some did welcome Jesus. The verse then clarifies what receiving Him means: “*to those who believe in his name*” (*v. 12*). To receive Jesus is to believe in His name, to trust Him as who He truly is. In the Bible, a person’s “name” represents their character and identity.

“*to them he gave the right to become God’s children*” (*v. 12*). “Right” can also be translated “authority” or “privilege.” Those who receive Jesus are given the privilege of becoming God’s children. This is a gift, not something earned. People are not automatically God’s children in this sense; they become His children by receiving Christ.

The next verse explains how this happens: they are “*born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God*” (*v. 13*). Becoming God’s child is not a matter of family heritage (“blood”), human desire (“the will of the flesh”), or human decision alone (“the will of man”). It is a work of God, a new birth that He brings about. Jesus will explain this new birth to Nicodemus in *John 3*.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals the heart of salvation: through faith in Jesus, people become children of God. This is more than forgiveness; it is adoption into God’s family. Paul writes, “*For you are all children of God, through faith in Christ Jesus*” (*Galatians 3:26*). Believers can call God “Father” and share in the inheritance of His children.

It also shows that salvation is both a gift and a response. God gives the right to become His children; people receive Christ and believe in His name. Both God’s initiative and human faith are involved, though the new birth itself is God’s work (v. 13).

Finally, the verse shows that God’s family is not limited by ethnicity or heritage. Some of “His own” rejected Him, but “as many as received him,” Jew or Gentile, became God’s children. This anticipates the inclusion of all nations in God’s family.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites everyone to receive Jesus and believe in His name. Becoming God’s child is not about religious background or good works but about trusting Jesus. Anyone can receive Him today.

It also gives believers a secure identity. They are children of God, loved and accepted by their heavenly Father. In times of insecurity, loneliness, or failure, they can remember who they are in Christ.

Finally, this verse calls believers to live as God’s children. Children often resemble their parents. As God’s children, believers can grow to reflect His character: His love, holiness, truth, and grace.

### *John 1:14* — The Word Became Flesh

> *“The Word became flesh and lived among us. We saw his glory, such glory as of the only born Son of the Father, full of grace and truth.”*
>
> — *John 1:14* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse is the climax of John’s Prologue. In verse 1, John declared that the Word was with God and was God. In verse 3, all things were made through Him. Now John states the astonishing truth: “*The Word became flesh and lived among us*” (*v. 14*).

“*The Word became flesh*” (*v. 14*). “Flesh” means full humanity, with a real human body, real human emotions, and real human limitations. The eternal Word, who was God, became a human being. This is called the incarnation, from a Latin word meaning “in flesh.” The Word did not merely appear to be human or temporarily inhabit a human body; He truly became human while remaining fully God. Some early teachers claimed Jesus only seemed to have a body, but John insists on His real flesh (*1 John 4:2*).

“*and lived among us*” (*v. 14*). The Greek word literally means “pitched His tent” or “tabernacled.” In the Old Testament, God’s presence dwelt among Israel in the tabernacle, a tent in the wilderness (*Exodus 25:8–9*; *40:34–35*). Now God’s presence dwelt among people in the person of Jesus. He is the true meeting place between God and humanity.

“*We saw his glory*” (*v. 14*). “We” refers to John and the other eyewitnesses. They saw Jesus’ glory, not only at the transfiguration but in His miracles, His love, His teaching, and supremely in His death and resurrection. In the Old Testament, God’s glory filled the tabernacle as a cloud. Now His glory was revealed in Jesus.

“*such glory as of the only born Son of the Father*” (*v. 14*). Jesus’ glory was the glory of the unique Son, sharing the Father’s nature. “Only born” (often translated “only begotten” or “one and only”) emphasizes His uniqueness.

“*full of grace and truth*” (*v. 14*). These words recall God’s self-description to Moses in *Exodus 34:6*, where God revealed Himself as “*abundant in loving kindness and truth*” (*Exodus 34:6*). Jesus embodies God’s steadfast love (grace) and faithfulness (truth). He is not grace without truth or truth without grace, but full of both.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals the wonder of the incarnation. The infinite God became a finite human being. The Creator entered His creation. The eternal Word was born as a baby, grew up, worked, ate, slept, suffered, and died. Paul describes this as Jesus emptying Himself and taking the form of a servant (*Philippians 2:6–8*).

It also reveals that God came near. He did not remain distant but came to live among His people. This fulfills the promise of Immanuel, “*God with us*” (*Matthew 1:23*). God understands human life from the inside.

Finally, the verse shows that the incarnation was necessary for salvation. Because Jesus became human, He could represent humanity and die for human sin. Because He is God, His life and death have infinite value. *Hebrews 2:14–17* explains that Jesus shared in flesh and blood so that through death He might destroy the power of death.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to marvel at God’s love. God loved the world so much that He came to live among people in Jesus. This love can fill believers with gratitude and worship.

It also brings comfort to believers in their struggles. Jesus experienced human life fully, including weakness, sorrow, temptation, and pain. He understands what believers face and can sympathize with their weaknesses (*Hebrews 4:15*).

Finally, this verse calls believers to reflect Jesus’ grace and truth. Many people lean toward either grace without truth, accepting everything, or truth without grace, being harsh and judgmental. Jesus was full of both. Believers can seek to speak truth with love and to show grace without compromising truth.

### *John 1:29* — The Lamb of God Who Takes Away the Sin of the World

> *“The next day, he saw Jesus coming to him, and said, Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!”*
>
> — *John 1:29* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These words were spoken by John the Baptist when he saw Jesus coming toward him at the Jordan River. The day before, religious leaders had asked John who he was, and he told them he was not the Messiah but a voice preparing the way for one who was coming. Now that one appeared.

“*Behold, the Lamb of God*” (*v. 29*). “Behold” means “Look!” John directed everyone’s attention to Jesus. “Lamb of God” was a rich image for Jewish listeners. Lambs were sacrificed in Israel’s worship. Each morning and evening, a lamb was offered in the temple (*Exodus 29:38–42*). At Passover, each family sacrificed a lamb, recalling how the blood of the Passover lamb protected Israel from judgment in Egypt (*Exodus 12*). *Isaiah 53:7* described the Servant of the Lord as “*a lamb that is led to the slaughter*” (*Isaiah 53:7*), who bore the sins of many. And in *Genesis 22:8*, Abraham told Isaac that God Himself would provide the lamb for the sacrifice.

By calling Jesus “the Lamb of God,” John identified Him as the sacrifice that God Himself provides. Jesus would die like a sacrificial lamb.

“*who takes away the sin of the world!*” (*v. 29*) “Takes away” means removes or carries off. Jesus would bear sin and remove it. “Sin” is singular, referring to the whole reality of human rebellion against God. “Of the world” shows the scope of His work: not only Israel’s sin but the sin of all humanity. Jesus’ sacrifice would be for the whole world.

John’s Gospel later shows that Jesus was crucified at the time the Passover lambs were being prepared (*John 19:14*), and that none of His bones were broken, like the Passover lamb (*John 19:36*; *Exodus 12:46*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals the central purpose of Jesus’ coming: to deal with sin by offering Himself as a sacrifice. The Old Testament sacrificial system pointed forward to Him. Hebrews explains that the blood of animals could not truly take away sins (*Hebrews 10:4*), but Jesus offered Himself once for all (*Hebrews 10:10–14*).

It also shows the universal scope of Jesus’ work. He takes away the sin “of the world.” His sacrifice is sufficient for every person, and the offer of forgiveness is extended to all. John later writes, “*He is the atoning sacrifice for our sins, and not for ours only, but also for the whole world*” (*1 John 2:2*).

Finally, the image of the Lamb shows the humility and gentleness of Jesus. The one who is the eternal Word, through whom all things were made, came as a lamb to be sacrificed. In Revelation, Jesus is pictured as the Lamb who was slain, now standing on the throne, worthy of all worship (*Revelation 5:6–12*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to look to Jesus for forgiveness. Whatever sins burden them, Jesus, the Lamb of God, has taken them away. They can come to Him in faith and receive forgiveness.

It also calls believers to point others to Jesus, as John the Baptist did. John did not draw attention to himself; he said, “Behold, the Lamb of God!” Believers can direct people to Jesus as the only one who can take away sin.

Finally, this verse invites believers to worship Jesus with gratitude. The Lamb of God gave Himself for them. Remembering His sacrifice can deepen love for Him and inspire lives of grateful obedience.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*John 1* reveals who Jesus is in the most profound terms. He is the eternal Word, who was with God and was God. Through Him all things were made. He is the light that shines in the darkness, the source of life. He became flesh and lived among us, full of grace and truth. He is the only Son who makes the Father known, the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world, the Son of God, and the King of Israel. Believers can respond with worship, trust, and wonder.

The chapter also shows how people respond to Jesus. Some, including many of His own people, rejected Him. But those who received Him and believed in His name were given the right to become God’s children. Everyone must decide how to respond. Believers can rejoice in their identity as God’s children and invite others to receive Jesus.

John the Baptist’s humility provides an example. He knew he was not the light, only a witness. He pointed people away from himself to Jesus. Believers can serve faithfully while directing attention to Christ.

Finally, the first disciples show how faith spreads. Jesus invited them to “come and see.” Andrew brought his brother Peter. Philip told Nathanael to “come and see.” Faith often spreads through personal invitation. Believers can invite their family and friends to come and see Jesus for themselves, trusting that He will reveal Himself to those who seek Him.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, You are the eternal Word, who was with God and is God. Through You all things were made, and in You is life and light. I worship You. Thank You that You became flesh and lived among us, full of grace and truth, so that I could see the glory of God and know the Father.

Thank You for giving me the right to become a child of God by receiving You and believing in Your name. You are the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world. Thank You for taking away my sin. Help me to point others to You, as John the Baptist did, and to invite my family and friends to come and see. Fill me with Your grace and truth, and let Your light shine through me in the darkness. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
