John · Chapter 2 of 21

# John — Chapter 2

Chapter Theme: New Wine and a New Temple

[Read John 2 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/JHN02.htm)

Main Teaching

At a wedding in Cana, Jesus turns water set aside for ritual washing into abundant, excellent wine, the first of His signs, revealing His glory so that His disciples believe. At Passover in Jerusalem, He drives the merchants out of the temple and declares that if this temple is destroyed He will raise it in three days, speaking of His own body. Jesus brings the joy of God’s new age and is Himself the true meeting place between God and people.

## Chapter Background and Story

*John 2* contains two events that introduce major themes of John’s Gospel. John calls Jesus’ miracles “signs,” because they point beyond themselves to reveal who Jesus is. The first sign, at Cana, shows Jesus bringing abundant joy and transforming the old into the new. The second event, the cleansing of the temple, shows that Jesus Himself replaces the temple as the place where people meet God. Both events concern Jewish religious practices, ceremonial washing jars and the Jerusalem temple, and both show Jesus fulfilling and surpassing them.

### The Wedding at Cana (*2:1–11*)

“*The third day*” (*v. 1*), counting from Jesus’ conversation with Nathanael, there was a wedding in Cana of Galilee, a village a few miles north of Nazareth. Nathanael came from Cana (*John 21:2*). Jesus’ mother was there, and Jesus and His disciples had also been invited.

Weddings in that culture were major community celebrations that could last a week. The groom’s family was responsible for providing food and drink for the guests. Running out of wine would have been a serious embarrassment, a social disgrace that could be remembered for years, and in some cases could even lead to legal complaints from guests who had given gifts.

When the wine ran out, Jesus’ mother told Him, “*They have no wine*” (*v. 3*). She seems to have expected Jesus to do something. Jesus replied, “*Woman, what does that have to do with you and me? My hour has not yet come*” (*v. 4*). Addressing His mother as “Woman” was not rude in that culture; it was a respectful but somewhat formal address. Jesus uses it again from the cross when He lovingly provides for her (*John 19:26*). His question suggests that His actions would be guided by His Father’s timing, not by family requests. “My hour” is an important theme in John’s Gospel. Jesus’ “hour” refers to the time of His death, resurrection, and glorification (*John 12:23*; *13:1*; *17:1*).

His mother did not argue. She said to the servants, “*Whatever he says to you, do it*” (*v. 5*). This verse is studied below.

Six stone water jars stood nearby, used “*after the Jews’ way of purifying*” (*v. 6*). Jews washed their hands and utensils before meals for ritual purity (*Mark 7:3–4*). Stone jars were used because, according to Jewish law, stone did not become ritually unclean as pottery could. Each jar held twenty or thirty gallons, so together they held about 120 to 180 gallons.

Jesus told the servants to fill the jars with water, and they filled them to the brim. Then He told them to draw some out and take it to the master of the banquet, who was in charge of the feast. The master tasted the water that had become wine, without knowing where it came from, though the servants knew. He called the bridegroom and said, “*Everyone serves the good wine first, and when the guests have drunk freely, then that which is worse. You have kept the good wine until now!*” (*v. 10*)

John concludes, “*This beginning of his signs Jesus did in Cana of Galilee, and revealed his glory; and his disciples believed in him*” (*v. 11*). This verse is studied below.

### Interlude in Capernaum (*2:12*)

After the wedding, Jesus went down to Capernaum with His mother, brothers, and disciples, and they stayed there a few days. Capernaum, on the shore of the Sea of Galilee, became Jesus’ base for much of His Galilean ministry.

### Cleansing the Temple (*2:13–22*)

When the Jewish Passover was near, Jesus went up to Jerusalem. John’s Gospel records Jesus attending several festivals in Jerusalem, showing that His ministry lasted about three years.

In the temple courts, Jesus found people selling oxen, sheep, and doves, and money changers sitting at their tables. Pilgrims needed animals that met the requirements for sacrifice, and they needed to exchange foreign currency for the Tyrian shekels used for the temple tax. These services were convenient, but they had turned the outer court, the only area where Gentiles could worship, into a noisy marketplace, and there was opportunity for exploitation.

Jesus made a whip of cords and drove them all out of the temple, with the sheep and oxen. He poured out the money changers’ coins and overturned their tables. To those selling doves, He said, “*Take these things out of here! Don’t make my Father’s house a marketplace!*” (*v. 16*) Jesus called the temple “my Father’s house,” claiming a unique relationship with God.

His disciples remembered *Psalm 69:9*: “*Zeal for your house will eat me up*” (*v. 17*). Jesus’ passion for God’s honor would consume Him, and ultimately it would lead to His death.

The Jewish authorities asked, “*What sign do you show us, seeing that you do these things?*” (*v. 18*) They wanted proof of His authority to act this way. Jesus answered, “*Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up*” (*v. 19*). This statement is studied below. They misunderstood, thinking He meant the physical temple, which had been under construction for forty-six years. (Herod the Great began rebuilding it around 20 B.C., and work continued for decades.) But John explains, “*But he spoke of the temple of his body*” (*v. 21*). After Jesus was raised from the dead, His disciples remembered what He had said and believed the Scripture and His words.

John places this event early in Jesus’ ministry, while Matthew, Mark, and Luke place a temple cleansing during His final week. Some scholars believe Jesus cleansed the temple twice, at the beginning and end of His ministry. Others think John placed the event early for theological reasons, to show from the start that Jesus replaces the temple. Either way, the meaning is the same: Jesus has authority over God’s house, and He Himself is the new meeting place between God and people.

### Many Believe, But Jesus Knows Their Hearts (*2:23–25*)

While Jesus was in Jerusalem during the Passover festival, many people believed in His name when they saw the signs He was doing. But Jesus “*didn’t entrust himself to them, because he knew everyone*” (*v. 24*). He did not need anyone’s testimony about people, “*for he himself knew what was in man*” (*v. 25*). There is a play on words in the Greek: many “believed” in Jesus, but Jesus did not “believe” (entrust) Himself to them. Their faith was based on miracles and may have been shallow. Jesus knew the human heart and knew that some who were impressed by signs would not truly follow Him. This prepares for the next chapter, where Nicodemus, one of these impressed observers, comes to Jesus at night.

## Important Verses Explained

### *John 2:5* — “*Whatever He Says to You, Do It*” (*v. 5*)

> *“His mother said to the servants, ‘Whatever he says to you, do it.’”*
>
> — *John 2:5* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These words were spoken by Jesus’ mother, Mary, to the servants at the wedding in Cana. The wedding celebration was in progress when the wine ran out, a serious embarrassment for the bridegroom’s family, who were responsible for providing for the guests. Mary told Jesus, “They have no wine.” She seems to have trusted that He could do something about it.

Jesus responded, “Woman, what does that have to do with you and me? My hour has not yet come.” His answer showed that He would act according to His Father’s timing and purposes, not simply because His mother asked. Yet Mary was not discouraged. She turned to the servants and said, “*Whatever he says to you, do it*” (*v. 5*).

Mary’s words show remarkable faith. She did not know exactly what Jesus would do, and she did not try to tell Him how to solve the problem. She simply trusted Him and instructed the servants to obey whatever He commanded.

Her words also echo *Genesis 41:55*, where Pharaoh told the starving Egyptians during a famine, “*Go to Joseph. What he says to you, do*” (*Genesis 41:55*). Joseph provided for the people’s needs; Jesus would provide for this wedding, and ultimately for all who come to Him.

The servants obeyed. When Jesus told them to fill six large stone jars with water, they filled them to the brim. When He told them to draw some out and take it to the master of the banquet, they did. Their obedience was part of the miracle. They did not understand what Jesus was doing, but they followed His instructions, and the water became wine.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse expresses the heart of discipleship: doing whatever Jesus says. Mary, the mother of Jesus, points people not to herself but to her Son. Her words are a fitting summary of faith: trust Jesus and obey Him.

It also shows that faith often involves obeying without fully understanding. The servants filled the jars with water and drew some out to serve, which must have seemed strange. But their obedience made them witnesses to Jesus’ first sign. Often, believers see God’s work only after they obey.

Finally, the verse shows the value of bringing needs to Jesus and then trusting His response. Mary brought the need to Jesus, accepted His answer, and trusted Him to act in His own way. Believers can do the same in prayer.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to commit to doing whatever Jesus says. His commands are found in Scripture: love God and neighbor, forgive, be generous, tell the truth, serve others, and follow Him. Believers can ask, “What is Jesus telling me to do?” and then obey, even when it is difficult or does not make sense to them.

It also encourages believers to bring their needs to Jesus and trust Him with the answer. Like Mary, they can tell Him honestly what is lacking, without dictating how He should respond, and then wait for His direction.

Finally, this verse reminds believers that obedience often comes before understanding. The servants did not know what Jesus would do until they obeyed. Believers may find that God reveals His work as they take steps of faithful obedience.

### *John 2:11* — The First Sign Revealed His Glory

> *“This beginning of his signs Jesus did in Cana of Galilee, and revealed his glory; and his disciples believed in him.”*
>
> — *John 2:11* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse concludes the story of the wedding at Cana. Jesus had turned about 120 to 180 gallons of water into wine, and the master of the banquet, not knowing where it came from, praised the bridegroom for saving the best wine until last. Most hosts served the best wine first and cheaper wine later, when guests were less likely to notice. This wine was excellent and abundant.

John comments, “*This beginning of his signs Jesus did in Cana of Galilee*” (*v. 11*). John calls Jesus’ miracles “signs,” a word he uses deliberately. A sign points beyond itself to something greater. Jesus’ miracles were not just displays of power; they revealed who He is. John’s Gospel records seven major signs before Jesus’ death and resurrection, and this is the first.

“*and revealed his glory*” (*v. 11*). “Glory” refers to the visible display of God’s presence, character, and power. In *John 1:14*, John wrote, “*We saw his glory*” (*John 1:14*). At Cana, Jesus’ glory was revealed in His power over creation, His generosity, and His care for people in need.

“*and his disciples believed in him*” (*v. 11*). The sign led to faith. The disciples, who had just begun following Jesus, saw His glory and trusted Him more deeply.

What did this sign reveal? First, Jesus’ power over creation: only the Creator can transform water into wine. Second, His abundant generosity: He provided far more than was needed, and of the highest quality. The Old Testament prophets pictured the age of the Messiah as a time of overflowing wine and joy (*Amos 9:13–14*; *Isaiah 25:6*). Third, the transformation of the old into the new: the water came from jars used for Jewish purification rituals, and Jesus turned it into the wine of celebration. He brings something better than the old ways of purification.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that Jesus’ miracles are meant to reveal His identity and lead to faith. John wrote his Gospel so that readers would believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God (*John 20:31*). Each sign is an invitation to see Jesus’ glory and trust Him.

It also shows that Jesus brings joy. His first sign was not at a funeral or in a synagogue, but at a wedding celebration. He saved a family from embarrassment and kept a celebration going. God’s kingdom is often pictured as a wedding feast (*Matthew 22:2*; *Revelation 19:7–9*). Jesus brings the joy of that kingdom into ordinary life.

Finally, the sign points to the new covenant. The water for purification represents the old system of ritual cleansing. Jesus transformed it into wine, which later, at the Last Supper, would represent His blood of the new covenant. Jesus brings a deeper cleansing and a greater joy than the old rituals could provide.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to look for Jesus’ glory in His works. When they read the Gospels or reflect on how God has worked in their lives, they can ask what these things reveal about Jesus and allow them to deepen their faith.

It also reminds believers that Jesus cares about ordinary human needs and joys. A wedding running out of wine was not a life-or-death crisis, yet Jesus cared. Believers can bring everyday concerns to Him, trusting that He cares about their lives.

Finally, this verse encourages believers to expect Jesus’ abundant generosity. He did not provide just enough wine; He provided an overflowing supply of the best wine. While God does not promise believers everything they want, He is generous, and His grace is more than sufficient.

### *John 2:19–21* — The Temple of His Body

> *“Jesus answered them, ‘Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.’ The Jews therefore said, ‘It took forty-six years to build this temple! Will you raise it up in three days?’ But he spoke of the temple of his body.”*
>
> — *John 2:19–21* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These verses record Jesus’ answer to the religious authorities after He cleansed the temple. During Passover, Jesus found merchants selling animals and money changers at their tables in the temple courts. He made a whip from cords, drove them out, overturned the tables, and said, “Don’t make my Father’s house a marketplace!”

The Jewish authorities challenged Him: “What sign do you show us, seeing that you do these things?” They wanted proof that He had authority to act this way.

Jesus answered, “*Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up*” (*v. 19*). He did not perform a miracle on the spot. Instead, He gave them a puzzling statement.

The authorities misunderstood: “*It took forty-six years to build this temple! Will you raise it up in three days?*” (*v. 20*) Herod the Great had begun a massive rebuilding of the temple around 20 B.C., and construction was still ongoing. To them, Jesus’ words seemed absurd.

But John explains, “*But he spoke of the temple of his body*” (*v. 21*). Jesus was speaking of His own body. The authorities would “destroy” it by having Him crucified, and He would raise it on the third day. His resurrection would be the sign that proved His authority.

Verse 22 adds that after Jesus was raised from the dead, His disciples remembered this statement and believed the Scripture and Jesus’ words. At the time, they did not understand, but the resurrection made everything clear.

Jesus’ words were later twisted and used against Him at His trial, where false witnesses claimed He had said He would destroy the temple (*Mark 14:58*), and they were thrown back at Him as He hung on the cross (*Mark 15:29*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses reveal that Jesus Himself is the true temple. In the Old Testament, the temple was the place where God’s presence dwelt among His people and where sacrifices were offered for sin. Jesus’ body is now the place where God dwells with humanity (*John 1:14*) and where the final sacrifice for sin was made. The physical temple was destroyed by the Romans in A.D. 70, but Jesus, the true temple, was raised and lives forever.

They also point to the resurrection as the ultimate sign. The authorities demanded a sign; Jesus pointed to His death and resurrection. Throughout the Gospels, the resurrection is the supreme proof of Jesus’ identity and authority (*Romans 1:4*).

Finally, these verses connect to the church. The New Testament teaches that believers, united to Christ, become God’s temple, the dwelling place of His Spirit (*1 Corinthians 3:16*; *6:19*; *Ephesians 2:21–22*). Through Jesus, God now dwells in His people.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses invite believers to meet God through Jesus. They do not need to travel to a particular building or perform certain rituals to come into God’s presence. Jesus is the meeting place between God and humanity. Through Him, believers can approach God anywhere.

They also give believers confidence in the resurrection. Jesus predicted His resurrection, and it happened. This gives assurance that His other words are trustworthy.

Finally, these verses remind believers that they are now part of God’s temple. Their bodies and their community are places where God’s Spirit dwells. This calls them to honor God in how they live, both individually and together as the church.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*John 2* shows Jesus revealing His glory in two very different settings: a joyful wedding and a corrupted temple. At Cana, Jesus showed His care for ordinary human needs, His power over creation, and His abundant generosity. He transformed water used for purification into the best wine, showing that He brings the joy of God’s new age. Believers can bring their everyday needs to Jesus, trust His care, and expect Him to bring joy and transformation.

Mary’s words to the servants, “Whatever he says to you, do it,” summarize the response Jesus desires. Believers can commit to obeying Jesus, even when His instructions do not make sense to them, trusting that obedience leads to seeing His glory.

The cleansing of the temple shows Jesus’ zeal for God’s honor and His authority over God’s house. He would not allow worship to be turned into a marketplace. Believers can examine whether their worship has become cluttered with distractions or commercial concerns, and they can ask Jesus to cleanse their hearts.

Jesus’ statement about the temple of His body points to His death and resurrection and reveals that He is the true meeting place between God and humanity. Believers can approach God through Him with confidence. Finally, the note that Jesus knew what was in every human heart calls believers to genuine faith that goes beyond being impressed by miracles, a faith that entrusts itself fully to Jesus.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for revealing Your glory at the wedding in Cana, caring for ordinary needs and bringing abundant joy. Help me to bring my needs to You and to trust You with the answer. Like Mary, I want to say, “Whatever You say to me, I will do.” Give me faith to obey even when I do not understand.

Thank You for Your zeal for God’s house. Cleanse my heart of anything that distracts from true worship. Thank You that You are the true temple, the place where I meet God, and that You were raised on the third day just as You said. You know what is in my heart. Make my faith genuine, not based only on signs, but on trusting You completely. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

John · Chapter 3 of 21

# John — Chapter 3

Chapter Theme: Born Anew: God’s Love and the Gift of Eternal Life

[Read John 3 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/JHN03.htm)

Main Teaching

Nicodemus, a respected Pharisee, comes to Jesus by night and learns that no one can see God’s kingdom without being born anew by the Spirit. Jesus explains that, like the bronze serpent Moses lifted up, the Son of Man must be lifted up so that whoever believes may have eternal life, because God so loved the world that He gave His only Son. When John the Baptist’s followers worry about Jesus’ growing popularity, John rejoices like the bridegroom’s friend and declares that Jesus must increase while he decreases.

## Chapter Background and Story

*John 3* contains one of the most famous conversations in the Bible and one of its most beloved verses, *John 3:16*. The chapter follows the end of *John 2*, where many in Jerusalem believed in Jesus because of His signs, but Jesus did not entrust Himself to them because “*he himself knew what was in man*” (*John 2:25*). Nicodemus is an example of such a person: impressed by Jesus’ signs, but not yet understanding who He is.

### Nicodemus Comes by Night (*3:1–2*)

Nicodemus was “*a man of the Pharisees*” (*v. 1*) and “*a ruler of the Jews*” (*v. 1*), meaning he was likely a member of the Sanhedrin, the ruling council in Jerusalem. Jesus later calls him “*the teacher of Israel*” (*v. 10*), suggesting he was a well-known teacher of the law. He was respected, educated, and devout.

He came to Jesus “*by night*” (*v. 2*). Perhaps he wanted to avoid being seen with a controversial teacher, or perhaps he wanted an uninterrupted conversation. In John’s Gospel, night and darkness often symbolize spiritual ignorance (*John 1:5*; *13:30*). Nicodemus came out of the darkness toward the light.

He began respectfully: “*Rabbi, we know that you are a teacher who has come from God, for no one can do these signs that you do, unless God is with him*” (*v. 2*). Nicodemus acknowledged Jesus as a God-sent teacher based on His miracles. But this was not yet full understanding of who Jesus is.

### You Must Be Born Anew (*3:3–8*)

Jesus responded directly: “*Most certainly I tell you, unless one is born anew, he can’t see God’s Kingdom*” (*v. 3*). This is studied below. The Greek word translated “anew” can mean “again” or “from above,” and Jesus may intend both.

Nicodemus took Jesus’ words literally: “*How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter a second time into his mother’s womb and be born?*” (*v. 4*) He may have understood that Jesus was speaking figuratively but wondered how an old man could start over completely.

Jesus explained, “*unless one is born of water and Spirit, he can’t enter into God’s Kingdom*” (*v. 5*). Christians have understood “water and Spirit” in several ways. Some see “water” as referring to physical birth and “Spirit” to spiritual birth. Others connect “water” with baptism, which was already being practiced by John and Jesus’ disciples (*John 3:22–23*). Many see it as a reference to *Ezekiel 36:25–27*, where God promised to sprinkle clean water on His people and give them a new heart and a new spirit, describing inner cleansing and renewal by God’s Spirit. Since Jesus rebuked Nicodemus as a teacher of Israel for not understanding (v. 10), He likely expected him to recognize this Old Testament promise. In any case, the emphasis is on spiritual cleansing and new life given by the Holy Spirit.

“*That which is born of the flesh is flesh. That which is born of the Spirit is spirit*” (*v. 6*). Human birth produces human life, but only the Spirit can produce spiritual life. Jesus then used an image: “*The wind blows where it wants to, and you hear its sound, but don’t know where it comes from and where it is going. So is everyone who is born of the Spirit*” (*v. 8*). In both Hebrew and Greek, the same word means “wind,” “breath,” and “spirit.” The Spirit’s work is like the wind: invisible and beyond human control, yet its effects are real and observable.

### Heavenly Things (*3:9–15*)

Nicodemus asked, “*How can these things be?*” (*v. 9*) Jesus replied, “*Are you the teacher of Israel, and don’t understand these things?*” (*v. 10*) Nicodemus, as a respected teacher, should have known the prophets’ promises of spiritual renewal.

Jesus said that He spoke of what He knew and had seen, yet people did not accept His testimony. If they did not believe when He spoke of earthly things, such as the new birth that happens on earth, how would they believe if He spoke of heavenly things? “*No one has ascended into heaven but he who descended out of heaven, the Son of Man*” (*v. 13*). Jesus alone came from heaven and can reveal heavenly truth.

Then He pointed to an Old Testament story: “*As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of Man be lifted up*” (*v. 14*). In *Numbers 21:4–9*, the Israelites complained against God in the wilderness, and venomous snakes bit them, and many died. God told Moses to make a bronze snake and put it on a pole. Anyone who was bitten could look at the bronze snake and live. Jesus said He must be “lifted up” in the same way. In John’s Gospel, “lifted up” refers to His crucifixion (*John 12:32–33*) and also to His exaltation. Just as the Israelites looked at the bronze snake and lived, people who look to Jesus in faith receive eternal life: “*that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life*” (*v. 15*).

### God So Loved the World (*3:16–21*)

Then comes perhaps the most famous verse in the Bible: “*For God so loved the world, that he gave his only born Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life*” (*v. 16*). This verse is studied below. (Scholars debate whether Jesus’ words to Nicodemus end at verse 15 or verse 21, with the rest being John’s reflection. Either way, these verses explain the meaning of what Jesus taught.)

“*For God didn’t send his Son into the world to judge the world, but that the world should be saved through him*” (*v. 17*). God’s purpose in sending Jesus was salvation, not condemnation. “*He who believes in him is not judged. He who doesn’t believe has been judged already*” (*v. 18*). Those who refuse to believe are already under condemnation, not because Jesus came to condemn them, but because they reject the only way of rescue.

Then John explains the nature of this judgment: people love darkness rather than light. This is studied below. Those who do evil hate the light and avoid it, so their deeds will not be exposed. But those who practice the truth come to the light, so that it may be seen that their deeds have been done in God.

### John the Baptist’s Final Testimony (*3:22–36*)

After this, Jesus and His disciples went into the Judean countryside, where they spent time and baptized. (*John 4:2* clarifies that Jesus Himself did not baptize; His disciples did.) John the Baptist was also baptizing at Aenon near Salim, where there was plenty of water, since he had not yet been put in prison.

A dispute arose between some of John’s disciples and a certain Jew about purification, perhaps about whose baptism was more effective. John’s disciples came to him concerned: the one John had testified about was now baptizing, and “*everyone is coming to him*” (*v. 26*). They seemed jealous on John’s behalf.

John answered with deep humility. A person can receive only what is given from heaven. He reminded them that he had said he was not the Messiah but was sent ahead of Him. He used the image of a wedding: the bride belongs to the bridegroom, and the friend of the bridegroom, the best man, rejoices when he hears the bridegroom’s voice. “*Therefore my joy is made full*” (*v. 29*). John was glad that people were going to Jesus. Then he said, “*He must increase, but I must decrease*” (*v. 30*). This verse is studied below.

The chapter closes with a reflection on Jesus’ heavenly origin and authority (vv. 31–36). The one who comes from above is above all. God has given Him the Spirit without measure. “*The Father loves the Son, and has given all things into his hand*” (*v. 35*). “*One who believes in the Son has eternal life, but one who disobeys the Son won’t see life, but the wrath of God remains on him*” (*v. 36*). Notice that believing and obeying are linked; true faith shows itself in obedience.

## Important Verses Explained

### *John 3:3* — You Must Be Born Anew

> *“Jesus answered him, ‘Most certainly I tell you, unless one is born anew, he can’t see God’s Kingdom.’”*
>
> — *John 3:3* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse is Jesus’ first response to Nicodemus, a Pharisee and respected teacher who came to Jesus at night. Nicodemus had opened with a compliment: he recognized that Jesus was a teacher sent from God, because no one could perform such signs unless God was with him. He seemed ready to engage Jesus in a respectful discussion between teachers.

But Jesus went straight to the heart of the matter: “*Most certainly I tell you, unless one is born anew, he can’t see God’s Kingdom*” (*v. 3*).

“*Most certainly I tell you*” (*v. 3*) (literally “Amen, amen”) marks a solemn, important statement.

“*unless one is born anew*” (*v. 3*). The Greek word “anothen” can mean “again” or “from above.” Nicodemus understood it as “again,” a second birth. Jesus likely intended both meanings: a person must be born again, and this new birth comes from above, from God. It is not something a person can produce by effort.

“*he can’t see God’s Kingdom*” (*v. 3*). “See” here means experience or enter (as verse 5 says, “enter into God’s Kingdom”). The kingdom of God is God’s reign, His saving rule and the life of the age to come. Without new birth, no one can participate in it.

This statement would have startled Nicodemus. As a devout Pharisee and a Jew, he likely assumed he already belonged to God’s people and would share in God’s kingdom. He kept God’s law carefully. But Jesus told him that even he needed to be born anew. Religious heritage, knowledge, and moral effort were not enough. He needed a completely new beginning from God.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse teaches that salvation requires an inner transformation that only God can accomplish. Human beings cannot reform themselves into God’s kingdom. They need new life from God, which the Holy Spirit gives. Paul describes this as becoming a new creation: “*if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation*” (*2 Corinthians 5:17*). Peter speaks of being born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus (*1 Peter 1:3*).

It also shows that everyone needs new birth, even the most religious. Nicodemus was respectable, educated, and devout, yet Jesus told him he must be born anew. Religious practice cannot substitute for spiritual rebirth.

Finally, the image of birth emphasizes God’s initiative. No one causes their own birth. In the same way, spiritual birth is God’s gift. *John 1:13* describes believers as born “*not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God*” (*John 1:13*). This new birth comes through faith in Jesus, as the rest of the chapter explains.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites everyone to consider whether they have been born anew. It is possible to grow up in church, know the Bible, and live morally without having experienced the new life God gives. Each person can come to Jesus in faith, asking for the new birth that only God can give.

It also encourages humility. No one is too good or too religious to need new birth. Believers can approach others, including religious people, with the understanding that everyone needs God’s transforming grace.

Finally, this verse offers hope for real change. Many people feel stuck in old patterns, unable to change themselves. The new birth means that God can give a fresh start and a new heart. Believers can trust the Spirit to keep transforming them.

### *John 3:16* — For God So Loved the World

> *“For God so loved the world, that he gave his only born Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life.”*
>
> — *John 3:16* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse is perhaps the most famous verse in the Bible. It comes in the context of Jesus’ conversation with Nicodemus. Jesus had just explained that people must be born anew by the Spirit, and that, as Moses lifted up the bronze serpent in the wilderness so that bitten people could look at it and live, the Son of Man must be lifted up so that whoever believes in Him may have eternal life.

Then comes this summary of the gospel: “*For God so loved the world*” (*v. 16*). “So” means “in this way” or “to such a degree.” God’s love is the source of salvation. “The world” in John’s Gospel often refers to humanity in rebellion against God (*John 1:10*; *7:7*). God loved not a perfect world but a sinful one that had turned away from Him. His love is not limited to one nation or group; it extends to the whole world.

“*that he gave his only born Son*” (*v. 16*). God’s love was shown in action: He gave His Son. “Gave” refers to sending Jesus into the world and, ultimately, giving Him up to death on the cross. “Only born Son” (often translated “only begotten” or “one and only”) emphasizes Jesus’ unique relationship with the Father. God gave the most precious gift possible. This recalls Abraham being asked to offer his only son Isaac (*Genesis 22:2*), but where God spared Isaac, He did not spare His own Son (*Romans 8:32*).

“*that whoever believes in him*” (*v. 16*). “Whoever” opens the invitation to everyone. “Believes in him” means trusting Jesus, relying on Him, committing oneself to Him. It is more than agreeing with facts about Jesus; it is personal trust.

“*should not perish, but have eternal life*” (*v. 16*). There are two possible destinies. “Perish” means to be lost or destroyed, to experience final separation from God. “Eternal life” is more than endless existence; it is the life of the age to come, a quality of life found in knowing God (*John 17:3*). It begins now and continues forever.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse summarizes the heart of the Christian faith. God’s love is the motivation, the giving of His Son is the means, faith is the response, and eternal life is the result. Every part of the gospel is contained in this one sentence.

It reveals the depth of God’s love. God did not love the world because it was lovable; He loved it despite its rebellion. Paul writes, “*But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us*” (*Romans 5:8*). God’s love is costly, self-giving, and undeserved.

It also shows that salvation is a gift received through faith. Eternal life is not earned by good works but received by believing in Jesus. The word “whoever” means that no one is excluded from the invitation.

Finally, the following verses (vv. 17–18) clarify that God’s purpose in sending Jesus was to save, not to condemn. Condemnation is the result of rejecting the gift, not the goal of God’s coming.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites every person to believe in Jesus and receive eternal life. God’s love extends to everyone, and the offer is open to “whoever believes.” Those who have not yet trusted Jesus can do so today.

It also gives believers assurance of God’s love. When they feel unworthy or unloved, they can remember that God loved the world so much that He gave His Son. His love for them is proven at the cross.

Finally, this verse calls believers to share God’s love with the world. If God loved the world this much, His people should love others too, sharing the good news of Jesus with everyone, regardless of background.

### *John 3:19* — Loving Darkness Rather Than Light

> *“This is the judgment, that the light has come into the world, and men loved the darkness rather than the light, for their works were evil.”*
>
> — *John 3:19* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse explains why some people reject Jesus. John has just said that God sent His Son not to condemn the world but to save it. Whoever believes in Him is not condemned, but whoever does not believe is condemned already, because they have not believed in the name of God’s only Son (v. 18).

Now John explains the nature of that condemnation: “*This is the judgment, that the light has come into the world, and men loved the darkness rather than the light, for their works were evil*” (*v. 19*).

“*the light has come into the world*” (*v. 19*). Jesus is the light. In *John 1:4–9*, He is described as the light that shines in the darkness and gives light to everyone. Later Jesus says, “*I am the light of the world*” (*John 8:12*). Light reveals, exposes, guides, and gives life.

“*and men loved the darkness rather than the light*” (*v. 19*). Many people preferred darkness. “Darkness” represents sin, ignorance, and separation from God. The problem was not lack of evidence or lack of opportunity. Light had come, but people loved darkness more.

“*for their works were evil*” (*v. 19*). The reason is moral, not intellectual. People who are doing evil prefer not to have their deeds exposed. The next verse explains: “*For everyone who does evil hates the light and doesn’t come to the light, lest his works would be exposed*” (*v. 20*). Coming to Jesus means having one’s sin revealed, and many people would rather hide.

But verse 21 offers contrast: “*But he who does the truth comes to the light, that his works may be revealed, that they have been done in God*” (*v. 21*). Those who are willing to live truthfully come to the light without fear.

This passage connects to Nicodemus, who came to Jesus “by night.” He was moving from darkness toward light. Later in John’s Gospel, he defends Jesus before the council (*John 7:50–51*) and helps bury Jesus’ body (*John 19:39*), suggesting that he eventually came fully into the light.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals that unbelief is often a matter of the heart and will, not simply a lack of information. People reject Jesus not because the light is unclear but because they love darkness. Sin is attractive and comfortable, and the light threatens to expose it.

It also shows that judgment is a consequence of people’s own choices. God sent the light to save, but those who reject the light condemn themselves by preferring darkness. The judgment is not arbitrary; it reflects the choice people make.

Finally, the verse shows that coming to the light requires honesty. To come to Jesus, people must be willing to have their sins exposed and dealt with. This is painful, but it leads to healing and life. John writes elsewhere, “*But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus Christ, his Son, cleanses us from all sin*” (*1 John 1:7*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to examine their own hearts. Are there areas of life they are hiding from God, preferring darkness to light? Coming into the light means confessing sin honestly and allowing God to deal with it.

It also helps believers understand why some people resist the gospel. Sometimes the issue is not intellectual objections but unwillingness to give up sin. Believers can pray for such people and share the good news with patience, trusting God to draw them to the light.

Finally, this verse encourages believers to live transparently. Those who have nothing to hide can live in the light with freedom. Honesty, integrity, and confession allow believers to experience the joy of walking in the light with God and others.

### *John 3:30* — He Must Increase, But I Must Decrease

> *“He must increase, but I must decrease.”*
>
> — *John 3:30* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These words were spoken by John the Baptist near the end of his ministry. John had been baptizing at Aenon near Salim, while Jesus and His disciples were baptizing in the Judean countryside. Some of John’s disciples became concerned. They came to John and said, “*Rabbi, he who was with you beyond the Jordan, to whom you have testified, behold, he baptizes, and everyone is coming to him*” (*v. 26*). They seemed jealous that Jesus was attracting more followers than John.

John’s response showed remarkable humility. He said that a person can receive only what is given from heaven. He reminded his disciples that he had told them he was not the Messiah, but one sent ahead of Him.

Then he used an image from a wedding. The bridegroom is the one who has the bride. The friend of the bridegroom (like a best man) does not compete with the groom; he rejoices to hear the bridegroom’s voice. John saw himself as the friend, and Jesus as the bridegroom. In the Old Testament, God is pictured as the husband of His people (*Isaiah 62:5*; *Hosea 2:19–20*). John was saying that Jesus is the true bridegroom of God’s people. John said, “*Therefore my joy is made full*” (*v. 29*).

Then he concluded: “*He must increase, but I must decrease*” (*v. 30*). The word “must” expresses necessity, part of God’s plan. Jesus’ influence and recognition would grow, and John’s would fade. John was not discouraged by this; he embraced it as God’s will and the fulfillment of his purpose.

This is the last time John the Baptist speaks in John’s Gospel. He was soon imprisoned and later executed by Herod (*Mark 6:14–29*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse expresses the right attitude for every believer and every servant of God. The goal of ministry and life is not self-promotion but making Jesus known. John found joy not in his own success but in Jesus’ increase.

It also shows freedom from envy and competition. John’s disciples were jealous, but John was content. He knew his role and was glad to fulfill it. Believers often compare themselves with others and feel threatened by others’ success. John’s example shows a better way: rejoicing whenever Christ is honored, whoever is used.

Finally, the verse describes a lifelong process. As believers grow in faith, Christ increases in their lives and self-centeredness decreases. Paul writes, “*it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me*” (*Galatians 2:20*). This is the path of spiritual maturity.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to examine their motives. Are they serving to make Jesus known or to gain recognition for themselves? John’s example encourages believers to point others to Christ and to find joy in His glory rather than their own.

It also helps believers deal with envy and competition, especially in ministry. When other believers or churches seem more successful, believers can rejoice that Jesus is being honored, rather than feeling threatened.

Finally, this verse can be a daily prayer: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” Believers can ask God to help them let go of pride, self-promotion, and selfishness, so that Christ is seen more clearly in their lives.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*John 3* presents the heart of the gospel. Nicodemus, a respected religious teacher, learned that even he needed to be born anew. Spiritual life is not achieved through religious effort, heritage, or knowledge but is given by God through the Holy Spirit. Everyone, no matter how religious, needs this new birth. Believers can examine whether they have experienced it and can trust the Spirit to keep transforming them.

The chapter reveals how new life comes: through faith in Jesus, who was lifted up on the cross like the bronze serpent in the wilderness. God so loved the world that He gave His only Son, so that whoever believes in Him will not perish but have eternal life. Believers can rest in God’s love, proven at the cross, and share this good news with everyone, since “whoever believes” includes all.

The chapter also explains why some reject Jesus: they love darkness rather than light because their deeds are evil. Believers can examine their hearts for areas they are hiding, come into the light through honest confession, and live with transparency and integrity.

Finally, John the Baptist’s testimony provides a model of humility. “He must increase, but I must decrease.” Believers can find joy in Christ’s glory rather than their own, rejoice when others are used by God, and let Christ grow more prominent in their lives day by day.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for teaching that I must be born anew. I cannot make myself new; only Your Spirit can give me new life. Give me a new heart and keep transforming me by Your Spirit.

Thank You that God so loved the world that He gave You, His only Son, so that whoever believes in You will not perish but have eternal life. I believe in You. Thank You for being lifted up on the cross for me. Help me to come into Your light, to confess what I have hidden, and to live honestly before You and others. Like John the Baptist, I pray that You would increase and I would decrease. Free me from pride and envy, and help me to find my joy in making You known. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

John · Chapter 4 of 21

# John — Chapter 4

Chapter Theme: Living Water for the Thirsty and Faith in Jesus’ Word

[Read John 4 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/JHN04.htm)

Main Teaching

Crossing barriers of ethnicity, religion, gender, and reputation, Jesus speaks with a Samaritan woman at a well, offers her living water that satisfies forever, reveals her past without condemning her, teaches that true worship is in spirit and truth, and declares that He is the Messiah. She tells her town, and many Samaritans believe that He is the Savior of the world. Back in Galilee, a royal official trusts Jesus’ word that his son will live, and the boy is healed at that very hour.

## Chapter Background and Story

*John 4* follows Jesus’ conversation with Nicodemus in *John 3*, and the contrast between the two encounters is striking. Nicodemus was a respected Jewish man, a religious leader and teacher, who came to Jesus at night. The Samaritan woman was an unnamed woman of a despised people, with a troubled personal history, who met Jesus at noon. Nicodemus struggled to understand; the woman came to faith and immediately told others. Jesus offers new life to both the respectable insider and the rejected outsider.

### Why Jesus Went Through Samaria (*4:1–6*)

The Pharisees heard that Jesus was gaining more disciples than John the Baptist (though Jesus Himself did not baptize; His disciples did). To avoid premature conflict, Jesus left Judea and returned to Galilee. John writes, “*He needed to pass through Samaria*” (*v. 4*). Samaria lay between Judea in the south and Galilee in the north. It was the most direct route, though some strict Jews avoided it by crossing the Jordan and traveling on the eastern side. The word “needed” may also suggest divine purpose: Jesus had an appointment in Samaria.

The hostility between Jews and Samaritans went back centuries. When the Assyrians conquered the northern kingdom of Israel in 722 B.C., they deported many Israelites and settled foreigners in the land (*2 Kings 17:24–41*). The remaining Israelites intermarried with these settlers, and their descendants became the Samaritans. Jews considered them mixed in race and corrupted in religion. The Samaritans accepted only the five books of Moses as Scripture and built their own temple on Mount Gerizim. Jews destroyed that temple around 128 B.C. By Jesus’ time, deep resentment existed on both sides.

Jesus came to the town of Sychar, near the land Jacob had given to his son Joseph (*Genesis 33:19*; *48:22*). Jacob’s well was there, a deep well that still exists today. Jesus, “*being tired from his journey*” (*v. 6*), sat down by the well. John, who emphasizes Jesus’ divinity, also shows His full humanity: He was tired and thirsty. It was about the sixth hour, around noon.

### The Conversation at the Well (*4:7–26*)

A Samaritan woman came to draw water. Women usually drew water in the cooler morning or evening and often went together. Coming alone at midday may suggest that she was avoiding others, perhaps because of her reputation.

Jesus said, “*Give me a drink*” (*v. 7*). The woman was astonished: “*How is it that you, being a Jew, ask for a drink from me, a Samaritan woman?*” (*v. 9*) John explains that Jews did not share things with Samaritans; some Jews believed that Samaritan vessels were ritually unclean. Jesus crossed three barriers at once: He spoke to a Samaritan, a woman (Jewish rabbis did not usually speak publicly with women), and someone with a questionable reputation.

Jesus answered, “*If you knew the gift of God, and who it is who says to you, ‘Give me a drink,’ you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water*” (*v. 10*). “Living water” was a common phrase for flowing water, such as a spring or stream, as opposed to stagnant water in a cistern. The woman took Him literally. Jesus had no bucket, and the well was deep. Was He greater than their ancestor Jacob, who gave them the well?

Jesus explained the difference between ordinary water and the water He gives. This is studied below. The woman said, “*Sir, give me this water, so that I don’t get thirsty, neither come all the way here to draw*” (*v. 15*). She still did not fully understand, but she was interested.

Then Jesus said, “*Go, call your husband, and come here*” (*v. 16*). She answered, “*I have no husband*” (*v. 17*). Jesus said she was right: she had had five husbands, and the man she was now with was not her husband. In that culture, women could not easily initiate divorce, so the woman may have been divorced by several husbands, widowed, or both. Her situation may have involved great pain as well as sin. Jesus did not condemn her harshly. He simply revealed that He knew her life completely.

The woman said, “*Sir, I perceive that you are a prophet*” (*v. 19*). Then she raised a religious question: Samaritans worshiped on Mount Gerizim, while Jews said Jerusalem was the place to worship. Some see this as an attempt to change the subject; others see a sincere question from a woman whose religious and personal life were both unsettled. Jesus took her question seriously. He said that a time was coming when people would worship the Father neither on that mountain nor in Jerusalem. He affirmed that salvation comes from the Jews, through God’s covenant with Israel and the Messiah who comes from Israel. But true worshipers would worship the Father in spirit and truth. This is studied below.

The woman said, “*I know that Messiah is coming, he who is called Christ. When he has come, he will declare to us all things*” (*v. 25*). The Samaritans expected a coming figure they called the Taheb, a prophet like Moses. Jesus answered, “*I am he, the one who speaks to you*” (*v. 26*). This is one of the clearest statements in the Gospels of Jesus revealing that He is the Messiah, and He made it to a Samaritan woman.

### The Woman’s Witness and the Harvest (*4:27–42*)

At that moment, the disciples returned and were surprised that Jesus was talking with a woman, but no one asked Him why. The woman left her water jar, went back to the town, and said, “*Come, see a man who told me everything that I have done. Can this be the Christ?*” (*v. 29*) The woman who may have avoided people now went to them eagerly. Leaving her water jar showed that something more important had captured her attention.

Meanwhile the disciples urged Jesus to eat. He said, “*I have food to eat that you don’t know about*” (*v. 32*). They wondered if someone had brought Him food. Jesus explained, “*My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work*” (*v. 34*). Doing the Father’s will nourished and satisfied Him more than physical food.

Then He spoke about the harvest, studied below. People from the town were coming out to Jesus across the fields. Many Samaritans believed in Him because of the woman’s testimony. They asked Him to stay, and He stayed two days. Many more believed because of His own words. They told the woman, “*Now we believe, not because of your speaking; for we have heard for ourselves, and know that this is indeed the Christ, the Savior of the world*” (*v. 42*). The title “Savior of the world” is significant. These were Samaritans, not Jews, and they recognized that Jesus came for everyone.

### Healing the Official’s Son (*4:43–54*)

After two days, Jesus went to Galilee. Although He had said that a prophet has no honor in his own country, the Galileans welcomed Him because they had seen what He did in Jerusalem at the Passover.

Jesus came again to Cana, where He had turned water into wine. A royal official, probably serving Herod Antipas, had a son who was sick in Capernaum, about twenty miles away. The official came to Jesus and begged Him to come and heal his son, who was near death.

Jesus said, “*Unless you people see signs and wonders, you will in no way believe*” (*v. 48*). The “you” is plural, addressing the people of Galilee in general who sought miracles. The official persisted: “*Sir, come down before my child dies*” (*v. 49*). Jesus said, “*Go your way. Your son lives*” (*v. 50*). This verse is studied below.

The official believed and started home. On the way, his servants met him with the news that his son was alive. He asked when the boy began to get better, and they said the fever left him at the seventh hour (about one in the afternoon) the day before, exactly when Jesus had spoken. The official and his whole household believed. John calls this “*the second sign that Jesus did*” (*v. 54*) after coming from Judea to Galilee, linking it with the first sign at the same village of Cana.

## Important Verses Explained

### *John 4:13–14* — Water That Satisfies Forever

> *“Jesus answered her, ‘Everyone who drinks of this water will thirst again, but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never thirst again; but the water that I will give him will become in him a well of water springing up to eternal life.’”*
>
> — *John 4:13–14* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus speaks these words to a Samaritan woman at Jacob’s well, near the town of Sychar. It was noon, and Jesus was tired and thirsty from His journey. When the woman came to draw water, He asked her for a drink, which surprised her because Jews did not usually associate with Samaritans. Jesus told her that if she knew who He was, she would ask Him, and He would give her “living water.” She took this literally, pointing out that He had no bucket and the well was deep.

Jesus then explained: “*Everyone who drinks of this water will thirst again*” (*v. 13*). Physical water satisfies only temporarily. The woman had come to this well many times and would have to keep coming back. In a deeper sense, the things people pursue to satisfy their inner needs, such as relationships, possessions, success, and pleasure, leave them thirsty again.

“*but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never thirst again*” (*v. 14*). The water Jesus gives satisfies the deepest thirst of the human soul. Those who receive it will never again be spiritually thirsty in the same desperate way, because their deepest need has been met.

“*but the water that I will give him will become in him a well of water springing up to eternal life*” (*v. 14*). This water does not have to be drawn from outside again and again. It becomes an inner spring, continually flowing up and leading to eternal life. Later in John’s Gospel, Jesus explains that the “living water” refers to the Holy Spirit, whom believers would receive (*John 7:37–39*).

The woman’s own life illustrated the truth of Jesus’ words. As the conversation revealed, she had had five husbands and was living with a man who was not her husband. She may have been searching for love, security, or worth in relationships, and each one left her thirsty again. Jesus offered her something that would truly satisfy.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses reveal that Jesus satisfies the deepest longings of the human heart. The Old Testament pictures God as the fountain of living waters. Through Jeremiah, God said His people had forsaken Him, “*the spring of living waters*” (*Jeremiah 2:13*), and dug for themselves “*broken cisterns that can’t hold water*” (*Jeremiah 2:13*). People often look to “broken cisterns” for satisfaction. Jesus offers the true spring.

They also connect with the promise of the Holy Spirit. Isaiah promised that God would pour water on the thirsty land and His Spirit on His people’s descendants (*Isaiah 44:3*). Jesus gives the Spirit, who dwells within believers, bringing life, renewal, and satisfaction from within.

Finally, the verses show that eternal life begins now. The spring “springing up to eternal life” is not only a future hope but a present reality. Those who receive Jesus experience the beginning of eternal life today.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses invite people to consider where they are seeking satisfaction. Many people go from one relationship, achievement, or pleasure to another, always thirsty again. Jesus offers lasting satisfaction. Anyone can come to Him and receive the living water He gives.

They also encourage believers to keep drinking from the spring. Although believers have received the Spirit, they can still drift into seeking satisfaction elsewhere. Through prayer, worship, Scripture, and fellowship, they can return to Jesus and be refreshed.

Finally, these verses offer hope to those who feel empty or ashamed. The Samaritan woman’s story shows that Jesus offers living water even to those whose lives are broken. No past is too complicated for His grace.

### *John 4:23–24* — Worship in Spirit and Truth

> *“But the hour comes, and now is, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, for the Father seeks such to be his worshipers. God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth.”*
>
> — *John 4:23–24* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These verses come in the middle of Jesus’ conversation with the Samaritan woman. Jesus had revealed that He knew about her five previous husbands and her current relationship. She recognized that He was a prophet and raised a question that had divided Jews and Samaritans for centuries: where should God be worshiped? Samaritans worshiped on Mount Gerizim, near Sychar, where their temple had once stood. Jews insisted that Jerusalem was the only proper place, according to God’s command (*Deuteronomy 12:5*; *2 Chronicles 6:6*).

Jesus answered that a time was coming when people would worship the Father neither on that mountain nor in Jerusalem. He affirmed that the Jews knew what they worshiped, “*for salvation is from the Jews*” (*v. 22*), since God had revealed Himself to Israel and the Messiah came from Israel. But location would no longer be the central issue.

“*But the hour comes, and now is*” (*v. 23*). The new era was both coming and already present in Jesus.

“*when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth*” (*v. 23*). “In spirit” means that worship is not limited to a physical place or external rituals but comes from the heart and is empowered by God’s Spirit. “In truth” means worship that is genuine and sincere, and also worship that is based on the truth of who God is, as revealed in Jesus, who is “*the truth*” (*John 14:6*).

“*for the Father seeks such to be his worshipers*” (*v. 23*). This is a remarkable statement. God is seeking worshipers. He takes the initiative to draw people to Himself.

“*God is spirit*” (*v. 24*). God is not limited to a physical body or location. He is present everywhere.

“*and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth*” (*v. 24*). Because God is spirit, worship must be spiritual and true, not merely physical, external, or tied to one place.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses reveal that true worship is a matter of the heart and of truth, not of location or ritual. Through Jesus, the true temple (*John 2:19–21*), people can worship God anywhere. The barrier between Jews and Samaritans, and between all peoples, is broken down. Anyone can worship the Father through Jesus.

They also reveal that God seeks worshipers. Jesus was seeking this woman, and through her, her whole town. God takes the initiative in drawing people to Himself.

Finally, “spirit and truth” belong together. Worship that is sincere but not based on truth can be misguided. Worship that is doctrinally correct but lacks heart is empty. True worship combines a sincere heart, empowered by the Spirit, with accurate knowledge of God revealed in Jesus.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses invite believers to examine their worship. Is it sincere, coming from the heart, or merely external? Is it based on the truth of who God is, as revealed in Scripture and in Jesus? Believers can ask God to help them worship with both spirit and truth.

They also free believers to worship God anywhere: at home, at work, in nature, or in church. While gathering with other believers is important, worship is not confined to a building. Every part of life can be offered to God.

Finally, these verses invite believers to set aside divisions about outward forms. Christians often disagree about worship styles and practices. While these matters have some importance, Jesus’ words remind believers that what matters most is worshiping God in spirit and truth.

### *John 4:35* — Fields Ready for Harvest

> *“Don’t you say, “There are yet four months until the harvest”? Behold, I tell you, lift up your eyes and look at the fields, that they are white for harvest already.”*
>
> — *John 4:35* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus speaks these words to His disciples after His conversation with the Samaritan woman. While Jesus spoke with her, the disciples had gone into town to buy food. When they returned, they were surprised to find Him talking with a Samaritan woman. The woman left her water jar and went back to town to tell people about Jesus. The disciples urged Jesus to eat, but He said His food was to do the will of the One who sent Him.

Then He said, “*Don’t you say, ‘There are yet four months until the harvest’?*” (*v. 35*) This may have been a common saying, meaning “There’s plenty of time,” or a reference to the actual season; grain was sown in winter and harvested about four months later.

“*Behold, I tell you, lift up your eyes and look at the fields, that they are white for harvest already*” (*v. 35*). At that very moment, the Samaritans from the town were coming out across the fields toward Jesus, likely wearing white garments. Jesus pointed to them as a harvest that was ready right now. The disciples did not need to wait four months; people were ready to receive Jesus immediately.

In the following verses, Jesus explained that the one who reaps receives wages and gathers a crop for eternal life, so that the sower and reaper rejoice together. He said, “*One sows, and another reaps*” (*v. 37*). Others had done the work of sowing (including the Old Testament prophets, John the Baptist, and the Samaritan woman herself), and the disciples would reap.

The result was remarkable: many Samaritans believed because of the woman’s testimony, and many more believed after hearing Jesus Himself.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse teaches that God is preparing people to receive the gospel, often in unexpected places. The disciples would never have expected a Samaritan town to be ready for harvest. Yet there it was. God works in hearts in ways believers cannot see.

It also teaches urgency. The harvest is ready now, not someday. Believers should not assume that people are not interested or that the time is not right. Many are ready to hear about Jesus.

Finally, the verse shows that God’s work involves many people. Some sow, some reap, and all rejoice together. No one does the work alone. Paul expresses the same idea: one plants, another waters, but God gives the growth (*1 Corinthians 3:6–9*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to “lift up their eyes” and notice the people around them who may be ready to hear about Jesus. Coworkers, neighbors, family members, and strangers may be more open than believers assume.

It also encourages believers not to delay sharing their faith. There is a tendency to think that the right time will come later. Jesus says the fields are ready now.

Finally, this verse encourages believers that their efforts are part of a larger work. Sometimes they sow and others reap; sometimes they reap where others have sown. Believers can rejoice together in what God is doing, whatever their part.

### *John 4:50* — Believing Jesus’ Word

> *“Jesus said to him, ‘Go your way. Your son lives.’ The man believed the word that Jesus spoke to him, and he went his way.”*
>
> — *John 4:50* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse describes the second sign Jesus performed in Cana of Galilee. A royal official, likely serving Herod Antipas, had a son who was very sick in Capernaum, about twenty miles away. Hearing that Jesus had returned to Galilee, the official traveled to Cana and begged Jesus to come down and heal his son, who was close to death.

Jesus responded with a rebuke directed at the people in general: “Unless you people see signs and wonders, you will in no way believe.” Many Galileans were interested in Jesus mainly because of His miracles. But the official did not give up. He pleaded, “Sir, come down before my child dies.”

Then Jesus said, “*Go your way. Your son lives*” (*v. 50*). Jesus did not go with him. He did not touch the boy or even see him. He simply spoke.

“*The man believed the word that Jesus spoke to him, and he went his way*” (*v. 50*). This is the key. The official had wanted Jesus to come with him, but he accepted Jesus’ word without any visible sign. He trusted that what Jesus said was true and started the long journey home.

The next day, his servants met him on the road with the news that his son was alive. The official asked when he began to recover, and they said the fever left him at the seventh hour, about one in the afternoon, the day before. That was exactly when Jesus had said, “Your son lives.” The official and his whole household believed.

The official’s faith grew in stages: first he believed enough to come to Jesus, then he believed Jesus’ word without seeing, and finally he and his household believed fully when they saw the result.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows the power of Jesus’ word. He did not need to be physically present to heal. His word alone accomplished His will, just as God’s word created the world (*Genesis 1:3*; *John 1:3*). This reveals Jesus’ divine authority.

It also shows the nature of faith. The official believed Jesus’ word before he saw the result. This is the kind of faith Jesus desires: trust in His word, not dependence on signs and wonders. Later, Jesus tells Thomas, “*Blessed are those who have not seen, and have believed*” (*John 20:29*).

Finally, the verse shows that faith grows. The official’s faith began with desperation, grew into trust in Jesus’ word, and became full belief that spread to his whole household. Faith often develops gradually through experience of God’s faithfulness.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to trust Jesus’ word. Believers today do not see Jesus physically, but they have His words in Scripture. They can trust His promises even when they do not yet see the results.

It also encourages believers to bring their urgent needs to Jesus, as the official did. They can pray boldly for those they love and trust Jesus to answer in His way.

Finally, this verse shows how faith can spread through a household. The official’s encounter with Jesus led his whole family to believe. Believers’ faith can influence their families and those around them.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*John 4* shows Jesus crossing barriers to reach people. He spoke with a Samaritan woman despite ethnic hostility, cultural rules about men and women, and her troubled reputation. Believers can follow His example by reaching out to people others avoid, crossing barriers of ethnicity, culture, and social status to share God’s love.

Jesus’ offer of living water speaks to everyone who is spiritually thirsty. Many people seek satisfaction in relationships, possessions, achievements, or pleasures that leave them thirsty again. Jesus offers lasting satisfaction through the Holy Spirit. Believers can drink deeply from Him and invite others to do the same.

The conversation about worship teaches that true worship is not about location or outward forms but about worshiping the Father in spirit and truth. Believers can worship God sincerely, based on the truth revealed in Jesus, in every part of their lives.

The Samaritan woman’s response shows the power of personal testimony. She simply told her town, “Come, see a man who told me everything that I have done.” Many believed because of her words and then came to believe through Jesus Himself. Believers can share what Jesus has done for them and invite others to come and see. And Jesus’ words about the harvest remind believers that people are often more ready to hear the gospel than they assume.

Finally, the royal official’s story teaches believers to trust Jesus’ word even before they see the outcome. Jesus’ word has power, and faith that trusts His word grows into deeper faith that can influence a whole household.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for crossing every barrier to reach people who were thirsty and broken. Thank You for offering living water that satisfies forever. I come to You with my thirst. Fill me with Your Spirit, and help me to stop seeking satisfaction in things that leave me empty.

Teach me to worship the Father in spirit and truth, with a sincere heart and in the truth You have revealed. Give me courage to tell others what You have done for me, as the Samaritan woman did. Open my eyes to see the fields that are ready for harvest around me. Help me to trust Your word even when I cannot yet see the answer, like the official who believed and went his way. Thank You that You are the Savior of the world. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
