John · Chapter 5 of 21

# John — Chapter 5

Chapter Theme: The Son Who Gives Life and the Witnesses Who Point to Him

[Read John 5 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/JHN05.htm)

Main Teaching

At the pool of Bethesda, Jesus heals a man who had been sick for thirty-eight years, and because He does it on the Sabbath, the religious leaders begin to seek His death. Jesus responds with one of His most important speeches about His relationship with the Father: the Son does what the Father does, gives life, and holds authority to judge. He then names the witnesses that testify about Him, John the Baptist, His works, the Father, and the Scriptures, and warns that refusing Him is refusing the life that the Scriptures promise.

## Chapter Background and Story

*John 5* marks a turning point in the Gospel. Until now, Jesus has met curiosity, misunderstanding, and growing faith. From this chapter on, open hostility begins. The healing at Bethesda leads directly to the first recorded plot to kill Jesus (*5:16–18*), and the long speech that follows explains why the conflict is so serious. The issue is not merely a broken Sabbath rule; it is who Jesus claims to be.

### The Pool of Bethesda (*5:1–9*)

Jesus went up to Jerusalem for “*a feast of the Jews*” (*v. 1*). John does not name the feast, and scholars have suggested Passover, Pentecost, Tabernacles, or another festival. By the sheep gate, north of the temple, was a pool called Bethesda, a name that may mean “house of mercy.” It had five covered porches. Archaeologists have uncovered a large double pool in this area with porticoes around it and a colonnade between the two basins, which matches John’s description well.

The porches were crowded with “*those who were sick, blind, lame, or paralyzed*” (*v. 3*). Verse 4, which explains that an angel stirred the water and the first person in was healed, appears in the World English Bible and in many later manuscripts but is absent from the earliest and most reliable ones. Many scholars believe it was added later as an explanation of the popular belief reflected in verse 7. Either way, the sick man’s words show what people there believed: when the water moved, the first one into the pool would be healed.

One man had been sick for thirty-eight years, longer than most people in that crowd had been alive. Jesus saw him, knew how long he had suffered, and asked, “*Do you want to be made well?*” (*v. 6*) This question is studied below. The man did not answer yes or no. He explained his helplessness: he had no one to put him into the pool, and someone always got there first. Jesus did not carry him to the water. He said, “*Arise, take up your mat, and walk*” (*v. 8*). At once the man was well, picked up his mat, and walked.

Then John adds the detail that drives the rest of the chapter: “*Now that day was a Sabbath*” (*v. 9*).

### Conflict over the Sabbath (*5:10–18*)

Religious leaders saw the healed man carrying his mat and told him, “*It is the Sabbath. It is not lawful for you to carry the mat*” (*v. 10*). The Law of Moses commanded rest on the Sabbath, and the prophets had warned against carrying burdens on that day (*Jeremiah 17:21–22*). Over time, teachers had developed detailed rules defining what counted as work, and carrying an object from one place to another was on the list. The leaders were so focused on the rule that they showed no joy at all that a man crippled for thirty-eight years was walking.

The man passed the responsibility to his healer, but he did not know Jesus’ name, because Jesus had slipped away into the crowd. Later Jesus found him in the temple and said, “*Behold, you are made well. Sin no more, so that nothing worse happens to you*” (*v. 14*). Jesus does not say that the man’s illness was caused by a specific sin; elsewhere He rejects that assumption (*John 9:2–3*). But He warns that there is something worse than thirty-eight years of paralysis: facing God’s judgment unrepentant. Physical healing was a gift; it was not the whole of what the man needed.

The man went and told the leaders that Jesus had healed him. We are not told why. It may have been innocent, or it may have been a way to protect himself. In contrast with the man born blind in *John 9*, who boldly defends Jesus, this man shows no clear sign of faith.

The leaders began to persecute Jesus. His answer was brief but explosive: “*My Father is still working, so I am working, too*” (*v. 17*). Jewish teachers agreed that God, in one sense, never stops working on the Sabbath: He continues to sustain the world, give life, and judge. Jesus claimed the same freedom for Himself, because the Father is His Father. John explains why this enraged them: He “*called God his own Father, making himself equal with God*” (*v. 18*). They understood exactly what He meant.

### The Son and the Father (*5:19–30*)

Jesus did not soften His claim. He explained it. He began, “*Most certainly, I tell you, the Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing*” (*v. 19*). This is not a confession of weakness. It describes a perfect unity of will and action. The Son never acts independently of the Father, and whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise. The Father loves the Son and shows Him everything, and He will show Him greater works than healing a lame man.

Jesus then names two works that belong to God alone: giving life and judging. “*For as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, even so the Son also gives life to whom he desires*” (*v. 21*). And the Father has given all judgment to the Son, “*that all may honor the Son, even as they honor the Father*” (*v. 23*). To dishonor the Son is to dishonor the Father who sent Him. There is no way to honor God while rejecting Jesus.

Verse 24, studied below, applies this to anyone who hears Jesus’ word. Verses 25–29 speak of two “hours.” The first is already present: “*the hour comes, and now is, when the dead will hear the Son of God’s voice; and those who hear will live*” (*v. 25*). This refers to people who are spiritually dead receiving new life when they hear and believe. The second hour is future: “*the hour comes in which all who are in the tombs will hear his voice*” (*v. 28*), and they will come out, some to the resurrection of life and some to the resurrection of judgment. This echoes *Daniel 12:2*.

Some readers wonder whether verse 29, which mentions “*those who have done good*” (*v. 29*) and “*those who have done evil*” (*v. 29*), teaches salvation by works. In context, Jesus has just said that eternal life comes by hearing His word and believing (*5:24*). Throughout John, the “work” God requires is to believe in the One He sent (*John 6:29*). The life a person lives reveals whether they have truly received that life; good deeds are the fruit of faith, not its price.

Jesus closes this section by returning to His dependence on the Father: “*I don’t seek my own will, but the will of my Father who sent me*” (*v. 30*).

### The Witnesses to Jesus (*5:31–47*)

In Jewish law, a matter had to be confirmed by two or three witnesses (*Deuteronomy 19:15*). Jesus acknowledges that if He were His only witness, His testimony would not be legally sufficient. So He calls His witnesses.

The first is John the Baptist. The leaders had sent messengers to question John (*John 1:19*), and he had testified to the truth. Jesus calls him “*the burning and shining lamp*” (*v. 35*), in whose light the people were glad to rejoice for a while. But Jesus does not ultimately depend on human testimony; He mentions John for their sake, “*that you may be saved*” (*v. 34*).

The second witness is Jesus’ works: “*the very works that I do, testify about me, that the Father has sent me*” (*v. 36*). The healing at Bethesda was one of those works.

The third witness is the Father Himself. Yet the leaders had never heard His voice or seen His form, and they did not have His word living in them, because they did not believe the One He sent.

The fourth witness is the Scriptures, studied below. Jesus then exposes the root problem: “*How can you believe, who receive glory from one another, and you don’t seek the glory that comes from the only God?*” (*v. 44*) Their concern for human approval kept them from receiving Him.

Finally, Jesus says that He will not need to accuse them before the Father. Moses, the one in whom they had placed their hope, would accuse them, “*for he wrote about me*” (*v. 46*). The Law itself pointed to Christ, in its promises, its sacrifices, and its promise of a prophet like Moses (*Deuteronomy 18:15*). To reject Jesus was, in the end, to disbelieve Moses.

## Important Verses Explained

### *John 5:6* — Do You Want to Be Made Well?

> *“When Jesus saw him lying there, and knew that he had been sick for a long time, he asked him, ‘Do you want to be made well?’”*
>
> — *John 5:6* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The scene is a crowded pool in Jerusalem, surrounded by porches full of people who were blind, lame, and paralyzed. They waited there day after day, hoping the water would move and they could be first into it. Among them lay a man who had been sick for thirty-eight years. John tells us that Jesus “*saw him lying there*” (*v. 6*) and “*knew that he had been sick for a long time*” (*v. 6*). Out of the whole crowd, Jesus went to him.

Jesus’ question may seem strange at first: “*Do you want to be made well?*” (*v. 6*) Surely anyone who had been sick that long would want healing. But the question is gentle and searching. After thirty-eight years, a person’s whole life is shaped around an illness. Hope can fade. The man may have stopped expecting anything to change. Healing would also mean a new life with new responsibilities: work, relationships, and a place in the community after decades of dependence.

The man’s answer shows where his hope had settled. He did not say yes. He explained why healing was impossible for him: “*Sir, I have no one to put me into the pool when the water is stirred up, but while I’m coming, another steps down before me*” (*v. 7*). He was thinking only of the pool and of his lack of help. He did not yet realize that the One standing in front of him did not need the pool at all.

Jesus did not argue with him or wait for a better answer. He simply spoke: “*Arise, take up your mat, and walk*” (*v. 8*). The power to heal came from Jesus’ word, not from the water or from the man’s ability to reach it. What the man could not do in thirty-eight years, Jesus did in a moment.

This healing also shows that Jesus’ grace does not depend on a person already having strong faith. The man did not know Jesus’ name (*5:13*). Jesus took the initiative, asked the question, and gave the healing.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Jesus’ question reveals His respect for the person in front of Him. He does not treat the man as a project or an object of pity. He speaks to him as someone whose desire matters. God’s grace is never forced upon people as if they were machines; He engages the heart, inviting a response even while He alone supplies the power.

The scene also shows the difference between human systems of hope and the grace of Christ. At the pool, healing (as people understood it) went to the fastest and strongest, to those with someone to help them. The weakest and loneliest were always left behind. Jesus reverses this. He goes to the one who has no one. The gospel is good news especially for those who cannot get themselves to the water.

Many interpreters also see a picture of spiritual helplessness here. Before Christ, human beings are not merely sick but, as Paul says, “*weak*” (*Romans 5:6*), unable to save themselves. Rescue comes not because we finally manage to reach the right place, but because the Son of God comes to us and speaks life.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Jesus’ question still speaks to people who have lived with something for a very long time: an illness, an addiction, a broken relationship, a habit of fear or bitterness. After years, it is possible to stop hoping, or to grow so used to a situation that change feels threatening. Jesus’ question invites honesty. He meets people in their long-standing need and asks whether they are willing to receive what He offers, even when it means a new way of living.

The man’s answer also reflects a common pattern: explaining why things cannot change instead of looking to the One who can change them. Many people rehearse the reasons they are stuck: no one helps, others always get ahead, the right moment has passed. Jesus does not depend on the conditions people think are necessary. He can work where every human option has failed.

This passage also gives comfort to those who feel overlooked. In a crowd of hurting people, Jesus noticed one man who had been waiting longer than almost anyone. He sees those whom others step over, and His compassion moves toward the forgotten. His people are called to do the same, noticing those who have no one to help them and bringing them the care of Christ.

### *John 5:17* — My Father Is Still Working

> *“But Jesus answered them, ‘My Father is still working, so I am working, too.’”*
>
> — *John 5:17* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After Jesus healed the man at the pool, the religious leaders confronted the man for carrying his mat on the Sabbath. When they learned that Jesus had healed him and told him to carry it, they began to persecute Jesus, “*because he did these things on the Sabbath*” (*v. 16*).

Jesus’ defense is short: “*My Father is still working, so I am working, too*” (*v. 17*). The Sabbath commemorated God resting from His work of creation (*Genesis 2:2–3*). Yet Jewish teachers recognized that God had not stopped all activity. Every Sabbath, babies are born, the sun rises, rain falls, and people die. God continues to sustain the universe, give life, and judge. If God stopped working, creation would collapse.

Jesus applies this to Himself. His Father works on the Sabbath, and so He works too. Healing the lame man was not a violation of the Sabbath’s purpose but a work of the same God who never ceases to care for His creation.

Notice the phrase “*My Father*” (*v. 17*). Jesus did not say “our Father,” as His disciples would later pray. He spoke of God as His own Father in a unique way, and He claimed the right to do what God does.

The leaders understood immediately. John writes that they sought all the more to kill Him, because He “*called God his own Father, making himself equal with God*” (*v. 18*). They did not misunderstand Him. Jesus never corrected them by saying, “You have taken Me wrongly.” Instead, He went on to explain how the Son and the Father work together.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse is one of the clearest early claims to deity in John’s Gospel. Jesus does not merely claim to be a prophet who heals by God’s power. He claims to share in God’s own ongoing work, and to stand in a relationship with the Father that gives Him the same authority over the Sabbath that God has. Jesus is not a rival to God or a second god; He is the Son who acts in perfect unity with the Father, as the following verses explain.

The verse also reveals the heart of the Sabbath. God gave the Sabbath as a gift of rest and a sign of His covenant, not as a burden that prevents mercy. Jesus says elsewhere that the Sabbath was made for people, not people for the Sabbath (*Mark 2:27*). On the Sabbath, God continues to do good, and so Jesus does good.

Finally, the verse shows that God is never idle in the world. Even when He seems silent, the Father is still at work, holding all things together and carrying out His purposes. Jesus’ ministry was the visible expression of the Father’s constant work of mercy.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse offers comfort to people who wonder whether God is doing anything in their situation. Jesus says that His Father is always working. Even when believers cannot see what He is doing, God has not stopped caring, sustaining, and working out His purposes. Times that seem quiet are not times when God is absent.

It also challenges a religion that values rules above people. The leaders cared more about a mat being carried than about a man being healed. Christians can fall into the same pattern, valuing traditions, preferences, or appearances more than the restoration of people. Jesus’ example calls His followers to keep mercy at the center of their faith.

Finally, the verse calls everyone to face Jesus’ claim. He did not present Himself as one good teacher among many. He spoke of God as His own Father and claimed to do God’s work. A person must decide whether that claim is true. If it is, Jesus deserves the same honor as the Father.

### *John 5:24* — Passed from Death into Life

> *“Most certainly I tell you, he who hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life, and doesn’t come into judgment, but has passed out of death into life.”*
>
> — *John 5:24* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus spoke these words in the middle of a long answer to religious leaders who wanted to kill Him. He had just explained that the Father gives the Son the authority to give life and to judge. Now He tells how a person receives that life.

“*he who hears my word and believes him who sent me*” (*v. 24*). Two actions are named: hearing and believing. “Hearing” means more than letting sounds enter the ears. It means listening and receiving what Jesus says. “Believing him who sent me” means trusting the Father who sent Jesus, which in John’s Gospel is inseparable from trusting Jesus Himself. To believe the Father is to accept His testimony about His Son.

Jesus then gives three promises. First, such a person “*has eternal life*” (*v. 24*). The verb is present tense. Eternal life is not only something to hope for after death; it is a present possession. In John, eternal life is the life of God Himself, knowing the Father and the Son (*John 17:3*).

Second, the believer “*doesn’t come into judgment*” (*v. 24*). Jesus has just said that the Father has given all judgment to the Son. The One who will judge the world promises that those who believe will not face condemnation. This does not mean believers will never give an account of their lives (*Romans 14:12*), but that they will not be condemned.

Third, the believer “*has passed out of death into life*” (*v. 24*). This too is described as already done. Before believing, a person is spiritually dead, separated from God. Through faith, that person crosses over, like someone moving from one country to another, from the realm of death into the realm of life.

Jesus begins this statement with “*Most certainly I tell you*” (*v. 24*), a solemn formula He uses to emphasize something of the greatest importance.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse is one of the clearest statements in the Bible of the assurance that belongs to those who trust in Christ. Salvation is not a reward for earning enough merit. It is received through hearing and believing. And it is not uncertain until the very end; Jesus speaks of life as already given, judgment as already removed, and the passage from death to life as already accomplished.

The verse also shows that eternal life is relational. It comes through hearing Jesus’ word and trusting the Father who sent Him. Life flows from being joined to the One who has life in Himself (*5:26*). Just as the dead man Lazarus would later come out of the tomb at Jesus’ voice (*John 11:43–44*), spiritually dead people come to life when they hear His word.

Paul expresses the same truth when he writes, “*There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus*” (*Romans 8:1*). Jesus’ words in *John 5:24* lie behind the confident hope of believers throughout history.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse gives believers confidence. Many Christians live with constant fear that they have not done enough to be accepted by God. Jesus says that those who hear His word and believe have eternal life now. Their security rests on His promise, not on the strength of their feelings on a particular day.

It also invites those who have not yet believed. The way to life is open: hear what Jesus says and trust the One who sent Him. There is no long list of achievements to complete first. The crossing from death to life happens through faith.

Finally, the verse shapes how believers live. Those who have passed from death into life no longer belong to the old realm. Eternal life is meant to be lived now, in fellowship with God, in growing obedience, and in love for others. The life Jesus gives begins today and continues forever.

### *John 5:39–40* — The Scriptures Testify About Jesus

> *“You search the Scriptures, because you think that in them you have eternal life; and these are they which testify about me. Yet you will not come to me, that you may have life.”*
>
> — *John 5:39–40* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Near the end of His speech, Jesus spoke to religious leaders who knew the Scriptures extremely well. Many of them had memorized large portions of the Law and studied it carefully every day. Jesus acknowledged this: “*You search the Scriptures, because you think that in them you have eternal life*” (*v. 39*). They believed that diligent study of the Law was the path to life in the age to come.

Then He said something startling: “*and these are they which testify about me*” (*v. 39*). The Scriptures they studied so carefully were pointing to Jesus. The promises to Abraham, the Passover lamb, the prophet like Moses, the king from David’s line, the suffering servant in Isaiah, all of them found their fulfillment in Him.

Yet the tragedy was this: “*Yet you will not come to me, that you may have life*” (*v. 40*). They held the map in their hands but refused to go to the destination. They studied the testimony while rejecting the One to whom it testified.

The problem was not lack of knowledge. It was unwillingness. The word “will not” describes a choice. Jesus explains part of the reason a few verses later: they were seeking glory from one another rather than the glory that comes from God (*5:44*).

The leaders were not wrong to search the Scriptures. Jesus never criticizes careful study of God’s Word. What He exposes is study that stops short of coming to Him.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses teach that Christ is the center of the whole Bible. After His resurrection, Jesus showed His disciples, beginning “*from Moses and from all the prophets*” (*Luke 24:27*), the things written about Himself. The Old Testament is not a collection of unrelated stories and laws; it is the unfolding of God’s plan that leads to Christ. Reading Scripture rightly means reading it with Him in view.

The verses also show that the Scriptures are not an end in themselves. They are God’s inspired Word and deserve deep reverence, but life is not found in the pages as such. Life is found in the Person to whom the pages point. Scripture’s purpose is to bring people to Christ.

Finally, the verses reveal that knowledge without surrender can become a barrier. It is possible to know much about the Bible and still refuse to come to the One it reveals. True understanding of Scripture leads to faith, humility, and worship.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to read the whole Bible with Jesus at the center. When reading the Old Testament stories, laws, psalms, and prophecies, believers can ask how they prepare for, point to, or are fulfilled in Christ. This makes the Bible a unified story rather than a collection of disconnected parts.

They also caution against Bible knowledge that does not lead to relationship. Studying Scripture can become an academic exercise, a source of pride, or a way to win arguments. The purpose of reading is to come to Jesus, to know Him, trust Him, and follow Him.

Finally, these verses speak to anyone who has heard about Jesus for years without coming to Him. Familiarity with religious things is not the same as life. Jesus’ invitation remains: come to Him and have life.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*John 5* shows that Jesus notices the people others overlook. At the crowded pool, He went to a man who had waited thirty-eight years with no one to help him. Many people today live with long-standing suffering and quiet despair. Jesus sees them, knows how long they have been there, and comes to them with power that does not depend on their strength. His followers are called to share that compassion, paying attention to those who have no one.

The chapter also warns against a faith that cares more about rules than about people. The religious leaders saw a mat being carried and missed a miracle. Believers today can become so focused on doing religion correctly that they fail to rejoice when God restores someone. Mercy, not mere rule-keeping, reflects the heart of the Father who is always working.

At the center of the chapter stands Jesus’ claim to be the Son who shares the Father’s work, gives life, and judges the world. This means that no one can honor God while dismissing Jesus. It also means that those who hear His word and believe can live with deep assurance. They have eternal life now, will not be condemned, and have already crossed from death into life.

Finally, *John 5* calls readers to let all the evidence lead them to Jesus. John the Baptist, Jesus’ works, the Father, and the Scriptures all testify about Him. It is possible to know the Bible well and still refuse to come to Christ, often because of concern for the approval of others. The chapter invites a humble response: seeking God’s approval more than people’s, reading Scripture to find Christ, and coming to Him to receive life.

## Chapter Prayer

Heavenly Father, thank You that You are always working, even when I cannot see what You are doing. Thank You for sending Your Son, who saw the man no one helped and spoke a word that made him well. Lord Jesus, You know the places in my life where I have waited a long time and stopped hoping. Help me to bring them honestly to You and to trust that Your power does not depend on my strength. Thank You that whoever hears Your word and believes the Father who sent You has eternal life and has passed from death into life. Let that promise give me peace and confidence. Keep me from caring more about rules or appearances than about people, and from seeking the praise of others instead of Your approval. Open my eyes to see You on every page of Scripture, and draw me to come to You for life. Give me Your compassion for those who are overlooked and alone. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

John · Chapter 6 of 21

# John — Chapter 6

Chapter Theme: Jesus, the Bread of Life Who Satisfies and Keeps His Own

[Read John 6 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/JHN06.htm)

Main Teaching

Jesus feeds five thousand people with five barley loaves and two fish, walks on the stormy sea to His disciples, and then explains the meaning of the sign in the synagogue at Capernaum: He Himself is the bread of life who came down from heaven. Those who come to Him will never be turned away, and those who receive Him by faith have eternal life. When many disciples find His words too hard and leave, Peter speaks for the Twelve: there is nowhere else to go, because Jesus has the words of eternal life.

## Chapter Background and Story

*John 6* is one of the longest chapters in the Gospel and one of the most important. It contains the only miracle, other than the resurrection, recorded in all four Gospels: the feeding of the five thousand. But John does more than tell the miracle. He records a long conversation and teaching that explains what the sign means. The chapter moves from great popularity, with a crowd wanting to make Jesus king, to great loss, as many disciples walk away.

### The Feeding of the Five Thousand (*6:1–15*)

Jesus crossed to the far side of the Sea of Galilee, and a large crowd followed because they had seen His healings. John notes that “*the Passover, the feast of the Jews, was at hand*” (*v. 4*). This detail matters. Passover remembered God’s rescue of Israel from Egypt, and the wilderness journey that followed included God’s gift of manna, bread from heaven. The whole chapter will connect Jesus with that story.

Seeing the crowd, Jesus asked Philip, “*Where are we to buy bread, that these may eat?*” (*v. 5*) John explains that Jesus asked this “*to test him, for he himself knew what he would do*” (*v. 6*). Philip calculated that two hundred denarii, about eight months’ wages for a laborer, would not buy enough for each person to have a little. Andrew found a boy with “*five barley loaves and two fish*” (*v. 9*), though he wondered what use they were among so many. Barley bread was the food of the poor. John alone mentions the boy and the barley, details that recall the prophet Elisha, who fed a hundred men with twenty barley loaves and had some left over (*2 Kings 4:42–44*).

Jesus had the people sit on the grass, about five thousand men, plus women and children (*Matthew 14:21*). He gave thanks and distributed the bread and fish, “*as much as they desired*” (*v. 11*). Everyone was filled. Then Jesus said, “*Gather up the broken pieces which are left over, that nothing be lost*” (*v. 12*). The disciples filled twelve baskets. The miracle was studied more fully at *Matthew 14:19–20* and *Mark 6:41–42*; John’s account emphasizes how the sign pointed to Jesus’ identity.

The people concluded, “*This is truly the prophet who comes into the world*” (*v. 14*), recalling the prophet like Moses promised in *Deuteronomy 18:15*. Some wanted to take Jesus by force and make Him king. They wanted a political Messiah who would feed them and free them from Rome. Jesus withdrew to the mountain alone. He would not accept a crown on their terms.

### Walking on the Sea (*6:16–21*)

That evening the disciples set out across the lake toward Capernaum. It was dark, a strong wind was blowing, and Jesus had not yet joined them. After rowing three or four miles, they saw Jesus walking on the sea and coming near the boat, and they were frightened. He said, “*It is I. Don’t be afraid*” (*v. 20*). The Greek words translated “It is I” are literally “I am,” the same words Jesus uses in His great “I am” sayings, echoing God’s name revealed to Moses (*Exodus 3:14*). This event is studied at *Matthew 14:27*. In John, when they received Him into the boat, “*Immediately the boat was at the land where they were going*” (*v. 21*).

### The Crowd Seeks Jesus (*6:22–34*)

The next day the crowd realized that Jesus was gone. They took boats to Capernaum and found Him. Jesus went straight to their motives: “*you seek me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves and were filled*” (*v. 26*). They had eaten the bread but missed the meaning. A “sign” points beyond itself, and they had seen only a free meal.

Jesus told them, “*Don’t work for the food which perishes, but for the food which remains to eternal life, which the Son of Man will give to you*” (*v. 27*). They asked what works God required. Jesus answered, “*This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent*” (*v. 29*). The one “work” God asks is faith in His Son.

The crowd then asked for a sign, pointing to Moses and the manna: “*He gave them bread out of heaven to eat*” (*v. 31*) (*Psalm 78:24*). Jesus corrected them. It was not Moses who gave the bread, but His Father, and the Father now gives “*the true bread out of heaven*” (*v. 32*), which “*comes down out of heaven and gives life to the world*” (*v. 33*). Like the Samaritan woman asking for living water (*John 4:15*), they said, “*Lord, always give us this bread*” (*v. 34*).

### “I Am the Bread of Life” (*6:35–51*)

Jesus answered with the first of His seven “I am” sayings in John, studied below. He explained that those whom the Father gives Him will come to Him, and He will never cast them out (also studied below). It is the Father’s will that He lose none of them but raise them up at the last day.

The crowd, now called “the Jews” by John (meaning the Jewish opponents in Galilee), grumbled, just as Israel grumbled in the wilderness (*Exodus 16:2*). They said, “*Isn’t this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know?*” (*v. 42*) They could not accept that someone so familiar had come down from heaven.

Jesus answered, “*No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him*” (*v. 44*). Coming to Jesus is not simply a human achievement; it is the result of God’s gracious work in the heart. Quoting *Isaiah 54:13*, He said, “*They will all be taught by God*” (*v. 45*). Everyone who truly listens to the Father comes to the Son.

Jesus then contrasted Himself with the manna. Their ancestors ate manna and died. But “*I am the living bread which came down out of heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever*” (*v. 51*). Then He added words that pointed to the cross: “*the bread which I will give for the life of the world is my flesh*” (*v. 51*).

### Eating His Flesh and Drinking His Blood (*6:52–59*)

The listeners argued, “*How can this man give us his flesh to eat?*” (*v. 52*) Instead of softening His language, Jesus intensified it, speaking of eating His flesh and drinking His blood. These words are studied below, together with the different ways Christians have understood them.

### Many Disciples Leave (*6:60–71*)

Even many of Jesus’ disciples, in the wider sense of those who had been following Him, said, “*This is a hard saying! Who can listen to it?*” (*v. 60*) Jesus asked whether this offended them. What would they think if they saw the Son of Man ascending to where He was before? Then He said, “*It is the spirit who gives life. The flesh profits nothing. The words that I speak to you are spirit, and are life*” (*v. 63*). His words cannot be understood on a merely physical level; they must be received spiritually, by faith, through the work of God’s Spirit.

“*At this, many of his disciples went back and walked no more with him*” (*v. 66*). The crowd that wanted to make Jesus king the day before had largely melted away. Jesus turned to the Twelve and asked whether they also wanted to leave. Peter’s answer is studied below.

The chapter ends on a sober note. Jesus said that He had chosen the Twelve, yet “*one of you is a devil*” (*v. 70*). John explains that He meant Judas Iscariot, who would betray Him. Even among the closest followers, not everyone truly believed.

## Important Verses Explained

### *John 6:35* — I Am the Bread of Life

> *“Jesus said to them, I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me will not be hungry, and whoever believes in me will never be thirsty.”*
>
> — *John 6:35* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These words come the day after Jesus fed five thousand people. The crowd had followed Him across the lake, hoping for more bread. They reminded Him that Moses gave their ancestors manna in the wilderness, and they asked Him for a similar sign. Jesus told them that the true bread from heaven was not manna but a gift from His Father that gives life to the world. When they asked for this bread, Jesus said, “*I am the bread of life*” (*v. 35*).

Bread was the most basic food in the ancient world. For most ordinary people, it made up the largest part of every meal. To call Himself “the bread of life” meant that Jesus is not an optional extra but the essential source of life for the soul. Just as the body cannot live without food, the soul cannot truly live without Him.

“*Whoever comes to me will not be hungry, and whoever believes in me will never be thirsty*” (*v. 35*). Notice the parallel between “comes to me” and “believes in me.” Coming to Jesus and believing in Him describe the same response. Those who do so find their deepest hunger and thirst satisfied.

This does not mean believers never feel spiritual longing again. Rather, the fundamental emptiness of a life apart from God is filled. Those who come to Jesus have found what they were made for. They continue to receive from Him, but they no longer search desperately for life elsewhere.

The crowd had wanted Jesus to keep giving them bread. Jesus offered them something far better: Himself.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This is the first of seven “I am” sayings in John’s Gospel, each with a picture of who Jesus is. The phrase “I am” echoes God’s self-revelation to Moses at the burning bush, “*I AM WHO I AM*” (*Exodus 3:14*). When Jesus says “I am,” He speaks with divine authority and reveals Himself as the One who meets humanity’s deepest needs.

The saying also shows that Jesus is greater than Moses and the manna. Manna sustained Israel in the wilderness for a time, but those who ate it eventually died (*6:49*). Jesus gives life that lasts forever. The manna pointed forward to Him; He is the true bread from heaven.

Finally, the saying reveals the generous heart of God. Bread was given freely to the Israelites every morning in the wilderness. Jesus is offered freely to all who will come. The invitation is wide: “whoever comes” and “whoever believes.”

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites people to look honestly at what they are depending on for life. Many people try to satisfy their inner hunger with success, relationships, possessions, entertainment, or approval. These things may be good gifts, but they cannot fill the soul. Jesus offers Himself as the bread that truly satisfies.

It also reminds believers that they need Jesus daily, just as the body needs food daily. The Israelites gathered manna each morning; they could not store up yesterday’s portion. In the same way, believers are sustained by continual fellowship with Christ through prayer, Scripture, worship, and trust.

Finally, the verse encourages believers to share this bread with others. The disciples distributed the loaves to the crowd. Followers of Jesus today are called to point a hungry world to the One who alone can satisfy, while also caring for people’s physical needs as Jesus did.

### *John 6:37* — I Will in No Way Throw Out

> *“All those whom the Father gives me will come to me. He who comes to me I will in no way throw out.”*
>
> — *John 6:37* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus spoke these words right after declaring that He is the bread of life. He had just told the crowd that although they had seen Him, they did not believe (*6:36*). Their unbelief did not mean that His mission was failing. He went on to explain how God’s purpose works.

“*All those whom the Father gives me will come to me*” (*v. 37*). Jesus describes those who believe as a gift from the Father to the Son. The Father’s plan to bring people to His Son will not fail. Those He gives will come.

Then comes the promise: “*He who comes to me I will in no way throw out*” (*v. 37*). The words “in no way” translate a strong Greek expression meaning “never, under any circumstances.” Jesus will not reject anyone who comes to Him. No one who genuinely comes will be turned away at the door.

The next verses show the security of this promise. Jesus came to do the Father’s will, and “*This is the will of my Father who sent me, that of all he has given to me I should lose nothing, but should raise him up at the last day*” (*v. 39*). Not only will Jesus receive those who come; He will keep them and raise them to eternal life.

This verse holds together two truths that people sometimes find hard to combine: God’s initiative in bringing people to Christ, and the open invitation to anyone who comes. Both are true. The Father gives, and people come. And those who come are welcomed.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse offers great comfort about the security of salvation. Believers do not hold on to Christ by their own strength alone; they are held by the Father’s gift and the Son’s commitment. Later Jesus says of His sheep, “*no one will snatch them out of my hand*” (*John 10:28*). Salvation rests on the faithfulness of God.

The verse also reveals the welcoming heart of Jesus. Many people fear that their sin, failure, or past is too great for Him to accept them. Jesus’ promise is that He will never throw out anyone who comes. The tax collectors, sinners, the Samaritan woman, and the thief on the cross all found this to be true.

Christians have discussed how God’s choosing and human responsibility relate to each other. Some emphasize God’s sovereign choice, while others emphasize that God’s grace enables all to respond and holds people responsible for their choice. This verse affirms both that God’s purpose is sure and that the invitation is real. No one who comes will be rejected.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse speaks to anyone who hesitates to come to Jesus because they feel unworthy. His promise is clear: He will in no way throw out the one who comes. A person does not need to clean up their life first. They come as they are, and He receives them.

It also gives assurance to believers who struggle with doubt. When believers are weighed down by their failures, they can rest in Christ’s promise that He loses none of those the Father has given Him. Their security is anchored not in the strength of their grip on Him but in His grip on them.

Finally, the verse shapes how the church receives people. If Jesus does not turn away those who come to Him, His people should not either. Churches are called to be places of welcome, where those who are seeking Christ find open arms.

### *John 6:53–56* — Eating His Flesh and Drinking His Blood

> *“Jesus therefore said to them, Most certainly I tell you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you don’t have life in yourselves. He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up at the last day. For my flesh is food indeed, and my blood is drink indeed. He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood lives in me, and I in him.”*
>
> — *John 6:53–56* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After Jesus said that the bread He would give for the life of the world was His flesh, His listeners argued among themselves: How could He give them His flesh to eat? Jesus did not explain His words away. Instead, He spoke even more strongly.

“*unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you don’t have life in yourselves*” (*v. 53*). To a Jewish audience, these words were shocking. The Law strictly forbade drinking blood (*Leviticus 17:10–14*). Taken literally and physically, Jesus’ words sounded like cannibalism. Many of His listeners were offended.

Jesus continued, “*He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up at the last day*” (*v. 54*). Notice how closely this parallels verse 40, where Jesus said that everyone who sees the Son and believes in Him has eternal life and will be raised up at the last day. Eating and drinking Him is connected to believing in Him.

“*He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood lives in me, and I in him*” (*v. 56*). The result of this eating and drinking is a deep, mutual union. Jesus lives in the believer, and the believer lives in Him. This is the language of abiding that Jesus will develop later in the image of the vine and the branches (*John 15:4–5*).

The reference to “flesh” and “blood” points to Jesus’ death. His body would be given and His blood poured out on the cross for the life of the world. To “eat” and “drink” means to receive personally, by faith, the benefits of His sacrificial death, and to depend on Him completely for life.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Christians have understood these verses in different ways, especially regarding their connection to the Lord’s Supper. Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox Christians see them as speaking directly of the Eucharist, in which believers truly receive Christ’s body and blood. Lutherans also affirm Christ’s real presence in the sacrament. Many Reformed and evangelical Christians understand the passage as speaking primarily of believing in Christ and receiving His sacrifice by faith, which the Lord’s Supper later expresses and signifies. Jesus had not yet instituted the Supper when He spoke these words, yet many Christians across traditions see a meaningful connection, since both speak of His body given and blood shed.

Whatever one’s view of the sacrament, all agree on the central meaning: eternal life comes through union with Christ in His death. It is not enough to admire Jesus as a teacher or to wish for His blessings. A person must receive Him personally and completely, depending on His sacrifice for life.

Jesus’ words in verse 63 also guide interpretation: “*The words that I speak to you are spirit, and are life*” (*v. 63*). His teaching is not about a merely physical act cut off from faith, but about receiving Him by the Spirit. The life He gives is spiritual and eternal.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses call believers to depend on Christ as completely as the body depends on food and drink. Faith is not a casual interest in Jesus but a receiving of Him into the center of life. Just as food becomes part of the body, Christ’s life becomes part of the believer’s life.

They also give deeper meaning to the Lord’s Supper. When believers share the bread and the cup, they remember Christ’s body given and blood shed, and they express their union with Him and with one another. However they understand the sacrament, Christians can come to it with reverence, faith, and gratitude.

Finally, these verses remind readers that Jesus’ teaching sometimes challenges and even offends. He did not adjust His words to keep the crowd. Believers today are called to receive His words even when they are difficult, trusting that they are spirit and life.

### *John 6:68–69* — To Whom Would We Go?

> *“Simon Peter answered him, ‘Lord, to whom would we go? You have the words of eternal life. We have come to believe and know that you are the Christ, the Son of the living God.’”*
>
> — *John 6:68–69* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After Jesus’ teaching about eating His flesh and drinking His blood, many of His followers found His words too hard and left. The large crowd that had wanted to make Him king just a day earlier was gone. Jesus turned to the Twelve and asked, “*You don’t also want to go away, do you?*” (*v. 67*) The question invited them to make their own decision.

Simon Peter answered for the group: “*Lord, to whom would we go?*” (*v. 68*) Peter did not claim to understand everything Jesus had said. His answer was not based on having solved every difficulty. It was based on knowing that there was no better alternative. Every other option would lead away from life.

“*You have the words of eternal life*” (*v. 68*). Jesus had just said that His words are spirit and life (*6:63*). Peter had come to recognize this. No other teacher, religion, or philosophy offered what Jesus offered.

“*We have come to believe and know that you are the Christ, the Son of the living God*” (*v. 69*). Peter’s confession rests on what the disciples had come to believe and know through their time with Jesus. They had seen His works, heard His teaching, and experienced His presence. Their faith was not blind; it was grounded in their experience of who He was.

This scene in John parallels Peter’s confession at Caesarea Philippi in the other Gospels (studied at *Matthew 16:16*), but here it comes at a moment of crisis, when many others were walking away.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Peter’s response shows the nature of mature faith. Faith does not mean having no unanswered questions. It means trusting Jesus even when His words are difficult, because one has come to know who He is. The disciples stayed not because they understood everything, but because they knew Him.

The confession also highlights Jesus’ identity. Peter calls Him “the Christ,” the promised Messiah, and in many manuscripts “the Son of the living God.” In some of the earliest manuscripts, Peter calls Him “the Holy One of God” instead; the World English Bible follows the manuscripts that read “the Son of the living God.” Both titles point to Jesus’ unique relationship with God and His divine mission.

The scene also reveals a sobering contrast. While Peter speaks for the Twelve, Jesus reveals that one of them, Judas, would betray Him. Outward association with Jesus is not the same as true faith. Faith is a personal response of trust and allegiance.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Many believers go through times when following Jesus is hard. His teaching may challenge their desires or their understanding, or life’s suffering may raise difficult questions. In those times, Peter’s words offer an anchor. Even when believers do not understand everything, they can say with Peter, “To whom would we go?” There is no one else with the words of eternal life.

This passage also encourages believers when others walk away from faith. It can be painful and confusing when friends or family members leave Jesus. Peter’s response shows that each person must decide for themselves, and that faithfulness is possible even when many turn back.

Finally, the passage invites honest reflection. Jesus did not pressure the Twelve to stay; He asked them a question. He still invites each person to decide whether they will follow Him. Those who have come to know Him can choose to stay, not out of mere habit, but because they have found in Him the words of eternal life.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*John 6* begins with a crowd that wanted bread and ends with a few disciples who wanted Jesus. Many people today come to God hoping for help with practical needs, and Jesus is compassionate toward those needs; He fed the hungry crowd generously. But He also calls people to see beyond the gifts to the Giver. The deepest need of every person is not merely food, health, or success, but Christ Himself, the bread of life.

The chapter also offers deep reassurance. Jesus promises that He will never throw out anyone who comes to Him, and that He will lose none of those the Father has given Him. Those who fear that they are too sinful or broken can come to Him without fear of rejection. Those who already believe can rest in His faithfulness to keep them and raise them up at the last day.

*John 6* teaches that eternal life comes through union with Christ in His death. His body given and His blood poured out are the source of life for the world. Receiving Him is not a matter of admiring Him from a distance but of depending on Him completely, as the body depends on food. The Lord’s Supper gives believers a regular, visible reminder of this union.

Finally, the chapter shows that following Jesus involves choice and sometimes cost. Many walked away when His words became difficult. Believers will also encounter teachings they find hard and seasons when faith is tested. In those moments, Peter’s words offer a faithful response: there is no one else to go to, because Jesus alone has the words of eternal life.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, You are the bread of life. Thank You for feeding the hungry crowd with compassion, and thank You even more for giving Yourself for the life of the world. Forgive me for the times I have wanted Your gifts more than I have wanted You. Satisfy the hunger of my soul with Your presence, and teach me to depend on You each day. Thank You for Your promise that You will never throw out anyone who comes to You. Help me to rest in that promise when I feel unworthy, and to trust that You will keep me and raise me up at the last day. When Your words are hard for me, give me the faith of Peter, who knew there was no one else to go to. You have the words of eternal life. Make me faithful when others turn away, and use me to share the bread of life with a hungry world. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

John · Chapter 7 of 21

# John — Chapter 7

Chapter Theme: Rivers of Living Water at the Feast of Booths

[Read John 7 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/JHN07.htm)

Main Teaching

At the Feast of Booths in Jerusalem, Jesus teaches openly in the temple while the city argues about who He is. He says that anyone willing to do God’s will can recognize that His teaching comes from God, and He calls people to judge rightly rather than by appearances. On the great final day of the feast, He cries out an invitation to the thirsty to come to Him and drink, promising rivers of living water, which John explains as the Holy Spirit. The crowd divides, the officers sent to arrest Him return amazed, and Nicodemus begins to speak up for Him.

## Chapter Background and Story

*John 7* takes place around the Feast of Booths, also called Tabernacles, one of the three great pilgrim festivals of Israel. For seven days, families lived in temporary shelters made of branches to remember how God cared for Israel during forty years in the wilderness (*Leviticus 23:33–43*). It was also a joyful harvest festival. By Jesus’ time, two ceremonies had become central: a daily procession in which a priest carried water from the Pool of Siloam and poured it out at the altar, accompanied by prayers for rain and readings from the prophets, and the lighting of great lamps in the temple courts. Both form the background for what Jesus says in *John 7* and 8.

The chapter is filled with questions and divided opinions. “Where is He?” “Is He a good man?” “How does He know so much?” “Is this the Christ?” “Can the Christ come from Galilee?” John shows that Jesus forces people to decide.

### Jesus and His Brothers (*7:1–9*)

Jesus remained in Galilee because the leaders in Judea wanted to kill Him (*5:18*). As the Feast of Booths approached, His brothers urged Him to go to Jerusalem and show Himself openly: “*If you do these things, reveal yourself to the world*” (*v. 4*). John adds a painful note: “*For even his brothers didn’t believe in him*” (*v. 5*). These were Jesus’ younger brothers, sons of Mary and Joseph, including James and Jude (*Mark 6:3*). Their advice sounds like that of people who wanted Jesus to become famous, without understanding His mission.

Jesus answered, “*My time has not yet come, but your time is always ready*” (*v. 6*). Throughout John, Jesus moves according to the Father’s timing, which leads toward His “hour” of death and glorification. His brothers could go to the feast whenever they liked, because the world did not hate them. But the world hated Jesus, “*because I testify about it, that its works are evil*” (*v. 7*).

There is great hope in this sad scene. After the resurrection, Jesus’ brothers became believers (*Acts 1:14*). James became a leader of the church in Jerusalem and is traditionally regarded as the author of the letter of James, and Jude is traditionally regarded as the author of the letter of Jude.

### Teaching in the Temple (*7:10–24*)

After His brothers left, Jesus went up privately. The crowds were whispering about Him. Some said, “*He is a good man*” (*v. 12*). Others said, “*Not so, but he leads the multitude astray*” (*v. 12*). Yet people were afraid to speak openly.

In the middle of the feast, Jesus began teaching publicly in the temple. The leaders were amazed: “*How does this man know letters, having never been educated?*” (*v. 15*) Jesus had not studied under a recognized rabbi. He answered that His teaching came from the One who sent Him, and that anyone willing to do God’s will would recognize it. This is studied below.

Jesus then confronted them directly. Moses gave them the law, yet none of them kept it, since they were seeking to kill Him. The crowd, apparently unaware of the leaders’ plans, replied, “*You have a demon! Who seeks to kill you?*” (*v. 20*)

Jesus referred back to the healing at Bethesda (*5:1–9*), the “*one work*” (*v. 21*) that had caused such controversy. He pointed out that they circumcised baby boys on the Sabbath when the eighth day fell on it, because the law required circumcision on the eighth day (*Leviticus 12:3*). If they allowed that work on the Sabbath, why were they angry that He made a man completely well on the Sabbath? He concluded with a call to right judgment, studied below.

### Is This the Christ? (*7:25–36*)

Some people of Jerusalem knew that the leaders wanted to kill Jesus, and they wondered why He was being allowed to speak openly. Could the rulers have concluded that He was the Christ? But they had an objection: “*we know where this man comes from, but when the Christ comes, no one will know where he comes from*” (*v. 27*). Some believed that the Messiah would appear suddenly from an unknown origin.

Jesus cried out that they did know where He came from in an earthly sense, but they did not know the One who sent Him. “*I know him, because I am from him, and he sent me*” (*v. 29*). His true origin was heavenly.

They tried to seize Him, “*but no one laid a hand on him, because his hour had not yet come*” (*v. 30*). Many in the crowd believed in Him, reasoning that the Messiah could hardly do more signs than He had done. The Pharisees and chief priests sent officers, the temple police, to arrest Him.

Jesus said that He would be with them only a little while longer and then return to the One who sent Him. “*You will seek me and won’t find me. You can’t come where I am*” (*v. 34*). His listeners misunderstood, wondering whether He planned to go to the Jews scattered among the Greeks. Ironically, the gospel would indeed go to the Greeks after His death and resurrection.

### The Great Invitation (*7:37–39*)

On the last and greatest day of the feast, after days of water ceremonies and prayers for rain, Jesus stood and cried out an invitation to the thirsty. This is studied below.

### Division and Unbelief (*7:40–52*)

The crowd divided. Some said, “*This is truly the prophet*” (*v. 40*). Others said, “*This is the Christ*” (*v. 41*). Others objected that the Messiah would not come from Galilee, since Scripture said He would be a descendant of David from Bethlehem (*Micah 5:2*). John’s readers know the irony: Jesus was born in Bethlehem and descended from David, though He grew up in Nazareth.

The officers returned without Jesus. When the leaders asked why, they answered, “*No man ever spoke like this man!*” (*v. 46*) The Pharisees scorned them and the crowd: “*But this multitude that doesn’t know the law is cursed*” (*v. 49*). Their contempt for ordinary people is striking.

Then Nicodemus, who had come to Jesus by night in *John 3*, spoke up: “*Does our law judge a man unless it first hears from him personally and knows what he does?*” (*v. 51*) It was a cautious defense, appealing to fairness rather than declaring faith. The others mocked him: “*Are you also from Galilee? Search and see that no prophet has arisen out of Galilee*” (*v. 52*). In fact, the prophet Jonah came from Gath Hepher in Galilee (*2 Kings 14:25*), so their claim was not even accurate. Nicodemus’s small step of courage would later grow; he would help bury Jesus’ body (*John 19:39*).

## Important Verses Explained

### *John 7:17* — Willing to Do God’s Will

> *“If anyone desires to do his will, he will know about the teaching, whether it is from God or if I am speaking from myself.”*
>
> — *John 7:17* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus was teaching in the temple courts during the Feast of Booths. The religious leaders were amazed at His knowledge because He had never studied under one of the recognized rabbis. In that culture, a teacher’s authority came from the teachers he had learned from. They wondered where Jesus’ learning came from.

Jesus answered, “*My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me*” (*v. 16*). He was not inventing new ideas or relying on human authorities. His teaching came directly from God.

Then He explained how a person could recognize this: “*If anyone desires to do his will, he will know about the teaching, whether it is from God or if I am speaking from myself*” (*v. 17*). The key is a willingness to do God’s will. Jesus says that understanding His teaching does not depend first on education or intellectual ability, but on the attitude of the heart. Those who truly want to obey God will recognize that Jesus’ words come from God.

This shows that knowing truth is not only a matter of the mind. A person who is unwilling to obey may find endless reasons to doubt. A person who sincerely wants to do God’s will is open to recognizing His voice.

In the next verse, Jesus offers another test: “*He who speaks from himself seeks his own glory, but he who seeks the glory of him who sent him is true*” (*v. 18*). Jesus did not seek His own glory but the Father’s. That is a mark of a true messenger.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals a deep connection between obedience and understanding. In Scripture, knowing God is never merely academic. *Psalm 111:10* says that the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom. A heart surrendered to God becomes able to perceive His truth. Resistance to God’s will often lies behind resistance to His Word.

It also shows that faith is not blind. Jesus invites people to test His teaching. Those who seek to do God’s will will come to know whether His teaching is from God. This is an invitation to honest seeking, not to a leap in the dark.

Finally, the verse highlights Jesus’ humility and unity with the Father. Though He is the eternal Word, He says His teaching is from the Father who sent Him. Jesus’ whole ministry was marked by seeking the Father’s glory rather than His own.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages anyone who has questions about Jesus. Questions are not a barrier to faith when they come from a sincere heart. Jesus promises that those who truly desire to do God’s will will come to know whether His teaching is from God. Honest seekers can approach His words with openness.

It also challenges believers to consider whether their struggles with Scripture are sometimes struggles of the will rather than the mind. When a teaching of Jesus is hard to accept, the difficulty may lie in unwillingness to obey. Surrender often opens the way to understanding.

Finally, the verse offers a test for any teacher or leader. Those who speak for God should seek His glory rather than their own. Believers can be wise in listening for teachers who point to Christ rather than to themselves.

### *John 7:24* — Judge Righteous Judgment

> *“Don’t judge according to appearance, but judge righteous judgment.”*
>
> — *John 7:24* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus spoke these words to people who were angry with Him for healing a man on the Sabbath (the healing at the pool of Bethesda in *John 5*). He pointed out their inconsistency. The Law required boys to be circumcised on the eighth day after birth. When the eighth day fell on a Sabbath, they circumcised the boy anyway, because they understood that the command to circumcise took priority. They performed this work on the Sabbath without hesitation.

Jesus argued that if they could perform circumcision, which affected one part of the body, on the Sabbath, they should not be angry that He “*made a man completely healthy on the Sabbath*” (*v. 23*). Restoring a whole person fulfills the purpose of God’s law.

Then He concluded, “*Don’t judge according to appearance, but judge righteous judgment*” (*v. 24*). They had looked at the outward appearance: a man carrying a mat, a healing done on the Sabbath. They had not looked deeper at what God was doing or at the purpose of the law. Their judgment was shallow and therefore wrong.

This verse is sometimes misunderstood as forbidding all judgment. But Jesus does not tell them to stop judging; He tells them to judge rightly. Right judgment looks beneath the surface, considers the truth, and is consistent and fair.

Jesus’ words echo the Law itself, which commanded Israel’s judges to judge fairly and not to show partiality (*Deuteronomy 16:18–19*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reflects God’s own way of seeing. When Samuel looked at Jesse’s sons, God told him that people look at the outward appearance, “*but the LORD looks at the heart*” (*1 Samuel 16:7*). God’s judgment is never superficial. Jesus calls people to share, as far as humans can, God’s concern for truth beneath the surface.

The verse also shows the danger of religious rule-keeping that misses the heart of God’s law. The leaders were so focused on external regulations that they could not recognize God’s mercy at work. Right judgment requires understanding the purpose of God’s commands, which is love for God and neighbor.

Finally, the verse invites people to judge Jesus Himself rightly. Many in the chapter judged Him by appearances: His Galilean background, His lack of formal training, His family. Right judgment looks at the evidence of His words, His works, and His character.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse challenges believers to resist quick, surface-level judgments about others. People are often judged by their appearance, background, accent, education, or social status. Jesus calls His followers to look deeper, to seek the truth, and to be fair.

It also calls believers to be consistent. The leaders accepted one kind of Sabbath work but condemned another that was even more merciful. Christians can apply standards to others that they do not apply to themselves. Righteous judgment is honest and consistent.

Finally, the verse reminds believers that discernment is still necessary. Jesus does not forbid all moral evaluation. Believers must distinguish truth from error and right from wrong. But they are called to do so carefully, humbly, and with God’s purposes of mercy in view.

### *John 7:37–39* — Rivers of Living Water

> *“Now on the last and greatest day of the feast, Jesus stood and cried out, ‘If anyone is thirsty, let him come to me and drink! He who believes in me, as the Scripture has said, from within him will flow rivers of living water.’ But he said this about the Spirit, which those believing in him were to receive. For the Holy Spirit was not yet given, because Jesus wasn’t yet glorified.”*
>
> — *John 7:37–39* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These words were spoken “*on the last and greatest day of the feast*” (*v. 37*) of Booths. Each morning of the festival, a priest led a procession to the Pool of Siloam, filled a golden pitcher with water, carried it back to the temple, and poured it out at the altar while the people sang. The ceremony remembered how God provided water from the rock in the wilderness and expressed prayers for rain for the coming year. Many also connected it with prophecies of water flowing from the temple (*Ezekiel 47:1–12*; *Zechariah 14:8*) and with Isaiah’s words, “*Therefore with joy you will draw water out of the wells of salvation*” (*Isaiah 12:3*).

On the climactic day, Jesus “*stood and cried out*” (*v. 37*). Teachers usually sat to teach, so His standing and crying out showed the urgency of His invitation: “*If anyone is thirsty, let him come to me and drink!*” (*v. 37*) While the people celebrated water poured out in a ceremony, Jesus offered the reality the ceremony pointed to. He Himself is the source of living water.

He continued, “*He who believes in me, as the Scripture has said, from within him will flow rivers of living water*” (*v. 38*). No single Old Testament verse says exactly these words; Jesus seems to be summarizing the promises of passages like *Isaiah 58:11*, *Ezekiel 47*, and *Zechariah 14:8*. The Greek is also ambiguous about whose “within” is meant. Many read it as describing the believer, from whom the Spirit’s life flows to others. Others read it as describing Christ, from whom the living water flows, like the water from the rock in the wilderness. Both readings are faithful to John’s message, since the Spirit flows from Christ to believers and through them to others.

John explains, “*But he said this about the Spirit, which those believing in him were to receive*” (*v. 39*). The Spirit had not yet been given in this new way, “*because Jesus wasn’t yet glorified*” (*v. 39*). In John’s Gospel, Jesus’ glorification refers to His death, resurrection, and return to the Father. After that, the Spirit would be poured out on all believers, as happened at Pentecost (*Acts 2*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This invitation reveals that Jesus is the fulfillment of everything the Feast of Booths celebrated. God gave Israel water in the wilderness; Jesus gives living water that satisfies the soul. The prophets promised a river flowing from God’s temple to bring life; Jesus is the true temple (*John 2:21*), and from Him the life-giving Spirit flows.

It also shows the generosity of God’s gift. Jesus does not speak of a trickle but of “rivers.” The Holy Spirit’s presence in believers is abundant, bringing life, renewal, and power. And the Spirit’s life does not stop with the individual; it flows outward to bless others.

Finally, the passage connects the gift of the Spirit with Jesus’ death and resurrection. The Spirit comes because Jesus was glorified through the cross. Every blessing believers receive from the Spirit flows from the finished work of Christ.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Jesus’ invitation is open to “anyone” who is thirsty. Many people today feel spiritually dry, weary, or empty. They may be surrounded by religious activity, as the crowd was at the feast, and still be thirsty. Jesus calls them to come to Him personally and drink.

This passage also encourages believers to depend on the Holy Spirit. The Christian life is not meant to be lived in human strength alone. The Spirit dwells in believers, renewing them, giving them joy, and enabling them to love and serve.

Finally, the image of rivers flowing outward reminds believers that God’s gifts are meant to be shared. When the Spirit fills a person, His life overflows in love, kindness, encouragement, and witness. Believers are called to be channels of the living water to a thirsty world.

### *John 7:46* — No Man Ever Spoke Like This Man

> *“The officers answered, ‘No man ever spoke like this man!’”*
>
> — *John 7:46* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Earlier in the feast, the chief priests and Pharisees had sent officers to arrest Jesus (*7:32*). These were the temple police, Levites responsible for keeping order in the temple. They were under the authority of the religious leaders and were expected to carry out orders.

When the officers returned empty-handed, the leaders demanded, “*Why didn’t you bring him?*” (*v. 45*) Their answer was simple: “*No man ever spoke like this man!*” (*v. 46*) They had gone to arrest Jesus, but as they listened to Him, they were so struck by His words that they could not bring themselves to seize Him.

This is a remarkable testimony. These officers were not disciples of Jesus. They had no reason to favor Him and every reason to obey their superiors. Yet His words had a power and authority they had never encountered.

The Pharisees responded with scorn, asking whether the officers had also been deceived and pointing out that none of the rulers believed in Him. They dismissed the crowds who followed Jesus as ignorant of the law. But the officers’ testimony stood.

The other Gospels also record that people were astonished at Jesus’ teaching, “*for he taught them as having authority, and not as the scribes*” (*Mark 1:22*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The officers’ words point to the unique authority of Jesus’ teaching. Other teachers quoted earlier authorities; Jesus spoke on His own authority, saying, “Most certainly I tell you.” His words carried the power of God because He is the Word made flesh (*John 1:14*). When He spoke, people encountered not just ideas but the presence of God.

The scene also shows how God can work in unexpected people. The religious experts rejected Jesus, while those sent to arrest Him were moved by His words. God’s truth is not limited to the educated or powerful. It reaches those with ears to hear.

Finally, the leaders’ response reveals the danger of pride. They assumed that because the rulers did not believe, Jesus could not be the Christ. Their trust in their own position kept them from considering the evidence.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites people to listen to Jesus’ words for themselves. Many people form opinions about Jesus based on what others say. The officers’ experience shows the power of actually hearing Him. Reading the Gospels with an open heart can bring people face to face with words unlike any other.

It also encourages believers to trust the power of Jesus’ words when sharing their faith. They do not need clever arguments to convince others. Pointing people to what Jesus said and did allows His words to do their work.

Finally, the leaders’ scorn for “this multitude” warns against spiritual pride. Believers can look down on those they consider less informed or less religious. Jesus’ words reached ordinary people and officers alike. His people should honor all whom He came to reach.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*John 7* shows that Jesus divides opinion. Some called Him good, others a deceiver; some said prophet, others Christ; some wanted to arrest Him, while others could not bring themselves to touch Him. People today also hold many opinions about Jesus. The chapter invites readers to look past rumor and appearances and to judge rightly, considering His words, His works, and His character.

The chapter also offers hope for families. Jesus’ own brothers did not believe in Him at first, yet later they became leaders in the church. Believers who grieve over family members who do not believe can take heart. God’s timing is not ours, and the story is not yet finished.

At the center of the chapter is Jesus’ great invitation: anyone who is thirsty can come to Him and drink. Religious celebrations, traditions, and ceremonies can point to God, but only Christ can satisfy the soul. Through His death and resurrection, He gives the Holy Spirit, who fills believers and flows out through them to others. Believers are invited to keep coming to Him and to live in dependence on the Spirit.

Finally, *John 7* encourages small steps of courage. Nicodemus did not make a bold confession, but he spoke up for fairness when others were condemning Jesus. Later his faith would become public. Believers may feel timid, but God honors faithful steps, and He can grow small courage into bold love.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, You stood in the temple and cried out for the thirsty to come to You and drink. I come to You now, thirsty and in need. Fill me with Your Holy Spirit, and let Your living water flow through me to others. Give me a heart that truly desires to do God’s will, so that I may recognize Your voice and understand Your teaching. Keep me from judging by appearances, and teach me to see people and situations as You see them, with truth and mercy. Thank You that no one ever spoke like You. Let Your words have their full authority in my life. I pray for family members and friends who do not yet believe; work in their hearts as You did in the hearts of Your own brothers. Give me courage to speak up for what is right and to honor You when others reject You. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
