John · Chapter 8 of 21

# John — Chapter 8

Chapter Theme: The Light of the World, the Truth That Frees, and the Eternal “I Am”

[Read John 8 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/JHN08.htm)

Main Teaching

Jesus refuses to condemn a woman caught in adultery, shaming her accusers with their own sin while calling her to leave her sin behind. In the temple He declares that He is the light of the world, and He tells those who believe that remaining in His word will make them true disciples who know the truth and are set free. The debate grows fierce as Jesus confronts slavery to sin and the refusal to hear Him, and it reaches its climax when He declares, “Before Abraham came into existence, I AM.”

## Chapter Background and Story

*John 8* continues the setting of the Feast of Booths in the temple courts. During the festival, four enormous golden lamps were lit in the Court of the Women, and it was said that their light shone over all Jerusalem. The celebration recalled the pillar of fire that guided Israel through the wilderness by night. Against that background, Jesus says, “I am the light of the world.”

The chapter contains some of the sharpest exchanges in the Gospels. John often uses the phrase “the Jews” to refer to the religious authorities and others in Jerusalem who opposed Jesus, not to the Jewish people as a whole. Jesus Himself, His disciples, and the first believers were Jewish, and many Jews in this very chapter believe in Him (*8:30*). These harsh words were spoken within a family argument among Jews about the meaning of their own Scriptures and the identity of their Messiah. They must never be used to justify contempt for Jewish people, as tragically has happened in history.

### A Woman Caught in Adultery (*7:53–8*:11)

A note on the text is needed here. The story of the woman caught in adultery (*7:53–8*:11) is not found in the earliest and most reliable Greek manuscripts of John, and in some later manuscripts it appears in other places, such as after *Luke 21:38*. For this reason, most modern Bibles place it in brackets or with a note. Many scholars nevertheless believe that it records a genuine event from Jesus’ life, preserved in the church’s memory, because it fits His character and teaching so well. The World English Bible includes it in its traditional place, and this commentary treats it with that understanding.

Jesus spent the night on the Mount of Olives and returned to the temple at dawn, where crowds gathered to hear Him. The scribes and Pharisees brought a woman and set her in the middle of the crowd. “*Teacher, we found this woman in adultery, in the very act*” (*v. 4*). They reminded Jesus that the Law of Moses commanded stoning in such cases (*Leviticus 20:10*; *Deuteronomy 22:22–24*) and asked what He said.

John explains their motive: “*They said this testing him, that they might have something to accuse him of*” (*v. 6*). It was a trap. If Jesus said to release her, they could accuse Him of disregarding the Law. If He said to stone her, He would contradict His reputation for mercy and might also defy Roman authorities, who did not permit Jews to carry out executions on their own (*John 18:31*). The trap also revealed their injustice. The Law required both the man and the woman to be punished, yet only the woman was brought. She was being used as a tool in their plan.

Jesus stooped and wrote on the ground with His finger. No one knows what He wrote. Some suggest He wrote the sins of the accusers, others a verse such as *Jeremiah 17:13*, others that He was simply refusing to be rushed. When they kept pressing Him, He stood and said, “*He who is without sin among you, let him throw the first stone at her*” (*v. 7*). Then He stooped and wrote again.

One by one, beginning with the oldest, they left. Jesus was left alone with the woman. His words to her are studied below.

### The Light of the World (*8:12–20*)

Jesus then declared, “*I am the light of the world*” (*v. 12*). This is studied below. The Pharisees objected that He was testifying about Himself, so His testimony was invalid. Jesus answered that His testimony was true because He knew where He came from and where He was going. And He was not alone: the Father who sent Him also testified about Him. The Law required two witnesses (*Deuteronomy 19:15*), and Jesus had two, Himself and His Father.

They asked, “*Where is your Father?*” (*v. 19*) Jesus replied, “*You know neither me nor my Father. If you knew me, you would know my Father also*” (*v. 19*). To know Jesus is to know the Father. He said these things in the treasury area of the temple, yet no one seized Him, “*because his hour had not yet come*” (*v. 20*).

### “Unless You Believe That I Am He” (*8:21–30*)

Jesus warned, “*I am going away, and you will seek me, and you will die in your sins*” (*v. 21*). His listeners wondered if He meant to take His own life. Jesus explained that they were from below and He was from above. Then He said, “*unless you believe that I am he, you will die in your sins*” (*v. 24*). The word “he” is not in the Greek; Jesus literally says, “unless you believe that I am.” This is another echo of God’s name, preparing for the climax of the chapter.

They asked, “*Who are you?*” (*v. 25*) Jesus said that He was what He had been telling them from the beginning. Then He spoke of the cross: “*When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am he*” (*v. 28*). His crucifixion, the moment of apparent defeat, would reveal who He truly is. He added, “*The Father hasn’t left me alone, for I always do the things that are pleasing to him*” (*v. 29*). As He spoke, “*many believed in him*” (*v. 30*).

### The Truth That Sets Free (*8:31–47*)

Jesus spoke to those who had believed in Him about what true discipleship involves. This is studied below. Some listeners objected that they were Abraham’s descendants and had never been slaves to anyone, which, considering Egypt, Babylon, and Rome, was a remarkable statement. Jesus answered, “*everyone who commits sin is the bondservant of sin*” (*v. 34*). A slave does not remain in the household forever, but a son does. “*If therefore the Son makes you free, you will be free indeed*” (*v. 36*).

The conversation became heated. They claimed Abraham as their father, but Jesus said that if they were truly Abraham’s children, they would act like Abraham, who welcomed God’s word. They were seeking to kill Him, which Abraham never did. They answered, “*We were not born of sexual immorality*” (*v. 41*), possibly hinting at rumors about Jesus’ birth. They claimed God as their Father.

Jesus said, “*If God were your father, you would love me, for I came out and have come from God*” (*v. 42*). Then came His strongest words: “*You are of your father the devil*” (*v. 44*). Jesus explained that the devil was a murderer from the beginning and the father of lies. Their desire to kill Jesus and their refusal of the truth showed whose will they were following. These words were addressed to specific opponents who were plotting murder, not to Jewish people as a group; Jesus also told Peter, His own disciple, “*Get behind me, Satan!*” (*Matthew 16:23*) when Peter opposed God’s plan. The point is that anyone who rejects the truth and plots evil is following the deceiver rather than God.

Jesus challenged them: “*Which of you convicts me of sin?*” (*v. 46*) No one could. He concluded, “*He who is of God hears the words of God*” (*v. 47*).

### Before Abraham Was, I AM (*8:48–59*)

The opponents accused Jesus of being a Samaritan and demon-possessed. Jesus calmly denied it and said that He honored His Father. Then He made a promise: “*if a person keeps my word, he will never see death*” (*v. 51*). They were outraged. Abraham died, and so did the prophets. “*Who do you make yourself out to be?*” (*v. 53*)

Jesus said that His Father glorified Him, and that “*Your father Abraham rejoiced to see my day. He saw it and was glad*” (*v. 56*). Abraham, through faith in God’s promises, looked forward to the coming of the promised Seed through whom all nations would be blessed (*Genesis 22:18*). His listeners protested that Jesus was not even fifty years old. How could He have seen Abraham? Jesus’ answer is studied below. The crowd picked up stones to throw at Him, but He slipped away from the temple.

## Important Verses Explained

### *John 8:10–11* — Neither Do I Condemn You

> *“Jesus, standing up, saw her and said, ‘Woman, where are your accusers? Did no one condemn you?’ She said, ‘No one, Lord.’ Jesus said, ‘Neither do I condemn you. Go your way. From now on, sin no more.’”*
>
> — *John 8:10–11* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The woman had been dragged before a crowd in the temple courts early in the morning, caught in adultery. Her accusers made her stand in the middle of everyone, publicly shamed, while they tried to trap Jesus. Under the Law, adultery was punishable by death. Her life seemed to hang on Jesus’ answer.

Jesus said that whoever was without sin should throw the first stone. One by one, the accusers left, beginning with the oldest. They were “*convicted by their conscience*” (*v. 9*). Perhaps the older ones were wise enough to recognize their own sins most quickly. At the end, only Jesus and the woman remained.

Jesus stood up and asked her, “*Woman, where are your accusers? Did no one condemn you?*” (*v. 10*) She answered, “*No one, Lord*” (*v. 11*). Then Jesus spoke words of astonishing grace: “*Neither do I condemn you*” (*v. 11*). The only person present who was truly without sin, and who therefore had the right to throw a stone, chose not to condemn her.

But Jesus did not stop there: “*Go your way. From now on, sin no more*” (*v. 11*). He did not pretend that what she had done was acceptable. He called it sin. But He gave her freedom from condemnation first, and then called her to a new life. Mercy came before the command, and the command flowed from the mercy.

It is worth noticing what Jesus did not do. He did not shame her further, lecture her in front of the crowd, or demand that she prove herself before He would show mercy. He treated her with dignity, addressing her directly and with respect.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This scene shows how Jesus holds together grace and truth (*John 1:14*). Grace: “Neither do I condemn you.” Truth: “From now on, sin no more.” Some people emphasize grace in a way that excuses sin; others emphasize truth in a way that crushes sinners. Jesus does neither. He forgives freely and calls to holiness.

It also shows how Jesus could release her from condemnation without setting aside God’s justice. Jesus Himself would soon bear the condemnation of sin on the cross. Paul writes, “*There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus*” (*Romans 8:1*). The mercy Jesus showed the woman was costly; it would be paid for at Calvary.

The scene also exposes the hypocrisy of self-righteous accusers. The scribes and Pharisees were eager to condemn someone else’s sin while ignoring their own, and they showed no concern for justice toward the man involved. Jesus’ words turned the spotlight on every heart. All have sinned, and none can stand as a sinless judge over others.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage offers deep comfort to anyone weighed down by shame. Some people carry the memory of sins that others know about, or that they fear others will discover. Jesus’ words are for them: He does not condemn those who come to Him. His forgiveness is not grudging or partial.

It also calls forgiven people to live differently. Jesus’ mercy is not permission to continue in sin but power to leave it behind. Gratitude for grace becomes the motivation for a changed life.

Finally, the passage challenges anyone who is quick to condemn others. Believers can easily focus on the visible sins of others while ignoring their own pride, harshness, or hidden failings. Jesus’ words invite humility. Those who know they have been forgiven are called to treat others with the same mercy, while still speaking the truth in love. At the same time, mercy toward sinners never means ignoring harm done to others; Jesus’ compassion for this woman included protecting her from violence and from those who were using her.

### *John 8:12* — I Am the Light of the World

> *“Again, therefore, Jesus spoke to them, saying, ‘I am the light of the world. He who follows me will not walk in the darkness, but will have the light of life.’”*
>
> — *John 8:12* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus spoke these words in the temple during or just after the Feast of Booths. During the feast, great golden lamps were lit in the temple courts, giving light to the whole city. These lamps reminded the people of the pillar of fire by which God led Israel through the wilderness at night (*Exodus 13:21*). Against this background, Jesus made a bold claim: “*I am the light of the world*” (*v. 12*).

Jesus does not say that He is one light among many, or a light for Israel only. He says that He is the light of the whole world. In the Old Testament, light is often associated with God Himself. “*The LORD is my light and my salvation*” (*Psalm 27:1*). Isaiah prophesied that God’s servant would be “*a light to the nations*” (*Isaiah 49:6*).

“*He who follows me will not walk in the darkness*” (*v. 12*). Darkness in Scripture represents sin, ignorance, confusion, danger, and separation from God. Without Jesus, people walk in darkness, unable to see their way. Following Him means walking in His light.

“*but will have the light of life*” (*v. 12*). Jesus does not only show the way; He gives life. The light He gives is the light that produces and sustains true life. Just as plants need sunlight to grow, people need the light of Christ to truly live.

The word “follows” is important. Jesus does not say, “He who admires Me,” but “He who follows Me.” Like the Israelites following the pillar of fire through the wilderness, believers follow Jesus step by step.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This is the second of Jesus’ “I am” sayings in John. It connects with the opening of the Gospel, where John wrote that in the Word “*was life, and the life was the light of men*” (*John 1:4*), and that “*The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness hasn’t overcome it*” (*John 1:5*). Jesus is the eternal light who has entered the world’s darkness.

The saying also points to Jesus’ role in revealing the truth about God and about people. Light exposes what is hidden. When people come to Jesus, their sin is revealed, but so is God’s grace. Those who love darkness avoid the light (*John 3:19–20*), but those who come to the light find life.

In the next chapter, Jesus demonstrates this claim by giving sight to a man born blind, saying again, “*I am the light of the world*” (*John 9:5*). His words and His works agree.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse offers guidance to people who feel lost or confused. Many people today are uncertain about the meaning of life, the right way to live, or the path ahead. Jesus offers Himself as the light. Following Him does not mean every question is answered at once, but it means walking with the One who sees the way clearly.

It also calls believers to follow Jesus daily. Light is given for walking. Believers walk in His light by listening to His words, obeying His teaching, and staying close to Him in prayer. When they wander from Him, they find themselves stumbling in darkness again.

Finally, the verse reminds believers of their calling. Jesus also told His disciples, “*You are the light of the world*” (*Matthew 5:14*). Believers reflect His light to others through lives of truth, goodness, and love.

### *John 8:31–32* — The Truth Will Make You Free

> *“Jesus therefore said to those Jews who had believed him, ‘If you remain in my word, then you are truly my disciples. You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.’”*
>
> — *John 8:31–32* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

As Jesus spoke about His relationship with the Father, many people believed in Him (*8:30*). Jesus then addressed these new believers, explaining what genuine discipleship involves: “*If you remain in my word, then you are truly my disciples*” (*v. 31*).

To “remain” in Jesus’ word means to continue in it, to live in it, and to keep returning to it. It is not a one-time decision but a lasting commitment. Initial belief is the beginning, but true disciples continue in His teaching over time.

“*You will know the truth*” (*v. 32*). Those who remain in Jesus’ word come to know the truth. This is not merely knowing facts but knowing reality as God sees it, and ultimately knowing Jesus Himself, who later says, “*I am the way, the truth, and the life*” (*John 14:6*).

“*and the truth will make you free*” (*v. 32*). This verse is often quoted in schools, libraries, and public buildings, usually to mean that knowledge or education liberates people. But Jesus means something deeper. The freedom He speaks of is freedom from the slavery of sin.

The listeners objected that they had never been slaves. Jesus explained, “*everyone who commits sin is the bondservant of sin*” (*v. 34*). Sin is not merely a series of bad actions; it is a power that enslaves. Then He promised, “*If therefore the Son makes you free, you will be free indeed*” (*v. 36*). True freedom comes through Jesus Himself.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses reveal that genuine faith shows itself in perseverance. Throughout John, some people “believed” in a shallow way and later turned away (*John 2:23–25*; *6:66*). In this very chapter, some who believed soon became hostile. Jesus teaches that true disciples continue in His word. Perseverance does not earn salvation, but it is evidence of genuine faith.

The passage also redefines freedom. Many people think of freedom as doing whatever they want. Jesus teaches that doing whatever one wants can be slavery, because sinful desires control the heart. True freedom is being released from sin’s power to live as God intended. Paul expresses the same idea: “*Stand firm therefore in the liberty by which Christ has made us free*” (*Galatians 5:1*).

Finally, the passage shows that truth and freedom are connected to a Person. The truth that frees is not an abstract idea but Jesus Himself and His word. Freedom comes through relationship with the Son, who has the authority to release slaves and make them members of God’s family.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to remain in Jesus’ word. Discipleship grows as believers read, study, and obey His teaching over time. Christians are called not only to begin well but to keep continuing in His word through every season of life.

They also offer hope to people who feel trapped. Many struggle with habits, addictions, fears, or patterns of sin they cannot break. Jesus promises real freedom. This freedom may come gradually, through the work of His Spirit, His word, and His people, but His promise is sure: those whom the Son sets free are free indeed.

Finally, these verses challenge cultural ideas of freedom. Believers can show that true freedom is not found in having no limits but in living in the truth. Life with Christ brings freedom from guilt, from slavery to sin, and from the fear of death.

### *John 8:58* — Before Abraham, I AM

> *“Jesus said to them, ‘Most certainly, I tell you, before Abraham came into existence, I AM.’”*
>
> — *John 8:58* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse comes at the end of a long, heated debate in the temple courts. Jesus had promised that whoever keeps His word will never see death. His opponents were outraged. Abraham, the father of the nation, had died, and so had the prophets. Was Jesus claiming to be greater than Abraham?

Jesus answered that Abraham rejoiced to see His day. The opponents responded, “*You are not yet fifty years old! Have you seen Abraham?*” (*v. 57*) Jesus was in His early thirties. Abraham had lived about two thousand years earlier. The claim seemed absurd.

Then Jesus said, “*Most certainly, I tell you, before Abraham came into existence, I AM*” (*v. 58*). Notice the contrast in the verbs. Abraham “came into existence”; he had a beginning. But Jesus does not say, “Before Abraham was, I was.” He says, “I AM.” He speaks of His existence as timeless and continuous, without beginning.

The phrase “I AM” recalls God’s revelation of His name to Moses at the burning bush: “*God said to Moses, “I AM WHO I AM,” and he said, “You shall tell the children of Israel this: ‘I AM has sent me to you.’”*” (*Exodus 3:14*) Jesus applies God’s own name to Himself.

The listeners understood what He meant. “*Therefore they took up stones to throw at him*” (*v. 59*). Stoning was the penalty for blasphemy (*Leviticus 24:16*). They recognized that Jesus was claiming to be God.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse is one of the clearest claims to deity in the Gospels. Jesus does not merely claim to be a prophet or a messenger from God. He claims eternal existence and identifies Himself with the God of Israel who revealed Himself to Moses. This fulfills John’s opening words: “*In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God*” (*John 1:1*).

It also shows that Jesus is the fulfillment of Abraham’s hope. God promised Abraham that all nations would be blessed through his offspring. Abraham looked forward to that promise and rejoiced. Jesus is the One in whom the promise is fulfilled. He is greater than Abraham, not as a rival, but as the eternal Lord whom Abraham trusted.

Finally, this verse forces a decision. As many have observed, someone who claims to be God is either mistaken, deceptive, or telling the truth. The opponents concluded that Jesus was a blasphemer. John wrote his Gospel so that readers would conclude that He is the eternal Son of God (*John 20:31*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites people to consider who Jesus really is. He cannot be reduced to a wise teacher, a moral example, or an inspiring figure. He claimed to be the eternal I AM. Each person must decide how to respond to that claim.

It also gives believers deep confidence. The Jesus they trust is not limited by time. He existed before Abraham, He is present now, and He will be forever. The One who promises that those who keep His word will never see death is the eternal Lord who has authority over life and death.

Finally, the verse calls believers to worship. If Jesus is the I AM, He deserves the worship that belongs to God alone. Believers can bring Him their praise, trust, and obedience, knowing that the Lord who spoke to Moses from the burning bush is the same Lord who walked among us and died for us.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*John 8* begins with a woman surrounded by accusers and ends with Jesus surrounded by people ready to stone Him. In between, Jesus reveals who He is and what He offers. To the woman, He offers freedom from condemnation and a call to a new life. Those who carry shame can come to Jesus and hear the same words: “Neither do I condemn you.” Those who are quick to condemn others are reminded that no one is without sin, and that mercy is the way of Christ.

The chapter presents Jesus as the light of the world. In a world of confusion and moral darkness, He offers light for the path and light that brings life. Following Him daily, listening to His word, and staying close to Him allow believers to walk in His light and reflect it to others.

*John 8* also teaches that true discipleship means remaining in Jesus’ word. The freedom He gives is not simply the freedom to do what we want but freedom from the slavery of sin. Many people who feel trapped by patterns they cannot break can take hope in His promise that those whom the Son sets free are free indeed.

Finally, the chapter brings readers face to face with Jesus’ claim to be the eternal I AM. This claim cannot be ignored or softened. It calls for worship from those who believe and a serious response from those who are still considering Him. And it reminds believers that the One who forgives, guides, and frees them is the eternal Lord, worthy of their whole trust.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, You are the eternal I AM, who existed before Abraham and who stands above all time. I worship You. Thank You that You did not condemn the woman who was brought before You in shame, and that You do not condemn those who come to You for mercy. Thank You for bearing the condemnation I deserved. Help me to leave behind my sin and to walk in the new life You give. You are the light of the world; lead me out of darkness and let me follow You each day. Keep me in Your word, so that I may truly be Your disciple and know the truth that sets me free. Where I am still bound by sin or fear, set me free indeed. Guard my heart from self-righteousness and from quick condemnation of others, and make me a person of grace and truth like You. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

John · Chapter 9 of 21

# John — Chapter 9

Chapter Theme: The Man Born Blind Receives Sight, and the Seeing Become Blind

[Read John 9 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/JHN09.htm)

Main Teaching

Jesus gives sight to a man who had been blind from birth, rejecting the assumption that his blindness was punishment for sin and revealing it instead as an occasion for God’s works to be displayed. As the healed man is questioned, pressured, and finally thrown out of the synagogue, his understanding of Jesus grows from “a man called Jesus” to “a prophet” to worship of the Son of God. Meanwhile the religious leaders, who claim to see, harden into deeper blindness.

## Chapter Background and Story

*John 9* is one of the most carefully told stories in the Gospels. It is almost like a drama in several scenes: Jesus and the blind man, the man and his neighbors, the man and the Pharisees, the Pharisees and his parents, the man and the Pharisees again, Jesus and the man, and finally Jesus and the Pharisees. As the scenes unfold, two movements happen at the same time. The man who was blind sees more and more clearly who Jesus is, while those who claim to see become more and more blind.

The chapter puts into action Jesus’ claim in *John 8:12*, “*I am the light of the world*” (*John 8:12*). He now shows it by giving light to eyes that had never seen.

### Who Sinned? (*9:1–7*)

As Jesus walked along, He saw a man who had been blind from birth. The disciples asked a common question of their time: “*Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?*” (*v. 2*) Many people believed that suffering was always the direct result of a specific sin. Some rabbis even speculated that a baby could sin in the womb, or that children suffered for their parents’ sins.

Jesus rejected both options. This is studied below. Then He said, “*I must work the works of him who sent me while it is day. The night is coming, when no one can work*” (*v. 4*). Jesus’ time on earth was limited, and He was committed to doing the Father’s work while He could. He added, “*While I am in the world, I am the light of the world*” (*v. 5*).

Jesus spat on the ground, made mud, and put it on the man’s eyes. Then He said, “*Go, wash in the pool of Siloam*” (*v. 7*). John explains that Siloam means “Sent.” This was the pool from which water was drawn for the ceremonies at the Feast of Booths. The detail also points to Jesus, who throughout John is the One “sent” by the Father. The man went, washed, and “*came back seeing*” (*v. 7*).

Why mud? Some see an echo of *Genesis 2:7*, where God formed the first man from the dust of the ground. Jesus, the Creator, now completes a man’s creation by forming eyes that work. Others note that saliva was sometimes used in ancient healing practices. What is clear is that Jesus involved the man in his healing; he had to go and wash, trusting the word of One he could not yet see.

### The Neighbors’ Questions (*9:8–12*)

The man’s neighbors could hardly believe it. Some said, “*Isn’t this he who sat and begged?*” (*v. 8*) Others said he only looked like the man. He kept saying, “*I am he*” (*v. 9*). When they asked how his eyes were opened, he told the story simply: “*A man called Jesus made mud, anointed my eyes, and said to me, ‘Go to the pool of Siloam and wash.’ So I went away and washed, and I received sight*” (*v. 11*). At this stage, Jesus is to him simply “a man called Jesus.” When asked where Jesus was, he said he did not know.

### The First Hearing before the Pharisees (*9:13–17*)

The neighbors brought the man to the Pharisees. John notes, “*It was a Sabbath when Jesus made the mud and opened his eyes*” (*v. 14*). Kneading dough, or by extension mud, was among the kinds of work forbidden on the Sabbath under the rules the teachers had developed, and so was healing in cases that were not life-threatening.

The Pharisees were divided. Some said, “*This man is not from God, because he doesn’t keep the Sabbath*” (*v. 16*). Others asked, “*How can a man who is a sinner do such signs?*” (*v. 16*) They asked the man his opinion, and he answered, “*He is a prophet*” (*v. 17*). His understanding was growing.

### The Parents Questioned (*9:18–23*)

The religious leaders did not believe that the man had really been born blind, so they called his parents. The parents confirmed that this was their son and that he had been born blind, but they would not say how he now saw or who had healed him. “*He is of age. Ask him. He will speak for himself*” (*v. 21*).

John explains their fear: “*the Jews had already agreed that if any man would confess him as Christ, he would be put out of the synagogue*” (*v. 22*). Being expelled from the synagogue meant being cut off from community, worship, and social life. It was a serious threat, and the parents chose safety over speaking the truth about what had happened to their own son.

### The Second Hearing (*9:24–34*)

The leaders called the man back and said, “*Give glory to God. We know that this man is a sinner*” (*v. 24*). “Give glory to God” was a formula used to urge someone to tell the truth (*Joshua 7:19*). They wanted him to agree that Jesus was a sinner. His reply is studied below.

When they asked him again how Jesus had healed him, he showed surprising boldness: “*I told you already, and you didn’t listen. Why do you want to hear it again? You don’t also want to become his disciples, do you?*” (*v. 27*) The leaders insulted him: “*You are his disciple, but we are disciples of Moses*” (*v. 28*). They said they did not know where Jesus came from.

The man, who had spent his life begging, now reasoned with the experts. It was amazing, he said, that they did not know where Jesus came from, since He had opened his eyes. God does not listen to sinners but to those who worship Him and do His will. “*Since the world began it has never been heard of that anyone opened the eyes of someone born blind*” (*v. 32*). His conclusion: “*If this man were not from God, he could do nothing*” (*v. 33*).

The leaders had no answer except contempt: “*You were altogether born in sins, and do you teach us?*” (*v. 34*) Then they threw him out. Ironically, they used the same assumption the disciples had made at the beginning, that his blindness proved his sinfulness.

### Jesus Finds the Man (*9:35–41*)

When Jesus heard that the man had been thrown out, He went and found him. This scene is studied below. The man came to faith and worshiped Jesus.

Jesus then said, “*I came into this world for judgment, that those who don’t see may see; and that those who see may become blind*” (*v. 39*). Some Pharisees nearby asked, “*Are we also blind?*” (*v. 40*) Jesus answered, “*If you were blind, you would have no sin; but now you say, ‘We see.’ Therefore your sin remains*” (*v. 41*). Those who admit their need can receive sight. Those who insist that they already see, and refuse the light, remain in their sin.

## Important Verses Explained

### *John 9:2–3* — That the Works of God Might Be Revealed

> *“His disciples asked him, ‘Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?’ Jesus answered, This man didn’t sin, nor did his parents, but that the works of God might be revealed in him.”*
>
> — *John 9:2–3* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

As Jesus and His disciples walked through Jerusalem, they saw a man who had been blind since birth. He was probably sitting by the road begging, since blind people had few other ways to survive. The disciples did not ask how they could help him. Instead, they asked a theological question: “*Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?*” (*v. 2*)

Their question reflected a widespread belief that suffering was always punishment for a particular sin. If someone was born blind, either the parents had sinned, or perhaps the child had somehow sinned before birth. The book of Job had already challenged this way of thinking, but it remained common.

Jesus answered, “*This man didn’t sin, nor did his parents*” (*v. 3*). Jesus was not saying that the man and his parents were sinless in general. He meant that the man’s blindness was not caused by a specific sin committed by him or his parents. The disciples’ assumption was wrong.

Then Jesus gave a new perspective: “*but that the works of God might be revealed in him*” (*v. 3*). Instead of looking backward to find someone to blame, Jesus looked forward to what God would do. This man’s life, which others saw only as a tragedy or a punishment, would become a place where God’s power and mercy would be displayed.

Jesus did not merely discuss the man’s situation. He acted, giving him sight.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This passage corrects a harmful view of suffering. While Scripture teaches that sin brought suffering into the world (*Genesis 3*), and that some specific sins bring painful consequences, it also teaches that not all suffering is a direct punishment for particular sins. Job suffered though he was righteous. Jesus also rejected the idea that people who died in disasters were worse sinners than others (*Luke 13:1–5*).

The passage also shows God’s ability to bring good out of suffering. This does not mean that God enjoys suffering or that every painful thing is good in itself. It means that God can work even in what is broken, displaying His glory through healing, comfort, endurance, or the hope of final restoration. Paul expresses a similar confidence: “*We know that all things work together for good for those who love God*” (*Romans 8:28*).

Finally, the passage reveals Jesus’ compassion and purpose. He came to do the works of the Father, and those works include restoring what is broken. This healing is a sign of the new creation, when God will wipe away every tear and heal every disease.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage warns against assuming that people’s suffering is their fault. When someone is sick, disabled, poor, or grieving, it is easy to look for someone to blame. Jesus’ response calls His followers to compassion rather than judgment. Instead of asking “Who sinned?”, believers can ask how God might be glorified through their love and care for the one who is suffering.

It also gives hope to people who live with long-term suffering, including disabilities they were born with. Their lives are not punishments, and they are not less valuable to God. God can display His works in many ways, through healing, through strength in weakness, through the love of others, and through the faith that perseveres.

Finally, the passage encourages believers to respond to suffering with action. Jesus did not stop at a theological answer; He helped the man. Believers are called to do the works of God while it is day, showing mercy to those in need.

### *John 9:25* — Though I Was Blind, Now I See

> *“He therefore answered, ‘I don’t know if he is a sinner. One thing I do know: that though I was blind, now I see.’”*
>
> — *John 9:25* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The man who had been born blind was standing before religious leaders for the second time. They had already questioned him, questioned his parents, and argued among themselves. Now they tried to pressure him to agree with their conclusion: “*Give glory to God. We know that this man is a sinner*” (*v. 24*). Because Jesus had healed on the Sabbath, they were sure He could not be from God.

The man answered, “*I don’t know if he is a sinner*” (*v. 25*). He did not claim to have answers to all their theological questions. He was not a trained scholar and did not try to debate their interpretation of the Sabbath laws.

“*One thing I do know: that though I was blind, now I see*” (*v. 25*). What he did know was his own experience. He had been blind all his life. Now he could see. No argument could change that fact.

This answer was simple but powerful. The religious leaders had knowledge, authority, and power, but they could not deny what had happened. The man’s testimony rested on the undeniable change in his life.

Throughout the chapter, the man shows growing courage. He began by simply describing what happened, then called Jesus a prophet, then challenged the leaders, and finally worshiped Jesus. His faith grew as he faced opposition.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The man’s words have become a picture of conversion. Spiritually, all people are born blind, unable to see God’s truth and glory. Paul writes that “*the god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelieving*” (*2 Corinthians 4:4*). When Christ opens a person’s eyes, they can say, “*though I was blind, now I see*” (*v. 25*). The well-known hymn “Amazing Grace” uses these very words.

The verse also shows the power of personal testimony. Theological arguments are important, but a transformed life speaks in a way that is hard to dismiss. The apostles also bore witness to what they had seen and heard (*1 John 1:1–3*).

Finally, the scene shows that faithfulness to the truth may cost something. The man’s honesty led to his being thrown out of the synagogue. His parents had chosen safety. He chose to tell the truth, and in losing his place in the community, he found Jesus.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers who feel unqualified to talk about their faith. They may not be able to answer every theological question or win every argument. But they can share what they know: what Jesus has done in their lives. A simple, honest testimony can be powerful.

It also reminds believers to remember what God has done for them. Gratitude grows when believers recall how Christ opened their eyes, forgave their sins, and changed their lives. These memories strengthen faith in difficult times.

Finally, the man’s courage challenges believers to stand for the truth even under pressure. Many people face social, family, or professional pressure to deny or downplay their faith. The man’s example shows that it is better to lose human approval than to deny what Christ has done.

### *John 9:35–38* — Lord, I Believe

> *“Jesus heard that they had thrown him out, and finding him, he said, ‘Do you believe in the Son of God?’ He answered, ‘Who is he, Lord, that I may believe in him?’ Jesus said to him, ‘You have both seen him, and it is he who speaks with you.’ He said, ‘Lord, I believe!’ and he worshiped him.”*
>
> — *John 9:35–38* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The man who had been healed had just been thrown out of the synagogue. For a first-century Jew, this meant being cut off from community life, worship, and relationships. He had received his sight, only to lose his place among his people. His own parents had refused to stand with him.

Then: “*Jesus heard that they had thrown him out, and finding him*” (*v. 35*). Jesus went looking for him. The man had not seen Jesus since he went to wash in the pool; he had been blind when Jesus spoke to him. Now Jesus sought him out.

Jesus asked, “*Do you believe in the Son of God?*” (*v. 35*) (Some early manuscripts read “Son of Man.”) The man answered, “*Who is he, Lord, that I may believe in him?*” (*v. 36*) He was ready to believe; he only needed to know who this person was.

Jesus said, “*You have both seen him, and it is he who speaks with you*” (*v. 37*). The words “you have seen him” are beautiful, since the man had been blind and could now see. The first face he could recognize as the face of his healer was the face of the Son of God.

“*He said, “Lord, I believe!” and he worshiped him*” (*v. 38*). The man’s faith reached its full expression. He began by calling Jesus “a man,” then “a prophet,” then “from God,” and now he worshiped Him as Lord.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This scene shows the seeking heart of Jesus. Just as a shepherd goes after a lost sheep, Jesus went after the man who had been cast out. In the next chapter, Jesus describes Himself as the Good Shepherd who knows His sheep and calls them by name (*John 10:3*, 11). Those whom the religious leaders rejected, Jesus welcomed.

The scene also shows that faith grows over time. The man did not understand everything at once. His understanding developed through his experience, his testimony, and the opposition he faced. When Jesus revealed Himself fully, he was ready to believe and worship.

The man’s worship is significant. In John’s Gospel, worship belongs to God alone. Jesus accepted the man’s worship without correction, confirming His divine identity. The man received both physical sight and spiritual sight, seeing Jesus for who He truly is.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage offers comfort to anyone who has been rejected for their faith or has been pushed out by others. Jesus seeks out those who are cast out. When people lose relationships, community, or status because of their faith in Him, Jesus comes to them and draws them closer.

It also encourages people whose faith is still growing. Not everyone understands everything about Jesus at once. Faith often grows step by step. Jesus patiently reveals Himself to those who are willing to believe.

Finally, the passage shows the right response to Jesus: belief and worship. Knowing facts about Jesus is not enough. The man’s response, “Lord, I believe,” followed by worship, is the response Jesus invites from everyone.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*John 9* teaches believers to look at suffering differently. Instead of searching for someone to blame, Jesus pointed to what God would do. Christians are called to respond to people who suffer, including those with lifelong disabilities, with compassion, dignity, and practical help, trusting that God can display His works even in situations that seem hopeless.

The chapter also celebrates the power of a changed life. The man who was healed could not answer every question, but he knew that he had been blind and now could see. Every believer has a story of what Christ has done. Sharing that story honestly and humbly can be a powerful witness, even when others oppose it.

*John 9* shows that faithfulness can be costly. The man’s parents chose safety over truth, while the man chose truth and was thrown out. Many believers face pressure to remain silent about Jesus. This chapter reminds them that Jesus seeks out those who suffer for His sake and draws them into deeper fellowship with Himself.

Finally, the chapter contains a sobering warning. Those who insist that they already see clearly, and refuse to admit their need, can remain blind. Spiritual sight begins with humility. Those who acknowledge their blindness can receive sight from Jesus, the light of the world, and grow in faith until they worship Him as Lord.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, You are the light of the world. Thank You for seeing the man born blind when others saw only a beggar or a theological question. Teach me to see suffering people with Your compassion, and keep me from blaming those who are already hurting. Thank You for opening my eyes to see You. Like the man You healed, I can say that once I was blind, but now I see. Give me courage to speak honestly about what You have done in my life, even when others oppose me or do not understand. When I feel rejected or pushed aside, remind me that You seek out those who are cast out. Keep me humble, so that I never claim to see while refusing Your light. Help my faith to grow until my whole life is worship of You, my Lord. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

John · Chapter 10 of 21

# John — Chapter 10

Chapter Theme: The Good Shepherd Who Lays Down His Life and Holds His Sheep Secure

[Read John 10 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/JHN10.htm)

Main Teaching

Jesus contrasts Himself with thieves, robbers, and hired hands. He is the door through which the sheep find salvation and pasture, and He is the Good Shepherd who knows His sheep by name and lays down His life for them of His own free will. At the Feast of Dedication, He declares that His sheep hear His voice and follow Him, that He gives them eternal life and no one can snatch them from His hand or the Father’s, and that He and the Father are one.

## Chapter Background and Story

*John 10* follows directly from *John 9*. The Pharisees had just thrown out the man born blind, treating him harshly instead of caring for him. Jesus, by contrast, sought him out. Now Jesus uses the familiar picture of shepherds and sheep to show the difference between false leaders who harm the flock and the true Shepherd who cares for it.

The image was deeply rooted in Israel’s Scriptures. God is called the Shepherd of Israel (*Psalm 80:1*), and David wrote, “*The LORD is my shepherd*” (*Psalm 23:1*). Israel’s kings and leaders were also called shepherds. In *Ezekiel 34*, God condemns the shepherds of Israel who fed themselves instead of the flock, who did not strengthen the weak or seek the lost, and He promises: “I myself will search for my sheep” and “I will set up one shepherd over them, and he will feed them, even my servant David” (*Ezekiel 34:11*, 23). Jesus’ words in *John 10* claim the fulfillment of that promise.

### The Shepherd and the Door (*10:1–6*)

In Palestine, sheep were often kept at night in a sheepfold, a walled enclosure of stone with a single opening. Sometimes several flocks shared a fold, with a gatekeeper watching the entrance. In the morning, each shepherd came and called his own sheep, and they recognized his voice and followed him out.

Jesus said that anyone who climbs into the fold some other way is “*a thief and a robber*” (*v. 1*), but the one who enters by the door is the shepherd. “*He calls his own sheep by name and leads them out*” (*v. 3*). Shepherds often gave their sheep names, and the sheep knew their shepherd’s voice. “*he goes before them; and the sheep follow him, for they know his voice*” (*v. 4*). Eastern shepherds led their flocks from the front rather than driving them from behind. The sheep would not follow a stranger.

The listeners did not understand what Jesus meant, so He explained further.

### I Am the Door (*10:7–10*)

Jesus said, “*I am the sheep’s door*” (*v. 7*). In some shepherds’ practice, especially in the open countryside, a fold had an opening but no gate, and the shepherd himself would lie across the entrance at night. Nothing could enter or leave except through him. Jesus is the only way into the safety of God’s flock.

“*All who came before me are thieves and robbers*” (*v. 8*). This does not refer to the true prophets, but to false messiahs and leaders who claimed to bring salvation and instead exploited the people. “*I am the door. If anyone enters in by me, he will be saved, and will go in and go out and will find pasture*” (*v. 9*). “Going in and out” was a Hebrew expression for living safely and freely (*Deuteronomy 28:6*). Through Jesus, the sheep find salvation, security, freedom, and nourishment. Verse 10 is studied below.

### I Am the Good Shepherd (*10:11–18*)

Jesus declared, “*I am the good shepherd*” (*v. 11*). This is studied below. He contrasted the Good Shepherd with the hired hand, who works for wages and does not own the sheep. When the wolf comes, the hired hand runs away, because he does not truly care for the sheep.

“*I am the good shepherd. I know my own, and I’m known by my own*” (*v. 14*). Jesus’ relationship with His sheep is personal and intimate, reflecting His relationship with the Father: “*even as the Father knows me, and I know the Father*” (*v. 15*).

Then He spoke of a wider flock: “*I have other sheep which are not of this fold. I must bring them also, and they will hear my voice. They will become one flock with one shepherd*” (*v. 16*). The “other sheep” are generally understood as Gentiles, people outside Israel, who would come to faith and join with Jewish believers in one people of God.

Jesus emphasized that His death would be voluntary: “*No one takes it away from me, but I lay it down by myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again*” (*v. 18*). His death would not be a tragic accident or a defeat. He would give His life freely, in obedience to the Father, and He would take it up again in resurrection.

The crowd was divided again. Some said He was demon-possessed and insane. Others said, “*It isn’t possible for a demon to open the eyes of the blind, is it?*” (*v. 21*)

### At the Feast of Dedication (*10:22–42*)

Some time later, perhaps two months, Jesus was in Jerusalem for “*the Feast of the Dedication*” (*v. 22*), which is known today as Hanukkah. It remembered the rededication of the temple in 164 B.C., after the Jewish leader Judas Maccabeus drove out the Syrian king Antiochus IV Epiphanes, who had desecrated the temple. The feast celebrated deliverance from foreign oppression, and it naturally stirred messianic hopes.

It was winter, and Jesus was walking in Solomon’s porch, a covered colonnade on the eastern side of the temple. The leaders surrounded Him and said, “*How long will you hold us in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly*” (*v. 24*). Jesus answered that He had told them, and that His works testified about Him, but they did not believe because they were not His sheep. Then He spoke of the security of His sheep, studied below, and declared, “*I and the Father are one*” (*v. 30*), also studied below.

The leaders picked up stones again. Jesus asked for which of His many good works they were stoning Him. They answered, “*We don’t stone you for a good work, but for blasphemy, because you, being a man, make yourself God*” (*v. 33*).

Jesus replied with an argument from *Psalm 82:6*: “*Isn’t it written in your law, ‘I said, you are gods’?*” (*v. 34*) In that psalm, God addresses human rulers and judges as “gods” because they were given authority to judge on God’s behalf, though they would die like men. Jesus reasons from the lesser to the greater: if Scripture, which “*can’t be broken*” (*v. 35*), could call such people “gods,” how could they accuse Him of blasphemy for calling Himself the Son of God, when He is the One the Father consecrated and sent into the world? Jesus was not reducing His claim to that of an ordinary human judge. He was showing that their charge of blasphemy did not take Scripture seriously, and He pointed again to His works: “*believe the works, that you may know and believe that the Father is in me, and I in the Father*” (*v. 38*).

They tried to seize Him, but He escaped. He went back across the Jordan to the place where John the Baptist had first baptized, where His ministry had begun. Many came to Him and said, “*John indeed did no sign, but everything that John said about this man is true*” (*v. 41*). “*Many believed in him there*” (*v. 42*).

## Important Verses Explained

### *John 10:10* — Life to the Full

> *“The thief only comes to steal, kill, and destroy. I came that they may have life, and may have it abundantly.”*
>
> — *John 10:10* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus had been describing how a shepherd cares for his sheep. In the morning, the shepherd comes to the sheepfold through the gate, calls his sheep by name, and leads them out to pasture. Then Jesus said that He is the door of the sheep: anyone who enters through Him will be saved and find pasture.

In contrast, He described the thief: “*The thief only comes to steal, kill, and destroy*” (*v. 10*). In context, the “thief” refers to false leaders who use people for their own purposes. The religious leaders who had just thrown out the healed blind man (*John 9*) were acting like thieves, harming the very sheep they were supposed to protect. Behind all such destructive influence stands the enemy of souls, whom Jesus called “*a murderer from the beginning*” (*John 8:44*).

Then Jesus said, “*I came that they may have life, and may have it abundantly*” (*v. 10*). Jesus’ purpose is the opposite of the thief’s. The thief takes; Jesus gives. The thief destroys; Jesus brings life.

The word “abundantly” means “more than enough,” overflowing, beyond what is necessary. Jesus does not offer a barely-surviving existence but life in its fullness. In John’s Gospel, this life is eternal life, the life of God shared with His people, which begins now and continues forever.

It is important to understand what Jesus means by “abundant life.” He does not promise wealth, comfort, or freedom from trouble. In this same Gospel, He tells His disciples that in the world they will have trouble (*John 16:33*). Abundant life is the richness of knowing God, being forgiven, being cared for by the Good Shepherd, and having a life filled with purpose, love, and hope.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse summarizes the purpose of Jesus’ coming. He came not to burden people but to give them life. *Psalm 23* describes the life of a sheep under the Lord’s care: green pastures, still waters, a restored soul, protection in the valley of the shadow of death, and a table prepared even in the presence of enemies. Jesus is the Shepherd who brings that life to reality.

The verse also helps believers discern between true and false voices. Any message, teacher, or influence that steals, kills, and destroys does not come from Christ. Jesus’ voice leads to life, freedom, and wholeness. This does not mean the Christian life is always easy, but its direction is always toward life.

Finally, the abundance Jesus offers flows from His sacrifice. In the very next verse He says that the Good Shepherd lays down His life for the sheep. The fullness of life believers receive was purchased at the cost of His death.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites people to consider what is truly giving them life. Many things promise fulfillment but leave people empty, enslaved, or harmed. Jesus offers life that is real and lasting. Believers can bring their whole lives to Him and receive the life He gives.

It also corrects distorted ideas about the Christian life. Some people imagine that following Jesus means a smaller, more restricted life. Jesus says the opposite: He came to give abundant life. His commands are not meant to rob people of joy but to lead them into true freedom and wholeness.

Finally, the verse calls Christian leaders to examine their leadership. Leaders in families, churches, and workplaces can either give life or take it. Those who follow the Good Shepherd are called to care for others in ways that nourish and protect, never to use people for their own gain. Leadership that harms, manipulates, or exploits the vulnerable is the work of a thief, not a shepherd.

### *John 10:11* — The Good Shepherd Lays Down His Life

> *“I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.”*
>
> — *John 10:11* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After describing Himself as the door of the sheep, Jesus used a second image: “*I am the good shepherd*” (*v. 11*). The word “good” here carries the sense of noble, excellent, or beautiful. Jesus is not only adequate as a shepherd; He is the ideal Shepherd, the one in whom all the qualities of a true shepherd are perfectly found.

“*The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep*” (*v. 11*). In Palestine, shepherding could be dangerous. Wolves, lions, bears, and thieves threatened the flock. David told King Saul that as a shepherd he had fought lions and bears to rescue his sheep (*1 Samuel 17:34–35*). A good shepherd was willing to put himself in danger to protect his flock.

Jesus goes further. He does not merely risk His life; He lays it down. This points directly to His death on the cross. The phrase “for the sheep” means on behalf of them, in their place. He would die so that they could live.

Jesus contrasts Himself with the hired hand, who works only for wages. When the wolf comes, the hired hand runs away, because the sheep are not his own and he does not truly care about them. Jesus owns His sheep, knows them, and loves them. He will not abandon them when danger comes.

Jesus says that His death is voluntary: “*No one takes it away from me, but I lay it down by myself*” (*v. 18*). He would not be a helpless victim of circumstances. He would give His life freely, out of love and obedience to the Father.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse is a clear statement of Jesus’ substitutionary death. The Shepherd dies for the sheep. Isaiah prophesied, “*All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all*” (*Isaiah 53:6*). Jesus is both the Shepherd who dies for the sheep and the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world (*John 1:29*).

It also fulfills God’s promise in *Ezekiel 34* to raise up a true shepherd for His people. The leaders of Israel had failed as shepherds, but God promised to shepherd His people Himself and to set over them a shepherd from David’s line. Jesus fulfills both: He is God Himself shepherding His people, and He is the promised Son of David.

Finally, the verse shows the depth of Christ’s love. He did not lay down His life for people who deserved it. He died for straying sheep, people who had wandered from God. This is the love Paul describes when he writes that “*God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us*” (*Romans 5:8*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse offers believers deep security. The Shepherd who laid down His life for them will not abandon them now. When they face fear, loss, or danger, they can trust that their Shepherd cares for them personally and will never run away.

It also sets the pattern for Christian leadership and love. Peter later urged church leaders to “*shepherd the flock of God which is among you*” (*1 Peter 5:2*) willingly and not for dishonest gain. Pastors, parents, and anyone responsible for others are called to sacrificial care, putting the good of those in their care above their own comfort.

Finally, this verse calls people to come to the Shepherd. Sheep that wander are in danger. Jesus has given His life to bring them back. No matter how far someone has strayed, the Good Shepherd invites them to return to His care.

### *John 10:27–28* — No One Will Snatch Them

> *“My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me. I give eternal life to them. They will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand.”*
>
> — *John 10:27–28* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These words were spoken during the Feast of Dedication in winter, as Jesus walked in Solomon’s porch in the temple. The religious leaders surrounded Him and demanded that He tell them plainly whether He was the Christ. Jesus answered that He had already told them, and His works testified about Him, but they did not believe because they were not His sheep.

Then He described His true sheep: “*My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me*” (*v. 27*). There are three marks here. They hear His voice, listening to and receiving His words. He knows them, with a personal knowledge that includes love and care. And they follow Him, trusting and obeying Him as their Shepherd.

Jesus then made a promise: “*I give eternal life to them*” (*v. 28*). Eternal life is His gift, not something His sheep earn. “*They will never perish*” (*v. 28*). The Greek uses a strong double negative: they will certainly not perish, ever.

“*and no one will snatch them out of my hand*” (*v. 28*). The word “snatch” is the same word used for the wolf snatching the sheep in verse 12. Wolves, thieves, and enemies of every kind may try, but they will not succeed. Jesus holds His sheep securely.

He added in the next verse: “*My Father who has given them to me is greater than all. No one is able to snatch them out of my Father’s hand*” (*v. 29*). The sheep are held in two hands, the Son’s and the Father’s. They are doubly secure.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses are among the strongest statements in Scripture of the security of those who belong to Christ. Their eternal life does not depend on their own ability to hold on, but on the power of the Son and the Father who hold them. Paul echoes this when he writes that nothing in all creation “*will be able to separate us from God’s love, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord*” (*Romans 8:39*).

The verses also connect security with relationship. The sheep who are secure are those who hear His voice and follow Him. Christians have discussed how these truths fit together. Some emphasize that true believers will never finally fall away, because God keeps them. Others emphasize the importance of continuing to follow Christ and warn against presuming on God’s grace. Both perspectives agree that the sheep who belong to Jesus are known by their following Him, and that their safety rests in His hands.

Finally, these verses reveal the tenderness of the Shepherd. “I know them” speaks of a personal, intimate relationship. Believers are not anonymous members of a crowd. The Shepherd knows each one by name.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses bring comfort to believers who fear losing their salvation or being overwhelmed by temptation, doubt, or suffering. Their security rests not on their strength but on Christ’s. When they feel weak, they can remember that they are held in the hands of the Son and the Father.

They also encourage believers to listen for the Shepherd’s voice. Jesus speaks through His word, by His Spirit, and through the fellowship of His people. Sheep learn to recognize their shepherd’s voice by spending time with him. Believers grow in recognizing Christ’s voice as they spend time in Scripture and prayer.

Finally, these verses call believers to follow. Hearing is not enough; Jesus’ sheep follow Him. Following means trusting Him with each step, going where He leads, and staying close to Him through every season.

### *John 10:30* — I and the Father Are One

> *“I and the Father are one.”*
>
> — *John 10:30* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus had just promised that no one could snatch His sheep out of His hand, and no one could snatch them out of the Father’s hand. The sheep are held securely by both the Son and the Father. Then He made this short but profound statement: “*I and the Father are one*” (*v. 30*).

The word “one” in Greek is neuter, not masculine. Jesus is not saying that He and the Father are one person; they are distinct, as the whole chapter shows (the Father gives, the Son receives; the Father sends, the Son is sent). Rather, He is saying that they are one in nature, purpose, and power. What the Son does, the Father does. To be held by the Son is to be held by the Father.

The religious leaders understood the meaning. They immediately picked up stones again to stone Him. When Jesus asked why, they answered, “*because you, being a man, make yourself God*” (*v. 33*). They understood that He was claiming divine equality.

Jesus did not withdraw His claim. He argued from Scripture that their charge of blasphemy was unjustified and pointed to His works as evidence that “*the Father is in me, and I in the Father*” (*v. 38*).

This verse summarizes what John’s Gospel teaches throughout: Jesus is fully one with the Father, yet distinct from Him. This is the foundation of what Christians later expressed in the doctrine of the Trinity.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse is central to the Christian understanding of who Jesus is. Jesus does not claim to be a second god alongside the Father, nor merely a good man in agreement with God. He claims a unity with the Father that only God could claim. The early church, reflecting on texts like this one, confessed that the Son is of one being with the Father, true God from true God.

It also shows that the security of believers rests on the unity of the Father and the Son. Because they are one, the believer held by the Son is held by the Father. There is no division in God’s purpose to save and keep His people.

Finally, the verse invites worship. If Jesus and the Father are one, then to know Jesus is to know God, and to honor Jesus is to honor God. As Jesus said earlier, “*He who doesn’t honor the Son doesn’t honor the Father who sent him*” (*John 5:23*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse assures believers that when they look at Jesus, they see the heart of God. His compassion, His truth, His mercy toward sinners, and His willingness to lay down His life all reveal what God is like. There is no hidden God behind Jesus who is different from Him.

It also gives believers a firm foundation for trust. The Shepherd who holds them is one with the all-powerful Father. Nothing can overpower Him. When believers face uncertainty, they can rest in the united love and power of the Father and the Son.

Finally, the verse calls believers to give Jesus the worship and trust that belong to God. He is not merely a teacher to admire but the Lord to adore, the One who is one with the Father.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*John 10* presents Jesus as the Good Shepherd who knows His sheep by name, leads them, protects them, and lays down His life for them. Believers can take deep comfort in this picture. They are not alone or forgotten. Their Shepherd knows them personally, cares for them more than any hired hand ever could, and has already proven His love by dying for them.

The chapter also helps believers recognize true and false shepherds. Some leaders and influences steal, kill, and destroy; Jesus gives life to the full. Believers can learn to listen for His voice, to follow Him, and to be wary of any voice that leads them away from Him. Those who lead others, whether in the church, the home, or elsewhere, are called to imitate the Good Shepherd: caring for the weak, seeking the lost, protecting the vulnerable, and never exploiting those in their care.

*John 10* offers a powerful assurance of security. Jesus’ sheep are held in His hand and in the Father’s hand, and no one can snatch them away. This truth gives believers peace when they face fear, temptation, or suffering. Their safety rests on the power and faithfulness of God, not on their own strength.

Finally, the chapter calls readers to respond to Jesus’ claim to be one with the Father. Many listeners rejected Him and picked up stones. Others believed. Jesus’ works and words still testify about Him. Each person is invited to hear His voice, come through Him as the door, and follow Him as the Good Shepherd who gives eternal life.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, You are the Good Shepherd. Thank You for knowing me by name and for laying down Your life for me. Thank You that You came not to steal and destroy, but to give life to the full. Teach me to recognize Your voice above all the other voices around me, and give me a heart that follows You wherever You lead. When I am afraid, remind me that I am held in Your hand and in the Father’s hand, and that no one can snatch me away. Guard me from false shepherds and from anything that would lead me away from You. If I lead or care for others in any way, make me a shepherd like You, gentle, faithful, and willing to sacrifice. Thank You that You and the Father are one, and that in You I see the heart of God. Bring Your other sheep into Your fold, so that there may be one flock and one Shepherd. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
