John · Chapter 11 of 21

# John — Chapter 11

Chapter Theme: The Resurrection and the Life at the Tomb of Lazarus

[Read John 11 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/JHN11.htm)

Main Teaching

When His friend Lazarus falls sick, Jesus deliberately waits, and Lazarus dies. Arriving four days later, Jesus meets grieving Martha with the declaration, “I am the resurrection and the life,” weeps with Mary and the mourners, and then calls Lazarus out of the tomb alive. This greatest of His signs leads many to believe, but it also moves the council to plan His death, as the high priest unknowingly prophesies that one man will die for the people.

## Chapter Background and Story

*John 11* records the seventh and climactic sign of the first half of John’s Gospel. Jesus has turned water into wine, healed an official’s son, healed a lame man, fed five thousand, walked on water, and given sight to a man born blind. Now He raises a man who has been dead for four days. This sign reveals Jesus as the Lord of life, and it also sets in motion the events that lead to His own death. The one who gives life to Lazarus will give His own life for the world.

The chapter is also deeply personal. It shows Jesus’ friendship with a family in Bethany, His love for them, His grief at their loss, and the different ways two sisters bring their pain to Him.

### The News of Lazarus’s Sickness (*11:1–16*)

Lazarus lived in Bethany, a village on the eastern slope of the Mount of Olives, about two miles from Jerusalem. His sisters were Martha and Mary. Luke describes an earlier visit to their home, when Martha was busy serving and Mary sat at Jesus’ feet (*Luke 10:38–42*). John identifies Mary as the one who anointed the Lord, an event he will describe in the next chapter.

The sisters sent a message to Jesus: “*Lord, behold, he for whom you have great affection is sick*” (*v. 3*). They did not ask Him to come; they trusted that His love would move Him. Jesus said, “*This sickness is not to death, but for the glory of God, that God’s Son may be glorified by it*” (*v. 4*). Lazarus would die, but death would not be the final outcome.

Then comes a surprising sequence, studied below: Jesus loved them, and so He stayed where He was two more days.

When Jesus finally said, “*Let’s go into Judea again*” (*v. 7*), the disciples objected. The leaders there had just tried to stone Him (*10:31*). Jesus answered with an image of walking in daylight: “*If a man walks in the day, he doesn’t stumble*” (*v. 9*). As long as His appointed time continued, He could walk safely in the Father’s will.

He said, “*Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, but I am going so that I may awake him out of sleep*” (*v. 11*). The disciples took Him literally, so He told them plainly, “*Lazarus is dead*” (*v. 14*). He added that He was glad for their sake that He had not been there, “*so that you may believe*” (*v. 15*).

Thomas, often remembered for his later doubts, showed loyal courage here: “*Let’s also go, that we may die with him*” (*v. 16*). He expected that going to Judea meant death for Jesus, and he was willing to share it.

### Jesus and Martha (*11:17–27*)

When Jesus arrived, Lazarus had been in the tomb four days. Jews buried their dead on the day of death, and there was a popular belief that the soul lingered near the body for three days. After four days, death was considered completely final. Many mourners had come from Jerusalem to comfort the sisters, as Jewish custom encouraged.

Martha, characteristically active, went out to meet Jesus while Mary stayed home. Her words carried both pain and faith: “*Lord, if you would have been here, my brother wouldn’t have died*” (*v. 21*). Yet she added, “*Even now I know that whatever you ask of God, God will give you*” (*v. 22*).

Jesus told her, “*Your brother will rise again*” (*v. 23*). Martha replied with the orthodox belief of many Jews of her day, based on texts like *Daniel 12:2*: “*I know that he will rise again in the resurrection at the last day*” (*v. 24*). Jesus then made one of His greatest statements, studied below. Martha answered with a full confession of faith: “*Yes, Lord. I have come to believe that you are the Christ, God’s Son, he who comes into the world*” (*v. 27*). Her confession is as complete as Peter’s in the other Gospels.

### Jesus and Mary (*11:28–37*)

Martha went to call Mary secretly: “*The Teacher is here and is calling you*” (*v. 28*). Mary rose quickly and went to Him, followed by the mourners, who thought she was going to the tomb to weep. She fell at Jesus’ feet and spoke the same words as Martha: “*Lord, if you would have been here, my brother wouldn’t have died*” (*v. 32*). But she did not add anything. She simply wept.

Jesus’ response to Mary was different from His response to Martha. With Martha, He spoke words of truth. With Mary, He shared her grief. When He saw her weeping and the mourners weeping, “*he groaned in the spirit and was troubled*” (*v. 33*). The Greek word translated “groaned” often expresses strong emotion, even indignation. Many interpreters believe Jesus was not only sad but also deeply moved with anger at death itself, the enemy that brings such sorrow into God’s world. He asked where Lazarus had been laid, and then came the shortest verse in the English Bible, studied below.

Some mourners said, “*See how much affection he had for him!*” (*v. 36*) Others said, “*Couldn’t this man, who opened the eyes of him who was blind, have also kept this man from dying?*” (*v. 37*)

### Lazarus Raised (*11:38–44*)

Still deeply moved, Jesus came to the tomb, a cave with a stone across the entrance. He said, “*Take away the stone*” (*v. 39*). Martha, practical as ever, objected that after four days there would be a stench. Jesus reminded her, “*Didn’t I tell you that if you believed, you would see God’s glory?*” (*v. 40*)

They removed the stone. Jesus looked up and prayed, thanking the Father for hearing Him. He said He prayed aloud for the sake of the crowd, “*that they may believe that you sent me*” (*v. 42*). Then He called Lazarus out. This is studied below.

### The Council’s Plot (*11:45–57*)

Many who saw what Jesus did believed in Him. But others went and reported to the Pharisees. The chief priests and Pharisees called a meeting of the Sanhedrin, the Jewish ruling council. They were alarmed: “*If we leave him alone like this, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation*” (*v. 48*). Their concern was political as well as religious. A popular messianic movement could provoke Rome to crush the nation and remove the leaders’ authority and the temple (“our place”).

Caiaphas, the high priest that year, spoke bluntly: “*You know nothing at all*” (*v. 49*). Then he said, “*it is advantageous for us that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation not perish*” (*v. 50*). Caiaphas meant this as cold political calculation: sacrifice one man to save the nation from Rome.

But John sees a deeper meaning: “*being high priest that year, he prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation*” (*v. 51*), “*and not for the nation only, but that he might also gather together into one the children of God who are scattered abroad*” (*v. 52*). Without knowing it, Caiaphas spoke the truth of the gospel. Jesus would indeed die in the place of others, not to save them from Rome, but to save them from sin and death, and to gather God’s children from every nation into one family.

From that day, the council planned to kill Jesus. The very miracle that gave Lazarus life led to the decision to put Jesus to death. Jesus withdrew to a town called Ephraim near the wilderness. As Passover approached, crowds in Jerusalem wondered whether He would come to the feast, and the leaders ordered that anyone who knew where He was should report it so they could arrest Him.

## Important Verses Explained

### *John 11:5–6* — Because He Loved Them, He Stayed

> *“Now Jesus loved Martha, and her sister, and Lazarus. When therefore he heard that he was sick, he stayed two days in the place where he was.”*
>
> — *John 11:5–6* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Lazarus was seriously ill in Bethany, and his sisters, Martha and Mary, sent word to Jesus. They described Lazarus as the one Jesus loved, trusting that this would be enough to bring Him quickly. Jesus was at that time across the Jordan, perhaps a day’s journey away.

John then writes, “*Now Jesus loved Martha, and her sister, and Lazarus*” (*v. 5*). John wants readers to be clear about this before telling what happened next. Jesus was not indifferent to this family. He loved each of them personally.

“*When therefore he heard that he was sick, he stayed two days in the place where he was*” (*v. 6*). The word “therefore” is surprising. We might expect John to say, “Jesus loved them, so He hurried to them.” Instead, John says that because He loved them, He stayed. His delay was not a lack of love but an expression of it.

By the time Jesus arrived, Lazarus had been dead four days. If Jesus had come at once, He might have healed Lazarus before he died, as He had healed many others. But Jesus had a greater purpose. He told His disciples that this sickness was for God’s glory (*11:4*) and that He was glad He had not been there, “*so that you may believe*” (*v. 15*).

The delay was painful for Martha and Mary. Both said to Jesus, “Lord, if you would have been here, my brother wouldn’t have died.” They did not understand why He had not come sooner. Yet Jesus’ delay led to a far greater revelation of His glory than a healing would have.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses teach that God’s delays are not denials of His love. Jesus’ love for this family was certain, yet His timing did not match their expectations. He allowed them to go through grief in order to give them something greater: a revelation of Himself as the resurrection and the life.

They also show that God’s purposes are larger than our immediate requests. Martha and Mary wanted their brother healed. Jesus intended to raise him from the dead, strengthen the faith of His disciples, and reveal His glory to many. What seemed like a failure to act became a moment of overwhelming grace.

Finally, these verses remind believers that Jesus knows the whole story while they see only part of it. The sisters could not see beyond the tomb. Jesus could. Faith trusts His love even when His timing seems hard to understand.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses speak to believers who are waiting for God to act. Many people pray for healing, help, or change and see no immediate answer. It can feel as though God is far away or does not care. John’s words offer assurance: Jesus’ love is not measured by the speed of His answers. He may delay because He loves, and because He has purposes that are not yet visible.

They also invite believers to be honest with God about their disappointment. Martha and Mary told Jesus exactly how they felt. He did not rebuke them. Believers can bring their questions and grief to Him, trusting His love even when they do not understand His timing.

Finally, these verses encourage patience and hope. God’s timing does not always bring the outcome people want in this life; not every sick loved one is healed. But believers can trust that God’s love is constant and that His final word is life, not death.

### *John 11:25–26* — I Am the Resurrection and the Life

> *“Jesus said to her, ‘I am the resurrection and the life. He who believes in me will still live, even if he dies. Whoever lives and believes in me will never die. Do you believe this?’”*
>
> — *John 11:25–26* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus had arrived in Bethany four days after Lazarus died. Martha went out to meet Him, grieving and confused. She told Jesus that if He had been there, her brother would not have died. Yet she still believed that God would give Jesus whatever He asked.

Jesus told her that her brother would rise again. Martha understood this as a reference to the final resurrection: “*I know that he will rise again in the resurrection at the last day*” (*v. 24*). She believed in the resurrection as a distant future event.

Jesus then said, “*I am the resurrection and the life*” (*v. 25*). He moved her faith from an event to a Person. Resurrection is not only something that will happen at the end of time; it is found in Jesus Himself. He does not merely promise resurrection; He is the resurrection.

He continued with two promises. First, “*He who believes in me will still live, even if he dies*” (*v. 25*). Believers will still face physical death, but death will not be the end. They will live again. Second, “*Whoever lives and believes in me will never die*” (*v. 26*). This refers to spiritual and eternal death. Those who believe in Jesus have eternal life that physical death cannot destroy.

Then Jesus asked Martha a personal question: “*Do you believe this?*” (*v. 26*) He did not only want her to understand the teaching; He wanted her to trust Him. Martha responded with a great confession of faith in Jesus as the Christ and the Son of God.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This is the fifth of Jesus’ “I am” sayings in John, and perhaps the most comforting. It declares that Jesus has power over death itself. He would prove it, first by raising Lazarus, and then, more completely, by rising from the dead Himself. Lazarus was raised to mortal life and would die again; Jesus was raised to immortal, glorified life, the first fruits of the final resurrection.

It also shows that eternal life is found in union with Christ. Life is not simply a gift separate from Jesus; it is participation in His life. Those who believe in Him share in His resurrection. Paul writes that believers have been raised with Christ and that their life is hidden with Christ in God (*Colossians 3:1–3*).

Finally, Jesus’ question to Martha shows that this truth demands a personal response. Believing in the resurrection as a doctrine is not the same as trusting Jesus as the resurrection and the life. Faith rests in Him.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses bring hope to those who grieve. When believers lose loved ones who trusted in Christ, they can grieve with hope, knowing that death is not the end. Jesus’ promise is that those who believe in Him will live, even though they die. Christian funerals often read these words for this reason.

They also help believers face their own mortality. Death is still an enemy, and it still brings sorrow. But for those in Christ, it is not final. Believers can live with courage, knowing that their future is secure in the One who is the resurrection and the life.

Finally, Jesus’ question to Martha is asked of every reader: “Do you believe this?” It is possible to hear these words many times without personally trusting Jesus. He invites each person to place their faith in Him for life beyond death.

### *John 11:35* — Jesus Wept

> *“Jesus wept.”*
>
> — *John 11:35* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After speaking with Martha, Jesus met Mary, who came out of the house weeping, followed by mourners from Jerusalem. Mary fell at His feet and said the same words Martha had said: if He had been there, her brother would not have died. Unlike Martha, she did not add a statement of faith. She simply wept.

John tells us that when Jesus saw her weeping, and the others weeping with her, “*he groaned in the spirit and was troubled*” (*v. 33*). He asked where Lazarus had been laid. The mourners said, “*Lord, come and see*” (*v. 34*).

Then: “*Jesus wept*” (*v. 35*). This is the shortest verse in most English Bibles, but it is one of the most profound. The word for Jesus’ weeping is different from the loud wailing of the mourners. It suggests quiet tears.

Why did Jesus weep, when He knew that He was about to raise Lazarus from the dead? He was not weeping because He had lost hope. He wept because He shared the sorrow of His friends. He was moved by their grief and by the painful reality of death itself, which brings such sorrow into the world God made.

The mourners noticed: “*See how much affection he had for him!*” (*v. 36*) Jesus’ tears showed His love.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals the full humanity of Jesus. The eternal Word, who was with God and was God, became flesh and felt human emotions, including grief. He was not distant from human pain. Hebrews says that we do not have a high priest who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses (*Hebrews 4:15*).

It also reveals the heart of God toward human suffering. Jesus is the perfect image of the Father. When He weeps at a grave, He shows that God is not indifferent to the sorrow of His people. God hates death and grieves with those who grieve.

Finally, Jesus’ tears show that faith and grief can exist together. Jesus knew He would raise Lazarus, yet He wept. Christians who know that their loved ones will be raised can still grieve. Paul writes that believers do not grieve “*like the rest, who have no hope*” (*1 Thessalonians 4:13*), but they do grieve. Hope does not cancel sorrow; it transforms it.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse brings great comfort to those who are grieving. Jesus understands sorrow. He does not stand at a distance from human pain but enters into it. Those who mourn can bring their tears to Him, knowing that He shares their grief.

It also gives believers permission to grieve. Some people feel that strong faith means never crying or always appearing joyful. But Jesus wept. Grief is a natural and right response to loss. Believers can weep honestly while still holding on to hope.

Finally, the verse teaches believers how to care for those who are grieving. Jesus did not rush to explain or correct Mary. He wept with her. Paul instructs believers to “*weep with those who weep*” (*Romans 12:15*). Sometimes the most loving response to someone’s pain is not words but presence and shared sorrow.

### *John 11:43–44* — Lazarus, Come Out!

> *“When he had said this, he cried with a loud voice, ‘Lazarus, come out!’ He who was dead came out, bound hand and foot with wrappings, and his face was wrapped around with a cloth. Jesus said to them, ‘Free him, and let him go.’”*
>
> — *John 11:43–44* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus stood before the tomb of Lazarus, a cave with a stone across the entrance. He had told them to remove the stone, despite Martha’s concern about the smell after four days. Jesus prayed aloud, thanking the Father for hearing Him, so that the crowd would believe that the Father had sent Him.

Then “*he cried with a loud voice, “Lazarus, come out!”*” (*v. 43*) Jesus did not use elaborate rituals. He spoke with authority. Many have observed that if Jesus had not called Lazarus by name, every grave might have opened at His command. Earlier, He had said, “*the hour comes in which all who are in the tombs will hear his voice*” (*John 5:28*). Here, one man in one tomb heard His voice.

“*He who was dead came out, bound hand and foot with wrappings, and his face was wrapped around with a cloth*” (*v. 44*). Lazarus emerged still wrapped in burial cloths. Jewish burial customs involved wrapping the body in strips of linen with spices. The sight must have been astonishing: a man four days dead walking out of his grave.

Jesus then gave a practical command: “*Free him, and let him go*” (*v. 44*). He involved the bystanders in the final step, removing the grave clothes and releasing Lazarus to his family.

This was not a resurrection to eternal, glorified life. Lazarus would eventually die again. But it was a powerful sign pointing to Jesus’ authority over death and to the final resurrection.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This miracle demonstrates that Jesus is truly the resurrection and the life, as He had just told Martha. His words have power to give life to the dead. What He did for Lazarus physically, He does spiritually for all who believe: He calls them out of spiritual death into new life. Paul writes that God made believers alive with Christ “*even when we were dead through our trespasses*” (*Ephesians 2:5*).

It also points forward to Jesus’ own resurrection. There are important differences. Lazarus came out bound in grave clothes; Jesus’ grave clothes were left lying in the tomb (*John 20:6–7*). Lazarus was raised to die again; Jesus was raised never to die again. Lazarus’s raising is a preview; Jesus’ resurrection is the victory.

The command “Free him, and let him go” can also be seen as a picture of the community’s role. Jesus gives life, but He calls others to help remove what still binds the one who has been raised. New believers often need the love and support of the church to grow in freedom.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage gives hope that no situation is beyond Jesus’ power. Lazarus had been dead four days, and everyone considered his case hopeless. Jesus called him out. Believers can bring situations that seem dead and hopeless to Christ, trusting that He has power to bring life, even if His timing and ways differ from what they expect.

It also encourages believers to pray for those who are spiritually dead. No one is too far gone for Jesus’ voice to reach. Believers can pray with confidence for friends and family who do not yet know Christ, trusting that His word has power to give life.

Finally, the passage calls believers to help others walk in freedom. Many people who have come to faith still carry the “grave clothes” of past habits, wounds, or fears. The church is called to come alongside them with patience and love, helping them grow into the freedom Christ has given.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*John 11* shows that Jesus’ love does not always look the way people expect. He loved Martha, Mary, and Lazarus, and yet He delayed. Believers who are waiting for God to act can take comfort that His delays are not signs of indifference. He sees the whole story and is working for His glory and their good, even when they cannot understand His timing.

The chapter also shows how Jesus meets people in grief. To Martha, He spoke truth about Himself. To Mary, He offered His tears. He meets each person in the way they need. Those who are grieving can bring their pain honestly to Him, knowing that He weeps with them and also speaks words of hope. Those who comfort others can learn from Him to listen, to share sorrow, and to point gently to hope.

At the center of the chapter is Jesus’ declaration that He is the resurrection and the life. For believers, death is real and painful, but it is not the end. Those who trust in Christ will live, even though they die. This truth gives courage in facing death, hope in grieving loved ones, and a reason to share the gospel with those who do not yet believe.

Finally, the chapter reveals that Jesus’ gift of life came at a cost. The raising of Lazarus led directly to the plot to kill Jesus. Caiaphas’s words, spoken in political calculation, became a prophecy of the gospel: one man would die for the people. The life believers receive comes through Jesus’ death in their place. That is the deepest reason for gratitude and worship.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, You are the resurrection and the life. Thank You that whoever believes in You will live, even though they die, and that death does not have the final word. When You seem slow to answer my prayers, help me to trust that Your love is real and that You see what I cannot see. Thank You for weeping at the tomb of Your friend, and for understanding the sorrow I carry. Meet me in my grief as You met Martha and Mary, with Your truth and with Your tears. Speak life into the places in my life and in the lives of those I love that seem dead and hopeless. Help me to come alongside others whom You have raised, helping them to walk in freedom. Thank You for dying in my place so that I could live. I believe that You are the Christ, the Son of God, who came into the world. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

John · Chapter 12 of 21

# John — Chapter 12

Chapter Theme: The Hour Has Come: Anointed, Welcomed, and Lifted Up

[Read John 12 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/JHN12.htm)

Main Teaching

Six days before Passover, Mary anoints Jesus’ feet with costly perfume in an act of extravagant love that prepares Him for burial. The next day crowds welcome Him into Jerusalem as King, and when Greeks come asking to see Him, Jesus announces that the hour of His glorification has arrived. Like a grain of wheat that must die to bear fruit, He will be lifted up on the cross and draw all people to Himself. The chapter closes the first half of John’s Gospel with a sober reflection on unbelief and a final appeal to believe in the light.

## Chapter Background and Story

*John 12* is a hinge in the Gospel. It concludes Jesus’ public ministry, which John has presented through seven signs and many conversations. From chapter 13 onward, Jesus will speak privately to His disciples and then go to the cross. Throughout the Gospel, Jesus has said, “My hour has not yet come” (*John 2:4*; *7:30*; *8:20*). In this chapter, He finally says, “The time has come” (*12:23*).

The chapter moves through three scenes: a dinner in Bethany, a royal welcome in Jerusalem, and a moment when Greeks seek Jesus. Then John reflects on why so many did not believe and records Jesus’ final public appeal.

### Mary Anoints Jesus (*12:1–11*)

Six days before Passover, Jesus returned to Bethany, the village where He had raised Lazarus. A dinner was given in His honor. Mark and Matthew place it in the house of Simon the leper (*Mark 14:3*), and John adds the details of the family: “*Martha served, but Lazarus was one of those who sat at the table with him*” (*v. 2*). The man who had been dead was now eating with Jesus.

Then Mary took a pound of very expensive perfume made from pure nard, a fragrant oil imported from the Himalayas, and anointed Jesus’ feet, wiping them with her hair. This is studied below. (Matthew and Mark describe her pouring perfume on His head; she likely anointed both His head and His feet. *Luke 7* records a different anointing earlier in Jesus’ ministry by a sinful woman in Galilee.)

Judas Iscariot objected: “*Why wasn’t this ointment sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?*” (*v. 5*) Three hundred denarii was about a year’s wages for a laborer. Judas’s words sounded generous, but John explains his real motive: “*he was a thief, and having the money box, used to steal what was put into it*” (*v. 6*). Judas, the treasurer of the group, was already showing the greed that would lead to betrayal.

Jesus defended Mary: “*Leave her alone. She has kept this for the day of my burial*” (*v. 7*). And He said, “*For you always have the poor with you, but you don’t always have me*” (*v. 8*). Jesus was not dismissing care for the poor; His words echo *Deuteronomy 15:11*, which commands generosity to the poor precisely because they will always be present. He was saying that this was a unique moment, the last opportunity to honor Him before His death.

A large crowd came to Bethany to see both Jesus and Lazarus. The chief priests then planned to kill Lazarus too, because many people were believing in Jesus because of him. Lazarus himself had become evidence that could not be ignored.

### The King Enters Jerusalem (*12:12–19*)

The next day, a great crowd of Passover pilgrims heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem. They took palm branches and went out to meet Him, shouting, “*Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel!*” (*v. 13*) Palm branches had become a symbol of national victory since the days of the Maccabees, who had freed Jerusalem from foreign rule. The words come from *Psalm 118:25–26*, a psalm sung at the great festivals. This event is studied at *Matthew 21:9*.

Jesus found a young donkey and sat on it, fulfilling *Zechariah 9:9*: “*Don’t be afraid, daughter of Zion. Behold, your King comes, sitting on a donkey’s colt*” (*v. 15*). A conquering king might ride a warhorse; Jesus came humbly, as a king of peace. John adds an honest note: “*His disciples didn’t understand these things at first, but when Jesus was glorified, then they remembered that these things were written about him*” (*v. 16*). Understanding came after the resurrection.

The crowd that had seen Lazarus raised kept telling about it, and many came out because of this sign. The Pharisees said to one another, “*See how you accomplish nothing. Behold, the world has gone after him*” (*v. 19*). Their words were an exaggeration, but also, unknowingly, a prophecy. The very next verses show “the world” coming.

### Greeks Seek Jesus (*12:20–36*)

Among the worshipers at the feast were some Greeks, probably Gentiles who worshiped the God of Israel. They came to Philip, who had a Greek name and came from Bethsaida, a town with Gentile influence, and said, “*Sir, we want to see Jesus*” (*v. 21*). Philip told Andrew, and together they told Jesus.

Jesus’ answer seems at first not to address their request: “*The time has come for the Son of Man to be glorified*” (*v. 23*). But the arrival of Gentiles seeking Him signaled that the moment had come for His death, which would open the way for all nations. He explained with the image of a grain of wheat, studied below.

Then Jesus revealed His inner anguish: “*Now my soul is troubled. What shall I say? ‘Father, save me from this time’? But I came to this time for this cause*” (*v. 27*). This is John’s equivalent of the Gethsemane prayer in the other Gospels (studied at *Mark 14:36*). Jesus felt the weight of what lay ahead, yet He chose the Father’s will. He prayed, “*Father, glorify your name!*” (*v. 28*) A voice came from heaven: “*I have both glorified it and will glorify it again*” (*v. 28*). Some in the crowd thought it was thunder; others thought an angel had spoken. Jesus said that the voice had come for their sake.

“*Now is the judgment of this world. Now the prince of this world will be cast out*” (*v. 31*). The cross, which looked like Satan’s victory, would actually be his defeat. Then Jesus spoke of being lifted up, studied below.

The crowd was confused. They had learned from Scripture that the Messiah would remain forever (perhaps from texts like *Psalm 89:36* and *Isaiah 9:7*). How could the Son of Man be lifted up? Jesus did not argue but urged them: “*Yet a little while the light is with you. Walk while you have the light, that darkness doesn’t overtake you*” (*v. 35*). “*While you have the light, believe in the light, that you may become children of light*” (*v. 36*). Then He left and hid Himself.

### The Tragedy of Unbelief (*12:37–43*)

John now steps back to reflect on Jesus’ public ministry: “*But though he had done so many signs before them, yet they didn’t believe in him*” (*v. 37*). He explains this unbelief by quoting two passages from Isaiah. The first is *Isaiah 53:1*: “*Lord, who has believed our report? To whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?*” (*v. 38*) The second is *Isaiah 6:10*, describing hearts hardened and eyes blinded. The same God who sends light also judges those who persistently reject it, so that their refusal becomes inability.

John adds a remarkable statement: “*Isaiah said these things when he saw his glory, and spoke of him*” (*v. 41*). In *Isaiah 6*, the prophet saw the Lord, high and lifted up, in the temple. John says that the glory Isaiah saw was the glory of Jesus. This is a powerful testimony to Jesus’ divine identity.

Yet not all rejected Him. Many even among the rulers believed, though they kept their faith secret. This is studied below.

### Jesus’ Final Public Appeal (*12:44–50*)

John closes the section with a summary of Jesus’ message. Jesus cried out, “*Whoever believes in me, believes not in me, but in him who sent me*” (*v. 44*). “*He who sees me sees him who sent me*” (*v. 45*). “*I have come as a light into the world, that whoever believes in me may not remain in the darkness*” (*v. 46*).

Jesus had come not to judge the world but to save it. Yet those who rejected Him would be judged by the very word He had spoken. His words were not His own invention; they came from the Father, “*I know that his commandment is eternal life*” (*v. 50*). The public ministry of Jesus ends with an invitation to believe and a warning not to refuse the light.

## Important Verses Explained

### *John 12:3* — The House Filled with Fragrance

> *“Therefore Mary took a pound of ointment of pure nard, very precious, and anointed Jesus’ feet and wiped his feet with her hair. The house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment.”*
>
> — *John 12:3* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This scene took place at a dinner in Bethany six days before Passover, given in Jesus’ honor. Lazarus, whom Jesus had raised from the dead, was at the table. Martha was serving. Mary, the sister who had once sat at Jesus’ feet to listen to His teaching (*Luke 10:39*), and who had fallen at His feet in grief after Lazarus died (*John 11:32*), now came to His feet again.

“*Therefore Mary took a pound of ointment of pure nard, very precious*” (*v. 3*). A Roman pound was about twelve ounces, a large amount of an extremely costly perfume. Nard came from a plant grown in the Himalayan mountains of India and had to be imported. Judas valued it at three hundred denarii, roughly a year’s wages for a laborer. This may have been Mary’s most valuable possession, perhaps kept for her own future.

“*and anointed Jesus’ feet and wiped his feet with her hair*” (*v. 3*). Anointing the feet was unusual; it was a humble act normally done by servants. A respectable woman in that culture did not usually let down her hair in public. Mary set aside her dignity in an act of humble, wholehearted devotion.

“*The house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment*” (*v. 3*). Mary’s act could not be hidden. The fragrance filled the whole house, touching everyone present.

Jesus explained the deeper meaning of her action: “*She has kept this for the day of my burial*” (*v. 7*). Whether Mary fully understood or not, she was preparing Jesus’ body for His death. The other Gospels record Jesus’ promise that her act would be remembered wherever the gospel is preached (studied at *Matthew 26:13*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Mary’s act is a picture of worship that holds nothing back. Love does not calculate the minimum required; it gives generously. Mary gave what was costly because she understood, more than the others, the worth of Jesus. Her gift expressed gratitude for her brother’s life and devotion to the One who was about to die.

The contrast with Judas is striking. Both looked at the same perfume. Mary saw a way to honor Jesus; Judas saw money. The scene reveals that the heart’s attitude toward Jesus shows itself in how a person uses what they have. Paul writes that believers are “*a sweet aroma of Christ to God*” (*2 Corinthians 2:15*), spreading the fragrance of the knowledge of Him everywhere.

The anointing also points to Jesus’ identity. The title “Christ” or “Messiah” means “Anointed One.” Kings and priests were anointed with oil. Mary anointed Jesus just before He entered Jerusalem as King and went to the cross as the Priest who offered Himself.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Mary’s devotion invites believers to consider what they are offering to Jesus. Some acts of love for Him may seem wasteful to others: time spent in worship, generosity toward His work, careers or plans surrendered to His call. When Jesus is worth everything, giving Him our best is not a waste.

The fragrance filling the house also reminds believers that genuine devotion affects others. A life given to Christ spreads His presence in families, workplaces, and communities, often in ways that cannot be measured.

Finally, the scene warns against criticizing the devotion of others. Judas used concern for the poor as a cover for his own greed. Believers can sometimes be quick to judge how others worship or give. Jesus defended Mary. He receives sincere love offered to Him, even when others misunderstand it.

### *John 12:24–26* — Unless a Grain of Wheat Dies

> *“Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit. He who loves his life will lose it. He who hates his life in this world will keep it to eternal life. If anyone serves me, let him follow me. Where I am, there my servant will also be. If anyone serves me, the Father will honor him.”*
>
> — *John 12:24–26* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Some Greeks had come to Jerusalem for the Passover and asked to see Jesus. When Philip and Andrew brought the request to Him, Jesus announced that His hour had come to be glorified. Then He explained what that glory would involve.

“*unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone*” (*v. 24*). A seed of wheat kept in a jar remains a single seed. It may be preserved, but it produces nothing. “*But if it dies, it bears much fruit*” (*v. 24*). When the seed is buried in the ground and its outer shell breaks down, new life sprouts, and a single seed becomes a stalk with many grains.

Jesus was speaking about His own death. He would be “buried in the earth,” and through His death, He would bring life to many, including the Greeks who were seeking Him and people from every nation.

Then He applied the principle to His followers: “*He who loves his life will lose it. He who hates his life in this world will keep it to eternal life*” (*v. 25*). “Hating” one’s life is a Hebrew way of expressing strong preference. It means loving God so much more than one’s own life in this world that self-interest is no longer the controlling priority. Those who cling to their lives for themselves will lose what matters most; those who give their lives to God will gain eternal life.

“*If anyone serves me, let him follow me. Where I am, there my servant will also be. If anyone serves me, the Father will honor him*” (*v. 26*). To serve Jesus is to follow Him, even on the path of self-giving. And there is a promise: those who serve Him will be with Him and will be honored by the Father.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The image of the grain of wheat reveals the meaning of the cross. Jesus’ death was not a tragic end but the planting of a seed that would produce an enormous harvest. His death and resurrection opened the way for people of all nations to receive eternal life. The church throughout history is the fruit of the seed that fell into the ground at Calvary.

The principle also shapes the life of every disciple. The pattern of Jesus’ life, death leading to life, becomes the pattern of the believer’s life. Similar teaching appears in the other Gospels (studied at *Mark 8:36* and *Matthew 16:24*), but here it is tied directly to the image of fruitful dying. Self-giving is not loss but the way to fruitfulness.

Finally, the promise of verse 26 shows God’s generous heart. Those who follow Jesus in self-giving service are not forgotten. The Father Himself honors them. This is not earned merit but the delight of a Father who honors those who honor His Son.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage challenges a culture that values self-preservation and self-promotion above all. Jesus teaches that fruitfulness comes through self-giving. Believers bear fruit when they lay down their own preferences, comfort, and ambitions to serve God and others.

It also brings meaning to sacrifice. Parents who give years to raising children, believers who serve quietly in their churches, people who care for aging relatives, and missionaries who leave home for the sake of the gospel are following the pattern of the grain of wheat. Their sacrifices are not wasted; they bear fruit.

Finally, the passage gives hope in times of loss. Sometimes God allows things in believers’ lives to “die,” such as plans, dreams, or comforts. These experiences are painful, but in God’s hands they can become seeds of new life and greater fruitfulness.

### *John 12:32* — I Will Draw All People to Myself

> *“And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.”*
>
> — *John 12:32* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus had just heard a voice from heaven responding to His prayer, “Father, glorify your name.” He told the crowd that the voice had come for their benefit and that now was the time for judgment on this world and for its ruler to be cast out. Then He said, “*And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself*” (*v. 32*).

John explains what Jesus meant: “*But he said this, signifying by what kind of death he should die*” (*v. 33*). Being “lifted up from the earth” refers to crucifixion. A crucified person was raised up on a cross above the ground. Jesus used this phrase earlier in John’s Gospel too, comparing His being lifted up to the bronze serpent Moses lifted up in the wilderness (*John 3:14*).

The phrase also has a double meaning. “Lifted up” can mean “exalted.” In John’s Gospel, the cross is not only Jesus’ humiliation but also His glorification. Through His death, Jesus would be exalted, leading to His resurrection and return to the Father.

“*will draw all people to myself*” (*v. 32*). This does not mean that every single person will be saved, since John’s Gospel clearly teaches that some reject Jesus (*12:48*). It means that Jesus will draw people of all kinds, from every nation, not only Jews but also Gentiles like the Greeks who had just asked to see Him. The cross would become the place where people from every background are drawn to God.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals the power of the cross. The cross was intended by Jesus’ enemies to destroy Him and His movement. Instead, it became the center of His saving work and the means by which He draws people to Himself. Paul writes that the message of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to those who are being saved “*it is the power of God*” (*1 Corinthians 1:18*).

It also shows the universal scope of the gospel. The Greeks who came to see Jesus represent the nations of the world. Through His death, Jesus would break down the barrier between Jews and Gentiles and gather one people for God from every tribe and language (*Ephesians 2:14–16*; *Revelation 5:9*).

Finally, the verse shows that salvation is Jesus’ work. He says, “I will draw.” Earlier He said that no one can come to Him unless the Father draws them (*John 6:44*). The Father and the Son work together to draw people through the message of the cross.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to keep the cross at the center of their message. It is tempting to present Christianity mainly as a source of practical wisdom or moral improvement. But Jesus said that He would draw people through being lifted up on the cross. The message of His sacrificial death and resurrection has power to draw people to God.

It also gives hope for those who seem far from God. Jesus draws all kinds of people to Himself. No background, nationality, or history puts someone beyond the reach of the cross.

Finally, this verse invites each reader to respond to Christ’s drawing. Many people feel a pull toward Jesus, a sense that He is calling them. That pull is His drawing, and it is an invitation to come to Him.

### *John 12:42–43* — Loving Human Praise

> *“Nevertheless, even many of the rulers believed in him, but because of the Pharisees they didn’t confess it, so that they wouldn’t be put out of the synagogue, for they loved men’s praise more than God’s praise.”*
>
> — *John 12:42–43* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

John has just explained that many people did not believe in Jesus despite all the signs He had done. He quoted Isaiah to show that their unbelief had been foretold. Then he added a qualification: “*Nevertheless, even many of the rulers believed in him*” (*v. 42*). Not everyone among the leaders rejected Jesus. Some recognized that He was from God.

“*but because of the Pharisees they didn’t confess it, so that they wouldn’t be put out of the synagogue*” (*v. 42*). These rulers kept their faith secret. They feared the consequences of openly confessing Jesus. *John 9* showed what could happen: the man born blind was thrown out of the synagogue for speaking in Jesus’ favor. Being expelled meant losing one’s place in religious and social life, and for rulers it would mean losing their position and influence.

Then John gives the reason behind their silence: “*for they loved men’s praise more than God’s praise*” (*v. 43*). Their problem was not only fear but misplaced love. They valued the approval of people more than the approval of God. Jesus had diagnosed the same problem earlier: “*How can you believe, who receive glory from one another, and you don’t seek the glory that comes from the only God?*” (*John 5:44*)

John does not say whether these secret believers ever came into the open. But he does tell of two rulers who later did: Joseph of Arimathea, who was a disciple “*but secretly for fear of the Jews*” (*John 19:38*), and Nicodemus. After the crucifixion, both came forward to give Jesus an honorable burial.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses reveal that the desire for human approval can be a powerful barrier to faithfulness. It is possible to believe something is true and still refuse to stand for it because of what others might think. Jesus taught that those who are ashamed of Him before others will find Him ashamed of them (*Mark 8:38*), and that those who confess Him before others will be confessed before the Father (*Matthew 10:32*).

They also show the difference between private conviction and public confession. Faith in Scripture is not only inward belief but also outward allegiance. Paul writes that “*with the mouth confession is made resulting in salvation*” (*Romans 10:10*). True faith eventually shows itself in a willingness to be identified with Jesus.

Yet the example of Joseph and Nicodemus offers hope. Even fearful, secret believers can grow in courage. The cross that seemed to end everything became the moment when they stepped into the open.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses invite believers to examine whose approval matters most to them. Many Christians feel pressure to hide their faith at work, at school, among friends, or in their families. Fear of rejection, ridicule, or loss can lead to silence. John’s words expose the root issue: loving human praise more than God’s praise.

They also encourage believers who struggle with fear. Courage often grows step by step. Believers can ask God to help them value His approval above all and to give them boldness to speak and live openly for Christ, with gentleness and respect.

Finally, these verses remind believers that standing for Christ may cost something, but His approval is worth far more than anything the world can offer. The praise of people is temporary; God’s “well done” lasts forever.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*John 12* invites believers to wholehearted devotion. Mary poured out her most valuable possession at Jesus’ feet, and the whole house was filled with fragrance. Love for Jesus does not calculate the least it can give. Believers are called to offer Him their best, their time, gifts, resources, and lives, trusting that nothing given to Him is wasted, even when others do not understand.

The chapter also teaches the pattern of the grain of wheat. Jesus’ death brought life to the world, and His followers are called to a similar pattern of self-giving. Fruitfulness comes not through clinging to life but through giving it away in love and service. The sacrifices made for Christ and for others are seeds that God uses to bring a harvest.

At the center of the chapter is the cross. Jesus was lifted up to draw all people to Himself. The message of His death and resurrection still has power to draw people from every background to God. Believers are called to keep the cross central in their faith and witness, trusting that Jesus Himself does the drawing.

Finally, *John 12* warns against the love of human praise. Many rulers believed in Jesus but stayed silent for fear of losing their place. Believers today face similar pressures. The chapter calls them to walk in the light while they have it, to seek God’s approval above all, and to grow in courage to confess Christ openly.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, You are the King who came humbly, riding on a donkey, and the grain of wheat who fell into the ground and died to bring life to the world. Thank You for being lifted up on the cross to draw people of every nation to Yourself, and for drawing me. Give me a heart like Mary’s, ready to pour out my best for You without counting the cost. Let my life spread the fragrance of Your love wherever I go. Teach me the way of the grain of wheat, so that I stop clinging to my own life and give myself in love and service. When I am tempted to hide my faith because I fear what others will think, forgive me, and help me to love Your praise more than the praise of people. Keep me walking in Your light and believing in You while I have the light. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

John · Chapter 13 of 21

# John — Chapter 13

Chapter Theme: Love to the End: The Servant Lord and the New Commandment

[Read John 13 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/JHN13.htm)

Main Teaching

On the night before His death, Jesus, fully aware of His divine authority, takes a towel and washes His disciples’ feet. He tells Peter that unless He washes him, Peter has no part with Him, and He calls all His followers to serve one another as He has served them. After Judas goes out into the night to betray Him, Jesus gives His disciples a new commandment: to love one another as He has loved them, so that everyone will know they are His disciples. He also gently warns Peter that he will deny Him three times.

## Chapter Background and Story

*John 13* begins the second half of John’s Gospel, often called the Book of Glory. In the first twelve chapters, Jesus ministered publicly through signs and teaching. Now, in chapters 13–17, He speaks privately with His disciples on the night before His crucifixion. These chapters, sometimes called the Upper Room Discourse or Farewell Discourse, contain some of the most tender and profound teaching in the Bible.

John does not describe the institution of the Lord’s Supper, which the other three Gospels record (studied at *Matthew 26:28* and *Mark 14:24*). Instead, he tells of something the others do not mention: Jesus washing His disciples’ feet. Both events reveal the meaning of His death, one through bread and cup, the other through a towel and basin.

### Jesus Washes the Disciples’ Feet (*13:1–11*)

John begins with a summary of Jesus’ heart, studied below. Then he sets the scene. The meal was underway. The devil had already put the idea of betrayal into Judas’s heart. And Jesus knew “*that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he came from God and was going to God*” (*v. 3*). John emphasizes that Jesus acted not from weakness but from full awareness of His authority and identity.

Then Jesus “*arose from supper, and laid aside his outer garments. He took a towel and wrapped a towel around his waist*” (*v. 4*). He poured water into a basin and began to wash the disciples’ feet. In that culture, people walked in sandals on dusty roads, and feet became dirty. Washing guests’ feet was usually done by the lowest household servant; some Jewish teachers said that even a Jewish servant should not be required to do it. Disciples might perform many services for their rabbi, but not this one. Luke records that the disciples had been arguing that same evening about which of them was the greatest (*Luke 22:24*). No one had volunteered to wash feet.

When Jesus came to Peter, Peter protested. This exchange is studied below. Jesus also said, “*You are clean, but not all of you*” (*v. 10*), because He knew who would betray Him.

### The Example of the Servant Lord (*13:12–20*)

After washing their feet, Jesus put His outer garment back on, returned to His place, and asked, “*Do you know what I have done to you?*” (*v. 12*) He then explained the lesson, studied below.

He added, “*a servant is not greater than his lord, neither is one who is sent greater than he who sent him*” (*v. 16*). If the Lord serves, His servants cannot consider themselves too important to serve. Then He gave a promise: “*If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them*” (*v. 17*). The blessing comes not from knowing but from doing.

Jesus made it clear that He was not speaking of all of them. He quoted *Psalm 41:9*: “*He who eats bread with me has lifted up his heel against me*” (*v. 18*). In the ancient Near East, sharing a meal was a sign of friendship and trust, so betrayal by a table companion was especially painful. Jesus told them ahead of time “*that when it happens, you may believe that I am he*” (*v. 19*). The betrayal would not take Him by surprise; it was part of the Father’s plan foretold in Scripture.

### Jesus Foretells His Betrayal (*13:21–30*)

Jesus was “*troubled in spirit*” (*v. 21*) and said plainly, “*one of you will betray me*” (*v. 21*). The disciples looked at one another, unsure whom He meant. At ancient banquets, guests reclined on couches around a low table, leaning on their left elbows. The disciple whom Jesus loved, traditionally identified as John, the author of the Gospel, was reclining next to Jesus. Peter signaled him to ask who it was.

Jesus answered quietly, “*It is he to whom I will give this piece of bread when I have dipped it*” (*v. 26*). Then He dipped the bread and gave it to Judas. Offering a morsel of bread to a guest was a sign of honor and friendship. Even at this moment, Jesus extended love to His betrayer. Judas had washed feet, and he now received bread from Jesus’ hand. Yet “*After the piece of bread, then Satan entered into him*” (*v. 27*). Judas had repeatedly chosen his path, and now he gave himself completely to it.

Jesus said, “*What you do, do quickly*” (*v. 27*). The others did not understand; they thought Jesus might be sending Judas, who kept the money box, to buy something for the feast or to give to the poor. Judas went out. John adds four of the most haunting words in his Gospel: “*It was night*” (*v. 30*). Judas left the light of the world and went out into the darkness.

### The New Commandment (*13:31–35*)

When Judas had left, Jesus said, “*Now the Son of Man has been glorified, and God has been glorified in him*” (*v. 31*). The events that would lead to His death had begun, and in them God would be glorified.

He spoke tenderly: “*Little children, I will be with you a little while longer*” (*v. 33*). This is the only time in John’s Gospel that Jesus calls His disciples “little children,” an expression of deep affection. He was about to leave them, and they could not follow Him yet. Then He gave them the new commandment, studied below.

### Peter’s Denial Foretold (*13:36–38*)

Peter asked, “*Lord, where are you going?*” (*v. 36*) Jesus told him that he could not follow now but would follow later. Peter insisted, “*Lord, why can’t I follow you now? I will lay down my life for you*” (*v. 37*). Peter meant it sincerely, but he did not know his own weakness.

Jesus answered, “*Will you lay down your life for me? Most certainly I tell you, the rooster won’t crow until you have denied me three times*” (*v. 38*). Peter’s failure is studied at *Mark 14:72*, and his restoration will be told in *John 21*. Jesus’ words “you will follow afterwards” (*John 13:36*) also contain a hidden promise: Peter would one day follow Jesus even in death (*John 21:18–19*).

## Important Verses Explained

### *John 13:1* — He Loved Them to the End

> *“Now before the feast of the Passover, Jesus, knowing that his time had come that he would depart from this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end.”*
>
> — *John 13:1* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse opens the second half of John’s Gospel and introduces everything that follows: the foot washing, the farewell teaching, the prayer, the arrest, the crucifixion, and the resurrection. It explains the motive behind it all.

“*Now before the feast of the Passover*” (*v. 1*). The setting is the evening before Passover. Passover remembered God’s deliverance of Israel from slavery in Egypt, when the blood of a lamb protected each household from judgment. Jesus, the Lamb of God (*John 1:29*), would die at Passover time.

“*Jesus, knowing that his time had come that he would depart from this world to the Father*” (*v. 1*). Throughout the Gospel, Jesus said that His “hour” had not yet come. Now it had. He would “depart from this world to the Father,” a gentle way of describing His death, resurrection, and ascension. For Jesus, death meant going home to the Father.

“*having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end*” (*v. 1*). “His own” are His disciples, those who belonged to Him. He had loved them throughout His ministry, and now He would love them “to the end.” The Greek phrase can mean both “to the end of His life” and “to the fullest extent,” completely and perfectly. Both meanings are true. Jesus loved His disciples until His final breath, and He loved them with a love that held nothing back.

Notice that Jesus’ thoughts at this moment were not focused on Himself, though He knew He would soon suffer terribly. His focus was on loving His disciples.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals that love is the key to understanding the cross. Jesus’ death was not merely an unfortunate event or a political execution. It was the supreme expression of His love. Later in this discourse, He says, “*Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends*” (*John 15:13*).

It also shows the faithfulness of Christ’s love. The disciples were about to fail Him. One would betray Him, one would deny Him three times, and all would scatter. Yet His love for them did not change. Christ’s love is not based on the worthiness of the ones He loves; it is rooted in His own character.

Finally, the verse reveals the security of belonging to Christ. Those whom Jesus calls “his own” are loved to the end. His love does not give up halfway. Paul expresses the same confidence when he writes that nothing can separate believers from the love of God in Christ (*Romans 8:38–39*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse assures believers that Christ’s love for them is complete and lasting. Many people fear that God’s love will run out, that their failures will eventually exhaust His patience. Jesus loved His disciples to the end, even knowing how they would fail. Believers can rest in the same steadfast love.

It also shows how Jesus faced suffering. Knowing that His hour had come, He spent His last evening loving others. Believers facing difficult times can follow His example, turning their attention outward in love even when their own burdens are heavy.

Finally, the verse calls believers to love others faithfully. Many relationships end when love becomes costly or disappointing. Jesus’ love endured betrayal, denial, and abandonment. His people are called to a love that perseveres, while still using wisdom and seeking safety where there is danger or abuse.

### *John 13:8* — If I Don’t Wash You

> *“Peter said to him, ‘You will never wash my feet!’ Jesus answered him, ‘If I don’t wash you, you have no part with me.’”*
>
> — *John 13:8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus had taken the place of a household servant, wrapping a towel around His waist and washing His disciples’ dusty feet. When He came to Simon Peter, Peter was shocked: “*Lord, do you wash my feet?*” (*v. 6*) In Peter’s mind, it was entirely wrong for his Lord and Teacher to do such a lowly task.

Jesus answered, “*You don’t know what I am doing now, but you will understand later*” (*v. 7*). The act had a deeper meaning that Peter would grasp only after the cross and resurrection.

Peter refused firmly: “*You will never wash my feet!*” (*v. 8*) His refusal came from a mixture of reverence and pride. He could not accept the idea of Jesus humbling Himself in this way.

Jesus’ reply was serious: “*If I don’t wash you, you have no part with me*” (*v. 8*). To have “a part” with Jesus means to share in His life, His fellowship, and His inheritance. Jesus was saying that unless Peter allowed Him to serve him in this way, Peter could not belong to Him.

Peter immediately swung to the other extreme: “*Lord, not my feet only, but also my hands and my head!*” (*v. 9*) Jesus explained that someone who has bathed only needs to wash their feet. A person who had bathed before going to a dinner would get only their feet dirty on the way. In the same way, the disciples were already “clean” through their relationship with Jesus, except for Judas, but they still needed the cleansing that comes through His continued service.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The foot washing points beyond itself to the cross. Jesus laid aside His garments, took the role of a servant, and cleansed His disciples. This mirrors what Paul describes in Philippians 2: Christ, though He existed in the form of God, “*emptied himself, taking the form of a servant*” (*Philippians 2:7*), and humbled Himself to death on a cross. The cleansing that truly makes a person clean is His sacrificial death.

Peter’s refusal reveals a common spiritual problem. Many people find it hard to receive grace. Pride prefers to serve rather than be served, to earn rather than receive. But no one can belong to Christ without first allowing Him to cleanse them. Salvation begins with receiving what He has done.

The distinction between a full bath and washing the feet has often been seen as a picture of the difference between the initial cleansing of salvation and the ongoing cleansing of daily confession. Believers who have been made clean through Christ still need to bring their daily sins to Him. John writes in his first letter, “*If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins*” (*1 John 1:9*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to humbly receive Christ’s grace. Some people struggle to accept that Jesus would serve and cleanse them. They feel they must first become worthy or do something to deserve it. Jesus insists that He must wash them, and that their part is to receive.

It also encourages believers to come to Christ regularly for cleansing. Daily life leaves the “dust” of sin, failure, and weariness. Believers do not need to be saved again each day, but they do need to bring their sins to Jesus in confession and receive His forgiveness.

Finally, Peter’s swing from refusal to excess reminds believers that Jesus knows exactly what they need. Believers do not need to dictate the terms of His grace. They can trust Him to give them what is right.

### *John 13:14–15* — Wash One Another’s Feet

> *“If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet. For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you.”*
>
> — *John 13:14–15* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After washing His disciples’ feet, Jesus put His outer garment back on and returned to His place at the table. Then He explained what He had done. He began by affirming His authority: “*You call me, ‘Teacher’ and ‘Lord.’ You say so correctly, for so I am*” (*v. 13*). Jesus was not denying His position by serving; He was showing what true authority looks like.

“*If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet*” (*v. 14*). If the One who is Lord and Teacher took the lowest place, then His followers have no excuse for refusing to serve one another. No act of service is beneath them.

“*For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you*” (*v. 15*). The word “example” means a pattern to be copied. Jesus’ act was a model of how His disciples should treat one another.

Some Christian traditions practice foot washing literally as a church ordinance, especially on Maundy Thursday, the day before Good Friday. Most Christians understand Jesus’ command as calling for humble, practical service of every kind. Either way, the point is the same: followers of Jesus are called to serve one another humbly.

Remember the setting. The disciples had just been arguing about which of them was the greatest (*Luke 22:24*). None of them had offered to wash feet. Jesus answered their argument not with a lecture but with a towel.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses reveal a new definition of greatness. In the world, greatness means being served. In God’s kingdom, greatness means serving. Jesus taught this earlier: “*For the Son of Man also came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many*” (*Mark 10:45*). The foot washing is a living illustration of that truth.

They also show that Christian service flows from what Christ has done. Jesus first washed the disciples’ feet, and then told them to wash one another’s. Believers serve because they have been served by Christ. Service is not a way to earn His love but a response to it.

Finally, these verses show that humility and authority are not opposites. Jesus served with full awareness of His divine authority (*13:3*). True humility is not denying one’s worth but using one’s position to serve others.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses call believers to look for ways to serve, especially in tasks that others avoid. In families, churches, and workplaces, there are always unseen, unglamorous jobs. Following Jesus means being willing to do them, not for recognition but out of love.

They also challenge attitudes of pride and status. Believers can be tempted to think some tasks are beneath them because of their education, position, or experience. Jesus, the Lord of all, washed dirty feet. No act of loving service is beneath His followers.

Finally, these verses encourage leaders to serve. Those with authority in churches, homes, and organizations are called to use their position to serve others rather than to be served. Servant leadership reflects the heart of Christ. It never means tolerating abuse, but it does mean that power exists to bless and protect others.

### *John 13:34–35* — Love One Another as I Have Loved You

> *“A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another. Just as I have loved you, you also love one another. By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.”*
>
> — *John 13:34–35* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After Judas left to betray Him, Jesus spoke tenderly to the remaining disciples, calling them “little children.” He told them that He would be with them only a little longer, and that where He was going they could not come. Then He gave them a commandment to guide them after He was gone.

“*A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another*” (*v. 34*). The command to love was not entirely new; the Law commanded, “*you shall love your neighbor as yourself*” (*Leviticus 19:18*). What was new?

“*Just as I have loved you, you also love one another*” (*v. 34*). The new standard is Jesus’ own love. The disciples had just seen that love in action: He had washed their feet, including the feet of the one who would betray Him. Within hours, He would lay down His life for them. The new commandment calls believers to love one another with the same self-giving, humble, sacrificial love.

“*By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another*” (*v. 35*). Jesus made love the identifying mark of His followers. People would recognize His disciples not primarily by their knowledge, their buildings, or their rituals, but by the way they loved one another.

This command focuses on love within the community of believers, “one another.” Elsewhere Jesus commands love for neighbors and even enemies. But here He emphasizes that the love among His people will be a witness to the world.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The new commandment is new because it is rooted in a new reality: the love of Christ revealed in His death. The cross sets a standard of love that the world had never seen. John later writes, “*By this we know love, because he laid down his life for us. And we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers*” (*1 John 3:16*).

It also reveals that the church’s love is a form of witness. In a divided world, a community of people from different backgrounds who genuinely love one another points to the reality of Christ. Early Christian writers reported that outsiders said of believers, “See how they love one another.” Jesus prayed that His followers would be one so that the world would believe (*John 17:21*).

Finally, the command shows that love is possible only because believers have first been loved. They cannot generate this love on their own. It flows from receiving Christ’s love and is produced by His Spirit (*Galatians 5:22*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This commandment calls believers to examine how they treat other Christians. It is easy to criticize, compete with, or ignore fellow believers, especially those with different personalities, backgrounds, or opinions. Jesus calls His followers to love one another as He loved them, with patience, forgiveness, and practical care.

It also reminds churches that their love is their witness. Programs, preaching, and buildings matter, but the world will recognize Jesus’ disciples by their love. Churches marked by division, gossip, or coldness obscure the gospel. Churches marked by love display it.

Finally, the commandment encourages believers to love in concrete ways. Jesus’ love was practical: He washed feet, fed the hungry, touched the sick, and gave His life. Believers can show love by serving, encouraging, forgiving, sharing resources, and standing with one another in hard times.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*John 13* shows the heart of Jesus on the night before His death. He loved His disciples to the end, knowing they would fail Him. Believers can rest in that same faithful love. Their failures do not exhaust Christ’s patience. He loves His own completely and to the end.

The chapter also shows that belonging to Christ begins with receiving His cleansing. Peter had to let Jesus wash his feet. Many people find it hard to receive grace, preferring to earn God’s favor or to serve Him on their own terms. Jesus calls everyone to humbly accept what He does for them, and to keep coming to Him for cleansing when the dust of daily sin builds up.

*John 13* teaches that true greatness is found in serving. The Lord and Teacher took a towel and washed feet. His followers are called to serve one another, especially in humble and unnoticed ways. Leaders in particular are called to follow His example, using their authority to bless and protect rather than to be served.

Finally, the chapter gives the new commandment: to love one another as Jesus has loved us. This love is the mark by which the world will recognize Jesus’ disciples. In a world full of division, a community of believers who love one another sacrificially is a powerful testimony to the reality of Christ. Each believer can contribute to that witness through patience, forgiveness, and practical care for others.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for loving Your own to the end, and for loving me with a love that does not give up. You knew the Father had given all things into Your hands, and still You took a towel and washed Your disciples’ feet. Humble my pride. Help me to receive Your cleansing, and to come to You each day for forgiveness. Teach me to follow Your example by serving others gladly, even in tasks no one else wants to do. Forgive me for the times I have sought to be great instead of seeking to serve. Fill me with Your love so that I may love my brothers and sisters as You have loved me. Let the love among Your people be so real that the world will know we belong to You. When I am confident in my own strength, as Peter was, keep me humble and dependent on You. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
