John · Chapter 14 of 21

# John — Chapter 14

Chapter Theme: Comfort for Troubled Hearts: The Way to the Father and the Promised Counselor

[Read John 14 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/JHN14.htm)

Main Teaching

On the night of His betrayal, Jesus comforts His anxious disciples. He promises that He is going to prepare a place for them in His Father’s house and will come again to take them to Himself. He declares that He is the way, the truth, and the life, that whoever has seen Him has seen the Father, and that He will send another Counselor, the Spirit of truth, to be with them forever. He leaves them His own peace, which is unlike anything the world can give.

## Chapter Background and Story

*John 14* continues Jesus’ farewell conversation in the upper room. The disciples had just heard devastating news. Jesus had said that one of them would betray Him, that He was going where they could not follow, and that Peter, their boldest member, would deny Him three times before morning (*13:21–38*). Their hearts were troubled. Everything they had built their lives around for three years seemed to be falling apart.

Jesus’ response is not to rebuke them but to comfort them. Much of chapter 14 is a series of promises: a place prepared, a way to the Father, answered prayer, the gift of the Spirit, the presence of the Father and the Son, and lasting peace. Along the way, three disciples, Thomas, Philip, and Judas (not Iscariot), ask questions that reveal their confusion, and each question leads to a deeper revelation.

### A Place Prepared (*14:1–4*)

Jesus began, “*Don’t let your heart be troubled. Believe in God. Believe also in me*” (*v. 1*). He then spoke of His Father’s house and of His return, studied below. He added, “*You know where I go, and you know the way*” (*v. 4*).

### The Way, the Truth, and the Life (*14:5–7*)

Thomas, honest as always, said, “*Lord, we don’t know where you are going. How can we know the way?*” (*v. 5*) Thomas thought in terms of places and roads. Jesus answered with one of His greatest statements, studied below. He added, “*If you had known me, you would have known my Father also. From now on, you know him and have seen him*” (*v. 7*).

### Seeing the Father (*14:8–14*)

Philip said, “*Lord, show us the Father, and that will be enough for us*” (*v. 8*). Perhaps he was thinking of Moses, who asked to see God’s glory (*Exodus 33:18*). Philip wanted a visible manifestation of God.

Jesus’ answer combines gentle disappointment with profound revelation: “*Have I been with you such a long time, and do you not know me, Philip? He who has seen me has seen the Father*” (*v. 9*). Philip had been looking at the Father’s revelation for three years without fully realizing it. Jesus is the perfect image of the Father. His words and works are the Father’s words and works: “*the Father who lives in me does his works*” (*v. 10*). If Philip found it hard to believe Jesus’ words, he could believe because of the works themselves.

Then Jesus made a remarkable promise: “*he who believes in me, the works that I do, he will do also; and he will do greater works than these, because I am going to my Father*” (*v. 12*). “Greater works” does not mean more spectacular miracles than raising the dead. It refers to the wider scope of the work the disciples would do after Jesus’ return to the Father and the coming of the Spirit. Jesus ministered in a small region for about three years; through His followers, the gospel would spread to the ends of the earth, and thousands would come to faith in a single day (*Acts 2:41*).

He added, “*Whatever you will ask in my name, I will do it, that the Father may be glorified in the Son*” (*v. 13*). To ask “in Jesus’ name” is not to use a magic formula but to pray as His representatives, according to His character and will, for the glory of the Father. John later explains, “*if we ask anything according to his will, he listens to us*” (*1 John 5:14*).

### Another Counselor (*14:15–24*)

“*If you love me, keep my commandments*” (*v. 15*). Love for Jesus shows itself in obedience, not as a way to earn His love but as a response to it. Jesus then promised the Holy Spirit, studied below.

He continued, “*I will not leave you orphans. I will come to you*” (*v. 18*). The disciples would not be abandoned like children without parents. “*Because I live, you will live also*” (*v. 19*). His resurrection would guarantee their life.

Judas, a different disciple from Judas Iscariot (probably the same person called Thaddaeus in Matthew and Mark), asked why Jesus would reveal Himself to them and not to the world. Jesus answered that He reveals Himself to those who love Him and keep His word: “*My Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him*” (*v. 23*). The word for “home” is related to the “homes” in the Father’s house in verse 2. Jesus is preparing a place for His people in the Father’s house, and meanwhile the Father and the Son make their home in His people.

### The Spirit’s Teaching and the Gift of Peace (*14:25–31*)

Jesus said that the Counselor, the Holy Spirit, “*will teach you all things, and will remind you of all that I said to you*” (*v. 26*). This promise applied especially to the apostles, who would preserve and explain Jesus’ teaching. It helps explain how John could write his Gospel decades later, with the Spirit bringing Jesus’ words to his memory and deepening his understanding. Then Jesus gave His peace, studied below.

Jesus said that if they loved Him, they would rejoice that He was going to the Father, “*for the Father is greater than I*” (*v. 28*). This does not mean that Jesus is less divine than the Father, since the same Gospel says the Word was God (*1:1*) and Jesus said, “I and the Father are one” (*10:30*). Christians have understood this statement as referring to Jesus’ role as the Son who was sent, who took on human nature and humbled Himself, and who was now returning to the glory He had with the Father before the world began (*17:5*).

Jesus said that the ruler of this world was coming, but “*he has nothing in me*” (*v. 30*). Satan had no claim on Jesus, because Jesus was without sin. Jesus would go to the cross not because Satan had power over Him but “*that the world may know that I love the Father*” (*v. 31*), in obedience to the Father’s command. Then He said, “*Arise, let’s go from here*” (*v. 31*). The conversation may have continued as they walked toward the Mount of Olives.

## Important Verses Explained

### *John 14:1–3* — I Will Come Again

> *“Don’t let your heart be troubled. Believe in God. Believe also in me. In my Father’s house are many homes. If it weren’t so, I would have told you. I am going to prepare a place for you. If I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and will receive you to myself; that where I am, you may be there also.”*
>
> — *John 14:1–3* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The disciples were shaken. Jesus had just told them that He was leaving, that one of them would betray Him, and that Peter would deny Him. Their world was collapsing. Into this moment, Jesus spoke words of comfort: “*Don’t let your heart be troubled*” (*v. 1*).

The word “troubled” means stirred up, agitated, disturbed. Jesus Himself had been troubled at the tomb of Lazarus (*11:33*), at the thought of the cross (*12:27*), and at the prediction of betrayal (*13:21*). He knew what it felt like. He did not tell the disciples that their situation was easy, but He showed them how to face it.

“*Believe in God. Believe also in me*” (*v. 1*). The remedy for a troubled heart is trust. The disciples already believed in God; now Jesus called them to trust Him in the same way. He placed Himself alongside God as the object of faith.

“*In my Father’s house are many homes*” (*v. 2*). The image of a father’s house suggests family, belonging, and permanence. “Many homes” means there is plenty of room. Older translations used the word “mansions,” which originally meant “dwelling places.” The emphasis is not on luxury but on belonging. “*If it weren’t so, I would have told you*” (*v. 2*). Jesus assures them that He has been honest with them.

“*I am going to prepare a place for you*” (*v. 2*). Jesus’ departure was not abandonment but preparation. Through His death, resurrection, and ascension, He would open the way into the Father’s presence.

“*If I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and will receive you to myself; that where I am, you may be there also*” (*v. 3*). This is a promise of Jesus’ return. The greatest joy of heaven is not the place itself but being with Jesus.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses give believers a clear hope for the future. Jesus will come again. Christians have often understood this primarily as His second coming at the end of the age, when He will gather His people (*1 Thessalonians 4:16–17*). Some also see a secondary application to the moment of a believer’s death, when they go to be with Christ (*Philippians 1:23*). In either case, the promise is that believers will be with Him forever.

The image of a wedding may also lie behind these words. In Jewish custom, after a betrothal, the bridegroom went to prepare a place for his bride, often an addition to his father’s house. When it was ready, he came to bring her home. The church is called the bride of Christ (*Ephesians 5:25–27*; *Revelation 19:7*).

Finally, these verses show that Jesus’ focus is relational. “*I will come again and will receive you to myself; that where I am, you may be there also*” (*v. 3*). Heaven is above all the presence of Jesus. This is the deepest longing of the believer and the deepest desire of Christ for His people (*John 17:24*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These words bring comfort to troubled hearts. Believers face many situations that stir up fear: illness, loss, uncertainty about the future, and the approach of death. Jesus’ remedy is trust in God and in Him. Believers can bring their troubled hearts to Christ and rest in His promises.

They also bring hope in the face of death. Christian funerals often include these verses because they remind mourners that believers who die go to the Father’s house, where Jesus has prepared a place for them. Death is not the end but a homecoming.

Finally, these verses help believers keep an eternal perspective. Life in this world is not the whole story. Jesus is preparing a place for His people and will come again. This hope gives strength to endure hardship and to live faithfully while waiting for His return.

### *John 14:6* — The Way, the Truth, and the Life

> *“Jesus said to him, I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father, except through me.”*
>
> — *John 14:6* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus had told His disciples that they knew the way to where He was going. Thomas, honest about his confusion, said, “*Lord, we don’t know where you are going. How can we know the way?*” (*v. 5*) Thomas was thinking of a physical destination and a road to get there.

Jesus answered, “*I am the way, the truth, and the life*” (*v. 6*). He did not give directions; He pointed to Himself. Jesus does not merely show the way; He is the way. He does not merely teach the truth; He is the truth. He does not merely give life; He is the life.

“The way”: Jesus is the path by which people come to God. Through His life, death, and resurrection, He has opened the way into the Father’s presence.

“The truth”: Jesus is the full and reliable revelation of God. In a world of confusion and lies, He is the reality of who God is and what God has done.

“The life”: Jesus is the source of eternal life. As He said to Martha, He is the resurrection and the life (*11:25*).

“*No one comes to the Father, except through me*” (*v. 6*). This is a clear and exclusive claim. Jesus is not one way among many. He is the only way to the Father. This is not because God is narrow or unkind, but because only Jesus has dealt with sin and opened the way to God.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This is the sixth of Jesus’ “I am” sayings in John. It brings together much of the Gospel’s message. John began by describing Jesus as the Word who was with God, full of grace and truth (*1:14*), and in whom was life (*1:4*). Now Jesus summarizes His identity in relation to the Father: He is the way to the Father, the truth about the Father, and the life of the Father.

The claim of exclusivity is often difficult for modern readers. But it flows from who Jesus is. If He is truly the Son of God who died for sins and rose again, then He alone can reconcile people to God. The apostles proclaimed the same truth: “*There is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven that is given among men, by which we must be saved!*” (*Acts 4:12*)

The verse is also deeply gracious. The way to God is not a long list of achievements or a secret path known only to a few. It is a Person who welcomes all who come. The exclusive claim is joined with a universal invitation: whoever comes to Him will not be cast out (*6:37*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse gives believers confidence. In a world of many religions and philosophies, Christians can trust that Jesus is the way to the Father. They do not need to search endlessly for truth; they can know the One who is the truth.

It also shapes how believers speak about their faith. Jesus’ claim is exclusive, but it should be shared with humility and love, never with arrogance. Believers do not claim to be better than others; they point to Jesus, who alone can bring anyone to God. Honest, gentle conversation and respect for people of other beliefs are fully consistent with confidence in Christ.

Finally, the verse invites believers to keep following Jesus as the way. Every day, believers face choices about how to live. Jesus is not only the way into God’s family but also the way of life within it. Following Him means trusting His truth and living by His life.

### *John 14:16–17* — Another Counselor, the Spirit of Truth

> *“I will pray to the Father, and he will give you another Counselor, that he may be with you forever: the Spirit of truth, whom the world can’t receive, for it doesn’t see him and doesn’t know him. You know him, for he lives with you and will be in you.”*
>
> — *John 14:16–17* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus was preparing His disciples for His departure. They had depended on His presence for three years. How would they continue without Him? Jesus answered with a promise: “*I will pray to the Father, and he will give you another Counselor, that he may be with you forever*” (*v. 16*).

The word “Counselor” translates the Greek word paraclete, which means “one called alongside.” It can refer to a legal advocate, a helper, a comforter, or an encourager. Different translations use different words, such as Helper, Comforter, or Advocate, because no single English word captures its full meaning.

The word “another” is important. Greek has two words for “another”: one meaning “another of a different kind,” and one meaning “another of the same kind.” Jesus uses the second. The Holy Spirit would be a Counselor just like Jesus, continuing His presence and ministry with the disciples.

“*that he may be with you forever*” (*v. 16*). Jesus would be with them only a short time longer, but the Spirit would remain with them forever.

“*the Spirit of truth, whom the world can’t receive, for it doesn’t see him and doesn’t know him*” (*v. 17*). The Spirit reveals truth, especially the truth about Jesus. The world, meaning humanity in rebellion against God, cannot receive Him because it does not recognize Him.

“*You know him, for he lives with you and will be in you*” (*v. 17*). The Spirit was already with the disciples through Jesus’ presence. After Jesus’ glorification, the Spirit would dwell within them.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses reveal the personal nature of the Holy Spirit. Jesus speaks of Him not as an impersonal force but as a Person, one who teaches, reminds, testifies, guides, and convicts (*14:26*; *15:26*; *16:8*, 13). He is the third Person of the Trinity, sent by the Father at the request of the Son.

They also show the intimacy of God’s presence with believers. Under the old covenant, God’s Spirit came upon certain people for particular tasks. Under the new covenant, the Spirit dwells within every believer. Paul writes that believers’ bodies are “*a temple of the Holy Spirit*” (*1 Corinthians 6:19*).

Finally, the promise shows that Jesus’ departure was not a loss but a gain. Later He says, “*It is to your advantage that I go away*” (*John 16:7*). While on earth, Jesus was present in one place at a time. Through the Spirit, He is present with all His people everywhere.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses assure believers that they are never alone. Many people feel isolated, especially in times of grief, fear, or transition. Jesus promised that the Spirit would be with His people forever. Believers can rely on the Spirit’s presence in every circumstance.

They also encourage believers to depend on the Spirit’s help. The Christian life is not meant to be lived in human strength. The Spirit teaches, guides, comforts, and empowers. Believers can ask for His help in understanding Scripture, resisting temptation, making decisions, and loving others.

Finally, these verses call believers to listen to the Spirit of truth. In a world full of conflicting voices, the Spirit guides believers into the truth about Jesus. He works especially through Scripture, which He inspired, helping believers understand and apply God’s Word.

### *John 14:27* — My Peace I Give to You

> *“Peace I leave with you. My peace I give to you; not as the world gives, I give to you. Don’t let your heart be troubled, neither let it be fearful.”*
>
> — *John 14:27* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus was near the end of His conversation with the disciples in the upper room. He had promised them a place in His Father’s house, the presence of the Holy Spirit, and the indwelling of the Father and the Son. Now He gave them a parting gift: “*Peace I leave with you. My peace I give to you*” (*v. 27*).

“Peace” (in Hebrew, shalom) was a common greeting and farewell. But Jesus meant much more than a polite goodbye. In Scripture, shalom means wholeness, well-being, and right relationship with God and others. Jesus was leaving them something real.

“My peace” is the peace Jesus Himself had. On the night of His betrayal, facing the cross, He was at peace because He trusted the Father completely. He was offering His disciples a share in that same peace.

“*not as the world gives, I give to you*” (*v. 27*). The world offers a kind of peace that depends on circumstances: the absence of conflict, financial security, good health, or comfort. That peace disappears when circumstances change. Jesus’ peace does not depend on circumstances. It comes from His presence and His promises.

“*Don’t let your heart be troubled, neither let it be fearful*” (*v. 27*). Jesus repeated the words He spoke at the beginning of the chapter (*14:1*). Because of His peace, His disciples did not need to be overwhelmed by fear.

The disciples were about to face the most frightening hours of their lives. Jesus’ peace was not a promise that nothing bad would happen, but a promise that they would not face it alone.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The peace Jesus gives is rooted in reconciliation with God. Paul writes, “*Being therefore justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ*” (*Romans 5:1*). Because Jesus has dealt with sin on the cross, those who trust Him are no longer enemies of God. This peace with God becomes the foundation for the peace of God in the heart.

It is also connected with the Holy Spirit, whom Jesus has just promised. Peace is part of the fruit of the Spirit (*Galatians 5:22*). The Spirit’s presence in believers produces a peace that surpasses understanding (*Philippians 4:7*).

Finally, this peace reflects the character of Jesus Himself. He faced betrayal, suffering, and death without losing His trust in the Father. His peace was not denial of reality but confidence in God within reality. That is the peace He gives His people.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse offers hope to people who struggle with anxiety and fear. Jesus’ peace is available even when circumstances are difficult. Believers can bring their worries to Him in prayer and receive His peace. This does not mean that feelings of fear disappear instantly, or that anxiety is always a sign of weak faith; anxiety can have many causes, and seeking help from doctors or counselors is wise and compatible with faith. But Jesus offers a deep anchor of peace that the storms of life cannot remove.

It also helps believers recognize false sources of peace. The world promises peace through wealth, entertainment, control, or escape. These things cannot give lasting peace. True peace comes from Christ.

Finally, the verse encourages believers to share Christ’s peace with others. Those who have received His peace can bring calm, comfort, and reconciliation into a troubled world, becoming peacemakers who reflect the heart of their Lord (*Matthew 5:9*).

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*John 14* speaks directly to troubled hearts. Jesus did not ignore His disciples’ fear or tell them to pretend everything was fine. He comforted them with promises. Believers today face many sources of fear and grief. This chapter invites them to bring their troubled hearts to Jesus and to trust Him as they trust God.

The chapter also gives believers a firm hope for the future. Jesus is preparing a place for His people in His Father’s house, and He will come again to bring them to Himself. This hope changes how believers face death and loss. Those who die in Christ are going home, and those who remain can grieve with hope.

*John 14* points to Jesus as the way, the truth, and the life. In a world of many voices and options, believers can rest in the confidence that Jesus is the way to the Father. This truth should be held with humility and shared with love, offering others the same welcome that Jesus offers.

Finally, the chapter promises the presence of the Holy Spirit and the gift of Christ’s peace. Believers are not orphans. The Spirit lives in them, teaches them, and reminds them of Jesus’ words. The Father and the Son make their home with those who love Jesus. And His peace, unlike the world’s peace, remains even in the storm. These promises allow believers to face each day with courage and calm.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, when my heart is troubled, help me to trust in God and to trust in You. Thank You for preparing a place for me in Your Father’s house, and for Your promise that You will come again and take me to be with You. You are the way, the truth, and the life. Thank You for opening the way to the Father and for showing me what He is like. Thank You for sending the Holy Spirit to be with me forever, so that I am never alone. Teach me by Your Spirit, remind me of Your words, and help me to love You by keeping Your commandments. Make Your home in my heart. Give me Your peace, the peace the world cannot give or take away, and calm my fears. Help me to share that peace with others who are troubled. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

John · Chapter 15 of 21

# John — Chapter 15

Chapter Theme: The True Vine: Remaining in Christ, Loving as Friends, Enduring the World’s Hatred

[Read John 15 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/JHN15.htm)

Main Teaching

Jesus describes Himself as the true vine, His Father as the farmer, and His disciples as branches. Fruitfulness comes only by remaining in Him, and the Father prunes fruitful branches so that they bear more. Jesus calls His disciples friends, commands them to love one another with the self-giving love He is about to show on the cross, and prepares them for the hatred of a world that hated Him first, promising that the Spirit of truth will testify about Him through them.

## Chapter Background and Story

*John 14* ended with Jesus saying, “Arise, let’s go from here” (*14:31*). Chapters 15–17 may have been spoken as Jesus and the disciples walked from the upper room through Jerusalem toward the Kidron Valley and the Mount of Olives, perhaps passing vineyards on the slopes, or the great golden vine that decorated the entrance to the temple sanctuary, a symbol of Israel. Or Jesus may have continued speaking before they left the room. Either way, the image of the vine would have been vivid to the disciples.

The chapter moves through three relationships: the disciples’ relationship with Jesus (abiding in the vine), their relationship with one another (love as friends), and their relationship with the world (hatred and witness).

### The Vine and the Branches (*15:1–8*)

Jesus said, “*I am the true vine, and my Father is the farmer*” (*v. 1*). This is the seventh and final “I am” saying in John’s Gospel. In the Old Testament, Israel was often pictured as God’s vine or vineyard (*Psalm 80:8–16*; *Isaiah 5:1–7*; *Jeremiah 2:21*). God planted it with care and looked for good fruit, but too often it produced wild grapes. Jesus calls Himself the “true” vine. He is the faithful Israel, the One who perfectly bears the fruit God desires, and all who are joined to Him become part of God’s true people. The Father’s care for the vine is studied below.

“*You are already pruned clean because of the word which I have spoken to you*” (*v. 3*). The Greek word for “pruned” and “clean” is the same word. Through Jesus’ teaching and their relationship with Him, the disciples had already been cleansed.

Jesus then called them to remain in Him, studied below. He warned, “*If a man doesn’t remain in me, he is thrown out as a branch and is withered; and they gather them, throw them into the fire, and they are burned*” (*v. 6*). Vine wood is useless for building or carving (*Ezekiel 15:2–5*). A branch that is cut off is good only for burning. This sobering warning shows that a mere outward connection to Jesus, without true union with Him, ends in judgment. Judas, who had walked with Jesus and then left, is a sobering example.

Jesus promised, “*If you remain in me, and my words remain in you, you will ask whatever you desire, and it will be done for you*” (*v. 7*). Those who remain in Him, and in whom His words remain, will desire what He desires. Their prayers will be shaped by His will. “*In this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit; and so you will be my disciples*” (*v. 8*). Fruitfulness is the evidence of true discipleship.

### Remaining in His Love (*15:9–17*)

Jesus spoke of the depth of His love: “*Even as the Father has loved me, I also have loved you. Remain in my love*” (*v. 9*). The love Jesus has for His disciples is the same love the Father has for Him. They are invited to remain, to live, in that love.

How do they remain in His love? “*If you keep my commandments, you will remain in my love, even as I have kept my Father’s commandments and remain in his love*” (*v. 10*). Obedience is not the way to earn Jesus’ love; it is the way to live within it. Jesus Himself lived in obedience to the Father, and that obedience was an expression of their loving relationship.

“*I have spoken these things to you, that my joy may remain in you, and that your joy may be made full*” (*v. 11*). Jesus’ commands are not meant to burden His disciples but to fill them with His joy.

He repeated the command He had given in *John 13:34*: “*This is my commandment, that you love one another, even as I have loved you*” (*v. 12*). Then He spoke of His friendship with them, studied below.

“*You didn’t choose me, but I chose you and appointed you, that you should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain*” (*v. 16*). In Jesus’ day, disciples usually chose which rabbi to follow. Jesus reversed this. He chose them, and He appointed them for a purpose: to go and bear lasting fruit. The disciples’ mission flowed from His initiative.

### The World’s Hatred (*15:18–25*)

Jesus then prepared the disciples for opposition, studied below. He reminded them of what He had said after washing their feet: “*A servant is not greater than his lord*” (*v. 20*). If the world persecuted Jesus, it would persecute them. If it kept His word, it would keep theirs.

The world’s hatred of Jesus was not caused by ignorance alone. Jesus said that if He had not come and spoken to them and done works no one else had done, they would not be guilty of this sin. But now they had seen and hated both Him and His Father. “*He who hates me, hates my Father also*” (*v. 23*). This fulfilled the Scripture, “*They hated me without a cause*” (*v. 25*), words found in *Psalms 35:19* and *69:4*, where David described the unjust hostility of his enemies. Jesus, the Son of David, experienced the same.

### The Witness of the Spirit and the Disciples (*15:26–27*)

Jesus closed this section with a promise. The Counselor, the Spirit of truth whom He would send from the Father, “*will testify about me*” (*v. 26*). The disciples too would testify, “*because you have been with me from the beginning*” (*v. 27*). The Spirit would bear witness to Jesus through the disciples’ witness. They were not left to defend Jesus in their own strength. The Spirit would work with them and through them.

## Important Verses Explained

### *John 15:1–2* — The Father Prunes the Branches

> *“I am the true vine, and my Father is the farmer. Every branch in me that doesn’t bear fruit, he takes away. Every branch that bears fruit, he prunes, that it may bear more fruit.”*
>
> — *John 15:1–2* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus was speaking to His disciples on the night before His crucifixion. He used an image they all understood: a vineyard. Vineyards covered the hillsides of Israel, and grapes were one of the most important crops. Every Israelite knew how much care a vineyard required.

“*I am the true vine, and my Father is the farmer*” (*v. 1*). Jesus is the vine, the main stem through which life flows. The Father is the farmer, the vinedresser who tends the vine with skill and care.

“*Every branch in me that doesn’t bear fruit, he takes away*” (*v. 2*). A vinedresser removes branches that are dead or unfruitful. Some interpreters understand “takes away” as describing those who seem to be connected to Jesus but have no real life in Him, like Judas. Others note that the Greek word can also mean “lifts up,” and suggest that the vinedresser lifts fallen branches off the ground so that they can receive sunlight and become fruitful. Both readings show the farmer’s active care for the vine.

“*Every branch that bears fruit, he prunes, that it may bear more fruit*” (*v. 2*). Pruning involves cutting back healthy branches, removing shoots that would drain energy without producing fruit. A pruned vine may look bare and wounded for a time, but it produces a much better harvest. Skilled vinedressers prune heavily because they know what the vine can become.

This verse shows that the Father is deeply involved in the lives of believers. He is not a distant observer but an attentive vinedresser, working to make His people more fruitful.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The image of pruning helps believers understand some of the painful experiences of life. God sometimes uses difficulties, discipline, and loss to remove what hinders growth. Hebrews teaches that God disciplines His children “*for our profit, that we may be partakers of his holiness*” (*Hebrews 12:10*). Pruning is not punishment but loving care with a purpose.

It also shows that fruitful believers are not exempt from pruning. In fact, it is the fruitful branches that are pruned. God’s work in a believer’s life is never finished. Even those who are growing will experience His shaping, so that they bear more fruit.

Finally, this image reveals God’s goal: fruit. Throughout Scripture, “fruit” refers to the evidence of a life connected to God, including Christlike character (*Galatians 5:22–23*), good works (*Colossians 1:10*), and the influence that brings others to faith. The Father’s work in His people is directed toward a life that reflects His goodness.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse helps believers interpret seasons of difficulty. Not every hardship is God’s pruning; some suffering comes from the brokenness of the world, from the wrongdoing of others, or from evil that God hates. But God can use painful experiences to shape His people. When believers face loss, disappointment, or difficult change, they can ask how God might be using it to make them more fruitful.

It also encourages believers to trust the Vinedresser. Pruning is painful, and it is not always clear why it is happening. But the Father is skilled and loving. He knows what He is doing and has a good purpose.

Finally, this verse invites believers to welcome God’s shaping. Sometimes believers cling to habits, attitudes, or priorities that drain their energy without producing fruit. They can invite God to remove what hinders their growth, trusting that His pruning leads to a fuller life.

### *John 15:5* — Apart from Me You Can Do Nothing

> *“I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.”*
>
> — *John 15:5* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus continued the image of the vine and branches. He had already told the disciples to remain in Him, as a branch remains in the vine (*15:4*). Now He made the picture explicit: “*I am the vine. You are the branches*” (*v. 5*).

A branch draws everything it needs from the vine: water, nutrients, and life. A branch does not produce fruit by trying hard; it bears fruit by staying connected. The fruit is the natural result of the vine’s life flowing through it.

“*He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit*” (*v. 5*). The word “remains” (sometimes translated “abides”) is a key word in this chapter, used many times. To remain in Jesus means to stay connected to Him in a continuing relationship of trust, love, and obedience. It is not a one-time decision but an ongoing life. Notice the mutual relationship: “remains in me and I in him.” The believer lives in Christ, and Christ lives in the believer.

The promise is “much fruit.” Jesus does not promise a small or barely-there result. Those who remain in Him will be fruitful.

“*for apart from me you can do nothing*” (*v. 5*). This is a strong statement. A branch cut off from the vine cannot produce even one grape. In the same way, believers cannot produce spiritual fruit apart from Christ. They may accomplish many things in human strength, but nothing of eternal value comes without Him.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals the secret of the Christian life: dependence on Christ. The Christian life is not primarily about trying harder but about staying closer. Paul expressed the same truth: “*it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me*” (*Galatians 2:20*). The life of Christ flows into believers through their union with Him.

It also humbles human pride. People like to think of themselves as self-sufficient. Jesus says that apart from Him, His disciples can do nothing. This is not an insult but a liberating truth. Believers do not have to produce fruit by their own strength. They need to stay connected to the One who does.

Finally, the verse shows that union with Christ is personal and mutual. Believers are “in Christ,” and Christ is “in” them. This union is made real by the Holy Spirit, who lives in believers and joins them to Christ.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to prioritize their relationship with Jesus. Remaining in Him involves practices such as prayer, reading and meditating on Scripture, worship, obedience, and fellowship with other believers. These are not ways to earn His love but ways to stay connected to the source of life.

It also brings relief to weary believers. Many Christians feel pressure to produce results through their own effort. Jesus’ words remind them that fruit comes from Him. When believers feel empty, the answer is not simply to work harder but to return to Christ and draw on His life.

Finally, this verse challenges self-reliance. Believers may be tempted to rely on their own talents, plans, or strength in ministry, work, or family life. Jesus calls them to depend on Him in everything. Even the smallest act of faithful service bears fruit when it flows from union with Him.

### *John 15:13–15* — Greater Love and True Friendship

> *“Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends. You are my friends if you do whatever I command you. No longer do I call you servants, for the servant doesn’t know what his lord does. But I have called you friends, for everything that I heard from my Father, I have made known to you.”*
>
> — *John 15:13–15* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus had just repeated His command that His disciples love one another as He had loved them. Then He described the greatest form of love: “*Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends*” (*v. 13*). There is no greater proof of love than giving one’s life for another.

Within hours, Jesus would demonstrate this love on the cross. He was not speaking theoretically. He was describing what He was about to do for these very disciples.

“*You are my friends if you do whatever I command you*” (*v. 14*). Friendship with Jesus shows itself in obedience. This is not a condition for earning friendship but a description of what His friends are like. Those who are truly His friends follow His teaching.

“*No longer do I call you servants, for the servant doesn’t know what his lord does*” (*v. 15*). A servant receives orders without explanation. He does his master’s will without being told the master’s plans.

“*But I have called you friends, for everything that I heard from my Father, I have made known to you*” (*v. 15*). Jesus had shared His heart and His Father’s purposes with them. He had brought them into His confidence. They were not merely servants but friends.

In the Old Testament, only a few were called God’s friends, such as Abraham (*Isaiah 41:8*; *James 2:23*) and Moses, with whom God spoke “*face to face, as a man speaks to his friend*” (*Exodus 33:11*). Jesus extends this privilege to all His disciples.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses reveal the heart of the gospel. Jesus laid down His life for His friends. Paul goes even further, noting that Christ died for us while we were still sinners and even enemies (*Romans 5:8*, 10). Christ’s love made enemies into friends. His death was the greatest act of love the world has ever known.

They also show the intimacy of the relationship between Jesus and His followers. Believers are still His servants in the sense that they belong to Him and obey Him; the apostles often called themselves servants of Christ. But they are more than servants. They are friends, invited to know His heart and share His purposes.

Finally, these verses show that love and obedience go together. Jesus’ friends do what He commands. This obedience is not cold duty but the natural response of friends who trust and love Him.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses invite believers to see themselves as friends of Jesus. Many Christians relate to God mainly as a distant master or judge. Jesus offers friendship. Believers can speak to Him openly in prayer, trust His heart, and enjoy His company.

They also set the standard for Christian love. Jesus’ love was sacrificial; He laid down His life. Believers may not be called to die for others, but they are called to lay down their lives in smaller ways every day: giving time, setting aside preferences, serving, forgiving, and caring for others’ needs.

Finally, these verses encourage believers to listen to Jesus. Friends share what is on their hearts. Jesus has made known to His disciples what He heard from the Father. Believers can grow in friendship with Jesus by listening to His words in Scripture and responding with trust and obedience.

### *John 15:18–19* — If the World Hates You

> *“If the world hates you, you know that it has hated me before it hated you. If you were of the world, the world would love its own. But because you are not of the world, since I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you.”*
>
> — *John 15:18–19* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After speaking about love within the community of disciples, Jesus turned to the opposition they would face. He wanted to prepare them so that they would not be shocked or discouraged.

“*If the world hates you, you know that it has hated me before it hated you*” (*v. 18*). In John’s Gospel, “the world” often refers to humanity organized in rebellion against God. Jesus had experienced this hatred. The religious leaders plotted to kill Him, the crowds turned against Him, and soon He would be crucified. His disciples should expect similar treatment.

The words “it has hated me before it hated you” offer comfort. The disciples would not be alone in their suffering. Jesus had walked the path first.

“*If you were of the world, the world would love its own*” (*v. 19*). If the disciples shared the world’s values and lived like the world, they would be accepted. People tend to welcome those who are like them.

“*But because you are not of the world, since I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you*” (*v. 19*). Jesus had chosen them out of the world. They now belonged to Him. Their new identity, values, and loyalty would set them apart and provoke opposition.

This does not mean that Christians should try to provoke hatred or should assume that every criticism is persecution. Sometimes believers are disliked because of their own unkindness or foolishness. Peter later warned believers not to suffer as wrongdoers, but if they suffer for being Christians, not to be ashamed (*1 Peter 4:15–16*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses reveal the cost of belonging to Christ. Following Jesus means being identified with Him, and that includes sharing in His rejection. Paul writes that “*all who desire to live godly in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution*” (*2 Timothy 3:12*). This is not a sign that something has gone wrong; it is part of what it means to follow a rejected Lord.

They also show the believer’s new identity. Jesus told His disciples, “*I chose you out of the world*” (*v. 19*). They still live in the world and are sent into it (*John 17:18*), but they no longer belong to it. Their identity is rooted in Christ.

Finally, these verses give perspective on suffering for Christ. Jesus said earlier, “*Blessed are you when people reproach you, persecute you, and say all kinds of evil against you falsely, for my sake*” (*Matthew 5:11*). Suffering for His name connects believers with Christ and with the faithful throughout history.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses prepare believers to expect opposition. Many Christians are surprised or discouraged when they face rejection, ridicule, or hostility because of their faith. Jesus’ words remind them that this is not unusual. He experienced it first.

They also encourage believers to examine their lives. If believers are never different from the world around them, it may be because they have absorbed the world’s values. Following Jesus involves living by a different standard, even when that brings misunderstanding.

Finally, these verses call believers to respond to hatred with love. Jesus did not respond to the world’s hatred with hatred. He prayed for those who crucified Him. Believers are called to bless those who persecute them and to continue bearing witness to Christ with gentleness and courage. Around the world today, many Christians face severe persecution; believers can remember them in prayer and stand with them.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*John 15* teaches that the Christian life is a life of union with Christ. Jesus is the vine, and believers are the branches. Fruitfulness does not come from trying harder in human strength but from remaining in Him. Believers can build their lives around staying connected to Jesus through prayer, Scripture, worship, obedience, and fellowship, trusting that His life will flow through them.

The chapter also helps believers understand God’s work in their lives. The Father is a skilled and loving vinedresser who prunes fruitful branches so they bear more fruit. Seasons of difficulty and loss can become times of growth when believers trust Him. Not every hardship is pruning, but God is able to use even painful experiences for good.

*John 15* calls believers to love one another with the self-giving love of Jesus, who laid down His life for His friends. It also offers believers the astonishing privilege of being Jesus’ friends, invited to know His heart and share His purposes. Love for others and friendship with Christ are bound together.

Finally, the chapter prepares believers for opposition. The world hated Jesus, and it may also reject those who follow Him. Believers do not need to be shocked or afraid. They are not alone; the Spirit of truth testifies about Jesus through them. They are called to remain faithful, to love even those who oppose them, and to bear witness to Christ with courage and grace.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, You are the true vine, and I am a branch. Apart from You, I can do nothing. Keep me close to You, and let Your life flow through me so that I bear fruit that glorifies the Father. Father, You are the vinedresser. When You prune me, help me to trust Your skill and Your love, even when it is painful. Thank You, Lord Jesus, for laying down Your life for Your friends, and for calling me Your friend. Teach me to remain in Your love by keeping Your commandments, and fill me with Your joy. Help me to love my brothers and sisters as You have loved me. When the world rejects me because I belong to You, give me courage and keep me from bitterness. Let Your Spirit testify about You through my words and my life. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

John · Chapter 16 of 21

# John — Chapter 16

Chapter Theme: Sorrow Turned to Joy and Peace in a Troubled World

[Read John 16 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/JHN16.htm)

Main Teaching

Jesus warns His disciples that they will face persecution, but He tells them that His going away is for their good, because He will send the Counselor. The Spirit will convict the world about sin, righteousness, and judgment, and will guide the disciples into all truth, glorifying Jesus. Their grief at His death will be like a woman’s labor pains, turning into a joy no one can take away. Jesus closes His farewell teaching with a promise: in the world they will have trouble, but they can take heart, because He has overcome the world.

## Chapter Background and Story

*John 16* completes Jesus’ farewell teaching before His great prayer in chapter 17. The disciples were filled with sorrow (*16:6*). Jesus had told them He was leaving, that the world would hate them, and that one of them would betray Him. Now He explains why His departure is necessary, what the Holy Spirit will do, and how their sorrow will become joy. The chapter ends with a frank prediction that the disciples will abandon Him, followed by one of the most comforting promises in the Bible.

### Warning of Persecution (*16:1–4*)

Jesus said, “*I have said these things to you so that you wouldn’t be caused to stumble*” (*v. 1*). He did not want His disciples to be caught off guard and lose their faith when hard times came. He spoke plainly: “*They will put you out of the synagogues. Yes, the time is coming that whoever kills you will think that he offers service to God*” (*v. 2*).

This prophecy was fulfilled in the early church. Stephen was stoned by religious leaders (*Acts 7*), and Saul of Tarsus persecuted Christians, convinced he was serving God (*Acts 26:9–11*; *Galatians 1:13–14*). Religious zeal without true knowledge of God can become cruel. Jesus explained, “*They will do these things because they have not known the Father nor me*” (*v. 3*).

Jesus had not told them these things at the beginning because He was with them and protected them. Now that He was leaving, they needed to be prepared.

### The Advantage of Jesus’ Departure (*16:5–15*)

The disciples were so overwhelmed with sorrow that they did not even ask where He was going. Jesus told them a surprising truth: His departure was for their benefit, because then He would send the Counselor. This is studied below, together with the Spirit’s work of convicting the world.

Jesus added, “*I still have many things to tell you, but you can’t bear them now*” (*v. 12*). The disciples could not yet understand everything. The Spirit would complete their understanding, guiding them into all truth. This is also studied below.

“*All things that the Father has are mine*” (*v. 15*). The Father, the Son, and the Spirit work together. The Spirit takes what belongs to the Son, which is also the Father’s, and makes it known to believers.

### A Little While (*16:16–24*)

Jesus said, “*A little while, and you will not see me. Again a little while, and you will see me*” (*v. 16*). The disciples were confused and whispered among themselves, “*What is this that he says, ‘A little while’? We don’t know what he is saying*” (*v. 18*). Jesus was referring to His death, when they would not see Him, and His resurrection, when they would see Him again. These events would happen within days.

Jesus explained with the image of childbirth, studied below. He also promised a new relationship in prayer: “*whatever you may ask of the Father in my name, he will give it to you*” (*v. 23*). “*Until now, you have asked nothing in my name. Ask, and you will receive, that your joy may be made full*” (*v. 24*). After the resurrection, the disciples would pray to the Father in Jesus’ name, on the basis of His finished work.

### The Father Himself Loves You (*16:25–33*)

Jesus said that He had been speaking in figures of speech, but the time was coming when He would speak plainly about the Father. Then He said something tender: “*I don’t say to you that I will pray to the Father for you*” (*v. 26*), “*for the Father himself loves you, because you have loved me, and have believed that I came from God*” (*v. 27*). Jesus does intercede for His people (*Romans 8:34*; *Hebrews 7:25*), but He wanted His disciples to know that they did not need to persuade a reluctant Father. The Father Himself loves them.

Jesus summarized His mission in one sentence: “*I came from the Father and have come into the world. Again, I leave the world and go to the Father*” (*v. 28*).

The disciples said that now they understood: “*By this we believe that you came from God*” (*v. 30*). Jesus answered with a gentle but sobering question: “*Do you now believe?*” (*v. 31*) He told them that very soon they would be scattered, each going his own way, and would leave Him alone. “*Yet I am not alone, because the Father is with me*” (*v. 32*). Jesus knew His disciples’ faith was real but weak. He did not reject them; He prepared them. His final words in this section are studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *John 16:7–8* — It Is to Your Advantage That I Go

> *“Nevertheless I tell you the truth: It is to your advantage that I go away; for if I don’t go away, the Counselor won’t come to you. But if I go, I will send him to you. When he has come, he will convict the world about sin, about righteousness, and about judgment;”*
>
> — *John 16:7–8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The disciples were filled with sorrow. Jesus had been their teacher, friend, and Lord for three years. They could not imagine life without Him. Now He was telling them He was going away.

Jesus said something that must have seemed impossible: “*Nevertheless I tell you the truth: It is to your advantage that I go away*” (*v. 7*). How could it be better for them that Jesus would leave? He explained: “*for if I don’t go away, the Counselor won’t come to you. But if I go, I will send him to you*” (*v. 7*).

While Jesus was on earth in His physical body, He could be in only one place at a time. Through the Holy Spirit, His presence would be with all His followers everywhere, at all times. The Spirit would live within each believer. This was a greater gift than having Jesus physically beside them.

Then Jesus described what the Spirit would do in the world: “*When he has come, he will convict the world about sin, about righteousness, and about judgment*” (*v. 8*). The word “convict” means to expose, to prove wrong, or to bring to the point of recognizing guilt. It is the work of a prosecutor who shows the truth of a case.

Jesus explained each part. The Spirit would convict the world “*about sin, because they don’t believe in me*” (*v. 9*). The deepest sin is rejecting Jesus. “*about righteousness, because I am going to my Father*” (*v. 10*). The world judged Jesus as a criminal, but His resurrection and return to the Father would prove that He was righteous. “*about judgment, because the prince of this world has been judged*” (*v. 11*). At the cross, Satan was defeated, and his judgment was sealed.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses reveal the Spirit’s essential role in salvation. No one comes to faith simply by human persuasion. The Spirit opens people’s eyes to their sin, to Christ’s righteousness, and to the reality of judgment. On the day of Pentecost, when Peter preached, the listeners “*were cut to the heart*” (*Acts 2:37*). That was the Spirit’s convicting work.

They also show how the cross and resurrection reverse the world’s verdict. The world declared Jesus guilty; God declared Him righteous by raising Him. The world thought it had defeated Him; in reality, the ruler of the world was defeated. The Spirit brings people to see this truth.

Finally, these verses offer comfort to believers. The Spirit’s presence is an advantage greater than Jesus’ physical presence. Believers are not living in a lesser age, longing for the days when Jesus walked the earth. They have the Spirit of Christ within them.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers in their witness. It is not their job to convict others of sin; that is the Spirit’s work. Believers are called to share the truth about Jesus with love, trusting the Spirit to work in people’s hearts. This frees them from the pressure of trying to force change in others.

They also help believers understand their own experience. Many believers remember a time when they became aware of their sin and their need for Christ. That awareness was the work of the Spirit. When believers feel the Spirit’s conviction today, it is an invitation to turn back to God, not a sign that God has rejected them.

Finally, these verses remind believers of the Spirit’s nearness. They can pray for the Spirit’s help in their witness, their struggles, and their daily walk, confident that He is present with them.

### *John 16:13* — He Will Guide You into All Truth

> *“However, when he, the Spirit of truth, has come, he will guide you into all truth, for he will not speak from himself; but whatever he hears, he will speak. He will declare to you things that are coming.”*
>
> — *John 16:13* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus told His disciples, “*I still have many things to tell you, but you can’t bear them now*” (*v. 12*). There was much more they needed to understand, but they were not yet ready. They had not yet seen the cross or the resurrection, and they had not yet received the Spirit.

Then He promised, “*However, when he, the Spirit of truth, has come, he will guide you into all truth*” (*v. 13*). The Spirit would lead them step by step into a fuller understanding of what Jesus had taught and done. The word “guide” suggests leading someone along a path, like a guide showing travelers the way.

“*for he will not speak from himself; but whatever he hears, he will speak*” (*v. 13*). The Spirit would not bring new teaching that contradicted Jesus. He would speak what He heard from the Father and the Son. His teaching would be in perfect harmony with Jesus’ words.

“*He will declare to you things that are coming*” (*v. 13*). The Spirit would help the disciples understand future events, including the meaning of Jesus’ death and resurrection and the hope of His return.

In the next verse, Jesus summarized the Spirit’s purpose: “*He will glorify me*” (*v. 14*). The Spirit’s work always points to Jesus.

This promise was given first to the apostles. The Spirit guided them to understand and record the truth about Jesus. The New Testament is the fruit of this guidance.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse helps explain the authority of the New Testament. The apostles did not simply remember Jesus’ words by human memory or develop their own theology. The Spirit guided them into all truth. The Gospels, letters, and Revelation preserve this Spirit-guided teaching. Peter writes that prophecy never came by human will, but “*holy men of God spoke, being moved by the Holy Spirit*” (*2 Peter 1:21*).

It also shows that the Spirit continues to illumine believers today. The Spirit does not give new revelation that adds to Scripture, but He helps believers understand and apply the truth Scripture contains. Paul prays that believers would receive “*a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him*” (*Ephesians 1:17*).

Finally, the verse gives a test for discerning spiritual teaching. The Spirit glorifies Jesus and speaks in harmony with His words. Any teaching that contradicts Jesus or draws attention away from Him does not come from the Spirit of truth.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to read Scripture with confidence. The Bible is not a collection of human opinions but the Spirit-guided record of God’s truth. Believers can trust it as their guide for faith and life.

It also invites believers to depend on the Spirit when they read. Understanding Scripture is not only an intellectual task. Believers can ask the Spirit to open their minds and hearts, to show them Jesus, and to help them apply what they read.

Finally, this verse helps believers discern truth in a confusing world. Many voices claim to speak for God. Believers can test them by asking whether they glorify Jesus and agree with His words as revealed in Scripture.

### *John 16:20–22* — Sorrow Turned into Joy

> *“Most certainly I tell you that you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice. You will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will be turned into joy. A woman, when she gives birth, has sorrow because her time has come. But when she has delivered the child, she doesn’t remember the anguish any more, for the joy that a human being is born into the world. Therefore you now have sorrow, but I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy away from you.”*
>
> — *John 16:20–22* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus had told His disciples that in a little while they would not see Him, and then in a little while they would see Him again. They were confused. Jesus explained: “*Most certainly I tell you that you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice*” (*v. 20*). Within hours, Jesus would be arrested and crucified. The disciples would grieve deeply, while His enemies would celebrate what they thought was their victory.

“*You will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will be turned into joy*” (*v. 20*). Jesus did not say that their sorrow would be replaced by something else. He said that the sorrow itself would be turned into joy. The very thing that caused their grief, His death, would become the source of their joy when they understood it through the resurrection.

Then He gave an illustration: “*A woman, when she gives birth, has sorrow because her time has come. But when she has delivered the child, she doesn’t remember the anguish any more, for the joy that a human being is born into the world*” (*v. 21*). Labor pain is real and intense. But it leads to new life, and the joy of holding the child surpasses the memory of the pain.

“*Therefore you now have sorrow, but I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy away from you*” (*v. 22*). Jesus would rise from the dead and see them again. Their joy would be permanent. No one, not their enemies, not persecution, not even death, could take it away.

This promise was fulfilled on Easter Sunday. When Jesus appeared to the disciples, “*The disciples therefore were glad when they saw the Lord*” (*John 20:20*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses reveal the pattern of the gospel: sorrow turned into joy, death turned into life. The cross, the darkest moment in history, became the source of salvation. What looked like defeat became victory.

The image of childbirth is used in the Old Testament for the painful arrival of God’s new age (*Isaiah 26:17–19*; *66:7–14*). Paul also describes creation itself as groaning in labor pains, waiting for the revelation of God’s children (*Romans 8:22*). The sufferings of the present are birth pains leading to the new creation.

Finally, these verses describe the unique nature of Christian joy. It is not dependent on circumstances. It is rooted in the risen Christ, and because He lives forever, the joy He gives cannot be taken away.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses bring hope to believers who are grieving. Sorrow is real, and Jesus does not dismiss it. He said His disciples would weep and lament. But for those who belong to Christ, sorrow is not the final word. God can turn sorrow into joy, sometimes in this life and fully in the life to come.

They also help believers understand suffering as part of a larger story. Like labor pains, some suffering leads to new life. Believers can hold on through painful seasons, trusting that God is bringing something good that is not yet visible.

Finally, these verses encourage believers to anchor their joy in Christ. Joy that depends on circumstances is easily lost. Joy that rests in the risen Lord cannot be taken away. Believers can return again and again to the truth of the resurrection as the foundation of their joy.

### *John 16:33* — I Have Overcome the World

> *“I have told you these things, that in me you may have peace. In the world you have trouble; but cheer up! I have overcome the world.”*
>
> — *John 16:33* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These are the final words of Jesus’ farewell teaching to His disciples. He had just told them that very soon they would be scattered and would abandon Him. Even so, He did not end with a rebuke but with a promise.

“*I have told you these things, that in me you may have peace*” (*v. 33*). Everything Jesus had taught them that evening, about the Father’s house, the way to the Father, the Holy Spirit, the vine and branches, the world’s hatred, and sorrow turned to joy, was meant to give them peace. Notice the words “in me.” Peace is found in Jesus, in union with Him.

“*In the world you have trouble*” (*v. 33*). Jesus did not promise His disciples an easy life. The word “trouble” refers to pressure, affliction, or distress. In the world, believers will face hardship, persecution, sickness, loss, and sorrow. This is a realistic promise.

“*but cheer up! I have overcome the world*” (*v. 33*). “Cheer up” can also be translated “take courage” or “take heart.” Jesus’ disciples can have courage, not because their circumstances are easy, but because Jesus has already won the victory. He spoke in the past tense, “I have overcome,” even though the cross was still ahead. His victory was certain.

Within hours, Jesus would be arrested, beaten, and crucified. To the world, it would look like total defeat. But through His death and resurrection, He would overcome sin, death, and Satan.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse holds together two realities that believers live in: “in me” and “in the world.” In the world, they face trouble. In Christ, they have peace. Both are true at the same time. Christian peace does not deny the reality of trouble; it rests in the deeper reality of Christ’s victory.

It also points to the victory of the cross and resurrection. Jesus overcame the world not by political power or military force but by obedient suffering and death. John later writes, “*This is the victory that has overcome the world: your faith*” (*1 John 5:4*). Believers share in Christ’s victory through faith in Him.

Finally, the verse reveals Jesus’ care for weak disciples. He knew they would fail Him that very night. Yet His final words to them were words of peace and courage. His love did not depend on their strength.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse prepares believers for hardship. Some people expect that following Jesus will make life easy, and they are disillusioned when trouble comes. Jesus was honest: in the world, His people will have trouble. Hardship is not a sign that God has abandoned them.

It also gives believers courage. Whatever troubles believers face, Jesus has overcome the world. Their circumstances do not have the final word. Christ’s victory is greater than any trouble.

Finally, the verse invites believers to seek peace in Christ. When troubles press in, believers can turn to Jesus in prayer, remember His promises, and rest in His victory. Peace is found not by escaping the world but by abiding in Him.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*John 16* prepares believers for a world that may oppose them. Jesus did not hide the cost of following Him. He spoke plainly about persecution so that His disciples would not be shaken when it came. Believers who face rejection or hostility can remember that Jesus warned them in advance, and that this does not mean God has abandoned them.

The chapter also reveals the gift of the Holy Spirit. Jesus said it was better for His disciples that He go away, so that the Spirit could come. The Spirit convicts the world, guides believers into truth, and glorifies Jesus. Believers can depend on the Spirit in their witness, their understanding of Scripture, and their daily walk, trusting that He is present with them.

*John 16* offers hope to those who are grieving. Jesus promised that His disciples’ sorrow would turn into joy, like a mother’s pain giving way to the joy of new life. Believers who mourn can hold on to the hope of the resurrection, knowing that the joy Christ gives cannot be taken away.

Finally, the chapter ends with a promise for every season: in the world there will be trouble, but Jesus has overcome the world. Believers can face hardship with courage and peace, not because life is easy, but because they are in Christ, who has already won the victory. They can also rest in the truth that the Father Himself loves them.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for telling Your disciples the truth about the trouble they would face, and for not leaving them without hope. Thank You for sending the Holy Spirit, who convicts the world, guides Your people into all truth, and glorifies You. Holy Spirit, open my eyes to the truth of Your Word and help me to see Jesus more clearly. When I grieve, remind me that You can turn sorrow into joy, and that the joy You give cannot be taken away. Thank You, Father, that You Yourself love me. When troubles press in, give me Your peace and help me to take courage, because You have overcome the world. Strengthen believers who suffer for Your name, and keep us all faithful until we see You face to face. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
