John · Chapter 17 of 21

# John — Chapter 17

Chapter Theme: The Prayer of Jesus for Himself, His Disciples, and All Who Will Believe

[Read John 17 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/JHN17.htm)

Main Teaching

Before going to the cross, Jesus lifts His eyes to heaven and prays. He asks the Father to glorify the Son so that the Son may glorify Him, and He defines eternal life as knowing the only true God and Jesus Christ whom He sent. He prays for His disciples to be kept from the evil one and made holy by God’s word of truth, and He prays for all future believers to be one, as the Father and the Son are one, so that the world may believe. He ends by asking that His people may be with Him and see His glory.

## Chapter Background and Story

*John 17* is the longest recorded prayer of Jesus. It is often called His High Priestly Prayer, because in it Jesus intercedes for His people as a priest stands before God on behalf of others. Just as the high priest in Israel carried the names of the twelve tribes on his breastplate into God’s presence (*Exodus 28:29*), Jesus brings His disciples, and all who will believe through them, before the Father.

The prayer comes at the end of Jesus’ farewell teaching, after He told His disciples, “I have overcome the world” (*16:33*). Within hours He would be arrested. Yet His prayer is not filled with fear. It is filled with confidence in the Father, love for His disciples, and concern for the glory of God. The disciples, and through John’s Gospel all readers, are allowed to listen as the Son speaks to the Father.

The prayer has three movements: Jesus prays for Himself (*17:1–5*), for His disciples (*17:6–19*), and for all future believers (*17:20–26*).

### Jesus Prays for Himself (*17:1–5*)

“*lifting up his eyes to heaven*” (*v. 1*), a common posture of prayer, Jesus said, “*Father, the time has come. Glorify your Son, that your Son may also glorify you*” (*v. 1*). Throughout John’s Gospel, Jesus’ “hour” or “time” referred to His death, resurrection, and return to the Father. Now it had arrived. Jesus asked to be glorified, not for selfish reasons, but so that He could glorify the Father. His glorification would come through the cross, where God’s love, justice, and saving power would be most fully revealed.

The Father had given the Son “*authority over all flesh*” (*v. 2*), so that He could give eternal life to all whom the Father had given Him. Jesus then defined eternal life, studied below.

“*I glorified you on the earth. I have accomplished the work which you have given me to do*” (*v. 4*). Jesus spoke as though His work were already complete, because He was about to finish it on the cross, where He would say, “It is finished” (*19:30*). Then He asked, “*Now, Father, glorify me with your own self with the glory which I had with you before the world existed*” (*v. 5*). This is a clear statement of Jesus’ eternal existence. Before creation, the Son shared the Father’s glory. In becoming human, He set aside the visible display of that glory. Now He would return to it.

### Jesus Prays for His Disciples (*17:6–19*)

Jesus prayed for the disciples whom the Father had given Him. He said that He had revealed the Father’s name to them, meaning that He had made known who God is. They had received His words and believed that the Father sent Him. Their faith was still weak, and that very night they would scatter, but Jesus spoke of them with confidence and affection.

“*I pray for them. I don’t pray for the world, but for those whom you have given me*” (*v. 9*). This does not mean Jesus did not care for the world; He came to save the world (*3:16–17*), and in verse 21 He prays that the world may believe. But at this moment, He prayed specifically for His disciples, who would face the world without His physical presence.

“*Holy Father, keep them through your name which you have given me, that they may be one, even as we are*” (*v. 11*). Jesus asked the Father to protect them and to keep them united. While He was with them, He had kept them, and none was lost “*except the son of destruction*” (*v. 12*), referring to Judas, whose betrayal fulfilled Scripture (*Psalm 41:9*).

Jesus prayed that His disciples would have His joy made full in them. He had given them the Father’s word, and the world hated them because they did not belong to it. His requests for their protection and holiness are studied below.

“*As you sent me into the world, even so I have sent them into the world*” (*v. 18*). The disciples were not to escape the world but to be sent into it, as Jesus had been. “*For their sakes I sanctify myself, that they themselves also may be sanctified in truth*” (*v. 19*). Jesus “sanctified” or set Himself apart for His sacrificial death, so that His disciples could be set apart for God.

### Jesus Prays for All Believers (*17:20–26*)

Then Jesus’ prayer reached across the centuries: “*Not for these only do I pray, but for those also who will believe in me through their word*” (*v. 20*). Every believer who has come to faith through the apostles’ message, preserved in the New Testament, was included in this prayer. His prayer for unity is studied below.

“*The glory which you have given me, I have given to them, that they may be one, even as we are one*” (*v. 22*). Jesus shares His glory with His people, the glory of being loved by the Father and of reflecting God’s character. The goal again is unity and witness: “*that the world may know that you sent me and loved them, even as you loved me*” (*v. 23*). The Father loves believers with the same love with which He loves His Son.

Jesus’ final requests are studied below. He concluded, “*Righteous Father, the world hasn’t known you, but I knew you; and these knew that you sent me*” (*v. 25*). “*I made known to them your name, and will make it known; that the love with which you loved me may be in them, and I in them*” (*v. 26*). The prayer ends where all of God’s purposes lead: the love of the Father dwelling in His people, and Christ Himself living in them.

## Important Verses Explained

### *John 17:3* — This Is Eternal Life

> *“This is eternal life, that they should know you, the only true God, and him whom you sent, Jesus Christ.”*
>
> — *John 17:3* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

At the beginning of His prayer, Jesus asked the Father to glorify the Son. He explained that the Father had given Him authority to give eternal life to all whom the Father had given Him. Then He defined what eternal life is.

“*This is eternal life, that they should know you, the only true God, and him whom you sent, Jesus Christ*” (*v. 3*). Many people think of eternal life mainly as living forever, an endless length of time after death. Jesus defines it differently. Eternal life is first of all a relationship: knowing God.

The word “know” in Scripture means more than knowing facts. It describes personal, intimate relationship. In the Old Testament, “knowing” God involved trust, love, and covenant faithfulness. To know God is to be in relationship with Him, to experience His love, and to live in fellowship with Him.

Jesus speaks of knowing “*the only true God*” (*v. 3*). In a world filled with many gods and idols, Israel confessed that there is one God (*Deuteronomy 6:4*). Jesus affirms this. He then adds, “*and him whom you sent, Jesus Christ*” (*v. 3*). Knowing God is inseparable from knowing Jesus. The Father is known through the Son He sent.

Because eternal life is knowing God, it begins now, not only after death. Those who know God through Jesus already possess eternal life (*John 5:24*). And because God is eternal, the relationship continues forever.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals that the heart of salvation is relationship with God. Forgiveness, adoption, and eternal life all serve this purpose: to bring people into knowing God. Through Jeremiah, God promised that in the new covenant, “*they will all know me, from their least to their greatest*” (*Jeremiah 31:34*). Jesus fulfills this promise.

It also shows the unity and distinction of the Father and the Son. Jesus speaks of “the only true God” and of Himself as the One sent. Yet knowing God involves knowing both. Elsewhere in John, Jesus says that whoever has seen Him has seen the Father (*14:9*). The Father and the Son are distinct, yet one.

Finally, the verse reveals the quality of eternal life. It is not merely endless existence, which could be a burden, but life filled with the presence and love of God. Eternal life is the life of God shared with His people.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to see their faith as a relationship, not merely a set of beliefs or rules. Christianity is about knowing God through Jesus Christ. Believers can grow in this relationship through prayer, Scripture, worship, obedience, and fellowship with other believers.

It also encourages believers to enjoy eternal life now. Eternal life is not only a future hope but a present reality. Every day, believers can experience the presence, love, and guidance of God.

Finally, the verse gives purpose to all spiritual activity. Bible study, church attendance, and service can become routine. Their true purpose is to know God more deeply. Believers can approach each practice with the desire to know the Father and the Son.

### *John 17:15–17* — Kept from the Evil One, Sanctified by the Truth

> *“I pray not that you would take them from the world, but that you would keep them from the evil one. They are not of the world, even as I am not of the world. Sanctify them in your truth. Your word is truth.”*
>
> — *John 17:15–17* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus was praying for His disciples, who would soon face the world without His physical presence. He had told them that the world hated them because they did not belong to it. One might expect Him to ask the Father to take them out of the world to protect them. Instead, He prayed, “*I pray not that you would take them from the world, but that you would keep them from the evil one*” (*v. 15*).

Jesus did not want His disciples to escape the world. They had a mission there. Instead, He asked that they would be protected from Satan, the evil one, who would try to destroy their faith, divide them, and draw them away from God.

“*They are not of the world, even as I am not of the world*” (*v. 16*). The disciples lived in the world but no longer belonged to it. Their identity, values, and loyalty were now rooted in God.

“*Sanctify them in your truth. Your word is truth*” (*v. 17*). To “sanctify” means to set apart for God, to make holy. Jesus asked the Father to make His disciples holy, and He named the means: God’s truth, which is His word.

God’s word is not merely true; it is truth itself, the reliable revelation of reality. Through His word, God shapes His people’s minds, hearts, and lives, making them more like Him.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses describe the Christian’s position in the world. Believers are “in the world” but “not of the world.” They are not to withdraw from the world in isolation, nor to be absorbed into it. They are to live in the world as people who belong to God, bringing His light into dark places.

They also reveal the means of spiritual growth. God sanctifies His people through His word. Paul writes that all Scripture is inspired by God and is profitable for teaching, reproof, correction, and instruction in righteousness (*2 Timothy 3:16–17*). As believers receive and obey God’s word, they are transformed.

Finally, these verses show the reality of spiritual warfare. Jesus prayed for protection from the evil one because the enemy is real and active. But believers are not left defenseless. Jesus Himself prays for them, and the Father keeps them.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to engage with the world rather than retreating from it. Christians are called to live faithfully in their workplaces, schools, neighborhoods, and communities, bringing the presence of Christ into every area of life.

They also call believers to stay rooted in God’s word. Living in the world without being shaped by it requires a steady diet of truth. Believers can make Scripture a regular part of their lives, allowing it to shape their thinking and choices.

Finally, these verses offer comfort in the face of spiritual attack. Believers may feel the pull of temptation, discouragement, or doubt. They can take heart that Jesus prayed for their protection from the evil one, and that He continues to intercede for them (*Hebrews 7:25*).

### *John 17:20–21* — That They May All Be One

> *“Not for these only do I pray, but for those also who will believe in me through their word, that they may all be one; even as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be one in us; that the world may believe that you sent me.”*
>
> — *John 17:20–21* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After praying for His disciples, Jesus extended His prayer to include all who would believe in Him in the future: “*Not for these only do I pray, but for those also who will believe in me through their word*” (*v. 20*). The apostles would preach and write about Jesus, and through their message, people in every generation would come to faith. Jesus prayed for all of them, including believers today.

His central request for them was this: “*that they may all be one*” (*v. 21*). Jesus prayed for the unity of His followers. He knew that the church would include people of many nations, cultures, and backgrounds. He prayed that they would be united.

He described the kind of unity He meant: “*even as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be one in us*” (*v. 21*). The model for Christian unity is the relationship between the Father and the Son: a relationship of love, mutual indwelling, and shared purpose. This is not a mere organizational unity but a deep spiritual oneness rooted in God Himself.

Then He gave the purpose: “*that the world may believe that you sent me*” (*v. 21*). The unity of believers is a witness to the world. When people see Christians from different backgrounds loving one another and living in harmony, it points to the truth of the gospel.

This unity does not mean that all believers must be identical. The Father and the Son are distinct Persons, yet perfectly one. Christian unity includes diversity.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This prayer reveals how deeply Jesus cares about the unity of His people. On the night before His death, one of His central prayers was that His followers would be one. Divisions among Christians grieve the heart of Christ.

It also shows that Christian unity is a gift and a calling. It is a gift because believers are already united in Christ through the Spirit. Paul urges believers to “*keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace*” (*Ephesians 4:3*). Believers do not create unity; they preserve and express what God has given.

Finally, the prayer connects unity with mission. The world’s belief in Jesus is linked to the unity of His followers. Division weakens the church’s witness; unity strengthens it.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This prayer challenges believers to pursue unity with other Christians. Churches and believers often divide over secondary issues, preferences, or personalities. Jesus calls His people to love one another, to seek reconciliation, and to work together for the gospel.

It also encourages humility. Believers in different traditions may disagree about important matters, and the prayer does not require pretending that truth does not matter, since Jesus has just prayed for His people to be sanctified in the truth. But it does call believers to recognize one another as members of the same family, to speak of one another with charity, and to cooperate where they can.

Finally, the prayer reminds believers that their relationships with one another are a witness to the world. The way Christians treat each other in families, churches, and communities can either draw people to Christ or push them away.

### *John 17:24* — That They May Be with Me and See My Glory

> *“Father, I desire that they also whom you have given me be with me where I am, that they may see my glory which you have given me, for you loved me before the foundation of the world.”*
>
> — *John 17:24* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Near the end of His prayer, Jesus expressed His deepest desire for His people: “*Father, I desire that they also whom you have given me be with me where I am*” (*v. 24*). Jesus wanted His followers to be with Him. This echoes His promise in *John 14:3*, where He said He would come again and take them to Himself so that where He is, they may be also.

“*that they may see my glory which you have given me*” (*v. 24*). Jesus wanted His followers to see His glory. During His earthly ministry, His glory was partly hidden. The disciples saw glimpses of it in His miracles, His transfiguration, and His love. But Jesus wanted them to see His glory fully, in heaven.

“*for you loved me before the foundation of the world*” (*v. 24*). The glory Jesus has is rooted in the eternal love of the Father for the Son. Before the world was created, the Father loved the Son. That love is the source of Jesus’ glory.

Notice the tone of this request. Jesus does not say, “I would like,” but “I desire.” It is a strong expression of His will. Jesus truly wants His people with Him.

This verse reveals that heaven is not merely a place of rest or reward. Its greatest joy is being with Jesus and beholding His glory.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals the heart of Jesus for His people. He does not merely tolerate them; He desires them to be with Him forever. The Bible ends with the same vision: “*Behold, God’s dwelling is with people*” (*Revelation 21:3*). The goal of salvation is eternal fellowship with God.

It also shows the eternal love within God. The Father loved the Son “before the foundation of the world.” Love did not begin with creation; it has always existed within the Triune God. Believers are invited to share in this eternal love (*17:26*).

Finally, the verse shapes the hope of believers. Paul writes that to depart and be with Christ is “*far better*” (*Philippians 1:23*). The hope of seeing Christ’s glory gives believers courage to face suffering and death.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse gives believers assurance of Jesus’ love. He wants them to be with Him. Believers who struggle with feelings of unworthiness can rest in the fact that Jesus Himself prayed for them to be with Him forever.

It also shapes how believers think about heaven. The center of heaven is not mansions or streets of gold but Jesus Himself. Believers can cultivate a longing for Him now by spending time in His presence through prayer and worship.

Finally, the verse brings comfort in grief. When believers lose loved ones who trusted in Christ, they can know that Jesus’ prayer has been answered for them: they are with Him, seeing His glory.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*John 17* lets believers listen to Jesus pray for them. Before going to the cross, He prayed for Himself, His disciples, and all who would believe through their message. This prayer reveals the heart of Christ for His people. Believers can take great comfort in knowing that Jesus prayed for them then and continues to intercede for them now.

The chapter defines eternal life as knowing God through Jesus Christ. This invites believers to treat their faith as a living relationship rather than a set of routines. Prayer, Scripture, worship, and obedience are all means of knowing God more deeply. Eternal life begins now and continues forever.

*John 17* also describes how believers are to live in the world: not removed from it, but not belonging to it either. They are sent into the world as Jesus was sent, kept by the Father from the evil one, and sanctified by God’s word of truth. Staying rooted in Scripture helps believers live faithfully in a world that often pulls them in other directions.

Finally, the chapter reveals Jesus’ deep desire for the unity of His people and for their eternal fellowship with Him. Christian unity, rooted in the love between the Father and the Son, is a powerful witness to the world. Believers are called to pursue love and harmony with other Christians, and to live with the hope of one day being with Jesus and seeing His glory.

## Chapter Prayer

Holy Father, thank You for the prayer Your Son prayed for His disciples and for all who would believe through their word, including me. Thank You that eternal life is knowing You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom You sent. Help me to know You more deeply each day. Keep me from the evil one, and sanctify me by Your truth, for Your word is truth. As You sent Jesus into the world, send me into my everyday world to live for You. Make Your people one, as You and the Son are one, so that the world may believe. Forgive us for our divisions, and teach us to love one another. Lord Jesus, thank You for desiring that I be with You and see Your glory. Fill me with that hope, and let the Father’s love for You dwell in me. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

John · Chapter 18 of 21

# John — Chapter 18

Chapter Theme: The King Who Gives Himself Up: Arrest, Denial, and Trial before Pilate

[Read John 18 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/JHN18.htm)

Main Teaching

In a garden across the Kidron Valley, Jesus steps forward to meet the soldiers who come to arrest Him, and at His words “I am he” they fall to the ground. He protects His disciples, tells Peter to put away his sword, and willingly drinks the cup the Father has given Him. While Jesus is questioned by Annas, Peter denies Him three times. Before Pilate, Jesus declares that His kingdom is not of this world and that He came to testify to the truth, yet the crowd chooses Barabbas instead.

## Chapter Background and Story

*John 18* begins the account of Jesus’ suffering and death, often called the Passion narrative. Matthew, Mark, and Luke also tell this story, and John’s account agrees with them in its main events. But John includes details the others do not mention, such as the soldiers falling to the ground, the name of the servant Malchus, the hearing before Annas, and a longer conversation between Jesus and Pilate. Throughout, John emphasizes that Jesus is not a helpless victim. He goes to the cross in full control, as the King who gives His life willingly.

The arrest in Gethsemane, Peter’s denial, and the trial before Pilate are also studied in *Matthew 26–27*, *Mark 14–15*, and *Luke 22–23*. The studies below focus on what John especially highlights.

### The Arrest in the Garden (*18:1–11*)

After His prayer, Jesus crossed the Kidron Valley, east of Jerusalem, to a garden on the slope of the Mount of Olives. The other Gospels call it Gethsemane. John notes that “*Jesus often met there with his disciples*” (*v. 2*), so Judas knew where to find Him. Jesus did not hide.

Judas came with “*a detachment of soldiers and officers from the chief priests and the Pharisees*” (*v. 3*). The word “detachment” usually refers to a Roman cohort, which could include several hundred soldiers, although only part of it may have come. The officers were the temple police. They carried lanterns, torches, and weapons, as if hunting a dangerous criminal hiding in the dark. Ironically, they came with lamps to find the Light of the world.

John writes that Jesus, “*knowing all the things that were happening to him*” (*v. 4*), went out to meet them. The encounter that followed is studied below.

Jesus asked the soldiers to let His disciples go. John comments that this fulfilled Jesus’ words: “*Of those whom you have given me, I have lost none*” (*v. 9*) (*John 17:12*). Even at His arrest, the Good Shepherd protected His sheep.

Then Simon Peter drew a sword and struck the high priest’s servant, cutting off his right ear. Only John names the servant, “*Malchus*” (*v. 10*), and only John names Peter as the one who struck. (Peter’s sword and Jesus’ response are studied at *Matthew 26:52*, and Luke tells us that Jesus healed the servant’s ear.) Jesus said to Peter, “*Put the sword into its sheath. The cup which the Father has given me, shall I not surely drink it?*” (*v. 11*) This is studied below.

### Before Annas, and Peter’s First Denial (*18:12–18*)

The soldiers seized Jesus and bound Him. They took Him first to Annas, the father-in-law of Caiaphas. Annas had been high priest from A.D. 6 to 15 and had been removed by the Romans, but he remained enormously influential. Five of his sons, as well as his son-in-law Caiaphas, served as high priest. Many Jews still regarded him as the rightful high priest. John reminds readers that Caiaphas was the one who had advised that “*it was expedient that one man should perish for the people*” (*v. 14*) (*11:50*).

Simon Peter and “*another disciple*” (*v. 15*) followed Jesus. This other disciple, who was known to the high priest, is often identified as John himself, though he does not name himself. He went into the courtyard and spoke to the woman at the door, who let Peter in.

The servant girl at the door asked Peter, “*Are you also one of this man’s disciples?*” (*v. 17*) Peter answered, “*I am not*” (*v. 17*). Inside the courtyard, it was cold, and the servants and officers had made a charcoal fire. Peter stood with them, warming himself. This charcoal fire will be echoed in *John 21:9*, where the risen Jesus restores Peter beside another charcoal fire.

### Jesus Questioned by Annas (*18:19–24*)

Annas questioned Jesus about His disciples and His teaching. Jesus answered, “*I spoke openly to the world. I always taught in synagogues and in the temple, where the Jews always meet. I said nothing in secret*” (*v. 20*). Under Jewish law, an accused person was not required to testify against himself; the case had to be established by witnesses. Jesus pointed Annas to the people who had heard Him: “*Ask those who have heard me what I said to them*” (*v. 21*).

One of the officers slapped Jesus: “*Do you answer the high priest like that?*” (*v. 22*) Jesus replied calmly, “*If I have spoken evil, testify of the evil; but if well, why do you beat me?*” (*v. 23*) Jesus did not respond with violence or insults, but He also did not pretend that the injustice was right. He named the wrong and asked for justice. Annas then sent Him, still bound, to Caiaphas.

### Peter’s Second and Third Denials (*18:25–27*)

Meanwhile, Peter was still warming himself by the fire. Others asked him, “*You aren’t also one of his disciples, are you?*” (*v. 25*) He denied it again: “*I am not*” (*v. 25*). Then a relative of Malchus, the man whose ear Peter had cut off, said, “*Didn’t I see you in the garden with him?*” (*v. 26*) Peter denied it a third time, “*and immediately the rooster crowed*” (*v. 27*).

Notice the contrast John creates. In the garden, Jesus said, “I am he.” In the courtyard, Peter said, “I am not.” Jesus faced His accusers with courage and truth; Peter, afraid, denied his Lord. Peter’s grief is studied at *Mark 14:72*, and his restoration will come in *John 21*.

### Jesus before Pilate (*18:28–40*)

Early in the morning, the leaders brought Jesus from Caiaphas to the Praetorium, the Roman governor’s headquarters in Jerusalem. John notes a striking irony: “*they themselves didn’t enter into the Praetorium, that they might not be defiled, but might eat the Passover*” (*v. 28*). Entering a Gentile’s house would make them ritually unclean and unable to celebrate the feast. They were careful about ritual purity while plotting the death of an innocent man.

Pilate, the Roman governor of Judea from A.D. 26 to 36, came out to them and asked, “*What accusation do you bring against this man?*” (*v. 29*) They avoided a direct answer: “*If this man weren’t an evildoer, we wouldn’t have delivered him up to you*” (*v. 30*). When Pilate told them to judge Him themselves, they replied, “*It is illegal for us to put anyone to death*” (*v. 31*). Under Roman rule, Jewish courts generally could not carry out the death penalty. John sees this as fulfilling Jesus’ prediction that He would be “lifted up” (*12:32–33*), since crucifixion was a Roman form of execution, while Jewish execution was usually by stoning.

Pilate went back inside and asked Jesus, “*Are you the King of the Jews?*” (*v. 33*) Jesus asked whether Pilate was asking on his own or because others had told him. Pilate answered, “*I’m not a Jew, am I? Your own nation and the chief priests delivered you to me. What have you done?*” (*v. 35*) Jesus’ answer about His kingdom, and Pilate’s question about truth, are studied below.

Pilate went out and declared, “*I find no basis for a charge against him*” (*v. 38*). He offered to release Jesus under the custom of releasing a prisoner at Passover. But the crowd shouted, “*Not this man, but Barabbas!*” (*v. 40*) John adds, “*Now Barabbas was a robber*” (*v. 40*). The word can also describe a violent rebel; Mark says Barabbas had committed murder in an uprising (*Mark 15:7*). The crowd chose a man of violence over the King of peace. The guilty man went free, and the innocent One was condemned in his place, a vivid picture of what Jesus’ death would accomplish.

## Important Verses Explained

### *John 18:4–6* — “I Am He”

> *“Jesus therefore, knowing all the things that were happening to him, went out and said to them, ‘Who are you looking for?’ They answered him, ‘Jesus of Nazareth.’ Jesus said to them, ‘I am he.’ Judas also, who betrayed him, was standing with them. When therefore he said to them, ‘I am he,’ they went backward and fell to the ground.”*
>
> — *John 18:4–6* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus had just finished praying with His disciples and had crossed the Kidron Valley to a garden where He often went. Judas, who knew the place, arrived with soldiers and temple officers carrying torches and weapons. They expected to search for Jesus in the dark garden.

But John says, “*Jesus therefore, knowing all the things that were happening to him, went out and said to them, “Who are you looking for?”*” (*v. 4*) Jesus did not hide or run. He stepped forward and took the initiative. He knew everything that would happen to Him, the betrayal, the trials, the beatings, the cross, and still He went out to meet them.

They answered, “*Jesus of Nazareth*” (*v. 5*). Jesus said, “*I am he*” (*v. 5*). In Greek, these words are literally “I am,” the same words Jesus had used in His great “I am” sayings, and especially when He said, “before Abraham came into existence, I AM” (*8:58*). John notes that Judas was standing with the soldiers, on the side of those who came to arrest Him.

Then something remarkable happened: “*When therefore he said to them, “I am he,” they went backward and fell to the ground*” (*v. 6*). The armed soldiers and officers, who had come to seize Jesus, were overwhelmed. They stepped back and fell down.

Jesus asked them again whom they were looking for, and again told them, “I am he.” Then He asked them to let His disciples go. He gave Himself up, but on His own terms, protecting His followers.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This scene reveals that Jesus went to the cross voluntarily. He had said, “*No one takes it away from me, but I lay it down by myself*” (*John 10:18*). The soldiers’ falling to the ground showed that they had no power over Him unless He allowed it. Jesus could have walked away, but He chose to be arrested.

It also reveals Jesus’ divine identity. The words “I am” echo God’s name revealed to Moses. When the soldiers heard them, they fell back, as people in Scripture often fell before the presence of God (*Ezekiel 1:28*; *Daniel 10:9*). For a moment, the divine majesty of Jesus was revealed.

Finally, the scene shows Jesus’ care for His disciples. Even as He was arrested, He thought of them: “let these go their way.” The Good Shepherd laid down His life for the sheep, beginning by stepping between them and danger.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage assures believers that Jesus was never a helpless victim. His suffering and death were a deliberate act of love. Believers can trust that the One who gave Himself for them did so willingly and with full knowledge of what it would cost.

It also reminds believers that Jesus is in control even in the darkest moments. The arrest looked like the triumph of evil, but Jesus was fulfilling the Father’s plan. When believers face situations that seem out of control, they can trust that Christ is still Lord.

Finally, the scene encourages believers to face difficulties with courage. Jesus went out to meet what was coming rather than running from it. With His strength, believers can face hard things honestly, trusting God’s purposes.

### *John 18:11* — The Cup the Father Has Given

> *“Jesus therefore said to Peter, ‘Put the sword into its sheath. The cup which the Father has given me, shall I not surely drink it?’”*
>
> — *John 18:11* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

When the soldiers came to arrest Jesus, Peter tried to defend Him. He drew a sword and struck the high priest’s servant, Malchus, cutting off his right ear. Peter had promised that he would lay down his life for Jesus (*13:37*), and he meant it. He was ready to fight.

But Jesus said to him, “*Put the sword into its sheath*” (*v. 11*). Jesus did not want His disciples to fight for Him. Earlier in the evening He had shown them the way of humble service, not violence.

Then He explained why: “*The cup which the Father has given me, shall I not surely drink it?*” (*v. 11*) In the Old Testament, a “cup” often symbolized a person’s destiny, especially suffering or God’s judgment (*Psalm 75:8*; *Isaiah 51:17*). In Gethsemane, the other Gospels record Jesus praying for the cup to pass from Him if possible, yet submitting to the Father’s will (studied at *Mark 14:36*). Now, in John, He speaks with settled resolve. He would drink the cup.

Notice that Jesus describes the cup as one “*which the Father has given me*” (*v. 11*). His suffering was not simply the result of human evil, though human evil was involved. It was part of the Father’s plan for salvation. Jesus trusted His Father even in giving Him this cup.

Peter’s way was the way of the sword. Jesus’ way was the way of the cross.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals Jesus’ perfect obedience to the Father. He had come to do the Father’s will (*John 6:38*), and now He would complete it by drinking the cup of suffering. Paul writes that Jesus “*humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross*” (*Philippians 2:8*).

The cup also represents the judgment that sin deserves. Jesus would drink the cup of God’s wrath against sin so that His people would not have to. Through His suffering, He would offer them the cup of salvation (*Psalm 116:13*) and the cup of the new covenant in His blood (*Luke 22:20*).

Finally, the verse shows that God’s kingdom does not advance by violence. Peter wanted to defend Jesus with a sword. But Jesus’ victory would come through self-sacrifice. His followers are called to the same way, overcoming evil with good.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to trust God when He allows them to face suffering. There may be times when believers are given a “cup” they would never have chosen: illness, loss, or hardship. Jesus’ example shows that it is possible to receive such a cup with trust in the Father’s love and purposes. This does not mean that every suffering is God’s direct will, or that believers should not seek relief or justice, but it does mean that God can be trusted within it.

It also challenges believers to reject violence as a means of advancing Christ’s cause. Throughout history, some have tried to defend or spread the faith by force. Jesus told Peter to put away his sword. His kingdom advances through truth, love, and self-giving.

Finally, the verse invites deep gratitude. Jesus drank the cup of suffering and judgment in the place of His people. Believers can thank Him for His willingness to suffer for them, and can respond with lives of love and obedience.

### *John 18:36* — My Kingdom Is Not of This World

> *“Jesus answered, ‘My Kingdom is not of this world. If my Kingdom were of this world, then my servants would fight, that I wouldn’t be delivered to the Jews. But now my Kingdom is not from here.’”*
>
> — *John 18:36* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus was standing before Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor. The religious leaders had brought Him to Pilate, hoping Rome would execute Him. Pilate’s main concern was whether Jesus was a political threat. He asked, “*Are you the King of the Jews?*” (*v. 33*) If Jesus claimed to be a king, He might be leading a rebellion against Caesar.

Jesus answered, “*My Kingdom is not of this world*” (*v. 36*). Jesus did not deny that He was a king. But His kingdom was different from the kingdoms Pilate knew. It did not come from the world, and it did not operate by the world’s methods.

He explained: “*If my Kingdom were of this world, then my servants would fight, that I wouldn’t be delivered to the Jews*” (*v. 36*). Earthly kings defend their power with armies. If Jesus were that kind of king, His followers would have fought to prevent His arrest. In fact, when Peter tried to fight, Jesus stopped him.

“*But now my Kingdom is not from here*” (*v. 36*). Jesus’ kingdom comes from God. Its source, authority, and character are heavenly.

“Not of this world” does not mean that Jesus’ kingdom has nothing to do with this world. Jesus’ kingdom affects every part of life, and one day it will fill the whole earth. But it does not originate in human power, and it does not advance by violence or political force.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals the nature of God’s kingdom. It is a kingdom of truth, love, and righteousness, ruled by a King who gives His life for His people. Its power is not the power of armies but the power of God’s Spirit. Paul writes that “*God’s Kingdom is not eating and drinking, but righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit*” (*Romans 14:17*).

It also shows the irony of the trial. Pilate represented the mightiest empire of the day, yet he stood before the true King of all. Rome would eventually fall, but Jesus’ kingdom would endure forever. Daniel had foreseen a kingdom set up by God that “*will never be destroyed*” (*Daniel 2:44*).

Finally, the verse clarifies the relationship between Christ’s kingdom and earthly governments. Christians are called to respect earthly authorities (*Romans 13:1–7*) and to seek the good of their communities. But their highest allegiance is to Christ, whose kingdom is not identical to any nation or political party.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse helps believers keep their priorities clear. It is easy to place hope in political leaders, parties, or movements. Christians may rightly engage in public life and work for justice, but they must remember that Christ’s kingdom is not built by human power. Their deepest hope rests in Him.

It also challenges believers to advance Christ’s cause by His methods. Jesus’ kingdom grows through truth spoken in love, through service, through faithful witness, and through the work of the Spirit, not through coercion, manipulation, or force.

Finally, the verse gives believers a sense of security. Earthly kingdoms rise and fall. Political situations change. But the kingdom of Christ cannot be shaken. Believers belong to a kingdom that will last forever.

### *John 18:37–38* — Testifying to the Truth

> *“Pilate therefore said to him, ‘Are you a king then?’ Jesus answered, ‘You say that I am a king. For this reason I have been born, and for this reason I have come into the world, that I should testify to the truth. Everyone who is of the truth listens to my voice.’ Pilate said to him, ‘What is truth?’ When he had said this, he went out again to the Jews, and said to them, I find no basis for a charge against him.”*
>
> — *John 18:37–38* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus had just told Pilate that His kingdom was not of this world. Pilate pressed further: “*Are you a king then?*” (*v. 37*) Jesus answered, “*You say that I am a king*” (*v. 37*), a way of acknowledging that Pilate’s words were correct while also suggesting that Pilate did not understand what kind of king He was.

Then Jesus explained His mission: “*For this reason I have been born, and for this reason I have come into the world, that I should testify to the truth*” (*v. 37*). Jesus came not to conquer territory but to bear witness to the truth, the truth about God, about humanity, about sin and salvation. Notice that He speaks of both being “born” and “coming into the world.” His birth was not His beginning; He came into the world from the Father.

“*Everyone who is of the truth listens to my voice*” (*v. 37*). Those who belong to the truth recognize Jesus’ voice. This echoes His words about the Good Shepherd: “My sheep hear my voice” (*10:27*). Jesus was inviting Pilate to listen.

Pilate responded, “*What is truth?*” (*v. 38*) We do not know Pilate’s tone. He may have spoken cynically, dismissing the idea that anyone could know the truth. He may have been weary of religious arguments, or politically calculating. What is clear is that he did not wait for an answer. He immediately went out to the crowd.

The irony is striking. Pilate asked “What is truth?” while standing face to face with the One who had said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (*14:6*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This passage shows that truth is ultimately personal. Truth is not merely a set of ideas but is revealed in Jesus Christ. John’s Gospel began by describing the Word made flesh as “*full of grace and truth*” (*John 1:14*). To know the truth is to know Jesus.

It also reveals the human tendency to avoid truth. Pilate asked the right question but did not stay for the answer. Many people are similar. They ask big questions about truth and meaning, but they do not want to face the answers if those answers would require change. Pilate’s political interests and fear of the crowd kept him from following the truth he had glimpsed.

Finally, the passage shows that Jesus’ kingship is exercised through truth. He rules not by force but by bearing witness to the truth and calling people to listen to His voice. Those who belong to the truth respond to Him.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage speaks to a world that often doubts whether truth can be known. Many people today echo Pilate’s question, “What is truth?” Believers can point them to Jesus, who is the truth and who testified to it. The answer to the question of truth is found in a Person.

It also challenges believers to listen to Jesus’ voice. Being “of the truth” means listening to Him and responding to what He says. Believers can examine whether they are truly listening to Jesus or, like Pilate, asking questions without wanting the answers.

Finally, the passage calls believers to bear witness to the truth as Jesus did. In a world of confusion and competing claims, believers are called to speak the truth about Christ with clarity, humility, and love, trusting that those who are of the truth will listen.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*John 18* shows that Jesus went to the cross willingly. He stepped forward to meet those who came to arrest Him, protected His disciples, and chose to drink the cup the Father had given Him. Believers can take deep comfort in knowing that His love for them was deliberate and complete. He was never a helpless victim, but the King who gave Himself for His people.

The chapter also offers both warning and hope through Peter’s denials. Peter had been bold in the garden, but in the courtyard, fear led him to deny Jesus three times. Believers can be strong in one moment and weak in the next. Yet John’s Gospel does not end with Peter’s failure; the same Jesus who foresaw his denial would restore him. Those who have failed the Lord can find hope that He does not abandon them.

*John 18* reveals the nature of Christ’s kingdom. It is not of this world, and it does not advance by the sword. Believers are called to follow Jesus’ way of truth, love, and self-sacrifice rather than relying on force or political power. Their highest hope is not in any earthly government but in the King whose kingdom will never end.

Finally, the chapter confronts readers with Pilate’s question: “What is truth?” Pilate turned away from the answer standing before him. Each person must decide whether they will listen to Jesus’ voice. Those who belong to the truth will hear Him and follow Him, even when it is costly.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for stepping forward in the garden and giving Yourself up for me. Thank You for protecting Your disciples, and for drinking the cup the Father gave You, so that I could receive the cup of salvation. When I face suffering I did not choose, help me to trust the Father as You did. Forgive me for the times I have denied You through my words, my silence, or my fear, and thank You that You restore those who fail. Teach me the ways of Your kingdom, which is not of this world. Keep me from trusting in power, force, or human approval, and help me to follow Your way of truth and love. You are the truth. Let me listen to Your voice, and give me courage to bear witness to You in a world that asks, “What is truth?” In Jesus’ name, Amen.

John · Chapter 19 of 21

# John — Chapter 19

Chapter Theme: Behold Your King: The Crucifixion and the Finished Work

[Read John 19 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/JHN19.htm)

Main Teaching

Pilate has Jesus flogged and presents Him to the crowd crowned with thorns, but the leaders demand His crucifixion, and Pilate, though convinced of His innocence, hands Him over. Jesus carries His cross to Golgotha, where He is crucified under a sign proclaiming Him King of the Jews in three languages. From the cross, He entrusts His mother to the beloved disciple, fulfills Scripture, and cries, “It is finished!” before giving up His spirit. Blood and water flow from His pierced side, and two secret disciples, Joseph and Nicodemus, give Him an honorable burial in a new tomb in a garden.

## Chapter Background and Story

*John 19* records the crucifixion of Jesus, the event toward which the whole Gospel has been moving. From the beginning, John the Baptist called Jesus “the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world” (*1:29*). Jesus spoke of being “lifted up” (*3:14*; *12:32*) and of His “hour” (*2:4*; *12:23*; *13:1*). Now the hour has come.

John tells the story as an eyewitness, the only one of the Twelve recorded as standing at the cross (*19:26*, 35). He emphasizes three themes throughout: Jesus is the true King, even as He is mocked and crucified; Jesus fulfills Scripture in detail; and Jesus dies as the Passover Lamb at the very time the Passover lambs were being prepared. Other aspects of the crucifixion are studied at *Matthew 27*, *Mark 15*, and *Luke 23*.

### “Behold, the Man!” (*19:1–7*)

Pilate had Jesus flogged. Roman flogging was brutal, done with a whip of leather straps embedded with pieces of bone or metal. It tore the skin and could even kill. Pilate may have hoped that this punishment would satisfy the crowd and allow him to release Jesus.

The soldiers mocked Jesus as a king. They twisted thorns into a crown, put a purple robe on Him, the color of royalty, and kept saying, “*Hail, King of the Jews!*” (*v. 3*) while slapping Him. Pilate brought Jesus out and said, “*Behold, I bring him out to you, that you may know that I find no basis for a charge against him*” (*v. 4*). Then: “*Behold, the man!*” (*v. 5*) Pilate perhaps meant to show the crowd a pitiful, beaten figure who posed no threat. But John’s readers hear a deeper meaning: here is the true Man, the Son of Man, the One in whom God’s purpose for humanity is fulfilled, suffering for humanity.

The chief priests and officers shouted, “*Crucify! Crucify!*” (*v. 6*) Pilate, for the third time in John’s account, declared that he found no basis for a charge. The leaders then revealed their real accusation: “*We have a law, and by our law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God*” (*v. 7*). *Leviticus 24:16* commanded death for blasphemy.

### Power from Above (*19:8–16*)

“*When therefore Pilate heard this saying, he was more afraid*” (*v. 8*). Romans were superstitious about divine beings, and Pilate’s wife had warned him about a dream concerning Jesus (*Matthew 27:19*). Pilate went back inside and asked Jesus, “*Where are you from?*” (*v. 9*) Jesus gave no answer. Pilate grew frustrated and reminded Jesus of his power. Jesus’ reply is studied below.

From then on Pilate tried to release Him, but the leaders played their strongest card: “*If you release this man, you aren’t Caesar’s friend! Everyone who makes himself a king speaks against Caesar!*” (*v. 12*) “Friend of Caesar” was an honorary title for loyal officials. A report to Emperor Tiberius that Pilate had released a rival king could end Pilate’s career, or his life.

Pilate brought Jesus out and sat on the judgment seat at a place called the Stone Pavement, Gabbatha in Aramaic. John notes the time: “*it was the Preparation Day of the Passover, at about the sixth hour*” (*v. 14*), around noon. This was the time when the Passover lambs began to be slaughtered in the temple. Pilate said, “*Behold, your King!*” (*v. 14*) The crowd shouted, “*Away with him! Away with him! Crucify him!*” (*v. 15*) Pilate asked, “*Shall I crucify your King?*” (*v. 15*) The chief priests answered, “*We have no king but Caesar!*” (*v. 15*) It was a shocking statement. Israel’s faith confessed that God alone was their true King (*Judges 8:23*; *1 Samuel 8:7*). In rejecting Jesus, the leaders declared their allegiance to a pagan emperor. Pilate handed Jesus over to be crucified. (Pilate’s decision is studied at *Mark 15:15*.)

### The Crucifixion (*19:17–24*)

Jesus went out “*bearing his cross*” (*v. 17*) to the place called the Place of a Skull, Golgotha in Aramaic (Calvary, from the Latin word for skull). The other Gospels tell us that Simon of Cyrene was forced to carry the cross for part of the way. John emphasizes that Jesus began by carrying it Himself, perhaps recalling Isaac, who carried the wood for his own sacrifice (*Genesis 22:6*).

There they crucified Him, with two others, one on each side, and Jesus in the middle. Crucifixion was one of the cruelest forms of execution ever devised. Victims were nailed or tied to a wooden cross and left to die slowly, often over many hours, from exhaustion, blood loss, and suffocation. It was meant to be public and shameful.

Pilate wrote a sign and placed it on the cross: “*JESUS OF NAZARETH, THE KING OF THE JEWS*” (*v. 19*). It was written in Hebrew (or Aramaic), Latin, and Greek, the languages of religion, government, and culture, so that everyone passing by could read it. The chief priests objected and wanted it changed to “He said, ‘I am King of the Jews.’” Pilate refused: “*What I have written, I have written*” (*v. 22*). Without intending it, Pilate proclaimed the truth to the world in its three great languages.

The soldiers divided Jesus’ clothes among themselves, as was customary for executioners. His tunic was seamless, woven in one piece from top to bottom, so instead of tearing it, they cast lots for it. John sees this as a fulfillment of *Psalm 22:18*: “*They parted my garments among them. They cast lots for my clothing*” (*v. 24*). *Psalm 22*, which begins with the cry “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (studied at *Matthew 27:46*), describes the suffering of a righteous sufferer in strikingly detailed ways. Some interpreters also see significance in the seamless tunic, since the high priest’s robe was woven without a seam (*Exodus 28:32*), pointing to Jesus as our great High Priest.

### Jesus and His Mother (*19:25–27*)

Standing near the cross were several women: Jesus’ mother, His mother’s sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene. Many of the disciples had fled, but these women remained, along with the beloved disciple. Jesus’ words to His mother and to this disciple are studied below.

### “It Is Finished” (*19:28–30*)

“*After this, Jesus, seeing that all things were now finished, that the Scripture might be fulfilled, said, “I am thirsty!”*” (*v. 28*) The One who had offered living water to the Samaritan woman (*4:10*) and invited the thirsty to come to Him (*7:37*) now experienced burning thirst. His words recall *Psalm 69:21*: “*In my thirst, they gave me vinegar to drink*” (*Psalm 69:21*). The soldiers put a sponge soaked in sour wine on a branch of hyssop and held it to His mouth. Hyssop was the plant used at the first Passover to spread the lamb’s blood on the doorposts (*Exodus 12:22*).

Then Jesus spoke His final word, studied below, and “*he bowed his head and gave up his spirit*” (*v. 30*). John’s wording emphasizes that Jesus actively gave up His spirit. No one took His life from Him; He laid it down (*10:18*).

### The Pierced Side (*19:31–37*)

It was the Day of Preparation, and the next day was a special Sabbath, because it fell during Passover week. The Law said that a body hanged on a tree should not remain there overnight (*Deuteronomy 21:22–23*), and the leaders did not want the bodies on the crosses during the holy day. They asked Pilate to have the legs of the crucified men broken, which would hasten death by making it impossible for them to push up and breathe.

The soldiers broke the legs of the two men crucified with Jesus. But when they came to Jesus, they saw that He was already dead, so they did not break His legs. Instead, one soldier pierced His side with a spear, “*and immediately blood and water came out*” (*v. 34*). This is studied below.

John saw this himself and testifies that it is true. He explains that these events fulfilled two Scriptures: “*A bone of him will not be broken*” (*v. 36*), a command given about the Passover lamb (*Exodus 12:46*; *Numbers 9:12*; compare *Psalm 34:20*), and “*They will look on him whom they pierced*” (*v. 37*) (*Zechariah 12:10*). Jesus died as the true Passover Lamb.

### The Burial (*19:38–42*)

Joseph of Arimathea, “*being a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews*” (*v. 38*), asked Pilate for Jesus’ body. (His courage is studied at *Mark 15:43*.) Nicodemus, “*who at first came to Jesus by night*” (*v. 39*), came too, bringing about a hundred Roman pounds of myrrh and aloes, roughly seventy-five pounds today. This was an enormous amount, the kind of burial fit for a king. Two men who had once been afraid to confess Jesus openly came forward at the moment when following Him seemed most dangerous and least rewarding. The secret believers described in *John 12:42* stepped into the light.

They wrapped Jesus’ body in linen cloths with the spices, according to Jewish burial custom. Near the place of crucifixion was a garden, and in the garden a new tomb where no one had ever been laid. Because the Sabbath was about to begin at sundown, and the tomb was nearby, they laid Jesus there. John’s Gospel began with creation (*1:1*), and the story of humanity began in a garden. Now the Lord is laid in a garden tomb, and in the next chapter, new creation will begin there.

## Important Verses Explained

### *John 19:11* — Power Given from Above

> *“Jesus answered, ‘You would have no power at all against me, unless it were given to you from above. Therefore he who delivered me to you has greater sin.’”*
>
> — *John 19:11* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Pilate had heard the religious leaders say that Jesus claimed to be the Son of God, and he became more afraid. He took Jesus inside and asked Him, “*Where are you from?*” (*v. 9*) Jesus gave no answer. Pilate already had the information he needed to know Jesus was innocent, and Jesus had already told him that His kingdom was not of this world.

Pilate grew frustrated: “*Aren’t you speaking to me? Don’t you know that I have power to release you and have power to crucify you?*” (*v. 10*) Pilate wanted Jesus to recognize his authority. As Roman governor, he held the power of life and death.

Jesus answered, “*You would have no power at all against me, unless it were given to you from above*” (*v. 11*). Pilate’s authority was real, but it was not ultimate. It had been given to him by God. Pilate thought he was in control, but he was only exercising power that God permitted.

Then Jesus added, “*Therefore he who delivered me to you has greater sin*” (*v. 11*). The one who “delivered” Jesus may refer to Caiaphas, the high priest, who handed Him over to Pilate, or more broadly to the religious leaders, or to Judas. They had greater knowledge of God and of the Scriptures, and they had deliberately rejected Jesus. Pilate was guilty too, but those who knew more bore greater responsibility.

Jesus, though beaten, bleeding, and standing before the most powerful man in the region, spoke with calm authority. He was the One truly in control.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse teaches that all earthly authority comes from God. Paul writes, “*For there is no authority except from God*” (*Romans 13:1*). Rulers are accountable to God for how they use the power He has given them. No earthly power is absolute.

It also shows God’s sovereignty over the events of the cross. Human beings acted freely and wickedly in condemning Jesus, yet God was working through these events to accomplish salvation. Peter later preached that Jesus was “*delivered up by the determined counsel and foreknowledge of God*” (*Acts 2:23*), and also that those who crucified Him did so by lawless hands. God’s sovereignty and human responsibility are both real.

Finally, the verse reveals that sin has degrees of guilt. All sin is serious, but those who sin with greater knowledge and deliberate rejection of the truth bear greater responsibility (*Luke 12:47–48*). This does not excuse anyone, but it shows God’s justice.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse brings comfort to believers who feel powerless before human authorities. Whether facing an unjust government, an abusive employer, or a corrupt system, believers can remember that earthly power is limited and accountable to God. No one has power over God’s people except what God permits, and He will judge all misuse of authority.

It also challenges those who hold authority. Parents, employers, church leaders, and officials all exercise power that God has entrusted to them. They will give an account for how they use it. Authority is a responsibility to serve, never a license to oppress.

Finally, the verse encourages believers to trust God’s purposes in dark times. The cross looked like the triumph of human injustice, but God was accomplishing salvation. When believers face suffering at the hands of others, they can trust that God is still at work.

### *John 19:26–27* — “Behold, Your Mother!”

> *“Therefore when Jesus saw his mother, and the disciple whom he loved standing there, he said to his mother, ‘Woman, behold, your son!’ Then he said to the disciple, ‘Behold, your mother!’ From that hour, the disciple took her to his own home.”*
>
> — *John 19:26–27* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Near the cross stood a small group of women who had followed Jesus, including His mother Mary. Most of the disciples had fled, but these women stayed. With them was “*the disciple whom he loved*” (*v. 26*), traditionally identified as John, the author of this Gospel.

Mary was watching her son die a terrible death. Years earlier, when she brought the infant Jesus to the temple, the old man Simeon had told her, “*a sword will pierce through your own soul*” (*Luke 2:35*). Now that prophecy was being fulfilled.

In the midst of His own agony, Jesus thought of His mother. He said to her, “*Woman, behold, your son!*” (*v. 26*) Calling her “woman” was not disrespectful in that culture; it was a polite form of address, the same He used at the wedding in Cana (*2:4*). He was entrusting her to the care of the beloved disciple.

Then He said to the disciple, “*Behold, your mother!*” (*v. 27*) Jesus was asking him to care for Mary as if she were his own mother. As the eldest son, Jesus had a responsibility to provide for His widowed mother. His brothers did not yet believe in Him (*7:5*). So He entrusted her to a disciple who would care for her faithfully.

John adds, “*From that hour, the disciple took her to his own home*” (*v. 27*). He obeyed immediately.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This scene shows Jesus’ perfect obedience to God’s law, including the command to honor one’s father and mother (*Exodus 20:12*). Even while bearing the sin of the world, Jesus fulfilled His earthly responsibilities with love.

It also points to the new family that Jesus creates. Through His death, believers become brothers and sisters in God’s family. Earlier, Jesus said that whoever does God’s will is His brother, sister, and mother (*Mark 3:35*). At the cross, He formed a new relationship between His mother and His disciple, a picture of the family of faith that would be born through His death and resurrection.

Some Christian traditions also see in this scene a special honor for Mary as a spiritual mother to believers. Others understand it primarily as Jesus’ personal care for His mother. All agree that it reveals Jesus’ love and His concern for those closest to Him, even in His suffering.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage teaches believers to care for their families, especially aging parents. Even in His suffering, Jesus made sure His mother would be provided for. Believers are called to honor and care for their parents, especially when they are vulnerable or alone. Paul writes that caring for one’s own family is a basic expression of faith (*1 Timothy 5:4*, 8).

It also reminds believers that the church is a family. Many people are without close family because of death, distance, or broken relationships. The church is called to care for widows, orphans, the elderly, and the lonely as family members in Christ.

Finally, the passage shows that suffering does not have to make a person self-focused. Jesus, in the worst pain imaginable, thought of others. With God’s help, believers who are suffering can still show love to those around them.

### *John 19:30* — “*It Is Finished!*” (*v. 30*)

> *“When Jesus therefore had received the vinegar, he said, ‘It is finished!’ Then he bowed his head and gave up his spirit.”*
>
> — *John 19:30* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus had been on the cross for several hours. He had been flogged, mocked, and nailed to a cross. Darkness had covered the land (*Matthew 27:45*). Knowing that everything was now accomplished, He said, “I am thirsty,” and was given sour wine.

Then He said, “*It is finished!*” (*v. 30*) In Greek, this is a single word: tetelestai. It was used in different settings with rich meaning. A servant might use it to report that a task was completed. An artist might use it of a finished work. In commercial documents, a related form was used to mark a debt as “paid in full.” A priest might use it to declare that a sacrificial animal was without blemish and acceptable.

Jesus’ words were not a cry of defeat, as if to say, “I am finished.” They were a cry of victory: “It is finished.” The work the Father had given Him to do was complete. He had said in His prayer, “*I have accomplished the work which you have given me to do*” (*John 17:4*). Now He declared that it was done.

What was finished? Jesus had perfectly obeyed the Father. He had fulfilled the Scriptures that spoke of His suffering. He had offered Himself as the sacrifice for sin. The price for sin had been fully paid.

“*Then he bowed his head and gave up his spirit*” (*v. 30*). Jesus did not have His life taken from Him. He bowed His head and gave up His spirit, laying down His life by His own will.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse declares the completeness of Christ’s work of salvation. Nothing needs to be added to what Jesus accomplished on the cross. Hebrews teaches that Jesus “*offered one sacrifice for sins forever*” (*Hebrews 10:12*) and then sat down at God’s right hand. The priests of the old covenant stood daily offering sacrifices that could never take away sin. Jesus offered Himself once, and His work is complete.

It also shows that salvation is a gift, not an achievement. If the work is finished, then believers cannot earn salvation by their own efforts. They can only receive it by faith. Paul writes, “*for by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God*” (*Ephesians 2:8*).

Finally, the verse reveals Jesus’ faithfulness to His mission. From the beginning, He came to do the Father’s will. He did not stop halfway or give up. He finished the work completely.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse brings deep rest to believers. Many people live with the burden of trying to earn God’s acceptance or make up for their sins. Jesus’ words declare that the work is finished. Believers can rest in what He has done, rather than trying to add to it.

It also brings assurance to those troubled by guilt. If Jesus has paid the debt of sin in full, then believers who trust in Him are forgiven completely. Their past failures do not need to define them. The debt has been paid.

Finally, the verse inspires gratitude and worship. Jesus finished the work at great cost to Himself. Believers can respond with thankful hearts, offering their lives in loving service, not to earn salvation but because it has been freely given.

### *John 19:34–35* — Blood and Water

> *“However, one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and immediately blood and water came out. He who has seen has testified, and his testimony is true. He knows that he tells the truth, that you may believe.”*
>
> — *John 19:34–35* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Because the next day was a special Sabbath during Passover, the religious leaders asked Pilate to have the legs of the crucified men broken. Breaking the legs prevented the victims from pushing up to breathe, so they would die quickly and the bodies could be removed before the Sabbath began.

The soldiers broke the legs of the two men crucified with Jesus. But when they came to Jesus, they found that He was already dead. To make certain, “*one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and immediately blood and water came out*” (*v. 34*). Some medical writers have suggested that the flow of blood and a clear, watery fluid could result from the effects of severe trauma, such as fluid collecting around the heart or lungs. Whatever the exact physical explanation, the event confirmed that Jesus had truly died.

This mattered greatly. Some early false teachers claimed that Jesus only seemed to have a physical body or only appeared to die. John insists that Jesus truly died a physical death.

John emphasizes that this is an eyewitness account: “*He who has seen has testified, and his testimony is true. He knows that he tells the truth, that you may believe*” (*v. 35*). John saw it with his own eyes. He wrote it down so that readers might believe.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Many Christians throughout history have seen deep symbolic meaning in the blood and water. In John’s Gospel, water is associated with new life and the Holy Spirit (*3:5*; *4:14*; *7:38–39*), and blood with the sacrificial death that gives life (*6:53–56*). From Jesus’ pierced side flowed both: the cleansing and life-giving gifts that come through His death. Some early Christian writers connected the water with baptism and the blood with the Lord’s Supper. John later writes that Jesus “*came by water and blood*” (*1 John 5:6*).

The event also fulfilled Scripture. Zechariah prophesied that God’s people “*will look to me whom they have pierced; and they shall mourn for him*” (*Zechariah 12:10*), and that a fountain would be opened to cleanse them from sin (*Zechariah 13:1*). The piercing of Jesus’ side points to the fountain of cleansing opened through His death.

Finally, the fact that Jesus’ legs were not broken links Him to the Passover lamb, whose bones were not to be broken (*Exodus 12:46*). Jesus is the true Passover Lamb, whose blood protects His people from judgment.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage assures believers that Jesus truly died. His death was not an illusion or a symbol only. He experienced real death so that believers could have real life. The reality of His death makes the reality of His resurrection all the more powerful.

It also invites believers to receive the cleansing and life that flow from the cross. The blood of Jesus cleanses from sin, and the life of the Spirit renews the heart. Believers can come to Christ daily for forgiveness and for the refreshing presence of His Spirit.

Finally, John’s eyewitness testimony encourages believers to trust the Gospel accounts. John was there. He wrote what he saw so that readers would believe. The Christian faith rests on historical events attested by eyewitnesses.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*John 19* presents Jesus as the true King, even as He is mocked and crucified. The crown of thorns, the purple robe, and the sign above the cross were meant as insults, but they proclaimed the truth. Believers are invited to see in the crucified Jesus the King who rules by self-giving love, and to give Him their allegiance above every other power.

The chapter also shows that Jesus’ death was the fulfillment of God’s plan. Scripture after Scripture was fulfilled in the details of His suffering. Pilate’s authority was given from above, and the cross, though carried out by sinful hands, accomplished God’s purpose of salvation. Believers can trust that God is at work even in the darkest events of history and of their own lives.

At the center of the chapter is Jesus’ cry, “It is finished!” His work of salvation is complete. Nothing needs to be added to it. Believers can rest in His finished work, receive forgiveness as a gift, and live in gratitude rather than in the anxious effort to earn God’s favor.

Finally, *John 19* shows that love and courage can grow even in dark times. Jesus cared for His mother from the cross. The women stayed when others fled. Joseph and Nicodemus, once secret disciples, came forward boldly to honor Jesus’ body. Believers can follow their example, caring for those closest to them, staying faithful when others leave, and stepping out of fear into open devotion to Christ.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, I stand in awe at Your cross. You were flogged, mocked, and crowned with thorns, yet You are the true King. Thank You for carrying Your cross and laying down Your life for me. Thank You that even in Your agony You cared for Your mother, and that You care for me in my weakness. When You cried, “It is finished,” You completed the work of salvation. Help me to rest in what You have done and to stop trying to earn what You have freely given. Thank You for the blood and water that flowed from Your side, for cleansing and new life. Forgive me for the times I have been a secret disciple out of fear, and give me the courage of Joseph and Nicodemus to honor You openly. I bow before You as my Savior and King. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
