John · Chapter 20 of 21

# John — Chapter 20

Chapter Theme: The Risen Lord Calls, Sends, and Is Confessed as “My Lord and My God”

[Read John 20 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/JHN20.htm)

Main Teaching

Early on the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene finds the tomb empty, and Peter and the beloved disciple see the grave clothes lying in place. Weeping outside the tomb, Mary meets the risen Jesus, who calls her by name and sends her to tell the disciples. That evening Jesus appears to the frightened disciples behind locked doors, gives them peace, breathes on them the Holy Spirit, and sends them as the Father sent Him. A week later, the doubting Thomas sees His wounds and confesses, “My Lord and my God!” John then tells his readers why he wrote: so that they may believe and have life in Jesus’ name.

## Chapter Background and Story

*John 20* tells of the resurrection of Jesus, the event on which the Christian faith stands or falls. Paul writes, “*If Christ has not been raised, your faith is vain; you are still in your sins*” (*1 Corinthians 15:17*). Each Gospel tells of the empty tomb and of Jesus’ appearances, focusing on different witnesses and details. John’s account is deeply personal. He describes four people coming to faith in the risen Jesus in different ways: the beloved disciple, who believes when he sees the grave clothes; Mary Magdalene, who recognizes Jesus when He speaks her name; the disciples, who rejoice when they see His hands and side; and Thomas, who moves from doubt to the highest confession in the Gospel.

The resurrection is also studied at *Matthew 28*, *Mark 16*, and *Luke 24*.

### The Empty Tomb (*20:1–10*)

“*on the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene went early, while it was still dark, to the tomb*” (*v. 1*). The first day of the week is Sunday. Jesus had been buried on Friday before sunset, and the Sabbath had passed. Mary Magdalene had been delivered by Jesus from seven demons (*Luke 8:2*) and had stood at the cross (*John 19:25*). Other women came with her, as the other Gospels report, and John hints at this when Mary says “we don’t know” (*John 20:2*).

She saw that the stone had been removed from the entrance. Assuming that someone had taken the body, she ran to Peter and the beloved disciple: “*They have taken away the Lord out of the tomb, and we don’t know where they have laid him!*” (*v. 2*) Grave robbery was common enough that, a few years later, a Roman emperor’s decree ordered the death penalty for disturbing tombs.

Peter and the other disciple ran to the tomb. The other disciple arrived first, looked in, and saw the linen cloths lying there, but did not enter. Peter, characteristically, went straight in. He saw the linen cloths lying, “*and the cloth that had been on his head, not lying with the linen cloths, but rolled up in a place by itself*” (*v. 7*). The grave clothes were not scattered, as they would have been if thieves had hurriedly unwrapped the body. And thieves would hardly have taken the time to unwrap the body and leave behind about seventy-five pounds of costly spices bound into the linen (*19:39–40*). The scene suggested that Jesus’ body had passed out of the wrappings, leaving them in place.

“*So then the other disciple who came first to the tomb also entered in, and he saw and believed*” (*v. 8*). He did not yet see Jesus, but he believed that He had risen. John adds honestly, “*For as yet they didn’t know the Scripture, that he must rise from the dead*” (*v. 9*). They had not yet understood passages like *Psalm 16:10* and *Isaiah 53:10–12* that pointed to the resurrection. Their belief came first from the evidence of the tomb; understanding of the Scriptures came later.

### Jesus Appears to Mary Magdalene (*20:11–18*)

Mary stayed outside the tomb, weeping. When she looked in, she saw two angels in white sitting where Jesus’ body had been, one at the head and one at the feet. They asked, “*Woman, why are you weeping?*” (*v. 13*) She answered that someone had taken her Lord.

Then she turned and saw Jesus standing there, but did not recognize Him. He asked, “*Woman, why are you weeping? Who are you looking for?*” (*v. 15*) She thought He was the gardener and asked Him to tell her where He had put the body. This moment, and what happened next, is studied below.

Jesus said, “*Don’t hold me, for I haven’t yet ascended to my Father*” (*v. 17*). Mary was clinging to Him, perhaps afraid of losing Him again. Jesus gently told her that their relationship would not return to what it had been before. He would ascend to the Father, and a new kind of relationship would begin through the Spirit. He gave her a mission: “*go to my brothers and tell them, ‘I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.’*” (*v. 17*) For the first time in John, Jesus calls His disciples “my brothers.” Through His death and resurrection, His Father has become their Father.

Mary went and announced to the disciples, “*she had seen the Lord*” (*v. 18*). In a culture where women’s testimony was often considered unreliable in court, the risen Jesus chose a woman to be the first witness of His resurrection. This detail is one reason many historians consider the accounts credible; it is not the kind of detail people would invent if they were creating a story to persuade others.

### Jesus Appears to the Disciples (*20:19–23*)

That evening, the disciples were gathered behind locked doors, “*for fear of the Jews*” (*v. 19*), that is, the authorities who had arranged Jesus’ death. Suddenly Jesus stood among them and said, “*Peace be to you*” (*v. 19*). This was the usual Jewish greeting, shalom, but on His lips it carried new meaning. These disciples had abandoned Him. He did not rebuke them. He gave them peace.

“*he showed them his hands and his side*” (*v. 20*). The marks of the nails and spear proved that it was truly Jesus, the same One who had been crucified. His resurrection body was real and physical, yet transformed, able to appear in a locked room. “*The disciples therefore were glad when they saw the Lord*” (*v. 20*), just as Jesus had promised that their sorrow would turn to joy (*16:20–22*). Then Jesus commissioned them and breathed on them, studied below.

Jesus also said, “*If you forgive anyone’s sins, they have been forgiven them. If you retain anyone’s sins, they have been retained*” (*v. 23*). Christians have understood these words in different ways. Roman Catholic and Orthodox traditions see in them the authority given to the church’s ministers to declare forgiveness in the sacrament of confession. Many Protestant traditions understand them as the authority given to the church to proclaim the gospel: when the church announces forgiveness through Christ, those who believe are truly forgiven, and those who reject Christ remain in their sins. All agree that only God can forgive sins (*Mark 2:7*), and that the church’s role is to declare and administer the forgiveness that God gives through Christ.

### Thomas Sees and Believes (*20:24–29*)

Thomas, one of the Twelve, was not with them when Jesus came. The others told him, “*We have seen the Lord!*” (*v. 25*) But Thomas would not believe without seeing and touching the wounds himself. A week later, Jesus appeared again, with Thomas present. This scene is studied below.

### The Purpose of the Gospel (*20:30–31*)

John concludes this chapter by explaining why he wrote his Gospel. This is studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *John 20:15–16* — “Mary”

> *“Jesus said to her, ‘Woman, why are you weeping? Who are you looking for?’ She, supposing him to be the gardener, said to him, ‘Sir, if you have carried him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him away.’ Jesus said to her, ‘Mary.’ She turned and said to him, ‘Rabboni!’ which is to say, ‘Teacher!’”*
>
> — *John 20:15–16* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Mary Magdalene had come to the tomb before dawn. She found it empty and assumed someone had stolen Jesus’ body. After Peter and the other disciple went home, she stayed outside the tomb, weeping. She had seen Jesus die. Now it seemed that even His body had been taken from her.

She turned around and saw a man standing there. “*Jesus said to her, “Woman, why are you weeping? Who are you looking for?”*” (*v. 15*) His question gently invited her to express her grief. Notice the words “Who are you looking for?” Jesus asked the same question at the beginning of His ministry to His first disciples (*1:38*) and at His arrest (*18:4*).

Mary did not recognize Him. Perhaps her eyes were blurred with tears, or it was still dim, or Jesus’ resurrection body was not immediately recognizable, as was true for the disciples on the road to Emmaus (*Luke 24:16*). “*She, supposing him to be the gardener*” (*v. 15*), asked Him to tell her where He had put the body so she could take it away.

Then “*Jesus said to her, “Mary.”*” (*v. 16*) One word, her name, spoken in the voice she knew. Instantly, she recognized Him. “*She turned and said to him, “Rabboni!” which is to say, “Teacher!”*” (*v. 16*) “Rabboni” is an Aramaic word meaning “my teacher,” a warm and personal form of address.

Mary went from deepest grief to overwhelming joy in a single moment, because Jesus called her by name.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This scene beautifully fulfills Jesus’ words about the Good Shepherd: “*He calls his own sheep by name and leads them out*” (*John 10:3*). Mary recognized the Shepherd when He spoke her name. Faith is not only accepting facts about Jesus; it is recognizing His voice and responding to Him personally.

It also shows the tenderness of the risen Lord. His first recorded appearance in John was not to a powerful leader or to the apostles, but to a grieving woman who had been delivered from much (*Luke 8:2*). He came to the one who loved Him and stayed when others went home.

The setting in a garden is also significant. Humanity’s story began in a garden, where sin brought death. Now, in a garden, the risen Jesus appears, the beginning of new creation. Mary’s mistake in thinking He was the gardener holds a deeper truth: He is the One who will restore God’s creation.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage brings comfort to those who grieve. Mary’s tears were real, and Jesus did not dismiss them. He came to her in her grief and asked about her sorrow. Believers who are weeping can know that the risen Lord sees them and comes near.

It also reminds believers that Jesus knows each of them personally. He calls His sheep by name. Believers are not anonymous faces in a crowd. The Lord knows their names, their stories, and their needs.

Finally, the passage encourages believers to listen for Jesus’ voice. Sometimes believers, like Mary, are so overwhelmed by grief or confusion that they do not recognize Jesus’ presence. He speaks through His word, His Spirit, and His people. When believers hear His voice, they can turn to Him in faith and joy.

### *John 20:21–22* — “*As the Father Has Sent Me, Even So I Send You*” (*v. 21*)

> *“Jesus therefore said to them again, ‘Peace be to you. As the Father has sent me, even so I send you.’ When he had said this, he breathed on them, and said to them, Receive the Holy Spirit!”*
>
> — *John 20:21–22* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

It was the evening of the first Easter. The disciples were gathered behind locked doors, afraid of the authorities. Jesus suddenly stood among them, said “Peace be to you,” and showed them the wounds in His hands and side. The disciples were filled with joy.

Then Jesus said again, “*Peace be to you. As the Father has sent me, even so I send you*” (*v. 21*). Throughout John’s Gospel, Jesus described Himself as the One sent by the Father. He came into the world to reveal the Father, to do His will, and to give His life for the world’s salvation. Now He sends His disciples into the world in the same way. They would continue His mission.

The pattern of Jesus’ sending shapes the disciples’ sending. He was sent in love, in humility, in obedience, and in dependence on the Father. The disciples would go in the same spirit. Jesus had already prayed, “*As you sent me into the world, even so I have sent them into the world*” (*John 17:18*).

“*When he had said this, he breathed on them, and said to them, “Receive the Holy Spirit!”*” (*v. 22*) The act of breathing recalls the creation of the first man, when God “*breathed into his nostrils the breath of life*” (*Genesis 2:7*). It also recalls Ezekiel’s vision of the valley of dry bones, where God’s breath brought the dead to life (*Ezekiel 37:9–10*). Jesus was giving new life and the power for mission through the Spirit.

Some see this as a first giving of the Spirit, followed by the fuller outpouring at Pentecost (*Acts 2*). Others see it as a symbolic act pointing forward to Pentecost. In either case, Jesus links the mission of the disciples with the gift of the Spirit.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This passage is John’s version of the Great Commission (compare *Matthew 28:19–20*). Its emphasis is on the pattern of mission: as the Father sent the Son, so the Son sends His people. Christian mission is a continuation of the mission of Jesus, carried out in His way and by His Spirit.

It also shows that mission flows from peace. Twice Jesus said, “Peace be to you.” The disciples were not sent out from fear or guilt, but from the peace that Jesus had won for them through His death and resurrection. Those who have peace with God are sent to share it.

Finally, the breathing of the Spirit points to new creation. The resurrection of Jesus begins God’s renewal of all things. The Spirit makes believers new creations (*2 Corinthians 5:17*) and empowers them to bring Christ’s life to the world.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage reminds believers that they are sent people. Every follower of Jesus is called to continue His mission in their own setting, whether at home, at work, at school, or across the world. Mission is not only for a few specialists; it is the calling of the whole church.

It also shapes how believers carry out their mission. Jesus was sent in humility, love, and obedience. Believers are called to serve others, speak truth with grace, and depend on the Father, just as Jesus did.

Finally, the passage encourages believers to rely on the Holy Spirit. The disciples were afraid and hiding behind locked doors. Jesus gave them peace and the Spirit. Believers who feel fearful or inadequate can trust that the same Spirit empowers them for the task to which they are sent.

### *John 20:27–29* — “My Lord and My God!”

> *“Then he said to Thomas, ‘Reach here your finger, and see my hands. Reach here your hand, and put it into my side. Don’t be unbelieving, but believing.’ Thomas answered him, ‘My Lord and my God!’ Jesus said to him, ‘Because you have seen me, you have believed. Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed.’”*
>
> — *John 20:27–29* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Thomas had not been with the other disciples when Jesus first appeared to them. When they told him, “We have seen the Lord!” he refused to believe. He said that unless he saw the nail marks in Jesus’ hands, put his finger into them, and put his hand into His side, he would not believe.

Thomas is often called “Doubting Thomas,” but he was not unusually skeptical. The other disciples had not believed the women’s report either (*Luke 24:11*). Thomas wanted the same evidence the others had received. Earlier in the Gospel, he had shown courage, saying, “Let’s also go, that we may die with him” (*John 11:16*), and honesty, asking, “How can we know the way?” (*John 14:5*).

A week later, the disciples were together again, and Thomas was with them. Jesus came, though the doors were locked, and stood among them. He turned to Thomas: “*Reach here your finger, and see my hands. Reach here your hand, and put it into my side. Don’t be unbelieving, but believing*” (*v. 27*). Jesus knew exactly what Thomas had said. He offered him the very evidence he had asked for. He did not reject Thomas for his doubts; He met him in them.

“*Thomas answered him, “My Lord and my God!”*” (*v. 28*) John does not say whether Thomas actually touched Jesus’ wounds. What he records is Thomas’s confession, the greatest confession of faith in the Gospel. Thomas called Jesus not only “Lord” but “God.”

Jesus responded, “*Because you have seen me, you have believed. Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed*” (*v. 29*). Jesus pronounced a special blessing on all future believers who would trust Him without seeing Him physically.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Thomas’s confession forms the climax of John’s Gospel. The Gospel began with the declaration, “*the Word was God*” (*John 1:1*). Now a disciple confesses that same truth to Jesus’ face: “My Lord and my God!” Jesus accepted this worship without correction, confirming His divine identity.

It also shows Jesus’ patience with honest doubt. Thomas’s doubt was not hardened unbelief but a struggle to believe something extraordinary. Jesus met him with gentleness and evidence. Doubt can become the doorway to deeper faith when it is brought honestly to Jesus.

Finally, the blessing on those who have not seen speaks to every reader of John’s Gospel. Peter later wrote to believers, “*whom, not having known, you love. In him, though now you don’t see him, yet believing, you rejoice greatly with joy that is unspeakable and full of glory*” (*1 Peter 1:8*). Faith that rests on the testimony of eyewitnesses is not second-class; it is blessed by Jesus Himself.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage encourages believers who struggle with doubt. Many Christians experience seasons of questioning. Thomas’s story shows that Jesus does not reject those who doubt. He meets them where they are. Believers can bring their questions honestly to Him, and to trusted fellow believers, and seek Him with an open heart.

It also invites every reader to make Thomas’s confession their own. It is not enough to know that Jesus rose from the dead as a historical fact. Thomas’s words are personal: “My Lord and my God.” Faith involves surrendering to Jesus as Lord and worshiping Him as God.

Finally, Jesus’ blessing gives believers confidence. Though they have not seen Jesus with their eyes, their faith is blessed. They believe through the testimony of those who saw, preserved in Scripture, and confirmed by the Spirit in their hearts.

### *John 20:31* — That You May Believe and Have Life

> *“but these are written that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name.”*
>
> — *John 20:31* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After recording Thomas’s confession and Jesus’ blessing on those who believe without seeing, John explained why he wrote his Gospel. He first acknowledged that he had not recorded everything: “*Therefore Jesus did many other signs in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book*” (*v. 30*). John selected certain signs and teachings for a specific purpose.

“*but these are written that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God*” (*v. 31*). John’s purpose was to lead readers to faith. He wanted them to believe two things about Jesus. First, that He is “the Christ,” the promised Messiah of Israel, the anointed King. Second, that He is “the Son of God,” sharing the Father’s nature and revealing Him.

Some ancient manuscripts have a verb form that could mean “that you may continue to believe.” This suggests that John may have written both to bring unbelievers to faith and to strengthen believers in their faith. Both purposes are fulfilled through his Gospel.

“*and that believing you may have life in his name*” (*v. 31*). The goal of believing is life, eternal life, the life of God shared with His people. This life is found “in his name,” meaning through Jesus Himself and all that He is and has done.

This verse is the key to understanding the whole Gospel. Every sign, conversation, and teaching John recorded was chosen to help readers believe in Jesus and receive life.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals that the Bible is written with a purpose. John did not write simply to record history or to satisfy curiosity. He wrote so that readers would encounter Jesus and believe. Scripture is God’s means of bringing people to faith. Paul writes that “*faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God*” (*Romans 10:17*).

It also shows that belief and life are connected. In John’s Gospel, believing is not merely agreeing with information. It is trusting Jesus personally and receiving Him. Those who believe receive the life He gives.

Finally, the verse summarizes the identity of Jesus as the whole Gospel presents it. Through seven signs, seven “I am” sayings, many conversations, and His death and resurrection, John has shown that Jesus is the Christ and the Son of God.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites every reader of John’s Gospel to respond. John has presented the evidence. The question is whether each reader will believe. Those who have not yet trusted Jesus are invited to believe in Him and receive life.

It also encourages believers to read the Gospel of John as a means of strengthening their faith. Returning to John’s account of Jesus’ signs and words can deepen trust, renew love, and refresh the soul.

Finally, the verse encourages believers to share the Gospel with others. John wrote so that others would believe. Believers can share the story of Jesus, invite friends to read the Gospels, and trust that God uses His word to bring people to life.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*John 20* proclaims that Jesus is risen. This changes everything. Death is not the end. Sin has been defeated. The One who was crucified is alive and reigns. Believers can live with hope, courage, and joy because the tomb is empty and Jesus lives.

The chapter shows that the risen Jesus meets people personally. He called Mary by name in her grief, gave peace to frightened disciples behind locked doors, and offered Thomas the evidence he needed for his doubts. Believers who are grieving, afraid, or struggling with doubt can know that Jesus comes to them as well, meeting them in their particular need.

*John 20* also reminds believers that they are sent. As the Father sent Jesus, Jesus sends His followers into the world, empowered by the Holy Spirit. The mission of Jesus continues through His people as they share His peace, proclaim forgiveness, and live out His love in every part of life.

Finally, the chapter calls each reader to make Thomas’s confession their own: “My Lord and my God!” John wrote his Gospel so that readers would believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and have life in His name. Believers are blessed when they trust Him without seeing, and they can keep returning to His word to deepen that faith and share it with others.

## Chapter Prayer

Risen Lord Jesus, thank You that the tomb is empty and that You are alive. Thank You for calling Mary by name in her grief, and for knowing my name too. When I weep, help me to hear Your voice and turn to You. Thank You for coming to Your frightened disciples with peace, and for showing them Your wounds. Breathe Your Holy Spirit on me, and send me into the world as the Father sent You. When I struggle with doubt, meet me as You met Thomas, and lead me to deeper faith. I confess with Thomas that You are my Lord and my God. Thank You for the blessing You give to those who have not seen and yet believe. Strengthen my faith through Your word, and help me to share it so that others may believe and have life in Your name. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

John · Chapter 21 of 21

# John — Chapter 21

Chapter Theme: Breakfast on the Shore: Peter Restored and Called to Follow

[Read John 21 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/JHN21.htm)

Main Teaching

Beside the Sea of Galilee, the risen Jesus meets seven disciples after a fruitless night of fishing, fills their net with a miraculous catch, and serves them breakfast over a charcoal fire. Then He asks Peter three times, “Do you love me?”, restoring the disciple who had denied Him three times and entrusting him with the care of His sheep. Jesus foretells the kind of death by which Peter will glorify God and calls him simply to follow, without comparing his path to anyone else’s. John closes his Gospel by affirming that his testimony is true and that Jesus did far more than could ever be written.

## Chapter Background and Story

*John 20* ended with what sounds like a conclusion: “these are written that you may believe” (*20:31*). Chapter 21 is often described as an epilogue. It ties up an important unfinished thread, Peter’s restoration after his denial, and it looks forward to the mission of the church and the future of two key apostles. All Greek manuscripts of John include this chapter, and its style and themes fit closely with the rest of the Gospel.

The setting moves from Jerusalem back to Galilee, where Jesus first called these men to follow Him. Matthew and Mark record that Jesus told the disciples He would meet them in Galilee (*Matthew 28:7*; *Mark 16:7*).

### A Night of Fishing (*21:1–3*)

Seven disciples were together by the Sea of Tiberias, another name for the Sea of Galilee: Simon Peter, Thomas, Nathanael, the sons of Zebedee (James and John), and two others. Peter said, “*I’m going fishing*” (*v. 3*), and the others joined him. Some see this as Peter returning to his old life in discouragement. Others think the disciples were simply waiting in Galilee as instructed and needed to eat and earn a living. Either way, the scene recalls the beginning of Peter’s discipleship. Fishing was usually done at night on the Sea of Galilee. “*That night, they caught nothing*” (*v. 3*).

### The Miraculous Catch (*21:4–14*)

At dawn, Jesus stood on the shore, though the disciples did not recognize Him. He called out, “*Children, have you anything to eat?*” (*v. 5*) “Children” was a friendly, familiar way of addressing them, a little like “lads” or “friends.” They answered, “No.” Jesus’ instruction and the result are studied below.

The beloved disciple recognized Him first: “*It’s the Lord!*” (*v. 7*) Peter, impulsive as ever, wrapped his outer garment around himself (he had stripped down for work) and jumped into the water to reach Jesus quickly. The others followed in the boat, dragging the net, since they were only about a hundred yards from shore.

On the shore, “*they saw a fire of coals there, with fish and bread laid on it*” (*v. 9*). The phrase “fire of coals” (a charcoal fire) appears in only one other place in the New Testament: the courtyard fire where Peter warmed himself as he denied Jesus (*18:18*). The scene of Peter’s failure is quietly echoed in the scene of his restoration.

Jesus told them to bring some of the fish they had caught. Peter dragged the net ashore, “*full of one hundred fifty-three great fish. Even though there were so many, the net wasn’t torn*” (*v. 11*). Many interpreters have looked for symbolic meaning in the number 153. One ancient suggestion is that it represents all the kinds of fish then known, pointing to the gospel reaching all nations. Others see no special symbolism, only the careful memory of an eyewitness who remembered counting the catch. Many also see in the unbroken net a picture of the church, which holds people of every nation without tearing apart.

Jesus said, “*Come and eat breakfast!*” (*v. 12*) The disciples knew it was the Lord, though they did not dare to ask Him. “*Then Jesus came and took the bread, gave it to them, and the fish likewise*” (*v. 13*). The risen Lord of glory served them breakfast, recalling His feeding of the five thousand by the same lake (*6:11*). John notes that this was the third time Jesus appeared to His disciples as a group after His resurrection.

### “Do You Love Me?” (*21:15–19*)

After breakfast, Jesus turned to Peter and asked him three times whether he loved Him. This conversation is studied below, along with Jesus’ prophecy of Peter’s death and His call to follow.

### “What About This Man?” (*21:20–23*)

Peter turned and saw the beloved disciple following them. He asked, “*Lord, what about this man?*” (*v. 21*) Jesus’ answer is studied below. John then corrects a rumor that had spread in the early church. Some believers had understood Jesus’ words to mean that this disciple would not die before Jesus returned. John explains that Jesus did not say that; He only said, “If I desire that he stay until I come, what is that to you?” The correction may suggest that the beloved disciple was very old, or had recently died, when the Gospel was completed.

### The Testimony of the Beloved Disciple (*21:24–25*)

“*This is the disciple who testifies about these things, and wrote these things. We know that his witness is true*” (*v. 24*). The “we” may be the church or a group of John’s companions who knew him and affirmed his testimony. The beloved disciple, traditionally identified as John the son of Zebedee, is the source and author of this Gospel.

The Gospel closes with a striking statement: “*There are also many other things which Jesus did, which if they would all be written, I suppose that even the world itself wouldn’t have room for the books that would be written*” (*v. 25*). John has selected only some of Jesus’ works and words. The full story of who Jesus is and what He has done can never be exhausted.

## Important Verses Explained

### *John 21:6* — Cast the Net on the Right Side

> *“He said to them, ‘Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some.’ They cast it therefore, and now they weren’t able to draw it in for the multitude of fish.”*
>
> — *John 21:6* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Seven disciples had fished all night on the Sea of Galilee and caught nothing. These were experienced fishermen. Peter, James, and John had grown up fishing on this lake. They knew where the fish were and how to catch them. Yet after a whole night of work, their nets were empty.

At dawn, a man on the shore called out and asked whether they had caught anything. They said no. Then He said, “*Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some*” (*v. 6*). From a human perspective, this advice made little sense. The disciples were the experts. A stranger on the shore could hardly know better than they did. Yet they obeyed.

“*They cast it therefore, and now they weren’t able to draw it in for the multitude of fish*” (*v. 6*). The net was suddenly so full that they could not haul it into the boat.

This event recalled something that had happened years earlier. Luke records that when Jesus first called Peter, Peter had also fished all night and caught nothing. Jesus told him to let down his nets, and they caught so many fish that the nets began to break (*Luke 5:4–7*). Then Jesus said, “*From now on you will be catching people*” (*Luke 5:10*). The beloved disciple seems to have recognized this pattern, and he said, “It’s the Lord!”

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This miracle shows the difference between working in human strength and working at Jesus’ word. The disciples were skilled, and they worked hard, but without Jesus, they caught nothing. When they obeyed His word, their nets were filled. Jesus had taught them, “*apart from me you can do nothing*” (*John 15:5*).

It also points to the mission of the church. The disciples had been called to be fishers of people. The great catch is a picture of the many who would come to faith through their witness after Jesus’ resurrection. The fruitfulness of mission depends on the Lord’s direction and power.

Finally, the miracle shows the generosity of the risen Christ. He did not merely give them enough for a meal; He gave them an abundance. He already had fish cooking on the fire, yet He invited them to bring some of what they had caught. He provides abundantly, and He also delights to include His followers in His work.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage speaks to believers who feel that their efforts are fruitless. Many people work hard in their families, churches, or jobs and see little result. The disciples’ empty nets remind believers that fruitfulness ultimately comes from Christ. Believers can bring their discouragement to Him and listen for His direction.

It also encourages obedience even when Jesus’ instructions seem unexpected. The disciples were experts, yet they followed the word of a stranger on the shore. Believers may sometimes find that God’s word challenges their experience or expectations. Obedience to Him leads to blessing.

Finally, the passage reminds believers that Jesus is present in ordinary life. He met His disciples not in the temple but at work, by the lake, at breakfast. He meets His people today in their daily tasks, offering His presence and guidance.

### *John 21:15–17* — “*Do You Love Me?*” (*v. 15*)

> *“So when they had eaten their breakfast, Jesus said to Simon Peter, ‘Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me more than these?’ He said to him, ‘Yes, Lord; you know that I have affection for you.’ He said to him, ‘Feed my lambs.’ He said to him again a second time, ‘Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me?’ He said to him, ‘Yes, Lord; you know that I have affection for you.’ He said to him, ‘Tend my sheep.’ He said to him the third time, ‘Simon, son of Jonah, do you have affection for me?’ Peter was grieved because he asked him the third time, ‘Do you have affection for me?’ He said to him, ‘Lord, you know everything. You know that I have affection for you.’ Jesus said to him, Feed my sheep.”*
>
> — *John 21:15–17* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After breakfast on the shore, Jesus turned to Simon Peter. Only days before, Peter had denied knowing Jesus three times beside a charcoal fire in the high priest’s courtyard. Now, beside another charcoal fire, Jesus spoke to him.

“*Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me more than these?*” (*v. 15*) Jesus called him “Simon, son of Jonah,” his original name, rather than “Peter,” the name Jesus had given him meaning “rock.” The phrase “more than these” may mean “more than these other disciples love Me,” recalling Peter’s earlier boast that even if all others fell away, he would not (*Matthew 26:33*). Or it may mean “more than these things,” such as fishing and boats. Either way, Jesus was asking Peter to examine his heart.

Peter answered, “*Yes, Lord; you know that I have affection for you*” (*v. 15*). Jesus said, “*Feed my lambs*” (*v. 15*).

Jesus asked a second time, and Peter gave the same answer. Jesus said, “*Tend my sheep*” (*v. 16*).

Then Jesus asked a third time: “*Simon, son of Jonah, do you have affection for me?*” (*v. 17*) “*Peter was grieved because he asked him the third time*” (*v. 17*). The third question surely reminded Peter of his three denials. He answered, “*Lord, you know everything. You know that I have affection for you*” (*v. 17*). Peter no longer boasted about his own loyalty. He appealed to Jesus’ knowledge of his heart. And Jesus said, “*Feed my sheep*” (*v. 17*).

The World English Bible translates two different Greek words for love here. In His first two questions, Jesus used the word agapao (translated “love”), and in the third question He used phileo (translated “have affection for”), the word Peter used each time. Some interpreters believe the change is significant, with Jesus coming down to Peter’s level. Others note that John often uses these words interchangeably and see the variation as stylistic. Either way, the central point is clear: three denials are answered by three affirmations of love, and each affirmation is followed by a commission.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This passage is a beautiful picture of restoration. Peter had failed badly, but Jesus did not reject him. He did not lecture him or demand a long period of proving himself. He invited him to affirm his love and then restored him to service. The grace of Christ is greater than our greatest failures.

It also shows that love for Jesus is the foundation of ministry. Jesus did not ask Peter about his skill, his knowledge, or even his courage. He asked about his love. Service flows from love for Christ. And love for Christ shows itself in caring for His people: “Feed my sheep.”

Finally, notice that Jesus calls them “my lambs” and “my sheep.” The flock belongs to Christ, not to Peter. Peter would serve as a shepherd under the Good Shepherd. Peter later wrote to church leaders, urging them to shepherd God’s flock willingly and humbly, and calling Jesus “*the chief Shepherd*” (*1 Peter 5:4*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage brings hope to anyone who has failed Jesus. Many believers carry guilt over moments when they denied Christ by their words, actions, or silence. Peter’s story shows that failure is not the end. Jesus seeks out those who have failed and restores them.

It also invites believers to examine their love for Jesus. The question “Do you love me?” is asked of every follower. Love for Christ is not measured by bold promises but by humble dependence on His knowledge of the heart and by faithful care for His people.

Finally, the passage reminds believers that loving Jesus means caring for others. Feeding and tending His sheep can take many forms: teaching, encouraging, serving, praying for, and supporting other believers. Every act of loving care for God’s people is an expression of love for Christ.

### *John 21:18–19* — “Follow Me”

> *“Most certainly I tell you, when you were young, you dressed yourself and walked where you wanted to. But when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will dress you and carry you where you don’t want to go. Now he said this, signifying by what kind of death he would glorify God. When he had said this, he said to him, ‘Follow me.’”*
>
> — *John 21:18–19* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After restoring Peter and giving him the task of caring for His sheep, Jesus spoke about Peter’s future: “*Most certainly I tell you, when you were young, you dressed yourself and walked where you wanted to*” (*v. 18*). As a young man, Peter had been independent, going where he wished and making his own choices.

“*But when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will dress you and carry you where you don’t want to go*” (*v. 18*). Jesus was describing a future in which Peter would lose his freedom. The phrase “stretch out your hands” was used in the ancient world to describe crucifixion.

John explains, “*Now he said this, signifying by what kind of death he would glorify God*” (*v. 19*). Peter would die as a martyr. Early Christian tradition reports that Peter was crucified in Rome during the persecution under Emperor Nero, around A.D. 64–68. One tradition says he asked to be crucified upside down, feeling unworthy to die in the same way as his Lord.

Notice the phrase “*he would glorify God*” (*v. 19*). Peter’s death would not be a tragedy without meaning. It would bring glory to God, just as Jesus’ death glorified the Father.

Then Jesus said to him, “*Follow me*” (*v. 19*). These were the same words Jesus spoke when He first called Peter by the lake years before (*Mark 1:17*). Now, after Peter’s failure and restoration, and knowing the cost, Jesus called him again.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This passage shows that following Jesus may lead to suffering. Peter had once promised to lay down his life for Jesus (*13:37*) but failed when the moment came. Now Jesus told him that he would indeed lay down his life, not in his own strength, but by God’s grace. The Peter who once denied Jesus would one day die for Him.

It also shows that God can be glorified in the death of His people. Death is still an enemy, but for believers it can become a final act of faithful witness. Paul wrote that he hoped Christ would be magnified in his body “*whether by life, or by death*” (*Philippians 1:20*).

Finally, the call “Follow me” summarizes the whole Christian life. It is not a one-time decision but a daily walk with Jesus wherever He leads, including through suffering. Peter’s restoration was not merely forgiveness; it was a renewed call to follow.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage reminds believers that following Jesus involves surrender. Like Peter, believers may have once lived as they pleased, going where they wanted. Following Christ means allowing Him to lead, even when His path goes where they would not choose.

It also encourages believers facing suffering, illness, or the losses of old age. Many people experience a loss of independence as they grow older, being “carried where they don’t want to go.” Even in such seasons, believers can glorify God through their faith, patience, and trust.

Finally, the passage renews Jesus’ call to every believer: “Follow me.” Whatever failures lie in the past, and whatever challenges lie ahead, the call remains the same. Each day, believers can respond by following Jesus with trust and love.

### *John 21:21–22* — “What Is That to You? You Follow Me”

> *“Peter, seeing him, said to Jesus, ‘Lord, what about this man?’ Jesus said to him, ‘If I desire that he stay until I come, what is that to you? You follow me.’”*
>
> — *John 21:21–22* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus had just told Peter that he would die a martyr’s death and called him to follow. Peter turned and saw the beloved disciple following them. He asked, “*Lord, what about this man?*” (*v. 21*) Peter wanted to know what would happen to this other disciple. Would he also suffer? Would his path be easier?

Jesus answered, “*If I desire that he stay until I come, what is that to you? You follow me*” (*v. 22*). Jesus’ answer was firm but not harsh. He told Peter, in effect, that the other disciple’s future was not Peter’s concern. Jesus had a plan for each of them. Peter’s responsibility was to follow Jesus himself.

The word “You” in “You follow me” is emphatic in Greek. Jesus was calling Peter to focus on his own walk with Him rather than comparing himself with others.

John adds that this saying led to a rumor among believers that the beloved disciple would not die before Jesus returned. He corrects this misunderstanding: Jesus did not say that he would not die; He only said, “If I desire that he stay until I come, what is that to you?”

Peter and John would have very different paths. Peter would die as a martyr, probably in Rome in the 60s. According to early Christian tradition, John lived to old age in Ephesus and died a natural death near the end of the first century. Both glorified God, but in different ways.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This passage teaches that each disciple has a unique calling. God does not lead all His people in the same way. Some suffer greatly; others are spared certain trials. Some have public ministries; others serve quietly. God’s plans for each person are His to decide. Paul writes that believers have different gifts according to the grace given to them (*Romans 12:6*).

It also reveals the danger of comparison. Comparing oneself with others can lead to envy, resentment, pride, or discouragement. Peter’s question shows a very human tendency. Jesus’ answer redirects attention to the most important thing: personal faithfulness to Him.

Finally, the mention of Jesus’ coming (“until I come”) points to the hope of His return. The Gospel ends with the expectation that Jesus will come again. Until then, His followers are called to follow Him faithfully, each in the path He gives.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage frees believers from the trap of comparison. It is easy to look at other Christians and wonder why their lives seem easier, why their gifts seem greater, or why they have been spared certain sufferings. Jesus’ words apply: “What is that to you? You follow me.” Each believer is responsible for their own faithfulness to Christ.

It also helps believers accept their unique path. God’s plan for one person may involve hardships that another person does not face. Trusting God’s wisdom and love means accepting His plan without demanding that it look like someone else’s.

Finally, the passage encourages believers to keep their eyes on Jesus. Distraction, comparison, and curiosity about others can pull attention away from Him. The call is simple and personal: follow Him.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*John 21* shows that the risen Jesus meets His people in ordinary life. He came to tired fishermen at dawn, after a night of failure, and served them breakfast. Believers can expect to meet Him not only in church but at work, at home, and in the routines of daily life. When their efforts feel fruitless, they can listen for His word and trust Him for fruitfulness.

The chapter is also a powerful story of restoration. Peter had denied Jesus three times, and Jesus restored him with three questions of love and three commissions to care for His sheep. Believers who have failed Christ can take heart. He does not discard His people when they fall. He invites them to renewed love and renewed service.

*John 21* reminds believers that love for Jesus is expressed in caring for His people. Feeding and tending His sheep is the calling not only of pastors but of every believer who encourages, serves, and supports others in their faith. Love for Christ and love for His church go together.

Finally, the chapter calls each believer to follow Jesus personally, without comparing their path to anyone else’s. Peter would die as a martyr; the beloved disciple would live long. Each glorified God in his own way. Believers today are invited to trust the path Jesus gives them, to follow Him faithfully until He comes, and to remember that His story is greater than all the books the world could hold.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for meeting Your disciples on the shore after their night of failure, and for meeting me in the ordinary places of my life. When my efforts seem empty, help me to listen for Your voice and to trust You for fruitfulness. Thank You for the grace You showed Peter, restoring him after his denial and calling him again to follow You. You know everything; You know that I love You, even when my love is weak. Restore me where I have failed You, and help me to show my love by caring for Your people. Give me courage to follow You wherever You lead, even when the path is hard or not what I would choose. Keep me from comparing my path with others, and help me to keep my eyes on You until You come again. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Book 5 of 27

# Acts

## About This Book

The Acts of the Apostles is the second volume of Luke’s two-part work. Like his Gospel, it is addressed to Theophilus, and it picks up exactly where the Gospel ends, with the risen Jesus and His ascension (*Acts 1:1–11*). Luke was a companion of Paul, and in several passages he writes “we,” showing that he was present for parts of Paul’s journeys (*Acts 16:10–17*; *20:5–21*:18; *27:1–28*:16). Acts covers about thirty years, from Jesus’ ascension around A.D. 30 to Paul’s house arrest in Rome in the early 60s. Many scholars date the book to the 60s–80s A.D.

## The Shape of the Book

Jesus’ words in *Acts 1:8* provide an outline: “you will be witnesses to me in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth.” Chapters 1–7 tell of the church in Jerusalem, beginning with the coming of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost. Chapters 8–12 describe the gospel spreading to Samaria, to an Ethiopian official, to the Roman centurion Cornelius, and to Antioch, along with the dramatic conversion of Saul of Tarsus. Chapters 13–28 follow Paul’s missionary journeys through Asia Minor and Greece, his arrest in Jerusalem, his trials, and his voyage to Rome. In the first half, Peter is the leading figure; in the second, Paul.

## Themes to Watch For

Acts is often called the Acts of the Holy Spirit, because the Spirit empowers, guides, and unites the church at every turn. Luke shows the gospel crossing one barrier after another, from Jews to Samaritans to Gentiles, until it reaches the capital of the empire. He highlights the preaching of the apostles, centered on Jesus’ death and resurrection; the prayer, generosity, and fellowship of the early believers; the suffering and courage of Christ’s witnesses; and God’s sovereign hand moving His word forward despite opposition. Again and again Luke reports that “the word of God increased.” The book ends with Paul in Rome proclaiming the kingdom of God “*with all boldness, without hindrance*” (*Acts 28:31*), an open ending that invites every generation to continue the story.

## Chapters

1.  [Acts 1](#c05_ACT_001.xhtml) — The Risen Lord Ascends and His Witnesses Wait and Pray
2.  [Acts 2](#c05_ACT_002.xhtml) — Pentecost: The Spirit Poured Out and the Church Born
3.  [Acts 3](#c05_ACT_003.xhtml) — Healing in the Name of Jesus and the Call to Repent
4.  [Acts 4](#c05_ACT_004.xhtml) — Bold Witness Before the Council and a Church United in Prayer and Generosity

Acts · Chapter 1 of 28

# Acts — Chapter 1

Chapter Theme: The Risen Lord Ascends and His Witnesses Wait and Pray

[Read Acts 1 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/ACT01.htm)

Main Teaching

For forty days after His resurrection, Jesus appears to His apostles, speaks about God’s kingdom, and tells them to wait in Jerusalem for the promised Holy Spirit. He declares that they will receive power and become His witnesses from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth, and then He is taken up into heaven, while angels promise that He will return in the same way. The disciples devote themselves to prayer together, and Matthias is chosen to replace Judas among the Twelve.

## Chapter Background and Story

Acts begins where Luke’s Gospel ends. In his first book, Luke wrote about “*all that Jesus began both to do and to teach*” (*v. 1*). The word “began” is important. Acts tells what Jesus continued to do and teach after His ascension, through His Spirit and His church. The main character of Acts is not merely Peter or Paul, but the risen Lord Jesus at work through the Holy Spirit.

### Forty Days of Teaching (*1:1–5*)

Luke reminds Theophilus that Jesus “*showed himself alive after he suffered, by many proofs, appearing to them over a period of forty days and speaking about God’s Kingdom*” (*v. 3*). The resurrection was not a vague feeling or a vision. Jesus appeared repeatedly to His followers, ate with them, and taught them. Paul lists many of these appearances, including one to more than five hundred people at once (*1 Corinthians 15:3–8*). The forty days recall other significant periods in Scripture, such as Israel’s forty years in the wilderness and Jesus’ forty days of testing.

Jesus’ theme during these days was “*God’s Kingdom*” (*v. 3*), the same message He had preached throughout His ministry. Now the disciples could understand it in light of the cross and resurrection.

Jesus commanded them, “*Don’t depart from Jerusalem, but wait for the promise of the Father*” (*v. 4*). The promise was the Holy Spirit, foretold by the prophets (*Joel 2:28–29*; *Ezekiel 36:26–27*) and by Jesus Himself (*John 14:16–17*; *Luke 24:49*). John the Baptist had baptized with water, but “*you will be baptized in the Holy Spirit not many days from now*” (*v. 5*).

### The Question about the Kingdom (*1:6–8*)

The disciples asked, “*Lord, are you now restoring the kingdom to Israel?*” (*v. 6*) Their question was natural. The prophets had promised a time when God would restore Israel, defeat its enemies, and establish His rule. Now that the Messiah had risen, surely that time had come?

Jesus did not dismiss the question, but He redirected it. This is studied below.

### The Ascension (*1:9–11*)

“*When he had said these things, as they were looking, he was taken up, and a cloud received him out of their sight*” (*v. 9*). In Scripture, a cloud often signals God’s presence and glory, as with the cloud that led Israel in the wilderness and filled the tabernacle (*Exodus 40:34*), and the cloud at Jesus’ transfiguration (*Luke 9:34–35*). The ascension was not Jesus disappearing into outer space, but His entering into the presence and glory of the Father, where He now reigns. The angels’ message is studied below.

The ascension is often overlooked, but it is an essential part of the gospel. Because Jesus ascended, He now reigns at the Father’s right hand (*Ephesians 1:20–22*), intercedes for His people (*Romans 8:34*; *Hebrews 7:25*), and pours out the Spirit (*Acts 2:33*).

### Waiting in Prayer (*1:12–14*)

The disciples returned to Jerusalem from the Mount of Olives, “*a Sabbath day’s journey away*” (*v. 12*), about two-thirds of a mile, the distance a Jew could walk on the Sabbath according to tradition. They gathered in the upper room where they were staying. Luke lists the eleven apostles, matching the list in *Luke 6:14–16* without Judas Iscariot. Their prayerful waiting is studied below.

### Matthias Chosen (*1:15–26*)

During these days, about one hundred twenty believers were gathered. Peter, who had denied Jesus only weeks before but had been restored (*John 21:15–19*), now stood up to lead. He explained that Judas’s betrayal had fulfilled Scripture, spoken by the Holy Spirit through David.

Luke includes a parenthetical description of Judas’s death. Judas “*obtained a field with the reward for his wickedness; and falling headlong, his body burst open*” (*v. 18*). Matthew records that Judas hanged himself and that the priests used his returned silver to buy a potter’s field (*Matthew 27:5–8*). The accounts are often harmonized by suggesting that the field was bought in Judas’s name with his money, and that after he hanged himself, his body fell and burst open. The field became known as “*Akeldama*” (*v. 19*), meaning “The field of blood.”

Peter quoted two psalms. *Psalm 69:25* speaks of the desolation of the dwelling of those who persecute the righteous, and *Psalm 109:8* says, “*Let another take his office*” (*v. 20*). Peter concluded that someone must take Judas’s place among the Twelve.

The qualifications were specific. The new apostle had to be someone who had accompanied them “*beginning from the baptism of John to the day that he was received up from us*” (*v. 22*), so that he could “*become a witness with us of his resurrection*” (*v. 22*). The apostles’ unique role was to be eyewitnesses of Jesus’ ministry and resurrection.

Two men were nominated: Joseph called Barsabbas (also called Justus) and Matthias. The believers prayed, “*You, Lord, who know the hearts of all men, show which one of these two you have chosen*” (*v. 24*). Then they cast lots, an Old Testament practice used to discern God’s will (*Proverbs 16:33*; *1 Chronicles 24:5*), and “*the lot fell on Matthias; and he was counted with the eleven apostles*” (*v. 26*).

The number twelve mattered. Jesus had chosen twelve apostles, corresponding to the twelve tribes of Israel (*Luke 22:30*). Restoring the Twelve showed that God’s plan to renew His people was continuing. After the Spirit came at Pentecost, the church never again is recorded casting lots to make decisions; instead, believers sought the Spirit’s guidance through prayer, Scripture, and counsel (*Acts 13:2*; *15:28*).

## Important Verses Explained

### *Acts 1:7–8* — Power to Be Witnesses

> *“He said to them, ‘It isn’t for you to know times or seasons which the Father has set within his own authority. But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you. You will be witnesses to me in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth.’”*
>
> — *Acts 1:7–8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The risen Jesus had spent forty days teaching His disciples about God’s kingdom. They gathered with Him on the Mount of Olives and asked whether He was now going to restore the kingdom to Israel. They were eager for God’s promises to be fulfilled, and they wanted to know when.

Jesus answered, “*It isn’t for you to know times or seasons which the Father has set within his own authority*” (*v. 7*). The timing of God’s final plans belongs to the Father. Jesus had said something similar about His return: no one knows the day or the hour (*Mark 13:32*). The disciples did not need a timetable; they needed a mission.

“*But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you*” (*v. 8*). Instead of focusing on when the kingdom would come in fullness, they were to receive the Spirit’s power. The word “power” refers to God’s strength working through them, enabling them to do what they could not do on their own.

“*You will be witnesses to me*” (*v. 8*). A witness is someone who tells what they have seen and heard. The disciples had seen Jesus’ life, death, and resurrection. Their task was to testify about Him. Notice that Jesus says “witnesses to me.” The focus of their message was not themselves, but Jesus.

“*in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth*” (*v. 8*). Their witness would spread outward in expanding circles: first Jerusalem, the city where Jesus was crucified; then the surrounding region of Judea; then Samaria, home of the people Jews usually avoided; and finally to the ends of the earth. This verse is the outline of the book of Acts.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses reveal that God’s kingdom advances through the Spirit-empowered witness of His people. The disciples expected a political restoration. Jesus pointed them to something larger: a kingdom that would include people of every nation, spreading not by force but by the testimony of those filled with the Spirit.

They also fulfill God’s ancient promise. God told Abraham that through his offspring, “*All the nations of the earth will be blessed*” (*Genesis 22:18*). Isaiah foresaw God’s servant as “*a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth*” (*Isaiah 49:6*). Through the witness of Jesus’ followers, this promise would be fulfilled.

Finally, these verses show that witness depends on the Spirit’s power. The disciples were ordinary people, fishermen and tax collectors, who had recently abandoned Jesus in fear. Their transformation into bold witnesses would be the work of the Holy Spirit.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses remind believers that they are called to be witnesses. Every follower of Jesus has a story of what He has done and can tell others about Him. Witnessing is not only for pastors or missionaries; it is the calling of the whole church.

They also encourage believers who feel inadequate. Many people hesitate to share their faith because they feel unqualified or afraid. Jesus’ promise is that the Spirit gives power. Believers can depend on Him for the courage and words they need.

Finally, these verses help believers keep a balanced view of the future. It is natural to wonder about the timing of Jesus’ return and the end of history. But Jesus redirects attention to the present mission. Rather than speculating about dates, believers are called to live as faithful witnesses wherever God places them, beginning where they live and reaching outward.

### *Acts 1:11* — This Jesus Will Come Back

> *“who also said, ‘You men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into the sky? This Jesus, who was received up from you into the sky, will come back in the same way as you saw him going into the sky.’”*
>
> — *Acts 1:11* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jesus had just finished speaking to His disciples on the Mount of Olives. As they watched, He was lifted up, and a cloud hid Him from their sight. The disciples kept staring into the sky, perhaps stunned, perhaps hoping He would reappear.

Then two men in white clothing stood beside them. Luke had described two men in dazzling clothing at the empty tomb as well (*Luke 24:4*). These were angels, God’s messengers.

They said, “*You men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into the sky?*” (*v. 11*) The question gently moved the disciples from staring to acting. They had been given a mission, and they needed to return to Jerusalem and wait for the Spirit.

Then came the promise: “*This Jesus, who was received up from you into the sky, will come back in the same way as you saw him going into the sky*” (*v. 11*). Notice the words “This Jesus.” The same Jesus who had lived among them, died, and risen would return. He would not be replaced by someone else. And He would come back “in the same way,” personally, visibly, and in glory, with the clouds.

Jesus Himself had spoken of His return: “*Then they will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and great glory*” (*Luke 21:27*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse affirms one of the central hopes of the Christian faith: the personal, visible return of Jesus Christ. The ancient creeds of the church confess that He “will come again in glory to judge the living and the dead.” Christians hold different views about the order of events surrounding His return, but they share the confident hope that He will come.

It also reveals the connection between the ascension and the second coming. Jesus left visibly and will return visibly. The time between His ascension and His return is the age of the church’s mission, the time for His witnesses to carry the gospel to the ends of the earth.

Finally, the angels’ question shows that hope in Christ’s return should lead to faithful action, not passive waiting. Believers are not called to stand staring into the sky but to live as faithful servants, ready for their Master’s return (*Luke 12:35–40*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse gives believers hope in a troubled world. History is not moving aimlessly. The same Jesus who ascended will return to set everything right, to judge with justice, and to make all things new.

It also calls believers to live with readiness. Jesus’ return could happen at any time. This should lead believers to live faithfully, to remain in His love, and to be ready to meet Him.

Finally, the angels’ gentle rebuke encourages believers not to become so focused on the future that they neglect the present. Some people become so absorbed in end-time speculation that they lose sight of their calling. The hope of Jesus’ return is meant to strengthen believers for faithful witness and service today.

### *Acts 1:14* — With One Accord in Prayer

> *“All these with one accord continued steadfastly in prayer and supplication, along with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus, and with his brothers.”*
>
> — *Acts 1:14* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After the ascension, the disciples returned to Jerusalem as Jesus had commanded and gathered in an upper room. Luke lists the eleven apostles by name. Then he tells us what they were doing: “*All these with one accord continued steadfastly in prayer and supplication*” (*v. 14*).

Two phrases stand out. First, “*with one accord*” (*v. 14*). The believers were united in heart and purpose. Only weeks before, the disciples had argued about who was greatest (*Luke 22:24*). Now they were united. This phrase appears repeatedly in Acts to describe the early church (*Acts 2:46*; *4:24*; *5:12*).

Second, “*continued steadfastly in prayer*” (*v. 14*). They did not pray once and then stop. They persevered in prayer. Jesus had told them to wait for the Spirit, and they waited by praying.

Luke also names others who were present: “*along with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus, and with his brothers*” (*v. 14*). The women who had followed Jesus, supported His ministry, stood at the cross, and discovered the empty tomb were part of this praying community. Mary, the mother of Jesus, was there. This is the last time she is mentioned by name in the New Testament, and she is found among those praying.

Jesus’ brothers were there too. During Jesus’ ministry, they had not believed in Him (*John 7:5*). After the resurrection, they became believers. Jesus had appeared to James (*1 Corinthians 15:7*), who would later become a leader of the church in Jerusalem.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that the church was born in prayer. Before the Spirit came at Pentecost, the believers prayed together. Throughout Acts, major events are preceded by prayer: the choosing of leaders (*6:6*), the sending of missionaries (*13:3*), and deliverance from prison (*12:5*). Prayer is the atmosphere in which God’s work moves forward.

It also reveals the unity of the early church. The group in the upper room included apostles, women, Jesus’ mother, and His formerly unbelieving brothers. People with very different backgrounds and histories were united in prayer. This unity was an answer to Jesus’ prayer that His followers would be one (*John 17:21*).

Finally, the verse shows the honor given to women in the early church. Women were not on the margins of this community; they were among its faithful members, praying alongside the apostles. Luke, who in his Gospel gave special attention to women followers of Jesus, continues to show their place in the church.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to make prayer central in their lives and churches. Before acting, the early church prayed. Believers today can seek God together in prayer, especially when they face decisions, challenges, or periods of waiting.

It also calls believers to unity. The phrase “with one accord” challenges churches divided by conflict, competition, or factions. Believers are called to be united in heart and purpose, setting aside differences for the sake of Christ.

Finally, the verse offers hope for families. Jesus’ brothers once doubted Him, but now they were praying among His followers. Believers who pray for family members who do not yet believe can take heart. God can change hearts, and those who once resisted Jesus can become His faithful followers.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Acts 1* reminds believers that Jesus is alive and active. Luke’s Gospel told what Jesus began to do and teach; Acts tells what He continues to do through His Spirit and His people. Believers today are part of this ongoing story. The risen Lord is still at work in the world, and He works through those who follow Him.

The chapter also gives believers a clear mission. Jesus did not satisfy His disciples’ curiosity about timing; He gave them a calling to be His witnesses, empowered by the Spirit, from their home city to the ends of the earth. Every believer can be a witness in their own setting, telling others about Jesus with the help of the Holy Spirit.

*Acts 1* offers hope for the future. The same Jesus who ascended will return in glory. This hope keeps believers from despair and calls them to live faithfully and expectantly. At the same time, the angels’ question reminds them not to stand staring into the sky, but to get on with the work Jesus has given.

Finally, the chapter shows the importance of prayer and unity. Before the Spirit came, the believers waited together in prayer, with one accord. Churches and individual believers today can follow their example, seeking God together, waiting on Him, and preparing for what He will do.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for showing Yourself alive after Your suffering, and for continuing Your work through Your Spirit and Your people. Thank You that You reign now at the Father’s right hand. When I am curious about times and seasons, help me to trust the Father’s plan and to focus on the mission You have given me. Fill me with the power of Your Holy Spirit, and make me Your witness in my home, my community, and wherever You send me. Thank You for the promise that You will come again in glory. Help me to live ready for Your return, not standing idle, but serving You faithfully. Teach me to pray with perseverance, and unite Your church in heart and purpose. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
