Acts · Chapter 2 of 28

# Acts — Chapter 2

Chapter Theme: Pentecost: The Spirit Poured Out and the Church Born

[Read Acts 2 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/ACT02.htm)

Main Teaching

On the day of Pentecost, the Holy Spirit comes on the gathered believers with the sound of a mighty wind and tongues like fire, and they declare God’s mighty works in the languages of pilgrims from many nations. Peter explains that this fulfills Joel’s prophecy and proclaims that the crucified Jesus has been raised and exalted as Lord and Christ. Cut to the heart, about three thousand people repent and are baptized, and the new community devotes itself to the apostles’ teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread, and prayer, sharing generously and praising God with glad hearts.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Acts 2* describes one of the most important events in the history of God’s people: the coming of the Holy Spirit and the birth of the church. Jesus had told His disciples to wait in Jerusalem for “the promise of the Father” (*1:4*). Ten days after His ascension, the promise was fulfilled.

The timing was significant. Pentecost, also called the Feast of Weeks, came fifty days after Passover (the name Pentecost comes from the Greek word for “fiftieth”). It was a harvest festival when the first fruits of the wheat harvest were offered to God (*Leviticus 23:15–21*). In later Jewish tradition, it was also associated with the giving of the Law at Mount Sinai. Jesus had died at Passover as the Passover Lamb; now, at Pentecost, the Spirit came to gather the first fruits of a great harvest of people, and to write God’s law on human hearts, as the new covenant promised (*Jeremiah 31:33*; *Ezekiel 36:26–27*).

### The Coming of the Spirit (*2:1–13*)

The believers were “*all with one accord in one place*” (*v. 1*). Suddenly a sound like a violent wind filled the house. In both Hebrew and Greek, the same word can mean “wind,” “breath,” and “spirit.” The wind recalls God’s breath giving life to Adam (*Genesis 2:7*) and to the dry bones in Ezekiel’s vision (*Ezekiel 37:9–14*). Then “*Tongues like fire appeared and were distributed to them, and one sat on each of them*” (*v. 3*). Fire often signals God’s presence in Scripture, as at the burning bush and on Mount Sinai (*Exodus 3:2*; *19:18*). John the Baptist had promised that Jesus would baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire (*Luke 3:16*). The Spirit came on each person individually, not only on the leaders. This is studied below.

Jerusalem was crowded with Jewish pilgrims from across the known world, as well as “*proselytes*” (*v. 10*), Gentiles who had converted to Judaism. When they heard the sound, a crowd gathered. They were astonished, because “*everyone heard them speaking in his own language*” (*v. 6*). Luke lists the nations from the east (Parthians, Medes, Elamites, Mesopotamia), from Asia Minor, from North Africa, from Rome, and from Crete and Arabia. These Galileans, who were often looked down on as uneducated, were declaring “*the mighty works of God*” (*v. 11*) in languages they had never learned.

Many interpreters see Pentecost as a reversal of the Tower of Babel (*Genesis 11:1–9*). At Babel, God confused human languages and scattered the nations because of their pride. At Pentecost, God overcame the barrier of language so that people from many nations could hear the gospel. Babel scattered; Pentecost gathered.

Some were amazed and asked, “*What does this mean?*” (*v. 12*) Others mocked: “*They are filled with new wine*” (*v. 13*).

### Peter’s Sermon (*2:14–36*)

Peter stood up with the eleven and addressed the crowd. The man who had denied Jesus in fear before a servant girl now spoke boldly before thousands. He began by dismissing the accusation of drunkenness: it was only “*the third hour of the day*” (*v. 15*), about nine in the morning.

Instead, he said, “*this is what has been spoken through the prophet Joel*” (*v. 16*). Peter quoted *Joel 2:28–32*, studied below. He then turned to his central message: Jesus of Nazareth.

“*Jesus of Nazareth, a man approved by God to you by mighty works and wonders and signs which God did by him among you, even as you yourselves know*” (*v. 22*). Peter appealed to what his audience had seen. Jesus’ ministry had been public.

Then he described Jesus’ death: “*him, being delivered up by the determined counsel and foreknowledge of God, you have taken by the hand of lawless men, crucified and killed*” (*v. 23*). Peter held together God’s sovereign plan and human responsibility. Jesus’ death was part of God’s plan, yet those who crucified Him were guilty. (“Lawless men” probably refers to the Roman authorities, who did not know God’s law.)

“*whom God raised up, having freed him from the agony of death, because it was not possible that he should be held by it*” (*v. 24*). Death could not keep its hold on the Author of life.

Peter supported this with *Psalm 16:8–11*, in which David says, “*you will not leave my soul in Hades, neither will you allow your Holy One to see decay*” (*v. 27*). Peter pointed out that David had died and was buried, and “*his tomb is with us to this day*” (*v. 29*). David’s body had decayed. So David must have been speaking as a prophet about his descendant, the Messiah, whom God had promised to place on his throne (*2 Samuel 7:12–13*). “*This Jesus God raised up, to which we all are witnesses*” (*v. 32*).

Peter then connected the resurrection with what the crowd was seeing: “*Being therefore exalted by the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this which you now see and hear*” (*v. 33*). The risen and ascended Jesus was the one pouring out the Spirit.

Peter quoted *Psalm 110:1*: “*The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit by my right hand*” (*v. 34*) until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet. Jesus Himself had used this psalm to show that the Messiah is greater than David (*Luke 20:41–44*). Peter’s conclusion is studied below.

### The Response (*2:37–41*)

The listeners “*were cut to the heart*” (*v. 37*) and asked, “*Brothers, what shall we do?*” (*v. 37*) Peter’s answer is studied below. “*Then those who gladly received his word were baptized. There were added that day about three thousand souls*” (*v. 41*). Jesus had promised that His disciples would do “greater works” after He went to the Father (*John 14:12*). On a single day, three thousand people came to faith.

### The Life of the Early Church (*2:42–47*)

Luke describes the life of the new community, studied below. He adds that “*Fear came on every soul, and many wonders and signs were done through the apostles*” (*v. 43*). The believers shared their possessions: “*All who believed were together, and had all things in common*” (*v. 44*). They “*sold their possessions and goods, and distributed them to all, according as anyone had need*” (*v. 45*). This sharing was voluntary, not commanded (*Acts 5:4* shows that property remained the owner’s to use). It was a spontaneous expression of love, so that no one among them was in need (*Acts 4:34*), fulfilling God’s desire for His people in *Deuteronomy 15:4*.

They met daily in the temple courts and in homes, eating together “*with gladness and singleness of heart*” (*v. 46*), “*praising God and having favor with all the people. The Lord added to the assembly day by day those who were being saved*” (*v. 47*). Notice who added people to the church: the Lord. Growth was His work.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Acts 2:4* — Filled with the Holy Spirit

> *“They were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak with other languages, as the Spirit gave them the ability to speak.”*
>
> — *Acts 2:4* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The believers were gathered together on the day of Pentecost, about one hundred twenty of them, praying as they had been doing since Jesus ascended (*1:14–15*). Suddenly the sound of a mighty wind filled the house, and something like flames of fire appeared and rested on each of them.

“*They were all filled with the Holy Spirit*” (*v. 4*). Notice the word “all.” The Spirit did not come only on the apostles or on the leaders, but on every believer present, men and women, young and old. This was something new. In the Old Testament, the Spirit came upon certain individuals, such as prophets, judges, and kings, for particular tasks. Moses had once said, “*I wish that all the LORD’s people were prophets, that the LORD would put his Spirit on them!*” (*Numbers 11:29*) At Pentecost, that wish was fulfilled.

“*and began to speak with other languages, as the Spirit gave them the ability to speak*” (*v. 4*). The believers spoke in languages they had not learned. The crowd of pilgrims from many nations heard them speaking in their own native languages. The Spirit gave them this ability; it was not something they produced on their own.

What did they speak about? The crowd said, “*we hear them speaking in our languages the mighty works of God!*” (*v. 11*) The gift of languages was used to praise God and declare His works. It was the beginning of the church’s witness to the nations.

This filling with the Spirit fulfilled Jesus’ promise: “*you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you*” (*Acts 1:8*). The Spirit came to empower them for witness.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Pentecost marks the beginning of a new era in God’s dealings with His people. The Spirit now dwells in all believers, uniting them to Christ and to one another. Paul later writes, “*For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body*” (*1 Corinthians 12:13*). Pentecost was the birthday of the church as a Spirit-filled community.

Christians hold different views on how Pentecost relates to believers today. Some traditions, especially Pentecostal and charismatic churches, emphasize that believers can and should experience a distinct filling or baptism of the Spirit, often accompanied by speaking in tongues, as a continuing gift. Other traditions see Pentecost as a unique, unrepeatable event that inaugurated the church, with all believers receiving the Spirit at conversion, and they understand the miraculous signs of Acts as especially tied to the apostolic era. Many Christians hold positions between these views. All agree that every believer has the Holy Spirit (*Romans 8:9*) and that believers are called to be continually filled with the Spirit (*Ephesians 5:18*).

Finally, the gift of languages shows God’s heart for all nations. The gospel would not be limited to one language or culture. From the very first day, the church was multilingual and multinational, pointing to the vision of Revelation: a great multitude “*out of every nation and of all tribes, peoples, and languages*” (*Revelation 7:9*) worshiping God.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse reminds believers that the Christian life is meant to be lived in the power of the Spirit. The disciples did not begin their mission by their own strength. They waited for the Spirit, and He empowered them. Believers today can depend on the Spirit’s help in their witness, their struggles, and their service.

It also challenges believers to value every member of the church. The Spirit was poured out on all believers, not only on the leaders. Every believer has been given the Spirit and has a part to play in God’s work.

Finally, the verse encourages believers to celebrate the diversity of the church. God’s people come from every nation and language. Churches can reflect this by welcoming people from different backgrounds, supporting the translation of Scripture, and sharing the gospel across cultural lines.

### *Acts 2:17–18* — I Will Pour Out My Spirit on All Flesh

> *“‘It will be in the last days, says God, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh. Your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your young men will see visions. Your old men will dream dreams. Yes, and on my servants and on my handmaidens in those days, I will pour out my Spirit, and they will prophesy.”*
>
> — *Acts 2:17–18* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Some in the crowd had mocked the believers, saying they were drunk. Peter stood up and explained that this was not drunkenness but the fulfillment of a prophecy given through the prophet Joel centuries earlier (*Joel 2:28–32*).

“*It will be in the last days, says God, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh*” (*v. 17*). Peter’s quotation begins with “in the last days,” words that are not in the original Hebrew of Joel but which Peter uses to interpret the moment. The “last days” are the final era of God’s plan, which began with Jesus’ coming and will be completed at His return. Believers have been living in the “last days” since Pentecost.

“All flesh” means all kinds of people. The Spirit would not be limited by age, gender, or social status. Joel’s prophecy continues: “*Your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your young men will see visions. Your old men will dream dreams*” (*v. 17*). Both sons and daughters, both young and old, would receive the Spirit.

“*Yes, and on my servants and on my handmaidens in those days, I will pour out my Spirit, and they will prophesy*” (*v. 18*). Even servants and slaves, both men and women, would receive the Spirit. In the ancient world, social status determined much of life. God’s Spirit would be poured out on everyone who belongs to Him, regardless of status.

“Prophesy” in this context means speaking God’s message under the Spirit’s inspiration. The believers at Pentecost were declaring the mighty works of God, a form of prophecy.

The quotation ends with the promise: “*whoever will call on the name of the Lord will be saved*” (*v. 21*). Peter goes on to show that “the Lord” on whom people must call is Jesus.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This prophecy reveals the generous, inclusive nature of the Spirit’s outpouring. Under the old covenant, the Spirit’s work was mostly limited to certain leaders. Under the new covenant, every believer, man or woman, young or old, rich or poor, receives the Spirit. Paul writes that in Christ “*There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free man, there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus*” (*Galatians 3:28*).

It also shows that Pentecost marks the arrival of the last days. The cosmic signs Joel describes, the sun darkened and the moon turned to blood, have been understood in different ways. Some connect them to the darkness at Jesus’ crucifixion (*Luke 23:44–45*); others see them as pointing to events before Christ’s return; others read them as vivid prophetic language for God’s dramatic intervention in history. All agree that Pentecost begins the age that leads to “the great and glorious day of the Lord.”

Finally, the passage shows God’s initiative. He says, “I will pour out.” The Spirit is God’s gift, not a human achievement.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses remind believers that the Spirit is given to all God’s people. No believer is too young, too old, too poor, or too insignificant to be used by God. Churches are called to recognize and encourage the gifts of all their members, including women, young people, the elderly, and those with little social status.

They also encourage believers to live with a sense of urgency. The last days have begun. Believers live between Pentecost and Christ’s return, a time of opportunity for the gospel to go to all nations.

Finally, these verses invite everyone to call on the name of the Lord. The promise is for “whoever.” No one is excluded from the offer of salvation. Believers can share this hope with confidence.

### *Acts 2:36–38* — Repent and Be Baptized

> *“‘Let all the house of Israel therefore know certainly that God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified.’ Now when they heard this, they were cut to the heart, and said to Peter and the rest of the apostles, ‘Brothers, what shall we do?’ Peter said to them, Repent and be baptized, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.”*
>
> — *Acts 2:36–38* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Peter had just finished explaining that Jesus, whom the people had crucified, had been raised from the dead and exalted to God’s right hand, and that He was the one pouring out the Spirit. Then he reached his conclusion: “*Let all the house of Israel therefore know certainly that God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified*” (*v. 36*).

“Lord” was the title used for God in the Greek translation of the Old Testament. “Christ” means Messiah, the anointed King. The One they had rejected and crucified was the Lord of all and the promised Messiah. The words “this Jesus whom you crucified” brought the message home personally.

“*Now when they heard this, they were cut to the heart*” (*v. 37*). The Holy Spirit convicted them of their sin, just as Jesus had promised (*John 16:8*). They asked, “*Brothers, what shall we do?*” (*v. 37*)

Peter answered, “*Repent and be baptized, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit*” (*v. 38*). “Repent” means to change one’s mind and turn around, turning from sin and from rejecting Jesus to trusting and following Him. “Be baptized” was the outward sign of this inner change, publicly identifying with Jesus. Baptism “in the name of Jesus Christ” meant baptism by His authority and into relationship with Him.

The promises were “the forgiveness of sins” and “the gift of the Holy Spirit.” The very people who had called for Jesus’ crucifixion could be forgiven and receive the Spirit.

Peter added, “*For the promise is to you and to your children, and to all who are far off, even as many as the Lord our God will call to himself*” (*v. 39*). The promise extended across generations and to people far away, which would later include the Gentiles.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses summarize the gospel response: repentance and faith, expressed in baptism, leading to forgiveness and the gift of the Spirit. Elsewhere in Acts, forgiveness is linked with faith (*10:43*) and with repentance (*3:19*), showing that these belong together.

Christians understand the relationship between baptism and forgiveness in different ways. Some traditions, including Roman Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, and Churches of Christ, see baptism as a means through which God gives forgiveness and new life. Many evangelical and Baptist traditions understand baptism as an outward sign and public confession of the forgiveness already received through faith. Others hold positions in between. All agree that forgiveness comes through Christ and is received by faith, and that baptism is commanded by Jesus and important for every believer.

The passage also shows the astonishing grace of God. These listeners had been part of the city that rejected and crucified Jesus only seven weeks earlier. Yet the offer of forgiveness was extended to them. No sin is too great for God’s grace when people repent and turn to Christ.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses show the right response to the gospel. Hearing about Jesus is not enough; it calls for a response. Those who recognize their sin and Jesus’ lordship are called to repent, turn to Him in faith, and be baptized as a public sign of belonging to Him.

They also bring hope to those who feel their sin is too great. Peter’s listeners had rejected the Messiah. Yet God offered them forgiveness and His Spirit. Anyone who turns to Christ can be forgiven, no matter what they have done.

Finally, these verses show the importance of baptism in the Christian life. Jesus commanded it (*Matthew 28:19*), and the early church practiced it immediately. Believers who have not been baptized are encouraged to consider Jesus’ command and to take this step of obedience.

### *Acts 2:42* — Devoted to Teaching, Fellowship, Bread, and Prayer

> *“They continued steadfastly in the apostles’ teaching and fellowship, in the breaking of bread, and prayer.”*
>
> — *Acts 2:42* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After Peter’s sermon, about three thousand people were baptized and joined the believers in a single day. Suddenly there was a large community of new believers who needed to grow in their faith. Luke tells us how they lived.

“*They continued steadfastly*” (*v. 42*). The word means to persist, to be devoted, to keep at something with determination. These new believers did not simply attend occasional meetings; they were committed.

Luke names four things they were devoted to.

“*in the apostles’ teaching*” (*v. 42*). The apostles had been with Jesus and had been taught by Him, including during the forty days after His resurrection. They passed on what Jesus taught and explained how the Scriptures pointed to Him. The new believers were eager to learn. Today, the apostles’ teaching is preserved in the New Testament.

“*and fellowship*” (*v. 42*). The Greek word koinonia means sharing, partnership, or communion. It includes spending time together, caring for one another, and sharing life and possessions, as the following verses describe.

“*in the breaking of bread*” (*v. 42*). This probably refers both to shared meals and to the Lord’s Supper, which in the early church was often celebrated as part of a meal. The believers remembered Jesus’ death as He had commanded (*Luke 22:19*).

“*and prayer*” (*v. 42*). In Greek, it is literally “the prayers,” which may include both the set times of prayer at the temple and their own times of prayer together. The church that had been born in prayer (*1:14*) continued in prayer.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse describes the essential marks of a healthy church. A church grounded in the apostles’ teaching stays faithful to the truth. A church marked by fellowship expresses love and unity. A church that breaks bread together remembers Christ’s death and lives in communion with Him. A church devoted to prayer depends on God.

These four practices are not merely activities; they are means by which believers are joined to Christ and to one another. Through the apostles’ teaching, believers hear Christ’s word. Through fellowship, they experience His love in His people. Through the breaking of bread, they remember His sacrifice. Through prayer, they speak with the Father in Jesus’ name.

The verse also shows that the Spirit’s coming led to a new kind of community. The Spirit did not produce isolated, individual believers but a family devoted to God and to one another. The result was gladness, generosity, and growth (*2:46–47*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse offers a pattern for every believer and every church. Believers can examine whether they are devoted to these four practices: learning God’s word, sharing life with other believers, regularly remembering Christ at His table, and praying together.

It also challenges a consumer approach to church. The early believers did not merely attend services; they devoted themselves to a shared life. Believers today can look for ways to be more deeply involved in their church community, through small groups, shared meals, service, and prayer.

Finally, the verse encourages churches to focus on what matters most. Programs and styles vary across cultures and generations, but these four practices remain central. Churches that return to the apostles’ teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread, and prayer will find themselves on the same path as the first believers.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Acts 2* shows what happens when God pours out His Spirit. Ordinary believers were filled with power, spoke of God’s mighty works, and became bold witnesses. Believers today have the same Spirit living within them. They can depend on Him for courage, wisdom, and love, and they can trust that God still works powerfully through ordinary people who are yielded to Him.

The chapter also centers on the message of Jesus. Peter’s sermon was about Jesus’ life, death, resurrection, and exaltation as Lord and Christ. The Spirit’s coming led directly to the proclamation of Jesus. Believers today are called to keep Jesus at the center of their message, sharing the good news that He died for sins, rose again, and offers forgiveness and the Holy Spirit to all who turn to Him.

*Acts 2* shows the right response to the gospel: repentance, faith, and baptism, leading to forgiveness and the gift of the Spirit. The offer of grace extended even to those who had rejected Jesus. No one is beyond the reach of God’s forgiveness. Anyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.

Finally, the chapter paints a picture of a Spirit-filled church: devoted to the apostles’ teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread, and prayer, sharing generously, meeting with gladness, and praising God. Churches today can be renewed by returning to these essentials, and believers can find joy in living as part of such a community.

## Chapter Prayer

Holy Spirit, thank You for coming at Pentecost and for living in all who belong to Jesus. Fill me afresh with Your power, so that I may speak of the mighty works of God and bear witness to Jesus with courage and love. Lord Jesus, thank You that You were raised from the dead and exalted as Lord and Christ, and that You pour out the Spirit on Your people. I repent of my sin and turn to You again. Thank You for the forgiveness You offer and the gift of Your Spirit. Make me devoted to Your word, to fellowship with Your people, to remembering Your death at Your table, and to prayer. Fill Your church with gladness, generosity, and unity, and add to us daily those who are being saved. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Acts · Chapter 3 of 28

# Acts — Chapter 3

Chapter Theme: Healing in the Name of Jesus and the Call to Repent

[Read Acts 3 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/ACT03.htm)

Main Teaching

At the temple gate called Beautiful, Peter and John meet a man lame from birth. Having no money to give, Peter heals him in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, and the man enters the temple walking, leaping, and praising God. When a crowd gathers, Peter insists that the healing came not from their own power but from the risen Jesus, whom the people had rejected but God had glorified. He calls them to repent and turn to God, so that their sins may be blotted out and times of refreshing may come.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Acts 2* ended with a summary of the early church’s life, including the note that “many wonders and signs were done through the apostles” (*2:43*). *Acts 3* now tells one of those signs in detail. The healing of the lame man leads to Peter’s second public sermon and, in chapter 4, to the first arrest of the apostles. Luke shows how the same pattern that marked Jesus’ ministry, mighty works, bold preaching, and opposition from the authorities, now continues through His followers.

### At the Beautiful Gate (*3:1–10*)

Peter and John were going up to the temple “*at the hour of prayer, the ninth hour*” (*v. 1*), about three in the afternoon, when the evening sacrifice was offered and crowds gathered to pray. The first believers were Jewish and continued to worship at the temple, seeing their faith in Jesus as the fulfillment of Israel’s hope.

A man “*lame from his mother’s womb*” (*v. 2*) was carried each day and laid at the gate called Beautiful, probably the great Nicanor Gate, made of polished Corinthian bronze, which led into the inner courts. Luke tells us later that he was over forty years old (*4:22*). Begging near the temple was a good strategy, since worshipers on their way to pray were often in a generous mood, and giving to the poor was considered an act of righteousness. But the man was stuck at the gate. People with his kind of disability were often excluded from the inner temple courts. He spent his life outside, looking in.

When he saw Peter and John, he asked them for money. Peter looked straight at him and said, “*Look at us*” (*v. 4*). The man looked up, “*expecting to receive something from them*” (*v. 5*). Peter’s response is studied below.

Peter took him by the right hand and raised him up. “*Immediately his feet and his ankle bones received strength*” (*v. 7*). Luke, the physician, includes these anatomical details. The man did not need weeks of learning to walk; he jumped up, stood, and walked. Then he “*entered with them into the temple, walking, leaping, and praising God*” (*v. 8*). The man who had always sat outside the gate now went inside to worship. Isaiah had prophesied that in the age of God’s salvation, “*the lame man will leap like a deer*” (*Isaiah 35:6*).

All the people recognized him as the beggar from the Beautiful Gate, and “*They were filled with wonder and amazement at what had happened to him*” (*v. 10*).

### Not by Our Own Power (*3:11–16*)

The man clung to Peter and John, and a crowd ran to them in Solomon’s Porch, the long covered colonnade where Jesus had once taught (*John 10:23*). Peter saw an opportunity and spoke. He immediately redirected attention away from himself: “*why do you marvel at this man? Why do you fasten your eyes on us, as though by our own power or godliness we had made him walk?*” (*v. 12*)

Peter then pointed them to God: “*The God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the God of our fathers, has glorified his Servant Jesus*” (*v. 13*). The title “Servant” recalls the suffering servant of *Isaiah 52:13–53:12*, of whom God said, “*he will be exalted and lifted up*” (*Isaiah 52:13*). Peter then confronted the people directly. They had handed Jesus over and denied Him before Pilate, even when Pilate wanted to release Him. They had denied “*the Holy and Righteous One and asked for a murderer to be granted to you*” (*v. 14*), choosing Barabbas instead of Jesus. Peter’s words about the source of the healing are studied below.

### Repent and Turn Again (*3:17–26*)

Peter softened his tone: “*Now, brothers, I know that you did this in ignorance, as did also your rulers*” (*v. 17*). Their guilt was real, but Peter recognized that they had not fully understood what they were doing. Jesus had prayed on the cross, “*Father, forgive them, for they don't know what they are doing*” (*Luke 23:34*). Their ignorance did not excuse them, but it left room for mercy.

Peter added that God had used even their sin to fulfill His plan: “*the things which God announced by the mouth of all his prophets, that Christ should suffer, he thus fulfilled*” (*v. 18*). Then he called them to respond, studied below.

Peter supported his appeal with Scripture. Moses had promised, “*The Lord God will raise up a prophet for you from among your brothers, like me. You shall listen to him in all things whatever he says to you*” (*v. 22*) (*Deuteronomy 18:15*). Jesus is that Prophet. Anyone who refused to listen to Him would be cut off from God’s people (*Deuteronomy 18:19*). All the prophets from Samuel onward had spoken of these days.

Peter reminded his listeners of their privilege: “*You are the children of the prophets, and of the covenant which God made with our fathers*” (*v. 25*). God had promised Abraham, “*All the families of the earth will be blessed through your offspring*” (*v. 25*) (*Genesis 22:18*). That promise was being fulfilled in Jesus. Peter concluded, “*God, having raised up his servant Jesus, sent him to you first to bless you, in turning away every one of you from your wickedness*” (*v. 26*). The word “first” hints that the blessing would also go beyond Israel to all the families of the earth. And the blessing itself is described as being turned away from sin.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Acts 3:6* — What I Have, That I Give You

> *“But Peter said, ‘I have no silver or gold, but what I have, that I give you. In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, get up and walk!’”*
>
> — *Acts 3:6* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

A man who had been unable to walk since birth sat every day at the temple gate called Beautiful, asking for money from people going in to pray. He had done this for years. When Peter and John came by, he asked them for a gift, as he asked everyone.

Peter looked at him intently and said, “Look at us.” The man looked up, expecting money. Then Peter said, “*I have no silver or gold*” (*v. 6*). The apostles were not wealthy. The early church had shared its possessions with those in need, and Peter likely had little money of his own.

“*but what I have, that I give you*” (*v. 6*). Peter had something far more valuable than money. He had the authority and power of Jesus.

“*In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, get up and walk!*” (*v. 6*) To act “in the name” of someone meant to act with that person’s authority, as their representative. Peter did not claim power of his own. He spoke in the name of Jesus, the One who had healed the lame during His ministry and who now reigned as the risen Lord. The mention of “Nazareth” connected this healing with the man Jesus whom many in Jerusalem had seen and heard.

Peter did not stop at words. “*He took him by the right hand and raised him up*” (*v. 7*). The healing was immediate and complete.

The man had asked for money to survive one more day. He received the ability to walk, a new life, and an encounter with the power of Jesus.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that the church’s greatest gift to the world is Jesus. Money and material help are important, and the early church gave generously to those in need. But the deepest need of every person is Christ Himself. The church may not always have silver and gold, but it always has the name of Jesus to share.

It also shows that the power of the early church came from the risen Christ. Peter healed in Jesus’ name, just as Jesus had promised that His followers would do works in His name (*John 14:12–14*). The healing demonstrated that Jesus was alive and active.

Finally, the healing is a sign of God’s kingdom. Isaiah had foretold that when God came to save His people, the lame would leap. The man walking and leaping in the temple courts was a living sign that the age of salvation had arrived through Jesus.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers who feel they have little to offer. Many believers do not have wealth, influence, or special talents. But every believer has something to give: the love of Christ, the message of the gospel, prayer, encouragement, and their own presence. What believers have in Christ is always worth sharing.

It also challenges believers to look at people the way Peter did. Many people walked past the lame man every day without truly seeing him. Peter stopped, looked at him, and engaged with him. Believers can learn to notice those who are overlooked and to offer them both practical help and the hope of Christ.

Finally, the verse reminds believers that God sometimes gives more than people ask for. The man asked for money and received healing. Believers can bring their needs to God with confidence, knowing that He is able to do far more than they ask or imagine (*Ephesians 3:20*).

### *Acts 3:15–16* — The Prince of Life

> *“and killed the Prince of life, whom God raised from the dead, to which we are witnesses. By faith in his name, his name has made this man strong, whom you see and know. Yes, the faith which is through him has given him this perfect soundness in the presence of you all.”*
>
> — *Acts 3:15–16* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After the lame man was healed, a crowd gathered in amazement. Peter quickly made it clear that he and John had not healed the man by their own power or holiness. He pointed instead to Jesus.

He reminded the people of what they had done. They had denied the Holy and Righteous One, asked for a murderer to be released, and “*killed the Prince of life*” (*v. 15*). The word translated “Prince” can also mean “Author,” “Originator,” or “Leader.” It describes someone who is the source or pioneer of something. Jesus is the source of life itself. The tragic irony is that people put to death the very One who gives life.

“*whom God raised from the dead, to which we are witnesses*” (*v. 15*). Human beings killed Him, but God raised Him. The apostles were eyewitnesses of the risen Christ.

Then Peter explained the healing: “*By faith in his name, his name has made this man strong, whom you see and know*” (*v. 16*). It was the name of Jesus, His power and authority, that healed the man. And this power was received “by faith.” Peter does not say whose faith; it may have been the faith of the apostles, or of the man, or both.

“*Yes, the faith which is through him has given him this perfect soundness in the presence of you all*” (*v. 16*). Notice that even faith comes “through him.” Faith is not a human achievement that earns healing; it is itself a gift that comes through Jesus. The healing was complete, “perfect soundness,” and public, done “in the presence of you all.”

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The title “Prince of life” reveals Jesus’ identity as the source and Lord of life. John’s Gospel says of the Word, “*In him was life*” (*John 1:4*). The One who gives life could not be held by death. His resurrection proves that He is the Author of life, and He gives life to all who trust in Him.

These verses also show the contrast between human rejection and divine vindication. People killed Jesus; God raised Him. This contrast appears again and again in the apostles’ preaching (*Acts 2:23–24*; *4:10*; *5:30*). God overturned the world’s verdict on Jesus.

Finally, the passage shows that faith and the name of Jesus work together. Faith is not a force in itself; its power lies in its object, Jesus. Even faith is received through Him. This keeps all the glory with Christ.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses remind believers that Jesus is the source of life. Whatever believers need, whether forgiveness, healing, strength, or hope, comes from Him. They can turn to Him as the Author of life in every situation.

They also teach believers to give God the credit for what He does through them. Peter refused to accept praise for the healing. When God works through believers, they are called to point others to Jesus rather than drawing attention to themselves.

Finally, these verses encourage believers to place their faith in Jesus Himself rather than in their own faith. Some people worry that their faith is too weak. The power is not in the strength of faith but in the One in whom faith is placed. Even small faith in a great Savior is enough to receive His help.

### *Acts 3:19–21* — Times of Refreshing

> *“Repent therefore, and turn again, that your sins may be blotted out, so that there may come times of refreshing from the presence of the Lord, and that he may send Christ Jesus, who was ordained for you before, whom heaven must receive until the times of restoration of all things, which God spoke long ago by the mouth of his holy prophets.”*
>
> — *Acts 3:19–21* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Peter had told the crowd that they had rejected and killed Jesus, the Prince of life, but that God had raised Him from the dead. He acknowledged that they had acted in ignorance, and that God had used their actions to fulfill what the prophets had foretold about the Messiah’s suffering. Now he called them to respond.

“*Repent therefore, and turn again*” (*v. 19*). “Repent” means to change one’s mind and heart. “Turn again” means to turn back to God. Together, these words describe a complete change of direction, turning away from sin and unbelief and turning toward God through faith in Jesus.

Peter then described what would follow. First, “*that your sins may be blotted out*” (*v. 19*). The image is of writing being wiped away from a page. In the ancient world, ink on papyrus could be wiped clean. God would erase their record of sin completely.

Second, “*so that there may come times of refreshing from the presence of the Lord*” (*v. 19*). Repentance leads to renewal. God’s presence brings refreshment, like cool water to a weary traveler.

Third, “*and that he may send Christ Jesus, who was ordained for you before*” (*v. 20*). Peter looked forward to Jesus’ return. Jesus had been appointed as the Messiah for Israel, and He would come again.

“*whom heaven must receive until the times of restoration of all things, which God spoke long ago by the mouth of his holy prophets*” (*v. 21*). Jesus is now in heaven, reigning at the Father’s right hand. He will remain there until the time when God restores everything, as the prophets foretold. This restoration includes the renewal of creation, the end of sin and death, and the fulfillment of all God’s promises.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show the full scope of salvation. It begins with personal repentance and forgiveness, continues with times of refreshing through God’s presence, and reaches its completion in the restoration of all things at Christ’s return. Salvation is personal, present, and future.

They also reveal that God’s plan includes the renewal of all creation. Paul writes that creation itself “*will be delivered from the bondage of decay into the liberty of the glory of the children of God*” (*Romans 8:21*). The prophets foresaw a renewed world where righteousness dwells, and Revelation describes a new heaven and a new earth (*Revelation 21:1–5*).

Finally, these verses show the urgency and hope of the gospel call. Peter’s listeners had rejected the Messiah, yet the door of repentance was open to them. God’s offer of forgiveness and refreshment is extended even to those who have resisted Him.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses invite everyone to repent and turn to God. Repentance is not only for people who have committed obvious sins; it is for all who need forgiveness and new life. Believers also continue to repent as God reveals areas of their lives that need to change.

They also promise refreshment. Many people are spiritually weary, burdened by guilt or by the pressures of life. Turning to God brings times of refreshing from His presence. Believers can return to Him regularly in confession, prayer, and worship to find renewal.

Finally, these verses give believers hope for the future. Jesus will return, and God will restore all things. The brokenness of the world is not permanent. Believers can live with hope, working for good now while waiting for the day when God makes everything new.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Acts 3* shows that the risen Jesus is still at work. The healing of the lame man demonstrated that Jesus’ power had not ended with His ascension; it continued through His followers. Believers today can trust that Christ is alive and active, and that He can work through ordinary people who act in His name.

The chapter also shows what the church has to offer the world. Peter had no silver or gold, but he had the name of Jesus. Believers may not always have material resources to give, but they always have Christ to share. They can offer both practical care and the hope of the gospel, paying attention to people who are often overlooked.

*Acts 3* models humility in ministry. Peter refused to take credit for the healing and pointed the crowd to Jesus. When God uses believers, they are called to give Him the glory, and to remember that even faith comes through Christ.

Finally, the chapter calls everyone to repent and turn to God. Peter’s listeners had rejected Jesus, yet they were offered forgiveness, refreshment, and a share in God’s future restoration. No one is beyond God’s mercy. Believers can respond to this call personally and share it with others, holding out the hope of sins blotted out and of a world one day made new.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, You are the Prince of life, whom God raised from the dead. Thank You that Your power did not end when You ascended, but continues through Your people. Help me to see the people around me who are overlooked, as Peter saw the man at the gate. When I feel that I have little to offer, remind me that I always have You to share. Keep me humble, so that I point others to You and never take the glory for myself. I repent of my sins and turn to You again. Thank You for blotting out my sins and for the times of refreshing that come from Your presence. Fill me with hope for the day when You return and restore all things. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Acts · Chapter 4 of 28

# Acts — Chapter 4

Chapter Theme: Bold Witness Before the Council and a Church United in Prayer and Generosity

[Read Acts 4 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/ACT04.htm)

Main Teaching

Peter and John are arrested for proclaiming the resurrection of Jesus. Filled with the Holy Spirit, Peter tells the council that the lame man was healed in the name of Jesus, whom they crucified and God raised, and declares that there is salvation in no other name. The leaders, astonished at the boldness of these ordinary men, order them to stop speaking about Jesus, but they answer that they cannot help telling what they have seen and heard. The church responds with prayer for boldness, the place is shaken, and the believers share everything so that no one among them is in need.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Acts 4* records the first official opposition to the church. The same council that condemned Jesus now confronts His apostles. Jesus had warned His disciples that they would be brought before rulers and authorities, and He had promised that the Holy Spirit would give them words to speak (*Luke 12:11–12*; *21:12–15*). In this chapter, that promise is fulfilled.

### Arrested for Preaching the Resurrection (*4:1–4*)

While Peter was still speaking to the crowd in Solomon’s Porch, the priests, the captain of the temple (the officer responsible for temple security), and the Sadducees arrived. They were “*upset because they taught the people and proclaimed in Jesus the resurrection from the dead*” (*v. 2*). The Sadducees were the priestly aristocracy who controlled the temple. They did not believe in the resurrection of the dead (*Luke 20:27*). The apostles’ message that Jesus had risen challenged both their beliefs and their authority.

They arrested Peter and John and held them overnight. But Luke notes that the message could not be locked up: “*many of those who heard the word believed, and the number of the men came to be about five thousand*” (*v. 4*). Opposition did not stop the growth of the church.

### Before the Council (*4:5–12*)

The next morning, the Sanhedrin gathered: the rulers, elders, and scribes. Luke names Annas, Caiaphas, John, Alexander, and other members of the high priest’s family. These were the same men who had examined Jesus only weeks earlier (*John 18:13*, 24). Now Peter and John stood before them.

They asked, “*By what power, or in what name, have you done this?*” (*v. 7*) Then “*Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit*” (*v. 8*), answered. The man who had denied Jesus before a servant girl now stood boldly before the highest court in the land. Peter pointed out that they were being questioned about “*a good deed done to a crippled man*” (*v. 9*). Then he declared that the healing had been done “*in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead*” (*v. 10*).

Peter quoted *Psalm 118:22*: “*the stone which was regarded as worthless by you, the builders, which has become the head of the corner*” (*v. 11*). Jesus had applied this verse to Himself after the parable of the wicked tenants (*Luke 20:17*). The religious leaders, the “*builders*” (*Luke 20:17*) of Israel, had rejected Jesus as useless, but God had made Him the cornerstone of His new temple, the foundation of everything. Peter’s conclusion is studied below.

### The Council’s Dilemma (*4:13–22*)

The leaders were astonished. Their reaction is studied below. They could not deny the miracle, since the healed man was standing right there. They sent the apostles out and discussed what to do. They admitted, “*a notable miracle has been done through them, as can be plainly seen by all who dwell in Jerusalem, and we can’t deny it*” (*v. 16*). Yet instead of considering whether the apostles’ message might be true, they decided to stop it from spreading: “*let’s threaten them, that from now on they don’t speak to anyone in this name*” (*v. 17*).

They called Peter and John back and ordered them not to speak or teach at all in the name of Jesus. The apostles’ answer is studied below. The council threatened them further but let them go, because the people were praising God for the healing of a man who had been lame for over forty years.

### The Church Prays (*4:23–31*)

When Peter and John were released, they went to the other believers and reported what had happened. The church’s response was to pray. Their prayer is studied below. They began by acknowledging God as the Creator: “*O Lord, you are God, who made the sky, the earth, the sea, and all that is in them*” (*v. 24*). Then they quoted *Psalm 2:1–2*, which speaks of the nations raging and the rulers plotting “*against the Lord, and against his Christ*” (*v. 26*). They saw this fulfilled in what had happened to Jesus: Herod, Pilate, the Gentiles, and the people of Israel had gathered against Him, “*to do whatever your hand and your counsel foreordained to happen*” (*v. 28*). Even the worst human rebellion could not overturn God’s plan.

### One Heart and Soul (*4:32–37*)

Luke describes the life of the church again: “*The multitude of those who believed were of one heart and soul. Not one of them claimed that anything of the things which he possessed was his own, but they had all things in common*” (*v. 32*). Their unity was not only spiritual but practical. They did not hold on to their possessions as if they belonged only to themselves.

“*With great power, the apostles gave their testimony of the resurrection of the Lord Jesus. Great grace was on them all*” (*v. 33*). The resurrection remained the center of the apostles’ message, and God’s grace was evident in the whole community.

“*For neither was there among them any who lacked*” (*v. 34*). This fulfilled God’s intention for Israel: “*there will be no poor with you*” (*Deuteronomy 15:4*). Property owners sold land or houses and brought the money to the apostles, who distributed it to those in need. This was voluntary and based on need, not a system that abolished private property; Peter later reminds Ananias that his property was his own to keep (*5:4*).

Luke introduces one man by name as an example: “*Joses, who by the apostles was also called Barnabas (which is, being interpreted, Son of Encouragement), a Levite, a man of Cyprus by race*” (*v. 36*). He sold a field and brought the money to the apostles. Barnabas will become one of the most important figures in Acts. He will vouch for Paul when others are afraid of him (*9:27*), encourage the new church in Antioch (*11:22–24*), and travel with Paul on his first missionary journey (*13:2*). His nickname fit him perfectly.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Acts 4:12* — No Other Name

> *“There is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven that is given among men, by which we must be saved!”*
>
> — *Acts 4:12* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Peter and John stood before the Sanhedrin, the same council that had condemned Jesus. They were being questioned about how they had healed a man who had been lame from birth. Peter explained that the man had been healed by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom the council had crucified and God had raised from the dead.

Then Peter moved from physical healing to spiritual salvation: “*There is salvation in no one else*” (*v. 12*). The Greek word for “salvation” is related to the word for being “made whole” or “healed” (*4:9*). The lame man had been made whole through Jesus’ name. In the same way, salvation, being made whole spiritually and rescued from sin and death, is found only in Jesus.

“*for there is no other name under heaven that is given among men, by which we must be saved!*” (*v. 12*) A “name” in Scripture represents a person’s identity, character, and authority. Peter declared that no other person, religion, or power in all the world can save. God has given only one name for salvation: Jesus.

Notice the word “given.” Salvation through Jesus is God’s gift to humanity. It is not a human invention or achievement. And notice the word “must.” Salvation is not optional; all people need it, and there is only one way to receive it.

Peter spoke these words to the most powerful religious leaders in Israel. He did not soften his message to avoid offense. He told them plainly that the Jesus they had rejected was the only Savior.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse expresses one of the central convictions of the Christian faith: Jesus is the only Savior. Jesus Himself said, “*No one comes to the Father, except through me*” (*John 14:6*). Paul writes, “*For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus*” (*1 Timothy 2:5*). The uniqueness of Christ flows from who He is, the Son of God, and what He has done, dying for sins and rising again.

It also shows that this exclusive claim is the foundation of a universal invitation. Because there is only one Savior, His salvation is offered to all. The name of Jesus is “given among men,” meaning it is available to all people everywhere. No one is excluded because of nationality, background, or past.

Finally, this verse shows the courage of the early church. Claiming that Jesus is the only Savior was unpopular then, as it often is now. The apostles proclaimed it anyway, because they believed it was true and because they loved those who needed to hear it.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse gives believers confidence in the gospel. In a world of many beliefs and spiritual options, believers can be sure that Jesus is the Savior. They do not need to search elsewhere for salvation.

It also calls believers to share this message with love and humility. The claim that Jesus is the only Savior can be offensive if spoken with arrogance. Believers are not better than others; they have simply received a gift that is offered to everyone. They can share it with gentleness and respect (*1 Peter 3:15*), honoring the people they speak with even when they disagree.

Finally, the verse encourages believers to pray and work for the spread of the gospel. If salvation is found only in Jesus, then sharing His name is the most loving thing believers can do. This motivates mission, evangelism, Bible translation, and support for those who carry the gospel to places where His name is not yet known.

### *Acts 4:13* — They Had Been with Jesus

> *“Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and had perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marveled. They recognized that they had been with Jesus.”*
>
> — *Acts 4:13* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The members of the Sanhedrin were among the most educated and powerful men in Israel. They were experts in the Law, trained in rabbinic schools, and accustomed to respect. Standing before them were Peter and John, two former fishermen from Galilee.

“*Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John*” (*v. 13*). “Boldness” means courage and freedom in speaking, especially in the face of danger. Peter and John did not cower before the council. They spoke clearly and confidently about Jesus.

“*and had perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marveled*” (*v. 13*). The words “unlearned and ignorant” do not mean that the apostles were foolish or illiterate. They mean that they had not received formal training in the rabbinic schools. They were laymen, not professional scholars. Yet they spoke with wisdom and power and used Scripture skillfully.

“*They recognized that they had been with Jesus*” (*v. 13*). The council remembered Jesus, who had also taught with authority without formal rabbinic training (*John 7:15*). They saw in Peter and John the same boldness and authority they had seen in Jesus. The apostles’ time with Jesus had shaped them.

The source of their boldness was also the Holy Spirit, who had filled Peter as he spoke (*4:8*). Their time with Jesus and the presence of His Spirit had transformed these ordinary men.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that God uses ordinary people. The apostles had no special credentials, yet God used them to turn the world upside down. Paul writes that God chose “*the foolish things of the world that he might put to shame those who are wise*” (*1 Corinthians 1:27*). God’s power is displayed through human weakness.

It also shows that time with Jesus transforms people. The apostles had spent three years with Jesus, listening to His teaching, watching His life, and learning His ways. That relationship changed them so deeply that others could see it. Paul describes believers being “*transformed into the same image from glory to glory*” (*2 Corinthians 3:18*) as they behold the Lord’s glory.

Finally, the verse shows the work of the Spirit in giving boldness. The same Peter who had denied Jesus in fear was now fearless. The difference was not merely his own resolve but the Spirit’s power.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers who feel unqualified. Many believers think they cannot share their faith or serve God because they lack education, training, or special gifts. God does not require credentials. He uses ordinary people who have been with Jesus and are filled with His Spirit.

It also invites believers to spend time with Jesus. Today, believers spend time with Him through prayer, reading Scripture, worship, and fellowship with other believers. As they do, they are shaped by Him, and others may notice the difference.

Finally, the verse challenges believers to consider what others see in them. The council recognized that Peter and John had been with Jesus. Believers can ask God to make their lives, words, and character reflect Him so clearly that others are drawn to Christ.

### *Acts 4:19–20* — We Can’t Help Telling What We Saw and Heard

> *“But Peter and John answered them, ‘Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, judge for yourselves, for we can’t help telling the things which we saw and heard.’”*
>
> — *Acts 4:19–20* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The Sanhedrin could not deny that a miracle had happened. Everyone in Jerusalem knew about it. But the leaders were determined to stop the message about Jesus from spreading. They called Peter and John back and “*commanded them not to speak at all nor teach in the name of Jesus*” (*v. 18*).

This was a serious command. The Sanhedrin had religious and civil authority, and disobeying it could lead to punishment. Peter and John had to choose between obeying human authorities and obeying God.

They answered, “*Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, judge for yourselves*” (*v. 19*). They respectfully but firmly pointed out that the council was asking them to disobey God. Jesus had commanded them to be His witnesses (*1:8*). They could not obey both.

“*for we can’t help telling the things which we saw and heard*” (*v. 20*). The apostles had seen Jesus’ life, death, and resurrection. They had heard His teaching. What they had experienced was so real and so important that they could not keep silent. It was not merely that they would not stop; they could not stop.

Notice the respectful tone of their answer. They did not insult the council or call for rebellion. They simply stated that they must obey God. Later, when the council again ordered them to stop, Peter said, “*We must obey God rather than men*” (*Acts 5:29*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses establish an important principle for believers: when human authorities command what God forbids, or forbid what God commands, believers must obey God. Scripture generally calls believers to respect and obey governing authorities (*Romans 13:1–7*; *1 Peter 2:13–17*). But this obedience has limits. God’s authority is higher than any human authority.

They also reveal the nature of true witness. The apostles spoke because they had encountered Jesus. Their witness was rooted in personal experience of real events. Christian witness is not repeating secondhand ideas but telling what God has done.

Finally, these verses show the inner compulsion of the gospel. The prophet Jeremiah once said that God’s word was like “*a burning fire shut up in my bones*” (*Jeremiah 20:9*), and he could not hold it in. The apostles felt the same. When people truly encounter Christ, they cannot help sharing Him.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to remain faithful to God even under pressure. In many parts of the world, believers face laws or threats that forbid them from sharing their faith. In other places, the pressure is social rather than legal. In every setting, believers are called to obey God first, while treating authorities with respect.

They also call believers to share what they have experienced. Every believer has a story of what Jesus has done in their life. Sharing this story is a natural and powerful form of witness.

Finally, these verses invite believers to examine their passion for Christ. The apostles could not help speaking about Him. If believers find it easy to stay silent about Jesus, they can ask God to renew their love for Him and their awareness of what He has done, so that their witness flows from a full heart.

### *Acts 4:29–31* — Grant Your Servants Boldness

> *“Now, Lord, look at their threats, and grant to your servants to speak your word with all boldness, while you stretch out your hand to heal; and that signs and wonders may be done through the name of your holy Servant Jesus. When they had prayed, the place was shaken where they were gathered together. They were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and they spoke the word of God with boldness.”*
>
> — *Acts 4:29–31* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After Peter and John were released and told the other believers about the council’s threats, the church gathered to pray. They did not complain, panic, or plan revenge. They lifted their voices to God together.

Their prayer began by acknowledging God’s sovereignty over creation and history. They quoted *Psalm 2*, which describes the nations and rulers raging against God and His anointed King, and they recognized that this had been fulfilled in the opposition to Jesus. Yet even this opposition had accomplished only what God had planned.

Then they made their request: “*Now, Lord, look at their threats*” (*v. 29*). They brought the threats before God, trusting Him to see and respond.

“*and grant to your servants to speak your word with all boldness*” (*v. 29*). Remarkably, they did not ask God to remove the danger or punish their enemies. They asked for boldness to keep speaking His word. Their concern was faithfulness, not safety.

“*while you stretch out your hand to heal; and that signs and wonders may be done through the name of your holy Servant Jesus*” (*v. 30*). They asked God to continue confirming His word through miracles, as He had done with the lame man.

God answered immediately: “*When they had prayed, the place was shaken where they were gathered together. They were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and they spoke the word of God with boldness*” (*v. 31*). The shaking of the place was a sign of God’s presence and power, recalling the shaking of Mount Sinai (*Exodus 19:18*). The believers were filled with the Spirit again, and God gave exactly what they had asked for: boldness.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This prayer shows how believers can respond to persecution. They turned first to God, acknowledging His sovereignty. They saw their situation in light of Scripture. They asked not for comfort but for courage to continue God’s work. This kind of prayer reflects deep trust in God’s purposes.

It also shows that the filling of the Spirit is not a one-time event. The believers had been filled at Pentecost, and they were filled again here. Paul later commands believers to “*be filled with the Spirit*” (*Ephesians 5:18*), using a verb that suggests continual filling. Believers need the Spirit’s fresh empowering for each new challenge.

Finally, the passage reveals the power of united prayer. The believers prayed together with one voice, and God answered powerfully. Throughout Acts, prayer precedes and accompanies the advance of the gospel.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This prayer offers a model for believers facing opposition or pressure. Instead of asking only for relief, believers can ask for boldness to remain faithful. They can bring their fears to God, remember His sovereignty, and ask for courage to keep speaking His word.

It also encourages believers to pray together. Many churches pray mainly for physical needs, which is good and right. The early church also prayed for boldness in witness. Believers can pray for one another’s courage and faithfulness, especially for those who face persecution.

Finally, the passage reminds believers that God answers prayer. The early church asked for boldness, and God gave it. Believers can pray with confidence, trusting that God hears and responds according to His will.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Acts 4* shows that faithful witness may bring opposition. Peter and John were arrested and threatened for proclaiming Jesus. Believers today may face resistance as well, whether through laws, social pressure, ridicule, or rejection. This chapter reminds them that opposition is not a sign that God has abandoned them; it is part of following a rejected and risen Lord.

The chapter also shows the source of the apostles’ courage. They had been with Jesus, and they were filled with the Holy Spirit. Believers today can grow in boldness by spending time with Jesus and depending on His Spirit. God uses ordinary people, not because of their credentials, but because of His presence in them.

*Acts 4* proclaims a clear message: there is salvation in no other name than Jesus. This truth gives believers confidence and urgency. They are called to share the name of Jesus with humility and love, trusting that He alone can save.

Finally, the chapter shows a church that responds to threats with prayer and to need with generosity. The believers prayed for boldness rather than safety, and God filled them with His Spirit. They shared their possessions so that no one was in need. Believers today can follow their example, praying together for courage, caring for one another practically, and encouraging one another like Barnabas.

## Chapter Prayer

Sovereign Lord, You made the heavens, the earth, the sea, and everything in them. Nothing happens outside Your hand. Thank You that there is salvation in Jesus, the name given among us by which we must be saved. Make me bold to speak of Him, and help me to share His name with humility and love. Let my life show that I have been with Jesus. When I face pressure to be silent, help me to obey You rather than people, and to speak respectfully but faithfully. Look at the threats Your people face around the world, and grant Your servants boldness. Fill me again with Your Holy Spirit. Make Your church one in heart and soul, generous with what we have, so that no one among us is in need. Raise up encouragers like Barnabas, and make me one of them. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
