Acts · Chapter 5 of 28

# Acts — Chapter 5

Chapter Theme: Holiness in the Church and Joy in Suffering for Jesus’ Name

[Read Acts 5 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/ACT05.htm)

Main Teaching

Ananias and Sapphira lie to the Holy Spirit about a gift they claim to have given in full, and both fall dead, filling the church with holy fear. The apostles perform many signs, multitudes believe, and when the jealous high priest jails them, an angel sets them free to keep preaching. Brought before the council again, Peter declares that God has exalted the crucified Jesus as Prince and Savior. The Pharisee Gamaliel warns the council that if this movement is from God, they cannot stop it. The apostles are flogged and leave rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer for Jesus’ name.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Acts 4* ended with a picture of a generous, united church, highlighted by Barnabas, who sold a field and gave the money to the apostles. *Acts 5* opens with a shocking contrast: a couple who pretend to be as generous as Barnabas while secretly holding back. The chapter then returns to the growing conflict between the apostles and the Jerusalem authorities. Throughout, Luke shows that the church faces danger from within, through hypocrisy, and from without, through persecution, and that God protects His church in both.

### Ananias and Sapphira (*5:1–11*)

Ananias and his wife Sapphira sold a piece of property. They kept back part of the money and brought the rest to the apostles, presenting it as if it were the full amount. Sapphira knew about the plan. Peter’s response is studied below.

When Peter confronted Ananias, he fell down and died. “*Great fear came on all who heard these things*” (*v. 5*). The young men wrapped his body and buried him. About three hours later, Sapphira came in, unaware of what had happened. Peter gave her an opportunity to tell the truth: “*Tell me whether you sold the land for so much*” (*v. 8*). She answered, “*Yes, for so much*” (*v. 8*), repeating the lie. Peter said, “*How is it that you have agreed together to tempt the Spirit of the Lord?*” (*v. 9*) She too fell down and died.

This is one of the most sobering stories in the New Testament. Many readers find it troubling. Several things help explain it. First, the sin was not keeping part of the money, which was entirely their right, but lying to God and to the church to gain a reputation for generosity they did not deserve. Second, this happened at the very beginning of the church’s life, when God’s presence was being powerfully revealed, much as Nadab and Abihu were struck down at the beginning of Israel’s worship in the tabernacle (*Leviticus 10:1–2*), and Achan was judged at the beginning of Israel’s conquest of the land (*Joshua 7*). Third, God’s judgment here was unusual, not His normal way of dealing with believers’ sins; elsewhere in Acts and the letters, sin in the church is addressed through confrontation, discipline, and restoration. The story shows how seriously God takes hypocrisy and deception among His people.

“*Great fear came on the whole assembly, and on all who heard these things*” (*v. 11*). This is the first time Luke uses the word “assembly” (often translated “church”) in Acts. The holy fear that came on the church was not terror of a cruel God, but a deep reverence for His holiness.

### Signs and Growth (*5:12–16*)

The apostles performed many signs and wonders. The believers met together “*with one accord in Solomon’s porch*” (*v. 12*). Luke notes that “*None of the rest dared to join them; however, the people honored them*” (*v. 13*). After what happened to Ananias and Sapphira, no one joined the church casually. Yet “*More believers were added to the Lord, multitudes of both men and women*” (*v. 14*).

People brought the sick into the streets, hoping that even Peter’s shadow would fall on them. Crowds came from towns around Jerusalem, bringing the sick and those tormented by unclean spirits, “*and they were all healed*” (*v. 16*). This recalls the ministry of Jesus, when people sought to touch even the fringe of His garment (*Mark 6:56*). The same power that worked through Jesus now worked through His apostles.

### Arrest and Angelic Release (*5:17–26*)

The high priest and the Sadducees “*laid hands on the apostles, then put them in public custody*” (*v. 18*). Luke says they were “*filled with jealousy*” (*v. 17*). The apostles’ popularity threatened their authority.

But “*an angel of the Lord opened the prison doors by night, and brought them out*” (*v. 19*). The irony is striking: the Sadducees did not believe in angels (*Acts 23:8*), yet an angel released their prisoners. The angel commanded, “*Go stand and speak in the temple to the people all the words of this life*” (*v. 20*). The gospel is a message of life.

At daybreak, the apostles were back in the temple teaching. When the council met and sent for the prisoners, the officers reported, “*We found the prison shut and locked, and the guards standing before the doors, but when we opened them, we found no one inside!*” (*v. 23*) The leaders were baffled. Then someone reported that the men were standing in the temple teaching the people. The captain brought them back, but without force, because the officers feared the people might stone them.

### Before the Council Again (*5:27–33*)

The high priest said, “*Didn’t we strictly command you not to teach in this name? Behold, you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching, and intend to bring this man’s blood on us*” (*v. 28*). His words were an unintentional compliment: the apostles had filled Jerusalem with their teaching. And the leaders, who had once said of Jesus, “*May his blood be on us and on our children!*” (*Matthew 27:25*), now resented being blamed for His death.

Peter and the apostles answered, “*We must obey God rather than men*” (*v. 29*), restating the principle they had expressed before (*4:19–20*). Then they proclaimed the gospel again, studied below. The council was furious and wanted to kill them.

### Gamaliel’s Advice (*5:34–40*)

A Pharisee named Gamaliel, “*a teacher of the law, honored by all the people*” (*v. 34*), stood up. Gamaliel was one of the most respected rabbis of his time, and the apostle Paul had studied under him (*Acts 22:3*). He had the apostles removed and gave the council advice, studied below.

The council accepted his advice. But they still had the apostles flogged, probably with the thirty-nine lashes prescribed by Jewish law (*Deuteronomy 25:3*; *2 Corinthians 11:24*), and ordered them again not to speak in Jesus’ name. The apostles’ response is studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Acts 5:3–4* — You Have Not Lied to Men, but to God

> *“But Peter said, ‘Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit and to keep back part of the price of the land? While you kept it, didn’t it remain your own? After it was sold, wasn’t it in your power? How is it that you have conceived this thing in your heart? You haven’t lied to men, but to God.’”*
>
> — *Acts 5:3–4* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The early church was marked by remarkable generosity. Believers sold property and gave the money to the apostles so that no one would be in need. Barnabas had just been praised for selling a field and giving the money (*4:36–37*). Ananias and his wife Sapphira also sold a piece of property, but they kept part of the money for themselves while pretending to give it all.

Peter, apparently given insight by the Holy Spirit, confronted Ananias: “*Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit and to keep back part of the price of the land?*” (*v. 3*) Peter identified the source of the deception: Satan had influenced Ananias’s heart. Yet Ananias was still responsible, as Peter’s next words show.

“*While you kept it, didn’t it remain your own? After it was sold, wasn’t it in your power?*” (*v. 4*) Peter made it clear that Ananias was under no obligation to sell the land or to give away the money. The property was his. The giving in the early church was voluntary. The problem was not that he kept some of the money.

“*How is it that you have conceived this thing in your heart? You haven’t lied to men, but to God*” (*v. 4*). The sin was deception. Ananias wanted the reputation of being generous without paying the full cost. He lied to the apostles and the church, but ultimately he lied to God.

Notice that Peter speaks of lying “to the Holy Spirit” in verse 3 and lying “to God” in verse 4. This passage is one of the places in Scripture that shows the Holy Spirit is God.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This passage reveals how seriously God views hypocrisy. Jesus repeatedly warned against hypocrisy, especially in religious matters. He criticized those who practiced their righteousness to be seen by others (*Matthew 6:1–4*). Ananias and Sapphira wanted to appear more generous than they were. Their sin was a performance of holiness without its reality.

It also shows that God sees the heart. Ananias could deceive people, but not God. The psalmist writes, “*For there is not a word on my tongue, but, behold, LORD, you know it altogether*” (*Psalm 139:4*). Nothing is hidden from God’s sight (*Hebrews 4:13*).

Finally, the passage shows that the church is God’s holy community. The Holy Spirit dwells in the church (*1 Corinthians 3:16–17*). To lie within the church is to lie in the presence of God. This calls believers to integrity and honesty in their life together.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage challenges believers to examine their motives. It is possible to do good things, such as giving, serving, or praying, in order to be seen and praised by others. God calls His people to serve with sincere hearts, not to build a reputation.

It also calls believers to honesty. Ananias and Sapphira lied about money, but the principle applies to all areas of life. Believers are called to be truthful with God, with the church, and with others, even when the truth is less impressive than a lie.

Finally, the passage reminds believers that giving is voluntary and should be done freely. Peter affirmed that Ananias had the right to keep his property. God does not want gifts given under pressure or for show. Paul writes, “*Let each man give according as he has determined in his heart, not grudgingly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver*” (*2 Corinthians 9:7*).

### *Acts 5:30–32* — Prince and Savior

> *“The God of our fathers raised up Jesus, whom you killed, hanging him on a tree. God exalted him with his right hand to be a Prince and a Savior, to give repentance to Israel, and remission of sins. We are his witnesses of these things; and so also is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him.”*
>
> — *Acts 5:30–32* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The apostles stood before the Sanhedrin for the second time. They had been arrested for preaching about Jesus, miraculously released from prison by an angel, and then found teaching in the temple again. The high priest accused them of disobeying the council’s orders. Peter answered that they must obey God rather than men. Then he proclaimed the gospel to the council.

“*The God of our fathers raised up Jesus, whom you killed, hanging him on a tree*” (*v. 30*). Peter connected Jesus with the God of Israel’s ancestors. The phrase “hanging him on a tree” recalls *Deuteronomy 21:23*, which says that anyone hanged on a tree is under God’s curse. The leaders thought that crucifixion proved Jesus was cursed. But God raised Him. Paul later explains that Christ became a curse for us to redeem us from the curse of the law (*Galatians 3:13*).

“*God exalted him with his right hand to be a Prince and a Savior*” (*v. 31*). “Prince” means leader or ruler. “Savior” means rescuer. The One the council rejected had been exalted by God to the highest position of authority and given the role of saving His people.

“*to give repentance to Israel, and remission of sins*” (*v. 31*). Notice that repentance itself is described as a gift. Jesus gives both the ability to turn from sin and the forgiveness that follows. Even the council members who had condemned Jesus could receive this gift.

“*We are his witnesses of these things; and so also is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him*” (*v. 32*). The apostles were eyewitnesses of Jesus’ resurrection. The Holy Spirit also bore witness through the miracles and through the transformed lives of believers. The Spirit is given to those who obey God, which in this context means those who respond to the gospel with faith.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses summarize the core of the apostles’ preaching: Jesus was killed, God raised Him, exalted Him, and now offers repentance and forgiveness through Him. This pattern appears throughout Acts. It shows that the resurrection and exaltation of Jesus are the foundation of the gospel.

They also show that repentance is a gift of God’s grace. People cannot turn from sin by their own strength alone. God grants repentance (*Acts 11:18*; *2 Timothy 2:25*), enabling people to turn to Him. This gives hope even for those who seem far from God.

Finally, the verses reveal the double witness to Jesus: human witnesses and the Holy Spirit. Jesus had promised that the Spirit would testify about Him and that the disciples would also testify (*John 15:26–27*). The Christian witness is never merely human; the Spirit works through it.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses remind believers of the heart of the gospel message. When believers share their faith, they can focus on what God has done in Jesus: His death, His resurrection, and His offer of forgiveness.

They also encourage believers to pray for those who seem resistant to the gospel. The council members were hostile, yet Peter offered them repentance and forgiveness. God can give repentance to anyone. Believers can pray that God would soften hearts and grant repentance to those they love.

Finally, these verses invite believers to rely on the Holy Spirit’s witness. Believers are not alone when they share Christ. The Spirit works alongside them, confirming the truth and drawing people to Jesus.

### *Acts 5:38–39* — If It Is of God

> *“Now I tell you, withdraw from these men and leave them alone. For if this counsel or this work is of men, it will be overthrown. But if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow it, and you would be found even to be fighting against God!”*
>
> — *Acts 5:38–39* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The council was so enraged by the apostles’ testimony that they wanted to kill them. Then Gamaliel, a highly respected Pharisee and teacher of the law, stood up and urged caution. He had the apostles taken outside and spoke to the council.

He reminded them of two earlier movements. A man named Theudas had gathered about four hundred followers, but he was killed and his followers scattered. Then Judas of Galilee had led a revolt at the time of the census, but he too was killed and his followers dispersed. (The Jewish historian Josephus also mentions a Judas the Galilean who led a revolt against Roman taxation around A.D. 6.)

From these examples, Gamaliel drew his conclusion: “*Now I tell you, withdraw from these men and leave them alone. For if this counsel or this work is of men, it will be overthrown*” (*v. 38*). If the movement was merely human, it would collapse on its own, like the movements of Theudas and Judas.

“*But if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow it, and you would be found even to be fighting against God!*” (*v. 39*) If the movement truly came from God, no human power could stop it, and opposing it would mean opposing God Himself.

The council accepted his advice. They did not kill the apostles, though they still had them beaten.

Gamaliel’s advice was wise in some ways. It was cautious, fair, and recognized God’s sovereignty. But it was also incomplete. He did not take the further step of examining whether Jesus was truly the Messiah. He chose to wait and see rather than to believe.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Gamaliel’s words, though spoken by someone who was not a follower of Jesus, express a deep truth: God’s work cannot be stopped by human opposition. The rest of Acts proves it. Despite persecution, imprisonment, beatings, and killings, the gospel spread from Jerusalem to Rome. Jesus had promised, “*I will build my assembly, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it*” (*Matthew 16:18*).

The passage also shows how God protects His people, sometimes through unexpected means. God used a respected Pharisee to save the apostles’ lives. God can use people who do not share believers’ faith to accomplish His purposes and protect His church.

Finally, Gamaliel’s warning about “fighting against God” applies to everyone. One of Gamaliel’s own students, Saul of Tarsus, would soon fight against the church, until Jesus confronted him on the road to Damascus and asked, “*why do you persecute me?*” (*Acts 9:4*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage gives believers confidence. When the church faces opposition, believers can remember that God’s work cannot be overthrown. Churches, movements, and individuals may struggle, but God’s purposes will prevail.

It also encourages humility in judging new movements or ideas. Gamaliel’s caution can be a helpful principle: time often reveals whether something is from God. At the same time, believers are called to test everything by Scripture, not merely to wait (*1 Thessalonians 5:21*; *1 John 4:1*).

Finally, the passage challenges anyone who is neutral about Jesus. Gamaliel recognized that the apostles’ movement might be from God, but he did not commit himself. Waiting to see is not the same as believing. Each person must decide how to respond to Jesus.

### *Acts 5:41–42* — Rejoicing to Suffer for His Name

> *“They therefore departed from the presence of the council, rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for Jesus’ name. Every day, in the temple and at home, they never stopped teaching and preaching Jesus, the Christ.”*
>
> — *Acts 5:41–42* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After Gamaliel’s advice, the council decided not to kill the apostles. But they did not let them go unpunished. They had them flogged. Jewish flogging was severe; it often consisted of thirty-nine lashes, which could leave the back torn and bleeding. Then the council commanded them again not to speak in the name of Jesus and released them.

How did the apostles respond? “*They therefore departed from the presence of the council, rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for Jesus’ name*” (*v. 41*). They rejoiced. They did not consider their suffering a disgrace but an honor. They were “counted worthy” to suffer for the One who had suffered for them.

This was not a strange reaction for the followers of Jesus. He had taught, “*Blessed are you when men hate you, and when they exclude and mock you, and throw out your name as evil, for the Son of Man’s sake*” (*Luke 6:22*). He had said that they should “*Rejoice in that day and leap for joy*” (*Luke 6:23*).

“*Every day, in the temple and at home, they never stopped teaching and preaching Jesus, the Christ*” (*v. 42*). The beating did not silence them. They continued teaching publicly in the temple and privately in homes. Their message was simple: Jesus is the Christ.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses reveal the transforming power of the gospel. The apostles had once fled in fear when Jesus was arrested. Now they rejoiced after being flogged for Him. This change was the work of the risen Christ and the Holy Spirit.

They also show that suffering for Christ is a privilege. Paul writes, “*it has been granted to you on behalf of Christ, not only to believe in him, but also to suffer on his behalf*” (*Philippians 1:29*). To suffer for Jesus is to share in His sufferings and to be identified with Him. Peter, who was among those beaten, later wrote to believers, “*But because you are partakers of Christ’s sufferings, rejoice*” (*1 Peter 4:13*).

Finally, the verses show the importance of both public and private ministry. The apostles taught in the temple, the public center of Jewish life, and in homes, where believers gathered. The gospel spread through both settings.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers who suffer for their faith. Many Christians around the world face persecution, including imprisonment, beatings, and loss of property. Others face rejection or ridicule. The apostles’ example shows that suffering for Christ can be met with joy, not because suffering is pleasant, but because it is an honor to be identified with Him.

They also challenge believers in places of relative safety. If the apostles rejoiced to suffer for Jesus, believers today can examine whether they are willing to accept even small costs for following Him, such as social awkwardness, criticism, or missed opportunities.

Finally, these verses call believers to persistence. The apostles never stopped teaching and preaching Jesus. Believers can continue to share Christ in public and in private, in their communities and in their homes, without giving up when it becomes difficult.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Acts 5* shows that God takes the holiness of His church seriously. Ananias and Sapphira wanted the reputation of generosity without its reality, and their deception was judged. Believers are called to integrity, honesty, and sincerity in their life together. God sees the heart, and He desires truth in the inner being.

The chapter also shows that God’s work cannot be stopped. The apostles were arrested, but an angel released them. The council threatened them, but they kept preaching. Even a respected Pharisee recognized that if this movement was from God, no one could overthrow it. Believers can take courage when the church faces opposition, knowing that God’s purposes will prevail.

*Acts 5* proclaims the heart of the gospel: Jesus, whom people rejected and killed, has been raised and exalted as Prince and Savior, offering repentance and forgiveness. This message is for everyone, even those who have resisted God. Believers can share it with confidence and pray that God would grant repentance to those they love.

Finally, the chapter shows the joy of suffering for Jesus’ name. The apostles rejoiced after being flogged, considering it an honor to suffer for Him. They never stopped teaching and preaching Jesus. Believers today can follow their example, accepting the costs of discipleship with joy and continuing faithfully in their witness, both publicly and at home.

## Chapter Prayer

Holy God, You see the heart, and nothing is hidden from You. Forgive me for the times I have tried to look better than I am, or have served to be seen by others. Make me honest and sincere before You and Your people. Thank You for the power of Your Spirit at work in the early church, and thank You that Your work cannot be overthrown by any human opposition. Lord Jesus, thank You that You were raised and exalted as Prince and Savior, and that You give repentance and forgiveness. Grant repentance to those I love who do not yet know You. Give me the joy of the apostles, who rejoiced to suffer for Your name. Help me never to stop speaking of You, in public and in my home. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Acts · Chapter 6 of 28

# Acts — Chapter 6

Chapter Theme: Serving Tables, Spreading the Word, and the Courage of Stephen

[Read Acts 6 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/ACT06.htm)

Main Teaching

As the church grows, Greek-speaking believers complain that their widows are being overlooked in the daily distribution of food. The apostles respond wisely, asking the church to choose seven Spirit-filled, wise men to oversee the work so that the apostles can devote themselves to prayer and the ministry of the word. The word of God spreads, and even many priests believe. One of the seven, Stephen, performs great signs and speaks with such wisdom that his opponents cannot answer him, so they bring false charges against him before the council, where his face shines like an angel’s.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Acts 6* is a transition chapter. It shows the church solving an internal problem and then introduces Stephen, whose speech and martyrdom in chapter 7 will lead to persecution that scatters the believers beyond Jerusalem (*8:1*). In this way, a dispute about food distribution leads indirectly to the spread of the gospel to Samaria and beyond.

The chapter also shows the growing diversity of the church. The early believers were all Jewish, but they came from different backgrounds. Luke calls one group “Hellenists” and the other “Hebrews.” The Hellenists were Greek-speaking Jews, many of whom had grown up outside Israel in places like Egypt, Asia Minor, or Cyprus, and had settled in Jerusalem. The Hebrews were Aramaic-speaking Jews native to Judea and Galilee. The two groups often worshiped in different synagogues and could feel culturally distant from each other.

### A Complaint about Widows (*6:1–7*)

“*Now in those days, when the number of the disciples was multiplying, a complaint arose from the Hellenists against the Hebrews, because their widows were neglected in the daily service*” (*v. 1*). Widows in the ancient world were especially vulnerable. Without a husband’s income, many depended on family or charity to survive. The Old Testament repeatedly commanded care for widows (*Deuteronomy 10:18*; *24:19–21*; *Isaiah 1:17*). The early church provided daily food for widows in need, but the Greek-speaking widows were being overlooked. Whether this was due to language barriers, cultural prejudice, or simple oversight as the church grew rapidly, it was a real problem.

The apostles’ response is studied below. They called the whole community together and asked them to choose seven men to oversee this ministry. The qualifications were spiritual and practical: “*seven men of good report, full of the Holy Spirit and of wisdom*” (*v. 3*). Meanwhile, the apostles would “*continue steadfastly in prayer and in the ministry of the word*” (*v. 4*).

The proposal “*pleased the whole multitude*” (*v. 5*). They chose seven men: Stephen, Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, and Nicolaus. All seven have Greek names, suggesting that most or all of them came from the Hellenist community, the very group whose widows had been neglected. The church responded to the complaint generously by placing the care of the neglected group in the hands of leaders who understood them. Nicolaus is described as “*a proselyte of Antioch*” (*v. 5*), a Gentile who had converted to Judaism before becoming a follower of Jesus. Already, the church’s leadership included someone from a Gentile background.

The seven were presented to the apostles, who “*prayed, they laid their hands on them*” (*v. 6*). The laying on of hands was a sign of commissioning and blessing, recalling Moses laying his hands on Joshua (*Numbers 27:18–23*). These seven are often regarded as the first deacons, since the Greek word for “service” (diakonia) is related to the word “deacon,” although Luke does not use that title for them here.

Luke concludes with another summary of growth, studied below.

### Stephen’s Ministry and Arrest (*6:8–15*)

Stephen, “*full of faith and power, performed great wonders and signs among the people*” (*v. 8*). Though he had been chosen to serve tables, his ministry was not limited to administration. God used him in powerful ways.

Opposition arose from members of “*the synagogue called “The Libertines”*” (*v. 9*), meaning “Freedmen,” probably descendants of Jews who had been taken to Rome as slaves and later freed. Others came from Cyrene and Alexandria in North Africa, and from Cilicia and Asia in what is now Turkey. Cilicia was the home province of Saul of Tarsus, who may well have been among those who debated Stephen.

“*They weren’t able to withstand the wisdom and the Spirit by which he spoke*” (*v. 10*). This fulfilled Jesus’ promise: “*for I will give you a mouth and wisdom which all your adversaries will not be able to withstand or to contradict*” (*Luke 21:15*).

Unable to win the argument, his opponents resorted to deception. They secretly persuaded men to say, “*We have heard him speak blasphemous words against Moses and God*” (*v. 11*). They stirred up the people, the elders, and the scribes, seized Stephen, and brought him before the council. False witnesses testified, “*This man never stops speaking blasphemous words against this holy place and the law*” (*v. 13*). They claimed he had said that Jesus would destroy the temple and change the customs of Moses.

The parallels with Jesus’ trial are striking. Jesus too was accused by false witnesses of speaking against the temple (*Mark 14:57–58*). Stephen’s experience mirrors his Lord’s. There may also be a kernel of truth behind the distorted charges: Stephen likely taught, as Jesus had, that God’s presence was not confined to the temple and that Jesus fulfilled the Law. Chapter 7 shows his reasoning.

The chapter ends with a remarkable image, studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Acts 6:1–3* — Choosing Servants Full of the Spirit and Wisdom

> *“Now in those days, when the number of the disciples was multiplying, a complaint arose from the Hellenists against the Hebrews, because their widows were neglected in the daily service. The twelve summoned the multitude of the disciples and said, It is not appropriate for us to forsake the word of God and serve tables. Therefore, select from among you, brothers, seven men of good report, full of the Holy Spirit and of wisdom, whom we may appoint over this business.”*
>
> — *Acts 6:1–3* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The church in Jerusalem was growing rapidly. Thousands had come to faith, and the community was sharing its resources so that no one was in need. Part of this care involved a daily distribution of food to widows. But a problem arose: “*a complaint arose from the Hellenists against the Hebrews, because their widows were neglected in the daily service*” (*v. 1*).

This complaint could have divided the young church along cultural lines. The Greek-speaking believers felt that their widows were being treated unfairly compared to those of the Aramaic-speaking majority.

The apostles took the complaint seriously. They called the whole community together and said, “*It is not appropriate for us to forsake the word of God and serve tables*” (*v. 2*). They were not saying that serving tables was beneath them. Jesus had taught them to serve, even washing their feet. Rather, they recognized that their particular calling was to teach and pray, and that they could not do everything.

They proposed a solution: “*Therefore, select from among you, brothers, seven men of good report, full of the Holy Spirit and of wisdom, whom we may appoint over this business*” (*v. 3*). The church would choose qualified people to take responsibility for this ministry.

Notice the qualifications. The men were to be “of good report,” meaning they had a good reputation and were trusted. They were to be “full of the Holy Spirit,” spiritually mature and led by God. And they were to be “full of wisdom,” able to handle practical matters fairly and wisely. Even a task like distributing food required spiritual leaders.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This passage shows that the church is called to care for the vulnerable fairly. God’s people have always been commanded to care for widows, orphans, and strangers. James writes, “*Pure religion and undefiled before our God and Father is this: to visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction*” (*James 1:27*). When some are neglected, the church must act.

It also shows that practical service is spiritual work. The seven were chosen for their spiritual qualities, not merely their administrative skills. All service in the church, whether teaching or serving meals, is ministry done in the power of the Spirit. Paul teaches that the church is one body with many members, each with different gifts (*1 Corinthians 12:4–7*).

Finally, the passage shows healthy leadership. The apostles listened to the complaint, involved the whole community in the solution, and shared responsibility with others. They did not ignore the problem, dismiss it, or try to handle everything themselves.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage encourages churches to pay attention to those who may be overlooked. In every community, some people, perhaps those from a minority culture, those who speak a different language, the elderly, or the disabled, can be neglected. Churches can ask whether everyone is being cared for fairly and take steps to address any gaps.

It also shows the value of listening to complaints. The apostles did not dismiss the Hellenists’ concern as divisive. They listened and responded. Leaders in churches, families, and organizations can learn from this example, treating concerns seriously and seeking fair solutions.

Finally, the passage reminds believers that every form of service matters. Those who serve in practical ways, such as cooking, cleaning, organizing, or caring for others, are doing spiritual work. Churches can honor and support these ministries and look for people of good character, spiritual maturity, and wisdom to lead them.

### *Acts 6:4* — Prayer and the Ministry of the Word

> *“But we will continue steadfastly in prayer and in the ministry of the word.”*
>
> — *Acts 6:4* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After proposing that seven men be chosen to oversee the distribution of food, the apostles explained their own focus: “*But we will continue steadfastly in prayer and in the ministry of the word*” (*v. 4*).

The apostles had been entrusted by Jesus with a unique responsibility. They were eyewitnesses of His life, death, and resurrection, and they had been commissioned to teach and proclaim His message (*Acts 1:8*, 21–22). With thousands of new believers in Jerusalem, the need for teaching was enormous.

They named two priorities. First, “*prayer*” (*v. 4*). The apostles knew that their ministry depended on God. Without prayer, their teaching would lack power. The church had been born in prayer (*1:14*) and continued to grow through prayer (*2:42*; *4:24–31*).

Second, “*the ministry of the word*” (*v. 4*). The word “ministry” here is the same Greek word used for the “service” of tables in verse 1. Both are forms of service. The apostles’ service was to teach and proclaim God’s word.

The phrase “continue steadfastly” means to be devoted, to persist, to keep at something. The apostles would not merely fit prayer and teaching into their schedule; they would give themselves fully to these tasks.

This was not a statement that serving tables was unimportant, but a recognition that the apostles needed to focus on the work God had especially given them.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse highlights the central importance of prayer and Scripture in the life of the church. Without the word, the church would lose its foundation. Without prayer, it would lose its dependence on God. Paul urged Timothy, a church leader, to “*preach the word; be urgent in season and out of season*” (*2 Timothy 4:2*).

It also shows that different people have different callings within the body of Christ. The apostles were called to prayer and the word; the seven were called to oversee practical care. Both callings were necessary. Paul writes that God gave some as apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors, and teachers, “*for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving, to the building up of the body of Christ*” (*Ephesians 4:12*).

Finally, the verse shows wisdom in managing time and energy. Even the apostles could not do everything. Recognizing one’s priorities and sharing responsibilities is part of faithful ministry.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages pastors and church leaders to prioritize prayer and the teaching of Scripture. Leaders are often pulled in many directions by administration, meetings, and urgent needs. The apostles’ example reminds them to protect time for prayer and for studying and teaching God’s word.

It also encourages churches to support their leaders in this focus. Congregations can share practical responsibilities so that those called to teach have time to prepare and pray.

Finally, the verse applies to every believer. All believers are called to pray and to know God’s word. Whatever their role, believers can make prayer and Scripture central in their lives, giving them priority rather than leaving them for whatever time is left over.

### *Acts 6:7* — The Word of God Increased

> *“The word of God increased and the number of the disciples greatly multiplied in Jerusalem. A great company of the priests were obedient to the faith.”*
>
> — *Acts 6:7* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After the church resolved the dispute about the widows and appointed the seven, Luke gives a summary of what happened next: “*The word of God increased and the number of the disciples greatly multiplied in Jerusalem*” (*v. 7*).

The phrase “the word of God increased” is unusual. Luke describes the word itself as growing, almost like a living thing. This phrase appears several times in Acts (*12:24*; *19:20*). It means that the message about Jesus spread more and more widely and had increasing influence.

The growth was connected to what had just happened. When the church dealt wisely with its internal problem, it was freed to focus on its mission. A divided church would have been distracted; a united church continued to grow.

Then Luke adds a remarkable detail: “*A great company of the priests were obedient to the faith*” (*v. 7*). The priests served in the temple. Many of the high priestly leaders were Sadducees who opposed the apostles. But there were thousands of ordinary priests who served in rotation (*Luke 1:8–9*), many of them not wealthy or powerful. A large number of these priests came to faith in Jesus.

The phrase “obedient to the faith” shows that believing in Jesus involves obedience. Faith is not just agreeing with ideas; it is submitting to Jesus as Lord.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows the power of God’s word. The gospel spread not because of clever strategies or human power, but because God’s word is living and active (*Hebrews 4:12*). Isaiah writes that God’s word “*will not return to me void, but it will accomplish that which I please*” (*Isaiah 55:11*).

It also shows that unity supports mission. When the church handled its problem with fairness and wisdom, it continued to grow. Jesus prayed that His followers would be one so that the world would believe (*John 17:21*). Division hinders witness; unity strengthens it.

Finally, the conversion of many priests shows that no group is beyond the reach of the gospel. The priests were closely tied to the temple system that had opposed Jesus. Yet many of them believed. This anticipates the conversion of Saul, a fierce opponent who would become an apostle.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to trust the power of God’s word. Believers may wonder whether their witness makes any difference. The word of God has power to grow and spread, often in ways believers cannot see.

It also reminds churches that dealing well with internal problems matters for their mission. Conflicts, complaints, and divisions can distract a church from its purpose. Handling them with wisdom, fairness, and humility allows the church to continue its work.

Finally, the verse encourages believers to pray for those who seem unlikely to believe. Many priests came to faith despite their leaders’ opposition. Believers can pray for people in every group, including those who seem resistant, trusting that God’s word can reach them.

### *Acts 6:15* — The Face of an Angel

> *“All who sat in the council, fastening their eyes on him, saw his face like it was the face of an angel.”*
>
> — *Acts 6:15* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Stephen had been brought before the Sanhedrin, the same council that had condemned Jesus and threatened the apostles. False witnesses had accused him of speaking against the temple and the Law of Moses. His life was in danger.

Then Luke records: “*All who sat in the council, fastening their eyes on him, saw his face like it was the face of an angel*” (*v. 15*). Everyone in the council stared at Stephen, and what they saw astonished them. His face shone with a heavenly radiance or calm. He did not look like a frightened man facing execution. He looked like a messenger from God’s presence.

This recalls Moses, whose face shone after he had been in God’s presence on Mount Sinai (*Exodus 34:29–35*). Stephen had been accused of speaking against Moses, but his face shone as Moses’ face had. The irony is powerful.

Stephen’s shining face was a sign that God was with him. He was “full of grace and power” (*6:8* in some translations), full of the Holy Spirit and wisdom. In this moment of danger, God’s presence was visible on him.

The council members saw it, but they did not change their minds. In the next chapter, after Stephen’s speech, they will stone him.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that God’s presence can sustain His people in the most difficult moments. Stephen faced false accusations and the threat of death, yet he was filled with peace and glory. Paul writes that believers “*with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory*” (*2 Corinthians 3:18*).

It also shows that faithfulness to Christ can reflect His glory even in suffering. Stephen’s face shone not because his circumstances were good, but because he was close to God. Peter later wrote that when believers are insulted for Christ, “*the Spirit of glory and of God rests on you*” (*1 Peter 4:14*).

Finally, the verse shows that seeing evidence of God is not the same as believing. The council saw Stephen’s face, yet they hardened their hearts. Faith requires a willingness to respond to what God reveals.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers who face opposition, false accusations, or danger. God’s presence can give them peace and strength. They do not have to face these trials alone.

It also invites believers to spend time in God’s presence. Moses’ face shone after being with God, and Stephen’s face shone because he was full of the Spirit. Believers who spend time with God in prayer, worship, and Scripture may find that His presence shapes their character and even how others see them.

Finally, the verse reminds believers that their calm and grace under pressure can be a witness. When believers respond to hostility with peace and love instead of fear or anger, others may see something of Christ in them, even if they do not immediately respond.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Acts 6* shows that even healthy churches face problems. The early church was growing and generous, yet some widows were being overlooked. The apostles responded by listening to the complaint, involving the whole community, and appointing Spirit-filled, wise leaders to address it. Churches today can learn from this example, paying attention to those who may be neglected and seeking fair, wise solutions.

The chapter also highlights the importance of different callings. The apostles devoted themselves to prayer and the ministry of the word, while the seven oversaw practical care. Both forms of service were essential and spiritual. Every believer has a role in the body of Christ, and all forms of service matter to God.

*Acts 6* shows that when the church handles problems well, the word of God continues to spread. The church grew, and many priests came to faith. Believers can trust the power of God’s word to reach people, including those who seem least likely to believe.

Finally, the chapter introduces Stephen, a man full of faith, power, the Holy Spirit, and wisdom. When he was falsely accused, his face shone like an angel’s. Believers who face opposition or injustice can find in Stephen an example of courage and peace, and can trust that God’s presence will sustain them.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord, thank You for caring about the widows who were overlooked, and for the wisdom You gave the early church to meet their needs. Open my eyes to those around me who are neglected or forgotten, and show me how to help. Thank You for the many ways Your people serve, both in teaching and in practical care. Help me to serve faithfully in whatever role You give me, and to honor those whose service is quiet and unseen. Make me devoted to prayer and to Your word. Let Your word increase in my life, in my church, and in my community. Fill me with Your Spirit and wisdom, as You filled Stephen, and when I face opposition or false accusation, give me Your peace and let Your presence be seen in me. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Acts · Chapter 7 of 28

# Acts — Chapter 7

Chapter Theme: Stephen’s Witness: God Is Not Confined, His People Resist, and the Martyr Sees Jesus Standing

[Read Acts 7 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/ACT07.htm)

Main Teaching

Accused of speaking against the temple and the Law, Stephen answers the council with a sweeping review of Israel’s history. He shows that God met His people far from the temple, through Abraham, Joseph, and Moses, and that Israel has repeatedly rejected the deliverers God sent, just as the council has now betrayed and murdered the Righteous One. Enraged, they drag him out to stone him. Full of the Holy Spirit, Stephen sees Jesus standing at God’s right hand, commits his spirit to Him, and prays for his killers’ forgiveness, while a young man named Saul looks on.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Acts 7* contains the longest speech in the book of Acts. Stephen had been charged with speaking against “this holy place and the law” and claiming that Jesus would destroy the temple and change the customs of Moses (*6:13–14*). Rather than defending himself point by point, Stephen retells the story of Israel. His speech makes two main points. First, God has never been confined to one place; He appeared to Abraham in Mesopotamia, was with Joseph in Egypt, spoke to Moses in the wilderness at the burning bush, and declared through the prophets that no building can contain Him. Second, Israel has a long history of rejecting the leaders God sent to rescue them: Joseph was sold by his brothers, Moses was pushed away, and the prophets were persecuted. In rejecting Jesus, the council was repeating the pattern.

Stephen is not attacking the Law or the temple as such. He honors Moses as God’s deliverer and the Law as “living revelations” (*7:38*). His point is that the true worship of God involves receiving the One God sends, and that the temple was always meant to point beyond itself.

### Abraham: God Speaks Outside the Land (*7:1–8*)

The high priest asked, “*Are these things so?*” (*v. 1*) Stephen began respectfully: “*Brothers and fathers, listen*” (*v. 2*). Then he spoke of “*The God of glory*” (*v. 2*) appearing to Abraham “*when he was in Mesopotamia*” (*v. 2*), far from the promised land. God called Abraham to leave his land and go to a place He would show him.

God gave Abraham a promise but “*no inheritance in it, no, not so much as to set his foot on*” (*v. 5*). Abraham lived by faith in a promise not yet fulfilled. God told him that his descendants would be strangers and slaves in a foreign land for four hundred years, and then God would bring them out to worship Him. God also gave Abraham the covenant of circumcision.

### Joseph: Rejected by His Brothers, but God Was with Him (*7:9–16*)

Stephen continued with Joseph, studied below. Jacob’s family came down to Egypt, “*seventy-five souls*” (*v. 14*). (*Genesis 46:27* in the Hebrew text says seventy; the Greek translation of Genesis, which Stephen as a Greek-speaking Jew would have used, says seventy-five, counting additional descendants of Joseph.) Jacob and the patriarchs died in Egypt and were buried in Shechem. Stephen’s summary combines details of the burial places of Abraham and Jacob (*Genesis 23*; *33:19*; *50:13*; *Joshua 24:32*), a compressed way of telling the story that is common in speeches. Notably, Shechem was in Samaria, outside Judea; even the burial places of the patriarchs were not in Jerusalem.

### Moses: Deliverer Rejected (*7:17–43*)

Stephen spent the most time on Moses, since he had been accused of speaking against him. He described Moses’ birth in a time of oppression, his rescue by Pharaoh’s daughter, and his education in all the wisdom of Egypt. At forty, Moses visited his fellow Israelites and defended one who was being mistreated. “*He supposed that his brothers understood that God, by his hand, was giving them deliverance; but they didn’t understand*” (*v. 25*). When he tried to make peace between two Israelites, one pushed him away: “*Who made you a ruler and a judge over us?*” (*v. 27*) Moses fled to Midian.

Forty years later, God appeared to Moses in a burning bush in the wilderness near Mount Sinai. God said, “*Take off your sandals, for the place where you stand is holy ground*” (*v. 33*). Stephen’s point is clear: holy ground was found in the desert, far from the temple, wherever God chose to reveal Himself.

Then Stephen drove home the parallel: “*This Moses whom they refused, saying, ‘Who made you a ruler and a judge?’—God has sent him as both a ruler and a deliverer*” (*v. 35*). The one the people rejected was the one God sent to save them. Moses himself had promised, “*The Lord our God will raise up a prophet for you from among your brothers, like me*” (*v. 37*). Stephen’s hearers would have understood the implication: Jesus is that Prophet, rejected by His people but sent by God.

Even after the exodus, Israel rejected Moses in their hearts and turned back toward Egypt. They made a golden calf and “*rejoiced in the works of their hands*” (*v. 41*). God gave them over to idolatry, as the prophet Amos later described (*Amos 5:25–27*).

### Tabernacle and Temple (*7:44–50*)

Stephen then addressed the temple. Israel had the tabernacle in the wilderness, made according to the pattern God showed Moses. It traveled with them into the land under Joshua and remained until the days of David. David wanted to build a dwelling for God, “*But Solomon built him a house*” (*v. 47*). Stephen’s conclusion about the temple is studied below.

### “You Always Resist the Holy Spirit” (*7:51–53*)

Stephen then turned directly to his accusers with strong words: “*You stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit! As your fathers did, so you do*” (*v. 51*). “Stiff-necked” was God’s own description of Israel at the golden calf (*Exodus 33:5*). “Uncircumcised in heart” echoes the prophets’ call for inner renewal (*Jeremiah 9:26*; *Deuteronomy 10:16*). The council members had the outward sign of the covenant but not its inner reality.

“*Which of the prophets didn’t your fathers persecute? They killed those who foretold the coming of the Righteous One, of whom you have now become betrayers and murderers*” (*v. 52*). They had received the Law, delivered through angels, but had not kept it.

These are harsh words, spoken by a Jewish believer to the leaders of his own people, in the tradition of the prophets who called Israel to repentance. They are not a condemnation of the Jewish people as a whole, and they must never be used to justify hatred or contempt for Jews.

### The Stoning of Stephen (*7:54–60*)

“*Now when they heard these things, they were cut to the heart, and they gnashed at him with their teeth*” (*v. 54*). The same phrase “cut to the heart” described the crowd at Pentecost who repented (*2:37*). Here, conviction led to rage instead. Stephen’s vision is studied below.

“*But they cried out with a loud voice and stopped their ears, then rushed at him with one accord*” (*v. 57*). They covered their ears, refusing to hear what they considered blasphemy. They dragged him out of the city and stoned him. Luke adds an important detail: “*The witnesses placed their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul*” (*v. 58*). This is the first mention of the man who would later become the apostle Paul. Stephen’s final words are studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Acts 7:9–10* — God Was with Joseph

> *“The patriarchs, moved with jealousy against Joseph, sold him into Egypt. God was with him and delivered him out of all his afflictions, and gave him favor and wisdom before Pharaoh, king of Egypt. He made him governor over Egypt and all his house.”*
>
> — *Acts 7:9–10* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

In his speech to the council, Stephen retold the story of Joseph, one of the twelve sons of Jacob. Joseph was his father’s favorite son, and his brothers hated him for it. Stephen said, “*The patriarchs, moved with jealousy against Joseph, sold him into Egypt*” (*v. 9*). The founders of Israel’s twelve tribes betrayed their own brother out of envy (*Genesis 37*).

But then come the key words: “*God was with him*” (*v. 9*). Joseph was far from home, sold as a slave, falsely accused, and thrown into prison. Yet God had not abandoned him. Genesis repeats this phrase several times: “The LORD was with Joseph” (*Genesis 39:2*, 21, 23).

“*and delivered him out of all his afflictions, and gave him favor and wisdom before Pharaoh, king of Egypt. He made him governor over Egypt and all his house*” (*v. 10*). God rescued Joseph from his troubles, gave him wisdom to interpret Pharaoh’s dreams, and raised him to be the second most powerful man in Egypt. Through Joseph, God saved his family, including the brothers who had betrayed him, from famine.

Stephen’s point was twofold. First, God was with Joseph in Egypt, far from the promised land and long before there was a temple. God’s presence is not limited to one place. Second, Joseph was rejected by his brothers but became their savior. This pattern points to Jesus, who was rejected by His own people but became the Savior of the world.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The story of Joseph is one of Scripture’s clearest pictures of how God works through suffering. Joseph later told his brothers, “*As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to save many people alive*” (*Genesis 50:20*). The same is true of the cross: what humans intended for evil, God used to bring salvation.

The passage also reveals the presence of God with His people in every circumstance. Joseph was in a pit, in slavery, in prison, and in a palace, and God was with him in each place. Jesus promised His followers, “*I am with you always, even to the end of the age*” (*Matthew 28:20*).

Finally, Joseph’s story shows a recurring pattern in Israel’s history: the deliverer God sends is often rejected first. Joseph, Moses, the prophets, and finally Jesus were all rejected by those they came to save. Stephen was showing the council that their rejection of Jesus fit this tragic pattern.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers who feel abandoned, betrayed, or far from home. Joseph’s circumstances were terrible, yet God was with him. Believers going through hardship can trust that God’s presence does not depend on their circumstances.

They also give hope that God can bring good out of evil. Believers may suffer because of the jealousy, cruelty, or betrayal of others. This does not make the wrong done to them good, and it does not mean they should stay in harmful situations. But God can work even through painful experiences to accomplish His purposes and bring blessing.

Finally, Joseph’s story encourages believers to forgive. Joseph eventually forgave the brothers who sold him. Through Christ’s strength, believers can release bitterness toward those who have wronged them, while trusting God to bring justice and redemption.

### *Acts 7:48–50* — The Most High Doesn’t Dwell in Temples Made with Hands

> *“However, the Most High doesn’t dwell in temples made with hands, as the prophet says, “heaven is my throne, and the earth a footstool for my feet. What kind of house will you build me?” says the Lord. “Or what is the place of my rest? Didn’t my hand make all these things?””*
>
> — *Acts 7:48–50* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Stephen had been accused of speaking against the temple. In his speech, he traced the history of God’s dwelling place among His people. Israel had the tabernacle in the wilderness, a portable tent built according to God’s pattern. It traveled with them for centuries. King David wanted to build a permanent house for God, and his son Solomon built the temple in Jerusalem.

Then Stephen said, “*However, the Most High doesn’t dwell in temples made with hands*” (*v. 48*). The temple was a gift from God and a place where He made His presence known. But God cannot be confined to any building. He is the “Most High,” above all creation.

Stephen quoted *Isaiah 66:1–2*: “*heaven is my throne, and the earth a footstool for my feet. What kind of house will you build me?’ says the Lord. ‘Or what is the place of my rest?*” (*v. 49*) “*Didn’t my hand make all these things?*” (*v. 50*) God made the whole universe. How could any human building contain Him?

Even Solomon understood this. When he dedicated the temple, he prayed, “*But will God in very deed dwell on the earth? Behold, heaven and the heaven of heavens can’t contain you; how much less this house that I have built!*” (*1 Kings 8:27*)

Stephen was not saying the temple was evil or worthless. He was saying that the religious leaders had made the temple into something it was never meant to be, treating it as though God’s presence were limited to it and as though defending the building were more important than receiving God’s Messiah.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This passage prepares the way for one of the great themes of the New Testament: God’s presence is no longer centered on a building but on a Person and a people. Jesus said, “*Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up*” (*John 2:19*), speaking of His body. He told the Samaritan woman that true worshipers would worship the Father in spirit and truth, not only in Jerusalem (*John 4:21–24*).

After Pentecost, God’s presence dwells in His people by the Holy Spirit. Paul writes, “*Don’t you know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit lives in you?*” (*1 Corinthians 3:16*) The church, made of people from every nation, is God’s temple.

Finally, the passage warns against confusing the symbol with the reality. Buildings, rituals, and traditions can be good gifts that point to God. But when they become more important than God Himself, or than obedience to Him, they become idols.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses remind believers that God can be worshiped anywhere. Church buildings are valuable places for gathering, but God is present wherever His people call on Him: in homes, workplaces, hospitals, prisons, and fields. Believers can live with a sense of His presence in every place.

They also caution believers against placing too much importance on buildings and traditions. Churches can become so focused on preserving their buildings, programs, or customs that they lose sight of their mission. God’s presence is with His people, not confined to their structures.

Finally, these verses invite believers to see themselves as God’s dwelling place. If the Spirit lives in believers, then their bodies and their communities are holy. This calls them to honor God with how they live and how they treat one another.

### *Acts 7:55–56* — Jesus Standing at the Right Hand of God

> *“But he, being full of the Holy Spirit, looked up steadfastly into heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing on the right hand of God, and said, ‘Behold, I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God!’”*
>
> — *Acts 7:55–56* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Stephen had finished his speech by accusing the council of resisting the Holy Spirit and murdering the Righteous One. The council members were furious. They gnashed their teeth at him in rage. In that moment of hatred and danger, Stephen’s eyes were lifted to heaven.

“*But he, being full of the Holy Spirit, looked up steadfastly into heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing on the right hand of God*” (*v. 55*). Stephen was given a vision of heaven. He saw God’s glory and Jesus at the place of highest honor and authority.

He told the council what he saw: “*Behold, I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God!*” (*v. 56*) The title “Son of Man” comes from *Daniel 7:13–14*, where one like a son of man comes before God and receives everlasting dominion. Jesus had used this title for Himself, and at His own trial before this very council, He had said, “*From now on, the Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of the power of God*” (*Luke 22:69*). Now Stephen declared that he could see it.

Notice that Stephen saw Jesus “standing,” not sitting. Elsewhere, Jesus is described as seated at God’s right hand (*Psalm 110:1*; *Hebrews 1:3*). Why was He standing? Interpreters have suggested several reasons. Jesus may have been standing to welcome His faithful witness into heaven. He may have been standing as an advocate or witness in Stephen’s defense, as Stephen stood before an earthly court. Or He may have been standing as a judge ready to act. Many find the first two explanations especially moving: the risen Lord rose to receive His servant.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This vision shows that Jesus is alive, exalted, and actively concerned for His people. Stephen was condemned by an earthly court, but heaven’s verdict was different. The Son of Man stood in his defense. Jesus had promised, “*everyone who confesses me before men, the Son of Man will also confess before the angels of God*” (*Luke 12:8*).

It also shows that the Holy Spirit strengthens believers in their darkest moments. Stephen was “full of the Holy Spirit.” The Spirit opened his eyes to see beyond his circumstances to the glory of God and the reigning Christ.

Finally, Stephen’s vision confirms the claim that so enraged the council. Jesus, whom they had condemned, was exactly where He said He would be: at the right hand of God. The council could not bear to hear it, and they covered their ears.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage brings comfort to believers who suffer for their faith. When the world condemns them, Jesus stands with them. They are not alone. The Lord they serve sees their faithfulness and is ready to welcome them.

It also encourages believers to look up in difficult times. Stephen fixed his eyes on heaven. Believers facing trials can lift their eyes to Jesus, remembering that He reigns and that their future is secure with Him. Hebrews urges believers to run with endurance, “*looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith*” (*Hebrews 12:2*).

Finally, this passage gives believers hope in the face of death. For Stephen, death was the moment of seeing Jesus and being welcomed by Him. Believers can face their own deaths with the same hope, knowing that Jesus is waiting for them.

### *Acts 7:59–60* — “Lord, Don’t Hold This Sin Against Them”

> *“They stoned Stephen as he called out, saying, ‘Lord Jesus, receive my spirit!’ He kneeled down and cried with a loud voice, ‘Lord, don’t hold this sin against them!’ When he had said this, he fell asleep.”*
>
> — *Acts 7:59–60* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The council members rushed at Stephen, dragged him out of the city, and began to stone him. Stoning was the penalty for blasphemy under the Law (*Leviticus 24:16*), though the Romans did not normally permit the Jewish council to carry out executions. This appears to have been a violent mob action as much as a legal sentence.

As the stones struck him, Stephen prayed: “*Lord Jesus, receive my spirit!*” (*v. 59*) These words echo Jesus’ prayer from the cross: “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!” (studied at *Luke 23:46*). Jesus addressed the Father; Stephen addressed Jesus. Stephen entrusted his spirit to Jesus, showing that he regarded Jesus as Lord over life and death.

Then “*He kneeled down and cried with a loud voice, “Lord, don’t hold this sin against them!”*” (*v. 60*) Even as he was being killed, Stephen prayed for those who were killing him. This echoes Jesus’ prayer from the cross: “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing” (studied at *Luke 23:34*). Stephen had learned from his Master not only how to live but how to die.

“*When he had said this, he fell asleep*” (*v. 60*). Luke describes Stephen’s death as falling asleep. This was a common way for early Christians to describe the death of believers, because they knew death was not the end. Those who “sleep” in Christ will awaken at the resurrection (*1 Thessalonians 4:13–16*).

Stephen became the first Christian martyr. The word “martyr” comes from the Greek word for “witness.” Stephen bore witness to Jesus with his life and his death.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Stephen’s death reflects the death of Jesus. Both were falsely accused, both were condemned by the same council, both committed their spirits to God, and both prayed for their executioners. Stephen’s life shows what it means to follow Christ fully, even to death.

His prayer for forgiveness reveals the heart of the gospel. Jesus taught His followers, “*love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who mistreat you and persecute you*” (*Matthew 5:44*). Stephen lived out this command in the most extreme circumstances.

God answered Stephen’s prayer in a remarkable way. Standing nearby, approving of his death, was Saul of Tarsus (*8:1*). Within a short time, Saul would meet the risen Jesus and become the apostle Paul. Many have seen Saul’s conversion as, in part, an answer to Stephen’s prayer. Augustine famously said that if Stephen had not prayed, the church would not have had Paul.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses challenge believers to forgive those who wrong them. Stephen forgave the people who were killing him. Most believers will never face such extreme circumstances, but they do face hurt, injustice, and betrayal. With Christ’s help, they can pray for those who wrong them and release bitterness. Forgiveness does not mean pretending wrong was not done, excusing abuse, or remaining in danger; it means entrusting justice to God and refusing to hold on to hatred.

They also give believers peace about death. Stephen entrusted his spirit to Jesus and “fell asleep.” For believers, death is not the end but a passage into the presence of Christ. Believers can face death with trust, committing themselves to the Lord.

Finally, Stephen’s prayer reminds believers that God can transform even the fiercest enemies of the gospel. Saul was present at Stephen’s death and approved of it, yet God turned him into the greatest missionary of the early church. Believers can pray for those who oppose the faith, trusting that God can change their hearts.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Acts 7* reminds believers that God is not confined to any place. He met Abraham in Mesopotamia, was with Joseph in Egypt, spoke to Moses in the wilderness, and now dwells with His people by His Spirit. Believers can trust that God is with them wherever they are, and they can worship Him in every place, not only in church buildings.

The chapter also warns against resisting God. Stephen showed that Israel had a long history of rejecting the deliverers God sent, from Joseph to Moses to the prophets to Jesus. Believers today can also be tempted to resist God’s Spirit, holding on to traditions, preferences, or pride rather than receiving what God is doing. Stephen’s speech calls for humble, open hearts.

*Acts 7* shows the courage of faithful witness. Stephen spoke the truth even when it cost him his life. Believers today may face pressure to remain silent about Christ. Stephen’s example encourages them to speak with conviction, grounded in Scripture and filled with the Spirit.

Finally, the chapter shows how a believer can face death. Stephen saw Jesus standing at God’s right hand, entrusted his spirit to Him, and prayed for his killers. Believers can face suffering and death with the same hope and forgiveness, knowing that Jesus stands with them and that God can bring life even from the death of His servants.

## Chapter Prayer

Most High God, heaven is Your throne and the earth is Your footstool. No building can contain You, yet You choose to dwell with Your people. Thank You for being with Joseph in his suffering, with Moses in the wilderness, and with me wherever I go. Forgive me for the times I have resisted Your Holy Spirit and held on to my own ways. Give me an open and humble heart. Lord Jesus, thank You that You reign at the right hand of God and that You stand with Your people when the world condemns them. When I face opposition, lift my eyes to see You. Teach me to forgive those who hurt me, as Stephen forgave those who killed him. When my time comes to die, help me to say, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” In Jesus’ name, Amen.
