Acts · Chapter 8 of 28

# Acts — Chapter 8

Chapter Theme: Scattered Believers Carry the Gospel to Samaria and Beyond

[Read Acts 8 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/ACT08.htm)

Main Teaching

After Stephen’s death, a fierce persecution led by Saul scatters the believers from Jerusalem, and wherever they go they preach the word. Philip proclaims Christ in Samaria with signs and great joy, and many believe, including a famous sorcerer named Simon. Peter and John come from Jerusalem, pray for the Samaritans to receive the Holy Spirit, and sternly rebuke Simon for trying to buy God’s gift. Then the Spirit leads Philip to a desert road where he explains Isaiah’s prophecy of the suffering servant to an Ethiopian official, who believes in Jesus, is baptized, and goes on his way rejoicing.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Acts 8* marks a major turning point. Until now, the gospel had been preached mainly in Jerusalem. Jesus had told His disciples that they would be His witnesses “in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth” (*1:8*). In this chapter, the gospel moves into Judea and Samaria, and through the Ethiopian official, it begins its journey to the ends of the earth. Strikingly, the means God uses to spread the gospel is persecution.

### Persecution and Scattering (*8:1–4*)

“*Saul was consenting to his death*” (*v. 1*). Saul approved of Stephen’s execution. That same day, “*A great persecution arose against the assembly which was in Jerusalem*” (*v. 1*). The believers were “*all scattered abroad throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except for the apostles*” (*v. 1*). The apostles stayed in Jerusalem, perhaps because the persecution focused especially on the Greek-speaking believers associated with Stephen, or because the apostles felt called to remain at the center.

“*Devout men buried Stephen and lamented greatly over him*” (*v. 2*). Even in a time of danger, believers honored Stephen and grieved openly. Faith does not erase grief.

Meanwhile, “*Saul ravaged the assembly, entering into every house and dragged both men and women off to prison*” (*v. 3*). The word “ravaged” describes a wild animal tearing its prey. Saul later admitted, “*beyond measure I persecuted the assembly of God and ravaged it*” (*Galatians 1:13*). The scattering of the believers is studied below.

### Philip in Samaria (*8:5–13*)

Philip, one of the seven chosen to serve the widows (*6:5*), went to “*the city of Samaria*” (*v. 5*) and “*proclaimed to them the Christ*” (*v. 5*). This was significant. Jews and Samaritans had been divided for centuries (*John 4:9*). Jesus had shown the way by speaking with a Samaritan woman and telling a parable about a good Samaritan. Now a Greek-speaking Jewish believer brought the gospel to Samaria. The Samaritans, who also expected a coming deliverer, listened eagerly.

The people paid close attention “*when they heard and saw the signs which he did*” (*v. 6*). Unclean spirits came out of many people, and many who were paralyzed or lame were healed. “*There was great joy in that city*” (*v. 8*).

Among them was a man named Simon who had practiced sorcery and amazed the people, “*making himself out to be some great one*” (*v. 9*). The people said of him, “*This man is that great power of God*” (*v. 10*). Later Christian writers called him “Simon Magus” (“Simon the magician”) and described him as a founder of false teachings, though Luke tells us only what happened in Samaria.

When the Samaritans believed Philip’s message about God’s kingdom and the name of Jesus, “*they were baptized, both men and women*” (*v. 12*). Simon himself believed and was baptized, and he followed Philip, amazed at the miracles. Whether Simon’s faith was genuine is uncertain; the following verses suggest his heart had not truly changed.

### Peter and John in Samaria (*8:14–25*)

When the apostles in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John. They prayed for the new believers to receive the Holy Spirit, laid hands on them, and the Spirit came. This unusual event is studied below.

Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands, and he offered them money: “*Give me also this power, that whomever I lay my hands on may receive the Holy Spirit*” (*v. 19*). Peter’s stern response is studied below. Simon asked Peter to pray for him. Luke does not tell us what happened to him afterward. His name gave rise to the word “simony,” which refers to buying or selling church offices or spiritual privileges.

Peter and John then returned to Jerusalem, preaching in many Samaritan villages along the way. John, who once wanted to call down fire on a Samaritan village (*Luke 9:54*), now brought them the good news.

### Philip and the Ethiopian Official (*8:26–40*)

An angel told Philip to go south to the road from Jerusalem to Gaza, “*This is a desert*” (*v. 26*). Philip left a successful ministry among crowds to go to a lonely road, and there he met one man.

“*there was a man of Ethiopia, a eunuch of great authority under Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who was over all her treasure*” (*v. 27*). “Ethiopia” in the ancient world referred to the kingdom of Kush, south of Egypt, in what is now Sudan. “Candace” was a title for the queen mother who ruled there, not a personal name. This official was the royal treasurer, a man of high rank. He had traveled about a thousand miles to worship in Jerusalem.

As a eunuch, he would have been excluded from full participation in the temple assembly (*Deuteronomy 23:1*), and as a foreigner, he could not enter the inner courts. Yet he had made the long journey, and he was reading the scroll of Isaiah on his way home. *Isaiah 56:3–5* contains a beautiful promise that God would give eunuchs who hold fast to His covenant “a name better than of sons and of daughters.” This man was about to experience its fulfillment.

The Spirit told Philip to go near the chariot. Philip ran and heard the man reading Isaiah aloud, as was customary in the ancient world. The conversation that followed is studied below.

After the official was baptized, “*the Spirit of the Lord caught Philip away, and the eunuch didn’t see him any more, for he went on his way rejoicing*” (*v. 39*). Philip appeared at Azotus (ancient Ashdod) and preached in all the towns along the coast until he reached Caesarea, where he apparently settled. Years later, Paul and Luke would stay at his house there (*Acts 21:8–9*).

Ancient Christian tradition says that the Ethiopian official brought the gospel back to his homeland. Whether or not that is so, his conversion shows the gospel beginning to reach “the uttermost parts of the earth.”

## Important Verses Explained

### *Acts 8:4* — Scattered Abroad, Preaching the Word

> *“Therefore those who were scattered abroad went around preaching the word.”*
>
> — *Acts 8:4* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After Stephen was killed, a great persecution broke out against the church in Jerusalem. Saul went from house to house, dragging believers off to prison. Many believers fled from Jerusalem to escape the danger, leaving their homes, jobs, and communities behind. They were scattered throughout Judea and Samaria.

Then Luke writes, “*Therefore those who were scattered abroad went around preaching the word*” (*v. 4*). The believers did not hide their faith or fall silent. Wherever they went, they shared the message about Jesus.

Notice who was doing the preaching. The apostles had stayed in Jerusalem (*8:1*). The ones scattered were ordinary believers, men and women who were not apostles or official leaders. Yet they spread the gospel everywhere they went.

The word “scattered” is related to the word for sowing seed. Like a farmer scattering seed across a field, God scattered His people, and the seed of the gospel took root in new places.

Persecution was meant to destroy the church. Instead, it spread the church. What the enemies of the gospel intended for harm, God used for the spread of His word.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows God’s sovereign power to bring good out of evil. The persecution was real and painful. Believers lost homes, freedom, and in some cases their lives. Yet God used it to fulfill Jesus’ command to be His witnesses in Judea and Samaria. Paul later wrote from prison that his imprisonment had “*turned out rather to the progress of the Good News*” (*Philippians 1:12*).

It also shows that the spread of the gospel is the work of all believers, not only leaders. Ordinary Christians who simply shared what they knew about Jesus carried the gospel far beyond Jerusalem. Throughout history, the church has often grown most through the everyday witness of ordinary believers.

Finally, the verse reveals the resilience of genuine faith. These believers had lost much, yet they did not lose their message. Their faith was not dependent on comfortable circumstances.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers who have been displaced, whether by persecution, war, economic hardship, or other circumstances. Many Christians today are refugees or migrants. Wherever they go, they can carry the gospel with them. God can use their scattering to spread His word.

It also reminds every believer that they are called to share their faith. Sharing Christ is not only the job of pastors or missionaries. Believers can speak about Jesus in their workplaces, neighborhoods, schools, and families.

Finally, the verse invites believers to see difficult circumstances differently. Changes that seem like losses, such as moving to a new place, changing jobs, or being separated from familiar communities, can become opportunities for new witness. God can use unexpected situations to bring the gospel to people who need it.

### *Acts 8:14–17* — The Samaritans Receive the Holy Spirit

> *“Now when the apostles who were at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them, who, when they had come down, prayed for them, that they might receive the Holy Spirit; for as yet he had fallen on none of them. They had only been baptized in the name of Christ Jesus. Then they laid their hands on them, and they received the Holy Spirit.”*
>
> — *Acts 8:14–17* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Philip had preached the gospel in Samaria, and many people had believed and been baptized. When the apostles in Jerusalem heard about it, “*they sent Peter and John to them*” (*v. 14*). This was an important moment. For centuries, Jews and Samaritans had been divided by hostility. Now Samaritans were believing in the Jewish Messiah.

When Peter and John arrived, they “*prayed for them, that they might receive the Holy Spirit*” (*v. 15*). Luke explains why: “*for as yet he had fallen on none of them. They had only been baptized in the name of Christ Jesus*” (*v. 16*). This was unusual. Normally in Acts, believers receive the Spirit when they believe (*2:38*; *10:44*).

“*Then they laid their hands on them, and they received the Holy Spirit*” (*v. 17*). The Spirit came on the Samaritan believers through the prayer and laying on of hands of the apostles. Something visible seems to have happened, since Simon “saw” that the Spirit was given (*8:18*).

Why the delay? Many interpreters believe God withheld the Spirit until the apostles came so that the Samaritan believers would be clearly united with the Jerusalem church. If the Samaritans had received the Spirit independently, the old division might have continued, with two separate churches. Instead, the apostles from Jerusalem welcomed the Samaritans into the one body of Christ, and the Samaritans received the Spirit through the leaders of the Jewish church.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This passage shows that the gospel breaks down barriers. Jews and Samaritans had been enemies for centuries. Through Christ, they became one family, sharing the same Spirit. Paul writes that Christ “*broke down the middle wall of separation*” (*Ephesians 2:14*).

Christians have understood this passage in different ways. Some traditions, particularly Pentecostal ones, see it as evidence that receiving the Holy Spirit in fullness can be a distinct experience after conversion. Some sacramental traditions see a connection to confirmation, in which a bishop lays on hands and prays for the Spirit. Many others see the delay as a unique event in the history of the early church, related to the Samaritans’ inclusion, rather than a pattern for every believer. All agree that the Holy Spirit is given to all who belong to Christ (*Romans 8:9*) and that the Spirit unites believers in one body.

Finally, the passage shows the importance of unity and connection in the church. The apostles did not view the Samaritan believers as a separate movement. They came, prayed, and welcomed them.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage challenges believers to reach across divisions. Many communities today are divided by ethnicity, culture, politics, or history. The gospel calls believers to cross these lines with love, as Philip, Peter, and John did. Churches can seek to welcome people from groups that have been divided from them.

It also encourages believers to value connection with the wider church. Local churches are part of the one body of Christ. Partnerships, fellowship, and mutual support across churches reflect the unity the Spirit creates.

Finally, the passage invites believers to pray for the Spirit’s work. Peter and John prayed for the Samaritans to receive the Spirit. Believers can pray for one another to be filled with the Spirit and to experience His presence and power.

### *Acts 8:20–22* — The Gift of God Cannot Be Bought

> *“But Peter said to him, May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money! You have neither part nor lot in this matter, for your heart isn’t right before God. Repent therefore of this, your wickedness, and ask God if perhaps the thought of your heart may be forgiven you.”*
>
> — *Acts 8:20–22* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Simon had been a famous sorcerer in Samaria before he believed and was baptized. When he saw that the Holy Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands, he offered them money and asked for the same power. As a magician, he may have been used to buying secret techniques from other practitioners. He seemed to view the Holy Spirit as a power he could purchase and use.

Peter’s response was severe: “*May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money!*” (*v. 20*) The Holy Spirit is a gift from God. Gifts cannot be bought. Simon’s offer showed that he completely misunderstood the nature of God’s grace.

“*You have neither part nor lot in this matter, for your heart isn’t right before God*” (*v. 21*). Peter saw that Simon’s heart was not right. He wanted power and prestige, not God Himself.

Yet Peter did not leave Simon without hope: “*Repent therefore of this, your wickedness, and ask God if perhaps the thought of your heart may be forgiven you*” (*v. 22*). Peter called Simon to repent and pray for forgiveness. The word “perhaps” does not mean God might refuse a truly repentant heart; it emphasizes the seriousness of Simon’s sin and the need for genuine repentance.

Peter added, “*For I see that you are in the poison of bitterness and in the bondage of iniquity*” (*v. 23*). Simon was still enslaved by sin.

Simon replied, “*Pray for me to the Lord, that none of the things which you have spoken happen to me*” (*v. 24*). His response seems more concerned with avoiding punishment than with a change of heart, but Luke does not tell us the outcome.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This passage reveals that God’s gifts cannot be purchased. Salvation, the Holy Spirit, and spiritual gifts are given freely by God’s grace. Isaiah invited people to come and buy “*without money and without price*” (*Isaiah 55:1*). Any attempt to buy God’s favor misunderstands grace.

It also shows the danger of seeking spiritual power for selfish purposes. Simon wanted to use God’s power to enhance his own reputation and influence. Throughout history, some people have tried to use religion for profit, fame, or control. God’s power is not for sale and cannot be used for personal gain.

Finally, the passage shows that outward participation does not guarantee a changed heart. Simon believed, was baptized, and followed Philip, yet his heart was not right before God. Jesus warned that not everyone who calls Him “Lord” truly knows Him (*Matthew 7:21–23*). True faith involves a transformed heart.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage warns against treating faith as a means to personal gain. Some people approach God mainly for what they can get: wealth, health, success, or influence. While God cares about people’s needs, He is not a tool to be used. Believers are called to seek God for who He is.

It also warns against the commercialization of spiritual things. Churches and ministries must be careful never to suggest that God’s blessings can be bought, or that giving money guarantees spiritual power or favor. Generosity is good, but God’s grace is free.

Finally, the passage encourages believers to examine their hearts. Simon’s outward actions seemed right, but his heart was not. Believers can ask God to search their hearts and to purify their motives, and they can trust that God forgives those who genuinely repent.

### *Acts 8:35–36* — Beginning from This Scripture, He Preached Jesus

> *“Philip opened his mouth, and beginning from this Scripture, preached to him about Jesus. As they went on the way, they came to some water; and the eunuch said, ‘Behold, here is water. What is keeping me from being baptized?’”*
>
> — *Acts 8:35–36* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The Ethiopian official was sitting in his chariot reading from the scroll of Isaiah. He was reading *Isaiah 53:7–8*, which describes someone who was led like a sheep to the slaughter, silent like a lamb before its shearer, humiliated and denied justice, whose life was taken from the earth.

Philip, led by the Spirit, ran up to the chariot and asked, “*Do you understand what you are reading?*” (*v. 30*) The official answered honestly, “*How can I, unless someone explains it to me?*” (*v. 31*) He invited Philip to sit with him.

The official asked, “*Who is the prophet talking about? About himself, or about someone else?*” (*v. 34*) This was a natural question. Jewish interpreters had different views. Some thought Isaiah was speaking about himself, others about the nation of Israel, others about a future figure.

“*Philip opened his mouth, and beginning from this Scripture, preached to him about Jesus*” (*v. 35*). Philip explained that the passage described Jesus, who was led to the slaughter, suffered in silence, was unjustly condemned, and died for the sins of others. *Isaiah 53* says that the servant was “pierced for our transgressions” and that “the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all.”

As they traveled, they came to some water, and the official said, “*Behold, here is water. What is keeping me from being baptized?*” (*v. 36*) He wanted to respond immediately to the good news. (Verse 37, which contains a confession of faith, appears in some later manuscripts but not in the earliest ones, which is why the World English Bible leaves it blank.) The chariot stopped, and Philip baptized him. The official went on his way rejoicing.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This passage shows that the Old Testament points to Jesus. *Isaiah 53*, written centuries before Jesus’ birth, describes His suffering and death with remarkable clarity. Jesus Himself taught that all the Scriptures testify about Him (*Luke 24:27*, 44). Philip’s method, beginning with a Scripture passage and showing how it is fulfilled in Jesus, is a model for understanding the Bible.

It also shows God’s care for individuals. Philip left a city-wide revival to speak with one man on a desert road. God cared about this one seeker, a foreigner and a eunuch who had been on the edges of Israel’s worship. Through Christ, he was fully welcomed into God’s people.

Finally, the official’s question, “What is keeping me from being baptized?”, has a powerful answer: nothing. His nationality, his status as a eunuch, and his distance from Jerusalem could not keep him out. In Christ, the barriers are removed.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage encourages believers to help others understand Scripture. Many people read the Bible but struggle to understand it. Believers can come alongside them, as Philip did, with patience and humility, explaining how the Bible points to Jesus.

It also encourages believers to follow the Spirit’s leading, even when it seems unusual. Philip went to a desert road because God told him to. Believers can be open to God’s prompting to speak with someone, visit someone, or help someone, trusting that God has prepared the way.

Finally, the passage invites anyone who feels excluded to come to Christ. The Ethiopian official was a foreigner and a eunuch, someone who had been kept at a distance from full participation in worship. In Jesus, he was welcomed completely. No one is too far away, too different, or too marginalized to be included in God’s family.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Acts 8* shows that God can use even persecution to spread the gospel. The believers who were scattered from Jerusalem preached the word wherever they went. Believers today who face hardship, displacement, or loss can trust that God is able to use their circumstances for His purposes, and they can carry the message of Jesus wherever they go.

The chapter also shows the gospel crossing barriers. Philip preached to the Samaritans, long despised by Jews, and Peter and John came to welcome them into the one church. Philip then explained the Scriptures to an Ethiopian official who had been on the margins of Israel’s worship. Believers today are called to reach across lines of ethnicity, culture, and social status, welcoming all into the family of God.

*Acts 8* also warns against trying to use God for selfish purposes. Simon wanted to buy spiritual power, but God’s gifts cannot be purchased. Believers can examine their motives, seeking God for who He is rather than for what they can gain, and they can trust that God forgives those who truly repent.

Finally, the chapter shows the joy of the gospel. There was great joy in Samaria, and the Ethiopian official went on his way rejoicing. When people encounter Jesus, their lives are filled with joy. Believers can share this joy by helping others understand the Scriptures and meet the Savior they reveal.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord God, thank You that no persecution or hardship can stop Your word from spreading. When my life is disrupted or I find myself in new places, help me to carry the message of Jesus with me. Thank You for breaking down the walls between Jews and Samaritans, and for welcoming the Ethiopian official into Your family. Show me the barriers I need to cross with Your love. Guard my heart from seeking You only for what I can gain, and purify my motives. Thank You that Your gifts are free and cannot be bought. Lead me by Your Spirit, as You led Philip, to people who are seeking You. Give me wisdom to explain Your word and to point others to Jesus. Fill me with the joy of Your salvation. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Acts · Chapter 9 of 28

# Acts — Chapter 9

Chapter Theme: The Persecutor Becomes a Preacher, and the Church Grows in Peace

[Read Acts 9 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/ACT09.htm)

Main Teaching

Saul of Tarsus, on his way to arrest believers in Damascus, is stopped by a blinding light and the voice of the risen Jesus asking why Saul is persecuting Him. Blind for three days, Saul waits and prays until a fearful disciple named Ananias obeys the Lord, calls him “Brother Saul,” and lays hands on him so that he regains his sight and is filled with the Spirit. Saul immediately begins proclaiming Jesus as the Son of God, escapes plots against his life, and is welcomed in Jerusalem through Barnabas. The church enjoys peace and growth, and Peter heals Aeneas and raises Tabitha from the dead.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Acts 9* tells one of the most important events in Christian history: the conversion of Saul, who would become the apostle Paul. Luke considers this event so important that he tells it three times in Acts (here, in 22:3–16, and in 26:9–18). Paul himself refers to it in his letters (*1 Corinthians 15:8–10*; *Galatians 1:13–17*; *Philippians 3:4–11*; *1 Timothy 1:12–16*).

Saul was born in Tarsus, a major city in the Roman province of Cilicia (in modern-day Turkey). He was a Jew of the tribe of Benjamin, a Pharisee, a Roman citizen by birth, and a student of the great rabbi Gamaliel in Jerusalem (*Acts 22:3*; *Philippians 3:5*). He was zealous for the Law and saw the followers of Jesus as a dangerous threat to Israel’s faith. He was present at Stephen’s death and led the persecution that followed.

### Saul on the Road to Damascus (*9:1–9*)

“*But Saul, still breathing threats and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord, went to the high priest*” (*v. 1*). Saul’s hostility was so intense that it was like the very air he breathed. He asked the high priest for letters to the synagogues in Damascus, about 150 miles north of Jerusalem, authorizing him to arrest any who belonged to “*the Way*” (*v. 2*) and bring them bound to Jerusalem. “The Way” was an early name for the Christian movement (*Acts 19:9*, 23; *24:14*), perhaps reflecting Jesus’ words, “*I am the way*” (*John 14:6*).

As Saul approached Damascus, “*suddenly a light from the sky shone around him*” (*v. 3*). Paul later said it was about noon and the light was brighter than the sun (*Acts 26:13*). He fell to the ground and heard a voice. This encounter is studied below.

The men traveling with Saul “*stood speechless, hearing the sound, but seeing no one*” (*v. 7*). (In *Acts 22:9*, Paul says they did not “*understand*” (*Acts 22:9*) or “hear” the voice; the Greek word can mean either hearing a sound or understanding speech, so they heard a sound but did not understand the words.)

Saul got up, but when he opened his eyes, he could see nothing. His companions led him by the hand into Damascus. The man who had come to drag others away in chains was now led like a helpless child. “*He was without sight for three days, and neither ate nor drank*” (*v. 9*). These three days of darkness and fasting were a time of profound reflection and repentance.

### Ananias Sent to Saul (*9:10–19*)

In Damascus lived a disciple named Ananias (not the same man as in chapter 5). The Lord spoke to him in a vision, telling him to go to a house on Straight Street and ask for Saul of Tarsus, who was praying. Saul had seen a vision of a man named Ananias coming to restore his sight. The street called Straight still exists in Damascus today.

Ananias was afraid: “*Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he did to your saints at Jerusalem*” (*v. 13*). He knew Saul had come with authority to arrest believers. His honesty with the Lord is understandable. The Lord’s answer is studied below.

Ananias obeyed. His greeting is also studied below. “*Immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he received his sight. He arose and was baptized*” (*v. 18*). Saul ate and regained his strength.

### Saul Preaches Christ (*9:19–31*)

Saul stayed with the believers in Damascus, and “*Immediately in the synagogues he proclaimed the Christ, that he is the Son of God*” (*v. 20*). This is the only time in Acts that the title “Son of God” appears in a summary of preaching. Those who heard him were amazed: “*Isn’t this he who in Jerusalem made havoc of those who called on this name?*” (*v. 21*) Saul grew stronger and confounded the Jews of Damascus, “*proving that this is the Christ*” (*v. 22*).

Paul writes in *Galatians 1:17–18* that after his conversion he went to Arabia (probably the Nabatean kingdom east and south of Damascus) and later returned to Damascus, and that three years passed before he went to Jerusalem. Luke’s phrase “*When many days were fulfilled*” (*v. 23*) covers this period.

Eventually, some Jews in Damascus plotted to kill him. They watched the city gates day and night. But Saul’s disciples “*took him by night and let him down through the wall, lowering him in a basket*” (*v. 25*). Paul later mentions this humbling escape as one of the things he “boasts” about in his weakness (*2 Corinthians 11:32–33*). The hunter had become the hunted.

When Saul came to Jerusalem, the believers were afraid of him. Barnabas’s role is studied below. Saul preached boldly in Jerusalem and debated with the Greek-speaking Jews, the same groups Stephen had debated, but they tried to kill him. The believers took him down to Caesarea and sent him home to Tarsus, where he would remain for several years until Barnabas brought him to Antioch (*11:25–26*).

Luke then summarizes: “*So the assemblies throughout all Judea, Galilee, and Samaria had peace and were built up. They were multiplied, walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit*” (*v. 31*). The persecution had ended with its leader’s conversion.

### Peter Heals Aeneas and Raises Tabitha (*9:32–43*)

Luke now turns back to Peter, who was traveling among the believers. At Lydda, near the coast, he found a man named Aeneas who had been paralyzed and bedridden for eight years. Peter said, “*Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you. Get up and make your bed!*” (*v. 34*) Peter made it clear that Jesus was the healer. Aeneas got up immediately, and many in the region turned to the Lord.

In nearby Joppa lived a disciple named Tabitha (Aramaic) or Dorcas (Greek), both meaning “gazelle.” “*This woman was full of good works and acts of mercy which she did*” (*v. 36*). She became sick and died. The believers sent for Peter. When he arrived, “*All the widows stood by him weeping, and showing the tunics and other garments which Dorcas had made while she was with them*” (*v. 39*). Dorcas had clothed the poor widows with her own hands. Her love was visible in every garment.

Peter sent everyone out, knelt, and prayed. Then he said, “*Tabitha, get up!*” (*v. 40*) The scene recalls Jesus raising Jairus’s daughter, when He put everyone out and said, “Talitha cumi” (*Mark 5:40–41*), words that differ from Peter’s by only one letter in Aramaic. She opened her eyes and sat up. Peter presented her alive to the believers and widows, and many in Joppa believed in the Lord.

Peter stayed in Joppa with “*a tanner named Simon*” (*v. 43*). Tanners worked with the skins of dead animals, which made them ritually unclean according to the Law. Many strict Jews avoided them. Peter’s willingness to stay with a tanner hints that God was already preparing him for the even greater barrier he would cross in the next chapter.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Acts 9:4–5* — “*Why Do You Persecute Me?*” (*v. 4*)

> *“He fell on the earth, and heard a voice saying to him, ‘Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?’ He said, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ The Lord said, I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.”*
>
> — *Acts 9:4–5* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Saul was traveling to Damascus with letters from the high priest, ready to arrest followers of Jesus and bring them back to Jerusalem in chains. He was convinced he was serving God. As he neared the city, a blinding light from heaven flashed around him.

“*He fell on the earth, and heard a voice saying to him, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?”*” (*v. 4*) The voice called him by name, twice, a pattern in Scripture that signals a personal and urgent call from God (*Genesis 22:11*; *Exodus 3:4*; *1 Samuel 3:10*).

Notice the question: “Why do you persecute me?” Saul had been persecuting the followers of Jesus, not Jesus Himself, or so he thought. But the voice identified completely with the believers. To attack them was to attack Him.

Saul asked, “*Who are you, Lord?*” (*v. 5*) He recognized that he was encountering a heavenly being, but he did not yet know who it was. The word “Lord” may have been a respectful address, but it soon took on its full meaning.

“*The Lord said, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.”*” (*v. 5*) In that moment, Saul’s entire understanding collapsed. The Jesus he believed was a dead false messiah was alive and speaking to him from heaven in glory. Everything he had believed about Jesus was wrong. Everything the believers had said was true.

The Lord then told him, “*But rise up and enter into the city, then you will be told what you must do*” (*v. 6*). The proud leader would now have to wait and receive instructions.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This encounter reveals the deep union between Christ and His people. Jesus said, “Why do you persecute me?” The church is the body of Christ (*1 Corinthians 12:27*). What happens to believers matters to Jesus personally. He feels their suffering. Jesus had taught that whatever is done to the least of His brothers is done to Him (*Matthew 25:40*).

It also shows that no one is beyond the reach of God’s grace. Saul was the church’s fiercest enemy, actively trying to destroy it. Yet Jesus appeared to him not in judgment but in mercy. Paul later wrote, “*Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am chief*” (*1 Timothy 1:15*).

Finally, the encounter shows that conversion is ultimately the work of God. Saul was not searching for Jesus; he was fighting against Him. Jesus took the initiative and confronted him. Paul later described himself as one whom God “*separated me from my mother’s womb, and called me through his grace*” (*Galatians 1:15*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage gives hope for those who seem far from God. Some people actively oppose the Christian faith. Saul’s story shows that God can transform even the most hostile heart. Believers can pray with hope for those who seem least likely to believe.

It also comforts believers who are persecuted or mistreated for their faith. Jesus identifies with them. Their suffering is His suffering. They are not forgotten.

Finally, the passage invites everyone to reconsider what they think about Jesus. Saul was certain he was right, but he was wrong. Many people today have firm opinions about Jesus without having truly encountered Him. Like Saul, they can ask, “Who are you, Lord?” and be open to His answer.

### *Acts 9:15–16* — A Chosen Vessel

> *“But the Lord said to him, ‘Go your way, for he is my chosen vessel to bear my name before the nations and kings, and the children of Israel. For I will show him how many things he must suffer for my name’s sake.’”*
>
> — *Acts 9:15–16* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The Lord had told Ananias, a disciple in Damascus, to go to Saul and restore his sight. Ananias was understandably afraid. He had heard about the harm Saul had done to believers in Jerusalem, and he knew Saul had come to Damascus with authority to arrest them. Going to Saul seemed dangerous, even foolish.

The Lord answered, “*Go your way, for he is my chosen vessel to bear my name before the nations and kings, and the children of Israel*” (*v. 15*). God had chosen Saul for a special purpose. A “vessel” is a container or instrument. Saul would carry the name of Jesus to others.

Notice the three groups: “the nations” (the Gentiles), “kings,” and “the children of Israel.” Saul would become the apostle to the Gentiles, carrying the gospel across the Roman world. He would also testify before kings and rulers, including King Agrippa and possibly Caesar. And he would continue to preach to his own Jewish people, often going first to the synagogue in each city.

Then the Lord added something sobering: “*For I will show him how many things he must suffer for my name’s sake*” (*v. 16*). Saul, who had made believers suffer, would now suffer for the name of Jesus. This was not revenge but the path of discipleship. Paul later described his sufferings in detail: beatings, imprisonments, shipwrecks, dangers, hunger, and sleepless nights (*2 Corinthians 11:23–28*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses reveal God’s sovereign choice and purpose. Saul did not choose God; God chose Saul. Paul later wrote that God’s grace toward him was undeserved and transforming: “*But by the grace of God I am what I am*” (*1 Corinthians 15:10*).

They also show that God’s choice is for service, not privilege. Saul was chosen to carry Christ’s name to others. Every believer is chosen by God for a purpose, to bear witness to Christ and to serve others.

Finally, these verses show that suffering is often part of faithful service. Jesus did not promise Saul an easy life. He promised suffering. Yet Paul later wrote that he considered his sufferings worth it, because through them he came to know Christ more deeply (*Philippians 3:10*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to see themselves as vessels for Christ. Every believer can carry the name of Jesus into their families, workplaces, and communities. God has a purpose for each life.

They also prepare believers to accept suffering as part of following Jesus. Faithful service does not guarantee comfort. Believers who suffer for their faith can remember that this has always been part of the path of discipleship, and that God is with them in it.

Finally, these verses encourage believers to trust God when He calls them to do something frightening. Ananias was afraid, but he obeyed. God may call believers to reach out to people they fear or to do things that feel risky. They can trust that God knows what He is doing.

### *Acts 9:17* — “*Brother Saul*” (*v. 17*)

> *“Ananias departed and entered into the house. Laying his hands on him, he said, ‘Brother Saul, the Lord, who appeared to you on the road by which you came, has sent me that you may receive your sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit.’”*
>
> — *Acts 9:17* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Ananias had every reason to be afraid of Saul. Saul had come to Damascus to arrest believers like him. But the Lord told Ananias that Saul was His chosen instrument, and so Ananias went.

“*Ananias departed and entered into the house*” (*v. 17*). He obeyed despite his fear. He walked into the house where the persecutor was staying.

“*Laying his hands on him, he said, “Brother Saul*” (*v. 17*). These two words are among the most beautiful in Acts. Ananias did not call him “Saul the persecutor” or “enemy.” He called him “Brother.” Saul had come to Damascus as an enemy of the church; now he was welcomed as a member of the family. Ananias touched the man who had come to bind believers, laying his hands on him in blessing.

“*the Lord, who appeared to you on the road by which you came, has sent me that you may receive your sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit*” (*v. 17*). Ananias explained that he had been sent by the same Lord who had appeared to Saul on the road. He came to bring healing and the gift of the Spirit.

Immediately something like scales fell from Saul’s eyes, and he could see again. He got up and was baptized.

Ananias is mentioned only briefly in Scripture, and we know little else about him. But his faithful obedience and his welcoming words made him a key figure in the conversion of the greatest missionary of the early church.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows the power of grace to transform relationships. Through Christ, an enemy becomes a brother. Paul later wrote that believers who were once alienated from God and from one another have been reconciled through the cross (*Ephesians 2:13–16*). Ananias’s words put that reconciliation into practice.

It also shows the importance of ordinary believers in God’s work. Ananias was not an apostle or a famous leader. He was simply a faithful disciple who listened to God and obeyed. God often uses unknown believers to accomplish great things.

Finally, the restoring of Saul’s sight is a picture of spiritual sight. Saul had been spiritually blind, unable to see that Jesus was the Messiah. Now his eyes were opened physically and spiritually. Paul later described his mission as opening people’s eyes, “*that they may turn from darkness to light*” (*Acts 26:18*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse challenges believers to welcome those whose past is troubling. When someone with a difficult history comes to faith, believers may be suspicious or hesitant. Ananias’s example encourages them to welcome new believers as brothers and sisters, trusting God’s work in their lives. At the same time, wisdom and appropriate safeguards remain important, especially where harm has been done to vulnerable people.

It also encourages believers to obey God even when they are afraid. Ananias’s fear was real, but his obedience was greater. Believers can follow his example, trusting God when He leads them into uncomfortable situations.

Finally, the verse reminds believers that small acts of faithfulness matter. A single visit, a word of welcome, or a prayer can change someone’s life and have effects far beyond what anyone can imagine.

### *Acts 9:26–27* — Barnabas Stands with Saul

> *“When Saul had come to Jerusalem, he tried to join himself to the disciples; but they were all afraid of him, not believing that he was a disciple. But Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles, and declared to them how he had seen the Lord on the way, and that he had spoken to him, and how at Damascus he had preached boldly in the name of Jesus.”*
>
> — *Acts 9:26–27* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After Saul’s conversion and his ministry in Damascus, he traveled to Jerusalem. He wanted to join the believers there. But “*they were all afraid of him, not believing that he was a disciple*” (*v. 26*). The believers in Jerusalem remembered Saul as the man who had dragged their friends and family members to prison. Some may have thought his conversion was a trick to infiltrate the church and arrest more believers.

Their fear was understandable. Saul had done real harm. Trust is not easily rebuilt.

“*But Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles*” (*v. 27*). Barnabas, whose name means “Son of Encouragement” (*4:36*), stepped forward. He took Saul by the hand, so to speak, and brought him to the apostles.

Barnabas “*declared to them how he had seen the Lord on the way, and that he had spoken to him, and how at Damascus he had preached boldly in the name of Jesus*” (*v. 27*). He told them Saul’s story: his encounter with Jesus and his bold preaching in Damascus. Barnabas vouched for him.

Because of Barnabas, Saul was accepted. He stayed with the apostles and preached boldly in Jerusalem.

Barnabas would continue to play a key role in Saul’s life. Later, he brought Saul from Tarsus to Antioch to help lead the growing church there, and the two traveled together on the first missionary journey (*Acts 11:25–26*; *13:2*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This passage shows the vital ministry of encouragement. Without Barnabas, Saul might have remained isolated and rejected by the Jerusalem church. Barnabas saw what God was doing in Saul’s life and stood with him when others would not. Paul later urged believers to “*exhort one another, and build each other up*” (*1 Thessalonians 5:11*).

It also shows the importance of advocacy in the church. Barnabas used his credibility to open a door for someone else. Those who are trusted can help others be welcomed, especially those who are new, different, or have a troubled past.

Finally, the passage shows that God often works through relationships. Saul’s transformation was God’s work, but God used Ananias and Barnabas to bring Saul into the community of believers. Faith grows within community.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage encourages believers to be like Barnabas. Many people in churches feel unwelcome, overlooked, or misunderstood, whether new believers, newcomers, or people with difficult histories. Believers can take the initiative to welcome them, listen to their stories, and help them find their place.

It also reminds believers that encouragement can change lives. A word of support or an act of trust can give someone the confidence to keep going. Barnabas’s encouragement helped launch the ministry of the greatest missionary in history.

Finally, the passage acknowledges that fear and caution are understandable. The Jerusalem believers had good reasons to be wary. Wisdom is needed in welcoming those with a history of harm. But fear should not have the final word when there is clear evidence of God’s transforming work.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Acts 9* shows that no one is beyond the reach of God’s grace. Saul, the fierce persecutor of the church, became its greatest missionary. Believers can pray with hope for those who seem far from God, even those who oppose the faith, knowing that Jesus can meet anyone and transform their life.

The chapter also shows how deeply Jesus identifies with His people. When Saul persecuted the believers, Jesus said, “Why do you persecute me?” Believers who suffer for their faith can take comfort in knowing that Jesus shares their suffering. Believers are also challenged to treat one another with care, since how they treat Christ’s people is how they treat Christ.

*Acts 9* highlights the importance of ordinary believers. Ananias obeyed despite his fear and welcomed Saul as a brother. Barnabas stood with Saul when others were afraid. Dorcas served widows with her hands. These faithful believers show that every act of obedience, welcome, and service matters in God’s kingdom.

Finally, the chapter shows a church growing in peace, walking in the fear of the Lord and the comfort of the Holy Spirit, with the power of Jesus at work through healing and restoration. Believers today can seek to be part of such a church: humble, encouraging, welcoming, and confident in the power of the risen Lord.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for meeting Saul on the road to Damascus and turning an enemy into a brother and an apostle. Thank You that no one is beyond the reach of Your grace. I pray for those I know who seem far from You or opposed to You; meet them as You met Saul. Thank You for identifying with Your people in their suffering. Make me a faithful vessel to carry Your name, even when it costs me. Give me the courage of Ananias to obey You when I am afraid, and the heart of Barnabas to welcome and encourage others. Help me, like Dorcas, to serve others with my hands. Build up Your church in peace, in the fear of the Lord, and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Acts · Chapter 10 of 28

# Acts — Chapter 10

Chapter Theme: God Shows No Favoritism: The Gospel Comes to the Gentiles

[Read Acts 10 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/ACT10.htm)

Main Teaching

God prepares two men at the same time. Cornelius, a devout Roman centurion, is told by an angel to send for Peter, while Peter, praying on a rooftop in Joppa, sees a vision of unclean animals and hears, “What God has cleansed, you must not call unclean.” Peter goes to Cornelius’s house, the home of a Gentile, and declares that God shows no favoritism. As he proclaims Jesus’ life, death, resurrection, and the forgiveness of sins for all who believe, the Holy Spirit falls on the Gentile listeners, and Peter has them baptized in the name of Jesus Christ.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Acts 10* is one of the great turning points of the New Testament. Until now, the church was made up of Jews and of Samaritans, who shared much of Israel’s heritage. The Ethiopian official was probably a God-fearer, a Gentile who worshiped Israel’s God. But the question of whether Gentiles could become full members of God’s people without first becoming Jews had not been faced directly. In this chapter, God answers that question, and Luke considers it so important that Peter retells the story in chapter 11 and refers to it again at the Jerusalem Council in chapter 15.

For Jews of Peter’s day, the separation between Jews and Gentiles was deep. The Law of Moses distinguished between clean and unclean foods (*Leviticus 11*), and these distinctions marked Israel as a people set apart. Over time, many Jews avoided entering Gentile homes or eating with Gentiles, to avoid being made ritually unclean. This made table fellowship between Jews and Gentiles extremely difficult. God was about to break down this wall.

### Cornelius’s Vision (*10:1–8*)

Cornelius lived in Caesarea, the Roman capital of the province of Judea, on the Mediterranean coast. He was “*a centurion of what was called the Italian Regiment*” (*v. 1*), a Roman officer commanding about a hundred soldiers. He was “*a devout man, and one who feared God with all his house, who gave gifts for the needy generously to the people, and always prayed to God*” (*v. 2*). Cornelius was a “God-fearer,” a Gentile who believed in the God of Israel, prayed, and gave to the poor, but who had not become a full convert to Judaism.

At about three in the afternoon, the time of evening prayer, an angel appeared to him in a vision: “*Your prayers and your gifts to the needy have gone up for a memorial before God*” (*v. 4*). The angel told him to send for Simon Peter in Joppa, who was staying with Simon the tanner by the sea. Cornelius immediately sent two servants and a devout soldier.

### Peter’s Vision (*10:9–23*)

The next day, as Cornelius’s messengers approached Joppa, Peter went up on the flat roof of the house to pray at noon. He became hungry, and while food was being prepared, he fell into a trance. He saw heaven opened and something like a great sheet being lowered by its four corners. In it were all kinds of animals, reptiles, and birds, including those the Law declared unclean.

A voice said, “*Rise, Peter, kill and eat!*” (*v. 13*) Peter protested: “*Not so, Lord; for I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean*” (*v. 14*). Peter’s reply shows his lifelong faithfulness to the food laws. The voice answered, studied below. This happened three times, and the sheet was taken back up to heaven. The threefold repetition may remind readers of Peter’s three denials and Jesus’ three questions in *John 21*; God was again patiently teaching Peter.

While Peter was puzzling over the vision, Cornelius’s men arrived at the gate. The Spirit told Peter, “*arise, get down, and go with them, doubting nothing; for I have sent them*” (*v. 20*). The timing was perfect. God had prepared both men.

The men explained that Cornelius, “*a righteous man and one who fears God, and well spoken of by all the nation of the Jews*” (*v. 22*), had been directed by an angel to invite Peter. Then Peter “*called them in and provided a place to stay*” (*v. 23*). Already, Peter was beginning to understand. He welcomed Gentiles as guests.

### Peter in Cornelius’s House (*10:24–33*)

The next day, Peter traveled to Caesarea with some believers from Joppa. Cornelius was waiting, having gathered his relatives and close friends. When Peter entered, Cornelius fell at his feet in reverence. Peter lifted him up: “*Stand up! I myself am also a man*” (*v. 26*). Peter refused to accept worship.

Then Peter said, “*You yourselves know how it is an unlawful thing for a man who is a Jew to join himself or come to one of another nation, but God has shown me that I shouldn’t call any man unholy or unclean*” (*v. 28*). Peter had understood the vision. It was not ultimately about food but about people. God was teaching him that no person should be considered unclean or beyond the reach of His grace.

Cornelius explained his vision and said, “*Now therefore we are all here present in the sight of God to hear all things that have been commanded you by God*” (*v. 33*). Cornelius and his household were eager to hear God’s word.

### Peter’s Sermon (*10:34–43*)

Peter began, “*Truly I perceive that God doesn’t show favoritism*” (*v. 34*). This opening is studied below. Peter then summarized the story of Jesus, studied in part below: His ministry beginning in Galilee after John’s baptism, His anointing with the Spirit and power, His healing of all who were oppressed by the devil, His death “*hanging him on a tree*” (*v. 39*), and His resurrection on the third day. God made Him known to chosen witnesses “*who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead*” (*v. 41*). Jesus commanded them to preach and to testify “*that this is he who is appointed by God as the Judge of the living and the dead*” (*v. 42*). Peter’s conclusion and what followed are studied below.

### The Spirit Poured Out on the Gentiles (*10:44–48*)

While Peter was still speaking, the Holy Spirit fell on all who were listening. The Jewish believers who had come with Peter “*were amazed*” (*v. 45*), “*because the gift of the Holy Spirit was also poured out on the Gentiles*” (*v. 45*). They heard the Gentiles “*speaking in other languages and magnifying God*” (*v. 46*), just as the disciples had at Pentecost. This is sometimes called “the Gentile Pentecost.”

Peter asked, “*Can anyone forbid these people from being baptized with water? They have received the Holy Spirit just like us*” (*v. 47*). God had already accepted these Gentiles by giving them His Spirit. The church could not refuse them baptism. Peter commanded them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ, and they asked him to stay with them for several days. Peter, the Jew who had never eaten anything unclean, now stayed in a Gentile home, sharing meals and fellowship.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Acts 10:15* — What God Has Cleansed

> *“A voice came to him again the second time, ‘What God has cleansed, you must not call unclean.’”*
>
> — *Acts 10:15* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Peter was on the roof of a house in Joppa, praying at noon. He became hungry, and while waiting for food, he fell into a trance. He saw a large sheet lowered from heaven, filled with all kinds of animals, including those that the Law of Moses called unclean, such as pigs, reptiles, and certain birds. Jews were forbidden to eat these animals (*Leviticus 11*).

A voice told Peter to kill and eat. Peter refused, saying he had never eaten anything unclean. He had kept these food laws all his life, as faithful Jews did.

Then the voice said, “*What God has cleansed, you must not call unclean*” (*v. 15*). God was declaring that the old distinctions between clean and unclean foods were no longer in force. Jesus had already pointed in this direction when He taught that what goes into a person’s mouth does not make them unclean, and Mark notes that by this Jesus declared “*making all foods clean*” (*Mark 7:19*). Now God made it clear to Peter in a vision.

But the vision was about more than food. While Peter was wondering what it meant, Gentile visitors arrived at the door. Peter soon understood: “*God has shown me that I shouldn’t call any man unholy or unclean*” (*v. 28*). The food laws had symbolized Israel’s separation from the nations. Now that God was welcoming the nations into His people through Christ, that separation was ending.

The vision was repeated three times, emphasizing its importance and helping Peter accept a truth that went against everything he had been taught.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals that God Himself has broken down the barriers between peoples. Through Christ, Gentiles are no longer outsiders. Paul writes that Christ “*abolished in his flesh the hostility, the law of commandments contained in ordinances*” (*Ephesians 2:15*), so that He might create one new people from Jews and Gentiles.

It also shows that God’s cleansing work is complete. What God has cleansed is truly clean. People cannot declare unclean those whom God has accepted. This applies to all who come to Christ: their sins are washed away, and they are welcomed fully into God’s family.

Finally, the verse shows that God sometimes has to challenge His people’s deeply held assumptions. Peter’s refusal came from sincere faithfulness to what he had been taught. God patiently showed him something new, not by contradicting His purposes, but by revealing how they were fulfilled in Christ.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse challenges believers to examine their attitudes toward others. Many believers, consciously or unconsciously, view certain groups as less worthy of God’s love, perhaps people of a different ethnicity, culture, social class, or background. God’s word to Peter applies: no one should be called unclean whom God has cleansed.

It also encourages believers who feel unworthy. Some people believe they are too sinful or too different to be accepted by God. God declares clean all who come to Him through Christ. Their past does not define them.

Finally, the verse invites believers to be open to God’s correction. Peter’s convictions were sincere, but God corrected him. Believers can ask God to show them where their attitudes need to change, and they can be humble enough to accept His correction through His word.

### *Acts 10:34–35* — God Doesn’t Show Favoritism

> *“Peter opened his mouth and said, Truly I perceive that God doesn’t show favoritism; but in every nation he who fears him and works righteousness is acceptable to him.”*
>
> — *Acts 10:34–35* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Peter stood in the home of Cornelius, a Roman centurion, surrounded by his Gentile family and friends. Only days before, he would never have entered such a house. Now, having seen God’s vision and heard Cornelius’s account, he began to speak.

“*Truly I perceive that God doesn’t show favoritism*” (*v. 34*). The word “perceive” suggests that Peter was coming to a new understanding. The phrase “show favoritism” literally means “receive faces,” judging people by their outward appearance, nationality, or status. Peter realized that God does not accept or reject people based on their ethnicity or background.

“*but in every nation he who fears him and works righteousness is acceptable to him*” (*v. 35*). God welcomes people from every nation who revere Him and seek to do what is right. Cornelius was an example: he feared God, prayed, and gave generously to the poor.

This verse does not mean that people are saved by their good works or that Jesus is unnecessary. Cornelius still needed to hear about Jesus, and the angel told him to send for Peter so that he could hear the message by which he would be saved (*Acts 11:14*). The point is that God is open to people of every nation and that ethnicity is no barrier to coming to Him. Those whose hearts are turned toward God, like Cornelius, are welcomed to receive the gospel and the salvation it brings through faith in Jesus (*10:43*).

Peter’s realization fulfilled what the Old Testament had already taught: God “*doesn’t respect persons or take bribes*” (*Deuteronomy 10:17*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses reveal the impartiality of God. God created all peoples and loves all peoples. His covenant with Israel was never meant to exclude the nations forever; it was meant to bring blessing to all nations (*Genesis 12:3*). In Christ, that purpose is fulfilled.

They also show that God’s salvation is for everyone. Paul writes that there is no distinction between Jew and Greek, “*for the same Lord is Lord of all, and is rich to all who call on him*” (*Romans 10:12*). The gospel is not a message for one culture or nation but for the whole world.

Finally, the verses challenge every form of prejudice within the church. James warns believers not to show favoritism, treating the rich better than the poor (*James 2:1–9*). If God does not show favoritism, His people must not either.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses call believers to reject prejudice and discrimination. Every person, of whatever nationality, ethnicity, class, or background, is equally precious to God. Churches are called to welcome all people and to treat them with equal respect and love.

They also encourage believers to share the gospel with everyone. Some believers unconsciously assume that certain people are unlikely to be interested in Jesus or unworthy of their effort. Peter’s experience shows that God may be preparing hearts in unexpected places.

Finally, these verses give hope to people who feel like outsiders. Many people feel that faith is for others, not for people like them. God shows no favoritism. Anyone from any nation can come to Him through Jesus.

### *Acts 10:38* — He Went About Doing Good

> *“how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power, who went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him.”*
>
> — *Acts 10:38* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

In his sermon at Cornelius’s house, Peter summarized the life and ministry of Jesus. His Gentile listeners had probably heard something about Jesus, since His ministry had been well known in Judea and Galilee. Peter explained who He was and what He had done.

“*how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power*” (*v. 38*). This anointing took place at Jesus’ baptism, when the Spirit descended on Him like a dove (*Luke 3:21–22*). The title “Christ” means “Anointed One.” Jesus was anointed by God for His mission.

“*who went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil*” (*v. 38*). This is a beautiful summary of Jesus’ life. He “went about doing good.” Wherever He went, He brought blessing: healing the sick, feeding the hungry, welcoming outcasts, teaching truth, and setting people free. His healing ministry was also a battle against evil. He freed people from the power of the devil.

“*for God was with him*” (*v. 38*). The source of Jesus’ power was God’s presence with Him. Jesus Himself said that He did nothing on His own but only what He saw the Father doing (*John 5:19*).

Peter then went on to describe Jesus’ death and resurrection. But he began with Jesus’ life of goodness. The One who died on the cross had spent His life doing good.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that Jesus’ ministry was a demonstration of God’s kingdom. When Jesus healed and delivered people, He was showing that God’s rule had come to overthrow the power of evil. He said, “*But if I by God’s finger cast out demons, then God’s Kingdom has come to you*” (*Luke 11:20*).

It also reveals the character of Jesus. He was not a distant teacher or a political revolutionary. He was full of compassion, moving toward people in need. His goodness was not passive; He “went about” doing good, actively seeking out those who needed help.

Finally, the verse shows that Jesus’ life is a pattern for His followers. Believers are called to imitate Christ, filled with the same Spirit, doing good to all people (*Galatians 6:10*) and opposing the works of evil.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to follow Jesus’ example of doing good. Believers can look for opportunities to help others in practical ways: caring for the sick, supporting the poor, encouraging the discouraged, and standing up for the oppressed.

It also reminds believers that their power comes from God’s presence. Jesus did good because God was with Him and He was anointed with the Spirit. Believers can rely on the same Spirit to empower them for good works.

Finally, the verse offers comfort to those who are oppressed, whether by spiritual forces, illness, or injustice. Jesus came to heal and set people free. Believers can bring their burdens to Him, trusting His power to help.

### *Acts 10:43–44* — Everyone Who Believes Receives Forgiveness

> *“All the prophets testify about him, that through his name everyone who believes in him will receive remission of sins. While Peter was still speaking these words, the Holy Spirit fell on all those who heard the word.”*
>
> — *Acts 10:43–44* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Peter was concluding his sermon to Cornelius and his household. He had described Jesus’ ministry, death, and resurrection, and had said that Jesus was appointed by God as the Judge of the living and the dead. Then he offered the good news.

“*All the prophets testify about him*” (*v. 43*). The Old Testament prophets pointed to Jesus. Isaiah, Jeremiah, and others had spoken of a coming Savior who would bring forgiveness. Peter’s message was the fulfillment of God’s long-promised plan.

“*that through his name everyone who believes in him will receive remission of sins*” (*v. 43*). “Remission” means forgiveness or release. This is the heart of the gospel: forgiveness of sins comes through Jesus, and it is available to “everyone who believes in him.” Not only Jews, but Gentiles. Not only the religious, but anyone. The only condition is believing in Jesus.

Then something remarkable happened: “*While Peter was still speaking these words, the Holy Spirit fell on all those who heard the word*” (*v. 44*). Peter had not finished his sermon. He had not given an invitation or laid hands on anyone. As soon as the listeners heard the message of forgiveness through faith in Jesus, God poured out His Spirit on them.

The Jewish believers with Peter were astonished. They heard these Gentiles speaking in tongues and praising God, just as the disciples had at Pentecost. God had given the Gentiles the same gift He had given the Jewish believers.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that salvation comes through faith in Jesus, not through ethnic identity or religious ritual. The Gentiles received the Spirit before they were circumcised or baptized, showing that God accepted them on the basis of faith alone. Peter later argued at the Jerusalem Council that God “*made no distinction between us and them, cleansing their hearts by faith*” (*Acts 15:9*).

They also show that God takes the initiative. The Spirit fell on the listeners while Peter was still speaking. God did not wait for the church to approve the Gentiles. He acted first, and the church followed by baptizing them.

Finally, the verses show the unity of the church. The same Spirit given to Jewish believers at Pentecost was given to Gentile believers in Caesarea. Paul writes that in one Spirit believers were all baptized into one body, “*whether Jews or Greeks*” (*1 Corinthians 12:13*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to share the simple message of forgiveness through faith in Jesus. The gospel is good news for everyone. Believers can share it with confidence, trusting that God’s Spirit works through His word.

They also give assurance to anyone who believes. Forgiveness is not earned by good works or religious rituals. It is received by faith in Jesus. Believers can rest in this assurance, knowing that their sins are forgiven.

Finally, these verses challenge believers to welcome those whom God has accepted. The Jewish believers were amazed that God had poured out His Spirit on the Gentiles. Believers today may also be surprised at whom God chooses to save. When God works in someone’s life, the church is called to welcome them fully.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Acts 10* shows that God shows no favoritism. He welcomes people from every nation who turn to Him through Jesus. Believers are called to reject every form of prejudice and to welcome all people as equally loved by God. Churches can reflect this by being places where people of every background feel at home.

The chapter also shows how God prepares hearts and directs His people. He spoke to Cornelius and to Peter at the same time, bringing them together for His purposes. Believers can trust that God is at work in the lives of people around them, and they can be attentive to His leading as they share their faith.

*Acts 10* reminds believers that God sometimes challenges their assumptions. Peter had to unlearn deeply held beliefs about who was clean and unclean. Believers can be open to God’s correction through His word, allowing Him to expand their understanding of His love and grace.

Finally, the chapter celebrates the heart of the gospel: through Jesus, everyone who believes receives forgiveness of sins. Jesus went about doing good, died, rose again, and now offers salvation to all. Believers can share this message with everyone, trusting that God’s Spirit can fall on anyone who hears and believes.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord God, thank You that You show no favoritism, and that in every nation You welcome those who turn to You. Forgive me for the times I have looked at others as less worthy of Your love. Teach me not to call anyone unclean whom You have cleansed. Thank You for preparing Cornelius’s heart and Peter’s heart at the same time; prepare my heart and lead me to those who are seeking You. Lord Jesus, thank You that You went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed. Fill me with Your Spirit so that I may do good as You did. Thank You for the forgiveness of sins that comes to everyone who believes in You. Make Your church a place where people of every nation are welcomed and loved. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
