Acts · Chapter 11 of 28

# Acts — Chapter 11

Chapter Theme: Repentance unto Life for the Gentiles and a New Church in Antioch

[Read Acts 11 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/ACT11.htm)

Main Teaching

When Peter returns to Jerusalem, some believers criticize him for eating with uncircumcised Gentiles. Peter tells them step by step how God led him to Cornelius and poured out the Holy Spirit on the Gentiles, and the church glorifies God, recognizing that He has granted the Gentiles repentance that leads to life. Meanwhile, scattered believers begin preaching to Greeks in Antioch, and a great number turn to the Lord. Barnabas encourages the new church, brings Saul to help teach, and the disciples are first called Christians. When a famine is foretold, the Antioch believers send relief to the believers in Judea.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Acts 11* shows how the church responded to the conversion of Cornelius and how the gospel took root in a major Gentile city. The chapter has two parts. First, Peter explains to the Jerusalem church why he baptized Gentiles (*11:1–18*). Second, Luke describes the founding of the church in Antioch, which would become the base for Paul’s missionary journeys (*11:19–30*).

### Peter Criticized (*11:1–3*)

News traveled quickly. “*the apostles and the brothers who were in Judea heard that the Gentiles had also received the word of God*” (*v. 1*). When Peter returned to Jerusalem, “*those who were of the circumcision contended with him*” (*v. 2*). This phrase refers to Jewish believers who believed that Gentiles needed to be circumcised and keep the Law of Moses to be part of God’s people.

Notice what they criticized: “*You went in to uncircumcised men and ate with them!*” (*v. 3*) Their concern was not primarily that Gentiles had believed, but that Peter had shared table fellowship with them. Eating together was a sign of acceptance and community. For many Jewish believers, this crossed a line they had been taught never to cross.

### Peter’s Explanation (*11:4–18*)

Peter did not respond with anger or defensiveness. “*But Peter began, and explained to them in order*” (*v. 4*). He told them exactly what had happened: the vision of the sheet with unclean animals, the voice saying, “What God has cleansed, don’t you call unclean,” the arrival of the three men, the Spirit’s instruction to go “*without discriminating*” (*v. 12*), and the angel’s message to Cornelius that Peter would bring “*words by which you will be saved, you and all your house*” (*v. 14*). Peter also mentioned that “*These six brothers also accompanied me*” (*v. 12*). He had witnesses.

Then Peter described the decisive moment: “*As I began to speak, the Holy Spirit fell on them, even as on us at the beginning*” (*v. 15*). He remembered Jesus’ promise that His followers would be baptized with the Holy Spirit. Peter’s conclusion and the church’s response are studied below.

### The Church in Antioch (*11:19–26*)

Luke now picks up the story of those who had been scattered by the persecution after Stephen’s death (*8:1*, 4). They traveled to Phoenicia (along the coast north of Israel), Cyprus (an island in the Mediterranean), and Antioch, “*speaking the word to no one except to Jews only*” (*v. 19*).

Antioch was the capital of the Roman province of Syria and the third-largest city in the Roman Empire, after Rome and Alexandria, with a population of perhaps half a million. It was a cosmopolitan city of many cultures and religions, known for both its wealth and its moral corruption.

“*But there were some of them, men of Cyprus and Cyrene, who, when they had come to Antioch, spoke to the Hellenists, preaching the Lord Jesus*” (*v. 20*). Here “Hellenists” probably means Greek-speaking Gentiles. These unnamed believers took a bold step, sharing the gospel directly with non-Jews. “*The hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number believed and turned to the Lord*” (*v. 21*).

The Jerusalem church sent Barnabas to Antioch. His ministry there is studied below. Barnabas then went to Tarsus to find Saul and brought him to Antioch. For a whole year, they taught many people. Then Luke adds a significant detail, studied below.

### Famine Relief (*11:27–30*)

Prophets came from Jerusalem to Antioch. One of them, Agabus, “*indicated by the Spirit that there should be a great famine all over the world, which also happened in the days of Claudius*” (*v. 28*). Claudius was the Roman emperor from A.D. 41 to 54. Ancient historians record several severe famines during his reign, including one in Judea around A.D. 46–48. The response of the Antioch church is studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Acts 11:17–18* — Who Was I to Withstand God?

> *“If then God gave to them the same gift as us when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I, that I could withstand God? When they heard these things, they held their peace and glorified God, saying, ‘Then God has also granted to the Gentiles repentance to life!’”*
>
> — *Acts 11:17–18* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Peter had been criticized by Jewish believers in Jerusalem for entering the home of uncircumcised Gentiles and eating with them. He explained carefully everything that had happened: his vision, the Spirit’s guidance, Cornelius’s vision, and the Holy Spirit falling on the Gentiles as Peter spoke.

Then Peter drew his conclusion: “*If then God gave to them the same gift as us when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I, that I could withstand God?*” (*v. 17*) God had given the Gentiles “the same gift,” the Holy Spirit, that He had given the Jewish believers at Pentecost. This showed that God had accepted them fully. If God had accepted them, how could Peter refuse to accept them? To oppose them would be to oppose God.

Notice that Peter emphasizes the gift was given “when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ.” The basis of acceptance for both Jews and Gentiles was faith in Jesus, not circumcision or keeping the Law.

The response of the critics was remarkable: “*When they heard these things, they held their peace and glorified God*” (*v. 18*). They stopped arguing and began praising God. Their minds were changed by the evidence of God’s work.

They said, “*Then God has also granted to the Gentiles repentance to life!*” (*v. 18*) “Repentance to life” means a turning to God that leads to eternal life. They recognized that repentance itself was God’s gift, and that God had given it to the Gentiles just as He had given it to the Jews.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This passage shows that the church must follow where God leads. The Jerusalem believers had their own assumptions, but when they saw clear evidence of God’s work, they submitted to it. The church does not decide whom God will accept; it recognizes and welcomes those whom God has already accepted.

It also reveals that salvation is a gift of God’s grace from beginning to end. Even repentance, turning from sin to God, is something God “grants.” Paul writes that God’s kindness leads people to repentance (*Romans 2:4*). No one can boast in their own repentance; it is God’s gift.

Finally, the passage shows a healthy way to handle disagreement in the church. Peter explained patiently, providing evidence and witnesses. The critics listened, changed their minds, and praised God. This pattern, honest discussion grounded in God’s work and word, leads to unity.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to welcome those whom God has accepted. Sometimes churches struggle to accept people who are different, whether culturally, socially, or in their background. If God has given someone faith and His Spirit, the church is called to welcome them fully.

They also model how to handle conflict. When believers disagree, they can follow Peter’s example: explaining carefully and humbly, and listening openly. They can also follow the Jerusalem believers’ example: being willing to change their minds when they see God at work.

Finally, these verses encourage gratitude for the gift of repentance. Believers who have turned to God can thank Him for granting them repentance and life. They can also pray for others, asking God to grant them the same gift.

### *Acts 11:23–24* — Barnabas Saw the Grace of God

> *“who, when he had come, and had seen the grace of God, was glad. He exhorted them all, that with purpose of heart they should remain near to the Lord. For he was a good man, and full of the Holy Spirit and of faith, and many people were added to the Lord.”*
>
> — *Acts 11:23–24* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

When the church in Jerusalem heard that many Gentiles in Antioch had believed, they sent Barnabas to investigate. This was a wise choice. Barnabas was from Cyprus, like some of those who had first preached in Antioch, and he was known for his generosity and encouragement (*4:36–37*; *9:27*).

“*who, when he had come, and had seen the grace of God, was glad*” (*v. 23*). Barnabas could have come with suspicion, looking for problems. Instead, he saw evidence of God’s grace in the lives of the new believers, and he rejoiced. He recognized that God was at work.

“*He exhorted them all, that with purpose of heart they should remain near to the Lord*” (*v. 23*). Barnabas encouraged the new believers to remain faithful to the Lord with determined hearts. New believers in a city like Antioch would face many temptations and pressures. Barnabas urged them to stay close to Jesus.

Luke then describes Barnabas’s character: “*For he was a good man, and full of the Holy Spirit and of faith*” (*v. 24*). Barnabas was a person of genuine goodness, spiritual maturity, and trust in God. Few people in Scripture are simply described as “a good man.”

“*and many people were added to the Lord*” (*v. 24*). Barnabas’s ministry bore fruit. Through his encouragement, the church continued to grow.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show the importance of recognizing God’s grace in others. Barnabas did not focus on what was missing in the new believers or on their differences from Jewish believers. He saw what God was doing, and he was glad. Paul similarly gave thanks for the grace of God at work in the churches (*1 Corinthians 1:4*).

They also highlight the importance of perseverance. Barnabas urged the believers to remain true to the Lord. Faith is not only a one-time decision but a lifelong commitment. Jesus said, “*Remain in me, and I in you*” (*John 15:4*).

Finally, Barnabas’s character shows that effective ministry flows from who a person is. His goodness, faith, and fullness of the Spirit made him a channel of God’s blessing. God uses people whose lives reflect His character.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to look for God’s grace in others. It is easy to notice faults, especially in people who are different. Believers can train themselves to see and celebrate what God is doing in the lives of others.

They also call believers to encourage one another to remain faithful. New believers especially need support and encouragement. Believers can follow Barnabas’s example, urging one another to stay close to the Lord through every season.

Finally, these verses invite believers to grow in character. Barnabas was a good man, full of the Spirit and faith. Believers can ask God to shape their character, knowing that genuine goodness and faith make a lasting impact.

### *Acts 11:26* — First Called Christians

> *“When he had found him, he brought him to Antioch. For a whole year they were gathered together with the assembly, and taught many people. The disciples were first called Christians in Antioch.”*
>
> — *Acts 11:26* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The church in Antioch was growing rapidly. Barnabas realized he needed help, so he went to Tarsus, about a hundred miles away, to find Saul. Saul had been sent to Tarsus after his conversion when his life was threatened in Jerusalem (*9:30*). He had probably been ministering there for several years.

“*When he had found him, he brought him to Antioch. For a whole year they were gathered together with the assembly, and taught many people*” (*v. 26*). Barnabas and Saul worked together for a full year, teaching the new believers. Teaching was essential for a church made up of many new believers from pagan backgrounds who needed to understand the Scriptures and the way of Jesus.

“*The disciples were first called Christians in Antioch*” (*v. 26*). The name “Christian” means “follower of Christ” or “belonging to Christ.” It may have been given by outsiders, possibly as a nickname. The church in Antioch included both Jews and Gentiles, so outsiders could not simply call them a Jewish sect. They needed a new name, and they chose one based on the person the believers constantly talked about: Christ.

The name appears only three times in the New Testament (here; *Acts 26:28*; *1 Peter 4:16*). The believers usually called themselves “disciples,” “brothers,” “saints,” or followers of “the Way.” But the name “Christian” stuck and became the name used throughout history.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that the identity of believers is centered on Christ. They were known not by their ethnicity, culture, or social status, but by their connection to Christ. Paul writes, “*where there can’t be Greek and Jew, circumcision and uncircumcision, barbarian, Scythian, bondservant, or free person; but Christ is all, and in all*” (*Colossians 3:11*).

It also shows the importance of teaching in the church. Barnabas and Saul spent a whole year teaching. Strong churches are built on solid teaching of God’s word. Jesus commanded His followers to make disciples, “*teaching them to observe all things that I commanded you*” (*Matthew 28:20*).

Finally, the verse shows that believers’ lives can be visible to the world. Outsiders noticed that these people were devoted to Christ. Their lives revealed their allegiance.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to consider whether their lives reflect the name “Christian.” The name means belonging to Christ. Believers can ask whether others would recognize them as followers of Jesus by their words, actions, and priorities.

It also encourages believers to value teaching. New believers need to be taught, and all believers continue to grow through learning God’s word. Churches can prioritize solid biblical teaching, and believers can commit themselves to learning.

Finally, the verse reminds believers that their identity in Christ is greater than any other identity. Ethnicity, nationality, culture, and social status matter, but they are not the deepest truth about a believer. Belonging to Christ unites believers across all differences.

### *Acts 11:29–30* — Sending Relief to the Brothers in Judea

> *“As any of the disciples had plenty, each determined to send relief to the brothers who lived in Judea; which they also did, sending it to the elders by the hands of Barnabas and Saul.”*
>
> — *Acts 11:29–30* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

A prophet named Agabus came to Antioch from Jerusalem and predicted, by the Spirit, that a severe famine would spread over the Roman world. This famine came during the reign of Emperor Claudius. In Judea, where many believers were already poor, a famine would be devastating.

The church in Antioch responded immediately: “*As any of the disciples had plenty, each determined to send relief to the brothers who lived in Judea*” (*v. 29*). Each believer gave according to their ability. No one was forced; each person decided what they could give. This followed the principle Paul later taught: “*For if the readiness is there, it is acceptable according to what you have, not according to what you don’t have*” (*2 Corinthians 8:12*).

Notice who they were helping: “the brothers who lived in Judea.” The Antioch church was largely Gentile; the Judean church was Jewish. Yet they saw each other as family. The Gentile believers who had received the gospel from Jewish believers now helped them in their time of need.

“*which they also did, sending it to the elders by the hands of Barnabas and Saul*” (*v. 30*). They did not merely intend to help; they actually sent the gift. They entrusted it to Barnabas and Saul, trusted leaders, who delivered it to the elders of the Jerusalem church. This is the first mention of “elders” in the church, leaders who oversaw the congregation.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that the unity of the church is expressed in practical love. Jews and Gentiles were one in Christ, and that unity was shown through generosity across ethnic and geographic lines. John writes, “*But whoever has the world’s goods and sees his brother in need, then closes his heart of compassion against him, how does God’s love remain in him?*” (*1 John 3:17*)

They also reveal a pattern of mutual blessing. The Gentiles had received spiritual blessings from the Jewish believers; now they shared material blessings. Paul later wrote that if the Gentiles have shared in the Jews’ spiritual blessings, “*they owe it to them also to serve them in material things*” (*Romans 15:27*).

Finally, these verses show responsible handling of money. The gift was carried by trusted leaders and delivered to the elders. Paul later took great care to handle financial gifts with integrity (*2 Corinthians 8:20–21*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to care for fellow believers in need, including those in other places and cultures. Many Christians around the world face poverty, famine, war, or persecution. Believers can give generously to support them.

They also show that giving should be according to ability. Not everyone can give the same amount. Each believer can decide what they are able to give, giving freely and cheerfully.

Finally, these verses highlight the importance of integrity in handling resources. Churches and ministries should be transparent and responsible with the gifts entrusted to them, ensuring that help reaches those who need it.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Acts 11* shows a church willing to change its mind when God reveals His will. The Jerusalem believers were troubled when Peter ate with Gentiles, but when they heard how God had poured out His Spirit, they praised Him. Believers today can follow this example, remaining humble and open to God’s leading, even when it challenges long-held assumptions.

The chapter also celebrates the spread of the gospel to new people and places. Unnamed believers from Cyprus and Cyrene shared Jesus with Gentiles in Antioch, and a great number believed. Every believer can share Christ with those around them, including people from different backgrounds, trusting that the Lord’s hand is with them.

*Acts 11* highlights the importance of encouragement and teaching. Barnabas saw the grace of God and encouraged the new believers to remain faithful. He and Saul taught the church for a year. Believers today need both encouragement to persevere and teaching to grow. Churches can provide both, and individual believers can be encouragers like Barnabas.

Finally, the chapter shows practical love across ethnic and geographic lines. The Antioch church, made up largely of Gentiles, sent relief to Jewish believers in Judea. Believers today can express their unity in Christ by giving generously to support fellow believers in need around the world.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord God, thank You for granting repentance that leads to life to people of every nation. Thank You for including me in Your family. Make me humble and willing to follow where You lead, even when it challenges my assumptions. Give me eyes like Barnabas to see Your grace at work in others, and a heart to encourage them to remain near to You. Let my life show that I belong to Christ, so that the name “Christian” fits me truly. Teach me through Your word and help me to grow. Make me generous, ready to share what I have with brothers and sisters in need, wherever they are. Unite Your church across every division by Your love. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Acts · Chapter 12 of 28

# Acts — Chapter 12

Chapter Theme: A Praying Church, a Delivered Apostle, and a Proud King Brought Low

[Read Acts 12 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/ACT12.htm)

Main Teaching

King Herod Agrippa I executes the apostle James and imprisons Peter, planning to put him on trial after Passover. While the church prays earnestly, an angel wakes Peter in his cell, his chains fall off, and he is led out through locked gates. Peter goes to the house where believers are praying, but they are slow to believe the servant girl who announces him. Later, Herod accepts the crowd’s praise as a god and is struck down. Herod dies, but the word of God continues to grow and multiply.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Acts 12* brings the first half of the book to a close. The focus has been on the church in Jerusalem and on Peter. After this chapter, Peter largely disappears from Acts (he reappears briefly at the Jerusalem Council in chapter 15), and the focus shifts to Paul and the mission to the Gentiles. The chapter shows the church facing persecution from the highest political authority in the region and shows God’s power over even the mightiest earthly rulers.

The “King Herod” in this chapter is Herod Agrippa I, grandson of Herod the Great, who had tried to kill the infant Jesus (*Matthew 2*), and nephew of Herod Antipas, who had executed John the Baptist and mocked Jesus at His trial (*Luke 23:6–12*). Herod Agrippa I was a friend of the Roman emperors Caligula and Claudius and ruled over a territory nearly as large as his grandfather’s from A.D. 41 to 44. He worked hard to please the Jewish population and present himself as devout.

### James Killed, Peter Arrested (*12:1–5*)

“*Now about that time, King Herod stretched out his hands to oppress some of the assembly*” (*v. 1*). Herod began a new wave of persecution. “*He killed James, the brother of John, with the sword*” (*v. 2*). James was one of the first disciples Jesus called and one of the inner three, with Peter and John, who witnessed the transfiguration and Jesus’ prayer in Gethsemane. Years earlier, James and John had asked to sit at Jesus’ right and left in His glory, and Jesus had asked whether they could drink the cup He would drink. They said they could, and Jesus said, “You will indeed drink my cup” (*Matthew 20:20–23*). James became the first of the Twelve to be martyred. Luke records his death in a single verse.

“*When he saw that it pleased the Jews, he proceeded to seize Peter also*” (*v. 3*). Herod’s motive was political: he wanted popularity. It was during “*the days of unleavened bread*” (*v. 3*), the week following Passover. Herod put Peter in prison under the guard of four squads of four soldiers each, intending to bring him out for public trial after the festival. He may have heard that the apostles had escaped from prison before (*5:19*) and taken extra precautions. The church’s response is studied below.

### Peter’s Miraculous Escape (*12:6–11*)

The night before Herod planned to bring him out, Peter was “*sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains*” (*v. 6*). Peter was asleep. Facing likely execution the next day, he slept peacefully, perhaps remembering Jesus’ words that he would live to old age (*John 21:18*).

“*And behold, an angel of the Lord stood by him, and a light shone in the cell*” (*v. 7*). The angel struck Peter on the side to wake him and said, “*Stand up quickly!*” (*v. 7*) Peter’s chains fell from his wrists. The angel told him to dress, put on his sandals and cloak, and follow. Peter obeyed, thinking he was seeing a vision. They passed the first and second guards and came to the iron gate leading to the city, “*which opened to them by itself*” (*v. 10*). They walked down a street, and the angel suddenly left. Peter’s realization is studied below.

### At the House of Mary (*12:12–17*)

Peter went to “*the house of Mary, the mother of John who was called Mark, where many were gathered together and were praying*” (*v. 12*). This John Mark would later travel with Paul and Barnabas and is traditionally regarded as the author of the Gospel of Mark. Mary’s house was large enough for many believers to gather, and it may have been a regular meeting place for the Jerusalem church.

A servant girl named Rhoda came to the gate. The scene that follows, one of the most charming in Acts, is studied below.

Peter told them how the Lord had brought him out of prison and said, “*Tell these things to James and to the brothers*” (*v. 17*). This James was the brother of Jesus, who had become a leader in the Jerusalem church (*15:13*; *Galatians 1:19*; *2:9*). Then Peter “*departed and went to another place*” (*v. 17*). Luke does not say where Peter went. He left Jerusalem to avoid Herod.

### Herod’s Death (*12:18–25*)

In the morning, there was great commotion among the soldiers. Herod searched for Peter and could not find him. He questioned the guards and ordered them executed, as Roman law often required when guards lost a prisoner. Then Herod went to Caesarea.

Herod had been angry with the people of Tyre and Sidon, coastal cities that depended on his territory for food. They sought peace through Blastus, the king’s chamberlain. On an appointed day, Herod put on his royal robes, sat on his throne, and gave a speech. The crowd shouted, “*The voice of a god, and not of a man!*” (*v. 22*) Herod’s response and its consequence are studied below.

The Jewish historian Josephus also records Herod Agrippa’s death in Caesarea in A.D. 44. He describes Herod wearing a robe made of silver that shone in the morning sun, the crowd hailing him as a god, Herod not rebuking them, and being struck immediately with severe abdominal pain, dying five days later. Josephus’s account closely matches Luke’s.

Barnabas and Saul returned from Jerusalem, where they had delivered the famine relief (*11:30*), and brought John Mark with them to Antioch. This sets the stage for the first missionary journey in chapter 13.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Acts 12:5* — Constant Prayer Was Made for Him

> *“Peter therefore was kept in the prison, but constant prayer was made by the assembly to God for him.”*
>
> — *Acts 12:5* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

King Herod had just executed the apostle James and arrested Peter. Herod planned to bring Peter before the people after Passover, almost certainly to execute him as well. Peter was held in prison under heavy guard, with sixteen soldiers assigned to him in rotating shifts. Escape seemed impossible.

“*Peter therefore was kept in the prison, but constant prayer was made by the assembly to God for him*” (*v. 5*). Notice the contrast: “Peter was kept in prison, but...” On one side was the power of the king, his soldiers, his chains, and his prison. On the other side was the church, praying.

The word “constant” can also be translated “earnestly” or “fervently.” It describes prayer that is intense and persistent, stretched out like a runner reaching for the finish line. Luke uses a related word to describe Jesus’ prayer in Gethsemane, when He prayed “*more earnestly*” (*Luke 22:44*).

The church had no political power, no army, and no influence with Herod. But they had access to God through prayer. They did not organize a protest or a rescue attempt. They prayed.

Their prayer was also communal: “by the assembly.” The believers gathered together to pray, as they had done from the beginning (*1:14*; *4:24*).

It is worth remembering that James had just been killed. The church had prayed, no doubt, for James too, and he had died. Yet they did not give up on prayer. They continued to pray earnestly for Peter.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that prayer is the church’s most powerful resource in times of crisis. Earthly rulers may seem all-powerful, but God rules over them. James writes, “*The insistent prayer of a righteous person is powerfully effective*” (*James 5:16*). The church in Jerusalem trusted that God could act when no human help was possible.

It also raises a difficult question: why was Peter delivered while James was killed? Scripture does not give a full answer. God’s purposes are sometimes beyond human understanding. Both men were faithful, and both were loved by God. James glorified God through his death, and Peter through his continued ministry. *Hebrews 11* describes believers who by faith escaped the sword and others who by faith were killed by the sword (*Hebrews 11:34*, 37). Both outcomes can be faithful, and God is present in both.

Finally, the verse shows the importance of persevering in prayer even after disappointment. The church had seen James die, yet they continued to pray. Faith keeps praying, even when previous prayers seem unanswered.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to pray earnestly in times of crisis. When believers face situations beyond their control, such as illness, injustice, or danger, they can turn to God in fervent, persistent prayer.

It also encourages believers to pray together. The church gathered to pray for Peter. Believers today can join with others to pray for those in need, especially for believers who are persecuted or imprisoned for their faith.

Finally, the verse offers comfort to those who have prayed and not received the answer they hoped for. God does not always answer as we wish, and some faithful believers suffer and die. Yet God is still good, still sovereign, and still worthy of trust. Believers can continue to pray, trusting God’s wisdom and love.

### *Acts 12:11* — Now I Truly Know

> *“When Peter had come to himself, he said, ‘Now I truly know that the Lord has sent out his angel and delivered me out of the hand of Herod, and from everything the Jewish people were expecting.’”*
>
> — *Acts 12:11* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Peter had been asleep in prison, chained between two soldiers, on the night before his likely execution. An angel woke him, his chains fell off, and he followed the angel past two sets of guards and through an iron gate that opened by itself. Throughout this, Peter thought he was dreaming or seeing a vision. Then the angel suddenly left him, and Peter found himself standing alone in a street of Jerusalem.

“*When Peter had come to himself*” (*v. 11*). The phrase means that Peter came to his senses, fully awake and aware. The cool night air and the empty street made it clear that this was really happening.

“*he said, “Now I truly know that the Lord has sent out his angel and delivered me out of the hand of Herod*” (*v. 11*). Peter recognized that his rescue was the Lord’s work. It was not luck or human cleverness. God had sent His angel.

“*and from everything the Jewish people were expecting*” (*v. 11*). Many people, including those who opposed the church, were expecting Peter’s execution. Herod had arrested him to please them. God had overturned their expectations.

Peter’s statement recalls *Psalm 34:7*: “*The LORD’s angel encamps around those who fear him, and delivers them*” (*Psalm 34:7*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that God’s deliverance can be so surprising that it seems unreal. Peter thought he was dreaming. Sometimes God’s answers to prayer are beyond what believers can imagine. Paul writes that God is able to do “*exceedingly abundantly above all that we ask or think*” (*Ephesians 3:20*).

It also shows that God is sovereign over earthly powers. Herod was a powerful king, supported by Rome, with soldiers and prisons at his command. Yet he could not hold Peter when God decided to release him. No human power can stand against God’s purposes.

Finally, the verse shows the importance of recognizing God’s work. Peter did not take credit for his escape or attribute it to chance. He acknowledged the Lord’s hand. Gratitude begins with recognizing what God has done.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to recognize God’s hand in their lives. Sometimes God’s help comes in ways that seem ordinary; sometimes it comes in extraordinary ways. Either way, believers can learn to say, “*Now I truly know that the Lord has sent out his angel and delivered me*” (*v. 11*), and give Him thanks.

It also gives hope to those who feel trapped. Peter was chained, guarded, and behind locked gates. Believers who feel trapped by circumstances can remember that God is able to open doors that seem permanently shut.

Finally, the verse reminds believers that human expectations do not limit God. Everyone expected Peter to die. God had other plans. Believers can trust that God’s purposes are not bound by what others predict or fear.

### *Acts 12:15–16* — “*You Are Crazy!*” (*v. 15*)

> *“They said to her, ‘You are crazy!’ But she insisted that it was so. They said, ‘It is his angel.’ But Peter continued knocking. When they had opened, they saw him and were amazed.”*
>
> — *Acts 12:15–16* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After his miraculous escape, Peter went to the house of Mary, the mother of John Mark, where many believers were gathered, praying. They were praying for Peter at that very moment. He knocked at the gate.

A servant girl named Rhoda came to answer. When she recognized Peter’s voice, she was so overjoyed that she forgot to open the gate. Instead, she ran inside to tell everyone that Peter was standing outside.

“*They said to her, “You are crazy!”*” (*v. 15*) The believers who were praying for Peter’s release did not believe that their prayer had been answered. They thought Rhoda was out of her mind.

“*But she insisted that it was so*” (*v. 15*). Rhoda kept insisting. She knew what she had heard.

“*They said, “It is his angel.”*” (*v. 15*) Some Jews believed that each person had a guardian angel who might look or sound like them (compare *Matthew 18:10*). Perhaps they thought Peter had already been killed and his angel had come.

“*But Peter continued knocking. When they had opened, they saw him and were amazed*” (*v. 16*). Peter was still standing outside, knocking. When they finally opened the gate, they were astonished.

This scene is both humorous and humbling. The believers were praying earnestly for Peter, but when God answered, they could not believe it.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This scene shows that God answers prayer even when believers’ faith is imperfect. The church prayed, but they did not fully expect God to answer. God answered anyway. His answers are not limited by the strength of human faith. Jesus taught that even faith as small as a mustard seed can move mountains (*Matthew 17:20*).

It also shows the honesty of Scripture. Luke does not present the early church as perfect. He shows their struggles and doubts. Believers today can take comfort in knowing that the early Christians, too, sometimes struggled to believe.

Finally, the scene honors a servant girl. Rhoda, a person of low social status, was the first to recognize the answer to the church’s prayer, and she held to the truth even when others dismissed her. Like the women at the empty tomb whose report was dismissed (*Luke 24:11*), Rhoda was right. God often reveals His work through those whom others overlook.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage encourages believers to pray with expectation. It is possible to pray faithfully while not really expecting God to answer. Believers can ask God to increase their faith so that they pray believing He will act.

It also comforts believers who struggle with doubt. God answered the church’s prayer despite their unbelief. Believers do not need perfect faith for God to hear them. They can bring their doubts to Him, like the father who said to Jesus, “*I believe. Help my unbelief!*” (*Mark 9:24*).

Finally, the passage reminds believers to listen to those whose voices are often ignored. Rhoda’s report was dismissed because she was young and a servant. Believers can learn to take seriously the testimony of all members of the community, regardless of their status.

### *Acts 12:23–24* — He Didn’t Give God the Glory

> *“Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him, because he didn’t give God the glory. Then he was eaten by worms and died. But the word of God grew and multiplied.”*
>
> — *Acts 12:23–24* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

King Herod Agrippa had executed James and imprisoned Peter. When Peter escaped, Herod had the guards executed and went to Caesarea. There, on an appointed day, he put on his royal robes, sat on his throne, and gave a speech to the people of Tyre and Sidon, who were seeking peace with him.

The people shouted, “*The voice of a god, and not of a man!*” (*v. 22*) They flattered Herod, perhaps because they depended on him for food. Herod did not reject their praise. He accepted being called a god.

“*Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him, because he didn’t give God the glory. Then he was eaten by worms and died*” (*v. 23*). Luke explains clearly why Herod died: he accepted the glory that belongs only to God. The same angel of the Lord who delivered Peter now struck Herod.

Contrast Herod with Peter, who refused worship when Cornelius bowed before him (*10:25–26*), and with Paul and Barnabas, who later tore their clothes when the people of Lystra tried to worship them (*14:14–15*).

Then comes a powerful contrast: “*But the word of God grew and multiplied*” (*v. 24*). Herod, the persecutor, died. The church he tried to destroy continued to grow. The king who wanted to stop the word of God was gone, but the word lived on.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that God will not share His glory with anyone. Through Isaiah, God declared, “*I will not give my glory to another*” (*Isaiah 42:8*). Herod’s pride brought judgment. Pride, especially the desire to be worshiped, is a grave sin because it takes what belongs to God alone.

They also show the outcome of opposing God’s people. Herod began the chapter killing James and imprisoning Peter. He ended the chapter dead. The chapter shows a dramatic reversal: the persecutor fell, and the persecuted church thrived.

Finally, verse 24 summarizes the message of Acts: God’s word cannot be stopped. Rulers rise and fall. Persecution comes and goes. But the word of God continues to grow and multiply. Isaiah writes, “*The grass withers, the flower fades; but the word of our God stands forever*” (*Isaiah 40:8*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses warn believers against pride. It is easy to accept praise that should go to God, taking credit for accomplishments, gifts, or successes that come from Him. Believers can practice giving God the glory, acknowledging that all good things come from Him.

They also encourage believers facing persecution. Those who oppose God’s people may seem powerful, but they are not in ultimate control. God is sovereign, and His purposes will prevail.

Finally, these verses give believers confidence in God’s word. No matter what happens in the world, God’s word will continue to grow. Believers can invest their lives in spreading His word, knowing that it will outlast every earthly power.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Acts 12* shows the power of a praying church. Facing the power of a king who had already killed one apostle, the believers turned to God in earnest prayer. God answered in a way they could hardly believe. Believers today can bring every crisis to God in prayer, together with other believers, trusting that He is able to act when no human help is possible.

The chapter also holds together two different outcomes: James was killed, and Peter was delivered. Believers will not always understand why God allows some to suffer and rescues others. But both outcomes are held within God’s loving purposes. Believers can trust Him when prayers are answered as they hoped, and when they are not.

*Acts 12* humbly reminds believers that even faithful pray-ers can struggle to believe. The church was astonished when Peter appeared at the door. God answers prayer even when faith is weak. Believers can bring their doubts to Him and ask Him to increase their faith, and they can learn to listen to the testimony of those, like Rhoda, whom others might overlook.

Finally, the chapter contrasts the fate of a proud king with the growth of God’s word. Herod accepted glory that belonged to God and was struck down, but the word of God grew and multiplied. Believers are called to give God the glory in everything, and they can live with confidence that His word will outlast every power that opposes it.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord God, thank You that You hear the prayers of Your people. When I face situations beyond my control, teach me to pray earnestly and to keep praying, together with my brothers and sisters. Thank You for delivering Peter from prison, and thank You for the faithfulness of James, who glorified You in his death. Help me to trust You when Your answers are not what I hoped, and to rejoice when You do more than I imagined. Forgive me for the times I have prayed without really expecting You to answer, and increase my faith. Guard my heart from pride, and help me always to give You the glory that belongs to You alone. Thank You that Your word grows and multiplies, and that no power on earth can stop it. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Acts · Chapter 13 of 28

# Acts — Chapter 13

Chapter Theme: Sent by the Spirit: The First Missionary Journey and the Good News of Justification

[Read Acts 13 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/ACT13.htm)

Main Teaching

While the church in Antioch worships and fasts, the Holy Spirit calls Barnabas and Saul to a special work, and the church sends them out. On Cyprus they meet a Roman governor who believes despite the opposition of a sorcerer. In Pisidian Antioch, Paul preaches in the synagogue, tracing Israel’s history to Jesus, the promised Son of David whom God raised from the dead, and announcing that through Him everyone who believes is forgiven and justified. When many Jews reject the message, Paul and Barnabas turn to the Gentiles, who rejoice and believe, and though the missionaries are driven out, the disciples are filled with joy and the Holy Spirit.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Acts 13* marks the beginning of the second half of the book. The focus shifts from Jerusalem and Peter to Antioch and Paul, and from the church’s spread in Judea and Samaria to its deliberate mission to the wider Gentile world. This chapter begins what is usually called Paul’s first missionary journey, which took place around A.D. 46–48 and covered the island of Cyprus and the region of Galatia in central Asia Minor (modern Turkey).

In this chapter, Luke begins calling Saul by his Roman name, Paul (*13:9*). Many Jews of the time had both a Hebrew name and a Greek or Latin name. As Saul began his mission to the Gentile world, he used the name that would be more familiar to them.

### The Spirit Sends Barnabas and Saul (*13:1–3*)

The church in Antioch had a remarkably diverse group of leaders: “*Barnabas, Simeon who was called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen the foster brother of Herod the tetrarch, and Saul*” (*v. 1*). Barnabas was a Levite from Cyprus. Simeon’s nickname “Niger” means “black,” suggesting he may have come from Africa. Lucius was from Cyrene in North Africa. Manaen had been raised in the court of Herod Antipas, the ruler who had executed John the Baptist. Saul was a former Pharisee from Tarsus. Their diversity reflected the multicultural church in Antioch. Their calling is studied below.

### Cyprus: The Proconsul Believes (*13:4–12*)

“*So, being sent out by the Holy Spirit*” (*v. 4*), Barnabas and Saul sailed to Cyprus, Barnabas’s home island, taking John Mark as their helper. They preached in the synagogues of Salamis and traveled across the island to Paphos, the Roman capital.

There they met “*a certain sorcerer, a false prophet, a Jew whose name was Bar Jesus*” (*v. 6*), also called Elymas. He was an advisor to the proconsul (the Roman governor), “*Sergius Paulus, a man of understanding*” (*v. 7*), who wanted to hear the word of God. But Elymas opposed them, trying to turn the proconsul from the faith.

Then “*Saul, who is also called Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit*” (*v. 9*), looked at Elymas and rebuked him sharply: “*You son of the devil, full of all deceit and all cunning, you enemy of all righteousness, will you not cease to pervert the right ways of the Lord?*” (*v. 10*) There is irony in this: the man called “Bar Jesus,” meaning “son of Joshua” or “son of salvation,” was in fact acting as a son of the devil. Paul declared that the hand of the Lord was against him, and he would be blind for a time. “*Immediately a mist and darkness fell on him. He went around seeking someone to lead him by the hand*” (*v. 11*). Paul himself had once been struck blind and led by the hand (*9:8*). The temporary blindness may have been meant, as in Paul’s case, to lead Elymas to repentance.

“*Then the proconsul, when he saw what was done, believed, being astonished at the teaching of the Lord*” (*v. 12*). A high Roman official came to faith.

### Perga: John Mark Leaves (*13:13*)

Paul and his companions sailed from Paphos to Perga in Pamphylia, on the southern coast of Asia Minor. There “*John departed from them and returned to Jerusalem*” (*v. 13*). Luke does not say why. Some suggest he was homesick, afraid of the dangerous journey inland, unhappy that Paul was taking the lead from his cousin Barnabas (*Colossians 4:10*), or uneasy about the mission to Gentiles. Whatever the reason, Paul saw it as desertion, and it would later cause a sharp disagreement between Paul and Barnabas (*Acts 15:37–39*). Yet later, Paul and Mark were reconciled, and Paul wrote, “*Take Mark, and bring him with you, for he is useful to me for service*” (*2 Timothy 4:11*).

### Paul’s Sermon in Pisidian Antioch (*13:14–41*)

From Perga, Paul and Barnabas traveled about one hundred miles inland, over the Taurus Mountains, to Antioch in Pisidia (a different city from Antioch in Syria). On the Sabbath, they went to the synagogue. After the reading from the Law and the Prophets, the synagogue leaders invited them to speak. This was a common custom, and visiting teachers were often invited to give a word of encouragement.

Paul’s sermon, the first of his recorded sermons, was addressed to “*Men of Israel, and you who fear God*” (*v. 16*), both Jews and Gentile God-fearers. He reviewed Israel’s history: God chose their ancestors, made them great in Egypt, led them out with mighty power, endured them in the wilderness for forty years, gave them the land of Canaan, provided judges, and then gave them kings. The first king, Saul, was removed, and God raised up David. God’s testimony about David is studied below.

“*From this man’s offspring, God has brought salvation to Israel according to his promise*” (*v. 23*). The promised descendant of David is Jesus. John the Baptist had prepared the way, saying he was not worthy to untie the sandals of the One coming after him.

Paul then explained that the people of Jerusalem and their rulers did not recognize Jesus or understand the prophets read every Sabbath, and so they fulfilled the prophecies by condemning Him. Though they found no grounds for death, they asked Pilate to execute Him. “*But God raised him from the dead*” (*v. 30*). Many witnesses saw Him.

Paul supported the resurrection with three Old Testament passages. *Psalm 2:7*: “*You are my Son. Today I have become your father*” (*v. 33*), which Paul understood to be fulfilled in Jesus’ resurrection, when God publicly declared Him to be the Son of God with power (*Romans 1:4*). *Isaiah 55:3*: “*I will give you the holy and sure blessings of David*” (*v. 34*). And *Psalm 16:10*: “*You will not allow your Holy One to see decay*” (*v. 35*). Like Peter at Pentecost (*Acts 2:29–31*), Paul pointed out that David died and his body decayed, but Jesus, whom God raised, did not.

Paul then announced the heart of the gospel, studied below. He closed with a warning from *Habakkuk 1:5* not to scoff at God’s work.

### Jews and Gentiles Respond (*13:42–52*)

As they left, the people begged them to speak again the next Sabbath. Many Jews and devout converts to Judaism followed Paul and Barnabas, who “*urged them to continue in the grace of God*” (*v. 43*).

The next Sabbath, “*almost the whole city was gathered together to hear the word of God*” (*v. 44*). But when some of the Jewish leaders saw the crowds, “*they were filled with jealousy*” (*v. 45*) and contradicted Paul, speaking abusively. Paul and Barnabas answered boldly: “*It was necessary that God’s word should be spoken to you first. Since indeed you thrust it from yourselves, and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles*” (*v. 46*). Paul’s pattern throughout his ministry was to go first to the synagogue, because the gospel was the fulfillment of God’s promises to Israel (*Romans 1:16*). When Jewish audiences rejected it, he turned to the Gentiles. Their response is studied below.

The Jewish leaders stirred up prominent women and leading men of the city to persecute Paul and Barnabas, and they were driven out. “*But they shook off the dust of their feet against them*” (*v. 51*), as Jesus had instructed His disciples to do when a town rejected them (*Luke 9:5*). They went on to Iconium. Yet the chapter ends on a note of joy: “*The disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit*” (*v. 52*). The new believers left behind were not discouraged.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Acts 13:2–3* — Separate Barnabas and Saul for Me

> *“As they served the Lord and fasted, the Holy Spirit said, ‘Separate Barnabas and Saul for me, for the work to which I have called them.’ Then, when they had fasted and prayed and laid their hands on them, they sent them away.”*
>
> — *Acts 13:2–3* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The church in Antioch had grown into a large and diverse community. Its leaders included prophets and teachers from different backgrounds. One day, “*As they served the Lord and fasted*” (*v. 2*). The word “served” here is often used of worship and priestly service. The leaders were devoting themselves to worship and prayer, and they were fasting, setting aside food to focus on God.

In this setting of worship, “*the Holy Spirit said, “Separate Barnabas and Saul for me, for the work to which I have called them.”*” (*v. 2*) Luke does not say how the Spirit spoke. It may have been through one of the prophets. The message was clear: God had a special task for Barnabas and Saul.

Notice the words “for me.” Barnabas and Saul were being set apart for God’s purposes. And notice “to which I have called them.” God had already called them; the church was recognizing and confirming that call. Saul had been told at his conversion that he would carry Christ’s name to the Gentiles (*9:15*).

“*Then, when they had fasted and prayed and laid their hands on them, they sent them away*” (*v. 3*). The church responded with more fasting and prayer. Then they laid their hands on Barnabas and Saul, a sign of blessing, commissioning, and identification. The church sent them out.

It is worth noting that the church sent two of its best leaders. Barnabas and Saul had been teaching the church for over a year. Sending them was a sacrifice. But the church in Antioch was willing to give up its best for the sake of God’s mission.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that mission begins with God. The Holy Spirit took the initiative, calling Barnabas and Saul. Mission is not merely a human strategy; it is God’s work, carried out through people He calls and sends. Jesus had said, “*As the Father has sent me, even so I send you*” (*John 20:21*).

They also show the role of the church in confirming and sending. The Spirit called, and the church responded by praying, laying on hands, and sending. Individual calling and community confirmation work together. Paul later asked, “*And how will they preach unless they are sent?*” (*Romans 10:15*)

Finally, these verses show the importance of worship, prayer, and fasting in discerning God’s will. The church heard the Spirit’s voice as they worshiped and fasted. Seeking God’s guidance involves drawing near to Him in devotion.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage churches to be places of worship, prayer, and fasting, where believers seek God’s direction together. Churches can set aside time to listen to God, especially when making important decisions.

They also encourage churches to be generous in sending. Antioch sent its best leaders. Churches today can support missionaries and new works, even when it means giving up gifted people or resources. A sending church shares in the fruit of the mission.

Finally, these verses invite each believer to be open to God’s calling. God calls people to many different kinds of service, at home and abroad. Believers can seek God’s guidance through prayer and the counsel of the church, ready to go where He leads.

### *Acts 13:22* — A Man After My Heart

> *“When he had removed him, he raised up David to be their king, to whom he also testified, “I have found David the son of Jesse, a man after my heart, who will do all my will.””*
>
> — *Acts 13:22* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

In his sermon in the synagogue at Pisidian Antioch, Paul reviewed Israel’s history to show how it led to Jesus. He described how God chose Israel’s ancestors, brought them out of Egypt, gave them the land, and provided judges. Then the people asked for a king, and God gave them Saul. But Saul disobeyed God, and God removed him.

“*When he had removed him, he raised up David to be their king*” (*v. 22*). God chose David, the youngest son of Jesse, a shepherd boy from Bethlehem, to be king.

Then Paul quoted God’s testimony about David: “*I have found David the son of Jesse, a man after my heart, who will do all my will*” (*v. 22*). These words combine phrases from *1 Samuel 13:14*, *Psalm 89:20*, and *Isaiah 44:28*. “A man after my heart” means a man whose heart was aligned with God’s heart, someone who loved God and sought to do His will.

David was not perfect. He committed serious sins, including adultery with Bathsheba and the murder of her husband Uriah (*2 Samuel 11*). But when confronted, David repented deeply (*Psalm 51*). His heart was turned toward God. Unlike Saul, who made excuses, David humbly confessed and sought God’s mercy.

Paul mentioned David because God had promised that the Messiah would come from David’s family. The next verse says, “*From this man’s offspring, God has brought salvation to Israel according to his promise*” (*v. 23*). Jesus is the Son of David, the King who fulfills all God’s promises to David.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows what God values in a person: a heart turned toward Him. When Samuel was looking for the next king, God told him that He does not look at outward appearance but at the heart (*1 Samuel 16:7*). David was chosen not because of his size, age, or status, but because of his heart.

It also shows that God’s purposes move forward through imperfect people. David’s failures were real and serious, yet God kept His promises to him. This reveals God’s grace and faithfulness.

Finally, the verse points to Jesus, the true King after God’s own heart. David’s heart was devoted to God, but imperfectly. Jesus perfectly did the Father’s will in everything. He is the Son of David who reigns forever, fulfilling God’s promise that David’s throne would endure (*2 Samuel 7:12–16*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to seek a heart after God’s heart. This means loving God, desiring to do His will, and responding to Him with humility and repentance when they fail. God is more concerned with the heart than with outward achievements.

It also encourages believers who have failed. David sinned greatly, yet his repentance was genuine, and God forgave him. Believers who have fallen can return to God with honest confession, trusting His mercy.

Finally, the verse reminds believers that Jesus is the King after God’s own heart. Believers can look to Him as their perfect example and their faithful King, the One in whom all God’s promises are fulfilled.

### *Acts 13:38–39* — Justified by Him

> *“Be it known to you therefore, brothers, that through this man is proclaimed to you remission of sins; and by him everyone who believes is justified from all things, from which you could not be justified by the law of Moses.”*
>
> — *Acts 13:38–39* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had shown his listeners in the synagogue that Jesus was the promised descendant of David, that He had been condemned and crucified, and that God had raised Him from the dead. Now Paul came to the heart of his message: what this means for them.

“*Be it known to you therefore, brothers, that through this man is proclaimed to you remission of sins*” (*v. 38*). “Remission” means forgiveness. Through Jesus, forgiveness is offered. Paul emphasized “this man,” Jesus, as the one through whom forgiveness comes.

“*and by him everyone who believes is justified from all things, from which you could not be justified by the law of Moses*” (*v. 39*). “Justified” is a legal term meaning “declared righteous” or “acquitted.” A person who is justified is declared not guilty before God and accepted as righteous. This is the first time in Acts that this key word, central to Paul’s letters, appears.

Notice three important points. First, justification is “by him,” through Jesus. Second, it is for “everyone who believes.” It is received by faith, not earned. Third, it covers “all things,” everything from which the Law of Moses could not free people. The Law could reveal sin and point to the need for forgiveness, but it could not make people fully right with God. Jesus does what the Law could not do.

These words were spoken in a synagogue, to Jews and God-fearers who honored the Law. Paul was not saying the Law was bad; he was saying that it could not justify. Only faith in Jesus brings complete forgiveness and right standing with God.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses summarize the gospel that Paul would explain in detail in his letters to the Romans and Galatians. Paul writes, “*We maintain therefore that a man is justified by faith apart from the works of the law*” (*Romans 3:28*). Justification is a gift of God’s grace received through faith in Christ.

They also show that justification is complete. Believers are justified “from all things.” There is no sin too great to be covered by Christ’s work. Paul writes, “*There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus*” (*Romans 8:1*).

Finally, these verses show the relationship between the Law and the gospel. The Law is good and holy, but it cannot save. It shows people their sin and their need for a Savior. The gospel announces that the Savior has come, and that through faith in Him, people are declared righteous.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses give believers assurance. Many people struggle with guilt and wonder whether they are truly accepted by God. Paul’s message is clear: everyone who believes in Jesus is justified from all things. Believers can rest in this complete forgiveness.

They also caution against trying to earn God’s acceptance. Some believers try to make themselves acceptable to God through rule-keeping, religious activity, or good works. These things have their place as expressions of love for God, but they cannot justify. Only faith in Christ does that.

Finally, these verses invite everyone to believe. Justification is offered to “everyone who believes.” No one is excluded. Believers can share this good news with confidence, knowing that it is for all.

### *Acts 13:47–48* — A Light for the Gentiles

> *“For so has the Lord commanded us, saying, “I have set you as a light for the Gentiles, that you should bring salvation to the uttermost parts of the earth.” As the Gentiles heard this, they were glad and glorified the word of God. As many as were appointed to eternal life believed.”*
>
> — *Acts 13:47–48* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul and Barnabas had preached in the synagogue in Pisidian Antioch, and the following Sabbath almost the whole city came to hear them. But some of the Jewish leaders became jealous and opposed them. Paul and Barnabas declared that since these leaders had rejected the message, they would turn to the Gentiles.

They explained their decision by quoting Scripture: “*For so has the Lord commanded us, saying, ‘I have set you as a light for the Gentiles, that you should bring salvation to the uttermost parts of the earth.’*” (*v. 47*) This quotation comes from *Isaiah 49:6*, which describes the mission of God’s Servant. The Servant would not only restore Israel but also bring God’s light to the nations. Paul and Barnabas saw their mission to the Gentiles as part of the Servant’s mission, which Jesus fulfilled and now carried out through His followers.

“*As the Gentiles heard this, they were glad and glorified the word of God*” (*v. 48*). The Gentiles rejoiced when they heard that the gospel was for them too. They had been on the outside of Israel’s covenant, but now they were invited in.

“*As many as were appointed to eternal life believed*” (*v. 48*). Many Gentiles believed. Luke describes them as those “appointed to eternal life.”

“*The Lord’s word was spread abroad throughout all the region*” (*v. 49*). The gospel spread throughout the surrounding area.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that the mission to the Gentiles was rooted in God’s original plan. From the beginning, God intended to bless all nations through Abraham’s offspring (*Genesis 12:3*). The prophets foresaw a day when God’s light would reach the ends of the earth. The church’s mission to the Gentiles was not a new idea but the fulfillment of Scripture.

The phrase “as many as were appointed to eternal life believed” has been understood in different ways. Many Christians, especially in the Reformed tradition, see it as teaching that God’s sovereign choice lies behind faith: those whom God had appointed believed. Others, especially in the Wesleyan and Arminian traditions, emphasize that the Greek word can mean “disposed” or “ordered” toward eternal life, describing those whose hearts were open to God’s call, and they stress human responsibility to respond. Both perspectives affirm that salvation is God’s gracious work and that people are called to believe. Notably, the previous verse described the opposing leaders as judging themselves unworthy of eternal life (*13:46*), highlighting human responsibility alongside God’s sovereignty.

Finally, the verses show the joy of the gospel. The Gentiles were glad and glorified God. The good news is truly good news that brings joy to those who receive it.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses remind believers that they are called to be a light to the nations. The mission given to the Servant and carried out by Paul continues through the church today. Believers can support and participate in sharing the gospel with people of every nation, both near and far.

They also encourage believers when some reject the message. Paul and Barnabas faced opposition, but they did not give up. They turned to others who were open. When some people reject the gospel, believers can continue to share it with others whose hearts God may be preparing.

Finally, these verses invite believers to rejoice in the gospel. Those who were once far from God have been brought near. Believers can join the Gentiles of Antioch in being glad and glorifying God’s word.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Acts 13* shows that God’s mission begins with God. The Holy Spirit called Barnabas and Saul, and the church in Antioch responded by praying, fasting, and sending them. Churches today can follow this example, seeking God’s direction in worship and prayer, recognizing those He calls, and generously sending and supporting them.

The chapter also shows that the gospel meets opposition. Elymas tried to turn the proconsul away from the faith, and jealous leaders in Pisidian Antioch stirred up persecution. Yet in both places, God’s word prevailed. Believers can face opposition with courage, trusting that God is at work even when others resist.

*Acts 13* presents the heart of the gospel in Paul’s first recorded sermon: Jesus, the Son of David, was crucified and raised, and through Him everyone who believes is forgiven and justified from all things. This message is for everyone, Jews and Gentiles alike. Believers can rest in the assurance of their justification and share this good news with confidence.

Finally, the chapter shows the gospel going to the nations as a light to the Gentiles. Even when Paul and Barnabas were driven out, the new believers were filled with joy and the Holy Spirit. Believers today can carry that light wherever they go, finding joy in the gospel and sharing it with all people.

## Chapter Prayer

Holy Spirit, thank You for calling and sending Your servants into the world. Make Your church a people who worship, fast, and pray, listening for Your voice. Show me where You are calling me to serve, and give me a willing heart to go. Thank You, Father, for David, a man after Your heart, and for Jesus, the Son of David, who fulfills all Your promises. Thank You that through Jesus my sins are forgiven and I am justified from all things, not by my own works but by faith in Him. Help me to rest in this grace and to share it with others. Make me a light to those around me, and fill me with joy and with the Holy Spirit, even when I face opposition. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
