Acts · Chapter 14 of 28

# Acts — Chapter 14

Chapter Theme: Through Many Hardships: Faithful Ministry, Rejected Worship, and a Door of Faith Opened

[Read Acts 14 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/ACT14.htm)

Main Teaching

In Iconium, Paul and Barnabas preach boldly, and many Jews and Greeks believe, until a plot to stone them drives them on. In Lystra, Paul heals a man lame from birth, and the crowd hails them as the gods Zeus and Hermes. Horrified, the apostles tear their clothes and urge the people to turn from idols to the living God who made all things and shows His kindness through rain and harvests. Soon after, opponents stone Paul and leave him for dead, but he rises and continues. Retracing their steps, Paul and Barnabas strengthen the new churches, appoint elders, and return to Antioch to report that God has opened a door of faith to the Gentiles.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Acts 14* completes the account of Paul’s first missionary journey. Paul and Barnabas travel through the Roman province of Galatia, visiting the cities of Iconium, Lystra, and Derbe, before retracing their route and returning to Antioch in Syria. These are likely the churches to which Paul later wrote his letter to the Galatians.

The chapter shows two important aspects of the mission. First, it shows how Paul addressed a pagan audience with no background in the Scriptures, beginning with God as Creator. Second, it shows Paul’s care for the new churches, strengthening them, warning them about suffering, and appointing leaders.

### Iconium: Belief and Division (*14:1–7*)

In Iconium, about ninety miles east of Pisidian Antioch, Paul and Barnabas went to the synagogue as usual, “*and so spoke that a great multitude both of Jews and of Greeks believed*” (*v. 1*). But unbelieving Jews stirred up the Gentiles and poisoned their minds against the believers.

Remarkably, opposition did not make them leave immediately: “*Therefore they stayed there a long time, speaking boldly in the Lord, who testified to the word of his grace, granting signs and wonders to be done by their hands*” (*v. 3*). The Lord confirmed the message of grace with miracles. Note the description of the gospel as “*the word of his grace*” (*v. 3*). At its heart, the gospel is a message of God’s undeserved kindness.

The city became divided. Some sided with the Jewish opponents, others with the apostles. When both Gentiles and Jews, along with their leaders, plotted to mistreat and stone them, Paul and Barnabas learned of it and fled to Lystra, Derbe, and the surrounding region, “*There they preached the Good News*” (*v. 7*). Jesus had told His disciples, “*When they persecute you in this city, flee into the next*” (*Matthew 10:23*). Fleeing danger was not cowardice but wisdom, and the mission continued in new places.

### Lystra: Healing and Mistaken Worship (*14:8–18*)

In Lystra, there was a man “*impotent in his feet, a cripple from his mother’s womb, who never had walked*” (*v. 8*). Luke uses three phrases to emphasize the severity of his condition. The man listened to Paul preaching. Paul “*fastening eyes on him and seeing that he had faith to be made whole*” (*v. 9*), said loudly, “*Stand upright on your feet!*” (*v. 10*) The man jumped up and began to walk. This healing closely parallels Peter’s healing of the lame man at the temple gate (*3:1–10*), showing that the same power worked through both apostles.

The crowd’s reaction was dramatic. They shouted in their local language, “*The gods have come down to us in the likeness of men!*” (*v. 11*) They called Barnabas “Jupiter” (Zeus in Greek), the chief of the gods, and Paul “Mercury” (Hermes), the messenger of the gods, because Paul did most of the speaking. There was a local legend that Zeus and Hermes had once visited the region disguised as humans and were refused hospitality by everyone except an elderly couple, who were rewarded while the others were punished. The people of Lystra may have been determined not to make the same mistake.

The priest of Zeus, whose temple stood at the city’s entrance, brought bulls and garlands to the gates to offer sacrifices. Because the crowd spoke Lycaonian, Paul and Barnabas may not have understood at first what was happening. When they realized, they “*tore their clothes*” (*v. 14*), a Jewish sign of grief and horror at blasphemy, and rushed into the crowd. Their message is studied below. Even so, “*they hardly stopped the multitudes from making a sacrifice to them*” (*v. 18*).

### Paul Stoned (*14:19–20*)

Then the mood turned. Opponents from Antioch and Iconium arrived and persuaded the crowd. The people who had wanted to worship Paul now stoned him and dragged him out of the city, thinking he was dead. This is studied below.

### Strengthening the Churches (*14:21–28*)

After preaching in Derbe and making many disciples, Paul and Barnabas did something surprising. Derbe was near the eastern edge of Galatia, and from there they could have taken a shorter route home through Paul’s home region of Cilicia. Instead, they went back through Lystra, Iconium, and Antioch, the very cities where they had been persecuted. Their purpose and their message are studied below.

“*When they had appointed elders for them in every assembly, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord on whom they had believed*” (*v. 23*). The new churches needed leaders. Paul and Barnabas appointed elders, mature believers who would shepherd and oversee each congregation. The word “appointed” can describe a process that involved the church; some interpreters note that it can mean choosing by a show of hands. Before leaving, the apostles prayed and fasted, entrusting the churches to the Lord. They knew that the churches ultimately belonged to Christ, not to them.

They traveled back through Pisidia and Pamphylia, preached in Perga (where they had apparently not preached on the way in), and sailed from Attalia to Antioch in Syria, “*from where they had been committed to the grace of God for the work which they had fulfilled*” (*v. 26*). Their report to the church is studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Acts 14:15–17* — Turn to the Living God

> *“‘Men, why are you doing these things? We also are men of the same nature as you, and bring you good news, that you should turn from these vain things to the living God, who made the sky, the earth, the sea, and all that is in them; who in the generations gone by allowed all the nations to walk in their own ways. Yet he didn’t leave himself without witness, in that he did good and gave you rains from the sky and fruitful seasons, filling our hearts with food and gladness.’”*
>
> — *Acts 14:15–17* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After Paul healed a lame man in Lystra, the crowd decided that Paul and Barnabas were gods in human form. The priest of Zeus prepared to offer sacrifices to them. Paul and Barnabas were horrified. They tore their clothes and rushed into the crowd.

“*Men, why are you doing these things? We also are men of the same nature as you*” (*v. 15*). Paul insisted that they were ordinary human beings, with the same weaknesses as everyone else. They were not to be worshiped.

“*and bring you good news, that you should turn from these vain things to the living God*” (*v. 15*). “Vain things” means worthless or empty things, referring to the idols the people worshiped. Paul called them to turn from these empty idols to “the living God,” the one true God who is alive and active.

“*who made the sky, the earth, the sea, and all that is in them*” (*v. 15*). Paul began with God as Creator. His audience in Lystra did not know the Jewish Scriptures, so Paul did not quote the prophets as he did in synagogues. He started with what they could see: the creation around them. This language echoes *Exodus 20:11* and *Psalm 146:6*.

“*who in the generations gone by allowed all the nations to walk in their own ways*” (*v. 16*). In the past, God allowed the nations to go their own way without the special revelation He had given Israel.

“*Yet he didn’t leave himself without witness, in that he did good and gave you rains from the sky and fruitful seasons, filling our hearts with food and gladness*” (*v. 17*). Even so, God had given evidence of Himself through His kindness in nature. Every rainfall, every harvest, every meal, and every moment of joy was a gift from the living God. Lystra was an agricultural region, and the people knew how much they depended on rain and good harvests.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that God reveals Himself through creation. Paul writes in Romans, “*For the invisible things of him since the creation of the world are clearly seen, being perceived through the things that are made, even his everlasting power and divinity*” (*Romans 1:20*). Even people without the Scriptures can see evidence of God in the world He made. This is often called “general revelation.”

They also reveal God’s kindness to all people. Jesus said that God “*makes his sun to rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the just and the unjust*” (*Matthew 5:45*). God’s goodness in providing food and joy is meant to lead people to seek Him.

Finally, these verses show the danger of idolatry. The people of Lystra wanted to worship Paul and Barnabas instead of the God who had healed the man. Humans are always tempted to worship created things instead of the Creator. Paul’s message calls everyone to turn from idols to the living God.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to see God’s goodness in everyday life. Food, rain, seasons, and gladness are all gifts from Him. Believers can cultivate gratitude by recognizing God’s hand in ordinary blessings.

They also show a wise way to share the gospel with people who do not know the Bible. Paul began with what his listeners could understand: creation and God’s kindness. Believers can start conversations about God by pointing to evidence of His goodness that others can see and experience.

Finally, these verses warn against the temptation to idolize people. Christians can sometimes put leaders, celebrities, or gifted individuals on pedestals. Paul and Barnabas refused to be worshiped. All glory belongs to God alone. Leaders, too, must resist the temptation to receive praise that belongs to God.

### *Acts 14:19–20* — Stoned, but Rising Again

> *“But some Jews from Antioch and Iconium came there, and having persuaded the multitudes, they stoned Paul and dragged him out of the city, supposing that he was dead. But as the disciples stood around him, he rose up, and entered into the city. On the next day he went out with Barnabas to Derbe.”*
>
> — *Acts 14:19–20* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The people of Lystra had tried to worship Paul and Barnabas as gods. Shortly afterward, opponents arrived from Pisidian Antioch and Iconium, cities where Paul had preached and faced opposition. They had traveled long distances to stop Paul’s ministry.

“*But some Jews from Antioch and Iconium came there, and having persuaded the multitudes, they stoned Paul and dragged him out of the city, supposing that he was dead*” (*v. 19*). The same crowd that had wanted to offer sacrifices to Paul now threw stones at him. Crowds can be fickle; praise can quickly turn to violence. They stoned Paul until they thought he was dead and dragged his body outside the city.

Paul later referred to this event in his list of sufferings: “*Once I was stoned*” (*2 Corinthians 11:25*). He may have carried scars from it for the rest of his life (*Galatians 6:17*).

“*But as the disciples stood around him, he rose up, and entered into the city*” (*v. 20*). The new believers gathered around Paul’s body, perhaps grieving, perhaps praying. Then Paul got up. Whether he had been unconscious or near death, his recovery was remarkable. And he went back into the city that had just tried to kill him.

“*On the next day he went out with Barnabas to Derbe*” (*v. 20*). The very next day, Paul continued his journey, traveling about sixty miles to Derbe to preach again.

It is worth remembering that Paul himself had once approved of the stoning of Stephen (*8:1*). Now he experienced stoning for the sake of the same Lord.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show the cost of faithful ministry. Jesus had said that Paul would suffer much for His name (*9:16*). Paul’s stoning in Lystra was one fulfillment of that prophecy. Following Jesus can bring suffering.

They also show God’s sustaining power. Paul was left for dead, yet he rose and continued his mission. Paul later wrote, “*We are pressed on every side, yet not crushed; perplexed, yet not to despair*” (*2 Corinthians 4:8*), “*pursued, yet not forsaken; struck down, yet not destroyed*” (*2 Corinthians 4:9*).

Finally, the image of the disciples gathered around Paul is significant. The new believers did not abandon him. They stood with him in his suffering. The church is a community that surrounds and supports those who suffer.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers who face hardship for their faith. Suffering for Christ is not a sign of failure. Paul was stoned, yet he continued. Believers can trust that God will sustain them through difficult times.

They also remind believers not to depend on the approval of crowds. Praise and popularity can quickly change. Believers are called to faithfulness to God, not to seeking human approval.

Finally, these verses encourage believers to stand with those who suffer. When fellow believers face persecution, illness, or loss, believers can gather around them, offering prayer, presence, and practical help.

### *Acts 14:22* — Through Many Afflictions into the Kingdom

> *“strengthening the souls of the disciples, exhorting them to continue in the faith, and that through many afflictions we must enter into God’s Kingdom.”*
>
> — *Acts 14:22* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After preaching in Derbe, Paul and Barnabas made a courageous decision. Instead of taking a shorter route home, they went back through Lystra, Iconium, and Pisidian Antioch, the very cities where they had faced persecution and where Paul had been stoned. They returned because the new believers needed them.

“*strengthening the souls of the disciples*” (*v. 22*). The new believers were young in the faith and surrounded by opposition. Paul and Barnabas strengthened them through teaching and encouragement.

“*exhorting them to continue in the faith*” (*v. 22*). They urged the believers to keep going, to remain faithful to Jesus. Faith is not only about beginning well but continuing to the end.

“*and that through many afflictions we must enter into God’s Kingdom*” (*v. 22*). Paul and Barnabas were honest with the new believers. They did not promise them an easy life. They told them that the path to God’s kingdom would involve many hardships. The word “afflictions” refers to pressures, troubles, and persecutions.

Notice the word “we.” Paul included himself. He was not telling others to endure what he himself avoided. He had just been stoned.

“God’s Kingdom” here refers to the full, future experience of God’s reign, which believers will enter at the end of their journey. Hardships are part of the road that leads there.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that suffering is a normal part of the Christian life. Jesus said, “*In the world you have trouble*” (*John 16:33*). Paul wrote to Timothy that all who want to live godly lives in Christ will be persecuted (*2 Timothy 3:12*). The Christian life is not a promise of comfort but of faithfulness and future glory.

It also shows that suffering has purpose. Paul writes, “*we also rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces perseverance*” (*Romans 5:3*). Hardships shape believers’ character and strengthen their hope. Paul also wrote that “*the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which will be revealed toward us*” (*Romans 8:18*).

Finally, the verse shows the importance of honest discipleship. Paul and Barnabas did not hide the cost of following Jesus. They prepared new believers for what was ahead. Honest teaching helps believers persevere when trouble comes.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse helps believers understand their struggles. When hardship comes, believers can remember that this is part of the journey, not a sign that God has abandoned them. The path to God’s kingdom goes through difficulty, but it leads to glory.

It also encourages believers to strengthen one another. Paul and Barnabas returned to dangerous places to encourage the new believers. Believers today can support and encourage those who are struggling, especially new believers who may not yet understand that hardships are part of following Jesus.

Finally, the verse challenges churches to teach honestly. Some messages promise that faith will bring health, wealth, and ease. Paul and Barnabas taught that the road to God’s kingdom involves many afflictions. Honest teaching prepares believers to endure and to find their hope in God rather than in comfortable circumstances.

### *Acts 14:27* — A Door of Faith to the Nations

> *“When they had arrived and had gathered the assembly together, they reported all the things that God had done with them, and that he had opened a door of faith to the nations.”*
>
> — *Acts 14:27* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After their long journey, Paul and Barnabas returned to Antioch in Syria, the church that had sent them out. They had traveled for perhaps two years, covering many hundreds of miles by land and sea. They had preached in many cities, seen many people come to faith, faced fierce opposition, and established new churches.

“*When they had arrived and had gathered the assembly together*” (*v. 27*). They called the whole church together. The church had sent them, prayed for them, and committed them to God’s grace. Now they deserved to hear what had happened.

“*they reported all the things that God had done with them*” (*v. 27*). Notice the emphasis. They did not report what they had done, but what God had done with them. They recognized that the mission’s success was God’s work. They were His instruments.

“*and that he had opened a door of faith to the nations*” (*v. 27*). The most important news was that God had opened a door for the Gentiles to come to faith. People who had worshiped idols had turned to the living God. The way into God’s family was open to all nations through faith in Jesus.

The image of a door is used elsewhere by Paul to describe opportunities for the gospel (*1 Corinthians 16:9*; *Colossians 4:3*). God opens doors that no one can shut (*Revelation 3:8*).

“*They stayed there with the disciples for a long time*” (*v. 28*). Paul and Barnabas rested and ministered in Antioch.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that mission is God’s work. Paul and Barnabas reported what God had done. Paul later wrote, “*I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase*” (*1 Corinthians 3:6*). Missionaries and ministers plant and water, but God gives the growth.

It also shows that faith is the door into God’s family. The door was opened “to the nations,” and it was a door “of faith.” Gentiles did not need to become Jews first. They entered through faith in Jesus. This would become the central issue in the next chapter, at the Jerusalem Council.

Finally, the verse shows the importance of accountability and partnership in mission. Paul and Barnabas reported back to the church that sent them. Missionaries and sending churches are partners. The church shares in the joy of what God has done through those it sends.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to give God the credit for what He does through them. When believers see good results from their efforts, they can recognize that God has worked with them and give Him the glory.

It also encourages churches to celebrate what God is doing in mission. Hearing reports of how God is working around the world can strengthen faith and inspire prayer and support.

Finally, the verse invites believers to look for doors God is opening. God opens opportunities for the gospel in neighborhoods, workplaces, and nations. Believers can pray for open doors and be ready to walk through them when God provides them.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Acts 14* shows that faithful ministry often involves both fruit and opposition. In Iconium, many believed, but the city was divided. In Lystra, a man was healed, but Paul was stoned. Believers today can expect both joy and difficulty as they share their faith. They can continue boldly, trusting that the Lord confirms the word of His grace.

The chapter also shows the importance of pointing people to the living God. When the crowd in Lystra tried to worship Paul and Barnabas, the apostles refused and pointed them to the Creator who gives rain, harvests, food, and gladness. Believers can help others see God’s goodness in everyday life, and they can resist every temptation to receive glory that belongs to God alone.

*Acts 14* teaches that hardship is part of the Christian journey. Paul and Barnabas told the new believers that through many afflictions they must enter God’s kingdom. Believers today can face struggles with honest expectations and confident hope, knowing that God sustains them and that glory awaits.

Finally, the chapter shows the care of Paul and Barnabas for the new churches. They returned to dangerous cities to strengthen believers, appointed elders, and entrusted the churches to the Lord. Then they reported to their sending church what God had done. Believers can follow this example, caring for others’ spiritual growth, supporting church leadership, and celebrating what God is doing in His mission.

## Chapter Prayer

Living God, You made the heavens, the earth, the sea, and everything in them. Thank You for the rain, the harvests, the food, and the gladness You give every day. Open my eyes to see Your kindness in ordinary things, and help me to point others to You. Guard me from seeking praise that belongs to You, and from placing any person on a pedestal. When following You brings hardship, strengthen me as You strengthened Paul, so that I can rise and continue. Help me to remember that through many afflictions I will enter Your kingdom, and that the glory to come is worth it all. Make me an encourager of other believers, and bless the leaders of Your church. Thank You for opening the door of faith to all nations. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Acts · Chapter 15 of 28

# Acts — Chapter 15

Chapter Theme: Saved by Grace: The Jerusalem Council and the Unity of Jews and Gentiles

[Read Acts 15 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/ACT15.htm)

Main Teaching

Some teachers from Judea insist that Gentile believers must be circumcised and keep the Law of Moses to be saved. The church sends Paul and Barnabas to Jerusalem, where the apostles and elders meet to consider the question. Peter testifies that God gave the Gentiles the Holy Spirit and cleansed their hearts by faith, declaring that Jews and Gentiles alike are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus. James shows that the prophets foretold the inclusion of the nations and proposes that Gentiles not be burdened, while asking them to avoid practices that would especially offend their Jewish brothers and sisters. A letter brings joy to the Gentile churches. The chapter closes with a sharp disagreement between Paul and Barnabas over John Mark.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Acts 15* records one of the most important meetings in church history, often called the Jerusalem Council. It took place around A.D. 49, after Paul’s first missionary journey. The question before the church was fundamental: Do Gentiles have to become Jews in order to become Christians? Specifically, must Gentile men be circumcised and must Gentile believers keep the whole Law of Moses, including its food laws and festivals, in order to be saved?

This was not a minor question. If the answer were yes, Christianity would remain a movement within Judaism, and Gentiles would have to adopt Jewish identity to follow Jesus. If the answer were no, the church would become a fellowship of Jews and Gentiles united by faith in Jesus alone. The answer would shape the gospel itself. Paul’s letter to the Galatians addresses the same issue with great urgency.

### The Dispute Arises (*15:1–5*)

“*Some men came down from Judea and taught the brothers, “Unless you are circumcised after the custom of Moses, you can’t be saved.”*” (*v. 1*) These teachers claimed that faith in Jesus was not enough; Gentiles also had to be circumcised. Paul and Barnabas strongly disagreed, and there was “*no small discord and discussion with them*” (*v. 2*). The church in Antioch decided to send Paul, Barnabas, and others to Jerusalem to consult with the apostles and elders.

On the way, they passed through Phoenicia and Samaria, “*declaring the conversion of the Gentiles. They caused great joy to all the brothers*” (*v. 3*). In Jerusalem, they were welcomed and reported what God had done. But “*some of the sect of the Pharisees who believed*” (*v. 5*) insisted that Gentile believers must be circumcised and keep the Law of Moses. These were genuine believers in Jesus who had come from the Pharisee tradition. They sincerely believed that God’s covenant required circumcision, as *Genesis 17* taught.

### Peter’s Testimony (*15:6–11*)

The apostles and elders gathered to consider the matter. “*When there had been much discussion*” (*v. 7*), Peter stood up. He reminded them of Cornelius: God had chosen Peter to bring the gospel to the Gentiles, and God, “*who knows the heart, testified about them, giving them the Holy Spirit, just like he did to us*” (*v. 8*). “*He made no distinction between us and them, cleansing their hearts by faith*” (*v. 9*). Peter’s conclusion is studied below.

### Barnabas and Paul’s Report (*15:12*)

“*All the multitude kept silence, and they listened to Barnabas and Paul reporting what signs and wonders God had done among the nations through them*” (*v. 12*). Their testimony confirmed Peter’s: God Himself was at work among the Gentiles, without requiring circumcision.

### James’s Judgment (*15:13–21*)

Then James spoke. This was James the brother of Jesus, the recognized leader of the Jerusalem church, known for his devotion to the Law. His support would carry great weight with the Jewish believers. He pointed to Scripture, studied below, and proposed a decision, also studied below.

James added, “*For Moses from generations of old has in every city those who preach him, being read in the synagogues every Sabbath*” (*v. 21*). Jewish communities existed throughout the Roman world, and Moses’ Law was read every week. Gentile believers needed to be sensitive to their Jewish neighbors and fellow believers, avoiding practices that would be especially offensive to them.

### The Letter to the Gentile Believers (*15:22–35*)

The apostles, elders, and whole church agreed. They chose two respected leaders, Judas called Barsabbas and Silas, to accompany Paul and Barnabas back to Antioch with a letter. The letter acknowledged that some had “*troubled you with words, unsettling your souls*” (*v. 24*), without authorization from the Jerusalem leaders. It commended Barnabas and Paul as “*men who have risked their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ*” (*v. 26*).

The letter’s key statement was: “*For it seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us, to lay no greater burden on you than these necessary things*” (*v. 28*). The decision was reached by the church together, guided by the Holy Spirit. It listed four things to avoid: “*things sacrificed to idols, from blood, from things strangled, and from sexual immorality*” (*v. 29*).

In Antioch, the church gathered and read the letter. “*When they had read it, they rejoiced over the encouragement*” (*v. 31*). The Gentile believers were relieved and joyful. They did not have to become Jews to belong to Christ. Judas and Silas, who were prophets, encouraged and strengthened the believers. (Verse 34, which says Silas stayed in Antioch, appears in some later manuscripts but not in the earliest ones.) Paul and Barnabas remained in Antioch, teaching and preaching with many others.

### Paul and Barnabas Separate (*15:36–41*)

Some time later, Paul suggested that they revisit the churches they had planted. Barnabas wanted to take John Mark, but Paul did not, because Mark had left them in Pamphylia (*13:13*). This disagreement is studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Acts 15:10–11* — Saved Through the Grace of the Lord Jesus

> *“Now therefore why do you tempt God, that you should put a yoke on the neck of the disciples which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear? But we believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they are.”*
>
> — *Acts 15:10–11* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The council in Jerusalem was debating whether Gentile believers needed to be circumcised and keep the Law of Moses. After much discussion, Peter stood up. He reminded the council how God had sent him to Cornelius, a Gentile, and how God had given the Holy Spirit to the Gentiles just as He had to the Jewish believers, cleansing their hearts by faith.

Then Peter asked, “*Now therefore why do you tempt God, that you should put a yoke on the neck of the disciples which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear?*” (*v. 10*) A “yoke” was a wooden frame placed on the necks of oxen to make them work. Rabbis spoke of taking on “the yoke of the Law.” Peter said that requiring Gentiles to keep the whole Law as a condition of salvation would place a burden on them that even the Jews had never been able to carry perfectly. To impose it would be to “tempt God,” testing Him by questioning what He had clearly shown.

“*But we believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they are*” (*v. 11*). This is the heart of Peter’s argument. Salvation comes “through the grace of the Lord Jesus,” God’s undeserved favor shown in Christ. And notice the order: Peter does not say “they are saved just as we are,” but “we are saved just as they are.” Jewish believers are saved in the same way as Gentile believers: by grace, not by keeping the Law.

These are the last words Peter speaks in the book of Acts. It is fitting that his final recorded statement is a clear declaration of salvation by grace.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses express the core truth of the gospel: salvation is by grace through faith, not by works of the Law. Paul writes, “*for by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God*” (*Ephesians 2:8*), “*not of works, that no one would boast*” (*Ephesians 2:9*). Both Jews and Gentiles stand before God on the same basis.

They also show the danger of adding requirements to the gospel. The teachers from Judea said, “*Unless you are circumcised after the custom of Moses, you can’t be saved*” (*v. 1*). This added a human requirement to God’s free gift. Whenever people add conditions to faith in Christ, whether religious rituals, cultural practices, or moral achievements, they distort the gospel. Paul wrote to the Galatians that there is no other gospel, but that some “*want to pervert the Good News of Christ*” (*Galatians 1:7*).

Finally, these verses show that the Law, while holy and good, cannot save. Peter acknowledged that no one had been able to carry its yoke perfectly. The Law reveals sin and points to the need for a Savior. Jesus offered a different yoke: “*For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light*” (*Matthew 11:30*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses free believers from trying to earn salvation. Many people, including Christians, live with a sense that they must prove themselves to God through good works, religious activity, or moral performance. Peter declares that believers are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus. They can rest in that grace.

They also challenge churches not to add unnecessary burdens to the gospel. Churches can unintentionally suggest that people must adopt certain cultural practices, dress codes, political views, or traditions to truly belong. The gospel requires only faith in Jesus. Churches can welcome people as they are, trusting God to transform them.

Finally, these verses encourage humility. Jewish believers had a rich heritage, but Peter acknowledged that they too were saved only by grace. No believer has grounds for pride. All stand before God as recipients of the same undeserved favor.

### *Acts 15:16–17* — Rebuilding the Tabernacle of David

> *““After these things I will return. I will again build the tabernacle of David, which has fallen. I will again build its ruins. I will set it up that the rest of men may seek after the Lord: all the Gentiles who are called by my name, says the Lord, who does all these things.””*
>
> — *Acts 15:16–17* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After Peter, Barnabas, and Paul had spoken, James, the leader of the Jerusalem church, addressed the council. He agreed with Peter that God had visited the Gentiles “to take out of them a people for his name” (*15:14*). Then he showed that this agreed with the words of the prophets.

James quoted *Amos 9:11–12*: “*After these things I will return. I will again build the tabernacle of David, which has fallen. I will again build its ruins. I will set it up*” (*v. 16*). The “tabernacle” (or “tent”) of David refers to David’s royal house, his dynasty and kingdom. By the time of Amos, David’s kingdom had been divided and weakened, and later it fell completely. Amos prophesied that God would one day restore it.

“*that the rest of men may seek after the Lord: all the Gentiles who are called by my name, says the Lord, who does all these things*” (*v. 17*). The purpose of rebuilding David’s house was that the Gentiles, the nations, would seek the Lord. The phrase “called by my name” means belonging to God, as His own people.

James understood that this prophecy was being fulfilled. Through Jesus, the Son of David, God was rebuilding David’s house. Jesus’ resurrection and reign as King restored David’s fallen dynasty. And as a result, Gentiles were seeking the Lord and becoming His people, not by becoming Jews, but as Gentiles “called by my name.”

James quoted the passage in a form close to the Greek translation of the Old Testament, which emphasizes the Gentiles seeking the Lord.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that the inclusion of the Gentiles was always part of God’s plan. It was not an afterthought or a departure from Israel’s hope. The prophets foresaw that when God restored David’s kingdom, the nations would come to Him. Isaiah, Micah, Zechariah, and others spoke of nations streaming to worship the Lord.

They also show the importance of Scripture in the church’s decision-making. The council did not decide based only on experience. Peter’s testimony and the reports of Paul and Barnabas showed what God was doing, but James confirmed it from the Scriptures. Experience and Scripture together guided the church.

Finally, these verses show that Jesus is the fulfillment of God’s promises to David. He is the King who reigns forever. Under His rule, Jews and Gentiles together become one people for God’s name.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to read Scripture in light of Christ. The promises of the Old Testament find their fulfillment in Jesus and His church. Believers can grow in understanding as they see how the whole Bible tells one story.

They also show a wise pattern for making decisions in the church. When believers face difficult questions, they can consider what God is doing, listen to testimony, and test everything by Scripture.

Finally, these verses invite believers from every nation to see themselves as part of God’s people. Gentile believers are not second-class members of God’s family. They are among those “called by my name,” included in God’s promises through Jesus.

### *Acts 15:19–20* — Don’t Trouble Those Who Turn to God

> *“Therefore my judgment is that we don’t trouble those from among the Gentiles who turn to God, but that we write to them that they abstain from the pollution of idols, from sexual immorality, from what is strangled, and from blood.”*
>
> — *Acts 15:19–20* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After showing that the prophets foretold the inclusion of the Gentiles, James gave his judgment: “*Therefore my judgment is that we don’t trouble those from among the Gentiles who turn to God*” (*v. 19*). The word “trouble” means to make difficult or to burden. James concluded that the church should not make it harder for Gentiles to come to God by requiring circumcision and the full observance of the Law of Moses.

This was a decisive moment. The leader of the Jerusalem church, known for his devotion to the Law, agreed with Peter and Paul that Gentiles did not need to become Jews to be saved.

But James added a request: “*but that we write to them that they abstain from the pollution of idols, from sexual immorality, from what is strangled, and from blood*” (*v. 20*). Four things were named.

First, “the pollution of idols,” meaning food offered to idols or participation in idol worship. Gentiles came from a world full of idol temples, and food sacrificed to idols was common.

Second, “sexual immorality.” Pagan culture was often permissive about sexual behavior, and some pagan worship included sexual practices.

Third and fourth, “what is strangled” and “blood.” These relate to food laws. Animals that were strangled still had their blood in them. The prohibition against eating blood went back to God’s command to Noah (*Genesis 9:4*), before the Law of Moses, and was deeply important to Jewish believers.

These requests were not conditions for salvation. Salvation was by grace through faith. Rather, they were ways for Gentile believers to avoid practices that were connected to idolatry or that would deeply offend Jewish believers, making fellowship between them possible. Jews and Gentiles in the church often shared meals together; these guidelines helped make that table fellowship possible.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show how the church balanced freedom and love. Gentile believers were free from the requirements of the Law, but they were asked to limit their freedom in certain areas for the sake of unity with Jewish believers. Paul later taught the same principle: believers should not use their freedom in ways that cause others to stumble (*Romans 14:13–21*; *1 Corinthians 8:9–13*).

They also show that some moral standards are not merely cultural. The prohibition of sexual immorality is not just a Jewish custom; it reflects God’s design for all people. Throughout the New Testament, believers are called to sexual purity (*1 Thessalonians 4:3–5*). Christians have generally understood the food-related requests as practical guidelines for that time and context, while the prohibitions against idolatry and sexual immorality remain permanent moral commands.

Finally, these verses show wise leadership. James sought a solution that upheld the gospel of grace while addressing the real concerns of Jewish believers. The decision preserved both truth and unity.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage churches to avoid placing unnecessary obstacles in the way of people coming to God. Believers can examine whether any of their expectations or traditions make it harder for others to come to Christ.

They also teach believers to use their freedom in love. In matters where Scripture gives freedom, believers can still choose to limit their freedom out of love for others, especially to avoid causing offense or harm to fellow believers.

Finally, these verses remind believers that freedom in Christ is not freedom to sin. Gentile believers were free from the Law’s ceremonies, but they were still called to turn from idolatry and sexual immorality. Grace frees believers from trying to earn salvation, and it also empowers them to live holy lives.

### *Acts 15:39–40* — A Sharp Disagreement

> *“Then the contention grew so sharp that they separated from each other. Barnabas took Mark with him and sailed away to Cyprus, but Paul chose Silas and went out, being commended by the brothers to the grace of God.”*
>
> — *Acts 15:39–40* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After the Jerusalem Council, Paul and Barnabas returned to Antioch. Some time later, Paul suggested that they go back and visit the churches they had planted on their first journey. Barnabas wanted to take his cousin John Mark with them (*Colossians 4:10*).

But Paul disagreed. Mark had left them partway through the first journey, at Pamphylia, and returned home (*13:13*). Paul did not think it wise to take someone who had abandoned the work before.

“*Then the contention grew so sharp that they separated from each other*” (*v. 39*). The disagreement was intense. These two men had worked closely together for years. Barnabas had vouched for Paul when others were afraid of him (*9:27*) and had brought him to Antioch (*11:25–26*). They had suffered together on their missionary journey. Now they parted ways.

“*Barnabas took Mark with him and sailed away to Cyprus*” (*v. 39*). Barnabas, true to his name as “Son of Encouragement,” gave Mark another chance.

“*but Paul chose Silas and went out, being commended by the brothers to the grace of God*” (*v. 40*). Paul chose Silas, one of the leaders who had brought the council’s letter to Antioch. The church commended them to God’s grace.

Luke does not say who was right. Both men had good reasons. Paul was concerned about the mission’s reliability; Barnabas was concerned about restoring a young man who had failed.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This passage shows the honesty of Scripture. Luke does not hide the conflict between two great leaders. Even godly believers can disagree sharply. The church is made up of real people with real differences.

It also shows that God can bring good out of disagreement. Instead of one missionary team, there were now two. Barnabas and Mark went to Cyprus, and Paul and Silas went through Syria and Cilicia. The mission expanded.

Finally, the story has a hopeful ending beyond this chapter. Mark grew into a faithful servant of Christ. He later worked with Peter, who called him “*my son*” (*1 Peter 5:13*), and is traditionally regarded as the author of the Gospel of Mark. Paul and Mark were reconciled. Near the end of his life, Paul wrote, “*Take Mark, and bring him with you, for he is useful to me for service*” (*2 Timothy 4:11*). Barnabas’s patience with Mark bore fruit, and Paul’s relationship with him was restored.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage reminds believers that disagreements are a normal part of life, even among faithful Christians. Believers do not need to pretend that conflict never happens. They can face disagreements honestly and seek to handle them with grace.

It also shows that sometimes believers may need to go separate ways in ministry, while still serving the same Lord. When believers cannot agree on a particular course of action, they can part with blessing rather than bitterness, trusting God to work through both paths.

Finally, the story encourages believers to give second chances. Mark had failed, but Barnabas believed in him, and he became a valuable servant of Christ. Believers can follow Barnabas’s example, encouraging those who have stumbled. And they can follow Paul’s example later in life, being willing to reconcile and to recognize growth in others.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Acts 15* declares that salvation is by grace through faith in Jesus, not by keeping the Law or adopting a particular culture. Jews and Gentiles are saved in the same way. Believers can rest in this grace, free from the burden of trying to earn God’s acceptance. They can also guard the gospel from additions that would turn it into a message of human effort.

The chapter also shows how the church can handle serious disagreements. The council listened to testimony, discussed openly, consulted Scripture, and reached a decision together with the guidance of the Holy Spirit. Churches today can follow this pattern when facing difficult questions, seeking both truth and unity.

*Acts 15* teaches believers to use their freedom in love. Gentile believers were free from the Law, but they were asked to avoid practices connected to idolatry and sexual immorality, and to be sensitive to the convictions of Jewish believers. Believers today can exercise their freedom in ways that build up others rather than causing them to stumble.

Finally, the chapter shows that even godly leaders can disagree sharply. Paul and Barnabas parted ways, yet God used both of them, and Mark, who had failed, was later restored. Believers can face conflict honestly, extend second chances, and trust God to bring good out of difficult situations.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You that I am saved through Your grace, not by my own efforts. Thank You that Jews and Gentiles, people of every nation, are saved in the same way, by faith in You. Guard me from adding burdens to Your gospel, and help me to welcome others as You have welcomed me. Give Your church wisdom when we face hard questions, and help us to listen to one another, to search the Scriptures, and to follow Your Spirit. Teach me to use my freedom in love, never causing others to stumble. When I disagree with fellow believers, help me to act with grace and humility. Make me like Barnabas, giving second chances to those who have failed, and like Paul, willing to be reconciled. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Acts · Chapter 16 of 28

# Acts — Chapter 16

Chapter Theme: Led by the Spirit into Europe: Lydia, a Freed Slave Girl, and a Jailer Saved

[Read Acts 16 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/ACT16.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul and Silas, now joined by Timothy, revisit the churches and are guided by the Holy Spirit through closed doors until a night vision calls them to Macedonia. In Philippi, the Lord opens the heart of Lydia, a businesswoman, and she and her household believe. Paul frees an enslaved girl from a spirit of divination, and her owners, angry at losing their income, have Paul and Silas beaten and jailed. At midnight they pray and sing hymns; an earthquake opens the doors, and the terrified jailer asks what he must do to be saved. He and his household believe in the Lord Jesus and are baptized, rejoicing.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Acts 16* begins Paul’s second missionary journey, around A.D. 49–52. In this chapter, the gospel crosses from Asia into Europe for the first time in Acts, as Paul and his companions travel to Macedonia, in what is now northern Greece. The church planted in Philippi would become one of Paul’s most beloved congregations; years later he wrote them the letter we call Philippians, full of joy and affection.

This chapter also contains the first of the “we” passages in Acts (*16:10–17*), in which Luke writes in the first person. This suggests that Luke joined Paul at Troas and traveled with him to Philippi.

### Timothy Joins Paul (*16:1–5*)

In Lystra, where Paul had been stoned on his first journey, he met “*a certain disciple was there, named Timothy, the son of a Jewess who believed, but his father was a Greek*” (*v. 1*). Timothy’s mother Eunice and grandmother Lois were believers who had taught him the Scriptures from childhood (*2 Timothy 1:5*; *3:15*). “*The brothers who were at Lystra and Iconium gave a good testimony about him*” (*v. 2*).

Paul wanted Timothy to join him. “*he took and circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those parts, for they all knew that his father was a Greek*” (*v. 3*). This may seem surprising, since Paul had just fought at the Jerusalem Council against requiring circumcision for Gentiles. But Timothy’s situation was different. He had a Jewish mother, and by Jewish standards he was considered Jewish. An uncircumcised Jew would have been a barrier to Paul’s ministry in synagogues. Paul circumcised Timothy not for salvation but to remove an obstacle to the gospel. Paul explained his approach: “*To the Jews I became as a Jew, that I might gain Jews*” (*1 Corinthians 9:20*). By contrast, Paul refused to circumcise Titus, a Gentile, when others insisted it was necessary (*Galatians 2:3*).

Timothy became one of Paul’s closest companions. Paul later called him “*my true child in faith*” (*1 Timothy 1:2*), and two New Testament letters are addressed to him.

As they traveled, they delivered the decisions of the Jerusalem Council, and “*the assemblies were strengthened in the faith, and increased in number daily*” (*v. 5*).

### The Spirit’s Guidance and the Macedonian Call (*16:6–10*)

Paul’s team tried to go in several directions but were prevented. This guidance is studied below.

### Lydia’s Conversion in Philippi (*16:11–15*)

The team sailed from Troas to Neapolis and traveled to “*Philippi, which is a city of Macedonia, the foremost of the district, a Roman colony*” (*v. 12*). Philippi was named after Philip II of Macedon, the father of Alexander the Great. As a Roman colony, it was settled by retired Roman soldiers and enjoyed special privileges. Its citizens were proud of their Roman identity.

Paul’s usual practice was to begin at the synagogue. But Philippi apparently had no synagogue, which required ten Jewish men. So on the Sabbath, the team “*went outside of the city by a riverside, where we supposed there was a place of prayer*” (*v. 13*). They found a group of women gathered for prayer. Lydia’s conversion is studied below.

### A Slave Girl Set Free (*16:16–24*)

As the team was going to the place of prayer, they met “*a certain girl having a spirit of divination*” (*v. 16*). The Greek literally says she had “a spirit of python,” a reference to the serpent associated with the oracle of Apollo at Delphi, where prophets were believed to speak the god’s messages. She “*brought her masters much gain by fortune telling*” (*v. 16*). She was a slave, exploited by her owners for profit.

She followed Paul and his companions, shouting, “*These men are servants of the Most High God, who proclaim to us a way of salvation!*” (*v. 17*) Her words were true, but coming from a spirit of divination, they could confuse people, linking the gospel with fortune-telling. “Most High God” could also be understood by pagans as Zeus or another deity. This went on for many days. Finally, Paul, “*becoming greatly annoyed*” (*v. 18*), turned and said to the spirit, “*I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her!*” (*v. 18*) It left her that very hour.

The girl was freed, but her owners were furious, “*when her masters saw that the hope of their gain was gone*” (*v. 19*). They cared more about their profits than about the girl’s freedom. They dragged Paul and Silas to the magistrates and accused them: “*These men, being Jews, are agitating our city*” (*v. 20*) “*and advocate customs which it is not lawful for us to accept or to observe, being Romans*” (*v. 21*). The accusation appealed to anti-Jewish prejudice and Roman pride. The real reason, lost profits, was hidden.

The crowd joined the attack, and the magistrates had Paul and Silas stripped and beaten with rods, a Roman punishment. Paul later mentioned that he had been beaten with rods three times (*2 Corinthians 11:25*). After a severe beating, they were thrown into prison, and the jailer put them in the inner cell with their feet fastened in stocks.

### Midnight Songs and an Earthquake (*16:25–34*)

What Paul and Silas did in prison, and what followed, is studied below.

### Paul Demands Justice (*16:35–40*)

In the morning, the magistrates sent officers to release Paul and Silas quietly. But Paul refused: “*They have beaten us publicly without a trial, men who are Romans, and have cast us into prison! Do they now release us secretly? No, most certainly, but let them come themselves and bring us out!*” (*v. 37*)

Roman citizens had legal rights, including the right to a trial before punishment. Beating a Roman citizen without trial was a serious crime. When the magistrates heard that Paul and Silas were Romans, they were alarmed. They came personally, apologized, escorted them out, and asked them to leave the city.

Why did Paul insist on this? He was not seeking revenge. By having the magistrates publicly acknowledge the injustice, Paul helped protect the young church in Philippi from being treated as a criminal group. Standing up for justice was not contrary to his faith; it served the gospel and protected vulnerable believers.

Paul and Silas went to Lydia’s house, encouraged the believers, and departed. The church in Philippi now included a wealthy businesswoman, a freed slave girl (presumably), and a Roman jailer with his household, a vivid picture of how the gospel unites people across social lines.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Acts 16:6–10* — Doors Closed and a Door Opened

> *“When they had gone through the region of Phrygia and Galatia, they were forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia. When they had come opposite Mysia, they tried to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit didn’t allow them. Passing by Mysia, they came down to Troas. A vision appeared to Paul in the night. There was a man of Macedonia standing, begging him and saying, ‘Come over into Macedonia and help us.’ When he had seen the vision, immediately we sought to go out to Macedonia, concluding that the Lord had called us to preach the Good News to them.”*
>
> — *Acts 16:6–10* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul, Silas, and Timothy had been visiting the churches from Paul’s first journey. Now they wanted to take the gospel to new regions. But something unusual happened.

“*When they had gone through the region of Phrygia and Galatia, they were forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia*” (*v. 6*). “Asia” here refers to the Roman province on the western coast of what is now Turkey, including the great city of Ephesus. It seemed like a natural place to go next. But the Holy Spirit said no. Luke does not say how; perhaps through a prophecy, circumstances, or an inner conviction.

“*When they had come opposite Mysia, they tried to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit didn’t allow them*” (*v. 7*). They tried another direction, north toward Bithynia. Again, the Spirit, here called “*the Spirit*” (*v. 7*) (some manuscripts read “the Spirit of Jesus”), prevented them.

Two doors had closed. They traveled west to Troas, a port city on the Aegean Sea. Then: “*A vision appeared to Paul in the night. There was a man of Macedonia standing, begging him and saying, “Come over into Macedonia and help us.”*” (*v. 9*)

“*When he had seen the vision, immediately we sought to go out to Macedonia, concluding that the Lord had called us to preach the Good News to them*” (*v. 10*). Notice the word “we.” Luke joins the story here. Notice also the word “concluding.” The team discussed the vision together and concluded that God was calling them to Macedonia. They acted immediately.

The Spirit’s “no” to Asia was not permanent. Later, Paul spent nearly three years in Ephesus, and the gospel spread throughout Asia (*19:10*). God’s timing was different from Paul’s.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that God guides His people both by closing doors and by opening them. Sometimes His guidance comes as a clear call; sometimes it comes as a series of closed doors. Proverbs says, “*A man’s heart plans his course, but the LORD directs his steps*” (*Proverbs 16:9*).

They also show that guidance often comes while believers are moving. Paul and his team were actively trying to serve God. They did not sit and wait for a vision; they made plans and took steps. God redirected them along the way.

Finally, these verses show the importance of community in discernment. Paul received the vision, but the team together “concluded” what it meant. God often guides through the shared wisdom of believers.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers who face closed doors. When plans fail or opportunities disappear, it can be discouraging. But God may be closing one door to lead toward another. Believers can trust that God is directing their steps, even through disappointment.

They also encourage believers to keep moving in faith. Paul did not stop serving when doors closed. He kept going until God made the direction clear. Believers can make plans and take faithful steps, staying open to God’s redirection.

Finally, these verses encourage believers to seek guidance together. Important decisions can be discussed with trusted believers who can help discern God’s will through prayer, Scripture, and wise counsel.

### *Acts 16:14* — The Lord Opened Her Heart

> *“A certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple, of the city of Thyatira, one who worshiped God, heard us. The Lord opened her heart to listen to the things which were spoken by Paul.”*
>
> — *Acts 16:14* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

In Philippi, there was no synagogue, so Paul and his companions went to a place by the river where they thought people would gather to pray. They found a group of women and sat down to talk with them.

“*A certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple, of the city of Thyatira, one who worshiped God, heard us*” (*v. 14*). Lydia was from Thyatira, a city in the province of Asia known for its purple dye. She was a businesswoman who sold expensive purple cloth, a luxury item worn by the wealthy and by royalty. She was likely wealthy and independent, since she had a household of her own.

Lydia “*worshiped God*” (*v. 14*). Like Cornelius, she was a Gentile who believed in the God of Israel. She was spiritually seeking, gathering with others to pray.

“*The Lord opened her heart to listen to the things which were spoken by Paul*” (*v. 14*). Lydia listened to Paul’s message, but her response was not merely the result of Paul’s persuasive speaking. The Lord opened her heart. God worked within her to help her understand and receive the gospel.

Then “*When she and her household were baptized*” (*v. 15*), she immediately showed hospitality: “*If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come into my house and stay*” (*v. 15*). She insisted, and they accepted. Her house became the first meeting place of the church in Philippi (*16:40*).

Interestingly, Paul’s vision was of “a man of Macedonia,” but the first convert in Macedonia was a woman from Asia, the very province where the Spirit had forbidden them to preach.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that conversion is the work of God. Paul preached, but the Lord opened Lydia’s heart. Jesus had said, “*No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him*” (*John 6:44*). Faith comes when God opens hearts to receive His word.

It also shows the importance of faithful preaching. God opened Lydia’s heart “to listen to the things which were spoken by Paul.” God uses the message of the gospel, shared by His people, to bring people to faith. Paul writes that faith comes by hearing the word of Christ (*Romans 10:17*).

Finally, the verse shows that the gospel transforms people’s use of their resources. Lydia immediately opened her home to the missionaries. Her conversion led to hospitality and generosity. Throughout the New Testament, believers’ homes became centers of church life.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to share the gospel with confidence, knowing that God is the one who opens hearts. Believers do not need to rely on their own persuasiveness. They can share faithfully and pray for God to work.

It also encourages believers to pray for those who are seeking. Lydia was already worshiping God and gathering to pray. Many people today are spiritually seeking. Believers can pray that God would open their hearts to the gospel.

Finally, the verse invites believers to use their homes and resources for God’s kingdom. Lydia’s home became a place of hospitality and fellowship. Believers can open their homes to others, offering welcome, meals, and a place for believers to gather.

### *Acts 16:25* — Praying and Singing at Midnight

> *“But about midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them.”*
>
> — *Acts 16:25* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul and Silas had been through a terrible day. They had freed a slave girl from a spirit of divination, and her owners had dragged them before the magistrates. A crowd attacked them. They were stripped, beaten severely with rods, and thrown into the inner prison, the darkest and most secure part, with their feet fastened in wooden stocks. Their backs were bleeding. They were in pain, in darkness, unable to move.

“*But about midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God*” (*v. 25*). In the middle of the night, in pain and chains, they prayed and sang. They did not complain, curse their captors, or despair. They worshiped God.

The hymns they sang may have been psalms, many of which speak of trusting God in times of trouble. For example, “*I will bless the LORD at all times. His praise will always be in my mouth*” (*Psalm 34:1*).

“*and the prisoners were listening to them*” (*v. 25*). The other prisoners heard them. In that dark place, they heard prayers and songs instead of groans and curses. Paul and Silas’s worship was a witness.

Then “*Suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken; and immediately all the doors were opened, and everyone’s bonds were loosened*” (*v. 26*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that joy in God does not depend on circumstances. Paul later wrote to the Philippians, the church founded in this very city, “*Rejoice in the Lord always! Again I will say, “Rejoice!”*” (*Philippians 4:4*) He had learned this joy in the Philippian jail.

It also shows that worship in suffering is a powerful witness. The prisoners were listening. People notice how believers respond to hardship. Praise in the midst of pain points to a God who is worthy of trust even in the darkest places.

Finally, the verse shows that God hears the prayers and praises of His people. The earthquake came as Paul and Silas worshiped. God is present with His people in their suffering and is able to act on their behalf.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to turn to God in prayer and praise during difficult times. When pain, fear, or injustice comes, believers can bring their hurts to God and choose to worship Him. This does not mean pretending everything is fine; many psalms of praise also include honest lament. It means trusting God enough to praise Him even in the darkness.

It also reminds believers that others are watching. Family members, coworkers, and friends notice how believers respond to suffering. Faithful worship in hard times can draw others to God.

Finally, the verse offers hope to those in “midnight” moments, times of deep darkness, whether illness, loss, depression, or imprisonment. God is present in those moments. Believers can pray and sing, trusting that He hears and is able to bring light and freedom.

### *Acts 16:30–31* — “*What Must I Do to Be Saved?*” (*v. 30*)

> *“brought them out, and said, ‘Sirs, what must I do to be saved?’ They said, ‘Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you will be saved, you and your household.’”*
>
> — *Acts 16:30–31* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

A great earthquake had shaken the prison. All the doors flew open, and all the prisoners’ chains came loose. The jailer woke up and saw the doors open. He assumed the prisoners had escaped. Under Roman law, a jailer who lost his prisoners could face execution. In despair, he drew his sword to kill himself.

But Paul shouted, “*Don’t harm yourself, for we are all here!*” (*v. 28*) None of the prisoners had escaped. Paul cared for the man who had locked him in the stocks.

The jailer called for lights, rushed in, and fell trembling before Paul and Silas. Then he brought them out and asked, “*Sirs, what must I do to be saved?*” (*v. 30*) This was the most important question anyone could ask. The jailer may have heard the slave girl’s words that these men proclaimed “a way of salvation” (*16:17*), or heard Paul and Silas praying and singing. Now, shaken by the earthquake and by the prisoners’ refusal to escape, he wanted to know how to be saved.

Paul and Silas answered, “*Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you will be saved, you and your household*” (*v. 31*). The answer was simple. Salvation comes through believing in Jesus as Lord and Christ. No rituals, payments, or achievements were required.

The promise included “your household.” This does not mean the jailer’s family would be saved automatically through his faith. Rather, the same offer was extended to everyone in his household. Paul and Silas “*spoke the word of the Lord to him, and to all who were in his house*” (*v. 32*). The household heard the message and believed.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses summarize the gospel in its simplest form: believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you will be saved. Salvation is not earned; it is received by faith. Paul writes, “*if you will confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved*” (*Romans 10:9*).

They also show the transformation that comes with faith. That same night, the jailer “*washed their stripes*” (*v. 33*), caring for the wounds of the men he had imprisoned. He was baptized with his household. He brought them into his home, gave them food, and “*rejoiced greatly with all his household, having believed in God*” (*v. 34*). The man who had been about to take his own life was now filled with joy.

Finally, these verses show that no one is beyond the reach of the gospel. The jailer was a Roman official, probably a retired soldier, part of the system that had beaten and imprisoned God’s servants. Yet he was saved. God’s grace reaches all kinds of people.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses give the clearest answer to life’s most important question. Anyone who asks, “What must I do to be saved?” can receive the same answer: believe in the Lord Jesus Christ. Believers can share this simple message with confidence.

They also show that faith changes lives. The jailer’s faith led to compassion, hospitality, and joy. Believers can let their faith shape how they treat others, especially those they once opposed or ignored.

Finally, these verses encourage believers to care even for those who mistreat them. Paul could have escaped but chose to stay, saving the jailer’s life. Believers can show grace and compassion to those who wrong them, opening the way for them to encounter Christ.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Acts 16* shows how God guides His people. Paul’s team faced closed doors before receiving a clear call to Macedonia. Believers today can trust God’s guidance through both closed and open doors, continuing to serve faithfully while staying open to His redirection, and seeking discernment together with other believers.

The chapter also shows that God opens hearts. Lydia listened, and the Lord opened her heart to receive the gospel. Believers can share their faith with confidence, praying for God to work in the hearts of those who hear. Like Lydia, those who believe can use their homes and resources to serve God’s people.

*Acts 16* shows the power of worship in suffering. Paul and Silas, beaten and chained, prayed and sang at midnight. Their worship became a witness. Believers facing their own dark moments can turn to God in prayer and praise, trusting that He hears them and is present with them.

Finally, the chapter shows the simple, life-changing power of the gospel. The jailer asked, “What must I do to be saved?” and received the answer: “Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ.” The gospel freed a slave girl from spiritual bondage, brought a businesswoman to faith, and transformed a jailer and his household. Believers can share this message with all kinds of people, and they can stand for justice, as Paul did, especially for the vulnerable.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord God, thank You for guiding Your servants through closed doors and open doors. When my plans are interrupted, help me to trust that You are directing my steps. Open the hearts of those around me who are seeking You, as You opened Lydia’s heart, and make me faithful to share Your word. Thank You for setting free those who are bound and exploited; give me compassion for the vulnerable and courage to stand for justice. When I find myself in a dark and painful place, teach me to pray and sing to You, as Paul and Silas did at midnight. Thank You for the simple and wonderful answer to the most important question: believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you will be saved. I believe in You, Lord Jesus. Fill my household with Your joy. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
