Acts · Chapter 17 of 28

# Acts — Chapter 17

Chapter Theme: Reasoning from the Scriptures and Speaking to the Seekers of Athens

[Read Acts 17 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/ACT17.htm)

Main Teaching

In Thessalonica, Paul reasons from the Scriptures that the Messiah had to suffer and rise, and many believe, but opponents accuse the believers of turning the world upside down and proclaiming another king, Jesus. In Berea, the people receive the word eagerly and examine the Scriptures daily. In Athens, distressed by a city full of idols, Paul speaks to philosophers at the Areopagus, proclaiming the unknown God as the Creator of all, who made every nation, is near to every person, and now commands all people everywhere to repent, because He will judge the world through the Man He raised from the dead. Some mock, some want to hear more, and some believe.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Acts 17* continues Paul’s second missionary journey. After leaving Philippi, Paul, Silas, and Timothy traveled west along the Via Egnatia, the great Roman road across Macedonia, to Thessalonica, and then to Berea. Paul then went south to Athens, the ancient center of Greek philosophy and culture.

The chapter shows Paul speaking to three very different audiences. In the synagogues of Thessalonica and Berea, he reasoned from the Hebrew Scriptures with Jews and God-fearing Gentiles. In Athens, he spoke to Greek philosophers who did not know the Scriptures, beginning instead with creation and with their own poets. His message was the same, but his approach adapted to his listeners.

### Thessalonica: “Another King, Jesus” (*17:1–9*)

Thessalonica was the capital of the Roman province of Macedonia, a large and prosperous port city. “*Paul, as was his custom, went in to them; and for three Sabbath days reasoned with them from the Scriptures*” (*v. 2*). His message: “*explaining and demonstrating that the Christ had to suffer and rise again from the dead, and saying, “This Jesus, whom I proclaim to you, is the Christ.”*” (*v. 3*) Many Jews expected a conquering Messiah, not a suffering one. Paul showed from passages like *Isaiah 53* and *Psalm 22* that the Messiah had to suffer and die, and from *Psalm 16* that He would rise. Then he declared that Jesus was that Messiah.

Some Jews were persuaded, along with “*of the devout Greeks a great multitude, and not a few of the chief women*” (*v. 4*). But opponents became jealous, gathered troublemakers from the marketplace, and started a riot. They attacked the house of Jason, where Paul was staying, and when they could not find Paul and Silas, they dragged Jason and other believers before the city officials. Their accusation is studied below. The officials took a security payment from Jason and released them. Paul’s letters to the Thessalonians, written soon afterward, show how deeply he loved this young church, which continued to face persecution (*1 Thessalonians 2:14*).

### Berea: Noble Examiners of Scripture (*17:10–15*)

The believers sent Paul and Silas away by night to Berea, about fifty miles away. There, too, they went to the synagogue. The Bereans’ response is studied below. Many believed, including prominent Greek women and men. But opponents from Thessalonica came to Berea and stirred up the crowds. The believers sent Paul to the coast, while Silas and Timothy stayed behind. Paul’s escorts brought him to Athens.

### Athens: A City Full of Idols (*17:16–21*)

Athens had been the intellectual capital of the ancient world, the city of Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle. By Paul’s time, its political power had faded, but it remained a center of philosophy, art, and religion. It was filled with temples, statues, and altars to many gods. An ancient writer joked that it was easier to find a god in Athens than a man.

“*Now while Paul waited for them at Athens, his spirit was provoked within him as he saw the city full of idols*” (*v. 16*). Paul was not impressed by the beauty of the art. He was deeply distressed that people were worshiping idols instead of the living God.

Paul reasoned in the synagogue with Jews and God-fearers, and in the marketplace (the agora) every day with anyone who happened to be there, much as Socrates had done centuries earlier. Some Epicurean and Stoic philosophers debated with him. Epicureans believed that the gods were distant and uninvolved in human affairs, and that the goal of life was pleasure, understood as tranquility and freedom from pain. Stoics believed that a divine reason pervaded the universe, and that the goal of life was to live in harmony with reason and accept one’s fate with self-control.

Some called Paul a “*babbler*” (*v. 18*), literally a “seed-picker,” a word for a bird that picks up scraps, used of someone who picks up bits of ideas without understanding them. Others said, “*He seems to be advocating foreign deities*” (*v. 18*), because he preached about Jesus and the resurrection. Some may have thought “Jesus” and “Resurrection” (anastasis in Greek) were a pair of new gods.

They brought him to the Areopagus, which could refer both to a hill near the Acropolis (the “Hill of Ares,” or Mars Hill) and to the council that met there, which oversaw matters of religion and education. Luke adds a slightly humorous note: “*Now all the Athenians and the strangers living there spent their time in nothing else, but either to tell or to hear some new thing*” (*v. 21*).

### Paul’s Speech at the Areopagus (*17:22–31*)

Paul began respectfully: “*You men of Athens, I perceive that you are very religious in all things*” (*v. 22*). He had noticed an altar with the inscription “*TO AN UNKNOWN GOD*” (*v. 23*). The Athenians, fearing they might have overlooked some deity, had built altars to unknown gods. Paul used this as a starting point: “*What therefore you worship in ignorance, I announce to you*” (*v. 23*).

Paul then described the true God. He is the Creator of the world and everything in it, “*being Lord of heaven and earth*” (*v. 24*), who “*doesn’t dwell in temples made with hands*” (*v. 24*). Standing within sight of the magnificent Parthenon, this was a bold statement. God “*isn’t served by men’s hands, as though he needed anything, seeing he himself gives to all life and breath and all things*” (*v. 25*). The gods of Greece were imagined as needing offerings and temples. The true God needs nothing; He is the giver of everything. Paul then spoke of God’s purpose for humanity, studied below.

Paul quoted Greek poets. “*For in him we live, move, and have our being*” (*v. 28*) is often attributed to the poet Epimenides, and “*For we are also his offspring*” (*v. 28*) comes from the poet Aratus, who was from Paul’s home region of Cilicia. Paul used their words to make his point: if we are God’s offspring, “*we ought not to think that the Divine Nature is like gold, or silver, or stone, engraved by art and design of man*” (*v. 29*). Living, personal beings cannot have been made by lifeless images. Paul’s conclusion is studied below.

### The Response (*17:32–34*)

“*Now when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked*” (*v. 32*). To Greek thinkers, the idea of bodily resurrection seemed foolish. Many believed the soul was immortal but the body was a prison to escape. Others said, “*We want to hear you again concerning this*” (*v. 32*). And some believed, “*including Dionysius the Areopagite, and a woman named Damaris, and others with them*” (*v. 34*). Dionysius was a member of the Areopagus council, a man of high standing. Damaris was a woman whom Luke considered worth naming. Paul’s ministry in Athens did not produce a large church, but it produced real fruit.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Acts 17:6–7* — Those Who Have Turned the World Upside Down

> *“When they didn’t find them, they dragged Jason and certain brothers before the rulers of the city, crying, ‘These who have turned the world upside down have come here also, whom Jason has received. These all act contrary to the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, Jesus!’”*
>
> — *Acts 17:6–7* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had preached in the synagogue in Thessalonica for three Sabbaths, and many people believed. But some of the Jewish leaders became jealous. They gathered troublemakers from the marketplace, formed a mob, and started a riot. They rushed to the house of Jason, where Paul and Silas were staying, but could not find them.

So “*they dragged Jason and certain brothers before the rulers of the city, crying, “These who have turned the world upside down have come here also,*” (*v. 6*). The accusation was meant as an insult. The opponents were saying that these men were troublemakers who caused disorder wherever they went. Yet their words were a remarkable testimony. In less than twenty years since the resurrection, the gospel had spread so widely that the believers were known for turning the world upside down.

“*whom Jason has received. These all act contrary to the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, Jesus!*” (*v. 7*) This was a serious political charge. In the Roman Empire, Caesar was the supreme ruler, and some emperors claimed divine honors. Proclaiming another king could be treated as treason.

The charge was false in the sense intended. Paul was not leading a political rebellion against Rome. But it contained a deep truth. Paul did proclaim Jesus as King, the Lord whose authority is above every earthly ruler. Jesus’ kingdom is not of this world (*John 18:36*), but it does claim the ultimate allegiance of every person.

The city officials were disturbed, but they released Jason and the others after taking a security payment.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that the gospel has the power to transform the world. The believers did not have political power, wealth, or armies. But the message of Jesus changed lives, families, and communities wherever it went. What looked like upheaval to opponents was the beginning of God’s new creation.

They also show the radical claim of the gospel: Jesus is King. The early Christian confession “Jesus is Lord” (*Romans 10:9*; *1 Corinthians 12:3*) had a direct challenge built into it, since Caesar also claimed to be lord. Christians honored earthly rulers (*Romans 13:1–7*; *1 Peter 2:17*), but they gave their highest loyalty to Christ.

Finally, the accusation shows a pattern seen throughout Acts and history: the gospel is often opposed with false or distorted charges. Jesus Himself was accused of claiming to be a rival king to Caesar (*Luke 23:2*; *John 19:12*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses challenge believers to consider whether their faith makes any difference in the world. The early believers were known for turning the world upside down. Believers today can ask God to make their faith active and transforming in their families, workplaces, and communities.

They also remind believers that Jesus is King over every area of life. Faith is not merely a private matter. Allegiance to Jesus shapes how believers think about money, work, relationships, justice, and politics. Believers are called to honor earthly authorities while giving their ultimate loyalty to Christ.

Finally, these verses encourage believers who face misunderstanding or false accusations. When believers live faithfully, others may misinterpret their motives. Believers can respond with patience, integrity, and trust in God, knowing that the early church faced the same.

### *Acts 17:11* — Examining the Scriptures Daily

> *“Now these were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, examining the Scriptures daily to see whether these things were so.”*
>
> — *Acts 17:11* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After being forced to leave Thessalonica, Paul and Silas went to Berea, a smaller town about fifty miles away. As usual, they went to the synagogue and taught about Jesus.

“*Now these were more noble than those in Thessalonica*” (*v. 11*). The word “noble” originally referred to people of high birth, but it came to describe people of noble character, open-minded and generous in spirit. The Bereans showed this character in two ways.

First, “*they received the word with all readiness of mind*” (*v. 11*). They listened eagerly. They did not reject Paul’s message out of hand or react with jealousy, as some in Thessalonica had done. They were open to hearing something new.

Second, they were “*examining the Scriptures daily to see whether these things were so*” (*v. 11*). They did not simply accept everything Paul said because he was a persuasive speaker. They studied the Hebrew Scriptures every day to see whether his claims about Jesus were true. They tested his teaching by God’s word.

These two qualities, eagerness and careful examination, belong together. The Bereans were neither closed-minded nor gullible. They were open to truth and committed to testing it.

“*Many of them therefore believed*” (*v. 12*). Their careful study led many of them to faith in Jesus.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows the importance of Scripture as the standard for truth. The Bereans tested even the teaching of an apostle by the Scriptures. Believers are called to test all teaching by God’s word. John writes, “*Beloved, don’t believe every spirit, but test the spirits, whether they are of God*” (*1 John 4:1*).

It also shows that faith and careful thinking go together. The Bereans examined the evidence and came to faith. Christianity does not ask people to believe blindly. It invites them to examine the Scriptures and see whether these things are so.

Finally, the verse shows that eagerness for God’s word is a mark of noble character. *Psalm 119* is filled with expressions of delight in God’s word: “*How I love your law! It is my meditation all day*” (*Psalm 119:97*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to read and study Scripture regularly. The Bereans examined the Scriptures daily. Believers can develop habits of reading the Bible, thinking about it, and applying it.

It also encourages believers to test what they hear. Sermons, books, podcasts, and social media are full of teaching about God. Believers can listen eagerly while also checking what they hear against Scripture. Good teachers welcome this kind of examination.

Finally, the verse invites seekers to examine the evidence for themselves. Those who are curious about Christianity can read the Scriptures and consider whether the claims about Jesus are true. God honors honest seeking.

### *Acts 17:26–27* — He Is Not Far from Each One of Us

> *“He made from one blood every nation of men to dwell on all the surface of the earth, having determined appointed seasons and the boundaries of their dwellings, that they should seek the Lord, if perhaps they might reach out for him and find him, though he is not far from each one of us.”*
>
> — *Acts 17:26–27* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul was speaking to the philosophers of Athens at the Areopagus. He had begun by telling them about the unknown God, the Creator of the world who does not live in temples or need anything from human hands. Now he explained God’s relationship with all humanity.

“*He made from one blood every nation of men to dwell on all the surface of the earth*” (*v. 26*). All people come from one ancestor. The Athenians were proud of their heritage and considered themselves superior to other peoples, whom they called “barbarians.” Paul taught that all nations share a common origin. Every human being is part of one human family.

“*having determined appointed seasons and the boundaries of their dwellings*” (*v. 26*). God is sovereign over history and geography. He determines the times of nations and the places where they live. Nothing about human history is outside His control.

“*that they should seek the Lord, if perhaps they might reach out for him and find him*” (*v. 27*). God’s purpose in creating and guiding the nations is that people would seek Him. The phrase “reach out for him” pictures someone groping in the dark, trying to find something by touch. Without God’s full revelation, people search for Him, sensing that He exists but not knowing Him clearly.

“*though he is not far from each one of us*” (*v. 27*). God is not distant or uninterested, as the Epicureans believed. He is near to every person. He is not hiding. He wants to be found.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses teach the unity and dignity of all humanity. Every person is made by God and descended from a common ancestor. This truth rules out racism, ethnic pride, and contempt for other peoples. Every person, of every nation, bears the image of God (*Genesis 1:27*) and is precious to Him.

They also reveal God’s desire for relationship with all people. God shaped human history so that people would seek Him. Jeremiah records God’s promise, “*You shall seek me, and find me, when you search for me with all your heart*” (*Jeremiah 29:13*). God’s nearness is an invitation.

Finally, these verses show God’s sovereignty over the nations. The rise and fall of empires, the movements of peoples, and the boundaries of countries are all within His purposes. This gives believers confidence that history is not random.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses call believers to treat every person with dignity. Since all people come from one ancestor and are made by God, there is no place for prejudice or discrimination. Believers can actively love and respect people of every nation, ethnicity, and background.

They also encourage believers to recognize that people around them may be seeking God. Many people sense that there is something more, that God exists, even if they do not know Him. Believers can be attentive to these signs of seeking and gently point people to Jesus.

Finally, these verses offer comfort to those who feel far from God. God is not far from anyone. He is near, ready to be found. Anyone can reach out to Him, and He will respond.

### *Acts 17:30–31* — Now He Commands All People Everywhere to Repent

> *“The times of ignorance therefore God overlooked. But now he commands that all people everywhere should repent, because he has appointed a day in which he will judge the world in righteousness by the man whom he has ordained; of which he has given assurance to all men, in that he has raised him from the dead.”*
>
> — *Acts 17:30–31* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had been explaining to the philosophers of Athens who the true God is: the Creator who needs nothing, who made all nations, who is near to every person, and who cannot be represented by images of gold, silver, or stone. Now he came to the climax of his speech.

“*The times of ignorance therefore God overlooked*” (*v. 30*). In the past, the nations did not have the full revelation of God. They worshiped idols in ignorance. God was patient during these times, not bringing immediate judgment. This does not mean ignorance was innocent, but that God showed forbearance.

“*But now he commands that all people everywhere should repent*” (*v. 30*). Something has changed. Now that God has revealed Himself fully through Jesus, the time of patience has given way to a clear command. Everyone, everywhere, must repent: turn from idols and sin to the living God.

“*because he has appointed a day in which he will judge the world in righteousness by the man whom he has ordained*” (*v. 31*). There is a coming day of judgment. God will judge the world fairly and justly, through a specific Man whom He has appointed. Paul does not name Him here, but his listeners would soon understand that he meant Jesus.

“*of which he has given assurance to all men, in that he has raised him from the dead*” (*v. 31*). The proof that this Man is God’s appointed judge is that God raised Him from the dead. The resurrection is God’s public confirmation of who Jesus is.

At this point, some of the listeners began to mock. The idea of a dead man being raised seemed foolish to them. Others wanted to hear more.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that the gospel calls for a response. It is not merely interesting information to be discussed. It is a command from God to repent. Paul’s message in Athens, like Peter’s at Pentecost, ended with a call to turn to God.

They also show that judgment is real and coming. God is patient, but He will not overlook sin forever. Jesus, the One who died for sinners, is also the One who will judge the world. This gives urgency to the call to repent. Paul later wrote, “*For we must all be revealed before the judgment seat of Christ*” (*2 Corinthians 5:10*).

Finally, these verses show the central place of the resurrection. Paul pointed to the resurrection as God’s proof. The resurrection confirms that Jesus is who He claimed to be and that God’s promises are true. Paul later wrote that if Christ has not been raised, faith is useless (*1 Corinthians 15:14–17*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses remind believers that the gospel calls everyone to repentance. Believers can share this message with kindness and respect, as Paul did, while also being clear that God calls all people everywhere to turn to Him.

They also encourage believers to live in light of the coming judgment. Knowing that Jesus will judge the world motivates believers to live faithfully and to share the gospel with urgency and love.

Finally, these verses encourage believers to expect different responses. Some mocked, some wanted to hear more, and some believed. When believers share their faith, they will meet the same range of responses. They can continue faithfully, trusting God with the results.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Acts 17* shows how the gospel can turn the world upside down. The early believers had no political power, yet their message about King Jesus transformed lives and communities. Believers today can live out their faith in ways that make a real difference, honoring earthly authorities while giving their ultimate allegiance to Christ.

The chapter also shows the importance of Scripture. Paul reasoned from the Scriptures in Thessalonica, and the Bereans examined the Scriptures daily to test what they heard. Believers can study God’s word regularly, receive it eagerly, and use it to test every teaching.

*Acts 17* provides a model for sharing faith with people who do not know the Bible. In Athens, Paul began with what his listeners knew, their altar to an unknown God and their own poets, and led them to the truth about the Creator, the unity of humanity, and Jesus’ resurrection. Believers can learn to understand the people around them, find points of connection, and clearly present the gospel.

Finally, the chapter calls everyone to respond. God is near to every person and commands all people everywhere to repent, because He has appointed a day of judgment through Jesus, whom He raised from the dead. Believers can share this message with respect, urgency, and love, accepting that some will mock, some will want to hear more, and some will believe.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord God, Creator of heaven and earth, You do not live in temples made with hands, and You need nothing from me, yet You give me life and breath and everything. Thank You that You made every nation from one ancestor, and that You are not far from any of us. Forgive me for the idols in my own heart. Help me to see people of every background as You see them, and to treat them with dignity and love. Give me a noble heart like the Bereans, eager to receive Your word and diligent in searching the Scriptures. Teach me to speak about You wisely, finding points of connection with those who do not yet know You. Thank You that You raised Jesus from the dead and appointed Him as the Judge of the world. I repent and turn to You again. Make my faith turn the world upside down for Your glory. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Acts · Chapter 18 of 28

# Acts — Chapter 18

Chapter Theme: Faithful Work in Corinth and the Ministry of Priscilla and Aquila

[Read Acts 18 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/ACT18.htm)

Main Teaching

In Corinth, Paul works as a tentmaker alongside Aquila and Priscilla, Jewish believers recently expelled from Rome, while preaching every Sabbath. When the synagogue rejects him, he turns to the Gentiles, and many Corinthians believe. The Lord tells Paul in a vision not to be afraid, because He has many people in that city, and Paul stays a year and a half. The Roman proconsul Gallio refuses to hear the case against him. Paul travels to Ephesus, Jerusalem, and Antioch, beginning his third journey, and Priscilla and Aquila gently teach the gifted preacher Apollos the way of God more accurately.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Acts 18* describes Paul’s ministry in Corinth, one of the most important cities of the Roman world. Corinth was the capital of the province of Achaia (southern Greece). It sat on a narrow strip of land between two seas, with ports on each side, making it a wealthy center of trade and travel. It was famous for its commerce, its athletic games, and its temples, including a temple to Aphrodite, the goddess of love. The city had such a reputation for immorality that “to act like a Corinthian” became a Greek expression for living immorally.

Paul founded a church in Corinth that would cause him both great joy and great concern. His letters to the Corinthians (1 and 2 Corinthians) address many problems in the church, including divisions, immorality, lawsuits, and confusion about worship and the resurrection.

The chapter also includes a valuable historical marker. Gallio, the brother of the philosopher Seneca, was proconsul of Achaia around A.D. 51–52, according to an inscription found at Delphi. This helps date Paul’s time in Corinth.

### Paul Meets Aquila and Priscilla (*18:1–4*)

Paul left Athens and came to Corinth, about fifty miles away. There he met “*a certain Jew named Aquila, a man of Pontus by race, who had recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had commanded all the Jews to depart from Rome*” (*v. 2*). The Roman historian Suetonius records that Emperor Claudius expelled Jews from Rome because of disturbances “at the instigation of Chrestus,” which many scholars believe refers to conflicts over Christ in the Jewish community there. This expulsion took place around A.D. 49. Aquila and Priscilla may already have been believers when they arrived in Corinth.

Paul’s work with them is studied below. Every Sabbath, Paul reasoned in the synagogue, persuading both Jews and Greeks.

### Paul Turns to the Gentiles (*18:5–8*)

When Silas and Timothy arrived from Macedonia, probably bringing a financial gift from the churches there (*2 Corinthians 11:9*; *Philippians 4:15*), Paul devoted himself fully to preaching, “*testifying to the Jews that Jesus was the Christ*” (*v. 5*). When the synagogue opposed him and spoke abusively, Paul “*shook out his clothing*” (*v. 6*), a gesture of separation, and said, “*Your blood be on your own heads! I am clean. From now on, I will go to the Gentiles!*” (*v. 6*) These words echo *Ezekiel 33:1–9*, where God told the prophet that a watchman who warned the people faithfully was not responsible for those who ignored the warning.

Paul moved next door, to the house of “*a certain man named Justus, one who worshiped God*” (*v. 7*). Remarkably, “*Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believed in the Lord with all his house*” (*v. 8*). Paul mentions baptizing Crispus personally (*1 Corinthians 1:14*). “*Many of the Corinthians, when they heard, believed and were baptized*” (*v. 8*).

### The Lord’s Encouragement (*18:9–11*)

Paul received a vision from the Lord, studied below. “*He lived there a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them*” (*v. 11*). This was one of Paul’s longest stays in any city.

### Before Gallio (*18:12–17*)

When Gallio became proconsul, some Jewish leaders brought Paul before his judgment seat, accusing him: “*This man persuades men to worship God contrary to the law*” (*v. 13*). Before Paul could even defend himself, Gallio dismissed the case. He saw it as a dispute about “*questions about words and names and your own law*” (*v. 15*), not a crime under Roman law. “*So he drove them from the judgment seat*” (*v. 16*).

Gallio’s decision was significant. By treating the Christian movement as a matter within Judaism, which was a legally recognized religion in the Roman Empire, he gave the church a measure of legal protection for years to come.

Then the crowd seized Sosthenes, the new synagogue ruler, and beat him in front of the court. “*Gallio didn’t care about any of these things*” (*v. 17*). Interestingly, a Sosthenes is mentioned as a “brother” with Paul when he wrote 1 Corinthians (*1 Corinthians 1:1*). If this is the same man, then another synagogue ruler came to faith.

### Paul’s Return and New Journey (*18:18–23*)

After staying many more days, Paul sailed for Syria with Priscilla and Aquila. At Cenchreae, the eastern port of Corinth, “*He shaved his head in Cenchreae, for he had a vow*” (*v. 18*). This was probably a Nazirite-type vow, a Jewish practice of special dedication to God (*Numbers 6:1–21*). Paul, though free from the Law as a requirement for salvation, still sometimes practiced Jewish customs as expressions of devotion.

In Ephesus, Paul reasoned in the synagogue, and the people asked him to stay longer. He declined, with words studied below. He left Priscilla and Aquila in Ephesus and sailed to Caesarea, greeted the church (probably in Jerusalem), and went down to Antioch. This ended his second journey. After some time, he set out again, traveling through Galatia and Phrygia, “*establishing all the disciples*” (*v. 23*). This marks the beginning of his third journey.

### Apollos (*18:24–28*)

Meanwhile, a Jew named Apollos came to Ephesus. He was from Alexandria in Egypt, a great center of learning with a large Jewish community. He was “*an eloquent man*” (*v. 24*) and “*mighty in the Scriptures*” (*v. 24*). He had been instructed in the way of the Lord and “*being fervent in spirit, he spoke and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus, although he knew only the baptism of John*” (*v. 25*). Apollos knew about Jesus, perhaps from disciples of John the Baptist, but his understanding was incomplete. He may not have known about the full significance of Jesus’ death and resurrection, Christian baptism, or the gift of the Holy Spirit. How Priscilla and Aquila helped him is studied below.

Apollos then went to Achaia, with a letter of recommendation from the believers in Ephesus. There “*he greatly helped those who had believed through grace*” (*v. 27*), “*for he powerfully refuted the Jews, publicly showing by the Scriptures that Jesus was the Christ*” (*v. 28*). Apollos became an important teacher in Corinth. Paul later wrote, “*I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase*” (*1 Corinthians 3:6*).

## Important Verses Explained

### *Acts 18:3* — By Trade They Were Tentmakers

> *“and because he practiced the same trade, he lived with them and worked, for by trade they were tent makers.”*
>
> — *Acts 18:3* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

When Paul arrived in Corinth, he was alone. Silas and Timothy were still in Macedonia. He needed a place to stay and a way to support himself. He met Aquila and Priscilla, a Jewish couple who had recently arrived from Rome.

“*and because he practiced the same trade, he lived with them and worked, for by trade they were tent makers*” (*v. 3*). Paul shared their trade. The word translated “tent makers” may refer to making tents from goat-hair cloth or to working with leather more generally. Jewish rabbis were expected to learn a trade so that they would not need to profit from teaching the Law. Paul had learned this trade, perhaps in his hometown of Tarsus, which was known for a goat-hair cloth called cilicium.

Paul worked with his hands to support himself while he preached. In his letters, he often mentions this. He told the Thessalonians, “*For you remember, brothers, our labor and travail; for working night and day, that we might not burden any of you, we preached to you the Good News of God*” (*1 Thessalonians 2:9*). In Corinth, he refused to accept financial support from the church, so that no one could accuse him of preaching for money (*1 Corinthians 9:12–18*; *2 Corinthians 11:7–9*).

Paul did not consider manual labor beneath him or a distraction from ministry. His workshop became a place of relationships. Working side by side with Aquila and Priscilla, he formed a lifelong partnership. They became some of his most trusted co-workers. Paul later wrote that they “*risked their own necks*” (*Romans 16:4*) for his life.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows the dignity of ordinary work. In the Greek world, many educated people looked down on manual labor. Paul, a highly educated former Pharisee, worked with his hands without shame. Scripture teaches that work is part of God’s good design for humanity (*Genesis 2:15*). All honest work can be done for God’s glory.

It also shows the integration of work and ministry. Paul did not see his tentmaking as separate from his calling. His work supported his ministry, gave him credibility, and created relationships. Believers who work in ordinary jobs are not second-class servants of God. Their workplaces can be places of witness and service.

Finally, the verse shows the value of partnership. Aquila and Priscilla were not apostles, but they became key partners in Paul’s ministry. They hosted churches in their home (*1 Corinthians 16:19*; *Romans 16:5*) and taught others. God uses partnerships of believers with different gifts and roles.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to see their work as meaningful. Whether believers work in offices, factories, fields, homes, or shops, their work can honor God. Paul wrote, “*And whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord, and not for men*” (*Colossians 3:23*).

It also encourages believers to see their workplaces as places of ministry. Paul formed deep relationships through his work. Believers can build friendships, show integrity, and share their faith with coworkers.

Finally, the verse encourages believers to support ministry in different ways. Some are called to full-time ministry supported by others. Others, like Paul in Corinth, may support themselves while serving. Both are valuable. Believers can also follow Aquila and Priscilla’s example of offering their homes and skills to support God’s work.

### *Acts 18:9–10* — “*Don't Be Afraid, but Speak*” (*v. 9*)

> *“The Lord said to Paul in the night by a vision, ‘Don’t be afraid, but speak and don’t be silent; for I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, for I have many people in this city.’”*
>
> — *Acts 18:9–10* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul’s ministry in Corinth had faced opposition. The synagogue leaders had opposed him and spoken abusively, and he had moved his teaching next door. Paul had faced violent opposition in nearly every city on his journey: he had been beaten and imprisoned in Philippi, driven out of Thessalonica and Berea, and mocked in Athens. He later wrote that he came to Corinth “*in weakness, in fear, and in much trembling*” (*1 Corinthians 2:3*). Even great apostles feel fear.

Then “*The Lord said to Paul in the night by a vision, “Don’t be afraid, but speak and don’t be silent;*” (*v. 9*). The Lord knew Paul’s fear and spoke directly to it. He gave Paul three commands: do not be afraid, keep speaking, and do not be silent. The repetition emphasizes that Paul should continue his ministry boldly.

The Lord gave three reasons. First, “*for I am with you*” (*v. 10*). The presence of Jesus was Paul’s greatest security. This echoes Jesus’ promise at the Great Commission: “*I am with you always*” (*Matthew 28:20*).

Second, “*and no one will attack you to harm you*” (*v. 10*). God promised protection during this time in Corinth. Paul would face opposition, but he would not be harmed.

Third, “*for I have many people in this city*” (*v. 10*). God had people in Corinth who would believe. They had not yet heard or responded, but God already knew them and considered them His. Paul’s preaching would be the means by which they would come to faith.

Encouraged by this vision, Paul stayed in Corinth for a year and a half.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that God cares for His servants’ fears. Paul was a bold apostle, yet he needed encouragement. God did not rebuke him for being afraid; He reassured him. Throughout Scripture, God often says “Do not be afraid” to His people, from Abraham to Joshua to Mary.

They also show the connection between God’s sovereignty and human responsibility. God said, “I have many people in this city.” He already knew who would believe. Yet Paul still needed to speak. God’s sovereign plan does not make evangelism unnecessary; it makes evangelism hopeful. Because God has people everywhere, believers can share the gospel with confidence that it will bear fruit.

Finally, these verses show the importance of Christ’s presence. The greatest encouragement was not a promise of success but the promise “I am with you.” Christ’s presence gives courage in every situation.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers who feel afraid to share their faith. Fear is a common experience, even for mature believers. God’s word to Paul applies to them: do not be afraid, keep speaking, for I am with you.

They also give believers hope for their communities. God has people in every city, neighborhood, and workplace, people He is drawing to Himself. Believers can share the gospel with hope, knowing that God is at work.

Finally, these verses remind believers to seek encouragement from the Lord. When believers feel discouraged or afraid, they can turn to God in prayer and Scripture, listening for His reassurance. He knows their fears and meets them with His presence.

### *Acts 18:21* — “*If God Wills*” (*v. 21*)

> *“but taking his leave of them, he said, ‘I must by all means keep this coming feast in Jerusalem, but I will return again to you if God wills.’ Then he set sail from Ephesus.”*
>
> — *Acts 18:21* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After his long stay in Corinth, Paul sailed to Ephesus with Priscilla and Aquila. Ephesus was a major city in the province of Asia, the same region where the Holy Spirit had earlier prevented Paul from preaching (*16:6*). Now Paul went to the synagogue in Ephesus and reasoned with the Jews.

The response was positive: “*When they asked him to stay with them a longer time, he declined*” (*v. 20*). This was unusual. In many cities, the synagogue had rejected Paul. Here they wanted him to stay. Yet Paul felt he needed to move on.

“*but taking his leave of them, he said, “I must by all means keep this coming feast in Jerusalem, but I will return again to you if God wills.”*” (*v. 21*) Some manuscripts mention the feast in Jerusalem; others do not. Either way, Paul felt he needed to go. But he promised to return “*if God wills*” (*v. 21*).

Paul made plans, but he held them humbly, recognizing that God’s will was greater than his own. He did return to Ephesus on his next journey and stayed for nearly three years (*19:1–10*; *20:31*). God did will it.

Paul often used this kind of language. He wrote to the Corinthians, “*But I will come to you shortly, if the Lord is willing*” (*1 Corinthians 4:19*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows the right attitude toward planning. Believers can and should make plans, but they hold them in submission to God’s will. James writes, “*For you ought to say, “If the Lord wills, we will both live, and do this or that.”*” (*James 4:15*) This is not a magic formula but a heartfelt recognition that God is sovereign over the future.

It also shows that God’s timing is often different from human timing. Earlier, the Spirit prevented Paul from going to Asia. Now an open door was there, but Paul could not stay. Later, God brought him back for an extended ministry. God’s timing was perfect.

Finally, the verse shows the humility of a great leader. Paul did not presume that his plans would succeed. He trusted God to direct his steps.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to make plans with humility. Believers can set goals and make decisions while acknowledging that God’s will may be different. This attitude brings peace, since believers do not have to control the future.

It also helps believers handle disappointment. When plans fall through, believers can trust that God’s will is good, even when they do not understand it.

Finally, the verse invites believers to pray about their plans. Before making major decisions, believers can seek God’s guidance and commit their plans to Him. Proverbs says, “*Commit your deeds to the LORD, and your plans shall succeed*” (*Proverbs 16:3*).

### *Acts 18:26* — Explaining the Way of God More Accurately

> *“He began to speak boldly in the synagogue. But when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside, and explained to him the way of God more accurately.”*
>
> — *Acts 18:26* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Apollos was a gifted Jewish teacher from Alexandria who came to Ephesus. He was eloquent, deeply knowledgeable in the Scriptures, and passionate. He taught accurately about Jesus, but his understanding was incomplete; he knew only the baptism of John. He may not have fully understood Jesus’ death and resurrection, Christian baptism, or the coming of the Holy Spirit.

“*He began to speak boldly in the synagogue*” (*v. 26*). Apollos was courageous and enthusiastic. He preached what he knew with conviction.

“*But when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside, and explained to him the way of God more accurately*” (*v. 26*). Priscilla and Aquila, the tentmakers who had worked with Paul in Corinth, heard Apollos preach. They recognized both his gifts and the gaps in his understanding.

Notice how they responded. They did not criticize him publicly or interrupt his preaching. They “took him aside,” speaking with him privately, possibly inviting him into their home. They “explained to him the way of God more accurately.” They filled in what he lacked, with gentleness and respect.

Notice also that Priscilla is named first here, as she often is in the New Testament. This may suggest that she was especially prominent in this teaching ministry. Both husband and wife taught Apollos together.

Apollos received their instruction humbly. A gifted, eloquent preacher was willing to learn from two tentmakers. Afterward, he became an even more effective minister, helping the believers in Achaia greatly.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows the importance of sound teaching. Apollos was gifted and sincere, but his understanding needed to be completed. Even passionate believers need to grow in their knowledge of God’s truth. Paul writes that God gives teachers to the church “*until we all attain to the unity of the faith, and of the knowledge of the Son of God*” (*Ephesians 4:13*).

It also shows a gracious way of correcting others. Priscilla and Aquila did not shame Apollos. They spoke privately, explained carefully, and built him up. Paul later wrote that believers should restore those who need correction “*in a spirit of gentleness*” (*Galatians 6:1*).

Finally, the verse shows that God uses ordinary believers, both men and women, to teach and strengthen others. Priscilla and Aquila were not apostles or official leaders in the usual sense, but they played a key role in the growth of the early church. Their home became a place where believers were taught and encouraged.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to help others grow in their understanding of God’s word. When believers see someone who sincerely loves God but has gaps in their understanding, they can come alongside them privately and gently, sharing what they know.

It also encourages believers to remain teachable. Apollos was gifted and knowledgeable, yet he was willing to learn. No believer ever outgrows the need to learn. Believers can welcome correction and instruction from others, even those who seem less impressive.

Finally, the verse encourages believers to use their homes for ministry. Priscilla and Aquila’s home became a place of teaching and hospitality. Believers can open their homes for Bible study, mentoring, and encouragement.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Acts 18* shows that ordinary work matters to God. Paul worked as a tentmaker alongside Aquila and Priscilla while preaching the gospel. Believers today can see their work as meaningful, doing it for God’s glory and using their workplaces as places to build relationships and share their faith.

The chapter also offers encouragement for those who are afraid. Paul came to Corinth in weakness and fear, and the Lord told him not to be afraid but to keep speaking, because He was with him and had many people in that city. Believers can take courage from Christ’s presence and share their faith with hope, knowing that God is at work in their communities.

*Acts 18* teaches humility in planning. Paul made plans but held them loosely, saying, “If God wills.” Believers can make plans while trusting God’s sovereignty and accepting His timing.

Finally, the chapter shows the value of gentle, private instruction. Priscilla and Aquila took Apollos aside and explained the way of God more accurately, and he became an even more effective minister. Believers can help one another grow, offering correction with gentleness and receiving it with humility, and they can use their homes as places of teaching and fellowship.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for the dignity of work. Help me to do my work wholeheartedly for You and to use my workplace as a place to love and serve others. When I am afraid, speak to me as You spoke to Paul: “*Don’t be afraid, but speak and don’t be silent*”; “*for I am with you*”. Thank You that You have people in my city whom You are drawing to Yourself; make me faithful to share Your word with them. Teach me to make plans humbly, always saying, “If God wills.” Give me the wisdom and gentleness of Priscilla and Aquila to help others grow in their understanding of You, and give me a teachable heart like Apollos, always ready to learn. Use my home and my life for Your kingdom. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Acts · Chapter 19 of 28

# Acts — Chapter 19

Chapter Theme: The Word of the Lord Grows Mighty in Ephesus

[Read Acts 19 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/ACT19.htm)

Main Teaching

In Ephesus, Paul meets about twelve disciples who knew only John’s baptism; he explains that John pointed to Jesus, and they are baptized in Jesus’ name and receive the Holy Spirit. Paul teaches for over two years, so that the whole province of Asia hears the word, and God works extraordinary miracles. When seven sons of Sceva try to use Jesus’ name like a magic spell, an evil spirit overpowers them, and fear spreads through the city. Many believers confess their practices and burn their valuable magic books. A silversmith named Demetrius, alarmed at losing business from shrines of Artemis, stirs up a city-wide riot, until the town clerk calms the crowd.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Acts 19* describes Paul’s ministry in Ephesus, the longest he stayed in any city during his missionary journeys, nearly three years (*20:31*). Ephesus was the capital of the Roman province of Asia and one of the largest cities in the empire, with perhaps 250,000 people. It was a major port and commercial center.

Ephesus was famous for the Temple of Artemis (called Diana by the Romans), one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. It was four times the size of the Parthenon in Athens. The Artemis of Ephesus was a fertility goddess, and her worship drew pilgrims from across the region. The city was also known as a center of magic and the occult. “Ephesian letters” were magical formulas sold as charms.

Paul’s ministry in Ephesus shows the gospel confronting this world of idolatry and magic, and the power of Jesus’ name overcoming spiritual darkness. Paul later wrote his letter to the Ephesians, and the church in Ephesus is addressed in *Revelation 2:1–7*.

### Disciples Who Knew Only John’s Baptism (*19:1–7*)

Paul arrived in Ephesus and found about twelve disciples. He asked them a question, and their conversation is studied below. When Paul laid his hands on them, “*the Holy Spirit came on them and they spoke with other languages and prophesied*” (*v. 6*). This experience recalls Pentecost (*Acts 2*), Samaria (*Acts 8*), and Cornelius’s household (*Acts 10*). In each case, a new group of people was clearly welcomed into the church through the gift of the Spirit.

### Two Years of Teaching (*19:8–10*)

As usual, Paul began in the synagogue, where “*he entered into the synagogue and spoke boldly for a period of three months, reasoning and persuading about the things concerning God’s Kingdom*” (*v. 8*). But when some became stubborn and spoke evil of the Way publicly, Paul withdrew with the disciples and taught daily in “*the school of Tyrannus*” (*v. 9*), probably a lecture hall rented out at certain hours. One early manuscript adds that Paul taught there from about eleven in the morning to four in the afternoon, the hottest part of the day when most people rested.

“*This continued for two years, so that all those who lived in Asia heard the word of the Lord Jesus, both Jews and Greeks*” (*v. 10*). People from all over the province came to Ephesus for business, and many heard the gospel. Paul’s co-workers also traveled to nearby cities. Churches were founded in places like Colossae, Laodicea, and Hierapolis (*Colossians 1:7*; *4:13*), probably during this time. The seven churches of Asia addressed in *Revelation 2–3* may have their roots in this period.

### Extraordinary Miracles (*19:11–12*)

“*God worked special miracles by the hands of Paul*” (*v. 11*). Notice that it was God who worked the miracles. Even “*handkerchiefs or aprons were carried away from his body to the sick, and the diseases departed from them, and the evil spirits went out*” (*v. 12*). These were probably the sweat cloths and work aprons Paul used as a tentmaker. Luke describes these miracles as “special” or “extraordinary.” They were not the usual pattern even in Paul’s ministry. In a city obsessed with magic, God demonstrated His power in a way that showed that Jesus is greater than any sorcery. (Compare the woman healed by touching the edge of Jesus’ garment in *Luke 8:44*, and the people healed by Peter’s shadow in *Acts 5:15*.)

### The Sons of Sceva (*19:13–17*)

Some traveling Jewish exorcists tried to use the name of Jesus as a magic formula. This incident is studied below.

### Burning the Magic Books (*19:18–20*)

The incident with the sons of Sceva led to deep repentance among believers, studied below.

### Paul’s Plans (*19:21–22*)

“*Paul determined in the Spirit, when he had passed through Macedonia and Achaia, to go to Jerusalem, saying, “After I have been there, I must also see Rome.”*” (*v. 21*) This is a turning point in Acts. From here on, Paul’s journey moves toward Jerusalem and ultimately Rome, the capital of the empire. The word “must” suggests a divine necessity. Paul sent Timothy and Erastus ahead to Macedonia while he stayed in Asia a little longer.

### The Riot in Ephesus (*19:23–41*)

“*About that time there arose no small disturbance concerning the Way*” (*v. 23*). A silversmith named Demetrius made silver shrines of Artemis, small models of the temple or the goddess that pilgrims bought as souvenirs or for worship. His concerns are studied below.

The craftsmen were enraged and began shouting, “*Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!*” (*v. 28*) The city filled with confusion. The crowd rushed into the great theater of Ephesus, which could hold about 25,000 people and whose ruins can still be seen today. They dragged Gaius and Aristarchus, Paul’s traveling companions from Macedonia, with them.

Paul wanted to go into the theater to address the crowd, but the disciples would not let him. Even some of the “*Asiarchs*” (*v. 31*), wealthy officials of the province who were his friends, sent word urging him not to go. That Paul had friends among the province’s leading citizens shows how widely his influence had spread.

“*Some therefore cried one thing, and some another, for the assembly was in confusion. Most of them didn’t know why they had come together*” (*v. 32*). Luke paints a picture of mob mentality. Some Jews pushed forward a man named Alexander, perhaps to explain that the Jews were not responsible for Paul’s teaching. But when the crowd realized he was a Jew, they shouted for about two hours, “*Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!*” (*v. 34*)

Finally, the town clerk, the chief civic official, calmed the crowd. He reminded them that Ephesus was the guardian of Artemis’s temple and of the image “*which fell down from Zeus*” (*v. 35*) (probably a meteorite believed to be sacred). Since no one could deny this, they should not act rashly. Paul’s companions were “*neither robbers of temples nor blasphemers of your goddess*” (*v. 37*). Paul had not insulted Artemis; he had simply preached the truth about the living God. If Demetrius had a complaint, the courts were open. The town clerk warned that the city could be accused of rioting by the Roman authorities. Then he dismissed the assembly.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Acts 19:4–5* — John Pointed to Jesus

> *“Paul said, ‘John indeed baptized with the baptism of repentance, saying to the people that they should believe in the one who would come after him, that is, in Christ Jesus.’ When they heard this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus.”*
>
> — *Acts 19:4–5* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

When Paul arrived in Ephesus, he met about twelve disciples. Something about them seemed incomplete, so he asked, “*Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?*” (*v. 2*) They answered, “*No, we haven’t even heard that there is a Holy Spirit*” (*v. 2*). They probably meant that they had not heard that the Holy Spirit had been given, since John the Baptist had spoken of the coming Spirit (*Luke 3:16*).

Paul asked, “*Into what then were you baptized?*” (*v. 3*) They said, “*Into John’s baptism*” (*v. 3*). These were disciples of John the Baptist, or people who had been taught by his followers, perhaps like Apollos before Priscilla and Aquila instructed him (*18:25*). They had repented and prepared for the Messiah, but they had not yet heard the full message about Jesus.

Paul explained: “*John indeed baptized with the baptism of repentance, saying to the people that they should believe in the one who would come after him, that is, in Christ Jesus*” (*v. 4*). John’s baptism was a baptism of repentance, preparing people for the coming Messiah. But John always pointed beyond himself. He told people to believe in the One coming after him. That One was Jesus.

“*When they heard this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus*” (*v. 5*). When they understood that Jesus was the One John had pointed to, they believed and were baptized in His name. This is the only place in the New Testament where people are recorded as being rebaptized. They had received John’s baptism, which looked forward to Jesus; now they received Christian baptism, which identified them with Jesus who had come.

Then Paul laid his hands on them, and the Holy Spirit came on them.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that John the Baptist’s ministry was always meant to lead to Jesus. John said, “*He must increase, but I must decrease*” (*John 3:30*). Repentance prepares the way, but faith in Jesus is the goal.

They also show the importance of a complete understanding of the gospel. These disciples were sincere, but their faith was incomplete. They needed to hear about Jesus, His death and resurrection, and the gift of the Spirit. Paul did not dismiss them; he patiently explained and led them into the fullness of faith.

Finally, these verses show the close connection between faith in Jesus, baptism in His name, and the gift of the Holy Spirit. These belong together in the Christian life. While Christians have different views about the exact timing and relationship of these elements, as discussed at *Acts 8:14–17*, all agree that every believer is meant to know Jesus, be baptized into Him, and live by His Spirit.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to make sure their faith is centered on Jesus. Some people have a religious background or a sincere desire to be good, but have not yet come to know Jesus personally. Believers can gently help them, as Paul did, to see that all true faith points to Christ.

They also encourage believers to seek the fullness of the Christian life. The Holy Spirit is given to all who believe in Jesus. Believers can depend on the Spirit, ask for His filling, and grow in His fruit.

Finally, these verses model patient, respectful teaching. Paul did not criticize the Ephesian disciples for what they lacked. He asked questions, listened, and explained. Believers can follow this approach when helping others grow in their understanding.

### *Acts 19:15* — “*Jesus I Know, and Paul I Know, but Who Are You?*” (*v. 15*)

> *“The evil spirit answered, ‘Jesus I know, and Paul I know, but who are you?’”*
>
> — *Acts 19:15* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

God was working extraordinary miracles through Paul in Ephesus. Even cloths that had touched Paul were taken to the sick, and they were healed and evil spirits left them. Ephesus was a city full of magic and exorcists, and some people noticed Paul’s power and wanted to copy it.

“*But some of the itinerant Jews, exorcists, took on themselves to invoke over those who had the evil spirits the name of the Lord Jesus, saying, “We adjure you by Jesus whom Paul preaches.”*” (*v. 13*) These traveling exorcists did not know Jesus personally. They treated His name like a magic formula, a word of power that would work if spoken correctly. Notice their words: “Jesus whom Paul preaches.” They did not know Jesus for themselves; they only knew about Him through Paul.

Among them were “*seven sons of one Sceva, a Jewish chief priest*” (*v. 14*). Sceva is not known from other sources; he may have been from a priestly family, or he may have claimed the title to impress people.

“*The evil spirit answered, “Jesus I know, and Paul I know, but who are you?”*” (*v. 15*) The evil spirit recognized Jesus’ authority and knew Paul as His servant. But it did not recognize these men. They had no relationship with Jesus and therefore no authority from Him.

The man with the evil spirit then attacked them, overpowered all seven, and beat them so badly that they ran out of the house naked and wounded.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that the power of Jesus’ name is not magic. The name of Jesus represents His person and authority. It cannot be used as a formula by those who do not know Him. Jesus warned that on the day of judgment many will say, “*Lord, Lord, didn’t we prophesy in your name, in your name cast out demons, and in your name do many mighty works?*” (*Matthew 7:22*) and He will say, “*I never knew you*” (*Matthew 7:23*).

It also shows that spiritual authority comes from relationship with Jesus. Paul had authority because he belonged to Jesus and served Him. The sons of Sceva had no such relationship. Believers have authority in Jesus’ name because they are united to Him by faith.

Finally, the verse shows the reality of spiritual forces. The evil spirit recognized Jesus and Paul. Scripture teaches that there is a real spiritual battle (*Ephesians 6:12*), and the forces of darkness must submit to Jesus’ authority, but only Jesus and those who truly belong to Him have power over them.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse warns against treating faith as a formula. Some people use Jesus’ name or religious practices as if they were magic, hoping to get results without a genuine relationship with Him. Prayer, worship, and the name of Jesus are not tools to manipulate God. They are expressions of trust in the One we know.

It also invites believers to examine whether they know Jesus personally or only know about Him. The sons of Sceva knew about “Jesus whom Paul preaches,” but they did not know Him. Believers can ask whether their faith is secondhand, based only on what others say, or whether they have a living relationship with Christ.

Finally, the verse gives believers confidence. Believers who truly belong to Jesus have nothing to fear from evil powers. Jesus has defeated them, and His people are under His protection.

### *Acts 19:18–20* — Burning the Books of Magic

> *“Many also of those who had believed came, confessing and declaring their deeds. Many of those who practiced magical arts brought their books together and burned them in the sight of all. They counted their price, and found it to be fifty thousand pieces of silver. So the word of the Lord was growing and becoming mighty.”*
>
> — *Acts 19:18–20* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The story of the sons of Sceva spread throughout Ephesus. “*Fear fell on them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was magnified*” (*v. 17*). People realized that the name of Jesus was not something to be used lightly. It was holy and powerful.

This led to a powerful response among believers: “*Many also of those who had believed came, confessing and declaring their deeds*” (*v. 18*). These were people who had already believed in Jesus, but had continued in some of their old practices, including magic. Now they came forward publicly, confessing what they had done.

“*Many of those who practiced magical arts brought their books together and burned them in the sight of all*” (*v. 19*). Ephesus was famous for its books of spells and charms. These new believers did not sell their magic books or hide them; they burned them publicly, making a clean break from their old way of life.

“*They counted their price, and found it to be fifty thousand pieces of silver*” (*v. 19*). A silver coin (a drachma) was about a day’s wage for a laborer. Fifty thousand days’ wages represented an enormous sum. These believers were willing to destroy something very valuable because they recognized it was incompatible with following Jesus.

“*So the word of the Lord was growing and becoming mighty*” (*v. 20*). The result was that the gospel spread even more powerfully. Genuine repentance strengthened the church’s witness.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that true faith leads to repentance from sin, including secret practices. These believers had believed in Jesus but had not fully left their old ways. When they saw the holiness of Jesus’ name, they brought their hidden practices into the light. John writes, “*If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness*” (*1 John 1:9*).

They also show that following Jesus may involve costly decisions. The believers burned books worth a fortune. Jesus taught that following Him means being willing to give up anything that stands in the way (*Mark 9:43–47*). Some things must be destroyed, not merely set aside.

Finally, these verses show that repentance strengthens the church’s witness. When believers turned decisively from sin, the word of the Lord grew mightily. A church that takes holiness seriously is a powerful testimony to the world.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to bring hidden sins into the light. Many believers have areas of their lives they keep secret, such as habits, practices, or attitudes that do not honor God. Confession to God, and where appropriate to trusted believers, brings freedom and healing (*James 5:16*).

They also challenge believers to make clean breaks with sin. It is not enough to reduce or hide sinful practices. Believers may need to remove things from their lives completely, such as certain media, habits, relationships, or possessions that draw them away from God. This may be costly, but freedom is worth it.

Finally, these verses encourage believers to take spiritual matters seriously. Involvement in the occult, such as fortune-telling, spells, or séances, is incompatible with following Jesus (*Deuteronomy 18:10–12*). Believers who have been involved in such practices can renounce them and trust in the power of Christ.

### *Acts 19:26–27* — When the Gospel Threatens Profits

> *“You see and hear that not at Ephesus alone, but almost throughout all Asia, this Paul has persuaded and turned away many people, saying that they are no gods that are made with hands. Not only is there danger that this our trade come into disrepute, but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis will be counted as nothing and her majesty destroyed, whom all Asia and the world worships.”*
>
> — *Acts 19:26–27* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul’s ministry in Ephesus had been so successful that it began to affect the city’s economy. A silversmith named Demetrius made silver models of the temple of Artemis, which he sold to worshipers and pilgrims. His business, and the business of many other craftsmen, depended on the worship of Artemis.

Demetrius called a meeting of the craftsmen and said, “*Sirs, you know that by this business we have our wealth*” (*v. 25*). He went straight to the issue: money.

“*You see and hear that not at Ephesus alone, but almost throughout all Asia, this Paul has persuaded and turned away many people, saying that they are no gods that are made with hands*” (*v. 26*). Paul had taught that idols made by human hands are not gods. As people turned to the living God, they stopped buying silver shrines. Demetrius’s words are a remarkable testimony to the spread of the gospel throughout the region.

“*Not only is there danger that this our trade come into disrepute, but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis will be counted as nothing and her majesty destroyed, whom all Asia and the world worships*” (*v. 27*). Demetrius combined economic concerns with religious and civic pride. He presented the threat to his business as a threat to the goddess and to the city’s honor.

His speech worked. The craftsmen were enraged and shouted, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” Soon the whole city was in an uproar.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that the gospel can threaten economic systems built on sin or idolatry. When people turn to Christ, their spending, priorities, and values change. Businesses that profit from things contrary to God’s ways may lose income. This happened in Philippi too, where the owners of the slave girl lost their profits (*16:19*).

They also show how financial interests can disguise themselves as religious or civic concerns. Demetrius’s real concern was money, but he framed it as devotion to Artemis and pride in the city. People often justify opposing what is right by appealing to tradition, identity, or patriotism when their real motive is self-interest.

Finally, these verses show that the gospel calls into question every idol. Paul taught that gods made with hands are not gods at all. This message challenged not only religious practices but the whole way of life built around them. Paul later wrote that believers had “*turned to God from idols, to serve a living and true God*” (*1 Thessalonians 1:9*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses invite believers to consider how their faith shapes their economic lives. Following Jesus may mean changing how believers earn, spend, and invest money, avoiding businesses or practices that profit from harm to others.

They also encourage believers to recognize when opposition to the gospel is driven by self-interest. Sometimes people oppose Christian values because those values threaten their profits or comfort. Believers can respond with wisdom and integrity, continuing to do what is right.

Finally, these verses challenge believers to identify the idols of their own culture. Modern idols may not be silver shrines, but they can include wealth, success, pleasure, or status. The gospel calls believers to turn from every idol to serve the living and true God.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Acts 19* shows the power of the gospel in a city full of idolatry and magic. Through Paul’s patient teaching over two years, the word of the Lord spread throughout the province of Asia. Believers today can trust that faithful, consistent teaching and witness bear fruit, even in places that seem resistant.

The chapter also shows that the name of Jesus is not a magic formula. The sons of Sceva tried to use Jesus’ name without knowing Him, and they were overpowered. Believers are called to know Jesus personally, not merely to know about Him. Their authority comes from belonging to Him.

*Acts 19* calls believers to genuine repentance. When believers in Ephesus saw the holiness of Jesus’ name, they confessed their practices and burned their costly books of magic. Believers today can bring hidden sins into the light, make clean breaks with anything that draws them away from God, and experience the freedom that comes through confession and forgiveness.

Finally, the chapter shows that the gospel can challenge economic and cultural systems. Demetrius saw his profits threatened as people turned from idols to the living God. Believers can let their faith shape how they use money and how they engage with their culture, recognizing and turning from the idols of their own time, while trusting that God’s word will continue to grow and prevail.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You that John the Baptist pointed to You, and that all true faith leads to You. Thank You for the gift of Your Holy Spirit. Help me to know You personally, not only to know about You, and keep me from treating Your name or Your ways as a formula. Your name is holy and powerful. Bring into the light any hidden sin in my life, and give me courage to confess it and to make a clean break, whatever it costs. Show me the idols of my own heart and culture, and help me to turn from them to serve You, the living and true God. Let my use of money and possessions reflect my faith in You. Let Your word grow and become mighty in my life, my church, and my city. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
