Acts · Chapter 20 of 28

# Acts — Chapter 20

Chapter Theme: Finishing the Race: Paul’s Farewell to the Ephesian Elders

[Read Acts 20 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/ACT20.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul travels through Macedonia and Greece, then meets the believers at Troas on the first day of the week, where he talks until midnight and raises a young man named Eutychus who falls from a window. Hurrying toward Jerusalem, he calls the elders of Ephesus to Miletus and gives a moving farewell. He reminds them of his humble, tearful, and faithful ministry, declares that he counts his life as nothing compared to finishing his race and testifying to God’s grace, charges them to shepherd the church Christ purchased with His blood, warns of wolves to come, and commends them to God and the word of His grace. They kneel, pray, and weep together as he departs.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Acts 20* marks the end of Paul’s third missionary journey and the beginning of his final journey to Jerusalem, which will lead to his arrest and eventually to Rome. During the months described briefly at the beginning of this chapter, Paul was collecting a financial gift from the Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem (*Romans 15:25–28*; *1 Corinthians 16:1–4*; *2 Corinthians 8–9*). The men listed in *Acts 20:4* were probably representatives of the churches who traveled with Paul to deliver the gift. During his three months in Greece, probably in Corinth, Paul likely wrote his letter to the Romans.

The heart of this chapter is Paul’s speech to the Ephesian elders at Miletus. It is the only speech in Acts addressed to Christian leaders, and it reveals Paul’s heart as a pastor. Many of its themes echo his letters, especially his letters to Timothy, who was later a leader in Ephesus.

### Journeys in Macedonia and Greece (*20:1–6*)

After the riot in Ephesus, Paul encouraged the disciples and left for Macedonia, where he strengthened the churches with many words. He then spent three months in Greece. When he learned of a plot against him as he was about to sail for Syria, he changed his route and traveled back through Macedonia.

He was accompanied by a group of men from different churches: Sopater from Berea, Aristarchus and Secundus from Thessalonica, Gaius from Derbe, Timothy, and Tychicus and Trophimus from Asia. The “we” passages resume in verse 5, indicating that Luke rejoined Paul at Philippi. They sailed from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread and joined the others at Troas.

### Eutychus Raised at Troas (*20:7–12*)

The gathering at Troas is studied below. During it, a young man named Eutychus, whose name means “fortunate,” was sitting in a window. “*As Paul spoke still longer, being weighed down by his sleep, he fell down from the third floor and was taken up dead*” (*v. 9*). Luke the physician says plainly that he was “taken up dead.” The many oil lamps in the upper room may have made the room warm and stuffy, adding to his drowsiness.

“*Paul went down and fell upon him, and embracing him said, “Don’t be troubled, for his life is in him.”*” (*v. 10*) Paul’s action recalls Elijah and Elisha, who stretched themselves over dead children and brought them back to life (*1 Kings 17:21*; *2 Kings 4:34*). Paul then went back upstairs, broke bread, ate, and kept talking until dawn. “*They brought the boy in alive, and were greatly comforted*” (*v. 12*).

### Journey to Miletus (*20:13–16*)

Paul’s companions sailed ahead to Assos, while Paul walked there by land, about twenty miles, perhaps wanting time alone to pray. Then they sailed together along the coast. Paul decided to sail past Ephesus, because “*he was hastening, if it were possible for him, to be in Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost*” (*v. 16*). A visit to Ephesus would have involved many people and delays.

### Paul’s Farewell Speech (*20:17–35*)

From Miletus, about thirty miles south of Ephesus, Paul sent for the elders of the Ephesian church. When they arrived, he spoke to them from his heart.

He reminded them of his conduct among them: “*serving the Lord with all humility, with many tears, and with trials which happened to me by the plots of the Jews*” (*v. 19*). He had not held back anything helpful: “*teaching you publicly and from house to house*” (*v. 20*). His message to everyone, Jews and Greeks, was “*repentance toward God and faith toward our Lord Jesus*” (*v. 21*).

Then he spoke of the future: “*Now, behold, I go bound by the Spirit to Jerusalem, not knowing what will happen to me there*” (*v. 22*), except that the Spirit warned him in every city that imprisonment and hardships awaited him. His attitude toward this is studied below.

He told them they would never see him again. He declared, “*I am clean from the blood of all men*” (*v. 26*), “*for I didn’t shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God*” (*v. 27*). Like the watchman in *Ezekiel 33*, Paul had faithfully warned and taught them. He had declared not only the parts of God’s message that were popular, but all of it.

His charge to the elders is studied below. He warned them, “*For I know that after my departure, vicious wolves will enter in among you, not sparing the flock*” (*v. 29*). “*Men will arise from among your own selves, speaking perverse things, to draw away the disciples after them*” (*v. 30*). False teachers would come from outside and arise from within. Paul’s later letters to Timothy show that this warning came true (*1 Timothy 1:3–7*; *2 Timothy 2:17–18*). He reminded them that for three years he had warned each of them “*night and day with tears*” (*v. 31*).

“*Now, brothers, I entrust you to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to build up and to give you the inheritance among all those who are sanctified*” (*v. 32*). Paul could not stay with them, but he left them in the best hands: God’s, and the word of His grace. Scripture would build them up and lead them to their eternal inheritance.

Paul concluded by reminding them of his example of hard work and generosity, studied below.

### A Tearful Farewell (*20:36–38*)

“*When he had spoken these things, he knelt down and prayed with them all*” (*v. 36*). “*They all wept freely, and fell on Paul’s neck and kissed him*” (*v. 37*), grieving most of all at his words that they would never see his face again. Then they accompanied him to the ship. The scene shows the deep love between Paul and the believers he had served. Ministry, for Paul, was not a job but a bond of love.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Acts 20:7* — Gathered on the First Day of the Week to Break Bread

> *“On the first day of the week, when the disciples were gathered together to break bread, Paul talked with them, intending to depart on the next day; and continued his speech until midnight.”*
>
> — *Acts 20:7* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul and his companions had arrived in Troas, a port city on the northwest coast of Asia Minor. They stayed there for seven days. On their last full day, the believers gathered together.

“*On the first day of the week, when the disciples were gathered together to break bread*” (*v. 7*). The “first day of the week” is Sunday, the day Jesus rose from the dead (*Luke 24:1*). This verse is one of the earliest pieces of evidence that Christians gathered for worship on Sunday. Paul also told the Corinthians to set aside money for the Jerusalem collection “*On the first day of every week*” (*1 Corinthians 16:2*), and John refers to “*the Lord's day*” (*Revelation 1:10*).

The purpose of their gathering was “to break bread.” This likely refers to the Lord’s Supper, possibly shared as part of a fellowship meal. Since *Acts 2:42*, breaking bread had been a central part of Christian gatherings.

Jewish days began at sunset, but Roman days began at midnight. Luke may be using either reckoning. Many believers worked during the day, since Sunday was not a day off in the Roman world, so they may have gathered in the evening after work.

“*Paul talked with them, intending to depart on the next day; and continued his speech until midnight*” (*v. 7*). Paul knew this was his last time with these believers, so he taught them for a long time. The believers were eager to listen. Even after Eutychus fell and was raised, Paul continued talking until dawn.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that Sunday became the day of Christian worship because of the resurrection. Jewish believers continued to honor the Sabbath, but the first day of the week, the day of Jesus’ resurrection, became the special day when believers gathered. It celebrated the beginning of the new creation.

It also shows the central place of the Lord’s Supper and teaching in Christian worship. The believers gathered to break bread, and Paul taught them. Word and sacrament, teaching and the Lord’s Supper, have been at the heart of Christian worship from the beginning.

Finally, the verse shows the eagerness of the early believers. They gathered after a day’s work and listened late into the night. Their hunger for God’s word and for fellowship is an example for believers in every generation.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to gather regularly for worship. Hebrews urges believers not to give up meeting together (*Hebrews 10:25*). Sunday worship connects believers with the resurrection of Jesus and with Christians throughout history.

It also encourages believers to value the Lord’s Supper and the teaching of God’s word. These are not empty rituals but means by which believers remember Christ, grow in faith, and share fellowship.

Finally, the verse invites believers to consider their own hunger for God. The believers at Troas listened until midnight and beyond. Believers can ask God to deepen their desire for His word and for fellowship with His people.

### *Acts 20:24* — That I May Finish My Race with Joy

> *“But these things don’t count; nor do I hold my life dear to myself, so that I may finish my race with joy, and the ministry which I received from the Lord Jesus, to fully testify to the Good News of the grace of God.”*
>
> — *Acts 20:24* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul was speaking to the elders of the church in Ephesus at Miletus. He told them he was going to Jerusalem, “*bound by the Spirit*” (*v. 22*), without knowing exactly what would happen there. But he did know one thing: “*the Holy Spirit testifies in every city, saying that bonds and afflictions wait for me*” (*v. 23*). In city after city, prophets and believers warned him that he would be arrested and suffer.

How did Paul respond? “*But these things don’t count; nor do I hold my life dear to myself*” (*v. 24*). Paul did not consider his own life, safety, or comfort to be the most important thing. He did not cling to his life. He had a greater goal.

“*so that I may finish my race with joy*” (*v. 24*). Paul often compared the Christian life to a race (*1 Corinthians 9:24–27*; *Philippians 3:13–14*). His goal was not to avoid suffering but to finish his race faithfully. And he wanted to finish it “with joy,” not with regret.

“*and the ministry which I received from the Lord Jesus, to fully testify to the Good News of the grace of God*” (*v. 24*). Paul’s ministry was given to him by Jesus. His task was to testify to “the Good News of the grace of God,” the message that God freely forgives and saves sinners through Jesus. This was Paul’s life purpose.

Years later, near the end of his life, Paul wrote to Timothy, “*I have fought the good fight. I have finished the course. I have kept the faith*” (*2 Timothy 4:7*). He did finish his race.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals the heart of a disciple whose life is fully surrendered to Christ. Paul did not value his life above his calling. Jesus taught, “*For whoever wants to save his life will lose it; and whoever will lose his life for my sake and the sake of the Good News will save it*” (*Mark 8:35*). Paul lived this out.

It also shows that the Christian life has a purpose and a goal. Paul did not drift through life. He knew what he was called to do and pursued it with focus. Every believer has a race to run and a ministry received from the Lord.

Finally, the verse shows the centrality of grace. Paul summarized his whole message as “the Good News of the grace of God.” Grace is the heart of the gospel: God’s undeserved favor shown in Christ. Paul, who had once persecuted the church, had experienced this grace powerfully himself.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse challenges believers to consider what they value most. Many people make comfort, safety, or success their highest goals. Paul’s example calls believers to value faithfulness to Christ above everything, even their own lives.

It also encourages believers to see their lives as a race with a purpose. Every believer has a ministry received from the Lord, a calling to serve Him and testify to His grace in their particular setting. Believers can ask God to show them their race and give them strength to run it.

Finally, the verse invites believers to aim for a joyful finish. At the end of life, the greatest joy will be to have been faithful to Christ. Believers can live today in a way that will bring joy, not regret, when their race is done.

### *Acts 20:28* — Shepherd the Flock Purchased with His Blood

> *“Take heed, therefore, to yourselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to shepherd the assembly of the Lord and God which he purchased with his own blood.”*
>
> — *Acts 20:28* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul was giving his final charge to the elders of the church in Ephesus. He knew he would never see them again, and he wanted to prepare them to lead the church after he was gone.

“*Take heed, therefore, to yourselves and to all the flock*” (*v. 28*). Paul gave two responsibilities. First, the elders must watch over themselves, their own lives, character, and faith. Leaders who neglect their own spiritual health cannot care for others well. Second, they must watch over “all the flock,” every member of the church.

“*in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers*” (*v. 28*). The elders’ authority came from the Holy Spirit. The church may have recognized and appointed them, but it was the Spirit who made them overseers. The word “overseers” (episkopoi) is related to the word later translated “bishop.” In this verse, “elders” (*20:17*) and “overseers” refer to the same people, showing that in the early church these terms described the same role.

“*to shepherd the assembly of the Lord and God*” (*v. 28*). Elders are shepherds. Their task is to feed, guide, protect, and care for God’s people, just as a shepherd cares for sheep. Notice that the church belongs to God, not to the elders. (Manuscripts differ here; some read “the church of God” and others “the church of the Lord.”)

“*which he purchased with his own blood*” (*v. 28*). The church was bought at the greatest possible price: the blood of Christ. This shows how precious the church is to God. The phrase may also be translated “with the blood of his own \[Son\].” Either way, it points to the cross.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows the high value God places on His church. The church is not a human organization; it is God’s flock, purchased by the blood of Christ. Peter writes that believers were redeemed “*with precious blood, as of a lamb without blemish or spot, the blood of Christ*” (*1 Peter 1:19*). Those who lead the church must treat it with the care that its value deserves.

It also shows the pattern of Christian leadership. Leaders are shepherds, following the example of Jesus, the Good Shepherd who laid down His life for the sheep (*John 10:11*). Peter urges elders to shepherd the flock “*not under compulsion, but voluntarily*” (*1 Peter 5:2*), not for money but eagerly, not domineering but being examples.

Finally, the verse shows that leaders must care for themselves as well as for others. Paul told Timothy, “*Pay attention to yourself and to your teaching*” (*1 Timothy 4:16*). Leaders who fall into sin or false teaching can harm the whole flock.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse calls church leaders to faithful, loving shepherding. Pastors and elders are called to care for every member of the church, teaching, guiding, protecting, and loving them. They are also called to guard their own hearts and lives.

It also calls all believers to value the church. Since Christ purchased the church with His blood, believers should not treat it lightly. They can love their church, pray for it, serve it, and seek its good.

Finally, the verse reminds believers that leaders are accountable to God. Church leaders are not owners of the flock but servants of the Chief Shepherd. Believers can pray for their leaders and support them, and leaders can lead with humility, knowing that the church belongs to God. Shepherds must never use their position to harm, control, or exploit those in their care.

### *Acts 20:35* — More Blessed to Give than to Receive

> *“In all things I gave you an example, that so laboring you ought to help the weak, and to remember the words of the Lord Jesus, that he himself said, “It is more blessed to give than to receive.””*
>
> — *Acts 20:35* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul concluded his farewell speech to the Ephesian elders by reminding them of his own example. He said, “*I coveted no one’s silver, gold, or clothing*” (*v. 33*). Paul had not ministered for money or material gain. “*You yourselves know that these hands served my necessities, and those who were with me*” (*v. 34*). He had worked as a tentmaker to support himself and his companions.

“*In all things I gave you an example, that so laboring you ought to help the weak*” (*v. 35*). Paul’s hard work was not only to support himself, but also to be able to help others. He showed the elders that leaders should work hard and use their resources to care for those in need, “the weak,” which may refer to the poor, the sick, or those who cannot support themselves.

“*and to remember the words of the Lord Jesus, that he himself said, ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’*” (*v. 35*) This saying of Jesus is not recorded in any of the four Gospels. It is one of the few sayings of Jesus preserved outside the Gospels. John wrote that Jesus did many things that were not written down (*John 21:25*), and the early church remembered some of His sayings through oral tradition.

The saying is simple but profound: giving brings greater blessing than receiving. The world often teaches that happiness comes from getting more. Jesus taught that true blessing comes from giving.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reflects the heart of God, who is the greatest giver. “*For God so loved the world, that he gave his only born Son*” (*John 3:16*). Jesus Himself gave His life for others. When believers give, they reflect the character of God.

It also shows that giving is a source of joy. Paul wrote that “*God loves a cheerful giver*” (*2 Corinthians 9:7*). Giving is not merely a duty but a privilege that brings blessing to both the giver and the receiver.

Finally, the verse shows that leaders should model generosity. Paul did not ask others to do what he was unwilling to do. He worked hard and gave generously. Leaders who live generously set an example for others to follow.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to be generous. Believers can look for opportunities to give their time, money, skills, and care to those in need. Giving is not reserved for the wealthy; everyone can give something.

It also challenges the values of a consumer culture. Many people seek happiness through acquiring more. Jesus’ words invite believers to find joy in giving. Believers can test this by practicing generosity and experiencing the blessing it brings.

Finally, the verse encourages believers to work hard so that they can help others. Paul wrote elsewhere that believers should work “*that he may have something to give to him who has need*” (*Ephesians 4:28*). Work is not only for personal provision but also for the blessing of others.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Acts 20* shows the importance of gathering for worship. The believers at Troas met on the first day of the week to break bread and hear God’s word, staying late into the night. Believers today can value regular worship, the Lord’s Supper, and the teaching of Scripture, coming with hunger for God and love for His people.

The chapter also presents Paul’s example of faithful ministry. He served with humility and tears, taught the whole counsel of God, and did not hold his life dear compared to finishing his race and testifying to God’s grace. Believers can ask God to give them the same focus, seeing their lives as a race with a purpose and aiming to finish with joy.

*Acts 20* contains a powerful charge to church leaders. Elders are called to watch over themselves and the whole flock, shepherding the church that Christ purchased with His blood, and protecting it from false teaching. Believers can pray for their leaders, and leaders can serve with humility and care, remembering that the church belongs to God.

Finally, the chapter calls believers to generosity. Paul worked hard to support himself and help the weak, and he reminded the elders of Jesus’ words: “It is more blessed to give than to receive.” Believers can find joy in giving and can entrust themselves, as Paul entrusted the Ephesians, to God and to the word of His grace.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for rising from the dead on the first day of the week, and for gathering Your people to break bread and hear Your word. Give me a hunger for worship and for Your truth. Help me, like Paul, to not hold my life dear compared to finishing the race You have given me, and to testify to the Good News of Your grace. Thank You for purchasing Your church with Your own blood. Bless the leaders of Your church; help them to watch over themselves and over the flock, and protect Your people from false teaching. Make me generous, finding joy in giving rather than receiving. I entrust myself to You and to the word of Your grace, which is able to build me up and give me an inheritance among Your people. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Acts · Chapter 21 of 28

# Acts — Chapter 21

Chapter Theme: Ready to Die for the Name of the Lord Jesus: Paul Arrives in Jerusalem

[Read Acts 21 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/ACT21.htm)

Main Teaching

As Paul sails toward Jerusalem, believers in Tyre and Caesarea warn him, and the prophet Agabus binds his own hands and feet with Paul’s belt to show that Paul will be arrested. Paul answers that he is ready not only to be bound but to die for the name of the Lord Jesus, and his friends say, “The Lord’s will be done.” In Jerusalem, James and the elders rejoice at what God has done among the Gentiles, and they ask Paul to join some men in a purification rite to show Jewish believers that he respects the Law. In the temple, Jews from Asia falsely accuse him of bringing a Gentile inside, a mob tries to kill him, and Roman soldiers rescue and arrest him.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Acts 21* marks a turning point in Paul’s life. The missionary journeys are over. From here to the end of Acts, Paul is a prisoner, first in Jerusalem, then in Caesarea, and finally in Rome. Yet even in chains, he continues to bear witness to Jesus before crowds, councils, governors, and kings, just as Jesus had said he would (*9:15*).

The chapter also echoes the journey of Jesus to Jerusalem in Luke’s Gospel. Like Jesus, Paul set his face to go to Jerusalem despite knowing that suffering awaited him (*Luke 9:51*). Like Jesus, he was warned by friends, handed over to the Gentiles, and accused by a crowd that shouted, “Away with him!” (compare *Luke 23:18*).

### Warnings Along the Way (*21:1–14*)

Paul and his companions sailed from Miletus past Cos and Rhodes to Patara, then crossed to Tyre in Phoenicia. There they found disciples and stayed seven days. These believers “*said to Paul through the Spirit that he should not go up to Jerusalem*” (*v. 4*). This raises a question: was Paul disobeying the Spirit by going? Most interpreters understand that the Spirit revealed to these believers that Paul would suffer in Jerusalem, and out of love they urged him not to go. Paul, however, had already been told that he was “bound by the Spirit” to go to Jerusalem (*20:22*). The Spirit revealed the danger; the believers drew their own conclusion about what Paul should do.

When it was time to leave, the believers, “*with wives and children*” (*v. 5*), walked them out of the city. “*Kneeling down on the beach, we prayed*” (*v. 5*). This tender scene shows the love that united believers who had just met.

They sailed on to Ptolemais and then to Caesarea, where they stayed at the house of “*Philip the evangelist, who was one of the seven*” (*v. 8*) (*6:5*). Philip had preached in Samaria and to the Ethiopian official (*Acts 8*). Nearly twenty years later, he was still serving the Lord in Caesarea. Luke notes that “*this man had four virgin daughters who prophesied*” (*v. 9*). The fulfillment of Joel’s prophecy, “your sons and your daughters will prophesy” (*2:17*), continued in the life of the church.

While they were there, the prophet Agabus came from Judea. This was the same prophet who had predicted the famine (*11:28*). Agabus took Paul’s belt, tied his own feet and hands with it, and said, “*The Holy Spirit says: ‘So the Jews at Jerusalem will bind the man who owns this belt, and will deliver him into the hands of the Gentiles.’*” (*v. 11*) Like Old Testament prophets who acted out their messages (*Isaiah 20:2–4*; *Jeremiah 13:1–11*), Agabus dramatized the prophecy. Paul’s response is studied below.

### Arrival in Jerusalem (*21:15–26*)

Paul and his companions traveled to Jerusalem, staying with Mnason of Cyprus, “*an early disciple*” (*v. 16*). In Jerusalem, “*the brothers received us gladly*” (*v. 17*). The next day, Paul met with James and the elders. Their conversation is studied below. Their request, and Paul’s response, are also studied below.

James and the elders also reminded Paul of the decision of the Jerusalem Council (*15:20*, 29): Gentile believers were not required to follow the Law of Moses, except to avoid certain practices. The concern here was not about Gentiles but about Jewish believers and Paul’s reputation among them.

### Riot in the Temple (*21:27–36*)

Near the end of the seven days of purification, Jews from the province of Asia, perhaps from Ephesus, saw Paul in the temple. Their accusation and its effects are studied below.

The crowd dragged Paul out of the temple, and the gates were shut. As they were trying to kill him, the commander of the Roman garrison heard that all Jerusalem was in an uproar. The Roman garrison was stationed in the Fortress of Antonia, which overlooked the temple courts, with stairs leading down into the courtyard. The commander immediately ran down with soldiers and centurions. When the crowd saw the soldiers, they stopped beating Paul.

The commander arrested Paul and ordered him to be bound with two chains, fulfilling Agabus’s prophecy. He asked who Paul was and what he had done, but the crowd was shouting different things, so he ordered Paul taken into the barracks. The violence was so great that the soldiers had to carry Paul up the stairs. The crowd followed, shouting, “*Away with him!*” (*v. 36*), the same cry the crowd had shouted at Jesus’ trial (*Luke 23:18*).

### Paul Asks to Speak (*21:37–40*)

As Paul was about to be taken into the barracks, he asked the commander in Greek, “*May I speak to you?*” (*v. 37*) The commander was surprised: “*Do you know Greek?*” (*v. 37*) He had assumed Paul was “*the Egyptian who before these days stirred up to sedition and led out into the wilderness the four thousand men of the Assassins*” (*v. 38*). The Jewish historian Josephus also tells of an Egyptian false prophet who led a large group to the Mount of Olives, promising that Jerusalem’s walls would fall at his command; the Roman governor Felix attacked them, and the Egyptian escaped.

Paul answered, “*I am a Jew from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no insignificant city. I beg you, allow me to speak to the people*” (*v. 39*). The commander gave permission. Paul, bruised and bound, stood on the stairs, motioned to the crowd, and when there was a great hush, he spoke to them “*in the Hebrew language*” (*v. 40*), probably Aramaic, the everyday language of Jews in Judea. His speech follows in chapter 22.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Acts 21:13–14* — Ready to Die for the Name of the Lord Jesus

> *“Then Paul answered, ‘What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die at Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus.’ When he would not be persuaded, we ceased, saying, ‘The Lord’s will be done.’”*
>
> — *Acts 21:13–14* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul was staying in Caesarea at the house of Philip the evangelist. The prophet Agabus had just bound his own hands and feet with Paul’s belt, declaring that the Jews in Jerusalem would bind Paul and hand him over to the Gentiles. When Paul’s companions, including Luke, and the local believers heard this, they “*begged him not to go up to Jerusalem*” (*v. 12*). They loved Paul and did not want him to suffer.

Paul’s response was emotional but firm: “*What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart?*” (*v. 13*) Their tears made the decision harder, not because Paul was unsure, but because he loved them and their grief pained him. The word “breaking” suggests pounding or crushing, as if their pleas were weakening his resolve.

“*For I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die at Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus*” (*v. 13*). Paul was willing not only to be arrested, as Agabus had prophesied, but even to die. He was motivated by “the name of the Lord Jesus,” his love and loyalty to Christ.

“*When he would not be persuaded, we ceased, saying, “The Lord’s will be done.”*” (*v. 14*) When Paul could not be persuaded, his friends stopped pleading. They submitted to God’s will, echoing the prayer of Jesus in Gethsemane: “*Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done*” (*Luke 22:42*).

This scene shows that both Paul and his friends acted out of love. His friends loved Paul and wanted to protect him. Paul loved Christ and was willing to suffer for Him. In the end, they all trusted God’s will.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show the cost of discipleship. Jesus called His followers to take up their cross and follow Him (*Luke 9:23*). Paul was willing to do exactly that. He had told the Ephesian elders that he did not count his life as precious to himself (*Acts 20:24*). Now that conviction was tested.

They also show how believers can respond when they disagree about God’s will. Paul’s friends sincerely believed he should not go; Paul sincerely believed he must. They expressed their concerns honestly, but in the end they trusted God. Believers can hold their own views while submitting to God’s sovereign will.

Finally, the phrase “The Lord’s will be done” is a powerful expression of faith. It is not resignation but trust. It acknowledges that God’s plans are wiser than human plans, even when they involve suffering.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses challenge believers to consider their willingness to suffer for Christ. Most believers will not face death for their faith, though many around the world do. But all believers may face costs: loss of reputation, relationships, opportunities, or comfort. Paul’s example encourages believers to be ready to follow Jesus whatever the cost.

They also encourage believers to support those who make costly decisions for Christ. Paul’s friends, though they disagreed, eventually supported him with the words, “The Lord’s will be done.” Believers can stand with fellow believers who follow God’s call, even when it is difficult.

Finally, these verses invite believers to pray, “The Lord’s will be done,” in their own lives. In times of uncertainty, illness, or difficult decisions, believers can entrust their lives to God’s will, trusting that He is good and wise.

### *Acts 21:19–20* — Glorifying God for What He Has Done

> *“When he had greeted them, he reported one by one the things which God had worked among the Gentiles through his ministry. They, when they heard it, glorified God. They said to him, You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews of those who have believed, and they are all zealous for the law.”*
>
> — *Acts 21:19–20* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had arrived in Jerusalem with representatives of the Gentile churches, bringing a generous gift for the poor believers there. The next day, he met with James, the leader of the Jerusalem church, and all the elders.

“*When he had greeted them, he reported one by one the things which God had worked among the Gentiles through his ministry*” (*v. 19*). Paul did not boast about his own achievements. He reported what “God had worked” through him. He described in detail how Gentiles had come to faith, churches had been planted, and lives had been changed.

“*They, when they heard it, glorified God*” (*v. 20*). The Jerusalem leaders responded with praise. They rejoiced that God was saving Gentiles. This was a beautiful moment of unity between the Jewish church in Jerusalem and the Gentile mission.

But then they raised a concern: “*You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews of those who have believed, and they are all zealous for the law*” (*v. 20*). Notice the word “brother.” The leaders affirmed their fellowship with Paul. They also pointed out that thousands of Jewish believers in Jerusalem were devoted to the Law of Moses. They still circumcised their sons, kept the food laws, and observed the festivals, as expressions of their Jewish identity and faithfulness.

These Jewish believers had heard rumors that Paul taught Jews living among Gentiles to abandon Moses, stop circumcising their children, and forsake Jewish customs. This was not true. Paul taught that Gentiles did not need to keep the Law to be saved, but he did not forbid Jewish believers from keeping their customs.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show the joy of the church when God works among the nations. The Jerusalem leaders glorified God for the Gentiles’ salvation. Believers can rejoice whenever God works, wherever and through whomever He works.

They also show the challenge of unity in a diverse church. Jewish believers and Gentile believers had different practices and sensitivities. Rumors and misunderstandings threatened to divide them. Unity required honest conversation, mutual respect, and a willingness to address concerns.

Finally, these verses show the importance of giving God the credit. Paul reported what God had done, and the leaders glorified God. In the church, all fruitfulness comes from God, and He deserves the praise.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to celebrate what God is doing in other places and through other people. Hearing reports of God’s work around the world, in other churches, or in other people’s lives can lead believers to praise God.

They also encourage believers to address misunderstandings honestly. Rumors and false reports can damage relationships in the church. Believers can speak directly and graciously with one another to clear up misunderstandings.

Finally, these verses remind believers to respect differences within the church. Believers from different cultures, traditions, and backgrounds may practice their faith in different ways. As long as these practices do not contradict the gospel, believers can respect and honor one another’s convictions.

### *Acts 21:26* — Becoming as a Jew to the Jews

> *“Then Paul took the men, and the next day purified himself and went with them into the temple, declaring the fulfillment of the days of purification, until the offering was offered for every one of them.”*
>
> — *Acts 21:26* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

James and the elders were concerned that Jewish believers in Jerusalem had heard false rumors that Paul taught Jews to abandon the Law of Moses. To address this, they made a suggestion. Four Jewish believers had taken a vow, probably a Nazirite vow, which involved abstaining from wine and not cutting one’s hair for a period of time, ending with offerings at the temple and the shaving of the head (*Numbers 6*). The leaders asked Paul to join these men in their purification rites and pay for their offerings. “*Then all will know that there is no truth in the things that they have been informed about you, but that you yourself also walk keeping the law*” (*v. 24*).

“*Then Paul took the men, and the next day purified himself and went with them into the temple, declaring the fulfillment of the days of purification, until the offering was offered for every one of them*” (*v. 26*). Paul agreed. He went through the purification ritual and supported the four men, showing publicly that he respected the Law and Jewish customs.

Some readers wonder whether Paul compromised his convictions. But this action was consistent with his principles. Paul taught that keeping the Law could not save anyone. But he never taught that Jewish believers had to stop observing their customs. He wrote, “*To the Jews I became as a Jew, that I might gain Jews; to those who are under the law, as under the law, that I might gain those who are under the law*” (*1 Corinthians 9:20*). Paul was willing to set aside his own freedom for the sake of unity and the gospel.

Paul had also previously taken a vow of his own (*18:18*), showing that he continued to value certain Jewish practices as expressions of devotion.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows Paul’s flexibility for the sake of the gospel. Paul was firm on the essentials of the gospel: salvation by grace through faith, not by works of the Law. But he was flexible on matters of practice that did not compromise the gospel. He was willing to adapt his behavior to remove obstacles for others.

It also shows the importance of peace in the church. Paul cooperated with James and the elders to maintain unity between Jewish and Gentile believers. Paul wrote, “*If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men*” (*Romans 12:18*).

Finally, the verse shows that good intentions do not always prevent conflict. Paul’s action was meant to calm tensions, but it ended up leading to his arrest. Believers can do what is right and wise, yet still face opposition. Faithfulness is not measured by outcomes but by obedience.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to be flexible in non-essential matters for the sake of others. Believers may have freedom in many areas, such as food, customs, or styles of worship. They can choose to set aside their preferences to build relationships and avoid unnecessary offense.

It also encourages believers to work for peace and unity in the church. Paul cooperated with the Jerusalem leaders to address misunderstanding. Believers can seek practical ways to build bridges between different groups in the church.

Finally, the verse reminds believers to distinguish between essential and non-essential matters. Believers must stand firm on the gospel itself, while being gracious and flexible on secondary issues.

### *Acts 21:28–29* — A False Accusation

> *“crying out, ‘Men of Israel, help! This is the man who teaches all men everywhere against the people, and the law, and this place. Moreover, he also brought Greeks into the temple and has defiled this holy place!’ For they had seen Trophimus the Ephesian with him in the city, and they supposed that Paul had brought him into the temple.”*
>
> — *Acts 21:28–29* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul was in the temple completing the days of purification with the four men who had taken a vow. He was doing exactly what James and the elders had suggested, showing his respect for the Law and the temple. But some Jews from the province of Asia saw him there. They may have been from Ephesus, where Paul had ministered for nearly three years and faced opposition.

They stirred up the crowd and seized Paul, “*crying out, “Men of Israel, help! This is the man who teaches all men everywhere against the people, and the law, and this place.*” (*v. 28*) These were serious charges: that Paul taught against the Jewish people, the Law of Moses, and the temple. They were similar to the charges against Stephen (*6:13*) and Jesus (*Mark 14:58*).

“*Moreover, he also brought Greeks into the temple and has defiled this holy place!*” (*v. 28*) This was the most inflammatory charge. Gentiles were allowed in the outer Court of the Gentiles, but a stone barrier separated it from the inner courts. Inscriptions in Greek and Latin warned that any Gentile who passed beyond the barrier would be responsible for his own death. Two of these warning inscriptions have been found by archaeologists.

Luke explains the reason for the accusation: “*For they had seen Trophimus the Ephesian with him in the city, and they supposed that Paul had brought him into the temple*” (*v. 29*). Trophimus was a Gentile believer from Ephesus who had traveled with Paul (*20:4*). The accusers had seen Paul with Trophimus in the city and assumed, without evidence, that Paul had brought him into the temple. It was false, but it was enough to start a riot.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show the danger of false assumptions and accusations. The accusers jumped to conclusions without checking the facts. Scripture warns against spreading false reports (*Exodus 23:1*) and calls believers to judge rightly (*John 7:24*). Rumors and assumptions can do tremendous harm.

They also show that faithful believers may face unjust accusations, as Jesus did. Jesus warned, “*Blessed are you when people reproach you, persecute you, and say all kinds of evil against you falsely, for my sake*” (*Matthew 5:11*).

Finally, there is a deep irony in the accusation. Paul was accused of bringing a Gentile past the barrier that separated Jews and Gentiles in the temple. Paul later wrote that Christ “*broke down the middle wall of separation*” (*Ephesians 2:14*) between Jews and Gentiles. Spiritually, Paul did proclaim that in Christ the barrier was removed, not by defiling the temple, but through the cross.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses warn believers against making assumptions about others. It is easy to jump to conclusions based on partial information. Believers can be careful to seek the truth before speaking or acting, and to refuse to spread rumors.

They also encourage believers who face false accusations. When believers are misunderstood or falsely accused, they can trust that God knows the truth and will vindicate them. Paul faced false accusations repeatedly, yet God used his trials to advance the gospel.

Finally, these verses remind believers of the unity that Christ brings. The barriers that once divided people have been broken down in Christ. Believers can live out this unity by welcoming people of every background into the fellowship of the church.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Acts 21* shows a disciple who was ready to suffer and even die for Jesus. Despite warnings and the tears of his friends, Paul went to Jerusalem. Believers today can ask God for the same readiness to follow Him whatever the cost, and can support one another with the prayer, “The Lord’s will be done.”

The chapter also shows the beauty of Christian fellowship. Believers in Tyre knelt and prayed with Paul on the beach. Philip welcomed him into his home. The Jerusalem church received him gladly. Believers can show the same love and hospitality to fellow believers, even those they have just met.

*Acts 21* models wisdom in maintaining unity. Paul reported what God had done, the Jerusalem leaders glorified God, and Paul willingly joined in a purification rite to address misunderstandings. Believers can celebrate God’s work, address concerns honestly, and be flexible in non-essential matters for the sake of peace.

Finally, the chapter shows that faithful believers may face unjust accusations. Paul was falsely accused and nearly killed, yet God protected him through the Roman soldiers. Believers can refuse to spread rumors, seek the truth, and trust God when they themselves are misunderstood, knowing that He can use even injustice to advance His purposes.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, give me the courage of Paul, who was ready not only to be bound but to die for Your name. When following You is costly, help me to trust You and to say with Your people, “The Lord’s will be done.” Thank You for the love of believers who pray together, open their homes, and welcome one another. Help me to show that same love. Teach me to rejoice whenever You are at work, and to give You the glory. Give me wisdom to be flexible in things that do not matter and firm in the truth of the gospel. Guard my tongue from spreading rumors or making false assumptions about others. When I am misunderstood or falsely accused, help me to trust You to bring the truth to light. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Acts · Chapter 22 of 28

# Acts — Chapter 22

Chapter Theme: Paul’s Testimony: From Zealous Persecutor to Witness for the Nations

[Read Acts 22 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/ACT22.htm)

Main Teaching

Standing on the barracks stairs, Paul speaks to the hostile crowd in their own language. He describes his zeal for the Law and his persecution of the Way, his encounter with the risen Jesus on the Damascus road, and Ananias’s call to be baptized and wash away his sins. When he tells how Jesus sent him to the Gentiles, the crowd erupts in fury. The Roman commander orders him flogged for questioning, but Paul asks whether it is lawful to scourge an uncondemned Roman citizen, and the commander, alarmed, brings him before the Jewish council instead.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Acts 22* contains the second of three accounts of Paul’s conversion in Acts (see also 9:1–19 and *26:9–18*). Each telling is shaped for its audience. Here Paul speaks to a crowd of Jews in Jerusalem who had just tried to kill him because they believed he had betrayed the Law and defiled the temple. Paul’s speech emphasizes his Jewish credentials, his zeal for God, and the role of Ananias, a respected, law-observant Jew. He wants his listeners to understand that his faith in Jesus did not come from rejecting the God of Israel but from an encounter with Him.

The conversion itself and Ananias’s welcome are studied at *Acts 9:4–5*, *9:15–16*, and *9:17*. The studies below focus on what this telling adds.

### “I Am Indeed a Jew” (*22:1–5*)

Paul began, “*Brothers and fathers, listen to the defense which I now make to you*” (*v. 1*). These were the same words Stephen had used to begin his speech (*7:2*). When the crowd heard Paul speaking in their own language, “*they were even more quiet*” (*v. 2*). His background and his past as a persecutor are studied below.

### The Damascus Road (*22:6–11*)

Paul described the light from heaven at about noon, the voice saying, “*Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?*” (*v. 7*), and his question, “*Who are you, Lord?*” (*v. 8*) The answer: “*I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you persecute*” (*v. 8*). Only here does Paul include the words “of Nazareth,” connecting the heavenly Lord with the man from Galilee whom Jerusalem had rejected.

Paul added a question not recorded in Acts 9: “*What shall I do, Lord?*” (*v. 10*) His first response to Jesus was a readiness to obey. The Lord told him to go into Damascus, where he would be told what to do. Blinded by “*the glory of that light*” (*v. 11*), Paul was led by the hand into the city.

### Ananias and Paul’s Commission (*22:12–16*)

Paul described Ananias as “*a devout man according to the law, well reported of by all the Jews who lived in Damascus*” (*v. 12*). To this audience, Ananias’s reputation as a law-observant Jew mattered. Ananias said, “*Brother Saul, receive your sight!*” (*v. 13*) and Paul could see.

Ananias then gave Paul his commission: “*The God of our fathers has appointed you to know his will, and to see the Righteous One, and to hear a voice from his mouth*” (*v. 14*). Notice that Ananias speaks of “the God of our fathers,” the God of Israel. The title “the Righteous One” was a messianic title (*Acts 3:14*; *7:52*). “*For you will be a witness for him to all men of what you have seen and heard*” (*v. 15*). Then came a call to respond, studied below.

### The Vision in the Temple (*22:17–21*)

Paul then described a vision he had in the temple after returning to Jerusalem, studied below. This account was especially significant because he was speaking in the temple area and had been accused of defiling it. Paul showed that he had prayed there and received a vision from God there.

### The Crowd’s Fury and Paul’s Citizenship (*22:22–30*)

“*They listened to him until he said that; then they lifted up their voice and said, “Rid the earth of this fellow, for he isn’t fit to live!”*” (*v. 22*) The crowd had listened quietly until Paul mentioned being sent to the Gentiles. The idea that God would send a Jewish messenger to the Gentiles, offering them equal standing in God’s people, was intolerable to them. They shouted, “*threw off their cloaks, and threw dust into the air*” (*v. 23*), signs of extreme rage and horror.

The Roman commander, who may not have understood Paul’s Aramaic speech, could not tell why the crowd was so angry. He ordered Paul to be brought into the barracks and “*examined by scourging*” (*v. 24*). Roman scourging was brutal, done with leather whips tipped with pieces of bone or metal; it was sometimes fatal. Paul’s question is studied below.

The commander asked whether Paul was really a Roman citizen. He said, “*I bought my citizenship for a great price*” (*v. 28*). Under Emperor Claudius, citizenship could sometimes be obtained through bribes. The commander’s name, Claudius Lysias (*23:26*), suggests he took the emperor’s name when he became a citizen. Paul replied, “*But I was born a Roman*” (*v. 28*). His father or an earlier ancestor must have received citizenship, perhaps for service to Rome. Being born a citizen carried more prestige than buying it.

The soldiers who were about to interrogate Paul withdrew immediately, and the commander was afraid because he had bound a Roman citizen. The next day, wanting to know exactly why Paul was being accused, he released him and ordered the chief priests and the whole council to assemble. He brought Paul before them.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Acts 22:3–4* — Zealous for God, Yet Persecuting the Way

> *“I am indeed a Jew, born in Tarsus of Cilicia, but brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel, instructed according to the strict tradition of the law of our fathers, being zealous for God, even as you all are today. I persecuted this Way to the death, binding and delivering into prisons both men and women,”*
>
> — *Acts 22:3–4* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul stood on the steps of the Roman barracks in Jerusalem, bruised from being beaten by the crowd and bound with chains. Below him was the crowd that had just tried to kill him. They believed he was a traitor who taught against the Law and had defiled the temple.

Paul began by establishing his background: “*I am indeed a Jew, born in Tarsus of Cilicia, but brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel*” (*v. 3*). Though born outside Israel, Paul was raised and educated in Jerusalem. He studied under Gamaliel, one of the most respected rabbis of the time (*5:34*). To sit “at the feet” of a teacher meant to be his student.

“*instructed according to the strict tradition of the law of our fathers*” (*v. 3*). Paul received rigorous training in the Law. He later described himself as “*a Hebrew of Hebrews; concerning the law, a Pharisee*” (*Philippians 3:5*).

“*being zealous for God, even as you all are today*” (*v. 3*). Paul acknowledged his listeners’ zeal. He did not insult them. He identified with them: he had once been just like them, passionate for God and for the Law.

Then he described how his zeal had expressed itself: “*I persecuted this Way to the death, binding and delivering into prisons both men and women*” (*v. 4*). Paul’s zeal had led him to persecute followers of Jesus, even to the point of death. He arrested both men and women. The high priest and the council could confirm this.

Paul was saying, in effect, “I understand your anger. I once felt the same way. I did what you are doing now. Let me tell you what changed me.”

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that zeal for God is not enough. Paul was sincerely zealous, yet he was fighting against God. He later wrote of his fellow Jews, “*For I testify about them that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge*” (*Romans 10:2*). Sincere religious passion can be misdirected when it is not guided by the truth about Jesus.

They also show the power of humble, empathetic witness. Paul did not attack his audience. He acknowledged their zeal and confessed his own past. By identifying with them, he hoped to open their hearts to his message. Paul wrote, “*I have become all things to all men, that I may by all means save some*” (*1 Corinthians 9:22*).

Finally, these verses show the depth of God’s grace. Paul had persecuted the church to death. Yet God saved him and made him an apostle. Paul later called himself the chief of sinners (*1 Timothy 1:15–16*), and said that God showed him mercy so that he could be an example of Christ’s patience to all who would believe.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses challenge believers to examine whether their zeal is guided by truth. Passion for God is good, but it must be shaped by Scripture and by the character of Jesus. Zeal that leads to hatred, violence, or harshness is not true zeal for God.

They also encourage believers to share their faith with empathy. When speaking with those who oppose the gospel, believers can acknowledge what is good in them and share honestly about their own journey. Humility and understanding can open doors that arguments cannot.

Finally, these verses give hope to those who feel their past is too dark. Paul had persecuted believers to death, yet God forgave and transformed him. No one’s past is beyond God’s grace.

### *Acts 22:16* — Arise, Be Baptized, and Wash Away Your Sins

> *“Now why do you wait? Arise, be baptized, and wash away your sins, calling on the name of the Lord.’”*
>
> — *Acts 22:16* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul was telling the crowd in Jerusalem about his conversion. He described how Jesus appeared to him on the road to Damascus, how he was blinded, and how a devout man named Ananias came to him. Ananias restored Paul’s sight and told him that God had appointed him to know His will, to see the Righteous One, and to be His witness to all people.

Then Ananias said, “*Now why do you wait?*” (*v. 16*) There was urgency in Ananias’s words. Paul had met the risen Lord and had received a commission. It was time to respond.

“*Arise, be baptized, and wash away your sins, calling on the name of the Lord*” (*v. 16*). Ananias gave Paul four instructions. First, “arise,” get up and act. Second, “be baptized,” publicly identify with Jesus through baptism. Third, “wash away your sins,” receive forgiveness and cleansing. Fourth, “calling on the name of the Lord,” turning to Jesus in faith and prayer.

The phrase “calling on the name of the Lord” echoes *Joel 2:32*, quoted by Peter at Pentecost: “*whoever will call on the name of the Lord will be saved*” (*Acts 2:21*). In the Old Testament, “the Lord” referred to the God of Israel. Here, Paul is told to call on the name of Jesus. This shows that the early church worshiped Jesus as Lord.

The image of washing recalls the Old Testament washings for purification. Through Christ, believers are made clean from their sins.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows the close connection between baptism, forgiveness, and faith. Christians have understood this connection in different ways. Some traditions see baptism as a means through which God grants forgiveness and cleansing. Others understand baptism as the outward sign that expresses the inner reality of cleansing received through faith, with the phrase “calling on the name of the Lord” showing that it is faith in Christ that saves. Paul himself later wrote of believers being washed, sanctified, and justified “*in the name of the Lord Jesus, and in the Spirit of our God*” (*1 Corinthians 6:11*). All Christians agree that forgiveness comes through Christ and that baptism is an important act of obedience and identification with Him.

It also shows the urgency of responding to Christ. Ananias asked, “Why do you wait?” When people come to know Jesus, they are called to respond without delay.

Finally, the verse shows the completeness of God’s cleansing. Paul had done terrible things, persecuting the church to death. Yet he could wash away his sins by calling on the Lord. God’s forgiveness is complete. Isaiah wrote, “*Though your sins are as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow*” (*Isaiah 1:18*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites anyone who has heard the gospel to respond. If someone knows the truth about Jesus but has not yet trusted Him, Ananias’s question applies: “Why do you wait?” Today is the day to call on the name of the Lord.

It also encourages believers who have not been baptized to consider Jesus’ command. Baptism is a way of publicly identifying with Christ and declaring one’s faith.

Finally, the verse brings comfort to those burdened by guilt. Through calling on Jesus, sins are washed away. Believers can trust that their sins, however great, have been cleansed by the blood of Christ.

### *Acts 22:19–21* — “I Will Send You Far from Here to the Gentiles”

> *“I said, “Lord, they themselves know that I imprisoned and beat in every synagogue those who believed in you. When the blood of Stephen, your witness, was shed, I also was standing by, consenting to his death, and guarding the cloaks of those who killed him.” ‘He said to me, “Depart, for I will send you out far from here to the Gentiles.”’”*
>
> — *Acts 22:19–21* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul was telling the crowd about a vision he had received in the temple soon after his conversion. While he was praying there, he fell into a trance and saw the Lord, who told him, “*Hurry and get out of Jerusalem quickly, because they will not receive testimony concerning me from you*” (*v. 18*).

Paul argued with the Lord. He thought his story would be especially convincing to the people of Jerusalem: “*Lord, they themselves know that I imprisoned and beat in every synagogue those who believed in you*” (*v. 19*). “*When the blood of Stephen, your witness, was shed, I also was standing by, consenting to his death, and guarding the cloaks of those who killed him*” (*v. 20*). Paul assumed that if the people saw such a dramatic change in a former persecutor, they would listen.

Notice that Paul called Stephen “your witness.” The Greek word for “witness” (martys) is the origin of the English word “martyr.” Stephen bore witness to Jesus with his life and death.

But the Lord answered, “*Depart, for I will send you out far from here to the Gentiles*” (*v. 21*). God had a different plan. Paul’s mission was not mainly to Jerusalem but to the nations.

When Paul said these words, the crowd erupted. They had listened quietly to his story about the vision on the road and about Ananias. But the mention of being sent to the Gentiles was too much. To them, it suggested that Gentiles could become God’s people on equal terms with Jews, without becoming Jews themselves.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that God’s plans are sometimes different from our own. Paul thought his testimony would persuade Jerusalem, but God knew the people would not accept it. God sent him elsewhere. God’s wisdom is greater than human reasoning. Isaiah writes, “*“For my thoughts are not your thoughts, and your ways are not my ways,” says the LORD*” (*Isaiah 55:8*).

They also show Paul’s grief over his past. Paul never forgot Stephen’s death. He carried the memory of his role in it. Yet his grief did not crush him; it shaped his understanding of grace. The man who held the cloaks of Stephen’s killers became the apostle to the Gentiles.

Finally, these verses show that the mission to the Gentiles came from Jesus Himself. Paul did not invent it. The Lord sent him. The crowd’s rage shows how radical this mission was, and how deeply it challenged the assumptions of the time.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to trust God’s direction even when it differs from their plans. Believers may think they know where they can be most useful, but God may send them elsewhere. Believers can bring their reasoning to God honestly, as Paul did, and then trust His wisdom.

They also show that God can use believers’ past failures for His purposes. Paul’s past as a persecutor did not disqualify him; it became part of his testimony to God’s grace. Believers can trust that God can redeem their past.

Finally, these verses challenge believers to embrace God’s heart for all people. The crowd could not accept that God would send His message to the Gentiles. Believers today can ask whether there are people they consider outside God’s concern, and ask God to give them His love for all nations.

### *Acts 22:25* — Is It Lawful to Scourge a Roman?

> *“When they had tied him up with straps, Paul asked the centurion who stood by, ‘Is it lawful for you to scourge a man who is a Roman, and not found guilty?’”*
>
> — *Acts 22:25* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After Paul’s speech, the crowd erupted in rage. The Roman commander still did not understand why they were so angry. He decided to find out by having Paul flogged, a common Roman method of extracting information from prisoners. Roman flogging was extremely brutal; the whip had leather straps with pieces of metal or bone attached, and it could tear the flesh and even cause death.

The soldiers stretched Paul out and tied him with straps, ready to whip him. Then “*Paul asked the centurion who stood by, “Is it lawful for you to scourge a man who is a Roman, and not found guilty?”*” (*v. 25*)

Roman law protected citizens from such treatment. It was illegal to flog a Roman citizen, and especially one who had not been tried and convicted. Violating these laws could bring severe penalties on the officials responsible.

The centurion immediately reported this to the commander: “*Watch what you are about to do, for this man is a Roman!*” (*v. 26*) The commander came and confirmed it with Paul. The soldiers withdrew, and the commander was alarmed that he had even bound a Roman citizen.

Paul had used his citizenship before, in Philippi, after he had already been beaten (*16:37*). This time he spoke up before the flogging began. Paul did not seek to suffer needlessly. When legal protections were available, he used them.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that it is not wrong for believers to use legal rights and protections. Paul was willing to suffer for Christ, but he did not seek suffering for its own sake. He used his rights as a Roman citizen to protect himself from unjust treatment. This was not a lack of faith but wise stewardship.

It also shows that God works through ordinary means, including governments and laws. Paul’s citizenship protected him and eventually enabled him to appeal to Caesar and be taken to Rome (*25:11*). God used Roman law to carry Paul to the center of the empire, fulfilling Jesus’ promise that Paul would testify in Rome (*23:11*).

Finally, the verse shows that justice matters. Paul’s question exposed an injustice: punishment without trial. Scripture calls for justice and fair treatment (*Deuteronomy 16:20*). Believers can stand for justice, both for themselves and for others.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse teaches believers that they may use legal rights to protect themselves and others from injustice. Believers who face mistreatment can seek protection through legal and lawful means. Following Christ does not require passively accepting abuse.

It also encourages believers to stand for justice for others. Many people around the world are punished without fair trials or denied basic rights. Believers can advocate for justice, especially for the vulnerable and the persecuted.

Finally, the verse encourages believers to trust God’s providence. God used Paul’s citizenship, an ordinary fact of his birth, for His purposes. God can use the circumstances of believers’ lives, including their nationality, education, and position, to advance His kingdom.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Acts 22* shows the power of personal testimony. Paul told the hostile crowd his own story: his zeal for God, his persecution of the church, his encounter with Jesus, and his calling. Every believer has a story of what God has done. Sharing it honestly and humbly can open hearts, even among those who disagree.

The chapter also shows that sincere zeal is not enough. Paul was passionate for God, yet he was fighting against Him until he met Jesus. Believers can ask God to guide their zeal by His truth, so that their passion leads to love and not to harm.

*Acts 22* calls people to respond to Jesus without delay. Ananias asked Paul, “Why do you wait? Arise, be baptized, and wash away your sins, calling on the name of the Lord.” Anyone who knows the truth about Jesus can respond to Him today, and believers can rest in the complete cleansing He gives.

Finally, the chapter shows that God’s mission is for all nations, and that God works through ordinary means like laws and citizenship. The crowd raged at the idea of God sending Paul to the Gentiles, but God’s plan would not be stopped. Believers can embrace God’s love for all people, use their rights wisely to stand against injustice, and trust that God directs their lives for His purposes.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for meeting Paul on the road to Damascus and turning a zealous persecutor into a witness for the nations. Guide my zeal by Your truth, so that my passion for You always leads to love. Give me courage to share my own story of what You have done, with humility and grace, even with those who oppose me. Thank You that through calling on Your name, my sins are washed away. Help me never to delay in responding to You. When Your plans differ from mine, help me to trust Your wisdom. Give me Your heart for people of every nation. Help me to use the rights and opportunities You have given me wisely, to stand for justice, and to serve Your purposes. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
