Acts · Chapter 23 of 28

# Acts — Chapter 23

Chapter Theme: “Cheer Up, Paul”: God’s Presence and Providence in the Midst of Plots

[Read Acts 23 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/ACT23.htm)

Main Teaching

Before the Jewish council, Paul declares that he has lived before God with a good conscience, is struck on the high priest’s orders, and responds sharply before apologizing out of respect for God’s law. When he identifies himself as a Pharisee on trial for the hope of the resurrection, the council divides. That night, the Lord stands beside Paul and tells him to take courage, because he must testify in Rome. More than forty men vow not to eat until they kill Paul, but his nephew uncovers the plot, and the Roman commander sends Paul under heavy guard to the governor Felix in Caesarea.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Acts 23* continues the story of Paul’s arrest in Jerusalem. The Roman commander, Claudius Lysias, still did not understand why the Jewish leaders were so hostile to Paul. In chapter 22, he planned to have Paul flogged to find out, but stopped when he learned that Paul was a Roman citizen. Now he brought Paul before the Sanhedrin, the Jewish ruling council, to discover the charges.

This chapter shows the danger Paul faced and God’s protection of him. Through a vision, through the courage of a young relative, and through the actions of a Roman commander, God kept Paul safe so that he could testify in Rome.

### Paul before the Council (*23:1–5*)

Paul began, “*Brothers, I have lived before God in all good conscience until today*” (*v. 1*). This statement is studied below. The high priest, Ananias, immediately ordered those standing near Paul to strike him on the mouth. This Ananias (a different man from the disciple in Damascus) was high priest from about A.D. 47 to 59. Josephus describes him as greedy and violent. He was later killed by Jewish rebels at the start of the war against Rome in A.D. 66.

Paul responded sharply: “*God will strike you, you whitewashed wall! Do you sit to judge me according to the law, and command me to be struck contrary to the law?*” (*v. 3*) A “whitewashed wall” was a wall that looked solid but was weak underneath, painted over to hide its cracks (*Ezekiel 13:10–16*). Jesus had called the Pharisees “*whitened tombs*” (*Matthew 23:27*). Paul pointed out the hypocrisy of a judge who broke the law while claiming to judge by it. The Law required fair trials (*Leviticus 19:15*; *Deuteronomy 25:1–2*). Paul’s words proved prophetic; Ananias died violently some years later.

Those standing nearby were shocked: “*Do you malign God’s high priest?*” (*v. 4*) Paul’s response is studied below.

### Pharisees and Sadducees Divided (*23:6–10*)

Paul recognized that the council included both Sadducees and Pharisees. He called out, “*Men and brothers, I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees. Concerning the hope and resurrection of the dead I am being judged!*” (*v. 6*) Paul was not merely using clever tactics. The resurrection was at the heart of his message. He was on trial because he proclaimed that Jesus had risen from the dead, and that through Him there would be a resurrection of the dead. As a Pharisee, Paul shared the Pharisees’ belief in the resurrection; now he knew it had begun in Jesus.

His statement divided the council. “*For the Sadducees say that there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit; but the Pharisees confess all of these*” (*v. 8*). Some of the Pharisees’ scribes stood up and said, “*We find no evil in this man. But if a spirit or angel has spoken to him, let’s not fight against God!*” (*v. 9*) Their words echoed Gamaliel’s warning in *Acts 5:39*. The argument became so violent that the commander feared Paul would be torn apart, so he ordered his soldiers to take Paul back to the barracks.

### The Lord Stands by Paul (*23:11*)

That night, the Lord appeared to Paul. This encouragement is studied below.

### The Plot to Kill Paul (*23:12–22*)

The next morning, more than forty men “*banded together and bound themselves under a curse, saying that they would neither eat nor drink until they had killed Paul*” (*v. 12*). They went to the chief priests and elders, asking them to request that the commander bring Paul to the council again, so that the conspirators could ambush and kill him on the way. That religious leaders cooperated with an assassination plot shows how far their hatred had gone.

How God revealed the plot is studied below. The commander took Paul’s nephew aside, heard the plot, and told him not to tell anyone.

### Sent to Caesarea (*23:23–35*)

The commander acted quickly. He ordered two centurions to prepare “*two hundred soldiers to go as far as Caesarea, with seventy horsemen and two hundred men armed with spears, at the third hour of the night*” (*v. 23*), about nine in the evening. Nearly half of the Jerusalem garrison was sent to protect one prisoner. They provided horses for Paul and took him to Felix, the governor.

The commander wrote a letter to Felix. It is the only letter in Acts from a Roman official. He explained that Paul had been seized by the Jews and was about to be killed when he rescued him, “*having learned that he was a Roman*” (*v. 27*). This was a slight bending of the truth; he had learned Paul was a Roman only later, when he was about to flog him. He wrote that Paul was accused “*about questions of their law, but not to be charged with anything worthy of death or of imprisonment*” (*v. 29*). Like Gallio in Corinth, a Roman official found Paul innocent of any crime under Roman law.

The soldiers brought Paul by night to Antipatris, about forty miles from Jerusalem. The next day, the foot soldiers returned to Jerusalem while the horsemen continued with Paul to Caesarea, about twenty-five miles farther. Felix read the letter, asked what province Paul was from, and said, “*I will hear you fully when your accusers also arrive*” (*v. 35*). He ordered Paul to be kept under guard in Herod’s palace, the governor’s headquarters built by Herod the Great.

Felix was governor of Judea from about A.D. 52 to 59. The Roman historian Tacitus wrote that he “exercised the power of a king with the mind of a slave.” He was known for cruelty and corruption.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Acts 23:1* — A Good Conscience Before God

> *“Paul, looking steadfastly at the council, said, ‘Brothers, I have lived before God in all good conscience until today.’”*
>
> — *Acts 23:1* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The Roman commander had brought Paul before the Sanhedrin, the highest Jewish court. These were the same leaders who had condemned Jesus and Stephen. Paul knew some of them; he had once worked with them to persecute the church.

“*Paul, looking steadfastly at the council*” (*v. 1*). Paul looked directly at the council members. He was not intimidated or ashamed.

“*said, “Brothers, I have lived before God in all good conscience until today.”*” (*v. 1*) Paul addressed them as “brothers,” fellow Jews. Then he made a bold statement: he had lived his life before God with a clear conscience.

What did Paul mean? He did not claim to be sinless. He knew he had persecuted the church, and he called himself the chief of sinners (*1 Timothy 1:15*). But he meant that he had always acted according to what he believed was right before God. Before his conversion, he persecuted the church sincerely, believing it was God’s will. After his conversion, he followed Jesus with the same sincerity. And now, having received forgiveness through Christ, his conscience was clear before God.

Paul later told Felix, “*In this I also practice always having a conscience void of offense toward God and men*” (*Acts 24:16*).

The high priest’s response was to have Paul struck on the mouth, perhaps because he considered Paul’s claim arrogant, or because he resented Paul’s confidence.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows the importance of a clear conscience. The conscience is the inner sense of right and wrong that God has given every person. Paul wrote that Gentiles show the work of the law written in their hearts, “*their conscience testifying with them*” (*Romans 2:15*). Living with a clear conscience means living in a way that one believes is pleasing to God.

It also shows that a sincere conscience is not always a correct one. Paul had once persecuted the church with a clear conscience, because his conscience was misinformed. The conscience must be shaped by God’s truth. Paul later wrote that he was “*not justified by this*” (*1 Corinthians 4:4*), meaning that a clear conscience does not prove one is right; only God is the final judge.

Finally, the verse shows the freedom that comes from forgiveness. Paul could speak of a clear conscience because Christ had cleansed him. Hebrews speaks of the blood of Christ cleansing “*your conscience from dead works to serve the living God*” (*Hebrews 9:14*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to live with a clear conscience. Believers can seek to do what is right before God and others, confessing and making things right when they fail. A clear conscience brings peace and boldness.

It also encourages believers to shape their conscience by Scripture. Since the conscience can be mistaken, believers need God’s word to inform and correct it. Regular reading of Scripture helps believers develop a conscience that agrees with God’s truth.

Finally, the verse offers freedom to those burdened by guilt. Through Christ, believers’ consciences can be cleansed. Those who have confessed their sins and trusted Christ can stand before God without shame, knowing that they are forgiven.

### *Acts 23:5* — Respect for Those in Authority

> *“Paul said, ‘I didn’t know, brothers, that he was high priest. For it is written, “You shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people.”’”*
>
> — *Acts 23:5* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

When Paul declared that he had lived with a good conscience before God, the high priest Ananias ordered him to be struck on the mouth. This was a violation of the law, which required a fair hearing. Paul responded angrily: “God will strike you, you whitewashed wall! Do you sit to judge me according to the law, and command me to be struck contrary to the law?”

Those standing nearby were shocked: “*Do you malign God’s high priest?*” (*v. 4*)

“*Paul said, “I didn’t know, brothers, that he was high priest.”*” (*v. 5*) Why didn’t Paul know? There are several possibilities. Paul had been away from Jerusalem for many years and may not have recognized Ananias. The meeting may have been informal, without the high priest wearing his official robes or sitting in his usual place. Paul may have had poor eyesight (*Galatians 4:15*; *6:11*). Or Paul may have been speaking ironically, meaning that a man who acted like that did not behave like a high priest. Most interpreters take Paul’s words at face value: he did not realize who had given the order.

“*For it is written, ‘You shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people.’*” (*v. 5*) Paul quoted *Exodus 22:28*. As soon as he realized he had spoken harshly to the high priest, he acknowledged that he should not have done so, because God’s law commands respect for those in authority.

Paul’s response is remarkable. He had been treated unjustly, yet he quickly acknowledged his error and submitted to God’s word.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows the importance of respecting authority, even when those in authority act wrongly. Scripture calls believers to honor those in positions of authority (*Romans 13:1–7*; *1 Peter 2:17*). This does not mean approving of their wrongdoing or obeying them when they command sin, but it does mean treating the office with respect.

It also shows the humility of a mature believer. Paul did not justify himself or make excuses. He recognized his mistake and quoted Scripture against himself. James writes that the wisdom from above is “*peaceful, gentle, reasonable*” (*James 3:17*).

Finally, the verse shows that even great believers sometimes react in anger. Paul was human. Under pressure and injustice, he spoke harshly. Jesus, when struck before the high priest, responded calmly (*John 18:22–23*). Paul’s quick acknowledgment shows the importance of humility and correction.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to speak respectfully about those in authority, including government leaders, employers, and church leaders, even when they disagree with them. Believers can challenge injustice while still showing respect.

It also encourages believers to acknowledge their mistakes quickly. When believers speak or act wrongly, they can admit it, apologize, and seek to make it right. Humility is a mark of spiritual maturity.

Finally, the verse reminds believers that respecting authority does not mean accepting injustice silently. Paul pointed out that the high priest was violating the law. Believers can stand for justice while maintaining respect, speaking the truth with grace.

### *Acts 23:11* — “*Cheer Up, Paul*” (*v. 11*)

> *“The following night, the Lord stood by him and said, ‘Cheer up, Paul, for as you have testified about me at Jerusalem, so you must testify also at Rome.’”*
>
> — *Acts 23:11* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had been through a terrible series of events. He had been attacked by a mob in the temple, nearly killed, arrested, bound in chains, nearly flogged, struck on the mouth, and caught in a violent argument in the council so fierce that the commander feared he would be torn apart. Now he was alone in the Roman barracks at night. He did not know what would happen next. He may have wondered whether his mission was over.

“*The following night, the Lord stood by him*” (*v. 11*). In Paul’s loneliest moment, the Lord came to him. Jesus did not send an angel or a message; He Himself stood by Paul.

“*and said, “Cheer up, Paul*” (*v. 11*). The words can also be translated “Take courage.” Jesus spoke words of comfort and encouragement. He knew Paul’s fears and discouragement.

“*for as you have testified about me at Jerusalem, so you must testify also at Rome.*” (*v. 11*) Jesus affirmed that Paul’s witness in Jerusalem had been faithful. Paul had testified to the crowd and to the council. Then Jesus gave a promise: Paul “must” testify in Rome. This was God’s plan, and it would not fail. Paul had longed to go to Rome (*19:21*; *Romans 1:10–15*). Now Jesus promised that he would.

This promise sustained Paul through everything that followed: two years in prison in Caesarea, trials before governors and a king, a dangerous voyage, and a shipwreck. Through it all, Paul knew he would reach Rome because Jesus had promised.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows the faithful presence of Jesus with His servants. Jesus had promised, “*I will in no way leave you, neither will I in any way forsake you*” (*Hebrews 13:5*). In Paul’s darkest moments, Jesus came to stand beside him. Paul later wrote of a time when everyone deserted him: “*But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me*” (*2 Timothy 4:17*).

It also shows that God’s purposes cannot be stopped. Paul faced mobs, councils, and assassination plots, but God had determined that he would testify in Rome. No human opposition could prevent it. The word “must” expresses divine necessity.

Finally, the verse shows that faithful witness is valued by Jesus. Jesus affirmed Paul’s testimony in Jerusalem, even though it had been rejected. Faithfulness, not success, is what Jesus honors.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse brings comfort to believers who are discouraged, lonely, or afraid. Jesus stands by His people in their darkest moments. Believers can turn to Him in prayer, trusting that He is present and that He cares.

It also encourages believers to trust God’s purposes. When circumstances seem to threaten God’s plans for their lives, believers can trust that God’s purposes will be accomplished. Nothing can stop what God has determined.

Finally, the verse encourages believers to remain faithful even when their witness seems unfruitful. Paul’s testimony in Jerusalem was rejected, yet Jesus affirmed it. Believers can trust that faithful witness is never wasted, even when they do not see the results.

### *Acts 23:16* — A Nephew Overhears the Plot

> *“But Paul’s sister’s son heard they were lying in wait, and he came and entered into the barracks and told Paul.”*
>
> — *Acts 23:16* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

More than forty men had sworn an oath not to eat or drink until they had killed Paul. They plotted with the chief priests and elders to ask the Roman commander to bring Paul to the council again, so they could ambush and kill him on the way. It was a well-organized conspiracy. Paul was in the barracks, unaware of the danger.

“*But Paul’s sister’s son heard they were lying in wait, and he came and entered into the barracks and told Paul*” (*v. 16*). This is the only mention in the New Testament of Paul’s family. We learn that Paul had a sister, and that her son was in Jerusalem. We do not know how he heard about the plot; perhaps he overheard conversations, or perhaps his family had connections with the religious leaders. Somehow, the news reached him, and he acted.

The young man went into the barracks and told Paul. Paul called a centurion and asked him to take his nephew to the commander. The commander took the young man by the hand, led him aside, and listened privately. Notice the commander’s kindness to the youth. The young man explained the plot and urged the commander not to agree to the request.

The commander believed him and acted immediately, sending Paul to Caesarea that night under heavy guard.

God had promised that Paul would testify in Rome. Here God fulfilled His promise through ordinary means: a young man who overheard a conversation and had the courage to act.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows God’s providence working through ordinary people and events. There was no angel, earthquake, or miraculous escape this time. God used a young man’s attentiveness and courage. Joseph told his brothers that God had used their actions for good (*Genesis 50:20*). God is sovereign over all events, both extraordinary and ordinary.

It also shows that God can use anyone. Paul’s nephew is not even named. He was young and probably unknown. Yet God used him to save the life of the great apostle. God often works through the faithfulness of unknown people.

Finally, the verse shows how God’s promises and human action work together. Jesus had promised that Paul would testify in Rome. That promise was fulfilled through the nephew’s courage, Paul’s wise response, and the commander’s decision. God’s sovereignty does not make human action unimportant; it works through it.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to look for God’s hand in ordinary events. God does not always work through miracles. He often works through conversations, timing, and the actions of ordinary people. Believers can learn to recognize His providence in everyday life.

It also encourages young people and those who feel insignificant. Paul’s nephew was a young man whose name we do not know, yet God used him to save Paul’s life. Believers of every age can be used by God when they act with courage and integrity.

Finally, the verse encourages believers to act when they see danger or injustice. The nephew could have stayed silent, but he took a risk to warn Paul. Believers can speak up to protect others, especially those who are vulnerable.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Acts 23* encourages believers to live with a clear conscience before God, shaped by His word and cleansed by Christ’s forgiveness. Paul stood before the council with confidence because his conscience was clear. Believers can pursue integrity in all areas of life, confessing quickly when they fail.

The chapter also shows the importance of humility and respect. When Paul spoke harshly to the high priest, he quickly acknowledged his error and quoted Scripture against himself. Believers can show respect to those in authority, even when they disagree, and can humbly admit when they are wrong.

*Acts 23* offers deep comfort in times of discouragement. In Paul’s loneliest moment, the Lord stood beside him and said, “Cheer up.” Believers can trust that Jesus stands beside them in their darkest hours, and that His purposes for their lives will be fulfilled.

Finally, the chapter shows God’s providence working through ordinary means. A young man overheard a plot, and a Roman commander acted to protect Paul. God fulfilled His promise without a miracle, through the courage of an unnamed person. Believers can look for God’s hand in everyday events and can be ready to act with courage when He gives them the opportunity.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for standing by Paul in his loneliest night and telling him to take courage. Stand by me when I am discouraged, afraid, or alone, and remind me that Your purposes for my life will not fail. Help me to live with a clear conscience before You, shaped by Your word and cleansed by Your forgiveness. When I speak or act wrongly, give me the humility to admit it quickly. Teach me to respect those in authority while still standing for what is right. Thank You for working through ordinary people and events, as You worked through Paul’s nephew. Open my eyes to see Your hand in everyday life, and give me courage to act when You call me to protect others. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Acts · Chapter 24 of 28

# Acts — Chapter 24

Chapter Theme: Righteousness, Self-Control, and the Judgment to Come: Paul before Felix

[Read Acts 24 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/ACT24.htm)

Main Teaching

The high priest and a hired orator named Tertullus accuse Paul before the governor Felix of being a troublemaker, a ringleader of the Nazarene sect, and a temple defiler. Paul calmly answers that the charges cannot be proven and confesses that he worships the God of his ancestors according to the Way, believing the Law and the Prophets and hoping for the resurrection of the righteous and the unrighteous. Felix postpones the case. Later, when Paul speaks to Felix and his wife Drusilla about faith in Christ, righteousness, self-control, and coming judgment, Felix becomes afraid and sends him away, hoping for a bribe, and leaves Paul in prison for two years.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Acts 24* records Paul’s trial before Antonius Felix, the Roman governor of Judea from about A.D. 52 to 59. Felix had been born a slave and freed, and he rose to power through the influence of his brother Pallas, a favorite of Emperor Claudius. The Roman historian Tacitus described him as cruel and lustful, ruling with the power of a king and the mind of a slave. His wife Drusilla, mentioned in this chapter, was the youngest daughter of Herod Agrippa I (the king who killed James in *Acts 12*). Felix had persuaded her to leave her first husband to marry him. She was probably only about twenty at the time.

The chapter shows Paul’s integrity and courage before a corrupt ruler. Paul answered the charges truthfully and calmly, and when given the opportunity to speak privately, he did not flatter Felix but spoke about righteousness, self-control, and judgment.

### The Accusation (*24:1–9*)

Five days after Paul arrived in Caesarea, the high priest Ananias came with some elders and a lawyer named Tertullus, a professional speaker familiar with Roman legal procedures. Tertullus began with flattery: “*Seeing that by you we enjoy much peace, and that prosperity is coming to this nation by your foresight*” (*v. 2*). This was a common courtroom technique, but it was far from the truth. Felix’s rule was marked by violent uprisings and brutal repression.

Then Tertullus made three charges. First, “*we have found this man to be a plague, an instigator of insurrections among all the Jews throughout the world*” (*v. 5*). This was a political charge: Paul was a troublemaker who stirred up riots, a serious accusation in the eyes of Rome, which valued order above all. Second, he called Paul “*a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes*” (*v. 5*). “Nazarenes” was a name for followers of Jesus of Nazareth. Third, “*He even tried to profane the temple, and we arrested him*” (*v. 6*). (Verse 7, which adds details about the commander Lysias taking Paul by force, appears in some later manuscripts but not the earliest.) The Jewish leaders joined in, affirming the charges.

### Paul’s Defense (*24:10–21*)

When Felix nodded for him to speak, Paul began respectfully but without flattery: “*Because I know that you have been a judge of this nation for many years, I cheerfully make my defense*” (*v. 10*). Paul simply acknowledged Felix’s experience.

Paul answered each charge. First, regarding stirring up trouble: it had been only twelve days since he went to Jerusalem to worship. “*In the temple they didn’t find me disputing with anyone or stirring up a crowd, either in the synagogues or in the city*” (*v. 12*). “*Nor can they prove to you the things of which they now accuse me*” (*v. 13*). Paul’s confession about the Way is studied below.

Regarding the temple: Paul had come to Jerusalem “*to bring gifts for the needy to my nation, and offerings*” (*v. 17*), referring to the collection from the Gentile churches. When the Jews from Asia found him in the temple, he was ritually purified, “*not with a mob, nor with turmoil*” (*v. 18*). Paul pointed out that the Jews from Asia, his original accusers, were not even present. Under Roman law, accusers had to appear in person; their absence was a serious weakness in the case.

Finally, Paul challenged his accusers to say what crime the council had found when he stood before them, unless it was his statement about the resurrection of the dead.

### Felix’s Response (*24:22–27*)

“*But Felix, having more exact knowledge concerning the Way, deferred them, saying, “When Lysias, the commanding officer, comes down, I will decide your case.”*” (*v. 22*) Felix knew something about the Christian movement, perhaps through his Jewish wife or through his years in Judea. He postponed the decision, which effectively left Paul in prison. He ordered that Paul be kept under guard but given some freedom, and that his friends be allowed to visit and care for him. Luke and others probably visited Paul during this time.

Some days later, Felix and Drusilla summoned Paul to hear him speak about faith in Christ Jesus. What followed is studied below. Felix’s motive for keeping Paul is also studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Acts 24:14–15* — Serving the God of Our Fathers According to the Way

> *“But this I confess to you, that according to the Way, which they call a sect, so I serve the God of our fathers, believing all things which are according to the law, and which are written in the prophets; having hope toward God, which these also themselves look for, that there will be a resurrection of the dead, both of the just and unjust.”*
>
> — *Acts 24:14–15* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul stood before Felix, the Roman governor, answering charges brought by the high priest and his lawyer. They had called Paul a troublemaker, a ringleader of the Nazarene sect, and a desecrator of the temple. Paul had denied causing any disturbance and pointed out that his accusers could not prove their charges. Then he made a positive statement about his faith.

“*But this I confess to you, that according to the Way, which they call a sect, so I serve the God of our fathers*” (*v. 14*). Paul freely admitted that he followed “the Way,” the name early Christians used for their faith. His accusers called it a “sect,” suggesting it was a dangerous splinter group. But Paul insisted that he worshiped the same God as his ancestors: the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Following Jesus was not abandoning Israel’s faith but fulfilling it.

“*believing all things which are according to the law, and which are written in the prophets*” (*v. 14*). Paul believed everything written in the Hebrew Scriptures. He was not rejecting the Law or the Prophets. He believed that they pointed to Jesus.

“*having hope toward God, which these also themselves look for, that there will be a resurrection of the dead, both of the just and unjust*” (*v. 15*). Paul shared the hope of the Pharisees and many Jews: that God would raise the dead. This resurrection would include both the righteous and the unrighteous. Jesus taught the same (*John 5:28–29*), as did the prophet Daniel (*Daniel 12:2*).

Paul’s point was that his faith was not a strange new religion but the fulfillment of Israel’s Scriptures and hope. This also mattered legally: Judaism was a recognized religion in the Roman Empire, so if Paul’s faith was part of the Jewish tradition, it was not illegal.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that Christianity is rooted in the Old Testament. The God of Israel is the God who sent Jesus. The promises of the Law and the Prophets are fulfilled in Him. Jesus Himself said, “*Don’t think that I came to destroy the law or the prophets. I didn’t come to destroy, but to fulfill*” (*Matthew 5:17*).

They also show the centrality of the resurrection hope. Paul’s whole message rested on the resurrection: Jesus’ resurrection, and the future resurrection of all the dead. Paul wrote that if there is no resurrection, faith is useless (*1 Corinthians 15:13–19*). The resurrection gives believers hope beyond death.

Finally, the mention of the resurrection of “both of the just and unjust” reminds readers that all people will face God. The resurrection is a hope for the righteous and a warning for the unrighteous. This gives urgency to the call to repent and believe.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to read the whole Bible, including the Old Testament, as God’s word that points to Christ. The Law and the Prophets are not outdated; they reveal God’s character and prepare the way for Jesus.

They also give believers confidence in their hope. The resurrection of the dead is not wishful thinking; it is a promise rooted in God’s word and confirmed by Jesus’ resurrection. Believers can face death and loss with hope.

Finally, these verses remind believers that everyone will one day stand before God. This truth calls believers to live faithfully and to share the gospel with love and urgency.

### *Acts 24:25* — Righteousness, Self-Control, and the Judgment to Come

> *“As he reasoned about righteousness, self-control, and the judgment to come, Felix was terrified, and answered, ‘Go your way for this time, and when it is convenient for me, I will summon you.’”*
>
> — *Acts 24:25* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Some days after Paul’s trial, Felix and his wife Drusilla sent for Paul to hear him speak about faith in Christ Jesus. Felix may have been curious about the movement he had heard about, or Drusilla, who was Jewish, may have been interested. This was a remarkable opportunity: a private audience with the most powerful man in the province.

What did Paul talk about? “*As he reasoned about righteousness, self-control, and the judgment to come*” (*v. 25*). Paul spoke about three topics, each of which applied directly to Felix and Drusilla.

“Righteousness”: Felix was known for injustice and cruelty. Paul spoke about God’s righteousness and the righteous life God requires, and the righteousness that God gives through faith in Christ.

“Self-control”: Felix and Drusilla had married after Felix persuaded her to leave her husband. Felix was known for his lust and indulgence. Paul spoke about mastering one’s desires.

“The judgment to come”: Felix was a judge, but he too would one day stand before God’s judgment. No earthly position would protect him.

Paul did not flatter Felix or avoid uncomfortable topics. He spoke the truth with courage.

“*Felix was terrified*” (*v. 25*). Felix felt the weight of Paul’s words. His conscience was stirred. He realized that he was guilty before God.

“*and answered, “Go your way for this time, and when it is convenient for me, I will summon you.”*” (*v. 25*) Instead of responding with repentance, Felix sent Paul away. He postponed the decision to a “convenient” time. As far as we know, that convenient time never came.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that the gospel addresses the whole person. Faith in Christ is not only about belief but also about righteousness, self-control, and accountability to God. The gospel calls people to turn from sin and to live under God’s rule.

It also shows the work of the Holy Spirit in convicting people. Jesus said that the Spirit would convict the world “*about sin, about righteousness, and about judgment*” (*John 16:8*). Paul’s words, empowered by the Spirit, brought Felix to fear.

Finally, the verse shows the danger of delay. Felix was terrified but postponed his response. Many people feel the conviction of the Spirit but put off responding, waiting for a more convenient time. Scripture warns, “*Behold, now is the acceptable time. Behold, now is the day of salvation*” (*2 Corinthians 6:2*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to speak the truth with courage, even to powerful people. Paul did not water down his message to please Felix. Believers can share the gospel faithfully, including its call to righteousness and its warning of judgment, with love and respect.

It also challenges anyone who feels conviction but delays responding. Many people sense that they need to turn to God but put it off. Felix’s story warns that delay can become permanent. When God speaks, the time to respond is now.

Finally, the verse invites believers to examine their own lives in light of righteousness, self-control, and judgment. These are not only for unbelievers to hear. Believers too are called to live righteously, practice self-control, and remember that they will give an account to God.

### *Acts 24:26–27* — Hoping for a Bribe

> *“Meanwhile, he also hoped that money would be given to him by Paul, that he might release him. Therefore also he sent for him more often and talked with him. But when two years were fulfilled, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus, and desiring to gain favor with the Jews, Felix left Paul in bonds.”*
>
> — *Acts 24:26–27* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Felix had been frightened by Paul’s words about righteousness, self-control, and judgment. Yet he did not repent. Instead, Luke reveals Felix’s true motive for keeping Paul around.

“*Meanwhile, he also hoped that money would be given to him by Paul, that he might release him*” (*v. 26*). Felix wanted a bribe. Paul had mentioned bringing a large gift to Jerusalem (*24:17*), and Felix may have thought Paul or his friends had access to money. Roman law forbade accepting bribes to release prisoners, but corrupt officials often did so.

“*Therefore also he sent for him more often and talked with him*” (*v. 26*). Felix sent for Paul frequently. Perhaps he hoped Paul would offer a bribe. Paul apparently never did. He refused to buy his freedom through corruption.

These conversations also show God’s patience. Felix heard the gospel again and again. He had many opportunities to respond. Yet he continued to resist.

“*But when two years were fulfilled, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus, and desiring to gain favor with the Jews, Felix left Paul in bonds*” (*v. 27*). Paul remained in prison for two years. Felix was recalled to Rome, probably because of his harsh handling of a conflict between Jews and Gentiles in Caesarea. Before leaving, Felix wanted to gain favor with the Jewish leaders, so he left Paul in prison instead of releasing him.

Two years is a long time. Paul could not travel, preach in new cities, or visit the churches. Yet his time was not wasted. He may have written letters, received visitors, and prayed. Some scholars think Luke may have gathered material for his Gospel during this time in Judea.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show the corruption of the human heart. Felix heard the gospel many times, yet his love for money and his desire for political advantage kept him from responding. Jesus warned, “*You aren’t able to serve God and Mammon*” (*Luke 16:13*). Felix chose money and power over God.

They also show Paul’s integrity. Paul could have tried to buy his freedom. He refused to compromise. He trusted God with his future rather than resorting to corruption.

Finally, these verses show that God’s timing is not always our timing. Paul waited two years in prison. Jesus had promised that Paul would testify in Rome (*23:11*), but the fulfillment took time. Waiting is part of the life of faith. Isaiah writes, “*But those who wait for the LORD will renew their strength*” (*Isaiah 40:31*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses warn against the love of money and the pursuit of power. Felix’s greed and desire for favor kept him from God. Believers can examine whether money, status, or approval is hindering their obedience to God.

They also encourage believers to maintain integrity, even when compromise would bring relief. Paul refused to pay a bribe, even though it might have meant freedom. Believers can trust God rather than resorting to dishonest means.

Finally, these verses encourage believers who are waiting. Some believers face long seasons of waiting: in illness, unemployment, difficult circumstances, or unanswered prayer. Paul’s two years in prison remind them that God’s purposes continue even in seasons of delay. Believers can use these times faithfully, trusting that God’s promises will be fulfilled.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Acts 24* shows how to respond to false accusations with truth and calm. Paul did not flatter Felix or attack his accusers. He answered each charge honestly and pointed out that the charges could not be proven. Believers facing unjust criticism can respond with the same honesty, respect, and confidence.

The chapter also shows that Christian faith is rooted in God’s earlier revelation. Paul worshiped the God of his ancestors, believed the Law and the Prophets, and hoped for the resurrection. Believers can read the whole Bible as one story pointing to Christ, and can hold firmly to the hope of the resurrection.

*Acts 24* contains a powerful warning about delay. Felix heard about righteousness, self-control, and the judgment to come, and he was terrified. Yet he said, “When it is convenient for me, I will summon you.” He never responded. Anyone who feels God’s conviction can respond today, not waiting for a convenient time that may never come.

Finally, the chapter shows Paul’s integrity during a long, unjust imprisonment. He refused to pay a bribe and waited two years, trusting God’s timing. Believers can maintain integrity under pressure, resist the love of money and power, and trust that God’s purposes continue even in seasons of waiting.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord God, thank You that the faith I have in Jesus is rooted in Your promises from the beginning. Thank You for the hope of the resurrection. When I face false accusations, give me calm and truthfulness, as You gave Paul. Give me courage to speak about righteousness, self-control, and the judgment to come, even to those who may not want to hear. Search my own heart, and help me to live righteously and with self-control, remembering that I will give an account to You. Keep me from delaying when Your Spirit convicts me; help me to respond to You now. Guard me from the love of money and the desire for power. When I must wait, help me to trust Your timing and to remain faithful. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Acts · Chapter 25 of 28

# Acts — Chapter 25

Chapter Theme: “I Appeal to Caesar”: God’s Plan Moves Through Courts and Kings

[Read Acts 25 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/ACT25.htm)

Main Teaching

The new governor Festus arrives, and the Jewish leaders immediately ask him to bring Paul to Jerusalem, planning to ambush him. Festus holds a hearing in Caesarea instead, where Paul insists he has done nothing against the Law, the temple, or Caesar. When Festus, seeking to please the leaders, suggests a trial in Jerusalem, Paul exercises his right as a Roman citizen and appeals to Caesar. Festus later explains the case to King Agrippa II, puzzled that the dispute concerns “one Jesus, who was dead, whom Paul affirmed to be alive,” and Paul is brought before a glittering assembly of rulers.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Acts 25* begins a new phase of Paul’s imprisonment. After two years in custody under Felix, Paul’s case is taken up by a new governor, Porcius Festus, who ruled Judea from about A.D. 59 to 62. Festus seems to have been a more honest administrator than Felix, though he too was concerned with keeping peace with the Jewish leaders. He died in office after only a few years.

The chapter also introduces King Herod Agrippa II, the son of Herod Agrippa I (who killed James in *Acts 12*), and his sister Bernice. Agrippa II ruled territories to the north and east of Judea and had authority over the temple, including the right to appoint the high priest. He was considered an expert in Jewish customs. Bernice lived with her brother, and their relationship was the subject of gossip in Rome. She later had a relationship with the Roman general Titus, who destroyed Jerusalem in A.D. 70.

Through these chapters, Luke shows the fulfillment of Jesus’ words that Paul would bear His name before kings (*9:15*), and Jesus’ promise that Paul would testify in Rome (*23:11*).

### Festus Visits Jerusalem (*25:1–5*)

Three days after arriving in the province, Festus went to Jerusalem. The high priest and the leading Jews immediately brought their charges against Paul. Even after two years, their hatred had not cooled. They asked Festus “*asking a favor against him, that he would summon him to Jerusalem, plotting to kill him on the way*” (*v. 3*). This was the same kind of ambush plot that had been planned two years earlier (*23:12–15*).

Festus refused. He said Paul would remain in Caesarea, and that the leaders could come there and present their accusations. Without knowing it, Festus protected Paul’s life.

### The Hearing before Festus (*25:6–12*)

After about ten days in Jerusalem, Festus returned to Caesarea and the next day convened the court. The Jewish leaders surrounded Paul, “*bringing against him many and grievous charges which they could not prove*” (*v. 7*). Paul’s defense is studied below.

“*But Festus, desiring to gain favor with the Jews, answered Paul and said, “Are you willing to go up to Jerusalem and be judged by me there concerning these things?”*” (*v. 9*) Festus wanted to please the Jewish leaders at the beginning of his rule. He may not have known about the plot, but Paul understood the danger. A trial in Jerusalem would be an opportunity for his enemies. Paul’s response, his appeal to Caesar, is studied below.

Festus conferred with his council and then declared, “*You have appealed to Caesar. To Caesar you shall go*” (*v. 12*). The emperor at this time was Nero, who had ruled since A.D. 54. In the early years of his reign, Nero’s government was considered fair and stable. His persecution of Christians came later, after the great fire of Rome in A.D. 64.

### Festus Consults King Agrippa (*25:13–22*)

Some days later, King Agrippa and Bernice arrived in Caesarea to welcome the new governor. Festus explained Paul’s case to Agrippa. He described how the Jewish leaders had asked for Paul’s condemnation, and how he had told them that Roman law required the accused to face his accusers and defend himself. This principle of fair trial is one of the great contributions of Roman law: “*it is not the custom of the Romans to give up any man to destruction before the accused has met the accusers face to face and has had opportunity to make his defense*” (*v. 16*). Festus’s puzzled summary of the case is studied below.

Agrippa said, “*I also would like to hear the man myself*” (*v. 22*). Like his great-uncle Herod Antipas, who had wanted to see Jesus (*Luke 23:8*), Agrippa was curious about Paul. Festus arranged a hearing for the next day.

### Paul before Agrippa and Bernice (*25:23–27*)

The scene of Paul’s appearance before this assembly is studied below. Festus introduced the case, explaining that he had found nothing deserving of death, but that he needed something to write to the emperor: “*For it seems to me unreasonable, in sending a prisoner, not to also specify the charges against him*” (*v. 27*). The governor was in an awkward position: he was sending a prisoner to Caesar without a clear charge. He hoped Agrippa, with his knowledge of Jewish matters, could help him.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Acts 25:8* — Neither Against the Law, the Temple, nor Caesar

> *“while he said in his defense, ‘Neither against the law of the Jews, nor against the temple, nor against Caesar, have I sinned at all.’”*
>
> — *Acts 25:8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul stood before the new governor, Festus, surrounded by the Jewish leaders who had come from Jerusalem. They brought many serious charges against him, but they could not prove any of them. Then Paul made his defense.

“*while he said in his defense, “Neither against the law of the Jews, nor against the temple, nor against Caesar, have I sinned at all.”*” (*v. 8*) Paul’s defense covered three areas.

“Against the law of the Jews”: Paul had been accused of teaching people to abandon the Law of Moses. But Paul had not done so. He taught that Gentiles did not need to keep the Law to be saved, but he respected the Law and did not forbid Jews from keeping it. He had even participated in a purification rite in the temple (*21:26*).

“Against the temple”: Paul had been accused of bringing a Gentile into the temple and defiling it. This was false. He had been in the temple as a ritually purified worshiper.

“Against Caesar”: This was the most dangerous charge from Rome’s perspective. Paul’s accusers may have suggested that he was a troublemaker who stirred up riots, or that by proclaiming Jesus as King, he was disloyal to Caesar. But Paul had not plotted rebellion or broken Roman law.

Paul’s defense was simple and direct: he was innocent in every area. He had nothing to hide.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows the integrity of Paul’s life. He could stand before religious and political authorities and declare that he had not wronged anyone. Peter later wrote that believers should live so that, though they are accused of evil, “*they may see your good works and glorify God in the day of visitation*” (*1 Peter 2:12*).

It also shows that Christianity is not inherently a threat to legitimate authority. Paul honored the Law, respected the temple, and did not rebel against Caesar. Christians are called to be good citizens, obeying the law and honoring rulers, as long as doing so does not require disobeying God (*Romans 13:1–7*; *Acts 5:29*).

Finally, the verse shows that faithfulness to Christ may still bring accusation. Paul was innocent, yet he was accused repeatedly. Jesus warned that His followers would be falsely accused (*Matthew 5:11*). Innocence does not always prevent opposition.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to live lives of integrity in every area: religious, social, and civic. Believers can seek to live so that, if accused, they can honestly say they have done no wrong.

It also encourages believers to be good citizens. Following Christ includes respecting laws, paying taxes, and contributing to the common good. Believers can show that faith in Jesus makes them better neighbors, not worse.

Finally, the verse comforts believers who are falsely accused. Paul faced repeated unjust charges, yet he responded calmly and truthfully. Believers can trust that God sees the truth and that their integrity will ultimately be vindicated.

### *Acts 25:11* — “*I Appeal to Caesar!*” (*v. 11*)

> *“For if I have done wrong and have committed anything worthy of death, I don’t refuse to die; but if none of those things is true that they accuse me of, no one can give me up to them. I appeal to Caesar!”*
>
> — *Acts 25:11* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Festus asked Paul whether he would be willing to go to Jerusalem and be tried there. Festus wanted to please the Jewish leaders, but Paul knew the danger. Two years earlier, more than forty men had sworn to kill him (*23:12*). If he went to Jerusalem, he might not survive the journey, and even if he did, he would not receive a fair trial.

Paul answered firmly: “*I am standing before Caesar’s judgment seat, where I ought to be tried. I have done no wrong to the Jews, as you also know very well*” (*v. 10*). Paul reminded Festus that he was a Roman citizen standing in a Roman court. He had done nothing wrong, and Festus knew it.

“*For if I have done wrong and have committed anything worthy of death, I don’t refuse to die*” (*v. 11*). Paul was not trying to escape justice. If he were guilty of a capital crime, he would accept the penalty. He was willing to die if he deserved it.

“*but if none of those things is true that they accuse me of, no one can give me up to them*” (*v. 11*). But since he was innocent, no one had the right to hand him over to his enemies as a political favor.

“*I appeal to Caesar!*” (*v. 11*) Roman citizens had the right to appeal their case to the emperor, the highest court in the empire. Once a citizen appealed, the provincial governor had to send the case to Rome. This appeal removed Paul from the jurisdiction of the local authorities and guaranteed that he would go to Rome.

Paul’s appeal was not only a legal maneuver. Jesus had promised that Paul would testify in Rome (*23:11*). The appeal was the means by which this promise would be fulfilled.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that God works through legal systems and human institutions. Paul’s Roman citizenship and the right of appeal became God’s means of bringing him to Rome. God is sovereign over all things, including governments and laws. Proverbs says, “*The king’s heart is in the LORD’s hand like the watercourses. He turns it wherever he desires*” (*Proverbs 21:1*).

It also shows that seeking justice is not contrary to faith. Paul was willing to suffer for Christ, but he did not accept injustice passively. He used the legal protections available to him. Believers may use legitimate means to protect themselves and others from injustice.

Finally, the verse shows Paul’s willingness to accept just consequences. He did not claim exemption from the law. He said that if he were guilty, he would accept death. Believers are not above the law; they are called to accept just consequences for wrongdoing while resisting injustice.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers who face injustice to seek fair treatment through legitimate means. Using legal rights, seeking protection, or appealing unfair decisions can be consistent with faithfulness to Christ. This includes seeking safety and legal protection in situations of abuse.

It also encourages believers to trust that God can use ordinary circumstances, such as legal processes, to accomplish His purposes. Believers may not see how God is working, but He can use even difficult situations to move His plans forward.

Finally, the verse reminds believers to be willing to accept responsibility for their actions. Paul did not ask to be spared if he was guilty. Believers can take responsibility for their wrongs while standing firm when they are innocent.

### *Acts 25:19* — “*One Jesus, Who Was Dead, Whom Paul Affirmed to Be Alive*” (*v. 19*)

> *“but had certain questions against him about their own religion and about one Jesus, who was dead, whom Paul affirmed to be alive.”*
>
> — *Acts 25:19* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

King Agrippa and his sister Bernice had come to Caesarea to welcome the new governor, Festus. During their visit, Festus told Agrippa about Paul’s case. He explained that the Jewish leaders had accused Paul, but that when they brought their charges, they did not accuse him of the crimes Festus expected.

“*but had certain questions against him about their own religion*” (*v. 19*). Festus saw the dispute as a religious disagreement among Jews. The word translated “religion” can also mean “superstition”; Festus may have been speaking politely to Agrippa, who was Jewish, but his view was that this was not a matter for Roman law.

“*and about one Jesus, who was dead, whom Paul affirmed to be alive*” (*v. 19*). Festus summarized the heart of the controversy. The dispute was about a man named Jesus. Everyone agreed that He had died. But Paul insisted that He was alive.

Festus’s words are a remarkable summary of the Christian message from the perspective of an outsider. He did not understand it, and he was perplexed by it. But he recognized that the central issue was the resurrection of Jesus. Everything depended on whether Jesus was dead or alive.

The phrase “one Jesus” shows that Festus knew little about Him. To the Roman governor, Jesus was just another name. But to Paul, Jesus was the risen Lord of all.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that the resurrection is the center of the Christian faith. The early church’s message was not merely that Jesus was a good teacher or that He died as a martyr. It was that He is alive. Paul wrote, “*If Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain, and your faith also is in vain*” (*1 Corinthians 15:14*).

It also shows that the resurrection forces a decision. Either Jesus is dead, or He is alive. If He is dead, Christianity is false. If He is alive, He is Lord, and everything changes. Festus did not know what to make of it. Every person must decide what they believe about the risen Jesus.

Finally, the verse shows that even outsiders recognized the core of the Christian message. The resurrection was not a later addition to Christianity. From the beginning, followers of Jesus proclaimed that He had risen from the dead.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites everyone to consider the central question: Is Jesus dead, or is He alive? This question matters more than any other. Believers can share the evidence for the resurrection and the difference it makes.

It also encourages believers to keep the resurrection at the center of their faith. The resurrection is not merely a doctrine to affirm on Easter; it is the foundation of hope, forgiveness, and new life every day.

Finally, the verse encourages believers to be patient with those who are perplexed by the gospel. Festus did not understand Paul’s message. Many people today find the resurrection hard to believe. Believers can explain it patiently and pray for God to open their understanding.

### *Acts 25:23* — Great Pomp and a Prisoner in Chains

> *“So on the next day, when Agrippa and Bernice had come with great pomp, and they had entered into the place of hearing with the commanding officers and the principal men of the city, at the command of Festus, Paul was brought in.”*
>
> — *Acts 25:23* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

King Agrippa had expressed interest in hearing Paul. Festus arranged a hearing for the next day. Luke describes the scene vividly.

“*So on the next day, when Agrippa and Bernice had come with great pomp*” (*v. 23*). The word “pomp” (in Greek, phantasia, from which we get “fantasy”) describes a grand display, a parade of wealth and status. Agrippa and Bernice arrived in their royal robes, with attendants and ceremony.

“*and they had entered into the place of hearing with the commanding officers and the principal men of the city*” (*v. 23*). The audience hall was filled with the most powerful people in Caesarea: the military commanders (there were five cohorts stationed in Caesarea, each with a commander) and the leading citizens of the city.

“*at the command of Festus, Paul was brought in*” (*v. 23*). Into this glittering assembly came Paul, a prisoner in chains (*26:29*). He had no wealth, no title, and no political power. He had been in prison for two years.

The contrast is striking. The powerful people in the room thought they were examining Paul. But in God’s eyes, Paul was the one with the most important message, and they were the ones being given an opportunity to hear the truth. Jesus had said that Paul would bear His name “*before the nations and kings*” (*Acts 9:15*). This prophecy was being fulfilled.

Within a few years, Festus would be dead, Agrippa’s kingdom would be gone, and the glory of this assembly would be forgotten. But Paul’s message would spread throughout the world.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows the contrast between worldly glory and true greatness. The world is impressed by wealth, power, and display. But God values faithfulness and truth. Paul wrote, “*while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal*” (*2 Corinthians 4:18*).

It also shows that God gives opportunities to hear the gospel to people of every status. Agrippa, Bernice, Festus, the commanders, and the leading citizens all heard Paul’s message. God reaches out to the powerful as well as the poor.

Finally, the verse shows the fulfillment of God’s promises. Jesus had promised that Paul would testify before kings. Even in chains, Paul was exactly where God wanted him to be.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers not to be impressed by worldly status. Wealth, power, and fame are temporary. Believers can value what God values: faithfulness, humility, and truth.

It also encourages believers who feel powerless. Paul was a prisoner in chains, yet he had the most important message in the room. Believers do not need status or power to have a meaningful witness. God can use them in any situation.

Finally, the verse invites believers to see every situation as an opportunity for witness. Paul was in chains before a king, yet he used the moment to share the gospel. Believers can look for opportunities to speak about Jesus wherever they find themselves, whether in humble or exalted settings.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Acts 25* shows the importance of integrity. Paul could declare that he had done nothing wrong against the Law, the temple, or Caesar. Believers can seek to live lives of integrity in every area, so that accusations against them have no basis.

The chapter also shows that it can be right to seek justice through legitimate means. Paul appealed to Caesar to avoid an unjust trial and an ambush. Believers facing injustice can use legal rights and protections, while being willing to accept just consequences for any real wrongdoing.

*Acts 25* highlights the center of the Christian faith: Jesus, who was dead, is alive. Even a perplexed Roman governor recognized that this was the heart of the matter. Believers can keep the resurrection at the center of their faith and witness, and patiently help others consider this all-important question.

Finally, the chapter contrasts worldly glory with true greatness. Agrippa and Bernice entered with great pomp, while Paul came in chains. Yet Paul had the message of eternal life. Believers can refuse to be impressed by status, trust that God’s promises are being fulfilled even in difficult circumstances, and look for opportunities to share Christ before people of every rank.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord God, thank You that You rule over governors, kings, and courts, and that You work through them to accomplish Your purposes. Help me to live with integrity in every area of my life, so that I can stand before others with a clear conscience. When I face injustice, give me wisdom to seek fair treatment and courage to stand firm. Thank You that Jesus, who was dead, is alive. Keep this truth at the center of my faith, and help me to share it with those who are perplexed by it. Guard me from being impressed by worldly pomp and status, and help me to value what You value. Whether I stand among the powerful or the powerless, give me courage to speak of Jesus. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
