Acts · Chapter 26 of 28

# Acts — Chapter 26

Chapter Theme: From Darkness to Light: Paul’s Testimony before King Agrippa

[Read Acts 26 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/ACT26.htm)

Main Teaching

Before King Agrippa, Bernice, Festus, and the leaders of Caesarea, Paul tells his story once more. He explains that he stands on trial for Israel’s hope in the resurrection, describes his former fury against the followers of Jesus, and recounts how the risen Lord confronted him and sent him to open the eyes of the nations, turning them from darkness to light and from Satan’s power to God. Festus shouts that Paul is out of his mind, but Paul appeals to Agrippa’s belief in the prophets. Agrippa asks whether Paul thinks he can make him a Christian so quickly, and Paul answers that he prays all his hearers would become as he is, except for his chains. The rulers agree that he has done nothing deserving death.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Acts 26* contains Paul’s final and fullest defense in Acts, and the third account of his conversion (see also *Acts 9* and 22). This telling is shaped for a royal audience. King Agrippa II was knowledgeable about Jewish customs and the Scriptures, so Paul speaks to him as someone who could understand. Paul also emphasizes his commission to the Gentiles and the content of his message more fully than in the earlier accounts.

The scene fulfills Jesus’ words that Paul would bear His name “before the nations and kings, and the children of Israel” (*9:15*), and that His followers would be brought before kings and governors for His name’s sake, as a testimony to them (*Luke 21:12–13*). Although Paul is technically defending himself, his speech is really a presentation of the gospel. He ends not by asking for release, but by inviting the king to believe.

The events of the Damascus road are studied at *Acts 9* and *Acts 22*. The studies below focus on what this telling adds.

### Paul’s Introduction (*26:1–3*)

Agrippa gave Paul permission to speak. Paul “*stretched out his hand*” (*v. 1*), a gesture used by orators to begin a speech. He said that he considered himself fortunate to make his defense before Agrippa, “*especially because you are expert in all customs and questions which are among the Jews*” (*v. 3*). He asked the king to listen patiently.

### Paul’s Life as a Pharisee and the Hope of Israel (*26:4–8*)

Paul reminded his audience that his life had been well known from his youth in Jerusalem. He had lived as a Pharisee, “*after the strictest sect of our religion*” (*v. 5*). Now he was on trial “*for the hope of the promise made by God to our fathers*” (*v. 6*), the hope that the twelve tribes served God day and night to attain. That hope was the coming of the Messiah and the resurrection of the dead. Paul’s question about the resurrection is studied below.

### Paul’s Former Hostility (*26:9–11*)

Paul confessed his past openly: “*I myself most certainly thought that I ought to do many things contrary to the name of Jesus of Nazareth*” (*v. 9*). He imprisoned many believers on the authority of the chief priests, and “*when they were put to death I gave my vote against them*” (*v. 10*). This may mean that Paul was a member of a council that voted for executions, or it may be a way of saying that he approved of them. He punished believers in synagogues and tried to force them to blaspheme, that is, to deny or curse Jesus. “*Being exceedingly enraged against them, I persecuted them even to foreign cities*” (*v. 11*).

### The Heavenly Vision (*26:12–18*)

Paul again described the light on the road to Damascus, “*brighter than the sun*” (*v. 13*), and the voice speaking in Hebrew (Aramaic). This account adds a phrase, studied below. Jesus’ commission to Paul, recorded here more fully than in the other accounts, is also studied below.

### Paul’s Obedience and Message (*26:19–23*)

“*Therefore, King Agrippa, I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision*” (*v. 19*). Paul had obeyed. He preached first in Damascus, then in Jerusalem, throughout Judea, and to the Gentiles, “*that they should repent and turn to God, doing works worthy of repentance*” (*v. 20*). Repentance is shown in a changed life. John the Baptist had taught the same: “*Therefore produce fruits worthy of repentance*” (*Luke 3:8*).

For this reason, Paul said, the Jews had seized him in the temple and tried to kill him. But “*Having therefore obtained the help that is from God, I stand to this day testifying both to small and great*” (*v. 22*). Paul had spoken to the humble and the powerful alike, and now he was speaking to a king. His message was nothing new; it was “*nothing but what the prophets and Moses said would happen*” (*v. 22*): “*how the Christ must suffer, and how, by the resurrection of the dead, he would be first to proclaim light both to these people and to the Gentiles*” (*v. 23*).

### Festus Interrupts (*26:24–27*)

At this point, Festus interrupted loudly: “*Paul, you are crazy! Your great learning is driving you insane!*” (*v. 24*) To a Roman, the idea of a crucified Messiah who rose from the dead and brought light to the nations sounded like madness. Paul wrote that the message of the cross is “*foolishness to Greeks*” (*1 Corinthians 1:23*).

Paul answered respectfully: “*I am not crazy, most excellent Festus, but boldly declare words of truth and reasonableness*” (*v. 25*). The gospel is not irrational; it is true and reasonable. Paul then turned to Agrippa: “*For the king knows of these things, to whom also I speak freely. For I am persuaded that none of these things is hidden from him, for this has not been done in a corner*” (*v. 26*). The events of Jesus’ life, death, and resurrection, and the growth of the church, were public knowledge. They had not happened in secret. Christianity rests on historical events that could be investigated.

Then Paul asked the king directly, “*King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know that you believe*” (*v. 27*). Agrippa’s response, and Paul’s reply, are studied below.

### The Verdict (*26:30–32*)

The king, the governor, Bernice, and those with them rose and withdrew. They agreed: “*This man does nothing worthy of death or of bonds*” (*v. 31*). Agrippa said to Festus, “*This man might have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar*” (*v. 32*). Paul’s innocence was confirmed again by the highest authorities. But because he had appealed to Caesar, he would go to Rome, exactly as Jesus had promised.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Acts 26:8* — Why Is It Incredible That God Raises the Dead?

> *“Why is it judged incredible with you if God does raise the dead?”*
>
> — *Acts 26:8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul was making his defense before King Agrippa, the Roman governor Festus, and the leading people of Caesarea. He explained that he had lived as a strict Pharisee and that he was on trial because of the hope God had promised to Israel’s ancestors, the hope that all twelve tribes longed to see fulfilled. That hope was the coming of the Messiah and the resurrection of the dead.

Then Paul asked a direct question: “*Why is it judged incredible with you if God does raise the dead?*” (*v. 8*) The word “you” is plural; Paul was addressing the whole audience, perhaps especially the Gentiles who found the idea of resurrection hard to believe.

Paul’s question went to the heart of the matter. Why should it seem impossible that God could raise the dead? If God created the universe and gave life to every living thing, why could He not give life again? The question is not whether resurrection is possible for humans, but whether it is possible for God.

Paul’s audience included people with different views. Agrippa was Jewish and familiar with the hope of resurrection. The Romans generally did not believe in bodily resurrection; many thought the soul might live on, but the body was gone forever. Paul challenged them all to consider the power of God.

This question prepared the way for Paul’s testimony. He had met Jesus, who had been raised from the dead. The resurrection was not a theory to him; it was the reason his whole life had changed.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that the resurrection is a matter of God’s power. Jesus told the Sadducees, who denied the resurrection, “*Isn’t this because you are mistaken, not knowing the Scriptures nor the power of God?*” (*Mark 12:24*) Those who believe in a Creator God have every reason to believe He can raise the dead.

It also shows that the resurrection is the fulfillment of Israel’s hope. Paul did not present it as a new idea. God had promised it through the prophets (*Isaiah 26:19*; *Daniel 12:2*; *Ezekiel 37*). Jesus’ resurrection was the first fruits of the resurrection of all God’s people (*1 Corinthians 15:20*).

Finally, the verse invites honest reflection. Many people dismiss the resurrection as impossible without considering who God is. Paul’s question challenges them to think again. If God exists, the resurrection is not incredible; it is exactly what we might expect from the Author of life.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to have confidence in the resurrection. In a world that often doubts the supernatural, believers can rest in the power of God, who raised Jesus and will raise His people.

It also gives believers a helpful question to ask others. When people say the resurrection is impossible, believers can gently ask Paul’s question: Why is it incredible that God could raise the dead? This can open a conversation about who God is.

Finally, the verse offers hope to those facing death or grieving loved ones. The God who raised Jesus has the power to raise all who belong to Him. Death is not the end.

### *Acts 26:14* — Kicking Against the Goads

> *“When we had all fallen to the earth, I heard a voice saying to me in the Hebrew language, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads.””*
>
> — *Acts 26:14* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul was retelling the story of his conversion to King Agrippa. He described the blinding light on the road to Damascus at noon, brighter than the sun. He and his companions fell to the ground.

“*I heard a voice saying to me in the Hebrew language, ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?*” (*v. 14*) Paul noted that the voice spoke in Hebrew (likely Aramaic), his native language. Jesus spoke to him personally.

Then Paul added something not recorded in the earlier accounts: “*It is hard for you to kick against the goads.*” (*v. 14*) A “goad” was a sharp pointed stick used by farmers to drive oxen. If an ox kicked against the goad, it would only hurt itself. This was a common proverb in the Greek world, meaning that it is useless and painful to resist a power greater than oneself.

What did Jesus mean? He was telling Paul that by persecuting the church, Paul was fighting against God, and it was only hurting himself. Some interpreters also think the phrase suggests that God had been working on Paul’s conscience before this moment. Perhaps Paul had been troubled by Stephen’s death, by the courage of the believers he persecuted, or by the Scriptures that pointed to a suffering Messiah. He may have been resisting these “goads” as he raged against the church.

Paul had been “exceedingly enraged” against the believers (*26:11*). Sometimes, the fiercer a person’s opposition, the more they are fighting against an inner conviction.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that resisting God is ultimately futile and painful. God is sovereign, and His purposes will prevail. Gamaliel had warned the council that if this movement was from God, they would find themselves fighting against God (*5:39*). Paul was doing exactly that, and it was harming him.

It also shows God’s patient pursuit of those who resist Him. God was not merely punishing Paul; He was calling him. The goads were meant to direct him, not to destroy him. God pursues people even when they run from Him, as He pursued Jonah and as the father waited for the prodigal son.

Finally, the verse reveals the inner struggle that can lie behind hostility to faith. Paul’s violent persecution may have been partly a way of silencing his own doubts. People who oppose the gospel most fiercely may sometimes be closest to the truth.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites everyone to consider whether they are resisting God. Some people sense God’s call, the conviction of their conscience, or the truth of the gospel, but they push back against it. Jesus’ words apply: resisting God only brings pain. Surrendering to Him brings freedom.

It also encourages believers to pray for those who oppose the faith. Paul was the fiercest opponent of the early church, yet God was at work in him. Believers can pray with hope for those who seem hostile, trusting that God may be “goading” their hearts.

Finally, the verse encourages believers to respond to God’s guidance in their own lives. Even believers can resist God’s direction in areas such as forgiveness, obedience, or calling. Believers can ask God to show them where they are resisting Him and give them grace to yield.

### *Acts 26:18* — From Darkness to Light

> *“to open their eyes, that they may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, that they may receive remission of sins and an inheritance among those who are sanctified by faith in me.’”*
>
> — *Acts 26:18* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul was telling King Agrippa what Jesus said to him on the road to Damascus. Jesus told him to stand up, because He had appeared to appoint him as a servant and a witness. Jesus promised to rescue him from both his own people and the Gentiles, to whom He was sending him. Then Jesus described Paul’s mission.

“*to open their eyes*” (*v. 18*). People without Christ are spiritually blind. They cannot see the truth about God. Paul’s message would open their eyes. Paul himself had been physically blinded and then received his sight, a picture of what happens spiritually when someone comes to Christ.

“*that they may turn from darkness to light*” (*v. 18*). Darkness represents sin, ignorance, and separation from God. Light represents truth, holiness, and life with God. Conversion is a turning from one realm to the other. Jesus is the light of the world (*John 8:12*).

“*and from the power of Satan to God*” (*v. 18*). Before coming to Christ, people are under the power of Satan, the enemy of God. Through the gospel, they are rescued and brought under the loving rule of God. Paul later wrote that God “*delivered us out of the power of darkness, and translated us into the Kingdom of the Son of his love*” (*Colossians 1:13*).

“*that they may receive remission of sins*” (*v. 18*). Those who turn to God receive forgiveness. Their sins are released and cancelled.

“*and an inheritance among those who are sanctified by faith in me*” (*v. 18*). They also receive a share in the inheritance of God’s people, all who have been made holy by faith in Jesus. This inheritance includes eternal life and every blessing God has promised.

Notice the final words: “by faith in me.” All of this comes through faith in Jesus.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse is one of the most complete descriptions of salvation in the New Testament. It includes illumination (eyes opened), conversion (turning from darkness to light), deliverance (from Satan’s power to God), forgiveness (remission of sins), and inheritance (a place among God’s people). All of it comes by faith in Jesus.

It also echoes the mission of God’s Servant in Isaiah, who was to be “*a light for the nations*” (*Isaiah 42:6*) and “*to open the blind eyes, to bring the prisoners out of the dungeon*” (*Isaiah 42:7*). Paul’s mission was a participation in the mission of Jesus, the true Servant.

Finally, the verse shows the reality of spiritual warfare. Salvation is not merely a change of opinion but a rescue from one kingdom to another. The gospel has the power to set people free from the power of Satan.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse helps believers understand what God has done for them. They were once in darkness, under Satan’s power, guilty of sin. Now their eyes have been opened, they live in the light, they belong to God, they are forgiven, and they have an inheritance. This should fill believers with gratitude and joy.

It also clarifies the mission of the church. Believers are called to share the gospel so that others’ eyes may be opened and they may turn from darkness to light. This is the most important work believers can do.

Finally, the verse gives hope to anyone who feels trapped in darkness. No one is too far gone. Through faith in Jesus, anyone can be brought from darkness to light, from Satan’s power to God, and receive forgiveness and a place among God’s people.

### *Acts 26:28–29* — “Become Such as I Am, Except for These Bonds”

> *“Agrippa said to Paul, ‘With a little persuasion are you trying to make me a Christian?’ Paul said, ‘I pray to God, that whether with little or with much, not only you, but also all that hear me today, might become such as I am, except for these bonds.’”*
>
> — *Acts 26:28–29* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had just asked King Agrippa directly, “Do you believe the prophets? I know that you believe.” This put Agrippa in a difficult position. If he said yes, Paul would argue that the prophets pointed to Jesus. If he said no, he would lose credibility with his Jewish subjects.

Agrippa avoided a direct answer: “*With a little persuasion are you trying to make me a Christian?*” (*v. 28*) The Greek can also be read as “In a short time you would persuade me to become a Christian?” Agrippa may have been brushing off Paul’s appeal with a joke, or expressing surprise at Paul’s boldness, or perhaps showing that he was more moved than he wanted to admit. Notice that he used the word “Christian,” one of only three times it appears in the New Testament.

Paul’s response was gracious and heartfelt: “*I pray to God, that whether with little or with much, not only you, but also all that hear me today, might become such as I am*” (*v. 29*). Paul did not care whether it took a short time or a long time. He prayed that the king, and everyone present, would become a follower of Jesus as he was.

Then Paul added, “*except for these bonds*” (*v. 29*). Paul was in chains. He wished his hearers to share his faith, his joy, his hope, and his forgiveness, but not his chains. Even as a prisoner, Paul considered himself more blessed than the king.

This was the high point of Paul’s defense. He was not asking for his own release. He was asking for the salvation of the people judging him.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show the heart of a true witness. Paul’s greatest desire was not his own freedom but others’ salvation. He wrote to the Romans, “*Brothers, my heart’s desire and my prayer to God is for Israel, that they may be saved*” (*Romans 10:1*). Paul’s love for people drove his witness, even in chains.

They also show that true freedom is found in Christ. Paul was physically bound, yet spiritually free. Agrippa was physically free and powerful, yet spiritually needy. Paul knew that knowing Christ was worth more than any earthly position. He wrote, “*I count all things to be a loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus, my Lord*” (*Philippians 3:8*).

Finally, Agrippa’s response shows how people can be close to faith but not come to it. He was familiar with the Scriptures and had heard the gospel clearly. Yet he deflected. Being “almost persuaded” is not the same as believing.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to love others enough to share Christ with them. Paul wanted everyone who heard him to become a Christian. Believers can ask God for the same desire for others’ salvation, praying for and speaking to people of every status.

They also remind believers of the treasure they have in Christ. Even when believers face hardship, illness, or loss, they possess something more valuable than anything the world can offer. Believers can rejoice in their faith even in difficult circumstances.

Finally, these verses challenge anyone who is “almost persuaded.” Agrippa heard the truth but did not respond. Those who have heard the gospel and are close to believing are invited not to delay, but to trust Christ fully.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Acts 26* shows the power of a changed life. Paul told the king how he had once raged against Jesus’ followers, and how the risen Lord had met him and transformed him. Every believer has a story of what God has done. Believers can share their testimony honestly, as Paul did, pointing to Jesus as the One who changed them.

The chapter also challenges people to take the resurrection seriously. Paul asked, “Why is it judged incredible with you if God does raise the dead?” The God who created life can give life again. Believers can rest in this hope and invite others to consider it.

*Acts 26* describes salvation in rich terms: eyes opened, darkness turned to light, freedom from Satan’s power, forgiveness of sins, and an inheritance among God’s people, all by faith in Jesus. Believers can rejoice in what God has done for them and join in His mission to bring others from darkness to light, calling them to repent and live lives that show their repentance.

Finally, the chapter shows the heart of true witness. Paul did not ask for his own release; he prayed that everyone who heard him would become as he was, except for his chains. Believers can ask God for this kind of love, sharing the gospel with people of every status, and inviting those who are “almost persuaded” to trust Christ fully.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for meeting Paul on the road to Damascus and for meeting me. Thank You for opening my eyes, turning me from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, forgiving my sins, and giving me an inheritance among Your people. I believe that God raises the dead, because You are risen. Where I have been kicking against the goads and resisting You, help me to yield to Your will. Give me courage to tell my story of what You have done, and to speak the truth boldly and reasonably. Fill my heart with Paul’s love for others, so that I long for everyone I meet to know You as I do. For those who are almost persuaded, I pray that they would come to You fully. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Acts · Chapter 27 of 28

# Acts — Chapter 27

Chapter Theme: Faith in the Storm: “I Believe God”

[Read Acts 27 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/ACT27.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul sails for Rome as a prisoner under a centurion named Julius. Against Paul’s warning, the ship leaves harbor late in the season and is caught in a violent storm that rages for two weeks, until all hope of being saved is gone. Paul stands among the terrified crew and passengers and tells them to take courage, because an angel of God has promised that all 276 aboard will survive. He prevents the sailors from abandoning ship, urges everyone to eat, gives thanks to God before them all, and breaks bread. The ship runs aground and breaks apart, but the centurion spares the prisoners for Paul’s sake, and everyone reaches land safely.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Acts 27* is one of the most detailed accounts of a sea voyage that survives from the ancient world. Luke writes in the first person (“we”), showing that he was on board. His descriptions of the route, the winds, the ship’s handling, and the nautical procedures are so precise that historians and sailors have studied this chapter to understand ancient navigation. One nineteenth-century sailor and scholar, James Smith, retraced the voyage and found Luke’s details accurate down to the depth soundings near Malta.

But the chapter is more than an exciting travel story. It shows God fulfilling His promise that Paul would testify in Rome (*23:11*), and it shows how a believer can respond to danger with faith, courage, and practical wisdom. Paul, the prisoner, becomes the true leader on the ship.

### Setting Out for Italy (*27:1–8*)

Paul and other prisoners were handed over to “*a centurion named Julius, of the Augustan band*” (*v. 1*). They sailed from Caesarea on a ship from Adramyttium, a port on the northwest coast of Asia Minor. Aristarchus from Thessalonica, who had been with Paul in Ephesus (*19:29*), came along, as did Luke.

At Sidon, “*Julius treated Paul kindly and gave him permission to go to his friends and refresh himself*” (*v. 3*). Throughout the voyage, Julius showed respect for Paul. The winds were against them, so they sailed along the coast to Myra, in Lycia, where Julius found “*a ship of Alexandria sailing for Italy*” (*v. 6*). This was probably a grain ship; Egypt supplied much of Rome’s grain, and the government contracted with private ships to carry it.

The sailing was slow and difficult. They reached Fair Havens, on the south coast of Crete.

### Paul’s Warning Ignored (*27:9–12*)

“*When much time had passed and the voyage was now dangerous because the Fast had now already gone by*” (*v. 9*). “The Fast” was the Day of Atonement, which fell in late September or October. Sailing on the Mediterranean was considered dangerous from mid-September to early November and was generally avoided from November to March.

Paul warned, “*Sirs, I perceive that the voyage will be with injury and much loss, not only of the cargo and the ship, but also of our lives*” (*v. 10*). Paul was an experienced traveler; he had already been shipwrecked three times (*2 Corinthians 11:25*). But “*the centurion gave more heed to the master and to the owner of the ship than to those things which were spoken by Paul*” (*v. 11*). It was natural to trust the professionals. The harbor at Fair Havens was not suitable for spending the winter, so the majority decided to try to reach Phoenix, a better harbor farther west on Crete.

### The Storm (*27:13–20*)

A gentle south wind made them think they could make it. But soon “*a stormy wind beat down from shore, which is called Euroclydon*” (*v. 14*), a violent northeasterly wind. The ship was caught and could not head into the wind, so they let it be driven along.

Behind a small island called Clauda (Cauda), they managed to secure the lifeboat, which was being towed behind the ship. They passed ropes under the ship to hold it together, a technique called “undergirding.” Fearing they would run aground on the Syrtis, dangerous sandbars off the coast of North Africa, they lowered the sea anchor (or the sails) and let the ship be driven.

The storm continued. The next day they threw cargo overboard. The third day they threw out the ship’s tackle with their own hands. Then came a moment of despair, studied below.

### Paul’s Message of Hope (*27:21–26*)

After a long time without food, Paul stood up among them. He began by gently reminding them that they should have listened to him, not to say “I told you so,” but to give credibility to what he was about to say. His message of hope is studied below.

### Approaching Land (*27:27–38*)

On the fourteenth night, as they were driven across the Adriatic Sea (the ancient name included the sea between Greece, Italy, and Africa), the sailors sensed they were nearing land, perhaps hearing breakers. They took soundings: twenty fathoms (about 120 feet), then fifteen fathoms (about 90 feet). Fearing they would hit rocks, they dropped four anchors from the stern and prayed for daylight.

The sailors’ attempt to escape, and Paul’s response, are studied below. As dawn approached, Paul urged everyone to eat, which is also studied below. Luke notes that there were “*two hundred seventy-six souls on the ship*” (*v. 37*). After eating, they lightened the ship further by throwing the grain into the sea.

### Shipwreck (*27:39–44*)

At daylight, they did not recognize the land, but they saw a bay with a beach. They cut the anchors, loosened the steering oars, raised the foresail, and headed for the beach. But “*coming to a place where two seas met, they ran the vessel aground*” (*v. 41*), probably a sandbar between two channels. The bow stuck fast, and the stern began to break apart in the pounding waves.

The soldiers planned to kill the prisoners so that none would escape. Under Roman law, guards who allowed prisoners to escape could face the same penalty the prisoners would have received. “*But the centurion, desiring to save Paul, stopped them from their purpose*” (*v. 43*). Julius had come to respect Paul. Because of Paul, all the prisoners were spared. Those who could swim jumped overboard first; the rest followed on planks and pieces of the ship. “*So they all escaped safely to the land*” (*v. 44*). God’s promise was fulfilled exactly: every life was saved, but the ship was lost.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Acts 27:20* — All Hope Was Taken Away

> *“When neither sun nor stars shone on us for many days, and no small storm pressed on us, all hope that we would be saved was now taken away.”*
>
> — *Acts 27:20* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The ship carrying Paul had been caught in a violent storm off the coast of Crete. For days, it had been driven by the wind, completely out of control. The crew had tied ropes around the ship to keep it from breaking apart, thrown cargo overboard, and even thrown away the ship’s equipment with their own hands. Nothing seemed to help.

“*When neither sun nor stars shone on us for many days*” (*v. 20*). Ancient sailors navigated by the sun during the day and the stars at night. Without them, the crew had no way of knowing where they were or which direction they were going. They were lost in the darkness and the storm.

“*and no small storm pressed on us*” (*v. 20*). The storm did not let up. It kept battering them day after day.

“*all hope that we would be saved was now taken away*” (*v. 20*). Luke, who was on the ship, includes himself in this despair. Everyone on board, the sailors, soldiers, prisoners, and passengers, had given up hope of survival. They expected to die.

This verse is honest about the reality of despair. Luke does not pretend that the believers on board felt no fear or hopelessness. Even people of faith can reach moments when circumstances seem completely hopeless.

Yet this moment of total despair was the moment God chose to speak hope through Paul.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that believers are not exempt from life’s storms. Paul was on a mission from God, traveling to Rome as Jesus had promised. Yet he still faced a terrible storm. Following God’s will does not guarantee calm seas. Jesus’ disciples also faced a storm while obeying His command to cross the lake (*Mark 4:35–41*).

It also shows that despair is a real human experience. Paul himself once wrote of being “*weighed down exceedingly, beyond our power, so much that we despaired even of life*” (*2 Corinthians 1:8*). Scripture does not shame those who feel hopeless; it meets them there.

Finally, the verse shows that God often speaks hope at the darkest moment. When all hope was gone, God gave a message of rescue. *Psalm 107* describes sailors in a storm who cried to the Lord: “*He makes the storm a calm, so that its waves are still*” (*Psalm 107:29*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse speaks to anyone who feels that all hope is gone. Some people face illness, loss, financial ruin, broken relationships, or depression so deep that they cannot see any way forward. Luke’s honesty shows that such feelings are part of human experience. Those who feel this way can bring their despair to God, and they should also seek help from others, including trusted believers, counselors, and doctors.

It also reminds believers that times of darkness do not mean God has abandoned them. The sun and stars were hidden, but they still existed. In the same way, God is still present and at work even when believers cannot see Him.

Finally, the verse encourages believers to be ready to bring hope to others. Paul was in the same storm, yet he became a source of hope for everyone on board. Believers who are suffering can still point others to God’s promises.

### *Acts 27:23–25* — “I Believe God”

> *“For there stood by me this night an angel, belonging to the God whose I am and whom I serve, saying, “Don’t be afraid, Paul. You must stand before Caesar. Behold, God has granted you all those who sail with you.” Therefore, sirs, cheer up! For I believe God, that it will be just as it has been spoken to me.”*
>
> — *Acts 27:23–25* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After many days in the storm, with everyone on board having given up hope, Paul stood up in the middle of the crew and passengers. He reminded them that they should have listened to his earlier warning. Then he said, “*Now I exhort you to cheer up, for there will be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship*” (*v. 22*).

Paul explained why he could be so confident: “*For there stood by me this night an angel, belonging to the God whose I am and whom I serve*” (*v. 23*). Notice how Paul described God: “whose I am and whom I serve.” Paul belonged to God, and he served God. In a ship full of people who worshiped many gods, Paul spoke of the one true God to whom he belonged.

The angel’s message: “*Don’t be afraid, Paul. You must stand before Caesar. Behold, God has granted you all those who sail with you.*” (*v. 24*) God’s purpose for Paul had not changed. He “must” stand before Caesar. The storm could not prevent it. And God had “granted” to Paul the lives of everyone on the ship. This suggests that Paul had been praying for them, and God had answered.

Then Paul said, “*Therefore, sirs, cheer up! For I believe God, that it will be just as it has been spoken to me*” (*v. 25*). This is the heart of the passage. Paul’s courage did not come from the weather, the ship, or the skill of the sailors. It came from trusting God’s word. “I believe God.”

Paul added, “*But we must run aground on a certain island*” (*v. 26*). God’s promise did not mean the journey would be easy. The ship would be wrecked. But everyone would live.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show the nature of faith: trusting God’s word even when circumstances seem to contradict it. The storm was still raging, and no one could see a way to survive. Yet Paul believed God. Abraham was described in the same way: “*Yet, looking to the promise of God, he didn’t waver through unbelief, but grew strong through faith, giving glory to God*” (*Romans 4:20*).

They also show the identity of a believer. Paul belonged to God and served God. This gave him stability in the storm. Believers who know whose they are can face any circumstance with confidence.

Finally, these verses show God’s mercy to unbelievers through His people. God spared everyone on the ship for Paul’s sake. Throughout Scripture, God blesses others through His people, as He blessed the nations through Abraham (*Genesis 12:3*) and spared cities for the sake of the righteous (*Genesis 18:26*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to anchor their faith in God’s word. In times of trouble, believers can hold on to God’s promises in Scripture. Like Paul, they can say, “*I believe God, that it will be just as it has been spoken to me*” (*v. 25*).

They also encourage believers to remember whose they are. Believers belong to God and serve Him. This identity gives them security and purpose in every storm.

Finally, these verses encourage believers to be sources of hope for others. Paul’s faith gave courage to everyone on board. Believers can share God’s promises with those around them who are afraid, offering hope rooted in God’s faithfulness.

### *Acts 27:31* — “*Unless These Stay in the Ship*” (*v. 31*)

> *“Paul said to the centurion and to the soldiers, ‘Unless these stay in the ship, you can’t be saved.’”*
>
> — *Acts 27:31* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

On the fourteenth night of the storm, the sailors sensed they were near land. They took soundings and found the water getting shallower. Fearing they would be wrecked on rocks in the dark, they dropped four anchors from the back of the ship and waited for daylight.

Then the sailors secretly tried to escape. “*As the sailors were trying to flee out of the ship and had lowered the boat into the sea, pretending that they would lay out anchors from the bow*” (*v. 30*). They lowered the lifeboat into the water, pretending they were going to drop more anchors from the front of the ship. In reality, they planned to row to shore and leave everyone else behind.

Paul noticed what was happening. He said to the centurion and the soldiers, “*Unless these stay in the ship, you can’t be saved*” (*v. 31*). The sailors were needed. Without their skill, no one would be able to bring the ship to land safely.

“*Then the soldiers cut away the ropes of the boat and let it fall off*” (*v. 32*). The soldiers acted immediately. They cut the ropes, and the lifeboat drifted away. Now everyone had to stay together.

This verse shows an interesting balance. God had promised that everyone would survive. Yet Paul still said, “Unless these stay in the ship, you can’t be saved.” God’s promise did not mean that human actions were unimportant. God would save them, but He would do it through the sailors’ skill and everyone’s cooperation.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows the relationship between God’s sovereignty and human responsibility. God had promised to save everyone, but He would accomplish it through human means. Faith in God’s promises does not mean doing nothing. It means acting wisely and faithfully, trusting God to work through those actions. Paul wrote, “*work out your own salvation with fear and trembling*” (*Philippians 2:12*), “*for it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure*” (*Philippians 2:13*).

It also shows the importance of community. Everyone on the ship needed one another. The sailors needed the others, and the others needed the sailors. No one could be saved by abandoning the group. The church is also a community in which believers need one another (*1 Corinthians 12:21*).

Finally, the verse shows Paul’s practical wisdom. Paul was not only a man of prayer and faith; he was also alert and practical. Faith and common sense work together.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to act responsibly while trusting God. Trusting God’s promises does not mean neglecting wise action. Believers can pray for healing and also see a doctor, pray for provision and also work, pray for safety and also take precautions.

It also encourages believers to stay committed to their communities. In difficult times, it can be tempting to abandon others and look out only for oneself. Paul’s words remind believers that they are bound together, and that faithfulness includes standing with others.

Finally, the verse encourages believers to be alert. Paul noticed the sailors’ deception and acted. Believers can pay attention to what is happening around them and speak up when others are in danger.

### *Acts 27:35* — He Gave Thanks to God in the Presence of All

> *“When he had said this and had taken bread, he gave thanks to God in the presence of all; then he broke it and began to eat.”*
>
> — *Acts 27:35* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

It was just before dawn on the fourteenth day of the storm. Everyone on the ship had been too afraid, seasick, or busy to eat properly for two weeks. They were exhausted and weak. Soon they would need all their strength to reach the shore.

Paul urged them to eat: “*Therefore I beg you to take some food, for this is for your safety; for not a hair will perish from any of your heads*” (*v. 34*). Paul cared about their physical needs. He repeated God’s promise that they would all be safe.

“*When he had said this and had taken bread, he gave thanks to God in the presence of all; then he broke it and began to eat*” (*v. 35*). Paul took bread, gave thanks to God, broke it, and ate. He did this publicly, in front of all 276 people, most of whom did not share his faith. In the middle of a storm, on a ship that was about to be wrecked, Paul thanked God.

Paul’s actions echo the way Jesus took bread, gave thanks, and broke it (*Luke 9:16*; *22:19*; *24:30*). This was not the Lord’s Supper, since most on board were not believers, but it was a meal marked by thanksgiving to God.

“*Then they all cheered up, and they also took food*” (*v. 36*). Paul’s faith and example encouraged everyone. They began to eat, and their spirits lifted.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows the power of thanksgiving in difficult times. Paul thanked God before the rescue had happened. He trusted God’s promise enough to give thanks in advance. Paul later wrote, “*In everything give thanks, for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus toward you*” (*1 Thessalonians 5:18*).

It also shows that faith can be a public witness. Paul gave thanks “in the presence of all.” He was not ashamed of his faith before soldiers, sailors, and prisoners. His simple act of thanksgiving pointed everyone to the God he trusted.

Finally, the verse shows that God cares for physical needs. Paul urged everyone to eat for their survival. Spiritual faith and practical care go together. God created human bodies and cares for their needs.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to give thanks to God even in hard times. Thanksgiving is not only for when life is going well. Believers can thank God for His presence, His promises, and the good gifts He provides, even in the middle of storms.

It also encourages believers to let their faith be seen. Paul gave thanks publicly. Believers can pray before meals, speak of God’s goodness, and live in a way that shows their trust in Him, even among people who do not share their faith.

Finally, the verse encourages believers to care for others’ practical needs. Paul made sure everyone ate. Believers can show God’s love by meeting the physical needs of those around them, especially in times of crisis.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Acts 27* shows that believers are not exempt from life’s storms. Paul was traveling according to God’s plan, yet he faced a terrible storm, darkness, and despair. Believers today may also face trials that seem overwhelming. This chapter assures them that God is present in the storm and that His purposes cannot be defeated.

The chapter also shows the power of faith in God’s word. When all hope was gone, Paul stood up and said, “I believe God, that it will be just as it has been spoken to me.” Believers can anchor themselves in God’s promises, remember whose they are and whom they serve, and offer that hope to others who are afraid.

*Acts 27* teaches that faith and responsible action go together. God had promised to save everyone, yet Paul insisted that the sailors stay on the ship and that everyone eat. Believers can trust God while acting wisely, staying committed to their communities, and caring for practical needs.

Finally, the chapter shows the witness of thanksgiving. Paul gave thanks to God in front of everyone before the rescue had come, and his example gave courage to all. Believers can give thanks in every circumstance, letting their trust in God be visible, and becoming, as Paul did, a source of hope and steadiness for those around them.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord God, You are the God to whom I belong and whom I serve. Thank You that You are present in every storm. When the sun and stars are hidden and all hope seems gone, help me to remember Your promises and to say with Paul, “I believe God.” Give me courage to bring hope to others who are afraid. Help me to trust You while acting wisely and responsibly, and to stand with others in hard times rather than looking out only for myself. Teach me to give thanks in every circumstance, even before I see Your rescue. Let my faith be visible to those around me, so that they too may take courage. Thank You that Your purposes cannot be defeated by any storm. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Acts · Chapter 28 of 28

# Acts — Chapter 28

Chapter Theme: Rome at Last: Boldly and Without Hindrance

[Read Acts 28 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/ACT28.htm)

Main Teaching

Shipwrecked on Malta, Paul and his companions are welcomed with unusual kindness. Paul survives a viper’s bite, heals the father of the island’s chief official and many others, and the islanders send them on with supplies. Arriving in Italy, Paul is met by believers from Rome, thanks God, and takes courage. In Rome, under house arrest, he meets with Jewish leaders and spends a whole day explaining Jesus from the Law and the Prophets. Some believe and some do not. The book closes with Paul living two years in his rented house, welcoming all who come, and proclaiming the kingdom of God and the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness, without hindrance.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Acts 28* completes Luke’s two-volume work. The Gospel of Luke began in Jerusalem with the announcement of Jesus’ birth; Acts ends in Rome, the capital of the empire, with the gospel being freely proclaimed. Jesus had said that His witnesses would go “to the uttermost parts of the earth” (*1:8*). Rome was not the end of the earth, but it was the center of the known world, and from there the gospel would spread in every direction.

The ending of Acts surprises many readers. We are not told the outcome of Paul’s trial before Caesar or how Paul died. Instead, Luke ends with Paul preaching freely. This open ending suggests that the story of Acts is not finished. The work of the Spirit through the church continues, and every generation of believers takes up the task.

### Kindness on Malta (*28:1–10*)

After the shipwreck, the survivors learned that they were on Malta, an island south of Sicily. Malta lies about 600 miles from Crete, the distance the ship had been driven by the storm. “*The natives showed us uncommon kindness; for they kindled a fire and received us all, because of the present rain and because of the cold*” (*v. 2*). The word Luke uses for the islanders is “barbarians,” which in Greek simply meant people who did not speak Greek. They welcomed 276 cold, wet, exhausted strangers with remarkable hospitality.

Paul, the great apostle, did not stand idle. He gathered sticks for the fire. When he laid them on the fire, “*a viper came out because of the heat and fastened on his hand*” (*v. 3*). The islanders assumed Paul must be a murderer. He had escaped the sea, but “*Justice has not allowed to live*” (*v. 4*). “Justice” (Dike) was a Greek goddess of justice and vengeance. The islanders believed that the gods would not let a guilty man escape. But Paul “*shook off the creature into the fire, and wasn’t harmed*” (*v. 5*). Jesus had promised His disciples that they would have authority over serpents (*Luke 10:19*). The islanders waited for him to swell up or drop dead. When nothing happened, “*they changed their minds and said that he was a god*” (*v. 6*). Their opinions swung from one extreme to the other, much as the people of Lystra had once tried to worship Paul (*Acts 14:11–18*).

Nearby was the estate of “*the chief man of the island, named Publius*” (*v. 7*), who welcomed them and entertained them for three days. An inscription found on Malta uses the same title, “chief man,” for the island’s Roman official, confirming Luke’s accuracy. Publius’s father was sick with fever and dysentery. “*Paul entered in to him, prayed, and laying his hands on him, healed him*” (*v. 8*). Notice that Paul prayed first; he made clear that healing came from God. Then the rest of the sick people on the island came and were healed. The islanders honored Paul and his companions and supplied them with what they needed for the journey.

Luke does not record Paul preaching on Malta, but it is likely that the gospel was shared there during the three months they stayed. Christian tradition holds that the church on Malta began with Paul’s visit.

### The Journey to Rome (*28:11–16*)

After three months, at the beginning of spring sailing season, they set sail on another Alexandrian ship that had wintered on the island. Its figurehead was “*The Twin Brothers*” (*v. 11*), Castor and Pollux, sons of Zeus who were believed to protect sailors. Luke may include this detail to contrast these supposed protectors with the true God who had protected them all.

They sailed to Syracuse in Sicily, then to Rhegium at the toe of Italy, and then to Puteoli, a major port near Naples. There they found believers, who urged them to stay a week. The gospel had already reached Italy before Paul.

“*So we came to Rome*” (*v. 14*). Luke states it simply. After years of longing, imprisonment, trials, a storm, and a shipwreck, Paul had arrived. The welcome he received is studied below.

In Rome, Paul “*was allowed to stay by himself with the soldier who guarded him*” (*v. 16*). He lived under house arrest, probably chained to a soldier at all times. The guards would have rotated, so over time many soldiers heard the gospel. Paul later wrote that his imprisonment had become known throughout the whole palace guard (*Philippians 1:13*).

### Paul and the Jewish Leaders in Rome (*28:17–29*)

Three days after arriving, Paul called together the leaders of the Jewish community in Rome. As always, he wanted to share the gospel with his own people first. He explained that he had done nothing against the Jewish people or their customs, but had been handed over to the Romans, who wanted to release him. When the Jewish leaders objected, he had been forced to appeal to Caesar, “*not that I had anything about which to accuse my nation*” (*v. 19*). Paul had no desire to bring charges against his people. “*For because of the hope of Israel I am bound with this chain*” (*v. 20*). The hope of Israel, the Messiah and the resurrection, was the reason for his chains.

The Jewish leaders said they had received no letters from Judea about Paul and no one had spoken against him. But they wanted to hear his views, “*For, as concerning this sect, it is known to us that everywhere it is spoken against*” (*v. 22*). Paul’s day of teaching is studied below.

When they disagreed among themselves and began to leave, Paul quoted *Isaiah 6:9–10*, the same passage Jesus had quoted about those who hear but do not understand (*Matthew 13:14–15*). “*For this people’s heart has grown callous. Their ears are dull of hearing. Their eyes they have closed*” (*v. 27*). Isaiah’s words, spoken centuries earlier, described the hardening of heart that keeps people from receiving God’s message. Paul concluded, “*Be it known therefore to you that the salvation of God is sent to the nations, and they will listen*” (*v. 28*).

This statement does not mean that God had rejected the Jewish people. Some of the Jewish leaders in Rome believed (*28:24*). Paul himself wrote that God has not rejected His people (*Romans 11:1–2*), and that he longed for their salvation (*Romans 10:1*). Throughout Acts, many thousands of Jews believed. But Paul recognized that as many rejected the message, the gospel would go forth to the Gentiles, who would receive it. (Verse 29 appears in some later manuscripts but not the earliest.)

### Two Years in Rome (*28:30–31*)

The final verses of Acts are studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Acts 28:2* — Uncommon Kindness

> *“The natives showed us uncommon kindness; for they kindled a fire and received us all, because of the present rain and because of the cold.”*
>
> — *Acts 28:2* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The ship carrying Paul had broken apart on the coast of an unknown island. All 276 people on board, sailors, soldiers, prisoners, and passengers, had swum or floated to shore on pieces of wreckage. They were soaked, cold, exhausted, and probably injured. It was raining. They had lost everything except their lives.

Then they learned that the island was called Malta. The people living there were not Greeks or Romans. Luke calls them “natives,” people who spoke their own language.

“*The natives showed us uncommon kindness*” (*v. 2*). The islanders could have been suspicious or hostile toward a large group of strangers, including prisoners and soldiers. Instead, they welcomed them warmly. The word translated “uncommon” means unusual or extraordinary. Their kindness went beyond what anyone would expect.

“*for they kindled a fire and received us all, because of the present rain and because of the cold*” (*v. 2*). Their kindness was practical. They built a fire to warm everyone. They “received us all,” welcoming everyone without discrimination. They cared for physical needs in a time of crisis.

Luke, a careful historian, made a point of recording this kindness. These islanders were not believers, yet they showed compassion to strangers in need. Their kindness opened the door for Paul’s ministry of healing on the island.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that kindness can be found among people of all backgrounds. The islanders were not part of God’s covenant people, yet they reflected something of God’s character. All people are made in God’s image (*Genesis 1:27*), and even those who do not know Him can show kindness and mercy. Jesus’ parable of the Good Samaritan shows that compassion can come from unexpected people (*Luke 10:30–37*).

It also shows God’s care for His people through others. God had promised that everyone on the ship would survive. Part of how He fulfilled that promise was through the kindness of the islanders. God often provides for His people through the generosity of others.

Finally, the verse shows the value of hospitality. Scripture repeatedly calls God’s people to welcome strangers. Hebrews says, “*Don’t forget to show hospitality to strangers, for in doing so, some have entertained angels without knowing it*” (*Hebrews 13:2*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to show kindness to strangers, especially those in need. Refugees, immigrants, travelers, and people affected by disasters often arrive with nothing. Believers can follow the islanders’ example of practical, generous welcome.

It also encourages believers to recognize and honor kindness wherever it appears, including among people who do not share their faith. Believers can be grateful for the goodness of others and see it as evidence of God’s common grace.

Finally, the verse reminds believers that small acts of kindness matter. Building a fire on a rainy day may seem simple, but it meant everything to people who had just escaped a shipwreck. Believers can look for practical ways to meet the needs of those around them.

### *Acts 28:15* — He Thanked God and Took Courage

> *“From there the brothers, when they heard of us, came to meet us as far as The Market of Appius and The Three Taverns. When Paul saw them, he thanked God and took courage.”*
>
> — *Acts 28:15* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After three months on Malta, Paul and his companions sailed to Italy. They landed at Puteoli and stayed a week with believers there. Then they traveled by land toward Rome along the Appian Way, the great Roman road.

“*From there the brothers, when they heard of us, came to meet us as far as The Market of Appius and The Three Taverns*” (*v. 15*). Word had reached the believers in Rome that Paul was coming. Some walked out to meet him. The Market of Appius was about forty-three miles from Rome; the Three Taverns was about thirty-three miles away. These believers traveled a long distance on foot to welcome Paul and escort him into the city, the way a city might go out to welcome an honored guest.

Paul had written his letter to the Romans about three years earlier, expressing his longing to visit them (*Romans 1:10–12*; *15:23–24*). He had never met most of them. Now they came out to meet him.

“*When Paul saw them, he thanked God and took courage*” (*v. 15*). Paul was arriving in Rome as a prisoner, facing trial before Caesar. He had been through storms and shipwreck. He may have wondered how he would be received. When he saw these believers who had come so far to welcome him, he thanked God and was encouraged.

Even the great apostle needed encouragement. The love of fellow believers renewed his strength.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows the power of Christian fellowship. Paul was strengthened by the presence and love of other believers. Paul wrote to the Romans, “*that is, that I with you may be encouraged in you, each of us by the other’s faith, both yours and mine*” (*Romans 1:12*). Believers need one another.

It also shows the importance of gratitude. Paul’s first response was to thank God. He recognized that these believers were God’s gift to him. Gratitude often leads to renewed courage.

Finally, the verse shows that even strong believers need encouragement. Paul had faced countless trials with faith and courage. Yet he still needed the support of others. No believer is meant to walk alone.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to support those who are facing difficulties. A visit, a phone call, a meal, or simply showing up can bring great encouragement. The Roman believers walked thirty or forty miles to meet Paul. Believers can make the effort to be present for others.

It also encourages believers to receive encouragement with gratitude. When others show love and support, believers can thank God for them and let that love renew their courage.

Finally, the verse reminds believers that everyone needs encouragement, including leaders. Pastors, missionaries, and other leaders may seem strong, but they also need the support and love of the church. Believers can look for ways to encourage those who serve them.

### *Acts 28:23–24* — Persuading Them Concerning Jesus from Morning until Evening

> *“When they had appointed him a day, many people came to him at his lodging. He explained to them, testifying about God’s Kingdom, and persuading them concerning Jesus, both from the law of Moses and from the prophets, from morning until evening. Some believed the things which were spoken, and some disbelieved.”*
>
> — *Acts 28:23–24* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had met with the leaders of the Jewish community in Rome and explained why he had been arrested. They wanted to hear more about his message, so they set a day to meet with him.

“*When they had appointed him a day, many people came to him at his lodging*” (*v. 23*). Many Jews came to the house where Paul was staying under guard. Even as a prisoner, Paul had a ministry. His home became a place of teaching.

“*He explained to them, testifying about God’s Kingdom, and persuading them concerning Jesus, both from the law of Moses and from the prophets, from morning until evening*” (*v. 23*). Paul spent the whole day teaching. He explained God’s kingdom, the reign of God that Jesus had announced and brought. He tried to persuade them about Jesus, using the Scriptures they knew: the Law of Moses and the Prophets. Paul showed how the Old Testament pointed to Jesus as the Messiah.

This was the same approach Jesus used with the disciples on the road to Emmaus: “*Beginning from Moses and from all the prophets, he explained to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself*” (*Luke 24:27*).

“*Some believed the things which were spoken, and some disbelieved*” (*v. 24*). The response was divided. Some were persuaded and believed in Jesus. Others did not. This mixed response had been typical throughout Paul’s ministry.

Paul’s patience is striking. He spent a whole day explaining and persuading. He did not give up quickly or present a short message. He took time to answer questions and work through the Scriptures with his listeners.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that the gospel is rooted in the Old Testament. Paul did not present Jesus as a new idea but as the fulfillment of everything the Law and the Prophets had promised. Jesus Himself said that the Scriptures testify about Him (*John 5:39*).

They also show the importance of patient, thoughtful evangelism. Paul reasoned and persuaded from morning until evening. He engaged people’s minds as well as their hearts. Peter urges believers to always be ready “*to give an answer to everyone who asks you a reason concerning the hope that is in you, with humility and fear*” (*1 Peter 3:15*).

Finally, these verses show that the same message receives different responses. Paul preached faithfully, but not everyone believed. The outcome depends on God’s work in hearts and on each person’s response. Faithful witnesses are responsible for faithfulness, not for results.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to know the Scriptures well enough to explain how they point to Jesus. Believers can study the Old Testament as well as the New, seeing how the whole Bible tells one story centered on Christ.

They also encourage believers to be patient when sharing their faith. Some people need time to consider the gospel. Believers can take time to listen, answer questions, and explain the Scriptures, rather than expecting quick decisions.

Finally, these verses comfort believers when some reject the message. Not everyone will believe. Believers can share faithfully, trust God with the results, and rejoice over those who do believe.

### *Acts 28:30–31* — With All Boldness, Without Hindrance

> *“Paul stayed two whole years in his own rented house and received all who were coming to him, preaching God’s Kingdom and teaching the things concerning the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness, without hindrance.”*
>
> — *Acts 28:30–31* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These are the final verses of the book of Acts. Paul had arrived in Rome as a prisoner. He was waiting for his trial before Caesar. Luke tells us what Paul did during this time.

“*Paul stayed two whole years in his own rented house*” (*v. 30*). Paul lived in a rented house, guarded by a soldier, for two years. He was not free to travel, but he was able to live in his own lodgings.

“*and received all who were coming to him*” (*v. 30*). Paul welcomed everyone who came to visit. Jews and Gentiles, believers and seekers, friends and strangers came to his house. His home became a center of ministry.

“*preaching God’s Kingdom and teaching the things concerning the Lord Jesus Christ*” (*v. 31*). Paul’s message remained the same as it had been from the beginning: the kingdom of God and the Lord Jesus Christ. Jesus had begun His ministry preaching the kingdom of God (*Luke 4:43*), and Acts began with Jesus teaching about the kingdom (*Acts 1:3*). Now Acts ends with Paul doing the same.

“*with all boldness, without hindrance*” (*v. 31*). The final words of Acts are significant. Paul preached “with all boldness,” with courage and freedom of speech. And he preached “without hindrance.” Even though Paul was in chains, the gospel was not chained. The Roman authorities did not stop him from teaching.

During this time, Paul probably wrote several letters, including Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, and Philemon, often called the Prison Letters. Through these letters, his ministry reached far beyond his rented house.

Luke does not tell us what happened next. Early Christian tradition says that Paul was released, traveled further, was arrested again, and was executed in Rome under Nero around A.D. 64–67. But Luke ends with the gospel going forward, unhindered.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that the gospel cannot be stopped. Paul was imprisoned, yet he preached freely. Paul wrote from prison, “*in which I suffer hardship to the point of chains as a criminal. But God’s word isn’t chained*” (*2 Timothy 2:9*). No human power can bind the word of God.

They also show the faithfulness of God’s promises. Jesus had told Paul that he would testify in Rome (*23:11*). Despite plots, trials, storms, shipwreck, and snakebite, Paul arrived in Rome and testified there. God’s promises are sure.

Finally, the open ending of Acts invites every reader into the story. The book does not end with a final conclusion but with the gospel going forward. The story of the church continues through every generation of believers who carry the message of the kingdom and of Jesus to the world.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers who face limitations. Paul could not travel, yet he used his situation to welcome visitors and write letters. Believers who are limited by illness, age, circumstances, or responsibilities can still serve God where they are, welcoming others and sharing their faith.

They also encourage believers to keep the gospel at the center. Paul’s message never changed: the kingdom of God and the Lord Jesus Christ. Believers can keep their focus on Jesus and His kingdom in all their witness.

Finally, these verses invite believers to see themselves as part of the continuing story of Acts. The Holy Spirit who empowered Peter and Paul still empowers the church today. Believers are called to carry the gospel boldly, trusting that God’s word cannot be hindered.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Acts 28* shows that kindness and hospitality reflect God’s heart. The people of Malta welcomed shipwrecked strangers with uncommon kindness. Believers can follow their example, offering practical welcome and care to strangers, refugees, and anyone in need, and can recognize and honor kindness wherever it appears.

The chapter also shows the importance of Christian fellowship. When believers from Rome walked out to meet Paul, he thanked God and took courage. Believers can encourage one another, especially those facing hardship, and can receive the encouragement of others with gratitude.

*Acts 28* models patient, Scripture-centered witness. Paul spent an entire day explaining Jesus from the Law and the Prophets. Some believed and some did not. Believers can grow in their knowledge of how the whole Bible points to Jesus, share their faith patiently, and trust God with the results.

Finally, the chapter ends with Paul preaching the kingdom of God and the Lord Jesus Christ boldly and without hindrance, even in chains. The book of Acts is open-ended because the story is still being written. Every believer is invited to take up the mission, empowered by the same Holy Spirit, carrying the good news of Jesus to the ends of the earth with confidence that God’s word cannot be chained.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord God, thank You for bringing Paul safely to Rome, just as You promised. Thank You that Your promises never fail. Make me a person of uncommon kindness, welcoming strangers and caring for those in need. Thank You for the believers who encourage me; help me to encourage others, especially those who are weary or facing hardship. Give me a deep knowledge of Your word, so that I can explain how the whole Bible points to Jesus, and give me patience when I share my faith. When I face limitations, help me to serve You where I am. Thank You that Your word is not chained. Fill me with Your Holy Spirit, and help me to proclaim Your kingdom and the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness, so that the story of Acts continues through my life. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Book 6 of 27

# Romans

## About This Letter

Paul wrote Romans around A.D. 57, probably from Corinth, near the end of his third missionary journey (*Acts 20:2–3*; *Romans 15:25–26*; *16:1*, 23). He had not yet visited Rome, but he hoped to stop there on his way to Spain and to receive the church’s support for that mission (*15:23–24*). The church in Rome included both Jewish and Gentile believers. Emperor Claudius had expelled Jews from Rome around A.D. 49 (*Acts 18:2*), and when they returned after his death in A.D. 54, they found congregations now led largely by Gentiles. Tensions between the two groups may lie behind much of the letter. Paul sent the letter by Phoebe, a servant of the church in Cenchreae (*Romans 16:1–2*).

## The Shape of the Letter

Romans is the most complete explanation of the gospel in the New Testament. After his greeting, Paul states his theme: the gospel is the power of God for salvation for everyone who believes, revealing God’s righteousness “from faith to faith” (*1:16–17*). He then shows that all people, Gentiles and Jews alike, are under sin (*1:18–3*:20), and that God’s righteousness is given as a gift through faith in Jesus Christ, whose death made atonement for sin (*3:21–4*:25). He describes the new life that results: peace with God, freedom from the reign of sin and death, and life in the Spirit, ending in the triumphant assurance that nothing can separate believers from God’s love (chapters 5–8). Chapters 9–11 address God’s faithfulness to Israel and His plan to show mercy to Jews and Gentiles alike. Chapters 12–16 describe how the gospel shapes daily life: living sacrifices, love in the church, relationships with authorities, and welcome across differences.

## Themes to Watch For

Look for the righteousness of God, both His own justice and the right standing He gives to sinners; justification by faith apart from works of the Law; the universal reach of sin and of grace; union with Christ in His death and resurrection; the work of the Holy Spirit; God’s faithfulness to His promises to Israel; and the call for Jewish and Gentile believers to welcome one another as Christ has welcomed them. Romans has shaped Christian thought perhaps more than any other book, from Augustine to Martin Luther to John Wesley, each of whom found new life through its pages.
