# Romans — Chapter 1

Chapter Theme: The Gospel of God’s Power and Humanity’s Need

[Read Romans 1 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/ROM01.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul introduces himself as a servant of Christ Jesus, set apart for the gospel God promised through the prophets concerning His Son, descended from David and declared Son of God in power by the resurrection. He expresses his longing to visit the believers in Rome and states his theme: he is not ashamed of the gospel, because it is God’s power for the salvation of everyone who believes, revealing a righteousness that is received by faith. Paul then begins to explain why everyone needs this gospel: God’s wrath is revealed against human ungodliness, because people have known God through creation yet refused to honor Him, exchanging the Creator for created things and falling into every kind of sin.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Romans 1* opens the most systematic letter Paul ever wrote. In ancient letters, the writer usually began with his name, the recipients, and a greeting. Paul follows this pattern, but he expands it dramatically, packing his greeting with a summary of the gospel. Then, after a personal section about his plans, he announces the theme of the whole letter (*1:16–17*) and begins his argument that all people need God’s saving righteousness (*1:18–3*:20).

### Paul’s Greeting and the Gospel of God’s Son (*1:1–7*)

Paul describes himself in three ways. He is “*a servant of Jesus Christ*” (*v. 1*); the word means “slave” or “bondservant,” someone wholly owned by and devoted to his master. He is “*called to be an apostle*” (*v. 1*), appointed by Christ Himself. And he is “*set apart for the Good News of God*” (*v. 1*). As a Pharisee, which means “separated one,” Paul had once been set apart for the Law; now he was set apart for the gospel.

This gospel is not new. God “*promised before through his prophets in the holy Scriptures*” (*v. 2*). Its subject is God’s Son, described in two ways. According to His human nature, He “*was born of the offspring of David according to the flesh*” (*v. 3*), fulfilling the promise of a Messiah from David’s line. And He “*was declared to be the Son of God with power according to the Spirit of holiness, by the resurrection from the dead*” (*v. 4*). Jesus did not become God’s Son at the resurrection; He was always the Son. But the resurrection publicly declared and displayed His identity in power.

Through Christ, Paul received grace and apostleship “*for obedience of faith among all the nations*” (*v. 5*). The phrase “obedience of faith” sums up the goal of Paul’s mission: faith that expresses itself in obedience to Christ. Paul’s greeting ends with his characteristic blessing: “*Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ*” (*v. 7*). Notice that Paul places Jesus alongside the Father as the source of grace and peace.

### Paul’s Longing to Visit Rome (*1:8–15*)

Paul thanked God that the Roman believers’ “*faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world*” (*v. 8*). Rome was the capital, and news of a church there spread widely. He prayed for them constantly and longed to visit, “*that I may impart to you some spiritual gift, to the end that you may be established*” (*v. 11*). Then he humbly added that the blessing would be mutual: “*that is, that I with you may be encouraged in you, each of us by the other’s faith, both yours and mine*” (*v. 12*).

He had often planned to come but had been prevented. He felt a debt to all people: “*I am debtor both to Greeks and to foreigners, both to the wise and to the foolish*” (*v. 14*). Having received the gospel, he owed it to everyone. So “*I am eager to preach the Good News to you also who are in Rome*” (*v. 15*).

### The Theme of the Letter (*1:16–17*)

Paul then announced the theme of the entire letter, studied below in two parts.

### God’s Wrath against Ungodliness (*1:18–32*)

Paul now began to explain why the gospel is necessary. Before describing the good news, he describes the bad news. The first part of this explanation, about God’s revelation in creation, is studied below, as is the “great exchange” of truth for a lie.

Paul then describes how God “gave them up” three times (*1:24*, 26, 28). This phrase describes God’s judgment in the present: when people persistently reject Him, God allows them to experience the consequences of their choices. Sin becomes its own punishment.

In verses 26–27, Paul speaks of same-sex sexual relations as an example of humanity’s turning away from God’s created design, describing them as contrary to “nature,” meaning God’s design in creation. These verses are part of Paul’s broader argument that all humanity has turned from the Creator. Christians in most traditions throughout history have understood these verses as teaching that sexual relations are intended for marriage between a man and a woman, while some modern interpreters have proposed other readings. Whatever one’s view, Paul’s argument does not single out one group as uniquely sinful. In the very next verses, he lists envy, deceit, gossip, arrogance, disobedience to parents, and unmercifulness, and in chapter 2 he turns to those who judge others, showing that all people stand in need of God’s grace. These verses must never be used to justify contempt, mockery, or mistreatment of anyone. Every person is made in God’s image and loved by Him.

Paul’s list of sins in verses 29–31 is sobering: “*being filled with all unrighteousness, sexual immorality, wickedness, covetousness, malice; full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, evil habits, secret slanderers*” (*v. 29*), “*backbiters, hateful to God, insolent, arrogant, boastful, inventors of evil things, disobedient to parents*” (*v. 30*), “*without understanding, covenant breakers, without natural affection, unforgiving, unmerciful*” (*v. 31*). The list includes sins that many people consider minor, such as gossip and boasting, alongside violent ones like murder. No one can read this list without finding themselves in it.

The chapter ends with a final observation: people know that God’s judgment is right, yet “*not only do the same, but also approve of those who practice them*” (*v. 32*). Approving and celebrating sin shows how deeply the human heart has been darkened.

This dark picture is not the end of the story. It prepares the way for the good news of chapter 3: “*for all have sinned, and fall short of the glory of God*” (*Romans 3:23*), “*being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus*” (*Romans 3:24*).

## Important Verses Explained

### *Romans 1:16* — Not Ashamed of the Gospel

> *“For I am not ashamed of the Good News of Christ, because it is the power of God for salvation for everyone who believes, for the Jew first, and also for the Greek.”*
>
> — *Romans 1:16* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had just told the believers in Rome how much he longed to visit them and preach the gospel there. Rome was the capital of the most powerful empire in the world, a city of wealth, culture, and military might. To many in Rome, the message of a crucified Jewish teacher who rose from the dead would seem foolish or even shameful. Crucifixion was the most humiliating form of execution, reserved for slaves and rebels.

Yet Paul declared, “*For I am not ashamed of the Good News of Christ*” (*v. 16*). He had been mocked in Athens, beaten in Philippi, and stoned in Lystra for this message. He was not embarrassed by it. He was proud to proclaim it.

Why? “*because it is the power of God for salvation*” (*v. 16*). The gospel is not merely good advice or interesting information. It is “the power of God.” The Greek word for power (dynamis) is related to the English word “dynamite.” Through the gospel, God acts with power to rescue people from sin and death.

“*for everyone who believes*” (*v. 16*). The gospel’s power is available to everyone, without exception. It is received by believing, by trusting in Jesus. No one is excluded because of nationality, background, or past.

“*for the Jew first, and also for the Greek*” (*v. 16*). The gospel came first to the Jewish people, because God had made His promises to them and the Messiah came from them. Then it went to the Gentiles (“Greeks” here meaning all non-Jews). Paul’s own ministry followed this pattern: he usually preached first in the synagogue, then to Gentiles. Both Jews and Gentiles are saved in the same way, by faith.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that the gospel is God’s power, not human wisdom. Paul wrote to the Corinthians that the message of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, “*but to us who are being saved it is the power of God*” (*1 Corinthians 1:18*). Lives are transformed not by clever arguments or programs but by the message of Christ crucified and risen.

It also shows the universal scope of salvation. “Everyone who believes” includes every nation, culture, and class. The gospel breaks down barriers between Jew and Gentile, rich and poor, educated and uneducated.

Finally, the verse shows that there is a temptation to be ashamed of the gospel. Jesus warned, “*For whoever will be ashamed of me and of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation, the Son of Man also will be ashamed of him*” (*Mark 8:38*). Paul’s declaration is a model of courageous faith.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse challenges believers to examine whether they are ashamed of the gospel. Many believers feel embarrassed to speak about Jesus at work, at school, or among friends, fearing ridicule or rejection. Paul’s example encourages them to speak with confidence, because the gospel is God’s power.

It also encourages believers to trust the gospel’s power. Believers do not need to make the message more impressive or acceptable. The simple message of Christ’s death and resurrection has power to save. Believers can share it with confidence that God will work through it.

Finally, the verse reminds believers that the gospel is for everyone. No one is too far gone, too different, or too sinful to be saved. Believers can share the gospel with all people, trusting that it is for “everyone who believes.”

### *Romans 1:17* — The Righteous Shall Live by Faith

> *“For in it is revealed God’s righteousness from faith to faith. As it is written, ‘But the righteous shall live by faith.’”*
>
> — *Romans 1:17* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had just declared that he was not ashamed of the gospel, because it is the power of God for salvation for everyone who believes. Now he explained why the gospel has this power.

“*For in it is revealed God’s righteousness*” (*v. 17*). The gospel reveals “God’s righteousness.” This phrase has a rich meaning. It refers to God’s own righteousness, His faithfulness, justice, and goodness. It also refers to the righteousness God gives to sinners, the right standing before Him that He grants as a gift. In the gospel, God shows that He is righteous and makes sinners righteous through faith in Christ. Paul will explain this more fully in *Romans 3:21–26*.

“*from faith to faith*” (*v. 17*). This phrase has been understood in several ways. It may mean “by faith from first to last,” that is, entirely by faith. It may mean from God’s faithfulness to human faith. Or it may mean from the faith of one person to the faith of another, as the gospel spreads. The main point is clear: this righteousness is received by faith, not by works.

“*As it is written, “But the righteous shall live by faith.”*” (*v. 17*) Paul quoted *Habakkuk 2:4*. In its original setting, Habakkuk was struggling to understand why God would allow the cruel Babylonians to conquer Judah. God answered that the righteous person would live by trusting Him, remaining faithful even when circumstances were confusing. Paul applies this verse to the gospel: those who are made righteous by faith will live, receiving eternal life, through faith.

This verse changed the course of history. Martin Luther, a sixteenth-century monk who was tormented by the fear that he could never be righteous enough for God, studied this verse and came to understand that God’s righteousness is a gift received by faith. He later wrote that he felt as if he had been born again and had entered paradise itself through open gates.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse introduces the central theme of Romans: justification by faith. People cannot make themselves righteous before God by their own efforts. But God gives righteousness as a gift to all who trust in Christ. Paul writes later, “*even the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ to all and on all those who believe*” (*Romans 3:22*).

It also shows that faith is not only the entrance to the Christian life but its whole character. “The righteous shall live by faith.” Believers begin by faith, continue by faith, and will finish by faith. Faith means trusting God and His promises, even when circumstances are difficult, as Habakkuk learned.

Finally, the verse shows the continuity between the Old and New Testaments. Paul grounds his message in Habakkuk. Justification by faith is not a new idea; it was always God’s way. Abraham himself was declared righteous by faith (*Genesis 15:6*; *Romans 4:3*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse brings freedom to those who feel they can never be good enough for God. Righteousness is not earned; it is received as a gift through faith in Christ. Believers can rest in this gift rather than striving anxiously to earn God’s approval.

It also calls believers to live by faith every day. Faith is not only for the moment of conversion. Believers are called to trust God in every circumstance, especially in times of confusion or suffering, as Habakkuk did.

Finally, the verse encourages believers to share this good news. Many people around them are burdened by guilt or by the fear that they are not good enough. The gospel reveals that God gives righteousness freely to all who believe.

### *Romans 1:20–21* — Without Excuse

> *“For the invisible things of him since the creation of the world are clearly seen, being perceived through the things that are made, even his everlasting power and divinity, that they may be without excuse. Because knowing God, they didn’t glorify him as God, and didn’t give thanks, but became vain in their reasoning, and their senseless heart was darkened.”*
>
> — *Romans 1:20–21* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After announcing the good news of the gospel, Paul began to explain why everyone needs it. He started with people who do not have the written Scriptures, the Gentile world. Did they know anything about God?

“*For the invisible things of him since the creation of the world are clearly seen, being perceived through the things that are made*” (*v. 20*). God is invisible; no one can see Him directly. But His creation reveals Him. When people look at the vastness of the sky, the beauty of the earth, the complexity of living things, and the order of the universe, they can perceive something of the God who made them.

“*even his everlasting power and divinity*” (*v. 20*). Creation reveals two things about God in particular: His “everlasting power,” the power needed to create and sustain the universe, and His “divinity,” that He is God, a being above and beyond creation.

“*that they may be without excuse*” (*v. 20*). Because God has revealed Himself in creation, no one can say they had no knowledge of Him at all. Everyone has received some light.

Then Paul described humanity’s response: “*Because knowing God, they didn’t glorify him as God, and didn’t give thanks*” (*v. 21*). People knew God through creation, but they did not honor Him as God or thank Him for His gifts. Ingratitude and refusal to worship are at the root of human sin.

“*but became vain in their reasoning, and their senseless heart was darkened*” (*v. 21*). When people turn from God, their thinking becomes empty and confused, and their hearts become darkened. Rejecting the light leads to deeper darkness.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses teach what is often called “general revelation”: God reveals Himself to all people through creation. *Psalm 19* says, “*The heavens declare the glory of God. The expanse shows his handiwork*” (*Psalm 19:1*). This revelation is not enough to show people the way of salvation through Christ, but it is enough to show them that God exists and deserves their worship.

They also reveal the root of sin. The fundamental human problem is not ignorance but rebellion: refusing to honor God and give Him thanks. Sin begins in the heart’s refusal to acknowledge God as God.

Finally, these verses show that rejecting God affects the mind. When people refuse the truth, their reasoning becomes futile. This helps explain why intelligent people can believe foolish things when they reject God. Paul writes that people “*Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools*” (*v. 22*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to see God’s glory in creation. Nature is not merely a collection of random processes; it is the handiwork of God. Believers can grow in worship by paying attention to the beauty and wonder of the world He made.

They also call believers to gratitude. Paul identifies ingratitude as one of the first steps away from God. Believers can cultivate thankfulness, regularly recognizing and thanking God for His gifts.

Finally, these verses help believers understand those who reject God. Many people know, at some level, that God exists, but they resist honoring Him. Believers can pray for them and gently point them to the God revealed in creation and, more fully, in Jesus Christ.

### *Romans 1:24–25* — Exchanging the Truth of God for a Lie

> *“Therefore God also gave them up in the lusts of their hearts to uncleanness, that their bodies should be dishonored among themselves; who exchanged the truth of God for a lie, and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever. Amen.”*
>
> — *Romans 1:24–25* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had explained that people knew God through creation but refused to honor Him or give Him thanks. Instead, they “*traded the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of an image of corruptible man, and of birds, four-footed animals, and creeping things*” (*v. 23*). They made idols and worshiped them instead of the true God.

Then Paul described God’s response: “*Therefore God also gave them up in the lusts of their hearts to uncleanness, that their bodies should be dishonored among themselves*” (*v. 24*). The phrase “God gave them up” is repeated three times in this chapter (*1:24*, 26, 28). It describes God’s judgment. When people persistently reject God, He allows them to go their own way and experience the consequences of their choices. He removes His restraining hand, and their desires lead them into deeper sin.

“*who exchanged the truth of God for a lie*” (*v. 25*). The “truth of God” is the truth about who God is and who people are in relation to Him. The “lie” is the idea that something other than God deserves worship. Every idol is a lie, promising what only God can give.

“*and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator*” (*v. 25*). This is the heart of idolatry: giving the worship that belongs to God to something He has made. In the ancient world, this meant statues and images. But it can include anything people put in God’s place: money, pleasure, power, success, relationships, or even oneself.

“*who is blessed forever. Amen.*” (*v. 25*) Even while describing humanity’s rebellion, Paul cannot help but praise God. The Creator remains worthy of eternal praise, whether or not people give it to Him.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that idolatry is the root of all other sins. When people stop worshiping God, they will worship something else. And what they worship shapes who they become. The psalmist writes of idols, “*Those who make them will be like them*” (*Psalm 115:8*).

They also show that God’s judgment can take the form of allowing people to have what they want. “God gave them up” means that He let them follow their own desires. This is a sobering truth: one of the most serious judgments is for God to let people go their own way. Yet even this judgment is meant to show people the emptiness of life without God and lead them back to Him.

Finally, these verses show that sin distorts human relationships and even the human body. When people reject the Creator, they misuse His good gifts. The rest of the chapter traces how turning from God leads to the breakdown of relationships and moral life.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses invite believers to examine their own hearts for idols. Idols today are rarely statues, but they can be anything that takes God’s place in one’s affections, trust, or priorities. Believers can ask God to reveal their idols and help them turn back to Him.

They also warn against believing the lie that anything other than God can truly satisfy. Every idol eventually disappoints. Believers can find their deepest satisfaction in worshiping and serving the Creator.

Finally, these verses encourage believers to respond to a broken world with compassion. Paul’s description of humanity applies to everyone, including believers before they knew Christ. Believers are not called to look down on others but to share the gospel, which has the power to rescue people from the lie and bring them back to the truth.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Romans 1* calls believers to be unashamed of the gospel. The message of Christ crucified and risen may seem foolish to the world, but it is the power of God for the salvation of everyone who believes. Believers can share it confidently, knowing that it is good news for every person, regardless of background.

The chapter also introduces the heart of Paul’s message: God’s righteousness is revealed in the gospel and received by faith. People cannot make themselves right with God; He gives righteousness as a gift. Believers can rest in this grace and live each day by faith, trusting God in every circumstance.

*Romans 1* also shows that God reveals Himself through creation, so that all people have some knowledge of Him. Yet humanity has refused to honor Him and give Him thanks, turning instead to idols. Believers can respond by cultivating gratitude and worship, seeing God’s glory in the world He made, and examining their own hearts for anything that has taken His place.

Finally, the chapter paints an honest picture of human sinfulness. Its list of sins includes things like envy, gossip, and arrogance alongside more obvious wrongs. No one escapes this description. This should lead believers not to pride or condemnation of others, but to humility and compassion, and to a deeper gratitude for the gospel, which is God’s answer to the brokenness of every human heart.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord God, I praise You as the Creator, who is blessed forever. Thank You for revealing Your eternal power and divine nature in the world You made. Forgive me for the times I have failed to honor You or give You thanks, and for the idols I have allowed to take Your place in my heart. Thank You for the gospel of Your Son, born of David’s line and declared to be the Son of God with power by His resurrection. Help me never to be ashamed of this good news, for it is Your power for the salvation of everyone who believes. Thank You for the righteousness You give by faith. Teach me to live by faith every day. Keep me from pride and from looking down on others, and fill me with compassion and a desire to share the gospel with all. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Romans · Chapter 2 of 16

# Romans — Chapter 2

Chapter Theme: No Partiality with God: The Judgment That Exposes Every Heart

[Read Romans 2 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/ROM02.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul turns from the obvious sins of the pagan world to those who judge others while doing the same things. God’s judgment is according to truth, and His kindness is meant to lead people to repentance, not to make them complacent. God will judge everyone impartially according to what they have done, whether they have the written Law or only the law written on their hearts. Paul then addresses those who rely on the Law and circumcision for confidence, showing that what matters before God is not outward identity but a heart circumcised by the Spirit.

## Chapter Background and Story

In *Romans 1:18–32*, Paul described the sins of the pagan world: idolatry, immorality, and a long list of evils. Many readers, especially Jewish readers who knew God’s Law, would have agreed with Paul’s description. They might even have felt morally superior to the Gentiles.

In *Romans 2*, Paul turns the spotlight around. He speaks to anyone who judges others, and then directly to the Jewish reader who relies on the Law. His purpose is to show that everyone, not only pagans, stands guilty before God. This prepares for his conclusion in chapter 3: “*we previously warned both Jews and Greeks that they are all under sin*” (*Romans 3:9*).

Paul uses a style of argument common in his time, called a diatribe, in which the writer addresses an imaginary conversation partner directly (“O man... you”). This makes the argument vivid and personal.

### The Judge Who Is Guilty (*2:1–5*)

Paul begins with a direct challenge to those who judge others, studied below. He continues: “*We know that the judgment of God is according to truth against those who practice such things*” (*v. 2*). God judges with perfect knowledge and fairness. “*Do you think this, O man who judges those who practice such things, and do the same, that you will escape the judgment of God?*” (*v. 3*) No one can escape God’s judgment by condemning others.

Paul then warns against misunderstanding God’s patience, studied below. Those who refuse to repent are “*treasuring up for yourself wrath in the day of wrath, revelation, and of the righteous judgment of God*” (*v. 5*). The image is of storing up treasure, but the treasure being accumulated is judgment.

### Judgment According to Works (*2:6–16*)

God “*will pay back to everyone according to their works*” (*v. 6*), quoting *Psalm 62:12* and *Proverbs 24:12*. This principle, and how it fits with Paul’s teaching on grace, is studied below. Paul repeats the phrase “*to the Jew first, and also to the Greek*” (*v. 9*), showing that judgment, like salvation (*Romans 1:16*), applies to all. “*For there is no partiality with God*” (*v. 11*).

Paul then explains how God judges those with and without the written Law: “*For as many as have sinned without the law will also perish without the law. As many as have sinned under the law will be judged by the law*” (*v. 12*). Gentiles who did not have the Law of Moses would be judged by the light they had; Jews who had the Law would be judged by it.

“*For it isn’t the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law will be justified*” (*v. 13*). Hearing the Law read in the synagogue every Sabbath did not make anyone righteous. What God requires is obedience. Paul will soon show that no one has perfectly obeyed (*3:10–20*), which is why everyone needs the righteousness that comes through faith.

Paul adds that Gentiles, though they do not have the written Law, sometimes “*do by nature the things of the law*” (*v. 14*). They “*show the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience testifying with them, and their thoughts among themselves accusing or else excusing them*” (*v. 15*). All people have a sense of right and wrong. Every culture has moral laws against murder, theft, and betrayal. Conscience is God’s witness within every person.

This judgment will take place “*in the day when God will judge the secrets of men, according to my Good News, by Jesus Christ*” (*v. 16*). God will judge not only outward actions but hidden things, motives, thoughts, and secrets. And He will judge through Jesus Christ, whom He has appointed as judge (*Acts 17:31*).

### The Jew Who Relies on the Law (*2:17–24*)

Paul now addresses his Jewish reader directly. He lists the privileges and claims of the Jewish people: “*Indeed you bear the name of a Jew, rest on the law, glory in God*” (*v. 17*), “*know his will, and approve the things that are excellent, being instructed out of the law*” (*v. 18*). They were confident that they were “*a guide of the blind, a light to those who are in darkness*” (*v. 19*), “*a corrector of the foolish, a teacher of babies*” (*v. 20*). These were real privileges. God had given Israel His Law and called them to be a light to the nations (*Isaiah 42:6*).

But privilege brings responsibility. Paul asks a series of piercing questions: “*You therefore who teach another, don’t you teach yourself? You who preach that a man shouldn’t steal, do you steal?*” (*v. 21*) “*You who say a man shouldn’t commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who abhor idols, do you rob temples?*” (*v. 22*) “*You who glory in the law, do you dishonor God by disobeying the law?*” (*v. 23*)

Paul quotes *Isaiah 52:5*: “*the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you*” (*v. 24*). When God’s people fail to live by His word, outsiders mock God. This applies to every generation of God’s people, including the church today.

Paul’s words are not an attack on the Jewish people as a whole. Paul was Jewish himself, and his point applies to all religious people who rely on their privileges rather than living in genuine obedience. Jesus spoke in similar terms to the religious leaders of His day (*Matthew 23*).

### True Circumcision (*2:25–29*)

Circumcision was the sign of God’s covenant with Abraham and his descendants (*Genesis 17:10–14*). It marked Jewish men as members of God’s people. Paul acknowledges that circumcision has value, “*if you are a doer of the law*” (*v. 25*). But if a person breaks the Law, their circumcision becomes meaningless. Conversely, if a Gentile keeps the Law’s requirements, God will regard him as if he were circumcised. Paul’s conclusion about true circumcision is studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Romans 2:1* — Condemning Yourself When You Judge

> *“Therefore you are without excuse, O man, whoever you are who judge. For in that which you judge another, you condemn yourself. For you who judge practice the same things.”*
>
> — *Romans 2:1* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

In *Romans 1*, Paul described the sins of people who rejected God: idolatry, immorality, envy, deceit, gossip, arrogance, and many more. Many readers would have nodded in agreement, thinking of the wickedness they saw around them in the pagan world. They might have felt that they were not like those people.

Then Paul turned to them: “*Therefore you are without excuse, O man, whoever you are who judge*” (*v. 1*). Paul addressed anyone who judges others, condemning their sins while feeling morally superior. Just as the pagans were “without excuse” (*1:20*), so are those who judge.

“*For in that which you judge another, you condemn yourself*” (*v. 1*). When people condemn others for sin, they show that they know what is right. But by that same standard, they condemn themselves, because they too have sinned.

“*For you who judge practice the same things*” (*v. 1*). Paul says that the judges do the same things. They may not commit every sin they condemn in exactly the same way, but they are guilty of the same kinds of sin: envy, pride, deceit, gossip, and others on Paul’s list in chapter 1. Jesus taught that anger is a form of murder and lust is a form of adultery (*Matthew 5:21–28*). No one stands above the list.

This does not mean that believers should never recognize sin or speak the truth. It means that they should never set themselves up as morally superior to others, as if they were not also sinners in need of grace.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse echoes Jesus’ teaching: “*Don’t judge, so that you won’t be judged*” (*Matthew 7:1*). Jesus warned against noticing the speck in another person’s eye while ignoring the log in one’s own (*Matthew 7:3–5*). Judging others is often a way of avoiding one’s own guilt.

It also shows that self-righteousness is a serious sin. The Pharisee in Jesus’ parable thanked God that he was not like other people, while the tax collector humbly asked for mercy (*Luke 18:9–14*). Jesus said that the tax collector, not the Pharisee, went home justified. God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble (*James 4:6*).

Finally, the verse prepares for the gospel. If everyone, including the moral and religious, is guilty, then everyone needs the same Savior. Paul is leading all his readers to the place where they can receive grace: the recognition of their own need.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse challenges believers to examine their attitudes toward others. It is easy to condemn the obvious sins of others while overlooking one’s own pride, gossip, or harshness. Believers can ask God to show them their own sin before they focus on the sins of others.

It also calls believers to humility. Believers are not better than others; they are forgiven sinners. This truth can soften their attitudes and help them speak to others with compassion rather than condemnation.

Finally, the verse encourages believers to approach moral issues with grace. Believers are still called to recognize sin and speak the truth in love. But they can do so as people who know their own need for mercy, pointing others to the same grace they have received.

### *Romans 2:4* — God’s Kindness Leads to Repentance

> *“Or do you despise the riches of his goodness, forbearance, and patience, not knowing that the goodness of God leads you to repentance?”*
>
> — *Romans 2:4* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul was addressing people who condemned others while committing the same sins. Perhaps they thought that because God had not punished them, they were safe. They may have assumed that God’s patience meant He approved of them.

Paul asked, “*Or do you despise the riches of his goodness, forbearance, and patience*” (*v. 4*)? God had been extraordinarily kind to them. “Goodness” refers to God’s kindness and generosity. “Forbearance” means holding back from immediate punishment. “Patience” means a long-suffering attitude, waiting rather than acting in anger. Paul calls these “riches,” treasures of grace.

To “despise” these riches means to treat them lightly, to take them for granted, or to misunderstand their purpose. Some people interpret God’s patience as indifference or weakness.

“*not knowing that the goodness of God leads you to repentance?*” (*v. 4*) God’s kindness has a purpose: to lead people to turn from their sins. God does not delay judgment because He does not care about sin. He delays because He wants people to repent. Peter writes, “*The Lord is not slow concerning his promise, as some count slowness; but he is patient with us, not wishing that anyone should perish, but that all should come to repentance*” (*2 Peter 3:9*).

The next verse warns what happens when people refuse: they store up wrath for themselves on the day of judgment.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals the heart of God. He is not eager to punish. He is rich in kindness, patient, and long-suffering. Every day that a person lives is an expression of God’s patience. The prophet Ezekiel records God’s words: “*I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live*” (*Ezekiel 33:11*).

It also shows that repentance is a response to God’s kindness, not merely to fear. People often think that repentance comes mainly from being frightened of punishment. While God’s warnings are real, Paul says that God’s goodness leads people to repentance. Recognizing how kind God has been can melt a hardened heart.

Finally, the verse warns against presuming on God’s patience. God’s patience is not unlimited. A day of judgment is coming. Those who misuse God’s kindness as an excuse to continue in sin will face the consequences.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to reflect on God’s kindness in their own lives. God has been patient with them, provided for them, and given them opportunities to know Him. Remembering His kindness can lead to gratitude and a renewed desire to turn from sin.

It also warns anyone who is presuming on God’s patience. Some people know they are living in ways that displease God, but they assume that because nothing bad has happened, everything is fine. God’s patience is an invitation to repent, not permission to continue.

Finally, the verse shapes how believers share the gospel. While warnings about judgment are part of the message, Paul shows that God’s goodness is what draws people to repentance. Believers can emphasize the kindness and love of God as they invite others to turn to Him.

### *Romans 2:6–8* — Judged According to Works

> *“who ‘will pay back to everyone according to their works:’ to those who by perseverance in well-doing seek for glory, honor, and incorruptibility, eternal life; but to those who are self-seeking and don’t obey the truth, but obey unrighteousness, will be wrath, indignation,”*
>
> — *Romans 2:6–8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul was explaining that God’s judgment is fair and impartial. Those who condemn others while doing the same things cannot escape. Now Paul states a principle of God’s judgment: God “*will pay back to everyone according to their works*” (*v. 6*). This principle appears throughout Scripture (*Psalm 62:12*; *Proverbs 24:12*; *Matthew 16:27*; *Revelation 22:12*).

Paul then describes two groups. First, “*to those who by perseverance in well-doing seek for glory, honor, and incorruptibility, eternal life*” (*v. 7*). Some people patiently continue doing good, seeking what God offers: glory, honor, and immortality. God gives them eternal life.

Second, “*but to those who are self-seeking and don’t obey the truth, but obey unrighteousness, will be wrath, indignation*” (*v. 8*). Some people live for themselves, rejecting the truth and following evil. They will face God’s anger.

These verses can seem confusing. Is Paul saying that people are saved by doing good works? That would contradict what he says later: “*Because by the works of the law, no flesh will be justified in his sight*” (*Romans 3:20*).

Interpreters have understood these verses in several ways. Some see Paul as describing the standard of judgment in principle: if anyone did persistently and perfectly do good, they would receive eternal life, but as Paul shows in chapter 3, no one does, so all need grace. Others see Paul as describing believers whose lives, transformed by grace, show the fruit of faith in persevering good works; their works do not earn salvation but reveal genuine faith. Both views agree that salvation is by grace through faith, and that genuine faith shows itself in a changed life.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that God takes human actions seriously. What people do matters to God. He is not indifferent to good and evil. Every person will give an account of their life (*2 Corinthians 5:10*).

They also show that the direction of a person’s life reveals their heart. Those who seek God’s glory and persevere in doing good show that they are oriented toward God. Those who live selfishly and reject the truth show that they are turned away from Him. James writes that faith without works is dead (*James 2:17*).

Finally, these verses prepare for the gospel. If God judges according to works, and if no one has perfect works, then everyone needs a righteousness that comes as a gift. This is exactly what Paul will explain in *Romans 3:21–26*: the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses remind believers that their lives matter to God. Believers are saved by grace, but they are called to live lives of persevering goodness. Paul writes elsewhere that believers are “*created in Christ Jesus for good works*” (*Ephesians 2:10*).

They also encourage believers to persevere. Paul speaks of those who “by perseverance in well-doing” seek glory and honor. Believers may grow weary, but they can keep going, trusting that God sees and rewards faithfulness (*Galatians 6:9*).

Finally, these verses warn against self-seeking. Living for oneself, rejecting God’s truth, and following evil leads to judgment. Believers can examine whether they are seeking God’s glory or their own, and ask God to turn their hearts toward Him.

### *Romans 2:28–29* — Circumcision of the Heart

> *“For he is not a Jew who is one outwardly, neither is that circumcision which is outward in the flesh; but he is a Jew who is one inwardly, and circumcision is that of the heart, in the spirit, not in the letter; whose praise is not from men, but from God.”*
>
> — *Romans 2:28–29* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had been speaking to Jewish readers who relied on their identity as God’s people, their possession of the Law, and their circumcision. Circumcision was the physical sign of God’s covenant with Abraham. Every Jewish boy was circumcised on the eighth day. It marked him as part of God’s chosen people.

But Paul made a striking statement: “*For he is not a Jew who is one outwardly, neither is that circumcision which is outward in the flesh*” (*v. 28*). Being part of God’s people is not only a matter of outward identity or physical signs. A person could be circumcised and still be far from God.

“*but he is a Jew who is one inwardly, and circumcision is that of the heart, in the spirit, not in the letter*” (*v. 29*). True belonging to God is inward. It involves a “circumcision of the heart,” a cutting away of sin and rebellion from within. This is done “in the spirit,” by the work of God’s Spirit, “not in the letter,” not merely by external rules.

This idea was not new. Moses had told Israel, “*Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no more stiff-necked*” (*Deuteronomy 10:16*). He also promised that God Himself would do this: “*The LORD your God will circumcise your heart*” (*Deuteronomy 30:6*). Jeremiah spoke of hearts that needed circumcision (*Jeremiah 4:4*).

“*whose praise is not from men, but from God*” (*v. 29*). There may be a wordplay here. The name “Jew” comes from “Judah,” which is related to the Hebrew word for “praise.” A true Jew is one whose praise comes from God, not from people.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that God looks at the heart. Outward religious identity, rituals, and signs have value, but they cannot replace a heart that truly belongs to God. Jesus said that the Pharisees honored God with their lips while their hearts were far from Him (*Matthew 15:8*).

They also point to the new covenant. God promised to give His people new hearts and to put His Spirit within them (*Ezekiel 36:26–27*). Through Christ, this promise is fulfilled. Paul writes that believers “*were also circumcised with a circumcision not made with hands*” (*Colossians 2:11*), through Christ.

Finally, these verses show that God’s people are defined by inner transformation, not outward markers. Paul later explains that Gentiles who believe are included in God’s people (*Romans 4:11–12*; *Galatians 3:7*). What matters is a heart transformed by God’s Spirit.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses challenge believers to examine whether their faith is merely outward. Church attendance, baptism, religious traditions, and Christian identity are valuable, but they cannot replace a heart that truly loves and obeys God. Believers can ask God to search their hearts and make their faith genuine.

They also encourage believers to seek God’s praise rather than human approval. It is easy to practice faith in ways that impress others. Paul reminds believers that what matters is God’s approval.

Finally, these verses encourage believers to depend on the Holy Spirit. Inner transformation is not something people can achieve on their own. It is the work of the Spirit. Believers can ask God to continue His work of cutting away sin from their hearts and making them new.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Romans 2* warns against judging others while ignoring one’s own sin. Those who condemn others often practice the same things. Believers are called to humility, recognizing that they too are sinners saved by grace. This does not mean ignoring sin, but approaching others with compassion rather than condemnation.

The chapter also reveals the kindness of God. His goodness, patience, and forbearance are meant to lead people to repentance. Believers can reflect on how kind God has been to them and respond with gratitude and a turning from sin. Those who presume on God’s patience are warned that a day of judgment is coming.

*Romans 2* teaches that God judges impartially and according to what people have done. He judges with perfect knowledge, including the secrets of the heart. Everyone, whether they have the written Law or only the law written on their conscience, will give an account to God. This truth prepares the way for the gospel: since no one has perfectly obeyed, all need the righteousness that comes through faith in Christ.

Finally, the chapter shows that what matters to God is the heart. Outward religion, identity, and rituals cannot replace a heart circumcised by the Spirit. Believers can seek genuine, inward faith, depend on the Spirit to transform them, and live for God’s praise rather than the praise of people.

## Chapter Prayer

Righteous God, You judge with perfect truth, and nothing is hidden from You. Forgive me for the times I have judged others while ignoring my own sin. Give me a humble heart that remembers my own need for Your mercy. Thank You for the riches of Your kindness, patience, and forbearance toward me. Let Your goodness lead me to repentance, and keep me from taking Your patience for granted. Help me to persevere in doing good, not to earn Your favor, but because Your grace has changed me. Search my heart, Lord, and make my faith real on the inside, not only on the outside. Circumcise my heart by Your Spirit, and help me to live for Your praise rather than the approval of others. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Romans · Chapter 3 of 16

# Romans — Chapter 3

Chapter Theme: All Have Sinned, and All Who Believe Are Justified Freely by Grace

[Read Romans 3 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/ROM03.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul answers objections about God’s faithfulness to Israel and then draws his conclusion: Jews and Gentiles alike are under sin, and no one is righteous before God. The Law cannot justify anyone; it reveals sin. But now God has revealed His righteousness apart from the Law, through faith in Jesus Christ, for all who believe. All have sinned and fall short of God’s glory, yet they are justified freely by His grace through the redemption in Christ Jesus, whom God presented as an atoning sacrifice. In this way God shows Himself both just and the One who justifies those who have faith in Jesus, leaving no room for boasting.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Romans 3* contains the turning point of Paul’s argument and some of the most important verses in the Bible. Since 1:18, Paul has been showing that all humanity, Gentiles and Jews alike, stand guilty before God. In 3:1–20 he completes this argument, answering objections and declaring the universal guilt of humanity. Then, in 3:21–26, comes the great announcement of the gospel: God’s righteousness has been revealed through faith in Jesus Christ. Many have called this passage the heart of the whole letter, and even of the whole Bible.

### Objections Answered (*3:1–8*)

If being Jewish and circumcised does not guarantee righteousness (*2:25–29*), a reader might ask, “*Then what advantage does the Jew have? Or what is the profit of circumcision?*” (*v. 1*) Paul answers, “*Much in every way! Because first of all, they were entrusted with the revelations of God*” (*v. 2*). Israel received the Scriptures, God’s covenants, and His promises. This was a great privilege.

But what if some Jews were unfaithful? Does their unfaithfulness cancel God’s faithfulness? “*May it never be! Yes, let God be found true, but every man a liar*” (*v. 4*). Even if every human being proved false, God would remain true. Paul quotes *Psalm 51:4*, David’s prayer of repentance, in which David acknowledges that God is right to judge him.

Paul then addresses a twisted argument: if human sin makes God’s righteousness shine more brightly, is it unfair for God to judge sinners? Some even slanderously accused Paul of teaching, “*Let’s do evil, that good may come*” (*v. 8*). Paul rejects this completely: “*Those who say so are justly condemned*” (*v. 8*). God’s grace never excuses sin.

### No One Is Righteous (*3:9–20*)

Paul then asks, “*What then? Are we better than they? No, in no way. For we previously warned both Jews and Greeks that they are all under sin*” (*v. 9*). “Under sin” means under sin’s power and guilt.

He supports this with a collection of Old Testament passages, mostly from the Psalms, studied below in part. They describe the corruption of the whole person: “*Their throat is an open tomb. With their tongues they have used deceit.*” (*v. 13*) (*Psalm 5:9*) “*Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness.*” (*v. 14*) (*Psalm 10:7*) “*Their feet are swift to shed blood.*” (*v. 15*) (*Isaiah 59:7*) The list moves from speech to violence to the root of it all: “*There is no fear of God before their eyes.*” (*v. 18*) (*Psalm 36:1*)

Paul explains the purpose of the Law: “*that every mouth may be closed, and all the world may be brought under the judgment of God*” (*v. 19*). Like a defendant who has no answer, every person stands silent before God’s judgment. “*Because by the works of the law, no flesh will be justified in his sight; for through the law comes the knowledge of sin*” (*v. 20*). The Law is like a mirror: it shows people their sin, but it cannot wash it away. Keeping the Law cannot make anyone right with God, because no one keeps it perfectly.

### The Righteousness of God Revealed (*3:21–26*)

Then come two of the most important words in Romans: “*But now*” (*v. 21*). After the long, dark description of human sin, Paul turns to God’s answer. “*apart from the law, a righteousness of God has been revealed, being testified by the law and the prophets*” (*v. 21*). God has provided a righteousness that does not come by keeping the Law. Yet it is not a departure from the Old Testament; the Law and the Prophets point to it.

“*even the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ to all and on all those who believe. For there is no distinction*” (*v. 22*). This righteousness comes through faith in Jesus. It is available to all who believe, without distinction between Jew and Gentile. (Some interpreters translate the phrase “through the faithfulness of Jesus Christ,” emphasizing Christ’s own faithful obedience; both readings affirm that salvation rests on Christ and is received by faith.) The rest of this passage is studied below.

### Boasting Excluded (*3:27–31*)

“*Where then is the boasting? It is excluded*” (*v. 27*). If salvation is God’s free gift, received by faith, no one can boast. Paul’s conclusion is studied below. Paul then shows that this truth means God is the God of Gentiles as well as Jews: “*since indeed there is one God who will justify the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith*” (*v. 30*). Because there is one God, there is one way of salvation for all people.

Finally, Paul anticipates an objection: “*Do we then nullify the law through faith? May it never be! No, we establish the law*” (*v. 31*). Faith does not destroy the Law; it fulfills its true purpose. The Law pointed to Christ and revealed humanity’s need for Him. In *Romans 4*, Paul will show that the Law itself teaches justification by faith through the example of Abraham. And in chapter 8, he will show that those who live by the Spirit fulfill the righteous requirement of the Law (*8:4*).

## Important Verses Explained

### *Romans 3:10–12* — There Is No One Righteous

> *“As it is written, ‘There is no one righteous; no, not one. There is no one who understands. There is no one who seeks after God. They have all turned away. They have together become unprofitable. There is no one who does good, no, not so much as one.’”*
>
> — *Romans 3:10–12* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had been building his case since *Romans 1:18* that all people, both Gentiles and Jews, are guilty before God. He had shown that the pagan world rejected God and fell into every kind of sin, and that those who judge others, including those who have God’s Law, are guilty too. Now he brings his argument to a conclusion with a series of quotations from the Old Testament.

“*As it is written, “There is no one righteous; no, not one.*” (*v. 10*) This quotation comes from *Psalm 14:1–3* and *Psalm 53:1–3*. No one, not a single person, is righteous before God by their own merit. Paul emphasizes “not one.” There are no exceptions.

“*There is no one who understands. There is no one who seeks after God.*” (*v. 11*) Sin affects the mind (“no one who understands”) and the will (“no one who seeks”). People do not naturally seek God on their own. When people do seek God, it is because God has first drawn them (*John 6:44*).

“*They have all turned away. They have together become unprofitable. There is no one who does good, no, not so much as one.*” (*v. 12*) All people have turned from God’s way. The word “unprofitable” was used of milk that has gone sour, or of fruit that has become rotten. Humanity has become spoiled, unable to fulfill its purpose.

These are strong words. They do not mean that people never do anything kind or good in a human sense. People can be generous, brave, and loving. But no one does good in the full sense God requires, with a perfect heart, for God’s glory, and consistently. Measured against God’s perfect standard, everyone falls short.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses describe what theologians often call the universal sinfulness of humanity. Sin is not merely a problem for some especially bad people; it is the condition of every human heart. The prophet Isaiah wrote, “*For we have all become like one who is unclean, and all our righteousness is like a polluted garment*” (*Isaiah 64:6*).

They also show that sin affects the whole person: mind, will, desires, words, and actions. This does not mean that people are as bad as they could possibly be, but that every part of human nature has been affected by sin.

Finally, these verses prepare the way for grace. Paul does not describe human sinfulness to make people despair, but to show them their need for a Savior. Only when people recognize that they cannot save themselves are they ready to receive God’s free gift.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses humble believers. No one can stand before God on the basis of their own goodness. Believers can lay down any pride in their own righteousness and depend completely on God’s grace.

They also help believers understand the world. The brokenness, violence, and injustice in the world are not surprising; they flow from the human heart. Believers can respond to evil with sorrow and with the hope of the gospel, which alone can change hearts.

Finally, these verses encourage believers to share the gospel with compassion. Everyone stands in the same need. Believers do not approach others as superior people, but as fellow sinners who have found mercy and want to share it.

### *Romans 3:23–24* — Justified Freely by His Grace

> *“for all have sinned, and fall short of the glory of God; being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus,”*
>
> — *Romans 3:23–24* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had just announced that God’s righteousness has been revealed through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe, with no distinction between Jews and Gentiles. Now he explains why there is no distinction.

“*for all have sinned, and fall short of the glory of God*” (*v. 23*). Everyone has sinned. Paul uses two verbs. “Have sinned” looks back at the past: everyone has committed sin. “Fall short” is in the present tense: everyone continues to fall short of God’s glory. “The glory of God” may refer to the perfect standard of God’s character, or to the glory God intended humans to share as His image bearers. Either way, everyone misses the mark.

“*being justified freely by his grace*” (*v. 24*). Then comes the good news. The same “all” who have sinned can be justified. “Justified” is a legal term meaning “declared righteous.” It is the verdict a judge gives when he declares someone not guilty. God declares sinners righteous.

How? “Freely by his grace.” The word “freely” means as a gift, without cost to the receiver. The same word is used in *John 15:25*, “*They hated me without a cause*” (*John 15:25*). Justification is given without any cause in the person receiving it. “Grace” is God’s undeserved favor. People do not earn it; God gives it.

“*through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus*” (*v. 24*). “Redemption” means release through the payment of a price. In the ancient world, it was used of buying the freedom of a slave or a prisoner. In the Old Testament, God redeemed Israel from slavery in Egypt. Through Christ, God redeems people from slavery to sin. The price was paid by Christ Himself through His death.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses summarize the gospel. All have sinned, and all who believe are justified freely by God’s grace through Christ. Salvation is entirely God’s gift. Paul writes, “*for by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God*” (*Ephesians 2:8*).

They also show that justification is a legal declaration. God does not merely help people become better; He declares them righteous in His sight. This is not a legal fiction, because it rests on the real work of Christ, who bore the penalty of sin. Believers are counted righteous because they are united to Christ, the Righteous One.

Finally, these verses show that the gift is free to the receiver but costly to the Giver. Grace is free, but redemption required a price. The cost was the life of God’s Son. Peter writes that believers were redeemed “*with precious blood, as of a lamb without blemish or spot, the blood of Christ*” (*1 Peter 1:19*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses bring freedom from guilt. Believers who trust in Christ are justified, declared not guilty, by God Himself. No accusation can stand against them. They can live with peace and confidence before God.

They also bring freedom from the pressure to earn God’s approval. Justification is free. Believers do not need to prove themselves to God. They can serve Him out of gratitude, not out of fear.

Finally, these verses level the ground among all people. Everyone has sinned, and everyone is saved in the same way. Believers can welcome others as fellow recipients of grace, regardless of their background or past.

### *Romans 3:25–26* — Just and the Justifier

> *“whom God sent to be an atoning sacrifice through faith in his blood, for a demonstration of his righteousness through the passing over of prior sins, in God’s forbearance; to demonstrate his righteousness at this present time, that he might himself be just and the justifier of him who has faith in Jesus.”*
>
> — *Romans 3:25–26* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had just said that sinners are justified freely by God’s grace through the redemption in Christ Jesus. Now he explains how God accomplished this.

“*whom God sent to be an atoning sacrifice through faith in his blood*” (*v. 25*). The phrase “atoning sacrifice” translates a word that refers to a sacrifice that turns away God’s wrath and removes sin. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament, the same word described the “mercy seat,” the cover of the Ark of the Covenant, where the high priest sprinkled blood on the Day of Atonement (*Leviticus 16:14–15*). Jesus is the true place where God’s mercy meets human sin. His blood, His death on the cross, makes atonement. This atonement is received “through faith.”

“*for a demonstration of his righteousness through the passing over of prior sins, in God’s forbearance*” (*v. 25*). Before Christ came, God had been patient with human sin. He did not punish every sin immediately. Someone might ask whether God was being unjust by letting sin go unpunished. The cross answers this question: God had not ignored sin; He was waiting to deal with it fully through Christ.

“*to demonstrate his righteousness at this present time, that he might himself be just and the justifier of him who has faith in Jesus*” (*v. 26*). This is the heart of the gospel. God faced what seemed like an impossible problem. If He is just, He must punish sin. If He is loving, He wants to forgive sinners. How can He do both? At the cross, God punished sin in Christ, so He remains just. And He forgives those who believe in Jesus, so He is the justifier. Justice and mercy meet at the cross.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses reveal the meaning of the cross. Jesus’ death was not merely an example of love or a tragic martyrdom. It was an atoning sacrifice in which God dealt with sin. Isaiah wrote of the suffering servant, “*But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed*” (*Isaiah 53:5*).

They also show that God’s love and justice are not in conflict. Some people imagine that God’s love means He overlooks sin, or that His justice means He has no mercy. The cross shows that God is perfectly just and perfectly loving. He takes sin seriously enough to judge it, and He loves sinners enough to bear that judgment Himself in His Son.

Finally, these verses show that atonement was God’s initiative. “God sent” Jesus. The Father did not have to be persuaded to love; He provided the sacrifice. John writes, “*In this is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins*” (*1 John 4:10*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses help believers understand why the cross was necessary. God could not simply overlook sin without compromising His justice. The cross shows how seriously God takes sin and how much He loves sinners. This should lead believers to worship and gratitude.

They also assure believers that their forgiveness is secure. God’s justice has been satisfied in Christ. When God forgives believers, He is not ignoring their sin; He has dealt with it fully. Believers can rest in complete forgiveness.

Finally, these verses call believers to reflect God’s character. God is both just and merciful. Believers are called to love justice and show mercy (*Micah 6:8*), taking wrong seriously while extending grace to others.

### *Romans 3:28* — Justified by Faith Apart from Works of the Law

> *“We maintain therefore that a man is justified by faith apart from the works of the law.”*
>
> — *Romans 3:28* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had just explained that God justifies sinners freely through the atoning sacrifice of Jesus. He asked, “Where then is the boasting?” and answered, “It is excluded.” If salvation is God’s gift, no one can take credit for it.

Then Paul gave his conclusion: “*We maintain therefore that a man is justified by faith apart from the works of the law*” (*v. 28*). “We maintain” means “we conclude” or “we hold firmly.” This is the summary of everything Paul has argued.

“A man is justified,” declared righteous before God, “by faith,” by trusting in Jesus Christ. “Apart from the works of the law,” without depending on keeping the commands of the Law of Moses. Faith is the means by which a person receives God’s gift.

Faith is not a work that earns salvation. It is like an empty hand that receives a gift. The value is not in the hand but in what it receives. Faith looks away from oneself to Christ.

Some readers wonder how this fits with *James 2:24*, which says that a person is justified by works and not by faith alone. Paul and James are addressing different issues. Paul is arguing against the idea that people can earn God’s acceptance by keeping the Law. James is arguing against a “faith” that is merely intellectual agreement and produces no change in life. Both agree that genuine faith in Christ saves, and that genuine faith shows itself in good works. Paul himself writes about “*faith working through love*” (*Galatians 5:6*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse expresses the doctrine of justification by faith, which was central to the Protestant Reformation of the sixteenth century. Martin Luther called it the article on which the church stands or falls. But the truth goes back to Abraham, who “*believed in the LORD, who credited it to him for righteousness*” (*Genesis 15:6*). Paul will develop this example in *Romans 4*.

It also shows that salvation is the same for all people. Since it is by faith, not by the Law, Gentiles can be saved without becoming Jews, and Jews are saved in the same way as Gentiles. Faith unites all believers on equal ground.

Finally, the verse excludes all boasting. No one can say, “I earned my salvation.” All the glory belongs to God. Paul writes, “*He who boasts, let him boast in the Lord*” (*1 Corinthians 1:31*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse brings rest to believers who are anxious about whether they have done enough for God. Justification is by faith, not by performance. Believers can stop striving to earn God’s acceptance and rest in what Christ has done.

It also protects believers from pride. Since salvation is a gift received by faith, believers have nothing to boast about except Christ. This humility can shape how they treat others.

Finally, the verse invites anyone to come to God. No one is required to clean up their life first or achieve a certain level of goodness. Anyone can be justified by trusting in Jesus. Believers can share this open invitation with everyone.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Romans 3* brings every reader face to face with the truth: there is no one righteous, not even one. All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God. This truth humbles everyone, the religious and the irreligious alike. Believers can lay aside every claim to self-righteousness and acknowledge their complete need for God’s grace.

The chapter also announces the good news: God’s righteousness has been revealed through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe. Sinners are justified freely by God’s grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus. Believers can rest in this gift, free from the guilt of sin and from the burden of trying to earn God’s acceptance.

*Romans 3* explains the meaning of the cross. Jesus is the atoning sacrifice through whom God deals with sin. At the cross, God shows that He is both just and the justifier of those who have faith in Jesus. Believers can worship God for His perfect justice and His overwhelming mercy, and they can reflect both in how they live.

Finally, the chapter excludes all boasting. Since salvation is by faith apart from works, no one can take credit for it. Jews and Gentiles, people of every background, are saved in the same way. Believers can welcome one another as fellow recipients of grace, share the gospel freely with everyone, and give all the glory to God.

## Chapter Prayer

Holy God, I confess that there is no one righteous, not even one, and that I too have sinned and fallen short of Your glory. Thank You that You have not left me in my sin. Thank You for revealing Your righteousness through faith in Jesus Christ, and for justifying me freely by Your grace through the redemption that is in Him. Lord Jesus, thank You for being the atoning sacrifice for my sins, bearing the judgment I deserved. Father, I praise You because You are both just and the One who justifies those who believe in Jesus. Take away every trace of pride in my heart, and help me to boast only in You. Help me to rest in Your grace and to share this good news with everyone, for there is no distinction. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
