Romans · Chapter 4 of 16

# Romans — Chapter 4

Chapter Theme: Abraham, the Father of All Who Believe

[Read Romans 4 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/ROM04.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul shows that justification by faith is not a new idea by pointing to Abraham, the father of Israel. Abraham believed God, and his faith was credited to him as righteousness, not because he earned it, but as a gift from the God who justifies the ungodly. David, too, celebrates the blessing of those whose sins are forgiven apart from works. Abraham was declared righteous before he was circumcised, so he is the father of all who believe, whether Jew or Gentile. Though he and Sarah were far past the age of having children, Abraham trusted God’s promise, giving glory to God, and his faith is a pattern for those who believe in the God who raised Jesus from the dead.

## Chapter Background and Story

In *Romans 3*, Paul declared that a person is justified by faith apart from the works of the Law (*3:28*). A Jewish reader might object: “Isn’t this a new teaching? What about Abraham, the father of our nation? Wasn’t he accepted by God because of his obedience and circumcision?” Abraham was the great example of righteousness in Jewish tradition. Some Jewish writings of the time praised Abraham for keeping the Law even before it was given.

Paul answers by turning to the Scriptures themselves. He shows that Abraham was justified by faith, not by works, and that this was true before he was circumcised. Abraham therefore becomes the father of all believers, both Jews and Gentiles. Paul’s argument in this chapter is careful and rooted in the text of Genesis.

### Abraham Justified by Faith (*4:1–8*)

Paul asks what Abraham discovered. “*For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about, but not toward God*” (*v. 2*). If Abraham had earned God’s acceptance, he could boast. But Scripture says otherwise, as studied below.

Paul then brings in a second witness: David, Israel’s great king. David “*pronounces blessing on the man to whom God counts righteousness apart from works*” (*v. 6*). Paul quotes *Psalm 32:1–2*, studied below. Having two witnesses was important in Jewish law (*Deuteronomy 19:15*). Abraham and David, the two most honored figures in Israel’s history, both testify to justification by faith.

### Before Circumcision (*4:9–12*)

Paul then asks whether this blessing is only for the circumcised. When was Abraham declared righteous? “*Not in circumcision, but in uncircumcision*” (*v. 10*). In Genesis, Abraham was declared righteous by faith in *Genesis 15*, but he was not circumcised until *Genesis 17*, at least fourteen years later. Circumcision came after his justification.

What, then, was circumcision? “*He received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of the faith which he had while he was in uncircumcision*” (*v. 11*). Circumcision was a sign and a seal, a visible confirmation of the righteousness Abraham already had by faith. It did not create his righteousness.

This means that Abraham is “*the father of all those who believe, though they might be in uncircumcision*” (*v. 11*). Gentile believers are Abraham’s spiritual children. And he is also “*the father of circumcision to those who not only are of the circumcision, but who also walk in the steps of that faith of our father Abraham*” (*v. 12*). Jewish believers who share Abraham’s faith are his children in the fullest sense.

### The Promise through Faith (*4:13–17*)

God’s promise to Abraham was that he and his descendants would inherit the world. “*For the promise to Abraham and to his offspring that he would be heir of the world wasn’t through the law, but through the righteousness of faith*” (*v. 13*). The promise was given about 430 years before the Law of Moses (*Galatians 3:17*). It could not depend on the Law.

If the promise depended on keeping the Law, no one would receive it, because “*the law produces wrath*” (*v. 15*). The Law reveals sin and brings judgment. “*For this cause it is of faith, that it may be according to grace, to the end that the promise may be sure to all the offspring*” (*v. 16*). Because the promise rests on grace received by faith, it is certain. If it depended on human performance, it would always be uncertain.

God had told Abraham, “*I have made you a father of many nations*” (*v. 17*) (*Genesis 17:5*). Abraham believed God, “*who gives life to the dead, and calls the things that are not, as though they were*” (*v. 17*). God can speak of things that do not yet exist as if they already did, because His word brings them into being.

### Abraham’s Faith (*4:18–22*)

Paul describes Abraham’s faith in vivid terms: “*Against hope, Abraham in hope believed*” (*v. 18*). From a human perspective, there was no hope. But Abraham’s hope was in God. “*Without being weakened in faith, he didn’t consider his own body, already having been worn out, (he being about a hundred years old), and the deadness of Sarah’s womb*” (*v. 19*). Abraham faced the facts honestly. He knew he and Sarah were too old to have children. But he did not let those facts weaken his faith. The rest of this description is studied below.

### Written for Us (*4:23–25*)

Paul concludes by applying Abraham’s story to his readers, studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Romans 4:3–5* — Faith Credited as Righteousness

> *“For what does the Scripture say? ‘Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him for righteousness.’ Now to him who works, the reward is not counted as grace, but as something owed. But to him who doesn’t work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is accounted for righteousness.”*
>
> — *Romans 4:3–5* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had argued that people are justified by faith, not by works. He knew that his Jewish readers would think of Abraham, the father of their nation, whom they regarded as the greatest example of righteousness. So Paul turned to Abraham’s story in Genesis.

“*For what does the Scripture say? “Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him for righteousness.”*” (*v. 3*) Paul quoted *Genesis 15:6*. God had promised Abraham, who was old and childless, that his descendants would be as numerous as the stars. Abraham believed God’s promise. And God “accounted” his faith as righteousness.

The word “accounted” (or “credited”) is a bookkeeping term. It means to put something into someone’s account. God credited righteousness to Abraham’s account because of his faith. Abraham did not earn it; God gave it.

Paul then explained the difference between earning and receiving: “*Now to him who works, the reward is not counted as grace, but as something owed*” (*v. 4*). When people work for an employer, their wages are not a gift; they are owed. If salvation were earned by works, God would owe it to people.

“*But to him who doesn’t work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is accounted for righteousness*” (*v. 5*). Salvation is not like wages. It is a gift received by faith. Notice the remarkable phrase: God “justifies the ungodly.” God does not justify people because they are already godly; He justifies those who are ungodly and trust in Him. This is the wonder of grace.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that justification by faith has always been God’s way. Abraham lived long before the Law of Moses, yet he was declared righteous by faith. The New Testament gospel is not a departure from the Old Testament but its fulfillment.

They also show the difference between grace and wages. Paul writes elsewhere, “*For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord*” (*Romans 6:23*). Humanity has earned only death. Eternal life comes as a free gift.

Finally, the phrase “justifies the ungodly” shows the depth of God’s grace. Many people think God accepts good people and rejects bad ones. The gospel teaches that God justifies those who know they are ungodly and trust in Him. Jesus said, “*I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance*” (*Luke 5:32*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses free believers from trying to earn God’s approval. Many people treat their relationship with God like a job, hoping that if they work hard enough, God will reward them. Paul teaches that salvation is not wages but a gift. Believers can receive it with gratitude.

They also bring hope to those who feel too sinful for God. God justifies the ungodly. No one is too far gone to receive His grace. Believers can share this hope with anyone.

Finally, these verses encourage believers to follow Abraham’s example of faith. Abraham believed God’s promise even when it seemed impossible. Believers can trust God’s promises in their own lives, knowing that faith is what God honors.

### *Romans 4:7–8* — Blessed Are Those Whose Sins Are Forgiven

> *“‘Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, whose sins are covered. Blessed is the man whom the Lord will by no means charge with sin.’”*
>
> — *Romans 4:7–8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After showing that Abraham was justified by faith, Paul brought in a second witness: King David. David was the greatest king in Israel’s history, a man after God’s own heart. But David had also committed terrible sins, including adultery with Bathsheba and the murder of her husband Uriah (*2 Samuel 11*).

Paul said that David “*pronounces blessing on the man to whom God counts righteousness apart from works*” (*v. 6*). Then he quoted *Psalm 32:1–2*.

“*Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, whose sins are covered*” (*v. 7*). The word “blessed” means happy, fortunate, deeply favored by God. The happiest people are not those who have never sinned, since no one fits that description, but those whose sins are forgiven. “Forgiven” means released, sent away. “Covered” means hidden from God’s judgment, as if under a covering. In the Old Testament, the word for atonement carries the idea of covering.

“*Blessed is the man whom the Lord will by no means charge with sin*” (*v. 8*). The Lord does not “charge” or “count” sin against this person. The same bookkeeping language is used here as in verse 3. Just as God credited righteousness to Abraham, He does not credit sin to those He forgives.

Notice that David speaks of this blessing apart from works. David did not earn forgiveness by doing good deeds. He received it by confessing his sin and trusting God’s mercy. *Psalm 32* describes how David felt crushed while he kept silent about his sin, and how he found relief when he confessed it: “*I acknowledged my sin to you*” (*Psalm 32:5*) and “*you forgave the iniquity of my sin*” (*Psalm 32:5*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that justification includes forgiveness. Being declared righteous means that God no longer counts a person’s sins against them. This is the heart of the good news. Paul writes, “*namely, that God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not reckoning to them their trespasses*” (*2 Corinthians 5:19*).

They also show that the happiest life is a forgiven life. Many people search for happiness in success, pleasure, or possessions. David discovered that true blessedness comes from having one’s sins forgiven and being right with God.

Finally, these verses show that even great sinners can be forgiven. David committed adultery and murder, yet God forgave him when he repented. No sin is beyond God’s mercy for those who turn to Him.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses invite believers to experience the joy of forgiveness. Believers who carry guilt can bring their sins to God, confess them honestly as David did, and receive His forgiveness. There is great freedom in knowing that God does not count their sins against them.

They also remind believers that God’s forgiveness is complete. When God forgives, He does not keep a record of sins. Believers do not need to keep punishing themselves for sins God has forgiven.

Finally, these verses encourage believers to extend forgiveness to others. Those who have been forgiven much are called to forgive others (*Colossians 3:13*). The joy of being forgiven can overflow into mercy toward those who have wronged them.

### *Romans 4:20–21* — Fully Assured That God Is Able

> *“Yet, looking to the promise of God, he didn’t waver through unbelief, but grew strong through faith, giving glory to God, and being fully assured that what he had promised, he was also able to perform.”*
>
> — *Romans 4:20–21* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul was describing Abraham’s faith. God had promised Abraham that he would be the father of many nations and that his descendants would be as numerous as the stars. But Abraham was about a hundred years old, and Sarah was about ninety and had never been able to have children. From a human point of view, the promise was impossible.

Paul said that Abraham did not ignore these facts. He considered his own body, which was “as good as dead,” and Sarah’s barrenness. He faced reality honestly. Yet he believed.

“*Yet, looking to the promise of God, he didn’t waver through unbelief, but grew strong through faith, giving glory to God*” (*v. 20*). Abraham kept his eyes on God’s promise. He did not waver between belief and unbelief. Instead, his faith grew stronger. And in trusting God, he gave glory to God.

Paul’s description is generous. Genesis shows that Abraham sometimes struggled; he laughed at the promise (*Genesis 17:17*) and tried to fulfill it through Hagar (*Genesis 16*). Yet over the whole course of his life, Abraham’s faith held firm and grew stronger. Paul focuses on the overall direction of his faith.

“*and being fully assured that what he had promised, he was also able to perform*” (*v. 21*). This is the heart of Abraham’s faith. He was “fully assured,” completely convinced, that God was able to do what He had promised. Abraham’s faith rested not on his own ability but on God’s power and faithfulness.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show the nature of true faith. Faith is not denying reality or pretending that difficulties do not exist. Abraham faced the facts. But faith looks beyond the facts to the God who is greater than any circumstance. Hebrews says, “*Now faith is assurance of things hoped for, proof of things not seen*” (*Hebrews 11:1*).

They also show that faith gives glory to God. When people trust God, they honor Him as faithful and powerful. Unbelief, by contrast, suggests that God cannot be trusted. Faith is an act of worship.

Finally, these verses show that faith can grow. Abraham “grew strong through faith.” Faith is not static; it can be strengthened through trusting God over time, especially in difficult circumstances.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers who face impossible situations. Believers may face illness, financial hardship, broken relationships, or long-delayed hopes. Like Abraham, they can acknowledge the difficulties honestly while trusting that God is able to do what He has promised.

They also encourage believers to focus on God’s promises. Abraham looked to “the promise of God.” Believers can strengthen their faith by meditating on God’s promises in Scripture and remembering His faithfulness.

Finally, these verses encourage believers who struggle with doubt. Abraham was not perfect; he had moments of weakness. Yet God honored his faith. Believers who struggle can bring their doubts to God and ask Him to strengthen their faith.

### *Romans 4:24–25* — Delivered for Our Trespasses, Raised for Our Justification

> *“but for our sake also, to whom it will be accounted, who believe in him who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead, who was delivered up for our trespasses, and was raised for our justification.”*
>
> — *Romans 4:24–25* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had been telling the story of Abraham’s faith. Abraham believed God’s promise, and his faith was credited to him as righteousness. Now Paul applied this story to his readers.

“*Now it was not written that it was accounted to him for his sake alone*” (*v. 23*). The story of Abraham was not recorded only for Abraham’s benefit. “*but for our sake also, to whom it will be accounted, who believe in him who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead*” (*v. 24*). The same thing that happened to Abraham happens to all who believe. Abraham believed in the God who could bring life from his and Sarah’s “dead” bodies. Believers today trust in the God who raised Jesus from the dead. Both kinds of faith trust God’s power to bring life out of death.

Then Paul summarized the gospel in one verse: “*who was delivered up for our trespasses, and was raised for our justification*” (*v. 25*). Jesus was “delivered up,” handed over to death, because of our sins. His death dealt with the problem of sin. This echoes *Isaiah 53:12*, which says the servant “*bore the sins of many*” (*Isaiah 53:12*).

And Jesus “was raised for our justification.” His resurrection showed that God accepted His sacrifice. It is God’s declaration that the work is complete. Because Jesus was raised, believers can be declared righteous. The death and resurrection of Jesus belong together; both are necessary for salvation.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that the Scriptures were written for believers in every generation. Paul says the same elsewhere: “*For whatever things were written before were written for our learning*” (*Romans 15:4*). The stories of the Old Testament are not merely ancient history; they speak to believers today.

They also summarize the heart of the gospel: Christ’s death and resurrection. Paul writes that the gospel is “*that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures*” (*1 Corinthians 15:3*), “*that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures*” (*1 Corinthians 15:4*). Salvation rests entirely on what Christ has done.

Finally, these verses show the connection between faith in the resurrection and justification. Believers are justified by trusting in the God who raised Jesus. The resurrection is not an optional extra in the Christian faith; it is central to salvation.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to read the Old Testament as God’s word for them. The stories of Abraham, Moses, David, and others were written to teach and encourage believers today.

They also invite believers to rest in what Christ has done. Jesus was delivered for their sins and raised for their justification. Believers can trust that their sins have been dealt with and that God has declared them righteous.

Finally, these verses call believers to place their faith in the God who raises the dead. The same God who brought life from Abraham and Sarah and who raised Jesus can bring life into situations that seem hopeless. Believers can trust Him with every part of their lives.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Romans 4* shows that justification by faith is God’s ancient way. Abraham, the father of Israel, was declared righteous because he believed God, not because of his works. David, too, celebrated the blessing of forgiveness apart from works. Believers today are justified in the same way: by trusting God, who justifies the ungodly.

The chapter also shows that Abraham is the father of all who believe. He was declared righteous before he was circumcised, so Gentile believers are his true children, along with Jewish believers who share his faith. Believers can see themselves as part of one family of faith that stretches back to Abraham and includes people of every nation.

*Romans 4* holds up Abraham as a model of faith. Facing impossible circumstances, he did not deny reality, but he looked to God’s promise, grew strong in faith, and gave glory to God, fully convinced that God was able to do what He had promised. Believers can follow his example, trusting God’s promises in their own difficulties and asking Him to strengthen their faith.

Finally, the chapter points to Jesus, who was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification. Believers can rest in His finished work, trusting in the God who raises the dead, and can rejoice in the blessing of sins forgiven and righteousness credited to them as a gift.

## Chapter Prayer

Faithful God, thank You for Abraham, who believed You and was counted righteous. Thank You that You justify the ungodly, and that I can be made right with You not by my works but by trusting You. Thank You for the joy David knew, the blessing of sins forgiven and no longer counted against me. Make me a true child of Abraham, walking in the steps of his faith. When I face situations that seem impossible, help me to look to Your promises, to grow strong in faith, and to give You glory, fully assured that You are able to do what You have promised. Lord Jesus, thank You for being delivered up for my sins and raised for my justification. I trust in the God who raises the dead. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Romans · Chapter 5 of 16

# Romans — Chapter 5

Chapter Theme: Peace with God, Hope That Does Not Disappoint, and Grace That Reigns

[Read Romans 5 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/ROM05.htm)

Main Teaching

Having been justified by faith, believers have peace with God and stand in His grace, rejoicing in the hope of His glory. They can even rejoice in suffering, because God uses it to produce endurance, character, and hope, a hope that will not disappoint because God’s love has been poured into their hearts by the Spirit. God proved His love by sending Christ to die for us while we were still sinners and enemies, and if He reconciled us through Christ’s death, He will surely save us through His life. Paul then contrasts Adam and Christ: through one man’s disobedience sin and death spread to all, but through one man’s obedience grace abounds, and where sin increased, grace overflowed even more.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Romans 5* marks a transition in Paul’s letter. In chapters 1–4, he explained how sinners are justified by faith. Now he begins to describe the results of justification: peace, hope, love, and the reign of grace. Chapters 5–8 explore the new life that believers have in Christ, ending with the triumphant declaration that nothing can separate them from God’s love (*8:38–39*).

The second half of chapter 5 contains one of the most important theological passages in the Bible, comparing Adam, the first man, with Christ. Paul shows that just as Adam’s sin affected all humanity, Christ’s obedience brings life to all who belong to Him.

### The Results of Justification (*5:1–11*)

Paul begins with a great “therefore.” Because believers have been justified by faith, as he has explained in chapters 3–4, they now experience peace with God, studied below. Their hope, even in suffering, is also studied below.

Paul then describes the love of God displayed in Christ’s death. “*For while we were yet weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly*” (*v. 6*). “Weak” means helpless, unable to save ourselves. “At the right time” means at the moment God had appointed in history (*Galatians 4:4*). Paul then highlights the astonishing nature of this love, studied below.

“*Much more then, being now justified by his blood, we will be saved from God’s wrath through him*” (*v. 9*). If God has already justified believers through Christ’s death, He will certainly save them from the coming judgment. “*For if while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, being reconciled, we will be saved by his life*” (*v. 10*). Paul reasons from the greater to the lesser: if God reconciled His enemies through Christ’s death, how much more will He save His friends through Christ’s risen life. Believers’ security rests on the living Christ, who continues to intercede for them (*Hebrews 7:25*).

“*Not only so, but we also rejoice in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received the reconciliation*” (*v. 11*). The deepest joy is not only in God’s gifts but in God Himself.

### Adam and Christ (*5:12–21*)

Paul now compares Adam and Christ. “*Therefore, as sin entered into the world through one man, and death through sin, so death passed to all men because all sinned*” (*v. 12*). Sin entered the world through Adam’s disobedience in the Garden of Eden (*Genesis 3*). Death followed as its consequence. And death spread to all people, because all sinned.

Christians have understood the relationship between Adam’s sin and humanity’s sin in different ways. Some emphasize that Adam acted as the representative of the whole human race, so that his guilt is counted to all. Others emphasize that Adam’s sin introduced a corrupted nature that all people inherit, so that all inevitably sin. Others emphasize that all people follow Adam’s pattern by sinning themselves. Many see truth in more than one of these perspectives. All agree that sin and death came through Adam and affect every human being.

Paul notes that sin existed even before the Law of Moses was given, since death reigned from Adam to Moses. Adam is “*a foreshadowing of him who was to come*” (*v. 14*). Adam was a “type” or pattern of Christ: just as one man’s action affected all humanity, so another man’s action would affect all who belong to Him.

But the comparison also involves contrast. “*But the free gift isn’t like the trespass*” (*v. 15*). Grace is far greater than sin. “*For if by the trespass of the one the many died, much more did the grace of God and the gift by the grace of the one man, Jesus Christ, abound to the many*” (*v. 15*). “*For if by the trespass of the one, death reigned through the one; so much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness reign in life through the one, Jesus Christ*” (*v. 17*). Notice that believers will not only escape death; they will “reign in life.” Paul’s summary of the comparison is studied below.

“*The law came in that the trespass might abound; but where sin abounded, grace abounded more exceedingly*” (*v. 20*). When the Law was given, it made sin more visible and showed how serious it was. But no matter how great sin became, God’s grace was greater still. The image is of a flood: sin rose high, but grace overflowed far above it.

“*that as sin reigned in death, even so grace might reign through righteousness to eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord*” (*v. 21*). Two kings are contrasted: sin, which reigned and brought death, and grace, which reigns and brings eternal life. Through Christ, grace has taken the throne.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Romans 5:1–2* — Peace with God

> *“Being therefore justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ; through whom we also have our access by faith into this grace in which we stand. We rejoice in hope of the glory of God.”*
>
> — *Romans 5:1–2* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had spent the first four chapters of Romans explaining how sinners are justified, declared righteous before God, through faith in Jesus Christ. Now he begins to describe what justification means for believers’ lives.

“*Being therefore justified by faith*” (*v. 1*). This summarizes everything Paul has taught. Believers have been declared righteous. This is a settled fact, not something that might happen in the future.

“*we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ*” (*v. 1*). The first result of justification is peace with God. Before justification, people are at war with God. Paul later says that we were “enemies” (*5:10*). Sin made people rebels against God and placed them under His judgment. But through Christ, the war is over. God has made peace. This is not merely a feeling of peace, but a real change in relationship.

“*through whom we also have our access by faith into this grace in which we stand*” (*v. 2*). Through Christ, believers have “access” to God’s grace. The word was used of being brought into the presence of a king. Believers can come into God’s presence freely. And they “stand” in grace. Grace is not a place they visit occasionally; it is where they live, their firm and secure position.

“*We rejoice in hope of the glory of God*” (*v. 2*). Believers look forward with joy to sharing in God’s glory. In *Romans 3:23*, Paul said that all have fallen short of the glory of God. Now believers can rejoice because they will one day share in that glory. “Hope” in the Bible is not wishful thinking; it is confident expectation based on God’s promises.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that justification changes a person’s relationship with God. Peace with God is the foundation of every other blessing. Paul writes, “*For he is our peace*” (*Ephesians 2:14*). Christ Himself is the peace between God and humanity.

They also show the security of believers. They “stand” in grace. Their position does not depend on their feelings or their performance on a given day. They are firmly established in God’s favor through Christ.

Finally, these verses show that the Christian life looks forward. Believers have peace now, stand in grace now, and look forward to glory in the future. The best is yet to come.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses bring assurance to believers who doubt whether God accepts them. Because they have been justified by faith, they have peace with God. The war is over. They can approach God with confidence, not fear.

They also invite believers to live in grace. Believers do not need to earn their place before God each day. They stand in grace. This frees them to serve God out of love, not out of anxiety.

Finally, these verses encourage believers to rejoice in hope. Whatever difficulties believers face now, they can look forward to sharing in God’s glory. This hope can bring joy even in hard times.

### *Romans 5:3–5* — Suffering Produces Hope

> *“Not only this, but we also rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces perseverance; and perseverance, proven character; and proven character, hope; and hope doesn’t disappoint us, because God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who was given to us.”*
>
> — *Romans 5:3–5* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had just said that believers rejoice in hope of the glory of God. Then he added something surprising: “*Not only this, but we also rejoice in our sufferings*” (*v. 3*). Believers can rejoice not only in their future hope but even in their present sufferings.

This does not mean that believers enjoy pain or pretend that suffering is pleasant. It means they can rejoice because of what God does through suffering. Paul explains: “*knowing that suffering produces perseverance*” (*v. 3*). Suffering, when faced with faith, produces “perseverance,” the ability to endure and keep going.

“*and perseverance, proven character; and proven character, hope*” (*v. 4*). Perseverance produces “proven character,” a character that has been tested and found genuine, like metal refined by fire. And proven character produces “hope.” Each step leads to the next, like a chain: suffering, perseverance, character, hope.

“*and hope doesn’t disappoint us*” (*v. 5*). This hope will not let believers down. It will not prove to be empty. The word can also mean “does not put us to shame.” Believers will not be embarrassed for having trusted God.

“*because God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who was given to us*” (*v. 5*). The reason believers can be sure of their hope is that they have experienced God’s love. The Holy Spirit has “poured” God’s love into their hearts, an image of abundance, like water poured out generously. This is the first mention of the Holy Spirit in Romans since chapter 1. Believers know they are loved by God because His Spirit assures them of it.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that God uses suffering for good in the lives of believers. James writes something similar: “*Count it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various temptations*” (*James 1:2*), “*knowing that the testing of your faith produces endurance*” (*James 1:3*). Suffering is not meaningless; God uses it to shape believers into the image of Christ.

They also show that Christian hope is grounded in God’s love. Hope is not based on positive thinking or favorable circumstances. It is based on the love of God, which the Spirit makes real in believers’ hearts. Because God loves them, believers can be sure He will fulfill His promises.

Finally, these verses show the work of the Holy Spirit in the believer’s inner life. The Spirit does not only give gifts or power; He fills believers’ hearts with the experience of God’s love. Paul later says that the Spirit testifies with believers’ spirits that they are God’s children (*Romans 8:16*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses help believers find meaning in suffering. When believers face illness, loss, disappointment, or hardship, they can trust that God is at work, producing endurance, character, and hope. This does not make suffering easy, but it gives it purpose. It also does not mean that believers should stay in situations of abuse or harm; God’s purposes in suffering never require accepting mistreatment.

They also encourage believers to persevere. Endurance is built over time. Believers who keep trusting God through difficulties will find their character strengthened and their hope deepened.

Finally, these verses invite believers to rest in God’s love. When believers feel discouraged or doubtful, they can remember that God’s love has been poured into their hearts by the Holy Spirit. They can ask the Spirit to renew their awareness of God’s love.

### *Romans 5:8* — While We Were Yet Sinners

> *“But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”*
>
> — *Romans 5:8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had been explaining the hope believers have because of God’s love. Now he shows how God proved that love.

He first said that Christ died for the ungodly at the right time, while we were weak and helpless (*5:6*). Then he made a comparison: “*For one will hardly die for a righteous man. Yet perhaps for a good person someone would even dare to die*” (*v. 7*). It is rare for anyone to give their life for another person, even for someone who is upright. Perhaps someone might be willing to die for a person who is especially good or kind to them. But this is unusual.

“*But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us*” (*v. 8*). God’s love is completely different. Christ did not die for good people. He died for “sinners,” people who had rebelled against God and did not deserve His love. “Commends” means proves, demonstrates, or shows clearly. The cross is the clearest proof of God’s love.

Notice the timing: “while we were yet sinners.” God did not wait for people to improve before sending Christ. He acted while they were still in their sin. His love was not a response to their goodness; it came first.

Notice also that Paul says “God commends his own love.” The death of Christ demonstrates God’s love. This shows the unity of the Father and the Son. The cross is not the Son persuading an unwilling Father to love; it is the Father’s love expressed through the Son’s sacrifice.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals the unconditional nature of God’s love. Human love is often based on the worth or attractiveness of the one loved. God’s love is based on His own character. John writes, “*We love him, because he first loved us*” (*1 John 4:19*).

It also shows the substitutionary nature of Christ’s death. Christ died “for us,” in our place and for our benefit. He took the penalty we deserved.

Finally, the verse provides the ultimate assurance of God’s love. When believers doubt that God loves them, they can look at the cross. God has already proven His love in the most costly way possible.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse brings comfort to anyone who feels unlovable. God’s love is not based on how good people are. He loved sinners enough to send His Son to die for them. No one is beyond the reach of His love.

It also challenges believers to love others as God loves. If God loved people while they were still sinners, believers are called to love others even when they do not deserve it, including enemies and those who are difficult to love.

Finally, the verse encourages believers to share the good news of God’s love. Many people believe they must earn God’s love. The gospel declares that God has already demonstrated His love through Christ’s death. This is the message the world needs to hear.

### *Romans 5:18–19* — One Act of Righteousness

> *“So then as through one trespass, all men were condemned; even so through one act of righteousness, all men were justified to life. For as through the one man’s disobedience many were made sinners, even so through the obedience of the one, many will be made righteous.”*
>
> — *Romans 5:18–19* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had been comparing Adam, the first man, with Jesus Christ. Through Adam’s sin, sin and death entered the world and spread to all people. But through Christ, grace and life have come. Now Paul summarizes the comparison.

“*So then as through one trespass, all men were condemned*” (*v. 18*). Adam’s single act of disobedience, eating the forbidden fruit in the Garden, brought condemnation to all humanity. All people share in the consequences of Adam’s sin.

“*even so through one act of righteousness, all men were justified to life*” (*v. 18*). Christ’s “one act of righteousness,” His obedient life culminating in His death on the cross, brings justification and life. Just as Adam’s act affected all who are connected to him, Christ’s act affects all who are connected to Him.

“*For as through the one man’s disobedience many were made sinners, even so through the obedience of the one, many will be made righteous*” (*v. 19*). Adam’s disobedience made many sinners. Christ’s obedience makes many righteous. Christ succeeded where Adam failed. Adam disobeyed in a garden of plenty; Christ obeyed in the garden of Gethsemane and on the cross.

The word “all” in verse 18 has been understood in different ways. Most Christians understand that Christ’s act makes justification available to all, or that it brings life to all who are “in Christ,” just as Adam’s act brought condemnation to all who are “in Adam.” Verse 17 speaks of “those who receive the abundance of grace,” showing that the gift must be received. Paul uses “all” to emphasize the universal scope of Christ’s work, which includes both Jews and Gentiles.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses teach that humanity is connected to either Adam or Christ. Paul writes elsewhere, “*For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive*” (*1 Corinthians 15:22*). Every person is born connected to Adam. Through faith, believers become connected to Christ.

They also show the importance of Christ’s obedience. Christ did not only die for sins; He lived a perfectly obedient life. His righteousness is credited to believers. They are “made righteous” through His obedience.

Finally, these verses show the greatness of Christ’s work. One act of Adam brought disaster to the whole human race. One act of Christ undid that disaster and brought something even greater: not merely a return to Eden, but eternal life and reigning with Christ.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses help believers understand their identity. Believers are no longer defined by Adam’s failure but by Christ’s success. They are “in Christ,” declared righteous through His obedience.

They also give believers hope in the face of sin and death. Adam brought sin and death, but Christ has overcome both. Believers can live with confidence that sin and death do not have the final word.

Finally, these verses encourage believers to share the gospel. All people are affected by Adam’s sin, and Christ’s work is offered to all. Believers can invite others to receive the abundance of grace and the gift of righteousness through Christ.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Romans 5* describes the blessings of justification. Believers have peace with God, access to His grace, and confident hope of sharing His glory. They do not need to live in fear of God’s judgment or wonder whether He accepts them. The war is over, and they stand firmly in His grace.

The chapter also transforms how believers view suffering. Suffering, faced with faith, produces endurance, character, and hope, a hope that will not disappoint because God’s love has been poured into believers’ hearts by the Holy Spirit. Believers can find meaning and even joy in hardship, trusting God to use it for their good, while never mistaking God’s purposes for permission for anyone to harm them.

*Romans 5* proclaims the greatness of God’s love. Christ died for us while we were still sinners, helpless and even enemies of God. This love is the foundation of believers’ assurance. If God reconciled them while they were enemies, He will certainly save them now that they are His children.

Finally, the chapter shows that grace is greater than sin. Adam’s disobedience brought sin and death to all, but Christ’s obedience brings righteousness and life. Where sin increased, grace overflowed. Believers can rejoice that grace now reigns, and they can live with confidence that no sin is too great for God’s grace to overcome.

## Chapter Prayer

Gracious God, thank You that I have been justified by faith and have peace with You through my Lord Jesus Christ. Thank You for bringing me into Your grace, where I now stand, and for the hope of sharing Your glory. When I face suffering, help me to trust that You are producing endurance, character, and hope in me. Pour Your love into my heart afresh by Your Holy Spirit. Thank You for proving Your love by sending Christ to die for me while I was still a sinner. Lord Jesus, thank You for Your perfect obedience, through which I am made righteous. I rejoice that where sin increased, Your grace overflowed even more. Let grace reign in my life, leading me to eternal life. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Romans · Chapter 6 of 16

# Romans — Chapter 6

Chapter Theme: Dead to Sin, Alive to God: Freedom from Sin’s Reign

[Read Romans 6 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/ROM06.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul answers a dangerous misunderstanding of grace: if grace increases where sin increases, should believers keep sinning? Absolutely not. Through baptism, believers have been united with Christ in His death and resurrection; their old self was crucified with Him so that they might walk in newness of life. They are to consider themselves dead to sin and alive to God, offering their bodies to God as instruments of righteousness, because sin is no longer their master. Everyone serves someone; once slaves of sin, believers are now set free to serve righteousness, and while the wages of sin is death, God’s free gift is eternal life in Christ Jesus.

## Chapter Background and Story

In *Romans 5:20*, Paul wrote, “*where sin abounded, grace abounded more exceedingly*” (*Romans 5:20*). Some might twist this truth to mean that sin does not matter, or even that sinning more would bring more grace. In *Romans 6*, Paul addresses this misunderstanding directly. He asks two similar questions: “Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound?” (*6:1*) and “Shall we sin because we are not under law but under grace?” (*6:15*). He answers both with a strong “May it never be!”

Paul’s answer is not merely to forbid sin. He explains that believers have been fundamentally changed through their union with Christ. They are no longer the same people. Their relationship to sin has been broken. This chapter is foundational for understanding Christian holiness: believers obey God not to earn salvation, but because they have been made new.

### Dead to Sin through Union with Christ (*6:1–11*)

Paul’s opening question and answer are studied below. He explains what happened to believers: “*Or don’t you know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?*” (*v. 3*) To be baptized “into Christ” means to be united with Him. And union with Christ includes union with His death. The meaning of this union is studied below.

“*For if we have become united with him in the likeness of his death, we will also be part of his resurrection*” (*v. 5*). The word “united” was used of plants grafted together so that they grow as one. Believers are joined to Christ in His death and will share in His resurrection.

“*knowing this, that our old man was crucified with him, that the body of sin might be done away with, so that we would no longer be in bondage to sin*” (*v. 6*). The “old man” refers to the person believers used to be before Christ, their old identity in Adam, under the power of sin. That old self was crucified with Christ. The “body of sin” may refer to human existence dominated by sin. The purpose is that believers would no longer be slaves to sin. “*For he who has died has been freed from sin*” (*v. 7*). Death ends all obligations. A dead person cannot be commanded by a former master.

“*But if we died with Christ, we believe that we will also live with him*” (*v. 8*). Christ’s resurrection was final: “*knowing that Christ, being raised from the dead, dies no more. Death no longer has dominion over him!*” (*v. 9*) “*For the death that he died, he died to sin one time; but the life that he lives, he lives to God*” (*v. 10*). Christ dealt with sin once for all and now lives forever to God. Paul’s application of this truth is studied below.

### Offering Yourselves to God (*6:12–14*)

Because of this new identity, Paul gives commands: “*Therefore don’t let sin reign in your mortal body, that you should obey it in its lusts*” (*v. 12*). Sin is no longer the rightful king, but it still tries to rule. Believers must refuse to let it.

“*Also, do not present your members to sin as instruments of unrighteousness, but present yourselves to God as alive from the dead, and your members as instruments of righteousness to God*” (*v. 13*). “Members” refers to the parts of the body, such as hands, feet, eyes, and tongue, and by extension all of one’s abilities. “Instruments” can also mean “weapons.” Believers can use their bodies either as weapons for sin or as weapons for righteousness. Each day, they choose whom they will serve with their bodies.

Then comes a promise: “*For sin will not have dominion over you, for you are not under law, but under grace*” (*v. 14*). Sin will not be the master of believers. Why? Because they are under grace, not law. The Law commanded but did not give power to obey. Grace frees believers from sin’s dominion and gives them a new life.

### Slaves of Righteousness (*6:15–23*)

Paul asks again, “*Shall we sin because we are not under law but under grace? May it never be!*” (*v. 15*) He uses the image of slavery, common in the Roman world, where perhaps a third of the population were slaves. “*Don’t you know that when you present yourselves as servants and obey someone, you are the servants of whomever you obey, whether of sin to death, or of obedience to righteousness?*” (*v. 16*) Everyone serves someone. There is no neutral ground. People either serve sin, which leads to death, or serve God, which leads to righteousness.

“*But thanks be to God that, whereas you were bondservants of sin, you became obedient from the heart to that form of teaching to which you were delivered*” (*v. 17*). Believers were once slaves to sin, but they have responded wholeheartedly to the gospel. Notice the phrase “from the heart.” Their obedience was not mere outward conformity but heartfelt.

“*Being made free from sin, you became bondservants of righteousness*” (*v. 18*). Freedom from sin does not mean freedom to do anything one wants. It means freedom to serve righteousness. True freedom is found in serving God.

Paul admits that he is using a human illustration “*because of the weakness of your flesh*” (*v. 19*). Slavery is an imperfect picture, since serving God is not oppressive but life-giving. Still, the illustration helps. Just as believers once gave themselves fully to sin, they should now give themselves fully to righteousness, “*for sanctification*” (*v. 19*), the process of becoming holy.

Paul asks them to consider the results of their former life: “*What fruit then did you have at that time in the things of which you are now ashamed? For the end of those things is death*” (*v. 21*). Sin promised much but produced shame and death. “*But now, being made free from sin and having become servants of God, you have your fruit of sanctification and the result of eternal life*” (*v. 22*). Serving God produces holiness and leads to eternal life. Paul’s final summary is studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Romans 6:1–2* — Shall We Continue in Sin?

> *“What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? May it never be! We who died to sin, how could we live in it any longer?”*
>
> — *Romans 6:1–2* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had just written that where sin increased, grace overflowed even more (*5:20*). God’s grace is greater than any sin. This is wonderful news. But Paul knew that some people might misuse it.

“*What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound?*” (*v. 1*) Someone might reason: “If God’s grace is shown most when there is the most sin, then the more I sin, the more grace I will receive. So why not keep sinning?” Paul had apparently been accused of teaching this (*3:8*).

“*May it never be!*” (*v. 2*) This is the strongest negative expression in Greek. It can be translated “Absolutely not!” or “God forbid!” Paul rejects the idea completely.

“*We who died to sin, how could we live in it any longer?*” (*v. 2*) Paul’s reason is that believers have “died to sin.” This does not mean that believers never sin or that they no longer feel the pull of temptation. It means that their relationship to sin has fundamentally changed. Sin is no longer their master. They have been separated from sin’s power. Living in sin would contradict who they now are.

The question is not “May I continue in sin?” but “How could I?” For someone who has died to sin, continuing to live in it makes no sense.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that grace is not a license to sin. True grace does not make people careless about sin; it changes them. Paul writes to Titus that God’s grace “*instructing us to the intent that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we would live soberly, righteously, and godly in this present age*” (*Titus 2:12*).

They also show that the gospel creates a new identity. Believers are not merely forgiven sinners who continue as before. They have died to sin and been raised to new life. Their identity has changed, and their behavior is meant to flow from that new identity.

Finally, these verses show that justification and sanctification belong together. God does not declare people righteous and then leave them unchanged. Those whom He justifies, He also begins to transform. Faith that does not change a person’s life is not genuine faith.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses warn believers against taking God’s grace for granted. It is possible to think, “God will forgive me anyway, so it doesn’t matter what I do.” Paul’s response is clear: those who have truly received grace do not want to keep living in sin.

They also encourage believers who struggle with sin. Believers have died to sin, which means sin’s power has been broken. They can fight against sin with confidence, knowing that they are no longer its slaves.

Finally, these verses invite believers to examine their attitude toward sin. Do they hate sin, or do they excuse it? A heart changed by grace grows to hate sin and love righteousness.

### *Romans 6:4* — Walking in Newness of Life

> *“We were buried therefore with him through baptism into death, that just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we also might walk in newness of life.”*
>
> — *Romans 6:4* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had asked whether believers should continue in sin so that grace might increase, and he had answered, “Absolutely not!” He explained that believers have died to sin. Now he explains how this happened: through union with Christ, pictured in baptism.

In the early church, baptism was often done by immersion, plunging the person under water and bringing them up again. This vividly pictured death, burial, and resurrection.

“*We were buried therefore with him through baptism into death*” (*v. 4*). When believers are baptized, they are identified with Christ’s death and burial. Just as Christ died and was buried, believers’ old way of life has died and been buried.

“*that just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father*” (*v. 4*). Christ did not stay in the tomb. He was raised by the glorious power of God the Father.

“*so we also might walk in newness of life*” (*v. 4*). Just as Christ rose to new life, believers are raised to live a new kind of life. “Walk” is a common biblical word for the way a person lives day by day. “Newness of life” means a life that is fresh and different, empowered by the risen Christ.

Christians understand baptism in different ways. Some see it as a means through which God unites believers with Christ. Others see it as an outward sign of a union with Christ that happens through faith. All agree that union with Christ in His death and resurrection is the foundation of the Christian life, and that baptism is the visible sign of this union.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that believers share in Christ’s death and resurrection. This is not just a symbol; it is a spiritual reality. Paul writes, “*I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me*” (*Galatians 2:20*).

It also shows that the Christian life is a new life. Believers do not merely try to improve their old life. They have been given a new life, powered by the same God who raised Jesus from the dead. Paul writes, “*Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new*” (*2 Corinthians 5:17*).

Finally, the verse shows the importance of baptism. Baptism is not merely a ritual; it is a powerful picture of the believer’s union with Christ. It marks the beginning of a new life and identity.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to remember their baptism. Baptism marks the moment of identification with Christ’s death and resurrection. Believers can recall that their old life has been buried and that they have been raised to walk in newness of life.

It also encourages believers to live differently. The new life is not merely a future hope; it is meant to be lived now, every day. Believers can ask God to help them walk in newness of life in their relationships, habits, words, and choices.

Finally, the verse brings hope to those who feel stuck in old patterns. The same power that raised Jesus from the dead is at work in believers. Change is possible. Believers can trust God to give them new life.

### *Romans 6:11* — Consider Yourselves Dead to Sin and Alive to God

> *“Thus consider yourselves also to be dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord.”*
>
> — *Romans 6:11* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had been explaining that believers were united with Christ in His death and resurrection. Christ died to sin once for all, and now He lives to God. Death no longer has any power over Him.

“*Thus consider yourselves also to be dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord*” (*v. 11*). This is the first command in *Romans 6*. Paul tells believers to “consider” themselves dead to sin and alive to God. The word “consider” is the same bookkeeping word used in *Romans 4* for “accounted” or “credited.” It means to count something as true, to reckon it to be so.

Believers are not told to make themselves dead to sin by their own effort. They are told to recognize what is already true because of their union with Christ. They have died to sin. They are alive to God. Now they must live in light of this reality.

“Dead to sin” means that sin no longer has authority over them. A dead person does not respond to commands. Sin may still call to believers, but they are no longer obligated to obey.

“Alive to God” means that believers now live in relationship with God, responsive to Him, living for Him.

“In Christ Jesus our Lord” shows that this new identity comes only through union with Christ.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that the Christian life begins with knowing who one is in Christ. Before Paul gives commands about behavior (*6:12–13*), he tells believers to understand their identity. Right living flows from right understanding. Believers do not obey to become new; they obey because they are new.

It also shows the importance of faith in the ongoing Christian life. Believers must believe what God says about them, even when their feelings or experiences seem to contradict it. Faith counts God’s word as true.

Finally, the verse shows that believers share in Christ’s victory. Just as Christ has defeated sin and death, believers share in His triumph. Their struggle against sin is not a battle to be won from scratch, but a battle in which the decisive victory has already been won.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers facing temptation to remember who they are. When temptation comes, believers can say, “I am dead to sin and alive to God in Christ. Sin is not my master.” This truth gives strength to resist.

It also encourages believers to think rightly about themselves. Many believers see themselves mainly as sinners who will always fail. While believers still struggle with sin, their deepest identity is that they are alive to God in Christ. This truth can bring hope and confidence.

Finally, the verse invites believers to live for God daily. Being “alive to God” means paying attention to Him, responding to Him, and living for His glory. Believers can ask each day how they can live for God in their particular circumstances.

### *Romans 6:23* — The Wages of Sin and the Free Gift of God

> *“For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.”*
>
> — *Romans 6:23* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had been comparing two kinds of servitude: slavery to sin and slavery to God. He had shown that serving sin produces shame and leads to death, while serving God produces holiness and leads to eternal life. Now he summarizes the whole chapter in one powerful verse.

“*For the wages of sin is death*” (*v. 23*). “Wages” were the regular payment given to soldiers or workers. They were earned. Sin pays its servants, and what it pays is death. Death here includes physical death, spiritual separation from God, and ultimately eternal separation from Him. Sin always pays what it promises, and its payment is death.

“*but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord*” (*v. 23*). In contrast to wages, which are earned, eternal life is a “free gift.” It cannot be earned. God gives it graciously. “Eternal life” is not only endless existence; it is the life of God, a relationship with Him that begins now and lasts forever. And it is found “in Christ Jesus our Lord,” through union with Him.

The contrast is striking: wages versus gift, sin versus God, death versus eternal life. Sin pays what is deserved; God gives what is not deserved.

This verse is one of the most well-known in the Bible because it summarizes the gospel so clearly.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows the seriousness of sin. Sin is not a minor problem; it leads to death. Genesis shows that death entered the world through sin (*Genesis 2:17*; *3:19*). Every death is a reminder of sin’s terrible cost.

It also shows the generosity of God. Eternal life is a gift. God does not wait for people to earn it, because they never could. He gives it freely through Christ. This gift cost God the life of His Son.

Finally, the verse shows that there are only two paths. Every person is either receiving sin’s wages or God’s gift. There is no middle ground. The choice is between death and life.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse helps believers share the gospel simply. Many people do not understand that sin leads to death or that eternal life is a free gift. This verse explains both truths in a few words.

It also reminds believers of the seriousness of sin. Even believers can treat sin lightly. Remembering that the wages of sin is death can motivate believers to turn from sin and live for God.

Finally, the verse fills believers with gratitude. They have received the free gift of eternal life, which they could never have earned. They can thank God every day for this gift and live in a way that honors the Giver.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Romans 6* makes clear that grace is not a license to sin. Those who have truly received God’s grace have died to sin and cannot continue to live in it as before. Believers can reject the idea that sin does not matter, and instead let God’s grace transform how they live.

The chapter also explains the foundation of the Christian life: union with Christ. Through faith, pictured in baptism, believers have died with Christ and been raised with Him to walk in newness of life. Their old self was crucified, so that they are no longer slaves to sin. Believers can remember their baptism and live in the reality of their new identity.

*Romans 6* calls believers to consider themselves dead to sin and alive to God, and to offer their bodies to God as instruments of righteousness. Each day, believers choose whom they will serve with their hands, eyes, tongues, and abilities. Because they are under grace, sin will not be their master. Believers can face temptation with confidence, knowing that sin’s power has been broken.

Finally, the chapter contrasts two kinds of servitude. Serving sin produces shame and leads to death; serving God produces holiness and leads to eternal life. The wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord. Believers can respond with gratitude for this gift and give themselves gladly to serving the God who has set them free.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You that I have been united with You in Your death and resurrection. Thank You that my old self was crucified with You, so that I no longer have to be a slave to sin. Keep me from ever treating Your grace as an excuse to sin. Help me to consider myself dead to sin and alive to God in You. Today I offer myself to You, and I offer my body, my hands, my eyes, my tongue, and my abilities as instruments of righteousness. When temptation comes, remind me that sin is not my master, because I am under grace. Thank You for setting me free to serve You. Thank You that though the wages of sin is death, You have given me the free gift of eternal life. Help me to walk in newness of life each day. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
