Romans · Chapter 7 of 16

# Romans — Chapter 7

Chapter Theme: The Holy Law, the Power of Sin, and the Cry for Deliverance

[Read Romans 7 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/ROM07.htm)

Main Teaching

Using the illustration of a marriage ended by death, Paul explains that believers have died to the Law through Christ so that they might belong to the risen Christ and bear fruit for God. The Law itself is holy, righteous, and good, but sin used the commandment to awaken desire and bring death. Paul then describes an intense inner struggle: wanting to do good but not doing it, delighting in God’s law inwardly while finding another power at work in the body. The chapter ends with the cry, “Who will deliver me out of the body of this death?” and the answer, “I thank God through Jesus Christ, our Lord!”

## Chapter Background and Story

*Romans 7* is one of the most discussed chapters in Paul’s letters. It answers two questions raised by chapter 6. First, Paul had said that believers are “not under law, but under grace” (*6:14*). How can believers be free from the Law that God Himself gave? Second, if the Law does not free people from sin, is the Law itself evil? Paul’s answer is that the Law is good, but sin is so powerful that it uses even the good Law to bring death. The problem is not the Law but human sinfulness. The solution is not trying harder to keep the Law but deliverance through Jesus Christ and life in the Spirit, which Paul describes in chapter 8.

### Released from the Law (*7:1–6*)

Paul begins with an illustration from marriage. The law binds a married woman to her husband as long as he lives. If he dies, she is free to marry another without being called an adulteress. Paul’s point is not to give teaching about marriage and divorce, which he addresses elsewhere (*1 Corinthians 7*), but to illustrate a principle: death ends legal obligations.

The application is studied below. Paul then contrasts the old life and the new: “*For when we were in the flesh, the sinful passions which were through the law worked in our members to bring out fruit to death*” (*v. 5*). “In the flesh” refers to life apart from Christ, dominated by sinful human nature. In that state, the Law actually stirred up sinful desires. “*But now we have been discharged from the law, having died to that in which we were held; so that we serve in newness of the spirit, and not in oldness of the letter*” (*v. 6*). Believers now serve God not by external rules written on stone, but by the new life of the Spirit written on their hearts (*2 Corinthians 3:6*; *Jeremiah 31:33*).

### Is the Law Sin? (*7:7–13*)

If the Law stirred up sinful passions, is the Law itself sinful? “*May it never be!*” (*v. 7*) The Law revealed sin: “*I wouldn’t have known coveting unless the law had said, “You shall not covet.”*” (*v. 7*) The tenth commandment (*Exodus 20:17*) is unique because it addresses inner desire rather than outward action. It exposes the heart.

“*But sin, finding occasion through the commandment, produced in me all kinds of coveting*” (*v. 8*). Sin is pictured as an active power that used the commandment as a base of operations. Being told not to do something can make people want it more. “*I was alive apart from the law once, but when the commandment came, sin revived and I died*” (*v. 9*). Paul may be describing his own experience as a child before becoming responsible for the Law, or Israel’s experience when the Law was given at Sinai, or Adam’s experience in the garden when he received God’s command. All three readings have been proposed, and each sheds light on the passage.

“*The commandment which was for life, this I found to be for death*” (*v. 10*). God gave the Law to show the way of life (*Leviticus 18:5*), but sin twisted it into an instrument of death. “*for sin, finding occasion through the commandment, deceived me, and through it killed me*” (*v. 11*). The word “deceived” recalls the serpent in Eden, who deceived Eve (*Genesis 3:13*). Paul’s conclusion about the Law is studied below.

### The Inner Struggle (*7:14–25*)

Paul now describes a painful inner conflict, studied below. Interpreters have long debated who the “I” in this passage is. Some believe Paul is describing his experience as a mature Christian, who still struggles with sin even while delighting in God’s law. They point to the present tense, Paul’s delight in God’s law (*7:22*), and the experience of many believers. Others believe Paul is describing life under the Law without the Spirit, perhaps his experience as a devout Jew before conversion, or the experience of anyone who tries to obey God by their own strength. They point to phrases like “sold under sin” (*7:14*) and “captivity under the law of sin” (*7:23*), which seem to contradict Paul’s description of believers as freed from sin in chapter 6, and to the fact that the Holy Spirit is not mentioned in this section but appears constantly in chapter 8. Still others see Paul speaking for Israel as a whole. Each view has strong supporters among faithful scholars.

Whatever view one takes, the passage shows that the Law alone cannot overcome sin, and that human willpower is not enough. Many believers recognize their own struggles in Paul’s words, and the passage points them to the only source of victory: Jesus Christ and the power of the Spirit.

Paul says, “*For we know that the law is spiritual, but I am fleshly, sold under sin*” (*v. 14*). The Law comes from God’s Spirit, but human nature is weak and enslaved. “*So now it is no more I that do it, but sin which dwells in me*” (*v. 17*). Paul is not excusing himself but describing sin as a foreign power living within. “*For I know that in me, that is, in my flesh, dwells no good thing. For desire is present with me, but I don’t find it doing that which is good*” (*v. 18*).

“*For I delight in God’s law after the inward person*” (*v. 22*), “*but I see a different law in my members, warring against the law of my mind, and bringing me into captivity under the law of sin which is in my members*” (*v. 23*). Two “laws” or principles are at war: the desire to obey God and the power of sin. Paul’s cry for help, and the answer, are studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Romans 7:4* — Joined to Another

> *“Therefore, my brothers, you also were made dead to the law through the body of Christ, that you would be joined to another, to him who was raised from the dead, that we might produce fruit to God.”*
>
> — *Romans 7:4* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had used an illustration from marriage. A woman is bound to her husband by law as long as he lives. If he dies, she is free to marry someone else. Death ends the legal bond.

Now Paul applied this to believers and the Law: “*Therefore, my brothers, you also were made dead to the law through the body of Christ*” (*v. 4*). Believers have died in relation to the Law. How? “Through the body of Christ,” meaning through Christ’s death on the cross. When Christ died, believers died with Him (*6:3–6*). The Law’s claim on them as a way of gaining righteousness ended.

“*that you would be joined to another, to him who was raised from the dead*” (*v. 4*). The purpose of this death was not to leave believers alone and free to do as they please. It was so that they could be “joined to another,” to belong to the risen Christ. Believers are like a bride joined to a new husband. The church is often pictured as the bride of Christ (*Ephesians 5:25–32*; *Revelation 19:7*).

“*that we might produce fruit to God*” (*v. 4*). The result of this new union is fruitfulness. A marriage produces children; union with Christ produces the fruit of a transformed life. Paul describes this fruit elsewhere: “*But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith*” (*Galatians 5:22*).

Notice the change from “you” to “we.” Paul includes himself. He too, though a devout Jew, had died to the Law through Christ and now belonged to Him.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that the Christian life is a relationship with Christ, not merely obedience to rules. The Law gave commands but could not give life. Union with the risen Christ gives both new life and the power to bear fruit.

It also shows that freedom from the Law is not freedom from righteousness. Believers are not set free to do whatever they want; they are set free to belong to Christ and bear fruit for God. Paul says that the righteous requirement of the Law is fulfilled in those who walk by the Spirit (*Romans 8:4*).

Finally, the verse shows the intimacy of believers’ relationship with Christ. The image of marriage speaks of love, belonging, and faithfulness. Believers are not merely Christ’s servants; they are united to Him in love.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to see their faith as a relationship with Christ. The Christian life is not primarily about keeping rules but about belonging to Jesus and living in His love.

It also frees believers from trying to earn God’s approval through rule-keeping. Believers have died to the Law as a way of salvation. They can rest in their union with Christ.

Finally, the verse calls believers to fruitfulness. Union with Christ is meant to produce a changed life. Believers can ask God to produce the fruit of the Spirit in them, in love, kindness, patience, and goodness.

### *Romans 7:12* — The Law Is Holy, Righteous, and Good

> *“Therefore the law indeed is holy, and the commandment holy, righteous, and good.”*
>
> — *Romans 7:12* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had explained that sin used the Law to stir up sinful desires and bring death. A reader might conclude that the Law itself was evil. Paul had already asked, “*Is the law sin? May it never be!*” (*v. 7*)

Now he gave his conclusion: “*Therefore the law indeed is holy, and the commandment holy, righteous, and good*” (*v. 12*). The Law of God is “holy,” because it comes from the holy God and reflects His character. Each commandment is “holy,” set apart by God. It is “righteous,” because it shows what is right and just. And it is “good,” because it was given for people’s benefit.

The problem was never the Law. The problem was sin, which took the good Law and used it to produce death. Paul compares it to a doctor’s diagnosis: an X-ray reveals a disease, but the X-ray does not cause it. The Law reveals sin, but it does not cause it. Sin, like a parasite, uses the Law for its own purposes.

“*Did then that which is good become death to me? May it never be! But sin, that it might be shown to be sin, was producing death in me through that which is good*” (*v. 13*). Sin is so evil that it can take something good and use it to destroy. This shows how deeply sinful sin really is: “*that through the commandment sin might become exceedingly sinful*” (*v. 13*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows the high value Paul placed on God’s Law. Paul is sometimes misunderstood as being against the Law. In fact, he honored it as holy, righteous, and good. The psalmist also delighted in God’s law: “*The LORD’s law is perfect, restoring the soul*” (*Psalm 19:7*).

It also shows that the Law has an important purpose, even though it cannot save. It reveals God’s character, shows people their sin, and points them to their need for Christ. Paul writes elsewhere that the Law was a guardian leading people to Christ (*Galatians 3:24*).

Finally, the verse shows the terrible power of sin. Sin can corrupt even the best things. This explains why people can misuse good gifts, including religion, Scripture, and morality, in harmful ways. The answer is not to reject good things but to be freed from sin’s power.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to honor God’s Law. While believers are not saved by keeping the Law, the moral commands of Scripture reveal God’s will and remain a guide for living. Believers can study and treasure God’s commands.

It also helps believers understand why rules alone cannot change hearts. Many people try to become better by following rules, but find that rules alone do not give power to obey. Believers need the transforming power of the Spirit.

Finally, the verse warns believers against being deceived by sin. Sin can make good things seem harmful and harmful things seem good. Believers can ask God for wisdom to recognize sin’s deceptions.

### *Romans 7:18–19* — The Good I Desire, I Don’t Do

> *“For I know that in me, that is, in my flesh, dwells no good thing. For desire is present with me, but I don’t find it doing that which is good. For the good which I desire, I don’t do; but the evil which I don’t desire, that I practice.”*
>
> — *Romans 7:18–19* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul was describing an intense inner struggle. He had said that the Law is spiritual, but he was “fleshly, sold under sin.” He did not understand his own actions. He wanted to do good, but he did not do it. He hated evil, but he did it.

“*For I know that in me, that is, in my flesh, dwells no good thing*” (*v. 18*). “Flesh” here refers to human nature as affected by sin. Paul is careful to say “in my flesh.” He does not say there is nothing good in him at all, since he desires to do good. But his sinful nature contains nothing good.

“*For desire is present with me, but I don’t find it doing that which is good*” (*v. 18*). The problem is not a lack of desire. Paul wants to do good. The problem is a lack of power. Desire alone is not enough.

“*For the good which I desire, I don’t do; but the evil which I don’t desire, that I practice*” (*v. 19*). This is the heart of the struggle. Paul wants to do good but fails. He does not want to do evil but does it anyway.

Many people throughout history have recognized themselves in these words. Even the Roman poet Ovid wrote, “I see the better things and approve them, but I follow the worse.” Human beings often know what is right and want to do it, yet find themselves unable to follow through.

As explained in the chapter background, Christians differ on whether Paul is describing the experience of a believer or of someone trying to live under the Law without the Spirit. Either way, the passage reveals that human willpower and the Law alone cannot defeat sin.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show the depth of human sinfulness. Sin is not merely a matter of bad choices; it is a power that dwells within, working against good intentions. Jesus said, “*The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak*” (*Matthew 26:41*).

They also show that knowledge and desire are not enough. Knowing what is right and wanting to do it do not guarantee success. People need a power beyond themselves. This sets the stage for *Romans 8*, where Paul describes the power of the Holy Spirit.

Finally, these verses show honesty about the struggle with sin. Paul does not pretend that the Christian life, or the moral life, is easy. Believers who struggle with sin are not alone; even the great apostle described this battle vividly.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses bring comfort to believers who struggle with sin. Many believers feel discouraged because they keep failing in the same areas. Paul’s words show that this struggle is real and common. Believers do not need to despair or pretend.

They also show that trying harder is not the full answer. Willpower alone cannot overcome sin. Believers need to depend on Christ and the Holy Spirit, as Paul will explain in chapter 8.

Finally, these verses encourage believers to be honest with God and with one another about their struggles. Confession brings sin into the light, where it loses some of its power (*James 5:16*; *1 John 1:9*). Believers can support one another in the fight against sin.

### *Romans 7:24–25* — Who Will Deliver Me?

> *“What a wretched man I am! Who will deliver me out of the body of this death? I thank God through Jesus Christ, our Lord! So then with the mind, I myself serve God’s law, but with the flesh, sin’s law.”*
>
> — *Romans 7:24–25* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had described an intense inner conflict: wanting to do good but failing, delighting in God’s law but finding another law at work within him, waging war and taking him captive to sin. Now he reaches a breaking point.

“*What a wretched man I am!*” (*v. 24*) The word “wretched” means miserable, distressed, worn out by struggle. Paul feels the full weight of his inability to overcome sin by his own strength.

“*Who will deliver me out of the body of this death?*” (*v. 24*) Paul does not ask “What will deliver me?” but “Who?” He knows he needs a person, a rescuer. “The body of this death” may refer to his physical body as the place where sin works, or to his whole existence under sin’s power, which leads to death. Some have compared it to an ancient punishment in which a murderer was chained to the corpse of his victim. Whatever the exact image, Paul feels trapped and needs rescue.

“*I thank God through Jesus Christ, our Lord!*” (*v. 25*) Suddenly, the cry of despair turns into a shout of thanksgiving. Paul knows who will deliver him: God, through Jesus Christ. Deliverance comes not from within but from outside, through Christ.

“*So then with the mind, I myself serve God’s law, but with the flesh, sin’s law*” (*v. 25*). Paul summarizes the struggle he has described. Some see this as describing the ongoing tension of the Christian life until final redemption; others see it as a summary of the situation apart from the Spirit, which *Romans 8* resolves. Either way, the answer is in Christ.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that the answer to sin is a Person, not a method. Paul does not find deliverance in better techniques, stronger willpower, or more rules. He finds it in Jesus Christ. Jesus said, “*If therefore the Son makes you free, you will be free indeed*” (*John 8:36*).

They also show that recognizing one’s helplessness is the doorway to deliverance. Paul’s cry, “What a wretched man I am!” is not a sign of failure but a step toward grace. Only those who know they need rescue will look for a Rescuer. Jesus said that He came not for the healthy but for the sick (*Mark 2:17*).

Finally, these verses show that deliverance includes both present and future. Christ delivers believers now from sin’s condemnation and gives them the Spirit’s power to resist sin. And He will deliver them completely in the future, when they receive resurrection bodies free from sin and death (*Romans 8:23*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers who feel overwhelmed by sin. When believers feel like crying out, “*What a wretched man I am!*” (*v. 24*) they can turn to Jesus. He is the answer to their struggle.

They also teach believers to move from despair to thanksgiving. Paul did not stay in his misery. He turned to Christ and gave thanks. Believers can do the same, remembering that they are not left alone in their struggle.

Finally, these verses point believers to *Romans 8*, which describes the power of the Spirit and the freedom of those who are in Christ. Believers who feel stuck in the struggle of *Romans 7* can move forward into the hope and victory of *Romans 8*.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Romans 7* teaches that believers have died to the Law through Christ and now belong to the risen Lord. Their relationship with God is not based on rule-keeping but on union with Christ, which produces fruit for God. Believers can rest in this relationship rather than trying to earn God’s approval through their own efforts.

The chapter also affirms that God’s Law is holy, righteous, and good. The Law reveals God’s character and shows people their sin. The problem is not the Law but sin, which uses even good things to bring death. Believers can honor God’s commands while recognizing that the commands alone cannot give the power to obey.

*Romans 7* describes the struggle with sin honestly. Many believers recognize themselves in Paul’s words: wanting to do good but failing, delighting in God’s law but feeling the pull of sin. This struggle is real. Believers do not need to hide it or despair over it. They can be honest with God and with trusted believers about their struggles.

Finally, the chapter points to the only answer: Jesus Christ. Paul’s cry, “Who will deliver me?” is answered with “I thank God through Jesus Christ, our Lord!” Believers can bring their struggles to Christ, trusting Him for forgiveness and for the power of the Spirit to live a new life, which Paul will describe in the next chapter.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord God, thank You that through the death of Christ I have been set free from the Law as a way of earning Your favor, and joined to Him who was raised from the dead. Make my life fruitful for You. Thank You for Your Law, which is holy, righteous, and good, and which shows me my need for You. I confess that I often fail to do the good I want to do, and I do the things I don’t want to do. I cannot overcome sin by my own strength. When I feel overwhelmed and cry out, “Who will deliver me?”, remind me that You have already answered through Jesus Christ my Lord. Thank You for Your forgiveness and for the power of Your Spirit. Lead me from struggle into thanksgiving and freedom. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Romans · Chapter 8 of 16

# Romans — Chapter 8

Chapter Theme: Life in the Spirit: No Condemnation and No Separation

[Read Romans 8 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/ROM08.htm)

Main Teaching

There is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, because the Spirit of life has set them free from the power of sin and death. God has done what the Law could not do by sending His Son as a sin offering, so that those who live by the Spirit fulfill the Law’s righteous requirement. The Spirit dwells in believers, gives life, leads them as God’s adopted children, and assures them that they can call God “Abba, Father.” Though they groan with all creation while awaiting final redemption, present sufferings cannot compare with the coming glory, and the Spirit helps them pray. God works all things for good for those who love Him, and nothing in all creation can separate them from His love in Christ Jesus.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Romans 8* is often called the summit of Paul’s letter, and many consider it one of the greatest chapters in the Bible. It completes the argument Paul began in chapter 5 about the new life of those who have been justified by faith. In chapter 6, Paul showed that believers have died to sin. In chapter 7, he showed that the Law, though holy, cannot give power over sin. Now, in chapter 8, he shows the answer: the Holy Spirit. The Spirit is mentioned only once in chapters 1–7 after the opening (*5:5*), but about twenty times in chapter 8.

The chapter begins with “no condemnation” (*8:1*) and ends with “no separation” (*8:39*). Between these two great statements, Paul describes the Spirit’s work, believers’ identity as God’s children, the hope of glory, and the unbreakable love of God.

### No Condemnation (*8:1–4*)

The chapter’s opening declaration is studied below. Paul explains how God accomplished this: “*For what the law couldn’t do, in that it was weak through the flesh, God did, sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin, he condemned sin in the flesh*” (*v. 3*). The Law could not save because sinful human nature could not obey it. So God sent His Son in a real human body, “in the likeness of sinful flesh,” though without sin Himself (*Hebrews 4:15*). The phrase “for sin” can be translated “as a sin offering.” On the cross, God condemned sin in Christ’s body. Sin was judged and its power broken.

The purpose: “*that the ordinance of the law might be fulfilled in us who don’t walk according to the flesh, but according to the Spirit*” (*v. 4*). Those who live by the Spirit fulfill what the Law truly required: love for God and neighbor (*Romans 13:8–10*).

### Flesh and Spirit (*8:5–13*)

Paul contrasts two ways of living. “*For those who live according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh, but those who live according to the Spirit, the things of the Spirit*” (*v. 5*). The “flesh” refers to human nature apart from God, dominated by sin. The “Spirit” refers to God’s Holy Spirit. What people set their minds on reveals which way they live. “*For the mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace*” (*v. 6*).

“*But you are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if it is so that the Spirit of God dwells in you. But if any man doesn’t have the Spirit of Christ, he is not his*” (*v. 9*). Every true believer has the Holy Spirit. The Spirit is not an extra blessing for a few; He is the mark of belonging to Christ. Notice that Paul uses “the Spirit of God” and “the Spirit of Christ” interchangeably, pointing to the unity of Father, Son, and Spirit.

“*But if the Spirit of him who raised up Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised up Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you*” (*v. 11*). The same Spirit who raised Jesus will one day raise believers’ bodies. This is a promise of the future resurrection.

Therefore, believers have an obligation, not to the flesh but to the Spirit. “*For if you live after the flesh, you must die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live*” (*v. 13*). Believers are called to “put to death” sinful practices, but they do this “by the Spirit,” not by willpower alone.

### Children of God (*8:14–17*)

“*For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are children of God*” (*v. 14*). Being led by the Spirit is the mark of God’s children. The Spirit’s witness to believers’ adoption is studied below.

“*and if children, then heirs—heirs of God and joint heirs with Christ, if indeed we suffer with him, that we may also be glorified with him*” (*v. 17*). As God’s children, believers will inherit everything God has promised, sharing in Christ’s inheritance. But the path to glory goes through suffering, just as it did for Christ.

### Future Glory (*8:18–25*)

“*For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which will be revealed toward us*” (*v. 18*). Paul, who suffered more than most (*2 Corinthians 11:23–28*), weighed his sufferings against the coming glory and concluded that there is no comparison.

Paul then describes creation itself waiting for this glory. “*For the creation waits with eager expectation for the children of God to be revealed*” (*v. 19*). The whole created world was “*subjected to vanity*” (*v. 20*), frustration and futility, because of human sin (*Genesis 3:17–19*). But it was subjected “*in hope*” (*v. 20*), “*that the creation itself also will be delivered from the bondage of decay into the liberty of the glory of the children of God*” (*v. 21*). God’s plan includes the renewal of the whole creation, not only the salvation of individual souls. “*For we know that the whole creation groans and travails in pain together until now*” (*v. 22*), like a woman in labor, whose pain leads to new life.

Believers groan too: “*Not only so, but ourselves also, who have the first fruits of the Spirit, even we ourselves groan within ourselves, waiting for adoption, the redemption of our body*” (*v. 23*). Believers already have the Spirit as “first fruits,” the first part of the harvest, which guarantees that the rest will come. But they still wait for the full experience of adoption, when their bodies will be raised and transformed. “*For we were saved in hope, but hope that is seen is not hope*” (*v. 24*). “*But if we hope for that which we don’t see, we wait for it with patience*” (*v. 25*).

### The Spirit’s Help and God’s Purpose (*8:26–30*)

The Spirit’s help in prayer and God’s purpose in all things are studied below. Paul then describes the unbreakable chain of God’s saving work: “*For whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brothers*” (*v. 29*). “*Whom he predestined, those he also called. Whom he called, those he also justified. Whom he justified, those he also glorified*” (*v. 30*). God’s purpose is to make believers like Jesus. Notice that “glorified” is in the past tense, even though glorification is still future. It is so certain that Paul speaks of it as already done.

Christians have understood “foreknew” and “predestined” in different ways. Some, especially in the Reformed tradition, understand that God chose specific people for salvation according to His sovereign will. Others, especially in Wesleyan and Arminian traditions, understand that God predestined those whom He foreknew would believe, or that He predestined the church as a whole to be conformed to Christ. Many note that “foreknew” in Scripture often means to know in a personal, loving relationship. All agree that salvation is God’s work from beginning to end, and that it gives believers deep security.

### More Than Conquerors (*8:31–39*)

Paul then asks a series of questions. “*What then shall we say about these things? If God is for us, who can be against us?*” (*v. 31*) No opposition can succeed against those whom God is for. “*He who didn’t spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how would he not also with him freely give us all things?*” (*v. 32*) If God gave His greatest gift, His Son, He will surely give everything else believers need.

“*Who could bring a charge against God’s chosen ones? It is God who justifies*” (*v. 33*). The judge has already declared them righteous. “*Who is he who condemns? It is Christ who died, yes rather, who was raised from the dead, who is at the right hand of God, who also makes intercession for us*” (*v. 34*). Christ, the only one who has the right to condemn, is the one who died for believers and now prays for them.

“*Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Could oppression, or anguish, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?*” (*v. 35*) Paul lists hardships he himself had experienced. He quotes *Psalm 44:22*: “*For your sake we are killed all day long. We were accounted as sheep for the slaughter*” (*v. 36*). Believers may suffer terribly. “*No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us*” (*v. 37*). Not “in spite of” these things, but “in” them, believers overcome through Christ’s love. The chapter’s conclusion is studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Romans 8:1–2* — No Condemnation

> *“There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus, who don’t walk according to the flesh, but according to the Spirit. For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus made me free from the law of sin and of death.”*
>
> — *Romans 8:1–2* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

*Romans 7* ended with Paul describing the struggle with sin and crying out, “What a wretched man I am! Who will deliver me?” He then gave thanks to God through Jesus Christ. Now, in *Romans 8*, Paul explains the deliverance believers have in Christ.

“*There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus*” (*v. 1*). “Condemnation” is a legal term meaning the verdict of guilty and the punishment that follows. For those in Christ, there is “no condemnation,” none at all. God will never condemn them. The word “now” emphasizes that this is a present reality, not only a future hope. Believers do not have to wait until the end of their lives to find out whether they will be condemned. The verdict has already been given.

Who receives this? “Those who are in Christ Jesus.” Being “in Christ” means being united to Him by faith. Everything that belongs to Christ, including His righteousness, belongs to those who are in Him. Since Christ cannot be condemned, those in Him cannot be condemned.

(Some later manuscripts add the words “who don’t walk according to the flesh, but according to the Spirit” to verse 1, as the World English Bible includes; the earliest manuscripts end the verse with “in Christ Jesus.” The phrase appears in all manuscripts at the end of verse 4.)

“*For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus made me free from the law of sin and of death*” (*v. 2*). Paul explains why there is no condemnation. Two “laws” or powers are contrasted. “The law of sin and of death” is the power of sin that Paul described in chapter 7, which leads to death. “The law of the Spirit of life” is the power of the Holy Spirit, who gives life. The Spirit has set believers free from sin’s power.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses express the heart of the gospel’s comfort. Believers are completely free from condemnation because Christ has taken their condemnation on Himself. Paul writes later in this chapter, “*Who is he who condemns? It is Christ who died*” (*v. 34*). The one who could condemn is the one who died for them.

They also show that freedom from condemnation and freedom from sin’s power go together. God not only declares believers not guilty; He also gives them His Spirit to free them from sin’s control. Justification and transformation are both part of salvation.

Finally, these verses show the centrality of union with Christ. Everything depends on being “in Christ Jesus.” Paul uses this phrase repeatedly in his letters. It describes the deep, personal union between believers and their Savior.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses bring deep comfort to believers who struggle with guilt. Many believers continue to feel condemned even after trusting Christ. Paul declares that there is no condemnation for those in Christ. Believers can rest in this truth, even when their feelings say otherwise.

They also encourage believers who feel trapped by sin. The Spirit of life has set them free from the law of sin and death. They are no longer slaves. They can rely on the Spirit’s power to resist sin and live a new life.

Finally, these verses invite believers to find their identity in Christ. They are not defined by their failures but by their union with Him. When believers are tempted to see themselves as condemned, they can remember who they are in Christ.

### *Romans 8:15–16* — “*Abba! Father!*” (*v. 15*)

> *“For you didn’t receive the spirit of bondage again to fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, ‘Abba! Father!’ The Spirit himself testifies with our spirit that we are children of God;”*
>
> — *Romans 8:15–16* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had just said that those who are led by the Spirit of God are God’s children. Now he explains the nature of this relationship.

“*For you didn’t receive the spirit of bondage again to fear*” (*v. 15*). Before coming to Christ, people lived as slaves, under the power of sin and the fear of judgment. Some may have related to God mainly through fear, like slaves afraid of a harsh master. The Spirit does not bring believers back into that kind of fearful slavery.

“*but you received the Spirit of adoption*” (*v. 15*). Instead, believers received “the Spirit of adoption.” In the Roman world, adoption was a legal act that gave an adopted child all the rights of a natural-born child, including the right to inherit. Adopted children received a new name, a new family, and a new status. Their old debts were canceled. Believers have been adopted into God’s family through the Spirit.

“*by whom we cry, “Abba! Father!”*” (*v. 15*) “Abba” is an Aramaic word for “father,” used by children to address their fathers with affection and trust. Jesus Himself used this word when He prayed in Gethsemane: “*Abba, Father*” (*Mark 14:36*). Believers can address God with the same intimate trust that Jesus had. The word “cry” suggests a heartfelt, sometimes urgent call, especially in times of need.

“*The Spirit himself testifies with our spirit that we are children of God*” (*v. 16*). The Holy Spirit confirms in believers’ hearts that they truly belong to God. This inner assurance is a gift of the Spirit. Believers do not have to wonder whether God accepts them; the Spirit bears witness that they are His children.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses reveal the intimacy of the relationship between believers and God. God is not a distant ruler but a loving Father. Through Christ, believers share in the relationship that Jesus has with the Father. Paul writes in Galatians, “*And because you are children, God sent out the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, “Abba, Father!”*” (*Galatians 4:6*)

They also show that fear is not the right foundation for a relationship with God. While believers rightly revere God, they do not need to live in terror of His rejection. John writes, “*There is no fear in love; but perfect love casts out fear*” (*1 John 4:18*).

Finally, these verses show the work of the Spirit in giving assurance. Assurance of salvation is not merely a conclusion drawn from evidence; it is also the inner witness of the Spirit. God wants His children to know that they belong to Him.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses invite believers to approach God as their loving Father. Believers can pray with confidence and trust, bringing their needs, fears, and joys to Him as children bring them to a caring parent.

They also bring comfort to those who have had difficult relationships with earthly fathers. Some people find it hard to think of God as a father because of painful experiences. God is the perfect Father, whose love is faithful, patient, and good. Believers can ask the Spirit to help them know God’s fatherly love.

Finally, these verses encourage believers who struggle with assurance. When doubts arise, believers can ask the Spirit to testify to their hearts that they are God’s children, and they can rest in the promises of God’s word.

### *Romans 8:26–28* — The Spirit Helps, and God Works for Good

> *“In the same way, the Spirit also helps our weaknesses, for we don’t know how to pray as we ought. But the Spirit himself makes intercession for us with groanings which can’t be uttered. He who searches the hearts knows what is on the Spirit’s mind, because he makes intercession for the saints according to God. We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, for those who are called according to his purpose.”*
>
> — *Romans 8:26–28* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had been describing the groaning of creation and of believers as they wait for the full redemption God has promised. Life in this world involves weakness, suffering, and longing. Now Paul describes how God helps believers in this condition.

“*In the same way, the Spirit also helps our weaknesses, for we don’t know how to pray as we ought*” (*v. 26*). Believers are weak, and sometimes they do not even know what to pray for. In times of confusion, grief, or suffering, words may fail. “*But the Spirit himself makes intercession for us with groanings which can’t be uttered*” (*v. 26*). The Holy Spirit prays on believers’ behalf, with deep longings that cannot be put into words. Believers are not alone in prayer; the Spirit carries their prayers to God.

“*He who searches the hearts knows what is on the Spirit’s mind, because he makes intercession for the saints according to God*” (*v. 27*). God the Father, who knows every heart, understands the Spirit’s prayers, because the Spirit always prays in line with God’s will.

Then comes one of the most beloved verses in the Bible: “*We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, for those who are called according to his purpose*” (*v. 28*). Paul does not say that all things are good. Suffering, loss, and sin are not good in themselves. But God works in all things, even painful ones, to bring about good for His people.

What is this “good”? The next verse explains: God’s purpose is that believers would be “*conformed to the image of his Son*” (*v. 29*). The ultimate good is becoming like Jesus and sharing His glory. Everything God allows in believers’ lives serves this purpose.

The promise is for “those who love God,” who are “called according to his purpose.” It describes believers, those who have responded to God’s call with love.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show the deep care of God for believers in their weakness. The Spirit prays for them, and the Father works in every circumstance for their good. Believers are surrounded by God’s care. Jesus also intercedes for them (*8:34*; *Hebrews 7:25*).

They also show that God’s purposes are larger than believers’ immediate comfort. The “good” God works toward is not necessarily ease or success, but conformity to Christ. Sometimes God uses hardship to make believers more like Jesus. Joseph told his brothers, “*As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good*” (*Genesis 50:20*).

Finally, these verses must be read with care. *Romans 8:28* is sometimes quoted too quickly to people who are suffering, as if it explains away their pain. Paul wrote these words in a passage about groaning and suffering. The verse is not a slogan to silence grief but a deep comfort that God is at work even in what is broken. Believers can grieve honestly while trusting God’s purposes.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers who do not know how to pray. In times of overwhelming pain or confusion, believers can come to God with sighs, tears, or silence, trusting that the Spirit is praying for them.

They also bring hope to believers in difficult circumstances. Whatever believers face, God is working for their good. They may not see how, and they may not understand why, but they can trust that God has not abandoned them.

Finally, these verses encourage believers to be gentle with those who are suffering. Rather than quickly quoting *Romans 8:28* to someone in pain, believers can first weep with them (*Romans 12:15*), pray with them, and, in time, gently share the hope that God is at work.

### *Romans 8:38–39* — Nothing Can Separate Us from God’s Love

> *“For I am persuaded that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor things present, nor things to come, nor powers, nor height, nor depth, nor any other created thing will be able to separate us from God’s love which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.”*
>
> — *Romans 8:38–39* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had been asking a series of questions: If God is for us, who can be against us? Who can bring a charge against God’s chosen ones? Who can condemn? Who can separate us from the love of Christ? He had listed many hardships: trouble, hardship, persecution, famine, nakedness, danger, and sword. And he had declared that in all these things, believers are more than conquerors through Christ who loved them.

Now Paul gives his final, triumphant answer: “*For I am persuaded*” (*v. 38*). Paul is completely convinced. This is not wishful thinking but deep certainty.

“*that neither death, nor life*” (*v. 38*). Neither dying nor the challenges of living can separate believers from God’s love.

“*nor angels, nor principalities*” (*v. 38*). No spiritual powers, whether good or evil, can separate them. “Principalities” probably refers to spiritual rulers, including evil forces (*Ephesians 6:12*).

“*nor things present, nor things to come, nor powers*” (*v. 38*). Nothing happening now and nothing that will happen in the future, no power of any kind, can separate them.

“*nor height, nor depth*” (*v. 39*). These words may refer to the farthest reaches of the universe, or to astrological powers that people in Paul’s day feared. Nothing in all of space can separate believers from God’s love.

“*nor any other created thing*” (*v. 39*). To make sure nothing is left out, Paul adds “any other created thing.” Everything except God is created, and nothing created can separate believers from Him.

“*will be able to separate us from God’s love which is in Christ Jesus our Lord*” (*v. 39*). God’s love is found “in Christ Jesus our Lord.” Because believers are in Christ, they are held in God’s love forever.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses express the ultimate security of believers. Their salvation does not depend on their own strength, but on God’s love, which cannot fail. Jesus said, “*I give eternal life to them. They will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand*” (*John 10:28*).

They also show the comprehensive nature of God’s love. Paul’s list covers every category: life and death, spiritual powers, time, space, and all creation. There is no situation, place, or power that lies outside the reach of God’s love.

Finally, these verses show that God’s love is found in Christ. It is not a general sentiment but a specific love revealed and secured through Jesus’ death and resurrection. Believers are held in this love because they are united to Christ.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses bring comfort to believers facing fear. Whether they fear death, illness, the future, spiritual attack, or any other danger, they can be sure that nothing will separate them from God’s love.

They also encourage believers in suffering. Paul wrote these words knowing that believers face trouble, persecution, and even death. Suffering does not mean that God’s love has failed. Believers can hold on to His love in their darkest moments.

Finally, these verses invite believers to rest in God’s love. Many believers live with anxiety about whether God still loves them, especially after failure. Paul’s words are clear: nothing can separate them from His love. Believers can live with confidence, joy, and peace.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Romans 8* begins with the declaration that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. Believers who struggle with guilt can rest in this truth. God has condemned sin in Christ, and the Spirit of life has set believers free from the power of sin and death. They can live without fear of God’s judgment.

The chapter also describes life in the Spirit. Every believer has the Spirit of God, who gives life, leads them, helps them put sinful practices to death, and assures them that they are God’s children. Believers can depend on the Spirit daily, setting their minds on the things of the Spirit and approaching God with the trust of children who cry, “Abba, Father.”

*Romans 8* gives believers hope in suffering. Present sufferings are not worth comparing with the glory to come. All creation groans, waiting for renewal, and believers groan too as they await the redemption of their bodies. Yet the Spirit helps them pray when they do not know how, and God works in all things for the good of those who love Him, shaping them into the image of His Son.

Finally, the chapter ends with the triumphant assurance that nothing can separate believers from God’s love in Christ. If God is for them, no one can stand against them. If God gave His own Son, He will give them everything they need. Believers can face every fear, hardship, and uncertainty with confidence that they are held forever in the love of God.

## Chapter Prayer

Heavenly Father, thank You that there is now no condemnation for me because I am in Christ Jesus. Thank You for sending Your Son to condemn sin and for giving me Your Spirit to set me free. Holy Spirit, lead me, help me to put to death what is sinful, and fill my heart with the assurance that I am a child of God. Abba, Father, thank You for adopting me into Your family. When I suffer, lift my eyes to the glory that is coming. When I do not know how to pray, thank You that Your Spirit prays for me. Help me to trust that You are working in all things for my good, making me more like Jesus. Thank You that nothing in all creation, not death or life, not present or future, not any power, will ever be able to separate me from Your love in Christ Jesus my Lord. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Romans · Chapter 9 of 16

# Romans — Chapter 9

Chapter Theme: God’s Faithful Word, Sovereign Mercy, and Paul’s Grief for Israel

[Read Romans 9 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/ROM09.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul expresses deep and unceasing sorrow for his fellow Israelites, who have received great privileges from God, including the Messiah Himself, yet many have not believed. He insists that God’s word has not failed, because God’s promises have always worked through His choice and calling, not merely physical descent, as seen with Isaac and Jacob. God is not unjust; He shows mercy as He chooses, like a potter with clay, and He has called a people from both Jews and Gentiles, as the prophets foretold. Paul concludes that Gentiles have obtained righteousness by faith, while many in Israel stumbled because they pursued it by works rather than by faith in the stone God laid in Zion.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Romans 9–11* forms a distinct section of the letter. Paul has just ended chapter 8 with the triumphant declaration that nothing can separate believers from God’s love. But a serious question arises: if God’s promises are so secure, what about Israel? God made great promises to Abraham’s descendants, yet most of Paul’s fellow Jews had not accepted Jesus as the Messiah. Had God’s word failed? Could Gentile believers trust God’s promises if He had apparently abandoned Israel?

In these three chapters, Paul wrestles with this question. Chapter 9 emphasizes God’s sovereign freedom and faithfulness. Chapter 10 emphasizes human responsibility to believe. Chapter 11 shows that God has not rejected Israel and that His plan includes a future for them. The section ends with a hymn of praise to God’s wisdom (*11:33–36*). These chapters must be read together.

These chapters have been the subject of intense discussion throughout church history, especially regarding election and predestination. They have also sometimes been misused to justify hostility toward Jewish people, which is a grievous distortion. Paul writes with tears for his own people and affirms God’s continuing love for them (*11:28–29*).

### Paul’s Sorrow for Israel (*9:1–5*)

Paul begins with a solemn oath of sincerity and a statement of grief, studied below. He then lists Israel’s privileges: “*who are Israelites; whose is the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the service, and the promises*” (*v. 4*). Israel was adopted as God’s son (*Exodus 4:22*). God’s glory dwelt among them in the tabernacle and temple. They received the covenants with Abraham, Moses, and David; the Law at Sinai; the worship of the temple; and the promises of the prophets. The climax of this list is studied below.

### God’s Word Has Not Failed (*9:6–13*)

“*But it is not as though the word of God has come to nothing. For they are not all Israel that are of Israel*” (*v. 6*). Paul explains that God’s promises were never based merely on physical descent. Not all of Abraham’s physical descendants were children of the promise. Abraham had two sons, Ishmael and Isaac, but God said, “*your offspring will be accounted as from Isaac*” (*v. 7*) (*Genesis 21:12*). “*That is, it is not the children of the flesh who are children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as heirs*” (*v. 8*).

Paul then gives a second example: Rebekah’s twins, Jacob and Esau. “*For being not yet born, neither having done anything good or bad, that the purpose of God according to election might stand, not of works, but of him who calls*” (*v. 11*), “*it was said to her, “The elder will serve the younger.”*” (*v. 12*) (*Genesis 25:23*). God’s choice did not depend on their works. “*Even as it is written, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.”*” (*v. 13*) (*Malachi 1:2–3*).

The phrase “Esau I hated” has troubled many readers. In Hebrew idiom, “love” and “hate” in such comparisons often mean “chose” and “did not choose,” or “loved more” and “loved less” (compare *Genesis 29:30–31*; *Luke 14:26*). In Malachi, the words refer to the nations descended from Jacob (Israel) and Esau (Edom). God chose Israel to carry His covenant purpose; He did not choose Edom for that role. The point is that God’s choice is free and based on His purpose, not on human merit.

### Is God Unjust? (*9:14–29*)

“*What shall we say then? Is there unrighteousness with God? May it never be!*” (*v. 14*) Paul quotes God’s words to Moses, studied below.

Paul gives the example of Pharaoh: “*For this very purpose I caused you to be raised up, that I might show in you my power, and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth*” (*v. 17*) (*Exodus 9:16*). “*So then, he has mercy on whom he desires, and he hardens whom he desires*” (*v. 18*). In Exodus, Pharaoh hardened his own heart, and God also hardened it (*Exodus 8:15*; *9:12*). God’s hardening confirmed Pharaoh’s own stubborn choices.

Paul anticipates an objection: “*Why does he still find fault? For who withstands his will?*” (*v. 19*) If God hardens people, how can He blame them? Paul responds with the image of the potter and the clay, drawn from *Isaiah 29:16*, *45:9*, and *Jeremiah 18:1–6*: “*But indeed, O man, who are you to reply against God? Will the thing formed ask him who formed it, “Why did you make me like this?”*” (*v. 20*) “*Or hasn’t the potter a right over the clay, from the same lump to make one part a vessel for honor, and another for dishonor?*” (*v. 21*) Paul does not fully answer the philosophical question. Instead, he reminds his readers that God is the Creator and humans are creatures. Humility is required before the mystery of God’s ways. In *Jeremiah 18*, the potter reshapes the clay in response to Israel’s repentance or rebellion, showing that God’s sovereignty works together with His responsiveness to human choices.

Paul then speaks of God’s patience: “*What if God, willing to show his wrath and to make his power known, endured with much patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction*” (*v. 22*), “*and that he might make known the riches of his glory on vessels of mercy, which he prepared beforehand for glory*” (*v. 23*)? God patiently endures those who oppose Him, giving time for repentance (*2:4*). And He shows the riches of His glory to those on whom He has mercy, “*us, whom he also called, not from the Jews only, but also from the Gentiles*” (*v. 24*).

Christians have understood this passage in different ways. Many in the Reformed tradition see it as teaching that God sovereignly chooses individuals for salvation, and that this choice rests on His mercy alone. Many in Wesleyan, Arminian, Catholic, and Orthodox traditions see Paul speaking mainly about God’s choice of peoples and roles in His plan, such as Israel and the church, and emphasize that God desires all to be saved (*1 Timothy 2:4*) and that people are responsible to believe, as chapter 10 makes clear. All agree that salvation is by God’s mercy, not human merit, and that God is just.

Paul quotes Hosea to show that God has called Gentiles to be His people: “*I will call them ‘my people,’ which were not my people; and her ‘beloved,’ who was not beloved.*” (*v. 25*) And he quotes Isaiah to show that only a remnant of Israel would be saved at that time: “*If the number of the children of Israel are as the sand of the sea, it is the remnant who will be saved*” (*v. 27*).

### The Stumbling Stone (*9:30–33*)

Paul draws his conclusion, studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Romans 9:2–3* — Great Sorrow and Unceasing Pain

> *“that I have great sorrow and unceasing pain in my heart. For I could wish that I myself were accursed from Christ for my brothers’ sake, my relatives according to the flesh”*
>
> — *Romans 9:2–3* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had just finished *Romans 8* with a triumphant declaration: nothing can separate believers from the love of God in Christ. One might expect Paul to continue in joy. Instead, he suddenly expresses deep grief.

He begins with a solemn affirmation: “*I tell the truth in Christ. I am not lying, my conscience testifying with me in the Holy Spirit*” (*v. 1*). Paul wants his readers to know that what he is about to say is completely sincere. Some might have thought that Paul, the apostle to the Gentiles, had turned his back on his own people. He insists that this is not so.

“*that I have great sorrow and unceasing pain in my heart*” (*v. 2*). Paul’s grief is “great” and “unceasing.” It is not a passing sadness but a constant ache.

Why? “*For I could wish that I myself were accursed from Christ for my brothers’ sake, my relatives according to the flesh*” (*v. 3*). Paul says he could almost wish to be “accursed,” cut off from Christ, if it would save his fellow Jews. This is an astonishing statement. Paul has just said that nothing can separate believers from Christ’s love. Yet he loves his people so much that he would be willing to give up his own salvation for them, if that were possible.

Paul’s words echo Moses, who prayed when Israel sinned with the golden calf: “*Yet now, if you will, forgive their sin—and if not, please blot me out of your book which you have written*” (*Exodus 32:32*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses reveal the heart of a true servant of God. Paul’s theology of God’s sovereignty did not make him cold or indifferent to the lost. Instead, it was joined with deep compassion and grief. Belief in God’s sovereign purposes should never make believers careless about those who do not know Christ.

They also reflect the heart of Christ. Jesus wept over Jerusalem because its people did not recognize Him (*Luke 19:41–44*). And Jesus did what Paul could only wish: He became a curse for others, bearing God’s judgment so that they could be saved (*Galatians 3:13*).

Finally, these verses show Paul’s love for the Jewish people. Paul never stopped loving his own people. Any use of Romans to justify hostility toward Jews contradicts Paul’s own heart. He prayed for their salvation (*10:1*) and believed that God had not rejected them (*11:1–2*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses challenge believers to care deeply about those who do not know Christ. It is easy to become comfortable in one’s own salvation and forget about others. Paul’s grief invites believers to pray for family members, friends, and neighbors who do not yet believe.

They also encourage believers to love people even when they reject the gospel. Paul did not become bitter toward those who opposed him. He loved them and longed for their salvation.

Finally, these verses call believers to reject every form of antisemitism. Paul loved his Jewish people deeply. Christians are called to honor the Jewish people, from whom the Messiah came, and to treat them with respect and love.

### *Romans 9:5* — Christ Who Is Over All, God Blessed Forever

> *“of whom are the fathers, and from whom is Christ as concerning the flesh, who is over all, God, blessed forever. Amen.”*
>
> — *Romans 9:5* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul was listing the privileges God had given Israel: adoption as God’s children, the glory of God’s presence, the covenants, the Law, the temple worship, and the promises. Now he names the greatest privileges of all.

“*of whom are the fathers*” (*v. 5*). The “fathers” are the patriarchs: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Israel descended from these men, to whom God made His great promises.

“*and from whom is Christ as concerning the flesh*” (*v. 5*). The Messiah Himself came from Israel. Jesus was born a Jew, a descendant of Abraham and David. “As concerning the flesh” refers to His human ancestry. As a man, Jesus was an Israelite.

“*who is over all, God, blessed forever. Amen*” (*v. 5*). This phrase is one of the clearest statements in Paul’s letters that Christ is God. Grammatically, the most natural reading is that Christ “is over all, God, blessed forever.” Some translations punctuate the verse differently, making the last part a separate praise to God the Father, but the World English Bible and most translations follow the reading that applies these words to Christ. The early church fathers widely read it this way.

Paul’s point is that Israel’s greatest privilege is that the Messiah, who is God Himself, came from their people. This makes their unbelief all the more painful to Paul.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse affirms both the humanity and the divinity of Christ. He came from Israel “according to the flesh,” fully human. And He is “over all, God, blessed forever,” fully divine. This truth is at the heart of Christian faith. John writes, “*The Word became flesh, and lived among us*” (*John 1:14*).

It also shows the honor God gave to Israel. The Savior of the world came from the Jewish people. Jesus said to the Samaritan woman, “*for salvation is from the Jews*” (*John 4:22*). Christians owe a great debt to Israel.

Finally, the verse leads to worship. Paul cannot speak of Christ without praising Him: “blessed forever. Amen.” Theology should always lead to doxology.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to worship Jesus as God. He is not merely a great teacher or prophet. He is “over all, God, blessed forever.” Believers can bring Him the worship and trust that belong to God alone.

It also encourages believers to appreciate the Jewish roots of their faith. Jesus was Jewish. The Scriptures, the covenants, and the promises came through Israel. Believers can study the Old Testament and honor the heritage they have received.

Finally, the verse reminds believers that true theology leads to praise. When believers learn more about who Jesus is, their response should be worship.

### *Romans 9:15–16* — Mercy on Whom He Has Mercy

> *“For he said to Moses, ‘I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion.’ So then it is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who has mercy.”*
>
> — *Romans 9:15–16* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had just explained that God chose Jacob over Esau before they were born, before they had done anything good or bad, so that His purpose would stand, based not on works but on His calling. This raised an obvious question: “*Is there unrighteousness with God?*” (*v. 14*) Is it fair for God to choose one person over another?

Paul’s answer is emphatic: “*May it never be!*” (*v. 14*) God is never unjust.

Then Paul quotes God’s words to Moses: “*For he said to Moses, “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion.”*” (*v. 15*) These words come from *Exodus 33:19*. Moses had asked to see God’s glory after Israel sinned with the golden calf. God responded by revealing His goodness and proclaiming His name, including His freedom to show mercy. Israel did not deserve mercy; they had just worshiped an idol. Yet God chose to show compassion.

“*So then it is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who has mercy*” (*v. 16*). Salvation does not depend on human desire (“him who wills”) or human effort (“him who runs”). It depends on God’s mercy.

The key word is “mercy.” Mercy, by definition, is not deserved. If anyone deserved God’s favor, it would not be mercy. God is not unjust when He shows mercy, because no one has a claim on it. Justice would mean everyone receiving what they deserve. Mercy means some receiving what they do not deserve.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that salvation is entirely God’s gracious work. No one can earn it or demand it. Paul wrote earlier that all have sinned (*3:23*). If God gave everyone what they deserved, no one would be saved. That anyone is saved is a display of mercy.

They also show God’s freedom. God is not obligated to show mercy to anyone. When He does, it is a free gift. This truth humbles believers, because their salvation is not based on anything in themselves.

As discussed in the chapter background, Christians differ on how God’s sovereign mercy relates to human choice. Some emphasize God’s choice of individuals; others emphasize God’s mercy offered to all and the human responsibility to respond. Paul himself holds both truths together: in chapter 9 he emphasizes God’s sovereignty, and in chapter 10 he emphasizes that “whoever will call on the name of the Lord will be saved” (*10:13*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses humble believers. Their salvation is not the result of their own goodness, wisdom, or effort. It is the result of God’s mercy. This truth leaves no room for pride.

They also fill believers with gratitude. God did not have to show them mercy, but He did. Believers can thank Him daily for His undeserved kindness.

Finally, these verses give hope. Since salvation depends on God’s mercy rather than human effort, no one is too sinful to be saved. Believers can pray for God’s mercy on those who seem far from Him.

### *Romans 9:30–32* — Righteousness by Faith, Not by Works

> *“What shall we say then? That the Gentiles, who didn’t follow after righteousness, attained to righteousness, even the righteousness which is of faith; but Israel, following after a law of righteousness, didn’t arrive at the law of righteousness. Why? Because they didn’t seek it by faith, but as it were by works of the law. They stumbled over the stumbling stone,”*
>
> — *Romans 9:30–32* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had been explaining God’s sovereign choice and mercy. Now he draws a conclusion that highlights human responsibility as well.

“*What shall we say then? That the Gentiles, who didn’t follow after righteousness, attained to righteousness, even the righteousness which is of faith*” (*v. 30*). The Gentiles had not been seeking a right relationship with God through the Law. They had been worshiping idols and living without God’s revelation. Yet many of them obtained righteousness, the righteousness that comes by faith in Christ.

“*but Israel, following after a law of righteousness, didn’t arrive at the law of righteousness*” (*v. 31*). Many in Israel had been earnestly pursuing righteousness through the Law. They were zealous for God. Yet they did not reach their goal.

“*Why? Because they didn’t seek it by faith, but as it were by works of the law*” (*v. 32*). The problem was not their zeal but their method. They tried to become righteous by keeping the Law, rather than by trusting God. Righteousness cannot be earned; it must be received by faith.

“*They stumbled over the stumbling stone*” (*v. 32*). The “stumbling stone” is Christ. Paul quotes *Isaiah 8:14* and *28:16* in the next verse: “*Behold, I lay in Zion a stumbling stone and a rock of offense; and no one who believes in him will be disappointed*” (*v. 33*). Jesus, the crucified Messiah, was a stumbling block to many in Israel (*1 Corinthians 1:23*). They expected a Messiah who would vindicate their righteousness, not one who died for sinners. But those who trust in Him will never be put to shame.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that human responsibility is real. Chapter 9 emphasizes God’s sovereignty, but here Paul makes clear that Israel stumbled “because they didn’t seek it by faith.” People are responsible for how they respond to God. Paul continues this theme in chapter 10.

They also show the surprising nature of grace. Those who were not seeking God found Him, while those who were seeking Him in the wrong way did not. Jesus told parables with the same theme: the tax collector went home justified rather than the Pharisee (*Luke 18:9–14*).

Finally, these verses show that Christ is either a foundation or a stumbling stone. For those who trust Him, He is a secure foundation. For those who reject Him, He becomes a stone of stumbling. Peter writes, “*For you who believe therefore is the honor, but for those who are disobedient*” (*1 Peter 2:7*), He is a stone of stumbling.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses warn believers against trying to earn God’s favor. Even sincere, zealous people can miss God if they rely on their own works rather than faith in Christ. Believers can examine whether they are trusting in their own goodness or in Christ alone.

They also encourage believers to share the gospel with those who seem far from God. The Gentiles were not seeking righteousness, yet they found it. People who seem uninterested in God may be among those who respond to the gospel.

Finally, these verses give assurance. “No one who believes in him will be disappointed.” Those who trust in Christ will never be put to shame. Believers can rest securely on Him as their foundation.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Romans 9* begins with Paul’s deep sorrow for his fellow Israelites. His understanding of God’s sovereignty did not make him indifferent; it was joined with tears and longing for their salvation. Believers can ask God for a similar compassion for those who do not yet know Christ, and they can firmly reject any attitude of contempt toward the Jewish people, from whom the Messiah came.

The chapter affirms that God’s word has not failed. God’s promises have always worked through His choice and calling, not merely through human descent or effort. Believers can trust that God is faithful to His promises, even when His ways are hard to understand.

*Romans 9* emphasizes God’s sovereign mercy. Salvation depends not on human desire or effort but on God who shows mercy. Believers can respond with humility, recognizing that their salvation is entirely a gift, and with gratitude for mercy they did not deserve. Where the chapter raises difficult questions about God’s choices, believers can approach them with humility before the Creator, remembering that Christians have understood these passages in different ways while agreeing that God is both just and merciful.

Finally, the chapter shows that righteousness is received by faith, not earned by works. Many who pursued righteousness through the Law stumbled over Christ, while many who were not seeking God found righteousness through faith. Believers can trust in Christ as their sure foundation, knowing that no one who believes in Him will be put to shame, and they can share this good news with everyone.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord God, You are faithful, and Your word never fails. Thank You for the privileges You gave to Israel, and for sending the Messiah through them, Jesus Christ, who is over all, God blessed forever. Give me a heart like Paul’s, full of love and longing for those who do not yet know You. Guard me from any contempt toward the Jewish people, and help me to honor the heritage of faith I have received through them. Thank You that my salvation depends on Your mercy, not on my own desire or effort. Keep me humble and grateful. When I struggle to understand Your ways, help me to trust You as the wise and good Potter. Thank You that no one who believes in Jesus will be put to shame. Make Him my sure foundation. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
