Romans · Chapter 10 of 16

# Romans — Chapter 10

Chapter Theme: The Word of Faith Is Near: Whoever Calls on the Lord Will Be Saved

[Read Romans 10 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/ROM10.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul prays for Israel’s salvation, acknowledging their zeal for God but explaining that they sought to establish their own righteousness rather than submitting to God’s righteousness, which is found in Christ, the goal of the Law. The righteousness of faith does not require impossible journeys to heaven or the depths; the word is near: confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised Him from the dead, and you will be saved. There is no distinction between Jew and Gentile, for whoever calls on the Lord’s name will be saved. This requires messengers to be sent, because faith comes from hearing the message about Christ, and God continues to stretch out His hands to His people.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Romans 10* continues Paul’s discussion of Israel that began in chapter 9. In chapter 9, Paul emphasized God’s sovereign freedom and mercy. In chapter 10, he emphasizes human responsibility: Israel’s failure to believe, and the need for the gospel to be proclaimed and received by faith. Both truths are held together in Paul’s thinking.

The chapter also contains one of the clearest summaries of how a person is saved (*10:9–10*) and one of the strongest calls to mission in the New Testament (*10:14–15*).

### Zeal Without Knowledge (*10:1–4*)

Paul begins with his heart’s desire: “*Brothers, my heart’s desire and my prayer to God is for Israel, that they may be saved*” (*v. 1*). Paul continued to pray for his people. His teaching about God’s sovereignty in chapter 9 did not stop him from praying earnestly for their salvation.

“*For I testify about them that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge*” (*v. 2*). Paul knew this from experience. He had been zealous for God himself, persecuting the church (*Galatians 1:14*; *Philippians 3:6*). Zeal is admirable, but it is not enough. It must be guided by true knowledge.

“*For being ignorant of God’s righteousness, and seeking to establish their own righteousness, they didn’t subject themselves to the righteousness of God*” (*v. 3*). Many in Israel did not understand that God’s righteousness is a gift received by faith. Instead, they tried to build their own righteousness through keeping the Law. In doing so, they did not submit to God’s way. Paul’s statement about Christ and the Law is studied below.

### The Word Is Near (*10:5–13*)

Paul contrasts two approaches to righteousness. “*For Moses writes about the righteousness of the law, “The one who does them will live by them.”*” (*v. 5*) (*Leviticus 18:5*). The way of the Law requires doing everything it commands. If anyone perfectly obeyed, they would live, but no one does.

“*But the righteousness which is of faith says this, “Don’t say in your heart, ‘Who will ascend into heaven?’ (that is, to bring Christ down);*” (*v. 6*) “*or, ‘Who will descend into the abyss?’ (that is, to bring Christ up from the dead.)”*” (*v. 7*). Paul draws on *Deuteronomy 30:11–14*, where Moses told Israel that God’s command was not too hard or far away; it was near them. Paul applies this to Christ. No one needs to climb to heaven to bring Christ down, because He has already come. No one needs to descend into the depths to bring Him back from the dead, because God has already raised Him. Salvation is not a matter of heroic human achievement.

“*But what does it say? “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart;” that is, the word of faith which we preach*” (*v. 8*). The gospel is near, accessible to everyone. Paul then explains what it calls for, studied below. He continues, “*For the Scripture says, “Whoever believes in him will not be disappointed.”*” (*v. 11*) (*Isaiah 28:16*). “*For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek; for the same Lord is Lord of all, and is rich to all who call on him*” (*v. 12*). One Lord rules over all people, and He is generous to all who call on Him. The universal promise is studied below.

### How Will They Hear? (*10:14–17*)

Paul then shows the necessity of proclaiming the gospel, studied below. “*But they didn’t all listen to the glad news. For Isaiah says, “Lord, who has believed our report?”*” (*v. 16*) (*Isaiah 53:1*). Not everyone who hears believes. “*So faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God*” (*v. 17*). Some manuscripts read “the word of Christ,” meaning the message about Christ. Faith is born when people hear the gospel.

### Israel Heard but Did Not Respond (*10:18–21*)

Has Israel heard? “*Yes, most certainly, “Their sound went out into all the earth, their words to the ends of the world.”*” (*v. 18*) Paul quotes *Psalm 19:4*, which speaks of creation’s witness to God, and applies it to the spread of the gospel. The message had gone out widely.

Did Israel understand? Paul quotes Moses: “*I will provoke you to jealousy with that which is no nation. I will make you angry with a nation void of understanding.*” (*v. 19*) (*Deuteronomy 32:21*). God would use the Gentiles’ faith to provoke Israel to jealousy, a theme Paul develops in chapter 11. And Isaiah: “*I was found by those who didn’t seek me. I was revealed to those who didn’t ask for me.*” (*v. 20*) (*Isaiah 65:1*). The Gentiles found God without seeking Him.

The chapter ends with a moving picture of God’s patience: “*But about Israel he says, “All day long I stretched out my hands to a disobedient and contrary people.”*” (*v. 21*) (*Isaiah 65:2*). God has not given up on His people. He stretches out His hands like a parent pleading with a child, inviting them to come. This prepares for chapter 11, where Paul shows that God has not rejected Israel.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Romans 10:4* — Christ, the Fulfillment of the Law

> *“For Christ is the fulfillment of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.”*
>
> — *Romans 10:4* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had been explaining why many of his fellow Jews had not believed in Jesus. They had a zeal for God, but they did not understand God’s way of righteousness. Instead of receiving righteousness as a gift, they tried to establish their own righteousness by keeping the Law.

Then Paul declared, “*For Christ is the fulfillment of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes*” (*v. 4*). The word translated “fulfillment” (telos in Greek) can mean “end,” “goal,” or “completion.” Both meanings are important.

Christ is the “goal” of the Law. The Law pointed forward to Him. The sacrifices, the priesthood, the temple, and the promises all found their fulfillment in Him. The Law was like a road leading to a destination, and Christ is that destination.

Christ is also the “end” of the Law as a way of gaining righteousness. Since Christ has come, people no longer try to become righteous by keeping the Law. Instead, they receive righteousness through faith in Him.

“*for righteousness to everyone who believes*” (*v. 4*). This righteousness is available to “everyone who believes,” Jew and Gentile alike. No one is excluded.

This does not mean the Law has no value. Paul has said that the Law is holy, righteous, and good (*7:12*). The moral teaching of the Law still reveals God’s will. But the Law is no longer the means of becoming right with God. That role belongs to Christ alone.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that the whole Old Testament points to Christ. Jesus said, “*Don’t think that I came to destroy the law or the prophets. I didn’t come to destroy, but to fulfill*” (*Matthew 5:17*). Christ is the center of God’s plan, and the Law finds its meaning in Him.

It also shows that righteousness is found only in Christ. Paul wrote to the Philippians that he wanted to be found in Christ, “*not having a righteousness of my own, that which is of the law, but that which is through faith in Christ, the righteousness which is from God by faith*” (*Philippians 3:9*).

Finally, the verse shows the universal scope of the gospel. Righteousness comes to “everyone who believes.” The Law had separated Jews from Gentiles; Christ unites them through faith.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse frees believers from trying to make themselves righteous through rule-keeping. Christ has done what the Law could not. Believers can rest in His righteousness.

It also encourages believers to read the Old Testament with Christ in view. The Law, the sacrifices, and the promises all point to Him. Seeing Christ in the Old Testament deepens understanding and worship.

Finally, the verse reminds believers that righteousness is available to everyone. No one needs to meet religious requirements first. Anyone who believes in Christ receives His righteousness.

### *Romans 10:9–10* — Confess and Believe

> *“that if you will confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For with the heart one believes resulting in righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made resulting in salvation.”*
>
> — *Romans 10:9–10* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had been explaining that righteousness by faith does not require impossible achievements. No one needs to climb to heaven or descend into the depths. The message is near, “in your mouth and in your heart.” Now Paul explains what this means.

“*that if you will confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord*” (*v. 9*). To “confess” means to declare openly, to say publicly. The confession is “Jesus is Lord.” In the Roman world, people were expected to say “Caesar is Lord.” For Christians to say “Jesus is Lord” was a bold declaration of loyalty to Jesus above all. In the Greek Old Testament, “Lord” was the word used for God’s name. To confess Jesus as Lord means to acknowledge His divine authority and to submit to Him.

“*and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead*” (*v. 9*). The heart, in Scripture, is the center of a person’s thoughts, feelings, and will. Believing “in your heart” means trusting with one’s whole being, not merely agreeing with an idea. The content of this belief is that God raised Jesus from the dead. The resurrection is central to the gospel.

“*you will be saved*” (*v. 9*). The result is salvation. This is God’s promise to all who confess and believe.

“*For with the heart one believes resulting in righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made resulting in salvation*” (*v. 10*). Paul explains the connection. Inner faith leads to righteousness, being right with God. Outer confession leads to salvation. These are not two separate steps but two sides of the same response: true faith in the heart naturally expresses itself in confession with the mouth.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses summarize how a person is saved. Salvation comes through faith in the risen Jesus as Lord. It is simple, but it is not shallow. Confessing Jesus as Lord means giving Him one’s whole life.

They also show that faith is both inward and outward. Genuine faith is not hidden; it is confessed. Jesus said, “*Everyone therefore who confesses me before men, I will also confess him before my Father who is in heaven*” (*Matthew 10:32*).

Finally, these verses show the centrality of the resurrection. Believing that God raised Jesus from the dead is essential. The resurrection proves that Jesus is who He claimed to be and that His sacrifice was accepted.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses give a clear answer to anyone who asks how to be saved. Believers can share this simple message: confess that Jesus is Lord, and believe in your heart that God raised Him from the dead.

They also encourage believers to confess their faith openly. Many believers keep their faith private. Paul’s words remind them that true faith is expressed in confession. Believers can speak openly about Jesus with gentleness and respect.

Finally, these verses invite believers to examine whether Jesus is truly Lord in their lives. Confessing Jesus as Lord means giving Him authority over every area: relationships, work, money, and choices. Believers can ask whether there are areas they have not yet surrendered to Him.

### *Romans 10:13* — Whoever Will Call on the Name of the Lord

> *“For, ‘Whoever will call on the name of the Lord will be saved.’”*
>
> — *Romans 10:13* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had just said that there is no distinction between Jew and Greek, because the same Lord is Lord of all and is generous to all who call on Him. Now he supports this with a quotation from Scripture.

“*For, “Whoever will call on the name of the Lord will be saved.”*” (*v. 13*) This verse comes from *Joel 2:32*. Peter also quoted it in his sermon on the day of Pentecost (*Acts 2:21*).

“Whoever” means anyone. There are no exceptions based on nationality, background, past sins, or social status. The promise is open to all.

“Call on the name of the Lord” means to cry out to God for help, to pray to Him in trust. In the Old Testament, it describes worship and dependence on God. In Joel, “the Lord” refers to Yahweh, the God of Israel. Paul applies it to Jesus, whom he has just called Lord (*10:9*). This shows that Paul regarded Jesus as fully divine, sharing the name and identity of Israel’s God.

“Will be saved” is the promise. Salvation is certain for those who call on the Lord.

This verse is beautifully simple. Salvation is not reserved for the religious elite or for those who have achieved great things. Anyone who calls on Jesus in faith will be saved.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows the universal offer of the gospel. God’s salvation is not limited to one people. It is offered to “whoever.” This fulfills God’s promise to Abraham that all nations would be blessed through him (*Genesis 12:3*).

It also shows the deity of Christ. By applying Joel’s words about Yahweh to Jesus, Paul shows that Jesus shares the identity of the one true God. Calling on Jesus is calling on God.

Finally, the verse shows that salvation requires a response. People must “call on the name of the Lord.” God offers salvation freely, but it must be received. This prepares for Paul’s questions in the next verses about how people can call on someone they have not heard of.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse brings hope to anyone who feels far from God. No matter what someone has done or where they come from, if they call on the name of the Lord, they will be saved.

It also encourages believers to pray with confidence. Believers can call on the Lord in every need, trusting that He hears and responds.

Finally, the verse motivates believers to share the gospel. If “whoever” calls on the Lord will be saved, then every person needs to hear about Him. Believers can share Jesus’ name with everyone they meet.

### *Romans 10:14–15* — How Beautiful Are the Feet

> *“How then will they call on him in whom they have not believed? How will they believe in him whom they have not heard? How will they hear without a preacher? And how will they preach unless they are sent? As it is written: ‘How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the Good News of peace, who bring glad tidings of good things!’”*
>
> — *Romans 10:14–15* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had just declared that whoever calls on the name of the Lord will be saved. But this raises a practical question: how can people call on someone they do not know? Paul asks a series of questions, each building on the one before.

“*How then will they call on him in whom they have not believed?*” (*v. 14*) People will not call on the Lord unless they believe in Him.

“*How will they believe in him whom they have not heard?*” (*v. 14*) People cannot believe in someone they have never heard of.

“*How will they hear without a preacher?*” (*v. 14*) People cannot hear unless someone tells them. “Preacher” here means anyone who proclaims the message, not only ordained ministers.

“*And how will they preach unless they are sent?*” (*v. 15*) Messengers must be sent. This is the beginning of the chain.

So the chain is: sent, preach, hear, believe, call, be saved. If any link is missing, the chain breaks.

“*As it is written: “How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the Good News of peace, who bring glad tidings of good things!”*” (*v. 15*) Paul quotes *Isaiah 52:7*. In Isaiah, the image is of a messenger running across the mountains to bring news of victory and the return from exile. To those waiting for good news, the dusty feet of the messenger look beautiful. Paul applies this to those who bring the gospel.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that God uses people to spread the gospel. God could have chosen to reveal Himself directly to every person, but He chose to use messengers. This is a great privilege and responsibility for believers. Jesus commissioned His followers to “*Go into all the world, and preach the Good News to the whole creation*” (*Mark 16:15*).

They also show the importance of sending. Some go, and others send. Churches that send and support missionaries are part of the chain of salvation. Paul relied on churches to send and support him (*Romans 15:24*; *Philippians 4:15–16*).

Finally, these verses show the beauty of the gospel. The message is “good news,” “glad tidings of good things.” Those who bring it are bringing the best news in the world.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses challenge believers to share the gospel. Many people around them have not heard or understood the good news of Jesus. Believers can be the messengers who tell them.

They also encourage believers to support mission. Not everyone is called to go to distant places, but everyone can participate by praying, giving, and encouraging those who go. Churches can make sending a priority.

Finally, these verses honor those who share the gospel. Pastors, missionaries, evangelists, and ordinary believers who share their faith are doing beautiful work. Believers can thank and support them, and they can see their own witness as part of this beautiful calling.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Romans 10* begins with Paul’s prayer for his people’s salvation. Like Paul, believers can pray earnestly for those who do not yet know Christ, including those who are religious but have not understood God’s gift of righteousness. Zeal for God is good, but it must be joined with knowledge of the truth.

The chapter also shows that Christ is the goal and fulfillment of the Law. Righteousness is not achieved by human effort but received through faith in Him. Believers can stop trying to establish their own righteousness and submit to God’s righteousness, found in Christ.

*Romans 10* gives a clear and simple message of salvation: confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord, and believe in your heart that God raised Him from the dead. Whoever calls on the name of the Lord will be saved, with no distinction between people. Believers can rest in this promise for themselves and share it confidently with others, while also confessing their faith openly.

Finally, the chapter calls believers to mission. People cannot call on someone they have not believed, believe in someone they have not heard of, or hear without someone telling them. Faith comes by hearing the message about Christ. Believers can share the gospel, support those who are sent, and remember that God, with outstretched hands, still invites all people to come to Him.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, I confess that You are Lord, and I believe in my heart that God raised You from the dead. Thank You for the promise that whoever calls on Your name will be saved. Thank You that You are the fulfillment of the Law and that I can receive Your righteousness by faith. Keep me from trying to establish my own righteousness. Give me a heart like Paul’s that prays for the salvation of others, especially my friends, family, and neighbors. Make me willing to share Your good news, and let my feet be beautiful as I bring glad tidings to others. Bless those who are sent to preach the gospel around the world, and show me how to support them. Thank You, Father, that You stretch out Your hands to all people. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Romans · Chapter 11 of 16

# Romans — Chapter 11

Chapter Theme: God Has Not Rejected His People: The Olive Tree and the Depth of God’s Wisdom

[Read Romans 11 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/ROM11.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul insists that God has not rejected Israel; he himself is an Israelite, and just as in Elijah’s day, there is a faithful remnant chosen by grace. Israel’s stumbling has opened the way of salvation to the Gentiles, and Paul hopes this will move his own people to jealousy and faith. Using the image of an olive tree, he warns Gentile believers, grafted in like wild branches, not to boast over the natural branches, because they stand only by faith, and God is able to graft the natural branches back in. Paul reveals a mystery: a partial hardening has come upon Israel until the full number of Gentiles comes in, and so all Israel will be saved, for God’s gifts and calling are irrevocable. The chapter ends in a hymn of praise to the unsearchable wisdom of God.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Romans 11* completes Paul’s discussion of Israel in chapters 9–11. In chapter 9, Paul showed that God’s word has not failed, because God’s promises work through His sovereign choice. In chapter 10, he showed that Israel is responsible for not believing the gospel. Now he answers the crucial question: Has God rejected His people? His answer is a resounding no.

This chapter is especially important for understanding the relationship between the church and the Jewish people. Paul warns Gentile Christians against arrogance toward Israel, affirms God’s ongoing love for the Jewish people, and expresses hope for their future. Sadly, throughout history, many Christians have ignored this teaching and treated Jewish people with contempt and cruelty. *Romans 11* stands as a rebuke to all such attitudes.

### A Remnant Chosen by Grace (*11:1–10*)

“*I ask then, did God reject his people? May it never be!*” (*v. 1*) Paul offers himself as proof: “*For I also am an Israelite, a descendant of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin*” (*v. 1*). If God had rejected Israel, Paul himself would not have been saved. “*God didn’t reject his people, whom he foreknew*” (*v. 2*).

Paul then points to Elijah. In a time of great unfaithfulness, Elijah complained that he alone was left faithful (*1 Kings 19:10*). But God answered, “*I have reserved for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal*” (*v. 4*). Elijah was not alone. God had preserved a faithful remnant. Paul’s application is studied below.

“*What then? That which Israel seeks for, that he didn’t obtain, but the chosen ones obtained it, and the rest were hardened*” (*v. 7*). Paul quotes *Deuteronomy 29:4* and *Isaiah 29:10* about a “spirit of stupor,” and *Psalm 69:22–23*. These passages describe God’s judgment on those who persistently reject Him. Yet Paul will show that this hardening is neither total nor final.

### Israel’s Stumbling and the Gentiles’ Salvation (*11:11–16*)

“*I ask then, did they stumble that they might fall? May it never be!*” (*v. 11*) Israel’s stumbling is not permanent. “*But by their fall salvation has come to the Gentiles, to provoke them to jealousy*” (*v. 11*). When many Jews rejected the gospel, the apostles turned to the Gentiles (*Acts 13:46*). God used Israel’s unbelief to bring salvation to the nations. And He intends the Gentiles’ salvation to make Israel jealous, drawing them back to Him.

“*Now if their fall is the riches of the world, and their loss the riches of the Gentiles, how much more their fullness!*” (*v. 12*) If Israel’s stumbling has brought such blessing, how much greater blessing will come when Israel returns. Paul magnified his ministry to the Gentiles, hoping it would provoke his own people to faith. “*For if the rejection of them is the reconciling of the world, what would their acceptance be, but life from the dead?*” (*v. 15*) Israel’s future acceptance will be like resurrection.

“*If the first fruit is holy, so is the lump. If the root is holy, so are the branches*” (*v. 16*). The “first fruit” and “root” probably refer to the patriarchs, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Because the root is holy, the whole tree belongs to God.

### The Olive Tree (*11:17–24*)

Paul then uses the image of an olive tree, studied below. He warns, “*True; by their unbelief they were broken off, and you stand by your faith. Don’t be conceited, but fear*” (*v. 20*). “*for if God didn’t spare the natural branches, neither will he spare you*” (*v. 21*). “*See then the goodness and severity of God. Toward those who fell, severity; but toward you, goodness, if you continue in his goodness; otherwise you also will be cut off*” (*v. 22*). God’s kindness should never be taken for granted. Those who stand by faith must continue in faith.

“*They also, if they don’t continue in their unbelief, will be grafted in, for God is able to graft them in again*” (*v. 23*). The door remains open for Israel. “*how much more will these, which are the natural branches, be grafted into their own olive tree?*” (*v. 24*) It is even more natural for the original branches to be restored.

### The Mystery: All Israel Will Be Saved (*11:25–32*)

Paul reveals a “mystery,” studied below. He then explains God’s attitude toward Israel: “*Concerning the Good News, they are enemies for your sake. But concerning the election, they are beloved for the fathers’ sake*” (*v. 28*). In relation to the gospel, many Jews were opposing it, which opened the door for the Gentiles. But in relation to God’s choice, they remain loved because of His promises to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. “*For the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable*” (*v. 29*). God does not take back His promises. This is good news for Israel, and also for all believers: God’s faithfulness to His promises is the foundation of their own security.

“*For as you in time past were disobedient to God, but now have obtained mercy by their disobedience*” (*v. 30*), “*even so these also have now been disobedient, that by the mercy shown to you they may also obtain mercy*” (*v. 31*). Gentiles and Jews alike receive mercy. “*For God has bound all to disobedience, that he might have mercy on all*” (*v. 32*). God has shown that all people, Jews and Gentiles, are disobedient, so that all might receive mercy rather than earning salvation. This verse does not teach that every individual will be saved regardless of faith, but that God’s mercy is offered to all without distinction.

### The Hymn of Praise (*11:33–36*)

Paul ends this section with a burst of worship, studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Romans 11:5–6* — A Remnant by Grace

> *“Even so too at this present time also there is a remnant according to the election of grace. And if by grace, then it is no longer of works; otherwise grace is no longer grace. But if it is of works, it is no longer grace; otherwise work is no longer work.”*
>
> — *Romans 11:5–6* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had asked whether God had rejected His people, Israel. He answered, “May it never be!” He pointed to himself, an Israelite who believed in Jesus. Then he pointed to Elijah’s time, when Elijah thought he was the only faithful person left, but God said He had kept seven thousand who had not worshiped Baal.

Now Paul applied this to his own time: “*Even so too at this present time also there is a remnant according to the election of grace*” (*v. 5*). A “remnant” is a small part that remains from a larger whole. In the Old Testament, God often preserved a faithful remnant even when most of the nation turned away (*Isaiah 10:20–22*). In Paul’s day, many Jews had believed in Jesus, including the apostles, the thousands at Pentecost, and many others. They were the remnant.

This remnant exists “according to the election of grace.” God chose them, and His choice was based on grace, not on their merit.

“*And if by grace, then it is no longer of works; otherwise grace is no longer grace*” (*v. 6*). Paul explains what grace means. If salvation were based on works, it would no longer be grace. Grace and works are opposites when it comes to earning salvation. Grace is God’s free gift; works are what people earn. If people could earn salvation, grace would not really be grace.

These verses show that God has always been faithful to His people, preserving a remnant by His grace. Even in times of widespread unbelief, God is at work.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show God’s faithfulness to His promises. Even when Israel as a whole turned away, God never abandoned His people completely. He always preserved a faithful remnant. This shows that God’s purposes cannot be defeated by human unfaithfulness.

They also show that salvation is entirely by grace. Paul writes elsewhere, “*not of works, that no one would boast*” (*Ephesians 2:9*). Grace cannot be mixed with merit. Either salvation is a free gift, or it is earned. It cannot be both.

Finally, these verses offer encouragement in times when faithfulness seems rare. Elijah felt alone, but he was not. God always has people who belong to Him, even when they are hidden.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers who feel isolated in their faith. Like Elijah, believers may sometimes feel that they are the only ones who remain faithful. God’s word to Elijah applies: He has others who belong to Him. Believers are not alone.

They also remind believers that their salvation is a gift of grace. No one can earn it. This truth humbles believers and fills them with gratitude.

Finally, these verses give hope for the future. God is always at work, preserving His people and drawing others to Himself. Believers can trust that God’s purposes will prevail, even in times of widespread unbelief.

### *Romans 11:17–18* — Don’t Boast over the Branches

> *“But if some of the branches were broken off, and you, being a wild olive, were grafted in among them and became partaker with them of the root and of the richness of the olive tree, don’t boast over the branches. But if you boast, remember that it is not you who support the root, but the root supports you.”*
>
> — *Romans 11:17–18* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul now uses a vivid image from agriculture to describe the relationship between Israel and Gentile believers: an olive tree. Olive trees were common in Israel and were an important source of food, oil, and income. The olive tree was also a symbol of Israel in the Old Testament (*Jeremiah 11:16*; *Hosea 14:6*).

“*But if some of the branches were broken off*” (*v. 17*). The “branches” are the people of Israel. Some of them were broken off because of unbelief. Notice that Paul says “some,” not all.

“*and you, being a wild olive, were grafted in among them*” (*v. 17*). Gentile believers are like branches from a wild olive tree, grafted into the cultivated tree. Grafting involves cutting a branch from one tree and inserting it into another so that it grows as part of it. Normally, farmers grafted cultivated branches onto wild trees, not the other way around. Paul acknowledges that what God has done is unusual, “contrary to nature” (*11:24*).

“*and became partaker with them of the root and of the richness of the olive tree*” (*v. 17*). Gentile believers now share in the root and the rich sap of the tree, the blessings God promised to Abraham and his descendants. They have been brought into the people of God.

“*don’t boast over the branches*” (*v. 18*). Paul warns Gentile believers not to feel superior to the Jews. They should not think that because some branches were broken off, they are better.

“*But if you boast, remember that it is not you who support the root, but the root supports you*” (*v. 18*). The Gentiles depend on Israel, not the other way around. The root, God’s covenant with Abraham and the patriarchs, supports the whole tree. Gentile believers owe their faith to God’s work through Israel.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show the unity of God’s people across history. The church is not a separate tree from Israel. Gentile believers are grafted into the same tree, sharing in the same promises. Paul writes, “*So then you are no longer strangers and foreigners, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and of the household of God*” (*Ephesians 2:19*).

They also show the danger of pride. Gentile believers were tempted to look down on Jews who had not believed. Paul warns that they stand only by faith and have no grounds for boasting. Pride is always a danger when people forget that everything they have is a gift.

Finally, these verses show that the Christian faith has Jewish roots. The Scriptures, the promises, the covenants, and the Messiah all came through Israel. Christians should honor this heritage, not despise it.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses call believers to humility. Believers are saved by grace, not by their own merit. They have no grounds to boast over anyone.

They also call believers to reject antisemitism. Throughout history, many Christians have treated Jewish people with contempt, persecution, and violence. Paul’s words condemn such attitudes. Christians are called to honor the Jewish people, pray for them, and treat them with love.

Finally, these verses encourage believers to appreciate their spiritual heritage. The Old Testament is not a book for someone else; it is part of believers’ own story. They can study it with gratitude, recognizing the root that supports them.

### *Romans 11:25–26* — And So All Israel Will Be Saved

> *“For I don’t desire you to be ignorant, brothers, of this mystery, so that you won’t be wise in your own conceits, that a partial hardening has happened to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, and so all Israel will be saved. Even as it is written, There will come out of Zion the Deliverer, and he will turn away ungodliness from Jacob.”*
>
> — *Romans 11:25–26* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had been explaining that some branches of the olive tree, the people of Israel, had been broken off because of unbelief, and that Gentiles had been grafted in. But he had said that God is able to graft the natural branches back in. Now he reveals something about the future.

“*For I don’t desire you to be ignorant, brothers, of this mystery, so that you won’t be wise in your own conceits*” (*v. 25*). A “mystery” in Paul’s letters is not something mysterious in the modern sense, but a truth once hidden that God has now revealed. Paul shares this mystery to keep Gentile believers from becoming proud.

“*that a partial hardening has happened to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in*” (*v. 25*). The hardening of Israel is “partial,” not complete; many Jews have believed. It is also temporary, “until” a certain point. That point is when “the fullness of the Gentiles has come in,” when the full number of Gentiles God intends to save have come to faith.

“*and so all Israel will be saved*” (*v. 26*). This is one of the most discussed phrases in Romans. Christians have understood it in several ways. Many believe it refers to a future turning of the Jewish people as a whole to faith in Jesus as the Messiah, perhaps near the time of Christ’s return. Others believe “all Israel” refers to all the elect among the Jewish people throughout history, saved one by one as they come to faith. Still others believe it refers to the whole people of God, both Jews and Gentiles, “*God’s Israel*” (*Galatians 6:16*). Each view is held by faithful interpreters. Many find the first view most natural in the context, since Paul has been distinguishing Israel from the Gentiles throughout the chapter. All agree that salvation comes only through faith in Jesus, and that God remains faithful to His promises to Israel.

“*Even as it is written, “There will come out of Zion the Deliverer, and he will turn away ungodliness from Jacob.*” (*v. 26*) Paul quotes *Isaiah 59:20–21* and *27:9*. The Deliverer, Christ, will remove sin from Jacob, that is, Israel. “*This is my covenant with them, when I will take away their sins.*” (*v. 27*) God’s covenant includes the forgiveness of Israel’s sins.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that God has a continuing purpose for the Jewish people. God has not replaced Israel or forgotten His promises. Paul writes, “*For the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable*” (*v. 29*).

They also show that God’s plan is bigger than any one moment in history. Israel’s partial hardening, the inclusion of the Gentiles, and the future salvation of Israel are all part of God’s unfolding purpose. God is working out His plan across centuries.

Finally, these verses show that salvation always comes through Christ. The Deliverer from Zion is the one who takes away sin. Whatever the exact meaning of “all Israel,” it is through faith in the Messiah that Israel will be saved, just as the Gentiles are.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to pray for the Jewish people. Paul longed for their salvation, and these verses give hope that God has not forgotten them.

They also call believers to humility. Paul revealed this mystery so that Gentile believers would not be “wise in your own conceits.” Believers should not think of themselves as superior to Israel or any other people.

Finally, these verses give believers confidence in God’s faithfulness. If God remains faithful to His promises to Israel despite their unbelief, He will also be faithful to His promises to all who belong to Him.

### *Romans 11:33–36* — The Depth of God’s Wisdom

> *“Oh the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and the knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past tracing out! ‘For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor?’ ‘Or who has first given to him, and it will be repaid to him again?’ For of him and through him and to him are all things. To him be the glory for ever! Amen.”*
>
> — *Romans 11:33–36* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had spent three chapters wrestling with one of the hardest questions of his time: how God’s promises to Israel fit with Israel’s unbelief and the inclusion of the Gentiles. He had explained God’s sovereign choice, Israel’s responsibility, the remnant, the olive tree, and the mystery of Israel’s future salvation. At the end of all this explanation, Paul does not simply conclude with a summary. He bursts into worship.

“*Oh the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and the knowledge of God!*” (*v. 33*) Paul is overwhelmed by God’s greatness. God’s riches, wisdom, and knowledge are like an ocean too deep to measure.

“*How unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past tracing out!*” (*v. 33*) God’s decisions and ways are beyond human understanding. People can understand some of what God reveals, but they can never fully grasp all of His ways. The phrase “past tracing out” pictures footprints that cannot be followed.

“*“For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor?”*” (*v. 34*) Paul quotes *Isaiah 40:13*. No one fully knows God’s mind, and no one has ever given Him advice. God does not need human counsel.

“*“Or who has first given to him, and it will be repaid to him again?”*” (*v. 35*) This echoes *Job 41:11*. No one has ever given God something that would put Him in their debt. Everything people have came from God first. Salvation is grace, not repayment.

“*For of him and through him and to him are all things*” (*v. 36*). Everything comes “from” God as its source, exists “through” God as its sustainer, and exists “for” God as its goal. God is the beginning, middle, and end of all things.

“*To him be the glory for ever! Amen.*” (*v. 36*) The only fitting response is to give God glory forever.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that theology should lead to worship. Paul did not study God’s ways merely to win arguments or satisfy curiosity. The more he understood, the more he was moved to praise. True knowledge of God always leads to adoration.

They also show the limits of human understanding. Paul had explained much, but he acknowledged that God’s ways are ultimately beyond full comprehension. This is not a failure of faith but an expression of it. Isaiah writes, “*For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways, and my thoughts than your thoughts*” (*Isaiah 55:9*).

Finally, these verses show that everything exists for God’s glory. This is the ultimate purpose of creation, history, and salvation. The whole plan of God, including His dealings with Israel and the Gentiles, leads to His glory.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses invite believers to respond to God’s truth with worship. When believers study Scripture and learn about God, they can pause to praise Him for His wisdom and greatness.

They also encourage believers to trust God when they do not understand. Many questions about God’s ways remain unanswered. Believers can rest in the knowledge that His wisdom is perfect, even when His ways are past finding out.

Finally, these verses call believers to live for God’s glory. Since everything is from Him, through Him, and to Him, believers can seek to honor Him in all they do, offering every part of their lives back to Him.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Romans 11* declares that God has not rejected His people. Even in times of widespread unbelief, God preserves a remnant chosen by grace. Believers who feel isolated in their faith can take heart, as Elijah did, that God always has people who belong to Him. And believers can rest in the truth that salvation is entirely by grace.

The chapter also warns Gentile believers against pride. They are like wild branches grafted into God’s olive tree, sharing in the rich root of God’s promises to Israel. They have no grounds to boast over the natural branches. Believers are called to humility, to gratitude for their spiritual heritage, and to the firm rejection of antisemitism in every form.

*Romans 11* gives hope for Israel’s future. A partial hardening has come upon Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles comes in, and so all Israel will be saved, because God’s gifts and calling are irrevocable. Believers can pray for the Jewish people with hope, trusting God’s faithfulness. And they can take comfort that the God who keeps His promises to Israel will keep His promises to them.

Finally, the chapter ends in worship. After wrestling with the deepest questions, Paul praises the depth of God’s wisdom and knowledge, His unsearchable judgments, and His untraceable ways. Believers can follow his example, letting their study of God lead to praise, trusting God when they do not understand, and living for the glory of the One from whom, through whom, and to whom are all things.

## Chapter Prayer

Faithful God, thank You that You have not rejected Your people and that Your gifts and calling are irrevocable. Thank You for preserving a remnant by grace in every generation, and for including me in Your family by grace alone. Keep me humble, remembering that I am a branch grafted in, supported by the root You planted. Forgive Your church for every arrogance and cruelty shown toward the Jewish people, and fill me with love for them. I pray that many would come to know Jesus as their Messiah. When I do not understand Your ways, help me to trust Your wisdom. Oh the depth of the riches of Your wisdom and knowledge! From You and through You and to You are all things. To You be the glory forever. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Romans · Chapter 12 of 16

# Romans — Chapter 12

Chapter Theme: Living Sacrifices: Transformed Minds and Genuine Love

[Read Romans 12 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/ROM12.htm)

Main Teaching

In light of God’s mercies, Paul urges believers to offer their whole selves to God as living sacrifices and to be transformed by the renewing of their minds rather than conforming to the pattern of this world. He calls them to think humbly about themselves and to use their different gifts for the good of the one body of Christ. He describes genuine love in practical detail: hating evil, clinging to good, honoring one another, serving with zeal, rejoicing in hope, persevering in trouble, praying faithfully, sharing with those in need, and practicing hospitality. Finally, he teaches believers to bless their persecutors, refuse revenge, leave judgment to God, and overcome evil with good.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Romans 12* marks a major turning point in the letter. In chapters 1–11, Paul explained the gospel: God’s righteousness revealed in Christ, justification by faith, life in the Spirit, and God’s faithful plan for Jews and Gentiles. Now, beginning with “Therefore,” Paul turns to how believers should live in response. Theology leads to practice; belief shapes behavior.

This pattern is typical of Paul’s letters. He first describes what God has done, then calls believers to live in light of it. The Christian life is not an effort to earn God’s mercy; it is a response to mercy already received.

### Living Sacrifices and Transformed Minds (*12:1–2*)

Paul’s appeal is studied below in two parts.

### Humble Service in the Body (*12:3–8*)

Paul begins his practical instruction with humility: “*not to think of yourself more highly than you ought to think; but to think reasonably, as God has apportioned to each person a measure of faith*” (*v. 3*). Believers are to have an honest and sober view of themselves, neither proud nor falsely humble, recognizing that whatever they have is God’s gift. His teaching on the body and its gifts is studied below.

### Genuine Love (*12:9–16*)

Paul then describes what love looks like in practice. “*Let love be without hypocrisy. Abhor that which is evil. Cling to that which is good*” (*v. 9*). “Without hypocrisy” means sincere, not pretended. The word was used of actors wearing masks. Christian love is not a performance. Genuine love also has moral strength: it hates evil and holds tightly to good. Love is not merely niceness; it seeks what is truly good for others.

“*In love of the brothers be tenderly affectionate to one another; in honor prefer one another*” (*v. 10*). Believers are family, and they should love one another with warm affection. They are to compete in showing honor to one another, each trying to honor the others more.

“*not lagging in diligence, fervent in spirit, serving the Lord*” (*v. 11*). Believers should not be lazy but zealous, with a spiritual fire. “Fervent” means boiling, burning with enthusiasm. And all service is ultimately for the Lord.

“*rejoicing in hope, enduring in troubles, continuing steadfastly in prayer*” (*v. 12*). Three short commands describe how believers face life. They rejoice because of their hope of glory (*5:2*). They endure when trouble comes (*5:3*). And they keep praying, persistently and faithfully.

“*contributing to the needs of the saints, and given to hospitality*” (*v. 13*). Love is practical. Believers share what they have with fellow believers in need. And they “pursue” hospitality, actively welcoming others, especially travelers and strangers. In the ancient world, inns were often unsafe or immoral, so Christian hospitality was vital for traveling believers.

“*Bless those who persecute you; bless, and don’t curse*” (*v. 14*). This echoes Jesus’ teaching (*Luke 6:28*). Believers are to speak blessing, not curses, over those who mistreat them.

“*Rejoice with those who rejoice. Weep with those who weep*” (*v. 15*). Love shares the emotions of others. It is sometimes harder to rejoice with others’ success than to weep with their sorrow, because envy can creep in. Love does both.

“*Be of the same mind one toward another. Don’t set your mind on high things, but associate with the humble. Don’t be wise in your own conceits*” (*v. 16*). Believers should live in harmony, not seeking status, but willing to associate with people of low position. They should not consider themselves wiser than others.

### Overcoming Evil with Good (*12:17–21*)

Paul’s teaching on responding to evil is studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Romans 12:1* — A Living Sacrifice

> *“Therefore I urge you, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service.”*
>
> — *Romans 12:1* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had spent eleven chapters explaining the gospel: God’s mercy toward sinners, justification by faith, the gift of the Holy Spirit, and God’s faithful plan for His people. He had ended chapter 11 with a hymn of praise to God’s wisdom. Now he turns to how believers should respond.

“*Therefore I urge you, brothers, by the mercies of God*” (*v. 1*). The word “therefore” connects everything that follows to what came before. Paul does not command believers to obey in order to earn God’s favor. He appeals to them “by the mercies of God,” the mercy they have already received. Obedience is a response to grace.

“*to present your bodies a living sacrifice*” (*v. 1*). In the Old Testament, worshipers brought animals to the temple as sacrifices. The animals were killed and offered on the altar. Paul calls believers to offer themselves as sacrifices, but “living” ones. They do not die on an altar; they live for God every day. “Bodies” refers to the whole person, including physical life. Faith is not only about the soul or the mind; it includes what believers do with their hands, feet, eyes, and tongues.

“*holy, acceptable to God*” (*v. 1*). The sacrifice is “holy,” set apart for God, and “acceptable,” pleasing to Him. Because of Christ’s sacrifice, believers’ offering of themselves is welcomed by God.

“*which is your spiritual service*” (*v. 1*). The word translated “spiritual” can also mean “reasonable” or “logical.” Considering everything God has done, offering oneself to Him is the only reasonable response. The word “service” also means “worship.” True worship is not only singing or attending church; it is offering one’s whole life to God.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that worship involves the whole of life. The Old Testament sacrifices pointed forward to Christ, who offered Himself once for all (*Hebrews 10:10–14*). Now that His sacrifice is complete, believers no longer bring animal sacrifices. Instead, they offer their lives in grateful response. Peter writes that believers are “*to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God through Jesus Christ*” (*1 Peter 2:5*).

It also shows that grace motivates obedience. Paul urges believers “by the mercies of God.” The deeper believers understand God’s mercy, the more they will want to give themselves to Him.

Finally, the verse shows that the body matters to God. Some ancient philosophies taught that the body was unimportant or even evil. Christianity teaches that God created the body, Christ took on a body, and believers will be raised in bodies. What believers do with their bodies is part of their worship.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse calls believers to offer every part of their lives to God. Work, relationships, rest, eating, speaking, and serving can all be acts of worship. Believers can begin each day by offering themselves to God afresh.

It also encourages believers to remember God’s mercy. When obedience feels difficult, believers can reflect on all that God has done for them. Gratitude for mercy fuels a willing heart.

Finally, the verse reminds believers that worship is more than a Sunday activity. While gathering for worship is important, true worship continues throughout the week, in every place and situation.

### *Romans 12:2* — Transformed by the Renewing of Your Mind

> *“Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.”*
>
> — *Romans 12:2* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After calling believers to offer themselves as living sacrifices, Paul describes how this happens in daily life.

“*Don’t be conformed to this world*” (*v. 2*). “This world” refers to the present age, the way of thinking and living that is opposed to God. To be “conformed” means to be shaped by an outside mold, like clay pressed into a form. Without realizing it, people can be shaped by the values, priorities, and assumptions of the culture around them.

“*but be transformed by the renewing of your mind*” (*v. 2*). Instead of being shaped from the outside, believers are to be “transformed” from the inside. The Greek word is metamorphoo, from which we get “metamorphosis,” the change of a caterpillar into a butterfly. The same word describes Jesus’ transfiguration (*Matthew 17:2*). This transformation happens through “the renewing of your mind,” a new way of thinking shaped by God’s truth.

Notice that this is something God does in believers, as the passive “be transformed” suggests, but believers participate by allowing their minds to be renewed. This happens through Scripture, prayer, worship, and the work of the Holy Spirit.

“*so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God*” (*v. 2*). The purpose of a renewed mind is to discern and approve God’s will. “Prove” means to test and recognize. As believers’ minds are renewed, they increasingly understand what God wants. God’s will is “good,” beneficial; “well-pleasing,” delightful to Him; and “perfect,” complete and lacking nothing.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that the Christian life involves a battle for the mind. What people think shapes how they live. Paul writes, “*whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable, whatever things are just, whatever things are pure, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report: if there is any virtue and if there is anything worthy of praise, think about these things*” (*Philippians 4:8*).

It also shows that transformation is a process. Renewal is ongoing. Believers are continually being transformed as they grow in Christ. Paul writes that believers are “*transformed into the same image from glory to glory*” (*2 Corinthians 3:18*).

Finally, the verse shows that knowing God’s will is connected to transformation. Many believers want to know God’s will for specific decisions. Paul teaches that as minds are renewed, believers become more able to recognize God’s will in all things.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse challenges believers to examine what is shaping their minds. Media, entertainment, social media, advertising, and cultural trends can subtly conform believers to the world’s patterns. Believers can be intentional about what they allow to influence their thinking.

It also encourages believers to fill their minds with God’s truth. Reading and meditating on Scripture, praying, and worshiping help renew the mind. Believers can make these practices regular parts of their lives.

Finally, the verse encourages believers who want to know God’s will. The way to discern God’s will is not mainly through searching for signs, but through a renewed mind that understands God’s word and character. As believers grow, they will increasingly recognize what pleases God.

### *Romans 12:4–6* — Many Members, One Body

> *“For even as we have many members in one body, and all the members don’t have the same function, so we, who are many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another, having gifts differing according to the grace that was given to us: if prophecy, let’s prophesy according to the proportion of our faith;”*
>
> — *Romans 12:4–6* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had just urged believers not to think too highly of themselves but to think with sober judgment. Now he explains why: every believer is part of a larger body.

“*For even as we have many members in one body, and all the members don’t have the same function*” (*v. 4*). A human body has many parts, such as eyes, hands, feet, and ears, and each has a different role. The parts are different, but they work together.

“*so we, who are many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another*” (*v. 5*). The church is like a body. Believers are many, but they are united as one in Christ. Each believer belongs to the others. Believers are not independent individuals; they are connected and need one another.

“*having gifts differing according to the grace that was given to us*” (*v. 6*). God has given each believer different gifts. These gifts are given “according to the grace,” showing that they are not earned but given freely by God.

Paul then lists several gifts. Prophecy, speaking God’s message for building up the church, should be exercised “*according to the proportion of our faith*” (*v. 6*). Service should be given to serving. Teaching, encouraging (exhorting), giving, leading, and showing mercy should all be done wholeheartedly. Each gift has an appropriate attitude: “*he who gives, let him do it with generosity; he who rules, with diligence; he who shows mercy, with cheerfulness*” (*v. 8*).

This list is not complete. Paul lists other gifts in *1 Corinthians 12* and *Ephesians 4*. The point is that every believer has a gift, and every gift is important for the health of the body.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show the unity and diversity of the church. Believers are united in Christ, yet they are different from one another. This diversity is not a problem but a gift. Paul writes, “*The eye can’t tell the hand, “I have no need for you,” or again the head to the feet, “I have no need for you.”*” (*1 Corinthians 12:21*)

They also show that every believer has a role. No one is unimportant in the body of Christ. Every gift, whether public or private, is valuable. Peter writes, “*As each has received a gift, employ it in serving one another, as good managers of the grace of God in its various forms*” (*1 Peter 4:10*).

Finally, these verses show that gifts are for the good of others. God gives gifts not to make individuals impressive but to build up the body. Believers use their gifts in service to one another.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to discover and use their gifts. Every believer has been given gifts by God. Believers can pray, seek counsel, and try different forms of service to discover how God has gifted them.

They also encourage believers to value others’ gifts. Believers may be tempted to think their own gifts are more important, or to feel inferior to those with more visible gifts. Every gift matters. Believers can honor and appreciate the diverse gifts in their church.

Finally, these verses call believers to serve wholeheartedly. Whatever their gift, believers can use it with diligence, generosity, and cheerfulness, knowing they are serving the Lord and His people.

### *Romans 12:17–21* — Overcome Evil with Good

> *“Repay no one evil for evil. Respect what is honorable in the sight of all men. If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men. Don’t seek revenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to God’s wrath. For it is written, ‘Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay, says the Lord.’ Therefore ‘If your enemy is hungry, feed him. If he is thirsty, give him a drink; for in doing so, you will heap coals of fire on his head.’ Don’t be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.”*
>
> — *Romans 12:17–21* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had been describing genuine love among believers. Now he turns to how believers should respond to those who wrong them, including enemies and persecutors.

“*Repay no one evil for evil. Respect what is honorable in the sight of all men*” (*v. 17*). When someone harms them, believers must not take revenge. Instead, they are to do what everyone recognizes as right and honorable.

“*If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men*” (*v. 18*). Believers should seek peace with everyone. Paul recognizes that this is not always possible; others may refuse peace. But believers should do everything within their power to live peaceably.

“*Don’t seek revenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to God’s wrath. For it is written, “Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay, says the Lord.”*” (*v. 19*) Paul quotes *Deuteronomy 32:35*. Believers do not need to take revenge because God will bring justice. They can leave the matter in God’s hands. Notice that Paul calls them “beloved”; this is a word of tenderness to people who have been hurt.

“*Therefore “If your enemy is hungry, feed him. If he is thirsty, give him a drink; for in doing so, you will heap coals of fire on his head.”*” (*v. 20*) Paul quotes *Proverbs 25:21–22*. Instead of revenge, believers are to do good to their enemies, meeting their practical needs. “Heaping coals of fire on his head” probably means causing the enemy to feel burning shame and remorse, which may lead to repentance. Some connect it to an Egyptian ritual in which a person carried coals on their head as a sign of repentance.

“*Don’t be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good*” (*v. 21*). This is the summary. When believers repay evil with evil, evil wins, because it has turned them into the same kind of person. But when they respond with good, they defeat evil.

It is important to understand what these verses do not mean. They do not mean that believers must stay in abusive or dangerous situations, or that they should not seek protection or justice through proper means. In the next chapter, Paul teaches that governing authorities are God’s servants to punish wrongdoing (*13:4*). Refusing personal revenge is fully compatible with seeking safety, reporting crimes, and pursuing justice through lawful authorities.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses reflect the teaching and example of Jesus. Jesus taught, “*love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who mistreat you and persecute you*” (*Matthew 5:44*). On the cross, He prayed for those who crucified Him. Believers follow His example.

They also show trust in God’s justice. Believers can refuse revenge not because wrongdoing does not matter, but because God will judge rightly. Leaving vengeance to God is an act of faith.

Finally, these verses show the power of goodness. Evil is not overcome by more evil, but by good. This is the way of the cross: Jesus overcame evil by self-giving love.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses challenge believers to respond to wrongs with goodness rather than revenge. When someone insults, cheats, or harms them, believers can refuse to retaliate and instead seek ways to do good.

They also encourage believers to pursue peace. In families, workplaces, churches, and communities, believers can work to resolve conflicts and build peace, doing everything within their power.

Finally, these verses free believers from the burden of revenge. Holding on to bitterness and plotting revenge consumes people. Believers can entrust justice to God, and where appropriate to lawful authorities, and find freedom in forgiveness, while still taking wise steps to protect themselves and others from harm.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Romans 12* calls believers to respond to God’s mercy by offering their whole lives as living sacrifices. Worship is not limited to church services; it includes everything believers do with their bodies, time, and abilities. Believers can begin each day by offering themselves to God in gratitude for His mercy.

The chapter also calls believers to be transformed by the renewing of their minds rather than conformed to the world. What shapes their thinking shapes their lives. Believers can be intentional about filling their minds with God’s truth through Scripture, prayer, and worship, so that they can discern and delight in God’s will.

*Romans 12* teaches that every believer is part of one body with many members. Each has gifts given by grace, to be used for the good of others. Believers can discover and use their gifts, value the gifts of others, and serve with humility, generosity, diligence, and cheerfulness. Their love for one another should be genuine, warm, practical, and hospitable.

Finally, the chapter teaches believers how to respond to evil. They are to bless those who persecute them, refuse revenge, pursue peace as far as it depends on them, and do good even to enemies, leaving justice to God. This is not weakness but strength: overcoming evil with good, following the way of Jesus, while still seeking safety and lawful justice where needed.

## Chapter Prayer

Merciful God, in view of all Your mercies, I offer myself to You today as a living sacrifice. Take my body, my time, my abilities, and my desires, and use them for Your glory. Keep me from being conformed to the patterns of this world, and transform me by renewing my mind with Your truth, so that I may know and delight in Your good, pleasing, and perfect will. Help me to think of myself humbly and to use the gifts You have given me to serve others in Your church. Make my love genuine, warm, and practical. Teach me to rejoice in hope, endure in trouble, and keep praying. When others wrong me, help me to bless rather than curse, to refuse revenge, and to trust You for justice. Help me to overcome evil with good. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
