Romans · Chapter 13 of 16

# Romans — Chapter 13

Chapter Theme: Honoring Authorities, Owing Love, and Waking Up to the Day

[Read Romans 13 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/ROM13.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul teaches that governing authorities exist under God’s ordering and serve as His servants for the good of society, rewarding what is good and restraining evil, so believers should submit to them, pay taxes, and give respect and honor. The only debt believers should always carry is the debt of love, because love does no harm to a neighbor and fulfills the whole Law. Paul then urges believers to wake up, because the night is almost over and the day of salvation is near. They are to cast off the works of darkness, put on the armor of light, and clothe themselves with the Lord Jesus Christ.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Romans 13* continues Paul’s practical teaching about how believers should live in response to God’s mercy. In chapter 12, he described life within the church and how to respond to those who wrong us. Now he turns to life in society: relationships with government, financial obligations, love for neighbors, and living in light of Christ’s return.

When Paul wrote this letter, the Roman emperor was Nero. In the early years of his reign (A.D. 54–59), Nero’s government was considered relatively stable and fair. His persecution of Christians came later, after the fire of Rome in A.D. 64. Paul himself benefited from Roman law at times, appealing to his citizenship for protection. Yet Paul also knew that rulers could be unjust; he had been beaten by Roman magistrates in Philippi.

*Romans 13:1–7* has been one of the most debated passages in Christian history regarding the relationship between believers and government. It must be read alongside the whole of Scripture, including passages where God’s people rightly refused to obey rulers who commanded sin (*Exodus 1:17*; *Daniel 3*; 6; *Acts 4:19–20*; *5:29*), and *Revelation 13*, which portrays a government that has become beastly and persecutes God’s people.

### Submission to Governing Authorities (*13:1–7*)

Paul’s teaching on authority is studied below. He continues: “*Therefore he who resists the authority withstands the ordinance of God; and those who withstand will receive to themselves judgment*” (*v. 2*). Rebelling against legitimate authority in general is resisting God’s order.

“*For rulers are not a terror to the good work, but to the evil*” (*v. 3*). Paul describes the purpose of government: to encourage good and restrain evil. “*for he is a servant of God to you for good. But if you do that which is evil, be afraid, for he doesn’t bear the sword in vain; for he is a servant of God, an avenger for wrath to him who does evil*” (*v. 4*). The “sword” represents the government’s authority to punish wrongdoing. In chapter 12, Paul told believers not to take personal revenge but to leave it to God’s wrath (*12:19*). Here, he shows that one way God exercises justice in the present is through governing authorities.

“*Therefore you need to be in subjection, not only because of the wrath, but also for conscience’ sake*” (*v. 5*). Believers submit not only to avoid punishment, but because their conscience recognizes that God has established government.

“*For this reason you also pay taxes, for they are servants of God’s service, continually doing this very thing*” (*v. 6*). Paying taxes is part of honoring God’s order. Jesus said, “*Give therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's*” (*Matthew 22:21*). “*Therefore give everyone what you owe: if you owe taxes, pay taxes; if customs, then customs; if respect, then respect; if honor, then honor*” (*v. 7*).

### The Debt of Love (*13:8–10*)

Paul then turns from what believers owe to the government to what they owe everyone. This is studied below.

### Wake Up! The Day Is Near (*13:11–14*)

Paul’s final appeal is studied below in two parts. In between, he describes the kind of behavior that belongs to the night: “*Let’s walk properly, as in the day; not in reveling and drunkenness, not in sexual promiscuity and lustful acts, and not in strife and jealousy*” (*v. 13*). Notice that Paul places “strife and jealousy” alongside drunkenness and sexual immorality. Sins of attitude and relationship are as serious as sins of the body.

This passage has a famous place in church history. In A.D. 386, a young man named Augustine was struggling with his sinful lifestyle and his inability to change. Sitting in a garden in Milan, he heard a child’s voice chanting, “Take up and read.” He opened a copy of Paul’s letters and read *Romans 13:13–14*. He later wrote that he needed to read no further, because a light of peace seemed to flood his heart and the darkness of his doubt vanished. Augustine became one of the most influential Christian thinkers in history.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Romans 13:1* — No Authority Except from God

> *“Let every soul be in subjection to the higher authorities, for there is no authority except from God, and those who exist are ordained by God.”*
>
> — *Romans 13:1* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had been describing how believers should live: offering themselves to God, loving one another, and responding to evil with good. Now he addresses how believers should relate to the government.

“*Let every soul be in subjection to the higher authorities*” (*v. 1*). “Every soul” means every person, including believers. “Higher authorities” refers to governing officials, those with civil authority. To be “in subjection” means to recognize their authority and cooperate with them.

“*for there is no authority except from God*” (*v. 1*). Paul explains why. All authority ultimately comes from God. Governments exist because God has ordained that human society should have order. Even rulers who do not know God hold their positions under His sovereign permission. Jesus told Pilate, “*You would have no power at all against me, unless it were given to you from above*” (*John 19:11*).

“*and those who exist are ordained by God*” (*v. 1*). The existing authorities have been put in place by God’s ordering. This does not mean that God approves of everything rulers do. It means that the institution of government is part of God’s design for human society, and that God is sovereign over who holds power.

This teaching would have been important for the believers in Rome. Some might have thought that because they belonged to Christ’s kingdom, they had no obligations to earthly rulers. Others might have been tempted to join the Jewish revolutionary movements that were growing at the time. Paul teaches that believers should be good citizens.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that God is sovereign over all human authority. Daniel declared that God “*removes kings, and sets up kings*” (*Daniel 2:21*). Earthly rulers are not ultimate; they are accountable to God.

It also shows that government has a God-given purpose: to promote good and restrain evil (*13:3–4*). When governments fulfill this purpose, they serve God, whether they know it or not.

Finally, the verse must be read in the context of all Scripture. Submission to authorities is the general rule, but it has limits. When rulers command what God forbids, believers must obey God rather than human authorities (*Acts 5:29*). The Hebrew midwives disobeyed Pharaoh’s command to kill babies (*Exodus 1:17*), Daniel continued to pray despite the king’s decree (*Daniel 6*), and the apostles kept preaching when ordered to stop (*Acts 4:19–20*). Believers throughout history have rightly resisted governments that committed grave injustice. Even then, believers are called to act with respect and without hatred, accepting the consequences when necessary. Christians also hold different views on how far believers may go in resisting unjust governments, and on matters such as participation in military or political action.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to be good citizens. Believers can obey laws, pay taxes, respect officials, and contribute to the common good. Their faith should make them better members of society.

It also encourages believers to pray for those in authority. Paul writes, “*I exhort therefore, first of all, that petitions, prayers, intercessions, and givings of thanks be made for all men*” (*1 Timothy 2:1*), “*for kings and all who are in high places, that we may lead a tranquil and quiet life in all godliness and reverence*” (*1 Timothy 2:2*). Believers can pray for leaders regardless of their political views.

Finally, the verse reminds believers that their ultimate allegiance is to God. Earthly authorities are under God’s authority. When human commands conflict with God’s commands, believers must follow God. This calls for wisdom, courage, and humility.

### *Romans 13:8–10* — Love Fulfills the Law

> *“Owe no one anything, except to love one another; for he who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law. For the commandments, ‘You shall not commit adultery,’ ‘You shall not murder,’ ‘You shall not steal,’ ‘You shall not covet,’ and whatever other commandments there are, are all summed up in this saying, namely, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ Love doesn’t harm a neighbor. Love therefore is the fulfillment of the law.”*
>
> — *Romans 13:8–10* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had just told believers to give everyone what they owe: taxes, revenue, respect, and honor. Now he speaks of one debt that can never be fully paid.

“*Owe no one anything, except to love one another*” (*v. 8*). Believers should pay their debts and not leave obligations unpaid. But there is one debt they will always owe: love. No matter how much they love others, they can never say, “I have loved enough.” Love is an ongoing debt.

“*for he who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law*” (*v. 8*). Love fulfills what the Law requires. The purpose of God’s commands is love.

“*For the commandments, “You shall not commit adultery,” “You shall not murder,” “You shall not steal,” “You shall not covet,” and whatever other commandments there are, are all summed up in this saying, namely, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”*” (*v. 9*) Paul quotes several of the Ten Commandments that deal with relationships with others. All of them are summed up in the command from *Leviticus 19:18* to love one’s neighbor as oneself. Jesus taught the same: the whole Law hangs on love for God and love for neighbor (*Matthew 22:37–40*).

“*Love doesn’t harm a neighbor. Love therefore is the fulfillment of the law*” (*v. 10*). Love never does wrong to another person. Someone who truly loves will not commit adultery, murder, steal, or covet. Love naturally fulfills these commands, not because it is following rules, but because it seeks the good of others.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that love is the heart of God’s Law. The commandments are not arbitrary rules; they describe what love looks like. When believers love, they fulfill God’s purposes. Paul writes, “*For the whole law is fulfilled in one word, in this: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”*” (*Galatians 5:14*)

They also show that love is more than a feeling. Love is defined by action: it does no harm to a neighbor. It keeps promises, respects life, honors property, and is content rather than covetous.

Finally, these verses show how believers fulfill the Law without being “under the Law.” Believers are not saved by keeping the Law (*3:28*), but through the Spirit, they fulfill the Law’s righteous requirement (*8:4*) by loving others. Love, produced by the Spirit, accomplishes what rule-keeping alone never could.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses remind believers that they always owe love. Believers can ask each day how they can show love to those around them, in their families, workplaces, churches, and communities.

They also encourage believers to pay their financial debts responsibly. Paul’s words “owe no one anything” encourage believers to avoid unpaid obligations and to be honest and faithful in financial matters.

Finally, these verses give believers a simple test for their actions. Before acting, believers can ask whether their choice will harm their neighbor. Love does no harm. This principle can guide decisions in many areas of life.

### *Romans 13:11–12* — The Night Is Far Gone

> *“Do this, knowing the time, that it is already time for you to awaken out of sleep, for salvation is now nearer to us than when we first believed. The night is far gone, and the day is near. Let’s therefore throw off the deeds of darkness, and let’s put on the armor of light.”*
>
> — *Romans 13:11–12* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had been describing how believers should live: submitting to authorities, paying what they owe, and loving their neighbors. Now he gives an urgent reason to live this way.

“*Do this, knowing the time*” (*v. 11*). Believers should live with awareness of the time in which they live, the time between Christ’s first coming and His return.

“*that it is already time for you to awaken out of sleep*” (*v. 11*). Paul uses the image of sleep for spiritual carelessness or laziness. It is time to wake up, to be alert and active.

“*for salvation is now nearer to us than when we first believed*” (*v. 11*). “Salvation” here refers to the final completion of salvation at Christ’s return, when believers will be fully redeemed. Every day brings that day closer.

“*The night is far gone, and the day is near*” (*v. 12*). The present age is like night, a time of spiritual darkness. But the night is almost over. The day, the age to come, when Christ returns and God’s kingdom comes in fullness, is about to dawn.

“*Let’s therefore throw off the deeds of darkness, and let’s put on the armor of light*” (*v. 12*). Just as people take off their nightclothes and put on their daytime clothes in the morning, believers are to throw off sinful behaviors that belong to the darkness and put on “the armor of light.” Notice the word “armor.” Living in the light involves spiritual battle. Believers need protection. Paul describes this armor more fully in *Ephesians 6:10–18* and *1 Thessalonians 5:8*.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that the hope of Christ’s return should shape how believers live now. Jesus taught His disciples to be watchful and ready for His return (*Matthew 24:42–44*). John writes, “*Everyone who has this hope set on him purifies himself, even as he is pure*” (*1 John 3:3*).

They also show that believers belong to the day, even though they live in the night. Paul writes, “*You are all children of light, and children of the day*” (*1 Thessalonians 5:5*). Believers already live by the light of the coming age, even though the darkness has not fully passed.

Finally, these verses show the urgency of the Christian life. Paul was not speculating about dates. He was calling believers to live with readiness and seriousness, knowing that the Lord’s return could come at any time.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses call believers to wake up spiritually. It is possible for believers to become spiritually drowsy, going through the motions without real devotion. Paul’s words call them to alertness, prayer, and active faithfulness.

They also encourage believers to examine their lives for “deeds of darkness.” Believers can ask God to show them behaviors, habits, or attitudes that belong to the night, and to help them throw these off.

Finally, these verses give believers hope. The night is far gone, and the day is near. Whatever darkness believers face, it will not last forever. Christ is coming, and with Him the fullness of salvation.

### *Romans 13:14* — Put On the Lord Jesus Christ

> *“But put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, for its lusts.”*
>
> — *Romans 13:14* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had urged believers to throw off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light. He had listed behaviors that belong to the night: wild parties, drunkenness, sexual immorality, sensuality, quarreling, and jealousy. Now he gives the positive alternative.

“*But put on the Lord Jesus Christ*” (*v. 14*). Instead of clothing themselves with sinful behavior, believers are to clothe themselves with Christ. This is a powerful image. Just as people put on clothes that cover them and shape how they appear, believers are to “put on” Christ so that His character covers and shapes their lives.

In one sense, believers have already put on Christ. Paul writes, “*For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ*” (*Galatians 3:27*). But here Paul commands believers to put on Christ, showing that this is also an ongoing, daily action. Believers continually choose to live out their identity in Christ.

Notice the full title: “the Lord Jesus Christ.” He is Lord, the one who rules; Jesus, the Savior; and Christ, the Messiah. Putting on Christ means submitting to Him as Lord and reflecting His character.

“*and make no provision for the flesh, for its lusts*” (*v. 14*). “Make no provision” means do not plan for or make room for the desires of the sinful nature. Believers should not set up situations that make it easy to sin. Instead of thinking about how to satisfy sinful desires, they should avoid giving those desires opportunity.

This is the verse Augustine read in the garden in Milan, which led to his conversion.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that the Christian life is not only about avoiding sin but about becoming like Christ. Holiness is not mainly a list of things not to do; it is a positive likeness to Jesus. Paul writes elsewhere, “*Put on therefore, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, a heart of compassion, kindness, lowliness, humility, and perseverance*” (*Colossians 3:12*).

It also shows practical wisdom in fighting sin. “Make no provision for the flesh” means being proactive. Believers should avoid situations, habits, and influences that feed sinful desires. Jesus spoke of radical measures to avoid sin (*Matthew 5:29–30*).

Finally, the verse shows the transforming power of God’s word. One verse changed Augustine’s life and, through him, influenced the whole history of Christian thought. God’s word has power to change hearts.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to “put on” Christ each day. Believers can begin each morning by consciously choosing to live as Christ would, in their thoughts, words, and actions, asking for His help to reflect His character.

It also encourages believers to be wise about temptation. Believers can identify situations, places, or habits that make sin easier, and take steps to avoid them. This might mean changing routines, setting boundaries on media use, or avoiding certain environments.

Finally, the verse brings hope to those who feel trapped in sin. Augustine had struggled for years to change. One verse, through the power of God’s Spirit, set him free. Believers who struggle can turn to God’s word and trust Him to transform them.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Romans 13* teaches believers to honor governing authorities as part of God’s ordering of human society. Governments exist to promote good and restrain evil. Believers can be good citizens who obey laws, pay taxes, and show respect, while praying for those in authority. At the same time, believers recognize that their ultimate allegiance is to God, and that when human commands conflict with God’s commands, they must obey God.

The chapter also teaches that love is the one debt believers can never finish paying. Love fulfills the whole Law, because love does no harm to a neighbor. Believers can let love guide their actions in every relationship, asking how they can seek the good of others.

*Romans 13* calls believers to wake up. The night is far gone, and the day of Christ’s return is near. Believers can live with alertness and urgency, throwing off the deeds of darkness and putting on the armor of light. Sins of attitude, such as quarreling and jealousy, are as serious as sins of the body.

Finally, the chapter calls believers to put on the Lord Jesus Christ and make no provision for sinful desires. The Christian life is about becoming like Christ, clothed with His character. Believers can begin each day by choosing to live as Christ would, avoiding situations that feed temptation, and trusting God’s word and Spirit to transform them, as He transformed Augustine.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord God, You are sovereign over all authorities, and every ruler is accountable to You. Help me to be a good citizen, honoring those in authority, obeying just laws, and paying what I owe. I pray for the leaders of my nation and my community; give them wisdom and justice. Give me courage to obey You first whenever human commands conflict with Yours. Thank You that love fulfills the Law. Help me to pay the debt of love every day, doing no harm to my neighbor. Wake me from spiritual drowsiness, for the night is far gone and the day is near. Help me to throw off the deeds of darkness and to put on the armor of light. Today I put on the Lord Jesus Christ. Help me to make no provision for sinful desires, and transform me by Your word and Spirit. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Romans · Chapter 14 of 16

# Romans — Chapter 14

Chapter Theme: Welcoming One Another Across Differences of Conscience

[Read Romans 14 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/ROM14.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul addresses disagreements in the Roman church over food and special days, urging believers to welcome those who are weak in faith without arguing over opinions. Those who feel free should not look down on those with stricter consciences, and those with stricter consciences should not judge the free, because God has welcomed both, and each serves the Lord. Believers belong to the Lord in life and death, and each will give an account to God, so they must stop judging one another and instead avoid placing stumbling blocks before others. The kingdom of God is not about food and drink but righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit, so believers should pursue what builds others up.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Romans 14* deals with a practical problem in the church in Rome. The congregation included believers from different backgrounds who disagreed about certain practices. Some believers, probably mostly Jewish believers and Gentiles influenced by Jewish customs, felt they should avoid certain foods (perhaps meat that might have been offered to idols or that was not prepared according to Jewish law) and should observe special days such as the Sabbath and festivals. Others, probably mostly Gentile believers and Jewish believers like Paul who understood their freedom in Christ, felt free to eat anything and to treat all days alike.

Paul calls the more cautious group “weak in faith” and the freer group, implicitly, “strong” (*15:1*). By “weak,” he does not mean that their faith in Christ was weak or that they were less committed. He means that their consciences were not yet fully persuaded of the freedom they had in Christ in these particular matters. Paul himself identifies with the “strong” (*15:1*), yet he spends most of the chapter urging the strong to be patient and loving toward the weak.

These issues are what later Christians have called “disputable matters” or “matters of conscience,” areas where Scripture does not give a clear command and sincere believers may differ. Paul is not addressing clear moral issues, such as those he lists in 1:29–31 or 13:13. Distinguishing between disputable matters and clear moral commands requires wisdom.

### Accept One Another (*14:1–12*)

Paul’s opening command is studied below. He describes the two groups: “*One man has faith to eat all things, but he who is weak eats only vegetables*” (*v. 2*). Then he gives instructions to each: “*Don’t let him who eats despise him who doesn’t eat. Don’t let him who doesn’t eat judge him who eats, for God has accepted him*” (*v. 3*). The temptation for the “strong” was to look down on the weak as narrow-minded. The temptation for the “weak” was to judge the strong as unspiritual or careless. Both attitudes are wrong, because God has welcomed both.

“*Who are you who judge another’s servant? To his own lord he stands or falls. Yes, he will be made to stand, for God has power to make him stand*” (*v. 4*). Each believer is the Lord’s servant, accountable to Him, not to other believers.

Paul then addresses special days: “*One man esteems one day as more important. Another esteems every day alike. Let each man be fully assured in his own mind*” (*v. 5*). In disputable matters, each believer should act with a clear conscience. “*He who observes the day, observes it to the Lord; and he who does not observe the day, to the Lord he does not observe it. He who eats, eats to the Lord, for he gives God thanks. He who doesn’t eat, to the Lord he doesn’t eat, and gives God thanks*” (*v. 6*). Both groups were trying to honor the Lord. Paul’s teaching on belonging to the Lord and on accountability is studied below.

### Don’t Cause Others to Stumble (*14:13–23*)

Paul then turns to the responsibility of the strong. “*I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean of itself; except that to him who considers anything to be unclean, to him it is unclean*” (*v. 14*). Paul agrees with the strong: no food is unclean in itself (*Mark 7:19*; *Acts 10:15*). But a person who believes something is wrong would sin against their own conscience by doing it.

“*Yet if because of food your brother is grieved, you walk no longer in love. Don’t destroy with your food him for whom Christ died*” (*v. 15*). If a strong believer’s freedom causes a weaker believer to stumble, the strong believer is not acting in love. Christ died for that weaker believer; how can a strong believer harm them over something as unimportant as food? Paul’s statement about the kingdom of God is studied below.

“*Don’t overthrow God’s work for food’s sake*” (*v. 20*). The “work of God” here is the weaker believer, whom God is building up. “*It is good to not eat meat, drink wine, nor do anything by which your brother stumbles, is offended, or is made weak*” (*v. 21*). Love is willing to give up freedom for the sake of others.

“*Do you have faith? Have it to yourself before God. Happy is he who doesn’t judge himself in that which he approves*” (*v. 22*). Strong believers can enjoy their freedom privately before God, without flaunting it in ways that harm others. “*But he who doubts is condemned if he eats, because it isn’t of faith; and whatever is not of faith is sin*” (*v. 23*). If someone does something while believing it is wrong, they sin, because they are acting against their conscience. Acting in faith means acting with confidence that God approves.

### A Note on the Doxology (*14:24–26*)

In the World English Bible, the closing doxology of Romans appears at the end of chapter 14 (*14:24–26*). In many other Bibles, these words appear at the end of chapter 16, as verses 25–27. Ancient manuscripts differ on where this doxology belongs; some place it after chapter 14, others after chapter 16, others in both places, and others after chapter 15. The words themselves are a beautiful hymn of praise: “*to the only wise God, through Jesus Christ, to whom be the glory forever! Amen*” (*v. 26*). The doxology praises God, who is able to strengthen believers through the gospel and who has revealed the mystery, kept hidden for ages, that all nations would come to the obedience of faith.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Romans 14:1* — Accept the One Who Is Weak in Faith

> *“Now accept one who is weak in faith, but not for disputes over opinions.”*
>
> — *Romans 14:1* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The church in Rome was made up of believers from different backgrounds. Some were Jewish and had grown up observing the food laws and the Sabbath. Others were Gentiles who had never followed those customs. Disagreements arose about what foods believers could eat and which days they should treat as special.

Paul begins his response with a clear command: “*Now accept one who is weak in faith*” (*v. 1*). “Accept” means to welcome, to receive warmly into fellowship. It is the same word used in 15:7, where Paul writes, “*Therefore accept one another, even as Christ also accepted you*” (*Romans 15:7*). Believers should welcome one another as Christ has welcomed them.

“One who is weak in faith” refers to a believer whose conscience is not fully persuaded of their freedom in Christ in certain matters. In this context, the “weak” were those who felt they had to avoid certain foods or observe special days. Their faith in Christ was real, but they had not yet understood all the implications of their freedom.

“*but not for disputes over opinions*” (*v. 1*). Believers should welcome the weak, but not in order to argue with them about their convictions. They should not welcome them only to try to change their minds or criticize their scruples. True welcome accepts people as they are.

This verse is the foundation for the rest of the chapter. Before Paul addresses the issues themselves, he establishes the priority of welcome.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reflects the welcoming heart of Christ. Jesus welcomed people of all kinds: tax collectors, sinners, the sick, the poor, children, and outcasts. His church is called to welcome as He did.

It also shows the importance of distinguishing between essential and non-essential matters. The gospel itself, salvation by grace through faith in Christ, is essential. But many practices, preferences, and opinions are matters where believers may differ. Wise believers learn to recognize the difference. A well-known saying, often attributed to early Christian writers, expresses it: “In essentials, unity; in non-essentials, liberty; in all things, charity.”

Finally, the verse shows that unity does not require uniformity. Believers do not need to agree on every question in order to be one in Christ. The church can include people with different convictions on disputable matters, united by their common faith and love.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse calls believers to welcome fellow Christians who see things differently. Believers today may disagree about matters such as styles of worship, alcohol, holidays, entertainment, diet, schooling choices, or other questions where Scripture does not give a clear command. Believers can welcome one another without requiring agreement on every point.

It also warns believers against using fellowship as an opportunity to argue. Some believers welcome others only to correct their opinions. Paul calls for genuine acceptance that does not quarrel over disputable matters.

Finally, the verse encourages humility. Believers who consider themselves “strong” may be tempted to look down on those with stricter consciences. Believers who are more cautious may be tempted to judge those who feel free. Both are called to welcome one another in love.

### *Romans 14:7–8* — We Are the Lord’s

> *“For none of us lives to himself, and none dies to himself. For if we live, we live to the Lord. Or if we die, we die to the Lord. If therefore we live or die, we are the Lord’s.”*
>
> — *Romans 14:7–8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had been explaining that believers who disagree about food and special days are all trying to honor the Lord. One person eats to the Lord and gives thanks; another abstains to the Lord and gives thanks. Both are living for Christ.

Now Paul states the principle behind this: “*For none of us lives to himself, and none dies to himself*” (*v. 7*). No believer lives only for themselves. Their lives are not their own. Everything they do, including their choices about food and days, is lived in relationship to the Lord.

“*For if we live, we live to the Lord. Or if we die, we die to the Lord*” (*v. 8*). Both life and death belong to the Lord. Believers live to honor Him, and when they die, they die belonging to Him.

“*If therefore we live or die, we are the Lord’s*” (*v. 8*). This is the heart of the matter. Believers belong to Christ. Whether they are strong or weak in conscience, whether they eat or abstain, whether they live or die, they are His.

In the next verse, Paul explains why: “*For to this end Christ died, rose, and lived again, that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living*” (*v. 9*). Christ’s death and resurrection established His lordship over all.

Because every believer belongs to the Lord, no believer has the right to judge another believer’s service. Each answers to Christ.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that the Christian life is centered on Christ’s lordship. Believers do not belong to themselves. Paul writes elsewhere, “*You are not your own*” (*1 Corinthians 6:19*), “*for you were bought with a price*” (*1 Corinthians 6:20*).

They also bring deep comfort about death. For believers, death is not the end of their belonging to Christ. They die “to the Lord” and remain His. Paul writes, “*For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain*” (*Philippians 1:21*).

Finally, these verses show that Christ’s lordship unites believers. Despite their differences, all believers belong to the same Lord. This shared belonging is the foundation for mutual acceptance.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses invite believers to live every part of life for the Lord. Eating, working, resting, relating, and choosing can all be done in honor of Christ. Believers can ask in each situation how they can live “to the Lord.”

They also bring peace in the face of death. Believers who fear death can remember that whether they live or die, they belong to the Lord. Death cannot take them from His care.

Finally, these verses encourage believers to respect one another’s convictions. Since every believer belongs to the Lord and lives for Him, believers can trust that others who differ from them are also seeking to honor Christ.

### *Romans 14:12–13* — Each Will Give Account; Do Not Cause Stumbling

> *“So then each one of us will give account of himself to God. Therefore let’s not judge one another any more, but judge this rather, that no man put a stumbling block in his brother’s way, or an occasion for falling.”*
>
> — *Romans 14:12–13* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had been urging believers not to judge or despise one another over disputable matters. He had reminded them that each believer belongs to the Lord. Then he pointed to the future: “*For we will all stand before the judgment seat of Christ*” (*v. 10*). Every believer will stand before Christ. Paul quoted *Isaiah 45:23*: every knee will bow and every tongue will confess to God.

“*So then each one of us will give account of himself to God*” (*v. 12*). Each believer will give an account “of himself,” not of others. Believers are not responsible for judging other believers’ service; they are responsible for their own.

This does not mean believers should never correct one another about clear sin; elsewhere Paul commands loving correction (*Galatians 6:1*). But in disputable matters, each believer is accountable to God for their own convictions and choices.

“*Therefore let’s not judge one another any more*” (*v. 13*). Since God is the judge, believers should stop judging one another over these matters.

“*but judge this rather, that no man put a stumbling block in his brother’s way, or an occasion for falling*” (*v. 13*). Paul uses a play on words. Instead of “judging” others, believers should “judge” or decide to avoid causing others to stumble. A “stumbling block” is something that causes another person to trip and fall, in this case, to sin against their conscience or to fall away from faith.

This verse shifts the focus from the weak to the strong. Strong believers should be careful not to use their freedom in ways that harm weaker believers.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that accountability to God should shape how believers treat one another. Knowing that each person will stand before Christ humbles believers and frees them from the burden of judging others.

They also show that love limits freedom. Paul writes elsewhere, “*But be careful that by no means does this liberty of yours become a stumbling block to the weak*” (*1 Corinthians 8:9*). True freedom is not insisting on one’s rights but using freedom in love.

Finally, these verses show that the spiritual welfare of others matters. Believers are not isolated individuals. Their choices affect fellow believers. Love considers how one’s actions will affect others’ faith.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to focus on their own accountability to God. Rather than evaluating others’ choices in disputable matters, believers can examine their own hearts and lives.

They also call believers to consider how their freedom affects others. A believer may be free to do something, but if it would cause a fellow believer to stumble, love may call them to set it aside, at least in that person’s presence.

Finally, these verses remind believers that they will stand before Christ. This truth can motivate them to live faithfully, to treat others with grace, and to leave judgment in God’s hands.

### *Romans 14:17–19* — Righteousness, Peace, and Joy in the Holy Spirit

> *“for God’s Kingdom is not eating and drinking, but righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. For he who serves Christ in these things is acceptable to God and approved by men. So then, let’s follow after things which make for peace, and things by which we may build one another up.”*
>
> — *Romans 14:17–19* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had been urging strong believers not to use their freedom in ways that harm weaker believers. He had said that if a believer’s eating grieves a brother, that believer is no longer walking in love. Now he puts the issue in perspective.

“*for God’s Kingdom is not eating and drinking*” (*v. 17*). The kingdom of God, God’s rule in the lives of His people, is not mainly about food and drink. These are secondary matters. Believers should not let them become the center of their faith or the cause of division.

“*but righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit*” (*v. 17*). The kingdom is about “righteousness,” right relationship with God and right living; “peace,” harmony with God and with one another; and “joy,” the deep gladness the Spirit gives. All of these come from the Holy Spirit. These are the things that truly matter.

“*For he who serves Christ in these things is acceptable to God and approved by men*” (*v. 18*). Those who serve Christ by pursuing righteousness, peace, and joy please God and earn the respect of others.

“*So then, let’s follow after things which make for peace, and things by which we may build one another up*” (*v. 19*). Believers are called to actively pursue peace and mutual upbuilding. “Build up” means to strengthen, like constructing a building. Believers should seek what strengthens one another’s faith rather than what tears it down.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show the true priorities of God’s kingdom. Religious people have often focused on outward practices, such as food, days, and rituals, while neglecting the weightier matters. Jesus criticized those who tithed spices but neglected “*the weightier matters of the law: justice, mercy, and faith*” (*Matthew 23:23*).

They also show the work of the Holy Spirit in the community. Righteousness, peace, and joy are the fruit of the Spirit. When the Spirit is at work, the church is marked by these qualities.

Finally, these verses show the importance of building up the church. Paul repeatedly emphasizes edification (*1 Corinthians 14:12*; *Ephesians 4:12*, 29). Believers’ words and actions should strengthen others, not weaken them.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses help believers keep perspective. Many conflicts in churches are over secondary matters. Believers can ask whether a disagreement truly concerns the gospel, or whether it is about preferences. The kingdom is about righteousness, peace, and joy, not about secondary matters.

They also encourage believers to pursue peace. Peace does not happen automatically; it requires effort. Believers can take steps to resolve conflicts, overlook minor offenses, and seek harmony.

Finally, these verses call believers to build one another up. Believers can encourage, support, and strengthen fellow believers through their words and actions, asking whether their choices will help or hinder others’ faith.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Romans 14* calls believers to welcome one another across differences of conscience. In matters where Scripture does not give clear commands, sincere believers may disagree. Believers are called to accept one another without arguing over opinions, neither looking down on those with stricter consciences nor judging those who feel free.

The chapter also reminds believers that they belong to the Lord in life and in death. Each believer lives for Christ and will give an account to Him. This truth frees believers from judging one another and calls them to focus on their own faithfulness. It also brings comfort: in life and in death, believers are the Lord’s.

*Romans 14* teaches that love limits freedom. Strong believers may be free to do certain things, but if their freedom would cause a weaker believer to stumble, love calls them to set it aside. Believers can consider how their choices affect others and avoid placing stumbling blocks in their path.

Finally, the chapter keeps believers focused on what matters most. The kingdom of God is not about food and drink but righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. Believers can pursue what makes for peace and builds others up, refusing to let secondary matters divide the body of Christ, while still standing firm on the clear teachings of the gospel.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for welcoming me into Your family. Help me to welcome others as You have welcomed me, especially those who see things differently than I do. Keep me from looking down on those whose consciences are stricter than mine, and from judging those who feel free where I do not. Thank You that in life and in death I belong to You. Remind me that I will give an account to You for my own life, and free me from the burden of judging others. Teach me to use my freedom in love, never placing a stumbling block in a brother’s or sister’s way. Help me to remember that Your kingdom is righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. Make me a person who pursues peace and builds others up. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Romans · Chapter 15 of 16

# Romans — Chapter 15

Chapter Theme: Welcome One Another as Christ Welcomed You, and Abound in Hope

[Read Romans 15 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/ROM15.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul calls the strong to bear with the weaknesses of the weak and to please their neighbors for their good, following the example of Christ, who did not please Himself. The Scriptures were written to give endurance, encouragement, and hope, and Paul prays that the church will live in harmony and glorify God with one voice. He urges Jews and Gentiles to welcome one another as Christ welcomed them, showing from Scripture that Christ came to confirm God’s promises to Israel and to bring the Gentiles to praise God. Paul prays that the God of hope will fill them with joy and peace. He then explains his ministry as a priestly service among the Gentiles, his plans to visit Rome on his way to Spain after delivering a gift to Jerusalem, and asks for their prayers.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Romans 15* completes Paul’s discussion of the “strong” and the “weak” begun in chapter 14, and then moves into the conclusion of the letter. Paul shares his plans, explains the purpose of his ministry, and asks for prayer. The chapter shows the heart of a pastor and missionary: deeply concerned for unity in the church, passionate about reaching those who have never heard of Christ, and humbly dependent on the prayers of others.

### Bearing with the Weak (*15:1–6*)

Paul’s call to the strong, grounded in the example of Christ, is studied below. His teaching on the purpose of Scripture is also studied below.

Paul then prays: “*Now the God of perseverance and of encouragement grant you to be of the same mind with one another according to Christ Jesus*” (*v. 5*), “*that with one accord you may with one mouth glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ*” (*v. 6*). Unity is not merely for the church’s comfort; it is for God’s glory. When believers who differ in background and conviction praise God together, they display His power to unite people in Christ.

### Christ, Servant of Jews and Gentiles (*15:7–13*)

Paul’s command to welcome one another is studied below. He explains that “*Christ has been made a servant of the circumcision for the truth of God, that he might confirm the promises given to the fathers*” (*v. 8*), “*and that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy*” (*v. 9*). Jesus came as a Jew and ministered mainly to Jews, fulfilling God’s promises to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. And through Him, the Gentiles are brought to praise God for His mercy.

Paul supports this with four Old Testament quotations, drawn from all parts of the Hebrew Scriptures: the Law, the Prophets, and the Writings. “*Therefore I will give praise to you among the Gentiles and sing to your name*” (*v. 9*) (*Psalm 18:49*; *2 Samuel 22:50*). “*Rejoice, you Gentiles, with his people*” (*v. 10*) (*Deuteronomy 32:43*). “*Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles! Let all the peoples praise him*” (*v. 11*) (*Psalm 117:1*). “*There will be the root of Jesse, he who arises to rule over the Gentiles; in him the Gentiles will hope*” (*v. 12*) (*Isaiah 11:10*). Jesse was the father of David; the “*root of Jesse*” (*Isaiah 11:10*) is the Messiah from David’s line. The whole Old Testament anticipates the day when Gentiles would join Israel in praising God.

Paul’s prayer for hope is studied below.

### Paul’s Ministry to the Gentiles (*15:14–21*)

Paul expresses confidence in the Roman believers: “*I myself am also persuaded about you, my brothers, that you yourselves are full of goodness, filled with all knowledge, able also to admonish others*” (*v. 14*). He has written boldly as a reminder, because of the grace God gave him “*that I should be a servant of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles, serving as a priest of the Good News of God, that the offering up of the Gentiles might be made acceptable, sanctified by the Holy Spirit*” (*v. 16*). Paul uses priestly language. Just as a priest offered sacrifices to God, Paul’s ministry was like presenting the Gentiles themselves as an offering to God, made holy by the Holy Spirit.

Paul boasts only in what Christ has done through him: “*For I will not dare to speak of any things except those which Christ worked through me for the obedience of the Gentiles, by word and deed*” (*v. 18*), “*in the power of signs and wonders, in the power of God’s Spirit; so that from Jerusalem and around as far as to Illyricum, I have fully preached the Good News of Christ*” (*v. 19*). Illyricum was a Roman province on the eastern coast of the Adriatic Sea, roughly modern-day Albania and the former Yugoslavia. Paul had planted churches in a vast arc stretching about 1,400 miles.

Paul’s guiding principle: “*yes, making it my aim to preach the Good News, not where Christ was already named, that I might not build on another’s foundation*” (*v. 20*). Paul was a pioneer. He wanted to take the gospel to places where people had never heard of Christ. He quotes *Isaiah 52:15*: “*They will see, to whom no news of him came. They who haven’t heard will understand*” (*v. 21*).

### Paul’s Travel Plans (*15:22–33*)

Paul had often been prevented from visiting Rome because he was busy preaching in new areas. But now that his work in the eastern Mediterranean was complete, he planned to visit Rome on his way to Spain. “*whenever I travel to Spain, I will come to you. For I hope to see you on my journey, and to be helped on my way there by you*” (*v. 24*). Spain was at the western edge of the known world. Paul hoped the Roman church would become a base of support for his mission there.

But first, Paul was going to Jerusalem with the collection from the churches of Macedonia and Achaia for the poor believers there. “*Yes, it has been their good pleasure, and they are their debtors. For if the Gentiles have been made partakers of their spiritual things, they owe it to them also to serve them in material things*” (*v. 27*). The gift expressed the unity of Jewish and Gentile believers.

Paul asked for prayer: “*Now I beg you, brothers, by our Lord Jesus Christ and by the love of the Spirit, that you strive together with me in your prayers to God for me*” (*v. 30*). The word “strive” suggests an athlete straining or a soldier fighting. Prayer is hard work. Paul asked them to pray that he would be rescued from unbelievers in Judea, that his gift would be accepted by the Jerusalem believers, and that he would come to Rome with joy.

God answered these prayers, though not in the way Paul expected. He was arrested in Jerusalem, but his life was preserved (*Acts 21–23*). He did come to Rome, but as a prisoner (*Acts 28*). Whether he ever reached Spain is uncertain; some early Christian writers suggest that he did, after being released from his first Roman imprisonment. Paul’s plans were held in God’s hands, as all believers’ plans are.

The chapter ends with a blessing: “*Now the God of peace be with you all. Amen*” (*v. 33*).

## Important Verses Explained

### *Romans 15:1–3* — Christ Did Not Please Himself

> *“Now we who are strong ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak, and not to please ourselves. Let each one of us please his neighbor for that which is good, to be building him up. For even Christ didn’t please himself. But, as it is written, ‘The reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me.’”*
>
> — *Romans 15:1–3* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had been addressing disagreements in the Roman church between the “strong,” who felt free to eat anything and treat all days alike, and the “weak,” whose consciences led them to avoid certain foods and observe special days. In chapter 14, he urged both groups to stop judging and despising each other. Now he speaks especially to the strong.

“*Now we who are strong ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak, and not to please ourselves*” (*v. 1*). Paul includes himself among the strong. He agreed that believers are free in these matters. But strength brings responsibility. The strong should “bear” the weaknesses of the weak, carrying their burdens patiently, like someone helping a person who cannot walk alone. They should not insist on their own preferences or rights.

“*Let each one of us please his neighbor for that which is good, to be building him up*” (*v. 2*). Instead of pleasing themselves, believers should seek to please their neighbors. This does not mean flattering people or doing whatever others want. It means seeking their “good,” their true benefit, and “building them up” in faith.

“*For even Christ didn’t please himself*” (*v. 3*). Paul gives the ultimate example: Christ. Jesus did not live to please Himself. He came to serve, to give His life for others. He set aside His own rights and comfort for the sake of others.

“*But, as it is written, “The reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me.”*” (*v. 3*) Paul quotes *Psalm 69:9*. In this psalm, a righteous sufferer says that the insults directed at God fell on him. Paul applies it to Christ, who bore the insults and hostility of those who rejected God. Christ took on suffering for the sake of others. If He did not please Himself, His followers should not insist on pleasing themselves.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that Christian strength is expressed in service. In the world, the strong often use their strength to dominate others. In Christ’s kingdom, the strong use their strength to support the weak. Paul writes, “*Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ*” (*Galatians 6:2*).

They also show that Christ is the pattern for Christian behavior. Paul repeatedly points to Christ’s example of self-giving love. He writes to the Philippians, “*each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others*” (*Philippians 2:4*), and then describes how Christ humbled Himself.

Finally, these verses show that love seeks the good of others, not merely their approval. Pleasing one’s neighbor “for that which is good” means caring about what truly helps them, which sometimes means gently challenging them, but always with love.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses challenge believers who are mature in faith to be patient with those who are still growing. Strong believers can set aside their own preferences to support others, rather than insisting on their freedom.

They also encourage believers to ask, “How can I build up others?” rather than “What do I want?” In relationships at home, at church, and at work, believers can look for ways to strengthen and encourage others.

Finally, these verses call believers to follow Christ’s example. When believers are tempted to please themselves, they can remember that Christ did not please Himself but gave His life for others.

### *Romans 15:4* — Written for Our Learning

> *“For whatever things were written before were written for our learning, that through perseverance and through encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope.”*
>
> — *Romans 15:4* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had just quoted *Psalm 69:9* to show that Christ did not please Himself. Now he explains why he quotes the Old Testament so often.

“*For whatever things were written before were written for our learning*” (*v. 4*). The Scriptures written “before,” the Old Testament, were written to teach believers. They are not merely ancient history or documents for another people. They were written with later readers in mind, including Christians.

“*that through perseverance and through encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope*” (*v. 4*). The Scriptures produce two things in believers: “perseverance,” the ability to endure difficulty, and “encouragement,” comfort and strength. Through these, believers have “hope.”

How do the Scriptures do this? They show how God has been faithful to His people throughout history. They tell of people like Abraham, Joseph, Moses, Ruth, David, and the prophets who trusted God through hardship. They record God’s promises and their fulfillment. When believers read these stories and promises, they are encouraged to endure and to hope.

This verse shows that the Old Testament remains valuable for Christians. While believers are not under the Law of Moses as a way of salvation, the Old Testament is still God’s word, given for their instruction. Paul writes elsewhere that the experiences of Israel “*were written for our admonition*” (*1 Corinthians 10:11*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals the purpose of Scripture: to give hope. God’s word is not merely information; it is a source of strength and encouragement for life. Paul writes to Timothy that all Scripture is inspired by God and is useful for teaching, correction, and training in righteousness (*2 Timothy 3:16–17*).

It also shows the unity of the Bible. The Old and New Testaments belong together. The Old Testament points to Christ, and the New Testament shows its fulfillment. Christians read the whole Bible as one story of God’s faithfulness.

Finally, the verse shows that hope is connected to God’s word. When believers feel hopeless, one of the best things they can do is turn to Scripture. God speaks through His word to renew hope.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to read the Old Testament. Some believers focus only on the New Testament, but the Old Testament was also written for their learning. Its stories, poetry, prophecies, and wisdom can teach and encourage them.

It also encourages believers to turn to Scripture in hard times. When believers face trials, they can read the stories of those who trusted God before them and the promises God has made. Scripture can give them endurance and hope.

Finally, the verse invites believers to read Scripture with expectation. God’s word is meant to produce hope. Believers can come to the Bible expecting God to speak, encourage, and strengthen them.

### *Romans 15:7* — Accept One Another as Christ Accepted You

> *“Therefore accept one another, even as Christ also accepted you, to the glory of God.”*
>
> — *Romans 15:7* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had been urging the strong and the weak in the Roman church to live in harmony. He had prayed that they would glorify God with one voice. Now he gives a clear command that summarizes everything he has said since 14:1.

“*Therefore accept one another*” (*v. 7*). “Accept” means to receive, to welcome, to bring into fellowship. This is the same word Paul used in 14:1: “accept one who is weak in faith.” Now he applies it to everyone: “one another.” Both strong and weak, Jewish and Gentile believers, are to welcome each other.

“*even as Christ also accepted you*” (*v. 7*). The standard and motive for welcome is Christ’s welcome. How did Christ receive them? Freely, by grace, while they were still sinners (*5:8*). He did not wait for them to become perfect or to agree on every question. He welcomed them as they were and began to transform them. Believers are to welcome one another in the same way.

“*to the glory of God*” (*v. 7*). The purpose of this mutual welcome is God’s glory. When believers welcome one another across differences, they display God’s grace and bring Him glory.

In the following verses, Paul explains how Christ welcomed both Jews and Gentiles. He came as a servant to the Jews, to confirm God’s promises to their ancestors, and He brought the Gentiles to glorify God for His mercy. Christ’s welcome reaches across every division.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that Christ’s welcome is the foundation of Christian community. Believers belong together because Christ has received each of them. They did not earn their place; they were welcomed by grace. This truth makes it impossible for any believer to look down on another.

It also shows that the church is meant to display God’s glory. When people from different backgrounds, cultures, and convictions welcome one another in love, the world sees the power of the gospel. Jesus prayed that His followers would be one “*that the world may believe that you sent me*” (*John 17:21*).

Finally, the verse shows that welcome is active. It is not enough to tolerate others; believers are to welcome them, embracing them as family. This involves warmth, hospitality, and genuine love.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse calls believers to welcome people who are different from them. Churches often divide along lines of culture, age, class, politics, or preferences. Believers can intentionally welcome those who are different, as Christ welcomed them.

It also reminds believers of their own welcome. When believers are tempted to judge or exclude others, they can remember how Christ received them: freely, graciously, and while they were still sinners.

Finally, the verse invites believers to see their welcome of others as an act of worship. When they receive one another in love, they bring glory to God. Hospitality, kindness, and inclusion are ways of honoring Him.

### *Romans 15:13* — The God of Hope

> *“Now may the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, that you may abound in hope in the power of the Holy Spirit.”*
>
> — *Romans 15:13* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had just quoted four Old Testament passages showing that God always intended for the Gentiles to praise Him alongside Israel. The last quotation, from Isaiah, ended with the words, “in him the Gentiles will hope.” Now Paul offers a prayer for his readers.

“*Now may the God of hope*” (*v. 13*). Paul describes God as “the God of hope.” God is the source of hope. He gives hope, and He is the object of hope. Believers’ hope rests in Him.

“*fill you with all joy and peace in believing*” (*v. 13*). Paul prays that God would fill them with “all joy and peace.” These are gifts of God, not merely feelings people create for themselves. And they come “in believing,” through faith. As believers trust God, He fills them with joy and peace.

“*that you may abound in hope*” (*v. 13*). The result is that believers would “abound,” overflow, in hope. Not just a little hope, but hope that spills over.

“*in the power of the Holy Spirit*” (*v. 13*). This is the work of the Holy Spirit. Hope is not produced by positive thinking or favorable circumstances. It is the Spirit’s work in believers’ hearts.

This beautiful prayer forms a fitting conclusion to the main teaching section of Romans. After discussing sin, justification, new life, God’s plan for Israel, and practical living, Paul prays that believers would be filled with joy, peace, and overflowing hope.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that hope is central to the Christian life. Paul has spoken of hope throughout Romans: Abraham’s hope against hope (*4:18*), the hope of glory (*5:2*), hope that does not disappoint (*5:5*), and the hope of creation’s renewal (*8:20–25*). Christian hope is confident expectation based on God’s promises.

It also shows that joy, peace, and hope come through faith. Believers do not produce these qualities by effort alone. As they trust God, He fills them. Faith is the channel through which God’s blessings flow.

Finally, the verse shows the work of the Trinity. The “God of hope” (the Father) fills believers with joy and peace as they believe (in Christ), so that they abound in hope “in the power of the Holy Spirit.” Father, Son, and Spirit work together to bring hope.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse is a prayer believers can pray for themselves and others. When believers feel discouraged, anxious, or hopeless, they can ask the God of hope to fill them with joy and peace.

It also encourages believers to trust God more deeply. Joy and peace come “in believing.” When believers focus on God’s promises and trust Him, they experience His joy and peace even in difficult circumstances.

Finally, the verse encourages believers to depend on the Holy Spirit. Hope is not something believers can manufacture. They can ask the Spirit to fill them with hope and to make that hope overflow to others.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Romans 15* calls the strong to bear with the weak and to seek the good of their neighbors rather than pleasing themselves. Christ is the ultimate example: He did not please Himself but bore the insults meant for God. Believers who are mature in faith can use their strength to support and build up others, setting aside their own preferences when love requires it.

The chapter also reminds believers that the Scriptures were written for their instruction, to give them endurance, encouragement, and hope. Believers can read the whole Bible, including the Old Testament, expecting God to strengthen them through it.

*Romans 15* calls believers to welcome one another as Christ has welcomed them. Christ came as a servant to Israel and brought the Gentiles to praise God for His mercy. Believers can welcome people of every background into their fellowship, and in doing so, bring glory to God. Paul’s prayer that the God of hope would fill believers with joy and peace reminds them that hope comes from God, through faith, by the power of the Spirit.

Finally, the chapter shows Paul’s heart for mission and his dependence on prayer. He longed to preach Christ where He had not been named, and he asked the Roman believers to strive together with him in prayer. Believers can share Paul’s passion for those who have never heard the gospel, support missionary work, and join in earnest prayer for those who carry the good news.

## Chapter Prayer

God of hope, fill me with all joy and peace as I trust in You, so that I may overflow with hope by the power of the Holy Spirit. Lord Jesus, You did not please Yourself but bore the reproaches meant for God. Help me to follow Your example, bearing with the weaknesses of others and seeking their good. Thank You for the Scriptures, written for my learning; give me endurance and encouragement through Your word. Thank You for welcoming me by Your grace. Help me to welcome others as You have welcomed me, for the glory of God. Give me Paul’s passion for those who have never heard of You, and teach me to pray earnestly for those who carry Your gospel to the ends of the earth. God of peace, be with me and with all Your people. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
