Romans · Chapter 16 of 16

# Romans — Chapter 16

Chapter Theme: A Family of Faithful Servants and a Final Warning

[Read Romans 16 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/ROM16.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul closes his letter by commending Phoebe, a servant of the church in Cenchreae who likely carried the letter, and by greeting a remarkable list of believers in Rome: men and women, Jews and Gentiles, slaves and free, many of whom labored hard in the Lord. Among them are Prisca and Aquila, who risked their lives for Paul, and Andronicus and Junia, notable among the apostles. Paul warns the church to watch out for those who cause divisions with smooth talk, urges them to be wise about good and innocent about evil, and promises that the God of peace will soon crush Satan under their feet. Greetings from Paul’s companions and a blessing of grace complete the letter.

## Chapter Background and Story

Many readers skip *Romans 16* because it seems to be just a list of names. But this chapter offers a rare and beautiful window into the life of the early church. After fifteen chapters of profound theology, Paul shows that the gospel creates a real community of people who love and serve one another. The names reveal a church that was diverse in background, gender, and social status, united in Christ.

Paul mentions about twenty-six people by name, plus several households and groups. Many of the names are Greek or Latin; some are common names for slaves or freed slaves in Rome. Some are Jewish. About a third are women, and Paul praises several of them for their hard work in ministry. Paul had never visited Rome, yet he knew many people there, probably because believers traveled widely in the Roman world, and some, like Prisca and Aquila, had lived elsewhere and returned to Rome after Claudius’s expulsion of the Jews ended.

### Commendation of Phoebe (*16:1–2*)

Paul’s commendation of Phoebe is studied below.

### Greetings to Believers in Rome (*16:3–16*)

“*Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus*” (*v. 3*). Prisca (Priscilla is a diminutive form) and her husband Aquila were tentmakers whom Paul had met in Corinth (*Acts 18:2–3*). They had taught Apollos the way of God more accurately (*Acts 18:26*). Paul says they “*risked their own necks for my life*” (*v. 4*). We do not know exactly when this happened, perhaps during the riot in Ephesus (*Acts 19*). Paul and all the Gentile churches owed them thanks. Prisca is often named before her husband, which may suggest her prominence in ministry.

“*Greet the assembly that is in their house*” (*v. 5*). The early church had no special buildings; believers met in homes. Prisca and Aquila hosted a house church in Rome, as they had done in Ephesus (*1 Corinthians 16:19*).

Paul greets Epaenetus, “*the first fruits of Achaia to Christ*” (*v. 5*) (or of Asia, in some manuscripts), the first convert in his region. He greets Mary, “*who labored much for us*” (*v. 6*). Andronicus and Junia are studied below.

Many of the greetings are warm and personal. Paul calls several people “beloved.” He greets those “*who are of the household of Aristobulus*” (*v. 10*) and “*them of the household of Narcissus, who are in the Lord*” (*v. 11*). These may have been slaves or servants in the households of prominent men, possibly including Narcissus, a powerful freed slave in the emperor’s household. The gospel had reached even into the households of the powerful.

“*Greet Tryphaena and Tryphosa, who labor in the Lord. Greet Persis, the beloved, who labored much in the Lord*” (*v. 12*). Tryphaena and Tryphosa may have been sisters, perhaps twins. Their names mean “dainty” and “delicate,” yet Paul describes them as hard workers for the Lord.

“*Greet Rufus, the chosen in the Lord, and his mother and mine*” (*v. 13*). Mark’s Gospel mentions that Simon of Cyrene, who carried Jesus’ cross, was “*the father of Alexander and Rufus*” (*Mark 15:21*). Mark, writing probably for believers in Rome, may have mentioned Rufus because he was known to them. If this is the same Rufus, his father carried Jesus’ cross. Rufus’s mother had cared for Paul like a mother.

“*Greet one another with a holy kiss*” (*v. 16*). The kiss was a common greeting in the ancient world among family and friends. Among believers, it expressed their family relationship in Christ. Today, believers in different cultures express this with a handshake, an embrace, or another warm greeting. “*The assemblies of Christ greet you*” (*v. 16*).

### A Warning about Divisive People (*16:17–20*)

Paul’s warning is studied below, along with his promise of victory.

### Greetings from Paul’s Companions (*16:21–24*)

Paul includes greetings from his companions in Corinth. “*Timothy, my fellow worker, greets you*” (*v. 21*), along with Lucius, Jason, and Sosipater. Then a surprise: “*I, Tertius, who write the letter, greet you in the Lord*” (*v. 22*). Tertius was Paul’s scribe or secretary, who wrote down the letter as Paul dictated it. This was common practice in the ancient world.

“*Gaius, my host and host of the whole assembly, greets you*” (*v. 23*). Gaius hosted Paul and the whole church in Corinth, probably the Gaius whom Paul had baptized (*1 Corinthians 1:14*). “*Erastus, the treasurer of the city, greets you*” (*v. 23*). Archaeologists in Corinth have found a first-century inscription reading, “Erastus, in return for his aedileship, laid this pavement at his own expense.” Many scholars believe this may be the same Erastus, a city official who became a believer.

“*The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all! Amen*” (*v. 24*). (In the World English Bible, the closing doxology that many Bibles place here as verses 25–27 appears at the end of chapter 14; see the note there.)

## Important Verses Explained

### *Romans 16:1–2* — Phoebe, Servant and Helper

> *“I commend to you Phoebe, our sister, who is a servant of the assembly that is at Cenchreae, that you receive her in the Lord in a way worthy of the saints, and that you assist her in whatever matter she may need from you, for she herself also has been a helper of many, and of my own self.”*
>
> — *Romans 16:1–2* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul begins the final chapter of Romans by introducing a woman named Phoebe. She was probably the person who carried this letter to Rome. In the ancient world, there was no postal service for private letters. Letters were carried by trusted travelers. Phoebe likely traveled from Corinth to Rome, a long and difficult journey, and may have read or explained the letter to the believers there.

“*I commend to you Phoebe, our sister*” (*v. 1*). Paul calls her “our sister,” a member of God’s family. He “commends” her, giving her a letter of recommendation so that the Roman believers would welcome and trust her.

“*who is a servant of the assembly that is at Cenchreae*” (*v. 1*). Cenchreae was the eastern port of Corinth. The word translated “servant” is diakonos, the same word that is sometimes translated “deacon” (*Philippians 1:1*; *1 Timothy 3:8–13*). Christians have understood this description of Phoebe in different ways. Some traditions understand that Phoebe held the recognized office of deacon in her church. Others understand the word in its general sense of “servant” or “minister,” describing her faithful service without implying a formal office. Either way, Paul clearly honors her as a valued servant of the church.

“*that you receive her in the Lord in a way worthy of the saints*” (*v. 2*). Paul asks the Roman believers to welcome her as fellow believers should welcome one another, with love and honor.

“*and that you assist her in whatever matter she may need from you*” (*v. 2*). They should help her with whatever she needed while in Rome.

“*for she herself also has been a helper of many, and of my own self*” (*v. 2*). The word “helper” can mean “patron” or “benefactor.” Phoebe had likely used her resources to support Paul and many others. She may have been a woman of some means, who provided hospitality, financial support, or legal protection.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show the important role of women in the early church. Phoebe was trusted with carrying the most theologically significant letter in the New Testament. She served the church and supported Paul’s ministry. Throughout this chapter, Paul greets many women who worked hard for the Lord.

They also show the value of generous service. Phoebe used what she had to help many people. Paul honored her for it. Jesus taught that greatness in His kingdom comes through service (*Mark 10:43–45*).

Finally, these verses show the importance of hospitality and mutual support. Paul asks the Roman believers to welcome and help Phoebe, just as she had helped others. The church is a network of mutual care, where believers support those who serve.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to honor those who serve in the church, both men and women. Many people serve faithfully behind the scenes, providing hospitality, financial support, and practical help. Believers can recognize and thank them.

They also encourage believers to use their resources to support God’s work. Phoebe was a helper of many. Believers can ask how they might use their homes, money, time, and skills to support others.

Finally, these verses encourage believers to welcome those who come to them in the Lord’s name. Missionaries, traveling ministers, and believers from other churches deserve warm welcome and practical help.

### *Romans 16:7* — Andronicus and Junia

> *“Greet Andronicus and Junia, my relatives and my fellow prisoners, who are notable among the apostles, who were also in Christ before me.”*
>
> — *Romans 16:7* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

In his long list of greetings, Paul mentions a pair of believers with special honor: “*Greet Andronicus and Junia, my relatives and my fellow prisoners*” (*v. 7*). “Relatives” may mean that they were Paul’s actual family members, or more likely that they were fellow Jews, since Paul uses this word for several people in this chapter (*16:11*, 21). They had been in prison with Paul at some point, suffering for the gospel.

“*who are notable among the apostles*” (*v. 7*). This phrase has been understood in two ways. Many interpreters understand it to mean that Andronicus and Junia were outstanding apostles themselves, in the broader sense of the word “apostle” as a commissioned messenger or missionary, not one of the Twelve. Others understand it to mean that they were well known to the apostles, respected by them. The Greek can be read either way, and scholars continue to discuss it.

Junia is a female name, and most ancient Christian writers understood her to be a woman. The early church leader John Chrysostom (around A.D. 400) praised her: “How great the devotion of this woman must have been, that she should be even counted worthy of the title of apostle!” Andronicus and Junia were likely a married couple who served together, like Prisca and Aquila.

“*who were also in Christ before me*” (*v. 7*). They became believers before Paul did. They may have been among the early believers in Jerusalem, perhaps even witnesses of the risen Christ, since Paul says that Jesus appeared to “*all the apostles*” (*1 Corinthians 15:7*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows the honor given to faithful servants who suffer for the gospel. Andronicus and Junia had been imprisoned for Christ. Paul honored them as fellow prisoners and as notable among the apostles.

It also shows the partnership of men and women in ministry. Throughout *Romans 16*, Paul greets both men and women who served the Lord. Andronicus and Junia, like Prisca and Aquila, appear to have served together as a couple. Christians hold different views about the roles of men and women in church leadership, but all can recognize from this chapter that women were valued partners in the work of the gospel.

Finally, the verse shows Paul’s humility. Andronicus and Junia were “in Christ before me.” Paul, the great apostle, honored those who had come to faith before him. He recognized that he was part of a larger story.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to honor those who have suffered for Christ. Many believers around the world are imprisoned for their faith. Believers can pray for them, support them, and remember their sacrifice.

It also encourages believers to appreciate the contributions of both men and women in the church. Whatever one’s view of specific leadership roles, believers can honor the faithful service of all who labor for the gospel.

Finally, the verse encourages believers to respect those who have walked with Christ longer. Paul honored those who were believers before him. Younger believers can learn from and honor those who have been faithful over many years.

### *Romans 16:17–18* — Watch Out for Those Who Cause Divisions

> *“Now I beg you, brothers, look out for those who are causing the divisions and occasions of stumbling, contrary to the doctrine which you learned, and turn away from them. For those who are such don’t serve our Lord Jesus Christ, but their own belly; and by their smooth and flattering speech they deceive the hearts of the innocent.”*
>
> — *Romans 16:17–18* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After his warm greetings, Paul suddenly gives a strong warning. He cared deeply about the Roman church and wanted to protect it from harm.

“*Now I beg you, brothers, look out for those who are causing the divisions and occasions of stumbling, contrary to the doctrine which you learned*” (*v. 17*). Believers should watch for people who cause divisions and create obstacles to faith. These people teach things “contrary to the doctrine which you learned,” contradicting the gospel Paul and others had taught. This is different from the disputable matters of chapter 14, where sincere believers disagreed about food and days. These people were promoting false teaching that undermined the gospel itself.

“*and turn away from them*” (*v. 17*). Believers should avoid such people, not giving them influence in the church.

“*For those who are such don’t serve our Lord Jesus Christ, but their own belly*” (*v. 18*). These people were not truly serving Christ. They served “their own belly,” their own appetites and desires. They may have been seeking money, power, recognition, or pleasure.

“*and by their smooth and flattering speech they deceive the hearts of the innocent*” (*v. 18*). They used pleasant, persuasive words and flattery to deceive people who were naive or unsuspecting. False teachers are often charming and persuasive. Their danger lies partly in how attractive they seem.

Paul does not name these people. They may not yet have arrived in Rome, but Paul knew from experience that such teachers often followed the spread of the gospel.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that the church must guard the truth. Paul had spent fifteen chapters explaining the gospel. He knew that false teaching could undermine everything. Jesus also warned, “*Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravening wolves*” (*Matthew 7:15*).

They also show that motives matter. False teachers serve their own desires rather than Christ. One way to recognize them is to look at their fruit: do they seek Christ’s glory or their own gain? Jesus said, “*By their fruits you will know them*” (*Matthew 7:16*).

Finally, these verses show that smooth speech is not the same as truth. Persuasiveness, charm, and flattery can deceive. Believers must test teaching by Scripture, not by how pleasing it sounds.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to be discerning. Not everyone who speaks in the name of Christ is serving Him. Believers can test teaching by comparing it with Scripture and by looking at the character and fruit of those who teach.

They also warn against being swayed by flattery and smooth speech. Some teachers today use charm, emotion, or flattery to gain followers. Believers can be wise, recognizing that truth is more important than eloquence.

Finally, these verses call believers to protect the unity of the church against those who would divide it through false teaching. At the same time, believers should be careful not to label every disagreement as false teaching. The difference between disputable matters (chapter 14) and teaching contrary to the gospel (chapter 16) is important.

### *Romans 16:19–20* — Wise in Good, Innocent in Evil

> *“For your obedience has become known to all. I rejoice therefore over you. But I desire to have you wise in that which is good, but innocent in that which is evil. And the God of peace will quickly crush Satan under your feet. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.”*
>
> — *Romans 16:19–20* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After warning about those who cause divisions, Paul encourages the Roman believers.

“*For your obedience has become known to all. I rejoice therefore over you*” (*v. 19*). The Roman church was known everywhere for its faithfulness to Christ. Paul rejoiced over them. He was not warning them because they were failing, but because he wanted to protect them.

“*But I desire to have you wise in that which is good, but innocent in that which is evil*” (*v. 19*). Paul wanted them to be experts in what is good, knowing God’s truth well and living it out. But he wanted them to be “innocent” in evil, inexperienced and unfamiliar with evil, not drawn into it. This echoes Jesus’ words: “*Therefore be wise as serpents, and harmless as doves*” (*Matthew 10:16*).

Being “innocent in evil” does not mean being naive or unaware of danger. Paul has just warned them about deceivers. It means not participating in evil, not being stained by it, while being wise enough to recognize it.

“*And the God of peace will quickly crush Satan under your feet*” (*v. 20*). This is a powerful promise. Behind the false teachers and divisions stands Satan, the enemy of God’s people. But God will defeat him. The language recalls *Genesis 3:15*, where God promised that the woman’s offspring would crush the serpent’s head. Christ has already won the decisive victory over Satan through His death and resurrection (*Colossians 2:15*). The final crushing will come at His return. And believers will share in that victory: Satan will be crushed “under your feet.”

Notice that the one who crushes Satan is “the God of peace.” God brings peace by defeating the enemy who causes division and destruction.

“*The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you*” (*v. 20*). Paul closes this section with a blessing of grace. Grace was the theme of his whole letter, and it remains believers’ strength and hope.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show the balance of Christian wisdom. Believers are called to be discerning without becoming cynical, knowledgeable about good without being fascinated by evil. Paul writes elsewhere, “*Brothers, don’t be children in thoughts, yet in malice be babies, but in thoughts be mature*” (*1 Corinthians 14:20*).

They also show that the battle against evil is ultimately God’s. Believers are called to resist evil, but the final victory belongs to God. The church can face opposition with confidence, knowing that Satan is a defeated enemy.

Finally, these verses connect the promise of victory with the first promise of the gospel in *Genesis 3:15*. From the beginning, God planned to defeat the serpent through the offspring of the woman. Christ fulfilled this promise, and believers share in His triumph.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to grow in wisdom about what is good. Believers can fill their minds with God’s truth and learn to recognize what pleases Him.

They also encourage believers to avoid unnecessary exposure to evil. While believers must be aware of the world around them, they do not need to immerse themselves in evil to understand it. Believers can be careful about what they watch, read, and participate in.

Finally, these verses give believers hope in spiritual battle. When believers face temptation, opposition, or the work of the enemy, they can trust that the God of peace will crush Satan under their feet. The victory is certain.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Romans 16* shows that the gospel creates a real community. After fifteen chapters of profound teaching, Paul greets a long list of real people: men and women, Jews and Gentiles, slaves and free, all serving the Lord together. Believers can see their own churches as families of brothers and sisters, valuing each person and their contributions.

The chapter also honors faithful service. Phoebe supported many, Prisca and Aquila risked their lives, Mary and Persis labored hard, Andronicus and Junia suffered imprisonment. Many served in ways that would otherwise have been forgotten. Believers can serve faithfully, knowing that God sees their work, and they can honor those who serve, including those whose work is often unnoticed.

*Romans 16* warns believers to watch out for those who cause divisions through teaching contrary to the gospel. Such people often use smooth words and flattery, serving their own desires rather than Christ. Believers can be discerning, testing teaching by Scripture, while still distinguishing between false teaching and disputable matters on which sincere believers differ.

Finally, the chapter calls believers to be wise in what is good and innocent in what is evil, and it promises that the God of peace will soon crush Satan under their feet. Believers can live with confidence that the battle belongs to God, that Christ has already won the victory, and that His grace will be with them always.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for building Your church as a family of faithful servants from every background. Thank You for Phoebe, Prisca and Aquila, Andronicus and Junia, and all whose names are written here, and for the many whose names are known only to You. Help me to serve faithfully in Your church, and to honor and support those who labor for Your gospel. Give me discernment to recognize teaching that is contrary to Your truth, and protect me from smooth words and flattery. Make me wise in what is good and innocent in what is evil. Thank You that the God of peace will crush Satan under our feet, and that Your victory is certain. May Your grace be with me and with all Your people. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Book 7 of 27

# 1 Corinthians

## About This Letter

Paul founded the church in Corinth during his second missionary journey, around A.D. 50–52, staying for a year and a half (*Acts 18:1–18*). Corinth was a wealthy, cosmopolitan port city, the capital of the Roman province of Achaia, famous for commerce, athletic games, and moral looseness. Paul wrote this letter from Ephesus around A.D. 53–55 (*1 Corinthians 16:8*), after receiving troubling reports from members of Chloe’s household (*1 Corinthians 1:11*) and a letter from the church with questions (*7:1*). Paul had already written them an earlier letter that has not survived (*5:9*).

## The Shape of the Letter

The first part of the letter (chapters 1–6) addresses problems Paul had heard about: divisions around favorite leaders, pride in human wisdom, a case of sexual immorality the church had tolerated, lawsuits between believers, and the misuse of Christian freedom. The second part (chapters 7–16) answers questions the Corinthians had asked, introduced by the phrase “now concerning”: marriage and singleness, food offered to idols, order in worship, the Lord’s Supper, spiritual gifts, and the resurrection of the dead. In the middle of his teaching on spiritual gifts, Paul writes his great chapter on love (chapter 13). He ends with instructions about a collection for the believers in Jerusalem and personal greetings.

## Themes to Watch For

Look for the message of the cross, which turns human wisdom and status upside down; the church as God’s temple and Christ’s body; the call to holiness in a permissive culture; the principle that freedom must be governed by love for others; the importance of order and edification in worship; the supremacy of love above every spiritual gift; and the certainty of the bodily resurrection, grounded in Christ’s own resurrection. Though written to a troubled church nearly two thousand years ago, 1 Corinthians speaks with striking relevance to believers living in proud, divided, and pleasure-seeking cultures today.

1 Corinthians · Chapter 1 of 16

# 1 Corinthians — Chapter 1

Chapter Theme: The Foolishness of the Cross and the Folly of Division

[Read 1 Corinthians 1 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/1CO01.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul greets the church in Corinth as people made holy in Christ, thanks God for His grace and gifts among them, and assures them that the faithful God will keep them to the end. Then he confronts the quarrels that have split the church into factions around favorite leaders, asking whether Christ is divided. He explains that the message of the cross looks foolish to the world but is the power of God for those being saved. God deliberately chose the weak and lowly to shame the proud, so that no one may boast before Him, and Christ Himself has become their wisdom, righteousness, holiness, and redemption.

## Chapter Background and Story

Corinth was a proud city. It had been destroyed by the Romans in 146 B.C. and rebuilt by Julius Caesar in 44 B.C. as a Roman colony. By Paul’s time, it was booming, filled with people seeking wealth, status, and advancement. Corinthians admired eloquent speakers, philosophers, and people of influence. This culture of status-seeking had seeped into the church. Believers were dividing into factions, each claiming a favorite teacher, and some were proud of their spiritual gifts and knowledge.

Paul writes to correct these attitudes. His central answer is the cross of Christ. The cross overturns the world’s values: it shows God’s power in weakness, His wisdom in what seems foolish, and His choice of the lowly rather than the proud. If believers understood the cross, they would stop boasting and stop dividing.

### Greeting and Thanksgiving (*1:1–9*)

Paul writes as “*called to be an apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God*” (*v. 1*), together with “*our brother Sosthenes*” (*v. 1*), who may be the synagogue leader mentioned in *Acts 18:17*. He addresses the church as “*those who are sanctified in Christ Jesus, called saints*” (*v. 2*). Despite their many problems, the Corinthian believers were “saints,” people set apart for God, because of their union with Christ. Holiness is first God’s gift, then a calling to live out.

Paul thanks God for the grace given to them. “*that in everything you were enriched in him, in all speech and all knowledge*” (*v. 5*). They were richly gifted. “*so that you come behind in no gift, waiting for the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ*” (*v. 7*). The Corinthians had many spiritual gifts, which Paul will discuss in chapters 12–14. But these gifts were meant to be used while waiting for Christ’s return, not as grounds for pride. Paul’s confidence in God’s faithfulness is studied below.

### Divisions in the Church (*1:10–17*)

Paul’s appeal for unity is studied below. He had heard “*by those who are from Chloe’s household, that there are contentions among you*” (*v. 11*). Chloe was probably a woman with a household that included servants or family members who traveled between Corinth and Ephesus.

The divisions: “*“I follow Paul,” “I follow Apollos,” “I follow Cephas,” and, “I follow Christ.”*” (*v. 12*) Some were loyal to Paul, who founded the church. Some preferred Apollos, the eloquent teacher from Alexandria (*Acts 18:24–28*). Some followed Cephas (Peter), perhaps Jewish believers who valued his connection to Jesus and the Jerusalem church. And some claimed to follow “Christ” alone, perhaps in a proud way that looked down on all human leaders.

Paul responds with sharp questions: “*Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized into the name of Paul?*” (*v. 13*) Christ cannot be divided into pieces. No human leader died for them. They were baptized into Christ’s name, not anyone else’s.

Paul is glad he baptized only a few of them, such as Crispus, Gaius, and the household of Stephanas, so that no one could claim to have been baptized into Paul’s name. “*For Christ sent me not to baptize, but to preach the Good News—not in wisdom of words, so that the cross of Christ wouldn’t be made void*” (*v. 17*). Paul does not belittle baptism; he simply emphasizes that his main calling was to preach. And he refused to rely on clever rhetoric, because that would distract from the power of the cross.

### The Message of the Cross (*1:18–25*)

Paul’s statement about the power of the cross is studied below. He quotes *Isaiah 29:14*: “*I will destroy the wisdom of the wise. I will bring the discernment of the discerning to nothing*” (*v. 19*). “*Where is the wise? Where is the scribe? Where is the debater of this age? Hasn’t God made foolish the wisdom of this world?*” (*v. 20*) The great thinkers of the world, with all their wisdom, could not find God. “*For seeing that in the wisdom of God, the world through its wisdom didn’t know God, it was God’s good pleasure through the foolishness of the preaching to save those who believe*” (*v. 21*).

“*For Jews ask for signs, Greeks seek after wisdom*” (*v. 22*), “*but we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Greeks*” (*v. 23*). Many Jews wanted miraculous proof of God’s power; a crucified Messiah seemed to contradict everything they expected, since Scripture said that anyone hanged on a tree was cursed (*Deuteronomy 21:23*). Many Greeks valued philosophy and eloquence; the idea that God would save the world through a crucified Jewish carpenter seemed absurd. Yet “*but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God*” (*v. 24*). “*because the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men*” (*v. 25*). What looks foolish and weak in God’s ways is far wiser and stronger than the best of human wisdom and power.

### God Chose the Lowly (*1:26–31*)

Paul’s reminder of their calling is studied below. He concludes: “*Because of him, you are in Christ Jesus, who was made to us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification, and redemption*” (*v. 30*). Everything believers need is found in Christ. He is their “wisdom,” the true wisdom that comes from God. He is their “righteousness,” the right standing they have before God. He is their “sanctification,” the holiness they are growing into. And He is their “redemption,” their full and final deliverance. “*that, as it is written, “He who boasts, let him boast in the Lord.”*” (*v. 31*) Paul quotes *Jeremiah 9:24*. Since everything comes from God, the only proper boasting is in Him.

## Important Verses Explained

### *1 Corinthians 1:9* — God Is Faithful

> *“God is faithful, through whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 1:9* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul began his letter to the Corinthians with thanksgiving. Despite all the problems he was about to address, including divisions, immorality, lawsuits, and confusion in worship, he thanked God for the grace He had given them. They had been enriched with spiritual gifts. And Paul expressed confidence that Christ “*will also confirm you until the end, blameless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ*” (*v. 8*).

How could Paul be so confident about such a troubled church? His answer: “*God is faithful*” (*v. 9*). Paul’s hope for the Corinthians did not rest on their performance, which was often poor. It rested on God’s faithfulness. God keeps His promises. He finishes what He starts.

“*through whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord*” (*v. 9*). God had called them into “fellowship” with His Son. The Greek word koinonia means sharing, partnership, or communion. Believers share life with Christ. They are united with Him, partners in His life, His sufferings, and His glory.

This fellowship was God’s initiative. He “called” them. And the God who called them would be faithful to keep them. Paul writes elsewhere, “*He who calls you is faithful, who will also do it*” (*1 Thessalonians 5:24*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that the security of believers rests on God’s character, not their own. The Corinthian church was deeply flawed, yet Paul was confident that God would keep them to the end. God’s faithfulness is greater than human failure. Paul writes, “*If we are faithless, he remains faithful; for he can’t deny himself*” (*2 Timothy 2:13*).

It also shows that salvation is relational. Believers are called into fellowship with Jesus Christ. The Christian life is not merely believing correct ideas or following rules; it is a shared life with the Son of God.

Finally, the verse shows Paul’s pastoral wisdom. Before correcting the Corinthians, he reminded them of God’s grace and faithfulness. Correction is easier to receive when it comes in the context of hope and affirmation.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse brings assurance to believers who feel weak or who have failed. Their hope does not rest on their own strength but on God’s faithfulness. He will keep them to the end.

It also invites believers to enjoy fellowship with Christ. Believers have been called into a shared life with Jesus. They can spend time with Him in prayer, Scripture, and worship, and they can share in His life throughout the day.

Finally, the verse shows a healthy way to approach difficult situations in the church. Before addressing problems, believers can remember and give thanks for God’s grace at work in others. This sets correction within the framework of hope.

### *1 Corinthians 1:10* — No Divisions Among You

> *“Now I beg you, brothers, through the name of our Lord, Jesus Christ, that you all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you, but that you be perfected together in the same mind and in the same judgment.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 1:10* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After his opening thanksgiving, Paul turns to the first major problem in the Corinthian church: divisions. He had heard from members of Chloe’s household that the believers were quarreling, splitting into groups around different leaders.

“*Now I beg you, brothers, through the name of our Lord, Jesus Christ*” (*v. 10*). Paul makes his appeal with great seriousness, “through the name of our Lord.” The name of Christ, in which all believers were baptized and which unites them, is the basis of his plea. He calls them “brothers,” reminding them that they are one family.

“*that you all speak the same thing*” (*v. 10*). Paul wants them to agree, to speak with one voice rather than shouting competing slogans.

“*and that there be no divisions among you*” (*v. 10*). The word “divisions” (schismata) describes a tear in a garment. The church was being torn apart. Paul wants this tearing to stop.

“*but that you be perfected together in the same mind and in the same judgment*” (*v. 10*). “Perfected together” was used of mending torn nets or setting broken bones. Paul wants the church to be repaired, restored to wholeness, sharing the same mind and purpose.

This does not mean believers must agree on every opinion. In *Romans 14* and *1 Corinthians 8–10*, Paul allows for differences in matters of conscience. But they should be united in their commitment to Christ, in their understanding of the gospel, and in their love for one another.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that unity is essential to the church. Jesus prayed that His followers would be one (*John 17:21*). Paul writes, “*being eager to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace*” (*Ephesians 4:3*). Division damages the church’s witness and grieves the heart of Christ.

It also shows that divisions often come from pride. The Corinthians were exalting human leaders, each group claiming to be better than the others. Paul’s answer throughout this chapter is the cross, which humbles all human pride.

Finally, the verse shows that unity is something believers must work toward. Paul uses the image of mending. Unity is not automatic; it requires effort, humility, and a shared focus on Christ.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse challenges believers to examine whether they contribute to division in their churches. Believers can be tempted to form groups around favorite pastors, teachers, styles, or opinions. Paul calls them to focus on Christ, who unites them.

It also encourages believers to work for reconciliation. When relationships in the church are torn, believers can seek to mend them through humility, forgiveness, and honest conversation.

Finally, the verse reminds believers that unity is rooted in Christ. Believers do not create unity by agreeing on everything; they preserve unity by remaining centered on Jesus and His gospel.

### *1 Corinthians 1:18* — The Word of the Cross

> *“For the word of the cross is foolishness to those who are dying, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 1:18* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had just said that Christ sent him to preach the gospel, “not in wisdom of words, so that the cross of Christ wouldn’t be made void.” The Corinthians admired eloquent speakers and impressive philosophy. Paul refused to rely on such things because he did not want to distract from the cross.

“*For the word of the cross is foolishness to those who are dying*” (*v. 18*). “The word of the cross” is the message that Jesus Christ was crucified for sinners. To many people, this message seems foolish. In the Roman world, crucifixion was the most shameful form of execution, reserved for slaves, rebels, and criminals. It was considered so horrible that polite Romans avoided even mentioning it. The idea that a crucified man could be the Savior of the world, or that God would save people through such a death, seemed absurd.

Notice the phrase “those who are dying.” People who reject the message of the cross are on the path to destruction. They see the cross as foolishness because they do not understand their need for it.

“*but to us who are being saved it is the power of God*” (*v. 18*). To those who believe, the cross is not foolish but powerful. Through the cross, God saves people, forgives sins, defeats evil, and brings new life. Notice the present tense, “being saved.” Salvation is a reality believers have now and are continuing to experience until its completion.

The same message produces opposite responses. To some it is foolishness; to others it is God’s power. The difference is not in the message but in how people receive it.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that the cross is central to the Christian faith. Paul writes later in this letter, “*For I determined not to know anything among you, except Jesus Christ and him crucified*” (*1 Corinthians 2:2*). The cross is not a side issue; it is the heart of the gospel.

It also shows that God’s ways often contradict human expectations. Humans expect power to look like strength, victory to look like triumph, and wisdom to look like cleverness. God revealed His power through weakness and His wisdom through what seemed foolish.

Finally, the verse shows that the gospel’s power is not in human presentation. Paul did not rely on eloquence or clever arguments. The power is in the message itself, because it is God’s power.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to keep the cross at the center of their faith and witness. In a world that values success, strength, and self-sufficiency, the message of a crucified Savior may seem foolish. Believers can proclaim it with confidence, knowing that it is God’s power.

It also helps believers understand why some people reject the gospel. To those who are perishing, the cross seems foolish. Believers can pray that God would open their eyes to see its power.

Finally, the verse encourages believers to rely on the gospel’s power rather than their own cleverness. Believers do not need to be eloquent or persuasive to share their faith. God works through the simple message of Christ crucified.

### *1 Corinthians 1:27–29* — God Chose the Foolish and the Weak

> *“but God chose the foolish things of the world that he might put to shame those who are wise. God chose the weak things of the world that he might put to shame the things that are strong. God chose the lowly things of the world, and the things that are despised, and the things that don’t exist, that he might bring to nothing the things that exist, that no flesh should boast before God.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 1:27–29* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had been explaining that the message of the cross seems foolish to the world but is the power of God. Now he asks the Corinthians to look at themselves as evidence of this truth.

“*For you see your calling, brothers, that not many are wise according to the flesh, not many mighty, and not many noble*” (*v. 26*). When God called the Corinthian believers, He did not mainly choose the educated, powerful, or aristocratic. Some believers in Corinth did have status, such as Crispus the synagogue ruler and Erastus the city treasurer. But “not many” did. Most were ordinary people, and many were slaves or freed slaves.

“*but God chose the foolish things of the world that he might put to shame those who are wise. God chose the weak things of the world that he might put to shame the things that are strong*” (*v. 27*). God deliberately chose those whom the world considered foolish and weak. Why? To shame the wise and the strong, to show that their wisdom and strength cannot save them.

“*God chose the lowly things of the world, and the things that are despised, and the things that don’t exist, that he might bring to nothing the things that exist*” (*v. 28*). God chose those who were looked down on, ignored, even regarded as nothing, in order to overturn the world’s values.

“*that no flesh should boast before God*” (*v. 29*). This is the purpose: so that no one can boast. If God had chosen only the wise, powerful, and noble, they might think they deserved salvation. By choosing the lowly, God shows that salvation is entirely His gift.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show God’s pattern throughout Scripture. He chose Abraham, an elderly man without children; Jacob, the younger son; Joseph, a slave; Moses, a man who could not speak well; David, the youngest shepherd boy; Mary, a young woman from an unimportant town. Jesus Himself was born in a stable and grew up in Nazareth. God consistently works through the unlikely.

They also show that the gospel humbles human pride. No one can say, “God chose me because I was smart, strong, or important.” Salvation is grace from beginning to end. Paul writes, “*not of works, that no one would boast*” (*Ephesians 2:9*).

Finally, these verses bring dignity to the lowly. The world may despise the poor, the uneducated, and the powerless. But God chooses them and uses them for His glory. In God’s kingdom, the last are first.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers who feel insignificant. Many believers think they have little to offer because they lack education, wealth, or status. God delights to use such people. Their weakness is not a barrier but an opportunity for God’s power.

They also challenge believers who are proud of their achievements. Education, wealth, and influence are not grounds for boasting before God. Believers with these gifts can use them humbly, recognizing that everything they have comes from Him.

Finally, these verses call believers to value people the world overlooks. Churches can honor the poor, the uneducated, and the marginalized, recognizing that God chooses and uses them. Believers can resist the temptation to favor the wealthy and influential.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*1 Corinthians 1* reminds believers that their security rests on God’s faithfulness. Despite the Corinthians’ many problems, Paul was confident that God would keep them to the end, because God is faithful. Believers who feel weak or have failed can rest in the faithfulness of the God who called them into fellowship with His Son.

The chapter also confronts division in the church. The Corinthians were splitting into factions around favorite leaders. Paul asks, “Is Christ divided?” Believers today can examine whether they are contributing to division by elevating leaders, preferences, or groups above Christ, and they can work to mend broken relationships.

*1 Corinthians 1* places the cross at the center of the Christian faith. The message of Christ crucified seems foolish to the world, but it is the power of God for those being saved. Believers can proclaim the cross with confidence, relying not on their own eloquence but on the power of God’s message.

Finally, the chapter shows that God chooses the lowly to shame the proud, so that no one can boast before Him. Christ Himself is believers’ wisdom, righteousness, holiness, and redemption. Believers can lay aside all pride, find their worth in Christ alone, honor those the world overlooks, and boast only in the Lord.

## Chapter Prayer

Faithful God, thank You for calling me into fellowship with Your Son, Jesus Christ. Thank You that my hope does not rest on my own strength but on Your faithfulness, and that You will keep me to the end. Forgive me for the times I have contributed to division in Your church by exalting people, preferences, or groups above Christ. Make me a peacemaker who helps mend what is torn. Thank You for the message of the cross, which seems foolish to the world but is Your power to save. Help me never to be ashamed of it. Thank You that You chose the weak and lowly, and that You chose me, not because of anything in me, but because of Your grace. Lord Jesus, You are my wisdom, righteousness, holiness, and redemption. Let me boast only in You. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

1 Corinthians · Chapter 2 of 16

# 1 Corinthians — Chapter 2

Chapter Theme: Christ Crucified and the Wisdom Revealed by the Spirit

[Read 1 Corinthians 2 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/1CO02.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul reminds the Corinthians that when he first came to them, he did not rely on impressive speech or philosophy, but resolved to know nothing among them except Jesus Christ and Him crucified. He came in weakness and fear, so that their faith would rest on God’s power rather than human wisdom. Yet there is a true wisdom that God has revealed, hidden from the rulers of this age who crucified the Lord of glory, and made known to believers by the Holy Spirit, who searches the depths of God. People without the Spirit cannot accept these things, but believers have received the Spirit and have the mind of Christ.

## Chapter Background and Story

In chapter 1, Paul showed that the message of the cross seems foolish to the world but is God’s power and wisdom. In chapter 2, he continues this theme by reminding the Corinthians of how he first preached to them, and by explaining that there is a true wisdom, God’s wisdom, which can only be understood through the Holy Spirit.

When Paul arrived in Corinth, he had just come from Athens, where he had spoken to philosophers at the Areopagus with mixed results (*Acts 17*). Some scholars think Paul resolved in Corinth to focus even more simply on the cross. Whether or not that is so, Paul’s approach in Corinth was deliberately plain. The Corinthians, who loved rhetoric and philosophy, may have later compared Paul unfavorably with the eloquent Apollos. Paul explains that his plainness was intentional.

### Paul’s Preaching in Corinth (*2:1–5*)

Paul’s description of his approach is studied below in two parts. In between, he describes his own condition: “*I was with you in weakness, in fear, and in much trembling*” (*v. 3*). Paul arrived in Corinth after being beaten in Philippi, driven out of Thessalonica and Berea, and mocked in Athens. He may have been physically weak, emotionally exhausted, and afraid of what might happen in another city. The Lord later appeared to him in a vision and said, “*Don't be afraid*” (*Acts 18:9*). Paul did not hide his weakness. He knew that God’s power is made perfect in weakness (*2 Corinthians 12:9*).

### God’s Hidden Wisdom (*2:6–9*)

Paul does not reject wisdom altogether. “*We speak wisdom, however, among those who are full grown, yet a wisdom not of this world nor of the rulers of this world who are coming to nothing*” (*v. 6*). There is a true wisdom that mature believers can understand. But it is different from the wisdom of this age and of its rulers, whose power is passing away.

“*But we speak God’s wisdom in a mystery, the wisdom that has been hidden, which God foreordained before the worlds for our glory*” (*v. 7*). A “mystery” in Paul’s writings is a truth God has now revealed that was previously hidden. God’s wisdom, His plan of salvation through Christ, was planned before the world was made, for the purpose of bringing believers to glory.

“*which none of the rulers of this world has known. For had they known it, they wouldn’t have crucified the Lord of glory*” (*v. 8*). The “rulers of this world” may refer to human rulers, such as Pilate, Herod, and the Jewish leaders, or to spiritual powers behind them, or both. They did not understand God’s plan. If they had, they would not have crucified Jesus, because the cross became the means of their defeat. Notice the title “the Lord of glory.” The one who was crucified is the glorious Lord Himself. The promise of verse 9 is studied below with verse 10.

### Revealed by the Spirit (*2:10–16*)

Paul explains that the Spirit reveals God’s wisdom, as studied below. He uses an analogy: “*For who among men knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man which is in him? Even so, no one knows the things of God except God’s Spirit*” (*v. 11*). Only a person knows their own thoughts. Only God’s Spirit knows God’s thoughts.

“*But we received not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit which is from God, that we might know the things that were freely given to us by God*” (*v. 12*). Believers have received God’s Spirit, who helps them understand the gifts God has given them. “*We also speak these things, not in words which man’s wisdom teaches but which the Holy Spirit teaches, comparing spiritual things with spiritual things*” (*v. 13*). Paul’s message came from the Spirit, not from human philosophy.

Paul’s contrast between the natural person and the spiritual person, and his claim that believers have the mind of Christ, is studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *1 Corinthians 2:2* — Jesus Christ and Him Crucified

> *“For I determined not to know anything among you except Jesus Christ and him crucified.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 2:2* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul was reminding the Corinthians of how he first preached the gospel to them. Corinth was a city that admired eloquent speakers and clever philosophers. Public speakers were celebrities, and people judged teachers by how impressive they sounded.

“*When I came to you, brothers, I didn’t come with excellence of speech or of wisdom, proclaiming to you the testimony of God*” (*v. 1*). Paul did not try to impress them with fancy speech or philosophical arguments. He simply proclaimed God’s message.

“*For I determined not to know anything among you except Jesus Christ and him crucified*” (*v. 2*). Paul made a deliberate decision. “Determined” means he resolved, he made up his mind. He chose to focus his message entirely on Jesus Christ, and specifically on His crucifixion.

This does not mean Paul never taught anything else. He taught about the resurrection, Christian living, the church, and many other topics. But everything was centered on Christ and the cross. The cross was the heart of his message, the lens through which he understood everything else.

Why did Paul focus on the cross? Because the cross is where God’s love, justice, power, and wisdom are most fully revealed. It is where sins are forgiven and sinners are reconciled to God. And the cross humbles human pride. The Corinthians were proud of their wisdom and status. The cross shows that salvation comes not through human achievement but through God’s grace in the death of His Son.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that the cross is the center of Christian faith and preaching. Paul writes elsewhere, “*But far be it from me to boast, except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ*” (*Galatians 6:14*). Everything in the Christian life flows from what Christ accomplished on the cross.

It also shows the power of simplicity. Paul could have used his education to impress the Corinthians. He was highly trained and could argue brilliantly. But he chose simplicity so that people’s faith would rest on God, not on him.

Finally, the verse shows that the person of Christ is inseparable from His work. Paul focused on “Jesus Christ and him crucified,” both who Jesus is and what He did. The gospel is not merely a set of ideas but a Person who died and rose for sinners.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse calls believers to keep Christ and the cross at the center of their faith. It is easy to drift toward focusing on secondary matters: programs, techniques, opinions, or personalities. Believers can return again and again to the cross.

It also encourages those who teach and preach. Pastors, teachers, and parents do not need to impress others with eloquence or clever ideas. The most powerful message they can share is Jesus Christ and Him crucified.

Finally, the verse invites believers to see everything through the lens of the cross. Suffering, relationships, forgiveness, humility, and service all take on new meaning in light of Christ’s sacrifice.

### *1 Corinthians 2:4–5* — Faith Resting on God’s Power

> *“My speech and my preaching were not in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power, that your faith wouldn’t stand in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 2:4–5* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had told the Corinthians that he came to them in weakness, fear, and much trembling. He was not a confident, polished speaker trying to impress them. He continued describing his preaching.

“*My speech and my preaching were not in persuasive words of human wisdom*” (*v. 4*). Paul did not rely on the techniques of persuasion that were popular in Corinth. Greek orators were trained in rhetoric, the art of persuasive speaking. They used clever arguments, emotional appeals, and impressive language to win audiences. Paul deliberately avoided relying on these methods.

“*but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power*” (*v. 4*). Instead, Paul’s preaching was accompanied by the Holy Spirit’s power. The Spirit convicted hearts, opened minds, and changed lives. There may also have been miraculous signs (*2 Corinthians 12:12*). The “demonstration” was the proof that the message came from God.

“*that your faith wouldn’t stand in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God*” (*v. 5*). Paul had a purpose. If the Corinthians had believed because of Paul’s eloquence, their faith would rest on Paul. If someone more eloquent came along, they might be swayed. But because their faith came through the Spirit’s power, it rested on God. Faith built on God is secure.

This was especially important in Corinth, where the believers were dividing into groups around favorite teachers. Paul wanted them to understand that their faith did not depend on any human teacher.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that genuine faith is the work of God, not human persuasion. Paul writes, “*and that our Good News came to you not in word only, but also in power, and in the Holy Spirit, and with much assurance*” (*1 Thessalonians 1:5*). Human words can inform and persuade, but only the Spirit can create saving faith.

They also show that God uses weakness to display His power. Paul came in weakness and fear, yet God worked powerfully through him. Paul later wrote that God told him, “*My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness*” (*2 Corinthians 12:9*).

Finally, these verses show the importance of the foundation of faith. Faith that rests on human wisdom can be shaken when that wisdom is challenged. Faith that rests on God’s power is secure.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers who feel weak or inadequate when sharing their faith. Believers do not need to be eloquent or persuasive. God’s Spirit does the work of convincing hearts. Believers can share simply and trust God.

They also caution believers against basing their faith on human personalities. Some believers’ faith depends heavily on a favorite pastor, speaker, or author. When that person disappoints them, their faith is shaken. Believers can make sure their faith rests on God Himself.

Finally, these verses encourage believers to pray for the Spirit’s power. When believers share the gospel, teach, or serve, they can ask the Holy Spirit to work through them, demonstrating God’s power in ways human effort cannot.

### *1 Corinthians 2:9–10* — What God Has Prepared, Revealed by the Spirit

> *“But as it is written, ‘Things which an eye didn’t see, and an ear didn’t hear, which didn’t enter into the heart of man, these God has prepared for those who love him.’ But to us, God revealed them through the Spirit. For the Spirit searches all things, yes, the deep things of God.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 2:9–10* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had explained that there is a true wisdom from God, hidden from the rulers of this world who crucified the Lord of glory. Now he quotes Scripture to describe this wisdom.

“*But as it is written, “Things which an eye didn’t see, and an ear didn’t hear, which didn’t enter into the heart of man, these God has prepared for those who love him.”*” (*v. 9*) This quotation is based on *Isaiah 64:4* and perhaps other Old Testament passages. It describes the blessings God has prepared for those who love Him. These blessings are beyond human perception. No eye has seen them, no ear has heard them, and no human mind has imagined them.

This verse is often quoted in reference to heaven, and that is a fitting application. The glories of the age to come are beyond imagination. But in this context, Paul is also speaking about God’s wisdom revealed in the gospel: the plan of salvation through the crucified Christ, which no human could have discovered or imagined on their own.

“*But to us, God revealed them through the Spirit*” (*v. 10*). Here is the wonderful news: what humans could never discover, God has revealed. He has made it known to believers through the Holy Spirit. Believers do not have to guess about God’s plan; He has shown it to them.

“*For the Spirit searches all things, yes, the deep things of God*” (*v. 10*). The Holy Spirit knows everything, even the deepest truths about God. Because the Spirit is God, He knows God’s thoughts completely. And He reveals them to believers.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show the limits of human knowledge and the necessity of revelation. Humans cannot discover God’s deepest truths by their own reasoning. God must reveal Himself. Jesus said, “*No one knows the Son, except the Father; neither does anyone know the Father, except the Son, and he to whom the Son desires to reveal him*” (*Matthew 11:27*).

They also show the role of the Holy Spirit as revealer. The Spirit inspired the Scriptures (*2 Peter 1:21*) and illuminates believers’ minds to understand them. Jesus promised that the Spirit would guide His disciples into all truth (*John 16:13*).

Finally, these verses inspire hope and wonder. God has prepared things for those who love Him that are beyond imagination. Whatever believers experience now is only a foretaste of what is to come.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to depend on the Holy Spirit when reading Scripture. Understanding God’s truth is not merely an intellectual exercise. Believers can ask the Spirit to open their minds and hearts to what God has revealed.

They also give believers hope in difficult times. Whatever believers face now, God has prepared good things for those who love Him, things beyond their imagination. This hope can sustain them through suffering.

Finally, these verses invite believers to grow in love for God. The promise is for “those who love him.” Believers can cultivate their love for God through worship, prayer, obedience, and gratitude.

### *1 Corinthians 2:14–16* — The Mind of Christ

> *“Now the natural man doesn’t receive the things of God’s Spirit, for they are foolishness to him; and he can’t know them, because they are spiritually discerned. But he who is spiritual discerns all things, and he himself is to be judged by no one. ‘For who has known the mind of the Lord that he should instruct him?’ But we have Christ’s mind.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 2:14–16* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had explained that God reveals His wisdom through the Holy Spirit, and that believers have received the Spirit so that they can understand what God has given them. Now he contrasts two kinds of people.

“*Now the natural man doesn’t receive the things of God’s Spirit, for they are foolishness to him*” (*v. 14*). The “natural man” refers to a person without the Holy Spirit, someone who lives only by natural human abilities. Such a person does not accept the things that come from God’s Spirit. They seem foolish.

“*and he can’t know them, because they are spiritually discerned*” (*v. 14*). The problem is not intelligence but spiritual perception. Spiritual truths can only be understood with the help of the Spirit. A person without the Spirit is like someone without sight trying to appreciate a painting.

“*But he who is spiritual discerns all things, and he himself is to be judged by no one*” (*v. 15*). The “spiritual” person is someone who has the Spirit. Such a person can evaluate all things with spiritual insight. And they cannot be properly judged by those without the Spirit, because unspiritual people do not understand spiritual things.

“*“For who has known the mind of the Lord that he should instruct him?” But we have Christ’s mind*” (*v. 16*). Paul quotes *Isaiah 40:13*. No one can instruct God or fully know His mind. Yet believers “have Christ’s mind.” Through the Spirit, believers share in Christ’s way of thinking. They can understand God’s purposes as revealed in Christ.

Paul’s words would also challenge the Corinthians. They considered themselves “spiritual,” but in the next chapter, Paul tells them they are still acting like “fleshly” people because of their jealousy and quarreling (*3:1–3*). Truly spiritual people show it by their humility and love.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show why some people cannot understand the gospel. It is not because the gospel is irrational, but because spiritual truth requires spiritual perception. Paul writes, “*in whom the god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelieving*” (*2 Corinthians 4:4*). Only the Spirit can open blind eyes.

They also show the privilege of believers. Believers have the mind of Christ. This does not mean they know everything or are never wrong. It means that through the Spirit, they can understand God’s truth, see things from His perspective, and grow in wisdom.

Finally, these verses show that spiritual maturity is measured by Christlikeness. Having the mind of Christ means thinking as He thinks: humble, loving, self-giving. Paul writes, “*Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus*” (*Philippians 2:5*), and then describes Christ’s humility.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses help believers be patient with those who do not understand the gospel. Spiritual truth may seem foolish to someone without the Spirit. Believers can pray for God to open their eyes rather than becoming frustrated.

They also encourage believers to rely on the Spirit for understanding. When believers read Scripture or face decisions, they can ask the Spirit to help them think with the mind of Christ.

Finally, these verses call believers to develop the mind of Christ. Believers can examine their thoughts and attitudes, asking whether they reflect Christ’s humility, love, and wisdom. Growing in the mind of Christ is a lifelong process.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*1 Corinthians 2* calls believers to keep Jesus Christ and Him crucified at the center of their faith and witness. Paul deliberately chose simplicity over eloquence so that the cross would not be emptied of its power. Believers today can resist the temptation to rely on impressive techniques or personalities, and instead point people clearly to Christ and His cross.

The chapter also shows that God works through weakness. Paul came to Corinth in weakness, fear, and trembling, yet God’s Spirit worked powerfully through him. Believers who feel inadequate can trust that God’s power is displayed in their weakness, and that faith built on God’s power is secure.

*1 Corinthians 2* teaches that God’s wisdom is revealed by the Holy Spirit. What no eye has seen and no ear has heard, God has revealed to those who love Him. Believers can depend on the Spirit to understand Scripture and God’s purposes, and they can live with hope, knowing that God has prepared things beyond imagination for those who love Him.

Finally, the chapter shows that believers have the mind of Christ. People without the Spirit may find the gospel foolish, but believers can understand spiritual truths through the Spirit. Believers can be patient with those who do not yet understand, and they can grow in thinking as Christ thinks, with humility, love, and wisdom.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, help me to keep You and Your cross at the center of my life. Like Paul, I want to know nothing except Jesus Christ and Him crucified. When I feel weak, afraid, or inadequate, remind me that Your power is made perfect in weakness. Let my faith rest not on human wisdom or impressive personalities but on the power of God. Holy Spirit, thank You for revealing the deep things of God. Open my mind and heart to understand Your word. Thank You for the wonderful things You have prepared for those who love You, things no eye has seen and no ear has heard. Help me to love You more. Give me the mind of Christ, so that I may think as He thinks and live as He lived. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
