1 Corinthians · Chapter 3 of 16

# 1 Corinthians — Chapter 3

Chapter Theme: God’s Field, God’s Building, God’s Temple

[Read 1 Corinthians 3 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/1CO03.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul tells the Corinthians that their jealousy and quarreling show they are still spiritually immature, like infants who need milk. Leaders such as Paul and Apollos are only servants; one plants and another waters, but God gives the growth. The church is God’s field and God’s building, and its only foundation is Jesus Christ. Each worker must build carefully, because the quality of every person’s work will be tested by fire on the day of judgment. The church is also God’s holy temple, where His Spirit dwells, and anyone who destroys it will face God’s judgment. So no one should boast in human leaders, because all things belong to believers, and they belong to Christ.

## Chapter Background and Story

In chapters 1–2, Paul contrasted the wisdom of the world with the wisdom of God revealed in the cross and made known by the Spirit. He ended chapter 2 by saying that “*we have Christ’s mind*” (*1 Corinthians 2:16*). The Corinthians probably liked that idea; they considered themselves spiritually advanced. Now Paul brings them down to earth. Their divisions over leaders show that they are not as spiritual as they think.

Paul uses three images for the church in this chapter: a field, a building, and a temple. Each image shows that the church belongs to God, not to any human leader, and that leaders are simply God’s servants.

### Spiritual Infants (*3:1–4*)

Paul’s diagnosis of the Corinthians’ condition is studied below.

### Servants Through Whom You Believed (*3:5–9*)

“*Who then is Apollos, and who is Paul, but servants through whom you believed, and each as the Lord gave to him?*” (*v. 5*) Paul and Apollos were not rivals or heads of competing parties. They were “servants” (diakonoi), people who wait on others. Each did the task the Lord assigned. The image of planting and watering is studied below.

“*Now he who plants and he who waters are the same, but each will receive his own reward according to his own labor*” (*v. 8*). Paul and Apollos had a common purpose. They were not competitors but partners. Each would be rewarded by God for faithful work.

“*For we are God’s fellow workers. You are God’s farming, God’s building*” (*v. 9*). Paul and Apollos work together with God, or as God’s co-workers. The church belongs to God: it is His field, which He cultivates, and His building, which He constructs.

### The Foundation and the Building (*3:10–15*)

Paul shifts from the farming image to a building image. “*According to the grace of God which was given to me, as a wise master builder I laid a foundation, and another builds on it. But let each man be careful how he builds on it*” (*v. 10*). Paul laid the foundation when he founded the church in Corinth. Others, like Apollos and later teachers, built on it. Each must be careful. The foundation and the testing of the work are studied below.

### God’s Temple (*3:16–17*)

Paul then uses his third image, the church as God’s temple, studied below.

### Don’t Boast in Men (*3:18–23*)

“*Let no one deceive himself. If anyone thinks that he is wise among you in this world, let him become a fool that he may become wise*” (*v. 18*). Those who think they are wise by the world’s standards need to humble themselves and accept God’s “foolish” message of the cross. Only then will they find true wisdom.

“*For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. For it is written, “He has taken the wise in their craftiness.”*” (*v. 19*) Paul quotes *Job 5:13*, and then *Psalm 94:11*: “*The Lord knows the reasoning of the wise, that it is worthless*” (*v. 20*).

“*Therefore let no one boast in men. For all things are yours*” (*v. 21*). The Corinthians were saying, “I belong to Paul,” or “I belong to Apollos.” Paul turns this upside down. They do not belong to these leaders; the leaders belong to them. “*whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas, or the world, or life, or death, or things present, or things to come. All are yours*” (*v. 22*). Every leader, every gift, even the whole world, life and death, present and future, all serve the good of believers. Why limit themselves to one leader when all God’s servants are given for their benefit?

“*and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s*” (*v. 23*). Believers belong to Christ, and Christ belongs to God. This is the true chain of belonging. Believers do not belong to human leaders; they belong to Christ.

## Important Verses Explained

### *1 Corinthians 3:1–3* — Still Infants in Christ

> *“Brothers, I couldn’t speak to you as to spiritual, but as to fleshly, as to babies in Christ. I fed you with milk, not with solid food, for you weren’t yet ready. Indeed, you aren’t ready even now, for you are still fleshly. For insofar as there is jealousy, strife, and factions among you, aren’t you fleshly, and don’t you walk in the ways of men?”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 3:1–3* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had just told the Corinthians that spiritual people understand God’s wisdom and have the mind of Christ. The Corinthians may have thought, “That’s us! We are spiritual.” But Paul quickly corrected them.

“*Brothers, I couldn’t speak to you as to spiritual, but as to fleshly, as to babies in Christ*” (*v. 1*). When Paul first came to Corinth, he had to speak to them as “fleshly,” not yet mature, like babies. This was natural; they were new believers. Paul still calls them “brothers,” showing that they were genuine believers. But they were spiritually young.

“*I fed you with milk, not with solid food, for you weren’t yet ready*” (*v. 2*). Paul used the image of feeding a child. Babies need milk; they are not ready for solid food. Paul had given them the basic truths of the gospel, the “milk,” because they were not ready for deeper teaching.

“*Indeed, you aren’t ready even now*” (*v. 2*). The surprising part is that years later, they were still not ready. They should have grown, but they had remained infants.

“*for you are still fleshly. For insofar as there is jealousy, strife, and factions among you, aren’t you fleshly, and don’t you walk in the ways of men?*” (*v. 3*) Paul gives the evidence of their immaturity: jealousy and quarreling. These behaviors are signs of living by the flesh, by sinful human nature, rather than by the Spirit. They were acting “in the ways of men,” like people who do not know God.

The Corinthians thought they were advanced because of their spiritual gifts and knowledge. But Paul measures maturity differently. Spiritual maturity is shown not by gifts or knowledge, but by love, humility, and unity.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that spiritual maturity is measured by character, not by gifts or knowledge. The Corinthians had many gifts (*1:7*), yet they were immature because of their jealousy and quarreling. Paul later writes that without love, even the greatest gifts are worthless (*13:1–3*).

They also show that believers are meant to grow. Just as babies should grow into adults, believers should grow into maturity in Christ. Hebrews makes a similar point: “*For although by this time you should be teachers, you again need to have someone teach you the rudiments of the first principles of the revelations of God*” (*Hebrews 5:12*). Growth is the normal path of the Christian life.

Finally, these verses show that division is a sign of immaturity. When believers fight over leaders, preferences, or status, they show that they are still living by worldly values. Mature believers seek unity and peace.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses invite believers to evaluate their own maturity. Believers can ask themselves whether their lives show jealousy, quarreling, and division, or love, humility, and unity. These qualities reveal true spiritual maturity more than knowledge or gifts.

They also encourage believers to keep growing. No believer should remain an infant. Believers can grow by studying Scripture, praying, obeying God, and learning from mature believers.

Finally, these verses remind leaders to be patient with those who are spiritually young. Paul adjusted his teaching to the Corinthians’ level of maturity. Teachers and mentors can meet people where they are while encouraging them to grow.

### *1 Corinthians 3:6–7* — God Gives the Growth

> *“I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase. So then neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 3:6–7* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The Corinthians were dividing into groups around different leaders, especially Paul and Apollos. Some preferred Paul, the founder of the church; others preferred Apollos, the eloquent teacher. Paul wanted them to understand the true role of these leaders.

He used an image from farming: “*I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase*” (*v. 6*). Paul had “planted” the church in Corinth, preaching the gospel there first and seeing people come to faith. Apollos had “watered,” coming later and teaching and strengthening the believers. Both had important roles. But neither could make anything grow. Only God gives growth.

Anyone who has grown a garden understands this. A gardener can plant seeds and water them faithfully, but the gardener cannot make the seeds sprout or grow. Life and growth come from God.

“*So then neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase*” (*v. 7*). Paul draws the conclusion. Compared to God, the planter and the waterer are nothing. They are simply servants. All the credit belongs to God.

This was a direct challenge to the Corinthians’ factions. If Paul and Apollos were simply servants, and God was the one who gave the growth, then it made no sense to divide over them. Believers should honor God, not human leaders.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that God is the source of all spiritual growth. Human efforts are important, since God uses people to plant and water, but the life-giving power belongs to God alone. Jesus told a parable about a farmer who scatters seed, and the seed grows “*he doesn’t know how*” (*Mark 4:27*).

They also show the humility that should mark Christian leaders. Paul, a great apostle, called himself “nothing” compared to God. Leaders should not seek glory for themselves but point people to God.

Finally, these verses show that different ministries work together. Planting and watering are both necessary. Different leaders have different roles, but they serve the same purpose. Paul writes, “he who plants and he who waters are the same” (*3:8*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses free believers from the pressure to produce results. Believers who share the gospel, teach, or serve may feel responsible for whether people grow. Paul reminds them that God gives the growth. Their job is to plant and water faithfully.

They also encourage believers who serve in less visible roles. Some plant; others water. Both are essential. Believers who serve faithfully behind the scenes are as important as those whose work is more visible.

Finally, these verses call believers to give God the glory. When churches grow or lives are changed, believers can thank God rather than exalting human leaders.

### *1 Corinthians 3:11–13* — The Foundation and the Testing Fire

> *“For no one can lay any other foundation than that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ. But if anyone builds on the foundation with gold, silver, costly stones, wood, hay, or straw, each man’s work will be revealed. For the Day will declare it, because it is revealed in fire; and the fire itself will test what sort of work each man’s work is.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 3:11–13* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had compared himself to a master builder who laid the foundation of the Corinthian church. Others were building on that foundation. He warned that each person must be careful how they build.

“*For no one can lay any other foundation than that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ*” (*v. 11*). The foundation of the church is Jesus Christ. There is no other foundation. Everything in the church must rest on Him: His person, His death and resurrection, His teaching. Any church built on another foundation is not truly a church.

“*But if anyone builds on the foundation with gold, silver, costly stones, wood, hay, or straw*” (*v. 12*). Paul describes different building materials. Gold, silver, and costly stones are valuable and durable; they survive fire. Wood, hay, and straw are cheap and burn easily. These materials represent the quality of work done in the church, the teaching, ministry, and influence of those who build. Some work is valuable and lasting; some is worthless and temporary.

“*each man’s work will be revealed. For the Day will declare it, because it is revealed in fire; and the fire itself will test what sort of work each man’s work is*” (*v. 13*). “The Day” refers to the day of judgment, when Christ returns. On that day, every person’s work will be tested by fire. Fire reveals the true quality of materials. Gold survives; straw is consumed.

Paul continues: “*If any man’s work remains which he built on it, he will receive a reward*” (*v. 14*). “*If any man’s work is burned, he will suffer loss, but he himself will be saved, but as through fire*” (*v. 15*). This passage is about believers who build on the foundation of Christ. Their salvation is not in question. But the quality of their work will be revealed. Those who built well will receive a reward; those who built poorly will lose their reward, though they themselves will be saved, like someone escaping a burning house.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that Christ is the only foundation for faith and the church. Peter writes, “*Behold, I lay in Zion a chief cornerstone, chosen and precious: He who believes in him will not be disappointed*” (*1 Peter 2:6*). Every true work of God rests on Christ.

They also show that believers will give an account for their work. Salvation is by grace, but believers’ service will be evaluated. Paul writes, “*For we must all be revealed before the judgment seat of Christ; that each one may receive the things in the body according to what he has done, whether good or bad*” (*2 Corinthians 5:10*).

Some traditions, especially the Roman Catholic Church, have connected this passage with the doctrine of purgatory, a state of purification after death. Many other Christians understand the passage as referring to the evaluation of believers’ works at Christ’s return, not to a period of purification. All agree that the passage teaches accountability for how believers build on the foundation of Christ.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to build their lives and ministries on Christ alone. Believers can examine whether their faith, teaching, and service are truly grounded in Him.

They also encourage believers to do work that lasts. Believers can ask whether their efforts are aimed at things of eternal value, such as faithful teaching, genuine love, and Christlike character, or at things that will not survive the test, such as self-promotion or shallow results.

Finally, these verses remind church leaders of their responsibility. Those who teach and lead will give an account for how they have built. Leaders can be careful to teach truth, serve faithfully, and build up the church with lasting materials.

### *1 Corinthians 3:16–17* — You Are God’s Temple

> *“Don’t you know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit lives in you? If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy him; for God’s temple is holy, which you are.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 3:16–17* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had compared the church to a field and a building. Now he uses a third, even more powerful image: “*Don’t you know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit lives in you?*” (*v. 16*)

In the ancient world, a temple was the dwelling place of a god. In Israel, the temple in Jerusalem was where God’s presence dwelt among His people. It was the holiest place on earth. Now Paul tells the Corinthians that they, the church, are God’s temple. God does not live in a building made of stones but in His people.

The word “you” is plural here. Paul is speaking about the whole church community, not individual believers. (In 6:19, he applies the same image to the individual believer’s body.) The church as a community is where God’s Spirit dwells.

“*If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy him*” (*v. 17*). This is a serious warning. In context, those who “destroy” God’s temple are those who damage the church through division, false teaching, or worldly behavior. The Corinthians’ factions were tearing God’s temple apart. God takes this seriously.

“*for God’s temple is holy, which you are*” (*v. 17*). God’s temple is holy, set apart for Him. Because the church is God’s temple, it is holy. This holiness is both a gift and a calling. The church belongs to God and must be treated with reverence.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show the incredible privilege of the church. God’s presence, once limited to the tabernacle and the temple in Jerusalem, now dwells in His people by the Holy Spirit. Paul writes, “*in whom the whole building, fitted together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord*” (*Ephesians 2:21*), “*in whom you also are built together for a habitation of God in the Spirit*” (*Ephesians 2:22*).

They also show how seriously God takes the unity and holiness of the church. Damaging the church is not a small matter. It is an attack on God’s dwelling place. This should cause believers to treat the church with great care.

Finally, these verses show that the church is more than a human organization. It is a spiritual reality, the dwelling place of God. When believers gather, God is present among them in a special way.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses call believers to treat the church with reverence. The church is God’s temple. Believers can honor it by protecting its unity, guarding its teaching, and living holy lives.

They also warn against harming the church. Gossip, division, false teaching, and selfish behavior can damage God’s temple. Believers can examine whether their words and actions build up or tear down the church.

Finally, these verses encourage believers to value gathering together. When believers meet, they are God’s temple, and His Spirit dwells among them. Believers can gather with expectation, aware of God’s presence.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*1 Corinthians 3* teaches that spiritual maturity is measured by love and unity, not by gifts or knowledge. The Corinthians were gifted, but their jealousy and quarreling showed that they were still infants. Believers can examine their own lives, asking whether they show the marks of maturity, and can commit themselves to growing in Christ.

The chapter also shows that leaders are servants, and God gives the growth. Paul planted, Apollos watered, but God made the church grow. Believers can stop dividing over human leaders and give all the glory to God. Those who serve can do so faithfully, trusting God for the results.

*1 Corinthians 3* teaches that Jesus Christ is the only foundation, and that each person’s work will be tested by fire. Believers can build their lives and ministries on Christ alone, using materials that last: faithful teaching, genuine love, and Christlike character. They will give an account for how they have built.

Finally, the chapter declares that the church is God’s holy temple, where His Spirit dwells. Believers can treat the church with reverence, protecting its unity and holiness. And they can remember that they belong not to any human leader but to Christ, and that in Him, all things are theirs.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord God, forgive me for the times I have acted like a spiritual infant, with jealousy, quarreling, and division. Help me to grow up in Christ, so that my life shows love, humility, and unity. Thank You for the leaders You have given Your church; help me to honor them as Your servants, without dividing over them. Thank You that You give the growth. Help me to plant and water faithfully, trusting You for the results. Lord Jesus, You are the only foundation. Help me to build my life on You with materials that will last. Holy Spirit, thank You for dwelling in Your church as Your temple. Help me to treat Your church with reverence and to protect its unity and holiness. Thank You that all things are mine because I belong to Christ, and Christ belongs to You. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

1 Corinthians · Chapter 4 of 16

# 1 Corinthians — Chapter 4

Chapter Theme: Faithful Stewards, Humble Hearts, and a Father’s Love

[Read 1 Corinthians 4 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/1CO04.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul tells the Corinthians to regard him and Apollos as servants of Christ and stewards of God’s mysteries, who must above all be faithful. He does not rely on human judgment or even his own, but on the Lord, who will reveal the motives of every heart when He comes. Paul confronts the Corinthians’ pride by reminding them that everything they have is a gift, and he contrasts their imagined status with the apostles’ humble suffering as fools for Christ. Writing not to shame them but as a loving father, he urges them to imitate him, sends Timothy to remind them of his ways in Christ, and warns that God’s kingdom is a matter of power, not talk.

## Chapter Background and Story

*1 Corinthians 4* concludes Paul’s long discussion of divisions in the church (chapters 1–4). The Corinthians had been comparing leaders, judging them by worldly standards, and boasting about their favorites. Some had also begun to criticize Paul, perhaps saying that he was less impressive than Apollos or that he was not coming back to Corinth.

Paul responds by explaining how leaders should be viewed, by exposing the Corinthians’ pride, and by appealing to them as their spiritual father. The chapter moves from sharp irony to tender affection, revealing both Paul’s frustration and his deep love for this church.

### Servants and Stewards (*4:1–5*)

Paul’s description of leaders as servants and stewards is studied below, as is his teaching on judgment. Paul says, “*But with me it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you, or by a human court. Yes, I don’t even judge my own self*” (*v. 3*). Paul was not overly concerned about the Corinthians’ opinion of him. He did not even trust his own judgment of himself. “*For I know nothing against myself. Yet I am not justified by this, but he who judges me is the Lord*” (*v. 4*). Paul’s conscience was clear, but a clear conscience did not prove he was innocent. Only the Lord’s judgment counted.

### Do Not Be Puffed Up (*4:6–13*)

Paul explains that he has applied these things to himself and Apollos as an example, “*that in us you might learn not to think beyond the things which are written, that none of you be puffed up against one another*” (*v. 6*). The phrase “*not to think beyond the things which are written*” (*v. 6*) may have been a familiar saying, urging believers to stay within the boundaries of Scripture and not go beyond it in pride. Paul’s piercing questions about gifts are studied below.

Paul then uses biting irony: “*You are already filled. You have already become rich. You have come to reign without us*” (*v. 8*). The Corinthians acted as if they had already arrived spiritually, as if they were already reigning like kings in God’s kingdom. Paul wishes it were true, so that he could reign with them!

Then he contrasts their imagined glory with the apostles’ reality: “*For I think that God has displayed us, the apostles, last of all, like men sentenced to death. For we are made a spectacle to the world, both to angels and men*” (*v. 9*). The image comes from a Roman triumphal procession, where captured prisoners condemned to death were displayed at the end of the parade, or from the arena, where condemned criminals fought to the death for public entertainment.

“*We are fools for Christ’s sake, but you are wise in Christ. We are weak, but you are strong. You have honor, but we have dishonor*” (*v. 10*). Paul’s irony is sharp. The Corinthians considered themselves wise, strong, and honored. The apostles were considered fools, weak, and disgraced.

Paul describes the apostles’ life: “*Even to this present hour we hunger, thirst, are naked, are beaten, and have no certain dwelling place*” (*v. 11*). “*We toil, working with our own hands. When people curse us, we bless. Being persecuted, we endure*” (*v. 12*). “*Being defamed, we entreat. We are made as the filth of the world, the dirt wiped off by all, even until now*” (*v. 13*). The words “filth” and “dirt wiped off” describe the scrapings and garbage people throw away. Yet in this humility, the apostles followed the way of Jesus, who blessed those who cursed Him and endured suffering.

### A Father’s Appeal (*4:14–21*)

Paul’s tone changes completely: “*I don’t write these things to shame you, but to admonish you as my beloved children*” (*v. 14*). His harsh words came from love. His appeal as their spiritual father is studied below.

Paul sent Timothy to them, “*who is my beloved and faithful child in the Lord, who will remind you of my ways which are in Christ, even as I teach everywhere in every assembly*” (*v. 17*). Timothy would remind them of Paul’s teaching and example, which were the same in every church.

Some in Corinth were arrogant, acting as if Paul would never come back. Paul assured them, “*But I will come to you shortly, if the Lord is willing. And I will know, not the word of those who are puffed up, but the power*” (*v. 19*). Paul would test whether their claims were backed by real spiritual power. “*For God’s Kingdom is not in word, but in power*” (*v. 20*). God’s kingdom is not about impressive talk but about the transforming power of God in people’s lives.

“*What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love and a spirit of gentleness?*” (*v. 21*) Paul gave them a choice. If they repented, he would come with gentleness. If not, he would come with discipline. Like a loving father, Paul preferred gentleness, but he was willing to discipline if necessary.

## Important Verses Explained

### *1 Corinthians 4:1–2* — Stewards Must Be Faithful

> *“So let a man think of us as Christ’s servants and stewards of God’s mysteries. Here, moreover, it is required of stewards that they be found faithful.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 4:1–2* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The Corinthians had been comparing and ranking their leaders, Paul, Apollos, and Peter, as if they were celebrities. Paul wanted them to understand how leaders should really be viewed.

“*So let a man think of us as Christ’s servants*” (*v. 1*). The word translated “servants” here originally described rowers on the lower deck of a ship, workers who simply followed orders. It came to mean any subordinate servant. Paul and other leaders are servants of Christ. They do not have their own agenda; they serve their Master.

“*and stewards of God’s mysteries*” (*v. 1*). A “steward” was a household manager, often a trusted slave, who took care of the master’s property and household. The steward did not own the property; he managed it on behalf of the owner. Paul and other leaders are stewards of “God’s mysteries,” the truths of the gospel that God has revealed. They are entrusted with God’s message and must manage it faithfully.

“*Here, moreover, it is required of stewards that they be found faithful*” (*v. 2*). The most important quality of a steward is faithfulness. A steward does not need to be impressive, eloquent, or popular. He needs to be faithful, reliable, trustworthy, carrying out the master’s wishes.

This was a different standard from the one the Corinthians used. They judged leaders by eloquence, charisma, and impressive appearance. Paul says God judges by faithfulness.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that ministry is stewardship. Leaders do not own the gospel or the church; they manage what God has entrusted to them. Peter writes, “*As each has received a gift, employ it in serving one another, as good managers of the grace of God in its various forms*” (*1 Peter 4:10*).

They also show that faithfulness is what God values most. Jesus told the parable of the talents, in which the master praised his servants: “*Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things*” (*Matthew 25:21*). God does not measure success by human standards but by faithfulness.

Finally, these verses show that every believer is a steward. Not only leaders, but every believer has been entrusted with gifts, time, resources, and the gospel itself. All will give an account for how they have managed what God has given.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses help believers view leaders correctly. Pastors and teachers are not celebrities to be idolized or competitors to be ranked. They are servants and stewards who answer to Christ. Believers can honor them while remembering that they are accountable to God.

They also encourage leaders to focus on faithfulness rather than popularity. Leaders can ask not “Am I impressive?” but “Am I faithful to what God has entrusted to me?”

Finally, these verses remind every believer of their stewardship. Believers can ask how faithfully they are managing their time, money, gifts, relationships, and opportunities to share the gospel. Faithfulness in small things matters to God.

### *1 Corinthians 4:5* — Judge Nothing Before the Time

> *“Therefore judge nothing before the time, until the Lord comes, who will both bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of the hearts. Then each man will get his praise from God.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 4:5* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had said that he was not concerned about being judged by the Corinthians or by any human court. He did not even judge himself, because although his conscience was clear, that did not make him innocent. The Lord is the one who judges.

“*Therefore judge nothing before the time, until the Lord comes*” (*v. 5*). The Corinthians had been passing judgment on their leaders, comparing them and declaring some better than others. Paul tells them to stop. It is not their place to make final judgments about the worth of God’s servants. That judgment belongs to the Lord, and it will happen when He returns.

“*who will both bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of the hearts*” (*v. 5*). When the Lord comes, He will reveal everything. Hidden things will be brought into the light. He will expose the motives of every heart. Human beings can see only outward actions; God sees the heart.

“*Then each man will get his praise from God*” (*v. 5*). This is a surprising and encouraging conclusion. Paul does not say “each will receive condemnation,” but “*each man will get his praise from God*” (*v. 5*). For faithful servants, the day of judgment will be a day of commendation. God will recognize and praise what was done faithfully, even what was hidden from human eyes.

This verse does not forbid all evaluation. Elsewhere, Paul calls the church to judge sin within the community (*5:12*) and to test teaching (*1 Thessalonians 5:21*). But it forbids the kind of final, condemning judgment of other people’s worth and motives that only God can make.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that only God can judge the heart. Humans see the outside; God sees the inside. Samuel was told, “*For man looks at the outward appearance, but the LORD looks at the heart*” (*1 Samuel 16:7*). Believers cannot fully know others’ motives, and they should not presume to.

It also shows that God will bring justice. Nothing hidden will remain hidden. Those who have served faithfully in secret will be recognized, and those who have hidden wrongdoing will be exposed. Jesus said, “*For nothing is hidden that will not be revealed, nor anything secret that will not be known and come to light*” (*Luke 8:17*).

Finally, the verse brings hope. God’s judgment is not only about punishment. For faithful believers, it includes praise. God delights to commend His servants.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse calls believers to stop passing final judgment on others. It is easy to assume the worst about people’s motives or to rank others as better or worse. Believers can leave the judgment of hearts to God.

It also encourages believers who feel misjudged. When others criticize or misunderstand them, believers can remember that God sees their hearts and will reveal the truth.

Finally, the verse encourages believers to serve faithfully, even in secret. God sees what others do not see, and He will praise faithfulness. Believers do not need human recognition; they can wait for God’s commendation.

### *1 Corinthians 4:7* — What Do You Have That You Did Not Receive?

> *“For who makes you different? And what do you have that you didn’t receive? But if you did receive it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 4:7* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The Corinthians were proud. They boasted about their favorite leaders, their spiritual gifts, their knowledge, and their wisdom. They were “puffed up,” inflated with self-importance, looking down on one another.

Paul asks three piercing questions.

“*For who makes you different?*” (*v. 7*) Who decided that you are better than others? What gives you the right to consider yourself superior? The answer implied is: no one. If there is any difference between believers, it is God’s doing, not theirs.

“*And what do you have that you didn’t receive?*” (*v. 7*) This question goes to the heart of human pride. Everything believers have, their life, abilities, opportunities, spiritual gifts, faith, and salvation, came from God. They received it as a gift. They did not create it themselves.

“*But if you did receive it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?*” (*v. 7*) If everything is a gift, why boast as if it were an achievement? Boasting about a gift makes no sense. It would be like a child boasting about a present they received, as if they had made it themselves.

These questions demolish pride. No one can boast before God, because everything is grace.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that everything is a gift from God. James writes, “*Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights*” (*James 1:17*). Life, breath, talents, opportunities, and salvation itself all come from God.

It also shows that pride is a form of forgetfulness. Proud people forget that what they have came from God. Humility is simply remembering the truth: everything is grace.

Finally, the verse shows that gifts are meant to lead to gratitude, not pride. When believers recognize that everything comes from God, their response should be thanksgiving and humble service, using their gifts to bless others.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse challenges believers to examine their hearts for pride. Believers can ask whether they take credit for things God has given them, such as their intelligence, abilities, success, or even spiritual growth.

It also encourages believers to respond to gifts with gratitude. Instead of boasting, believers can thank God for every good thing in their lives.

Finally, the verse helps believers treat others with respect. If everything is a gift, then no believer is inherently better than another. Believers can honor others’ gifts without envy and use their own gifts without pride.

### *1 Corinthians 4:15–16* — Imitate Me

> *“For though you have ten thousand tutors in Christ, you don’t have many fathers. For in Christ Jesus, I became your father through the Good News. I beg you therefore, be imitators of me.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 4:15–16* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had just used sharp irony to expose the Corinthians’ pride. Now his tone becomes tender. He explains that he wrote these hard words not to shame them but to warn them as his beloved children.

“*For though you have ten thousand tutors in Christ, you don’t have many fathers*” (*v. 15*). A “tutor” (paidagogos) was a slave in a wealthy household who supervised a child’s education and conduct. Children might have many tutors over the years, but only one father. The Corinthians had many teachers, perhaps more than they needed, but only one spiritual father.

“*For in Christ Jesus, I became your father through the Good News*” (*v. 15*). Paul had brought them to faith by preaching the gospel. In this sense, he was their spiritual father. He did not mean that he replaced God as Father, but that he had a unique role in their spiritual birth. His relationship with them was not that of a hired teacher but of a loving parent.

“*I beg you therefore, be imitators of me*” (*v. 16*). Children learn by imitating their parents. Paul urged the Corinthians to follow his example. This may seem proud, but Paul’s example was one of humility, service, and suffering for Christ, the very opposite of the Corinthians’ pride. He writes later, “*Be imitators of me, even as I also am of Christ*” (*1 Corinthians 11:1*). Paul was not asking them to imitate him instead of Christ, but to imitate him as he imitated Christ.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show the deep love that should mark spiritual leadership. Paul was not a distant teacher but a father who loved his children. His correction came from love. Hebrews says, “*For whom the Lord loves, he disciplines*” (*Hebrews 12:6*).

They also show the importance of example in discipleship. People learn not only from teaching but from seeing faith lived out. Paul did not only teach; he lived what he taught, and he invited others to follow his example.

Finally, these verses show that Christian maturity is passed on through relationships. Paul sent Timothy, his “beloved and faithful child,” to remind the Corinthians of his ways. Faith is often passed from one generation to the next through mentoring relationships.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage mature believers to invest in others. Believers can serve as spiritual mothers and fathers to younger believers, guiding them with love, patience, and example.

They also challenge believers to live in a way that others can imitate. Believers can ask whether their lives reflect Christ in a way that would help others grow if they followed their example.

Finally, these verses encourage believers to look for godly examples. Believers can find mature believers whose lives reflect Christ and learn from them, imitating their faith (*Hebrews 13:7*).

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*1 Corinthians 4* teaches that leaders are servants of Christ and stewards of God’s mysteries, and that what God requires most is faithfulness. Believers can view their leaders through this lens, honoring them as servants rather than idolizing them as celebrities. And every believer can see themselves as a steward, faithfully managing the gifts and opportunities God has given.

The chapter also warns against judging others before the time. Only the Lord sees the hidden motives of the heart, and He will reveal them when He comes. Believers can leave final judgment to God, trusting that He will bring justice and that faithful servants will receive His praise.

*1 Corinthians 4* exposes pride with a simple question: What do you have that you did not receive? Everything believers have is a gift from God. This truth leads to gratitude and humility. Paul’s description of the apostles’ suffering shows that following Christ often involves weakness, hardship, and dishonor in the world’s eyes, the opposite of the pride the Corinthians displayed.

Finally, the chapter shows Paul’s tender love as a spiritual father. His correction came from love, and he invited the Corinthians to imitate him as he imitated Christ. Believers can invest in younger believers as spiritual mothers and fathers, live in a way that others can follow, and remember that God’s kingdom is a matter not of talk but of transforming power.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for entrusting me with Your gospel and with the gifts You have given me. Help me to be a faithful steward, more concerned with faithfulness than with being impressive. Keep me from judging others before the time, and help me to leave the judgment of hearts to You. Thank You that You see what others do not see, and that You will praise those who serve You faithfully. Humble me, Lord. Remind me that everything I have, I have received from You. Turn my pride into gratitude. Give me the heart of Paul, who suffered for Your sake and blessed those who cursed him. Make me a spiritual father or mother to others, and help me to live in a way that others can imitate as I imitate You. Let my faith be not just in words but in Your power. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

1 Corinthians · Chapter 5 of 16

# 1 Corinthians — Chapter 5

Chapter Theme: A Holy Church: Discipline for Restoration and Christ Our Passover

[Read 1 Corinthians 5 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/1CO05.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul confronts a shocking case of sexual immorality that the Corinthian church has tolerated, a man living with his father’s wife, and rebukes the church for being proud instead of grieving. He instructs them to remove the man from their fellowship, handing him over to Satan with the hope that he will ultimately be saved. Using the image of yeast at Passover, Paul explains that tolerated sin spreads through the whole community, and that because Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed, the church must live in sincerity and truth. He clarifies that believers are not to withdraw from unbelievers in the world, but must not tolerate unrepentant, flagrant sin among those who claim to follow Christ.

## Chapter Background and Story

In chapters 1–4, Paul addressed the problem of divisions in the church. Now he turns to another serious problem: moral failure that the church was ignoring. Corinth was known for sexual immorality, and some believers apparently thought that Christian freedom meant they could live however they pleased. Others may have been so proud of their spiritual gifts and knowledge that they overlooked sin among them.

Paul’s instructions in this chapter are about church discipline, the process by which a church responds to a member who persists in serious, unrepentant sin. This is a difficult subject. Throughout history, church discipline has sometimes been misused harshly, and sometimes neglected entirely. Paul’s teaching shows that discipline is meant to protect the church’s holiness and, ultimately, to restore the sinner. Jesus Himself gave instructions for addressing sin within the community (*Matthew 18:15–17*), beginning privately and gently.

It is also important to note what this chapter does not teach. Church discipline is not a substitute for reporting crimes to proper authorities, and it must never be used to protect abusers or silence victims. In cases of abuse, the safety of the vulnerable comes first, and civil authorities must be involved (*Romans 13:1–4*).

### Shocking Immorality and Proud Tolerance (*5:1–5*)

Paul’s confrontation of this situation, and his instructions, are studied below.

### A Little Yeast (*5:6–8*)

The image of yeast and Christ as our Passover is studied below.

### Judging Those Inside, Not Outside (*5:9–13*)

Paul clarifies a misunderstanding about an earlier letter, studied below. He concludes, “*For what do I have to do with also judging those who are outside? Don’t you judge those who are within?*” (*v. 12*) “*But those who are outside, God judges. “Put away the wicked man from among yourselves.”*” (*v. 13*) Paul quotes a phrase that appears several times in Deuteronomy (*Deuteronomy 17:7*; *19:19*; *22:21*, 24). God’s people are responsible for holiness within their own community. People outside the church are under God’s judgment, not the church’s.

This chapter’s story has a hopeful sequel. Many interpreters believe that *2 Corinthians 2:5–11* refers to this same man. If so, the discipline worked. The man repented, and Paul urged the church to forgive him, comfort him, and reaffirm their love for him, “*lest by any means such a one should be swallowed up with his excessive sorrow*” (*2 Corinthians 2:7*). The goal of discipline is always restoration.

## Important Verses Explained

### *1 Corinthians 5:1–2* — Mourning Rather Than Pride

> *“It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you, and such sexual immorality as is not even named among the Gentiles, that one has his father’s wife. You are arrogant, and didn’t mourn instead, that he who had done this deed might be removed from among you.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 5:1–2* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had heard a report about the church in Corinth that shocked him. “*It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you, and such sexual immorality as is not even named among the Gentiles, that one has his father’s wife*” (*v. 1*). A man in the church was in a sexual relationship with his father’s wife, probably his stepmother. This was forbidden in the Law of Moses (*Leviticus 18:8*) and was considered shameful even in pagan Roman society, where such relationships were illegal. The Corinthian church was tolerating something that even unbelievers condemned.

Paul says that the woman was “his father’s wife,” not “his mother,” which suggests she was his stepmother. Paul does not address her, which suggests she was not a member of the church.

“*You are arrogant*” (*v. 2*). The church’s response made the problem worse. They were “arrogant,” puffed up. Perhaps they were proud of their tolerance, thinking that their freedom in Christ allowed anything. Perhaps they were so proud of their spiritual gifts that they ignored moral failures. Whatever the reason, their pride blinded them to the seriousness of sin.

“*and didn’t mourn instead, that he who had done this deed might be removed from among you*” (*v. 2*). Paul says they should have “mourned.” The right response to serious sin in the church is grief, the kind of sorrow people feel at a death. Instead of boasting, they should have grieved and taken action to remove the man from their fellowship.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that sin in the church is serious. The church is God’s holy temple (*3:16–17*). Tolerating serious, unrepentant sin damages the community and dishonors God.

They also show that pride can blind people to sin. The Corinthians were so focused on their own status that they did not see the danger in their midst. Pride often leads people to excuse sin, either in themselves or in others.

Finally, these verses show the right response to sin: grief. Sin should not be celebrated, excused, or ignored. It should be mourned. Jesus said, “*Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted*” (*Matthew 5:4*). Godly sorrow over sin leads to repentance and healing.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses challenge churches that ignore serious sin. Some churches avoid addressing sin because they fear conflict or want to appear tolerant. Paul’s words remind them that love sometimes requires confronting sin.

They also challenge believers to examine their own attitudes. Do they excuse sin in themselves or others? Do they feel grief over sin, or have they become indifferent? Believers can ask God to give them His heart toward sin.

Finally, these verses call for humility. The Corinthians’ pride kept them from seeing clearly. Believers can ask God to keep them humble, so that they can see sin for what it is and respond with sorrow and appropriate action.

### *1 Corinthians 5:5* — Delivered to Satan, That the Spirit May Be Saved

> *“you are to deliver such a one to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 5:5* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had told the Corinthians that they should have removed the immoral man from their fellowship. Now he gives specific instructions. When the church gathered in the name of the Lord Jesus, with Paul present in spirit and the power of the Lord among them, they were to take action.

“*you are to deliver such a one to Satan*” (*v. 5*). This is a strong expression. It means to remove the man from the fellowship of the church, putting him outside the community where God’s people gather and are protected. Outside the church is the world, which Paul elsewhere describes as under the influence of Satan (*2 Corinthians 4:4*; *1 John 5:19*). The man would no longer enjoy the protection and fellowship of God’s people.

“*for the destruction of the flesh*” (*v. 5*). This phrase has been understood in different ways. Some interpret “flesh” as the sinful nature: being removed from the church would lead the man to see the destructive results of his sin, so that his sinful desires would be “destroyed” through repentance. Others interpret it as physical suffering or illness that might result from being outside God’s protection, which could lead him to repentance. Either way, the purpose is redemptive.

“*that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus*” (*v. 5*). This is the ultimate goal. Paul hoped that the discipline would bring the man to repentance, so that he would be saved on the day of Christ’s return. The purpose of discipline was not to destroy the man but to save him.

This shows that church discipline, rightly practiced, is an act of love. Like a doctor who must sometimes cause pain to heal, the church sometimes must take difficult action for the good of the person who is in danger.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that the goal of discipline is restoration. Paul does not want the man to be lost; he wants him to be saved. Hebrews writes, “*All chastening seems for the present to be not joyous but grievous; yet afterward it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it*” (*Hebrews 12:11*).

It also shows the seriousness of being outside the church. The community of believers is a place of protection, fellowship, and spiritual nourishment. Being removed from it is a serious matter, meant to awaken a person to their danger.

Finally, the verse shows that discipline must be done with authority and care. Paul instructed the church to act “in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ” and “with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ.” Discipline is not about personal revenge or power; it is a solemn act done under Christ’s authority, with the goal of healing.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse reminds churches that discipline is sometimes necessary. When a member persists in serious, unrepentant sin, the church may need to take loving but firm action. This should be done carefully, following Jesus’ instructions in *Matthew 18:15–17*, beginning with private conversation and moving to more formal steps only if necessary.

It also reminds churches that discipline must always aim at restoration. The goal is never to punish or shame but to bring the person to repentance and back into fellowship. Churches can pray for those under discipline and welcome them back when they repent.

Finally, this verse warns against misusing discipline. Discipline should never be used to control people, silence those who raise legitimate concerns, or protect leaders from accountability. It should be practiced humbly, fairly, and in the spirit of Christ.

### *1 Corinthians 5:6–8* — Christ Our Passover

> *“Your boasting is not good. Don’t you know that a little yeast leavens the whole lump? Purge out the old yeast, that you may be a new lump, even as you are unleavened. For indeed Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed in our place. Therefore let’s keep the feast, not with old yeast, neither with the yeast of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 5:6–8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had instructed the Corinthians to remove the immoral man from their fellowship. Now he explains why this was so important, using an image from the Jewish Passover.

“*Your boasting is not good. Don’t you know that a little yeast leavens the whole lump?*” (*v. 6*) Yeast (or leaven) spreads through dough. Just a small amount can make a whole batch rise. Paul uses this image to show that tolerated sin spreads. If the church allowed this sin to continue, it would influence others and corrupt the whole community.

“*Purge out the old yeast, that you may be a new lump, even as you are unleavened*” (*v. 7*). Before Passover, Jewish families searched their homes and removed all yeast. During the Feast of Unleavened Bread that followed Passover, they ate bread made without yeast, remembering how Israel left Egypt in haste (*Exodus 12:15–20*). Paul tells the Corinthians to remove the “old yeast,” the sin in their midst, so that they can be a “new lump,” a fresh batch of dough. He adds, “even as you are unleavened.” In Christ, they had already been made new. Now they needed to live like it.

“*For indeed Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed in our place*” (*v. 7*). Here is the reason. At the first Passover, a lamb was sacrificed, and its blood protected Israel from judgment (*Exodus 12*). Christ is the true Passover lamb. He was sacrificed so that His people would be delivered from sin and judgment. Since Christ has been sacrificed, believers are now celebrating the feast, living in the new life He has given.

“*Therefore let’s keep the feast, not with old yeast, neither with the yeast of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth*” (*v. 8*). The whole Christian life is like a festival, a celebration of Christ’s sacrifice. Believers celebrate it not with the “yeast” of evil and wickedness, but with the “unleavened bread” of sincerity and truth, living honest and holy lives.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show the deep connection between Christ’s death and the Passover. Jesus was crucified at Passover time. John the Baptist called Him “*the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world*” (*John 1:29*). His blood delivers believers from judgment, just as the lamb’s blood delivered Israel in Egypt.

They also show that sin has a spreading influence. Sin is never purely private; it affects others. Paul writes elsewhere, “*A little yeast grows through the whole lump*” (*Galatians 5:9*). Churches and individuals must take sin seriously because of its power to spread.

Finally, these verses show that the Christian life is a celebration. Because Christ our Passover has been sacrificed, believers live in joy and freedom. Holiness is not a burden but a fitting way to celebrate the feast.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to remove “old yeast” from their lives. Believers can ask God to show them sinful attitudes and habits that need to be removed, knowing that these can spread and affect others.

They also encourage churches to take holiness seriously. Tolerating sin is not love; it allows sin to spread and harm the whole community. Churches can address sin with humility and grace, seeking the health of the whole body.

Finally, these verses invite believers to celebrate Christ’s sacrifice. Every day, believers can remember that Christ, their Passover, was sacrificed for them. They can live with sincerity and truth as an expression of joy and gratitude.

### *1 Corinthians 5:9–11* — Not Leaving the World

> *“I wrote to you in my letter to have no company with sexual sinners; yet not at all meaning with the sexual sinners of this world, or with the covetous and extortionists, or with idolaters, for then you would have to leave the world. But as it is, I wrote to you not to associate with anyone who is called a brother who is a sexual sinner, or covetous, or an idolater, or a slanderer, or a drunkard, or an extortionist. Don’t even eat with such a person.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 5:9–11* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had written an earlier letter to the Corinthians, which has not survived. In it, he had told them not to associate with sexually immoral people. Apparently, the Corinthians had misunderstood him.

“*I wrote to you in my letter to have no company with sexual sinners*” (*v. 9*). Some Corinthians may have thought Paul meant they should avoid all immoral people, including unbelievers. That would have been impossible in Corinth.

“*yet not at all meaning with the sexual sinners of this world, or with the covetous and extortionists, or with idolaters, for then you would have to leave the world*” (*v. 10*). Paul clarifies that he did not mean believers should cut themselves off from unbelievers. If they tried to avoid every immoral, greedy, dishonest, or idolatrous person in the world, they would have to leave the world entirely. Believers are called to live in the world and to be a light to it. Jesus Himself ate with tax collectors and sinners.

“*But as it is, I wrote to you not to associate with anyone who is called a brother who is a sexual sinner, or covetous, or an idolater, or a slanderer, or a drunkard, or an extortionist. Don’t even eat with such a person*” (*v. 11*). Paul’s instruction was about people who claim to be believers, “anyone who is called a brother,” but who persist in serious, unrepentant sin. Notice that the list includes not only sexual sins but also greed, idolatry, slander, drunkenness, and swindling. All these are serious.

“Don’t even eat with such a person” means not sharing close fellowship with them, including the fellowship meals of the church, which often included the Lord’s Supper. The goal was to make clear that their behavior was incompatible with following Christ, in the hope that they would repent.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that believers are called to be in the world but not of the world. Jesus prayed, “*I pray not that you would take them from the world, but that you would keep them from the evil one*” (*John 17:15*). Believers are not to withdraw from society but to be a holy presence within it.

They also show the difference between how the church relates to unbelievers and to those who claim to be believers. The church does not judge unbelievers; it loves them and shares the gospel with them. But within the church, believers are accountable to one another.

Finally, these verses show that a variety of sins are serious. Paul’s list includes greed, slander, and drunkenness alongside sexual immorality. Churches sometimes focus on certain sins while ignoring others. Paul’s list shows that all persistent, unrepentant sin is serious.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to engage with the world. Believers should not isolate themselves from unbelievers. They can build friendships, show love, and share the gospel with people of all kinds, just as Jesus did.

They also call believers to hold one another accountable. Within the church, believers are responsible to help one another live faithfully. This involves loving correction, encouragement, and, when necessary, discipline.

Finally, these verses warn against hypocrisy. Churches can be quick to condemn some sins while tolerating others, such as greed, gossip, and slander. Believers can take all sin seriously, beginning with their own.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*1 Corinthians 5* teaches that the church must take sin seriously. The Corinthian church tolerated shocking immorality and was even proud of its tolerance. Paul called them to mourn instead. Believers today can ask God to give them His heart toward sin: not indifference, not harsh condemnation, but grief that leads to repentance and healing.

The chapter also teaches that church discipline, rightly practiced, is an act of love aimed at restoration. Removing an unrepentant member from fellowship is a serious step, meant to awaken them to their danger and lead them back to God. Churches can practice discipline humbly and carefully, following Jesus’ teaching, praying for restoration, and welcoming back those who repent. Discipline must never be used to control, silence, or protect wrongdoers, and abuse must always be reported to proper authorities.

*1 Corinthians 5* reminds believers that Christ our Passover has been sacrificed. Because of His sacrifice, believers are a new lump, free from the old yeast of sin. Sin spreads like yeast, so believers can remove it from their lives and communities, celebrating Christ’s sacrifice with sincerity and truth.

Finally, the chapter clarifies that believers should not withdraw from unbelievers in the world. They are called to live among all kinds of people, showing love and sharing the gospel. Within the church, however, believers are accountable to one another. Believers can engage the world with love while holding one another to the standards of Christ, beginning with themselves.

## Chapter Prayer

Holy God, You are pure and righteous, and Your church is Your holy temple. Forgive me for the times I have excused sin, in myself or in others, or have been proud when I should have mourned. Give me Your heart toward sin, a heart that grieves and seeks healing. Help Your church to practice correction with humility, love, and wisdom, always aiming at restoration. Protect the vulnerable, and guard Your church from those who would misuse authority. Lord Jesus, thank You for being sacrificed as our Passover Lamb. Help me to remove the old yeast of sin from my life, and to celebrate Your sacrifice with sincerity and truth. Help me to live in the world as a light, loving those who do not know You, while walking faithfully with Your people. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
