1 Corinthians · Chapter 6 of 16

# 1 Corinthians — Chapter 6

Chapter Theme: Washed, Sanctified, Justified: Honoring God with the Body

[Read 1 Corinthians 6 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/1CO06.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul rebukes the Corinthians for taking disputes with fellow believers before pagan courts, reminding them that believers will one day judge the world and asking why they would not rather be wronged than harm their own brothers. He warns that those who persist in unrighteousness will not inherit God’s kingdom, but rejoices that some of them who once lived that way have been washed, sanctified, and justified in the name of Jesus and by the Spirit. Responding to slogans the Corinthians used to justify immorality, Paul teaches that the body belongs to the Lord, will be raised, and is united to Christ. He calls them to flee sexual immorality, because their bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit and they were bought with a price.

## Chapter Background and Story

*1 Corinthians 6* continues Paul’s response to problems in the Corinthian church. In chapter 5, he addressed a case of sexual immorality the church had tolerated. Now he addresses two more issues: lawsuits between believers and the misuse of Christian freedom to justify sexual sin.

The Corinthians had absorbed some of their culture’s attitudes. In Roman society, lawsuits were common, and wealthier people often used the courts to their advantage over the poor. Some Greek philosophies taught that the body was unimportant, or that what people did with their bodies did not affect their souls. Some Corinthians seem to have reasoned that because they were spiritual, physical actions, including sexual immorality, did not matter. Paul firmly rejects this thinking.

### Lawsuits Among Believers (*6:1–8*)

“*Dare any of you, having a matter against his neighbor, go to law before the unrighteous, and not before the saints?*” (*v. 1*) Paul is shocked that believers were suing one another in pagan courts. “*Don’t you know that the saints will judge the world? And if the world is judged by you, are you unworthy to judge the smallest matters?*” (*v. 2*) Believers will share in Christ’s judgment of the world at the end of the age (*Daniel 7:22*; *Matthew 19:28*; *Revelation 20:4*). If they will judge the world, surely they can settle small disputes among themselves. “*Don’t you know that we will judge angels? How much more, things that pertain to this life?*” (*v. 3*)

“*I say this to move you to shame. Isn’t there even one wise man among you who would be able to decide between his brothers?*” (*v. 5*) The Corinthians prided themselves on their wisdom, yet they could not find anyone wise enough to settle a dispute. Paul’s further rebuke is studied below.

### Who Will Inherit the Kingdom (*6:9–11*)

Paul’s warning and his words of hope are studied below.

### The Body Belongs to the Lord (*6:12–20*)

The Corinthians apparently had slogans that they used to justify their behavior. Paul quotes them and then corrects them. The first slogan is studied below. The second: “*“Foods for the belly, and the belly for foods,”*” (*v. 13*) Some Corinthians argued that just as the stomach is made for food, the body is made for sexual satisfaction, so sexual activity is as natural and unimportant as eating. Paul responds: “*but God will bring to nothing both it and them. But the body is not for sexual immorality, but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body*” (*v. 13*). The body is not merely a physical machine; it belongs to the Lord.

“*Now God raised up the Lord, and will also raise us up by his power*” (*v. 14*). The body matters to God because He will raise it. Christianity teaches the resurrection of the body, not merely the survival of the soul. What believers do with their bodies matters because their bodies have an eternal future.

“*Don’t you know that your bodies are members of Christ? Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? May it never be!*” (*v. 15*) Believers are united to Christ, body and spirit. Corinth was notorious for prostitution, some of it associated with pagan temples. To join one’s body to a prostitute would be to involve Christ in that union.

“*Or don’t you know that he who is joined to a prostitute is one body? For, “The two”, he says, “will become one flesh.”*” (*v. 16*) Paul quotes *Genesis 2:24*, God’s design for marriage. Sexual union creates a deep bond, a “one flesh” union, that God intended only for marriage. “*But he who is joined to the Lord is one spirit*” (*v. 17*). Believers have an even deeper union with Christ.

Paul’s command to flee immorality, and his teaching that the body is a temple, are studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *1 Corinthians 6:7–8* — Why Not Rather Be Wronged?

> *“Therefore it is already altogether a defect in you that you have lawsuits one with another. Why not rather be wronged? Why not rather be defrauded? No, but you yourselves do wrong and defraud, and that against your brothers.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 6:7–8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had been rebuking the Corinthians for taking their disputes with fellow believers to pagan courts. Lawsuits were common in Corinth, and they were often used by the powerful to take advantage of the weak. The Corinthian believers were bringing these practices into the church.

“*Therefore it is already altogether a defect in you that you have lawsuits one with another*” (*v. 7*). The very existence of lawsuits among believers was a failure. Even before considering who was right or wrong, the fact that believers were suing one another showed that something had gone wrong in their relationships. The word “defect” can also mean “defeat.” They had already lost, regardless of the court’s verdict.

“*Why not rather be wronged? Why not rather be defrauded?*” (*v. 7*) Paul asks a radical question. Would it not be better to accept being wronged or cheated than to take a fellow believer to court? This reflects Jesus’ teaching about turning the other cheek and giving up one’s coat (*Matthew 5:39–40*). Love is willing to suffer loss rather than harm a brother or sister.

“*No, but you yourselves do wrong and defraud, and that against your brothers*” (*v. 8*). Worse still, some of them were the ones doing the wronging and cheating, and they were doing it to their own spiritual family.

It is important to understand what Paul is addressing. He is speaking about civil disputes between believers over “the smallest matters” (*6:2*), things like property and money, which could be resolved within the church. He is not saying that crimes, such as abuse, violence, or serious fraud, should be hidden from civil authorities. In *Romans 13*, Paul teaches that governing authorities are God’s servants to punish wrongdoing. Victims of crime should be protected, and crimes should be reported. Paul’s concern here is believers using courts to pursue their own advantage against one another over everyday disputes.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that the church should be a place of reconciliation. Believers have access to God’s wisdom and are called to love one another. They should be able to resolve disputes in ways that reflect Christ’s love, rather than through adversarial lawsuits.

They also show the radical nature of Christian love. Love is willing to suffer loss for the sake of others. Jesus suffered the greatest wrong of all, yet He did not retaliate. Peter writes of Christ, “*When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. When he suffered, he didn’t threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously*” (*1 Peter 2:23*).

Finally, these verses show that public conflict between believers damages the church’s witness. When believers drag one another into court, unbelievers see a church that is no different from the world.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to resolve conflicts with fellow believers through conversation, reconciliation, and mediation, rather than through lawsuits, whenever possible. Many churches and Christian organizations offer mediation services to help believers settle disputes.

They also challenge believers to be willing to accept loss for the sake of peace. Believers can ask whether insisting on their rights is worth damaging a relationship or the church’s witness.

Finally, these verses must not be misused to silence victims. When someone has been abused, defrauded on a large scale, or harmed by criminal behavior, they should seek protection and justice through proper authorities. Paul’s teaching addresses believers seeking advantage over one another in ordinary disputes, not the covering up of crimes.

### *1 Corinthians 6:9–11* — Such Were Some of You

> *“Or don’t you know that the unrighteous will not inherit God’s Kingdom? Don’t be deceived. Neither the sexually immoral, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor male prostitutes, nor homosexuals, nor thieves, nor covetous, nor drunkards, nor slanderers, nor extortionists, will inherit God’s Kingdom. Some of you were such, but you were washed. You were sanctified. You were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and in the Spirit of our God.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 6:9–11* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had just said that some Corinthians were wronging and cheating their own brothers. Now he gives a serious warning.

“*Or don’t you know that the unrighteous will not inherit God’s Kingdom? Don’t be deceived*” (*v. 9*). Those who live in persistent, unrepentant sin will not inherit God’s kingdom. Paul says, “Don’t be deceived,” because some Corinthians apparently believed that how they lived did not matter.

Paul then lists types of behavior that characterize the unrighteous: “*Neither the sexually immoral, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor male prostitutes, nor homosexuals*” (*v. 9*), “*nor thieves, nor covetous, nor drunkards, nor slanderers, nor extortionists, will inherit God’s Kingdom*” (*v. 10*). The list includes sexual sins, idolatry, theft, greed, drunkenness, verbal abuse, and swindling. Notice how broad the list is. Greed and slander are listed alongside sexual sins.

The two Greek words translated “male prostitutes” and “homosexuals” in the World English Bible (malakoi and arsenokoitai) have been the subject of much discussion. Most Christian traditions throughout history have understood them as referring to the passive and active partners in male same-sex sexual relations, in line with *Leviticus 18:22* and *20:13*, from which the second word appears to be formed. Some modern interpreters have proposed narrower meanings, such as exploitative relationships. Whatever view one holds, the point of Paul’s list is that everyone is included in the need for God’s grace.

Then comes one of the most hopeful verses in the New Testament: “*Some of you were such, but you were washed. You were sanctified. You were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and in the Spirit of our God*” (*v. 11*). Some of the Corinthian believers had once lived in these ways. But they had been changed. Three words describe the change.

“Washed”: They had been cleansed from their sins. Their guilt and shame had been washed away.

“Sanctified”: They had been set apart as holy, belonging to God.

“Justified”: They had been declared righteous before God.

All this happened “in the name of the Lord Jesus, and in the Spirit of our God.” Salvation is the work of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that genuine faith leads to a changed life. Those who claim to follow Christ while persisting in unrepentant sin are deceiving themselves. Paul writes elsewhere, “*those who practice such things will not inherit God’s Kingdom*” (*Galatians 5:21*).

They also show the transforming power of the gospel. “*Some of you were such*” (*v. 11*). The Corinthian church included former idolaters, thieves, drunkards, swindlers, and people who had been involved in sexual sin of every kind. Christ had washed them clean. No sin is too great for His grace.

Finally, these verses show that past sins do not define believers. They “were” such people, but they are no longer. Their identity is now defined by what Christ has done: washed, sanctified, justified.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses warn believers against thinking that how they live does not matter. Grace is not permission to continue in sin. Believers can examine their lives and turn from any persistent sin.

They also bring hope to anyone burdened by their past. No matter what someone has done, Christ can wash them clean. Believers who struggle with shame over past sins can remember: “*Some of you were such, but you were washed*” (*v. 11*).

Finally, these verses call believers to humility and compassion. Every believer was once in need of washing. The church is not a group of people who never sinned; it is a community of sinners who have been forgiven. Believers can treat everyone, whatever their struggles, with dignity and compassion, offering the hope of the gospel rather than contempt.

### *1 Corinthians 6:12* — All Things Are Lawful, but Not All Are Helpful

> *“‘All things are lawful for me,’ but not all things are expedient. ‘All things are lawful for me,’ but I will not be brought under the power of anything.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 6:12* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The Corinthians had a slogan: “*“All things are lawful for me,”*” (*v. 12*). This may have originally come from Paul’s own teaching about freedom in Christ. Paul taught that believers are not saved by keeping the Law and are free from its ceremonial requirements. But some Corinthians twisted this teaching to mean that they could do anything they wanted, including sexual immorality.

Paul responds with two qualifications.

“*but not all things are expedient*” (*v. 12*). The word “expedient” means beneficial, helpful, or profitable. Even if something is permitted, it may not be good. Believers should ask not only “Is this allowed?” but “Is this helpful? Does it build me up and help others?”

“*“All things are lawful for me,” but I will not be brought under the power of anything*” (*v. 12*). Paul repeats the slogan and adds a second qualification. Even if something is permitted, believers should not let it control them. Freedom that leads to addiction or slavery is not true freedom. There is a wordplay in Greek: “All things are in my power, but I will not be put under the power of anything.”

Paul is not denying Christian freedom. He is showing that true freedom is not the right to do whatever one wants. True freedom is the ability to choose what is good and to remain free from slavery to anything.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that Christian freedom has limits. Believers are free from the Law as a way of salvation, but they are not free to sin. Paul writes, “*For you, brothers, were called for freedom. Only don’t use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love be servants to one another*” (*Galatians 5:13*).

It also shows that anything can become an idol or an addiction. Even good things, such as food, entertainment, work, or technology, can become masters if believers are not careful. True freedom means not being controlled by anything except Christ.

Finally, the verse shows the importance of wisdom in Christian living. The question is not merely “What is permitted?” but “What is wise, helpful, and edifying?”

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse helps believers make wise decisions. When considering an activity, believers can ask: Is it beneficial? Does it build me up? Does it help others? Could it control me?

It also encourages believers to examine areas where they may be losing their freedom. Habits involving screens, food, substances, shopping, or anything else can become masters. Believers can ask God for help in breaking free from anything that controls them.

Finally, the verse warns against using freedom as an excuse. Some people justify harmful behavior by saying, “I’m free in Christ.” True freedom in Christ leads to holiness, not license.

### *1 Corinthians 6:18–20* — Your Body Is a Temple of the Holy Spirit

> *“Flee sexual immorality! ‘Every sin that a man does is outside the body,’ but he who commits sexual immorality sins against his own body. Or don’t you know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God? You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. Therefore glorify God in your body and in your spirit, which are God’s.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 6:18–20* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had explained that believers’ bodies are members of Christ, and that sexual union with a prostitute would join Christ’s members to her. Now he gives a clear command.

“*Flee sexual immorality!*” (*v. 18*) Paul does not say “resist” or “manage” sexual immorality, but “flee” it. Run away from it, as Joseph ran from Potiphar’s wife (*Genesis 39:12*). Some temptations are best handled by getting away from them.

“*“Every sin that a man does is outside the body,” but he who commits sexual immorality sins against his own body*” (*v. 18*). This may be another Corinthian slogan that Paul quotes and corrects. Sexual sin is unique in that it involves the body in a deep way, uniting it with another person. It affects the whole person.

“*Or don’t you know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God?*” (*v. 19*) In chapter 3, Paul said that the church as a community is God’s temple. Here he applies the same image to the individual believer’s body. The Holy Spirit lives in each believer. The body is the place where God dwells.

“*You are not your own*” (*v. 19*), “*for you were bought with a price*” (*v. 20*). Believers do not belong to themselves. They were purchased, like slaves bought in a marketplace, but the price was the blood of Christ (*1 Peter 1:18–19*). They now belong to God.

“*Therefore glorify God in your body and in your spirit, which are God’s*” (*v. 20*). Because believers belong to God, they should honor Him with their bodies. (The words “and in your spirit, which are God’s” appear in some later manuscripts; the earliest end with “glorify God in your body.”) This includes sexual purity, but also every way believers use their bodies: what they eat, how they care for their health, how they work, and how they treat others.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that the body matters to God. Christianity is not a religion that despises the body. God created the body, Christ took on a human body, the Holy Spirit dwells in believers’ bodies, and believers will be raised in glorified bodies. The body is holy.

They also show that believers belong to God. They were bought with the price of Christ’s blood. This is both a humbling truth and a liberating one. Believers are not their own masters, but they belong to a loving God who paid the highest price for them.

Finally, these verses show God’s good design for sexuality. Sexual union is a powerful gift meant to unite husband and wife in a one-flesh relationship (*Genesis 2:24*). Outside of marriage, it damages the person and dishonors God. Believers who have sinned sexually can find forgiveness and healing in Christ (*1 Corinthians 6:11*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses call believers to sexual purity. Believers can flee situations, relationships, media, and thoughts that lead to sexual sin. Fleeing may mean setting boundaries, changing habits, or seeking accountability.

They also remind believers to care for their bodies as temples of the Holy Spirit. This includes physical health, rest, and avoiding substances that harm the body. Believers can honor God in how they treat their bodies.

Finally, these verses offer hope and dignity. Many people have been hurt or ashamed because of sexual sin, whether their own or others’ sins against them. The body that has been hurt is still a temple of the Holy Spirit. Christ offers forgiveness, healing, and restoration. Those who have been victims of sexual abuse bear no guilt for what was done to them; God sees their pain, and His people should offer them care and protection.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*1 Corinthians 6* calls believers to resolve disputes with one another in ways that reflect Christ’s love. Instead of using courts to gain advantage over fellow believers in ordinary disputes, believers can seek reconciliation and mediation, and can be willing to accept loss for the sake of peace. This never means hiding crimes or abuse, which must be reported to proper authorities.

The chapter also warns that those who persist in unrighteousness will not inherit God’s kingdom. Grace is not permission to sin. Yet the chapter offers great hope: “*Some of you were such, but you were washed. You were sanctified. You were justified*” (*v. 11*). No one is beyond the reach of Christ’s cleansing. Believers can treat others with compassion, remembering that they too have been washed.

*1 Corinthians 6* teaches that Christian freedom has limits. Not everything permitted is helpful, and believers should not be mastered by anything. Believers can make wise choices, asking whether something builds them up and keeps them free.

Finally, the chapter teaches that believers’ bodies belong to the Lord. They are members of Christ and temples of the Holy Spirit, bought with the price of Christ’s blood. Believers are called to flee sexual immorality and to glorify God with their bodies in every area of life, finding forgiveness and healing in Christ when they have failed.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You that though I was once lost in sin, I have been washed, sanctified, and justified in Your name and by Your Spirit. Thank You that my past does not define me. Help me to resolve conflicts with my brothers and sisters in love, and give me the grace to accept loss rather than harm others. Teach me to use my freedom wisely, asking what is helpful and refusing to be mastered by anything but You. Thank You that my body is a temple of the Holy Spirit and that I was bought with a price. Help me to flee sexual immorality and every temptation that would dishonor You. Heal those who carry shame or have been hurt, and let Your church be a place of compassion and restoration. Help me to glorify You with my body in all I do. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

1 Corinthians · Chapter 7 of 16

# 1 Corinthians — Chapter 7

Chapter Theme: Marriage, Singleness, and Serving the Lord in Every Calling

[Read 1 Corinthians 7 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/1CO07.htm)

Main Teaching

Responding to questions from the Corinthians, Paul affirms both marriage and singleness as good gifts from God. Within marriage, husband and wife belong to each other and should not deprive one another of intimacy, except by mutual agreement for a time of prayer. Paul wishes others could share his gift of singleness, which frees a person for undivided devotion to the Lord, but he says it is better to marry than to burn with desire. Passing on the Lord’s command, he teaches that married believers should not divorce, and that a believer married to an unbeliever should not leave if the unbeliever is willing to stay, though the believer is not bound if the unbeliever departs. Believers should serve God faithfully in whatever situation they were called, remembering that the present form of this world is passing away.

## Chapter Background and Story

With chapter 7, Paul begins answering questions the Corinthians had written to him. The phrase “Now concerning” introduces each new topic (*7:1*, 25; *8:1*; *12:1*; *16:1*, 12). The first questions concern marriage, sexual relations, singleness, divorce, and remarriage.

The Corinthian church faced pressures from two opposite directions. Some, as chapters 5 and 6 show, believed that sexual freedom was acceptable. Others seem to have gone to the opposite extreme, believing that sexual relations, even within marriage, were unspiritual. They may have been influenced by philosophies that saw the body and physical pleasure as inferior to the spirit. Some may have been considering abstaining from sex within marriage, or even divorcing their spouses in order to be more “spiritual.” Paul addresses both errors.

This chapter must be read carefully. Paul distinguishes between commands from the Lord (*7:10*), his own apostolic guidance (*7:12*, 25), and his personal preferences (*7:7*, 40). He also speaks in light of a particular “present distress” (*7:26*), which may refer to persecution, famine, or the general hardships of that time. And his teaching on marriage and divorce must be read alongside Jesus’ teaching (*Matthew 5:31–32*; *19:3–12*; *Mark 10:2–12*) and the rest of Scripture. Christians hold differing views on some questions this chapter raises, especially about divorce and remarriage.

One principle applies throughout: nothing in this chapter requires anyone to remain in a situation of abuse or danger. Scripture’s teaching on marriage assumes love, faithfulness, and the protection of each spouse (*Ephesians 5:25–29*). A person facing abuse should seek safety and help, and churches must protect them.

### Mutual Belonging in Marriage (*7:1–9*)

“*Now concerning the things about which you wrote to me: it is good for a man not to touch a woman*” (*v. 1*). Many interpreters believe this was a slogan from the Corinthians’ letter, which Paul quotes and then qualifies, as he did with the slogans in chapter 6. Some Corinthians were saying that it was best to avoid sexual relations entirely. Paul responds: “*But, because of sexual immoralities, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband*” (*v. 2*). Given the temptations around them, marriage is the right context for sexual desire. Paul’s teaching on mutual belonging is studied below, as is his teaching on singleness as a gift.

### Married Believers and Divorce (*7:10–16*)

Paul’s teaching for married believers, passing on the Lord’s command, is studied below. He then addresses mixed marriages, where one spouse had become a believer and the other had not. “*But to the rest I—not the Lord—say, if any brother has an unbelieving wife, and she is content to live with him, let him not leave her*” (*v. 12*). Paul speaks here with apostolic authority on a situation Jesus did not directly address during His earthly ministry. “*The woman who has an unbelieving husband, and he is content to live with her, let her not leave her husband*” (*v. 13*).

Some believers may have worried that being married to an unbeliever made them or their children unclean. Paul reassures them: “*For the unbelieving husband is sanctified in the wife, and the unbelieving wife is sanctified in the husband. Otherwise your children would be unclean, but now they are holy*” (*v. 14*). This does not mean the unbelieving spouse is saved automatically. It means that the marriage is not defiled, and the believing spouse’s presence brings God’s influence into the home. The children are not excluded from God’s people. Paul’s teaching about when the unbeliever leaves is studied below.

### Remain in Your Calling (*7:17–24*)

Paul then gives a general principle: “*Only, as the Lord has distributed to each man, as God has called each, so let him walk. So I command in all the assemblies*” (*v. 17*). Coming to faith does not require believers to change their outward circumstances. They can serve God where they are.

He applies this to circumcision: “*Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing, but what matters is keeping God’s commandments*” (*v. 19*). Ethnic identity markers do not make someone more or less acceptable to God.

He also applies it to slavery: “*Were you called being a bondservant? Don’t let that bother you, but if you get an opportunity to become free, use it*” (*v. 21*). Slavery was widespread in the Roman Empire. Paul encourages slaves not to despair, because their worth before God does not depend on their social status. But he also encourages them to gain freedom if they can. “*For he who was called in the Lord being a bondservant is the Lord’s free man. Likewise he who was called being free is Christ’s bondservant*” (*v. 22*). In Christ, a slave is spiritually free, and a free person is Christ’s servant. “*You were bought with a price. Don’t become bondservants of men*” (*v. 23*). Paul’s teaching contains the seeds that would later lead many Christians to oppose slavery entirely, recognizing that it is incompatible with the dignity of people redeemed by Christ (compare *Philemon 16*; *1 Timothy 1:10*, which condemns slave traders).

### Concerning the Unmarried (*7:25–40*)

“*Now concerning virgins, I have no commandment from the Lord, but I give my judgment as one who has obtained mercy from the Lord to be trustworthy*” (*v. 25*). Paul gives his advice to those who had never married. “*Therefore I think that because of the distress that is on us, it’s good for a man to remain as he is*” (*v. 26*). Because of the difficult times, Paul thought it wise to remain unmarried. But “*But if you marry, you have not sinned. If a virgin marries, she has not sinned*” (*v. 28*). Marriage is not sinful; it simply brings additional responsibilities and troubles in hard times.

“*But I say this, brothers: the time is short*” (*v. 29*). Believers should live with an awareness that this world is temporary. “*For the mode of this world passes away*” (*v. 31*). Marriage, sorrow, joy, buying, and using the world are all real, but none is ultimate. Believers should hold them loosely.

Paul explains his preference for singleness: “*He who is unmarried is concerned for the things of the Lord, how he may please the Lord*” (*v. 32*); “*but he who is married is concerned about the things of the world, how he may please his wife*” (*v. 33*). Married people rightly care about their spouses’ needs; this is not sinful but part of the calling of marriage. Unmarried people can focus more fully on the Lord. “*This I say for your own benefit, not that I may ensnare you, but for that which is appropriate, and that you may attend to the Lord without distraction*” (*v. 35*). Paul is not trying to restrict them but to help them serve the Lord wholeheartedly.

Verses 36–38 address a man and “his virgin,” which may refer to a father and his daughter or to an engaged couple. Either way, Paul says that marrying is good, and not marrying is also good, or even better in the present circumstances.

“*A wife is bound by law for as long as her husband lives; but if the husband is dead, she is free to be married to whomever she desires, only in the Lord*” (*v. 39*). Widows may remarry, but they should marry a believer. Paul adds his opinion that she might be happier remaining single, “*and I think that I also have God’s Spirit*” (*v. 40*).

## Important Verses Explained

### *1 Corinthians 7:3–5* — Mutual Belonging in Marriage

> *“Let the husband give his wife the affection owed her, and likewise also the wife her husband. The wife doesn’t have authority over her own body, but the husband does. Likewise also the husband doesn’t have authority over his own body, but the wife does. Don’t deprive one another, unless it is by consent for a season, that you may give yourselves to fasting and prayer, and may be together again, that Satan doesn’t tempt you because of your lack of self-control.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 7:3–5* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Some in the Corinthian church apparently believed that sexual relations were unspiritual, even within marriage. Some married couples may have been abstaining from intimacy in an effort to be more holy. Paul corrects this.

“*Let the husband give his wife the affection owed her, and likewise also the wife her husband*” (*v. 3*). Both husband and wife have a responsibility to meet each other’s needs for intimacy. This is mutual. Paul gives the same instruction to both.

“*The wife doesn’t have authority over her own body, but the husband does. Likewise also the husband doesn’t have authority over his own body, but the wife does*” (*v. 4*). In marriage, husband and wife belong to each other. This was a remarkable statement in the ancient world, where husbands were usually considered to have rights over their wives, but not the reverse. Paul affirms complete mutuality: the husband’s body belongs to his wife just as much as hers belongs to him.

This mutual belonging is not about control or demands. It is about self-giving love. Each spouse gives themselves to the other, seeking the other’s good. It never justifies coercion, force, or abuse, which violate the love and respect that Scripture requires in marriage (*Ephesians 5:25–33*; *1 Peter 3:7*).

“*Don’t deprive one another, unless it is by consent for a season, that you may give yourselves to fasting and prayer, and may be together again, that Satan doesn’t tempt you because of your lack of self-control*” (*v. 5*). Couples should not withhold intimacy from each other. There may be times when they agree to abstain for a short period for prayer. But this should be by mutual agreement, temporary, and followed by coming together again. Prolonged abstinence can expose them to temptation.

“*But this I say by way of concession, not of commandment*” (*v. 6*). Paul allows temporary abstinence for prayer but does not command it.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that sexual intimacy within marriage is good. God created it as a gift for husband and wife. Genesis says, “*Therefore a man will leave his father and his mother, and will join with his wife, and they will be one flesh*” (*Genesis 2:24*). The Song of Songs celebrates marital love. Paul affirms this goodness against those who considered it unspiritual.

They also show the equality and mutuality of husband and wife. In a culture where women often had few rights, Paul taught that husband and wife have equal responsibilities to each other in this area. Each belongs to the other.

Finally, these verses show that marriage requires self-giving love. The focus is not on getting but on giving. Each spouse considers the other’s needs. Paul writes elsewhere that husbands should love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her (*Ephesians 5:25*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage married couples to honor each other through intimacy. Intimacy is not merely physical; it is an expression of love, commitment, and unity. Couples can seek to meet each other’s needs with tenderness and care.

They also encourage couples to communicate. Times of abstinence should be by mutual agreement. Couples can talk openly about their needs and seek to understand each other.

Finally, these verses must never be used to justify coercion. Mutual belonging means mutual love and respect. Any form of pressure, force, or abuse violates God’s design. Couples facing difficulties in this area, whether physical, emotional, or relational, can seek help from trusted counselors, doctors, or pastors.

### *1 Corinthians 7:7–8* — Each Has His Own Gift

> *“Yet I wish that all men were like me. However, each man has his own gift from God, one of this kind, and another of that kind. But I say to the unmarried and to widows, it is good for them if they remain even as I am.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 7:7–8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had just been discussing marriage and the importance of intimacy between husband and wife. Now he shares his personal perspective.

“*Yet I wish that all men were like me*” (*v. 7*). Paul was unmarried at this time. He may have never married, or he may have been a widower. He found his single life a great blessing because it allowed him to serve the Lord without the responsibilities of a family. He wished others could experience the same freedom.

“*However, each man has his own gift from God, one of this kind, and another of that kind*” (*v. 7*). But Paul recognized that not everyone has the same gift. Both marriage and singleness are gifts from God. Some people are gifted for marriage; others are gifted for singleness. Neither is better in God’s eyes. Each person should recognize and embrace the gift God has given them.

“*But I say to the unmarried and to widows, it is good for them if they remain even as I am*” (*v. 8*). Paul encouraged those who were unmarried or widowed to consider remaining single, as he was.

“*But if they don’t have self-control, let them marry. For it’s better to marry than to burn with passion*” (*v. 9*). However, if they struggled with strong sexual desire, they should marry. “Burn with passion” means being consumed by sexual desire. Marriage is God’s good provision for this desire.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that singleness is a valuable gift, not a lesser state. In many cultures, then and now, singleness is seen as a failure or a problem to be solved. Paul, along with Jesus, who was also unmarried, shows that a single life can be full, fruitful, and devoted to God. Jesus spoke of those who are single “*for the Kingdom of Heaven’s sake*” (*Matthew 19:12*).

They also show that marriage is a gift. Paul does not disparage marriage. He recognizes that it is God’s good design for many people. Both marriage and singleness can be lived for God’s glory.

Finally, these verses show that God gives different gifts to different people. Believers should not compare themselves with others or feel pressure to conform to one pattern. Each can embrace the calling God has given.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage single believers. Singleness is not a waiting room or a second-class status. Single believers can embrace their gift, using their freedom to serve God and others with undivided devotion.

They also encourage churches to honor single people. Churches often focus on families and couples, sometimes leaving single people feeling overlooked. Churches can value, include, and support single members, recognizing their gifts and contributions.

Finally, these verses encourage believers to seek God’s guidance about marriage. Some are called to marriage, others to singleness. Believers can pray, seek counsel, and trust God’s wisdom in this important area.

### *1 Corinthians 7:10–11* — The Lord’s Command on Divorce

> *“But to the married I command—not I, but the Lord—that the wife not leave her husband (but if she departs, let her remain unmarried, or else be reconciled to her husband), and that the husband not leave his wife.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 7:10–11* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul now turns to married believers. Some in Corinth may have been considering divorce, perhaps believing that marriage was unspiritual, or that they could serve God better without a spouse.

“*But to the married I command—not I, but the Lord—that the wife not leave her husband*” (*v. 10*). Paul emphasizes that this is not merely his opinion. It is a command from the Lord Jesus Himself, who taught that marriage is a lifelong union and that divorce was not God’s original intention (*Mark 10:2–12*; *Matthew 19:3–9*). “*What therefore God has joined together, let no man separate*” (*Mark 10:9*).

“*(but if she departs, let her remain unmarried, or else be reconciled to her husband), and that the husband not leave his wife*” (*v. 11*). Paul recognizes that separation may sometimes happen. If it does, the person should either remain unmarried or seek reconciliation. The goal is restoration of the marriage, where that is possible and safe. The same instruction applies to husbands: they should not divorce their wives.

Christians have understood this teaching in different ways. Many believe that divorce is permitted in certain circumstances, such as sexual unfaithfulness, which Jesus mentions in *Matthew 5:32* and *19:9*, and desertion by an unbelieving spouse, which Paul addresses in *1 Corinthians 7:15*. Many also believe that serious abuse and persistent cruelty destroy the covenant of marriage and may justify divorce. Others hold stricter views. Some traditions do not permit remarriage after divorce while a former spouse is living; others do in certain circumstances. These are serious questions, and believers facing them should seek wise counsel from their church.

What all should agree on is this: God’s design is for marriage to be a lifelong covenant of love and faithfulness, and no one is required by this teaching to remain in a situation where they or their children are in danger. Separation for safety in a case of abuse is not disobedience to God. Paul’s own words, “if she departs,” recognize that separation sometimes occurs. Churches must never pressure victims of abuse to return to danger.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that marriage is sacred. God designed it as a lifelong covenant reflecting His faithful love for His people and Christ’s love for the church (*Ephesians 5:31–32*). Divorce breaks something precious; through Malachi, God links the breaking of the marriage covenant with unfaithfulness and violence (*Malachi 2:14–16*).

They also show that reconciliation is often the goal. Paul encourages separated spouses to seek reconciliation where possible. Many marriages that seemed broken have been restored through repentance, forgiveness, and God’s grace.

Finally, these verses must be read alongside God’s concern for the oppressed. Throughout Scripture, God defends the vulnerable and condemns violence and cruelty (*Psalm 11:5*; *Malachi 2:16*). The command not to divorce was never meant to trap people in abuse. God’s design for marriage includes the safety and dignity of both spouses.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage married believers to honor their commitment. Marriage takes work, patience, and forgiveness. Couples facing difficulties can seek help from counselors, pastors, and mature believers, and they can pray for God’s grace to strengthen their marriage.

They also encourage believers to support marriages in their churches. Churches can offer marriage preparation, counseling, and encouragement, helping couples build strong relationships.

Finally, these verses call churches to care well for those affected by divorce and those in harmful marriages. Divorced people should be treated with compassion, not condemnation. Victims of abuse should be protected, believed, and helped to safety. Churches should never use these verses to keep anyone in danger.

### *1 Corinthians 7:15–16* — God Has Called Us to Peace

> *“Yet if the unbeliever departs, let there be separation. The brother or the sister is not under bondage in such cases, but God has called us in peace. For how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife?”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 7:15–16* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had been addressing believers married to unbelievers. In many cases, one spouse had come to faith after the marriage, while the other had not. Paul said that if the unbelieving spouse was willing to stay, the believer should not seek divorce. The believer’s presence would bring God’s influence into the home.

But what if the unbeliever did not want to stay? “*Yet if the unbeliever departs, let there be separation*” (*v. 15*). If the unbelieving spouse chose to leave the marriage, the believer should let them go. The believer cannot force the unbeliever to stay.

“*The brother or the sister is not under bondage in such cases*” (*v. 15*). In this situation, the believing spouse is not “bound.” Christians have understood this phrase in different ways. Many understand it to mean that the believer is free from the marriage and may remarry, since the marriage has been broken by the unbeliever’s departure. Others understand it more narrowly, as meaning that the believer is not obligated to pursue the unbeliever or prevent the separation, without necessarily implying freedom to remarry.

“*but God has called us in peace*” (*v. 15*). God’s desire for His people is peace. Believers should not live in constant conflict, trying to hold together a marriage the other person has abandoned. Peace is God’s purpose.

“*For how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife?*” (*v. 16*) This verse can be read in two ways. It may mean that believers should stay in the marriage if possible, because they might lead their spouse to faith. Or it may mean that believers should not hold on to a departing spouse with the hope of converting them, since they cannot know whether that will happen. Either way, the believer can trust God with the outcome.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that God’s design includes peace. While marriage is meant to be lifelong, God does not call His people to endless conflict when a spouse chooses to leave. Paul writes elsewhere, “*If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men*” (*Romans 12:18*).

They also show that believers cannot control others’ choices. A believer can be faithful, loving, and committed, but they cannot force an unbelieving spouse to stay. Paul releases them from responsibility for a decision that was not theirs.

Finally, these verses show God’s care for believers in painful situations. Being abandoned by a spouse is deeply painful. Paul’s words bring comfort: the believer is not under bondage, and God has called them to peace.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses bring comfort to believers whose spouses have left them. Believers who have been abandoned can release the guilt of a decision that was not theirs, trust God with their future, and seek His peace.

They also encourage believers married to unbelievers to live faithfully. Peter writes that believing wives may win their husbands “*without a word*” (*1 Peter 3:1*) by their conduct. Believers can show Christ’s love in their marriages, praying for their spouses’ salvation.

Finally, these verses encourage churches to support believers in mixed marriages and those who have been abandoned. These situations bring unique challenges. Churches can offer understanding, prayer, practical help, and wise counsel.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*1 Corinthians 7* affirms that both marriage and singleness are good gifts from God. Neither is superior in His eyes. Married believers can honor their spouses with self-giving love, including the gift of intimacy, which God created to be good. Single believers can embrace their gift, using their freedom to serve the Lord with undivided devotion. Churches can honor and include people in every season of life.

The chapter also teaches that marriage is meant to be a lifelong covenant. The Lord’s command is that married believers should not divorce, and that separated spouses should seek reconciliation where possible. At the same time, believers abandoned by an unbelieving spouse are not bound, for God has called His people to peace. Believers facing difficult questions about divorce and remarriage can seek wise counsel, and churches must ensure that no one is ever pressured to remain in abuse or danger.

*1 Corinthians 7* teaches believers to serve God in whatever circumstances they were called. Their worth before God does not depend on their marital status, ethnicity, or social position. Each can live faithfully where God has placed them, while taking opportunities to improve their situation when appropriate.

Finally, the chapter reminds believers that the present form of this world is passing away. Marriage, joy, sorrow, and possessions are real, but none is ultimate. Believers can hold all these things loosely, devoting themselves to the Lord without distraction, and living with an eternal perspective.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord God, thank You for the gifts of marriage and singleness, and for calling each of Your people to serve You in different ways. Help married believers to love their spouses with self-giving, faithful love, and to honor one another in every way. Strengthen marriages that are struggling, bring reconciliation where it is possible and safe, and protect all who are in danger. Comfort those who have been abandoned or who carry the pain of divorce, and give them Your peace. Help single believers to embrace their calling and to serve You with undivided devotion, and make Your church a family where everyone belongs. Teach me to serve You faithfully in whatever situation You have called me, remembering that this world is passing away and that I belong to You. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

1 Corinthians · Chapter 8 of 16

# 1 Corinthians — Chapter 8

Chapter Theme: Knowledge Puffs Up, but Love Builds Up

[Read 1 Corinthians 8 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/1CO08.htm)

Main Teaching

Answering a question about food sacrificed to idols, Paul agrees that idols are nothing and that there is only one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things exist. But he warns that knowledge alone can make people proud, while love builds others up. Not every believer has this knowledge; some, who once worshiped idols, would feel their consciences defiled by eating such food. If believers with knowledge eat in idol temples and lead weaker believers to violate their consciences, they sin against those for whom Christ died, and against Christ Himself. Paul declares that he would rather never eat meat again than cause a brother to stumble.

## Chapter Background and Story

*1 Corinthians 8* begins a three-chapter discussion (chapters 8–10) of a question the Corinthians had asked: Can believers eat food that has been sacrificed to idols?

This was a practical issue in Corinth. Much of the meat sold in the marketplace came from animals sacrificed in pagan temples. Part of the animal was burned on the altar, part went to the priests, and the rest was often sold in the market or eaten at feasts in the temple dining rooms. Social life in Corinth often revolved around such meals. Trade guilds, family celebrations, and civic events were frequently held in temple banquet halls. Refusing to attend could mean social isolation or economic loss.

Some Corinthian believers argued that since idols are not real gods, eating food offered to them was meaningless; they could eat freely, even in temple dining halls. Others, especially those who had recently left idol worship, felt that eating such food would draw them back into idolatry and violate their consciences.

Paul’s answer is nuanced. In chapter 8, he agrees that idols are nothing, but he emphasizes that love must govern the use of knowledge and freedom. In chapter 9, he gives his own example of setting aside his rights for the sake of others. In chapter 10, he warns against participating in idol worship and gives practical guidelines about eating.

### Knowledge and Love (*8:1–3*)

Paul’s opening principle is studied below.

### One God and One Lord (*8:4–6*)

“*Therefore concerning the eating of things sacrificed to idols, we know that no idol is anything in the world, and that there is no other God but one*” (*v. 4*). Paul agrees with the Corinthians who have knowledge: idols are not real gods. There is only one God. This reflects the great confession of Israel, the Shema: “*Hear, Israel: The LORD is our God. The LORD is one*” (*Deuteronomy 6:4*).

“*For though there are things that are called “gods”, whether in the heavens or on earth—as there are many “gods” and many “lords”—*” (*v. 5*). In the Roman world, people worshiped many gods and called many rulers “lord.” Paul acknowledges that these so-called gods exist in people’s minds and practices, and later he warns that demons stand behind idol worship (*10:20*). Paul’s great confession is studied below.

### Concern for the Weak (*8:7–13*)

“*However, that knowledge isn’t in all men. But some, with consciousness of an idol until now, eat as of a thing sacrificed to an idol, and their conscience, being weak, is defiled*” (*v. 7*). Not every believer has fully grasped that idols are nothing. Some who had worshiped idols for years still associated the food with idol worship. If they ate it, they felt that they were participating in idolatry, and their consciences were troubled.

“*But food will not commend us to God. For neither, if we don’t eat are we the worse, nor if we eat are we the better*” (*v. 8*). Food itself does not make anyone more or less acceptable to God. Eating or not eating is spiritually neutral.

“*But be careful that by no means does this liberty of yours become a stumbling block to the weak*” (*v. 9*). However, freedom must be exercised carefully. “*For if a man sees you who have knowledge sitting in an idol’s temple, won’t his conscience, if he is weak, be emboldened to eat things sacrificed to idols?*” (*v. 10*) If a weaker believer saw a stronger believer eating in a pagan temple, they might be encouraged to do the same, even though their conscience told them it was wrong. The consequences, and Paul’s own resolution, are studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *1 Corinthians 8:1–3* — Knowledge Puffs Up, Love Builds Up

> *“Now concerning things sacrificed to idols: We know that we all have knowledge. Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up. But if anyone thinks that he knows anything, he doesn’t yet know as he ought to know. But anyone who loves God is known by him.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 8:1–3* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The Corinthians had asked Paul about eating food sacrificed to idols. Some of them believed they had special knowledge on this subject. They knew that idols were not real gods, so they felt free to eat such food without concern.

“*Now concerning things sacrificed to idols: We know that we all have knowledge*” (*v. 1*). The phrase “we all have knowledge” may be a slogan from the Corinthians’ letter. Paul agrees that they have knowledge, but he immediately qualifies it.

“*Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up*” (*v. 1*). Knowledge alone can make people proud. The word “puffs up” pictures something inflated, like a balloon, full of air but empty inside. The Corinthians were proud of their knowledge, and it was making them arrogant toward those who did not share it. Love, on the other hand, “builds up.” It strengthens others, like a builder constructing a house. Love uses knowledge to help others, not to feel superior.

“*But if anyone thinks that he knows anything, he doesn’t yet know as he ought to know*” (*v. 2*). People who think they have everything figured out do not truly understand. True knowledge includes humility, recognizing how much one does not know.

“*But anyone who loves God is known by him*” (*v. 3*). Paul shifts the focus. What matters most is not what people know, but whether they love God. And those who love God are known by Him. Being known by God, having a relationship with Him, is far more important than having knowledge about Him.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that love is greater than knowledge. Paul later writes in this same letter, “*If I have the gift of prophecy, and know all mysteries and all knowledge*” (*1 Corinthians 13:2*), “*but don’t have love, I am nothing*” (*1 Corinthians 13:2*). Knowledge is valuable, but without love, it becomes a source of pride and division.

They also show that true knowledge leads to humility. The more people truly understand, the more they recognize the limits of their understanding. Pride in knowledge is a sign of shallow understanding.

Finally, these verses show that being known by God is the heart of faith. Paul writes, “*But now that you have come to know God, or rather to be known by God*” (*Galatians 4:9*). Salvation is not merely knowing facts about God; it is being in a relationship with Him in which He knows and loves His people.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses challenge believers who are knowledgeable about the Bible or theology. Knowledge is good, but it must be joined with love. Believers can ask whether their knowledge makes them humble and loving, or proud and critical.

They also encourage believers to use their knowledge to build others up. Instead of using knowledge to win arguments or feel superior, believers can use it to help others grow in faith.

Finally, these verses remind believers that what matters most is loving God and being known by Him. Believers can focus on deepening their relationship with God, not merely accumulating information about Him.

### *1 Corinthians 8:6* — One God, the Father, and One Lord, Jesus Christ

> *“yet to us there is one God, the Father, of whom are all things, and we for him; and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we live through him.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 8:6* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had agreed with the Corinthians that idols are nothing and that there is only one God. He acknowledged that people in the Roman world worshiped many so-called gods and lords. Now he gives a powerful confession of Christian faith.

“*yet to us there is one God, the Father, of whom are all things, and we for him*” (*v. 6*). For believers, there is one God, the Father. All things come “from” Him; He is the Creator and source of everything. And believers exist “for” Him; He is their purpose and goal.

“*and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we live through him*” (*v. 6*). There is also one Lord, Jesus Christ. All things came into being “through” Him; He was the agent of creation. And believers live “through” Him; He is the means of their salvation and new life.

This verse is remarkable. Paul is adapting the Shema, the central confession of Israel’s faith: “*Hear, Israel: The LORD is our God. The LORD is one*” (*Deuteronomy 6:4*). In the Greek translation of the Old Testament, the word for “LORD” is kyrios. Paul takes this confession and expands it to include Jesus. “One God” is the Father; “one Lord” is Jesus Christ. Paul includes Jesus within the identity of the one God of Israel, while distinguishing Him from the Father.

This is one of the earliest and clearest statements of what Christians later called the doctrine of the Trinity. There is one God, yet the Father and the Son are distinct Persons, both sharing the divine identity.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that Jesus is fully divine. He shares in the work of creation, which belongs to God alone. John writes, “*All things were made through him. Without him, nothing was made that has been made*” (*John 1:3*). Paul writes, “*For by him all things were created*” (*Colossians 1:16*).

It also shows that Christian faith is monotheistic. Christians do not worship many gods. They worship one God, revealed as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. This confession set early Christians apart in a world of many gods.

Finally, the verse shows the purpose of human life. All things are from God and for God. Believers live through Christ. Their lives have meaning and direction because they belong to the one true God.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to worship Jesus as Lord. He is not merely a great teacher or prophet. He is the one Lord through whom all things were made. Believers can give Him the honor and trust that belong to God.

It also encourages believers to reject modern idols. People today may not worship statues, but they often give ultimate allegiance to money, success, pleasure, power, or human leaders. Believers confess that there is one God and one Lord, and they can give their highest loyalty to Him alone.

Finally, the verse gives believers a sense of purpose. All things are from God and for Him, and believers live through Christ. Every part of life, including work, relationships, and leisure, can be lived for God’s glory.

### *1 Corinthians 8:11–12* — Sinning Against Christ

> *“And through your knowledge, he who is weak perishes, the brother for whose sake Christ died. Thus, sinning against the brothers, and wounding their conscience when it is weak, you sin against Christ.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 8:11–12* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had explained that some believers had the knowledge that idols are nothing, while others did not. If a believer with knowledge ate in an idol’s temple, a weaker believer who saw them might be encouraged to eat too, even though their conscience told them it was wrong.

“*And through your knowledge, he who is weak perishes, the brother for whose sake Christ died*” (*v. 11*). Paul describes the serious consequences. The weaker believer could be “destroyed” or “ruined.” This does not necessarily mean losing salvation, but it describes serious spiritual harm. Acting against their conscience could draw them back into idolatry, damage their faith, or lead them away from Christ.

Notice how Paul describes this weaker believer: “the brother for whose sake Christ died.” Christ valued this person so much that He gave His life for them. How could a stronger believer harm someone so precious to Christ over something as unimportant as food?

“*Thus, sinning against the brothers, and wounding their conscience when it is weak, you sin against Christ*” (*v. 12*). Using freedom in a way that harms a fellow believer is not neutral; it is sin. And it is not only sin against the brother, but sin against Christ Himself. Jesus identifies with His people. When believers harm one another, they harm Christ.

This echoes what Jesus said to Saul on the road to Damascus: “*why do you persecute me?*” (*Acts 9:4*). Jesus is so united with His people that what is done to them is done to Him.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show the value of every believer. Each one is a person for whom Christ died. This gives every believer immense worth, regardless of how mature, knowledgeable, or strong they are.

They also show the seriousness of causing others to stumble. Jesus warned, “*Whoever will cause one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him if he were thrown into the sea with a millstone hung around his neck*” (*Mark 9:42*). Believers have a responsibility to care for one another’s spiritual welfare.

Finally, these verses show the union between Christ and His people. Christ is so identified with believers that sinning against them is sinning against Him. This should lead believers to treat one another with the same care and reverence they would show to Christ.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to consider how their actions affect others. Believers may have the freedom to do certain things, but they should ask whether their actions might harm a weaker believer.

They also call believers to value every fellow believer. Every person in the church is someone for whom Christ died. Believers can treat one another with care and respect, especially those who are new or struggling in their faith.

Finally, these verses remind believers that how they treat others matters to Christ. Believers can examine their relationships, asking whether they have harmed anyone through careless words or actions, and seeking to make things right.

### *1 Corinthians 8:13* — I Will Eat No Meat

> *“Therefore, if food causes my brother to stumble, I will eat no meat forever more, that I don’t cause my brother to stumble.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 8:13* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had explained that believers with knowledge should be careful not to cause weaker believers to stumble. Now he gives his personal resolution.

“*Therefore, if food causes my brother to stumble, I will eat no meat forever more, that I don’t cause my brother to stumble*” (*v. 13*). Paul says that if eating meat would cause a fellow believer to fall into sin, he would never eat meat again. This is a remarkable statement. Paul knew that he had the freedom to eat. He agreed that idols are nothing and food does not affect a person’s standing with God. Yet he was willing to give up his freedom entirely for the sake of a brother.

Paul’s statement is a strong expression of love. He was not speaking about all situations; he would eat meat when it did not cause harm. But when his freedom threatened another person’s faith, love took priority.

This verse prepares for chapter 9, where Paul explains how he gave up many rights for the sake of the gospel and others. He writes there, “*For though I was free from all, I brought myself under bondage to all, that I might gain the more*” (*1 Corinthians 9:19*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that love is willing to sacrifice. Christian freedom is real, but it is not the highest value. Love for others is greater. Jesus Himself set aside His rights and privileges for the sake of others (*Philippians 2:5–8*).

It also shows that Christian maturity is measured by love, not by freedom. The Corinthians who had knowledge thought they were mature because they felt free to eat. Paul shows that true maturity is shown in willingness to give up freedom for the sake of others.

Finally, the verse shows Paul’s example as a leader. He did not ask others to do what he was unwilling to do. He modeled the self-giving love he taught.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse challenges believers to consider whether there are freedoms they should give up for the sake of others. This might involve choices about alcohol, entertainment, or other activities. If a believer’s freedom might lead someone else into sin or harm their faith, love may call them to set it aside, at least in certain settings.

It also encourages believers to prioritize relationships over rights. Believers can ask not only “Am I allowed to do this?” but “Will this help or harm others?”

Finally, the verse encourages believers to follow Paul’s example. Leaders, parents, and mature believers can model self-giving love, showing others that following Christ means putting others first.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*1 Corinthians 8* teaches that knowledge without love leads to pride, while love builds others up. Believers can value knowledge and grow in understanding, but they must always use their knowledge in love, seeking to strengthen others rather than to feel superior. What matters most is loving God and being known by Him.

The chapter also contains a powerful confession: there is one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ. Believers can worship Jesus as the Lord through whom all things were made, and reject every idol, ancient or modern, that competes for their allegiance.

*1 Corinthians 8* calls believers to care for those whose consciences are weaker. Every believer is someone for whom Christ died. Using freedom in a way that harms a fellow believer is sin against Christ Himself. Believers can consider how their actions affect others and be willing to limit their freedom out of love.

Finally, the chapter shows Paul’s example of self-giving love. He was willing to give up meat forever rather than cause a brother to stumble. Believers can follow his example, prioritizing love over rights and modeling for others what it means to follow Christ, who gave up everything for us.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord God, You are the one God, the Father, from whom all things come and for whom I live. Lord Jesus, You are the one Lord, through whom all things were made and through whom I live. I worship You. Forgive me for the times my knowledge has made me proud rather than loving. Help me to use what I know to build others up. Thank You that I am known by You. Give me a heart that values every brother and sister for whom Christ died. Keep me from using my freedom in ways that cause others to stumble. Teach me to put love above my rights, as Paul did, and as You did when You gave Yourself for me. Help me to reject every idol and to live for You alone. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
