1 Corinthians · Chapter 9 of 16

# 1 Corinthians — Chapter 9

Chapter Theme: Giving Up Rights for the Sake of the Gospel and Running to Win

[Read 1 Corinthians 9 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/1CO09.htm)

Main Teaching

Continuing his teaching on freedom and love, Paul offers his own example. As an apostle, he has every right to receive financial support from the churches, a right supported by common sense, the Law of Moses, and the Lord’s own command. Yet he has chosen not to use this right, enduring hardship so as not to hinder the gospel. He feels compelled to preach and finds his reward in offering the gospel free of charge. Though free, he has made himself a servant to all, becoming all things to all people so that by all means he might save some. Finally, using the image of athletes, he urges believers to run with purpose and self-discipline for an imperishable prize.

## Chapter Background and Story

*1 Corinthians 9* may seem at first like a change of subject. In chapter 8, Paul was discussing food offered to idols. In chapter 10, he will return to that topic. But chapter 9 is not a digression. Paul is giving his own life as an example of the principle he taught in chapter 8: believers should be willing to give up their rights for the sake of others.

The chapter also suggests that some Corinthians were questioning Paul’s authority as an apostle. Perhaps they thought that because he worked as a tentmaker and did not accept their money, he was not a real apostle, or that he was less important than other leaders who received support. Paul answers by showing that he had every right to support, but chose not to use it for the sake of the gospel.

### Paul’s Rights as an Apostle (*9:1–14*)

Paul begins with a series of questions: “*Am I not free? Am I not an apostle? Haven’t I seen Jesus Christ, our Lord? Aren’t you my work in the Lord?*” (*v. 1*) Paul had seen the risen Christ on the road to Damascus (*Acts 9*), a key qualification for an apostle (*Acts 1:21–22*). And the Corinthian church itself was proof of his apostleship: “*for you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord*” (*v. 2*).

Paul then lists rights that apostles have. “*Have we no right to eat and to drink?*” (*v. 4*) Apostles had the right to be provided with food and drink by the churches. “*Have we no right to take along a wife who is a believer, even as the rest of the apostles, and the brothers of the Lord, and Cephas?*” (*v. 5*) Other apostles, Jesus’ brothers, and Peter traveled with their wives, supported by the churches. This verse tells us that Peter was married (compare *Mark 1:30*). “*Or have only Barnabas and I no right to not work?*” (*v. 6*) Paul and Barnabas worked to support themselves, but they had the right not to.

Paul supports these rights with examples from everyday life: “*What soldier ever serves at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard, and doesn’t eat of its fruit? Or who feeds a flock, and doesn’t drink from the flock’s milk?*” (*v. 7*) Workers naturally benefit from their work.

He also appeals to Scripture: “*For it is written in the law of Moses, “You shall not muzzle an ox while it treads out the grain.”*” (*v. 9*) (*Deuteronomy 25:4*). An ox treading grain should be allowed to eat some of it. If God cares about oxen, how much more does He care about His workers? “*Yes, it was written for our sake*” (*v. 10*). “*If we sowed to you spiritual things, is it a great thing if we reap your fleshly things?*” (*v. 11*)

He points to the temple: those who served in the temple received food from the offerings (*Numbers 18:8–31*). And most importantly: “*Even so the Lord ordained that those who proclaim the Good News should live from the Good News*” (*v. 14*). Jesus Himself taught this (*Luke 10:7*; *Matthew 10:10*). Paul makes clear that it is right for churches to support those who serve them.

Yet Paul did not use this right, as studied below.

### Paul’s Reason for Refusing Support (*9:15–18*)

“*But I have used none of these things, and I don’t write these things that it may be done so in my case; for I would rather die, than that anyone should make my boasting void*” (*v. 15*). Paul was not writing to ask for money. He would rather die than lose his “boast,” his joy in preaching without charge. His sense of calling is studied below.

“*What then is my reward? That when I preach the Good News, I may present the Good News of Christ without charge, so as not to abuse my authority in the Good News*” (*v. 18*). Paul’s reward was the joy of offering the gospel freely, making clear that he was not in it for money. In Corinth, where traveling teachers often charged fees and many were suspected of greed, this mattered greatly.

### All Things to All People (*9:19–23*)

“*For though I was free from all, I brought myself under bondage to all, that I might gain the more*” (*v. 19*). Paul was free, not bound by anyone. Yet he voluntarily made himself a servant to everyone, in order to win more people to Christ.

He gives examples: “*To the Jews I became as a Jew, that I might gain Jews; to those who are under the law, as under the law, that I might gain those who are under the law*” (*v. 20*). Among Jews, Paul observed Jewish customs, such as when he circumcised Timothy (*Acts 16:3*) or took a vow (*Acts 21:26*). “*to those who are without law, as without law (not being without law toward God, but under law toward Christ), that I might win those who are without law*” (*v. 21*). Among Gentiles, Paul did not insist on Jewish customs. But he was never lawless; he was always under the law of Christ, the law of love. His summary statement is studied below.

### Running to Win (*9:24–27*)

Paul closes with an image from athletics, studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *1 Corinthians 9:12* — That We May Cause No Hindrance to the Gospel

> *“If others partake of this right over you, don’t we yet more? Nevertheless we didn’t use this right, but we bear all things, that we may cause no hindrance to the Good News of Christ.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 9:12* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had just made a strong case that apostles have the right to receive financial support from the churches they serve. He used examples from soldiers, farmers, and shepherds, and he cited the Law of Moses. The Corinthians themselves had supported other teachers.

“*If others partake of this right over you, don’t we yet more?*” (*v. 12*) Other teachers had received support from the Corinthian church. If they had this right, surely Paul, the founder of the church, had it even more.

“*Nevertheless we didn’t use this right*” (*v. 12*). But Paul and his co-workers had chosen not to use this right. They supported themselves through their own work, such as tentmaking.

“*but we bear all things, that we may cause no hindrance to the Good News of Christ*” (*v. 12*). They endured hardship, working long hours and sometimes going without, so that nothing would get in the way of the gospel. In a city where many teachers charged fees and were suspected of greed, Paul did not want anyone to think he preached for money. He wanted the gospel to be clearly free.

The word “hindrance” pictures something that cuts into a road and blocks the way forward. Paul did not want anything, even his legitimate rights, to block people from coming to Christ.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that the gospel is more important than personal rights. Paul had a genuine right to support, but he valued the progress of the gospel more. Jesus said, “*For the Son of Man also came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many*” (*Mark 10:45*).

It also shows that believers should consider how their actions affect their witness. Even legitimate actions can become obstacles to the gospel in certain situations. Paul wisely considered how his choices would be perceived.

Finally, the verse connects to the discussion of food offered to idols. Just as Paul gave up his right to support, believers should be willing to give up their right to eat certain foods if it would harm others.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to consider whether any of their rights or freedoms are hindering the gospel. Believers can ask whether their behavior, lifestyle, or choices might make it harder for others to hear and receive the good news.

It also encourages Christian workers to maintain integrity with money. Paul’s example shows the importance of avoiding even the appearance of greed. Ministers and ministries can be transparent and careful with finances so that the gospel is not discredited.

Finally, the verse affirms that churches should support those who serve them. Paul’s choice was his own; he clearly taught that those who preach the gospel should be supported. Churches can generously care for their pastors and missionaries.

### *1 Corinthians 9:16* — Woe to Me If I Don’t Preach

> *“For if I preach the Good News, I have nothing to boast about, for necessity is laid on me; but woe is to me if I don’t preach the Good News.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 9:16* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had explained that he chose not to accept payment for preaching so that he could offer the gospel free of charge. Now he explains why preaching itself gave him nothing to boast about.

“*For if I preach the Good News, I have nothing to boast about, for necessity is laid on me*” (*v. 16*). Paul could not take credit for preaching, because he had no choice. God had laid it on him as a necessity. On the road to Damascus, Jesus had commissioned him to preach to the Gentiles (*Acts 26:16–18*). Preaching was not a career choice; it was a divine calling.

“*but woe is to me if I don’t preach the Good News*” (*v. 16*). If Paul failed to preach, he would be disobeying God’s call. “Woe” is a strong word of warning, used by the prophets to describe coming judgment. Paul felt the weight of his calling so deeply that he could not imagine not preaching.

This echoes the experience of Old Testament prophets. Jeremiah said that God’s word was like “*a burning fire shut up in my bones*” (*Jeremiah 20:9*), and he could not hold it in. Amos said, “*The Lord GOD has spoken. Who can but prophesy?*” (*Amos 3:8*).

Paul’s reward, then, was not in preaching itself, which was his duty, but in preaching freely, giving up his right to payment (*9:17–18*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that the gospel is a stewardship entrusted to believers. Paul writes in the next verse, “*But if not of my own will, I have a stewardship entrusted to me*” (*v. 17*). Believers do not own the gospel; they are entrusted with it and responsible to share it.

It also shows the compelling nature of God’s call. When God calls someone, the call is not optional. Paul felt compelled to preach. Peter and John said, “*for we can’t help telling the things which we saw and heard*” (*Acts 4:20*).

Finally, the verse shows that faithful service is not a reason for pride. Paul could not boast about preaching, because it was what God required. Jesus taught that servants who do what they are commanded should say, “*We are unworthy servants. We have done our duty*” (*Luke 17:10*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to take their calling seriously. Every believer has been entrusted with the gospel and called to share it in some way. Believers can ask God to give them a sense of urgency about sharing Christ with others.

It also reminds believers that service is not a reason for pride. When believers serve faithfully, they are simply doing what God has called them to do. Their service is a response to grace, not a way to earn credit.

Finally, the verse encourages those called to ministry. Pastors, missionaries, and others in ministry may face discouragement. Remembering God’s call can sustain them through difficult times.

### *1 Corinthians 9:22* — All Things to All People

> *“To the weak I became as weak, that I might gain the weak. I have become all things to all men, that I may by all means save some.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 9:22* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had explained that although he was free, he made himself a servant to all people in order to win more of them to Christ. He gave examples: among Jews, he lived as a Jew; among Gentiles, he lived as a Gentile, while always remaining under the law of Christ.

“*To the weak I became as weak, that I might gain the weak*” (*v. 22*). The “weak” here probably refers to believers with sensitive consciences, like those discussed in chapter 8. Paul limited his freedom for their sake, becoming like them so that he could help them.

“*I have become all things to all men, that I may by all means save some*” (*v. 22*). This is Paul’s summary. He adapted himself to different people and cultures, so that by every possible means, he might bring some to salvation.

This does not mean Paul compromised the gospel or his moral convictions. He never became an idolater to reach idolaters or sinned to reach sinners. He remained “under law toward Christ” (*9:21*). What he adapted were customs, practices, and approaches that did not affect the truth of the gospel. He was flexible in method but firm in message.

“*Now I do this for the sake of the Good News, that I may be a joint partaker of it*” (*v. 23*). Paul did everything for the gospel’s sake, so that he might share in its blessings with others.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows the heart of missionary love. Paul was willing to set aside his own preferences, comfort, and culture to reach others. This is what Christ did in the incarnation: He became human to reach humanity. John writes, “*The Word became flesh, and lived among us*” (*John 1:14*).

It also shows the importance of understanding others. To become “*all things to all men*” (*v. 22*), Paul had to understand different cultures, customs, and ways of thinking. Effective witness requires listening, learning, and empathy.

Finally, the verse shows that the goal of flexibility is salvation. Paul adapted “that I may by all means save some.” His flexibility was not about being popular or comfortable; it was about bringing people to Christ.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to adapt their approach to reach others. Believers can learn about the cultures, interests, and concerns of people around them, and they can find ways to connect with them, while remaining faithful to the gospel.

It also encourages believers to set aside personal preferences for the sake of others. Believers might change how they dress, what they eat, or how they spend their time in order to build relationships and remove barriers to the gospel.

Finally, the verse warns against compromise. Believers should be flexible in methods but never in the message. They can adapt to others without abandoning biblical truth or moral convictions.

### *1 Corinthians 9:24–27* — Run to Win the Imperishable Crown

> *“Don’t you know that those who run in a race all run, but one receives the prize? Run like that, so that you may win. Every man who strives in the games exercises self-control in all things. Now they do it to receive a corruptible crown, but we an incorruptible. I therefore run like that, not aimlessly. I fight like that, not beating the air, but I beat my body and bring it into submission, lest by any means, after I have preached to others, I myself should be disqualified.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 9:24–27* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul closes this chapter with an image the Corinthians knew well. Corinth hosted the Isthmian Games every two years, one of the great athletic festivals of the ancient world, second only to the Olympic Games. Athletes trained intensely for these events.

“*Don’t you know that those who run in a race all run, but one receives the prize? Run like that, so that you may win*” (*v. 24*). In a race, many runners compete, but only one wins. Paul is not saying that only one believer will be saved. He is saying that believers should run with the same determination as athletes who want to win.

“*Every man who strives in the games exercises self-control in all things*” (*v. 25*). Athletes in the Isthmian Games had to train for ten months and follow strict diets and disciplines. They gave up many pleasures to prepare for competition.

“*Now they do it to receive a corruptible crown, but we an incorruptible*” (*v. 25*). The winners of the Isthmian Games received a crown made of pine or wilted celery, which would soon wither. Yet athletes disciplined themselves intensely for this temporary prize. Believers run for an “incorruptible” crown, eternal life and reward from God, which will never fade (*2 Timothy 4:8*; *1 Peter 5:4*).

“*I therefore run like that, not aimlessly. I fight like that, not beating the air*” (*v. 26*). Paul ran with purpose, not wandering aimlessly. He fought like a boxer who lands his punches, not one who swings wildly at the air.

“*but I beat my body and bring it into submission, lest by any means, after I have preached to others, I myself should be disqualified*” (*v. 27*). Paul disciplined himself, keeping his body and its desires under control. He did not want to preach to others and then fail to live what he preached. “Disqualified” was a term used for athletes who broke the rules and were rejected from the competition. Paul took seriously the need for self-discipline and faithfulness.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that the Christian life requires discipline. Salvation is a free gift, but living the Christian life involves effort, self-control, and perseverance. Paul writes, “*exercise yourself toward godliness*” (*1 Timothy 4:7*).

They also show the value of eternal rewards. Athletes discipline themselves for temporary prizes. Believers have far greater motivation: an eternal crown. Hebrews urges believers to “*run with perseverance the race that is set before us*” (*Hebrews 12:1*).

Finally, these verses show Paul’s humility and seriousness. Even the great apostle did not assume that he could relax. He knew the danger of preaching to others while neglecting his own walk with God.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to run their race with purpose. Believers can set spiritual goals, such as growing in prayer, Bible reading, service, and character, and pursue them with determination.

They also encourage self-discipline. Believers can identify areas where they need greater self-control, such as their time, eating, spending, media use, or speech, and ask God for help in disciplining themselves.

Finally, these verses remind believers to keep their eyes on the eternal prize. When the Christian life feels difficult, believers can remember that they are running for a crown that will never fade.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*1 Corinthians 9* shows that believers should be willing to give up their rights for the sake of the gospel. Paul had every right to receive financial support, but he chose not to use it so that nothing would hinder the gospel. Believers can consider whether any of their rights, freedoms, or choices might be obstacles to others coming to Christ.

The chapter also affirms that churches should support those who serve them. Paul’s arguments from common sense, the Law, and the Lord’s command show that it is right for churches to care for their pastors and missionaries. Paul’s choice not to accept support was his own, made for the sake of the gospel in his particular situation.

*1 Corinthians 9* calls believers to become all things to all people, adapting their approach to reach others while remaining faithful to Christ. Believers can learn about the people around them, build bridges across cultural differences, and set aside their own preferences, all for the purpose of bringing people to salvation.

Finally, the chapter calls believers to run their race with purpose and self-discipline. Like athletes training for a prize, believers can discipline themselves for the incorruptible crown of eternal life. They can pursue spiritual growth with determination and guard against preaching to others while neglecting their own walk with God.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for setting aside Your rights and becoming a servant to save me. Help me to follow Your example, giving up my own rights and preferences when they would hinder others from knowing You. Give me Paul’s sense of urgency about sharing the gospel, and help me never to treat it as optional. Make me flexible in how I reach others, willing to become all things to all people, while remaining faithful to Your truth. Bless and provide for those who serve Your church and carry Your gospel. Help me to run my race with purpose, not aimlessly, and to discipline myself for the crown that will never fade. Keep me from preaching to others while neglecting my own walk with You. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

1 Corinthians · Chapter 10 of 16

# 1 Corinthians — Chapter 10

Chapter Theme: Warnings from Israel, a Way of Escape, and Doing All for God’s Glory

[Read 1 Corinthians 10 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/1CO10.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul warns the Corinthians not to presume on their spiritual privileges, pointing to Israel in the wilderness, who experienced God’s deliverance and provision yet fell into idolatry, immorality, testing God, and grumbling, and perished. These things were written as examples, so believers who think they stand should take care not to fall, trusting that God is faithful and will provide a way of escape in every temptation. Paul then forbids participation in idol feasts, because sharing in the Lord’s Supper unites believers with Christ, and pagan sacrifices involve fellowship with demons. He closes with practical guidance about food bought in the market or served by unbelievers, summed up in the principle: whatever you do, do it all for the glory of God, seeking the good of others.

## Chapter Background and Story

*1 Corinthians 10* concludes Paul’s discussion of food offered to idols (chapters 8–10). In chapter 8, he said that idols are nothing and food does not bring people closer to God, but believers should not use their freedom in a way that harms weaker believers. In chapter 9, he gave his own example of giving up rights for the sake of others. Now he warns about the real danger of idolatry and gives practical guidelines.

Some Corinthians apparently felt spiritually secure. They had been baptized and shared in the Lord’s Supper. They believed that because idols were nothing, they could attend feasts in pagan temples without danger. Paul shows that this confidence was misplaced. Spiritual privileges do not protect people who willfully participate in idolatry.

### Lessons from Israel’s History (*10:1–11*)

Paul reminds the Corinthians of Israel’s experience in the wilderness. “*our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea*” (*v. 1*). God led Israel with a pillar of cloud and brought them through the Red Sea (*Exodus 13:21*; *14:22*). “*and were all baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea*” (*v. 2*). Their passage through the sea under the cloud was like a baptism, uniting them with Moses as their leader. “*and all ate the same spiritual food*” (*v. 3*), the manna (*Exodus 16*), “*and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank of a spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ*” (*v. 4*). God provided water from the rock (*Exodus 17:6*; *Numbers 20:11*). Paul sees Christ present with Israel, the source of their spiritual sustenance. Some Jewish traditions spoke of a rock that followed Israel through the wilderness; Paul’s point is that Christ was with them throughout their journey.

Israel had experiences similar to Christian baptism and the Lord’s Supper. Yet “*However with most of them, God was not well pleased, for they were overthrown in the wilderness*” (*v. 5*). Despite their privileges, most of that generation died in the wilderness and never entered the promised land.

“*Now these things were our examples, to the intent we should not lust after evil things as they also lusted*” (*v. 6*). Paul lists four sins of Israel. Idolatry: “*Don’t be idolaters, as some of them were. As it is written, “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play.”*” (*v. 7*) This refers to the golden calf (*Exodus 32:6*), when Israel ate a feast and engaged in revelry before an idol, exactly the kind of thing that happened at pagan temple feasts in Corinth. Sexual immorality: “*Let’s not commit sexual immorality, as some of them committed, and in one day twenty-three thousand fell*” (*v. 8*) (*Numbers 25:1–9*, where Israelite men joined Moabite women in sexual immorality and idol worship). Testing God: “*Let’s not test Christ, as some of them tested, and perished by the serpents*” (*v. 9*) (*Numbers 21:5–6*). Grumbling: “*Don’t grumble, as some of them also grumbled, and perished by the destroyer*” (*v. 10*) (*Numbers 14*; 16).

(*Numbers 25:9* records twenty-four thousand deaths; Paul’s figure of twenty-three thousand may refer to those who died “in one day,” or may be a rounded number. Ancient writers often used approximate figures.)

“*Now all these things happened to them by way of example, and they were written for our admonition, on whom the ends of the ages have come*” (*v. 11*). Believers live in the last era of history, the time between Christ’s first and second comings. Israel’s history serves as a warning for them.

### A Warning and a Promise (*10:12–13*)

Paul’s warning and his promise about temptation are studied below.

### Flee from Idolatry (*10:14–22*)

“*Therefore, my beloved, flee from idolatry*” (*v. 14*). Paul tells them to run away from idolatry, just as he told them to flee sexual immorality (*6:18*). His teaching on the Lord’s Supper is studied below.

“*Consider Israel according to the flesh. Don’t those who eat the sacrifices participate in the altar?*” (*v. 18*) In Israel, those who ate the sacrifices shared in the worship at the altar. Eating was participation.

“*What am I saying then? That a thing sacrificed to idols is anything, or that an idol is anything?*” (*v. 19*) Paul has not changed his view that idols are nothing in themselves. “*But I say that the things which the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God, and I don’t desire that you would have fellowship with demons*” (*v. 20*). Behind idol worship stand demonic powers (*Deuteronomy 32:17*). Participating in pagan worship meant entering into fellowship with these spiritual forces.

“*You can’t both drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You can’t both partake of the table of the Lord and of the table of demons*” (*v. 21*). Believers cannot be loyal to Christ and participate in idol worship. “*Or do we provoke the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than he?*” (*v. 22*) God is a jealous God, who will not share His people’s worship with idols (*Exodus 20:5*). It is foolish to test Him.

### Practical Guidelines (*10:23–33*)

Paul returns to a Corinthian slogan, studied below. He then gives practical advice. “*Whatever is sold in the butcher shop, eat, asking no question for the sake of conscience*” (*v. 25*), “*for “the earth is the Lord’s, and its fullness.”*” (*v. 26*) (*Psalm 24:1*). Meat sold in the market could be eaten freely. Believers did not need to investigate whether it had been offered to idols. Everything belongs to God.

“*But if one of those who don’t believe invites you to a meal, and you are inclined to go, eat whatever is set before you, asking no questions for the sake of conscience*” (*v. 27*). Believers could accept invitations to unbelievers’ homes and eat what was served. But “*But if anyone says to you, “This was offered to idols,” don’t eat it for the sake of the one who told you, and for the sake of conscience*” (*v. 28*). If someone pointed out that the food had been offered to idols, perhaps an unbeliever testing the Christian’s loyalty or a weaker believer troubled by it, the believer should not eat it, out of consideration for that person’s conscience. Paul’s summary principle is studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *1 Corinthians 10:12–13* — God Will Make a Way of Escape

> *“Therefore let him who thinks he stands be careful that he doesn’t fall. No temptation has taken you except what is common to man. God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted above what you are able, but will with the temptation also make the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 10:12–13* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had just reminded the Corinthians of Israel’s history. The Israelites had experienced God’s deliverance at the Red Sea, eaten manna from heaven, and drunk water from the rock. Yet many of them fell into idolatry, sexual immorality, testing God, and grumbling, and they died in the wilderness.

“*Therefore let him who thinks he stands be careful that he doesn’t fall*” (*v. 12*). Some Corinthians were overconfident. They believed that because they had been baptized and shared in the Lord’s Supper, they were safe, no matter what they did. Paul warns them: those who think they are standing firm should be careful. Overconfidence is dangerous. Pride comes before a fall (*Proverbs 16:18*).

But Paul does not leave them in fear. He immediately gives a promise.

“*No temptation has taken you except what is common to man*” (*v. 13*). The temptations believers face are not unique. Others have faced the same struggles. Believers are not alone.

“*God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted above what you are able*” (*v. 13*). God is faithful. He sets limits on temptation. He will not allow believers to face temptation beyond what they can bear, with His help.

“*but will with the temptation also make the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it*” (*v. 13*). With every temptation, God provides a way out. This does not always mean the temptation disappears. It means God gives believers the strength and the means to resist it and endure it without falling into sin. The “way of escape” may be fleeing the situation, calling a friend, turning to prayer, remembering Scripture, or simply saying no.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses balance warning and assurance. Believers should not be overconfident, assuming they cannot fall. But neither should they despair, believing temptation is too strong. God is faithful. Peter writes, “*the Lord knows how to deliver the godly out of temptation*” (*2 Peter 2:9*).

They also show that temptation is not sin. Being tempted is a common human experience; even Jesus was tempted (*Hebrews 4:15*). Sin occurs when people give in to temptation. God provides the strength to resist.

Finally, these verses show God’s faithful care. He knows His people’s limits. He does not abandon them to temptation but walks with them through it and provides a way out. This is part of His loving fatherhood.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses warn believers against spiritual pride. No believer is beyond temptation or immune from falling. Believers can stay humble, watchful, and dependent on God.

They also encourage believers facing temptation. Whatever temptation they face, they are not alone, and God will provide a way of escape. Believers can look for that way out: leaving a situation, setting boundaries, seeking accountability, or turning to God in prayer.

Finally, these verses encourage believers who feel that their temptation is too great. God is faithful. With His help, they can resist. If they fall, they can confess and receive forgiveness (*1 John 1:9*), and keep walking with Him.

### *1 Corinthians 10:16–17* — Sharing in the Body and Blood of Christ

> *“The cup of blessing which we bless, isn’t it a sharing of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, isn’t it a sharing of the body of Christ? Because there is one loaf of bread, we, who are many, are one body; for we all partake of the one loaf of bread.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 10:16–17* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had told the Corinthians to flee from idolatry. Some of them were attending feasts in pagan temples, believing that because idols were nothing, it did not matter. Paul now explains why participating in such feasts was incompatible with following Christ.

“*The cup of blessing which we bless, isn’t it a sharing of the blood of Christ?*” (*v. 16*) In the Lord’s Supper, believers drink from the cup. “The cup of blessing” was a phrase used at Jewish Passover meals for the cup over which a blessing was spoken. Jesus used such a cup at the Last Supper. When believers drink it, they have “sharing” (koinonia) in the blood of Christ. They participate in the benefits of His death.

“*The bread which we break, isn’t it a sharing of the body of Christ?*” (*v. 16*) When believers eat the bread, they share in the body of Christ. They are united with Him.

“*Because there is one loaf of bread, we, who are many, are one body; for we all partake of the one loaf of bread*” (*v. 17*). The one loaf symbolizes the unity of believers. Although there are many of them, they all eat from the same loaf, showing that they are one body in Christ. The Lord’s Supper unites believers not only with Christ but with one another.

Paul’s point is that eating is participation. If eating the Lord’s Supper means sharing in Christ, then eating at a pagan sacrifice means sharing in what that sacrifice represents. Believers cannot share in both.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show the deep meaning of the Lord’s Supper. It is not merely a reminder of a past event; it is a “sharing” in Christ. Christians have understood this sharing in different ways. Some traditions believe that Christ’s body and blood are truly present in the bread and cup. Others believe Christ is spiritually present, nourishing believers by faith. Others understand the Supper mainly as a memorial and proclamation of His death. All agree that the Supper is a sacred act that unites believers with Christ and with one another.

They also show the unity of the church. The one loaf represents the one body. Believers who share the Lord’s Supper together declare that they belong to one another. This makes divisions in the church especially serious, as Paul will discuss in chapter 11.

Finally, these verses show that worship involves loyalty. Believers cannot divide their worship between Christ and idols. Jesus said, “*No one can serve two masters*” (*Matthew 6:24*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to approach the Lord’s Supper with reverence. When believers share the bread and cup, they participate in Christ and His sacrifice. They can come with gratitude, faith, and self-examination.

They also call believers to unity. The Lord’s Supper declares that believers are one body. Believers can examine whether there are divisions or broken relationships that need to be healed.

Finally, these verses challenge believers to give their undivided loyalty to Christ. Believers can examine whether they are trying to serve Christ while also giving their hearts to other things that compete for their worship.

### *1 Corinthians 10:23–24* — Not All Things Build Up

> *“‘All things are lawful for me,’ but not all things are profitable. ‘All things are lawful for me,’ but not all things build up. Let no one seek his own, but each one his neighbor’s good.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 10:23–24* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul returns to a slogan the Corinthians liked to use: “*“All things are lawful for me,”*” (*v. 23*). He had addressed this slogan in 6:12 in the context of sexual immorality. Now he addresses it in the context of food and freedom.

“*but not all things are profitable*” (*v. 23*). Even if something is permitted, it may not be beneficial. Believers should consider whether an action is good for them and for others.

“*“All things are lawful for me,” but not all things build up*” (*v. 23*). Paul repeats the slogan and adds a second qualification. Even if something is permitted, it may not “build up,” strengthen others’ faith or the community. In 6:12, Paul’s second point was about not being mastered by anything. Here it is about edification, the good of others.

“*Let no one seek his own, but each one his neighbor’s good*” (*v. 24*). This is the guiding principle. Believers should not seek only their own good, comfort, or freedom. They should seek the good of others.

These verses summarize the whole discussion of chapters 8–10. Freedom is real, but love governs it. The question is not only “Am I allowed?” but “Will this help others?”

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that Christian freedom is shaped by love. Paul writes elsewhere, “*each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others*” (*Philippians 2:4*). Love considers others before self.

They also show that the Christian life is not merely about avoiding sin but about building up others. Believers can ask not only “Is this wrong?” but “Is this good? Does it help others grow?”

Finally, these verses show the pattern of Christ. Jesus did not seek His own good but the good of others, even to the point of death. His followers are called to the same self-giving love.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses give believers a helpful test for decisions. Before acting, believers can ask: Is this beneficial? Will this build others up? Am I seeking my own good or my neighbor’s good?

They also encourage believers to think beyond themselves. In a culture that emphasizes individual rights and self-fulfillment, believers can consider how their choices affect their families, churches, and communities.

Finally, these verses encourage believers to seek opportunities to help others. Seeking a neighbor’s good is not only about avoiding harm but about actively doing good, encouraging, serving, and supporting others.

### *1 Corinthians 10:31* — Do All to the Glory of God

> *“Whether therefore you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 10:31* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had been giving practical guidelines about eating food that may have been offered to idols. Believers could eat food bought in the market without asking questions. They could eat at unbelievers’ homes. But if someone pointed out that the food had been offered to idols, they should refrain for the sake of that person’s conscience.

Now Paul states the principle that governs everything: “*Whether therefore you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God*” (*v. 31*).

This verse applies to every area of life. Eating and drinking are the most ordinary activities. If even these can be done for God’s glory, then everything can. “Whatever you do” includes work, rest, relationships, conversations, recreation, and every decision.

To do something “to the glory of God” means to do it in a way that honors Him, shows His worth, and reflects His character. It means doing it with gratitude, in obedience to Him, in love for others, and with awareness that He is the source of all good things.

Paul continues: “*Give no occasion for stumbling, whether to Jews, to Greeks, or to the assembly of God*” (*v. 32*). Glorifying God includes not causing others to stumble. “*even as I also please all men in all things, not seeking my own profit, but the profit of the many, that they may be saved*” (*v. 33*). Paul’s goal in everything was the salvation of others.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that all of life is worship. There is no division between sacred and secular for believers. Everything can be done for God’s glory. Paul writes, “*Whatever you do, in word or in deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him*” (*Colossians 3:17*).

It also shows the purpose of human life. People were created to glorify God. The Westminster Shorter Catechism famously begins, “Man’s chief end is to glorify God, and to enjoy him forever.” Believers find their deepest purpose in living for God’s glory.

Finally, the verse shows that glorifying God involves love for others. Paul connects glorifying God with not causing others to stumble and seeking their salvation. God is glorified when His people love one another and point others to Him.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to see every part of life as an opportunity to glorify God. Washing dishes, studying, working, exercising, and resting can all be done for His glory. Believers can begin each day by offering everything to Him.

It also gives believers a guide for decisions. When unsure about a choice, believers can ask, “Will this glorify God?” This question can clarify many decisions.

Finally, the verse encourages believers to live with gratitude. Glorifying God in eating and drinking means receiving food as His gift and thanking Him for it. Believers can practice gratitude in all things, recognizing that every good gift comes from God.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*1 Corinthians 10* warns believers not to presume on their spiritual privileges. Israel experienced God’s deliverance and provision, yet many fell into idolatry, immorality, testing God, and grumbling. These things were written as warnings. Believers who think they stand firm should be careful not to fall, staying humble and watchful.

The chapter also offers a wonderful promise: no temptation is beyond what is common to humanity, and God is faithful. He will not allow believers to be tempted beyond what they can bear, and He will provide a way of escape. Believers facing temptation can look for that way out and trust God’s strength.

*1 Corinthians 10* teaches that the Lord’s Supper is a sharing in the body and blood of Christ, and that believers cannot share in both the Lord’s table and the table of demons. Believers can come to the Lord’s Supper with reverence and give their undivided loyalty to Christ, fleeing every form of idolatry.

Finally, the chapter gives practical wisdom for living in freedom. Not everything permitted is beneficial or builds others up. Believers should seek their neighbor’s good, not merely their own. And in everything, from eating and drinking to the greatest decisions, believers can do all for the glory of God, giving no cause for stumbling and seeking the salvation of others.

## Chapter Prayer

Faithful God, thank You for the warnings You have given through Israel’s history. Keep me humble, so that I never think I stand so firmly that I cannot fall. Thank You that no temptation I face is beyond what others have faced, and that You will not let me be tempted beyond what I can bear. Show me the way of escape when temptation comes, and give me strength to take it. Lord Jesus, thank You for the cup of blessing and the broken bread, which unite me with You and with Your people. Help me to give You my undivided loyalty and to flee every form of idolatry. Teach me to seek my neighbor’s good rather than my own. Whether I eat or drink or whatever I do, help me to do it all for Your glory. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

1 Corinthians · Chapter 11 of 16

# 1 Corinthians — Chapter 11

Chapter Theme: Honor in Worship and the Meaning of the Lord’s Supper

[Read 1 Corinthians 11 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/1CO11.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul addresses two problems in the Corinthians’ worship gatherings. First, he gives instruction about head coverings for men and women who pray and prophesy, grounding it in honor, creation, and the mutual dependence of men and women in the Lord. Second, he rebukes the church because their gatherings for the Lord’s Supper have become occasions of division, where the wealthy feast while the poor go hungry. He reminds them of the words Jesus spoke on the night He was betrayed, explains that the Supper proclaims the Lord’s death until He comes, and calls each believer to examine themselves and discern the Lord’s body, so that they come together in love rather than for judgment.

## Chapter Background and Story

*1 Corinthians 11* begins a section of the letter (chapters 11–14) about the church’s worship gatherings. In Corinth, believers met in homes, often in the houses of wealthier members. Worship included prayer, prophecy, teaching, singing, and a shared meal that included the Lord’s Supper.

The first issue Paul addresses, head coverings, is one of the most difficult passages in Paul’s letters for modern readers. The customs involved were closely tied to the culture of the first century, and scholars still debate exactly what Paul meant by several phrases. The second issue, the abuse of the Lord’s Supper, is clearer and contains the earliest written account of Jesus’ words at the Last Supper.

The chapter begins with a sentence that probably belongs with chapter 10: “*Be imitators of me, even as I also am of Christ*” (*v. 1*). Paul had just described how he gave up his rights to seek the good of others. He invites the Corinthians to follow his example as he follows Christ.

### Head Coverings in Worship (*11:2–16*)

Paul begins with praise: “*Now I praise you, brothers, that you remember me in all things, and hold firm the traditions, even as I delivered them to you*” (*v. 2*). Then he explains: “*But I would have you know that the head of every man is Christ, and the head of the woman is man, and the head of Christ is God*” (*v. 3*). The word “head” has been understood in different ways. Many interpreters understand it to mean authority, so that Paul is describing an order of leadership: Christ, man, woman. Others understand “head” to mean source or origin, since Paul goes on to say that woman came from man in creation (*11:8*, 12) and Christ came from God. Notice that the relationship between Christ and God involves both equality and order; Christ is fully God, yet He submitted to the Father. Whatever “head” means, it does not imply that women are of lesser worth.

Paul then speaks of men and women praying and prophesying. “*Every man praying or prophesying, having his head covered, dishonors his head*” (*v. 4*). “*But every woman praying or prophesying with her head uncovered dishonors her head*” (*v. 5*). Notice that Paul assumes women pray and prophesy in the gathered church. His concern is how they do so. In Corinthian culture, a married woman’s head covering was a sign of modesty and respectability. A woman appearing publicly without it might be seen as immodest or as rejecting her marriage. For men, covering the head in worship was associated with certain pagan religious practices.

Paul appeals to creation: “*For a man indeed ought not to have his head covered, because he is the image and glory of God, but the woman is the glory of the man*” (*v. 7*). “*For man is not from woman, but woman from man*” (*v. 8*); “*for man wasn’t created for the woman, but woman for the man*” (*v. 9*). Paul refers to *Genesis 2*, where the woman was created from the man to be his partner. “*For this cause the woman ought to have authority over her own head, because of the angels*” (*v. 10*). This difficult verse has been interpreted in many ways. Some think the angels observe the church’s worship and care about proper order (compare *1 Corinthians 4:9*; *Ephesians 3:10*). Many note that the Greek says the woman ought to have authority “over” her head, which may mean she has the right to pray and prophesy, exercising her own authority with appropriate honor. Paul then balances his teaching, as studied below.

Paul also appeals to what was natural and customary: “*Doesn’t even nature itself teach you that if a man has long hair, it is a dishonor to him?*” (*v. 14*) “*But if a woman has long hair, it is a glory to her, for her hair is given to her for a covering*” (*v. 15*). “Nature” here may mean the natural order of things or the customs that had become second nature in their culture. He concludes, “*But if any man seems to be contentious, we have no such custom, neither do God’s assemblies*” (*v. 16*).

Christians today apply this passage in different ways. Some churches practice head coverings for women in worship, believing the instruction is still binding. Most understand the head covering as a cultural expression of a deeper principle, honoring God and one another, maintaining appropriate distinctions between men and women, and avoiding behavior that would bring shame on the church, which can be expressed in different ways in different cultures. Christians also differ on how this passage relates to women’s roles in church leadership. What is clear is that Paul cares about honor, order, and the mutual dependence of men and women in the Lord.

### Abuses at the Lord’s Supper (*11:17–22*)

Paul’s tone changes: “*But in giving you this command I don’t praise you, because you come together not for the better but for the worse*” (*v. 17*). Their gatherings were doing more harm than good. “*For first of all, when you come together in the assembly, I hear that divisions exist among you*” (*v. 18*). The divisions here seem to be social and economic. “*For there also must be factions among you, that those who are approved may be revealed among you*” (*v. 19*). Divisions reveal who is genuinely faithful.

“*When therefore you assemble yourselves together, it is not the Lord’s supper that you eat*” (*v. 20*). “*For in your eating each one takes his own supper first. One is hungry, and another is drunken*” (*v. 21*). In a Roman home, the wealthier guests might eat in the dining room, arriving early with plenty of food and wine, while poorer members, including slaves who had to work until evening, arrived late and found little or nothing left. The meal meant to express unity in Christ had become a display of social inequality.

“*What, don’t you have houses to eat and to drink in? Or do you despise God’s assembly and put them to shame who don’t have enough?*” (*v. 22*) By humiliating the poor, they were despising the church itself. Paul refuses to praise them.

### The Institution of the Lord’s Supper (*11:23–26*)

Paul reminds them of Jesus’ words, studied below.

### Examine Yourselves (*11:27–34*)

Paul’s warning about eating unworthily is studied below. He adds, “*For this cause many among you are weak and sickly, and not a few sleep*” (*v. 30*). Paul links some illness and even death in the church to their abuse of the Supper. This does not mean all sickness is caused by sin (*John 9:2–3*), but in this case, God was disciplining His people. “*But when we are judged, we are disciplined by the Lord, that we may not be condemned with the world*” (*v. 32*). God’s discipline is meant to restore, not to destroy.

Paul gives a practical solution: “*Therefore, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another*” (*v. 33*). “*But if anyone is hungry, let him eat at home, lest your coming together be for judgment*” (*v. 34*). The gathering should reflect the unity and love of Christ’s body.

## Important Verses Explained

### *1 Corinthians 11:11–12* — Not Independent, but All from God

> *“Nevertheless, neither is the woman independent of the man, nor the man independent of the woman, in the Lord. For as woman came from man, so a man also comes through a woman; but all things are from God.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 11:11–12* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had been discussing head coverings in worship and had pointed to the order of creation, saying that woman was created from man and for man (*Genesis 2*). Some readers might have taken this to mean that men are superior to women. Paul immediately guards against that misunderstanding.

“*Nevertheless, neither is the woman independent of the man, nor the man independent of the woman, in the Lord*” (*v. 11*). The word “nevertheless” signals a strong balancing statement. “In the Lord,” in the new life believers share in Christ, men and women are not independent of each other. They belong together. They need each other.

“*For as woman came from man, so a man also comes through a woman*” (*v. 12*). In creation, the first woman came from the first man. But ever since, every man has been born of a woman. If one were to argue for male priority from creation, one would have to admit that every man owes his life to a mother. The relationship is mutual.

“*but all things are from God*” (*v. 12*). Ultimately, both men and women come from God. Neither is the source of the other’s worth. Both are created by God, in His image (*Genesis 1:27*), and both depend on Him.

These verses show that whatever distinctions Paul has in mind, they exist within a deeper equality and mutual dependence. Men and women are partners, not rivals.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses reflect the creation account, where God created humanity as male and female, both in His image: “*God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them*” (*Genesis 1:27*). Both men and women bear the full dignity of God’s image.

They also reflect the new creation in Christ. Paul writes, “*There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free man, there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus*” (*Galatians 3:28*). In Christ, men and women share equally in salvation, the Spirit, and the inheritance of God’s children.

Finally, these verses show that God is the source of all. Human relationships, including those between men and women, find their meaning in God, who made all things and to whom all things belong.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage mutual respect between men and women. Believers can honor one another as equally created in God’s image and equally redeemed by Christ, recognizing that they need each other.

They also guard against using Scripture to belittle women. Any interpretation of this chapter that treats women as inferior contradicts Paul’s own words here. Churches can value, include, and honor women’s gifts and contributions.

Finally, these verses encourage partnership in marriage, family, and church. Men and women can work together, each contributing their gifts, in humble dependence on God and one another.

### *1 Corinthians 11:23–25* — “Do This in Memory of Me”

> *“For I received from the Lord that which also I delivered to you, that the Lord Jesus on the night in which he was betrayed took bread. When he had given thanks, he broke it and said, ‘Take, eat. This is my body, which is broken for you. Do this in memory of me.’ In the same way he also took the cup after supper, saying, ‘This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink, in memory of me.’”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 11:23–25* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had rebuked the Corinthians for turning the Lord’s Supper into a selfish meal where some went hungry while others got drunk. To correct them, he reminded them of what the Lord’s Supper truly means.

“*For I received from the Lord that which also I delivered to you*” (*v. 23*). Paul passed on what he had received. The words “received” and “delivered” were used for passing on sacred tradition. Paul received this teaching through the earliest believers, and ultimately from the Lord Himself. This passage, written around A.D. 54, is the earliest written account of the Last Supper, older than the Gospels.

“*that the Lord Jesus on the night in which he was betrayed took bread*” (*v. 23*). Paul sets the scene: the night of betrayal. Even as Judas was betraying Him, Jesus gave His disciples this gift.

“*When he had given thanks, he broke it and said, “Take, eat. This is my body, which is broken for you. Do this in memory of me.”*” (*v. 24*) Jesus gave thanks, broke the bread, and identified it with His body given for His disciples. The word for “given thanks” is eucharisteo, from which comes “Eucharist,” a name many Christians use for the Lord’s Supper.

“*In the same way he also took the cup after supper, saying, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink, in memory of me.”*” (*v. 25*) The cup represents the new covenant, the promise God made through Jeremiah to forgive His people’s sins and write His law on their hearts (*Jeremiah 31:31–34*). This covenant is sealed by Jesus’ blood, His death on the cross.

Twice Jesus said, “Do this in memory of me.” The Supper is a remembrance. But in Scripture, remembering is more than recalling a past event. It is bringing it into the present, participating in its meaning, as Israel “remembered” the Passover by celebrating it each year.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that the Lord’s Supper is centered on Christ’s sacrifice. His body was broken and His blood poured out for His people. The Supper keeps the cross at the center of the church’s life. The meaning of Jesus’ covenant blood is studied at *Matthew 26:28* and *Mark 14:24*.

They also show that the Supper is a gift from Jesus Himself. It was not invented by the church; Jesus instituted it and commanded His followers to continue it. Christians across all traditions celebrate it, though they understand Christ’s presence in it in different ways.

Finally, these verses show the grace of Jesus. On the night He was betrayed, abandoned, and arrested, He gave His disciples a meal of love. He gave Himself for those who would fail Him.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to participate faithfully in the Lord’s Supper. Jesus commanded it, and believers can obey with gratitude, remembering His sacrifice.

They also encourage believers to remember Christ’s death often, not only at the Lord’s Supper. Believers can reflect regularly on the cross and what it means for their lives.

Finally, these verses call believers to approach the Supper with the same self-giving love Jesus showed. The Corinthians were using the meal selfishly. Believers can come to the table in a spirit of humility, gratitude, and love for one another.

### *1 Corinthians 11:26* — Proclaiming the Lord’s Death Until He Comes

> *“For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 11:26* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had just recounted Jesus’ words at the Last Supper. Now he explains what happens when believers celebrate the Supper.

“*For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death*” (*v. 26*). The Lord’s Supper is a proclamation. Every time believers share the bread and cup, they declare the message of the cross. The Supper is a visible sermon, announcing that Jesus died for sinners.

The word “proclaim” is the same word used for preaching the gospel. The Supper does not merely remind believers privately; it announces publicly that Christ died.

“*until he comes*” (*v. 26*). The Supper also looks forward. Believers celebrate it “until he comes,” until Jesus returns. It is a meal for the time between His first coming and His second coming. Jesus said at the Last Supper that He would not drink of the fruit of the vine again until He drank it new in His Father’s kingdom (*Matthew 26:29*). The Supper anticipates the great banquet at the end of the age, the marriage supper of the Lamb (*Revelation 19:9*).

So the Lord’s Supper looks in three directions: backward to the cross, upward to the risen Lord who is present with His people, and forward to His return.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that the Lord’s Supper is a central act of Christian witness. In every generation, as believers gather at the table, they proclaim the death of Christ. This has continued for two thousand years, in every nation and language.

It also shows that the Christian life is lived in hope. Believers do not only look back to the cross; they look forward to Christ’s return. The Supper is a foretaste of the future feast, when Christ’s people will be gathered with Him forever.

Finally, the verse connects the Supper to the gospel. The death of Christ is the heart of the good news. Every celebration of the Supper is a reminder of that good news and an invitation to receive it.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to see the Lord’s Supper as an act of proclamation. When believers share in it, they declare their faith in Christ’s death. It is an opportunity to remember and to witness.

It also encourages believers to live in hope of Christ’s return. The Supper reminds them that history is moving toward a glorious conclusion. Believers can live with expectation and readiness.

Finally, the verse reminds believers that their whole lives can proclaim Christ’s death. The Supper is one way of proclaiming it, but believers can also proclaim it through words of witness and lives of self-giving love.

### *1 Corinthians 11:28–29* — Examine Yourself and Discern the Body

> *“But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of the bread and drink of the cup. For he who eats and drinks in an unworthy way eats and drinks judgment to himself if he doesn’t discern the Lord’s body.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 11:28–29* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had warned that “*whoever eats this bread or drinks the Lord’s cup in a way unworthy of the Lord will be guilty of the body and the blood of the Lord*” (*v. 27*). Eating “in an unworthy way” does not mean that only perfect people can take the Supper. No one is worthy in that sense; the Supper is for sinners saved by grace. In context, eating in an unworthy way meant treating the Supper carelessly and selfishly, as the Corinthians were doing by humiliating the poor and getting drunk.

“*But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of the bread and drink of the cup*” (*v. 28*). Before taking the Supper, each believer should examine their heart and life. Are they coming with faith in Christ? Are they treating fellow believers with love? Are there sins they need to confess or relationships they need to make right? Notice that after examining themselves, believers are to eat. Self-examination is not meant to keep believers away from the table but to prepare them to come rightly.

“*For he who eats and drinks in an unworthy way eats and drinks judgment to himself if he doesn’t discern the Lord’s body*” (*v. 29*). “Discerning the body” has been understood in two ways, and both are likely included. It may mean recognizing the significance of the bread as representing Christ’s body given for them. It may also mean recognizing the church as the body of Christ (*10:17*; *12:27*), and treating fellow believers with love. The Corinthians were failing to discern the body by despising the poor members of the church.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that the Lord’s Supper is holy. It is not an ordinary meal. It represents Christ’s body and blood and the unity of His people. Treating it carelessly dishonors Christ.

They also show the importance of self-examination in the Christian life. Believers are called to regularly examine their hearts and lives. The psalmist prayed, “*Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts*” (*Psalm 139:23*).

Finally, these verses show that love for fellow believers is connected to communion with Christ. Believers cannot rightly share the body and blood of Christ while despising His body, the church. Jesus taught that believers should be reconciled with others before bringing their offering to God (*Matthew 5:23–24*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to prepare their hearts before taking the Lord’s Supper. Believers can take time to pray, confess sin, and reflect on Christ’s sacrifice.

They also encourage believers to examine their relationships. Before coming to the table, believers can ask whether there is anyone they need to forgive or seek forgiveness from, and whether they are treating all members of the church with love and honor.

Finally, these verses encourage believers who feel unworthy. The Supper is not for perfect people but for sinners who trust in Christ. Self-examination leads not to staying away but to coming humbly, receiving grace, and renewing commitment to Christ and His people.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*1 Corinthians 11* shows that worship should be marked by honor, order, and respect. Paul’s teaching about head coverings reflected the customs of his day, and Christians apply it in different ways. But its underlying principles remain: honoring God in worship, avoiding what brings shame on the church, and recognizing that men and women are mutually dependent in the Lord, both coming from God and both created in His image.

The chapter also confronts division in the church. The Corinthians’ gatherings had become places where the wealthy feasted and the poor went hungry. Believers today can examine whether their churches reflect social divisions or the unity of Christ’s body, and they can make sure that every member, especially the poor and overlooked, is honored and cared for.

*1 Corinthians 11* contains the earliest written account of Jesus’ words at the Last Supper. The bread represents His body broken for His people; the cup represents the new covenant in His blood. Believers can celebrate the Supper faithfully, remembering Christ’s sacrifice, proclaiming His death, and looking forward to His return.

Finally, the chapter calls believers to examine themselves before coming to the Lord’s table and to discern the Lord’s body. Believers can prepare their hearts through confession and reconciliation, coming not as perfect people but as forgiven sinners, and treating one another with the love that the Supper proclaims.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for the gift of Your Supper, given on the night You were betrayed. Thank You for Your body broken for me and Your blood poured out to seal the new covenant. Help me to remember You, not only at Your table but every day. As I share in the bread and cup, let me proclaim Your death until You come. Search my heart before I come, and show me any sin I need to confess or relationship I need to make right. Help me to discern Your body, both in the bread and in Your people, and to honor every brother and sister, especially the poor and overlooked. Thank You that men and women are created in Your image and need each other in You. Make Your church a place of honor, love, and unity. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
