1 Corinthians · Chapter 12 of 16

# 1 Corinthians — Chapter 12

Chapter Theme: One Spirit, Many Gifts, One Body

[Read 1 Corinthians 12 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/1CO12.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul begins answering the Corinthians’ questions about spiritual gifts by establishing that genuine Spirit-led speech confesses “Jesus is Lord.” There are many kinds of gifts, services, and workings, but the same Spirit, Lord, and God gives them all, and each is given for the common good. Using the picture of a human body, Paul shows that the church is one body with many members, all baptized by one Spirit. No member should feel it does not belong because it is different, and no member should look down on another as unnecessary. God gives special honor to the parts that seem weaker, so that members care for one another, suffering and rejoicing together. Not everyone has the same gift, and Paul points them toward a still more excellent way.

## Chapter Background and Story

*1 Corinthians 12–14* addresses another question the Corinthians had written about: spiritual gifts. The Corinthian church was richly gifted (*1:7*), but the gifts had become a source of pride and division. Some believers apparently valued the more spectacular gifts, especially speaking in tongues, above others. Those with these gifts may have considered themselves more spiritual, while those without them may have felt inferior.

Paul’s answer has three parts. In chapter 12, he teaches that all gifts come from the same Spirit and serve the one body. In chapter 13, he shows that love is greater than any gift. In chapter 14, he gives practical instructions for using gifts, especially prophecy and tongues, in orderly worship that builds up the church.

Christians today hold different views about some of the gifts Paul lists. Some, often called cessationists, believe that certain gifts, such as prophecy, tongues, and miraculous healing, were given mainly to establish the church in the apostolic age and are no longer given in the same way. Others, often called continuationists, including Pentecostal and charismatic Christians, believe that all the gifts continue today. Many hold views in between. All agree that the Spirit gives gifts to every believer for the good of the church, and that love must govern their use.

### The Test of the Spirit (*12:1–3*)

Paul’s opening principle is studied below.

### Varieties of Gifts, One Source (*12:4–11*)

Paul’s teaching on the unity behind the variety is studied below. He then lists examples of gifts. “*For to one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, and to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit*” (*v. 8*). A “word of wisdom” may be a Spirit-given insight into how to apply God’s truth; a “word of knowledge” may be Spirit-given understanding of God’s truth or of a situation. “*to another faith by the same Spirit, and to another gifts of healings by the same Spirit*” (*v. 9*). “Faith” here is not saving faith, which all believers have, but a special gift of trust in God for extraordinary things. “*and to another workings of miracles, and to another prophecy, and to another discerning of spirits, to another different kinds of languages, and to another the interpretation of languages*” (*v. 10*). “Prophecy” is speaking a message from God for the church’s encouragement and building up (*14:3*). “Discerning of spirits” is the ability to tell whether a message or influence comes from God or from another source. “Different kinds of languages,” often called “tongues,” is speaking in languages one has not learned, and “interpretation” is the ability to explain the meaning.

“*But the one and the same Spirit produces all of these, distributing to each one separately as he desires*” (*v. 11*). The Spirit decides who receives which gift. No one can boast about their gift, because it was given, not earned.

### One Body, Many Members (*12:12–26*)

“*For as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, being many, are one body; so also is Christ*” (*v. 12*). The church is the body of Christ. “*For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Greeks, whether bond or free; and were all given to drink into one Spirit*” (*v. 13*). Every believer has been baptized by the Spirit into the one body, regardless of ethnicity or social status. All have been given the Spirit to drink, like water that refreshes and gives life.

Paul then imagines parts of the body talking. “*If the foot would say, “Because I’m not the hand, I’m not part of the body,” it is not therefore not part of the body*” (*v. 15*). Some believers felt that because they did not have certain gifts, they did not belong. Paul says they do. “*If the whole body were an eye, where would the hearing be?*” (*v. 17*) A body needs different parts. “*But now God has set the members, each one of them, in the body, just as he desired*” (*v. 18*). God has arranged the body according to His wisdom.

Paul’s teaching about the weaker members and mutual care is studied below.

### You Are the Body of Christ (*12:27–31*)

Paul’s declaration is studied below with verse 26. He then lists roles in the church: “*God has set some in the assembly: first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then miracle workers, then gifts of healings, helps, governments, and various kinds of languages*” (*v. 28*). “Helps” may refer to acts of assistance and service; “governments” to administration or guidance. Notice that tongues appears last. The Corinthians may have placed it first, but Paul does not.

“*Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Are all miracle workers?*” (*v. 29*) “*Do all have gifts of healings? Do all speak with various languages? Do all interpret?*” (*v. 30*) The expected answer to each question is no. Not every believer has every gift, and no single gift is required of all.

“*But earnestly desire the best gifts. Moreover, I show a most excellent way to you*” (*v. 31*). The “best gifts” are those that most build up the church, such as prophecy (*14:1*, 5). But even greater than seeking gifts is the “most excellent way,” the way of love, which Paul describes in chapter 13.

## Important Verses Explained

### *1 Corinthians 12:3* — “*Jesus Is Lord*” (*v. 3*) by the Holy Spirit

> *“Therefore I make known to you that no man speaking by God’s Spirit says, ‘Jesus is accursed.’ No one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ but by the Holy Spirit.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 12:3* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul begins his teaching on spiritual gifts by reminding the Corinthians of their past: “*You know that when you were heathen, you were led away to those mute idols, however you might be led*” (*v. 2*). Before they knew Christ, many of the Corinthians had worshiped idols. Pagan worship sometimes included ecstatic experiences, where worshipers felt carried away by spiritual forces. The Corinthians knew what it was like to be “led” by spiritual powers. Not every spiritual experience comes from God.

So how can believers tell whether something comes from the Holy Spirit? Paul gives a basic test: “*Therefore I make known to you that no man speaking by God’s Spirit says, “Jesus is accursed.”*” (*v. 3*) The Holy Spirit would never lead anyone to curse Jesus. Any message that dishonors Christ is not from God’s Spirit. Some interpreters think that someone in Corinth may have actually spoken against Jesus while claiming to be inspired, perhaps distinguishing between the earthly Jesus and a spiritual Christ.

“*No one can say, “Jesus is Lord,” but by the Holy Spirit*” (*v. 3*). Anyone can say the words “Jesus is Lord,” but no one can truly confess Jesus as Lord, with genuine faith and submission, except by the work of the Holy Spirit. “Jesus is Lord” was the earliest Christian confession (*Romans 10:9*). It meant acknowledging Jesus as the divine Lord and giving Him one’s allegiance, in a world where Caesar demanded to be called lord.

This verse sets the foundation for the whole discussion of gifts. The most important evidence of the Spirit’s work is not spectacular gifts, but the confession that Jesus is Lord. Every believer who truly confesses Jesus as Lord has the Holy Spirit.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that the Holy Spirit always glorifies Jesus. Jesus said of the Spirit, “*He will glorify me*” (*John 16:14*). The Spirit’s work is centered on Christ. Any spiritual experience, gift, or teaching that draws attention away from Jesus or contradicts His lordship is not from the Spirit.

It also shows that faith itself is the work of the Spirit. No one can truly confess Jesus as Lord by human effort alone. Every believer’s faith is evidence of the Spirit’s work in their life.

Finally, the verse shows that all believers are equal in the most important sense. Every believer who confesses Jesus as Lord does so by the Spirit. There are no first-class and second-class Christians. Some may have more visible gifts, but all have the Spirit.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse helps believers evaluate spiritual experiences and teachings. Believers can ask: Does this honor Jesus as Lord? Does it agree with what Scripture teaches about Him? If not, it does not come from the Holy Spirit.

It also encourages believers who feel spiritually inferior. Every believer who truly confesses Jesus as Lord has the Holy Spirit. Spectacular gifts are not the measure of spirituality.

Finally, the verse invites believers to confess Jesus as Lord in every area of their lives. Confessing Jesus as Lord is not only a statement of belief; it is a commitment to follow Him in everything.

### *1 Corinthians 12:4–7* — Different Gifts, the Same Spirit, for the Common Good

> *“Now there are various kinds of gifts, but the same Spirit. There are various kinds of service, and the same Lord. There are various kinds of workings, but the same God who works all things in all. But to each one is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the profit of all.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 12:4–7* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The Corinthian church had many spiritual gifts, but they had become a source of competition and pride. Some believers valued certain gifts above others and looked down on those who did not have them. Paul explains the true nature of gifts.

“*Now there are various kinds of gifts, but the same Spirit*” (*v. 4*). The gifts are different, but they all come from the same Holy Spirit. The word “gifts” (charismata) is related to the word “grace” (charis). Gifts are expressions of God’s grace.

“*There are various kinds of service, and the same Lord*” (*v. 5*). Gifts are also “service.” They are not for showing off but for serving others. And all service is done for the same Lord, Jesus Christ.

“*There are various kinds of workings, but the same God who works all things in all*” (*v. 6*). Gifts are also “workings,” expressions of God’s power at work. And it is the same God who works in all believers.

Notice the threefold pattern: the same Spirit, the same Lord, the same God. Paul connects the gifts to the Holy Spirit, the Lord Jesus, and God the Father. The unity of the Triune God is the foundation for the unity of the church. The variety of gifts reflects the richness of God; the unity of the source reflects the oneness of God.

“*But to each one is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the profit of all*” (*v. 7*). Two important truths. First, “to each one.” Every believer has been given some gift, some way the Spirit shows Himself through them. No believer is left out. Second, “for the profit of all.” Gifts are given for the common good, to benefit the whole church, not for personal glory.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that the diversity of gifts reflects the nature of God. Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are distinct Persons yet one God. The church, with its many members and gifts, reflects this unity in diversity.

They also show that every believer has a role. Peter writes, “*As each has received a gift, employ it in serving one another*” (*1 Peter 4:10*). No believer is meant to be a spectator in the church.

Finally, these verses show that gifts are for others. The purpose of every gift is the common good. Gifts used for self-promotion or to make others feel inferior are being misused.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage every believer to recognize that they have a gift. Believers can ask God to show them how He has gifted them and look for ways to serve others.

They also encourage believers to use their gifts for the good of others. Believers can ask not “How does this gift make me look?” but “How can this gift help others?”

Finally, these verses encourage believers to value different gifts. A church needs many kinds of gifts. Believers can appreciate and honor gifts that are different from their own.

### *1 Corinthians 12:21–22* — The Weaker Members Are Necessary

> *“The eye can’t tell the hand, ‘I have no need for you,’ or again the head to the feet, ‘I have no need for you.’ No, much rather, those members of the body which seem to be weaker are necessary.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 12:21–22* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had been using the image of a human body to describe the church. He had addressed believers who felt they did not belong because they were different. Now he addresses the opposite problem: believers who thought others were unnecessary.

“*The eye can’t tell the hand, “I have no need for you,” or again the head to the feet, “I have no need for you.”*” (*v. 21*) If an eye said to the hand, “I don’t need you,” it would forget that without hands, the eye could see things but never pick them up. If the head said to the feet, “I don’t need you,” it would forget that without feet, the head could never go anywhere. Every part of the body needs the others.

In the church, some believers with prominent gifts may have looked down on others, thinking they did not need them. Paul says this is foolish. Every member is needed.

“*No, much rather, those members of the body which seem to be weaker are necessary*” (*v. 22*). Paul goes further. The parts of the body that “seem” weaker are actually essential. Think of the heart, lungs, or brain. They are hidden and delicate, yet absolutely necessary for life.

Paul continues: “*Those parts of the body which we think to be less honorable, on those we bestow more abundant honor*” (*v. 23*). People take special care of the parts of the body they consider less presentable, clothing them with modesty. “*But God composed the body together, giving more abundant honor to the inferior part*” (*v. 24*). God has arranged the church so that those who seem less important receive special honor.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that every believer is valuable. No one in the church is unnecessary. Paul has already said that God chose the weak and lowly (*1:27–28*). God gives special honor to those the world overlooks.

They also show the danger of pride in the church. Believers with prominent gifts or positions can be tempted to look down on others. Paul’s words humble them: they need those they might consider less important.

Finally, these verses show God’s heart for the weak. Throughout Scripture, God cares for the poor, the widow, the orphan, and the stranger. In the church, those who seem weak are given special honor.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses challenge believers to value every member of the church. Believers can ask whether they have overlooked or undervalued certain people, such as the elderly, children, people with disabilities, the poor, or those with less visible gifts.

They also encourage believers who feel weak or insignificant. They are necessary to the body of Christ. Their presence, prayers, and service matter.

Finally, these verses encourage churches to give special care and honor to those who are often overlooked. Churches can make sure that all members are included, valued, and given opportunities to serve.

### *1 Corinthians 12:26–27* — Suffering and Rejoicing Together

> *“When one member suffers, all the members suffer with it. When one member is honored, all the members rejoice with it. Now you are the body of Christ, and members individually.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 12:26–27* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had explained that God arranged the body so that there would be no division, but that members would have the same care for one another. Now he describes what this care looks like.

“*When one member suffers, all the members suffer with it*” (*v. 26*). In a human body, when one part is injured, the whole body feels it. A stubbed toe can make the whole body wince. In the church, when one believer suffers, the whole community should share in that suffering. Believers are not isolated individuals; they are connected.

“*When one member is honored, all the members rejoice with it*” (*v. 26*). Likewise, when one member is honored or blessed, the whole body rejoices. There is no room for jealousy. One believer’s joy is everyone’s joy.

“*Now you are the body of Christ, and members individually*” (*v. 27*). Paul states the truth plainly. The church is not merely like a body; it is the body of Christ. Christ is present in the world through His church. And each believer is a member, an essential part of this body.

This was a powerful truth for the divided Corinthian church. Instead of competing over gifts, they were called to care for one another, suffering and rejoicing together, because they were one body.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show the deep connection between believers. Paul writes, “*Rejoice with those who rejoice. Weep with those who weep*” (*Romans 12:15*). Christian community is not a gathering of individuals but a body united by the Spirit.

They also show the dignity of the church. The church is the body of Christ, the visible presence of Christ in the world. Jesus identified so closely with His church that He said to Saul, “*why do you persecute me?*” (*Acts 9:4*).

Finally, these verses show that each believer has a place. “Members individually” means that every believer is a distinct and valued part of the body. No one is lost in the crowd.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to share one another’s sorrows. When a fellow believer is sick, grieving, or struggling, believers can show care through prayer, visits, meals, and practical help.

They also encourage believers to rejoice in one another’s blessings. When a fellow believer is honored, succeeds, or experiences joy, believers can celebrate with them, free from jealousy.

Finally, these verses remind believers of the persecuted church. Believers around the world suffer for their faith. Because the church is one body, believers everywhere can share their suffering through prayer and support.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*1 Corinthians 12* teaches that the most important evidence of the Holy Spirit is the confession that Jesus is Lord. Every believer who truly confesses Jesus has the Spirit. Believers can evaluate spiritual experiences and teachings by asking whether they honor Christ, and they can reject any idea that some believers are second-class because they lack certain gifts.

The chapter also teaches that there are many different gifts, but they all come from the same Spirit, Lord, and God, and every believer has been given a gift for the common good. Believers can discover and use their gifts to serve others, honoring the gifts of others rather than competing with them. Though Christians differ on whether certain gifts continue today, all can agree that God equips every believer to serve.

*1 Corinthians 12* describes the church as one body with many members. No member should feel that they do not belong because they are different, and no member should look down on others as unnecessary. God gives special honor to those who seem weaker. Churches can make sure that every member, especially those often overlooked, is valued, included, and cared for.

Finally, the chapter calls believers to suffer and rejoice together. When one member suffers, all suffer; when one is honored, all rejoice. Believers are the body of Christ, and each is a member. They can care for one another deeply, and they can seek the most excellent way, the way of love that Paul describes in the next chapter.

## Chapter Prayer

Holy Spirit, thank You that I can confess Jesus as Lord only by Your work in me. Thank You for the gifts You give to each believer for the good of all. Show me how You have gifted me, and help me to use my gifts to serve others, not to draw attention to myself. Thank You for placing me in the body of Christ. When I feel that I do not belong, remind me that You have set me where I am. When I am tempted to look down on others, remind me that I need them. Help me to honor those who seem weaker and to care for every member of Your church. Teach me to suffer with those who suffer and rejoice with those who rejoice. Unite Your church in love, and show us the most excellent way. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

1 Corinthians · Chapter 13 of 16

# 1 Corinthians — Chapter 13

Chapter Theme: The Most Excellent Way: Love That Never Fails

[Read 1 Corinthians 13 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/1CO13.htm)

Main Teaching

In the middle of his teaching on spiritual gifts, Paul shows the Corinthians “a most excellent way.” Without love, even the most impressive gifts, knowledge, faith, and sacrifice are worthless. Paul then describes love: patient, kind, free from envy and pride, not rude or self-seeking, not easily angered or keeping a record of wrongs, delighting in truth, and always protecting, trusting, hoping, and persevering. Spiritual gifts are temporary and partial, suited to this present age, but love never fails. Now believers see as in a dim mirror, but one day they will see face to face. Faith, hope, and love remain, and the greatest of these is love.

## Chapter Background and Story

*1 Corinthians 13* is one of the most famous passages in the Bible. It is often read at weddings, and its words are frequently quoted as a beautiful poem about love. But it was written in a specific context: a church divided by pride over spiritual gifts. The Corinthians were competing over who had the most impressive gifts, especially speaking in tongues. They were knowledgeable and gifted, but they were not loving.

Paul places this chapter between chapter 12, which teaches that all gifts come from one Spirit for the good of one body, and chapter 14, which gives practical instructions for using gifts in worship. Chapter 13 is the heart of the argument. It shows that love is the goal of every gift and the test of every believer’s spirituality.

The Greek word Paul uses for love throughout this chapter is agape. In Christian usage, agape describes the self-giving love of God, a love that seeks the good of others regardless of their worthiness. It is the love God showed in sending His Son (*John 3:16*; *Romans 5:8*) and the love believers are called to show one another (*John 13:34*).

The chapter has three movements: the necessity of love (*13:1–3*), the character of love (*13:4–7*), and the permanence of love (*13:8–13*). Each is studied below.

### The Necessity of Love (*13:1–3*)

Paul lists the gifts and actions the Corinthians most admired and shows that without love, they are worthless.

### The Character of Love (*13:4–7*)

Paul describes love not by defining it abstractly but by describing what it does and does not do. Many readers have noticed that this description perfectly fits Jesus Christ. Reading the passage with “Jesus” in place of “love” shows a portrait of Him: Jesus is patient and kind, does not envy or boast, and so on. It is also a mirror for believers, showing how far they have yet to grow.

Several of the qualities Paul lists directly address the Corinthians’ problems. They were envious and proud (*3:3*; *4:6*), rude and self-seeking at the Lord’s Supper (*11:21*), quick to take one another to court (*6:1–8*), and tolerant of sin (*5:1–2*). Love would heal all these problems.

### The Permanence of Love (*13:8–13*)

“*Love never fails*” (*v. 8*). The word “fails” means falls, collapses, or comes to an end. Love never ends. In contrast, spiritual gifts are temporary, as studied below.

“*When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I felt as a child, I thought as a child. Now that I have become a man, I have put away childish things*” (*v. 11*). Paul compares the present age to childhood and the coming age to adulthood. Spiritual gifts are suited to the “childhood” of the church in this present age. When maturity comes, they will no longer be needed. There may also be a gentle rebuke here: the Corinthians’ obsession with gifts and status was childish (*3:1*).

## Important Verses Explained

### *1 Corinthians 13:1–3* — Without Love, Nothing

> *“If I speak with the languages of men and of angels, but don’t have love, I have become sounding brass or a clanging cymbal. If I have the gift of prophecy, and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but don’t have love, I am nothing. If I give away all my goods to feed the poor, and if I give my body to be burned, but don’t have love, it profits me nothing.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 13:1–3* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The Corinthians were proud of their spiritual gifts. Some spoke in tongues, some prophesied, some had great knowledge or faith, and some were generous. They measured spirituality by these gifts. Paul shows them that something is far more important.

“*If I speak with the languages of men and of angels, but don’t have love, I have become sounding brass or a clanging cymbal*” (*v. 1*). Speaking in tongues was the gift the Corinthians prized most. Paul says that even if he could speak every human language and even the language of angels, without love it would be mere noise. “Sounding brass” and “clanging cymbal” were instruments used in pagan worship, making loud but meaningless sounds. Corinth was famous for its bronze work. Without love, even the most spiritual speech is empty noise.

“*If I have the gift of prophecy, and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but don’t have love, I am nothing*” (*v. 2*). Prophecy, understanding of deep truths, knowledge, and mountain-moving faith are all valuable gifts. Jesus Himself spoke of faith that could move mountains (*Matthew 17:20*). Yet without love, a person with all these gifts is “nothing.”

“*If I give away all my goods to feed the poor, and if I give my body to be burned, but don’t have love, it profits me nothing*” (*v. 3*). Even the most extreme acts of generosity and sacrifice, giving away everything to the poor or even dying as a martyr, gain nothing without love. (Some manuscripts read “that I may boast” instead of “to be burned.”) It is possible to do impressive things for wrong reasons, such as pride, guilt, or a desire for recognition.

Paul uses the word “I” throughout. He is not pointing fingers at others; he is applying the principle to himself.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that love is the essential quality of the Christian life. Gifts, knowledge, and even sacrifice are worthless without it. Jesus taught that the greatest commandments are to love God and love one’s neighbor (*Matthew 22:37–40*). Everything else depends on these.

They also show that God looks at motives. Two people may do the same outward action, but if one does it out of love and the other out of pride, God sees the difference. Jesus warned against doing good deeds to be seen by others (*Matthew 6:1–4*).

Finally, these verses show that spiritual gifts are not a measure of spiritual maturity. The Corinthians had many gifts but little love. True maturity is shown in love.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses challenge believers to examine their motives. Believers can ask why they serve, give, teach, or use their gifts. Is it out of love for God and others, or out of a desire for recognition, approval, or control?

They also encourage believers to value love above impressive abilities. Churches sometimes admire gifted speakers, talented musicians, or successful leaders without asking whether they are loving. Love is what matters most.

Finally, these verses encourage believers who feel they have few gifts. Every believer can love. Love is available to all, and it is what gives meaning to everything else.

### *1 Corinthians 13:4–7* — What Love Is and Does

> *“Love is patient and is kind. Love doesn’t envy. Love doesn’t brag, is not proud, doesn’t behave itself inappropriately, doesn’t seek its own way, is not provoked, takes no account of evil; doesn’t rejoice in unrighteousness, but rejoices with the truth; bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, and endures all things.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 13:4–7* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul now describes the character of love. He lists fifteen qualities, some positive and some negative.

“*Love is patient and is kind*” (*v. 4*). “Patient” means long-suffering, slow to anger, enduring people’s faults without giving up on them. “Kind” means actively doing good to others. Patience endures; kindness acts.

“*Love doesn’t envy*” (*v. 4*). Love does not resent others’ gifts, success, or blessings. It rejoices when others are blessed.

“*Love doesn’t brag, is not proud*” (*v. 4*). Love does not boast about itself or inflate its own importance. The Corinthians were “puffed up” (*4:6*, 18; *5:2*; *8:1*). Love is humble.

“*doesn’t behave itself inappropriately*” (*v. 5*). Love is not rude. It respects others and behaves with courtesy and consideration.

“*doesn’t seek its own way*” (*v. 5*). Love is not self-seeking. It considers the needs and interests of others.

“*is not provoked*” (*v. 5*). Love is not easily angered or irritated. It does not have a short temper.

“*takes no account of evil*” (*v. 5*). Love does not keep a record of wrongs. It does not store up grievances to bring up later. This is the language of forgiveness.

“*doesn’t rejoice in unrighteousness, but rejoices with the truth*” (*v. 6*). Love does not take pleasure in wrongdoing, including the failures of others. It celebrates what is true and right. Love and truth go together.

“*bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, and endures all things*” (*v. 7*). “Bears all things” can mean “covers” or “protects,” like a roof that shelters. Love protects others and does not expose their faults unnecessarily. “Believes all things” means that love is not cynical; it is ready to believe the best. “Hopes all things” means love does not give up hope for others. “Endures all things” means love perseveres through difficulty.

It is important to understand verse 7 rightly. “Bears all things” and “believes all things” do not mean that love tolerates abuse, ignores danger, or believes lies. Love “rejoices with the truth” (*13:6*) and “doesn’t rejoice in unrighteousness.” Genuine love protects the vulnerable and confronts evil. Love may require setting boundaries, seeking safety, and holding wrongdoers accountable. Love for an abuser may include refusing to enable their sin. These verses describe love’s generous, hopeful character, not a demand that anyone remain in harm’s way.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses describe the love of God shown in Jesus Christ. Jesus was patient with His slow-learning disciples, kind to sinners, free from envy and pride, never rude or self-seeking, slow to anger, forgiving, rejoicing in truth, and enduring the cross. John writes, “*He who doesn’t love doesn’t know God, for God is love*” (*1 John 4:8*).

They also show that love is active, not merely a feeling. Paul describes love by its actions and attitudes. Love is something people do, choices they make each day.

Finally, these verses show that love is the fruit of the Spirit. No one can love like this by their own strength. Paul writes, “*But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith*” (*Galatians 5:22*). The Holy Spirit produces this love in believers as they walk with Him.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses give believers a mirror for their relationships. Believers can read the list slowly and ask where they need to grow: in patience with their family, in kindness toward coworkers, in freedom from envy, in forgiveness, in hope for difficult people.

They also give a description of what to look for in relationships. Marriages, friendships, and church communities can be measured by these qualities. Where love is present, these qualities will be growing.

Finally, these verses encourage believers to ask God for His love. When believers recognize how far they fall short, they can ask the Holy Spirit to fill them with Christ’s love and to produce this fruit in their lives.

### *1 Corinthians 13:8–10* — Love Never Fails

> *“Love never fails. But where there are prophecies, they will be done away with. Where there are various languages, they will cease. Where there is knowledge, it will be done away with. For we know in part and we prophesy in part; but when that which is complete has come, then that which is partial will be done away with.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 13:8–10* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Having described the character of love, Paul now shows its permanence. The Corinthians valued spiritual gifts highly. Paul shows that gifts are temporary, but love is eternal.

“*Love never fails*” (*v. 8*). Love will never end. It will continue forever, into eternity.

“*But where there are prophecies, they will be done away with. Where there are various languages, they will cease. Where there is knowledge, it will be done away with*” (*v. 8*). In contrast, the gifts the Corinthians prized will come to an end. Prophecy, tongues, and knowledge are valuable now, but they are temporary.

“*For we know in part and we prophesy in part*” (*v. 9*). Present knowledge and prophecy are incomplete. They give believers a partial understanding of God’s truth.

“*but when that which is complete has come, then that which is partial will be done away with*” (*v. 10*). When “that which is complete” comes, the partial gifts will no longer be needed.

What is “that which is complete” (sometimes translated “the perfect”)? Most interpreters understand it as the return of Christ and the fullness of God’s kingdom, when believers will see God face to face (*13:12*). Some, especially those who believe certain gifts have ceased, understand it as the completion of the New Testament or the maturity of the church. Paul’s description in verse 12 of seeing “face to face” and knowing fully seems to point most naturally to the age to come. Either way, the main point is clear: gifts are temporary, but love is eternal.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that love belongs to eternity. In heaven, there will be no need for prophecy, since believers will see God directly; no need for tongues, since all will understand; and no need for partial knowledge, since believers will know fully. But love will continue forever, because God is love.

They also show the humility believers should have about their knowledge. All present knowledge is partial. Even the most learned theologian knows only in part. This should keep believers humble and open to learning.

Finally, these verses show why love should be the priority. If gifts are temporary and love is eternal, believers should invest most in what will last forever.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to prioritize love. Gifts, knowledge, and accomplishments will pass away, but love lasts forever. Believers can invest their time and energy in loving God and others.

They also encourage humility. All believers know only in part. They can hold their opinions with humility, listen to others, and avoid arrogance about their understanding.

Finally, these verses give hope. The partial and imperfect will one day give way to the complete and perfect. Believers can look forward to that day with joy.

### *1 Corinthians 13:12–13* — Face to Face; the Greatest Is Love

> *“For now we see in a mirror, dimly, but then face to face. Now I know in part, but then I will know fully, even as I was also fully known. But now faith, hope, and love remain—these three. The greatest of these is love.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 13:12–13* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had compared the present age to childhood and the coming age to adulthood. Now he uses another image.

“*For now we see in a mirror, dimly, but then face to face*” (*v. 12*). Ancient mirrors were made of polished bronze, a product for which Corinth was famous. Even the best mirrors gave a dim, imperfect reflection. In this life, believers know God, but only partially, as if looking at a dim reflection. But one day, they will see Him “face to face,” directly and clearly. This recalls God’s words about Moses, with whom He spoke “mouth to mouth” and not in riddles (*Numbers 12:8*).

“*Now I know in part, but then I will know fully, even as I was also fully known*” (*v. 12*). Now believers know God partially. In the future, they will know Him fully, just as God already knows them fully. God knows His people completely, every thought, weakness, and need, and He loves them. One day, they will know Him with similar clarity.

“*But now faith, hope, and love remain—these three*” (*v. 13*). Paul names three virtues that last. “Faith” is trust in God. “Hope” is confident expectation of God’s promises. “Love” is self-giving devotion to God and others. These three appear together often in Paul’s letters (*1 Thessalonians 1:3*; *5:8*; *Colossians 1:4–5*).

“*The greatest of these is love*” (*v. 13*). Why is love greatest? Faith will one day become sight, and hope will be fulfilled, but love will continue forever. And love is the very nature of God Himself. God does not have faith or hope, but God is love (*1 John 4:8*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show the glorious future of believers. One day, they will see God face to face. John writes, “*we know that when he is revealed, we will be like him; for we will see him just as he is*” (*1 John 3:2*). The deepest longing of the human heart will be satisfied.

They also show that God already knows His people fully. There is nothing hidden from Him, and yet He loves them. This is a source of deep security. Believers do not need to hide or pretend before God.

Finally, these verses show that love is the greatest virtue because it reflects God’s nature and lasts forever. Everything else serves love. Gifts, knowledge, faith, and hope all find their purpose in love.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers who struggle with unanswered questions. In this life, believers see dimly. They will not understand everything. But one day, they will know fully. Believers can trust God with what they do not yet understand.

They also bring comfort to believers who feel unknown or misunderstood. God knows them fully and loves them completely. They can rest in His knowledge and love.

Finally, these verses call believers to make love their highest priority. Faith and hope are essential, but love is greatest. Believers can ask each day how they can grow in love for God and for others.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*1 Corinthians 13* teaches that without love, even the most impressive gifts and sacrifices are worthless. Believers can examine their motives, asking whether their service, giving, and use of gifts flow from love or from pride and the desire for recognition. Every believer, whatever their gifts, can love.

The chapter also gives a beautiful and searching description of love. Love is patient and kind, free from envy, pride, rudeness, and selfishness, slow to anger, forgiving, rejoicing in truth, protecting, trusting, hoping, and persevering. This is a portrait of Jesus and a mirror for believers. Believers can read it slowly, identify where they need to grow, and ask the Holy Spirit to produce this love in them. True love always rejoices in truth and never requires anyone to remain in abuse; it protects the vulnerable.

*1 Corinthians 13* teaches that spiritual gifts are temporary, but love never fails. All present knowledge is partial; one day believers will see God face to face and know Him fully, just as He knows them. This truth encourages humility about what believers know now, and hope for what they will know then.

Finally, the chapter declares that faith, hope, and love remain, and the greatest of these is love. Love reflects the very nature of God, who is love. Believers can make love their highest aim, in their families, friendships, churches, and communities, investing in what will last forever.

## Chapter Prayer

Loving God, You are love, and You have shown Your love to me in Jesus Christ. Forgive me for the times I have valued gifts, knowledge, or recognition more than love. Without love, I am nothing. Fill me with Your love by Your Holy Spirit. Make me patient and kind. Free me from envy, boasting, and pride. Keep me from rudeness and selfishness, from a quick temper and a record of wrongs. Help me to rejoice in the truth, to protect, to trust, to hope, and to persevere, as Jesus did. Thank You that You know me fully and love me completely. I long for the day when I will see You face to face. Until then, help me to live by faith, hope, and love, and above all, by love. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

1 Corinthians · Chapter 14 of 16

# 1 Corinthians — Chapter 14

Chapter Theme: Gifts That Build Up the Church in Orderly Worship

[Read 1 Corinthians 14 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/1CO14.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul urges the Corinthians to pursue love and to desire spiritual gifts, especially prophecy, because prophecy speaks understandable words that build up, encourage, and comfort the church, while uninterpreted tongues benefit only the speaker. He compares unclear speech to an instrument that gives an uncertain sound and calls believers to pray and sing with both the spirit and the mind. Worship should help outsiders recognize that God is truly present. Paul gives practical guidelines: everything should be done to build up the church, speakers should take turns, tongues should be interpreted, prophecies should be weighed, and order should prevail, because God is not a God of confusion but of peace.

## Chapter Background and Story

*1 Corinthians 14* is the practical conclusion of Paul’s teaching on spiritual gifts. In chapter 12, he showed that all gifts come from one Spirit for the good of one body. In chapter 13, he showed that love is greater than any gift. Now he applies these principles to the church’s worship gatherings.

The specific problem was that the Corinthians were overvaluing speaking in tongues. Their gatherings had apparently become chaotic, with many people speaking in tongues at once, without interpretation, so that no one could understand. Visitors would think the believers were out of their minds. Paul does not forbid tongues; he values them and speaks in tongues himself (*14:18*). But he insists that public worship must be understandable and must build up the whole church.

The guiding principle of the chapter is “edification,” building up. Paul uses this word and its related forms repeatedly (*14:3*, 4, 5, 12, 17, 26). The question for every activity in worship is: Does this build up the church?

As noted in chapter 12, Christians hold different views on whether the gifts of tongues and prophecy continue today and how they should be practiced. Whatever one’s view, the principles of this chapter, love, understanding, edification, and order, apply to all worship.

### Prophecy and Tongues (*14:1–5*)

“*Follow after love and earnestly desire spiritual gifts, but especially that you may prophesy*” (*v. 1*). Love comes first, but believers should also desire gifts, especially prophecy. The comparison between prophecy and tongues is studied below.

“*Now I desire to have you all speak with other languages, but even more that you would prophesy. For he is greater who prophesies than he who speaks with other languages, unless he interprets, that the assembly may be built up*” (*v. 5*). Paul values tongues, but in public worship, prophecy is more useful, unless tongues are interpreted.

### The Need for Understanding (*14:6–19*)

Paul uses illustrations. “*Even lifeless things that make a sound, whether pipe or harp, if they didn’t give a distinction in the sounds, how would it be known what is piped or harped?*” (*v. 7*) Music needs distinct notes to make sense. “*For if the trumpet gave an uncertain sound, who would prepare himself for war?*” (*v. 8*) Soldiers needed clear trumpet calls to know whether to advance or retreat. “*So also you, unless you uttered by the tongue words easy to understand, how would it be known what is spoken? For you would be speaking into the air*” (*v. 9*).

“*If then I don’t know the meaning of the language, I would be to him who speaks a foreigner, and he who speaks would be a foreigner to me*” (*v. 11*). Speaking in an unknown language creates distance rather than fellowship.

“*So also you, since you are zealous for spiritual gifts, seek that you may abound to the building up of the assembly*” (*v. 12*). The Corinthians were eager for gifts. Paul redirects that eagerness toward building up the church.

“*Therefore let him who speaks in another language pray that he may interpret*” (*v. 13*). Paul’s teaching on praying with spirit and mind is studied below.

“*I thank my God, I speak with other languages more than you all*” (*v. 18*). Paul was not against tongues. He spoke in tongues more than any of them. “*However, in the assembly I would rather speak five words with my understanding, that I might instruct others also, than ten thousand words in another language*” (*v. 19*). In the gathered church, a few words that others can understand are worth more than thousands they cannot.

### Signs for Believers and Unbelievers (*14:20–25*)

“*Brothers, don’t be children in thoughts, yet in malice be babies, but in thoughts be mature*” (*v. 20*). The Corinthians’ fascination with tongues was a sign of immaturity. They should be innocent of evil but mature in their thinking.

Paul quotes *Isaiah 28:11–12*, where God warned that He would speak to unbelieving Israel through foreign invaders whose language they could not understand, as a sign of judgment. “*Therefore other languages are for a sign, not to those who believe, but to the unbelieving; but prophesying is for a sign, not to the unbelieving, but to those who believe*” (*v. 22*). Uninterpreted tongues can be a sign of judgment to unbelievers, leaving them confused and outside. “*If therefore the whole assembly is assembled together and all speak with other languages, and unlearned or unbelieving people come in, won’t they say that you are crazy?*” (*v. 23*)

But prophecy has the opposite effect: “*But if all prophesy, and someone unbelieving or unlearned comes in, he is reproved by all, and he is judged by all*” (*v. 24*). “*And thus the secrets of his heart are revealed. So he will fall down on his face and worship God, declaring that God is among you indeed*” (*v. 25*). Clear, Spirit-given words can convict the heart of an unbeliever and lead them to worship. This is one of the great goals of worship: that outsiders would recognize that God is truly present.

### Orderly Worship (*14:26–40*)

Paul’s guiding principle is studied below. He gives specific guidelines for tongues: “*If any man speaks in another language, let there be two, or at the most three, and in turn; and let one interpret*” (*v. 27*). “*But if there is no interpreter, let him keep silent in the assembly, and let him speak to himself and to God*” (*v. 28*).

For prophecy: “*Let two or three of the prophets speak, and let the others discern*” (*v. 29*). Prophecies must be evaluated. Not every claimed message from God is accepted automatically; it must be tested by Scripture and by the discernment of the church (*1 Thessalonians 5:20–21*; *1 John 4:1*). “*But if a revelation is made to another sitting by, let the first keep silent*” (*v. 30*). “*For you all can prophesy one by one, that all may learn and all may be exhorted*” (*v. 31*). “*The spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets*” (*v. 32*). The Holy Spirit does not force people to speak uncontrollably. Those who prophesy can control themselves and wait their turn. Paul’s statement about God’s character is studied below.

Verses 34–35 are among the most debated in Paul’s letters: “*Let the wives be quiet in the assemblies, for it has not been permitted for them to be talking except in submission, as the law also says*” (*v. 34*), “*if they desire to learn anything. “Let them ask their own husbands at home, for it is shameful for a wife to be talking in the assembly.”*” (*v. 35*) Paul has already assumed that women pray and prophesy in the gathered church (*11:5*), so he cannot mean that women must be completely silent at all times. Christians have understood these verses in several ways. Some understand them as forbidding women from evaluating prophecies or teaching with authority in the church. Others understand them as addressing a specific problem of disruptive questions or chatter during worship, perhaps by wives who were less educated and were interrupting to ask questions. Some interpreters note that the World English Bible places part of verse 35 in quotation marks, suggesting that Paul may be quoting a Corinthian view, which he then challenges in verse 36. A few ancient manuscripts place these verses after verse 40, and some scholars question whether they were originally in this location. Faithful Christians hold different conclusions on these verses and on the roles of women in church leadership. Whatever view one holds, the surrounding context emphasizes orderly worship that builds up everyone, and Paul elsewhere honors women as co-workers in the gospel (*Romans 16*).

“*What!? Was it from you that the word of God went out? Or did it come to you alone?*” (*v. 36*) Paul reminds the Corinthians that they are not the source of God’s word, and they should not act independently of the other churches. “*If any man thinks himself to be a prophet or spiritual, let him recognize the things which I write to you, that they are the commandment of the Lord*” (*v. 37*). Truly spiritual people will recognize Paul’s teaching as coming from the Lord.

“*Therefore, brothers, desire earnestly to prophesy, and don’t forbid speaking with other languages*” (*v. 39*). “*Let all things be done decently and in order*” (*v. 40*).

## Important Verses Explained

### *1 Corinthians 14:3–4* — Building Up, Encouraging, Comforting

> *“But he who prophesies speaks to men for their edification, exhortation, and consolation. He who speaks in another language edifies himself, but he who prophesies edifies the assembly.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 14:3–4* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had urged the Corinthians to pursue love and to desire spiritual gifts, especially prophecy. Now he explains why prophecy is so valuable in the gathered church.

First, he describes speaking in tongues: “*For he who speaks in another language speaks not to men, but to God, for no one understands, but in the Spirit he speaks mysteries*” (*v. 2*). When someone speaks in tongues without interpretation, they are speaking to God, and no one else understands. Paul does not say this is bad; prayer to God is good. But it does not help others in the church.

“*But he who prophesies speaks to men for their edification, exhortation, and consolation*” (*v. 3*). Prophecy speaks to people in words they can understand. Paul describes three purposes. “Edification” means building people up, strengthening their faith. “Exhortation” means encouraging, urging, or challenging people to live faithfully. “Consolation” means comforting those who are hurting.

“*He who speaks in another language edifies himself, but he who prophesies edifies the assembly*” (*v. 4*). Tongues build up the individual; prophecy builds up the whole church. Since gifts are given “for the profit of all” (*12:7*), gifts that build up the church are more valuable in public worship.

Prophecy in the New Testament is not always predicting the future. It is speaking a message from God that applies His truth to people’s lives. Some Christians see this gift as continuing in Spirit-prompted words of encouragement and insight; others see its function now fulfilled mainly through the faithful preaching and teaching of Scripture. In either case, its purpose is to build up, encourage, and comfort.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that the purpose of spiritual gifts is to serve others. Love seeks the good of others (*13:5*). A gift that builds up the church is an expression of love.

They also show the importance of understanding in worship. God’s word must be understood to transform lives. Throughout Scripture, God speaks so that His people can hear and respond. Nehemiah records that the Levites read the Law “*distinctly; and they gave the sense, so that they understood the reading*” (*Nehemiah 8:8*).

Finally, these verses describe what the church needs: building up, encouragement, and comfort. Every believer needs these things. Words spoken in the Spirit can strengthen weak faith, encourage the discouraged, and comfort the grieving.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to use their words to build others up. Whether in formal ministry or everyday conversation, believers can speak words that strengthen, encourage, and comfort. Paul writes, “*Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear*” (*Ephesians 4:29*).

They also encourage churches to prioritize what builds up the whole community. Worship services, programs, and activities can be evaluated by whether they strengthen the faith of the people.

Finally, these verses encourage believers to seek gifts that serve others. Believers can ask God not only for gifts that bless them personally, but for gifts that help others grow.

### *1 Corinthians 14:15* — With the Spirit and with the Understanding

> *“What should I do? I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the understanding also. I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the understanding also.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 14:15* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had been explaining that speaking in tongues without interpretation does not help others understand. He also pointed out that it does not engage the speaker’s own mind: “*For if I pray in another language, my spirit prays, but my understanding is unfruitful*” (*v. 14*). When someone prays in tongues, their spirit is praying, but their mind is not producing understandable words.

“*What should I do? I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the understanding also*” (*v. 15*). Paul’s answer is not to choose one or the other, but to do both. He will pray with his spirit, the deep, Spirit-led part of his being, and with his understanding, his mind and thoughts.

“*I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the understanding also*” (*v. 15*). The same applies to singing. Worship should engage both the heart and the mind. Singing with the spirit means singing with deep, Spirit-filled devotion. Singing with the understanding means knowing what one is singing and meaning it.

Paul explains why this matters for others: “*Otherwise, if you bless with the spirit, how will he who fills the place of the unlearned say the “Amen” at your giving of thanks, seeing he doesn’t know what you say?*” (*v. 16*) In the early church, when someone prayed, others would say “Amen,” meaning “So be it,” agreeing with the prayer. But they could only agree if they understood it. “*For you most certainly give thanks well, but the other person is not built up*” (*v. 17*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that worship involves the whole person. God is not honored by mindless emotion or by cold intellect alone. Jesus said that true worshipers worship “*in spirit and truth*” (*John 4:24*). The greatest commandment calls people to love God with all their heart, soul, mind, and strength (*Mark 12:30*).

It also shows that worship is communal. Public prayer and singing should be understandable so that others can join in, agree, and be built up. Worship is not only a private experience but a shared act of the body of Christ.

Finally, the verse shows that the Spirit and the mind work together. The Holy Spirit does not bypass the mind; He renews it (*Romans 12:2*). Spiritual experience and understanding belong together.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to engage both heart and mind in worship. When singing, believers can pay attention to the words, thinking about their meaning, while also offering their hearts to God.

It also encourages believers to pray thoughtfully. Prayer can be deeply heartfelt while also being clear and meaningful. Believers can bring both their emotions and their thoughts to God.

Finally, the verse encourages churches to make worship understandable. Songs, prayers, and teaching should be clear enough for people to understand and join in, including newcomers and those unfamiliar with church language.

### *1 Corinthians 14:26* — Let All Things Be Done to Build Up

> *“What is it then, brothers? When you come together, each one of you has a psalm, has a teaching, has a revelation, has another language, or has an interpretation. Let all things be done to build each other up.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 14:26* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had been explaining the value of gifts that people can understand. Now he gives practical instructions for the church’s gatherings.

“*What is it then, brothers? When you come together, each one of you has a psalm, has a teaching, has a revelation, has another language, or has an interpretation*” (*v. 26*). Paul describes a worship gathering in which many people participate. One person brings a “psalm,” a song of praise, perhaps from the Psalms or a new song. Another brings a “teaching,” instruction from God’s word. Another has a “revelation,” a message from God. Another speaks in tongues, and another interprets. Worship in the early church was participatory, with many members contributing.

“*Let all things be done to build each other up*” (*v. 26*). Here is the guiding principle. Whatever is done in worship should build up the church. Every song, teaching, prayer, and gift should strengthen the faith of the people.

This principle does not require that every church follow exactly the same pattern of worship. Churches today worship in many different ways, from liturgical services to informal gatherings. But in every setting, the question remains: Does this build up the people of God?

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that every believer has something to contribute. Worship is not a performance by a few for an audience of many. The whole body participates, each member bringing their gift. Paul writes elsewhere about believers “*teaching and admonishing one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs*” (*Colossians 3:16*).

It also shows that worship has a purpose beyond personal experience. While worship is directed to God, it also builds up the church. When believers gather, they strengthen one another’s faith.

Finally, the verse shows that love governs worship. Building up others is an expression of love (*8:1*). Worship that is self-centered or chaotic fails to love; worship that builds up others fulfills it.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to come to worship ready to contribute. Believers can come not only to receive but also to give: a song, a prayer, a word of encouragement, a gift of service.

It also encourages churches to make room for the participation of members. Churches can find ways for members to share their gifts in worship and in other gatherings.

Finally, the verse gives a test for worship practices. Churches can ask of every part of their worship: Does this build up the people? Does it help them know and love God?

### *1 Corinthians 14:33* — Not a God of Confusion but of Peace

> *“for God is not a God of confusion but of peace, as in all the assemblies of the saints.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 14:33* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had been giving instructions for orderly worship: tongues should be limited and interpreted, prophets should take turns, and prophecies should be evaluated. He had said that “*The spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets*” (*v. 32*), meaning that those who prophesy can control themselves. The Holy Spirit does not make people speak uncontrollably.

Now he gives the reason for these instructions: “*for God is not a God of confusion but of peace*” (*v. 33*). Worship should reflect the character of God. God is not chaotic or disorderly. He is a God of peace, harmony, and order. When worship is chaotic, with everyone speaking at once and no one understanding, it does not reflect God’s character.

The word “peace” here is the opposite of “confusion” or “disorder.” It means harmony, order, and well-being. God’s work brings peace.

“*as in all the assemblies of the saints*” (*v. 33*). This principle applies not only to Corinth but to all the churches. The Corinthians were not free to make up their own rules; they were part of a wider family of churches.

Paul concludes the chapter with a summary: “*Let all things be done decently and in order*” (*v. 40*). Worship should be done in a fitting and orderly way.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that worship reflects the character of God. Since God is a God of peace and order, His people’s worship should reflect these qualities. In creation, God brought order out of chaos (*Genesis 1:2*). His Spirit brings order, not confusion.

It also shows that spiritual freedom and order are not opposites. The Corinthians may have thought that the Spirit’s work was shown in wild, uncontrolled behavior. Paul teaches that the Spirit produces self-control (*Galatians 5:23*). True spiritual freedom works within order.

Finally, the verse shows that God’s peace should mark the church. Jesus said, “*Peace I leave with you. My peace I give to you*” (*John 14:27*). Churches marked by peace reflect the presence of the Prince of Peace.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages churches to pursue orderly worship. Order does not mean rigidity or lack of joy. It means that worship is conducted in a way that allows people to understand, participate, and be built up.

It also encourages believers to exercise self-control in worship. Whatever one’s tradition or style, believers can worship in ways that are considerate of others.

Finally, the verse encourages believers to seek peace in all of life. God is a God of peace. Believers can bring His peace into their homes, workplaces, and communities, avoiding unnecessary chaos and conflict.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*1 Corinthians 14* teaches that the purpose of spiritual gifts in worship is to build up the church. Prophecy is especially valuable because it speaks understandable words that strengthen, encourage, and comfort. Believers can seek gifts that serve others and use their words to build up, encourage, and comfort those around them.

The chapter also emphasizes understanding in worship. Paul would rather speak five words that others can understand than ten thousand in an unknown language. Believers can worship with both spirit and mind, singing and praying with heartfelt devotion and clear understanding, and churches can make worship accessible to all, including newcomers and outsiders, so that they may recognize that God is truly present.

*1 Corinthians 14* shows that worship is participatory. When believers gather, each may bring a song, a teaching, or another gift. Believers can come ready to contribute, and churches can make room for the gifts of their members. Everything should be done to build up the church.

Finally, the chapter teaches that God is not a God of confusion but of peace. Worship should be done decently and in order, reflecting God’s character. Believers can exercise self-control, honor one another, test what is spoken by Scripture, and pursue the peace and order that the Spirit produces, whatever the style or tradition of their worship.

## Chapter Prayer

Holy Spirit, thank You for the gifts You give to build up Your church. Help me to pursue love above all, and to desire gifts that strengthen, encourage, and comfort others. Teach me to worship You with both my spirit and my understanding, offering You my heart and my mind. When Your people gather, help me to come ready to contribute, not only to receive. Let my words build others up. Give Your church wisdom to worship in ways that are clear, orderly, and welcoming, so that those who come in may recognize that You are truly among us. You are not a God of confusion but of peace. Fill Your church with Your peace, and let everything be done decently and in order, for Your glory. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
