1 Corinthians · Chapter 15 of 16

# 1 Corinthians — Chapter 15

Chapter Theme: Christ Is Risen: The Gospel and the Hope of the Resurrection

[Read 1 Corinthians 15 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/1CO15.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul reminds the Corinthians of the gospel that saves them: Christ died for our sins, was buried, and was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, appearing to Peter, the Twelve, more than five hundred believers, James, the apostles, and finally Paul himself. Some in Corinth were denying the resurrection of the dead, so Paul shows that if the dead are not raised, Christ is not raised, faith is empty, and believers are still in their sins. But Christ has indeed been raised as the first fruits of all who belong to Him, and He will reign until every enemy, including death, is destroyed. Paul explains that the resurrection body will be imperishable, glorious, powerful, and spiritual, and that at the last trumpet the dead will be raised and the living changed. Death will be swallowed up in victory, so believers can stand firm, knowing their labor in the Lord is not in vain.

## Chapter Background and Story

*1 Corinthians 15* is the longest and fullest treatment of the resurrection in the Bible. Paul writes it because some Corinthian believers were saying that “*there is no resurrection of the dead*” (*v. 12*). They probably did not deny that Jesus rose. But influenced by Greek thinking, which often viewed the body as a prison for the soul, they may have found the idea of a bodily resurrection unappealing or absurd. Some may have believed that the “resurrection” was a purely spiritual experience that had already happened (compare *2 Timothy 2:18*), or that only the soul would survive death.

Paul responds by showing that the resurrection of believers is inseparable from the resurrection of Christ, and that both are essential to the gospel. The chapter moves from the historical fact of Christ’s resurrection (*15:1–11*), to the consequences of denying the resurrection (*15:12–19*), to the certainty and order of the resurrection (*15:20–28*), to practical arguments (*15:29–34*), to the nature of the resurrection body (*15:35–49*), and finally to the triumphant victory over death (*15:50–58*).

### The Gospel of the Risen Christ (*15:1–11*)

Paul’s summary of the gospel, with its list of witnesses, is studied below. Paul then describes his own unworthiness: “*For I am the least of the apostles, who is not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the assembly of God*” (*v. 9*). “*But by the grace of God I am what I am. His grace which was given to me was not futile, but I worked more than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me*” (*v. 10*). Paul’s apostleship, like his salvation, was entirely a gift of grace.

### If Christ Is Not Raised (*15:12–19*)

Paul draws out the consequences of denying the resurrection. “*But if there is no resurrection of the dead, neither has Christ been raised*” (*v. 13*). If the dead cannot be raised, then Christ was not raised either. “*If Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith also is in vain*” (*v. 14*). “*Yes, we are also found false witnesses of God*” (*v. 15*). If the resurrection did not happen, the apostles were lying about God. The further consequences, and Paul’s triumphant answer, are studied below.

### The Order of the Resurrection (*15:20–28*)

“*For since death came by man, the resurrection of the dead also came by man*” (*v. 21*). “*For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive*” (*v. 22*). As in *Romans 5*, Paul contrasts Adam and Christ. Adam brought death; Christ brings resurrection life to all who are “in Christ.”

“*But each in his own order: Christ the first fruits, then those who are Christ’s at his coming*” (*v. 23*). The resurrection happens in stages. Christ was raised first. Believers will be raised when He returns. “*Then the end comes, when he will deliver up the Kingdom to God the Father, when he will have abolished all rule and all authority and power*” (*v. 24*).

“*For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet*” (*v. 25*). Christ is reigning now, and He will continue until every enemy is defeated (*Psalm 110:1*). “*The last enemy that will be abolished is death*” (*v. 26*). Death is an enemy, not a friend. It entered the world through sin, and it will be destroyed.

“*When all things have been subjected to him, then the Son will also himself be subjected to him who subjected all things to him, that God may be all in all*” (*v. 28*). This verse does not mean the Son is inferior in nature to the Father; the Son is fully God. It describes the Son’s role in God’s plan: having completed His saving work, He presents the kingdom to the Father, so that God may be all in all. Christians have long understood this as reflecting the loving order within the Trinity, in which the Son, equal with the Father, delights to glorify Him.

### Living in Light of the Resurrection (*15:29–34*)

“*Or else what will they do who are baptized for the dead? If the dead aren’t raised at all, why then are they baptized for the dead?*” (*v. 29*) This is one of the most puzzling verses in the New Testament; scholars have proposed dozens of interpretations. Some think certain Corinthians were being baptized on behalf of believers who had died without baptism; Paul mentions the practice without approving it, simply pointing out that it makes no sense if there is no resurrection. Others think it refers to people who were baptized because of the testimony of believers who had died, hoping to be reunited with them. The Christian church has never adopted a practice of baptism for the dead. Paul’s point is clear: the resurrection gives meaning to Christian practice.

“*Why do we also stand in jeopardy every hour?*” (*v. 30*) “*I die daily*” (*v. 31*). Paul faced danger and death every day. “*If I fought with animals at Ephesus for human purposes, what does it profit me?*” (*v. 32*) Paul may be speaking figuratively of fierce human opponents. “*If the dead are not raised, then “let’s eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.”*” (*v. 32*) (*Isaiah 22:13*). Without the resurrection, the only logical approach would be to live for pleasure.

“*Don’t be deceived! “Evil companionships corrupt good morals.”*” (*v. 33*) Paul quotes a well-known saying from the Greek poet Menander. Those who denied the resurrection were having a corrupting influence. “*Wake up righteously and don’t sin, for some have no knowledge of God. I say this to your shame*” (*v. 34*).

### The Resurrection Body (*15:35–49*)

Paul answers the question, “*How are the dead raised?*” (*v. 35*) and, “*With what kind of body do they come?*” (*v. 35*) He uses the image of a seed: “*You foolish one, that which you yourself sow is not made alive unless it dies*” (*v. 36*). “*That which you sow, you don’t sow the body that will be, but a bare grain*” (*v. 37*). A seed is buried and dies, but from it comes a plant that is far more glorious than the seed. There is continuity, since the plant comes from the seed, and transformation, since the plant is very different from the seed.

Paul then notes that God has made many kinds of bodies, earthly and heavenly, each with its own glory. The resurrection body is described below.

“*So also it is written, “The first man Adam became a living soul.” The last Adam became a life-giving spirit*” (*v. 45*). Adam received life from God (*Genesis 2:7*); Christ, the “last Adam,” gives life. “*As we have borne the image of those made of dust, let’s also bear the image of the heavenly*” (*v. 49*). Believers who now bear Adam’s earthly image will one day bear Christ’s heavenly image.

### Victory over Death (*15:50–58*)

“*Now I say this, brothers, that flesh and blood can’t inherit God’s Kingdom; neither does the perishable inherit imperishable*” (*v. 50*). Human bodies in their present, mortal state cannot enter God’s eternal kingdom. They must be transformed.

“*Behold, I tell you a mystery. We will not all sleep, but we will all be changed*” (*v. 51*), “*in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound and the dead will be raised incorruptible, and we will be changed*” (*v. 52*). Not all believers will die before Christ returns. But all, whether living or dead, will be transformed. It will happen instantly. Paul describes the same event in *1 Thessalonians 4:16–17*. “*For this perishable body must become imperishable, and this mortal must put on immortality*” (*v. 53*). Paul’s song of victory is studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *1 Corinthians 15:3–8* — Christ Died, Was Buried, Was Raised, and Appeared

> *“For I delivered to you first of all that which I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve. Then he appeared to over five hundred brothers at once, most of whom remain until now, but some have also fallen asleep. Then he appeared to James, then to all the apostles, and last of all, as to the child born at the wrong time, he appeared to me also.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 15:3–8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul begins by reminding the Corinthians of the gospel he had preached to them, which they had received, in which they stood, and by which they were saved. Then he summarizes it.

“*For I delivered to you first of all that which I also received*” (*v. 3*). “First of all” means “of first importance.” This is the heart of the Christian message. Paul did not invent it; he “received” it and “delivered” it, the language of passing on sacred tradition. Many scholars believe verses 3–5 are an early Christian creed that Paul learned within a few years of Jesus’ resurrection, perhaps when he visited Peter in Jerusalem (*Galatians 1:18*).

“*that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures*” (*v. 3*). Christ’s death was not an accident or a tragedy. He died “for our sins,” as a sacrifice to take away sin. And this happened “according to the Scriptures,” fulfilling prophecies like *Isaiah 53*.

“*that he was buried*” (*v. 4*). His burial confirmed that He truly died.

“*that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures*” (*v. 4*). The verb “was raised” is in a tense that emphasizes a lasting result: He was raised and remains alive. This too fulfilled Scripture (*Psalm 16:10*; *Hosea 6:2*; and the sign of Jonah, *Matthew 12:40*).

Then Paul lists witnesses. “*and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve*” (*v. 5*). Peter (Cephas) and the Twelve saw the risen Jesus (*Luke 24:34*; *John 20:19–29*). “*Then he appeared to over five hundred brothers at once, most of whom remain until now, but some have also fallen asleep*” (*v. 6*). More than five hundred people saw Him at the same time. Most were still alive when Paul wrote, about twenty-five years later. Paul was saying, in effect, “You can ask them.” “*Then he appeared to James, then to all the apostles*” (*v. 7*). James, Jesus’ brother, who had not believed during Jesus’ ministry, saw the risen Lord and became a leader of the church. “*and last of all, as to the child born at the wrong time, he appeared to me also*” (*v. 8*). Paul saw the risen Christ on the road to Damascus. He describes himself as “born at the wrong time,” perhaps meaning that he came to faith abnormally, after the other apostles, or that he was like a stillborn child, spiritually dead until Christ gave him life.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses summarize the core of the Christian faith: Christ died for our sins and was raised. Everything else in Christianity depends on these facts. This message was taught from the very beginning of the church.

They also show that the resurrection is a historical event, attested by many witnesses. Christianity does not rest on myths or private visions but on public events that people saw. Luke writes that Jesus “*showed himself alive after he suffered, by many proofs*” (*Acts 1:3*).

Finally, these verses show that the gospel fulfills Scripture. The death and resurrection of Christ were the climax of God’s plan revealed throughout the Old Testament.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses give believers a clear summary of the gospel to share with others. Believers can explain the good news simply: Christ died for our sins, was buried, and was raised on the third day, as the Scriptures foretold.

They also give believers confidence in their faith. The resurrection was witnessed by many people. Believers can trust that their faith rests on solid historical ground.

Finally, these verses remind believers that the gospel transforms lives. James, who once doubted, and Paul, who once persecuted, became faithful witnesses after seeing the risen Christ. The same risen Christ can transform anyone today.

### *1 Corinthians 15:17–20* — But Now Christ Has Been Raised

> *“If Christ has not been raised, your faith is vain; you are still in your sins. Then they also who are fallen asleep in Christ have perished. If we have only hoped in Christ in this life, we are of all men most pitiable. But now Christ has been raised from the dead. He became the first fruit of those who are asleep.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 15:17–20* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Some Corinthians were saying there is no resurrection of the dead. Paul shows what would follow if that were true.

“*If Christ has not been raised, your faith is vain; you are still in your sins*” (*v. 17*). If Christ was not raised, faith in Him is useless. Believers would still be guilty of their sins, because the resurrection is God’s proof that Christ’s sacrifice was accepted (*Romans 4:25*). A dead Savior cannot save.

“*Then they also who are fallen asleep in Christ have perished*” (*v. 18*). Believers who had died would have perished, lost forever, with no hope of life beyond the grave.

“*If we have only hoped in Christ in this life, we are of all men most pitiable*” (*v. 19*). If Christianity offers hope only for this life, believers are to be pitied more than anyone. They have given up worldly pleasures, faced persecution, and sacrificed much, all for a false hope.

Then Paul turns from this dark possibility to glorious reality: “*But now Christ has been raised from the dead*” (*v. 20*). These are among the most triumphant words in the Bible. The resurrection is not a theory or a wish; it is a fact.

“*He became the first fruit of those who are asleep*” (*v. 20*). “First fruits” refers to the first portion of the harvest, which was offered to God (*Leviticus 23:10–11*). The first fruits were a promise that the rest of the harvest was coming. Christ’s resurrection is the first fruits; the resurrection of believers is the full harvest that will follow. Interestingly, the Feast of First Fruits fell on the day after the Sabbath following Passover, the very day Jesus rose.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that the resurrection is essential to Christianity. Without it, there is no forgiveness, no hope, and no gospel. Christianity stands or falls on this one event.

They also show that believers’ future resurrection is guaranteed by Christ’s resurrection. Because Christ was raised as the first fruits, all who belong to Him will follow. Jesus said, “*Because I live, you will live also*” (*John 14:19*).

Finally, these verses show that Christian hope reaches beyond this life. Believers are not merely hoping for a better life now; they are looking forward to resurrection and eternal life. This hope gives meaning to sacrifice and suffering.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses give believers confidence in the face of death. Because Christ was raised, believers who die are not lost. They will be raised as Christ was raised.

They also assure believers that their sins are forgiven. Because Christ was raised, His sacrifice was accepted, and believers are no longer in their sins.

Finally, these verses encourage believers to live with eternal hope. The sacrifices believers make for Christ are not wasted. Their hope is not only for this life but for eternity.

### *1 Corinthians 15:42–44* — Raised Imperishable, Glorious, Powerful

> *“So also is the resurrection of the dead. The body is sown perishable; it is raised imperishable. It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power. It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. There is a natural body and there is also a spiritual body.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 15:42–44* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Someone had asked, “*How are the dead raised?*” (*v. 35*) and “*With what kind of body do they come?*” (*v. 35*) Paul had answered with the image of a seed that dies and becomes a plant. Now he describes the resurrection body directly, using four contrasts.

“*So also is the resurrection of the dead. The body is sown perishable; it is raised imperishable*” (*v. 42*). The present body is like a seed “sown” in the ground at burial. It is “perishable,” subject to sickness, aging, decay, and death. The resurrection body will be “imperishable,” never again subject to decay or death.

“*It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory*” (*v. 43*). The present body, especially in death, is “in dishonor,” weak and humbled. The resurrection body will be “in glory,” radiant and beautiful.

“*It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power*” (*v. 43*). The present body is weak, limited, tired, and vulnerable. The resurrection body will be powerful.

“*It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. There is a natural body and there is also a spiritual body*” (*v. 44*). The present body is “natural,” suited to life in this present age. The resurrection body will be “spiritual.” This does not mean it will be non-physical or ghostly. Jesus’ resurrection body could be touched and could eat (*Luke 24:39–43*). “Spiritual” means a body fully empowered and directed by the Holy Spirit, suited to the life of the age to come.

There is continuity between the present body and the resurrection body, just as there is continuity between a seed and a plant. The same person will be raised. But there will also be glorious transformation.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that God’s salvation includes the body. Christianity does not teach merely that souls escape to heaven. It teaches that God will raise and transform human bodies. Paul writes that Christ “*will change the body of our humiliation to be conformed to the body of his glory*” (*Philippians 3:21*).

They also show the pattern of Jesus’ resurrection. Jesus’ risen body was real and physical, yet transformed. The disciples recognized Him, touched Him, and ate with Him, yet He could appear and disappear. Believers’ resurrection bodies will be like His.

Finally, these verses bring great hope. Every weakness, illness, disability, and limitation of the present body will be overcome. The resurrection body will be glorious and powerful, free from pain and death.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses bring comfort to those who suffer in their bodies. Believers with illness, disability, chronic pain, or the weaknesses of aging can look forward to resurrection bodies free from all suffering.

They also encourage believers to honor their present bodies. The body matters to God. Believers can care for their bodies and use them for His glory, knowing that God will one day transform them.

Finally, these verses bring hope at funerals. When believers bury loved ones who trusted in Christ, they are planting seeds that will rise in glory. Grief is real, but it is grief filled with hope.

### *1 Corinthians 15:55–58* — Death, Where Is Your Sting?

> *“‘Death, where is your sting? Hades, where is your victory?’ The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law. But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the Lord’s work, because you know that your labor is not in vain in the Lord.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 15:55–58* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had described the moment when, at the last trumpet, the dead will be raised and the living changed, when the perishable will put on the imperishable and the mortal will put on immortality. Then the Scripture will be fulfilled: “*Death is swallowed up in victory*” (*v. 54*) (*Isaiah 25:8*).

Paul then taunts death, using words from *Hosea 13:14*: “*“Death, where is your sting? Hades, where is your victory?”*” (*v. 55*) Death once seemed all-powerful. But now Paul mocks it, because it has been defeated. A “sting” is like the stinger of a scorpion or bee, which causes pain and death. Death’s sting has been removed.

“*The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law*” (*v. 56*). What makes death so terrible is sin. Sin brings guilt and judgment, making death the gateway to condemnation. And the Law gives sin its power, because the Law reveals sin and pronounces judgment on it.

“*But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ*” (*v. 57*). But Christ has dealt with sin. He died for sins and rose again, removing death’s sting. Through Him, believers have victory over sin, the Law’s condemnation, and death. This victory is a gift from God.

Then Paul draws a practical conclusion: “*Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the Lord’s work, because you know that your labor is not in vain in the Lord*” (*v. 58*). Because of the resurrection, believers can stand firm, not shaken by doubt or opposition. They can give themselves fully to the Lord’s work. And they can know that nothing done for the Lord is wasted. The resurrection guarantees that their work has eternal value.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that death has been defeated. Death is still an enemy, and believers still die. But for those in Christ, death has lost its sting. It is no longer a gateway to judgment but to eternal life. Jesus said, “*I am the resurrection and the life. He who believes in me will still live, even if he dies*” (*John 11:25*).

They also show that victory is a gift. Believers do not defeat death by their own strength. God gives the victory through Jesus Christ. All the glory belongs to Him.

Finally, these verses show that the resurrection gives meaning to life now. Because believers will be raised, their present work for the Lord matters. Nothing done in His name is wasted.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses bring hope to those facing death. Believers can face their own death, and the death of loved ones who trusted Christ, with confidence that death has been defeated.

They also encourage believers to stand firm. When doubts or difficulties come, believers can remember the resurrection and remain steadfast in their faith.

Finally, these verses encourage believers in their service. Believers who serve faithfully, often without seeing results or recognition, can know that their labor in the Lord is never in vain. Every act of faithfulness matters for eternity.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*1 Corinthians 15* reminds believers of the gospel of first importance: Christ died for our sins, was buried, and was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures. This message was witnessed by many and has been passed down from the beginning. Believers can hold firmly to it, share it clearly, and trust that it rests on solid ground.

The chapter shows that the resurrection is essential to the Christian faith. If Christ was not raised, faith is futile and believers are still in their sins. But Christ has been raised, the first fruits of all who belong to Him. Believers can live with confidence that their sins are forgiven and that those who have died in Christ will be raised.

*1 Corinthians 15* describes the glorious resurrection body: imperishable, glorious, powerful, and spiritual. Believers who suffer in their bodies can look forward to complete renewal. Those who grieve can do so with hope, knowing that loved ones who died in Christ are like seeds that will rise in glory.

Finally, the chapter declares that death has been swallowed up in victory through Jesus Christ. Death’s sting has been removed. Because of this, believers can be steadfast and immovable, always abounding in the Lord’s work, knowing that their labor in the Lord is not in vain.

## Chapter Prayer

Risen Lord Jesus, thank You that You died for my sins, were buried, and were raised on the third day according to the Scriptures. Thank You for the many witnesses who saw You alive, and for the grace that made Paul, and me, Your servant. I rejoice that You have been raised as the first fruits, and that all who belong to You will be raised at Your coming. Thank You that my sins are forgiven and that death is not the end. When I grieve, fill me with hope. When I suffer in my body, remind me of the imperishable, glorious body You will give me. Death, where is your sting? Thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ. Help me to stand firm, immovable, always abounding in Your work, knowing that my labor in You is never in vain. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

1 Corinthians · Chapter 16 of 16

# 1 Corinthians — Chapter 16

Chapter Theme: Generous Giving, Open Doors, and Courage Rooted in Love

[Read 1 Corinthians 16 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/1CO16.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul closes his letter with practical instructions. He asks the Corinthians to set aside money regularly on the first day of each week for the collection for poor believers in Jerusalem, to be carried by approved representatives. He shares his travel plans, explaining that he will remain in Ephesus because a great door for effective work has opened despite many opponents. He asks them to welcome Timothy and explains Apollos’s plans. Then he gives a short, powerful charge: be watchful, stand firm in the faith, be courageous and strong, and do everything in love. He commends faithful servants like Stephanas, sends greetings, adds a personal note in his own hand, and closes with the ancient prayer, “Come, Lord!”

## Chapter Background and Story

Letters in the ancient world often ended with travel plans, instructions, greetings, and a farewell. Paul follows this pattern, but even his practical closing words are full of spiritual meaning. This chapter shows Paul as an organizer, a planner, a friend, and a pastor who cared about the practical details of church life.

The collection for Jerusalem mentioned here was a major project of Paul’s ministry. The believers in Jerusalem were poor, perhaps because of famine, persecution, and the economic hardships of the time. Paul gathered gifts from the Gentile churches of Galatia, Macedonia, and Achaia to help them (*Romans 15:25–27*; *2 Corinthians 8–9*). This gift expressed the unity of Jewish and Gentile believers in one body. Paul writes more about it in *2 Corinthians 8–9*.

### The Collection for the Saints (*16:1–4*)

“*Now concerning the collection for the saints*” (*v. 1*). This is another topic the Corinthians had asked about. Paul’s instructions about regular giving are studied below. He adds: “*When I arrive, I will send whoever you approve with letters to carry your gracious gift to Jerusalem*” (*v. 3*). Paul did not want to handle the money himself without accountability. The church would choose trustworthy representatives to carry it. “*If it is appropriate for me to go also, they will go with me*” (*v. 4*). Paul was careful about financial integrity (*2 Corinthians 8:20–21*).

### Paul’s Travel Plans (*16:5–12*)

Paul planned to visit Corinth after passing through Macedonia, and perhaps to spend the winter there. “*For I do not wish to see you now in passing, but I hope to stay a while with you, if the Lord permits*” (*v. 7*). As always, Paul held his plans humbly, subject to the Lord’s will. In fact, his plans later changed, causing some Corinthians to question his reliability (*2 Corinthians 1:15–17*). The reason he was staying in Ephesus is studied below.

“*Now if Timothy comes, see that he is with you without fear, for he does the work of the Lord, as I also do*” (*v. 10*). Timothy was young (*1 Timothy 4:12*) and perhaps timid (*2 Timothy 1:7*). The Corinthian church could be difficult. Paul urged them to welcome him and not to look down on him. “*Therefore let no one despise him*” (*v. 11*).

“*Now concerning Apollos the brother, I strongly urged him to come to you with the brothers, but it was not at all his desire to come now*” (*v. 12*). Notice how Paul speaks of Apollos: “the brother.” Some Corinthians had divided into factions around Paul and Apollos (*1:12*), but Paul and Apollos were not rivals. Paul urged Apollos to visit, though Apollos decided to wait, perhaps to avoid stirring up the divisions further.

### Final Exhortations (*16:13–18*)

Paul’s charge to the church is studied below. He then commends the household of Stephanas, “*the first fruits of Achaia*” (*v. 15*), who had “*set themselves to serve the saints*” (*v. 15*). Paul asks the church to “*be in subjection to such, and to everyone who helps in the work and labors*” (*v. 16*). Those who serve faithfully deserve respect. Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus had come to Paul from Corinth, perhaps carrying the church’s letter. “*For they refreshed my spirit and yours. Therefore acknowledge those who are like that*” (*v. 18*). Faithful believers who refresh others should be honored.

### Greetings and Farewell (*16:19–24*)

“*The assemblies of Asia greet you. Aquila and Priscilla greet you warmly in the Lord, together with the assembly that is in their house*” (*v. 19*). Priscilla and Aquila, who had worked with Paul in Corinth (*Acts 18:2–3*), were now in Ephesus, hosting a church in their home. “*All the brothers greet you. Greet one another with a holy kiss*” (*v. 20*).

“*This greeting is by me, Paul, with my own hand*” (*v. 21*). Paul usually dictated his letters to a scribe (*Romans 16:22*), but he often wrote the final greeting himself, as a personal touch and a sign of authenticity (*Galatians 6:11*; *Colossians 4:18*; *2 Thessalonians 3:17*). The closing prayer is studied below. “*The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with you*” (*v. 23*). “*My love to all of you in Christ Jesus. Amen*” (*v. 24*). After all his corrections and rebukes, Paul’s final word is love.

## Important Verses Explained

### *1 Corinthians 16:2* — Regular, Proportionate Giving

> *“On the first day of every week, let each one of you save as he may prosper, that no collections are made when I come.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 16:2* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul was collecting money from the Gentile churches to help the poor believers in Jerusalem. He had given the same instructions to the churches in Galatia, and now he gave them to the Corinthians.

“*On the first day of every week*” (*v. 2*). The first day of the week, Sunday, was the day believers gathered to worship, because it was the day of Jesus’ resurrection (*Acts 20:7*). Paul asked them to set aside their gifts each week. This made giving a regular part of worship.

“*let each one of you save as he may prosper*” (*v. 2*). Every believer was to participate: “each one of you.” No one was excluded, whether rich or poor. And each was to give “as he may prosper,” in proportion to their income. Those who had more would give more; those who had less would give less. Giving was to be proportionate, not a fixed amount for everyone.

The phrase “save” or “put aside” suggests that believers set the money aside, perhaps at home or in a common fund, so that it would be ready when Paul arrived.

“*that no collections are made when I come*” (*v. 2*). Paul did not want to have to pressure people to give when he arrived. Regular, planned giving would mean the gift was ready. It also meant giving would be thoughtful and generous rather than rushed and emotional.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that giving is an act of worship. By connecting giving with the first day of the week, Paul made it part of believers’ regular worship. Giving is a way of honoring God with what He has provided.

It also shows principles for Christian giving: it should be regular, personal, proportionate, and planned. Paul later wrote, “*Let each man give according as he has determined in his heart, not grudgingly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver*” (*2 Corinthians 9:7*).

Finally, the verse shows that giving expresses the unity of the church. The Gentile believers in Corinth were giving to Jewish believers in Jerusalem whom they had never met. Generosity crossed ethnic and geographic boundaries, showing that believers are one body.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to give regularly. Rather than giving only when they feel moved, believers can plan their giving as part of their worship and budget.

It also encourages proportionate giving. Each believer can give according to what God has provided. This means that giving is possible for everyone, whatever their income.

Finally, the verse encourages believers to support those in need beyond their own community. Believers can give to help the poor, support persecuted Christians, and assist believers around the world.

### *1 Corinthians 16:9* — A Great Door and Many Adversaries

> *“for a great and effective door has opened to me, and there are many adversaries.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 16:9* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul was writing from Ephesus. He planned to visit Corinth, but not immediately. He explained, “*But I will stay at Ephesus until Pentecost*” (*v. 8*).

Why? “*for a great and effective door has opened to me*” (*v. 9*). God had given Paul a great opportunity in Ephesus. The image of a “door” is used elsewhere in Paul’s letters for opportunities to preach the gospel (*2 Corinthians 2:12*; *Colossians 4:3*). During Paul’s time in Ephesus, the gospel spread throughout the province of Asia (*Acts 19:10*). The door was “great,” a large opportunity, and “effective,” leading to real results.

“*and there are many adversaries*” (*v. 9*). At the same time, Paul faced many opponents. *Acts 19* describes the opposition in Ephesus, including a riot led by silversmiths whose business was threatened (*Acts 19:23–41*). Paul may also have faced other dangers there (*1 Corinthians 15:32*; *2 Corinthians 1:8–9*).

Notice that Paul mentions the open door and the opponents together. For Paul, opposition was not a sign that he should leave. It was often a sign that God was at work. Where the gospel advances, opposition often arises.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that God opens doors for His work. Opportunities for the gospel come from Him. Jesus says to the church in Philadelphia, “*Behold, I have set before you an open door, which no one can shut*” (*Revelation 3:8*).

It also shows that opportunity and opposition often go together. When God is working powerfully, the enemy often resists. Believers should not be surprised or discouraged by opposition.

Finally, the verse shows Paul’s wisdom in discerning God’s leading. Paul did not leave Ephesus simply because there was opposition. He stayed because the door was open. Believers can look for where God is opening doors and walk through them, even when it is difficult.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to look for open doors. God may give believers opportunities to share their faith, serve others, or start new ministries. Believers can pray for open doors and be ready to walk through them.

It also encourages believers not to be discouraged by opposition. When believers face resistance in serving God, it may be a sign that God is at work. Believers can persevere, trusting Him.

Finally, the verse encourages believers to discern God’s leading. Not every difficulty is a sign to quit, and not every opportunity is from God. Believers can seek God’s wisdom through prayer, Scripture, and counsel to know when to stay and when to move on.

### *1 Corinthians 16:13–14* — Stand Firm, Be Strong, Do All in Love

> *“Watch! Stand firm in the faith! Be courageous! Be strong! Let all that you do be done in love.”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 16:13–14* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

As Paul brought his letter to a close, he gave a short, powerful set of commands that sum up much of what he had written.

“*Watch!*” (*v. 13*) Be alert, awake, on guard. The Corinthians faced dangers: false teaching, division, immorality, and pride. They needed to be watchful. Jesus also told His followers to watch (*Mark 13:37*).

“*Stand firm in the faith!*” (*v. 13*) Do not be shaken or moved. Hold on to the truth of the gospel. Paul had just written about standing firm in the resurrection hope (*15:1*, 58).

“*Be courageous!*” (*v. 13*) The Greek word means to act like a mature person, to be brave. The Corinthians had been acting like spiritual children (*3:1*; *14:20*). Paul called them to maturity and courage.

“*Be strong!*” (*v. 13*) Be strengthened, empowered. Strength comes not from oneself but from the Lord (*Ephesians 6:10*).

These four commands sound like a military charge, calling soldiers to readiness and courage. But Paul immediately balances them:

“*Let all that you do be done in love*” (*v. 14*). Everything, all their watchfulness, firmness, courage, and strength, must be done in love. Without love, strength can become harshness, firmness can become stubbornness, and courage can become pride. Paul had written a whole chapter on love (chapter 13). Now he summarizes: let everything be done in love.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show the balance of Christian character. Believers are called to be strong and courageous, standing firm for the truth. But they are also called to love. Strength without love is harsh; love without strength is weak. Christ combined both perfectly.

They also summarize the whole letter. The Corinthians needed to be watchful against error, firm in the gospel, mature rather than childish, strong in the Lord, and above all loving. These commands address every problem Paul had confronted.

Finally, these verses show that love is the governing principle of the Christian life. Paul writes elsewhere, “*Above all these things, walk in love, which is the bond of perfection*” (*Colossians 3:14*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to be spiritually alert. Believers can be watchful against temptation, false teaching, and the gradual drift away from God.

They also encourage believers to stand firm and be courageous. In a world that often opposes Christian faith, believers need courage to hold to the truth and live it out.

Finally, these verses remind believers that everything must be done in love. When believers stand for truth, defend the faith, or confront wrong, they can do so with love: speaking the truth in love (*Ephesians 4:15*), with gentleness and respect (*1 Peter 3:15*).

### *1 Corinthians 16:22* — “*Come, Lord!*” (*v. 22*)

> *“If any man doesn’t love the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be cursed. Come, Lord!”*
>
> — *1 Corinthians 16:22* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had written his final greeting with his own hand. Then he added a solemn statement and a prayer.

“*If any man doesn’t love the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be cursed*” (*v. 22*). This is a serious warning. To “be cursed” (anathema) means to be under God’s judgment. Paul had written a letter full of correction. Now he reminds the Corinthians that what ultimately matters is love for the Lord Jesus. Those who do not love Him are outside His blessing. This warning would have challenged anyone in Corinth who was merely going through the motions without genuine love for Christ.

“*Come, Lord!*” (*v. 22*) Paul then prays a short prayer. In the original, it is an Aramaic phrase, “Maranatha,” which Paul did not translate. It may be read as “Our Lord, come!” or “Our Lord has come.” Most interpreters understand it as a prayer for Christ’s return. Its use in Aramaic, the language of the earliest Jewish believers, shows that this was one of the earliest Christian prayers, probably used in worship. Revelation ends with the same prayer: “*Amen! Yes, come, Lord Jesus*” (*Revelation 22:20*).

This prayer shows that the early believers longed for Christ’s return. They lived with expectation. Paul had just written about the resurrection that will happen at Christ’s coming (*15:23*, 51–52). Now he prays for that day to come.

Notice also that the prayer was addressed to Jesus as “Lord.” The earliest Aramaic-speaking Jewish believers prayed to Jesus, showing that they regarded Him as divine.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that love for Jesus is the heart of the Christian faith. It is not enough to know about Jesus or belong to a church. Jesus asked Peter, “Do you love me?” (*John 21:15–17*). Love for Christ is the mark of a true disciple.

It also shows that Christian hope is centered on Christ’s return. The early church prayed eagerly for Jesus to come back. This hope gave them courage in suffering and purpose in daily life.

Finally, the verse shows that the earliest believers worshiped Jesus. Praying “Come, Lord” in Aramaic shows that from the very beginning, Jewish believers addressed Jesus as Lord in prayer.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to examine their love for Jesus. Believers can ask whether their faith is driven by genuine love for Him, or whether it has become routine.

It also encourages believers to pray for Christ’s return. Believers can join the early church in praying “Come, Lord!” with longing and expectation.

Finally, the verse encourages believers to live in light of His coming. Believers who long for Christ’s return will want to live faithfully, love others, and share the gospel while there is time.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*1 Corinthians 16* shows that practical matters are part of faithful Christian living. Paul’s instructions about giving show that generosity should be regular, proportionate, planned, and part of worship. Believers can give faithfully to support the church and help those in need, including believers far away, and those who handle gifts should do so with integrity and accountability.

The chapter also shows that God opens doors for His work, often alongside opposition. Paul stayed in Ephesus because a great door had opened, even though there were many adversaries. Believers can look for opportunities God provides and persevere through resistance, holding their plans humbly, “if the Lord permits.”

*1 Corinthians 16* calls believers to be watchful, stand firm in the faith, be courageous, be strong, and do everything in love. This short charge summarizes the whole letter. Believers can stand for truth with courage while making love the governing principle of all they do. They can also honor those who serve faithfully and refresh others, like Stephanas and his household.

Finally, the chapter ends with a prayer: “Come, Lord!” Love for the Lord Jesus is the heart of the Christian faith, and hope in His return gives believers courage and purpose. Believers can examine their love for Christ, pray eagerly for His coming, and live each day in light of that hope, held by the grace of the Lord Jesus.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for the practical wisdom of this letter and for Your care for every part of Your people’s lives. Make me a generous giver, setting aside regularly what You have given me to bless others. Open doors for Your gospel, and give me courage to walk through them even when there is opposition. Help me to be watchful, to stand firm in the faith, to be courageous and strong, and above all, to do everything in love. Thank You for those who serve faithfully and refresh my spirit; help me to honor them and to be like them. Fill my heart with love for You, Lord Jesus, and with longing for Your return. Come, Lord! May Your grace be with me and with all Your people. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Book 8 of 27

# 2 Corinthians

## About This Letter

Paul wrote 2 Corinthians from Macedonia around A.D. 55–56, some months after 1 Corinthians (*2 Corinthians 2:13*; *7:5*). In between, his relationship with the Corinthian church had been strained. Paul had made a “painful visit” to Corinth (*2:1*), and he had written a “severe letter” with many tears (*2:4*; *7:8*), which has probably not survived. When Titus brought news that most of the church had repented and longed to see Paul, Paul was overjoyed (*7:6–16*). But a group of visiting teachers, whom Paul ironically calls the “very best apostles” (*11:5*), were still undermining his ministry, boasting of their credentials and mocking Paul’s weakness.

## The Shape of the Letter

The letter has three main parts. In chapters 1–7, Paul explains his changed travel plans, celebrates the church’s repentance, and describes the nature of true Christian ministry: a ministry of the new covenant, of the Spirit, of glory, and of reconciliation, carried in fragile “clay jars” so that its power is clearly from God. In chapters 8–9, he encourages the Corinthians to complete their gift for the poor believers in Jerusalem, with some of the New Testament’s richest teaching on generosity. In chapters 10–13, he defends his apostleship against the false apostles, reluctantly “boasting” in his sufferings and weakness, and preparing for his third visit.

## Themes to Watch For

2 Corinthians is the most personal of Paul’s letters, revealing his heart, his tears, his anxieties, and his deep love for a difficult church. Watch for God’s comfort in affliction, the glory of the new covenant, treasure in clay jars, the hope of a heavenly dwelling, the new creation, the ministry of reconciliation, cheerful and generous giving, and above all, the power of God made perfect in weakness. In a world that admires strength and success, 2 Corinthians shows that God works most powerfully through humble, suffering servants who depend on His grace.

2 Corinthians · Chapter 1 of 13

# 2 Corinthians — Chapter 1

Chapter Theme: The God of All Comfort and the Yes of His Promises

[Read 2 Corinthians 1 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/2CO01.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul opens his letter by praising the Father of mercies and God of all comfort, who comforts His people in every trouble so that they can comfort others. He tells of a crushing affliction in Asia that made him despair of life, which taught him to rely not on himself but on God who raises the dead, and he thanks the Corinthians for their prayers. Paul then explains his changed travel plans, insisting that he did not act carelessly, because the gospel he preached is not “yes and no.” In Christ, all God’s promises are “Yes,” and God has anointed, sealed, and given His Spirit as a guarantee to those who belong to Him. Paul delayed his visit to spare them pain, for he is not a ruler over their faith but a worker for their joy.

## Chapter Background and Story

2 Corinthians is Paul’s most personal letter. Between 1 and 2 Corinthians, Paul’s relationship with the church had gone through a painful time. He had made a brief, sorrowful visit to Corinth that did not go well (*2:1*). He had written a severe letter “out of much affliction and anguish of heart... with many tears” (*2:4*). He had changed his travel plans, and some Corinthians accused him of being unreliable. Meanwhile, rival teachers were questioning his authority.

Paul begins not by defending himself but by praising God. The theme of comfort in suffering runs through the opening chapter. The word “comfort” (paraklesis, related to the Holy Spirit’s title “Counselor” or “Comforter”) appears ten times in verses 3–7 alone.

### Greeting (*1:1–2*)

Paul writes as “*an apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God*” (*v. 1*), together with “*Timothy our brother*” (*v. 1*), to the church in Corinth and “*all the saints who are in the whole of Achaia*” (*v. 1*), the whole Roman province of southern Greece. “*Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ*” (*v. 2*).

### The God of All Comfort (*1:3–7*)

Paul’s praise is studied below. He continues: “*For as the sufferings of Christ abound to us, even so our comfort also abounds through Christ*” (*v. 5*). Believers share in Christ’s sufferings as they follow Him in a world that opposed Him. But in the same way, they share abundantly in His comfort. “*But if we are afflicted, it is for your comfort and salvation. If we are comforted, it is for your comfort, which produces in you the patient enduring of the same sufferings which we also suffer*” (*v. 6*). Paul’s sufferings and comforts were not only for himself; they benefited the Corinthians. “*Our hope for you is steadfast, knowing that, since you are partakers of the sufferings, so you are also of the comfort*” (*v. 7*).

### Delivered from Deadly Peril (*1:8–11*)

Paul’s account of his affliction in Asia is studied below. He adds, “*you also helping together on our behalf by your supplication; that, for the gift given to us by means of many, thanks may be given by many persons on your behalf*” (*v. 11*). Paul valued the Corinthians’ prayers. When many people pray, God’s answer leads many people to give thanks.

### Paul’s Integrity and Changed Plans (*1:12–24*)

“*For our boasting is this: the testimony of our conscience that in holiness and sincerity of God, not in fleshly wisdom but in the grace of God, we behaved ourselves in the world, and more abundantly toward you*” (*v. 12*). Paul’s conscience was clear. He had acted with integrity, by God’s grace, not by worldly scheming.

Paul had planned to visit Corinth twice, once on his way to Macedonia and again on his way back (*1:15–16*). But he changed his plans. Some accused him of being fickle: “*When I therefore planned this, did I show fickleness? Or the things that I plan, do I plan according to the flesh, that with me there should be the “Yes, yes” and the “No, no?”*” (*v. 17*) They suggested Paul said “yes” and “no” at the same time, making promises he did not keep.

Paul answers by pointing to God’s faithfulness: “*But as God is faithful, our word toward you was not “Yes and no.”*” (*v. 18*) “*For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was preached among you by us—by me, Silvanus, and Timothy—was not “Yes and no,” but in him is “Yes.”*” (*v. 19*) The message Paul preached was completely reliable, because Christ Himself is God’s “Yes.” This is studied below, together with God’s work of establishing believers.

“*But I call God for a witness to my soul, that to spare you, I didn’t come to Corinth*” (*v. 23*). Paul explains the real reason for his changed plans: he wanted to spare them another painful visit. He did not want to come with harshness. “*We don’t control your faith, but are fellow workers with you for your joy. For you stand firm in faith*” (*v. 24*). Paul did not see himself as a ruler over their faith. He was a co-worker for their joy. Leaders in the church are not meant to dominate believers but to serve their growth and joy.

## Important Verses Explained

### *2 Corinthians 1:3–4* — The God of All Comfort

> *“Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our affliction, that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction, through the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God.”*
>
> — *2 Corinthians 1:3–4* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had been through great suffering. He had faced deadly danger in Asia, conflict with the Corinthian church, and opposition from false teachers. Yet he begins his letter not with complaints but with praise.

“*Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ*” (*v. 3*). “Blessed” means praised. Paul praises God, describing Him in relation to Jesus. God is not a distant deity; He is the Father of the Lord Jesus Christ.

“*the Father of mercies and God of all comfort*” (*v. 3*). Paul gives God two beautiful titles. He is “the Father of mercies,” the source of all compassion. And He is the “God of all comfort,” the source of every kind of comfort. Every comfort believers receive ultimately comes from Him.

“*who comforts us in all our affliction*” (*v. 4*). God does not always remove affliction, but He comforts His people in it. The word “comfort” means more than sympathy. It includes encouragement, strength, and help. And God comforts “in all” afflictions. No trouble is too great or too small for His comfort.

“*that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction, through the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God*” (*v. 4*). God’s comfort has a purpose beyond the one who receives it. Those whom God comforts become able to comfort others. Believers who have been through suffering and received God’s comfort can share that comfort with others who are hurting. They understand, and they can point others to the same God.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses reveal the compassionate heart of God. He is the Father of mercies, who cares about His children’s pain. Isaiah writes, “*As one whom his mother comforts, so I will comfort you*” (*Isaiah 66:13*). God’s comfort is personal and tender.

They also show that suffering can have purpose. God does not waste His people’s pain. Through suffering, they receive comfort that equips them to help others. A person who has grieved, been ill, or faced loss can often comfort others in a way that no one else can.

Finally, these verses show the connection between receiving and giving. Believers receive comfort from God and pass it on. The church becomes a community of comfort, in which people who have been comforted comfort others.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to turn to God in their suffering. Whatever believers face, God is the God of all comfort. They can bring their pain to Him in prayer, through Scripture, and through the support of other believers.

They also encourage believers to use their experiences to comfort others. Believers who have walked through grief, illness, divorce, loss, depression, or other hardships can reach out to others facing similar trials, sharing the comfort they received.

Finally, these verses encourage believers to see that their pain can have meaning. While suffering is never good in itself, God can use it to make believers more compassionate and more able to help others.

### *2 Corinthians 1:8–9* — Trusting God Who Raises the Dead

> *“For we don’t desire to have you uninformed, brothers, concerning our affliction which happened to us in Asia: that we were weighed down exceedingly, beyond our power, so much that we despaired even of life. Yes, we ourselves have had the sentence of death within ourselves, that we should not trust in ourselves, but in God who raises the dead,”*
>
> — *2 Corinthians 1:8–9* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul wanted the Corinthians to know about a terrible experience he had gone through. “*For we don’t desire to have you uninformed, brothers, concerning our affliction which happened to us in Asia*” (*v. 8*). “Asia” refers to the Roman province in western Asia Minor, where Ephesus was located. Paul does not say exactly what happened. It may have been the riot in Ephesus (*Acts 19*), a serious illness, imprisonment, or severe persecution.

“*that we were weighed down exceedingly, beyond our power, so much that we despaired even of life*” (*v. 8*). The pressure was crushing, far beyond Paul’s ability to endure. He expected to die. This is remarkable honesty from a great apostle. Paul did not pretend to be unshakable. He admitted that he reached the point of despair.

“*Yes, we ourselves have had the sentence of death within ourselves*” (*v. 9*). Paul felt as though he had received a death sentence. Humanly speaking, there was no way out.

“*that we should not trust in ourselves, but in God who raises the dead*” (*v. 9*). But Paul saw a purpose in this experience. It taught him not to rely on himself, his strength, wisdom, or resources, but on God. And not just any idea of God, but the God “who raises the dead.” If God can raise the dead, He can deliver from any danger. And even if death comes, God will raise His people.

“*who delivered us out of so great a death, and does deliver, on whom we have set our hope that he will also still deliver us*” (*v. 10*). God rescued Paul. Paul speaks of God’s deliverance in the past, present, and future: He delivered, He does deliver, and He will deliver.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that even strong believers can reach the end of their own resources. Paul, who had faced so much, was overwhelmed. This honesty gives permission to believers who feel crushed. Despair is a human experience, even for those with great faith.

They also show that God can use extreme hardship to teach dependence on Him. When people are strong, they are tempted to rely on themselves. When they are brought to the end of their strength, they learn to rely on God. Paul later wrote, “*For when I am weak, then am I strong*” (*2 Corinthians 12:10*).

Finally, these verses show that the resurrection is the foundation of hope. God raises the dead. This truth gives believers hope in every situation, because no situation is beyond the power of the God who raised Jesus.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses comfort believers who feel overwhelmed. Paul despaired of life itself, yet God delivered him. Believers who feel crushed can be honest with God about their despair and turn to Him for help. They can also reach out to others for support, including trusted believers, counselors, or medical professionals when needed.

They also encourage believers to rely on God rather than themselves. When believers face situations beyond their strength, they can see them as opportunities to trust God more deeply.

Finally, these verses give believers hope for the future. God has delivered in the past, He delivers now, and He will deliver again. Believers can set their hope on Him.

### *2 Corinthians 1:20* — All God’s Promises Are “*Yes*” (*v. 20*) in Christ

> *“For however many are the promises of God, in him is the ‘Yes.’ Therefore also through him is the ‘Amen’, to the glory of God through us.”*
>
> — *2 Corinthians 1:20* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Some Corinthians had accused Paul of being unreliable because he changed his travel plans. They suggested that his word could not be trusted. Paul responded by pointing to the reliability of the gospel he preached and of Jesus Christ Himself.

He had said that Jesus Christ, whom he preached, was not “Yes and no,” but in Him is “Yes.” Now he explains: “*For however many are the promises of God, in him is the “Yes.”*” (*v. 20*) God made many promises throughout Scripture: to Abraham, to David, through the prophets. He promised a Savior, forgiveness of sins, the gift of the Spirit, a new covenant, eternal life, and the renewal of all things. Every one of these promises finds its fulfillment in Jesus Christ. In Him, God says “Yes” to all His promises.

“*Therefore also through him is the “Amen”, to the glory of God through us*” (*v. 20*). “Amen” means “so be it” or “it is true.” When believers say “Amen” in worship, they affirm God’s promises. Because Christ has fulfilled God’s promises, believers respond with “Amen,” giving glory to God. In the early church, believers would say “Amen” together when prayers were offered and Scripture was read.

Paul’s point is that the message he preached is completely reliable, because it is about Jesus, in whom God’s promises are fulfilled. Paul himself might change travel plans, but the gospel never changes.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that Jesus is the fulfillment of all God’s promises. The whole Old Testament points to Him. Jesus said, “*that all things which are written in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms concerning me must be fulfilled*” (*Luke 24:44*).

It also shows the faithfulness of God. God keeps His promises. Believers can trust every promise in Scripture because God has proven His faithfulness in Christ. Paul writes, “*He who didn’t spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how would he not also with him freely give us all things?*” (*Romans 8:32*)

Finally, the verse shows that worship is a response to God’s faithfulness. Believers say “Amen” to God’s promises, affirming their trust and giving Him glory.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to trust God’s promises. When believers read promises in Scripture, they can know that God will keep them, because in Christ, His answer is “Yes.”

It also encourages believers to be people of their word. Paul defended his integrity. Believers, who follow a faithful God, can strive to be reliable and honest in their own promises.

Finally, the verse invites believers to say “Amen” with faith. When believers hear God’s promises, they can respond with heartfelt agreement and praise.

### *2 Corinthians 1:21–22* — Anointed, Sealed, and Given the Spirit

> *“Now he who establishes us with you in Christ and anointed us is God, who also sealed us and gave us the down payment of the Spirit in our hearts.”*
>
> — *2 Corinthians 1:21–22* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had been explaining that God’s promises are “Yes” in Christ. Now he describes what God has done for believers, using four images.

“*Now he who establishes us with you in Christ and anointed us is God*” (*v. 21*). First, God “establishes” believers. The word means to make firm, secure, and stable. God strengthens believers in their relationship with Christ. Notice “us with you”: Paul and the Corinthians were established together.

Second, God “anointed” believers. In the Old Testament, prophets, priests, and kings were anointed with oil as a sign of being set apart for God’s service. The title “Christ” means “Anointed One.” Believers share in Christ’s anointing through the Holy Spirit. John writes that believers “*have an anointing from the Holy One*” (*1 John 2:20*).

“*who also sealed us*” (*v. 22*). Third, God has “sealed” believers. In the ancient world, a seal was a mark of ownership and authenticity, pressed into wax on a document or package. A seal showed who owned something and protected it from tampering. Believers are marked as belonging to God. Paul writes elsewhere that believers “*were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit*” (*Ephesians 1:13*).

“*and gave us the down payment of the Spirit in our hearts*” (*v. 22*). Fourth, God has given the Holy Spirit as a “down payment.” The Greek word (arrabon) was used in business for a deposit or first installment that guaranteed the rest of the payment would come. The Holy Spirit in believers’ hearts is God’s guarantee that He will complete everything He has promised, including the resurrection and eternal life.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that salvation is God’s work. God establishes, anoints, seals, and gives the Spirit. Believers’ security rests on what God has done, not on their own strength.

They also show the work of the Holy Spirit. The Spirit anoints, seals, and guarantees. The Spirit is God’s presence in believers, the mark of belonging to Him, and the foretaste of the glory to come.

Finally, these verses show the Trinity at work. God (the Father) establishes believers in Christ (the Son) and gives them the Spirit. Salvation involves all three Persons of the Trinity.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses bring assurance to believers who doubt. God has established them, anointed them, sealed them as His own, and given them the Spirit as a guarantee. Their salvation is secure in His hands.

They also encourage believers to live as those set apart for God. They have been anointed for His service and sealed as His possession. Believers can live in a way that reflects whose they are.

Finally, these verses give believers hope. The Spirit is a down payment, a foretaste of what is to come. The joy, peace, and presence of God that believers experience now are just the beginning of what they will experience in eternity.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*2 Corinthians 1* reveals God as the Father of mercies and the God of all comfort. He comforts His people in every affliction, so that they can comfort others. Believers can bring their pain to God and receive His comfort, and they can use their experiences of suffering and comfort to help others who are hurting.

The chapter also shows that even strong believers can reach the point of despair. Paul was crushed beyond his strength and expected to die, yet God delivered him. Through this, Paul learned not to rely on himself but on God who raises the dead. Believers who feel overwhelmed can be honest with God and others, and can set their hope on the God who delivers, past, present, and future.

*2 Corinthians 1* declares that all God’s promises are “Yes” in Christ. Every promise God has made is fulfilled in Jesus. Believers can trust God’s promises, respond with “Amen,” and strive to be people of integrity whose word can be trusted.

Finally, the chapter assures believers that God has established them, anointed them, sealed them, and given them the Spirit as a guarantee. Their security rests in God’s work. And like Paul, those who serve in the church can do so not as rulers over others’ faith, but as fellow workers for their joy.

## Chapter Prayer

Blessed be You, God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort. Thank You for comforting me in all my troubles. Help me to comfort others with the comfort I have received from You. When I am crushed beyond my strength, teach me not to rely on myself but on You, the God who raises the dead. Thank You for delivering me in the past; I trust You to deliver me now and in the future. Thank You that all Your promises are “Yes” in Christ. I gladly agree with Your promises and give You glory. Thank You for establishing me in Christ, anointing me, sealing me as Your own, and giving me Your Spirit as a guarantee. Make me a person of integrity and a fellow worker for the joy of others. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
