2 Corinthians · Chapter 2 of 13

# 2 Corinthians — Chapter 2

Chapter Theme: Tears, Forgiveness, and the Fragrance of Christ

[Read 2 Corinthians 2 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/2CO02.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul explains that he did not return to Corinth because he did not want another painful visit, and that his severe letter was written with many tears out of deep love, not to cause grief. A man who had caused trouble in the church had been disciplined by the majority and had repented, so Paul urges the church to forgive him, comfort him, and reaffirm their love, so that Satan will not take advantage of them. Paul describes his restlessness when he could not find Titus, and then bursts into thanks to God, who leads His people in Christ’s triumphal procession and spreads the fragrance of the knowledge of Christ through them, a fragrance of life to some and death to others. Paul insists that he does not peddle God’s word for profit but speaks sincerely before God.

## Chapter Background and Story

*2 Corinthians 2* continues Paul’s explanation of his relationship with the Corinthians during a difficult period. Paul had made a “painful visit” to Corinth, during which someone in the church apparently opposed or insulted him publicly (*2:5*; *7:12*). Instead of returning, Paul wrote a severe letter, sometimes called the “tearful letter,” calling the church to deal with the situation. He then waited anxiously for news through his co-worker Titus.

Some interpreters connect the man who caused grief with the immoral man of *1 Corinthians 5*; others believe he was a different person who had personally opposed Paul. Either way, the church had disciplined him, and he had repented. Paul now urges them to restore him.

### A Letter Written with Tears (*2:1–4*)

“*But I determined this for myself, that I would not come to you again in sorrow*” (*v. 1*). Paul chose not to make another painful visit. “*For if I make you grieve, then who will make me glad but he who is made to grieve by me?*” (*v. 2*) Paul’s joy was bound up with theirs. Hurting them meant hurting himself. Paul’s description of how he wrote is studied below.

### Forgive and Comfort the Offender (*2:5–11*)

“*But if any has caused sorrow, he has caused sorrow not to me, but in part (that I not press too heavily) to you all*” (*v. 5*). The man’s offense had hurt the whole church, not only Paul. Paul does not name him or describe his offense; he protects the man’s dignity. “*This punishment which was inflicted by the many is sufficient for such a one*” (*v. 6*). The church had disciplined the man, and the discipline had done its work. It was enough. Paul’s call to forgiveness, and his warning about Satan, are studied below.

### Anxiety and Triumph (*2:12–17*)

“*Now when I came to Troas for the Good News of Christ, and when a door was opened to me in the Lord*” (*v. 12*), “*I had no relief for my spirit, because I didn’t find Titus my brother, but taking my leave of them, I went out into Macedonia*” (*v. 13*). Paul had an opportunity to preach in Troas, but he was so anxious to hear how the Corinthians had responded to his letter that he could not rest. He left to find Titus. Even the great apostle felt deep anxiety for the people he loved. (He resumes this story in 7:5–7.)

Then Paul suddenly breaks into praise, studied below. He concludes: “*For we are not as so many, peddling the word of God. But as of sincerity, but as of God, in the sight of God, we speak in Christ*” (*v. 17*). The word “peddling” describes a dishonest merchant who waters down wine to make more profit. Some teachers used the word of God for financial gain, altering the message to please audiences. Paul spoke with sincerity, as one sent by God, aware that God was watching.

## Important Verses Explained

### *2 Corinthians 2:4* — Written with Many Tears

> *“For out of much affliction and anguish of heart I wrote to you with many tears, not that you should be made to grieve, but that you might know the love that I have so abundantly for you.”*
>
> — *2 Corinthians 2:4* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had written a severe letter to the Corinthians, calling them to deal with someone in the church who had caused serious trouble. Some Corinthians may have thought that Paul wrote it out of anger or a desire to control them. Paul explains his true feelings.

“*For out of much affliction and anguish of heart I wrote to you with many tears*” (*v. 4*). Paul wrote with deep distress. “Affliction” means pressure or trouble; “anguish of heart” means intense inner pain. He wrote “with many tears.” Writing that letter was painful for him.

“*not that you should be made to grieve*” (*v. 4*). Paul’s purpose was not to hurt them. He did not enjoy confrontation or causing pain.

“*but that you might know the love that I have so abundantly for you*” (*v. 4*). The letter was an expression of love. Paul cared enough about them to confront what was wrong. His love was “abundant,” overflowing.

This verse shows that hard words can be loving words. Paul confronted the Corinthians because he loved them, not because he wanted to dominate them. Love sometimes requires difficult conversations.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that true love includes correction. Proverbs says, “*The wounds of a friend are faithful*” (*Proverbs 27:6*). A friend who never challenges you may not truly care about you. Paul’s willingness to confront showed his love.

It also shows the heart of a godly leader. Paul did not confront casually or harshly. He did it with tears, with deep sorrow and love. Godly correction comes from a broken heart, not from pride or anger.

Finally, the verse reflects the heart of God. God disciplines His people because He loves them (*Hebrews 12:6*). His correction comes from love and aims at their good.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to speak the truth in love when correction is needed. In families, friendships, and churches, love sometimes requires honest, difficult conversations. Believers can approach such conversations with humility, prayer, and genuine care.

It also encourages believers to examine their motives before confronting others. Are they speaking out of love, or out of anger, pride, or a desire to control? Paul’s tears show the right spirit.

Finally, the verse encourages believers to receive correction well. When others confront believers lovingly, it may be painful, but it can be a sign of genuine care. Believers can listen with humility.

### *2 Corinthians 2:7–8* — Forgive, Comfort, and Reaffirm Your Love

> *“so that, on the contrary, you should rather forgive him and comfort him, lest by any means such a one should be swallowed up with his excessive sorrow. Therefore I beg you to confirm your love toward him.”*
>
> — *2 Corinthians 2:7–8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

A man in the Corinthian church had caused serious harm. The church had disciplined him, and the discipline had been effective; he had repented. Paul said that the punishment had been enough. Now it was time for something else.

“*so that, on the contrary, you should rather forgive him and comfort him*” (*v. 7*). The church should stop punishing the man and instead forgive him and comfort him. Discipline is never meant to last forever. Once a person repents, the church should restore them.

“*lest by any means such a one should be swallowed up with his excessive sorrow*” (*v. 7*). Paul was concerned that the man might be overwhelmed by grief and guilt. Excessive sorrow could lead to despair, perhaps even to giving up on faith altogether. The church needed to welcome him back before that happened.

“*Therefore I beg you to confirm your love toward him*” (*v. 8*). Paul urged them to “confirm” or “reaffirm” their love. The word was used for a formal, public decision. The church should publicly welcome the man back, making clear that he was loved and accepted. Forgiveness should be visible and real.

This shows that the purpose of church discipline is always restoration. Discipline that continues after repentance becomes harsh and unloving.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show the heart of God toward repentant sinners. God does not hold grudges against those who turn to Him. He forgives completely and welcomes them home. The father in Jesus’ parable ran to embrace his returning son (*Luke 15:20*).

They also show that forgiveness includes comfort and love. It is not enough to stop punishing someone. True forgiveness actively restores relationship, offering comfort and affection.

Finally, these verses show the danger of excessive sorrow. Godly sorrow leads to repentance (*7:10*). But excessive sorrow, which continues after repentance, can lead to despair. Believers need to know that they are forgiven and loved.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to forgive those who repent. When someone who has wronged believers genuinely turns from their sin, believers can forgive them, comfort them, and restore the relationship as far as is wise.

They also encourage churches to restore repentant members. Churches that practice discipline must also practice restoration, welcoming back those who repent with genuine love.

Finally, these verses must be applied with wisdom. Forgiveness does not mean ignoring consequences or placing someone in a position where they could harm others again. In cases of abuse, forgiveness can coexist with boundaries, accountability, and protection of the vulnerable. Forgiveness restores fellowship; it does not require trust to be restored instantly or safeguards to be removed.

### *2 Corinthians 2:10–11* — Not Ignorant of Satan’s Schemes

> *“Now I also forgive whomever you forgive anything. For if indeed I have forgiven anything, I have forgiven that one for your sakes in the presence of Christ, that no advantage may be gained over us by Satan, for we are not ignorant of his schemes.”*
>
> — *2 Corinthians 2:10–11* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had urged the Corinthians to forgive the man who had repented. Now he joins in that forgiveness.

“*Now I also forgive whomever you forgive anything*” (*v. 10*). Paul stood with the church in forgiving the man. Even though the man had personally offended Paul, Paul was ready to forgive.

“*For if indeed I have forgiven anything, I have forgiven that one for your sakes in the presence of Christ*” (*v. 10*). Paul’s forgiveness was “for your sakes,” for the good of the church, and “in the presence of Christ,” sincere before the Lord who sees all things.

“*that no advantage may be gained over us by Satan, for we are not ignorant of his schemes*” (*v. 11*). Paul explains why forgiveness matters so much. Satan, the enemy of God’s people, looks for opportunities to harm the church. If the church refused to forgive, Satan could use that unforgiveness to cause division, bitterness, and despair. The man might be driven away from the faith, and the church might become harsh and divided.

“Schemes” means plans, plots, or strategies. Satan has many tactics. One of them is to use unforgiveness. Believers who are aware of this can resist it.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that unforgiveness gives Satan an opportunity. Paul writes elsewhere, “*Don’t let the sun go down on your wrath*” (*Ephesians 4:26*), “*and don’t give place to the devil*” (*Ephesians 4:27*). Bitterness and unforgiveness open doors to the enemy.

They also show that spiritual warfare is real. Satan works to divide churches, discourage believers, and destroy relationships. Believers need to be aware of his schemes, without fear but with wisdom.

Finally, these verses show that forgiveness is a weapon against the enemy. When believers forgive, they defeat Satan’s plans to divide and destroy. Forgiveness reflects the grace of God and builds up the church.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to forgive quickly. Holding grudges and nursing bitterness can give the enemy an opportunity to cause harm. Believers can release resentment and choose to forgive.

They also encourage believers to be aware of spiritual realities. When conflicts arise in families or churches, believers can recognize that the enemy may be at work, seeking to divide. They can respond with prayer, humility, and forgiveness.

Finally, these verses encourage believers to stand together. Paul joined the church in forgiving. Unity in forgiveness strengthens the church against the enemy’s schemes.

### *2 Corinthians 2:14–16* — The Fragrance of Christ

> *“Now thanks be to God who always leads us in triumph in Christ, and reveals through us the sweet aroma of his knowledge in every place. For we are a sweet aroma of Christ to God in those who are being saved and in those who perish: to the one a stench from death to death, to the other a sweet aroma from life to life. Who is sufficient for these things?”*
>
> — *2 Corinthians 2:14–16* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had been describing his anxiety while waiting for Titus. Suddenly, he breaks into praise.

“*Now thanks be to God who always leads us in triumph in Christ*” (*v. 14*). Paul uses the image of a Roman triumphal procession. When a Roman general won a great victory, he paraded through the streets of Rome in a triumphal procession, followed by his soldiers and the captives he had taken. Paul pictures God as the victorious general, leading His people in Christ’s triumph. Paul may see himself as one of God’s captives, conquered by Christ and now displayed in His victory. Despite all his troubles, Paul is part of Christ’s triumphant march.

“*and reveals through us the sweet aroma of his knowledge in every place*” (*v. 14*). In triumphal processions, incense was burned, filling the air with fragrance. Paul says that God spreads the fragrance of the knowledge of Christ through His people. Wherever believers go, they carry the fragrance of Christ.

“*For we are a sweet aroma of Christ to God in those who are being saved and in those who perish*” (*v. 15*). Believers are a pleasing aroma to God. And this aroma reaches two groups of people: those being saved and those perishing.

“*to the one a stench from death to death, to the other a sweet aroma from life to life*” (*v. 16*). To those who reject Christ, the fragrance smells like death. For captives in a Roman procession, the incense meant that they were headed for execution. To those who receive Christ, the fragrance is life-giving. The same message produces opposite responses.

“*Who is sufficient for these things?*” (*v. 16*) Who is adequate for such an important task? Paul will answer in 3:5–6: their sufficiency comes from God.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that believers share in Christ’s victory. Even when believers face hardship, they are part of Christ’s triumphal procession. His victory over sin and death is certain, and they share in it.

They also show the influence of believers. Believers carry the fragrance of Christ wherever they go. Their words, actions, and character reveal something of Him. Paul writes elsewhere that believers should walk in love, “*even as Christ also loved us and gave himself up for us, an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweet-smelling fragrance*” (*Ephesians 5:2*).

Finally, these verses show the seriousness of the gospel. The message of Christ is a matter of life and death. People’s response to it determines their eternal destiny. This is why Paul asked, “Who is sufficient for these things?”

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to give thanks in all circumstances. Even when believers are anxious or troubled, they can thank God for leading them in Christ’s triumph.

They also encourage believers to spread the fragrance of Christ. Believers can ask whether their lives give off the fragrance of Christ’s love, grace, and truth in their homes, workplaces, and communities.

Finally, these verses help believers understand different responses to the gospel. Some will be drawn to Christ; others will reject Him. Believers do not need to be discouraged when some respond negatively. They can faithfully share the fragrance of Christ, trusting God with the results.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*2 Corinthians 2* shows that love sometimes requires difficult words. Paul wrote his severe letter with many tears, not to hurt the Corinthians but to show his abundant love. Believers can speak hard truths when necessary, but always with humility, prayer, and genuine love, and they can receive correction from others with the same humility.

The chapter also teaches that the goal of discipline is restoration. Once the offender repented, Paul urged the church to forgive, comfort, and reaffirm their love for him, so that he would not be overwhelmed by sorrow. Believers can forgive those who repent and welcome them back, while using wisdom about boundaries and protecting the vulnerable.

*2 Corinthians 2* warns that unforgiveness gives Satan an opportunity. Believers should not be ignorant of his schemes to divide and destroy. Forgiveness defeats those schemes and builds up the church.

Finally, the chapter celebrates that God leads His people in Christ’s triumph and spreads the fragrance of Christ through them. Believers carry the aroma of Christ wherever they go. They can live in a way that reveals Christ, share the gospel sincerely without peddling it, and trust God for the results, knowing that their sufficiency comes from Him.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord God, thank You for Paul’s example of love that speaks hard truths with tears. Help me to speak the truth in love, and to receive correction with humility. Give me a forgiving heart. When those who have wronged me repent, help me to forgive them, comfort them, and show them love, while giving me wisdom to protect myself and others where needed. Keep me from bitterness and unforgiveness, so that Satan gains no advantage over me. Thank You for leading me in Christ’s triumph, even when I am anxious or troubled. Spread the fragrance of the knowledge of Christ through my life wherever I go. Help me to share Your word sincerely, as one who speaks in Your sight. My sufficiency is from You. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

2 Corinthians · Chapter 3 of 13

# 2 Corinthians — Chapter 3

Chapter Theme: The Surpassing Glory of the New Covenant

[Read 2 Corinthians 3 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/2CO03.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul says he needs no letters of recommendation, because the Corinthian believers themselves are a letter from Christ, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God on human hearts. His adequacy for ministry comes not from himself but from God, who has made him a minister of a new covenant of the Spirit, which gives life. Comparing the old covenant given through Moses with the new, Paul shows that if the ministry that brought condemnation came with glory, so that Moses’ face shone, the ministry of the Spirit and righteousness has far greater and lasting glory. A veil still lies over hearts when the old covenant is read, but whenever anyone turns to the Lord, the veil is removed. Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom, and believers, beholding the Lord’s glory, are being transformed into His image.

## Chapter Background and Story

In *2 Corinthians 2:16*, Paul asked, “*Who is sufficient for these things?*” (*2 Corinthians 2:16*) In chapter 3, he answers. His sufficiency for ministry comes from God, who has made him a servant of the new covenant.

Paul was writing in a context where rival teachers had come to Corinth with letters of recommendation, perhaps from churches in Judea. They may have emphasized the Law of Moses and questioned Paul’s credentials. Paul responds by comparing the old covenant given through Moses with the new covenant in Christ. He does not despise the old covenant; he acknowledges that it came with glory. But the new covenant has a greater and more lasting glory.

Paul draws on the story of *Exodus 34:29–35*. When Moses came down from Mount Sinai after speaking with God, his face shone with God’s glory. The Israelites were afraid to come near him. After speaking God’s words to them, Moses put a veil over his face. He removed the veil when he went in to speak with the Lord again. Paul uses this story to illustrate the difference between the two covenants.

### A Letter Written on Hearts (*3:1–3*)

“*Are we beginning again to commend ourselves? Or do we need, as do some, letters of commendation to you or from you?*” (*v. 1*) In the ancient world, travelers often carried letters of recommendation to introduce them to new communities (*Acts 18:27*; *Romans 16:1*). The rival teachers in Corinth apparently boasted of theirs. Paul’s answer is studied below.

### Sufficiency from God (*3:4–6*)

“*Such confidence we have through Christ toward God*” (*v. 4*). Paul is confident, but his confidence is not in himself. His explanation is studied below.

### The Greater Glory (*3:7–11*)

Paul compares the two covenants. “*But if the service of death, written engraved on stones, came with glory, so that the children of Israel could not look steadfastly on the face of Moses for the glory of his face, which was passing away*” (*v. 7*), “*won’t service of the Spirit be with much more glory?*” (*v. 8*) The old covenant, written on stone tablets, came with glory. God’s glory was so real that Moses’ face shone. But it was a “service of death” because the Law, though holy, exposed sin and brought condemnation to those who could not keep it (*Romans 7:10*). The glory on Moses’ face was fading.

“*For if the service of condemnation has glory, the service of righteousness exceeds much more in glory*” (*v. 9*). The old covenant revealed condemnation; the new covenant brings righteousness. “*For most certainly that which has been made glorious has not been made glorious in this respect, by reason of the glory that surpasses*” (*v. 10*). The new covenant’s glory is so great that the old covenant’s glory seems faint by comparison, like a candle in the light of the sun. “*For if that which passes away was with glory, much more that which remains is in glory*” (*v. 11*). The old covenant was temporary; the new covenant is permanent.

Paul is not saying that the Law was bad. He has called it “*holy, righteous, and good*” (*Romans 7:12*). But the Law could not give life. The new covenant, through Christ and the Spirit, does what the Law could not.

### Unveiled Faces (*3:12–18*)

“*Having therefore such a hope, we use great boldness of speech*” (*v. 12*), “*and not as Moses, who put a veil on his face so that the children of Israel wouldn’t look steadfastly on the end of that which was passing away*” (*v. 13*). Paul interprets Moses’ veil as hiding the fading of the glory. Paul, by contrast, speaks openly and boldly about the gospel.

“*But their minds were hardened, for until this very day at the reading of the old covenant the same veil remains, because in Christ it passes away*” (*v. 14*). Paul uses the veil as an image. When the Law of Moses is read in synagogues, many do not understand that it points to Christ. It is as if a veil covers their understanding. “*But to this day, when Moses is read, a veil lies on their heart*” (*v. 15*). Paul writes this with grief, as he did in *Romans 9–11*, not with contempt. He himself once had this veil. The removal of the veil, and the transformation that follows, are studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *2 Corinthians 3:2–3* — A Letter of Christ Written on Hearts

> *“You are our letter, written in our hearts, known and read by all men, being revealed that you are a letter of Christ, served by us, written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God; not in tablets of stone, but in tablets that are hearts of flesh.”*
>
> — *2 Corinthians 3:2–3* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Rival teachers had come to Corinth with letters of recommendation. They may have suggested that Paul needed such letters to prove his authority. Paul responds with a beautiful image.

“*You are our letter, written in our hearts, known and read by all men*” (*v. 2*). The Corinthian church itself was Paul’s letter of recommendation. Their transformed lives proved that his ministry was genuine. This letter was “written in our hearts,” meaning Paul carried them in his heart with love. And it was “known and read by all,” since everyone could see what God had done in Corinth.

“*being revealed that you are a letter of Christ, served by us*” (*v. 3*). Ultimately, the letter was from Christ. Christ was the author; Paul was simply the one who delivered it, the servant who “wrote it down.”

“*written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God*” (*v. 3*). This letter was not written with ink on paper, but by the Holy Spirit. The Spirit had changed the Corinthians’ lives.

“*not in tablets of stone, but in tablets that are hearts of flesh*” (*v. 3*). This alludes to the Ten Commandments, written on stone tablets at Sinai. God’s new covenant is written on human hearts. The prophets had promised this. Ezekiel wrote that God would remove the heart of stone and give a heart of flesh (*Ezekiel 36:26*). Jeremiah wrote that God would write His law on their hearts (*Jeremiah 31:33*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that transformed lives are the best evidence of genuine ministry. Credentials, titles, and recommendations have their place, but what truly matters is whether God is changing people’s lives.

They also show the fulfillment of the new covenant. God promised through Jeremiah, “*I will put my law in their inward parts, and I will write it in their heart*” (*Jeremiah 31:33*). Through the Holy Spirit, this promise is fulfilled in believers.

Finally, these verses show that every believer is a “letter” that others read. The way believers live communicates something about Christ to those around them.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses remind believers that their lives are a message to the world. People “read” believers’ lives, often before they read the Bible. Believers can ask what message their lives communicate about Christ.

They also encourage those in ministry. The fruit of ministry is not measured by credentials or recognition but by changed lives. Pastors, teachers, and servants can find joy in seeing God at work in people.

Finally, these verses encourage believers to depend on the Spirit for transformation. Change is not merely a matter of following rules written on stone, but of the Spirit writing God’s ways on the heart.

### *2 Corinthians 3:5–6* — Our Sufficiency Is from God

> *“not that we are sufficient of ourselves to account anything as from ourselves; but our sufficiency is from God, who also made us sufficient as servants of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit. For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.”*
>
> — *2 Corinthians 3:5–6* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

In the previous chapter, Paul had asked, “Who is sufficient for these things?” The task of spreading the fragrance of Christ, bringing life to some and death to others, was enormous. Now he answers.

“*not that we are sufficient of ourselves to account anything as from ourselves*” (*v. 5*). Paul admits that he is not adequate in his own strength. He cannot claim any credit for his ministry.

“*but our sufficiency is from God*” (*v. 5*). Paul’s adequacy came from God. God equipped him for the task.

“*who also made us sufficient as servants of a new covenant*” (*v. 6*). God made Paul a “servant” (minister) of a “new covenant.” The new covenant is God’s promise to forgive sins and write His law on hearts, sealed by the blood of Jesus (*Luke 22:20*).

“*not of the letter but of the Spirit*” (*v. 6*). The old covenant was a covenant of “the letter,” written laws. The new covenant is a covenant of “the Spirit,” in which God’s Spirit transforms hearts.

“*For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life*” (*v. 6*). “The letter,” the written law by itself, “kills.” This does not mean the Law is evil, but that the Law alone cannot give life. It commands but does not empower; it reveals sin and pronounces judgment. “The Spirit gives life.” The Holy Spirit gives new life, empowering believers to live in a way that pleases God.

This verse is sometimes misused to mean that believers should ignore the plain meaning of Scripture in favor of their own “spiritual” interpretations. That is not Paul’s point. He is contrasting the old covenant of law with the new covenant of the Spirit.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that all ministry depends on God. No one is adequate on their own for the work of the gospel. Jesus said, “*apart from me you can do nothing*” (*John 15:5*). God supplies what His servants need.

They also show the difference between law and Spirit. Law alone can show what is right but cannot change the heart. The Spirit changes the heart and gives power to obey. Paul writes, “*For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus made me free from the law of sin and of death*” (*Romans 8:2*).

Finally, these verses show the greatness of the new covenant. Believers live under a covenant of life, empowered by the Spirit. This is a privilege that even the greatest Old Testament saints looked forward to.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers who feel inadequate. Many believers feel unqualified to share their faith, serve in the church, or lead others. Their sufficiency comes from God. He equips those He calls.

They also warn against relying on rules alone for spiritual growth. Rules have their place, but lasting change comes through the Spirit. Believers can depend on the Spirit to transform them from within.

Finally, these verses encourage those in ministry to stay humble. Any fruit in their ministry is God’s work, not theirs. They can serve with confidence in God and humility about themselves.

### *2 Corinthians 3:16–17* — The Veil Removed; Freedom in the Spirit

> *“But whenever someone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away. Now the Lord is the Spirit; and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty.”*
>
> — *2 Corinthians 3:16–17* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had been explaining that when the Law of Moses is read, a “veil” covers the hearts of many, keeping them from understanding that it points to Christ. Now he describes how this veil is removed.

“*But whenever someone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away*” (*v. 16*). This echoes *Exodus 34:34*, where Moses removed his veil whenever he went in before the Lord. Paul applies it to anyone who turns to Christ. When a person turns to the Lord in faith, the veil is lifted. They can now see the truth, understand the Scriptures, and behold God’s glory in Christ.

Notice “whenever someone.” This is available to anyone, Jew or Gentile. Paul himself had once been veiled, persecuting the church, until he met the risen Christ and “*something like scales fell from his eyes*” (*Acts 9:18*).

“*Now the Lord is the Spirit*” (*v. 17*). This phrase has been understood in different ways. Many interpreters understand Paul to mean that “the Lord” in the Exodus passage, to whom Moses turned, is now experienced through the Spirit. The Spirit makes the Lord present to believers. Paul is not confusing the Persons of the Trinity; he speaks elsewhere of “the Spirit of the Lord,” showing that he distinguishes them while emphasizing their unity.

“*and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty*” (*v. 17*). Where the Spirit is present, there is freedom: freedom from the veil, from condemnation, from the power of sin, from fear, and from the burden of trying to earn God’s favor. Believers are free to approach God, to see His glory, and to live for Him.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that understanding God’s truth requires turning to Christ. Without Christ, the Scriptures remain veiled. With Christ, they open up. Jesus opened His disciples’ minds to understand the Scriptures (*Luke 24:45*).

They also show that the Spirit brings freedom. Jesus said, “*If therefore the Son makes you free, you will be free indeed*” (*John 8:36*). This freedom is not license to sin but liberty to live as God’s children.

Finally, these verses offer hope for all who are veiled. Paul wrote with grief about those whose hearts were veiled, but he also wrote with hope: whenever anyone turns to the Lord, the veil is removed.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to pray for those who do not yet understand the gospel. Only the Lord can remove the veil. Believers can pray for friends and family members that their eyes would be opened.

They also invite believers to enjoy their freedom in Christ. Believers can approach God without fear, confident in His grace. They are free from condemnation and free to live for Him.

Finally, these verses encourage believers to read Scripture with dependence on the Spirit. When believers turn to the Lord as they read, He removes the veil and helps them understand His word.

### *2 Corinthians 3:18* — Transformed from Glory to Glory

> *“But we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as from the Lord, the Spirit.”*
>
> — *2 Corinthians 3:18* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had explained that when people turn to the Lord, the veil is removed, and where the Spirit is, there is freedom. Now he describes what happens to believers whose faces are unveiled.

“*But we all, with unveiled face*” (*v. 18*). “We all” includes every believer, not just Moses or apostles. In the old covenant, only Moses saw God’s glory with an unveiled face. In the new covenant, every believer can.

“*seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror*” (*v. 18*). The phrase can mean “beholding” or “reflecting” the glory of the Lord. Believers see the glory of the Lord, revealed in Jesus Christ, through the gospel. Paul writes in the next chapter of “*the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ*” (*2 Corinthians 4:6*). As in a mirror, the view is real but not yet complete (compare *1 Corinthians 13:12*).

“*are transformed into the same image*” (*v. 18*). As believers behold the Lord’s glory, they are changed into His likeness. The word “transformed” is metamorphoo, the same word used for Jesus’ transfiguration (*Matthew 17:2*) and in *Romans 12:2*. Believers are gradually being made like Jesus.

“*from glory to glory*” (*v. 18*). This transformation is progressive, increasing step by step. Unlike Moses’ fading glory, believers’ glory increases. It continues throughout life and will be completed when Christ returns.

“*even as from the Lord, the Spirit*” (*v. 18*). This transformation is the work of the Spirit. Believers do not transform themselves by willpower. As they behold Christ, the Spirit changes them.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows God’s purpose for believers: to make them like Christ. Paul writes, “*For whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son*” (*Romans 8:29*). Transformation into Christ’s likeness is the goal of the Christian life.

It also shows how transformation happens: by beholding Christ. People become like what they gaze upon. As believers spend time looking at Jesus through Scripture, prayer, and worship, the Spirit makes them more like Him.

Finally, the verse shows that transformation is gradual. Believers are being changed “from glory to glory.” Growth takes time. Believers should not be discouraged by slow progress; God is at work.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to spend time beholding Christ. Reading the Gospels, meditating on Scripture, worshiping, and praying all help believers see the glory of the Lord. As they do, the Spirit transforms them.

It also encourages patience in spiritual growth. Transformation is a lifelong process. Believers can trust that God is changing them, even when progress seems slow.

Finally, the verse gives believers hope. One day, the transformation will be complete. John writes, “*we will be like him; for we will see him just as he is*” (*1 John 3:2*). Until then, believers can keep looking to Jesus, being changed from glory to glory.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*2 Corinthians 3* shows that transformed lives are the best evidence of genuine ministry. The Corinthian believers were a letter from Christ, written by the Spirit on their hearts. Believers today are “letters” that others read. They can ask what their lives communicate about Christ.

The chapter also teaches that believers’ sufficiency comes from God. No one is adequate in themselves for the work of the gospel. God makes His servants sufficient as ministers of the new covenant. Believers who feel unqualified can trust God to equip them.

*2 Corinthians 3* celebrates the surpassing glory of the new covenant. The old covenant came with glory, but it was a ministry of condemnation and its glory faded. The new covenant is a ministry of the Spirit and righteousness, with a glory that surpasses and remains. The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life. Believers can rejoice in the privilege of living under the new covenant.

Finally, the chapter shows that when anyone turns to the Lord, the veil is removed, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom. Believers, beholding the Lord’s glory with unveiled faces, are being transformed into His image from glory to glory. Believers can spend time beholding Christ, trusting the Spirit to change them, and praying for others to turn to the Lord and have the veil removed.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord God, thank You for writing Your word on my heart by Your Spirit. Make my life a letter of Christ that others can read. I confess that I am not sufficient in myself for anything You call me to do. My sufficiency is from You. Thank You for making me a servant of the new covenant, which brings life and righteousness through Your Spirit. Thank You that the veil is removed when I turn to You, and that where Your Spirit is, there is freedom. Remove the veil from the hearts of those I love who do not yet know You. Help me to behold Your glory in the face of Jesus Christ, and by Your Spirit, transform me into His image from glory to glory. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

2 Corinthians · Chapter 4 of 13

# 2 Corinthians — Chapter 4

Chapter Theme: Treasure in Clay Jars and an Eternal Weight of Glory

[Read 2 Corinthians 4 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/2CO04.htm)

Main Teaching

Because God in His mercy has given him this ministry, Paul does not lose heart. He refuses deceit and openly proclaims the truth, knowing that the god of this age has blinded unbelievers’ minds, but that the God who said “*Light will shine out of darkness*” (*v. 6*) has shone in believers’ hearts to reveal His glory in the face of Christ. This treasure is held in fragile clay jars, so that its surpassing power is clearly from God. Though hard-pressed, perplexed, persecuted, and struck down, Paul is never crushed, abandoned, or destroyed, carrying Jesus’ death in his body so that Jesus’ life may be revealed. Though his outer self is wasting away, his inner self is renewed daily, and his momentary troubles are achieving an eternal glory, so he fixes his eyes on what is unseen and eternal.

## Chapter Background and Story

*2 Corinthians 4* continues Paul’s description of Christian ministry under the new covenant. In chapter 3, he described its surpassing glory. Now he explains how that glorious ministry is carried out by weak, suffering people. Paul’s opponents in Corinth may have pointed to his sufferings and unimpressive appearance as evidence that he was not a true apostle. Paul turns this around: his weakness shows that the power at work in his ministry comes from God.

This chapter is one of the most encouraging passages in the New Testament for believers who are suffering, weary, or growing old.

### Not Losing Heart (*4:1–6*)

“*Therefore, seeing we have this ministry, even as we obtained mercy, we don’t faint*” (*v. 1*). Paul received his ministry as an act of mercy. He did not earn it. Because it came from God’s mercy, he did not give up, despite the difficulties.

“*But we have renounced the hidden things of shame, not walking in craftiness nor handling the word of God deceitfully, but by the manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man’s conscience in the sight of God*” (*v. 2*). Paul refused to use deceptive methods or to twist God’s word. He simply proclaimed the truth openly, before God and every person’s conscience.

“*Even if our Good News is veiled, it is veiled in those who are dying*” (*v. 3*). Some did not believe. But this was not because Paul hid the gospel. “*in whom the god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelieving, that the light of the Good News of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God, should not dawn on them*” (*v. 4*). “The god of this world” refers to Satan, who has influence over the present evil age (*John 12:31*; *Ephesians 2:2*). He blinds people so that they cannot see the glory of Christ. Christ is “the image of God,” the perfect revelation of who God is (*Colossians 1:15*). Paul’s message and God’s light are studied below.

### Treasure in Clay Jars (*4:7–15*)

The treasure in fragile vessels, and Paul’s description of his sufferings, are studied below. “*For we who live are always delivered to death for Jesus’ sake, that the life also of Jesus may be revealed in our mortal flesh*” (*v. 11*). “*So then death works in us, but life in you*” (*v. 12*). Paul’s sufferings brought life to others. His willingness to endure hardship for the gospel resulted in the Corinthians’ salvation.

“*But having the same spirit of faith, according to that which is written, “I believed, and therefore I spoke.” We also believe, and therefore we also speak*” (*v. 13*). Paul quotes *Psalm 116:10*, a psalm of someone who trusted God in great distress and was delivered. Like the psalmist, Paul believed, and so he spoke. Faith leads to proclamation, even in suffering.

“*knowing that he who raised the Lord Jesus will raise us also through Jesus, and will present us with you*” (*v. 14*). Paul’s confidence rested on the resurrection. The God who raised Jesus will raise believers and bring them together into His presence.

“*For all things are for your sakes, that the grace, being multiplied through the many, may cause the thanksgiving to abound to the glory of God*” (*v. 15*). Everything Paul endured was for the good of others, so that God’s grace would reach more people, resulting in more thanksgiving and more glory to God.

### Renewed Day by Day (*4:16–18*)

Paul’s conclusion is studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *2 Corinthians 4:5–6* — Light Shining Out of Darkness

> *“For we don’t preach ourselves, but Christ Jesus as Lord, and ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake, seeing it is God who said, ‘Light will shine out of darkness,’ who has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.”*
>
> — *2 Corinthians 4:5–6* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had explained that Satan blinds the minds of unbelievers so that they cannot see the glory of Christ. Now he describes what he preaches and how God opens blind eyes.

“*For we don’t preach ourselves, but Christ Jesus as Lord*” (*v. 5*). Paul did not promote himself. His message was not about his own importance, wisdom, or achievements. He proclaimed Jesus Christ as Lord, the One who rules over all.

“*and ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake*” (*v. 5*). Paul saw himself as a servant (literally “slave”) of the Corinthians, for Jesus’ sake. He served them because he served Jesus. Ministry is not about status but service.

“*seeing it is God who said, “Light will shine out of darkness,”*” (*v. 6*). Paul refers to creation. In *Genesis 1:3*, God said, “*Let there be light*” (*Genesis 1:3*), and light shone in the darkness. The same God who created light at the beginning of the world now creates light in human hearts.

“*who has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ*” (*v. 6*). Just as God spoke light into existence at creation, He shines light into the hearts of those who believe. This light gives “the knowledge of the glory of God.” And this glory is seen “in the face of Jesus Christ.” To know God, people must look at Jesus. In Jesus, God’s glory is fully revealed.

Paul may have been thinking of his own conversion. On the road to Damascus, a blinding light from heaven shone around him, and he saw the glory of the risen Christ (*Acts 9:3*). God shone light into his darkened heart.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that conversion is a new creation. Just as God created light out of darkness, He creates spiritual light in darkened hearts. Paul writes, “*Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation*” (*2 Corinthians 5:17*).

They also show that God’s glory is revealed in Jesus. Jesus said, “*He who has seen me has seen the Father*” (*John 14:9*). People who want to know what God is like can look at Jesus.

Finally, these verses show the right focus of ministry. Ministry is not about promoting oneself but proclaiming Jesus as Lord and serving others for His sake.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers to keep Jesus at the center of their witness. When believers share their faith, the focus should be on Jesus, not on themselves.

They also encourage believers to pray for those who are spiritually blind. Only God can shine light into darkened hearts. Believers can pray for God to open the eyes of those they love.

Finally, these verses invite believers to keep looking at Jesus. The knowledge of God’s glory is found in the face of Jesus Christ. Believers can grow in knowing God by studying the life, words, and work of Jesus in the Gospels.

### *2 Corinthians 4:7* — Treasure in Clay Jars

> *“But we have this treasure in clay vessels, that the exceeding greatness of the power may be of God and not from ourselves.”*
>
> — *2 Corinthians 4:7* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had just described the glorious light of the knowledge of God in the face of Jesus Christ, which God has shone into believers’ hearts. This is an incredible treasure. Now he describes the containers that hold it.

“*But we have this treasure in clay vessels*” (*v. 7*). In the ancient world, clay jars were ordinary, inexpensive, and fragile. They were used for everyday purposes, such as storing water, oil, or grain. Sometimes people hid valuable things like coins in clay jars, since no one would expect treasure in such ordinary containers. The Dead Sea Scrolls, discovered in 1947, had been preserved in clay jars for nearly two thousand years.

Paul says that the treasure of the gospel is held in “clay vessels,” meaning ordinary, weak human beings. Paul himself was not physically impressive (*10:10*). He suffered illness, persecution, and hardship. He was a fragile container for a priceless treasure.

“*that the exceeding greatness of the power may be of God and not from ourselves*” (*v. 7*). Why would God put such a great treasure in such weak containers? So that it is clear that the power comes from God, not from the human messengers. If the messengers were impressive, people might think the power came from them. Because they are weak, the power is obviously God’s.

This was an important answer to Paul’s critics. They pointed to his weakness as evidence that he was not a true apostle. Paul says his weakness actually proves that God is at work.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that God works through weakness. Throughout Scripture, God used weak and unlikely people: Moses, who could not speak well; Gideon, the least in his family; David, the youngest son; and the fishermen who became apostles. Paul writes, “*God chose the weak things of the world that he might put to shame the things that are strong*” (*1 Corinthians 1:27*).

It also shows the value of the gospel. The gospel is a “treasure,” more valuable than anything the world can offer. Jesus compared the kingdom of heaven to treasure hidden in a field (*Matthew 13:44*).

Finally, the verse keeps believers humble. Whatever good is done through them comes from God’s power, not their own. All the glory belongs to Him.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers who feel weak or ordinary. God does not need impressive people; He uses ordinary “clay jars.” Believers’ weaknesses do not disqualify them from serving God. They may even make God’s power more visible.

It also encourages believers to value the gospel. The good news of Jesus is a priceless treasure. Believers can treasure it, guard it, and share it.

Finally, the verse encourages humility. When God works through believers, they can give Him the credit. The power belongs to God, not to the clay jar.

### *2 Corinthians 4:8–10* — Pressed but Not Crushed

> *“We are pressed on every side, yet not crushed; perplexed, yet not to despair; pursued, yet not forsaken; struck down, yet not destroyed; always carrying in the body the putting to death of the Lord Jesus, that the life of Jesus may also be revealed in our body.”*
>
> — *2 Corinthians 4:8–10* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had just said that believers hold the treasure of the gospel in fragile clay jars, so that the power is clearly God’s. Now he describes what life in a clay jar is like, using four contrasts.

“*We are pressed on every side, yet not crushed*” (*v. 8*). “Pressed” means squeezed, under pressure from all sides. Paul faced pressure constantly. But he was not “crushed,” completely flattened.

“*perplexed, yet not to despair*” (*v. 8*). Paul was sometimes confused, not knowing what to do or why things were happening. But he did not give up hope. In Greek, there is a play on words: “at a loss, but not utterly at a loss.”

“*pursued, yet not forsaken*” (*v. 9*). Paul was hunted by enemies. But he was never abandoned by God.

“*struck down, yet not destroyed*” (*v. 9*). Paul was knocked down, as in a fight. But he was not destroyed. He got back up. This was literally true; he had been stoned and left for dead, then got up and went back into the city (*Acts 14:19–20*).

“*always carrying in the body the putting to death of the Lord Jesus, that the life of Jesus may also be revealed in our body*” (*v. 10*). Paul’s sufferings were a way of sharing in Jesus’ suffering and death. But through these sufferings, the life of the risen Jesus was revealed. God’s power sustained Paul, showing that Jesus is alive.

Notice the pattern: in each pair, the first part describes real hardship, and the second part describes God’s sustaining power. Paul does not deny the hardships. But he declares that they do not have the final word.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that the Christian life involves real suffering. Paul does not pretend that following Jesus is easy. Believers may be pressed, perplexed, persecuted, and struck down.

They also show that God’s power sustains believers in suffering. God does not always remove hardship, but He keeps His people from being destroyed by it. Jesus promised, “*I will in no way leave you, neither will I in any way forsake you*” (*Hebrews 13:5*).

Finally, these verses show the pattern of death and resurrection in the Christian life. Believers share in Jesus’ sufferings, and they also share in His life. Through their weakness, the life of the risen Jesus is displayed.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses encourage believers in hard times. Believers may feel pressed, confused, attacked, or knocked down. But God has not abandoned them. They are not crushed, not in despair, not forsaken, and not destroyed.

They also encourage honesty about struggles. Paul admitted that he was perplexed and struck down. Believers do not need to pretend everything is fine. They can be honest about their difficulties while holding on to God’s faithfulness.

Finally, these verses encourage believers to see their sufferings as opportunities for Christ’s life to be revealed. When believers endure hardship with faith, others can see the power of the risen Jesus at work in them.

### *2 Corinthians 4:16–18* — Renewed Day by Day

> *“Therefore we don’t faint, but though our outward person is decaying, yet our inward person is renewed day by day. For our light affliction, which is for the moment, works for us more and more exceedingly an eternal weight of glory, while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.”*
>
> — *2 Corinthians 4:16–18* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul had been describing his sufferings and the hope of resurrection. Now he draws a conclusion.

“*Therefore we don’t faint*” (*v. 16*). Paul repeats what he said at the beginning of the chapter (*4:1*). Despite everything, he does not give up.

“*but though our outward person is decaying, yet our inward person is renewed day by day*” (*v. 16*). Paul contrasts two parts of his life. The “outward person,” his physical body and earthly life, was “decaying,” wearing out. Suffering, persecution, illness, and age were taking their toll. But the “inward person,” his spirit, his life in God, was being “renewed day by day.” While his body weakened, his inner life grew stronger.

“*For our light affliction, which is for the moment, works for us more and more exceedingly an eternal weight of glory*” (*v. 17*). Paul calls his afflictions “light” and “for the moment.” This is remarkable, considering what he endured (*11:23–28*). His sufferings were not light in themselves; they seem light only when compared to the glory to come. And they are “for the moment,” temporary compared to eternity. These afflictions are producing “an eternal weight of glory.” The word “weight” contrasts with “light.” The glory to come is weighty, substantial, and far greater than the suffering.

“*while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen*” (*v. 18*). Paul’s secret was where he fixed his eyes. He did not focus on visible circumstances, his suffering and problems. He focused on the unseen realities: God, Christ, and the eternal glory to come.

“*For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal*” (*v. 18*). Visible things, including suffering, possessions, and even physical bodies, are temporary. Invisible things, God and eternal life, last forever.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that God renews believers inwardly even as they age or suffer outwardly. The psalmist says that God renews strength like the eagle’s (*Psalm 103:5*). Isaiah writes, “*But those who wait for the LORD will renew their strength*” (*Isaiah 40:31*).

They also show that present suffering produces future glory. Paul writes in Romans, “*For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which will be revealed toward us*” (*Romans 8:18*). Suffering is not meaningless; God uses it to prepare believers for glory.

Finally, these verses show the importance of perspective. What believers focus on shapes how they experience life. Those who focus only on visible circumstances may lose heart. Those who fix their eyes on eternal realities find strength to endure.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses bring hope to believers who are aging, ill, or suffering. Even as the body weakens, God renews the inner person day by day. Believers can seek this daily renewal through prayer, Scripture, and fellowship with God.

They also encourage believers to keep an eternal perspective. When troubles feel heavy, believers can remember that they are temporary, and that God is using them to prepare an eternal glory far greater.

Finally, these verses encourage believers to fix their eyes on the unseen. Believers can focus on God’s presence, His promises, and the hope of eternal life, rather than being overwhelmed by visible circumstances. This does not mean ignoring real problems or pain, but seeing them in the light of eternity.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*2 Corinthians 4* encourages believers not to lose heart. Paul faced constant hardship, yet he did not give up, because his ministry came from God’s mercy and his hope rested in God’s power. Believers who feel discouraged can remember that they have received mercy and that God is at work.

The chapter also shows that the treasure of the gospel is held in fragile clay jars. God uses weak, ordinary people so that it is clear the power comes from Him. Believers who feel inadequate can trust that God works through their weakness, and they can keep Jesus, not themselves, at the center of their witness.

*2 Corinthians 4* describes the reality of suffering and the faithfulness of God. Believers may be pressed, perplexed, persecuted, and struck down, but they are not crushed, in despair, forsaken, or destroyed. Through their sufferings, the life of Jesus is revealed. Believers can be honest about their struggles while trusting God’s sustaining power.

Finally, the chapter offers deep hope to those who are suffering or aging. Though the outer person is wasting away, the inner person is being renewed day by day. Present troubles, though real, are light and momentary compared to the eternal weight of glory they are producing. Believers can fix their eyes on what is unseen and eternal, finding strength to endure.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord God, thank You for shining Your light into my heart and showing me Your glory in the face of Jesus Christ. Thank You for entrusting the treasure of the gospel to an ordinary clay jar like me. Let Your power be seen in my weakness. When I am pressed on every side, keep me from being crushed. When I am perplexed, keep me from despair. When I feel attacked, remind me that You will never forsake me. When I am struck down, raise me up. Let the life of Jesus be revealed in me. Though my outer self is wasting away, renew my inner self day by day. Help me to see my troubles in the light of eternity, and to fix my eyes not on what is seen, but on what is unseen and eternal. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
