2 Corinthians · Chapter 8 of 13

# 2 Corinthians — Chapter 8

Chapter Theme: The Grace of Giving

[Read 2 Corinthians 8 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/2CO08.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul encourages the Corinthians to complete the collection they had begun for the poor believers in Jerusalem. He holds up the example of the Macedonian churches, who gave joyfully and beyond their means out of deep poverty because they first gave themselves to the Lord. The ultimate pattern for giving is Jesus Christ, who though rich became poor so that others might become rich. Paul explains that giving should be willing and proportionate, aimed at mutual care, and handled with careful integrity.

## Chapter Background and Story

Chapters 8 and 9 turn to a practical matter that was close to Paul’s heart: the collection for the believers in Jerusalem. The church there was largely poor. Famine had struck Judea in the 40s (*Acts 11:28–30*), and many Jewish believers may have lost family support or employment because of their faith in Jesus. At the Jerusalem council, the leaders had asked Paul to “*remember the poor*” (*Galatians 2:10*), which he said he was eager to do.

Over several years, Paul gathered gifts from the Gentile churches he had founded, in Galatia, Macedonia, and Achaia, the province that included Corinth (*1 Corinthians 16:1–4*; *Romans 15:25–27*). For Paul, this collection was more than charity. It was a powerful sign of unity between Jewish and Gentile believers. The Gentiles had received spiritual blessings through the Jewish people; now they could share material blessings in return (*Romans 15:27*).

The Corinthians had been among the first to show interest in the collection a year earlier. But during the conflict with Paul, their giving appears to have stalled. Now that the relationship has been restored (chapter 7), Paul gently encourages them to finish what they started. These two chapters contain the New Testament’s most extended teaching on giving, and Paul handles the subject with remarkable tact. He never uses the ordinary word for money. Instead he speaks of “grace,” “fellowship,” “service,” and “blessing.”

### The Example of Macedonia (*8:1–6*)

“*Moreover, brothers, we make known to you the grace of God which has been given in the assemblies of Macedonia*” (*v. 1*). The churches of Macedonia included Philippi, Thessalonica, and Berea. Paul calls their generosity “the grace of God.” Their giving was not their own achievement; it was evidence of God’s grace at work in them.

“*how in a severe ordeal of affliction, the abundance of their joy and their deep poverty abounded to the riches of their generosity*” (*v. 2*). The Macedonian believers were suffering persecution (*1 Thessalonians 1:6*; *2:14*) and were very poor. Yet joy and poverty combined to overflow in generosity. “*For according to their power, I testify, yes and beyond their power, they gave of their own accord*” (*v. 3*), “*begging us with much entreaty to receive this grace and the fellowship in the service to the saints*” (*v. 4*). Paul did not have to persuade them. They pleaded for the privilege of giving. The secret of their generosity, given in verse 5, is studied below.

Encouraged by this example, Paul urged Titus, who had already begun the work in Corinth, to help them complete it (v6).

### Abounding in This Grace (*8:7–15*)

“*But as you abound in everything—in faith, utterance, knowledge, all earnestness, and in your love to us—see that you also abound in this grace*” (*v. 7*). The Corinthians prized spiritual gifts, especially speech and knowledge (*1 Corinthians 1:5*). Paul gently suggests that generosity belongs on that list too.

“*I speak not by way of commandment, but as proving through the earnestness of others the sincerity also of your love*” (*v. 8*). Paul does not order them to give. He wants their gift to be a genuine expression of love. The supreme example of giving, Christ Himself, is studied below.

Paul offers advice. The Corinthians had begun with eagerness a year earlier; now they should finish. The principle of giving according to what one has is studied below.

“*For this is not that others may be eased and you distressed*” (*v. 13*), “*but for equality. Your abundance at this present time supplies their lack, that their abundance also may become a supply for your lack, that there may be equality*” (*v. 14*). Paul is not asking the Corinthians to impoverish themselves so that others can live in ease. He is describing mutual care within the family of God. At present, the Corinthians have more and Jerusalem has less. Another time, it may be the reverse. The goal is that no one in God’s family should go without what they need.

He illustrates this with the story of the manna in the wilderness: “*As it is written, “He who gathered much had nothing left over, and he who gathered little had no lack.”*” (*v. 15*) In *Exodus 16:18*, when the Israelites gathered manna, each family ended up with what it needed. God’s provision was shared so that no one was in want. Paul sees the church’s generosity as continuing that pattern.

### Integrity in Handling Money (*8:16–24*)

Paul then describes the team he is sending to Corinth to receive the gift. Titus himself was eager to go (“*But thanks be to God, who puts the same earnest care for you into the heart of Titus*” (*v. 16*)). With him went “*the brother whose praise in the Good News is known throughout all the assemblies*” (*v. 18*), a respected believer chosen by the churches. Paul does not name him, and scholars have suggested various candidates, such as Luke or Barnabas, but no one knows for certain. A third brother, tested and proven earnest, also went (v22). Paul’s reasons for this careful arrangement are studied below.

“*As for Titus, he is my partner and fellow worker for you. As for our brothers, they are the apostles of the assemblies, the glory of Christ*” (*v. 23*). “Apostles” here means messengers or representatives sent by the churches, not apostles in the sense of the Twelve. Paul closes by asking the Corinthians to show these men the proof of their love (v24).

## Important Verses Explained

### *2 Corinthians 8:5* — First They Gave Themselves to the Lord

> *“This was not as we had expected, but first they gave their own selves to the Lord, and to us through the will of God.”*
>
> — *2 Corinthians 8:5* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul has just described the astonishing generosity of the Macedonian churches. They were poor and suffering, yet they gave beyond their ability and even begged for the opportunity to help. Now Paul explains what made it possible.

“This was not as we had expected.” Paul had expected something modest from such poor churches, perhaps even hoped to spare them. Instead, they surpassed every expectation.

The reason is that “first they gave their own selves to the Lord.” Before they gave any money, they gave themselves. Their generosity flowed from surrender. Once a person has given their whole life to God, giving possessions becomes a natural expression of that deeper commitment.

They also gave themselves “to us through the will of God.” They committed themselves to Paul and his mission, trusting that this was God’s will for them. Their partnership with Paul was an outworking of their devotion to the Lord.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals the true source of Christian generosity. Giving is not first a financial matter but a spiritual one. Where the heart belongs to God, the wallet follows. Jesus said, “*for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also*” (*Matthew 6:21*). The Macedonians show the other side of that truth: when the heart is given to God, treasure is released for His purposes.

Paul makes the same point in *Romans 12:1*, where he urges believers to present their bodies as a living sacrifice. The offering God wants most is not a portion of what people have but the whole of who they are. Gifts of money, time, and talent are meaningful because they express that deeper offering.

It is also striking that their generosity flowed from joy (v2). Self-giving to the Lord produced not grim duty but overflowing gladness. Those who know they belong to God find freedom in letting go of what they own.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Conversations about giving often begin with percentages, budgets, or needs. Those are important, but this verse suggests starting at a deeper place. The first question is not “How much should I give?” but “Have I given myself to the Lord?” When that question is settled, decisions about money become a matter of worship rather than reluctant obligation.

This verse also guards against giving as a substitute for surrender. It is possible to give money while holding back one’s heart, or to use generosity to feel spiritually secure. The Macedonians reversed that order. Their lives belonged to God first, and their gifts followed.

### *2 Corinthians 8:9* — Though He Was Rich, He Became Poor

> *“For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that you through his poverty might become rich.”*
>
> — *2 Corinthians 8:9* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

In the middle of a practical discussion about a financial collection, Paul suddenly points to the heart of the gospel. He does not command the Corinthians to give. Instead he reminds them of what Christ has given.

“Though he was rich.” Before He came to earth, the Son of God shared the glory, honor, and riches of heaven with the Father (*John 17:5*). “Yet for your sakes he became poor.” He took on human nature, was born in humble circumstances, lived without a home of His own (*Luke 9:58*), and finally gave up His life on the cross.

The purpose of His poverty was “that you through his poverty might become rich.” The riches Paul has in mind are spiritual: forgiveness, reconciliation with God, adoption as God’s children, the gift of the Spirit, and eternal life. Christ’s self-emptying became the source of every blessing believers enjoy.

Paul’s logic is simple. The Corinthians have received unimaginable riches through Christ’s self-giving. How could they hold back from giving to fellow believers in need?

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse is a compact summary of the incarnation and the cross. Paul expresses the same truth more fully in *Philippians 2:5–8*, where Christ, who existed in the form of God, emptied Himself, took the form of a servant, and humbled Himself to death on a cross. The eternal Son chose to step down from glory into human weakness and suffering for the sake of others.

It is important to read “become rich” in its context. Paul is not promising that believers will become financially wealthy by following Christ. Paul himself lived in poverty (*2 Corinthians 6:10*; *11:27*). The riches in view are the riches of grace. Some modern teaching has used this verse to argue that Christ’s death guarantees material prosperity, but that reading overlooks Paul’s own life and the point of the passage, which is to encourage generosity toward the poor, not the pursuit of wealth.

The verse also shows that Christian giving is shaped by Christ’s example. He did not give out of surplus but gave Himself. His people imitate Him, in their measure, when they give sacrificially for the good of others.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

The most powerful motivation for generosity is not guilt or pressure but gratitude. When believers remember how much Christ gave up for them, their own giving becomes a joyful response. A heart that dwells on the grace of the Lord Jesus becomes more open-handed.

This verse also challenges the common assumption that the goal of life is accumulation. Christ moved from riches to poverty for the sake of others. That does not mean every believer is called to poverty, but it does mean that wealth is held for the sake of others, and that downward steps taken in love, such as sharing, simplifying, or serving the poor, follow the pattern of Christ.

### *2 Corinthians 8:12* — Acceptable According to What You Have

> *“For if the readiness is there, it is acceptable according to what you have, not according to what you don’t have.”*
>
> — *2 Corinthians 8:12* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul has just urged the Corinthians to finish the giving they began a year earlier. Now he explains the standard by which God views their gift.

“If the readiness is there,” meaning if there is a willing heart, then the gift “is acceptable according to what you have, not according to what you don’t have.” God does not measure giving by the size of the amount but by the willingness behind it in relation to what a person actually has.

This principle frees people from comparison. A wealthy person and a poor person cannot give the same amount, and God does not expect them to. Each gives in proportion to their means. Paul made the same point in *1 Corinthians 16:2*, asking each one to “*save as he may prosper*” (*1 Corinthians 16:2*).

The principle also guards against unhealthy pressure. Paul does not want anyone to go into debt or neglect their own family’s needs in order to give. As verse 13 says, the goal is not that others should be relieved while the givers are burdened.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Jesus illustrated this principle when He watched a poor widow put two small coins into the temple treasury. He said she had given more than all the others, because they gave out of their abundance, but she gave out of her poverty (*Mark 12:41–44*). God sees the heart and the cost, not just the amount.

This verse also reflects the character of God, who is not a harsh taskmaster demanding what people do not have. He gives first and receives gladly whatever is offered in love. The willingness of the heart matters to Him more than the size of the gift. When God asked for offerings for the tabernacle, He said to receive them “*from everyone whose heart makes him willing*” (*Exodus 25:2*). The theme runs throughout Scripture.

At the same time, Paul does not use this principle as an excuse for half-hearted giving. Willingness must lead to action; that is why he urges the Corinthians to “complete the doing” (v11). The ideal is a willing heart that follows through.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

People with limited income sometimes feel their gifts do not matter. This verse affirms that small gifts given willingly are fully acceptable to God. A modest offering from someone with little is precious in His sight.

For those with greater means, the same principle calls for proportionate generosity. Giving “according to what you have” means that as resources increase, generosity can grow too. And for everyone, the verse encourages finishing what was promised. Good intentions to give, serve, or help are worth following through on.

### *2 Corinthians 8:20–21* — Honorable in the Sight of God and People

> *“We are avoiding this, that any man should blame us concerning this abundance which is administered by us. Having regard for honorable things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men.”*
>
> — *2 Corinthians 8:20–21* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul explains why he arranged for several trusted men, including one chosen by the churches themselves, to accompany the collection. He wanted to avoid any suspicion that he might misuse the money.

“We are avoiding this, that any man should blame us concerning this abundance which is administered by us.” The collection was a large sum. Paul’s opponents had already questioned his motives, perhaps suggesting he was using the collection for his own benefit (*2 Corinthians 12:16–18*). By involving others, Paul made the process transparent.

Verse 21 states the principle: “Having regard for honorable things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men.” It is not enough to be honest before God privately. Those who handle money for others must also act in ways that are visibly honest and accountable.

This verse echoes *Proverbs 3:4*, which speaks of finding favor and good understanding in the sight of God and man.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Paul’s approach shows that integrity is not only about avoiding wrongdoing but also about avoiding the appearance of wrongdoing where possible. The reputation of the gospel was at stake. If Christian leaders were seen as greedy or careless with money, people would be turned away from Christ.

Paul’s practice also shows humility. He did not insist that people simply trust him because he was an apostle. He welcomed accountability. Leaders who resist oversight, especially in financial matters, place themselves and their communities at risk. Leaders who invite oversight protect both themselves and the people they serve.

Throughout Scripture, God cares deeply about honest dealing. *Leviticus 19:35–36* calls for just weights and measures. Jesus warned against devouring widows’ houses (*Mark 12:40*). Paul’s careful handling of the collection reflects God’s own justice and faithfulness.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Churches, ministries, and charities today can follow Paul’s model by having more than one person handle funds, keeping clear records, being transparent about how money is used, and welcoming outside review. These practices are not signs of distrust but expressions of care for the community and for the reputation of Christ.

The same principle applies to individuals. Believers who manage money for others, whether as treasurers, executors, business partners, or employees, should act in ways that are honorable “in the sight of men” as well as before God. Clear records, honest communication, and openness to accountability help build trust and honor God.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

Second Corinthians 8 presents giving not as a burden but as a grace, something God works in His people. The Macedonian believers had every reason to hold back. They were poor and persecuted. Yet they gave joyfully and beyond their means because they had first given themselves to the Lord. Their example shows that generosity flows from surrender and joy, not from surplus.

The heart of the chapter is Christ Himself. He was rich and became poor so that others could become rich in God’s grace. Every act of Christian giving is a small reflection of His great self-giving. When believers remember the grace of the Lord Jesus, giving becomes an act of gratitude rather than pressure.

Paul also gives practical wisdom. Giving should be willing, not coerced. It should be proportionate to what a person has, so no one need feel ashamed of a small gift or burdened beyond their means. Its goal is mutual care within the family of God, so that those who have more help those who have less, knowing the situation may someday be reversed. And good intentions should be carried through to completion.

Finally, the chapter calls for integrity in handling money. Paul took care to be transparent and accountable, protecting the reputation of the gospel. Churches and individuals can follow his example by handling resources honestly and openly. In all these ways, the way believers use money becomes a witness to the generous grace of God.

## Chapter Prayer

Generous God, thank You for the grace of my Lord Jesus Christ, who though He was rich became poor for my sake, so that through His poverty I might become rich in Your love. Before I offer You anything else, I give myself to You again. Free my heart from clinging to what I have, and fill me with the joy that overflows in generosity. Help me to give willingly and according to what You have given me, without comparison and without pressure. Open my eyes to the needs of brothers and sisters near and far, and let my abundance meet their lack. Help me to follow through on the good I intend to do. Make me honest and transparent in everything I handle, so that my life honors You in the sight of others. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

2 Corinthians · Chapter 9 of 13

# 2 Corinthians — Chapter 9

Chapter Theme: God Loves a Cheerful Giver

[Read 2 Corinthians 9 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/2CO09.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul continues his encouragement about the collection for Jerusalem, asking the Corinthians to have their promised gift ready so it will be a willing offering and not something extracted under pressure. Using the image of sowing and reaping, he teaches that generous giving leads to a generous harvest, that each person should give as they have decided in their heart, and that God loves a cheerful giver. God is able to supply everything needed for every good work, and generosity overflows in thanksgiving to God, binding believers together. Paul closes with praise for God’s indescribable gift.

## Chapter Background and Story

Chapter 9 continues the subject of chapter 8: the collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem. Some scholars think chapter 9 was originally a separate note, perhaps sent to the wider churches of Achaia, because Paul introduces the subject again as if afresh. Others see it as a natural continuation, in which Paul moves from the practical arrangements of chapter 8 to the deeper spiritual principles behind giving. Either way, the chapter fits the situation well.

Paul is in Macedonia, and he has been boasting to the Macedonians about the Corinthians’ eagerness. Their early zeal had even inspired the Macedonians to give (v2). Now Paul is concerned that when he arrives in Corinth, possibly with Macedonian companions, the Corinthians’ gift might not be ready, which would embarrass both him and them. So he sends Titus and the brothers ahead to help them prepare.

But Paul does not want them to give simply to avoid embarrassment. He wants their gift to be cheerful, willing, and generous. So he moves beyond logistics to explain how God views giving and what God does through it. The chapter ends not with a request for money but with an outburst of thanksgiving to God.

### Getting Ready (*9:1–5*)

“*It is indeed unnecessary for me to write to you concerning the service to the saints*” (*v. 1*). Paul tactfully says he hardly needs to write, since he knows their readiness. “*for I know your readiness, of which I boast on your behalf to those of Macedonia, that Achaia has been prepared for the past year. Your zeal has stirred up very many of them*” (*v. 2*). Achaia was the Roman province that included Corinth. The Corinthians’ early enthusiasm had inspired others.

Paul explains that he is sending the brothers ahead “*so that our boasting on your behalf may not be in vain in this respect, that, just as I said, you may be prepared*” (*v. 3*). He imagines the embarrassment if Macedonians came with him and found nothing ready (v4).

“*I thought it necessary therefore to entreat the brothers that they would go before to you and arrange ahead of time the generous gift that you promised before, that the same might be ready as a matter of generosity, and not of greediness*” (*v. 5*). The word translated “generous gift” is literally “blessing.” Paul wants their gift prepared in advance so that it will be a true blessing, freely given, rather than something squeezed out at the last moment. “Not of greediness” may mean that it should not look like Paul is greedily extracting it, or that the Corinthians should not give stingily, holding back.

### Sowing and Reaping (*9:6–11*)

Paul then explains the principles behind generous giving. The sowing image, the cheerful giver, and God’s ability to supply are studied below.

“*As it is written, “He has scattered abroad. He has given to the poor. His righteousness remains forever.”*” (*v. 9*) Paul quotes *Psalm 112:9*, which describes the righteous person who gives generously to the poor. Such a person’s righteousness endures. Generosity is not wasted; it has lasting value before God.

“*Now may he who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food, supply and multiply your seed for sowing, and increase the fruits of your righteousness*” (*v. 10*). Paul draws on *Isaiah 55:10*, where God gives seed to the sower and bread to the eater. God is the source of every resource. He provides both what is needed for daily life and what can be “sown” in generosity. As believers give, God increases the “fruits of your righteousness,” the good results that flow from righteous living.

“*you being enriched in everything for all generosity, which produces thanksgiving to God through us*” (*v. 11*). God enriches His people not so they can hoard but so they can be generous. And generosity leads to thanksgiving to God.

### Thanksgiving to God (*9:12–15*)

Paul now describes the wider results of the collection. “*For this service of giving that you perform not only makes up for lack among the saints, but abounds also through much giving of thanks to God*” (*v. 12*). The gift meets real physical needs, but it also produces something more: an overflow of thanksgiving.

“*seeing that through the proof given by this service, they glorify God for the obedience of your confession to the Good News of Christ and for the generosity of your contribution to them and to all*” (*v. 13*). The Jewish believers in Jerusalem would see in this gift proof that the Gentile believers had truly received the gospel. Their faith was not just words; it showed in action. This would cause the Jerusalem believers to glorify God.

“*while they themselves also, with supplication on your behalf, yearn for you by reason of the exceeding grace of God in you*” (*v. 14*). The gift would create bonds of affection and prayer between Jewish and Gentile believers who had never met. The collection was building unity in the body of Christ. Paul’s closing words of praise are studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *2 Corinthians 9:6* — Sowing Bountifully

> *“Remember this: he who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly. He who sows bountifully will also reap bountifully.”*
>
> — *2 Corinthians 9:6* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul uses an image every farmer in the ancient world understood. A farmer who scatters only a little seed will harvest only a little grain. A farmer who sows generously can expect a generous harvest. The amount of the harvest is connected to the amount of the sowing.

Paul applies this to giving. Giving is like sowing seed. It may look like loss in the moment, the way scattering seed on the ground looks like throwing it away. But sowing is the way to a harvest. Those who give sparingly will reap sparingly; those who give generously will reap generously.

The word translated “bountifully” is literally “with blessings.” Paul is describing giving that comes from a generous, blessing-filled spirit, not a grudging or minimal one.

What is the harvest? Paul explains in the following verses: God’s grace abounding, sufficiency for every good work, the increase of the “fruits of your righteousness,” and an overflow of thanksgiving to God (vv8–12). The harvest includes spiritual blessing, the good that comes to others, and God’s provision for continued generosity.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The principle of sowing and reaping appears throughout Scripture. *Proverbs 11:24–25* says that one who scatters still increases, and the liberal soul shall be made fat. Jesus said, “*Give, and it will be given to you*” (*Luke 6:38*). Paul uses the same principle in *Galatians 6:7–9* to speak about the whole of life: whatever a person sows, that they will also reap.

It is important to read this verse carefully. Some teaching today presents giving as a financial investment that guarantees a larger financial return, encouraging people to give in order to get rich. That is not Paul’s point. He himself gave everything and remained poor (*2 Corinthians 6:10*; *11:27*). The motive he commends is cheerful love, not profit. And the harvest he describes is mainly spiritual and relational: righteousness, thanksgiving, unity, and God’s provision of “all sufficiency” for doing good. God may well provide materially for generous people, but He does so that they can keep giving, not so they can accumulate.

This verse, then, assures believers that generosity is never wasted. What is given in love is not lost; it is sown into God’s field, and He brings the harvest.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Many people hesitate to give because they fear they will not have enough. This verse invites a different perspective. Generosity is not a loss but a sowing, and God is faithful to bring a harvest, sometimes in ways that are seen quickly and sometimes in ways seen only later.

This applies not only to money but to time, encouragement, hospitality, and service. A person who is generous with kindness tends to find kindness growing around them. A church that sows generously in its community often sees spiritual fruit. The invitation is to sow with an open hand and trust God with the harvest.

### *2 Corinthians 9:7* — God Loves a Cheerful Giver

> *“Let each man give according as he has determined in his heart, not grudgingly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.”*
>
> — *2 Corinthians 9:7* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul now speaks about the attitude behind giving. “Let each man give according as he has determined in his heart.” Giving is a personal decision made thoughtfully before God. Paul does not set an amount or a percentage. Each believer is to consider prayerfully what to give and then follow through.

Giving should be “not grudgingly.” That means not with sorrow or reluctance, as if each coin were being torn away. It should also be “not … under compulsion,” meaning not because of outside pressure, manipulation, or fear of what others will think.

“For God loves a cheerful giver.” The Greek word for “cheerful” is related to our English word “hilarious,” though it means glad and joyful rather than comical. God delights in giving that flows from a joyful heart.

This phrase likely echoes a line found in the Greek version of *Proverbs 22:8–9*, which speaks of God blessing a cheerful and generous person.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

God Himself is the most cheerful giver. He gives sunlight and rain to all (*Matthew 5:45*), gives His Spirit to those who ask (*Luke 11:13*), and gave His only Son for the world (*John 3:16*). When His people give cheerfully, they reflect His character.

This verse also reveals what God cares about most in giving. He does not need anyone’s money. What He values is the heart. A small gift given gladly pleases Him more than a large gift given resentfully. This is why pressure tactics and manipulation have no place in Christian giving. Leaders who shame, threaten, or guilt people into giving violate the spirit of this verse.

The freedom described here is not a license to give nothing. Paul has just encouraged generous sowing. The point is that generosity is meant to be the free and joyful response of a heart that has been touched by grace, not a tax imposed from outside.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse encourages believers to make giving a thoughtful, prayerful decision rather than an impulse or a reluctant afterthought. Deciding in advance, as Paul urged in *1 Corinthians 16:2*, helps giving become intentional and joyful.

It also offers freedom to anyone who has felt pressured or manipulated into giving. God does not want gifts extracted by guilt. Believers may decline appeals that use high-pressure tactics, and they can give with a clear conscience according to what they have decided before God.

Cheerfulness in giving often grows as a person reflects on God’s generosity. When the heart is filled with gratitude, letting go of resources becomes less of a struggle and more of a joy.

### *2 Corinthians 9:8* — All Grace Abounding

> *“And God is able to make all grace abound to you, that you, always having all sufficiency in everything, may abound to every good work.”*
>
> — *2 Corinthians 9:8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul anticipates a natural worry: “If I give generously, will I have enough for myself?” His answer is this verse, which is full of the word “all”: “all grace,” “always,” “all sufficiency,” “everything,” “every good work.”

“God is able.” The emphasis is on God’s power. He is not limited. He is able to make all grace abound to His people. “Grace” here includes God’s favor and every kind of provision, spiritual and material.

The result is that believers will have “all sufficiency in everything.” The word “sufficiency” was used by Greek philosophers to describe self-sufficiency, a person not needing anything from others. Paul gives it a new meaning: God-sufficiency. Believers have enough because God supplies them.

The purpose is that they “may abound to every good work.” God’s provision is not just for personal comfort; it equips His people to do good. He supplies so that they can keep giving and serving.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse expresses a deep trust in God’s provision, the same trust Jesus taught when He said not to be anxious about food or clothing but to seek first God’s kingdom, and all these things would be added (*Matthew 6:31–33*). Paul expresses a similar confidence in *Philippians 4:19*, after the Philippians had generously supported him: God will supply every need according to His riches in glory in Christ Jesus.

“Sufficiency” does not mean luxury. Paul himself knew how to be content in need and in plenty (*Philippians 4:11–12*). God’s promise is to provide what is needed for life and for good works, not necessarily everything a person might want. Contentment and generosity go together: those who are content with God’s provision are free to give.

This verse also shows that God’s grace is the source of all good works. Believers do not produce generosity or service from their own resources. God makes grace abound, and from that abundance, good works overflow.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Fear of scarcity is one of the strongest barriers to generosity. This verse speaks directly to that fear. God is able to provide enough, both for one’s needs and for the good He calls His people to do. That does not mean giving recklessly or ignoring responsibilities to family; Scripture also calls believers to provide for their households (*1 Timothy 5:8*). But it does mean they can give without being ruled by anxiety.

This verse also invites believers to view their resources as tools for “every good work.” Whatever God supplies, whether income, skills, time, or opportunities, can be put to use in serving others. God’s provision is meant to flow through His people, not just to them.

### *2 Corinthians 9:15* — Thanks Be to God for His Unspeakable Gift

> *“Now thanks be to God for his unspeakable gift!”*
>
> — *2 Corinthians 9:15* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After two chapters about giving, Paul ends with a burst of praise. He thinks of the gifts the Corinthians will give, the thanksgiving it will produce in Jerusalem, and the unity it will create between Jewish and Gentile believers. And all of it points him to the greatest gift of all.

“His unspeakable gift” means a gift so great it cannot be fully described in words. Paul does not say exactly what the gift is, but in the context of the letter, most interpreters see it as God’s gift of His Son, Jesus Christ, along with all the grace that comes through Him. Paul had already pointed to this in *2 Corinthians 8:9*: Christ became poor so that believers might become rich.

This verse places all human giving in its proper light. Every gift believers give is a response to the far greater gift God has given. Generosity begins and ends in thanksgiving to God.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The ending of this chapter shows that for Paul, giving is ultimately an act of worship. The collection was not merely a financial transaction or relief effort; it was part of God’s work of uniting His people and drawing praise to His name.

The word “unspeakable” reminds believers that God’s gift in Christ exceeds human understanding. *John 3:16* expresses the same wonder: God so loved the world that He gave His only Son. *Romans 8:32* asks how God, who did not spare His own Son, will not also with Him freely give all things. All other gifts flow from this one.

It is fitting that Paul ends with thanks rather than with an appeal. Generosity is sustained not by repeated pressure but by renewed gratitude. When believers dwell on God’s indescribable gift, their hearts are moved to give.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

It is easy to approach giving as a duty to be calculated rather than a response of worship. This verse invites believers to start and end every decision about giving with thanksgiving. Before considering what to give, they can pause to remember what God has given them in Christ.

Gratitude also changes daily life. People who regularly thank God for His gift tend to become more content, more generous, and less anxious. A habit of thanksgiving, in prayer, at meals, and in conversation, keeps the heart focused on God’s goodness and makes generosity a natural overflow.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

Second Corinthians 9 completes Paul’s teaching on giving with a vision that is both practical and deeply spiritual. Practically, Paul encourages planning ahead. The Corinthians had promised a gift, and he wanted it ready, so that their generosity would be freely given rather than hastily gathered under pressure. Believers today can likewise make thoughtful, prayerful decisions about giving and follow through on what they intend.

Spiritually, Paul shows that giving is like sowing seed. What is given in love is not lost; God brings a harvest of righteousness, thanksgiving, and continued provision. This should not be confused with a promise of financial gain in exchange for donations. The harvest Paul describes is that God supplies “all sufficiency” so that His people can keep doing good, and that their generosity produces praise to God and unity among His people.

The attitude behind giving matters to God. He loves a cheerful giver. Gifts given grudgingly or under pressure miss the heart of what God desires. This frees believers from manipulation and invites them into the joy of giving freely. It also comforts those who fear scarcity: God is able to make all grace abound, providing what they need and enabling them to share.

Finally, the chapter points to the source of all generosity: God’s indescribable gift in Jesus Christ. Every act of giving is an echo of His giving. When believers remember that gift, their hearts overflow with thanksgiving, and thanksgiving overflows in generosity. In this way, giving becomes worship, and worship builds up the whole body of Christ.

## Chapter Prayer

Gracious and generous God, thank You for Your indescribable gift, Your Son Jesus Christ, and for every blessing that flows from Him. Teach me to give the way You give, freely, joyfully, and with love. Help me to decide in my heart what to give and to follow through with gladness, not reluctance or pressure. When I am afraid there will not be enough, remind me that You are able to make all grace abound to me, so that I have what I need and can abound in every good work. Let what I sow in generosity bring a harvest of righteousness and thanksgiving to You. Bind me together in love with Your people near and far. Fill my heart with gratitude so that my whole life becomes an offering of praise. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

2 Corinthians · Chapter 10 of 13

# 2 Corinthians — Chapter 10

Chapter Theme: Spiritual Weapons and Authority for Building Up

[Read 2 Corinthians 10 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/2CO10.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul, appealing by the meekness and gentleness of Christ, answers critics who said he was bold in letters but weak in person. He explains that though he lives in a human body, he does not fight with worldly weapons; his weapons are mighty through God to demolish strongholds and bring every thought captive to Christ. His authority was given by the Lord for building up, not tearing down. Refusing the foolishness of measuring himself against others, he resolves to boast only in the Lord, since true approval comes from the Lord’s commendation.

## Chapter Background and Story

With chapter 10, the tone of 2 Corinthians changes sharply. Chapters 1–9 ended with warmth, reconciliation, and thanksgiving. Chapters 10–13 are forceful, ironic, and at times sharply confrontational. Paul defends his apostleship against a group he will later ironically call “*the very best apostles*” (*2 Corinthians 11:5*), sometimes rendered “super-apostles”, who had come into the Corinthian church and were undermining him.

Scholars have offered several explanations for this shift. Some believe chapters 10–13 were originally a separate letter, perhaps the “severe letter” mentioned in *2 Corinthians 2:4*, later combined with chapters 1–9. Others think they were written after chapters 1–9, when Paul received fresh news that the situation had worsened. Still others think Paul wrote the whole letter at once and deliberately turned in the final section to address the minority who still opposed him, after having addressed the majority who had repented. Each view has thoughtful supporters, and the message of these chapters is clear whichever view one takes.

The critics in Corinth were impressive by worldly standards. They were polished speakers, proud of their Jewish heritage and their spiritual experiences, and they accepted financial support. They mocked Paul as weak in person, unimpressive in speech, and inconsistent. Paul’s response in these chapters is a powerful lesson in what true spiritual authority looks like.

### The Gentleness of Christ (*10:1–2*)

Paul begins with an appeal grounded in the character of Christ, studied below. He then adds a warning: “*Yes, I beg you that I may not, when present, show courage with the confidence with which I intend to be bold against some, who consider us to be walking according to the flesh*” (*v. 2*). “Walking according to the flesh” means living by merely human motives and methods. Paul’s critics accused him of being driven by worldly concerns. Paul hopes the church will deal with the problem so that he will not need to confront it forcefully when he arrives.

### Weapons Not of the Flesh (*10:3–6*)

“*For though we walk in the flesh, we don’t wage war according to the flesh*” (*v. 3*). Paul admits he lives in a human body with all its weakness. But his ministry is not fought with human weapons such as manipulation, eloquence designed to impress, political maneuvering, or force. The nature of his weapons is studied below.

“*and being in readiness to avenge all disobedience when your obedience is made full*” (*v. 6*). Once the church as a whole has returned to faithful obedience, Paul is ready to deal with those who persist in rebellion. He wants the community to be restored first.

### Authority for Building Up (*10:7–11*)

“*Do you look at things only as they appear in front of your face? If anyone trusts in himself that he is Christ’s, let him consider this again with himself, that even as he is Christ’s, so we also are Christ’s*” (*v. 7*). The Corinthians were judging by appearances. Some claimed a special connection to Christ. Paul reminds them that he belongs to Christ just as much. The purpose of his authority is studied below.

Paul then quotes what his critics were saying: “*For, “His letters”, they say, “are weighty and strong, but his bodily presence is weak, and his speech is despised.”*” (*v. 10*) This is one of the few descriptions of Paul’s appearance and speaking style in the New Testament, and it comes from his opponents. Whether Paul suffered from a physical ailment, lacked rhetorical polish, or simply refused to put on a show, he did not fit the Greek ideal of an impressive orator. In *1 Corinthians 2:1–4*, Paul said he deliberately avoided persuasive words of human wisdom when he first came to Corinth.

“*Let such a person consider this, that what we are in word by letters when we are absent, such are we also in deed when we are present*” (*v. 11*). Paul insists that he is consistent. His gentleness in person was not weakness, and his boldness in writing was not empty.

### Boasting in the Lord (*10:12–18*)

Paul refuses to compare himself with the self-promoting critics, an approach studied below. Instead, he speaks of the sphere God assigned him. “*But we will not boast beyond proper limits, but within the boundaries with which God appointed to us, which reach even to you*” (*v. 13*). God had given Paul the task of preaching to the Gentiles, and Corinth was within that area. Paul had founded the church there (*Acts 18:1–11*). The critics, by contrast, had moved into a church someone else had planted and were claiming credit for its life.

“*not boasting beyond proper limits in other men’s labors, but having hope that as your faith grows, we will be abundantly enlarged by you in our sphere of influence*” (*v. 15*), “*so as to preach the Good News even to the parts beyond you, not to boast in what someone else has already done*” (*v. 16*). Paul longed to take the gospel further west, to places where Christ had not yet been preached (*Romans 15:20–24*). He hoped that as the Corinthian church matured, it would become a base for that mission.

Paul then quotes *Jeremiah 9:24*, as he did in *1 Corinthians 1:31*: “*But “he who boasts, let him boast in the Lord.”*” (*v. 17*) “*For it isn’t he who commends himself who is approved, but whom the Lord commends*” (*v. 18*). Self-promotion means nothing in the end. The only approval that truly matters is the Lord’s.

## Important Verses Explained

### *2 Corinthians 10:1* — The Humility and Gentleness of Christ

> *“Now I Paul, myself, entreat you by the humility and gentleness of Christ, I who in your presence am lowly among you, but being absent am bold toward you.”*
>
> — *2 Corinthians 10:1* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul opens this forceful section of the letter in a surprising way. Before confronting his critics, he appeals to the Corinthians “by the humility and gentleness of Christ.” The word translated “humility” can also mean meekness: strength under control, a refusal to use power harshly. “Gentleness” means a gracious, reasonable, considerate spirit.

Paul’s critics had turned his gentleness into an accusation. They said he was “lowly” in person, timid and unimpressive, and bold only when writing from a distance. Paul accepts the description of himself as lowly in their presence, but he explains its source: he was following the example of Christ.

By beginning with Christ’s gentleness, Paul shows the spirit in which he wants to approach the conflict. He does not want to be harsh. He would far prefer that the Corinthians respond to a gentle appeal.

“Now I Paul, myself” is an emphatic, personal way of speaking. Paul is putting his whole self behind this appeal.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Jesus described Himself in similar terms: “*for I am gentle and humble in heart*” (*Matthew 11:29*). Though He had all authority, He came riding on a donkey (*Matthew 21:5*), washed His disciples’ feet (*John 13:1–15*), and did not break a bruised reed (*Matthew 12:20*). His gentleness was not weakness but the deliberate choice of infinite strength to serve and heal.

The Corinthians, influenced by the values of their culture, admired dominance, eloquence, and self-assertion. They mistook gentleness for weakness. Paul’s appeal turns those values upside down. True spiritual authority looks like Christ, and Christ’s authority was expressed in meekness and gentleness.

This verse is also a model for anyone who must address conflict. Paul begins not with threats but with the character of Christ. Firmness has its place, as the rest of the chapter shows, but it should rise out of gentleness, not replace it.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Many cultures still prize forcefulness and admire people who dominate rooms and conversations. Believers may be tempted to see gentleness as weakness. This verse calls them to see it as Christlikeness. Gentleness in speech, in parenting, in leadership, and in disagreement reflects the heart of Jesus.

When conflict arises, beginning gently is wise. A calm, respectful approach often opens hearts that harshness would close. Gentleness does not mean avoiding hard truths or allowing harm to continue; it means speaking those truths in a way that reflects Christ’s character.

### *2 Corinthians 10:4–5* — Taking Every Thought Captive

> *“for the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh, but mighty before God to the throwing down of strongholds, throwing down imaginations and every high thing that is exalted against the knowledge of God and bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ,”*
>
> — *2 Corinthians 10:4–5* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul uses military language. A “stronghold” was a fortress, a fortified position that defended a city. Ancient armies used siege weapons to break down such walls. Paul says his weapons are not ordinary human weapons, but they are “mighty before God,” powerful because God works through them, and able to throw down fortresses.

What fortresses does Paul mean? He explains in verse 5: “imaginations,” meaning reasonings, arguments, or ways of thinking, and “every high thing that is exalted against the knowledge of God.” These are the proud ideas and attitudes that set themselves up against God’s truth. In Corinth, these included worldly wisdom, pride in status, and the critics’ claims that undermined the gospel Paul preached.

Paul’s goal is “bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ.” Like a soldier taking prisoners, Paul seeks to bring every thought under Christ’s lordship. Ideas that oppose God are not just defeated; they are brought into submission to Christ.

What are Paul’s weapons? He does not list them here, but elsewhere he mentions “*the armor of righteousness*” (*2 Corinthians 6:7*) and, in *Ephesians 6:13–18*, truth, righteousness, the gospel, faith, salvation, the word of God, and prayer. These are spiritual weapons, and they work through God’s power.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This passage reveals that the deepest battles in the Christian life are often battles of the mind. False ideas about God, about oneself, and about the world can become strongholds that keep people from freedom. Pride, lies, and deceptive reasoning can build walls against the knowledge of God.

The gospel is God’s power to tear down those walls. Paul does not rely on clever arguments designed to impress, as his critics did. He relies on the truth of Christ crucified and risen, proclaimed in the power of the Spirit (*1 Corinthians 2:1–5*). Truth, spoken in love and empowered by God, has a power that human cleverness does not.

These verses have often been applied to the inner life of believers as well. Thoughts of fear, bitterness, shame, temptation, or despair can be brought before Christ and measured against His truth. This does not mean simply suppressing thoughts but submitting them to Christ, asking whether they agree with what God has revealed, and replacing lies with truth. Paul gives a similar instruction in *Philippians 4:8*, encouraging believers to think on whatever is true, honorable, just, pure, and lovely.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers face many ideas that are “exalted against the knowledge of God,” in media, education, culture, and sometimes in their own thinking. These verses encourage them to engage those ideas with the truth of Scripture, prayer, and the gospel rather than with mockery, anger, or worldly tactics.

On a personal level, taking thoughts captive can be a daily practice. When a destructive thought arises, such as “God could never forgive me” or “I am worthless,” a believer can bring it before Christ and set it beside what God says. For persistent patterns of anxious or harmful thoughts, help from wise counselors, pastors, or medical professionals can also be part of how God brings healing. Taking thoughts captive is not about willpower alone but about bringing the mind under Christ’s loving rule.

### *2 Corinthians 10:8* — Authority for Building Up, Not Tearing Down

> *“For even if I boast somewhat abundantly concerning our authority, which the Lord gave for building you up and not for casting you down, I will not be ashamed,”*
>
> — *2 Corinthians 10:8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul acknowledges that he might seem to boast a lot about his authority. But he explains the nature of that authority. It was given by “the Lord,” not by himself or by human institutions. And it was given “for building you up and not for casting you down.”

The image is of construction. Paul’s role was to build the church, to strengthen faith, encourage growth, and help believers become what God intended. His authority was not a tool for controlling people, intimidating them, or demolishing them.

Paul says he will “not be ashamed” of this authority, because it is real and given by God. But verse 9 adds that he does not want to seem as though he is trying to terrify them with his letters. His strong words are meant to help, not to frighten.

Paul will repeat this principle near the end of the letter, saying that the Lord gave him authority “*for building up and not for tearing down*” (*2 Corinthians 13:10*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse sets a standard for every form of spiritual leadership. Authority in the church is real, but its purpose is always the good of the people. Jesus taught that the rulers of the nations lord it over people, but it must not be so among His followers; whoever wants to be great must be a servant (*Mark 10:42–45*). Peter likewise urged elders to shepherd God’s flock not by lording it over them but by being examples (*1 Peter 5:2–3*).

When authority is used to control, manipulate, silence, or harm people, it has departed from its God-given purpose. Paul’s critics in Corinth were doing exactly this. Paul later says they enslaved, exploited, and even struck the Corinthians (*2 Corinthians 11:20*). Spiritual authority that tears people down is a distortion of the authority Christ gives.

This principle provides a clear test for discerning healthy leadership. Leaders who build people up, point them to Christ, respect their consciences, and seek their good reflect God’s design. Leaders who demand unquestioning loyalty, use fear, or exploit others do not.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Anyone who holds authority, whether as a parent, pastor, teacher, employer, or ministry leader, can measure their use of it by this verse. The question is not “Am I in charge?” but “Am I building people up?” Authority used well leaves people stronger, freer, and closer to God.

This verse also offers clarity to people who have experienced spiritual abuse, where leaders used God’s name to control or harm them. That kind of treatment contradicts the purpose of authority Christ gives. Such harm should be named, those affected deserve care and protection, and wrongdoing should be reported to appropriate church bodies or authorities. No one is obligated to submit to leadership that is tearing them down.

### *2 Corinthians 10:12* — The Foolishness of Comparison

> *“For we are not bold to number or compare ourselves with some of those who commend themselves. But they themselves, measuring themselves by themselves, and comparing themselves with themselves, are without understanding.”*
>
> — *2 Corinthians 10:12* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul’s critics promoted themselves by measuring themselves against one another and against Paul. They set up their own standards, such as eloquence, impressive appearance, or ecstatic experiences, and then judged themselves superior because they met those standards.

Paul says he will not even join in that game. “We are not bold to number or compare ourselves with some of those who commend themselves.” There is gentle irony here. Paul pretends to be too timid to compete with such impressive people.

Then he exposes the problem: “measuring themselves by themselves, and comparing themselves with themselves, are without understanding.” Their standard was circular. They invented a measuring stick based on themselves and then praised themselves for measuring up. It is like a person who defines success by their own qualities and then declares themselves successful.

Paul refuses this way of thinking. He measures his ministry by the task God gave him (v13) and seeks only the Lord’s approval (v18).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Comparison is a deep and constant temptation in human life. It can lead to pride when a person feels superior or to despair when they feel inferior. Either way, it focuses attention on oneself and on others rather than on God.

Scripture repeatedly warns against this. *Galatians 6:4* encourages each person to test their own work, so that they can take pride in themselves alone and not in comparison with someone else. When Peter asked Jesus about John’s future, Jesus replied, “*What is that to you? You follow me*” (*John 21:22*). Each believer is accountable to the Lord for the calling given to them, not for someone else’s.

The only true measuring stick is God’s. He alone sees the heart and knows the calling He has given. That is why Paul concludes, “it isn’t he who commends himself who is approved, but whom the Lord commends” (v18). Freedom from comparison comes from caring most about the Lord’s approval.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

In an age of social media, comparison has become constant. People compare their homes, bodies, careers, families, and even their churches and ministries with what they see in others. This verse names that habit as foolish, not because others do not matter, but because comparison measures by the wrong standard.

Believers can find freedom by turning their attention to the specific calling God has given them and to His approval. A small, faithful ministry in an obscure place is not less valuable than a large, celebrated one. The question to bring before God is not “How do I measure up to others?” but “Am I faithful in what You have given me?”

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

Second Corinthians 10 offers a portrait of true spiritual strength. Paul’s critics thought him weak because he was gentle, unimpressive in appearance, and plain in speech. Paul answers that his gentleness came from Christ Himself, and that his real power lay elsewhere. Believers today are invited to see gentleness, humility, and meekness not as weaknesses to overcome but as the very character of Jesus.

The chapter also reminds believers that their deepest battles are spiritual and often take place in the mind. Pride, lies, and ideas set against God can become strongholds. These are not defeated by worldly methods such as manipulation, mockery, or force, but by God’s truth, prayer, and the gospel. Each day, believers can bring their thoughts captive to Christ, testing them against His word and replacing lies with truth.

Paul’s teaching on authority is especially important. Authority given by Christ exists for building people up, never for tearing them down. Leaders in homes, churches, and workplaces can test their leadership by this standard. And those who have been harmed by leaders who misused authority can know that such misuse contradicts God’s design, and that seeking safety, help, and accountability is right.

Finally, the chapter frees believers from the trap of comparison. Measuring oneself against others leads only to pride or discouragement. Paul measured himself by God’s calling and sought only the Lord’s commendation. Those who boast only in the Lord can serve faithfully in whatever place God has given them, content to let Him be the judge of their work.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, You are gentle and lowly in heart, and Your strength is shown in humility. Make me more like You. Teach me to approach conflict with Your gentleness, and to speak truth without harshness. Tear down every stronghold in my mind that stands against the knowledge of God: every lie, every proud thought, every fear that denies Your goodness. Help me bring each thought captive to obey You. If You have given me any measure of authority, let me use it only to build others up, never to control or harm. Protect those who have been wounded by the misuse of power, and bring them healing. Free me from comparing myself with others, and let me be content to seek Your approval alone. May all my boasting be in You. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
