2 Corinthians · Chapter 11 of 13

# 2 Corinthians — Chapter 11

Chapter Theme: Godly Jealousy and Boasting in Weakness

[Read 2 Corinthians 11 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/2CO11.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul, jealous for the Corinthians with a godly jealousy, fears that just as the serpent deceived Eve, their minds may be led away from sincere devotion to Christ by teachers preaching another Jesus. He explains why he preached to them free of charge and exposes his rivals as false apostles who disguise themselves as servants of righteousness. Then, playing the part of a fool, he “boasts” in a list of his sufferings, hardships, and daily concern for the churches, showing that true apostleship is marked by weakness and sacrifice, not by impressive displays.

## Chapter Background and Story

In chapter 11, Paul continues his defense against the rival teachers in Corinth. They boasted about their credentials, their Jewish heritage, their eloquence, and their spiritual experiences. Many in the church were impressed. Paul finds himself in an awkward position. He does not want to boast, because boasting in oneself is foolish and contrary to the gospel (*2 Corinthians 10:17–18*). But if he says nothing, the Corinthians may be drawn away by these teachers.

So Paul adopts a deliberate strategy, sometimes called the “Fool’s Speech,” which runs from 11:1 to 12:13. He announces that he will “boast” like a fool, playing his opponents’ game. But he turns the game upside down. Instead of boasting about achievements and status, he boasts about beatings, shipwrecks, dangers, sleeplessness, and weakness. The very things the world would consider signs of failure become, in Paul’s hands, evidence of true service to a crucified Lord.

The chapter is full of irony, and at times it is painfully personal. It also gives the most detailed list of Paul’s sufferings anywhere in the New Testament, many of which are not recorded in the book of Acts.

### A Godly Jealousy (*11:1–4*)

“*I wish that you would bear with me in a little foolishness, but indeed you do bear with me*” (*v. 1*). Paul asks the Corinthians to put up with his “foolishness,” the boasting he is about to do. His reason, a jealous love for their devotion to Christ, is studied below.

“*For if he who comes preaches another Jesus whom we didn’t preach, or if you receive a different spirit which you didn’t receive, or a different “good news” which you didn’t accept, you put up with that well enough*” (*v. 4*). The rival teachers were presenting a distorted version of the faith. We do not know every detail of what they taught, but their “Jesus” seems to have been a figure of power and glory without the cross, and their “spirit” seemed to produce pride and impressive displays rather than humility and love. The Corinthians were tolerating it far too easily.

### Preaching Free of Charge (*11:5–12*)

“*For I reckon that I am not at all behind the very best apostles*” (*v. 5*). “Very best apostles” (sometimes rendered “super-apostles”) is Paul’s ironic name for his rivals. “*But though I am unskilled in speech, yet I am not unskilled in knowledge*” (*v. 6*). Paul admits he lacked the polished speaking skills that Greek audiences admired, but he did not lack knowledge of God’s truth.

One of the charges against Paul was that he refused payment from the Corinthians. In Greek culture, teachers of high status charged fees or accepted patronage. Refusing support might have seemed like an insult, or a sign that Paul’s teaching was of little worth. “*Or did I commit a sin in humbling myself that you might be exalted, because I preached to you God’s Good News free of charge?*” (*v. 7*) Paul’s question is heavy with irony.

“*I robbed other assemblies, taking wages from them that I might serve you*” (*v. 8*). “Robbed” is a deliberate exaggeration. Paul means that other churches, especially in Macedonia, supported him while he served in Corinth (v9; see *Philippians 4:15–16*). He did this so that he would not be a burden to the Corinthians and so that no one could accuse him of preaching for money.

“*Why? Because I don’t love you? God knows*” (*v. 11*). Paul’s refusal of their support was not a lack of love. “*But what I do, that I will continue to do, that I may cut off opportunity from those who desire an opportunity, that in which they boast, they may be recognized just like us*” (*v. 12*). The rivals wanted to claim they were on the same level as Paul. By preaching for free, Paul made it clear that he was not in ministry for gain, and he exposed the difference between himself and them.

### False Apostles (*11:13–15*)

Paul now speaks bluntly about who these rivals really are. This passage is studied below.

### The Fool’s Boast (*11:16–21*)

“*I say again, let no one think me foolish. But if so, yet receive me as foolish, that I also may boast a little*” (*v. 16*). Paul knows that what he is about to do is not the way of the Lord (v17), but the Corinthians have pushed him into it. “*Seeing that many boast after the flesh, I will also boast*” (*v. 18*).

“*For you bear with the foolish gladly, being wise*” (*v. 19*). Paul’s irony is sharp: the Corinthians, who think themselves so wise, gladly put up with fools.

Then comes a startling description of how the rivals treated the church: “*For you bear with a man if he brings you into bondage, if he devours you, if he takes you captive, if he exalts himself, or if he strikes you on the face*” (*v. 20*). These leaders were controlling, exploitative, manipulative, arrogant, and possibly even physically violent. The Corinthians tolerated all of it, perhaps mistaking domination for strength. It is a sobering picture of spiritual abuse, and Paul’s words make clear that such behavior is a mark of false leadership, not of true servants of Christ.

“*To my shame, I speak as though we had been weak*” (*v. 21*). With deep irony, Paul says he must admit he was too “weak” to treat them that way. Then he begins his boast.

### Paul’s Credentials and Sufferings (*11:22–33*)

“*Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they the offspring of Abraham? So am I*” (*v. 22*). The rivals boasted of their Jewish heritage. Paul’s heritage was just as strong (see *Philippians 3:5*). But then he turns to the true marks of a servant of Christ, which are studied below.

Paul ends the chapter with an unusual story. “*In Damascus the governor under King Aretas guarded the Damascenes’ city, desiring to arrest me*” (*v. 32*). “*I was let down in a basket through a window by the wall, and escaped his hands*” (*v. 33*). This event, also described in *Acts 9:23–25*, happened soon after Paul’s conversion. In the Roman world, a soldier who was first to climb over an enemy’s wall received a special crown for bravery. Paul’s “achievement” was the reverse: he was let down the wall in a basket, escaping in the dark. It is a fitting climax to his boasting in weakness, and it prepares for chapter 12, where God will teach him that power is made perfect in weakness.

## Important Verses Explained

### *2 Corinthians 11:2–3* — Sincere and Pure Devotion to Christ

> *“For I am jealous over you with a godly jealousy. For I promised you in marriage to one husband, that I might present you as a pure virgin to Christ. But I am afraid that somehow, as the serpent deceived Eve in his craftiness, so your minds might be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ.”*
>
> — *2 Corinthians 11:2–3* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul explains why he is willing to act “foolishly” by boasting. It is because of love. “I am jealous over you with a godly jealousy.” This is not the petty jealousy of envy but the protective jealousy of someone who loves deeply and will not let what is precious be stolen away.

Paul uses an image from ancient marriage customs. Marriages were often arranged in two stages: first a betrothal, which was a binding commitment, and later the wedding itself, when the bride was presented to her husband. Paul sees himself like a father who has promised his daughter in marriage. When he preached the gospel in Corinth, he betrothed the church to Christ. Now he longs to present the church to Christ as a pure bride at His coming.

But he fears that something is threatening this. Verse 3 explains: “as the serpent deceived Eve in his craftiness, so your minds might be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ.” In *Genesis 3*, the serpent did not attack Eve with force; he deceived her with clever words that twisted God’s command and cast doubt on God’s goodness. Paul fears the rival teachers are doing the same thing, leading the Corinthians away from their wholehearted devotion to Christ.

“The simplicity that is in Christ” refers to single-minded, sincere devotion. The danger was not that the Corinthians would openly reject Christ, but that their love for Him would become divided and diluted.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The image of God’s people as a bride runs throughout Scripture. In the Old Testament, God speaks of Israel as His bride and grieves over her unfaithfulness (*Hosea 2:19–20*; *Jeremiah 2:2*). In the New Testament, the church is the bride of Christ (*Ephesians 5:25–27*), and history ends with the marriage supper of the Lamb (*Revelation 19:7–9*). Paul’s godly jealousy reflects God’s own jealousy, His passionate desire for His people’s undivided love (*Exodus 34:14*).

The reference to Eve warns that the greatest spiritual danger is often deception rather than open attack. False teaching seldom announces itself as false. It usually sounds reasonable, attractive, even spiritual. It may keep the name of Jesus while changing who He is. This is why believers need to stay rooted in the truth of the gospel as it was first delivered.

The word “simplicity” does not mean that the Christian faith is simplistic. It means sincerity and singleness of heart. Devotion to Christ is meant to be wholehearted, not divided between Christ and other loyalties.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers today encounter many messages about Jesus that may sound appealing but differ from the Jesus of Scripture: a Jesus who promises wealth but not the cross, a Jesus who affirms everything but transforms nothing, or a Jesus reshaped to fit a political or cultural agenda. Paul’s warning invites careful discernment, measuring every teaching against the apostolic gospel.

This verse also speaks to the heart. Devotion to Christ can be slowly diluted by many good and not-so-good things: busyness, entertainment, ambition, or worry. Returning regularly to Scripture, prayer, and worship helps keep love for Christ sincere and pure, like a bride whose heart belongs to her beloved.

### *2 Corinthians 11:13–15* — Disguised as Angels of Light

> *“For such men are false apostles, deceitful workers, masquerading as Christ’s apostles. And no wonder, for even Satan masquerades as an angel of light. It is no great thing therefore if his servants also masquerade as servants of righteousness, whose end will be according to their works.”*
>
> — *2 Corinthians 11:13–15* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul now speaks plainly. The rival teachers are “false apostles, deceitful workers, masquerading as Christ’s apostles.” They claim to be sent by Christ, but they are not. Their work is deceptive, and their appearance of authority is a disguise.

Paul explains that this should not surprise anyone: “even Satan masquerades as an angel of light.” Satan does not usually appear in an obviously evil form. He often presents himself as something good, beautiful, or enlightening. Since their master disguises himself this way, it is no surprise that his servants disguise themselves as “servants of righteousness.”

The phrase “whose end will be according to their works” is a solemn warning. Their disguise may fool people now, but God sees through it, and they will be judged according to what they have actually done.

Paul’s harsh language here is reserved for those who were deliberately leading the church away from the true gospel and exploiting it (v20). He is not describing believers who simply disagree with him on secondary matters.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses teach an important principle of discernment: evil often looks good. Jesus warned about false prophets who come in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves, and He said they would be recognized by their fruits (*Matthew 7:15–20*). Outward appearance, charisma, success, and even religious language are not reliable signs of genuine ministry.

How can believers discern? Paul’s letter offers several tests. Does the teaching proclaim the same Jesus, the crucified and risen Lord (*11:4*)? Does the leader serve or exploit (*11:20*)? Does the ministry produce humility, love, and holiness, or pride and division? Do the leader’s life and motives reflect the character of Christ? True servants of Christ are marked by the cross; false ones are marked by self-exaltation.

It is also important to apply this passage carefully. It does not license believers to label everyone they disagree with as a servant of Satan. Paul’s judgment here concerns people who were distorting the gospel itself and harming the church. Discernment should be humble, careful, and rooted in Scripture.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers should not be naïve about leaders, teachers, or movements simply because they appear impressive, successful, or spiritual. It is wise to look beneath the surface: at the message they preach, the way they treat people, the way they handle money and power, and the fruit their ministry produces over time.

At the same time, believers should not live in suspicion of every leader. Many faithful servants of Christ are humble and trustworthy. The goal is wise discernment, not cynicism. When a teacher’s message or behavior raises concerns, comparing it with Scripture and seeking counsel from mature believers is a wise step.

### *2 Corinthians 11:23–27* — The Marks of a True Servant

> *“Are they servants of Christ? (I speak as one beside himself.) I am more so: in labors more abundantly, in prisons more abundantly, in stripes above measure, and in deaths often. Five times I received forty stripes minus one from the Jews. Three times I was beaten with rods. Once I was stoned. Three times I suffered shipwreck. I have been a night and a day in the deep. I have been in travels often, perils of rivers, perils of robbers, perils from my countrymen, perils from the Gentiles, perils in the city, perils in the wilderness, perils in the sea, perils among false brothers; in labor and travail, in watchings often, in hunger and thirst, in fastings often, and in cold and nakedness.”*
>
> — *2 Corinthians 11:23–27* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul’s rivals called themselves servants of Christ. Paul responds, “I am more so,” and then lists not his successes but his sufferings. He says he is speaking “as one beside himself,” because boasting feels like madness to him.

The list is staggering. “Forty stripes minus one” was the punishment of synagogue discipline under *Deuteronomy 25:3*, which limited a beating to forty lashes; thirty-nine were given to avoid accidentally exceeding the limit. Paul received this punishment five times, a sign that he kept returning to synagogues to preach to his own people despite their opposition. “Beaten with rods” was a Roman punishment; *Acts 16:22–23* records one such beating at Philippi. “Once I was stoned” refers to Lystra, where he was left for dead (*Acts 14:19*). He had been shipwrecked three times, all before the shipwreck recorded in *Acts 27*, and had once spent a night and a day adrift at sea.

Verse 26 describes constant danger while traveling: rivers that flooded, robbers on lonely roads, hostility from both Jews and Gentiles, danger in cities and wilderness and at sea, and betrayal by false believers. Verse 27 adds hard work, sleepless nights, hunger, thirst, cold, and lack of clothing.

Paul is not complaining. He is showing what genuine service to Christ has cost him. His credentials are written on his body.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Paul’s sufferings reflect the pattern of Christ, who was despised, beaten, and crucified. Jesus told His disciples that a servant is not greater than his master; if they persecuted Him, they would persecute His followers too (*John 15:20*). Paul’s life showed this truth vividly. At his conversion, the Lord said He would show Paul how much he must suffer for His name (*Acts 9:16*).

This list overturns the values of Paul’s critics. They measured spiritual authority by power, eloquence, and success. Paul measures it by faithfulness in suffering. This is not because suffering is good in itself, but because a willingness to suffer for Christ and for others shows a love that is real. Paul endured all of this so that people could hear the gospel.

The list also reveals how much of Paul’s life is hidden from the record in Acts. Many of these sufferings are mentioned nowhere else. Paul did not publicize his hardships until he was forced to. True servants of Christ often endure much that is unseen by others but fully known to God.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

In many places, following Christ still brings serious persecution. Believers in such places stand in the line of Paul, and Christians elsewhere are called to pray for them, support them, and speak up for them (*Hebrews 13:3*).

For believers who face lesser hardships, such as misunderstanding, sacrifice, or difficulty in serving, Paul’s example offers perspective and encouragement. Hardship endured for Christ is not a sign of failure or of God’s absence. It may be a sign of faithful service.

This passage also reshapes how believers evaluate ministry and leadership. The most faithful servants of Christ are not necessarily the most visible or celebrated. Often they are those who have quietly given themselves, at great cost, for the sake of others.

### *2 Corinthians 11:28–30* — Anxiety for the Churches and Boasting in Weakness

> *“Besides those things that are outside, there is that which presses on me daily: anxiety for all the assemblies. Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is caused to stumble, and I don’t burn with indignation? If I must boast, I will boast of the things that concern my weakness.”*
>
> — *2 Corinthians 11:28–30* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After listing the outward dangers and hardships of his ministry, Paul names a burden that may have weighed on him even more: “that which presses on me daily: anxiety for all the assemblies.” Every day, Paul carried the churches on his heart. He worried about their faith, their unity, their struggles, and the threats they faced.

Verse 29 shows how personally he felt this. “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” When a believer struggled, Paul felt it with them. “Who is caused to stumble, and I don’t burn with indignation?” When someone was led into sin or harmed in their faith, Paul burned with grief and anger on their behalf.

Then Paul states the principle that will guide the rest of his “boasting”: “If I must boast, I will boast of the things that concern my weakness.” Paul will not boast of his strength, his achievements, or his status. He will boast only in the things that show his weakness, because in those things the power of God is most clearly seen.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Paul’s “anxiety for all the assemblies” shows the heart of a true shepherd. His care was not professional or distant. He loved the churches as a parent loves children, and he felt their pain as his own. This reflects the heart of Christ, the Good Shepherd, who knows His sheep and lays down His life for them (*John 10:11–14*).

Elsewhere Paul tells believers not to be anxious about anything but to bring everything to God in prayer (*Philippians 4:6*). These two teachings fit together. Paul felt the weight of concern for the churches, and he brought that weight to God constantly in prayer, as his letters show. Godly concern does not mean carrying burdens alone; it means carrying them to God.

Boasting in weakness is one of the central themes of 2 Corinthians. It anticipates the Lord’s words to Paul in the next chapter: “*my power is made perfect in weakness*” (*2 Corinthians 12:9*). Weakness is not something to hide. It is the place where God’s strength is displayed.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Pastors, parents, teachers, and caregivers often carry daily concern for those in their care. Paul’s honesty affirms that such burdens are real and heavy. They are not a sign of weak faith but of love. At the same time, those burdens are meant to be brought to God in prayer, and shared with others, so that no one is crushed under them alone.

Paul’s example also encourages empathy. Believers can choose to feel with those who are weak and to be moved when others are harmed. Indifference to the struggles of others is not Christlike; compassion is.

Finally, this passage invites believers to stop hiding their weaknesses behind a polished image. Admitting limitations, struggles, and needs can open the door for God’s power and for genuine fellowship with others.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

Second Corinthians 11 is a passionate defense of true devotion to Christ against counterfeit versions of the faith. Paul’s godly jealousy shows how deeply he loved the church and how seriously he took the danger of deception. Like Eve in the garden, believers can be led away not by open attack but by clever words that subtly change the message. The call is to keep a sincere and pure devotion to Christ, staying rooted in the gospel as Scripture presents it.

The chapter also teaches discernment about leaders. False apostles can look impressive and sound spiritual. They may even present themselves as angels of light. But their fruit gives them away: they exploit, control, exalt themselves, and harm the people they claim to serve. Paul’s description of how the Corinthians tolerated abusive leaders is a warning for churches today. Spiritual abuse should never be tolerated or excused. Those who have experienced it deserve to be heard, protected, and cared for, and those who commit it must be held accountable.

Paul’s list of sufferings redefines what success in ministry looks like. The true marks of a servant of Christ are not wealth, fame, or eloquence, but faithful love that is willing to sacrifice for others. Believers can take courage in their own hardships, remembering that suffering for Christ is not a sign of failure.

Finally, Paul shows a better way to boast. Instead of hiding his weakness, he highlights it, because weakness is where God’s power is revealed. Believers can be honest about their limitations, carry the burdens of others with compassion, and bring every concern to God, trusting that His strength will be shown in their weakness.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, You are my Bridegroom and my King. Keep my heart sincere and pure in devotion to You. Guard me from deception, from every message that offers another Jesus or another gospel, and from anything that would divide my love for You. Give me discernment to see beneath outward appearances and wisdom to recognize those who truly serve You. Protect Your church from leaders who exploit and harm, and bring healing and justice to those who have been wounded. Thank You for the faithful servants who have suffered so that the gospel could reach the world; strengthen those who suffer for Your name today. Give me a heart that feels the weakness of others and burns with compassion when they are harmed. Teach me to boast not in my strength but in my weakness, so that Your power may be seen. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

2 Corinthians · Chapter 12 of 13

# 2 Corinthians — Chapter 12

Chapter Theme: My Grace Is Sufficient for You

[Read 2 Corinthians 12 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/2CO12.htm)

Main Teaching

Continuing his reluctant boasting, Paul describes a man in Christ caught up to the third heaven, then turns at once to the thorn in the flesh God allowed to keep him from pride. When he pleaded three times for its removal, the Lord answered that His grace is sufficient and His power is made perfect in weakness, so Paul learned to delight in weakness, for when he is weak, then he is strong. He reminds the Corinthians of the signs of an apostle done among them, assures them he seeks not their possessions but them, and expresses his fear of finding unrepented sin when he comes.

## Chapter Background and Story

Chapter 12 continues the “Fool’s Speech” that Paul began in chapter 11. His rivals in Corinth boasted about extraordinary spiritual experiences: visions, revelations, and displays of power. They may have suggested that Paul’s lack of such boasting showed he was spiritually inferior.

Paul responds by describing an experience more extraordinary than anything they could claim. Yet he tells it in a strange, indirect way, speaking of “a man in Christ” rather than saying “I.” And he quickly moves from the vision to something far less glamorous: a painful, humbling affliction that God refused to remove. This is the heart of the chapter, and indeed one of the central messages of the whole letter. The power of Christ is most clearly seen not in human strength but in human weakness.

The chapter then turns back to Paul’s relationship with the Corinthians. He is preparing for a third visit and is worried about what he will find. His love for them shines through, along with his fear that sin and division may still be present.

### Visions and Revelations (*12:1–6*)

“*It is doubtless not profitable for me to boast, but I will come to visions and revelations of the Lord*” (*v. 1*). Paul has no interest in boasting, but the situation forces him to speak.

“*I know a man in Christ who was caught up into the third heaven fourteen years ago—whether in the body, I don’t know, or whether out of the body, I don’t know; God knows*” (*v. 2*). Almost all interpreters agree that Paul is speaking about himself (see v7), but he refers to himself in the third person to distance himself from any sense of personal glory. Fourteen years before writing would place this experience around AD 42, during the years Paul spent in Syria and Cilicia before his missionary journeys, a period about which Acts says little.

“The third heaven” was a way of describing the very presence of God, beyond the sky (the first heaven) and the realm of the stars (the second). Paul also calls it “Paradise” (v4), the word Jesus used when He promised the dying thief, “*today you will be with me in Paradise*” (*Luke 23:43*). Paul honestly does not know whether he was taken there bodily or only in spirit. He leaves that to God.

“*how he was caught up into Paradise and heard unspeakable words, which it is not lawful for a man to utter*” (*v. 4*). What Paul heard was too sacred to repeat. Unlike the rival teachers, who apparently made much of their experiences, Paul kept this silent for fourteen years.

“*On behalf of such a one I will boast, but on my own behalf I will not boast, except in my weaknesses*” (*v. 5*). Paul is willing to speak about the experience as something God did, but he will not use it to build his own reputation. “*But I refrain, so that no man may think more of me than that which he sees in me or hears from me*” (*v. 6*). Paul wants to be evaluated by his life and teaching, not by private experiences that others cannot test.

### The Thorn in the Flesh (*12:7–10*)

Paul now turns from the heights of heaven to the reality of his weakness. The thorn, his prayers, the Lord’s answer, and Paul’s response are studied below.

### The Signs of an Apostle (*12:11–13*)

“*I have become foolish in boasting. You compelled me, for I ought to have been commended by you, for I am in no way inferior to the very best apostles, though I am nothing*” (*v. 11*). Paul ends his boasting with a gentle rebuke. The Corinthians should have defended him. Instead, they forced him to defend himself. Yet he adds “though I am nothing,” a reminder that all he is comes from God’s grace (*1 Corinthians 15:10*).

“*Truly the signs of an apostle were worked among you in all perseverance, in signs and wonders and mighty works*” (*v. 12*). When Paul founded the church in Corinth, God confirmed his message with miraculous works. Notice that Paul mentions “perseverance” first. Endurance through hardship was itself a sign of genuine apostleship. Paul does not dwell on the miracles; he simply reminds the Corinthians that they saw them.

“*For what is there in which you were made inferior to the rest of the assemblies, unless it is that I myself was not a burden to you? Forgive me this wrong!*” (*v. 13*) Once again, irony. The only “wrong” Paul did was refusing to take their money.

### Not Yours, but You (*12:14–18*)

Paul announces his third visit and explains his continued refusal to accept support from them. His heart for them is studied below.

Some apparently accused Paul of trickery, suggesting that while he refused money personally, he used the collection to take advantage of them. “*Even so, I myself didn’t burden you. But you might say that being crafty, I caught you with deception*” (*v. 16*). Paul answers by pointing to Titus and the brother who had gone with him: “*Did Titus take any advantage of you? Didn’t we walk in the same spirit? Didn’t we walk in the same steps?*” (*v. 18*) Their conduct was above reproach, and the Corinthians knew it.

### Fears for the Coming Visit (*12:19–21*)

“*Again, do you think that we are excusing ourselves to you? In the sight of God we speak in Christ. But all things, beloved, are for your edifying*” (*v. 19*). Paul’s defense is not about protecting his own reputation. It is for their good, for building them up.

Then he voices his fears. “*For I am afraid that perhaps when I come, I might find you not the way I want to, and that I might be found by you as you don’t desire, that perhaps there would be strife, jealousy, outbursts of anger, factions, slander, whisperings, proud thoughts, or riots*” (*v. 20*). These were the very sins that had troubled the church from the beginning (*1 Corinthians 1:10–11*; *3:3*). “*that again when I come my God would humble me before you, and I would mourn for many of those who have sinned before now, and not repented of the uncleanness, sexual immorality, and lustfulness which they committed*” (*v. 21*). Paul does not anticipate their sin with anger alone but with mourning. A shepherd grieves over sheep who have wandered. He would feel humbled by their failure, because he loved them as his own.

## Important Verses Explained

### *2 Corinthians 12:7–8* — A Thorn in the Flesh

> *“By reason of the exceeding greatness of the revelations, that I should not be exalted excessively, a thorn in the flesh was given to me: a messenger of Satan to torment me, that I should not be exalted excessively. Concerning this thing, I begged the Lord three times that it might depart from me.”*
>
> — *2 Corinthians 12:7–8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After describing his extraordinary vision, Paul explains that it came with a cost. “By reason of the exceeding greatness of the revelations, that I should not be exalted excessively, a thorn in the flesh was given to me.” The danger after such an experience was pride. To keep Paul humble, a “thorn in the flesh” was given to him.

The word translated “thorn” can refer to a sharp stake or splinter. It suggests something painful, persistent, and difficult to ignore. “In the flesh” probably means it affected his body or his earthly life.

Paul also calls it “a messenger of Satan to torment me.” This is striking. The thorn was “given” to Paul, and the purpose stated is God’s purpose of keeping him humble, yet the agent of the torment was Satan. As in the story of Job, Satan intended harm, but God used even this for good.

Paul responded by praying. “I begged the Lord three times that it might depart from me.” He did not passively accept it. He earnestly asked for relief, repeatedly.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

What was Paul’s thorn? Scripture does not say, and many suggestions have been made. Some think it was a physical illness, perhaps an eye disease (see *Galatians 4:13–15*, where Paul mentions a bodily illness and says the Galatians would have given him their eyes), recurring malaria, or another chronic condition. Others think it was persistent opposition from enemies of the gospel, since the Old Testament sometimes describes enemies as thorns in the side (*Numbers 33:55*). Still others have suggested a spiritual struggle or temptation. Because Paul does not name it, believers with many different kinds of suffering have been able to find themselves in his story.

Paul’s three prayers echo Jesus in Gethsemane, who prayed three times that the cup might pass from Him, while submitting to the Father’s will (*Mark 14:32–41*). Like Jesus, Paul brought his honest request to God, and like Jesus, he received an answer different from what he asked.

This passage holds together two truths. God is sovereign, able to use even evil and suffering for good purposes (*Genesis 50:20*; *Romans 8:28*). And suffering is real and painful, and believers are free to plead for relief. Paul did not pretend the thorn was pleasant, and he did not stop praying because he believed God was in control.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Many believers carry their own “thorn”: a chronic illness, a disability, a painful relationship, ongoing opposition, or a struggle that will not go away. Paul’s example gives permission to pray honestly and persistently for relief. Asking God to remove suffering is not a lack of faith; it is an expression of trust in His power and care.

This passage also guards against simplistic explanations of suffering. Paul’s thorn was not a punishment for sin, nor was it a sign of weak faith. It came to one of the most faithful servants of God. Those who suffer should not be told their pain is their fault or that more faith would surely remove it. God may heal, and believers should pray for healing, but He may also, as with Paul, give grace to endure.

### *2 Corinthians 12:9* — My Grace Is Sufficient

> *“He has said to me, ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.’ Most gladly therefore I will rather glory in my weaknesses, that the power of Christ may rest on me.”*
>
> — *2 Corinthians 12:9* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After Paul’s three prayers, the Lord answered. But the answer was not, “Yes, I will remove it.” It was, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.”

“My grace is sufficient for you.” God’s grace, His favor, presence, and strength, would be enough for Paul to live with the thorn. The tense of the verb “has said” in Greek suggests that this word continued to stand for Paul; it was a lasting answer he could keep returning to.

“For my power is made perfect in weakness.” The word “perfect” means brought to completion or fully displayed. God’s power is most clearly shown when human strength runs out. When Paul could not rely on his own strength, the power of Christ was seen more plainly.

Paul’s response is remarkable: “Most gladly therefore I will rather glory in my weaknesses, that the power of Christ may rest on me.” Instead of resenting his weakness, Paul embraced it, because it made room for Christ’s power. The phrase “rest on me” uses a word related to “tent” or “dwelling,” suggesting that Christ’s power would dwell over Paul like God’s presence over the tabernacle.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse is the heart of 2 Corinthians. The whole letter has wrestled with the question of what true strength looks like. The rival teachers displayed power through eloquence, impressive appearance, and visions. Paul’s life was marked by suffering, weakness, and humility. Here the Lord Himself declares which kind of life displays His power: the life that depends on His grace.

This pattern is seen throughout Scripture. God reduced Gideon’s army to three hundred men so that Israel could not boast in its own strength (*Judges 7:2*). He chose David, the youngest son, over his impressive brothers (*1 Samuel 16:7*). He chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong (*1 Corinthians 1:27*). Supremely, He accomplished salvation through the weakness of the cross, which Paul calls the power of God (*1 Corinthians 1:18*).

“Sufficient” is a beautiful word. It does not promise an abundance of comfort or the removal of every hardship. It promises enough: enough strength for today, enough grace for this trial. Like the manna in the wilderness, God’s grace is given as it is needed, and it is always enough.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

When prayers for relief seem to go unanswered, this verse offers a different kind of answer. God may not remove every hardship, but He promises His grace will be enough to carry His people through it. That grace often comes day by day, as strength for the next step.

Many people feel ashamed of their weakness, whether physical, emotional, or spiritual. This verse transforms weakness from something to hide into a place where Christ’s power can rest. Believers who live with limitations can serve God faithfully, and often their dependence on Him becomes a powerful testimony to others.

This verse also challenges cultures, and churches, that celebrate only strength, success, and polish. Those who are weak, struggling, or limited are not second-class members of God’s family. Often they show most clearly what God’s grace can do.

### *2 Corinthians 12:10* — When I Am Weak, Then I Am Strong

> *“Therefore I take pleasure in weaknesses, in injuries, in necessities, in persecutions, and in distresses, for Christ’s sake. For when I am weak, then am I strong.”*
>
> — *2 Corinthians 12:10* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul draws a conclusion from the Lord’s answer. Because God’s power is made perfect in weakness, Paul says, “I take pleasure in weaknesses, in injuries, in necessities, in persecutions, and in distresses, for Christ’s sake.”

This list summarizes the kinds of hardship Paul described in chapter 11. “Weaknesses” are human limitations. “Injuries” can also mean insults or mistreatment. “Necessities” are hardships and times of need. “Persecutions” are attacks because of faith. “Distresses” are situations of crushing pressure.

Paul does not take pleasure in these things because he enjoys pain. He takes pleasure in them “for Christ’s sake,” because they are endured in serving Christ and because they become occasions for Christ’s power to be revealed.

Then comes the famous paradox: “For when I am weak, then am I strong.” When Paul’s own strength failed, he was cast on Christ’s strength. In that dependence, he found a strength far greater than his own.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This paradox lies at the center of the Christian life. Jesus said that whoever wants to save their life will lose it, but whoever loses their life for His sake will find it (*Matthew 16:25*). He said the last will be first and the humble will be exalted. Paul’s statement belongs with these sayings of Jesus. The kingdom of God reverses the values of the world.

This does not mean believers should seek out suffering or make themselves weak on purpose. Paul did not go looking for hardship; it came to him as he served Christ. Nor does this verse mean that every kind of suffering should simply be accepted. Paul himself sought to escape danger when possible (*2 Corinthians 11:32–33*), appealed to his legal rights (*Acts 22:25*), and prayed for relief. People facing abuse or harm should seek safety. Paul’s point is that, when weakness and hardship come in the course of following Christ, they need not be signs of defeat. They can become occasions for God’s power.

The strength Paul describes is not the absence of weakness but the presence of Christ in it. *Philippians 4:13* expresses the same truth: “*I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me*” (*Philippians 4:13*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Many people feel that they must be strong, capable, and self-sufficient. When weakness comes, through illness, loss, failure, or exhaustion, it can feel like everything is falling apart. This verse offers a new way to see those moments. They can become the very places where believers experience Christ’s strength most deeply.

This truth also brings freedom in serving others. Believers do not need to wait until they feel strong or competent to be useful to God. Often God uses people precisely when they feel inadequate, because then it is clear that the power belongs to Him.

### *2 Corinthians 12:15* — Spend and Be Spent

> *“I will most gladly spend and be spent for your souls. If I love you more abundantly, am I loved the less?”*
>
> — *2 Corinthians 12:15* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul has just explained, once again, why he will not accept financial support from the Corinthians: “*for I seek not your possessions, but you*” (*v. 14*). He compares himself to a parent. Parents save up for their children, not the other way around. Paul sees himself as the spiritual father of the Corinthian church (*1 Corinthians 4:15*), and he wants to give to them, not take from them.

Then he says, “I will most gladly spend and be spent for your souls.” Paul is willing to spend everything he has, his money, energy, and time, and to be spent himself, giving his very life for their spiritual good. And he will do this “most gladly,” not grudgingly.

His question that follows is full of pain: “If I love you more abundantly, am I loved the less?” Paul’s love for them was great, but they seemed to love him less in return. Yet his love did not depend on being loved back.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Paul’s words reflect the heart of Christ, who gave Himself fully for people who did not love Him in return. *Romans 5:8* says that God commended His love toward us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. Paul’s willingness to love without return was a reflection of the love he had received.

This verse also contrasts sharply with the rival teachers, who devoured and exploited the Corinthians (*2 Corinthians 11:20*). False shepherds take from the flock; true shepherds give themselves for the flock. Jesus described the same contrast in *John 10:10–11*: the thief comes to steal and destroy, but the good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep.

The phrase “not your possessions, but you” captures the essence of genuine ministry and genuine love. Healthy love seeks the good of the other person, not what can be gained from them.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse provides a measure for love in every setting: in families, friendships, churches, and ministry. Is the goal to receive something from others, or to seek their good? Love that says, “*I seek not your possessions, but you*” (*v. 14*), gives freely without calculating return.

It also brings comfort to those who love others who do not love them back, such as parents of wayward children, spouses in difficult seasons, or pastors serving unappreciative congregations. Paul knew that pain. His example shows that love can keep giving even when it is not returned, because it is rooted in Christ’s love. At the same time, love does not require anyone to remain in a situation of abuse or exploitation; seeking another person’s good can include setting healthy boundaries.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

Second Corinthians 12 brings the letter’s central message into focus: God’s power is made perfect in weakness. Paul could have boasted about his extraordinary vision of Paradise, but he chose instead to speak about the thorn in his flesh. God did not remove it despite Paul’s earnest prayers, but He gave him something greater: the assurance that His grace was sufficient.

This chapter speaks to anyone living with ongoing hardship. Believers are free to pray boldly and persistently for relief, as Paul did, and God often does heal and deliver. But when relief does not come, God’s grace is still enough. Weakness is not a sign of His absence or of a lack of faith. It can be the very place where Christ’s power rests most clearly.

The chapter also challenges the way people measure spiritual maturity and leadership. Paul refused to build his reputation on spiritual experiences others could not test. He wanted to be known by his life and teaching. Believers today can be cautious about leaders who emphasize their own extraordinary experiences, and they can value humility, faithfulness, and character above spectacle.

Paul’s love for the Corinthians offers a model of selfless care. He sought them, not their possessions, and was willing to spend and be spent for their good, even when his love was not returned. Finally, his grief over unrepented sin reminds believers that sin harms the community and that a loving leader mourns over it. The call is to repentance, not out of fear, but because God’s grace is sufficient to forgive, restore, and strengthen.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You that Your grace is sufficient for me and that Your power is made perfect in weakness. I bring You the thorns in my life, the pains and struggles that will not go away, and I ask You for relief. Yet if You choose not to remove them, give me grace to endure and let Your power rest on me. Teach me not to hide my weakness or be ashamed of it, but to depend on You in it. Guard me from pride, and keep me from seeking my own glory. Give me a love like Paul’s, a love that seeks the good of others rather than what I can gain from them, a love willing to spend and be spent. Where there is unconfessed sin in my life, lead me to repentance. When I am weak, be my strength. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

2 Corinthians · Chapter 13 of 13

# 2 Corinthians — Chapter 13

Chapter Theme: Examine Yourselves and Live in Peace

[Read 2 Corinthians 13 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/2CO13.htm)

Main Teaching

As Paul prepares for his third visit, he warns that he will deal firmly with unrepentant sin, because Christ, who was crucified in weakness but lives by the power of God, is powerful among them. He calls the Corinthians to examine themselves to see whether they are in the faith, and he prays that they will do what is right, even if he seems to fail. Paul closes with a call to rejoice, mature, be comforted, agree, and live in peace, and with a blessing that names the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit.

## Chapter Background and Story

The final chapter of 2 Corinthians brings the letter to a close with a mixture of firm warning and warm blessing. Paul is about to visit Corinth for the third time. His first visit founded the church (*Acts 18*). His second was the “painful visit” mentioned in *2 Corinthians 2:1*. Now he is coming again, and he wants the church to be ready.

Throughout chapters 10–12, Paul has defended his apostleship against critics who claimed he was weak. In this chapter he answers one final challenge. The Corinthians wanted “proof” that Christ was speaking through him (v3). Paul says they will have it, but he hopes he will not need to show it through discipline. He would much rather see them repent and grow strong.

The chapter ends with one of the most beloved blessings in Christian worship, a closing benediction that names Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together. After all the conflict and hard words of this letter, Paul’s last word is grace, love, and fellowship.

### Firm Warning (*13:1–4*)

“*This is the third time I am coming to you. “At the mouth of two or three witnesses shall every word be established.”*” (*v. 1*) Paul quotes *Deuteronomy 19:15*, the principle that any accusation must be confirmed by two or three witnesses. He may mean that when he arrives, any charges against members of the church will be handled fairly, with proper evidence, not on the basis of rumor. He may also be suggesting that his three visits serve as three witnesses or warnings. Either way, he signals that matters will be dealt with justly.

“*I have warned previously, and I warn again, as when I was present the second time, so now, being absent, I write to those who have sinned before now and to all the rest that if I come again, I will not spare*” (*v. 2*). Paul has been patient, but patience has a purpose. If those who persist in sin do not repent, he will act.

“*seeing that you seek a proof of Christ who speaks in me who is not weak, but is powerful in you*” (*v. 3*). The Corinthians wanted evidence of Christ’s power in Paul. Paul reminds them that Christ is not weak among them. The relationship between weakness and power in Christ’s life and Paul’s is studied below.

### Examine Yourselves (*13:5–10*)

Paul turns the Corinthians’ demand back on them. They have been testing him; now they need to test themselves. This call is studied below.

“*But I hope that you will know that we aren’t disqualified*” (*v. 6*). Paul is confident that if they examine themselves honestly, they will recognize that his ministry is genuine, since their very faith came through it.

“*Now I pray to God that you do no evil; not that we may appear approved, but that you may do that which is honorable, though we may seem to have failed*” (*v. 7*). This is a remarkable prayer. Paul cares more about the Corinthians’ doing right than about his own reputation. If they repent and do what is good, he will not need to show his authority, and he may seem “weak” to his critics. He is willing to look like a failure if it means they are faithful.

“*For we can do nothing against the truth, but for the truth*” (*v. 8*). Paul’s authority is bound to the truth. He cannot use it for any purpose other than the gospel and the good of the church.

“*For we rejoice when we are weak and you are strong. We also pray for this: your becoming perfect*” (*v. 9*). The word translated “perfect” means being restored, mended, or made complete. It was used of setting broken bones or mending nets. Paul prays for the church’s restoration.

“*For this cause I write these things while absent, that I may not deal sharply when present, according to the authority which the Lord gave me for building up and not for tearing down*” (*v. 10*). Paul wrote this letter so that, when he arrives, he can come in gentleness rather than severity. He repeats the principle from *2 Corinthians 10:8*: his authority exists for building up.

### Final Greetings and Blessing (*13:11–14*)

Paul’s closing words, studied below, gather up the whole letter’s hopes for the church. “*Greet one another with a holy kiss*” (*v. 12*). In that culture, a kiss on the cheek was a common greeting among family and friends. Paul calls it “holy” because it expressed the family love of believers, who had become brothers and sisters in Christ. “*All the saints greet you*” (*v. 13*). The believers in Macedonia, where Paul was writing, send their greetings too. The Corinthian church was part of a much larger family. The closing blessing is studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *2 Corinthians 13:4* — Crucified in Weakness, Living by God’s Power

> *“For he was crucified through weakness, yet he lives through the power of God. For we also are weak in him, but we will live with him through the power of God toward you.”*
>
> — *2 Corinthians 13:4* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The Corinthians wanted proof of Christ’s power in Paul. Paul answers by pointing to Christ Himself. “He was crucified through weakness.” At the cross, Jesus appeared utterly weak. He was arrested, mocked, beaten, and executed as a criminal. He did not call down angels or defend Himself. To onlookers, it looked like total defeat.

“Yet he lives through the power of God.” The weakness of the cross was not the end. God raised Jesus from the dead by His mighty power. The crucified one is now the risen Lord.

Paul says the same pattern is true in his own life. “For we also are weak in him.” Paul shares in Christ’s weakness through his sufferings and limitations. “But we will live with him through the power of God toward you.” Just as Christ lives by God’s power, Paul too will act in God’s power when he comes to Corinth. His weakness is real, but it is not the whole story.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse summarizes the theology of the whole letter. The life of a believer follows the shape of Christ’s life: weakness and death, followed by resurrection power. Paul said it earlier: “*always carrying in the body the putting to death of the Lord Jesus, that the life of Jesus may also be revealed in our body*” (*2 Corinthians 4:10*).

The cross shows that God’s power does not work the way human power works. Human power dominates and displays itself. God’s power was revealed through the self-giving weakness of the crucified Christ, and then through His resurrection. As Paul wrote in *1 Corinthians 1:25*, the weakness of God is stronger than men.

This means that weakness, when joined to Christ, is never final. Every grave, failure, and sorrow can be followed by God’s resurrection power. Believers live in hope because the pattern of Christ’s life is the pattern of their own.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

When believers feel weak, defeated, or overwhelmed, this verse reminds them that weakness is not the end of the story. Christ’s weakness led to resurrection, and those who are in Him share in His life through the power of God.

This verse also offers a pattern for leadership and service. Paul did not try to prove his authority through displays of power. He pointed to the cross and the resurrection. Believers can serve with humility, trusting that God’s power works through them most clearly when they rely on Him rather than on their own strength or status.

### *2 Corinthians 13:5* — Examine Yourselves

> *“Examine your own selves, whether you are in the faith. Test your own selves. Or don’t you know about your own selves, that Jesus Christ is in you?—unless indeed you are disqualified.”*
>
> — *2 Corinthians 13:5* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The Corinthians had spent a great deal of energy examining Paul, questioning his credentials, his speaking, his motives, and his authority. Now Paul turns the question around. “Examine your own selves, whether you are in the faith. Test your own selves.”

The word “test” was used for testing metals to see whether they were genuine. Paul asks the Corinthians to look honestly at their own lives to see whether their faith is real.

“Or don’t you know about your own selves, that Jesus Christ is in you?” This question expects a positive answer. Paul believes that most of them will recognize that Christ is indeed living in them. Their faith came through Paul’s preaching, and the Spirit’s presence among them was evidence that the gospel was real.

“Unless indeed you are disqualified.” This is a sober warning. If someone examines their life and finds no evidence of Christ, no faith, no love, no repentance, no fruit of the Spirit, that is a serious matter that should lead them to turn to Christ.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Self-examination is a regular theme in Scripture. Paul told the Corinthians to examine themselves before taking the Lord’s Supper (*1 Corinthians 11:28*). The psalmist prayed, “*Search me, God, and know my heart*” (*Psalm 139:23*). Healthy self-examination looks at one’s life in the light of God’s truth.

It is important to understand what this examination is meant to do. It is not meant to produce endless anxiety or doubt. Paul fully expected that the Corinthians would find Christ in them. The goal is honest assurance, not fear. Assurance of salvation rests ultimately on Christ’s work and God’s promises (*Romans 8:38–39*; *1 John 5:13*), but genuine faith also shows itself in a changed life, and examining that evidence can confirm faith or reveal a need to turn to God.

Different Christian traditions place different emphases here. Some stress that believers should look mainly to Christ’s promises rather than to their own performance, since looking too much at oneself can lead to discouragement. Others stress the importance of examining the fruit of one’s life. Both emphases have value, and Paul’s words hold them together: look honestly at yourself, and look for Christ in you.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

It is often easier to evaluate others than to evaluate oneself. Like the Corinthians, believers can spend much energy critiquing leaders, churches, or fellow Christians while neglecting their own hearts. This verse calls for a turn inward, an honest look at one’s own faith, love, and obedience.

This examination can be done prayerfully, perhaps by reading a passage like *Galatians 5:22–23* or *1 Corinthians 13* and asking God to show where growth is needed. For those who struggle with constant doubt about their salvation, it is helpful to remember that the goal is to find Christ in them, not to find perfection. Even weak faith, placed in Christ, is genuine faith. Those who find no evidence of faith at all can take the examination as an invitation to come to Christ today.

### *2 Corinthians 13:11* — Rejoice, Be Perfected, Live in Peace

> *“Finally, brothers, rejoice! Be perfected. Be comforted. Be of the same mind. Live in peace, and the God of love and peace will be with you.”*
>
> — *2 Corinthians 13:11* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

As Paul closes this intense letter, he gives a series of brief, warm instructions.

“Rejoice!” The word can also mean “farewell,” as it was a common way to say goodbye, but Paul likely intends both meanings. After all the tension, he calls them to joy.

“Be perfected.” This is related to the word in verse 9 meaning restored or mended. Paul calls them to put things right, to let God repair what has been broken in their community.

“Be comforted.” This may also mean “be encouraged” or “listen to my appeal.” Paul wants them to receive the comfort and exhortation of this letter.

“Be of the same mind.” The church had been divided. Paul calls them to unity, to share the same purpose and commitment to Christ.

“Live in peace.” Conflict had marked the church for a long time. Paul urges them to pursue peace with one another.

Then comes the promise: “and the God of love and peace will be with you.” When believers pursue love and peace, they experience the presence of the God who is Himself love and peace.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These five instructions form a summary of what Paul has hoped for the Corinthians throughout both letters. He wanted them to be a joyful, restored, encouraged, united, and peaceful community. These are not merely human goals; they reflect the character of God.

The title “the God of love and peace” appears only here in the New Testament, though Paul often speaks of “the God of peace” (*Romans 15:33*; *Philippians 4:9*). It reminds the Corinthians that their divisions and conflicts were contrary to the nature of the God they worshiped. A community that reflects God’s character will be marked by love and peace.

The order is also worth noting. The promise of God’s presence comes with the call to pursue love and peace. This does not mean God’s love is earned by good behavior, but that a community living in harmony experiences His presence more fully, while a community torn by conflict grieves the Spirit (*Ephesians 4:30–32*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These five short commands offer a practical guide for any church, family, or friendship that has been through conflict. Rejoice in what God has done. Allow God to restore what is broken. Receive encouragement. Seek unity around what matters most. Pursue peace actively.

Being “of the same mind” does not mean everyone must agree on every opinion. It means sharing a common commitment to Christ and to one another, so that differences do not become divisions. Peace may require humility, forgiveness, and patience. Where peace is not possible because of ongoing harm or abuse, safety must come first, but wherever reconciliation is possible, believers can pursue it, trusting that the God of love and peace will be with them.

### *2 Corinthians 13:14* — Grace, Love, and Fellowship

> *“The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, God’s love, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all. Amen.”*
>
> — *2 Corinthians 13:14* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul ends the letter with a blessing that has been used in Christian worship for centuries. It names three gifts and three persons.

“The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ.” Grace is God’s undeserved favor, shown most fully in Jesus, who became poor so that others might become rich (*2 Corinthians 8:9*). Paul begins with grace because it is through Christ that people come to know God’s love.

“God’s love.” This is the Father’s love, the source of salvation. God’s love sent His Son and reconciled the world to Himself (*2 Corinthians 5:18–19*).

“The fellowship of the Holy Spirit.” “Fellowship” means sharing, participation, or communion. The Holy Spirit brings believers into fellowship with God and with one another. It can mean both the fellowship the Spirit creates among believers and believers’ participation in the Spirit Himself.

“Be with you all.” Paul’s blessing is for everyone in the church, including those who had opposed him. His final word is not condemnation but grace.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse is one of the clearest expressions in the New Testament of what the church later came to describe as the Trinity: one God in three persons, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Paul does not explain the doctrine here, but he names the three persons side by side as the source of every blessing. *Matthew 28:19* does something similar when Jesus commands baptism in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

The order is interesting. Paul mentions Christ first, then God the Father, then the Spirit. This reflects how believers come to know God. Through the grace of Christ, they discover the love of the Father, and they enter into the fellowship of the Spirit.

For a church divided by conflict, this blessing was especially fitting. The very life of God is a life of love and fellowship. The Corinthians were being invited into that divine fellowship and called to reflect it in their relationships with one another.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Many churches use this blessing at the end of worship services. It can also be a daily prayer for oneself and others. Praying it reminds believers that every blessing comes from the Father, the Son, and the Spirit, and that their life together is meant to reflect God’s own life of love.

This verse also shows how to end a difficult conversation or season. After sharp words and painful conflict, Paul ends with grace, love, and fellowship. Even when correction is necessary, the final word for God’s people is His blessing. Believers can follow this example in their own relationships, letting grace have the last word.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

Second Corinthians 13 brings together the firmness and the tenderness of Paul’s ministry. He warns the Corinthians that unrepented sin will be dealt with, and he insists that matters be handled fairly, on the testimony of witnesses. Yet his deepest desire is not to exercise discipline but to see the church restored. He would rather appear weak than have to act harshly, because his authority exists for building up, not tearing down. This offers a model for any leader, parent, or friend who must address wrongdoing: be honest and firm, act justly, and always aim for restoration.

The chapter also calls each believer to self-examination. It is easy to evaluate others and neglect one’s own heart. Paul invites the Corinthians, and readers today, to look honestly at their lives and find Christ living in them. This is not meant to produce fear but to bring assurance and, where needed, repentance. Even weak faith, resting in Christ, is real faith.

Paul’s reflection on Christ’s weakness and power reminds believers that weakness is never the final word. Christ was crucified in weakness, but He lives by the power of God. Those who are united with Him share in both, so they can face their own weaknesses with hope.

Finally, the letter ends with a call to rejoice, be restored, be encouraged, be united, and live in peace, followed by a blessing that names Father, Son, and Spirit. After a letter full of conflict and hard truths, the last word is grace. Believers can carry this blessing into their own relationships, letting the grace of Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Spirit shape how they live together.

## Chapter Prayer

Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, thank You for the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, for Your boundless love, and for the fellowship of Your Spirit. Search my heart and show me whether I am living in the faith; let me find Christ living in me, and lead me to repentance wherever I have wandered. Thank You that Christ was crucified in weakness but lives by Your power, and that my weakness is not the end of my story. Help me to care more about others doing what is right than about how I appear. Give me joy, restore what is broken in me and in my relationships, comfort me, unite me with Your people, and make me a peacemaker. May the God of love and peace be with me and with all Your people. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Book 9 of 27

# Galatians

## About This Letter

Paul wrote Galatians to churches in the Roman province of Galatia, in what is now central Turkey. Many scholars believe these were the churches of Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra, and Derbe, which Paul founded on his first missionary journey (*Acts 13–14*); others think the letter was sent to ethnic Galatians farther north, whom Paul visited later (*Acts 16:6*; *18:23*). Depending on which view is right, the letter was written either around A.D. 48–49, making it perhaps Paul’s earliest surviving letter, or in the mid-50s.

After Paul left, other teachers arrived who insisted that Gentile believers must be circumcised and keep the Law of Moses in order to belong fully to God’s people. Paul saw this as a different gospel altogether, one that would make Christ’s death unnecessary. Galatians is his urgent, passionate response. It is the only one of Paul’s letters to churches that skips the usual words of thanksgiving and goes straight to the problem.

## The Shape of the Letter

In chapters 1–2, Paul defends the gospel he preached by telling his own story: his life in Judaism, his call by God, his independence from the Jerusalem leaders, their recognition of his ministry, and his public confrontation with Peter at Antioch. In chapters 3–4, he argues from Scripture and experience that people are made right with God by faith in Christ, as Abraham was, and not by the works of the Law; believers are God’s adopted children and heirs, free rather than enslaved. In chapters 5–6, he shows what this freedom looks like in practice: not a license for selfishness but a life led by the Spirit, marked by love, the fruit of the Spirit, and bearing one another’s burdens.

## Themes to Watch For

Watch for the grace of God that calls people freely, justification by faith in Christ rather than by works of the Law, the promise to Abraham fulfilled in Christ, the meaning of the Law and its purpose, adoption as God’s children, the unity of all believers in Christ regardless of ethnicity, social status, or sex, freedom in Christ, life in the Spirit, and the cross as the believer’s only boast. Galatians has sometimes been called the charter of Christian freedom. It shows that the gospel is not Christ plus anything else, but Christ alone, received by faith and lived out in love.
