Galatians · Chapter 1 of 6

# Galatians — Chapter 1

Chapter Theme: There Is No Other Gospel

[Read Galatians 1 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/GAL01.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul opens his letter by affirming that his apostleship came directly from Jesus Christ and God the Father, and that Christ gave Himself for our sins to rescue us from this present evil age. Astonished that the Galatians are turning so quickly to a different gospel, he declares that there is no other good news and that anyone who preaches another should be under God’s curse. He explains that the gospel he preached came by revelation from Jesus Christ, telling how God transformed him from a violent persecutor of the church into a preacher of the faith he once tried to destroy.

## Chapter Background and Story

Paul had planted the churches of Galatia with great joy. When he first arrived there, he was ill, yet the Galatians welcomed him as if he were an angel of God, even as Christ Jesus Himself (*Galatians 4:13–14*). Many believed the gospel and received the Holy Spirit. They were mostly Gentiles who had turned from idols to the living God.

After Paul moved on, other teachers came. They taught that Gentile believers needed to be circumcised and to observe the Law of Moses, including its calendar and food laws, to be full members of God’s people. These teachers may have presented themselves as representatives of the Jerusalem church, and they seem to have questioned Paul’s authority, suggesting that he was a second-hand apostle who had watered down the message to please Gentiles.

Paul’s response is the most urgent and emotional of all his letters. He does not begin with thanksgiving, as he usually does. Instead, after a brief greeting, he expresses astonishment and alarm. For Paul, the issue was not a minor disagreement about religious customs. It was about the heart of the gospel: whether people are made right with God by faith in Christ alone, or by Christ plus the works of the Law.

### Greeting (*1:1–5*)

“*Paul, an apostle—not from men, nor through man, but through Jesus Christ, and God the Father, who raised him from the dead—*” (*v. 1*). From the very first sentence, Paul answers the charge that his authority came secondhand. He was not appointed by a human committee or sent by a human church. He was commissioned directly by the risen Christ on the road to Damascus (*Acts 9:3–6*). The mention of the resurrection is significant: Paul’s apostleship came from the risen Lord.

“*and all the brothers who are with me, to the assemblies of Galatia*” (*v. 2*). The letter was written to several churches in the region. Notice that Paul offers no words of praise here, unlike most of his letters. The greeting of grace and peace, and Christ’s rescuing work, are studied below.

### No Other Gospel (*1:6–10*)

Paul expresses his amazement that the Galatians are turning away so quickly. This section is studied below.

### The Gospel by Revelation (*1:11–12*)

“*But I make known to you, brothers, concerning the Good News which was preached by me, that it is not according to man*” (*v. 11*). “*For I didn’t receive it from man, nor was I taught it, but it came to me through revelation of Jesus Christ*” (*v. 12*). Paul is not saying he never learned anything from other believers. In *1 Corinthians 15:3*, he says he passed on what he had received about Christ’s death and resurrection. His point here is that the core of his gospel, that the crucified Jesus is the risen Lord and that salvation comes by grace through faith to Jew and Gentile alike, was revealed to him by Christ Himself. He did not invent it, and he did not receive it as an approved message from human authorities.

### Paul’s Former Life (*1:13–14*)

“*For you have heard of my way of living in time past in the Jews’ religion, how that beyond measure I persecuted the assembly of God and ravaged it*” (*v. 13*). Paul does not hide his past. Acts tells how he approved of Stephen’s death and went from house to house dragging believers off to prison (*Acts 8:1–3*). “*I advanced in the Jews’ religion beyond many of my own age among my countrymen, being more exceedingly zealous for the traditions of my fathers*” (*v. 14*). Paul had been more devoted to the Law and the traditions than the teachers now troubling the Galatians. He knew that path from the inside, which makes his testimony all the more powerful.

### Called by Grace (*1:15–24*)

God’s call of Paul, studied below, changed everything. Afterward, Paul did not rush to Jerusalem for approval. “*nor did I go up to Jerusalem to those who were apostles before me, but I went away into Arabia. Then I returned to Damascus*” (*v. 17*). “Arabia” probably refers to the Nabataean kingdom, south and east of Damascus. Paul may have gone there to pray and reflect, to preach, or both. Some have noted that Mount Sinai was traditionally located in Arabia (*Galatians 4:25*), and that Paul, like Elijah, may have gone to the place where God gave the Law to reflect on its fulfillment in Christ.

“*Then after three years I went up to Jerusalem to visit Peter, and stayed with him fifteen days*” (*v. 18*). The word translated “visit” suggests getting to know someone, perhaps learning from him about Jesus’ earthly life. “*But of the other apostles I saw no one except James, the Lord’s brother*” (*v. 19*). James was the brother of Jesus who became a leader of the Jerusalem church (*Acts 15:13*). Paul’s contact with the Jerusalem leaders was brief and personal; he did not receive his commission from them.

“*Now about the things which I write to you, behold, before God, I’m not lying*” (*v. 20*). Paul takes an oath because the accusations against him were serious.

“*Then I came to the regions of Syria and Cilicia*” (*v. 21*). Cilicia included Paul’s hometown, Tarsus (*Acts 9:30*). “*I was still unknown by face to the assemblies of Judea which were in Christ*” (*v. 22*), “*but they only heard, “He who once persecuted us now preaches the faith that he once tried to destroy.”*” (*v. 23*) “*So they glorified God in me*” (*v. 24*). The churches in Judea did not know Paul personally, but the news of his transformation led them to praise God. The very believers he had once attacked now rejoiced because of what God had done in him.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Galatians 1:3–5* — Christ Gave Himself to Rescue Us

> *“Grace to you and peace from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ, who gave himself for our sins, that he might deliver us out of this present evil age, according to the will of our God and Father— to whom be the glory forever and ever. Amen.”*
>
> — *Galatians 1:3–5* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul’s greeting is short, but it is packed with the gospel. “Grace to you and peace” was Paul’s usual greeting, combining a Greek word of greeting (grace) with the Hebrew greeting (shalom, peace). Both come “from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ.”

Then Paul adds something he does not usually include in a greeting. He describes what Christ has done: He “gave himself for our sins.” Jesus did not merely give teaching or an example. He gave Himself, His very life, as a sacrifice for sins.

The purpose was “that he might deliver us out of this present evil age.” The word “deliver” means to rescue, as one would rescue someone from danger. “This present evil age” refers to the world as it is now, under the power of sin, death, and evil forces. Christ came to rescue people from that domain and bring them into God’s new age.

All of this happened “according to the will of our God and Father.” Salvation was not an accident or a backup plan. It was God’s purpose from the beginning. And so Paul bursts into praise: “to whom be the glory forever and ever. Amen.”

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Paul packs the core of his argument into this greeting. If Christ gave Himself for our sins, then nothing more is needed to deal with sin. The teachers in Galatia were implying that faith in Christ was not enough and that the Law must be added. Paul’s opening words already answer them: Christ’s self-giving is sufficient.

The idea of “two ages” was common in Jewish thought. There was the present age, marked by sin and suffering, and the age to come, when God would set all things right. Paul teaches that in Christ, the age to come has already broken into the present. Believers still live in the present age, but they have been rescued from its power and belong to the new creation (*Galatians 6:15*). This is why returning to the Law as a way of being right with God would be a step backward into the old age.

The closing praise reminds readers that the goal of salvation is God’s glory. Paul cannot describe what Christ has done without breaking into worship.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Many people feel trapped by the patterns of this present age: addictions, anxieties, injustices, and the pull of sin. This verse proclaims that Christ came to rescue. His self-giving love is powerful enough to deliver people from what holds them captive.

It also reminds believers that their salvation rests not on what they do but on what Christ has done. On days when they feel they have not done enough, they can return to this truth: He gave Himself for their sins. Their response is not anxious striving but grateful worship, giving glory to God forever.

### *Galatians 1:6–8* — No Other Gospel

> *“I marvel that you are so quickly deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ to a different ‘good news’, but there isn’t another ‘good news.’ Only there are some who trouble you and want to pervert the Good News of Christ. But even though we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you any ‘good news’ other than that which we preached to you, let him be cursed.”*
>
> — *Galatians 1:6–8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Instead of giving thanks, as he usually does at this point in a letter, Paul expresses astonishment. “I marvel that you are so quickly deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ.” The word “deserting” was used of soldiers abandoning their post or of someone changing allegiance. The Galatians were not just changing an opinion; they were turning away from God Himself, who had called them by grace.

They were turning “to a different ‘good news’.” But Paul immediately corrects himself: “there isn’t another ‘good news.’” There is only one gospel. What the false teachers were offering was not good news at all; it was a distortion. “There are some who trouble you and want to pervert the Good News of Christ.” These teachers were causing confusion and twisting the message.

Then Paul makes a startling statement. Even if he himself, or an angel from heaven, preached a different gospel, that person should be “cursed.” The word refers to being placed under God’s judgment. Paul repeats it in verse 9 for emphasis.

Paul is not saying that the truth of the gospel depends on him. On the contrary, he says the gospel is so fixed and certain that even he, the one who preached it, has no authority to change it.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Why does Paul react so strongly? Because the gospel is about how people are made right with God and saved from judgment. If the message is distorted, people are led away from the only way of salvation. Adding the works of the Law as a requirement for acceptance with God would mean that Christ’s death was not enough. Paul will say this directly in *Galatians 2:21*: if righteousness came through the Law, then Christ died for nothing.

This passage also shows that a message can keep Christian language and still be “another gospel.” The false teachers likely spoke about Jesus and claimed to follow Him. Their error was adding something to faith in Christ as a requirement for belonging to God. Paul warns that “Christ plus” anything turns grace into something else.

The reference to “an angel from heaven” is striking. Spiritual experiences, visions, and claims of new revelation must all be tested by the gospel already given. No experience, however impressive, can override the truth revealed in Christ.

At the same time, Paul’s severe words are directed at those who distort the core of the gospel, not at believers who differ on secondary matters. Paul himself was flexible in many practices (*1 Corinthians 9:19–23*) and urged patience with differing convictions (*Romans 14*). His curse is reserved for those who corrupt the message of salvation by grace through faith.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

In every generation, there are messages that add to the gospel. Some suggest that believers must follow certain rules, achieve certain experiences, belong to a certain group, or meet certain cultural standards to be truly accepted by God. Others subtract from the gospel, removing the cross, sin, or Christ’s lordship. Paul’s warning calls believers to hold firmly to the one gospel: Christ crucified and risen, received by grace through faith.

This passage also encourages careful listening. Not every teaching that uses the name of Jesus is faithful to Him. Believers can test what they hear by Scripture, asking whether it points to Christ’s finished work as the basis of salvation or quietly adds human requirements.

### *Galatians 1:10* — Pleasing God Rather Than People

> *“For am I now seeking the favor of men, or of God? Or am I striving to please men? For if I were still pleasing men, I wouldn’t be a servant of Christ.”*
>
> — *Galatians 1:10* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul’s opponents apparently accused him of being a people-pleaser. They may have said he dropped the requirement of circumcision to make the gospel easier for Gentiles to accept. Paul answers with a pointed question: “For am I now seeking the favor of men, or of God?”

The harsh words he has just written (vv8–9) are proof that he is not trying to please people. No one seeking popularity would pronounce a curse on those who distort the gospel.

“For if I were still pleasing men, I wouldn’t be a servant of Christ.” The word “still” may refer to Paul’s former life, when he sought the approval of religious leaders and advanced in Judaism. Now, as a servant of Christ, his goal is to please God alone. A servant’s task is to do the master’s will, not to win the approval of others.

Paul is not saying he never cares how people feel or that he tries to offend. Elsewhere he says he seeks to please others for their good and for the sake of the gospel (*1 Corinthians 10:33*). The point here is about ultimate loyalty. When pleasing people conflicts with faithfulness to Christ, Christ must come first.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Jesus warned His disciples about the danger of seeking human approval. He said, “*How can you believe, who receive glory from one another, and you don’t seek the glory that comes from the only God?*” (*John 5:44*) The desire for approval can quietly shape what people believe, say, and do, pulling them away from truth.

Paul’s freedom from people-pleasing came from his identity as a “servant of Christ.” He belonged to a Master whose approval mattered more than anyone else’s. That gave him courage to speak hard truths, endure rejection, and stand firm when others disagreed.

This verse also explains why the gospel cannot be adjusted to suit popular opinion. The message of Christ crucified has always been offensive to some and foolish to others (*1 Corinthians 1:23*). Those who preach it faithfully will sometimes disappoint people. Faithfulness to Christ means accepting that cost.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

The desire to be liked is strong in everyone. It can lead believers to stay silent when they should speak, to compromise convictions to fit in, or to measure their worth by others’ opinions. This verse invites a reorientation: the most important approval is God’s.

This does not mean being harsh or careless about others’ feelings. Believers are called to speak the truth in love (*Ephesians 4:15*). But when faced with a choice between pleasing people and being faithful to Christ, Paul’s example points the way. There is great freedom in living for an audience of One.

### *Galatians 1:15–16* — Called by His Grace

> *“But when it was the good pleasure of God, who separated me from my mother’s womb and called me through his grace, to reveal his Son in me, that I might preach him among the Gentiles, I didn’t immediately confer with flesh and blood,”*
>
> — *Galatians 1:15–16* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After describing his violent past, Paul turns to what God did. “But when it was the good pleasure of God.” The turning point in Paul’s life was not his own decision but God’s gracious initiative.

God “separated me from my mother’s womb.” Even before Paul was born, God had set him apart for a purpose. This echoes the calls of the prophets. God told Jeremiah that before he was born He had set him apart as a prophet to the nations (*Jeremiah 1:5*), and the Servant in *Isaiah 49:1* says the LORD called him from the womb.

God “called me through his grace.” Paul did not earn his calling. He was actively persecuting the church when God called him. His calling was pure grace.

The purpose of this call was “to reveal his Son in me, that I might preach him among the Gentiles.” God revealed Jesus to Paul, both outwardly on the Damascus road and inwardly in his heart. And the purpose of this revelation was mission: Paul was to proclaim Christ among the non-Jewish nations.

“I didn’t immediately confer with flesh and blood.” “Flesh and blood” means human beings. Paul did not need human approval to begin obeying God’s call.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Paul’s story is a powerful illustration of the gospel he preached. He was not made right with God through his zeal for the Law. In fact, his zeal had led him to persecute God’s people. He was saved and called entirely by grace. This is exactly what Paul wants the Galatians to understand: if the most zealous Law-keeper needed grace, then no one can be made right with God by the Law.

The phrase “reveal his Son in me” is notable. Paul speaks not only of seeing Christ but of Christ being revealed within him. This anticipates *Galatians 2:20*, where Paul says Christ lives in him. The gospel is not just information about Christ; it is a personal encounter with Him that transforms a person from within.

Paul’s calling to the Gentiles is also part of God’s ancient plan. God promised Abraham that all nations would be blessed through him (*Genesis 12:3*), and Paul will develop this theme in chapter 3. His mission to the Gentiles was the fulfillment of God’s long-standing purpose.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Some people believe their past is too dark for God to use them. Paul’s story shows otherwise. God called a violent persecutor and made him the greatest missionary of the early church. No one is beyond the reach of God’s grace.

This passage also shows that God’s call has a purpose. He reveals His Son to people not only for their own salvation but so that they might share Christ with others. Every believer’s story of grace becomes part of God’s mission in the world.

Finally, Paul’s confidence in God’s call encourages believers to obey God without waiting for every human approval. Wise counsel is valuable, as Paul himself later sought (*Galatians 2:2*). But a clear call from God, confirmed by Scripture and the community of faith over time, does not depend on popularity.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Galatians 1* sets the tone for a letter about the heart of the gospel. Paul begins by reminding his readers that Christ gave Himself for our sins to rescue us from this present evil age. This is the foundation of everything. Salvation is God’s work, accomplished in Christ, according to the Father’s will. Nothing needs to be added to it.

Because the gospel is so precious, Paul guards it fiercely. He is astonished that the Galatians are turning to a message that adds human requirements to faith in Christ. His strong words warn believers in every age to hold fast to the one true gospel. Messages that add rules, rituals, or achievements as conditions for God’s acceptance, or that remove the cross and Christ’s lordship, are not good news at all. Believers can test every teaching by asking whether it rests on Christ’s finished work.

Paul’s example of pleasing God rather than people encourages believers to live with courage and integrity. The approval that matters most is God’s. That frees believers to speak truth with love even when it is unpopular, and to resist the pressure to shape their faith around others’ opinions.

Finally, Paul’s testimony shows the transforming power of grace. The persecutor became a preacher, and the churches that once feared him glorified God because of him. Whatever a person’s past, God’s grace can call, change, and use them. Every believer’s story of grace can bring glory to God and point others to Christ.

## Chapter Prayer

Father, thank You for the gift of Your Son, who gave Himself for my sins to rescue me from this present evil age. To You be the glory forever and ever. Keep me faithful to the one true gospel. Guard my heart against every message that adds to Your grace or takes away from Christ. Give me discernment to recognize distortions of the truth, and courage to hold fast to what You have revealed. Free me from the need to please people, and let my deepest desire be to please You as a servant of Christ. Thank You that You call people by Your grace, even those with the darkest pasts. Reveal Your Son in me more and more, and use my story to bring glory to You and to point others to Jesus. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Galatians · Chapter 2 of 6

# Galatians — Chapter 2

Chapter Theme: Justified by Faith, Crucified with Christ

[Read Galatians 2 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/GAL02.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul describes his visit to Jerusalem, where the leading apostles, James, Peter, and John, recognized his gospel to the Gentiles, refused to require that the Greek believer Titus be circumcised, and gave him the right hand of fellowship. He then recounts how he publicly confronted Peter at Antioch when Peter withdrew from eating with Gentile believers out of fear. From that confrontation, Paul states the heart of the gospel: a person is justified not by the works of the Law but through faith in Jesus Christ. He has been crucified with Christ, and Christ now lives in him, for if righteousness came through the Law, Christ died for nothing.

## Chapter Background and Story

In chapter 1, Paul showed that his gospel came directly from Christ and not from the Jerusalem apostles. But this raised a question: Did the Jerusalem leaders agree with Paul, or were they on the side of the teachers troubling the Galatians? In chapter 2, Paul shows that the leading apostles fully recognized his gospel and his mission to the Gentiles.

He then tells a painful story. At Antioch, a church where Jewish and Gentile believers shared meals together, Peter at first joined freely in table fellowship with Gentiles. But when certain people arrived from Jerusalem, Peter pulled back. Other Jewish believers followed, even Barnabas. Paul saw that this was not a minor matter of social custom. By refusing to eat with Gentile believers, Peter was implying that they were second-class members of God’s family unless they adopted Jewish law. That contradicted the gospel.

Paul’s account of his words to Peter flows into one of the most important passages in all his letters, a summary of justification by faith and of the believer’s union with Christ.

### Recognition in Jerusalem (*2:1–10*)

“*Then after a period of fourteen years I went up again to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus also with me*” (*v. 1*). The fourteen years are counted either from Paul’s conversion or from his first visit to Jerusalem. Scholars debate whether this visit is the famine relief visit of *Acts 11:27–30* or the Jerusalem Council of *Acts 15*. Either way, the issue at stake was the same: must Gentile believers keep the Law of Moses?

“*I went up by revelation, and I laid before them the Good News which I preach among the Gentiles, but privately before those who were respected, for fear that I might be running, or had run, in vain*” (*v. 2*). Paul did not go for permission; he went because God directed him. But he wanted the unity of the church to be clear. If the Jerusalem leaders rejected his gospel, the church would be split into two, and his work among the Gentiles could be undermined.

“*But not even Titus, who was with me, being a Greek, was compelled to be circumcised*” (*v. 3*). Titus was a test case. He was a Gentile believer, and the Jerusalem leaders did not require him to be circumcised. This was strong evidence that Paul’s gospel was accepted.

“*This was because of the false brothers secretly brought in, who stole in to spy out our liberty which we have in Christ Jesus, that they might bring us into bondage*” (*v. 4*), “*to whom we gave no place in the way of subjection, not for an hour, that the truth of the Good News might continue with you*” (*v. 5*). Some people pretending to be believers had pushed for Titus to be circumcised. Paul refused to yield, not out of stubbornness, but to protect the freedom of the gospel for Gentiles like the Galatians.

“*But from those who were reputed to be important—whatever they were, it makes no difference to me; God doesn’t show partiality to man—they, I say, who were respected imparted nothing to me*” (*v. 6*). Paul respected the Jerusalem leaders, but he knew that God does not judge by status. The leaders added nothing to his gospel.

Instead, they recognized that God was working through Paul among the Gentiles just as He was working through Peter among the Jews (vv7–8). “*and when they perceived the grace that was given to me, James and Cephas and John, those who were reputed to be pillars, gave to Barnabas and me the right hand of fellowship, that we should go to the Gentiles, and they to the circumcision*” (*v. 9*). “Cephas” is the Aramaic form of Peter’s name. The right hand of fellowship was a sign of partnership and agreement. The leaders divided the mission field, not the gospel. “*They only asked us to remember the poor—which very thing I was also zealous to do*” (*v. 10*). This concern for the poor led to the collection Paul gathered for Jerusalem (*2 Corinthians 8–9*).

### Confrontation at Antioch (*2:11–14*)

The conflict with Peter, and what it reveals about the gospel, is studied below.

### Justified by Faith (*2:15–21*)

Paul’s words to Peter turn into a summary of the gospel. “*“We, being Jews by nature and not Gentile sinners*” (*v. 15*). Jewish people often spoke of Gentiles as “sinners” because they did not have or keep the Law. Paul begins from that common viewpoint and then shows that even Jewish believers had to be justified the same way as Gentiles: through faith in Christ. This central teaching is studied below.

“*But if while we sought to be justified in Christ, we ourselves also were found sinners, is Christ a servant of sin? Certainly not!*” (*v. 17*) Paul’s opponents might argue that abandoning the Law to eat with Gentiles made Jewish believers “sinners” and that Christ was therefore promoting sin. Paul rejects this completely. “*For if I build up again those things which I destroyed, I prove myself a law-breaker*” (*v. 18*). The real wrongdoing would be to rebuild the Law as a way of being right with God after having torn it down as that way. That was exactly what Peter was doing at Antioch.

“*For I through the law died to the law, that I might live to God*” (*v. 19*). The Law itself, by exposing sin and pronouncing its sentence of death, led Paul to Christ, who bore that sentence. In union with Christ’s death, Paul died to the Law as a means of righteousness, so that he could live for God. His union with Christ and his conclusion about grace are studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Galatians 2:11–14* — Walking Uprightly According to the Truth of the Gospel

> *“But when Peter came to Antioch, I resisted him to his face, because he stood condemned. For before some people came from James, he ate with the Gentiles. But when they came, he drew back and separated himself, fearing those who were of the circumcision. And the rest of the Jews joined him in his hypocrisy, so that even Barnabas was carried away with their hypocrisy. But when I saw that they didn’t walk uprightly according to the truth of the Good News, I said to Peter before them all, If you, being a Jew, live as the Gentiles do, and not as the Jews do, why do you compel the Gentiles to live as the Jews do?”*
>
> — *Galatians 2:11–14* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Antioch, in Syria, was home to the first large church with many Gentile members (*Acts 11:19–26*). Jewish and Gentile believers there ate together, including, most likely, the Lord’s Supper. For Jews who followed strict interpretations of the food laws, eating with Gentiles was a serious issue, because Gentile food might not be prepared according to the Law and because close table fellowship with Gentiles was widely avoided.

When Peter came to Antioch, he ate freely with Gentile believers. This was consistent with what God had shown him in his vision and at the house of Cornelius (*Acts 10:28*). But when “some people came from James,” Peter “drew back and separated himself, fearing those who were of the circumcision.” These visitors may have pressured Jewish believers to keep separate from Gentiles. Peter’s fear of their disapproval led him to change his behavior.

The effect spread. “The rest of the Jews joined him in his hypocrisy, so that even Barnabas was carried away.” Barnabas, Paul’s partner in the Gentile mission, was swept along. The church was being divided into two groups at the table.

Paul saw that this was not merely about food. It was about “the truth of the Good News.” By withdrawing, Peter was sending a message: Gentile believers were not fully acceptable unless they lived like Jews. So Paul confronted him publicly: “If you, being a Jew, live as the Gentiles do, and not as the Jews do, why do you compel the Gentiles to live as the Jews do?”

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This story shows that the gospel has social consequences. If all believers are justified by faith in Christ alone, then they all belong equally to God’s family and should share the same table. Separating from fellow believers on the basis of ethnicity or religious custom denies the gospel in practice, even if it is affirmed in words.

Paul calls Peter’s actions “hypocrisy,” which literally means play-acting. Peter knew the truth; he had acted on it. But fear made him act as though he believed something else. This is a sobering reminder that even mature believers and respected leaders can fail when they fear others’ disapproval. Peter, who had once denied Jesus out of fear, struggled again with the same weakness.

It is also important to see what happened later. Peter was not destroyed by this confrontation. At the Jerusalem Council, he spoke powerfully for salvation by grace for Gentiles (*Acts 15:7–11*), and in his own letter he speaks warmly of “*our beloved brother Paul*” (*2 Peter 3:15*). Honest correction, received humbly, can strengthen relationships rather than end them.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Churches today can still divide along lines of ethnicity, class, culture, or politics, sometimes without noticing. This passage calls believers to examine whether their practices, such as whom they welcome, sit with, eat with, and include, reflect the truth that all believers are one in Christ.

This story also shows the danger of fear of others’ opinions. Peter knew what was right but changed his behavior under social pressure. Believers face similar pressures to distance themselves from people others look down on. Faithfulness to the gospel sometimes requires the courage to stay at the table.

Finally, Paul’s example shows that loving correction is sometimes necessary, even with respected leaders. When public behavior harms others and contradicts the gospel, it may need to be addressed openly. Such correction should be motivated by concern for the truth and for those being harmed, not by pride.

### *Galatians 2:16* — Justified Through Faith in Jesus Christ

> *“yet knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, even we believed in Christ Jesus, that we might be justified by faith in Christ and not by the works of the law, because no flesh will be justified by the works of the law.”*
>
> — *Galatians 2:16* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse is one of the clearest statements of the gospel in Paul’s letters. He uses the word “justified” three times. To be justified means to be declared righteous, to be put right with God, to be accepted by Him as being in the right. It is a legal term, like a judge’s verdict, but it also describes the restoration of a relationship.

Paul says that “a man is not justified by the works of the law.” “Works of the law” refers to doing what the Law of Moses commands. In the context of Galatians, Paul has especially in view the practices that marked Jews as distinct from Gentiles, such as circumcision, food laws, and Sabbath observance, but the principle applies to any attempt to be right with God through law-keeping.

Instead, a person is justified “through faith in Jesus Christ.” Paul emphasizes that even Jewish believers like himself and Peter, who had the Law, “believed in Christ Jesus, that we might be justified by faith in Christ.”

He ends with a reason drawn from *Psalm 143:2*: “because no flesh will be justified by the works of the law.” No human being can be made right with God by keeping the Law, because everyone falls short of it (*Romans 3:20*, 23).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The phrase translated “faith in Jesus Christ” can also be translated “the faithfulness of Jesus Christ.” Scholars have debated this for many years. Those who prefer “faithfulness of Christ” see Paul emphasizing Christ’s faithful obedience to the Father, even to death, as the basis of justification. Those who prefer “faith in Christ” see Paul emphasizing the believer’s trust in Christ. In this verse, Paul clearly speaks of believers trusting in Christ (“we believed in Christ Jesus”), so both ideas are present: believers are justified because of Christ’s faithful work, received through their faith in Him.

This verse was at the center of the Protestant Reformation in the sixteenth century, when Martin Luther and others found in it freedom from trying to earn God’s favor through religious works. Christians from many traditions agree that salvation is God’s gracious gift received through faith, though they have sometimes described the relationship between faith, works, and the sacraments in different ways. In recent decades, some scholars have emphasized that Paul’s argument in Galatians concerns not only individual salvation but also whether Gentiles can belong fully to God’s people without becoming Jews. Both concerns are present. Justification by faith means that every person, Jew or Gentile, comes to God on the same basis, and therefore all believers belong together.

Faith in this sense is not a work that earns salvation. It is trusting reliance on Christ, receiving what He has done. Genuine faith will produce a changed life (*Galatians 5:6*), but the changed life is the fruit of justification, not its basis.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Many people, including many churchgoers, live with a quiet belief that they must earn God’s acceptance by being good enough, religious enough, or disciplined enough. This verse offers freedom. God’s acceptance comes through faith in Christ, not through a record of achievements. Believers can rest in what Christ has done.

This truth also humbles. If no one is justified by works, then no believer can look down on another as less worthy. Everyone stands before God on the same ground: the grace of God received through faith. That truth should shape how believers treat those of different backgrounds, as Paul’s confrontation with Peter shows.

### *Galatians 2:20* — Christ Lives in Me

> *“I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself up for me.”*
>
> — *Galatians 2:20* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This is one of the most personal and beloved verses in Paul’s letters. “I have been crucified with Christ.” When Christ died, Paul died with Him. This is not a physical death but a spiritual union. Paul’s old life, the life of trying to be right with God by his own efforts and living for himself, came to an end at the cross.

“And it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” The center of Paul’s life has changed. He still has his own personality, but the driving force of his life is now the risen Christ living in him by the Holy Spirit.

“That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God.” Paul still lives in a human body, with its limitations and struggles. But he lives that life by trusting in Christ day by day.

“Who loved me and gave himself up for me.” Paul makes it deeply personal. Christ did not only love the world in general; He loved Paul specifically and gave Himself for him. The great love of God becomes intensely personal at the cross.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Paul develops this idea of union with Christ in many places. In *Romans 6:3–11*, he explains that believers were baptized into Christ’s death and raised to walk in newness of life. In *Colossians 3:3*, he says, “*For you died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God*” (*Colossians 3:3*). The Christian life is not merely imitation of Christ from a distance; it is participation in His life.

In the context of Galatians, this verse explains why returning to the Law makes no sense. The person who has died with Christ has died to the Law as a means of righteousness (v19). Their new life is not lived by law-keeping but by faith in the Son of God and by the power of Christ living in them.

The phrase “who loved me and gave himself up for me” is the only place in Paul’s letters where he speaks so directly of Christ’s love for him in the singular. It reveals the personal heart behind Paul’s theology. Everything he taught flowed from the wonder of being loved by Christ.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse changes how believers understand their identity. They are not simply people trying to be better. They are people who have died with Christ and in whom Christ now lives. Their old self does not have the final word. This truth can bring hope to those who feel trapped by their past or their failures.

It also shapes daily living. Each day can be lived “by faith in the Son of God,” trusting Him for strength, guidance, and grace in ordinary tasks and struggles. The Christian life is not lived by willpower alone but by reliance on Christ who lives within.

Finally, this verse invites every believer to receive Christ’s love personally. It is one thing to know that God loves the world; it is another to say, that the Son of God “*loved me and gave himself up for me*” (*v. 20*). That personal assurance can steady the heart in seasons of doubt, loneliness, or shame.

### *Galatians 2:21* — If Righteousness Came Through the Law, Christ Died for Nothing

> *“I don’t reject the grace of God. For if righteousness is through the law, then Christ died for nothing!”*
>
> — *Galatians 2:21* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul concludes his argument with a powerful statement. “I don’t reject the grace of God.” The teachers in Galatia were, in effect, setting aside God’s grace by insisting that the Law must be added to faith in Christ. Paul refuses to do that.

Then he gives the decisive reason: “For if righteousness is through the law, then Christ died for nothing!” If people could be made right with God by keeping the Law, then there would have been no need for Christ to die. His death would have been pointless.

This shows how serious the issue in Galatia was. Adding the Law as a requirement for righteousness did not simply add a few extra rules. It undermined the very reason for the cross.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The cross is the measure of how serious sin is and how great God’s grace is. If human effort could solve the problem of sin, God would not have given His Son. The fact that Christ died shows that no other way was sufficient. To trust in anything other than Christ for righteousness is, in effect, to say that His death was unnecessary.

Paul is not saying the Law is bad. In chapter 3 he will explain that the Law had a good purpose: it revealed sin and guided God’s people until Christ came. But it was never meant to be the means by which people are made right with God. That role belongs to Christ alone.

This verse also shows that grace and self-justification cannot be combined. A person either receives righteousness as a gift through Christ or tries to earn it through works. Mixing the two turns grace into something else. As Paul wrote in *Romans 11:6*, if it is by grace, it is no longer of works.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can slip into thinking that their standing with God depends on their performance, such as how much they pray, serve, or avoid sin. Those things are good fruits of faith, but they are not the basis of righteousness. This verse calls believers back to the cross as the only foundation of their acceptance with God.

This verse also encourages gratitude. Christ did not die for nothing. His death accomplished what no human effort ever could. Remembering this can turn anxious striving into grateful obedience, and it honors the immense cost of God’s grace.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Galatians 2* shows that the gospel unites people. The leaders in Jerusalem recognized that the same God was at work through Peter among Jews and through Paul among Gentiles. They gave Paul the right hand of fellowship, and they did not require Gentile believers to become Jews. The gospel creates one family from people of every background.

The confrontation at Antioch warns that this unity can be undermined by fear and social pressure, even among respected leaders. When Peter withdrew from Gentile believers, he denied in practice what he believed in principle. Churches today can examine their own practices to see whether they welcome and include all believers equally, and believers can find courage to stand with those others exclude.

At the heart of the chapter is the truth that people are justified through faith in Jesus Christ, not by the works of the Law. No one earns God’s acceptance. Everyone receives it as a gift through Christ. This truth brings freedom from anxious striving and humility that rules out looking down on others.

Finally, Paul’s words “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” describe the inner reality of the Christian life. Believers have died to the old way of self-effort and now live by faith in the Son of God, who loved them and gave Himself for them. Holding on to grace honors the cross. If righteousness came through the Law, Christ would have died for nothing, but He did not die in vain. His death is the source of new life for all who believe.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You that I am made right with God not by my own works but through faith in You. Thank You that You loved me and gave Yourself up for me. I have been crucified with You; let it be no longer I who live, but You who live in me. Teach me to live each day by faith in You. Keep me from setting aside Your grace by trusting in my own efforts. Give me the courage to stand for the truth of the gospel, even when I feel pressure to please others. Help me to welcome and stand with all Your people, whatever their background, and never to treat any of them as second-class members of Your family. Make me humble enough to receive correction and wise enough to offer it in love. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Galatians · Chapter 3 of 6

# Galatians — Chapter 3

Chapter Theme: Children of Abraham Through Faith

[Read Galatians 3 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/GAL03.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul reminds the Galatians that they received the Holy Spirit by believing the message about Christ crucified, not by keeping the Law, and asks why they would now try to finish by human effort what began by the Spirit. He shows from Scripture that Abraham was counted righteous by faith and that God promised to bless all nations through him. Christ redeemed us from the Law’s curse by becoming a curse for us, so that Abraham’s blessing could come to the Gentiles. The Law, given centuries after the promise, could not cancel it; it served as a guardian until Christ came. Now all who believe are God’s children, clothed with Christ, one in Him, and heirs of the promise.

## Chapter Background and Story

In chapters 1 and 2, Paul defended the gospel by telling his own story. In chapter 3, he turns to two kinds of evidence: the Galatians’ own experience and the testimony of Scripture.

The teachers troubling the Galatians likely appealed heavily to Abraham. In *Genesis 17*, God commanded Abraham and his descendants to be circumcised as the sign of the covenant. The teachers probably argued that anyone who wanted to be counted among Abraham’s children, and so share in God’s blessing, needed to be circumcised and keep the Law given through Moses.

Paul meets this argument head-on. He goes back to Abraham, but to an earlier moment: *Genesis 15*, where Abraham believed God and was counted righteous, years before he was circumcised. He also points to God’s promise in *Genesis 12* that all nations would be blessed through Abraham. Paul argues that the true children of Abraham are those who share Abraham’s faith, and that this blessing comes to the nations through Christ.

The chapter also addresses an obvious question: If righteousness does not come through the Law, why did God give the Law at all? Paul’s answer gives one of the most important explanations in the New Testament of the Law’s purpose.

### The Galatians’ Experience (*3:1–5*)

“*Foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you not to obey the truth, before whose eyes Jesus Christ was openly portrayed among you as crucified?*” (*v. 1*) Paul’s language is strong. “Bewitched” suggests they had fallen under a kind of spell. When Paul preached among them, he proclaimed Christ crucified so vividly that it was as if a public notice had been posted before their eyes. How could they turn away from such a clear message? Paul’s questions about how they received the Spirit are studied below.

“*Did you suffer so many things in vain, if it is indeed in vain?*” (*v. 4*) The Galatians had apparently suffered for their faith, perhaps persecution of the kind recorded in *Acts 14:2*, 19, 22. Would they now throw all that away? Paul still hopes it is not in vain.

“*He therefore who supplies the Spirit to you and does miracles among you, does he do it by the works of the law, or by hearing of faith?*” (*v. 5*) God was continuing to work powerfully among them, even miraculously. All this came through faith, not through Law-keeping.

### The Example of Abraham (*3:6–9*)

“*Even so, Abraham “believed God, and it was counted to him for righteousness.”*” (*v. 6*) Paul quotes *Genesis 15:6*, the same verse he uses in *Romans 4:3*. Abraham was counted righteous because he trusted God’s promise, not because of his works. “*Know therefore that those who are of faith are children of Abraham*” (*v. 7*). Being a child of Abraham is not a matter of physical descent or of circumcision, but of sharing Abraham’s faith.

“*The Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, preached the Good News beforehand to Abraham, saying, “In you all the nations will be blessed.”*” (*v. 8*) Paul quotes *Genesis 12:3*. From the very beginning, God’s plan included the Gentiles. Scripture “*preached the Good News beforehand to Abraham*” (*v. 8*). “*So then, those who are of faith are blessed with the faithful Abraham*” (*v. 9*).

### The Curse of the Law and Christ’s Redemption (*3:10–14*)

“*For as many as are of the works of the law are under a curse. For it is written, “Cursed is everyone who doesn’t continue in all things that are written in the book of the law, to do them.”*” (*v. 10*) Paul quotes *Deuteronomy 27:26*. The Law required complete obedience, and it pronounced a curse on those who failed to keep it. Since no one keeps the Law perfectly, those who rely on the Law for righteousness place themselves under its curse.

“*Now that no man is justified by the law before God is evident, for, “The righteous will live by faith.”*” (*v. 11*) Paul quotes *Habakkuk 2:4*, as he does in *Romans 1:17*. Even in the Old Testament, life before God was by faith. “*The law is not of faith, but, “The man who does them will live by them.”*” (*v. 12*) Quoting *Leviticus 18:5*, Paul notes that the Law operates on the principle of doing. It is a different principle from faith. How Christ removes the curse is studied below.

### The Promise and the Law (*3:15–22*)

Paul uses an illustration from ordinary life. “*Brothers, speaking of human terms, though it is only a man’s covenant, yet when it has been confirmed, no one makes it void or adds to it*” (*v. 15*). Once a legal agreement or will has been ratified, no one can add new conditions to it later. In the same way, God made a binding promise to Abraham.

“*Now the promises were spoken to Abraham and to his offspring. He doesn’t say, “To descendants”, as of many, but as of one, “To your offspring”, which is Christ*” (*v. 16*). The Hebrew word for “offspring” (or “seed”) can refer to one person or to many descendants. Paul sees its ultimate fulfillment in one descendant, Christ, through whom all of Abraham’s true offspring are gathered (v29).

“*Now I say this: A covenant confirmed beforehand by God in Christ, the law, which came four hundred thirty years after, does not annul, so as to make the promise of no effect*” (*v. 17*). The Law came centuries after the promise to Abraham. It could not change the terms of a promise God had already made. “*For if the inheritance is of the law, it is no more of promise; but God has granted it to Abraham by promise*” (*v. 18*). The inheritance is a gift.

“*Then why is there the law? It was added because of transgressions, until the offspring should come to whom the promise has been made*” (*v. 19*). This is the natural question. Paul says the Law was “added because of transgressions.” It made sin clear as a violation of God’s will (*Romans 4:15*; *5:20*), and it restrained sin in Israel’s life. But it was temporary, meant to last “until the offspring should come,” that is, until Christ. Paul notes that it was given through angels and a mediator, Moses (see *Acts 7:53*; *Hebrews 2:2*), while the promise came directly from God.

“*Is the law then against the promises of God? Certainly not! For if there had been a law given which could make alive, most certainly righteousness would have been of the law*” (*v. 21*). The Law is not opposed to God’s promises. But it could not give life. Only God’s Spirit, given through Christ, can do that. “*But the Scripture imprisoned all things under sin, that the promise by faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe*” (*v. 22*). Scripture shows that everyone is under sin, so that the promise comes to all in the same way: through faith in Christ.

### Under a Guardian; Children of God (*3:23–29*)

The Law’s role as a guardian and the believer’s new identity as God’s child are studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Galatians 3:2–3* — Begun in the Spirit

> *“I just want to learn this from you: Did you receive the Spirit by the works of the law, or by hearing of faith? Are you so foolish? Having begun in the Spirit, are you now completed in the flesh?”*
>
> — *Galatians 3:2–3* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul asks the Galatians to think about their own experience. “Did you receive the Spirit by the works of the law, or by hearing of faith?” The Galatians knew how they had come to faith. They had heard the gospel of Christ crucified, believed it, and received the Holy Spirit. They had not first been circumcised or kept the Law. The Spirit came to them as a gift when they believed.

The phrase “hearing of faith” could mean hearing that leads to faith, or hearing the message about faith. Either way, the Spirit came through receiving the gospel by faith, not through religious performance.

Then Paul asks: “Are you so foolish? Having begun in the Spirit, are you now completed in the flesh?” “The flesh” here refers to human effort, especially relying on outward religious acts like circumcision. The Galatians had begun their new life by the power of God’s Spirit. Now they were trying to bring it to completion by their own efforts. Paul sees this as completely backward.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The gift of the Holy Spirit was the great sign, promised by the prophets, that God’s new age had come (*Joel 2:28–29*; *Ezekiel 36:26–27*). For Paul, the presence of the Spirit is the clearest evidence that someone belongs to God (*Romans 8:9*). The Galatians already had the Spirit, which proved they already belonged fully to God’s people. Nothing needed to be added.

This passage also shows that the Christian life is not “begun by grace and finished by effort.” It is lived from beginning to end by the Spirit through faith. Believers do grow, work, and obey, but they do so by the Spirit’s power, not by self-reliant striving. Paul will develop this in chapter 5, where he describes walking by the Spirit and bearing the Spirit’s fruit.

There is a temptation in every generation to think that, having been saved by grace, believers must now prove themselves or maintain their standing through their own performance. Paul’s question exposes that error.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Many believers start their Christian life with joy and dependence on God, but over time drift into a performance-based faith, measuring their worth by how well they keep spiritual disciplines or rules. This passage invites them to return to the beginning. The same Spirit who gave them new life is the one who will complete the work (*Philippians 1:6*).

This does not make effort unimportant. Prayer, Scripture reading, worship, and obedience matter. But they are ways of keeping in step with the Spirit, not ways of earning God’s acceptance. Believers can approach these practices with freedom and joy, relying on God’s power rather than their own.

### *Galatians 3:13–14* — Christ Became a Curse for Us

> *“Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us. For it is written, ‘Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree,’ that the blessing of Abraham might come on the Gentiles through Christ Jesus, that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith.”*
>
> — *Galatians 3:13–14* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul has just explained that everyone who relies on the Law for righteousness is under a curse, because no one keeps it perfectly. Now he announces the good news: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law.”

“Redeemed” means bought back or set free by paying a price. In the ancient world, the word was used for freeing slaves or captives. Christ paid the price to set people free from the curse of the Law.

How did He do it? By “having become a curse for us.” Christ took the curse on Himself. Paul supports this with *Deuteronomy 21:23*: “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree.” In Israel, the body of an executed criminal was sometimes hung on a tree as a sign that he was under God’s judgment. Jesus was crucified on a wooden cross, and in this way He took the place of one under the curse.

Verse 14 explains the purpose. First, “that the blessing of Abraham might come on the Gentiles through Christ Jesus.” Through Christ, the promise to bless all nations is fulfilled. Second, “that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith.” The blessing of Abraham includes the gift of the Holy Spirit, received by faith.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses express the heart of substitution: Christ took what belonged to others so that they might receive what belonged to Him. This is the same “great exchange” Paul describes in *2 Corinthians 5:21*. Christ, who never sinned, bore the curse that sin deserves, so that those who were under the curse could receive God’s blessing.

For many Jews in Paul’s day, the idea of a crucified Messiah was a contradiction. How could someone under God’s curse be God’s chosen one? Paul himself once thought this way. But after meeting the risen Christ, he understood: Jesus was under the curse not for His own sin but for others. The cross, which looked like God’s rejection, was actually God’s way of rescuing His people.

Notice that the blessing reaches both Jews and Gentiles. The “us” who were redeemed from the curse of the Law likely refers first to Jewish people, who were under the Law. But the result is that the blessing reaches the Gentiles too, and “we,” all believers, receive the Spirit by faith. In Christ, Jew and Gentile share one blessing.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Many people carry a deep sense of being under condemnation, haunted by guilt, shame, or the feeling that God is against them. This passage proclaims that Christ has borne the curse. For those who trust in Him, there is no curse left to bear. As Paul writes in *Romans 8:1*, there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.

This truth also calls for worship and gratitude. Christ willingly took the curse on Himself out of love. Remembering the cost of redemption can deepen love for Him and strengthen the desire to live for Him, not out of fear, but in thankfulness.

### *Galatians 3:24–25* — The Law as Our Guardian

> *“So that the law has become our tutor to bring us to Christ, that we might be justified by faith. But now that faith has come, we are no longer under a tutor.”*
>
> — *Galatians 3:24–25* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul uses an image familiar in the Greek and Roman world. The word translated “tutor” (sometimes “guardian” or “schoolmaster”) referred to a household servant, often a slave, who was responsible for a child’s supervision and discipline. This servant escorted the child to and from school, watched over their behavior, and sometimes punished them. The tutor was not the teacher but a supervisor. And once the child came of age, the tutor’s role ended.

Paul says the Law played this role for God’s people. In verse 23 he explains that before faith came, “we were kept in custody under the law.” The Law guarded, restrained, and disciplined God’s people for a time.

“So that the law has become our tutor to bring us to Christ, that we might be justified by faith.” The phrase “to bring us to Christ” can mean either “leading us to Christ” or “until Christ came.” Both ideas fit. The Law prepared the way for Christ and served until He came.

“But now that faith has come, we are no longer under a tutor.” Now that Christ has come and faith in Him has been revealed, the Law’s guardianship has ended. God’s people have come of age.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This image shows both the value and the limits of the Law. The Law was good and served a necessary purpose. It revealed God’s holiness, exposed sin, restrained wrongdoing, and pointed forward to Christ through its sacrifices and promises. Paul never dismisses it as worthless.

But the Law was temporary in its role as guardian. It was never meant to be the final stage of God’s dealings with His people. Its job was to bring them safely to the time of maturity, when they would receive the full rights of children (*Galatians 4:1–7*). Returning to the guardian now would be like an adult insisting on being escorted to school by a childhood supervisor.

This does not mean that God’s moral will has been abolished. Paul will say that love fulfills the Law (*Galatians 5:14*), and that those who walk by the Spirit bear the fruit that no law condemns (*Galatians 5:22–23*). Christians have differed on how exactly the Old Testament Law applies to believers today, but they broadly agree that the moral character of God revealed in the Law remains, while believers are no longer under the Law as a covenant system for righteousness. They live under Christ, by the Spirit.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

The Old Testament Law remains a precious part of Scripture. Believers can read it to learn about God’s holiness, His justice, His care for the poor and vulnerable, and His plan of redemption that points to Christ. It still teaches, warns, and guides.

At the same time, this passage frees believers from living as though they were still under a guardian. Their relationship with God is not that of a child under constant supervision but of mature children who know and love their Father. Obedience flows from the Spirit’s life within, not from external rules alone.

### *Galatians 3:26–29* — All One in Christ Jesus

> *“For you are all children of God, through faith in Christ Jesus. For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ. There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free man, there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus. If you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring and heirs according to promise.”*
>
> — *Galatians 3:26–29* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul now describes the new identity of believers. “For you are all children of God, through faith in Christ Jesus.” The Galatians did not need to become Jews to become God’s children. They were already His children through faith in Christ. The word “all” is important: every believer, without exception, is a child of God.

“For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ.” In baptism, believers are united with Christ. Paul uses the image of putting on clothes. Just as clothing covers a person, Christ now surrounds and defines those who belong to Him.

Then comes one of the most remarkable statements in the New Testament: “There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free man, there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus.” These three pairs represented the deepest divisions of the ancient world: ethnic and religious, social and economic, and gender. Paul declares that in Christ, none of these divisions determine a person’s standing before God. All are equally God’s children, equally clothed with Christ, equally heirs.

“If you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring and heirs according to promise.” Because Christ is the true offspring of Abraham (v16), all who belong to Him are Abraham’s offspring too. The Gentile believers in Galatia did not need circumcision to be Abraham’s children. They already were, through Christ.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This passage reveals the social power of the gospel. In the ancient world, a Jewish man might thank God daily that he was not a Gentile, a slave, or a woman, a prayer known from later Jewish writings and reflecting attitudes common in the period. Greek writers expressed similar sentiments. Paul’s statement directly overturns such thinking. In Christ, all have equal access to God and equal dignity as His children.

Paul does not mean that ethnic, social, or gender differences disappear. Jews remained Jews and Gentiles remained Gentiles; men and women remained men and women. Christians from different traditions have discussed how this verse relates to questions such as roles in marriage and church leadership, and they have reached different conclusions on those questions. But all agree that this verse affirms the full and equal standing of every believer before God. No one is a second-class member of God’s family because of their ethnicity, social status, or sex.

Over time, this vision helped transform societies. It challenged racial and ethnic prejudice in the church, and it planted seeds that would later grow into Christian opposition to slavery. The church has not always lived up to it, but the vision stands as a call to repentance and renewal.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage challenges every form of division and prejudice within the church. Believers of every ethnic group, economic level, and both sexes belong to one family. Churches can ask whether their life together reflects this unity: whether all are welcomed, valued, heard, and included.

It also gives each believer a secure identity. In a world that ranks people by race, wealth, education, or appearance, the gospel declares that every believer is a child of God, clothed with Christ, and an heir of God’s promises. That identity cannot be taken away by others’ opinions.

Finally, this passage calls believers to treat one another accordingly. If all are one in Christ, then contempt, favoritism, and exclusion have no place among God’s people. The family of God is meant to display to the world a unity that only Christ can create.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Galatians 3* reminds believers how their life with God began and how it continues. The Galatians received the Holy Spirit by believing the message of Christ crucified, not by keeping the Law. Paul warns them not to try to finish by human effort what God began by His Spirit. Believers today face the same temptation to drift from grace into performance. The Christian life, from start to finish, is lived by faith and by the power of the Spirit.

The chapter also shows that God’s plan has always been one of grace and faith. Abraham was counted righteous because he believed God, and God promised that all nations would be blessed through him. That promise is fulfilled in Christ, who took the curse of the Law on Himself so that the blessing of Abraham could reach the whole world. Those burdened by guilt can rest in the truth that Christ has borne the curse.

Paul’s explanation of the Law helps believers read the Old Testament rightly. The Law was a good guardian that revealed sin and pointed to Christ, but it was never the way to become righteous before God. Now that Christ has come, believers live as mature children of God, guided by the Spirit.

Finally, the chapter gives a breathtaking vision of unity. In Christ, there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female, for all are one in Christ Jesus. Every believer is a child of God, clothed with Christ, and an heir of the promise. This truth calls the church to welcome all equally and to reject every form of prejudice and exclusion, displaying the unity that the gospel creates.

## Chapter Prayer

Father, thank You that I received Your Spirit not by my own works but by believing the message of Christ crucified. Keep me from trying to complete by my own effort what You began by Your Spirit. Thank You that, like Abraham, I am counted righteous through faith. Thank You, Lord Jesus, for becoming a curse for me, so that I could be free from condemnation and receive the blessing of Abraham and the promise of the Spirit. Thank You for the Law that showed me my need and led me to You. Thank You that I am Your child, clothed with Christ, and an heir of Your promises. Help me to treat every believer as my brother or sister, whatever their background, status, or circumstances. Make Your church a living picture of our oneness in Christ Jesus. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
