Galatians · Chapter 4 of 6

# Galatians — Chapter 4

Chapter Theme: No Longer Slaves, but Children and Heirs

[Read Galatians 4 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/GAL04.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul explains that before Christ came, God’s people were like underage heirs, no better off than slaves. But when the fullness of time came, God sent His Son, born of a woman and under the Law, to redeem those under the Law so that they might be adopted as God’s children, and He sent the Spirit of His Son into their hearts crying, “Abba, Father.” Paul pleads with the Galatians not to return to slavery, recalls their warm welcome when he first came to them in illness, and longs for Christ to be formed in them. Using the story of Hagar and Sarah, he shows that believers are children of promise and of freedom.

## Chapter Background and Story

Chapter 4 continues Paul’s argument from chapter 3. He has shown that believers are children of God and heirs of the promise to Abraham through faith in Christ (*Galatians 3:26–29*). Now he develops what it means to be a child and heir, and he warns the Galatians about the folly of going back to a state of slavery.

The chapter moves through three sections. First, Paul uses an illustration from inheritance law to explain the difference between life before Christ and life in Christ (*4:1–11*). Second, he makes a heartfelt personal appeal, reminding the Galatians of their relationship with him (*4:12–20*). Third, he offers a figurative reading of the story of Abraham’s two sons, Ishmael and Isaac, to show that believers in Christ are children of the free woman, heirs of God’s promise (*4:21–31*).

Throughout, the key contrast is between slavery and sonship, bondage and freedom. Paul is deeply concerned that the Galatians, who had been set free, were on the verge of putting themselves back into chains.

### Heirs Under Guardians (*4:1–3*)

“*But I say that so long as the heir is a child, he is no different from a bondservant, though he is lord of all*” (*v. 1*), “*but is under guardians and stewards until the day appointed by the father*” (*v. 2*). In the ancient world, a young heir to a great estate had no more freedom than a household slave until he came of age. He was under the authority of guardians and managers until the time his father had set.

“*So we also, when we were children, were held in bondage under the elemental principles of the world*” (*v. 3*). “Elemental principles” translates a word that can mean basic principles, the ABCs of something, or the elemental spiritual forces believed to govern the world. Paul seems to use it broadly for the basic, immature religious systems people lived under before Christ, whether the Law for Jews or pagan religion for Gentiles. Both were forms of bondage compared with the freedom of God’s children.

### God Sent His Son and His Spirit (*4:4–7*)

These central verses are studied below.

### Do Not Turn Back (*4:8–11*)

“*However at that time, not knowing God, you were in bondage to those who by nature are not gods*” (*v. 8*). Before they believed, the Galatians had worshiped idols. The question in verse 9 is studied below.

“*You observe days, months, seasons, and years*” (*v. 10*). The Galatians had begun to keep the Jewish religious calendar, such as Sabbaths, new moons, and festivals, as requirements for righteousness. Paul is not condemning the observance of special days in itself; in *Romans 14:5–6* he allows believers freedom on such matters. His concern is that the Galatians were treating these observances as necessary to be right with God, which was a return to bondage. “*I am afraid for you, that I might have wasted my labor for you*” (*v. 11*).

### A Personal Appeal (*4:12–20*)

Paul’s tone becomes tender and personal. “*I beg you, brothers, become as I am, for I also have become as you are. You did me no wrong*” (*v. 12*). Paul, a Jew, had lived like a Gentile among them, free from the Law’s requirements, in order to reach them. Now he asks them to become like him, free in Christ.

“*but you know that because of weakness in the flesh I preached the Good News to you the first time*” (*v. 13*). Paul had first come to Galatia because of an illness. We do not know what it was. Some suggest malaria, which was common along the coast, leading him to travel to the higher, cooler region. Others connect it with his eyes because of verse 15. “*That which was a temptation to you in my flesh, you didn’t despise nor reject; but you received me as an angel of God, even as Christ Jesus*” (*v. 14*). In the ancient world, illness was often seen as a sign of divine displeasure, and some people might have spat or turned away from someone sick. The Galatians did not. They welcomed Paul warmly.

“*What was the blessing you enjoyed? For I testify to you that, if possible, you would have plucked out your eyes and given them to me*” (*v. 15*). Their love had been so great they would have given him anything, perhaps literally their own eyes if his illness affected his sight. “*So then, have I become your enemy by telling you the truth?*” (*v. 16*) Paul is pained that their affection has cooled because he told them the truth.

“*They zealously seek you in no good way. No, they desire to alienate you, that you may seek them*” (*v. 17*). The false teachers were courting the Galatians, but for selfish reasons. They wanted to cut them off from Paul so the Galatians would depend on them. Paul’s deep longing for them is studied below.

### Hagar and Sarah (*4:21–31*)

“*Tell me, you that desire to be under the law, don’t you listen to the law?*” (*v. 21*) “The law” here means the books of Moses, including Genesis. Paul turns to a story from Genesis to make his point.

“*For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by the servant, and one by the free woman*” (*v. 22*). Abraham’s first son, Ishmael, was born to Hagar, Sarah’s Egyptian servant, when Abraham and Sarah tried to fulfill God’s promise by human means (*Genesis 16*). His second son, Isaac, was born to Sarah, the free woman, in her old age, as God had promised (*Genesis 21*). “*However, the son by the servant was born according to the flesh, but the son by the free woman was born through promise*” (*v. 23*).

“*These things contain an allegory, for these are two covenants. One is from Mount Sinai, bearing children to bondage, which is Hagar*” (*v. 24*). Paul uses the story figuratively. Hagar represents the covenant from Mount Sinai, the Law, which, when used as a way of being right with God, produces bondage. “*For this Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia, and answers to the Jerusalem that exists now, for she is in bondage with her children*” (*v. 25*). “The Jerusalem that exists now” refers to the religious system centered on the Law that the false teachers were promoting. “*But the Jerusalem that is above is free, which is the mother of us all*” (*v. 26*). The heavenly Jerusalem, God’s new covenant community, is free, and all believers are her children.

“*For it is written, “Rejoice, you barren who don’t bear. Break out and shout, you who don’t travail. For the desolate women have more children than her who has a husband.”*” (*v. 27*) Paul quotes *Isaiah 54:1*, a promise of joy to a desolate Jerusalem after exile. Just as Sarah, once barren, became the mother of a great people, so God’s new community, born by His promise, would have countless children.

“*Now we, brothers, as Isaac was, are children of promise*” (*v. 28*). Believers, like Isaac, were born by God’s power and promise, not by human effort. “*But as then, he who was born according to the flesh persecuted him who was born according to the Spirit, so also it is now*” (*v. 29*). Jewish tradition interpreted *Genesis 21:9* as Ishmael mocking or mistreating Isaac. Paul sees a parallel in how the false teachers were pressuring the Galatian believers.

“*However, what does the Scripture say? “Throw out the servant and her son, for the son of the servant will not inherit with the son of the free woman.”*” (*v. 30*) Quoting Sarah’s words in *Genesis 21:10*, Paul calls the Galatians to reject the false teaching that would bring them into bondage. “*So then, brothers, we are not children of a servant, but of the free woman*” (*v. 31*).

It is important to read this passage carefully. Paul is contrasting two ways of relating to God, by human effort under the Law or by God’s promise and Spirit, and he is addressing false teachers within the church. He is not condemning the Jewish people as a whole, whom he loved deeply and for whom he prayed (*Romans 9:1–5*; *10:1*). Nor should this passage be used to demean Hagar or her descendants. Genesis shows God’s tender care for Hagar: He saw her in her distress, called her by name, and promised to bless her son (*Genesis 16:7–13*; *21:17–20*). Hagar is the only person in Scripture who gives God a name, calling Him “*You are a God who sees*” (*Genesis 16:13*). Paul’s figurative use of the story makes a point about covenants, not about the worth of persons.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Galatians 4:4–5* — When the Fullness of Time Came

> *“But when the fullness of the time came, God sent out his Son, born to a woman, born under the law, that he might redeem those who were under the law, that we might receive the adoption as children.”*
>
> — *Galatians 4:4–5* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These verses describe the turning point of history. “When the fullness of the time came” means when the time set by the Father had arrived, like the date appointed for an heir to come of age (v2). God had been preparing for this moment for centuries.

“God sent out his Son.” The Son existed before He was sent. He came from the Father into the world. This shows Christ’s divine origin.

“Born to a woman.” Jesus was fully human, born as every human being is born. This phrase emphasizes His real humanity.

“Born under the law.” Jesus was born a Jew, circumcised on the eighth day, and lived under the Law of Moses. He kept it perfectly.

The purpose is twofold: “that he might redeem those who were under the law,” setting them free from its bondage and curse (*Galatians 3:13*), and “that we might receive the adoption as children.” Through Christ, people who were like slaves become God’s adopted children with full rights in His family.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses are a compact summary of the incarnation. The eternal Son of God became fully human and entered fully into the human condition, including life under the Law, in order to rescue those who were under it. He stood where they stood so that He could bring them where He is.

The phrase “fullness of the time” suggests that God prepared the world for Christ’s coming. Many have noted that the first century provided remarkable conditions for the spread of the gospel: a common language (Greek), Roman roads and relative peace, Jewish communities scattered throughout the empire with synagogues and the Scriptures, and widespread longing for spiritual truth. More importantly, it was the moment God had appointed in His plan, the moment when the promises to Abraham and the prophets would be fulfilled.

“Adoption” was a significant legal practice in the Roman world. An adopted son received a new identity, a new name, and full rights of inheritance, and his old debts were canceled. Paul uses this image to describe what God does for believers. They are not merely forgiven servants; they are beloved children with a full place in the family.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses remind believers that God’s timing is purposeful. He sent His Son at exactly the right moment. In seasons when God seems slow, believers can trust that He is working toward the fullness of His time in their lives as well.

They also invite believers to rest in their identity as God’s adopted children. Adoption is not a lesser form of belonging; it is a deliberate choice of love. Those who feel unwanted, rejected, or out of place can know that God chose to bring them into His family at great cost, through the sending of His Son.

### *Galatians 4:6–7* — The Spirit Cries, “*Abba, Father*” (*v. 6*)

> *“And because you are children, God sent out the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father!’ So you are no longer a bondservant, but a son; and if a son, then an heir of God through Christ.”*
>
> — *Galatians 4:6–7* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

God not only sent His Son to make people His children; He also sent His Spirit to make them know it. “Because you are children, God sent out the Spirit of his Son into your hearts.”

The Spirit is called “the Spirit of his Son.” The same Spirit who filled Jesus now lives in believers, and He shares with them Jesus’ own relationship with the Father.

The Spirit cries out, “Abba, Father!” “Abba” is an Aramaic word for father, used by children and adults for their own fathers. It expresses closeness, trust, and affection. Jesus used this word when He prayed in Gethsemane (*Mark 14:36*). Now believers, by the Spirit, can address God the same way.

“So you are no longer a bondservant, but a son; and if a son, then an heir of God through Christ.” Paul switches from “you” plural to “you” singular, making it personal for each reader. Each believer is no longer a slave but a child, and therefore an heir. In the ancient world, “son” was the legal term for an heir; Paul applies it to all believers, men and women alike (see *Galatians 3:28*; *2 Corinthians 6:18*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show the cooperation of the Father, Son, and Spirit in salvation. The Father sent the Son to redeem, and the Father sent the Spirit to dwell in believers’ hearts. Salvation is the work of the whole Trinity, bringing people into the very life of God.

Paul writes something very similar in *Romans 8:15–16*, where he says believers received the Spirit of adoption, by whom they cry “Abba! Father!”, and the Spirit testifies with their spirit that they are God’s children. Assurance of belonging to God is not only a matter of reasoning; it is also the inner witness of the Spirit, who draws believers to pray to God as Father.

The contrast between slave and child is central. A slave serves out of obligation and fear, never sure of their place. A child belongs, is loved, and will inherit. Returning to the Law as a way of being right with God would be like a child choosing to live as a slave. Paul cannot imagine why anyone would do that.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Many believers relate to God more like servants than children. They work hard to please Him, fear His disapproval, and are unsure of their standing. These verses invite them into the warmth of a child’s relationship with a loving Father. Prayer can be the simple, trusting cry of “Abba, Father.”

For people whose earthly fathers were absent, harsh, or abusive, the word “father” may be painful. God is not like a harmful earthly father. He is the perfect Father, full of love, faithfulness, and care. The Spirit can gradually heal the wounds of the past and teach the heart to trust God as the Father it has always needed.

Being an heir also gives hope. Believers have a future inheritance in God that cannot be lost. Their present struggles are not the whole story; they are heirs of God through Christ.

### *Galatians 4:9* — Known by God

> *“But now that you have come to know God, or rather to be known by God, why do you turn back again to the weak and miserable elemental principles, to which you desire to be in bondage all over again?”*
>
> — *Galatians 4:9* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul reminds the Galatians of the change that had happened in their lives. “But now that you have come to know God.” Once they had worshiped idols (v8); now they knew the true God.

Then Paul corrects himself: “or rather to be known by God.” The more important truth is not that they had come to know God, but that God had come to know them. In the Bible, to be “known” by God means more than His awareness of someone. It means being personally chosen, loved, and claimed by Him.

Paul’s question follows: “why do you turn back again to the weak and miserable elemental principles, to which you desire to be in bondage all over again?” Having been known and loved by the living God, why would they return to the “weak and miserable” religious systems that could never save them? Paul is astonished that they would trade such a relationship for bondage.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The phrase “known by God” is deeply comforting. A believer’s relationship with God depends ultimately not on how well they know Him, which is always partial, but on His knowledge and love of them, which is complete and steadfast. Paul writes similarly in *1 Corinthians 8:3*: “*But anyone who loves God is known by him*” (*1 Corinthians 8:3*). And Jesus said of His sheep, “*I know them*” (*John 10:27*).

Paul’s surprising grouping of Jewish Law observance with pagan religion as “elemental principles” needs careful reading. He is not saying the Law was the same as idolatry. The Law was given by God and was holy (*Romans 7:12*). His point is that any religious system, whether pagan rituals or the Law, when used as the means of being right with God apart from Christ, leaves people in bondage. Only Christ sets people free.

The word “weak” echoes *Romans 8:3*, which says the Law was weak through the flesh. The Law could not give the power to obey. “Miserable” or “poor” means it could not provide the riches that come only through Christ.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

There are seasons when believers feel distant from God or unsure of how well they know Him. This verse turns attention to what matters most: God knows them. His knowledge is personal, loving, and secure. That can steady the heart when feelings fluctuate.

This verse also warns against drifting back into old patterns of bondage. These might be religious, such as relying on rituals or rule-keeping for acceptance, or they might be the idols of the culture, such as success, approval, or pleasure. Having been known by God, believers are invited to live in the freedom of His love rather than returning to what cannot satisfy.

### *Galatians 4:19* — Until Christ Is Formed in You

> *“My little children, of whom I am again in travail until Christ is formed in you—”*
>
> — *Galatians 4:19* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul’s appeal reaches its most tender point. “My little children.” He speaks with the affection of a parent. He was their spiritual father (or here, mother), since they came to faith through his ministry.

“Of whom I am again in travail.” Paul uses the image of childbirth. He had already gone through the pain of bringing them to faith once. Now, because they were in danger of turning away, he feels as if he must go through labor pains all over again.

“Until Christ is formed in you.” Paul’s goal is not merely that they agree with correct doctrine but that Christ Himself would take shape in their lives. “Formed” was used of a baby developing in the womb. Paul longs for Christ’s character to grow in them until it is fully developed.

Verse 20 adds his frustration: he wishes he could be with them and speak in a different tone, because he is perplexed about them. Letters can be easily misunderstood; Paul longs for face-to-face conversation.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reveals the goal of all Christian ministry and the goal of the Christian life: Christlikeness. Paul expresses the same aim elsewhere. Believers are being transformed into Christ’s image (*2 Corinthians 3:18*), predestined to be conformed to the image of God’s Son (*Romans 8:29*), and called to grow to the full stature of Christ (*Ephesians 4:13*).

It is remarkable that Paul, a man, uses the image of a mother in labor. He also describes himself as a nursing mother caring for her children in *1 Thessalonians 2:7*. These images show the intensity and tenderness of his love. True spiritual leadership is not cold or authoritarian; it involves deep, costly, nurturing love.

The process of Christ being formed in a believer takes time. Like a baby in the womb, it grows gradually and cannot be rushed. It also involves pain, both for those who are growing and for those who love and serve them.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse gives a clear goal for spiritual growth. The aim is not simply knowing more, doing more, or being more religious. It is Christ being formed in the heart: His love, humility, patience, purity, and faithfulness becoming part of who a person is.

It also shows what it means to care for others spiritually. Parents, mentors, pastors, and friends who invest in others’ faith often experience something like Paul’s labor pains: prayers, tears, patience, and disappointment along the way. This is part of love. Those who feel weary in this work can take heart that Paul felt the same, and that God is faithful to complete what He begins.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Galatians 4* celebrates the identity of believers as God’s adopted children. Before Christ, people lived like heirs who were still under guardians, no better off than slaves. But when the time was right, God sent His Son, born of a woman and under the Law, to redeem them and give them the full rights of children. He also sent His Spirit into their hearts, so that they can call God “Abba, Father.” This means believers can approach God with the confidence and affection of children, not with the fear of servants.

This identity changes everything. Believers are no longer slaves to sin, to empty religion, or to the expectations of others. They are known by God, loved by Him, and heirs of His promises. Paul’s warning against returning to bondage applies today whenever believers drift into trying to earn God’s approval or chase the false securities of the world.

Paul’s personal appeal also shows the heart of genuine Christian love. He remembered the Galatians’ kindness when he was sick, grieved when their affection cooled, and longed like a mother in labor for Christ to be formed in them. This reveals the goal of spiritual growth, Christlikeness, and the patient, costly love required to help others grow.

Finally, the story of Hagar and Sarah, read figuratively, reminds believers that they are children of promise and of freedom. Their life with God rests not on human achievement but on God’s faithful promise. At the same time, the original story reminds readers that God sees and cares for the overlooked and the mistreated, as He did for Hagar. Believers who have been made free in Christ are called to stand firm in that freedom and to extend His care to others.

## Chapter Prayer

Abba, Father, thank You that when the time was right You sent Your Son, born of a woman and born under the Law, to redeem me and make me Your child. Thank You for sending the Spirit of Your Son into my heart, so that I can call You Father. Help me to live as Your beloved child and heir, not as a fearful servant. Thank You that I am known by You; when I feel distant, remind me that Your love holds me. Keep me from turning back to anything that would put me in bondage again. Form Christ in me, day by day, until His character fills my life. Give me patient, tender love for those I help to grow in faith. Thank You that I am a child of promise and of freedom. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Galatians · Chapter 5 of 6

# Galatians — Chapter 5

Chapter Theme: Freedom in Christ and the Fruit of the Spirit

[Read Galatians 5 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/GAL05.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul calls the Galatians to stand firm in the freedom Christ has won and not return to slavery under the Law, warning that seeking righteousness through circumcision means falling away from grace. In Christ, what counts is faith working through love. Yet freedom is not a license for selfishness; it is the freedom to serve one another in love, which fulfills the whole Law. Paul describes the conflict between the flesh and the Spirit, lists the works of the flesh, and then describes the fruit the Spirit produces: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control. Those who live by the Spirit are called to keep in step with the Spirit.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Galatians 5* is the turning point of the letter. In chapters 1–4, Paul defended the gospel of grace and argued that believers are justified by faith in Christ, not by the works of the Law. Now he turns to the practical question: What does this freedom look like in daily life?

There were two dangers in Galatia. The first was legalism: the belief that one must keep the Law, especially circumcision, to be right with God. Paul addresses this in 5:1–12. The second danger was the opposite: if believers are not under the Law, might they live however they please? Paul addresses this in 5:13–26. His answer is that Christian freedom is not freedom to indulge selfish desires but freedom to love. The power for this new life is not the Law but the Holy Spirit.

This chapter contains some of the most beloved and practical teaching in Paul’s letters, especially the description of the fruit of the Spirit.

### Stand Firm in Freedom (*5:1–6*)

Paul’s opening call to freedom is studied below. He then speaks very directly. “*Behold, I, Paul, tell you that if you receive circumcision, Christ will profit you nothing*” (*v. 2*). Paul is not condemning circumcision as a physical act. He himself had Timothy circumcised for practical reasons of ministry (*Acts 16:3*). His point is that if the Galatians accepted circumcision as necessary for righteousness, they would be trusting in something other than Christ, and Christ would be of no benefit to them.

“*Yes, I testify again to every man who receives circumcision that he is a debtor to do the whole law*” (*v. 3*). Circumcision was the entrance into a whole system. Those who relied on it for righteousness would be obligated to keep the entire Law perfectly. “*You are alienated from Christ, you who desire to be justified by the law. You have fallen away from grace*” (*v. 4*). To seek righteousness through the Law is to step away from the realm of grace. Christians have discussed what “fallen away from grace” implies for questions of whether salvation can be lost, and they have answered differently. But all agree on Paul’s main point: grace and law-righteousness cannot be mixed. One must choose which to rely on.

“*For we through the Spirit, by faith wait for the hope of righteousness*” (*v. 5*). Believers wait in hope for the final declaration of their righteousness at Christ’s return, and they wait through the Spirit and by faith, not by works.

“*For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision amounts to anything, but faith working through love*” (*v. 6*). This is a key verse. Neither being circumcised nor being uncircumcised gives anyone an advantage before God. What matters is faith, and genuine faith shows itself in love. Paul’s teaching that we are justified by faith alone never meant that faith stands alone without producing love.

### Who Hindered You? (*5:7–12*)

“*You were running well! Who interfered with you that you should not obey the truth?*” (*v. 7*) Paul uses the image of a race. The Galatians had started well, but someone had cut in on them. “*This persuasion is not from him who calls you*” (*v. 8*). The new teaching did not come from God. “*A little yeast grows through the whole lump*” (*v. 9*). A small amount of false teaching can spread and corrupt a whole community (see *1 Corinthians 5:6*).

“*I have confidence toward you in the Lord that you will think no other way. But he who troubles you will bear his judgment, whoever he is*” (*v. 10*). Paul trusts that the Galatians will return to the truth. Those who are leading them astray will answer to God.

“*But I, brothers, if I still preach circumcision, why am I still persecuted? Then the stumbling block of the cross has been removed*” (*v. 11*). Some apparently claimed that Paul himself preached circumcision in some settings. Paul answers that if he did, he would not be persecuted. The message of the cross is offensive precisely because it says that nothing people can do, not even religious rituals, can earn salvation.

“*I wish that those who disturb you would cut themselves off*” (*v. 12*). This is one of Paul’s harshest statements. The phrase can mean “castrate themselves,” a biting comment directed at those so obsessed with circumcision. Some pagan priests in the region practiced self-castration, and Paul may be suggesting that the false teachers’ insistence on cutting the flesh was no better than pagan ritual. His sharp words show how seriously he took their harm to the Galatians. It is a moment of raw frustration and anger at those who were endangering his spiritual children.

### Called to Freedom and Love (*5:13–15*)

Paul’s teaching on the purpose of freedom is studied below. “*But if you bite and devour one another, be careful that you don’t consume one another*” (*v. 15*). The conflict in Galatia had become vicious. Paul warns that a community that fights like wild animals will destroy itself.

### Walking by the Spirit (*5:16–26*)

Paul now describes the inner conflict between the flesh and the Spirit, and the remedy, which are studied below. He then lists the works of the flesh. “*Now the deeds of the flesh are obvious, which are: adultery, sexual immorality, uncleanness, lustfulness*” (*v. 19*), “*idolatry, sorcery, hatred, strife, jealousies, outbursts of anger, rivalries, divisions, heresies*” (*v. 20*), “*envy, murders, drunkenness, orgies, and things like these*” (*v. 21*). The list includes sexual sins, religious sins, social sins, and sins of excess. Notice how many involve broken relationships: hatred, strife, jealousy, anger, rivalries, divisions, and envy. These were exactly the problems tearing the Galatian church apart. Paul warns that “*those who practice such things will not inherit God’s Kingdom*” (*v. 21*). He is describing a settled pattern of life, not an occasional failure that a believer repents of.

The fruit of the Spirit, which stands in contrast to these works, is studied below. “*Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and lusts*” (*v. 24*). At conversion, believers decisively rejected the old way of life, nailing it to the cross with Christ (see *Galatians 2:20*). “*If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit*” (*v. 25*). The word “walk” here means to keep in line or keep in step, like soldiers marching in formation. Since the Spirit has given believers life, they are to follow His lead in daily conduct. “*Let’s not become conceited, provoking one another, and envying one another*” (*v. 26*). Pride and competition are among the clearest signs of the flesh at work in a church.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Galatians 5:1* — Stand Firm in Freedom

> *“Stand firm therefore in the liberty by which Christ has made us free, and don’t be entangled again with a yoke of bondage.”*
>
> — *Galatians 5:1* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse summarizes everything Paul has said so far. “Stand firm therefore in the liberty by which Christ has made us free.” The purpose of Christ’s work was freedom. He did not set people free so they could be put back into another form of slavery.

Freedom here means freedom from the Law as a means of being right with God, freedom from the curse of the Law, freedom from sin’s power, and freedom from the “elemental principles” that once held them captive (*Galatians 4:3*, 9). Believers have been set free to live as God’s children.

“Stand firm” means to hold one’s ground, like a soldier refusing to retreat. The Galatians were being pressured to give up their freedom. Paul calls them to resist.

“Don’t be entangled again with a yoke of bondage.” A yoke was a wooden frame placed on the necks of animals to make them pull loads. In Jewish teaching, the Law was sometimes called a “yoke.” Peter described it at the Jerusalem Council as a yoke that neither the fathers nor his generation had been able to bear (*Acts 15:10*). Paul warns the Galatians not to put that yoke back on their necks as a way to earn righteousness. The word “again” reminds them that before Christ they had already lived under a different kind of bondage, the bondage of idolatry.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Freedom is one of the great themes of the gospel. Jesus announced that He came to proclaim release to the captives (*Luke 4:18*). He said, “*If therefore the Son makes you free, you will be free indeed*” (*John 8:36*). Christian freedom is not merely political or social freedom, though it has implications for both. It is the deep, inner freedom of being right with God and released from the condemnation and power of sin.

Jesus also spoke of a yoke, but a very different one. He said, “*Take my yoke upon you and learn from me*” (*Matthew 11:29*), and “*my yoke is easy, and my burden is light*” (*Matthew 11:30*). Following Christ is not a yoke of bondage but a yoke of rest. His people do not live without direction; they follow Him. But their following comes from love and grace, not from fear and obligation.

Freedom must be guarded. It is possible to lose the joy and experience of freedom by drifting back into legalism, fear, or performance-based religion. That is why Paul says “stand firm.”

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Many believers live under burdens Christ never placed on them: expectations of perfection, rules invented by people, or constant fear of failing God. This verse invites them to stand in the freedom Christ has given. Their acceptance with God is secure in Christ, and they do not need to earn it.

Standing firm sometimes means resisting pressure from others who want to add requirements to the gospel. It can also mean resisting inner voices that whisper that God’s love must be earned. Believers can return again and again to the truth that Christ has made them free.

At the same time, freedom in Christ is not a reason to look down on believers who have different convictions about secondary matters. Paul’s concern is about the gospel itself, not about every personal practice. Believers can stand firm in grace while extending grace to others.

### *Galatians 5:13–14* — Freedom to Serve in Love

> *“For you, brothers, were called for freedom. Only don’t use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love be servants to one another. For the whole law is fulfilled in one word, in this: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’”*
>
> — *Galatians 5:13–14* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul has strongly defended Christian freedom. Now he guards against a misunderstanding. “For you, brothers, were called for freedom.” Freedom is God’s calling for His people. “Only don’t use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh.” The word “opportunity” was used of a military base of operations, a foothold from which to launch an attack. Paul warns that freedom must not become a foothold for selfish desires.

Instead, “through love be servants to one another.” This is a beautiful paradox. Believers have been set free from slavery, and now they are called to serve one another, not out of compulsion, but freely and lovingly. True freedom is not freedom from others but freedom for others.

Verse 14 explains: “For the whole law is fulfilled in one word, in this: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’” Paul quotes *Leviticus 19:18*. The Law that the false teachers were so concerned about is fulfilled not by circumcision or calendar observance but by love. When believers love their neighbors, they accomplish what the Law was aiming at all along.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Jesus taught that the greatest commandments are to love God with all one’s heart and to love one’s neighbor as oneself (*Mark 12:29–31*). Paul says something similar in *Romans 13:8–10*: love is the fulfillment of the Law. The Law’s commands against adultery, murder, theft, and coveting are all ways of describing what love does and does not do.

This shows that Christian freedom is not lawlessness. Believers are free from the Law as a means of righteousness, but they are not free from the call to love. In fact, the Spirit empowers them to love in a way the Law alone could never produce. As Paul says in *Romans 8:4*, the righteous requirement of the Law is fulfilled in those who walk according to the Spirit.

The example of Christ shapes this teaching. Jesus, though free and Lord of all, took the form of a servant and washed His disciples’ feet (*John 13:12–15*). He used His freedom to serve. His followers are called to do the same.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Some people think of freedom as the right to do whatever they want. This passage presents a different vision: freedom is the ability to love and serve without fear, compulsion, or selfishness. Believers can use their freedom to care for others in practical ways, such as meeting needs, sharing burdens, and offering kindness.

When believers are unsure what to do in a particular situation, the law of love offers guidance. Does this action serve my neighbor’s good? Does it express love? These questions can guide decisions about time, money, speech, and conduct, especially in matters where Scripture gives no specific command.

Paul’s warning in verse 15 also applies to modern churches and communities. When believers bite and devour one another through gossip, criticism, and conflict, they harm the whole body. Love calls for patience, forgiveness, and building one another up.

### *Galatians 5:16–18* — Walk by the Spirit

> *“But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you won’t fulfill the lust of the flesh. For the flesh lusts against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh; and these are contrary to one another, that you may not do the things that you desire. But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law.”*
>
> — *Galatians 5:16–18* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

How can believers live in freedom without falling into selfishness? Paul’s answer is not more rules but the Holy Spirit. “Walk by the Spirit, and you won’t fulfill the lust of the flesh.”

To “walk” is to live day by day. Walking by the Spirit means living in dependence on the Spirit, following His guidance, and drawing on His power. When believers do this, they will not carry out the desires of the flesh.

“The flesh” in Paul’s letters often refers not to the physical body but to human nature turned in on itself and away from God, the source of selfish and sinful desires. Even after coming to Christ, believers still feel its pull.

Verse 17 describes the inner conflict: “the flesh lusts against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh; and these are contrary to one another.” There is a real struggle in the believer’s life. The Spirit pulls toward God and love; the flesh pulls toward self and sin. The phrase “that you may not do the things that you desire” may mean that the Spirit prevents believers from simply following the flesh’s desires, or that the conflict keeps believers from doing all the good they wish. Either way, the Christian life involves struggle.

Verse 18 brings assurance: “But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law.” Those who follow the Spirit’s leading do not need the Law as an external guardian. The Spirit leads them into the life the Law described.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This passage shows that the Christian life is not passive. There is a real battle. Believers are not yet perfect, and the flesh still exerts its pull. Paul describes a similar struggle in *Romans 7* and 8. But the struggle itself is a sign of life. Before coming to Christ, there was no Spirit to oppose the flesh. Now there is.

The answer to the flesh is not trying harder under the Law, which only exposes and sometimes stirs up sin (*Romans 7:8*). The answer is walking by the Spirit. The Spirit gives new desires, new power, and a new direction. As believers yield to Him, the flesh loses its grip.

Christians have described this process in different ways. Some emphasize a decisive work of the Spirit that gives victory over sin; others emphasize a lifelong, gradual process of growth. Paul’s language includes both a decisive break (v24) and an ongoing walk (v25). Both are part of the Spirit’s work.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Every believer knows the struggle Paul describes: wanting to do right and feeling the pull of selfishness, anger, lust, or pride. This passage offers both realism and hope. The struggle is normal, but believers are not left to fight alone. The Spirit lives in them.

Walking by the Spirit can be practiced in simple ways: beginning the day in prayer, asking for the Spirit’s help in moments of temptation, listening to Scripture, and paying attention to the Spirit’s quiet promptings toward love and holiness. Over time, these small steps shape a life.

When believers fail, as all do, they need not despair. The presence of the struggle shows that the Spirit is at work. They can confess, receive forgiveness, and keep walking.

### *Galatians 5:22–23* — The Fruit of the Spirit

> *“But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.”*
>
> — *Galatians 5:22–23* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After listing the “deeds of the flesh,” Paul describes something entirely different: “the fruit of the Spirit.” Notice the contrast between “deeds” and “fruit.” Deeds are things people produce by their own effort. Fruit is something that grows naturally from a living source. The qualities Paul lists are not achievements but the result of the Spirit’s life within believers.

Notice also that Paul says “fruit,” singular. These nine qualities are not separate fruits that believers can choose among. They are one harvest, growing together.

Love comes first, because it is the foundation of all the others (*1 Corinthians 13:13*). Joy is a deep gladness in God that does not depend on circumstances. Peace is a settled calm that comes from trusting God, and also harmony with others. Patience is the ability to endure difficult people and situations without giving up or lashing out. Kindness is a gracious, generous attitude toward others. Goodness is moral uprightness that actively does good. “Faith” here likely means faithfulness, being trustworthy and reliable. Gentleness, or meekness, is strength under control, a humble and considerate spirit. Self-control is mastery over one’s desires and impulses.

“Against such things there is no law.” No law forbids these qualities. They fulfill everything the Law aimed at.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The fruit of the Spirit is a portrait of Jesus Christ. He perfectly displayed love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control. As the Spirit forms Christ in believers (*Galatians 4:19*), these qualities grow in them.

The image of fruit has deep roots in Scripture. *Psalm 1* describes the righteous person as a tree planted by streams of water, bearing fruit in season. Jesus said He is the vine and His followers are the branches; those who remain in Him bear much fruit (*John 15:5*). Fruit grows through connection to the source. Believers bear the fruit of the Spirit by remaining connected to Christ.

Fruit also grows slowly. It takes time, seasons, and sometimes pruning. Believers should not be discouraged if they do not see full maturity immediately. The Spirit is patient, and growth is real even when it is gradual.

This list contrasts sharply with the works of the flesh. Many of the works of the flesh destroy relationships; nearly all of the fruit of the Spirit builds them up. The Spirit’s work creates community, harmony, and love.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage offers a beautiful picture of what a Spirit-filled life looks like. It is not measured mainly by spiritual gifts, religious activity, or dramatic experiences, but by character. Believers can ask God to grow these qualities in them and can notice where each is growing or lacking.

Because these qualities are fruit, the way to grow them is not mainly by gritting one’s teeth but by staying close to Christ through prayer, Scripture, worship, and fellowship. As believers abide in Him, the Spirit produces what they could not produce alone.

This list also provides a helpful way to evaluate leaders, movements, and teachings. Do they produce love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control? Or do they produce strife, division, pride, and envy? The fruit reveals the source.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Galatians 5* shows what Christian freedom looks like. Christ has set believers free, and they are called to stand firm in that freedom. They do not need to earn God’s acceptance through religious rituals or rule-keeping. Anything added to faith in Christ as a requirement for righteousness leads back into bondage. What matters is faith working through love.

But freedom is not a license for selfishness. Paul calls believers to use their freedom to serve one another in love, which fulfills the whole Law. Freedom is not freedom from others but freedom for others. This vision challenges both legalism, which adds rules, and license, which ignores God’s call to holiness and love.

The key to living this way is the Holy Spirit. Believers face a real struggle between the flesh and the Spirit, but they are not left to fight in their own strength. As they walk by the Spirit, keeping in step with His leading, the desires of the flesh lose their power. The works of the flesh, such as immorality, hatred, strife, jealousy, anger, and division, give way to the fruit of the Spirit.

That fruit, love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control, is a portrait of Christ Himself. It grows gradually as believers stay connected to Him. It is the true mark of a Spirit-filled life and community. In a world full of conflict and selfishness, a church that displays this fruit becomes a living testimony to the freedom and love of Christ.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for setting me free. Help me to stand firm in the freedom You have given me, and keep me from being entangled again in any yoke of bondage. Let my faith work through love. Teach me to use my freedom not to serve myself but to serve others with a willing and joyful heart. Forgive me for the times I have bitten and devoured others with my words. Holy Spirit, I want to walk by You today. When the desires of my flesh pull at me, strengthen me to follow Your leading. Grow Your fruit in me: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control. Keep me connected to Christ, the true vine, so that my life bears fruit that honors Him and blesses others. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Galatians · Chapter 6 of 6

# Galatians — Chapter 6

Chapter Theme: Bearing Burdens and Boasting in the Cross

[Read Galatians 6 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/GAL06.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul shows how life in the Spirit works out in community: gently restoring those caught in sin, bearing one another’s burdens to fulfill the law of Christ, examining one’s own work rather than comparing, and supporting those who teach. He warns that people reap what they sow, encourages believers not to grow weary in doing good, and urges them to do good to everyone, especially fellow believers. Writing the conclusion in his own hand, Paul exposes the motives of the false teachers and declares that he will boast only in the cross of Christ, through which the world has been crucified to him, because what matters is a new creation.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Galatians 6* completes the practical section that began in chapter 5. Paul has described the freedom of believers and the contrast between the works of the flesh and the fruit of the Spirit. Now he shows what Spirit-led living looks like in the everyday life of a church. The Galatian believers had been “biting and devouring” one another (*Galatians 5:15*). Paul gives them a very different vision: a community that restores, supports, shares, and does good.

Then, in verse 11, Paul takes the pen from the scribe who had been writing his words and writes the closing lines himself. In the ancient world, letters were often dictated, and the author would add a personal note at the end to confirm authenticity. Paul uses his closing to summarize the whole letter. He contrasts the false teachers, who wanted to boast in outward religious achievements, with his own boast in the cross of Christ.

### Restoring and Bearing Burdens (*6:1–5*)

Paul’s instructions about restoring those caught in sin and bearing burdens are studied below.

“*For if a man thinks himself to be something when he is nothing, he deceives himself*” (*v. 3*). Pride makes it impossible to bear others’ burdens, because a proud person thinks they are above such things. “*But let each man examine his own work, and then he will have reason to boast in himself, and not in someone else*” (*v. 4*). Instead of comparing themselves with others, believers should honestly evaluate their own lives before God. Any satisfaction should come from faithfulness to their own calling, not from feeling superior to others.

“*For each man will bear his own burden*” (*v. 5*). This might seem to contradict verse 2, but Paul uses different words. In verse 2, “burdens” refers to heavy loads too much for one person to carry alone. In verse 5, the word refers to a pack, the normal load each person carries, such as their own responsibility before God. Believers help one another with crushing burdens, while each remains responsible for their own life and calling.

### Sharing with Teachers (*6:6*)

“*But let him who is taught in the word share all good things with him who teaches*” (*v. 6*). Those who receive teaching in God’s word should support their teachers, including materially. Paul had chosen not to accept support from some churches for strategic reasons (*1 Corinthians 9:12–15*), but he affirmed the principle that those who teach the gospel should be supported (*1 Corinthians 9:14*). In Galatia, this may also have been a gentle encouragement to support faithful teachers rather than the false teachers who were drawing attention to themselves.

### Sowing and Reaping (*6:7–10*)

The principle of sowing and reaping, and the call not to grow weary, are studied below.

### Paul’s Closing in His Own Hand (*6:11–18*)

“*See with what large letters I write to you with my own hand*” (*v. 11*). Paul’s large handwriting may have been due to poor eyesight (see *Galatians 4:15*), to his lack of practice as a scribe, or to his desire to emphasize these final words, much as someone today might use bold or capital letters.

“*As many as desire to make a good impression in the flesh compel you to be circumcised, just so they may not be persecuted for the cross of Christ*” (*v. 12*). Paul exposes the false teachers’ motives. They wanted to look good to others, perhaps to Jewish communities who might otherwise persecute them for associating with uncircumcised Gentiles. By getting the Gentile believers circumcised, they could avoid the offense of the cross.

“*For even they who receive circumcision don’t keep the law themselves, but they desire to have you circumcised, so that they may boast in your flesh*” (*v. 13*). The false teachers did not even keep the whole Law themselves. Their real goal was to boast in the number of Gentiles they had brought into conformity, as trophies of their influence. Paul’s own boast is studied below.

“*For in Christ Jesus neither is circumcision anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation*” (*v. 15*). This repeats *Galatians 5:6* in new words. Outward religious marks do not matter. What matters is the new creation that God brings about in Christ, transforming people from within and beginning the renewal of all things (*2 Corinthians 5:17*).

“*As many as walk by this rule, peace and mercy be on them, and on God’s Israel*” (*v. 16*). “This rule” is the principle Paul just stated: the cross and the new creation are what count. Interpreters differ on the meaning of “God’s Israel.” Some understand it as a description of the whole church, Jewish and Gentile believers together, as the true people of God in Christ (compare *Galatians 3:29*). Others think Paul is extending a blessing to Jewish believers specifically, or to the Jewish people whom he hoped would yet turn to Christ (*Romans 11:26*). Whatever the precise reference, Paul’s blessing of peace and mercy reflects God’s faithfulness to His promises.

“*From now on, let no one cause me any trouble, for I bear the marks of the Lord Jesus branded on my body*” (*v. 17*). The false teachers wanted to put the mark of circumcision on the Galatians’ bodies. Paul bore different marks: the scars from beatings, stoning, and persecution suffered for Christ (*2 Corinthians 11:23–25*). In the ancient world, slaves were sometimes branded with their owner’s mark. Paul’s scars showed that he belonged to Jesus.

“*The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers. Amen*” (*v. 18*). The letter that began with grace (*Galatians 1:3*) ends with grace. Despite the sharp words throughout, Paul still calls them “brothers.” His final word is a blessing.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Galatians 6:1–2* — Restore Gently and Bear One Another’s Burdens

> *“Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted. Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.”*
>
> — *Galatians 6:1–2* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul now shows what walking by the Spirit looks like when someone in the community falls into sin. “Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault.” The word “caught” suggests being overtaken or surprised by sin, like someone tripped up. Paul is describing a believer who has stumbled.

“You who are spiritual must restore such a one.” “Spiritual” here means those who are walking by the Spirit and bearing His fruit (*Galatians 5:22–25*), not people who think themselves superior. The word “restore” was used for setting a broken bone or mending a torn fishing net. The goal is healing, not punishment or humiliation.

“In a spirit of gentleness.” Gentleness is part of the fruit of the Spirit (*Galatians 5:23*). Restoration must be done kindly and humbly.

“Looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.” Those who help others must stay humble and watchful, knowing that they too are vulnerable to temptation. Pride can be its own form of falling.

Verse 2 widens the principle: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.” Believers are to help carry the heavy loads others face, whether temptations, sorrows, needs, or struggles. In doing this, they fulfill “the law of Christ,” which is the law of love that Christ taught and lived (*John 13:34*; *Galatians 5:14*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

“The law of Christ” is a striking phrase in a letter that warns so strongly against returning to the Law of Moses. Paul is not introducing a new set of rules. He is pointing to Christ’s way of love. Christ bore the heaviest burden of all, the sin of the world, on the cross. His followers imitate Him when they help carry the burdens of others.

This passage gives a model for how churches should respond to sin among their members. Jesus taught a similar approach in *Matthew 18:15–17*, beginning with private, gentle conversation and aiming at restoration. The goal is always to bring the person back to health and fellowship, not to shame them. *James 5:19–20* likewise speaks of the great good done when someone turns a wanderer back.

At the same time, gentle restoration does not mean ignoring serious harm. When sin involves abuse or crimes against others, those harmed must be protected, and appropriate authorities must be involved. Restoration of the offender’s relationship with God never requires the victim to stay at risk or to keep silent. Gentleness toward the one who has fallen goes together with justice and care for those who have been hurt.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

When a fellow believer stumbles, the natural reactions are often gossip, judgment, or avoidance. This passage calls for something better: a humble, gentle effort to help them return. That might mean a private conversation, an offer of support, prayer together, or walking alongside them as they rebuild.

Bearing one another’s burdens can take many practical forms: bringing meals to a grieving family, helping someone through a financial crisis, sitting with a friend in depression, or being an accountability partner for someone fighting temptation. These simple acts of love fulfill the law of Christ.

The warning to “look to yourself” is also important. Those who help others should remain humble, aware of their own weaknesses, and careful not to place themselves in situations of temptation.

### *Galatians 6:7–8* — Whatever a Person Sows, They Will Reap

> *“Don’t be deceived. God is not mocked, for whatever a man sows, that he will also reap. For he who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption. But he who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life.”*
>
> — *Galatians 6:7–8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul uses another image from farming. “Don’t be deceived. God is not mocked, for whatever a man sows, that he will also reap.” Just as a farmer who plants wheat harvests wheat, the choices people make produce corresponding results. No one can fool God by sowing one thing and expecting to reap another.

“God is not mocked” means God cannot be outwitted or treated with contempt. People may think they can live however they please without consequences, but God’s moral order stands.

Verse 8 describes two kinds of sowing. “He who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption.” To sow to the flesh means investing one’s life in selfish desires, the works of the flesh listed in *Galatians 5:19–21*. The harvest is “corruption,” decay and ruin. “But he who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life.” To sow to the Spirit means investing one’s life in what pleases God, following the Spirit’s leading. The harvest is eternal life.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The principle of sowing and reaping runs throughout Scripture (*Job 4:8*; *Proverbs 22:8*; *Hosea 8:7*). It reflects the moral order God has built into His world. Choices matter, and they have consequences, both in this life and in eternity.

This principle might seem to contradict Paul’s teaching that salvation is by grace through faith. But Paul sees no contradiction. Eternal life is God’s gift through Christ, received by faith. Yet genuine faith, through the Spirit, leads to a life that “sows to the Spirit.” A life that persistently sows to the flesh shows that the person is not walking with God. Paul is not teaching salvation by works but describing the direction of a life.

It is also important not to apply this principle mechanically. Not every hardship is a direct result of someone’s own sin. Jesus rejected that idea in *John 9:1–3*, and Job’s suffering was not caused by his wrongdoing. The principle describes the general moral order and the final outcome of a life, not a formula to explain every difficulty.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Every day, people sow seeds through their choices: what they watch, how they spend money, how they treat others, how they use their time, and what they feed their minds. This verse invites believers to consider what kind of harvest those seeds will produce. Small choices, repeated over time, shape a life.

This principle offers both warning and hope. It warns that sinful habits will eventually produce painful harvests. But it also promises that faithful choices, such as prayer, honesty, kindness, and generosity, will produce a good harvest. Sowing to the Spirit is never wasted.

For those who have sown poorly in the past, the gospel offers forgiveness and a fresh start. Consequences may remain, but God’s grace allows them to begin sowing to the Spirit today.

### *Galatians 6:9–10* — Do Not Grow Weary in Doing Good

> *“Let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season if we don’t give up. So then, as we have opportunity, let’s do what is good toward all men, and especially toward those who are of the household of the faith.”*
>
> — *Galatians 6:9–10* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Farmers know that harvest does not come immediately. There is a long season of waiting between sowing and reaping. Paul applies this to doing good. “Let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season if we don’t give up.”

Doing good can be tiring. People may not notice or appreciate it. Results may be slow. Paul acknowledges the danger of weariness and discouragement. But he promises that a harvest will come “in due season,” at the right time, God’s time. The condition is perseverance: “if we don’t give up.”

Verse 10 draws the practical conclusion: “So then, as we have opportunity, let’s do what is good toward all men, and especially toward those who are of the household of the faith.” Believers should use the opportunities they have to do good to everyone, not just to fellow Christians. At the same time, they have a special responsibility toward their spiritual family, “the household of the faith.”

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses connect with the sowing image of verses 7–8. Doing good is sowing to the Spirit, and the harvest is sure, even when it is delayed. Paul expresses similar encouragement in *1 Corinthians 15:58*, urging the Corinthians to keep working, “*because you know that your labor is not in vain in the Lord*” (*1 Corinthians 15:58*).

The phrase “as we have opportunity” suggests both readiness and urgency. Opportunities to do good come and go. Life is short, and the time to act is now.

The order of “all men” and “*especially toward those who are of the household of the faith*” (*v. 10*) reflects a balance. Christian love is not limited to fellow believers; it reaches out to all people, as Jesus taught in the parable of the Good Samaritan (*Luke 10:25–37*). Yet the church is a family, and family members have particular responsibilities to care for one another. In Galatia, the church’s internal conflict made this reminder especially important.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Many believers grow weary in doing good: parents raising children, caregivers looking after aging relatives, volunteers serving in thankless roles, pastors laboring in difficult places. This verse speaks directly to them. Their work is not in vain. The harvest will come in God’s time.

Weariness is not the same as failure. Sometimes rest, help from others, and renewed time with God are needed to continue. Jesus Himself withdrew to rest and pray. Perseverance does not mean ignoring one’s limits; it means not abandoning the good work God has given.

Believers can also look for opportunities to do good each day, toward neighbors, coworkers, strangers, and especially toward fellow believers in need. Small acts of kindness, faithfully repeated, can produce a harvest far greater than anyone expects.

### *Galatians 6:14* — Boasting Only in the Cross

> *“But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.”*
>
> — *Galatians 6:14* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

In contrast to the false teachers, who wanted to boast in the number of Gentiles they had circumcised, Paul declares, “But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

In the Roman world, the cross was an object of horror and shame. It was the most humiliating form of execution, reserved for slaves and rebels. No one would ever boast about a cross. Yet Paul says the cross is his only boast. Everything he values, his forgiveness, his righteousness, his relationship with God, comes from Christ’s death on the cross.

“Through which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.” “The world” here refers to the whole system of values, status, and religious achievement that stands apart from God. Through the cross, that world has lost its power and attraction for Paul. It is as if the world is dead to him and he is dead to it. He no longer looks to the world for his identity, approval, or security.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse sums up the whole letter. The false teachers offered a religion of outward achievement: circumcision, calendar observance, and a good impression. Paul offers the cross, where all human achievement is set aside and God’s grace is everything. Boasting in the cross means acknowledging that salvation is entirely God’s gift.

Paul makes a similar statement in *1 Corinthians 2:2*: “*For I determined not to know anything among you except Jesus Christ and him crucified*” (*1 Corinthians 2:2*). And in *Philippians 3:7–8*, he says he counts everything as loss compared with knowing Christ. For Paul, the cross was not just the means of salvation but the center of his whole life and identity.

The double crucifixion, “the world... crucified to me, and I to the world,” echoes *Galatians 2:20* (“I have been crucified with Christ”) and *Galatians 5:24* (“Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh”). Union with Christ in His death breaks the grip of self, flesh, and world, and opens the way to the new creation (v15).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

People are always tempted to boast in something: achievements, appearance, wealth, education, family background, spiritual accomplishments, or even church involvement. This verse calls believers to a different boast. Their worth and hope rest not on what they have done but on what Christ has done for them on the cross.

Being crucified to the world means that its values no longer control a believer’s life. Popularity, success, and status lose their power to define them. This brings tremendous freedom. Believers can live for God’s approval, serve humbly, and endure rejection, because their identity is anchored in the cross.

This verse also invites believers to keep the cross central in their faith, worship, and witness. The message of Christ crucified is still the power of God for salvation, and it remains the only true ground for boasting.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Galatians 6* shows how the freedom and life of the Spirit shape a Christian community. When a believer falls into sin, those walking by the Spirit should restore them gently and humbly, aiming at healing rather than shame, while also ensuring that anyone who has been harmed is protected and cared for. Believers are called to bear one another’s burdens, fulfilling the law of Christ, the law of self-giving love that He displayed on the cross.

The chapter also calls for honest self-examination instead of comparison. Each person is responsible for their own life and calling before God. At the same time, the community supports those who teach God’s word and shares good things with them.

Paul’s teaching on sowing and reaping reminds believers that their choices matter. Sowing to the flesh leads to decay; sowing to the Spirit leads to eternal life. This is not salvation by works, but a description of the direction and outcome of a life. For those who grow weary in doing good, Paul offers a promise: the harvest will come in due season. Believers can keep seizing opportunities to do good to all people, especially to their spiritual family.

Finally, Paul closes the letter by pointing to the cross. The false teachers wanted to boast in outward achievements, but Paul boasts only in the cross of Christ. There, the world’s values lost their hold on him, and he found his identity in Christ. What matters is not religious performance but the new creation God brings about. This is the heart of the gospel: grace, received through faith, producing new life in Christ.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, You carried the heaviest burden of all when You bore my sin on the cross. Make me willing to carry the burdens of others. When a brother or sister stumbles, give me a gentle and humble spirit to help restore them, and keep me watchful over my own heart. Free me from comparing myself with others. Help me to sow to the Spirit in the choices I make each day. When I grow weary in doing good, renew my strength and remind me that the harvest will come in Your time. Show me the opportunities You give me to do good to everyone, especially to Your family. Far be it from me to boast in anything except Your cross. Let the world lose its grip on my heart, and make me a new creation in You. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Book 10 of 27

# Ephesians

## About This Letter

Ephesians presents itself as a letter from Paul, written while he was a prisoner for the Lord (*Ephesians 3:1*; *4:1*; *6:20*). The traditional view, held by most Christians through history, is that Paul wrote it during his Roman imprisonment around A.D. 60–62, at about the same time as Colossians and Philemon, and that Tychicus carried it to its readers (*6:21–22*). Some modern scholars think it was written after Paul’s death by a close follower who summarized his teaching, because its style and emphases differ somewhat from his earlier letters. Others answer that differences of purpose, setting, and the use of a secretary explain the change in style. Either way, the church has received Ephesians as Scripture from the earliest centuries.

Paul had spent nearly three years in Ephesus, a great city of the Roman province of Asia and home to the famous temple of Artemis (*Acts 19*). Yet the letter contains few personal greetings, and the words “at Ephesus” in 1:1 are missing from some of the earliest manuscripts. For this reason, many think Ephesians was a circular letter intended for several churches in the region, with Ephesus as the leading city.

## The Shape of the Letter

Ephesians falls into two halves. Chapters 1–3 celebrate what God has done in Christ: every spiritual blessing, chosen and adopted, redeemed and sealed with the Spirit, raised from spiritual death by grace through faith, and brought together, Jew and Gentile, into one new people, one household, and one temple. Paul prays twice for his readers to grasp these riches and the immeasurable love of Christ. Chapters 4–6 show how to live in light of this calling: in unity and maturity as one body, putting off the old self and putting on the new, walking in love and light, being filled with the Spirit, honoring Christ in households, and standing firm in the armor of God.

## Themes to Watch For

Watch for the phrase “in Christ” and its many variations, God’s eternal plan to bring all things together under Christ, the riches of grace, salvation as a gift and not by works, the church as Christ’s body, bride, household, and temple, the breaking down of the dividing wall between Jew and Gentile, the mystery now revealed, the power of the risen Christ at work in believers, unity in diversity of gifts, the new life of holiness and love, and the reality of spiritual warfare. Ephesians lifts the reader’s eyes to the cosmic scope of God’s purpose and then brings that vision down to everyday relationships at home, at work, and in the church.
