Ephesians · Chapter 1 of 6

# Ephesians — Chapter 1

Chapter Theme: Every Spiritual Blessing in Christ

[Read Ephesians 1 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/EPH01.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul opens with a great hymn of praise to God, who has blessed believers with every spiritual blessing in Christ. Before the foundation of the world, God chose them to be holy and destined them for adoption as His children. In Christ they have redemption through His blood and the forgiveness of sins, and God has made known His plan to unite all things in Christ. Believers have been sealed with the promised Holy Spirit as the guarantee of their inheritance. Paul then prays that they will have the eyes of their hearts enlightened to know the hope of their calling, the riches of God’s inheritance, and the immense power that raised Christ from the dead and seated Him above every authority as head over all things for the church.

## Chapter Background and Story

Ephesians begins differently from many of Paul’s letters. There is no crisis to address, no false teaching to correct in the opening lines. Instead, after a short greeting, Paul bursts into praise. Verses 3–14 form a single, long sentence in the original Greek, overflowing with one blessing after another. It reads like a hymn, celebrating the work of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

The believers who first received this letter lived in the shadow of the great temple of Artemis in Ephesus, in a culture full of magic, astrology, and fear of spiritual powers (*Acts 19:18–19*). Many of them had once lived in dread of forces they could not control. Paul’s opening chapter lifts their eyes to see that God’s purposes stretch from before the creation of the world to the end of the ages, and that the risen Christ reigns far above every power. Their lives are held securely in the plan of a loving God.

The chapter has two parts: the great blessing (*1:3–14*) and Paul’s prayer for his readers (*1:15–23*).

### Greeting (*1:1–2*)

“*Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God, to the saints who are at Ephesus, and the faithful in Christ Jesus*” (*v. 1*). “Saints” means holy ones, those set apart for God. Paul uses it for all believers, not just a special few. They are “faithful,” or believing, and they are “in Christ Jesus,” a phrase that will echo throughout the letter. “*Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ*” (*v. 2*).

### The Father’s Blessing: Chosen and Adopted (*1:3–6*)

The opening blessing and God’s choice of His people are studied below. “*having predestined us for adoption as children through Jesus Christ to himself, according to the good pleasure of his desire*” (*v. 5*). God planned beforehand that believers would be adopted as His children. This was not a reluctant decision but “the good pleasure of his desire.” God delighted to bring people into His family. “*to the praise of the glory of his grace, by which he freely gave us favor in the Beloved*” (*v. 6*). The purpose of it all is the praise of God’s grace. “The Beloved” is Christ, the Father’s beloved Son (*Matthew 3:17*). Believers are accepted because they are in Him.

### The Son’s Work: Redemption and God’s Plan (*1:7–12*)

Redemption through Christ’s blood is studied below. “*which he made to abound toward us in all wisdom and prudence*” (*v. 8*), “*making known to us the mystery of his will, according to his good pleasure which he purposed in him*” (*v. 9*). In Paul’s letters, a “mystery” is not a puzzle but a truth once hidden and now revealed by God. The mystery here is God’s plan for history.

“*to an administration of the fullness of the times, to sum up all things in Christ, the things in the heavens and the things on the earth, in him*” (*v. 10*). This is one of the grandest statements in the Bible. God’s purpose is to bring everything together under Christ as head. A world fractured by sin, divided between heaven and earth, between peoples and nations, will one day be reunited and set right in Christ.

“*We were also assigned an inheritance in him, having been foreordained according to the purpose of him who does all things after the counsel of his will*” (*v. 11*), “*to the end that we should be to the praise of his glory, we who had before hoped in Christ*” (*v. 12*). “We who had before hoped in Christ” may refer to Jewish believers, who first hoped in the Messiah, as distinct from the Gentile believers addressed in verse 13 as “you also.”

### The Spirit’s Seal (*1:13–14*)

The sealing of believers with the Spirit is studied below.

### Paul’s Prayer (*1:15–23*)

“*For this cause I also, having heard of the faith in the Lord Jesus which is among you and the love which you have toward all the saints*” (*v. 15*), “*don’t cease to give thanks for you, making mention of you in my prayers*” (*v. 16*). Faith in the Lord and love for fellow believers go together; they are the twin marks of genuine Christian life. “*that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give to you a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him*” (*v. 17*). Paul’s first prayer is not for their circumstances but for their knowledge of God. The content of his prayer is studied below.

“*which he worked in Christ when he raised him from the dead and made him to sit at his right hand in the heavenly places*” (*v. 20*), “*far above all rule, authority, power, dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age, but also in that which is to come*” (*v. 21*). The resurrection and ascension of Christ display God’s power. Christ reigns above every spiritual power, every authority, every name, now and forever. For believers who once feared spiritual forces, this was profoundly reassuring.

“*He put all things in subjection under his feet, and gave him to be head over all things for the assembly*” (*v. 22*), “*which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all in all*” (*v. 23*). Paul echoes *Psalm 8:6*, where God put all things under humanity’s feet. That psalm finds its fulfillment in Christ. And Christ’s supreme authority is exercised “for the assembly,” the church. The church is His body, so closely united with Him that it is called His “fullness.” The one who fills the whole universe with His presence fills the church in a special way.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Ephesians 1:3–4* — Blessed and Chosen in Christ

> *“Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ, even as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we would be holy and without defect before him in love,”*
>
> — *Ephesians 1:3–4* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul begins with praise: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.” To “bless” God means to praise Him, to speak well of Him. Paul then explains why: God “has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ.”

“Every spiritual blessing” means every blessing that comes from the Holy Spirit and belongs to the life of God’s kingdom. Nothing believers need for their spiritual life has been withheld. “In the heavenly places” refers to the spiritual realm where Christ reigns. Though believers live on earth, they already share in the blessings of heaven through their union with Christ. And all these blessings come “in Christ.” They are found in Him and given through Him.

Verse 4 names the first blessing: God “chose us in him before the foundation of the world.” Before God created anything, He had a plan to have a people for Himself. That choice was made “in him,” in Christ.

The purpose of the choice was “that we would be holy and without defect before him in love.” God chose His people so that they would belong to Him, be set apart for Him, and be made blameless in His sight. The phrase “in love” may describe God’s love in choosing, or the love in which believers are to live. Both are true.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The idea that God “chose” His people before creation has been discussed by Christians for centuries, and different traditions understand it in different ways. Some, often called Reformed or Calvinist, understand it to mean that God, in His sovereign grace, chose particular individuals for salvation, not on the basis of anything in them. Others, often called Arminian or Wesleyan, understand it to mean that God chose Christ and all who would be in Christ by faith, foreseeing their response, so that election is corporate and conditional on faith. Still others emphasize that the choice is of a people, the church, in Christ, rather than of isolated individuals. Each view seeks to honor both God’s sovereign grace and human responsibility, and all agree that salvation originates in God’s loving initiative, not in human merit.

What is clear in this passage is the tone. Paul does not present election as a cause for anxiety or speculation, but as a reason for praise. Believers’ salvation was not an afterthought. God’s love for them reaches back before time began. It is grounded “in Christ,” so that believers can look to Christ for assurance rather than trying to look into God’s secret plans.

The goal of election is holiness. God did not choose people so that they could live however they please, but so that they would become holy and blameless. Election and transformation go together.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Many people struggle with feelings of being unwanted, overlooked, or accidental. These verses proclaim that believers were chosen in love before the world began. Their lives have meaning within God’s eternal purpose. That truth can bring deep security and peace.

These verses also invite praise. Paul begins not with requests or instructions but with worship. Believers can cultivate the habit of thanking God for spiritual blessings that cannot be taken away, even when earthly circumstances are hard.

Finally, being chosen calls for holiness. Those who have been chosen in love are invited to live lives that reflect God’s character, not to earn His choice, but in grateful response to it.

### *Ephesians 1:7* — Redemption Through His Blood

> *“In him we have our redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses, according to the riches of his grace”*
>
> — *Ephesians 1:7* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Having described the Father’s choice, Paul turns to the work of the Son. “In him we have our redemption through his blood.” Redemption means release by the payment of a price. In the ancient world, it was used for freeing slaves or prisoners of war. In the Old Testament, God redeemed Israel from slavery in Egypt (*Exodus 6:6*). Now, through Christ, believers are set free from slavery to sin.

The price was Christ’s “blood,” that is, His sacrificial death on the cross. His life was given in exchange for theirs.

Paul then defines this redemption as “the forgiveness of our trespasses.” “Trespasses” are wrongful steps, the ways people have crossed God’s boundaries. Through Christ’s death, these are forgiven, completely and freely.

All of this is “according to the riches of his grace.” God does not forgive grudgingly or in small amounts. He forgives out of the overflowing wealth of His grace.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Notice that Paul says “we have” redemption. It is a present possession, not merely a future hope. Believers are already forgiven and set free.

The reference to Christ’s blood connects with the entire sacrificial system of the Old Testament, where the shedding of blood signified life given for life (*Leviticus 17:11*). *Hebrews 9:22* states that without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness. Jesus is the fulfillment of every sacrifice, the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world (*John 1:29*).

The phrase “the riches of his grace” is characteristic of Ephesians, which speaks often of God’s riches: riches of His glory (*1:18*; *3:16*), riches of His mercy (*2:4*), and the unsearchable riches of Christ (*3:8*). God is not poor in grace. His forgiveness is not measured out sparingly but poured out abundantly.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Many believers carry lingering guilt over past sins, even after confessing them. This verse declares that forgiveness is a present reality, secured by Christ’s blood and given according to the riches of God’s grace. No sin is too great for that grace.

Knowing the cost of redemption also deepens gratitude. Forgiveness is free to the one who receives it, but it was costly to the one who gave it. Remembering the cross can move believers to love Christ more deeply and to extend forgiveness to others, as Paul urges later in this letter (*Ephesians 4:32*).

### *Ephesians 1:13–14* — Sealed with the Holy Spirit

> *“In him you also, having heard the word of the truth, the Good News of your salvation—in whom, having also believed, you were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, who is a pledge of our inheritance, to the redemption of God’s own possession, to the praise of his glory.”*
>
> — *Ephesians 1:13–14* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul now turns to the work of the Holy Spirit and to the Gentile believers (“you also”). He traces their journey. First, they “heard the word of the truth, the Good News of your salvation.” Then they “believed.” And when they believed, they “were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit.”

In the ancient world, a seal was a mark made in wax or clay, often with a signet ring. It showed ownership, authenticity, and protection. A sealed document or package belonged to its owner and was guarded from tampering. The Holy Spirit is God’s seal on believers, marking them as His own and guaranteeing their security.

The Spirit is called “the promised Holy Spirit” because God had promised through the prophets to pour out His Spirit (*Ezekiel 36:27*; *Joel 2:28*), and Jesus promised to send the Spirit to His disciples (*John 14:16–17*; *Acts 1:4–5*).

Verse 14 says the Spirit “is a pledge of our inheritance.” The word “pledge” was used in business for a down payment, a first installment guaranteeing that the full payment would follow (see *2 Corinthians 1:22*; *5:5*). The Spirit is the first portion of the inheritance believers will fully receive in the future. His presence now guarantees the rest.

This continues “to the redemption of God’s own possession, to the praise of his glory.” Believers belong to God, and He will bring them to full and final redemption.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses complete the Trinitarian pattern of the opening hymn. The Father chose and adopted (vv3–6), the Son redeemed and revealed God’s plan (vv7–12), and the Spirit seals and guarantees (vv13–14). Each section ends with a refrain about the praise of God’s glory (vv6, 12, 14). Salvation is the work of the one God in three persons, and its goal is His glory.

The sealing of the Spirit provides great assurance. Believers’ security does not rest on the strength of their feelings or the consistency of their performance but on God’s mark of ownership. Paul repeats this in *Ephesians 4:30*, calling believers not to grieve the Holy Spirit, “in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.”

The idea of “inheritance” points forward. What believers experience of God now, His presence, peace, and power through the Spirit, is real but partial. It is a foretaste of the fullness to come, when God’s people will see Him face to face and creation itself will be renewed.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Many believers struggle with doubts about whether they truly belong to God. These verses offer assurance rooted in God’s action. Those who have heard and believed the gospel have been sealed by the Spirit. God has marked them as His own.

The Spirit’s presence also gives hope in difficult times. The joy, comfort, and love believers experience through the Spirit, even in hardship, are a down payment on the inheritance to come. Whatever is lost or painful now, the best is yet ahead.

Finally, because believers are God’s possession, sealed by His Spirit, they are invited to live in a way that honors their Owner. This is not a burden but a privilege: they belong to the God who loves them.

### *Ephesians 1:18–19* — The Eyes of Your Hearts Enlightened

> *“having the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know what is the hope of his calling, and what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints, and what is the exceeding greatness of his power toward us who believe, according to that working of the strength of his might”*
>
> — *Ephesians 1:18–19* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul’s prayer for the believers is that they would see more clearly. He prays for “the eyes of your hearts” to be “enlightened.” In biblical language, the “heart” is the center of a person: mind, will, and emotions together. Paul prays that God would open the inner eyes of their understanding so they can grasp spiritual realities.

He prays that they would know three things.

First, “what is the hope of his calling.” God has called them, and that calling comes with a sure hope: the future glory God has prepared for His people.

Second, “what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints.” This can mean either the inheritance believers will receive, or the inheritance God has in His people. Many interpreters favor the second: God regards His people as His treasured inheritance, His own possession (*Deuteronomy 32:9*). Believers are precious to God.

Third, “what is the exceeding greatness of his power toward us who believe.” Paul piles up words for power, “working,” “strength,” “might,” to describe how vast it is. This power is directed “toward us who believe.”

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Paul’s prayer shows that the great need of believers is not simply to receive new blessings but to understand the blessings they already have. They have already been blessed with every spiritual blessing (v3), but they need spiritual sight to grasp it. This kind of understanding comes only by God’s revelation through the Spirit (*1 Corinthians 2:9–12*).

The measure of God’s power at work in believers is the resurrection and ascension of Christ (vv20–21). The same power that raised Jesus from the dead and seated Him above every authority is at work in those who believe. This is not power for showing off but power for transformation, perseverance, and victory over sin and evil.

Paul’s prayer also teaches believers how to pray for one another. He does not pray mainly for health, comfort, or success, though those things are good to pray for. He prays for deeper knowledge of God, hope, an awareness of being treasured, and experience of His power. These are the riches that last.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can pray this prayer for themselves and for others. Asking God to open the eyes of the heart is a way of seeking a deeper, more personal grasp of His truth, beyond simply knowing facts about Him.

This prayer also brings encouragement. When believers feel powerless against temptation, discouragement, or fear, they can remember that the same power that raised Christ from the dead is at work in them. When they feel insignificant, they can remember that God regards His people as His glorious inheritance.

Finally, the hope of God’s calling can steady believers through hard times. Their future is secure in Christ, who reigns above every power. Whatever happens now, God’s purposes will not fail.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Ephesians 1* lifts believers’ eyes to see the vast scope of God’s love and purpose. Before the world was made, God chose His people in Christ to be holy and blameless, and He destined them for adoption as His children. This truth gives deep security. Believers are not accidents or afterthoughts. They are loved, chosen, and welcomed into God’s family, all to the praise of His glorious grace.

In Christ, believers have redemption through His blood and the forgiveness of their sins, according to the riches of God’s grace. Guilt and shame no longer define them. And God has revealed His great plan: to bring all things together under Christ. This means that history is not random. A broken and divided world is moving toward healing and unity in Christ.

The Holy Spirit seals believers as God’s own possession and serves as the guarantee of their future inheritance. In times of doubt or suffering, believers can rest in this assurance. God has marked them as His, and He will complete what He has begun.

Finally, Paul’s prayer teaches believers what to seek most: open eyes to know God, His hope, His treasured love for His people, and His resurrection power. Christ reigns far above every authority and power, and He is head over all things for the church. Whatever believers face, they can live with confidence, gratitude, and praise, knowing that they are held in the purposes of a God whose power and love have no limit.

## Chapter Prayer

Blessed be You, God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, for blessing me with every spiritual blessing in Christ. Thank You for choosing me in love before the foundation of the world and for adopting me as Your child. Thank You, Lord Jesus, for redeeming me through Your blood and forgiving all my trespasses according to the riches of Your grace. Thank You, Holy Spirit, for sealing me as God’s own and for being the guarantee of my inheritance. Open the eyes of my heart, so that I may know the hope of Your calling, the riches of Your glorious inheritance in Your people, and the immeasurable greatness of Your power toward those who believe. Help me to live with confidence that Christ reigns above every power, and let my whole life be to the praise of Your glory. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Ephesians · Chapter 2 of 6

# Ephesians — Chapter 2

Chapter Theme: Saved by Grace and Made One in Christ

[Read Ephesians 2 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/EPH02.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul describes the human condition apart from God: dead in sins, following the ways of the world and the evil one, and by nature under God’s wrath. But God, rich in mercy and great in love, made believers alive with Christ, raised them up, and seated them with Him. Salvation is by grace through faith, a gift of God and not the result of works, and believers are God’s workmanship created for good works. Paul then shows that Christ has broken down the dividing wall between Jews and Gentiles, making peace through the cross and creating one new people. Gentile believers are no longer strangers but fellow citizens and members of God’s household, being built together into a holy temple where God lives by His Spirit.

## Chapter Background and Story

In chapter 1, Paul celebrated God’s eternal plan and prayed that believers would know the immense power that raised Christ from the dead. In chapter 2, he shows that same power at work in two ways. First, God raised individual believers from spiritual death to life (*2:1–10*). Second, God brought together two groups that had been deeply divided, Jews and Gentiles, into one new people (*2:11–22*).

The division between Jews and Gentiles was one of the deepest in the ancient world. It was religious, cultural, and social. In the temple in Jerusalem, a stone barrier separated the Court of the Gentiles from the inner courts, with inscriptions warning that any Gentile who passed beyond it would be put to death. Paul himself had been arrested after being falsely accused of bringing a Gentile, Trophimus the Ephesian, past that barrier (*Acts 21:27–29*). When Paul writes of Christ breaking down “the middle wall of separation,” his readers in Ephesus would have known exactly the kind of wall he meant.

This chapter contains one of the most famous summaries of the gospel in the Bible (*2:8–9*) and one of the most powerful visions of reconciliation between peoples.

### Dead in Sins (*2:1–3*)

“*You were made alive when you were dead in transgressions and sins*” (*v. 1*). Paul’s description of life apart from God is stark. People were not merely sick or weak; they were spiritually dead, unable to respond to God on their own.

“*in which you once walked according to the course of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit who now works in the children of disobedience*” (*v. 2*). Three forces held people captive. “The course of this world” refers to the values and patterns of a society that has turned from God. “The prince of the power of the air” refers to Satan, whom ancient people pictured as ruling the realm between earth and heaven. He is “the spirit who now works” in those who disobey God.

“*We also all once lived among them in the lusts of our flesh, doing the desires of the flesh and of the mind, and were by nature children of wrath, even as the rest*” (*v. 3*). The third force is the flesh, the sinful human nature turned in on itself. Paul includes himself and other Jewish believers (“we also all”). Everyone, Jew and Gentile alike, was under God’s righteous judgment. “Children of wrath” means people who, by their sinful condition, deserved God’s judgment against sin.

### But God (*2:4–7*)

Two of the most hopeful words in Scripture begin verse 4. God’s merciful action is studied below. “*and raised us up with him, and made us to sit with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus*” (*v. 6*). Believers are united with Christ not only in His resurrection but also in His ascension. In a spiritual sense, they already share His victory and His place of authority. “*that in the ages to come he might show the exceeding riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus*” (*v. 7*). Throughout eternity, God’s people will be living displays of His grace and kindness.

### By Grace Through Faith (*2:8–10*)

These central verses are studied below.

### Strangers Brought Near (*2:11–13*)

“*Therefore remember that once you, the Gentiles in the flesh, who are called “uncircumcision” by that which is called “circumcision” (in the flesh, made by hands)*” (*v. 11*). Paul asks the Gentile believers to remember where they came from. Jews often referred to Gentiles dismissively as “the uncircumcision.”

“*that you were at that time separate from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of the promise, having no hope and without God in the world*” (*v. 12*). Paul lists five losses. Gentiles had been without the Messiah, outside God’s covenant people, strangers to His promises, without hope, and without God. They had many gods, but not the true God.

“*But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off are made near in the blood of Christ*” (*v. 13*). Another great turning point. Through Christ’s death, those who were far from God have been brought near.

### Christ Our Peace (*2:14–18*)

How Christ made peace between Jew and Gentile is studied below. “*He came and preached peace to you who were far off and to those who were near*” (*v. 17*). Paul echoes *Isaiah 57:19*, where God promises peace to those far and near. Through the apostles’ preaching, the risen Christ continued to proclaim peace. “*For through him we both have our access in one Spirit to the Father*” (*v. 18*). Jew and Gentile now approach God on the same basis, through the same Son, by the same Spirit, to the same Father.

### God’s Household and Temple (*2:19–22*)

“*So then you are no longer strangers and foreigners, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and of the household of God*” (*v. 19*). Gentile believers are no longer outsiders or resident aliens with limited rights. They are full citizens and family members.

“*being built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone*” (*v. 20*). The church rests on the teaching of the apostles and prophets. “Prophets” here probably refers to New Testament prophets, since they are listed after the apostles (see *Ephesians 3:5*; *4:11*). Christ is the cornerstone, the stone that determined the position and alignment of the whole building (*Psalm 118:22*; *1 Peter 2:6*).

“*in whom the whole building, fitted together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord*” (*v. 21*); “*in whom you also are built together for a habitation of God in the Spirit*” (*v. 22*). Ephesus had the magnificent temple of Artemis. Jerusalem had God’s temple, with its barrier that excluded Gentiles. Paul announces a new temple, made not of stone but of people, Jew and Gentile together. God Himself lives in it by His Spirit. And it is still growing, as more people are added and the church matures.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Ephesians 2:4–5* — But God, Rich in Mercy

> *“But God, being rich in mercy, for his great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead through our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ—by grace you have been saved—”*
>
> — *Ephesians 2:4–5* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After describing humanity’s desperate condition, dead in sins, enslaved, and under judgment, Paul turns with two powerful words: “But God.” Everything changes because of God’s action.

Paul describes God’s character in three ways. He is “rich in mercy.” Mercy is compassion toward those in misery, withholding the punishment they deserve. God has an abundance of it. His action flows “for his great love with which he loved us.” God’s love was the motive. And this love reached people “even when we were dead through our trespasses.” God did not wait for people to improve or reach out to Him. He loved them while they were still dead in sin.

What did God do? He “made us alive together with Christ.” Just as God raised Jesus from physical death, He raised believers from spiritual death. They were given new life, the very life of the risen Christ.

Paul cannot resist adding a parenthetical exclamation: “by grace you have been saved.” He will repeat it in verse 8. Grace means God’s undeserved favor. Dead people cannot raise themselves. Salvation must be entirely God’s gift.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The phrase “But God” appears at turning points throughout Scripture. Joseph told his brothers, “*you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good*” (*Genesis 50:20*). Paul wrote in *Romans 5:8*, “*But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us*” (*Romans 5:8*). These words mark the moment when human hopelessness meets divine intervention.

The description of humanity as “dead” is significant for understanding grace. If people were merely sick, they might cooperate with a doctor. If they were drowning, they might reach for a rope. But the dead can do nothing. Christian traditions have discussed how this truth relates to human response to the gospel, but all agree that new life begins with God’s initiative. Faith itself is a response made possible by His grace.

That God “*made us alive together with Christ*” (*v. 5*) also points to union with Christ. What happened to Christ, death, resurrection, and ascension, happens to believers in Him. They share His life now and will share His glory in the future.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

For anyone who feels spiritually lifeless, trapped in patterns of sin, or hopeless about change, these verses proclaim good news. God specializes in bringing the dead to life. No one is too far gone for His mercy.

These verses also humble believers. Their new life is entirely a gift. They did not raise themselves. That truth guards against pride and cultivates gratitude and compassion toward those who have not yet experienced God’s grace. Every believer was once dead in sin; the difference is God’s mercy.

### *Ephesians 2:8–9* — Saved by Grace Through Faith

> *“for by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works, that no one would boast.”*
>
> — *Ephesians 2:8–9* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These are among the most well-known verses in the Bible. Paul repeats what he said in verse 5, “by grace you have been saved,” and now he explains it more fully.

“By grace”: salvation comes from God’s free, undeserved favor. It is not earned, purchased, or achieved.

“You have been saved”: in Greek this verb describes a completed action with lasting results. Believers have been rescued and remain saved.

“Through faith”: faith is the means by which people receive God’s gift. Faith is not a work that earns salvation; it is the empty hand that receives it, trusting in Christ.

“And that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God.” The word “that” likely refers to the whole package of salvation by grace through faith. None of it originates from human effort. It is entirely God’s gift.

“Not of works, that no one would boast.” If salvation came by works, people could take credit for it. But because it is a gift, no one can boast before God. Everyone stands on the same ground, receiving mercy they did not deserve.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses capture the heart of the gospel that Paul preached everywhere. They echo his teaching in *Romans 3:23–28* and *Galatians 2:16*. Salvation is not a reward for good behavior or religious devotion. It is a rescue from God, received through trust in Christ.

Different Christian traditions have explored how faith itself relates to God’s grace. Some emphasize that even faith is God’s gift, produced by the Spirit. Others emphasize that God enables people to respond freely in faith. Both agree that faith is not a meritorious work and that the credit for salvation belongs to God alone.

The phrase “that no one would boast” shows the purpose of grace. God designed salvation in a way that removes all human pride. This is fitting, because pride was at the root of humanity’s original rebellion. Grace levels everyone. The most moral person and the most notorious sinner come to God the same way: as recipients of mercy.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Many people, including many who attend church, believe deep down that they must earn God’s approval. They try to balance their bad deeds with good ones or measure their standing by how religious they feel. These verses bring freedom: salvation is a gift to be received, not a wage to be earned.

This truth also brings stability. If salvation depended on human performance, it would rise and fall with each success and failure. But because it rests on God’s grace, believers can have assurance even on their worst days.

Finally, these verses shape how believers see others. No one has grounds for spiritual superiority. Those who have received grace are called to extend it humbly to others, remembering where they came from.

### *Ephesians 2:10* — Created for Good Works

> *“For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them.”*
>
> — *Ephesians 2:10* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Right after saying that salvation is “not of works,” Paul explains where good works fit in. “For we are his workmanship.” The word for “workmanship” can mean something made, a creation, or even a work of art. It is the root of the English word “poem.” Believers are God’s masterpiece, carefully crafted by Him.

“Created in Christ Jesus.” Salvation is a new creation. God has not just patched up the old life; He has created something new in Christ (*2 Corinthians 5:17*).

“For good works.” Good works are not the root of salvation, but they are its fruit. God saved people so that they would do good. Salvation and good works go together, but in the right order.

“Which God prepared before that we would walk in them.” God has already prepared good works for His people to do. Like a path laid out ahead of time, these works are part of His plan. Believers simply need to walk in them.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Verses 8–10 hold together two truths that are sometimes separated. Salvation is entirely by grace, not by works. And salvation results in good works. Those who emphasize only the first may neglect holiness and service. Those who emphasize only the second may fall into trying to earn salvation. Paul keeps both together. James makes a complementary point when he says that faith without works is dead (*James 2:17*). Genuine faith always produces a changed life.

The idea that God has prepared good works in advance is deeply encouraging. It means that believers’ lives have purpose. Every act of kindness, faithfulness, service, and love can be part of what God planned. This does not mean every detail is scripted, but it does mean that God has a purpose for each believer’s life and equips them to fulfill it.

Being God’s “workmanship” also speaks of dignity. Each believer is a work of the divine Artist. God is shaping them, sometimes through difficult seasons, into something beautiful that displays His glory.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Many people wonder whether their lives matter. This verse declares that believers are God’s handiwork, created for a purpose. Their everyday lives, at home, at work, in their neighborhoods, can be filled with good works God has prepared for them.

This verse also offers freedom. Believers do not need to strive anxiously to find significant things to do. They can walk day by day in the path God prepares, paying attention to the opportunities He places before them, such as a neighbor in need, a coworker who is struggling, or a chance to show kindness.

Finally, this verse reminds believers that they are works in progress. God is still shaping them. When they feel unfinished or flawed, they can trust the skill and patience of the Artist.

### *Ephesians 2:14–16* — He Is Our Peace

> *“For he is our peace, who made both one, and broke down the middle wall of separation, having abolished in his flesh the hostility, the law of commandments contained in ordinances, that he might create in himself one new man of the two, making peace, and might reconcile them both in one body to God through the cross, having killed the hostility through it.”*
>
> — *Ephesians 2:14–16* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul now explains how Jew and Gentile were brought together. “For he is our peace.” Christ does not merely bring peace; He Himself is peace. In His person and work, He reconciles people to God and to one another.

He “made both one, and broke down the middle wall of separation.” The two groups, Jews and Gentiles, have become one. The “middle wall of separation” was the barrier of hostility between them, symbolized by the literal wall in the temple courts that kept Gentiles out.

Verse 15 explains how: He abolished “in his flesh the hostility, the law of commandments contained in ordinances.” Through His death, Christ set aside the Law as a system of regulations that separated Jews from Gentiles, such as circumcision, food laws, and purity rules. These had marked Israel as distinct, but they had also become a source of division and hostility.

The purpose: “that he might create in himself one new man of the two, making peace.” Christ did not make Gentiles into Jews or Jews into Gentiles. He created a new humanity, a new people that includes both.

Verse 16 adds that He reconciled “them both in one body to God through the cross, having killed the hostility through it.” The cross reconciles people to God and to each other at the same time. On the cross, hostility itself was put to death.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This passage shows that the gospel has both vertical and horizontal dimensions. Reconciliation with God leads to reconciliation among people. Those who are at peace with God through Christ are called to live at peace with one another. The church is meant to be a community where ancient divisions are overcome.

Paul’s words about the Law need careful reading. He is not saying that God’s moral commands have been abolished. Elsewhere, he affirms that the Law is holy and that love fulfills it (*Romans 7:12*; *13:8–10*). What Christ abolished was the Law as a dividing wall, the system of ceremonial regulations that separated Jews and Gentiles and could not make anyone right with God.

“One new man” is a remarkable phrase. The church is not just an organization or a mixture of groups; it is a new humanity created in Christ. This new humanity reflects God’s original purpose for the human race, now restored. Ethnic and cultural identities remain, but they no longer divide or determine standing before God.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Divisions between ethnic groups, nations, classes, and political tribes remain deep in today’s world, and sometimes they run through churches. This passage calls believers to see these divisions in the light of the cross. Christ has broken down the dividing walls. Churches that welcome people of every background into one family display the power of the gospel.

This calling is practical. It may involve building friendships across cultural lines, listening to the experiences of believers from different backgrounds, repenting of prejudice, and working for justice and reconciliation. It also involves humility, recognizing that every group stands equally in need of grace.

On a personal level, Christ is also the source of peace in strained relationships. Those who have been reconciled to God through the cross can seek reconciliation with others, as far as it is possible and safe, trusting that Christ is able to bring peace where hostility once ruled.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Ephesians 2* tells the story of salvation in two great movements. The first is personal. Every human being, apart from God, was spiritually dead, enslaved to the world, the devil, and the flesh, and under judgment. “But God,” rich in mercy and great in love, made believers alive with Christ and raised them up with Him. This is entirely a gift of grace, received through faith, not earned by works. No one can boast; everyone stands in need of mercy. Believers can rest in the security of this gift, and they can extend the same grace humbly to others.

At the same time, grace is not idle. Believers are God’s workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works that God has prepared. Their daily lives become the setting for acts of love and service that reflect His character. Salvation by grace leads naturally to a life of good works.

The second movement is communal. Christ has broken down the wall of hostility between Jews and Gentiles, creating one new people and reconciling both to God through the cross. Those who were once strangers are now fellow citizens and members of God’s household. The church is a living temple, built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ as the cornerstone, and God dwells within it by His Spirit.

This vision calls the church to be a place where every dividing wall comes down. Believers are invited to welcome one another across lines of ethnicity, culture, class, and background, to pursue reconciliation, and to display to the world the peace that only Christ can bring.

## Chapter Prayer

Gracious God, I was dead in my sins, but You, rich in mercy and great in love, made me alive with Christ. Thank You that I have been saved by grace through faith, not by my own works, so that I have nothing to boast of but You. Thank You that I am Your workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works You prepared beforehand. Help me to walk in them each day. Lord Jesus, You are our peace. You broke down the dividing wall and made us one new people through Your cross. Tear down every wall of hostility in my heart. Help me to welcome all whom You have welcomed, and to seek peace and reconciliation wherever I can. Build Your church into a holy temple where You are pleased to live by Your Spirit. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Ephesians · Chapter 3 of 6

# Ephesians — Chapter 3

Chapter Theme: The Mystery Revealed and the Love That Surpasses Knowledge

[Read Ephesians 3 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/EPH03.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul, a prisoner for the sake of the Gentiles, explains the mystery God revealed to him: through the gospel, Gentiles are fellow heirs with Israel, members of the same body, and sharers in the same promise in Christ. Though he considers himself the least of all God’s people, he was given the grace of proclaiming the unsearchable riches of Christ, so that through the church God’s wisdom would be displayed even to the powers in the heavenly places. Paul then kneels before the Father and prays that believers would be strengthened by the Spirit, that Christ would dwell in their hearts, and that, rooted and grounded in love, they would grasp the vast love of Christ and be filled with all the fullness of God. He closes with praise to the God who is able to do far more than we ask or imagine.

## Chapter Background and Story

Paul begins chapter 3 as if he is about to pray: “For this cause I, Paul...” But he interrupts himself to explain his own role in God’s plan, and he does not return to the prayer until verse 14. This digression, from verse 2 to verse 13, explains the “mystery” of the gospel and Paul’s calling to proclaim it.

Paul was writing as a prisoner, probably in Rome, where he was under house arrest awaiting trial (*Acts 28:16*, 30–31). He had been arrested in Jerusalem precisely because of his ministry to the Gentiles (*Acts 21:27–36*; *22:21–22*). So when he calls himself “the prisoner of Christ Jesus on behalf of you Gentiles,” he means it literally. His chains were the direct result of his commitment to bringing the gospel to people like the Ephesians.

The chapter ends with one of the most beautiful prayers in the Bible and a soaring doxology. Together they form the climax of the first half of Ephesians, before Paul turns to practical instructions in chapter 4.

### Paul’s Stewardship of the Mystery (*3:1–5*)

“*For this cause I, Paul, am the prisoner of Christ Jesus on behalf of you Gentiles*” (*v. 1*). Paul does not see himself as Rome’s prisoner but as Christ’s. His imprisonment is part of Christ’s purpose.

“*if it is so that you have heard of the administration of that grace of God which was given me toward you*” (*v. 2*). “Administration” translates a word meaning stewardship or management of a household. God had entrusted Paul with a special responsibility: to dispense God’s grace to the Gentiles.

“*how that by revelation the mystery was made known to me, as I wrote before in few words*” (*v. 3*). Paul had already touched on this in chapters 1 and 2. “*which in other generations was not made known to the children of men, as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets in the Spirit*” (*v. 5*). The Old Testament did speak of Gentiles being blessed through Abraham and turning to the LORD (*Genesis 12:3*; *Isaiah 49:6*). What had not been fully revealed was the way it would happen: Gentiles joining God’s people on equal terms, without becoming Jews, united in one body in Christ. The content of the mystery is studied below.

### The Least of All Saints (*3:7–13*)

“*of which I was made a servant according to the gift of that grace of God which was given me according to the working of his power*” (*v. 7*). Paul’s ministry was a gift of grace and empowered by God. Paul’s humble description of himself and his calling is studied below.

“*and to make all men see what is the administration of the mystery which for ages has been hidden in God, who created all things through Jesus Christ*” (*v. 9*). The God who created all things through Christ has now revealed His plan for all things in Christ.

“*to the intent that now through the assembly the manifold wisdom of God might be made known to the principalities and the powers in the heavenly places*” (*v. 10*). This is a breathtaking statement. The church, a community of reconciled Jews and Gentiles, is God’s showcase to the spiritual powers of the universe. “Manifold” means many-colored or multifaceted, like a richly embroidered fabric. When angels and spiritual powers look at the church, they see God’s wisdom in bringing together people who had been divided. “*according to the eternal purpose which he accomplished in Christ Jesus our Lord*” (*v. 11*).

“*In him we have boldness and access in confidence through our faith in him*” (*v. 12*). Because of Christ, believers can approach God freely and confidently, without fear. “*Therefore I ask that you may not lose heart at my troubles for you, which are your glory*” (*v. 13*). Paul did not want his readers to be discouraged by his imprisonment. His sufferings were for their benefit and showed how much God valued them.

### Paul’s Prayer (*3:14–19*)

“*For this cause, I bow my knees to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ*” (*v. 14*). Jews usually stood to pray (*Mark 11:25*; *Luke 18:11*, 13). Kneeling suggested special earnestness and humility. “*from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named*” (*v. 15*). In Greek there is a wordplay: “Father” is *pater*, and “family” is *patria*. Every family takes its name and existence from God, the ultimate Father. The content of Paul’s prayer is studied below.

### Doxology (*3:20–21*)

Paul’s closing praise is studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Ephesians 3:6* — Fellow Heirs, Fellow Members, Fellow Partakers

> *“that the Gentiles are fellow heirs and fellow members of the body, and fellow partakers of his promise in Christ Jesus through the Good News,”*
>
> — *Ephesians 3:6* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse states the content of the mystery Paul has been describing. “That the Gentiles are fellow heirs and fellow members of the body, and fellow partakers of his promise in Christ Jesus through the Good News.”

In Greek, Paul uses three words that all begin with the same prefix, meaning “together with.” The Gentiles are “co-heirs,” “co-members of the body,” and “co-sharers of the promise.” The repetition emphasizes complete equality and partnership.

“Fellow heirs” means Gentiles share the same inheritance as Jewish believers. They are not second-class heirs who receive a lesser portion.

“Fellow members of the body” means Gentiles are part of the same body, the church, with Christ as its head. They are not attached loosely from the outside; they are members of one organism.

“Fellow partakers of his promise” means the promises God made to Abraham and Israel now belong to Gentile believers as well.

All of this happens “in Christ Jesus” and “through the Good News.” Union with Christ, received through the gospel, is what brings Gentiles into this full belonging.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse expresses the revolutionary nature of the gospel. For centuries, the distinction between Israel and the nations had been fundamental. Israel was God’s chosen people, set apart by covenant, Law, and temple. Gentiles could join Israel by becoming proselytes, but they had to adopt the Law and its customs. The mystery revealed in Christ is that Gentiles become full members of God’s people simply by faith in Christ, without becoming Jews.

This does not mean God has abandoned Israel or that Jewish identity is erased. Paul elsewhere insists that God’s gifts and calling to Israel are irrevocable (*Romans 11:29*), and that Gentile believers have been grafted into Israel’s olive tree (*Romans 11:17–24*). The church is not a replacement for Israel but the fulfillment of God’s promise that through Abraham all nations would be blessed. Christians have different views on how the church and Israel relate in God’s ongoing plan, but they share the conviction that in Christ, Jew and Gentile are one family.

This mystery reveals God’s heart for all peoples. From the beginning, His plan was to gather a family from every nation, tribe, people, and language (*Revelation 7:9*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Many believers feel like outsiders in their churches, perhaps because of their background, culture, past, or social status. This verse declares that in Christ, every believer is a full heir, a full member, and a full partaker of God’s promises. No one is a second-class Christian.

This verse also challenges churches to embody this equality. Do people of every background feel fully welcomed, included, and valued? Are some treated as more important than others? The gospel calls the church to reflect God’s design of full and equal belonging in Christ.

### *Ephesians 3:8* — The Unsearchable Riches of Christ

> *“To me, the very least of all saints, was this grace given, to preach to the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ,”*
>
> — *Ephesians 3:8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul describes himself with remarkable humility: “the very least of all saints.” In Greek, Paul creates a new word, something like “leaster” or “less than the least.” He is not merely saying he is the least of the apostles (as in *1 Corinthians 15:9*); he says he is less than the least of all God’s people.

Why did Paul think of himself this way? He never forgot that he had once persecuted the church (*1 Timothy 1:13–15*). He was deeply aware that his calling was not something he deserved.

“Was this grace given.” Paul’s ministry was a gift. God chose the least likely person to carry the gospel to the Gentiles.

The purpose: “to preach to the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ.” “Unsearchable” means something so vast that it can never be fully explored or traced out, like footprints that cannot be tracked to their end. The riches of Christ, His grace, love, wisdom, and power, are inexhaustible.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows the connection between humility and grace. Paul’s sense of his own unworthiness did not make him timid or ineffective. On the contrary, it made him all the more amazed at God’s grace and all the more eager to share it. Those who know they have received grace freely are often the most passionate about offering it to others.

The phrase “unsearchable riches of Christ” reminds believers that no one ever exhausts the treasure of knowing Christ. Even the apostle Paul, after years of ministry and deep revelation, saw himself standing at the edge of an ocean. Every believer can keep discovering more of Christ throughout life and eternity.

Paul’s humility is genuine, not false modesty. He does not deny God’s work in his life; in other places he defends his apostleship vigorously. But he attributes everything to grace. As he said in *1 Corinthians 15:10*, “*by the grace of God I am what I am*” (*1 Corinthians 15:10*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Some believers feel unqualified to serve God or to share their faith because of their past or their weaknesses. Paul’s example shows that God delights in using unlikely people. A sense of unworthiness, rightly held, can become a channel for grace rather than an obstacle.

This verse also invites believers to keep exploring the riches of Christ. Faith is not meant to become stale or routine. Through Scripture, prayer, worship, and fellowship, there is always more to discover of His love and wisdom.

### *Ephesians 3:16–19* — Rooted and Grounded in Love

> *“that he would grant you, according to the riches of his glory, that you may be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner person, that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith, to the end that you, being rooted and grounded in love, may be strengthened to comprehend with all the saints what is the width and length and height and depth, and to know Christ’s love which surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled with all the fullness of God.”*
>
> — *Ephesians 3:16–19* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul’s prayer has several connected requests, each building on the last.

First, that God would grant them “according to the riches of his glory” to be “strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner person.” The “inner person” is the heart, the spiritual center of a person. Paul prays for inner strength that comes from the Holy Spirit, measured not by human limits but by the riches of God’s glory.

Second, “that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith.” Christ already lives in believers, but “dwell” suggests settling down and being fully at home. Paul prays that Christ would be completely at home in every part of their lives.

Third, that they would be “rooted and grounded in love.” Paul mixes two images: a tree with deep roots and a building with a solid foundation. Love is the soil in which believers grow and the foundation on which they stand.

Fourth, that they would “be strengthened to comprehend with all the saints what is the width and length and height and depth.” Paul is speaking of the dimensions of Christ’s love. It is wide enough to embrace all people, long enough to last forever, high enough to lift people to heaven, and deep enough to reach the lowest places of human sin and suffering. And this understanding comes “with all the saints.” It is grasped in community, not alone.

Fifth, “to know Christ’s love which surpasses knowledge.” This is a paradox. Believers are to know what is beyond knowing. They can experience Christ’s love truly, even though they can never measure it fully.

Finally, “that you may be filled with all the fullness of God.” This is the ultimate goal: to be filled with God’s own life, love, and character.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This prayer reveals what matters most in the Christian life. Paul does not pray for his readers’ circumstances, comfort, or success. He prays for inner strength, the indwelling of Christ, deep roots in love, and an ever-growing experience of Christ’s love. These are the things that sustain believers through every circumstance.

The image of being “rooted” in love is especially rich. Roots draw nourishment and provide stability. A tree with deep roots can withstand storms and drought (*Psalm 1:3*; *Jeremiah 17:7–8*). Believers who are rooted in Christ’s love can withstand the storms of life because their security does not depend on circumstances.

The phrase “with all the saints” is important. The love of Christ is so vast that no single believer can grasp it alone. Each believer, with their own experience of grace, contributes to the church’s shared understanding. Believers need one another to know the love of Christ more fully.

“Filled with all the fullness of God” does not mean believers become divine. It means they are filled with God’s presence and transformed to reflect His character, as much as human beings can, now partially and one day fully.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can pray this prayer for themselves and for others regularly. It is a prayer that reaches beyond surface needs to the deepest needs of the heart.

Many people live with an inner emptiness or insecurity, trying to fill it with achievement, relationships, possessions, or approval. This prayer points to the only source that can truly fill the heart: the love of Christ and the fullness of God. Being rooted and grounded in love provides a security that nothing else can give.

The call to grasp Christ’s love “with all the saints” also encourages believers to share their experiences of God’s love with one another. Testimony, fellowship, and worship together help each believer see more of the width, length, height, and depth of that love.

### *Ephesians 3:20–21* — Exceedingly Abundantly Above All We Ask

> *“Now to him who is able to do exceedingly abundantly above all that we ask or think, according to the power that works in us, to him be the glory in the assembly and in Christ Jesus to all generations, forever and ever. Amen.”*
>
> — *Ephesians 3:20–21* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After praying for such great things, Paul might have worried that he was asking too much. Instead, he bursts into praise, declaring that God is able to do even more.

“Now to him who is able to do exceedingly abundantly above all that we ask or think.” Paul piles up words to express the abundance of God’s ability. God can do more than believers ask. He can do more than they can even imagine. And He can do it “exceedingly abundantly,” far beyond every limit.

“According to the power that works in us.” This is not abstract power far away. It is the same power that raised Christ from the dead (*Ephesians 1:19–20*), now at work within believers.

“To him be the glory in the assembly and in Christ Jesus to all generations, forever and ever. Amen.” The goal of everything is God’s glory. And that glory is displayed in two places: in the church and in Christ Jesus. The church, as the body of Christ, is the place where God’s glory shines in the world, now and forever.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This doxology closes the first half of Ephesians. After three chapters of celebrating God’s grace, plan, and power, Paul ends with praise. Theology leads to worship. The more believers understand of God, the more they are moved to glorify Him.

The phrase “above all that we ask or think” does not mean God will give believers everything they want. Rather, it means that His purposes and power exceed human imagination. Sometimes He answers prayers in unexpected ways, doing something deeper and better than what was asked. His ability is unlimited, and His wisdom determines how it is used.

The mention of glory “in the assembly” is striking. The church, with all its flaws, is the place God has chosen to display His glory. This gives dignity and purpose to the ordinary life of local congregations. When believers love one another, worship together, and serve their communities, God’s glory is seen.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

When believers face situations that seem impossible, such as broken relationships, persistent struggles, or overwhelming needs, this verse reminds them that God is able to do far more than they can imagine. They can pray boldly, trusting His power and wisdom.

This verse also lifts believers’ expectations of what God can do in and through His church. Local congregations may seem small or ordinary, but they are the place where God has chosen to display His glory. Believers can serve with hope, knowing that God’s power is at work among them.

Finally, this doxology invites believers to make praise a habit. Every prayer, every reflection on God’s goodness, can end as Paul’s does: “to him be the glory... forever and ever.”

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Ephesians 3* reveals the mystery hidden for ages and now made known in Christ: Gentiles are fellow heirs, fellow members of the body, and fellow partakers of God’s promise. In Christ, people of every background belong fully to God’s family. This truth calls churches to welcome all believers as full and equal members and to display God’s wisdom by living as one reconciled people.

Paul’s example shows that God uses unlikely people. Though he saw himself as the least of all God’s people, he was entrusted with the privilege of proclaiming the unsearchable riches of Christ. Believers who feel unqualified can take heart. God’s grace, not human merit, equips people for His work. And the riches of Christ are inexhaustible, inviting believers to keep exploring them throughout their lives.

The heart of this chapter is Paul’s prayer. He asks that believers would be strengthened by the Spirit in their inner being, that Christ would make His home in their hearts, and that, rooted and grounded in love, they would grasp the immeasurable love of Christ and be filled with God’s fullness. This is a prayer for the deepest needs of the human heart, and believers can pray it for themselves and for one another. To be rooted in Christ’s love is to have a security that no storm can shake.

Finally, the chapter ends with praise to the God who is able to do far more than anyone can ask or imagine. His power is at work in His people, and His glory is displayed in the church and in Christ Jesus. Believers can face every challenge with bold prayer, confident hope, and a heart full of worship.

## Chapter Prayer

Father, I bow before You, from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named. Thank You for revealing the mystery of Your grace: that people from every nation are fellow heirs, members of one body, and sharers in Your promise in Christ. Thank You that You use the least likely people to share the unsearchable riches of Christ. Strengthen me with power through Your Spirit in my inner being. Let Christ make His home in my heart through faith. Root me and ground me in love. Give me, together with all Your people, the strength to grasp how wide and long and high and deep is the love of Christ, and to know this love that surpasses knowledge, so that I may be filled with all Your fullness. Now to You, who are able to do far more than all I ask or think, according to Your power at work in me, be the glory in the church and in Christ Jesus to all generations, forever and ever. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
