Ephesians · Chapter 4 of 6

# Ephesians — Chapter 4

Chapter Theme: Walking Worthy in Unity and New Life

[Read Ephesians 4 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/EPH04.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul urges believers to live worthily of their calling, with humility, gentleness, patience, and love, eagerly keeping the unity the Spirit creates, because there is one body, one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, and one God and Father of all. The risen Christ has given gifts to His people, including apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds, and teachers, to equip every believer for service so that the whole body grows to maturity in Christ, speaking the truth in love. Paul then calls believers to put off the old self, with its darkened and deceitful ways, and put on the new self created to be like God, replacing lies with truth, theft with generosity, harmful words with words that build up, and bitterness with kindness and forgiveness, just as God in Christ forgave them.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Ephesians 4* marks the turning point of the letter. In chapters 1–3, Paul celebrated what God has done: chosen, redeemed, raised, and united His people in Christ. Now, beginning with the word “therefore,” he explains how believers should live in light of all that. Christian ethics flows from Christian identity. Paul does not say, “Live this way so that God will accept you,” but “God has made you His people; now live like it.”

The chapter has two main sections. First, Paul focuses on the unity and growth of the church (*4:1–16*). The church is one body made up of many members, each with gifts from Christ, growing together toward maturity. Second, he describes the personal transformation that marks the new life in Christ (*4:17–32*). Believers are to put off the old way of life they once lived and put on the new self, created to be like God.

The original readers lived in a city full of idolatry, magic, sexual immorality, and economic exploitation. Many had come out of that world. Paul’s instructions helped them see what it meant to live differently, not as isolated individuals, but as members of a new community.

### Walk Worthily in Unity (*4:1–6*)

“*I therefore, the prisoner in the Lord, beg you to walk worthily of the calling with which you were called*” (*v. 1*). “Walk” again means to live day by day. To walk “worthily” means to live in a way that fits or matches one’s calling, like a person whose actions suit their position. The qualities that mark this walk, and the call to keep unity, are studied below.

“*There is one body and one Spirit, even as you also were called in one hope of your calling*” (*v. 4*), “*one Lord, one faith, one baptism*” (*v. 5*), “*one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in us all*” (*v. 6*). Paul lists seven “ones” that form the foundation of Christian unity. The list includes the Spirit, the Lord Jesus, and God the Father, the three persons of the Trinity. Believers are united not by their preferences or opinions but by these shared realities. The church does not create unity; it receives it from God and is called to guard it.

### Gifts for Building Up the Body (*4:7–16*)

“*But to each one of us, the grace was given according to the measure of the gift of Christ*” (*v. 7*). Unity does not mean sameness. Each believer receives a particular gift of grace from Christ.

“*Therefore he says, “When he ascended on high, he led captivity captive, and gave gifts to people.”*” (*v. 8*) Paul adapts *Psalm 68:18*, which pictures God ascending Mount Zion in triumph after victory, receiving tribute from captives. Paul applies it to Christ’s ascension. Having triumphed over sin, death, and evil powers, the risen Christ now distributes gifts to His people.

“*Now this, “He ascended”, what is it but that he also first descended into the lower parts of the earth?*” (*v. 9*) Interpreters understand “the lower parts of the earth” in different ways. Some see it as Christ’s descent to earth in the incarnation, the earth itself being “lower” than heaven. Others see it as His burial or His descent to the realm of the dead (see *1 Peter 3:18–19*). Others connect it with the coming of the Spirit at Pentecost. The main point is that the one who humbled Himself is now exalted. “*He who descended is the one who also ascended far above all the heavens, that he might fill all things*” (*v. 10*).

The gifts Christ gave to the church are studied below. “*until we all attain to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to a full grown man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ*” (*v. 13*). The goal is maturity. The church is to grow up together until it reflects Christ fully.

“*that we may no longer be children, tossed back and forth and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the trickery of men, in craftiness, after the wiles of error*” (*v. 14*). Immature believers are like small boats on a stormy sea, pushed around by every new teaching. Maturity brings stability.

“*but speaking truth in love, we may grow up in all things into him who is the head, Christ*” (*v. 15*). Truth and love belong together. Truth without love can be harsh and wounding; love without truth can be weak and deceptive. The church grows when its members speak honestly and lovingly to one another.

“*from whom all the body, being fitted and knit together through that which every joint supplies, according to the working in measure of each individual part, makes the body increase to the building up of itself in love*” (*v. 16*). Paul describes the church as a living body. Each part contributes, and each joint provides support. Growth happens when every member does its part, and the result is a body built up in love.

### The Old Life and the New (*4:17–24*)

“*This I say therefore, and testify in the Lord, that you no longer walk as the rest of the Gentiles also walk, in the futility of their mind*” (*v. 17*). Paul uses “Gentiles” here to describe those who do not know God. His readers were Gentiles by birth, but they were no longer to live as their pagan neighbors did.

“*being darkened in their understanding, alienated from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them, because of the hardening of their hearts*” (*v. 18*). Paul traces a sad progression. Hardened hearts lead to ignorance, which leads to darkened understanding and separation from God’s life. “*They, having become callous, gave themselves up to lust, to work all uncleanness with greediness*” (*v. 19*). When people lose their sensitivity to God, they abandon themselves to self-indulgence, always wanting more.

“*But you didn’t learn Christ that way*” (*v. 20*), “*if indeed you heard him and were taught in him, even as truth is in Jesus*” (*v. 21*). The phrase “learn Christ” is unusual. Believers do not merely learn about Christ; they learn Christ Himself, His character and His way. The transformation that follows is studied below.

### Practical Holiness (*4:25–32*)

Paul now gives specific examples of putting off the old and putting on the new. Each has a negative command, a positive replacement, and a reason.

“*Therefore, putting away falsehood, speak truth each one with his neighbor, for we are members of one another*” (*v. 25*). Lying harms the body, because believers are connected like parts of one body. Deceiving another believer is like one hand deceiving the other.

“*“Be angry, and don’t sin.” Don’t let the sun go down on your wrath*” (*v. 26*), “*and don’t give place to the devil*” (*v. 27*). Paul quotes *Psalm 4:4*. Anger is not always sinful. God Himself is angry at injustice, and Jesus was angry at the corruption of the temple (*Mark 11:15–17*) and at hardness of heart (*Mark 3:5*). Anger at wrong, including anger at abuse and injustice, can be right. But anger can easily become sinful when it turns into bitterness, revenge, or cruelty. “Don’t let the sun go down on your wrath” encourages dealing with anger promptly rather than nursing it. Unresolved anger gives the devil a foothold. This does not mean every conflict must be fully resolved by sunset, or that those who have been seriously harmed must pretend all is well; it means not allowing anger to settle in and harden into hatred.

“*Let him who stole steal no more; but rather let him labor, producing with his hands something that is good, that he may have something to give to him who has need*” (*v. 28*). Notice the transformation. The thief does not just stop stealing; he becomes a worker and then a giver. The new life moves from taking, to earning, to sharing.

“*Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear*” (*v. 29*). “Corrupt” means rotten, like spoiled fruit. Words can either decay and spread harm, or they can build up and give grace. Believers are called to choose words that fit the need of the moment and bless the hearer.

“*Don’t grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption*” (*v. 30*). The Holy Spirit is a person who can be grieved. When believers harm one another through lies, anger, theft, or corrupt speech, they grieve the Spirit who lives in them and unites them. The call to replace bitterness with kindness and forgiveness is studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Ephesians 4:2–3* — Keeping the Unity of the Spirit

> *“with all lowliness and humility, with patience, bearing with one another in love, being eager to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.”*
>
> — *Ephesians 4:2–3* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul describes what it looks like to walk worthily of one’s calling. He lists four qualities.

“Lowliness and humility.” In the Greek and Roman world, humility was often seen as weakness, the attitude of a slave. Christianity transformed it into a virtue, modeled by Christ who humbled Himself (*Philippians 2:5–8*). Humility means not thinking too highly of oneself and putting others first.

“With patience.” Patience means being slow to anger and willing to endure others’ faults and slowness without giving up on them.

“Bearing with one another in love.” This means putting up with one another’s weaknesses, quirks, and irritations, not grudgingly, but lovingly. Every community includes people who are difficult at times, and everyone is difficult to someone.

Then Paul gives the goal: “being eager to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.” The word “eager” means making every effort, being diligent. Unity is not automatic; it must be guarded actively. Notice that it is “the unity of the Spirit.” The Spirit has already created unity among believers. Their task is to keep it, protect it, and not destroy it. Peace is the “bond,” like a cord or ligament, that holds the body together.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that Christian unity is both a gift and a task. It is a gift because the Spirit has made all believers one in Christ (*Ephesians 2:14–18*). It is a task because sin, pride, and selfishness constantly threaten to break it apart. Jesus prayed for the unity of His followers, “*that they may all be one*” (*John 17:21*), so that the world would believe. Unity among believers is a powerful witness to the gospel.

The qualities Paul lists are the very qualities of Christ. He was gentle and lowly in heart (*Matthew 11:29*), patient with His disciples’ slowness, and bore with their failures in love. When believers display these qualities, they reflect Christ to one another and to the world.

Unity does not mean uniformity, as Paul will show in the following verses about diverse gifts. Nor does it mean ignoring serious error or harm. It means a shared commitment to Christ and to one another, expressed in humility, patience, and love, so that differences do not become divisions.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Churches, families, and friendships are often damaged not by major doctrinal disputes but by pride, impatience, and small irritations allowed to grow. These verses call believers to practice humility, patience, and forbearance in everyday relationships. That might mean letting minor offenses go, listening before reacting, or assuming the best about others.

Keeping the unity of the Spirit also requires effort. When tension arises, believers can take initiative to seek peace, through honest conversation, apology, or forgiveness. Bearing with one another in love does not mean tolerating abuse or ignoring harm, but it does mean extending the same grace believers have received.

### *Ephesians 4:11–12* — Equipping the Saints for Ministry

> *“He gave some to be apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, shepherds and teachers; for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving, to the building up of the body of Christ,”*
>
> — *Ephesians 4:11–12* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul lists the gifts the ascended Christ gave to the church. Notice that the gifts are people. Christ gave the church “apostles,” “prophets,” “evangelists,” and “shepherds and teachers.”

Apostles were those sent by Christ to establish the church and lay its foundation (*Ephesians 2:20*). Prophets spoke God’s revelation and encouragement to the church. Evangelists proclaimed the gospel and helped spread the faith to new people and places (Philip is called an evangelist in *Acts 21:8*). “Shepherds and teachers” may describe one role, pastors who teach, or two closely related roles. “Shepherd” is the word often translated “pastor.” These leaders care for, guide, protect, and teach God’s people.

Verse 12 explains the purpose of these gifts. They were given “for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving, to the building up of the body of Christ.” The word “perfecting” means equipping, preparing, or restoring, like mending nets or setting a bone. Leaders are to equip “the saints,” all believers, for “the work of serving,” or ministry. The result is that the body of Christ is built up.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This passage overturns the idea that ministry is only for professional clergy. Leaders are given to equip all believers to serve. Every member of the church has a part in the work of ministry. Pastors and teachers succeed not when they do all the work themselves but when they help others grow and serve.

Christians differ on how these roles continue today. Many believe that apostles and prophets in the foundational sense belonged to the first generation of the church, while their functions continue in other forms, such as missionaries and church planters, and those who encourage and exhort. Others believe the gifts of apostle and prophet continue in the church today in a similar way to the New Testament, though not adding new Scripture. Evangelists, pastors, and teachers are recognized across nearly all traditions. Whatever the view, Paul’s main point is clear: Christ provides leaders so that the whole church can be equipped and built up.

The fact that these gifts come from the ascended Christ is also important. Church leadership is not merely a human institution. It is Christ’s provision for His people, and leaders are accountable to Him for how they serve.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Every believer has a role in the work of ministry. Serving is not just for pastors or leaders. Believers can ask how God has gifted them, whether in teaching, encouraging, serving practically, giving, showing hospitality, or caring for others, and how they can use those gifts to build up the body.

For church leaders, this passage provides a clear job description: equip others. Healthy leadership empowers people, trains them, and releases them to serve, rather than controlling or doing everything alone.

This passage also encourages believers to value and support faithful leaders who help them grow, and to receive their teaching and care with gratitude.

### *Ephesians 4:22–24* — Put Off the Old, Put On the New

> *“that you put away, as concerning your former way of life, the old man that grows corrupt after the lusts of deceit, and that you be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who in the likeness of God has been created in righteousness and holiness of truth.”*
>
> — *Ephesians 4:22–24* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul uses the image of changing clothes. Believers are to “put away” the old self and “put on” the new self.

“The old man” refers to the old self, the person a believer was before coming to Christ, shaped by sin and self-centeredness. Paul describes it as the old man “*that grows corrupt after the lusts of deceit*” (*v. 22*). The old self is decaying, and its desires are deceptive. They promise satisfaction but lead to ruin.

“Be renewed in the spirit of your mind.” Between putting off and putting on, there is the renewal of the mind. Transformation is not merely external behavior change. It involves a new way of thinking, renewed by God’s Spirit and truth (see *Romans 12:2*).

“Put on the new man, who in the likeness of God has been created in righteousness and holiness of truth.” The new self is a new creation, made to be like God. It is marked by righteousness, doing what is right, and holiness, being set apart for God. And it is rooted in truth, in contrast to the deceit of the old self.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

In *Colossians 3:9–10*, Paul uses similar language, saying that believers have already put off the old self and put on the new. In *Ephesians 4*, he speaks of it as an ongoing practice. Both are true. At conversion, believers decisively became new people in Christ. Each day, they live out that reality by continuing to set aside old habits and embrace new ones.

The new self is the new man “*who in the likeness of God has been created*” (*v. 24*). This recalls *Genesis 1:26–27*, where humanity was created in God’s image. Sin marred that image, but in Christ it is being restored. The goal of the Christian life is to become more fully what God created humans to be.

Renewal of the mind is the key. Old habits are rooted in old ways of thinking. As believers fill their minds with God’s truth, through Scripture, prayer, and Christian community, their thinking changes, and their behavior follows.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Change can feel slow and difficult. Old habits, attitudes, and reactions do not disappear overnight. This passage encourages believers to see transformation as a daily practice of putting off what belongs to the old life and putting on what belongs to the new.

Practical steps may include recognizing the lies behind certain behaviors and replacing them with God’s truth, avoiding situations that feed old desires, and intentionally practicing new habits of kindness, honesty, and generosity. Help from trusted believers, and in some situations from counselors or support groups, can also be part of this process.

Most of all, believers can remember that the new self is already theirs in Christ. They are not trying to become someone they are not; they are learning to live as who they truly are.

### *Ephesians 4:31–32* — Kind, Tenderhearted, Forgiving

> *“Let all bitterness, wrath, anger, outcry, and slander be put away from you, with all malice. And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you.”*
>
> — *Ephesians 4:31–32* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul concludes this chapter with a list of things to put away and things to put on.

Verse 31 lists attitudes and behaviors that destroy relationships. “Bitterness” is a settled resentment that refuses to let go of hurts. “Wrath” is a sudden outburst of rage. “Anger” here is a lasting, smoldering hostility. “Outcry” refers to shouting and quarreling. “Slander” is speaking evil of others. “Malice” is a desire to harm. Paul says all of these must be “put away.”

Verse 32 describes what should replace them. “Be kind to one another.” Kindness is generous goodness toward others. “Tender hearted” means compassionate, deeply moved by others’ needs. “Forgiving each other” means releasing others from the debt of their wrongs.

The reason is given at the end: “just as God also in Christ forgave you.” Believers forgive because they have been forgiven. God’s forgiveness of them, through Christ’s death, is both the motivation and the model for their forgiveness of others.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Jesus taught that those who have been forgiven much should forgive others. In the parable of the unforgiving servant, a man forgiven a huge debt refused to forgive a small one, and Jesus said that such a heart contradicts the mercy it has received (*Matthew 18:21–35*). When believers remember how much God has forgiven them, it becomes possible to forgive others.

Forgiveness is often misunderstood. Biblical forgiveness means releasing the desire for revenge and entrusting justice to God (*Romans 12:19*). It does not mean pretending the wrong did not happen, excusing it, or immediately restoring trust. Forgiveness is not the same as reconciliation, which requires repentance and rebuilt trust. And forgiveness does not require a person to remain in danger. Someone who has suffered abuse can forgive while also seeking safety, setting boundaries, and pursuing justice through proper authorities. Forgiveness is often a process, not a single moment, especially for deep wounds.

The words “kind” and “tender hearted” reflect the character of God, who is kind even to the ungrateful and evil (*Luke 6:35*) and full of compassion. As believers forgive and show kindness, they reflect their Father’s character.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Bitterness can poison a person’s heart and relationships for years. This passage invites believers to bring their hurts to God and begin the process of letting go of resentment. That process may involve prayer, honest conversation, time, and sometimes the help of a pastor or counselor.

Kindness and compassion can be practiced in small, daily ways: a gentle word, a patient response, a thoughtful act of help. These small choices shape relationships and reflect God’s character.

When forgiveness feels impossible, believers can remember the cross. God forgave them at great cost. That truth does not make forgiveness easy, but it makes it possible, and it reminds believers that they never forgive alone. The Spirit helps them do what they cannot do on their own.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Ephesians 4* shows how believers live out their high calling in Christ. The first emphasis is unity. Believers are one body, with one Spirit, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, and one God and Father. The Spirit has already made them one; their task is to guard that unity through humility, gentleness, patience, and love. In a world full of division, a church that bears with one another in love bears powerful witness to Christ.

The second emphasis is growth. The risen Christ has given leaders to equip all believers for ministry, so that the whole body grows toward maturity. Every believer has a part to play. As the church speaks the truth in love and each member contributes, the body is built up and becomes stable, no longer tossed around by every new idea.

The third emphasis is transformation. Believers are called to put off the old self, with its deceitful desires and darkened thinking, and to put on the new self, created to be like God in righteousness and holiness. This involves the renewal of the mind and practical changes in daily life: telling the truth instead of lying, dealing with anger before it becomes sin, working and giving instead of stealing, speaking words that build up rather than tear down.

Finally, the chapter calls believers to replace bitterness, rage, and malice with kindness, compassion, and forgiveness, forgiving others as God in Christ has forgiven them. This forgiveness does not excuse wrongdoing or require anyone to stay in harm’s way, but it releases the heart from the poison of resentment. As believers live this way, they honor the Spirit who lives in them and display the beauty of the new life in Christ.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, You have called me to a life worthy of Your name. Make me humble, gentle, and patient, bearing with others in love. Help me to guard the unity Your Spirit has created among Your people. Thank You for the gifts You have given Your church; show me how You have equipped me to serve, and help me to build up others. Teach me to speak the truth in love. Renew my mind by Your truth. Help me to put off my old self and put on the new self, created to be like God in righteousness and holiness. Guard my words, so that they build up and give grace. Holy Spirit, I do not want to grieve You. Remove all bitterness, rage, and malice from my heart. Make me kind and tenderhearted, and give me grace to forgive others as God in Christ has forgiven me. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Ephesians · Chapter 5 of 6

# Ephesians — Chapter 5

Chapter Theme: Walking in Love, Light, and Wisdom

[Read Ephesians 5 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/EPH05.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul calls believers to imitate God as beloved children and to walk in love as Christ loved them and gave Himself for them. Because they were once darkness but are now light in the Lord, they must turn from sexual immorality, impurity, and greed, and live as children of light, exposing the deeds of darkness. They are to live wisely, making the most of their time, and to be filled with the Spirit, which shows itself in worship, thanksgiving, and mutual submission out of reverence for Christ. Paul then describes Christian marriage as a living picture of Christ and the church: wives are to submit to their husbands as to the Lord, and husbands are to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Ephesians 5* continues the practical teaching that began in chapter 4. Paul has called believers to put off the old self and put on the new. Now he describes what that new life looks like using three images: walking in love (*5:1–6*), walking in light (*5:7–14*), and walking in wisdom (*5:15–21*). He then begins a section on Christian households (*5:22–6*:9), starting with marriage.

The city of Ephesus, like most Greek and Roman cities, was marked by widespread sexual immorality, often connected with pagan religion. Feasts in honor of gods could include drunkenness and sexual excess. Greed and exploitation were common in commerce. Against this background, Paul’s call to purity, generosity, and Spirit-filled worship was strikingly countercultural.

His teaching on marriage was also shaped by its setting. In the Roman world, husbands held enormous legal power over their wives. Moral philosophers wrote “household codes” instructing wives, children, and slaves to obey, but they rarely placed demands on the husband. Paul’s household instructions take that familiar form and transform it. He addresses wives directly as moral agents, places all relationships under Christ, and gives husbands the demanding command to love their wives with the self-sacrificing love of Christ.

### Imitators of God, Walking in Love (*5:1–6*)

The call to imitate God and walk in love is studied below.

“*But sexual immorality, and all uncleanness or covetousness, let it not even be mentioned among you, as becomes saints*” (*v. 3*). Paul sets a high standard. These sins should not even be associated with God’s people. “Covetousness” is greed, the restless desire for more. It is listed alongside sexual sins because both are forms of selfish grasping.

“*nor filthiness, nor foolish talking, nor jesting, which are not appropriate, but rather giving of thanks*” (*v. 4*). “Jesting” here refers to crude or vulgar joking, not to healthy humor. Instead of speech that degrades, believers are to be people of thanksgiving.

“*Know this for sure, that no sexually immoral person, nor unclean person, nor covetous man (who is an idolater), has any inheritance in the Kingdom of Christ and God*” (*v. 5*). Paul calls greed a form of idolatry, because it makes possessions into a god. He is describing people whose lives are characterized by these sins, not believers who struggle and repent. “*Let no one deceive you with empty words, for because of these things the wrath of God comes on the children of disobedience*” (*v. 6*). Some were apparently teaching that such sins did not matter. Paul warns against being misled.

### Children of Light (*5:7–14*)

“*Therefore don’t be partakers with them*” (*v. 7*). “*For you were once darkness, but are now light in the Lord. Walk as children of light*” (*v. 8*). Paul does not say believers were once “in” darkness but that they “were” darkness. Now they “are” light. Their identity has changed completely.

“*for the fruit of the Spirit is in all goodness and righteousness and truth*” (*v. 9*), “*proving what is well pleasing to the Lord*” (*v. 10*). Light produces fruit: goodness, righteousness, and truth. Believers are to discern and test what pleases the Lord.

“*Have no fellowship with the unfruitful deeds of darkness, but rather even reprove them*” (*v. 11*). Believers should not participate in evil but should expose it. Light naturally reveals what darkness hides. “*But all things, when they are reproved, are revealed by the light, for everything that reveals is light*” (*v. 13*).

This principle is important for the life of the church. Hiding wrongdoing, especially abuse, in order to protect a reputation is a deed of darkness. Bringing such things into the light, with care for those who have been harmed and through proper channels and authorities, is part of walking as children of light.

“*Therefore he says, “Awake, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.”*” (*v. 14*) This may be a line from an early Christian hymn, perhaps sung at baptisms, drawing on themes from *Isaiah 60:1*. It calls people to wake from spiritual sleep and receive the light of Christ.

### Walking in Wisdom and Filled with the Spirit (*5:15–21*)

Paul’s call to live wisely and use time well is studied below. “*Therefore, don’t be foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is*” (*v. 17*). Wisdom means understanding God’s will and living by it. The call to be filled with the Spirit, and what that produces, is studied below.

### Marriage: A Picture of Christ and the Church (*5:22–33*)

Paul’s teaching on wives and husbands is studied below. “*“For this cause a man will leave his father and mother and will be joined to his wife. Then the two will become one flesh.”*” (*v. 31*) Paul quotes *Genesis 2:24*, the foundational text on marriage, which Jesus also quoted (*Matthew 19:5*). Marriage is a covenant union so close that husband and wife become one.

“*This mystery is great, but I speak concerning Christ and the assembly*” (*v. 32*). Paul reveals that marriage, from the beginning, was designed to point beyond itself to the relationship between Christ and His people. Human marriage is a living parable of Christ’s love for the church. “*Nevertheless each of you must also love his own wife even as himself; and let the wife see that she respects her husband*” (*v. 33*). Paul returns to the practical. Love and respect are the twin pillars of a Christian marriage.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Ephesians 5:1–2* — Imitators of God, Walking in Love

> *“Be therefore imitators of God, as beloved children. Walk in love, even as Christ also loved us and gave himself up for us, an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweet-smelling fragrance.”*
>
> — *Ephesians 5:1–2* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse follows directly from the end of chapter 4, where Paul urged believers to forgive one another as God in Christ forgave them. Now he says, “Be therefore imitators of God, as beloved children.”

Children naturally imitate their parents. They copy their words, gestures, and habits. Paul says believers, as God’s beloved children, should imitate their heavenly Father. What does that look like? Verse 2 explains: “Walk in love.”

The model of this love is Christ: “even as Christ also loved us and gave himself up for us.” Christ’s love was not merely a feeling. It was self-giving. He gave His very life.

Paul describes Christ’s self-giving as “an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweet-smelling fragrance.” In the Old Testament, sacrifices that pleased God were described as a pleasing aroma (*Genesis 8:21*; *Leviticus 1:9*). Christ’s sacrifice on the cross was the perfect offering, fully pleasing to God.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

It is remarkable that Paul calls believers to imitate God. In one sense, God is utterly beyond human imitation. But God has revealed Himself in Jesus Christ, so believers can see what God’s love looks like in human form. Jesus said, “*just as I have loved you, you also love one another*” (*John 13:34*).

The phrase “beloved children” is important. Believers do not imitate God in order to become His children; they imitate Him because they already are His beloved children. The motivation is not fear but love. A child who knows they are loved naturally wants to be like the parent who loves them.

Christ’s sacrifice is the measure of love. It is not merely kindness when it is convenient but costly self-giving for the good of others. This is the love believers are called to walk in, a love that forgives, serves, and puts others first.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse provides a simple guide for daily life: imitate God by walking in love. In each relationship and situation, believers can ask how Christ’s self-giving love would act here. That might mean patience with a difficult family member, generosity toward someone in need, or forgiveness toward someone who has caused hurt.

It also reminds believers of their identity. They are God’s beloved children. Living from that security frees them to love others without needing to earn approval or protect themselves at all costs.

### *Ephesians 5:15–16* — Redeeming the Time

> *“Therefore watch carefully how you walk, not as unwise, but as wise, redeeming the time, because the days are evil.”*
>
> — *Ephesians 5:15–16* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“Therefore watch carefully how you walk, not as unwise, but as wise.” Paul calls believers to pay careful attention to how they live. Life should not be lived carelessly or thoughtlessly. Wisdom means understanding God’s ways and applying them to daily choices.

“Redeeming the time.” The word “redeem” means to buy back or buy up, like a merchant seizing a good opportunity in the market. “Time” here refers to opportunities, moments that can be used for good. Believers are to make the most of every opportunity God gives them.

“Because the days are evil.” Paul recognized that the world is full of evil influences and that time is limited. In such a world, opportunities to do good, to share the gospel, and to grow in faith should not be wasted.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The Bible often speaks of life’s brevity. *Psalm 90:12* prays, “*So teach us to count our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom*” (*Psalm 90:12*). *James 4:14* reminds readers that life is a vapor that appears for a little while and then vanishes. Wisdom includes recognizing that time is a gift to be stewarded for God’s purposes.

“The days are evil” does not mean believers should withdraw from the world in fear. Rather, it means that in a world darkened by sin, the light of believers is especially needed. Every opportunity to love, serve, and witness matters.

This wisdom is not anxious busyness. Jesus Himself rested, withdrew to pray, and enjoyed meals with friends. Redeeming the time means using it well for God’s purposes, which includes rest, worship, and relationships, not just productivity.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

In an age of endless distractions, these verses invite believers to examine how they use their time. Hours can slip away through mindless scrolling, entertainment, or busyness that does not matter. Redeeming the time means being intentional about what fills each day.

This might mean setting aside regular time for prayer and Scripture, prioritizing relationships with family and friends, looking for opportunities to serve, or saying no to activities that crowd out what matters most. Wisdom also means recognizing God-given opportunities when they appear, such as a conversation with someone in need or an open door to share faith, and seizing them.

### *Ephesians 5:18–21* — Be Filled with the Spirit

> *“Don’t be drunken with wine, in which is dissipation, but be filled with the Spirit, speaking to one another in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs; singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord; giving thanks always concerning all things in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ to God, even the Father; subjecting yourselves to one another in the fear of Christ.”*
>
> — *Ephesians 5:18–21* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul contrasts two kinds of influence. “Don’t be drunken with wine, in which is dissipation.” Drunkenness leads to “dissipation,” a wasteful, reckless, out-of-control life. In the pagan festivals of the time, drunkenness was often part of worship, believed to bring people into contact with the gods.

“But be filled with the Spirit.” Instead of being controlled by wine, believers are to be filled and influenced by the Holy Spirit. In Greek, this command is in the present tense, meaning “keep on being filled.” It is a continual experience, not a one-time event.

Paul then describes what a Spirit-filled life looks like through four results.

First, “speaking to one another in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs.” The Spirit produces worship that builds up the community.

Second, “singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord.” Worship is not only outward but from the heart.

Third, “giving thanks always concerning all things in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ to God, even the Father.” The Spirit produces a grateful heart.

Fourth, “subjecting yourselves to one another in the fear of Christ.” The Spirit produces humility and mutual submission, a willingness to put others before oneself out of reverence for Christ.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Being filled with the Spirit is not mainly about dramatic experiences, though the Spirit may sometimes work in powerful ways. According to Paul, the evidence of being Spirit-filled is worship, gratitude, and humble relationships. These are the marks of a community in which the Spirit is at work.

The phrase “giving thanks always concerning all things” does not mean thanking God for evil itself, such as abuse, injustice, or tragedy. It means giving thanks in every circumstance, trusting that God is present and working even in hard times (*1 Thessalonians 5:18*). Gratitude flows from confidence in God’s goodness.

Verse 21 is a bridge to the household teaching that follows. In Greek, verse 22 does not even have its own verb; it borrows “subjecting” from verse 21. Mutual submission is the umbrella over all the relationships Paul goes on to describe. Every believer is called to humble, other-centered living, out of reverence for Christ.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Many people turn to alcohol, entertainment, or other substances to escape stress or find joy. Paul points to a better source: the Holy Spirit. Believers can ask regularly to be filled with the Spirit and can make room for Him through prayer, worship, and Scripture.

The fruit of the Spirit-filled life can be cultivated. Singing to God, alone and together, nurtures the heart. Practicing gratitude, perhaps by naming specific blessings each day, shapes perspective. Mutual submission shows up in everyday humility: listening, serving, deferring to others, and refusing to insist on one’s own way.

### *Ephesians 5:22–25* — Marriage Shaped by Christ’s Love

> *“Wives, be subject to your own husbands, as to the Lord. For the husband is the head of the wife, as Christ also is the head of the assembly, being himself the savior of the body. But as the assembly is subject to Christ, so let the wives also be to their own husbands in everything. Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the assembly and gave himself up for her,”*
>
> — *Ephesians 5:22–25* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul now applies the principle of mutual submission (v21) to marriage. He addresses wives first: “Wives, be subject to your own husbands, as to the Lord.” The word “subject” means to arrange oneself under, to yield or defer. Paul grounds this in the wife’s relationship with Christ: it is “as to the Lord,” an expression of her devotion to Him.

“For the husband is the head of the wife, as Christ also is the head of the assembly, being himself the savior of the body.” Paul compares the husband’s role to Christ’s role as head of the church. Importantly, Christ is described as “savior,” the one who gives His life for the body.

Then Paul addresses husbands, and this is where his teaching most sharply differs from the culture around him. “Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the assembly and gave himself up for her.” The standard for husbands is Christ’s self-sacrificing love. Christ did not use His position to dominate the church; He died for her. Husbands are called to the same kind of costly, self-giving love. In the verses that follow, Paul adds that husbands should love their wives as their own bodies, nourishing and cherishing them (vv28–29).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Christians have understood this passage in different ways, and both views are held by sincere believers who take Scripture seriously. Many, often called complementarians, understand “headship” to mean that husbands have a God-given responsibility of loving, servant leadership in the home, and that wives are called to respond to that leadership with respect and support. Others, often called egalitarians, emphasize that verse 21 calls all believers to mutual submission, understand “head” here primarily in terms of source, care, and self-giving rather than authority, and see Paul’s instructions as working within the structures of his time while planting the seeds of full partnership. Both views agree that husbands and wives are equal in dignity and worth before God (*Galatians 3:28*; *1 Peter 3:7*), and that the model for the husband is Christ’s self-giving love.

What this passage never teaches is that a husband may control, demean, or harm his wife. A husband who uses this passage to justify domination or abuse has completely reversed its meaning. Christ’s headship is expressed in sacrifice, not in force. Likewise, a wife’s submission is “as to the Lord,” which means it can never require her to sin, to accept abuse, or to place herself or her children in danger. Abuse in any form is a grievous sin that breaks the marriage covenant’s purpose. A spouse who is being abused should seek safety and help, and churches must protect and support victims rather than urging them to stay in harm’s way.

The deepest point of this passage is that marriage is a picture of the gospel (v32). Christ’s love for His people, self-giving, faithful, purifying, and nourishing, is the pattern for marriage. The church’s trusting response to Christ is also part of the picture. A marriage shaped by these realities becomes a living testimony to God’s love.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

For married believers, this passage invites reflection on how their marriage can reflect Christ’s love. For husbands, the question is whether their love is self-giving: do they put their wife’s good above their own comfort, listen to her, cherish her, and serve her? For wives, the question is whether they honor and support their husband as an expression of their devotion to Christ. For both, the call to mutual submission (v21) means humble, other-centered love.

Couples who hold different views on headship and roles can still agree on the heart of the passage: marriage is to be marked by Christlike love, respect, faithfulness, and mutual care. Wise counsel, honest communication, and prayer together can help couples work out these principles in their particular situation.

For those whose marriages are marked by control, fear, or abuse, this passage offers no support for that harm. God’s design is a relationship of love and safety. Seeking help from trusted pastors, counselors, domestic violence services, and, when necessary, legal authorities is a right and wise step.

For those who are single, widowed, or divorced, this passage still speaks. It reveals the love Christ has for every member of His church. Every believer is cherished, nourished, and loved by Christ, who gave Himself for them.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Ephesians 5* calls believers to a life that reflects the character of God. As His beloved children, they are to imitate Him by walking in love, the self-giving love Christ showed when He gave Himself for them. This love shapes every relationship and every choice.

Believers are also called to walk as children of light. Once they were darkness; now they are light in the Lord. This means turning from sexual immorality, impurity, and greed, which damage both the self and others, and choosing goodness, righteousness, and truth. Children of light also expose the deeds of darkness rather than covering them up, which includes refusing to hide abuse or wrongdoing within the church.

The chapter calls for wisdom in how believers use their time. In a world full of distraction and evil, every opportunity to love, serve, and witness is precious. Believers can live intentionally, making the most of each day.

At the heart of the chapter is the call to be continually filled with the Spirit. The evidence is not mainly dramatic experiences but worship, gratitude, and mutual submission out of reverence for Christ. This Spirit-filled life shapes even the most intimate relationship, marriage. Husbands are called to love their wives with Christ’s self-sacrificing love, and wives are called to honor their husbands as an expression of their devotion to Christ. Marriage becomes a living picture of Christ’s love for His church. It is never a license for control or harm, but a covenant of love, safety, and faithfulness that points to the greatest love of all.

## Chapter Prayer

Father, I am Your beloved child. Help me to imitate You by walking in love, just as Christ loved me and gave Himself for me. Thank You that I was once darkness but am now light in the Lord. Keep me from sexual immorality, impurity, and greed, and help me to live in goodness, righteousness, and truth. Give me courage to bring hidden wrongs into the light and compassion for those who have been harmed. Teach me to live wisely and to make the most of the time You give me. Fill me continually with Your Holy Spirit, so that my life overflows with worship, thanksgiving, and humble love for others. Bless marriages with Christlike love, respect, and faithfulness, and protect all who are in danger in their homes. Thank You, Lord Jesus, for loving Your church and giving Yourself for her. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Ephesians · Chapter 6 of 6

# Ephesians — Chapter 6

Chapter Theme: Faithful at Home and Strong in the Lord

[Read Ephesians 6 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/EPH06.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul continues his teaching on Christian households, calling children to obey and honor their parents and fathers not to provoke their children but to bring them up in the Lord’s training and instruction. He addresses servants and masters, reminding both that they serve one Master in heaven who shows no favoritism. Then Paul calls believers to be strong in the Lord and to put on the full armor of God, because their struggle is not against flesh and blood but against spiritual forces of evil. Truth, righteousness, the gospel of peace, faith, salvation, and the word of God equip them to stand firm, all undergirded by persistent prayer. The letter closes with a request for prayer, news of Tychicus, and a blessing of peace and grace.

## Chapter Background and Story

The final chapter of Ephesians completes Paul’s teaching on household relationships, which began in *Ephesians 5:22*, and then turns to the spiritual battle every believer faces.

In the Roman world, a household included not only parents and children but often servants or slaves as well. Roman fathers had near-absolute legal authority over their children, and slaves had very few rights. Paul writes within that world, but he addresses each member of the household as a responsible person before God, and he places demands on those with power (fathers and masters) that the culture rarely placed on them. Every relationship is brought under the lordship of Christ.

The section on spiritual armor (*6:10–20*) is one of the most vivid passages in Paul’s letters. Paul was writing as a prisoner, probably chained to a Roman soldier (v20; *Acts 28:16*, 20). He may have looked at that soldier’s equipment and seen in it a picture of the spiritual resources God provides. For the Ephesian believers, many of whom had once practiced magic and lived in fear of spiritual powers (*Acts 19:18–19*), this passage offered both a sober warning and great encouragement. The powers of evil are real, but Christ has already triumphed over them (*Ephesians 1:20–22*), and believers can stand firm in His strength.

### Children and Parents (*6:1–4*)

“*Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right*” (*v. 1*). Paul addresses children directly, which shows that they were present when the letter was read in the church gathering. Children were members of the community, not mere bystanders. “In the Lord” frames their obedience as part of their relationship with Christ.

“*“Honor your father and mother,” which is the first commandment with a promise*” (*v. 2*): “*“that it may be well with you, and you may live long on the earth.”*” (*v. 3*) Paul quotes the fifth commandment (*Exodus 20:12*; *Deuteronomy 5:16*). Honoring parents is a lifelong calling that continues into adulthood, even when obedience in the childhood sense no longer applies. It involves respect, gratitude, and care for parents, especially in their old age.

Obedience “in the Lord” never requires a child to do what is wrong, and this verse never justifies abuse by parents. Children who are being harmed need protection, and adults who know of abuse should act to protect them and report it to the proper authorities. Honoring parents who have caused deep harm may look very different, involving forgiveness and respect for their humanity while keeping healthy boundaries. Paul’s instruction to fathers is studied below.

### Servants and Masters (*6:5–9*)

“*Servants, be obedient to those who according to the flesh are your masters, with fear and trembling, in singleness of your heart, as to Christ*” (*v. 5*). Slavery was woven into the structure of the Roman Empire. A large portion of people in cities like Ephesus were enslaved. Roman slavery was not identical to the race-based chattel slavery of later centuries; people became slaves through war, debt, birth, or abandonment, and some could gain freedom. But it was still a system of ownership in which human beings could be bought, sold, beaten, and exploited.

Paul did not have the power to abolish this system, and his instructions address believers living within it. He calls enslaved believers to serve faithfully, not as people-pleasers, “*but as servants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart*” (*v. 6*), “*with good will doing service as to the Lord and not to men*” (*v. 7*). Their ultimate identity is not “slave” but “servant of Christ.” “*knowing that whatever good thing each one does, he will receive the same good again from the Lord, whether he is bound or free*” (*v. 8*). Christ sees and rewards their faithful work, even when earthly masters do not.

“*You masters, do the same things to them, and give up threatening, knowing that he who is both their Master and yours is in heaven, and there is no partiality with him*” (*v. 9*). This was radical. Masters were to treat slaves with the same good will, stop using threats, and remember that they themselves had a Master in heaven who would judge them impartially. In God’s eyes, master and slave stood on equal ground.

It is important to be clear: this passage does not endorse slavery as God’s design. Scripture condemns kidnapping and trading in human beings (*Exodus 21:16*; *1 Timothy 1:10*), and Paul encouraged slaves to gain their freedom if they could (*1 Corinthians 7:21*). The gospel’s declaration that all are one in Christ (*Galatians 3:28*) and that every person bears God’s image planted seeds that, in time, led many Christians to oppose and work to end slavery. Tragically, others in later centuries misused passages like this to defend the enslavement of Africans and others, a terrible distortion of Scripture that Christians must reject and repent of. Today, the principles Paul gives apply especially to work: employees can serve faithfully as to the Lord, and employers must treat workers justly, without threats or exploitation, remembering that they too answer to God.

### The Armor of God (*6:10–17*)

Paul’s call to be strong in the Lord, and his description of the spiritual struggle and the armor God provides, are studied below.

### Prayer (*6:18–20*)

The call to persistent prayer is studied below. “*Pray for me, that utterance may be given to me in opening my mouth, to make known with boldness the mystery of the Good News*” (*v. 19*), “*for which I am an ambassador in chains; that in it I may speak boldly, as I ought to speak*” (*v. 20*). Paul does not ask for release from prison. He asks for boldness to proclaim the gospel. An ambassador normally enjoyed honor and immunity; Paul, Christ’s ambassador, was in chains. Yet he saw even his imprisonment as an opportunity to make Christ known (*Philippians 1:12–14*).

### Closing Greetings (*6:21–24*)

“*But that you also may know my affairs, how I am doing, Tychicus, the beloved brother and faithful servant in the Lord, will make known to you all things*” (*v. 21*). Tychicus was a trusted coworker from the province of Asia (*Acts 20:4*) who also carried the letter to the Colossians (*Colossians 4:7–8*). “*I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that you may know our state and that he may comfort your hearts*” (*v. 22*).

“*Peace be to the brothers, and love with faith, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ*” (*v. 23*). “*Grace be with all those who love our Lord Jesus Christ with incorruptible love. Amen*” (*v. 24*). The letter ends as it began, with grace and peace (*Ephesians 1:2*). “Incorruptible love” means love that is sincere, undying, and unfailing.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Ephesians 6:4* — Bringing Up Children in the Lord

> *“You fathers, don’t provoke your children to wrath, but nurture them in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.”*
>
> — *Ephesians 6:4* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After addressing children, Paul turns to fathers. In the Roman world, fathers had nearly unlimited legal power over their children. They could discipline harshly, arrange marriages, and in some circumstances even reject newborn children. Paul’s instruction would have been surprising.

“You fathers, don’t provoke your children to wrath.” Fathers are not to exasperate their children through harshness, unfairness, constant criticism, favoritism, excessive demands, or inconsistency. Such treatment produces anger, discouragement, and resentment. *Colossians 3:21* adds the reason: so that children will not lose heart.

“But nurture them in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.” “Nurture” means to bring up, to feed and care for, to help grow. “Discipline” refers to training, including correction when needed. “Instruction” means teaching and guidance through words. Both are to be “of the Lord,” shaped by His character and His ways.

Though Paul addresses fathers, who held the most authority in the household, the principle applies to mothers and all who raise children.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reflects God’s own way of parenting His children. *Hebrews 12:5–11* describes God’s discipline as an expression of love, aimed at our good, so that we may share His holiness. God does not provoke His children with cruelty; He corrects, teaches, and patiently nurtures them.

The Old Testament also emphasizes parents’ responsibility to teach children about God. *Deuteronomy 6:6–7* instructs parents to impress God’s commands on their children, talking about them at home and on the road, when they lie down and when they rise. Faith is meant to be woven into the fabric of family life.

This verse also limits parental authority. Parents are accountable to God for how they treat their children. Authority is given for nurture, not for domination. Harsh, abusive, or neglectful treatment contradicts this command and grieves God, who has a special concern for the vulnerable, including children (*Mark 9:36–37*; *10:13–16*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Parents can examine their own patterns: Do they listen to their children? Do they discipline fairly and consistently, explaining the reasons? Do they encourage more than they criticize? Do they apologize when they are wrong? These practices help children feel loved and secure.

Bringing children up in the Lord’s instruction includes reading Scripture together, praying together, talking openly about faith, and modeling a genuine relationship with God. Children learn as much from what they see as from what they hear.

For those who were raised by harsh or absent parents, this verse affirms that such treatment was not God’s design. God can bring healing, and He offers Himself as the perfect Father. For those who are raising children now, God offers grace for mistakes and wisdom for the journey.

### *Ephesians 6:10–12* — Our Struggle Is Not Against Flesh and Blood

> *“Finally, be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might. Put on the whole armor of God, that you may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil. For our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against the principalities, against the powers, against the world’s rulers of the darkness of this age, and against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.”*
>
> — *Ephesians 6:10–12* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“Finally, be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might.” Paul does not tell believers to be strong in themselves. Their strength comes from the Lord, the same mighty power that raised Christ from the dead (*Ephesians 1:19–20*).

“Put on the whole armor of God, that you may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil.” “Wiles” means schemes, strategies, or tricks. The devil does not usually attack openly. He works through deception, temptation, discouragement, and division. God provides the armor believers need to stand against these schemes.

Verse 12 explains the nature of the struggle: “For our wrestling is not against flesh and blood.” The ultimate enemies of believers are not other human beings. They are “the principalities... the powers... the world’s rulers of the darkness of this age, and... the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.” These terms describe spiritual beings opposed to God, who work behind the scenes of human evil.

“Wrestling” suggests close, personal struggle. The Christian life involves real spiritual conflict.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This passage teaches that evil in the world is not merely the result of human choices or social systems, though those are real. Behind them are spiritual forces that oppose God and His people. Jesus confronted these forces throughout His ministry, casting out demons and resisting Satan’s temptations. Through His death and resurrection, He disarmed the powers and triumphed over them (*Colossians 2:15*).

Christians in different traditions understand spiritual warfare in somewhat different ways. Some emphasize direct encounters with demonic forces; others emphasize the ways evil works through temptation, deception, and unjust structures. Both perspectives recognize that evil is real and personal, and that believers must rely on God’s strength rather than their own.

The statement “our wrestling is not against flesh and blood” has an important implication: people are not the ultimate enemy. Even those who oppose or harm believers are not the true foe. This should shape how believers treat others, with love, prayer, and a desire for their redemption, even while standing firm against evil and seeking justice for harm done.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers face real spiritual struggles: temptations that seem to come at the worst moments, discouragement that whispers lies, divisions that tear relationships apart. This passage helps believers recognize these struggles for what they are and respond with God’s strength rather than their own.

It also changes how believers view conflict with others. When tension arises in a family, church, or community, it helps to remember that the real enemy is not the other person. This can lead to more patience, prayer, and grace, while still addressing wrongs honestly.

Finally, this passage brings hope. The powers of evil are real, but they are not equal to God. Christ reigns far above them all, and believers stand in His strength.

### *Ephesians 6:14–17* — The Whole Armor of God

> *“Stand therefore, having the utility belt of truth buckled around your waist, and having put on the breastplate of righteousness, and having fitted your feet with the preparation of the Good News of peace, above all, taking up the shield of faith, with which you will be able to quench all the fiery darts of the evil one. And take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God;”*
>
> — *Ephesians 6:14–17* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul describes six pieces of armor, drawing on the equipment of a Roman soldier and on images from Isaiah, where God Himself is pictured as a warrior wearing righteousness as a breastplate and salvation as a helmet (*Isaiah 59:17*).

“The utility belt of truth.” A soldier’s belt held his clothing in place and secured other equipment. Truth, both the truth of God’s word and a life of honesty, holds everything else together.

“The breastplate of righteousness.” The breastplate protected the heart and vital organs. Righteousness includes the right standing believers have through Christ and the righteous living that flows from it. It guards the heart against accusation and corruption.

“Having fitted your feet with the preparation of the Good News of peace.” Roman soldiers wore sturdy sandals with hobnails for grip. The gospel of peace gives believers firm footing and readiness to move forward with the message of Christ.

“The shield of faith, with which you will be able to quench all the fiery darts of the evil one.” Roman shields were large and could be soaked in water to put out flaming arrows. Faith, trust in God’s promises, extinguishes the attacks of the evil one, such as lies, doubts, accusations, and temptations.

“The helmet of salvation.” The helmet protected the head. The assurance of salvation guards the mind against despair and doubt.

“The sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.” This is the only offensive weapon in the list. The word translated “word” often refers to a specific spoken word. When Jesus was tempted in the wilderness, He answered each temptation with Scripture (*Matthew 4:1–11*). The Spirit enables believers to use God’s word against the enemy.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Every piece of armor is ultimately found in Christ. He is the truth (*John 14:6*), our righteousness (*1 Corinthians 1:30*), our peace (*Ephesians 2:14*), the object of our faith, our salvation, and the living Word (*John 1:1*). To put on the armor of God is, in a sense, to put on Christ (*Romans 13:14*).

The armor is primarily defensive. Paul’s repeated command is to “stand” (vv11, 13, 14). Believers are not called to go looking for battles with spiritual forces but to stand firm in the victory Christ has already won. Their task is to hold their ground, not to win the war, which Christ has already won.

The armor is also communal. The commands are plural, addressed to the whole church. Roman soldiers fought in formation, their shields locked together. Believers stand together, supporting and protecting one another.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can “put on” the armor daily through practical habits: committing to truth and honesty; resting in Christ’s righteousness rather than their own performance; being ready to share the gospel of peace; trusting God’s promises when doubts or accusations come; remembering their secure salvation; and filling their minds with Scripture so that the Spirit can bring it to mind when needed.

When temptation or discouragement strikes, believers can respond as Jesus did, with God’s word. Memorizing key passages of Scripture equips the heart for such moments.

Believers also need one another. Standing firm is easier in community, where others pray, encourage, and help carry the shield of faith when one is weak.

### *Ephesians 6:18* — Praying at All Times in the Spirit

> *“with all prayer and requests, praying at all times in the Spirit, and being watchful to this end in all perseverance and requests for all the saints.”*
>
> — *Ephesians 6:18* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Prayer is not listed as a piece of armor, but it is woven through the whole passage. It is how believers put on the armor and stay alert in the battle.

Paul uses the word “all” four times: “all prayer and requests,” “at all times,” “all perseverance,” and “all the saints.” Prayer is to be comprehensive and constant.

“With all prayer and requests” includes every kind of prayer: praise, thanksgiving, confession, and specific requests.

“Praying at all times in the Spirit.” Prayer is not limited to set times but can be a continual conversation with God throughout the day. “In the Spirit” means prayer guided and empowered by the Holy Spirit (*Romans 8:26–27*).

“Being watchful to this end in all perseverance.” Believers must stay alert and keep praying, not giving up. Jesus told His disciples to watch and pray (*Mark 14:38*).

“And requests for all the saints.” Prayer is not only for oneself but for all of God’s people. Believers support one another in the spiritual battle by praying for each other.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Prayer is the posture of dependence. In the spiritual battle, believers do not rely on their own strength, wisdom, or effort. They rely on God. Prayer acknowledges that dependence and draws on His power.

Praying “in the Spirit” reminds believers that even prayer is a gift of grace. The Spirit helps them pray when they do not know what to say, interceding with groans too deep for words (*Romans 8:26*). Prayer is not a technique to master but a relationship to enjoy.

Praying for “all the saints” reflects the communal nature of the Christian life. Believers are members of one body. When one suffers, all suffer. Through prayer, they carry one another’s burdens and stand together against the enemy.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Many believers struggle to pray consistently. This verse encourages them to see prayer not as an occasional duty but as an ongoing conversation with God throughout the day: in the car, at work, while doing chores, in moments of worry or joy.

Setting aside regular times for focused prayer is also valuable. Some find it helpful to keep a list of people and needs to pray for, including fellow believers in their church and Christians around the world who face persecution.

Perseverance matters. Some prayers take years to be answered. This verse encourages believers to keep praying, staying alert and trusting God’s timing.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Ephesians 6* completes Paul’s picture of the Christian life by showing how faith shapes the home, the workplace, and the unseen spiritual battle.

In the home, children are called to obey and honor their parents, and parents are called to nurture their children with patient discipline and instruction in the Lord, without provoking them to anger. Parental authority is a trust from God, given for the children’s good, never a license for harshness or abuse. Honoring parents remains a lifelong calling, shaped by wisdom where there has been harm.

In the workplace, Paul’s words to servants and masters, written within the unjust system of Roman slavery, are not an endorsement of that system. Their lasting principles apply to every form of work: serve faithfully, as to the Lord, whether anyone is watching or not; and if you have authority over others, treat them justly, without threats or exploitation, knowing that you too answer to a Master in heaven who shows no favoritism.

Above all, the chapter reminds believers that they face a real spiritual battle. Their ultimate enemies are not other people but spiritual forces of evil. They cannot win this struggle in their own strength, but they can stand firm in the Lord’s mighty power, clothed in the armor He provides: truth, righteousness, the gospel of peace, faith, salvation, and the word of God. All of this is sustained by persistent prayer, for themselves and for all of God’s people.

The letter ends with grace and peace. Whatever believers face at home, at work, or in the spiritual realm, they are held in the love of God, strengthened by His Spirit, and secure in Christ, who reigns above every power.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord, I want my home, my work, and my whole life to honor You. Help me to honor my parents and to treat the children in my care with patience, kindness, and faithful instruction in Your ways. Protect every child who is in danger, and heal those who carry wounds from childhood. In my work, help me to serve faithfully as unto You, and if I have authority over others, help me to treat them with justice and respect. Make me strong in You and in the strength of Your might. Clothe me with the whole armor of God: truth, righteousness, the gospel of peace, faith, salvation, and Your word. When the enemy attacks with lies and temptations, help me to stand firm. Teach me to pray at all times in the Spirit, for myself and for all Your people, and give boldness to all who proclaim the gospel. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Book 11 of 27

# Philippians

## About This Letter

Philippi was a Roman colony in Macedonia, in northern Greece, settled by retired Roman soldiers and proud of its Roman citizenship and customs. Paul founded the church there around A.D. 49–50 on his second missionary journey, after a vision of a man from Macedonia pleading for help (*Acts 16:9–10*). Its first members included Lydia, a businesswoman who sold purple cloth, a slave girl set free from an oppressive spirit, and a jailer who came to faith after an earthquake opened the prison where Paul and Silas had been singing hymns at midnight (*Acts 16:11–40*).

Paul wrote this letter from prison, most likely in Rome around A.D. 60–62, though some scholars suggest an earlier imprisonment in Ephesus or Caesarea. The Philippians had sent him a gift by the hand of Epaphroditus, who became gravely ill while with Paul and then recovered. Paul writes to thank them, to update them on his situation, to send Epaphroditus home, and to encourage them in unity and joy.

## The Shape of the Letter

In chapter 1, Paul thanks God for the Philippians’ partnership in the gospel, explains how his imprisonment has advanced the gospel, and reflects on life and death: to live is Christ, and to die is gain. In chapter 2, he calls them to unity and humility, holding up the example of Christ, who emptied Himself and became obedient to death on a cross, and then commends Timothy and Epaphroditus as examples of selfless service. In chapter 3, he warns against those who trust in the flesh and tells how he counted all his former advantages as loss compared with knowing Christ, pressing on toward the goal. In chapter 4, he urges two women leaders to agree, calls the church to rejoice always and not be anxious, and thanks the Philippians for their generous gift, testifying that he has learned contentment in Christ who strengthens him.

## Themes to Watch For

Philippians is often called the letter of joy; words for joy and rejoicing appear again and again, even though Paul writes in chains. Watch for partnership in the gospel, the mind of Christ and His humility, unity in the church, the surpassing worth of knowing Christ, the hope of resurrection and heavenly citizenship, freedom from anxiety through prayer, contentment in every circumstance, and the peace of God that guards the heart. Philippians shows that joy in Christ does not depend on comfortable circumstances but on a living relationship with the Lord who is near.
