Philippians · Chapter 1 of 4

# Philippians — Chapter 1

Chapter Theme: To Live Is Christ

[Read Philippians 1 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/PHP01.htm)

Main Teaching

Writing from prison, Paul thanks God with joy for the Philippians’ partnership in the gospel and expresses confidence that God, who began a good work in them, will complete it. He prays that their love will abound in knowledge and discernment. Paul explains that his imprisonment has actually advanced the gospel, and he rejoices that Christ is being proclaimed, even by some with poor motives. Facing the possibility of death, he declares that for him to live is Christ and to die is gain, though he expects to remain for their sake. He urges them to live worthily of the gospel, standing firm together without fear, knowing that suffering for Christ is part of their calling.

## Chapter Background and Story

When Paul wrote this letter, he was in chains, probably under house arrest in Rome, awaiting a trial that could end in his execution (*Acts 28:16*, 30–31). Yet the letter overflows with joy. Paul’s circumstances were uncertain and difficult, but his confidence in Christ was not shaken.

The church at Philippi held a special place in Paul’s heart. From the very beginning, they had supported his ministry with their prayers and gifts (*Philippians 4:15–16*). They had recently sent Epaphroditus with another gift, and Paul writes partly to thank them. He addresses them with deep affection, and his tone throughout is warm and personal.

The Philippians also faced challenges. They were experiencing opposition from outsiders (*1:28–30*), and there were tensions within the church that threatened their unity (*2:1–4*; *4:2–3*). Paul’s words in this chapter encourage them to see their circumstances, and his, in light of God’s purposes.

### Greeting (*1:1–2*)

“*Paul and Timothy, servants of Jesus Christ, to all the saints in Christ Jesus who are at Philippi, with the overseers and servants*” (*v. 1*). Paul does not call himself an apostle here, as he does in most letters. With this beloved church, he did not need to assert his authority. He simply calls himself a servant, or slave, of Christ. “Overseers” (sometimes translated bishops) and “servants” (sometimes translated deacons) were the church’s leaders; this is one of the earliest references to these roles. “*Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ*” (*v. 2*).

### Thanksgiving and Confidence (*1:3–8*)

“*I thank my God whenever I remember you*” (*v. 3*), “*always in every request of mine on behalf of you all, making my requests with joy*” (*v. 4*), “*for your partnership in furtherance of the Good News from the first day until now*” (*v. 5*). “Partnership” translates *koinonia*, often rendered “fellowship.” It means sharing in something together. The Philippians had shared in Paul’s mission through prayer, financial support, and their own witness. Paul’s confidence about God’s continuing work in them is studied below.

“*It is even right for me to think this way on behalf of all of you, because I have you in my heart, because both in my bonds and in the defense and confirmation of the Good News, you all are partakers with me of grace*” (*v. 7*). Even in prison and on trial, Paul felt the Philippians were with him. “*For God is my witness, how I long after all of you in the tender mercies of Christ Jesus*” (*v. 8*). Paul’s love for them was not merely his own; it was the deep compassion of Christ flowing through him.

### Paul’s Prayer (*1:9–11*)

Paul’s prayer for their growth in love and discernment is studied below.

### The Gospel Advances Through Chains (*1:12–18*)

“*Now I desire to have you know, brothers, that the things which happened to me have turned out rather to the progress of the Good News*” (*v. 12*). The Philippians may have worried that Paul’s imprisonment was a disaster for the gospel. Paul assures them the opposite is true. “Progress” was a word used for an army clearing a path through difficult terrain.

“*so that it became evident to the whole palace guard, and to all the rest, that my bonds are in Christ*” (*v. 13*). The “palace guard” was the Praetorian Guard, the elite soldiers of the emperor. Paul was chained to these soldiers in shifts, and they came to understand that he was imprisoned not for a crime but for Christ. The gospel was reaching the heart of the empire. Later in the letter, Paul even sends greetings from believers “*of Caesar’s household*” (*Philippians 4:22*).

“*and that most of the brothers in the Lord, being confident through my bonds, are more abundantly bold to speak the word of God without fear*” (*v. 14*). Paul’s courage in chains inspired other believers to speak boldly.

“*Some indeed preach Christ even out of envy and strife, and some also out of good will*” (*v. 15*). Not everyone preaching in Rome had pure motives. Some were rivals of Paul who hoped to increase his distress. Others preached out of love. “*What does it matter? Only that in every way, whether in pretense or in truth, Christ is proclaimed. I rejoice in this, yes, and will rejoice*” (*v. 18*). Paul’s response is remarkable. These preachers were not teaching false doctrine, as the troublemakers in Galatia were; they were preaching Christ, though with selfish motives. Paul cared more about Christ being known than about his own reputation.

### To Live Is Christ (*1:19–26*)

“*For I know that this will turn out to my salvation through your prayers and the supply of the Spirit of Jesus Christ*” (*v. 19*). “Salvation” here may mean deliverance from prison or, more broadly, his final vindication before God, whatever the outcome of his trial. “*according to my earnest expectation and hope, that I will in no way be disappointed, but with all boldness, as always, now also Christ will be magnified in my body, whether by life or by death*” (*v. 20*). Paul’s one concern was that Christ would be honored through him, whether he lived or died. His famous statement about life and death is studied below.

“*But if I live on in the flesh, this will bring fruit from my work; yet I don’t know what I will choose*” (*v. 22*). “*But I am hard pressed between the two, having the desire to depart and be with Christ, which is far better*” (*v. 23*). “*Yet to remain in the flesh is more needful for your sake*” (*v. 24*). Paul is torn. Personally, he longs to be with Christ. But for the sake of the churches, it would be better for him to remain. “*Having this confidence, I know that I will remain, yes, and remain with you all for your progress and joy in the faith*” (*v. 25*). Paul expected to be released, and many believe he was, for a time, before a later imprisonment and death.

### Living Worthy of the Gospel (*1:27–30*)

Paul’s call to live worthily of the gospel is studied below. “*and in nothing frightened by the adversaries, which is for them a proof of destruction, but to you of salvation, and that from God*” (*v. 28*). The Philippians’ courage in the face of opposition was itself a sign. It showed that God was with them.

“*Because it has been granted to you on behalf of Christ, not only to believe in him, but also to suffer on his behalf*” (*v. 29*). This is a surprising statement. Paul says suffering for Christ is something “granted,” a gift of grace, just as faith is. To suffer for Christ is to share in His sufferings and to be counted worthy of His name (*Acts 5:41*). “*having the same conflict which you saw in me and now hear is in me*” (*v. 30*). The Philippians had seen Paul beaten and imprisoned in their own city (*Acts 16:22–24*). Now they shared the same struggle.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Philippians 1:6* — He Who Began a Good Work

> *“being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ.”*
>
> — *Philippians 1:6* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul expresses his confidence about the Philippians’ future. “Being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ.”

“He who began a good work” is God. The “good work” is God’s work of salvation and transformation in their lives. It began when they first believed the gospel, as told in *Acts 16*, when Lydia’s heart was opened by the Lord and the jailer and his household believed.

God “will complete it.” The word means to bring to completion, to finish. God does not abandon what He starts. He will continue His work in them until it is finished.

“Until the day of Jesus Christ” refers to Christ’s return. God’s work in believers continues throughout their lives and will be brought to perfection when Christ comes again.

Paul’s confidence is not in the Philippians’ strength but in God’s faithfulness.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse expresses the faithfulness of God in salvation. Salvation is not something God starts and then leaves believers to finish on their own. He is committed to completing it. *Romans 8:29–30* describes the same unbreakable chain: those whom God called, He justified, and those He justified, He also glorified.

Christian traditions have discussed how this promise relates to human responsibility and whether believers can fall away. Some emphasize God’s preserving grace, holding that God will certainly keep all true believers to the end. Others emphasize that believers must continue in faith, while God faithfully supplies the grace to do so. Both affirm that God is faithful and that believers’ hope rests in Him, not in themselves. Paul himself holds both together: in *Philippians 2:12–13*, he calls believers to work out their salvation, because God is the one working in them.

This verse also reminds believers that they are works in progress. God’s work in them is real but not yet finished. They should expect growth over time, not instant perfection.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Many believers become discouraged by their slow progress or repeated failures. This verse offers hope: God has not given up on them. The work He began, He will finish. Their growth depends ultimately on His faithfulness, not on their perfection.

This verse also encourages patience with others. Fellow believers, children, friends, and new Christians are all works in progress. God is at work in them too, even when change seems slow. Believers can pray for one another with confidence, trusting God to complete what He has started.

### *Philippians 1:9–11* — Love Abounding in Knowledge and Discernment

> *“This I pray, that your love may abound yet more and more in knowledge and all discernment, so that you may approve the things that are excellent, that you may be sincere and without offense to the day of Christ, being filled with the fruits of righteousness which are through Jesus Christ, to the glory and praise of God.”*
>
> — *Philippians 1:9–11* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul tells the Philippians what he prays for them. “This I pray, that your love may abound yet more and more in knowledge and all discernment.” The Philippians already showed love, but Paul prays for it to overflow even more. And he wants their love to be guided by “knowledge” and “discernment.” Love is not merely a feeling; it needs understanding and wisdom to act well.

“So that you may approve the things that are excellent.” Discerning love helps believers recognize what truly matters, to test and choose what is best, not just what is good or acceptable.

“That you may be sincere and without offense to the day of Christ.” “Sincere” means pure, with no hidden mixture. “Without offense” means not causing others to stumble and living blamelessly. Paul looks ahead to Christ’s return as the time when their lives will be fully revealed.

“Being filled with the fruits of righteousness which are through Jesus Christ, to the glory and praise of God.” The goal is a life full of the good results of right living, produced through Christ’s work in them, all bringing glory to God.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This prayer shows that love and knowledge are not opposed. Some think of love as purely emotional and knowledge as cold and intellectual. Paul unites them. Love without knowledge can be naïve or misguided. Knowledge without love is empty and prideful (*1 Corinthians 8:1*; *13:2*). Mature Christian love is wise, discerning, and thoughtful.

“Discernment” is the ability to perceive moral and spiritual realities, to recognize what is true, good, and wise in particular situations. It is developed through Scripture, prayer, the Spirit’s guidance, and experience (*Hebrews 5:14*). Discerning love knows how to help without enabling harm, how to forgive while still protecting the vulnerable, and how to speak truth graciously.

The phrase “through Jesus Christ” reminds believers that the fruit of righteousness is not produced by their own efforts alone. It comes through union with Christ, the vine (*John 15:5*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This prayer can shape how believers pray for themselves and others. Rather than praying only for circumstances, they can pray for overflowing love guided by wisdom, for the ability to recognize what is best, and for lives that bring glory to God.

Discerning love has practical applications. It helps parents know when to say yes and when to say no. It helps friends know how to support someone without enabling destructive behavior. It helps churches care for people wisely and protect the vulnerable. Love that grows in knowledge and discernment makes wise choices about time, money, relationships, and priorities.

### *Philippians 1:21* — To Live Is Christ, and to Die Is Gain

> *“For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.”*
>
> — *Philippians 1:21* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This short verse captures the heart of Paul’s life. “For to me to live is Christ.” For Paul, life meant Christ. Christ was the center, purpose, and joy of his existence. Everything he did, he did for Christ, through Christ, and with Christ.

“And to die is gain.” If Paul’s life was all about Christ, then death could only bring him more of Christ. Death would mean being with Christ in a fuller way (v23). So even death, which most people fear as the ultimate loss, was gain for Paul.

Paul was not being morbid or wishing for death. He was expressing complete confidence in Christ. Whether he lived or died, he could not lose, because Christ was his treasure.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse challenges every believer to ask what fills in the blank: “For to me to live is \_\_\_\_.” If the answer is money, success, comfort, or relationships, then death is loss, because those things are left behind. Only when Christ is the center of life can death be gain.

Paul’s confidence rests on the resurrection of Christ. Because Jesus conquered death, death has lost its sting (*1 Corinthians 15:55–57*). For those who belong to Christ, death is not the end but a passage into His presence. Paul says in verse 23 that to depart and be with Christ is “far better.” In *2 Corinthians 5:8*, he says that to be absent from the body is to be at home with the Lord.

At the same time, Paul valued life. He wanted to remain for the sake of others. This verse does not encourage despising life or seeking death. It expresses a perspective in which both life and death are held in Christ’s hands. It is important to say clearly that this verse is not about ending one’s own life. Paul chose to remain and serve, and God calls His people to cherish the life He has given. Anyone who is struggling with thoughts of death or self-harm should reach out right away to a trusted person, a pastor, a doctor, or a crisis line for help.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to make Christ the center of their lives. That does not mean neglecting work, family, or responsibilities, but living all of them for Christ, with Christ at the heart.

It also brings comfort in the face of death. Believers who are facing serious illness, aging, or the loss of loved ones can hold on to this truth: for those in Christ, death is gain. It is not the end but the doorway to being with Christ. Grief is still real, and it is right to mourn, but believers grieve with hope (*1 Thessalonians 4:13*).

Finally, this verse frees believers from fear. If neither life nor death can separate them from Christ, they can live boldly, serving God and others without being controlled by fear of loss.

### *Philippians 1:27* — Living Worthy of the Gospel

> *“Only let your way of life be worthy of the Good News of Christ, that whether I come and see you or am absent, I may hear of your state, that you stand firm in one spirit, with one soul striving for the faith of the Good News;”*
>
> — *Philippians 1:27* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“Only let your way of life be worthy of the Good News of Christ.” The phrase translated “way of life” comes from a word related to citizenship. It means to live as a citizen. Philippi was a Roman colony, and its citizens were proud of their Roman citizenship. Paul calls the believers to live as citizens of a greater kingdom, in a way that fits the gospel. He will develop this idea further in *Philippians 3:20*: “*our citizenship is in heaven*” (*Philippians 3:20*).

“That whether I come and see you or am absent, I may hear of your state.” Paul wants them to live faithfully whether or not he is present to see it.

“That you stand firm in one spirit, with one soul striving for the faith of the Good News.” Paul describes the church as a united team. “Stand firm” suggests soldiers holding their position. “With one soul” means sharing the same purpose and commitment. “Striving” was used for athletes competing together. The Philippians were to work side by side, like teammates, for the sake of the gospel.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The gospel is not only a message to believe but a way of life to live. Those who have received the good news of Christ are called to live in a way that reflects it. This includes personal holiness, but Paul especially emphasizes unity. A divided church contradicts the gospel of reconciliation.

The image of citizenship is powerful. Just as Roman citizens in Philippi lived by Roman laws and customs far from Rome, believers live by the values of God’s kingdom while living in the world. Their loyalty is ultimately to Christ, their King.

Unity in this verse is not uniformity. It is a shared commitment to the gospel that allows believers to stand together and work together despite differences in personality, background, or opinion. Paul will develop this further in chapter 2.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can ask whether their way of life fits the gospel they believe. Does their conduct at home, work, and in the community reflect the grace, love, and truth of Christ? Living worthily of the gospel is not about earning salvation but about letting the gospel shape everything.

This verse also calls churches to unity in mission. Believers are not meant to compete with one another but to work together, side by side, for the sake of the gospel. Small disagreements can be set aside for the sake of shared purpose. When churches work together in love, they bear powerful witness to Christ.

Finally, living worthily “whether I come... or am absent” reminds believers that faithfulness does not depend on being watched. Integrity means living the same way in private as in public.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Philippians 1* shows that joy and confidence in Christ do not depend on circumstances. Paul was in prison, facing a possible death sentence, and some of his fellow preachers were trying to make his situation worse. Yet he overflowed with thanksgiving, prayer, and joy. His secret was that Christ was the center of his life.

Believers can share Paul’s confidence that God, who began a good work in them, will complete it. This truth gives hope when they feel discouraged by slow progress or repeated failure, and it encourages patience with others who are still growing. Like Paul, they can pray for themselves and others to grow in love that is wise and discerning, able to recognize what is best and to produce the fruit of righteousness.

Paul’s perspective on his imprisonment invites believers to see their own difficulties differently. What seems like a setback may become an opportunity for the gospel. Paul’s chains opened doors to the emperor’s guard and gave courage to other believers. God can use hard circumstances for His purposes.

At the heart of the chapter is Paul’s declaration: “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.” When Christ is the center of life, death loses its terror, and life gains meaning. Believers can live boldly, serving others, standing firm together, and striving side by side for the gospel. Even suffering for Christ can be seen as a privilege. Whatever comes, life or death, joy or hardship, Christ is enough.

## Chapter Prayer

Father, thank You for the people You have given me as partners in the gospel. I am confident that You, who began a good work in me, will carry it on to completion until the day of Christ Jesus. Let my love abound more and more in knowledge and discernment, so that I may approve what is excellent and be filled with the fruit of righteousness that comes through Jesus Christ, to Your glory and praise. When my circumstances are hard, help me to trust that You can use them to advance the gospel. Make Christ the center of my life, so that I can say, “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.” Help me to live as a citizen of Your kingdom, standing firm with my brothers and sisters in one spirit, and to be unafraid in the face of opposition. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Philippians · Chapter 2 of 4

# Philippians — Chapter 2

Chapter Theme: The Mind of Christ

[Read Philippians 2 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/PHP02.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul appeals to the Philippians to complete his joy by being united in love and purpose, doing nothing from selfish ambition but in humility counting others more significant than themselves. He holds up the supreme example of Christ Jesus, who, though He existed in the form of God, emptied Himself, took the form of a servant, and humbled Himself to death on a cross, and whom God therefore highly exalted, so that every knee will bow and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord. Paul calls them to work out their salvation, since God is at work in them, and to shine as lights in a dark world. He then commends Timothy and Epaphroditus as living examples of the selfless, Christlike care he has described.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Philippians 2* follows directly from Paul’s call at the end of chapter 1 to stand firm “*in one spirit, with one soul*” (*Philippians 1:27*). The church at Philippi was facing opposition from outside, but there were also signs of tension within. Later in the letter, Paul urges two women, Euodia and Syntyche, to agree in the Lord (*Philippians 4:2*). Rivalry, pride, and self-interest were threatening the church’s unity.

Paul’s answer is not merely to tell them to get along. He points them to Christ. Verses 6–11 form one of the most beautiful and profound passages about Jesus in the entire Bible. Many scholars believe it may be an early Christian hymn, perhaps sung in worship, which Paul quotes or composed himself. It traces Christ’s journey from the glory of God, down to the humiliation of the cross, and back up to exaltation as Lord of all.

Paul then gives practical instructions and introduces two coworkers, Timothy and Epaphroditus, whose lives embody the humility and self-giving love of Christ.

### A Call to Unity and Humility (*2:1–4*)

“*If therefore there is any exhortation in Christ, if any consolation of love, if any fellowship of the Spirit, if any tender mercies and compassion*” (*v. 1*). The “if” here means “since.” Paul lists blessings the Philippians have already experienced: encouragement in Christ, comfort from His love, fellowship in the Spirit, and compassion. Because they have received these, they should share them with one another.

“*make my joy full by being like-minded, having the same love, being of one accord, of one mind*” (*v. 2*). Paul piles up phrases for unity. He is not asking them to agree on every opinion but to share the same love and purpose. The humility that makes unity possible is studied below.

### The Example of Christ (*2:5–11*)

“*Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus*” (*v. 5*). Believers are to share the attitude, the mindset, that Christ had. The description of Christ’s humility and exaltation is studied below.

### Working Out Salvation (*2:12–13*)

This call to obedience, grounded in God’s work within, is studied below.

### Shining as Lights (*2:14–18*)

“*Do all things without complaining and arguing*” (*v. 14*), “*that you may become blameless and harmless, children of God without defect in the middle of a crooked and perverse generation, among whom you are seen as lights in the world*” (*v. 15*). Complaining and arguing were exactly what Israel did in the wilderness (*Exodus 16:7–8*; *Numbers 14:27*). Paul echoes *Deuteronomy 32:5*, where Moses described “*a perverse and crooked generation*” (*Deuteronomy 32:5*). Believers are called to be different: to shine like stars in a dark night sky.

“*holding up the word of life, that I may have something to boast in the day of Christ that I didn’t run in vain nor labor in vain*” (*v. 16*). “Holding up” can mean holding fast to the word of life or holding it out to others. Both fit. Believers cling to the gospel and offer it to the world.

“*Yes, and if I am poured out on the sacrifice and service of your faith, I am glad and rejoice with you all*” (*v. 17*). Paul uses the image of a drink offering, wine poured out on a sacrifice in Old Testament worship (*Numbers 28:7*). He sees his possible death as an offering poured out alongside the Philippians’ own sacrifice of faith and service. Even facing death, he rejoices. “*In the same way, you also should be glad and rejoice with me*” (*v. 18*).

### Timothy and Epaphroditus (*2:19–30*)

“*But I hope in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy to you soon, that I also may be cheered up when I know how you are doing*” (*v. 19*). Timothy had been with Paul when the church at Philippi was founded (*Acts 16:1–3*, 12). “*For I have no one else like-minded, who will truly care about you*” (*v. 20*). “*For they all seek their own, not the things of Jesus Christ*” (*v. 21*). Timothy was a rare example of selfless concern for others. “*But you know that he has proved himself. As a child serves a father, so he served with me in furtherance of the Good News*” (*v. 22*). Timothy’s character had been tested and proven over many years.

“*But I thought it necessary to send to you Epaphroditus, my brother, fellow worker, fellow soldier, and your apostle and servant of my need*” (*v. 25*). Epaphroditus was the messenger the Philippians had sent with their gift to Paul. “Apostle” here means messenger or delegate. Paul gives him five titles of honor.

“*since he longed for you all, and was very troubled because you had heard that he was sick*” (*v. 26*). “*For indeed he was sick nearly to death, but God had mercy on him, and not on him only, but on me also, that I might not have sorrow on sorrow*” (*v. 27*). Epaphroditus nearly died while serving Paul. Notice that Paul, who had seen God work miracles of healing (*Acts 19:11–12*), did not heal Epaphroditus at will. His recovery was God’s mercy. And Paul does not hide his own grief; he would have experienced “sorrow on sorrow.” Grief is not a sign of weak faith.

“*Receive him therefore in the Lord with all joy, and hold such people in honor*” (*v. 29*), “*because for the work of Christ he came near to death, risking his life to supply that which was lacking in your service toward me*” (*v. 30*). The word for “risking” was used for gamblers who staked everything. In later centuries, some Christians who cared for the sick during plagues were called “the gamblers,” after this verse. Epaphroditus is another example of the mind of Christ: putting others first at great cost.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Philippians 2:3–4* — Counting Others Better Than Yourself

> *“doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself; each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.”*
>
> — *Philippians 2:3–4* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul now names the attitudes that destroy unity and the attitudes that build it.

“Doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit.” “Rivalry” means selfish ambition, the desire to promote oneself at others’ expense. “Conceit” means empty pride, a hollow sense of self-importance. Both put self at the center.

“But in humility, each counting others better than himself.” Humility here means a lowly view of oneself in relation to others, a willingness to put others first. “Counting others better” does not mean believing that everyone else is more talented or more valuable. It means treating others as more important, giving their needs and interests priority.

“Each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.” Notice the word “also.” Paul does not say believers should neglect their own needs entirely. He says they should not look only to their own interests but also pay attention to the interests of others.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

In the Greek and Roman world, humility was generally not considered a virtue. It was the attitude expected of slaves and the lower classes. Honor, status, and self-promotion were highly valued. Christianity transformed humility into a virtue because of the example of Christ, who though He was God, humbled Himself.

These verses describe the opposite of what comes naturally to sinful human beings. People are inclined to put themselves first, to compete, to compare, and to seek recognition. The gospel reverses this. Jesus taught that the greatest must be the servant of all (*Mark 10:43–45*), and He washed His disciples’ feet (*John 13:1–15*).

Humility is not self-hatred or thinking poorly of oneself. It is freedom from self-preoccupation. A humble person is secure enough in God’s love that they do not need to promote themselves, and so they are free to care about others. Humility also does not mean allowing oneself to be abused or exploited. Christ’s humility was a free choice of love, not a submission to cruelty. Caring for others’ interests includes caring for one’s own safety and the safety of others.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses can transform relationships at home, at work, and in church. In conversations, believers can listen more than they speak. In decisions, they can consider how choices will affect others. In conflicts, they can seek to understand the other person’s perspective. In service, they can do tasks no one notices.

Selfish ambition can show up in subtle ways: needing credit, competing for attention, feeling envious of others’ success, or quietly tearing others down. Humility looks for ways to celebrate others, support them, and help them succeed.

A practical question for each day is: “Whose interests can I put ahead of my own today?” Small acts of humble service build unity and reflect the mind of Christ.

### *Philippians 2:6–8* — He Emptied Himself

> *“who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.”*
>
> — *Philippians 2:6–8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul describes the greatest example of humility in history: Jesus Christ.

“Who, existing in the form of God.” Before He became human, Christ existed as God. “Form” here refers to the true nature and essence of something. Christ was fully God.

“Didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped.” Christ did not cling to His divine privileges or use them for His own advantage. He did not regard His equality with God as something to hold on to for Himself.

“But emptied himself.” This phrase has been much discussed. Most Christian interpreters understand it to mean that Christ did not give up His divine nature, but that He laid aside His heavenly glory and the full use of His divine privileges by becoming human. He “emptied himself” by what He took on, not by what He lost.

“Taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men.” The one who existed in the form of God took on the form of a slave. He became truly human.

“And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” Christ’s humility went even further. As a human, He obeyed the Father all the way to death, and not just any death, but crucifixion, the most shameful and painful form of execution, reserved for slaves and criminals.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This passage describes a downward journey of stunning humility: from equality with God, to the form of a servant, to human likeness, to obedience, to death, to death on a cross. Every step went lower. The Creator became a creature. The Lord became a servant. The Holy One died the death of a criminal.

This is the central mystery of the Christian faith: the incarnation. The eternal Son of God became fully human without ceasing to be fully God. Early church councils, such as the Council of Chalcedon in A.D. 451, worked carefully to express this truth: Christ is one person with two natures, fully divine and fully human. Passages like this one were foundational to those confessions.

The reason Paul includes this passage is practical. He wants the Philippians to have “this mind” (v5). If Christ, who had every right to be served, chose to serve, then His followers should do the same. Christ’s humility is the pattern for Christian relationships.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

When believers struggle with pride, a desire for recognition, or an unwillingness to serve, this passage offers both a challenge and a comfort. The challenge is to follow Christ’s example of laying aside privileges for the sake of others. The comfort is that Christ understands every human weakness and suffering, because He entered fully into human life, even to death.

This passage can also shape how believers think about rights and privileges. Christ had every right to stay in glory, but He gave it up for others. Believers may be called at times to set aside their preferences, comforts, or rights in order to serve others well. This is not because their needs do not matter, but because love sometimes chooses the lower place.

Finally, this passage leads to worship. Reflecting on the depth of Christ’s humility can deepen gratitude and love for Him.

### *Philippians 2:9–11* — Every Knee Will Bow

> *“Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, those on earth, and those under the earth, and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.”*
>
> — *Philippians 2:9–11* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Christ’s downward journey is followed by an upward one. “Therefore God also highly exalted him.” Because Christ humbled Himself, God lifted Him to the highest place. The resurrection and ascension were God’s vindication of His obedient Son.

“And gave to him the name which is above every name.” In the ancient world, a name represented a person’s character and authority. The name given to Jesus is the highest name of all. Verse 11 reveals what it is: “Lord.” In the Greek Old Testament, “Lord” was the word used to translate God’s personal name, Yahweh, often written as “the LORD.”

“That at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, those on earth, and those under the earth.” Every being in the universe, angels, humans, and even the dead or the spiritual powers below, will one day bow before Jesus.

“And that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.” All creation will acknowledge His lordship. And this brings glory not only to Jesus but to the Father.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Paul is echoing *Isaiah 45:23*, where God declares, “*to me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall take an oath*” (*Isaiah 45:23*). In Isaiah, these words refer to the LORD, the one true God, who says He will not share His glory with another. Paul applies them to Jesus. This is a powerful statement of Christ’s divinity. The honor that belongs to God alone is given to Jesus, and it brings glory to the Father.

The confession “Jesus Christ is Lord” was the earliest Christian creed (*Romans 10:9*; *1 Corinthians 12:3*). In the Roman world, people were expected to declare “Caesar is Lord.” Christians who confessed Jesus as Lord were making a bold claim: He, not Caesar, is the true ruler of all.

Christians have discussed what it means that “every knee will bow.” Most understand it to mean that all will eventually acknowledge Christ’s lordship, some joyfully in worship, others unwillingly at the final judgment. Some hope that it points toward a wider reconciliation of all things. All agree that Christ’s lordship is universal and that the wise response is to bow before Him willingly now.

This passage also reveals a principle of God’s kingdom: the way up is down. Jesus taught that those who humble themselves will be exalted (*Luke 14:11*). Christ’s own story is the supreme example.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage invites believers to confess Jesus as Lord now, willingly and joyfully. That confession is not merely words; it means submitting every area of life to His authority.

It also brings hope. In a world where injustice, evil, and suffering seem to prevail, this passage declares that Jesus will be acknowledged as Lord by all. The final word belongs to Him.

Finally, it encourages those who choose humility. Choosing the lower place, serving without recognition, and setting aside one’s rights can feel like loss. But God honors humility, as He honored His Son. Believers can trust God to lift them up in His time.

### *Philippians 2:12–13* — Work Out Your Salvation

> *“So then, my beloved, even as you have always obeyed, not only in my presence, but now much more in my absence, work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in you both to will and to work for his good pleasure.”*
>
> — *Philippians 2:12–13* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“So then, my beloved.” Paul draws a practical conclusion from Christ’s example. “Even as you have always obeyed, not only in my presence, but now much more in my absence.” The Philippians had a history of faithfulness. Paul encourages them to continue, whether or not he is present.

“Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling.” This does not mean “work for your salvation,” as if they had to earn it. Paul has made clear that salvation is a gift (*Philippians 3:9*). To “work out” means to bring to completion, to live out in practice what God has already given. The phrase “your own” is plural in Greek, so Paul may especially have in mind the church’s shared life: working out what salvation means for their community, including their unity. “With fear and trembling” means with reverence, seriousness, and humble dependence on God.

Verse 13 explains why they can do this: “For it is God who works in you both to will and to work for his good pleasure.” God is at work within believers. He shapes their desires (“to will”) and empowers their actions (“to work”). Their effort is possible because of His prior work.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses hold together two truths that might seem to be in tension: human effort and divine grace. Believers are called to work, to obey, to grow, and to put their salvation into practice. Yet the power for all of this comes from God. It is not that God does part and believers do part. God works in them, and therefore they work.

This balance guards against two errors. One is passivity, the idea that because salvation is a gift, believers need not make any effort to grow. The other is self-reliance, the idea that spiritual growth depends entirely on human willpower. Paul rejects both. Believers work hard, but they do so in dependence on God’s power, knowing that every good desire and action is His gift.

Christian traditions have expressed this relationship in different ways, but all affirm that sanctification, growth in holiness, involves both God’s grace and human response. The motivation is not fear of losing God’s favor but reverent gratitude for His work.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can approach spiritual growth with both seriousness and confidence. Seriousness, because growth requires real effort: choosing obedience, building habits of prayer and Scripture, resisting temptation, and seeking reconciliation. Confidence, because God Himself is at work in them, giving them both the desire and the ability to do His will.

When believers feel weak or unmotivated, they can ask God to work in them “to will,” to give them the desire to obey. When they feel unable, they can ask God to work in them “to work,” to give them the strength. Growth is a partnership in which God always takes the lead.

For churches, this verse invites working out together what salvation means in community: how to love one another, resolve conflicts, and live in unity under Christ.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Philippians 2* calls believers to have the mind of Christ. In a world that celebrates self-promotion, competition, and status, Paul urges humility: doing nothing out of selfish ambition or empty pride, treating others as more important, and looking out for their interests as well as one’s own.

The reason for this humility is Christ Himself. Though He existed in the form of God, He did not cling to His privileges. He emptied Himself, took the form of a servant, became human, and humbled Himself to death on a cross. God therefore exalted Him and gave Him the name above every name, so that every knee will bow and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord. The way of Christ is the way of humble self-giving, and it is the way God honors.

This chapter also shows how believers grow. They work out their salvation with reverence, not to earn God’s favor, but because God is already at work in them, giving them the desire and the power to do His will. As they do, they shine like lights in a dark world, holding out the word of life, without complaining or arguing.

Finally, Paul offers living examples. Timothy genuinely cared for others’ welfare rather than his own interests. Epaphroditus risked his life to serve. These ordinary believers showed what the mind of Christ looks like in everyday life. Believers today can follow their example, serving others with humble, self-giving love that reflects the Lord who gave everything for them.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, You existed in the form of God, yet You did not cling to Your glory. You emptied Yourself, took the form of a servant, and humbled Yourself to death on a cross. I bow before You and confess that You are Lord, to the glory of God the Father. Give me Your mind. Free me from selfish ambition and empty pride. Teach me to count others as more important and to care for their interests as well as my own. Father, thank You that You are at work in me, giving me both the desire and the strength to do Your will. Help me to work out my salvation with reverence, without complaining or arguing, shining as a light in this world and holding out the word of life. Make me like Timothy and Epaphroditus, caring deeply and serving faithfully for the sake of Christ. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Philippians · Chapter 3 of 4

# Philippians — Chapter 3

Chapter Theme: Knowing Christ and Pressing On

[Read Philippians 3 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/PHP03.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul warns the Philippians against those who insist on circumcision and confidence in the flesh. He lists his own impressive religious credentials but declares that he counts them all as loss compared with the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus his Lord. He wants to gain Christ and be found in Him, with a righteousness that comes from God through faith, and to know the power of Christ’s resurrection and the fellowship of His sufferings. Not yet perfect, Paul forgets what lies behind and presses on toward the goal of God’s upward call in Christ. He urges the Philippians to follow his example, warns against those whose minds are set on earthly things, and reminds them that their citizenship is in heaven, from where they await the Savior who will transform their bodies to be like His glorious body.

## Chapter Background and Story

Chapter 3 begins with “Finally,” as if Paul were about to end the letter, but then he turns sharply to a warning. Some scholars think Paul received news that prompted this change of tone, or that he simply turned to a concern he had been meaning to address. Either way, the warning is serious.

The danger Paul names is similar to the one he confronted in Galatians. Teachers were traveling among the churches insisting that Gentile believers must be circumcised and keep the Law of Moses in order to be fully right with God. There is no clear sign that these teachers had already gained influence in Philippi, but Paul wants to protect the church before they do.

Paul responds by telling his own story. He had more reason than anyone to trust in his religious achievements. Yet he had discovered something infinitely better: knowing Christ. This chapter contains some of the most personal and passionate words Paul ever wrote, revealing the heart of his faith.

### A Warning (*3:1–3*)

“*Finally, my brothers, rejoice in the Lord! To write the same things to you, to me indeed is not tiresome, but for you it is safe*” (*v. 1*). Joy in the Lord is a safeguard against false teaching. Those who rejoice in Christ are less likely to look for security elsewhere.

“*Beware of the dogs; beware of the evil workers; beware of the false circumcision*” (*v. 2*). Paul’s language is sharp. Some Jewish people of the time used “dogs” as an insulting term for Gentiles, whom they regarded as unclean. Paul turns the term around and applies it to the false teachers themselves. “Evil workers” points to their emphasis on works of the Law. “False circumcision” translates a word meaning “mutilation,” a biting wordplay on “circumcision.” Paul is not attacking the Jewish people in general, whom he loved deeply (*Romans 9:1–5*), nor Jewish believers in Jesus. He is warning against particular teachers who were distorting the gospel by requiring Gentile believers to be circumcised to be saved.

“*For we are the circumcision, who worship God in the Spirit, and rejoice in Christ Jesus, and have no confidence in the flesh*” (*v. 3*). True circumcision is not a physical mark but a heart transformed by God (*Deuteronomy 30:6*; *Romans 2:28–29*). Believers worship by the Spirit, boast in Christ, and put no confidence in human achievement.

### Paul’s Credentials (*3:4–6*)

“*though I myself might have confidence even in the flesh. If any other man thinks that he has confidence in the flesh, I yet more*” (*v. 4*). Paul lists seven credentials, the first four inherited and the last three chosen.

“*circumcised the eighth day, of the stock of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews; concerning the law, a Pharisee*” (*v. 5*). He was circumcised on the eighth day as the Law required (*Leviticus 12:3*), so he was not a convert. He was born an Israelite. He came from the tribe of Benjamin, which had produced Israel’s first king, Saul, after whom Paul was named, and which remained loyal to David’s line. He was “a Hebrew of Hebrews,” raised in a family that kept its Hebrew language and customs. He was a Pharisee, a member of the strictest party in keeping the Law.

“*concerning zeal, persecuting the assembly; concerning the righteousness which is in the law, found blameless*” (*v. 6*). His zeal was so intense that he persecuted the church. By the standards of outward Law-keeping, no one could fault him.

### Counting All as Loss (*3:7–11*)

Paul’s dramatic reassessment of his credentials, and his longing to know Christ, are studied below.

“*and be found in him, not having a righteousness of my own, that which is of the law, but that which is through faith in Christ, the righteousness which is from God by faith*” (*v. 9*). This verse summarizes the gospel Paul preached. There are two kinds of righteousness: one that comes from one’s own Law-keeping, and one that comes from God as a gift through faith in Christ. Paul had once relied on the first. Now he rejoices in the second.

### Pressing On (*3:12–16*)

“*Not that I have already obtained, or am already made perfect; but I press on, that I may take hold of that for which also I was taken hold of by Christ Jesus*” (*v. 12*). Paul is honest. He has not arrived. He is still growing. But he presses on, because Christ first took hold of him on the road to Damascus. His pursuit of Christ is a response to Christ’s pursuit of him. His determination to keep running is studied below.

“*Let us therefore, as many as are perfect, think this way. If in anything you think otherwise, God will also reveal that to you*” (*v. 15*). “Perfect” here means mature. Mature believers know they are not yet perfect in the absolute sense. Paul trusts God to correct those who see things differently. “*Nevertheless, to the extent that we have already attained, let’s walk by the same rule. Let’s be of the same mind*” (*v. 16*). Believers should live consistently with what they already understand.

### Citizens of Heaven (*3:17–21*)

“*Brothers, be imitators together of me, and note those who walk this way, even as you have us for an example*” (*v. 17*). Paul invites them to follow his example, not because he is perfect, but because he is pressing toward Christ. Mature believers provide models for others.

“*For many walk, of whom I told you often, and now tell you even weeping, as the enemies of the cross of Christ*” (*v. 18*), “*whose end is destruction, whose god is the belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who think about earthly things*” (*v. 19*). Paul now warns against a different danger: people who lived self-indulgently, controlled by their appetites. They may have claimed to be Christians but rejected the way of the cross. Notice that Paul speaks of them with tears. He does not condemn them with satisfaction but grieves over them. Heavenly citizenship and the hope of resurrection are studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Philippians 3:7–8* — Counting All Things Loss for Christ

> *“However, I consider those things that were gain to me as a loss for Christ. Yes most certainly, and I count all things to be a loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus, my Lord, for whom I suffered the loss of all things, and count them nothing but refuse, that I may gain Christ”*
>
> — *Philippians 3:7–8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul has just listed his impressive religious credentials. Now he makes a stunning declaration. “However, I consider those things that were gain to me as a loss for Christ.” Paul uses the language of an accountant. Before meeting Christ, he placed these achievements in the “profit” column. Now he has moved them to the “loss” column.

In verse 8, he goes even further. “I count all things to be a loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus, my Lord.” Not just his religious achievements, but everything, all things, is loss compared with the surpassing value of knowing Christ. Notice how personal it is: “Christ Jesus, my Lord.”

“For whom I suffered the loss of all things.” Paul had literally lost much for Christ: his status as a respected Pharisee, his career, perhaps his family’s support, his comfort and safety.

“And count them nothing but refuse.” The word translated “refuse” was a strong, even crude term, meaning garbage, dung, or what is thrown to the dogs. Paul uses it deliberately. Compared with Christ, everything else is worthless.

“That I may gain Christ.” The goal is not just to give things up but to gain something infinitely better: Christ Himself.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Paul is not saying that his heritage, education, and devotion were evil in themselves. Being an Israelite was a privilege (*Romans 9:4–5*). The problem was that he had trusted in these things for his standing before God. When he met Christ, he saw that his own righteousness could never compare with the righteousness God gives through Christ.

Jesus described the kingdom of God as a treasure hidden in a field. A man who found it sold everything he had with joy to buy that field (*Matthew 13:44*). Paul had found that treasure. Giving up everything was not a grim sacrifice; it was a joyful exchange.

The phrase “knowledge of Christ Jesus, my Lord” refers not just to knowing facts about Christ but knowing Him personally. In the Bible, to “know” someone often means to have an intimate relationship with them. This relationship is what Paul valued above everything.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Every believer has things they might be tempted to trust in or treasure above Christ: achievements, reputation, education, wealth, family background, religious activity, or moral record. This passage invites honest reflection: What am I relying on for my worth and my standing before God?

These things are not necessarily bad. Education, family, and work can be good gifts. But they become dangerous when they replace Christ as the source of identity and security. Paul invites believers to hold everything loosely and to treasure Christ above all.

For those who have lost much, through illness, financial hardship, broken relationships, or persecution, this passage offers comfort. No loss can take away the surpassing worth of knowing Christ. In Him, believers have a treasure that cannot be lost.

### *Philippians 3:10–11* — Knowing Christ and the Power of His Resurrection

> *“that I may know him and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings, becoming conformed to his death, if by any means I may attain to the resurrection from the dead.”*
>
> — *Philippians 3:10–11* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul now describes what he longs for. “That I may know him.” Paul had known Christ for many years, yet he still longed to know Him more. The Christian life is a growing relationship.

“And the power of his resurrection.” Paul wants to experience the same power that raised Jesus from the dead, power that gives new life, overcomes sin, and sustains believers in hardship.

“And the fellowship of his sufferings.” Paul also wants to share in Christ’s sufferings. This may seem strange, but Paul understood that following Christ means walking His path, which includes suffering for His sake. Sharing in His sufferings brings a deep fellowship with Him.

“Becoming conformed to his death.” Paul wants his life to be shaped like Christ’s death: self-giving, humble, and obedient to the Father. This echoes the mind of Christ described in *Philippians 2:5–8*.

“If by any means I may attain to the resurrection from the dead.” Paul’s hope is the final resurrection. The words “if by any means” do not express doubt about his salvation but humility and eager longing. He presses on toward that day.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses reveal the pattern of the Christian life: death and resurrection. Just as Christ suffered, died, and rose again, believers share in His sufferings and death, and they will share in His resurrection. Paul expresses the same idea in *Romans 8:17*: believers are heirs with Christ, if they suffer with Him so that they may also be glorified with Him.

The order here is interesting. Paul mentions resurrection power before sufferings. Believers do not endure suffering in their own strength. The power of Christ’s resurrection enables them to share in His sufferings with faith and hope.

This passage does not mean that believers should seek out suffering or that all suffering is noble. Suffering caused by abuse, injustice, or neglect is evil and should be resisted and addressed. Paul’s focus is on suffering that comes because of faithfulness to Christ, and on the way God uses all hardships to conform believers to the image of His Son.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

The desire to know Christ more is at the heart of spiritual growth. Believers can nurture this desire through Scripture, prayer, worship, and obedience. Knowing Christ is not a task to be completed but a lifelong journey.

When believers face hardship, these verses offer a different perspective. Suffering is not a sign that God has abandoned them. It can be a place of deep fellowship with Christ, who also suffered. And resurrection power is available to sustain them through it.

Finally, these verses point to hope. Whatever believers endure now, the resurrection is coming. Death and suffering do not have the final word.

### *Philippians 3:13–14* — Forgetting What Is Behind, Pressing On

> *“Brothers, I don’t regard myself as yet having taken hold, but one thing I do: forgetting the things which are behind and stretching forward to the things which are before, I press on toward the goal for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.”*
>
> — *Philippians 3:13–14* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul uses the image of a runner in a race. “Brothers, I don’t regard myself as yet having taken hold.” He has not yet reached the finish line.

“But one thing I do.” Paul is single-minded. His whole life is focused on one goal.

“Forgetting the things which are behind.” A runner who keeps looking back will lose speed and may stumble. Paul does not dwell on the past, neither his past achievements, which might make him proud, nor his past failures, such as his persecution of the church, which might weigh him down. This does not mean erasing memory, but refusing to let the past control the present.

“And stretching forward to the things which are before.” The image is of a runner straining forward, every muscle stretched toward the finish.

“I press on toward the goal for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.” The goal is the finish line, and the prize is what awaits there: the fullness of life with Christ. “The high calling” may refer to God’s call to come up to receive the prize, as winners in ancient games were called up to the platform to receive their crowns.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses describe the Christian life as a race that requires perseverance and focus. *Hebrews 12:1–2* uses the same image, calling believers to run with endurance the race set before them, looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith. The goal is Christ Himself.

“Forgetting the things which are behind” is profoundly freeing. Many believers are held back by past failures, regrets, or wounds. Paul had a past that could have crushed him with guilt: he had persecuted and imprisoned believers. But he had received God’s forgiveness, and he refused to let that past define him. Others are held back by past successes, resting on what they once achieved. Paul refused that too.

This does not mean ignoring the past entirely. Remembering God’s faithfulness, learning from mistakes, and making amends for harm done are all important. Healing from trauma may require carefully revisiting painful memories with wise help. The point is not to be paralyzed or defined by the past, but to move forward in Christ.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers who feel stuck in guilt over past sins can take hold of God’s forgiveness and move forward. Christ’s grace covers the past, and the future is open.

Those who are tempted to coast on past spiritual experiences or achievements can hear Paul’s call to keep pressing on. Spiritual growth does not stop; there is always more of Christ to know.

Single-mindedness also matters. Many things compete for believers’ attention and energy. Paul’s “one thing I do” invites believers to examine their priorities and focus on what matters most: knowing and following Christ.

### *Philippians 3:20–21* — Our Citizenship Is in Heaven

> *“For our citizenship is in heaven, from where we also wait for a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will change the body of our humiliation to be conformed to the body of his glory, according to the working by which he is able even to subject all things to himself.”*
>
> — *Philippians 3:20–21* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

In contrast to those whose minds are set on earthly things (v19), Paul reminds believers of their true identity. “For our citizenship is in heaven.” Philippi was a Roman colony. Its citizens, though living far from Rome, held Roman citizenship, followed Roman laws, and took pride in their Roman identity. Paul says believers are like a colony of heaven on earth. Their true homeland is heaven, and they live by its values.

“From where we also wait for a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ.” The citizens of Philippi looked to the Roman emperor, who was often called “savior” and “lord.” Believers look to a greater Savior and Lord: Jesus Christ. They wait eagerly for His return.

“Who will change the body of our humiliation to be conformed to the body of his glory.” When Christ returns, He will transform believers’ bodies. The “body of our humiliation” refers to the present body, weak, subject to sickness, aging, and death. It will be changed to be like Christ’s resurrection body, glorious and imperishable (*1 Corinthians 15:42–44*).

“According to the working by which he is able even to subject all things to himself.” The same power by which Christ will bring all things under His rule will be used to transform His people.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses express the hope that sustains believers. Their identity is not defined by their earthly nationality, social status, or circumstances, but by their citizenship in God’s kingdom. This gives them both freedom and responsibility. They are free from being controlled by the world’s values, and they are called to live as faithful representatives of heaven.

Heavenly citizenship does not mean withdrawing from earthly life. Paul himself used his Roman citizenship when it served the gospel (*Acts 16:37*; *22:25–29*), and he encouraged believers to be good citizens (*Romans 13:1–7*). But their ultimate loyalty belongs to Christ.

The promise of a transformed body affirms that God cares about the physical body. Christian hope is not escape from the body but its redemption. The resurrection body will be real and physical, yet free from weakness, sin, and death. This hope gives dignity to the present body and comfort to those who suffer from illness, disability, or aging.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can ask whether their lives reflect their heavenly citizenship. Are their priorities, values, and choices shaped by God’s kingdom or by the culture around them? Living as citizens of heaven means honoring Christ as King in every area of life.

This passage also offers hope to those who struggle with physical weakness, chronic pain, disability, or the effects of aging. The present body is not the final word. Christ will transform it into a glorious body like His own.

Finally, believers can live with eager expectation. The Savior is coming. That hope can strengthen them to endure hardship, resist temptation, and live faithfully in the meantime.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Philippians 3* calls believers to find their deepest joy, security, and identity in Christ alone. Paul warns against trusting in religious achievements or human credentials for standing before God. He himself had every reason to boast, yet he counted all of it as loss compared with the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus his Lord. True righteousness does not come from human effort but from God through faith in Christ.

This invites honest reflection on what each believer relies on. Achievements, reputation, family background, education, and religious activity can all become substitutes for Christ. Paul calls believers to treasure Christ above all, to long to know Him more, to experience the power of His resurrection, and to share in His sufferings.

Paul also models perseverance. He had not yet arrived, but he pressed on, forgetting what lay behind and straining toward the goal. Believers can let go of past failures, receiving God’s forgiveness, and refuse to rest on past successes. The race is not finished, and there is always more of Christ to know.

Finally, the chapter lifts believers’ eyes to their true home. Their citizenship is in heaven, and they eagerly wait for their Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform their weak bodies into glorious bodies like His. This hope gives strength to live faithfully now, to endure suffering, and to reject the pull of a life focused only on earthly things. Christ is the treasure, the goal, and the hope of every believer.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, I want to know You. Help me to count everything as loss compared with the surpassing worth of knowing You as my Lord. Forgive me for trusting in my own achievements, reputation, or goodness. Thank You that my righteousness comes not from myself but from God through faith in You. Let me know the power of Your resurrection and the fellowship of Your sufferings. Help me to let go of what lies behind, both my failures and my successes, and to press on toward the goal of Your upward call. Keep my mind from being set on earthly things. Remind me that my citizenship is in heaven, and fill me with eager hope as I wait for Your return, when You will transform my weak body to be like Your glorious body. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
