Philippians · Chapter 4 of 4

# Philippians — Chapter 4

Chapter Theme: Joy, Peace, and Contentment in Christ

[Read Philippians 4 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/PHP04.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul urges the Philippians to stand firm in the Lord and pleads with two women who had labored with him, Euodia and Syntyche, to agree in the Lord. He calls the church to rejoice in the Lord always, to let their gentleness be known, and not to be anxious about anything but to bring every request to God with thanksgiving, promising that God’s peace, which surpasses understanding, will guard their hearts and minds. He encourages them to think about whatever is true, honorable, just, pure, lovely, and praiseworthy. Thanking them for their generous gift, Paul testifies that he has learned to be content in every circumstance and can do all things through Christ who strengthens him, and he assures them that God will supply all their needs according to His riches in glory.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Philippians 4* brings the letter to a close with practical encouragement, a personal plea for unity, and heartfelt thanks. Paul has been building toward these instructions throughout the letter. He has called the church to stand firm together (*Philippians 1:27*), to have the humble mind of Christ (*2:5*), and to press on toward the goal (*3:14*). Now he addresses a specific conflict, gives guidance for the inner life, and expresses gratitude for the Philippians’ partnership.

The church at Philippi had supported Paul generously from the beginning. When he left Macedonia, they were the only church that shared with him financially, and they sent help to him more than once in Thessalonica (vv15–16). Most recently, they had sent Epaphroditus with a gift to Paul in prison. This chapter contains Paul’s thank-you note, but it is far more than a polite acknowledgment. It reveals the secret of Paul’s contentment and joy.

### Stand Firm (*4:1*)

“*Therefore, my brothers, beloved and longed for, my joy and crown, stand firm in the Lord in this way, my beloved*” (*v. 1*). Paul piles up words of affection. The Philippians are his “joy and crown,” the victor’s wreath awarded in ancient games. They are the reward of his labor (*1 Thessalonians 2:19–20*). He calls them to stand firm, drawing on everything he has said about heavenly citizenship and the hope of Christ’s return.

### A Plea for Unity (*4:2–3*)

“*I exhort Euodia, and I exhort Syntyche, to think the same way in the Lord*” (*v. 2*). Paul names two women in the church who were in disagreement. He addresses each one individually, showing respect and impartiality; he does not take sides. He asks them to “think the same way in the Lord,” echoing his call to have the mind of Christ (*Philippians 2:2*, 5). The goal is not that they agree on every opinion, but that they share a common commitment to Christ that overcomes their conflict.

“*Yes, I beg you also, true partner, help these women, for they labored with me in the Good News with Clement also, and the rest of my fellow workers, whose names are in the book of life*” (*v. 3*). Paul asks a trusted member of the church, perhaps a leader, to help them reconcile. These women were not minor figures. They had “labored” alongside Paul in spreading the gospel, using a word that suggests struggling side by side like athletes. Women played significant roles in the church at Philippi from its beginning, starting with Lydia, the first convert in Europe (*Acts 16:14–15*). Paul honors these women’s ministry even as he urges them toward unity. Their names, he says, are written in “the book of life,” God’s record of His people (*Revelation 3:5*; *20:12*).

### Rejoice and Be Gentle (*4:4–5*)

The call to rejoice always is studied below. “*Let your gentleness be known to all men. The Lord is at hand*” (*v. 5*). “Gentleness” describes a gracious, reasonable, forbearing spirit, a willingness to yield rather than insist on one’s rights. It should be visible to everyone. “The Lord is at hand” may mean that the Lord is near in presence, or that His return is near. Both truths encourage gentleness and calm.

### Prayer, Peace, and Right Thinking (*4:6–9*)

Paul’s teaching on anxiety, prayer, and peace, and his call to think on what is good, are studied below. “*Do the things which you learned, received, heard, and saw in me, and the God of peace will be with you*” (*v. 9*). Paul encourages them to put into practice what they have seen in him. Right thinking must lead to right living. And the result is not only the peace of God (v7) but the God of peace Himself, present with them.

### Contentment and Thanks (*4:10–20*)

“*But I rejoice in the Lord greatly that now at length you have revived your thought for me; in which you did indeed take thought, but you lacked opportunity*” (*v. 10*). Paul rejoices in their gift. They had always cared for him but had not had the chance to show it for a while. Paul’s testimony about contentment is studied below.

“*However you did well that you shared in my affliction*” (*v. 14*). Paul does not want them to think he did not value their gift. Their giving was a way of sharing in his struggles.

“*You yourselves also know, you Philippians, that in the beginning of the Good News, when I departed from Macedonia, no assembly shared with me in the matter of giving and receiving but you only*” (*v. 15*). “*For even in Thessalonica you sent once and again to my need*” (*v. 16*). The Philippians had a long history of generosity.

“*Not that I seek for the gift, but I seek for the fruit that increases to your account*” (*v. 17*). Paul uses business language. Their giving was like an investment that would bring spiritual return to them.

“*But I have all things and abound. I am filled, having received from Epaphroditus the things that came from you, a sweet-smelling fragrance, an acceptable and well-pleasing sacrifice to God*” (*v. 18*). Paul describes their gift as an offering to God, like the fragrant sacrifices of the Old Testament. Giving to support God’s work is an act of worship.

“*My God will supply every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus*” (*v. 19*). The Philippians had met Paul’s needs; now God will meet theirs. Notice that the promise is “every need,” not every desire. And God’s supply is measured “according to his riches in glory,” not according to human limitations. This promise was given to a generous church that had sacrificed to support God’s work.

“*Now to our God and Father be the glory forever and ever! Amen*” (*v. 20*).

### Final Greetings (*4:21–23*)

“*Greet every saint in Christ Jesus. The brothers who are with me greet you*” (*v. 21*). “*All the saints greet you, especially those who are of Caesar’s household*” (*v. 22*). “Caesar’s household” refers to the large staff of servants, officials, and workers in the emperor’s service. The gospel had reached into the heart of the Roman Empire, even as Paul sat in chains. “*The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen*” (*v. 23*).

## Important Verses Explained

### *Philippians 4:4* — Rejoice in the Lord Always

> *“Rejoice in the Lord always! Again I will say, ‘Rejoice!’”*
>
> — *Philippians 4:4* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This is one of the most famous commands in Scripture, and Paul repeats it for emphasis: “Rejoice in the Lord always! Again I will say, ‘Rejoice!’”

“In the Lord” is the key. Paul is not commanding believers to feel happy about every circumstance. He is commanding them to rejoice in the Lord, in who He is and what He has done. Circumstances change, but the Lord does not.

“Always” means in every season, not only when things go well. Paul wrote these words from prison, facing a possible death sentence. If he could rejoice there, believers can rejoice anywhere.

Paul repeats the command, “Again I will say,” perhaps because he knew how hard it is. Joy does not come naturally in hard times. It must be chosen and cultivated.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Christian joy is different from happiness. Happiness often depends on what happens. Joy is a deep gladness rooted in God’s character, His promises, and His presence. It can coexist with sorrow. Paul described himself as “*sorrowful yet always rejoicing*” (*2 Corinthians 6:10*). Jesus Himself, “*for the joy that was set before him endured the cross*” (*Hebrews 12:2*).

Joy is part of the fruit of the Spirit (*Galatians 5:22*). It is not something believers produce by sheer willpower but something the Spirit grows in them as they focus on the Lord. The theme of joy runs throughout Philippians: Paul rejoices in prayer (*Philippians 1:4*), in the preaching of Christ (*1:18*), in the possibility of being poured out (*2:17*), and in the Philippians’ generosity (*4:10*).

This command does not mean believers should deny grief or pretend to be happy when they are hurting. Scripture is full of laments, honest cries of pain to God. Joy in the Lord is compatible with tears. It is the steady confidence that, whatever happens, the Lord is good, present, and faithful.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Rejoicing in the Lord can be practiced in concrete ways: reflecting on God’s character, remembering His past faithfulness, thanking Him for specific blessings, singing songs of praise, and meditating on His promises. These habits help joy grow even when circumstances are hard.

For those going through grief, depression, or deep pain, this command is not a demand to feel happy. It is an invitation to hold on to the Lord, even in tears. Honest lament and quiet trust can be forms of rejoicing in the Lord. Those who struggle with ongoing depression may also need support from friends, pastors, and medical or counseling care, which God can use as part of His healing.

### *Philippians 4:6–7* — Do Not Be Anxious; God’s Peace Will Guard You

> *“In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.”*
>
> — *Philippians 4:6–7* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“In nothing be anxious.” Paul addresses a universal human struggle: worry. Anxiety pulls the mind in many directions, imagining worst-case scenarios and trying to control what cannot be controlled.

Instead, Paul offers an alternative: “but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God.” The word “everything” matches “nothing.” Nothing is too big or too small to bring to God. “Prayer” is a general word for talking with God. “Petition” means specific requests. “With thanksgiving” reminds believers to thank God even as they ask, remembering His past faithfulness.

The result is in verse 7: “And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.” God’s peace is not the absence of problems but a deep calm that comes from trusting Him. It “surpasses all understanding,” meaning it goes beyond what human reasoning can explain or produce. It may come even when circumstances have not changed.

“Will guard” is a military term. Philippi was a Roman colony with soldiers stationed there. Paul pictures God’s peace standing guard like a soldier over the heart and mind, protecting them from fear and anxiety.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Jesus also taught His followers not to be anxious, reminding them that their heavenly Father knows what they need and cares for them more than for the birds and flowers (*Matthew 6:25–34*). Peter wrote, “*casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you*” (*1 Peter 5:7*). The remedy for anxiety is not mere positive thinking but trust in a loving God expressed through prayer.

Notice that Paul does not promise that God will give believers everything they ask for. He promises God’s peace. Sometimes God changes circumstances; sometimes He changes the heart. Either way, His peace guards those who bring their concerns to Him.

It is important to understand that this command is not a condemnation of people who struggle with anxiety disorders or mental health conditions. Anxiety can have physical, emotional, and situational causes, and many faithful believers experience it. Paul himself admitted to “*anxiety for all the assemblies*” (*2 Corinthians 11:28*). This passage offers a path of hope: bringing worries to God in prayer. For many, that path also includes help from doctors, counselors, and trusted friends, which God can use for healing. Seeking such help is not a lack of faith.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

When anxiety rises, believers can turn worries into prayers. Naming specific concerns before God, asking for His help, and thanking Him for what He has already done can shift the focus from the problem to the One who is greater than the problem.

Some find it helpful to name their worries and pray through them one by one, or to pause throughout the day to bring concerns to God as they arise. Thanksgiving is especially powerful: remembering God’s past faithfulness builds confidence for the present.

For those whose anxiety is persistent or overwhelming, prayer can be joined with other forms of care: rest, community, and professional help. God’s peace can come through many means, and He is present in all of them.

### *Philippians 4:8* — Think About These Things

> *“Finally, brothers, whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable, whatever things are just, whatever things are pure, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report: if there is any virtue and if there is anything worthy of praise, think about these things.”*
>
> — *Philippians 4:8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Having addressed anxiety, Paul turns to the thought life. What believers think about shapes their hearts and lives.

He lists eight qualities to focus on. “True”: what is real and honest, in contrast to lies and deception. “Honorable”: what is worthy of respect, dignified, and serious. “Just”: what is right and fair. “Pure”: what is morally clean and wholesome. “Lovely”: what is beautiful, pleasing, and attractive in a good sense. “Of good report”: what is admirable and well spoken of. “Virtue”: moral excellence. “Worthy of praise”: what deserves commendation.

“Think about these things.” The word means to consider carefully, to dwell on, to let one’s mind rest on. Paul is not just telling believers to avoid bad thoughts but to deliberately fill their minds with good ones.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse reflects a principle found throughout Scripture: the mind shapes the life. *Proverbs 4:23* urges, “*Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life*” (*Proverbs 4:23*). *Romans 12:2* calls believers to be transformed by the renewing of their minds. What people consistently think about influences what they desire, how they feel, and how they act.

Many of the qualities Paul lists were also valued by Greek moral philosophers. Paul affirms that whatever is genuinely true, good, and beautiful, wherever it is found, is worth dwelling on. All truth and beauty ultimately come from God. Believers can appreciate goodness in creation, art, literature, music, and human kindness, recognizing God as their source.

Above all, these qualities describe Christ Himself. He is true, honorable, just, pure, lovely, and worthy of praise. Thinking on these things ultimately leads the mind to Him.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

In an age of constant information, news, and entertainment, believers face a flood of input that can fill their minds with fear, anger, impurity, or despair. This verse invites careful choices about what to read, watch, and listen to.

It also encourages a deliberate habit of focusing on good things: reading Scripture, noticing beauty in creation, remembering acts of kindness, appreciating what is true and admirable in others. This is not denial of evil but a refusal to let evil dominate the mind.

When negative or harmful thoughts arise, believers can redirect their minds by asking: Is this true? Is it honorable? Is it pure? Is it worth dwelling on? This simple test, practiced over time, can reshape thought patterns and bring peace.

### *Philippians 4:11–13* — The Secret of Contentment

> *“Not that I speak because of lack, for I have learned in whatever state I am, to be content in it. I know how to be humbled, and I also know how to abound. In any and all circumstances I have learned the secret both to be filled and to be hungry, both to abound and to be in need. I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me.”*
>
> — *Philippians 4:11–13* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul has just thanked the Philippians for their gift, but he wants them to know that his joy does not depend on receiving it. “Not that I speak because of lack, for I have learned in whatever state I am, to be content in it.”

“I have learned.” Contentment did not come naturally to Paul. It was learned through experience, often painful experience.

“To be content.” The word was used by Greek philosophers, especially the Stoics, to describe self-sufficiency, being independent of outward circumstances. Paul gives it a new meaning. His contentment comes not from self-sufficiency but from Christ-sufficiency.

Verse 12 describes the range of Paul’s experiences: “I know how to be humbled, and I also know how to abound.” He had known poverty and plenty, hunger and fullness. “I have learned the secret.” The word suggests being initiated into a mystery. Paul had discovered something that many never learn.

Verse 13 reveals the secret: “I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me.” In context, “all things” refers especially to facing every circumstance with contentment, whether need or abundance. Christ gives Paul the strength to live faithfully and contentedly in any situation.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

*Philippians 4:13* is one of the most quoted verses in the Bible, often used as a motto for achieving goals or winning competitions. While Christ does strengthen believers for many tasks, the primary meaning in context is the strength to be content in every circumstance, including hunger, need, and hardship. Paul is not promising that believers can accomplish anything they set their minds on; he is testifying that Christ gives the strength to endure and remain faithful whatever life brings.

Contentment is a rare and precious virtue. First Timothy 6:6 says that godliness with contentment is great gain. *Hebrews 13:5* urges believers to be content with what they have, because God has said, “*I will in no way leave you, neither will I in any way forsake you*” (*Hebrews 13:5*). Contentment flows from knowing that God is present and sufficient.

Paul’s contentment also guards against two dangers. In poverty, it guards against despair and envy. In abundance, it guards against pride and self-reliance. Both extremes test faith, and Christ gives strength for both.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Many people believe they will be content when they have a little more: more money, a better job, a bigger house, a relationship, or recognition. This passage reveals that contentment is not found in circumstances but in Christ. It is learned over time as believers trust Him in both lean and plentiful seasons.

Learning contentment can involve practicing gratitude for what one has, resisting comparison with others, simplifying desires, and regularly reminding oneself of God’s presence and promises. Contentment does not mean passivity; Paul still worked hard and gladly received help. It means not being controlled by circumstances.

When believers face hardship, *Philippians 4:13* is a powerful promise: Christ will give them the strength they need to endure. Whatever comes, they are not alone.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Philippians 4* gathers the themes of the letter into practical wisdom for daily life. It begins with a call to stand firm in the Lord and a plea for unity between two faithful women whose conflict was harming the church. Paul’s approach is a model for handling disagreements: speak to each person with respect, appeal to their shared commitment to Christ, and invite others to help bring reconciliation.

The chapter then gives guidance for the inner life. Believers are called to rejoice in the Lord always, not by denying pain, but by anchoring their joy in the unchanging goodness of God. They are invited to bring every worry to God in prayer, with thanksgiving, and to receive His peace, which guards the heart and mind beyond human understanding. For those who struggle with anxiety, this is a gentle invitation, and it can go hand in hand with other forms of help God provides.

Paul also teaches believers to guard their thoughts, focusing on whatever is true, honorable, just, pure, lovely, and praiseworthy. What fills the mind shapes the life. Believers can make wise choices about what they take in and deliberately dwell on what is good.

Finally, Paul shares the secret of contentment. Whether in need or in plenty, he had learned to be content, because Christ gave him strength for every circumstance. This frees believers from the endless pursuit of “more” and from despair in times of lack. And God, who supplies every need according to His riches in Christ, invites His people to give generously, trusting Him to care for them. Joy, peace, right thinking, and contentment are all found in the same place: in Christ, who is near.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord, I want to rejoice in You always, in every season and every circumstance. When I am anxious, help me to bring every worry to You in prayer, with thanksgiving, and guard my heart and mind with Your peace that surpasses all understanding. Where I am in conflict with others, give me humility and help me to seek unity in You. Let my gentleness be evident to all. Fill my mind with whatever is true, honorable, just, pure, lovely, and praiseworthy. Teach me the secret of contentment, whether I have little or much, and strengthen me through Christ to face all things. Make me generous like the Philippians, and help me trust that You will supply every need according to Your riches in glory in Christ Jesus. To You be the glory forever. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Book 12 of 27

# Colossians

## About This Letter

Colossae was a small town in the Lycus River valley of Phrygia, in what is now southwestern Turkey, about a hundred miles east of Ephesus and close to the larger cities of Laodicea and Hierapolis. Paul had not visited the church there himself (*Colossians 2:1*). It was founded by Epaphras, a native of Colossae who had probably come to faith during Paul’s long ministry in Ephesus, when, as *Acts 19:10* says, “all those who lived in Asia heard the word of the Lord Jesus”. Epaphras later visited Paul in prison and brought news of the church (*Colossians 1:7–8*; *4:12–13*).

The letter presents itself as written by Paul, together with Timothy, while Paul was a prisoner (*4:3*, 10, 18). Most Christians through history have held that Paul wrote it during his Roman imprisonment around A.D. 60–62, at the same time as Philemon and Ephesians; Tychicus and Onesimus carried it (*4:7–9*). Some modern scholars think a follower of Paul wrote it in his name, pointing to differences in style and emphasis, while many others find these differences fully explained by the subject matter and circumstances.

Epaphras’s report included a concern. Some teachers were urging the Colossian believers toward a mix of practices: strict food and festival rules, harsh treatment of the body, the worship of angels, claims to special visions, and a “philosophy” based on human tradition and spiritual forces (*2:8*, 16–23). The exact nature of this teaching is debated, but its effect was to suggest that Christ alone was not enough.

## The Shape of the Letter

In chapter 1, Paul gives thanks for the Colossians’ faith, prays for their growth in knowledge and fruitfulness, and celebrates the supremacy of Christ in a great hymn: He is the image of the invisible God, the one through whom and for whom all things were created, the head of the church, and the one through whom God reconciled all things by the blood of His cross. In chapter 2, he warns against empty philosophy and human regulations, declaring that in Christ the fullness of deity dwells bodily and that believers are complete in Him, having been buried and raised with Him. In chapters 3 and 4, he shows what life in Christ looks like: setting the mind on things above, putting off the old self and putting on the new, letting Christ’s peace and word dwell richly, living faithfully in households and at work, devoting themselves to prayer, and speaking graciously to outsiders.

## Themes to Watch For

Watch for the supremacy and sufficiency of Christ, the fullness of God dwelling in Him, His victory over every spiritual power, reconciliation through the cross, union with Christ in His death and resurrection, the mystery of “Christ in you, the hope of glory,” freedom from human rules and spiritual intimidation, the new self being renewed in the image of its Creator, thankfulness, and doing everything in the name of the Lord Jesus. Colossians answers every claim that believers need something more than Christ: in Him they have been made full.

Colossians · Chapter 1 of 4

# Colossians — Chapter 1

Chapter Theme: The Supremacy of Christ

[Read Colossians 1 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/COL01.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul thanks God for the Colossians’ faith, love, and hope, which grew from the gospel that Epaphras brought them, and prays that they will be filled with the knowledge of God’s will, live in a way that pleases Him, and be strengthened with patience and joy. He celebrates what the Father has done: rescuing believers from the domain of darkness and transferring them into the kingdom of His beloved Son. Then, in a majestic hymn, Paul proclaims that Christ is the image of the invisible God, the one through whom and for whom all things were created, the one who holds all things together, the head of the church, and the one through whom God reconciled all things by the blood of His cross. Paul rejoices to serve this gospel and to proclaim the mystery now revealed: Christ in you, the hope of glory.

## Chapter Background and Story

Paul had never visited Colossae, but he had heard about the church through Epaphras, who had planted it. The report was largely encouraging: the Colossians had genuine faith and love. But there was also a danger. Some teachers were pressing a mixture of ideas that, whatever their details, made Christ seem insufficient. They suggested that believers needed special knowledge, visions, strict rules, or the help of angels and spiritual powers to reach spiritual fullness.

Paul’s response begins not with an attack on the false teaching but with a glorious portrait of Christ. If the Colossians truly understood who Christ is, they would see that nothing else is needed. Verses 15–20 are often called the “Christ hymn” of Colossians. They may have been an early Christian hymn or confession that Paul quotes or composed. They contain some of the highest statements about Christ in the New Testament.

### Thanksgiving (*1:3–8*)

“*We give thanks to God the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, praying always for you*” (*v. 3*), “*having heard of your faith in Christ Jesus and of the love which you have toward all the saints*” (*v. 4*), “*because of the hope which is laid up for you in the heavens, of which you heard before in the word of the truth of the Good News*” (*v. 5*). Faith, love, and hope appear together here, as they do in *1 Corinthians 13:13* and *1 Thessalonians 1:3*. Faith is directed toward Christ, love toward fellow believers, and hope toward what God has prepared. Notice that hope comes first in Paul’s reasoning: their faith and love spring from the secure hope “laid up” for them in heaven.

“*which has come to you, even as it is in all the world and is bearing fruit and growing, as it does in you also, since the day you heard and knew the grace of God in truth*” (*v. 6*). The gospel is alive. Like a healthy plant, it bears fruit and grows wherever it goes. The Colossians were part of a worldwide movement.

“*even as you learned from Epaphras our beloved fellow servant, who is a faithful servant of Christ on your behalf*” (*v. 7*), “*who also declared to us your love in the Spirit*” (*v. 8*). Paul affirms Epaphras as a trustworthy teacher. The gospel the Colossians had received from him was the true gospel. They did not need a different one.

### Paul’s Prayer (*1:9–12*)

“*For this cause, we also, since the day we heard this, don’t cease praying and making requests for you, that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding*” (*v. 9*). The false teachers offered special knowledge. Paul prays for true knowledge: understanding God’s will, with spiritual wisdom. This knowledge is practical; its purpose is a changed life.

“*that you may walk worthily of the Lord, to please him in all respects, bearing fruit in every good work and increasing in the knowledge of God*” (*v. 10*). Knowledge leads to living in a way that pleases the Lord, which leads to good works and to deeper knowledge of God. It is a growing cycle.

“*strengthened with all power, according to the might of his glory, for all endurance and perseverance with joy*” (*v. 11*). God’s mighty power is given not only for dramatic deeds but for endurance and patience. And endurance is to be accompanied by joy.

“*giving thanks to the Father, who made us fit to be partakers of the inheritance of the saints in light*” (*v. 12*). Believers did not qualify themselves. The Father made them fit to share in the inheritance of God’s people. The rescue that made this possible is studied below.

### The Supremacy of Christ (*1:15–20*)

The great hymn about Christ is studied below in two parts.

### Reconciled and Presented Holy (*1:21–23*)

“*You, being in past times alienated and enemies in your mind in your evil deeds*” (*v. 21*), “*yet now he has reconciled in the body of his flesh through death, to present you holy and without defect and blameless before him*” (*v. 22*). The cosmic reconciliation described in the hymn becomes personal. The Colossians were once far from God and hostile toward Him. Now, through Christ’s death in His real, physical body, they have been reconciled. The goal is that they will stand before God holy, without defect, and free from accusation.

“*if it is so that you continue in the faith, grounded and steadfast, and not moved away from the hope of the Good News which you heard, which was proclaimed in all creation under heaven, of which I, Paul, was made a servant*” (*v. 23*). Paul encourages perseverance. Those who are truly reconciled will continue in the faith, firmly established like a building on a foundation, not shifting away to other teachings. Christian traditions have different views on whether a true believer can finally fall away, but all agree on the practical call here: hold fast to the gospel you received.

### Paul’s Ministry and the Mystery (*1:24–29*)

“*Now I rejoice in my sufferings for your sake, and fill up on my part that which is lacking of the afflictions of Christ in my flesh for his body’s sake, which is the assembly*” (*v. 24*). This is a difficult verse. Paul does not mean that Christ’s sacrifice for sin was incomplete; he has just said that Christ reconciled all things through His cross. Most interpreters understand Paul to mean that Christ’s people continue to suffer in the world as they carry the gospel, and that these sufferings are in some sense Christ’s own, since He is united with His body. Jesus asked Paul on the Damascus road, “*why do you persecute me?*” (*Acts 9:4*). There is a measure of suffering appointed for the church before the end, and Paul gladly bore his share for others’ sake.

“*of which I was made a servant according to the stewardship of God which was given me toward you to fulfill the word of God*” (*v. 25*), “*the mystery which has been hidden for ages and generations. But now it has been revealed to his saints*” (*v. 26*). The content of the mystery, and Paul’s goal in ministry, are studied below.

“*for which I also labor, striving according to his working, which works in me mightily*” (*v. 29*). Paul worked hard, but the energy came from God working powerfully in him.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Colossians 1:13–14* — Rescued from Darkness into the Kingdom

> *“who delivered us out of the power of darkness, and translated us into the Kingdom of the Son of his love, in whom we have our redemption, the forgiveness of our sins.”*
>
> — *Colossians 1:13–14* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul describes what God the Father has done for believers. “Who delivered us out of the power of darkness.” “The power of darkness” refers to the realm where sin, evil, and spiritual forces opposed to God hold people captive. God has rescued believers from that realm. The word “delivered” suggests a rescue from danger, like being pulled out of a burning building.

“And translated us into the Kingdom of the Son of his love.” “Translated” means transferred, moved from one place to another. In the ancient world, conquering kings sometimes moved whole populations from one land to another. God has moved believers out of the kingdom of darkness and into the kingdom of His beloved Son. They have a new King and a new home.

Verse 14 explains what this means: “in whom we have our redemption, the forgiveness of our sins.” Redemption means being set free by the payment of a price. In Christ, believers have been set free, and the heart of that freedom is the forgiveness of their sins.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses describe salvation as a change of kingdoms. Before Christ, people lived under the dominion of darkness. They were not merely making bad choices; they were under a power they could not escape on their own. Jesus described His mission in similar terms: He came to bind the strong man and plunder his house (*Mark 3:27*), and to set the captives free (*Luke 4:18*).

The phrase “the Son of his love” emphasizes the Father’s love for the Son. Believers are brought into the kingdom of the one the Father loves supremely, and in Him they too are loved.

Notice that both verbs are in the past tense. The rescue and transfer have already happened. Believers do not need to fear the powers of darkness or seek special rituals to protect themselves from spiritual forces, as the false teachers in Colossae may have suggested. They already belong to Christ’s kingdom.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Many people live in fear of spiritual forces, bad luck, curses, or unseen powers. These verses declare that believers have been rescued from the dominion of darkness and now belong to Christ. They do not need to live in fear.

This truth also changes identity. Believers are citizens of Christ’s kingdom. Their loyalty, values, and hope belong to Him. When old patterns of sin or fear try to pull them back, they can remember that they no longer live under the old ruler.

Finally, these verses remind believers of the heart of salvation: the forgiveness of sins. Whatever burdens of guilt a person carries, they can be lifted in Christ.

### *Colossians 1:15–17* — The Image of the Invisible God

> *“He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation. For by him all things were created in the heavens and on the earth, visible things and invisible things, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers. All things have been created through him and for him. He is before all things, and in him all things are held together.”*
>
> — *Colossians 1:15–17* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul begins the great hymn with breathtaking statements about Christ.

“He is the image of the invisible God.” God is spirit and cannot be seen with human eyes. But in Christ, the invisible God has been made visible. An image is an exact representation. To see Christ is to see what God is like. Jesus said, “*He who has seen me has seen the Father*” (*John 14:9*).

“The firstborn of all creation.” This phrase does not mean that Christ was the first being created. In the Bible, “firstborn” often refers to rank and inheritance, the one who holds the place of honor and authority. God said of David, who was the youngest son, “*I will also appoint him my firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth*” (*Psalm 89:27*). Christ holds supreme rank over all creation.

Verse 16 explains why: “For by him all things were created.” Christ is not part of creation; He is the Creator. “In the heavens and on the earth, visible things and invisible things, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers.” Everything, including every spiritual power the false teachers feared or honored, was made by Christ. “All things have been created through him and for him.” Christ is the agent of creation and its goal. Everything exists for His glory.

Verse 17: “He is before all things, and in him all things are held together.” Christ existed before creation. And He continues to hold the universe together. Without Him, everything would fall apart.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses make some of the highest claims about Christ anywhere in Scripture. They echo *John 1:1–3*, which says that the Word was with God and was God, and that all things were made through Him. They also echo *Hebrews 1:2–3*, which says that God made the universe through the Son and that the Son upholds all things by the word of His power.

In the early centuries of the church, some teachers, such as Arius in the fourth century, argued that “firstborn of all creation” meant that Christ was a created being, the first and highest of God’s creatures. The church rejected this view at the Council of Nicaea in A.D. 325, affirming that the Son is “begotten, not made,” fully God, of one being with the Father. The very next verse supports this, because it says all things were created by Him; He cannot be both the Creator of all things and one of the created things.

For the Colossians, these verses answered the false teaching directly. Angels and spiritual powers are not rivals to Christ or necessary mediators. They are His creations, under His authority. Believers who have Christ have the Creator of all things.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses invite believers to see Christ in His full glory. He is not merely a great teacher or a good example. He is the Creator of the universe, the one who holds all things together, and the one for whom everything exists. That vision of Christ should lead to worship.

It also brings security. The one who holds the universe together holds believers’ lives together too. When life feels chaotic or falling apart, believers can remember that “in him all things are held together.”

Finally, these verses give meaning to all of life. If all things were created for Christ, then work, relationships, creativity, and the beauty of the natural world all find their purpose in Him. Every part of life can be lived for His glory.

### *Colossians 1:18–20* — Head of the Church and Reconciler of All Things

> *“He is the head of the body, the assembly, who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in all things he might have the preeminence. For all the fullness was pleased to dwell in him, and through him to reconcile all things to himself by him, whether things on the earth or things in the heavens, having made peace through the blood of his cross.”*
>
> — *Colossians 1:18–20* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The second part of the hymn moves from creation to new creation.

“He is the head of the body, the assembly.” Christ is the head of the church, which is His body. As the head directs and gives life to the body, Christ leads and sustains His people.

“Who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead.” Christ is the beginning of the new creation. He is the “firstborn from the dead,” the first to rise from the dead with a resurrection body, never to die again. His resurrection is the first of many; all who belong to Him will follow (*1 Corinthians 15:20–23*).

“That in all things he might have the preeminence.” Christ is first in everything, in creation and in redemption.

Verse 19: “For all the fullness was pleased to dwell in him.” God, in all His fullness, chose to dwell in Christ. The false teachers may have used the word “fullness” for a series of spiritual beings or levels between God and humanity. Paul says the fullness of God is found entirely in Christ.

Verse 20: “and through him to reconcile all things to himself by him, whether things on the earth or things in the heavens, having made peace through the blood of his cross.” God’s purpose is to reconcile all things to Himself through Christ. The means of reconciliation is “the blood of his cross,” Christ’s sacrificial death.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The hymn presents Christ as supreme in two creations: the original creation (vv15–17) and the new creation (vv18–20). He is the firstborn of all creation and the firstborn from the dead. He is the Creator and the Redeemer.

The reconciliation of “all things” is a vast vision. Sin did not only break the relationship between humanity and God; it disordered the whole creation (*Romans 8:19–22*). Through the cross, God is setting everything right. Christians have understood this in different ways. Most understand it to mean that God will restore creation and bring all things under Christ’s rightful rule, with every hostile power defeated and subdued (*Colossians 2:15*). Some hope it points to the eventual salvation of all people, though most Christian traditions have held that Scripture also teaches a final judgment for those who reject Christ. All agree that the cross is the center of God’s plan to heal a broken world.

The phrase “made peace through the blood of his cross” is remarkable. Peace with God and the healing of creation come not through human effort, special knowledge, or spiritual rituals, but through Christ’s sacrifice.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses call believers to let Christ have first place in everything: their priorities, their affections, their decisions, and their worship. If He is preeminent in the universe, He should be preeminent in their lives.

They also bring hope in a broken world. Injustice, suffering, environmental damage, and broken relationships are not the final word. Through the cross, God is reconciling all things. Believers can work for peace, justice, and the care of creation as signs of the reconciliation Christ is bringing.

Finally, these verses remind believers that Christ’s resurrection guarantees their own. He is the firstborn from the dead, and those who belong to Him will share His resurrection life.

### *Colossians 1:27–28* — Christ in You, the Hope of Glory

> *“to whom God was pleased to make known what are the riches of the glory of this mystery among the Gentiles, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory. We proclaim him, admonishing every man and teaching every man in all wisdom, that we may present every man perfect in Christ Jesus;”*
>
> — *Colossians 1:27–28* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul describes the mystery God has now revealed. In Paul’s letters, a “mystery” is a truth once hidden in God’s plan but now made known. God was “pleased to make known what are the riches of the glory of this mystery among the Gentiles.”

What is the mystery? “Christ in you, the hope of glory.” The astonishing truth is that Christ Himself lives in His people, including Gentiles who were once far from God. Through the Holy Spirit, the Lord of all creation dwells in ordinary believers. And His presence within them is the guarantee of future glory. Because Christ is in them now, they can be sure they will share His glory when He returns.

Verse 28 describes Paul’s response: “We proclaim him.” Paul’s message is not a philosophy, a set of rules, or a spiritual technique. It is a person: Christ. “Admonishing every man and teaching every man in all wisdom.” Admonishing means warning and correcting; teaching means instructing in truth. Both are needed.

“That we may present every man perfect in Christ Jesus.” “Perfect” here means mature, complete. Paul’s goal is that every believer would grow to full maturity in Christ. Notice the repetition of “every man,” three times in this verse. The false teachers may have offered special knowledge to a select few. Paul’s gospel is for everyone.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

“Christ in you” is one of the most profound truths of the Christian faith. Believers are not only forgiven and declared righteous; they are indwelt by Christ Himself. Jesus promised that He and the Father would come and make their home with those who love Him (*John 14:23*). Paul wrote, “*Christ lives in me*” (*Galatians 2:20*). This indwelling presence is the source of transformation, strength, and hope.

The phrase “the hope of glory” links the present and the future. Christ’s presence in believers now is the down payment of the glory they will share with Him forever. *Colossians 3:4* says, “*When Christ, our life, is revealed, then you will also be revealed with him in glory*” (*Colossians 3:4*).

Paul’s goal of presenting “every man perfect in Christ” shows that spiritual maturity is not for an elite few but for all believers. Every person who belongs to Christ can grow toward maturity, and the church’s ministry exists to help them.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers who feel spiritually inadequate or unimportant can take great comfort in this truth: Christ Himself lives in them. They are not ordinary in God’s eyes. They carry the presence of the Lord of the universe.

This truth also gives hope. Whatever struggles, weaknesses, or sufferings believers face, Christ in them is the guarantee of future glory. The present is not the final chapter.

Finally, Paul’s ministry goal can shape the way believers serve one another. In families, friendships, and churches, the aim is to help every person grow to maturity in Christ, through teaching, encouragement, and loving correction. No one is beyond growth, and no one should be left behind.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Colossians 1* lifts believers’ eyes to see the greatness of Jesus Christ. Paul begins by thanking God for the Colossians’ faith, love, and hope, and by praying that they will grow in knowledge, fruitfulness, endurance, and joy. These prayers remind believers what matters most: knowing God’s will, living in a way that pleases Him, and finding strength for patient endurance.

The chapter then reveals what God has done. He has rescued believers from the domain of darkness and transferred them into the kingdom of His beloved Son, where they have redemption and forgiveness. They do not need to fear spiritual powers or seek special rituals for protection. They belong to Christ.

At the heart of the chapter is a majestic portrait of Christ. He is the image of the invisible God, the Creator of all things, the one who holds the universe together, the head of the church, the firstborn from the dead, and the one in whom all the fullness of God dwells. Through His cross, God is reconciling all things to Himself. This vision of Christ answers every claim that believers need something more. In Christ, they have everything.

Finally, Paul celebrates the mystery now revealed: Christ in you, the hope of glory. The Lord of all creation lives in His people and guarantees their future glory. This truth gives every believer dignity, hope, and purpose. Like Paul, believers can proclaim Christ, help one another grow to maturity, and labor with the strength that God supplies. Christ is supreme, Christ is sufficient, and Christ is in His people.

## Chapter Prayer

Father, thank You for rescuing me from the domain of darkness and bringing me into the kingdom of Your beloved Son, in whom I have redemption and the forgiveness of my sins. Fill me with the knowledge of Your will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding, so that I may live in a way that pleases You, bear fruit in every good work, and grow in knowing You. Strengthen me with all power for endurance and patience with joy. Lord Jesus, You are the image of the invisible God, the Creator of all things, and the one who holds all things together. You are the head of the church and the firstborn from the dead. Take first place in every part of my life. Thank You for making peace through the blood of Your cross. Thank You that You live in me, my hope of glory. Help me to proclaim You and to help others grow to maturity in You. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Colossians · Chapter 2 of 4

# Colossians — Chapter 2

Chapter Theme: Complete in Christ

[Read Colossians 2 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/COL02.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul tells the Colossians how he struggles in prayer for them, longing that they be encouraged, united in love, and given full understanding of Christ, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden. He urges them, as they received Christ Jesus the Lord, to keep walking in Him, rooted and built up in Him, and to beware of empty philosophy based on human tradition rather than on Christ. In Christ the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily, and in Him believers have been made full. They have been spiritually circumcised, buried and raised with Him, made alive, and forgiven, because God canceled the record of debt against them by nailing it to the cross and disarmed the spiritual powers. So they must not let anyone judge them by food laws and festivals, which were shadows of Christ, or disqualify them through false humility, angel worship, and harsh rules that cannot restrain the flesh.

## Chapter Background and Story

In chapter 1, Paul presented a majestic portrait of Christ as supreme over all creation and the one through whom God reconciled all things. In chapter 2, he applies that truth to the danger facing the Colossian church. If Christ is supreme and sufficient, then believers do not need anything else to reach spiritual fullness.

The teaching Paul warns against is not described in full, and scholars have reconstructed it in different ways. It seems to have combined elements of Jewish practice (circumcision, food laws, Sabbaths, festivals), ascetic discipline (harsh treatment of the body), mystical experiences (visions), and reverence for angels or spiritual powers. Its teachers presented it as a “philosophy,” a path to deeper wisdom and spiritual maturity. Its underlying message was that faith in Christ was a good start but not enough.

Paul’s answer is clear and powerful. In Christ, believers already have everything. They do not need to add rules, rituals, or experiences to be complete. They need to stay rooted in the Christ they first received.

### Paul’s Struggle for Them (*2:1–5*)

“*For I desire to have you know how greatly I struggle for you and for those at Laodicea, and for as many as have not seen my face in the flesh*” (*v. 1*). Paul had never met these believers, but he struggled for them, likely in intense prayer (see *Colossians 4:12*). Laodicea was a nearby city; Paul wanted this letter shared there too (*4:16*).

“*that their hearts may be comforted, they being knit together in love, and gaining all riches of the full assurance of understanding, that they may know the mystery of God, both of the Father and of Christ*” (*v. 2*), “*in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden*” (*v. 3*). The false teachers offered hidden knowledge. Paul declares that all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are already hidden in Christ. “Hidden” does not mean inaccessible, but stored up, like treasure in a vault, available to all who are in Him.

“*Now I say this that no one may delude you with persuasiveness of speech*” (*v. 4*). The false teachers were persuasive. Paul warns the Colossians not to be fooled by impressive arguments. “*For though I am absent in the flesh, yet I am with you in the spirit, rejoicing and seeing your order, and the steadfastness of your faith in Christ*” (*v. 5*). Paul uses military language: “order” and “steadfastness” describe soldiers in disciplined ranks, standing firm.

### Rooted in Christ (*2:6–7*)

These verses, at the heart of this chapter, are studied below.

### Beware of Empty Philosophy (*2:8*)

“*Be careful that you don’t let anyone rob you through his philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the elemental spirits of the world, and not after Christ*” (*v. 8*). “Rob” means to take captive, to carry off as plunder. The false teachers would make the Colossians their captives. Paul is not condemning all careful thinking or philosophy as such. He condemns “vain deceit,” empty and deceptive teaching rooted in human tradition and “the elemental spirits of the world,” rather than in Christ. As in *Galatians 4:3*, “elemental spirits” may mean the basic principles of religion or the spiritual powers thought to govern the world.

### Fullness and Freedom in Christ (*2:9–15*)

The fullness of deity in Christ, and the believer’s fullness in Him, are studied below. “*In him you were also circumcised with a circumcision not made with hands, in the putting off of the body of the sins of the flesh, in the circumcision of Christ*” (*v. 11*). The false teachers may have urged physical circumcision. Paul says believers have already received a spiritual circumcision performed by Christ Himself: the cutting away of the old sinful nature.

“*having been buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him through faith in the working of God, who raised him from the dead*” (*v. 12*). Baptism pictures union with Christ in His burial and resurrection (*Romans 6:3–4*). Believers have died to the old life and been raised to new life, through faith in the God who raised Jesus. What God has done in canceling their debt and defeating the powers is studied below.

### Do Not Be Judged by Shadows (*2:16–19*)

The issue of food laws and festivals is studied below. “*Let no one rob you of your prize by self-abasement and worshiping of the angels, dwelling in the things which he has not seen, vainly puffed up by his fleshly mind*” (*v. 18*). “Rob you of your prize” uses an athletic image: an umpire disqualifying a runner. The false teachers claimed spiritual superiority based on extreme self-denial, angel worship, and visions. “Worshiping of the angels” may mean worshiping angels directly or claiming to join in the worship angels offer. Either way, it shifted attention from Christ. Paul notes the irony: their supposed humility actually made them proud.

“*and not holding firmly to the Head, from whom all the body, being supplied and knit together through the joints and ligaments, grows with God’s growth*” (*v. 19*). The fundamental problem was that they had lost connection with Christ, the Head. True spiritual growth comes only from Him, as the body is nourished and held together through its connection to the Head.

### Dead to Human Rules (*2:20–23*)

“*If you died with Christ from the elemental spirits of the world, why, as though living in the world, do you subject yourselves to ordinances*” (*v. 20*), “*“Don’t handle, nor taste, nor touch”*” (*v. 21*). Paul mimics the rules of the false teachers. Believers have died with Christ and been freed from such regulations. Why would they submit to them again?

“*(all of which perish with use), according to the precepts and doctrines of men?*” (*v. 22*) These rules concern things that perish, like food. Jesus taught that what goes into the body does not defile a person, but what comes out of the heart (*Mark 7:14–23*). These are human commands, not God’s.

“*These things indeed appear like wisdom in self-imposed worship, humility, and severity to the body, but aren’t of any value against the indulgence of the flesh*” (*v. 23*). This is an important insight. Harsh rules and self-punishment may look impressive and spiritual. But they cannot change the heart or truly restrain sinful desires. Only union with Christ and the power of His Spirit can do that, as Paul will show in chapter 3.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Colossians 2:6–7* — Rooted and Built Up in Him

> *“As therefore you received Christ Jesus the Lord, walk in him, rooted and built up in him and established in the faith, even as you were taught, abounding in it in thanksgiving.”*
>
> — *Colossians 2:6–7* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These verses summarize Paul’s counsel to the Colossians. “As therefore you received Christ Jesus the Lord, walk in him.” When they first believed, they received Christ, not just a teaching about Him, but Christ Himself as Lord. Now they are to “walk” in Him, living each day in union with Him. The way they began is the way they should continue. They did not receive Christ through rules or rituals, and they should not try to grow that way either.

Paul then uses several images. “Rooted”: like a tree whose roots go deep into the soil, drawing nourishment and stability. The tense in Greek suggests something already done: they have been rooted in Christ once for all. “Built up in him”: like a building rising on a firm foundation. This is ongoing: they are being built up continually. “Established in the faith”: made firm, stable, and secure in the truth of the gospel. “Even as you were taught”: the gospel they learned from Epaphras was sufficient. They did not need new teachers with new doctrines.

“Abounding in it in thanksgiving.” The result of being rooted in Christ is overflowing gratitude. Thanksgiving is a recurring theme in Colossians, appearing in every chapter.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses describe the whole Christian life in a few words. It begins with receiving Christ, continues by walking in Him, grows by being rooted and built up in Him, stands firm through being established in the faith, and overflows in thanksgiving.

The image of roots is especially rich. *Psalm 1:3* describes the righteous person as “*like a tree planted by the streams of water, that produces its fruit in its season*” (*Psalm 1:3*). *Jeremiah 17:8* says the one who trusts in the LORD is like a tree whose roots reach the stream, not fearing when heat comes. Jesus spoke of seed that fell on rocky ground and withered because it had no root (*Mark 4:5–6*, 16–17). Deep roots in Christ provide stability in the storms of life and nourishment for growth.

The combination of being “rooted” (a past, completed action) and “built up” (an ongoing process) reflects the shape of the Christian life. Believers are already fully united with Christ, and they are continually growing in Him. Both are true at once.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers grow deep roots in Christ through regular practices that keep them connected to Him: reading and meditating on Scripture, prayer, worship, fellowship with other believers, and obedience. These are not ways of earning God’s favor, but ways of drawing nourishment from Christ, just as roots draw from the soil.

When new teachings, trends, or spiritual fads come along, promising something more than Christ, these verses call believers back to the gospel they first received. The way forward is not adding something new, but going deeper into Christ.

Finally, thanksgiving is both a sign and a source of healthy roots. Believers who regularly give thanks find their faith strengthened and their hearts steadied. Gratitude keeps attention focused on what God has already given in Christ.

### *Colossians 2:9–10* — The Fullness of Deity Dwells in Him

> *“For in him all the fullness of the Deity dwells bodily, and in him you are made full, who is the head of all principality and power.”*
>
> — *Colossians 2:9–10* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul gives the reason believers should not look beyond Christ. “For in him all the fullness of the Deity dwells bodily.” Everything that God is, all of His divine nature, lives in Christ. Not a portion, not a reflection, but all the fullness. And it dwells in Him “bodily,” in His real, physical human body. In Jesus, God became fully present in human form.

“And in him you are made full.” Because the fullness of God dwells in Christ, and believers are in Christ, they share in that fullness. They are complete in Him. They do not lack anything they need for spiritual life and growth.

“Who is the head of all principality and power.” Christ rules over every spiritual power and authority. The false teachers may have suggested that believers needed to honor or appease these powers. Paul says Christ is their head. Believers who have Christ do not need to look to any other power.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse is one of the clearest statements of the full divinity of Christ in the New Testament. It goes beyond saying that Christ reveals God or represents God. It says that the full divine nature dwells in Him. Combined with the word “bodily,” it affirms that Jesus is both fully God and fully human, the truth the church later expressed in its creeds.

This truth answered the false teaching directly. Some thinkers of the time believed that God’s “fullness” was spread out among many spiritual beings, and that people needed to climb a ladder of spiritual experiences or intermediaries to reach God. Paul says no: all of God’s fullness is in Christ. There is no higher level to reach, no other mediator needed (*1 Timothy 2:5*).

“In him you are made full” is a great comfort. Believers are not spiritually second-class or incomplete. They are not waiting for some extra experience or special knowledge to become truly spiritual. They have Christ, and in Him they have all they need. This does not mean they have reached maturity; growth continues. But they have the source of everything.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Many believers feel that something is missing in their spiritual lives. They may be tempted to chase new experiences, techniques, or teachings that promise to take them to a higher level. This verse assures them that in Christ, they are already complete. Growth comes not from looking elsewhere but from going deeper into Him.

This truth also brings freedom from fear. Christ is the head over every spiritual power. Believers do not need to fear unseen forces, curses, or spiritual threats. They belong to the one who rules over all.

Finally, this verse invites worship. In Jesus, the fullness of God has come near. To know Jesus is to know God.

### *Colossians 2:13–15* — Nailed to the Cross

> *“You were dead through your trespasses and the uncircumcision of your flesh. He made you alive together with him, having forgiven us all our trespasses, wiping out the handwriting in ordinances which was against us. He has taken it out of the way, nailing it to the cross. Having stripped the principalities and the powers, he made a show of them openly, triumphing over them in it.”*
>
> — *Colossians 2:13–15* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul describes what God has done for believers through Christ.

“You were dead through your trespasses and the uncircumcision of your flesh.” Before Christ, the Colossians, mostly Gentiles, were spiritually dead and outside God’s covenant people.

“He made you alive together with him, having forgiven us all our trespasses.” God gave them new life together with Christ and forgave all their sins. Notice Paul’s shift from “you” to “us”: he includes himself among the forgiven.

Verse 14: “wiping out the handwriting in ordinances which was against us.” The “handwriting” was a term for a handwritten certificate of debt, like an IOU. Humanity owed God a debt of obedience that it could not pay. The record of that debt, with its legal demands, stood against us. God wiped it out. “He has taken it out of the way, nailing it to the cross.” When Jesus was crucified, the charge against Him was nailed to the cross above His head (*John 19:19*). Paul pictures God nailing humanity’s record of debt to the cross. Christ paid it in full.

Verse 15: “Having stripped the principalities and the powers, he made a show of them openly, triumphing over them in it.” The spiritual powers that held humanity captive were disarmed. The image is of a Roman triumphal procession, in which a victorious general paraded defeated enemies through the streets, stripped of their weapons. The cross, which looked like Christ’s defeat, was actually His victory over every hostile power.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show the cross from two angles. First, it is the place of forgiveness. The debt of sin has been canceled completely. There is no record left against those who are in Christ (*Romans 8:1*). Second, it is the place of victory. The powers of evil, which used sin and accusation to hold people captive, have been disarmed and defeated.

The two are connected. The spiritual powers’ main weapon against humanity is accusation: pointing to the record of sin. When that record is canceled, the powers lose their grip. *Revelation 12:10–11* describes Satan as “*the accuser of our brothers*” (*Revelation 12:10*), who is overcome “*because of the Lamb’s blood*” (*Revelation 12:11*).

This passage directly addresses the fear of spiritual powers that may have troubled the Colossians. They did not need to appease or worship angels or other spiritual beings. Those powers had already been publicly defeated by Christ at the cross.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Many believers live under a sense of unpaid debt, feeling they must somehow make up for their failures. This passage declares that the debt has been canceled and nailed to the cross. Nothing remains to be paid. Believers can live in the freedom of complete forgiveness.

When feelings of accusation or condemnation arise, whether from one’s own conscience, from others, or from the enemy, believers can remember the cross. The record has been wiped out. That does not mean ignoring wrongdoing or the need to make things right with people who have been harmed, but it does mean that guilt before God has been fully dealt with.

This passage also brings courage. Whatever spiritual opposition believers face, Christ has already triumphed. They stand in His victory.

### *Colossians 2:16–17* — The Shadow and the Substance

> *“Let no one therefore judge you in eating or drinking, or with respect to a feast day or a new moon or a Sabbath day, which are a shadow of the things to come; but the body is Christ’s.”*
>
> — *Colossians 2:16–17* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul draws a practical conclusion. “Let no one therefore judge you in eating or drinking, or with respect to a feast day or a new moon or a Sabbath day.” The false teachers were pressuring the Colossians to follow food laws and to observe the Jewish religious calendar, including annual festivals, monthly new moon celebrations, and the weekly Sabbath, as requirements for spiritual maturity. Paul says believers should not let anyone condemn them for not keeping these practices.

Verse 17 explains why: “which are a shadow of the things to come; but the body is Christ’s.” A shadow is cast by a real object. It has an outline of the real thing but no substance of its own. The Old Testament food laws and festivals were shadows that pointed forward to Christ. Now that the reality has come, believers do not need to cling to the shadows as a means of standing with God.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The idea of shadow and reality appears also in *Hebrews 8:5* and *10:1*, which describe the Old Testament priesthood and sacrifices as shadows of heavenly realities fulfilled in Christ. The Passover pointed to Christ, our Passover Lamb (*1 Corinthians 5:7*). The Sabbath rest pointed to the true rest found in Him (*Matthew 11:28*; *Hebrews 4:9–10*). The food laws pointed to the holiness that Christ provides.

Christians hold different views about the Sabbath today. Some believe the Sabbath principle continues, observed on Sunday as the Lord’s Day in honor of the resurrection. Others believe a weekly day of rest is a wise practice but not a binding law. Others keep the seventh-day Sabbath as an act of faithfulness. Paul’s point in this passage is not to forbid observing special days, which he allows elsewhere (*Romans 14:5–6*), but to forbid anyone from judging others or making these observances requirements for being right with God or spiritually mature.

The key phrase is “the body is Christ’s,” meaning the substance, the reality, belongs to Christ. Everything the shadows pointed to is fulfilled in Him.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers today may face pressure to follow rules that are not required by the gospel: particular diets, religious observances, styles of worship, or spiritual disciplines presented as necessary for real Christianity. This passage frees believers from being judged by such standards. Their standing with God rests on Christ alone.

At the same time, believers are free to practice disciplines and observances that help them grow, such as setting aside a day for rest and worship, fasting, or following the church calendar, as long as they do not treat these as requirements for God’s acceptance or use them to judge others.

The image of shadow and substance also invites believers to read the Old Testament with fresh eyes, seeing how its laws, festivals, and sacrifices point to Christ. Every shadow finds its substance in Him.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Colossians 2* calls believers to find their completeness in Christ alone. All the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in Him. All the fullness of God dwells in Him bodily. And in Him, believers have been made full. They do not need to add special knowledge, rituals, rules, or spiritual experiences to become complete.

The way forward in the Christian life is the same as the way it began. As believers received Christ Jesus the Lord, so they are to walk in Him, rooted and built up in Him, established in the faith, and overflowing with thanksgiving. Deep roots in Christ provide stability when new teachings and spiritual fads come along promising something more.

This chapter also celebrates the completeness of Christ’s work on the cross. Believers have been spiritually circumcised, buried and raised with Christ, made alive, and forgiven. The record of debt against them has been wiped out and nailed to the cross. The spiritual powers have been disarmed and publicly defeated. Believers can live free from guilt, accusation, and fear.

Finally, Paul warns against those who would judge believers by food laws, festivals, or harsh disciplines, or who claim spiritual superiority through visions and angel worship. These things are shadows, and the substance is Christ. Human rules may look wise, but they have no power to change the heart. True growth comes only from holding fast to Christ, the Head, from whom the whole body is nourished and grows with the growth that God gives.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in You, and all the fullness of God dwells in You bodily. Thank You that in You I have been made complete. As I received You as Lord, help me to walk in You day by day, rooted and built up in You, established in the faith, and overflowing with thanksgiving. Guard me from empty philosophy and deceptive teaching that would draw me away from You. Thank You that I was buried with You and raised with You, that You made me alive and forgave all my sins, and that You canceled the record of debt against me by nailing it to the cross. Thank You for triumphing over every power of darkness. Free me from the judgments of others and from rules that cannot change my heart. Help me to hold fast to You, my Head, and to grow with the growth that comes from God. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
