Colossians · Chapter 3 of 4

# Colossians — Chapter 3

Chapter Theme: Set Your Minds on Things Above

[Read Colossians 3 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/COL03.htm)

Main Teaching

Since believers have been raised with Christ, Paul calls them to seek and set their minds on the things above, where Christ is seated, because their life is hidden with Christ in God and they will appear with Him in glory. They are to put to death the earthly ways of sexual immorality, impurity, evil desire, and greed, and to put away anger, malice, slander, and lies, because they have put off the old self and put on the new self, renewed in the image of its Creator, in whom ethnic and social divisions lose their power, for Christ is all and in all. As God’s chosen and beloved people, they are to clothe themselves with compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, patience, forgiveness, and above all love, letting Christ’s peace rule and His word dwell richly among them, and doing everything in the name of the Lord Jesus with thanksgiving. Paul then applies this new life to households and to work, calling all to serve the Lord Christ.

## Chapter Background and Story

In chapter 2, Paul warned the Colossians against teachers who promoted rules and rituals as the path to spiritual maturity: “*Don’t handle, nor taste, nor touch*” (*Colossians 2:21*). Paul said these regulations look wise but have no power to restrain sinful desires (*2:23*). That raises a natural question: If rules cannot transform the heart, what can?

Chapter 3 answers that question. The power for holy living comes not from human rules but from union with Christ. Believers have died with Christ and been raised with Him. Their life is now bound up with His. As they set their minds on Christ, they are empowered to put off the old way of life and put on the new.

This chapter closely parallels *Ephesians 4–6*, which was likely written at about the same time. Both letters describe putting off the old self and putting on the new, the importance of worship and thanksgiving, and the shape of Christian households. Colossians expresses many of these truths in a shorter, more compact form.

### Seek the Things Above (*3:1–4*)

The call to seek and set the mind on things above is studied below. “*When Christ, our life, is revealed, then you will also be revealed with him in glory*” (*v. 4*). Christ is not merely part of believers’ lives; He is their life. Right now, their true life is hidden. But when Christ returns, it will be revealed, and they will share His glory.

### Put to Death and Put Away (*3:5–11*)

“*Put to death therefore your members which are on the earth: sexual immorality, uncleanness, depraved passion, evil desire, and covetousness, which is idolatry*” (*v. 5*). “Members which are on the earth” refers to the parts of the old nature still at work in believers. Paul uses strong language: “put to death.” These are not habits to be managed but sins to be killed. The list moves from outward acts to inner desires. As in *Ephesians 5:5*, greed is called idolatry because it makes things into a god.

“*For these things’ sake the wrath of God comes on the children of disobedience*” (*v. 6*). “*You also once walked in those, when you lived in them*” (*v. 7*). The Colossians had once lived this way, but no longer.

“*but now you must put them all away: anger, wrath, malice, slander, and shameful speaking out of your mouth*” (*v. 8*). The second list focuses on sins of the temper and tongue, those that destroy relationships. “Put away” uses the image of taking off dirty clothes.

“*Don’t lie to one another, seeing that you have put off the old man with his doings*” (*v. 9*), “*and have put on the new man, who is being renewed in knowledge after the image of his Creator*” (*v. 10*). Here Paul says believers have already put off the old self and put on the new, decisively at conversion. Now they are to live in line with what is already true. The new self is “being renewed,” an ongoing process of becoming more like Christ, who is the image of God (*Colossians 1:15*). God is restoring in believers the image that sin had damaged (*Genesis 1:26–27*).

“*where there can’t be Greek and Jew, circumcision and uncircumcision, barbarian, Scythian, bondservant, or free person; but Christ is all, and in all*” (*v. 11*). In the new humanity, the divisions of the old world lose their power. “Greek and Jew” was a religious and ethnic divide. “Barbarian” was a Greek term for anyone who did not speak Greek. “Scythian” referred to people from the region north of the Black Sea, regarded by Greeks and Romans as the most uncivilized of all. “Bondservant or free person” was the deepest social divide. In Christ, none of these labels determines a person’s worth or standing. Christ is everything, and He lives in all His people equally.

### Put On the New Clothing (*3:12–17*)

The qualities believers are to put on, the role of peace and the word of Christ, and the call to do all in Jesus’ name are studied below.

### Christian Households (*3:18–4*:1)

“*Wives, be in subjection to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord*” (*v. 18*). “*Husbands, love your wives, and don’t be bitter against them*” (*v. 19*). This is a shorter version of Paul’s teaching in *Ephesians 5:22–33*, which is discussed more fully there. “As is fitting in the Lord” places the wife’s response within her relationship with Christ, which means it can never require her to sin or to endure abuse. Husbands are commanded to love their wives and not to be harsh or bitter toward them. In a culture where husbands held great power, this was a significant limit on that power. Christians hold different views on the roles of husbands and wives, but all agree that marriage must be marked by love, respect, and safety, never by control or harm.

“*Children, obey your parents in all things, for this pleases the Lord*” (*v. 20*). “*Fathers, don’t provoke your children, so that they won’t be discouraged*” (*v. 21*). As in *Ephesians 6:1–4*, children are addressed as members of the church, and fathers are warned against harshness that crushes a child’s spirit. “In all things” assumes parents who are guiding their children in the Lord; it never requires a child to do wrong or to submit to abuse.

“*Servants, obey in all things those who are your masters according to the flesh, not just when they are looking, as men pleasers, but in singleness of heart, fearing God*” (*v. 22*). As in *Ephesians 6:5–9*, Paul addresses believers living within the Roman system of slavery. This passage does not endorse slavery as God’s design; the principles behind the gospel, including the equality of all in Christ that Paul has just declared in verse 11, eventually led many Christians to oppose slavery. Paul’s words are pastoral guidance for those living within a system they could not change. Their lasting principle for work is studied below. “*But he who does wrong will receive again for the wrong that he has done, and there is no partiality*” (*v. 25*). God judges impartially. This warning applies to both slaves and masters, as *Colossians 4:1* shows.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Colossians 3:1–3* — Your Life Is Hidden with Christ in God

> *“If then you were raised together with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated on the right hand of God. Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth. For you died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.”*
>
> — *Colossians 3:1–3* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“If then you were raised together with Christ.” The “if” means “since.” Believers have been united with Christ in His resurrection (*Colossians 2:12*). This is not a future hope only; it is already true in a spiritual sense.

“Seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated on the right hand of God.” Since believers have been raised with Christ, they should pursue the things of His kingdom. “Seated on the right hand of God” describes Christ’s position of supreme authority (*Psalm 110:1*). The things “above” are the realities of His kingdom: His righteousness, His love, His purposes.

“Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth.” This goes deeper than seeking; it concerns the whole direction of one’s thinking. “Things that are on the earth” does not mean the physical world is evil. It means the values and pursuits of life apart from God, such as the sinful desires listed in verse 5, or the human regulations criticized in chapter 2.

“For you died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.” Believers died with Christ to their old way of life. Their new life is now “hidden with Christ in God.” “Hidden” means both secure and not yet fully visible. Their life is kept safe in God, where no one can take it. And its full glory is not yet seen; it will be revealed when Christ returns (v4).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses describe the foundation of Christian ethics. Believers are not trying to become new people through their own efforts. They already are new people, raised with Christ. Their task is to live out who they already are. This is why rules alone cannot produce holiness: holiness flows from identity, from union with the risen Christ.

Setting the mind on things above is not escapism. It does not mean ignoring earthly responsibilities or the needs of the world. In fact, the rest of the chapter shows that a heavenly mind leads to very practical, earthly changes: kindness, forgiveness, faithful work, and loving relationships. Those whose minds are set on Christ become more useful on earth, not less.

The phrase “your life is hidden with Christ in God” is deeply comforting. A believer’s true life cannot be destroyed by suffering, failure, loss, or even death. It is safe with Christ, held in God Himself. Jesus said that no one can snatch His sheep out of His hand or the Father’s hand (*John 10:28–29*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Every day, believers’ minds are pulled toward many concerns: work, money, relationships, news, entertainment, and worries. These verses invite them to deliberately turn their minds toward Christ and His kingdom. This might involve beginning the day with prayer and Scripture, pausing during the day to remember Christ’s presence, and evaluating priorities in light of eternity.

When believers feel insecure, these verses remind them that their life is hidden with Christ in God. Their identity and future are secure in Him, regardless of what happens on earth.

Setting the mind on things above also helps in moments of temptation. When the pull of old desires is strong, remembering that one has died and been raised with Christ can bring strength to choose differently.

### *Colossians 3:12–14* — Clothed with Compassion and Love

> *“Put on therefore, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, a heart of compassion, kindness, lowliness, humility, and perseverance; bearing with one another, and forgiving each other, if any man has a complaint against any; even as Christ forgave you, so you also do. Above all these things, walk in love, which is the bond of perfection.”*
>
> — *Colossians 3:12–14* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Having described what to “put away,” Paul now describes what to “put on.” He begins with believers’ identity: “as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved.” These three titles were once used for Israel (*Deuteronomy 7:6–8*). Now they belong to all who are in Christ, Jew and Gentile. Believers are chosen by God, set apart for Him, and deeply loved. Their new behavior flows from this identity.

Paul lists qualities to “put on,” like clothing. “A heart of compassion”: deep, heartfelt mercy for others. “Kindness”: goodness shown in practical ways. “Lowliness” or humility: not thinking too highly of oneself. “Humility,” which may also be translated “gentleness” or “meekness”: a gentle, considerate spirit. “Perseverance” or patience: enduring others’ faults without anger.

Verse 13 describes how these qualities work in practice: “bearing with one another, and forgiving each other, if any man has a complaint against any; even as Christ forgave you, so you also do.” Believers will have complaints against one another. Paul does not pretend otherwise. But they are called to bear with each other’s weaknesses and to forgive, following Christ’s example.

Verse 14: “Above all these things, walk in love, which is the bond of perfection.” Love is like the outer garment or belt that holds all the others together. It is “the bond of perfection,” the tie that binds everything into complete unity.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These qualities are the character of Christ Himself. He was compassionate toward the suffering, kind to the outcast, humble and gentle in heart, and patient with His slow-to-learn disciples. When believers put on these qualities, they are putting on Christ (*Romans 13:14*; *Galatians 3:27*).

The command to forgive “even as Christ forgave you” sets the measure for forgiveness. Christ forgave completely, freely, and at great cost. Believers who have received such forgiveness are called to extend it to others. As discussed in *Ephesians 4:32*, forgiveness does not mean excusing wrongdoing, immediately restoring trust, or remaining in danger. It means releasing the desire for revenge and entrusting justice to God, while still seeking safety and accountability where needed.

Love as “the bond of perfection” echoes *1 Corinthians 13*, where Paul says that without love, even the greatest gifts are nothing. Love is not just one virtue among many; it is the one that unites all the others and makes them complete.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

The image of putting on clothing suggests a daily choice. Each morning, believers can ask God to help them clothe themselves with compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience for the day ahead.

These qualities are especially tested in close relationships, where complaints and irritations naturally arise. Believers can practice bearing with others’ quirks and weaknesses, letting go of minor offenses, and forgiving more serious ones, remembering how much Christ has forgiven them.

When forgiveness feels hard, believers can begin by praying for the person who hurt them, asking God for help, and seeking wise counsel. Forgiveness is often a process, and God’s grace is sufficient for each step.

### *Colossians 3:15–16* — The Peace and Word of Christ

> *“And let the peace of God rule in your hearts, to which also you were called in one body, and be thankful. Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly; in all wisdom teaching and admonishing one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your heart to the Lord.”*
>
> — *Colossians 3:15–16* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“And let the peace of God rule in your hearts.” The word “rule” was used of an umpire in athletic contests, the one who made decisions and settled disputes. Paul pictures God’s peace acting as the umpire in believers’ hearts, guiding decisions and settling conflicts. Some manuscripts read “the peace of Christ.”

“To which also you were called in one body.” This peace is not only personal but communal. Believers were called into one body, the church, and peace is meant to govern their relationships with one another.

“And be thankful.” Again, Paul emphasizes thanksgiving.

Verse 16: “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly.” “The word of Christ” may mean the message about Christ, the gospel, or Christ’s own teaching. It is to “dwell” in believers, to live there, to be at home, and to do so “richly,” abundantly.

“In all wisdom teaching and admonishing one another.” When Christ’s word dwells richly in believers, they are able to teach and encourage one another, and to warn and correct one another, with wisdom.

“With psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your heart to the Lord.” Worship through song is one way the word of Christ dwells in believers and is shared among them. Singing teaches, encourages, and expresses gratitude. “With grace in your heart” can also mean “with thankfulness in your hearts.”

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses describe a community shaped by Christ. His peace governs their relationships, His word fills their hearts, and their worship overflows in song and thanksgiving. This is a picture of a healthy church.

The parallel passage in *Ephesians 5:18–19* says that being “*filled with the Spirit*” (*Ephesians 5:18*) leads to speaking to one another in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs. Here, letting the word of Christ dwell richly produces the same result. The Spirit and the word work together. The Spirit fills believers as they are saturated in Christ’s word.

Singing has always been central to the worship of God’s people. Israel sang the Psalms; the early church sang hymns about Christ (perhaps including *Colossians 1:15–20* and *Philippians 2:6–11*). Songs carry truth into the heart and memory in a way that teaching alone sometimes cannot.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

When facing decisions or conflicts, believers can ask whether a choice leads toward the peace of Christ. Sometimes a lack of peace signals that something needs to be reconsidered. This is not merely a feeling, but a discernment grounded in Scripture and prayer.

Letting the word of Christ dwell richly involves regular, deep engagement with Scripture: reading, studying, memorizing, and meditating on it. As it fills the heart, it shapes thinking, speech, and relationships.

Believers can also make singing part of their spiritual life, both in church and in private. Songs of worship can teach, comfort, and strengthen faith. Encouraging one another through words of Scripture and songs of praise builds up the whole community.

### *Colossians 3:23–24* — Work Heartily as for the Lord

> *“And whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the reward of the inheritance; for you serve the Lord Christ.”*
>
> — *Colossians 3:23–24* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul’s words here were addressed first to enslaved believers, whose work was often unrewarded and unnoticed. But the principle applies to all believers in every kind of work. “And whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men.”

“Whatever you do” covers every kind of work: paid or unpaid, important or ordinary, seen or unseen. “Work heartily” means wholeheartedly, with energy and sincerity, from the soul. “As for the Lord and not for men.” The ultimate audience of a believer’s work is the Lord. Even when human supervisors are unfair or unappreciative, believers can work as an offering to Christ.

Verse 24 gives the motivation: “knowing that from the Lord you will receive the reward of the inheritance; for you serve the Lord Christ.” Enslaved people in the Roman world could not legally inherit property. Paul tells them that they will receive an inheritance from the Lord. Their faithful work is seen by God and will be rewarded. “For you serve the Lord Christ”: whatever their earthly status, their true Master is Christ.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This passage transforms the meaning of work. In the ancient world, manual labor was often looked down upon, especially by the wealthy. Paul declares that all work done for Christ has dignity and eternal significance. Cooking, cleaning, building, farming, caring for children, managing accounts: all can be done as service to the Lord.

This passage also brings justice into view. Verse 25 warns that wrongdoers will be repaid, and *Colossians 4:1* commands masters to treat their servants justly and fairly, knowing that they too have a Master in heaven. Paul does not ask the oppressed to work faithfully while ignoring the sins of the oppressor. God sees both, and He judges impartially.

Working “as for the Lord” does not mean accepting exploitation as God’s will. Believers may seek fair treatment, better conditions, and justice in the workplace. But whatever their circumstances, they can find dignity and purpose in offering their work to Christ.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Many people find their work tedious, unappreciated, or frustrating. These verses offer a new perspective: every task can be an act of worship. Believers can work with excellence and integrity, not to impress others, but to honor Christ.

This truth also brings freedom from the need for recognition. When work goes unnoticed by others, believers can remember that the Lord sees and will reward faithful service.

For those in positions of authority, these verses and the following verse call for fair and just treatment of those who work for them. Employers, managers, and leaders answer to Christ for how they treat others.

Finally, this passage encourages believers who do unpaid work, such as caring for family members, volunteering, or serving in church, that their labor matters deeply to God.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Colossians 3* reveals the true source of holy living: union with the risen Christ. Rules and rituals cannot change the heart, but believers who have died and been raised with Christ have a new life. That life is hidden with Christ in God, secure and safe, and it will be revealed in glory when He returns. Believers are called to seek the things above and to set their minds on Christ.

From that heavenly focus come very practical changes. Believers are to put to death sexual immorality, impurity, evil desire, and greed, and to put away anger, malice, slander, and lies. They have already put off the old self and put on the new, which is being renewed in the image of its Creator. In this new humanity, ethnic and social divisions lose their power, for Christ is all and in all.

As God’s chosen, holy, and beloved people, believers are to clothe themselves with compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience, bearing with one another and forgiving as Christ forgave them. Above all, they are to put on love, which binds everything together. Christ’s peace is to rule their hearts, His word is to dwell in them richly, and their worship is to overflow in songs and thanksgiving. Whatever they do, in word or deed, they are to do it in the name of the Lord Jesus.

This new life reaches into homes and workplaces. Marriages are to be marked by love and respect, never by harshness or harm. Parents are to raise children without provoking them. And in every kind of work, believers can work wholeheartedly as for the Lord, knowing that He sees, He rewards, and He judges with perfect fairness. All of life becomes worship when it is offered to Christ.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You that I have been raised with You and that my life is hidden with You in God. Help me to seek the things above and set my mind on You. Give me grace to put to death what belongs to my old life and to put away anger, malice, slander, and lies. Thank You that I am being renewed in Your image, and that in You there are no divisions that separate Your people. As one chosen, holy, and beloved, help me to clothe myself with compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience. Teach me to bear with others and to forgive as You have forgiven me. Above all, fill me with love. Let Your peace rule in my heart and Your word dwell in me richly. Whatever I do today, in word or deed, let me do it in Your name, giving thanks to the Father through You. Help me to work heartily, as for You and not for others. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Colossians · Chapter 4 of 4

# Colossians — Chapter 4

Chapter Theme: Devoted to Prayer and Gracious in Speech

[Read Colossians 4 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/COL04.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul completes his household teaching by calling masters to treat their servants justly and fairly, remembering that they too have a Master in heaven. He urges the Colossians to devote themselves to prayer with watchfulness and thanksgiving, asking God to open doors for the gospel. They are to act wisely toward outsiders, making the most of every opportunity, and to let their speech always be gracious and seasoned with salt. Paul closes with greetings from a remarkable group of coworkers, including Tychicus, Onesimus, Aristarchus, Mark, Luke, and Epaphras, who wrestles in prayer for the Colossians to stand mature and fully assured in God’s will. He sends greetings to Laodicea, gives a charge to Archippus, and signs the letter in his own hand, asking them to remember his chains.

## Chapter Background and Story

The final chapter of Colossians moves from instructions about relationships inside the Christian household to relationships with the wider world, and then to personal greetings that reveal the network of believers who worked alongside Paul.

The list of names at the end is easy to skip, but it is full of stories. Several of these people appear elsewhere in the New Testament. Onesimus is the runaway slave whose story is told in the letter to Philemon, written at the same time. Mark is the young man who once abandoned Paul and Barnabas but was later restored to ministry. Luke is the physician who wrote the Gospel of Luke and Acts. Demas would later desert Paul (*2 Timothy 4:10*). These names remind readers that the gospel spread through real people with real histories, strengths, and failures.

### Masters and Servants (*4:1*)

Paul’s instruction to masters completes the household section and is studied below.

### Devoted to Prayer (*4:2–4*)

The call to steadfast prayer is studied below.

### Wise and Gracious Toward Outsiders (*4:5–6*)

Paul’s guidance for interacting with those outside the church is studied below.

### Tychicus and Onesimus (*4:7–9*)

“*All my affairs will be made known to you by Tychicus, the beloved brother, faithful servant, and fellow bondservant in the Lord*” (*v. 7*). Tychicus also carried the letter to the Ephesians (*Ephesians 6:21–22*). “*I am sending him to you for this very purpose, that he may know your circumstances and comfort your hearts*” (*v. 8*).

“*together with Onesimus, the faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you. They will make known to you everything that is going on here*” (*v. 9*). Onesimus was a slave who had run away from his master, Philemon, a member of the Colossian church. While away, he met Paul and became a believer. Now Paul was sending him back, carrying the letter to Philemon in which Paul asked Philemon to receive him “*no longer as a slave, but more than a slave, a beloved brother*” (*Philemon 1:16*). Notice how Paul describes Onesimus here: not as a runaway, but as “the faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you.” The gospel had transformed both his life and his standing.

### Greetings from Paul’s Companions (*4:10–14*)

“*Aristarchus, my fellow prisoner, greets you, and Mark the cousin of Barnabas (concerning whom you received instructions, “if he comes to you, receive him”)*” (*v. 10*). Aristarchus was from Thessalonica and had traveled with Paul through dangerous times, including the riot in Ephesus and the voyage to Rome (*Acts 19:29*; *27:2*). Mark had once left Paul and Barnabas partway through their first missionary journey (*Acts 13:13*). Paul later refused to take him on the second journey, which led to a sharp disagreement with Barnabas (*Acts 15:37–39*). Now Mark is with Paul again and commended to the churches. Later, Paul would write that Mark was “*useful to me for service*” (*2 Timothy 4:11*). Mark’s story is one of failure followed by restoration.

“*and Jesus who is called Justus. These are my only fellow workers for God’s Kingdom who are of the circumcision, men who have been a comfort to me*” (*v. 11*). “Jesus” was a common Jewish name (the Greek form of Joshua). These three were Jewish believers who worked with Paul. Their loyalty was a great comfort to him.

Epaphras’s prayer ministry is noted in verses 12–13 and reflected in the study of prayer below. “*For I testify about him that he has great zeal for you, and for those in Laodicea, and for those in Hierapolis*” (*v. 13*). These three cities were close neighbors in the Lycus valley.

“*Luke the beloved physician and Demas greet you*” (*v. 14*). This verse tells us that Luke was a doctor. Since he is not among those “of the circumcision” (v11), he was likely a Gentile, making him the only Gentile author of a New Testament book. Demas is mentioned without comment. Sadly, he would later abandon Paul, “*having loved this present world*” (*2 Timothy 4:10*).

### Greetings and Instructions (*4:15–18*)

“*Greet the brothers who are in Laodicea, with Nymphas and the assembly that is in his house*” (*v. 15*). Early churches met in homes. Some ancient manuscripts read “Nympha” and “her house,” indicating a woman who hosted a church, much as Lydia did in Philippi (*Acts 16:15*, 40). Women who hosted churches in their homes likely played significant roles in their communities.

“*When this letter has been read among you, cause it to be read also in the assembly of the Laodiceans, and that you also read the letter from Laodicea*” (*v. 16*). Paul’s letters were meant to be read aloud in church gatherings and shared with other churches. “The letter from Laodicea” may be a letter Paul wrote to Laodicea that has not survived, or it may be the letter we know as Ephesians, if that letter circulated among the churches of the region.

“*Tell Archippus, “Take heed to the ministry which you have received in the Lord, that you fulfill it.”*” (*v. 17*) Archippus is also mentioned in *Philemon 1:2*, perhaps as a member of Philemon’s household. He had received a ministry from the Lord, and Paul publicly encourages him to complete it.

“*I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand. Remember my chains. Grace be with you. Amen*” (*v. 18*). Paul takes the pen from his secretary and signs the letter himself. As he writes, his hand may have been weighed down by the chain. “Remember my chains” is both a request for prayer and a reminder of the cost of the gospel. And his final word, as always, is grace.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Colossians 4:1* — Masters, Treat Others Justly

> *“Masters, give to your servants that which is just and equal, knowing that you also have a Master in heaven.”*
>
> — *Colossians 4:1* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse completes Paul’s teaching on households, which began in *Colossians 3:18*. Having addressed servants, Paul now addresses masters. “Masters, give to your servants that which is just and equal.”

“Just” means right and fair. “Equal” can mean fair or equitable, and it may even suggest treating servants as equals in some sense. In the Roman world, slaves had almost no legal rights, and masters could treat them however they wished. Paul places a moral obligation on masters to treat their servants with justice and fairness.

The reason: “knowing that you also have a Master in heaven.” Masters were not ultimately in charge. They too were servants of a higher Master, the Lord Jesus Christ. They would answer to Him for how they treated those under their authority. This places masters and servants on the same level before God.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows how the gospel begins to undermine unjust structures from within. Paul did not have the power to abolish Roman slavery, but he set principles in motion that would challenge it. If masters must treat slaves justly and fairly, if both are brothers in Christ (*Philemon 1:16*), if in Christ there is neither slave nor free (*Colossians 3:11*), then the very foundations of slavery are called into question. Over centuries, Christians drew on these truths in the fight to end slavery, even as others tragically misused Scripture to defend it.

The principle behind this verse applies to all relationships of power. Those who have authority, whether employers, managers, government officials, parents, teachers, or church leaders, are accountable to God for how they use it. God sees, and He judges impartially (*Colossians 3:25*). Authority is a stewardship, not a license for exploitation.

This verse also reflects the character of God, who is just and who defends the oppressed. The Old Testament repeatedly commands fair treatment of workers, such as paying wages promptly (*Deuteronomy 24:14–15*), and the prophets condemned those who exploited laborers (*Jeremiah 22:13*). James warns that the wages withheld from workers cry out to God (*James 5:4*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Employers, supervisors, and anyone with authority over others can ask whether they are treating people “justly and fairly.” This includes fair wages, safe working conditions, honest communication, respect, and freedom from abuse or harassment.

This verse also offers hope to those who are treated unjustly. God sees, and every person with power answers to a Master in heaven. Believers who face unfair treatment at work may pursue justice through appropriate means, trusting that God cares about their situation.

Finally, this verse reminds all believers that whatever authority they hold, they hold it under Christ. Remembering that they too have a Master can keep them humble, fair, and kind.

### *Colossians 4:2–4* — Continue Steadfastly in Prayer

> *“Continue steadfastly in prayer, watching in it with thanksgiving, praying together for us also, that God may open to us a door for the word, to speak the mystery of Christ, for which I am also in bonds, that I may reveal it as I ought to speak.”*
>
> — *Colossians 4:2–4* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“Continue steadfastly in prayer.” The word means to persist, to be devoted to, to hold fast. Prayer is not an occasional activity but a constant commitment.

“Watching in it with thanksgiving.” “Watching” means being alert and attentive, like a guard on duty. Jesus told His disciples to watch and pray (*Mark 14:38*). Believers are to pray with their eyes open, aware of spiritual realities and of the needs around them. And their prayers are to be filled with thanksgiving, as thankfulness runs throughout Colossians.

Verse 3: “praying together for us also, that God may open to us a door for the word, to speak the mystery of Christ, for which I am also in bonds.” Paul asks for prayer, but not for release from prison. He asks for open doors to share the gospel. “The mystery of Christ” is the gospel now revealed, that Christ dwells in His people, including Gentiles (*Colossians 1:27*). Paul was in chains because he proclaimed it.

Verse 4: “that I may reveal it as I ought to speak.” Paul asks for clarity, to be able to explain the gospel well.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Paul’s request shows his priorities. Though in chains, his greatest concern was the spread of the gospel. He believed that God opens doors for the message, and that prayer is part of how those doors open. Elsewhere he speaks of “a great and effective door” opened for him (*1 Corinthians 16:9*) and of a door opened by the Lord (*2 Corinthians 2:12*).

The combination of persistence, watchfulness, and thanksgiving forms a healthy pattern for prayer. Persistence keeps believers praying even when answers are slow. Watchfulness keeps them spiritually alert. Thanksgiving keeps them aware of God’s goodness and guards against discouragement.

Paul’s humility is also evident. He, the great apostle, asks the Colossians to pray for him. Every believer, no matter how mature or gifted, needs the prayers of others. Prayer binds believers together in a shared mission.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses invite believers to make prayer a regular, devoted part of life, not only in times of crisis. Setting aside time each day for prayer, praying throughout the day, and joining with others in prayer all help build a steadfast prayer life.

Believers can also pray specifically for open doors for the gospel: for opportunities to share their faith with friends, neighbors, and coworkers, and for missionaries and church leaders around the world. They can pray for clarity and boldness for those who teach and preach.

Thanksgiving can transform prayer. Beginning or ending prayer by thanking God for specific blessings keeps the heart grateful and hopeful.

### *Colossians 4:5–6* — Wisdom and Gracious Speech Toward Outsiders

> *“Walk in wisdom toward those who are outside, redeeming the time. Let your speech always be with grace, seasoned with salt, that you may know how you ought to answer each one.”*
>
> — *Colossians 4:5–6* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul turns to how believers should relate to people outside the church. “Walk in wisdom toward those who are outside.” Believers should live wisely in front of those who do not share their faith, aware that their conduct reflects on Christ.

“Redeeming the time.” As in *Ephesians 5:16*, this means making the most of every opportunity. Believers should be alert to chances to show kindness, demonstrate integrity, and share their faith.

Verse 6: “Let your speech always be with grace, seasoned with salt.” “With grace” means gracious, kind, pleasant, and filled with God’s grace. “Seasoned with salt” means flavorful, interesting, and wholesome. In the ancient world, salt preserved food and enhanced its taste. Believers’ words should be engaging and beneficial, not bland, harsh, or corrupt.

“That you may know how you ought to answer each one.” Every person is different, with different questions, needs, and backgrounds. Gracious, thoughtful speech allows believers to respond appropriately to each individual.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses describe a winsome, thoughtful witness. Paul does not call believers to aggressive or argumentative evangelism, but to wise living and gracious speech. First Peter 3:15–16 gives similar counsel: always be ready to give an answer to anyone who asks about the hope within, but do so with gentleness and respect.

Jesus modeled this kind of engagement. He spoke differently to different people: gently to the woman at the well (*John 4*), boldly to the religious leaders, compassionately to the grieving, and thoughtfully to seekers like Nicodemus (*John 3*). He knew “*how you ought to answer each one*” (*v. 6*).

The image of salt also connects with Jesus’ teaching that His followers are “*the salt of the earth*” (*Matthew 5:13*). Their presence and words should preserve what is good and add the flavor of God’s kingdom to the world around them.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers interact with people outside the church every day: at work, at school, in their neighborhoods, and online. These verses invite them to consider how their conduct and words reflect Christ. Are they honest, kind, and trustworthy? Do their words build up or tear down?

Online conversations especially can become harsh and divisive. Gracious speech means engaging respectfully even with those who disagree, listening well, and speaking truth with kindness.

Believers can also prepare to share their faith thoughtfully. That might mean learning to explain the gospel clearly, listening carefully to others’ questions, and responding with humility rather than having a rehearsed speech for everyone. Wisdom and grace open doors that arguments often close.

### *Colossians 4:12* — Wrestling in Prayer

> *“Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ, salutes you, always striving for you in his prayers, that you may stand perfect and complete in all the will of God.”*
>
> — *Colossians 4:12* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul sends greetings from Epaphras, the founder of the Colossian church. “Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ.” Epaphras was from Colossae. Paul calls him a servant, or slave, of Christ, a title Paul usually used for himself and Timothy.

“Always striving for you in his prayers.” The word for “striving” comes from athletic contests and suggests intense effort, like a wrestler in a match. It is related to the English word “agonize.” Epaphras was not praying casually. He prayed with deep effort and earnestness.

What did he pray for? “That you may stand perfect and complete in all the will of God.” “Perfect” means mature. “Complete” means fully assured, convinced. Epaphras prayed that the Colossians would stand firm, grow to maturity, and be fully confident in God’s will, not swayed by false teaching.

Verse 13 adds that Epaphras had great zeal and concern not only for the Colossians but also for the believers in Laodicea and Hierapolis.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Epaphras is a model of pastoral prayer. Separated from his church by distance and perhaps by imprisonment (he is called Paul’s “fellow prisoner” in *Philemon 1:23*), he could not be present with them. But he could pray. And he prayed with intensity, persistence, and love.

His prayer echoes Paul’s prayers in this letter: that the Colossians would be filled with the knowledge of God’s will (*Colossians 1:9*), grow to maturity in Christ (*1:28*), and be established in the faith (*2:7*). Epaphras shared Paul’s goal for the church.

This verse shows that prayer is real work. Jesus Himself prayed with such intensity in Gethsemane that His sweat became like drops of blood (*Luke 22:44*). Prayer can be costly. It requires time, focus, and love. But it is one of the most powerful ways to serve others.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Many believers cannot be physically present with those they love: children who have moved away, friends in distant places, missionaries overseas, or believers in persecuted churches. Epaphras’s example shows that prayer bridges that distance. Believers can wrestle in prayer for those they love, asking God to help them stand firm and grow mature.

This verse also challenges believers to deepen their prayer lives. Prayer does not always feel easy or natural. Sometimes it requires effort and perseverance. Setting aside time, using Scripture as a guide, and praying for specific people and needs can help.

Finally, Epaphras’s prayers for the believers in Laodicea and Hierapolis show a heart that reached beyond his own congregation. Believers can pray not only for their own church but for other churches and believers in their region and around the world.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Colossians 4* brings the letter to a close with practical wisdom and a glimpse into the community that surrounded Paul. It begins by completing the household teaching: those with authority must treat others justly and fairly, remembering that they too answer to a Master in heaven. This principle applies to every relationship of power today, from the workplace to the home to the church. Authority is a stewardship, and God sees how it is used.

The chapter then calls believers to a life of steadfast prayer, marked by watchfulness and thanksgiving. Paul, though in chains, asked not for release but for open doors to share the gospel and for clarity to speak it well. Believers can pray the same way for themselves and for others who carry the gospel.

Paul also teaches believers how to relate to those outside the church: with wisdom in their conduct, making the most of every opportunity, and with speech that is gracious and seasoned with salt. A thoughtful, kind, engaging witness opens hearts more effectively than harsh argument.

Finally, the list of names at the end reminds believers that the gospel advances through ordinary people. Onesimus, a runaway slave, became a beloved brother. Mark, who once failed, was restored to useful service. Luke, a doctor, became a faithful companion and writer. Epaphras wrestled in prayer for his church. Demas, sadly, would later fall away. Each name is a reminder that God works through imperfect people, that failure need not be final, and that faithfulness to the end matters. Through it all, the final word is grace.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord, You are the Master over all. Help me to treat everyone under my care or authority with justice and fairness, remembering that I answer to You. Make me devoted to prayer, watchful and thankful. Open doors for the gospel in my life and in the lives of those who serve You around the world, and give clarity and boldness to all who proclaim Your word. Help me to walk wisely toward those who do not yet know You, making the most of every opportunity. Let my speech always be gracious and seasoned with salt, so that I may know how to answer each person. Thank You for the faithful believers who have gone before me and for the way You restore those who have failed. Teach me to wrestle in prayer for others, that they may stand mature and fully assured in Your will. Let Your grace be with me always. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Book 13 of 27

# 1 Thessalonians

## About This Letter

Thessalonica was the capital of the Roman province of Macedonia, a busy port city on the great Roman road called the Via Egnatia. Paul, Silas, and Timothy brought the gospel there around A.D. 49–50, soon after leaving Philippi. Some Jews and many God-fearing Greeks and prominent women believed. But opposition quickly rose, a mob attacked the house of a believer named Jason, and Paul and Silas had to leave the city by night after only a short stay (*Acts 17:1–10*).

Paul worried about the young church he had been forced to leave behind. From Athens he sent Timothy back to strengthen them, and when Timothy returned with good news of their faith and love, Paul wrote this letter, probably from Corinth around A.D. 50–51 (*1 Thessalonians 3:1–6*; *Acts 18:5*). Most scholars agree that it is one of Paul’s earliest letters, and perhaps the oldest book of the New Testament.

## The Shape of the Letter

In chapters 1–3, Paul gives thanks for the Thessalonians’ faith, love, and hope, recalls how they turned to God from idols, defends the sincerity and gentleness of his ministry among them, and shares his joy at Timothy’s report. In chapters 4–5, he gives instruction: to live in holiness and sexual purity, to love one another, to work quietly with their own hands, and to grieve with hope for believers who have died, because the Lord Himself will descend from heaven and the dead in Christ will rise. He reminds them that the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night, so they should live as children of light, and he closes with a series of short commands about church life, prayer, joy, and thanksgiving.

## Themes to Watch For

Watch for the triad of faith, love, and hope, the joy of believers who received the word in the midst of suffering, Paul’s model of gentle and sacrificial ministry, holiness as God’s will, brotherly love, the dignity of honest work, the hope of Christ’s return and the resurrection of the dead, readiness and watchfulness, encouragement of one another, and the call to rejoice always, pray without ceasing, and give thanks in everything. First Thessalonians shows the warm heart of a pastor for a young, persecuted church, and it offers lasting comfort to all who grieve.

## Chapters

3.  [1 Thessalonians 3](#c13_1TH_003.xhtml) — Standing Firm and Growing in Love
4.  [1 Thessalonians 4](#c13_1TH_004.xhtml) — Holy Living and the Hope of Resurrection

1 Thessalonians · Chapter 1 of 5

# 1 Thessalonians — Chapter 1

Chapter Theme: Faith, Love, and Hope That Others Can See

[Read 1 Thessalonians 1 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/1TH01.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul, Silas, and Timothy thank God for the Thessalonian believers, remembering their work produced by faith, their labor prompted by love, and their endurance inspired by hope in Christ. They are confident that God has chosen these believers, because the gospel came to them not only in words but with power, with the Holy Spirit, and with deep conviction. Though they received the message in the midst of severe suffering, they welcomed it with joy from the Holy Spirit and became an example to believers throughout Greece. Everyone was talking about how they turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God and to wait for His Son from heaven, Jesus, who rescues from the coming wrath.

## Chapter Background and Story

Paul’s time in Thessalonica had been short and stormy. *Acts 17* tells how he preached in the synagogue for three Sabbaths, explaining from the Scriptures that the Messiah had to suffer and rise from the dead and that Jesus is the Messiah. Some Jews were persuaded, along with a large number of God-fearing Greeks and many leading women. But jealous opponents formed a mob, dragged a believer named Jason before the city officials, and accused the missionaries as men who had “*turned the world upside down*” (*Acts 17:6*) and who proclaimed another king, Jesus (*Acts 17:7*). Paul and Silas left that night for Berea.

Paul was anxious about the new believers. They had received only a few weeks of teaching before he was forced to leave, and they were facing persecution from their own neighbors. He longed to go back but was prevented (*1 Thessalonians 2:17–18*). So he sent Timothy to check on them. When Timothy returned with good news, Paul was overjoyed, and he wrote this letter.

Chapter 1 is a thanksgiving overflowing with joy and encouragement. Paul wants the Thessalonians to know that their faith is genuine, that God is at work among them, and that their example is inspiring believers far beyond their city.

### Greeting (*1:1*)

“*Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, to the assembly of the Thessalonians in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ*” (*v. 1*). Silvanus is the Roman form of the name Silas, Paul’s companion on his second journey (*Acts 15:40*). Paul does not call himself an apostle here; he simply writes as one of three coworkers. The church is “in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.” Notice how naturally Paul places the Father and Jesus side by side as the source of the church’s life and of grace and peace. Even in this very early letter, Jesus is honored alongside God.

### Faith, Love, and Hope (*1:2–3*)

Paul’s thanksgiving for their faith, love, and hope is studied below.

### Chosen and Transformed (*1:4–7*)

“*We know, brothers loved by God, that you are chosen*” (*v. 4*). Paul is confident that the Thessalonians belong to God. The basis of his confidence is studied below.

“*You became imitators of us and of the Lord, having received the word in much affliction, with joy of the Holy Spirit*” (*v. 6*). The Thessalonians followed the example of the missionaries and of Jesus Himself. Like Jesus, they suffered for their faith. And yet they had joy, a joy given by the Holy Spirit that did not depend on circumstances.

“*so that you became an example to all who believe in Macedonia and in Achaia*” (*v. 7*). Macedonia was northern Greece; Achaia was southern Greece, including Corinth and Athens. This young church, only months old, had already become a model for other believers. The word “example” was used for a pattern or mold that shaped something else.

### A Faith That Spreads (*1:8–10*)

“*For from you the word of the Lord has been declared, not only in Macedonia and Achaia, but also in every place your faith toward God has gone out, so that we need not say anything*” (*v. 8*). “Has been declared” suggests a sound ringing out, like a trumpet blast or a thunderclap echoing across the hills. Thessalonica was on a major trade route, and travelers carried the news of the Thessalonians’ faith far and wide. Their conversion was the talk of the region. The content of that report, their turning from idols and their waiting for Christ, is studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *1 Thessalonians 1:3* — Work of Faith, Labor of Love, Perseverance of Hope

> *“remembering without ceasing your work of faith and labor of love and perseverance of hope in our Lord Jesus Christ, before our God and Father.”*
>
> — *1 Thessalonians 1:3* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

When Paul prayed for the Thessalonians, he remembered three things about them. Each is a pair: a visible action and its invisible source.

“Your work of faith.” Their faith was not just an idea; it produced action. Faith in Christ led them to do things they had never done before: turn from idols, gather with other believers, speak about Jesus, and live differently.

“Labor of love.” The word “labor” suggests hard, wearying toil. Their love was not merely a warm feeling. It worked hard for others, even when it was exhausting.

“Perseverance of hope in our Lord Jesus Christ.” Their hope in Christ, especially in His return (v10), gave them the strength to endure persecution and hardship. “Perseverance” means steadfast endurance, bearing up under pressure without giving up.

“Before our God and Father.” All of this was lived out in God’s presence and noticed by Him.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Faith, love, and hope appear together throughout Paul’s letters (*1 Corinthians 13:13*; *Colossians 1:4–5*; *1 Thessalonians 5:8*). They form a portrait of genuine Christian life. Faith looks to what God has done in Christ. Love reaches out to others in the present. Hope looks forward to what God will do when Christ returns. Together, they embrace past, present, and future.

This verse also shows the connection between inner reality and outward action. Faith produces work, love produces labor, and hope produces endurance. James makes a similar point: faith without works is dead (*James 2:17*). Genuine faith, love, and hope always show themselves in life.

Notice that hope is focused on “our Lord Jesus Christ.” Christian hope is not vague optimism. It is confident expectation rooted in a person: the risen Lord who will return. That hope gave the Thessalonians strength to endure suffering.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to consider how their faith, love, and hope show up in daily life. Faith might show in trusting God enough to obey Him in a difficult decision. Love might show in tiring, unglamorous service, such as caring for an aging parent, helping a struggling neighbor, or serving in a ministry that no one notices. Hope might show in steady endurance through illness, loss, or opposition.

It also encourages believers who feel worn out by serving others. Paul calls it a “labor” of love because it is hard. Such labor is not wasted; it is noticed by God.

Finally, this verse provides a pattern for encouraging others. Like Paul, believers can notice and thank God for the faith, love, and hope they see in fellow believers, and tell them so.

### *1 Thessalonians 1:5* — Not in Word Only, but in Power

> *“and that our Good News came to you not in word only, but also in power, and in the Holy Spirit and with much assurance. You know what kind of men we showed ourselves to be among you for your sake.”*
>
> — *1 Thessalonians 1:5* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul explains how he knows the Thessalonians are chosen by God. It is because of how the gospel came to them.

“Our Good News came to you not in word only.” The missionaries did speak words; they preached and taught. But the gospel was more than words.

“But also in power.” God’s power was at work. This may include miraculous signs, but it especially refers to the power of God changing hearts and lives. The gospel is “*the power of God for salvation*” (*Romans 1:16*).

“And in the Holy Spirit.” The Spirit was active, convicting hearts, opening eyes, and producing faith.

“And with much assurance.” This could refer to the deep conviction with which the missionaries preached, or to the full assurance the Thessalonians received when they believed. Both were true.

“You know what kind of men we showed ourselves to be among you for your sake.” The missionaries’ lives matched their message. Their character and conduct were part of their testimony. Paul will describe this in detail in chapter 2.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that genuine conversion is the work of God. The missionaries did not convert the Thessalonians through persuasive speech or clever techniques. The Holy Spirit worked through their words with power and conviction. Paul says something similar in *1 Corinthians 2:4–5*: his message was not with persuasive words of wisdom but with a demonstration of the Spirit and of power, so that faith would rest on God’s power, not human wisdom.

The connection between election (“you are chosen,” v4) and the gospel’s power is important. Paul did not have a secret list of the chosen. He recognized God’s choosing by its fruit: the Spirit’s power in their conversion and their transformed lives (vv6–10). Election is not a cold doctrine for speculation but a warm assurance for believers, seen in the evidence of God’s work.

The final phrase reminds readers that the messengers’ lives matter. The gospel came “in word” and was confirmed by the lives of those who carried it.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers who share their faith can take comfort that the results do not depend on their eloquence. God’s Spirit works through simple, honest words. At the same time, they can pray for the Spirit’s power and assurance whenever they speak about Christ.

This verse also reminds believers that their lives are part of their witness. People notice whether a believer’s conduct matches their words. Integrity, kindness, and humility give credibility to the message.

For those who wonder whether God is truly at work in their lives, this verse points to the evidence: a heart that responded to the gospel, a growing love for God and others, and a changed life. These are signs of God’s choosing and power.

### *1 Thessalonians 1:9–10* — Turned to God from Idols

> *“For they themselves report concerning us what kind of a reception we had from you, and how you turned to God from idols to serve a living and true God, and to wait for his Son from heaven, whom he raised from the dead: Jesus, who delivers us from the wrath to come.”*
>
> — *1 Thessalonians 1:9–10* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

People throughout the region were reporting two things: the warm welcome the Thessalonians gave the missionaries, and the remarkable change in their lives.

“How you turned to God from idols.” The Thessalonians had worshiped the many gods of the Greek and Roman world. Thessalonica had temples to various gods, and the emperor was also honored as divine. Turning from these gods was costly. Idol worship was woven into family life, trade guilds, civic festivals, and social gatherings. Leaving it behind could mean losing friendships, business, and social standing.

“To serve a living and true God.” Idols were lifeless and false. The Thessalonians now served the God who is alive and real.

“And to wait for his Son from heaven.” Their new life had a forward focus. They eagerly awaited Jesus’ return.

“Whom he raised from the dead: Jesus.” The one they awaited is the risen Jesus, proof that God has power over death.

“Who delivers us from the wrath to come.” Jesus rescues His people from the coming judgment of God against sin.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses give a compact summary of Christian conversion: turning, serving, and waiting. Conversion is a turning, a change of direction, away from false gods toward the true God. It leads to service, a life devoted to God. And it involves waiting, an eager expectation of Christ’s return.

Notice the order: they turned “to God from idols.” The movement toward God came first. It was the beauty and truth of God in Christ that drew them away from idols. People do not usually give up false gods simply because they are told to; they let go when they discover something better.

The phrase “the wrath to come” reminds readers that God will judge evil. But the good news is that Jesus delivers His people from that judgment, because He bore it Himself on the cross (*Romans 5:9*). This hope gave the Thessalonians courage in the face of persecution.

This passage also introduces a theme that runs through both letters to the Thessalonians: the return of Christ. Paul will develop it more fully in chapters 4 and 5.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Idols today may not be statues in temples, but they are just as real. Anything that takes God’s place as the source of security, identity, or ultimate hope can become an idol: money, success, relationships, appearance, comfort, or approval. These verses invite believers to examine their hearts and to turn from anything that competes with God.

Turning from idols can be costly, as it was for the Thessalonians. It may mean changing habits, relationships, or priorities. But it leads to serving the living and true God, who gives life and joy.

Waiting for Christ’s return also shapes daily life. It gives hope in suffering, perspective in success, and urgency in sharing the gospel. Believers live each day in light of the day when Jesus will return.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

First Thessalonians 1 paints a portrait of a young church whose faith was genuine and contagious. Only months old, facing persecution from their neighbors, these believers displayed faith that worked, love that labored, and hope that endured. Their example inspired believers throughout Greece and beyond.

Their story reminds believers today that the Christian life is not merely a matter of belief but of transformation. Faith, love, and hope are invisible, but they show themselves in visible ways: in obedience, in tireless service, and in steady endurance. Believers can ask how these qualities are being expressed in their own lives, and they can encourage others by noticing and celebrating the work of God in them.

The chapter also shows that conversion is God’s work. The gospel came to Thessalonica not merely in words but in power, in the Holy Spirit, and with deep conviction. Those who share their faith can rely on God’s power rather than their own skill, while letting their lives confirm their message.

Finally, the Thessalonians’ story shows what conversion looks like: turning to God from idols, serving the living and true God, and waiting for His Son from heaven. Believers today can examine their hearts for modern idols and turn from them to the God who is alive. And they can live with eager hope, knowing that Jesus, who rose from the dead, will return and will deliver His people from the coming wrath. Even in suffering, they can have joy given by the Holy Spirit.

## Chapter Prayer

Father, thank You for the gospel that comes not in word only but in power, in the Holy Spirit, and with deep conviction. Thank You for the faith, love, and hope You have planted in Your people. Let my faith be seen in my work, my love in my labor, and my hope in my endurance. When I face hardship for following You, give me joy from Your Holy Spirit. Show me any idols in my heart that compete with You, and help me to turn from them to serve You, the living and true God. Make my life an example that encourages others in their faith, and let the message of Your grace ring out from my life to those around me. Help me to wait eagerly for Your Son from heaven, Jesus, whom You raised from the dead and who rescues us from the wrath to come. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
