1 Thessalonians · Chapter 2 of 5

# 1 Thessalonians — Chapter 2

Chapter Theme: A Ministry of Integrity and Tender Love

[Read 1 Thessalonians 2 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/1TH02.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul reminds the Thessalonians how he and his companions came to them after being mistreated in Philippi and boldly proclaimed the gospel despite opposition. Their message was not driven by error, impure motives, or trickery, and they did not use flattery, greed, or a desire for praise; they spoke to please God, who tests hearts. Instead, they were gentle like a nursing mother, sharing not only the gospel but their very lives, working night and day so as not to be a burden, and encouraging each believer like a father to live worthily of God. Paul thanks God that the Thessalonians received the message as God’s word, which is at work in them, even as they suffered from their own countrymen. Though forcibly separated from them, Paul longs to see them, for they are his glory and joy.

## Chapter Background and Story

After Paul left Thessalonica, his opponents apparently tried to discredit him. They may have said he was just another traveling teacher, of whom there were many in the Roman world, who used clever speech to win followers and money, and then fled at the first sign of trouble. Since Paul had left so suddenly and had not returned, some may have wondered whether he really cared.

In chapter 2, Paul answers these suspicions by reminding the Thessalonians of what they had seen with their own eyes. Again and again he says, “you know” and “you remember.” He appeals to their own experience of how he and his companions lived among them. The chapter gives one of the most beautiful pictures of Christian ministry in the New Testament: bold yet gentle, truthful yet tender, hard-working and selfless.

The chapter also includes a difficult passage (vv14–16) about opposition from some of Paul’s Jewish contemporaries. It must be read carefully in its historical setting, as explained below.

### Boldness in the Face of Opposition (*2:1–2*)

“*For you yourselves know, brothers, our visit to you wasn’t in vain*” (*v. 1*), “*but having suffered before and been shamefully treated, as you know, at Philippi, we grew bold in our God to tell you the Good News of God in much conflict*” (*v. 2*). In Philippi, Paul and Silas had been beaten with rods, thrown into prison, and fastened in stocks, even though Paul was a Roman citizen (*Acts 16:22–24*, 37). Many would have given up. But they went straight to Thessalonica and preached boldly. Their courage came “in our God,” not from themselves.

### Pure Motives (*2:3–6*)

“*For our exhortation is not of error, nor of uncleanness, nor in deception*” (*v. 3*). Paul denies three charges: that his message was false, that his motives were impure, and that his methods were deceptive. His commitment to pleasing God is studied below.

“*For neither were we at any time found using words of flattery, as you know, nor a cloak of covetousness (God is witness)*” (*v. 5*), “*nor seeking glory from men (neither from you nor from others), when we might have claimed authority as apostles of Christ*” (*v. 6*). Traveling speakers in the ancient world often flattered audiences to win their favor and money. Paul did none of this. He could have insisted on his rights as an apostle, including financial support, but he chose not to.

### Gentle as a Mother, Encouraging as a Father (*2:7–12*)

Paul describes the character of his ministry using family images, which are studied below. “*For you remember, brothers, our labor and travail; for working night and day, that we might not burden any of you, we preached to you the Good News of God*” (*v. 9*). Paul worked as a tentmaker (*Acts 18:3*), probably starting before dawn and continuing late, so that he could support himself while preaching. He did not want anyone to think he was preaching for money.

“*You are witnesses with God how holy, righteously, and blamelessly we behaved ourselves toward you who believe*” (*v. 10*). Paul’s conduct was open to inspection by both God and the Thessalonians.

### Receiving God’s Word (*2:13*)

The Thessalonians’ reception of the gospel as God’s word is studied below.

### Suffering from Their Own Countrymen (*2:14–16*)

“*For you, brothers, became imitators of the assemblies of God which are in Judea in Christ Jesus; for you also suffered the same things from your own countrymen, even as they did from the Jews*” (*v. 14*). The Thessalonian believers, mostly Gentiles, were being persecuted by their own fellow citizens. Paul compares their experience with that of the Jewish believers in Judea, who had been persecuted by fellow Jews.

Verses 15 and 16 contain some of the harshest words in Paul’s letters, and they must be read with great care. Paul speaks of those “*who killed both the Lord Jesus and their own prophets, and drove us out, and don’t please God, and are contrary to all men*” (*v. 15*), “*forbidding us to speak to the Gentiles that they may be saved*” (*v. 16*). Paul is not speaking about the Jewish people as a whole. He was himself a Jew, as were Jesus, the apostles, and the first believers in Judea whom he is praising in this very passage. He is speaking specifically about those Jewish leaders and opponents who had rejected Jesus and were actively trying to stop the gospel from reaching the Gentiles, the same opponents who had driven Paul out of Thessalonica (*Acts 17:5–10*). His words echo the language of Israel’s own prophets, who spoke sharply against those in their own nation who persecuted God’s messengers (*Nehemiah 9:26*; *Matthew 23:29–37*).

Elsewhere, Paul expresses deep love and grief for his fellow Jews, saying he would be willing to be cut off from Christ for their sake (*Romans 9:1–5*), and he insists that God has not rejected His people (*Romans 11:1–2*, 29). Tragically, passages like this have been misused over the centuries to fuel hatred and violence against Jewish people. Such use is a terrible distortion of Scripture and has no place in Christian faith. The New Testament teaches that all humanity, Jew and Gentile alike, shares responsibility for sin, and that Jesus laid down His life willingly for all (*John 10:17–18*; *Romans 3:23*).

“*But wrath has come on them to the uttermost*” (*v. 16*). Interpreters understand this phrase in different ways. It may refer to a recent event, such as a disaster in Judea, or it may describe the certainty of God’s judgment on those who oppose His work, spoken as if already accomplished.

### Longing to See Them (*2:17–20*)

“*But we, brothers, being bereaved of you for a short season in presence, not in heart, tried even harder to see your face with great desire*” (*v. 17*). “Bereaved” is the word for being orphaned. Paul felt the separation as painfully as a parent separated from children, or children torn from parents.

“*because we wanted to come to you—indeed, I, Paul, once and again—but Satan hindered us*” (*v. 18*). Paul tried more than once to return, but was blocked. We do not know exactly what hindered him; perhaps the bond Jason had posted (*Acts 17:9*), ongoing opposition, or illness. Paul saw spiritual opposition behind these obstacles.

“*For what is our hope, or joy, or crown of rejoicing? Isn’t it even you, before our Lord Jesus at his coming?*” (*v. 19*) “*For you are our glory and our joy*” (*v. 20*). Paul’s greatest joy is not his own achievements but the people he has brought to Christ. When Jesus returns, these believers will be his “crown,” like the wreath given to a victorious athlete.

## Important Verses Explained

### *1 Thessalonians 2:4* — Pleasing God, Who Tests Our Hearts

> *“But even as we have been approved by God to be entrusted with the Good News, so we speak—not as pleasing men, but God, who tests our hearts.”*
>
> — *1 Thessalonians 2:4* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul explains the foundation of his ministry. “Even as we have been approved by God to be entrusted with the Good News.” God had tested Paul and his companions and found them fit to be trusted with the gospel. The gospel did not belong to them; it was entrusted to them, like a valuable treasure given to a steward.

“So we speak—not as pleasing men, but God.” Because the gospel was God’s message entrusted to them, their aim was to please God, not people. They did not change the message to make it more appealing or soften it to avoid offense.

“Who tests our hearts.” God sees not only what people say and do but why they do it. He examines motives. Paul lived with an awareness that God knew his heart completely.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse expresses a theme that runs throughout Paul’s letters. In *Galatians 1:10*, he asked, “*am I striving to please men? For if I were still pleasing men, I wouldn’t be a servant of Christ*” (*Galatians 1:10*). True servants of God care most about God’s approval.

The idea that God “tests” hearts appears often in Scripture. *Jeremiah 17:10* says, “*I, the LORD, search the mind. I try the heart*” (*Jeremiah 17:10*). *Psalm 139:23* prays, “*Search me, God, and know my heart*” (*Psalm 139:23*). God’s testing is not meant to catch people out but to refine them, like metal purified in fire.

Being “entrusted” with the gospel also carries responsibility. Stewards must be faithful (*1 Corinthians 4:2*). Those who share the gospel are not free to change it. They are responsible to God for passing it on accurately and faithfully.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Everyone faces the temptation to please people: to say what others want to hear, to seek approval, or to avoid conflict at the cost of truth. This verse calls believers to live for an audience of One. When God’s approval matters most, believers are free to speak truth with love, to stand firm in convictions, and to serve without needing applause.

This verse also invites believers to examine their motives. Why do they serve, give, or speak about their faith? Is it to be seen, praised, or rewarded by others, or to please God? God tests hearts, and believers can ask Him to purify their motives.

Finally, every believer has been entrusted with the gospel in some way. Parents pass it on to children, friends share it with friends, and churches proclaim it to their communities. Faithfulness to the message is a sacred trust.

### *1 Thessalonians 2:7–8* — Gentle as a Nursing Mother

> *“But we were gentle among you, like a nursing mother cherishes her own children. Even so, affectionately longing for you, we were well pleased to impart to you not the Good News of God only, but also our own souls, because you had become very dear to us.”*
>
> — *1 Thessalonians 2:7–8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul uses a beautiful image to describe how he and his companions treated the Thessalonians. “But we were gentle among you, like a nursing mother cherishes her own children.”

A nursing mother cares for her infant with tenderness, patience, and self-giving love. She feeds her child from her own body, attends to its needs day and night, and holds it close. Paul says the missionaries treated the new believers with that same tender care. They did not act like distant authorities or demanding teachers.

Some ancient manuscripts read “we were infants among you” instead of “we were gentle among you.” In Greek, the two words differ by only one letter. If “infants” is correct, Paul would be saying that he and his companions were innocent and without guile, like little children. Most translations prefer “gentle,” which fits the image of a mother that follows.

Verse 8: “Even so, affectionately longing for you, we were well pleased to impart to you not the Good News of God only, but also our own souls, because you had become very dear to us.” The missionaries did not just deliver a message and leave. They shared their lives. They opened their hearts, spent time with the believers, and loved them deeply.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This image is remarkable, especially coming from Paul, a man trained as a strict Pharisee. He chooses a mother’s tenderness to describe his ministry. Throughout Scripture, God also describes His love in motherly terms: “*As one whom his mother comforts, so I will comfort you*” (*Isaiah 66:13*). Jesus longed to gather Jerusalem’s children “*even as a hen gathers her chicks*” (*Matthew 23:37*). Paul’s ministry reflected the tender heart of God.

Verse 8 shows that the gospel is not just information to transfer. It is best shared within relationships of genuine love. The missionaries gave both the message and themselves. This mirrors Christ, who not only taught the truth but gave His life for His people.

Gentleness in ministry does not mean weakness. Paul was bold in preaching (v2) and firm in exhorting (v11). But his boldness was wrapped in tenderness. Truth and love belong together.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Those who lead, teach, or care for others can learn from Paul’s example. Gentleness, patience, and tender care create an environment where people can grow. Harshness and impatience, on the other hand, often wound and discourage.

This passage also challenges believers to share not only the gospel but their lives. Inviting people into homes, listening to their struggles, celebrating their joys, and walking with them through hard seasons are ways of showing the love of Christ. People are often more open to the message when they experience the messenger’s love.

For those who serve in demanding roles, such as parents, caregivers, teachers, or ministry leaders, the image of the nursing mother may feel exhausting. It is a reminder that this kind of love is costly, and that those who give it need God’s strength and the support of others.

### *1 Thessalonians 2:11–12* — Encouraging Like a Father

> *“As you know, we exhorted, comforted, and implored every one of you, as a father does his own children, to the end that you should walk worthily of God, who calls you into his own Kingdom and glory.”*
>
> — *1 Thessalonians 2:11–12* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul now uses a second family image. “As you know, we exhorted, comforted, and implored every one of you, as a father does his own children.”

A good father guides, encourages, and challenges his children. Paul uses three verbs. “Exhorted” means urged or encouraged to action. “Comforted” means consoled and strengthened, especially in difficulty. “Implored” means testified or charged earnestly, insisting on what is important.

“Every one of you.” Paul’s care was personal. He did not just preach to crowds; he gave attention to individuals.

Verse 12 gives the goal: “to the end that you should walk worthily of God, who calls you into his own Kingdom and glory.” Paul wanted the believers to live in a way that reflected the God who had called them. And God’s call is not only to a moral life but into His own kingdom and glory. The believers’ present lives were to be shaped by their future destiny.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The images of mother and father together show the fullness of Paul’s care. A mother’s tenderness and a father’s guidance are both needed. Paul offered both. Good spiritual leadership includes nurturing care and clear direction.

Paul’s goal was not merely to make converts but to help them grow into mature disciples who live “worthily of God.” The same phrase appears in *Colossians 1:10* and *Ephesians 4:1*. A life worthy of God is not about earning His favor but about reflecting His character as His children.

The phrase “who calls you into his own Kingdom and glory” reminds believers that God’s call is active and ongoing (“calls,” present tense). God is continually inviting His people into His kingdom and glory. Their future is secure, and their present lives are meant to be shaped by that future.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Parents, mentors, pastors, and friends can follow Paul’s example of personal, fatherly care: encouraging people to grow, comforting them in hardship, and urging them earnestly toward what is right. This kind of care pays attention to individuals, not just groups.

This verse also reminds believers of their high calling. God calls them into His kingdom and glory. That calling gives dignity to everyday life and motivates believers to live in a way that honors Him.

For those who did not have good fathers, this image may be painful. God can provide spiritual fathers and mothers in the church who offer the care that was missing, and above all, God Himself is the perfect Father.

### *1 Thessalonians 2:13* — Received as the Word of God

> *“For this cause we also thank God without ceasing that when you received from us the word of the message of God, you accepted it not as the word of men, but as it is in truth, God’s word, which also works in you who believe.”*
>
> — *1 Thessalonians 2:13* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul thanks God for how the Thessalonians responded to the gospel. “When you received from us the word of the message of God, you accepted it not as the word of men, but as it is in truth, God’s word.”

The Thessalonians heard the gospel through human messengers, Paul, Silas, and Timothy. But they recognized it as more than human opinion or philosophy. They accepted it as God’s own word. Paul affirms that this is exactly what it was: “as it is in truth, God’s word.”

“Which also works in you who believe.” God’s word is not dead or inactive. It works. It is at work in believers, changing their hearts, shaping their lives, and producing faith, love, and hope. The word “works” is related to the English word “energy.”

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse expresses a high view of the gospel and of the apostolic message. Though spoken by human beings, it carries divine authority. Paul says something similar in *Galatians 1:11–12*: the gospel he preached was not of human origin but came by revelation of Jesus Christ. Christians have recognized the apostolic writings as Scripture because they bear this divine authority (*2 Peter 3:15–16*).

The idea that God’s word is active echoes many passages. *Isaiah 55:10–11* says that God’s word does not return to Him empty but accomplishes what He desires. *Hebrews 4:12* says that God’s word is “*living and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword*” (*Hebrews 4:12*). When believers receive God’s word, it goes to work within them.

The key is how the word is received. The Thessalonians received it with faith, as God’s word. Those who hear the word merely as human opinion may not experience its power. Faith opens the heart to the word’s transforming work.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to approach Scripture not as an ordinary book but as God’s word. Reading the Bible with that conviction changes how it is read: with attention, humility, expectancy, and a willingness to obey.

It also encourages believers that God’s word is at work in them, even when they do not feel it. Regular reading, hearing, and meditating on Scripture allows it to shape their thinking and transform their lives over time.

Finally, this verse encourages those who teach and preach. When they faithfully proclaim God’s word, they can trust that it carries God’s power. The results depend not on their skill but on the living word itself.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

First Thessalonians 2 offers a rich portrait of Christian ministry and Christian love. Paul and his companions came to Thessalonica after being beaten and imprisoned in Philippi, yet they preached boldly. Their message was true, their motives were pure, and their methods were honest. They sought to please God, who tests hearts, rather than people. They did not use flattery or seek money or praise.

At the same time, their boldness was wrapped in tenderness. They were gentle like a nursing mother and encouraging like a father. They shared not only the gospel but their very lives, working night and day so as not to burden anyone. Their example calls believers today to combine truth and love, courage and gentleness, in every relationship and every form of service.

The Thessalonians, in turn, received the message not as human words but as God’s word, and that word was at work in them. Believers today can approach Scripture with the same faith and expectancy, trusting that God’s word is living and active.

The chapter also reminds believers that faithfulness often brings opposition. The Thessalonians suffered from their own neighbors, just as the believers in Judea had. Paul’s sharp words about those who opposed the gospel must be read carefully; they are aimed at specific persecutors, not at the Jewish people, whom Paul loved and for whom he prayed. Believers must reject every misuse of these words to justify prejudice.

Finally, Paul’s longing for the Thessalonians shows the depth of his love. They were his hope, his joy, and his crown. In the same way, believers can find their deepest joy not in their own achievements but in the people they love and help toward Christ.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord, You have entrusted Your gospel to Your people. Help me to be faithful to it, speaking not to please others but to please You, who test my heart. Purify my motives and free me from flattery, greed, and the desire for praise. Make me bold when I face opposition, and gentle in the way I treat others. Teach me to care for people with the tenderness of a nursing mother and to encourage them like a faithful father, sharing not only Your message but my life. Help me to receive Your word as it truly is, Your word and not merely human words, and let it be at work in me. Protect me from prejudice of every kind, and fill me with love for all people. Thank You for the joy of seeing others grow in faith. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

1 Thessalonians · Chapter 3 of 5

# 1 Thessalonians — Chapter 3

Chapter Theme: Standing Firm and Growing in Love

[Read 1 Thessalonians 3 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/1TH03.htm)

Main Teaching

Unable to bear the uncertainty any longer, Paul stayed alone in Athens and sent Timothy to strengthen and encourage the Thessalonians, so that no one would be shaken by their troubles, which Paul had told them to expect. When Timothy returned with good news of their faith and love and their warm memories of Paul, Paul was deeply comforted in his own distress, saying that now he really lives, since they are standing firm in the Lord. He overflows with thanksgiving, prays earnestly to see them again and supply what is lacking in their faith, and asks the Lord to make their love increase and overflow, and to strengthen their hearts to be blameless in holiness at the coming of the Lord Jesus with all His holy ones.

## Chapter Background and Story

After being driven out of Thessalonica, Paul went to Berea, where opponents from Thessalonica followed and stirred up trouble again (*Acts 17:10–14*). Believers took Paul to Athens for safety, while Silas and Timothy stayed behind for a time. In Athens, Paul was alone in a city full of idols (*Acts 17:16*).

Paul’s anxiety for the young church grew. They had been believers for only a few weeks when he left. They were facing persecution. Would their faith survive? Had the pressure been too much? Had the “tempter” succeeded in drawing them away? Paul could not go himself, so he sent Timothy, his trusted young coworker, back to Thessalonica.

Chapter 3 tells what happened next. Timothy returned with wonderful news, and Paul’s relief and joy overflow into thanksgiving and prayer. This chapter shows the heart of a pastor who suffers when his people suffer and rejoices when they stand firm.

### Sending Timothy (*3:1–5*)

“*Therefore when we couldn’t stand it any longer, we thought it good to be left behind at Athens alone*” (*v. 1*). Paul’s concern became unbearable. He chose to be alone in Athens, a hard place for him, so that Timothy could go to the Thessalonians. The phrase “left behind” is the same word used for being abandoned or bereaved. It was a real sacrifice. The purpose of Timothy’s mission, and the reality of suffering for the faith, are studied below.

“*For this cause I also, when I couldn’t stand it any longer, sent that I might know your faith, for fear that by any means the tempter had tempted you, and our labor would have been in vain*” (*v. 5*). “The tempter” is Satan, who seeks to use suffering to pull believers away from faith. Paul knew that hardship can either strengthen or weaken faith. He feared that, under pressure, the young believers might have given up.

### Timothy’s Good News (*3:6–10*)

“*But Timothy has just now come to us from you, and brought us glad news of your faith and love, and that you have good memories of us always, longing to see us, even as we also long to see you*” (*v. 6*). “Brought glad news” is the same word used for preaching the gospel. Timothy’s report was good news indeed. The Thessalonians were still standing in faith and love, and they still loved Paul and longed to see him, despite the accusations of his opponents. Paul’s response is studied below.

“*For what thanksgiving can we give again to God for you, for all the joy with which we rejoice for your sakes before our God*” (*v. 9*), “*night and day praying exceedingly that we may see your face and may perfect that which is lacking in your faith?*” (*v. 10*) Paul cannot thank God enough. Yet he also recognizes that their faith, while genuine, was still young and incomplete. He prays “exceedingly,” with great intensity, for the chance to return and teach them more. “Perfect” here means to complete, to supply what is missing, or to mend, like repairing nets. Chapters 4 and 5 will begin to supply some of what was lacking.

### Paul’s Prayer (*3:11–13*)

“*Now may our God and Father himself, and our Lord Jesus Christ, direct our way to you*” (*v. 11*). In Greek, the verb “direct” is singular, even though it has two subjects, the Father and the Lord Jesus. This small grammatical detail suggests how closely Paul linked the Father and the Son, acting together as one. Paul’s prayer for their love and holiness is studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *1 Thessalonians 3:2–4* — Appointed to Suffer

> *“and sent Timothy, our brother and God’s servant in the Good News of Christ, to establish you and to comfort you concerning your faith, that no one would be moved by these afflictions. For you know that we are appointed to this task. For most certainly, when we were with you, we told you beforehand that we are to suffer affliction, even as it happened, and you know.”*
>
> — *1 Thessalonians 3:2–4* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul describes Timothy and his mission. Timothy was “our brother and God’s servant in the Good News of Christ.” Some manuscripts read “God’s fellow worker.” Paul honors Timothy as a trusted partner.

Timothy was sent “to establish you and to comfort you concerning your faith.” “Establish” means to strengthen, to make firm, like adding supports to a building. “Comfort” can also mean encourage or exhort. Timothy’s task was to help the Thessalonians stand firm in their faith.

The reason: “that no one would be moved by these afflictions.” The word “moved” was used of a dog wagging its tail, and came to mean being flattered or being shaken and unsettled. Paul did not want the believers to be shaken loose from their faith by the persecution they were enduring.

“For you know that we are appointed to this task.” Suffering is not an accident or a sign that something has gone wrong. It is part of the calling of Christ’s followers. The word “appointed” means set or destined.

Verse 4: “For most certainly, when we were with you, we told you beforehand that we are to suffer affliction, even as it happened, and you know.” Paul had warned them in advance that following Christ would bring suffering. Now his words had come true. This should not shake their faith; it should confirm it.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The New Testament is honest about suffering. Jesus told His disciples, “*In the world you have trouble; but cheer up! I have overcome the world*” (*John 16:33*). Paul and Barnabas told new believers that through many afflictions we must enter into God’s kingdom (*Acts 14:22*). Peter wrote that believers should not be surprised at fiery trials, as though something strange were happening (*1 Peter 4:12*).

Why would believers be “appointed” to suffer? Not because God delights in their pain, but because they follow a crucified Lord in a world that is hostile to Him. Suffering for Christ’s sake is a sign of belonging to Him (*John 15:18–20*). And God uses suffering to strengthen faith, produce endurance, and make believers more like Christ (*Romans 5:3–5*; *James 1:2–4*).

Paul’s practice of warning new believers about suffering is wise. Faith that expects only comfort is easily shaken when trouble comes. Faith that has been prepared for hardship can stand firm. This is one reason Paul sent Timothy: to remind them of what they had already been told.

It is important to distinguish suffering for Christ’s sake from suffering caused by abuse or injustice that can be escaped. Scripture does not call believers to remain in abusive situations or to accept mistreatment that could be stopped. Paul himself escaped danger when he could (*Acts 9:23–25*; *17:10*). The suffering Paul describes here is persecution for faith, which believers endure with courage while still seeking safety and justice where possible.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers who face opposition, misunderstanding, or hardship because of their faith can take comfort that this is not unusual. It does not mean God has abandoned them. Jesus and the apostles told His followers to expect it.

This passage also encourages believers to strengthen one another, as Timothy did. When someone is going through hardship, a visit, a phone call, a word of encouragement from Scripture, or a reminder of God’s faithfulness can help them stand firm.

Finally, those who teach new believers can follow Paul’s example by being honest about the cost of following Christ. Preparing people for hardship helps their faith grow deep roots.

### *1 Thessalonians 3:7–8* — Now We Live

> *“For this cause, brothers, we were comforted over you in all our distress and affliction through your faith. For now we live, if you stand fast in the Lord.”*
>
> — *1 Thessalonians 3:7–8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul describes the effect of Timothy’s report. “For this cause, brothers, we were comforted over you in all our distress and affliction through your faith.” Paul himself was going through hardship. He was facing opposition in Corinth, where he was now ministering (*Acts 18:5–6*). But the news of the Thessalonians’ faith brought him comfort in the middle of his own troubles.

Verse 8: “For now we live, if you stand fast in the Lord.” This is a striking statement. Paul says that the Thessalonians’ faithfulness gives him new life. While he was anxious about them, it was as if he could hardly breathe. Now that he knows they are standing firm, he feels truly alive again.

“Stand fast in the Lord.” This is the heart of Paul’s desire for them. He wants them to remain firm, steady, and unshaken, not in their own strength, but “in the Lord.”

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses reveal the deep bond between Paul and the churches he founded. Their spiritual welfare was so closely tied to his own that their faith gave him life. This is what it means to be part of the body of Christ: when one member suffers, all suffer; when one is honored, all rejoice (*1 Corinthians 12:26*).

There is also a beautiful reversal here. Paul sent Timothy to comfort and strengthen the Thessalonians (v2). But the result was that the Thessalonians comforted Paul. In the body of Christ, encouragement flows both ways. Leaders strengthen their people, and people strengthen their leaders.

John expressed a similar joy: “*I have no greater joy than this: to hear about my children walking in truth*” (*3 John 1:4*). Those who invest in others’ faith find their deepest joy in seeing that faith flourish.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers may not realize how much their faithfulness encourages others. Parents, pastors, mentors, and friends who have invested in someone’s faith are deeply comforted when they hear that person is standing firm. A simple message of gratitude or an update on how one is growing can bring great encouragement to those who have cared for them.

This passage also invites believers to carry others on their hearts the way Paul did. Caring deeply about others’ spiritual welfare, praying for them, and rejoicing in their growth reflect the love of Christ.

Finally, for those in hard seasons, this passage shows that good news about others’ faith can bring comfort and renewed strength. Fellowship with other believers, even from a distance, can lift a weary heart.

### *1 Thessalonians 3:12–13* — Abounding in Love, Blameless in Holiness

> *“May the Lord make you to increase and abound in love toward one another and toward all men, even as we also do toward you, to the end he may establish your hearts blameless in holiness before our God and Father at the coming of our Lord Jesus with all his saints.”*
>
> — *1 Thessalonians 3:12–13* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul’s prayer has two requests.

First, “May the Lord make you to increase and abound in love toward one another and toward all men, even as we also do toward you.” Paul prays that their love would grow and overflow, like a river overflowing its banks. Their love is to reach “one another,” fellow believers, and “all men,” including those outside the church, even their persecutors. Paul points to his own love for them as an example.

Second, “to the end he may establish your hearts blameless in holiness before our God and Father.” Paul prays that God would strengthen their hearts so that they would be holy and blameless. “Hearts” refers to the inner person, the source of thoughts, desires, and choices.

“At the coming of our Lord Jesus with all his saints.” Paul looks forward to Christ’s return. “Saints” means holy ones. It may refer to angels who accompany Christ (*Matthew 25:31*), to believers who have died and will return with Him (*1 Thessalonians 4:14*), or to both. The goal is that the Thessalonians would be ready to stand before God on that day.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This prayer shows the connection between love and holiness. Paul prays first for love to abound, and then for hearts to be established in holiness. The two go together. Holiness is not cold rule-keeping; it is a heart filled with love for God and others. And genuine love leads to holy living. Paul says elsewhere that love is the fulfillment of the Law (*Romans 13:10*).

Notice that Paul asks the Lord to do this work. Love and holiness are not simply human achievements. They are the fruit of God’s work in the heart. Believers participate through their choices and efforts, but God provides the growth.

The mention of Christ’s coming gives this prayer its urgency and its hope. Believers live now in light of that day. The prospect of standing before God motivates holy living, not out of fear, but out of a desire to be ready to meet the Lord they love.

The phrase “toward all men” is important. The Thessalonians were being persecuted by their neighbors. Paul prays that their love would extend even to those who mistreated them, following the teaching of Jesus to love one’s enemies (*Matthew 5:44*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This prayer is a wonderful one for believers to pray for themselves, their families, and their churches. It asks for growing, overflowing love and for hearts made firm in holiness.

Love “toward all men” challenges believers to look beyond their own circles. It includes neighbors, coworkers, strangers, people of other faiths, and even those who are hostile. Such love does not mean approving of wrongdoing or accepting abuse, but it does mean seeking others’ good, praying for them, and treating them with kindness and respect.

Living in light of Christ’s return can shape daily decisions. Believers can ask whether their choices, relationships, and priorities reflect hearts that are ready to meet Him. This perspective brings both seriousness and hope to everyday life.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

First Thessalonians 3 reveals the heart of a loving pastor and the reality of a faith tested by suffering. Paul could not bear the uncertainty about the young believers in Thessalonica, so he gave up the comfort of Timothy’s companionship and sent him to strengthen them. His example shows the sacrificial love that leaders, parents, and friends can have for those in their care.

The chapter is honest about suffering. Paul had told the Thessalonians from the beginning that followers of Christ are appointed to face affliction. Hardship for the sake of faith is not a sign that God has abandoned His people. Believers can prepare one another for this reality and strengthen one another when it comes, as Timothy did. At the same time, suffering for faith is different from abuse or injustice that can and should be escaped or stopped.

When Timothy returned with good news, Paul was overjoyed. The Thessalonians’ faithfulness gave him new life in the middle of his own troubles. This shows the deep bond within the body of Christ: one believer’s faithfulness encourages others, and encouragement flows in both directions. Believers can share good news of their growth with those who have invested in them and can carry others on their hearts in prayer.

Finally, Paul’s prayer sets out what matters most: love that increases and overflows to everyone, and hearts made firm in holiness before God at the coming of the Lord Jesus. Believers can pray this prayer for themselves and for others, living each day in love and in readiness for Christ’s return.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord, thank You for those who have strengthened and encouraged me in my faith. When I face hardship for following You, keep me from being shaken. Remind me that You told us to expect trouble in this world, and that You have overcome the world. Help me to strengthen others when they struggle, and give me a heart that cares deeply about their faith. Thank You for the joy of seeing others stand firm in You. Make my love increase and overflow toward my brothers and sisters and toward all people, even those who oppose me. Strengthen my heart, so that I may be blameless in holiness before You, our God and Father, at the coming of our Lord Jesus with all His holy ones. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

1 Thessalonians · Chapter 4 of 5

# 1 Thessalonians — Chapter 4

Chapter Theme: Holy Living and the Hope of Resurrection

[Read 1 Thessalonians 4 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/1TH04.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul urges the Thessalonians to keep growing in the way of life that pleases God. God’s will is their sanctification: to avoid sexual immorality, to control their bodies in holiness and honor, and not to wrong one another, because God has called them to holiness and given them His Holy Spirit. They already love one another, but Paul urges them to love even more, to aim at a quiet life, to mind their own affairs, and to work with their hands so as to earn the respect of outsiders. Then he comforts them about believers who have died. Christians grieve, but not like those without hope, because Jesus died and rose again, and when the Lord Himself descends from heaven with a shout and the trumpet of God, the dead in Christ will rise first, and those still alive will be caught up together with them to meet the Lord, and so they will be with the Lord forever.

## Chapter Background and Story

In chapter 3, Paul prayed that he might return to Thessalonica to “perfect that which is lacking” in their faith (*1 Thessalonians 3:10*). Since he could not yet come, chapters 4 and 5 begin to supply some of that teaching. Paul addresses three areas where the young church needed guidance: sexual holiness, love and work, and the hope of Christ’s return.

Each area reflected the challenges of their situation. They had come out of a pagan culture where sexual immorality was widely accepted, even connected with some forms of worship. Some may have stopped working, perhaps out of excitement that Christ would return soon, and were depending on others. And some members of the church had died since Paul left, leaving the believers grieving and confused. Would those who had died miss out when Christ returned?

Paul’s answers are practical and full of hope. The final section of this chapter (*4:13–18*) is one of the most important passages in the New Testament about Christ’s return and the resurrection of believers, and it has comforted grieving Christians for two thousand years.

### Living to Please God (*4:1–2*)

“*Finally then, brothers, we beg and exhort you in the Lord Jesus, that as you received from us how you ought to walk and to please God, that you abound more and more*” (*v. 1*). The Thessalonians were already living to please God. Paul urges them to keep growing. The Christian life is never static. “*For you know what instructions we gave you through the Lord Jesus*” (*v. 2*). These instructions came with the authority of the Lord.

### Sexual Holiness (*4:3–8*)

The call to sexual purity is studied below. “*that no one should take advantage of and wrong a brother or sister in this matter; because the Lord is an avenger in all these things, as also we forewarned you and testified*” (*v. 6*). Sexual sin is not merely a private matter. It wrongs others, such as a spouse, a future spouse, or the person drawn into sin. Sexual exploitation and abuse are serious wrongs against real people, and God Himself takes up the cause of those who are wronged. Those who have been harmed are never to blame for another’s sin against them.

“*For God called us not for uncleanness, but in sanctification*” (*v. 7*). “*Therefore he who rejects this doesn’t reject man, but God, who has also given his Holy Spirit to you*” (*v. 8*). This teaching is not merely Paul’s opinion. To reject it is to reject God. And God has given His Holy Spirit to empower believers to live holy lives. The Spirit is called “holy,” and He makes His people holy.

### Love and Honest Work (*4:9–12*)

“*But concerning brotherly love, you have no need that one write to you. For you yourselves are taught by God to love one another*” (*v. 9*), “*for indeed you do it toward all the brothers who are in all Macedonia. But we exhort you, brothers, that you abound more and more*” (*v. 10*). The Thessalonians already loved one another and extended their love to believers throughout Macedonia. “Taught by God” may echo *Jeremiah 31:33–34* and *Isaiah 54:13*, which promised that God’s people would be taught by Him directly. Still, love can always grow. The call to quiet, honest work is studied below.

### Grieving with Hope (*4:13–18*)

Paul’s comfort to those grieving the death of believers, and his description of Christ’s return, are studied below. “*For this we tell you by the word of the Lord, that we who are alive, who are left until the coming of the Lord, will in no way precede those who have fallen asleep*” (*v. 15*). “By the word of the Lord” may refer to a saying of Jesus not recorded in the Gospels, to a revelation given to Paul, or to Jesus’ teaching in passages such as *Matthew 24:30–31*. Paul’s point is that believers who die before Christ returns will not miss out. In fact, they will rise first.

Paul uses “we” in verse 15, which may suggest he hoped to be alive when Christ returned. Yet elsewhere he contemplates his own death (*2 Corinthians 5:8*; *Philippians 1:21–23*). The New Testament writers lived in eager expectation of Christ’s return without knowing its timing, as Jesus Himself taught (*Matthew 24:36*).

“*Therefore comfort one another with these words*” (*v. 18*). The purpose of this teaching is comfort, not speculation. Paul does not give these words to satisfy curiosity about the end times but to give hope to the grieving.

## Important Verses Explained

### *1 Thessalonians 4:3–5* — This Is the Will of God: Your Sanctification

> *“For this is the will of God: your sanctification, that you abstain from sexual immorality, that each one of you know how to control his own body in sanctification and honor, not in the passion of lust, even as the Gentiles who don’t know God,”*
>
> — *1 Thessalonians 4:3–5* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Many people wonder, “What is God’s will for my life?” Paul gives a clear answer here: “For this is the will of God: your sanctification.” Sanctification means being made holy, set apart for God, and growing to be more like Him. Whatever else God’s will includes, it certainly includes this.

Paul then applies this to a specific area: “that you abstain from sexual immorality.” The word translated “sexual immorality” refers broadly to any sexual activity outside of marriage between a husband and wife. In the Greek and Roman world, sexual freedom for men was widely accepted, including relationships with slaves and prostitutes. Christian teaching was strikingly different.

Verse 4: “that each one of you know how to control his own body in sanctification and honor.” The phrase “control his own body” is literally “possess his own vessel.” Interpreters understand “vessel” either as one’s own body, meaning learning self-control, or as one’s wife, meaning taking a wife in holiness and honor rather than lust. Either way, Paul calls for sexual conduct marked by holiness and respect.

Verse 5: “not in the passion of lust, even as the Gentiles who don’t know God.” Paul contrasts the Christian way with the way of those who do not know God, who are driven by uncontrolled desire. Believers are called to something different because they know God.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The Bible presents sexuality as a good gift of God, created for the covenant of marriage between a husband and wife (*Genesis 2:24*; Song of Songs; *Hebrews 13:4*). Sexual immorality distorts that gift. It treats people as objects for gratification rather than as persons made in God’s image, and it breaks the trust and faithfulness that God designed sexuality to express.

Sanctification is both God’s work and a believer’s calling. God sanctifies His people through His Spirit (v8; *2 Thessalonians 2:13*), and believers respond by choosing holiness in their daily lives. Self-control is part of the fruit of the Spirit (*Galatians 5:23*), not merely willpower.

This teaching should be held with compassion. Many people carry deep regret about past sexual sin, and many have been harmed by others’ sexual sin, including abuse. The gospel offers forgiveness and cleansing to all who repent (*1 Corinthians 6:9–11*), and healing to those who have been wounded. Victims of sexual abuse are not guilty of the sin committed against them, and they deserve care, protection, and justice. Believers who struggle with sexual temptation are not alone; the call to holiness comes with the promise of God’s Spirit and the support of His people.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Modern culture often treats sexual choices as purely personal and without moral weight. This passage calls believers to see their bodies and their sexuality as belonging to God and to live in a way that honors Him and respects others.

Practical steps toward sexual holiness might include guarding what one watches and reads, setting healthy boundaries in relationships, being accountable to trusted friends, and seeking help for struggles with pornography or compulsive behavior. Marriage is to be honored and protected through faithfulness.

For those who have failed, God’s grace is greater than any sin. Confession, repentance, and renewed commitment can begin a new path. For those who have been harmed, this passage affirms that God takes their suffering seriously and is their defender.

### *1 Thessalonians 4:11–12* — A Quiet Life and Honest Work

> *“and that you make it your ambition to lead a quiet life, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands, even as we instructed you, that you may walk properly toward those who are outside, and may have need of nothing.”*
>
> — *1 Thessalonians 4:11–12* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul gives practical advice for daily living. “Make it your ambition to lead a quiet life.” This is an unusual phrase. Ambition usually means striving for prominence. Paul says believers should strive to live quietly, peacefully, without seeking attention or stirring up trouble.

“And to do your own business.” Believers should take care of their own responsibilities rather than meddling in others’ affairs.

“And to work with your own hands, even as we instructed you.” Many Greeks looked down on manual labor as fit only for slaves. Paul affirms the dignity of work. He himself worked with his hands as a tentmaker (*1 Thessalonians 2:9*).

Verse 12 gives two reasons. First, “that you may walk properly toward those who are outside.” When believers live quietly, responsibly, and industriously, they earn the respect of their neighbors and give the gospel a good reputation. Second, “and may have need of nothing.” By working, believers can provide for themselves and not depend unnecessarily on others.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This passage suggests that some believers in Thessalonica had stopped working. Perhaps they thought Christ’s return was so close that work no longer mattered. Perhaps some were relying on wealthier believers’ generosity. Paul addresses this more strongly in *2 Thessalonians 3:6–12*.

The Christian hope of Christ’s return does not lead to idleness. It leads to faithful, ordinary living. Jesus told parables about servants who were found faithfully working when their master returned (*Matthew 24:45–46*). Waiting for Christ means living responsibly in the present.

Work is part of God’s good design for humanity. Before sin entered the world, God placed Adam in the garden “*to cultivate and keep it*” (*Genesis 2:15*). Work done well, with integrity, is a way of honoring God, serving others, and reflecting His creative character.

This teaching does not condemn those who cannot work because of illness, disability, age, or circumstances beyond their control. Scripture calls the church to care generously for those in genuine need (*Acts 4:34–35*; *1 Timothy 5:3–16*). Paul’s concern is for those who are able to work but choose not to.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

In a culture that often prizes attention, fame, and constant activity, the call to “lead a quiet life” offers a refreshing alternative. Believers can find contentment in faithful, ordinary lives without needing to be noticed.

Minding one’s own business also matters. Gossip, meddling, and unnecessary involvement in others’ affairs cause harm. Believers can focus on their own responsibilities while still caring for others in appropriate ways.

Work, whether paid or unpaid, can be done as service to God. Doing honest work well, being reliable, and providing for oneself and one’s family are part of a Christian witness that earns the respect of others.

### *1 Thessalonians 4:13–14* — Grieving with Hope

> *“But we don’t want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who have fallen asleep, so that you don’t grieve like the rest, who have no hope. For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep in Jesus.”*
>
> — *1 Thessalonians 4:13–14* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Some believers in Thessalonica had died since Paul left. The church was grieving, and they may have feared that their loved ones would miss out on Christ’s return. Paul writes to comfort them.

“But we don’t want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who have fallen asleep.” “Fallen asleep” is a gentle way of speaking about death for believers. Sleep is temporary; those who sleep will wake. Jesus used the same image when He spoke of Lazarus (*John 11:11*) and of Jairus’s daughter (*Mark 5:39*).

“So that you don’t grieve like the rest, who have no hope.” Paul does not say believers should not grieve. Grief is natural and right. Jesus Himself wept at the tomb of Lazarus (*John 11:35*). But Christian grief is different. It is grief mixed with hope. Many people in the ancient world had little hope beyond death. Some inscriptions on tombs expressed despair. Believers grieve, but they grieve with hope.

Verse 14 gives the reason: “For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep in Jesus.” The resurrection of Jesus is the foundation of Christian hope. Because He died and rose, those who belong to Him will rise too. When Jesus returns, God will bring with Him those believers who have died.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show the deep connection between Christ’s resurrection and the believer’s future. Paul develops this more fully in *1 Corinthians 15*, where he calls Christ “*the first fruit of those who are asleep*” (*1 Corinthians 15:20*). Just as the first fruit of a harvest guarantee the rest, Christ’s resurrection guarantees the resurrection of all who are in Him.

The phrase “fallen asleep in Jesus” is tender. Believers who die are still “in Jesus.” Death does not separate them from Christ (*Romans 8:38–39*). Paul says elsewhere that to be absent from the body is to be at home with the Lord (*2 Corinthians 5:8*). Christians have discussed exactly what happens between death and the final resurrection, but all agree that believers who die are safe with Christ and will rise when He returns.

Grief with hope is one of the distinctive marks of Christian faith. It does not deny the pain of loss. It does not tell grieving people to “get over it” or to stop crying. It holds sorrow and hope together. Believers can mourn deeply while trusting that death is not the end.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Those who have lost believing loved ones can take great comfort in these verses. Their loved ones are not lost forever. They have “fallen asleep in Jesus,” and they will rise when He returns. The separation is real and painful, but it is temporary.

This passage also gives permission to grieve. Believers do not need to hide their tears or pretend to be fine. Grief is an expression of love. Christian hope does not remove grief; it gives it a different shape.

Those who walk alongside grieving people can follow Paul’s example by offering both presence and hope: sitting with them in their sorrow and gently reminding them of the resurrection, without rushing them through their grief. For those whose grief becomes overwhelming, support from pastors, counselors, and grief groups can also be part of how God brings comfort.

### *1 Thessalonians 4:16–17* — The Lord Himself Will Descend

> *“For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel and with God’s trumpet. The dead in Christ will rise first, then we who are alive, who are left, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air. So we will be with the Lord forever.”*
>
> — *1 Thessalonians 4:16–17* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul describes the return of Christ. “For the Lord himself will descend from heaven.” Not an angel or a representative, but Jesus Himself will come. The same Jesus who ascended into heaven will return (*Acts 1:11*).

His coming will be accompanied by three sounds: “with a shout, with the voice of the archangel and with God’s trumpet.” These may be three descriptions of one great announcement. In the Old Testament, trumpets announced God’s presence and gathered His people (*Exodus 19:16*; *Isaiah 27:13*). Christ’s return will be public and unmistakable.

“The dead in Christ will rise first.” Believers who have died will be raised to new, resurrection life before anything else happens.

Verse 17: “then we who are alive, who are left, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air.” Believers who are still living when Christ returns will be “caught up,” snatched up suddenly, together with the resurrected believers. Clouds in Scripture often signal God’s presence (*Exodus 13:21*; *Daniel 7:13*; *Acts 1:9*).

“So we will be with the Lord forever.” This is the ultimate hope. Whatever the details, the final result is eternal fellowship with Christ.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Christians have understood the details of these verses in different ways, and faithful believers hold a range of views.

Some believe these verses describe a “rapture,” in which believers are taken up to meet Christ and then taken to heaven before a period of tribulation on earth. Others believe the “catching up” happens at the same time as Christ’s visible return at the end of history, after a time of tribulation, so that believers rise to meet Him and then accompany Him back to earth. Supporters of this second view point out that the word translated “to meet” was often used in the ancient world for citizens going out of a city to greet an arriving king or official and then escorting him back into the city. Still others emphasize that this passage, like much biblical language about the end, uses vivid imagery to describe a glorious reality whose exact details cannot be fully mapped out.

Whatever view one holds, all Christians agree on the central truths: Jesus will personally and visibly return; believers who have died will be raised; living believers will be transformed; and all of God’s people will be together with the Lord forever. These truths are meant to bring comfort and hope, not division or fear.

The phrase “together with them” is also precious. Believers who are alive will be reunited with those who have died. The church will be gathered as one family in the presence of Christ.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses give believers a sure hope for the future. History is not heading toward meaningless chaos. It is heading toward the return of Christ, when death will be defeated and God’s people will be with Him forever.

This hope brings comfort in grief, courage in suffering, and perspective in daily life. Believers can face hardships, aging, and even death with confidence, knowing that the best is yet to come.

Because Christians hold different views on the details, this passage also invites humility and charity. Believers can discuss and study these questions with interest while remembering that Paul’s purpose was comfort. The central message, “we will be with the Lord forever,” unites all believers.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

First Thessalonians 4 shows that the Christian life is shaped by both present holiness and future hope. God’s will for His people is their sanctification, being made holy in every area of life, including sexuality. Believers are called to honor God with their bodies, to exercise self-control, and never to wrong or exploit others. This call comes with the gift of God’s Holy Spirit, who empowers holy living, and with the grace that forgives and heals those who have fallen or been harmed.

The chapter also calls believers to love one another more and more, to lead quiet and peaceful lives, to mind their own responsibilities, and to work honestly. These ordinary virtues earn the respect of outsiders and give the gospel a good name. Waiting for Christ’s return does not make work unimportant; it makes faithfulness in daily life all the more meaningful.

Finally, the chapter offers deep comfort to those who grieve. Believers grieve, but not like those who have no hope. Because Jesus died and rose again, those who have fallen asleep in Him will rise. When the Lord Himself descends from heaven, the dead in Christ will rise first, and those who are alive will join them to meet the Lord. Christians hold different views on the details, but they share the same glorious hope: “So we will be with the Lord forever.” Believers are called to comfort one another with these words, holding sorrow and hope together until the day when every tear is wiped away.

## Chapter Prayer

Holy God, Your will is my sanctification. Make me holy in every part of my life, including my body and my desires. Help me to honor You in purity and to treat others with respect, never taking advantage of anyone. Thank You for Your Holy Spirit, who empowers me to live in a way that pleases You. Heal those who have been harmed by the sins of others, and forgive and restore those who have fallen. Teach me to love my brothers and sisters more and more, to live quietly, to do my work faithfully, and to be a good witness to those outside the church. Thank You, Lord Jesus, that You died and rose again. Comfort all who grieve with the hope of the resurrection. I look forward to the day when You will descend from heaven, when the dead in Christ will rise, and when we will be with You forever. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
