1 Timothy · Chapter 3 of 6

# 1 Timothy — Chapter 3

Chapter Theme: Leaders of Character and the Mystery of Godliness

[Read 1 Timothy 3 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/1TI03.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul affirms that desiring to serve as an overseer is a noble aspiration, and he describes the character such a leader must have: above reproach, faithful in marriage, self-controlled, sensible, respectable, hospitable, able to teach, not given to drunkenness, not violent but gentle, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money, managing his household well, not a recent convert, and well thought of by outsiders. Deacons, too, must be dignified, honest, not addicted to wine or greedy, holding the faith with a clear conscience, tested first, and faithful in their households; the women mentioned with them must be dignified, not slanderers, sober, and faithful in all things. Paul explains that he writes so that Timothy will know how people ought to conduct themselves in God’s household, the church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth, and he closes with a hymn celebrating the great mystery of godliness revealed in Christ.

## Chapter Background and Story

The church in Ephesus was being damaged by false teachers, some of whom may have been leaders within the church. When leaders go astray, the whole community suffers. So Paul gives Timothy clear guidance about the kind of people who should lead God’s people.

Paul describes two kinds of church leaders. “Overseers” (sometimes translated “bishops”) were responsible for leading, teaching, and caring for the church. In the New Testament, the term seems to be used interchangeably with “elders” (*Titus 1:5–7*; *Acts 20:17*, 28). “Servants” (often translated “deacons”) assisted in practical ministry and care. The exact structure of church leadership has developed differently in various Christian traditions, but the qualifications Paul lists remain a standard for leaders in every tradition.

What is striking about Paul’s list is how little it focuses on gifts, talent, or charisma, and how much it focuses on character. Only one item, being “good at teaching,” concerns ability. The rest concern the kind of person a leader is: at home, in the church, and in the community. Paul wants leaders whose lives display the gospel they proclaim.

### Qualifications for Overseers (*3:1–7*)

The opening of Paul’s list is studied below. “*one who rules his own house well, having children in subjection with all reverence*” (*v. 4*); “*(for how could someone who doesn’t know how to rule his own house take care of God’s assembly?)*” (*v. 5*) The home is a proving ground for leadership. A leader’s family life shows whether they can care for others with wisdom, patience, and love. “With all reverence” may describe the children’s respectful conduct or the father’s dignified manner of leading. Paul is not demanding perfect children; even godly parents may have children who struggle. The concern is a leader’s faithful, loving management of the household, not harsh control.

“*not a new convert, lest being puffed up he fall into the same condemnation as the devil*” (*v. 6*). New believers need time to grow. Putting them in leadership too quickly can lead to pride, the very sin that brought judgment on the devil.

“*Moreover he must have good testimony from those who are outside, to avoid falling into reproach and the snare of the devil*” (*v. 7*). A leader’s reputation in the wider community matters. If outsiders know a leader to be dishonest or immoral, the church’s witness suffers, and the leader becomes vulnerable to the devil’s traps.

### Qualifications for Deacons (*3:8–13*)

Paul’s instructions for deacons are studied below. “*Their wives in the same way must be reverent, not slanderers, temperate, and faithful in all things*” (*v. 11*). The Greek word here simply means “women.” It may refer to the wives of deacons, as the WEB translates it, or to women who served as deacons themselves. Those who favor the second reading point to Phoebe, whom Paul calls a “servant,” the same word as “deacon,” of the church at Cenchreae (*Romans 16:1*), and note that Paul does not give a similar instruction about the wives of overseers. Christians in different traditions have understood the verse in both ways. Either way, Paul expects these women to share the same high standard of character.

“*Let servants be husbands of one wife, ruling their children and their own houses well*” (*v. 12*). “*For those who have served well gain for themselves a good standing and great boldness in the faith which is in Christ Jesus*” (*v. 13*). Faithful service brings respect and deepens confidence in the faith.

### The Household of God (*3:14–15*)

The purpose of Paul’s instructions and the identity of the church are studied below.

### The Mystery of Godliness (*3:16*)

The hymn about Christ is studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *1 Timothy 3:1–3* — The Character of an Overseer

> *“This is a faithful saying: someone who seeks to be an overseer desires a good work. The overseer therefore must be without reproach, the husband of one wife, temperate, sensible, modest, hospitable, good at teaching; not a drinker, not violent, not greedy for money, but gentle, not quarrelsome, not covetous;”*
>
> — *1 Timothy 3:1–3* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“This is a faithful saying: someone who seeks to be an overseer desires a good work.” Paul affirms that wanting to serve as a church leader is good. Leadership is described as “a good work,” not a position of honor to grasp but a task of service.

Then Paul lists qualities a leader must have.

“Without reproach”: no one can rightly accuse them of serious wrongdoing. This is the summary quality; the rest explain it.

“The husband of one wife”: literally “a one-woman man.” This has been understood in several ways. Most interpreters agree it means, at minimum, a man who is faithful in marriage, not polygamous and not unfaithful. Some also understand it to exclude men who have divorced and remarried, though many others believe it does not, especially when the divorce occurred before conversion, for reasons Scripture permits, or when the person was the victim of abandonment or abuse. Some understand it to require that an overseer be married; most do not, since Paul himself was unmarried. The heart of the requirement is sexual and marital faithfulness.

“Temperate”: clear-minded, balanced, not given to excess. “Sensible”: self-controlled, wise in judgment. “Modest”: well-behaved, respectable. “Hospitable”: literally “a lover of strangers,” welcoming others into one’s home. “Good at teaching”: able to explain and defend the faith.

Verse 3 lists what a leader must not be. “Not a drinker”: not addicted to alcohol. “Not violent”: not a bully or physically aggressive. “Not greedy for money.” The positive alternative is “gentle,” gracious and forbearing. “Not quarrelsome”: not argumentative or contentious. “Not covetous”: not a lover of money.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This list shows that Christian leadership is fundamentally about character. Jesus taught that the greatest among His followers must be the servant of all (*Mark 10:43–45*). Peter urged elders to shepherd God’s flock willingly, not for shameful gain, and not lording it over others but being examples (*1 Peter 5:2–3*).

The qualities Paul lists are not unique to leaders. They are marks of Christian maturity that all believers are called to pursue. What makes leaders different is that they must already display these qualities consistently, because their example shapes others.

The exclusion of violent and quarrelsome people is important. Leaders who intimidate, bully, or abuse others are not qualified for leadership in Christ’s church, no matter how gifted they may be. Gentleness is a requirement, not an option. Churches have sometimes overlooked serious character flaws in gifted leaders, with devastating results for those harmed. This passage calls the church to take character seriously.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Churches can use this passage when choosing and evaluating leaders. Character, faithfulness, gentleness, and integrity should matter more than charisma, eloquence, or popularity. Leaders who become violent, abusive, greedy, or unfaithful should be held accountable and, when necessary, removed from leadership, with care and protection for those who have been harmed.

For those who aspire to leadership, this passage provides a roadmap for growth. The desire to lead is good, but it must be accompanied by a commitment to grow in character.

For all believers, these qualities describe what Christian maturity looks like: self-control, hospitality, gentleness, contentment, and faithfulness. Every believer can pursue them.

### *1 Timothy 3:8–10* — Deacons: Tested and Trustworthy

> *“Servants, in the same way, must be reverent, not double-tongued, not addicted to much wine, not greedy for money, holding the mystery of the faith in a pure conscience. Let them also first be tested; then let them serve if they are blameless.”*
>
> — *1 Timothy 3:8–10* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul turns to deacons, or “servants.” The word was used for those who waited on tables or served others. In *Acts 6:1–6*, the apostles appointed seven men to oversee the daily distribution of food to widows, a role many see as an early form of the deacon ministry.

“Servants, in the same way, must be reverent.” “Reverent” means dignified, worthy of respect, serious about their responsibilities.

“Not double-tongued”: not saying one thing to one person and something different to another. Deacons, who often moved among many households, needed to be honest and consistent in their speech.

“Not addicted to much wine, not greedy for money.” Deacons may have handled funds for the poor. Integrity with money was essential.

Verse 9: “holding the mystery of the faith in a pure conscience.” Deacons must hold firmly to the truth of the gospel, and their lives must match their beliefs. “The mystery of the faith” is the gospel, once hidden and now revealed.

Verse 10: “Let them also first be tested; then let them serve if they are blameless.” Before being given responsibility, deacons should be observed over time to see whether their character is consistent.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The qualifications for deacons parallel those for overseers, with the notable absence of the requirement to be “good at teaching.” Deacons served mainly in practical ministry. Yet their role was no less important. Serving others in practical ways is a sacred calling, reflecting Christ, who came “*not to be served but to serve*” (*Mark 10:45*).

The requirement of testing reflects wisdom. Character is revealed over time. Paul later warns Timothy not to lay hands on anyone hastily (*1 Timothy 5:22*). Churches protect themselves and their people by carefully observing potential leaders before appointing them.

“Holding the mystery of the faith in a pure conscience” again links belief and behavior. Throughout 1 Timothy, Paul emphasizes that sound doctrine and a clear conscience belong together (*1:5*, 19).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Every form of service in the church, whether leading worship, welcoming guests, managing finances, caring for the sick, teaching children, or cleaning the building, is a ministry. Those who serve in these ways can do so with dignity and seriousness, as service to Christ.

Churches can wisely give people opportunities to serve in smaller ways before entrusting them with greater responsibility. This allows character and faithfulness to be observed and gives people room to grow.

The call to be “not double-tongued” applies to all believers. Speaking honestly and consistently, without gossip or flattery, builds trust and reflects the truthfulness of God.

### *1 Timothy 3:15* — The Pillar and Ground of the Truth

> *“but if I wait long, that you may know how men ought to behave themselves in God’s house, which is the assembly of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth.”*
>
> — *1 Timothy 3:15* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul explains why he has written these instructions. He hoped to visit Timothy soon, but if he was delayed, he wanted Timothy to know “how men ought to behave themselves in God’s house.” The word “men” here means people generally. Paul’s instructions are about how the whole church community should live.

Paul then describes the church in three ways.

“God’s house.” The church is God’s household, His family. Believers are brothers and sisters, and God is their Father. This is why the qualifications for leaders focus so much on how they manage their own households.

“The assembly of the living God.” The church belongs to the living God, not to dead idols like those worshiped in Ephesus, especially Artemis. God is present and active among His people.

“The pillar and ground of the truth.” A pillar holds up a building; a foundation, or “ground,” supports it from below. The church’s role is to uphold, support, and display the truth of the gospel to the world. The great temple of Artemis in Ephesus was famous for its more than one hundred huge pillars. Paul presents the church as a living temple whose pillars hold up God’s truth.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse gives a high view of the church. It is not merely a human organization or a social club. It is God’s household and the community through which His truth is upheld in the world.

The church does not create truth. Truth comes from God and is revealed in Christ and in Scripture. But the church is called to hold it up, guard it, and proclaim it. When the church is faithful, the truth is visible to the world. When the church compromises, the truth is obscured.

This verse also explains why conduct matters. The church upholds the truth not only by teaching it but by living it. When believers live in love, holiness, and integrity, they display the truth. When they live in hypocrisy, division, or immorality, they undermine it. This is why Paul cares so deeply about the character of leaders and the behavior of the church.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can see their local church not as a place they attend but as a household they belong to. Each member has a role in upholding the truth, both by holding to sound teaching and by living in ways that reflect it.

This verse also calls churches to take seriously their responsibility to teach and guard the truth. In a world full of competing claims, the church should be a place where the gospel is clearly proclaimed and faithfully lived.

Finally, this verse invites believers to treat one another as family. In God’s household, members care for one another, support one another, and work together to display the truth of God to the world.

### *1 Timothy 3:16* — The Mystery of Godliness

> *“Without controversy, the mystery of godliness is great: God was revealed in the flesh, justified in the spirit, seen by angels, preached among the nations, believed on in the world, and received up in glory.”*
>
> — *1 Timothy 3:16* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul closes this chapter with what appears to be an early Christian hymn or creed. “Without controversy, the mystery of godliness is great.” “Without controversy” means “beyond question” or “as we all confess.” “The mystery of godliness” is the revealed truth that produces godliness, and its heart is Christ Himself.

The hymn has six lines, likely arranged in pairs:

“God was revealed in the flesh.” Some manuscripts read “He who was revealed.” Either way, the line describes the incarnation: the eternal Son of God became human.

“Justified in the spirit.” Christ was vindicated, shown to be righteous, by the Spirit, especially through His resurrection (*Romans 1:4*).

“Seen by angels.” The angels witnessed His resurrection and exaltation.

“Preached among the nations.” The gospel of Christ was proclaimed to Gentiles throughout the world.

“Believed on in the world.” People everywhere put their faith in Him.

“Received up in glory.” Christ ascended to heaven and was exalted at the Father’s right hand.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This hymn summarizes the whole story of Christ: His incarnation, resurrection, exaltation, proclamation, reception by faith, and ascension. It moves between earth and heaven: flesh and spirit, angels and nations, world and glory. Christ unites heaven and earth.

The placement of this hymn is significant. Paul has just called the church “the pillar and ground of the truth.” Now he states that truth: it is Christ. The truth the church upholds is not a set of abstract ideas but a person, Jesus Christ, revealed in the flesh and received up in glory.

The phrase “mystery of godliness” also connects belief with life. Knowing Christ produces godliness. The false teachers in Ephesus offered speculations that produced controversy (*1:4*). The true mystery, Christ Himself, produces godliness.

Early Christians often expressed their faith in hymns and creeds like this one, singing and confessing together the great truths of the gospel (*Philippians 2:6–11*; *Colossians 1:15–20*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This hymn invites believers to worship. The story of Christ, God revealed in human flesh, vindicated, proclaimed, believed, and glorified, is the greatest story ever told. Believers can meditate on each line and praise God for what it reveals.

It also reminds believers that the center of their faith is a person. Doctrine matters because it tells the truth about Christ. Godliness grows from knowing Him.

Finally, the line “preached among the nations, believed on in the world” encourages believers to take part in God’s mission. The story of Christ is meant to be told to everyone.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

First Timothy 3 shows that the church’s leaders must be people of godly character. Paul’s lists for overseers and deacons focus overwhelmingly on who a person is rather than what they can do: faithful in marriage, self-controlled, wise, hospitable, gentle, honest, not violent, not quarrelsome, not greedy, respected at home and in the community, and tested over time. Churches today can apply these standards carefully when choosing leaders and hold leaders accountable, especially when there are signs of abuse, greed, or deceit, always protecting those who have been harmed.

These qualities are not only for leaders. They describe Christian maturity, and every believer can pursue them. Faithful service, whether in leading, teaching, or practical ministry, is a good work that honors God.

Paul also gives a rich vision of the church: God’s household, the assembly of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth. The church upholds God’s truth not only by teaching it but by living it. Believers can treat their local church as a family they belong to and take part in upholding the truth through faithful lives.

Finally, the chapter closes with a hymn about Christ: revealed in the flesh, vindicated by the Spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among the nations, believed in throughout the world, and taken up in glory. This is the truth the church upholds and the source of all godliness. Believers can respond with worship and with a renewed commitment to share this great mystery with the world.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for the gift of Your church, God’s household, the assembly of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth. Raise up leaders of godly character for Your people: faithful, gentle, wise, hospitable, honest, and free from the love of money. Protect Your church from leaders who would harm, and bring healing to those who have been hurt. Shape my own character, so that I may be above reproach, self-controlled, gentle, and faithful in every part of my life. Help me to serve others with dignity and joy, as You came not to be served but to serve. Thank You for the great mystery of godliness: that You were revealed in the flesh, vindicated by the Spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among the nations, believed on in the world, and taken up in glory. Let my life uphold and display Your truth. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

1 Timothy · Chapter 4 of 6

# 1 Timothy — Chapter 4

Chapter Theme: Train Yourself in Godliness

[Read 1 Timothy 4 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/1TI04.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul warns that the Spirit has clearly said some will abandon the faith, following deceiving spirits and teachings that come from demons, spread by hypocritical liars whose consciences are seared. These teachers forbid marriage and demand abstinence from certain foods, though everything God created is good and is to be received with thanksgiving, made holy by God’s word and prayer. Paul urges Timothy to teach this truth and to reject godless myths, training himself in godliness, which has value for both this life and the life to come. Though young, Timothy is to be an example to believers in speech, conduct, love, faith, and purity, to devote himself to the public reading of Scripture, preaching, and teaching, not to neglect his spiritual gift, and to watch his life and doctrine closely, for in doing so he will save both himself and his hearers.

## Chapter Background and Story

The false teachers in Ephesus had a particular emphasis. In addition to their myths and speculations (*1 Timothy 1:4*), they promoted a strict form of self-denial. They forbade marriage and required people to avoid certain foods. This kind of teaching, often called asceticism, appeared in various forms in the ancient world. Some believed that the physical world, including the body, sexuality, and food, was inferior or even evil, and that true spirituality meant escaping or denying it as much as possible.

Paul strongly rejects this view. God created the physical world, and He declared it good (*Genesis 1:31*). Marriage and food are His gifts. The problem is not God’s creation but the sinful misuse of it. True godliness is not achieved by rejecting God’s gifts but by receiving them with thanksgiving and living for Him.

In the second half of the chapter, Paul turns to Timothy personally. Timothy may have felt intimidated by older and more assertive opponents. Paul encourages him to focus on his own spiritual growth, to set an example, and to remain faithful in teaching the truth.

### A Warning About Deception (*4:1–3*)

“*But the Spirit says expressly that in later times some will fall away from the faith, paying attention to seducing spirits and doctrines of demons*” (*v. 1*). “The Spirit says expressly” may refer to prophecies given in the early church, or to Jesus’ warnings about false prophets (*Mark 13:22*). “Later times” refers to the period between Christ’s first coming and His return, the time in which Paul and Timothy were living and in which the church still lives. Behind false teaching, Paul sees spiritual deception. It is not merely a human error; demonic forces are at work.

“*through the hypocrisy of men who speak lies, branded in their own conscience as with a hot iron*” (*v. 2*). The false teachers were hypocrites. Their consciences had been “branded,” either seared until they no longer felt anything, or marked as belonging to Satan, the way slaves were branded with their owner’s mark. Either way, these teachers had silenced their consciences.

“*forbidding marriage and commanding to abstain from foods which God created to be received with thanksgiving by those who believe and know the truth*” (*v. 3*). Paul identifies two specific teachings: a ban on marriage and restrictions on food. God’s purpose is studied below.

### Training in Godliness (*4:6–10*)

“*If you instruct the brothers of these things, you will be a good servant of Christ Jesus, nourished in the words of the faith and of the good doctrine which you have followed*” (*v. 6*). Timothy’s own spiritual health depends on being continually nourished by the truth. A good teacher is first a good learner. Paul’s call to spiritual training is studied below.

“*This saying is faithful and worthy of all acceptance*” (*v. 9*). “*For to this end we both labor and suffer reproach, because we have set our trust in the living God, who is the Savior of all men, especially of those who believe*” (*v. 10*). Paul’s hard work and suffering are motivated by hope in the living God. The phrase “Savior of all men, especially of those who believe” has been understood in several ways. Some understand it to mean that God is the preserver and benefactor of all people, giving them life and providing for them, while He is Savior in a special, eternal sense to believers. Others understand it to mean that God’s saving work is offered to all and is sufficient for all, but becomes effective for those who believe. A few understand it to mean that God will ultimately save all people, though most Christian traditions have not held this view, given Scripture’s teaching about judgment. All agree that God’s kindness extends to everyone and that believers have a special relationship with Him as their Savior.

### An Example to Believers (*4:11–16*)

“*Command and teach these things*” (*v. 11*). Paul’s personal encouragement to Timothy, and his charge to watch his life and teaching, are studied below.

“*Until I come, pay attention to reading, to exhortation, and to teaching*” (*v. 13*). “Reading” refers to the public reading of Scripture in worship, a practice inherited from the synagogue (*Luke 4:16–20*; *Acts 13:15*). In a time when most people did not own copies of Scripture, hearing it read aloud was essential. “Exhortation” is preaching that applies Scripture and encourages people to act on it. “Teaching” is instruction in doctrine. Together, these form the heart of the church’s ministry of the word.

“*Don’t neglect the gift that is in you, which was given to you by prophecy with the laying on of the hands of the elders*” (*v. 14*). Timothy had received a spiritual gift for ministry, confirmed by prophetic words and by the elders’ laying on of hands (see also *1 Timothy 1:18*; *2 Timothy 1:6*). Paul urges him not to let it lie unused. Gifts must be exercised and developed.

## Important Verses Explained

### *1 Timothy 4:4–5* — Everything God Created Is Good

> *“For every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving. For it is sanctified through the word of God and prayer.”*
>
> — *1 Timothy 4:4–5* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul answers the false teachers who forbade marriage and certain foods. “For every creature of God is good.” Everything God made is good. This echoes the creation account, where God repeatedly saw that what He had made was good, and at the end, “*very good*” (*Genesis 1:31*).

“And nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving.” God’s gifts, such as food and marriage, are not to be refused as if they were unspiritual or evil. They are to be received gratefully.

Verse 5: “For it is sanctified through the word of God and prayer.” “Sanctified” means set apart for God’s purposes, made holy. God’s word declares His creation good and gives guidelines for its proper use. Prayer, including the giving of thanks before meals, acknowledges God as the giver and dedicates His gifts to His glory.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This passage affirms the goodness of creation, a fundamental Christian conviction. The physical world is not evil or inferior. God made it, sustains it, and will one day renew it (*Romans 8:19–21*; *Revelation 21:1–5*). The incarnation itself, in which the Son of God took on a human body, affirms the goodness of physical life. The resurrection of the body confirms that God intends to redeem, not discard, His physical creation.

Jesus declared all foods clean (*Mark 7:18–19*), and Peter learned through a vision that he should not call unclean what God has made clean (*Acts 10:15*). Marriage, too, is a gift of God from the beginning (*Genesis 2:18–24*), honored by Jesus (*John 2:1–11*; *Matthew 19:4–6*).

This does not mean that every use of God’s gifts is right. Gluttony, drunkenness, and sexual immorality misuse God’s good gifts. And individuals may choose, for good reasons, to fast, to remain single, or to abstain from certain foods for health or conscience (*1 Corinthians 7:7*; *Romans 14:1–6*). Paul’s point is that such choices must never be imposed as requirements for spirituality, and God’s gifts must never be treated as evil in themselves.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can enjoy God’s good gifts, food, friendship, marriage, beauty, creativity, rest, with gratitude, seeing them as expressions of His generosity. A simple habit like giving thanks before meals can transform ordinary moments into acts of worship.

This passage also guards against spiritual pride based on self-denial. Some believers may feel more spiritual because of what they avoid. While self-discipline has value, true godliness is not measured by how much one denies oneself but by how faithfully one lives for God.

For those who have been taught that their bodies, desires, or physical needs are shameful, this passage brings freedom. God made the body good. Its desires are to be directed rightly, not despised.

### *1 Timothy 4:7–8* — Exercise Yourself Toward Godliness

> *“But refuse profane and old wives’ fables. Exercise yourself toward godliness. For bodily exercise has some value, but godliness has value in all things, having the promise of the life which is now and of that which is to come.”*
>
> — *1 Timothy 4:7–8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“But refuse profane and old wives’ fables.” Paul tells Timothy to reject the myths the false teachers were spreading. “Old wives’ fables” was a common expression for silly, superstitious tales. Paul is not insulting older women; he is using a familiar phrase for foolish stories.

“Exercise yourself toward godliness.” The word “exercise” is the root of the English word “gymnasium.” Greek culture valued athletic training highly. Every city had a gymnasium where young men trained their bodies. Paul uses this image for spiritual training. Godliness does not happen automatically; it requires discipline, effort, and consistent practice.

Verse 8: “For bodily exercise has some value, but godliness has value in all things.” Paul does not dismiss physical exercise; it has “some value.” But its value is limited to this life. Godliness, by contrast, “has value in all things.”

“Having the promise of the life which is now and of that which is to come.” Godliness benefits a person now, in this life, and for eternity. It shapes character, relationships, and peace in the present, and it prepares a person for eternal life with God.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The idea of spiritual training is common in Paul’s letters. In *1 Corinthians 9:24–27*, he compares the Christian life to running a race and says he disciplines his body so that he will not be disqualified. *Hebrews 5:14* speaks of those whose senses have been trained by practice to distinguish good from evil.

Godliness, which Paul mentions often in the Pastoral Letters, means a life oriented toward God, shaped by reverence for Him and expressed in holy living. It is not something earned but cultivated, a response to grace that grows through practice.

The contrast with the false teachers is important. They promoted physical disciplines, like avoiding certain foods and abstaining from marriage, as the path to spirituality. Paul redirects Timothy’s attention to the training that truly matters: growing in godliness through the word, prayer, and obedience.

Spiritual training is not a way of earning God’s favor. It is a way of positioning oneself to receive God’s grace and be transformed by it. Practices such as prayer, Scripture reading, worship, fellowship, service, and self-examination are like an athlete’s training: they build strength and endurance over time.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Many people invest significant time and money in physical fitness. Paul affirms that this has value. But he invites believers to give even greater attention to spiritual training.

Practical spiritual disciplines might include daily time in Scripture and prayer, regular worship with other believers, periods of silence or fasting, memorizing Scripture, serving others, and confessing sin. Like physical exercise, these practices may feel difficult at first but become more natural with time.

Believers can also be encouraged that the benefits of godliness are both present and eternal. Growing in godliness brings peace, wisdom, and joy now, and it prepares them for life with God forever.

### *1 Timothy 4:12* — An Example in Word, Life, Love, Faith, and Purity

> *“Let no man despise your youth; but be an example to those who believe, in word, in your way of life, in love, in spirit, in faith, and in purity.”*
>
> — *1 Timothy 4:12* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“Let no man despise your youth.” Timothy was probably in his thirties, which in the ancient world was considered young for a leader, especially compared with the elders of the church. Some may have looked down on him or dismissed his authority because of his age.

Paul’s solution is not for Timothy to demand respect but to earn it through his example. “But be an example to those who believe.” Timothy is to be a model that other believers can follow.

Paul lists five areas. “In word”: in his speech, which should be truthful, gracious, and edifying. “In your way of life”: in his conduct, his everyday behavior. “In love”: in his care for others. “In faith”: in his trust in God and his faithfulness. “In purity”: in his moral integrity, especially sexual purity.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that spiritual authority comes from character more than from age or position. Timothy did not need to be older to be respected. He needed to live in a way that showed the reality of his faith.

Scripture contains many examples of young people whom God used powerfully: Joseph, Samuel, David, Jeremiah, Daniel, and Mary. God told Jeremiah, “*Don't say, 'I am a child'*” (*Jeremiah 1:7*). Youth is not a barrier to faithful service.

The five areas Paul lists cover every part of life: speech, behavior, relationships, inner trust, and moral integrity. They describe a whole life shaped by Christ. An example is not merely something one tells others to do but something one shows them by living it.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Young believers can take this verse to heart. They do not need to wait until they are older to serve God or to influence others. They can be examples now, in how they speak, how they live, how they love, how they trust God, and how they keep themselves pure.

Older believers can also learn from this verse. Rather than dismissing younger believers, they can encourage and support them, recognizing the gifts God has given them.

For anyone in leadership, this verse is a reminder that the most powerful form of influence is example. People notice how leaders live, and that often speaks louder than their words.

### *1 Timothy 4:15–16* — Watch Your Life and Teaching

> *“Be diligent in these things. Give yourself wholly to them, that your progress may be revealed to all. Pay attention to yourself and to your teaching. Continue in these things, for in doing this you will save both yourself and those who hear you.”*
>
> — *1 Timothy 4:15–16* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“Be diligent in these things. Give yourself wholly to them, that your progress may be revealed to all.” Paul urges Timothy to throw himself fully into his ministry and spiritual growth. “Progress” was a word for advancing, like a pioneer cutting a path forward. As Timothy grows, others will see it.

Verse 16: “Pay attention to yourself and to your teaching.” Timothy must keep a close watch on two things: his own life and his teaching. Both are important. A leader with sound doctrine but a corrupt life does great harm, and so does a leader with a good life but false teaching.

“Continue in these things.” Faithfulness is not a one-time effort but a lifelong commitment.

“For in doing this you will save both yourself and those who hear you.” By persevering in godly living and sound teaching, Timothy will continue in salvation himself and will be the means through which others hear the gospel and are saved.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The phrase “save both yourself and those who hear you” does not mean that Timothy earns salvation by his efforts. Salvation is by grace through faith. But Scripture also teaches that those who are saved persevere in faith, and that God uses the faithful proclamation of the gospel to save others (*Romans 10:14–17*). Timothy’s faithfulness is the means God uses for his own perseverance and for the salvation of his hearers.

The pairing of life and teaching is a central theme of the Pastoral Letters. False teachers had wrong doctrine and wrong lives. Faithful leaders must have both sound doctrine and godly lives. Jesus warned against teachers who say but do not do (*Matthew 23:3*). Paul calls Timothy to integrity: his life and his teaching must match.

“Pay attention to yourself” is a reminder that leaders must care for their own souls. Those who serve others can neglect their own spiritual health. Paul tells Timothy to keep watch over himself first.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse applies especially to pastors, teachers, and leaders, but all believers can benefit from it. Everyone teaches in some way, whether to children, friends, coworkers, or through their example. And everyone’s life speaks.

Believers can regularly examine both their beliefs and their behavior. Are their beliefs rooted in Scripture? Is their life consistent with what they believe? Regular self-examination, honest friendships, and accountability help keep both in check.

For those in ministry, caring for one’s own soul is not selfish but essential. Rest, prayer, personal study of Scripture, and relationships of accountability help leaders stay healthy so they can continue to serve others well.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

First Timothy 4 warns that some will abandon the faith, deceived by teachings that ultimately come from the enemy. In Ephesus, these teachings forbade marriage and certain foods, presenting self-denial as the path to holiness. Paul responds by affirming the goodness of God’s creation: everything God made is good and is to be received with thanksgiving, made holy by God’s word and prayer. Believers today can enjoy God’s gifts gratefully, while guarding against both indulgence and false asceticism.

The chapter also calls believers to spiritual training. Just as athletes train their bodies, believers are to train themselves in godliness. Physical exercise has some value, but godliness has value in every way, bringing blessing in this life and the life to come. Practices such as prayer, Scripture reading, worship, and service help believers grow.

Paul’s personal encouragement to Timothy speaks to every believer, especially the young. Age is not a barrier to faithful service. Timothy was to be an example in speech, conduct, love, faith, and purity. He was to devote himself to the public reading of Scripture, preaching, and teaching, not to neglect his spiritual gift, and to throw himself wholeheartedly into his calling.

Finally, Paul’s charge to “pay attention to yourself and to your teaching” reminds all believers, and especially leaders, that both life and doctrine matter. Faithfulness in both brings blessing to oneself and to others. Persevering in godly living and sound teaching is the path God uses to keep His people and to bring others to salvation.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord, guard me from deception and from every teaching that leads people away from You. Thank You that everything You created is good. Help me to receive Your gifts with thanksgiving and to use them for Your glory. Train me in godliness. Give me discipline to pursue You through prayer, Scripture, worship, and service, and let my growth be seen in every part of my life. Make me an example to others in my speech, my conduct, my love, my faith, and my purity. Help me not to neglect the gifts You have given me, but to use them faithfully. Keep me watchful over my own life and over what I believe and teach. Let my life and my words point others to You, the living God, the Savior of all people, especially of those who believe. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

1 Timothy · Chapter 5 of 6

# 1 Timothy — Chapter 5

Chapter Theme: Caring for God’s Family with Honor and Justice

[Read 1 Timothy 5 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/1TI05.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul instructs Timothy to treat members of the church as family: older men as fathers, younger men as brothers, older women as mothers, and younger women as sisters, with complete purity. He gives detailed guidance for caring for widows, urging families to care for their own relatives and declaring that anyone who fails to provide for their household has denied the faith. The church is to support widows who are truly alone and devoted to God, while younger widows are encouraged to remarry. Paul then turns to elders: those who lead well, especially in preaching and teaching, deserve double honor and fair support, accusations against them must be confirmed by witnesses, and those who persist in sin must be rebuked publicly. Timothy is to act without partiality, not to appoint leaders hastily, and to keep himself pure, trusting that both sins and good works will eventually come to light.

## Chapter Background and Story

First Timothy 5 deals with practical questions of church life. How should a young leader relate to people of different ages and sexes? How should the church care for vulnerable members, especially widows? And how should leaders be honored, supported, and, when necessary, held accountable?

Widows were among the most vulnerable people in the ancient world. Women often depended on husbands or sons for financial support. When a husband died and there was no family to help, a widow could fall into poverty. From the beginning, the church cared for widows (*Acts 6:1*; *9:39*). But by the time of this letter, questions had arisen. Some families were neglecting their own widowed relatives and leaving the church to support them. Some younger widows on the church’s support list were becoming idle and spreading gossip. Paul gives guidance so that the church can care well for those in genuine need while encouraging families to fulfill their responsibilities.

The second half of the chapter addresses elders. Since false teaching had arisen partly through leaders, Timothy needed guidance on how to honor faithful elders and how to deal fairly with accusations against them.

### The Church as Family (*5:1–2*)

Paul’s instructions on relating to others as family are studied below.

### Caring for Widows (*5:3–16*)

“*Honor widows who are widows indeed*” (*v. 3*). “Honor” includes respect and, in this context, financial support. “Widows indeed” are those who are truly alone and without family to care for them.

“*But if any widow has children or grandchildren, let them learn first to show piety toward their own family and to repay their parents, for this is acceptable in the sight of God*” (*v. 4*). Caring for aging parents and grandparents is a form of godliness. It repays them for the care they once gave. The principle of family responsibility is studied below.

“*Now she who is a widow indeed and desolate, has her hope set on God and continues in petitions and prayers night and day*” (*v. 5*). The true widow has placed her hope in God. Like Anna in the temple (*Luke 2:36–37*), she devotes herself to prayer. “*But she who gives herself to pleasure is dead while she lives*” (*v. 6*). In contrast, a widow who lives for self-indulgence is spiritually dead even though she is physically alive.

“*Let no one be enrolled as a widow under sixty years old, having been the wife of one man*” (*v. 9*), “*being approved by good works, if she has brought up children, if she has been hospitable to strangers, if she has washed the saints’ feet, if she has relieved the afflicted, and if she has diligently followed every good work*” (*v. 10*). There seems to have been an official list of widows who received ongoing support and who, in turn, served the church through prayer and good works. To be enrolled, a widow had to be at least sixty, faithful in marriage, and known for good works such as hospitality, humble service, and care for the suffering. “Washed the saints’ feet” refers to humble acts of service, following Jesus’ example (*John 13:14*).

“*But refuse younger widows, for when they have grown wanton against Christ, they desire to marry*” (*v. 11*), “*having condemnation, because they have rejected their first pledge*” (*v. 12*). Enrolled widows may have pledged to remain unmarried and devote themselves to the Lord’s service. Younger widows who made such a pledge might later want to remarry, breaking their promise. Paul is not condemning remarriage; in verse 14 he encourages it. His concern is the breaking of a pledge.

“*Besides, they also learn to be idle, going about from house to house. Not only idle, but also gossips and busybodies, saying things which they ought not*” (*v. 13*). Some younger widows supported by the church had become idle and were spreading gossip, possibly including the false teaching circulating in Ephesus.

“*I desire therefore that the younger widows marry, bear children, rule the household, and give no occasion to the adversary for insulting*” (*v. 14*). Paul encourages younger widows to remarry and build households. This directly counters the false teachers who forbade marriage (*1 Timothy 4:3*). “*For already some have turned away after Satan*” (*v. 15*).

“*If any man or woman who believes has widows, let them relieve them, and don’t let the assembly be burdened, that it might relieve those who are widows indeed*” (*v. 16*). Believers with widowed relatives should care for them, so that the church’s resources can go to those who have no one else.

### Honoring and Correcting Elders (*5:17–25*)

Paul’s teaching on supporting and holding elders accountable is studied below.

“*Lay hands hastily on no one. Don’t be a participant in other people’s sins. Keep yourself pure*” (*v. 22*). “Lay hands” refers to appointing leaders. Timothy should not rush to appoint anyone. If he appoints an unqualified person who then does harm, he shares in the responsibility.

“*Be no longer a drinker of water only, but use a little wine for your stomach’s sake and your frequent infirmities*” (*v. 23*). This personal note shows Paul’s care for Timothy’s health. Timothy may have been avoiding wine entirely, perhaps to distance himself from those who drank excessively or in reaction to the false teachers’ asceticism. Water in the ancient world was often unsafe. Paul advises a little wine as medicine. This verse also shows that physical health matters and that using ordinary means, like medicine, is not a lack of faith.

“*Some men’s sins are evident, preceding them to judgment, and some also follow later*” (*v. 24*). “*In the same way also there are good works that are obvious, and those that are otherwise can’t be hidden*” (*v. 25*). Some people’s sins are obvious; others only come to light over time. The same is true of good works. This is why Timothy should not appoint leaders hastily. Over time, the truth about a person’s character will become clear.

## Important Verses Explained

### *1 Timothy 5:1–2* — Treating One Another as Family

> *“Don’t rebuke an older man, but exhort him as a father; the younger men as brothers; the elder women as mothers; the younger as sisters, in all purity.”*
>
> — *1 Timothy 5:1–2* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul gives Timothy guidance on relating to different members of the church. “Don’t rebuke an older man, but exhort him as a father.” The word “rebuke” here means to speak harshly or to strike with words. Timothy, as a younger leader, should not speak harshly to older men. Instead, he should appeal to them respectfully, as he would to his own father.

“The younger men as brothers.” Younger men should be treated as equals and companions, with brotherly affection.

“The elder women as mothers.” Older women deserve the respect, honor, and care one would give one’s own mother.

“The younger as sisters, in all purity.” Younger women should be treated as sisters, with complete moral purity. Timothy was to avoid any hint of impropriety, flirtation, or exploitation.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This passage reflects the deep truth that the church is a family. Believers are brothers and sisters in Christ, children of one Father (*Ephesians 2:19*; *1 Timothy 3:15*). Jesus said that whoever does the will of God is His brother, sister, and mother (*Mark 3:35*). This family identity shapes how believers treat one another: with respect, affection, and care.

The instruction “in all purity” is especially important. Leaders hold positions of trust, and those who are younger or vulnerable must be protected. Treating younger women as sisters means seeking their good and protecting them, never using a position of spiritual authority to pursue personal desires. Tragically, leaders in the church have sometimes abused their positions, causing deep harm. This verse sets a clear standard: any such behavior is a violation of the family love that should mark God’s household.

Paul’s guidance about correcting older men shows wisdom. Even when correction is needed, it should be given with respect. Leadership in the church is not about dominating others but about serving them as family.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can think of their church as a family and treat its members accordingly. This means showing respect and care to older members, friendship and support to peers, and protection and purity toward those who are younger or vulnerable.

When correction is needed, believers can approach it as family members would, with gentleness, respect, and a desire for the person’s good, rather than with harshness.

Churches can also take practical steps to ensure that relationships between leaders and members are safe and pure, such as clear boundaries, accountability, transparency, and policies that protect children and vulnerable adults. These practices honor the family nature of the church.

### *1 Timothy 5:8* — Providing for One’s Own

> *“But if anyone doesn’t provide for his own, and especially his own household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.”*
>
> — *1 Timothy 5:8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul makes a strong statement about family responsibility. “But if anyone doesn’t provide for his own, and especially his own household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.”

“Provide for” means to think ahead and care for the needs of others. “His own” refers to relatives in general, and “his own household” refers especially to immediate family members living in the same home.

Those who neglect their family’s needs have “denied the faith.” Their actions contradict the faith they profess. And they are “worse than an unbeliever,” because even many unbelievers care for their families. In the Greek and Roman world, caring for aging parents was a widely accepted duty. A believer who failed to do so would fall below the moral standard of the surrounding culture.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that faith is not merely a matter of words or religious activity. It must be expressed in practical care for others, beginning at home. *James 2:15–17* makes a similar point: if a brother or sister lacks food and clothing and someone says, “Go in peace,” without giving them what they need, that faith is dead.

Jesus Himself criticized religious leaders who used religious vows as an excuse to avoid supporting their parents (*Mark 7:9–13*). The fifth commandment, “Honor your father and mother,” includes caring for them in their old age.

This verse applies to those who are able to provide but choose not to. It does not condemn those who, because of poverty, illness, disability, or other circumstances, are unable to provide all that their families need. In those situations, the church and wider community are called to help.

It also does not require anyone to remain in or return to an abusive situation in order to “provide.” Caring for family members who have caused serious harm may look different, sometimes involving support at a safe distance or through others.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can consider how they are caring for their families, including aging parents, children, spouses, and extended relatives in need. This may involve financial support, practical help, time, or emotional care.

Caring for aging parents can be demanding, and caregivers often need support themselves. Churches can come alongside families who are caring for elderly or disabled relatives, offering practical help, respite, and encouragement.

This verse also reminds believers that faith begins at home. Generosity to the wider world is good, but it should not come at the expense of neglecting one’s own family.

### *1 Timothy 5:17–18* — Double Honor for Faithful Elders

> *“Let the elders who rule well be counted worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in the word and in teaching. For the Scripture says, ‘You shall not muzzle the ox when it treads out the grain.’ And, ‘The laborer is worthy of his wages.’”*
>
> — *1 Timothy 5:17–18* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul turns to church leaders. “Let the elders who rule well be counted worthy of double honor.” Elders who lead faithfully and effectively deserve “double honor,” which likely includes both respect and financial support. The word “honor” was used in verse 3 to include material support for widows.

“Especially those who labor in the word and in teaching.” Elders who work hard at preaching and teaching deserve special recognition. “Labor” suggests hard, exhausting work.

Verse 18 supports this with two quotations. “You shall not muzzle the ox when it treads out the grain.” This comes from *Deuteronomy 25:4*. In ancient farming, oxen walked over harvested grain to separate it from the stalks. The Law said they should not be muzzled, so they could eat as they worked. Paul uses this same verse in *1 Corinthians 9:9* to argue that those who work for the gospel should be supported.

“The laborer is worthy of his wages.” This is a saying of Jesus, recorded in *Luke 10:7*. Remarkably, Paul places it alongside a quotation from the Old Testament and introduces both with “the Scripture says.” This suggests that Jesus’ words, and perhaps Luke’s Gospel, were already being recognized as Scripture.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This passage teaches that faithful leaders should be supported. Those who devote themselves to preaching, teaching, and caring for God’s people should not be left in want. Paul himself sometimes gave up this right for the sake of the gospel (*1 Corinthians 9:12–18*), but he affirmed it as a principle.

At the same time, this honor is for those who “rule well.” It is not automatic. Leaders who are faithful, diligent, and godly deserve honor. Those who misuse their position do not.

The use of Jesus’ words as Scripture is significant for understanding how the early church viewed the teachings of Jesus. From very early on, His words carried the same authority as the Old Testament.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Churches can honor faithful leaders through respect, encouragement, prayer, and fair financial support. Pastors and teachers who labor faithfully in the word should not be underpaid or overworked to the point of exhaustion.

Believers can also express appreciation to those who teach and lead them, through words of thanks, practical help, or simply praying for them.

At the same time, honor should not become blind loyalty. Leaders are worthy of honor when they lead well. Honoring leaders includes holding them to the high standards God sets, as the following verses show.

### *1 Timothy 5:19–21* — Fair Accountability Without Partiality

> *“Don’t receive an accusation against an elder except at the word of two or three witnesses. Those who sin, reprove in the sight of all, that the rest also may be in fear. I command you in the sight of God, and the Lord Jesus Christ, and the chosen angels, that you observe these things without prejudice, doing nothing by partiality.”*
>
> — *1 Timothy 5:19–21* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul gives guidance for handling accusations against elders. “Don’t receive an accusation against an elder except at the word of two or three witnesses.” Leaders are often targets of criticism, sometimes unfair. This instruction protects them from malicious gossip or unfounded attacks. It follows the Old Testament principle that a matter must be established by two or three witnesses (*Deuteronomy 19:15*).

Verse 20: “Those who sin, reprove in the sight of all, that the rest also may be in fear.” When an elder is found to have sinned, and especially when they persist in it, the matter should be addressed openly before the church. Leaders are not above accountability. Public correction shows that sin is taken seriously and warns others.

Verse 21: “I command you in the sight of God, and the Lord Jesus Christ, and the chosen angels, that you observe these things without prejudice, doing nothing by partiality.” Paul gives this charge with great solemnity. Timothy must handle these matters fairly, without favoritism. He must not protect a leader because of friendship, popularity, or status, nor condemn someone because of personal dislike.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses balance two concerns: protecting leaders from false accusations and protecting the church from leaders who sin. Both matter. A church that believes every accusation harms innocent leaders. A church that protects leaders at all costs harms those who suffer from their sin.

The requirement of “two or three witnesses” must be understood rightly. It means that accusations should be carefully investigated and confirmed by evidence, not that only accusations with multiple eyewitnesses should be taken seriously. Many forms of serious wrongdoing, especially sexual abuse, often happen in private, with no other witnesses. In such cases, evidence can include patterns of behavior, multiple independent reports, and other corroborating information. Crimes such as abuse must be reported to civil authorities, who are equipped to investigate, and churches must never use this verse as a reason to dismiss or silence victims. Protecting the vulnerable is a clear biblical priority.

The command to act “without partiality” is crucial. Throughout Scripture, God condemns favoritism in judgment (*Leviticus 19:15*; *James 2:1–9*). Church leaders must be held to the same standard as everyone else, and in some ways a higher one (*James 3:1*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Churches need clear, fair processes for handling accusations against leaders. These processes should protect people from false accusations while ensuring that genuine wrongdoing is investigated thoroughly and addressed openly. Independent investigation and outside accountability can help ensure fairness.

Believers can resist gossip and rumors about leaders, while also refusing to ignore credible concerns. If someone has been harmed by a leader, their account deserves to be taken seriously, and they deserve care, protection, and support.

Finally, these verses call for courage. Addressing sin in leaders is difficult, especially when those leaders are popular or powerful. But faithfulness to God and love for the church require it.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

First Timothy 5 shows how the church can live as God’s family. Members are to treat one another as fathers, mothers, brothers, and sisters, with respect, affection, and complete purity. This family identity shapes every relationship and calls leaders especially to protect those who are younger or vulnerable.

The chapter gives careful guidance for caring for widows, which reveals principles that apply to every form of care for the vulnerable. Families have a primary responsibility to care for their own, and failing to do so contradicts the faith. The church should support those who are truly alone, while wisely encouraging those who are able to build their own lives. Faith is expressed in practical care, beginning at home.

Paul also teaches that faithful leaders deserve double honor, including respect and fair support, especially those who labor in preaching and teaching. Jesus’ own words, “The laborer is worthy of his wages,” support this principle.

At the same time, leaders are not above accountability. Accusations against them should be carefully investigated, and those who persist in sin should be corrected openly, without partiality or favoritism. This principle must never be used to silence victims or dismiss reports of abuse; serious wrongdoing must be taken seriously and reported to the proper authorities. Churches that honor faithful leaders and hold all leaders accountable reflect God’s justice and protect His people.

## Chapter Prayer

Father, thank You that Your church is a family. Help me to treat others in Your household with respect, affection, and purity, as fathers and mothers, brothers and sisters. Give me a heart to care for those who are vulnerable, especially widows, the elderly, and those who are alone. Help me to provide faithfully for my own family and to support those who care for aging or disabled loved ones. Thank You for faithful leaders who labor in Your word; help me to honor and support them. Give Your church wisdom and courage to hold leaders accountable, without partiality, and to protect and care for anyone who has been harmed. Keep me pure, and help me to live in such a way that my good works honor You. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
