1 Timothy · Chapter 6 of 6

# 1 Timothy — Chapter 6

Chapter Theme: Godliness with Contentment Is Great Gain

[Read 1 Timothy 6 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/1TI06.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul instructs believing servants to honor their masters so that God’s name and the teaching are not slandered, especially when their masters are fellow believers. He warns again against false teachers who are proud, love controversy, and think godliness is a way to get rich. In contrast, godliness with contentment is great gain, because we brought nothing into the world and can take nothing out; with food and clothing we can be content. Those who want to be rich fall into temptation and harmful desires, for the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. Paul charges Timothy, as a man of God, to flee these things, pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, endurance, and gentleness, and fight the good fight of faith until Christ appears. He tells Timothy to command the rich not to be proud or trust in uncertain riches but to hope in God, be rich in good works, and be generous. He ends by urging Timothy to guard what has been entrusted to him.

## Chapter Background and Story

The final chapter of 1 Timothy gathers several themes from the letter: the conduct of believers in society, the danger of false teachers, and Timothy’s personal faithfulness. But the theme that dominates the chapter is money. The false teachers in Ephesus apparently saw religion as a path to financial gain (v5). Ephesus was a wealthy commercial city, and the temple of Artemis functioned as a major bank. The pull of wealth was strong.

Paul responds with some of the most important teaching in the New Testament on contentment, greed, and generosity. He addresses both those who want to become rich and those who already are. His words are as relevant today, in a world shaped by consumerism and the pursuit of wealth, as they were in first-century Ephesus.

### Servants and Masters (*6:1–2*)

“*Let as many as are bondservants under the yoke count their own masters worthy of all honor, that the name of God and the doctrine not be blasphemed*” (*v. 1*). As in *Ephesians 6:5–9* and *Colossians 3:22–4:1*, Paul addresses believers living within the system of Roman slavery. His concern is that the conduct of Christian slaves would not bring dishonor on the gospel. If believing slaves became rebellious or disrespectful, outsiders might accuse Christianity of undermining society, and the gospel’s reputation would suffer.

“*Those who have believing masters, let them not despise them because they are brothers, but rather let them serve them, because those who partake of the benefit are believing and beloved. Teach and exhort these things*” (*v. 2*). Some slaves with Christian masters may have thought that, since they were now brothers in Christ, they no longer needed to serve faithfully. Paul says their shared faith should make them serve even more willingly.

As discussed in the commentary on *Ephesians 6*, these instructions are pastoral guidance for believers living in an unjust system that they could not change. They are not an endorsement of slavery. The same letter condemns slave-trading (*1 Timothy 1:10*), and Paul encouraged slaves to gain their freedom when possible (*1 Corinthians 7:21*). The gospel’s teaching that all are equal in Christ eventually helped lead many Christians to work for the abolition of slavery. Today, these verses can guide believers in how to work faithfully and honorably, always with the understanding that exploitation and abuse in any workplace are wrong.

### False Teachers and the Love of Gain (*6:3–5*)

“*If anyone teaches a different doctrine and doesn’t consent to sound words, the words of our Lord Jesus Christ, and to the doctrine which is according to godliness*” (*v. 3*), “*he is conceited, knowing nothing, but obsessed with arguments, disputes, and word battles, from which come envy, strife, insulting, evil suspicions*” (*v. 4*), “*constant friction of people of corrupt minds and destitute of the truth, who suppose that godliness is a means of gain. Withdraw yourself from such*” (*v. 5*). Paul describes the false teachers’ character. They were proud, ignorant, and obsessed with controversy. Their teaching produced envy, conflict, insults, and suspicion. And they used religion to make money. “Sound words” means healthy teaching, the opposite of the sickly, quarrelsome teaching of these men. Notice that Paul specifically mentions “the words of our Lord Jesus Christ” as the standard.

### Contentment and the Love of Money (*6:6–10*)

Paul’s teaching on contentment and the dangers of wealth is studied below.

### Fight the Good Fight (*6:11–16*)

Paul’s charge to Timothy is studied below. “*I command you before God who gives life to all things, and before Christ Jesus who before Pontius Pilate testified the good confession*” (*v. 13*), “*that you keep the commandment without spot, blameless until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ*” (*v. 14*). Jesus made a faithful confession before Pilate, affirming that He was a king whose kingdom is not of this world (*John 18:33–37*). Timothy is to be equally faithful.

“*which at the right time he will show, who is the blessed and only Ruler, the King of kings and Lord of lords*” (*v. 15*). “*He alone has immortality, dwelling in unapproachable light, whom no man has seen nor can see, to whom be honor and eternal power. Amen*” (*v. 16*). Paul breaks into praise. In a city where Artemis was worshiped and the emperor was honored as divine, Paul declares that God alone is the true Ruler, the King of kings and Lord of lords. He alone has immortality by nature. He dwells in light so brilliant no human can approach it. To Him belongs all honor and eternal power.

### Instructions for the Rich (*6:17–19*)

Paul’s charge to the wealthy is studied below.

### Guard the Deposit (*6:20–21*)

“*Timothy, guard that which is committed to you, turning away from the empty chatter and oppositions of what is falsely called knowledge*” (*v. 20*), “*which some profess, and thus have wandered from the faith. Grace be with you. Amen*” (*v. 21*). “That which is committed to you” is a deposit, like money left in someone’s safekeeping. The gospel has been entrusted to Timothy, and he must guard it faithfully. “What is falsely called knowledge” may refer to the false teachers’ claims to special insight. Paul ends with grace. The word “you” in the final blessing is plural, suggesting that the letter was meant to be shared with the whole church.

## Important Verses Explained

### *1 Timothy 6:6–8* — Godliness with Contentment

> *“But godliness with contentment is great gain. For we brought nothing into the world, and we certainly can’t carry anything out. But having food and clothing, we will be content with that.”*
>
> — *1 Timothy 6:6–8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The false teachers thought godliness was a means of financial gain (v5). Paul turns this idea around. “But godliness with contentment is great gain.” Godliness does bring great gain, not necessarily money, but something far more valuable, when it is combined with contentment.

“Contentment” means being satisfied with what one has, free from the restless desire for more. The word was used by Greek philosophers for self-sufficiency. For Paul, contentment comes not from self-sufficiency but from Christ’s sufficiency (*Philippians 4:11–13*).

Verse 7 gives the reason: “For we brought nothing into the world, and we certainly can’t carry anything out.” Every person enters life with nothing and leaves with nothing. Job said the same thing after losing everything: “*Naked I came out of my mother’s womb, and naked will I return there*” (*Job 1:21*). Possessions are temporary.

Verse 8: “But having food and clothing, we will be content with that.” The word for “clothing” can include shelter. Paul is describing basic necessities. Having what one needs to live, believers can be content.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Contentment is a rare and precious virtue. Our culture often encourages the opposite: constant dissatisfaction, the desire for more and better, and comparison with others. Advertising thrives on making people feel that they lack something. The Bible offers a different way.

Contentment is not laziness or indifference to legitimate needs. Nor does it mean that poverty is good or that believers should not work to improve their circumstances or help others out of poverty. It means not being controlled by the desire for more. *Hebrews 13:5* urges believers to be free from the love of money and content with what they have, because God has promised never to leave or forsake them. The deepest source of contentment is God’s presence.

Jesus taught His followers not to store up treasures on earth but in heaven (*Matthew 6:19–21*), and not to worry about food and clothing, because their heavenly Father knows what they need (*Matthew 6:25–33*). Contentment flows from trust in God’s provision.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can cultivate contentment by practicing gratitude for what they have, resisting the pressure to compare themselves with others, and reflecting on the temporary nature of possessions.

Practical steps might include limiting exposure to advertising, simplifying one’s lifestyle, distinguishing between needs and wants, and regularly thanking God for His provision. Contentment can also be strengthened by remembering that one’s identity and security come from God, not from what one owns.

For those who struggle with real financial hardship, this passage is not a call to accept injustice or neglect. Believers and churches are called to help meet one another’s needs. But even in hardship, contentment in God’s presence can bring peace.

### *1 Timothy 6:9–10* — The Love of Money

> *“But those who are determined to be rich fall into a temptation, a snare, and many foolish and harmful lusts, such as drown men in ruin and destruction. For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. Some have been led astray from the faith in their greed, and have pierced themselves through with many sorrows.”*
>
> — *1 Timothy 6:9–10* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul now warns about the dangers of wanting to be rich. “But those who are determined to be rich fall into a temptation, a snare, and many foolish and harmful lusts, such as drown men in ruin and destruction.”

Notice that Paul speaks of those “determined to be rich,” those whose goal and desire is wealth. This desire leads to three dangers. It brings “temptation,” pressures to compromise and cut corners. It becomes “a snare,” a trap that catches and holds. And it leads to “many foolish and harmful lusts,” desires that are both senseless and destructive. The end result is like drowning: “ruin and destruction.”

Verse 10: “For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil.” This verse is often misquoted as “money is the root of all evil.” But Paul does not say money itself is evil. He says the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. Greed can lead to lying, stealing, exploitation, broken relationships, and countless other sins.

“Some have been led astray from the faith in their greed, and have pierced themselves through with many sorrows.” The pursuit of money has caused some to abandon their faith. And it brings pain: anxiety, broken relationships, regret, and emptiness.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Jesus warned repeatedly about the dangers of wealth. He said, “*You can't serve both God and Mammon*” (*Matthew 6:24*). He told the parable of the rich fool, who stored up wealth but was not rich toward God (*Luke 12:16–21*). He said it is hard for the rich to enter the kingdom of God (*Mark 10:23–25*). And He described how the deceitfulness of riches can choke the word of God (*Mark 4:19*).

The love of money is a form of idolatry (*Colossians 3:5*). It places wealth in the position that belongs to God, as the source of security, identity, and happiness. When money becomes an idol, it demands sacrifices: time, relationships, integrity, and faith.

The image of those who have “*pierced themselves through with many sorrows*” (*v. 10*) is vivid. Those who pursue wealth often discover that it does not satisfy. Instead, it brings pain. *Ecclesiastes 5:10* says that whoever loves money will never be satisfied with money.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can examine their hearts for the love of money. Signs might include constant worry about finances, envy of others’ wealth, willingness to compromise integrity for financial gain, neglect of relationships for the sake of work, or difficulty being generous.

This passage does not condemn working hard, earning a good income, or saving responsibly. Scripture commends diligence and wise planning (*Proverbs 6:6–8*; *21:20*). The problem is when money becomes the goal rather than a tool.

Generosity is one of the most effective antidotes to the love of money. Regularly giving to God’s work and to those in need loosens money’s grip on the heart.

### *1 Timothy 6:11–12* — Flee, Follow, Fight

> *“But you, man of God, flee these things, and follow after righteousness, godliness, faith, love, perseverance, and gentleness. Fight the good fight of faith. Take hold of the eternal life to which you were called, and you confessed the good confession in the sight of many witnesses.”*
>
> — *1 Timothy 6:11–12* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul turns to Timothy personally. “But you, man of God.” This title was used in the Old Testament for prophets and leaders like Moses, Samuel, and Elijah. Paul honors Timothy as one who belongs to God and serves Him.

“Flee these things.” Timothy must run away from the love of money and the corrupt behavior of the false teachers.

“And follow after righteousness, godliness, faith, love, perseverance, and gentleness.” Fleeing is not enough. Timothy must pursue godly qualities. “Righteousness” is doing what is right. “Godliness” is reverence for God shown in life. “Faith” is trust in God, or faithfulness. “Love” is self-giving care for others. “Perseverance” is steadfast endurance. “Gentleness” is a meek and humble spirit.

Verse 12: “Fight the good fight of faith.” The Christian life involves struggle. The word for “fight” was used for athletic contests, suggesting effort, discipline, and determination.

“Take hold of the eternal life to which you were called.” Timothy is to grasp firmly the eternal life God has given him, living in light of it.

“And you confessed the good confession in the sight of many witnesses.” Timothy had publicly declared his faith, perhaps at his baptism or ordination. He is to remain faithful to that confession.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses describe the Christian life with three verbs: flee, follow, and fight. Believers must flee from sin and temptation (*2 Timothy 2:22*; *1 Corinthians 6:18*; *10:14*). They must pursue godly character. And they must fight the good fight of faith, standing firm against everything that opposes it.

The list of qualities to pursue overlaps with the fruit of the Spirit (*Galatians 5:22–23*). These are not achievements earned by effort alone but qualities the Spirit produces as believers cooperate with His work.

“Take hold of the eternal life” is a striking phrase. Eternal life is already given to believers, yet they are called to grasp it, to live in its reality. This is the tension of the Christian life: believers already possess salvation, and they are called to live it out fully.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can ask what they need to flee from: greed, pride, sexual temptation, bitterness, or other sins. Fleeing may mean avoiding certain places, people, media, or situations.

They can also ask what qualities they need to pursue. Rather than simply avoiding sin, the Christian life is an active pursuit of godliness, love, and faithfulness.

The call to “fight the good fight” reminds believers that the Christian life is not always easy. There will be struggles, temptations, and discouragement. But it is a good fight, worth fighting, and God gives strength for it.

### *1 Timothy 6:17–19* — Rich in Good Works

> *“Charge those who are rich in this present age that they not be arrogant, nor have their hope set on the uncertainty of riches, but on the living God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy; that they do good, that they be rich in good works, that they be ready to distribute, willing to share; laying up in store for themselves a good foundation against the time to come, that they may lay hold of eternal life.”*
>
> — *1 Timothy 6:17–19* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul now addresses those who are already wealthy. He does not tell them to give away everything, nor does he condemn them for being rich. Instead, he gives them instructions.

“Charge those who are rich in this present age that they not be arrogant.” Wealth can lead to pride, a sense of superiority over others. The rich must guard against this.

“Nor have their hope set on the uncertainty of riches.” Wealth is uncertain. It can be lost through economic collapse, theft, illness, or disaster. *Proverbs 23:5* says that riches sprout wings and fly away. The rich should not trust in their wealth.

“But on the living God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy.” Hope should be placed in God, who is the source of every good gift. Notice that God gives things “to enjoy.” Paul does not say wealth is evil or that believers should feel guilty about enjoying God’s gifts.

Verse 18: “that they do good, that they be rich in good works, that they be ready to distribute, willing to share.” The rich are to use their wealth to do good, becoming “rich” in a different sense, rich in good deeds. They should be generous and eager to share.

Verse 19: “laying up in store for themselves a good foundation against the time to come, that they may lay hold of eternal life.” Generosity is like storing up treasure for eternity. It reflects and strengthens a life focused on what truly lasts.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This passage gives a balanced view of wealth. Being rich is not a sin in itself, but it brings special temptations and responsibilities. The rich must avoid pride and misplaced trust and must use their wealth generously.

Jesus taught similar principles. He told His followers to store up treasures in heaven (*Matthew 6:19–20*) and to use worldly wealth to make friends for eternity (*Luke 16:9*). Zacchaeus, after meeting Jesus, gave half his possessions to the poor and repaid those he had cheated (*Luke 19:8*). His generosity was a sign of his transformed heart.

The phrase “who richly provides us with everything to enjoy” is a beautiful reminder of God’s generosity. God is not stingy. He delights to give good gifts. Believers who recognize this become generous themselves.

“Laying up in store... a good foundation against the time to come” does not mean buying salvation through good works. Salvation is by grace. Rather, generosity shows where one’s heart is and reflects a life oriented toward eternity.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

By global standards, many people in wealthy nations are “rich in this present age.” This passage speaks directly to them. Believers can guard against pride, place their hope in God rather than in savings or investments, and use their resources generously.

Generosity can take many forms: giving to the church, supporting missions, helping the poor, funding ministries, sharing possessions, and showing hospitality. It can also include giving time, skills, and attention.

Believers can also enjoy God’s gifts with gratitude. Paul does not call for guilt over every pleasure, but for a heart that receives God’s gifts thankfully and shares them freely.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

First Timothy 6 speaks powerfully to a world shaped by the pursuit of wealth. Paul warns against false teachers who saw religion as a way to make money, and he offers a better path: godliness with contentment is great gain. Since people bring nothing into the world and take nothing out, believers can be content with what they need, trusting God’s provision.

The chapter also warns that the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. Those who are determined to become rich fall into temptation, traps, and harmful desires that can destroy their lives and lead them away from faith. Believers can examine their hearts, resist greed, and practice generosity as a remedy against money’s grip.

Paul’s charge to Timothy applies to every believer: flee from sin, pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, endurance, and gentleness, and fight the good fight of faith. Believers are called to take hold of the eternal life God has given them and to remain faithful to their confession until Christ appears.

For those who are wealthy, the instructions are clear: do not be proud, do not trust in uncertain riches, hope in God who richly provides everything to enjoy, and be rich in good works, generous, and willing to share. In this way, believers lay up a foundation for the future and take hold of true life.

Finally, Paul urges Timothy to guard what has been entrusted to him. Every believer has received the treasure of the gospel. Guarding it faithfully, living it out, and passing it on are among the greatest responsibilities and privileges of the Christian life.

## Chapter Prayer

Father, You richly provide me with everything to enjoy. Thank You for Your generosity. Teach me that godliness with contentment is great gain. Free me from the love of money and the restless desire for more. Remind me that I brought nothing into this world and can take nothing out. Help me to be content with what I have and to trust You for what I need. Guard me from pride and from placing my hope in uncertain riches. Make me rich in good works, generous, and eager to share. Help me to flee from sin and to pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, endurance, and gentleness. Give me strength to fight the good fight of faith and to take hold of eternal life. You are the blessed and only Ruler, the King of kings and Lord of lords. To You be honor and eternal power. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Book 16 of 27

# 2 Timothy

## About This Letter

Second Timothy is Paul’s last known letter, written from prison in Rome shortly before his death. His circumstances were very different from his earlier, gentler house arrest (*Acts 28:30–31*). Now he was chained like a criminal (*2 Timothy 1:16*; *2:9*), many of his friends had deserted him (*1:15*; *4:10*, 16), and he expected to be executed soon: “the time of my departure has come” (*4:6*). Early Christian tradition holds that Paul was beheaded in Rome during the persecution under the emperor Nero, around A.D. 64–67.

As with 1 Timothy and Titus, most Christians through history have accepted the letter as Paul’s own, while some modern scholars think a follower wrote it in his name; others note that its intensely personal details, names, and requests are hard to explain unless Paul wrote it. Timothy was still serving in Ephesus, where false teaching continued to threaten the church. Paul writes to encourage his beloved son in the faith to be strong, to suffer for the gospel without shame, to guard and pass on the truth, and to come to him quickly before winter.

## The Shape of the Letter

In chapter 1, Paul thanks God for Timothy’s sincere faith, urges him to fan into flame the gift of God, reminds him that God gave a spirit of power, love, and self-control rather than fear, and calls him not to be ashamed of the gospel or of Paul’s chains. In chapter 2, he calls Timothy to be strong in grace and to entrust the teaching to faithful people, using images of a soldier, an athlete, a farmer, a worker who correctly handles the word of truth, and a vessel for honorable use, and urging gentleness toward opponents. In chapter 3, he warns that difficult times will come, describes the character of people in the last days, and points Timothy to his own example and to the God-breathed Scriptures, which are able to make him wise for salvation. In chapter 4, Paul solemnly charges Timothy to preach the word in season and out of season, looks back on his own life as a finished race and forward to the crown of righteousness, and closes with personal requests and greetings.

## Themes to Watch For

Watch for courage instead of fear, suffering for the gospel, the power of God’s grace, guarding the good deposit and passing it on to others, endurance, the trustworthiness of God even when people are faithless, the inspiration and usefulness of Scripture, the call to preach, faithfulness to the end, and the hope of the crown of righteousness. Second Timothy is a father’s farewell to his son in the faith, and it speaks to every believer who wants to finish well.

## Chapters

2.  [2 Timothy 2](#c16_2TI_002.xhtml) — Strong in Grace, Faithful in the Word
3.  [2 Timothy 3](#c16_2TI_003.xhtml) — Difficult Times and the God-Breathed Scriptures
4.  [2 Timothy 4](#c16_2TI_004.xhtml) — Finishing the Race and Keeping the Faith

2 Timothy · Chapter 1 of 4

# 2 Timothy — Chapter 1

Chapter Theme: Not a Spirit of Fear

[Read 2 Timothy 1 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/2TI01.htm)

Main Teaching

Writing from prison near the end of his life, Paul thanks God for Timothy, remembers his tears, and recalls the sincere faith that first lived in Timothy’s grandmother Lois and mother Eunice. He urges Timothy to fan into flame the gift of God, for God has not given a spirit of fear but of power, love, and self-control. Timothy must not be ashamed of the testimony about the Lord or of Paul’s chains, but share in suffering for the gospel by God’s power. God saved and called His people by His own purpose and grace, given in Christ before time began and now revealed through Christ, who abolished death and brought life and immortality to light. Paul is not ashamed, because he knows whom he has believed and is convinced He is able to guard what has been entrusted to Him. He urges Timothy to hold to sound teaching and guard the good deposit, and he contrasts those who deserted him with Onesiphorus, who sought him out and was not ashamed of his chains.

## Chapter Background and Story

When Paul wrote this letter, he was in a cold Roman prison, chained and facing death. He knew his time was short (*2 Timothy 4:6*). Many of his companions had left him. He longed to see Timothy one more time.

Timothy, meanwhile, was still in Ephesus, dealing with false teachers and the pressures of leadership. He may have been tempted toward fear or discouragement. Christianity was increasingly dangerous. Nero’s persecution had made it costly to be associated with the faith, and even more costly to be associated with a prisoner like Paul. Some believers had distanced themselves from Paul to protect themselves.

In this chapter, Paul writes with deep tenderness to encourage Timothy to be courageous. He reminds him of his spiritual heritage, of the gift God gave him, of the power of the gospel, and of the faithfulness of God. The chapter is a call to boldness rooted in grace.

### Thanksgiving and Remembrance (*1:1–5*)

“*Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God, according to the promise of the life which is in Christ Jesus*” (*v. 1*). Even facing death, Paul speaks of “the promise of the life which is in Christ Jesus.” Death would not end his life; it would bring him into the fullness of life with Christ.

“*to Timothy, my beloved child: Grace, mercy, and peace, from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord*” (*v. 2*). In 1 Timothy, Paul called him “my true child”; here, “my beloved child.” The affection is deep.

“*I thank God, whom I serve as my forefathers did, with a pure conscience. How unceasing is my memory of you in my petitions, night and day*” (*v. 3*) “*longing to see you, remembering your tears, that I may be filled with joy*” (*v. 4*). Paul’s service to God continued the faith of his Jewish ancestors; he saw faith in Christ as the fulfillment of that heritage. He remembers Timothy’s tears, perhaps from their last parting. He longs to see him again. Timothy’s spiritual heritage is studied below.

### Fan into Flame the Gift (*1:6–7*)

Paul’s call to stir up the gift, and his reminder about the spirit God gives, are studied below.

### Do Not Be Ashamed (*1:8–12*)

Paul’s call to unashamed courage and his description of the gospel are studied below. “*For this I was appointed as a preacher, an apostle, and a teacher of the Gentiles*” (*v. 11*). Paul’s whole life was devoted to proclaiming this gospel. Paul’s confidence in the face of suffering is studied below.

### Guard the Good Deposit (*1:13–14*)

“*Hold the pattern of sound words which you have heard from me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus*” (*v. 13*). A “pattern” is a model or outline, like an architect’s sketch. Timothy is to keep Paul’s teaching as his standard. And he is to hold it “in faith and love,” not coldly or harshly, but with trust in Christ and love for people.

“*That good thing which was committed to you, guard through the Holy Spirit who dwells in us*” (*v. 14*). The gospel is a precious deposit entrusted to Timothy. He cannot guard it in his own strength, but he can guard it through the Holy Spirit, who lives in him and in all believers.

### Deserters and a Faithful Friend (*1:15–18*)

“*This you know, that all who are in Asia turned away from me, of whom are Phygelus and Hermogenes*” (*v. 15*). “Asia” refers to the Roman province whose capital was Ephesus. Many believers there, perhaps out of fear, had distanced themselves from Paul. This does not necessarily mean they abandoned the faith, but they abandoned Paul in his hour of need. This must have been deeply painful.

“*May the Lord grant mercy to the house of Onesiphorus, for he often refreshed me, and was not ashamed of my chain*” (*v. 16*), “*but when he was in Rome, he sought me diligently and found me*” (*v. 17*) “*(the Lord grant to him to find the Lord’s mercy in that day); and in how many things he served at Ephesus, you know very well*” (*v. 18*). In contrast, Onesiphorus was a faithful friend. When he came to Rome, he searched hard for Paul, which may have been difficult and dangerous in a large city full of prisons, and when he found him, he refreshed him. He was not ashamed of Paul’s chains. Some interpreters think Onesiphorus may have died, since Paul prays for his household and for mercy for him “in that day.” Whatever the case, his loyalty stands as a beautiful example of courageous friendship.

## Important Verses Explained

### *2 Timothy 1:5* — A Sincere Faith Passed Down

> *“having been reminded of the sincere faith that is in you, which lived first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice and, I am persuaded, in you also.”*
>
> — *2 Timothy 1:5* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul remembers Timothy’s faith. “Having been reminded of the sincere faith that is in you.” “Sincere” means without hypocrisy, genuine, unmasked. Timothy’s faith was real.

“Which lived first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice.” Timothy’s faith had been passed down through two generations of women. *Acts 16:1* tells us that Timothy’s mother was a Jewish believer and his father was Greek. His father may not have been a believer. Timothy’s mother and grandmother had taught him the Scriptures from childhood (*2 Timothy 3:15*), and they had come to faith in Christ, probably during Paul’s first visit to Lystra (*Acts 14:6–20*).

“And, I am persuaded, in you also.” Paul is confident that the same genuine faith now lives in Timothy.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse highlights the powerful role of family in passing on faith. Lois and Eunice did not have public ministries recorded in Scripture, but their faithful influence shaped one of the most important leaders of the early church. They taught Timothy the Scriptures, modeled genuine faith, and prepared him to receive the gospel.

The Old Testament emphasizes the responsibility of parents to teach their children about God (*Deuteronomy 6:6–7*; *Psalm 78:4–7*). Lois and Eunice fulfilled that calling. Their example also shows that faith can thrive even in a home where not everyone shares it.

At the same time, faith cannot simply be inherited. Each generation must come to genuine faith for themselves. Paul says the faith “lived first” in Lois and Eunice and now lives in Timothy. It was the same faith, but Timothy had to make it his own.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Parents, grandparents, and other family members can have a profound influence on the faith of children. Teaching them Scripture, praying with them, living out a genuine faith, and creating a home where faith is natural and real can plant seeds that bear fruit for generations.

This verse also encourages those who are raising children in homes where not everyone shares their faith. Eunice’s husband was likely not a believer, yet her faith shaped Timothy. Faithful influence matters.

For those who did not grow up in a home of faith, this verse is not a cause for discouragement. God can call anyone to faith. And they can become the first generation to pass faith on to those who come after them.

### *2 Timothy 1:6–7* — Power, Love, and Self-Control

> *“For this cause, I remind you that you should stir up the gift of God which is in you through the laying on of my hands. For God didn’t give us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control.”*
>
> — *2 Timothy 1:6–7* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“For this cause, I remind you that you should stir up the gift of God which is in you through the laying on of my hands.” “Stir up” means to rekindle, to fan into flame. The image is of a fire that has burned low and needs to be stirred so that it blazes again. Timothy had received a spiritual gift for ministry when Paul and the elders laid hands on him (*1 Timothy 4:14*). Paul urges him to keep it burning brightly.

Verse 7: “For God didn’t give us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control.” Timothy may have been naturally timid, and the dangers of the time could make anyone afraid. Paul reminds him that the Spirit God gives is not a spirit of cowardice.

Instead, God gives a spirit “of power”: the strength to serve, to speak, and to endure. “Of love”: care for others that motivates courageous action. And “of self-control”: a sound, disciplined, sensible mind, able to think clearly under pressure.

The word “spirit” may refer to the Holy Spirit or to the disposition God gives. Most interpreters see a reference to the Holy Spirit, who produces these qualities in believers.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Fear is a natural human response to danger, and Scripture does not condemn every feeling of fear. Even Jesus felt deep distress in Gethsemane (*Mark 14:33–34*). But fear must not control God’s people or keep them from obeying God. The Bible repeatedly commands, “Don’t be afraid,” because God is with His people (*Joshua 1:9*; *Isaiah 41:10*).

The three qualities Paul names balance one another. Power without love can become harsh. Love without power can become weak. And both need self-control, a clear and disciplined mind. Together they describe a healthy, courageous, Christlike character.

The image of fanning a flame suggests that spiritual gifts and passion can grow dim through neglect, discouragement, or fear. They need to be stirred up through prayer, use, and reliance on the Spirit.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Many believers struggle with fear: fear of failure, rejection, conflict, the future, or speaking about their faith. This verse reminds them that God’s Spirit gives power, love, and a sound mind. They can ask Him to strengthen them in moments of fear.

Believers can also “stir up” their gifts by using them. Gifts grow through practice. Those who have let their passion for God or their sense of calling grow cold can ask God to rekindle it and take small steps of obedience.

For those who struggle with anxiety disorders or persistent fear, this verse is not a rebuke. God understands human frailty. His Spirit brings comfort and strength, and help from counselors, doctors, and trusted friends can also be part of how He brings peace.

### *2 Timothy 1:8–10* — Do Not Be Ashamed of the Gospel

> *“Therefore don’t be ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, nor of me his prisoner; but endure hardship for the Good News according to the power of God, who saved us and called us with a holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace, which was given to us in Christ Jesus before times eternal, but has now been revealed by the appearing of our Savior, Christ Jesus, who abolished death, and brought life and immortality to light through the Good News.”*
>
> — *2 Timothy 1:8–10* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“Therefore don’t be ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, nor of me his prisoner.” In the Roman world, being associated with a condemned prisoner was shameful and dangerous. Paul urges Timothy not to be ashamed of the gospel or of Paul himself. Notice that Paul calls himself “his prisoner,” the Lord’s prisoner, not Rome’s.

“But endure hardship for the Good News according to the power of God.” Rather than avoiding suffering, Timothy should share in it, relying on God’s power.

Verse 9 describes God: “who saved us and called us with a holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace.” Salvation is entirely God’s work. He saved believers and called them to a holy life, not because of anything they had done but because of His own purpose and grace.

“Which was given to us in Christ Jesus before times eternal.” God’s grace was planned and given in Christ before the world began.

Verse 10: “but has now been revealed by the appearing of our Savior, Christ Jesus, who abolished death, and brought life and immortality to light through the Good News.” What God planned from eternity has now been revealed in history through Jesus’ coming. Christ “abolished death,” broke its power, through His death and resurrection. And He “brought life and immortality to light,” revealing the eternal life God offers through the gospel.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses explain why believers need not be ashamed of the gospel, even when it brings suffering. The gospel is the message of God’s eternal purpose, His grace given before time began, and Christ’s victory over death. It is the most glorious news in the world.

Paul wrote in *Romans 1:16*, “*For I am not ashamed of the Good News of Christ, because it is the power of God for salvation for everyone who believes*” (*Romans 1:16*). Jesus also warned that whoever is ashamed of Him and His words, He will be ashamed of when He comes in glory (*Mark 8:38*).

The statement that Christ “abolished death” does not mean that believers will not die physically. It means that death has been defeated and no longer has the final word. Paul writes in *1 Corinthians 15:54–57* that death has been swallowed up in victory through Christ. For believers, death is no longer an enemy to be feared but a doorway to life.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

In many places today, being openly Christian can bring ridicule, social exclusion, or even persecution. These verses encourage believers not to be ashamed of the gospel or of fellow believers who suffer for it. Standing with persecuted Christians, through prayer, advocacy, and support, is a way of living out this command.

Believers can also take comfort that their salvation does not depend on their works. God saved them by His grace, planned before time began. This security gives courage to face hardship.

Finally, the truth that Christ has abolished death gives hope in the face of mortality. Believers can face illness, aging, and death with confidence, because Christ has brought life and immortality to light.

### *2 Timothy 1:12* — I Know Whom I Have Believed

> *“For this cause I also suffer these things. Yet I am not ashamed, for I know him whom I have believed, and I am persuaded that he is able to guard that which I have committed to him against that day.”*
>
> — *2 Timothy 1:12* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“For this cause I also suffer these things.” Paul’s imprisonment and suffering were the result of his faithfulness in preaching the gospel.

“Yet I am not ashamed.” Despite chains, desertion, and approaching death, Paul is not ashamed.

“For I know him whom I have believed.” Paul’s confidence does not rest on an idea or a set of beliefs alone, but on a person: Jesus Christ. He knows Christ personally, and he trusts Him completely. Notice that Paul does not say “I know what I have believed,” but “whom.”

“And I am persuaded that he is able to guard that which I have committed to him against that day.” Paul has entrusted something to Christ, his life, his soul, his ministry, his future. He is convinced that Christ is able to keep it safe until “that day,” the day of Christ’s return and judgment. Some interpreters understand the phrase as “what He has entrusted to me,” referring to the gospel; either way, Paul’s confidence is in Christ’s ability to guard it.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse expresses the heart of Christian assurance. It is not rooted in one’s own strength, performance, or circumstances, but in the character and power of Christ. Paul knew Christ. He had walked with Him for decades. He had experienced His faithfulness in shipwrecks, beatings, imprisonments, and betrayals. Now, at the end of his life, he could say with confidence that Christ would keep what he had entrusted to Him.

This truth echoes Jesus’ promise in *John 10:28–29* that no one can snatch His sheep out of His hand or the Father’s hand. It also echoes *Jude 1:24*, which praises God as the one who is able to keep believers from stumbling and present them blameless before His glory.

The image of entrusting something to another’s care is powerful. Believers can entrust their lives, their loved ones, their futures, and their deepest fears to Christ, knowing He is able to guard them.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

When believers face suffering, uncertainty, or fear, they can say with Paul, “*I know him whom I have believed*” (*v. 12*). Their confidence rests in Christ’s faithfulness, not in their circumstances.

Knowing Christ personally is the foundation of this confidence. Believers can deepen that knowledge through prayer, Scripture, worship, and obedience, so that, like Paul, they have a history of walking with Him to draw on in hard times.

Believers can also practice entrusting things to Christ: placing their worries, plans, and loved ones in His hands in prayer, and trusting Him to guard them.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

Second Timothy 1 is a call to courage rooted in grace. Paul, facing death in prison and abandoned by many, wrote to encourage Timothy not to give in to fear. His words speak to every believer who faces pressure, danger, or discouragement because of their faith.

The chapter begins by honoring the faith passed down through Timothy’s grandmother and mother. Family influence can be a powerful channel of faith, and believers can invest in the spiritual lives of the next generation through teaching, prayer, and example.

Paul then urges Timothy to fan into flame the gift God has given him, reminding him that God’s Spirit is not a spirit of fear but of power, love, and self-control. Believers can ask God to rekindle their passion and courage, and they can use their gifts faithfully.

Paul calls Timothy not to be ashamed of the gospel or of those who suffer for it, but to share in suffering by God’s power. The gospel is worth it: it reveals God’s eternal grace and Christ’s victory over death. Believers can stand with persecuted Christians and live boldly, knowing that death has been defeated.

At the heart of the chapter is Paul’s confession: “I know him whom I have believed, and I am persuaded that he is able to guard that which I have committed to him.” Believers can rest their whole lives in Christ’s faithful care. They are called to hold to sound teaching in faith and love, to guard the gospel through the Holy Spirit, and, like Onesiphorus, to be faithful friends who are not ashamed to stand with those who suffer.

## Chapter Prayer

Father, thank You for those who have passed on the faith to me, and help me to pass it on to others. Stir up the gifts You have given me, and rekindle my love for You and my courage to serve. Thank You that You have not given me a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control. When I am afraid, fill me with Your Spirit. Help me never to be ashamed of the gospel or of those who suffer for it. Thank You that You saved me and called me by Your grace, not by my works, and that Christ Jesus has abolished death and brought life and immortality to light. Lord Jesus, I know whom I have believed, and I trust that You are able to guard all that I have entrusted to You until that day. Help me to guard the truth through Your Spirit, and make me a faithful friend to those who need encouragement. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

2 Timothy · Chapter 2 of 4

# 2 Timothy — Chapter 2

Chapter Theme: Strong in Grace, Faithful in the Word

[Read 2 Timothy 2 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/2TI02.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul urges Timothy to be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus and to entrust what he has learned to faithful people who will teach others. Using images of a soldier, an athlete, and a farmer, he calls Timothy to share in suffering, to compete by the rules, and to work hard. Paul tells him to remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, for whose gospel Paul is chained, though God’s word is not chained. A trustworthy saying reminds believers that if they die with Christ they will live with Him, and that even if they are faithless, He remains faithful. Timothy must avoid quarrels about words, be a worker who correctly handles the word of truth, shun godless chatter like that of Hymenaeus and Philetus, flee youthful desires, pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace, and, as the Lord’s servant, be kind to everyone, able to teach, patient, and gentle in correcting opponents, in hope that God may grant them repentance.

## Chapter Background and Story

In chapter 1, Paul urged Timothy not to be afraid or ashamed, but to guard the gospel entrusted to him. In chapter 2, he explains how Timothy can do this. He must rely on grace, pass on the truth to others, endure hardship, teach the word accurately, live a pure life, and deal gently with those who oppose him.

The false teaching in Ephesus had taken a specific form. Two men, Hymenaeus and Philetus, were teaching that “the resurrection is already past” (v18). They may have meant that the only resurrection was a spiritual one, already experienced at conversion, so there would be no future bodily resurrection. This teaching was undermining the faith of some believers. Paul responds by pointing Timothy to the risen Christ and to faithful teaching of the word.

Throughout the chapter, Paul uses vivid images from everyday life: soldiers, athletes, farmers, workers, and household vessels. Each one illustrates an aspect of faithful Christian life and ministry.

### Strong in Grace, Passing On the Truth (*2:1–2*)

“*You therefore, my child, be strengthened in the grace that is in Christ Jesus*” (*v. 1*). Timothy’s strength would not come from himself but from Christ’s grace. “Be strengthened” is in the passive voice: Timothy is to let himself be continually strengthened by God’s grace. The call to pass on the truth is studied below.

### Soldier, Athlete, Farmer (*2:3–7*)

“*You therefore must endure hardship as a good soldier of Christ Jesus*” (*v. 3*). Soldiers expect hardship. They endure difficult conditions, long marches, and danger for the sake of their mission. “*No soldier on duty entangles himself in the affairs of life, that he may please him who enrolled him as a soldier*” (*v. 4*). A soldier on active duty does not get distracted by civilian business. His focus is on pleasing his commanding officer. Believers are to stay focused on pleasing Christ.

“*Also, if anyone competes in athletics, he isn’t crowned unless he has competed by the rules*” (*v. 5*). In the Greek games, athletes had to train according to strict rules and compete honestly. Breaking the rules meant disqualification. Faithfulness requires integrity, following God’s ways, not shortcuts.

“*The farmer who labors must be the first to get a share of the crops*” (*v. 6*). Farmers work long and hard, often waiting patiently for a harvest. The one who works should share in the harvest. Faithful labor will be rewarded.

“*Consider what I say, and may the Lord give you understanding in all things*” (*v. 7*). Paul invites Timothy to reflect on these images. Understanding comes from the Lord, but it requires thoughtful consideration.

### Remember Jesus Christ (*2:8–10*)

“*Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, of the offspring of David, according to my Good News*” (*v. 8*). Against the false teaching that the resurrection was past, Paul points to the risen Christ. Jesus’ resurrection is the center of the gospel. “Of the offspring of David” emphasizes His human descent and His identity as the promised Messiah.

“*in which I suffer hardship to the point of chains as a criminal. But God’s word isn’t chained*” (*v. 9*). Paul was chained like a criminal. But the word of God could not be chained. Even from prison, Paul was writing letters, and the gospel was spreading. “*Therefore I endure all things for the chosen ones’ sake, that they also may obtain the salvation which is in Christ Jesus with eternal glory*” (*v. 10*). Paul endured suffering so that others could hear the gospel and be saved.

### A Trustworthy Saying (*2:11–13*)

This early Christian saying is studied below.

### A Worker Approved by God (*2:14–19*)

“*Remind them of these things, charging them in the sight of the Lord that they don’t argue about words to no profit, to the subverting of those who hear*” (*v. 14*). Arguments over words, debates that produce nothing good, harm those who listen. The positive alternative is studied below.

“*But shun empty chatter, for it will go further in ungodliness*” (*v. 16*), “*and those words will consume like gangrene, of whom is Hymenaeus and Philetus*” (*v. 17*): “*men who have erred concerning the truth, saying that the resurrection is already past, and overthrowing the faith of some*” (*v. 18*). False teaching spreads like gangrene, a disease that eats away healthy flesh. Hymenaeus, mentioned in *1 Timothy 1:20*, and Philetus were teaching that the resurrection had already happened, denying the future bodily resurrection that Paul defends in *1 Corinthians 15*.

“*However, God’s firm foundation stands, having this seal: “The Lord knows those who are his,” and, “Let every one who names the name of the Lord depart from unrighteousness.”*” (*v. 19*) Despite false teaching, God’s work is secure. His church is like a building with a solid foundation. On that foundation is a seal with two inscriptions. The first, “The Lord knows those who are his,” echoes *Numbers 16:5*, from the story of Korah’s rebellion. God knows His true people. The second, perhaps drawing on passages such as *Isaiah 52:11*, calls those who belong to the Lord to turn from wickedness. God’s knowing and human obedience go together.

### Vessels for Honorable Use (*2:20–23*)

“*Now in a large house there are not only vessels of gold and of silver, but also of wood and of clay. Some are for honor and some for dishonor*” (*v. 20*). In a wealthy household, some containers were made of precious metals and used for special occasions; others were made of wood or clay and used for ordinary or unpleasant tasks. “*If anyone therefore purges himself from these, he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified, and suitable for the master’s use, prepared for every good work*” (*v. 21*). Those who cleanse themselves from false teaching and sin become useful to God, ready for His purposes.

“*Flee from youthful lusts; but pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace with those who call on the Lord out of a pure heart*” (*v. 22*). “Youthful lusts” may include sexual temptation, but also impatience, love of argument, and desire for recognition, which often mark the young. Timothy should run from them and pursue godly qualities, together with other sincere believers. “*But refuse foolish and ignorant questionings, knowing that they generate strife*” (*v. 23*).

### The Lord’s Servant (*2:24–26*)

The character of the Lord’s servant toward opponents is studied below. “*and they may recover themselves out of the devil’s snare, having been taken captive by him to do his will*” (*v. 26*). Those who oppose the truth are caught in a trap. The goal of gentle correction is that they would come to their senses and escape.

## Important Verses Explained

### *2 Timothy 2:2* — Entrusting the Truth to Faithful People

> *“The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men who will be able to teach others also.”*
>
> — *2 Timothy 2:2* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul gives Timothy a plan for passing on the gospel. “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses.” Timothy had heard Paul’s teaching many times, in many settings, with many others present. It was not secret or private teaching but the public gospel that many could confirm.

“Commit the same things to faithful men.” “Commit” means to entrust, like a deposit placed in safekeeping. “Faithful men” means trustworthy people; the word for “men” can include both men and women. They must be people of proven faithfulness.

“Who will be able to teach others also.” The goal is not just that these people would learn the truth, but that they would pass it on.

This verse describes four generations of faith: Paul, Timothy, faithful people, and others. The gospel is to be passed from one generation to the next, like a relay race in which each runner hands the baton to the next.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse expresses God’s plan for spreading the gospel through the ages. Jesus trained twelve disciples, who trained others, who trained others, and the chain has continued for two thousand years. Every believer today has received the gospel because someone passed it on.

Paul knew he was about to die. He wanted to ensure that the gospel would continue to be taught faithfully after he was gone. This verse is a reminder that the church must always be preparing the next generation of teachers and leaders.

The emphasis on “faithful” is significant. Paul does not say “talented” or “eloquent,” but “faithful.” Character and trustworthiness are the most important qualifications for those who will teach others. This echoes the qualifications for overseers in *1 Timothy 3*.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Every believer can take part in passing on the faith. This might mean teaching children, mentoring a younger believer, leading a small group, or simply sharing what one has learned with a friend. Discipleship is not only for pastors.

Churches can intentionally invest in training future leaders and teachers, identifying faithful people and equipping them to teach others.

Believers can also reflect on those who passed the faith on to them, giving thanks for them and asking whom they can invest in next.

### *2 Timothy 2:11–13* — If We Are Faithless, He Remains Faithful

> *“This saying is trustworthy: ‘For if we died with him, we will also live with him. If we endure, we will also reign with him. If we deny him, he also will deny us. If we are faithless, he remains faithful; for he can’t deny himself.’”*
>
> — *2 Timothy 2:11–13* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul introduces another “trustworthy saying,” probably an early Christian hymn or creed. It has four lines.

“For if we died with him, we will also live with him.” Believers have died with Christ, both in their union with His death at conversion (*Romans 6:3–8*) and possibly in martyrdom for His sake. Those who die with Him will share His resurrection life.

“If we endure, we will also reign with him.” Those who persevere in faith through suffering will share in Christ’s rule in His coming kingdom (*Revelation 3:21*).

“If we deny him, he also will deny us.” This is a solemn warning. Jesus said, “*whoever denies me before men, I will also deny him before my Father who is in heaven*” (*Matthew 10:33*). Those who persistently and finally reject Christ will be rejected by Him.

“If we are faithless, he remains faithful; for he can’t deny himself.” This line is surprising. One might expect, “If we are faithless, He will be faithless to us.” Instead, it declares that Christ remains faithful even when His people fail. His faithfulness is rooted in His own character; He cannot be untrue to Himself.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The third and fourth lines seem to be in tension. How can Christ deny those who deny Him, and yet remain faithful to those who are faithless? Many interpreters see a difference between “denying” Christ, a deliberate, final rejection, and being “faithless,” a weakness or failure of trust. Peter denied Jesus three times out of fear, yet Jesus restored him (*John 21:15–19*). His denial was a failure of courage, not a final rejection. Jesus remained faithful to him.

Others understand the fourth line to mean that Christ remains faithful to His word, both His promises and His warnings. If people are faithless, He remains true to what He has said. Either way, the line is a powerful statement of Christ’s unchanging character.

This saying offers both warning and comfort. It warns against deliberately and finally rejecting Christ. And it comforts those who struggle with weak faith, failure, and doubt. Christ’s faithfulness does not depend on theirs. He holds on even when they are weak.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers who have stumbled or failed, who have doubted or wavered, can find great comfort in this saying. Christ remains faithful. His love and promises do not depend on their perfect faithfulness. Like Peter, they can return to Him and be restored.

At the same time, this saying calls believers to endure. The Christian life involves perseverance through hardship, and those who endure will reign with Christ.

The saying also invites believers to reflect on Christ’s character. He cannot deny Himself. His faithfulness is as certain as His nature. This is the foundation of Christian hope.

### *2 Timothy 2:15* — Correctly Handling the Word of Truth

> *“Give diligence to present yourself approved by God, a workman who doesn’t need to be ashamed, properly handling the Word of Truth.”*
>
> — *2 Timothy 2:15* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

In contrast to those who argue about words (v14), Paul gives Timothy a positive goal. “Give diligence to present yourself approved by God.” “Give diligence” means to make every effort, to be eager and earnest. Timothy’s aim is to be “approved by God,” tested and found genuine, like metal that has passed the test of purity.

“A workman who doesn’t need to be ashamed.” Timothy is to be like a skilled worker whose work is excellent, so that he has no reason to be embarrassed when it is inspected.

“Properly handling the Word of Truth.” The phrase “properly handling” literally means “cutting straight.” It was used for cutting a straight road, plowing a straight furrow, or a stonemason cutting a stone accurately. Timothy is to handle God’s word accurately, interpreting and teaching it correctly, not twisting it or using it carelessly.

“The Word of Truth” refers to the gospel and the Scriptures, God’s true message.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse emphasizes the importance of careful, faithful study and teaching of Scripture. The false teachers in Ephesus were mishandling the word, leading people astray. Timothy was to do the opposite: to handle it with care and accuracy.

“Approved by God” is the key. The goal is not to impress people, win arguments, or gain a reputation, but to please God. Teachers of the word will one day give an account to Him (*James 3:1*; *Hebrews 13:17*).

Handling the word correctly involves understanding its context, its meaning to its original readers, its place in the whole story of Scripture, and its application today. It requires diligence, humility, prayer, and dependence on the Holy Spirit.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

All believers, not only teachers, can seek to handle God’s word carefully. This means reading Scripture regularly, studying it thoughtfully, considering its context, comparing Scripture with Scripture, and seeking to understand what God is truly saying, rather than using verses to support preconceived ideas.

Those who teach, whether in churches, small groups, or homes, have a special responsibility to prepare diligently, study carefully, and present God’s word faithfully.

This verse also encourages humility. Believers can ask God for wisdom and be willing to learn from others, recognizing that understanding Scripture is a lifelong journey.

### *2 Timothy 2:24–25* — Gentle Toward All, Patient in Correction

> *“The Lord’s servant must not quarrel, but be gentle toward all, able to teach, patient, in gentleness correcting those who oppose him. Perhaps God may give them repentance leading to a full knowledge of the truth,”*
>
> — *2 Timothy 2:24–25* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul describes how “the Lord’s servant” should treat others, especially those who oppose the truth.

“The Lord’s servant must not quarrel.” Timothy must not be argumentative or combative. Even when defending the truth, he should avoid needless fighting.

“But be gentle toward all.” Kindness should mark his attitude to everyone, including opponents.

“Able to teach.” He must be capable of explaining the truth clearly.

“Patient.” The word means bearing evil without resentment, enduring wrongs patiently.

Verse 25: “in gentleness correcting those who oppose him.” When correction is needed, it should be done gently, not harshly. The goal is restoration, not humiliation.

“Perhaps God may give them repentance leading to a full knowledge of the truth.” The ultimate change in a person’s heart is God’s work. Timothy cannot force anyone to repent. But by gentle correction, he can be the means through which God grants repentance.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This passage gives a model for handling disagreement and opposition that is very different from the combative spirit often seen today. The Lord’s servant is not a fighter but a gentle, patient teacher. This reflects the character of Christ, who was gentle and humble in heart (*Matthew 11:29*), and of God, who is patient, not wanting anyone to perish (*2 Peter 3:9*).

The hope that “God may give them repentance” shows that opponents are not enemies to be defeated but captives to be freed (v26). Their real enemy is the devil, who has trapped them. The goal is their rescue.

This does not mean ignoring error or never speaking firmly. Paul elsewhere speaks strongly against false teaching. But the manner matters. Truth spoken with harshness often hardens hearts; truth spoken with gentleness can open them.

It also does not mean tolerating abuse or harmful behavior. Gentleness in correction is compatible with firm boundaries, accountability, and, when necessary, protecting others from harm.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

In a culture marked by angry debates, especially online, believers can stand out by refusing to quarrel and by engaging others with kindness and patience. This does not mean abandoning convictions but expressing them with gentleness and respect (*1 Peter 3:15*).

When believers need to correct someone, whether a child, a friend, a coworker, or a fellow church member, they can ask whether they are doing it gently and patiently, with the goal of restoration.

Believers can also pray for those who oppose the faith, asking God to grant them repentance and understanding, remembering that God changes hearts, not arguments alone.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

Second Timothy 2 shows how to remain faithful in difficult times. It begins with grace: Timothy is to be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus, not in his own strength. From that foundation, he is to pass on the truth to faithful people who will teach others. Every believer has a part in this chain of faithfulness, receiving the gospel and passing it on.

Paul’s images of the soldier, athlete, and farmer describe the Christian life as one of focus, integrity, endurance, and hard work. Believers are called to endure hardship, to avoid distraction from their mission, to live by God’s rules, and to work patiently, trusting that faithful labor will bear fruit.

At the center of the chapter is a call to remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead. His resurrection is the foundation of hope and the answer to false teaching. Though Paul was chained, God’s word was not. The trustworthy saying reminds believers that those who die and endure with Christ will live and reign with Him, and that even when they are faithless, He remains faithful.

Paul also calls Timothy to handle God’s word accurately, to avoid useless arguments, to flee youthful desires, and to pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace. Those who cleanse themselves from what dishonors God become vessels for honorable use, ready for every good work.

Finally, the Lord’s servant must not be quarrelsome but kind to all, able to teach, patient, and gentle in correcting opponents, trusting God to grant repentance. This calls believers to engage a contentious world with the gentleness and patience of Christ.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, strengthen me in Your grace. Help me to pass on the truth I have received to others who will teach others also. Make me like a good soldier who endures hardship, an athlete who competes with integrity, and a farmer who works patiently for the harvest. I remember You, risen from the dead, and I thank You that Your word cannot be chained. Thank You that even when I am faithless, You remain faithful. Help me to endure and to share in Your life. Make me a worker approved by God, handling Your word of truth correctly. Cleanse me, so that I may be a vessel for honorable use, ready for every good work. Help me to flee youthful desires and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace. Make me gentle, patient, and kind toward all, especially toward those who oppose me, and grant them repentance and knowledge of the truth. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
