2 Timothy · Chapter 3 of 4

# 2 Timothy — Chapter 3

Chapter Theme: Difficult Times and the God-Breathed Scriptures

[Read 2 Timothy 3 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/2TI03.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul warns Timothy that in the last days there will be difficult times, when people will be lovers of themselves, lovers of money, proud, abusive, ungrateful, unholy, heartless, and lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God, having an outward form of godliness but denying its power. Such people prey on the vulnerable and oppose the truth, as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, but their folly will be exposed. In contrast, Timothy has followed Paul’s teaching, way of life, faith, patience, love, and endurance through persecutions, from which the Lord rescued him. All who want to live a godly life in Christ will be persecuted, while evil people go from bad to worse. Timothy must continue in what he has learned, remembering the holy Scriptures he has known from childhood, which are able to make him wise for salvation through faith in Christ. All Scripture is God-breathed and useful for teaching, rebuking, correcting, and training in righteousness, so that the servant of God may be thoroughly equipped for every good work.

## Chapter Background and Story

In chapter 2, Paul urged Timothy to remain faithful amid false teaching. In chapter 3, he describes the broader moral and spiritual climate in which Timothy is serving, and he points Timothy to the two great resources that will keep him steady: the example of faithful believers and the Scriptures.

“The last days” in the New Testament refers to the whole period between Christ’s first coming and His return (*Acts 2:16–17*; *Hebrews 1:2*). Paul is not describing only a distant future. He tells Timothy to “turn away from these” (v5), showing that such people were already present. Every generation of believers has seen these patterns, though they may intensify as the end approaches.

This chapter contains one of the most important statements in the Bible about the nature and purpose of Scripture (vv16–17). Paul, facing death, wanted Timothy to know that God’s word would sustain him when Paul was gone.

### Difficult Times (*3:1–5*)

The description of people in the last days is studied below.

### Predators and Opponents of the Truth (*3:6–9*)

“*For some of these are people who creep into houses and take captive gullible women loaded down with sins, led away by various lusts*” (*v. 6*), “*always learning and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth*” (*v. 7*). The false teachers used manipulative methods. They “crept into” households, perhaps when husbands were away, and targeted people who were spiritually vulnerable, weighed down by guilt and easily swayed. Paul is not making a statement about women in general; in this setting, many women had limited access to education and were therefore more vulnerable to manipulative teachers. Paul’s anger is directed at those who prey on the vulnerable. Spiritual predators who exploit people’s guilt, loneliness, or need are a serious danger in every age. Such people were “always learning,” always hearing new ideas, but never coming to the truth.

“*Even as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, so these also oppose the truth, men corrupted in mind, who concerning the faith are rejected*” (*v. 8*). Jannes and Jambres are not named in the Old Testament, but Jewish tradition gave these names to Pharaoh’s magicians who opposed Moses by imitating his miracles (*Exodus 7:11–12*, 22). The false teachers were like them: counterfeits who opposed God’s truth.

“*But they will proceed no further. For their folly will be evident to all men, as theirs also came to be*” (*v. 9*). Pharaoh’s magicians eventually failed; they could not reproduce the plague of gnats and admitted, “*This is God’s finger*” (*Exodus 8:19*) (*Exodus 8:18–19*). Likewise, false teachers will eventually be exposed.

### Paul’s Example (*3:10–13*)

“*But you followed my teaching, conduct, purpose, faith, patience, love, steadfastness*” (*v. 10*), “*persecutions, and sufferings—those things that happened to me at Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra. I endured those persecutions. The Lord delivered me out of them all*” (*v. 11*). In contrast to the false teachers, Timothy had followed Paul closely. He knew Paul’s teaching, his way of life, his goals, and his character. Antioch in Pisidia, Iconium, and Lystra were cities on Paul’s first missionary journey, where he faced intense opposition and was even stoned and left for dead (*Acts 13:50*; *14:5*, 19). Lystra was Timothy’s hometown, so he may have witnessed these sufferings himself. The Lord rescued Paul each time. The reality of persecution for all believers is studied below.

“*But evil men and impostors will grow worse and worse, deceiving and being deceived*” (*v. 13*). Deception is a downward spiral. Those who deceive others end up deceived themselves.

### Continue in the Scriptures (*3:14–17*)

Paul’s call to remain in the Scriptures and his teaching about their nature and purpose are studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *2 Timothy 3:1–5* — A Form of Godliness Without Its Power

> *“But know this: that in the last days, grievous times will come. For men will be lovers of self, lovers of money, boastful, arrogant, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy, without natural affection, unforgiving, slanderers, without self-control, fierce, not lovers of good, traitors, headstrong, conceited, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God, holding a form of godliness but having denied its power. Turn away from these, also.”*
>
> — *2 Timothy 3:1–5* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“But know this: that in the last days, grievous times will come.” “Grievous” means difficult, dangerous, or hard to bear. The word was used for wild, fierce animals and for dangerous seas.

Paul then lists nineteen characteristics of people in these times. The list begins and ends with misplaced love: “lovers of self,” “lovers of money,” and “lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God.” At the root of these problems is love turned in the wrong direction, away from God and others and toward self.

The list includes pride (“boastful, arrogant”), harmful speech (“blasphemers,” “slanderers”), broken family relationships (“disobedient to parents,” “without natural affection”), ingratitude (“unthankful”), lack of holiness (“unholy”), hard hearts (“unforgiving”), lack of self-control, cruelty (“fierce”), hatred of good, betrayal (“traitors”), recklessness (“headstrong”), and conceit.

Verse 5 is especially striking: “holding a form of godliness but having denied its power.” These people look religious on the outside. They may attend worship, use spiritual language, and claim to follow God. But their lives deny the transforming power of true faith. Their religion is an outward shell without inner reality.

“Turn away from these, also.” Timothy is to avoid being influenced by such people.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This list is sobering because it describes not only the world outside the church but also people who claim to be religious. The most dangerous form of godlessness is the one that wears the mask of godliness. Jesus warned against hypocrisy, comparing religious hypocrites to whitened tombs that look beautiful outside but are full of death inside (*Matthew 23:27–28*).

The list also shows that sin is fundamentally a problem of love. When people love themselves, money, and pleasure more than God, every other relationship becomes distorted. Jesus taught that the greatest commandments are to love God with all one’s heart and to love one’s neighbor as oneself (*Mark 12:29–31*). The sins in this list are the opposite of those two commandments.

Believers can recognize these patterns in the world around them, and humbly, in their own hearts as well. Self-love, greed, pride, and ingratitude are temptations for everyone. The remedy is the “power” of true godliness: the transforming work of the Holy Spirit, who produces love for God and others.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Many of the traits Paul lists are visible in modern culture: self-promotion, consumerism, broken families, harsh speech, ingratitude, and the pursuit of pleasure. Believers can recognize these patterns without despair, knowing that Scripture anticipated them.

This passage also calls for self-examination. Believers can ask whether their faith is merely outward or whether it has transforming power in their lives. Does their faith make them more loving, grateful, self-controlled, and humble?

Finally, “turn away from these” calls for wisdom in relationships. Believers are called to love everyone, but they should be careful about being influenced by people whose lives deny the power of godliness, and they should protect themselves and others from those who are manipulative or abusive.

### *2 Timothy 3:12* — All Who Desire to Live Godly Will Suffer Persecution

> *“Yes, and all who desire to live godly in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution.”*
>
> — *2 Timothy 3:12* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul makes a simple but challenging statement. “Yes, and all who desire to live godly in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution.”

“All” means every believer, not just apostles or leaders. “Who desire to live godly” refers to those who are serious about following Christ, who want their lives to reflect His character. “In Christ Jesus” means in union with Him.

Such people “will suffer persecution.” Persecution can take many forms: physical violence, imprisonment, loss of property, social rejection, ridicule, discrimination, or pressure from family or society. Its intensity varies greatly from place to place and time to time. But some form of opposition is a normal part of following Christ.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Jesus told His followers to expect persecution. He said, “*If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you*” (*John 15:20*). He also said, “*Blessed are those who have been persecuted for righteousness' sake, for theirs is the Kingdom of Heaven*” (*Matthew 5:10*). The world that rejected Christ will often reject those who follow Him.

Why does godliness provoke opposition? A godly life exposes sin by contrast (*John 3:19–20*). It challenges the values of a world that loves self, money, and pleasure. And there is a spiritual enemy who opposes God’s people (*Ephesians 6:12*).

This truth should not lead believers to seek persecution or to see every difficulty as persecution. Some hardships come from one’s own foolishness or unkindness (*1 Peter 4:15*). True persecution comes because of faithfulness to Christ. Paul also shows that God often delivers His people (v11), though sometimes deliverance comes through death into His presence (*2 Timothy 4:18*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers in many parts of the world face severe persecution for their faith. This verse calls Christians everywhere to remember them, pray for them, and support them (*Hebrews 13:3*).

For those who face milder forms of opposition, such as ridicule, exclusion, or pressure to compromise, this verse is a reminder that such experiences are not strange. They are part of following Christ. Believers can respond with courage, grace, and love.

This verse also offers perspective. If following Christ were always easy and comfortable, it might be a sign that faith had become merely a “form of godliness.” Faithful living may bring cost, but it also brings the joy of sharing in Christ’s sufferings and the promise of His reward.

### *2 Timothy 3:14–15* — Remain in What You Have Learned

> *“But you remain in the things which you have learned and have been assured of, knowing from whom you have learned them. From infancy, you have known the holy Scriptures which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus.”*
>
> — *2 Timothy 3:14–15* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

In contrast to the deceivers who keep going from bad to worse, Paul urges Timothy: “But you remain in the things which you have learned and have been assured of.” Timothy should hold firmly to the truth he has received, not be swayed by new or false teaching.

“Knowing from whom you have learned them.” Timothy learned the faith from trustworthy people: his grandmother Lois, his mother Eunice (*2 Timothy 1:5*), and Paul. The character of his teachers confirmed the truth of their teaching.

Verse 15: “From infancy, you have known the holy Scriptures.” Since early childhood, Timothy had been taught the Scriptures, which at that time meant the Old Testament. Jewish children often began learning the Scriptures at a very young age.

“Which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus.” The Scriptures point to Christ. They give wisdom that leads to salvation, not through mere knowledge, but through faith in Jesus.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show the importance of continuing in the faith one has received. The false teachers offered novelty; Paul urges faithfulness. This does not mean refusing to learn or grow, but it does mean staying rooted in the truth of the gospel rather than chasing every new idea.

The phrase “from infancy” highlights the value of teaching children Scripture. Seeds planted in childhood can bear fruit throughout life. *Proverbs 22:6* says, “*Train up a child in the way he should go, and when he is old he will not depart from it*” (*Proverbs 22:6*).

Paul’s description of the Scriptures as able to make one “wise for salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus” shows how the Old Testament points to Christ. Jesus said that the Scriptures testify about Him (*John 5:39*), and after His resurrection He explained to His disciples how all the Scriptures spoke of Him (*Luke 24:27*, 44–47). The purpose of Scripture is to lead people to faith in Christ.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can stay grounded in the truths they have learned, especially in times when new teachings or cultural pressures challenge the faith. This involves regularly returning to Scripture and to the core truths of the gospel.

Parents, grandparents, and churches can invest in teaching children Scripture from an early age. Reading Bible stories, memorizing verses, and talking about God’s word at home can shape a child’s life.

Believers can also read the whole Bible, including the Old Testament, with an eye toward Christ, seeing how its stories, laws, and prophecies prepare for and point to Him.

### *2 Timothy 3:16–17* — All Scripture Is God-Breathed

> *“Every Scripture is God-breathed and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness, that each person who belongs to God may be complete, thoroughly equipped for every good work.”*
>
> — *2 Timothy 3:16–17* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This is one of the most important statements in the Bible about Scripture itself.

“Every Scripture is God-breathed.” The Greek word, *theopneustos*, literally means “breathed out by God.” Scripture is not merely human writing that God approves; it comes from God Himself. Though written by human authors in their own styles and contexts, its ultimate source is God. Peter says that the prophets spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit (*2 Peter 1:20–21*).

“And profitable.” Because Scripture comes from God, it is useful. Paul names four ways.

“For teaching”: instructing in truth, showing what to believe.

“For reproof”: exposing error and sin, showing what is wrong.

“For correction”: restoring to the right path, showing how to make it right.

“For instruction in righteousness”: training in godly living, showing how to stay on the right path.

Verse 17 gives the purpose: “that each person who belongs to God may be complete, thoroughly equipped for every good work.” Scripture prepares believers fully for whatever God calls them to do. “Thoroughly equipped” was used for a ship fully outfitted for a voyage or a wagon fully loaded for a journey.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

When Paul wrote these words, “Scripture” primarily referred to the Old Testament. But the early church soon recognized the writings of the apostles as Scripture as well. Peter refers to Paul’s letters alongside “*the other Scriptures*” (*2 Peter 3:16*) (*2 Peter 3:15–16*), and Paul quotes a saying of Jesus as Scripture (*1 Timothy 5:18*). Christians believe that the whole Bible, Old and New Testaments, is God-breathed.

Christians have described the nature of Scripture’s authority and inspiration in various ways, but they broadly agree that Scripture is God’s word, trustworthy, and the authority for Christian faith and life. The fact that Scripture is “God-breathed” means that, when believers read it, they hear God speaking.

The four uses of Scripture form a complete cycle: teaching shows the right path, reproof shows where one has left it, correction shows how to get back, and training shows how to stay on it. Scripture is not merely information; it is God’s tool for shaping His people.

The goal is not just knowledge but good works. Scripture equips believers to live and serve well. Knowledge of the Bible that does not lead to transformed living misses its purpose.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Because Scripture is God-breathed, believers can approach it with reverence, expecting God to speak through it. Regular reading, study, meditation, and memorization of Scripture allow it to shape their minds and hearts.

Believers can welcome all four functions of Scripture: learning truth, being confronted with sin, receiving correction, and being trained in righteousness. This requires humility and openness, especially when Scripture challenges one’s thinking or behavior.

Finally, believers can remember that the purpose of Scripture is to equip them for good works. As they read, they can ask not only “What does this mean?” but also “How is God calling me to live?”

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

Second Timothy 3 describes difficult times, marked by people who love themselves, money, and pleasure more than God, who display a form of godliness while denying its power. These patterns appear in every age, and believers can recognize them in the world and, with humility, in their own hearts. The remedy is not mere religious appearance but the transforming power of true faith.

The chapter also warns about manipulative teachers who prey on the vulnerable. Churches can protect people from such predators by teaching the truth clearly, caring for those who are struggling, and being watchful for those who would exploit others.

Paul’s example offers a different path. Timothy had followed Paul’s teaching, conduct, faith, patience, love, and endurance in suffering. All who want to live godly lives in Christ will face persecution in some form, but the Lord is faithful to deliver. Believers can endure opposition with courage and pray for persecuted Christians around the world.

Finally, the chapter points to the great resource that sustains believers: the Scriptures. They are able to make people wise for salvation through faith in Christ. All Scripture is God-breathed and useful for teaching, reproof, correction, and training in righteousness, equipping God’s people for every good work. In times of confusion, deception, and difficulty, believers can remain in what they have learned, staying rooted in God’s word and letting it shape their lives.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord, the times are often difficult, and many love themselves, money, and pleasure more than You. Guard my heart from these things, and let my faith be not merely an outward form but a life filled with Your power. Protect the vulnerable from those who would deceive and exploit them. Thank You for faithful examples who have shown me what it means to follow You. When I face opposition for living a godly life, give me courage and grace, and strengthen my brothers and sisters who suffer persecution around the world. Help me to remain in what I have learned and to treasure Your Scriptures, which make me wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus. Thank You that all Scripture is breathed out by You. Teach me, correct me, and train me in righteousness through Your word, so that I may be fully equipped for every good work. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

2 Timothy · Chapter 4 of 4

# 2 Timothy — Chapter 4

Chapter Theme: Finishing the Race and Keeping the Faith

[Read 2 Timothy 4 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/2TI04.htm)

Main Teaching

In the presence of God and of Christ Jesus, who will judge the living and the dead, Paul solemnly charges Timothy to preach the word, to be ready in season and out of season, and to correct, rebuke, and encourage with great patience and careful teaching, because a time is coming when people will not tolerate sound teaching but will gather teachers to say what their itching ears want to hear. Timothy must stay clear-minded, endure hardship, do the work of an evangelist, and fulfill his ministry. Paul, aware that his death is near, declares that he has fought the good fight, finished the race, and kept the faith, and that the crown of righteousness awaits him and all who have longed for Christ’s appearing. He asks Timothy to come quickly, bringing Mark, his cloak, and his scrolls, and tells how everyone deserted him at his first defense, yet the Lord stood by him and strengthened him. He closes with greetings and confidence that the Lord will bring him safely into His heavenly kingdom.

## Chapter Background and Story

These are likely the last words Paul ever wrote. He was in a Roman prison, probably the harsh Mamertine prison or another place of severe confinement, awaiting execution. Winter was approaching, and he was cold (v13, 21). Most of his companions were gone. Some had left for ministry elsewhere; others had abandoned him. He had already faced a preliminary hearing, and no one had stood with him (v16).

Yet the chapter is not one of despair. It overflows with faith, hope, and purpose. Paul gives Timothy a final, solemn charge to preach the word. He looks back on his life with gratitude and looks forward with confidence to his reward. And he shows, in his personal requests and greetings, that even at the end, he cared deeply about people, about his friends, his work, and the mission of the gospel.

This chapter is one of the most moving in the New Testament. It shows how a faithful servant of Christ faces death: not with fear, but with confidence in the Lord who stood by him.

### The Charge to Preach (*4:1–5*)

“*I command you therefore before God and the Lord Jesus Christ, who will judge the living and the dead at his appearing and his Kingdom*” (*v. 1*). Paul’s charge is given in the presence of God and Christ, the judge of all. Timothy’s ministry will be evaluated by the Lord at His return. The content of the charge, and the warning about itching ears, are studied below.

### Paul’s Farewell (*4:6–8*)

“*For I am already being offered, and the time of my departure has come*” (*v. 6*). “Being offered” uses the image of a drink offering, wine poured out on the altar as part of a sacrifice (*Numbers 15:5–10*). Paul sees his life, and soon his death, as an offering poured out to God (see *Philippians 2:17*). “Departure” was used for loosening a ship from its moorings, or for soldiers striking their tents to move on. Death, for Paul, is not an end but a departure to a new destination. His reflection on his life and his hope are studied below.

### Personal Requests (*4:9–15*)

“*Be diligent to come to me soon*” (*v. 9*), “*for Demas left me, having loved this present world, and went to Thessalonica; Crescens to Galatia; and Titus to Dalmatia*” (*v. 10*). Demas had once been Paul’s coworker (*Colossians 4:14*; *Philemon 1:24*). But he loved “this present world” and abandoned Paul. Crescens and Titus had gone to other places, probably for ministry. Dalmatia was on the eastern coast of the Adriatic Sea.

“*Only Luke is with me. Take Mark and bring him with you, for he is useful to me for service*” (*v. 11*). Luke, the beloved physician, remained faithful to the end. And Mark, who had once deserted Paul and Barnabas (*Acts 13:13*; *15:37–39*), is now “useful” for ministry. This is a beautiful picture of restoration. The young man who failed has become a valued coworker, and Paul, who once refused to take him, now asks for him.

“*But I sent Tychicus to Ephesus*” (*v. 12*). Tychicus may have carried this letter and taken Timothy’s place in Ephesus so that Timothy could come.

“*Bring the cloak that I left at Troas with Carpus when you come—and the books, especially the parchments*” (*v. 13*). Paul needed his cloak for the cold winter in prison. He also wanted his books and parchments, possibly copies of the Scriptures, his own notes, or legal documents. Even near death, Paul wanted to keep reading and studying. These small human details show that Paul was a real person with real needs.

“*Alexander the coppersmith did much evil to me. The Lord will repay him according to his deeds*” (*v. 14*). “*Beware of him, for he greatly opposed our words*” (*v. 15*). Alexander may be the same person mentioned in *1 Timothy 1:20*. He had caused Paul serious harm, perhaps by testifying against him. Paul does not seek revenge; he entrusts justice to the Lord, echoing *Psalm 62:12*. But he warns Timothy to be careful.

### The Lord Stood by Me (*4:16–18*)

The story of Paul’s first defense is studied below. “*And the Lord will deliver me from every evil work and will preserve me for his heavenly Kingdom. To him be the glory forever and ever. Amen*” (*v. 18*). Paul does not expect to be rescued from death. He expects to be rescued through death into Christ’s heavenly kingdom. Even facing execution, he ends with praise.

### Final Greetings (*4:19–22*)

“*Greet Prisca and Aquila, and the house of Onesiphorus*” (*v. 19*). Prisca (Priscilla) and Aquila were longtime coworkers who had risked their lives for Paul (*Romans 16:3–4*). Onesiphorus had refreshed Paul in prison (*2 Timothy 1:16–18*).

“*Erastus remained at Corinth, but I left Trophimus at Miletus sick*” (*v. 20*). Paul had seen God work miracles of healing, yet he left Trophimus sick. Not every illness was healed, even in the apostolic age. This shows that God’s healing is according to His will, and that sickness is not necessarily a sign of lack of faith.

“*Be diligent to come before winter. Eubulus salutes you, as do Pudens, Linus, Claudia, and all the brothers*” (*v. 21*). “Before winter” is urgent. Once winter came, sea travel stopped, and Timothy would not be able to reach Rome until spring, possibly too late. Linus may be the same Linus who, according to early church tradition, later became a leader of the church in Rome.

“*The Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Grace be with you. Amen*” (*v. 22*). Paul’s final written words are a blessing of the Lord’s presence and grace. The “you” in the last sentence is plural, extending the blessing to the whole church.

## Important Verses Explained

### *2 Timothy 4:2* — Preach the Word

> *“preach the word; be urgent in season and out of season; reprove, rebuke, and exhort with all patience and teaching.”*
>
> — *2 Timothy 4:2* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This is the heart of Paul’s charge to Timothy. “Preach the word.” The “word” is the message of the gospel and the Scriptures, which Paul has just described as God-breathed (*2 Timothy 3:16*). “Preach” means to proclaim publicly, like a herald announcing a king’s message.

“Be urgent in season and out of season.” Timothy must be ready at all times, whether the moment seems convenient or not, whether people are receptive or not. He should not wait for ideal circumstances.

Paul then describes three ways of applying the word. “Reprove”: convince people of the truth and expose error. “Rebuke”: confront sin directly and call for repentance. “Exhort”: encourage, comfort, and urge people to follow God.

“With all patience and teaching.” This ministry must be done with great patience, not giving up on people, and with careful teaching, explaining the truth clearly. Correction without patience can become harsh; correction without teaching can become empty.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse summarizes the calling of every minister of the gospel and, in a broader sense, the calling of the whole church. The church exists to proclaim God’s word. *Romans 10:14–17* asks how people can believe without hearing and how they can hear without someone preaching. Faith comes from hearing the message about Christ.

The phrase “in season and out of season” acknowledges that there will be times when preaching the truth is unpopular. Faithful ministry does not depend on popularity. It depends on faithfulness to God, who will judge the living and the dead (v1).

The balance of reproof, rebuke, and exhortation reflects the full ministry of God’s word. Scripture comforts the afflicted and challenges the comfortable. Faithful preaching does both, always with patience and careful teaching.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Pastors and teachers can take this charge to heart, making the preaching and teaching of God’s word central to their ministry, being faithful whether or not it is welcomed, and combining truth with patience.

Every believer can also “preach the word” in a broader sense: sharing the gospel with others, encouraging fellow believers with Scripture, and speaking truth with love when needed. Being ready “in season and out of season” means being prepared to speak about Christ whenever opportunities arise.

Churches can value faithful biblical preaching and support those who give their lives to it, recognizing that God’s word is the source of spiritual life and growth.

### *2 Timothy 4:3–5* — Itching Ears and a Faithful Ministry

> *“For the time will come when they will not listen to the sound doctrine, but having itching ears, will heap up for themselves teachers after their own lusts, and will turn away their ears from the truth, and turn away to fables. But you be sober in all things, suffer hardship, do the work of an evangelist, and fulfill your ministry.”*
>
> — *2 Timothy 4:3–5* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul explains why preaching the word is urgent. “For the time will come when they will not listen to the sound doctrine.” “Sound doctrine” means healthy teaching that nourishes spiritual life. People will reject it.

“But having itching ears, will heap up for themselves teachers after their own lusts.” “Itching ears” describes a craving to hear something pleasing, new, or exciting. Instead of seeking the truth, people will gather teachers who tell them what they want to hear, teachers who match their own desires.

Verse 4: “and will turn away their ears from the truth, and turn away to fables.” They will reject the truth in favor of myths, appealing stories with no basis in reality.

Verse 5: “But you be sober in all things.” In contrast, Timothy must keep a clear head, not swayed by popular trends. “Suffer hardship”: he must endure difficulty. “Do the work of an evangelist”: he must keep proclaiming the gospel to those who have not believed. “Fulfill your ministry”: he must complete the task God has given him.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This passage describes a temptation that exists in every age: preferring comfortable lies to uncomfortable truth. People naturally gravitate toward messages that affirm their desires and avoid messages that challenge them. The prophets of Israel faced this: the people said to the seers, “Don’t see!” and to the prophets, “*Don't prophesy to us right things. Tell us pleasant things*” (*Isaiah 30:10*).

The phrase “heap up for themselves teachers” suggests that people will not lack teachers. There will be many, offering a variety of appealing messages. The problem is not a lack of preaching but a lack of truth.

Paul’s response is not to compete by offering more pleasing messages. It is to remain faithful, clear-minded, willing to suffer, and committed to the gospel. Faithfulness is measured not by popularity but by obedience to God.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers today have access to an endless supply of teachers, sermons, podcasts, books, and videos. This can be a great blessing, but it also creates the temptation to choose teachers based on what one wants to hear. This passage invites believers to examine their own hearts: Do they seek truth, even when it challenges them, or do they seek affirmation of what they already want?

Pastors and teachers can resist the pressure to tell people what they want to hear. Faithful ministry speaks the truth with love, even when it is unpopular.

The call to “do the work of an evangelist” reminds all believers that sharing the gospel is part of every Christian’s calling. In a world that often prefers myths, the truth of Christ is needed more than ever.

### *2 Timothy 4:7–8* — I Have Kept the Faith

> *“I have fought the good fight. I have finished the course. I have kept the faith. From now on, the crown of righteousness is stored up for me, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will give to me on that day; and not to me only, but also to all those who have loved his appearing.”*
>
> — *2 Timothy 4:7–8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul looks back on his life with three statements.

“I have fought the good fight.” Paul’s life had been a struggle against sin, error, opposition, and suffering. He had not given up. The phrase may also suggest an athletic contest, such as wrestling. It was a “good” fight, one worth fighting.

“I have finished the course.” Paul uses the image of a runner who has completed the race. He did not quit halfway. He ran to the finish line.

“I have kept the faith.” Paul guarded the gospel entrusted to him and remained faithful to Christ to the end. He did not abandon or distort the truth.

Verse 8 looks forward. “From now on, the crown of righteousness is stored up for me.” In Greek athletic games, winners received a crown, or wreath, of leaves that soon withered. Paul looks forward to a crown that will never fade. “The crown of righteousness” may mean the crown that is righteousness itself, or the crown given as a reward for a righteous life.

“Which the Lord, the righteous judge, will give to me on that day.” Earthly judges had condemned Paul, but the righteous Judge would vindicate him. “That day” is the day of Christ’s return.

“And not to me only, but also to all those who have loved his appearing.” This crown is not only for apostles. It is for all who have longed for Christ’s return and lived in light of it.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses express the hope of every believer: to finish well. Paul did not claim to be perfect (*Philippians 3:12*). But he had remained faithful. His confidence was not in his own achievements but in the Lord, the righteous judge, who would reward faithfulness.

The phrase “those who have loved his appearing” is beautiful. It describes believers whose hearts are set on Christ’s return, who long to see Him. This love shapes how they live. Those who love His appearing live in a way that prepares for it.

Jesus also spoke of crowns and rewards for faithful servants (*Revelation 2:10*; *3:11*). These rewards are not earned by merit in a way that replaces grace; they are God’s gracious acknowledgment of the fruit His grace has produced in believers’ lives. *James 1:12* speaks of the crown of life promised to those who love God.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses invite every believer to consider how they want to finish their life. Will they be able to say, “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith”? Finishing well requires daily faithfulness over a lifetime.

For those near the end of life, or facing serious illness, these verses offer hope. Death is not the end but the finish line, and the crown of righteousness awaits all who love Christ’s appearing.

For those discouraged in the middle of the race, these verses offer encouragement to keep going. The fight is good, the race is worth finishing, and the reward is sure.

### *2 Timothy 4:16–17* — The Lord Stood by Me

> *“At my first defense, no one came to help me, but all left me. May it not be held against them. But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me, that through me the message might be fully proclaimed, and that all the Gentiles might hear. So I was delivered out of the mouth of the lion.”*
>
> — *2 Timothy 4:16–17* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul describes his “first defense,” probably a preliminary hearing before a Roman court. “At my first defense, no one came to help me, but all left me.” In Roman courts, the accused could have supporters or advocates stand with them. When Paul stood trial, no one stood beside him. Perhaps they were afraid of being associated with a condemned man.

“May it not be held against them.” Like Jesus on the cross (*Luke 23:34*) and Stephen at his death (*Acts 7:60*), Paul prays for those who abandoned him. He does not hold their failure against them.

Verse 17: “But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me.” When everyone else left, the Lord was present. He gave Paul strength.

“That through me the message might be fully proclaimed, and that all the Gentiles might hear.” Even at his trial, Paul preached the gospel. His defense became an opportunity to proclaim Christ before Roman officials and possibly a large audience.

“So I was delivered out of the mouth of the lion.” This may be a figure of speech for being saved from great danger, echoing *Psalm 22:21* or *Daniel 6*, or it may refer to escaping immediate execution at that first hearing. Paul was spared, for the moment.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses capture one of the most painful and most comforting experiences in the Christian life: being abandoned by people but upheld by God. Jesus experienced this when His disciples fled at His arrest (*Mark 14:50*). Paul experienced it at his trial. Believers may experience it when friends, family, or fellow church members fail them.

Paul’s response is a model of grace. He does not become bitter. He prays for those who failed him. He focuses on the Lord’s faithfulness rather than human failure.

The promise that the Lord stands by His people is found throughout Scripture. God told Joshua, “*I will not fail you nor forsake you*” (*Joshua 1:5*). Jesus promised, “*I am with you always, even to the end of the age*” (*Matthew 28:20*). *Hebrews 13:5–6* echoes this: God will never leave His people, so they can say, “The Lord is my helper.”

Even in his darkest moment, Paul’s concern was the gospel. He saw his trial as an opportunity for the message to be “fully proclaimed.” This shows the depth of his devotion.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Many believers have experienced being let down or abandoned by others in their time of need. This passage offers comfort: the Lord stands by His people, even when everyone else leaves.

Paul’s example also shows how to respond to those who fail us. Forgiveness, rather than bitterness, frees the heart. This does not mean ignoring real harm or trusting people who are unsafe, but it does mean releasing resentment and entrusting the situation to God.

Finally, Paul’s focus on the gospel, even at his trial, invites believers to see their own difficult moments as opportunities to testify about Christ. God can use even the hardest circumstances for His purposes.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

Second Timothy 4 contains Paul’s final charge and farewell. In the presence of God and Christ, who will judge the living and the dead, Paul urges Timothy to preach the word, ready in season and out of season, correcting, rebuking, and encouraging with great patience and careful teaching. This charge applies to pastors and teachers, and in a broader sense to every believer called to share God’s truth.

Paul warns that people will turn away from sound teaching and gather teachers who tell them what they want to hear. In a world full of appealing messages, believers are called to seek the truth even when it challenges them, and leaders are called to speak it faithfully even when it is unpopular.

Facing death, Paul could say, “I have fought the good fight. I have finished the course. I have kept the faith.” He looked forward to the crown of righteousness, which the Lord will give to all who love His appearing. His example invites every believer to finish well, staying faithful through daily obedience until the end.

The chapter also shows Paul’s humanity. He was cold, lonely, abandoned by many, and still eager to read and to see his friends. He celebrated Mark’s restoration, warned Timothy about a dangerous opponent, and acknowledged that not every sick friend was healed. Most of all, he testified that when everyone else deserted him, the Lord stood by him and strengthened him. Believers can find comfort in that same faithful presence, forgive those who fail them, and trust that the Lord will bring them safely into His heavenly kingdom. To Him be the glory forever and ever.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, You will judge the living and the dead at Your appearing. Help me to be faithful to Your word, ready in season and out of season, speaking truth with patience and love. Guard me from itching ears that want to hear only what pleases me, and give me a love for sound teaching. Help me to endure hardship, to share the gospel, and to fulfill the calling You have given me. I want to finish well. Give me strength to fight the good fight, to finish the race, and to keep the faith. Fill me with love for Your appearing. When others fail me or leave me, stand by me and strengthen me, as You did for Paul. Help me to forgive those who let me down. Thank You for restoring those who have failed, as You restored Mark. Rescue me from every evil and bring me safely into Your heavenly kingdom. To You be the glory forever and ever. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Book 17 of 27

# Titus

## About This Letter

Titus was a Gentile believer, a Greek, who became one of Paul’s trusted coworkers. Paul took him to Jerusalem as a living example that Gentile believers did not need to be circumcised (*Galatians 2:1–3*), and later sent him on delicate missions to Corinth, where Titus helped restore the strained relationship between Paul and the church and organized the collection for Jerusalem (*2 Corinthians 7:6–7*, 13–15; *8:6*, 16–17).

According to this letter, Paul and Titus had worked together on the island of Crete, in the Mediterranean south of Greece, and Paul had left Titus there to “set in order the things that were lacking” and to appoint elders in every town (*Titus 1:5*). The churches were young, the culture had a reputation for dishonesty and laziness, and false teachers, especially some from a Jewish background who insisted on rules and myths, were upsetting whole households.

Like 1 and 2 Timothy, Titus is one of the Pastoral Letters. Most Christians through history have held that Paul wrote it after his release from his first Roman imprisonment, around A.D. 62–64; some modern scholars think a later follower wrote it in his name. Paul planned to spend the winter at Nicopolis, on the western coast of Greece, and asked Titus to join him there (*3:12*).

## The Shape of the Letter

In chapter 1, Paul greets Titus, describes the qualifications for elders, who must be blameless in character and able to teach sound doctrine, and warns against rebellious, deceptive teachers who must be silenced. In chapter 2, he instructs Titus to teach what fits sound doctrine to older men, older women, younger women, younger men, and servants, so that God’s teaching may be made attractive, because the grace of God has appeared, training believers to renounce ungodliness and live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives while waiting for the appearing of Jesus Christ. In chapter 3, he urges believers to be good citizens, gentle and courteous to all, remembering that God saved them not because of their righteous works but by His mercy, through the washing of rebirth and renewal by the Holy Spirit, and he calls them to devote themselves to good works and avoid foolish controversies.

## Themes to Watch For

Watch for the close link between sound doctrine and godly living, the character of leaders, the grace of God that both saves and trains, the hope of Christ’s appearing, salvation by mercy rather than works, the renewing work of the Holy Spirit, devotion to good works, and the call to make the gospel attractive by the way believers live. Titus shows that the gospel transforms not only individuals but households, churches, and whole communities.

2.  [Titus 2](#c17_TIT_002.xhtml) — The Grace That Trains Us to Live Godly Lives

Titus · Chapter 1 of 3

# Titus — Chapter 1

Chapter Theme: Sound Leaders for a Godly Church

[Read Titus 1 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/TIT01.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul greets Titus as a servant of God and apostle, whose mission is to further the faith of God’s chosen people and their knowledge of the truth that leads to godliness, all resting on the hope of eternal life promised by God, who cannot lie. He reminds Titus that he left him in Crete to put things in order and appoint elders in every town. These leaders must be blameless, faithful in marriage, with households of good reputation, not arrogant, quick-tempered, drunken, violent, or greedy, but hospitable, lovers of good, self-controlled, upright, holy, and disciplined, holding firmly to the trustworthy message so they can encourage others with sound teaching and correct those who oppose it. Paul warns against many rebellious, empty talkers and deceivers who were upsetting whole households for dishonest gain and who must be silenced and sharply rebuked so they may become sound in the faith. To the pure all things are pure, but those who are corrupt claim to know God while denying Him by their actions.

## Chapter Background and Story

Crete is a large island in the Mediterranean Sea, south of Greece. People from Crete were present in Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost (*Acts 2:11*), and Paul’s ship stopped at Crete on his voyage to Rome (*Acts 27:7–13*). The book of Acts does not record Paul planting churches there, so this ministry likely took place after his release from his first Roman imprisonment.

The churches in Crete were young and needed structure and leadership. Titus’s task was to appoint elders in every town and to deal with false teachers who were causing serious harm. These teachers were especially “of the circumcision,” Jewish in background, and they promoted “Jewish fables and commandments of men” (v14), likely a mixture of speculative stories and human rules, perhaps similar to the problems in Ephesus. They were also motivated by money (v11).

Crete had a poor reputation in the ancient world. Greek writers used the word “to Cretanize” to mean “to lie.” Paul’s instructions show that the gospel was meant to transform even a culture known for dishonesty, through leaders of godly character and through sound teaching that produces godly living.

### Greeting (*1:1–4*)

“*Paul, a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ, according to the faith of God’s chosen ones and the knowledge of the truth which is according to godliness*” (*v. 1*). Paul’s purpose as an apostle is to build up the faith of God’s people and their knowledge of the truth. Notice that truth is connected with godliness. Sound doctrine and godly living belong together; this is the theme of the whole letter. The foundation of Paul’s ministry, the hope of eternal life, is studied below.

“*but in his own time revealed his word in the message with which I was entrusted according to the commandment of God our Savior*” (*v. 3*). God’s promise, made before time began, was revealed at the right time through the preaching of the gospel.

“*to Titus, my true child according to a common faith: Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ our Savior*” (*v. 4*). Titus was Paul’s “true child” in the faith, probably converted through Paul’s ministry. Notice that both “God” and “the Lord Jesus Christ” are called “Savior” in this letter (*1:3*, 4; *2:10*, 13; *3:4*, 6).

### Appointing Elders (*1:5–9*)

“*I left you in Crete for this reason, that you would set in order the things that were lacking and appoint elders in every city, as I directed you*” (*v. 5*). “Set in order” was a medical term for setting a broken bone. Titus’s job was to bring health and order to the young churches.

“*if anyone is blameless, the husband of one wife, having children who believe, who are not accused of loose or unruly behavior*” (*v. 6*). As in *1 Timothy 3*, the qualifications focus on character. “Blameless” means no one can rightly bring a serious charge against him. “The husband of one wife” means faithful in marriage (see the discussion at *1 Timothy 3:2*). “Having children who believe” may mean children who are believers, or children who are “faithful,” trustworthy and well-behaved. Interpreters differ. Either way, the leader’s household should reflect his faith, though even godly parents cannot control every choice their adult children make.

“*For the overseer must be blameless, as God’s steward, not self-pleasing, not easily angered, not given to wine, not violent, not greedy for dishonest gain*” (*v. 7*). An overseer is “God’s steward,” managing God’s household, not his own. He must not be arrogant, hot-tempered, a heavy drinker, violent, or greedy. These are exactly the traits that harm those in one’s care.

“*but given to hospitality, a lover of good, sober minded, fair, holy, self-controlled*” (*v. 8*). Positively, he must be welcoming, love what is good, be sensible, just, devoted to God, and disciplined. The leader’s role regarding sound teaching is studied below.

### Silencing False Teachers (*1:10–14*)

“*For there are also many unruly men, vain talkers and deceivers, especially those of the circumcision*” (*v. 10*), “*whose mouths must be stopped: men who overthrow whole houses, teaching things which they ought not, for dishonest gain’s sake*” (*v. 11*). The false teachers were rebellious, full of empty talk, and deceptive. They were “overthrowing whole houses,” disrupting entire families, perhaps house churches. And they did it for money.

“*One of them, a prophet of their own, said, “Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, and idle gluttons.”*” (*v. 12*) Paul quotes a Cretan poet, traditionally identified as Epimenides, who lived around the sixth century B.C. and was regarded by some as a prophet. This was a well-known saying about Crete’s reputation.

“*This testimony is true. For this cause, reprove them sharply, that they may be sound in the faith*” (*v. 13*). Paul is not endorsing ethnic stereotypes as a way of judging individuals. He is applying the poet’s observation to the false teachers, whose behavior fit the saying exactly. Scripture never permits believers to judge people by the reputation of their nationality or ethnicity; in Christ, every person is to be known and valued as an individual made in God’s image, and the Cretan believers were full members of God’s family. Paul’s goal, even in sharp rebuke, is restoration: “that they may be sound in the faith.”

“*not paying attention to Jewish fables and commandments of men who turn away from the truth*” (*v. 14*). The false teaching included myths and human rules. Jesus also warned against putting human traditions above God’s commands (*Mark 7:6–8*).

### Pure and Impure (*1:15–16*)

Paul’s statements about purity and about those whose deeds deny God are studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Titus 1:2* — The Hope of Eternal Life from God, Who Cannot Lie

> *“in hope of eternal life, which God, who can’t lie, promised before time began;”*
>
> — *Titus 1:2* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul describes the foundation of his ministry. Everything he does is “in hope of eternal life.” Eternal life is not just endless existence but the life of God’s kingdom, a life of knowing and enjoying God forever (*John 17:3*). Believers already begin to experience it now, and they will know it fully when Christ returns.

This hope rests on God’s promise: “which God, who can’t lie, promised before time began.” Before the world was created, God planned and promised eternal life to His people. And His promise is certain, because God cannot lie.

The contrast with Crete is striking. The Cretans were known as liars (v12). God is the opposite. He is completely truthful. His word can always be trusted.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The truthfulness of God is a foundation of Christian faith. *Numbers 23:19* says, “*God is not a man, that he should lie*” (*Numbers 23:19*). *Hebrews 6:18* says that it is impossible for God to lie, and that His promise and oath give strong encouragement to those who have taken refuge in Him. Jesus called Himself “*the truth*” (*John 14:6*).

Because God cannot lie, every promise He has made is sure. The promise of eternal life is not a wish or a guess. It is as certain as God’s character.

The phrase “before time began” points to God’s eternal purpose. Salvation was not an afterthought or a response to unexpected events. It was God’s plan from the beginning, revealed in history through Christ (*2 Timothy 1:9–10*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

In a world full of broken promises, misinformation, and deception, believers can rest in the truthfulness of God. Whatever He has said, He will do.

This truth brings comfort in times of doubt or fear. When believers wonder whether God’s promises are real, they can remember that God cannot lie. His word is the most reliable foundation for life.

It also calls believers to reflect God’s truthfulness in their own speech and lives. As children of the God who cannot lie, they are called to be people of honesty and integrity.

### *Titus 1:9* — Holding Fast to the Faithful Word

> *“holding to the faithful word which is according to the teaching, that he may be able to exhort in the sound doctrine, and to convict those who contradict him.”*
>
> — *Titus 1:9* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul describes an essential quality of church leaders. They must be “holding to the faithful word which is according to the teaching.” The “faithful word” is the trustworthy message of the gospel, as it was taught by the apostles. Leaders must hold onto it firmly, like someone gripping something valuable.

Why? “That he may be able to exhort in the sound doctrine, and to convict those who contradict him.” Leaders have two tasks with regard to teaching. First, they must “exhort,” or encourage, believers with “sound doctrine,” healthy teaching that nourishes spiritual life. Second, they must “convict,” or refute, those who oppose the truth, showing them their error.

A leader who does not hold firmly to the truth cannot do either. He will have nothing solid to offer believers and no basis for correcting error.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that church leadership is not only about character but also about teaching. Leaders must know and hold to the truth. In a church threatened by false teaching, as Crete was, this was essential. Leaders were the first line of defense.

The two tasks, encouraging and refuting, reflect the full ministry of God’s word. Encouragement builds up those who believe; refutation protects them from error. Both are acts of love: love for the flock and love for the truth.

“Sound doctrine” is a key phrase in the Pastoral Letters. The word “sound” means healthy. Just as healthy food nourishes the body, healthy teaching nourishes the soul. False teaching, by contrast, is like a disease (*2 Timothy 2:17*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Churches can seek leaders who know Scripture well, hold firmly to the gospel, and can explain it clearly. Training and equipping leaders in sound teaching is an important investment.

All believers can also hold fast to the faithful word. Knowing the core truths of the faith helps believers encourage one another and recognize error when they encounter it.

When correcting error, believers can follow the pattern of *2 Timothy 2:24–25*: with gentleness and patience, aiming for restoration, while still being clear about the truth.

### *Titus 1:15* — To the Pure, All Things Are Pure

> *“To the pure, all things are pure, but to those who are defiled and unbelieving, nothing is pure; but both their mind and their conscience are defiled.”*
>
> — *Titus 1:15* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The false teachers were apparently teaching rules about purity, perhaps about foods or rituals, similar to those in Colossae and Ephesus (*Colossians 2:20–23*; *1 Timothy 4:3*). They taught that certain things defiled people.

Paul responds: “To the pure, all things are pure.” For those whose hearts have been cleansed by Christ, God’s good gifts, such as food and the ordinary things of life, are not defiling. They can be received with thanksgiving.

“But to those who are defiled and unbelieving, nothing is pure.” For those whose hearts are corrupt and who do not believe, even good things become occasions for sin. Their impurity is not in the things themselves but in their hearts.

“But both their mind and their conscience are defiled.” The problem is internal. Their thinking and their moral sense have been corrupted.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse echoes Jesus’ teaching that it is not what goes into a person that defiles them, but what comes out of the heart (*Mark 7:14–23*). Purity is a matter of the heart, not merely of external rules. Paul makes a similar point in *Romans 14:14*, 20: nothing is unclean in itself, and all food is clean.

This does not mean that “anything goes” for believers. Paul is talking about matters like food and ritual purity, not moral sin. Sexual immorality, greed, and cruelty are always wrong. The point is that external rules cannot make a person pure; only a cleansed heart can.

The verse also shows that the condition of the heart shapes how a person sees the world. A pure heart sees God’s good gifts as good. A corrupt heart twists even good things into opportunities for sin. Jesus said that the eye is the lamp of the body; if it is healthy, the whole body is full of light (*Matthew 6:22–23*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can be free from legalistic rules that treat God’s good gifts as defiling. They can enjoy food, rest, creativity, and the ordinary pleasures of life with gratitude, as gifts from God.

At the same time, this verse invites believers to examine their hearts. Purity is not achieved by avoiding certain things but by having a heart cleansed by Christ and directed toward Him.

This verse also warns against assuming that outward religious rules make someone holy. A person may follow many rules and still have a corrupt heart. True holiness begins within.

### *Titus 1:16* — Professing God but Denying Him by Deeds

> *“They profess that they know God, but by their deeds they deny him, being abominable, disobedient, and unfit for any good work.”*
>
> — *Titus 1:16* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul ends the chapter with a sobering description of the false teachers. “They profess that they know God.” They claimed to know God, perhaps even to have special knowledge of Him.

“But by their deeds they deny him.” Their actions contradicted their words. Their lives showed that they did not really know God.

“Being abominable, disobedient, and unfit for any good work.” Paul uses strong words. Their behavior was detestable in God’s sight. They were disobedient to God’s will. And they were “unfit for any good work,” literally “disqualified,” like a coin that fails the test of genuineness. They could not do the good works that true faith produces.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse expresses a theme that runs throughout Titus: genuine faith is shown by godly living. Paul will emphasize good works repeatedly in this letter (*2:7*, 14; *3:1*, 8, 14). The false teachers had words without works; true believers are to have both.

Jesus warned about those who say “Lord, Lord” but do not do the will of His Father (*Matthew 7:21–23*). He also said that people would be known by their fruit (*Matthew 7:16–20*). James wrote that faith without works is dead (*James 2:17*). John said that whoever claims to know God but does not keep His commandments is a liar (*1 John 2:4*).

This does not mean that salvation is earned by good works. Paul will make clear in *Titus 3:5* that God saves “*not by works of righteousness, which we did ourselves*” (*Titus 3:5*). But those who are truly saved will show it in their lives. Good works are the evidence of genuine faith, not its cause.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to examine whether their lives match their words. It is easy to profess faith; it is harder to live it. Do their actions, relationships, and choices reflect the God they claim to know?

It also offers a test for evaluating teachers and leaders. Words alone are not enough. A leader whose life contradicts their teaching should be approached with caution, no matter how persuasive their message.

Finally, this verse encourages believers to pursue good works, not to earn God’s favor, but as the natural fruit of knowing Him. A life full of good works shows the reality of faith to a watching world.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Titus 1* shows that the health of a church depends on sound teaching and godly leaders. Paul begins by grounding his whole ministry in the hope of eternal life promised by God, who cannot lie. Believers can rest in that same hope, trusting every promise of the God whose word never fails, and they can reflect His truthfulness in their own lives.

Paul then describes the kind of leaders the church needs: blameless in character, faithful in marriage, with households that reflect their faith, not arrogant, hot-tempered, drunken, violent, or greedy, but hospitable, self-controlled, upright, and devoted to God. They must hold firmly to the trustworthy message so they can encourage believers with sound teaching and correct those who oppose it. Churches can use these standards when choosing leaders, giving character and faithfulness priority over charisma.

The chapter also warns against false teachers who disrupt households, promote human rules, and seek dishonest gain. They must be confronted, with the goal of restoration. Paul’s use of a well-known saying about Crete is not permission for ethnic stereotyping; the gospel calls believers to see each person as an individual created and loved by God.

Finally, Paul teaches that purity is a matter of the heart, not external rules, and that those who claim to know God must show it in their actions. Believers can enjoy God’s good gifts with gratitude and pursue a life in which their words and deeds both bear witness to the God they know.

## Chapter Prayer

Father, thank You for the hope of eternal life, which You, who cannot lie, promised before time began. Help me to trust every promise You have made and to reflect Your truthfulness in my own life. Raise up leaders in Your church who are blameless in character, gentle, self-controlled, and faithful to Your word. Give them wisdom to encourage Your people with sound teaching and courage to correct error with love. Protect families and churches from those who would deceive them for their own gain. Cleanse my heart, so that I may see Your good gifts as good and receive them with thanksgiving. Let my life match my words, so that my deeds show that I truly know You. Make me fit for every good work. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
