Titus · Chapter 2 of 3

# Titus — Chapter 2

Chapter Theme: The Grace That Trains Us to Live Godly Lives

[Read Titus 2 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/TIT02.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul instructs Titus to teach what fits sound doctrine, giving practical guidance for each group in the church. Older men are to be sober, dignified, self-controlled, and sound in faith, love, and endurance. Older women are to be reverent, not slanderers or slaves to wine, but teachers of what is good, training younger women to love their husbands and children and to live self-controlled, pure, kind lives, so that God’s word is not maligned. Younger men are to be self-controlled, and Titus himself must be an example of good works and sound, dignified teaching. Servants are to be trustworthy so that they adorn the teaching about God our Savior. All of this flows from the grace of God, which has appeared bringing salvation to all people and training believers to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions and to live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives while waiting for the blessed hope, the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ, who gave Himself to redeem and purify a people for His own possession, eager to do good works.

## Chapter Background and Story

Chapter 1 contrasted godly leaders with false teachers whose lives denied the God they professed to know. Chapter 2 turns to the whole church. Paul’s concern is that every believer, young and old, men and women, free and enslaved, would live in a way that fits sound doctrine.

The repeated purpose in this chapter is the church’s witness. Paul wants believers to live so “that God’s word may not be blasphemed” (v5), so that opponents “may be ashamed, having no evil thing to say about us” (v8), and so that believers “may adorn the doctrine of God, our Savior, in all things” (v10). In a culture with a poor moral reputation, transformed lives would make the gospel attractive.

The instructions reflect the household structures of the first century. Christians today apply them in different ways to modern families and societies, as explained below. But the theological heart of the chapter, verses 11–14, is a timeless summary of how God’s grace saves and transforms His people.

### Older Men (*2:1–2*)

“*But say the things which fit sound doctrine*” (*v. 1*), “*that older men should be temperate, sensible, sober minded, sound in faith, in love, and in perseverance*” (*v. 2*). In contrast to the false teachers, Titus is to teach what fits healthy doctrine. Older men are to be clear-headed, dignified, self-controlled, and spiritually healthy in faith, love, and endurance. These are the marks of mature believers who can be examples to others.

### Older and Younger Women (*2:3–5*)

The instructions for older and younger women are studied below.

### Younger Men and Titus’s Example (*2:6–8*)

“*Likewise, exhort the younger men to be sober minded*” (*v. 6*). Younger men are given one instruction: self-control. This word appears again and again in Titus (*1:8*; *2:2*, 5, 6, 12). It means having a sound, disciplined mind and mastering one’s impulses, an especially important quality for young people. Titus’s own example is studied below.

### Servants (*2:9–10*)

“*Exhort servants to be in subjection to their own masters and to be well-pleasing in all things, not contradicting*” (*v. 9*), “*not stealing, but showing all good fidelity, that they may adorn the doctrine of God, our Savior, in all things*” (*v. 10*). As in *Ephesians 6*, *Colossians 3*, and *1 Timothy 6*, Paul addresses believers living within the Roman system of slavery. His instructions are pastoral guidance for people in a system they could not change, not an endorsement of slavery, which the gospel’s teaching about the equal dignity of all in Christ eventually helped to overturn (see the discussion at *Ephesians 6:5–9*). Petty theft by slaves was common in the ancient world. By being honest and trustworthy, believing servants could “adorn” the gospel, making it beautiful and attractive, like jewelry that enhances its wearer. This is a remarkable thought: those with the lowest social status could display the beauty of God’s teaching. Today, the principle applies to all who work: honesty and faithfulness at work can make the gospel attractive to others.

### The Grace of God and the Blessed Hope (*2:11–14*)

The theological heart of the chapter is studied below in two parts.

### Teach with Authority (*2:15*)

“*Say these things and exhort and reprove with all authority. Let no one despise you*” (*v. 15*). Titus is to teach these truths, encourage believers, and correct those who need it, with the authority that comes from God’s word. Like Timothy (*1 Timothy 4:12*), he should not let anyone dismiss him.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Titus 2:3–5* — Older Women Teaching What Is Good

> *“and that older women likewise be reverent in behavior, not slanderers nor enslaved to much wine, teachers of that which is good, that they may train the young wives to love their husbands, to love their children, to be sober minded, chaste, workers at home, kind, being in subjection to their own husbands, that God’s word may not be blasphemed.”*
>
> — *Titus 2:3–5* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul gives instructions for older women. “Older women likewise be reverent in behavior.” Their manner of life should reflect devotion to God, like those who serve in a holy place.

“Not slanderers”: they should not spread gossip or speak evil of others. “Nor enslaved to much wine”: heavy drinking was a common problem, and older women, like older men, were to be self-controlled.

“Teachers of that which is good.” Older women have a vital teaching ministry. They are to model and teach goodness, especially to younger women.

Verse 4: “that they may train the young wives to love their husbands, to love their children.” Older women are to mentor younger women in the practical art of loving their families. Love can be learned and strengthened through example and encouragement.

Verse 5: “to be sober minded, chaste, workers at home, kind, being in subjection to their own husbands.” Younger women are encouraged to be self-controlled, pure, diligent in caring for their households, kind, and respectful toward their husbands.

“That God’s word may not be blasphemed.” The purpose is the reputation of the gospel. In a culture that would judge Christianity by how its followers lived, faithful family life would honor God’s word.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This passage shows the value of mentoring relationships between generations. Older believers have wisdom and experience that younger believers need. The church is meant to be a community where the older help the younger grow, not only through formal teaching but through friendship and example.

Christians apply the specific instructions in different ways. Many Christians understand “workers at home” and “being in subjection to their own husbands” as describing a lasting pattern for marriage and family, with the wife’s primary sphere in the home and a loving, voluntary respect for her husband’s leadership. Others understand these instructions as applying timeless principles, such as diligence, faithfulness, kindness, and respect, within the household structures of the first century, and believe they can be expressed in various ways in modern families where both spouses may work outside the home and share leadership. Both views affirm the dignity and value of women and of homemaking, and both agree that the purpose is a faithful witness to the gospel.

What this passage never teaches is that women must accept mistreatment. “Being in subjection to their own husbands” is set within the broader New Testament teaching that husbands must love their wives as Christ loved the church (*Ephesians 5:25*) and never be harsh with them (*Colossians 3:19*). A wife is never required to submit to abuse, to sin, or to danger. Abuse breaks the very purpose of marriage, and those facing it should seek safety and help.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Churches can encourage intentional mentoring between generations. Older women and men can invest in younger believers, sharing wisdom about faith, marriage, parenting, work, and life. Younger believers can seek out older mentors and learn from their experience.

The call to avoid slander and excessive drinking applies to everyone. Gossip and addiction harm individuals and communities. Believers can guard their speech and practice self-control.

Families can reflect on how their homes display the gospel, through love, kindness, faithfulness, and mutual respect. The way believers treat their spouses and children can make God’s word attractive to a watching world.

### *Titus 2:7–8* — An Example in Everything

> *“In all things show yourself an example of good works. In your teaching, show integrity, seriousness, incorruptibility, and soundness of speech that can’t be condemned, that he who opposes you may be ashamed, having no evil thing to say about us.”*
>
> — *Titus 2:7–8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul now speaks directly to Titus. “In all things show yourself an example of good works.” Titus is to be a model, not only in what he teaches but in how he lives. His good works should be visible to all.

“In your teaching, show integrity.” His teaching should be pure, not corrupted by false ideas or wrong motives. “Seriousness”: dignified, treating God’s truth with respect. “Incorruptibility”: genuine and sincere.

Verse 8: “and soundness of speech that can’t be condemned.” His words should be healthy and beyond reproach, so that no one can legitimately criticize them.

“That he who opposes you may be ashamed, having no evil thing to say about us.” The goal is that even opponents of the faith would have no grounds for accusation. If they look for something wrong, they will find nothing, and they will be embarrassed.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This passage emphasizes that leaders must lead by example. Jesus criticized religious leaders who said but did not do (*Matthew 23:3*). Paul repeatedly urged believers to follow his example as he followed Christ (*1 Corinthians 11:1*; *Philippians 3:17*). Example is one of the most powerful forms of teaching.

The concern for how outsiders view the church runs throughout this chapter and the New Testament. Peter wrote that believers should live such good lives among unbelievers that, even if accused of wrongdoing, their good deeds would be seen and God glorified (*1 Peter 2:12*). The church’s integrity is part of its witness.

This does not mean believers can avoid all criticism. Jesus was criticized despite His perfect life. But believers should ensure that any criticism they receive is not justified by their own wrongdoing.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Everyone who teaches or leads, whether parents, pastors, small group leaders, or mentors, can examine whether their life matches their words. Integrity is more persuasive than eloquence.

Believers can also consider how their conduct appears to those outside the church. Are they honest, kind, and fair? Do their words build up rather than tear down? A consistent, gracious life can disarm critics and open hearts to the gospel.

Finally, this passage encourages believers to speak with care, choosing words that are sound, wise, and beyond reproach, especially when discussing faith or responding to critics.

### *Titus 2:11–12* — The Grace That Trains Us

> *“For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to all men, instructing us to the intent that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we would live soberly, righteously, and godly in this present age;”*
>
> — *Titus 2:11–12* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul now gives the reason behind all his practical instructions. “For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to all men.” God’s grace, His undeserved favor, has appeared in history in the person of Jesus Christ. Like the sun rising over the horizon, grace has shone into the world. And it brings salvation to “all men,” to people of every kind: old and young, men and women, free and enslaved, Jew and Gentile.

Verse 12 describes what grace does. It is “instructing us.” The word means training, like a parent training a child or a coach training an athlete. Grace does not only save; it also teaches.

Grace trains believers to do two things. First, “denying ungodliness and worldly lusts”: saying no to everything that dishonors God and to selfish desires shaped by a world that ignores God. Second, to “live soberly, righteously, and godly in this present age”: to live with self-control (in relation to oneself), with righteousness (in relation to others), and with godliness (in relation to God).

“In this present age” means now, in the midst of everyday life, not just in the future.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This passage shows that grace is not only the starting point of the Christian life but also its ongoing power. Some people think of grace as merely forgiveness, while holy living depends on human effort. Paul teaches that grace itself trains believers to live godly lives. Grace is not a license to sin (*Romans 6:1–2*); it is the power to live free from sin.

The three-part description of the godly life, sober, righteous, and godly, covers every relationship. Sobriety governs a person’s inner life; righteousness governs their relationships with others; godliness governs their relationship with God. Grace transforms all three.

The phrase “bringing salvation to all men” has been understood in different ways, as discussed at *1 Timothy 2:4*. At minimum, it means that God’s grace is offered to people of every kind and background, without distinction.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can approach spiritual growth not as a grim struggle to earn God’s approval but as a response to grace. God has already shown them favor. That grace now teaches them to say no to sin and yes to godliness.

When facing temptation, believers can remember that grace instructs them, “*denying ungodliness and worldly lusts*” (*v. 12*), to live godly lives. Grace gives both the motivation and the power to resist.

Believers can also look at every area of life: personal habits, relationships, and devotion to God, asking how grace is shaping them to live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives.

### *Titus 2:13–14* — Our Great God and Savior, Jesus Christ

> *“looking for the blessed hope and appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ, who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity and purify for himself a people for his own possession, zealous for good works.”*
>
> — *Titus 2:13–14* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul continues: believers live godly lives while “looking for the blessed hope and appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ.”

“The blessed hope” is the return of Christ. It is “blessed” because it brings joy and completes salvation. Believers wait for it with eager expectation.

“Appearing of the glory” describes Christ’s return in splendor. The first appearing was of grace (v11); the second will be of glory.

“Our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ.” Most scholars and translations understand this phrase as referring to one person: Jesus Christ is “our great God and Savior.” This is one of the clearest statements in the New Testament that Jesus is God.

Verse 14 describes what Christ did: “who gave himself for us.” He gave His own life. The purpose was twofold: “that he might redeem us from all iniquity,” setting us free from the power and guilt of sin, “and purify for himself a people for his own possession.” Christ is creating a people who belong to Him, cleansed and set apart.

“Zealous for good works.” This people is marked by enthusiasm for doing good.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses connect Christ’s first and second comings. His first coming brought grace and salvation; His second will bring glory. Believers live between these two appearings, trained by grace and looking forward in hope.

The title “our great God and Savior” is significant. In the Roman world, emperors were sometimes called “god” and “savior.” Paul declares that the true God and Savior is Jesus Christ. This reflects the church’s conviction that Jesus is fully divine, a conviction expressed in *John 1:1*, *Romans 9:5*, *Hebrews 1:8*, and *2 Peter 1:1*.

The phrase “a people for his own possession” echoes God’s words to Israel at Mount Sinai: “*you shall be my own possession from among all peoples*” (*Exodus 19:5*). Peter applies similar language to the church (*1 Peter 2:9*). Through Christ, God is gathering a treasured people from every nation.

The goal is a people “zealous for good works.” Salvation is not by works (*Titus 3:5*), but it produces a passion for doing good. Grace saves, trains, and fills believers with zeal for good deeds.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

The hope of Christ’s return can shape how believers live now. Knowing that He will appear in glory gives motivation to live godly lives, endurance in hardship, and joy in waiting.

The truth that Jesus is “our great God and Savior” invites worship. Believers can honor Him not only as a teacher or example but as God Himself, who gave Himself for them.

Finally, being “a people for his own possession” gives believers a deep sense of belonging. They are treasured by Christ, purchased by His sacrifice. This identity can inspire them to be “zealous for good works,” eagerly looking for ways to serve others and reflect His love.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Titus 2* shows that sound doctrine must lead to godly living in every part of life. Paul gives practical instructions for older men, older women, younger women, younger men, and servants, each designed to help believers live in a way that honors God and makes the gospel attractive. Christians apply the specific household instructions in different ways today, but the underlying principles are clear: self-control, faithfulness, kindness, integrity, and love.

The chapter also highlights the value of mentoring across generations. Older believers can teach and model what is good, helping younger believers grow in faith and in loving their families. Leaders, like Titus, are called to be examples in everything, with teaching and lives beyond reproach.

A recurring purpose runs through the chapter: the reputation of the gospel. When believers live faithfully, even those with the lowest status in society can “adorn” the teaching about God, making it beautiful to others. The way believers live at home and at work is part of their witness.

At the heart of the chapter is the grace of God. Grace has appeared in Jesus Christ, bringing salvation to all people. That same grace trains believers to say no to ungodliness and to live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives now. And it fills them with hope as they wait for the appearing of the glory of their great God and Savior, Jesus Christ, who gave Himself to redeem them and make them His own people, eager to do good. Grace saves, grace trains, and grace gives hope.

## Chapter Prayer

Gracious God, thank You that Your grace has appeared in Jesus Christ, bringing salvation to people of every kind. Let Your grace train me to say no to ungodliness and worldly desires and to live a self-controlled, upright, and godly life in this present age. Help me to be an example of good works and to speak with integrity. Bless the relationships between generations in Your church; help the older to teach what is good and the younger to learn with humility. Let my home and my work adorn the teaching about You, our Savior. Protect every home from harm and fill families with love and respect. I wait with joy for the blessed hope, the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ. Thank You, Lord Jesus, for giving Yourself to redeem me and make me Your own. Make me zealous for good works. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Titus · Chapter 3 of 3

# Titus — Chapter 3

Chapter Theme: Saved by Mercy, Devoted to Good Works

[Read Titus 3 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/TIT03.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul tells Titus to remind believers to be subject to rulers and authorities, to be obedient and ready for every good work, to speak evil of no one, to avoid quarreling, and to be gentle and courteous toward all people. They should remember that they too were once foolish, disobedient, enslaved to passions, and full of malice and envy. But when the kindness and love of God our Savior appeared, He saved them, not because of righteous things they had done, but because of His mercy, through the washing of rebirth and renewal by the Holy Spirit, whom He poured out richly through Jesus Christ, so that, justified by His grace, they might become heirs with the hope of eternal life. Paul wants Titus to stress these truths so that believers will devote themselves to good works, while avoiding foolish controversies and warning divisive people. He closes with travel plans, a request to help Zenas and Apollos, and a final encouragement for believers to do good works that meet urgent needs.

## Chapter Background and Story

In the final chapter of Titus, Paul turns from relationships within the church to relationships with the wider world. How should believers in Crete relate to their rulers, their neighbors, and those outside the faith? Crete, like much of the Roman world, had a reputation for unruliness, and its people may have resented Roman rule. Believers were to be different: peaceful, gentle, and devoted to doing good.

The motivation for this kind of life is not human goodness but God’s mercy. In verses 3–7, Paul gives one of the richest summaries of salvation in the New Testament. He reminds believers what they once were, what God has done, and what they now have. Because God has been kind to them, they are to be kind to others.

The chapter, and the letter, ends with an emphasis on good works. Paul mentions them three times (vv1, 8, 14). Believers are saved not by good works, but for good works.

### Good Citizens and Gentle Neighbors (*3:1–2*)

Paul’s instructions about relating to authorities and to all people are studied below.

### What God Has Done (*3:3–7*)

“*For we were also once foolish, disobedient, deceived, serving various lusts and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful, and hating one another*” (*v. 3*). Paul includes himself: “we were also once.” Before God’s grace, believers were foolish, rebellious, deceived, enslaved to their desires, and filled with hatred. This memory keeps them humble and gentle toward those who are still in that condition. God’s saving work is studied below.

### Devoted to Good Works (*3:8–11*)

The call to devote oneself to good works is studied below. “*but shun foolish questionings, genealogies, strife, and disputes about the law; for they are unprofitable and vain*” (*v. 9*). As in *1 Timothy 1:4* and *2 Timothy 2:23*, Paul warns against pointless debates. Speculative arguments about genealogies and fine points of the Law were producing conflict, not godliness.

“*Avoid a factious man after a first and second warning*” (*v. 10*), “*knowing that such a one is perverted and sinful, being self-condemned*” (*v. 11*). A “factious man” is someone who stirs up division, creating parties and splits in the church. Paul gives a clear process: warn him once, then a second time. If he persists, have nothing more to do with him. This follows the pattern Jesus taught in *Matthew 18:15–17*. The person who continues in divisiveness after repeated warnings shows by his own behavior that something is wrong.

### Final Instructions (*3:12–15*)

“*When I send Artemas to you, or Tychicus, be diligent to come to me to Nicopolis, for I have determined to winter there*” (*v. 12*). Paul planned to send a replacement so that Titus could join him. Nicopolis was a city on the western coast of Greece. Tychicus is mentioned in several of Paul’s letters as a trusted messenger (*Ephesians 6:21*; *Colossians 4:7*; *2 Timothy 4:12*). Artemas is mentioned only here.

“*Send Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their journey speedily, that nothing may be lacking for them*” (*v. 13*). Zenas was a lawyer, perhaps an expert in Roman law or in the Jewish Law. Apollos was the eloquent teacher from Alexandria who had ministered in Ephesus and Corinth (*Acts 18:24–28*; *1 Corinthians 3:6*). Titus and the Cretan believers were to help them on their journey with supplies and support, a practical expression of Christian hospitality.

“*Let our people also learn to maintain good works to meet necessary needs, that they may not be unfruitful*” (*v. 14*). Supporting traveling ministers was one example of good works. Believers were to “learn” to do good, to make it a habit, so that their lives would be fruitful.

“*All who are with me greet you. Greet those who love us in faith. Grace be with you all. Amen*” (*v. 15*). Paul ends with greetings and a blessing of grace for “all,” the whole church.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Titus 3:1–2* — Ready for Every Good Work

> *“Remind them to be in subjection to rulers and to authorities, to be obedient, to be ready for every good work, to speak evil of no one, not to be contentious, to be gentle, showing all humility toward all men.”*
>
> — *Titus 3:1–2* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul tells Titus to remind believers of their responsibilities in society. “Remind them to be in subjection to rulers and to authorities, to be obedient.” Believers should respect and obey the government in matters of civil order. Paul gives similar teaching in *Romans 13:1–7*.

“To be ready for every good work.” Believers should be eager to contribute to the good of their communities.

Verse 2 describes how they should treat everyone. “To speak evil of no one”: not slandering or insulting anyone, including rulers and unbelievers. “Not to be contentious”: not argumentative or quarrelsome. “To be gentle”: reasonable and gracious. “Showing all humility toward all men”: treating everyone with courtesy, gentleness, and consideration.

The phrase “toward all men” is important. These attitudes are not just for fellow believers but for everyone, including those who disagree with them, oppose them, or behave badly.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses describe a Christian presence in society that is respectful, constructive, and gracious. Believers are not to be rebellious troublemakers but people who contribute to the common good. *Jeremiah 29:7* instructed the exiles in Babylon to seek the peace of the city and pray for it. Peter wrote that believers should honor everyone and honor the king (*1 Peter 2:17*).

Submission to authorities has limits. When rulers command what God forbids, believers must obey God rather than people (*Acts 5:29*). Christians throughout history have resisted unjust laws and protected the oppressed. But in ordinary matters, believers are to be law-abiding and respectful.

The command to “speak evil of no one” is challenging, especially in a culture where harsh speech about leaders and opponents is common. Believers can disagree, advocate for justice, and oppose wrongdoing, but they are to do so without slander, insults, or contempt.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can be good citizens: obeying laws, paying taxes, participating in their communities, and seeking the common good. Being “ready for every good work” might mean volunteering, helping neighbors, supporting local schools, or caring for those in need.

These verses also challenge how believers speak about others, especially in political discussions and on social media. Believers can express their views honestly while avoiding slander, insults, and contempt. Gentleness and courtesy toward everyone, including opponents, reflect the character of Christ.

When believers must oppose injustice, they can do so with courage and with grace, standing firmly for what is right while treating others with respect.

### *Titus 3:4–5* — Saved by His Mercy

> *“But when the kindness of God our Savior and his love toward mankind appeared, not by works of righteousness which we did ourselves, but according to his mercy, he saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewing by the Holy Spirit,”*
>
> — *Titus 3:4–5* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After describing what believers once were (v3), Paul describes what God did. “But when the kindness of God our Savior and his love toward mankind appeared.” The words “kindness” and “love toward mankind” describe God’s generous goodwill toward humanity. The second word is the root of the English word “philanthropy.” God’s love for humanity “appeared” in the coming of Jesus Christ.

Verse 5: “not by works of righteousness which we did ourselves.” God did not save people because of their good deeds. Even their best efforts could not earn salvation.

“But according to his mercy.” Salvation flows from God’s mercy, His compassion toward those who do not deserve it.

“He saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewing by the Holy Spirit.” God saved believers by washing them and giving them new life. “Regeneration” means new birth, being born again (*John 3:3–5*). “Renewing” means being made new. Both are the work of the Holy Spirit.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses are among the clearest statements in Scripture that salvation is by God’s mercy, not human works. They echo *Ephesians 2:8–9*: “for by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works.”

“The washing of regeneration” has been understood in different ways. Many Christian traditions, including Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, and Anglican traditions, see a reference to baptism, through which God works to cleanse and give new life. Other traditions, including many Baptist and evangelical churches, understand the washing as the inner cleansing of the heart by the Holy Spirit, which baptism outwardly pictures. Both views agree that new birth and renewal are God’s work by the Holy Spirit, not human achievement.

The contrast between verse 3 and verses 4–5 is striking. Believers were once hateful and hated, but God was kind and loving toward them. They did not deserve His mercy, yet He saved them. This is the gospel: God’s undeserved love reaching people at their worst.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can rest in the truth that their salvation does not depend on their performance. On days when they feel they have failed, they can remember that God saved them according to His mercy, not their works.

This truth also shapes how believers treat others. Remembering that they too were once foolish and disobedient, they can be gentle and patient with those who are still far from God. Their own salvation by mercy calls them to show mercy.

Believers can also give thanks for the work of the Holy Spirit, who has given them new birth and continues to renew them day by day.

### *Titus 3:6–7* — Poured Out Richly, Heirs of Hope

> *“whom he poured out on us richly through Jesus Christ our Savior; that being justified by his grace, we might be made heirs according to the hope of eternal life.”*
>
> — *Titus 3:6–7* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul continues describing God’s saving work. The Holy Spirit is the one “whom he poured out on us richly through Jesus Christ our Savior.” God did not give the Spirit sparingly. He poured Him out abundantly, as He promised through the prophet Joel (*Joel 2:28*) and fulfilled at Pentecost (*Acts 2:17*, 33). The Spirit comes “through Jesus Christ,” who sends Him to His people.

Notice that all three persons of the Trinity are involved: God the Father saves (v4–5), the Holy Spirit renews (v5–6), and Jesus Christ is the one through whom the Spirit is poured out (v6).

Verse 7 gives the purpose: “that being justified by his grace, we might be made heirs according to the hope of eternal life.” “Justified” means declared righteous, put right with God. This happens “by his grace,” as a gift. And the result is that believers become “heirs.” They will inherit eternal life. Right now, they have the hope of it; one day they will possess it fully.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses summarize the whole of salvation: God’s kindness, mercy, new birth, the Spirit’s renewal, justification by grace, and the inheritance of eternal life. It is a complete picture, from beginning to end, all God’s gracious work.

Being “heirs” is a rich image. Paul uses it often (*Romans 8:16–17*; *Galatians 4:7*). Heirs receive their inheritance not because they earned it but because of their relationship with the one who gives it. Believers are God’s children and therefore heirs of all He has promised.

The word “richly” emphasizes God’s generosity. He does not hold back. The Spirit is given in abundance, and with Him comes every spiritual blessing. Believers do not need to fear that God’s supply will run out.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can find assurance in these verses. They have been justified by grace, made heirs, and given a sure hope. Their standing with God is secure, based on His grace rather than their achievements.

The rich outpouring of the Spirit invites believers to depend on Him daily. He is not given sparingly. They can ask for His help, guidance, and strength with confidence.

Finally, the hope of eternal life can shape how believers face difficulties. Whatever they lose or suffer now, they are heirs of an inheritance that cannot be taken away.

### *Titus 3:8* — Careful to Maintain Good Works

> *“This saying is faithful, and concerning these things I desire that you insist confidently, so that those who have believed God may be careful to maintain good works. These things are good and profitable to men;”*
>
> — *Titus 3:8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“This saying is faithful.” This phrase likely refers to the summary of salvation in verses 4–7. It is trustworthy and true.

“And concerning these things I desire that you insist confidently.” Paul wants Titus to teach these truths firmly and clearly. The gospel of grace is not to be mentioned once and then left behind; it must be stressed repeatedly.

“So that those who have believed God may be careful to maintain good works.” The purpose of emphasizing grace is that believers will devote themselves to doing good. The word “careful” means to think about, to give attention to. Believers are to be intentional about good works, not leaving them to chance.

“These things are good and profitable to men.” Good works benefit others and the community. They are not merely private acts of piety but practical help to people.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows the right relationship between grace and good works. Grace comes first. Believers are saved by mercy, not works (v5). But grace leads to good works. In fact, Paul says that emphasizing grace is what produces good works. Some fear that teaching grace will make people careless about holiness. Paul teaches the opposite: grace, rightly understood, motivates believers to do good.

This echoes *Ephesians 2:10*: “*For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them*” (*Ephesians 2:10*). Believers are saved by grace for good works.

The phrase “profitable to men” connects good works with love for others. Christian good works are not mainly about religious rituals but about meeting real needs, as verse 14 emphasizes. They are the practical expression of the kindness and love that God has shown.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can be intentional about doing good. This might involve setting aside time and resources for serving others, looking for needs in their community, supporting ministries that help the poor, or showing kindness to neighbors and coworkers.

Churches can emphasize both grace and good works, teaching that salvation is God’s free gift and encouraging believers to respond with lives of practical love.

This verse also offers a test of genuine faith. Those who truly believe God’s grace will be marked by care for others. A faith that produces no good works should lead to honest self-examination.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Titus 3* shows how believers should live in the world: as good citizens, ready for every good work, speaking evil of no one, avoiding quarrels, and showing gentleness and courtesy to all people. This kind of life stands out in a world full of conflict and harsh words. Believers can respect authorities, contribute to the common good, and engage even their opponents with grace, while still standing firmly for justice.

The motivation for this life is the memory of God’s mercy. Believers were once foolish, disobedient, and enslaved to their desires, filled with malice and hatred. But God’s kindness and love appeared in Jesus Christ. He saved them not because of their righteous works, but because of His mercy, through new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit, poured out richly through Christ. Justified by grace, they are now heirs with the hope of eternal life.

This gospel of grace does not make believers careless. On the contrary, Paul insists on it so that believers will devote themselves to good works that meet real needs. Grace saves, and grace produces a life of practical love.

Finally, the chapter calls believers to avoid pointless controversies and to deal wisely with those who cause division. Instead, they are to focus on what is good and profitable: the gospel and the good works it produces. In this way, the kindness of God that appeared in Christ continues to appear through His people in the world.

## Chapter Prayer

God our Savior, thank You for the kindness and love You showed when You appeared in Jesus Christ. I remember that I was once foolish, disobedient, and enslaved to my own desires, yet You saved me, not because of anything I had done, but because of Your mercy. Thank You for washing me, giving me new birth, and renewing me by Your Holy Spirit, whom You poured out richly through Jesus Christ. Thank You that I am justified by Your grace and an heir of eternal life. Help me to be a good citizen and a gentle neighbor, ready for every good work. Guard my tongue from speaking evil of anyone, and keep me from quarrels. Make me courteous and kind to all people. Let Your grace move me to devote myself to good works that meet real needs, so that my life may be fruitful for Your glory. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Book 18 of 27

# Philemon

## About This Letter

Philemon is the shortest and most personal of Paul’s letters. Paul wrote it from prison, probably in Rome around A.D. 60–62, at the same time as Colossians, and nearly all scholars agree that Paul himself wrote it. It is addressed to Philemon, a believer in Colossae in whose home a church met, and also to Apphia, Archippus, and the whole house church.

The letter concerns Onesimus, a slave who belonged to Philemon. Onesimus had left his master, perhaps running away, perhaps after wronging him in some way, and possibly seeking out Paul to plead his case. While with Paul, Onesimus became a believer and a beloved helper. Under Roman law, a runaway slave could face severe punishment. Paul sends Onesimus back to Philemon, carrying this letter, in which Paul appeals to Philemon to receive Onesimus not merely as a slave but as a beloved brother in the Lord, and offers to pay anything Onesimus owes.

## The Shape of the Letter

After a warm greeting, Paul thanks God for Philemon’s love and faith, which have refreshed the hearts of the believers. Rather than commanding, Paul appeals to Philemon on the basis of love, as an old man and a prisoner, on behalf of Onesimus, whose name means “useful,” and who has become truly useful. Paul expresses his wish to have kept Onesimus with him but sends him back so that Philemon’s kindness may be freely given. He suggests that God may have allowed the separation so that Philemon might have Onesimus back forever, as a brother. Paul asks Philemon to welcome Onesimus as he would welcome Paul himself, to charge any debt to Paul’s account, and to do even more than Paul asks. He closes with a request for a guest room and greetings from his companions.

## Themes to Watch For

Watch for the transforming power of the gospel in a single life, reconciliation between people separated by wrongs and by social status, the new family of God in which a slave and his master are brothers, love that appeals rather than commands, forgiveness, the willingness to bear another’s debt, and the quiet ways the gospel undermines the foundations of slavery. In a few short lines, Philemon offers a living picture of what Christ has done for us: He stands between us and the one we have wronged and says, “Put that to my account.”

## Chapters

1.  [Philemon 1](#c18_PHM_001.xhtml) — Receive Him as a Beloved Brother

Philemon · Chapter 1 of 1

# Philemon — Chapter 1

Chapter Theme: Receive Him as a Beloved Brother

[Read Philemon 1 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/PHM01.htm)

Main Teaching

Paul, writing from prison, greets Philemon, a dear coworker whose home hosts a church, and thanks God for his love and faith, which have refreshed the hearts of the believers. Although Paul could command him, he appeals to him in love on behalf of Onesimus, Philemon’s slave, who became Paul’s spiritual son while Paul was in chains. Once “useless” to Philemon, Onesimus is now truly useful. Paul sends him back, though he would have liked to keep him, so that Philemon’s goodness would be freely chosen. Perhaps Onesimus was separated for a while so that Philemon could have him back forever, no longer as a slave but more than a slave, a beloved brother. Paul asks Philemon to welcome Onesimus as he would welcome Paul himself, and to charge anything Onesimus owes to Paul’s account. Confident that Philemon will do even more than he asks, Paul requests a guest room and sends greetings from his companions.

## Chapter Background and Story

Philemon was a believer in Colossae, probably a man of some wealth, since he owned at least one slave and had a house large enough for a church to meet in. He had likely come to faith through Paul’s ministry, perhaps during Paul’s years in Ephesus (v19; *Acts 19:10*). Apphia may have been his wife, and Archippus perhaps his son or a church leader (*Colossians 4:17*).

Onesimus was a slave in Philemon’s household. At some point, he left. He may have run away, perhaps taking money or property with him (v18). Some scholars suggest instead that he sought out Paul deliberately, as a friend of his master, to plead for help after a dispute, which was a recognized practice in Roman law. Either way, Onesimus ended up with Paul in prison, heard the gospel, and became a believer. He then served Paul faithfully.

Now Paul faced a delicate situation. Under Roman law, a runaway slave could be severely punished, branded, or even executed. Paul could not simply keep Onesimus without Philemon’s consent. So he sent Onesimus back, together with Tychicus, carrying this letter (*Colossians 4:7–9*). The letter is a masterpiece of tact, love, and gospel-shaped persuasion.

This letter also raises the question of how the gospel relates to slavery. Paul does not explicitly command Philemon to free Onesimus, though many readers believe that is what he hints at when he says Philemon will do “even beyond what I say” (v21). What Paul does is even more revolutionary in its implications: he insists that Onesimus be received as “a beloved brother,” as Paul himself would be received. Once a master sees his slave as a brother in Christ and an equal before God, the foundations of slavery begin to crumble. Early Christian tradition suggests that Onesimus may later have become a leader in the church; a bishop of Ephesus named Onesimus is mentioned in a letter written by Ignatius of Antioch in the early second century, though whether he is the same person is uncertain.

### Greeting (*1:1–3*)

“*Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus, and Timothy our brother, to Philemon, our beloved fellow worker*” (*v. 1*), “*to the beloved Apphia, to Archippus our fellow soldier, and to the assembly in your house*” (*v. 2*): “*Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ*” (*v. 3*). Paul calls himself “a prisoner of Christ Jesus” rather than an apostle. He comes not with authority but in humility. The letter is addressed not only to Philemon but to his household and the church, so the request will be heard by the whole community.

### Thanksgiving for Philemon’s Love (*1:4–7*)

Paul’s thanksgiving and prayer for Philemon are studied below.

### Paul’s Appeal for Onesimus (*1:8–14*)

Paul’s appeal, and the transformation of Onesimus, are studied below. “*I am sending him back. Therefore receive him, that is, my own heart*” (*v. 12*). Paul’s love for Onesimus is deep. Sending him back is like sending part of himself.

“*whom I desired to keep with me, that on your behalf he might serve me in my chains for the Good News*” (*v. 13*). “*But I was willing to do nothing without your consent, that your goodness would not be as of necessity, but of free will*” (*v. 14*). Paul could have kept Onesimus. But he wanted Philemon’s kindness to be freely given, not forced. Love that is coerced is not love.

### More Than a Slave (*1:15–16*)

Paul’s reflection on God’s purpose in the separation is studied below.

### Put It to My Account (*1:17–20*)

Paul’s offer to bear Onesimus’s debt is studied below. “*Yes, brother, let me have joy from you in the Lord. Refresh my heart in the Lord*” (*v. 20*). Philemon had refreshed the hearts of many believers (v7). Now Paul asks him to refresh Paul’s heart by welcoming Onesimus.

### Confidence and Greetings (*1:21–25*)

“*Having confidence in your obedience, I write to you, knowing that you will do even beyond what I say*” (*v. 21*). Paul expresses confidence that Philemon will do more than he asks. Many readers understand this as a gentle hint that Philemon should free Onesimus, perhaps so that he can return to serve with Paul.

“*Also, prepare a guest room for me, for I hope that through your prayers I will be restored to you*” (*v. 22*). Paul hoped to be released from prison and to visit Colossae. This request also meant that Paul would see for himself how Philemon had responded.

“*Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, greets you*” (*v. 23*), “*as do Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, my fellow workers*” (*v. 24*). The same companions are mentioned in *Colossians 4:10–14*. “*The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen*” (*v. 25*).

## Important Verses Explained

### *Philemon 1:4–7* — Love That Refreshes Hearts

> *“I thank my God always, making mention of you in my prayers, hearing of your love and of the faith which you have toward the Lord Jesus and toward all the saints, that the fellowship of your faith may become effective in the knowledge of every good thing which is in us in Christ Jesus. For we have much joy and comfort in your love, because the hearts of the saints have been refreshed through you, brother.”*
>
> — *Philemon 1:4–7* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul begins with thanksgiving. “I thank my God always, making mention of you in my prayers.” Paul regularly prayed for Philemon.

Verse 5: “hearing of your love and of the faith which you have toward the Lord Jesus and toward all the saints.” Philemon was known for his love and faith, directed both toward Jesus and toward fellow believers.

Verse 6 states Paul’s prayer: “that the fellowship of your faith may become effective in the knowledge of every good thing which is in us in Christ Jesus.” This verse is difficult to translate, but its meaning seems to be that Paul prays Philemon’s shared faith, his partnership with other believers, would become active and effective, leading to a fuller understanding of every good thing believers have in Christ. In other words, Paul prays that Philemon’s faith would show itself in action, and that as it does, he would understand more deeply the riches of life in Christ.

Verse 7: “For we have much joy and comfort in your love, because the hearts of the saints have been refreshed through you, brother.” Philemon’s love had brought joy and encouragement to many believers. “Hearts” here is a strong word meaning the deepest emotions. “Refreshed” means given rest, like a weary traveler finding relief.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This thanksgiving sets the stage for Paul’s request. Philemon was known for refreshing others with his love. Now Paul will ask him to extend that same love to Onesimus. Paul is not asking Philemon to become someone different, but to act consistently with who he already is.

Verse 6 connects faith with action. Faith is not merely private belief; it becomes “effective” when it is expressed in love and generosity. *James 2:14–17* makes a similar point. As believers put their faith into action, they come to know more fully the good things they have in Christ.

The description of Philemon as one who refreshes hearts is a beautiful picture of Christian love. Some people leave others drained; others leave them refreshed. Philemon was the second kind. His hospitality, generosity, and kindness renewed the spirits of those around him.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can ask whether their love refreshes others. Do people leave their company encouraged, strengthened, and renewed? Hospitality, kindness, listening, and practical help are ways of refreshing others’ hearts.

Believers can also pray for one another as Paul prayed for Philemon: that their faith would become active and effective, expressed in love and good works.

Finally, this passage shows the value of encouragement. Paul tells Philemon how much his love has meant. Believers can take time to tell others how they have been encouraged by them.

### *Philemon 1:8–11* — Useless Became Useful

> *“Therefore though I have all boldness in Christ to command you that which is appropriate, yet for love’s sake I rather appeal to you, being such a one as Paul, the aged, but also a prisoner of Jesus Christ. I appeal to you for my child Onesimus, whom I have become the father of in my chains, who once was useless to you, but now is useful to you and to me.”*
>
> — *Philemon 1:8–11* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul now begins his request. “Therefore though I have all boldness in Christ to command you that which is appropriate.” As an apostle, Paul could have commanded Philemon to do the right thing.

Verse 9: “yet for love’s sake I rather appeal to you.” Instead of commanding, Paul appeals on the basis of love. He describes himself as “Paul, the aged, but also a prisoner of Jesus Christ.” Some interpreters read “the aged” as “an ambassador,” since the Greek words are very similar. Either way, Paul presents himself not as a powerful authority but as an old man in chains, appealing to a friend.

Verse 10: “I appeal to you for my child Onesimus, whom I have become the father of in my chains.” Paul finally names Onesimus, after carefully preparing Philemon’s heart. He calls Onesimus “my child,” because Onesimus had come to faith through Paul while Paul was in prison.

Verse 11: “who once was useless to you, but now is useful to you and to me.” This is a wordplay. “Onesimus” means “useful” or “profitable.” He had not lived up to his name. He had been useless, perhaps even harmful, to Philemon. But now, transformed by Christ, he is truly useful.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Paul’s approach shows the power of love over authority. He could have demanded obedience, but he chose to appeal. Love invites rather than compels. This reflects the way God Himself often works, drawing people with kindness rather than forcing them (*Romans 2:4*; *Hosea 11:4*).

The transformation of Onesimus is a picture of what the gospel does. Those who were once “useless,” lost in sin, unable to fulfill their purpose, are made new in Christ. Paul himself had been transformed from persecutor to apostle. Onesimus was transformed from runaway slave to beloved brother and faithful helper. Christ makes people what God intended them to be.

The fact that Onesimus came to faith while Paul was in chains shows that God works in unexpected places. Paul’s imprisonment, which seemed like a setback, became the setting for a life changed by grace.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can follow Paul’s example by appealing to others with love rather than demanding with authority, especially in delicate situations. Gentle persuasion often achieves more than force.

This passage also offers hope to anyone who feels “useless,” whether because of past failures, broken relationships, or wasted years. In Christ, people are made new and given purpose. No one is beyond His transforming power.

Finally, believers can look for God at work in difficult circumstances. Like Paul in prison, they may find that hardship becomes an opportunity for God to change lives.

### *Philemon 1:15–16* — No Longer as a Slave, but a Beloved Brother

> *“For perhaps he was therefore separated from you for a while that you would have him forever, no longer as a slave, but more than a slave, a beloved brother—especially to me, but how much rather to you, both in the flesh and in the Lord.”*
>
> — *Philemon 1:15–16* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul offers a new way of looking at what happened. “For perhaps he was therefore separated from you for a while that you would have him forever.” Notice the gentle word “perhaps.” Paul does not claim to know God’s purposes for certain, but he suggests that God may have used Onesimus’s departure for good. Notice also the passive phrase “was separated,” as if God was quietly at work in the events. Onesimus was gone “for a while,” but now Philemon could have him “forever,” as a brother for eternity.

Verse 16: “no longer as a slave, but more than a slave, a beloved brother.” This is the heart of the letter. Philemon is to receive Onesimus not merely as a returning slave but as something far greater: a brother in Christ, beloved.

“Especially to me, but how much rather to you, both in the flesh and in the Lord.” Onesimus was dear to Paul, and he should be even dearer to Philemon, both “in the flesh,” in their everyday human relationship, and “in the Lord,” as fellow believers.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show how God can work through human failures and wrongs for good, much as Joseph said to his brothers, “*you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good*” (*Genesis 50:20*). This does not excuse wrongdoing, but it shows that God’s purposes can prevail even through it.

The phrase “a beloved brother” is radical. In the Roman world, slaves were legally considered property. Paul declares that in Christ, Onesimus is Philemon’s brother, equal before God (*Galatians 3:28*; *Colossians 3:11*). If Philemon truly received Onesimus as a beloved brother, the relationship of master and slave would be transformed from within, and its foundations would be undermined.

“Both in the flesh and in the Lord” means this brotherhood was not only spiritual but practical. It would change how Philemon treated Onesimus in daily life, not only on Sundays.

This passage, along with the rest of the New Testament’s teaching on human dignity, helped plant the seeds that eventually led many Christians to work for the abolition of slavery. Tragically, others in later centuries ignored this teaching and used Scripture to defend slavery, a grave distortion that the church must reject.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses challenge believers to see one another as family, regardless of social status, background, or past wrongs. In the church, there are no second-class members. Employers and employees, rich and poor, people of every ethnic background, are brothers and sisters in Christ.

They also encourage believers to look for God’s purposes in painful situations. A broken relationship, a departure, or a loss may, in God’s hands, become an opportunity for something new and lasting.

Finally, these verses invite believers to examine whether their faith changes how they treat people “in the flesh,” in daily life. True brotherhood in Christ shows up in practical respect, kindness, and justice.

### *Philemon 1:17–19* — Put That to My Account

> *“If then you count me a partner, receive him as you would receive me. But if he has wronged you at all or owes you anything, put that to my account. I, Paul, write this with my own hand: I will repay it (not to mention to you that you owe to me even your own self besides).”*
>
> — *Philemon 1:17–19* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Paul makes his request explicit. “If then you count me a partner, receive him as you would receive me.” Paul identifies himself completely with Onesimus. Whatever welcome Philemon would give Paul, he should give Onesimus.

Verse 18: “But if he has wronged you at all or owes you anything, put that to my account.” Onesimus may have stolen from Philemon or caused him financial loss. Paul offers to take responsibility for the debt. Whatever Onesimus owes, Philemon can charge to Paul.

Verse 19: “I, Paul, write this with my own hand: I will repay it.” Paul writes this promise himself, like signing a legal IOU. He is serious.

“Not to mention to you that you owe to me even your own self besides.” With gentle humor, Paul reminds Philemon that he owes Paul far more, his very life in Christ, since he likely came to faith through Paul’s ministry. Paul does not insist on it, but the reminder adds weight to his appeal.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses offer one of the most beautiful pictures of the gospel in the New Testament. Onesimus had wronged his master and owed a debt he could not pay. Paul stepped in as his advocate, identified himself with Onesimus, and offered to pay the debt himself. Philemon was asked to receive Onesimus as he would receive Paul.

This is exactly what Christ has done for sinners. Humanity has wronged God and owes a debt it cannot pay. Christ stands between sinners and God as their advocate (*1 John 2:1*). He identifies with them, takes their debt upon Himself, and pays it in full at the cross (*Colossians 2:14*). And God receives sinners as He receives His beloved Son, because they are in Him (*Ephesians 1:6*). Martin Luther once said that all of us are God’s Onesimus.

This passage also shows what reconciliation can cost. Paul was willing to pay personally so that two people could be reconciled. True reconciliation sometimes requires someone to absorb a cost, whether financial, emotional, or relational.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can marvel at the grace of Christ, who has said to the Father, “Put that to my account,” taking their debt of sin upon Himself. This truth can bring deep assurance and gratitude.

Believers can also follow Paul’s example by helping others be reconciled. This might involve mediating conflicts, standing with someone who has done wrong and is seeking to make things right, or even bearing some cost to help restore a relationship.

At the same time, reconciliation should never pressure someone to return to a dangerous or abusive situation. Paul’s appeal assumed that Philemon was a believer known for his love, and that Onesimus would be safe and welcomed as a brother. Reconciliation must always protect the dignity and safety of all involved.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

Philemon is a short letter with a powerful message about the transforming power of the gospel in real relationships. Paul appeals to Philemon, a believer known for refreshing the hearts of others, to welcome back Onesimus, a slave who had wronged him but who had since become a believer and a beloved helper to Paul.

The letter shows how the gospel changes people. Onesimus, whose name means “useful,” had once been useless to his master. But in Christ, he became truly useful. No one is beyond the reach of God’s grace, and those who have failed can be made new.

The letter also shows how the gospel changes relationships. Paul asks Philemon to receive Onesimus not merely as a slave but as a beloved brother, both in everyday life and in the Lord. This vision of brotherhood across the deepest social divisions planted seeds that would one day help bring down the institution of slavery. Believers today are called to see every fellow believer as family, regardless of status or past wrongs, and to let that family bond shape how they treat one another.

Paul’s method is also instructive. Rather than commanding, he appeals in love, wanting Philemon’s kindness to be freely given. He is willing to take Onesimus’s debt upon himself so that reconciliation can happen. In this, Paul reflects Christ, who stands between sinners and God and says, “Put that to my account.” Believers who have received such grace are called to extend it, helping others be reconciled and treating one another with the welcoming love they have received from God.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for standing in my place, taking my debt upon Yourself, and bringing me to the Father as one He welcomes and loves. Make my love like Philemon’s, refreshing the hearts of those around me. Help my faith to become active and effective in love. Thank You that You make the useless useful and give new life to those who have failed. Help me to see every believer as a beloved brother or sister, whatever their status, background, or past. Give me humility to appeal with love rather than demand with power, and courage to help others be reconciled, even when it costs me something. Keep me always mindful of the safety and dignity of every person. Let the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with my spirit, and with all Your people. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Book 19 of 27

# Hebrews

## About This Letter

Hebrews is unlike any other book in the New Testament. It begins without a greeting, like a sermon, and ends with personal notes, like a letter. Its author calls it “*the word of exhortation*” (*Hebrews 13:22*), and it may have been a sermon written down and sent to a congregation the author knew well.

No one knows for certain who wrote Hebrews. The author never names himself. Some in the early church thought Paul wrote it, and for many centuries it was printed among his letters, but its style and approach are quite different from Paul’s, and the author says he received the gospel from those who heard the Lord (*2:3*), which Paul insisted he did not (*Galatians 1:12*). Other suggestions have included Barnabas, Apollos, Luke, Silas, and Priscilla. The early Christian scholar Origen famously concluded that only God knows who wrote it. What is clear is that the author was a gifted teacher, deeply versed in the Greek Old Testament, who knew Timothy (*Hebrews 13:23*).

The first readers seem to have been Jewish believers in Jesus, though the letter speaks to all Christians. They had endured persecution in the past, including public insult, imprisonment, and the loss of property (*Hebrews 10:32–34*), but now they were weary and tempted to drift away, perhaps to return to the familiar practices of Judaism and avoid further suffering. The letter was probably written before A.D. 70, since it speaks of the sacrificial system as though it were still operating, and never mentions the destruction of the temple. Some suggest it was sent to believers in Rome (*Hebrews 13:24*).

## The Shape of the Letter

Hebrews alternates between teaching and warning. It shows that Jesus is superior to the angels (chapters 1–2), to Moses (chapter 3), and to Joshua, offering a greater rest (chapter 4). It then presents Jesus as the great high priest, sympathetic to our weakness, appointed in the order of Melchizedek (chapters 5–7), who serves in the true heavenly sanctuary, mediates a better covenant, and offered Himself once for all as the perfect sacrifice for sin (chapters 8–10). Chapter 11 celebrates the faith of the Old Testament saints, chapter 12 calls believers to run their race with endurance, looking to Jesus, and to receive God’s discipline as His children, and chapter 13 gives practical instructions for life together. Along the way come five solemn warnings against drifting, unbelief, falling away, willful sin, and refusing God’s voice.

## Themes to Watch For

Watch for the word “better”: Jesus is a better revelation, a better high priest, the mediator of a better covenant with better promises, offering a better sacrifice, and leading His people to a better country. Watch also for the full divinity and full humanity of Christ, His sympathy with human weakness, the once-for-all sufficiency of His sacrifice, access to God’s throne of grace, the danger of hardening one’s heart, the meaning of faith, endurance in suffering, and the unshakable kingdom. Hebrews shows how the whole Old Testament points to Christ and calls weary believers to hold fast to Him.
