Hebrews · Chapter 1 of 13

# Hebrews — Chapter 1

Chapter Theme: God Has Spoken by His Son

[Read Hebrews 1 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/HEB01.htm)

Main Teaching

In the past God spoke to His people through the prophets in many ways, but in these last days He has spoken by His Son, whom He appointed heir of all things and through whom He made the universe. The Son is the radiance of God’s glory and the exact imprint of His nature, upholding all things by His powerful word. After making purification for sins, He sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high, having become far superior to the angels. Using a chain of Old Testament quotations, the author shows that the Son holds a name and position no angel has ever had: He is called God’s Son, worshiped by angels, addressed as God whose throne lasts forever, the eternal Creator who never changes, and the one invited to sit at God’s right hand. Angels, by contrast, are ministering spirits sent to serve those who will inherit salvation.

## Chapter Background and Story

Hebrews opens without any greeting, name, or thanksgiving. It plunges straight into its great theme: Jesus Christ is God’s final and supreme word to humanity. The first four verses, a single long sentence in Greek, form one of the most majestic descriptions of Christ in the Bible.

The first readers were believers, probably Jewish Christians, who were tempted to drift away from Christ, perhaps back to the familiar practices of the temple and the Law. The author wants them to see that turning away from Jesus would mean turning away from the very fullness of what God had been promising all along. Everything God had said through the prophets, the Law, the priesthood, and the sacrifices pointed forward to Christ.

Why does the author spend so much time comparing Jesus with angels? In Jewish tradition, angels were believed to have played a role in giving the Law at Mount Sinai (*Acts 7:53*; *Galatians 3:19*; *Hebrews 2:2*). Angels were highly honored, and some may have been tempted to see Jesus as a kind of angel or to give angels too much importance. The author shows from Scripture that the Son is far above all angels. If the message delivered through angels was serious, how much more the message delivered by the Son.

### God’s Final Word (*1:1–4*)

The opening verses about God speaking through His Son, and the Son’s glory, are studied below. “*having become as much better than the angels as the more excellent name he has inherited is better than theirs*” (*v. 4*). The word “better” appears here for the first time; it will become a key word throughout Hebrews. The “name” the Son has inherited is the title “Son” itself, as the following verses show, a title and a position no angel holds.

### Greater Than the Angels (*1:5–14*)

The author now quotes seven Old Testament passages, mostly from the Psalms, to show the Son’s superiority.

“*For to which of the angels did he say at any time, “You are my Son. Today I have become your father?” and again, “I will be to him a Father, and he will be to me a Son?”*” (*v. 5*) The first quotation is from *Psalm 2:7*, a royal psalm about God’s anointed King. The second is from *2 Samuel 7:14*, God’s promise to David about his royal descendant. Both point ultimately to the Messiah. God never spoke to any angel this way. The phrase “Today I have become your father” is applied in the New Testament to Jesus’ resurrection and enthronement (*Acts 13:33*), when He was publicly declared to be God’s Son with power (*Romans 1:4*). It does not mean that the Son began to exist at that moment; verse 2 has already said He was active in creation.

“*When he again brings in the firstborn into the world he says, “Let all the angels of God worship him.”*” (*v. 6*) This quotation comes from the Greek version of *Deuteronomy 32:43* (see also *Psalm 97:7*). “Firstborn” refers to the Son’s rank and inheritance, as in *Colossians 1:15*. Angels do not receive worship; they give it to the Son. Since Scripture teaches that only God is to be worshiped (*Exodus 20:3–5*; *Revelation 22:8–9*), this verse points to the Son’s divinity.

“*Of the angels he says, “He makes his angels winds, and his servants a flame of fire.”*” (*v. 7*) Quoting *Psalm 104:4*, the author shows that angels are servants, powerful and glorious like wind and fire, but created and changeable. The contrast with the Son is studied below.

“*And, “You, Lord, in the beginning, laid the foundation of the earth. The heavens are the works of your hands.*” (*v. 10*) “*They will perish, but you continue. They all will grow old like a garment does.*” (*v. 11*) “*You will roll them up like a mantle, and they will be changed; but you are the same. Your years won’t fail.”*” (*v. 12*) *Psalm 102:25–27* originally addresses the LORD as Creator. The author applies it to the Son. He is the eternal Creator. The universe will wear out like old clothing and be replaced, but the Son will remain the same forever. *Hebrews 13:8* says, “*Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever*” (*Hebrews 13:8*).

“*But which of the angels has he told at any time, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet?”*” (*v. 13*) The final quotation is from *Psalm 110:1*, the Old Testament verse most often quoted in the New Testament. God invites the Messiah to sit at His right hand, the place of supreme honor and authority, until every enemy is defeated. No angel has ever been given that invitation. The role of angels is studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Hebrews 1:1–2* — God Has Spoken to Us by His Son

> *“God, having in the past spoken to the fathers through the prophets at many times and in various ways, has at the end of these days spoken to us by his Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom also he made the worlds.”*
>
> — *Hebrews 1:1–2* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The letter begins with God speaking. “God, having in the past spoken to the fathers through the prophets at many times and in various ways.” Throughout the Old Testament, God revealed Himself to Israel’s ancestors. He spoke “at many times,” over many centuries, and “in various ways”: through dreams, visions, laws, history, poetry, prophecy, and direct encounters. Each revelation was true, but each was partial.

“Has at the end of these days spoken to us by his Son.” Now God has spoken in a new and final way. “The end of these days” refers to the last era of history, which began with Christ’s coming. God’s final word is not a message delivered by a messenger but a person: His Son.

The author then describes the Son. “Whom he appointed heir of all things.” Everything belongs to the Son. He is the rightful owner and ruler of all creation.

“Through whom also he made the worlds.” The Son was the agent of creation. The word for “worlds” can also mean “ages,” including all of time and history. The Son is not part of creation but its Maker (*John 1:3*; *Colossians 1:16*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses establish the central claim of Hebrews: Jesus is God’s supreme and final revelation. The prophets spoke truly, but they spoke in fragments. In Jesus, God has spoken fully. John’s Gospel expresses the same truth: “*No one has seen God at any time. The only born Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has declared him*” (*John 1:18*). Jesus Himself said, “*He who has seen me has seen the Father*” (*John 14:9*).

This does not mean the Old Testament is unimportant. Hebrews quotes it constantly and treats it as God’s own word. But the Old Testament finds its fulfillment and its fullest meaning in Christ. Every promise, picture, and prophecy points to Him.

The description of the Son as both “heir of all things” and the one “*through whom also he made the worlds*” (*v. 2*) shows that Christ stands at both the beginning and the end of history. All things came through Him and all things are headed toward Him.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

If God has spoken by His Son, then the most important thing anyone can do is listen to Him. Believers can make knowing Jesus, through the Gospels and the whole of Scripture, the center of their spiritual lives.

This truth also brings confidence. People often wonder what God is like and whether He has spoken. Hebrews answers clearly: God has spoken, and His clearest word is Jesus. Those who want to know God can look to Him.

Finally, believers can read the Old Testament with new eyes, seeing how the many partial revelations of the past prepare for and point to Christ.

### *Hebrews 1:3* — The Radiance of God’s Glory

> *“His Son is the radiance of his glory, the very image of his substance, and upholding all things by the word of his power, who, when he had by himself purified us of our sins, sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high,”*
>
> — *Hebrews 1:3* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse describes who the Son is and what He has done.

“His Son is the radiance of his glory.” Just as sunlight streams from the sun, the Son shines forth God’s glory. The light and the sun cannot be separated; to see the light is to see the sun. In Jesus, the glory of God shines into the world.

“The very image of his substance.” The word for “image” was used for the impression a seal makes in wax or the stamp on a coin. The Son exactly represents God’s being. Everything God is, the Son reveals perfectly.

“And upholding all things by the word of his power.” The Son not only created the universe; He sustains it moment by moment. His powerful word holds everything in existence and carries it toward its goal.

“Who, when he had by himself purified us of our sins.” Here the description turns from cosmic glory to the cross. The Creator and Sustainer of the universe made purification for sins. He did it “by himself,” through His own sacrifice.

“Sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high.” After completing His work, the Son sat down in the place of supreme honor beside God the Father. Sitting down signals that His work of purification is finished. Old Testament priests never sat down, because their work was never done (*Hebrews 10:11–12*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse is one of the clearest statements in Scripture of the Son’s divine nature. He is not merely like God or sent by God; He is the radiance of God’s glory and the exact representation of His being. The early church drew on verses like this when it confessed that the Son is “God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God,” as the Nicene Creed puts it.

The verse also holds together the Son’s majesty and His humility. The one who upholds the universe is the same one who purified sins, which in the language of Hebrews means through His death as a sacrifice. The glory of God is seen most clearly at the cross, where the Son gave Himself for sinners.

The phrase “sat down” anticipates one of the major themes of Hebrews: the finished, once-for-all nature of Christ’s sacrifice. Nothing more needs to be added. Believers do not need to repeat sacrifices or earn their cleansing. Christ has done it, and He has sat down.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers who want to know what God is like can look at Jesus. His compassion, holiness, truth, and love are the exact representation of God’s character.

This verse also brings security. The one who holds the universe together holds believers’ lives together too. When life feels chaotic, they can remember that all things are upheld by His powerful word.

Finally, the truth that Christ has completed the work of purification brings peace. Believers do not need to carry the guilt of sins that Christ has already cleansed. They can rest in His finished work.

### *Hebrews 1:8–9* — Your Throne, O God, Is Forever

> *“But of the Son he says, ‘Your throne, O God, is forever and ever. The scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your Kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your fellows.’”*
>
> — *Hebrews 1:8–9* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

In contrast to the angels, who are servants (v7), the author quotes *Psalm 45:6–7* about the Son.

“But of the Son he says, ‘Your throne, O God, is forever and ever.’” The Son is addressed as “God.” His throne is eternal. *Psalm 45* was originally a royal wedding song for Israel’s king, but its language goes beyond any human king, and the author of Hebrews sees its fulfillment in Christ, the eternal King.

“The scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your Kingdom.” A scepter symbolized a king’s authority. The Son’s rule is marked by justice and righteousness.

Verse 9: “You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity.” The Son’s character is perfectly righteous. He loves what is right and hates what is evil.

“Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your fellows.” Kings were anointed with oil as a sign of their appointment. The Son is anointed with “the oil of gladness,” a sign of joy and favor, above all others.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This passage is remarkable because it calls the Son “God” while also speaking of “God, your God.” This reflects the mystery of the Trinity: the Son is fully God, and yet He is distinct from the Father. The New Testament holds these truths together in passages such as *John 1:1* (“the Word was with God, and the Word was God”) and *Titus 2:13* (“our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ”).

The Son’s eternal throne also fulfills God’s promise to David that his descendant’s throne would be established forever (*2 Samuel 7:13*, 16). Jesus is the son of David and the Son of God, the eternal King who rules in righteousness.

The connection between righteousness and joy is also significant. The Son loves righteousness, and He is anointed with gladness. Holiness and joy are not opposites. True joy is found in loving what is good.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses invite believers to worship Jesus as God and to trust His rule. In a world where earthly rulers come and go, often ruling unjustly, Christ’s throne is eternal and His scepter is righteous. Believers can find hope in His just and unending reign.

They also invite believers to share the Son’s love for righteousness and hatred of evil. Following Christ means loving what He loves and rejecting what He rejects.

Finally, the “oil of gladness” reminds believers that life with Christ is meant to be joyful. Holiness is not a grim burden but the path to the deepest joy.

### *Hebrews 1:14* — Ministering Spirits

> *“Aren’t they all serving spirits, sent out to do service for the sake of those who will inherit salvation?”*
>
> — *Hebrews 1:14* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The chapter ends with a question that sums up the role of angels. “Aren’t they all serving spirits, sent out to do service for the sake of those who will inherit salvation?”

Angels are “serving spirits.” They are not rulers or objects of worship. They are servants of God.

They are “sent out to do service.” God sends them on missions.

“For the sake of those who will inherit salvation.” Remarkably, angels serve believers. Those who belong to Christ are heirs of salvation, and God’s mighty angels are sent to help them.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse puts angels in their proper place. They are glorious and powerful beings, but they are servants, not the Son. And astonishingly, they serve God’s people. Scripture gives many examples: angels protected Elisha (*2 Kings 6:15–17*), shut the lions’ mouths for Daniel (*Daniel 6:22*), strengthened Jesus in Gethsemane (*Luke 22:43*), freed Peter from prison (*Acts 12:7–11*), and encouraged Paul in the storm (*Acts 27:23–24*). *Psalm 91:11* says that God will put His angels in charge of His people to guard them.

This truth has two applications. First, believers should not worship angels or seek to communicate with them as though they were mediators. Only the Son is worthy of worship, and He is the one mediator between God and humanity (*1 Timothy 2:5*). Second, believers can take comfort that God cares for them in ways they often cannot see. His servants are at work on their behalf.

The phrase “those who will inherit salvation” also points forward. Salvation has a present and a future dimension. Believers already have it, and they will inherit it fully when Christ returns.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can trust that God cares for them even when they cannot see His hand. His protection and provision often come in ways they never notice.

This verse also guards against unhealthy fascination with angels. In some popular spirituality, angels receive attention and devotion that belong only to God. Hebrews keeps the focus where it belongs: on the Son.

Finally, the description of believers as “those who will inherit salvation” reminds them of their great future. They are heirs. Their inheritance is secure, and God Himself, with all His angels, is committed to bringing them safely to it.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Hebrews 1* lifts believers’ eyes to the greatness of Jesus Christ. God once spoke through the prophets in many partial ways, but now He has spoken fully and finally through His Son. The Son is the heir of all things, the Creator of the universe, the radiance of God’s glory, and the exact representation of His being. He holds all things together by His powerful word. And He has made purification for sins and sat down at the right hand of God, His work complete.

This vision of Christ calls for worship. Scripture shows that the Son is far greater than the angels. He alone is called God’s Son; the angels worship Him; He is addressed as God whose throne is forever; He is the unchanging Creator; and He alone is invited to sit at God’s right hand. Angels, glorious as they are, are servants sent to help God’s people.

For believers who are weary or tempted to drift, this chapter offers a powerful reason to hold fast. There is no greater word, no greater revelation, no greater Savior than Jesus. Turning away from Him would mean turning away from God’s final word. Believers can listen to Him, trust Him, and rest in His finished work.

The chapter also brings comfort. The one who upholds the universe upholds the lives of His people. His throne is eternal and His rule is righteous. And God’s angels are at work on behalf of those who will inherit salvation. Whatever believers face, they belong to the Son, who is the same yesterday, today, and forever.

## Chapter Prayer

Father, thank You for speaking to us, not only through the prophets but fully and finally through Your Son. Lord Jesus, You are the radiance of God’s glory and the exact representation of His being. You made the universe and You uphold all things by Your powerful word. Thank You for purifying me from my sins by Your own sacrifice and for sitting down at the right hand of the Majesty on high, Your work complete. I worship You, as all the angels of God worship You. Your throne is forever, and Your scepter is righteous. Help me to love what You love and to listen to Your voice above every other. Thank You for caring for me in ways I cannot see. Keep me from drifting, and hold me fast to You, my unchanging Lord. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Hebrews · Chapter 2 of 13

# Hebrews — Chapter 2

Chapter Theme: Do Not Drift, and Behold Our Brother and High Priest

[Read Hebrews 2 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/HEB02.htm)

Main Teaching

Because the Son is so much greater than the angels, believers must pay careful attention to what they have heard, so they do not drift away. If the message delivered by angels was binding, how much more serious it would be to neglect the great salvation first announced by the Lord and confirmed by God through signs, wonders, and gifts of the Spirit. God has not placed the coming world under angels but under humanity, as *Psalm 8* says, and although we do not yet see all things under human rule, we see Jesus, made for a little while lower than the angels, now crowned with glory and honor because He suffered death for everyone. Jesus shared fully in human flesh and blood so that by His death He might destroy the one who has the power of death, the devil, and free those held in slavery by the fear of death. He became like His brothers and sisters in every way so that He could be a merciful and faithful high priest, making atonement for sins, and because He Himself suffered when tempted, He is able to help those who are tempted.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Hebrews 2* contains the first of five warning passages in the letter (*2:1–4*; *3:7–4*:13; *5:11–6*:12; *10:26–39*; *12:14–29*). These warnings are addressed to believers who were tempted to drift away from Christ. They are serious, but they are spoken in love, by a pastor who wants his readers to hold fast and reach the goal.

After the warning, the chapter turns to a surprising truth. Chapter 1 emphasized the Son’s divine glory, far above the angels. Chapter 2 emphasizes His humanity. For a time, He was made lower than the angels. He shared human flesh and blood, suffered, was tempted, and died. Some of the first readers may have found it hard to believe that a crucified man could be the glorious Son of God. The author explains that Jesus’ humanity and suffering were not a contradiction of His glory but the very path by which He brought many children to glory.

This chapter introduces a central theme of Hebrews: Jesus as our high priest. Because He became fully human, He understands human weakness and can represent humanity before God.

### Do Not Drift Away (*2:1–4*)

The first warning is studied below.

### Jesus Crowned with Glory (*2:5–9*)

“*For he didn’t subject the world to come, of which we speak, to angels*” (*v. 5*). “The world to come” is the new creation that God is bringing, which has already begun in Christ. God did not appoint angels to rule it.

“*But one has somewhere testified, saying, “What is man, that you think of him? Or the son of man, that you care for him?*” (*v. 6*) “*You made him a little lower than the angels. You crowned him with glory and honor.*” (*v. 7*) “*You have put all things in subjection under his feet.”*” (*v. 8*) The author quotes *Psalm 8:4–6*. This psalm marvels at God’s care for human beings and celebrates the honor God gave humanity at creation: to rule over the world as His representatives (*Genesis 1:26–28*). “Somewhere” does not mean the author had forgotten where the quotation came from; it was a common way of quoting a well-known passage, emphasizing God as the speaker rather than the human author.

“*For in that he subjected all things to him, he left nothing that is not subject to him. But now we don’t yet see all things subjected to him*” (*v. 8*). God’s purpose was that humanity would rule over all creation. But that is not what we see. Sin, death, suffering, and chaos show that humanity has failed to fulfill its calling. The world is not yet as God intended. How Jesus fulfills this purpose is studied below.

### The Pioneer of Salvation (*2:10–13*)

The meaning of Jesus’ suffering is studied below. “*For both he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one, for which cause he is not ashamed to call them brothers*” (*v. 11*). Jesus, who makes people holy, and those He makes holy share the same origin, whether that means they share one Father, God, or share one human nature. Because of this, Jesus is “not ashamed” to call them His brothers and sisters. This is a stunning statement: the radiance of God’s glory (*Hebrews 1:3*) is not embarrassed to be family with weak and sinful people.

“*saying, “I will declare your name to my brothers. Among the congregation I will sing your praise.”*” (*v. 12*) “*Again, “I will put my trust in him.” Again, “Behold, here I am with the children whom God has given me.”*” (*v. 13*) The author quotes *Psalm 22:22*, the psalm Jesus prayed on the cross, which moves from suffering to praise among God’s people. He also quotes *Isaiah 8:17–18*, where the prophet trusts God and stands with the children God has given him. In each case, the speaker identifies with God’s people and stands among them.

### Destroying the Power of Death (*2:14–16*)

Jesus’ victory over death and the devil is studied below. “*For most certainly, he doesn’t give help to angels, but he gives help to the offspring of Abraham*” (*v. 16*). Jesus did not become an angel to help angels. He became human, a descendant of Abraham, to help humanity. “The offspring of Abraham” refers to all who share Abraham’s faith (*Galatians 3:7*, 29).

### A Merciful and Faithful High Priest (*2:17–18*)

The chapter’s climax, introducing Jesus as high priest, is studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Hebrews 2:1–3* — So Great a Salvation

> *“Therefore we ought to pay greater attention to the things that were heard, lest perhaps we drift away. For if the word spoken through angels proved steadfast, and every transgression and disobedience received a just penalty, how will we escape if we neglect so great a salvation—which at the first having been spoken through the Lord, was confirmed to us by those who heard,”*
>
> — *Hebrews 2:1–3* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“Therefore we ought to pay greater attention to the things that were heard, lest perhaps we drift away.” The word “therefore” connects this warning to chapter 1. Because the Son is so great, believers must listen carefully to His message. The danger is drifting. The word was used for a boat that slips its mooring and drifts away from the harbor, or for a ring slipping off a finger. Drifting is usually not a dramatic decision but a gradual, almost unnoticed movement away.

Verse 2: “For if the word spoken through angels proved steadfast, and every transgression and disobedience received a just penalty.” “The word spoken through angels” is the Law given at Sinai, which Jewish tradition said was delivered through angels (*Acts 7:53*; *Galatians 3:19*). That Law was binding, and disobedience was punished.

Verse 3: “how will we escape if we neglect so great a salvation.” If ignoring the Law brought consequences, how much more serious is neglecting the salvation brought by the Son? Notice the word “neglect.” The danger is not necessarily open rejection but carelessness, failing to give the gospel the attention it deserves.

“Which at the first having been spoken through the Lord, was confirmed to us by those who heard.” This salvation was first proclaimed by Jesus Himself, and then confirmed by eyewitnesses who heard Him.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This warning is gentle in tone but serious in content. The author includes himself: “we ought,” “lest we drift,” “how will we escape.” He is not condemning his readers from a distance but standing alongside them.

The image of drifting is powerful. Spiritual decline is often slow. A believer may stop gathering with other believers, stop praying, stop reading Scripture, or grow indifferent, without ever consciously deciding to abandon faith. Over time, they find themselves far from where they once were. Jesus described seed choked by “*the cares of this age, and the deceitfulness of riches, and the lusts of other things*” (*Mark 4:19*).

The remedy is “greater attention.” Believers anchor themselves by giving careful, ongoing attention to the gospel: hearing it, remembering it, and responding to it.

Verse 4 adds that God confirmed this message “by signs and wonders, by various works of power, and by gifts of the Holy Spirit, according to his own will.” The gospel came with God’s own testimony. It is not merely a human idea but God’s word.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can ask whether they are drifting. Have prayer, Scripture, worship, and fellowship become less important than they once were? Has indifference crept in? Recognizing drift is the first step toward returning.

Practical anchors include regular time in Scripture, consistent participation in a church community, honest friendships with other believers, and habits of prayer. These help believers “pay greater attention” to the gospel.

This warning also highlights the greatness of salvation. The gospel is not a small matter to be treated casually. It is “so great a salvation,” worth our full attention and devotion.

### *Hebrews 2:9–10* — Crowned with Glory Through Suffering

> *“But we see him who has been made a little lower than the angels, Jesus, because of the suffering of death crowned with glory and honor, that by the grace of God he should taste of death for everyone. For it became him, for whom are all things and through whom are all things, in bringing many children to glory, to make the author of their salvation perfect through sufferings.”*
>
> — *Hebrews 2:9–10* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The author has just said that we do not yet see all things subject to humanity (v8). “But we see him.” Though humanity has failed, there is one human being in whom God’s purpose is fulfilled: Jesus.

“Who has been made a little lower than the angels.” Jesus, the eternal Son, became human. For a time, He took a position lower than the angels, entering human weakness and mortality.

“Because of the suffering of death crowned with glory and honor.” Through His death and resurrection, Jesus was exalted. He now holds the glory and honor that *Psalm 8* describes. He is the true human being, ruling as God intended.

“That by the grace of God he should taste of death for everyone.” Jesus died “for everyone.” His death was an act of God’s grace, on behalf of all humanity. “Taste of death” means to experience death fully.

Verse 10: “For it became him, for whom are all things and through whom are all things, in bringing many children to glory, to make the author of their salvation perfect through sufferings.” “It became him” means it was fitting, appropriate to God’s character. God’s purpose is “bringing many children to glory,” leading His people to share in Christ’s glory. Jesus is “the author,” also translated “pioneer” or “champion,” of their salvation: the one who goes ahead, opens the way, and leads others along it.

“Perfect through sufferings.” This does not mean Jesus was ever morally imperfect. “Perfect” in Hebrews means complete, fully qualified for His role. Through suffering, Jesus became fully equipped to be the Savior and high priest of His people.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses explain why the Son of God suffered. Suffering was not a defeat or a contradiction of His glory; it was the path to glory, both for Him and for His people. Jesus said that the Messiah had to suffer these things and then enter His glory (*Luke 24:26*). *Philippians 2:8–9* says that because Jesus humbled Himself to death on a cross, God highly exalted Him.

The idea of Jesus as “author” or “pioneer” is rich. In the ancient world, the word could describe a founder of a city, a leader of an expedition, or a hero who blazes a trail. Jesus goes ahead of His people through suffering and death into glory, and He brings them with Him. *Hebrews 12:2* calls Him “*the author and perfecter of faith*” (*Hebrews 12:2*).

“For everyone” emphasizes the breadth of Christ’s death. His grace reaches all people, and His invitation is open to all.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

When believers look at the world and see suffering, injustice, and brokenness, they may wonder whether God’s purposes are failing. These verses say: “But we see Jesus.” In Him, God’s purpose is already being fulfilled, and He will bring it to completion.

These verses also give meaning to believers’ own suffering. Jesus walked the path of suffering to glory, and He leads His people along it. Their suffering is not meaningless; it is part of the journey He has already traveled, and it leads to glory.

Finally, believers can rest in the truth that Jesus tasted death for them. Because He has gone through death, they need not face it alone.

### *Hebrews 2:14–15* — Freed from the Fear of Death

> *“Since then the children have shared in flesh and blood, he also himself in the same way partook of the same, that through death he might bring to nothing him who had the power of death, that is, the devil, and might deliver all of them who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage.”*
>
> — *Hebrews 2:14–15* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“Since then the children have shared in flesh and blood, he also himself in the same way partook of the same.” God’s children are human beings with physical bodies, subject to weakness and death. So Jesus became fully human too. He did not merely appear human; He truly shared human nature.

“That through death he might bring to nothing him who had the power of death, that is, the devil.” The purpose of Jesus’ becoming human was to die, and through His death to defeat the devil. “Bring to nothing” means to make powerless, to break the grip of. The devil “had the power of death” in the sense that he uses death, and the fear of death, to hold humanity captive. Sin leads to death, and the devil accuses sinners. Jesus’ death dealt with sin, and so broke the devil’s hold.

Verse 15: “and might deliver all of them who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage.” The fear of death enslaves people. It shapes their choices, fuels their anxieties, and keeps them from living freely. Jesus came to set them free.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that the incarnation and the cross belong together. The Son became human in order to die, and He died in order to destroy the power of death. This is the great paradox of the gospel: death was defeated by death. Jesus went into death and came out the other side, breaking its power for all who belong to Him.

The fear of death is one of the deepest human fears. People spend enormous energy avoiding it, denying it, or trying to escape it. Many philosophies and religions have tried to address it. The gospel offers something unique: not merely a way to cope with death, but a victory over it. Paul wrote, “*Death is swallowed up in victory*” (*1 Corinthians 15:54*) and “*Death, where is your sting?*” (*1 Corinthians 15:55*).

This does not mean believers will never feel fear or sorrow in the face of death. Jesus Himself wept at Lazarus’s tomb and was deeply troubled in Gethsemane. But death no longer has the final word. For believers, it is a defeated enemy and a doorway into the presence of Christ.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers who struggle with fear of death, their own or that of loved ones, can find comfort here. Jesus has entered death and defeated it. Those who belong to Him do not need to be enslaved by fear.

Freedom from the fear of death also brings freedom to live. Those who are not ruled by fear can take risks for the gospel, serve others sacrificially, and face suffering with courage.

Finally, these verses remind believers that Jesus truly shared their humanity. He knows what it is to have a body, to feel pain, and to face death. He understands.

### *Hebrews 2:17–18* — A Merciful and Faithful High Priest

> *“Therefore he was obligated in all things to be made like his brothers, that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest in things pertaining to God, to make atonement for the sins of the people. For in that he himself has suffered being tempted, he is able to help those who are tempted.”*
>
> — *Hebrews 2:17–18* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“Therefore he was obligated in all things to be made like his brothers.” To accomplish His mission, Jesus had to become like His people in every way, sharing their human nature, experiences, and struggles, though without sin (*Hebrews 4:15*).

“That he might become a merciful and faithful high priest in things pertaining to God.” This is the first time Hebrews calls Jesus a high priest, a theme it will develop at length. In Israel, the high priest represented the people before God. Jesus became human so that He could represent humanity perfectly.

He is “merciful”: compassionate toward human weakness, understanding and gentle. He is “faithful”: completely trustworthy and reliable in His service to God.

“To make atonement for the sins of the people.” The high priest’s central task was to offer sacrifices for sin, especially on the Day of Atonement. Jesus made atonement by offering Himself (*Hebrews 9:11–14*).

Verse 18: “For in that he himself has suffered being tempted, he is able to help those who are tempted.” Jesus experienced real temptation, and it involved real suffering. Because He knows what temptation feels like, He is able to help those who face it.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses reveal the heart of Christ toward His people. He is not a distant, unfeeling priest. He is merciful. He knows human weakness from the inside. He experienced hunger, exhaustion, grief, rejection, betrayal, pain, and temptation. And so He understands.

The word “atonement” refers to dealing with sin so that the relationship between God and humanity can be restored. Some translations use “propitiation,” which emphasizes turning away God’s righteous wrath against sin; others use “expiation,” which emphasizes removing sin itself. Both ideas are part of what Christ accomplished. Through His sacrifice, sin is dealt with and reconciliation with God is made possible.

Jesus’ temptation was real. He was tempted in the wilderness (*Matthew 4:1–11*), in Gethsemane (*Mark 14:32–42*), and throughout His life. The fact that He never sinned does not mean the temptations were easy. In fact, He felt the full force of temptation in a way that those who give in never do. That is why He can help.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

When believers face temptation, they can turn to Jesus with confidence. He understands exactly what they are facing, and He is able and willing to help. They do not need to hide from Him in shame.

When believers feel weak or struggle with failure, they can remember that their high priest is merciful. He does not look down on them with contempt but with compassion.

This passage also invites believers to bring every part of their human experience to Jesus: their pain, their struggles, their fears. Because He has shared their humanity, nothing they bring to Him is foreign to Him.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Hebrews 2* begins with a loving but serious warning: pay close attention to the gospel so that you do not drift away. Spiritual drift is usually gradual and often unnoticed. Believers can guard against it by staying anchored to Christ through Scripture, prayer, worship, and fellowship. The salvation they have received is “so great” that it deserves their full attention.

The chapter then reveals the wonder of Christ’s humanity. God created humanity to rule over creation, but we do not yet see that purpose fulfilled. “But we see Jesus,” who became lower than the angels for a time, tasted death for everyone, and is now crowned with glory and honor. Through His suffering, He became the pioneer of salvation, leading many sons and daughters to glory. He is not ashamed to call them His brothers and sisters.

Jesus shared fully in human flesh and blood so that, through His death, He could break the power of the devil and free those enslaved by the fear of death. Believers no longer need to live in bondage to that fear. They can face death, and life, with courage and hope.

Finally, the chapter introduces Jesus as a merciful and faithful high priest, who made atonement for sins and who, having suffered when tempted, is able to help those who are tempted. Whatever believers face, they have a Savior who understands, who sympathizes, and who stands ready to help.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, keep me from drifting away from You. Help me to pay close attention to the great salvation You have brought, and anchor my heart in Your word. Thank You for becoming lower than the angels for a time, for tasting death for everyone, and for being crowned with glory and honor. Thank You that You are not ashamed to call me Your brother or sister. Thank You for sharing my flesh and blood, and for breaking the power of the devil and setting me free from the fear of death. When I am tempted, help me to turn to You, knowing that You understand and are able to help. Thank You that You are a merciful and faithful high priest who has made atonement for my sins. Lead me, with all Your people, into glory. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Hebrews · Chapter 3 of 13

# Hebrews — Chapter 3

Chapter Theme: Greater Than Moses, and Today If You Hear His Voice

[Read Hebrews 3 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/HEB03.htm)

Main Teaching

The author calls believers, who share in a heavenly calling, to fix their thoughts on Jesus, the apostle and high priest of their confession. Jesus was faithful to God, just as Moses was faithful in God’s house, but Jesus deserves greater honor, as the builder of a house has more honor than the house itself. Moses was faithful as a servant in God’s house, pointing to what was to come; Christ is faithful as the Son over God’s house, and believers are that house if they hold firmly to their confidence and hope. Quoting *Psalm 95*, the author warns them not to harden their hearts as Israel did in the wilderness, when the people who had seen God’s works for forty years rebelled and could not enter His rest because of unbelief. He urges them to watch out for an unbelieving heart that turns away from the living God and to encourage one another every day, as long as it is called “Today,” so that none are hardened by sin’s deceitfulness.

## Chapter Background and Story

After showing that Jesus is greater than the angels (chapters 1–2), the author now compares Jesus with Moses. For Jewish readers, few figures were more honored than Moses. He led Israel out of slavery in Egypt, received the Law at Mount Sinai, built the tabernacle according to God’s instructions, and spoke with God “*mouth to mouth*” (*Numbers 12:8*) (*Numbers 12:7–8*). In *Numbers 12:7*, God Himself says of Moses, “*He is faithful in all my house*” (*Numbers 12:7*).

The author does not criticize Moses. On the contrary, he honors Moses’ faithfulness. But he shows that Jesus is greater, as a son is greater than a servant and a builder is greater than a house.

The second half of the chapter draws on one of the most painful episodes in Israel’s history. After God rescued Israel from Egypt, the people repeatedly complained and rebelled in the wilderness. At Kadesh, when they were on the edge of the promised land, they refused to enter because they did not trust God to give them victory (*Numbers 13–14*). As a result, that generation wandered for forty years and died in the wilderness. *Psalm 95* recalls this event as a warning. The author applies it to his readers, who were also tempted to turn back because of fear and hardship.

### Consider Jesus (*3:1–2*)

The call to fix one’s thoughts on Jesus is studied below.

### Son Over the House (*3:3–6*)

“*For he has been counted worthy of more glory than Moses, because he who built the house has more honor than the house*” (*v. 3*). “*For every house is built by someone; but he who built all things is God*” (*v. 4*). A builder deserves more honor than the building. “House” here means household or family, the people of God. Moses was part of God’s household; Jesus, as God, is its builder. Verse 4 connects the builder of the house with God, the builder of all things, pointing again to Jesus’ divine role (*Hebrews 1:2*, 10). The contrast between Moses as servant and Christ as Son is studied below.

### Today, If You Will Hear His Voice (*3:7–11*)

The warning from *Psalm 95* is studied below. “*where your fathers tested me and tried me, and saw my deeds for forty years*” (*v. 9*). “*Therefore I was displeased with that generation, and said, ‘They always err in their heart, but they didn’t know my ways.’*” (*v. 10*) “*As I swore in my wrath, ‘They will not enter into my rest.’”*” (*v. 11*) Israel had seen God’s mighty works: the plagues in Egypt, the parting of the Red Sea, manna from heaven, water from the rock. Yet they kept testing Him. Their problem was a heart problem: “they always err in their heart.” God’s oath, “they will not enter into my rest,” refers to the promised land, the place of rest God had prepared for them. In chapter 4, the author will explain that God’s “rest” points beyond Canaan to a deeper rest that remains for God’s people.

### Encourage One Another Daily (*3:12–15*)

The warning against an unbelieving heart and the call to daily encouragement are studied below. “*For we have become partakers of Christ, if we hold the beginning of our confidence firm to the end*” (*v. 14*). Believers share in Christ. The phrase “if we hold... firm to the end” shows that genuine participation in Christ is shown by perseverance. As discussed elsewhere, Christians understand the relationship between perseverance and salvation in different ways: some emphasize that those truly in Christ will certainly persevere because God keeps them, while others emphasize that believers must continue in faith and can fall away. Both take this call to endurance seriously.

“*while it is said, “Today if you will hear his voice, don’t harden your hearts, as in the rebellion.”*” (*v. 15*) The author repeats the key line from *Psalm 95*.

### Unbelief Kept Them Out (*3:16–19*)

“*For who, when they heard, rebelled? Wasn’t it all those who came out of Egypt led by Moses?*” (*v. 16*) “*With whom was he displeased forty years? Wasn’t it with those who sinned, whose bodies fell in the wilderness?*” (*v. 17*) “*To whom did he swear that they wouldn’t enter into his rest, but to those who were disobedient?*” (*v. 18*) “*We see that they weren’t able to enter in because of unbelief*” (*v. 19*). The author asks a series of questions to drive the point home. The very people who had experienced God’s great rescue from Egypt were the ones who rebelled. Having a great spiritual beginning does not guarantee finishing well. The root problem was unbelief, a refusal to trust God’s promise, which showed itself in disobedience.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Hebrews 3:1–2* — Consider Jesus

> *“Therefore, holy brothers, partakers of a heavenly calling, consider the Apostle and High Priest of our confession: Jesus, who was faithful to him who appointed him, as also Moses was in all his house.”*
>
> — *Hebrews 3:1–2* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“Therefore, holy brothers, partakers of a heavenly calling.” The author reminds his readers of their identity. They are “holy,” set apart for God. They are “brothers,” family members, as Jesus Himself is not ashamed to call them (*Hebrews 2:11*). And they share in “a heavenly calling,” an invitation from God that comes from heaven and leads to heaven.

“Consider the Apostle and High Priest of our confession: Jesus.” “Consider” means to fix one’s thoughts on, to look closely and carefully. Believers are to focus their attention on Jesus.

Jesus is called “the Apostle,” the only time this title is used for Him in the New Testament. An apostle is one who is sent. Jesus was sent by God to represent God to humanity. He is also “High Priest,” one who represents humanity before God. In Jesus, God comes to us, and in Jesus, we come to God.

“Of our confession” means Jesus is the one whom believers publicly confess and trust.

Verse 2: “who was faithful to him who appointed him, as also Moses was in all his house.” Jesus was completely faithful to the Father who sent Him, just as Moses was faithful in his role.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse summarizes the whole message of Hebrews in one command: consider Jesus. The readers were struggling with discouragement, fear, and the temptation to drift. The remedy was not first to try harder but to look at Jesus more closely. *Hebrews 12:2* echoes this: “*looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith*” (*Hebrews 12:2*).

The two titles, Apostle and High Priest, together capture Jesus’ role as mediator. As Apostle, He brings God’s word to humanity (*Hebrews 1:1–2*). As High Priest, He brings humanity to God (*Hebrews 2:17*). He bridges the gap between God and people completely.

The comparison with Moses begins with honor. Moses was faithful, and so was Jesus. The author does not diminish Moses to exalt Jesus; he shows that Jesus fulfills and surpasses all that Moses represented.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

When believers are discouraged, confused, or tempted to give up, the first step is to “consider Jesus”: to fix their thoughts on who He is and what He has done. This might involve reading the Gospels, meditating on passages about Christ, or simply pausing in prayer to remember His faithfulness.

Believers can also remember their identity: holy, part of God’s family, and sharing in a heavenly calling. Their lives have a purpose and destination beyond this world.

Finally, Jesus’ faithfulness to the Father is an example for believers. Like Him, they can be faithful in the tasks and relationships God has given them.

### *Hebrews 3:5–6* — Moses the Servant, Christ the Son

> *“Moses indeed was faithful in all his house as a servant, for a testimony of those things which were afterward to be spoken, but Christ is faithful as a Son over his house. We are his house, if we hold fast our confidence and the glorying of our hope firm to the end.”*
>
> — *Hebrews 3:5–6* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“Moses indeed was faithful in all his house as a servant.” Moses was a faithful servant in God’s household, Israel. “Servant” here is an honorable title, used for someone trusted with important responsibilities.

“For a testimony of those things which were afterward to be spoken.” Moses’ ministry pointed forward. The Law, the tabernacle, and the sacrifices were a witness to things that would be revealed later, in Christ. Jesus said, “*if you believed Moses, you would believe me; for he wrote about me*” (*John 5:46*).

Verse 6: “but Christ is faithful as a Son over his house.” Jesus’ relationship to God’s household is different. He is not a servant in the house but the Son over it, the heir and master.

“We are his house.” Believers are God’s household. The church is God’s family, the place where He dwells.

“If we hold fast our confidence and the glorying of our hope firm to the end.” Belonging to God’s house is shown by holding firmly to confidence and hope in Christ until the end.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The contrast between servant and son shows the superiority of the new covenant over the old. Under Moses, God’s people had the Law and the tabernacle, which were good but pointed beyond themselves. In Christ, they have the reality those things pointed to. Jesus is not another servant in the line of Moses and the prophets; He is the Son, the one the whole household belongs to.

The statement “we are his house” is profound. In the Old Testament, God’s “house” could mean the tabernacle or temple where He dwelt. Now His house is His people. As Paul writes, believers are being built together into a dwelling place for God (*Ephesians 2:21–22*).

The phrase “if we hold fast” is the first of several in Hebrews that emphasize perseverance. Faith is not a one-time event but an ongoing confidence that holds firm to the end.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can read the Old Testament with appreciation, recognizing Moses and the Law as faithful witnesses that point to Christ. The Law is not discarded; it is fulfilled.

Being part of God’s house gives believers a deep sense of belonging. They are not strangers but members of God’s household, under the care of Christ the Son.

The call to “hold fast our confidence” invites believers to persevere, especially in seasons of doubt or difficulty. Confidence in Christ is not maintained by feelings but by continually returning to the truth of who He is and what He has promised.

### *Hebrews 3:7–8* — Do Not Harden Your Hearts

> *“Therefore, even as the Holy Spirit says, Today if you will hear his voice, don’t harden your hearts as in the rebellion, in the day of the trial in the wilderness,”*
>
> — *Hebrews 3:7–8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“Therefore, even as the Holy Spirit says.” The author introduces a quotation from *Psalm 95:7–11*. Notice that he says “the Holy Spirit says,” in the present tense. Although the psalm was written centuries earlier, the author believes the Spirit is still speaking through it to believers now.

“Today if you will hear his voice.” God is speaking. The question is whether people will listen. “Today” emphasizes urgency. The opportunity to respond is now.

Verse 8: “don’t harden your hearts as in the rebellion, in the day of the trial in the wilderness.” The “rebellion” and “trial” refer to the events at Meribah and Massah, where Israel complained about lack of water and tested God (*Exodus 17:1–7*), and more broadly to the wilderness generation’s repeated unbelief, especially their refusal to enter the promised land (*Numbers 14*).

To “harden the heart” is to become resistant to God, unresponsive to His voice, stubborn in unbelief. A hard heart refuses to trust or obey.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Hardening of the heart is a process. It often begins with small acts of resistance to God’s voice: ignoring conviction, delaying obedience, choosing one’s own way. Over time, the heart becomes less sensitive. Pharaoh’s story in Exodus shows a heart that grew harder with each refusal (*Exodus 8:15*, 32).

The word “today” is central to this chapter and the next. Each day brings a new opportunity to hear and respond to God. But the opportunity is not unlimited. The wilderness generation missed their chance and died in the wilderness. Paul echoes this urgency: “*Behold, now is the acceptable time. Behold, now is the day of salvation*” (*2 Corinthians 6:2*).

The fact that the Holy Spirit “says” these words today shows that Scripture is living. God speaks through it to every generation (*Hebrews 4:12*). When believers read Scripture, they are not merely reading ancient history; they are hearing God’s voice.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can ask whether there are areas of their lives where they have been resisting God’s voice: a conviction they have ignored, a step of obedience they have delayed, or a sin they have refused to give up. Today is the day to respond.

Keeping a soft heart involves regular practices of listening to God: reading Scripture, praying, confessing sin, and responding quickly when God speaks.

This passage also brings hope. As long as it is “today,” it is not too late. God is still speaking, and His invitation to trust and obey is still open.

### *Hebrews 3:12–13* — Encourage One Another Every Day

> *“Beware, brothers, lest perhaps there might be in any one of you an evil heart of unbelief, in falling away from the living God; but exhort one another day by day, so long as it is called ‘today’, lest any one of you be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin.”*
>
> — *Hebrews 3:12–13* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“Beware, brothers, lest perhaps there might be in any one of you an evil heart of unbelief, in falling away from the living God.” The author warns believers to watch carefully. The danger is “an evil heart of unbelief,” a heart that does not trust God. Unbelief is not merely intellectual doubt but a heart that refuses to rely on God. It leads to “falling away from the living God,” turning away from Him.

Notice the phrase “any one of you.” The author is concerned for every individual in the community. No one should be left behind.

Verse 13 gives the remedy: “but exhort one another day by day, so long as it is called ‘today.’” “Exhort” means to encourage, to urge, to come alongside. Believers are to encourage one another daily, not occasionally.

“Lest any one of you be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin.” Sin is deceitful. It promises pleasure, freedom, or satisfaction, but it leads to bondage and death. It hardens hearts gradually, often without the person realizing it. Encouragement from others helps protect against this deception.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This passage shows that perseverance in faith is not only an individual responsibility but a community one. Believers need one another. Alone, a person can be deceived by sin and drift away without noticing. In community, believers can see warning signs in one another, offer encouragement, and help each other stay on course. *Ecclesiastes 4:9–10* says that two are better than one, because if one falls, the other can lift him up.

“The deceitfulness of sin” is a powerful phrase. Sin rarely presents itself as destructive. It disguises itself as something good or harmless. Eve was deceived by the serpent (*Genesis 3:13*). Paul speaks of “the deceitful lusts” of the old self (*Ephesians 4:22*). Encouragement from others helps believers see clearly.

The call to encourage “day by day” emphasizes regular, ongoing involvement in one another’s lives. Sunday gatherings are important, but this passage envisions believers caring for one another throughout the week.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can take active roles in encouraging others: sending a message of encouragement, calling a friend who is struggling, praying with someone, or gently speaking up when they see someone drifting.

This passage also invites believers to welcome encouragement and correction from others. Being part of a small group, having trusted friends, or meeting regularly with a mentor can provide the daily encouragement this passage describes.

Finally, believers can be aware of sin’s deceitfulness in their own lives. Sin often justifies itself. Honest friends who speak truth in love are a gift from God in resisting that deception.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Hebrews 3* calls believers to fix their thoughts on Jesus, the Apostle and High Priest of their confession. When they are weary or discouraged, the first remedy is to look at Him more closely. Jesus is faithful, and He is greater than Moses, as a builder is greater than a house and a son is greater than a servant. Moses faithfully pointed forward; Jesus is the Son over God’s house, and believers are that house.

The chapter also contains a serious warning drawn from Israel’s history. The generation that came out of Egypt had seen God’s mighty works, yet they hardened their hearts in unbelief and could not enter the land of rest. Their story warns believers that a strong beginning does not guarantee a faithful ending. Unbelief, a refusal to trust God’s promises, can lead people away from the living God.

The remedy is twofold. First, believers must listen to God’s voice “today,” responding with soft and trusting hearts, not delaying obedience. Second, they must encourage one another daily, so that no one is hardened by the deceitfulness of sin. Perseverance is a community effort. Believers need each other to stay on course.

As long as it is called “today,” God’s invitation stands. Believers can hold fast their confidence and hope to the end, trusting the faithful Son who leads His household, and helping one another reach the rest He has promised.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, You are the Apostle and High Priest of our confession, faithful to the Father in everything. Help me to fix my thoughts on You. Thank You that You are the Son over God’s house and that I belong to that house. Help me to hold fast my confidence and hope to the end. Holy Spirit, as You speak today, give me a heart that hears and obeys. Keep me from hardening my heart through unbelief or delayed obedience. Guard me from the deceitfulness of sin. Make me an encourager of others, day by day, so that none of us falls away from the living God. Thank You that it is still “today,” and that Your invitation is still open. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Hebrews · Chapter 4 of 13

# Hebrews — Chapter 4

Chapter Theme: Entering God’s Rest and Drawing Near to the Throne of Grace

[Read Hebrews 4 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/HEB04.htm)

Main Teaching

The promise of entering God’s rest still stands, so believers should take care that none of them falls short of it. Israel heard good news in the wilderness, but it did not benefit them because they did not combine it with faith. God’s rest goes back to creation, when He rested on the seventh day, and because *Psalm 95* still speaks of “today” long after Joshua led Israel into Canaan, it is clear that a deeper Sabbath rest remains for the people of God, in which they rest from their own works as God did from His. Believers must make every effort to enter that rest, for God’s word is living and active, sharper than any double-edged sword, judging the thoughts and attitudes of the heart, and nothing is hidden from God’s sight. Since believers have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, they should hold firmly to their faith. He is able to sympathize with their weaknesses, having been tempted in every way as they are, yet without sin, so they can approach the throne of grace with confidence to receive mercy and find grace to help in their time of need.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Hebrews 4* continues the reflection on *Psalm 95* begun in chapter 3. The wilderness generation failed to enter God’s “rest,” the promised land, because of unbelief. The author now asks: Does that promise of rest still apply? And what exactly is God’s “rest”?

His answer draws on three Old Testament moments. First, at creation, God rested on the seventh day after finishing His work (*Genesis 2:2*). Second, under Joshua, Israel entered Canaan, the land of rest. Third, centuries later, through David in *Psalm 95*, God still spoke of entering His rest “today.” If Joshua had already given Israel the complete rest God intended, why would God speak of another day of rest so long afterward? The author concludes that the rest of Canaan was a picture of a greater rest still to come: a Sabbath rest for God’s people, sharing in God’s own rest.

The chapter then turns from warning to encouragement. God’s word searches the heart, and nothing is hidden from Him. That might seem frightening. But believers have a great high priest who understands their weakness and invites them to come boldly to God’s throne of grace.

### The Promise Still Stands (*4:1–2*)

“*Let’s fear therefore, lest perhaps anyone of you should seem to have come short of a promise of entering into his rest*” (*v. 1*). The promise of rest is still open, but it can be missed. “Fear” here is a healthy concern, a seriousness about not falling short. Why Israel missed the promise is studied below.

### The Sabbath Rest That Remains (*4:3–11*)

“*For we who have believed do enter into that rest, even as he has said, “As I swore in my wrath, they will not enter into my rest;” although the works were finished from the foundation of the world*” (*v. 3*). Believers “do enter” that rest. It is both present and future. God’s rest has existed since creation, when His works were completed.

“*For he has said this somewhere about the seventh day, “God rested on the seventh day from all his works;”*” (*v. 4*) “*and in this place again, “They will not enter into my rest.”*” (*v. 5*) The author connects *Genesis 2:2* with *Psalm 95:11*. God’s “*rest*” (*Genesis 2:2*) is His own Sabbath rest, which He invites His people to share.

“*Seeing therefore it remains that some should enter into it, and they to whom the good news was preached before failed to enter in because of disobedience*” (*v. 6*), “*he again defines a certain day, “today”, saying through David so long a time afterward (just as has been said), “Today if you will hear his voice, don’t harden your hearts.”*” (*v. 7*) Since the wilderness generation failed to enter, and since God spoke again through David many centuries later, the opportunity to enter His rest is still open.

“*For if Joshua had given them rest, he would not have spoken afterward of another day*” (*v. 8*). In Greek, “Joshua” and “Jesus” are the same name. Joshua led Israel into Canaan, but that was not the final rest. Jesus leads God’s people into the true rest. The Sabbath rest that remains, and the call to enter it, are studied below.

### The Living Word (*4:12–13*)

The searching power of God’s word is studied below.

### Our Great High Priest (*4:14–16*)

“*Having then a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus, the Son of God, let’s hold tightly to our confession*” (*v. 14*). Israel’s high priest passed through the curtain into the Most Holy Place once a year. Jesus has “passed through the heavens” into the very presence of God. Because He is there for us, believers should hold firmly to their faith. His sympathy and the invitation to the throne of grace are studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Hebrews 4:2* — The Word Mixed with Faith

> *“For indeed we have had good news preached to us, even as they also did, but the word they heard didn’t profit them, because it wasn’t mixed with faith by those who heard.”*
>
> — *Hebrews 4:2* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“For indeed we have had good news preached to us, even as they also did.” Both the wilderness generation and present believers received good news from God. For Israel, it was the promise of the land. For believers, it is the gospel of Christ.

“But the word they heard didn’t profit them.” The promise did not benefit Israel. They heard it but did not receive its blessing.

“Because it wasn’t mixed with faith by those who heard.” The problem was not the message but the response. They heard God’s promise but did not combine it with trust. The word “mixed” suggests blending ingredients together, like food that is eaten and digested. The word must be received with faith to do its work.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that hearing God’s word is not enough. Many people hear the gospel but are not changed by it. Jesus’ parable of the sower makes the same point: the same seed falls on different soils, and only the good soil, the heart that hears and receives the word, bears fruit (*Matthew 13:18–23*). James urges believers to be doers of the word and not hearers only (*James 1:22*).

Faith is the essential link between God’s promise and its fulfillment in a person’s life. Faith does not earn the promise; it receives it. Without faith, even the greatest promises of God remain unclaimed.

This verse also shows that religious privilege does not guarantee spiritual blessing. Israel had seen miracles and received God’s word directly. Yet they missed the promise. Believers today who have heard the gospel many times must still respond with ongoing faith.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers who regularly hear sermons, read Scripture, or attend Bible studies can ask whether they are “mixing” what they hear with faith. Are they trusting God’s promises and acting on His word, or simply hearing it?

When reading Scripture, believers can pause to respond: thanking God for His promises, confessing where they have fallen short, and asking for faith to trust and obey.

For those who have heard the gospel but have never truly trusted Christ, this verse is an invitation. The good news is for them, and it becomes theirs when they receive it with faith.

### *Hebrews 4:9–10* — A Sabbath Rest for the People of God

> *“There remains therefore a Sabbath rest for the people of God. For he who has entered into his rest has himself also rested from his works, as God did from his.”*
>
> — *Hebrews 4:9–10* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“There remains therefore a Sabbath rest for the people of God.” This is the conclusion of the author’s argument. The rest of Canaan was not the final rest. A deeper, fuller rest still remains. The author uses a special word, “Sabbath rest,” which links God’s rest at creation with the rest He offers His people.

Verse 10: “For he who has entered into his rest has himself also rested from his works, as God did from his.” Entering God’s rest means ceasing from one’s own works, just as God rested from His creative work on the seventh day.

What does it mean to rest from one’s works? In the context of Hebrews, it likely means ceasing from the effort to make oneself right with God through one’s own deeds, especially through the sacrifices and rituals of the old covenant. Believers rest in the finished work of Christ, who has “by himself purified us of our sins” and sat down (*Hebrews 1:3*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The “Sabbath rest” has both a present and a future dimension. In the present, believers enter God’s rest by trusting Christ (v3). They no longer strive to earn God’s favor; they rest in His grace. Jesus said, “*Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest*” (*Matthew 11:28*).

In the future, believers will enter God’s rest fully, in the new creation, when every struggle and sorrow is over. *Revelation 14:13* speaks of the dead who die in the Lord, that they may “*rest from their labors*” (*Revelation 14:13*).

This rest does not mean inactivity. God’s “rest” after creation did not mean He stopped sustaining the world (*John 5:17*). It means completion, satisfaction, and enjoyment. Believers’ rest in Christ is not idleness but freedom from anxious striving, a settled peace in God.

Christians hold different views on how the weekly Sabbath relates to this passage. Some see the weekly day of rest and worship as a continuing sign of the rest Christ gives. Others see the Sabbath as fulfilled in Christ, while still valuing regular rest. Either way, this passage points beyond any single day to the rest found in Christ.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Many believers live with a constant sense of spiritual pressure, as if they must prove themselves to God. This passage invites them to rest. Christ has done the work. They can stop striving to earn what He has freely given.

Physical rest also matters. Regular rhythms of rest, worship, and refreshment, such as a weekly day set apart, can be a way of practicing trust in God and enjoying His gifts.

Finally, the promise of a future rest gives hope to those who are weary. The struggles of this life will end, and God’s people will enter His perfect rest.

### *Hebrews 4:12–13* — Living and Active

> *“For the word of God is living and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing even to the dividing of soul and spirit, of both joints and marrow, and is able to discern the thoughts and intentions of the heart. There is no creature that is hidden from his sight, but all things are naked and laid open before the eyes of him to whom we must give an account.”*
>
> — *Hebrews 4:12–13* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“For the word of God is living and active.” God’s word is not dead words on a page. It is alive, because God Himself speaks through it. It is “active,” or effective, accomplishing what God intends (*Isaiah 55:10–11*).

“And sharper than any two-edged sword.” A two-edged sword cuts deeply and precisely. God’s word cuts through excuses, pretenses, and self-deception.

“Piercing even to the dividing of soul and spirit, of both joints and marrow.” The word penetrates to the deepest parts of a person. These phrases describe its ability to reach the innermost being, not to provide a precise analysis of human makeup.

“And is able to discern the thoughts and intentions of the heart.” The word judges not only outward actions but inner thoughts and motives. It reveals what is really in the heart.

Verse 13: “There is no creature that is hidden from his sight, but all things are naked and laid open before the eyes of him to whom we must give an account.” Nothing is hidden from God. Everything is exposed before Him. “Laid open” was used for a wrestler gripping an opponent by the neck, or for exposing the throat of a sacrificial animal. It conveys complete exposure. Every person will give an account to God.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses follow the warning about Israel’s unbelief. God’s word is what Israel heard and failed to believe. And it is the word that confronts every reader. Through Scripture, God searches the heart and exposes hidden unbelief, disobedience, and sin.

This might seem frightening. But the purpose of exposure is healing. A surgeon cuts in order to heal. God’s word reveals sin so that it can be confessed and forgiven. The verses that follow (vv14–16) immediately point to the high priest who offers mercy and grace.

The phrase “to whom we must give an account” reminds believers of the final judgment. Everyone will stand before God. This truth should lead to honesty before God now. Since He already sees everything, there is no point in hiding. Believers can bring everything into the light, trusting His mercy.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can approach Scripture expecting God to speak, not only to inform but to search and transform their hearts. Reading the Bible prayerfully, with openness to correction, allows God’s word to do its work.

When Scripture convicts, believers can respond with honesty and repentance rather than defensiveness. The word’s sharpness is meant for healing, not destruction.

The truth that nothing is hidden from God can bring both sobriety and relief. Sobriety, because believers will give an account. Relief, because they do not need to pretend. God already knows everything, and He still invites them to come to Him.

### *Hebrews 4:15–16* — Approach the Throne of Grace with Confidence

> *“For we don’t have a high priest who can’t be touched with the feeling of our infirmities, but one who has been in all points tempted like we are, yet without sin. Let’s therefore draw near with boldness to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and may find grace for help in time of need.”*
>
> — *Hebrews 4:15–16* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“For we don’t have a high priest who can’t be touched with the feeling of our infirmities.” Jesus is not distant or unfeeling. He sympathizes with human weakness. He knows what it feels like to be weary, hungry, sorrowful, rejected, and in pain.

“But one who has been in all points tempted like we are, yet without sin.” Jesus faced temptation in every area of human life. He experienced the full force of temptation. But He never sinned. His sinlessness does not make Him less sympathetic; it means He felt the full pressure of temptation without ever giving in.

Verse 16: “Let’s therefore draw near with boldness to the throne of grace.” Because Jesus is a sympathetic high priest, believers can come to God with confidence. God’s throne, which could be a throne of judgment, has become a “throne of grace” for those who come through Christ.

“That we may receive mercy and may find grace for help in time of need.” At the throne of grace, believers receive mercy for their failures and grace for their struggles. “In time of need” means at the moment it is needed, timely help.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses are among the most comforting in the Bible. They hold together two truths that might seem to conflict: God’s holiness, which sees everything (v13), and Christ’s sympathy, which understands everything (v15). The God who searches the heart is also the God who welcomes the weak through His Son.

In the Old Testament, the people could not approach God directly. Only the high priest could enter the Most Holy Place, and only once a year, with blood (*Leviticus 16*). Now, through Jesus, every believer can draw near to God with confidence. The curtain has been torn (*Mark 15:38*). Access is open.

“Boldness” does not mean arrogance. It means freedom and confidence, the assurance that one is welcome. Believers come not because they deserve to, but because their high priest has made the way.

The pairing of mercy and grace is significant. Mercy is not receiving the punishment one deserves. Grace is receiving the help one does not deserve. At the throne, believers receive both.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

When believers feel weak, tempted, or ashamed, they can come to God boldly through Christ. They do not need to clean themselves up first. They can come as they are, trusting that Jesus understands and that God’s throne is a throne of grace.

Believers can make this a regular practice: bringing their struggles, temptations, failures, and needs to God in prayer, expecting to receive mercy and grace.

This passage also shapes how believers see Jesus. He is not a stern judge waiting to condemn, but a sympathetic high priest who knows their weakness and stands ready to help. That knowledge can transform their relationship with Him.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Hebrews 4* offers both a sober warning and a glorious invitation. The warning is that God’s promise of rest can be missed. Israel heard good news but did not combine it with faith, and so they did not enter. Believers today must also receive God’s word with faith, not simply hear it.

The invitation is that a Sabbath rest remains for the people of God. This rest is God’s own rest, first glimpsed at creation, pictured in the promised land, and now offered fully in Christ. Believers enter it by trusting Christ and ceasing from their own efforts to earn God’s favor. They will enter it fully in the new creation. Those who are weary from striving can rest in what Christ has done.

The chapter also reminds believers that God’s word is living and active, searching the heart and exposing what is hidden. Everything is laid open before God. This truth calls for honesty, repentance, and readiness to give an account.

But the chapter ends with deep comfort. Believers have a great high priest, Jesus the Son of God, who has passed through the heavens. He sympathizes with their weaknesses, having been tempted in every way, yet without sin. Because of Him, they can approach the throne of grace with confidence, to receive mercy and find grace to help in their time of need. Whatever they face, they are welcome before God through Christ.

## Chapter Prayer

Father, thank You for the promise of rest that still stands for Your people. Help me to receive Your word with faith, not merely to hear it. Teach me to rest from my own striving and to trust in the finished work of Christ. Thank You that a Sabbath rest remains for Your people, and that one day I will enter it fully. Let Your living and active word search my heart, expose what is hidden, and heal what is broken. Thank You, Lord Jesus, that You are my great high priest, that You understand my weaknesses, and that You were tempted in every way, yet without sin. Give me confidence to draw near to the throne of grace, to receive mercy for my failures and grace for every time of need. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
