Hebrews · Chapter 5 of 13

# Hebrews — Chapter 5

Chapter Theme: A High Priest Who Learned Obedience Through Suffering

[Read Hebrews 5 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/HEB05.htm)

Main Teaching

Every high priest is chosen from among people to represent them before God, offering gifts and sacrifices for sins, and because he shares their weakness, he can deal gently with the ignorant and wayward. No one takes this honor for himself; he must be called by God, as Aaron was. Likewise, Christ did not exalt Himself to become high priest; God appointed Him, saying, “You are my Son,” and “You are a priest forever, after the order of Melchizedek.” During His earthly life, Jesus offered prayers and petitions with loud cries and tears to the One who could save Him from death, and He was heard because of His reverent submission. Although He was a Son, He learned obedience through what He suffered, and having been made perfect, He became the source of eternal salvation for all who obey Him. The author then pauses, rebuking his readers for being slow to learn: they ought to be teachers by now, but they still need milk rather than solid food, which belongs to the mature, whose senses are trained by practice to distinguish good from evil.

## Chapter Background and Story

In *Hebrews 4:14–16*, the author introduced Jesus as “*a great high priest*” (*Hebrews 4:14*) who sympathizes with human weakness. Now he begins to explain in detail what makes Jesus a true high priest. This theme will dominate chapters 5–10.

In ancient Israel, the high priest held a special role. He was descended from Aaron, Moses’ brother, and he represented the people before God. Once a year, on the Day of Atonement, he entered the Most Holy Place of the tabernacle or temple to offer blood for the sins of the people (*Leviticus 16*). He was the mediator between a holy God and a sinful people.

For Jewish readers, a question naturally arose: How could Jesus be a high priest? He was from the tribe of Judah, not Levi, and not descended from Aaron. The author answers by pointing to *Psalm 110:4*, where God declares the Messiah to be “a priest forever, after the order of Melchizedek.” Melchizedek was a mysterious king-priest who met Abraham in *Genesis 14*. The author will explain his significance more fully in chapter 7.

At the end of chapter 5, the author pauses. He wants to teach about Melchizedek, but he is concerned that his readers have become spiritually sluggish. This leads into the third warning passage of the letter, which continues into chapter 6.

### The Role of a High Priest (*5:1–4*)

The qualities of a high priest, especially gentleness toward the weak, are studied below. “*Because of this, he must offer sacrifices for sins for the people, as well as for himself*” (*v. 3*). Human high priests were sinners too. On the Day of Atonement, the high priest first offered a sacrifice for his own sins before offering one for the people (*Leviticus 16:6*, 11). Jesus, being sinless, did not need to offer for Himself (*Hebrews 7:27*).

“*Nobody takes this honor on himself, but he is called by God, just like Aaron was*” (*v. 4*). The high priesthood was not a position anyone could grab for themselves. When Korah and others rebelled against Aaron’s priesthood, God judged them (*Numbers 16*). The high priest had to be appointed by God.

### Christ Appointed by God (*5:5–6*)

“*So also Christ didn’t glorify himself to be made a high priest, but it was he who said to him, “You are my Son. Today I have become your father.”*” (*v. 5*) Jesus did not seize the role of high priest. He was appointed by the Father. The author quotes *Psalm 2:7*, already cited in *Hebrews 1:5*, linking Jesus’ sonship with His priesthood.

“*As he says also in another place, “You are a priest forever, after the order of Melchizedek.”*” (*v. 6*) *Psalm 110:4* is central to Hebrews. The same psalm that invites the Messiah to sit at God’s right hand (*Psalm 110:1*; *Hebrews 1:13*) also declares Him a priest forever. Jesus is both King and Priest. His priesthood is “forever,” unlike the Levitical priests who died and were replaced. And it is “after the order of Melchizedek,” a different kind of priesthood than Aaron’s.

### Learning Obedience Through Suffering (*5:7–10*)

Jesus’ prayers and His learning obedience through suffering are studied below. “*named by God a high priest after the order of Melchizedek*” (*v. 10*). The author returns to Melchizedek, preparing for chapter 7.

### A Call to Maturity (*5:11–14*)

The author’s rebuke and call to spiritual maturity are studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Hebrews 5:1–2* — Dealing Gently with the Wayward

> *“For every high priest, being taken from among men, is appointed for men in things pertaining to God, that he may offer both gifts and sacrifices for sins. The high priest can deal gently with those who are ignorant and going astray, because he himself is also surrounded with weakness.”*
>
> — *Hebrews 5:1–2* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The author describes what a high priest is. “For every high priest, being taken from among men, is appointed for men in things pertaining to God.” A high priest is a human being, chosen from among the people, to act on their behalf before God. He is their representative.

“That he may offer both gifts and sacrifices for sins.” His main task is to offer offerings to God, especially sacrifices that deal with sin.

Verse 2: “The high priest can deal gently with those who are ignorant and going astray.” The phrase “deal gently” describes a balanced, moderate response, neither harsh nor indulgent. The high priest does not overreact in anger nor ignore sin. He responds with patience and understanding.

“Those who are ignorant and going astray” are people who sin through ignorance or weakness, wandering like lost sheep. In the Old Testament, sacrifices were provided especially for unintentional sins (*Leviticus 4*; *Numbers 15:27–29*).

“Because he himself is also surrounded with weakness.” The high priest can be gentle because he understands weakness from personal experience. He too struggles.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This description of a high priest shows what kind of mediator humanity needs: someone who represents us, who deals with our sin, and who understands our weakness. Human high priests met this need partially. Jesus meets it perfectly.

Jesus shares human nature fully and understands weakness (*Hebrews 2:17*; *4:15*). But unlike human priests, His gentleness does not come from personal sin; it comes from His perfect compassion and His experience of temptation and suffering. He is both completely holy and completely understanding.

The quality of gentleness toward the wayward is a model for all who care for others spiritually. Jesus did not crush bruised reeds or snuff out smoldering wicks (*Matthew 12:20*). He treated sinners with compassion, as with the woman caught in adultery (*John 8:1–11*) and with Peter after his denial (*John 21:15–19*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers who feel they have wandered or failed can take comfort in knowing that their high priest deals gently with the wayward. They can come back to Him without fear of harsh rejection.

Those in positions of spiritual leadership, such as pastors, parents, mentors, and friends, can follow this example. Responding to others’ failures with gentleness, patience, and understanding, while still taking sin seriously, reflects the heart of Christ.

Remembering one’s own weakness also helps believers treat others with compassion. Those who know they too are “surrounded with weakness” are less likely to judge harshly.

### *Hebrews 5:7–8* — Prayers with Loud Cries and Tears

> *“He, in the days of his flesh, having offered up prayers and petitions with strong crying and tears to him who was able to save him from death, and having been heard for his godly fear, though he was a Son, yet learned obedience by the things which he suffered.”*
>
> — *Hebrews 5:7–8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These verses give a vivid picture of Jesus’ humanity. “He, in the days of his flesh.” This refers to Jesus’ earthly life.

“Having offered up prayers and petitions with strong crying and tears to him who was able to save him from death.” Jesus prayed with intense emotion, with loud cries and tears. This most clearly recalls Gethsemane, where Jesus was deeply distressed and prayed that the cup might pass from Him (*Mark 14:32–36*), as discussed in the study of *Mark 14:36*. It may also recall His cry from the cross (*Mark 15:34*).

“And having been heard for his godly fear.” God heard Jesus’ prayer because of His reverent submission. But God did not spare Him from dying. How was He “heard”? Many understand it to mean that God answered by raising Him from the dead, saving Him out of death rather than from death. Others understand it to mean that God gave Jesus the strength to submit to His will (*Luke 22:43*). Either way, Jesus’ prayer was not unanswered; it was answered in God’s way.

Verse 8: “though he was a Son, yet learned obedience by the things which he suffered.” Jesus was always obedient; He never sinned. But He “learned” obedience in the sense of experiencing what obedience costs in a world of suffering. As a human being, He grew in obedience through each trial, culminating in His obedience to death on the cross (*Philippians 2:8*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses reveal the depth of Jesus’ identification with human suffering. He did not glide through life untouched by pain. He wept. He cried out. He felt fear and anguish. His sinlessness did not make Him less human; it made Him fully what humanity was meant to be, even in suffering.

This shows that strong emotion in prayer is not a lack of faith. Jesus Himself prayed with loud cries and tears. The Psalms are full of such prayers. Believers can bring their deepest anguish to God honestly.

“Though he was a Son” is significant. One might expect that the Son of God would be exempt from suffering. But He was not. His sonship did not shield Him from suffering; rather, His suffering was part of His perfect obedience as the Son. This gives dignity to believers’ suffering. They too are God’s children, and their suffering does not mean God has rejected them (*Hebrews 12:5–11*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

When believers face anguish, fear, or grief, they can pray honestly, with tears if need be. Jesus did, and He understands.

Believers can also trust that God hears their prayers, even when the answer is not what they asked. Jesus was heard, and God’s answer was resurrection. God’s answers to believers’ prayers may also come in ways they cannot yet see.

Finally, this passage encourages believers to see their own trials as opportunities to grow in obedience and trust. Like Jesus, they can learn through what they suffer, relying on the Father throughout.

### *Hebrews 5:9* — The Source of Eternal Salvation

> *“Having been made perfect, he became to all of those who obey him the author of eternal salvation,”*
>
> — *Hebrews 5:9* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“Having been made perfect.” As explained at *Hebrews 2:10*, “*perfect*” (*Hebrews 2:10*) does not mean that Jesus was ever morally flawed. It means He was made complete, fully qualified for His role as Savior and high priest. Through His suffering and obedience, culminating in His death and resurrection, He completed everything needed to save His people.

“He became to all of those who obey him the author of eternal salvation.” “Author” here means “source” or “cause.” Jesus is the one from whom eternal salvation flows. This salvation is “eternal,” lasting forever, in contrast to the temporary effects of the old sacrifices.

“To all of those who obey him.” Salvation is for those who respond to Jesus with obedience. In Hebrews, obedience is closely connected with faith (*Hebrews 3:18–19*). Those who truly trust Jesus will follow Him.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows the connection between Jesus’ obedience and our salvation. Jesus learned obedience through suffering (v8), and He became the source of salvation for those who obey Him. His perfect obedience is the basis of our salvation; our obedience is the response to His saving work.

This does not mean salvation is earned by obedience. Hebrews teaches clearly that salvation comes through Christ’s sacrifice (*Hebrews 9:12*, 26; *10:10*, 14). But genuine faith always leads to obedience. Jesus said, “*If you love me, keep my commandments*” (*John 14:15*). Obedience is the evidence of faith, not its replacement.

The word “eternal” is important in Hebrews. Christ brings “*eternal salvation*” (*v. 9*), “*eternal redemption*” (*Hebrews 9:12*), and “*the eternal inheritance*” (*Hebrews 9:15*), through “*the eternal Spirit*” (*Hebrews 9:14*). What He provides is permanent and complete.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can rest in the security of eternal salvation. What Christ has accomplished cannot be undone. It is not a temporary fix but a permanent gift.

This verse also calls believers to respond to Christ with obedience. Faith is not merely agreement with ideas but a commitment to follow Jesus. Believers can ask how they are obeying Him in their daily lives.

Finally, this verse invites gratitude. Jesus suffered and obeyed perfectly so that He could become the source of salvation. Everything believers have flows from Him.

### *Hebrews 5:12–14* — From Milk to Solid Food

> *“For although by this time you should be teachers, you again need to have someone teach you the rudiments of the first principles of the revelations of God. You have come to need milk, and not solid food. For everyone who lives on milk is not experienced in the word of righteousness, for he is a baby. But solid food is for those who are full grown, who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern good and evil.”*
>
> — *Hebrews 5:12–14* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The author pauses to address his readers’ spiritual condition. In verse 11 he says that he has much to say about Melchizedek, but it is hard to explain, because they have “become dull of hearing.” The problem is not that the subject is too difficult but that the readers have become sluggish, slow to listen and learn.

Verse 12: “For although by this time you should be teachers, you again need to have someone teach you the rudiments of the first principles of the revelations of God.” These believers had been Christians long enough that they should have been mature enough to teach others. Instead, they needed to relearn the basics.

“You have come to need milk, and not solid food.” Milk is for babies; solid food is for those who are grown. Spiritually, they were still infants.

Verse 13: “For everyone who lives on milk is not experienced in the word of righteousness, for he is a baby.” Those who remain on milk are unskilled in understanding and applying God’s word.

Verse 14: “But solid food is for those who are full grown, who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern good and evil.” Mature believers have trained their spiritual senses through constant practice. Like athletes, they have exercised their ability to distinguish what is good from what is evil.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This passage shows that spiritual growth is expected. God does not intend believers to remain spiritual infants. Paul similarly rebuked the Corinthians for being “babies in Christ” who still needed milk (*1 Corinthians 3:1–2*). Peter urged believers to crave pure spiritual milk so that they could grow (*1 Peter 2:2*). The goal is maturity.

Spiritual maturity is not merely about knowing more facts. It is about learning “*to discern good and evil*” (*v. 14*), the practical wisdom to apply God’s word to life. This discernment develops “by reason of use,” through practice. Just as physical muscles grow stronger through exercise, spiritual discernment grows through regularly applying God’s word in real decisions.

The readers’ spiritual sluggishness was connected to their temptation to drift away. Believers who stop growing are more vulnerable to falling away. Growth is a safeguard.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can ask whether they are growing spiritually or have become stagnant. Have they moved beyond the basics of the faith into deeper understanding and practice?

Growth requires intentional effort: studying Scripture more deeply, learning from mature believers, applying God’s word to everyday decisions, and serving others. Teaching others is also a sign and a means of maturity.

This passage is not meant to shame new believers. Everyone begins with milk, and that is good and right. The concern is for those who have been believers for a long time and have stopped growing. For them, the invitation is to move forward, to hunger for solid food, and to train their spiritual senses through practice.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Hebrews 5* explains what makes Jesus a true high priest. A high priest represents people before God, offers sacrifices for sins, and deals gently with the wayward because he understands weakness. And he must be appointed by God. Jesus fulfills every requirement perfectly. He did not exalt Himself but was appointed by the Father as Son and as a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.

The chapter also offers a moving picture of Jesus’ humanity. During His earthly life, He prayed with loud cries and tears, especially in Gethsemane. Although He was the Son, He learned obedience through suffering. Through that obedience, He was made perfect, fully qualified as the source of eternal salvation for all who obey Him. Believers can bring their own anguish to God honestly, trusting that He hears, as He heard Jesus.

Because Jesus deals gently with the wayward, believers who have wandered can return to Him without fear. And those who care for others can follow His example of gentle, patient understanding.

Finally, the chapter calls believers to spiritual maturity. Those who have been believers for some time should not remain spiritual infants, needing milk, but should grow into those who can handle solid food, with senses trained by practice to discern good and evil. Growth guards against drifting and prepares believers to help others grow as well.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for being my great high priest, appointed by the Father and faithful forever. Thank You that You deal gently with the weak and wayward. When I wander, draw me back with Your compassion. Thank You for praying with loud cries and tears in the days of Your flesh, and for learning obedience through what You suffered. When I am in anguish, help me to pray honestly, trusting that the Father hears. Thank You that You are the source of eternal salvation. Help me to respond to You with faithful obedience. Keep me from becoming dull of hearing or spiritually stagnant. Give me a hunger for solid food, and train my senses through practice to discern good from evil, so that I may grow to maturity and help others grow as well. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Hebrews · Chapter 6 of 13

# Hebrews — Chapter 6

Chapter Theme: Press On to Maturity, Anchored in Hope

[Read Hebrews 6 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/HEB06.htm)

Main Teaching

The author urges his readers to move beyond the elementary teachings about Christ, such as repentance, faith, baptisms, laying on of hands, resurrection, and judgment, and press on to maturity. He then gives a sobering warning: those who have been enlightened, tasted the heavenly gift, shared in the Holy Spirit, and tasted God’s word and the powers of the coming age, and then fall away, cannot be brought back to repentance, since they are crucifying the Son of God all over again and holding Him up to contempt. Like land that receives rain, those who produce good fruit receive God’s blessing, while those who produce only thorns face judgment. Yet the author is confident of better things for his readers, because God will not forget their work and love in serving His people. He urges them to show the same diligence to the end and to imitate those who inherit the promises through faith and patience, like Abraham, to whom God made a promise and confirmed it with an oath. By these two unchangeable things, God’s promise and His oath, believers who have fled to Him for refuge have strong encouragement to hold fast to the hope set before them, a hope that is a sure and steady anchor for the soul, entering behind the curtain where Jesus has gone ahead as forerunner, a high priest forever.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Hebrews 6* continues the warning that began in *Hebrews 5:11*. The author had been about to explain Jesus’ priesthood in the order of Melchizedek, but he paused because his readers had become spiritually sluggish. Now he urges them to grow up and warns them of the danger of falling away.

Verses 4–6 contain one of the most debated passages in the New Testament. Sincere Christians have understood it in several ways, and the commentary below presents those views fairly. It is important to read the whole chapter together. The author’s purpose was not to make his readers doubt their salvation but to shake them out of spiritual complacency and then to reassure them. The warning is followed immediately by words of confidence (v9) and by one of the most beautiful passages about Christian hope in Scripture (vv13–20).

### Moving Beyond the Basics (*6:1–3*)

The call to press on to maturity is studied below. “*This will we do, if God permits*” (*v. 3*). Growth depends on God’s enabling. The author intends to move forward in his teaching, trusting God to help.

### The Danger of Falling Away (*6:4–8*)

The warning is studied below. “*For the land which has drunk the rain that comes often on it and produces a crop suitable for them for whose sake it is also tilled, receives blessing from God*” (*v. 7*); “*but if it bears thorns and thistles, it is rejected and near being cursed, whose end is to be burned*” (*v. 8*). The author uses an agricultural image. Land that receives abundant rain should produce a good crop. If it produces only thorns, it is useless. The image echoes *Isaiah 5:1–7*, where God’s vineyard produced wild grapes, and Jesus’ parable of the sower (*Matthew 13:3–9*). The rain represents God’s blessings; the crop represents the fruit of a life that has received them.

### Confidence of Better Things (*6:9–12*)

“*But, beloved, we are persuaded of better things for you, and things that accompany salvation, even though we speak like this*” (*v. 9*). After the stern warning, the author speaks tenderly. He calls them “beloved” and expresses confidence that their lives show signs of genuine salvation. The warning was meant to shake them, not to condemn them. God’s faithfulness to remember their love is studied below.

“*We desire that each one of you may show the same diligence to the fullness of hope even to the end*” (*v. 11*), “*that you won’t be sluggish, but imitators of those who through faith and perseverance inherited the promises*” (*v. 12*). The author wants every one of them to keep going with the same zeal they once showed. “Sluggish” is the same word translated “dull” in *Hebrews 5:11*. The remedy for spiritual sluggishness is to imitate those who have persevered in faith and patience, a theme that will be developed in chapter 11.

### God’s Unchangeable Promise (*6:13–20*)

“*For when God made a promise to Abraham, since he could swear by no one greater, he swore by himself*” (*v. 13*), “*saying, “Surely blessing I will bless you, and multiplying I will multiply you.”*” (*v. 14*) After Abraham was willing to offer Isaac, God confirmed His promise with an oath (*Genesis 22:16–17*). Since there is no one greater than God, He swore by Himself.

“*Thus, having patiently endured, he obtained the promise*” (*v. 15*). Abraham waited many years for the promise to be fulfilled. He is an example of faith and patience (v12).

“*For men indeed swear by a greater one, and in every dispute of theirs the oath is final for confirmation*” (*v. 16*). Among humans, an oath settles disputes and confirms commitments. God accommodated Himself to human practice to give His people full assurance. The meaning of God’s promise and oath, and the anchor of hope, are studied below.

“*where as a forerunner Jesus entered for us, having become a high priest forever after the order of Melchizedek*” (*v. 20*). Jesus has gone ahead as a “forerunner,” a scout who goes before others to prepare the way. He entered God’s presence on behalf of His people. This brings the author back to Melchizedek, the subject of chapter 7.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Hebrews 6:1–2* — Press On to Maturity

> *“Therefore leaving the teaching of the first principles of Christ, let’s press on to perfection—not laying again a foundation of repentance from dead works, of faith toward God, of the teaching of baptisms, of laying on of hands, of resurrection of the dead, and of eternal judgment.”*
>
> — *Hebrews 6:1–2* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“Therefore leaving the teaching of the first principles of Christ, let’s press on to perfection.” The author does not mean abandoning the basics of the faith, but building on them. A builder does not keep laying the foundation; once it is laid, he builds the walls. “Perfection” here means maturity, spiritual adulthood.

“Not laying again a foundation.” The author lists six foundational teachings, in three pairs.

“Of repentance from dead works, of faith toward God.” The starting point of the Christian life: turning from sinful or useless works that lead to death, and trusting God.

“Of the teaching of baptisms, of laying on of hands.” The word “baptisms” is plural. It may refer to instruction about the difference between Christian baptism and other ritual washings practiced in Judaism, or to baptism in water and in the Spirit. “Laying on of hands” was used in the early church for blessing, healing, commissioning for ministry, and receiving the Spirit (*Acts 8:17*; *13:3*; *1 Timothy 4:14*).

“Of resurrection of the dead, and of eternal judgment.” The future hope of believers: the resurrection of the body and God’s final judgment.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These six teachings were basic truths that new believers learned, many of which had roots in Judaism. Jewish believers would have been familiar with repentance, faith in God, ritual washings, laying on of hands, resurrection, and judgment. What made Christian teaching distinctive was how these truths were fulfilled and transformed in Christ.

The danger the author faced was that his readers might cling to these basic teachings, perhaps understood in a way that did not require full commitment to Christ, and never move on to understand the deeper truths about Jesus as high priest and mediator of the new covenant. Moving forward meant growing in understanding of Christ’s work.

The foundation is essential, but it is not the whole building. Believers need to keep growing in their understanding of Christ, in their obedience, and in their love.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can ask whether they have moved beyond the basics of the faith. This is not about abandoning foundational truths but about building on them: deepening understanding of Scripture, growing in character, and maturing in service.

Practical steps toward maturity might include studying Scripture more deeply, learning about the whole story of the Bible, reading books that explain Christian teaching, participating in serious discussion with other believers, and applying God’s word to every area of life.

This passage also encourages patience with new believers, who need the foundation laid well. But for those who have walked with Christ for years, the call is to press on.

### *Hebrews 6:4–6* — The Warning Against Falling Away

> *“For concerning those who were once enlightened and tasted of the heavenly gift, and were made partakers of the Holy Spirit, and tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come, and then fell away, it is impossible to renew them again to repentance; seeing they crucify the Son of God for themselves again, and put him to open shame.”*
>
> — *Hebrews 6:4–6* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The author describes people who have experienced remarkable spiritual blessings. They were “once enlightened”: they had come to understand the gospel. They “tasted of the heavenly gift”: they had experienced God’s grace. They “were made partakers of the Holy Spirit”: they had shared in the Spirit’s work. They “tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come”: they had experienced the truth of Scripture and the miraculous signs that accompanied the gospel (*Hebrews 2:4*).

“And then fell away.” These people turned away from Christ, deliberately abandoning the faith.

“It is impossible to renew them again to repentance.” The author says that, having rejected Christ after such experiences, they cannot be brought back to repentance.

“Seeing they crucify the Son of God for themselves again, and put him to open shame.” By rejecting Christ after knowing Him, they join those who crucified Him, publicly treating Him with contempt.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Christians have understood this passage in several ways.

Some, often in the Arminian or Wesleyan tradition, believe the passage describes genuine believers who can truly fall away from salvation through deliberate, persistent rejection of Christ. They see the warning as describing a real possibility.

Others, often in the Reformed tradition, believe the passage describes people who were closely associated with the Christian community and experienced many blessings of the gospel, but who never truly trusted Christ. Like Judas, they tasted but did not truly receive. Their falling away reveals that their faith was never genuine (*1 John 2:19*).

Others believe the passage describes a hypothetical situation. They understand the author to be saying, in effect, “If a true believer were to fall away, there would be no other way back, because Christ’s sacrifice is the only one.” The warning functions to keep believers from even moving in that direction.

Still others note that the verb tense in verse 6 suggests an ongoing action, “while they keep on crucifying the Son of God.” On this reading, repentance is impossible as long as they continue in deliberate rejection of Christ.

All of these views agree on several important points. The passage describes a deliberate, settled rejection of Christ, not the ordinary struggles, doubts, and failures of believers. It is a serious warning meant to keep believers from drifting. And there is no other sacrifice for sin apart from Christ (*Hebrews 10:26*). If someone rejects Him, there is nowhere else to go.

It is also important to say this: people who are worried that they have committed this sin, who long to return to God and grieve over their failures, are showing the very opposite of the hardened rejection the passage describes. The desire to repent is itself a sign of God’s grace at work. Peter denied Jesus three times and was fully restored (*John 21:15–19*). Anyone who wants to come to Christ will be welcomed (*John 6:37*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage calls believers to take their faith seriously. Spiritual blessings, church involvement, and religious experiences are not the same as continuing faith in Christ. Believers are called to hold fast to Him.

At the same time, this passage should not produce paralyzing fear in believers who struggle with sin or doubt. The author himself goes on to express confidence in his readers (v9). The warning is meant to wake people up, not to crush tender consciences.

Those who are anxious that they have fallen beyond God’s reach can bring that anxiety to God and to trusted believers. The very desire to return is a sign that God is drawing them. His invitation stands: “*Draw near with boldness to the throne of grace*” (*Hebrews 4:16*).

### *Hebrews 6:10* — God Will Not Forget Your Work

> *“For God is not unrighteous, so as to forget your work and the labor of love which you showed toward his name, in that you served the saints, and still do serve them.”*
>
> — *Hebrews 6:10* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After the warning, the author encourages his readers. “For God is not unrighteous, so as to forget your work and the labor of love which you showed toward his name.”

God is just. He will not overlook the good the readers have done. Their “work” and “labor of love” were done “toward his name,” that is, for God’s sake and for His glory.

“In that you served the saints, and still do serve them.” Their love was expressed in practical service to fellow believers. *Hebrews 10:33–34* describes how they had stood with those who were persecuted and had joyfully accepted the loss of their property. And they were still serving.

This service was evidence of genuine faith. It was one of the “things that accompany salvation” (v9).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that God notices and values acts of love. Jesus said that even a cup of cold water given to one of His followers will not go unrewarded (*Matthew 10:42*). In the parable of the sheep and the goats, He said that whatever is done for the least of His brothers and sisters is done for Him (*Matthew 25:40*).

The phrase “toward his name” is important. Service to fellow believers is service to God. Love for God is shown in love for His people.

This verse also offers assurance. The readers’ practical love was a sign that God was at work in them. Genuine faith produces love, and love produces service. When believers see such fruit in their lives, they can be encouraged that their faith is real.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers who serve in quiet, unnoticed ways, caring for the sick, helping the poor, encouraging the discouraged, supporting fellow believers, can take comfort that God sees and will not forget.

This verse also encourages believers to keep serving. The readers had served in the past and were still serving. Faithful, ongoing love is a mark of genuine faith.

Finally, believers can see service to others as service to God’s name. Every act of love done for His people honors Him.

### *Hebrews 6:18–19* — An Anchor for the Soul

> *“that by two immutable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we may have a strong encouragement, who have fled for refuge to take hold of the hope set before us. This hope we have as an anchor of the soul, a hope both sure and steadfast and entering into that which is within the veil,”*
>
> — *Hebrews 6:18–19* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“That by two immutable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie.” The “two immutable things” are God’s promise and His oath. Both are unchangeable. Since it is impossible for God to lie, His promise and His oath are absolutely certain.

“We may have a strong encouragement, who have fled for refuge to take hold of the hope set before us.” Believers are described as those who have “fled for refuge.” This may recall the cities of refuge in the Old Testament, where someone who had accidentally killed another person could flee for safety (*Numbers 35:9–15*). Believers have fled to God for safety, and they hold onto the hope He has set before them.

Verse 19: “This hope we have as an anchor of the soul, a hope both sure and steadfast.” An anchor keeps a ship from drifting in a storm. Christian hope is like that anchor. It is “sure,” reliable and secure, and “steadfast,” firm and unshakable. It keeps the soul steady when life is turbulent.

“And entering into that which is within the veil.” In the temple, a thick curtain, or veil, separated the Most Holy Place, where God’s presence dwelt, from the rest of the sanctuary. Only the high priest could enter, once a year. The anchor of hope is fixed not in the sea floor but in heaven itself, in God’s very presence.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This passage connects back to the warning about drifting (*Hebrews 2:1*). The remedy for drifting is an anchor. Believers who are tempted to drift away can hold fast to the hope that is anchored in God’s presence.

The image is striking. Ordinarily, an anchor is dropped down into the depths. Christian hope is anchored upward, in heaven, where Jesus has entered as forerunner (v20). Because Jesus is there, believers’ hope is secure. Their future is tied to Him.

The certainty of God’s promise is the foundation of this hope. Christian hope is not wishful thinking but confident expectation based on the character of God, who cannot lie. *Titus 1:2* speaks of “*hope of eternal life, which God, who can't lie, promised before time began*” (*Titus 1:2*).

The early Christians loved this image. The anchor, often shaped to suggest a cross, was one of the earliest Christian symbols, found in the catacombs of Rome.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

When life feels stormy, through illness, loss, uncertainty, or fear, believers can hold onto the anchor of hope. Their hope is not in circumstances but in God’s unchangeable promise and in Jesus, who has gone ahead into God’s presence.

This hope can steady believers who are tempted to drift spiritually. Remembering God’s promises and Christ’s presence in heaven can renew their commitment.

Believers can also reflect on what they are anchoring their lives to. Many people anchor their hope in wealth, relationships, health, or success, all of which can shift. Only hope anchored in God’s presence is truly sure and steadfast.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Hebrews 6* calls believers to keep growing. The foundational truths of the faith, repentance, faith, baptism, laying on of hands, resurrection, and judgment, are essential, but they are a foundation to build on. Believers are called to press on to maturity, growing in their understanding of Christ and in their obedience to Him.

The chapter contains a serious warning about falling away. Christians have understood it in different ways, but all agree that it describes a deliberate, settled rejection of Christ, and that there is no other way of salvation apart from Him. The warning is meant to wake up the complacent, not to crush the tender-hearted. Those who long to return to God and grieve over their sins are showing the very sign of grace that the passage’s subjects lacked.

The chapter then turns to encouragement. God will not forget His people’s work and love in serving others. Their practical love is evidence of genuine faith. Believers can keep serving, knowing that God sees, and they can imitate those who have inherited God’s promises through faith and patience, like Abraham.

Finally, the chapter offers a beautiful image of hope. God’s promise and His oath are unchangeable, and He cannot lie. Believers who have fled to Him for refuge have a hope that is an anchor for the soul, sure and steadfast, fixed in God’s very presence, where Jesus has gone ahead as forerunner and high priest. Whatever storms they face, they are anchored in Him.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord, help me to press on to maturity, building on the foundation of faith You have laid in my life. Keep me from spiritual sluggishness and from drifting away from You. Guard my heart against any hardening, and keep me faithful to Christ. Where I have been afraid that I have gone too far from You, remind me that You welcome all who come to You, and that the desire to return is Your grace at work in me. Thank You that You do not forget the love and service of Your people. Help me to keep serving with diligence until the end. Thank You for Your unchangeable promise and oath, and that it is impossible for You to lie. Thank You for the hope that anchors my soul, sure and steadfast, fixed in Your presence where Jesus has gone ahead of me. Hold me fast. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Hebrews · Chapter 7 of 13

# Hebrews — Chapter 7

Chapter Theme: A Priest Forever After the Order of Melchizedek

[Read Hebrews 7 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/HEB07.htm)

Main Teaching

Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, met Abraham after a battle, blessed him, and received a tenth of the spoils from him. His name means “king of righteousness” and his title “king of peace,” and because Scripture records no genealogy, birth, or death for him, he resembles the Son of God as a priest who remains forever. His greatness is shown in that Abraham, the ancestor of the Levitical priests, gave him a tenth and received his blessing. If perfection could have come through the Levitical priesthood, there would have been no need for a different priest in the order of Melchizedek. Jesus, from the tribe of Judah, became a priest not by ancestry but by the power of an indestructible life, as *Psalm 110* declares. The former regulation was set aside because it was weak and could make nothing perfect, and a better hope has been introduced, through which believers draw near to God. Because God confirmed Jesus’ priesthood with an oath, He is the guarantee of a better covenant. Unlike the many priests who died, Jesus lives forever, so He is able to save completely those who come to God through Him, since He always lives to intercede for them. He is the high priest we need: holy, blameless, pure, exalted above the heavens, who offered Himself once for all.

## Chapter Background and Story

Melchizedek appears only twice in the Old Testament. In *Genesis 14:17–20*, after Abraham rescued his nephew Lot by defeating a coalition of kings, Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, came out with bread and wine, blessed Abraham, and received a tenth of the plunder. Then he disappears from the story. Centuries later, in *Psalm 110:4*, God declares to David’s Lord, the Messiah, “You are a priest forever, after the order of Melchizedek.”

These two brief passages become the foundation of one of the most profound arguments in the New Testament. The author of Hebrews wants to show that Jesus is a true high priest, even though He was not descended from Aaron or from the tribe of Levi. *Psalm 110* shows that God always intended a different kind of priesthood: one that combined kingship and priesthood, that was based on God’s oath rather than ancestry, and that would last forever.

This chapter can feel complex to modern readers, but its message is simple and powerful: Jesus is a better high priest than any who came before, and because He lives forever, He can save completely all who come to God through Him.

### Who Was Melchizedek? (*7:1–3*)

The description of Melchizedek is studied below.

### Greater Than Abraham and Levi (*7:4–10*)

“*Now consider how great this man was, to whom even Abraham the patriarch gave a tenth out of the best plunder*” (*v. 4*). Abraham was the revered founder of Israel. Yet he gave a tenth to Melchizedek, acknowledging Melchizedek’s greater position.

“*They indeed of the sons of Levi who receive the priest’s office have a commandment to take tithes from the people according to the law, that is, of their brothers, though these have come out of the body of Abraham*” (*v. 5*), “*but he whose genealogy is not counted from them has accepted tithes from Abraham, and has blessed him who has the promises*” (*v. 6*). Under the Law, the Levitical priests received tithes from their fellow Israelites. But Melchizedek, who was not a Levite, received tithes from Abraham himself.

“*But without any dispute the lesser is blessed by the greater*” (*v. 7*). In the ancient world, the one who gives a blessing has greater standing than the one who receives it. Melchizedek blessed Abraham, showing his superiority.

“*Here people who die receive tithes, but there one receives tithes of whom it is testified that he lives*” (*v. 8*). The Levitical priests were mortal. Melchizedek, because Scripture records no death for him, is presented as one who “lives,” pointing to the eternal priesthood of Christ.

“*We can say that through Abraham even Levi, who receives tithes, has paid tithes*” (*v. 9*), “*for he was yet in the body of his father when Melchizedek met him*” (*v. 10*). The author uses a way of thinking common in the ancient world: descendants were considered present in their ancestor. In a sense, Levi, the ancestor of the priests, paid tithes to Melchizedek through Abraham. So Melchizedek’s priesthood is greater than Levi’s. The author signals that this is a figure of speech: “We can say.”

### A Change in the Priesthood (*7:11–19*)

“*Now if perfection was through the Levitical priesthood (for under it the people have received the law), what further need was there for another priest to arise after the order of Melchizedek, and not be called after the order of Aaron?*” (*v. 11*) If the Levitical priesthood could have brought people into complete relationship with God, why would God, through David, speak of a new priest of a different order? The promise of a new priest shows that the old one was not final.

“*For the priesthood being changed, there is of necessity a change made also in the law*” (*v. 12*). The priesthood and the Law were tied together. A new priesthood means a new covenant arrangement. Chapter 8 will develop this.

“*For he of whom these things are said belongs to another tribe, from which no one has officiated at the altar*” (*v. 13*). “*For it is evident that our Lord has sprung out of Judah, about which tribe Moses spoke nothing concerning priesthood*” (*v. 14*). Jesus descended from Judah, the royal tribe of David (*Matthew 1:1–3*; *Revelation 5:5*), not from Levi. Under the Law, He could not have been a priest. His priesthood rests on a different basis.

“*This is yet more abundantly evident, if after the likeness of Melchizedek there arises another priest*” (*v. 15*), “*who has been made, not after the law of a fleshly commandment, but after the power of an endless life*” (*v. 16*); “*for it is testified, “You are a priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek.”*” (*v. 17*) Levitical priests became priests because of a legal requirement about physical descent. Jesus became a priest through “the power of an endless life,” His resurrection life that can never end. Why the old regulation was set aside is studied below.

### Confirmed by an Oath (*7:20–22*)

“*Inasmuch as he was not made priest without the taking of an oath*” (*v. 20*) “*(for they indeed have been made priests without an oath), but he with an oath by him that says of him, “The Lord swore and will not change his mind, ‘You are a priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek.’”*” (*v. 21*) The Levitical priests were appointed without an oath. But God swore an oath when He appointed the Messiah as priest. As *Hebrews 6:17–18* explained, God’s oath makes His purpose unchangeable.

“*By so much, Jesus has become the guarantee of a better covenant*” (*v. 22*). A “guarantee” is a pledge or surety, one who stands behind a promise to ensure it is kept. Jesus guarantees the new covenant. This is the first mention of the “better covenant,” which chapter 8 will explain.

### A Priest Who Lives Forever (*7:23–28*)

Jesus’ eternal priesthood and His perfect character are studied below. “*For the law appoints men as high priests who have weakness, but the word of the oath, which came after the law, appoints a Son forever who has been perfected*” (*v. 28*). The contrast is complete. The Law appointed weak, mortal, sinful men. God’s oath, given after the Law through David, appointed the Son, perfect and eternal.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Hebrews 7:1–3* — Melchizedek, King of Righteousness and Peace

> *“For this Melchizedek, king of Salem, priest of God Most High, who met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him, to whom also Abraham divided a tenth part of all (being first, by interpretation, ‘king of righteousness’, and then also ‘king of Salem’, which means ‘king of peace’, without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but made like the Son of God), remains a priest continually.”*
>
> — *Hebrews 7:1–3* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The author summarizes the story from *Genesis 14*. Melchizedek was “king of Salem, priest of God Most High.” Salem is generally identified with Jerusalem (*Psalm 76:2*). Remarkably, Melchizedek was both a king and a priest, a combination not permitted in Israel, where kings came from Judah and priests from Levi.

He “met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him.” And Abraham gave him “a tenth part of all,” a tithe.

Verse 2 explains the meaning of his name and title. “Melchizedek” means “king of righteousness.” “King of Salem” means “king of peace,” since “Salem” is related to the Hebrew word *shalom*. Righteousness and peace come together in him.

Verse 3: “without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life.” In Genesis, Melchizedek appears suddenly, with no mention of his parents, ancestors, birth, or death. This was unusual, especially for a priest, since priests in Israel had to prove their descent from Aaron.

“But made like the Son of God, remains a priest continually.” Because of the silence of Scripture about his origins and death, Melchizedek serves as a picture, a foreshadowing, of the Son of God, whose priesthood truly has no beginning or end.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Interpreters have understood Melchizedek in different ways. Most understand him to have been a real human king and priest, and believe the author is drawing a lesson from what Scripture says and does not say about him. The silence about his genealogy and death makes him a fitting picture of Christ’s eternal priesthood. Note that the author says Melchizedek was “made like the Son of God,” not that the Son was made like Melchizedek: Christ is the reality, and Melchizedek is the picture. Some interpreters, especially in earlier centuries, have suggested that Melchizedek was an appearance of the pre-incarnate Christ, though most do not hold this view. Either way, he points to Jesus.

Melchizedek’s names are significant. Jesus is the true King of righteousness and King of peace. Isaiah prophesied that the Messiah would be called “Prince of Peace” and would reign in justice and righteousness (*Isaiah 9:6–7*). In Christ, righteousness and peace meet. *Psalm 85:10* says, “*Righteousness and peace have kissed each other*” (*Psalm 85:10*).

The bread and wine Melchizedek brought (*Genesis 14:18*) have reminded many Christians of the Lord’s Supper, though Hebrews does not mention this connection.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Melchizedek’s story shows that God was preparing for Christ long before He came. Even in an obscure episode in Genesis, God placed a picture of His Son. Believers can read the Old Testament with expectation, looking for the ways it points to Christ.

The names “king of righteousness” and “king of peace” remind believers that in Christ they have both. He makes them righteous before God and brings them peace with God (*Romans 5:1*). They can rest in His reign.

Finally, Melchizedek’s eternal priesthood, pictured in the silence of Scripture, points to the security believers have in Christ, whose priesthood will never end.

### *Hebrews 7:18–19* — A Better Hope

> *“For there is an annulling of a foregoing commandment because of its weakness and uselessness (for the law made nothing perfect), and a bringing in of a better hope, through which we draw near to God.”*
>
> — *Hebrews 7:18–19* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“For there is an annulling of a foregoing commandment because of its weakness and uselessness.” The “foregoing commandment” is the regulation in the Law about the Levitical priesthood. It has been set aside, not because it was evil, but because it was “weak” and “useless” for bringing people fully to God.

Verse 19: “(for the law made nothing perfect).” The Law could not bring people to complete fellowship with God. It could reveal sin, regulate worship, and point to Christ, but it could not cleanse the conscience or make people truly right with God (*Hebrews 10:1–4*).

“And a bringing in of a better hope, through which we draw near to God.” Something better has come: a hope based on Christ’s priesthood. Through Him, believers “draw near to God.” This was the very thing the old system could not fully accomplish.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The phrase “draw near to God” is central to Hebrews. Under the old covenant, access to God was limited. The people stood outside; priests entered the Holy Place; only the high priest entered the Most Holy Place, once a year. Now, through Christ, all believers can draw near (*Hebrews 4:16*; *10:19–22*).

The “weakness” of the Law is not a criticism of God, who gave it. The Law did exactly what God intended: it revealed His holiness, exposed sin, and prepared for Christ. Paul says the Law was weak “*through the flesh*” (*Romans 8:3*), because sinful humans could not keep it. It was a tutor leading to Christ (*Galatians 3:24*).

The “better hope” is one of many “better” things in Hebrews: a better covenant (*7:22*), better promises (*8:6*), better sacrifices (*9:23*), a better possession (*10:34*), a better country (*11:16*), and a better resurrection (*11:35*). In every case, Christ brings what the old covenant could only anticipate.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers do not need to rely on religious rituals or rules to draw near to God. Through Christ, they can come to Him directly and confidently.

This passage also helps believers appreciate the Old Testament without being bound by its regulations. The Law served a good purpose, and its moral principles reflect God’s character, but its priestly system has been fulfilled in Christ.

Finally, the “better hope” invites believers to live with confidence. Their hope is not in their own ability to keep rules, but in Christ, who has opened the way to God.

### *Hebrews 7:24–25* — Able to Save Completely

> *“But he, because he lives forever, has his priesthood unchangeable. Therefore he is also able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, seeing that he lives forever to make intercession for them.”*
>
> — *Hebrews 7:24–25* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Verse 23 noted that there were many Levitical priests because death kept each one from continuing. Over the centuries, priests died and were replaced.

Verse 24: “But he, because he lives forever, has his priesthood unchangeable.” Jesus will never die again. His priesthood is permanent. He will never be replaced.

Verse 25: “Therefore he is also able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him.” “To the uttermost” can mean completely, fully, or forever. Jesus saves entirely: every part of a person, for all time. There is no limit to His saving power.

“Those who draw near to God through him.” Salvation comes to those who approach God through Jesus.

“Seeing that he lives forever to make intercession for them.” Jesus continually prays for His people. He stands before the Father on their behalf, representing them, pleading for them, and applying the benefits of His sacrifice to them.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This is one of the most comforting verses in Scripture. Jesus’ intercession is ongoing. He did not save His people once and then leave them. He continues to work on their behalf. *Romans 8:34* says that Christ Jesus, who died and was raised, is at the right hand of God and is interceding for us. First *John 2:1* says that if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.

Jesus’ intercession was foreshadowed in His earthly ministry. He prayed for Peter that his faith would not fail (*Luke 22:31–32*). He prayed for His disciples and for all who would believe through them (*John 17:9*, 20). That same intercession continues now.

“To the uttermost” means that no sin is too great, no situation too hopeless, no person too far gone. Jesus is able to save completely. And because He lives forever, His saving work will never end.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers who feel weak, tempted, or overwhelmed can take comfort that Jesus is praying for them right now. They are not alone in their struggles.

This verse also offers hope to anyone who feels beyond saving. Jesus is able to save “to the uttermost.” There is no limit to His power or His grace.

Finally, believers can rest in the permanence of Christ’s priesthood. Their salvation does not depend on a human priest who might fail or die. It rests on the living Christ, who never changes.

### *Hebrews 7:26–27* — Holy, Blameless, and Offered Once for All

> *“For such a high priest was fitting for us: holy, guiltless, undefiled, separated from sinners, and made higher than the heavens; who doesn’t need, like those high priests, to offer up sacrifices daily, first for his own sins, and then for the sins of the people. For he did this once for all, when he offered up himself.”*
>
> — *Hebrews 7:26–27* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“For such a high priest was fitting for us.” Jesus is exactly the high priest we need. The author describes Him with five phrases.

“Holy”: devoted to God, pure in character. “Guiltless”: innocent, without evil or deceit. “Undefiled”: morally pure, untouched by sin. “Separated from sinners”: though He lived among sinners and befriended them, He was different from them in His sinlessness, and now He is exalted above them. “Made higher than the heavens”: exalted to the highest place, at God’s right hand.

Verse 27: “who doesn’t need, like those high priests, to offer up sacrifices daily, first for his own sins, and then for the sins of the people.” Human high priests had to offer sacrifices repeatedly, and they had to offer for their own sins first. Jesus had no sins of His own.

“For he did this once for all, when he offered up himself.” Jesus’ sacrifice was “once for all,” complete and never to be repeated. And remarkably, He was both the priest and the sacrifice. He offered Himself.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses introduce a major theme that chapters 9 and 10 will develop: the sufficiency of Christ’s single sacrifice. Under the old covenant, sacrifices had to be repeated endlessly, because they could not truly take away sin (*Hebrews 10:1–4*, 11). Christ’s sacrifice was different. It was offered once, and it was enough.

The fact that Jesus is both priest and sacrifice is unique. In the old system, the priest offered an animal. Jesus offered His own life. He is the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world (*John 1:29*), and He is the High Priest who offers that Lamb.

Jesus’ sinlessness is essential. A sinful priest would need a sacrifice for himself. A sinful sacrifice would be unacceptable. Jesus, being holy and blameless, is both the perfect priest and the perfect offering (*1 Peter 1:18–19*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can rest in the finished work of Christ. His sacrifice was once for all. Nothing needs to be added. They do not need to earn God’s forgiveness through repeated efforts or rituals.

This passage also invites worship. Jesus is holy, blameless, and exalted, and He offered Himself for sinners. His love and sacrifice deserve wholehearted praise.

Finally, believers can find confidence in approaching God. Their high priest is perfect, and His sacrifice is complete. They can draw near to God with assurance.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Hebrews 7* shows that Jesus is a better high priest than any who came before. Through the mysterious figure of Melchizedek, king of righteousness and king of peace, God foreshadowed a priest who would combine kingship and priesthood, whose priesthood would rest not on ancestry but on God’s oath, and who would remain a priest forever. Jesus fulfills this picture perfectly.

The chapter explains that the Levitical priesthood, though given by God, could not bring perfection. It was weak because it depended on mortal, sinful men and could not fully cleanse or bring people near to God. In Christ, a better hope has been introduced, through which believers can draw near to God. Jesus guarantees a better covenant.

At the heart of the chapter is a glorious truth: because Jesus lives forever, He is able to save completely those who come to God through Him, and He always lives to intercede for them. Believers are never alone. Their high priest is praying for them right now. No sin is too great and no situation too hopeless for His saving power.

Finally, Jesus is exactly the high priest we need: holy, blameless, pure, separated from sinners, and exalted above the heavens. Unlike the old priests, He did not need to offer sacrifices repeatedly or for His own sins. He offered Himself once for all. Believers can rest in His finished work, draw near to God with confidence, and worship the King of righteousness and peace who is their eternal priest.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, You are the true King of righteousness and King of peace, a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek. Thank You that Your priesthood rests on the power of an indestructible life and on the Father’s unchangeable oath. Thank You for bringing a better hope, through which I can draw near to God. Thank You that You are the guarantee of a better covenant. I praise You that You are able to save completely those who come to God through You, and that You always live to intercede for me. When I am weak, remind me that You are praying for me. Thank You that You are holy, blameless, and pure, and that You offered Yourself once for all as the perfect sacrifice. Help me to rest in Your finished work and to draw near to God with confidence. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
