Hebrews · Chapter 8 of 13

# Hebrews — Chapter 8

Chapter Theme: The Mediator of a Better Covenant

[Read Hebrews 8 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/HEB08.htm)

Main Teaching

The main point of all that has been said is this: believers have a high priest who has taken His seat at the right hand of God’s throne in heaven, where He serves in the true sanctuary set up by the Lord, not by human hands. Earthly priests served in a sanctuary that was only a copy and shadow of the heavenly one, as God showed when He told Moses to build the tabernacle according to the pattern shown on the mountain. Jesus’ ministry is far superior, because He mediates a better covenant founded on better promises. If the first covenant had been without fault, there would have been no need for a second. Quoting *Jeremiah 31*, the author shows that God Himself promised a new covenant, different from the one made at the exodus, in which He would put His laws in His people’s minds and write them on their hearts, be their God, make Himself known to all of them from the least to the greatest, and forgive their sins and remember them no more. By calling this covenant “new,” God made the first one obsolete, and what is obsolete is ready to disappear.

## Chapter Background and Story

The author begins this chapter by summarizing his argument: “the main point is this.” Jesus is a high priest, and He serves not on earth but in heaven. The rest of the chapter develops two connected ideas: Jesus serves in a better sanctuary, and He mediates a better covenant.

A covenant is a binding relationship established by God with His people, with promises and commitments. The “first covenant” in Hebrews is the covenant God made with Israel at Mount Sinai after the exodus, often called the Mosaic or old covenant (*Exodus 19–24*). It included the Law, the priesthood, the tabernacle, and the sacrifices. It was a gracious gift of God, but Israel repeatedly broke it.

Centuries later, during the dark days before the Babylonian exile, God spoke through the prophet Jeremiah. Though Israel had broken the covenant, God promised a new covenant that would succeed where the old had failed, because God Himself would change His people’s hearts (*Jeremiah 31:31–34*). Jesus announced at the Last Supper that this new covenant was established in His blood (*Luke 22:20*). *Hebrews 8* contains the longest Old Testament quotation in the New Testament, and it is this promise.

### The Main Point (*8:1–2*)

The author’s summary is studied below.

### A Better Ministry (*8:3–6*)

“*For every high priest is appointed to offer both gifts and sacrifices. Therefore it is necessary that this high priest also have something to offer*” (*v. 3*). A priest must offer something. Jesus’ offering, as the author has already said and will explain, is Himself (*Hebrews 7:27*).

“*For if he were on earth, he would not be a priest at all, seeing there are priests who offer the gifts according to the law*” (*v. 4*). Jesus was from the tribe of Judah, so under the Law He could not serve as a priest in the earthly temple (*Hebrews 7:13–14*). His priesthood belongs to a different realm. The heavenly sanctuary and the better covenant are studied below.

### The Promise of a New Covenant (*8:7–13*)

“*For if that first covenant had been faultless, then no place would have been sought for a second*” (*v. 7*). The first covenant was not evil, but it was inadequate to accomplish everything God intended, because it depended on a sinful people who could not keep it.

“*For finding fault with them, he said, “Behold, the days are coming”, says the Lord, “that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah*” (*v. 8*). Notice the words “with them.” The fault was not mainly in the covenant itself but in the people who broke it. God promised a new covenant to the whole of His people, both the northern kingdom (Israel) and the southern kingdom (Judah).

“*not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers in the day that I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt; for they didn’t continue in my covenant, and I disregarded them,” says the Lord*” (*v. 9*). The new covenant would be different from the Sinai covenant, which Israel did not keep. The image of God taking Israel “by the hand” is tender, like a father leading a child. Yet the people turned away. The content of the new covenant is studied below.

“*In that he says, “A new covenant”, he has made the first obsolete. But that which is becoming obsolete and grows aged is near to vanishing away*” (*v. 13*). By promising a new covenant, God showed that the old one was temporary. If Hebrews was written before A.D. 70, the author may have been anticipating the destruction of the temple, which ended the sacrificial system. The old covenant’s role as a system of priesthood and sacrifice was fulfilled and passing away, because its purpose was complete in Christ.

It is important to read this carefully. The author is not saying that God has rejected the Jewish people. The new covenant was promised “with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah,” and Jesus and His first followers were Jewish. Gentiles are welcomed into this covenant through Christ (*Ephesians 2:11–13*). Christians understand the relationship between Israel and the church in different ways, but Paul insists that God has not rejected His people (*Romans 11:1–2*, 29). What has become obsolete is the old covenant’s system of priesthood and sacrifice as the way of relating to God, not God’s love for Israel.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Hebrews 8:1–2* — The Main Point

> *“Now in the things which we are saying, the main point is this: we have such a high priest, who sat down on the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in the heavens, a servant of the sanctuary and of the true tabernacle which the Lord pitched, not man.”*
>
> — *Hebrews 8:1–2* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“Now in the things which we are saying, the main point is this.” The author pauses to summarize. Everything he has said about Melchizedek, the priesthood, and the oath comes down to one central truth.

“We have such a high priest.” Believers have a high priest, the one the author has described: eternal, sinless, sympathetic, able to save completely.

“Who sat down on the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in the heavens.” He has taken His seat in the place of supreme honor and authority, beside God the Father. Sitting down shows that His sacrificial work is finished (*Hebrews 10:11–12*). “The Majesty” is a reverent way of referring to God.

Verse 2: “a servant of the sanctuary and of the true tabernacle which the Lord pitched, not man.” Jesus ministers in the heavenly sanctuary, the true tabernacle, which God Himself set up. The earthly tabernacle was built by human hands according to God’s instructions. The heavenly one is the reality it pictured.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The heart of Hebrews is not a doctrine but a person: Jesus, our high priest at God’s right hand. Everything else serves this main point. When believers are weary, confused, or tempted to drift, the author directs them to this central truth.

Jesus is both seated and serving. He is seated because His sacrifice is complete. He is serving because He continues to minister on behalf of His people, interceding for them (*Hebrews 7:25*) and applying the benefits of His sacrifice to them.

“The true tabernacle” does not mean the earthly one was false. “True” here means real, genuine, the ultimate reality. The earthly tabernacle was a true copy; the heavenly one is the original. Jesus serves in the very presence of God.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

When the Christian life feels complicated, believers can return to the main point: they have a high priest at God’s right hand. Everything rests on Him.

This truth brings confidence. Believers’ access to God does not depend on an earthly building, ritual, or human priest. Jesus represents them in God’s very presence.

Finally, the image of Jesus seated at God’s right hand invites rest. His work is finished. Believers do not need to complete it; they can trust it.

### *Hebrews 8:5* — A Copy and Shadow of Heavenly Things

> *“who serve a copy and shadow of the heavenly things, even as Moses was warned by God when he was about to make the tabernacle, for he said, ‘See, you shall make everything according to the pattern that was shown to you on the mountain.’”*
>
> — *Hebrews 8:5* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The earthly priests “serve a copy and shadow of the heavenly things.” The tabernacle and its worship were a copy, a sketch or model, of heavenly realities. And they were a shadow, an outline that indicates something real but is not the real thing itself.

“Even as Moses was warned by God when he was about to make the tabernacle.” When God gave Moses instructions for the tabernacle, He told him to follow a specific design.

“For he said, ‘See, you shall make everything according to the pattern that was shown to you on the mountain.’” This quotation comes from *Exodus 25:40*. God showed Moses a pattern on Mount Sinai, and the tabernacle was built according to it. The pattern pointed to heavenly reality.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that the Old Testament system of worship was not an end in itself. It was designed by God to point beyond itself. Every detail, the altar, the lampstand, the table of bread, the curtain, the ark, the sacrifices, was a picture of spiritual truths that would be fulfilled in Christ.

*Colossians 2:17* uses similar language: the festivals and Sabbaths were “a shadow of the things to come; but the body is Christ’s.” The shadow is real and meaningful, but it gives way to the substance when the substance arrives.

This understanding helps believers read the Old Testament with appreciation. The tabernacle and sacrifices are not irrelevant. They teach about God’s holiness, the seriousness of sin, the need for atonement, and the way God provides access to Himself. And they all point to Jesus.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can read the Old Testament descriptions of the tabernacle and sacrifices not as tedious details but as rich pictures of Christ. Each element teaches something about what Jesus has done.

This verse also reminds believers that physical buildings, rituals, and religious practices are not the ultimate reality. Churches and worship practices can be valuable, but their purpose is to point to God, not to replace Him.

Finally, believers can live with their eyes on heavenly realities. The things of this world are, in a sense, shadows. What is lasting is found in God’s presence, where Christ is.

### *Hebrews 8:6* — A Better Covenant on Better Promises

> *“But now he has obtained a more excellent ministry, by as much as he is also the mediator of a better covenant, which on better promises has been given as law.”*
>
> — *Hebrews 8:6* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“But now he has obtained a more excellent ministry.” Jesus’ priestly work is superior to that of the earthly priests.

“By as much as he is also the mediator of a better covenant.” A mediator brings two parties together and establishes an agreement between them. Moses was the mediator of the old covenant (*Galatians 3:19*). Jesus is the mediator of the new covenant, which is “better.”

“Which on better promises has been given as law.” The new covenant is established on better promises. These promises are listed in verses 10–12: an inner transformation of the heart, a personal relationship with God, a universal knowledge of God, and complete forgiveness of sins.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Why is the new covenant better? Not because the old covenant was bad, but because the new covenant accomplishes what the old could only point toward. The old covenant gave God’s Law on tablets of stone; the new covenant writes it on the heart. The old covenant had repeated sacrifices that could not fully remove sin; the new covenant brings a once-for-all sacrifice that cleanses completely. The old covenant had a human mediator; the new has the Son of God.

Jesus is the mediator of this covenant in a unique way. He not only announces it; He establishes it through His own blood (*Hebrews 9:15*; *Luke 22:20*). And He guarantees it (*Hebrews 7:22*). The new covenant is secure because it rests on Him.

The word “better” is a key word in Hebrews. Every comparison points to Christ as the fulfillment of what came before. Believers have something better than the greatest privileges of the old covenant.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can appreciate the privileges they have under the new covenant: direct access to God, the Spirit’s work in their hearts, and complete forgiveness. These are not small blessings but the fulfillment of centuries of hope.

This verse also reminds believers that their relationship with God rests on Jesus, the mediator. Their confidence is not in their own faithfulness but in His.

Finally, the “better promises” invite trust. God’s promises in the new covenant are sure, because they rest on Christ’s finished work. Believers can build their lives on them.

### *Hebrews 8:10–12* — Written on the Heart

> *“‘For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days,’ says the Lord: ‘I will put my laws into their mind; I will also write them on their heart. I will be their God, and they will be my people. They will not teach every man his fellow citizen and every man his brother, saying, “Know the Lord,” for all will know me, from their least to their greatest. For I will be merciful to their unrighteousness. I will remember their sins and lawless deeds no more.’”*
>
> — *Hebrews 8:10–12* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

These verses describe the content of the new covenant promised in *Jeremiah 31:33–34*. There are four great promises.

First, inner transformation. “I will put my laws into their mind; I will also write them on their heart.” Under the old covenant, the Law was written on stone tablets, outside the people. Under the new covenant, God writes His law inside, on the heart. People do not merely know what God commands; they are changed so that they desire to do His will. This is the work of the Holy Spirit (*Ezekiel 36:26–27*; *2 Corinthians 3:3*).

Second, a personal relationship. “I will be their God, and they will be my people.” This was always God’s goal (*Exodus 6:7*; *Leviticus 26:12*). In the new covenant, it is fully realized.

Third, universal knowledge of God. “They will not teach every man his fellow citizen and every man his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord,’ for all will know me, from their least to their greatest.” Under the old covenant, knowledge of God was often mediated through priests and prophets. Under the new covenant, every member of God’s people knows Him personally, regardless of status or age. This does not mean teachers are no longer needed (*Hebrews 5:12*), but that every believer has a direct, personal relationship with God.

Fourth, complete forgiveness. “For I will be merciful to their unrighteousness. I will remember their sins and lawless deeds no more.” This is the foundation of the other promises. God forgives completely and permanently. When He says He will “*remember their sins and lawless deeds no more*” (*v. 12*), it does not mean He forgets in the sense of losing information, but that He will never hold those sins against His people again.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These promises describe the heart of the gospel. God does not simply give people better rules; He gives them new hearts. He does not merely forgive some sins temporarily; He forgives all sins permanently. He does not keep His people at a distance; He makes Himself known to each one.

The promise of forgiveness is placed last in the list, but it is the foundation of everything. The word “for” at the beginning of verse 12 shows that the inner transformation and the personal knowledge of God are possible because God has forgiven sins. Chapters 9 and 10 will explain how this forgiveness is secured through Christ’s sacrifice.

These promises were made to Israel, and they have begun to be fulfilled through Jesus, the Messiah of Israel. Through Him, Gentiles also share in these blessings (*Romans 11:17*; *Ephesians 3:6*). Many Christians believe the promises also look forward to a future fulfillment for the people of Israel (*Romans 11:25–27*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can thank God that their obedience is not merely an external effort to follow rules. God has written His law on their hearts, giving them new desires to love and obey Him. When they struggle, they can ask the Spirit to strengthen what He has begun in them.

The promise that “all will know me” assures every believer, no matter how young, uneducated, or new to the faith, that they can know God personally. They do not need to go through a special class of people to have a relationship with Him.

Finally, the promise “I will remember their sins and lawless deeds no more” brings deep peace. Believers who are haunted by past sins can rest in God’s complete forgiveness. If God does not hold their sins against them, they can stop holding those sins against themselves.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Hebrews 8* summarizes the main point of the letter’s teaching about Christ: believers have a high priest who has sat down at the right hand of God’s throne in heaven and serves in the true sanctuary that the Lord Himself set up. When the Christian life feels complicated or discouraging, believers can return to this central truth. Everything rests on Jesus, their high priest in God’s presence.

The chapter explains that the earthly tabernacle and its worship were a copy and shadow of heavenly realities. They were good and meaningful, designed by God to point to Christ. Believers can read the Old Testament with fresh eyes, seeing how its details reveal the work of Jesus.

Jesus is the mediator of a better covenant, established on better promises. God foretold this new covenant through Jeremiah, promising to write His laws on His people’s hearts, to be their God, to make Himself known to all of them, and to forgive their sins and remember them no more. These promises describe the heart of the gospel: a new heart, a personal relationship with God, and complete forgiveness.

Believers can live in the joy and confidence of these promises. They can rely on the Spirit’s work within them, approach God personally, and rest in the assurance that their sins are forgiven and forgotten. The old covenant system has given way to the new, not because God’s love for Israel has ended, but because His promises have been fulfilled in Jesus, the Messiah of Israel and the Savior of the world.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, You are my high priest, seated at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in heaven. Thank You that You serve in the true sanctuary, in the very presence of God, on my behalf. Thank You for the tabernacle and sacrifices of the old covenant, which pointed to You, and for fulfilling all they foreshadowed. Thank You for being the mediator of a better covenant, established on better promises. Write Your law on my heart, and give me a desire to love and obey You. Thank You that You are my God and I am Yours, and that I can know You personally. Thank You that You have forgiven my sins and will remember them no more. Help me to live in the freedom and joy of that forgiveness. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Hebrews · Chapter 9 of 13

# Hebrews — Chapter 9

Chapter Theme: The Blood of Christ and the Once-for-All Sacrifice

[Read Hebrews 9 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/HEB09.htm)

Main Teaching

The first covenant had regulations for worship and an earthly sanctuary, with the Holy Place and, behind the second curtain, the Most Holy Place containing the ark of the covenant. Priests served daily in the outer room, but only the high priest entered the inner room, once a year, with blood offered for himself and for the people’s sins. The Holy Spirit showed by this that the way into God’s presence had not yet been opened, and that those gifts and sacrifices could not perfect the conscience of the worshiper. But Christ came as high priest of the good things now arrived, entering the greater, perfect tabernacle not made with hands, not with the blood of goats and calves but with His own blood, once for all, obtaining eternal redemption. If animal sacrifices could cleanse outwardly, how much more will Christ’s blood, offered through the eternal Spirit, cleanse our consciences from dead works so we may serve the living God. He is the mediator of a new covenant, ratified by His death, since without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness. Christ entered heaven itself to appear for us before God, offering Himself once at the culmination of the ages to remove sin, and just as people die once and then face judgment, Christ was offered once to bear the sins of many and will appear a second time to bring salvation to those who eagerly wait for Him.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Hebrews 9* continues the comparison between the old covenant and the new, focusing on the place of worship and the sacrifice offered there. To understand this chapter, it helps to picture the tabernacle that Israel built in the wilderness (*Exodus 25–40*).

The tabernacle was a portable tent surrounded by a courtyard. Inside the tent were two rooms. The first, the Holy Place, contained a lampstand, a table with the bread of the Presence, and the altar of incense near the curtain. The second, the Most Holy Place (or Holy of Holies), contained the ark of the covenant, a gold-covered chest holding the tablets of the Law, a jar of manna, and Aaron’s staff that had budded. Its lid, called the mercy seat or atonement cover, was guarded by two golden cherubim. God’s presence was understood to dwell above the mercy seat.

A thick curtain separated the two rooms. Priests entered the Holy Place daily for their duties. But only the high priest could enter the Most Holy Place, and only once a year, on the Day of Atonement (*Leviticus 16*). He brought the blood of a sacrificed bull for his own sins and the blood of a goat for the sins of the people, and sprinkled it on and before the mercy seat.

The author of Hebrews sees in this arrangement a powerful lesson. The system itself showed that access to God was limited and that sin had not yet been fully dealt with. Christ’s sacrifice changed everything.

### The Earthly Sanctuary (*9:1–5*)

“*Now indeed even the first covenant had ordinances of divine service and an earthly sanctuary*” (*v. 1*). The old covenant had a God-given system of worship. “*For a tabernacle was prepared. In the first part were the lamp stand, the table, and the show bread, which is called the Holy Place*” (*v. 2*). “*After the second veil was the tabernacle which is called the Holy of Holies*” (*v. 3*), “*having a golden altar of incense and the ark of the covenant overlaid on all sides with gold, in which was a golden pot holding the manna, Aaron’s rod that budded, and the tablets of the covenant*” (*v. 4*). The golden altar of incense actually stood just in front of the curtain in the Holy Place (*Exodus 30:6*), but it was closely connected with the Most Holy Place, especially on the Day of Atonement, when the high priest took incense from it into the inner room (*Leviticus 16:12–13*). The author may be describing its function rather than its exact location; some translations render the word as “censer.” “*and above it cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy seat, of which things we can’t speak now in detail*” (*v. 5*). The author does not want to explain every detail; his focus is on the main point.

### Limited Access (*9:6–10*)

“*Now these things having been thus prepared, the priests go in continually into the first tabernacle, accomplishing the services*” (*v. 6*), “*but into the second the high priest alone, once in the year, not without blood, which he offers for himself and for the errors of the people*” (*v. 7*). Access to God’s presence was severely restricted: one man, one day a year, and always with blood.

“*The Holy Spirit is indicating this, that the way into the Holy Place wasn’t yet revealed while the first tabernacle was still standing*” (*v. 8*). The very structure of the tabernacle taught a lesson. As long as the curtain stood and the old system continued, the way into God’s presence was not yet open to all.

“*This is a symbol of the present age, where gifts and sacrifices are offered that are incapable, concerning the conscience, of making the worshiper perfect*” (*v. 9*), “*being only (with foods and drinks and various washings) fleshly ordinances, imposed until a time of reformation*” (*v. 10*). The old sacrifices dealt with outward, ritual purity, but they could not cleanse the conscience, the inner sense of guilt before God. They were temporary, “until a time of reformation,” the time when Christ would set things right.

### Christ’s Better Sacrifice (*9:11–14*)

Christ’s entrance into the true sanctuary and the power of His blood are studied below.

### The Mediator of a New Covenant (*9:15–22*)

“*For this reason he is the mediator of a new covenant, since a death has occurred for the redemption of the transgressions that were under the first covenant, that those who have been called may receive the promise of the eternal inheritance*” (*v. 15*). Christ’s death redeems people from sins committed under the first covenant, which the animal sacrifices could not fully remove. As a result, God’s people receive their eternal inheritance.

“*For where a last will and testament is, there must of necessity be the death of him who made it*” (*v. 16*). “*For a will is in force where there has been death, for it is never in force while he who made it lives*” (*v. 17*). The Greek word for “covenant” can also mean “will” or “testament.” The author makes a play on words: a will takes effect only after the death of the one who made it. In the same way, the new covenant took effect through Christ’s death.

“*Therefore even the first covenant has not been dedicated without blood*” (*v. 18*). “*For when every commandment had been spoken by Moses to all the people according to the law, he took the blood of the calves and the goats, with water and scarlet wool and hyssop, and sprinkled both the book itself and all the people*” (*v. 19*), “*saying, “This is the blood of the covenant which God has commanded you.”*” (*v. 20*) At Mount Sinai, Moses ratified the covenant with sacrificial blood (*Exodus 24:3–8*). Jesus echoed these words at the Last Supper: “*This is my blood of the new covenant*” (*Mark 14:24*). “*He sprinkled the tabernacle and all the vessels of the ministry in the same way with the blood*” (*v. 21*). The principle that underlies all of this is studied below.

### Once for All (*9:23–28*)

“*It was necessary therefore that the copies of the things in the heavens should be cleansed with these, but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these*” (*v. 23*). The earthly tabernacle was cleansed with animal blood. The heavenly realities required a better sacrifice. The idea of “cleansing” heavenly things is mysterious; it may mean that Christ’s sacrifice opened the way into God’s presence for sinners, removing every barrier.

“*For Christ hasn’t entered into holy places made with hands, which are representations of the true, but into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God for us*” (*v. 24*). Christ did not enter a copy but the reality: heaven itself. And He is there “for us,” representing His people before God.

“*nor yet that he should offer himself often, as the high priest enters into the holy place year by year with blood not his own*” (*v. 25*), “*or else he must have suffered often since the foundation of the world. But now once at the end of the ages, he has been revealed to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself*” (*v. 26*). The high priest had to repeat the sacrifice every year. If Christ’s sacrifice worked the same way, He would have had to suffer repeatedly throughout history. But His sacrifice was once for all, at the climax of history, and it removes sin completely. The final verses are studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Hebrews 9:11–12* — Eternal Redemption Through His Own Blood

> *“But Christ having come as a high priest of the coming good things, through the greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made with hands, that is to say, not of this creation, nor yet through the blood of goats and calves, but through his own blood, entered in once for all into the Holy Place, having obtained eternal redemption.”*
>
> — *Hebrews 9:11–12* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“But Christ having come as a high priest of the coming good things.” Christ is the high priest of the “good things” that the old covenant only anticipated. Some manuscripts read “the good things that have come,” emphasizing that these blessings are already present.

“Through the greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made with hands, that is to say, not of this creation.” Christ ministers in a sanctuary greater than the earthly tabernacle, not built by human hands or belonging to this created world. This is the heavenly reality, God’s own presence.

Verse 12: “nor yet through the blood of goats and calves, but through his own blood.” The high priest entered with the blood of animals. Christ entered with His own blood, the blood of His sacrificial death.

“Entered in once for all into the Holy Place.” Not once a year, but once for all time. His entrance into God’s presence was decisive and complete.

“Having obtained eternal redemption.” “Redemption” means release by payment of a price. Christ’s death secured a redemption that is “eternal,” permanent, never needing to be repeated.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses capture the contrast between the old and new covenants. The old high priest entered an earthly sanctuary, with animal blood, every year, achieving temporary and outward cleansing. Christ entered the heavenly sanctuary, with His own blood, once for all, achieving eternal redemption.

The phrase “his own blood” emphasizes the cost of salvation. Christ did not offer something outside Himself. He gave His own life. First Peter 1:18–19 says believers were redeemed “*not with corruptible things like silver or gold*” (*1 Peter 1:18*) “*but with precious blood, as of a lamb without blemish or spot, the blood of Christ*” (*1 Peter 1:19*).

“Once for all” is one of the great themes of Hebrews (*7:27*; *9:12*, 26, 28; *10:10*). Christ’s sacrifice does not need to be repeated or supplemented. It is complete and sufficient forever.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can rest in the completeness of their redemption. It is “eternal,” not temporary or fragile. Nothing can undo what Christ has accomplished.

This truth also frees believers from trying to add to Christ’s work. They do not need to earn forgiveness through repeated efforts, rituals, or self-punishment. Christ has paid the price once for all.

Finally, the costliness of Christ’s sacrifice, His own blood, invites deep gratitude and love. Believers were bought at a great price (*1 Corinthians 6:20*), and they can live in a way that honors the One who redeemed them.

### *Hebrews 9:14* — Cleansing the Conscience

> *“how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without defect to God, cleanse your conscience from dead works to serve the living God?”*
>
> — *Hebrews 9:14* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Verse 13 sets up the comparison: “For if the blood of goats and bulls, and the ashes of a heifer sprinkling those who have been defiled, sanctify to the cleanness of the flesh.” The old sacrifices made people ritually clean, outwardly fit to take part in worship. “The ashes of a heifer” refers to a special cleansing ritual for people who had touched a dead body (*Numbers 19*).

Verse 14: “how much more will the blood of Christ.” If animal blood had some cleansing effect, how much greater is the power of Christ’s blood.

“Who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without defect to God.” Christ offered Himself willingly, empowered by the Holy Spirit. He was “without defect,” sinless, the perfect sacrifice, like the unblemished animals required by the Law (*Leviticus 22:21*).

“Cleanse your conscience from dead works to serve the living God.” Christ’s blood does what animal blood never could: it cleanses the conscience, the inner person. “Dead works” may refer to sinful deeds that lead to death, or to religious rituals that cannot give life. Either way, believers are set free from them to serve the living God.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse addresses one of the deepest human needs: a clean conscience. Many people carry guilt that no ritual, effort, or self-improvement can remove. The old sacrifices could cleanse outwardly, but they could not reach the heart. Christ’s sacrifice cleanses the conscience itself.

Notice the involvement of the whole Trinity. Christ offered Himself, through the eternal Spirit, to God the Father. Salvation is the work of Father, Son, and Spirit together.

The goal of cleansing is service. Believers are not cleansed merely to feel better but to “serve the living God.” A clean conscience frees them from paralyzing guilt and enables them to live for God with joy and freedom.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers who are burdened by guilt, even after confessing their sins, can take hold of this promise. Christ’s blood cleanses the conscience. They do not need to carry guilt that He has already removed.

This verse also invites believers to examine whether they are relying on “dead works,” religious activity or self-effort, to feel right with God. True cleansing comes only from Christ.

Finally, a cleansed conscience leads to service. Believers can ask how God is calling them to serve Him, freed from guilt and empowered by His Spirit.

### *Hebrews 9:22* — Without the Shedding of Blood

> *“According to the law, nearly everything is cleansed with blood, and apart from shedding of blood there is no remission.”*
>
> — *Hebrews 9:22* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“According to the law, nearly everything is cleansed with blood.” Under the Law, blood was used to purify the tabernacle, the priests, the people, and the objects of worship. The word “nearly” acknowledges some exceptions; for example, some things were cleansed with water or fire (*Numbers 31:22–23*), and very poor people could offer flour instead of an animal for certain sin offerings (*Leviticus 5:11–13*).

“And apart from shedding of blood there is no remission.” “Remission” means forgiveness, the release from sin’s penalty. The general principle of the Law was that forgiveness required the shedding of blood.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Why blood? In the Old Testament, blood represents life. *Leviticus 17:11* says, “*For the life of the flesh is in the blood. I have given it to you on the altar to make atonement for your souls*” (*Leviticus 17:11*). The shedding of blood means the giving of a life. Sin brings death (*Romans 6:23*), and forgiveness requires that a life be given in place of the sinner.

This principle points to the cross. The animal sacrifices were temporary and could not truly take away sin (*Hebrews 10:4*), but they taught that forgiveness is costly. Jesus fulfilled this principle by giving His own life. His blood was shed so that sins could be forgiven. At the Last Supper, He said, “*This is my blood of the new covenant, which is poured out for many for the remission of sins*” (*Matthew 26:28*).

This truth shows the seriousness of sin and the greatness of God’s love. Sin is not a small matter that can be overlooked. It requires the giving of a life. And God Himself, in Christ, gave that life.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Some people find the language of blood and sacrifice uncomfortable. But it reveals something important: forgiveness is not cheap. It cost Christ His life. Understanding this deepens appreciation for God’s grace.

Believers can also take comfort in this verse. Because Christ’s blood has been shed, forgiveness is available. They do not need to offer anything else. The price has been paid.

Finally, this verse invites believers to take sin seriously. If sin required the death of the Son of God, it is not something to treat lightly. Gratitude for forgiveness leads to a desire to turn from sin.

### *Hebrews 9:27–28* — Once to Die, and Christ Will Appear a Second Time

> *“Inasmuch as it is appointed for men to die once, and after this, judgment, so Christ also, having been offered once to bear the sins of many, will appear a second time, not to deal with sin, but to save those who are eagerly waiting for him.”*
>
> — *Hebrews 9:27–28* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The author draws a parallel. “Inasmuch as it is appointed for men to die once, and after this, judgment.” Every person dies once. There is no second chance at life, no reincarnation. After death comes judgment before God.

Verse 28: “so Christ also, having been offered once to bear the sins of many.” Just as people die once, Christ died once. His single death was enough to “bear the sins of many,” taking their sins upon Himself, as *Isaiah 53:12* foretold: “*he bore the sins of many*” (*Isaiah 53:12*).

“Will appear a second time, not to deal with sin, but to save those who are eagerly waiting for him.” Christ will come again. His first coming dealt with sin through His sacrifice. His second coming will not be to deal with sin again, because that work is finished. He will come to complete the salvation of His people, bringing them into the fullness of eternal life.

“Those who are eagerly waiting for him.” Believers are those who long for Christ’s return.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses echo the Day of Atonement. On that day, the people waited outside while the high priest entered the Most Holy Place. When he came back out, it was a sign that the sacrifice had been accepted and the people were forgiven. In the same way, Christ has entered God’s presence with His sacrifice, and believers wait for Him to come out, that is, to return, bringing the full blessing of salvation.

The reality of death and judgment is sobering. Every person will one day stand before God. But for those who trust in Christ, this is not a cause for terror, because Christ has already borne their sins. *Romans 8:1* says, “*There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus*” (*Romans 8:1*). Judgment for believers is not about whether they will be condemned, but the final revelation of Christ’s saving work.

The phrase “eagerly waiting” describes the posture of believers. They are not afraid of Christ’s return; they long for it. It will be the day their salvation is complete.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses remind everyone that life is a single, unrepeatable opportunity. Death is certain, and judgment follows. This truth calls for seriousness about how one lives and what one believes.

For believers, these verses bring hope. Christ has borne their sins, and He will return to bring them into the fullness of salvation. They can face death and judgment with confidence, not fear.

Finally, believers can cultivate an eager expectation of Christ’s return. That hope shapes daily life, giving perspective in hardship, motivation for holiness, and joy in waiting.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Hebrews 9* shows that the old covenant’s system of worship, though God-given, was limited. The tabernacle itself taught that access to God was restricted: only one high priest, once a year, with animal blood. Its sacrifices could cleanse outwardly but could not cleanse the conscience. They pointed forward to something better.

Christ fulfilled all that the tabernacle and sacrifices foreshadowed. He entered not an earthly sanctuary but heaven itself, not with animal blood but with His own, not repeatedly but once for all, securing eternal redemption. His blood, offered through the eternal Spirit, cleanses believers’ consciences from dead works so that they may serve the living God. Those who carry guilt can find complete cleansing in Him.

The chapter also explains why Christ’s death was necessary. A covenant, like a will, takes effect through death. And without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness. Sin is serious, and forgiveness is costly. Christ gave His life so that sins could be forgiven. Believers can respond with gratitude, take sin seriously, and rest in the fact that the price has been fully paid.

Finally, the chapter points to the future. Just as people die once and then face judgment, Christ was offered once to bear the sins of many, and He will appear a second time, not to deal with sin, but to bring salvation to those who eagerly wait for Him. Believers can live with confidence and hope, cleansed by His blood and longing for His return.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You that You entered not an earthly sanctuary but heaven itself, not with the blood of animals but with Your own blood, once for all, securing eternal redemption for me. Thank You that Your blood, offered through the eternal Spirit, cleanses my conscience from dead works so that I may serve the living God. Free me from guilt that You have already removed, and help me to serve You with joy. Thank You that You are the mediator of a new covenant, and that through Your death I receive the promise of an eternal inheritance. Help me to take sin seriously and to treasure the forgiveness You purchased at such cost. Thank You that You appear in the presence of God for me now. I wait eagerly for the day You will appear a second time to bring salvation to all who long for You. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Hebrews · Chapter 10 of 13

# Hebrews — Chapter 10

Chapter Theme: One Sacrifice Forever, So Let Us Draw Near

[Read Hebrews 10 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/HEB10.htm)

Main Teaching

The Law was only a shadow of the good things to come, and its sacrifices, repeated year after year, could never make worshipers perfect; in fact, they served as an annual reminder of sins, because the blood of bulls and goats cannot take sins away. Quoting *Psalm 40*, the author shows that Christ came to do God’s will by offering His body, and by that will believers have been made holy through His offering once for all. While earthly priests stood daily offering the same sacrifices, Christ offered one sacrifice for sins forever and sat down at God’s right hand, for by one offering He has perfected forever those being made holy, as the new covenant promised: “I will remember their sins and their iniquities no more.” Since believers now have confidence to enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus, through the new and living way He opened through the curtain of His flesh, they should draw near to God with sincere hearts and full assurance, hold firmly to their hope, and stir one another up to love and good works, not neglecting to meet together. The author warns that those who deliberately keep on sinning after knowing the truth have no other sacrifice left, only judgment. He reminds his readers of their earlier endurance under persecution and urges them not to throw away their confidence, for they need endurance, and they are not among those who shrink back but among those who have faith and are saved.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Hebrews 10* brings the author’s long explanation of Christ’s priesthood and sacrifice to its climax. Chapters 7–9 compared Christ’s priesthood, covenant, and sanctuary with those of the old covenant. Now the focus is on the sacrifice itself. Why were the old sacrifices repeated endlessly? Because they could not truly deal with sin. Why does Christ’s sacrifice never need to be repeated? Because it is perfect and complete.

Then, at verse 19, the author turns from teaching to application. If all this is true, what should believers do? The answer is a series of encouragements: draw near to God, hold fast to hope, and encourage one another. This is followed by the fourth warning in Hebrews, and then by a warm reminder of the readers’ past faithfulness and a call to endurance.

The readers had once suffered public persecution, including insults, imprisonment, and the confiscation of their property, and they had endured it joyfully (vv32–34). But now, years later, some were growing weary, and some had stopped gathering with other believers (v25). The author wants them to remember who they are and to keep going.

### The Inadequacy of the Old Sacrifices (*10:1–4*)

“*For the law, having a shadow of the good to come, not the very image of the things, can never with the same sacrifices year by year, which they offer continually, make perfect those who draw near*” (*v. 1*). As *Hebrews 8:5* explained, the Law was a shadow. It outlined the shape of good things to come but did not contain their reality.

“*Or else wouldn’t they have ceased to be offered, because the worshipers, having been once cleansed, would have had no more consciousness of sins?*” (*v. 2*) If the sacrifices had truly removed sin, there would have been no need to repeat them. Their repetition proved their inadequacy.

“*But in those sacrifices there is a yearly reminder of sins*” (*v. 3*). Rather than removing guilt, the annual Day of Atonement reminded people that sin remained.

“*For it is impossible that the blood of bulls and goats should take away sins*” (*v. 4*). Animal sacrifices could not ultimately remove human sin. They were signs pointing to the sacrifice that could.

### I Have Come to Do Your Will (*10:5–10*)

“*Therefore when he comes into the world, he says, “You didn’t desire sacrifice and offering, but you prepared a body for me.*” (*v. 5*) “*You had no pleasure in whole burnt offerings and sacrifices for sin.*” (*v. 6*) “*Then I said, ‘Behold, I have come (in the scroll of the book it is written of me) to do your will, O God.’”*” (*v. 7*) The author quotes *Psalm 40:6–8*, following the Greek version, which reads “you prepared a body for me” where the Hebrew reads “my ears you have opened.” He places these words in the mouth of Christ as He comes into the world. God did not ultimately desire animal sacrifices; He desired obedience. Christ came with a body prepared for Him, to do God’s will perfectly, even to the point of offering that body on the cross.

“*Previously saying, “Sacrifices and offerings and whole burnt offerings and sacrifices for sin you didn’t desire, neither had pleasure in them” (those which are offered according to the law)*” (*v. 8*), “*then he has said, “Behold, I have come to do your will.” He takes away the first, that he may establish the second*” (*v. 9*). Christ set aside the old system of sacrifices and established the new way: His own obedient sacrifice. The result is studied below.

### One Sacrifice Forever (*10:11–18*)

“*Every priest indeed stands day by day serving and offering often the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins*” (*v. 11*), “*but he, when he had offered one sacrifice for sins forever, sat down on the right hand of God*” (*v. 12*), “*from that time waiting until his enemies are made the footstool of his feet*” (*v. 13*). The contrast is vivid. Priests stood, because their work was never finished. There were no chairs in the tabernacle. Christ sat down, because His work was complete. He now waits for the final defeat of all His enemies, as *Psalm 110:1* promised. The result of His one offering is studied below.

“*The Holy Spirit also testifies to us, for after saying*” (*v. 15*), “*“This is the covenant that I will make with them after those days,” says the Lord, “I will put my laws on their heart, I will also write them on their mind;” then he says*” (*v. 16*), “*“I will remember their sins and their iniquities no more.”*” (*v. 17*) The author returns to *Jeremiah 31*, quoted in *Hebrews 8*, and emphasizes its final promise: complete forgiveness.

“*Now where remission of these is, there is no more offering for sin*” (*v. 18*). If sins are completely forgiven, no further sacrifice is needed. This is the conclusion of the whole argument of chapters 7–10.

### Let Us Draw Near (*10:19–25*)

The great call to draw near, hold fast, and encourage one another is studied below. “*let’s hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering; for he who promised is faithful*” (*v. 23*). Believers can hold firmly to their hope because their hope rests on God’s faithfulness, not their own.

### A Warning Against Deliberate Sin (*10:26–31*)

“*For if we sin willfully after we have received the knowledge of the truth, there remains no more a sacrifice for sins*” (*v. 26*), “*but a certain fearful expectation of judgment, and a fierceness of fire which will devour the adversaries*” (*v. 27*). This is the fourth warning in Hebrews, closely related to *Hebrews 6:4–6*. “Sin willfully” describes deliberate, persistent sin, continuing to sin knowingly as a settled way of life, ultimately rejecting Christ. Since Christ’s sacrifice is the only sacrifice for sin, those who reject it have nowhere else to turn.

“*A man who disregards Moses’ law dies without compassion on the word of two or three witnesses*” (*v. 28*). “*How much worse punishment do you think he will be judged worthy of who has trodden under foot the Son of God, and has counted the blood of the covenant with which he was sanctified an unholy thing, and has insulted the Spirit of grace?*” (*v. 29*) The author describes this sin in the strongest terms: trampling the Son of God, treating His blood as worthless, and insulting the Spirit of grace. This is not the stumbling of a weak believer but the defiant rejection of Christ.

“*For we know him who said, “Vengeance belongs to me. I will repay,” says the Lord. Again, “The Lord will judge his people.”*” (*v. 30*) “*It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God*” (*v. 31*). The author quotes *Deuteronomy 32:35–36*. God is the living God, and His judgment is real.

As with *Hebrews 6:4–6*, Christians understand this warning in different ways: as describing true believers who can fall away, as describing those who professed faith without truly possessing it, or as a real warning that God uses to keep His people from falling away. All agree that it describes deliberate, settled rejection of Christ, not the ordinary failures that every believer experiences and confesses. Believers who are grieved by their sins and want to turn back to God are not the people this passage describes. For them, the promise of *1 John 1:9* stands: if we confess our sins, He is faithful and righteous to forgive us.

### Remember and Endure (*10:32–39*)

“*But remember the former days, in which, after you were enlightened, you endured a great struggle with sufferings*” (*v. 32*): “*partly, being exposed to both reproaches and oppressions, and partly, becoming partakers with those who were treated so*” (*v. 33*). Soon after coming to faith, the readers had endured public insult and persecution, and they had stood with others who were suffering.

“*For you both had compassion on me in my chains and joyfully accepted the plundering of your possessions, knowing that you have for yourselves a better possession and an enduring one in the heavens*” (*v. 34*). They had cared for prisoners and joyfully accepted the loss of their property, because they knew they had a better and lasting possession in heaven. (Some manuscripts read “compassion on the prisoners” rather than “on me in my chains.”)

“*Therefore don’t throw away your boldness, which has a great reward*” (*v. 35*). “*For you need endurance so that, having done the will of God, you may receive the promise*” (*v. 36*). The readers had shown great courage before. Now they must not abandon it. What they need is endurance.

“*“In a very little while, he who comes will come and will not wait.*” (*v. 37*) “*But the righteous one will live by faith. If he shrinks back, my soul has no pleasure in him.”*” (*v. 38*) The author quotes *Habakkuk 2:3–4*, the same passage Paul quotes in *Romans 1:17* and *Galatians 3:11*. Christ’s return is near. The righteous live by faith and do not shrink back.

“*But we are not of those who shrink back to destruction, but of those who have faith to the saving of the soul*” (*v. 39*). The author ends with confidence. He believes his readers are among those who will persevere in faith. This verse leads directly into the great chapter on faith that follows.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Hebrews 10:10* — Sanctified Once for All

> *“by which will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.”*
>
> — *Hebrews 10:10* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“By which will we have been sanctified.” “Which will” refers to God’s will, which Christ came to do (v9). Because Christ obeyed the Father’s will perfectly, believers have been “sanctified,” made holy, set apart for God, cleansed from sin.

“Through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ.” The means of sanctification is Christ’s sacrifice, the offering of His physical body on the cross. *Psalm 40* spoke of a body prepared for Him (v5); He offered that body for His people.

“Once for all.” This phrase appears again. Christ’s sacrifice does not need to be repeated. It was offered once, and its effect is permanent.

Notice the tense: “we have been sanctified.” This is a completed action. Believers are already set apart as holy in God’s sight because of what Christ has done.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

In Hebrews, “sanctified” often refers to the definitive act by which believers are set apart and made acceptable to God through Christ’s sacrifice. This is sometimes called “positional” or “definitive” sanctification. It is complete and secure. Believers are holy in God’s sight because of Christ.

At the same time, verse 14 speaks of “those who are being sanctified,” an ongoing process. Believers are already holy in their standing before God, and they are being made holy in their character day by day. Both are true, and both rest on Christ’s sacrifice.

This verse also connects Christ’s obedience with His sacrifice. Christ did not merely die; He came to do God’s will, and His death was the climax of a life of perfect obedience. God desired obedience more than sacrifice (*1 Samuel 15:22*). In Christ, perfect obedience and perfect sacrifice come together.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can rest in the truth that they have been made holy in God’s sight through Christ’s sacrifice. Their standing before God does not depend on how well they performed today. It rests on what Christ did once for all.

This truth also motivates holy living. Those who have been set apart for God are called to live as people who belong to Him. Their identity shapes their behavior.

Finally, believers can follow Christ’s example of doing God’s will. Like Him, they can say, “I have come to do your will,” offering their own bodies as living sacrifices (*Romans 12:1*).

### *Hebrews 10:14* — Perfected Forever

> *“For by one offering he has perfected forever those who are being sanctified.”*
>
> — *Hebrews 10:14* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“For by one offering he has perfected forever those who are being sanctified.”

“By one offering”: a single sacrifice, Christ’s death on the cross.

“He has perfected forever”: He has made believers complete, fully qualified to stand in God’s presence, permanently. “Perfected” here means brought to the goal God intended: a right relationship with Him, with sin fully dealt with.

“Those who are being sanctified”: believers who are in the process of being made holy. The perfection is complete; the sanctification is ongoing.

This verse holds together two truths. Believers are already perfected in their standing before God, forever. And they are still being made holy in their daily lives.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This is one of the most remarkable statements in the New Testament. One offering accomplished what centuries of sacrifices could not. The old sacrifices could never make worshipers perfect (*Hebrews 10:1*). Christ’s single sacrifice has made believers perfect forever.

The combination of “perfected forever” and “being sanctified” gives believers both security and direction. Security, because their acceptance with God is complete and permanent, resting on Christ’s finished work. Direction, because they are on a journey of growth, becoming in practice what they already are in Christ.

This truth guards against two errors. One is anxiety, fearing that one’s standing with God depends on one’s performance. The other is complacency, thinking that because one is accepted, growth does not matter. Hebrews affirms both full acceptance and ongoing transformation.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers who struggle with insecurity before God can hold onto this verse. By one offering, Christ has perfected them forever. Their failures do not undo His work.

At the same time, believers can embrace the ongoing process of being made holy. They can grow in love, obedience, and character, not to earn acceptance, but because they are already accepted.

When believers fall, they can return to this truth: Christ’s offering is sufficient. They do not need another sacrifice. They need only to confess and receive the forgiveness already secured.

### *Hebrews 10:19–22* — A New and Living Way

> *“Having therefore, brothers, boldness to enter into the holy place by the blood of Jesus, by the way which he dedicated for us, a new and living way, through the veil, that is to say, his flesh, and having a great priest over God’s house, let’s draw near with a true heart in fullness of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience and having our body washed with pure water,”*
>
> — *Hebrews 10:19–22* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The author now turns from teaching to application. “Having therefore, brothers, boldness to enter into the holy place by the blood of Jesus.” Under the old covenant, only the high priest could enter the Most Holy Place, once a year, trembling. Now every believer has “boldness,” confidence and freedom, to enter God’s presence. The basis is “the blood of Jesus.”

Verse 20: “by the way which he dedicated for us, a new and living way, through the veil, that is to say, his flesh.” Jesus opened a way into God’s presence. It is “new,” never available before, and “living,” because it is through the living Christ. The curtain that once blocked the way is compared to Jesus’ flesh. When His body was torn on the cross, the way was opened. The Gospels record that at the moment of Jesus’ death, the temple curtain was torn from top to bottom (*Mark 15:38*).

Verse 21: “and having a great priest over God’s house.” Believers have Jesus as their high priest, who rules over God’s household.

Verse 22 gives the call: “let’s draw near with a true heart in fullness of faith.” Believers should approach God with sincerity and full confidence.

“Having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience.” Just as priests were sprinkled with blood to be consecrated, believers’ hearts have been cleansed by Christ’s blood from a guilty conscience.

“And having our body washed with pure water.” This likely refers to baptism, the outward sign of inner cleansing, or more broadly to the cleansing that comes through Christ.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses describe the greatest privilege of the new covenant: direct access to God. What was once reserved for one man on one day a year is now open to every believer at every moment. This is the fulfillment of everything the tabernacle pointed toward.

The image of the curtain as Christ’s flesh is profound. The barrier between God and humanity was removed through Christ’s body, offered on the cross. The way into God’s presence passes through the cross.

The call to “draw near” is an invitation to intimate fellowship with God. Believers do not need to stand at a distance. They can come close, speak freely, and enjoy His presence. This is what *Hebrews 4:16* described as approaching the throne of grace with boldness.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can draw near to God in prayer and worship with confidence, not because they are worthy, but because Jesus has opened the way. They can come to Him at any time, in any circumstance.

This passage invites believers to come with sincerity, a “true heart,” and with full assurance of faith. They do not need to approach God with doubt about whether they are welcome. They are welcome through Christ.

Believers who feel unclean or unworthy can remember that their hearts have been sprinkled clean by Christ’s blood. Their conscience can be at rest.

### *Hebrews 10:24–25* — Stir Up One Another to Love and Good Works

> *“Let’s consider how to provoke one another to love and good works, not forsaking our own assembling together, as the custom of some is, but exhorting one another, and so much the more as you see the Day approaching.”*
>
> — *Hebrews 10:24–25* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After calling believers to draw near to God and hold fast to hope, the author calls them to care for one another.

“Let’s consider how to provoke one another to love and good works.” “Consider” means to think carefully, to give attention to. Believers are to think about how to encourage one another. “Provoke” usually has a negative meaning, but here it is positive: to stir up, to stimulate, to spur on. Believers are to inspire one another toward love and good deeds.

Verse 25: “not forsaking our own assembling together, as the custom of some is.” Some of the readers had stopped meeting with other believers, perhaps out of fear of persecution, discouragement, or indifference. The author urges them not to give up gathering together.

“But exhorting one another.” When believers gather, they encourage one another.

“And so much the more as you see the Day approaching.” “The Day” is the day of Christ’s return. As it draws nearer, gathering and encouragement become even more important.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that the Christian life is not lived alone. Believers need one another. Drawing near to God (v22) and holding fast to hope (v23) are sustained by community (vv24–25). *Hebrews 3:13* made a similar point: “exhort one another day by day... lest any one of you be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin.”

The three verses form a pattern: faith (v22), hope (v23), and love (v24). These are the three great Christian virtues (*1 Corinthians 13:13*), and they flourish in community.

Gathering together was not merely a religious duty for the early Christians. It was where they worshiped, prayed, heard the Scriptures, shared the Lord’s Supper, and supported one another (*Acts 2:42–47*). To abandon the gathering was to cut oneself off from the means God uses to sustain faith.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can take regular gathering with other believers seriously. Participating in a local church, through worship, small groups, and fellowship, provides encouragement and accountability that are hard to find alone.

Believers can also think intentionally about how to encourage others: a word of affirmation, an invitation to serve together, a reminder of God’s promises, or an example of love and generosity.

For those who have drifted from Christian community because of hurt, busyness, or discouragement, this passage is a gentle invitation to return. And for churches, it is a call to be communities where people are genuinely encouraged and spurred on, where those who have been wounded find care, and where no one is left alone.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Hebrews 10* brings the great argument of Hebrews to its climax. The old sacrifices, repeated year after year, could never take away sins; they were only a shadow. But Christ came to do God’s will, offering His own body once for all. By that single sacrifice, believers have been made holy, and by one offering He has perfected forever those who are being sanctified. He has sat down at God’s right hand because His work is complete. Where sins are forgiven, no further sacrifice is needed.

This truth gives believers both security and freedom. They do not need to earn God’s acceptance or repeat sacrifices. Their standing before God is complete and permanent in Christ. At the same time, they are being made holy day by day, growing into what they already are.

Because of what Christ has done, believers can draw near to God with confidence, through the new and living way He opened through His flesh. They can come with sincere hearts and full assurance, cleansed from a guilty conscience. They can hold fast their hope, because God is faithful. And they can stir one another up to love and good works, faithfully gathering together and encouraging one another, especially as the day of Christ’s return approaches.

The chapter also contains a solemn warning against deliberately and persistently rejecting Christ, because there is no other sacrifice for sin. This warning is meant to keep believers from drifting, not to crush those who struggle and long for God. Finally, the author reminds his readers of their past courage in suffering and calls them to endure. They are not those who shrink back, but those who have faith and are saved.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for coming into the world to do the Father’s will and for offering Your body once for all. Thank You that by Your one sacrifice I have been made holy and perfected forever, and that You are making me holy day by day. Thank You that You sat down at the right hand of God because Your work is finished, and that my sins are remembered no more. Thank You for opening a new and living way into God’s presence through Your flesh. Help me to draw near with a sincere heart and full assurance of faith. Help me to hold fast to my hope, for You who promised are faithful. Show me how to stir up others to love and good works, and keep me faithful in gathering with Your people. Guard me from drifting, give me endurance, and keep me among those who have faith and are saved. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
