Hebrews · Chapter 11 of 13

# Hebrews — Chapter 11

Chapter Theme: The Great Cloud of Faithful Witnesses

[Read Hebrews 11 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/HEB11.htm)

Main Teaching

Faith is the assurance of things hoped for and the conviction of things not seen, and by it the people of old received God’s approval. By faith we understand that God created the universe by His word. The author then traces faith through the generations: Abel offered a better sacrifice, Enoch pleased God and was taken up, and Noah built the ark, for without faith it is impossible to please God, since whoever comes to Him must believe that He exists and rewards those who seek Him. Abraham obeyed God’s call and went out not knowing where he was going, living as a foreigner in tents while looking for the city whose builder is God; Sarah received power to conceive because she considered God faithful. These all died in faith without receiving what was promised, seeing it from a distance and confessing that they were strangers on earth seeking a better, heavenly country, and God is not ashamed to be called their God. Abraham offered Isaac, trusting God could raise the dead; Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph looked to the future; Moses’ parents hid him, and Moses chose mistreatment with God’s people over the passing pleasures of sin, valuing the reproach of Christ above Egypt’s treasures. By faith Israel crossed the Red Sea, Jericho’s walls fell, and Rahab was spared. Many others conquered kingdoms and escaped death, while others were tortured, mocked, imprisoned, and killed, the world not being worthy of them. All of them were commended for their faith, yet they did not receive the promise, because God had planned something better, so that only together with us would they be made complete.

## Chapter Background and Story

At the end of chapter 10, the author quoted *Habakkuk 2:4*: “the righteous one will live by faith,” and assured his readers that they were “of those who have faith to the saving of the soul” (*Hebrews 10:38–39*). Chapter 11 explains what that faith looks like by giving a long series of examples from Israel’s history.

This chapter is sometimes called the “Hall of Faith.” It moves from creation to the patriarchs, to Moses and the exodus, to the conquest of Canaan, and then to a rapid summary of judges, kings, prophets, and martyrs. The repeated phrase “by faith” ties it together.

The purpose of this chapter is pastoral. The readers were weary and tempted to give up because of hardship. The author reminds them that God’s people have always lived by faith, trusting God’s promises before seeing them fulfilled, often in the midst of suffering. Many of these heroes of faith did not see the fulfillment of God’s promises in their lifetimes. Yet they persevered. The readers are called to do the same.

### What Faith Is (*11:1–3*)

The definition of faith is studied below. “*For by this, the elders obtained approval*” (*v. 2*). “The elders” are the people of faith in the Old Testament. God approved of them because of their faith.

“*By faith we understand that the universe has been framed by the word of God, so that what is seen has not been made out of things which are visible*” (*v. 3*). Faith begins with creation. God made the universe by His word (*Genesis 1*; *Psalm 33:6*). What is visible came from what is invisible: God’s command. Believers know this not by observation but by faith in God’s revelation.

### Faith Before the Flood (*11:4–7*)

“*By faith Abel offered to God a more excellent sacrifice than Cain, through which he had testimony given to him that he was righteous, God testifying with respect to his gifts; and through it he, being dead, still speaks*” (*v. 4*). Abel’s offering was accepted and Cain’s was not (*Genesis 4:3–5*). The difference lay in Abel’s faith. Though Abel was murdered, his faith still speaks. *Hebrews 12:24* will say that Jesus’ blood speaks better than Abel’s.

“*By faith Enoch was taken away, so that he wouldn’t see death, and he was not found, because God translated him. For he has had testimony given to him that before his translation he had been well pleasing to God*” (*v. 5*). *Genesis 5:24* says that Enoch walked with God and was no more, because God took him. Enoch did not experience death. The principle that underlies his life is studied below.

“*By faith Noah, being warned about things not yet seen, moved with godly fear, prepared a ship for the saving of his house, through which he condemned the world and became heir of the righteousness which is according to faith*” (*v. 7*). Noah believed God’s warning about a flood he had never seen and built the ark, a huge project that must have looked foolish to others. His obedient faith saved his family and exposed the unbelief of the world around him.

### The Faith of Abraham and Sarah (*11:8–19*)

“*By faith Abraham, when he was called, obeyed to go out to the place which he was to receive for an inheritance. He went out, not knowing where he went*” (*v. 8*). God called Abraham to leave his homeland for a land God would show him (*Genesis 12:1–4*). He obeyed without knowing his destination. Faith often means obeying God without seeing the whole path.

“*By faith he lived as an alien in the land of promise, as in a land not his own, dwelling in tents with Isaac and Jacob, the heirs with him of the same promise*” (*v. 9*). “*For he was looking for the city which has foundations, whose builder and maker is God*” (*v. 10*). Even in the promised land, Abraham lived in tents, like a foreigner. He never owned the land except for a burial plot (*Genesis 23*). His hope reached beyond Canaan to a permanent city built by God.

“*By faith even Sarah herself received power to conceive, and she bore a child when she was past age, since she counted him faithful who had promised*” (*v. 11*). Sarah had laughed in disbelief at first (*Genesis 18:12*), but she came to trust God’s promise. The miracle of Isaac’s birth rested on God’s faithfulness. (Some interpreters read this verse as referring to Abraham’s faith, with Sarah included; the Greek is ambiguous.) “*Therefore as many as the stars of the sky in multitude, and as innumerable as the sand which is by the sea shore, were fathered by one man, and him as good as dead*” (*v. 12*). From one elderly couple came a nation as numerous as the stars.

The pilgrim faith of the patriarchs is studied below.

“*By faith, Abraham, being tested, offered up Isaac. Yes, he who had gladly received the promises was offering up his only born son*” (*v. 17*), “*to whom it was said, “Your offspring will be accounted as from Isaac,”*” (*v. 18*) “*concluding that God is able to raise up even from the dead. Figuratively speaking, he also did receive him back from the dead*” (*v. 19*). God’s command to offer Isaac (*Genesis 22*) seemed to contradict His promise that Abraham’s descendants would come through Isaac. Abraham resolved the tension by trusting that God could raise Isaac from the dead. In a sense, he did receive Isaac back from death when God provided a ram instead. This story foreshadows God’s own Son, offered and raised.

### Faith Looking Forward (*11:20–22*)

“*By faith Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau, even concerning things to come*” (*v. 20*). “*By faith Jacob, when he was dying, blessed each of the sons of Joseph, and worshiped, leaning on the top of his staff*” (*v. 21*). “*By faith Joseph, when his end was near, made mention of the departure of the children of Israel, and gave instructions concerning his bones*” (*v. 22*). At the end of their lives, the patriarchs looked forward to God’s future. Joseph, though he had become a ruler in Egypt, asked that his bones be carried to the promised land (*Genesis 50:24–25*), trusting God would fulfill His promise.

### The Faith of Moses and Israel (*11:23–31*)

“*By faith Moses, when he was born, was hidden for three months by his parents, because they saw that he was a beautiful child; and they were not afraid of the king’s commandment*” (*v. 23*). Moses’ parents defied Pharaoh’s order to kill Hebrew baby boys (*Exodus 1:22–2:2*). Their faith gave them courage to risk their lives.

“*By faith Moses, when he had grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter*” (*v. 24*), “*choosing rather to share ill treatment with God’s people than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a time*” (*v. 25*), “*considering the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt; for he looked to the reward*” (*v. 26*). Moses could have enjoyed the wealth and status of Egypt’s royal court. Instead, he identified with the enslaved Israelites. “The reproach of Christ” means the kind of disgrace that God’s anointed people suffer, a disgrace Christ Himself would later bear fully. Moses valued it more than Egypt’s treasures, because he looked to God’s reward.

“*By faith he left Egypt, not fearing the wrath of the king; for he endured, as seeing him who is invisible*” (*v. 27*). Moses persevered because he saw, by faith, the invisible God. “*By faith he kept the Passover and the sprinkling of the blood, that the destroyer of the firstborn should not touch them*” (*v. 28*). The Passover lamb’s blood protected Israel, pointing ahead to Christ, our Passover (*1 Corinthians 5:7*).

“*By faith they passed through the Red Sea as on dry land. When the Egyptians tried to do so, they were swallowed up*” (*v. 29*). “*By faith the walls of Jericho fell down after they had been encircled for seven days*” (*v. 30*). “*By faith Rahab the prostitute didn’t perish with those who were disobedient, having received the spies in peace*” (*v. 31*). Rahab was a Canaanite and a prostitute, an outsider in every way. Yet she trusted Israel’s God, sheltered the spies, and was saved (*Joshua 2*; *6:22–25*). She became an ancestor of King David and of Jesus (*Matthew 1:5*). Her inclusion shows that God welcomes anyone who turns to Him in faith.

### Triumph and Suffering (*11:32–40*)

“*What more shall I say? For the time would fail me if I told of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel, and the prophets—*” (*v. 32*). The author runs out of time to tell every story. Notice that some of these figures had serious flaws: Gideon was fearful, Samson was impulsive and immoral, and Jephthah made a rash and tragic vow. Their inclusion does not mean their sins are approved. It shows that God works through imperfect people who, at key moments, trusted Him.

“*who through faith subdued kingdoms, worked out righteousness, obtained promises, stopped the mouths of lions*” (*v. 33*), “*quenched the power of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, from weakness were made strong, grew mighty in war, and caused foreign armies to flee*” (*v. 34*). These phrases recall victories and rescues: Daniel in the lions’ den (*Daniel 6*), his friends in the fiery furnace (*Daniel 3*), and many others. The other side of faith’s story, suffering without rescue, is studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Hebrews 11:1* — The Assurance of Things Hoped For

> *“Now faith is assurance of things hoped for, proof of things not seen.”*
>
> — *Hebrews 11:1* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse describes what faith is. It is not a complete definition, but it captures the essence of faith as Hebrews presents it.

“Now faith is assurance of things hoped for.” “Assurance” translates a word that can mean foundation, confidence, or even a title deed, a legal document guaranteeing ownership. Faith gives substance and certainty to what believers hope for. Believers do not yet possess the fullness of God’s promises, but faith makes them confident those promises are real and will be fulfilled.

“Proof of things not seen.” “Proof” means conviction or evidence. Faith is convinced of realities that cannot be seen with physical eyes: God Himself, Christ in heaven, the future kingdom, and God’s unseen work in the present.

Faith, then, looks in two directions: forward to what is promised but not yet received, and upward to what is real but not yet seen.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Faith in Hebrews is not blind belief or wishful thinking. It is confident trust in God, based on His character and His word. The heroes of this chapter believed God because they knew Him to be faithful (v11). Their faith rested on God’s promises, which *Hebrews 6:18* calls unchangeable.

Faith is also not merely intellectual agreement. In every example in this chapter, faith leads to action: offering, building, leaving, obeying, refusing, choosing. Faith that does not act is not the kind of faith Hebrews celebrates. James makes the same point: faith without works is dead (*James 2:17*).

Paul expresses a similar thought in *2 Corinthians 4:18*: “*we don't look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal*” (*2 Corinthians 4:18*). Faith fixes its eyes on what lasts.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can ask what they are hoping for and whether their hope rests on God’s promises. Faith gives them confidence that what God has promised, forgiveness, His presence, resurrection, and eternal life, is real and certain.

Faith also helps believers live in light of unseen realities. Though they cannot see God, they can trust that He is present, active, and good. This trust can shape decisions, give courage, and bring peace.

Finally, believers can let their faith lead to action. Like the people in this chapter, they can obey God’s call, make sacrifices, and choose faithfulness, trusting in what they cannot yet see.

### *Hebrews 11:6* — Without Faith It Is Impossible to Please God

> *“Without faith it is impossible to be well pleasing to him, for he who comes to God must believe that he exists, and that he is a rewarder of those who seek him.”*
>
> — *Hebrews 11:6* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

This verse explains why Enoch pleased God (v5) and states a principle for everyone.

“Without faith it is impossible to be well pleasing to him.” No one can please God without faith. Good deeds, religious activities, or moral efforts that do not come from trust in God cannot please Him. Faith is essential.

“For he who comes to God must believe that he exists.” The first requirement is to believe that God is real. Approaching God begins with trusting that He is there.

“And that he is a rewarder of those who seek him.” The second requirement is to believe that God is good, that He responds to those who genuinely seek Him. God is not indifferent or hostile. He rewards those who come to Him.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse shows that faith is relational. It is not merely believing facts about God but coming to Him, seeking Him, and trusting Him. The two beliefs described here, that God exists and that He rewards seekers, are the foundation of a relationship with Him.

The idea that God rewards those who seek Him runs throughout Scripture. God said through Jeremiah, “*You shall seek me, and find me, when you search for me with all your heart*” (*Jeremiah 29:13*). Jesus said, “*Seek, and you will find*” (*Matthew 7:7*). The greatest reward is God Himself. He told Abraham, “*I am your shield, your exceedingly great reward*” (*Genesis 15:1*).

Faith pleases God because it honors Him. It takes God at His word, trusts His character, and depends on Him. Unbelief, by contrast, treats God as unreliable or unimportant.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites everyone to seek God, believing that He is real and that He responds. For those who are searching or doubting, it offers hope: God rewards those who sincerely seek Him.

For believers, this verse reminds them that pleasing God is not about religious performance but about trusting Him. Their everyday trust, in prayer, in obedience, in waiting, pleases Him.

Finally, believers can grow in faith by continuing to seek God through prayer, Scripture, and worship, confident that He will reward them with Himself.

### *Hebrews 11:13–16* — Strangers and Pilgrims Seeking a Better Country

> *“These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them and embraced them from afar, and having confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth. For those who say such things make it clear that they are seeking a country of their own. If indeed they had been thinking of that country from which they went out, they would have had enough time to return. But now they desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed of them, to be called their God, for he has prepared a city for them.”*
>
> — *Hebrews 11:13–16* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“These all died in faith, not having received the promises.” Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Sarah died without seeing the full fulfillment of God’s promises. They never saw their descendants become a great nation or possess the land fully.

“But having seen them and embraced them from afar.” Like travelers glimpsing a distant city on the horizon, they saw the promises by faith and welcomed them.

“And having confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth.” They openly acknowledged that this world was not their true home. Abraham called himself “*a stranger and a foreigner*” (*Genesis 23:4*), and Jacob spoke of his life as a pilgrimage (*Genesis 47:9*).

Verse 14: “For those who say such things make it clear that they are seeking a country of their own.” By calling themselves strangers, they showed that they were looking for a homeland.

Verse 15: “If indeed they had been thinking of that country from which they went out, they would have had enough time to return.” They could have gone back to Mesopotamia. But they did not, because they were looking for something better.

Verse 16: “But now they desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one.” Their hope reached beyond any earthly land to a heavenly home.

“Therefore God is not ashamed of them, to be called their God.” God proudly identified Himself as “*the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob*” (*Exodus 3:6*).

“For he has prepared a city for them.” God has a home ready for His people.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses describe the pilgrim nature of the life of faith. Believers live in this world but are not fully at home here. Their true citizenship is in heaven (*Philippians 3:20*). Peter calls believers “*foreigners and pilgrims*” (*1 Peter 2:11*). This identity frees them from clinging too tightly to earthly security and helps them endure hardship, knowing that something better awaits.

The fact that these patriarchs died without receiving the promises does not mean their faith failed. Faith does not require seeing the fulfillment. It trusts God’s promises even when they lie beyond one’s lifetime.

“God is not ashamed of them” is a beautiful phrase. These were imperfect people, yet God was glad to be called their God, because they trusted Him. The same is true for believers today. *Hebrews 2:11* says Jesus is not ashamed to call them His brothers and sisters.

The “city” God has prepared is described at the end of Scripture as the new Jerusalem, coming down from heaven, where God dwells with His people (*Revelation 21:2–3*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can hold earthly things loosely, recognizing that this world is not their final home. This perspective can bring freedom from materialism, anxiety about status, and fear of loss.

At the same time, being pilgrims does not mean withdrawing from the world. Abraham lived among the Canaanites, blessed others, and engaged with his neighbors. Believers can work, love, and serve faithfully here while looking forward to their true home.

For those who are waiting for God’s promises and have not yet seen them fulfilled, these verses bring encouragement. The great heroes of faith also waited, and many died before seeing the fulfillment. God is faithful, and His promises are sure.

### *Hebrews 11:35–38* — Of Whom the World Was Not Worthy

> *“Women received their dead by resurrection. Others were tortured, not accepting their deliverance, that they might obtain a better resurrection. Others were tried by mocking and scourging, yes, moreover by bonds and imprisonment. They were stoned. They were sawn apart. They were tempted. They were slain with the sword. They went around in sheep skins and in goat skins; being destitute, afflicted, ill-treated— of whom the world was not worthy—wandering in deserts, mountains, caves, and the holes of the earth.”*
>
> — *Hebrews 11:35–38* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After describing faith’s victories (vv33–35a), the author turns to another side of faith’s story. “Women received their dead by resurrection.” This recalls the widow of Zarephath and the Shunammite woman, whose sons were raised by Elijah and Elisha (*1 Kings 17:17–24*; *2 Kings 4:18–37*).

“Others were tortured, not accepting their deliverance, that they might obtain a better resurrection.” Some people of faith were not rescued. They chose torture rather than deny God, because they trusted in a better resurrection, eternal life with God. This may recall the Jewish martyrs during the persecution under Antiochus IV in the second century B.C., whose stories were well known.

Verse 36: “Others were tried by mocking and scourging, yes, moreover by bonds and imprisonment.” Jeremiah was beaten and imprisoned (*Jeremiah 20:2*; *37:15*).

Verse 37: “They were stoned.” Zechariah son of Jehoiada was stoned in the temple court (*2 Chronicles 24:20–21*). “They were sawn apart.” Jewish tradition says the prophet Isaiah was killed this way. “They were tempted. They were slain with the sword.” “They went around in sheep skins and in goat skins; being destitute, afflicted, ill-treated.” Prophets like Elijah lived in poverty and hardship.

Verse 38: “of whom the world was not worthy.” The world rejected and mistreated them, but in reality, the world was not worthy of such people. “Wandering in deserts, mountains, caves, and the holes of the earth.” Many faithful people lived as fugitives.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses are a vital part of the chapter. They show that faith does not always lead to visible success or deliverance in this life. Some people of faith conquered kingdoms and escaped death; others were tortured and killed. Both groups had genuine faith. God’s faithfulness is not measured by whether He rescues His people from every hardship in this life.

This truth corrects any teaching that suggests faith always produces health, wealth, or victory. Jesus Himself, the supreme example of faith, was crucified. Many of His followers have suffered and died for Him. Faith trusts God both in deliverance and in suffering, because its hope is ultimately in “a better resurrection.”

“Of whom the world was not worthy” is a powerful reversal of values. The world may despise those who suffer for their faith, but in God’s eyes, they are the truly honored ones.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers who are suffering, even after praying for deliverance, can find comfort here. Their suffering does not mean their faith is weak or that God has abandoned them. Many of the greatest believers in history suffered greatly.

These verses also call believers to remember and pray for persecuted Christians around the world, many of whom endure imprisonment, violence, and loss for their faith. They stand in this line of faithful witnesses.

Finally, these verses invite believers to see their lives in light of eternity. A “better resurrection” awaits. Whatever they lose for Christ’s sake in this life will be more than restored in the life to come.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Hebrews 11* teaches what faith is and what it looks like. Faith is the assurance of things hoped for and the conviction of things not seen. It trusts God’s promises before they are fulfilled and believes in unseen realities. Without faith it is impossible to please God, because whoever comes to Him must believe that He exists and rewards those who seek Him.

The chapter shows faith in action across many generations. Abel offered a better sacrifice; Enoch walked with God; Noah built the ark; Abraham left his home without knowing where he was going and offered Isaac, trusting God to raise the dead; Sarah trusted God’s promise; Moses chose suffering with God’s people over Egypt’s treasures; Israel crossed the Red Sea; and Rahab, an outsider, was saved by faith. These were imperfect people, but they trusted God at crucial moments.

Many of them died without receiving what was promised. They saw it from a distance and lived as strangers and pilgrims, seeking a better, heavenly country. God was not ashamed to be called their God, and He has prepared a city for them. Believers today can live with the same pilgrim hope, holding earthly things loosely while serving faithfully in the world.

Finally, the chapter honestly acknowledges that faith does not always bring deliverance in this life. Some conquered kingdoms and escaped death; others were tortured, imprisoned, and killed, people of whom the world was not worthy. Both groups had true faith. All were commended, and all await the fulfillment of God’s promises together with believers today. This great cloud of witnesses calls believers to keep trusting God, whatever comes.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord God, thank You for the faith You give, the assurance of things hoped for and the conviction of things not seen. Help me to believe that You exist and that You reward those who seek You. Give me faith like Abraham’s, to obey when I do not know where You are leading. Give me faith like Moses’, to choose faithfulness to You over the passing pleasures of sin. Help me to live as a stranger and pilgrim on earth, seeking the better country You have prepared. When I wait for promises I have not yet seen fulfilled, keep me trusting. When I face hardship that You do not remove, give me faith to endure, looking to the better resurrection. Strengthen Your persecuted people around the world, of whom the world is not worthy. Thank You that You are not ashamed to be called our God. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Hebrews · Chapter 12 of 13

# Hebrews — Chapter 12

Chapter Theme: Run the Race, Looking to Jesus

[Read Hebrews 12 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/HEB12.htm)

Main Teaching

Surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, believers are to throw off every weight and the sin that entangles them, and run with endurance the race set before them, fixing their eyes on Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith, who for the joy before Him endured the cross, despising its shame, and sat down at God’s right hand. Considering how He endured hostility, they will not grow weary. The hardships they face are the loving discipline of a Father who treats them as His children, training them to share His holiness; though painful at the time, discipline later produces the peaceful fruit of righteousness. So they should strengthen weak hands and knees, pursue peace with everyone and the holiness without which no one will see the Lord, watch that no one falls short of God’s grace or lets a bitter root grow, and not be like Esau, who traded his birthright for a single meal. Believers have not come to the terrifying, untouchable mountain of Sinai, but to Mount Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem, to joyful angels, to the church of the firstborn, to God the Judge of all, to the spirits of the righteous made perfect, and to Jesus, mediator of a new covenant, whose blood speaks a better word than Abel’s. Therefore they must not refuse the One who speaks from heaven. God will shake earth and heaven once more, removing what can be shaken, but believers are receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken, so they should be thankful and worship God with reverence and awe, for our God is a consuming fire.

## Chapter Background and Story

Chapter 11 ended with a long list of faithful people who endured hardship, many without receiving what was promised in their lifetimes. Chapter 12 turns that history into a call to action. The readers are now running the same race. The heroes of faith surround them like a great crowd in a stadium. And at the finish line is Jesus Himself.

The readers were weary. They had endured persecution in the past (*Hebrews 10:32–34*), but now they were growing tired and discouraged, perhaps facing new pressures. The author gives them three encouragements: look to Jesus, who endured far more; understand hardship as the loving discipline of a Father; and remember the glorious reality they have come to in Christ.

The chapter ends with the fifth and final warning in Hebrews: do not refuse the God who speaks. But it also contains one of the most glorious descriptions of the believer’s privileges in all of Scripture (vv22–24).

### Running the Race (*12:1–3*)

The call to run with endurance, looking to Jesus, is studied below. “*For consider him who has endured such contradiction of sinners against himself, that you don’t grow weary, fainting in your souls*” (*v. 3*). When believers are tempted to give up, they can think about Jesus, who endured hostility from sinners far greater than anything they face. Considering Him renews strength.

“*You have not yet resisted to blood, striving against sin*” (*v. 4*). The readers had suffered, but not yet to the point of death, as Jesus and many of the faithful in chapter 11 had. This is not a rebuke but a perspective: their struggle, though real, has not yet demanded everything.

### The Father’s Discipline (*12:4–13*)

“*You have forgotten the exhortation which reasons with you as with children, “My son, don’t take lightly the chastening of the Lord, nor faint when you are reproved by him*” (*v. 5*); “*for whom the Lord loves, he disciplines, and chastises every son whom he receives.”*” (*v. 6*) The author quotes *Proverbs 3:11–12*. God’s discipline is not a sign of rejection but of love. He treats believers as His children.

“*It is for discipline that you endure. God deals with you as with children, for what son is there whom his father doesn’t discipline?*” (*v. 7*) “*But if you are without discipline, of which all have been made partakers, then you are illegitimate, and not children*” (*v. 8*). In the ancient world, a father invested in training his legitimate children and heirs. A child who received no training might be one the father did not acknowledge as his own. God’s discipline shows that believers truly belong to Him.

“*Furthermore, we had the fathers of our flesh to chasten us, and we paid them respect. Shall we not much rather be in subjection to the Father of spirits and live?*” (*v. 9*) If people respect human fathers who trained them, how much more should they submit to God, the Father of their spirits, whose discipline leads to life. The purpose and fruit of discipline are studied below.

“*Therefore lift up the hands that hang down and the feeble knees*” (*v. 12*), “*and make straight paths for your feet, so what is lame may not be dislocated, but rather be healed*” (*v. 13*). Drawing on *Isaiah 35:3* and *Proverbs 4:26*, the author pictures weary runners whose arms droop and knees buckle. They are to take courage, strengthen themselves, and make the path straight, not only for themselves but for weaker members of the community, so that those who are “lame” are healed rather than injured further.

### Pursue Peace and Holiness (*12:14–17*)

The call to peace, holiness, and watchfulness is studied below. “*lest there be any sexually immoral person or profane person, like Esau, who sold his birthright for one meal*” (*v. 16*). Esau traded his birthright, his inheritance as firstborn, for a bowl of stew (*Genesis 25:29–34*). He valued immediate satisfaction above God’s blessing. “Profane” means treating sacred things as common.

“*For you know that even when he afterward desired to inherit the blessing, he was rejected, for he found no place for a change of mind though he sought it diligently with tears*” (*v. 17*). Later, Esau wanted the blessing, but it had been given to Jacob (*Genesis 27:30–40*). His tears could not undo his choice. “No place for a change of mind” likely means he could not reverse the consequences or change his father’s decision. The warning is that some choices have lasting consequences. This is not meant to frighten those who sincerely seek God’s forgiveness; God always welcomes the repentant. It warns against treating God’s gifts with contempt.

### Sinai and Zion (*12:18–24*)

“*For you have not come to a mountain that might be touched and that burned with fire, and to blackness, darkness, storm*” (*v. 18*), “*the sound of a trumpet, and the voice of words; which those who heard it begged that not one more word should be spoken to them*” (*v. 19*), “*for they could not stand that which was commanded, “If even an animal touches the mountain, it shall be stoned”.*” (*v. 20*) “*So fearful was the appearance that Moses said, “I am terrified and trembling.”*” (*v. 21*) When God gave the Law at Mount Sinai, the scene was terrifying: fire, darkness, storm, trumpet blasts, and God’s voice (*Exodus 19:16–19*; *20:18–21*; *Deuteronomy 9:19*). The people were kept at a distance. Even Moses trembled.

“*But you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to innumerable multitudes of angels*” (*v. 22*), “*to the festal gathering and assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven, to God the Judge of all, to the spirits of just men made perfect*” (*v. 23*), “*to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, and to the blood of sprinkling that speaks better than that of Abel*” (*v. 24*). In contrast, believers have come to Mount Zion, the heavenly city. Notice the tense: “you have come.” By faith, believers already belong to this heavenly reality. They are part of a joyful celebration with countless angels and the whole church, “the firstborn,” whose names are written in heaven. They come to God, the Judge of all, and to the righteous of past ages, now made perfect. And they come to Jesus, whose blood speaks a better word than Abel’s. Abel’s blood cried out for justice (*Genesis 4:10*); Jesus’ blood speaks of forgiveness and reconciliation.

### An Unshakable Kingdom (*12:25–29*)

“*See that you don’t refuse him who speaks. For if they didn’t escape when they refused him who warned on the earth, how much more will we not escape who turn away from him who warns from heaven*” (*v. 25*), “*whose voice shook the earth then, but now he has promised, saying, “Yet once more I will shake not only the earth, but also the heavens.”*” (*v. 26*) This is the final warning in Hebrews. At Sinai, God’s voice shook the earth. He promised through the prophet Haggai to shake heaven and earth once more (*Haggai 2:6*).

“*This phrase, “Yet once more” signifies the removing of those things that are shaken, as of things that have been made, that those things which are not shaken may remain*” (*v. 27*). God’s final shaking will remove everything temporary, leaving only what is eternal. The believer’s response is studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Hebrews 12:1–2* — Looking to Jesus

> *“Therefore let’s also, seeing we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, lay aside every weight and the sin which so easily entangles us, and let’s run with perseverance the race that is set before us, looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising its shame, and has sat down at the right hand of the throne of God.”*
>
> — *Hebrews 12:1–2* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“Therefore let’s also, seeing we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses.” The “witnesses” are the people of faith described in chapter 11. They surround believers like a crowd in a stadium. They are witnesses not mainly in the sense of spectators watching, but of those who bear witness, by their lives, that faith in God is worth it.

“Lay aside every weight and the sin which so easily entangles us.” Runners in the ancient games stripped off anything that would slow them down. Believers must lay aside “every weight,” things that may not be sinful in themselves but hinder their progress, and “the sin which so easily entangles,” sin that wraps around them like a long robe tangling a runner’s legs.

“And let’s run with perseverance the race that is set before us.” The Christian life is a race, not a sprint but a long-distance run requiring endurance. Each believer has a race “set before” them by God.

Verse 2: “looking to Jesus.” Runners fix their eyes on the finish line. Believers fix their eyes on Jesus.

“The author and perfecter of faith.” Jesus is the “author,” the pioneer or champion who blazed the trail of faith, and the “perfecter,” the one who completed it perfectly and who brings His people’s faith to completion.

“Who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising its shame.” Jesus endured the agony and humiliation of crucifixion because He looked beyond it to the joy that would follow: the joy of accomplishing salvation, of returning to the Father, and of bringing many children to glory. He “despised the shame,” refusing to let the disgrace of the cross stop Him.

“And has sat down at the right hand of the throne of God.” Jesus finished His race and now reigns in glory.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses describe the heart of Christian endurance. The secret is not willpower but focus: looking to Jesus. He is both the model and the source of faith. He ran the race before His people, and He runs with them now.

The word “joy” is striking in connection with the cross. Jesus did not enjoy suffering, but He endured it for the joy beyond it. This gives believers a pattern for their own hardships: looking beyond present pain to the joy God has promised.

The phrase “the race that is set before us” suggests that each believer’s race is unique. God sets the course. Some face more obvious hardships than others. But all are called to run with endurance and to keep their eyes on Jesus.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can ask what weights are slowing them down. These might include distractions, unhealthy relationships, misplaced priorities, or habits that are not sinful in themselves but hinder their spiritual growth. They can also identify specific sins that tend to entangle them and ask for God’s help to put them off.

When believers are weary, discouraged, or tempted to quit, they can look to Jesus. Reading the Gospels, meditating on His endurance, and remembering His victory can renew their strength.

Finally, believers can remember that they are not alone. The faithful of past generations show that the race can be run. And Jesus Himself waits at the finish line.

### *Hebrews 12:10–11* — The Peaceful Fruit of Righteousness

> *“For they indeed for a few days disciplined us as seemed good to them, but he for our profit, that we may be partakers of his holiness. All chastening seems for the present to be not joyous but grievous; yet afterward it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.”*
>
> — *Hebrews 12:10–11* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The author compares human fathers with God. “For they indeed for a few days disciplined us as seemed good to them.” Human fathers disciplined their children for a limited time, during childhood, and according to their own judgment, which was not always perfect.

“But he for our profit, that we may be partakers of his holiness.” God’s discipline is always for believers’ good. Its goal is that they would share in His holiness, becoming more like Him.

Verse 11: “All chastening seems for the present to be not joyous but grievous.” Discipline is painful. The author does not pretend otherwise.

“Yet afterward it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.” Over time, discipline produces good results: righteousness and peace. “Trained” is the athletic word from which “gymnasium” comes. Discipline is like an athlete’s training, difficult but strengthening.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

“Discipline” in Hebrews means training, not merely punishment. It includes all the ways God shapes His children, especially through hardship. The readers’ sufferings, including persecution, were being used by God to train them. This does not mean God causes every evil; persecution came from human sin. But God uses even hardship for His children’s good (*Romans 8:28*; *James 1:2–4*).

It is very important to read this passage rightly. It describes God’s perfect, loving discipline, not human abuse. The author acknowledges that human fathers disciplined “as seemed good to them,” that is, imperfectly. This passage must never be used to justify harsh treatment, abuse, or violence toward children or anyone else. God’s discipline is always loving, always purposeful, and always for good. Human discipline that harms, humiliates, or terrorizes is not a reflection of God’s character. Those who have been abused, whether by parents, spouses, or leaders, should know that God does not approve of what was done to them, and that seeking safety and help is right.

The promise of “the peaceful fruit of righteousness” gives hope. Believers may not understand their hardships now, but God is producing something good in them. *Romans 5:3–5* describes a similar process: suffering produces endurance, endurance produces character, and character produces hope.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

When believers face hardships, they can ask not only “Why is this happening?” but also “What is God teaching me through this?” Hardship can become a means of growth, deepening trust, patience, and holiness.

Believers can also be honest about pain. The author admits that discipline is “not joyous but grievous.” Faith does not require pretending that hard things are pleasant.

Finally, believers can hold onto hope. The fruit of discipline often comes “afterward.” What seems painful and pointless now may later produce peace and righteousness.

### *Hebrews 12:14–15* — Pursue Peace and Holiness

> *“Follow after peace with all men, and the sanctification without which no man will see the Lord, looking carefully lest there be any man who falls short of the grace of God, lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you and many be defiled by it,”*
>
> — *Hebrews 12:14–15* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“Follow after peace with all men.” “Follow after” means to pursue eagerly, to chase. Believers are to actively seek peace with everyone, not just fellow believers, as far as it depends on them (*Romans 12:18*).

“And the sanctification without which no man will see the Lord.” Believers must also pursue holiness. “Sanctification” here means holiness of life. Those who do not pursue holiness will not see the Lord. This does not mean that holiness earns salvation, which Hebrews has clearly shown comes through Christ’s sacrifice. It means that genuine faith always produces a growing holiness, and those who reject holiness show that they do not truly know God. Jesus said, “*Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God*” (*Matthew 5:8*).

Verse 15: “looking carefully lest there be any man who falls short of the grace of God.” Believers are to watch over one another, making sure no one drifts away from God’s grace.

“Lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you and many be defiled by it.” Bitterness is like a poisonous root. It may start small, but it grows and spreads, affecting many people. This phrase echoes *Deuteronomy 29:18*, which warns against a root bearing bitter poison among God’s people.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Peace and holiness go together. Peace without holiness can become compromise, tolerating sin for the sake of avoiding conflict. Holiness without peace can become harshness, judging others without love. Believers are called to pursue both.

The call to watch over one another is a community responsibility. As in *Hebrews 3:12–13* and *10:24–25*, believers are responsible for one another’s spiritual well-being. They are to notice when someone is drifting and help them return.

Bitterness is especially dangerous because it spreads. A bitter person can poison a whole community through gossip, resentment, and division. Paul urges believers to put away all bitterness and to forgive one another as God in Christ forgave them (*Ephesians 4:31–32*). Addressing bitterness, including bitterness arising from real hurts, is important for the health of both individuals and communities. Healing may require honest acknowledgment of wrongs, forgiveness, and sometimes the help of a counselor or pastor.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can ask whether they are actively pursuing peace in their relationships. Are there conflicts they need to address, apologies to make, or bridges to rebuild?

They can also examine their pursuit of holiness. Are there areas of life they have not surrendered to God? Holiness is not perfection, but it is a direction of life.

Finally, believers can watch for bitterness in their own hearts. Unresolved hurt can turn into bitterness that poisons relationships. Bringing those hurts to God, seeking healing, and choosing to forgive can uproot bitterness before it spreads.

### *Hebrews 12:28–29* — A Kingdom That Cannot Be Shaken

> *“Therefore, receiving a Kingdom that can’t be shaken, let’s have grace, through which we serve God acceptably, with reverence and awe, for our God is a consuming fire.”*
>
> — *Hebrews 12:28–29* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“Therefore, receiving a Kingdom that can’t be shaken.” God will one day shake heaven and earth, removing everything temporary (vv26–27). But believers are receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken. God’s kingdom is eternal and secure. Notice the present tense: believers are already receiving it.

“Let’s have grace, through which we serve God acceptably.” The phrase can also be translated “let us be thankful.” The right response to receiving an unshakable kingdom is gratitude, which leads to serving God in a way that pleases Him.

“With reverence and awe.” Worship should be marked by reverence and holy fear. Though believers have bold access to God through Christ (*Hebrews 4:16*; *10:19*), they should never treat Him lightly.

Verse 29: “for our God is a consuming fire.” This phrase comes from *Deuteronomy 4:24*. God is holy, and His holiness consumes everything impure. The God of the new covenant is the same holy God who appeared at Sinai.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses bring together the security and the seriousness of the Christian life. Believers are receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken. Everything else in the world, governments, economies, institutions, and even the physical universe, can and will be shaken. But God’s kingdom will stand forever. *Daniel 2:44* prophesied that God would set up a kingdom that would never be destroyed.

At the same time, the God who gives this kingdom is a consuming fire. The new covenant brings believers near to God, but it does not make Him less holy. Grace does not cancel reverence; it deepens it. Those who understand how much God has given and how holy He is will respond with both gratitude and awe.

The call to serve God “acceptably” means worshiping Him in ways that please Him. *Hebrews 13:15–16* will explain that acceptable worship includes praise, confession of His name, doing good, and sharing with others.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

In a world where so much feels unstable, believers can rest in the security of God’s kingdom. Whatever is shaken in their lives, whether health, finances, relationships, or nations, God’s kingdom remains.

This truth calls for gratitude. Believers can cultivate thankfulness in prayer and worship, remembering the unshakable kingdom they are receiving.

Finally, believers can approach God with both confidence and reverence. They are welcome in His presence through Christ, but He is holy. Worship that combines joy and awe honors the God who is both loving and a consuming fire.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Hebrews 12* calls weary believers to keep running. Surrounded by a great cloud of witnesses who proved that faith is worth it, they are to throw off every weight and entangling sin and run with endurance the race God has set before them. The key is to look to Jesus, the pioneer and perfecter of faith, who endured the cross for the joy set before Him and is now seated at God’s right hand. When believers grow tired, they can consider Him.

The chapter also helps believers understand hardship. God uses the trials of life as loving discipline, training His children to share in His holiness. Discipline is painful at the time, but later it produces the peaceful fruit of righteousness. This describes God’s perfect love, never human abuse, which God opposes. Believers can face hardship with honesty and hope, trusting that God is at work.

Believers are called to strengthen one another, to pursue peace with everyone and the holiness without which no one will see the Lord, to watch that no one falls short of grace, and to guard against bitterness and against despising God’s gifts like Esau.

Finally, the chapter reminds believers of their glorious privilege. They have not come to the terrifying mountain of Sinai, but to Mount Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem, to joyful angels, to the whole church, to God the Judge of all, and to Jesus, whose blood speaks a better word than Abel’s. They must not refuse the God who speaks from heaven. They are receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken, so they can respond with gratitude and worship God with reverence and awe, for He is a consuming fire.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, You are the author and perfecter of my faith. Help me to throw off every weight and the sin that so easily entangles me, and to run with endurance the race You have set before me, keeping my eyes on You. Thank You for enduring the cross for the joy set before You. When I grow weary, help me to consider You. Father, when I face hardship, help me to trust that You are training me in love to share in Your holiness, and let it produce the peaceful fruit of righteousness. Heal those who have been wounded by harsh and unloving treatment. Help me to pursue peace with everyone and holiness of life, and guard my heart from bitterness. Thank You that I have come to Mount Zion and to Jesus, whose blood speaks a better word. Thank You for a kingdom that cannot be shaken. Fill me with gratitude, and help me to worship You with reverence and awe. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Hebrews · Chapter 13 of 13

# Hebrews — Chapter 13

Chapter Theme: Living as Those Who Belong to an Unshakable Kingdom

[Read Hebrews 13 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/HEB13.htm)

Main Teaching

The author closes with practical instructions for the community: keep loving one another as brothers and sisters, show hospitality to strangers, remember prisoners and the mistreated as if suffering with them, honor marriage and keep it pure, and stay free from the love of money, content with what you have, because God has promised never to leave or forsake His people, so they can say, “The Lord is my helper; I will not fear.” Believers should remember the leaders who taught them and imitate their faith, for Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever. They should not be carried away by strange teachings about foods but be strengthened by grace. Since Jesus suffered outside the city gate to make His people holy through His own blood, they should go to Him outside the camp, bearing His disgrace, for they have no lasting city here but seek the one to come. Through Him they offer a sacrifice of praise and do good and share, which pleases God. They are to obey and submit to their leaders, who keep watch over their souls, and pray for the author. He closes with a beautiful blessing, praying that the God of peace, who brought back from the dead our Lord Jesus, the great Shepherd of the sheep, through the blood of the eternal covenant, would equip them with everything good to do His will, followed by personal news and greetings.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Hebrews 12* ended with the call to worship God acceptably with reverence and awe, as those receiving an unshakable kingdom (*Hebrews 12:28*). Chapter 13 shows what that acceptable worship looks like in daily life. It is not only what happens in a gathering for worship; it is love, hospitality, compassion, faithfulness in marriage, contentment, loyalty to Christ, praise, generosity, and respect for faithful leaders.

The chapter has a different style from the rest of the letter. It reads more like the end of a typical New Testament letter, with practical exhortations, a request for prayer, a blessing, and personal greetings. Yet it continues the main themes of Hebrews: Christ’s once-for-all sacrifice, the contrast between earthly and heavenly realities, and the call to endure.

The readers were facing the temptation to return to the familiar securities of their former religious life, perhaps the temple, its sacrifices, and its food regulations. The author calls them instead to follow Jesus “outside the camp,” accepting the disgrace that comes with belonging to Him, because their true city lies ahead.

### Love in Practice (*13:1–4*)

“*Let brotherly love continue*” (*v. 1*). The readers had shown love before (*Hebrews 6:10*; *10:33–34*). Now they must keep it going. Love is not a one-time act but an ongoing way of life. The calls to hospitality and compassion are studied below.

“*Let marriage be held in honor among all, and let the bed be undefiled; but God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterers*” (*v. 4*). Marriage is to be honored by everyone, both by those who are married and by those who are not. “The bed” refers to sexual union, which should be kept pure within marriage. This counters both the sexual immorality common in the surrounding culture and any teaching that treated marriage as unspiritual (*1 Timothy 4:3*). Faithfulness in marriage honors God; adultery and sexual immorality break covenant trust and harm others. Honoring marriage also means that no one should be harmed within it; marriages marked by abuse dishonor God’s design, and those in danger should seek safety and help.

### Contentment and Courage (*13:5–6*)

The call to contentment and its foundation in God’s promise are studied below.

### Faithful Leaders and an Unchanging Christ (*13:7–9*)

“*Remember your leaders, men who spoke to you the word of God, and considering the results of their conduct, imitate their faith*” (*v. 7*). These were likely the leaders who first brought the gospel to the readers, some of whom may have died, perhaps as martyrs. The readers should remember them, reflect on the outcome of their lives, and follow their example of faith. The unchanging nature of Christ is studied below.

“*Don’t be carried away by various and strange teachings, for it is good that the heart be established by grace, not by foods, through which those who were so occupied were not benefited*” (*v. 9*). Some were teaching that spiritual strength came through eating or avoiding certain foods, perhaps relating to Jewish food laws or to sacrificial meals. The author says the heart is strengthened by God’s grace, not by food rules.

### Outside the Camp (*13:10–14*)

“*We have an altar from which those who serve the holy tabernacle have no right to eat*” (*v. 10*). The “altar” may refer to the cross, or more broadly to Christ’s sacrifice. Those who still rely on the old sacrificial system do not share in the benefits of Christ’s sacrifice.

“*For the bodies of those animals, whose blood is brought into the holy place by the high priest as an offering for sin, are burned outside of the camp*” (*v. 11*). On the Day of Atonement, the bodies of the sacrificed animals were burned outside the camp (*Leviticus 16:27*).

“*Therefore Jesus also, that he might sanctify the people through his own blood, suffered outside of the gate*” (*v. 12*). Jesus was crucified outside the walls of Jerusalem (*John 19:17*, 20). Like the sin offering, He was taken “outside” as an outcast. There, through His own blood, He made His people holy.

“*Let’s therefore go out to him outside of the camp, bearing his reproach*” (*v. 13*). Believers are called to leave behind the security of the old religious system and of the world’s approval and to identify with Jesus, even if it brings disgrace. Following Christ may mean rejection by those who once accepted them.

“*For we don’t have here an enduring city, but we seek that which is to come*” (*v. 14*). This echoes *Hebrews 11:10*, 13–16. Believers are pilgrims seeking the city God has prepared. Earthly cities, even Jerusalem, are not their final home.

### Sacrifices That Please God (*13:15–16*)

“*Through him, then, let’s offer up a sacrifice of praise to God continually, that is, the fruit of lips which proclaim allegiance to his name*” (*v. 15*). Christ’s once-for-all sacrifice has ended the need for animal sacrifices. But believers still offer sacrifices: praise to God, offered through Jesus, continually. “The fruit of lips” echoes *Hosea 14:2*.

“*But don’t forget to be doing good and sharing, for with such sacrifices God is well pleased*” (*v. 16*). Acts of kindness and generosity are also sacrifices that please God. Worship includes both praise and practical love.

### Leaders and Prayer (*13:17–19*)

“*Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they watch on behalf of your souls, as those who will give account, that they may do this with joy and not with groaning, for that would be unprofitable for you*” (*v. 17*). Believers are to follow and respect faithful leaders, whose role is to care for their souls and who will give an account to God. Cooperating with them makes their work a joy. This instruction assumes leaders who are teaching God’s word and caring for the flock, like those described in verse 7. It does not require obedience to leaders who command sin, teach falsehood, or abuse their position. Leaders are themselves accountable to God, and the New Testament consistently warns against leaders who lord it over others (*1 Peter 5:2–3*). When leaders cause harm, believers should seek help and accountability, not silent submission.

“*Pray for us, for we are persuaded that we have a good conscience, desiring to live honorably in all things*” (*v. 18*). “*I strongly urge you to do this, that I may be restored to you sooner*” (*v. 19*). The author asks for prayer. Something was preventing him from visiting, and he hoped their prayers would help him return.

### Benediction and Greetings (*13:20–25*)

The closing blessing is studied below. “*But I exhort you, brothers, endure the word of exhortation, for I have written to you in few words*” (*v. 22*). The author calls his letter “the word of exhortation,” perhaps describing it as a sermon. He asks them to receive it patiently. Its “few words” may seem an understatement, but compared with all that could be said about Christ, it is brief.

“*Know that our brother Timothy has been freed, with whom, if he comes shortly, I will see you*” (*v. 23*). Timothy, Paul’s coworker, had been imprisoned and released. This is the only mention of Timothy’s imprisonment in the New Testament.

“*Greet all of your leaders and all the saints. The Italians greet you*” (*v. 24*). “The Italians” may mean believers in Italy, suggesting the author was writing from there, or Italian believers living elsewhere and sending greetings home, suggesting the letter was sent to Rome. “*Grace be with you all. Amen*” (*v. 25*).

## Important Verses Explained

### *Hebrews 13:2–3* — Hospitality and Compassion

> *“Don’t forget to show hospitality to strangers, for in doing so, some have entertained angels without knowing it. Remember those who are in bonds, as bound with them, and those who are ill-treated, since you are also in the body.”*
>
> — *Hebrews 13:2–3* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“Don’t forget to show hospitality to strangers.” Hospitality was vital in the ancient world, especially for traveling believers who needed safe places to stay. The word means “love of strangers.” Believers are to welcome people they do not know.

“For in doing so, some have entertained angels without knowing it.” This recalls Abraham, who welcomed three visitors who turned out to be messengers of God (*Genesis 18:1–8*), and Lot, who sheltered two angels (*Genesis 19:1–3*). Hospitality may bring unexpected blessing.

Verse 3: “Remember those who are in bonds, as bound with them.” Believers who were imprisoned for their faith depended on others for food, clothing, and encouragement. The readers had done this before (*Hebrews 10:34*). They are to keep remembering prisoners as if they themselves were in chains.

“And those who are ill-treated, since you are also in the body.” Believers should care for those who are suffering, remembering that they too are vulnerable, living in physical bodies that can suffer. It may also mean “since you too are part of the body,” the body of Christ, where the suffering of one member affects all.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that love for one another must extend beyond the familiar. Hospitality reaches out to strangers. Compassion reaches out to prisoners and the suffering. Jesus said that those who welcome strangers and visit prisoners are serving Him (*Matthew 25:35–40*).

The phrase “as bound with them” calls for empathy, imagining oneself in another’s situation. Believers are not to remember the suffering from a comfortable distance but to identify with them. Paul expresses a similar idea: “*When one member suffers, all the members suffer with it*” (*1 Corinthians 12:26*).

Hospitality in Scripture is not about impressive entertaining but about generous welcome. It was a mark of God’s people in the Old Testament (*Leviticus 19:33–34*) and a qualification for church leaders (*1 Timothy 3:2*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can practice hospitality by welcoming newcomers at church, inviting people into their homes, helping refugees and immigrants, and showing kindness to strangers. It does not require a large house or elaborate meals, only an open heart.

Believers can also remember those who are imprisoned, including Christians persecuted for their faith around the world, and those in local prisons. Prayer, letters, advocacy, and support for prison ministries are ways to do this.

Finally, believers can show compassion to anyone who is suffering, mistreated, or overlooked, remembering that they share the same human frailty and belong to the same body of Christ.

### *Hebrews 13:5–6* — I Will Never Leave You

> *“Be free from the love of money, content with such things as you have, for he has said, ‘I will in no way leave you, neither will I in any way forsake you.’ So that with good courage we say, ‘The Lord is my helper. I will not fear. What can man do to me?’”*
>
> — *Hebrews 13:5–6* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“Be free from the love of money.” Greed was a constant temptation, especially for those who had lost property through persecution (*Hebrews 10:34*). Believers are to keep their lives free from the desire for wealth.

“Content with such things as you have.” Contentment means being satisfied with what God provides.

“For he has said, ‘I will in no way leave you, neither will I in any way forsake you.’” The reason for contentment is God’s presence. This promise echoes God’s words to Israel and Joshua (*Deuteronomy 31:6*, 8; *Joshua 1:5*). In Greek, it is very emphatic: “I will never, ever leave you; I will never, never forsake you.”

Verse 6: “So that with good courage we say, ‘The Lord is my helper. I will not fear. What can man do to me?’” Quoting *Psalm 118:6*, the author shows that God’s presence produces courage. If the Lord is their helper, believers need not fear what people can do.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses connect money, contentment, and God’s presence. People often seek security in money because they fear being without resources. But true security comes from God’s promise never to leave His people. Those who have God have everything they need.

This truth was especially important for the readers, who had already lost possessions and might face more loss. God’s promise assured them that, whatever they lost, they would never lose Him.

The quotation from *Psalm 118* shows that God’s presence produces courage. People can harm the body, take possessions, and cause suffering, but they cannot separate believers from God. Jesus said not to fear those who can kill the body but cannot kill the soul (*Matthew 10:28*). Paul declared that nothing can separate believers from the love of God in Christ (*Romans 8:35–39*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can examine their relationship with money. Are they driven by the desire for more? Do they find their security in savings or possessions? This verse invites them to find their security in God instead.

When believers face financial loss, uncertainty, or fear, they can hold onto God’s promise: “I will in no way leave you.” His presence is the one thing that can never be taken away.

This promise also brings courage in the face of opposition or danger. Believers can say with confidence, “The Lord is my helper; I will not fear.”

### *Hebrews 13:8* — The Same Yesterday, Today, and Forever

> *“Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever.”*
>
> — *Hebrews 13:8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever.”

“Yesterday”: Jesus was faithful in the past, during His earthly ministry, in His death and resurrection, and in the lives of the leaders who first taught the readers (v7).

“Today”: Jesus is the same now. He is still faithful, still the great high priest interceding for His people, still able to save completely.

“And forever”: Jesus will never change. His character, His promises, and His love will remain the same for all eternity.

This verse comes right after the call to remember past leaders (v7) and right before a warning against strange teachings (v9). Leaders come and go, and teachings change, but Jesus remains the same.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse echoes *Hebrews 1:12*, where the Son is described as unchanging: “you are the same. Your years won’t fail.” The unchangeableness of Christ is a mark of His divinity. God says, “*For I, the LORD, don't change*” (*Malachi 3:6*). Jesus shares that unchanging nature.

This verse is also a strong reason not to be swayed by new teachings. If Jesus is the same, the gospel about Him does not change. Believers do not need to search for new revelations or novel ideas. The Christ their first leaders proclaimed is the same Christ today.

The unchanging Christ also means that everything He did and promised in the Gospels is still true. His compassion for the suffering, His forgiveness of sinners, His power over evil, and His welcome to the outcast are all as real today as they were then.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

In a world of constant change, believers can find stability in Christ. Relationships change, circumstances shift, and leaders pass away, but Jesus remains the same.

When believers read the Gospels, they can know that the Jesus they meet there is the same Jesus who is with them now. His love, power, and faithfulness have not diminished.

This verse also helps believers evaluate new teachings. Anything that contradicts the unchanging gospel of Christ should be rejected, however new or appealing it may seem.

### *Hebrews 13:20–21* — The God of Peace and the Great Shepherd

> *“Now may the God of peace, who brought again from the dead the great shepherd of the sheep with the blood of an eternal covenant, our Lord Jesus, make you complete in every good work to do his will, working in you that which is well pleasing in his sight, through Jesus Christ, to whom be the glory forever and ever. Amen.”*
>
> — *Hebrews 13:20–21* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The author closes with a beautiful prayer of blessing.

“Now may the God of peace.” God is the source of peace, wholeness, and reconciliation.

“Who brought again from the dead the great shepherd of the sheep.” This is the only explicit mention of the resurrection in Hebrews. God raised Jesus from the dead. Jesus is “the great shepherd,” greater than Moses, who led Israel like a shepherd (*Isaiah 63:11*), and the fulfillment of Jesus’ own words: “*I am the good shepherd*” (*John 10:11*).

“With the blood of an eternal covenant.” Jesus’ resurrection is connected to His sacrifice. His blood established the new covenant, which is eternal and will never be replaced.

“Our Lord Jesus.” He is the Lord of His people.

Verse 21: “make you complete in every good work to do his will.” The author prays that God would equip believers with everything they need to do His will. “Make you complete” can mean to restore, to repair, or to prepare.

“Working in you that which is well pleasing in his sight, through Jesus Christ.” God Himself works in believers, producing what pleases Him. He does it through Jesus Christ.

“To whom be the glory forever and ever. Amen.” All glory belongs to God, through Christ, forever.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This benediction gathers up the major themes of Hebrews: God’s peace, Christ’s resurrection, His role as shepherd and leader, His blood, the eternal covenant, and God’s work in believers. It is a summary of the gospel in the form of a prayer.

The prayer shows the balance between God’s work and believers’ responsibility. Believers are called to do God’s will, but God equips them to do it and works in them what pleases Him. This echoes *Philippians 2:12–13*: believers work out their salvation, for God is at work in them, both to will and to do His good pleasure.

The image of Jesus as “the great shepherd of the sheep” is tender. Throughout Hebrews, Jesus has been presented as high priest and Son. Here He is the Shepherd who leads, protects, feeds, and cares for His flock. For weary believers, this image brings comfort: they are not alone; their Shepherd leads them.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can pray this benediction for themselves and others. It is a prayer for God’s peace, for equipping to do His will, and for His work within them.

When believers feel inadequate for what God is calling them to do, they can take comfort that God equips them “in every good work” and works in them what pleases Him. They do not serve in their own strength.

Finally, believers can rest in the care of their great Shepherd. The one who rose from the dead leads them, protects them, and will bring them safely home.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Hebrews 13* shows what it looks like to live as people who are receiving an unshakable kingdom. Acceptable worship to God is not only what happens in a gathering but also love for one another, hospitality to strangers, compassion for prisoners and the mistreated, faithfulness in marriage, and freedom from the love of money. These are practical expressions of faith.

At the heart of the chapter are two great promises. First, God has said, “I will in no way leave you, neither will I in any way forsake you.” This promise frees believers from the love of money and gives them courage to say, “The Lord is my helper; I will not fear.” Second, Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever. In a changing world, believers can rest in His unchanging faithfulness and resist teachings that depart from the gospel.

The chapter calls believers to follow Jesus “outside the camp,” accepting the disgrace that comes with belonging to Him, because they have no lasting city here but seek the one to come. They offer God sacrifices of praise and sacrifices of doing good and sharing, which please Him. They honor faithful leaders who care for their souls, while remembering that leaders, too, are accountable to God and must never abuse their trust.

The letter closes with a rich blessing: may the God of peace, who brought back from the dead our Lord Jesus, the great Shepherd of the sheep, through the blood of the eternal covenant, equip believers with everything good to do His will, working in them what pleases Him. Believers can walk forward with confidence, led by their Shepherd, equipped by God, and secure in His unchanging love.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord God, help me to keep loving my brothers and sisters, to show hospitality to strangers, and to remember those who are imprisoned and mistreated as though I were suffering with them. Help me to honor marriage and to keep my life free from the love of money. Thank You for Your promise that You will never leave me nor forsake me. The Lord is my helper; I will not fear. Thank You that Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever. Keep me from strange teachings, and strengthen my heart by grace. Help me to follow Jesus outside the camp, bearing His disgrace, seeking the city that is to come. Accept my sacrifice of praise, and make me generous in doing good and sharing. Now, God of peace, who brought back from the dead our Lord Jesus, the great Shepherd of the sheep, through the blood of the eternal covenant, equip me with everything good to do Your will, and work in me what is pleasing in Your sight, through Jesus Christ, to whom be the glory forever and ever. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Book 20 of 27

# James

## About This Letter

The letter of James was written by “*James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ*” (*James 1:1*). Most Christians through history have identified him as James the brother of Jesus. During Jesus’ ministry, His brothers did not believe in Him (*John 7:5*), but after the resurrection Jesus appeared to James (*1 Corinthians 15:7*), and James became a leading figure in the Jerusalem church (*Acts 12:17*; *15:13–21*; *21:18*; *Galatians 1:19*; *2:9*). He was known for his deep devotion and prayer. According to the Jewish historian Josephus, he was put to death in Jerusalem around A.D. 62.

James writes “to the twelve tribes which are in the Dispersion,” most likely Jewish believers in Jesus scattered beyond the land of Israel, perhaps after the persecution that followed Stephen’s death (*Acts 8:1*; *11:19*). Many scholars believe it is one of the earliest New Testament writings, perhaps from the A.D. 40s; others date it closer to James’s death. Some modern scholars think a later writer used James’s name, while many others find the letter’s simple Jewish-Christian setting fits the brother of Jesus well.

James reads much like the wisdom books of the Old Testament, such as Proverbs, and like the Sermon on the Mount. Its short, vivid sayings and images echo the teaching of Jesus again and again.

## The Shape of the Letter

James moves quickly from topic to topic, returning often to a few great themes. Chapter 1 teaches joy in trials, asking God for wisdom, the source of temptation, God’s good gifts, and the call to be doers of the word, not hearers only. Chapter 2 condemns favoritism toward the rich and insists that faith without works is dead. Chapter 3 warns about the power of the tongue and contrasts earthly wisdom with the wisdom from above. Chapter 4 exposes the roots of conflict, calls for humble submission to God, and warns against judging others and boasting about tomorrow. Chapter 5 confronts rich oppressors, encourages patience until the Lord’s coming, and closes with teaching on honest speech, prayer for the sick, confession, and restoring those who wander.

## Themes to Watch For

Watch for genuine faith that shows itself in action, endurance in trials, wisdom from God, the danger and power of words, care for the poor and the vulnerable, warnings against favoritism and the arrogance of wealth, humility before God, patience, and the power of prayer. James has sometimes been thought to conflict with Paul’s teaching on faith, but the two writers address different problems: Paul insists that no one is made right with God by works, and James insists that the faith that saves is never a faith that does nothing.

2.  [James 2](#c20_JAS_002.xhtml) — Faith Without Favoritism, Faith That Works
