James · Chapter 4 of 5

# James — Chapter 4

Chapter Theme: Humble Yourselves Before the Lord

[Read James 4 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/JAS04.htm)

Main Teaching

James asks where the fights and quarrels among believers come from, and answers that they come from desires battling within them. They want what they do not have, so they quarrel and fight; they do not have because they do not ask God, and when they ask, they ask with wrong motives, to spend on their own pleasures. Friendship with the world, adopting its values, is hostility toward God, like spiritual adultery. Yet God gives more grace, opposing the proud but giving grace to the humble. So believers must submit to God, resist the devil, draw near to God, cleanse their hands and purify their hearts, grieve over their sin, and humble themselves before the Lord, who will lift them up. They must not speak evil against or judge one another, because there is only one Lawgiver and Judge. James then rebukes those who confidently plan their business ventures as if they controlled the future, reminding them that life is a mist that appears briefly and vanishes; they should say instead, “*If the Lord wills, we will both live, and do this or that*” (*v. 15*). Finally, anyone who knows the right thing to do and fails to do it commits sin.

## Chapter Background and Story

*James 3* ended by contrasting earthly wisdom, which produces envy, selfish ambition, and disorder, with heavenly wisdom, which produces peace. Chapter 4 shows what earthly wisdom looks like in practice: fights, quarrels, envy, and pride. The community James addressed was apparently troubled by conflict, perhaps over status, resources, or influence.

James diagnoses the root of these conflicts: selfish desires. He then calls believers to repentance, using some of the strongest language in his letter. But his call is full of hope. God gives more grace. Those who humble themselves will be lifted up. Those who draw near to God will find Him drawing near to them.

The final section addresses a different but related form of pride: the arrogance of planning life as though one were in control. James was likely speaking to merchants who traveled from city to city to trade. Their problem was not planning itself, but planning without reference to God.

### The Source of Conflict (*4:1–3*)

The source of fights and the problem of wrong motives in prayer are studied below.

### Friendship with the World (*4:4–6*)

“*You adulterers and adulteresses, don’t you know that friendship with the world is hostility toward God? Whoever therefore wants to be a friend of the world makes himself an enemy of God*” (*v. 4*). James uses the image of adultery, which the Old Testament prophets often used for Israel’s unfaithfulness to God (*Hosea 1–3*; *Jeremiah 3:20*). God’s people are like a bride pledged to Him. When they give their love to the world, its values, priorities, and pleasures, they are being unfaithful. “The world” here does not mean creation or people, whom God loves (*John 3:16*), but the system of values and desires opposed to God (*1 John 2:15–17*).

“*Or do you think that the Scripture says in vain, “The Spirit who lives in us yearns jealously”?*” (*v. 5*) This verse is difficult. James does not quote a specific Old Testament verse, but summarizes a biblical theme. Interpreters understand it in two main ways. It may mean that God jealously longs for the spirit He placed in human beings, wanting their undivided devotion, as a faithful husband longs for his wife’s love (*Exodus 20:5*; *34:14*). Or it may mean that the human spirit, left to itself, tends toward envy. The first reading fits the context of spiritual adultery well: God’s love is a jealous love that will not share His people with rivals. The call to humility and drawing near is studied below.

### Do Not Judge One Another (*4:11–12*)

“*Don’t speak against one another, brothers. He who speaks against a brother and judges his brother, speaks against the law and judges the law. But if you judge the law, you are not a doer of the law but a judge*” (*v. 11*). Slander and harsh judgment of fellow believers break the royal law of love (*James 2:8*). Those who judge others in this way place themselves above the law, acting as if they were the lawgiver rather than those under the law.

“*Only one is the lawgiver, who is able to save and to destroy. But who are you to judge another?*” (*v. 12*) God alone is the Lawgiver and Judge. He alone has the authority and knowledge to judge rightly. This does not forbid all discernment or correction; Scripture calls believers to recognize sin and to restore those who fall (*Galatians 6:1*; *Matthew 18:15*). It forbids condemning, slandering, and setting oneself up as judge over others’ hearts. Jesus taught, “*Don't judge, so that you won't be judged*” (*Matthew 7:1*).

### Boasting About Tomorrow (*4:13–17*)

The warning against arrogant planning and the sin of omission are studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *James 4:1–3* — The Source of Quarrels

> *“Where do wars and fightings among you come from? Don’t they come from your pleasures that war in your members? You lust, and don’t have. You murder and covet, and can’t obtain. You fight and make war. You don’t have, because you don’t ask. You ask, and don’t receive, because you ask with wrong motives, so that you may spend it on your pleasures.”*
>
> — *James 4:1–3* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“Where do wars and fightings among you come from?” James asks a direct question about the conflicts in the community. “Wars and fightings” describe ongoing quarrels and disputes.

“Don’t they come from your pleasures that war in your members?” The conflicts come from within. “Pleasures” means desires for gratification. These desires are at war within people, and they spill out into conflicts with others.

Verse 2: “You lust, and don’t have.” People desire things they do not have. “You murder and covet, and can’t obtain.” James may be speaking literally of violence that arises from desire, or he may use “murder” in the sense Jesus did, of hatred and anger in the heart (*Matthew 5:21–22*). Coveting, wanting what belongs to others, leads to frustration. “You fight and make war.” The inner war becomes an outer war.

“You don’t have, because you don’t ask.” Instead of bringing their needs to God, people try to grab what they want through conflict.

Verse 3: “You ask, and don’t receive, because you ask with wrong motives, so that you may spend it on your pleasures.” Even when they pray, their prayers are selfish. They want God to fulfill their desires for their own pleasure, not for His purposes.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses give a profound analysis of human conflict. Whether in families, churches, workplaces, or nations, conflicts often arise from unsatisfied desires: for possessions, power, status, recognition, or control. When people do not get what they want, they fight.

The remedy is not to suppress all desire but to bring desires to God. Prayer is the alternative to grasping and fighting. Jesus taught His followers to ask the Father for their needs (*Matthew 7:7–11*).

But prayer itself can be corrupted. When people pray only for their own pleasure, treating God as a means to satisfy their desires, their prayers go unanswered. True prayer seeks God’s will and glory, as Jesus taught: “*Your will be done*” (*Matthew 6:10*). First *John 5:14* says that if we ask anything according to His will, He hears us.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

When believers find themselves in conflict, they can look inward and ask what desires are driving it. Is it a desire for control, recognition, comfort, or getting their own way? Recognizing the root can open the door to resolution.

Believers can also bring their desires to God in prayer instead of trying to seize what they want. Honest prayer about desires, disappointments, and needs is healthy.

Finally, believers can examine their motives in prayer. Are they seeking God’s will or only their own pleasure? Prayer that aligns with God’s purposes, seeking His kingdom first, is prayer that He delights to answer.

### *James 4:6–8* — Grace for the Humble

> *“But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’ Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you. Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, you sinners. Purify your hearts, you double-minded.”*
>
> — *James 4:6–8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After the strong rebuke of verses 1–5, James offers hope. “But he gives more grace.” However great the problem of worldliness and pride, God’s grace is greater. He gives grace upon grace.

“Therefore it says, ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’” James quotes *Proverbs 3:34* (in the Greek version). Peter quotes the same verse (*1 Peter 5:5*). God opposes those who exalt themselves, but He pours out grace on those who humble themselves.

Verse 7: “Be subject therefore to God.” Humility means submitting to God, placing oneself under His authority.

“Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.” Submitting to God and resisting the devil go together. The devil is real and active, but he is not all-powerful. When believers stand firm against him in God’s strength, he flees.

Verse 8: “Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you.” This is a wonderful promise. When believers come close to God, He comes close to them. He is not distant or reluctant.

“Cleanse your hands, you sinners. Purify your hearts, you double-minded.” Drawing near to God involves turning from sin. “Hands” represent actions; “hearts” represent inner desires and motives. Both need cleansing. “Double-minded” describes those whose loyalty is divided between God and the world (*James 1:8*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses describe the path of repentance and restoration. It begins with God’s grace, which is greater than any sin. It continues with humility, submission to God, and resistance to the devil. It leads to intimacy with God, as believers draw near and He draws near to them. And it involves genuine change, the cleansing of actions and the purifying of hearts.

Verses 9–10 continue: “Lament, mourn, and weep... Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you.” James calls for genuine sorrow over sin, not a shallow apology. This sorrow is not meant to last forever; it leads to God’s lifting up. Jesus said that those who humble themselves will be exalted (*Luke 14:11*).

The promise “draw near to God, and he will draw near to you” reveals God’s eagerness for fellowship. Like the father in the parable of the prodigal son, who ran to meet his returning son (*Luke 15:20*), God responds to every step toward Him.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

When believers feel distant from God, they can take a step toward Him, through prayer, confession, Scripture, or worship, trusting His promise to draw near.

Humility is the doorway to grace. Believers can practice humility by acknowledging their dependence on God, confessing their sins honestly, and submitting their plans and desires to Him.

When believers face temptation or spiritual attack, they can resist the devil, standing firm in God’s strength, refusing to give in, and trusting that he will flee.

### *James 4:13–15* — If the Lord Wills

> *“Come now, you who say, ‘Today or tomorrow let’s go into this city and spend a year there, trade, and make a profit.’ Yet you don’t know what your life will be like tomorrow. For what is your life? For you are a vapor that appears for a little time and then vanishes away. For you ought to say, ‘If the Lord wills, we will both live, and do this or that.’”*
>
> — *James 4:13–15* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“Come now, you who say, ‘Today or tomorrow let’s go into this city and spend a year there, trade, and make a profit.’” James addresses merchants who made confident plans: where they would go, how long they would stay, what they would do, and what they would gain. Their plans left God out completely.

Verse 14: “Yet you don’t know what your life will be like tomorrow.” No one knows the future. Illness, accident, economic change, or death can overturn the best-laid plans.

“For what is your life? For you are a vapor that appears for a little time and then vanishes away.” Life is like morning mist or a puff of breath on a cold day. It appears briefly and then disappears. Human life is fragile and short.

Verse 15: “For you ought to say, ‘If the Lord wills, we will both live, and do this or that.’” Instead of presumptuous planning, believers should plan with humility, acknowledging that their lives and plans depend on God’s will.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

James is not condemning planning. Scripture commends wise planning (*Proverbs 21:5*). Paul made travel plans, often adding “*if the Lord permits*” (*1 Corinthians 16:7*) (see also *Acts 18:21*). The problem is arrogance: planning as if one controls the future and does not need God.

Jesus told a parable about a rich man who planned to build bigger barns and enjoy his wealth for many years, but God said, “*You foolish one, tonight your soul is required of you*” (*Luke 12:20*) (*Luke 12:16–21*). The man’s plans left God out, and his life ended suddenly.

The image of life as a vapor appears throughout Scripture. *Psalm 39:5* says that every person is but a breath. Ecclesiastes repeatedly calls life “vanity,” a word that means vapor or breath. This is not meant to make believers despair, but to make them wise, valuing each day and depending on God.

Saying “If the Lord wills” is not meant to be a superstitious formula, but an expression of a heart that submits all plans to God.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can make plans for their careers, families, finances, and futures, but they can hold those plans with humility, praying about them and remaining open to God’s direction.

Remembering that life is short can help believers prioritize what truly matters: relationships, faithfulness, love, and eternal things. It can also free them from anxiety about the future, since the future is in God’s hands.

When plans change unexpectedly, through illness, loss, or disappointment, believers can trust that God is still in control. His will is good, even when it differs from their plans.

### *James 4:17* — Knowing to Do Good

> *“To him therefore who knows to do good and doesn’t do it, to him it is sin.”*
>
> — *James 4:17* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

James ends the chapter with a short but powerful statement. “To him therefore who knows to do good and doesn’t do it, to him it is sin.”

Sin is not only doing wrong things. It is also failing to do right things. When a person knows what is good and has the opportunity to do it but chooses not to, that failure is sin.

This verse may connect to the previous section. Those who know they should depend on God and acknowledge His will, but continue in arrogant self-reliance, are sinning. But it also states a general principle.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Christians sometimes distinguish between “sins of commission,” doing what is wrong, and “sins of omission,” failing to do what is right. James emphasizes that both are real sins.

Jesus’ parables highlight sins of omission. In the parable of the good Samaritan, the priest and Levite did no active harm to the wounded man, but they passed by without helping (*Luke 10:30–37*). In the parable of the sheep and the goats, those condemned are not accused of doing evil but of failing to feed the hungry, welcome the stranger, clothe the naked, and visit the sick and imprisoned (*Matthew 25:41–46*).

This verse also connects with James’s emphasis on being doers of the word (*James 1:22*) and on faith that works (*James 2:14–26*). Knowledge without action is not enough. Knowing God’s will brings responsibility to do it.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can ask whether there are good things they know they should do but have been putting off: a kindness to show, a person to forgive, a need to meet, a conversation to have, or a step of obedience to take.

This verse is not meant to produce guilt over every possible good deed left undone. No one can meet every need. But it calls believers to respond to the specific opportunities God places before them.

Believers can pray for sensitivity to God’s leading and courage to act on what they know is right, trusting that God will give them the strength to obey.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*James 4* exposes the roots of conflict. Fights and quarrels come from desires warring within people. When they want what they do not have, they fight instead of asking God, or they pray with selfish motives. Believers can look beneath their conflicts to the desires driving them, and bring those desires honestly to God.

James warns that friendship with the world, embracing its values and priorities, is like spiritual adultery against God, who jealously desires His people’s undivided love. But God gives more grace. He opposes the proud and gives grace to the humble. The path back to God is humility: submitting to Him, resisting the devil, drawing near to God, cleansing actions and purifying hearts, grieving over sin, and humbling oneself before the Lord, who will lift up the humble. God promises to draw near to those who draw near to Him.

The chapter also warns against speaking evil of and judging one another. God alone is the Lawgiver and Judge. Believers can practice discernment and loving correction without slander or condemnation.

Finally, James warns against arrogant planning that leaves God out. Life is a vapor that appears briefly and vanishes. Believers can plan wisely while saying, “If the Lord wills,” holding their futures in humble dependence on God. And they are reminded that knowing the good and failing to do it is sin. Faith acts on what it knows.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord, search my heart and show me the desires that cause conflict in my relationships. Forgive me for fighting to get what I want instead of bringing my needs to You, and for praying with selfish motives. Keep me from friendship with the world and give me an undivided love for You. Thank You that You give more grace, and that You give grace to the humble. I submit myself to You. Help me to resist the devil. I draw near to You; thank You for drawing near to me. Cleanse my hands and purify my heart. Keep me from slandering or judging others. Help me to hold my plans humbly, remembering that my life is a vapor and that my future is in Your hands. Give me courage to do the good that I know I should do. I humble myself before You, trusting You to lift me up. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

James · Chapter 5 of 5

# James — Chapter 5

Chapter Theme: Patience, Prayer, and Restoring the Wanderer

[Read James 5 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/JAS05.htm)

Main Teaching

James issues a fierce warning to the rich who hoard wealth and exploit others: their riches are rotting, their clothes moth-eaten, their gold corroded, and the withheld wages of their workers cry out to the Lord of Armies, while they live in luxury and condemn the innocent. He then turns to the believers who suffer and urges them to be patient until the Lord’s coming, like a farmer waiting for the rain and harvest, strengthening their hearts because the Lord’s coming is near. They should not grumble against one another, but follow the example of the prophets and of Job, whose endurance revealed that the Lord is full of compassion and mercy. Their yes should be yes and their no, no, without oaths. Those who suffer should pray, the cheerful should sing, and the sick should call the elders to pray over them and anoint them with oil in the Lord’s name; the prayer of faith will restore the sick, and any sins will be forgiven. Believers are to confess their sins to one another and pray for one another, because the prayer of a righteous person is powerful, as Elijah’s prayers were. Finally, whoever brings back a wanderer from the truth saves a soul from death and covers a multitude of sins.

## Chapter Background and Story

James’s readers were largely poor believers, many of them working in fields owned by wealthy landowners. In the first-century world, agricultural laborers were often paid daily, and withholding their wages could mean their families went hungry. The Law of Moses commanded that workers be paid promptly (*Leviticus 19:13*; *Deuteronomy 24:14–15*). Yet many wealthy landowners exploited their workers, sometimes using the courts to oppress them (*James 2:6*).

The first section of this chapter (vv1–6) is addressed to these wealthy oppressors, in the style of the Old Testament prophets, who denounced injustice against the poor. Whether or not the rich would ever hear James’s words, the believers who did would be reassured that God sees and will judge.

The rest of the chapter turns to the believers themselves. They are to be patient in suffering, honest in their speech, and faithful in prayer. James ends his letter not with a formal greeting but with a call to restore those who wander from the truth.

### Warning to the Rich (*5:1–6*)

“*Come now, you rich, weep and howl for your miseries that are coming on you*” (*v. 1*). James echoes the prophets who warned of coming judgment on oppressors (*Isaiah 13:6*; *Amos 6:1–7*). “*Your riches are corrupted and your garments are moth-eaten*” (*v. 2*). “*Your gold and your silver are corroded, and their corrosion will be for a testimony against you and will eat your flesh like fire. You have laid up your treasure in the last days*” (*v. 3*). Wealth that is hoarded decays. Jesus warned against storing up treasure on earth, where moth and rust destroy (*Matthew 6:19–20*). Gold and silver do not literally rust, but James uses the image to show that hoarded wealth is worthless. The corrosion is evidence against the rich, showing that they kept what should have been used to help others. “In the last days” means they are hoarding when the end is near, foolishly preparing for the wrong future. The cry of the unpaid workers is studied below.

“*You have lived in luxury on the earth, and taken your pleasure. You have nourished your hearts as in a day of slaughter*” (*v. 5*). The rich indulged themselves without restraint, like cattle fattening themselves on the very day they will be slaughtered, unaware of the judgment coming.

“*You have condemned and you have murdered the righteous one. He doesn’t resist you*” (*v. 6*). The rich used their power, including courts, to condemn and even cause the death of innocent people who had no power to resist. Some interpreters also see an allusion to Jesus, the Righteous One, who did not resist those who condemned Him (*Acts 3:14*; *7:52*).

James is not condemning wealth itself, but the hoarding, exploitation, luxury, and injustice that often accompany it. Scripture elsewhere calls the wealthy to be generous and rich in good works (*1 Timothy 6:17–19*).

### Patience Until the Lord Comes (*5:7–11*)

The call to patience is studied below. “*Don’t grumble, brothers, against one another, so that you won’t be judged. Behold, the judge stands at the door*” (*v. 9*). Suffering can make people irritable and quick to complain about one another. James warns against this. The Judge is near, “at the door,” ready to enter.

“*Take, brothers, for an example of suffering and of perseverance, the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord*” (*v. 10*). The prophets suffered for faithfully speaking God’s word (*Matthew 5:12*; *Hebrews 11:36–38*). They are examples of patient endurance.

“*Behold, we call them blessed who endured. You have heard of the perseverance of Job and have seen the Lord in the outcome, and how the Lord is full of compassion and mercy*” (*v. 11*). Job lost his wealth, his children, and his health. He questioned and lamented, but he did not abandon God. At the end of his story, God restored him (*Job 42:10–17*). “The outcome” shows God’s purpose: He is full of compassion and mercy. Job’s example shows that endurance does not mean silent, emotionless acceptance. Job cried out honestly to God. Endurance means holding on to God even while struggling.

### Honest Speech (*5:12*)

“*But above all things, my brothers, don’t swear—not by heaven, or by the earth, or by any other oath; but let your “yes” be “yes”, and your “no”, “no”, so that you don’t fall into hypocrisy*” (*v. 12*). This echoes Jesus’ teaching in *Matthew 5:33–37*. People often swore oaths to make their statements seem more trustworthy, or used clever oaths to avoid commitment. Jesus and James call for simple, consistent honesty. Believers should be so truthful that their word needs no oath to back it up. Christians have differed on whether this forbids all oaths, such as in a court of law, or only careless and deceptive oaths; most understand the main point to be honesty in everyday speech.

### Prayer, Healing, and Confession (*5:13–18*)

“*Is any among you suffering? Let him pray. Is any cheerful? Let him sing praises*” (*v. 13*). Every circumstance of life can be brought to God. In hardship, believers pray. In joy, they praise. The study below explores prayer for the sick and the power of prayer.

“*Elijah was a man with a nature like ours, and he prayed earnestly that it might not rain, and it didn’t rain on the earth for three years and six months*” (*v. 17*). “*He prayed again, and the sky gave rain, and the earth produced its fruit*” (*v. 18*). Elijah was an ordinary human being, with weaknesses and fears like everyone else. After his great victory on Mount Carmel, he became so discouraged that he asked to die (*1 Kings 19:4*). Yet his prayers were powerful. *1 Kings 17–18* records the drought and the rain that followed his prayers. James’s point is that God answers the prayers of ordinary believers, not only spiritual heroes.

### Restoring the Wanderer (*5:19–20*)

The call to restore those who wander is studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *James 5:4* — The Cry of the Unpaid Worker

> *“Behold, the wages of the laborers who mowed your fields, which you have kept back by fraud, cry out; and the cries of those who reaped have entered into the ears of the Lord of Armies.”*
>
> — *James 5:4* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“Behold, the wages of the laborers who mowed your fields, which you have kept back by fraud, cry out.” The rich landowners had hired workers to harvest their fields but had refused to pay them, or had cheated them. James pictures the withheld wages themselves crying out, like a witness testifying against the rich.

“And the cries of those who reaped have entered into the ears of the Lord of Armies.” The workers’ cries for justice have reached God. “The Lord of Armies” (often translated “the Lord of Hosts”) is a title emphasizing God’s supreme power. He commands the armies of heaven. The oppressed may seem powerless, but their cause is heard by the most powerful One of all.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

God’s law specifically protected workers. “*You shall not oppress a hired servant who is poor and needy*” (*Deuteronomy 24:14*)... “*In his day you shall give him his wages, neither shall the sun go down on it, for he is poor and sets his heart on it, lest he cry against you to the LORD, and it be sin to you*” (*Deuteronomy 24:15*). James echoes this law. When workers are cheated, their cry rises to God.

The image of a cry reaching God’s ears appears throughout Scripture. Abel’s blood cried out from the ground (*Genesis 4:10*). Israel’s cry in Egypt reached God, and He came down to rescue them (*Exodus 3:7–8*). God hears the cries of the oppressed.

This passage shows that economic injustice is a spiritual issue. How people treat workers, pay wages, and use wealth matters to God. The prophets repeatedly condemned those who exploited the poor (*Amos 2:6–7*; *Micah 2:1–2*; *Jeremiah 22:13*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers who employ others, whether as business owners, managers, or simply as people who hire help, are called to pay fair wages promptly and treat workers justly.

Believers can also consider how their purchasing and investment choices affect workers elsewhere. Supporting fair labor practices and opposing exploitation reflect God’s concern for the worker.

For those who have been cheated or exploited, this verse brings comfort: God hears their cry. They can seek justice through proper means and trust that the Lord of Armies is on the side of the oppressed.

### *James 5:7–8* — Patient Like a Farmer

> *“Be patient therefore, brothers, until the coming of the Lord. Behold, the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, being patient over it, until it receives the early and late rain. You also be patient. Establish your hearts, for the coming of the Lord is at hand.”*
>
> — *James 5:7–8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“Be patient therefore, brothers, until the coming of the Lord.” After warning the rich, James turns to the suffering believers. They are to be patient, enduring hardship without giving up, until Christ returns. The word for patience suggests a long-suffering endurance, the ability to hold on for a long time.

“Behold, the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, being patient over it, until it receives the early and late rain.” In the land of Israel, the “early rain” came in autumn, softening the ground for planting. The “late rain” came in spring, helping the crops mature before harvest. Farmers could not hurry the rain or the harvest. They had to wait patiently, trusting that it would come.

Verse 8: “You also be patient. Establish your hearts, for the coming of the Lord is at hand.” Believers are to strengthen their hearts, standing firm and steady. The reason: “the coming of the Lord is at hand.” Christ’s return is near, and with it, justice and reward.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The image of the farmer teaches several lessons about patience. First, patience involves waiting for something that is certain. The farmer knows the rain will come; believers know Christ will return. Second, patience involves active faithfulness. The farmer does not sit idle; he works while he waits. Believers continue serving God while they wait. Third, patience trusts in God’s timing. The farmer cannot control the rain; believers cannot control the timing of Christ’s return or the end of their suffering.

“The coming of the Lord is at hand” has been the hope of believers in every generation. The New Testament writers lived with eager expectation of Christ’s return, without knowing its timing (*Matthew 24:36*). From God’s perspective, the time is short (*2 Peter 3:8–9*). The nearness of His coming gives believers strength to endure.

The call to “establish your hearts” reminds believers that patience is not passive resignation. It requires inner strength, rooted in trust in God.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers facing long seasons of hardship, illness, waiting, or injustice can take encouragement from the farmer. God’s timing is not theirs, but His promises are sure.

Patience can be cultivated through prayer, remembering God’s past faithfulness, and fixing hope on Christ’s return. Believers can ask God to strengthen their hearts when they feel like giving up.

Finally, believers can continue to be faithful in the meantime, working, serving, and loving others, as the farmer continues to work while waiting for the harvest.

### *James 5:14–16* — The Prayer of Faith

> *“Is any among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the assembly, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and the prayer of faith will heal him who is sick, and the Lord will raise him up. If he has committed sins, he will be forgiven. Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed. The insistent prayer of a righteous person is powerfully effective.”*
>
> — *James 5:14–16* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“Is any among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the assembly.” Those who are sick are encouraged to ask the church’s leaders to come and pray. The initiative is with the sick person, and the response comes from the community’s leaders.

“And let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord.” Oil was used in the ancient world both as medicine (*Luke 10:34*) and as a symbol of God’s presence and blessing. Jesus’ disciples anointed the sick with oil and healed them (*Mark 6:13*). The anointing is done “in the name of the Lord,” that is, by His authority and in dependence on Him.

Verse 15: “and the prayer of faith will heal him who is sick, and the Lord will raise him up.” The healing comes from the Lord in response to prayer offered in faith. “Raise him up” may mean restore to health or lift from the sickbed.

“If he has committed sins, he will be forgiven.” Sometimes, though not always, sickness may be connected with sin. If so, God offers forgiveness.

Verse 16: “Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed.” Healing is connected with confession and mutual prayer. Honest confession among believers brings healing, spiritual and sometimes physical.

“The insistent prayer of a righteous person is powerfully effective.” The prayers of those who are right with God are powerful. “Righteous” here does not mean perfect but one who lives in faithful relationship with God.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses teach that God cares about the sick and responds to prayer. Christians have practiced anointing and prayer for the sick throughout history, though in different ways. Some traditions see anointing of the sick as a sacrament; others practice it as an act of prayer and faith; others emphasize prayer without anointing. All take seriously the call to pray for the sick.

It is important to read these verses alongside the rest of Scripture. Not every sickness is healed in this life, even when believers pray in faith. Paul left Trophimus sick in Miletus (*2 Timothy 4:20*); Timothy had frequent illnesses (*1 Timothy 5:23*); Paul himself lived with a thorn in the flesh that God did not remove (*2 Corinthians 12:7–9*). When healing does not come, it is not necessarily because of weak faith or unconfessed sin. Jesus rejected the assumption that sickness is always caused by personal sin (*John 9:1–3*). Ultimately, every believer will be “raised up” at the resurrection, when all sickness will be healed forever.

Prayer for healing also does not exclude medical care. Oil was itself a common medicine. Luke was a physician (*Colossians 4:14*). Seeking medical treatment and praying for healing go together; God often heals through doctors, medicine, and care.

The call to confess sins to one another highlights the healing power of honesty and community. Hidden sin can weigh heavily on a person, affecting their spiritual, emotional, and even physical well-being (*Psalm 32:3–5*). Confession to trusted believers, combined with prayer, brings release and healing. Such confession should take place in safe, trustworthy relationships, never under pressure or in settings where it could be misused.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers who are sick can ask church leaders and fellow believers to pray for them. There is no shame in asking for prayer. And believers can respond when others ask, coming alongside the sick with prayer and care.

Believers can pray in faith for healing while also seeking medical help, trusting God to work through both. When healing does not come, they can hold onto God’s compassion and the hope of the resurrection, and they should never blame the sick person for a lack of faith.

Finally, believers can practice honest confession in trusted relationships, such as with a close friend, mentor, or pastor, and pray for one another. Confession and prayer bring healing and strengthen community.

### *James 5:19–20* — Turning Back the Wanderer

> *“Brothers, if any among you wanders from the truth and someone turns him back, let him know that he who turns a sinner from the error of his way will save a soul from death and will cover a multitude of sins.”*
>
> — *James 5:19–20* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

James ends his letter with a call to restoration. “Brothers, if any among you wanders from the truth.” “Wanders” suggests drifting or straying, like a sheep wandering from the flock. James speaks of someone “among you,” a member of the community who has drifted from the truth, whether in belief or in behavior.

“And someone turns him back.” Another believer helps bring the wanderer back. Every believer can play this role.

Verse 20: “let him know that he who turns a sinner from the error of his way will save a soul from death.” Bringing someone back from wandering is a matter of life and death. Persisting in sin leads to spiritual death (*James 1:15*). Restoring a wanderer rescues them.

“And will cover a multitude of sins.” The wanderer’s sins are covered, that is, forgiven, when they turn back to God. *Proverbs 10:12* says, “*love covers all wrongs*” (*Proverbs 10:12*), and Peter writes that “*love covers a multitude of sins*” (*1 Peter 4:8*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

James ends his letter not with a formal farewell but with a pastoral concern for those who stray. This reflects God’s heart. Jesus told the parable of the shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine sheep to search for the one that is lost (*Luke 15:3–7*). God does not give up on those who wander.

This passage also shows that believers are responsible for one another. As *Hebrews 3:13* says, believers are to encourage one another daily so that no one is hardened by sin. Paul writes that those who are spiritual should gently restore someone caught in sin (*Galatians 6:1*).

Restoration requires love, humility, and courage. It is not about condemning or shaming the wanderer, but about lovingly helping them find their way back. The goal is life and forgiveness.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can watch for those in their community who are drifting from faith, perhaps no longer attending, struggling with doubt, or slipping into harmful patterns. A phone call, a visit, a kind word, or an invitation can make a difference.

Restoring a wanderer requires gentleness and patience. Believers can listen, show love, share truth humbly, and pray for them, trusting God to work.

Those who have wandered themselves can take comfort that the door is always open. God welcomes those who return, and their sins are covered by His grace.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*James 5* begins with a strong warning against wealthy people who hoard riches, live in luxury, and exploit their workers. God hears the cries of the oppressed, and He will judge injustice. Believers are called to use their resources justly and generously, to pay fair wages, and to care for those who are exploited.

The chapter then encourages suffering believers to be patient until the Lord comes, like a farmer waiting for rain and harvest. They are to strengthen their hearts, avoid grumbling against one another, and follow the example of the prophets and of Job, whose story shows that the Lord is full of compassion and mercy. Endurance means holding on to God even while struggling honestly.

James calls for simple honesty in speech, letting “yes” mean yes and “no” mean no. He encourages believers to bring every situation to God: to pray in suffering, to praise in joy, and to call for prayer when sick. The prayer of a righteous person is powerful, as Elijah’s prayers were. Believers can pray for healing while also seeking medical care, trusting God’s compassion even when healing does not come in this life.

Confession and mutual prayer bring healing to individuals and communities. And the letter ends with a call to restore those who wander from the truth. Believers are responsible for one another. Those who lovingly turn a wanderer back save a soul from death and cover a multitude of sins. In this way, James’s practical wisdom comes to its goal: a community of genuine faith, marked by justice, patience, honesty, prayer, and restoring love.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord of Armies, You hear the cries of the oppressed. Give me a heart for justice, and help me to use whatever resources I have generously and fairly. Keep me from hoarding, greed, and self-indulgence. When I suffer, give me patience like a farmer waiting for the rain, and strengthen my heart, for Your coming is near. Keep me from grumbling against others. Thank You that You are full of compassion and mercy, as You showed to Job. Make my words honest and simple. Teach me to pray in every circumstance, to praise You in joy, and to ask for prayer when I am weak. I pray for all who are sick; heal them according to Your will, and comfort those who are not healed in this life with the hope of the resurrection. Give me courage to confess my sins and to pray for others. And make me a restorer of those who wander, bringing them back to You with love. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Book 21 of 27

# 1 Peter

## About This Letter

First Peter presents itself as written by “*Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ*” (*1 Peter 1:1*), with the help of Silvanus, also known as Silas (*5:12*). Peter was the fisherman from Galilee whom Jesus called to follow Him, who confessed Jesus as the Christ, denied Him three times on the night of His arrest, and was restored by the risen Lord to feed His sheep (*John 21:15–19*). He became a leading apostle in Jerusalem and later traveled widely. Early Christian tradition holds that he died as a martyr in Rome during Nero’s persecution in the mid-60s A.D. Most Christians through history have accepted the letter as Peter’s own; some modern scholars think it was written later by his followers, while many others point out that Silvanus’s help easily explains its polished Greek.

The letter is sent to believers “living as foreigners” scattered across five Roman provinces in what is now Turkey (*1:1*). Many were Gentiles who had turned from their former way of life (*1:14*, 18; *4:3–4*). Because they no longer joined in pagan festivals, idolatry, and immorality, their neighbors viewed them with suspicion, mocked them, and slandered them. They faced social rejection and the threat of wider persecution. Peter writes from “Babylon” (*5:13*), probably a symbolic name for Rome, to encourage them to stand firm.

## The Shape of the Letter

Chapter 1 praises God for a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus, an imperishable inheritance, and a faith refined by trials, and it calls believers to holiness and sincere love because they were redeemed by the precious blood of Christ. Chapter 2 describes believers as living stones built into a spiritual house, a chosen people and royal priesthood, and calls them to honorable conduct among unbelievers, respect for authorities, and patient endurance of unjust suffering, following the example of Christ, who bore our sins on the cross. Chapter 3 addresses wives and husbands, calls all believers to unity, compassion, and blessing in return for insult, and explains how Christ suffered for sins once for all. Chapter 4 urges believers to live for God’s will, to love deeply, to use their gifts, and not to be surprised by fiery trials but to rejoice in sharing Christ’s sufferings. Chapter 5 instructs elders to shepherd God’s flock willingly and humbly, calls all to clothe themselves with humility, to cast their anxieties on God, and to resist the devil, and closes with greetings.

## Themes to Watch For

Watch for living hope, suffering and glory, the example of Christ’s suffering, holiness, the believer’s identity as God’s chosen people and exiles in the world, good conduct that silences slander, submission and respect within the structures of society, humility, love that covers sins, God’s care for the anxious, and the true grace of God in which believers stand. First Peter is a letter of hope for Christians who feel like outsiders in their own culture.

1 Peter · Chapter 1 of 5

# 1 Peter — Chapter 1

Chapter Theme: A Living Hope and a Holy Life

[Read 1 Peter 1 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/1PE01.htm)

Main Teaching

Peter greets God’s chosen people living as foreigners scattered through Asia Minor, chosen by the Father, set apart by the Spirit, for obedience to Jesus Christ. He praises God, who in His great mercy has given believers new birth into a living hope through Jesus’ resurrection, and into an inheritance that can never perish, spoil, or fade, kept in heaven for them while they are guarded by God’s power through faith. Though they suffer grief in various trials, these trials prove their faith genuine, more precious than gold refined by fire. Though they have not seen Jesus, they love Him and rejoice with inexpressible joy. The prophets searched carefully to understand this salvation, and even angels long to look into it. So believers are to prepare their minds, set their hope fully on the grace coming at Christ’s revelation, and be holy in all their conduct, because God is holy. They should live in reverent fear as foreigners, knowing they were redeemed not with silver or gold but with the precious blood of Christ, the spotless Lamb. Having been purified and born again through the living and enduring word of God, they are to love one another deeply from the heart.

## Chapter Background and Story

Peter writes to believers who felt like outsiders. Many of them had been Gentiles who once took part in the idolatry and immorality of their culture. When they turned to Christ, everything changed. They stopped joining in pagan festivals and immoral practices, and their neighbors were surprised and offended (*1 Peter 4:3–4*). They were slandered, mocked, and treated with suspicion. Some may have lost jobs, friendships, or family relationships.

Peter calls them “foreigners” or “exiles” (v1, 17). This is not mainly a description of their geographical location but of their spiritual identity. They belong to God’s kingdom, so they no longer fully belong to the world around them. Like Israel in exile, they live in a land that is not their true home.

Peter begins not with instructions about suffering but with praise. Before he tells them how to live, he reminds them of who they are and what they have: a living hope, an imperishable inheritance, a salvation the prophets longed to see, and a precious redemption. Hope is the foundation for holiness and endurance.

### Greeting (*1:1–2*)

“*Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, to the chosen ones who are living as foreigners in the Dispersion in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia*” (*v. 1*). These were Roman provinces in Asia Minor, modern-day Turkey. The believers are “chosen,” God’s own people, and yet “living as foreigners,” not fully at home in the world.

“*according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, in sanctification of the Spirit, that you may obey Jesus Christ and be sprinkled with his blood: Grace to you and peace be multiplied*” (*v. 2*). Notice the work of the whole Trinity. The Father chose them according to His foreknowledge. The Spirit set them apart. And they were chosen for obedience to Jesus Christ and for cleansing by His blood. “Sprinkled with his blood” recalls the ceremony at Mount Sinai, where Moses sprinkled the people with blood to seal the covenant (*Exodus 24:7–8*). Believers belong to the new covenant established by Christ’s blood.

### A Living Hope (*1:3–5*)

Peter’s praise for the living hope is studied below. “*who by the power of God are guarded through faith for a salvation ready to be revealed in the last time*” (*v. 5*). Not only is the inheritance kept safe for believers; believers are kept safe for the inheritance. God’s power guards them, like a military garrison protecting a city. Their faith is the means through which God’s protection works.

### Joy in Trials (*1:6–9*)

Peter’s teaching on trials and joy is studied below. “*whom, not having known, you love. In him, though now you don’t see him, yet believing, you rejoice greatly with joy that is unspeakable and full of glory*” (*v. 8*), “*receiving the result of your faith, the salvation of your souls*” (*v. 9*). Peter had seen Jesus with his own eyes; his readers had not. Yet they loved Him and trusted Him, and they experienced a joy too deep for words. Jesus said to Thomas, “*Blessed are those who have not seen, and have believed*” (*John 20:29*).

### The Prophets and the Angels (*1:10–12*)

“*Concerning this salvation, the prophets sought and searched diligently. They prophesied of the grace that would come to you*” (*v. 10*), “*searching for who or what kind of time the Spirit of Christ which was in them pointed to when he predicted the sufferings of Christ and the glories that would follow them*” (*v. 11*). The Old Testament prophets spoke of the Messiah’s suffering and glory (*Isaiah 53*; *Psalm 22*), but they did not fully understand when or how it would happen. Notice that “the Spirit of Christ” was in the prophets, showing Christ’s existence before His birth.

“*To them it was revealed that they served not themselves, but you, in these things, which now have been announced to you through those who preached the Good News to you by the Holy Spirit sent out from heaven; which things angels desire to look into*” (*v. 12*). The prophets were serving future generations, including these believers. And the salvation now revealed is so wonderful that even angels long to look into it, like someone bending down to peer intently at something. Believers have received what prophets longed for and angels marvel at.

### Called to Be Holy (*1:13–21*)

“*Therefore prepare your minds for action. Be sober, and set your hope fully on the grace that will be brought to you at the revelation of Jesus Christ—*” (*v. 13*). “Prepare your minds for action” is literally “gird up the loins of your mind,” an image of tucking up a long robe into a belt so one can move quickly. Believers are to be mentally alert, self-controlled, and focused on hope.

“*as children of obedience, not conforming yourselves according to your former lusts as in your ignorance*” (*v. 14*). Before they knew Christ, they lived according to their desires. Now, as obedient children of God, they are not to be shaped by those old patterns. The call to holiness is studied below.

“*If you call on him as Father, who without respect of persons judges according to each man’s work, pass the time of your living as foreigners here in reverent fear*” (*v. 17*). Believers call God “Father,” a term of intimate relationship. But He is also an impartial Judge. Believers live their lives as temporary residents in this world with reverence for Him. The precious redemption that motivates this reverence is studied below.

“*who was foreknown indeed before the foundation of the world, but was revealed in this last age for your sake*” (*v. 20*), “*who through him are believers in God, who raised him from the dead and gave him glory, so that your faith and hope might be in God*” (*v. 21*). Christ’s sacrifice was planned before creation and revealed in history. Because God raised Him and glorified Him, believers’ faith and hope rest securely in God.

### Love One Another Deeply (*1:22–25*)

The call to love and the enduring word are studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *1 Peter 1:3–4* — Born Again to a Living Hope

> *“Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to his great mercy caused us to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, to an incorruptible and undefiled inheritance that doesn’t fade away, reserved in Heaven for you,”*
>
> — *1 Peter 1:3–4* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Peter begins with a burst of praise. “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.” To “bless” God means to praise and thank Him.

“Who according to his great mercy.” The reason for praise is God’s mercy, His compassion toward those who do not deserve it. It is “great” mercy, abundant and overflowing.

“Caused us to be born again.” God has given believers a new birth, a new beginning, a new life. This echoes Jesus’ words to Nicodemus: “*You must all be born anew*” (*John 3:7*).

“To a living hope.” The result of new birth is hope, but not a vague or uncertain hope. It is a “living” hope, active, vibrant, and sure, because it is connected to a living Savior.

“Through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead.” The foundation of this hope is the resurrection. Because Jesus rose from the dead, believers have a sure hope of life beyond death.

Verse 4: “to an incorruptible and undefiled inheritance that doesn’t fade away, reserved in Heaven for you.” Believers also have an inheritance. It is “incorruptible,” it cannot decay or be destroyed. It is “undefiled,” pure and untouched by evil. It “doesn’t fade away,” never losing its beauty. And it is “reserved in Heaven,” kept safe by God for His people.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

For Peter, this hope was deeply personal. After Jesus’ crucifixion, Peter’s hope had died. He had denied Jesus and watched Him die. But on the third day, everything changed. The risen Jesus appeared to Peter (*1 Corinthians 15:5*) and restored him. Peter knew from experience what it means to be given a living hope through the resurrection.

The inheritance contrasts with earthly inheritances. In the Old Testament, Israel’s inheritance was the land of Canaan, which could be lost through war, exile, or disobedience. Earthly wealth can be stolen, lost, or destroyed. Believers’ inheritance is in heaven, beyond the reach of decay, corruption, or loss. Jesus told His followers to store up treasures in heaven, where moth and rust do not destroy (*Matthew 6:20*).

For readers who had lost status, friendships, or possessions because of their faith, this hope was precious. Whatever they lost on earth, their true inheritance was secure.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can begin each day, like Peter, by praising God for His mercy and the hope He has given them. Gratitude for what God has done shapes how they face the challenges ahead.

When believers face loss, disappointment, or uncertainty, they can remember that they have a living hope rooted in Christ’s resurrection and an inheritance that can never be taken away.

This hope also gives believers courage to live differently from the world around them. Their security does not depend on the approval of others or the stability of earthly circumstances.

### *1 Peter 1:6–7* — Faith Refined Like Gold

> *“In this you greatly rejoice, though now for a little while, if need be, you have been grieved in various trials, that the proof of your faith, which is more precious than gold that perishes, even though it is tested by fire, may be found to result in praise, glory, and honor at the revelation of Jesus Christ—”*
>
> — *1 Peter 1:6–7* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“In this you greatly rejoice.” “This” refers to the living hope and inheritance just described. Believers have great reason for joy.

“Though now for a little while, if need be, you have been grieved in various trials.” At the same time, they are experiencing grief because of trials. Peter does not deny the pain. But he puts it in perspective: it is “for a little while,” brief compared with eternity. “If need be” suggests that trials are not random; God allows them for a purpose.

Verse 7: “that the proof of your faith, which is more precious than gold that perishes, even though it is tested by fire.” In the ancient world, gold was refined by heating it in fire, which melted away impurities and left pure gold. Trials are like that fire. They test faith and purify it. Genuine faith is more precious than gold, because gold eventually perishes, but faith lasts forever.

“May be found to result in praise, glory, and honor at the revelation of Jesus Christ.” When Christ returns, tested and proven faith will result in praise, glory, and honor, both for God and, by His grace, for believers.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This passage holds together joy and grief. Believers can “greatly rejoice” even while being “grieved.” Christian joy does not deny sorrow; it exists alongside it, rooted in hope.

The image of refining fire appears throughout Scripture. Job said, “*When he has tried me, I will come out like gold*” (*Job 23:10*). Malachi spoke of the Lord as a refiner’s fire who purifies His people (*Malachi 3:2–3*). Trials reveal what is genuine and strengthen it.

This passage is similar to *James 1:2–4*, which also speaks of joy in trials because they produce endurance. Both apostles teach that God uses hardship to strengthen faith. This does not mean God causes all suffering, or that suffering is good in itself. Much suffering comes from human sin or a broken world. But God can use even painful experiences to refine His people.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

When believers face trials, they can hold onto both grief and hope. They can honestly acknowledge their pain while trusting that God is at work.

Believers can also see their trials as temporary. Compared with eternity, even long hardships are “for a little while.” This perspective can bring endurance.

Finally, believers can trust that their tested faith is precious to God. Every time they continue to trust Him through difficulty, their faith is being refined, and it will result in praise, glory, and honor when Christ returns.

### *1 Peter 1:15–16* — Be Holy, for I Am Holy

> *“but just as he who called you is holy, you yourselves also be holy in all of your behavior, because it is written, ‘You shall be holy, for I am holy.’”*
>
> — *1 Peter 1:15–16* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“But just as he who called you is holy, you yourselves also be holy in all of your behavior.” God, who called believers to Himself, is holy: completely pure, set apart, without any sin or evil. Believers are to reflect His holiness in “all” of their behavior, every area of life.

Verse 16: “because it is written, ‘You shall be holy, for I am holy.’” Peter quotes Leviticus, where God repeatedly commanded Israel to be holy because He is holy (*Leviticus 11:44–45*; *19:2*; *20:7*). The standard of holiness is God Himself.

“Holy” means set apart for God. It includes moral purity, but it is more than avoiding sin. It means belonging to God and reflecting His character in every part of life.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

In Leviticus, God’s call to holiness was given to Israel, whom He had redeemed from Egypt and brought into covenant with Himself. Peter applies it to believers, whom God has redeemed through Christ. The pattern is the same: God first redeems, then calls His people to live as His own.

Holiness flows from relationship. Believers are not holy in order to become God’s people; they are called to be holy because they already are His people. Like children who resemble their father, believers are to reflect the character of their heavenly Father.

The phrase “in all of your behavior” shows that holiness is not limited to religious activities. It touches work, relationships, speech, entertainment, finances, and private thoughts. Every part of life belongs to God.

Holiness is not achieved by human effort alone. The Spirit sanctifies believers (*1 Peter 1:2*), and God’s grace trains them to live godly lives (*Titus 2:11–12*). Believers cooperate with God’s work, but He is the one who makes them holy.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can ask whether there are areas of their lives that they have not surrendered to God. Holiness invites them to bring every area under His lordship.

Holiness may make believers different from the world around them, as it did for Peter’s readers. This difference is not about being self-righteous or judgmental, but about reflecting God’s beautiful character.

Finally, believers can pursue holiness with hope, not fear. God, who calls them to be holy, is also the one who makes them holy by His Spirit.

### *1 Peter 1:22–23* — Love One Another from the Heart

> *“Seeing you have purified your souls in your obedience to the truth through the Spirit in sincere brotherly affection, love one another from the heart fervently, having been born again, not of corruptible seed, but of incorruptible, through the word of God, which lives and remains forever.”*
>
> — *1 Peter 1:22–23* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“Seeing you have purified your souls in your obedience to the truth through the Spirit.” When believers responded to the gospel in faith and obedience, their souls were cleansed. This cleansing came through the truth of the gospel and the work of the Spirit.

“In sincere brotherly affection.” The purpose of this cleansing is genuine love for fellow believers. “Sincere” means without hypocrisy. “Brotherly affection” is the love that family members share.

“Love one another from the heart fervently.” “Fervently” means earnestly, intensely, with effort, like stretching out to reach something. Believers are to love one another deeply and wholeheartedly, not superficially.

Verse 23: “having been born again, not of corruptible seed, but of incorruptible, through the word of God, which lives and remains forever.” Believers have been born again, given new life, not through human, perishable seed, but through God’s imperishable word. This new birth makes them family, brothers and sisters who share the same spiritual life.

Verses 24–25 quote *Isaiah 40:6–8*: “All flesh is like grass... but the Lord’s word endures forever.” Human life and glory fade like grass, but God’s word lasts forever. The gospel preached to the believers is that eternal word.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses connect new birth with love. Because believers have been born into God’s family through His word, they are family. Family members are called to love one another deeply. Jesus said that His disciples would be known by their love for one another (*John 13:35*).

The contrast between perishable and imperishable seed shows the difference between natural and spiritual life. Natural life comes from human parents and ends in death. Spiritual life comes from God’s word and lasts forever. *James 1:18* also describes God giving believers new birth through “the word of truth.”

The emphasis on God’s enduring word is important for believers facing pressure. The world’s opinions, values, and powers are like grass that withers. God’s word remains. Believers can build their lives on it.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can examine whether their love for fellow believers is sincere and earnest. Is it genuine, or merely polite? Do they make an effort to love those who are difficult, different, or in need?

Loving “from the heart fervently” might mean investing time in relationships, forgiving offenses, supporting those who are struggling, and showing hospitality.

Believers can also anchor their lives in God’s enduring word. In a world of shifting opinions and fading glory, Scripture remains a firm foundation. Reading, studying, and obeying it nourishes the new life God has given.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

First Peter 1 begins with praise. God, in His great mercy, has given believers new birth into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus, and into an inheritance that can never perish, spoil, or fade. They are guarded by God’s power through faith. For those who feel like outsiders in their culture or who have lost much for their faith, this hope is a secure anchor.

The chapter honestly acknowledges that believers face trials that bring grief. But these trials are temporary, and God uses them to refine faith, which is more precious than gold. Believers can rejoice even in sorrow, loving and trusting the Jesus they have not yet seen, and they can marvel that they have received a salvation the prophets searched for and angels long to look into.

Because of this hope, believers are called to holiness. They are to prepare their minds, set their hope fully on the grace coming at Christ’s return, and be holy in all their conduct, because God is holy. They live as foreigners in this world, with reverence for the Father who judges impartially, remembering that they were redeemed not with silver or gold but with the precious blood of Christ, the spotless Lamb.

Finally, having been born again through God’s living and enduring word, believers are to love one another deeply from the heart. Human glory fades like grass, but God’s word lasts forever. Believers can build their lives, their hope, and their love on that unshakable foundation.

## Chapter Prayer

Blessed be You, God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Thank You that in Your great mercy You caused me to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus from the dead. Thank You for an inheritance that can never perish, spoil, or fade, kept in heaven for me, and for guarding me by Your power through faith. When I face trials, help me to trust that You are refining my faith like gold. Though I have not seen Jesus, I love Him, and I rejoice in Him. Help me to set my hope fully on the grace that will come when He is revealed. Make me holy in all my conduct, as You are holy. Thank You that I was redeemed not with silver or gold but with the precious blood of Christ. Help me to love my brothers and sisters deeply from the heart, and to build my life on Your word, which endures forever. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
