1 Peter · Chapter 2 of 5

# 1 Peter — Chapter 2

Chapter Theme: Living Stones, a Chosen People, and the Example of Christ

[Read 1 Peter 2 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/1PE02.htm)

Main Teaching

Peter urges believers to rid themselves of malice, deceit, hypocrisy, envy, and slander, and like newborn babies to crave the pure milk of God’s word so they may grow. Coming to Christ, the living Stone rejected by people but chosen and precious to God, they are being built as living stones into a spiritual house and a holy priesthood offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God. For those who believe, Christ is the precious cornerstone; for those who reject Him, He is a stone that makes them stumble. Believers are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, God’s own possession, called out of darkness into His marvelous light to declare His praises; once they were not a people, but now they are God’s people and have received mercy. As foreigners and exiles, they must abstain from sinful desires and live such good lives among unbelievers that, though slandered, their good deeds will lead others to glorify God. For the Lord’s sake they are to submit to human authorities, live as free people who are servants of God, and honor everyone. Servants are to respect their masters, even harsh ones, since enduring unjust suffering with a clear conscience pleases God. In this they follow Christ, who suffered for them, leaving an example: He did not sin, did not retaliate, but entrusted Himself to the righteous Judge, and He bore our sins in His body on the cross so that we might die to sin and live for righteousness. By His wounds we are healed, and we have returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of our souls.

## Chapter Background and Story

In chapter 1, Peter reminded believers of their living hope and called them to holiness and love. In chapter 2, he describes their identity as God’s people and how that identity should shape their lives in a hostile society.

The believers Peter wrote to were often slandered as “evildoers” (v12). Their neighbors may have accused them of being antisocial, disloyal to the empire, or immoral, because they no longer joined in civic religious festivals and pagan practices. Peter’s answer is twofold. First, believers must remember who they are: God’s chosen, precious people, with a dignity no one can take away. Second, they must live honorably, so that slander is shown to be false and others are drawn to glorify God.

The second half of the chapter begins a section on how believers should relate to authorities and social structures (*2:13–3*:7). This section includes instructions for servants, many of whom were enslaved people in Roman households, about enduring unjust treatment. These instructions must be read carefully in their historical setting, as explained below. Peter grounds everything in the example of Christ, who suffered unjustly for others.

### Craving Spiritual Milk (*2:1–3*)

“*Putting away therefore all wickedness, all deceit, hypocrisies, envies, and all evil speaking*” (*v. 1*). Before growth, there must be removal. These sins, malice, deceit, hypocrisy, envy, and slander, destroy the sincere love Peter called for in *1 Peter 1:22*. “*as newborn babies, long for the pure spiritual milk, that with it you may grow*” (*v. 2*), “*if indeed you have tasted that the Lord is gracious*” (*v. 3*). Babies instinctively crave milk. Believers, born again through God’s word (*1:23*), should crave that word with the same intensity. “Pure spiritual milk” is God’s word, the nourishment that helps them grow. Peter echoes *Psalm 34:8*: “*Oh taste and see that the LORD is good*” (*Psalm 34:8*). Those who have tasted God’s goodness will want more.

### Living Stones (*2:4–8*)

The image of living stones and a spiritual house is studied below. “*Because it is contained in Scripture, “Behold, I lay in Zion a chief cornerstone, chosen and precious. He who believes in him will not be disappointed.”*” (*v. 6*) Peter quotes *Isaiah 28:16*. Christ is the cornerstone of God’s new temple, chosen and precious.

“*For you who believe therefore is the honor, but for those who are disobedient, “The stone which the builders rejected has become the chief cornerstone,”*” (*v. 7*) “*and, “a stumbling stone and a rock of offense.” For they stumble at the word, being disobedient, to which also they were appointed*” (*v. 8*). Peter quotes *Psalm 118:22*, which Jesus applied to Himself (*Mark 12:10*), and *Isaiah 8:14*. The same stone that is a foundation for believers is a stumbling stone for those who reject it. People stumble because they refuse to obey the word. “To which also they were appointed” has been understood in different ways: some see it as God’s sovereign appointment of judgment for unbelief, others as the appointed consequence of disobedience. Either way, unbelief brings its own downfall.

### A Chosen People (*2:9–10*)

The great description of believers’ identity is studied below.

### Living Honorably Among Unbelievers (*2:11–12*)

The call to good conduct among unbelievers is studied below.

### Submission to Authorities (*2:13–17*)

“*Therefore subject yourselves to every ordinance of man for the Lord’s sake: whether to the king, as supreme*” (*v. 13*), “*or to governors, as sent by him for vengeance on evildoers and for praise to those who do well*” (*v. 14*). Believers are to respect and obey civil authorities “for the Lord’s sake,” as part of their witness and obedience to God. The emperor at the time was likely Nero. Government’s God-given role is to punish wrongdoing and commend good (*Romans 13:1–7*). Submission to authorities has limits: when rulers command what God forbids, believers must obey God rather than people (*Acts 5:29*).

“*For this is the will of God, that by well-doing you should put to silence the ignorance of foolish men*” (*v. 15*). Good conduct silences false accusations. “*Live as free people, yet not using your freedom for a cloak of wickedness, but as bondservants of God*” (*v. 16*). Believers are truly free in Christ, but their freedom is not an excuse for evil. They use it to serve God.

“*Honor all men. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honor the king*” (*v. 17*). This short verse summarizes Christian social ethics. Every person deserves honor, because each bears God’s image. Fellow believers deserve love. God deserves reverent fear. And the king deserves honor, but notice that only God receives “fear.” The emperor is honored, but God alone is worshiped.

### Servants and Unjust Suffering (*2:18–20*)

“*Servants, be in subjection to your masters with all respect, not only to the good and gentle, but also to the wicked*” (*v. 18*). “Servants” here refers to household slaves, who made up a large part of the Roman population and had few rights. Many early Christians were slaves. Peter addresses them directly as moral agents, members of God’s people with dignity and responsibility.

“*For it is commendable if someone endures pain, suffering unjustly, because of conscience toward God*” (*v. 19*). “*For what glory is it if, when you sin, you patiently endure beating? But if when you do well, you patiently endure suffering, this is commendable with God*” (*v. 20*). Peter acknowledges that some masters were harsh and that slaves were sometimes beaten unjustly. In a situation they could not escape, believing slaves could endure with a clear conscience before God, and God would see and commend them.

These verses must be read with great care. Peter is giving pastoral comfort to people trapped in an unjust system that they had no power to leave. He is not approving of slavery, and he is not saying that abuse is acceptable or that victims should stay in abusive situations when they can escape. Scripture elsewhere condemns slave-trading (*1 Timothy 1:10*), encourages slaves to gain freedom when possible (*1 Corinthians 7:21*), and calls masters to treat slaves justly (*Colossians 4:1*). Tragically, these verses have sometimes been misused to tell victims of domestic abuse or exploitation to stay and endure. That is a serious misuse of Scripture. God is a God of justice who hears the cry of the oppressed. Those who are being abused should seek safety and help, and those who know of abuse should act to protect victims. What Peter’s words do offer is the assurance that God sees unjust suffering, that it is never meaningless to Him, and that those who suffer can find strength in Christ, who suffered unjustly too.

### The Example of Christ (*2:21–25*)

Christ’s example and His sin-bearing death are studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *1 Peter 2:4–5* — Living Stones in a Spiritual House

> *“Come to him, a living stone, rejected indeed by men, but chosen by God, precious. You also as living stones are built up as a spiritual house, to be a holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.”*
>
> — *1 Peter 2:4–5* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“Come to him, a living stone.” Jesus is described as a “living stone.” Stones are normally lifeless, but Christ is alive, risen from the dead. He is the foundation stone of God’s new temple.

“Rejected indeed by men, but chosen by God, precious.” People rejected Jesus; the religious leaders condemned Him and the crowds called for His crucifixion. But God chose Him and values Him as precious.

Verse 5: “You also as living stones are built up as a spiritual house.” Believers, too, are living stones. As they come to Christ, they are built together into a “spiritual house,” a temple where God dwells. The church is not a building of stone but a living community.

“To be a holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.” Believers are not only the temple; they are also its priests. Every believer has access to God and the privilege of serving Him. Their sacrifices are “spiritual”: praise, prayer, good works, generosity, and lives offered to God (*Romans 12:1*; *Hebrews 13:15–16*). These are acceptable to God because they are offered through Jesus Christ.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This image would have been powerful for Peter, whose name means “rock” or “stone.” Jesus had said, “*On this rock I will build my assembly*” (*Matthew 16:18*). Peter now applies the image of stones to all believers. The church is built on Christ, the cornerstone, and every believer is a stone in the building.

In the Old Testament, God dwelt in the tabernacle and then in the temple in Jerusalem. Only priests from Aaron’s family could serve there. Now God dwells in His people, and every believer is a priest. This is sometimes called “the priesthood of all believers.” It does not eliminate the need for leaders and teachers, but it affirms that every believer has direct access to God and a role in His service.

The phrase “living stones” also emphasizes that the church is not static. It is growing, alive, and being built. Each believer contributes to the whole.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can see themselves as part of something larger than themselves. They are living stones in God’s spiritual house, connected to other believers and built together on Christ.

They can also embrace their priestly calling. Every believer can approach God directly in prayer and can offer Him spiritual sacrifices: worship, praise, acts of kindness, generosity, and faithful service in daily life.

Finally, those who feel rejected by others can remember that Christ was also rejected by people but chosen and precious to God. Believers, too, are precious to Him.

### *1 Peter 2:9–10* — A Chosen People, a Royal Priesthood

> *“But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God’s own possession, that you may proclaim the excellence of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light. In the past, you were not a people, but now are God’s people, who had not obtained mercy, but now have obtained mercy.”*
>
> — *1 Peter 2:9–10* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

In contrast to those who stumble (v8), Peter describes the identity of believers with titles once given to Israel (*Exodus 19:5–6*; *Deuteronomy 7:6*; *Isaiah 43:20–21*).

“But you are a chosen race.” Believers are chosen by God. Their identity does not depend on ethnicity but on God’s choice.

“A royal priesthood.” They are priests who serve the King, and they share in His royal dignity.

“A holy nation.” They are set apart for God, a people distinct from the world.

“A people for God’s own possession.” They belong to God. They are His treasured people.

“That you may proclaim the excellence of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light.” The purpose of this identity is to declare God’s praises, to make known His wonderful character and works. God has brought them out of the darkness of sin and ignorance into the light of His truth and love.

Verse 10: “In the past, you were not a people, but now are God’s people, who had not obtained mercy, but now have obtained mercy.” Peter echoes *Hosea 1:6–10* and *2:23*. Many of his readers were Gentiles who had once been outside God’s people. Now, by His mercy, they belong to Him.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses describe the dignity and purpose of God’s people. Believers who were slandered, rejected, and treated as outsiders by their society are told that in God’s eyes they are chosen, royal, holy, and treasured. Their identity is defined not by how the world sees them but by how God sees them.

The titles applied to believers were first given to Israel at Mount Sinai. In Christ, Gentile believers share in these privileges alongside Jewish believers. Christians have understood the relationship between Israel and the church in different ways, but Paul affirms that Gentile believers are grafted into God’s people (*Romans 11:17*) without replacing Israel, whose calling remains (*Romans 11:29*).

The purpose of this identity is mission: to “proclaim the excellence” of God. Believers are not chosen merely for their own benefit but to be a light to the world, declaring God’s goodness by their words and lives.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers who feel insignificant, rejected, or overlooked can rest in their true identity. They are chosen, royal, holy, and God’s own possession.

This identity also gives purpose. Believers can look for ways to declare God’s praises in their families, workplaces, and communities, sharing the good news of how He brought them out of darkness into light.

Finally, believers can remember the mercy they have received. They were once outside God’s people, but now they belong. That memory can keep them humble and eager to welcome others.

### *1 Peter 2:11–12* — Good Conduct Among the Nations

> *“Beloved, I beg you as foreigners and pilgrims to abstain from fleshly lusts which war against the soul, having good behavior among the nations, so in that of which they speak against you as evildoers, they may see your good works and glorify God in the day of visitation.”*
>
> — *1 Peter 2:11–12* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“Beloved, I beg you as foreigners and pilgrims.” Peter speaks tenderly (“beloved”) and urgently (“I beg you”). He reminds believers that they are “foreigners and pilgrims,” temporary residents in this world, with their true home in God’s kingdom.

“To abstain from fleshly lusts which war against the soul.” Sinful desires are like an enemy army attacking the soul. Believers must resist them.

Verse 12: “having good behavior among the nations.” “The nations” means unbelievers, the surrounding society. Believers are to live honorably, with conduct that is good, attractive, and admirable.

“So in that of which they speak against you as evildoers.” Unbelievers were slandering them, accusing them of wrongdoing.

“They may see your good works and glorify God in the day of visitation.” Over time, believers’ good deeds will be seen, and some who once accused them may come to glorify God. “The day of visitation” may mean the day God visits people with salvation, when they come to faith, or the final day of judgment, when all will acknowledge God.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses describe the believer’s posture in a hostile world. They are not to retreat or retaliate, but to live in such a way that their lives speak for themselves. Jesus taught, “*Let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven*” (*Matthew 5:16*).

The phrase “foreigners and pilgrims” connects with the theme of exile that runs through 1 Peter. Believers live in the world but are not shaped by it. They have different values, priorities, and hopes. This difference may bring misunderstanding, but it also makes their lives a witness.

The early church grew remarkably in the face of persecution, partly because of the way Christians lived: caring for the poor, the sick, and abandoned infants, showing love across social barriers, and enduring suffering with grace. Their good conduct drew many to faith.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can ask how their conduct appears to those outside the faith. Are they known for honesty, kindness, generosity, and integrity? Or does their behavior give others reasons to reject the gospel?

When believers face criticism or misunderstanding because of their faith, they can respond not with anger but with consistent goodness, trusting that God will vindicate them in His time.

Finally, believers can resist sinful desires, recognizing them as enemies of the soul, and pursue lives that honor God and draw others to Him.

### *1 Peter 2:21–24* — Following in His Steps

> *“For you were called to this, because Christ also suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow his steps, who didn’t sin, ‘neither was deceit found in his mouth.’ When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. When he suffered, he didn’t threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously. He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we, having died to sins, might live to righteousness. You were healed by his wounds.”*
>
> — *1 Peter 2:21–24* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“For you were called to this, because Christ also suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow his steps.” Following Christ includes the possibility of suffering. Christ suffered “for us,” on our behalf. He also left “an example,” literally a pattern used to teach children to write letters by tracing over them. Believers are to trace His steps.

Verse 22: “who didn’t sin, ‘neither was deceit found in his mouth.’” Quoting *Isaiah 53:9*, Peter emphasizes Christ’s innocence. He suffered unjustly.

Verse 23: “When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. When he suffered, he didn’t threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously.” Jesus did not retaliate against those who insulted and tortured Him. He did not threaten revenge. Instead, He entrusted Himself to God, the righteous Judge, who would make all things right.

Verse 24: “He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree.” Christ’s suffering was not only an example; it was a sacrifice. He carried our sins in His own body on the cross (“the tree”).

“That we, having died to sins, might live to righteousness.” The purpose was transformation. Through His death, believers are freed from sin’s power to live righteous lives.

“You were healed by his wounds.” Quoting *Isaiah 53:5*, Peter declares that Christ’s wounds bring healing, especially the healing of the soul from sin. For enslaved readers, who knew the pain of beatings, the image of Christ’s wounds bringing healing would have been especially moving.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses combine two aspects of Christ’s suffering: example and substitution. As an example, Christ shows believers how to respond to unjust suffering: without sin, without retaliation, entrusting themselves to God. As a substitute, Christ bore believers’ sins, doing for them what they could not do for themselves. The example would be crushing without the substitution; the substitution gives power to follow the example.

Peter draws heavily on *Isaiah 53*, the prophecy of the Suffering Servant. Peter, who once rebuked Jesus for speaking of His suffering (*Mark 8:31–33*), now understands that the cross was the center of God’s plan.

Christ’s example of not retaliating does not mean passive acceptance of all injustice. Jesus spoke truth boldly, confronted wrongdoing, and challenged those who struck Him unjustly (*John 18:22–23*). His refusal to retaliate means He did not seek personal revenge but entrusted judgment to God. Believers, too, can seek justice through proper means and protect themselves and others from harm, while refusing personal vengeance.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

When believers are insulted or treated unfairly, they can follow Christ’s example: refusing to insult back, refusing to threaten or seek revenge, and entrusting themselves to God, who judges justly. This is difficult, but Christ’s strength makes it possible.

At the same time, following Christ’s example does not require staying in situations of abuse. Seeking safety and justice is consistent with entrusting oneself to God.

Finally, believers can find healing in Christ’s wounds. Whatever wounds they carry, from their own sin or from what others have done to them, Christ’s suffering brings healing and restoration. They have returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of their souls (v25), who cares for them completely.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

First Peter 2 tells believers who they are. They are living stones, built together on Christ, the living Stone, into a spiritual house. They are a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices to God. They are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, God’s own possession, called out of darkness into His marvelous light. Though the world may reject or slander them, they are precious to God.

This identity gives believers purpose: to grow by craving the pure milk of God’s word, to declare God’s praises, and to live as foreigners and pilgrims, resisting sinful desires. Their good conduct among unbelievers can silence false accusations and lead others to glorify God.

Peter calls believers to respect human authorities for the Lord’s sake, within the limits of obedience to God, to use their freedom to serve God, and to honor everyone. His instructions to servants who suffered unjustly offer comfort to people in situations they could not escape, assuring them that God sees and values their faithful endurance. These words must never be used to keep anyone in abuse; God is on the side of the oppressed, and seeking safety is right.

At the heart of the chapter is Christ, who suffered unjustly, did not retaliate, and entrusted Himself to the righteous Judge. He bore our sins in His body on the cross so that we might die to sin and live for righteousness. By His wounds believers are healed. Whatever they face, they can follow in His steps and rest in the care of the Shepherd and Overseer of their souls.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, You are the living Stone, rejected by people but chosen and precious to God. Thank You for making me a living stone in Your spiritual house and a priest who can offer spiritual sacrifices to God. Give me a hunger for the pure milk of Your word, that I may grow. Thank You that I am chosen, part of a royal priesthood and a holy nation, Your own possession, called out of darkness into Your marvelous light. Help me to declare Your praises. As a foreigner and pilgrim in this world, help me to resist sinful desires and to live in a way that leads others to glorify You. When I am insulted or treated unjustly, help me to follow Your example, refusing to retaliate and entrusting myself to the righteous Judge. Protect all who suffer abuse and lead them to safety. Thank You for bearing my sins in Your body on the cross. By Your wounds I am healed. You are the Shepherd and Overseer of my soul. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

1 Peter · Chapter 3 of 5

# 1 Peter — Chapter 3

Chapter Theme: Blessing Instead of Insult, Hope Ready to Explain

[Read 1 Peter 3 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/1PE03.htm)

Main Teaching

Peter instructs wives to submit to their own husbands so that unbelieving husbands may be won over by their pure and reverent conduct, and to cultivate the lasting beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit rather than relying on outward adornment, following the example of holy women like Sarah, doing good without giving way to fear. Husbands are to live with their wives in an understanding way, showing them honor as fellow heirs of the gracious gift of life, so that nothing hinders their prayers. All believers are to be like-minded, sympathetic, loving, compassionate, and humble, not repaying evil for evil or insult for insult, but blessing, because they were called to inherit a blessing, as *Psalm 34* teaches. Even if they suffer for doing right, they are blessed and need not fear. They are to honor Christ as Lord in their hearts, always ready to give a reason for their hope with gentleness and respect, keeping a clear conscience so that slanderers are put to shame. It is better to suffer for doing good than for doing evil, for Christ suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring us to God, being put to death in the flesh but made alive in the Spirit. Peter speaks of Christ proclaiming to the spirits in prison, of Noah’s family saved through water as a picture of baptism, which saves through the resurrection of Jesus Christ, who is now at God’s right hand with all powers subject to Him.

## Chapter Background and Story

First Peter 3 continues the section on how believers should live within the social structures of their world (*2:13–3*:7). Peter has addressed relationships with governing authorities and with masters. Now he addresses wives and husbands. He then broadens his instructions to all believers, especially regarding how to respond to hostility and suffering.

Peter’s original readers lived in a world where a wife was expected to share her husband’s religion. A woman who became a Christian while her husband remained a pagan was in a difficult and sometimes dangerous position. Her faith might be seen as rebellion against her husband and against social order. Peter’s advice is aimed at helping such women live faithfully and wisely, in a way that might win their husbands to Christ.

The chapter ends with one of the most difficult passages in the New Testament (vv18–22), about Christ preaching to “the spirits in prison.” Interpreters have offered several explanations, which are presented below. The main point is clear: Christ’s suffering led to victory, and believers who suffer with Him share in that victory.

### Wives and Husbands (*3:1–7*)

“*In the same way, wives, be in subjection to your own husbands, so that, even if any don’t obey the Word, they may be won by the behavior of their wives without a word*” (*v. 1*), “*seeing your pure behavior in fear*” (*v. 2*). Peter has in mind especially wives whose husbands did not believe. Rather than trying to argue them into faith, these wives could win them through godly lives. “Without a word” does not mean the wives could never speak of their faith, but that their conduct would speak powerfully.

“*Let your beauty come not from the outward adorning of braiding your hair, and of wearing gold ornaments or of putting on fine clothing*” (*v. 3*), “*but from the hidden person of the heart, in the incorruptible adornment of a gentle and quiet spirit, which is very precious in God’s sight*” (*v. 4*). In the Roman world, elaborate hairstyles and jewelry were marks of wealth and status (see *1 Timothy 2:9–10*). Peter is not forbidding all care for appearance, but redirecting attention to inner beauty, which never fades and which God treasures. “A gentle and quiet spirit” describes a calm, trusting heart, not a weak personality. It is a quality Jesus Himself displayed (*Matthew 11:29*), and it is fitting for every believer.

“*For this is how in the past the holy women who hoped in God also adorned themselves, being in subjection to their own husbands*” (*v. 5*). “*So Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord, whose children you now are if you do well and are not put in fear by any terror*” (*v. 6*). Sarah is presented as an example of a woman who hoped in God. Notice the closing phrase: “not put in fear by any terror.” Peter acknowledges that these women might face intimidation, and he encourages them not to be ruled by fear.

Christians understand the instructions to wives in different ways, as they do the similar passages in *Ephesians 5* and *Colossians 3*. Some see a lasting pattern of a wife’s voluntary respect for her husband’s loving leadership. Others see Peter applying the gospel within first-century household structures, with the lasting principles being faithfulness, respect, inner beauty, and courage. Both views agree on several crucial points. A wife’s submission is “*for the Lord’s sake*” (*1 Peter 2:13*) and never requires her to sin. It never requires her to accept abuse. Peter himself recognizes that wives might face “terror” and tells them not to be ruled by fear. A wife facing abuse should seek safety and help, and the church must protect and support her rather than urging her to remain in danger.

“*You husbands, in the same way, live with your wives according to knowledge, giving honor to the woman as to the weaker vessel, as also being joint heirs of the grace of life, that your prayers may not be hindered*” (*v. 7*). The instructions to husbands are studied below.

### Blessing Instead of Retaliation (*3:8–12*)

The call to unity and blessing is studied below. “*For, “He who would love life and see good days, let him keep his tongue from evil and his lips from speaking deceit.*” (*v. 10*) “*Let him turn away from evil and do good. Let him seek peace and pursue it.*” (*v. 11*) “*For the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and his ears open to their prayer; but the face of the Lord is against those who do evil.”*” (*v. 12*) Peter quotes *Psalm 34:12–16*, a psalm David wrote after escaping danger. A good life involves controlling the tongue, turning from evil, doing good, and actively pursuing peace. God watches over the righteous and hears their prayers.

### Suffering for Doing Good (*3:13–17*)

“*Now who will harm you if you become imitators of that which is good?*” (*v. 13*) Generally, those who do good are less likely to be harmed. “*But even if you should suffer for righteousness’ sake, you are blessed. “Don’t fear what they fear, neither be troubled.”*” (*v. 14*) Even if they do suffer, they are blessed. Jesus said, “*Blessed are those who have been persecuted for righteousness' sake*” (*Matthew 5:10*). Peter adapts *Isaiah 8:12*: believers need not share the fears of those around them. The call to be ready to explain their hope is studied below.

“*For it is better, if it is God’s will, that you suffer for doing what is right than for doing evil*” (*v. 17*). Suffering for wrongdoing is deserved; suffering for doing good shares in Christ’s experience and is commendable to God.

### Christ’s Suffering and Victory (*3:18–22*)

Christ’s once-for-all suffering is studied below.

“*in whom he also went and preached to the spirits in prison*” (*v. 19*), “*who before were disobedient when God waited patiently in the days of Noah while the ship was being built. In it, few, that is, eight souls, were saved through water*” (*v. 20*). These verses have puzzled readers throughout church history. There are three main interpretations. Some believe that between His death and resurrection, Christ went to the realm of the dead and proclaimed His victory, either announcing judgment or offering the gospel, to the spirits of those who died in Noah’s time. Others believe that the pre-incarnate Christ, through the Spirit, preached through Noah to the people of Noah’s day, who are now “spirits in prison.” Still others, noting that “spirits” in the New Testament often refers to angelic beings, believe that the risen Christ proclaimed His victory to fallen angels, connected in Jewish tradition with the days of Noah (*Genesis 6:1–4*; *2 Peter 2:4–5*; *Jude 1:6*). Whichever view is correct, the main point is that Christ’s suffering led to triumph over every hostile power.

“*This is a symbol of baptism, which now saves you—not the putting away of the filth of the flesh, but the answer of a good conscience toward God—through the resurrection of Jesus Christ*” (*v. 21*). Noah’s family passed through the waters of the flood and were brought safely to a new world. Baptism is a picture of this: passing through water into new life. Peter clarifies that baptism does not save by physically washing the body. What saves is the reality baptism signifies: a pledge or appeal to God from a good conscience, made possible “through the resurrection of Jesus Christ.” Christians understand the role of baptism in salvation differently, but all agree that its power comes from Christ’s death and resurrection, received by faith.

“*who is at the right hand of God, having gone into heaven, angels and authorities and powers being made subject to him*” (*v. 22*). Christ has ascended and reigns over every spiritual power. Believers who suffer can take courage: their Lord is victorious.

## Important Verses Explained

### *1 Peter 3:7* — Husbands, Honor Your Wives

> *“You husbands, in the same way, live with your wives according to knowledge, giving honor to the woman as to the weaker vessel, as also being joint heirs of the grace of life, that your prayers may not be hindered.”*
>
> — *1 Peter 3:7* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“You husbands, in the same way, live with your wives according to knowledge.” Husbands are to live with their wives in an understanding way, knowing them, considering their needs, perspectives, and feelings, and treating them wisely and thoughtfully.

“Giving honor to the woman.” Husbands are to show their wives honor, respect, and value. In a culture where women were often treated as inferior, this was a significant command.

“As to the weaker vessel.” This phrase likely refers to physical strength, since women are generally physically weaker than men, and perhaps to women’s more vulnerable social and legal position in the ancient world. It does not mean women are morally, intellectually, or spiritually weaker. The point is that husbands must never take advantage of greater physical or social power, but use it to protect and honor their wives.

“As also being joint heirs of the grace of life.” Husbands and wives are equal heirs of God’s grace and eternal life. Spiritually, they stand side by side before God.

“That your prayers may not be hindered.” A husband who mistreats his wife damages his relationship with God. His prayers will be hindered.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse balances the instructions to wives. While wives are called to respect their husbands, husbands are called to understand and honor their wives. Both are accountable to God for how they treat each other.

The phrase “joint heirs of the grace of life” is a powerful affirmation of equality. In God’s eyes, husband and wife are equally His children and equally heirs of His promises (*Galatians 3:28*). This truth transforms how a husband should treat his wife: not as a possession or subordinate, but as a fellow heir of grace.

The warning that prayers will be hindered shows how seriously God takes the treatment of wives. A man cannot mistreat his wife and expect to have a healthy relationship with God. *Malachi 2:13–16* also connects God’s refusal to accept offerings with men’s unfaithfulness to their wives.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Husbands can ask whether they truly understand their wives: listening to them, considering their needs, and seeking to know their hearts. Understanding requires time, attention, and humility.

Husbands can show honor through words of appreciation, respect for their wives’ opinions and gifts, faithfulness, and protection. Any form of control, harshness, or abuse is completely contrary to this verse and dishonors God.

Married couples can remember that they are joint heirs of grace, equally loved by God. Praying together, serving together, and growing together in faith reflects this shared inheritance.

### *1 Peter 3:8–9* — Blessing Instead of Insult

> *“Finally, all of you be like-minded, compassionate, loving as brothers, tenderhearted, courteous, not rendering evil for evil or insult for insult; but instead blessing, knowing that you were called to this, that you may inherit a blessing.”*
>
> — *1 Peter 3:8–9* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Peter now addresses all believers. “Finally, all of you be like-minded.” Believers should share a common purpose and commitment to Christ.

“Compassionate”: sharing in others’ feelings, rejoicing with those who rejoice and weeping with those who weep.

“Loving as brothers”: showing the affection of family members.

“Tenderhearted”: having a heart of mercy and kindness.

“Courteous”: or humble-minded, not proud or arrogant.

Verse 9: “not rendering evil for evil or insult for insult.” When believers are wronged or insulted, they are not to retaliate.

“But instead blessing.” Instead of repaying evil, they are to bless, speaking well of those who hurt them, praying for them, and seeking their good.

“Knowing that you were called to this, that you may inherit a blessing.” Believers are called to bless others, and they themselves will inherit God’s blessing.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This teaching echoes Jesus’ words: “*bless those who curse you, and pray for those who mistreat you*” (*Luke 6:28*). Paul taught the same: “*Bless those who persecute you; bless, and don't curse*” (*Romans 12:14*), and “*Repay no one evil for evil*” (*Romans 12:17*).

Peter had personally learned this lesson. When soldiers came to arrest Jesus, Peter drew a sword and cut off a man’s ear (*John 18:10*). Jesus rebuked him and healed the man. Later, Peter watched Jesus endure insults and suffering without retaliation (*1 Peter 2:23*). Now Peter teaches what he learned.

Blessing those who insult us is not natural. It requires the Spirit’s power. But it reflects the character of God, who blessed us when we were His enemies (*Romans 5:10*). It also breaks the cycle of retaliation and opens the door to reconciliation.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

When believers are insulted, criticized, or mistreated, they can choose not to respond in kind. This might mean pausing before reacting, refusing to speak harshly, and praying for the person who hurt them.

Blessing those who hurt us does not mean pretending the hurt did not happen or allowing ongoing abuse. Believers can set boundaries and seek justice while still refusing hatred and revenge.

Believers can also cultivate the qualities Peter lists: unity, compassion, love, tenderness, and humility, especially in their church communities, where these qualities build strong relationships.

### *1 Peter 3:15–16* — Always Ready to Give an Answer

> *“But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts. Always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you a reason concerning the hope that is in you, with humility and fear, having a good conscience. Thus, while you are spoken against as evildoers, they may be disappointed who curse your good way of life in Christ.”*
>
> — *1 Peter 3:15–16* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts.” Many manuscripts read “sanctify Christ as Lord in your hearts.” To “sanctify” means to set apart, to honor as holy. Believers are to give Christ the place of supreme honor in their hearts. When Christ is Lord, fear of others loses its power.

“Always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you a reason concerning the hope that is in you.” The word “answer” (*apologia*) means a defense or explanation, as in a court of law. Believers should be prepared to explain why they have hope. People will notice their hope, especially in suffering, and some will ask about it.

“With humility and fear.” Believers should explain their faith with gentleness, not arrogance or aggression, and with respect, both for the person asking and for God.

Verse 16: “having a good conscience.” Believers should live in a way that is consistent with their message.

“Thus, while you are spoken against as evildoers, they may be disappointed who curse your good way of life in Christ.” When believers live with integrity, those who slander them will be put to shame, because their accusations will be shown to be false.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This passage has been foundational for Christian “apologetics,” the practice of explaining and defending the faith. But notice the context. Peter is writing to believers facing hostility. The questions they receive may come from curious people or from critics. In either case, believers should be ready.

What they are to explain is not primarily a philosophical system but “the hope that is in you.” Their hope, rooted in Christ’s resurrection (*1 Peter 1:3*), is what makes them different. When people see believers facing suffering with hope, they will want to know why.

The manner of the answer is as important as its content. Gentleness and respect reflect Christ’s character. An argumentative, arrogant, or harsh defense of the faith contradicts the message. Paul similarly urges believers to let their speech be gracious, “*seasoned with salt*” (*Colossians 4:6*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can prepare to explain their hope. This might involve thinking through how they came to faith, what Christ means to them, and why they believe the gospel is true. They do not need to be experts, but they should be ready to share honestly.

Believers can also ask whether their lives display hope. Do people see something different in how they face difficulties?

Finally, when believers talk about their faith, they can do so with gentleness and respect, listening well, answering honestly, and treating others with dignity, even those who disagree or criticize.

### *1 Peter 3:18* — The Righteous for the Unrighteous

> *“Because Christ also suffered for sins once, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring you to God, being put to death in the flesh, but made alive in the Spirit,”*
>
> — *1 Peter 3:18* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“Because Christ also suffered for sins once.” Christ’s suffering was “for sins,” dealing with sin through His death. And it happened “once,” never needing to be repeated, as Hebrews also emphasizes (*Hebrews 9:26–28*; *10:10*).

“The righteous for the unrighteous.” Christ, who was completely righteous, suffered in the place of the unrighteous. He took the penalty that sinners deserved.

“That he might bring you to God.” The purpose of Christ’s death was reconciliation, bringing people into God’s presence and relationship with Him. Sin had separated people from God; Christ’s death removes the barrier.

“Being put to death in the flesh, but made alive in the Spirit.” Christ died physically, in His human body. But He was raised to life by the Spirit, or in the realm of the Spirit, His resurrection life.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse is one of the clearest summaries of the gospel in the New Testament. It explains the meaning of the cross: substitution (“the righteous for the unrighteous”), sufficiency (“once”), and purpose (“*that he might bring you to God*” (*v. 18*)).

The phrase “the righteous for the unrighteous” expresses what theologians call substitutionary atonement. Christ took the place of sinners. *Isaiah 53:5–6*, which Peter quoted in chapter 2, says the Servant was wounded for our transgressions and the LORD laid on Him the iniquity of us all. Paul writes that God made Christ, who knew no sin, to be sin for us (*2 Corinthians 5:21*).

“That he might bring you to God” shows that salvation is not only about forgiveness but about relationship. Christ’s death opens the way for sinners to come home to God.

In the context of 1 Peter, this verse also serves as encouragement. Christ suffered unjustly, but His suffering led to victory and resurrection. Believers who suffer for doing good follow the same path, from suffering to glory.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can rest in the truth that Christ suffered once for all their sins. Nothing needs to be added. They are forgiven and brought to God.

This verse also invites believers to marvel at Christ’s love. He, the righteous one, suffered for the unrighteous, including them. That love can inspire gratitude and devotion.

Finally, when believers suffer unjustly, they can remember that Christ did too, and that His suffering led to resurrection. Their suffering is not the end of the story.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

First Peter 3 shows how faith shapes the closest relationships and how believers should respond to hostility. Wives with unbelieving husbands are encouraged to win them through godly conduct and the lasting beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, not ruled by fear. Christians differ in how they apply these instructions today, but all agree that they never require a woman to sin or to remain in danger. Husbands are called to live with their wives in an understanding way, honoring them as equal heirs of God’s grace, knowing that mistreating their wives hinders their prayers.

All believers are called to unity, compassion, love, tenderness, and humility. When they are insulted or wronged, they are to bless instead of retaliating, because they were called to inherit a blessing. They can seek peace, control their tongues, and trust that God’s eyes are on the righteous.

Even when believers suffer for doing good, they are blessed and need not fear. They are to honor Christ as Lord in their hearts and always be ready to explain the hope within them, with gentleness and respect, living with a clear conscience so that slander is put to shame.

At the center of the chapter is Christ, who suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring us to God. He died, was raised, and now reigns at God’s right hand over every power. Whatever believers face, they belong to the victorious Christ, and their suffering, like His, leads to glory.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, You suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring me to God. Thank You for Your love and for Your victory over every power. Bless marriages with understanding, honor, faithfulness, and mutual respect, and protect all who live in fear in their homes. Give me the beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, precious in Your sight. Make me like-minded with Your people, compassionate, loving, tenderhearted, and humble. When I am insulted or wronged, help me to bless rather than retaliate. Teach me to keep my tongue from evil and to seek peace. Help me to honor You as Lord in my heart and to be ready to explain the hope I have, with gentleness and respect. When I suffer for doing good, keep me from fear, and remind me that You reign at the right hand of God. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

1 Peter · Chapter 4 of 5

# 1 Peter — Chapter 4

Chapter Theme: Living for God’s Will and Sharing Christ’s Sufferings

[Read 1 Peter 4 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/1PE04.htm)

Main Teaching

Since Christ suffered in the flesh, believers are to arm themselves with the same attitude, living the rest of their earthly lives not for human desires but for the will of God. They have spent enough time in the past in the reckless behavior of their surrounding culture, and their former companions are surprised and slander them for no longer joining in, but those slanderers will give account to God, the Judge of the living and the dead. Because the end of all things is near, believers should be clear-minded and self-controlled for prayer, love one another deeply, since love covers a multitude of sins, offer hospitality without grumbling, and use whatever gift they have received to serve others as good stewards of God’s grace, speaking as one who speaks God’s words and serving with the strength God provides, so that God may be glorified through Jesus Christ. They should not be surprised by the fiery trial testing them, but rejoice that they share in Christ’s sufferings, so they will be overjoyed when His glory is revealed. If they are insulted for Christ’s name, they are blessed, for the Spirit of glory rests on them. They must not suffer as wrongdoers, but if they suffer as Christians, they should not be ashamed but glorify God. Judgment begins with God’s household, so those who suffer according to God’s will should entrust themselves to their faithful Creator and keep doing good.

## Chapter Background and Story

First Peter 4 continues the theme of suffering that runs through the letter. Peter has shown that Christ suffered unjustly and was vindicated (*1 Peter 3:18–22*). Now he applies this to his readers’ situation. They were suffering because they had changed their way of life. Former friends who once joined them in drunken parties, immorality, and idol worship now found them strange and spoke against them.

Peter calls this suffering a “fiery trial” (v12). Some scholars think this refers to the intensifying persecution of Christians in the Roman Empire, perhaps under Nero, who blamed Christians for the great fire of Rome in A.D. 64. Others think it describes the ongoing social hostility believers faced. Either way, Peter wants his readers to understand that suffering for Christ is not strange or unexpected. It is a sharing in Christ’s own sufferings, and it leads to glory.

In the middle of the chapter, Peter gives practical instructions for life in the Christian community: prayer, love, hospitality, and the use of spiritual gifts. In times of pressure, believers need one another more than ever.

### Living for God’s Will (*4:1–6*)

“*Therefore, since Christ suffered for us in the flesh, arm yourselves also with the same mind; for he who has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sin*” (*v. 1*), “*that you no longer should live the rest of your time in the flesh for the lusts of men, but for the will of God*” (*v. 2*). Believers are to “arm themselves,” like soldiers putting on armor, with the same attitude Christ had: a willingness to suffer rather than sin. “He who has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sin” is a difficult phrase. It may mean that those willing to suffer for Christ have made a decisive break with sin, or that union with Christ in His death frees believers from sin’s power (*Romans 6:7*). Either way, the goal is to live for God’s will rather than human desires.

“*For we have spent enough of our past time doing the desire of the Gentiles, and having walked in lewdness, lusts, drunken binges, orgies, carousings, and abominable idolatries*” (*v. 3*). Peter describes the lifestyle many of his readers had left behind. “Gentiles” here means those who do not know God. Enough time had been wasted on such things.

“*They think it is strange that you don’t run with them into the same excess of riot, speaking evil of you*” (*v. 4*). Former companions were surprised and offended that believers no longer joined them. Their surprise turned to slander. “*They will give account to him who is ready to judge the living and the dead*” (*v. 5*). Those who slander believers will answer to God.

“*For to this end the Good News was preached even to the dead, that they might be judged indeed as men in the flesh, but live as to God in the spirit*” (*v. 6*). This verse is difficult. Many interpreters understand “the dead” to mean believers who heard the gospel while alive and have since died. Though they were “judged” by people, perhaps condemned or mocked, or though they experienced physical death, they now live with God. Others connect this verse with *1 Peter 3:19*, seeing a proclamation to the dead. Most favor the first reading, which offers comfort: believers who died, even if mocked or persecuted, are alive to God.

### Love and Service in the Last Days (*4:7–11*)

“*But the end of all things is near. Therefore be of sound mind, self-controlled, and sober in prayer*” (*v. 7*). Since Christ’s resurrection, the world has entered its final age. Believers should live with clear minds and self-control so they can pray well. Prayer requires alertness, not panic or distraction. The call to love, hospitality, and service is studied below.

### The Fiery Trial (*4:12–19*)

The call not to be surprised by suffering is studied below. “*But let none of you suffer as a murderer, or a thief, or an evil doer, or a meddler in other men’s matters*” (*v. 15*). Not all suffering is suffering for Christ. Those who suffer because of their own wrongdoing should not claim to be persecuted. Interestingly, Peter includes “meddler” in the list. Even believers can bring trouble on themselves by interfering in others’ affairs.

“*But if one of you suffers for being a Christian, let him not be ashamed; but let him glorify God in this matter*” (*v. 16*). The name “Christian” was first used in Antioch (*Acts 11:26*) and was likely a label outsiders used, sometimes with contempt. Peter says believers should not be ashamed of it. Suffering for bearing Christ’s name is an honor.

“*For the time has come for judgment to begin with the household of God. If it begins first with us, what will happen to those who don’t obey the Good News of God?*” (*v. 17*) “*“If it is hard for the righteous to be saved, what will happen to the ungodly and the sinner?”*” (*v. 18*) God’s judgment, like a refining fire, begins with His own people, purifying them through trials (see *Ezekiel 9:6*; *Malachi 3:1–3*). If God’s people go through refining trials, how much more serious will judgment be for those who reject the gospel? Peter quotes *Proverbs 11:31* (in the Greek version). The salvation of the righteous comes through difficulty, not because God is weak, but because the path to glory passes through suffering, as it did for Christ. The chapter’s closing call to trust God is studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *1 Peter 4:8* — Love Covers a Multitude of Sins

> *“And above all things be earnest in your love among yourselves, for love covers a multitude of sins.”*
>
> — *1 Peter 4:8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“And above all things be earnest in your love among yourselves.” Of all the instructions Peter gives, love comes first. “Earnest” means intense, fervent, constant, stretched out, like an athlete straining toward the finish line. Believers are to love one another deeply and wholeheartedly.

“For love covers a multitude of sins.” Peter draws on *Proverbs 10:12*: “*love covers all wrongs*” (*Proverbs 10:12*). Love covers sins by forgiving them, overlooking minor offenses, and refusing to keep a record of wrongs (*1 Corinthians 13:5*). Where there is love, people do not hold grudges or expose others’ faults unnecessarily.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

In times of pressure and persecution, communities can become tense. People may become irritable, critical, or divided. Peter calls believers to deep love, which holds communities together.

“Love covers a multitude of sins” does not mean that love ignores serious sin or hides wrongdoing that harms others. It does not mean covering up abuse or crime. Scripture calls for confronting sin, protecting the vulnerable, and seeking justice (*Matthew 18:15–17*; *Ephesians 5:11*). Rather, it means that love is quick to forgive, slow to take offense, and willing to overlook the everyday faults and irritations that come with living in community. It means not broadcasting others’ failures or holding them against them.

Love also covers sin in the sense that God’s love, shown in Christ, covers believers’ sins. Those who have received such love are called to extend it to others.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can make love their top priority in relationships, especially within the church. This might mean being patient with difficult people, forgiving offenses, and refusing to gossip about others’ faults.

When conflicts arise, believers can ask whether the issue is serious enough to address or whether love can simply overlook it. Many minor offenses can be covered by love.

At the same time, believers should distinguish between covering minor faults and covering serious wrongdoing. Love protects the vulnerable, and that sometimes requires bringing harm into the light.

### *1 Peter 4:10–11* — Good Stewards of God’s Grace

> *“As each has received a gift, employ it in serving one another, as good managers of the grace of God in its various forms. If anyone speaks, let it be as it were the very words of God. If anyone serves, let it be as of the strength which God supplies, that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ, to whom belong the glory and the dominion forever and ever. Amen.”*
>
> — *1 Peter 4:10–11* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“As each has received a gift.” Every believer has received at least one gift from God. No one is left out.

“Employ it in serving one another.” Gifts are not for personal advantage or display but for serving others.

“As good managers of the grace of God in its various forms.” A “manager” or steward was a household servant entrusted with the master’s resources. Believers are stewards of God’s grace, which comes in many different forms. Each gift is a piece of God’s grace to be used for others.

Verse 11 gives two broad categories of gifts. “If anyone speaks, let it be as it were the very words of God.” Those with speaking gifts, such as teaching, preaching, or encouraging, should speak faithfully, as those who are delivering God’s message, not their own opinions.

“If anyone serves, let it be as of the strength which God supplies.” Those with serving gifts, such as helping, giving, leading, or showing mercy, should serve in God’s strength, not their own.

“That in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ.” The ultimate purpose of every gift is God’s glory.

“To whom belong the glory and the dominion forever and ever. Amen.”

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This passage teaches that every believer is gifted and responsible. Paul describes spiritual gifts in *Romans 12:6–8* and *1 Corinthians 12*, emphasizing that every member of the body of Christ has a role. Peter makes the same point more simply: whatever gift you have, use it to serve others.

The image of stewardship is important. Gifts belong to God, not to the believer. They are entrusted for a purpose. Jesus’ parable of the talents warns against burying God’s gifts out of fear or laziness (*Matthew 25:14–30*).

The emphasis on God’s strength is freeing. Believers do not serve in their own power. When they feel inadequate, they can rely on the strength God supplies. And when they succeed, the glory goes to God, not to themselves.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can ask what gifts God has given them and how they are using them to serve others. Gifts might include teaching, encouraging, hospitality, administration, generosity, compassion, craftsmanship, music, prayer, or many others.

Those who speak, whether in teaching, preaching, or simply encouraging a friend, can seek to speak faithfully to God’s word. Those who serve can rely on God’s strength rather than their own.

Finally, believers can aim for God’s glory in all their service, not seeking recognition for themselves but pointing others to Him.

### *1 Peter 4:12–14* — Do Not Be Surprised by the Fiery Trial

> *“Beloved, don’t be astonished at the fiery trial which has come upon you to test you, as though a strange thing happened to you. But because you are partakers of Christ’s sufferings, rejoice, that at the revelation of his glory you also may rejoice with exceeding joy. If you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed, because the Spirit of glory and of God rests on you. On their part he is blasphemed, but on your part he is glorified.”*
>
> — *1 Peter 4:12–14* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“Beloved, don’t be astonished at the fiery trial which has come upon you to test you.” Peter addresses his readers tenderly as “beloved.” He tells them not to be surprised by intense suffering, a “fiery trial.” Like fire refining metal (*1 Peter 1:7*), this trial tests and purifies their faith.

“As though a strange thing happened to you.” Suffering for Christ is not unusual or foreign. It is part of following Him.

Verse 13: “But because you are partakers of Christ’s sufferings, rejoice.” Believers who suffer for Christ share in His sufferings. This is a reason for joy, not because suffering is pleasant, but because it unites them with Christ.

“That at the revelation of his glory you also may rejoice with exceeding joy.” When Christ returns in glory, those who shared His sufferings will share His joy. Present suffering leads to future joy.

Verse 14: “If you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed.” Those who are insulted because they belong to Christ are blessed, echoing Jesus’ words in *Matthew 5:11–12*.

“Because the Spirit of glory and of God rests on you.” The Holy Spirit, who brings God’s glory, rests on suffering believers. Just as God’s glory rested on the tabernacle (*Exodus 40:34–35*), His Spirit rests on His suffering people.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Jesus warned His followers that they would face persecution (*John 15:18–20*). Paul wrote that all who want to live godly lives in Christ will be persecuted (*2 Timothy 3:12*). Suffering for Christ is not a sign of God’s absence but of belonging to Him.

The idea of sharing in Christ’s sufferings is found throughout the New Testament. Paul longed to know “*the fellowship of his sufferings*” (*Philippians 3:10*). This does not mean believers add to Christ’s atoning work, which was complete. It means they share His experience of rejection by a hostile world and His path from suffering to glory.

The promise that “the Spirit of glory... rests on you” is deeply comforting. In the very moment of insult and suffering, God’s presence and glory are with His people. Stephen, as he was being stoned, saw the glory of God and Jesus standing at His right hand (*Acts 7:55–56*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers who face ridicule, rejection, or persecution because of their faith can remember that this is not strange. They are sharing in Christ’s experience, and God’s Spirit rests on them.

Believers can find joy even in difficult circumstances, not by denying the pain, but by remembering that they belong to Christ and that glory awaits.

This passage also calls believers to stand with persecuted Christians around the world, praying for them, supporting them, and speaking up for them.

### *1 Peter 4:19* — Entrust Your Souls to a Faithful Creator

> *“Therefore let them also who suffer according to the will of God in doing good entrust their souls to him, as to a faithful Creator.”*
>
> — *1 Peter 4:19* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Peter concludes the chapter with practical advice for those who suffer. “Therefore let them also who suffer according to the will of God.” Their suffering is not outside God’s control. God allows it for His purposes.

“In doing good.” While suffering, believers should keep doing good. Suffering is not an excuse to stop living faithfully.

“Entrust their souls to him.” “Entrust” means to commit something valuable into someone’s safekeeping, like depositing treasure. Believers are to place their whole lives into God’s hands.

“As to a faithful Creator.” God is the Creator, who made all things and sustains them. And He is faithful, completely trustworthy. The one who made them will take care of them.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse echoes Christ’s example. On the cross, Jesus prayed, “*Father, into your hands I commit my spirit*” (*Luke 23:46*), quoting *Psalm 31:5*. Peter earlier described how Jesus “*committed himself to him who judges righteously*” (*1 Peter 2:23*). Believers follow His example by entrusting themselves to God.

“Faithful Creator” is a unique title in the New Testament. It combines God’s power as Creator with His reliability. The God who created the universe has the power to care for His people, and He is faithful to do so. Nothing is outside His control, and He will never abandon those who trust Him.

The phrase “according to the will of God” does not mean God delights in suffering or that all suffering is His direct will. It means that even suffering is within His sovereign purposes, and He can bring good from it.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

When believers face suffering, they can pray as Jesus did, entrusting their lives into God’s hands. This act of trust brings peace, even when circumstances do not change.

Believers can also continue doing good, even when life is hard. Faithfulness in suffering is a powerful testimony.

Finally, believers can remember that their Creator is faithful. The God who made them knows them, loves them, and will care for them. Their lives are safe in His hands.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

First Peter 4 calls believers to live for God’s will rather than for human desires, arming themselves with the same mind Christ had when He suffered. When former friends find their new way of life strange and speak against them, believers can remember that those who slander them will give account to God, and that their own lives are hidden with Him.

Because the end of all things is near, believers are called to clear-minded prayer and, above all, to deep, earnest love for one another, love that covers a multitude of sins. They are to show hospitality without grumbling and to use every gift God has given them to serve others as good stewards of His varied grace, speaking His words faithfully and serving in His strength, so that God is glorified in everything.

Peter also prepares believers for suffering. They should not be surprised by fiery trials, as if something strange were happening. Suffering for Christ is a sharing in His sufferings, and it leads to joy when His glory is revealed. Those insulted for His name are blessed, because the Spirit of glory rests on them. They should not suffer for wrongdoing, but if they suffer as Christians, they need not be ashamed.

Finally, those who suffer according to God’s will are to entrust their lives to their faithful Creator and keep doing good. Like Christ, who committed His spirit into the Father’s hands, believers can rest their lives in the care of the God who made them and will never fail them.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, You suffered in the flesh for me. Help me to arm myself with the same mind, living not for my own desires but for the will of God. When others find my faith strange or speak against me, keep me steady. Because the end of all things is near, make me clear-minded and faithful in prayer. Above all, fill me with deep love for my brothers and sisters, love that covers a multitude of sins. Make me hospitable without grumbling. Show me the gifts You have given me, and help me to use them to serve others in Your strength, so that God may be glorified in everything. When fiery trials come, help me not to be surprised, but to rejoice that I share in Your sufferings. Strengthen all who are insulted and persecuted for Your name. Into the hands of my faithful Creator I entrust my life. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
