1 Peter · Chapter 5 of 5

# 1 Peter — Chapter 5

Chapter Theme: Humble Shepherds, Watchful Believers, and the God of All Grace

[Read 1 Peter 5 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/1PE05.htm)

Main Teaching

Peter, writing as a fellow elder and a witness of Christ’s sufferings, urges the elders to shepherd God’s flock willingly, eagerly, and not for dishonest gain, not lording it over those in their care but being examples to them, and promises that when the Chief Shepherd appears they will receive an unfading crown of glory. Younger people are to respect the elders, and all believers are to clothe themselves with humility toward one another, because God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble. Humbling themselves under God’s mighty hand, they can cast all their anxiety on Him, because He cares for them. They must be alert and sober, because their enemy the devil prowls like a roaring lion looking for someone to devour; they are to resist him, firm in faith, knowing that believers throughout the world face the same sufferings. After they have suffered a little while, the God of all grace, who called them to His eternal glory in Christ, will Himself restore, confirm, strengthen, and establish them. Peter closes by noting that he wrote with Silvanus’s help to testify that this is the true grace of God, and sends greetings from the church in “Babylon” and from Mark, his son in the faith.

## Chapter Background and Story

In the final chapter of his letter, Peter turns to the leaders of the churches. In times of suffering and pressure, good leadership is essential. Shepherds who care for the flock, protect it, and set a good example help believers stand firm. Poor leaders, who serve for selfish reasons or dominate others, cause great harm.

Peter writes with personal authority and humility. He calls himself a “fellow elder,” placing himself alongside the leaders rather than above them. He was a “witness of the sufferings of Christ,” having been present during Jesus’ ministry and arrest, though he had failed Jesus at the crucial moment. After the resurrection, Jesus had commissioned Peter three times to “*Feed my sheep*” (*John 21:17*) (*John 21:15–17*). Now Peter passes that charge on to other shepherds.

The chapter then gives final instructions to all believers about humility, trust, and spiritual watchfulness, before closing with a beautiful promise of God’s restoring grace.

### Shepherding the Flock (*5:1–4*)

“*Therefore I exhort the elders among you, as a fellow elder and a witness of the sufferings of Christ, and who will also share in the glory that will be revealed*” (*v. 1*): Peter’s appeal is grounded in his own experience and hope. He saw Christ suffer, and he will share in His glory. The charge to elders is studied below.

“*When the chief Shepherd is revealed, you will receive the crown of glory that doesn’t fade away*” (*v. 4*). Jesus is “the chief Shepherd.” Elders are under-shepherds, serving under Him and accountable to Him. When He returns, faithful shepherds will receive a reward: a crown of glory that never fades. Athletes in ancient games received wreaths of leaves that soon withered; this crown lasts forever.

### Clothed with Humility (*5:5–7*)

“*Likewise, you younger ones, be subject to the elder. Yes, all of you clothe yourselves with humility and subject yourselves to one another; for “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.”*” (*v. 5*) Younger believers are to respect the leaders. But humility is required of everyone. “Clothe yourselves” uses a word for tying on an apron, the garment a servant wore. Peter may have been remembering the night Jesus tied a towel around Himself and washed the disciples’ feet, including Peter’s (*John 13:4–5*). The quotation from *Proverbs 3:34* is also found in *James 4:6*, where it is discussed more fully. The call to humble oneself and cast anxieties on God is studied below.

### Resisting the Devil (*5:8–9*)

The warning about the devil is studied below.

### The God of All Grace (*5:10–11*)

God’s promise of restoration is studied below. “*To him be the glory and the power forever and ever. Amen*” (*v. 11*). The promise leads naturally to praise.

### Final Greetings (*5:12–14*)

“*Through Silvanus, our faithful brother, as I consider him, I have written to you briefly, exhorting and testifying that this is the true grace of God in which you stand*” (*v. 12*). Silvanus, also called Silas, was Paul’s companion on his missionary journeys (*Acts 15:40*; *1 Thessalonians 1:1*). He may have helped Peter write the letter or carried it to the churches. Peter summarizes his whole letter: it testifies to “the true grace of God.” Believers are to stand firm in it.

“*She who is in Babylon, chosen together with you, greets you. So does Mark, my son*” (*v. 13*). “She who is in Babylon” most likely refers to the church in Rome. Babylon, the city that had exiled God’s people in the Old Testament, became a symbol for Rome, the center of worldly power (*Revelation 17–18*). Believers in Rome were, like Peter’s readers, exiles in a foreign land. “Mark, my son” refers to John Mark, author of the Gospel of Mark, whom Peter regarded as a spiritual son. Early tradition holds that Mark’s Gospel was based on Peter’s preaching.

“*Greet one another with a kiss of love. Peace be to all of you who are in Christ Jesus. Amen*” (*v. 14*). The letter ends with a call to show love to one another and a blessing of peace for all who are in Christ.

## Important Verses Explained

### *1 Peter 5:2–3* — Shepherd the Flock of God

> *“shepherd the flock of God which is among you, exercising the oversight, not under compulsion, but voluntarily; not for dishonest gain, but willingly; not as lording it over those entrusted to you, but making yourselves examples to the flock.”*
>
> — *1 Peter 5:2–3* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“Shepherd the flock of God which is among you.” Elders are shepherds. Their job is to feed, guide, protect, and care for God’s people. Notice that it is “the flock of God,” not the elders’ own flock. The people belong to God, and elders care for them on His behalf.

“Exercising the oversight.” Elders watch over the flock, paying attention to its needs and dangers.

Peter then gives three contrasts describing how elders should lead.

“Not under compulsion, but voluntarily.” Elders should serve willingly, not because they feel forced or pressured. Some manuscripts add “according to God,” meaning as God would have them serve.

“Not for dishonest gain, but willingly.” Elders should not serve for money or personal advantage, but eagerly, with enthusiasm for the work.

Verse 3: “not as lording it over those entrusted to you, but making yourselves examples to the flock.” Elders should not dominate, control, or bully those in their care. Instead, they should lead by example, living in a way others can follow.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses describe Christlike leadership. Jesus, the Good Shepherd, laid down His life for the sheep (*John 10:11*). He did not come to be served but to serve (*Mark 10:45*). He warned His disciples against leaders who “lord it over” others, saying it must not be so among them (*Mark 10:42–43*). Peter, who heard those words, now passes them on.

The three temptations Peter names, reluctance, greed, and domination, have afflicted church leaders throughout history. Some lead out of duty without love. Some seek financial gain or status. Some use spiritual authority to control and harm. Each distorts the shepherd’s calling.

The final phrase, “making yourselves examples to the flock,” shows that true leadership is about influence through character, not force through position. Paul similarly urged believers to imitate him as he imitated Christ (*1 Corinthians 11:1*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Church leaders can examine their motives and methods. Are they serving willingly and eagerly? Are they free from the desire for personal gain? Are they leading by example rather than by control?

Churches can use this passage to evaluate their leaders and to establish structures of accountability. Leaders who dominate, manipulate, or abuse their authority contradict this passage, and those affected deserve protection and care.

All believers who lead in any capacity, whether as parents, managers, teachers, or ministry leaders, can apply these principles: serving willingly, avoiding selfish gain, and leading by example rather than domination.

### *1 Peter 5:6–7* — Cast All Your Anxiety on Him

> *“Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time, casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you.”*
>
> — *1 Peter 5:6–7* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God.” God’s “mighty hand” is a common biblical image for His power, especially His power to deliver His people, as when He rescued Israel from Egypt (*Exodus 3:19–20*; *Deuteronomy 26:8*). Believers are to submit humbly to God’s power, trusting His purposes even in suffering.

“That he may exalt you in due time.” God will lift up the humble at the right time, His time. Believers may not see it immediately, but God will vindicate and honor those who trust Him.

Verse 7: “casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you.” “Casting” means throwing, as one might throw a heavy load off one’s shoulders. Believers are to throw all their anxieties, worries, and burdens onto God. The word “all” includes everything, large and small.

“Because he cares for you.” The reason believers can do this is that God personally cares for them. He is not distant or indifferent. He is concerned about their lives.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses connect humility and trust. Anxiety often comes from trying to carry burdens that belong to God, from trying to control what cannot be controlled. Humility acknowledges that God is in control and that believers depend on Him. Casting anxieties on God is an act of humility.

This echoes *Psalm 55:22*: “*Cast your burden on the LORD, and he will sustain you*” (*Psalm 55:22*). Jesus taught His followers not to be anxious about their lives, because their heavenly Father knows what they need (*Matthew 6:25–34*). Paul wrote, “*In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God*” (*Philippians 4:6*).

“He cares for you” is one of the most comforting phrases in Scripture. For believers who felt rejected by society and threatened by persecution, it was a reminder that the God of the universe cared personally for each of them.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can practice casting their anxieties on God through prayer, naming their worries specifically and handing them over to Him. This may need to be done repeatedly, as anxieties return.

Humility can help reduce anxiety. Accepting that one cannot control everything and trusting God with the outcome brings freedom.

For those who struggle with ongoing anxiety, this passage offers comfort, not condemnation. God cares about their struggles. Alongside prayer, seeking help from trusted friends, counselors, or medical professionals can be part of how God provides care.

### *1 Peter 5:8–9* — Resist the Roaring Lion

> *“Be sober and self-controlled. Be watchful. Your adversary, the devil, walks around like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour. Withstand him steadfast in your faith, knowing that your brothers who are in the world are undergoing the same sufferings.”*
>
> — *1 Peter 5:8–9* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“Be sober and self-controlled. Be watchful.” Believers need to stay alert and clear-minded. Spiritual danger is real.

“Your adversary, the devil, walks around like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour.” The devil is believers’ adversary, their enemy and accuser. Peter compares him to a lion that roars and prowls, looking for prey. Lions often hunt animals that are isolated, weak, or unaware. The devil seeks to destroy believers’ faith, often through fear, discouragement, temptation, or division.

Verse 9: “Withstand him steadfast in your faith.” Believers are to resist the devil, standing firm. The weapon is faith, trust in God. James gives a similar promise: “*Resist the devil, and he will flee from you*” (*James 4:7*).

“Knowing that your brothers who are in the world are undergoing the same sufferings.” Believers are not alone. Christians everywhere face similar struggles. This knowledge brings comfort and solidarity.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Peter knew from experience how the devil works. Jesus had warned him, “*Satan asked to have all of you, that he might sift you as wheat*” (*Luke 22:31*), “*but I prayed for you, that your faith wouldn’t fail*” (*Luke 22:32*). That night, Peter fell asleep instead of watching and praying, and then denied Jesus three times. Peter learned the hard way the importance of being alert.

The image of a roaring lion suggests that the devil may use fear and intimidation. The persecution Peter’s readers faced could feel like a lion’s roar, meant to frighten them into abandoning their faith. But believers can stand firm, because Christ has already defeated the devil (*Colossians 2:15*; *Hebrews 2:14*).

The reminder that believers worldwide face similar sufferings counters one of the devil’s tactics: isolation. When believers feel alone in their struggles, they are more vulnerable. Knowing that others share their experiences strengthens them.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can stay spiritually alert through prayer, Scripture, and fellowship. These practices help them recognize and resist temptation, discouragement, and deception.

When believers feel attacked by fear, doubt, or temptation, they can resist by holding firmly to their faith in God, reminding themselves of His promises, and refusing to give in.

Believers can also remember that they are part of a worldwide family. Connecting with other believers, sharing struggles, and praying for persecuted Christians around the world brings strength and solidarity.

### *1 Peter 5:10* — The God of All Grace Will Restore You

> *“But may the God of all grace, who called you to his eternal glory by Christ Jesus, after you have suffered a little while, perfect, establish, strengthen, and settle you.”*
>
> — *1 Peter 5:10* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Peter ends his instructions with a magnificent promise. “But may the God of all grace.” God is the source of every kind of grace believers need: saving grace, sustaining grace, strengthening grace.

“Who called you to his eternal glory by Christ Jesus.” God’s purpose for believers is glory, eternal and shared with Christ. Their present suffering is not the end of the story.

“After you have suffered a little while.” Suffering is real, but it is temporary. Compared with eternal glory, it lasts only “a little while.”

“Perfect, establish, strengthen, and settle you.” God Himself will do four things for His suffering people. “Perfect” means restore, repair, or make complete, like mending a torn net or setting a broken bone. “Establish” means make firm and stable. “Strengthen” means give power and endurance. “Settle” means place on a solid foundation, so that nothing can shake them.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse summarizes the hope of the whole letter. Believers suffer, but their suffering is temporary. God is the God of all grace, who has called them to eternal glory. And He Himself will restore and strengthen them.

The four verbs are a powerful picture of God’s work. He repairs what is broken. He makes firm what is shaky. He gives strength to the weak. He establishes believers on an unshakable foundation. This promise speaks to every kind of suffering: physical, emotional, relational, and spiritual.

For Peter, these words were deeply personal. Jesus had told him, “*when once you have turned again, establish your brothers*” (*Luke 22:32*). Peter had failed, but the God of all grace had restored and established him. Now Peter promises the same to his readers.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers who are suffering can hold onto this promise. Their suffering is real, but it is “a little while.” God is the God of all grace, and He will restore, establish, strengthen, and settle them.

This verse also invites believers to look beyond their present circumstances to the eternal glory God has called them to. That perspective brings hope and endurance.

Finally, believers can trust that God Himself is at work in them. They do not need to restore themselves. The God of all grace will do it.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

First Peter 5 begins with a charge to leaders. Elders are to shepherd God’s flock willingly, eagerly, and without greed, not domineering over those in their care but setting an example. Leaders serve under Jesus, the Chief Shepherd, who will reward faithfulness with an unfading crown of glory. Churches today can value and hold accountable leaders who serve in this way, and protect those harmed by leaders who do not.

All believers are called to clothe themselves with humility, serving one another as Jesus did when He washed His disciples’ feet. God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble. Humbling themselves under God’s mighty hand, believers can cast all their anxieties on Him, because He cares for them personally.

The chapter also warns of spiritual danger. The devil prowls like a roaring lion, seeking to devour. Believers must stay alert and sober, resisting him firm in their faith, remembering that believers around the world share the same struggles. They are not alone.

Finally, Peter gives a promise that summarizes the whole letter. After believers have suffered a little while, the God of all grace, who called them to eternal glory in Christ, will Himself restore, establish, strengthen, and settle them. This is the true grace of God, and believers are called to stand firm in it.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, You are the Chief Shepherd. Raise up shepherds for Your church who serve willingly and eagerly, without greed, not lording it over others but leading by example. Protect Your people from leaders who would harm them. Clothe me with humility, and help me to serve others as You served Your disciples. I humble myself under Your mighty hand. I cast all my anxieties on You, because You care for me. Keep me alert and self-controlled, and help me to resist the devil, standing firm in faith. Strengthen my brothers and sisters around the world who suffer for Your name. God of all grace, You have called me to Your eternal glory in Christ. After I have suffered a little while, restore me, establish me, strengthen me, and settle me. To You be the power forever and ever. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Book 22 of 27

# 2 Peter

## About This Letter

Second Peter presents itself as a letter from “*Simon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ*” (*2 Peter 1:1*), written near the end of his life, when he knew his death was approaching, as Jesus had told him (*1:14*; *John 21:18–19*). Peter refers to being an eyewitness of Jesus’ transfiguration (*1:16–18*), to an earlier letter he had written (*3:1*), and to the letters of “our beloved brother Paul” (*3:15*).

Of all the New Testament books, 2 Peter’s authorship has been the most debated. Some early Christians hesitated to accept it, and many modern scholars believe it was written after Peter’s death by someone in his circle, pointing to its different Greek style from 1 Peter and its close similarities with the letter of Jude. Others defend Peter’s authorship, noting that he may have used a different secretary, that the letter’s personal claims are clear, and that the church came to recognize it as Scripture. If Peter wrote it, it dates to the mid-60s A.D., shortly before his martyrdom in Rome.

The letter was written to believers threatened by false teachers who denied the Lord’s return and the coming judgment, mocked the idea that Christ would come again, and used grace as an excuse for immorality and greed.

## The Shape of the Letter

Chapter 1 reminds believers that God’s divine power has given them everything needed for life and godliness, calls them to add virtue upon virtue to their faith, and grounds the faith in eyewitness testimony of Christ’s glory and in the prophetic Scriptures given by the Holy Spirit. Chapter 2 vividly exposes false teachers, their greed, arrogance, and immorality, and shows from Old Testament examples that God knows how to rescue the godly and judge the wicked. Chapter 3 answers those who scoff at Christ’s return, explaining that God’s apparent delay is His patience, since He does not want anyone to perish, and that the day of the Lord will come like a thief, bringing new heavens and a new earth where righteousness dwells; therefore believers should live holy lives, guard against error, and grow in grace and knowledge.

## Themes to Watch For

Watch for growth in godliness, the reliability of the apostolic witness and of Scripture, the danger of false teaching that leads to immoral living, God’s justice and mercy, the certainty of Christ’s return, God’s patience that gives time for repentance, the hope of a new creation, and the closing call to grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. Second Peter is a farewell reminder to remember what is true and to keep growing.

## Chapters

2.  [2 Peter 2](#c22_2PE_002.xhtml) — False Teachers and the God Who Rescues

2 Peter · Chapter 1 of 3

# 2 Peter — Chapter 1

Chapter Theme: Everything Needed for Life and Godliness

[Read 2 Peter 1 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/2PE01.htm)

Main Teaching

Peter greets those who have received a faith as precious as the apostles’ through the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ. God’s divine power has given believers everything they need for life and godliness through knowing Him, and through His great and precious promises they share in the divine nature and escape the corruption of the world caused by sinful desire. For this reason, they are to make every effort to add to their faith goodness, knowledge, self-control, endurance, godliness, brotherly affection, and love; these qualities keep them from being ineffective and unfruitful in knowing Christ, while those who lack them are shortsighted and have forgotten their cleansing. They are to confirm their calling and election, and so receive a rich welcome into Christ’s eternal kingdom. Knowing that his death is near, Peter wants to keep reminding them of these truths. The apostles did not follow cleverly invented stories when they spoke of Christ’s power and coming; they were eyewitnesses of His majesty, hearing the Father’s voice on the holy mountain. Believers also have the prophetic word made more certain, a lamp shining in a dark place until the day dawns, for no prophecy of Scripture came by human will, but people spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.

## Chapter Background and Story

Peter writes this letter knowing that his death is near (v14). Jesus had told him, years earlier, that he would one day be bound and led where he did not want to go, indicating the kind of death by which he would glorify God (*John 21:18–19*). Early Christian tradition says Peter was crucified in Rome during Nero’s persecution.

Like Paul’s final letter, 2 Timothy, this is a farewell message. Peter’s main concern is that after his death, believers would remember the truth and continue growing in their faith. False teachers were already at work, as chapter 2 will describe, and Peter wants to strengthen believers against them.

In chapter 1, Peter lays a positive foundation before he addresses the false teaching. He reminds believers of the resources God has given them, calls them to grow in Christlike character, and assures them that the faith rests on solid ground: the eyewitness testimony of the apostles and the God-given Scriptures.

### Greeting (*1:1–2*)

“*Simon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ, to those who have obtained a like precious faith with us in the righteousness of our God and Savior, Jesus Christ*” (*v. 1*): Peter uses his full name, Simon Peter, the name Jesus gave him (*Matthew 16:17–18*). He writes to believers who have received a faith “as precious” as the apostles’. Those who never saw Jesus in the flesh have the same faith and the same standing before God as those who walked with Him. Notice the phrase “our God and Savior, Jesus Christ,” a clear statement that Jesus is God (compare *Titus 2:13*).

“*Grace to you and peace be multiplied in the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord*” (*v. 2*). “Knowledge” is a key word in 2 Peter. It means not merely information, but personal, growing knowledge of God through Christ. This true knowledge contrasts with the false “knowledge” of the false teachers.

### God’s Power and Promises (*1:3–4*)

The resources God has given believers are studied below.

### Growing in Godly Character (*1:5–11*)

The call to add virtues to faith is studied below. “*For he who lacks these things is blind, seeing only what is near, having forgotten the cleansing from his old sins*” (*v. 9*). Those who fail to grow are spiritually shortsighted, seeing only what is immediately in front of them. They have forgotten that they were cleansed from their past sins, and so they live as though that cleansing did not matter.

“*Therefore, brothers, be more diligent to make your calling and election sure. For if you do these things, you will never stumble*” (*v. 10*). God has called and chosen believers. They are to “make it sure,” confirming it, showing its reality by a growing godly life. This does not mean believers secure their own salvation by effort. God’s call and choice are His work. But growing godliness is the evidence and confirmation of that call. Those who grow in these qualities will not fall away.

“*For thus you will be richly supplied with the entrance into the eternal Kingdom of our Lord and Savior, Jesus Christ*” (*v. 11*). The result is a rich welcome into Christ’s eternal kingdom, like a victorious athlete or a returning hero welcomed home with celebration.

### Peter’s Reminder (*1:12–15*)

“*Therefore I will not be negligent to remind you of these things, though you know them and are established in the present truth*” (*v. 12*). Peter’s readers already knew these truths, but they needed reminders. Believers often need to hear familiar truths again, not because they are new but because they are easily forgotten.

“*I think it right, as long as I am in this tent, to stir you up by reminding you*” (*v. 13*), “*knowing that the putting off of my tent comes swiftly, even as our Lord Jesus Christ made clear to me*” (*v. 14*). Peter compares his body to a tent, a temporary dwelling (see *2 Corinthians 5:1*). He knows he will soon “put it off,” a gentle image for death.

“*Yes, I will make every effort that you may always be able to remember these things even after my departure*” (*v. 15*). Peter wanted his teaching to outlive him. This letter is part of that effort. Some early Christian tradition also connects Peter’s desire here with the Gospel of Mark, which was said to preserve Peter’s preaching.

### Eyewitnesses and the Prophetic Word (*1:16–21*)

The apostles’ eyewitness testimony and the reliability of Scripture are studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *2 Peter 1:3–4* — Partakers of the Divine Nature

> *“seeing that his divine power has granted to us all things that pertain to life and godliness, through the knowledge of him who called us by his own glory and virtue, by which he has granted to us his precious and exceedingly great promises; that through these you may become partakers of the divine nature, having escaped from the corruption that is in the world by lust.”*
>
> — *2 Peter 1:3–4* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“Seeing that his divine power has granted to us all things that pertain to life and godliness.” God’s power has given believers everything they need for spiritual life and for living in a way that pleases Him. Nothing essential is missing.

“Through the knowledge of him who called us by his own glory and virtue.” These resources come through knowing God personally. He called believers by displaying His own glory and goodness, especially in Christ.

Verse 4: “by which he has granted to us his precious and exceedingly great promises.” Through His glory and goodness, God has given believers wonderful promises: forgiveness, His presence, the Spirit, eternal life, and the return of Christ.

“That through these you may become partakers of the divine nature.” Through God’s promises, believers share in God’s own nature. This does not mean believers become God or lose their humanity. It means they share in God’s moral character, His holiness, love, and goodness, and in His eternal life. They are being transformed to reflect Him.

“Having escaped from the corruption that is in the world by lust.” Believers have escaped the moral decay that sinful desire produces in the world.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses describe the abundant provision God has made for His people. Believers do not need to search for some secret knowledge or special experience to live godly lives, as the false teachers may have suggested. God has already given them everything they need in Christ.

“Partakers of the divine nature” is one of the most remarkable phrases in the New Testament. It describes the goal of salvation: not only forgiveness but transformation, sharing in God’s own life and character. Eastern Orthodox Christians have emphasized this as “theosis,” or becoming like God by grace. Other traditions speak of sanctification and union with Christ. All agree that believers do not become divine in essence, but they are made new and conformed to God’s character. Paul speaks of believers being transformed into Christ’s image (*2 Corinthians 3:18*) and conformed to the image of God’s Son (*Romans 8:29*).

The contrast between “the divine nature” and “the corruption that is in the world” shows two directions a life can take. One leads toward God’s holiness and life; the other leads toward decay and death.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers who feel inadequate for living a godly life can take heart. God’s power has given them everything they need. They do not need to look elsewhere; they need to draw on what God has already provided in Christ.

Believers can also treasure God’s promises. Reading, remembering, and trusting His promises nourishes the new life within them.

Finally, believers can embrace the goal of becoming more like God in character, growing in love, holiness, and goodness, knowing that this is God’s purpose for them.

### *2 Peter 1:5–8* — Add to Your Faith

> *“Yes, and for this very cause adding on your part all diligence, in your faith supply moral excellence; and in moral excellence, knowledge; and in knowledge, self-control; and in self-control, perseverance; and in perseverance, godliness; and in godliness, brotherly affection; and in brotherly affection, love. For if these things are yours and abound, they make you to not be idle or unfruitful in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ.”*
>
> — *2 Peter 1:5–8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“Yes, and for this very cause adding on your part all diligence.” Because God has given believers everything they need, they are to respond with effort. God’s provision does not make human effort unnecessary; it makes it possible.

Peter then lists qualities to “supply,” or add, building one upon another, like a chain or a ladder.

“In your faith supply moral excellence.” Faith is the foundation. To it believers add “moral excellence,” or virtue, goodness of character.

“And in moral excellence, knowledge.” Practical understanding of God and His ways.

Verse 6: “and in knowledge, self-control.” The ability to master one’s desires. Notice that true knowledge leads to self-control, unlike the false teachers’ “knowledge,” which led to indulgence.

“And in self-control, perseverance.” Endurance, steadfastness under pressure.

“And in perseverance, godliness.” Reverence for God expressed in life.

Verse 7: “and in godliness, brotherly affection.” Love for fellow believers, the warm affection of family.

“And in brotherly affection, love.” The highest virtue: self-giving love for all, the love of God Himself.

Verse 8: “For if these things are yours and abound, they make you to not be idle or unfruitful in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ.” When these qualities are present and growing, believers will be productive and fruitful in their relationship with Christ.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This list resembles the fruit of the Spirit (*Galatians 5:22–23*). It begins with faith and ends with love, the two great foundations of the Christian life. Paul writes that faith works through love (*Galatians 5:6*). Peter’s list describes the path from one to the other.

The list is not a rigid sequence in which one virtue must be complete before the next begins. Rather, each quality supports and enriches the others, and all grow together. The image is of a choir or a dance, with each part contributing to the whole. The Greek word for “supply” was used for a wealthy patron who generously funded a choir or a festival. Believers are to “fund” their faith generously with these qualities.

This passage holds together God’s work and human effort. God has given everything needed (vv3–4); believers make every effort to grow (v5). Paul expresses the same balance: “work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in you” (*Philippians 2:12–13*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can use this list as a guide for spiritual growth. Which qualities are growing in their lives? Which need more attention? They can ask God to help them grow in each one.

Growth requires effort: “all diligence.” Believers can cultivate these qualities through Scripture, prayer, practicing self-control, persevering through difficulty, serving others, and choosing love.

Finally, believers can find encouragement in the promise of verse 8. Those who grow in these qualities will be fruitful and effective. Their lives will make a difference.

### *2 Peter 1:16–18* — Eyewitnesses of His Majesty

> *“For we didn’t follow cunningly devised fables when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of his majesty. For he received from God the Father honor and glory when the voice came to him from the Majestic Glory, ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.’ We heard this voice come out of heaven when we were with him on the holy mountain.”*
>
> — *2 Peter 1:16–18* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“For we didn’t follow cunningly devised fables when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.” The false teachers apparently claimed that the apostles’ message about Christ’s return was a myth, an invented story. Peter denies this firmly. The apostles did not make up clever stories.

“But we were eyewitnesses of his majesty.” Peter had personally seen Christ’s glory.

Verse 17: “For he received from God the Father honor and glory when the voice came to him from the Majestic Glory, ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.’” Peter refers to the transfiguration, when Jesus’ appearance was changed and He shone with glory on a mountain, and the Father’s voice declared His identity (*Matthew 17:1–8*; *Mark 9:2–8*). “The Majestic Glory” is a reverent way of referring to God.

Verse 18: “We heard this voice come out of heaven when we were with him on the holy mountain.” Peter, James, and John were there. They saw and heard. The transfiguration was a preview of Christ’s glory at His return.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The Christian faith is rooted in history, not myth. The apostles bore witness to what they had seen and heard (*1 John 1:1–3*; *Acts 4:20*). Their testimony was not secondhand speculation but firsthand experience. Many of them, including Peter, died for this testimony. People do not usually die for what they know to be invented.

The transfiguration is significant because it gave the apostles a glimpse of Christ’s glory and confirmed His identity as God’s beloved Son. It also pointed forward to His coming in glory. The false teachers denied Christ’s return; Peter answers that he had already seen a preview of that glory.

This passage also highlights the role of the Father’s voice. The same voice spoke at Jesus’ baptism (*Matthew 3:17*). God Himself testified to who Jesus is.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can be confident that their faith rests on reliable testimony. The Gospels record what eyewitnesses saw and heard. Christianity is not built on myths but on historical events.

When believers face doubts or encounter claims that the Christian faith is merely a story, they can remember the apostles’ eyewitness testimony, which they were willing to die for.

Believers can also look forward with confidence to Christ’s return in glory. The transfiguration was a glimpse of what is to come.

### *2 Peter 1:20–21* — Carried Along by the Holy Spirit

> *“knowing this first, that no prophecy of Scripture is of private interpretation. For no prophecy ever came by the will of man, but holy men of God spoke, being moved by the Holy Spirit.”*
>
> — *2 Peter 1:20–21* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

In verse 19, Peter says that believers also have “the more sure word of prophecy,” the Old Testament prophecies about Christ, which are confirmed by the apostles’ testimony. Believers should pay attention to these prophecies, “as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star arises in your hearts.” The prophetic word gives light in a dark world until Christ returns.

Verse 20: “knowing this first, that no prophecy of Scripture is of private interpretation.” This may mean that prophecy did not originate from the prophet’s own interpretation of events, or that individuals should not interpret Scripture in isolation, apart from its divine source and the community of faith. The context, especially verse 21, favors the first meaning: the prophets did not simply share their own ideas.

Verse 21: “For no prophecy ever came by the will of man, but holy men of God spoke, being moved by the Holy Spirit.” Scripture did not originate with human decision. The prophets spoke from God, “moved,” literally “carried along,” by the Holy Spirit, like a ship carried by the wind.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses, along with *2 Timothy 3:16*, are among the most important biblical statements about the inspiration of Scripture. Scripture is both human and divine. Human authors wrote in their own languages, styles, and circumstances. But they were carried along by the Holy Spirit, so that what they wrote was God’s word.

This is why believers can trust Scripture. It is not merely human opinion or religious reflection. It is God speaking through human authors. The false teachers apparently twisted or rejected Scripture (*2 Peter 3:16*). Peter affirms its divine origin and authority.

The image of Scripture as “a lamp shining in a dark place” is beautiful. The world can be spiritually dark, confusing, and full of competing voices. God’s word gives light to guide believers until Christ, who calls Himself “*the bright and morning star*” (*Revelation 22:16*), returns and the full light of day arrives.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can approach Scripture with reverence and trust, knowing it comes from God. Reading it regularly, studying it carefully, and obeying it are ways of paying attention to the lamp God has given.

When believers face confusion or darkness, they can turn to Scripture for light and guidance.

Finally, believers can read Scripture humbly, seeking to understand what God intended, and doing so in community with other believers, so that their interpretation is guided by the Spirit and by the wisdom of the church.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

Second Peter 1 reminds believers of the rich resources God has given them. His divine power has granted everything needed for life and godliness, and through His great and precious promises they share in His nature, escaping the corruption of the world. They do not need to search for anything beyond what God has provided in Christ.

Because of this provision, believers are called to make every effort to grow. To their faith they add goodness, knowledge, self-control, endurance, godliness, brotherly affection, and love. As these qualities grow, believers become fruitful and effective in their knowledge of Christ. They confirm their calling and election and look forward to a rich welcome into Christ’s eternal kingdom.

Peter, facing death, wanted his readers to remember these truths. Believers today also need regular reminders of what they already know, because familiar truths are easily forgotten.

Finally, the chapter shows that the Christian faith rests on solid ground. The apostles were eyewitnesses of Christ’s majesty, hearing the Father’s voice on the mountain of transfiguration. And believers have the prophetic Scriptures, given not by human will but by people carried along by the Holy Spirit. These Scriptures are a lamp shining in a dark place until the day dawns and the morning star rises in their hearts. Believers can trust them, study them, and live by them.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord, thank You that Your divine power has given me everything I need for life and godliness, and that through Your precious promises I can share in Your nature and escape the corruption of the world. Help me to make every effort to grow: adding to my faith goodness, knowledge, self-control, endurance, godliness, brotherly affection, and love. Keep me from being unfruitful or forgetful of the cleansing You have given me. Thank You for the apostles who saw Your majesty and bore faithful witness. Thank You for Scripture, given by holy men carried along by the Holy Spirit. Let Your word be a lamp shining in the dark places of my life, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in my heart. Remind me again and again of what is true. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

2 Peter · Chapter 2 of 3

# 2 Peter — Chapter 2

Chapter Theme: False Teachers and the God Who Rescues

[Read 2 Peter 2 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/2PE02.htm)

Main Teaching

Just as false prophets arose among God’s people in the past, false teachers will arise among believers, secretly introducing destructive heresies, even denying the Master who bought them, and bringing swift destruction on themselves. Many will follow their sensual ways, causing the way of truth to be slandered, and in their greed they will exploit people with made-up stories. Their judgment is certain, as Old Testament examples show: God did not spare the angels who sinned, the ancient world in Noah’s day, or the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah, yet He rescued Noah and righteous Lot. The Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials and to hold the unrighteous for judgment. Peter vividly describes the false teachers: arrogant, bold in slandering spiritual powers, like unreasoning animals, reveling in pleasure, with eyes full of adultery, never ceasing from sin, enticing unstable people, trained in greed, following the path of Balaam who loved the wages of wrongdoing. They are springs without water and mists driven by a storm, promising freedom while themselves slaves of corruption. For those who have known the way of righteousness and then turned back, the last state is worse than the first.

## Chapter Background and Story

In chapter 1, Peter grounded the faith in the apostles’ eyewitness testimony and the Spirit-given Scriptures. In chapter 2, he turns to the danger threatening the churches: false teachers from within the community. This chapter has many similarities with the letter of Jude, and the two letters may draw on shared material or one may have used the other.

The false teachers Peter describes were not open opponents of the church. They were insiders who “secretly” brought in their teaching (v1) and who joined in the church’s fellowship meals (v13). Their errors were both doctrinal and moral. They denied the Lord, apparently rejecting His authority and His return (*3:3–4*). And they lived immoral, greedy lives, using the message of grace and freedom as a cover for indulgence.

Peter’s language in this chapter is strong and vivid. He uses images of animals, dry springs, and storm clouds to expose the emptiness and danger of these teachers. His purpose is protective: he wants believers to recognize false teaching and stay away from it. At the same time, he reassures believers that God knows how to rescue the godly.

### False Teachers Among You (*2:1–3*)

The arrival and character of false teachers is studied below.

### God’s Judgment and Rescue (*2:4–10*a)

“*For if God didn’t spare angels when they sinned, but cast them down to Tartarus, and committed them to pits of darkness to be reserved for judgment*” (*v. 4*). “Tartarus” was a Greek term for the deepest part of the underworld, a place of punishment. Peter refers to angels who sinned, likely connected in Jewish tradition with *Genesis 6:1–4* and the days before the flood (see also *Jude 1:6*). Even powerful spiritual beings did not escape God’s judgment.

“*and didn’t spare the ancient world, but preserved Noah with seven others, a preacher of righteousness, when he brought a flood on the world of the ungodly*” (*v. 5*). God judged the ancient world through the flood (*Genesis 6–8*), but He preserved Noah and his family, eight people in all. Noah is called “a preacher of righteousness,” suggesting that he warned his generation.

“*and turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah into ashes, condemned them to destruction, having made them an example to those who would live in an ungodly way*” (*v. 6*), “*and delivered righteous Lot, who was very distressed by the lustful life of the wicked*” (*v. 7*) “*(for that righteous man dwelling among them was tormented in his righteous soul from day to day with seeing and hearing lawless deeds)*” (*v. 8*). The destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah (*Genesis 19*) became a lasting example of God’s judgment. Scripture describes the sins of these cities in several ways: violent sexual immorality, including the attempted assault on Lot’s guests, as well as arrogance, abundance without care for the poor and needy (*Ezekiel 16:49*), and widespread lawlessness. Lot is called “righteous,” even though Genesis shows his serious flaws. He was distressed by the evil around him, and God rescued him.

Peter’s examples show a pattern: God judges the wicked and rescues the righteous. This pattern is the basis for the reassurance studied below.

“*but chiefly those who walk after the flesh in the lust of defilement and despise authority. Daring, self-willed, they are not afraid to speak evil of dignitaries*” (*v. 10*). The false teachers are especially guilty because they indulge their sinful desires and reject authority, including God’s authority. “Dignitaries” likely refers to spiritual beings, perhaps angels or even evil powers.

### The Character of the False Teachers (*2:10*b–19)

“*whereas angels, though greater in might and power, don’t bring a slanderous judgment against them before the Lord*” (*v. 11*). Even powerful angels do not speak arrogantly against other spiritual beings; they leave judgment to God (see *Jude 1:9*). The false teachers, by contrast, speak recklessly about things they do not understand.

“*But these, as unreasoning creatures, born natural animals to be taken and destroyed, speaking evil in matters about which they are ignorant, will in their destroying surely be destroyed*” (*v. 12*). Like animals driven by instinct, the false teachers act without reason or understanding. Their destructive ways will lead to their own destruction.

“*receiving the wages of unrighteousness; people who count it pleasure to revel in the daytime, spots and defects, reveling in their deceit while they feast with you*” (*v. 13*). They indulged openly, even in the daytime, which was considered especially shameless. They took part in the church’s fellowship meals, but they were like stains or blemishes on the community.

“*having eyes full of adultery, and who can’t cease from sin, enticing unsettled souls, having a heart trained in greed, accursed children!*” (*v. 14*) Their eyes constantly looked for opportunities for sexual sin. They preyed on spiritually unstable people. They had trained their hearts in greed, the way an athlete trains the body. Spiritual predators who exploit vulnerable people sexually or financially are a real danger in every age, and churches must be watchful to protect those at risk.

“*Forsaking the right way, they went astray, having followed the way of Balaam the son of Beor, who loved the wages of wrongdoing*” (*v. 15*); “*but he was rebuked for his own disobedience. A speechless donkey spoke with a man’s voice and stopped the madness of the prophet*” (*v. 16*). Balaam was a prophet hired to curse Israel for money (*Numbers 22–24*). God rebuked him through his donkey, which spoke to him. Balaam later led Israel into idolatry and immorality (*Numbers 31:16*; *Revelation 2:14*). He is a symbol of religious leaders who use spiritual gifts for financial gain.

“*These are wells without water, clouds driven by a storm, for whom the blackness of darkness has been reserved forever*” (*v. 17*). To a thirsty traveler, a dry well is a bitter disappointment. Clouds driven away by the wind promise rain but bring none. The false teachers promised much but delivered nothing.

“*For, uttering great swelling words of emptiness, they entice in the lusts of the flesh, by licentiousness, those who are indeed escaping from those who live in error*” (*v. 18*). They used impressive-sounding words to lure new believers, those just escaping from their old ways, back into immorality. Their false promise of freedom is studied below.

### Worse Than Before (*2:20–22*)

The danger of turning back is studied below. “*But it has happened to them according to the true proverb, “The dog turns to his own vomit again,” and “the sow that has washed to wallowing in the mire.”*” (*v. 22*) The first proverb comes from *Proverbs 26:11*; the second was a common saying. Both describe returning to filth after being cleansed. These vivid images show the tragedy of those who turn back to their old way of life.

## Important Verses Explained

### *2 Peter 2:1–3* — False Teachers Among You

> *“But false prophets also arose among the people, as false teachers will also be among you, who will secretly bring in destructive heresies, denying even the Master who bought them, bringing on themselves swift destruction. Many will follow their immoral ways, and as a result, the way of the truth will be maligned. In covetousness they will exploit you with deceptive words: whose sentence now from of old doesn’t linger, and their destruction will not slumber.”*
>
> — *2 Peter 2:1–3* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“But false prophets also arose among the people.” In Israel’s history, false prophets claimed to speak for God but led people astray (*Jeremiah 23:16–22*; *Deuteronomy 13:1–5*). Peter has just said that true prophecy comes from God (*2 Peter 1:21*). Now he warns that false prophets have always existed.

“As false teachers will also be among you.” In the church, there will be false teachers. Jesus and Paul gave similar warnings (*Matthew 7:15*; *Acts 20:29–30*).

“Who will secretly bring in destructive heresies.” They will not announce themselves as false teachers. They will slip their teaching in quietly. “Heresies” are teachings that depart from the true faith. They are “destructive,” leading to spiritual ruin.

“Denying even the Master who bought them.” “Master” is a word used for an owner of slaves. Christ bought believers with His blood (*1 Corinthians 6:20*; *1 Peter 1:18–19*). The false teachers deny His authority, living as though He were not their Master.

“Bringing on themselves swift destruction.” Their judgment is certain.

Verse 2: “Many will follow their immoral ways, and as a result, the way of the truth will be maligned.” False teachers attract followers, especially when their teaching permits indulgence. Their immoral behavior brings shame on the gospel, giving outsiders reason to mock “the way of the truth.”

Verse 3: “In covetousness they will exploit you with deceptive words.” They are motivated by greed. They use clever, fabricated stories to make money from their followers.

“Whose sentence now from of old doesn’t linger, and their destruction will not slumber.” Their judgment, announced long ago, is not idle or asleep. It is coming.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This passage teaches that false teaching is often found within the church, not just outside it. It also shows the typical marks of false teachers: secretive methods, denial of Christ’s authority, immoral living, many followers, damage to the gospel’s reputation, and greed. Many of these marks are moral, not just doctrinal. False belief and immoral living often go together.

The phrase “the Master who bought them” is significant. It shows that the false teachers had at least professed to belong to Christ. Christians have discussed what this means for the scope of Christ’s redemption. Some understand it to mean that Christ’s death was for all people, including those who reject Him; others understand it as describing the false teachers’ claim to be redeemed. Either way, their denial of Christ is especially serious because they claimed to know Him.

The warning that the way of truth would be “maligned” shows how leaders’ failures affect the whole church’s witness. When leaders are exposed for immorality or greed, outsiders often blame the gospel itself.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can be discerning about teachers, preachers, and leaders. Not everyone who claims to speak for God does. Believers can test teaching by Scripture and look at the fruit of a teacher’s life: Do they honor Christ as Lord? Do they live with integrity? Are they motivated by love for people or by money and power?

Churches can protect their members by teaching sound doctrine, holding leaders accountable, and being alert to signs of exploitation.

Finally, believers can remember that their lives affect how others view the gospel. Living with integrity honors “the way of the truth.”

### *2 Peter 2:9* — The Lord Knows How to Rescue the Godly

> *“then the Lord knows how to deliver the godly out of temptation and to keep the unrighteous under punishment for the day of judgment,”*
>
> — *2 Peter 2:9* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After the examples of Noah and Lot, Peter draws a conclusion. “Then the Lord knows how to deliver the godly out of temptation.” “Temptation” here means trial or testing. God knows how to rescue His faithful people from difficult and dangerous situations. He rescued Noah from the flood and Lot from Sodom.

“And to keep the unrighteous under punishment for the day of judgment.” God also knows how to hold the wicked accountable. They will face judgment on the final day.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse is a source of deep comfort for believers surrounded by evil. Like Lot, who was distressed by the lawlessness around him, believers today may feel troubled by the wickedness in the world. Peter assures them that God knows what He is doing. He has not lost control. He will rescue His people and judge evil in His time.

God’s rescue may take different forms. Sometimes He delivers His people from danger in this life. Sometimes He sustains them through it. And ultimately, He will deliver them completely at Christ’s return. Paul expresses similar confidence: “*The Lord will deliver me from every evil work and will preserve me for his heavenly Kingdom*” (*2 Timothy 4:18*).

This verse also shows that God’s judgment and God’s salvation go together. He is both just and merciful. He judges evil and rescues the righteous.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers facing trials, temptations, or a hostile environment can trust that the Lord knows how to rescue them. He may not always rescue them in the way or timing they expect, but He is faithful.

This verse also helps believers when they are troubled by evil that seems to go unpunished. God sees, and He will judge. Believers can leave justice to Him, while still working for what is right.

Finally, like Lot, believers can allow evil to grieve them rather than becoming comfortable with it. A tender conscience that is distressed by wickedness is a sign of righteousness.

### *2 Peter 2:19* — Promising Freedom, Enslaved to Corruption

> *“promising them liberty, while they themselves are bondservants of corruption; for a man is brought into bondage by whoever overcomes him.”*
>
> — *2 Peter 2:19* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“Promising them liberty.” The false teachers promised freedom, perhaps freedom from moral rules, freedom to indulge, freedom from accountability. They may have twisted the message of grace to mean that believers could live however they pleased.

“While they themselves are bondservants of corruption.” But the false teachers themselves were slaves, enslaved to the very desires they claimed freed people. Their “freedom” was actually bondage.

“For a man is brought into bondage by whoever overcomes him.” Whatever controls a person is that person’s master. Those who are controlled by lust, greed, or addiction are slaves to those things, no matter how free they claim to be.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse exposes one of the oldest lies: that freedom means doing whatever one wants. In reality, giving in to sinful desires leads to bondage. Jesus said, “*Everyone who commits sin is the bondservant of sin*” (*John 8:34*). Paul wrote that people are slaves to whatever they obey, whether sin leading to death or obedience leading to righteousness (*Romans 6:16*).

True freedom is found in Christ. Jesus said, “*If therefore the Son makes you free, you will be free indeed*” (*John 8:36*). This freedom is not the freedom to sin but the freedom from sin’s power, the freedom to become what God created people to be. Paul warns believers not to use their freedom as an opportunity for the flesh (*Galatians 5:13*).

The false teachers’ promise of freedom was especially dangerous for new believers who had just escaped their old way of life (v18). They were being lured back into the bondage they had just left.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Many messages in today’s culture promise freedom through indulgence: “Do whatever feels good,” “Follow your desires,” “No one can tell you what to do.” This verse invites believers to look more closely. What masters a person enslaves them.

Believers can examine their own lives. Are there habits, desires, or substances that control them? True freedom may involve seeking help to break free from addictions or destructive patterns.

Finally, believers can embrace the true freedom Christ offers: freedom from sin’s power and freedom to live for God.

### *2 Peter 2:20–21* — Worse Than the First

> *“For if, after they have escaped the defilement of the world through the knowledge of the Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, they are again entangled in it and overcome, the last state has become worse for them than the first. For it would be better for them not to have known the way of righteousness, than after knowing it, to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them.”*
>
> — *2 Peter 2:20–21* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“For if, after they have escaped the defilement of the world through the knowledge of the Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, they are again entangled in it and overcome.” Peter describes people who came to know Christ and escaped the moral corruption of the world. But then they became entangled in it again, like an animal caught in a net, and were overcome.

“The last state has become worse for them than the first.” Their final condition is worse than before they knew Christ. Jesus used similar words in His parable about an unclean spirit that returns with seven others, so that the person’s last state is worse than the first (*Matthew 12:43–45*).

Verse 21: “For it would be better for them not to have known the way of righteousness, than after knowing it, to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them.” Knowing the truth and then turning away from it brings greater responsibility and greater judgment. It would have been better never to have known.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Like the warnings in *Hebrews 6:4–6* and *10:26–31*, this passage describes a serious danger: turning away from Christ after knowing Him. Christians understand such passages in different ways. Some believe they describe genuine believers who fall away. Others believe they describe people who had outward knowledge of Christ without genuine faith, whose turning back shows that they never truly belonged to Him (*1 John 2:19*). All agree that the warning is real and serious.

The principle is that greater knowledge brings greater responsibility. Jesus said, “*To whomever much is given, of him will much be required*” (*Luke 12:48*). Those who have heard and understood the gospel are more accountable than those who never heard it.

The specific context is important. Peter is speaking of the false teachers and their followers, who had known the way of righteousness and then deliberately returned to immorality and denied Christ’s authority. This is different from a believer who struggles with sin, confesses it, and seeks God’s help.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage is a sober warning not to take the knowledge of Christ lightly. Believers can guard their hearts, stay connected to Christian community, and continue growing in faith, so that they are not drawn back into their old way of life.

At the same time, this passage should not cause despair for believers who struggle with sin. The difference between a struggling believer and those Peter describes is the heart’s direction. Those who grieve over sin and long for God are not the ones who have turned their backs on Him.

Finally, believers can pray for and gently seek those who have drifted away from the faith. God’s mercy is great, and He welcomes those who return.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

Second Peter 2 is a strong warning about false teachers within the church. They introduce destructive ideas secretly, deny the authority of the Master who bought them, live immoral lives, exploit people out of greed, and bring disgrace on the way of truth. They promise freedom but are themselves enslaved to corruption. They prey on unstable and vulnerable people.

Believers today can learn to recognize such teachers by their doctrine and by their lives. Do they honor Christ as Lord? Do they live with integrity, or do they show patterns of greed, sexual immorality, and arrogance? Churches can protect their members, especially the vulnerable, by teaching sound doctrine, holding leaders accountable, and responding swiftly to exploitation.

Amid this warning, Peter offers great reassurance. God’s past actions prove that He knows how to rescue the godly and to hold the wicked accountable. He rescued Noah from the flood and Lot from Sodom. He will rescue His people today and judge evil in His time.

Finally, Peter warns of the danger of turning back after knowing the way of righteousness. True freedom is found not in indulging sinful desires but in Christ, who frees people from sin’s power. Believers can hold fast to Christ, grow in Him, and help those who have drifted to return.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, You are the Master who bought me with Your blood. Help me to honor You as Lord in every part of my life. Give me discernment to recognize false teaching and wisdom to see the fruit of those who teach. Protect Your church from leaders who exploit others through greed and immorality, and protect the vulnerable from those who would prey on them. Thank You that You know how to rescue the godly from trials, as You rescued Noah and Lot. When I am distressed by the evil around me, help me to trust that You see and that You will judge. Guard me from the false promise of freedom that leads to bondage. Set me truly free, and keep me from turning back to my old ways. Draw back those who have wandered. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
