2 Peter · Chapter 3 of 3

# 2 Peter — Chapter 3

Chapter Theme: The Promise of His Coming

[Read 2 Peter 3 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/2PE03.htm)

Main Teaching

In this second letter, Peter again stirs believers to remember the words of the prophets and the commandment of the Lord given through the apostles. He warns that in the last days scoffers will come, following their own desires and mocking, “Where is the promise of his coming?” claiming everything continues as it always has. But they deliberately forget that God created the heavens and earth by His word and that the world was once destroyed by the flood; by the same word, the present heavens and earth are reserved for fire and judgment. With the Lord, one day is like a thousand years and a thousand years like one day. He is not slow in keeping His promise but patient, not wanting anyone to perish but all to come to repentance. The day of the Lord will come like a thief, when the heavens will pass away and the earth and its works will be exposed. Since everything will be dissolved, believers should live holy and godly lives as they wait for and hasten the day of God, looking for new heavens and a new earth where righteousness dwells. They should strive to be found at peace, spotless and blameless, regarding the Lord’s patience as salvation, as Paul also wrote, though some twist his letters as they twist other Scriptures. Peter closes by warning them to guard against error and to grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.

## Chapter Background and Story

The false teachers described in chapter 2 apparently mocked the idea that Christ would return. Perhaps they argued that since the first generation of believers was dying and Christ had not come, the promise must be false. If there was no return, there would be no judgment, and so there would be no reason to live a holy life. Their denial of the second coming supported their immoral lifestyle.

Peter answers this challenge directly. He shows that God has acted in history before and will act again. He explains that God’s timing is different from human timing and that His apparent delay is actually an expression of His patience and mercy. And he describes the glorious future God has promised: a new heavens and a new earth where righteousness is at home.

This chapter is Peter’s final word. It ends not with fear but with a call to growth and a burst of praise to Jesus Christ.

### Remember the Words (*3:1–2*)

“*This is now, beloved, the second letter that I have written to you; and in both of them I stir up your sincere mind by reminding you*” (*v. 1*) “*that you should remember the words which were spoken before by the holy prophets and the commandment of us, the apostles of the Lord and Savior*” (*v. 2*). The “second letter” suggests 1 Peter was the first. Peter wants his readers to remember two sources of truth: the Old Testament prophets and the teaching of the apostles, which carries the authority of the Lord Jesus. Together, these form the foundation of the faith (*Ephesians 2:20*).

### The Scoffers (*3:3–7*)

The mockers’ challenge and Peter’s answer are studied below. “*For they willfully forget that there were heavens from of old, and an earth formed out of water and amid water by the word of God*” (*v. 5*), “*by which means the world that existed then, being overflowed with water, perished*” (*v. 6*). The scoffers claimed nothing ever changes. But they deliberately ignored two great events. First, God created the world by His word (*Genesis 1*). Second, God judged the world by the flood (*Genesis 6–8*). The world has not continued unchanged; God has intervened before.

“*But the heavens that exist now and the earth, by the same word have been stored up for fire, being reserved against the day of judgment and destruction of ungodly men*” (*v. 7*). The same word that created and judged the world in the past has reserved the present world for a future judgment. Just as the first world was judged by water, the present world will face judgment by fire.

### God’s Patience (*3:8–9*)

The explanation of God’s timing and patience is studied below.

### The Day of the Lord and the New Creation (*3:10–13*)

The description of the day of the Lord and the new creation is studied below.

### Living in Light of the Promise (*3:14–18*)

“*Therefore, beloved, seeing that you look for these things, be diligent to be found in peace, without defect and blameless in his sight*” (*v. 14*). Since believers are waiting for these things, they should make every effort to live at peace with God and others, spotless and blameless, ready to meet Christ.

“*Regard the patience of our Lord as salvation; even as our beloved brother Paul also, according to the wisdom given to him, wrote to you*” (*v. 15*), “*as also in all of his letters, speaking in them of these things. In those, there are some things that are hard to understand, which the ignorant and unsettled twist, as they also do to the other Scriptures, to their own destruction*” (*v. 16*). God’s patience is an opportunity for salvation. Peter notes that Paul taught the same (*Romans 2:4*). Peter calls Paul “our beloved brother,” showing warm respect, even though they had once had a sharp disagreement (*Galatians 2:11–14*). He admits that some of Paul’s writings are hard to understand, and that untaught and unstable people twist them, just as they twist “the other Scriptures.” This is one of the earliest indications that Paul’s letters were being recognized as Scripture.

“*You therefore, beloved, knowing these things beforehand, beware, lest being carried away with the error of the wicked, you fall from your own steadfastness*” (*v. 17*). Forewarned is forearmed. Since believers know about false teaching, they should guard themselves so they are not swept away by it. The closing call to growth is studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *2 Peter 3:3–4* — Where Is the Promise of His Coming?

> *“knowing this first, that in the last days mockers will come, walking after their own lusts and saying, ‘Where is the promise of his coming? For, from the day that the fathers fell asleep, all things continue as they were from the beginning of the creation.’”*
>
> — *2 Peter 3:3–4* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“Knowing this first, that in the last days mockers will come.” “The last days” refers to the whole period between Christ’s first and second coming. Peter warns that scoffers will appear, people who ridicule God’s promises.

“Walking after their own lusts.” Their mockery is connected to their lifestyle. They want to live according to their own desires, and denying Christ’s return removes any sense of accountability.

Verse 4: “and saying, ‘Where is the promise of his coming?’” They mock the promise of Christ’s return, pointing out that it has not happened yet.

“For, from the day that the fathers fell asleep, all things continue as they were from the beginning of the creation.” “The fathers” may refer to the first generation of Christians who had died, or to the patriarchs of Israel. The scoffers argued that the world goes on as it always has; there is no sign of divine intervention, so there is no reason to expect it in the future.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The scoffers’ argument is essentially that the world is a closed system where nothing changes and God does not intervene. Peter shows that this assumption ignores history. God created the world, and God judged the world in the flood. He has acted decisively before, and He will act again.

There is also a moral dimension. Peter notes that the scoffers follow “their own lusts.” People who do not want to be accountable to God often find reasons to deny His involvement in the world. Unbelief is sometimes driven not by evidence but by desire.

Scoffing at Christ’s return has continued throughout history, and it remains common today. Many people dismiss the idea that Jesus will return. Peter’s words help believers understand that such mockery was predicted and does not disprove God’s promise.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

When believers encounter skepticism or mockery about Christ’s return, they need not be shaken. Peter warned that scoffers would come. Their presence actually confirms Scripture’s reliability.

Believers can also examine their own hearts. Do they live as though Christ will return? Or have they, perhaps unconsciously, begun to assume that life will simply go on as it always has? Remembering Christ’s promised return can shape how they live.

Finally, believers can respond to skeptics with gentleness and respect, explaining the hope they have (*1 Peter 3:15*), rather than with defensiveness or anger.

### *2 Peter 3:8–9* — The Lord Is Patient

> *“But don’t forget this one thing, beloved, that one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day. The Lord is not slow concerning his promise, as some count slowness; but he is patient with us, not wishing that anyone should perish, but that all should come to repentance.”*
>
> — *2 Peter 3:8–9* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“But don’t forget this one thing, beloved, that one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day.” Peter draws on *Psalm 90:4*. God does not experience time as humans do. He is eternal. What seems like a long delay to people is not a delay to Him. A thousand years is like a single day in His sight.

Verse 9: “The Lord is not slow concerning his promise, as some count slowness.” God is not late. He is not failing to keep His word. People may think He is slow, but they are measuring Him by human standards.

“But he is patient with us.” The real reason for the apparent delay is God’s patience.

“Not wishing that anyone should perish, but that all should come to repentance.” God is giving people time to turn to Him. He does not want anyone to be destroyed. He wants everyone to repent and be saved.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses transform how believers understand the waiting period before Christ’s return. What looks like delay is actually mercy. Every day that passes is another opportunity for people to repent and come to God. This echoes *1 Timothy 2:4*, which says God desires all people to be saved, and *Ezekiel 33:11*, where God says He takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked.

God’s patience has a purpose, but it is not unlimited. The day of the Lord will come (v10). God’s patience is an invitation to respond now, not a reason to delay.

As discussed at *1 Timothy 2:4*, Christians understand God’s desire for all to be saved in relation to His sovereignty in different ways. But all agree that God’s heart is merciful, that His invitation is genuine, and that His patience gives people real opportunity to repent.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers who wonder why Christ has not yet returned can find the answer here: God is patient, giving people time to repent. This perspective can transform impatience into gratitude and mission.

Believers can use this time well, sharing the gospel with those who do not yet know Christ, so that more people will come to repentance.

For those who have not yet turned to God, these verses are an invitation. God’s patience is giving them time, but that time will not last forever. Today is the day to respond.

### *2 Peter 3:10–13* — New Heavens and a New Earth

> *“But the day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night, in which the heavens will pass away with a great noise, and the elements will be dissolved with fervent heat; and the earth and the works that are in it will be burned up. Therefore, since all these things will be destroyed like this, what kind of people ought you to be in holy living and godliness, looking for and earnestly desiring the coming of the day of God, which will cause the burning heavens to be dissolved, and the elements will melt with fervent heat? But, according to his promise, we look for new heavens and a new earth, in which righteousness dwells.”*
>
> — *2 Peter 3:10–13* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“But the day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night.” The day of the Lord, the day of Christ’s return and God’s final judgment, will come suddenly and unexpectedly, as Jesus Himself said (*Matthew 24:43–44*; *1 Thessalonians 5:2*).

“In which the heavens will pass away with a great noise, and the elements will be dissolved with fervent heat; and the earth and the works that are in it will be burned up.” Peter describes cosmic upheaval. “The elements” may mean the basic components of the physical world, or the heavenly bodies. Some ancient manuscripts read “the earth and the works that are in it will be found,” or “laid bare,” meaning exposed before God’s judgment.

Verse 11: “Therefore, since all these things will be destroyed like this, what kind of people ought you to be in holy living and godliness.” The prospect of this day should shape how believers live now. Since this world is temporary, believers should live holy and godly lives.

Verse 12: “looking for and earnestly desiring the coming of the day of God.” Believers eagerly anticipate this day. The word translated “earnestly desiring” can also mean “hastening.” Believers may in some way hasten Christ’s return through holy living, prayer, and spreading the gospel (*Matthew 24:14*).

Verse 13: “But, according to his promise, we look for new heavens and a new earth, in which righteousness dwells.” The goal is not destruction for its own sake, but renewal. God has promised new heavens and a new earth (*Isaiah 65:17*; *66:22*; *Revelation 21:1*). In this new creation, righteousness will be at home. Evil, injustice, and suffering will be gone.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Christians have understood these verses in different ways. Some believe the present universe will be completely destroyed and replaced with an entirely new creation. Others believe the fire describes a purifying judgment that will cleanse and renew the existing creation, much as the flood judged the world without annihilating the earth. They point to *Romans 8:19–22*, which speaks of creation itself being set free from decay, and to the reading “laid bare” in verse 10. Both views agree that the present world, as it is now, marred by sin, will come to an end, and that God will bring a new creation where righteousness dwells.

The phrase “in which righteousness dwells” describes the heart of the new creation. It will be a world where everything is right: relationships with God, with one another, and with creation itself. This is the fulfillment of every longing for justice and peace.

The connection between future hope and present living is central. Because believers know where history is heading, they are called to live holy lives now. Hope is not escapism; it is motivation.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can hold the things of this world loosely, knowing that they are temporary. Possessions, achievements, and status will not last. What lasts is a life of holiness and godliness.

Believers can also look forward with hope to the new creation. Every injustice, sorrow, and suffering will be made right. This hope can sustain them through hard times.

Finally, believers can live in a way that “hastens” Christ’s return: praying for His kingdom to come, sharing the gospel, and living holy lives that reflect the righteousness of the world to come.

### *2 Peter 3:18* — Grow in Grace and Knowledge

> *“But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. To him be the glory both now and forever. Amen.”*
>
> — *2 Peter 3:18* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Peter’s final instruction is simple and profound. “But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.”

“Grow.” The Christian life is not static. Believers are meant to keep growing, maturing, and deepening.

“In the grace.” Believers grow in their experience and understanding of God’s undeserved favor. They grow in receiving grace and in extending it to others.

“And knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.” They grow in personal knowledge of Jesus, knowing Him more deeply, not just knowing about Him.

“To him be the glory both now and forever. Amen.” Peter ends with praise to Jesus Christ. Glory belongs to Him, now and in eternity.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse is the antidote to false teaching. The false teachers twisted grace into an excuse for sin and claimed a false knowledge. Peter calls believers to grow in true grace and true knowledge. Growth in grace and knowledge protects believers from being carried away by error (v17).

Notice that Peter ends his letter, and perhaps his life’s writing, with praise to Jesus. Glory is given to Christ “both now and forever,” literally “to the day of eternity.” This doxology, directed to Christ, shows that Peter worshiped Jesus as God. The fisherman who once denied Jesus now gives Him eternal glory.

This verse also echoes the beginning of the letter, which spoke of “grace” and “knowledge” (*2 Peter 1:2–3*). The whole letter is framed by this call: know Christ more, and grow in His grace.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can ask whether they are growing. Are they knowing Christ more deeply? Are they experiencing and extending His grace more fully? Growth comes through Scripture, prayer, worship, fellowship, service, and obedience.

Growth is a lifelong process. No matter how long believers have followed Christ, there is always more of His grace to experience and more of Him to know.

Finally, believers can make Peter’s closing words their own, giving glory to Jesus Christ now and forever. Worship is both the goal and the source of growth.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

Second Peter 3 addresses those who mock the promise of Christ’s return. Scoffers claim that nothing ever changes, so there is no reason to expect God to intervene. But they forget that God created the world by His word and judged it through the flood. The same word has reserved the present world for judgment. Believers need not be shaken by such mockery; Peter predicted it.

The chapter explains why Christ has not yet returned. With the Lord, a day is like a thousand years. He is not slow but patient, not wanting anyone to perish but all to come to repentance. Every day is an expression of His mercy and an opportunity for people to turn to Him. Believers can use this time to share the gospel, and those who have not yet turned to God can respond today.

The day of the Lord will come suddenly, like a thief. The present world will come to an end, and God will bring new heavens and a new earth where righteousness dwells. Christians understand the details in different ways, but all share this hope. And this hope shapes how believers live: in holiness and godliness, at peace, without spot or blame, eagerly looking forward to the day of God.

Finally, Peter warns believers to guard against error and to grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. The best protection against false teaching is growing in the true knowledge of Christ. And Peter’s last word is praise: to Jesus be the glory, now and forever.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for the promise of Your coming. When I hear people mock that promise, keep me steady. Help me to remember that with You a day is like a thousand years, and that You are not slow, but patient, not wanting anyone to perish but all to come to repentance. Thank You for Your patience with me. Give me a heart for those who do not yet know You, and help me to share the good news while there is time. I look forward to the new heavens and the new earth, where righteousness dwells. Help me to live a holy and godly life as I wait, at peace, without spot or blame. Guard me from error, and help me to grow in Your grace and in the knowledge of You, my Lord and Savior. To You be the glory, both now and forever. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Book 23 of 27

# 1 John

## About This Letter

First John does not name its author, but from the earliest times Christians have recognized it as the work of John, the apostle and “the disciple whom Jesus loved,” who also wrote the Gospel of John. Its vocabulary and themes, light and darkness, truth and lies, life, love, abiding, and believing that Jesus is the Christ, closely match the Gospel. The author writes as an eyewitness who heard, saw, and touched “*the Word of life*” (*1 John 1:1*). Some scholars attribute the letters to a close disciple of John in a community shaped by his teaching. According to early tradition, John spent his later years in Ephesus, and this letter may have been written there toward the end of the first century, around A.D. 85–95, to churches in the surrounding region.

The letter was written after a painful split in the community. Some members had left the fellowship (*1 John 2:19*) and were teaching a different message. They apparently denied that Jesus is the Christ come in the flesh (*2:22*; *4:2–3*), perhaps claiming that the divine Christ only seemed to be human or only came upon the man Jesus temporarily. They also claimed to know God and to be without sin, while showing little love for fellow believers. Those who remained were confused and unsettled. John writes to reassure them that they truly know God and have eternal life.

## The Shape of the Letter

First John does not follow a simple outline. It moves in circles, returning again and again to three great tests of genuine faith: right belief about Jesus, obedience to God’s commands, and love for one another. It opens with the testimony of eyewitnesses to the Word of life and the message that God is light. It calls believers to walk in the light, confess their sins, keep God’s commands, and love one another. It warns against loving the world and against antichrists who deny the Son. It celebrates the love of the Father who calls believers His children and promises that when Christ appears they will be like Him. It urges believers to test the spirits, declares that God is love and that perfect love casts out fear, and closes with the assurance that those who believe in the Son have eternal life, that God hears their prayers, and that they should keep themselves from idols.

## Themes to Watch For

Watch for fellowship with God and with one another, light and darkness, confession and forgiveness, Jesus as our Advocate and atoning sacrifice, the commandment to love, the danger of the world, the truth about Jesus come in the flesh, the identity of believers as God’s children, love shown in action, God’s love as the source of ours, overcoming the world through faith, and assurance of eternal life. First John was written “that you may know that you have eternal life” (*5:13*), and it offers a warm and searching picture of life in God’s family.

1 John · Chapter 1 of 5

# 1 John — Chapter 1

Chapter Theme: Walking in the Light

[Read 1 John 1 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/1JN01.htm)

Main Teaching

John begins by testifying to what he and the other apostles heard, saw with their own eyes, and touched with their hands: the Word of life, the eternal life that was with the Father and was revealed to them. They proclaim it so that their readers may share in their fellowship, which is fellowship with the Father and His Son Jesus Christ, and so that their joy may be complete. The message they heard from Christ is that God is light, and in Him there is no darkness at all. Anyone who claims fellowship with God but walks in darkness is lying. But if believers walk in the light, as God is in the light, they have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus cleanses them from all sin. Those who claim to have no sin deceive themselves, but if they confess their sins, God is faithful and just to forgive them and cleanse them from all unrighteousness. Those who claim they have not sinned make God a liar.

## Chapter Background and Story

First John begins without a greeting, much like the opening of John’s Gospel. In fact, the first verses deliberately echo the Gospel’s prologue: “*In the beginning was the Word*” (*John 1:1*). John wants his readers to know from the start that the message they believe is rooted in real, physical encounters with Jesus, the eternal Word who became flesh.

This emphasis was important because some false teachers were denying that Jesus truly came in a physical body (*1 John 4:2–3*). Influenced by ideas that treated the physical world as inferior, they may have taught that the divine Christ only appeared to be human, or that He was separate from the man Jesus. John counters this by stressing that the apostles heard, saw, looked at, and touched Him.

The second half of the chapter addresses another error. The false teachers apparently claimed to have special fellowship with God while living in moral darkness, and they claimed to be without sin. John insists that fellowship with God, who is light, requires walking in the light, and that honesty about sin is essential.

### The Word of Life (*1:1–4*)

John’s testimony about the Word of life is studied below. “*And we write these things to you, that our joy may be fulfilled*” (*v. 4*). Some manuscripts read “your joy.” Either way, John’s joy, and his readers’, is made complete when they share in fellowship with God and with one another. Jesus spoke of His joy being made full in His disciples (*John 15:11*; *17:13*).

### God Is Light (*1:5–7*)

The message that God is light, and what it means to walk in the light, are studied below. “*If we say that we have fellowship with him and walk in the darkness, we lie and don’t tell the truth*” (*v. 6*). This is the first of three “if we say” statements (vv6, 8, 10), each exposing a false claim. Claiming to know God while living in sin is a lie. John is blunt because the false teachers were making exactly this claim.

### Confessing Our Sins (*1:8–10*)

“*If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us*” (*v. 8*). The second false claim is to have no sin, perhaps meaning to have no sinful nature, or to think sin no longer matters. Such a claim is self-deception. The promise of forgiveness for those who confess is studied below.

“*If we say that we haven’t sinned, we make him a liar, and his word is not in us*” (*v. 10*). The third false claim is to have never sinned. This contradicts God’s word, which declares that all have sinned (*Romans 3:23*). To deny one’s sin is to call God a liar, since He has said all people sin and has sent His Son to deal with it.

## Important Verses Explained

### *1 John 1:1–3* — That Which We Have Seen and Touched

> *“That which was from the beginning, that which we have heard, that which we have seen with our eyes, that which we saw, and our hands touched, concerning the Word of life (and the life was revealed, and we have seen, and testify, and declare to you the life, the eternal life, which was with the Father, and was revealed to us); that which we have seen and heard we declare to you, that you also may have fellowship with us. Yes, and our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son, Jesus Christ.”*
>
> — *1 John 1:1–3* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“That which was from the beginning.” The Word existed from the beginning, before creation, as *John 1:1* says. He is eternal.

“That which we have heard, that which we have seen with our eyes, that which we saw, and our hands touched.” John piles up sensory experiences. The apostles heard Jesus teach. They saw Him with their own eyes. They looked at Him carefully, observing Him over time. They even touched Him. After the resurrection, Jesus invited His disciples to touch Him to prove He was not a ghost (*Luke 24:39*; *John 20:27*).

“Concerning the Word of life.” Jesus is the Word who gives life and who is life itself.

Verse 2: “and the life was revealed, and we have seen, and testify, and declare to you the life, the eternal life, which was with the Father, and was revealed to us.” The eternal life that existed with the Father became visible in Jesus. The apostles witnessed it and now proclaim it.

Verse 3: “that which we have seen and heard we declare to you, that you also may have fellowship with us.” The apostles share their testimony so that others can join their fellowship. “Fellowship” means sharing, partnership, a common life.

“Yes, and our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son, Jesus Christ.” This fellowship is not merely human friendship. It is a shared life with God Himself.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses affirm two essential truths about Jesus. First, He is eternal: He existed “from the beginning” and was “with the Father.” Second, He is fully human: He could be heard, seen, and touched. Jesus is both God and man. The false teachers denied His true humanity; John insists on it.

The Christian faith is grounded in eyewitness testimony. The apostles were not sharing ideas or theories but reporting what they had experienced. Peter made the same claim (*2 Peter 1:16*). This historical foundation gives believers confidence.

The goal of the apostolic testimony is fellowship. God’s purpose in sending His Son was not only to forgive sins but to bring people into relationship with Himself and with one another. The Christian life is a shared life, with the Father, the Son, and fellow believers.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can be confident that their faith rests on real events witnessed by real people. When doubts arise, they can return to the eyewitness testimony recorded in Scripture.

This passage also invites believers to experience fellowship with God. Faith is not merely believing facts but entering into a relationship with the Father through the Son.

Finally, believers can value fellowship with other believers. The Christian life is not meant to be lived alone. Sharing life with other believers, in worship, prayer, and friendship, is part of God’s design.

### *1 John 1:5* — God Is Light

> *“This is the message which we have heard from him and announce to you, that God is light, and in him is no darkness at all.”*
>
> — *1 John 1:5* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“This is the message which we have heard from him and announce to you.” The apostles received this message from Jesus and pass it on.

“That God is light.” Light is one of Scripture’s great images for God. Light represents truth, purity, holiness, goodness, and revelation. Where light shines, darkness is exposed and driven away.

“And in him is no darkness at all.” There is no evil, falsehood, or impurity in God. He is completely good, completely true, completely holy. The emphasis is strong: “no darkness at all.”

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This short verse is foundational for everything that follows in the letter. Because God is light, those who have fellowship with Him must walk in the light. Darkness and light cannot coexist.

The image of light runs throughout Scripture. At creation, God said, “*Let there be light*” (*Genesis 1:3*). The psalmist wrote, “*The LORD is my light and my salvation*” (*Psalm 27:1*). Jesus said, “*I am the light of the world*” (*John 8:12*). In the new creation, there will be no need for the sun, because God’s glory will be its light (*Revelation 21:23*).

The truth that God has “no darkness at all” brings great comfort. God is never deceptive, never cruel, never unjust. He can be trusted completely. His character is purely good.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can trust God completely, knowing there is no darkness in Him. When life is confusing or painful, they can hold onto the truth that God is good and true.

This verse also calls believers to examine their own lives. Are there areas of darkness, hidden sin, deception, or dishonesty, that need to be brought into God’s light?

Finally, believers can reflect God’s light in the world, living lives of truth, goodness, and love that point others to Him.

### *1 John 1:7* — Cleansed by the Blood of Jesus

> *“But if we walk in the light as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanses us from all sin.”*
>
> — *1 John 1:7* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“But if we walk in the light as he is in the light.” To “walk” means to live, to conduct one’s daily life. Walking in the light means living in honesty, openness, and obedience before God, with nothing hidden.

“We have fellowship with one another.” When believers live in the light, they can have genuine fellowship with one another. Honesty and openness make true relationships possible.

“And the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanses us from all sin.” Walking in the light does not mean being sinless. It means living honestly before God, including being honest about sin. And as believers do so, Jesus’ blood, His sacrificial death, keeps cleansing them from all sin. The verb is in the present tense: it continually cleanses.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse holds together two truths that might seem to be in tension: walking in the light and needing cleansing from sin. Walking in the light is not about perfection; it is about honesty and direction. Believers who walk in the light still sin, but they do not hide it. They bring it into the light, where Christ’s blood cleanses it.

“The blood of Jesus” refers to His sacrificial death on the cross. As Hebrews explains, His blood was offered once for all and is sufficient to cleanse completely (*Hebrews 9:14*; *10:10*). That cleansing is ongoing for believers as they walk with Him.

The connection between walking in the light and fellowship with one another is significant. Hidden sin damages relationships. Honesty, confession, and forgiveness build genuine community. *James 5:16* also connects confession to one another with healing.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can practice walking in the light by being honest with God about their sins, struggles, and failures, rather than hiding them or pretending.

This openness can also extend to trusted fellow believers. Having a few people with whom one can be honest about struggles brings support, accountability, and deeper fellowship.

Finally, believers can rest in the ongoing cleansing of Christ’s blood. They do not need to carry guilt. As they walk in the light, Christ keeps cleansing them.

### *1 John 1:9* — If We Confess Our Sins

> *“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”*
>
> — *1 John 1:9* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“If we confess our sins.” To “confess” means to say the same thing as God about our sins: to agree with Him that they are wrong, to acknowledge them honestly, without excuses.

“He is faithful.” God keeps His promises. He has promised to forgive those who confess, and He will.

“And righteous.” God’s forgiveness is also just. This might seem surprising, since forgiving sin might seem to overlook justice. But God forgives justly, because Christ has already paid the penalty for sin (*1 John 2:2*). God is not ignoring sin; He has dealt with it in Christ.

“To forgive us the sins.” God releases believers from the guilt of their sins.

“And to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” Beyond forgiveness, God cleanses, purifying believers from the stain and effects of sin. “All” means nothing is left out.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse is one of the most comforting promises in Scripture. It assures believers that confession leads to forgiveness and cleansing every time, not because they deserve it, but because God is faithful and just.

The words “faithful and righteous” show that forgiveness rests on God’s character and on Christ’s work. God is faithful to His promise, and He is just because the penalty has already been paid. Believers can be completely confident that confessed sin is forgiven.

Confession is not a way of earning forgiveness. It is the honest acknowledgment that opens the heart to receive what God freely gives. David experienced this: “*I acknowledged my sin to you*” (*Psalm 32:5*)... “*and you forgave the iniquity of my sin*” (*Psalm 32:5*). *Proverbs 28:13* says, “He who conceals his sins doesn’t prosper, but whoever confesses and renounces them finds mercy.”

This verse is written to believers. It shows that believers still sin and still need to confess. Confession is a regular part of the Christian life, not a one-time event at conversion.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can make confession a regular habit, bringing their sins honestly to God in prayer, naming them specifically, and receiving His forgiveness.

When believers struggle with guilt over confessed sin, they can return to this promise. God is faithful and just to forgive. They do not need to keep punishing themselves for what God has forgiven.

Finally, believers can extend the same forgiveness to others. Having received such generous forgiveness, they are called to forgive those who wrong them (*Ephesians 4:32*). This does not mean ignoring harm or abuse, but it does mean releasing bitterness and revenge.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

First *John 1* grounds the Christian faith in what the apostles heard, saw, and touched: Jesus Christ, the eternal Word of life who became truly human. Believers can rest their faith on this historical testimony. The goal of the apostles’ message was fellowship, a shared life with the Father, with His Son Jesus Christ, and with one another, leading to complete joy.

The central message is that God is light, and in Him there is no darkness at all. He is completely good, true, and holy. Those who claim to know Him must walk in the light, living in honesty and openness before Him. Claiming fellowship with God while living in darkness is a lie.

Walking in the light does not mean being sinless. John is clear that anyone who claims to be without sin is self-deceived. Rather, walking in the light means honesty about sin. As believers live openly before God, they enjoy fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus keeps cleansing them from all sin.

The chapter offers a beautiful promise: if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from all unrighteousness. Believers can bring their sins honestly to God, confident that He will forgive. They can live free from hidden guilt, in the light of His love, and extend the same forgiveness to others.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, You are the Word of life, eternal with the Father, who became truly human so that we could hear, see, and touch You. Thank You for the testimony of those who walked with You. Thank You for bringing me into fellowship with the Father and with You, and with Your people. Father, You are light, and in You there is no darkness at all. Help me to walk in the light, living honestly before You, with nothing hidden. Keep me from deceiving myself about my sin. I confess my sins to You now, trusting that You are faithful and just to forgive me and cleanse me from all unrighteousness. Thank You that the blood of Jesus cleanses me from all sin. Help me to forgive others as You have forgiven me. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

1 John · Chapter 2 of 5

# 1 John — Chapter 2

Chapter Theme: Knowing God, Loving One Another, and Remaining in Him

[Read 1 John 2 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/1JN02.htm)

Main Teaching

John writes so that his dear children will not sin, but if anyone does sin, they have an Advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, who is the atoning sacrifice for their sins and for the sins of the whole world. People show they know God by keeping His commands; whoever claims to know Him but disobeys is a liar, while those who obey have God’s love made complete in them and should walk as Jesus walked. The old command that is also new is to love one another; whoever claims to be in the light but hates a brother or sister is still in darkness, but whoever loves remains in the light. John encourages children, fathers, and young people in their forgiveness, knowledge of God, and victory over the evil one. He warns believers not to love the world or its desires of the flesh, desires of the eyes, and pride in possessions, because the world is passing away, but whoever does God’s will lives forever. Many antichrists have already come, some of whom left the fellowship, showing they never truly belonged; the liar is the one who denies that Jesus is the Christ, denying the Father and the Son. Believers have an anointing from the Holy One and know the truth; they should let what they heard from the beginning remain in them, so they will remain in the Son and the Father and have confidence, not shame, when He appears.

## Chapter Background and Story

In chapter 1, John declared that God is light and that believers must walk in the light, confessing their sins. Chapter 2 continues these themes and introduces several of the “tests” that run through the letter. How can believers know they truly know God? John gives three answers: they obey God’s commands, they love one another, and they believe the truth about Jesus.

The false teachers who had left the community claimed to know God, but their lives and beliefs showed otherwise. They did not obey God’s commands, they did not love the believers, and they denied that Jesus is the Christ. John wants to reassure the faithful believers who remained that they truly belong to God, while warning them not to be led astray.

Throughout the chapter, John speaks with tender affection, calling his readers “my little children” and “beloved.” He writes as an elderly apostle, a spiritual father to the churches.

### Our Advocate (*2:1–2*)

Jesus as Advocate and atoning sacrifice is studied below.

### Knowing Him by Obedience (*2:3–6*)

“*This is how we know that we know him: if we keep his commandments*” (*v. 3*). Obedience is evidence of genuine relationship with God. “*One who says, “I know him,” and doesn’t keep his commandments, is a liar, and the truth isn’t in him*” (*v. 4*). Claiming to know God while living in disobedience is self-deception. “*But God’s love has most certainly been perfected in whoever keeps his word. This is how we know that we are in him*” (*v. 5*): “God’s love” may mean love for God or God’s love working in a person; obedience shows that God’s love has reached its goal in them. The call to walk as Jesus walked is studied below.

### The Old and New Commandment (*2:7–11*)

“*Brothers, I write no new commandment to you, but an old commandment which you had from the beginning. The old commandment is the word which you heard from the beginning*” (*v. 7*). The command to love is not new; the readers had heard it from the beginning of their Christian lives, and it was already in the Law (*Leviticus 19:18*).

“*Again, I write a new commandment to you, which is true in him and in you, because the darkness is passing away and the true light already shines*” (*v. 8*). Yet it is also new, because Jesus gave it new meaning: “*Just as I have loved you, you also love one another*” (*John 13:34*). It is fulfilled in Christ and now being lived out in His people. The new age has dawned; darkness is fading. The contrast between love and hatred is studied below.

### Words to Every Stage of Faith (*2:12–14*)

“*I write to you, little children, because your sins are forgiven you for his name’s sake*” (*v. 12*). “*I write to you, fathers, because you know him who is from the beginning. I write to you, young men, because you have overcome the evil one. I write to you, little children, because you know the Father*” (*v. 13*). “*I have written to you, fathers, because you know him who is from the beginning. I have written to you, young men, because you are strong, and the word of God remains in you, and you have overcome the evil one*” (*v. 14*). John addresses believers at different stages. “Little children” may refer to all believers or to new believers; their sins are forgiven and they know the Father. “Fathers” are mature believers who have known Christ deeply over time. “Young men” are those in the vigor of faith, strong in God’s word and victorious over the evil one. These are words of affirmation and encouragement. John writes not because he doubts them but because he is confident in God’s work in them. Though the WEB uses “men,” the encouragement applies to believers of every sex and age.

### Do Not Love the World (*2:15–17*)

The warning against loving the world is studied below.

### Antichrists (*2:18–27*)

“*Little children, these are the end times, and as you heard that the Antichrist is coming, even now many antichrists have arisen. By this we know that it is the final hour*” (*v. 18*). “The final hour” refers to the last age, the period between Christ’s first and second comings. John’s readers had heard that “the Antichrist” would come, a figure of opposition to Christ (compare the “man of sin” in *2 Thessalonians 2:3–4*). John says that “many antichrists” have already appeared. Christians understand this in different ways: some believe a single future Antichrist will appear before Christ’s return, preceded by many lesser “antichrists”; others see “antichrist” mainly as a spirit or pattern of opposition present throughout history. John’s main concern is practical: anyone who denies the truth about Jesus is acting in the spirit of antichrist.

“*They went out from us, but they didn’t belong to us; for if they had belonged to us, they would have continued with us. But they left, that they might be revealed that none of them belong to us*” (*v. 19*). The false teachers had left the community. Their departure revealed that they had never truly belonged.

“*You have an anointing from the Holy One, and you all have knowledge*” (*v. 20*). The “anointing” is the Holy Spirit, given by Christ, “the Holy One.” The false teachers may have claimed special knowledge for a select few; John insists that all believers have the Spirit and know the truth. “*I have not written to you because you don’t know the truth, but because you know it, and because no lie is of the truth*” (*v. 21*).

“*Who is the liar but he who denies that Jesus is the Christ? This is the Antichrist, he who denies the Father and the Son*” (*v. 22*). “*Whoever denies the Son doesn’t have the Father. He who confesses the Son has the Father also*” (*v. 23*). The false teachers denied that Jesus is the Christ, perhaps separating the human Jesus from the divine Christ. To deny the Son is to lose the Father too, because the Father is known only through the Son (*John 14:6–9*).

“*Therefore, as for you, let that remain in you which you heard from the beginning. If that which you heard from the beginning remains in you, you also will remain in the Son, and in the Father*” (*v. 24*). “*This is the promise which he promised us, the eternal life*” (*v. 25*). Believers do not need new teachings. They need to hold on to the gospel they first received.

“*These things I have written to you concerning those who would lead you astray*” (*v. 26*). “*As for you, the anointing which you received from him remains in you, and you don’t need for anyone to teach you. But as his anointing teaches you concerning all things, and is true, and is no lie, and even as it taught you, you will remain in him*” (*v. 27*). John does not mean believers need no teachers at all; he himself is teaching them. He means they do not need the false teachers’ supposed new revelations. The Spirit, who taught them the truth of the gospel, continues to guide them in it.

### Remain in Him (*2:28–29*)

“*Now, little children, remain in him, that when he appears, we may have boldness and not be ashamed before him at his coming*” (*v. 28*). “Remain,” or “abide,” is a key word in John’s writings (*John 15:4–10*). Believers are to stay connected to Christ, so that when He returns, they will meet Him with confidence rather than shame.

“*If you know that he is righteous, you know that everyone who practices righteousness has been born of him*” (*v. 29*). A family resemblance shows who belongs to God. Those born of God reflect His righteousness.

## Important Verses Explained

### *1 John 2:1–2* — Jesus Our Advocate and Atoning Sacrifice

> *“My little children, I write these things to you so that you may not sin. If anyone sins, we have a Counselor with the Father, Jesus Christ, the righteous. And he is the atoning sacrifice for our sins, and not for ours only, but also for the whole world.”*
>
> — *1 John 2:1–2* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“My little children, I write these things to you so that you may not sin.” John has just said that everyone sins (*1 John 1:8–10*). But he does not want his readers to think sin is acceptable. His goal is that they would not sin.

“If anyone sins, we have a Counselor with the Father, Jesus Christ, the righteous.” When believers do sin, they are not left without help. They have a “Counselor,” an Advocate, like a defense lawyer who speaks on their behalf. Jesus stands before the Father representing them. He is “the righteous,” perfectly sinless, and therefore able to plead for sinners.

Verse 2: “And he is the atoning sacrifice for our sins.” Jesus is not only the Advocate but also the sacrifice. His death dealt with sin, satisfying God’s justice and removing guilt. The word translated “atoning sacrifice” has been rendered “propitiation” (turning away God’s righteous wrath against sin) or “expiation” (removing sin itself). Both ideas are present: through Christ’s sacrifice, sin is removed and God’s justice is satisfied.

“And not for ours only, but also for the whole world.” Christ’s sacrifice is not limited to one group. It is sufficient for the whole world. The gospel is for everyone.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses hold together two truths: the call not to sin and the provision for when we do. The gospel does not make sin acceptable, but it also does not leave believers without hope when they fail.

Jesus as Advocate is a beautiful image. When believers sin, they might fear that God will reject them. But Jesus stands with them before the Father. *Hebrews 7:25* says He always lives to make intercession for them. *Romans 8:34* asks, “Who is he who condemns? It is Christ who died... who also makes intercession for us.”

The phrase “for the whole world” has been understood in different ways. Some understand it to mean that Christ died for every person without exception, making salvation available to all. Others understand it to mean that Christ died for people from every nation, not only Jews or one community. All agree that the gospel is to be offered freely to everyone and that no one is beyond the reach of Christ’s sacrifice.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can aim not to sin, taking holiness seriously. But when they do sin, they need not despair. They can come to the Father through Jesus, their Advocate, confessing their sin and trusting His sacrifice.

This passage also gives confidence in sharing the gospel. Christ’s sacrifice is for the whole world. There is no person to whom believers cannot say, “Christ died for sins, and you can be forgiven.”

Finally, believers can find comfort in knowing that Jesus is on their side. He is not their accuser but their Advocate.

### *1 John 2:6* — Walk as He Walked

> *“he who says he remains in him ought himself also to walk just like he walked.”*
>
> — *1 John 2:6* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“He who says he remains in him.” Many people claim to have a relationship with God, to “remain,” or abide, in Him.

“Ought himself also to walk just like he walked.” Those who make this claim should live as Jesus lived. “Walk” means to conduct one’s life. Jesus is the model for how believers should live.

How did Jesus walk? He walked in obedience to the Father, in love for others, in humility, in compassion for the suffering, in truthfulness, and in self-giving sacrifice.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse sets a high standard: the life of Jesus Himself. Believers are not called merely to follow rules but to follow a person. Peter wrote that Christ left an example so that believers should follow in His steps (*1 Peter 2:21*). Paul urged believers to imitate him as he imitated Christ (*1 Corinthians 11:1*).

This standard is not achieved by human effort alone. Believers “remain in him,” and from that connection, Christ’s life flows through them. Jesus said, “*Remain in me, and I in you. As the branch can't bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you, unless you remain in me*” (*John 15:4*). Walking as Jesus walked is the fruit of abiding in Him.

The word “ought” indicates obligation, but it is an obligation that flows from relationship. Those who truly know Christ will want to become like Him.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can study the life of Jesus in the Gospels, observing how He treated people, how He responded to opposition, how He prayed, and how He obeyed the Father. These observations become a pattern for their own lives.

In daily situations, believers can ask, “How would Jesus respond here?” This question can shape how they treat difficult people, how they use their time and money, and how they respond to temptation.

Finally, believers can remember that walking as Jesus walked depends on remaining in Him. Prayer, Scripture, worship, and fellowship keep them connected to the source of His life.

### *1 John 2:9–10* — Love Remains in the Light

> *“He who says he is in the light and hates his brother is in the darkness even until now. He who loves his brother remains in the light, and there is no occasion for stumbling in him.”*
>
> — *1 John 2:9–10* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“He who says he is in the light and hates his brother is in the darkness even until now.” Someone may claim to be in the light, to know God and live in His truth. But if they hate a fellow believer, they are still in darkness, no matter what they claim.

Verse 10: “He who loves his brother remains in the light, and there is no occasion for stumbling in him.” In contrast, those who love their fellow believers live in the light. “No occasion for stumbling” may mean that they will not stumble themselves, or that they will not cause others to stumble. Love keeps the path clear.

Verse 11 adds: “But he who hates his brother is in the darkness, and walks in the darkness, and doesn’t know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes.” Hatred blinds people. They lose their way and cannot see clearly.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

John makes love a test of genuine faith. It is not enough to claim to be in the light; love proves it. Hatred, even when hidden behind religious claims, reveals darkness. John will return to this theme repeatedly (*1 John 3:14–15*; *4:20*).

“Brother” refers to fellow believers, members of God’s family, both men and women. John’s focus is on love within the community, which was threatened by division. But Jesus also taught love for neighbors and enemies (*Luke 6:27–36*), so love in the church is meant to overflow to all.

The image of darkness blinding the eyes is striking. Hatred distorts perception. People filled with resentment or bitterness often misjudge others and make poor decisions. Love, by contrast, brings clarity and keeps people on the right path.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can examine their hearts for hatred, resentment, or bitterness toward fellow believers. These attitudes are incompatible with walking in the light.

When conflicts arise, believers can seek reconciliation, forgive offenses, and choose love, even when it is difficult. Love does not require pretending that wrongs did not happen or remaining in harmful situations, but it does require letting go of hatred.

Finally, believers can let love guide their perception. Seeing others through eyes of love brings clarity, compassion, and understanding.

### *1 John 2:15–17* — Do Not Love the World

> *“Don’t love the world or the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the Father’s love isn’t in him. For all that is in the world—the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life—isn’t the Father’s, but is the world’s. The world is passing away with its lusts, but he who does God’s will remains forever.”*
>
> — *1 John 2:15–17* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“Don’t love the world or the things that are in the world.” “The world” here does not mean God’s good creation or the people He loves (*John 3:16*). It means the system of values, desires, and priorities that is opposed to God, human society organized without Him.

“If anyone loves the world, the Father’s love isn’t in him.” Love for the world and love for God compete. A heart devoted to the world’s values cannot be fully devoted to God.

Verse 16 describes what is in the world. “The lust of the flesh”: desires for physical pleasure and gratification apart from God’s design. “The lust of the eyes”: desires stirred by what one sees, covetousness and greed. “And the pride of life”: arrogance about one’s possessions, achievements, or status, boasting in what one has.

“Isn’t the Father’s, but is the world’s.” These desires do not come from God.

Verse 17: “The world is passing away with its lusts, but he who does God’s will remains forever.” The world and its desires are temporary. Those who do God’s will have a life that lasts forever.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The three temptations John describes appear throughout Scripture. In the Garden of Eden, Eve saw that the fruit was good for food (desire of the flesh), pleasing to the eyes (desire of the eyes), and desirable to make one wise (pride) (*Genesis 3:6*). Jesus faced similar temptations in the wilderness: to turn stones into bread, to receive the world’s kingdoms, and to make a spectacular display of His status (*Matthew 4:1–11*). Where Adam and Eve failed, Jesus triumphed.

The contrast between what passes away and what remains is crucial. People who invest their lives in temporary things will lose them. Those who do God’s will invest in what lasts forever. Jesus taught the same: “*For what does it profit a man to gain the whole world, and forfeit his life?*” (*Mark 8:36*).

This warning does not mean believers must reject all enjoyment of life. God gives good gifts to enjoy (*1 Timothy 6:17*). The problem is loving those gifts more than the Giver, or pursuing desires in ways contrary to His will.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can examine what captures their hearts. Are they driven by the pursuit of pleasure, possessions, or status? These are powerful forces in modern culture, amplified by advertising and social media.

Believers can resist these pressures by cultivating love for God, through worship, Scripture, prayer, and service, and by practicing contentment, generosity, and humility.

Finally, believers can live with eternity in view. The things of this world are passing away. Investing in God’s will, through love, faithfulness, and service, brings rewards that last forever.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

First *John 2* offers both comfort and challenge. The comfort is that believers who sin have an Advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, who is the atoning sacrifice for their sins and for the sins of the whole world. When they fail, they can come to the Father through Him.

The challenge is that genuine faith shows itself in a changed life. Those who know God keep His commands and walk as Jesus walked. Those who are in the light love their brothers and sisters; hatred reveals darkness, no matter what a person claims. Believers can examine their lives by these tests, not to produce anxiety, but to grow in assurance and faithfulness.

John encourages believers at every stage of faith, reminding them that their sins are forgiven, that they know the Father, and that they have overcome the evil one. He warns them not to love the world, with its desires of the flesh, desires of the eyes, and pride in possessions, because the world is passing away, while those who do God’s will live forever.

Finally, John warns about those who deny that Jesus is the Christ, showing the spirit of antichrist. Believers have the anointing of the Holy Spirit and know the truth. They need not chase new teachings. They can remain in what they heard from the beginning, remaining in the Son and in the Father, so that when Christ appears, they will meet Him with confidence and not shame.

## Chapter Prayer

Father, thank You that when I sin, I have an Advocate with You, Jesus Christ the righteous, who is the atoning sacrifice for my sins and for the sins of the whole world. Help me not to sin, and help me to keep Your commands. Teach me to walk as Jesus walked, in love, humility, and obedience. Remove any hatred or bitterness from my heart, and help me to love my brothers and sisters, so that I may remain in the light. Thank You that my sins are forgiven and that I know You. Keep me from loving the world, its pleasures, its possessions, and its pride. Help me to do Your will, which lasts forever. Guard me from every teaching that denies the truth about Your Son. Thank You for the anointing of Your Spirit. Help me to remain in Christ, so that I may have confidence when He appears. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
