1 John · Chapter 3 of 5

# 1 John — Chapter 3

Chapter Theme: Children of God, Loving in Deed and Truth

[Read 1 John 3 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/1JN03.htm)

Main Teaching

John marvels at the great love the Father has given, that believers should be called children of God, which they truly are, though the world does not recognize them. What they will be has not yet been revealed, but when Christ appears they will be like Him, for they will see Him as He is, and everyone with this hope purifies themselves as He is pure. Sin is lawlessness, and Christ appeared to take away sins and to destroy the devil’s works; those born of God do not keep on living in sin, because God’s seed remains in them. The children of God are known by doing what is right and by loving their brothers and sisters. Believers are not to be like Cain, who murdered his brother, and should not be surprised if the world hates them. They know they have passed from death to life because they love one another; whoever hates a brother or sister is a murderer at heart. Love is known in this: Christ laid down His life for us, and so we ought to lay down our lives for one another, not loving with words only, but with actions and in truth, sharing with those in need. In this way believers reassure their hearts before God, who is greater than their hearts and knows everything. God’s command is to believe in the name of His Son Jesus Christ and to love one another, and those who obey remain in Him, knowing it by the Spirit He has given.

## Chapter Background and Story

At the end of chapter 2, John said that those who practice righteousness have been born of God (*1 John 2:29*). The idea of being “born of God” leads him to celebrate one of the most wonderful truths of the gospel: believers are God’s children.

From this truth, John draws two practical implications. First, God’s children resemble their Father in righteousness. They do not continue in a settled pattern of sin. Second, God’s children love one another. Love is the family resemblance that marks them as God’s own.

John’s readers had been shaken by the departure of false teachers, who claimed special spiritual status but did not live righteously or love the community. John reassures the faithful believers that they truly belong to God, and he gives them clear signs by which to recognize genuine faith. He also addresses believers whose consciences trouble them, assuring them that God is greater than their hearts.

### See What Love (*3:1–3*)

The wonder of being God’s children is studied below. “*Everyone who has this hope set on him purifies himself, even as he is pure*” (*v. 3*). The hope of seeing Christ and becoming like Him motivates purity now. Those who look forward to meeting Him want to be ready.

### Children of God Do Not Continue in Sin (*3:4–10*)

“*Everyone who sins also commits lawlessness. Sin is lawlessness*” (*v. 4*). Sin is not a minor matter. It is rebellion against God’s law, a rejection of His authority.

“*You know that he was revealed to take away our sins, and no sin is in him*” (*v. 5*). Christ came to remove sin, and He Himself was sinless. “*Whoever remains in him doesn’t sin. Whoever sins hasn’t seen him and doesn’t know him*” (*v. 6*). The meaning of these strong statements is studied below.

“*Little children, let no one lead you astray. He who does righteousness is righteous, even as he is righteous*” (*v. 7*). The false teachers may have claimed that behavior did not matter. John warns against being deceived: righteousness is shown in action.

The relationship between being born of God and sin is studied below.

“*In this the children of God are revealed, and the children of the devil. Whoever doesn’t do righteousness is not of God, neither is he who doesn’t love his brother*” (*v. 10*). Two tests reveal who belongs to God: doing what is right and loving fellow believers. These are not ways of earning God’s favor but signs of a genuine relationship with Him.

### Love One Another (*3:11–15*)

“*For this is the message which you heard from the beginning, that we should love one another*” (*v. 11*)— “*unlike Cain, who was of the evil one and killed his brother. Why did he kill him? Because his deeds were evil, and his brother’s righteous*” (*v. 12*). Cain killed Abel out of jealousy, because Abel’s offering was accepted and his own was not (*Genesis 4:1–8*). Cain is the opposite of brotherly love. Hatred and murder come from the evil one.

“*Don’t be surprised, my brothers, if the world hates you*” (*v. 13*). Just as Cain hated Abel because Abel was righteous, the world may hate believers. Jesus warned of this (*John 15:18–19*).

“*We know that we have passed out of death into life, because we love the brothers. He who doesn’t love his brother remains in death*” (*v. 14*). Love is evidence of new life. Those who love have moved from spiritual death to life. Jesus said that whoever hears His word and believes has passed from death to life (*John 5:24*).

“*Whoever hates his brother is a murderer, and you know that no murderer has eternal life remaining in him*” (*v. 15*). Hatred is murder in the heart. Jesus taught the same, saying that anger and insults are connected to murder (*Matthew 5:21–22*). A life characterized by hatred is incompatible with eternal life. This does not mean that a person who has felt anger or even committed murder can never be forgiven; the gospel offers forgiveness to all who repent, as Paul’s own story shows. It means that a heart settled in hatred does not have God’s life within it.

### Love in Action (*3:16–18*)

The definition of love and the call to love in deed and truth are studied below.

### Confidence Before God (*3:19–24*)

The assurance God gives to troubled consciences is studied below. “*Beloved, if our hearts don’t condemn us, we have boldness toward God*” (*v. 21*); “*so whatever we ask, we receive from him, because we keep his commandments and do the things that are pleasing in his sight*” (*v. 22*). When believers’ consciences are clear, they can approach God with confidence in prayer. Answered prayer is connected with obedience, not because obedience earns answers, but because those who obey God desire what He desires and pray according to His will (*1 John 5:14*).

“*This is his commandment, that we should believe in the name of his Son, Jesus Christ, and love one another, even as he commanded*” (*v. 23*). John summarizes God’s command in two parts: believe in Jesus and love one another. Faith and love belong together.

“*He who keeps his commandments remains in him, and he in him. By this we know that he remains in us, by the Spirit which he gave us*” (*v. 24*). Those who obey God live in mutual relationship with Him. The Holy Spirit within them is the evidence that God dwells in them.

## Important Verses Explained

### *1 John 3:1–2* — Called Children of God

> *“See how great a love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God! For this cause the world doesn’t know us, because it didn’t know him. Beloved, now we are children of God. It is not yet revealed what we will be; but we know that when he is revealed, we will be like him, for we will see him just as he is.”*
>
> — *1 John 3:1–2* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“See how great a love the Father has given to us.” John invites his readers to look and marvel. The phrase “how great” suggests something astonishing, a love from beyond this world. God’s love is not merely shown but “given,” lavished on believers as a gift.

“That we should be called children of God!” The evidence of God’s love is that He calls believers His children. This is not just a title; it is a reality. Some manuscripts add “and we are.”

“For this cause the world doesn’t know us, because it didn’t know him.” The world does not recognize believers as God’s children because it did not recognize Jesus as God’s Son. Believers should not expect the world to understand them.

Verse 2: “Beloved, now we are children of God.” Believers are God’s children now, not only in the future. This is their present identity.

“It is not yet revealed what we will be.” There is more to come. Believers’ future glory has not yet been fully revealed.

“But we know that when he is revealed, we will be like him, for we will see him just as he is.” When Christ returns, believers will be transformed to be like Him. Seeing Christ in His glory will complete their transformation.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses describe the wonder of adoption. Believers were once separated from God, but now they are His children, loved and welcomed into His family. Paul writes that believers have received “*the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, 'Abba! Father!'*” (*Romans 8:15*). *John 1:12* says that to all who received Jesus, He gave the right to become children of God.

The phrase “now we are children of God” gives believers a secure identity. Their status does not depend on their feelings, achievements, or others’ opinions. It rests on God’s love.

The promise “we will be like him” is the ultimate hope of believers. They are being transformed now (*2 Corinthians 3:18*), but on the day of Christ’s return, the transformation will be complete. Paul says the same: Christ will transform their lowly bodies to be like His glorious body (*Philippians 3:21*). They will see Him face to face (*1 Corinthians 13:12*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers who struggle with feelings of worthlessness or rejection can rest in this truth: they are God’s children, deeply loved. Their identity is secure.

When believers feel misunderstood or rejected by the world, they can remember that the world also did not recognize Jesus. Being misunderstood is not a sign that they do not belong to God.

Finally, the hope of seeing Christ and becoming like Him can shape daily life. It gives believers a reason to pursue purity and to endure hardship, knowing that glory awaits.

### *1 John 3:8–9* — The Son Came to Destroy the Works of the Devil

> *“He who sins is of the devil, for the devil has been sinning from the beginning. To this end the Son of God was revealed: that he might destroy the works of the devil. Whoever is born of God doesn’t commit sin, because his seed remains in him, and he can’t sin, because he is born of God.”*
>
> — *1 John 3:8–9* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“He who sins is of the devil, for the devil has been sinning from the beginning.” In context, “he who sins” refers to someone who lives in a settled pattern of sin. Such a life reflects the devil’s character, since he has been sinning from the beginning.

“To this end the Son of God was revealed: that he might destroy the works of the devil.” Jesus came to undo everything the devil has done: sin, deception, bondage, and death.

Verse 9: “Whoever is born of God doesn’t commit sin, because his seed remains in him, and he can’t sin, because he is born of God.” Those born of God do not live in ongoing, habitual sin. God’s “seed,” His life or His word or His Spirit planted within them, remains in them and changes them. They “can’t sin” in the sense that they cannot continue comfortably in a life of sin, because God’s nature within them resists it.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses must be read alongside *1 John 1:8–10*, where John says that anyone who claims to be without sin deceives themselves, and *2:1*, where he provides for believers who do sin. John is not teaching that believers become sinless in this life. That would contradict his earlier statements.

Most interpreters understand John to be describing the direction and pattern of a believer’s life. The Greek verbs in verses 6 and 9 are in the present tense, which often indicates ongoing, habitual action. Believers still sin, but they do not live in settled, unrepentant sin. When they sin, they confess and turn back. Their new nature, God’s seed within them, will not allow them to be comfortable in sin.

Other interpreters suggest that John is describing the ideal of the new nature, which does not sin, or that he is countering false teachers who claimed sin did not matter. All agree that genuine faith produces a life that is increasingly free from sin’s dominion.

The statement that the Son of God was revealed “*that he might destroy the works of the devil*” (*v. 8*) is a powerful summary of His mission. Through His life, death, and resurrection, Jesus defeated the devil and set people free (*Hebrews 2:14–15*; *Colossians 2:15*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can take comfort that struggling with sin does not mean they are not God’s children. The very fact that sin troubles them shows God’s seed is at work in them.

At the same time, these verses call believers not to make peace with sin. Patterns of sin that a believer refuses to confront are serious. Believers can bring those patterns to God, confess them, seek help from others, and rely on the Spirit’s power to change.

Finally, believers can rejoice that Jesus came to destroy the devil’s works. No sin, addiction, or bondage is too strong for Him.

### *1 John 3:16–18* — Love in Deed and Truth

> *“By this we know love, because he laid down his life for us. And we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers. But whoever has the world’s goods and sees his brother in need, then closes his heart of compassion against him, how does God’s love remain in him? My little children, let’s not love in word only, or with the tongue only, but in deed and truth.”*
>
> — *1 John 3:16–18* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“By this we know love, because he laid down his life for us.” What is love? John points to the cross. Jesus gave His life for us. That is the definition and model of love.

“And we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers.” Because Christ loved this way, believers should love one another the same way, being willing to give their lives for one another.

Verse 17 makes it practical: “But whoever has the world’s goods and sees his brother in need, then closes his heart of compassion against him, how does God’s love remain in him?” Most believers will not be asked to die for others. But they will often see fellow believers in need. If they have resources and refuse to help, how can they claim that God’s love is in them?

Verse 18: “My little children, let’s not love in word only, or with the tongue only, but in deed and truth.” Love is not just words or feelings. It is shown in action and in sincerity.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This passage moves from the greatest act of love to the most ordinary. Christ’s death on the cross is the ultimate demonstration of love. But love is also shown in daily, practical ways: sharing food, money, time, and care with those in need.

Interestingly, the reference “*1 John 3:16*“ parallels “*John 3:16*.” Both speak of God’s love shown in giving. *John 3:16* shows God’s love for the world; *1 John 3:16* shows how believers should love one another in response.

James makes a similar point: if someone sees a brother or sister in need and says only “Go in peace,” without helping, what good is that? Faith without works is dead (*James 2:15–17*). Love that does not act is not genuine love.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can look for practical ways to love others: providing a meal for someone who is struggling, helping with bills, offering a ride, spending time with someone who is lonely, or giving to those in need.

This passage also challenges believers to examine whether their love is only in words. It is easy to say “I’ll pray for you” or “Let me know if you need anything.” Genuine love takes initiative and acts.

Finally, believers can remember Christ’s example. His love was costly. Following Him means being willing to sacrifice for others, whether time, money, comfort, or convenience.

### *1 John 3:19–20* — God Is Greater Than Our Heart

> *“And by this we know that we are of the truth and persuade our hearts before him, because if our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart, and knows all things.”*
>
> — *1 John 3:19–20* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“And by this we know that we are of the truth and persuade our hearts before him.” “By this” refers to loving in deed and truth (v18). When believers see genuine love in their lives, they gain assurance that they belong to the truth. This assurance can quiet their hearts before God.

Verse 20: “because if our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart, and knows all things.” Sometimes believers’ consciences accuse them. They feel guilty, unworthy, or uncertain of their standing with God. John reassures them: God is greater than their heart. He knows everything, including their genuine faith, their love, and their desire to please Him. His knowledge is more complete and more merciful than their self-condemnation.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses are a gift to sensitive consciences. Some believers struggle with constant self-condemnation, even after confessing their sins. They wonder whether they are truly saved. John points them away from their feelings to God’s greater knowledge.

“God is greater than our heart” can be understood in two ways. It may mean God is more merciful than our self-condemning hearts, seeing the genuine faith and love that we overlook. Or it may mean God knows everything, so nothing can be hidden from Him. Both are true and both comfort. God sees the whole picture, and He is merciful.

Peter’s restoration illustrates this. After denying Jesus, Peter was asked three times, “Do you love me?” Finally Peter said, “*Lord, you know everything. You know that I have affection for you*” (*John 21:17*). Peter appealed to Jesus’ complete knowledge. God knows the heart better than we know ourselves.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers who struggle with guilt or doubt about their salvation can bring their accusing hearts to God. They can confess any sin and then rest in His forgiveness, trusting that He is greater than their feelings.

Believers can also look for evidence of God’s work in their lives, such as love for others, desire to obey, and faith in Christ, which can bring assurance.

For those who struggle with severe and persistent guilt, scrupulosity, or anxiety, help from a wise pastor or counselor can be valuable. God’s grace is greater than any accusing voice.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

First *John 3* begins with wonder. The Father has lavished His love on believers, calling them His children, and that is what they truly are. Though the world does not recognize them, their identity is secure. And when Christ appears, they will be like Him, for they will see Him as He is. This hope motivates them to pursue purity now.

God’s children resemble their Father. They do not live in settled, unrepentant sin, because God’s seed remains in them. Christ came to destroy the works of the devil, and His power is at work in them. Believers still struggle and still need to confess their sins, but the direction of their lives is toward righteousness.

God’s children also love one another. Hatred is murder in the heart, but love is evidence of passing from death to life. True love is defined by Christ, who laid down His life for us. Believers are called to love the same way, not only in words but in practical actions, sharing with those in need.

Finally, the chapter offers assurance to troubled consciences. When believers’ hearts condemn them, God is greater than their hearts and knows everything. Those who believe in Jesus and love one another can rest in His mercy, with confidence in prayer and the assurance of His Spirit living within them.

## Chapter Prayer

Father, thank You for the great love You have given me, that I should be called Your child, and that I truly am. When the world does not understand me, remind me that I belong to You. Thank You for the hope that when Christ appears, I will be like Him and see Him as He is. Help me to purify myself as He is pure. Thank You, Lord Jesus, that You came to destroy the works of the devil. Free me from every pattern of sin, and let Your life grow in me. Teach me to love as You loved, laying down my life for others. Give me eyes to see those in need and a heart to act, loving not only in words but in deeds and truth. When my heart condemns me, remind me that You are greater than my heart and know all things. Help me to believe in the name of Your Son and to love others, as You have commanded. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

1 John · Chapter 4 of 5

# 1 John — Chapter 4

Chapter Theme: God Is Love

[Read 1 John 4 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/1JN04.htm)

Main Teaching

John warns believers not to believe every spirit but to test the spirits, because many false prophets have gone out into the world. Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God, while every spirit that denies this is the spirit of antichrist. Believers belong to God and have overcome the false prophets, because the One who is in them is greater than the one who is in the world. Then John turns to love: love comes from God, and everyone who loves has been born of God and knows God, while whoever does not love does not know God, because God is love. God showed His love by sending His one and only Son into the world so that we might live through Him; this is love, not that we loved God, but that He loved us and sent His Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins. Since God loved us so much, we ought to love one another. No one has seen God, but when we love one another, God lives in us and His love is made complete in us, and we know this by the Spirit He has given. Whoever lives in love lives in God, and love made complete gives confidence on the day of judgment. There is no fear in love; perfect love drives out fear. We love because He first loved us. Anyone who claims to love God but hates a brother or sister is a liar, for whoever loves God must also love their brother and sister.

## Chapter Background and Story

First *John 4* contains some of the most beautiful words ever written about love. It also contains a sober warning about spiritual deception. The two belong together. The false teachers had distorted the truth about Jesus and had shown no love for the believers. John responds by teaching believers how to recognize false spirits and by describing the true nature of God’s love.

In the ancient world, many people claimed to speak by the inspiration of spirits. Prophets, teachers, and religious leaders often claimed special spiritual insight. Some of the false teachers in John’s community may have claimed that the Spirit gave them new revelations about Jesus. John tells believers not to accept every spiritual claim but to test it by its teaching about Christ.

The second half of the chapter is a meditation on love. Its central statement, “God is love,” appears twice (vv8, 16). John shows that God’s love was revealed most clearly when He sent His Son, that this love should flow through believers to one another, and that love casts out fear.

### Test the Spirits (*4:1–6*)

The call to test the spirits and the victory of believers over false prophets are studied below. “*They are of the world. Therefore they speak of the world, and the world hears them*” (*v. 5*). False teachers speak from the world’s perspective, and so the world listens to them. Their message is popular because it matches what people already want to hear.

“*We are of God. He who knows God listens to us. He who is not of God doesn’t listen to us. By this we know the spirit of truth, and the spirit of error*” (*v. 6*). “We” here refers to the apostles, who bore witness to Christ. Those who belong to God receive the apostolic teaching. This becomes another test: does a teaching agree with the apostles’ message, preserved in the New Testament?

### God Is Love (*4:7–12*)

“*Beloved, let’s love one another, for love is of God; and everyone who loves has been born of God and knows God*” (*v. 7*). Love comes from God. Those who truly love, with the self-giving love God shows, reveal that they have been born of God.

“*He who doesn’t love doesn’t know God, for God is love*” (*v. 8*). This is one of the most profound statements in Scripture. God does not merely love; He is love. Love is His very nature. Everything He does flows from love, including His justice and His holiness. Because God is love, those who know Him will love. A person who does not love has not truly come to know Him. The way God revealed His love is studied below.

“*Beloved, if God loved us in this way, we also ought to love one another*” (*v. 11*). God’s love for us is both the model and the motive for our love for one another.

“*No one has seen God at any time. If we love one another, God remains in us, and his love has been perfected in us*” (*v. 12*). God is invisible, but His love becomes visible when believers love one another. Love among believers is how the invisible God is made known in the world. Jesus said that all people would know His disciples by their love for one another (*John 13:35*).

### Living in Love (*4:13–17*)

“*By this we know that we remain in him and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit*” (*v. 13*). The Holy Spirit within believers assures them that they belong to God.

“*We have seen and testify that the Father has sent the Son as the Savior of the world*” (*v. 14*). John again appeals to eyewitness testimony. Jesus is “the Savior of the world,” a title the Samaritans gave Him (*John 4:42*) and one that Roman emperors claimed for themselves.

“*Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God remains in him, and he in God*” (*v. 15*). Right belief about Jesus is a mark of genuine relationship with God.

“*We know and have believed the love which God has for us. God is love, and he who remains in love remains in God, and God remains in him*” (*v. 16*). Believers know God’s love by experience and trust it by faith. To live in love is to live in God.

“*In this, love has been made perfect among us, that we may have boldness in the day of judgment, because as he is, even so we are in this world*” (*v. 17*). When God’s love reaches its goal in believers, they can face the day of judgment with confidence rather than fear. “As he is, even so we are” may mean that believers, united with Christ, share His standing before the Father, or that they reflect His love in the world.

### Love Casts Out Fear (*4:18–21*)

The power of love over fear is studied below. “*If a man says, “I love God,” and hates his brother, he is a liar; for he who doesn’t love his brother whom he has seen, how can he love God whom he has not seen?*” (*v. 20*) “*This commandment we have from him, that he who loves God should also love his brother*” (*v. 21*). Love for God and love for others cannot be separated. It is easy to claim love for an invisible God, but that love is tested by how one treats visible people. Jesus joined the two great commandments, love for God and love for neighbor (*Mark 12:29–31*).

## Important Verses Explained

### *1 John 4:1–3* — Test the Spirits

> *“Beloved, don’t believe every spirit, but test the spirits, whether they are of God, because many false prophets have gone out into the world. By this you know the Spirit of God: every spirit who confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is of God, and every spirit who doesn’t confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is not of God; and this is the spirit of the Antichrist, of whom you have heard that it comes. Now it is in the world already.”*
>
> — *1 John 4:1–3* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“Beloved, don’t believe every spirit, but test the spirits, whether they are of God.” “Spirit” here refers to the spiritual source behind a teacher or prophet. Not every claim of spiritual inspiration comes from God. Believers are to test such claims.

“Because many false prophets have gone out into the world.” False prophets were already active, as Jesus had warned (*Matthew 24:11*, 24).

Verse 2: “By this you know the Spirit of God: every spirit who confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is of God.” The key test is what a teacher says about Jesus. The true Spirit leads people to confess that Jesus Christ came in a real human body. This truth was being denied by the false teachers, who apparently taught that the divine Christ only appeared to be human or was separate from the man Jesus.

Verse 3: “and every spirit who doesn’t confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is not of God; and this is the spirit of the Antichrist, of whom you have heard that it comes. Now it is in the world already.” Denying the incarnation is the mark of the spirit of antichrist. This spirit was already at work in John’s day.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This passage teaches that spiritual experiences and claims must be tested. Paul gave similar instructions: “*Test all things, and hold firmly that which is good*” (*1 Thessalonians 5:21*). Not every voice that claims to speak for God actually does.

The test John gives centers on Jesus. The incarnation, God becoming truly human in Jesus Christ, is at the heart of the gospel. If Jesus did not truly become human, He could not truly die for human sins or be raised as the firstfruits of a new humanity. Any teaching that undermines the truth about Jesus’ identity is not from God.

This test applies broadly. Believers can evaluate teachings, spiritual movements, and claims of revelation by asking: What does this say about Jesus? Does it affirm that He is fully God and fully human, crucified and risen? Does it exalt Him or diminish Him? Does it agree with the apostolic witness in Scripture?

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers encounter many spiritual voices today: teachers, books, podcasts, social media influencers, and movements claiming spiritual insight. Not all of them are from God. Believers can test what they hear by Scripture, especially by what it teaches about Jesus.

Testing the spirits is not about being suspicious of everything. It is about being wise and discerning, holding fast to what is true and rejecting what is false.

Believers can also be humble in this process, seeking the counsel of mature believers and the wisdom of the wider church when evaluating new teachings.

### *1 John 4:4* — Greater Is He Who Is in You

> *“You are of God, little children, and have overcome them, because greater is he who is in you than he who is in the world.”*
>
> — *1 John 4:4* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“You are of God, little children.” Believers belong to God. They are His children.

“And have overcome them.” Believers have overcome the false prophets. They did not fall for the false teaching. They remained faithful to the truth.

“Because greater is he who is in you than he who is in the world.” The reason for their victory is not their own strength. It is because God, who lives in them by His Spirit, is greater than the evil one, “he who is in the world,” who inspires the false prophets.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse is one of the great promises of Scripture. Believers may feel weak and vulnerable in the face of spiritual opposition, deception, temptation, and hostility. But they are not alone. God Himself dwells in them, and He is infinitely greater than any spiritual power opposed to Him.

The victory described here is already won. Believers “have overcome.” This is because Christ has already defeated the devil (*Colossians 2:15*; *Hebrews 2:14*). Believers share in His victory. Jesus said, “*Cheer up! I have overcome the world*” (*John 16:33*).

This does not mean believers will never face struggles or that they can be careless. But it does mean they can face spiritual opposition with confidence rather than fear. The One in them is greater.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

When believers face temptation, deception, or spiritual attack, they can remember that God in them is greater than any opposing force. They do not need to fear.

This verse also brings comfort to believers who feel overwhelmed by the evil in the world. Evil is real, but it is not supreme. God is greater.

Finally, believers can rely on God’s strength rather than their own. Their victory comes from Him.

### *1 John 4:9–10* — This Is Love

> *“By this God’s love was revealed in us, that God has sent his only born Son into the world that we might live through him. In this is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins.”*
>
> — *1 John 4:9–10* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“By this God’s love was revealed in us, that God has sent his only born Son into the world that we might live through him.” God’s love was made visible in a specific act: He sent His only Son into the world. The purpose was that we might “live through him,” receiving eternal life through Jesus.

Verse 10: “In this is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us.” True love is defined not by human love for God but by God’s love for humanity. God took the initiative. He loved us first, even when we did not love Him.

“And sent his Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins.” The greatest expression of God’s love is the cross, where Jesus became the sacrifice that dealt with our sins.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses echo *John 3:16*: “*For God so loved the world, that he gave his only born Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life.*” (*John 3:16*) God’s love is not abstract or sentimental. It is shown in a costly, concrete act: the gift of His Son.

The phrase “not that we loved God” is humbling. Human love for God is always a response. God’s love came first, and it came to people who were not seeking Him. Paul writes that “*while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us*” (*Romans 5:8*).

The connection between love and atonement is significant. Some people think of God’s love and His justice as opposites. But the cross shows them united. God’s love provided the sacrifice that satisfied His justice. Love is not ignoring sin; love is dealing with sin at great cost.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can find the measure of God’s love for them at the cross. When they doubt that God loves them, they can look at what He gave.

This truth also shapes how believers love others. True love is self-giving, initiating, and costly. It does not wait for others to love first. It reaches out, even to those who do not deserve it.

Finally, believers can rest in the fact that their relationship with God is grounded in His love, not theirs. Their love for Him may waver, but His love for them is steadfast.

### *1 John 4:18–19* — Perfect Love Casts Out Fear

> *“There is no fear in love; but perfect love casts out fear, because fear has punishment. He who fears is not made perfect in love. We love him, because he first loved us.”*
>
> — *1 John 4:18–19* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

“There is no fear in love.” Love and fear are opposites in this context. The fear John has in mind is the fear of punishment, the fear of standing before God in judgment (v17).

“But perfect love casts out fear.” “Perfect” means complete, mature, fully developed. When God’s love reaches its goal in a believer’s life, it drives out the dread of punishment. Those who know they are fully loved by God need not be afraid of Him.

“Because fear has punishment.” Fear is connected with the expectation of punishment. It belongs to those who expect condemnation.

“He who fears is not made perfect in love.” Someone still gripped by the fear of punishment has not yet fully grasped or experienced God’s love.

Verse 19: “We love him, because he first loved us.” Some ancient manuscripts lack the word “him,” which makes the statement even broader. All human love, for God and for others, is a response to God’s prior love.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses describe the freedom that God’s love brings. Many people relate to God out of fear, afraid of His anger, afraid of failing, afraid of rejection. John says that God’s love removes that kind of fear. *Romans 8:15* says believers did not receive a spirit of slavery to fear but the Spirit of adoption. *Romans 8:1* says there is no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus.

This does not remove the fear of the Lord in the sense of reverence and awe (*Proverbs 9:10*; *Hebrews 12:28*). Believers still honor God as holy and majestic. What is removed is the terror of punishment, because Christ has borne the punishment.

“We love him, because he first loved us” is a simple but profound summary of the Christian life. Believers do not generate love by their own efforts. They receive God’s love and then reflect it. The more they understand how much God loves them, the more they are able to love.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers who relate to God mainly out of fear can bring that fear to Him and ask Him to fill them with the assurance of His love. Meditating on passages about God’s love, such as this one, *John 3:16*, and *Romans 8:31–39*, can help.

As believers grow in confidence of God’s love, they can approach Him freely in prayer, confess their sins without dread, and live without the constant fear of rejection.

Finally, believers can let God’s love flow through them to others. Those who know they are deeply loved are free to love others generously, without fear.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

First *John 4* begins with a call to discernment. Not every spiritual voice is from God. Believers are to test the spirits by what they teach about Jesus: Do they confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh? Do they agree with the apostolic witness? The spirit of antichrist is already at work in the world, but believers have overcome it, because the One who is in them is greater than the one who is in the world.

The heart of the chapter is the declaration that God is love. His love was revealed when He sent His only Son into the world, that we might live through Him, and gave Him as the atoning sacrifice for our sins. This is what love is: not that we loved God, but that He loved us first. Because God loved us this way, we ought to love one another. When we do, the invisible God becomes visible in His people.

Love also brings confidence. Those who live in God’s love can face the day of judgment without fear, because perfect love drives out fear. Believers can approach God not with dread, but with the trust of children who know they are loved.

Finally, the chapter insists that love for God and love for others cannot be separated. Anyone who claims to love God but hates a brother or sister is a liar. Believers love because God first loved them, and they show that love in how they treat the people around them.

## Chapter Prayer

Father, give me discernment to test every spirit and to hold fast to the truth that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh. Thank You that the One who is in me is greater than the one who is in the world. Thank You that You are love, and that You showed Your love by sending Your only Son into the world so that I might live through Him. Thank You that You loved me first, and that Jesus is the atoning sacrifice for my sins. Fill me with Your love so that I may love others as You have loved me. Let Your love be made complete in me, and cast out every fear of punishment. Help me to approach You with confidence as Your beloved child. Keep me from claiming to love You while failing to love my brothers and sisters. I love because You first loved me. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

1 John · Chapter 5 of 5

# 1 John — Chapter 5

Chapter Theme: Faith That Overcomes and the Assurance of Eternal Life

[Read 1 John 5 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/1JN05.htm)

Main Teaching

John ties together the great threads of his letter: faith, love, and obedience. Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God, and everyone who loves the Father loves His children. Loving God means keeping His commandments, and His commandments are not burdensome, because everyone born of God overcomes the world through faith. Jesus came by water and blood, and the Spirit, the water, and the blood all testify to Him. God Himself has given testimony about His Son: He has given us eternal life, and this life is in His Son. Whoever has the Son has life. John wrote so that believers may know they have eternal life. He assures them that God hears prayers made according to His will, encourages them to pray for a brother or sister who sins, and closes with three great certainties: those born of God are kept from the evil one, believers belong to God, and the Son of God has come so that we may know the true God. His final word is a tender warning: keep yourselves from idols.

## Chapter Background and Story

The last chapter of 1 John gathers up everything the letter has said. Throughout, John has given believers tests by which they can know they truly belong to God: right belief about Jesus, obedience to God’s commands, and love for one another. Here he shows that these three are not separate. Faith in Jesus brings new birth; new birth produces love for God’s children; love for God shows itself in obedience. All of it is the work of God in those who trust His Son.

The false teachers who had left the community had unsettled the believers who remained. They may have claimed a superior knowledge of God and implied that ordinary believers lacked something essential. John writes to give the faithful firm ground under their feet. His purpose is stated plainly in verse 13: he wants them to know that they have eternal life.

The chapter also touches on two passages that have prompted much discussion over the centuries: the testimony of “water and blood” (vv6–8) and the “sin leading to death” (vv16–17). John’s original readers likely understood these references quickly; modern readers do well to consider the main interpretations with humility.

### Faith, Love, and Obedience Together (*5:1–5*)

“*Whoever believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God. Whoever loves the Father also loves the child who is born of him*” (*v. 1*). Faith in Jesus as the Christ is the evidence of new birth. And new birth places a person in God’s family. Just as a child who loves a parent will also care for the parent’s other children, so the one who loves God the Father will love His other children.

“*By this we know that we love the children of God, when we love God and keep his commandments*” (*v. 2*). Earlier John said that love for one another proves love for God (*4:20*). Now he says that love for God and obedience to His commands prove genuine love for God’s children. The two run in both directions. True love for people is not sentimental approval of whatever they do; it is shaped by God’s own will. The victory of faith over the world is studied below.

### The Testimony About the Son (*5:6–12*)

“*This is he who came by water and blood, Jesus Christ; not with the water only, but with the water and the blood. It is the Spirit who testifies, because the Spirit is the truth*” (*v. 6*). This verse has been understood in several ways. The most widely held view is that “water” refers to Jesus’ baptism, where His public ministry began and the Father declared Him to be His Son, and “blood” refers to His death on the cross. John insists that Jesus Christ came “not with the water only, but with the water and the blood.” This may answer a false teaching, associated in early church history with a teacher named Cerinthus, that the divine Christ came upon the man Jesus at His baptism but left Him before His crucifixion, so that only a human being died. John rejects this firmly: the One who was baptized is the same One who died, Jesus Christ the Son of God.

Others connect the water and blood with the water and blood that flowed from Jesus’ side when He was pierced on the cross (*John 19:34*), a sign that He truly died. Still others see a reference to baptism and the Lord’s Supper in the church’s life. These views are not entirely exclusive, but the first fits best with John’s emphasis that Jesus Christ came in the flesh and truly died.

“*For there are three who testify:*” (*v. 7*) “*the Spirit, the water, and the blood; and the three agree as one*” (*v. 8*). In Jewish law, a matter was established by two or three witnesses (*Deuteronomy 19:15*). The baptism, the cross, and the ongoing witness of the Holy Spirit together confirm who Jesus is.

Some older English translations, such as the King James Version, include additional words in verses 7–8 that speak of the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit bearing witness in heaven. These words are not found in the early Greek manuscripts and appear to have been added much later, which is why the World English Bible and most modern translations do not include them. The doctrine of the Trinity does not rest on this addition; it is taught throughout the New Testament (for example, *Matthew 28:19*; *2 Corinthians 13:14*).

“*If we receive the witness of men, the witness of God is greater; for this is God’s testimony which he has testified concerning his Son*” (*v. 9*). People accept human testimony every day, in courts, in business, and in ordinary life. How much more should they accept the testimony of God Himself?

“*He who believes in the Son of God has the testimony in himself. He who doesn’t believe God has made him a liar, because he has not believed in the testimony that God has given concerning his Son*” (*v. 10*). The believer carries God’s testimony within, through the inner witness of the Spirit. To reject that testimony is to treat God as untrustworthy. The content of God’s testimony is studied below.

### Confidence in Prayer (*5:13–17*)

The assurance of eternal life and confidence in prayer are studied below. “*If anyone sees his brother sinning a sin not leading to death, he shall ask, and God will give him life for those who sin not leading to death. There is sin leading to death. I don’t say that he should make a request concerning this*” (*v. 16*). “*All unrighteousness is sin, and there is sin not leading to death*” (*v. 17*).

These verses are among the most debated in John’s letters. John encourages believers to pray for a fellow believer caught in sin, and he promises that God will give that person life. But he also mentions a “sin leading to death,” and he does not command prayer about it.

Interpreters have understood this in several ways. Many see the “sin leading to death” in light of the letter’s own context: the deliberate, settled rejection of Jesus Christ shown by the false teachers who denied that Jesus is the Christ come in the flesh and walked away from the fellowship (*2:19*, 22). Such persistent rejection of the only source of life leads to spiritual death. Others think John means sin that results in physical death as a divine judgment, as when some believers in Corinth became sick and died (*1 Corinthians 11:30*) or in the account of Ananias and Sapphira (*Acts 5:1–11*). Still others connect it with Jesus’ warning about blasphemy against the Holy Spirit (*Mark 3:28–29*).

Several things are clear. John does not give believers a list for deciding who is beyond hope, and he does not forbid prayer for anyone; he simply says he is not commanding it in that case. His main point is positive: believers should pray for one another when they see sin. The context also reassures. A person who is troubled by their sin and wants to turn to God shows that they have not hardened their heart against Him. Every sin is serious, “all unrighteousness is sin,” but not every sin places a person beyond the reach of God’s mercy.

### Three Certainties and a Final Warning (*5:18–21*)

“*We know that whoever is born of God doesn’t sin, but he who was born of God keeps himself, and the evil one doesn’t touch him*” (*v. 18*). As in chapter 3, John means that the one born of God does not go on living in a settled pattern of sin. The phrase “he who was born of God keeps himself” is read in two ways. Many interpreters understand “he who was born of God” as a reference to Jesus, the eternal Son, who keeps the believer safe; a number of ancient manuscripts read “keeps him” rather than “keeps himself,” which supports this reading. Others take it as the believer, who guards their own life. Either way, the evil one cannot lay hold of those who belong to God.

“*We know that we are of God, and the whole world lies in the power of the evil one*” (*v. 19*). John draws a clear line. Believers belong to God, while the world system that rejects God remains under the sway of the evil one. This is not a reason for pride or fear, but for clear thinking about where true life is found.

“*We know that the Son of God has come and has given us an understanding, that we know him who is true; and we are in him who is true, in his Son Jesus Christ. This is the true God and eternal life*” (*v. 20*). Against the false teachers who claimed special knowledge, John declares that true understanding comes from the Son of God. Believers know the true God and live in union with Him through Jesus Christ. The final sentence, “This is the true God and eternal life,” is understood by many interpreters as a direct statement that Jesus Christ is the true God, matching the opening of John’s Gospel (*John 1:1*). Others read it as referring to the Father. Both readings affirm that eternal life is found only in knowing the true God through His Son.

“*Little children, keep yourselves from idols*” (*v. 21*). The letter ends abruptly with a tender but serious warning. In a city like Ephesus, filled with temples, idols were everywhere. But John likely also means any false image of God, including the distorted Jesus of the false teachers. An idol is anything that takes the place of the true God. Having shown believers the true God in Jesus Christ, John urges them not to turn aside to any substitute.

## Important Verses Explained

### *1 John 5:3–5* — The Faith That Overcomes the World

> *“For this is loving God, that we keep his commandments. His commandments are not grievous. For whatever is born of God overcomes the world. This is the victory that has overcome the world: your faith. Who is he who overcomes the world, but he who believes that Jesus is the Son of God?”*
>
> — *1 John 5:3–5* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

John begins by defining love for God in practical terms: “For this is loving God, that we keep his commandments.” Love for God is not only a feeling or a profession; it shows itself in a life that follows His ways. Jesus said the same thing: “*If you love me, keep my commandments*” (*John 14:15*).

Then John adds an encouraging word: “His commandments are not grievous.” God’s commands are not crushing burdens. This does not mean obedience is always easy, but that God’s commands are good, wise, and given in love. Jesus said, “*For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light*” (*Matthew 11:30*).

Why are God’s commands not burdensome? Verse 4 explains: “For whatever is born of God overcomes the world.” The new birth gives believers a new nature and a new power. They are not trying to obey God in their own strength. God’s life in them enables them to live for Him.

John then names the means of this victory: “This is the victory that has overcome the world: your faith.” Faith in Jesus is the victory. It is not a vague optimism, but trust in a specific Person. Verse 5 makes this explicit: the one who overcomes the world is the one who “believes that Jesus is the Son of God.”

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

In John’s writings, “the world” often means human society organized in rebellion against God, with its values, pressures, and lies (*2:15–17*). The world tempts believers to love what is passing away, to fear what others think, and to doubt God’s truth. Overcoming the world means not being conquered by these pressures.

This victory is rooted in Christ’s own victory. On the night before His death, Jesus told His disciples, “*In the world you have trouble; but cheer up! I have overcome the world*” (*John 16:33*). Believers overcome because they are joined by faith to the One who has already overcome. Notice that John says the victory “has overcome,” in the past tense. The decisive battle has already been won at the cross and the empty tomb.

This does not mean believers never struggle or fail. It means the world no longer has final authority over them. Faith keeps returning them to Christ, and in Him they share His victory. Each time a believer chooses trust over fear, truth over deception, and obedience over compromise, that victory is displayed again.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers face many pressures that can feel overwhelming: cultural expectations, temptations, discouragement, and the constant noise of voices that push God aside. This passage reminds them that they do not face these pressures alone or without power. Through faith in Jesus, they already share in His victory.

When obedience to God feels heavy, believers can remember that His commands are not meant to crush them but to lead them into life. God does not ask His children to do what He will not also give them strength to do.

The key to overcoming is not trying harder in one’s own strength, but trusting Jesus more deeply. Faith grows as believers spend time with God in His Word, in prayer, and in fellowship with other believers who remind them of who Jesus is.

### *1 John 5:11–13* — That You May Know You Have Eternal Life

> *“The testimony is this: that God gave to us eternal life, and this life is in his Son. He who has the Son has the life. He who doesn’t have God’s Son doesn’t have the life. These things I have written to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life, and that you may continue to believe in the name of the Son of God.”*
>
> — *1 John 5:11–13* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After speaking of God’s testimony about His Son, John tells us what that testimony says: “that God gave to us eternal life, and this life is in his Son.” Eternal life is a gift from God. It is not earned. And it is found in only one place: in Jesus.

Verse 12 states the consequence simply: “He who has the Son has the life. He who doesn’t have God’s Son doesn’t have the life.” Eternal life is not a separate thing that can be possessed apart from Jesus. To have Jesus, through faith, is to have life. To be without Him is to be without life.

Verse 13 gives John’s purpose in writing the whole letter: “These things I have written to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life.” John wants believers to have assurance. He does not want them to live in constant uncertainty about their standing with God.

John’s Gospel was written so that people might believe and have life (*John 20:31*). His letter was written so that those who already believe might know they have that life.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

In Scripture, eternal life is not only life that lasts forever. It is a quality of life: the life of God Himself, shared with His people. Jesus defined it in His prayer: “*This is eternal life, that they should know you, the only true God, and him whom you sent, Jesus Christ*” (*John 17:3*). Eternal life begins now, in a living relationship with God, and continues forever.

Assurance is grounded first in God’s own testimony. Believers do not rest their confidence on their feelings, which change, or on their performance, which is imperfect. They rest it on what God has said about His Son. If God has promised life to all who have the Son, then those who trust the Son can know they have life.

The tests John has given throughout the letter, believing the truth about Jesus, obeying God’s commands, and loving fellow believers, are not hurdles to earn life. They are signs that confirm life is present. A person who trusts Jesus, wants to obey Him, and loves His people can take comfort that God’s life is at work in them.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Many sincere believers struggle with doubts about whether they are truly saved. This passage offers a solid foundation. Assurance does not depend on having a perfect life or never feeling doubt. It depends on whether a person has the Son, trusting in Jesus Christ as Savior and Lord.

When doubts arise, believers can return to God’s promise rather than looking only inward. They can remind themselves that God has promised life to whoever has the Son, that they have put their trust in His Son, and that they can therefore rest in His word.

At the same time, this passage gives a loving and sober invitation to anyone who does not yet have the Son. Life is offered freely in Jesus, and no one is beyond the reach of this gift.

### *1 John 5:14–15* — Confidence When We Pray

> *“This is the boldness which we have toward him, that if we ask anything according to his will, he listens to us. And if we know that he listens to us, whatever we ask, we know that we have the petitions which we have asked of him.”*
>
> — *1 John 5:14–15* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

John moves from assurance of eternal life to confidence in prayer: “This is the boldness which we have toward him, that if we ask anything according to his will, he listens to us.” The word “boldness” means freedom and confidence in speaking. Believers can come to God openly, without fear, as children come to a loving Father.

The promise has an important qualification: “according to his will.” Prayer is not a way of getting God to do whatever we want. It is bringing our requests into line with what God desires. When we ask according to His will, He hears us.

Verse 15 adds: “And if we know that he listens to us, whatever we ask, we know that we have the petitions which we have asked of him.” To be heard by God, in the sense John means, is to have the request granted. If God hears a prayer that agrees with His will, the answer is certain, even if it does not come immediately or in the form we expected.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This promise is not a blank check. It is an invitation into partnership with God. Jesus taught His disciples to pray, “*Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven*” (*Matthew 6:10*). He Himself prayed in Gethsemane, “*However, not what I desire, but what you desire*” (*Mark 14:36*). True prayer seeks God’s will above our own.

How do believers know God’s will? Much of it is revealed in Scripture: God wills that believers grow in holiness (*1 Thessalonians 4:3*), that they be filled with the Spirit, that the gospel spread, that His people love one another. When believers pray for these things, they can pray with full confidence. In matters Scripture does not directly address, believers can bring their requests honestly and trust God to answer in the way that is truly best.

The Holy Spirit also helps believers in prayer. Paul writes that the Spirit intercedes for believers according to the will of God (*Romans 8:26–27*). Prayer is not a lonely effort to guess what God wants; it is a relationship in which God Himself helps His children to pray.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Many people pray hesitantly, unsure whether God is listening. This passage assures believers that God does hear them. They can approach Him with boldness, not because they deserve to be heard, but because they are His children through Jesus.

Praying according to God’s will can shape what believers pray for. As they grow in knowing Scripture, their prayers increasingly reflect God’s priorities: growth in Christlikeness, the good of others, the spread of the gospel, and the coming of His kingdom.

When an answer seems delayed or different from what was hoped, believers can trust that God has heard and that His will is good. Unanswered prayer, from our perspective, is often an answer we do not yet understand.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

First *John 5* brings the whole letter to a confident and hopeful close. It shows that faith, love, and obedience belong together. Those who believe that Jesus is the Christ have been born of God; those born of God love God’s children; and love for God shows itself in keeping His commandments. These commands are not burdensome, because God’s own life in His children gives them strength to obey.

The chapter calls believers to live as overcomers. The world presses hard with its values, temptations, and fears, but faith in Jesus is the victory that overcomes it. Believers are not left to fight in their own strength. They share in the victory Christ has already won.

John also wants believers to rest in assurance. God has testified about His Son, and His testimony is that eternal life is in Jesus. Whoever has the Son has life. Believers do not need to live in anxious uncertainty. They can know that they have eternal life, because God’s word is true.

This assurance leads naturally to bold, trusting prayer. Believers can bring their requests to God, knowing that He listens when they pray according to His will. They can also pray for fellow believers who stumble, asking God to restore them, rather than standing at a distance in judgment.

Finally, John reminds believers to guard their hearts. Having come to know the true God through His Son, they are to keep themselves from every idol, anything that would take God’s place in their hearts or distort the truth about who He is.

## Chapter Prayer

Father, thank You that everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of You, and that You have made me part of Your family. Teach me to love You by keeping Your commandments, and to love Your children with a sincere heart. Thank You that Your commands are not a burden, and that faith in Jesus is the victory that overcomes the world. Thank You for Your testimony about Your Son, and for the gift of eternal life that is found in Him. Help me to rest in the assurance that I have life because I have the Son. Give me boldness in prayer, and shape my desires so that I ask according to Your will. Teach me to pray for my brothers and sisters when they stumble. Keep me safe from the evil one, and guard my heart from every idol, so that I may know You, the true God, and live for You alone. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
