Book 24 of 27

# 2 John

## About This Letter

Second John is one of the shortest books in the Bible, short enough to fit on a single sheet of papyrus. Its author calls himself simply “*The elder*” (*2 John 1:1*). From early times Christians have identified this elder with John the apostle, the author of the Gospel of John and 1 John, though some ancient writers and modern scholars suggest a respected leader named John the Elder who belonged to the same circle. The letter’s language and concerns closely match 1 John: truth, love, the commandment heard from the beginning, and the danger of deceivers who deny that Jesus Christ came in the flesh. It was likely written around the same time as 1 John, toward the end of the first century, probably from Ephesus.

The letter is addressed to “the chosen lady and her children.” Some readers take this as a real Christian woman and her family. Many others understand it as a warm, figurative way of addressing a local church and its members, especially since the letter closes with greetings from “the children of your chosen sister,” likely the elder’s own congregation. Either way, the message is meant for a community of believers.

## The Shape of the Letter

After a greeting that joins truth and love, the elder rejoices that some of the church’s members are walking in truth. He reminds them of the commandment they have had from the beginning, to love one another, and explains that love means walking according to God’s commandments. He then warns them about deceivers who deny that Jesus Christ came in the flesh, urges them to remain in the teaching of Christ, and tells them not to welcome or support those who bring a different teaching. He closes by expressing his hope to visit them in person.

## Themes to Watch For

Watch for the close bond between truth and love, walking in obedience, the danger of deception about Jesus’ true humanity, remaining in the teaching of Christ, the importance of discernment in hospitality, and the joy of fellowship face to face. Second John shows that love without truth becomes empty, and truth without love becomes harsh; the Christian life holds both together.

## Chapters

1.  [2 John 1](#c24_2JN_001.xhtml) — Walking in Truth and Love

2 John · Chapter 1 of 1

# 2 John — Chapter 1

Chapter Theme: Walking in Truth and Love

[Read 2 John 1 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/2JN01.htm)

Main Teaching

The elder writes to “the chosen lady and her children,” whom he loves in truth, along with all who know the truth. He rejoices that some of her children are walking in truth, as the Father commanded, and he asks them to keep the commandment they have had from the beginning: to love one another. Love means walking according to God’s commandments. He warns that many deceivers have gone out into the world who do not confess that Jesus Christ came in the flesh; such a person is the deceiver and the antichrist. Believers must watch themselves so that they do not lose what they have worked for, but receive a full reward. Anyone who goes beyond the teaching of Christ and does not remain in it does not have God, but whoever remains in the teaching has both the Father and the Son. If someone comes bringing a different teaching, the church should not receive that person into the house or give a welcome, because doing so shares in their evil work. The elder has much more to say, but he hopes to visit and speak face to face so that their joy may be complete.

## Chapter Background and Story

Second John is a short pastoral letter written to protect a church that the elder loved. In the first century, traveling teachers and missionaries moved from town to town, relying on the hospitality of believers. Churches met in homes, so welcoming a traveling teacher often meant giving that person a place to stay, a meal, and an opportunity to teach the gathered church. This was a beautiful practice that helped spread the gospel. But it also created an opening for false teachers to gain influence.

The same deceivers described in 1 John, those who denied that Jesus Christ came in the flesh, were apparently traveling among the churches. The elder writes to warn this congregation before they arrive. His letter weaves together two words again and again: truth and love. He wants the church to love one another deeply, and he wants that love to be guarded by the truth about Jesus.

### Greeting in Truth and Love (vv1–3)

“*The elder, to the chosen lady and her children, whom I love in truth, and not I only, but also all those who know the truth*” (*v. 1*). The elder’s love for this church is not mere affection. It is love “in truth,” rooted in their shared faith in Jesus. And it is not his love alone. All who know the truth share this bond. The gospel creates a family of love that reaches across cities and congregations.

“*for the truth’s sake, which remains in us, and it will be with us forever:*” (*v. 2*) The truth is not just a set of ideas but a living reality that “remains” in believers. In John’s writings, truth is closely connected with Jesus Himself, who said, “*I am the way, the truth, and the life*” (*John 14:6*). Because the truth remains in believers, their fellowship has a permanent foundation.

“*Grace, mercy, and peace will be with us, from God the Father and from the Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of the Father, in truth and love*” (*v. 3*). Most New Testament greetings express a wish or prayer for grace and peace. Here the elder states it as a confident promise: grace, mercy, and peace “will be with us.” These gifts come from both the Father and the Son, and they are experienced “in truth and love,” the two themes that will shape the entire letter.

### The Commandment of Love (vv4–6)

The elder’s joy over believers walking in truth and his appeal to love one another are studied below.

### Watch Out for Deceivers (vv7–11)

The warning about deceivers, the call to remain in Christ’s teaching, and the instruction about hospitality are studied below.

### Hope to Meet Face to Face (vv12–13)

“*Having many things to write to you, I don’t want to do so with paper and ink, but I hope to come to you and to speak face to face, that our joy may be made full*” (*v. 12*). The elder has more to say, but he prefers to say it in person. Letters are valuable, but nothing replaces being together. Christian fellowship is meant to be personal and embodied, and the elder expects that their joy will be complete when they meet.

“*The children of your chosen sister greet you*” (*v. 13*). The letter closes with greetings from “the children of your chosen sister,” likely the members of the elder’s own church. Two congregations, joined in Christ, send love to one another like sisters in one family.

## Important Verses Explained

### *2 John 1:4–6* — Walking in Truth, Walking in Love

> *“I rejoice greatly that I have found some of your children walking in truth, even as we have been commanded by the Father. Now I beg you, dear lady, not as though I wrote to you a new commandment, but that which we had from the beginning, that we love one another. This is love, that we should walk according to his commandments. This is the commandment, even as you heard from the beginning, that you should walk in it.”*
>
> — *2 John 1:4–6* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The elder begins with joy: “I rejoice greatly that I have found some of your children walking in truth.” He has heard that members of the church are living out the truth of the gospel. “Walking” is a biblical picture of daily conduct. Walking in truth means living in a way that matches what one believes about Jesus.

He notes that this is “even as we have been commanded by the Father.” Walking in truth is not just a good idea; it is what God the Father asks of His children.

In verse 5, the elder makes a gentle appeal: “Now I beg you, dear lady, not as though I wrote to you a new commandment, but that which we had from the beginning, that we love one another.” There is nothing novel about this command. It goes back to Jesus Himself, who told His disciples to love one another as He had loved them (*John 13:34*).

Verse 6 explains what this love looks like: “This is love, that we should walk according to his commandments.” Love is not a vague feeling. It is shown by living the way God directs. And God’s central command is to walk in love.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses show that truth and love are inseparable. Some people emphasize truth and become cold, harsh, or proud. Others emphasize love and become willing to set truth aside. The elder holds both together. The church that walks in truth must also walk in love, and genuine love walks according to God’s commands.

There is a beautiful circle in verse 6. Love means obeying God’s commands, and God’s command is that we love. Love and obedience define each other. This reflects Jesus’ teaching that the whole law hangs on loving God and loving neighbor (*Matthew 22:37–40*).

The elder’s appeal to what was “from the beginning” is also significant. The false teachers likely claimed new insights that went beyond the original message. The elder points back to what the church first received from Jesus and the apostles. True spiritual growth does not leave the original gospel behind; it goes deeper into it.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers today can take encouragement that faithful living brings joy to others. Those who invest in a church, a family, or the faith of others rejoice when they see people walking in truth.

This passage also invites believers to keep truth and love together in every relationship. Speaking truth without love can wound. Offering love without truth can mislead. In families, friendships, and church life, believers are called to be both truthful and loving, as Jesus was full of grace and truth (*John 1:14*).

Love, as the elder defines it, is practical. It shows itself in obedience to God: patience, kindness, honesty, forgiveness, faithfulness, and care. These are the everyday ways believers walk in love.

### *2 John 1:7–9* — Remain in the Teaching of Christ

> *“For many deceivers have gone out into the world, those who don’t confess that Jesus Christ came in the flesh. This is the deceiver and the Antichrist. Watch yourselves, that we don’t lose the things which we have accomplished, but that we receive a full reward. Whoever transgresses and doesn’t remain in the teaching of Christ doesn’t have God. He who remains in the teaching has both the Father and the Son.”*
>
> — *2 John 1:7–9* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The elder now explains why he has stressed truth: “For many deceivers have gone out into the world, those who don’t confess that Jesus Christ came in the flesh.” These deceivers denied that Jesus truly became human. They may have taught that He only seemed to have a body or that the divine Christ was separate from the man Jesus. The elder calls such a person “the deceiver and the Antichrist,” meaning one who opposes the true Christ.

In verse 8 he warns: “Watch yourselves, that we don’t lose the things which we have accomplished, but that we receive a full reward.” The church has labored in faith, love, and service. If they are led away by false teaching, they could lose the fruit of that labor. He wants them to receive a full reward.

Verse 9 gives the test: “Whoever transgresses and doesn’t remain in the teaching of Christ doesn’t have God.” The word “transgresses” can also be understood as “goes ahead” or “goes beyond.” The false teachers claimed to have advanced beyond the basic message about Jesus. But going beyond Christ’s teaching means leaving God behind. In contrast, “He who remains in the teaching has both the Father and the Son.”

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The incarnation, the truth that the eternal Son of God became a real human being, is at the heart of the Christian faith. If Jesus did not truly come in the flesh, He could not truly die for sins or rise bodily from the dead. The salvation of human beings depends on Jesus being both fully God and fully human. That is why the elder takes this denial so seriously.

“The teaching of Christ” may mean the teaching about Christ, or the teaching Christ Himself gave. Both are true. The apostles passed on what Jesus taught and what He revealed about Himself. To remain in this teaching is to remain in relationship with the Father and the Son. Truth is not merely information; it is the way of knowing God personally.

The warning against “going beyond” is a needed caution. Christians should grow in understanding, but growth that departs from the apostolic witness about Jesus is not progress. The safest path forward in faith is always deeper into Christ, not beyond Him.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Many voices today offer new ideas about Jesus. Some reduce Him to a wise teacher, others to a symbol or a spiritual force. Believers can test such ideas by Scripture: Does this teaching affirm that Jesus is the Son of God who truly became human, died, and rose again?

The call to “watch yourselves” is also personal. Every believer needs to guard their heart and mind, staying rooted in Scripture and in a community that faithfully teaches it. This is not fearfulness, but wisdom.

Believers can also take comfort in the promise of verse 9. Those who remain in the teaching of Christ have both the Father and the Son. There is no higher spiritual knowledge to chase. In Jesus, believers already have everything they need for life and godliness.

### *2 John 1:10–11* — Discernment in Welcoming Teachers

> *“If anyone comes to you and doesn’t bring this teaching, don’t receive him into your house, and don’t welcome him, for he who welcomes him participates in his evil deeds.”*
>
> — *2 John 1:10–11* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The elder now gives a practical instruction: “If anyone comes to you and doesn’t bring this teaching, don’t receive him into your house, and don’t welcome him.” This refers to traveling teachers who came to churches expecting hospitality and an opportunity to teach. The elder tells the church not to give such teachers a home base or a platform.

Verse 11 explains why: “for he who welcomes him participates in his evil deeds.” Supporting a false teacher, giving them lodging, resources, and official approval, would make the church a partner in spreading what destroys faith.

The phrase “don’t welcome him” refers to a formal greeting of acceptance that signaled endorsement and fellowship, not ordinary politeness.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This instruction must be read carefully in its setting. In the first century, churches met in homes. Receiving a teacher “into your house” meant inviting them into the gathered church and sponsoring their ministry. The elder is not forbidding believers from showing basic kindness, courtesy, or compassion to people who disagree with them. Elsewhere Scripture calls believers to love their enemies, to do good to all people, and to show hospitality to strangers (*Luke 6:27*; *Galatians 6:10*; *Hebrews 13:2*).

What the elder forbids is giving active support and endorsement to those who are spreading a message that denies Christ. Love for the church requires protecting it from teaching that would lead people away from Jesus. Shepherds protect sheep from wolves (*Acts 20:28–30*).

This passage also shows that hospitality, though a precious Christian virtue, must be practiced with discernment. Truth guides love. The same letter that urges believers to love one another also urges them not to lend their homes and resources to the spread of falsehood.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers and churches today can apply this passage by being thoughtful about whom they support and promote. Inviting someone to teach, sharing their materials, funding their work, or giving them a platform implies endorsement. Churches have a responsibility to be discerning about what they help spread.

This passage does not justify rudeness, hostility, or refusing friendship to people with different beliefs. Believers are called to be gracious and kind to everyone, including those who do not share their faith. Many people come to Christ because believers showed them patient love and welcome.

The balance the elder teaches is wise: warm love for people and firm loyalty to the truth about Jesus. Believers can show kindness to all while refusing to become partners in spreading what denies Christ.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

Second John is brief, but its message is rich. It shows that truth and love belong together. The elder loves this church “in truth,” rejoices that its members are walking in truth, and calls them to keep the commandment they have had from the beginning: to love one another. Love, in turn, means walking according to God’s commands. Neither truth nor love can be set aside without losing the other.

The letter also calls believers to be watchful. Deceivers were spreading a false message about Jesus, denying that He truly came in the flesh. Today, too, believers meet many ideas about who Jesus is. They are called to remain in the teaching of Christ, testing every message by the witness of Scripture. Those who remain in His teaching have both the Father and the Son.

This watchfulness shapes how believers use their influence and resources. Hospitality and generosity are good gifts, but they should not be used to promote teaching that leads people away from Jesus. At the same time, believers can show genuine kindness to all people, holding truth firmly while extending grace freely.

Finally, the letter ends with a longing for personal fellowship. The elder wants to see his friends face to face so that their joy may be complete. Believers today can value the gift of being together, investing in real relationships within the body of Christ, where truth and love are lived out side by side.

## Chapter Prayer

Father, thank You for the truth that remains in us and will be with us forever, and for the grace, mercy, and peace that come from You and from Your Son, Jesus Christ. Help me to walk in truth and to keep the commandment I have heard from the beginning, to love others as You have loved me. Teach me that love means walking according to Your commands. Guard my heart and mind from every deception about Jesus, and keep me rooted in the teaching of Christ, so that I may have both the Father and the Son. Give me wisdom and discernment in what I support and share, and give me a gracious and kind heart toward all people. Thank You for the joy of fellowship with Your people, and draw us together in truth and love. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Book 25 of 27

# 3 John

## About This Letter

Third John is the shortest book in the New Testament by word count, and the most personal of John’s letters. Like 2 John, it comes from “*The elder*” (*3 John 1:1*), traditionally identified with the apostle John, writing near the end of the first century, probably from Ephesus. Unlike 2 John, it is addressed to a named individual: Gaius, a dear friend and faithful believer in a nearby church. Gaius was a common name, and we cannot be sure whether he is the same as any other Gaius mentioned in the New Testament.

The letter gives a rare glimpse into the everyday life of the early churches. Traveling missionaries went out from the elder’s community to preach the gospel, depending on the hospitality of local believers. Gaius had welcomed them generously. But a church leader named Diotrephes refused to receive them, rejected the elder’s authority, spread false accusations, and even expelled members who wanted to show hospitality. The elder writes to encourage Gaius, to commend a man named Demetrius, and to address the problem Diotrephes was causing.

## The Shape of the Letter

The elder greets Gaius warmly and prays for his well-being. He rejoices to hear that Gaius walks in the truth, and he praises Gaius for his faithful hospitality to traveling missionaries, urging him to continue sending them on their way in a manner worthy of God. He then describes the behavior of Diotrephes, who loves to be first, and promises to deal with it when he comes. He urges Gaius to imitate what is good rather than what is evil, commends Demetrius, and closes with his hope to see Gaius soon and speak face to face.

## Themes to Watch For

Watch for walking in the truth, the joy of seeing others grow in faith, the value of Christian hospitality, partnership in gospel work, the danger of selfish ambition in church leadership, the importance of a good testimony, and the gift of personal fellowship. Third John shows that the truth of the gospel is lived out in ordinary acts of generosity, humility, and faithfulness.

## Chapters

1.  [3 John 1](#c25_3JN_001.xhtml) — Faithful Hospitality and Humble Leadership

3 John · Chapter 1 of 1

# 3 John — Chapter 1

Chapter Theme: Faithful Hospitality and Humble Leadership

[Read 3 John 1 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/3JN01.htm)

Main Teaching

The elder writes to his beloved friend Gaius, praying that he may prosper and be in good health just as his soul prospers. He rejoices greatly at reports that Gaius is walking in the truth, saying that he has no greater joy than to hear that his children are walking in the truth. He commends Gaius for his faithful service to traveling believers, even strangers, who have testified about his love before the church, and urges him to send them on their way in a manner worthy of God. These missionaries went out for the sake of the Name, accepting nothing from unbelievers, so believers ought to support such people and become fellow workers for the truth. In contrast, Diotrephes, who loves to be first, refuses to welcome the elder’s messengers, spreads wicked accusations, refuses to receive the brothers, and even throws out of the church those who want to welcome them. The elder urges Gaius not to imitate what is evil but what is good, for whoever does good is from God. He commends Demetrius, who is well spoken of by everyone and by the truth itself. He hopes to see Gaius soon and speak face to face, and he sends a blessing of peace.

## Chapter Background and Story

Third John is a personal letter, much like a note between friends. Yet it addresses an important matter: how churches should treat those who travel to spread the gospel, and how leaders should use their position.

In the early church, missionaries and teachers traveled from city to city, often with little money. They relied on believers in each place to give them food, lodging, and help for the next stage of their journey. This was not a small kindness. Without such hospitality, the spread of the gospel would have been much slower. Believers who welcomed these travelers became partners in their mission.

Second John warned against welcoming false teachers. Third John shows the other side: the importance of welcoming true servants of the gospel. Taken together, the two letters teach that hospitality should be generous and also discerning.

### Greeting and Joy (vv1–4)

“*The elder to Gaius the beloved, whom I love in truth*” (*v. 1*). The elder’s affection for Gaius is warm and personal. He calls him “beloved” four times in this short letter (vv1, 2, 5, 11). Their friendship is rooted in shared faith, love “in truth.”

The elder’s prayer for Gaius and his joy over believers walking in truth are studied below.

### Faithful Hospitality (vv5–8)

Gaius’s faithful service to traveling believers is studied below.

### The Problem of Diotrephes (vv9–10)

“*I wrote to the assembly, but Diotrephes, who loves to be first among them, doesn’t accept what we say*” (*v. 9*). The elder had written an earlier letter to the church, but Diotrephes refused to accept it. The root problem is named clearly: Diotrephes “loves to be first.” He wanted control and prominence. This is the opposite of the servant leadership Jesus taught (*Mark 10:42–45*).

“*Therefore, if I come, I will call attention to his deeds which he does, unjustly accusing us with wicked words. Not content with this, he doesn’t receive the brothers himself, and those who would, he forbids and throws out of the assembly*” (*v. 10*). Diotrephes’s behavior was harmful in several ways. He spread false and malicious accusations. He refused hospitality to the traveling missionaries. He prevented others from showing hospitality, and he expelled from the church those who tried. His love of position led him to use his power to control others.

The elder does not respond with secret maneuvering or harsh counterattacks. He intends to come in person and bring Diotrephes’s actions into the open. Wrongdoing by leaders is not to be hidden but addressed honestly, with the truth brought to light.

### Imitate What Is Good (vv11–12)

The call to imitate what is good is studied below. “*Demetrius has the testimony of all, and of the truth itself; yes, we also testify, and you know that our testimony is true*” (*v. 12*). Demetrius may have been the carrier of this letter or one of the traveling missionaries. The elder commends him strongly. Everyone speaks well of him; his life matches the truth; and the elder himself adds his own testimony. In contrast to Diotrephes, Demetrius is a model of a trustworthy servant.

### Closing (vv13–14)

“*I had many things to write to you, but I am unwilling to write to you with ink and pen;*” (*v. 13*) “*but I hope to see you soon. Then we will speak face to face. Peace be to you. The friends greet you. Greet the friends by name*” (*v. 14*). As in 2 John, the elder prefers personal conversation to writing. He closes with a blessing of peace. The words “Greet the friends by name” show the personal care that marked the early church. Believers were not anonymous members of a crowd, but known and loved individuals.

## Important Verses Explained

### *3 John 1:2–4* — No Greater Joy

> *“Beloved, I pray that you may prosper in all things and be healthy, even as your soul prospers. For I rejoiced greatly when brothers came and testified about your truth, even as you walk in truth. I have no greater joy than this: to hear about my children walking in truth.”*
>
> — *3 John 1:2–4* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The elder begins with a prayer for his friend: “Beloved, I pray that you may prosper in all things and be healthy, even as your soul prospers.” This was a common way of beginning letters in the ancient world, but the elder fills it with Christian meaning. He prays for Gaius’s overall well-being and physical health, and he notes that Gaius’s soul is already prospering. Gaius is spiritually healthy, and the elder wishes that the rest of his life would match.

In verse 3, the elder explains his joy: “For I rejoiced greatly when brothers came and testified about your truth, even as you walk in truth.” Traveling believers had returned with reports about Gaius. His life matched the truth he believed.

Verse 4 expresses the elder’s deepest joy: “I have no greater joy than this: to hear about my children walking in truth.” The elder likely calls Gaius and others his “children” because he had led them to faith or nurtured them spiritually. Nothing pleased him more than seeing them live faithfully.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Verse 2 has sometimes been used to teach that God always wills financial wealth and perfect health for believers. That reading goes beyond what the verse says. It is a friend’s prayer for another’s well-being, similar to wishing someone good health in a letter. It shows that God cares about the whole person, body and soul, and that it is right to pray for one another’s health and circumstances. But it does not promise that faithful believers will never be poor or sick. Scripture also shows faithful believers enduring illness, hardship, and lack (*2 Corinthians 12:7–10*; *Philippians 4:11–13*; *2 Timothy 4:20*).

The elder’s priority is clear: the prosperity of the soul comes first. He measures Gaius’s life by his faithfulness to the truth, not by his wealth or status.

His joy in verse 4 reveals the heart of a true spiritual leader. His greatest satisfaction is not personal success, influence, or recognition, but the faithfulness of those he cares for. This echoes Paul, who told the believers in Thessalonica, “*For you are our glory and our joy*” (*1 Thessalonians 2:20*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can follow the elder’s example by praying for the whole well-being of others: their health, their circumstances, and especially their spiritual lives. It is good to pray for practical needs, and it is even more important to pray that people’s souls prosper.

This passage also encourages believers to examine what brings them the greatest joy. Parents, mentors, pastors, and friends can find deep joy in seeing those they love walk in truth. Investing in others’ faith brings lasting rewards.

Finally, Gaius’s example shows that faith is seen in how one lives. Others noticed that he walked in truth. Believers today can pray that their lives, too, will bear witness to the truth they believe.

### *3 John 1:5–8* — Fellow Workers for the Truth

> *“Beloved, you do a faithful work in whatever you accomplish for those who are brothers and strangers. They have testified about your love before the assembly. You will do well to send them forward on their journey in a way worthy of God, because for the sake of the Name they went out, taking nothing from the Gentiles. We therefore ought to receive such, that we may be fellow workers for the truth.”*
>
> — *3 John 1:5–8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The elder praises Gaius’s hospitality: “Beloved, you do a faithful work in whatever you accomplish for those who are brothers and strangers.” Gaius had welcomed traveling believers, even those he had never met before. His care for them was an act of faithfulness to God.

In verse 6, the elder notes that these travelers “have testified about your love before the assembly.” Gaius’s kindness had become known in the elder’s church. The elder then urges him: “You will do well to send them forward on their journey in a way worthy of God.” To “send them forward” meant providing what they needed for the next part of their trip: food, money, supplies, perhaps companions.

Verse 7 explains why they deserve support: “because for the sake of the Name they went out, taking nothing from the Gentiles.” These missionaries traveled for the sake of Jesus’ name. They refused to accept support from unbelievers, perhaps so that no one could accuse them of preaching for profit.

Verse 8 draws the conclusion: “We therefore ought to receive such, that we may be fellow workers for the truth.” Those who support missionaries share in their work.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Hospitality is a deeply biblical virtue. Abraham welcomed strangers who turned out to be messengers from God (*Genesis 18*; *Hebrews 13:2*). Jesus said that whoever receives one of His messengers receives Him (*Matthew 10:40*). Hospitality is not merely good manners; it is a way of serving Christ.

The phrase “in a way worthy of God” sets a high standard. Believers should treat God’s servants as they would want to treat God Himself. Support should be generous, thoughtful, and given with honor.

The idea of being “fellow workers for the truth” reveals something important about the body of Christ. Not everyone is called to travel and preach. But everyone can share in the mission. Those who give, host, pray, and encourage are partners in the work, and they share in its fruit. The mission of the church is a shared endeavor.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers today can practice this kind of hospitality in many ways: welcoming visiting missionaries, opening their homes to fellow believers, supporting those who serve in ministry, and showing kindness to strangers.

Supporting gospel work is not reserved for a few. Through prayer, giving, encouragement, and practical help, every believer can become a fellow worker for the truth. Small acts of generosity, a meal, a room, a gift, a note of encouragement, can strengthen those who labor for the gospel.

This passage also encourages believers to support those who serve with integrity, who go out “for the sake of the Name” rather than for personal gain.

### *3 John 1:11* — Imitate What Is Good

> *“Beloved, don’t imitate that which is evil, but that which is good. He who does good is of God. He who does evil hasn’t seen God.”*
>
> — *3 John 1:11* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After describing the harmful behavior of Diotrephes, the elder gives Gaius a simple instruction: “Beloved, don’t imitate that which is evil, but that which is good.” People naturally imitate those around them, especially leaders. The elder urges Gaius not to follow the example of Diotrephes, but to follow what is good.

He then gives a principle: “He who does good is of God.” Doing good is a sign that a person belongs to God. Then he adds the opposite: “He who does evil hasn’t seen God.” A person who habitually does evil shows that they do not truly know God.

These words echo the teaching of 1 John, where right actions, especially love, reveal whether a person truly knows God (*1 John 3:10*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse recognizes the power of example. Diotrephes was a church leader, and his example could lead others astray. Leaders shape the culture of a community. That is why Scripture holds leaders to a high standard of character (*1 Timothy 3:1–7*; *1 Peter 5:2–3*).

But this verse also places responsibility on every believer. Gaius was not obligated to imitate Diotrephes just because Diotrephes held a position of authority. Believers are called to imitate what is good, not simply whoever is in charge. Position does not make behavior right.

The connection between doing good and knowing God is a theme throughout John’s writings. Those who have truly seen God, through faith in Jesus, are transformed by that encounter. Their lives begin to reflect His goodness. A life marked by persistent evil, especially by pride, control, and mistreatment of others, reveals that a person has not truly known God, whatever position they hold.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers today are surrounded by examples, some good and some harmful, in churches, workplaces, families, and public life. This verse calls them to be thoughtful about whom they imitate. Not every leader, influencer, or popular figure is worth following.

The contrast between Diotrephes and Demetrius gives a clear picture. One loved to be first and used power to control and exclude. The other was well spoken of by all and lived according to the truth. Believers can seek out and follow leaders who show humility, integrity, and love, and they can aim to be such examples for others.

This verse also gives courage to those who find themselves in communities where leaders behave badly. Believers are not required to follow harmful examples or remain silent about wrongdoing. Like the elder, they can bring wrong into the light in a truthful and appropriate way. Where a leader is mistreating or controlling people, believers should seek help from trusted leaders and, where needed, from outside authorities. And in every situation, they can choose to do what is good.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

Third John shows how the truth of the gospel is lived out in everyday life. Gaius walked in the truth, and others could see it. The elder’s greatest joy was to hear that those he loved were walking faithfully. Believers today can pray for one another’s whole well-being, body and soul, and find their deepest joy in seeing others grow in faith.

The letter also highlights the importance of hospitality and partnership in the gospel. Gaius welcomed traveling believers, even strangers, and sent them on their way in a manner worthy of God. In doing so, he became a fellow worker for the truth. Believers today can share in God’s mission through generous support of those who serve, open homes, practical help, and faithful prayer.

The example of Diotrephes is a sober warning. His love of being first led him to reject others, spread false accusations, and control the church. Pride and selfish ambition can damage any community, including churches. Leaders and members alike are called to the humility of Jesus, who came not to be served but to serve.

Finally, the letter calls believers to imitate what is good. Those who do good show that they belong to God. Like Demetrius, believers can seek to live in such a way that their lives bear witness to the truth, and like the elder, they can value the joy of personal fellowship, knowing and greeting one another by name.

## Chapter Prayer

Father, thank You for the joy of walking in the truth and for the friends You have given me in Your family. Help me to care for the whole well-being of others, and above all to pray that their souls prosper. Give me a generous and welcoming heart, so that I may serve Your people faithfully and become a fellow worker for the truth. Guard me from the love of being first, from pride and selfish ambition, and make me humble like Jesus, who came to serve. Help me to imitate what is good and not what is evil, and let my life bear a good testimony to Your truth. Thank You for the gift of fellowship, and teach me to know and love Your people by name. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Book 26 of 27

# Jude

## About This Letter

The author introduces himself as “*Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ, and brother of James*” (*Jude 1:1*). The James he mentions is almost certainly the well-known leader of the Jerusalem church, the brother of Jesus. That would make Jude, or Judas, one of the brothers of Jesus named in the Gospels (*Matthew 13:55*; *Mark 6:3*). Like James, Jude did not believe in Jesus during His earthly ministry (*John 7:5*), but after the resurrection he became a follower and later a traveling servant of the gospel (*1 Corinthians 9:5*). Remarkably, he does not call himself the brother of the Lord, but a servant of Jesus Christ. The letter is often dated somewhere between A.D. 60 and 80. Its recipients are not named, but its heavy use of Old Testament stories and Jewish traditions suggests readers who were familiar with Jewish teaching, perhaps a mostly Jewish Christian community.

Jude had hoped to write about the salvation all believers share, but news of a danger forced him to change his plans. Certain people had slipped into the church who turned God’s grace into an excuse for immoral living and rejected the authority of Jesus Christ. Jude writes an urgent appeal for believers to contend for the faith. His letter shares much material with *2 Peter 2*, and many scholars believe one writer drew on the other or that both drew on a common source.

## The Shape of the Letter

After a warm greeting, Jude explains his purpose: to urge believers to contend for the faith once for all delivered to the saints. He then describes the ungodly intruders and reminds his readers of examples of God’s judgment from the past: Israel in the wilderness, angels who abandoned their place, and Sodom and Gomorrah. He compares the intruders to Cain, Balaam, and Korah, and uses vivid images from nature to describe their emptiness. He quotes a prophecy attributed to Enoch and reminds believers that the apostles foretold such mockers. Then he turns to the faithful with encouragement: build yourselves up in the faith, pray in the Holy Spirit, keep yourselves in God’s love, and show mercy to those who waver. The letter closes with one of the most beloved doxologies in Scripture.

## Themes to Watch For

Watch for contending for the faith, the danger of turning grace into license, God’s certain judgment on ungodliness, the importance of remembering Scripture, the security of believers who are kept by God, practices that sustain faith, mercy toward those who doubt, and praise to the God who is able to keep His people from stumbling. Jude’s brief letter is both a sober warning and a tender reassurance.

## Chapters

1.  [Jude 1](#c26_JUD_001.xhtml) — Contend for the Faith and Keep Yourselves in God’s Love

Jude · Chapter 1 of 1

# Jude — Chapter 1

Chapter Theme: Contend for the Faith and Keep Yourselves in God’s Love

[Read Jude 1 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/JUD01.htm)

Main Teaching

Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James, writes to those who are called, loved by God the Father, and kept for Jesus Christ. He had wanted to write about the salvation they share, but he felt compelled instead to urge them to contend for the faith that was once for all entrusted to God’s people. Certain ungodly people have slipped in secretly; they pervert the grace of God into a license for immorality and deny Jesus Christ, our only Master and Lord. Jude reminds his readers of God’s judgment in the past: on Israelites in the wilderness who did not believe, on angels who abandoned their proper place, and on Sodom and Gomorrah. The intruders reject authority, slander what they do not understand, and follow the way of Cain, the error of Balaam, and the rebellion of Korah. They are like hidden reefs, waterless clouds, fruitless trees, wild waves, and wandering stars. Enoch prophesied judgment on such people, and the apostles foretold that scoffers would come in the last time. But Jude urges the faithful to build themselves up in their most holy faith, pray in the Holy Spirit, keep themselves in God’s love, and wait for the mercy of Jesus Christ that leads to eternal life. They should show mercy to those who doubt and rescue others from the fire. The letter ends in praise to the God who is able to keep them from stumbling and to present them blameless before His glory with great joy.

## Chapter Background and Story

Jude is a short letter with an urgent tone. It reads like a warning sounded by a watchman. Its language is vivid and strong, full of images from nature and stories from the Old Testament and Jewish tradition. Yet beneath its warnings lies deep pastoral care. Jude begins and ends by assuring believers that they are loved and kept by God.

The intruders Jude describes were not outsiders attacking the church from without. They had slipped in among the believers and were taking part in the church’s fellowship meals. They apparently taught that God’s grace freed them to live however they pleased, especially in sexual matters. They rejected spiritual authority, claimed special insight through dreams, and caused divisions. Jude does not engage their arguments in detail. Instead, he shows from Scripture that such behavior has always come under God’s judgment, and he strengthens the faithful to stand firm.

### Greeting (vv1–2)

“*Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ, and brother of James, to those who are called, sanctified by God the Father, and kept for Jesus Christ:*” (*v. 1*) Jude describes believers in three beautiful ways. They are “called,” invited by God into relationship with Him. They are “sanctified by God the Father”; many manuscripts read beloved in God the Father instead, and both ideas express God’s tender care. And they are “kept for Jesus Christ,” protected and preserved until the day they meet Him. Before Jude says anything about danger, he reminds believers of their security in God. This theme of being “kept” returns at the end of the letter (vv21, 24).

“*May mercy, peace, and love be multiplied to you*” (*v. 2*). Jude prays not merely that believers will have these gifts, but that they will be multiplied, poured out in abundance.

### The Call to Contend and the Danger Within (vv3–4)

The call to contend for the faith and the description of the intruders are studied below.

### Examples of Judgment from the Past (vv5–7)

“*Now I desire to remind you, though you already know this, that the Lord, having saved a people out of the land of Egypt, afterward destroyed those who didn’t believe*” (*v. 5*). Jude’s first example is Israel in the wilderness. God rescued His people from Egypt, but many who experienced that rescue later refused to trust Him and died in the desert (*Numbers 14:26–35*). Being part of God’s people outwardly is not the same as genuine, persevering faith.

“*Angels who didn’t keep their first domain, but deserted their own dwelling place, he has kept in everlasting bonds under darkness for the judgment of the great day*” (*v. 6*). The second example concerns angels who abandoned their proper place. Many interpreters connect this with *Genesis 6:1–4*, where “*God’s sons*” (*Genesis 6:2*) took human wives, a passage that ancient Jewish writings, such as the book of 1 Enoch, interpreted as angels sinning by crossing the boundary God had set. Others understand Jude to refer more generally to the original rebellion of angels against God. Either way, the point is clear: even angels who rejected God’s order face judgment. Notice the wordplay: those who did not “keep” their position are now “kept” in chains for judgment.

“*Even as Sodom and Gomorrah and the cities around them, having in the same way as these given themselves over to sexual immorality and gone after strange flesh, are shown as an example, suffering the punishment of eternal fire*” (*v. 7*). The third example is Sodom and Gomorrah, cities destroyed for their wickedness (*Genesis 19*). Scripture describes their sins in several ways, including arrogance, neglect of the poor, and sexual immorality (*Ezekiel 16:49–50*). Jude highlights their sexual immorality and their pursuit of “strange flesh.” Interpreters understand this phrase in different ways: some see a reference to the men of Sodom seeking sexual relations with angelic visitors, matching the example of angels crossing boundaries in verse 6, while others see a broader reference to sexual sin outside God’s design. The common thread in all three examples is rebellion against the boundaries God has set, followed by judgment.

### The Character of the Intruders (vv8–16)

“*Yet in the same way, these also in their dreaming defile the flesh, despise authority, and slander celestial beings*” (*v. 8*). The intruders claimed revelations through dreams to justify their behavior. They indulged in immorality, rejected the authority of the Lord, and spoke contemptuously about spiritual beings.

“*But Michael, the archangel, when contending with the devil and arguing about the body of Moses, dared not bring against him an abusive condemnation, but said, “May the Lord rebuke you!”*” (*v. 9*) This account does not appear in the Old Testament. According to early church writers, it came from a Jewish work known as the Assumption of Moses or Testament of Moses. Jude uses a story familiar to his readers to make a point: even Michael, a mighty archangel, did not presume to pronounce judgment on the devil in his own authority, but left judgment to the Lord. The intruders, by contrast, arrogantly slandered spiritual realities. Jude’s use of such traditions does not mean he regarded these books as Scripture; Paul also cited non-biblical sources when they illustrated truth (*Acts 17:28*).

“*But these speak evil of whatever things they don’t know. They are destroyed in these things that they understand naturally, like the creatures without reason*” (*v. 10*). The intruders mocked what they did not understand, and they were ruled by their instincts like animals, which led them to ruin.

“*Woe to them! For they went in the way of Cain, and ran riotously in the error of Balaam for hire, and perished in Korah’s rebellion*” (*v. 11*). Jude points to three Old Testament figures. Cain murdered his brother out of envy and rejected God’s correction (*Genesis 4*). Balaam was willing to lead Israel into sin for money (*Numbers 22–25*; *31:16*). Korah rebelled against the leadership God had appointed through Moses and was destroyed (*Numbers 16*). The intruders show the same jealousy, greed, and rebellion. Jude speaks of Korah’s rebellion as though the intruders have already “perished” in it, so certain is their judgment.

“*These are hidden rocky reefs in your love feasts when they feast with you, shepherds who without fear feed themselves; clouds without water, carried along by winds; autumn trees without fruit, twice dead, plucked up by the roots;*” (*v. 12*) “*wild waves of the sea, foaming out their own shame; wandering stars, for whom the blackness of darkness has been reserved forever*” (*v. 13*). Jude paints five vivid pictures. The intruders are like hidden reefs that can wreck a ship, endangering the church’s fellowship meals, the “love feasts.” They are like shepherds who feed only themselves. They are like clouds that promise rain but bring none, trees that bear no fruit even at harvest time, waves that churn up only foam and filth, and stars that wander from their course and vanish into darkness. Each image shows something that looks promising but is empty or dangerous.

“*About these also Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesied, saying, “Behold, the Lord came with ten thousands of his holy ones,*” (*v. 14*) “*to execute judgment on all, and to convict all the ungodly of all their works of ungodliness which they have done in an ungodly way, and of all the hard things which ungodly sinners have spoken against him.”*” (*v. 15*) Jude quotes a prophecy found in the book of 1 Enoch (*1:9*), a Jewish writing well known in his day. Enoch himself is the man who “*walked with God*” (*Genesis 5:24*). By quoting this passage, Jude affirms the truth of its message: the Lord will come with His holy ones to judge the ungodly. Quoting a writing does not necessarily mean treating the whole work as Scripture; Jude draws on a familiar text whose message agreed with what Scripture teaches about the Lord’s coming judgment.

“*These are murmurers and complainers, walking after their lusts—and their mouth speaks proud things—showing respect of persons to gain advantage*” (*v. 16*). The intruders grumbled, followed their desires, boasted, and flattered people when it served their interests.

### Remember and Persevere (vv17–23)

“*But you, beloved, remember the words which have been spoken before by the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ.*” (*v. 17*) “*They said to you, “In the last time there will be mockers, walking after their own ungodly lusts.”*” (*v. 18*) Jude turns to the faithful with “But you, beloved.” The appearance of such people should not shake their faith. The apostles had warned that scoffers would come (*Acts 20:29–30*; *2 Timothy 3:1–5*; *2 Peter 3:3*).

“*These are those who cause divisions and are sensual, not having the Spirit*” (*v. 19*). The intruders may have claimed to be spiritual, but Jude says they do not have the Spirit at all. Their divisiveness and their focus on natural desires show it.

The call to keep oneself in God’s love and to show mercy are studied below.

### Doxology (vv24–25)

The closing praise to God is studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Jude 1:3–4* — Contend for the Faith

> *“Beloved, while I was very eager to write to you about our common salvation, I was constrained to write to you exhorting you to contend earnestly for the faith which was once for all delivered to the saints. For there are certain men who crept in secretly, even those who were long ago written about for this condemnation: ungodly men, turning the grace of our God into indecency, and denying our only Master, God, and Lord, Jesus Christ.”*
>
> — *Jude 1:3–4* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jude tells his readers that he had planned a different letter: “while I was very eager to write to you about our common salvation.” He wanted to celebrate the salvation all believers share. But circumstances changed: “I was constrained to write to you exhorting you to contend earnestly for the faith which was once for all delivered to the saints.”

“Contend earnestly” translates a word that pictures an athlete straining in a contest or a soldier fighting a battle. Jude calls believers to make a determined effort to defend and preserve the faith.

“The faith” here means the body of truth about Jesus Christ that God has revealed. It was “once for all delivered,” meaning it was given completely and does not need to be replaced or updated. “The saints” are all God’s people.

Verse 4 explains why this is urgent: “For there are certain men who crept in secretly.” These people had entered the church unnoticed. They were “turning the grace of our God into indecency,” using God’s grace as an excuse for immoral living, and “denying our only Master, God, and Lord, Jesus Christ,” rejecting His authority over their lives.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses teach that the Christian faith has content. It is not merely a feeling or a personal preference, but a revealed message about who God is and what He has done in Jesus Christ. This message was entrusted to the church through the apostles and is preserved in Scripture. Believers are its stewards, not its inventors.

The danger Jude describes is subtle. The intruders did not openly deny grace; they twisted it. They took the wonderful truth that God forgives freely and turned it into permission to sin. Paul faced the same distortion: “*What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound?*” (*Romans 6:1*) His answer, and Jude’s, is a firm no. True grace does not leave people in sin; it trains them to say no to ungodliness (*Titus 2:11–12*).

Jude also shows that denying Christ can be done not only with words but with life. To reject His lordship by living in defiance of Him is a practical denial of who He is. Faith and obedience belong together.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Contending for the faith does not mean being harsh, argumentative, or unkind. Jude himself, as the letter goes on, calls for mercy toward those who doubt. Contending means holding firmly to the truth of the gospel, knowing it well, living it faithfully, and refusing to let it be quietly changed into something else.

Believers today can contend for the faith by studying Scripture carefully, being part of churches that teach it faithfully, and gently correcting distortions when they appear, especially distortions that make grace an excuse for sin.

This passage also invites personal reflection. Believers can examine whether they are treating God’s grace as a gift that leads to holiness, or as a reason to excuse what God calls wrong. Grace is free, but it is never cheap.

### *Jude 1:20–21* — Keep Yourselves in God’s Love

> *“But you, beloved, keep building up yourselves on your most holy faith, praying in the Holy Spirit. Keep yourselves in God’s love, looking for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ to eternal life.”*
>
> — *Jude 1:20–21* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After describing the intruders, Jude turns to the faithful: “But you, beloved.” He gives them four instructions for staying strong.

First, “keep building up yourselves on your most holy faith.” The faith is like a foundation, and believers are to keep building their lives upon it through learning, worship, and obedience.

Second, they are to keep “praying in the Holy Spirit.” This means praying with the help and guidance of the Spirit, depending on Him rather than on mere human effort (*Romans 8:26*; *Ephesians 6:18*).

Third, in verse 21: “Keep yourselves in God’s love.” Believers cannot make God love them; He already does. But they can remain in the place where His love is enjoyed, staying close to Him and walking in His ways.

Fourth, they are to keep “looking for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ to eternal life.” They wait with hope for the return of Christ, when His mercy will bring them fully into eternal life.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses balance the beginning of the letter. In verse 1, Jude said that believers are “kept for Jesus Christ” by God. Now he says, “Keep yourselves in God’s love.” Both are true. God keeps His people, and His people respond by keeping themselves in His love. God’s protection does not make human effort unnecessary; it makes it possible. Jesus said something similar: “*Even as the Father has loved me, I also have loved you. Remain in my love*” (*John 15:9*).

The four instructions also reveal the Trinity at work in the Christian life. Believers pray in the Holy Spirit, keep themselves in the love of God the Father, and wait for the mercy of the Lord Jesus Christ. The whole life of faith is lived in relationship with the triune God.

Notice that Jude’s answer to the danger of false teaching is not anxious suspicion but positive spiritual growth. The best defense against error is a strong and growing faith, rooted in truth, sustained by prayer, and secure in God’s love.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can build themselves up in the faith by regularly reading and studying Scripture, learning sound teaching, worshiping with other believers, and putting what they learn into practice.

They can pray in the Holy Spirit by asking for His help, listening for His guidance, and depending on Him when they do not know what to pray.

Keeping oneself in God’s love means staying close to Him through daily trust and obedience, and turning away from anything that draws the heart away from Him. When believers drift, they can return quickly, knowing that God’s love has not changed.

Looking for Christ’s mercy gives believers hope. Whatever difficulties they face now, they can live with expectation, knowing that Jesus will return and bring them into the fullness of eternal life.

### *Jude 1:22–23* — Mercy for Those Who Waver

> *“On some have compassion, making a distinction, and some save, snatching them out of the fire with fear, hating even the clothing stained by the flesh.”*
>
> — *Jude 1:22–23* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jude now tells believers how to care for others affected by the false teaching. “On some have compassion, making a distinction.” Some people in the church were doubting or wavering. They needed mercy and patient help, not harsh condemnation.

Verse 23 continues: “and some save, snatching them out of the fire with fear.” Others were in greater danger, closer to being drawn into destructive sin. Believers are to act urgently, like someone pulling a person from a burning building.

Jude adds a caution: “hating even the clothing stained by the flesh.” Those who help others must be careful not to be drawn into sin themselves. They are to love the person while hating the sin that defiles.

The Greek manuscripts of these verses vary, and some translations describe two groups of people while others describe three. But the main teaching is the same: believers are to respond to those affected by error with discerning mercy, urgent rescue, and careful holiness.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

After strong words about judgment, Jude calls for mercy. This reflects the heart of God, who is rich in mercy and does not want anyone to perish (*2 Peter 3:9*). Those who receive mercy are called to show mercy. Believers who have just been told to wait for “the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ” (v21) are now to extend that mercy to others.

The phrase “making a distinction” shows that wisdom is needed. Not every situation is the same. Some people need gentle patience as they work through honest doubts. Others need urgent intervention. Love takes the time to understand where each person is.

The warning to hate “the clothing stained by the flesh” reflects the reality that sin can be contagious. Paul gave a similar caution when he urged believers to restore those caught in sin gently, while watching themselves so that they would not also be tempted (*Galatians 6:1*). Mercy and holiness go together.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers today will meet people who are wrestling with doubt, confused by false ideas, or drifting into harmful choices. This passage calls them to respond with compassion. Doubt is not the same as unbelief, and many who struggle with questions need patient friends who will walk with them.

At the same time, there are moments that call for urgency, when someone is in serious spiritual or moral danger. Love does not stay silent when a person is heading toward destruction. It speaks and acts with courage.

Those who help others should also guard their own hearts, seeking accountability and staying close to God. Helping someone out of the fire does not mean stepping into it.

### *Jude 1:24–25* — Able to Keep You from Stumbling

> *“Now to him who is able to keep them from stumbling, and to present you faultless before the presence of his glory in great joy, to God our Savior, who alone is wise, be glory and majesty, dominion and power, both now and forever. Amen.”*
>
> — *Jude 1:24–25* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Jude ends his letter with a hymn of praise. After warning about danger, he lifts believers’ eyes to God: “Now to him who is able to keep them from stumbling.” God is able to protect His people from falling away. Their security rests not on their own strength but on His power.

God is also able “to present you faultless before the presence of his glory in great joy.” One day believers will stand before God, not ashamed, but blameless, because of what Christ has done. And this will be an occasion of “great joy,” both for them and for God.

In verse 25, Jude gives glory “to God our Savior, who alone is wise.” All praise belongs to Him: “glory and majesty, dominion and power.” And this praise extends across all time, “both now and forever.”

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This doxology is one of the most comforting passages in Scripture. Jude has spoken of those who fell: Israelites in the wilderness, rebellious angels, the cities of the plain, Cain, Balaam, Korah, and the intruders. A reader might wonder whether they too could fall. Jude’s answer is to point to God, who is able to keep His people from stumbling.

The letter thus ends where it began. In verse 1, believers are “kept for Jesus Christ.” In verse 21, they are to keep themselves in God’s love. And in verse 24, God is able to keep them from stumbling. God’s keeping power surrounds the whole life of faith.

The picture of being presented “faultless” with “great joy” is rich with grace. Believers will not stand before God on the basis of their own record, but clothed in the righteousness of Christ (*2 Corinthians 5:21*). The joy of that day will be the joy of a Father welcoming His children home, and of a Savior presenting the people He redeemed.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers who feel weak or worry about falling away can take great comfort in this passage. Their perseverance does not finally depend on their own strength, but on the God who is able to keep them. They can bring their fears to Him and trust Him to hold them fast.

This doxology also invites worship. When believers face difficult times or troubling news, they can do what Jude did: turn their hearts to praise God for who He is and what He is able to do. Worship shifts the focus from fear to faith.

Finally, believers can live with hope, knowing that one day they will stand before God’s glory, not in shame but in great joy. That future can shape how they live today, with confidence, gratitude, and a desire to honor Him.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

Jude’s letter calls believers to take the faith seriously. The message of the gospel has been entrusted once for all to God’s people, and believers are called to contend for it, to hold it firmly, live it faithfully, and refuse to let it be twisted. Jude warns especially against turning God’s grace into an excuse for sin. Grace is a free gift, but it leads to a transformed life.

The letter also reminds believers that God’s judgment is real. The examples of Israel in the wilderness, the rebellious angels, and Sodom and Gomorrah show that God does not ignore rebellion. The images of empty clouds, fruitless trees, and wandering stars warn against a faith that looks impressive but has no substance. Believers can let these warnings lead them to examine their hearts and walk humbly with God.

Yet Jude’s main concern is not to frighten but to strengthen. He calls the faithful to build themselves up in their most holy faith, pray in the Holy Spirit, keep themselves in God’s love, and wait for the mercy of Jesus Christ. These practices keep believers rooted and growing, even when error surrounds them.

Jude also calls for mercy. Those who doubt need compassion. Those in danger need urgent help. Believers are to reach out with love, while guarding their own hearts from sin.

Above all, Jude points believers to the God who is able to keep them from stumbling and to present them faultless before His glory with great joy. Their security rests in Him. This truth gives courage to face any challenge and leads naturally to praise.

## Chapter Prayer

Father, thank You that I am called, loved by You, and kept for Jesus Christ. Give me courage to contend for the faith once for all delivered to Your people, and keep me from ever turning Your grace into an excuse for sin. Guard my heart from pride, rebellion, and empty religion. Help me to build my life on my most holy faith, to pray in the Holy Spirit, to keep myself in Your love, and to wait with hope for the mercy of my Lord Jesus Christ. Give me compassion for those who doubt and courage to help those in danger, while keeping my own heart pure. Thank You that You are able to keep me from stumbling and to present me faultless before Your glory with great joy. To You, the only wise God our Savior, be glory and majesty, dominion and power, now and forever. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Book 27 of 27

# Revelation

## About This Book

The book of Revelation opens with its own title: “*This is the Revelation of Jesus Christ*” (*Revelation 1:1*). The word “revelation” translates the Greek word *apokalypsis*, meaning an unveiling or disclosure. Revelation pulls back the curtain so that God’s people can see what is happening behind the events of history: the risen Christ ruling over His church, God reigning from His throne, evil being judged, and all things being made new.

The author calls himself John, a servant of Jesus Christ and a brother and companion of the believers in suffering (*1:9*). From the second century onward, most Christians identified him with John the apostle, the author of the Gospel and letters of John. Some ancient and modern scholars, noting differences in style, suggest another prophet named John who was well known to the churches of Asia. John received the visions while exiled on Patmos, a small island off the coast of modern Turkey, “because of God’s Word and the testimony of Jesus Christ.” Most scholars date the book to the reign of the emperor Domitian, around A.D. 95, though some date it earlier, near the time of Nero in the late 60s.

Revelation was first sent to seven real churches in the Roman province of Asia. These congregations faced pressure from many directions: hostility from neighbors, the demand to honor the emperor as a god, economic pressure to take part in trade guilds tied to idol worship, false teachers within, and, for some, the dangers of comfort and complacency. Revelation was written to strengthen these believers to remain faithful to Jesus, whatever the cost.

## How to Read Revelation

Revelation combines three kinds of writing. It is a letter, addressed to churches with real needs. It is a prophecy, a message from God calling His people to faithfulness. And it is an apocalypse, a type of Jewish and Christian writing that uses vivid symbols and visions to reveal heavenly realities. Readers in John’s day were familiar with this kind of imagery from books like Daniel, Ezekiel, and Zechariah. Revelation contains hundreds of allusions to the Old Testament, and much of its imagery is explained by those earlier Scriptures.

Because the book is full of symbols, numbers, and visions, it is important to read it carefully. Some symbols are explained in the text itself, such as the lampstands, which are churches (*1:20*), or the dragon, which is Satan (*12:9*). Numbers often carry symbolic meaning: seven suggests completeness, twelve suggests God’s people, and a thousand suggests a vast multitude or a long period. Readers do well to ask what each image meant to the original readers before asking how it applies today.

Christians have read Revelation in several main ways. The **preterist** view understands most of the book as describing events in the first century, such as the persecution of the church by Rome and the fall of Jerusalem or of the Roman Empire. The **historicist** view sees Revelation as a broad overview of church history from the first century to the return of Christ. The **futurist** view holds that most of the book, especially chapters 4–22, describes events that will take place in the period leading up to Christ’s return. The **idealist**, or spiritual, view sees the book as portraying timeless truths about the conflict between God and evil that apply in every age. Many readers today combine elements of these views, recognizing that Revelation spoke directly to its first readers, reveals patterns that recur throughout history, and points ahead to the final victory of Christ.

Christians also hold different views about the thousand years described in chapter 20, and about how the events of the book relate to one another in time. Sincere and faithful believers differ on these questions. This commentary presents the main interpretations fairly while focusing on what all agree the book clearly teaches.

## The Shape of the Book

Revelation opens with a vision of the risen Christ standing among His churches (chapter 1), followed by His messages to seven churches in Asia (chapters 2–3). John is then taken up into heaven to see God’s throne and the Lamb who was slain, who alone is worthy to open the sealed scroll (chapters 4–5). The opening of seven seals, the sounding of seven trumpets, and the pouring out of seven bowls portray God’s judgments on a rebellious world, with interludes that show God’s protection of His people (chapters 6–16). The central chapters reveal the spiritual conflict behind history: the dragon, the beast from the sea, and the beast from the land, opposed by the Lamb and His faithful followers (chapters 12–14). The fall of Babylon, the great city that represents human pride and opposition to God, is announced and mourned (chapters 17–18). Then heaven rejoices, Christ returns as the rider on the white horse, Satan is bound and finally defeated, and the dead are judged (chapters 19–20). The book ends with a vision of the new heaven and new earth, the holy city, the new Jerusalem, where God dwells with His people forever (chapters 21–22).

## Themes to Watch For

Watch for the sovereignty of God, who sits on the throne; the Lamb who was slain and conquered through His sacrifice; the call to faithful witness and endurance; worship in heaven and on earth; the reality of spiritual conflict; God’s righteous judgment on evil; the protection of God’s people; the fall of every power that opposes God; the return of Christ; and the hope of a renewed creation where God wipes every tear away. Revelation is not meant to frighten God’s people or to fuel speculation, but to give them hope and courage. Its central message is that Jesus Christ has conquered, and that those who belong to Him will share His victory.
