Revelation · Chapter 4 of 22

# Revelation — Chapter 4

Chapter Theme: The Throne Room of Heaven

[Read Revelation 4 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/REV04.htm)

Main Teaching

After the messages to the churches, John sees a door standing open in heaven and hears the voice like a trumpet inviting him to come up and see what must take place. In the Spirit, he sees a throne in heaven with One seated on it, shining like jasper and carnelian, surrounded by a rainbow like an emerald. Around the throne are twenty-four other thrones with twenty-four elders dressed in white and wearing golden crowns. From the throne come flashes of lightning and peals of thunder, and before it burn seven lamps of fire, the seven Spirits of God. In front of the throne is something like a sea of glass, clear as crystal. Around the throne are four living creatures, full of eyes, resembling a lion, an ox, a man, and a flying eagle. Each has six wings, and day and night they never stop saying, Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come. Whenever they give glory, honor, and thanks to the One on the throne, the twenty-four elders fall down and worship Him, casting their crowns before the throne and declaring that He is worthy to receive glory, honor, and power, because He created all things and by His will they exist.

## Chapter Background and Story

With chapter 4, Revelation moves from earth to heaven. In chapters 2 and 3, John saw the churches struggling with persecution, compromise, and complacency. Now he is shown the reality behind and above all earthly events: God reigning on His throne. Before John sees any of the judgments that follow, he sees the One who rules over all.

This vision would have been deeply encouraging to the first readers. The Roman emperor sat on a throne, surrounded by attendants and receiving honor from his subjects. Some emperors were even hailed as “lord and god.” *Revelation 4* shows that the true throne is in heaven, and the true Lord and God is the One who created all things.

The scene draws on earlier visions of God’s throne in the Old Testament, especially *Isaiah 6*, *Ezekiel 1*, and *Daniel 7*. It is a picture of worship at the center of all reality.

### The Open Door and the Invitation (*4:1–2*a)

“*After these things I looked and saw a door opened in heaven; and the first voice that I heard, like a trumpet speaking with me, was one saying, “Come up here, and I will show you the things which must happen after this.”*” (*v. 1*) The voice is the same trumpet-like voice John heard in 1:10, the voice of the risen Christ. The open door invites John into heaven’s perspective.

Some futurist interpreters, especially those who hold a pretribulation view, see John’s being called up to heaven as a picture of the church being taken up before the tribulation, noting that the word “church” (or “assembly”) does not appear again in chapters 4–19 until the end of the book. Most other interpreters see this as John’s personal visionary experience, similar to the prophets who were shown heavenly scenes, and point out that God’s people (called “saints” and “servants”) remain present on earth throughout the following chapters. What is clear is that John is given a heavenly vantage point to understand what happens on earth.

“*Immediately I was in the Spirit. Behold, there was a throne set in heaven, and one sitting on the throne*” (*v. 2*) The vision of the throne and the One seated on it is studied below.

### The Elders and the Throne (*4:4–6*a)

“*Around the throne were twenty-four thrones. On the thrones were twenty-four elders sitting, dressed in white garments, with crowns of gold on their heads*” (*v. 4*). The twenty-four elders have been understood in several ways. Many interpreters see them as representing the whole people of God, perhaps the twelve tribes of Israel and the twelve apostles together (compare 21:12–14). Others see them as a high order of angels who serve in God’s heavenly court. Their white garments suggest purity, their thrones suggest a share in God’s rule, and their golden crowns suggest victory. Whatever their exact identity, they lead heaven in worship.

“*Out of the throne proceed lightnings, sounds, and thunders. There were seven lamps of fire burning before his throne, which are the seven Spirits of God*” (*v. 5*). Lightning and thunder recall God’s appearance at Mount Sinai (*Exodus 19:16*), showing His awesome power and holiness. The seven lamps represent the Holy Spirit in His fullness (compare 1:4; *Zechariah 4:2–6*).

“*Before the throne was something like a sea of glass, similar to crystal. In the middle of the throne, and around the throne were four living creatures full of eyes before and behind*” (*v. 6*). The sea of glass may recall the “expanse” like crystal above the living creatures in *Ezekiel 1:22*, or the great bronze basin called “the sea” in Solomon’s temple (*1 Kings 7:23*). In the ancient world, the sea often symbolized chaos and danger. Here it is calm and still as glass before God’s throne, suggesting that nothing threatens His rule.

### The Four Living Creatures (*4:6*b–8)

“*The first creature was like a lion, the second creature like a calf, the third creature had a face like a man, and the fourth was like a flying eagle*” (*v. 7*). These creatures resemble the cherubim in *Ezekiel 1* and the seraphim in *Isaiah 6*. Their four forms have been understood to represent the noblest of created beings: the lion among wild animals, the ox among domestic animals, humanity as the crown of creation, and the eagle among birds. Together they may represent all creation worshiping God. Being “full of eyes” suggests constant watchfulness and knowledge. In later Christian tradition, these four figures came to be used as symbols of the four Gospel writers, though that is a later application rather than John’s original meaning. Their unceasing song is studied below.

### The Elders’ Worship (*4:9–11*)

“*When the living creatures give glory, honor, and thanks to him who sits on the throne, to him who lives forever and ever,*” (*v. 9*) The worship of the living creatures leads the elders to join in. The elders’ response is studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Revelation 4:2–3* — A Throne in Heaven

> *“Immediately I was in the Spirit. Behold, there was a throne set in heaven, and one sitting on the throne that looked like a jasper stone and a sardius. There was a rainbow around the throne, like an emerald to look at.”*
>
> — *Revelation 4:2–3* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

When John enters heaven in the Spirit, the first thing he sees is a throne: “Behold, there was a throne set in heaven, and one sitting on the throne.” The throne is the center of the whole vision. Everything else in the chapter is arranged around it.

John does not describe the appearance of the One on the throne in human terms. Instead, he uses the language of precious stones: He “looked like a jasper stone and a sardius.” Jasper was a brilliant, often clear stone, and sardius (carnelian) was a deep red stone. John can only describe God’s glory by comparison with the most dazzling things he knows.

Then he adds: “There was a rainbow around the throne, like an emerald to look at.” A rainbow encircles the throne, glowing with a green light.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The throne is one of the central images of Revelation. The word appears more than forty times in the book. The repeated message is that God reigns. No matter what chaos unfolds on earth, no matter how powerful earthly rulers appear, God is seated on His throne, and His rule is unshaken.

John’s reluctance to describe God’s form reflects the reverence of Scripture. Ezekiel, seeing a similar vision, spoke only of “*the appearance of the likeness of the LORD’s glory*” (*Ezekiel 1:28*). God is beyond human description. Precious stones and light are the closest comparisons.

The rainbow is especially meaningful. After the flood, God placed a rainbow in the sky as a sign of His covenant promise never again to destroy the earth by flood (*Genesis 9:12–17*). A rainbow also surrounded the throne in Ezekiel’s vision (*Ezekiel 1:28*). Around the throne from which judgments will come, there is a reminder of God’s mercy and faithfulness. His judgments will be just, but His covenant love remains.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

When life feels chaotic or frightening, believers can remember that there is a throne in heaven, and it is not empty. God reigns over every nation, every circumstance, and every moment of history. This truth brings stability and peace.

This vision also invites believers to worship. Before asking God for help or seeking answers about the future, believers can pause to behold who He is: glorious, holy, and faithful.

The rainbow reminds believers that God’s power is always joined to His promises. They can trust that the One who rules over all is also the God who keeps His covenant with His people.

### *Revelation 4:8* — Holy, Holy, Holy

> *“The four living creatures, each one of them having six wings, are full of eyes around and within. They have no rest day and night, saying, ‘Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God, the Almighty, who was and who is and who is to come!’”*
>
> — *Revelation 4:8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The four living creatures each have “six wings” and are “full of eyes around and within.” These details recall the seraphim in Isaiah’s vision (*Isaiah 6:2*) and the cherubim in Ezekiel’s vision (*Ezekiel 1:18*; *10:12*).

Their worship never stops: “They have no rest day and night.” Their song is constant: “Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God, the Almighty, who was and who is and who is to come!”

They declare three things about God. He is holy, utterly pure and set apart from all that is sinful and created. He is “the Lord God, the Almighty,” all-powerful and sovereign over all. And He is eternal, the One “who was and who is and who is to come.”

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The threefold “holy” echoes the song of the seraphim in “*Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of Armies! The whole earth is full of his glory!*” (*Isaiah 6:3*) In Hebrew, repetition is a way of emphasizing something. Saying “holy” three times expresses the highest degree of holiness. Holiness is at the very heart of who God is. Many Christians have also seen in the threefold “holy” a hint of the Trinity, though the primary meaning is the supreme holiness of God.

The phrase “who was and who is and who is to come” emphasizes God’s eternal nature. He existed before all things, He is present now, and He will come to complete His purposes. The order here, beginning with “who was,” highlights God’s faithfulness through all of history.

The fact that these creatures worship “day and night” without rest shows that worship is not an occasional activity in heaven but the constant atmosphere. Worship is the proper response of all creation to its Creator, and it will be the joy of God’s people forever.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This verse invites believers to grow in their awareness of God’s holiness. In a culture that often treats God casually or ignores Him altogether, believers can recover a sense of awe and reverence.

Recognizing God’s holiness also leads to humility. Like Isaiah, who cried out about his own uncleanness when he saw God’s holiness (*Isaiah 6:5*), believers become aware of their need for God’s grace. Yet through Christ, they are invited to approach the holy God with confidence.

Believers can join heaven’s worship in their own lives, in personal devotion, in gathered worship, and in daily living. Every act of praise on earth echoes the unending song of heaven.

### *Revelation 4:10–11* — Worthy Are You, Our Lord and God

> *“the twenty-four elders fall down before him who sits on the throne and worship him who lives forever and ever, and throw their crowns before the throne, saying, ‘Worthy are you, our Lord and God, the Holy One, to receive the glory, the honor, and the power, for you created all things, and because of your desire they existed and were created!’”*
>
> — *Revelation 4:10–11* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

When the living creatures give glory to God, the twenty-four elders respond. They “fall down before him who sits on the throne and worship him who lives forever and ever.” Falling down is a posture of complete humility and reverence.

Then they “throw their crowns before the throne.” The crowns they wear, symbols of honor and victory, are laid down before God. They acknowledge that every honor they have comes from Him and belongs to Him.

Their song, in verse 11, declares: “Worthy are you, our Lord and God, the Holy One, to receive the glory, the honor, and the power.” The reason for God’s worthiness is given: “for you created all things, and because of your desire they existed and were created!”

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The title “our Lord and God” is striking. The Roman emperor Domitian is reported to have demanded to be addressed as “our lord and god.” The heavenly worshipers give this title to the true God alone. This would have encouraged believers who were pressured to honor the emperor as divine. There is only one who truly deserves such worship.

The basis of God’s worthiness in this chapter is creation. He made all things, and everything exists because of His will. Creation is not an accident; it is the expression of God’s purpose and desire. Because He is the Creator, He is the rightful owner and ruler of all things. In chapter 5, the song will add a second reason for worship: redemption through the Lamb.

The casting of crowns teaches something about the nature of worship. Even the highest honors given to God’s servants are to be returned to Him. True worship recognizes that all good things come from God and exist for His glory.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can follow the example of the elders by giving God the honor He deserves. Every achievement, gift, and success can be laid before Him with gratitude, recognizing that He is the source of all good things.

This passage also gives believers a foundation for their sense of worth and purpose. They exist because God willed it. Their lives are not accidents. They were created by a loving Creator, for His glory.

Recognizing God as Creator can also shape how believers treat the world around them. Creation belongs to God and reflects His glory. Believers can care for it, enjoy it with thanksgiving, and see in it reasons to worship.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Revelation 4* lifts believers’ eyes from the struggles of earth to the throne of heaven. Before any of the book’s judgments unfold, John sees that God reigns. This is the foundation for everything that follows. Whatever happens in history, whatever trials believers face, God is seated on His throne, and His rule cannot be shaken.

The chapter also shows that worship is the center of heaven. The living creatures cry “holy” day and night, and the elders cast their crowns before the throne. Believers are invited to join this worship now, with reverence for God’s holiness, gratitude for His creation, and humble surrender of every honor to Him.

The vision encourages believers to trust God’s character. His throne is surrounded by a rainbow, the sign of His covenant faithfulness. His holiness is perfect. His power is unlimited. He is eternal, the One who was and is and is to come. Believers can rest in His care and live with confidence, knowing that the One who created all things holds all things in His hands.

Finally, the chapter challenges every rival claim to ultimate authority. Earthly rulers, systems, and powers may demand loyalty and honor, but only God is worthy to be called “our Lord and God.” Believers are called to give Him first place in their hearts and lives.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord God Almighty, You are seated on the throne of heaven, and Your rule cannot be shaken. When my world feels uncertain, help me to lift my eyes to You and remember that You reign. You are holy, holy, holy, the One who was and is and is to come. Fill me with awe at Your holiness and gratitude for Your faithfulness. Thank You that You created all things, and that I exist because of Your will. I lay before You every honor, every gift, and every success, for they all belong to You. Teach me to worship You with my whole life, joining the song of heaven. You alone are worthy, my Lord and my God, to receive glory, honor, and power. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Revelation · Chapter 5 of 22

# Revelation — Chapter 5

Chapter Theme: The Lamb Who Is Worthy

[Read Revelation 5 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/REV05.htm)

Main Teaching

In the right hand of the One seated on the throne, John sees a scroll written on both sides and sealed with seven seals. A mighty angel asks who is worthy to break the seals and open the scroll, but no one in heaven, on earth, or under the earth can open it or even look inside. John weeps bitterly. Then one of the elders tells him not to weep, because the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has triumphed and is able to open the scroll. When John looks, he sees not a lion but a Lamb, standing as though it had been slain, in the center of the throne, with seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven Spirits of God sent out into all the earth. The Lamb takes the scroll, and the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fall down before Him, holding harps and golden bowls of incense, which are the prayers of God’s people. They sing a new song: He is worthy to take the scroll and open its seals, because He was slain, and with His blood He purchased people for God from every tribe, language, people, and nation, and made them a kingdom and priests to serve God, and they will reign on the earth. Then countless angels join in, proclaiming that the Lamb who was slain is worthy to receive power, wealth, wisdom, strength, honor, glory, and blessing. Finally every creature in heaven, on earth, under the earth, and in the sea praises the One on the throne and the Lamb forever, and the elders fall down and worship.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Revelation 5* continues the heavenly vision of chapter 4. In chapter 4, God is worshiped as Creator. In chapter 5, the focus shifts to the Lamb, Jesus Christ, who is worshiped as Redeemer. Together these two chapters form one great vision of the throne room of heaven, and they provide the foundation for everything that follows in the book.

The central question of the chapter is: Who is worthy to open the scroll? The answer reveals the heart of the Christian faith. The One who is worthy is the Lamb who was slain. His victory came not through military force or political power, but through sacrificial death. This is the key to understanding all of Revelation: God’s purposes are accomplished through the cross.

### The Sealed Scroll (*5:1–4*)

“*I saw, in the right hand of him who sat on the throne, a book written inside and outside, sealed shut with seven seals*” (*v. 1*). The “book” is a scroll, the usual form of written documents in John’s day. It is written on both sides, suggesting that its contents are complete. It is sealed with seven seals, meaning it is fully secured and can only be opened by someone with proper authority.

What does the scroll represent? Interpreters have offered several views. Many see it as God’s plan for history, His purposes of judgment and redemption that will bring the world to its intended end. Others see it as a kind of title deed to creation, which the rightful heir alone can claim. Others connect it with the sealed scroll in *Daniel 12:4*, which contained revelation about the end times, or with the scroll of lament and judgment in *Ezekiel 2:9–10*. In each view, the scroll contains God’s purposes for bringing history to its goal, and the opening of its seals sets those purposes in motion.

“*I saw a mighty angel proclaiming with a loud voice, “Who is worthy to open the book, and to break its seals?”*” (*v. 2*) “*No one in heaven above, or on the earth, or under the earth, was able to open the book or to look in it*” (*v. 3*). The search covers all creation, and no one is found worthy. No angel, no human ruler, no prophet, and no spiritual power has the authority to carry out God’s purposes for the world.

“*Then I wept much, because no one was found worthy to open the book or to look in it*” (*v. 4*). John’s tears are not merely disappointment. If no one can open the scroll, then God’s purposes of justice and redemption will remain unfulfilled. Evil will continue unchecked, and the suffering of God’s people will have no resolution.

### The Lion Who Is a Lamb (*5:5–7*)

The elder’s announcement and John’s vision of the Lamb are studied below. “*Then he came, and he took it out of the right hand of him who sat on the throne*” (*v. 7*). The Lamb takes the scroll directly from God’s hand. This simple action has enormous meaning. The Lamb has authority to carry out God’s plan for history, and He shares the authority of the One on the throne.

### The New Song (*5:8–10*)

“*Now when he had taken the book, the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell down before the Lamb, each one having a harp, and golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints*” (*v. 8*). The worship that was given to God in chapter 4 is now given to the Lamb. This shows that Jesus is fully divine, worthy of the same worship as God the Father. The harps represent praise. The golden bowls of incense are explained as “the prayers of the saints.” The prayers of God’s people, often offered in suffering and weakness, rise before God’s throne like fragrant incense (*Psalm 141:2*). These prayers will play an important role later in the book (*Revelation 8:3–5*). The song itself is studied below.

### All Creation Worships (*5:11–14*)

“*I looked, and I heard something like a voice of many angels around the throne, the living creatures, and the elders. The number of them was ten thousands of ten thousands, and thousands of thousands,*” (*v. 11*) The circle of worship widens. Countless angels join the song. The number is meant to express a multitude beyond counting (compare *Daniel 7:10*).

“*saying with a loud voice, “Worthy is the Lamb who has been killed to receive the power, wealth, wisdom, strength, honor, glory, and blessing!”*” (*v. 12*) The angels ascribe seven qualities to the Lamb, a number of completeness. Every form of honor and power belongs to Him.

“*I heard every created thing which is in heaven, on the earth, under the earth, on the sea, and everything in them, saying, “To him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be the blessing, the honor, the glory, and the dominion, forever and ever! Amen!”*” (*v. 13*) Finally, all creation joins in. The worship of the One on the throne and the worship of the Lamb are united. They receive the same praise, together, forever.

“*The four living creatures said, “Amen!” Then the elders fell down and worshiped*” (*v. 14*). The scene ends as the living creatures affirm the praise with “Amen,” and the elders fall down in worship. The circle of worship that began around the throne has expanded to include the entire universe.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Revelation 5:5–6* — The Lion Who Is a Lamb

> *“One of the elders said to me, ‘Don’t weep. Behold, the Lion who is of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has overcome: he who opens the book and its seven seals.’ I saw in the middle of the throne and of the four living creatures, and in the middle of the elders, a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain, having seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven Spirits of God, sent out into all the earth.”*
>
> — *Revelation 5:5–6* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

As John weeps, one of the elders speaks to him: “Don’t weep.” There is someone who can open the scroll. The elder describes Him with two titles from the Old Testament.

He is “the Lion who is of the tribe of Judah.” This recalls Jacob’s blessing in *Genesis 49:9–10*, where Judah is called a lion’s cub and promised that the scepter will not depart from him. The Lion of Judah is the promised King from the line of Judah.

He is also “the Root of David.” This recalls *Isaiah 11:1* and *11:10*, which promise that a shoot will come from the stump of Jesse, David’s father, and that the Root of Jesse will stand as a banner for the nations. Jesus is the promised descendant of David who will reign forever.

The elder announces that this One “has overcome.” His victory qualifies Him to open the scroll.

Then John turns to see the Lion, and he sees something unexpected: “a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain.” The Lion is a Lamb. And the Lamb bears the marks of death, yet He is standing, alive.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This is one of the most important moments in all of Revelation. John hears about a Lion, but he sees a Lamb. The Messiah’s victory did not come through force or violence, as many expected, but through sacrificial death. Jesus conquered by dying for His people. The Lion of Judah won His triumph as the Lamb of God.

The image of the Lamb recalls the Passover lamb, whose blood protected Israel from judgment and whose sacrifice marked their deliverance from Egypt (*Exodus 12*). It also recalls *Isaiah 53:7*, where the Servant of the Lord is led like a lamb to the slaughter. John the Baptist had pointed to Jesus and said, “*Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!*” (*John 1:29*) The word “Lamb” appears about twenty-nine times in Revelation, more than any other title for Jesus.

The Lamb is “standing,” showing that He is risen and alive. Yet He bears the marks of having been slain. His death is not hidden but is the very basis of His glory. The “seven horns” represent complete power, since horns symbolized strength in the Old Testament. The “seven eyes, which are the seven Spirits of God, sent out into all the earth” represent complete knowledge and the presence of the Holy Spirit throughout the world.

The Lamb stands “in the middle of the throne.” He shares God’s own place of rule. The crucified Jesus is now enthroned as Lord of all.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage shows that God’s power is revealed in the cross. The world values strength, force, and domination. But Jesus conquered through self-giving love. Believers are called to follow the Lamb, overcoming evil not by imitating the world’s methods, but by faithfulness, truth, and sacrificial love.

When believers weep over the brokenness of the world or the apparent triumph of evil, they can hear the elder’s words: “Don’t weep.” The Lamb has conquered. History is in His hands.

Believers can also find comfort in the Lamb’s wounds. The One who reigns over all still bears the marks of His suffering. He understands pain and sacrifice, and His wounds are the source of their healing and hope.

### *Revelation 5:9–10* — Purchased from Every Nation

> *“They sang a new song, saying, ‘You are worthy to take the book and to open its seals, for you were killed, and bought us for God with your blood out of every tribe, language, people, and nation, and made us kings and priests to our God; and we will reign on the earth.’”*
>
> — *Revelation 5:9–10* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The living creatures and elders sing “a new song.” In the Old Testament, a new song was sung to celebrate a fresh act of God’s salvation (*Psalm 96:1*; *98:1*; *Isaiah 42:10*). The death and resurrection of the Lamb is the greatest act of salvation in history, and it calls for a new song.

The song begins: “You are worthy to take the book and to open its seals.” Then it gives the reason: “for you were killed, and bought us for God with your blood.” The Lamb’s death was a purchase. His blood was the price paid to redeem people for God.

These people come “out of every tribe, language, people, and nation.” The Lamb’s redemption is not limited to one nation or group. It reaches every part of humanity.

Verse 10 describes what the Lamb has made them: “and made us kings and priests to our God.” The redeemed share in God’s rule and serve Him in worship. Then comes a promise: “and we will reign on the earth.”

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The idea of being “bought” or redeemed recalls the practice of buying a slave’s freedom or redeeming property that had been lost. Humanity was in bondage to sin and death. Jesus paid the price of redemption with His own blood (*1 Corinthians 6:20*; *1 Peter 1:18–19*). Those He redeemed now belong to God.

The global scope of redemption is one of the great themes of Revelation. God promised Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him (*Genesis 12:3*). That promise is fulfilled through the Lamb, who has redeemed people from every culture, language, and nation. The church is not meant to be a single ethnic or cultural group but a diverse family united in worship of the Lamb. This vision leaves no room for racial or ethnic pride or prejudice among God’s people.

The promise that the redeemed will “reign on the earth” points to the future renewal of creation. God’s purpose is not to abandon the earth but to restore it. His people will share in Christ’s reign over a renewed world (*Revelation 22:5*). Interpreters differ on how this reign relates to the thousand years of chapter 20 and to the new creation of chapters 21–22, but all agree that God’s people will share in Christ’s victory and rule.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can rejoice that they have been purchased by the blood of the Lamb. Their worth and identity come from the price He paid. They belong to God.

This passage calls believers to embrace the global and diverse nature of God’s family. Every tribe, language, people, and nation is represented around the throne. Believers can celebrate this diversity now, welcoming people of all backgrounds, rejecting prejudice, and supporting the spread of the gospel to every people.

The promise of reigning on the earth gives believers hope. The present world, with its injustice and suffering, is not the end of the story. God’s people will one day share in Christ’s righteous rule over a renewed creation. This hope encourages faithful living now.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Revelation 5* reveals the heart of the gospel. The central question of history, who is worthy to carry out God’s purposes, is answered by the Lamb who was slain. Jesus is the Lion of Judah, the Root of David, the promised King. But He conquered not through force but through sacrificial death. His cross is the key to history.

This chapter invites believers to see the world through the lens of the Lamb. When evil seems strong and God’s purposes seem hidden, they can remember that the Lamb has conquered and holds the scroll of history in His hands. There is no need for despair. God’s purposes will be fulfilled.

The chapter also calls believers to follow the way of the Lamb. Just as Jesus overcame through self-giving love, His people are called to overcome evil not with the world’s weapons, but with faithfulness, truth, and love.

Believers can rejoice in their redemption. They were purchased by the Lamb’s blood from every tribe, language, people, and nation, and made into a kingdom and priests to serve God. This gives them a secure identity, a purpose in worship and service, and a sense of belonging to a worldwide family.

Finally, the chapter calls believers to join the worship of heaven. The prayers of God’s people rise before the throne like incense, and all creation sings the praise of the One on the throne and the Lamb. Believers can add their voices to this song, now and forever.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, You are the Lion of the tribe of Judah and the Root of David, and You are the Lamb who was slain. Thank You that You conquered not by force, but by giving Your life for me. Thank You that with Your blood You purchased me for God, and that You have redeemed people from every tribe, language, people, and nation. Help me to love and welcome all whom You have redeemed. When I weep over the brokenness of the world, remind me that You hold history in Your hands and that You have overcome. Teach me to follow Your way of faithful, sacrificial love. Receive my prayers like incense before Your throne. You are worthy to receive power, wealth, wisdom, strength, honor, glory, and blessing. With all creation, I worship You and the One who sits on the throne, forever and ever. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Revelation · Chapter 6 of 22

# Revelation — Chapter 6

Chapter Theme: The Opening of the Seals

[Read Revelation 6 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/REV06.htm)

Main Teaching

The Lamb begins to open the seven seals of the scroll. As He opens the first four, each of the four living creatures calls out, and four horsemen ride out. The first rides a white horse, holding a bow, wearing a crown, and going out to conquer. The second rides a red horse and is given power to take peace from the earth so that people kill one another. The third rides a black horse and holds a pair of scales, while a voice announces prices that signal severe scarcity, yet the oil and wine are not to be harmed. The fourth rides a pale horse; his name is Death, and Hades follows him, and they are given authority over a fourth of the earth to kill by sword, famine, plague, and wild beasts. When the Lamb opens the fifth seal, John sees under the altar the souls of those who were killed for the word of God and their testimony. They cry out, asking how long until God judges and avenges their blood. Each is given a white robe and told to rest a little longer until the number of their fellow servants who will be killed is complete. When the sixth seal is opened, there is a great earthquake; the sun turns black, the moon turns like blood, the stars fall, the sky recedes like a scroll, and every mountain and island is moved. People of every rank hide in caves and call on the mountains to fall on them and hide them from the face of the One on the throne and from the wrath of the Lamb, for the great day of their wrath has come, and who can stand?

## Chapter Background and Story

In chapter 5, the Lamb received the sealed scroll. Now He begins to open it. As each seal is broken, a new scene unfolds. The opening of the seals is the first of three series of seven judgments in Revelation, followed by the seven trumpets (chapters 8–11) and the seven bowls (chapters 15–16).

A key point to notice is who opens the seals: the Lamb. The events that follow are not random disasters or the work of evil powers acting freely. They unfold under the authority of the crucified and risen Christ. Even the troubles of history are within His control.

### How the Seals Are Understood

Interpreters understand the seals in several ways. **Futurist** interpreters generally see them as events of a future period of tribulation before Christ’s return. **Preterist** interpreters connect them with events of the first century, such as wars, famines, and the persecution of Christians under Rome. **Historicist** interpreters have linked them with successive stages in the history of the Roman Empire and the church. **Idealist** interpreters see them as describing conditions that mark the whole period between Christ’s first and second comings: war, conflict, scarcity, death, persecution, and the certainty of final judgment.

Many readers notice that the first four seals closely resemble Jesus’ teaching in *Matthew 24*, *Mark 13*, and *Luke 21*, where He describes wars, famines, earthquakes, persecution, and cosmic signs as “*the beginning of birth pains*” (*Matthew 24:8*). On this reading, the seals depict the kind of suffering that will mark history until the end, leading up to the final day of judgment in the sixth seal. The four horsemen also echo *Zechariah 1:8–11* and *6:1–8*, where horses of different colors are sent out over the earth by God.

### The Four Horsemen (*6:1–8*)

The first horseman is studied below.

“*When he opened the second seal, I heard the second living creature saying, “Come!”*” (*v. 3*) “*Another came out, a red horse. To him who sat on it was given power to take peace from the earth, and that they should kill one another. There was given to him a great sword*” (*v. 4*). The red horse represents war and bloodshed. The Roman Empire boasted of the “Pax Romana,” the peace of Rome, but this rider takes peace from the earth. Human beings turn against one another in violence. Notice the repeated phrase “was given”: this rider acts only by permission. His power is limited by God.

“*When he opened the third seal, I heard the third living creature saying, “Come and see!” And behold, a black horse, and he who sat on it had a balance in his hand*” (*v. 5*). “*I heard a voice in the middle of the four living creatures saying, “A choenix of wheat for a denarius, and three choenix of barley for a denarius! Don’t damage the oil and the wine!”*” (*v. 6*) The black horse represents famine and economic hardship. The scales were used to measure food. A choenix was roughly a quart, about a day’s ration for one person, and a denarius was about a day’s wage for a laborer. These prices are many times higher than normal. A worker’s whole wage would buy only enough wheat for himself, or enough cheaper barley for a small family. The command not to harm the oil and wine may suggest that the famine is limited, or it may highlight an injustice in which basic foods become unaffordable while luxuries remain available to the wealthy. Either way, the voice from among the living creatures shows that even this hardship has limits set by God.

“*When he opened the fourth seal, I heard the fourth living creature saying, “Come and see!”*” (*v. 7*) “*And behold, a pale horse, and the name of he who sat on it was Death. Hades followed with him. Authority over one fourth of the earth, to kill with the sword, with famine, with death, and by the wild animals of the earth was given to him*” (*v. 8*). The word translated “pale” describes a sickly greenish-gray color, the color of a corpse. The rider is named Death, and Hades, the realm of the dead, follows him. The four means of death, sword, famine, plague (“death”), and wild beasts, echo God’s “four severe judgments” in *Ezekiel 14:21*. Again, the destruction is limited: one fourth of the earth. And it was “given” to him. Death itself acts only within limits set by God, and Christ holds the keys of Death and Hades (*Revelation 1:18*).

### The Cry of the Martyrs (*6:9–11*)

The fifth seal is studied below.

### The Great Day of Wrath (*6:12–17*)

“*I saw when he opened the sixth seal, and there was a great earthquake. The sun became black as sackcloth made of hair, and the whole moon became as blood*” (*v. 12*). “*The stars of the sky fell to the earth, like a fig tree dropping its unripe figs when it is shaken by a great wind*” (*v. 13*). “*The sky was removed like a scroll when it is rolled up. Every mountain and island was moved out of its place*” (*v. 14*).

The sixth seal uses imagery drawn from the Old Testament prophets, who described the day of the Lord with cosmic signs: the sun darkened, the moon turned to blood, the stars falling, and the heavens rolled up like a scroll (*Isaiah 13:10*; *34:4*; *Joel 2:31*; *Haggai 2:6*). Jesus used the same language to describe the time of His coming (*Matthew 24:29*).

Interpreters understand these images in different ways. Some take them as literal cosmic upheavals at the end of the age. Others understand them as prophetic symbols for the collapse of earthly powers and the shaking of the whole order of the world, since the prophets used such language for the fall of nations like Babylon and Edom. Still others see both: symbolic language that points to a real, final, world-shaking day of judgment. In every view, the sixth seal portrays the overturning of everything human beings thought was stable, as God comes in judgment. The response of humanity is studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Revelation 6:1–2* — The Rider on the White Horse

> *“I saw that the Lamb opened one of the seven seals, and I heard one of the four living creatures saying, as with a voice of thunder, ‘Come and see!’ Then a white horse appeared, and he who sat on it had a bow. A crown was given to him, and he came out conquering, and to conquer.”*
>
> — *Revelation 6:1–2* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The Lamb opens the first seal, and one of the four living creatures calls out with a voice like thunder: “Come and see!” The command may be addressed to John, inviting him to look, or to the rider, summoning him to go out.

Then John sees “a white horse,” and its rider “had a bow.” The rider is given a crown, and “he came out conquering, and to conquer.” He is a conqueror on a mission of conquest.

Unlike the other three riders, this one’s identity is not obvious, and interpreters have understood him in different ways.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Some interpreters see this rider as Christ, or as the victorious spread of the gospel. They point out that white in Revelation usually represents purity and victory, and that Christ later appears on a white horse (*19:11*). Jesus also said that the gospel would be preached to all nations before the end (*Matthew 24:14*). On this view, the first seal shows the gospel going out victoriously even as war, famine, and death follow.

Many other interpreters see the rider as a symbol of conquest and militarism, or as a false messiah or deceiving power that imitates Christ. They note that the other three riders all represent destructive forces, so the first likely does as well. The bow may recall the Parthians, mounted archers who were Rome’s feared enemies on its eastern border. Jesus warned that many would come in His name and deceive many, and that this would come before wars and famines (*Matthew 24:4–7*). On this view, the white horse represents a deceptive imitation of Christ’s victory, the conquering ambition that leads to war, famine, and death.

The second view fits more naturally with the pattern of the four horsemen as a group, though both views agree on an essential truth: all of these forces are released by the Lamb and remain under His authority.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can learn from this passage to be discerning. Not everything that looks victorious or pure is from God. Conquering powers, political movements, and charismatic leaders can promise peace and glory while leading to destruction. Jesus’ warning not to be deceived remains urgent.

At the same time, believers can take comfort that even the forces of conquest and destruction do not act independently of God. The Lamb opens the seals. History is under His control, and nothing can separate His people from His love.

This passage also invites believers to place their hope in the true Conqueror, Jesus Christ, whose victory comes through the cross and whose kingdom brings true and lasting peace.

### *Revelation 6:9–11* — How Long, O Lord?

> *“When he opened the fifth seal, I saw underneath the altar the souls of those who had been killed for the Word of God, and for the testimony of the Lamb which they had. They cried with a loud voice, saying, ‘How long, Master, the holy and true, until you judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?’ A long white robe was given to each of them. They were told that they should rest yet for a while, until their fellow servants and their brothers, who would also be killed even as they were, should complete their course.”*
>
> — *Revelation 6:9–11* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

When the Lamb opens the fifth seal, the scene shifts from earth to heaven. John sees “underneath the altar the souls of those who had been killed for the Word of God, and for the testimony of the Lamb which they had.” These are martyrs, believers who were killed because of their faithfulness to God’s word and their witness to Jesus.

They are “underneath the altar.” In the Old Testament sacrificial system, the blood of sacrifices was poured out at the base of the altar (*Leviticus 4:7*). The martyrs’ lives have been poured out like an offering to God.

They cry out in verse 10: “How long, Master, the holy and true, until you judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?” They are not asking for personal revenge. They are appealing to God, the holy and true Judge, to bring justice.

In verse 11, each of them is given “a long white robe,” a sign of victory, purity, and honor. They are told to “rest yet for a while.” Their prayer will be answered, but not yet. More of their fellow believers will also suffer and die before God’s justice is complete.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The cry “How long?” echoes the prayers of God’s people throughout Scripture (*Psalm 13:1–2*; *79:5–10*; *Habakkuk 1:2*). It is not a cry of unbelief but of faith. The martyrs know that God is “holy and true.” They trust that He will judge justly. Their question is about timing, not about whether justice will come.

This passage shows that God takes injustice seriously. The suffering of His people is not forgotten. Their blood cries out to Him, as Abel’s blood cried out from the ground (*Genesis 4:10*). God will act. Many interpreters see the later judgments in Revelation, especially the trumpets that follow the prayers of the saints (*Revelation 8:3–5*), as God’s answer to this very cry.

The instruction to “rest yet for a while” acknowledges a painful mystery. God’s timing is not always what His people would choose. Yet the martyrs are not left without comfort. They are given white robes and invited to rest. They are safe in God’s presence, honored, and assured that justice will come. Their deaths were not defeats; they were victories.

It is worth noticing that the martyrs entrust vengeance to God rather than taking it themselves. This matches the teaching of the New Testament: “*Don’t seek revenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to God’s wrath. For it is written, “Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay, says the Lord.”*” (*Romans 12:19*)

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Many believers around the world today suffer and die for their faith. This passage assures them, and all believers, that God sees their suffering and will bring justice. Their faithfulness is honored in heaven.

Believers who face injustice of any kind can bring their cries to God, as the martyrs did. It is not wrong to ask “How long?” Honest lament is part of faithful prayer. Believers can pour out their grief and longing for justice to the God who is holy and true.

At the same time, this passage calls believers to leave vengeance in God’s hands. Rather than seeking revenge, they can trust God to judge rightly, work for justice by lawful and loving means, and continue to bear faithful witness, even under pressure.

### *Revelation 6:15–17* — Who Is Able to Stand?

> *“The kings of the earth, the princes, the commanding officers, the rich, the strong, and every slave and free person, hid themselves in the caves and in the rocks of the mountains. They told the mountains and the rocks, ‘Fall on us, and hide us from the face of him who sits on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb, for the great day of his wrath has come, and who is able to stand?’”*
>
> — *Revelation 6:15–17* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

When the sixth seal is opened and the world is shaken, people of every rank try to hide: “The kings of the earth, the princes, the commanding officers, the rich, the strong, and every slave and free person, hid themselves in the caves and in the rocks of the mountains.” No social position, wealth, or power can protect them.

They cry out in verse 16: “Fall on us, and hide us from the face of him who sits on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb.” They would rather be crushed by mountains than face God.

Verse 17 explains their terror: “for the great day of his wrath has come, and who is able to stand?” The day of judgment has arrived, and no one can stand on their own strength before a holy God.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The phrase “the wrath of the Lamb” is striking. Lambs are usually symbols of gentleness. But the Lamb who was slain for sinners is also the Judge of all. Those who reject His sacrifice will face His judgment. God’s wrath is not uncontrolled anger, but His holy and just opposition to evil. The same Jesus who offers grace will hold the world accountable.

The cry for the mountains to fall on them echoes *Hosea 10:8* and Jesus’ words to the women of Jerusalem (*Luke 23:30*). It shows the terror of facing God without having been reconciled to Him. The list of people, from kings to slaves, shows that judgment comes to all. Every human being will stand before God.

The question “who is able to stand?” is answered in the very next chapter. *Revelation 7* shows the servants of God sealed for protection and a great multitude standing before the throne, clothed in white robes washed in the blood of the Lamb. Those who belong to the Lamb can stand. Their confidence rests not on their own righteousness, but on His sacrifice.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage is a sober reminder that God’s judgment is real. Every person will one day stand before Him. Wealth, power, and status will make no difference. The only question will be whether one belongs to the Lamb.

For those who trust in Christ, this passage is not a cause for terror but for gratitude. They do not need to hide from God’s face, because the Lamb has borne their judgment. They can approach God with confidence because of His grace.

This passage also gives believers urgency in sharing the gospel. The day of the Lord will come. The good news is that the Lamb who will judge the world is the same Lamb who died to save it, and He invites all to come to Him while there is time.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Revelation 6* shows that the troubles of history, war, famine, disease, and death, are real, but they are not out of control. The Lamb opens the seals. Each rider acts only by permission and within limits. Believers can face the turmoil of the world with confidence that Christ holds history in His hands.

The chapter also warns against deception. The rider on the white horse may represent a false conqueror who imitates Christ. Believers are called to discern carefully and to place their hope only in the true King, whose victory comes through the cross.

The cry of the martyrs reminds believers that God sees the suffering of His people. Injustice will not have the final word. Believers can bring their honest laments to God, asking “How long?” while trusting Him to bring justice in His time. They can leave vengeance in His hands and continue to bear faithful witness.

Finally, the sixth seal reminds believers that a day of judgment is coming when every human power will be shaken. On that day, no one will be able to stand on their own. But those who belong to the Lamb, washed in His blood, will stand before the throne. This truth calls believers to rest in His grace and to share the good news with others while there is time.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, Lamb of God, thank You that history is in Your hands. When I see war, famine, sickness, and death in the world, help me to remember that nothing happens outside Your authority. Guard me from every deception, and keep my hope fixed on You, the true Conqueror. I lift up to You all who suffer for their faith around the world; comfort them, strengthen them, and bring Your justice in Your perfect time. When I cry out, “How long?” help me to trust that You are holy and true. Teach me to leave vengeance in Your hands. Thank You that because You bore my judgment, I do not need to hide from Your face, but can stand before You by Your grace. Give me a heart to share this hope with others. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Revelation · Chapter 7 of 22

# Revelation — Chapter 7

Chapter Theme: Sealed by God and Standing Before the Throne

[Read Revelation 7 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/REV07.htm)

Main Teaching

Between the sixth and seventh seals, the action pauses. John sees four angels holding back the four winds of the earth so that no harm comes to land, sea, or trees. Another angel rises from the east with the seal of the living God and calls out that no harm should be done until the servants of God have been sealed on their foreheads. John hears the number of those sealed: 144,000, twelve thousand from each of the twelve tribes of Israel. Then he looks and sees a great multitude that no one could count, from every nation, tribe, people, and language, standing before the throne and the Lamb, wearing white robes and holding palm branches. They cry out that salvation belongs to God on the throne and to the Lamb. All the angels, elders, and living creatures fall on their faces and worship God. One of the elders asks John who these people in white robes are, and then explains: they have come out of the great tribulation; they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb. Therefore they are before God’s throne and serve Him day and night, and He will shelter them with His presence. They will never again hunger or thirst, nor will the sun or scorching heat strike them, for the Lamb at the center of the throne will be their shepherd and lead them to springs of living water, and God will wipe away every tear from their eyes.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Revelation 6* ended with a terrifying question: “*for the great day of his wrath has come, and who is able to stand?*” (*Revelation 6:17*) Chapter 7 answers that question. Before the seventh seal is opened, the action pauses to show that God’s people are protected and that a vast multitude will stand before His throne.

This pattern of pausing between the sixth and seventh items appears again with the trumpets (*10:1–11*:14). These interludes reassure believers that, whatever judgments fall on the world, God knows and keeps His own.

### The Winds Held Back (*7:1*)

“*After this, I saw four angels standing at the four corners of the earth, holding the four winds of the earth, so that no wind would blow on the earth, or on the sea, or on any tree*” (*v. 1*). The “four corners” and “four winds” are ways of describing the whole earth in every direction (compare *Jeremiah 49:36*; *Zechariah 6:5*). The winds may represent the destructive forces of judgment, perhaps connected with the four horsemen of chapter 6. The angels hold them back. Judgment is restrained until God’s purposes for His people are accomplished.

### The Sealing of God’s Servants (*7:2–8*)

The sealing of God’s servants and the 144,000 are studied below.

“*of the tribe of Judah twelve thousand were sealed, of the tribe of Reuben twelve thousand, of the tribe of Gad twelve thousand,*” (*v. 5*) The list of tribes in verses 5–8 is unusual. Judah is listed first, rather than Reuben, Jacob’s firstborn, probably because the Messiah, the Lion of the tribe of Judah (*5:5*), came from Judah. The tribe of Dan is missing, and Joseph and his son Manasseh are both included, while Ephraim is not named. Interpreters have suggested several reasons for Dan’s absence. Dan was associated with idolatry in Israel’s history (*Judges 18:30*; *1 Kings 12:28–30*), and some early Christian writers connected Dan with the coming of antichrist, though Scripture does not teach this. Others think the list simply reflects one of the many ways the tribes were arranged in the Old Testament, which vary considerably. The point of the list is clearly the completeness of God’s people, with twelve tribes of twelve thousand each.

### The Great Multitude (*7:9–12*)

The vision of the great multitude is studied below.

“*All the angels were standing around the throne, the elders, and the four living creatures; and they fell on their faces before his throne, and worshiped God,*” (*v. 11*) “*saying, “Amen! Blessing, glory, wisdom, thanksgiving, honor, power, and might, be to our God forever and ever! Amen.”*” (*v. 12*) The whole heavenly court responds to the multitude’s praise with worship of its own. Seven qualities are ascribed to God, expressing complete and perfect praise, just as seven were ascribed to the Lamb in 5:12.

### Who Are These? (*7:13–17*)

“*One of the elders answered, saying to me, “These who are arrayed in the white robes, who are they, and where did they come from?”*” (*v. 13*) The elder asks a question so that he can explain the vision. John responds humbly: “*I told him, “My lord, you know.”*” (*v. 14*) The elder’s explanation is studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Revelation 7:2–4* — Sealed on Their Foreheads

> *“I saw another angel ascend from the sunrise, having the seal of the living God. He cried with a loud voice to the four angels to whom it was given to harm the earth and the sea, saying, ‘Don’t harm the earth, the sea, or the trees, until we have sealed the bondservants of our God on their foreheads!’ I heard the number of those who were sealed, one hundred forty-four thousand, sealed out of every tribe of the children of Israel:”*
>
> — *Revelation 7:2–4* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

John sees “another angel ascend from the sunrise, having the seal of the living God.” In the ancient world, a seal was a mark of ownership and protection. Kings and officials used seals to mark documents and property as their own and to guarantee that they were not tampered with.

The angel cries out to the four angels holding back the winds: “Don’t harm the earth, the sea, or the trees, until we have sealed the bondservants of our God on their foreheads!” Before judgment falls, God marks His servants as His own.

Then John hears the number of those sealed: “one hundred forty-four thousand, sealed out of every tribe of the children of Israel.” Twelve thousand are sealed from each of the twelve tribes.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The sealing recalls *Ezekiel 9*, where a man with a writing kit marks the foreheads of those in Jerusalem who grieve over its sins, so that they are spared when judgment comes. It also recalls the Passover, when the blood of the lamb on the doorposts protected Israel’s households (*Exodus 12:13*). In the New Testament, believers are said to be sealed with the Holy Spirit as a mark that they belong to God (*2 Corinthians 1:22*; *Ephesians 1:13*; *4:30*).

The seal does not mean that God’s servants will escape all suffering. Many believers in Revelation suffer and even die for their faith. But it means that they belong to God, that He knows them, and that nothing can separate them from Him or destroy their eternal life. Later in the book, those who follow the beast receive a different mark on their foreheads or hands (*13:16–17*). Every person ultimately bears the mark of the one they serve.

The identity of the 144,000 has been understood in several ways. Some futurist interpreters understand them as a specific group of Jewish believers in Jesus during a future time of tribulation, perhaps serving as witnesses to the world. Others see them as Jewish Christians in the early church. Many interpreters, across several traditions, understand the 144,000 as a symbolic picture of the whole people of God, both Jewish and Gentile believers, described in terms of Israel’s twelve tribes. They note that the number is built from twelve (the tribes) times twelve (perhaps the apostles) times a thousand (a vast number), expressing completeness. They also note that John hears the number of the 144,000 and then sees a countless multitude, just as he heard about a Lion and then saw a Lamb (*5:5–6*). On this view, the 144,000 and the great multitude are two ways of describing the same people: God’s complete and ordered people, and His vast, international family.

Whatever view one holds, this passage affirms God’s faithfulness to Israel and His intention to keep a complete people for Himself. It should never be used to diminish the place of the Jewish people in God’s purposes, nor to suggest that only a limited number of people can be saved.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can take great comfort in knowing that they are sealed by God. They belong to Him, and He knows them by name. Whatever happens in the world, their identity and destiny are secure.

This passage also reminds believers that God’s protection is not always protection from suffering, but protection through suffering. Believers may face trials, but they will never be lost.

Finally, the contrast between the seal of God and the mark of the beast invites believers to consider whose mark they bear. Every life is shaped by some ultimate loyalty. Believers are called to live as those who belong wholly to God.

### *Revelation 7:9–10* — A Great Multitude from Every Nation

> *“After these things I looked, and behold, a great multitude which no man could count, out of every nation and of all tribes, peoples, and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb, dressed in white robes, with palm branches in their hands. They cried with a loud voice, saying, ‘Salvation be to our God, who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!’”*
>
> — *Revelation 7:9–10* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After hearing the number of the sealed, John looks and sees “a great multitude which no man could count.” The crowd is so vast that it cannot be numbered.

This multitude comes “out of every nation and of all tribes, peoples, and languages.” Every ethnic group, every culture, and every language is represented.

They are “standing before the throne and before the Lamb.” In chapter 6, people cried out, “who is able to stand?” Here is the answer: these people stand, not in fear, but in worship.

They are “dressed in white robes,” symbols of purity and victory, “with palm branches in their hands.” Palm branches were used in celebrations of victory and in the Jewish Feast of Tabernacles. They were also waved when Jesus entered Jerusalem (*John 12:13*).

They cry out with a loud voice: “Salvation be to our God, who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!” They give all the credit for their salvation to God and the Lamb.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This vision is the fulfillment of God’s promise to Abraham that through him all the families of the earth would be blessed (*Genesis 12:3*). It also fulfills the promise that Abraham’s descendants would be as countless as the stars (*Genesis 15:5*). The people of God are not small or limited. They form a vast multitude beyond counting.

The diversity of the multitude is important. People from every nation, tribe, people, and language stand together before the throne. Their cultural differences are not erased; they are still recognized as coming from every nation and language. But they are united in worship of the one God and the Lamb. This is the goal toward which the church moves: a diverse family united in Christ.

The song of the multitude places salvation entirely in God’s hands. They do not praise themselves for their faithfulness or endurance. “Salvation” belongs to God and to the Lamb. This is the heart of the gospel: salvation is a gift of grace.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This vision gives believers a glimpse of their future and their family. They will one day stand with believers from every nation and language before God’s throne. This can shape how they view people from other cultures now: as fellow members of the same family, or as people whom God invites into it.

Churches can reflect this vision by welcoming people of all backgrounds, rejecting prejudice, and supporting the work of sharing the gospel with every people group.

This passage also reminds believers to give God all the credit for their salvation. Their place before the throne will not be earned by their own goodness but given by God’s grace through the Lamb.

### *Revelation 7:14–17* — Washed in the Blood of the Lamb

> *“I told him, ‘My lord, you know.’ He said to me, ‘These are those who came out of the great suffering. They washed their robes and made them white in the Lamb’s blood. Therefore they are before the throne of God, and they serve him day and night in his temple. He who sits on the throne will spread his tabernacle over them. They will never be hungry or thirsty any more. The sun won’t beat on them, nor any heat; for the Lamb who is in the middle of the throne shepherds them and leads them to springs of life-giving waters. And God will wipe away every tear from their eyes.’”*
>
> — *Revelation 7:14–17* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The elder explains who the multitude are: “These are those who came out of the great suffering.” They have passed through great trial and have come out on the other side.

Then he says: “They washed their robes and made them white in the Lamb’s blood.” It is a startling image: blood that makes robes white. Their purity comes not from their own efforts but from the sacrifice of Jesus.

Verse 15 describes their new life: “Therefore they are before the throne of God, and they serve him day and night in his temple.” And God “will spread his tabernacle over them,” sheltering them with His presence.

Verse 16 promises: “They will never be hungry or thirsty any more. The sun won’t beat on them, nor any heat.” Every form of suffering will be removed.

Verse 17 gives the reason: “for the Lamb who is in the middle of the throne shepherds them and leads them to springs of life-giving waters. And God will wipe away every tear from their eyes.”

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

“The great suffering,” often translated “the great tribulation,” has been understood in different ways. Futurist interpreters often see it as a specific period of intense tribulation before Christ’s return. Others understand it as the suffering that God’s people experience throughout the church age, which Jesus said His followers would face (*John 16:33*; *Acts 14:22*). Preterists connect it with the persecutions of the first century. In every view, the multitude has endured suffering and come through it into God’s presence.

The image of robes made white in blood expresses the heart of the gospel. Sin stains, and no human effort can make a person clean. But the blood of Jesus, His sacrificial death, cleanses completely (*1 John 1:7*). Isaiah had promised: “*Though your sins are as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow*” (*Isaiah 1:18*).

The promises of verses 15–17 draw on *Isaiah 49:10* and *Isaiah 25:8*. God’s presence shelters His people like the tabernacle in the wilderness. Their suffering ends. And the Lamb becomes their Shepherd. The image is beautiful: the Lamb who was slain now shepherds His flock, leading them to springs of living water, as in *Psalm 23*. And God Himself wipes away every tear. This tender promise is repeated at the climax of the book (*Revelation 21:4*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage offers deep comfort to those who are suffering. Whatever trials believers face now, there will be a day when God wipes every tear from their eyes. Hunger, thirst, pain, and sorrow will be no more.

Believers who feel stained by sin or shame can find hope in the image of robes washed white in the Lamb’s blood. No stain is too deep for Christ’s cleansing. They can come to Him in faith and receive His forgiveness.

The picture of the Lamb as Shepherd invites believers to trust Him now. He leads His people to springs of living water, not only in the future but in the present, through His word, His Spirit, and His presence. Believers can follow Him daily, confident that He knows the way.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Revelation 7* answers the question raised at the end of chapter 6: Who is able to stand? Those who belong to God and have been washed in the blood of the Lamb will stand before His throne. This truth gives believers deep security and hope.

The sealing of God’s servants reminds believers that they belong to God. They are marked as His own. Whatever judgments fall on the world, God knows and keeps His people. His protection may not spare them from all suffering, but it guarantees that they will never be lost.

The vision of the great multitude shows the wonderful scope of God’s salvation. People from every nation, tribe, people, and language will stand together before the throne. Believers are part of this vast, diverse family. They can welcome others, reject prejudice, and join in God’s mission to every people.

The elder’s explanation reminds believers that their salvation rests on the Lamb’s sacrifice. Their robes are made white not by their own goodness but by His blood. And their future is glorious: they will serve God in His presence, sheltered by Him, free from all suffering, shepherded by the Lamb, and comforted by God, who will wipe away every tear.

## Chapter Prayer

Father, thank You that You have sealed me as Your own, and that nothing can separate me from Your care. Thank You for the vast multitude from every nation, tribe, people, and language whom You have redeemed through the Lamb. Help me to love all who belong to Your family and to share Your good news with every people. Thank You that my robes have been washed white in the blood of the Lamb, and that my salvation comes from You alone. When I face suffering, remind me that one day I will stand before Your throne, sheltered by Your presence, free from hunger, thirst, and pain. Lord Jesus, be my Shepherd now; lead me to springs of living water. And until the day You wipe away every tear, hold me close and give me hope. Salvation belongs to You, our God, and to the Lamb. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
