Revelation · Chapter 8 of 22

# Revelation — Chapter 8

Chapter Theme: Silence in Heaven and the First Four Trumpets

[Read Revelation 8 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/REV08.htm)

Main Teaching

When the Lamb opens the seventh seal, there is silence in heaven for about half an hour. John sees the seven angels who stand before God, and seven trumpets are given to them. Another angel with a golden censer stands at the altar and is given much incense to offer with the prayers of all God’s people on the golden altar before the throne. The smoke of the incense rises with the prayers before God. Then the angel fills the censer with fire from the altar and throws it on the earth, and there are peals of thunder, rumblings, flashes of lightning, and an earthquake. The seven angels prepare to sound their trumpets. At the first trumpet, hail and fire mixed with blood are hurled to the earth, and a third of the earth, a third of the trees, and all the green grass are burned up. At the second, something like a great mountain burning with fire is thrown into the sea; a third of the sea becomes blood, a third of sea creatures die, and a third of the ships are destroyed. At the third, a great star named Wormwood falls from the sky, burning like a torch, onto a third of the rivers and springs, making the waters bitter so that many people die. At the fourth, a third of the sun, moon, and stars are struck, so that a third of the day and night are without light. Then John sees an eagle flying in midair and crying, Woe, woe, woe to those who live on the earth, because of the three trumpets yet to sound.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Revelation 8* opens the second series of seven judgments: the trumpets. In the Old Testament, trumpets were sounded to announce God’s presence (*Exodus 19:16*, 19), to call His people to assembly, to sound the alarm in war, and to herald the day of the Lord (*Joel 2:1*). The trumpet judgments are warnings that call the world to repentance before the final day.

The trumpets closely resemble the plagues God sent on Egypt before the exodus: hail and fire, water turned to blood, darkness, locusts. Just as those plagues revealed God’s power over the false gods of Egypt and led to the liberation of His people, the trumpets reveal His power over a world in rebellion and point toward the final deliverance of His people.

### How the Trumpets Relate to the Seals

Interpreters have understood the relationship between the seals, trumpets, and bowls in different ways. Some see them as a single sequence of events, one following another in time, with the seventh seal containing the seven trumpets and the seventh trumpet containing the seven bowls. Others see them as overlapping cycles that describe the same period from different angles, each ending with a picture of the end (*6:12–17*; *11:15–19*; *16:17–21*) and each growing in intensity. A notable feature supports the second view: the seals affect a fourth of the earth (*6:8*), the trumpets a third, and the bowls the whole, showing an increasing intensity rather than simply a new set of events. Many readers combine these insights, seeing real progression toward the end while recognizing that the cycles also repeat and deepen the same themes.

### The Seventh Seal and the Prayers of the Saints (*8:1–5*)

The silence in heaven and the offering of the prayers of the saints are studied below.

“*I saw the seven angels who stand before God, and seven trumpets were given to them*” (*v. 2*). These seven angels appear to be a special group who stand in God’s presence, ready to carry out His commands. Jewish tradition spoke of seven archangels, including Gabriel, who said to Zechariah, “*I am Gabriel, who stands in the presence of God*” (*Luke 1:19*).

“*The seven angels who had the seven trumpets prepared themselves to sound*” (*v. 6*). The scene is set. The prayers of God’s people have risen before Him, and now His response begins.

### The Third Woe Announced (*8:13*)

“*I saw, and I heard an eagle, flying in mid heaven, saying with a loud voice, “Woe! Woe! Woe to those who dwell on the earth, because of the other blasts of the trumpets of the three angels, who are yet to sound!”*” (*v. 13*) An eagle flies high overhead where all can see and hear it, announcing three woes for the three remaining trumpets. The eagle may also call to mind a bird of prey circling, a sign of coming judgment (compare *Matthew 24:28*). “Those who dwell on the earth” is a phrase Revelation uses for people who are hostile to God and settled in the world’s ways, as distinct from God’s people (compare *Revelation 6:10*; *13:8*). The warning shows that the coming judgments will be even more severe than the first four.

Yet even this cry of woe carries mercy within it. A warning is given before the blow falls. Throughout Scripture, God sends warnings so that people may turn and live (*Ezekiel 33:11*). The eagle’s cry, like the trumpets themselves, gives the world one more opportunity to listen. The tragedy, as chapter 9 will show, is that many refuse.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Revelation 8:1* — Silence in Heaven

> *“When he opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven for about half an hour.”*
>
> — *Revelation 8:1* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After all the drama of the first six seals and the loud worship of chapter 7, the opening of the seventh seal brings something surprising: “there was silence in heaven for about half an hour.”

Heaven, which has been filled with songs, cries, and thunder, falls completely silent. The silence lasts “about half an hour,” a brief but noticeable pause.

This silence prepares for what follows. The seventh seal does not reveal a new disaster directly. Instead, it opens into the seven trumpets.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Interpreters have suggested several meanings for this silence, and they may all contain truth. First, silence is a fitting response to God’s coming in judgment. The prophets called for silence before the Lord: “*But the LORD is in his holy temple. Let all the earth be silent before him!*” (*Habakkuk 2:20*) (see also *Zephaniah 1:7*; *Zechariah 2:13*). The silence expresses awe at the holiness and seriousness of God’s judgments.

Second, the silence may allow the prayers of the saints to be heard. In Jewish tradition, the temple worship included times of silence when incense was offered and the people prayed. The very next verses describe the prayers of God’s people rising before Him. It is as though all heaven falls silent to listen to the prayers of the suffering saints.

Third, the silence creates a dramatic pause before the next series of judgments, much like the hush before a storm breaks. It heightens the sense that something momentous is about to happen.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

In a world full of noise, this passage invites believers to recover the practice of silence before God. Worship is not only singing and speaking; it also includes stillness, reverence, and awe. Believers can make space in their lives to be quiet before God, to listen, and to wonder at His holiness.

The connection between silence and prayer is also encouraging. If heaven falls silent to hear the prayers of God’s people, then believers can be confident that their prayers matter to God. He listens.

Finally, this silence reminds believers to take God’s judgments seriously. They are not to be treated lightly or as entertainment. They call for humility, reverence, and repentance.

### *Revelation 8:3–5* — Prayers Rising Like Incense

> *“Another angel came and stood over the altar, having a golden censer. Much incense was given to him, that he should add it to the prayers of all the saints on the golden altar which was before the throne. The smoke of the incense, with the prayers of the saints, went up before God out of the angel’s hand. The angel took the censer, and he filled it with the fire of the altar, then threw it on the earth. Thunders, sounds, lightnings, and an earthquake followed.”*
>
> — *Revelation 8:3–5* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

John sees “another angel” with “a golden censer,” a container for burning incense. He stands at the golden altar before the throne. In the temple in Jerusalem, a golden altar of incense stood before the curtain leading to the Most Holy Place, and incense was burned there every morning and evening.

The angel is given “much incense,” which he adds “to the prayers of all the saints.” Verse 4 describes the result: “The smoke of the incense, with the prayers of the saints, went up before God out of the angel’s hand.” The prayers of God’s people rise into His presence, mingled with fragrant incense.

Then in verse 5, the angel fills the censer “with the fire of the altar,” and throws it on the earth. Immediately there are “thunders, sounds, lightnings, and an earthquake.” The prayers that went up to God now come down to earth in the form of His powerful response.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This passage reveals the power of prayer in God’s purposes. The prayers of the saints, including the cry of the martyrs in 6:10, “How long?”, have risen before God’s throne. Now God answers. The trumpet judgments that follow are, in part, God’s response to the prayers of His people for justice and for His kingdom to come.

The image of prayer as incense appears elsewhere in Scripture. David prayed, “*Let my prayer be set before you like incense*” (*Psalm 141:2*). In *Revelation 5:8*, the elders hold golden bowls of incense, “*which are the prayers of the saints*” (*Revelation 5:8*). Prayers are precious to God, a fragrant offering that delights Him.

The added incense from the angel may suggest that the prayers of God’s people are made acceptable and powerful before God through His grace. Believers do not pray in their own worthiness but through the mediation of Christ (*Hebrews 7:25*).

The fire thrown on the earth recalls *Ezekiel 10:2*, where burning coals from among the cherubim are scattered over Jerusalem in judgment. The thunder, lightning, and earthquake recall God’s appearance at Sinai. Heaven’s response to prayer shakes the earth.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage encourages believers to pray with confidence. Their prayers are not lost or ignored. They rise before God like incense, and He hears and answers. Even prayers that seem to go unanswered for a long time are gathered before His throne.

Believers can pray especially for God’s kingdom to come and His justice to be done, as Jesus taught (*Matthew 6:10*). These prayers are part of God’s plan to set the world right.

This passage also shows that prayer is not a small or passive activity. It is part of the way God works in the world. Ordinary believers, praying faithfully, take part in God’s great purposes.

### *Revelation 8:7–12* — The First Four Trumpets

> *“The first sounded, and there followed hail and fire, mixed with blood, and they were thrown to the earth. One third of the earth was burned up, and one third of the trees were burned up, and all green grass was burned up. The second angel sounded, and something like a great burning mountain was thrown into the sea. One third of the sea became blood, and one third of the living creatures which were in the sea died. One third of the ships were destroyed. The third angel sounded, and a great star fell from the sky, burning like a torch, and it fell on one third of the rivers, and on the springs of water. The name of the star is ‘Wormwood.’ One third of the waters became wormwood. Many people died from the waters, because they were made bitter. The fourth angel sounded, and one third of the sun was struck, and one third of the moon, and one third of the stars, so that one third of them would be darkened; and the day wouldn’t shine for one third of it, and the night in the same way.”*
>
> — *Revelation 8:7–12* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The first four trumpets bring judgments on the natural world. At the first trumpet, “hail and fire, mixed with blood” fall on the earth, burning a third of the earth and trees and all the green grass. This recalls the seventh plague on Egypt, when hail and fire fell (*Exodus 9:23–25*).

At the second trumpet, “something like a great burning mountain was thrown into the sea.” A third of the sea becomes blood, a third of sea creatures die, and a third of ships are destroyed. This recalls the first plague, when the Nile turned to blood (*Exodus 7:20–21*).

At the third trumpet, “a great star fell from the sky, burning like a torch,” onto the rivers and springs. Its name is “Wormwood,” a bitter plant. A third of the waters become bitter, and many people die.

At the fourth trumpet, a third of the sun, moon, and stars are darkened. This recalls the ninth plague, the darkness over Egypt (*Exodus 10:21–23*).

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The repeated phrase “one third” is significant. These judgments are severe but partial. They do not destroy everything. They are warnings, meant to call people to repentance before final judgment comes. Even in judgment, God shows patience.

The images have been interpreted in different ways. Some take them as literal future events: ecological disasters, perhaps involving meteors or volcanic eruptions. Some historicist interpreters have linked them to invasions that struck the Roman Empire. Many interpreters see them as symbols of the ways God’s judgment affects every part of creation that sinful humanity depends on: land, sea, fresh water, and light. The burning mountain may echo *Jeremiah 51:25*, where Babylon is called a destroying mountain that God will make a burnt mountain. Wormwood recalls *Jeremiah 9:15*, where God warns that He will give His unfaithful people wormwood to eat and poisoned water to drink. Rejecting God turns life’s sweetness to bitterness.

The connection with the plagues of Egypt is the key. In Exodus, the plagues showed that the gods of Egypt were powerless and that the Lord alone is God. They also preceded the deliverance of God’s people. The trumpets carry the same message: the powers of this world cannot stand against God, and He will deliver His people.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can see in these judgments a reminder that the created world depends on God. Land, sea, water, and light are His gifts. When humanity turns from Him, the effects ripple through all of life. This truth encourages gratitude for God’s gifts and responsible care for His creation.

The partial nature of these judgments reveals God’s patience. He does not desire anyone to perish but wants all to come to repentance (*2 Peter 3:9*). Believers can share this message of patience and invitation with others.

Finally, this passage reminds believers that God is greater than all the powers of the world. Like Israel in Egypt, they can trust that He will deliver them, even when the world around them is shaken.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Revelation 8* begins with silence. Heaven pauses in awe before God’s judgments, and in that silence the prayers of the saints rise before Him. Believers can learn to be still before God, to approach Him with reverence, and to trust that He listens to their prayers.

The chapter shows that prayer is powerful. The prayers of God’s people, mingled with incense, rise before His throne, and God answers by acting on the earth. Believers can pray faithfully for God’s kingdom to come and His justice to be done, knowing that their prayers are part of His purposes.

The first four trumpets reveal that God’s judgments affect every part of creation. They echo the plagues of Egypt and show that the powers of this world cannot stand against Him. Yet these judgments are partial, a sign of God’s patience and a call to repentance.

Finally, the eagle’s cry of woe reminds believers that the time is serious. A world that rejects God faces increasing judgment. This calls believers to live faithfully, to pray for those who do not know God, and to share the hope of the gospel while there is still time.

## Chapter Prayer

Holy God, teach me to be still before You, in awe of Your holiness and power. Thank You that my prayers rise before You like incense, and that You hear every prayer of Your people. Help me to pray with faith for Your kingdom to come and Your will to be done on earth as it is in heaven. Thank You for Your patience, which gives time for repentance. Make me grateful for the gifts of Your creation and faithful in caring for them. When the world is shaken, help me to trust that You are greater than every power, and that You will deliver Your people. Give me a heart that longs for others to turn to You, and use me to share Your hope while there is time. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Revelation · Chapter 9 of 22

# Revelation — Chapter 9

Chapter Theme: The Locusts from the Abyss and the Armies from the Euphrates

[Read Revelation 9 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/REV09.htm)

Main Teaching

When the fifth angel sounds his trumpet, John sees a star that had fallen from heaven to earth, and it is given the key to the shaft of the abyss. When the abyss is opened, smoke rises like a great furnace, darkening the sun and the air, and out of the smoke come locusts given power like scorpions. They are told not to harm the grass or trees, but only the people who do not have the seal of God on their foreheads. They are not allowed to kill, only to torment for five months, and in those days people will seek death but not find it. The locusts look like horses prepared for battle, with crowns like gold, human faces, women’s hair, lions’ teeth, iron breastplates, and wings that roar like chariots; their king is the angel of the abyss, called Abaddon in Hebrew and Apollyon in Greek, meaning Destroyer. This is the first woe. When the sixth angel sounds, a voice from the golden altar commands that the four angels bound at the great river Euphrates be released. They had been prepared for that very hour to kill a third of mankind. John hears that the mounted troops number two hundred million. The horses have heads like lions, and from their mouths come fire, smoke, and sulfur, which kill a third of mankind; their tails are like snakes with heads that cause harm. Yet the rest of mankind who survive these plagues do not repent of worshiping demons and idols, nor of their murders, sorceries, sexual immorality, and thefts.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Revelation 9* describes the fifth and sixth trumpets, which are also the first two of the three “woes” announced by the eagle in 8:13. These judgments are more intense than the first four. While the first four trumpets affected the natural world, the fifth and sixth strike human beings directly, and they involve demonic forces.

The imagery in this chapter is among the most vivid and strange in the whole book. Locusts with human faces and scorpion tails, armies of two hundred million, horses breathing fire: these pictures are meant to be terrifying. They draw heavily on the Old Testament, especially the locust plague of *Joel 1–2*, where an army of locusts is described like horses and chariots, and the plague of locusts in Egypt (*Exodus 10:12–15*).

### How the Fifth and Sixth Trumpets Are Understood

These images have been interpreted in many ways. Some **futurist** interpreters take them as literal future events, either supernatural demonic creatures or, in some modern readings, descriptions of modern warfare seen through ancient eyes. **Historicist** interpreters have linked the locusts and the armies with various invasions that struck the Roman Empire and Christendom from the east over the centuries. **Preterist** interpreters connect them with first-century events, such as the threat of the Parthian armies beyond the Euphrates or the turmoil surrounding the Jewish war with Rome. **Idealist** interpreters understand them as symbols of the demonic torment and destructive violence that sin unleashes in every age, and of God’s permitting such forces to judge a world that has rejected Him.

All of these approaches share important common ground. The forces described are real and destructive, they are demonic in character, and yet they act only within limits set by God. And the purpose of these judgments is to call people to repentance, a purpose the world tragically refuses.

### The Locusts from the Abyss (*9:1–12*)

The opening of the abyss and the limits placed on the locusts are studied below.

“*They were given power, not to kill them, but to torment them for five months. Their torment was like the torment of a scorpion when it strikes a person*” (*v. 5*). The torment is limited in both severity and time. “Five months” may correspond to the natural life span of a locust, or the season in which locusts typically appear, suggesting a limited period.

“*In those days people will seek death, and will in no way find it. They will desire to die, and death will flee from them*” (*v. 6*). The torment is so severe that people long for death. This is a picture of the misery that comes when people are handed over to the destructive forces they have chosen to serve.

“*The shapes of the locusts were like horses prepared for war. On their heads were something like golden crowns, and their faces were like people’s faces*” (*v. 7*). “*They had hair like women’s hair, and their teeth were like those of lions*” (*v. 8*). “*They had breastplates like breastplates of iron. The sound of their wings was like the sound of many chariots and horses rushing to war*” (*v. 9*). “*They have tails like those of scorpions, with stingers. In their tails they have power to harm men for five months*” (*v. 10*). The description combines features from different creatures into a nightmarish image. Joel had described locusts that look like horses and sound like chariots (*Joel 2:4–5*), with teeth like a lion’s (*Joel 1:6*). Each feature adds to the sense of menace: they are organized like an army, they claim authority (crowns), they have an intelligent and almost human quality (faces), they are fierce (lions’ teeth), they are protected (iron breastplates), and they are overwhelming (the roar of chariots).

“*They have over them as king the angel of the abyss. His name in Hebrew is “Abaddon”, but in Greek, he has the name “Apollyon”.*” (*v. 11*) Natural locusts have no king (*Proverbs 30:27*), but these do. “Abaddon” in Hebrew and “Apollyon” in Greek both mean “Destruction” or “Destroyer.” Some identify this angel with Satan; others see him as a powerful demonic being under Satan. Some scholars note that “Apollyon” may also be a play on the name of the god Apollo, whom the emperor Domitian liked to be associated with. If so, John may be hinting that the powers worshiped by the empire are actually destructive.

“*The first woe is past. Behold, there are still two woes coming after this*” (*v. 12*).

### The Armies from the Euphrates (*9:13–19*)

“*The sixth angel sounded. I heard a voice from the horns of the golden altar which is before God,*” (*v. 13*) The voice comes from the golden altar where the prayers of the saints were offered (*8:3–5*). This judgment, too, is connected with God’s response to the prayers of His people.

“*saying to the sixth angel who had the trumpet, “Free the four angels who are bound at the great river Euphrates!”*” (*v. 14*) The Euphrates River marked the eastern boundary of the Roman Empire and, in the Old Testament, the boundary of the land promised to Israel. Beyond it lay the lands of Israel’s great enemies, Assyria and Babylon, and in John’s day the feared Parthian Empire. Invasion from beyond the Euphrates was a symbol of overwhelming judgment.

“*The four angels were freed who had been prepared for that hour and day and month and year, so that they might kill one third of mankind*” (*v. 15*). The four angels are bound until released. They are evil powers held in restraint by God. The precise timing, “that hour and day and month and year,” shows that God is sovereign over the exact moment of judgment.

“*The number of the armies of the horsemen was two hundred million. I heard the number of them*” (*v. 16*). The Greek literally speaks of two myriads of myriads, a vast army beyond imagining. In John’s world, such a number was almost unthinkable and likely symbolizes an overwhelming, innumerable force.

“*Thus I saw the horses in the vision and those who sat on them, having breastplates of fiery red, hyacinth blue, and sulfur yellow; and the horses’ heads resembled lions’ heads. Out of their mouths proceed fire, smoke, and sulfur*” (*v. 17*). “*By these three plagues, one third of mankind was killed: by the fire, the smoke, and the sulfur, which proceeded out of their mouths*” (*v. 18*). “*For the power of the horses is in their mouths and in their tails. For their tails are like serpents, and have heads; and with them they harm*” (*v. 19*). Fire and sulfur recall the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah (*Genesis 19:24*) and point to the fiery judgment of the lake of fire (*Revelation 19:20*; *20:10*). Like the locusts, these horses are monstrous, combining lion and serpent. They are demonic powers of death. The world’s refusal to repent is studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Revelation 9:1–4* — The Abyss Opened, God’s People Protected

> *“The fifth angel sounded, and I saw a star from the sky which had fallen to the earth. The key to the pit of the abyss was given to him. He opened the pit of the abyss, and smoke went up out of the pit, like the smoke from a burning furnace. The sun and the air were darkened because of the smoke from the pit. Then out of the smoke came locusts on the earth, and power was given to them, as the scorpions of the earth have power. They were told that they should not hurt the grass of the earth, neither any green thing, neither any tree, but only those people who don’t have God’s seal on their foreheads.”*
>
> — *Revelation 9:1–4* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

When the fifth angel sounds, John sees “a star from the sky which had fallen to the earth.” In Revelation, stars sometimes represent angels (*1:20*). This fallen star is given “the key to the pit of the abyss.” The abyss, or bottomless pit, is the place where evil spirits are confined (*Luke 8:31*; *Revelation 20:1–3*).

Notice that the key “was given to him.” He does not seize it. Even the opening of the abyss happens only by God’s permission.

When the abyss is opened, “smoke went up out of the pit, like the smoke from a burning furnace,” darkening the sun and the air. Out of the smoke come locusts with the power of scorpions.

Verse 4 contains a crucial limit: “They were told that they should not hurt the grass of the earth, neither any green thing, neither any tree, but only those people who don’t have God’s seal on their foreheads.” The locusts are not ordinary insects; they leave plants alone. And they cannot harm those who belong to God.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The fallen star has been understood in different ways. Some see it as Satan, who fell from heaven (*Luke 10:18*; *Isaiah 14:12*). Others see it as an angel sent by God to carry out His command, since an angel later holds the key to the abyss and binds Satan (*Revelation 20:1*). Either way, the key is given by God. Evil can only act within the boundaries He sets.

The most important truth in this passage is the protection of God’s people. The servants of God were sealed in chapter 7 precisely so that they would be protected from these judgments. The demonic forces released from the abyss cannot touch those who bear God’s seal. This echoes the Exodus, where the plagues struck Egypt but God protected His people in Goshen (*Exodus 8:22–23*; *9:4*, 26).

This does not mean believers will never suffer. Revelation is clear that many will suffer persecution and even death. But it means that the demonic torment unleashed on a rebellious world has no power over those who belong to God. Spiritual darkness cannot claim them, because they belong to Christ.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can take comfort in knowing that evil spiritual forces are real but limited. They act only within the boundaries God allows, and they cannot ultimately harm those who belong to Him. As John wrote, “*greater is he who is in you than he who is in the world*” (*1 John 4:4*).

This passage also reminds believers that life apart from God is not neutral. When people reject God, they open themselves to forces that torment and destroy. Sin promises freedom but leads to bondage and misery. This can move believers to compassion for those trapped in destructive patterns and to pray for their freedom.

Finally, believers can rest in the seal of God. Their security does not depend on their own strength but on the One who has marked them as His own.

### *Revelation 9:20–21* — They Did Not Repent

> *“The rest of mankind, who were not killed with these plagues, didn’t repent of the works of their hands, that they wouldn’t worship demons, and the idols of gold, and of silver, and of brass, and of stone, and of wood, which can’t see, hear, or walk. They didn’t repent of their murders, their sorceries, their sexual immorality, or their thefts.”*
>
> — *Revelation 9:20–21* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After all the devastation of the six trumpets, John records a tragic response: “The rest of mankind, who were not killed with these plagues, didn’t repent of the works of their hands.”

They continued to worship “demons, and the idols of gold, and of silver, and of brass, and of stone, and of wood, which can’t see, hear, or walk.” They kept trusting in lifeless idols that could not help them, and behind those idols stood demonic powers.

Verse 21 lists their other sins: “They didn’t repent of their murders, their sorceries, their sexual immorality, or their thefts.” The worship of false gods led to the breakdown of moral life: violence, occult practices, immorality, and dishonesty.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses reveal the purpose of the trumpet judgments: to bring people to repentance. God’s judgments in history are warnings, calls to turn back before final judgment comes. But the hardened human heart refuses to turn.

This echoes the story of Pharaoh, who hardened his heart again and again in spite of the plagues (*Exodus 7–11*). It also shows a pattern described by Paul in Romans 1: when people exchange the glory of God for idols, they are given over to every kind of wrongdoing (*Romans 1:21–32*). Idolatry and immorality are closely connected. What people worship shapes how they live.

The description of idols that “can’t see, hear, or walk” echoes *Psalm 115:4–8* and *Daniel 5:23*, which mock idols as powerless. The prophets pointed out the foolishness of trusting in things made by human hands. Yet behind idolatry lies something more sinister: demonic powers that deceive and enslave (*1 Corinthians 10:19–20*).

The word “sorceries” translates a Greek word related to “pharmakeia,” which referred to magic, witchcraft, and the use of drugs or potions in occult practices. It represents any attempt to manipulate spiritual powers apart from God.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage is a sobering reminder of the hardness of the human heart. Suffering alone does not always lead people to God. Many people, even in the face of great hardship, continue to cling to what cannot save them. Believers can pray earnestly for hearts to be softened, knowing that only God’s grace can bring true repentance.

The list of idols may seem ancient, but idolatry takes many forms today. Money, success, pleasure, power, technology, and even good things can become idols when they take God’s place. Believers can examine their own hearts and turn from anything that competes with God for their trust and devotion.

Finally, this passage highlights the urgency of repentance. God’s patience is great, but it is not endless. Today is the day to turn to Him. Believers can share this message with love, urging others to turn to the God who forgives and restores.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Revelation 9* reveals the destructive power of evil when it is unleashed on a world that has rejected God. The locusts from the abyss and the armies from the Euphrates are terrifying images of demonic torment and violent destruction. These are not merely ancient fantasies but pictures of what happens when people turn from God and open themselves to the powers of darkness.

Yet the chapter also shows that these powers are limited. The key to the abyss is given by God. The locusts are told whom they may and may not harm. Their torment lasts for a limited time. The four angels are released only at the precise hour God has set. Evil is real, but it is never in control.

Most comforting of all, those who bear God’s seal are protected. The demonic forces cannot harm them. Believers can face spiritual darkness with confidence, knowing that they belong to Christ and that He is greater than every power of evil.

The chapter ends with a tragic warning. In spite of all these judgments, people refuse to repent. They cling to idols and continue in violence, sorcery, immorality, and theft. Believers can learn from this to take sin seriously, to examine their own hearts for idols, and to respond quickly to God’s call to repentance. They can also pray for those who are hardened, asking God to open their eyes and draw them to Himself.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord God, thank You that You are sovereign over every power, and that even the forces of darkness act only within the limits You set. Thank You that I bear Your seal and belong to You, and that no evil power can take me from Your hand. Protect me from the deceptions of the enemy, and keep me close to You. Search my heart for every idol, anything that takes Your place, and give me grace to turn from it. Soften my heart so that I respond quickly when You call me to repent. I pray for those who are trapped in destructive patterns and who cling to things that cannot save them; open their eyes, break their chains, and draw them to Yourself. Give me compassion, courage, and urgency to share Your hope. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Revelation · Chapter 10 of 22

# Revelation — Chapter 10

Chapter Theme: The Mighty Angel and the Little Scroll

[Read Revelation 10 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/REV10.htm)

Main Teaching

Between the sixth and seventh trumpets, John sees another mighty angel coming down from heaven, wrapped in a cloud, with a rainbow over his head, a face like the sun, and legs like pillars of fire. He holds a little scroll lying open in his hand. Planting his right foot on the sea and his left foot on the land, he gives a loud shout like a lion’s roar, and the seven thunders speak. John is about to record what they said, but a voice from heaven tells him to seal up what the seven thunders have said and not to write it. The angel then raises his right hand to heaven and swears by the eternal Creator of heaven, earth, and sea that there will be no more delay: when the seventh angel sounds his trumpet, the mystery of God will be accomplished, just as He announced to His servants the prophets. The voice from heaven tells John to take the open scroll from the angel’s hand. When John asks for it, the angel tells him to take it and eat it: it will be sweet as honey in his mouth but will turn his stomach sour. John eats it, and it is just as the angel said. Then John is told that he must prophesy again about many peoples, nations, languages, and kings.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Revelation 10* is an interlude between the sixth and seventh trumpets, just as chapter 7 was an interlude between the sixth and seventh seals. After the terrifying judgments of chapter 9 and the tragic refusal of humanity to repent, the action pauses. This pause focuses on John’s calling as a prophet and on the message God’s people are to proclaim.

The chapter draws heavily on the call of the prophet Ezekiel, who was also given a scroll to eat (*Ezekiel 2:8–3:3*), and on *Daniel 12*, where an angel raises his hand and swears by the One who lives forever about the time of the end (*Daniel 12:7*). John is presented as standing in the line of the great prophets, receiving a fresh commission to speak God’s word to the world.

This interlude continues into chapter 11, where the two witnesses are described. Together, chapters 10 and 11 show the role of God’s people as prophetic witnesses in a hostile world.

### The Mighty Angel (*10:1–3*)

“*I saw a mighty angel coming down out of the sky, clothed with a cloud. A rainbow was on his head. His face was like the sun, and his feet like pillars of fire*” (*v. 1*). This angel is described in glorious terms. The cloud, rainbow, shining face, and pillars of fire recall the description of the risen Christ in chapter 1 and of God’s throne in chapter 4. Because of this, some interpreters have suggested that this angel is Christ Himself. However, Revelation consistently calls him “another angel” and “a mighty angel” (compare 5:2), and he swears by God rather than receiving worship. Most interpreters therefore understand him as a powerful angel who reflects the glory of God, much as Moses’ face shone after being in God’s presence. The cloud and pillars of fire also recall the presence of God leading Israel through the wilderness.

“*He had in his hand a little open book. He set his right foot on the sea, and his left on the land*” (*v. 2*). The little scroll is open, unlike the sealed scroll of chapter 5. Some interpreters see it as the same scroll the Lamb opened, now unsealed and ready to be proclaimed; others see it as a smaller message, a portion of God’s plan given to John to declare. The angel’s stance on both sea and land shows that his message concerns the whole world.

“*He cried with a loud voice, as a lion roars. When he cried, the seven thunders uttered their voices*” (*v. 3*). The roar of a lion recalls the prophets’ description of God’s voice: “*The lion has roared. Who will not fear? The Lord GOD has spoken. Who can but prophesy?*” (*Amos 3:8*) The seven thunders respond, perhaps echoing *Psalm 29*, where the voice of the Lord thunders seven times over creation.

### The Sealed Thunders and the Oath (*10:4–7*)

The command to seal up the thunders and the angel’s oath are studied below.

### The Bitter-Sweet Scroll (*10:8–11*)

“*The voice which I heard from heaven, again speaking with me, said, “Go, take the book which is open in the hand of the angel who stands on the sea and on the land.”*” (*v. 8*) John is commanded to take the scroll himself. He is not merely to observe; he is to receive the message personally.

It is worth noticing what has just happened in the story. In chapter 9, the world refused to repent in spite of severe judgments. Now, rather than immediately sounding the final trumpet, God renews the prophetic witness. Judgment alone does not soften hard hearts, so God sends His word again through His servants. This pattern reveals God’s heart: even near the end, He continues to call people to Himself through the testimony of His people.

The eating of the scroll and the renewed commission are studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Revelation 10:4* — Seal Up What the Thunders Said

> *“When the seven thunders sounded, I was about to write; but I heard a voice from the sky saying, ‘Seal up the things which the seven thunders said, and don’t write them.’”*
>
> — *Revelation 10:4* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

When the seven thunders speak, John is ready to record their message: “When the seven thunders sounded, I was about to write.” He has been faithfully writing everything he sees and hears, as Christ commanded (*1:11*, 19).

But this time he is stopped: “I heard a voice from the sky saying, ‘Seal up the things which the seven thunders said, and don’t write them.’” The message of the thunders is not to be shared. John is to keep it hidden.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This is one of the most intriguing moments in Revelation. Interpreters have offered several explanations. Some suggest that the seven thunders announced another series of judgments, which God in His mercy cancelled or chose not to reveal, perhaps in light of the delay ending (*10:6*). Others suggest the message was simply too sacred or too overwhelming to be written, like Paul’s experience of hearing “*unspeakable words, which it is not lawful for a man to utter*” (*2 Corinthians 12:4*).

Whatever the content, this verse teaches an important truth: God has not revealed everything. Even in a book of revelation, some things remain hidden. Moses said, “*The secret things belong to the LORD our God; but the things that are revealed belong to us and to our children forever*” (*Deuteronomy 29:29*).

This should shape how believers read Revelation and all prophecy. There are limits to what humans know about God’s plans. Those who claim to have every detail of the future figured out are going beyond what God has revealed. Humility is fitting when studying the things of God.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can rest in the fact that God knows what they do not. They do not need to understand every detail of the future to trust Him. What God has revealed is enough for faith and obedience.

This verse also gives a healthy caution against speculation. Throughout history, many people have made confident predictions about the end times that proved to be wrong. Believers can study prophecy with humility, holding firmly to what is clear and holding loosely to what is uncertain.

Finally, this verse invites believers to trust God’s wisdom in what He chooses to reveal and to conceal. His silence is not neglect; it is part of His perfect wisdom and care.

### *Revelation 10:5–7* — No More Delay

> *“The angel whom I saw standing on the sea and on the land lifted up his right hand to the sky and swore by him who lives forever and ever, who created heaven and the things that are in it, the earth and the things that are in it, and the sea and the things that are in it, that there will no longer be delay, but in the days of the voice of the seventh angel, when he is about to sound, then the mystery of God is finished, as he declared to his servants the prophets.”*
>
> — *Revelation 10:5–7* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The mighty angel “lifted up his right hand to the sky,” a gesture used when taking a solemn oath. He swears “by him who lives forever and ever, who created heaven and the things that are in it, the earth and the things that are in it, and the sea and the things that are in it.” God is described as the eternal Creator of all things. The oath is made in the name of the One who has authority over everything.

The content of the oath is: “that there will no longer be delay.” The time of waiting is coming to an end.

Verse 7 explains: “but in the days of the voice of the seventh angel, when he is about to sound, then the mystery of God is finished, as he declared to his servants the prophets.” When the seventh trumpet sounds, God’s hidden plan, His “mystery,” will be brought to completion.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This oath answers the cry of the martyrs in *Revelation 6:10*: “*How long, Master, the holy and true*” (*Revelation 6:10*)? They were told to wait “*yet for a while*” (*Revelation 6:11*). Now the angel declares that the waiting is nearly over. God has heard His people’s prayers, and He will act.

The scene closely parallels *Daniel 12:7*, where an angel raises both hands to heaven and swears by Him who lives forever that it will be “*for a time, times, and a half*” (*Daniel 12:7*). In Daniel, the end was still sealed and future. In Revelation, the angel announces that its fulfillment is at hand.

“The mystery of God” in the New Testament refers to God’s plan, once hidden but now revealed in Christ (*Romans 16:25*; *Ephesians 3:3–6*; *Colossians 1:26–27*). It includes His plan to unite all things in Christ, to bring Gentiles and Jews together in one people, and to establish His kingdom fully. This mystery was “declared to his servants the prophets,” meaning that it fulfills what God promised throughout Scripture. The word translated “declared” is related to the word for preaching the good news. God’s plan is gospel, good news.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers who grow weary of waiting for God to set things right can take comfort in this oath. God’s timing may seem slow, but He has sworn that the delay will end. His purposes will be completed.

This passage also reminds believers that God’s plan is good news. The completion of the mystery of God means the fulfillment of His promises: the defeat of evil, the vindication of His people, and the establishment of His kingdom.

Because God is the Creator of heaven, earth, and sea, nothing lies outside His authority. Believers can trust that the One who made all things will also bring all things to their intended goal.

### *Revelation 10:9–11* — Sweet in the Mouth, Bitter in the Stomach

> *“I went to the angel, telling him to give me the little book. He said to me, ‘Take it and eat it. It will make your stomach bitter, but in your mouth it will be as sweet as honey.’ I took the little book out of the angel’s hand, and ate it. It was as sweet as honey in my mouth. When I had eaten it, my stomach was made bitter. They told me, ‘You must prophesy again over many peoples, nations, languages, and kings.’”*
>
> — *Revelation 10:9–11* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

John goes to the angel and asks for the little scroll. The angel says: “Take it and eat it. It will make your stomach bitter, but in your mouth it will be as sweet as honey.”

In verse 10, John obeys: “I took the little book out of the angel’s hand, and ate it. It was as sweet as honey in my mouth. When I had eaten it, my stomach was made bitter.”

Then in verse 11, John receives a fresh commission: “You must prophesy again over many peoples, nations, languages, and kings.” Having taken in God’s message, he must now proclaim it to the whole world.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Eating the scroll is a symbolic act. It means fully taking in God’s message, making it part of oneself before speaking it to others. Ezekiel had the same experience: God gave him a scroll to eat, and “*it was as sweet as honey in my mouth*” (*Ezekiel 3:3*). Jeremiah also said, “*Your words were found, and I ate them. Your words were to me a joy and the rejoicing of my heart*” (*Jeremiah 15:16*).

The scroll is sweet because God’s word is good. It reveals His love, His faithfulness, His victory, and His plan to make all things new. The psalmist declared that God’s words are sweeter than honey (*Psalm 19:10*; *119:103*).

But the scroll also turns bitter. God’s message includes judgment on a rebellious world and suffering for His people. To carry this message is a heavy burden. Prophets throughout Scripture wept over the messages they had to deliver. Jesus Himself wept over Jerusalem. The bitterness may also point to the suffering that faithful witnesses will face, as chapter 11 goes on to describe.

The commission to prophesy “over many peoples, nations, languages, and kings” shows that God’s message is for the whole world. Some translate it “about” many peoples, emphasizing that the rest of the book concerns the nations. Either way, John’s message has global significance, just as the church’s witness does.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage calls believers to take in God’s word deeply, not merely to read it or study it from a distance, but to make it part of their lives. Before speaking God’s word to others, they must receive it themselves.

Believers can also expect that God’s word will be both sweet and bitter. It brings joy, hope, comfort, and life. But it also confronts sin, calls for sacrifice, and sometimes leads to suffering. Faithful believers embrace both, trusting that God’s word is good even when it is hard.

Finally, believers share in John’s commission. The church is called to bear witness to Christ among all peoples, nations, languages, and leaders. This calling is both a privilege and a responsibility. Believers can pray for courage and compassion as they speak God’s truth in love.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Revelation 10* pauses the judgments to focus on God’s message and the messenger who carries it. The mighty angel, glorious and powerful, stands on sea and land, showing that God’s word concerns the whole world.

The sealing of the seven thunders reminds believers that God has not revealed everything. They can trust Him with what remains hidden, study prophecy with humility, and focus on what God has made clear.

The angel’s oath assures believers that God’s purposes will be completed. The waiting will end. The mystery of God, His plan to bring all things together in Christ, will be fulfilled. This gives hope to all who long for God to set the world right.

The eating of the scroll calls believers to receive God’s word fully, to let it shape them inwardly before they speak it outwardly. God’s word is sweet, full of grace and promise, but it can also be bitter, carrying hard truths and the cost of faithfulness. Like John, believers are called to bear witness to the nations, sharing God’s message with courage, honesty, and love.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord God, Creator of heaven, earth, and sea, You live forever, and Your purposes will surely be fulfilled. Thank You that the waiting will end and that Your plan in Christ will be completed. Help me to trust You with what You have not revealed, and to hold firmly to what You have made clear. Give me a hunger for Your word. Let me take it in deeply, so that it shapes my heart and my life. Thank You that Your word is sweeter than honey. When it is hard and costly, give me grace to receive it and obey it. Give me courage and love to bear witness to Christ among the people around me and to the nations. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Revelation · Chapter 11 of 22

# Revelation — Chapter 11

Chapter Theme: The Two Witnesses and the Seventh Trumpet

[Read Revelation 11 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/REV11.htm)

Main Teaching

John is given a measuring rod and told to measure the temple of God, the altar, and those who worship there, but to leave out the outer court, because it has been given to the nations, who will trample the holy city for forty-two months. God will empower His two witnesses, clothed in sackcloth, to prophesy for 1,260 days. They are the two olive trees and the two lampstands that stand before the Lord of the earth. No one can harm them until their work is done: fire comes from their mouths to consume their enemies, and they have power to shut the sky, turn waters into blood, and strike the earth with plagues. When they have finished their testimony, the beast that comes up from the abyss will attack, overpower, and kill them. Their bodies will lie in the street of the great city, which is figuratively called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was crucified. For three and a half days people from every nation will gaze on their bodies and refuse them burial, and the inhabitants of the earth will celebrate and exchange gifts. But after three and a half days, the breath of life from God enters them, they stand up, and terror strikes those who see them. A loud voice from heaven calls them to come up, and they ascend in a cloud as their enemies watch. At that moment a great earthquake strikes; a tenth of the city falls, seven thousand people are killed, and the survivors are terrified and give glory to the God of heaven. Then the seventh angel sounds his trumpet, and loud voices in heaven proclaim that the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Messiah, and He will reign forever. The twenty-four elders fall on their faces and worship, thanking God for taking His great power and beginning to reign, for the time has come to judge the dead, to reward His servants, and to destroy those who destroy the earth. God’s temple in heaven is opened, and the ark of His covenant is seen, with lightning, thunder, an earthquake, and a great hailstorm.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Revelation 11* continues the interlude that began in chapter 10. In chapter 10, John was commissioned to prophesy. In chapter 11, the prophetic witness of God’s people is portrayed through the image of two witnesses. The chapter then closes with the sounding of the seventh trumpet and a great announcement of God’s kingdom.

This is one of the most debated chapters in Revelation. Its images, the measuring of the temple, the forty-two months, the two witnesses, the great city, are understood in different ways by different interpreters. Yet its central message is clear: God protects His people, empowers them to bear witness, allows them to suffer, and vindicates them in the end. And His kingdom will triumph over the kingdoms of this world.

### Measuring the Temple (*11:1–2*)

“*A reed like a rod was given to me. Someone said, “Rise and measure God’s temple, and the altar, and those who worship in it.*” (*v. 1*) “*Leave out the court which is outside of the temple, and don’t measure it, for it has been given to the nations. They will tread the holy city under foot for forty-two months.*” (*v. 2*)

Measuring in the prophets is a sign of ownership, protection, or preparation for rebuilding (*Ezekiel 40–42*; *Zechariah 2:1–5*). John is told to measure the temple, the altar, and the worshipers, marking them as God’s own. The outer court, however, is left out and given over to the nations.

Interpreters understand this in several ways. Some **futurists** see a literal rebuilt temple in Jerusalem in a future period. Some **preterists** relate it to the temple in Jerusalem before its destruction in A.D. 70. Many interpreters understand the temple symbolically as the people of God, since the New Testament often describes the church as God’s temple (*1 Corinthians 3:16*; *2 Corinthians 6:16*; *Ephesians 2:21*). On this reading, God’s people are spiritually protected even as they are outwardly exposed to persecution, much like the sealing in chapter 7.

“Forty-two months” equals three and a half years, the same as 1,260 days (v3) and “a time, times, and half a time” (*12:14*). This period comes from *Daniel 7:25* and *12:7*, where it describes a limited time of persecution of God’s people. Some take it as a literal three and a half years in the future. Others understand it as a symbolic number for the whole period of the church’s witness and suffering between Christ’s first and second comings: a limited period, half of seven, a broken and incomplete time that will come to an end.

### The Two Witnesses (*11:3–14*)

The identity and ministry of the two witnesses, and their death and vindication, are studied below.

“*Their dead bodies will be in the street of the great city, which spiritually is called Sodom and Egypt, where also their Lord was crucified*” (*v. 8*). “The great city” is described in symbolic terms. It is “spiritually,” or figuratively, called Sodom, known for its wickedness, and Egypt, known for its oppression of God’s people. It is also identified as the place “where also their Lord was crucified,” which points to Jerusalem. Elsewhere in Revelation, “the great city” refers to Babylon, the symbol of the world system opposed to God (*16:19*; *17:18*). Many interpreters therefore see the great city as a picture of every human society that rejects God, including the Jerusalem that rejected Jesus, the Rome that persecuted the church, and the world in every age that opposes God’s witnesses.

“*In that day there was a great earthquake, and a tenth of the city fell. Seven thousand people were killed in the earthquake, and the rest were terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven*” (*v. 13*). This verse is remarkable. In contrast to the sixth trumpet, where survivors did not repent (*9:20–21*), here the survivors “gave glory to the God of heaven.” Some interpreters see this as genuine repentance and conversion; others see it as a terrified acknowledgment of God’s power without true faith. The proportions are notable: in the Old Testament, judgment often left only a remnant of a tenth or seven thousand (*Isaiah 6:13*; *1 Kings 19:18*). Here the pattern is reversed. Only a tenth fall, and the great majority survive and give glory to God. Many see this as a sign that the faithful witness and vindication of God’s people will lead many to turn to Him.

“*The second woe is past. Behold, the third woe comes quickly*” (*v. 14*).

### The Seventh Trumpet (*11:15–19*)

The great announcement at the seventh trumpet and the elders’ song are studied below.

“*God’s temple that is in heaven was opened, and the ark of the Lord’s covenant was seen in his temple. Lightnings, sounds, thunders, an earthquake, and great hail followed*” (*v. 19*). The ark of the covenant was the most sacred object in Israel’s worship, kept in the Most Holy Place. It represented God’s presence and His covenant with His people. It had been lost when Babylon destroyed the temple. Now John sees it in heaven, a sign that God’s covenant with His people remains and that access to His presence is open. The lightning, thunder, earthquake, and hail mark this as a climactic moment, as at the end of the seals (*8:5*) and the bowls (*16:18–21*).

## Important Verses Explained

### *Revelation 11:3–6* — Two Witnesses Empowered by God

> *“I will give power to my two witnesses, and they will prophesy one thousand two hundred sixty days, clothed in sackcloth. These are the two olive trees and the two lamp stands, standing before the Lord of the earth. If anyone desires to harm them, fire proceeds out of their mouth and devours their enemies. If anyone desires to harm them, he must be killed in this way. These have the power to shut up the sky, that it may not rain during the days of their prophecy. They have power over the waters, to turn them into blood, and to strike the earth with every plague, as often as they desire.”*
>
> — *Revelation 11:3–6* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

God says: “I will give power to my two witnesses, and they will prophesy one thousand two hundred sixty days, clothed in sackcloth.” Their mission is to bear witness, speaking God’s message. Sackcloth was a rough garment worn in mourning and repentance. Their message is a call to repent.

Verse 4 describes them: “These are the two olive trees and the two lamp stands, standing before the Lord of the earth.” This recalls *Zechariah 4*, where two olive trees supply oil to a lampstand, representing Zerubbabel the governor and Joshua the high priest, God’s anointed servants (*Zechariah 4:11–14*). In Revelation, lampstands represent churches (*Revelation 1:20*).

Verses 5–6 describe their power. No one can harm them during their ministry: “fire proceeds out of their mouth and devours their enemies.” They have power “to shut up the sky, that it may not rain,” like Elijah (*1 Kings 17:1*). And they have power “over the waters, to turn them into blood, and to strike the earth with every plague,” like Moses in Egypt.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The identity of the two witnesses has been widely discussed. Some interpreters believe they are two individual prophets who will appear in the future, often identified as Moses and Elijah, because of the miracles described, or as Enoch and Elijah, because neither experienced ordinary death. Others identify them with figures in the early church, such as Peter and Paul. Many interpreters understand the two witnesses as a symbol of the witnessing church, the people of God bearing testimony to Christ in the world. They note that the witnesses are called “two lamp stands,” and lampstands in Revelation represent churches. Two may also reflect the biblical requirement of two witnesses for valid testimony (*Deuteronomy 19:15*), and the fact that Jesus sent His disciples out two by two.

Whether individuals or a symbol of the church, the witnesses share the character of Moses and Elijah, the great representatives of the Law and the Prophets. They speak God’s word with power. Their ministry is protected by God until it is complete. The “fire” from their mouths likely represents the power of God’s word, as when God told Jeremiah, “*I will make my words in your mouth fire*” (*Jeremiah 5:14*).

The key point is that God’s witnesses are invincible until their work is done. No opposition can stop the testimony God has appointed. This is a powerful encouragement for believers facing opposition.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers today share in the calling of the two witnesses. The church is called to bear faithful witness to Christ in the world, speaking God’s truth, calling people to repentance, and shining as a lampstand in the darkness.

This passage encourages believers that their witness is empowered by God. They do not speak in their own strength but by the Spirit, like the oil that fed Zechariah’s lampstand: “*Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit*” (*Zechariah 4:6*).

Believers can also take courage that God protects His witnesses until their work is done. They do not need to live in fear. Their lives are in God’s hands, and nothing can cut short the work He has given them.

### *Revelation 11:7–12* — Killed, Raised, and Vindicated

> *“When they have finished their testimony, the beast that comes up out of the abyss will make war with them, and overcome them, and kill them. Their dead bodies will be in the street of the great city, which spiritually is called Sodom and Egypt, where also their Lord was crucified. From among the peoples, tribes, languages, and nations, people will look at their dead bodies for three and a half days, and will not allow their dead bodies to be laid in a tomb. Those who dwell on the earth will rejoice over them, and they will be glad. They will give gifts to one another, because these two prophets tormented those who dwell on the earth. After the three and a half days, the breath of life from God entered into them, and they stood on their feet. Great fear fell on those who saw them. I heard a loud voice from heaven saying to them, ‘Come up here!’ They went up into heaven in a cloud, and their enemies saw them.”*
>
> — *Revelation 11:7–12* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

When the witnesses “have finished their testimony,” their protection is lifted. “The beast that comes up out of the abyss will make war with them, and overcome them, and kill them.” This is the first mention of the beast, who will be described in detail in chapter 13. Evil seems to win.

The world’s response is cruel. People “will not allow their dead bodies to be laid in a tomb,” a terrible insult in the ancient world. “Those who dwell on the earth will rejoice over them, and they will be glad. They will give gifts to one another.” The world celebrates the silencing of God’s witnesses, “because these two prophets tormented those who dwell on the earth.” Their message of truth was unwelcome.

But the story does not end there. “After the three and a half days, the breath of life from God entered into them, and they stood on their feet.” God raises them from the dead. “Great fear fell on those who saw them.”

Then “a loud voice from heaven” says, “Come up here!” and “they went up into heaven in a cloud, and their enemies saw them.” The witnesses are publicly vindicated.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The story of the two witnesses follows the pattern of Jesus’ own life. Like Jesus, they bear witness, are killed in the city “where also their Lord was crucified,” are raised after three days (here, three and a half), and ascend to heaven in a cloud (*Acts 1:9*). The witnesses share in their Lord’s suffering, death, resurrection, and vindication.

“The breath of life from God entered into them” recalls *Ezekiel 37*, where God breathes life into a valley of dry bones and they stand on their feet, a vast army. It also recalls the creation of Adam, when God breathed into him the breath of life (*Genesis 2:7*). God is the giver of life, and death cannot hold those who belong to Him.

The three and a half days of apparent defeat are brief compared with the 1,260 days of witness. Evil’s triumph is short-lived. The world’s celebration turns to terror as God reverses the verdict.

Whether one understands the witnesses as individuals or as the church, the message is the same: faithful witnesses may be silenced and even killed, but God will raise and vindicate them. Their apparent defeat is not the end of the story.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers who suffer for their faith can take courage from this passage. Faithful witness may lead to rejection, mockery, and even death. The world may celebrate when God’s people are silenced. But God has the final word.

This passage also reminds believers that the pattern of the Christian life is the pattern of Jesus: faithful witness, suffering, death, and resurrection. Believers are called to follow Him, trusting that suffering is not the end.

Finally, believers can hold on to the hope of resurrection. The breath of life from God will one day enter all who belong to Him. Death will not have the last word for any of God’s people.

### *Revelation 11:15–18* — The Kingdom of Our Lord

> *“The seventh angel sounded, and great voices in heaven followed, saying, ‘The kingdom of the world has become the Kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ. He will reign forever and ever!’ The twenty-four elders, who sit on their thrones before God’s throne, fell on their faces and worshiped God, saying: ‘We give you thanks, Lord God, the Almighty, the one who is and who was, because you have taken your great power and reigned. The nations were angry, and your wrath came, as did the time for the dead to be judged, and to give your bondservants the prophets, their reward, as well as to the saints and those who fear your name, to the small and the great, and to destroy those who destroy the earth.’”*
>
> — *Revelation 11:15–18* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

When the seventh angel sounds, there are “great voices in heaven” proclaiming: “The kingdom of the world has become the Kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ. He will reign forever and ever!”

This is the great announcement of the whole book. The kingdom of the world, all the power and authority that human beings and evil forces have claimed, now belongs to God and His Messiah.

In verses 16–17, the twenty-four elders fall on their faces and worship: “We give you thanks, Lord God, the Almighty, the one who is and who was, because you have taken your great power and reigned.”

Verse 18 describes what this reign means: “The nations were angry, and your wrath came, as did the time for the dead to be judged.” God’s reign brings judgment on the rebellious, reward for “your bondservants the prophets,” “the saints and those who fear your name, to the small and the great,” and destruction for “those who destroy the earth.”

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This announcement fulfills the hope of the whole Bible. *Psalm 2* described the nations raging against the Lord and His anointed, while God laughs from heaven and establishes His King. *Daniel 7* foresaw that the kingdom would be given to the Son of Man and to the holy ones. Here, that kingdom is declared to have come.

Notice a subtle change in God’s title. Earlier He was called the One “who is and who was and who is to come” (*1:4*, 8; *4:8*). Now the elders say only “the one who is and who was.” The phrase “who is to come” is missing, because He has come. His reign is now fully established.

Interestingly, the seventh trumpet does not describe a final battle or catastrophe. It describes worship. The ultimate goal of history is not destruction but the reign of God, celebrated by His people.

The phrase “to destroy those who destroy the earth” is significant. God’s judgment is aimed at those who ruin His creation, whether through violence, oppression, idolatry, or greed. God is not the destroyer of His world; He is its restorer. His judgment removes those who corrupt it so that it can be made new.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can live with confident hope. However powerful the kingdoms of this world may seem, they will not last. The kingdom of God and of His Christ will reign forever. This truth can give believers courage, perspective, and peace.

This passage also calls believers to worship. The elders respond to God’s reign with thanksgiving. Believers can thank God now for His sovereignty and for the certainty of His coming kingdom.

The promise of reward for “the small and the great” assures believers that no act of faithfulness is forgotten. Whether their service is visible or hidden, God will reward those who fear His name.

Finally, God’s concern for “those who destroy the earth” reminds believers that His creation matters to Him. They can honor Him by caring for His world and by opposing what corrupts and destroys it.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Revelation 11* portrays the calling and destiny of God’s witnesses. Measured and protected by God, they bear testimony in a hostile world. Like Moses and Elijah, they speak with power. Like Jesus, they suffer, die, and are raised. Believers today share in this calling. They are lampstands, called to shine Christ’s light, empowered by the Spirit, protected until their work is done.

The chapter is honest about the cost of witness. The world may reject, mock, and even kill God’s messengers, and it may celebrate their silencing. But God has the final word. He raises His witnesses and vindicates them before their enemies. Believers can bear witness with courage, knowing that their faithfulness is never wasted.

The chapter also shows that faithful witness can lead others to God. After the vindication of the witnesses, many give glory to the God of heaven. Believers can hope and pray that their witness, even through suffering, will draw others to Christ.

Finally, the seventh trumpet declares the triumph of God’s kingdom. The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ, and He will reign forever. This is the hope that sustains God’s people through every trial. Believers can live in that hope, worship God with thanksgiving, and look forward to the day when His reign is fully revealed.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord God Almighty, thank You that You know and protect Your people. Make me a faithful witness, a lampstand that shines with the light of Christ. Fill me with Your Spirit, so that I speak Your truth not by my own might or power, but by Your Spirit. When faithfulness brings rejection or suffering, give me courage to follow Jesus in the way of the cross, trusting that You will raise and vindicate Your people. Use the witness of Your church to draw many to give You glory. Thank You that the kingdom of the world will become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ, and that He will reign forever and ever. I give You thanks, for You have taken Your great power and reigned. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
