Revelation · Chapter 15 of 22

# Revelation — Chapter 15

Chapter Theme: The Song of Moses and the Song of the Lamb

[Read Revelation 15 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/REV15.htm)

Main Teaching

John sees another great and marvelous sign in heaven: seven angels with the seven last plagues, for with them God’s wrath is completed. He sees what looks like a sea of glass glowing with fire, and standing beside it are those who have been victorious over the beast, its image, and the number of its name. They hold harps given by God and sing the song of God’s servant Moses and of the Lamb: Great and marvelous are Your deeds, Lord God Almighty; just and true are Your ways, King of the nations. Who will not fear You, Lord, and bring glory to Your name? For You alone are holy. All nations will come and worship before You, for Your righteous acts have been revealed. After this, the temple in heaven, the tabernacle of the covenant law, is opened. Out come the seven angels with the seven plagues, dressed in clean, shining linen with golden sashes around their chests. One of the four living creatures gives them seven golden bowls filled with the wrath of God, who lives forever. The temple fills with smoke from the glory of God and His power, and no one can enter it until the seven plagues are completed.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Revelation 15* is a short chapter, but it is full of meaning. It introduces the third and final series of seven judgments, the seven bowls, which will be poured out in chapter 16. These are called “the seven last plagues,” because with them God’s wrath is completed.

Before the bowls are poured out, however, John is shown a scene of worship. Those who have overcome the beast stand beside a sea of glass and sing a song of praise. As in earlier parts of Revelation, worship comes before judgment. The faithful are shown safe in God’s presence before the final judgments fall on the world.

The chapter is filled with echoes of the exodus. God’s people stand beside a sea, as Israel stood beside the Red Sea after their deliverance from Egypt. They sing the song of Moses, as Israel sang after crossing the sea (*Exodus 15*). The plagues recall the plagues on Egypt. And the temple is described as “the tabernacle of the testimony,” recalling the tent of meeting in the wilderness, which was filled with God’s glory (*Exodus 40:34–35*). Revelation presents the final victory of God’s people as a new and greater exodus.

### The Seven Last Plagues (*15:1*)

“*I saw another great and marvelous sign in the sky: seven angels having the seven last plagues, for in them God’s wrath is finished*” (*v. 1*). This is the third “sign” in heaven, following the woman (*12:1*) and the dragon (*12:3*). The bowls are the “last” plagues, because they complete God’s judgment on a rebellious world. The word “finished” means brought to its goal. God’s wrath is not endless rage; it has a purpose and an end. Once these judgments are complete, the way will be open for the new creation.

Modern readers sometimes find talk of God’s wrath uncomfortable. But in Scripture, God’s wrath is not a loss of temper or a cruel streak in His character. It is the settled, holy opposition of a good God to everything that destroys what He loves: violence, oppression, idolatry, and the deception that enslaves people. A God who never opposed evil would not be good. Revelation shows that God’s wrath is measured, purposeful, and always joined with patience, giving time and warning before it falls. And the gospel declares that Jesus Himself bore God’s judgment on the cross for all who trust Him, so that believers can say with Paul that they have been “*saved from God’s wrath through him*” (*Romans 5:9*).

The seven bowls are closely connected with the seals and trumpets, but they are more intense. The seals affected a fourth of the earth, the trumpets a third, but the bowls affect the whole. This progression suggests that God’s judgments increase in severity as the end approaches, while also giving repeated opportunities for repentance before the final outpouring.

### The Victors Beside the Sea of Glass (*15:2–4*)

The victors and their song are studied below.

### The Temple Opened (*15:5–8*)

The opening of the heavenly temple and the giving of the bowls are studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Revelation 15:2* — Victorious Over the Beast

> *“I saw something like a sea of glass mixed with fire, and those who overcame the beast, his image, and the number of his name, standing on the sea of glass, having harps of God.”*
>
> — *Revelation 15:2* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

John sees “something like a sea of glass mixed with fire.” The sea of glass first appeared before God’s throne in chapter 4, calm and clear like crystal. Now it is “mixed with fire,” perhaps reflecting the fire of judgment about to fall, or the fiery trials through which God’s people have passed.

Standing on or beside the sea of glass are “those who overcame the beast, his image, and the number of his name.” These are believers who refused to worship the beast or receive its mark. In chapter 13, the beast seemed to conquer them (*13:7*). Now they are revealed as the true victors.

They are “having harps of God,” instruments given by God for worship. They are ready to sing.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The phrase “those who overcame the beast” is striking. On earth, many of these believers may have been imprisoned, excluded from economic life, or killed. By worldly standards, they lost. But in heaven’s perspective, they won. They overcame the beast not by defeating it in battle, but by refusing to bow to it. Their faithfulness was their victory.

This reflects one of the central messages of Revelation: victory belongs to those who remain faithful to the Lamb, even unto death. As chapter 12 declared, “*They overcame him because of the Lamb’s blood, and because of the word of their testimony. They didn’t love their life, even to death*” (*Revelation 12:11*).

The image of standing beside a sea recalls Israel at the Red Sea. The sea that had seemed to block their escape became the means of their deliverance and the destruction of their enemies. In the same way, the trials that seemed to threaten God’s people have become the setting for their victory. They stand safely on the other side.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers who are struggling to remain faithful in the face of pressure can take courage from this vision. Faithfulness may look like loss in the eyes of the world, but in God’s eyes it is victory. Every time a believer refuses to compromise, they share in Christ’s triumph.

This passage also invites believers to look beyond their present circumstances to their future. Those who are faithful will one day stand in God’s presence with harps of praise, safe on the far side of every trial.

Finally, this vision encourages believers to redefine success. In God’s kingdom, success is not measured by power, wealth, or popularity, but by faithful loyalty to Christ.

### *Revelation 15:3–4* — Great and Marvelous Are Your Works

> *“They sang the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying, ‘Great and marvelous are your works, Lord God, the Almighty! Righteous and true are your ways, you King of the nations. Who wouldn’t fear you, Lord, and glorify your name? For you only are holy. For all the nations will come and worship before you. For your righteous acts have been revealed.’”*
>
> — *Revelation 15:3–4* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The victors “sang the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb.” This is one song, celebrating God’s deliverance in both the exodus and the work of Christ.

The song begins: “Great and marvelous are your works, Lord God, the Almighty!” God’s deeds are amazing and powerful. Then: “Righteous and true are your ways, you King of the nations.” God’s actions are always just and faithful, and He rules over every nation.

Verse 4 continues with a question: “Who wouldn’t fear you, Lord, and glorify your name?” The obvious answer is that everyone should. “For you only are holy.” God alone is perfectly holy.

The song ends with a great promise: “For all the nations will come and worship before you. For your righteous acts have been revealed.”

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The song of Moses in *Exodus 15* celebrated God’s victory over Pharaoh at the Red Sea. Another song of Moses, in *Deuteronomy 32*, celebrated God’s faithfulness and justice. The song in *Revelation 15* brings these together with the song of the Lamb, celebrating the greater deliverance accomplished through Christ’s death and resurrection. The exodus from Egypt was a preview of the greater exodus from sin, death, and the power of evil.

Interestingly, the song does not mention the victors themselves. It is entirely about God. The redeemed do not boast in their own faithfulness. They praise God’s works, ways, holiness, and righteous acts. This is the mark of true worship.

The words of the song are woven from Old Testament texts. “Great and marvelous are your works” echoes *Psalm 111:2* and *139:14*. “Righteous and true are your ways” echoes *Deuteronomy 32:4*. “Who wouldn’t fear you” echoes *Jeremiah 10:7*. “All the nations will come and worship before you” echoes *Psalm 86:9*: “*All nations you have made will come and worship before you, Lord. They shall glorify your name*” (*Psalm 86:9*).

The last line contains a remarkable hope. Even in the context of final judgment, the song looks forward to a day when all nations will worship God. Revelation consistently holds out the hope that people from every nation will turn to God. Judgment does not cancel this hope; it clears the way for its fulfillment.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This song gives believers words for worship. They can praise God for His great and marvelous works in creation, in history, and in their own lives. They can affirm that His ways are righteous and true, even when they do not fully understand them.

The focus of this song on God, rather than on the worshipers, can shape how believers worship. True worship turns attention away from ourselves and toward God’s greatness, holiness, and goodness.

This passage also encourages believers to trust God’s justice. When the world seems unjust, they can hold on to the truth that God’s ways are righteous and true. In the end, His righteous acts will be revealed to all.

Finally, believers can share the hope that all nations will come and worship God. This hope can fuel prayer and mission, as believers long for people from every nation to know and worship the true God.

### *Revelation 15:5–8* — The Temple Filled with Glory

> *“After these things I looked, and the temple of the tabernacle of the testimony in heaven was opened. The seven angels who had the seven plagues came out, clothed with pure, bright linen, and wearing golden sashes around their chests. One of the four living creatures gave to the seven angels seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God, who lives forever and ever. The temple was filled with smoke from the glory of God and from his power. No one was able to enter into the temple until the seven plagues of the seven angels would be finished.”*
>
> — *Revelation 15:5–8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After the song, John looks and sees that “the temple of the tabernacle of the testimony in heaven was opened.” The tabernacle was the tent where God dwelt among Israel in the wilderness. It was called the “tabernacle of the testimony” because it housed the ark containing the tablets of the law, God’s covenant testimony (*Exodus 38:21*).

The seven angels come out “clothed with pure, bright linen, and wearing golden sashes around their chests.” Their clothing resembles that of priests and of Christ Himself in chapter 1.

In verse 7, “One of the four living creatures gave to the seven angels seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God, who lives forever and ever.” The bowls are golden, like the bowls of incense that held the prayers of the saints (*5:8*).

Verse 8 describes the temple: “The temple was filled with smoke from the glory of God and from his power.” So intense is God’s presence that “No one was able to enter into the temple until the seven plagues of the seven angels would be finished.”

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The opening of the temple shows that the judgments come directly from God’s presence. They are not random disasters or the work of evil forces, but holy acts of a holy God. The angels who carry out the judgments come from the sanctuary, dressed in priestly purity.

The connection with the “testimony,” God’s covenant law, is significant. The judgments that follow are the outworking of God’s justice according to His covenant. God is faithful to His word, both in blessing those who trust Him and in judging those who persistently reject Him.

The golden bowls recall the golden bowls of incense in 5:8, which held the prayers of the saints. Many interpreters see a connection: the prayers of God’s people for justice and for His kingdom to come are now answered in the outpouring of these bowls.

The smoke filling the temple recalls moments when God’s glory filled the tabernacle and the temple so that no one could enter (*Exodus 40:34–35*; *1 Kings 8:10–11*; *Isaiah 6:4*). God’s glory is overwhelming. The fact that no one can enter until the plagues are finished may suggest that the time for intercession has passed; judgment must now take its course. It is a solemn moment.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage reminds believers of the holiness and majesty of God. His presence is so glorious that no one can stand before it on their own. Yet through Christ, believers have been given access to God’s presence (*Hebrews 10:19–22*). This is a privilege to be received with gratitude and reverence.

The solemnity of this scene also calls believers to take seriously the reality of God’s judgment. God is patient, but there will come a time when the opportunity for repentance ends. This truth gives urgency to sharing the gospel and to responding to God’s call today.

Finally, believers can trust that God’s judgments are holy and just. They come from His presence and reflect His perfect character. Believers do not need to fear that God will act unjustly. They can rest in His righteousness.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Revelation 15* shows that before God’s final judgments fall, His people are safe in His presence, singing His praise. Those who overcame the beast, often at great cost, stand beside the sea of glass like Israel after the exodus, celebrating God’s deliverance. Believers can take courage that faithfulness, even when it looks like defeat, is true victory.

The song of Moses and the Lamb gives believers a model for worship. It focuses entirely on God: His great and marvelous works, His righteous and true ways, His holiness, and His coming glory among the nations. Believers can make this song their own, praising God in every season and trusting His justice even when they cannot see it.

The chapter also calls believers to reverence. The heavenly temple, filled with the smoke of God’s glory, reminds them of the overwhelming holiness of God. His judgments are holy and just, flowing from His perfect character. Believers can approach Him with awe and gratitude, knowing that through Christ they have been given access to His presence.

Finally, the chapter holds out hope for the nations. Even as final judgment approaches, the song looks forward to a day when all nations will come and worship God. Believers can pray and work toward that day, sharing the good news with people from every nation.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord God Almighty, great and marvelous are Your works, and righteous and true are Your ways. You alone are holy, King of the nations. Who would not fear You and glorify Your name? Thank You for the victory You give to those who remain faithful, even when it costs them everything. Help me to see faithfulness as true success, and give me courage to refuse every compromise. Teach me to worship You with a heart focused on Your greatness, not my own. Thank You that through Jesus I have access to Your holy presence; help me to come with reverence and gratitude. I long for the day when all nations will come and worship before You. Use my life to point others to You. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Revelation · Chapter 16 of 22

# Revelation — Chapter 16

Chapter Theme: The Seven Bowls of God’s Wrath

[Read Revelation 16 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/REV16.htm)

Main Teaching

A loud voice from the temple commands the seven angels to pour out the seven bowls of God’s wrath on the earth. The first bowl brings ugly, festering sores on those who bear the mark of the beast and worship its image. The second turns the sea into blood like that of a dead person, and every living thing in the sea dies. The third turns the rivers and springs into blood, and the angel in charge of the waters declares that God is just in these judgments, for those who shed the blood of His people and prophets have been given blood to drink; the altar responds that His judgments are true and just. The fourth bowl is poured on the sun, which scorches people with fire, yet they curse God and refuse to repent and glorify Him. The fifth is poured on the throne of the beast, plunging its kingdom into darkness; people gnaw their tongues in agony and curse God, but do not repent of their deeds. The sixth dries up the Euphrates River to prepare the way for the kings from the east. John sees three impure spirits like frogs coming out of the mouths of the dragon, the beast, and the false prophet; they are demonic spirits performing signs, gathering the kings of the whole world for battle on the great day of God Almighty. Jesus declares that He comes like a thief and blesses those who stay awake and keep their clothes. The kings are gathered to the place called Armageddon. The seventh bowl is poured into the air, and a loud voice from the throne says, It is done! There are lightning, thunder, and a severe earthquake unlike any before. The great city splits into three parts, the cities of the nations collapse, and God remembers Babylon the great and gives her the cup of His fury. Every island flees, the mountains disappear, and huge hailstones fall, yet people curse God because of the plague.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Revelation 16* describes the seven bowls of God’s wrath, the last of the three series of judgments. These bowls complete God’s wrath (*15:1*). They are swift and severe, poured out one after another with no interlude, unlike the seals and trumpets. The bowls strike the whole earth rather than a portion of it.

The bowl judgments closely parallel both the trumpets and the plagues of Egypt. The first bowl brings sores, like the sixth plague (*Exodus 9:8–12*). The second and third turn water to blood, like the first plague (*Exodus 7:17–21*). The fifth brings darkness, like the ninth plague (*Exodus 10:21–23*). The seventh brings hail, like the seventh plague (*Exodus 9:22–26*). Frogs, the second plague of Egypt, appear as unclean spirits (*Exodus 8:1–15*). Just as the plagues on Egypt exposed the powerlessness of Pharaoh and his gods and led to Israel’s deliverance, the bowls expose the powerlessness of the beast and lead to the final deliverance of God’s people.

As with the seals and trumpets, interpreters understand the bowls in various ways: as literal future judgments in the last days, as judgments on Rome and the first-century world, as symbols of God’s ongoing judgments in history, or as a combination. What all agree on is that the bowls portray God’s righteous and complete judgment on a world that persistently refuses to repent.

### The First Four Bowls (*16:1–9*)

“*I heard a loud voice out of the temple, saying to the seven angels, “Go and pour out the seven bowls of the wrath of God on the earth!”*” (*v. 1*) The command comes from the temple, from God Himself.

“*The first went, and poured out his bowl into the earth, and it became a harmful and painful sore on the people who had the mark of the beast, and who worshiped his image*” (*v. 2*). The first bowl falls specifically on the beast’s followers. Those who received the beast’s mark now receive painful sores. Their choice of allegiance brings its consequences.

“*The second angel poured out his bowl into the sea, and it became blood as of a dead man. Every living thing in the sea died*” (*v. 3*). Under the second trumpet, a third of the sea became blood (*8:8–9*). Now the judgment is complete: every living thing in the sea dies.

“*The third poured out his bowl into the rivers and springs of water, and they became blood*” (*v. 4*). Fresh water, essential for life, also becomes blood. The response of the angel of the waters and the altar is studied below.

“*The fourth poured out his bowl on the sun, and it was given to him to scorch men with fire*” (*v. 8*). “*People were scorched with great heat, and people blasphemed the name of God who has the power over these plagues. They didn’t repent and give him glory*” (*v. 9*). The sun, God’s gift of light and warmth, becomes an instrument of judgment. Notice that people recognize God as the One who controls these plagues, yet instead of repenting, they curse Him. This tragic response is repeated three times in the chapter (vv9, 11, 21). It contrasts with the call of the eternal gospel in *Revelation 14:7*: “*Fear the Lord, and give him glory*” (*Revelation 14:7*). God’s people are promised the opposite: “*They will never be hungry or thirsty any more. The sun won’t beat on them, nor any heat*” (*Revelation 7:16*).

### The Fifth and Sixth Bowls (*16:10–16*)

“*The fifth poured out his bowl on the throne of the beast, and his kingdom was darkened. They gnawed their tongues because of the pain,*” (*v. 10*) “*and they blasphemed the God of heaven because of their pains and their sores. They still didn’t repent of their works*” (*v. 11*). The fifth bowl strikes the very center of the beast’s power, its throne. The beast’s kingdom, which seemed so mighty, is plunged into darkness. Those who followed it are left in agony. Yet still they will not repent.

“*The sixth poured out his bowl on the great river, the Euphrates. Its water was dried up, that the way might be prepared for the kings that come from the sunrise*” (*v. 12*). The Euphrates was the eastern boundary of the Roman Empire, beyond which lay the feared Parthian armies. The drying of the river recalls the drying of the Red Sea and the Jordan for Israel, but here it opens the way for invading armies. It may also recall the way the Persian king Cyrus captured ancient Babylon by diverting the Euphrates. The gathering of the kings and the battle of Armageddon are studied below.

### The Seventh Bowl (*16:17–21*)

The declaration “It is done” is studied below.

“*There were lightnings, sounds, and thunders; and there was a great earthquake such as has not happened since there were men on the earth—so great an earthquake and so mighty*” (*v. 18*). The signs that accompanied the end of the seals (*8:5*) and the trumpets (*11:19*) appear again, now at their greatest intensity. This earthquake is the greatest in human history, shaking the foundations of the world.

“*The great city was divided into three parts, and the cities of the nations fell. Babylon the great was remembered in the sight of God, to give to her the cup of the wine of the fierceness of his wrath*” (*v. 19*). The great city, Babylon, is shattered. God has not forgotten her sins. Her judgment will be described in detail in chapters 17 and 18.

“*Every island fled away, and the mountains were not found*” (*v. 20*). “*Great hailstones, about the weight of a talent, came down out of the sky on people. People blasphemed God because of the plague of the hail, for this plague was exceedingly severe*” (*v. 21*). A talent weighed roughly 75 to 100 pounds (35 to 45 kilograms). The hailstones recall the seventh plague of Egypt and the hailstones God sent against Israel’s enemies in *Joshua 10:11*. The world is shaken to its foundations, yet people still curse God. Their hearts are hardened beyond repentance.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Revelation 16:5–7* — True and Righteous Are Your Judgments

> *“I heard the angel of the waters saying, ‘You are righteous, who are and who were, O Holy One, because you have judged these things. For they poured out the blood of saints and prophets, and you have given them blood to drink. They deserve this.’ I heard the altar saying, ‘Yes, Lord God, the Almighty, true and righteous are your judgments.’”*
>
> — *Revelation 16:5–7* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After the waters are turned to blood, John hears “the angel of the waters,” an angel responsible for the waters of the earth. Rather than protesting the judgment, the angel praises God: “You are righteous, who are and who were, O Holy One, because you have judged these things.”

Verse 6 explains why the judgment is just: “For they poured out the blood of saints and prophets, and you have given them blood to drink. They deserve this.” Those who shed the blood of God’s people now receive blood to drink. The punishment fits the crime.

In verse 7, another voice responds from the altar: “Yes, Lord God, the Almighty, true and righteous are your judgments.” The altar is where the souls of the martyrs cried out for justice (*6:9–10*) and where the prayers of the saints were offered (*8:3–5*). Now the altar affirms that God’s justice has come.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

These verses are crucial for understanding the bowl judgments. Without them, the judgments might seem harsh or arbitrary. But the angel and the altar declare that God’s judgments are righteous. They are not random acts of anger but just responses to real evil, especially the persecution and murder of God’s people.

Notice that God is called the One “who are and who were.” As in 11:17, the phrase “who is to come” is missing. God has come in judgment. His promised intervention is happening.

The principle of fitting punishment appears throughout Scripture. Those who shed innocent blood are repaid with blood. This reflects God’s justice: evil is not ignored, and those who cause suffering will answer for it. The martyrs’ cry, “How long?” (*6:10*), is finally answered.

The response from the altar is moving. Those who suffered and died for their faith, whose prayers rose from the altar, now affirm that God’s judgments are true and righteous. They are not bitter or vengeful. They simply confirm that God has done what is right.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

These verses assure believers that God sees injustice and will set it right. Those who suffer at the hands of others, especially for their faith, can trust that God will not ignore their pain. Justice will come.

This passage also invites believers to trust God’s character when His judgments seem hard to understand. The angel and the altar affirm that God’s judgments are always true and righteous. Believers can hold on to this truth even when they do not understand everything.

Finally, this passage reminds believers that they do not need to take revenge. God Himself will judge rightly. Believers can leave justice in His hands, pray for those who harm them, and continue to bear witness with love.

### *Revelation 16:13–16* — Gathering for Armageddon

> *“I saw coming out of the mouth of the dragon, and out of the mouth of the beast, and out of the mouth of the false prophet, three unclean spirits, something like frogs; for they are spirits of demons, performing signs, which go out to the kings of the whole inhabited earth, to gather them together for the war of that great day of God the Almighty. ‘Behold, I come like a thief. Blessed is he who watches, and keeps his clothes, so that he doesn’t walk naked, and they see his shame.’ He gathered them together into the place which is called in Hebrew, ‘Harmagedon’.”*
>
> — *Revelation 16:13–16* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

John sees “three unclean spirits, something like frogs” coming out of the mouths of “the dragon,” “the beast,” and “the false prophet.” This is the first time the second beast is called “the false prophet,” which describes his role of deceiving people. The frogs come from their mouths, suggesting deceptive words and propaganda.

Verse 14 explains: “for they are spirits of demons, performing signs.” They go out “to the kings of the whole inhabited earth, to gather them together for the war of that great day of God the Almighty.” Through deception, the powers of evil gather the world’s rulers for a final rebellion against God.

Verse 15 interrupts with a word from Jesus: “Behold, I come like a thief. Blessed is he who watches, and keeps his clothes, so that he doesn’t walk naked, and they see his shame.” This is a call to readiness for believers.

Verse 16 names the gathering place: “He gathered them together into the place which is called in Hebrew, ‘Harmagedon’.” This is often spelled “Armageddon.”

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The unclean spirits are a picture of deception that leads people into rebellion against God. Throughout Revelation, the dragon and the beasts work through lies and false signs. The final rebellion is driven by deception. People are led to believe they can fight against God and win.

“Harmagedon” likely means “mountain of Megiddo.” Megiddo was a city overlooking the plain of Jezreel in northern Israel, the site of many famous battles in Israel’s history (*Judges 5:19*; *2 Kings 23:29*). There is no actual mountain called Megiddo, which has led many interpreters to see the name as symbolic: the place of the final decisive battle between God and the forces of evil. Some futurist interpreters expect a literal battle in that region of Israel in the last days. Others see Armageddon as a symbol of the final confrontation between God and all the powers that oppose Him, wherever and however it takes place. Some connect “mountain” with Mount Zion or Mount Carmel, where Elijah confronted the prophets of Baal.

Notably, the battle itself is not described here. When the confrontation is finally narrated (*19:11–21*; *20:7–10*), there is no real battle at all. Christ simply defeats His enemies by the word of His mouth. The gathering of the world’s armies is futile.

Jesus’ words in verse 15 are the third blessing in Revelation. In the middle of this terrifying scene, Christ speaks directly to His people, urging them to stay awake and spiritually clothed. The image recalls His warning to Sardis (*3:3*) and Laodicea (*3:18*). The danger for believers is not the armies of Armageddon, but spiritual sleepiness and unpreparedness.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage warns believers about the power of deception. Lies, propaganda, and false signs can lead whole nations into rebellion against God. Believers are called to test what they hear, hold to the truth of Scripture, and resist voices that stir up hostility toward God and His people.

The blessing in verse 15 is the most practical part of this passage for believers. Rather than speculating about the details of Armageddon, believers are called to watchfulness. They can stay spiritually awake through prayer, Scripture, and faithful living, and they can remain clothed in Christ’s righteousness, ready for His return.

Believers can also take comfort that the final confrontation between God and evil is not a close contest. The kings of the earth gather, but their rebellion is doomed. Christ will triumph.

### *Revelation 16:17* — It Is Done

> *“The seventh poured out his bowl into the air. A loud voice came out of the temple of heaven, from the throne, saying, ‘It is done!’”*
>
> — *Revelation 16:17* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The seventh angel pours out his bowl “into the air.” The air was sometimes thought of as the realm of evil spiritual powers (*Ephesians 2:2*). This final bowl affects the whole atmosphere surrounding the earth.

Then “A loud voice came out of the temple of heaven, from the throne, saying, ‘It is done!’” The voice comes from God Himself. With the seventh bowl, God’s judgment on the world is complete.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The declaration “It is done!” echoes Jesus’ cry from the cross: “*It is finished*” (*John 19:30*). At the cross, Jesus completed the work of salvation, bearing the judgment for sin. Here, God completes the work of judgment on those who have rejected that salvation. The two declarations belong together. Because of the cross, judgment and salvation are both brought to completion.

These words also anticipate the moment in *Revelation 21*, when God makes all things new and declares, “*I am the Alpha and the Omega, the Beginning and the End*” (*Revelation 21:6*). The completion of judgment opens the way for the new creation. Evil must be removed before God’s renewed world can be fully established.

This verse shows that history is moving toward a goal. God’s purposes are not endless cycles of judgment and suffering. There will be an end. God will finish what He has begun.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can take comfort in the certainty that God’s purposes will be completed. The struggles of this life, the suffering of His people, and the apparent triumph of evil will not go on forever. One day God will say, “It is done.”

This verse also points believers back to the cross. Jesus’ cry, “It is finished,” means that everything needed for their salvation has been accomplished. They do not need to add anything. They can rest in His finished work.

Finally, believers can live with hope, knowing that the end of judgment means the beginning of the new creation. The God who completes His judgment will also complete His promise to make all things new.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Revelation 16* portrays the final outpouring of God’s judgment on a world in rebellion. The bowls strike the beast’s followers, the sea, the waters, the sun, the beast’s throne, the Euphrates, and the air. Like the plagues of Egypt, they expose the powerlessness of every false god and every proud power. Believers can take courage that no power on earth can stand against God.

The chapter also reveals the tragic hardness of the human heart. Three times people curse God and refuse to repent. Suffering alone does not lead people to God. This should move believers to pray earnestly for those who are hardened and to share the gospel with urgency and love while there is time.

The voices of the angel and the altar remind believers that God’s judgments are true and righteous. God sees injustice, especially the suffering of His people, and He will set things right. Believers can trust His justice and leave vengeance in His hands.

In the middle of the chapter, Jesus speaks directly to His people: “Behold, I come like a thief. Blessed is he who watches.” Rather than being consumed by fear or speculation about the end, believers are called to stay spiritually awake and ready. And they can rest in the promise that God will bring all things to completion. One day He will say, “It is done,” and the way will be open for the new creation.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord God Almighty, true and righteous are Your judgments. Thank You that You see every injustice and every tear, and that You will set all things right. Help me to trust Your justice and to leave vengeance in Your hands. Soften my heart so that I never harden it against You. I pray for those who resist You; open their eyes and draw them to repentance while there is still time. Guard me from deception, and keep me watchful and ready for the return of Jesus. Clothe me in His righteousness, so that I may stand unashamed before Him. Thank You that Jesus cried, “It is finished,” and that His work for my salvation is complete. I look forward to the day when You will say, “It is done,” and make all things new. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Revelation · Chapter 17 of 22

# Revelation — Chapter 17

Chapter Theme: The Great Prostitute and the Beast

[Read Revelation 17 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/REV17.htm)

Main Teaching

One of the seven angels with the bowls invites John to see the judgment of the great prostitute who sits by many waters, with whom the kings of the earth committed adultery and by whose wine the inhabitants of the earth were made drunk. Carried in the Spirit into a wilderness, John sees a woman sitting on a scarlet beast covered with blasphemous names, with seven heads and ten horns. She is dressed in purple and scarlet, glittering with gold, jewels, and pearls, and holds a golden cup filled with abominable things and the filth of her immorality. On her forehead is written a mysterious name: Babylon the Great, the Mother of Prostitutes and of the Abominations of the Earth. She is drunk with the blood of God’s holy people and of those who bore witness to Jesus, and John is greatly astonished. The angel explains the mystery. The beast once was, now is not, and will come up out of the abyss and go to its destruction, and the inhabitants of the earth will be astonished. The seven heads are seven hills on which the woman sits, and also seven kings: five have fallen, one is, and one is yet to come for a little while. The beast is an eighth king who belongs to the seven and goes to destruction. The ten horns are ten kings who will receive authority for one hour along with the beast; they will wage war against the Lamb, but the Lamb will triumph over them because He is Lord of lords and King of kings, and with Him will be His called, chosen, and faithful followers. The waters where the prostitute sits are peoples, multitudes, nations, and languages. The beast and the ten horns will turn on the prostitute, hate her, strip her, devour her, and burn her with fire, for God has put it into their hearts to accomplish His purpose until His words are fulfilled. The woman is the great city that rules over the kings of the earth.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Revelation 17* and 18 describe the judgment of Babylon the great, which was announced in 14:8 and *16:19*. Chapter 17 introduces Babylon as a luxurious prostitute riding on the beast, and explains her relationship to the beast and the kings of the earth. Chapter 18 describes her fall and the mourning of those who profited from her.

The image of a city as a woman is common in Scripture. Jerusalem is often called “the daughter of Zion.” When cities or nations were unfaithful to God or led others into idolatry and exploitation, the prophets sometimes described them as prostitutes. Isaiah used this image for Tyre, a great trading city (*Isaiah 23:15–18*), and Nahum used it for Nineveh, the capital of Assyria (*Nahum 3:4*). The prophets even used it for Jerusalem when it turned from God (*Ezekiel 16*). The image is about spiritual unfaithfulness and the seductive power of wealth and idolatry. It is not a statement about women in general, and it should never be used to demean women.

### Who Is Babylon?

The identity of Babylon has been understood in several ways. Most interpreters believe that for John’s first readers, Babylon pointed to **Rome**. The city was famously built on seven hills (v9), it ruled over the kings of the earth (v18), it was the center of vast wealth and trade, and it persecuted Christians. Peter also appears to use “Babylon” as a code name for Rome (*1 Peter 5:13*). Some **preterist** interpreters instead identify Babylon with **Jerusalem**, which had rejected Christ and persecuted His followers, noting that the “great city” in 11:8 was where the Lord was crucified. Some **futurist** interpreters expect a future world system centered in a literal city, possibly a rebuilt Babylon in Iraq or another great world capital. **Idealist** interpreters see Babylon as a symbol of every human society, economic system, and culture that seduces people away from God through wealth, pleasure, and power, and persecutes those who remain faithful.

During the Reformation and afterward, some Protestant writers identified Babylon with the Roman Catholic Church. Most interpreters today, including many Protestants, regard that identification as a product of the bitter conflicts of that era rather than the meaning of the text. Revelation’s warnings about Babylon apply to every form of worldly seduction and should not be turned into a weapon against other Christians.

Many readers combine these perspectives. Babylon was Rome for John’s readers; she reappears in different forms throughout history wherever human societies make wealth and power their gods; and she will face final judgment when Christ returns.

### The Vision of the Woman (*17:1–6*)

The description of the woman is studied below.

### The Mystery of the Beast (*17:7–14*)

“*The angel said to me, “Why do you wonder? I will tell you the mystery of the woman and of the beast that carries her, which has the seven heads and the ten horns.*” (*v. 7*) John is astonished, perhaps because the woman is so impressive and glamorous. The angel gently corrects him: there is no need to be awed by her. Her secret will be revealed.

“*The beast that you saw was, and is not; and is about to come up out of the abyss and to go into destruction. Those who dwell on the earth and whose names have not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world will marvel when they see that the beast was, and is not, and shall be present*” (*v. 8*). The description “was, and is not, and shall be present” is a parody of God’s title, “who is and who was and who is to come” (*1:4*). The beast imitates God’s eternal existence, but its destiny is destruction. This recalls the healed fatal wound in 13:3.

“*Here is the mind that has wisdom. The seven heads are seven mountains on which the woman sits*” (*v. 9*). “*They are seven kings. Five have fallen, the one is, and the other has not yet come. When he comes, he must continue a little while*” (*v. 10*). “*The beast that was, and is not, is himself also an eighth, and is of the seven; and he goes to destruction*” (*v. 11*). The seven heads have a double meaning: seven hills, a clear reference to Rome, and seven kings. Interpreters have tried to identify the seven kings with specific Roman emperors, but the lists differ depending on where one starts counting and which emperors are included. Others understand the seven kings symbolically as the complete succession of world empires that oppose God, with the beast as the final embodiment of them all. Still others see a reference to the legend of Nero returning. The main point is clear: the time remaining for the beast’s rule is short, and its end is destruction.

“*The ten horns that you saw are ten kings who have received no kingdom as yet, but they receive authority as kings with the beast for one hour*” (*v. 12*). “*These have one mind, and they give their power and authority to the beast*” (*v. 13*). The ten horns echo *Daniel 7:7*, 24. They may represent client kings allied with Rome, future rulers allied with the antichrist, or symbolically, all the rulers of the earth who give their power to the beast. Their authority lasts only “one hour,” a very short time. The Lamb’s victory over them is studied below.

### The Prostitute’s Downfall (*17:15–18*)

“*He said to me, “The waters which you saw, where the prostitute sits, are peoples, multitudes, nations, and languages.*” (*v. 15*) Ancient Babylon was built on the Euphrates and its canals (*Jeremiah 51:13*). Here the waters are interpreted as the peoples of the world. Babylon’s influence extends over all nations. The beast’s turning on the prostitute is studied below.

“*The woman whom you saw is the great city which reigns over the kings of the earth.”*” (*v. 18*) The angel identifies the woman as a city, the great city that dominates the world’s rulers. For John’s readers, this pointed to Rome. Its larger meaning reaches to every such city and system in history.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Revelation 17:3–6* — The Woman on the Scarlet Beast

> *“He carried me away in the Spirit into a wilderness. I saw a woman sitting on a scarlet-colored beast, full of blasphemous names, having seven heads and ten horns. The woman was dressed in purple and scarlet, and decked with gold and precious stones and pearls, having in her hand a golden cup full of abominations and the impurities of the sexual immorality of the earth. And on her forehead a name was written, ‘MYSTERY, BABYLON THE GREAT, THE MOTHER OF THE PROSTITUTES AND OF THE ABOMINATIONS OF THE EARTH.’ I saw the woman drunken with the blood of the saints and with the blood of the martyrs of Jesus. When I saw her, I wondered with great amazement.”*
>
> — *Revelation 17:3–6* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The angel carries John “in the Spirit into a wilderness.” There he sees “a woman sitting on a scarlet-colored beast, full of blasphemous names, having seven heads and ten horns.” The beast is the same beast from the sea described in chapter 13. The woman rides it, suggesting that she is supported by its power and appears to control it.

Verse 4 describes her appearance: she is “dressed in purple and scarlet, and decked with gold and precious stones and pearls.” Purple and scarlet were expensive dyes worn by royalty and the wealthy. She is dazzling and luxurious.

She holds “a golden cup full of abominations and the impurities of the sexual immorality of the earth.” Her cup looks valuable on the outside but is filled with filth inside.

In verse 5, “on her forehead a name was written”: “MYSTERY, BABYLON THE GREAT, THE MOTHER OF THE PROSTITUTES AND OF THE ABOMINATIONS OF THE EARTH.” Her name reveals her true identity: she is the source of corruption and idolatry.

Verse 6 adds the most shocking detail: “I saw the woman drunken with the blood of the saints and with the blood of the martyrs of Jesus.” Beneath her beauty, she is a murderer of God’s people.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The woman presents a striking contrast with other women in Revelation. The woman in chapter 12, clothed with the sun, represents God’s faithful people. The bride of the Lamb in chapters 19 and 21, clothed in fine linen, represents the redeemed church. The prostitute, dressed in luxury, represents the world’s seductive system that opposes God. The contrast invites readers to ask which “woman” they belong to: the faithful bride or the seductive prostitute.

The prostitute’s appeal lies in her beauty, wealth, and pleasure. She offers prosperity, status, and enjoyment. But what she offers is ultimately poison. Her golden cup holds abominations. This reflects the way sin often looks attractive while bringing ruin.

Her drunkenness with the blood of the saints reveals the violent side of worldly power. Societies that worship wealth and pleasure often turn against those who refuse to join them. In John’s day, Rome’s prosperity was accompanied by the persecution of Christians. Throughout history, systems built on greed and power have crushed the vulnerable and silenced faithful witnesses.

The wilderness setting is significant. In chapter 12, the woman representing God’s people fled to the wilderness for protection. Now John is taken to the wilderness to see Babylon clearly. From a place set apart from the world’s glamour, he can see the prostitute for what she really is.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage calls believers to see through the glamour of the world. Wealth, luxury, status, and pleasure can be enticing. Advertising, entertainment, and culture often present them as the path to happiness. But Revelation reveals that the world’s system, when it sets itself against God, is ultimately corrupt and destructive.

Believers can examine their own hearts for ways they have been seduced by worldly values. They can ask whether their desires, spending, and goals are shaped more by Babylon than by the kingdom of God.

This passage also reminds believers to care for those who are crushed by systems of greed and power. Babylon’s luxury was built on exploitation. Believers can stand with the vulnerable, pursue justice, and refuse to profit from oppression.

### *Revelation 17:14* — The Lamb Will Overcome

> *“These will war against the Lamb, and the Lamb will overcome them, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings; and those who are with him are called, chosen, and faithful.”*
>
> — *Revelation 17:14* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The ten kings, united with the beast, “will war against the Lamb.” All the forces of the world gather against Christ.

But the outcome is certain: “the Lamb will overcome them.” The reason is given: “for he is Lord of lords and King of kings.” No king or lord can stand against the One who rules over all kings and lords.

The verse ends with a description of those who are with the Lamb: “those who are with him are called, chosen, and faithful.”

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse is a brief preview of the final victory described in 19:11–21, where Christ appears as the rider on the white horse with the title “*KING OF KINGS AND LORD OF LORDS*” (*Revelation 19:16*). The outcome of the war is never in doubt.

The title “Lord of lords and King of kings” was used in the Old Testament for God (*Deuteronomy 10:17*; *Daniel 2:47*). Applying it to the Lamb affirms that Jesus shares God’s supreme authority. In a world where emperors claimed to be lords, this was a bold declaration that Jesus alone is the true Lord.

The Lamb conquers as the Lamb. His victory is rooted in His sacrificial death and resurrection. The weapons of the world, armies, alliances, and power, cannot defeat the One who conquered through the cross.

Those with the Lamb are described with three words. They are “called,” invited by God’s grace. They are “chosen,” selected by God for His purposes. And they are “faithful,” remaining loyal to Christ to the end. The first two describe God’s initiative; the third describes their response. God calls and chooses, and His people respond with faithfulness.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can live with confidence in Christ’s victory. Whatever powers seem to dominate the world, the Lamb will overcome them. He is Lord of lords and King of kings, and no human authority can stand against Him.

This verse also reminds believers of their identity. They are called and chosen by God, not because of their own merit but because of His grace. And they are called to be faithful, remaining loyal to Christ in every circumstance.

Believers can find encouragement in standing “with him.” They are not alone in the struggle. They stand with the victorious Lamb, sharing in His triumph.

### *Revelation 17:16–17* — Evil Destroys Itself

> *“The ten horns which you saw, they and the beast will hate the prostitute, will make her desolate, will strip her naked, will eat her flesh, and will burn her utterly with fire. For God has put in their hearts to do what he has in mind, to be of one mind, and to give their kingdom to the beast, until the words of God should be accomplished.”*
>
> — *Revelation 17:16–17* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

In a surprising twist, the beast and the ten kings turn against the prostitute. They “will hate the prostitute, will make her desolate, will strip her naked, will eat her flesh, and will burn her utterly with fire.” The very powers that supported her now destroy her.

Verse 17 reveals who is behind this: “For God has put in their hearts to do what he has in mind, to be of one mind, and to give their kingdom to the beast, until the words of God should be accomplished.” God uses the plans of evil powers to accomplish His purposes.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This passage reveals a profound truth about evil: it is self-destructive. The alliance between the prostitute and the beast was based on mutual exploitation. Such alliances do not last. In the end, evil turns on itself. History has many examples of corrupt powers that collapsed from within, betrayed by their own allies.

The description of the prostitute’s destruction draws on the prophets, especially *Ezekiel 16:37–41* and *23:25–29*, where Jerusalem’s former lovers turn against her. The violent language reflects the horror of judgment on a corrupt system; it describes the downfall of a city and its way of life, not a pattern for how people should be treated.

Verse 17 shows God’s sovereignty over even the most evil plans. The kings think they are acting on their own, but God is using their actions to accomplish His word. This echoes the way God used the Assyrians and Babylonians in the Old Testament to bring judgment, even though those nations acted out of their own pride and cruelty (*Isaiah 10:5–15*). God does not cause evil, but He rules over it and turns it to serve His purposes.

The phrase “until the words of God should be accomplished” assures readers that everything is moving toward the fulfillment of God’s plan. Nothing happens outside His purposes.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage gives believers hope when evil seems strong and united. Evil alliances are unstable. Corrupt systems eventually collapse. Believers do not need to fear that evil will last forever.

It also reminds believers that God is sovereign even over the plans of the wicked. When believers see evil at work in the world, they can trust that God is still in control and that His purposes will be accomplished.

Finally, this passage warns against placing trust in worldly power. Those who rely on the beast and its allies will eventually be betrayed. True security is found only in the Lamb, who never betrays His people.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Revelation 17* pulls back the curtain on Babylon, the seductive world system that opposes God. Dressed in luxury and holding a golden cup, she looks beautiful and powerful. But her cup is full of corruption, and she is drunk with the blood of God’s people. Believers are called to see through her glamour and recognize the emptiness and danger of a life built on wealth, pleasure, and power apart from God.

The chapter contrasts Babylon with the faithful people of God and the bride of the Lamb. Every person must choose which they will belong to. Believers are called to be faithful to Christ, refusing the world’s seductions and standing with the vulnerable who are crushed by systems of greed.

The chapter also reveals that the beast’s power is temporary and destined for destruction. The kings who ally with it have authority for only one hour. The Lamb, who is Lord of lords and King of kings, will overcome them, and His called, chosen, and faithful people will share His victory.

Finally, the chapter shows that God is sovereign even over evil. Corrupt alliances turn on themselves, and God uses even the plans of the wicked to accomplish His word. Believers can live with confidence, knowing that history is moving toward the fulfillment of God’s purposes and the triumph of the Lamb.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord Jesus, You are Lord of lords and King of kings. Open my eyes to see through the glamour of the world and its empty promises. Guard my heart from being seduced by wealth, pleasure, and power, and keep me faithful to You alone. Help me to care for those who are exploited and crushed by systems of greed, and to stand for justice in Your name. Thank You that I am called and chosen by Your grace; make me faithful to the end. When evil seems strong, remind me that its power is temporary and that You rule over all things. Thank You that You will overcome every power that sets itself against You, and that I stand with You in Your victory. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Revelation · Chapter 18 of 22

# Revelation — Chapter 18

Chapter Theme: The Fall of Babylon

[Read Revelation 18 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/REV18.htm)

Main Teaching

An angel with great authority comes down from heaven, lighting up the earth with his splendor, and cries out that Babylon the great has fallen and become a home for demons and every impure spirit, because the nations drank the maddening wine of her immorality, the kings committed adultery with her, and the merchants grew rich from her excessive luxury. Another voice from heaven calls God’s people to come out of her so that they will not share in her sins or receive her plagues, for her sins are piled up to heaven and God has remembered her crimes. She is to be paid back double for her deeds, and given as much torment and grief as the glory and luxury she gave herself, for in her heart she boasts that she sits as a queen, is not a widow, and will never mourn. Therefore her plagues will overtake her in one day: death, mourning, and famine, and she will be consumed by fire, for mighty is the Lord God who judges her. The kings of the earth who shared her luxury will weep and mourn as they see the smoke of her burning, standing far off in terror and crying, Woe, woe, great city, in one hour your doom has come. The merchants will weep because no one buys their cargoes anymore: gold, silver, jewels, fine fabrics, precious woods, ivory, spices, foods, animals, and even the bodies and souls of human beings. The sea captains and sailors will also mourn, crying out that the city that made them rich has been brought to ruin in one hour. Heaven, God’s people, apostles, and prophets are called to rejoice, for God has judged her for the way she treated them. Then a mighty angel throws a boulder like a great millstone into the sea, declaring that Babylon will be thrown down with such violence and never found again. Music, craftsmanship, the sound of the mill, the light of the lamp, and the voices of bride and bridegroom will never be heard in her again, for her merchants were the world’s important people, by her magic spell all nations were led astray, and in her was found the blood of prophets, of God’s people, and of all who have been slaughtered on the earth.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Revelation 18* describes the fall of Babylon in vivid, poetic language. Chapter 17 revealed Babylon as a seductive prostitute riding the beast. Chapter 18 portrays her collapse and the reactions of those who loved her. It reads like a funeral song, a lament over a fallen city, combined with a call to rejoice in God’s justice.

The chapter draws heavily on the Old Testament prophets’ laments over proud cities: Babylon (*Isaiah 13–14*, 47; *Jeremiah 50–51*) and Tyre (*Ezekiel 26–28*). Tyre was a great trading city, and *Ezekiel 27* lists its many merchandise and mourns its fall in terms very similar to *Revelation 18*. John takes these prophecies against ancient cities and applies them to the Babylon of his own day and of the end of the age.

For John’s first readers, the chapter would have been a startling message. Rome seemed eternal, wealthy, and invincible. It controlled the trade of the known world, and many people prospered from its economy. Revelation declares that this great city, and every system like it, will fall suddenly and completely.

### The Announcement of Babylon’s Fall (*18:1–3*)

“*After these things, I saw another angel coming down out of the sky, having great authority. The earth was illuminated with his glory*” (*v. 1*). The angel is so glorious that his presence lights up the earth. His authority to announce Babylon’s fall comes from God.

“*He cried with a mighty voice, saying, “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great, and she has become a habitation of demons, a prison of every unclean spirit, and a prison of every unclean and hated bird!*” (*v. 2*) The repetition “Fallen, fallen” echoes *Isaiah 21:9*. The once-glorious city becomes a desolate ruin, a haunt for unclean spirits and scavenger birds. This echoes the prophets’ descriptions of fallen cities becoming homes for wild animals (*Isaiah 13:21–22*; *34:11–15*; *Jeremiah 50:39*).

“*For all the nations have drunk of the wine of the wrath of her sexual immorality, the kings of the earth committed sexual immorality with her, and the merchants of the earth grew rich from the abundance of her luxury.”*” (*v. 3*) Three groups are named: the nations, the kings, and the merchants. They all participated in Babylon’s corruption and profited from it. Her “sexual immorality” refers primarily to spiritual unfaithfulness, her idolatry and seduction of the nations away from God, joined with her economic exploitation.

### The Call to Come Out (*18:4–8*)

The call to come out of Babylon and the reasons for her judgment are studied below.

“*Return to her just as she returned, and repay her double as she did, and according to her works. In the cup which she mixed, mix to her double*” (*v. 6*). The call for repayment echoes *Jeremiah 50:29* and *Psalm 137:8*. “Double” may mean a full and fitting repayment, as in *Isaiah 40:2*. This is not addressed to God’s people as a command to take revenge, but is a declaration of God’s just judgment. Babylon will receive what she has done to others.

### The Laments of Kings, Merchants, and Sailors (*18:9–19*)

“*The kings of the earth who committed sexual immorality and lived wantonly with her will weep and wail over her, when they look at the smoke of her burning,*” (*v. 9*) “*standing far away for the fear of her torment, saying, ‘Woe, woe, the great city, Babylon, the strong city! For your judgment has come in one hour.’*” (*v. 10*) The kings mourn not out of love for Babylon, but because they have lost the source of their power and pleasure. They stand “far away,” unwilling to share her fate. Her fall comes “in one hour,” suddenly and unexpectedly.

The merchants’ lament is studied below.

“*For in an hour such great riches are made desolate.’ Every ship master, and everyone who sails anywhere, and mariners, and as many as gain their living by sea, stood far away,*” (*v. 17*) “*and cried out as they looked at the smoke of her burning, saying, ‘What is like the great city?’*” (*v. 18*) “*They cast dust on their heads, and cried, weeping and mourning, saying, ‘Woe, woe, the great city, in which all who had their ships in the sea were made rich by reason of her great wealth!’ For she is made desolate in one hour*” (*v. 19*). The sailors and shipmasters also lament. Their cry, “What is like the great city?”, echoes the world’s worship of the beast: “*Who is like the beast?*” (*Revelation 13:4*). They had treated Babylon as incomparable, but she has fallen. Casting dust on their heads was a sign of deep grief (*Ezekiel 27:30*).

Notice that all three groups mourn what they have lost financially. None of them mourns the sins of Babylon or the blood of the saints she shed. Their grief is entirely self-centered.

### Heaven Rejoices (*18:20*)

“*“Rejoice over her, O heaven, you saints, apostles, and prophets, for God has judged your judgment on her.”*” (*v. 20*) In contrast to the earth’s mourning, heaven is called to rejoice. God’s people rejoice not out of cruelty, but because justice has finally been done. Babylon persecuted them, and God has vindicated them. The cry of the martyrs in 6:10 has been answered.

### The Millstone (*18:21–24*)

“*A mighty angel took up a stone like a great millstone and cast it into the sea, saying, “Thus with violence will Babylon, the great city, be thrown down, and will be found no more at all.*” (*v. 21*) This symbolic act echoes *Jeremiah 51:63–64*, where Jeremiah told Seraiah to tie a stone to his scroll of prophecy against Babylon and throw it into the Euphrates, declaring that Babylon would sink and never rise again. A great millstone, thrown into the sea, disappears forever. So will Babylon.

“*The voice of harpists, minstrels, flute players, and trumpeters will be heard no more at all in you. No craftsman of whatever craft will be found any more at all in you. The sound of a mill will be heard no more at all in you*” (*v. 22*). “*The light of a lamp will shine no more at all in you. The voice of the bridegroom and of the bride will be heard no more at all in you, for your merchants were the princes of the earth; for with your sorcery all the nations were deceived*” (*v. 23*). The ordinary sounds of city life fall silent: music, craftsmanship, grinding grain, lamplight, and wedding celebrations. This echoes *Jeremiah 25:10*. The silence is haunting. A city once full of life is now empty.

Two reasons are given. First, “your merchants were the princes of the earth.” Babylon’s merchants had become the world’s elite, and wealth had become the measure of greatness. Second, “with your sorcery all the nations were deceived.” Babylon used deception and spiritual seduction to lead the nations astray.

“*In her was found the blood of prophets and of saints, and of all who have been slain on the earth.”*” (*v. 24*) The final charge is the most serious. Babylon is guilty of shedding the blood of God’s people and of all who have been killed unjustly on the earth. Babylon represents every system of violence and oppression in history.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Revelation 18:4–5* — Come Out of Her, My People

> *“I heard another voice from heaven, saying, Come out of her, my people, that you have no participation in her sins, and that you don’t receive of her plagues, for her sins have reached to the sky, and God has remembered her iniquities.”*
>
> — *Revelation 18:4–5* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

A voice from heaven calls out: “Come out of her, my people.” God’s people are urged to separate themselves from Babylon.

Two reasons are given. First, “that you have no participation in her sins.” If they remain entangled with Babylon, they will share in her corruption. Second, “that you don’t receive of her plagues.” If they share in her sins, they will also share in her judgment.

Verse 5 explains why judgment is coming: “for her sins have reached to the sky, and God has remembered her iniquities.” Babylon’s sins have piled up so high that they reach heaven itself. God has not forgotten them.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This call echoes the prophets’ commands to God’s people to flee from ancient Babylon: “*My people, go away from the middle of her, and each of you save yourselves from the LORD’s fierce anger*” (*Jeremiah 51:45*) (see also *Isaiah 48:20*; *52:11*). In the Old Testament, the call was to physically leave the city before its destruction. In Revelation, the call is primarily spiritual and moral.

For John’s readers, “coming out” did not necessarily mean physically leaving Rome or their cities. It meant refusing to participate in Babylon’s idolatry, immorality, greed, and exploitation. It meant living by different values, even while living in the midst of the world. Jesus prayed that His disciples would be in the world but not of it (*John 17:15–16*). Paul urged believers not to be conformed to the world but transformed by the renewing of their minds (*Romans 12:2*).

The phrase “her sins have reached to the sky” recalls the tower of Babel (*Genesis 11:4*), whose builders wanted to reach the heavens. Babel and Babylon share the same name in Hebrew. Human pride, building upward in defiance of God, eventually reaches heaven not in glory but in judgment.

“God has remembered her iniquities” means that God takes note and will act. For the persecuted, this was a comfort. God had not forgotten what Babylon had done.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers today live within societies that can resemble Babylon in many ways: consumerism, the pursuit of luxury, the exploitation of the vulnerable, and the worship of wealth and power. This passage calls believers to “come out” spiritually: to refuse to make these values their own.

Coming out of Babylon may involve practical choices: how believers spend their money, what they consume, where they invest, how they treat workers and the poor, and what they allow to shape their desires. It means living with generosity, simplicity, justice, and contentment.

This call is not a call to withdraw from the world in fear or pride. Believers are still called to love their neighbors, work for the good of their communities, and bear witness to Christ. But they are called to do so as citizens of God’s kingdom, not as captives of Babylon.

### *Revelation 18:7–8* — Pride Before the Fall

> *“However much she glorified herself and grew wanton, so much give her of torment and mourning. For she says in her heart, “I sit a queen, and am no widow, and will in no way see mourning.” Therefore in one day her plagues will come: death, mourning, and famine; and she will be utterly burned with fire, for the Lord God who has judged her is strong.”*
>
> — *Revelation 18:7–8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

Verse 7 describes Babylon’s attitude: “she glorified herself and grew wanton.” She lived for her own glory and indulged in luxury without limit. Therefore, the voice says, “so much give her of torment and mourning.”

Babylon’s inner boast is revealed: “For she says in her heart, ‘I sit a queen, and am no widow, and will in no way see mourning.’” She believes she is secure, powerful, and untouchable. She thinks nothing bad can ever happen to her.

Verse 8 announces the result: “Therefore in one day her plagues will come: death, mourning, and famine; and she will be utterly burned with fire.” Her confidence will be shattered suddenly. The reason: “for the Lord God who has judged her is strong.”

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Babylon’s boast echoes the words of ancient Babylon in *Isaiah 47*, who said, “*I will be a princess forever*” (*Isaiah 47:7*), and “*I won’t sit as a widow, neither will I know the loss of children*” (*Isaiah 47:8*). Isaiah declared that both losses would come upon her in a moment, in one day. Revelation applies this same prophecy to the Babylon of John’s day and beyond.

The heart of Babylon’s sin is pride and self-glorification. She believes she is self-sufficient and secure apart from God. This is the same attitude Christ rebuked in the Laodicean church: “*I am rich, and have gotten riches, and have need of nothing*” (*Revelation 3:17*). Pride blinds people to their true condition and their need for God.

The suddenness of Babylon’s fall is emphasized repeatedly: “in one day” (v8), “in one hour” (vv10, 17, 19). The proud often believe that their security will last forever. But God can bring down the mighty in a moment. As Proverbs says, “*Pride goes before destruction, and an arrogant spirit before a fall*” (*Proverbs 16:18*).

The final phrase, “the Lord God who has judged her is strong,” reminds readers that Babylon’s strength is nothing compared with God’s. She thought she was invincible, but she is no match for the Almighty.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage warns against the pride that assumes nothing bad could ever happen to us. Wealth, success, and comfort can create a false sense of security. Believers are called to humility, recognizing that every good thing comes from God and that true security is found only in Him.

Believers can also examine their own hearts for self-glorification. Living for one’s own glory, comfort, and pleasure is the spirit of Babylon. Living for God’s glory and the good of others is the spirit of the kingdom.

Finally, this passage encourages believers not to be intimidated by proud and powerful systems. However secure they seem, they can fall in a moment. God alone is truly strong.

### *Revelation 18:11–13* — Merchandise and Human Lives

> *“The merchants of the earth weep and mourn over her, for no one buys their merchandise any more: merchandise of gold, silver, precious stones, pearls, fine linen, purple, silk, scarlet, all expensive wood, every vessel of ivory, every vessel made of most precious wood, and of brass, and iron, and marble; and cinnamon, incense, perfume, frankincense, wine, olive oil, fine flour, wheat, cattle, sheep, horses, chariots, and people’s bodies and souls.”*
>
> — *Revelation 18:11–13* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The merchants of the earth “weep and mourn over her, for no one buys their merchandise any more.” Their grief is economic. Babylon was their best customer, and now she is gone.

Verses 12–13 list the merchandise that flowed into Babylon. The list includes precious metals and stones (“gold, silver, precious stones, pearls”), luxurious fabrics (“fine linen, purple, silk, scarlet”), expensive building materials (“expensive wood,” “ivory,” “brass, and iron, and marble”), spices and perfumes (“cinnamon, incense, perfume, frankincense”), food (“wine, olive oil, fine flour, wheat”), animals (“cattle, sheep, horses”), and vehicles (“chariots”).

The list ends with a shocking item: “people’s bodies and souls.” Human beings themselves were traded as merchandise.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This list closely resembles the list of Tyre’s trade goods in *Ezekiel 27:12–24*. It also reflects the actual luxury trade of the Roman Empire. Rome imported goods from across the known world: silk from China, spices from India, ivory from Africa, marble from Greece. Much of this trade served the luxury of the wealthy elite.

The list moves from luxury goods to basic necessities to living creatures and finally to human beings. The final item, “people’s bodies and souls,” exposes the moral horror at the heart of Babylon’s economy. The Roman Empire depended heavily on slavery. Millions of people were bought and sold as property. The phrase “bodies and souls” emphasizes that these were not mere “bodies,” as slave traders often called them, but human beings with souls, made in God’s image.

By placing human beings at the end of a list of commodities, Revelation exposes the dehumanizing logic of an economy driven by greed. When profit becomes the ultimate value, people are reduced to products. God condemns this. Scripture elsewhere condemns kidnapping and trafficking in people (*Exodus 21:16*; *1 Timothy 1:10*). Revelation’s judgment on Babylon includes judgment on every system that treats human beings as merchandise. Passages like this stand firmly against every form of slavery and human trafficking, and any attempt to use Scripture to defend such practices is a terrible distortion of God’s word.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage challenges believers to consider the human cost of the economic systems they participate in. Today, human trafficking, forced labor, and exploitation of workers continue around the world. Many products are made through unjust labor practices. Believers can seek to learn about these issues, make thoughtful choices as consumers, and support efforts to end exploitation.

This passage also warns against the love of luxury. The merchants grieved because their profits were lost, not because of the injustice they had supported. Believers can examine whether their own desires for comfort and luxury have made them indifferent to the suffering of others.

Most importantly, this passage reminds believers that every human being has infinite worth in God’s eyes. No person is merchandise. Believers can honor the dignity of every person, especially the poor, the vulnerable, and the exploited, treating them as people for whom Christ died.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Revelation 18* announces the fall of Babylon, the great city that seduced the nations with wealth, luxury, and idolatry and persecuted God’s people. Her fall comes suddenly, in one hour, and it is complete. The sounds of her life fall silent, and she is thrown down like a millstone into the sea, never to rise again.

The chapter calls believers to “come out” of Babylon. They live in societies shaped by greed, pride, and the pursuit of luxury, but they are called to refuse Babylon’s values. This means living with humility, generosity, contentment, and justice, and refusing to profit from the exploitation of others.

The laments of the kings, merchants, and sailors reveal the emptiness of a life built on wealth. They mourn their lost profits, but not Babylon’s sins or the blood of the saints. Believers are called to set their hearts on treasures that cannot be lost, treasures in heaven.

The list of Babylon’s merchandise, ending with “people’s bodies and souls,” exposes the moral horror of systems that treat human beings as commodities. Believers are called to honor the dignity of every person and to stand against exploitation and trafficking.

Finally, the chapter calls heaven and God’s people to rejoice in God’s justice. Babylon’s fall is not a tragedy for those who belong to God. It is the vindication of the persecuted and the end of oppression. Believers can live with confidence that every proud and oppressive system will one day fall, and God’s kingdom will stand forever.

## Chapter Prayer

Lord God, You are strong, and every proud power will fall before You. Open my eyes to the ways the values of Babylon have shaped my heart. Call me out of greed, pride, and the love of luxury, and teach me to live with humility, generosity, and contentment. Guard me from the pride that says nothing bad can happen to me, and help me to find my security in You alone. Give me a heart that honors the dignity of every person, and use me to stand against exploitation and injustice. I pray for all who are trafficked, enslaved, or exploited; rescue them and bring them freedom. Help me to set my heart on treasures that last forever. Thank You that You will judge every oppressive system and vindicate Your people. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
