Revelation · Chapter 19 of 22

# Revelation — Chapter 19

Chapter Theme: The Wedding of the Lamb and the Return of the King

[Read Revelation 19 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/REV19.htm)

Main Teaching

After the fall of Babylon, John hears what sounds like a great multitude in heaven shouting, Hallelujah! Salvation, glory, and power belong to our God, for His judgments are true and just; He has judged the great prostitute who corrupted the earth and has avenged the blood of His servants. The twenty-four elders and four living creatures fall down and worship, and a voice from the throne calls all God’s servants, small and great, to praise Him. Then the great multitude, sounding like rushing waters and loud thunder, cries out that the Lord God Almighty reigns, and that the wedding of the Lamb has come and His bride has made herself ready, clothed in fine linen, bright and clean, which stands for the righteous acts of God’s holy people. The angel tells John to write that those invited to the wedding supper of the Lamb are blessed. When John falls at the angel’s feet to worship him, the angel stops him, saying that he is a fellow servant and that John must worship God. Then heaven opens, and John sees a white horse whose rider is called Faithful and True, who judges and wages war with justice. His eyes are like blazing fire, He wears many crowns, and He has a name no one knows but He Himself. He is dressed in a robe dipped in blood, and His name is the Word of God. The armies of heaven, dressed in fine white linen, follow Him on white horses. From His mouth comes a sharp sword to strike down the nations; He will rule them with an iron scepter and tread the winepress of God’s wrath. On His robe and thigh is written: King of kings and Lord of lords. An angel standing in the sun calls the birds to the great supper of God. The beast, the kings of the earth, and their armies gather to make war against the rider and His army, but the beast and the false prophet are captured and thrown alive into the lake of fire, and the rest are killed by the sword that comes from the rider’s mouth.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Revelation 19* is a turning point. After the long descriptions of judgment on Babylon and the beast’s kingdom, heaven erupts in praise. Then the moment the whole book has been anticipating arrives: Christ returns in glory to defeat His enemies and establish His reign.

The chapter has two main parts. The first is a scene of worship in heaven (vv1–10), celebrating God’s judgment on Babylon and announcing the wedding of the Lamb. The second is the vision of Christ’s return as the rider on the white horse (vv11–21), defeating the beast, the false prophet, and their armies.

The chapter presents two contrasting feasts. The first is the wedding supper of the Lamb, a feast of joy for those who belong to Him. The second is “the great supper of God,” a grim image of judgment on those who opposed Him. Every person will be present at one of these two feasts.

### Hallelujah! (*19:1–5*)

“*After these things I heard something like a loud voice of a great multitude in heaven, saying, “Hallelujah! Salvation, power, and glory belong to our God;*” (*v. 1*) “*for his judgments are true and righteous. For he has judged the great prostitute who corrupted the earth with her sexual immorality, and he has avenged the blood of his servants at her hand.”*” (*v. 2*) “Hallelujah” is a Hebrew word meaning “Praise the LORD.” This is the only chapter in the New Testament where it appears, and it appears four times here (vv1, 3, 4, 6). It recalls the “Hallelujah Psalms” (*Psalms 146–150*) and the psalms that celebrated God’s victory over His enemies (*Psalms 113–118*).

The multitude praises God for two reasons. His judgments are “true and righteous,” and He has “avenged the blood of his servants.” The call of heaven to rejoice over Babylon (*18:20*) is now answered. The cry of the martyrs, “How long?” (*6:10*), has finally been answered in full.

“*A second said, “Hallelujah! Her smoke goes up forever and ever.”*” (*v. 3*) Babylon’s destruction is final. The smoke rising forever echoes *Isaiah 34:10*, describing the lasting ruin of Edom. Babylon will never rise again.

“*The twenty-four elders and the four living creatures fell down and worshiped God who sits on the throne, saying, “Amen! Hallelujah!”*” (*v. 4*) This is the last appearance of the elders and the living creatures in Revelation. They began the worship of heaven in chapter 4, and now they affirm God’s final victory.

“*A voice came from the throne, saying, “Give praise to our God, all you his servants, you who fear him, the small and the great!”*” (*v. 5*) All of God’s people, regardless of status, are invited to join the praise. “The small and the great” includes everyone, from the humblest believer to the most prominent.

### The Wedding of the Lamb (*19:6–10*)

The announcement of the wedding and the blessing on those invited are studied below.

### The Rider on the White Horse (*19:11–16*)

The vision of Christ’s return is studied below.

### The Defeat of the Beast (*19:17–21*)

“*I saw an angel standing in the sun. He cried with a loud voice, saying to all the birds that fly in the sky, “Come! Be gathered together to the great supper of God,*” (*v. 17*) “*that you may eat the flesh of kings, the flesh of captains, the flesh of mighty men, and the flesh of horses and of those who sit on them, and the flesh of all men, both free and slave, small and great.”*” (*v. 18*) This grim image comes from *Ezekiel 39:17–20*, where God invites birds and beasts to a feast on the fallen armies of Gog. In the ancient world, being left unburied and eaten by birds was the ultimate disgrace. The “great supper of God” stands in stark contrast to the “wedding supper of the Lamb.” Those who refused the invitation to the Lamb’s wedding feast become the feast for the birds. The image is deliberately shocking, underscoring the seriousness of rejecting God.

“*I saw the beast, the kings of the earth, and their armies, gathered together to make war against him who sat on the horse and against his army*” (*v. 19*). This is the gathering described in 16:14–16, the battle of Armageddon. The forces of evil assemble for their final stand against Christ.

“*The beast was taken, and with him the false prophet who worked the signs in his sight, with which he deceived those who had received the mark of the beast and those who worshiped his image. These two were thrown alive into the lake of fire that burns with sulfur*” (*v. 20*). Remarkably, there is no description of a battle. The beast and the false prophet are simply captured. The great confrontation that the world’s armies prepared for is over before it begins. The lake of fire, mentioned here for the first time, is the place of final judgment (*20:10*, 14–15).

“*The rest were killed with the sword of him who sat on the horse, the sword which came out of his mouth. So all the birds were filled with their flesh*” (*v. 21*). Christ defeats His enemies with the sword from His mouth, His word. Interpreters differ on how literally to understand this scene. Some expect a literal battle at Christ’s return. Many understand the sword from His mouth as showing that Christ’s victory is won not by physical weapons but by the power of His word, the same word that spoke creation into being and will judge the world. In either case, the victory belongs entirely to Christ, and it is complete.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Revelation 19:6–8* — The Wedding of the Lamb Has Come

> *“I heard something like the voice of a great multitude, and like the voice of many waters, and like the voice of mighty thunders, saying, ‘Hallelujah! For the Lord our God, the Almighty, reigns! Let’s rejoice and be exceedingly glad, and let’s give the glory to him. For the wedding of the Lamb has come, and his wife has made herself ready.’ It was given to her that she would array herself in bright, pure, fine linen, for the fine linen is the righteous acts of the saints.”*
>
> — *Revelation 19:6–8* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

John hears a great sound: “something like the voice of a great multitude, and like the voice of many waters, and like the voice of mighty thunders.” The praise of heaven is overwhelming in its volume and joy.

The multitude cries: “Hallelujah! For the Lord our God, the Almighty, reigns!” God’s reign is now fully revealed. Every rival power has fallen.

Verse 7 continues: “Let’s rejoice and be exceedingly glad, and let’s give the glory to him. For the wedding of the Lamb has come, and his wife has made herself ready.” The long-awaited wedding is at hand. The bride is the people of God, the church.

Verse 8 describes her clothing: “It was given to her that she would array herself in bright, pure, fine linen, for the fine linen is the righteous acts of the saints.” Her wedding garment represents the righteous deeds of God’s people.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The image of God’s people as His bride runs throughout Scripture. In the Old Testament, God called Israel His bride and Himself her husband (*Isaiah 54:5*; *62:5*; *Hosea 2:19–20*). In the New Testament, Jesus called Himself the bridegroom (*Mark 2:19–20*), and Paul described the church as the bride of Christ, whom He loved and gave Himself for (*Ephesians 5:25–27*; *2 Corinthians 11:2*). The wedding of the Lamb is the fulfillment of this great love story: the complete and joyful union of Christ and His people.

The bride contrasts sharply with the prostitute of chapters 17–18. The prostitute was dressed in purple, scarlet, gold, and jewels, the gaudy luxury of the world. The bride is dressed in simple, bright, pure linen. The prostitute’s beauty was a cover for corruption. The bride’s beauty is genuine purity.

Notice the balance in verse 8. The bride “has made herself ready,” and yet her clothing “was given to her.” Her righteousness is both a gift and a response. Believers are made righteous through Christ, as a gift of grace. And their lives, transformed by grace, produce righteous deeds. These deeds do not earn salvation, but they are the beautiful evidence of God’s work in them (*Ephesians 2:8–10*).

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage gives believers a glorious hope. The story of history ends not in tragedy but in a wedding celebration. Believers will be united with Christ in perfect love and joy forever.

This hope can shape how believers live now. Like a bride preparing for her wedding, believers can prepare for Christ’s return by growing in holiness and love. Every act of faithfulness, kindness, and righteousness is part of their wedding garment.

This passage also reminds believers that Christ loves His church deeply. Despite the church’s failures and weaknesses, Christ will present her as a radiant bride. Believers can love the church as Christ does, working for her purity and unity.

### *Revelation 19:9–10* — Invited to the Wedding Supper

> *“He said to me, ‘Write, “Blessed are those who are invited to the wedding supper of the Lamb.”’ He said to me, ‘These are true words of God.’ I fell down before his feet to worship him. He said to me, ‘Look! Don’t do it! I am a fellow bondservant with you and with your brothers who hold the testimony of Jesus. Worship God, for the testimony of Jesus is the Spirit of Prophecy.’”*
>
> — *Revelation 19:9–10* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

The angel tells John: “Write, ‘Blessed are those who are invited to the wedding supper of the Lamb.’” This is the fourth blessing in Revelation. Those invited to the wedding celebration are truly blessed. Then the angel adds: “These are true words of God.”

John is so overwhelmed that he falls at the angel’s feet to worship him. But the angel immediately stops him: “Look! Don’t do it! I am a fellow bondservant with you and with your brothers who hold the testimony of Jesus. Worship God.”

The angel explains: “for the testimony of Jesus is the Spirit of Prophecy.” True prophecy points to Jesus.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

Jesus often described the kingdom of God as a great feast or wedding banquet (*Matthew 8:11*; *22:1–14*; *Luke 14:15–24*). At the Last Supper, He told His disciples that He would not drink wine again until He drank it new with them in His Father’s kingdom (*Matthew 26:29*). The wedding supper of the Lamb is that promised celebration.

The invitation is the key. In Jesus’ parables, many were invited to the feast, but some refused (*Matthew 22:1–10*). The blessing belongs to those who accept the invitation. The gospel is God’s invitation to the wedding supper, and it is offered freely to all.

John’s mistake in worshiping the angel is a powerful lesson. Even an apostle could be tempted to give worship to a glorious messenger rather than to God. The angel firmly refuses. Angels, prophets, and church leaders are all fellow servants. Only God is worthy of worship. This also guards against any temptation to venerate angels in place of God (*Colossians 2:18*).

The phrase “the testimony of Jesus is the Spirit of Prophecy” has been understood in two ways. It may mean that the testimony about Jesus is the essence of all prophecy; all true prophecy points to Him. Or it may mean that those who bear witness to Jesus are speaking by the Spirit of prophecy. Both are true. Jesus is the center of God’s revelation.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can rejoice that they are invited to the wedding supper of the Lamb. This is not an invitation they earned, but a gift of grace. They can respond with gratitude and joy.

This passage also encourages believers to extend the invitation to others. The gospel is an invitation to a feast. Believers can share it with warmth and joy, inviting others to come.

The angel’s refusal of worship reminds believers to keep their worship focused on God alone. It is possible to admire spiritual leaders, gifted teachers, or spiritual experiences in a way that takes the place of God. Believers are called to honor others as fellow servants, while giving worship to God alone.

Finally, believers can remember that all true prophecy and spiritual teaching points to Jesus. They can evaluate any message by whether it exalts Christ and bears witness to Him.

### *Revelation 19:11–16* — Faithful and True, King of Kings

> *“I saw heaven opened, and behold, a white horse, and he who sat on it is called Faithful and True. In righteousness he judges and makes war. His eyes are a flame of fire, and on his head are many crowns. He has names written and a name written which no one knows but he himself. He is clothed in a garment sprinkled with blood. His name is called ‘The Word of God.’ The armies which are in heaven, clothed in white, pure, fine linen, followed him on white horses. Out of his mouth proceeds a sharp, double-edged sword that with it he should strike the nations. He will rule them with an iron rod. He treads the wine press of the fierceness of the wrath of God, the Almighty. He has on his garment and on his thigh a name written, ‘KING OF KINGS AND LORD OF LORDS.’”*
>
> — *Revelation 19:11–16* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

John sees “heaven opened,” and there is “a white horse, and he who sat on it is called Faithful and True.” This is Christ returning in glory. “In righteousness he judges and makes war.” His judgment and warfare are always just.

Verse 12 describes Him: “His eyes are a flame of fire,” seeing all things clearly. “On his head are many crowns,” showing His supreme authority. And “He has names written and a name written which no one knows but he himself,” pointing to the mystery of His divine nature.

In verse 13, “He is clothed in a garment sprinkled with blood. His name is called ‘The Word of God.’”

Verse 14 describes His army: “The armies which are in heaven, clothed in white, pure, fine linen, followed him on white horses.”

Verse 15 describes His power: “Out of his mouth proceeds a sharp, double-edged sword that with it he should strike the nations. He will rule them with an iron rod. He treads the wine press of the fierceness of the wrath of God, the Almighty.”

Verse 16 gives His title: “He has on his garment and on his thigh a name written, ‘KING OF KINGS AND LORD OF LORDS.’”

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This is the climactic vision of Christ in Revelation. The Lamb who was slain now comes as the conquering King. Many interpreters see this as the description of Christ’s second coming, the return that Jesus promised (*Matthew 24:30*; *Acts 1:11*). Some idealist interpreters understand it more broadly as a symbolic portrayal of Christ’s victory over evil, but most interpreters across traditions see here the visible, personal return of Christ at the end of the age.

His names reveal His identity. “Faithful and True” contrasts with the deceptive beast and false prophet. “The Word of God” connects with *John 1:1*, where Jesus is the eternal Word who was with God and was God. “KING OF KINGS AND LORD OF LORDS” declares His supreme authority over every earthly ruler. The hidden name suggests that there is more to Christ than any human can fully understand.

The robe “sprinkled with blood” has been understood in two ways. Some see it as the blood of His enemies, drawing on *Isaiah 63:1–3*, where the divine warrior’s garments are stained from treading the winepress. Others note that the robe is bloodstained before the battle begins, and see it as His own blood, shed on the cross. On this view, the King comes as the Lamb who was slain; His victory is grounded in His sacrifice. Both meanings may be present: the One who shed His blood for His people now comes to judge those who rejected Him.

The armies of heaven are dressed in white linen, the same clothing as the bride (*19:8*). They may be angels, the redeemed, or both (compare 17:14). Notably, they carry no weapons and do not fight. Christ alone wins the victory with the sword of His mouth, His word.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage gives believers great confidence. The same Jesus who came in humility, who was crucified and rose again, will return in glory. Every injustice will be judged, every enemy defeated, and every promise fulfilled.

The name “Faithful and True” invites believers to trust Christ completely. In a world full of broken promises and lies, He is utterly reliable. Everything He has said will come to pass.

The fact that Christ wins by the sword of His mouth reminds believers that God’s word is powerful. They can trust the power of His word to accomplish His purposes and can rely on it in their own lives.

Finally, the title “KING OF KINGS AND LORD OF LORDS” calls believers to give Him their full allegiance. No earthly ruler, nation, or cause deserves the loyalty that belongs to Him.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Revelation 19* is a chapter of celebration and victory. Heaven rejoices over God’s just judgment on Babylon and proclaims that the Lord God Almighty reigns. Believers can join this praise now, worshiping God for His justice, His power, and His faithfulness.

The chapter announces the wedding of the Lamb. The story of history ends in a celebration of love, as Christ and His people are united forever. Believers can live with joyful hope, preparing themselves like a bride by growing in holiness and righteous living, knowing that their wedding garment is ultimately a gift of grace.

The blessing on those invited to the wedding supper reminds believers that the gospel is an invitation. They can respond with gratitude and share the invitation with others. At the same time, the angel’s refusal of worship calls believers to keep their worship centered on God alone.

The vision of the rider on the white horse gives believers confidence in Christ’s return. The Lamb who was slain will return as King of kings and Lord of lords. He is Faithful and True, and He will defeat every enemy by the power of His word. The beast and the false prophet, who seemed so powerful, will be captured without a fight.

The two suppers in this chapter, the wedding supper of the Lamb and the great supper of God, present a solemn choice. Believers are called to accept God’s invitation, to live in readiness for Christ’s return, and to share His invitation with urgency and love.

## Chapter Prayer

Hallelujah! Salvation, glory, and power belong to You, Lord God Almighty, for Your judgments are true and righteous. Thank You that You reign, and that every power that opposes You will fall. Lord Jesus, thank You that You love Your church as a bridegroom loves his bride, and that You are preparing us for the wedding supper of the Lamb. Clothe me in Your righteousness, and help me to live a life of faithful, righteous deeds that honor You. Thank You for the invitation to Your feast; help me to share it joyfully with others. Keep my worship centered on You alone. I look forward to the day when You return, Faithful and True, King of kings and Lord of lords. Come, Lord Jesus. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Revelation · Chapter 20 of 22

# Revelation — Chapter 20

Chapter Theme: The Thousand Years and the Final Judgment

[Read Revelation 20 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/REV20.htm)

Main Teaching

John sees an angel coming down from heaven with the key to the abyss and a great chain. He seizes the dragon, the ancient serpent who is the devil and Satan, binds him for a thousand years, throws him into the abyss, and locks and seals it so that he can no longer deceive the nations until the thousand years are ended; after that he must be released for a short time. John sees thrones on which those given authority to judge are seated, and the souls of those who had been beheaded for their testimony about Jesus and for the word of God, who had not worshiped the beast or its image or received its mark. They come to life and reign with Christ for a thousand years. The rest of the dead do not come to life until the thousand years are ended. This is the first resurrection, and those who share in it are blessed and holy; the second death has no power over them, and they will be priests of God and of Christ and reign with Him. When the thousand years are over, Satan is released and goes out to deceive the nations in the four corners of the earth, Gog and Magog, gathering them for battle in numbers like the sand of the sea. They march across the earth and surround the camp of God’s people, the city He loves, but fire comes down from heaven and devours them. The devil is thrown into the lake of burning sulfur, where the beast and the false prophet were thrown. Then John sees a great white throne and Him who is seated on it; earth and sky flee from His presence. The dead, great and small, stand before the throne, and books are opened, including the book of life. The dead are judged according to what they have done, as recorded in the books. The sea, death, and Hades give up their dead, and each person is judged. Then death and Hades are thrown into the lake of fire, the second death. Anyone whose name is not found written in the book of life is thrown into the lake of fire.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Revelation 20* is one of the most discussed chapters in the Bible. It describes a period of a thousand years, often called the “millennium,” from the Latin word for a thousand years. During this time Satan is bound, and faithful believers reign with Christ. At the end of the thousand years, Satan is released, leads a final rebellion, and is defeated forever. The chapter closes with the final judgment before the great white throne.

Christians throughout history have held different views about the thousand years. These differences are not about whether Christ will return, whether there will be a resurrection and final judgment, or whether Satan will be defeated. All orthodox Christians affirm these things. The differences concern the timing and nature of the thousand years and how they relate to Christ’s return. Sincere, faithful believers hold each of these views, and they have long been held side by side within the church.

### The Main Views of the Thousand Years

**Premillennialism** holds that Christ will return before (“pre-”) the thousand years and will then reign on earth for a literal or extended period before the final judgment and the new creation. Premillennialists read *Revelation 20* as following chronologically after Christ’s return in chapter 19. This view was common in the early church, held by writers such as Justin Martyr and Irenaeus. Among premillennialists, **historic premillennialists** generally see the church going through the final tribulation before Christ returns, while **dispensational premillennialists** generally hold that the church will be taken up before a seven-year tribulation, and that the millennium will include the fulfillment of specific promises to the nation of Israel.

**Amillennialism** holds that the thousand years is a symbolic number representing the present age, the period between Christ’s first and second comings. On this view, Satan was bound by Christ’s victory at the cross so that he cannot prevent the gospel from going to the nations (*Matthew 12:29*), and believers who have died now reign with Christ in heaven. The “first resurrection” is understood as either spiritual new birth or the entrance of believers into Christ’s presence at death. This view was taught by Augustine and has been widely held in Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, and Reformed traditions. Many amillennialists see chapter 20 as recapitulating, or retelling from a new angle, the history of the church age rather than following chapter 19 in time.

**Postmillennialism** holds that Christ will return after (“post-”) the thousand years, which is understood as a long period in which the gospel spreads and transforms the world, leading to a time of great righteousness and peace before Christ’s return. This view was popular among many Protestants in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.

Each view has strengths and difficulties, and each is held by thoughtful, Bible-believing Christians. This commentary will note how each view reads key verses, while focusing on the truths all believers share.

### Satan Bound (*20:1–3*)

“*I saw an angel coming down out of heaven, having the key of the abyss and a great chain in his hand*” (*v. 1*). “*He seized the dragon, the old serpent, who is the devil and Satan, who deceives the whole inhabited earth, and bound him for a thousand years,*” (*v. 2*) “*and cast him into the abyss, and shut it and sealed it over him, that he should deceive the nations no more until the thousand years were finished. After this, he must be freed for a short time*” (*v. 3*).

The binding of Satan is described with strong language: seized, bound, thrown, locked, and sealed. Satan, who seemed so powerful in earlier chapters, is overpowered by a single angel. The purpose of the binding is specific: “that he should deceive the nations no more.”

Premillennialists understand this as a complete removal of Satan’s influence on earth during a future thousand-year reign of Christ. Amillennialists understand it as a restriction on Satan’s power that began with Christ’s victory at the cross and resurrection, so that he can no longer prevent the nations from hearing the gospel, as he once held them in darkness. They point to Jesus’ words about binding the strong man (*Matthew 12:29*), His statement that He saw Satan fall like lightning (*Luke 10:18*), and the declaration that the ruler of this world is cast out (*John 12:31*). Both views agree that Satan’s power is limited by God and that he will be finally defeated.

The phrase “he must be freed for a short time” shows that even Satan’s release is under God’s control. “Must” points to God’s purpose.

### The Reign of the Saints (*20:4–6*)

The reign with Christ and the first resurrection are studied below.

### Satan’s Final Defeat (*20:7–10*)

“*And after the thousand years, Satan will be released from his prison*” (*v. 7*) “*and he will come out to deceive the nations which are in the four corners of the earth, Gog and Magog, to gather them together to the war, whose number is as the sand of the sea*” (*v. 8*). Gog and Magog come from *Ezekiel 38–39*, where Gog of the land of Magog leads a vast coalition of nations against God’s people and is destroyed by God. In Revelation, Gog and Magog represent all the nations of the earth gathered in a final rebellion against God. Their vast number shows the scale of the rebellion.

The fact that people rebel even after a long period of Satan’s binding is sobering. It shows that the problem of evil lies not only in Satan’s deception but also in the human heart. Even in ideal conditions, humanity apart from God’s grace turns away from Him.

“*They went up over the width of the earth and surrounded the camp of the saints and the beloved city. Fire came down out of heaven from God and devoured them*” (*v. 9*). “The camp of the saints” recalls Israel camped in the wilderness. “The beloved city” is the city of God’s people, the holy city. The enemies surround it, but there is no battle. Fire from heaven ends the rebellion instantly, as in *Ezekiel 38:22* and *39:6*. Some interpreters see this battle as the same as the battle described in *Revelation 19:17–21* and *16:14–16*, retold from a different angle; others see it as a separate, later event. Either way, God wins effortlessly.

The final defeat of the devil is studied below.

### The Great White Throne (*20:11–15*)

The final judgment is studied below.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Revelation 20:4–6* — Reigning with Christ

> *“I saw thrones, and they sat on them, and judgment was given to them. I saw the souls of those who had been beheaded for the testimony of Jesus and for the word of God, and such as didn’t worship the beast nor his image, and didn’t receive the mark on their forehead and on their hand. They lived and reigned with Christ for a thousand years. The rest of the dead didn’t live until the thousand years were finished. This is the first resurrection. Blessed and holy is he who has part in the first resurrection. Over these, the second death has no power, but they will be priests of God and of Christ, and will reign with him one thousand years.”*
>
> — *Revelation 20:4–6* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

John sees “thrones,” and those seated on them are given authority to judge. He also sees “the souls of those who had been beheaded for the testimony of Jesus and for the word of God.” These are martyrs, along with all who “didn’t worship the beast nor his image, and didn’t receive the mark.” They are the faithful who refused to compromise.

These faithful believers “lived and reigned with Christ for a thousand years.” Those who seemed to lose everything on earth now share in Christ’s reign.

Verse 5 adds: “The rest of the dead didn’t live until the thousand years were finished. This is the first resurrection.”

Verse 6 pronounces a blessing: “Blessed and holy is he who has part in the first resurrection. Over these, the second death has no power, but they will be priests of God and of Christ, and will reign with him one thousand years.” This is the fifth blessing in Revelation.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This passage answers the cry of the martyrs in 6:9–11. Those who were killed for their faith are not forgotten. They are vindicated and honored, reigning with Christ. The scene also fulfills *Daniel 7:22*, where judgment is given in favor of the saints and they possess the kingdom.

Interpreters understand “the first resurrection” in different ways. Premillennialists generally see it as a bodily resurrection of believers at Christ’s return, before the thousand-year reign; the rest of the dead are raised a thousand years later for the final judgment. Amillennialists generally understand it as a spiritual resurrection, either the new birth of believers (*Ephesians 2:5–6*; *Colossians 3:1*) or the entrance of believers’ souls into Christ’s presence at death, where they reign with Him now; the second, bodily resurrection comes at Christ’s return. Each view seeks to be faithful to the text and to the wider teaching of Scripture.

What all agree on is the wonderful promise to those who belong to Christ: “the second death has no power” over them. The second death is the lake of fire (v14), final separation from God. Believers may die physically, but they will never experience the second death. They will be “priests of God and of Christ,” serving Him in His presence, and they will reign with Him. The promise to the overcomers in Smyrna (*2:11*) and Laodicea (*3:21*) is fulfilled.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers who suffer for their faith can take great comfort in this passage. Their faithfulness is seen and honored by God. Those who lose their lives for Christ will reign with Him.

This passage also gives all believers a secure hope. Whatever view of the millennium they hold, they can rejoice that the second death has no power over them. Their future is life with Christ, not judgment.

The promise that believers will be priests and reign with Christ gives dignity and purpose to the Christian life. Believers are not merely rescued; they are called to share in Christ’s rule and service. This future calling can shape how they live now: serving faithfully, worshiping wholeheartedly, and representing Christ in the world.

Finally, the different views of the millennium invite believers to hold their interpretations with humility and charity. Christians can discuss these questions honestly while maintaining unity around the central truths of Christ’s return, the resurrection, and the final judgment.

### *Revelation 20:10* — The Devil’s Final Defeat

> *“The devil who deceived them was thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur, where the beast and the false prophet are also. They will be tormented day and night forever and ever.”*
>
> — *Revelation 20:10* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

After the final rebellion is crushed, “The devil who deceived them was thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur, where the beast and the false prophet are also.”

The deceiver, who has led humanity astray since the garden of Eden, is finally removed. He joins the beast and the false prophet, who were thrown into the lake of fire in 19:20.

The verse ends: “They will be tormented day and night forever and ever.” The judgment of Satan is complete and permanent.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse marks the final fulfillment of God’s promise in *Genesis 3:15*, that the offspring of the woman would crush the serpent’s head. From the first pages of the Bible, Satan has been the deceiver and accuser. Now he is defeated forever.

The unholy trinity, the dragon, the beast, and the false prophet, are all removed. The forces that deceived the nations, persecuted God’s people, and opposed God’s purposes will never trouble creation again.

Jesus spoke of “*the eternal fire which is prepared for the devil and his angels*” (*Matthew 25:41*). The lake of fire was prepared for Satan and his allies. Human beings who share their fate do so because they chose to follow them rather than God. As noted earlier, Christians hold different understandings of the nature of final punishment, but all agree that Satan’s defeat is total and final.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can take courage from knowing that Satan’s defeat is certain. Though he still deceives and accuses, his time is limited, and his end is sure. Believers do not need to live in fear of him.

This verse also reminds believers that evil will not last forever. Every deception, every accusation, and every work of the enemy will be brought to an end. This hope can sustain believers through every spiritual battle.

Believers can resist the devil now, standing firm in faith (*James 4:7*; *1 Peter 5:8–9*), knowing that the victory belongs to Christ and that the enemy’s final destiny has already been decided.

### *Revelation 20:11–15* — The Great White Throne

> *“I saw a great white throne and him who sat on it, from whose face the earth and the sky fled away. There was found no place for them. I saw the dead, the great and the small, standing before the throne, and they opened books. Another book was opened, which is the book of life. The dead were judged out of the things which were written in the books, according to their works. The sea gave up the dead who were in it. Death and Hades gave up the dead who were in them. They were judged, each one according to his works. Death and Hades were thrown into the lake of fire. This is the second death, the lake of fire. If anyone was not found written in the book of life, he was cast into the lake of fire.”*
>
> — *Revelation 20:11–15* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

John sees “a great white throne and him who sat on it.” The throne is great, showing God’s supreme authority, and white, showing His perfect purity and justice. The presence of God is so overwhelming that “the earth and the sky fled away. There was found no place for them.” The old creation passes away before the Judge.

In verse 12, John sees “the dead, the great and the small, standing before the throne.” Every person, regardless of status, stands before God. “They opened books.” Then “Another book was opened, which is the book of life.” The dead are “judged out of the things which were written in the books, according to their works.”

Verse 13 shows that no one is left out: “The sea gave up the dead who were in it. Death and Hades gave up the dead who were in them.” Everyone is raised and judged.

Verse 14 announces the end of death itself: “Death and Hades were thrown into the lake of fire. This is the second death, the lake of fire.”

Verse 15 gives the final verdict: “If anyone was not found written in the book of life, he was cast into the lake of fire.”

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This is the final judgment that Scripture repeatedly promises (*Daniel 7:9–10*; *Matthew 25:31–46*; *Romans 2:5–16*; *2 Corinthians 5:10*). Every human being will stand before God and give an account. No one will escape, and no one will be judged unfairly.

There are two kinds of books. “The books” record the deeds of every person. God’s judgment is according to works, meaning it takes into account how each person has lived. No one is judged arbitrarily. Yet “the book of life” is also opened. This is the book that records those who belong to the Lamb (*13:8*; *21:27*). Ultimately, it is the book of life that determines each person’s destiny.

This reveals the heart of the gospel. If people were judged only by their deeds, no one could stand, for all have sinned (*Romans 3:23*). But those whose names are written in the Lamb’s book of life are saved by grace, through the Lamb who was slain. Their deeds still matter, as evidence of genuine faith and as the basis of reward, but their salvation rests on Christ.

The destruction of death and Hades is a glorious moment. Paul wrote, “*The last enemy that will be abolished is death*” (*1 Corinthians 15:26*). Death, the great enemy of humanity since the fall, is finally destroyed. Never again will anyone die.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage reminds every person that they will one day stand before God. This is a sobering truth. It gives weight and meaning to every choice and every action. Life matters, because God will judge it.

For believers, this passage brings assurance rather than terror. Their names are written in the Lamb’s book of life. They will not face condemnation, because Christ has borne it for them (*John 5:24*; *Romans 8:1*). They can approach the final judgment with confidence in His grace.

This passage also gives urgency to sharing the gospel. Everyone will stand before the great white throne. Believers can lovingly invite others to trust in Christ, so that their names too may be written in the book of life.

Finally, believers can rejoice in the promise that death will be destroyed. Every grave will be emptied, and death will be no more. This hope can comfort those who grieve and give courage to those who face death.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Revelation 20* describes the final defeat of evil and the final judgment of all people. Though Christians hold different views about the thousand years, all affirm the central truths of this chapter: Satan’s power is limited and will be completely destroyed, faithful believers will reign with Christ, and every person will stand before God’s throne.

The chapter invites believers to hold their views about the millennium with humility and to maintain unity with fellow believers who see these things differently. What matters most is not settling every detail, but trusting the Christ who will return and reign.

The chapter gives deep comfort to those who suffer for their faith. Those who refused to worship the beast and were even put to death will live and reign with Christ. The second death has no power over them. Their faithfulness is honored forever.

The chapter also shows that evil is rooted not only in Satan’s deception but in the human heart. Even after a long period of Satan’s binding, the nations rebel when he is released. This reminds believers of their deep need for God’s transforming grace.

Finally, the great white throne calls every person to take God’s judgment seriously. All will stand before Him, and only those whose names are written in the Lamb’s book of life will escape the second death. Believers can rest in His grace, live with integrity, and share the gospel with urgency and love, looking forward to the day when death itself is destroyed.

## Chapter Prayer

Almighty God, thank You that Satan’s power is limited by You, and that his final defeat is certain. Thank You for the promise that those who belong to Christ will reign with Him, and that the second death has no power over them. Help me to hold my understanding of Your plans with humility, and to love and stand with all who trust in Christ, even when we see some things differently. Thank You that my name is written in the Lamb’s book of life, not because of my own goodness, but because of His grace. Help me to live with integrity, knowing that I will stand before You. Give me compassion and urgency to share the good news, so that others may also find life in Christ. I rejoice that death itself will be destroyed, and I look forward to the day when it is no more. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Revelation · Chapter 21 of 22

# Revelation — Chapter 21

Chapter Theme: A New Heaven, a New Earth, and the Holy City

[Read Revelation 21 in the World English Bible](https://ebible.org/engwebp/REV21.htm)

Main Teaching

John sees a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and earth have passed away, and there is no longer any sea. He sees the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride beautifully dressed for her husband. A loud voice from the throne announces that God’s dwelling place is now among His people: He will live with them, they will be His people, and God Himself will be with them as their God. He will wipe every tear from their eyes, and there will be no more death, mourning, crying, or pain, for the old order of things has passed away. The One on the throne says, I am making everything new, and tells John to write, for these words are trustworthy and true. He is the Alpha and the Omega, the Beginning and the End, and He will give water without cost from the spring of the water of life to the thirsty. Those who overcome will inherit all this; He will be their God and they will be His children. But the cowardly, unbelieving, vile, murderers, sexually immoral, those who practice magic arts, idolaters, and all liars will have their place in the lake of fire, the second death. One of the seven angels shows John the bride, the wife of the Lamb, carrying him in the Spirit to a great, high mountain to see the holy city, Jerusalem, coming down from God and shining with His glory. It has a great high wall with twelve gates bearing the names of the twelve tribes of Israel, guarded by twelve angels, and twelve foundations bearing the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb. The angel measures the city with a golden rod: it is a cube, about 12,000 stadia in length, width, and height, and its wall is 144 cubits thick. The city is pure gold, like clear glass; its foundations are adorned with every kind of precious stone; its twelve gates are twelve pearls; and its great street is pure gold, like transparent glass. John sees no temple in the city, because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple. It needs no sun or moon, for the glory of God gives it light and the Lamb is its lamp. The nations will walk by its light, and the kings of the earth will bring their splendor into it. Its gates will never be shut, for there will be no night there. Nothing impure will ever enter it, but only those whose names are written in the Lamb’s book of life.

## Chapter Background and Story

*Revelation 21* brings the story of the Bible to its glorious goal. After the judgments, the battles, and the final defeat of evil, John sees what God has been working toward all along: a new heaven and a new earth, where God dwells with His people forever. This is not an escape from creation, but its renewal. The Bible begins with God creating the heavens and the earth (*Genesis 1:1*) and ends with God making all things new.

This vision answers every longing of the human heart and every promise of Scripture. The garden of Eden, where God walked with humanity, is restored and surpassed. The tabernacle and temple, where God’s presence dwelt among Israel, find their fulfillment in a city where God dwells with all His people. Jerusalem, the city of God, is made new. And the curse that began in *Genesis 3* is finally removed.

The vision draws heavily on the prophets, especially *Isaiah 65–66*, which promised new heavens and a new earth, and *Ezekiel 40–48*, which described a renewed temple and city. It uses rich, symbolic imagery to describe a reality beyond human imagination. As with the rest of Revelation, the images communicate truth about the beauty, security, and glory of God’s eternal home.

### All Things New (*21:1–8*)

“*I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth have passed away, and the sea is no more*” (*v. 1*). Christians have understood the “new heaven and new earth” in two main ways. Some believe the present creation will be completely destroyed and replaced by a new one. Many others believe that the present creation will be purified and renewed, transformed rather than discarded, just as believers’ bodies will be raised and transformed rather than replaced (*Romans 8:19–23*; *1 Corinthians 15:42–44*). Both views affirm that the new creation will be free from sin, death, and every effect of the curse.

“The sea is no more” does not mean that God dislikes oceans. In Revelation and the Old Testament, the sea often symbolizes chaos, danger, and evil. The beast rose out of the sea (*13:1*). For John, exiled on the island of Patmos, the sea was also what separated him from his churches. In the new creation, everything the sea represented, chaos, threat, and separation, will be gone.

“*I saw the holy city, New Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared like a bride adorned for her husband*” (*v. 2*). The holy city “comes down” from heaven. God’s people do not climb up to heaven; God brings heaven down to earth. The city is described as a bride, connecting it with the wedding of the Lamb in chapter 19. The city is not merely a place where God’s people live; in a sense, it is God’s people, the bride of Christ, in their perfected state. Its beauty contrasts with Babylon, the prostitute city.

God’s dwelling with His people and His promise to make all things new are studied below.

“*He who overcomes, I will give him these things. I will be his God, and he will be my son*” (*v. 7*). The promises to the overcomers in the seven messages (chapters 2–3) are all fulfilled here. The overcomer inherits everything, and the greatest inheritance is a relationship with God as His child. This echoes God’s covenant promise to David concerning his son (*2 Samuel 7:14*), now extended to all God’s people.

“*But for the cowardly, unbelieving, sinners, abominable, murderers, sexually immoral, sorcerers, idolaters, and all liars, their part is in the lake that burns with fire and sulfur, which is the second death.”*” (*v. 8*) This sobering verse reminds readers that the new creation is holy. Those who persist in rejecting God and clinging to evil have no place in it. “The cowardly” likely refers to those who denied Christ under pressure, refusing to stand with Him, in contrast to the overcomers. The list describes the character of those who followed the beast. This verse is not a list to make believers despair, since many believers were once such people and have been washed and made new (*1 Corinthians 6:9–11*). It is a warning to those who refuse God’s invitation, and a call to everyone to turn to Him while there is time.

### The Holy City (*21:9–21*)

“*One of the seven angels who had the seven bowls which were loaded with the seven last plagues came, and he spoke with me, saying, “Come here. I will show you the bride, the Lamb’s wife.”*” (*v. 9*) “*He carried me away in the Spirit to a great and high mountain, and showed me the holy city, Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God,*” (*v. 10*) The same kind of angel who showed John the prostitute (*17:1*) now shows him the bride. The parallel is deliberate. John was carried into a wilderness to see Babylon; now he is carried to a great, high mountain to see the new Jerusalem, recalling *Ezekiel 40:2*.

“*having the glory of God. Her light was like a most precious stone, like a jasper stone, clear as crystal;*” (*v. 11*) The city shines with God’s own glory. The jasper stone recalls the appearance of God on His throne (*4:3*).

“*having a great and high wall with twelve gates, and at the gates twelve angels, and names written on them, which are the names of the twelve tribes of the children of Israel*” (*v. 12*). “*On the east were three gates, and on the north three gates, and on the south three gates, and on the west three gates*” (*v. 13*). “*The wall of the city had twelve foundations, and on them twelve names of the twelve Apostles of the Lamb*” (*v. 14*). The gates bear the names of the twelve tribes of Israel, and the foundations bear the names of the twelve apostles. The city unites the people of God from the old covenant and the new. God’s people are one people, built on the foundation of Israel’s story and the apostles’ witness to Christ (*Ephesians 2:19–22*). The gates face every direction, open to people from every part of the world.

“*He who spoke with me had for a measure a golden reed to measure the city, its gates, and its walls*” (*v. 15*). “*The city is square. Its length is as great as its width. He measured the city with the reed: twelve thousand twelve stadia. Its length, width, and height are equal*” (*v. 16*). “*Its wall is one hundred forty-four cubits, by the measure of a man, that is, of an angel*” (*v. 17*). Twelve thousand stadia is about 1,400 miles (2,200 kilometers), roughly the size of the known Mediterranean world. The city is a perfect cube. The only other perfect cube in Scripture is the Most Holy Place in Solomon’s temple (*1 Kings 6:20*), where God’s presence dwelt. The whole city is now the Most Holy Place. God’s presence fills everything. The numbers, twelve thousand and 144 (twelve times twelve), symbolize the completeness of God’s people.

“*The construction of its wall was jasper. The city was pure gold, like pure glass*” (*v. 18*). “*The foundations of the city’s wall were adorned with all kinds of precious stones. The first foundation was jasper, the second sapphire, the third chalcedony, the fourth emerald,*” (*v. 19*) “*the fifth sardonyx, the sixth sardius, the seventh chrysolite, the eighth beryl, the ninth topaz, the tenth chrysoprase, the eleventh jacinth, and the twelfth amethyst*” (*v. 20*). “*The twelve gates were twelve pearls. Each one of the gates was made of one pearl. The street of the city was pure gold, like transparent glass*” (*v. 21*). The materials are dazzling: gold, precious stones, and pearls. The twelve stones resemble the stones on the breastplate of Israel’s high priest, which bore the names of the twelve tribes (*Exodus 28:17–21*). Isaiah also promised that God would rebuild Jerusalem with precious stones (*Isaiah 54:11–12*). Gold “like transparent glass” describes a purity and beauty beyond anything on earth. These images express the incomparable beauty and value of God’s eternal home. What the world treasures most becomes the pavement of God’s city.

### The Glory of the City (*21:22–27*)

The absence of a temple and the light of God’s glory are studied below.

“*The nations will walk in its light. The kings of the earth bring the glory and honor of the nations into it*” (*v. 24*). “*Its gates will in no way be shut by day (for there will be no night there),*” (*v. 25*) “*and they shall bring the glory and the honor of the nations into it so that they may enter*” (*v. 26*). This is a beautiful picture of the redeemed nations. The kings of the earth, who once served the beast and mourned Babylon, are now seen bringing their glory into God’s city. The best of human culture, redeemed and purified, is brought as an offering to God (*Isaiah 60:3–11*). The gates are never shut, a sign of perfect security; in ancient cities gates were closed at night for protection, but there is no night and no danger.

“*There will in no way enter into it anything profane, or one who causes an abomination or a lie, but only those who are written in the Lamb’s book of life*” (*v. 27*). The city is perfectly holy. Nothing impure can enter. Only those whose names are in the Lamb’s book of life, those redeemed by His blood, will live there.

## Important Verses Explained

### *Revelation 21:3–4* — God Will Dwell with His People

> *“I heard a loud voice out of heaven saying, ‘Behold, God’s dwelling is with people; and he will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God. He will wipe away every tear from their eyes. Death will be no more; neither will there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain any more. The first things have passed away.’”*
>
> — *Revelation 21:3–4* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

A loud voice from the throne announces: “Behold, God’s dwelling is with people.” The word for “dwelling” is related to the word for “tabernacle” or “tent.” God will pitch His tent among His people.

The voice continues: “and he will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God.” This is the heart of the new creation: God and His people living together in perfect relationship.

Verse 4 describes what this means: “He will wipe away every tear from their eyes. Death will be no more; neither will there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain any more. The first things have passed away.” All the sorrows of this present life will be gone forever.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

This verse fulfills the central promise of the whole Bible. God’s covenant promise was always, “*I will walk among you, and will be your God, and you will be my people*” (*Leviticus 26:12*) (see also *Jeremiah 31:33*; *Ezekiel 37:27*). In the tabernacle and temple, God dwelt among Israel, but His presence was hidden behind a curtain. In Jesus, “*The Word became flesh, and lived among us*” (*John 1:14*), literally “tabernacled” among us. Through the Holy Spirit, God dwells in His people now. But in the new creation, God’s presence will be fully and openly with His people forever.

The tender image of God wiping away every tear is deeply personal. God does not merely end suffering from a distance. He personally comforts each of His children. This promise echoes *Isaiah 25:8*: “*He has swallowed up death forever! The Lord GOD will wipe away tears from off all faces*” (*Isaiah 25:8*).

The list of things that will be no more, death, mourning, crying, and pain, includes everything that makes this world so hard. These are the effects of sin and the curse. In the new creation, they will be completely removed. “The first things have passed away.” The old order of sin and suffering will be gone forever.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage offers deep comfort to all who suffer. Those who grieve the loss of loved ones, those who live with chronic pain, those who weep over injustice, and those who struggle with sorrow can hold on to the promise that God will wipe away every tear. Their suffering is real, but it is not permanent.

This hope does not make present suffering insignificant, and it does not mean believers should hide their grief. Jesus wept at the tomb of Lazarus. But it means that grief is not the end of the story. Believers can grieve with hope.

This passage also reminds believers that the greatest gift of the new creation is God Himself. Heaven is not mainly about streets of gold or the absence of pain, wonderful as those are. It is about being with God. Believers can begin to enjoy His presence now, through prayer, worship, and the indwelling Spirit, as a foretaste of what is to come.

### *Revelation 21:5–6* — I Am Making All Things New

> *“He who sits on the throne said, ‘Behold, I am making all things new.’ He said, ‘Write, for these words of God are faithful and true.’ He said to me, I am the Alpha and the Omega, the Beginning and the End. I will give freely to him who is thirsty from the spring of the water of life.”*
>
> — *Revelation 21:5–6* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

For the first time in Revelation, God Himself speaks directly from the throne: “Behold, I am making all things new.” God is the one who renews creation. He is not making new things, but making all things new, restoring and transforming what He created.

He tells John: “Write, for these words of God are faithful and true.” These promises are completely reliable.

In verse 6, God declares: “I am the Alpha and the Omega, the Beginning and the End.” He is the source of all things and the goal of all things.

Then He makes an invitation: “I will give freely to him who is thirsty from the spring of the water of life.” Life with God is a free gift for all who thirst for it.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

“I am making all things new” echoes *Isaiah 43:19* and *65:17*, where God promises to do a new thing and create new heavens and a new earth. Paul declared that this renewal has already begun in those who belong to Christ: “*Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new*” (*2 Corinthians 5:17*). The new creation that will be fully revealed at the end has already begun in the lives of believers.

The present tense, “I am making,” suggests that God’s work of renewal is ongoing. He is at work now, and He will complete His work at the end.

The title “the Alpha and the Omega, the Beginning and the End” appears at the start of Revelation (*1:8*) and here near its close. God was there at the beginning of creation, and He will be there at its completion. History is not random. It begins and ends with God.

The offer of the water of life “freely” is an echo of *Isaiah 55:1*, where God invites everyone who thirsts to come and drink without money. It also echoes Jesus’ words to the Samaritan woman and His invitation at the feast in Jerusalem (*John 4:10–14*; *7:37–38*). Eternal life is a gift of grace, not something earned. All that is required is thirst, a recognition of one’s need, and coming to God to receive.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

Believers can find hope in knowing that God is making all things new. Whatever is broken in their lives, relationships, bodies, or world, God’s renewing work is underway and will be completed.

This passage also invites believers to live as part of God’s new creation now. Those who are in Christ are already new creations. They can live in the newness of life He gives, leaving behind old patterns of sin and embracing the life of the Spirit.

Finally, the offer of the water of life is for everyone who thirsts. Believers can come to God again and again to receive His life. And they can share this invitation with others, telling them that God’s gift is free to all who come.

### *Revelation 21:22–23* — No Temple, No Sun

> *“I saw no temple in it, for the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb are its temple. The city has no need for the sun or moon to shine, for the very glory of God illuminated it and its lamp is the Lamb.”*
>
> — *Revelation 21:22–23* (WEB)

#### Simple Explanation

John notices something surprising about the holy city: “I saw no temple in it.” In the ancient world, every great city had temples, and Jerusalem’s identity was centered on its temple. But the new Jerusalem has none.

The reason is given: “for the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb are its temple.” God’s presence is not confined to one building. He fills the whole city. The entire city is His dwelling.

Verse 23 adds another surprise: “The city has no need for the sun or moon to shine, for the very glory of God illuminated it and its lamp is the Lamb.” God’s own glory is the city’s light. The Lamb is its lamp.

#### Deeper Spiritual Meaning

The temple in Israel was where God’s presence dwelt among His people, but access was limited. Only priests could enter the holy place, and only the high priest could enter the Most Holy Place, once a year. The temple was a sign of God’s presence, but also of the barrier between a holy God and sinful people.

In the new creation, that barrier is completely gone. There is no need for a temple, because God and the Lamb are present everywhere. Every part of the city is holy, and every person has direct access to God. This fulfills what Jesus began when He said that true worshipers would worship the Father in spirit and truth, not in one location (*John 4:21–24*), and what was signified when the temple curtain was torn at His death (*Matthew 27:51*).

Notice that “the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb” are named together as the temple. The Lamb shares fully in God’s presence and glory. This is one of many places in Revelation where Jesus is honored as fully divine.

The absence of sun and moon recalls *Isaiah 60:19–20*: “*The sun will be no more your light by day, nor will the brightness of the moon give light to you, but the LORD will be your everlasting light, and your God will be your glory*” (*Isaiah 60:19*). In *Genesis 1*, God created light before He created the sun. He is the true source of light. In the new creation, His glory shines directly. There is no darkness at all.

#### Applying This Teaching to Life Today

This passage reveals the goal of all worship: direct, unhindered fellowship with God. Believers can look forward to a day when nothing stands between them and God. Even now, through Christ, they can draw near to Him with confidence (*Hebrews 10:19–22*).

The image of God’s glory as the city’s light invites believers to let God be their light now. In a dark world, they can walk in the light of His presence and reflect His light to others. Jesus said, “*I am the light of the world. He who follows me will not walk in the darkness, but will have the light of life*” (*John 8:12*).

Finally, this passage reminds believers that the center of eternity is God and the Lamb. All of heaven’s beauty points to them. Believers can center their lives on God now, making Him their greatest joy, as He will be forever.

## How to Apply This Chapter to Life Today

*Revelation 21* shows believers the goal toward which all of history is moving: a new heaven and a new earth where God dwells with His people forever. This vision is the ultimate hope of every believer. Whatever they face now, this is their future.

The heart of this hope is God’s presence. He will dwell with His people, and they will be His people. He will wipe away every tear. Death, mourning, crying, and pain will be no more. Believers can hold on to these promises in times of suffering and grief, knowing that their sorrow is real but temporary.

God is making all things new. This renewal has already begun in those who are in Christ, and it will be completed at the end. Believers can live as part of His new creation now, and they can come to Him again and again for the water of life, which He gives freely to all who thirst.

The holy city reveals the beauty, security, and holiness of God’s eternal home. It unites God’s people from Israel and the church, welcomes the redeemed from every nation, and is filled with God’s glory. There is no temple, because God and the Lamb are present everywhere, and no need for sun, because God’s glory is its light.

Finally, the chapter reminds believers that the city is holy. Only those whose names are written in the Lamb’s book of life will enter. This calls believers to rest in Christ’s grace, to live in holiness, and to extend God’s invitation to others, so that they too may drink from the water of life and enter the city of God.

## Chapter Prayer

Almighty God, thank You for the hope of a new heaven and a new earth, where You will dwell with Your people forever. Thank You that You will wipe away every tear, and that death, mourning, crying, and pain will be no more. Comfort all who are grieving and suffering today with this promise. Thank You that You are making all things new, and that in Christ I am already part of Your new creation. When I am thirsty, help me to come to You for the water of life, freely given. Let Your glory be my light, and let the Lamb be my lamp. Make me holy, and help me to invite others into Your city. I long for the day when I will see You face to face and live in Your presence forever. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
